**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL THE MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION EXTANT THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, ACCORDING TO THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS, COMPARED WITH ONE ANOTHER AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES, AND VERY CAREFULLY CORRECTED; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED WITH ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE MOST EXTENSIVE EDITIONS COMPLETED DURING THE LAST THREE CENTURIES; PROVIDED WITH PARTICULAR ANALYTICAL INDEXES FOLLOWING INDIVIDUAL VOLUMES OR AUTHORS OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ORNAMENTED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY ARRANGED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AS ALSO WITH TITLES DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING ITS SUBJECT-MATTER; EXPANDED WITH WORKS BOTH DUBIOUS AND APOCRYPHAL, YET POSSESSING SOME AUTHORITY with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched by two copious general indexes: the first, namely, an index of subjects, so that, upon consulting it, whatever each of the Fathers wrote on any subject may be seen at a glance; the other, an index of Holy Scripture, by which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in what places in their works. A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others, if one considers: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and the number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the entire course of the work, the modest price, and above all this single, methodical, and chronological collection of six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**SECOND SERIES, IN WHICH APPEAR THE FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND WRITERS OF THE LATIN CHURCH FROM GREGORY THE GREAT TO INNOCENT III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been published in two editions: one Latin, the other Greco-Latin.—The two hundred and sixty volumes of the Latin edition are sold for 1,300 francs; the thirteen hundred volumes of the Greco-Latin edition for 8,000 francs.—The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are given in it only in Latin translation.**

## The Twelfth Century

### The Complete Works of the Venerable Hildebert

First bishop of Le Mans, then archbishop of Tours,

both published and unpublished; to which have been added the little works of Marbod, bishop of Rennes, Hildebert’s equal.

Those hitherto published appear here enlarged, while the more numerous works not previously published are issued; all are collated with manuscript codices and are here and there illustrated with notes, through the labor and diligence of Dom Antoine Beaugendre, priest and monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, of the Congregation of Saint Maur; newly edited with notes and with very many genuine works added, drawn from manuscript codices, through the care and diligence of J. J. Bourassé, canon of the metropolitan church of Tours; under the editorship of J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# [Works of Hildebert of Le Mans]

[Col. 0009]

## To the Most Eminent Lord, Lord César d’Estrées, Cardinal Bishop of Albano, Duke and Peer of France, Commander of the Royal Orders, Abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, etc.

What has occurred in recent centuries, most eminent Prince of the Church—namely, that, under the patronage of princely men, certain distinguished remains of antiquity and marvels of a more perfect art, which had long lain buried under ruins through the injury of time, have been brought forth for public benefit and delight—I consider has happily happened to me, while under your favorable auspices I have undertaken to rescue from cockroaches and moths the works of the Venerable Hildebert, first bishop of Le Mans and afterwards archbishop of Tours. For what could be more just? What more useful to professors of Christian piety? What, finally, could be more pleasing to all men of letters than to restore to public light the writings of a bishop most renowned in his own age, whom almost all writers of that period celebrated in their encomia, and whom Bernard, one man in place of all, did not hesitate, amid the Church’s more difficult storms, to call “a great pillar of the Church”?

> [Note: [Col. 0009] Epistle 124, Mabillon edition. In this edition it is printed as no. 44 of Book II.]

Hildebert had rightly and deservedly won so great an encomium from a most holy man, who was never a flatterer either of kings or even of supreme pontiffs: not merely because of his ever unconquered spirit in defending the sacred rights of the Church, not only because of the fame of his most holy life, flying everywhere abroad, but also because of his always Catholic and excellent writings of every kind. As Orderic Vitalis, Hildebert’s own equal, testifies, they were “carried to Rome by Roman cardinals who were then frequenting Gaul, and were judged worthy of admiration in the schools of eloquent men and by the teachers of the Romans themselves.”

> [Note: [Col. 0009] *Ecclesiastical History*, Book X, p. 770.]

And indeed, not undeservedly. “He flourished incomparably,” says the same ancient author, “in learning both sacred and secular letters,” since he “spoke with elegance and wisdom alike concerning Christ and the Church, the body and the soul, the deeds of the saints and their virtues, the praise of virtues and the rebuke of vices.”

> [Note: [Col. 0009] As above.]

These are those outstanding writings which, through the course of almost seven centuries, lay hidden beneath dust through the injury of adverse times—to the great detriment, surely, of Christian piety and the republic of letters. These are the works for whose restoration to the light which they had once enjoyed the wishes of distinguished scholars had for so many years pleaded. These, I say, seemed spontaneously to call for a helping hand, that they might at last be drawn from their deeper hiding places.

[Col. 0011]

Hildebert at last congratulates himself that, for these his works, he has found that hand in you, most eminent Cardinal, while I have dared to extend him my own hand, though trembling, yet strengthened by your most illustrious name.

It was indeed a bold undertaking—lest I disguise anything—and one beyond the powers of myself, an old man of eighty: to attempt to recall from darkness into public light the works of a “great priest and one exalted in the word of glory.”

> [Note: [Col. 0011] Thus Bernard calls Hildebert in the epistle cited above.]

But what would not even the languor of a slower intellect have promised itself under the most secure protection of Your Eminence? What would not even an age more worn down by years have dared? I hoped all the more confidently that you would not refuse me this, because there is no one who has not happily experienced your kindly disposition toward all men of letters. It was therefore enough that those to whom I had vowed obedience so many years ago, moved by your benefits toward our congregation and toward this monastery also, and recognizing that I had long been moved by the signs of your good will toward me, assured me of that kindness with which you deign to embrace us. Thus strength almost dead might revive at your name, celebrated throughout Europe; and a mind distrustful indeed of its own smallness, but trusting in the most powerful patronage of Your Eminence, might undertake anything, daring to hope that whatever little service it could offer in publishing and restoring to their proper brilliance the works of the Venerable Hildebert would not be unwelcome to you.

Accordingly, there came back to our memory those happy days which we saw, when, in the very first down of youth, we beheld the Sorbonne—already most celebrated by so many distinctions—standing amazed at your learning. Barely in the second year after the twentieth of your life, it gloried, applauding itself, in placing the highest laurel of learning upon your head, when it saw so many fruits already swelling in their spring blossoms: precocious indeed, yet already wholly ripe, had age permitted it, for the sacred purple.

Neither the Sorbonne itself, therefore, nor all France failed, a few years later, to marvel at this exceptional distinction of your singular learning, crowned with sacred mitres. For you were such—as I may address you in Hildebert’s own words to Saint Anselm—“as was suited for pastoral watchfulness: one to whom nothing was now lacking for fullness of righteousness, nothing for completeness of learning.”

> [Note: [Col. 0011] Epistle 13, Book II of this edition, p. 94.]

For nothing less was foretold by that love of religion which you had imbibed from your very breast; nothing less by that tireless and most ardent zeal for the house of God which you already professed and later exercised so happily; nothing less, finally, by that most sagacious and clear-sighted industry and integrity in handling even then affairs of every kind, however weighty—qualities which you had received from a parent equally wise and courageous, and by which you were one day to restore peace and tranquility to the flock entrusted to you, indeed to the whole Gallican Church.

France felt itself far too narrow for this prudence, so wondrous and so manifold in practical affairs; Rome envied us it; she saw it and was astonished. And Rome—indeed, all Europe—beheld with admiration the man whom the distinguished Church of Laon had revered as a bishop wholly diligent in episcopal duties, tireless in visiting the churches within his jurisdiction, most vigilant in forming the morals of his clergy toward discipline and piety, and, further, in founding through his own liberality a seminary; whom it had also revered as the foremost founder of a hospice throughout the whole diocese for receiving needy persons of whatever rank, age, or region, and as a most kindly shepherd. Rome and all Europe saw him, amid the differing Gallican bishops in a matter of the greatest ecclesiastical importance, as an exceedingly industrious and prudent envoy of peace.

Undoubtedly no less wonder was stirred throughout the world by that supreme modesty of yours: when, through the most powerful joint efforts of both kings, you were summoned to the purple, you had scarcely entered the City before choosing rather to wait out the whole and complete course of a year—one troubled by various commotions, even at the risk, perhaps, of losing so great a dignity—than to depart by the breadth of a nail from the commands of your king and lord, commands which you could easily have interpreted to your own advantage. Thus it came about that the purple which, with such admirable moderation of spirit and mastery over yourself, you had declined as though it were voluntarily flattering you, you afterwards obtained more gloriously.

[Col. 0013]

From this arose that highest esteem which you attained among the supreme pontiff and all the purple-clad Fathers; from this grew the favor bestowed upon you by the greatest of all kings; and from this finally came that most discerning choice by which he made you a spectacle to the world through so many embassies in Italy, Germany, Spain, and Portugal, having found you everywhere the most devoted and perceptive administrator of his affairs—as he had formerly found your father a most courageous defender.

Such a patron does our Hildebert, as though restored to life, seek in you, while he rises again almost unknown into a new world. What could be more glorious for him? What safer? For what protection against any detractors might this bishop, restored to the world, not hope from a bishop most learned, perceptive, and just? What aid might he not expect from the most powerful house of Estrées itself, throughout which sacred mitres shine as they deserve, and which is illustrious throughout the world for victories by land and sea and for military honors, and those of the highest rank? What service, finally, might the “bishop of all reverence”—for Bernard again thus calls Hildebert—fail to hope for from an eminent cardinal who, radiant at last in the sacred purple, has devoted his whole self to the Church, king, and country, and who—what we proclaim only with submissive yet exultant spirits—has deigned to show himself so kindly disposed toward us, as soon as this our royal abbey of Saint-Germain was entrusted to him by the most munificent king, a most equitable judge of merit, if ever there was one, even while he was unaware of it?

> [Note: [Col. 0013] Epistle 123, Mabillon edition; printed here as no. 44 of Book II.]

Chiefly through you, most eminent Prince of the Church, may we therefore glory and rejoice: we whom you bind entirely to yourself by so many marks of kindness; whom you raise and encourage by your exhortations to studies that may perhaps one day prove useful, however modestly, to the Catholic world; and whom, finally, you enrich and support by your liberality for the adornment of the house of God.

Meanwhile, until some more celebrated occasion and one worthier of the observance due from us to you presents itself, allow our Hildebert, most eminent Cardinal, to stand as a pledge of our grateful mind toward you.

And, lest you doubt the sincerity of our intention, kindly receive his equal and most intimate friend, Marbod, bishop of Rennes, himself likewise restored to life for this purpose: that in the mouth of two bishops, beyond all exception, the word of our most humble reverence toward you may stand fixed and firm. I mean Marbod, that bishop once conspicuous for life and writings, who deserved to ascend from the chair of humane letters, in which Angers had formerly flourished, to the episcopal chair. He sat in it so piously and so holily that, having while alive been considered, like his equal and familiar friend Hildebert, among the most renowned of learned men, after death he deserved, like Hildebert himself, to be inscribed in the catalogues of the saints of Gaul.

> [Note: [Col. 0013] The *Gallican Martyrology* of the bishop of Toul.]

He also, most eminent Bishop, as though rising from the tomb in which, near the end of his life, having voluntarily resigned the episcopate, he had buried himself with Christ, now comes forth new from the old through these slight labors of ours, so that he may speak to Your Eminence through his little works, several of which have recently been discovered. He trusts that they will be the more pleasing to you because he suppliantly offers you a truer image of that venerable old age in which you flourish, painted as if by a prophetic brush; for by his words we may proclaim concerning you what, even in this present age and before our own eyes,

> We behold vigorous, distinguished old men flourishing,  
> Who, with mindful heart and eloquent tongue, recount  
> Deeds newly performed and the examples of their forebears, worthy of imitation.

> [Note: [Col. 0013] Marbod, in Book X of the *Chapters*, chapter “On Old Age.”]

To be sure:

> Nor does age deprive you of bodily strength;  
> Your intellect and mind are vigorous, and grow with time.  
> Nor has advancing age brought you contempt,  
> But greater reverence has grown for your gray head.

Indeed, most eminent Bishop, that reverence due to you for so many titles has grown, and will grow without measure among all, while you repay, as though with a hundredfold return, in the splendor of so many virtues and graces that honor which the Apostolic See has deservedly conferred upon you in its sacred purple.

[Col. 0015]

It will grow while the Most Christian King himself—and what a king!—does not cease to honor, support, and praise you as a minister most ready for every service and sincerely devoted to him with all your heart. Finally, that venerable dignity and distinction of countenance and whole person in which you flourish, and that obliging and lovable courtesy that shines in your eyes, will gain you the regard and bind to you the hearts of all. Yet nowhere, I shall venture to say, will that reverence grow more than among us, whom you cherish so wholly as your own with such fatherly care, whom you protect so kindly, and whom you do not cease to honor with so many marks of good will.

Meanwhile, I shall count myself happy if I may hope that this, whatever it may be, the last fruit of the solitude granted me in the final period of my life, will not be tasteless to you. Happy, I say, if you do not disdain to look with those kind eyes which are your custom upon this slight memorial of my more sincere obedience toward you. Hence arise my ardent prayers, and those also of my brethren: that God, the best and greatest, for the honor of His Church, for the glory and prosperity of the king and kingdom, and for the protection and consolation of all good men, may add still further long and happy years to you, ever in health—even patriarchal years, drawn from our own allotted span. This, in the name of our whole congregation and in his own, he vows from his heart.

Your Eminence’s

Most devoted and obedient  
**Brother Antoine BeauGendre**, Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur.

From your monastery of Saint-Germain.

[Col. 0017]

# Preface to the New Edition of the Works of the Venerable Hildebert, Bishop of Le Mans and Subsequently Archbishop of Tours

Being about to publish anew the works of the Venerable Hildebert, we have judged it right to preface a few remarks concerning the birth and beginnings of so great a bishop; concerning his alleged monastic profession, which Dom Antoine Beaugendre maintained less correctly; and concerning the accusation which authors, and indeed authors not undistinguished, have often and repeatedly not been ashamed to renew against his manner of life while he was archdeacon of Le Mans. In this preliminary notice we shall explain more fully to the kindly reader what has been added to this new edition: poems hitherto unpublished, drawn from manuscript codices and for the first time made public; letters and addresses extracted from various books, all of which escaped the earlier editor; documents taken from cartularies; and notes chiefly drawn from Benedictine sources. Nor should it be omitted that we had before us a copy of Hildebert’s work enlarged and corrected with notes and emendations by Dom Beaugendre himself, the learned Benedictine editor.

Following in the footsteps of our predecessor, we have appended to the works of the Venerable Hildebert, in this new edition, the little works of Marbod, bishop of Rennes.

Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans and afterwards archbishop of Tours, was a man most learned in divine Scripture and second to none of his time in secular learning; keen of intellect and highly eloquent in speech. For ecclesiastical liberty and holy discipline he suffered much; he excelled in piety, shone in virtues, and was renowned for writings both in verse and in prose. He was born at Lavardin, at Mont-Auré, in the district of Vendôme and diocese of Le Mans, of pious and honorable, though not wealthy, parents: in 1055 according to Mabillon (*Analect.*, vol. III, p. 303), but in 1057 according to Dom Beaugendre (*Works of Ven. Hildebert*, p. XVII). If, however, one trusted Jean Maan, it would be 1054 (*Ecclesiastical Metropolis of Tours*, p. 103). But because, when he was brought to the episcopal see of Le Mans in 1097, the unanimous reckoning of scholars (*Gallia Christiana*, Sammarthani, vol. II, p. 516) and the *Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans* testify that Hildebert had not then completed his fortieth year, he must have been born in 1057.

In his *Bibliothèque*, p. 190, Lacroix du Maine, a learned man misled by Hildebert’s surname, asserted that he sprang from the family of the lords of the castle of Lavardin. Dom Henri Lambron de Lignim, highly skilled in heraldry, adopted the same opinion in the work entitled *Armorial of the Archbishops of Tours* (Tours, octavo, 1854). In contrast, Bayle, *Dictionary*, vol. III, p. 343, note E, excessively credulous of Menage’s statements (*Menage*, vol. III, p. 176), asserts that he was raised from an undistinguished family. We learned the truth concerning his birth from a charter first published by the distinguished Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. VII, p. 209, from which it is evident that Hildebert’s father belonged to the equestrian order. In the same document we find his brothers Solomon, Drogo, and Geoffrey. Geoffrey, the youngest, was received at a still tender age to be educated in Marmoutier, near Tours, in the time of Abbot Albert.

[Col. 0019]

Abbot Albert was on familiar terms with Hildebert’s father. He came to the court of Count Geoffrey at Vendôme and asserted for his monastery possession of a mill on the bank of the Loir River, in the presence, says the charter, of men eminent in secular rank: Solomon of Lavardin, Odo of Lignières, and Hugh called “the Eating Breton.”

> [*History of Marmoutier*, manuscript, vol. I, p. 34; Library of Tours, no. 675.]

Hildebert, the elder in birth and more outstanding in ability, being destined for the ecclesiastical state, applied himself from childhood to the divine sciences and liberal arts. No one can fail to know how much he advanced in all these things who has read his works carefully, or merely sampled anything from his writings. After William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Kings of England*, Book III, p. 113, Maan of Tours, Dom Beaugendre, and very many others affirm that he was a pupil of Berengar, whether in the school of Tours or of Angers. But on what basis does not sufficiently appear, since Hildebert himself nowhere mentions this teacher.

That he wrote an epitaph upon Berengar’s death, when already bishop of Le Mans, and praised the archdeacon of Angers in the most ample terms, does not certainly prove that he had been Berengar’s pupil. In the funeral poem, when an opportunity presented itself, Hildebert says nothing of having had the use of so great a master. Nevertheless, Dom Rangeart, proceeding further in his manuscript *History of the University of Angers*, p. 20, asserts that Hildebert, as a youth, heard Berengar teaching at Angers and subsequently became a canon of the Church of Angers. But this is less correct, or at least not sufficiently established by authentic documents.

He never fell into Berengarian errors. He always professed orthodox doctrine concerning the sacred Eucharist, as is evident from his eloquent *Treatise on the Eucharist*, his *Explanation of the Mass*, his poem on the sacrifice of the Mass, his poem on the Holy Eucharist, and his various sermons scattered throughout his works. He vigorously defended the Catholic faith concerning Transubstantiation and the Real Presence. It should also be observed that the word *Transsubstantiatio* (“Transubstantiation”), which the Church now uses against sacramentarian heretics, is found for the first time among his theological writings. He speaks thus of communion:

> Communion bestows joys upon the holy followers of Christ,  
> By which the Lord’s true body is made present under bread.

> [From a Tours manuscript.]

Do not be excessively surprised that the bishop sang Berengar’s praise, perhaps in words exceeding due measure. The Chronicle of Tours says of the celebrated man:

> “Then Berengar, departing from Rome, came to Tours; and there, on the island called Saint-Cosmas, renouncing the pomps of the world, he served the Lord continually for almost eight years. Several other canons of Blessed Martin, instructed by the Holy Spirit and by his salutary admonition, changed their clothing and withdrew to that island.”

And shortly afterwards:

> “In the same year died Master Berengar the grammarian, faithful and truly Catholic.”

Thus Jean de Majoris. William of Malmesbury, Book I, chapter 3, however, adds:

> “Although Berengar, in the first heat of youth, made himself notorious by defending certain heresies, in a more austere age he recovered his senses so fully that some regard him as a saint without reservation.”

> [Note: [Col. 0019] On Berengar of Tours, see the manuscript *History of Saint Martin of Tours*, Library of Tours, vol. I.—Maan, *Church of Tours*, p. 104.—*Chronicles of Tours*, published by the Archaeological Society of Tours, Tours, Ladevèze, 1854.]

Having been instructed in the first elements of letters and having pursued the study of the sciences with no small distinction, Hildebert turned, in the schools then flourishing, to the study of sacred learning. Most who wrote about the life of our bishop relate that Hildebert went to the monastery of Cluny, where, under Saint Hugh as abbot, studies of sacred theology were flourishing especially. Some writers affirm that he assumed the monastic habit; others deny it. Dom Beaugendre took the greatest care to bring together all the testimonies of authors favoring the former opinion.

André Duchesne of Tours, in his notes on the *Life of Saint Hugh*, p. 83, says: “Hildebert was first a monk of Cluny and a pupil of that same Saint Hugh.” Jean Maan and the Sammarthani brothers in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, followed this opinion. It is attacked by the authors of the *Literary History of France*, vol. XI, p. 252, and by Simon, canon of the Church of Saint George at Vendôme, in the *History of Vendôme*, vol. III.

André Duchesne does not seem to have examined carefully his assertion concerning Hildebert’s monasticism. Without first weighing the matter, he followed the *Chronicle of Cluny*, compiled in 1485, at the command of Dom James of Amboise, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, by Dom Francis of Rivo of Cluny, its grand prior. Thus his conjecture concerning Hildebert’s monastic profession rests upon such an argument. No one can fail to see that all these things are recent and consequently weaker. On the other hand, reasons of grave importance are raised, and it is impossible to oppose them.

Hildebert wrote the life of Saint Hugh. How could he have passed over in silence that he had had such a master, learned sacred disciplines under the guidance of so illustrious an abbot, and enrolled himself in the Benedictine order? Moreover, all contemporary writers are silent concerning Hildebert’s monasticism, although they speak repeatedly of so great a man and extol him with the highest praises: such as Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, who calls him “a great priest and one exalted in the word of glory,” and “a great pillar of the Church.”

If one investigates carefully the author of the *Life of the Holy Abbot of Cluny*, one hears him confessing in the course of his history that he had not seen Blessed Hugh until, traveling to Rome with Hoël, bishop of Le Mans, he had stopped at the monastery of Cluny. When the man of great holiness addressed Hoël with great kindness, he repeatedly turned his eyes toward Hildebert the archdeacon, and at last deigned gently to address him in these words:

> “Only do not fail the grace of God; for it is foreseen that you will by no means remain in the rank in which you now serve.”

A short time passed, and the event followed the prophecy. For in the following year the archdeacon obtained episcopal dignity.

> “We heard this; we saw it while present; in that conversation we became sharers in the prayers of that blessed man. Fame had revealed to us certain things about his holiness, certain things about his gentleness, and certain things also about those qualities to which judgment assigns blame and virtue grants the prerogative of increase. Yet, observing the vigilance of the shepherd from the conduct of his flock, we found them more abundant.”

> [*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 923.]

Here he speaks only of having seen him. Who, then, could persuade himself that an alumnus of Blessed Odo, his pupil and monk, would have discovered more abundant, indeed almost all, things from the conduct of the flock, and learned the rest by the revelation of fame?

Two little verses of Peter of Poitiers are also adduced; they would settle the entire controversy if they certainly concerned Hildebert:

> There also came forth the sweet pupil of Julian,  
> Who governed well the Church of Tours.

But who could now number him among the Cluniacs? For he could scarcely—indeed, perhaps not at all—have been admitted, under the practice and custom of the Church of Le Mans at that time, to the office of master of its schools, had he devoted himself to Cluniac observances and bound himself by a religious vow. Hence, as Dom Mabillon says, “It does not appear to me that Hildebert was ever a monk of Cluny, neither before nor after his episcopate, although he himself expressed a desire to embrace the regular life, if the Roman Pontiff had granted permission: ‘I should long ago have embraced his bosom as one accused, had the pope, when consulted, permitted the burden of a bishop to be lightened’” (*Hildebert*, letter to Hugh). Thus Dom Beaugendre’s extensive argument entirely collapses.

But to return to Peter of Poitiers: in calling Hildebert an alumnus of Saint Julian, he did not express his meaning sufficiently. For two celebrated churches dedicated to Blessed Julian are found: the first at Le Mans, the latter at Tours, both resplendent in the eleventh century through the learning of the sciences and the brilliance of Christian virtues. The author of the panegyric upon Abbot Hugh more probably intended the cathedral church of the city of Le Mans.

Although you are free to embrace that opinion. In any case, our Hildebert had spread such a reputation of himself everywhere—indeed, for the extraordinary keenness of his intellect and the excellence of his learning—that Hoel, bishop of Le Mans, placed him over the schools of the cathedral church. So great and widespread was the fame of the learned schoolmaster that very many hearers flocked from every quarter around their teacher’s chair. How long he held this mastership is unknown. In the year of the Lord 1092, and in the thirty-fifth year of his life, the same bishop Hoel elevated him to the archdeaconry; and he worthily held this distinguished office for five years, as he himself notes (Letter 21, Book III, to William, abbot of Saint-Vincent).

Thus, as [Col. 0023] the archdeacon’s already excellent reputation for learning and for the skill of governing others increased day by day throughout his life, when Hoel died Hildebert appeared worthy to hold the pastoral staff and govern the church of Le Mans. The greater and better part of clergy and people, unanimously voting, elected him bishop at the age of forty. Almost the sole opponent was Count Elias, who favored the dean of the church, named Geoffrey, a native of Brittany, together with a few canons. Yet Count Elias was a religious man who feared God; he soon restrained his anger, recognized that the election had been canonically made, and approved it.

Hildebert was not immediately ordained bishop. A terrible storm arose against him. The hostile clergy of Le Mans, who had taken Geoffrey’s side, accused him of the most disgraceful crimes. Ivo, bishop of Chartres, the keenest defender of ecclesiastical discipline, who at that time in Gaul acted almost as the public judge of all causes, gave a hearing to the accusation and wrote to the bishop-elect that he should withdraw from the election if he were in fact guilty. Dom Beaugendre, Dom Bondonnet, Jean Maan, and Simon defend our prelate against the grave charge, and with unshakable arguments. Since the learned authors of the *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. XI, pp. 254 ff., have carefully handled the same question against Baronius and other writers of no small reputation, we have thought it right to assert anew the innocence of the holy bishop and to lay the Benedictine work before all eyes.

From Ivo’s letter it is easily inferred that Hildebert was painted in the blackest colors by a hostile hand and defamed for sexual immorality with women:

> “I have heard concerning you things that cause me grief and horror. If they are true, you will not be able to provide governance for the people, but will increase their danger. For certain persons of importance in the church of Le Mans, who testify that they know your former life, say that you loosened the reins of chastity beyond measure, so that, after receiving the archdeaconry, with a rabble of little women lying at your side, you begot a great multitude of boys and girls. But you know that one who is raised to the summit of pastoral responsibility ought to possess proven chastity.”

And shortly afterward:

> “If all this is so, dearest brother, it is dangerous for you and, in my judgment, will produce endless trouble. Therefore take counsel for yourself according to the testimony of your conscience: either honorably and prudently complete what you have begun, or, providing for your salvation, desist.”

These are Ivo’s words. He adds that a bishop must show himself blameless in all things; that one who has fallen must be deprived of rank and never promoted to higher dignities; and that all clergy in holy orders, after a fault, must be excluded from the Church or at least removed from the exercise of their orders. Hildebert’s accusers alleged that his election had been tumultuous and contrary to their wishes, and that their canonical opposition had been disregarded. Deeply moved by these and similar allegations, the bishop of Chartres urged Hildebert to renounce the election, provide for his soul, and prudently consider the welfare of the people of Le Mans while there was still time.

Relying upon Ivo’s letter as though it were established testimony, Baronius, in his *Annals* under the year 1088, charges Hildebert with a corrupt and dissolute life. Others afterward followed him rashly, never weighing or examining the original testimony. The most bitter enemies of divine and ecclesiastical affairs adopted the same account, repeating the calumny again and again, all too delighted to declaim against a priest honored with the highest dignities of the Church. Moreover, Baronius (same year, nos. 15, 20), offended that Berengar had been praised and eulogized more than was proper by Hildebert in a funeral epitaph, thereupon launches an unjust suspicion against the author. He says that the archdeacon of Le Mans, who spoke such things in praise of an arch-heretic, was remarkable neither for soundness of faith nor for integrity of morals. He then produces the previously mentioned letter of the bishop of Chartres, from which, he says, it is evident that Berengar’s disciple had loosened the reins of chastity beyond measure.

The same judgment strikes both the praised man and his praiser. But who does not see that such a manner of reasoning is defective? According to prudent writers who adhere to the rules of sound criticism, an accused person must not be judged guilty until he is certainly discovered to be guilty of the crime. Baronius ought surely to have acted otherwise: Berengar may perhaps be extolled beyond measure in praise, but Hildebert ought not thereby to have been defamed.

Corvaisier, in his *History of the Bishops of Le Mans*, pp. 389 ff., in the same [Col. 0025] error fell into the same error and went further. Supported by no authority at all—for he had no testimony from the preceding authors—he wrote that Ivo came to Le Mans, visited the bishop recently elected, and then rebuked him, now with exhortations, now with harsher words, to abandon his looser life and renounce a mode of conduct by which he had brought destruction upon himself and scandal upon Christ’s faithful. Then, paying little or no attention to other authors’ opinion, without even touching upon the arguments for Hildebert’s vindication, however lightly, he lends an attentive ear only to those who assert that Hildebert had been a sinner before his episcopate. On p. 394 he endeavors to support the falsehood by the authority of the necrology of the Church of Saint-Pierre de la Cour, where mention is made of a certain Gervase, allegedly the natural son of our Hildebert.

In his *History of Sablé*, Ménage acted no less unjustly toward our bishop, although he says little concerning him. Bayle, in vol. III of his *Dictionary*, pp. 341–342, did not omit the accusation made against the bishop. Perhaps he speaks of Hildebert only in order to bring forward both Ivo’s letter and a spurious letter attributed to Hildebert against the Roman curia.

Since the letter of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, appears to be the sole origin of the calumny so often circulated against the memory of the archdeacon of Le Mans, a sure way of repelling the calumny would be to demonstrate that it is forged and wholly unworthy of belief. Juret, in his notes on Ivo’s letters, pp. 208–209, asserts that Letter 177 was addressed to a certain Aldebert, not to Hildebert; but this is less cautiously said, since our prelate is also found called Aldebert in a document from Nantes of the year 1105, published by the author of the *History of Brittany*, p. 264, among the miscellaneous records, and by Dom Edmond Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, p. 316. Moreover, he is called Aldebert in letters and charters, especially in a letter written in Hildebert’s own hand to Ranulf, bishop of Durham. Besides, no archdeacon of this name is found in Ivo of Chartres’s time.

> “Certainly, anyone who obstinately denies that the letter was written concerning Hildebert must, in Sirmond’s judgment, be regarded as wishing to be believed with his eyes shut” (Sirmond, on Geoffrey, Book III, Letter 13).

The learned Mabillon uses almost the same words in *Annals*, Book LXIX, no. 59. No one of serious judgment can fail to recognize the authority of these most learned men. Nevertheless, Dom Beaugendre brings forward arguments not to be despised by which he endeavors to prove the letter spurious, p. XIX. Whatever may be thought of its authenticity, the accusation nevertheless proves no less false: Ivo invokes the letters of enemies of the bishop-elect, by whose counsel he had not been elected nor with whose assent. Thus falls the entire argument against our bishop, erected by adversaries combining their forces. Ivo was deceived regarding the archdeacon of Le Mans, just as Marbod, bishop of Rennes, and Geoffrey, abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, were deceived regarding Robert of Arbrissel, founder of the monastery of Fontevraud.

It also seems worth noting that Ivo, a man readily ardent in ecclesiastical matters and vigorous in polemical controversy, does not speak absolutely but uses words that are almost expressions of doubt: “Certain persons say”; “If these things are true”; “If they are so.” Later, once more certain concerning Hildebert’s virtues, Ivo repeatedly commends him as a well-conducted and devout bishop, and more frequently calls him his friend. We do not think it necessary to bring forward the almost innumerable testimonies of contemporary writers, all of whom sing the praises of our Hildebert.

William Rufus, king of England, also made many attempts to disturb Hildebert’s election and ordination. He maintained that the county of Le Mans lay under his dominion and that the entire affair neither ought to have reached nor could reach its conclusion without his being consulted. Indignant that Count Elias alone had intervened, he wished to render the archdeacon’s election void. But Ralph, archbishop of Tours, consecrated the bishop-elect in the church of Le Mans and installed him in possession of his see in 1097, on the very feast of the Nativity of the Lord.

A question concerning the year of his ordination has been raised by some scholars. Hildebert’s name appears among the subscriptions of the bishops who attended the Council of Saintes, held, according to Labbe, *Councils*, vol. X, p. 604, in 1096 on the second day of March, and according to Mabillon in 1097, *Annals*, Book LXIX, no. 64. If this is so, how could Hildebert have attended the council of 1096 adorned with episcopal insignia, when only in 1097 [Col. 0027] was he consecrated bishop by the metropolitan of Tours? Labbe seems to have calculated the year of the council erroneously. Mabillon’s opinion, however, is readily explained: at that time the year began with the feast of Easter, and consequently the year 1097 had not yet elapsed on the second day of March.

Hildebert had reached his fortieth year when he sat upon the episcopal throne; and scarcely had he canonically obtained possession of his dignity when he commendably proposed for himself a rule of life to follow, described by the author of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans*. (See below, *Extracts from the Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans*.)

We shall not linger longer over Hildebert’s holy manner of conduct, one indeed worthy of a bishop. In 1125, when Gilbert, archbishop of Tours, had died, Hildebert, almost seventy years old, was appointed in his place. He died at Tours on 18 December 1134. He was buried in the metropolitan church, whose foundations he himself had laid, and lies on the right-hand side of the altar.

Here we have thought it appropriate to add certain facts concerning the history of the Church of Tours that Dom Beaugendre omitted.

Before Hildebert assumed the governance and episcopate of the church of Tours, a certain Master Geoffrey—for so he is called in authentic documents—had already gathered many men, inhabitants of a devout solitude, in the forest of Blémars, in the territory of Chartres. For this reason Rainald Ancherius, Hugh Lombard, Hardouin Conan, Gano of Baugency, and his son Garnier devoutly bestowed upon him whatever serfs and dependents they held thereabouts. A small sacred building of wood was constructed there for Saint Mary Magdalene, and the place immediately became a populous hermitage of anchorites, under Geoffrey’s direction.

But when Hildebert had recently been appointed to the church of Tours, he could not tolerate their considerable departure from the rule of solitary life. He therefore dismissed them at once; moving to a neighboring place called Fontaines, he summoned Cistercian monks in 1127, whose fame had already spread widely through the great holiness of their Bernard. By Hildebert’s order and approval they established a monastery. So that they might live together, Reginald called “of the Castle,” within whose lordship lay the estates already granted to the hermit Geoffrey, finally granted them the lordship and rights of tenancy over these, adding La Lande, a noble neighboring estate, in 1140. Theobald, count of Blois, the superior lord of these possessions by the higher and prior right, and Hugh, archbishop of Tours, afterward confirmed this. On these matters see Maan, *Metropolitan Church of Tours*, p. 111.

When Count Richin died about this time, Fulk the Younger, his son by Bertrada—he was the fifth count of Anjou of that name—took possession of the county of Tours about 1115. Energetic in arms and equally devoted to Christian piety, he wished the church of Tours to be maintained safe and sound. He confirmed to Hugh of Calvimont Amboise, which Geoffrey, the brother of Elizabeth, had given his sister as dowry.

Richin had begotten Geoffrey Martel by his second wife Hermengarde, daughter of Archambaud of Bourbon. Having soon repudiated her and given her in marriage to William of Jaligny, he joined Bertrada to himself in marriage; by her he fathered Fulk before she was carried off by King Philip. William of Jaligny, moreover, had by Hermengarde a daughter Elizabeth. Betrothed to Hugh, son of Sulpice of Amboise, she received from her brother Geoffrey as dowry the other portion of the castle of Amboise which the people of Amboise had not yet obtained from the counts of Anjou. In this way Hugh became the first universal lord of Amboise, though he was already lord of Calvimont.

He restored to Hugh himself Mont-Richard, long unjustly taken from the lords of Calvimont. He left the castle of Preuilly, which he had captured in war, to Prince Echinard, after he had overcome him by arms in rebellion and he had turned to a better course. He bought Bazon’s Mount from John; when John, repenting of the transaction, refused to surrender it, Fulk took it by force of arms. He performed many other deeds of the same sort, splendidly and courageously, while he governed the county of Tours. Because of these deeds, after Baldwin II, king of Jerusalem, had died without male heirs, he was sought by the wishes of all the nobles and of the whole Christian knighthood; and, with the permission of Louis the Fat, king of the Franks, after receiving from Hildebert in the metropolitan church of Tours the insignia of holy knighthood on Pentecost itself, and after appointing his son Geoffrey, called Plantagenet, count of Tours, Anjou, and Le Mans, he departed for Jerusalem in 1127. At last he married Baldwin’s elder daughter and heiress of the kingdom and was hailed king of Jerusalem in 1131.

[Col. 0029] No one can fail to see how important the above-mentioned facts are for understanding well many matters in both the acts and writings of Archbishop Hildebert. We now turn to an account of those things which render this latest edition of the works of the Venerable Hildebert fuller and more accurate.

1. Dom Antoine Beaugendre published 121 letters of the Venerable Hildebert, arranged in order in three books. Letter 45 of Book II is not Hildebert’s, but merely a fragment of Saint Jerome’s letter to Demetrias. Two others, if the authors of the *Histoire littéraire*, vol. XI, p. 308, are to be believed, are by Odo, abbot of Saint-Pierre. In an appendix Dom Beaugendre also published three further letters, which came to his notice only after all the others had been printed.

The first, written to Thurstan, archbishop-elect of York in Great Britain, dates from about 1125. The second contains an answer to a question concerning a moral case proposed by Marbod, bishop of Rennes, and W., archdeacon of Anjou. Here it should be noted that Dom Luc d’Achery first published this letter in the *Spicilegium* and attributed it to Marbod, whereas Dom Beaugendre presents it as Hildebert’s. The latter seems wholly unaware of the former’s opinion; had he known it, he would surely have examined it. In the complicated and rather obscure questions concerning medieval authors, the source and origin of errors is easily discovered in the fact that ancient writers frequently—indeed almost always—indicate names merely by initial letters. Dom Luc d’Achery, an exceptionally sharp-sighted writer, saw the letter M and read “Marbod”; whereas Dom Antoine Beaugendre read “to Marbod.” Thus one regarded Marbod as the author of the letter and the other as its recipient. The former had a copy from the hand of the most learned d’Hérouval; the latter, from that of Étienne Baluze, an exceptionally knowledgeable scholar.

It seems more probable that this letter belongs to Hildebert, since Marbod would not have written of himself, “Marbod, by God’s grace venerable bishop of Rennes,” whereas one might properly write to him, “To Marbod, by God’s grace venerable bishop of Rennes.” We therefore agree with Dom Beaugendre that this letter was written by our Hildebert; but at what time is uncertain.

The third letter was addressed to R., that is, Ranulf, bishop of Durham, in 1099. The Benedictine editor received it from Dom Loyaute, a most discerning investigator of Tours antiquities, although he himself did not find it among the many manuscripts he is known to have possessed. We have placed these three letters immediately after Letter 34 of Book III, as nos. 35, 36, and 37; before them we have placed in a note Dom Beaugendre’s notice, so that the literary account in the Benedictine authors’ *Histoire littéraire de la France* clearly agrees in our latest edition with Dom Beaugendre’s edition.

Finally, from Antonio Muratori’s *Anecdota* we have taken two unpublished letters which he himself extracted from Ambrosian manuscripts; we include them here as nos. 38 and 39. That very learned man also printed three others together, but because they had already been published by Antoine Beaugendre, we carefully collated them and found Beaugendre’s text much more accurate. In Hildebert’s Letter 4—which is Letter 10 in the Ambrosian manuscript and Letter 40, Book II, p. 145, in Antoine Beaugendre’s edition—very many passages are found incorrectly transcribed by Muratori. The following words may suffice as an example:

> “When, in accordance with your command, we had fixed a day for them to plead their case, Agnes herself pleaded that she could not come to the hearing, both because of the shortness of the time and because of the place to which she could not bring her advocates, and especially because her brother Guy of Laval was at war with the count.”

Thus Dom Beaugendre, from the manuscript of Évreux. But Dom Muratori has:

> “When, in accordance with our command, we had fixed a day for them to plead their case, A. herself pleaded that she could not come to the hearing, because of the shortness of the time, because of the place to which she could not bring her advocates, and especially because her brother W. de Javalle had [a dispute] with Count Guerrin.”

A manuscript of very high quality, contemporary with Hildebert, was supplied to us by our friend André Salmon of Tours, a most devoted student of humane letters. It contains forty written letters. We collated all of them with the letters already printed and found none unpublished, although we read a note inserted on the last page in a hand not that of the ancient author, as follows:

> “Letters are lacking from this fortieth through the eighty-third and last; all of them are printed in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. But this one, beginning *Successisse [Col. 0031] confitebor* [‘I shall confess that I succeeded’], is not found among the printed letters.”

We found this letter included among the letters of Book III as no. 34.

In vol. XI, p. 308, of the *Histoire littéraire de la France* one reads the following note:

> “Thomas Bodley gave the University of Oxford, among other works, a manuscript codex in which are included 178 letters of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans.”

The *Catalogue of the Bodleian Library*, p. 92, no. 1872, is cited. This gave us hope of publishing fifty-three new letters of Hildebert. We wrote from Tours in May 1854 to the distinguished H. O. Coxe, librarian of the Bodleian Library. He replied that manuscript no. 1872, which he had in hand, contained only five letters of Hildebert, the last of which also seemed incomplete. The error arose because a printer, through carelessness, printed the following incorrectly: “Letters of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, 178,” instead of “a letter of Hildebert, [on] folio 178 of the codex.” The letters found in the Bodleian manuscript are nos. 7, 8, 18, 17, and 25 of Dom Beaugendre’s edition, and that manuscript was written toward the end of the twelfth century.

In order to illuminate obscure questions, especially concerning the time at which certain letters were written, we shall append to the texts notes taken from Benedictine books, largely extracted from *Histoire littéraire*, vol. XI. These notes, like all our additions, are marked with a cross in this form: +.

A spurious letter of Hildebert is found among the Magdeburg Centuriators. In the book *Le mystère d’iniquité dévoilé* [*The Mystery of Iniquity Unveiled*], Dom Coeffeteau established its forged character with clear arguments. Hence it is certain how seriously Illyricus, Viguier, Duplessis-Mornay, and Bayle erred.

2. Next come charters granted by Hildebert. Since they can scarcely be separated from the letters, the nature of the material gives them a more fitting place after them. They are certainly very numerous; Dom Beaugendre published only six. We have added three, published for the first time from cartularies, as nos. 7, 8, and 9. Two, namely nos. 10 and 11, occur in Dom Edmond Martène’s *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, pp. 579 and 606. Finally, we drew nos. 12 and 13 from the *Miscellanea* of Étienne Baluze, vol. III, Mansi’s folio edition.

See Dom Beaugendre’s index for the six charters printed under his care.

We found the seventh and eighth among the documents appended to the *History of Marmoutier near Tours*, by Edmond Martène, manuscript vol. II, pp. 64 and 182. That manuscript belongs to the library of the city of Tours. It should be observed here that the documents appended in the same manuscript history, which belongs to the Imperial Library of Paris, are not the same as those in ours. The seventh charter contains Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans’s, gift of the church of Saint George of the Wood (*de Nemore*). The eighth bears the title: “Letter of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, concerning the churches of Mayenne and Sceaux,” and was granted in the year of the Lord 1120.

The ninth, extracted from the cartulary of the distinguished church of Le Mans called the *White Book of the Chapter*, no. CCXVIII, was sent to us by the learned Dom Pitra, who stated that this *White Book* would soon be made public by Dom René J.-F. Lottin, canon of Le Mans. The tenth charter, granted about the year 1100, bears the following title: “Instrument concerning the agreement made between the canons of Saint-Julien of Le Mans and the monks of Saint-Vincent.” The eleventh is given to the monastery of Saint-Victor, and Hildebert confirms to its monks churches granted by laymen, in the year of the Lord 1116. The twelfth charter was written in 1114 for the benefit of the monks of Marmoutier near Tours. The thirteenth and final charter supplies Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans’s, confirmation concerning the church of Torciacum, commonly Torcé.

3. Dom Beaugendre publicly published 140 sermons, to which must be added the sermon for Palm Sunday at the end of Marbod’s works. We shall append two sermons discovered by Dom Muratori in an Ambrosian manuscript: the first for Advent, the second for the Council of Chartres. Thus this latest edition will contain 143 sermons.

4. There follow: (1) the *Life of Saint Radegund*, queen of the Franks; (2) the *Life of the Most Holy [Col. 0033] Father Hugh*, abbot of Cluny. Into both Lives we have inserted divisions into chapters, with summaries, and have placed after each chapter notes from the Bollandists’ *Acts of the Saints*.

5. Next comes the *Book on the Complaint and Conflict of Flesh and Spirit, or Soul*. We have found nothing to add except a note indicating that this same book was at one time designated under the title *The Conflagration* (*Incendium*). From this someone might perhaps, though erroneously, suppose that there are two works by Hildebert.

6. Afterward comes the *Moral Philosophy on the Honorable and the Useful*. Dom Beaugendre first published this book from Colbert manuscript 2662 and Victorine manuscript no. 759. We publish it again, however, much fuller and more correct than before, from a manuscript in the library of the seminary of Padua, with explanatory notes. Hildebert’s work holds the first place in the Paduan manuscript and is entitled *Introduction to Moral Philosophy* (*Isagoge ad moralem philosophiam*). This new annotated edition of the *Moral Philosophy* was most kindly provided to us by the learned and ardent lover of humane letters, Dom Vincenzo De Vit of Stresa on Lake Maggiore, in the Kingdom of Piedmont. He dedicated it to the eminent Joseph Valentinelli, director of Saint Mark’s Library in Venice. No one can fail to see that the Paduan manuscript is of the highest quality and should be preferred to the Colbertine and Victorine manuscripts if he merely compares the text now published by De Vit with that edited by Dom Beaugendre.

7. There follows the little book *On the Four Virtues of Honorable Life*.

8. This little book is followed by the *Theological Treatise*, a work altogether admirable for learning, method, elegance of style, and precision of expression. Whether it is Hildebert’s is doubted by the authors of the *Histoire littéraire*, vol. XI, pp. 362–365, and denied by the authors of the following volume, pp. 29–37. The latter attribute it to Hugh of Saint-Victor. Yet because most manuscripts—including manuscripts of very high quality and nearly contemporary with Hildebert—affirm that the *Theological Treatise* is Hildebert’s, we commit it to print on the authority of the manuscripts and wholly renew the text of the edition of 1708.

9. There follows a *Brief Treatise on the Sacrament of the Altar*.

10. Then the *Book on the Explanation of the Mass*.

11. Afterward, verses on the mystery of the Mass, to which we have added five unpublished lines from Tours manuscript no. 115, under the title “On the Change of Places in the Mass”; other verses on the sacrament of the altar; and finally, “On the New Sacrifice Abrogating the Old.”

12. The *Book on the Holy Eucharist* follows. The frequently cited authors of the *Histoire littéraire*, vol. XI, maintain that the poem on the Holy Eucharist is by Peter the Painter, as are the other verses on the sacrament of the altar. In Saint-Germain manuscript no. 658 one reads: “Of Master Peter the Painter, canon of Saint-Omer, on the sacraments of the altar.” (See the work mentioned above, p. 371.)

13. The poem *On the Works of the Six Days* is not Hildebert’s, according to the authors of the work mentioned above (p. 372), but Bishop Theobald’s; so also is the *Physiologus*, as may be seen in the book of Dom Jean Lebeuf, canon of Auxerre, *Historical Dissertations on Paris*, vol. II, p. 66 ff. Dom Polycarp Leyser, however, in his *Library of Medieval Poets*, does not deny that the poem on the Six Days belongs to the bishop of Le Mans, and he published the verses *On the Destruction of Troy* under Hildebert’s name because they immediately followed the book *On the Works of the Six Days* in a manuscript. To the section “On Sirens and the Onocentaur” we have added a note restoring the term *Onocentaurus* from the text of Isaiah and Saint Jerome and correcting certain words.

14 and 15. Poems *On the Order of the World* and *On the Adornment of the World*.

16. We have found nothing to add to the poem on the books of Kings.

17. A moral application of various passages of Holy Scripture. In Tours manuscript no. 117, five lines concerning the sacrifice of Isaac are read differently, and perhaps better; we have added them as the tenth section. The same manuscript does not contain the first two lines of section 45, which Dom Beaugendre incorrectly inserted here. These two lines are elegiac couplets and can in no way belong under that heading. The other lines are hexameters, under the title “The instruments hung upon the willows by the people of God.” So that nothing may be lost, we have collected the fragment and sent it here:

### On Christ’s Twofold Nature

The divinity united to our nature is shown forth:  
Thus in Christ are together both riches and poverty.

[Col. 0035] In the manuscript mentioned above we found two unpublished sections, which we have added as nos. L and LI, with these titles:

1. What is signified by the fact that the solemnity of Easter was celebrated for forty days.
2. What is signified by the fact that the people, while free, received grain for food, but when made slaves received it for seed.

From the New Testament, section XIV is given twice, on p. 1226 and p. 1363. We have taken care to remove one.

To the other subjects of the verses, in section VII we have added two unpublished lines from Tours manuscript no. 115.

18. A little book of Christian inscriptions. This little book is entirely new and unpublished. No expert in archaeological matters is unaware that in former times sacred buildings were painted on every side, and that all the chief articles of the Christian faith, the historical acts of sacred Scripture, and the deeds of the blessed, now triumphant in heaven, were depicted in form and colors upon their walls. In Gaul, especially in the eleventh century, the custom prevailed of adorning churches within by an almost royal display of painted images.

Prudentius says in *Peristephanon*, Hymn XII, lines 47–48:

> The place has royal splendor; a good prince consecrated these halls,  
> And lavished the resources of great wealth on their surroundings.

Here *lusit* means “painted.” One may cite this example:

> Therefore it seemed to us a useful work  
> To adorn all the house of Felix with holy painting.  
> (Saint Paulinus, *On the Feast of Saint Felix*, Poem IX, lines 580 ff.)

Not only walls but ceilings, vaults, and even pavements were decorated with colors or mosaic work, so that wherever the faithful looked they had sacred images before their eyes. The Fathers wished minds to be directed toward piety and devout meditation through the harmonious variety of colors and the wondrous splendor of light (Gori, *Ancient Diptychs*, vol. III, p. 261). On painting sacred images, compare Saint Basil, Homily 17 on the martyr Barlaam, and Homily 19 on the Forty Martyrs, vol. II, pp. 141 and 149; Saint Gregory of Nyssa, *Oration on Saint Theodore the Martyr*, vol. II, p. 1011; Saint John Chrysostom, *Encomium on Saint Meletius*, Homily 47, vol. VII, p. 191; Saint Augustine, *On the Solemnity of Stephen the Martyr*, Sermon 316, chapter 5, vol. V, part II, col. 1270; Prudentius, Hymns IX and XI; Saint Paulinus, Letter 32 to Severus, no. 2; idem, *On the Feast of Saint Felix*, Poem X, lines 10 ff. and 171 ff.

Beneath these paintings were set forth sentences drawn from the Scriptures or Christian inscriptions, by which all who possessed the art of reading were exhorted to cultivate virtues and imitate the courageous examples of the saints.

Furthermore, apostles, prophets, and other martyrs, confessors, or doctors of the New Covenant were distinguished from one another at first glance by their attributes. In the outstanding work recently published by the learned Dom Didron under the title Ἑρμηνεία τοῦ ζωγράφου (*The Painter’s Guide*), one may see that Greek painters distinguish every figure by the particular text of an inscription. We already know very many examples in Western churches of these pious inscriptions, which always accompany and explain the figures.

Our Hildebert, easily foremost in sacred poetry, composed many inscriptions of this kind. Not all have perished through the ravages of time. By God’s permission, we have extracted very many from Tours manuscript no. 117 new numbering, 164 old numbering, and now publish them for the first time. Dom Beaugendre had some before him and inserted them among the short poems, scattered and, as it were, without method. The inscriptions already printed we retain arranged in their proper order; and the unpublished ones, no. LV, we have arranged as follows:

1. God’s eternity.  
2. Adam’s sin.  
3. What is signified by the Lord’s saying to the serpent: “You shall crawl upon breast and belly.”  
4. Patriarchs of the Old Testament.  
5. The holy man Job.  
6. Moses strikes the rock in the wilderness.  
7. The Rod of Jesse.  
7 bis. On the Virgin Mother of God.  
8. Angels announce to the shepherds that the Savior has been born.  
9. Christ as an infant in a manger.  
[Col. 0037] 10. On Christ’s twofold nature.  
11. The infant Christ is suckled by the Virgin.  
12. The Magi come from the East.  
13. The Magi worship Christ.  
14. The Magi before Herod.  
15. Shepherds worship the Savior.  
16. Elizabeth greets Mary.  
17. The Blessed Virgin Mary visits Elizabeth.  
18. The Pharisee and the tax collector.  
19. The narrow way that leads to heaven.  
20. Christ remits the sins of the woman caught in adultery.  
21. Christ heals the sick: the pool of Siloam.  
22. The paralytic healed by Christ.  
23. Lazarus rises from the tomb.  
24. Christ enters Jerusalem in triumph.  
25. Christ feeds the apostles with Holy Communion in the upper room.  
26. Christ washes the disciples’ feet in the upper room.  
27. Christ is betrayed by Judas.  
28. Christ’s Passion.  
29. The women at Christ’s tomb.  
30. By his death Christ frees humankind from eternal death.  
31. Death conquered by Christ’s death.  
32. Where Christ’s image is painted.  
33. The Virgin, Christ’s mother, standing beside the cross.  
34. On Christ hanging upon the cross.  
35. The human being redeemed through Christ’s death.  
36. The cross drenched with Christ’s blood.  
37. Christ speaking to the redeemed human being.  
38. On the Messiah, son of the Virgin.  
39. The lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered.  
40. He reconciled sinners to God.  
41. Christ, Son of the eternal Father.  
42. On Christ’s cross.  
43. Beneath Christ’s image.  
44. The twelve apostles.  
45. Christ speaking to the apostles.  
46. The saints in paradise.  
47. On the Eucharist.  
48. On Holy Communion.  
49. On sleep.  
50. On old age.  
51. Against depraved habits.  
52. On confidence amid dangers.  
53. Modesty in clothing.  
54. On the human condition.  
55. From the sayings of Saint Gregory.

To this little book we have appended, under no. 56, an unpublished poem *On the Conception of Blessed Mary*, extracted from the Tours manuscript, which would more properly be entitled *On the Annunciation, the Conception, and the Nativity of Christ*; and, under no. 57, Hildebert’s verses to Blessed Mary, printed from manuscript codex 3550 of the Imperial Library of Paris among the additions to vol. XI of the *Histoire littéraire*, by members of the Institute of France. Finally, under no. 57, we have also added some unpublished little verses, from the aforesaid Tours codex, on the fifteen signs during the fifteen days before the Day of Judgment, which Jerome mentions in the *Annals of the Hebrews*, although it is doubtful whether they are Hildebert’s. Yet, since they immediately follow a Hildebertian poem, we believed that they should be attributed to him.

Before proceeding to other matters, we here produce two little verses found among the works attributed to Hildebert, in which the year is mentioned when Jerusalem was, with God’s favor, wrested from the hands of the unbelievers by the Franks and other Christian soldiers adorned with the sign of the cross:

> In the year eleven hundred lacking one,  
> The Franks take Jerusalem by mighty strength.

[Col. 0039] 19. There follow: 1. verses on Saint Susanna; 2. on the Maccabees; 3. on Saint Vincent; 4. the Passion of Saint Agnes, virgin and martyr; 5. on the Finding of the Holy Cross; 6. the Life of Blessed Mary of Egypt.

20. The Benedictine authors (*Histoire littéraire*, vol. XI) report that Hildebert’s work entitled *Lament of the Sinful Soul* mourns the soul’s departure and declares that departure most desirable.

We found it in manuscript codex no. 656 under its new numbering, and 222 under its old numbering, in the library of the city of Tours, and here publish it for the first time. Although composed in little verses ending in the same rhythm or sound, it may perhaps not be judged unworthy of our Hildebert if attention is paid to the piety breathed and inspired by its sentiments.

21. A History of Muhammad and a book called *Mathematicus* are described in Tours manuscript no. 117.

22. A little book called *The Flowering Aspect*. Among the miscellaneous poems is given the *Epitaph of Suger*, Abbot of Saint-Denis, but less correctly under Hildebert’s name. For the bishop of Le Mans became archbishop of Tours and died in 1134, whereas Abbot Suger died in 1152. It is therefore clear that the epitaph was not composed by Hildebert. To it we have appended the *Epitaph of William de Ros*, which is attributed to Hildebert (see *Histoire littéraire*, vol. IX, pp. 331–332). At the end we have added six unpublished little verses, under the titles: 1. *On Death*; 2. *To the Miser*. Finally, among the miscellaneous poems we have inserted six elegiac verses on Lucretia, which we read in Tours codex 61, after Berengar’s epitaph.

23. We have restored to Hildebert the poem entitled *On the Destruction of Troy*. Polycarp Leyser published it from a Leipzig manuscript codex in his book entitled *History of the Poets and Poems of the Middle Ages*, Halle-Magdeburg, 1721, p. 398 and following. There it is immediately joined to verses *On the Creation of the World and the Works of the Six Days*.

24. Among the works of Philip, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance, are found certain Hildebertian poems, which here first appear openly under their author’s name:

1. *Verses of the Bridegroom against His Bride.* 2. *The Bride’s Reply.* 3. *The Judge’s Reply.* 4. *On the Praises of Samson.* 5. *Epitaph of the Bishop of Sens.* 6. *Epitaph of the Kings of Jerusalem.* 7. *Epitaph of the Abbot of Clairvaux.* 8. *On Fortune’s Wheel.* 9. *That the Arts Avail Little without Money.*

25. Hildebert’s Aesopic fables. A medieval author, using the pseudonym Romulus, rewrote Phaedrus’s fables in looser prose under the pretext of imitating Aesop’s fables, entirely overturning the author’s style. Yet to discerning readers Phaedrus’s fables plainly show themselves and retain the savor of a poet of good repute. Hildebert, having Romulus’s book before him, an eloquent poet and elegant writer, removes the pedestrian manner and adorns it with excellent verse. Hence, in the schools of Gaul, Italy, and Spain during the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, Hildebert’s fables, bearing Aesop’s name, were handled by pupils together with the works of Virgil and Horace. In the fourteenth century these fables were translated from Latin into French and were always presented with great praise.

That Hildebert had before him the text of Romulus rather than Phaedrus’s genuine verses is clearer to anyone who reads his book attentively. Only sixty Hildebertian fables have happily come down to our time; the others remain hidden. They agree very well with the first three books of Romulus, according to the Ulm and Dijon manuscripts.

When Phaedrus’s genuine fables were first made public by J. Chifflet, Hildebert’s fables gradually fell into neglect, and today are scarcely known even to scholars.

Whoever wishes may readily find these fables in the work of D. Robert, entitled *Unpublished Fables of the Twelfth, Thirteenth, and Fourteenth Centuries*, 2 vols., octavo, Paris, 1825.

Let us now proceed to the works of our author that are lacking.

[Col. 0041]

## Doubtful or Spurious Works of the Venerable Hildebert, or Works That Are Missing

From Hildebert, *Works*, p. 171, we learn that he himself wrote a *History of the Miracles of the Church of Exeter*, at the request of a certain Clarembald, canon or monk of that same church. In epistle 3 of book III, addressed to that same Clarembald, one may see what Hildebert himself declares concerning the work sent to him.

Sanderus indicates a manuscript codex in the library of Cambron Abbey (*Bibliotheca Belgica manuscripta*, part I, p. 357), in which are found certain homilies on the Twelve Prophets under Hildebert’s name, and four most useful letters. If he had told us the names of those to whom those letters were written, we should certainly have known whether they occur among the Hildebertian letters edited by D. Beaugendre. The homilies, however, have become known to us only through this mention.

The same Sanderus (*ibid.*, part II, p. 119) states that in volume 123 of the manuscripts of the monastery of Loz or Loo, of the Cistercian Order near Lille in Flanders, there is a poem which he mentions in the following words under this title: “Heroic verses, which, as is apparent from the style, are by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, *On the Analogy of the Sacraments of the Eucharist, Baptism, and Marriage with Their Figures*.” We know nothing else of that poem.

Peter the Chanter (*Petrus Cantor*, p. 325), in the work entitled *The Abbreviated Word*, records the following four little verses, without however giving the author’s name:

> Ah! With what anxious labor each person  
> Hastens to a physician through love of the flesh!  
> Of the soul’s diseases, with no complaint,  
> Slow healing follows the sick soul.

But Dom George Galopin, monk of Saint-Ghislain, in a marginal note identifies these verses as Hildebertian and extracted from a poem entitled *The Conflagration*. Yet no poem by our author bears such a title. Whether such a poem ever existed is wholly unknown. Nevertheless, the poem which Dom George Galopin calls *The Conflagration* seems to be none other than the partly metrical and partly prose treatise *On the Conflict of Flesh and Soul*, in which the four little verses quoted above are found.

Philip of Bergamo, in the *Supplement to the Chronicle*, under the year 1106, p. 289, says of Hildebert: “He also wrote, in most elegant metre, a very useful exposition upon the whole Psalter.” Philip indeed cites Vincent of Beauvais, who says absolutely nothing about this poem. Did Philip see the poem? He does not affirm it. But since he praises Hildebert as most learned in scriptural knowledge, perhaps he attributed to him another’s work.

Jean Bouchet (*Annals of Aquitaine*, p. 29) represents the author of the *Life of Saint Hilary* as a certain Hildebrand, bishop of Le Mans, and cites his words while investigating the place of Saint Hilary’s burial. Bouchet certainly means our Hildebert under the name Hildebrand. Perhaps Hildebert wrote the *Life of Blessed Hilary*, or rewrote one already composed in a more elegant style, just as he recast the *Life of Blessed Radegund* into a better form. We suspect this, but do not affirm it, since we have learned it only from Bouchet, who represents our prelate as polishing this work twenty years after his death: “in the time,” he says, “of Henry, king of the English, and his wife Eleanor, when they were lords of Aquitaine.” No one fails to know that Henry ascended the throne in 1154, upon Stephen’s death, and married Eleanor in 1151, after she had been repudiated by Louis the Younger. (*Henry of Ghent*, *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 8, scholium, p. 118.)

The learned Le Mire, in his scholium on chapter 8, *On the Ecclesiastical Writers of Henry the Great*, attributes to our Hildebert a letter written to the Carthusians of Mont-Dieu (*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. IX, p. 233). Quite wrongly, indeed; for the author of the letter mentioned above died before the foundation of that monastery, which occurred in 1137, and therefore three years after Hildebert’s death.

Decker, *On Anonymous Writers*, p. 106, where he sets out conjectures on anonymous authors, says after Goldast that some persons falsely attribute to Hildebert the work entitled *On the Corrupt State of the Church*, whose author is Nicholas of Clamanges, archdeacon of Bayeux, who assumed Hildebert’s person and name. Certain less attentive writers, or persons little learned in the affairs of the twelfth and fifteenth centuries, may have erred.

Hildebert appears to have been the author of a *Collection of Canons*, since in a letter to the bishop of [Col. 0043] Memoria he openly asserts that he wrote such a book (epistle 27, book II). Who the bishop of Memoria was is unknown; yet the above-mentioned letter is certainly Hildebertian. D. Beaugendre believes that the bishop was named Malch, a former monk of Winchester made bishop in the province of Munster on the island of Ireland, according to Saint Bernard in the *Life of Blessed Malachy*. That prelate had written to Hildebert, announcing the death of Queen Matilda and commending to his prayers the soul of the queen lately deceased. Was he instead Gillebert, bishop of the city of Limerick in Ireland and legate in those regions? Whatever may be the name of the bishop and bishopric, Hildebert wrote to him in these words:

> “The excerpts from the decrees, which we have resolved to arrange in one volume, have not yet been brought to their conclusion. For this work requires a mind free from cares—a freedom of which the episcopal office has deprived us. We have nevertheless already completed part of it; and, in order to accomplish what remains, we shall lay aside the bishopric. When completed, it shall come into your hands, and there will be no need for your legate to weary himself by coming all the way to us to carry it. It will be our duty to send it to you by one of our own.”

From this it is evident that Hildebert did not complete the work he had begun because of the continual and importunate cares of his bishopric, and that he left it unfinished until Queen Matilda’s death in 1118. Did Hildebert complete his work? What became of the completed work? Does it survive, or has it perished? D. Beaugendre suspects that the work begun by Hildebert was completed by Ivo, bishop of Chartres, who, being at ease in the diocese of Chartres, never relaxed his labor. But the editor forgets that Ivo died in 1115, and therefore could not have finished a work which had not yet reached completion in 1118. D. Beaugendre himself affirms that the letter to the bishop of Memoria was written in 1118 or 1119, and that Matilda, queen of the English, died in 1118. We therefore conclude that the *Collection of Canons* bearing Ivo’s name is not Hildebertian, and that epistle 53 of book III is neither the preface to this work nor Hildebert’s offspring. (On books of canons, see *Histoire littéraire*, vol. XI, pp. 407, 408, and 409.)

D. Doujat speaks of certain capitularies of Hildebert, without producing anything from them. More probably the reference is to the synodal statutes which he composed while governing the Church of Le Mans. D. Thiers reported certain fragments of them in his minor works, from which D. Beaugendre concludes that he had seen a copy. The Benedictine editor himself labored greatly, but vainly, to see such a copy.

Casimir Oudin (*Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, p. 995) speaks at length of Hildebertian works preserved in various libraries of England. Among them some seem unpublished, and wholly escaped D. Beaugendre, although others seem to have been made public under different titles. The following do not appear to have been known hitherto: 1. A *Narrative on the Genealogy of the Savior*, in the manuscript codex of Charles Theyer, no. 15, containing letters and sermons of the same author; 2. A *Book on the Prefiguration of Christ and the Church*, in hexameter verse, in William Landi’s manuscript 28, no. 10; 3. An *Elegy in which Theology Addresses the Synagogue*, in the same codex.

At Tours, 13 September, on the feast of Saint Lidoire, bishop of Tours.

J.-J. BOURASSÉ,  
Canon of the Metropolitan Church of Tours.

[Col. 0045]

## PREFACE OF D. BEAUGENDRE

[Col. 0045A] Being about to give to public light, reduced into one body, the letters and other works of the Venerable Hildebert—whatever we could extract from various manuscripts and gather from editions scattered here and there—we judged it worthwhile to render an account to the kindly reader of our purpose and of the plan of this modest undertaking. But first, since we intend to say more about Hildebert in his Life, we have thought it necessary to state briefly what manner of man and how great a prelate he was, so that it may thereby be apparent what fruit may be hoped for from his labors, no small part of which has perished, certainly to the great loss of scholarship.
