Born, indeed, as the ancient *Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans* relate [Note: [Col. 0045D] Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. III.], of parents of moderate but honorable condition, he is said from childhood to have applied himself to humane letters under the master Berengar [Col. 0045B], and afterward, under Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, to sacred studies and at the same time to piety under the monastic habit. Having been excellently trained in these disciplines, and at length famous even among distant persons for his reputation in sacred eloquence, he was called by Hoel, the most devout no less than prudent bishop of Le Mans, first to the office of schoolmaster, then to that of archdeacon; finally, upon Hoel’s death, he was elected his successor by the votes of clergy and people.

Raised to that height only by the steps of virtue and learning, and established by the merit of holiness as though on a firm foundation of grace, he conducted himself so admirably that Saint Bernard—himself the marvel and oracle of his age—both revered him as a man deserving every reverence and did not hesitate to call him a great pillar of the Church. Nor without good reason. For that most holy abbot knew him to be distinguished not only for virtues expressive and breathing Christian piety and priestly holiness, but had found him a most courageous defender of the Church’s immunities both by example and by writing. The Church of Le Mans and the metropolitan church of Tours had experienced that neither the loss of all his possessions, nor repeated exiles, nor most unjust imprisonments, nor bodily sufferings inflicted by any magnates, could turn him from the sacred purpose of justice. When Pope Paschal II, their supreme pontiff, was treacherously detained by Emperor Henry IV together with his clergy, those churches had embraced Hildebert in defense of him; and amid the disturbance at Rome, almost the whole Church had applauded and marveled at so vigorous a champion. [Col. 0045D]

From this arose the reputation for learning, courage, and outstanding holiness which he had gained among all good and learned men, whether by his various writings, sacred sermons, or examples of virtue. Hence also came the wishes of many scholars, who often declared that it would be most welcome to them if Hildebert’s various little works—of which, as he himself says, he frequently makes mention in his letters—might somehow be extracted from the repositories of renowned libraries.

Nor did the endeavors of certain learned men, who seemed like standard-bearers and leaders to prepare and open the way for us in this task, contribute little to urging us to search for them. Above all, the illustrious Stephen Baluze, renowned for so many monuments of fine letters, produced this effect upon us; for in the preface to the works of Lupus Servatus, abbot of Ferrières, which he published in 1664, he had promised that he would someday publish Hildebert’s works also. No one would deny how excellently and successfully that most discerning man would have performed the task, had he not, occupied with studies of greater importance, left this undertaking to another. Yet our plan so little displeased him that he declared that, had leisure permitted, he would himself have lent us a hand. [Col. 0046B]

We shall not deny that Father Jacques Homey, an Augustinian of the community called Bourges, encouraged us. In his learned *Supplement to the Fathers*, printed at Paris in 1684, he brought to light certain little works, both prose and verse, which he had discovered; and, from more manuscripts than we ourselves may perhaps have been able to inspect, we established with absolute certainty that they were wholly genuine works of Hildebert. He annotated, however, only those letters of the Venerable Hildebert which he had read in the printed libraries of the Fathers.

What prevented us from undertaking this task was not so much the inconveniences of an approaching age already octogenarian at that time, now, God granting, passed through, as the very weight of so great an undertaking. Yet, sustained by the aid of almighty God—to whose glory we were bound and rejoiced to offer at least what remained to us of a life and sight already fleeing away—and trusting at once in the aid and indulgence of learned friends, we undertook this arduous work, in the small amount of leisure granted us outside our regular exercises, and with strength failing day by day. And indeed God, best and greatest, helped this perhaps overbold endeavor of ours beyond expectation. [Col. 0046C]

For while, through repeated reading of Hildebert’s letters published in the *Library of the Fathers*, we received no less a sense of piety than of harmless delight, and while we were rendering them into the vernacular tongue for the consolation of our solitude—as perhaps someday useful to devout persons of either sex—which, God granting, we have done according to our measure and may, with his favor, perhaps publish, we sometimes hesitated in resolving difficulties that arose. We did not neglect to have recourse to manuscript codices as though to originals; indeed, we often found this necessary. While laboring over their examination, we encountered more letters than had until then been committed to print in the three editions of the *Library of the Fathers*, and even in the latest Lyons edition. It is astonishing that in that edition letters already published both in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium* and elsewhere were omitted. [Col. 0047A]

Since Hildebert himself testifies in various places in his letters that he published various little works, we judged it not useless, indeed beneficial to the commonwealth of letters, if we searched for them with the utmost diligence possible and brought to public light whatever might be found—light which, as is clear from the multitude of manuscripts themselves, they had formerly enjoyed. Thus Hildebert, in epistle 3 of the newly ordered book III, to Clarembald, testifies that he wrote a *History of the Miracles of the Church of Exeter*, which, in his native modesty, he submits to Clarembald’s correction; and we could nowhere recover it, despite applying every diligence. Thus in epistle 15 of the same book, to Reginald, monk of Saint Augustine, he writes that he gladly embraces the fact that Reginald had inserted in his work certain propositions of his modest talent, as he calls them, its daughters, or little portions of his verses. Finally, not to be too lengthy, in epistle 30 of book III, to William, bishop of Winchester, he says that he was greatly pleased that William requested his little works to be sent to him. [Col. 0047B]

Warned and stirred, therefore, by these and other words, as it were Hildebert’s own, we set ourselves to investigate and search out his works from the shelves of distinguished libraries. Guided by the counsel of friends who patronized sound learning, and relying upon their aid, we have collated the works already published against the testimony of thirteen or more manuscripts of excellent authority and almost contemporary date, with all the accuracy we could; where we found errors in the editions, we corrected them by comparison with those manuscripts; we observed variant readings; and we have now first brought to light certain works recently discovered in them and not previously published. [Col. 0047C]

For this purpose the most learned Messrs. Clément and Boyvin, administrators under the most illustrious and learned Abbé Le Tellier, chief prefect of that truly royal and richly furnished library, most kindly lent us two manuscripts. From the exceedingly well-stocked Colbert Library, the most learned M. Duchesne, their diligent keeper, very courteously provided us with six others, and afterward, in his kindness, supplied several more for Hildebert’s metrical little works. From the celebrated library of Saint-Victor, the learned M. Perruquier, administrator to M. de Wion d’Herouval—regular canon, librarian, and doctor of the Sorbonne of that royal monastery—provided two more, with the latter’s consent and in accordance with the hereditary disposition toward helping all scholars which he had inherited from his distinguished father. Father Denis Sammarthanus, prior of the monastery of Saint-Ouen at Rouen, of our Congregation of Saint-Maur and celebrated among scholars for his new edition of Saint Gregory and other labors, granted us another from that monastery’s library. [Col. 0047D]

But among all the manuscripts which we were permitted to see, and which were almost all either contemporary with Hildebert himself or at least approached closely to his time, we obtained scarcely any of better authority or greater extent than the one which our most friendly and ardent lover of sound learning, Father Gabriel Pouget, prior of the monastery of Saint-Taurin at Évreux in our congregation, took care to send us. This manuscript codex was one of those among many others, both handwritten and printed, with which the highly select private library of the most eminent Cardinal du Perron had formerly been furnished—at that time bishop of Évreux and abbot of Saint-Taurin, afterward archbishop of Sens. In order that this library should not perish after his death or, as often happens, be dispersed to the public’s loss, the first monks of our congregation in that monastery purchased it entire from his heirs at a price certainly not small, immediately after they had been admitted there for its reform.

We thought it proper to note this in order that greater confidence might be placed in that manuscript, since it is known to have come from the library of a man both most learned and a most vigorous defender of the Catholic faith: the most eminent Cardinal du Perron, whom heterodox Christians experienced as such by the very frequent defeat or conversion of their own adherents, and whom orthodox Christians celebrated as such, to God’s glory and the Church’s edification, because of his repeatedly won victories. For scarcely anything is found in manuscripts which came to us from any source that is absent from this Évreux manuscript, whereas it contains much that is lacking in the others. [Col. 0048C]

Moreover, the distinguished advocate M. Logé of the sovereign court lent us two manuscripts of excellent authority from his own collection. He had received them from another most learned advocate of the same court, M. Loyaute, who had undertaken and had already begun the publication of Hildebert’s letters. Below we shall append Loyaute’s learned notes on eighteen of Hildebert’s letters, received from the aforesaid M. Logé; and without doubt he would have carried the work through to its completion had he not died prematurely.

Furthermore, among the letters of Hildebert which we had recently discovered, as we thought, from the aforementioned Évreux manuscript, we found that Father Luc d’Achery—whose memory is dear and illustrious among scholars and all good people—had inserted ten in number into vol. IV of his *Spicilegium*. One of them, however, beginning *Successisse*, is found there through the printer’s carelessness inserted twice; another, beginning *Jocunditas mihi*, appears in all editions, namely at the end of the eleventh letter of book I, or letter 61, to the bishop of Chartres. Thus D’Achery published there only eight previously unpublished letters, which he testifies had been pointed out and sent to him from a manuscript codex by the illustrious and most learned Lanfranc Bigot, distinguished to all scholars during his lifetime by learning and kindness. [Col. 0048D]

But because this man, most reverent toward venerable antiquity, considered it a matter of conscience to alter even the slightest stroke from the original manuscript, numerous scribal errors and frequent gaps had entered it, obscuring or greatly confusing its sense and intelligibility. We therefore took care to correct those errors by comparison with the more correct Évreux manuscript. We considered this especially necessary, for example, in epistle 22 of book II, the apology for Pope Paschal II, in which D’Achery’s *Spicilegium* contains almost as many lacunae as lines, and the sense is for the most part truncated or entangled. By comparison with the aforementioned Évreux manuscript, we have sought, as well as we could, to restore clarity and brightness to it. [Col. 0049A]

We were indeed somewhat congratulating ourselves that, beyond the eight letters mentioned as edited by Father D’Achery and found in the Évreux manuscript, we had found fourteen others in the same manuscript. But when we examined his *Spicilegium* more carefully, we were glad to discover that they too had not escaped that very sagacious man’s diligence. He had relegated them, as though on their return from exile, to an appendix at the end of the last volume, having extracted them from that one manuscript of Foucarmont; and it was very pleasing to us to be able to collate all of them with the Évreux manuscript, where alone we had found them.

Thus we added to the letters published in the *Libraries of the Fathers* those which had nowhere been published, together with nine others which, when the printing of the preceding letters had already been completed, we recovered from the collections of certain scholars and from the archives of our monasteries, and were compelled to consign to an appendix. [Col. 0049B]

Accordingly, whereas only eighty-three letters had been numbered in all editions of the *Library of the Fathers*, including the latest Lyons edition, we make public one hundred and twenty-one, after adding thirty-nine—if, however, one wishes to include among them epistle 15 of book II. We found this in none of the twelve manuscripts which we used and discovered it to be merely a fragment of Saint Jerome’s letter to Demetrias, which the three editors of the *Library of the Fathers*, one after another, had placed in their editions as Hildebert’s seventy-ninth letter. We collated Hildebert’s other letters against thirteen manuscript codices of excellent authority, not without tedious labor; noted their variant readings; reworked several summaries; indicated, insofar as could be inferred from the history of those times, when they were composed and to whom they were addressed; and supplied notes where it seemed necessary—would that we had done so successfully. [Col. 0049C–D]

We do not doubt, however, that many more of Hildebert’s letters have escaped the diligence of collectors. This is made nearly certain by the long intervals, sometimes of several years, during which we know of no letter written by him. Yet it is not probable that a prelate renowned, as Baronius says, throughout so many regions for holiness and prudence, passed such periods without writing letters, as occasion offered and as the various affairs in which he was entangled even to the final peril of his life seemed to require, to persons of every rank. Those who are more discerning or more fortunate than we, and who perhaps discover these letters or any part of them, should not begrudge them to the common good of scholarship, but should publish them for the edification of believers, in Christian charity and honor. [Col. 0050A]

Meanwhile, so far as concerns ourselves, since, as Pliny says, it is the mark of honorable modesty to confess through whom one has profited, we shall not deny that the *Supplement to the Fathers* of the aforementioned Father Jacques Homey was of use to us. In it he inserted certain works of Hildebert, both prose and verse, discovered by himself. Chief among these is the book *On Complaint*, or *On the Conflict of Flesh and Spirit*, which he had drawn from the manuscript of Saint-Victor at Paris alone, no. 272. We have collated it with Royal manuscript no. 4103 and the Évreux manuscript no. 19, which Homey probably had not had available and which alone, among the manuscripts we saw, contain it; and we publish it in a more correct form as an entirely genuine work of Hildebert. [Col. 0050B]

Moreover, in the aforesaid *Supplement to the Fathers*, the above-mentioned Homey added notes to the letters, certainly not unlearned ones. Yet, though we acknowledge that some light shone upon us from them, we did not adhere to them so closely that we did not occasionally depart from them when reason seemed to require it.

But in order to give the student of this collection an appropriate overview of what we have done in assembling it, and in what order, it is right that we should set this out.

[Col. 0050C] It was not our purpose to publish only those little works of Hildebert which we had recently discovered and extracted from various manuscripts, but to make public in one body absolutely all of them, both those long ago published and those still unpublished as recently found. The published works we revised according to manuscript codices; the unpublished ones we extracted from the manuscripts themselves after comparing them with one another. Thus we publish all of them, as corrected as our diligence could make them, whether composed by Hildebert in prose or in verse. The prose works, as more excellent, will hold first place; the verse works, second.

Among the works produced in prose, his letters stand out especially. They have been celebrated by the greatest learned men for their remarkable learning, sweet style, lucid speech, and pleasing and praiseworthy concision—as Saint Bernard says of them [Note: [Col. 0049D] Epistle 123.]. [Col. 0050D]

Then follow Hildebert’s sermons, one hundred and forty in number, whereas formerly only three were found in the various editions of the *Library of the Fathers*, even in the latest Lyons edition. All, as the reading itself will show, are full of theological and orthodox doctrine, distinguished by words and meanings of sacred Scripture that breathe and inspire sincere piety, and by their teaching of ancient rites of the Church. To extract, examine, and transcribe them from the best manuscripts was a labor not small, though most welcome, and together with the letters they constitute the larger and more excellent part of Hildebert’s works. [Col. 0051A]

Thereafter we have appended his various prose works. At their head stands the *Life of Saint Radegund the Queen*, composed by Hildebert, which our Father Mabillon kindly lent us from his papers. He had published its preface in vol. III of his *Analecta*, intending to produce the whole work if occasion ever presented itself; but when at last the opportunity arose through our present edition, he transferred this task to us while occupied with more weighty matters. This work has nowhere hitherto been published.

It is followed by the *Life of Saint Hugh, Abbot of Cluny*, which Hildebert composed at the urging—or, as Hildebert himself calls it, the command—of Pons, Saint Hugh’s successor in office, though not in holiness. It was published in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, and is also read in Surius under 29 April in the Cologne edition of 1618. [Col. 0051B]

Added to this is the book *On Complaint*, or *On the Conflict of Flesh and Spirit*, discussed above, partly prose and partly verse, in imitation of Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy*. I might perhaps have suspected that this treatise is the very same one which the most learned Dupin, in the second part of his *Ecclesiastical History* for the twelfth century, noted among the doubtful works of Hugh du Foliet, or more probably du Fouloy, under the title *Discourse between Flesh and Spirit*. Hugh was not, as Dupin thought, a monk of Corbie, but a regular canon, as our M. Élie le Doux, professor of theology, suggested to us and demonstrated learnedly from the Corbie manuscript of Hugh’s own works. At our request he examined that manuscript most exactly and found in it not the least trace of this *Discourse*. [Col. 0051C]

This treatise is followed by *Moral Philosophy*, or *Treatise on the Useful and the Honorable*, divided into four books and hitherto unpublished. We extracted it from Colbert manuscript no. 2662, approximately six hundred years old, and another, older Victorine manuscript, no. 759. It is composed solely from various sayings of Seneca, Cicero, Tacitus, and other philosophers and writers of the ancient school. Hildebert’s poem *On the Four Virtues of the Honorable Life*, extracted from Colbert manuscript no. 6327 of approximately the same age, has such great affinity with it, even in wording, that we judged it should be joined to the preceding work. [Col. 0051D]

There follows a theological treatise, which we found among Hildebert’s other indubitable works in a manuscript of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Lyre, of our Order and Congregation of Saint-Maur, approximately six hundred years old and thus nearly contemporary with Hildebert. From this one may not altogether rashly infer, as we shall explain more fully below, that the scholastic theologians later than Hildebert—Robert Pullus and Peter Lombard themselves—derived both the subject matter and the method of their doctrine from him.

[Col. 0052A] We have added to this a brief indeed, but excellent and most learned, treatise On the Sacrament of the Altar, which in the Colbert manuscript, no. 2662, immediately followed the treatise On the Honorable and the Useful. There the doctrine of the sacred Eucharist is expressed in such a manner that, by this fact alone, it could be proved beyond dispute how far Hildebert was from Berengar’s errors. If to it are joined the following moral Exposition of the Sacred Vestments and Ceremonies of the Mass, the metrical book On the Mystery of the Mass, and another On the Sacred Eucharist, it will not seem surprising that the ancient author of the Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans asserted that, when Hildebert approached the altar to celebrate the most holy mysteries, he was wholly moved to tears, and thus, in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart, offered the saving victim before the divine countenance. [Col. 0052B] Certainly no one can perceive that feeling and affection of devotion unless he firmly believes, with a sincere and inward conviction, what the Catholic Church believes and teaches concerning this sacred mystery. Nor would it be irrelevant to disclose what impelled us to investigate his sermons.

Indeed, we could not sufficiently wonder that only three sermons of this bishop and preacher, most celebrated in his own time, had been published. Orderic Vitalis, nearly his contemporary, testifies in Book X of his *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 770, that he continually devoted himself to good pursuits in both teaching and conduct. Moreover, the *Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans*, from Mabillon’s *Analecta*, vol. III, portray him as a wise preparer of spices, [Col. 0052C] making a honey-sweet drink from the flowers of Holy Scripture and diligently dispensing it to his hearers, sometimes in writing and sometimes by living speech. When he spoke in church, the people indeed listened most devoutly, but the clergy more attentively, because he spoke the Latin language with a certain greater fluency and vivacity.

Hence also that magnificent title with which St Bernard honoured Hildebert when writing him a letter, no. 124 among Bernard’s letters, which he addresses thus: “To the great priest and one exalted in the word of glory”—that is, to an exceedingly eloquent preacher, who was accustomed to disseminate the word of God only in an altogether glorious manner, for God’s honour and the edification of the faithful.

Further, that Hildebert always applied himself most diligently [Col. 0052D] to preaching the word of God seems evident both from the ecclesiastical offices entrusted to him before his episcopate and from the episcopal dignity itself to which he was raised. Before becoming bishop, who can believe that Hoel, a most wise bishop, elevated him first to be master of the schools of his Church at Le Mans, and then archdeacon, unless his reputation had recommended him—a reputation which, while still residing at Cluny at the feet of St Hugh, he had already gained for himself by many distinguished sermons, whether addressed to monks or to the people? Would a bishop renowned for prudence, as the *Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans* proclaim Hoel to have been, have set over the schools of his church and his clergy a man whom he had not found [Col. 0053A] eminently fit for preaching the word of God? Would he have raised to the archdeaconry a man whom he recognized, as the chief administrator of his own episcopal ministry, to be tongueless and a mute dog, unable to bark? Finally, would the clergy and people of Le Mans, by unanimous agreement, have advanced him to the episcopal throne unless long experience had shown them him to be most skilled in the art of preaching, which is the bishops’ chief and essential office?

This same point can be demonstrated with certainty from many passages of his letters and other shorter works; but Hildebert himself puts it beyond doubt in his epigram to Matilda, queen of the English, whom he addresses thus:

> He who is accustomed, before men, to be more eloquent than Cicero  
>   
> [Col. 0053B] is less fluent when he comes before God.  
>   
> Thus I, when I address the common crowd with an eloquent tongue,  
> could speak more before your countenance.  
>   
> I was struck dumb by your majesty, and, ranging over all of you  
> with wandering eye, etc.

It is clear from this not only that Hildebert was accustomed to preach to the mixed multitude, but also that he bore Christ’s name eloquently and successfully before kings and princes of the earth. They surely listened to him all the more willingly because he never ceased to instruct them, with the learning and freedom proper to a bishop, in moral and Christian precepts by means of mystical allegories, admirably supported and elucidated by testimonies from Holy Scripture.

Although, therefore, certain truly learned men who judged Hildebert’s works to be outstanding and otherwise most worthy of public light [Col. 0053C] did not greatly praise his sermons, this probably happened because they had been able to see only a very few of them: namely, only those three which have hitherto appeared in the *Libraries of the Fathers*. Yet other learned men did not fail to judge even his published sermons worthy of regard, since they found them pious, woven almost wholly from the texts of Holy Scripture, and breathing the charity and zeal of a most watchful shepherd. Thus, perhaps by a fairer judgment, moved by the loss of Hildebert’s sermons, they desired that they should be recovered and published wherever fortune might permit. Complying with their wishes, while we laboured to uncover his other minor works here [Col. 0053D] and there, we did not neglect the care of his sermons; and at length, with no small labour but, as we thought, with greater benefit to the faithful, we extracted more than one hundred and forty from the manuscripts listed above.

Besides the three sermons published in the *Libraries of the Fathers*, we had found four others in an Évreux manuscript. When we found one of these in the Victorine manuscript, no. 272, we corrected it by comparing the two.

The Reverend Father Dom Thomas Blampin, prior of the abbey of Saint-Remi at Reims, very kindly sent us another from a manuscript of that abbey. He was celebrated, despite his native modesty, as the principal author of the new edition of St Augustine. Thus, after finding these five sermons, a desire came upon us to seek out the rest; and this was certainly not unsuccessful. For in the first manuscript codex of our own Saint-Germain library that came to hand, we found several sermons. We inferred them to be Hildebert’s because among them we discovered the sermon beginning, “Isaiah, instructed by the Holy Spirit,” which three manuscripts—our Saint-Germain manuscript no. 381, that of Évreux no. 19, and the Victorine no. 272—likewise attribute to Hildebert. [Col. 0054A]

[Col. 0054B] We next found others in another Victorine manuscript, no. 468. The first sermon encountered there begins, “Say to the faint-hearted”; the three editions of the *Library of the Fathers*—the Paris, Cologne, and new Lyons editions—attribute it to Hildebert. Yet it differs in this respect: in this manuscript it is almost a quarter longer than, and more correct than, the published text. Taking this sermon, therefore, as it were as a lawful token leading the way, we examined the rest; from similarity of style and the character of the arguments, as far as the keenness of our little talent could penetrate—as Hildebert speaking of himself would say—we judged them to be Hildebert’s.

Since this search had not been wholly unlucky, we turned to examine others, and not in vain. For the Reverend Father Dom Hervaeus Menard, prior of the monastery of Saint-Albin at Angers, of our congregation and a most ardent lover of humane letters, sent us a manuscript codex of excellent authority, nearly contemporary with Hildebert himself, in which we counted many sermons [Col. 0054C] that, from comparison of style, we did not doubt were his legitimate offspring.

It should be noted that some in this series also slipped in among the sermons of Peter Comestor. But in the judgment of several learned men, we thought it more probable that Hildebert’s sermons had been inserted back among Comestor’s sermons by various collectors than that Comestor’s own sermons had been inserted among Hildebert’s. For Comestor had scarcely passed the bounds of childhood when Hildebert died. Hildebert, according to the more probable opinion, died in 1134; but Comestor, as the most learned Dupin and other scholarly men observed, did not die until 1198. It is therefore more probable that Hildebert’s sermons, by which he had then acquired a great name [Col. 0054D] for himself, collected and written down by some from his lips, were mingled with Comestor’s, rather than Comestor’s with Hildebert’s.

The same should be thought of the sermons of Peter of Blois, among which some are found that are attributed to Comestor, though they are truly Hildebert’s. For since Peter of Blois died only about the year 1200, and was thus scarcely out of his cradle when Hildebert departed this life—in 1134, as we noted above—it is fairer to suppose that many of Peter of Blois’s sermons were inserted among Hildebert’s than that Hildebert’s were inserted among those of Blois.

Moreover, most of the sermons are found both among Comestor’s and among those of Blois; from reading them it is clear that the preacher was a bishop. Yet this [Col. 0055A] can belong neither to Comestor nor to Blois, but fits Hildebert excellently. In Sermon 130, with his native modesty, he laments that he has been burdened with the weight of this dignity in these words: “See, brothers, that such was the will of our Lord: that he appointed me, though an unworthy sinner, not by my merits but by his mercy, to govern this Church, and entrusted to me the care of you and of the others belonging to this see. For a bishop or archbishop ought attentively to guard the peoples committed to him,” etc.

Possessing this episcopal jurisdiction and authority, he delivered Sermons 88, 89, and the following twelve: sometimes in synods to subordinate pastors and rectors of parishes, or curates; sometimes at the ordination of clerics whom he was to ordain. These sermons could properly be delivered only by a bishop, speaking with pontifical authority and by the obligation of his office. No one will deny that this could belong neither to Peter Comestor nor to Peter of Blois.

Led by these reasons, therefore, we judged the sermons from the manuscript of Saint-Albin at Angers to deserve publication together with the rest by all the greater right, because, from their conformity of style and thought when compared with his other works, we considered them almost beyond doubt to be Hildebert’s genuine offspring. [Col. 0055B]

This is what had to be stated concerning the works Hildebert wrote in prose. We must now preface something concerning the metrical works which he composed.

Perhaps someone may wonder that a man burdened with so many and such great affairs as the writers of his deeds represent Hildebert to have been should have composed so many poems, [Col. 0055C] so many epigrams, so many verses of every kind, that they grew to a total of ten thousand lines or more. But the wonder will cease if one considers the character of his talent, diligently cultivated from childhood in humane letters; if one considers how, from his youth, he always abhorred idleness; and finally, how much leisure, even against his will, was afforded him by the vexations and exiles inflicted upon him by the civic magistrates of Le Mans—as he calls them, that is, the city’s chief officials—or by the repeated and prolonged imprisonments, though unjust, inflicted by the kings of England or Count Rotrou.

The *Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans* expressly testify that he spent all his early years so fully upon good studies that [Col. 0055D] among all the clerics of that region he was considered outstanding in literary pursuits: one who had diligently devoted himself to literary studies from childhood, whose mind, trained in worthy arts, could not be idle; whose writings, both prose and verse, were most splendidly published and widely disseminated in many places; and whose fame had grown far and wide even to the ends of the world. Orderic Vitalis says the same in Book X of his *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 770:

> This sacred hero, Hildebert, devoted to the study both of divine and secular letters, flourished in our time as an incomparable maker of verse, and composed many poems equal or superior to ancient poetry. The ardent zeal of philosophers desires to investigate them subtly and to acquire them diligently above gold and topaz. [Col. 0056A] From Roman cardinals, who often make their way to Gaul … very many poems of Hildebert are carried to Rome, where they are judged worthy of admiration by the schools of the witty and the teachers of the Romans.

For, while in youth he remained at Cluny at the feet of St Hugh the abbot, he had willingly exercised himself in cultivating the more polished Muses. Yet he generally devoted their service only to serious and sacred subjects; and it seems probable that, while he was held in chains, he employed this honourable kind of solace either to console his solitude or to mitigate the weariness of imprisonment.

In this he especially imitated bishops famous for piety and for their celebrated name in the Church: in the Greek Church, [Col. 0056B] Amphilochius, Theodore the Studite, above all St Gregory Nazianzen, and many others; and in the Latin Church, Paulinus of Nola, Sidonius Apollinaris of Auvergne, Alcimus Avitus of Vienne, Theodulf of Orléans, and six hundred others whom it would be tiresome to enumerate. They did not hesitate even to illuminate Holy Scripture itself with metrical commentaries; they conveyed sacred doctrines and the evangelical precepts themselves to the Christian people in verse, for easier use by the memory; and they celebrated in poetry the deeds of saints and the triumphs of martyrs.

Emulating these men, Hildebert rendered several sacred books in verse; he illustrated various passages of Holy Scripture in metrical moral expositions for the edification of the faithful; he expounded the sacred mysteries of the Eucharist itself in several treatises in compressed expression; and he sang of the victories of many martyrs and of the virtues of more illustrious blessed persons. [Col. 0056C]

So far was this from being a fault to be imputed to him that, on the contrary, fairer judges among the men of his age celebrated him with immense praise because he had turned wholly to sacred uses that poetic vein in which he was exceptionally strong.

Further, that Hildebert did not always observe the strict measure of syllables with such scrupulous precision, no fair reader will refuse to pardon, if he attends rather to the weight of the meaning and gravity of the thoughts, worthy of a devout bishop, than to syllabic quantity, which befits a mere grammarian. For he knew the familiar saying:

> The Church often disregards the rules of grammar.

Nevertheless, in most verses, and sometimes in whole poems, Hildebert composed with strictness—indeed, with a strictness far greater than that of the poetry of our own age. What could be stricter than enclosing verses within such narrow confines as the custom of that age had established: that not only must each verse end in the same rhythm or sound, but in every hemistich, or half-line, or even in the third part of each line, the same sound of words must always recur? [Col. 0056D] Yet Hildebert observed this most exactly in many poems, including longer ones: for example, in the *Life of Blessed Mary of Egypt*, [Col. 0057A] of nearly a thousand lines; in the poem *On St Vincent*, of almost five hundred verses; in the *Panegyric of the Maccabees*; and in most others. How difficult this method is, even our more expert professors of poetic art will not deny. When they endeavour to try it by their own efforts, they will acknowledge how great an abundance of varied Latin it requires, and how much labour in turning and returning phrases.

Far be it, therefore, that anyone should judge our Hildebert’s Muse deformed because of certain minor blemishes of quantity. Far be it that the refinement and ease of our more polished age should charge him with the barbarism of a later age. We do admit that he sometimes, though rarely, employed humbler modes of versifying or forms of expression. In rendering Holy Scripture in verse, he judged this at times more suitable for the understanding of simpler persons, considering that in this manner they might be more easily committed to memory and held more firmly there, and as being more exalted than verses requiring the empty ornaments of poetry or secular eloquence in order to win their due reverence. [Col. 0057B]

But when he treated more human subjects—for example, when he celebrated encomia of kings and nobles of whatever rank, or set forth moral precepts free from the constraints of resounding rhythm and meter—he knew admirably how to raise the tragic buskin. A fair reader will confess that nothing could have issued more floridly even from that fabulous Parnassus. Let him consider what Hildebert composed *On the Works of the Six Days*, *On the Adornment of the World*, *On Susanna*, [Col. 0057C] *On the Kings and Queens of England*, *On His Own Exile*, *On True Friendship*, *On the Mathematician*, and other works of this kind; he will marvel that nothing nobler, nothing sweeter from Helicon, could have flowed forth.

What we say here about Hildebert, we consider rightly to be said also of Marbod, bishop of Rennes, whose shorter works we shall append to those of Hildebert. Although Marbod, accustomed to the usage accepted in his time, generally published rhythmic verses ending with a similar sound, whenever he could throw off that heavy yoke, he produced verses no less elegant than those which perhaps the more polished poets of our own age could compose. Thus he seems himself to have disapproved of what he had written in youth under such strict laws of sound, when, at the beginning of the *Book of Ten Chapters*, he warns, having reached his sixtieth year, above all against this:

> Neglecting the weight of things,  
> let us pursue sweet-sounding meters and well-shaped words.

And he advises:

> Let the strength of things, subdued by the rule of words,  
> be preserved; and let the melody of words abound beneath the matters themselves.  
>   
> This, he says, I seemed then to pursue with unremitting effort;  
> but now riper age counsels me better:  
> that it should be content with easy usefulness, as is fitting,  
> and should endeavour to avoid superfluous labour. [Col. 0057D]

He in fact accomplished this successfully in the above-mentioned *Book of Ten Chapters*, in the *Book on Gems*, the book *On the Ornaments of Words*, the sermon *On Solitude*, and other epigrams. In these, without observing any pattern of that [Col. 0058A] resounding rhythm, he distinguished the subjects he treated by the gravity of his thoughts, ease of expression, and various figures of a more solid eloquence.

We shall not delay in disclosing to the kindly reader the sources from which we drew so many hitherto unknown poems of Hildebert and Marbod. They are seventeen manuscript codices, obtained from different places, all judged by experts either contemporary with Hildebert or nearly so. They were kindly lent to us by most distinguished men born for the good of the republic of letters. Not all manuscripts contained every poem; rather, one supplied these, another those, and several supplied the same works. Yet all were of excellent authority in the judgment of experts and could be trusted without scruple, so that even where only one contained a particular work, it nevertheless seemed wholly beyond doubt from its style and thought that it was Hildebert’s. Where several codices contained the same text, diligent comparison among them yielded a purer and more correct text. [Col. 0058B]

From the Royal Library, its most learned custodians, Messrs Clemens and Boyvin, lent us manuscript no. 413 with the same courtesy with which they had supplied two manuscripts for revising the letters. From the Colbert Library, the distinguished Monsieur Duchesne, its most watchful administrator, provided five: manuscripts nos. 1050, 1367, 3019, 6101, and 6327. Through the help of our Dom Edmund Martene, renowned for so many sacred collections, [Col. 0058C] certain texts came to us from an excellent manuscript of the metropolitan church of Saint-Gatien at Tours, and others from two manuscripts of Marmoutier.

But the book entitled *Floridus aspectus*, and many other items—most of which were not found elsewhere—were generously furnished from his own museum, richly supplied with manuscripts of interest, by the most distinguished and learned physician of Tours, Monsieur Jacques du Poirier, a man always ready to assist literary studies. This was done through the aforementioned Reverend Father Dom Edmund Martene, who most diligently examined, collated, and noted variant readings in whatever he transmitted to us from Tours.

Yet the manuscripts which supplied us with the greatest number of Hildebert’s poems were especially the codex of Saint-Taurin at Évreux, the Peronne manuscript mentioned above, and another manuscript codex from the monastery of Saint-Marien at Auxerre, of the Premonstratensian Order. The most learned Reverend Father Dom Hubert Maillard, prior of Saint-Germain at Auxerre, obtained this for us from the prior of that monastery. In it we discovered three thousand or more lines, found almost nowhere else; and likewise in the Évreux manuscript we found many things reported in no other manuscript—the same manuscript, that is, which we used for the letters and other prose works. [Col. 0058D] Finally, we gleaned a few items from a manuscript of Jumièges and another of Bec, later than the rest indeed, but both about four hundred years old or more.

First, it should be observed that several poems were placed at the end of the works of Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, which manuscripts and even printed editions prove to be Hildebert’s. For example, the *Passion of St Agnes* is attributed to Hildebert in the manuscript of Saint-Marien at Auxerre, as it is by the most learned Rosweyde and, after him, Barthius, Book XXX of the *Commentaries of Adversaria*. Such are the verses *On the Destruction of Rome* and *Rome’s Reply*, the verses *On a Wicked Woman* and *On the Incarnation of the Word*. All these are ascribed to Hildebert in the Évreux manuscript, the royal manuscripts, and others. [Col. 0059A]

Second, it should be observed that Hildebert always held so firmly to the orthodox faith that he strove not only with all the strength of his mind to repress the heresies emerging in his time and their authors, and by pontifical authority to expel them from his territories, but also, as it were, to have condemned beforehand [Col. 0059B] those which arose long afterward concerning Christ’s grace.

Thus in Sermon 111 he says that grace never fails those who hope in God, and that assisting grace never deserts a person, even one falling daily. In Sermon 39, treating the justification of man, he says that it is twofold: one kind makes a person just; the other is done by the just person. The first is effected by God through the infusion of grace; the second by human cooperation of free choice, which he asserts to be wholly voluntary: “For,” he says, “we are not, in relation to God who justifies, a dead instrument, as a sword to a soldier or an axe to a craftsman; rather, our voluntary cooperation intervenes in it.”

Finally, in Letter 16, Book I, he says that God’s grace is most ready in service to human beings and, as it were, sworn to obedience to them. [Col. 0059C] From this he concludes that God wills all people to become good because he wills all people to be saved: for them he prepares grace upon which they may rely, distributes means that may assist them, and offers rewards by which they may be stirred. Hence one may legitimately infer that Hildebert truly believed that God denies to no human being sufficient means for salvation, since he expressly says in Sermon 31 that Christ’s death would have benefited either thief also, if they had so willed.

These and similar statements occur everywhere and repeatedly in Hildebert’s various writings. From them one may rightly infer how far he was from those troublesome opinions, justly condemned by the Church, which stirred up so much disturbance and discord a hundred years ago.

If, therefore, in Hildebert’s works anything occurs on these matters that is somewhat harsher concerning human difficulty in doing good, far be it from us to suppose that he believed God’s commands ever impossible for human beings, or that the grace by which they become possible is lacking to them. Rather, it is to be understood only of that very great difficulty arising from sin which the Apostle himself lamented that he experienced, when he said, “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish it” (Rom. 7); and, “For the good which I will, I do not do; but the evil which I do not will, that I do” (*ibid.*). [Col. 0059D] The holy Fathers and orthodox interpreters never understood these words as referring to genuine impossibility, but to the utmost difficulty which we daily experience in acting rightly because of the concupiscence predominant through sin.

[Col. 0060A] Third, it should be observed that we made an error in wording in the note on the verses *On Faith in the Holy Trinity*, when we said that they should be placed among doubtful works. Someone might therefore infer that the other works which follow are doubtful works of Hildebert; this we did not intend, nor ought we to have intended, since nothing is more certain than that the book *On His Exile* is his genuine offspring, as are all the other poems, whether preceding or following, which we extracted from the best manuscripts. In place, therefore, of the words “among doubtful works,” one should read: “though doubtful—and it alone among the undoubted poems of Hildebert which we present.”

Equipped, therefore, with all these manuscripts, we set about this new recension of Hildebert’s works already published and publication of the much greater number never published anywhere. We could accomplish this only with wearisome exertion of mind, indeed of body as well. For in the *Library of the Fathers* we found almost nothing printed continuously except Hildebert’s eighty-two letters and the metrical book *On the Mystery of the Mass*. It would have been wrong to detach them from it, and we lacked the opportunity, customary in preparing other editions, to extract them thence, or a supply of copies which could afterward, if desired, be cut apart so that we might conveniently note our observations in the margin or at the edge. [Col. 0060B] Instead, all things—both published and unpublished—had to be copied out exactly by us alone and without any assistance, as did the far more numerous new unpublished works which we searched out from manuscripts. A fair reader will surely judge that we could not have accomplished this without immense labour and persistent diligence. Yet, God granting it, we have completed it wholly, according to our ability, for his honour and the edification of the faithful—and, we hope, correctly.

Moreover, after time had passed and Hildebert’s letters had already been printed, we learned that the most distinguished and learned Monsieur Loyauté, a celebrated advocate in the supreme court of the Paris Parlement, had formerly begun to labour upon elucidating Hildebert’s letters. He had died about fifty years earlier, to the great loss of the republic of letters. We approached the close friend of the distinguished Monsieur Logé—himself another eminent advocate in the same court and keeper of Loyauté’s papers—and earnestly requested that, if he had any of them to hand that could contribute to the public benefit, [Col. 0060D] he would kindly grant them to us. [Col. 0060C]

As a man born to support humane learning, he willingly did so in his kindness. Consequently, we were able to recover three new letters or diplomas, with learned notes on eighteen of Hildebert’s letters which the said Monsieur Loyauté, prevented by death, had been unable to finish; and also further notes on Hildebert’s *Life*, written by the ancient author of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans*. We judged it better to reserve for an appendix those three letters restored to us, together with three others granted us by the distinguished Monsieur Baluze and, finally, three which came to us from the archives of the monasteries of Saint-Vincent at Le Mans and of Évron, rather than withhold them from the scholarly reader. [Col. 0061A]

Yet we cannot but lament the loss of the venerable Hildebert’s other minor works, which he himself often mentions in his letters: for example, the *History of the Miracles of the Church of Exeter*, mentioned in Letter 3, Book III, to Clarembald; and many others of which he speaks here and there. We had entertained no small hope of someday finding Hildebert’s synodal statutes for the diocese of Le Mans, and we spared no effort in seeking them out. Jean-Baptiste Thiers had formerly cited some fragments of them in his works; therefore we were convinced that he had possessed either the autograph or at least a copy of them, which at death he had left to his heirs. But after the most diligent search, we laboured in vain. We obtained from it nothing except the hope that, if someone either more shrewd or more fortunate than ourselves should someday discover this sacred monument of ancient discipline, he would not delay in presenting it, for the public benefit, to those who ardently desired it.

Furthermore, many learned men urged us to append to the aforesaid works of Hildebert the shorter works of Marbod, bishop of Rennes, Hildebert’s contemporary and friend. [Col. 0061B] Since these were so rare that we could scarcely—indeed, hardly at all—obtain [Col. 0061C] a single copy from even the better furnished libraries of France, namely one from the celebrated library of the Mazarin College, printed at Rennes in 1524 in an old typeface now obsolete and offensive to eyes accustomed to clearer characters, scholarly men especially persuaded us to contribute our labour toward discovering what had never appeared and giving greater brightness to the old material itself.

Accordingly, complying with their wishes, we examined that Mazarin copy, kindly granted us by the most learned Monsieur Colau, librarian of the college, and compared what it contained with the few manuscripts we could find. We gathered certain items scattered here and there elsewhere, and discovered certain new works also, which, so far as we know, have never been published. We have deferred fuller discussion of these to the preface to Marbod’s own works. [Col. 0061D]

To all these works of the venerable Hildebert, as well as to Marbod’s shorter works, we added our notes where they seemed necessary and insofar as it was granted us to attain conclusions from the various histories and events of that age, or even from more probable conjectures. We submitted them—especially for a most willing examination of the letters of Hildebert—to our very dear and learned Reverend Father Dom René Massuet, of our Congregation of Saint-Maur, long since emeritus professor of sacred theology. We frankly acknowledge that we profited not a little from his learning.

For we are not persons presumptuous enough to cling too stubbornly to our own opinion. Rather, measuring ourselves by ourselves and comparing ourselves with ourselves, we are not ashamed—as our Hildebert modestly wrote of himself to Pope Honorius II [Note: [Col. 0061D] Letter 41, Book II]—“we are not ashamed, I say, to consider or acknowledge our measure.” [Col. 0062A] We shall most gladly imitate him, who, although most celebrated among the learned men of his age, always most humbly and modestly submitted all his writings, as can be shown from many passages in them, to the judgment of skilled friends. With far greater reason, conscious of our own slenderness, we have offered our writings, such as they are, to kindly and learned friends for examination and correction.

Meanwhile, with our Hildebert in the prologue to the *Life of St Hugh*, we shall confess that pardon must be sought because we have dared to precede men of fuller learning in publishing his works. We trust that it will not be denied to an old man nearly at life’s end, who has endeavoured to employ in this way the leisure granted him by his superiors during the last stage of his life: namely, so that he might contribute, in accordance with the wishes of many learned men and toward some benefit and edification of the faithful, to the discovery and publication of the writings of a bishop no less devout than learned. [Col. 0062B]

And if he has unwittingly expressed anything less skilfully, less accurately, or even—far be it!—less Catholicly, he submits it all, ready to amend it, not only to the judgment of his mother, the Catholic and Roman Church, but also to that of any learned Catholic, whose correction he will again receive as a favour, in the words of his Hildebert. [Col. 0062C] For he well knows that what should be dutiful, and welcome to a prudent writer, is not the criticism of envious critics biting in every direction, but the kindly correction of faithful and learned friends.

We think it necessary here to warn the reader not to linger over Hildebert’s citations of Holy Scripture, since he very often quoted its words not according to the Vulgate, but according to the version of the Seventy Interpreters, which was in some use in his age, though for the most part to the same meaning. Many further examples could have been supplied. Secondly, we have sometimes, though very rarely, added or altered certain words for easier understanding, [Col. 0062D] but only where the sense plainly led us to believe that they had been accidentally omitted or changed by careless copyists. Whenever this has occurred—which was exceedingly rare—we enclosed additions or alterations within square brackets `[ ]`, lest we be accused of rashness for inserting our own words in place of those of the author himself. Thirdly, when we found some expression of the author that seemed, in our judgment, inconsistent with the sense, we did not dare alter it in the text itself; rather, in brackets in the text, or in notes marked with the letter *f*—that is, *forte*, “perhaps”—we supplied what we thought the more suitable reading, without prejudicing the judgment of a reader who may think better. Finally, the reader will observe that we have written Hildebert’s name with the letter [Col. 0063A] H. We were moved to do so by the plurality of manuscripts, which almost all prefix that letter to I; although, for brevity’s sake, we should rather have omitted it, with the most learned Sirmond in his notes on [Col. 0064A] Geoffrey of Vendôme, and with certain manuscripts, though these are far fewer.

[Col. 0063]

[NOTE.]

List of manuscript codices which we have used for the edition and recension of the works of the Venerable Hildebert—first bishop of Le Mans, then archbishop of Tours—and of Marbod, bishop of Rennes; and which we have indicated at the head of each work.

Four from Itegius, namely 4080, 4103, 4105; the Royal manuscript of Saint-Amand, 274; ten Colbert manuscripts, namely 1168, 1050, 1367, 2131, 2662, 3019, 4017, 5133, 6101, 6327; one Évreux manuscript, Perronianus 19; one from Saint-Remi; four from Saint-Victor in Paris, namely 272, 292, 905, 468; one Clermont manuscript, 41; three Saint-Germain manuscripts, 125, 381, 383; one from Saint-Ouen at Rouen; one from Saint-Albin at Angers; one distinguished manuscript of Beauvais Cathedral; two from the collegiate church of Sainte-Radegonde at Poitiers; one from the distinguished cathedral of Saint-Gatien at Tours; two from Marmoutier, namely 103 and 121; one from Saint-Marien at Auxerre; two from Jumièges, 77 and 98; two from Bec, 98 and 197; one belonging to the distinguished Dr. du Poirier, physician of Tours; two belonging to the distinguished M. Loyauté, one of which is noted as having belonged to the church of Grandmont; one from Lire; one from Saint-Evroult at Ouche.

In all, forty-two manuscripts: a few of the more recent are at least four hundred years old; the far greater number are either contemporary with Hildebert and Marbod, or nearly so.

[Col. 0063]

LIFE OF THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT, FIRST BISHOP OF LE MANS, THEN ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS, compiled from his writings and ancient records.

[Col. 0063B] Hildebert was born in 1057, not 1054 as some suppose, to devout parents of moderate means, in the castle of Lavarzin or Lavardin, at Golden Mount, in the district of Vendôme. For, since all agree in placing his accession to the see of Le Mans in 1097, while the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans* attest that he had not then completed his fortieth year, a backward calculation makes it necessary that he was born in 1057. [Note: [Col. 0063C] Mabillon, *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, *Annals*, vol. III.]

They report that from boyhood he was instructed in learning and the liberal arts; and no one who has read his works in prose or verse can deny that he devoted himself with especial distinction, for that age, to humane letters. His teacher was chiefly Berengar, then renowned for his learning; and Hildebert boasts that whatever charm, wit, or eloquence he attained, he received from that master. Yet he was not so incautious as childhood commonly is that he imbibed his master’s error. For he borrowed nothing from Berengar’s pernicious teaching concerning the sacred [Col. 0063C] Eucharist, but in his writings on so great a mystery he puts forward an uncorrupted and sound doctrine. [Note: [Col. 0063C] This is clear from his most learned treatise *On the [Col. 0064C] Sacred Eucharist*, from his *Explanation of the Mass*, from the poem *On the Sacrifice of the Mass*, and another *On the Sacred Eucharist*, from his sermons, and elsewhere.] Nevertheless, he was not ungrateful to his teacher. Once he had learned with certainty of Berengar’s sincere, though late, repentance, he composed a funeral lament for him and adorned the man with praises—perhaps more than was warranted.

Having thus passed the first years of youth, he applied himself to the study of sacred literature. At this time he is said to have entered the sacred monastery of Cluny, which flourished under Saint Hugh as abbot in the renown of every branch of learning. Some writers of no small repute maintain that he embraced the monastic state; others deny it. We shall present the testimony of both sides in such a manner as not to appear to incline unduly toward either.

[Col. 0064B] André du Chesne, a most discerning investigator of antiquities, says in his notes on the *Life of Saint Hugh*, p. 83: “Hildebert was first a monk of Cluny and a disciple of that same Saint Hugh.” The authors of *Gallia Christiana*, the brothers de Sainte-Marthe, support the same opinion in their account of the bishops of Le Mans. We pass over more recent writers, since they seem perhaps to have adopted the opinion of their predecessors without sufficiently weighing the matter. But the weightier testimony adduced on this point is that of the *Chronicle of Cluny*, compiled by Dom François de Rivo, then grand prior of Cluny, at the command of Dom Jacques d’Amboise, who was abbot of Cluny in 1485. This chronicle is found in the *Library of Cluny*, published in 1614. There one reads:

> “Hildebert was the disciple and monk of Saint Hugh, and was at last promoted to the episcopal dignity of the Church of Le Mans, and thereafter translated to the archiepiscopal Church of Tours. He was an [Col. 0064C] illustrious and most learned man, particularly in the writing of verse; he also elegantly composed the life of the aforesaid Saint Hugh, his lord and abbot.”

Since this chronicle was compiled, as may be supposed, from older records that perished in the repeated conflagrations of the monastery of Cluny, in the devastations inflicted upon it by heterodox persons, and consequently in the plundering of its library, this would seem to furnish by far the gravest ground for believing that Hildebert was a monk. Add to this Hildebert’s devotion to Saint Benedict, whose Rule was so familiar to him that he very often inserted whole clauses from it into his discourse as though they arose naturally from the matter at hand; his devotion to Benedictines, and especially to Cluniacs, whom he generally addresses as his brothers and companions; and to abbots, [Col. 0065A] whom, full of reverence, he calls his fathers, prelates, and lords. [Note: [Col. 0065D] Epistles 14 and 20, book I; 25, 50, and 51, book II; sermons 70, 119, 120, and more than twenty others.] Certainly, whenever the Benedictine order is under discussion, he appears to treat of a matter familiar and domestic to himself; he even calls it [Note: [Col. 0065D] Sermon 64.] “our order and our religious profession.” He calls the monastery itself—in which, he declares, he and the other monks to whom he speaks have left all things—[Note: [Col. 0065D] “Consider,” he says in sermon 121, “the dignity of our order . . . reflect what the black garment and the tonsure signify.”] “a garden enclosed by wall, rule, and vow, and a fountain sealed with the seal of Saint Benedict.” [Note: [Col. 0066D] In the *Explanation of the Mass*; sermon 121.] Who, in light of these things, would not think Hildebert a monk, and indeed a Benedictine?

Nevertheless, serious reasons and arguments stand against the assertion that he was a monk. If he had professed the monastic life under Saint Hugh as abbot, would Hildebert have passed this over in silence in the *Life* of Hugh which he wrote? Would all his contemporaries, peers, and all writers from the twelfth through the fifteenth century have omitted mention of his monastic profession when speaking of him? Since, therefore, no one before the writer of the Cluniac Chronicle has said that Hildebert was a monk—at least among those whose writings survive—it may be suspected that the chronicler asserted Hildebert’s monastic status not on ancient testimony but by conjecture and opinion.

[Col. 0065B] Another argument is brought against Hildebert’s monastic profession, though in my judgment it has no such great weight. It is a decree cited by Jacobus de Grassi, a monk of Monte Cassino, in part II of the *Golden Decisions*, book III, chapter 12, which provides that no one of a different profession and habit may be promoted to ecclesiastical dignities. Yet, they argue, this was always observed in the Church of Le Mans, where Hildebert was first scholasticus, or master of the schools, and then archdeacon. But this argument fails in every respect. For innumerable examples—which it would take too long to list—show that the decree was not widely observed: monks were transferred not only to episcopal sees, which is commonplace enough, [Col. 0065C] but also appointed to archdeaconries and other dignities of cathedral churches. On this subject consult our Mabillon, preface to the fifth century of the Order of Saint Benedict, §6, no. 130, where he cites as examples Ansbert, a monk of Arras made archdeacon of Cambrai; Usuard, at once abbot and archdeacon; Peter of Montmajour, cellarer at Marseille and archdeacon of Aix; and several others. Mabillon proves that this practice continued into the eleventh century—the very century of Hildebert—when Bishop Hoël of Le Mans appointed him scholasticus of the Church of Le Mans and subsequently archdeacon. A noteworthy trace of this practice survives in the distinguished Church of Chartres, where the royal abbey of Saint-Pierre-en-Vallée, by virtue of archidiaconal jurisdiction over several churches of the diocese, granted to it by several bishops of Chartres and confirmed by supreme pontiffs, [Col. 0065D] still enjoys the privilege that it is summoned to diocesan assemblies only under the title of the archdeaconry of Saint-Pierre-en-Vallée. [Note: [Col. 0066D] Bishops of Chartres: Renaud, 1215; Gautier, 1225; supreme pontiffs Honorius III, 1221; Innocent IV, 1247.]

Let this brief discussion of Hildebert’s monastic profession suffice. Every learned reader may now freely embrace whichever side he prefers.

Hildebert was appointed by Hoël, bishop of Le Mans, who had been moved by the fame of his learning, to preside over the schools of Le Mans. How many years he served as scholasticus is unknown. But in 1092, at the age of thirty-five, the same Bishop Hoël chose him as archdeacon; according to Hildebert himself, in an epistle [Col. 0066A] to William, abbot of Saint-Vincent, he performed that office for five years.

By these stages the distinguished man prepared his path to the honor of the episcopate. When the most worthy bishop Hoël had died, Hildebert, then forty years old, was appointed in his place in 1097. Yet he was not ordained bishop without some division of parties. For, as Orderic Vitalis says, *Ecclesiastical History*, book X, p. 770:

> “Elias, count of Le Mans, chose Geoffrey the Breton, dean of the same church, for the episcopate; but the clergy, acting beforehand, compelled Hildebert of Lavardin, the archdeacon, to sit in the pontifical chair, and sang with jubilant loud voices: ‘We praise thee, O God,’ and the other things required by ecclesiastical custom in the election of a bishop. When Elias learned this, he was greatly angered and wished to resist. But when the clergy told him, ‘You ought not to prefer your election to the Church’s election,’ he was reverent and, because he feared God, kept silence; and lest a deadly schism arise among the members of the Church, he assented to the canons.”

[Col. 0066B] But here we must pause in order to complain that Cardinal Baronius, in his *Annals* under the year 1088, no. 4, was somewhat too harsh toward our bishop. Since Baronius observed that Hildebert’s epitaph for his master Berengar was full of praise and commendation, and since he was most zealous for sound faith, he seems to cast some stain upon Hildebert for extolling with so many encomia a man accused of having corrupted the faith. He also employs the testimony of Ivo of Chartres to state that Hildebert, after receiving the dignity of archdeacon, lived a rather lax life. The first stain may be washed away in Baronius’s own words: these are signs of a friendship that, in poetic tribute to a friend and teacher, indulged itself more than was fitting. Certainly something must be granted to affection, and the words of a pupil praising his teacher are not always to be taken literally.

As for the letter of Ivo of Chartres in which Hildebert [Col. 0066C] is said to have lived laxly even after becoming archdeacon, many arguments prove it spurious. First, it is found in very few manuscript copies. There are six royal codices of Ivo of Chartres’s letters; only one contains that letter, and it places it next to last. Likewise, of nine Colbert manuscripts, only one contains the same letter, also next to last, and seemingly written in a second hand. It is entirely absent from our Saint-Germain manuscript of Ivo’s letters. In the Victorine, or Saint-Victor, manuscript it is addressed not to Hildebert but to Adalbert; Ivo’s name is absent; it is written after other letters but with a blank page left between, so that it appears to concern another matter. Since it is absent from almost all the codices and, in those in which it occurs, is not in its proper order but relegated among the last letters—though by subject matter and chronology it ought to have ranked among the first—and since the name is likewise [Col. 0066D] read differently, the learned men Juret, Souchet, Bondonnet, and Jean de Maun rightly judge it should be rejected as spurious. The distinguished Antoine Pagi also defends Hildebert under the year 1097.

Even if that letter of Ivo of Chartres were authentic and genuine, anyone who weighs the force of the arguments will judge it untrustworthy if he considers the circumstances of that time. For, as the sequence of events makes clear, it was written when factions were in fierce conflict: some demanded Hildebert, appointed by clergy and people, while others demanded Geoffrey the dean, selected by Count Elias, [Col. 0067A] as bishop of Le Mans. And, as usually happens in such disputes, slanders and insults were hurled back and forth against the bishop favored by either party. Therefore, what is stated in the letter—whether it is Ivo of Chartres’s or someone else’s—must be treated as rumors and abuse spread by the opposite party, as is clear even from its words:

> “Beyond all measure Hildebert had loosened the rein of chastity, to such an extent that after becoming archdeacon, with a crowd of little women lying at his side, he begot a great multitude of boys and girls.”

These allegations had plainly been spread by Geoffrey’s supporters in order to make Hildebert odious; they were so outrageous that even the author of the letter, whoever he was, seems not to have believed them. He says: “Consult the testimony of your conscience, so that you may either honorably and cautiously bring your undertakings to completion, or, having regard for your salvation, voluntarily withdraw.” Indeed, he indicates that these slanders came only from some of Hildebert’s opponents when [Col. 0067B] he says, as if in doubt: “For some say concerning the leading men of the Church of Le Mans”; and, “If these things are true”; and everywhere, “if this is so”—that is, from those who stood on the side of Geoffrey and Count Elias. That these charges were fabricated is demonstrated by the agreement of the clergy and people of Le Mans in electing Hildebert. For who can believe that a man whose unchastity and foulness revealed themselves in so many and such manifest signs would have been sought by the wishes of so vast a multitude?

To return to Ivo of Chartres: many passages in his letters speak far more favorably of Hildebert’s moral integrity, [Note: [Col. 0067D] “We think well of your religious character.” Ivo of Chartres, epistle 167.] where he addresses Hildebert as his friend and as a bishop “of good morals and religious character.” Hence perhaps arises the suspicion that one of Geoffrey’s party wrote such a letter under Ivo of Chartres’s forged name in order to damage Hildebert’s reputation. Indeed, Baronius himself, as though he made little of the testimony of malicious persons, calls Hildebert [Col. 0067C] “a man of great holiness and a most vigorous defender of the liberty of the Church,” under the year 1088. He evidently follows the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, which state: “After the death of Hoël, Hildebert, on account of his merit in learning and integrity, was appointed in his place by the common assent of clergy and people.” The distinguished M. Loyauté concurs with our opinion concerning Hildebert’s moral integrity in the notes on Hildebert which he prepared many years ago and which we have appended at the end.

Having passed this obstacle, let us return to the beginnings of Hildebert’s episcopate. Raised to the throne, he found everything beset by thorns: the faction of Count Elias, opposed to him even with Elias’s support, and factious men eager to cause disturbance. Nor did he fare better with William Rufus, king of England. Claiming that the county of Le Mans belonged to his dominion, William was offended that Hildebert had accepted an office conferred at Count Elias’s mere pleasure and without consulting him. [Col. 0067D] He therefore began to exert every effort to disrupt and annul Hildebert’s election. But his effort was futile: in 1097, on Christmas Day itself, Hildebert was solemnly consecrated by Raoul, archbishop of Tours.

When William learned this, angered against both bishop and count, he ravaged the bishop’s estates and villages in the territory of Le Mans and made war on Count Elias. Though inferior in strength, the count gathered an army and advanced to meet William. Battle was joined; Elias was defeated, captured, led to Rouen, and thrown into prison loaded with chains and irons.

But Count Fulk, who had recently become betrothed to Elias’s daughter, hurried with troops to the city, so as to forestall William’s desire to seize Le Mans. With the people’s support, he took possession of it; then, leaving his son there with a garrison, he returned to his own lands. King William, supported by only a small party of citizens, brought up his forces and attempted to take the city by deceit and treachery. On the same expedition he burned Coulaines, an estate of the bishop of Le Mans. But when the conspiracy was discovered, the townsmen marched out of the walls to attack the king. On learning this, he slipped away by night.

Meanwhile Count Elias, weary of his long imprisonment and fearing that Fulk might surrender Le Mans to the king by agreement and leave him in chains, obtained from King William the summoning of Hildebert and the leading men of the city to Rouen. He hoped that, out of pity for him, they would accept some terms of peace, however unfair. They came; and, since no other means of agreement remained, they surrendered the city to William. After settling affairs and leaving a garrison, William crossed to England.

Released from prison, Elias withdrew to a castle of his domain [Col. 0068B] named La Flèche. But mindful of injury and eager for revenge, he fortified all the castles that remained to him. Then, having enrolled soldiers and summoned allies, he brought his forces to the city. He routed the English and citizens who came out to fight, pursued the fugitives closely, occupied the city, besieged the citadel, and attacked it with engines and military missiles. The besieged resisted vigorously in return and hurled burning projectiles, by which the whole city and its suburbs were consumed by fire. Nevertheless the count pressed on with his operations and did not cease attacking the citadel until William—who, upon hearing the news, had again crossed over into Normandy—arrived with an army, drove out Elias, and recovered the city. He restrained his troops, greedy for plunder, with gifts; then, leaving a garrison, again departed for England.

Amid these tumults, Hildebert’s grief of mind can scarcely be described. He saw the city burned, the Church’s fields devastated, the clergy scattered, and his flock reduced to distress. Moreover, those enemies and slanderers who had assailed his accession to the episcopate [Col. 0068C] with calumnies, thinking they had found an opportunity, prepared new devices and denounced him to the king as the author of the disturbances. They falsely alleged that Elias had begun the war by Hildebert’s counsel and aid, and that the people had been stirred to revolt. The enraged king, indignant toward Hildebert, offered him these alternatives and compelled him to choose which he preferred: either to demolish the towers of the church that overlooked the citadel, or to go to England and clear himself of the charge of treason before the bishops. Preferring to face danger rather than inflict any injury upon his church, the bishop crossed to England. There, the situation changed: no mention was made of treason, no accusation of betrayal was brought forward, for the charge collapsed of itself and no ground remained even for suspicion. But the king began to insist that he demolish the towers, testing his constancy with repeated threats and setting before the resister evils and hardships. When he made little progress by this means, he tried another course. [Col. 0068D] He promised many gifts and rewards if Hildebert would comply, and promised to bestow much upon the tomb of Saint Julian, apostle of Le Mans. Hildebert, however, sought to soften the king by acts of service, lest he more gravely provoke him, and to delay the matter, hoping through frequent offices and prayers to draw him from his purpose. He then asked permission to return to his church, saying that further delay would harm his flock; and at last he obtained leave to return.

Upon his return, Hildebert placed in the treasury the sacred vessels and vestments acquired in England for adorning the church. He then attempted to repair the damage inflicted during the war, although this was difficult: the fields had been ravaged, the treasury exhausted, the clergy scattered in every direction, and the worship and service of the church almost abandoned. While Hildebert was occupied with these matters, a new and more grievous storm arose. The king again pressed him and ordered the towers demolished; he afflicted the reluctant [Col. 0069A] bishop with every sort of evil. He commanded Hildebert’s subjects and diocesan faithful not to render their bishop due obedience; he ordered all the bishop’s estates again devastated, the episcopal house itself plundered, and its furnishings carried off—“not even the mitres left,” as Hildebert says. Not content with this, he revived the fabricated charge of treason and ordered Hildebert, bound hand and foot, to be carried to a foul prison. Not even such hardships broke Hildebert: he preferred to lie for a whole year in misery and the most wretched condition rather than accept the offered condition of proving his innocence by touching red-hot iron, because this was forbidden by the sacred canons. The Church had rightly abolished that custom, formerly used in earlier centuries, because those who employed such a mode of proof seemed both to tempt God and to risk the oppression of innocent persons. Hildebert refused to undergo such a trial, on his own judgment and on that of his friend Ivo of Chartres, who addressed the imprisoned bishop thus in epistle 74:

> “Therefore act courageously, and do not furnish in your own person an example harmful to others, both future and present. For if you suffer anything contrary to justice, you shall be cleansed and tested through tribulation; and through the testing you shall obtain mercy.”

Amid these events William Rufus, king of England, perhaps in punishment for such cruelty toward a servant of God, perished miserably. While hunting, he was struck in the heart and killed by an arrow carelessly loosed, it is thought, by one of his retainers named Walter Tirel. [Note: [Col. 0069D] In the year 1099, 2 August.] When the unhappy death of William Rufus became known, Count Elias regained courage and besieged the English stationed in the citadel of Le Mans.
