Since they expected no aid from Henry I, William’s younger brother, who had seized the kingdom after killing his other brother Robert, they considered it a fortunate provision that Elias allowed them to return [Col. 0069C] to their own country “with life and limb safe and sound.” [Note: [Col. 0069D] *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans.*]

Shortly after the unfortunate death of King William Rufus, Hildebert was released from prison, but found Henry, William’s successor, no milder. Following in his dead brother’s footsteps, Henry ordered the towers of the church to be demolished. Because the bishop did not obey, he again forced him to cross to England, in order to clear himself in episcopal assemblies of the frequently renewed charge of treason. Upon arriving there, Hildebert found the prince’s anger inflamed and the hatred of all stirred against him. Thus, deprived once more of all his possessions, he was reduced to such utter want that, being unable through poverty to attend the Council of Poitiers, he was compelled to offer this excuse to the legates of the Apostolic See. [Note: [Col. 0069D] Epistle to John and Benedict, apostolic legates.]

Yet amid so many adversities the good shepherd Hildebert did not neglect to provide his sheep with the nourishment of sacred doctrine. Having learned how gloriously Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, had triumphed over the Greeks who denied the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, [Col. 0069D] he earnestly asked Anselm to commit to writing the arguments by which, in a public disputation before the supreme pontiff at the Council of Bari, he had refuted their errors. Saint Anselm nobly granted this request. Thus the whole Church owes that outstanding treatise of Saint Anselm, *On the Holy Spirit*, to Hildebert’s concern and entreaty. This is clear from their reciprocal letters, namely 9, 11, and 13 of book II, and from [Col. 0070A] William of Jumièges, *Norman History*, book VI, chapter 9.

Hildebert was harassed not only by the hatred of both kings but also by the insults of the consuls, as he calls them, of Le Mans. Seeking Henry’s favor, they did not cease for three whole years to vex the bishop. Overwhelmed by so many evils, he set out for Rome, both to find some consolation with the common father and, with his authorization, to resign his bishopric and withdraw to Cluny, there to spend the remainder of his life in peace in monastic exercises. “He would have embraced his bosom,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0069D] Epistle 7, book III, alternatively numbered 24.] “as a defendant embraces an altar, had the pope, once consulted, permitted him to lay aside the burden of the episcopate.” But while Paschal II was making his way by another route into France for the Second Council of Troyes, Hildebert, unaware of this, nevertheless arrived at Rome in the pope’s absence. From there he went to Naples, [Note: [Col. 0069D] See below the notes of M. Loyauté on this passage.] where he was received with the highest honor by the duke of Apulia, by the duke’s uncle Roger, count of Sicily, by all the [Col. 0070B] bishops, and by the leading men of the province; he was loaded with gifts worthy of royal magnificence. Returning to Le Mans, he distributed these partly among the city’s various churches and partly spent them in repairing the ruins of the cathedral church and episcopal residences, and in relieving the poor.

While following the pope on his journey to Troyes, he arrived at the island of Lérins, or Saint-Honorat. At that time savage pirates, on the holy day of Pentecost itself, had utterly overthrown the monastery from its foundations and slaughtered almost all the monks in a cruel massacre. Hildebert, as he recounts in the above-cited letter, [Note: [Col. 0069D] Epistle 7, alternatively numbered 24, book III. It is indeed remarkable that, among so many writers who have written on the affairs of the very famous monastery of Saint-Honorat [Col. 0070D] at Lérins, no one except Hildebert himself mentions this devastation. Yet he must be given unquestioning credence, as Baronius himself gave it under the year 1107, for he relates nothing here except what he himself saw at great peril to his own life, and he escaped from the bloody hands of the pirates only, as it were, by a miracle.] escaped safely. With favorable wind, he then made for Maguelonne and afterwards Savigny. There he met Paschal, who had formerly been a monk there, disclosed to him his intention of resigning the episcopate and embracing monastic life, and requested leave to fulfill his vow. But Paschal, moved by the man’s character, learning, energy, and care for souls, [Col. 0070C] not only dissuaded him from this resolution, but by an express apostolic mandate in writing sent him back to his church and pastoral responsibilities. Hildebert, lamenting that he must love his own lot and complaining of the supreme pontiff’s unyielding determination in this matter, was compelled to obey.

A diploma of Paschal II, issued in the fifteenth indiction, on 25 May 1107, is found in the *Library of Cluny*, in a case between the abbot of Cluny and Saint-Pierre of Chartres. Among the venerable bishops present at the judgment, Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, is expressly named.

Thus he returned to Le Mans, though unwillingly, and found the city at last enjoying profound peace. For Elias, by arms and with the help of Fulk Rechin, count of Anjou, who had married Elias’s daughter Eremburga, had defeated Henry I, king of England, and restored the city to his own dominion.

But while, peace having been established in 1110, the city of Le Mans was recovering a little from its former disasters, an enemy sowed tares in the Lord’s field. This was a certain hypocrite named Henry, who, acting as a wolf during the shepherd’s absence, had infected the sheep so thoroughly with false doctrines that the heretical man, by craft, by a certain natural eloquence, and by gifts, drew even the clergy to his side. It must nevertheless be admitted that Hildebert himself gave some occasion to this evil through insufficient caution. For that most cunning Henry had deceived the bishop so thoroughly under a feigned appearance of piety that, as Hildebert was preparing to go to Rome, [Col. 0071A] suspecting nothing in the man that savored of heresy or wickedness, and indeed thinking him moved by a genuine zeal to win souls, he granted him permission to preach in his diocese and ordered the archdeacons to deal very kindly with him and not hinder his ministry of preaching. Hence came the infection of evil and freer scope for the heretical man to spread his errors. Since he possessed some ability in speaking, he had won over by his eloquence and deceits not merely the lowest common people but many leading citizens and even clerics, so that they regarded him as a new apostle. Deceived by his wiles, they declared infant baptism useless; good works of no benefit to adults; churches not to be built but those already built to be destroyed; saints neither to be venerated nor invoked; hymns not to be sung in church; images and relics of saints to be trampled underfoot; crosses everywhere to be broken; and other ravings of that sort belonging to the followers of the ancient heretic Vigilantius. Though these doctrines had long been utterly extinguished, [Col. 0071B] innovators of this age fiercely defend them.

Yet there were not lacking those who resisted the rising heresy. The sounder part of the clergy, groaning over such great evils and not awaiting the bishop’s return, had prohibited Henry from exercising the ministry of preaching, driven him from the limits of the diocese, excommunicated the heretical man by an authoritative written decree, and proscribed him. At last, fearing Hildebert’s arrival, whom he did not doubt would be hostile to him, Henry withdrew from the city and retired to the town of Saint-Calais.

On his return Hildebert found many people deceived by the fraud of this wicked man and imbued with his impious teaching. Their newly introduced doctrines concerning the Christian faith so pleased them that they would neither hear their shepherd’s voice nor receive his blessing; indeed, they reviled him when he applied a healing hand. Hildebert, patiently bearing them because of his natural gentleness and striving gradually to recall them to sounder judgment, confronted the heretical man. [Col. 0071C] He contended with him with such authority, learning, and eloquence that he publicly convicted him of ignorance, wickedness, and depravity, expelled him from the whole diocese, and happily brought the wandering sheep back to the folds of the Catholic faith.

Once this pestilential and most hostile heretic had been driven out and banished far from his borders, peace was finally restored to the city, both by Hildebert’s own efforts and by those of Count Elias. Hildebert enjoyed the revenues of the episcopal domain for several years; but a severe storm soon followed this modest tranquility. For Elias died on 11 July 1110. Hildebert himself performed the funeral rites, and Elias was honorably buried in the basilica of Saint-Pierre-de-la-Couture. By hereditary right Fulk, count of Anjou, succeeded him, having married Eremburga, Elias’s daughter. But Fulk rendered homage and fealty for the county of Le Mans to Louis VI, surnamed the Fat, king of the Franks. Henry I, king of England, angrily claiming that this obedience was owed to himself, declared war on Fulk. Robert, count of Bellême, Henry’s bitterest enemy, took Henry’s side. Although aided by the forces of Count Rotrou Mauritanensis, his son-in-law, Robert was no match for Fulk’s army and was defeated; Rotrou himself was captured and handed over by Fulk to his enemy Robert of Bellême—though a kinsman—for close custody and, as Robert hoped, an immense ransom (1111).

Here, shut up in the great tower of the castle of Le Mans, Rotrou suspected Bishop Hildebert and Hugh, then dean of Le Mans, of having caused his captivity; and, thirsting for revenge, he set about entrapping them both by a dreadful and unheard-of deceit. Hildebert himself relates this in Letter 17 of Book II, formerly 39, in these words [Note: Col. 0071D: Written about the year 1110.]:

> “By the living God, and the Son of God, and the Spirit of them both, I shall not lie. Rotrou was held in the tower of Le Mans; I went to him, as he trembled through fear of death. Then he made confession to me, arranged the affairs of his household, made his will, and distributed gifts to churches. So that this might remain inviolate, he obtained, upon my entreaties, that I myself should go to his mother, bear witness to the will, and forbid anyone to presume to diminish it or attempt in any way to annul it. What the count requested was done: I went—would that I had never set foot there. The count’s mother received me with a kiss, applauded the will, and gave thanks that I had come by the count’s favor. Neither son nor mother denies that the matter happened thus; on that very day a plot against me was begun. You would have said that Christ’s betrayal had been repeated: on Thursday I was received with a kiss; on Friday, as though I were going with Christ to the cross, I was insultingly seized and put in public custody. They even divided my clothes among themselves, after distributing my horses among those who run freely to crime, but not to honorable action even for payment.
>
> “Now in the castle where these things were done was the bishop of Chartres, a man of venerable authority [Note: Col. 0072D: Ivo, namely.]; but among the authors of the crime authority had no authority. In a contrite spirit he approached Hubert—for that is the name of the prince of the Pharisees—and at first soothed that beast; but a beast admits no reason. Then he openly accused him of sacrilege, beseeched him seasonably, rebuked him unseasonably. Finally, he delivered him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, bound as he ought to have been with the bond of anathema: ‘For all this his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out’ (Isa. III.15). Religious abbots also, and anchorites perfected in name, gathered at the stone and found a stone: not that stone from which God raises up children to Abraham, but one in which there is no moisture, in which the seed of God’s word has no root: ‘For all this his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.’
>
> “At last a message was sent to Count Rotrou; my seizure and his dishonor were reported to him. At first he spoke in his heart and with a divided heart; at length he announced that I was to be released and satisfaction made to the Church. And lest he be thought to speak deceitfully, he sent to his mother hair cut from his head, adding that Humbert had inflicted upon him no less an injury in my person than if he had cut away the rest: ‘For all this his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.’
>
> “Therefore I turn to you, my dearest brethren, my fellow priests, my lords and friends. I ask you to pray for me, to take care for me, to stand beside me in compassion. For my own ransom I do nothing.”

It is indeed remarkable with what firmness of spirit Hildebert bore this violence inflicted upon him, and with what zeal, lest the rights of the Church and clergy should be violated, he resisted being ransomed, together with his dean, at any price. This was what Humbert, Count Rotrou’s seneschal, earnestly sought to exact from them both: that man, the eager instrument of the count’s vengeance and unscrupulous contriver of his schemes. Since neither the exhortations, prayers, or threats of the then renowned Ivo, bishop of Chartres, nor even the threat of anathema, could induce him to release the prisoners [Col. 0072D], he subjected them also to cruel tortures, kept them always fettered and oppressed with iron, and transferred them to the castle of Mortagne in the diocese of Séez. From there Hildebert wrote to Rabod, then bishop of Séez, to seek aid, or at least consolation, from a friendly fellow bishop.

Such grief over the captivity of their bishop seized clergy and people of Le Mans that they attempted everything to obtain the prisoners’ release. Hence private lamentations; hence publicly celebrated fasts; hence solemn supplications proclaimed; hence, finally, clerics prepared even to pawn, sell, or break up the crosses themselves and sacred vessels for the ransom of their captive shepherd. When Hildebert learned this, caring more for the Church’s honor and freedom than for his own, he opposed it with all his strength, as is evident from the aforesaid letter, which throughout, but especially toward its end [Col. 0073A], breathes forth a man truly apostolic. For he says:

> “Once redeemed by Christ’s blood, I do not seek to be redeemed again. That blood is my redemption; that blood is my price. It is unworthy that he whose price is without price should be brought under a price. Infamous is the ransom by which the Church’s liberty perishes. . . . I certainly do not value life so highly as to love it because it is brief and redeemed. . . . May my death benefit the Church, which, while I presided over it alive, I did not benefit. It belongs to a pontiff, if not to live, at least to die, for all.”

Such was that most valiant defender of ecclesiastical liberty even amid tortures. While Humbert, the diligent servant of Count Rotrou’s vengeance and avarice, wished to extort a ransom from the imprisoned men, and Hildebert and Hugh, the most steadfast defenders of the Church’s rights, refused to pay anything for freedom taken from them by a monstrous sacrilege, both were held for several years in a grim prison, and were repeatedly tortured and vainly harassed by Humbert [Col. 0073B]. At last peace was made between Louis the Fat, king of the Franks, and Henry I, king of the English, and likewise between those who had adhered to either side; the prisoners on both sides were released. Thus Count Rotrou was restored from the prison at Le Mans, and Bishop Hildebert with his dean Hugh from that of Mortagne (in the year 1118).

It is probable that, after the disturbances had been quieted, Hildebert was at last received into favor by Henry I, king of the English. For he addressed to him the consolatory letter which is Letter 12 of Book I, concerning the lamentable drowning of Henry’s sons, said to have occurred on 25 November 1120; and afterward several other letters on behalf of his friends, such as Letters 13 and 20 of Book III, which also breathe a degree of familiarity—the token of a sincere reconciliation.

Finally released from chains, Hildebert attempted to repair the damage caused by so many disturbances and to recall to a sounder mind the people, scattered and imbued with corrupt morals [Col. 0073C]. Since the example of clerics commonly contributes much to the instruction of the people, he endeavored, by his example and by his counsels, to bring the canons of the Church of Le Mans—who during the time of war and disturbances had wandered far from the true rule of piety—to better conduct. This was his chief concern; this, as it were, the sum of affairs to which he attended first. Yet he did not judge matters concerning the Church’s outward furnishing, restoration of buildings, and enlargement to be neglected. Indeed, he exerted himself so vigorously in these things that it is astonishing that a man more than once stripped of all his possessions and reduced to extreme poverty could have accomplished what is recorded in the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*. If there is room for conjecture, he could have amassed, from here and there, the great wealth and sums of money which he is said to have spent in erecting buildings and adorning churches only through the generosity of kings, bishops, and magnates whom he visited in the various circumstances of his life and by whom he is reported to have been highly esteemed.

Accordingly, the author of the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, cited above, says:

> “Although, sitting with Mary at the Lord’s feet, he would, if possible, have chosen continually to devote himself to the sweetness of contemplation, nevertheless, when the necessity of pastoral office compelled him to pass to Martha’s solicitude, it cannot be said how diligently and vigorously he attended to outward ministrations, striving with untiring industry to restore what the negligence of his predecessors had either destroyed or left undone. For he immediately began, from the foundations, to build with praiseworthy workmanship the chapter-house, of which there had for a long time been absolutely none there; he suitably illuminated it on every side with glass windows and caused it to be covered with vaulted work. He intended to do many other things, had he not been hindered by the onset of great tribulations.”

The same author continues, recounting Hildebert’s return from England:

> “From there he brought two precious cymbals, an excellent cloak of rich cloth, and two silver basins, with other ornaments, with which our church is adorned even to this day.”

And, after inserting certain matters, he describes his journey through Apulia:

> “When he proceeded to Apulia and Sicily, everyone showed him honor and reverence as though to an angel of God. For the duke of Apulia and his uncle Roger, count of Sicily, having heard of the bishop’s reputation for learning and uprightness, received him with the greatest honor and incredible reverence. Duke Roger himself prepared with his own hands three hundred pounds of precious incense, and sent it through Hildebert to blessed Julian, together with a large quantity of balsam, five precious cloths, silver and gilded cruets, and a silver censer whose workmanship surpassed its material. Roger, count of Sicily, likewise assigned one hundred ounces of gold for the work of blessed Julian and ten pounds of Le Mans currency for the sustenance of the canons. In those same regions there was a holy and noble matron, often inspired by an angelic vision, who had built a monastery in honor and in the name [Col. 0074B] of our most gracious patron Julian. She bestowed the grace of honorable hospitality upon the bishop’s companions, unacquainted with the route and wandering through every byway amid the darkness of night, and sent a certain cloth to our church. . . .
>
> “Moreover, Hildebert himself, honored with many gifts of various kinds by the bishops and other magnates of the same province, at last returned to his Church with peace and joy. By prudent distribution he gave a great part of what he brought with him to the churches of the city; the rest he spent abundantly on restoring the church and building episcopal residences. He transferred those residences from the western side to the eastern side of the church and established them in fitting workmanship beside the church of Saint Saviour, on the site where the hall of Lord Bishop Gervais had formerly stood. In an estate of his bishopric called Viriacum, about three miles from the city, he also built a stone hall with chambers and a hall, and enlarged it with lands, vineyards, and tithes.”

The same author adds the magnificent gifts which Count Helias of Le Mans—formerly Hildebert’s bitterest enemy, then his closest friend—bestowed, at Hildebert’s urging, upon the Church of blessed Julian, its canons, and the whole clergy:

> “By his counsel and diligent exhortation, the generous Count Helias adorned with gold and silver the bed in which the holy limbs of blessed Julian rest. He also granted to our church everything that his predecessors, Count Hugh son of Herbert, King William of the English, and Count Hugh son of the marquis, had in their times bestowed upon that church: namely, the *diablagium*, customary dues, exactions, and whatever they were said to possess, justly or unjustly, within the cloister, the episcopal residences, the settlements, and throughout all the land of the canons contained within Quinta, except robbery and arson. Besides this, he granted whatever his father-in-law Gervais of Château-du-Loir [Col. 0074D] had conferred upon blessed Julian in the land of the bishop and canons beyond the river Aune. Again, he ordained that all priests and clerics should be free and exempt from every customary due and public exaction. For the building of our church he gave one hundred and forty-seven gold pieces; for making the daily censer, two marks of silver; and to the canons, five marks. Moreover, when dying, he left fifty ounces of pure gold to blessed Julian for making a cross; from it Hildebert afterward fashioned a great cross resplendent with gems and decorative settings. From that time, therefore, he applied himself more diligently to building the church.”

When all matters belonging to divine worship had been properly and magnificently completed, Hildebert prepared to dedicate, with solemn rite, the church which he had completed, under the invocation of Mary, most blessed Mother of God; the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius; and Saint Julian the martyr. Having therefore invited several of the more illustrious prelates of that age, and they having assembled on the octave of Easter in the year 1120, with several abbots and many persons from neighboring churches, he proceeded to complete the church’s dedication. At that ceremony Archbishop Guillebert of Tours, as metropolitan, consecrated the high altar in honor [Note: Col. 0075D: Thus the author of the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*.] and in the name of the Lord Saviour, blessed Mary his mother, and the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. Geoffrey, archbishop of Rouen, formerly dean of Le Mans, consecrated the altar of the tomb of blessed Julian in his honor and name. Renaud of Martigné, bishop of Angers and afterward archbishop of Reims, consecrated the altar of the Crucified One, in honor of the Saviour and the Holy Cross. Our Hildebert consecrated the altar in the upper and more distinguished crypt, in honor and in the name of glorious Mary, ever virgin, and of all the saints. Marbod, bishop of Rennes, worn out by old age, “deprived of the sight of his eyes, but supporting the body’s infirmity with strength of mind and wisdom” [Col. 0075B], consecrated the altar in the right-hand limb of the church, in remembrance and honor of Saints Peter and Paul and all the apostles.

The same author reports that Count Fulk of Anjou, [supplied: son] of Fulk, and his wife Aremburga attended this solemn consecration of the mother church. In the presence of the bishops, and especially of Hildebert, they promised to confer several gifts from their property. This they actually accomplished a few days later, when, before the altar itself of Saint Julian, they gave to his church and canons a fair [Note: Col. 0076D: Commonly, *droit de foire*, “fair-right.”], to be held in the city of Le Mans for three consecutive days, with many other outstanding rights there specified. To confirm this gift:

> “The count himself,” says the author, “taking up his son Geoffrey and lifting him from the ground in his arms, placed him upon the altar of blessed Julian, offering to him both the boy himself and, through him and in him, adding the aforesaid benefaction, while the people heard: ‘To you, Saint Julian, I entrust my son and my land; be the protector and defender of both.’”

Leaving the said boy upon the altar, he withdrew bathed in abundant tears, intending shortly thereafter, as he had planned, to depart for Jerusalem. We have judged this entirely singular rite of offering particularly worthy of notice, as a striking monument of the sincere devotion of that count and his wife.

The writer of the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans* further recounts the magnificent gifts presented to the Church of Saint Julian by Geoffrey, son of Geoffrey of Mayenne. He was living in Apulia, where he had acquired almost immeasurable wealth. Among this his chapel, or chaplaincy, held the principal place, furnished with many relics and enriched for sacred worship with precious vestments and vessels of gold and silver. He had vowed that he would someday bestow all these things upon Saint Julian, and he notified the venerable Hildebert by letters that he should send to him those whom he judged fit for the task, to bring all these things back to Le Mans. When the pious bishop learned this, he spared no expense to enrich his church with so many sacred gifts. Accordingly, having abundantly provided funds for so great a journey, he sent there the principal men of his chapter: namely Gervais, Paganellus the archdeacon, and Hugh of Lavardin, archpriest.

> “They,” says the author, “performing the business entrusted to them and receiving everything, without difficulty, as that man, Geoffrey, had commanded, returned with those ornaments by a prosperous journey to our church, divine grace accompanying them. When the bishop learned of their arrival, he joyfully went out beyond the city to meet them with ecclesiastical array and a festive procession of clergy and people. Receiving gifts so holy and precious with the veneration they deserved [Col. 0076A], amid the immense rejoicing of clergy and people, he placed them in the sacristy of the mother church.
>
> “There was a certain golden panel bearing an image of Saint Demetrius the martyr, wrought with marvellous skill, whose marvellous excellence of workmanship surpassed even its golden material. There was also a treasure beyond comparison, a treasure to be desired: namely, an ounce of the same martyr, with a tooth of Saint John the Baptist and a certain hair of the Mother of God; also a portable altar-panel of gold and silver, clad on both sides in sheets of beaten gold. Within it, indeed, is enclosed one of the ribs of Stephen the protomartyr. Then there were two books, one of the Gospels and the other a missal, most elegantly decorated with the purest gold and silver; moreover, two silver candlesticks, excellently gilded but still better made, with a silver censer, two likewise gilded staffs, a silver cross bright with gold and gems, and a silver chalice gilded inside and out; likewise two precious chasubles adorned with excellent gold brocade, two bronze episcopal rings, two silk copes, a small pallium, an altar-cloth, an alb, a stole, and a maniple.”

After this author has recounted Geoffrey’s fortunate return to Le Mans and his solemn and festive reception by Hildebert and the whole clergy, he says of Hildebert:

> “Encouraged by such great benefits of divine grace, Hildebert himself also began, according to his ability, to act as a fellow worker with divine goodness, and laudably adorned the church with books, cloths, copes, priestly and Levitical instruments, most precious choir-hangings or tapestries, and doors before the choir. He also honorably restored, as the times permitted, the altar-panel of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius together with Saint Julian, partly from the silver which Lord Bishop Hoel, his predecessor of blessed memory, had left for this work, and partly from what he himself had acquired elsewhere. From his own resources he also made two caskets [Col. 0076C], most beautifully overlaid with gold and silver, in which he carefully deposited relics of Saints Turibius and Victor, as well as Saint Innocent and other bishops of our Church, and of Saint Tenestina and Ada, and Saint Hilary the priest.”

The same author then relates how solicitous he was for the deliverance of deceased canons from purgatorial flames by prayer, and what benefits he bestowed upon the living; and finally says:

> “He also newly founded and covered with vaulted work a treasury together with a vestry, for the preservation and protection of the church’s ornaments, lest the relics of the saints or the church’s treasure should ever be exposed to a popular fire or robbery.”

These are the statements of the author of the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans* concerning the buildings completed by Hildebert for the Church’s adornment and the magnificent gifts bestowed by Hildebert himself. The same author also maintains that in his time the abbey of Saint George of the Wood was restored, while the monastery of Carnia, the church of the Fountain of Saint Martin, the church of the Fountain of Gihard, the church of Saint Martin of Lucé, and the church of Saint Mary of Belle-Lieu were founded anew. John Maan, historiographer of the metropolitan church of Tours and its canon and precentor, reports that this last was raised, endowed with the distinguished institution of a monastery of Augustinian canons, and dedicated by Hildebert in 1115.

Hildebert labored not merely to adorn and enrich his own church, and the other churches both of the city and the diocese of Le Mans. His affection was also always directed toward his Benedictines, especially the neighboring monks of Saint Vincent in the suburb of Le Mans, whom he especially calls his brothers and sons. For them he obtained various gifts from kings and magnates, or bestowed them himself, and granted them several churches. Moved by devout feeling toward Saint Domnolus, bishop of Le Mans and founder of that monastery, at the request and advice of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris [Note: Col. 0077D: Bondonnet, *History of the Bishops of Le Mans*, p. 195.], he was the first reverently to open the saint’s sacred tomb, about the year 1124. The younger Fulk, count of Anjou, was present, together with a great multitude from the entire region and its magnates; all were eyewitnesses of miracles worked by God in that solemnity at the invocation of Saint Domnolus.

In the following year, 1125, after Gilbert, archbishop of Tours, had died, Hildebert was appointed to his place, although nearly seventy years old and reluctant. For when, as bishop of Le Mans and therefore the first among the suffragan bishops by the privilege of his see [Note: Col. 0077D: Thus Hildebert is described by Geoffrey of Vendôme, Letter 2, Book III; Sirmond says in his notes: “For just as, in the province of Belgica Secunda, the city of Châlons is next in rank after the metropolitan see, so in Lyonnaise III the city of Le Mans is first after the metropolitan see of Tours [Col. 0078D]. Hence the bishop of Le Mans is the first bishop of that province.”], he had come to Tours to administer the vacant metropolitan church, he was elected archbishop by the unanimous agreement of clergy and people. This election was approved and ratified by Louis VI, then king of the Franks, called the Fat; shortly afterward it was confirmed by Honorius II [Col. 0077B], to whom Hildebert’s holiness and outstanding gifts for the government of souls had become known.

Orderic Vitalis, in Book X, p. 770, of his *Ecclesiastical History*, recounts this in the following words:

> “After the death of Gilbert, archbishop of Tours, Hildebert was elected by clergy and people; by God’s will he passed from the eminence of Le Mans to the metropolitan see. He was gentle and religious, and zealous for learning in both sacred and secular letters,” etc.

“For,” as the frequently cited *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans* relates, “neither the exaltation of the honor conferred upon him, nor an abundance of wealth, nor the enticement of carnal luxury cast him down.” And indeed, just as, while bishop of Le Mans, he had diminished nothing—as the same author attests—from his frugality in food and drink, the hardness of his bed, the roughness of his hair-shirt, vigils, and prayers, by which perhaps, while living as a monk, he had learned to subdue his body; so neither in the archbishopric, though now almost worn out with age, did he relax his customary exercises of penance [Col. 0077C]. Thus always sparing toward himself, allowing nature’s necessities very little, lavish toward the poor with his possessions, munificent to churches, courteous and agreeable to all, he nevertheless remained an ever-watchful shepherd toward the people entrusted to his care.

Hence, in reforming the morals of clergy and people, or forming them for the better, he overcame the coldness of advancing age by a most ardent zeal that never grew cold. This is evident both from the *Acts* already mentioned and from various sermons which, whether as bishop or archbishop, he delivered to the people or in frequent synods to the subordinate pastors of his diocese, filled with remarkable learning and piety. Thus, by those effective words and compelling arguments which we observe everywhere in his sermons, he inspired teachableness in the sheep and diligence in the shepherds.

Meanwhile, in order to lead others by his example, he turned his attention to rooting out from the Lord’s field the tares that infested all Armorica. With the compliance of his suffragan bishops—one only resisting, Baldwin of Dol—he undertook, despite his advanced age, the visitation of the churches subject to his metropolitan see [Col. 0077D], and carried it out with the greatest benefit to the people. Ever watchful over ecclesiastical affairs and the governance of peoples, he summoned a provincial council at Nantes. Besides the bishops of the province, the more eminent abbots of those regions were summoned from various places, together with men especially distinguished for learning and piety, so that he might restore the Church of that province, almost ruined in form; restore fallen discipline; and by ecclesiastical authority bring back to better conduct ecclesiastical morals that had strayed from piety [Col. 0078A].

Above all, he sought to abolish incestuous marriages, dissolve the foul marriages of priests, and especially remove that shameful and inveterate custom by which the offspring of such sacrilegious marriages came to canonries and even to priesthoods as though by hereditary right. By a solemn decree of the Fathers, with the penalty of anathema pronounced, he proscribed these abuses [Note: Col. 0078D: Letter to Honorius II.].

Nor did he merely set ecclesiastical affairs in order; he also labored to relieve the burden of the people. He induced Conan, then count of Brittany, to renounce voluntarily, in the council itself and into the hands of the Fathers, two established rights that weighed most heavily upon the populace. When either spouse, husband or wife, first died, all the movable goods of the deceased passed to the count’s treasury, to the serious injury of the children. No less an injustice was inflicted upon wretched shipwreck victims, for whatever remained to them, whether from their merchandise or the remnants of their ship’s equipment, was all claimed by the count’s treasury [Col. 0078B]. Yet the archbishop, by his innate eloquence, so persuaded the count that he himself, renouncing such unjust imposts, earnestly requested that the penalty of anathema be imposed upon those who resisted.

It is remarkable how short a time our bishop required to accomplish these splendid deeds: all that pertained to the council was completed and brought to an end in three days. Hildebert reported the acts of the council to Pope Honorius II, so that he might strengthen them by his authority and decree. Honorius most willingly granted this, issuing at the Lateran, on 21 May of the same year, a letter to all suffragan bishops of the metropolitan church of Tours [Note: Col. 0078D: See among Pope Honorius’s letters, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXVI, the letter entitled “To the Suffragan Bishops of the Metropolitan Church of Tours.”]. After praising Hildebert, he commanded that whatever had been decreed in that Council of Nantes be observed without challenge. These letters—both Hildebert’s to Honorius II and Honorius II’s to all the suffragan bishops of the metropolitan church of Tours—were inserted among Hildebert’s letters by all the libraries of the Fathers; all collectors of councils likewise included them in their collections. Labbe himself does so in his collection, assigning this Council of Nantes with us to the year 1127.

In the same year, 1127, toward the end of October—namely 23 October, the tenth day before the Kalends of November—Hildebert went to Redon with his suffragans, at the invitation and earnest request of Hervé, then abbot of Redon, to reconcile and, as it were, consecrate anew the church of the monastery of Redon. The occasion for this most celebrated consecration had been provided by the rebellion of Oliver of Pontchâteau against Conan, duke of Brittany. To suppress and avenge the plundering and murders of this most crafty man, Conan gathered forces and besieged him, a fugitive in the church of Redon itself—though he had long before kept him imprisoned at Nantes for this very reason. Oliver, as is customary with men of this criminal sort, had polluted the church with six hundred sacrileges; and he who had already long inflicted very many injuries upon the monastery of Redon and its possessions had made its sanctuary a den of robbers [Col. 0078D].

Accordingly, Hervé the abbot and the monks frequently and repeatedly complained to the bishops and to Duke Conan himself. At last moved by them, although he had permitted the profanation of the holy place only from zeal for justice, the duke repented of the deed and, conscious also of certain injuries which he himself had at times caused the monks, wrote, through Hervé himself, abbot of Redon, a letter full of most humble petitions to the supreme pontiff, asking pardon. We hope that it will not displease the diligent reader for this letter to be produced, in order that it may appear from it with how great reverence the princes of Brittany formerly treated the apostolic see even while they possessed sovereign authority [Col. 0079A]. The distinguished Monsieur Baluze kindly lent us from his papers both this letter, once drawn from the cartulary of Redon and full of religious feeling and filial reverence, and the whole account of the matter. We later observed that neither had escaped the discerning attention of our learned Monsieur Alexis Lobineau, who published them among the proofs appended to his distinguished *History of Brittany*, recently issued [Note: Col. 0079D: *History of Brittany*, vol. II, p. 279.].

Thus runs that letter of Duke Conan to the supreme pontiff:

> “To his Honorius and lord of all Christians, his least son Conan, duke of the Bretons, greeting. Holy Father, I beseech your fatherhood: if I have offended in any matter, or shall offend, correct me as a tender son with a light rod. For I shall always obey you in all things. Moreover, the abbey of Saint Saviour at Redon, which the Emperor Louis the Pious of blessed memory once built in Lesser Brittany, which is now mine, and joined under Saint Pope Leo to the proper right of blessed Peter [Col. 0079B], I and my predecessors have hitherto preserved in fidelity to you. But, since Breton faithlessness has accumulated, I cannot henceforth preserve it as I ought. Therefore I restore it to you free, as the pious Emperor Louis gave it, grant it all its rights, and beg you to do justice concerning its wrongdoers. Farewell.”

Then, from the same cartulary of Redon, the whole sequence of the matter—here reproduced in full because it especially concerns Hildebert—is narrated as follows:

> “Conan, duke of the Bretons, sent this letter through the venerable Hervé, abbot of Redon, and William, prior of Saint-Melaine, to the aforesaid lord pope, in the year of the Savior’s Incarnation 1126. Receiving it, the holy pope ordered that it be read before the holy Roman senate and certain bishops of our regions, namely Guy of Le Mans, Ulger of Angers, and William of Poitiers, and preserved in the palace with our privilege. He asked the abbot who the wrongdoers were, what wrong had been committed, and for what cause it had occurred. The abbot reported everything to him in order.
>
> “When the pious pope heard these things, recoiling in horror from so great a crime, he directed by letter Gerald, legate of Angoulême, Hildebert, archbishop of Tours, and all the bishops of Brittany by name, to restrain the wrongdoers with episcopal severity until every injury done to the church, and all things wickedly taken from it, both possessions and other goods, should be restored. To the abbot and monks, as his most special sons, he entrusted his own authority in showing mercy to the guilty. Having confirmed all the church’s privileges, he also appended his seal. He further granted that the abbot might summon whatever persons he wished for the consecration of the altar and purification of the church.
>
> “Accordingly, he summoned the archbishop of Tours with all his suffragan bishops and abbots. They assembled at Redon on 23 October, and, with Prince Conan present with his mother [Col. 0079D], all the magnates of Brittany, almost all the monks and clerics, and a great multitude of people, consecrated with the utmost reverence the altar in honor of the Saviour of the world, his Mother, the blessed Peter and Paul, Saint Marcellinus, pope and martyr, and all God’s saints. They purified the church from the uncleanness committed there by those under siege.
>
> “But while these things were being prepared, Bricius, bishop of Nantes, who styled himself archdeacon of the abbey, presumed to seek a share of the offering; likewise all the canons of Vannes sought a share for themselves and their bishop. At the chapter’s advice, the abbot submitted judgment concerning these matters to the archbishop, bishops, and abbots. But they, fearing to incur Roman indignation, evaded judgment; and so, defeated and rebuked by the archbishop for their presumption, they fell silent.”

> “This consecration was celebrated (and this is from the aforesaid cartulary of Redon), and this wicked dispute was settled, in the year from the beginning of the world 5079, from the Incarnation of Christ 1126, epact 17, indiction 1, moon 15, on Sunday, 10 Kalends of November [23 October], with God as author, while the angels rejoiced, all the saints were glad, and the ministry was jointly celebrated by Hildebert, archbishop of Tours; the bishops Hamelin of Rennes, Donoal of Aleth, Gallus of Léon, and Robert of Cornouaille; and the assisting abbots Hervaeus of Redon, Hervaeus of Saint-Melaine, Gautier of Machecoul, and Ivo of Sacméel [Note: [Col. 0079D] Commonly Saint-Gildas-des-Bois.]; while countless monks and clerics prayed; and Conan the prince stood by with his mother Ermengard and many of his nobles, namely Geoffrey and Alan, proconsuls of Porhoët; Elven of Elven; Jarnogon son of Rioc; Pagan of Malestroit; Guetenoc of Rieux [Note: [Col. 0079D] Rieux.]; Oliver of Pontchâteau [Note: [Col. 0080D] Pont-chasteau.]; Savaric of Dung; Garsire of Rais [Note: [Col. 0080D] Rais.], with his son Harcuid; Guetenoc of Ancenis; Geoffrey of Châteaubriant; Senebrun of Bains; Haimo of Guérche; Ralph of Montfort; and many other nobles, together with a great crowd of both sexes—all praising God and execrating the impious petition of the archdeacon and the canons.”

From the foregoing, therefore, it is clear that Hervaeus, abbot of Redon and bearer of Conan’s letter, went to Rome in 1126 in order to lay before the supreme pontiff the grievances or injuries inflicted upon his church and monastery. Received there most graciously, and having obtained a sealed confirmation of his monastery’s privileges, together with letters of recommendation addressed to Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and then apostolic legate, and to Hildebert the metropolitan, he returned to his monastery near the end of that same year.

After that year had elapsed and 1127 had begun, it is probable that Hildebert held the Council of Nantes mentioned above [Col. 0080C]. In June of the same year he obtained and received from Honorius II its confirmation. Once this had been published and accepted throughout all Armorica, the aforesaid Abbot Hervaeus asked him to come to his church, defiled by sacrileges, in order to purify, reconcile, and consecrate it anew. At the end of that same year—namely, at the close of October—Hildebert most willingly performed this task, having summoned his suffragan bishops.

Yet a charter concerning the donation to the church of land at Ballac by Oliver of Pont, who had at last come to his senses, introduces some obscurity into the chronological sequence. The year 1126 is assigned to it; nevertheless, the same charter declares that it was made on the day after the consecration of the high altar of the church of Redon by Hildebert of Tours. We think this difficulty can be resolved only by charging the copyist with an error: through the careless omission of a single stroke, he wrote 1125 instead of the year 1127 [Col. 0080D], as frequently happens.

It will not be irrelevant to reproduce in full that charter of Oliver, in which the reader may observe the distinctive manner in which donations to churches were made in that age. The same will need to be observed below in another charter of Guegon, concerning the consecration of the altar of the chapel of Saint Mary Magdalene for the infirmary at Redon, solemnly performed by Hildebert himself five years later. Oliver’s charter reads as follows:

> “In the year from the Incarnation 1126, epact 17, indiction 1, the aforesaid Oliver, son of Jarnogon of Pont, greatly abhorring the sins of his youth—for he was a man of remarkable fierceness and shed much blood—came, with the other barons, to the consecration of the high altar of this most holy monastery of Redon. This consecration was performed by Hildebert, metropolitan of Tours, and his suffragan bishops, by command of Pope Honorius.  
> 
> Meanwhile, reflecting upon both the greatness of his sin and the frightfulness of the torments of Gehenna, as well as upon the glory of eternal recompense, and remembering also that divine mercy had delivered him from the prison at Nantes, where he had been held captive with other barons under Count Conan, he had vowed that, if the Saviour of the world delivered him from that distress, he would give to his deliverers the place called Ballac, in the parish of Pirriac.  
> 
> It happened that, in that prison, Abbot Hervaeus came down to him to offer consolation and, on the day after the aforesaid consecration, received from his hand the gift which he had vowed, together with certain of his retainers, namely Albin and Lambert. Oliver then freely approached the newly consecrated altar [Col. 0081B], summoned Abbot Hervaeus and the monks, and in the presence of the venerable persons invested that altar and the present church with this gift by his own hand, in the following manner:
>
> ‘I, Oliver, son of Jarnogon of Pont, inflamed with hope and desire for the heavenly blessing and inheritance, for the salvation of the souls of my parents, and for the safety and salvation of myself and my brothers, today give and firmly grant to the Saviour of the whole world, in this his church of Redon, the place called Ballac, with its entire appurtenance, as it is known to have been possessed by my ancestors and by me by hereditary right. From this place, and from everything which belongs to me therein by right, as I have said, I make a free, exempt, and undisturbed alms-gift upon this altar, by my own hand, to Abbot Hervaeus and his successors, to possess forever and in peace.’
>
> This was done on Monday, the sixteenth moon, 9 Kalends of November [24 October]. Witnesses to this transaction are Abbot Hervaeus himself [Col. 0081C], Abbot Gautier of Machecoul, and Abbot Simon of Sacméel. Of the monks there were Robert the physician, Ralph, James, William, and Hubert the hermit. Of the laymen: Oliver, Albin, Lambert, and William son of Geoffrey.”

At about this time, or a few years earlier, the most celebrated and holy Order of Fontevraud began. Its first abbess at its chief monastery was the venerable Petronilla of Chamillé, or Chamilly. Moved by the fame of the eminent holiness, learning, and prudence of the venerable Hildebert, which had spread throughout the Christian world, she sought and obtained him from Pope Honorius II, then supreme pontiff, as her defender and patron.

For she had herself experienced his outstanding moderation and wisdom in the dispute between Peter, bishop of Poitiers, and Hildebert concerning the tithes of Condat. The matter had been amicably settled through Gerard of Angoulême, then legate of the Holy See; and the abbess of Fontevraud herself was involved in that case [Col. 0081D]. Hildebert’s patronage and goodwill were certainly not without benefit to the nuns of the convent of Fontevraud. As long as he lived, he cherished them most lovingly in temporal as well as spiritual matters.

His assistance in temporal matters is evident from his letter to Henry I, king of England, in whose realm the Order of Fontevraud had perhaps already extended its branches. In it he pleads concerning a certain alms bestowed upon nuns there already admitted. Through a letter to Honorius II, he also humbly requests confirmation both of this grant and of another made to them by Henry himself [42, alternatively 20, book III; 69, book II]. This is likewise clear from charters issued expressly for their benefit or at least subscribed by Hildebert. According to the learned letters of Father Soris the elder, visitor of the Order of Fontevraud, more than forty such documents are counted in the cartulary of Fontevraud and are carefully and devoutly preserved.

His spiritual care may especially be inferred from his many letters [Col. 0082A], breathing and inspiring the solid piety in which he excelled. He repeatedly sent these to noble and devout nuns who had vowed themselves there to Christ; from his attentive and frequent visits to them and repeated conversations, by which he confirmed them in their holy purpose and kindled them toward the perfection of their vocation; and, finally, from the close and devout bond which he maintained until Robert of Arbrissel’s most pious death with that venerable man, their most holy father. Thereafter he proved himself an outstanding eulogist of Robert, as appears from his epitaph, recently discovered in the royal manuscript of Saint-Amand (Elnone), about six hundred years old, full of remarkable praises of him. That epitaph alone, as an invincible apology, could shame the more insolent detractors from the venerable memory of that most devout man and impose silence upon them. In that funeral poem Hildebert says of him:

> His breastplate wore down his side; parching thirst, his throat;  
> 
> Harsh hunger, his stomach; wakeful care, his eyes.  
> 
> The flesh was worn away under the laws of reason, its mistress;  
> 
> Nor did the flesh cease anywhere to be further deprived, etc.

These verses are reproduced here in full among Hildebert’s metrical works.

Although Hildebert had ascended the throne of the metropolitan see of Tours only with the assent and permission of Louis VI, king of the Franks, surnamed the Fat, he nevertheless incurred the king’s indignation shortly afterward—when, as he says in Letter 34, Book II, he had spent scarcely a year in that metropolitan see. He himself recounts the entire matter in the letter mentioned.

At the very beginning of his archiepiscopate, he found the offices of dean and archdeacon vacant through the deaths of their previous holders. He conferred both upon various clerics of his church whom he judged better suited to discharge those duties, but not upon those whom the king himself had chosen and named. Hildebert did not accept the latter as being less fit for the office [Col. 0082C].

Although, throughout this affair, he fixed his attention principally upon God’s glory, the dignity of the Church, and the salvation of the souls entrusted to him, and always stood firm in his decision, it is remarkable with what modesty and reverence he treated the king—who otherwise had deserved exceedingly well of the Church and had everywhere proved a most vigorous defender against domestic petty tyrants rising throughout the realm. In this business, however, the king was perhaps excessively credulous toward unjust ministers. Though injured, the bishop behaved with restraint.

Letters 33 and 34 of Book II should be consulted. In the first, he says mournfully:

> “With the most serene king, exhortation is needed rather than rebuke; counsel rather than command; instruction rather than the rod. He ought to have been approached in these ways and reverently instructed, lest he expend his arrows upon an aged priest; lest he void canonical enactments; lest he persecute the ashes of a Church already buried—ashes in which I eat the bread of sorrow, in which I drink the cup of mourning, and from which to be rescued and escape is to pass from death to life.”

And, wishing to furnish an example to posterity in similar cases and to restrain the rash attempts of restless men who, under a pretended zeal for piety, stubbornly oppose royal authority, he says:

> “Yet amid these straits anger never so triumphed over me that I would ever wish to raise a cry against the Lord’s anointed, or seek his peace by a strong hand and the arm of the Church. There is another way,” he continues, “by which, Christ leading, I may more directly attain that peace with him. I shall cast my thought upon the Lord, and he will grant me the desire of my heart,” etc.

Indeed, after he had set forth and defended, with great integrity and apostolic freedom but with still greater reverence, the rights of his church before the king himself and his council, though he suffered rebuff, he nevertheless defended them so effectively—by his own prayers, the intervention of Henry I, king of England, whose favor he had regained, and the support of the supreme pontiff’s legate with the king—that Louis finally consented. He permitted those promoted by Hildebert to the dignities of dean and archdeacon to retain their offices, and restored to the Church of Tours, though under burdensome conditions, the provostship which he had taken from it [Col. 0083A].

Soon afterward, however, the tranquility which Hildebert had secured for himself in his see and church by such efforts was disturbed (1129). Ralph, whom he had made dean of his church, corrected certain canons by ecclesiastical discipline, as Hildebert says in Letter 38, Book II, in the exercise of his deanery. Some of them burned with such implacable hatred toward him that they attempted by every possible means to inflame the king’s mind—which was already hostile because the deanery had been assumed without consulting him—through accusations and, in Hildebert’s words, “mutilations.” One of them in particular, named Nicholas, further tried to blacken the dean’s name everywhere by calumnies.

A lay brother of the dean, deeply enraged by this, unexpectedly seized Nicholas and, entirely without the dean’s knowledge, blinded him—or, as Hildebert says in the aforesaid Letter 38, Book II, “cut him off and dismembered him” [Col. 0083B]. When the mutilated Nicholas complained to Hildebert, asserting that the deed had been perpetrated only on the counsel and instigation of the dean and another canon named Herbert, but did not produce adequate proof for the accusation, Hildebert nevertheless wished to remove the scandal which this charge had spread among the faithful. Therefore, with the bishop of Le Mans present and seated beside him, together with several abbots and other religious and wise men, he pronounced sentence requiring the dean to undergo canonical purgation with the seventh hand of his order.

Ralph and Herbert, confident of their innocence, complied: each produced six fellow priests of unblemished reputation, who publicly attested their innocence under oath along with them. But Nicholas neither accepted Hildebert’s sentence nor the judgment of Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, then legate of the supreme pontiff, to whom the decision of the matter had been entrusted by papal authority and at the parties’ request. Nicholas therefore appealed to the supreme pontiff himself.

As Ralph was travelling to Rome to plead his cause before him, carrying letters of recommendation from Hildebert, he was miserably murdered on the road. He seems to have been killed by his opponents, although the real authors of the murder could never be clearly discovered [Col. 0083C].

It can scarcely be told how greatly Hildebert was grieved by the killing of his dean Ralph, cruelly and, as appeared, treacherously inflicted. Ralph was a man of outstanding integrity, zealous for ecclesiastical discipline and a most vigorous assailant of vices. This moral integrity earned him the hatred of clerics and finally brought about his destruction.

Since the dilatory appeal to the Apostolic See by the aforesaid mutilated Nicholas had given occasion for this crime, Hildebert took the opportunity in Letter 41 of Book II to explain how great were the dangers threatening God’s Church from appeals of this kind—which he calls frivolous—and from their too ready reception by the Roman court:

> “While,” he says, “episcopal vigor grows weak, and the abundance of crimes receives increase through impunity.”

Some believed that Pope Honorius II did not receive this very favorably, but wrongly. For he always showed Hildebert honorable signs of singular esteem and goodwill, and Hildebert always found him compliant with his wishes in all things.

This was especially evident when Baldric, bishop of Dol, to whom Urban II had personally granted the use of the pallium, died. His successor Geoffrey wished to enjoy the same prerogative as if it were owed by right to his church. Hildebert, on the contrary, maintained that this distinction belonged solely to the Church of Tours as metropolitan of all Armorica. In Letter 35 of Book II [Col. 0084A], he appealed to the supreme pontiff, ready, though worn out by age, to present himself at Rome before him and vigorously defend his church’s right against Geoffrey, bishop of Dol.

Yet he did not live to see the end of this dispute. It was not settled until 1144, when, after protracted contentions on both sides under three pontiffs, Pope Lucius II decreed that Hugh, Hildebert’s successor, was metropolitan of all Brittany. He declared the Church of Dol, like those of Tréguier and Saint-Brieuc, subject and suffragan to him. He also solemnly invested Hugh with metropolitan jurisdiction by the delivery of a wooden staff bearing a lead plate, inscribed in a sort of spiral line with certain Roman letters and characters. Our learned Dom Alexis Lobineau represented a finely engraved image of this distinctive object in his excellent History of Brittany, vol. II, among various seals of that age, no. 48 near the end, from the treasury of the eminent metropolitan church of Tours [Col. 0084B], where it is still devoutly preserved.

How great Hildebert’s name and authority were in the Church in that age is especially shown by the famous dispute between the antipope Anacletus and Innocent II, the legitimate pontiff, concerning the supreme pontificate. Saint Bernard, chosen by the unanimous agreement of the cardinals as something like the supreme arbiter of so great a controversy, earnestly sought Hildebert’s support.

At first Hildebert had favored Peter Leonis, or Anacletus, because he had been elected by more votes: he had obtained twenty-one votes, whereas Innocent had obtained only seventeen. Having learned this, Hildebert in good faith adhered to Anacletus, who had been elected first by a plurality of votes.

Saint Bernard observed this, and also how consequential it would be if Hildebert—whose reputation for piety and learning had spread almost throughout the whole Church and who was metropolitan of all Brittany—together with his suffragan bishops, should desert Innocent. Bernard therefore sent him an altogether moving letter to turn him away from Anacletus and bring him back to Innocent as the legitimate pontiff; and he did indeed bring him back.

For Saint Bernard and Hildebert had entered many years before into a bond of holy friendship, as is clear from Letter 18, Book III, of Hildebert to Saint Bernard, in which he earnestly asked admission, as he puts it, “within the sanctuary” of Bernard’s friendship; and from Letter 19 of the same book, Saint Bernard’s letter to Hildebert, entirely honeyed and radiant with his praises. Hence, in the aforesaid letter written to Hildebert concerning that very celebrated dispute, Bernard says that, as to an intimate friend and acquaintance, he offers him what he judged just and useful to the Church:

> “Lest so great a pillar of the Church,” he says, “should come to be shaken.”

Readily accepting these warnings, Hildebert drew all Armorica, both by counsel and example, to the side of Innocent, the legitimate pontiff [Col. 0084D], and thereafter steadfastly adhered to him with all of it (1130).

Even amid the frequent sufferings of illness which afflicted him during the final years of his pontificate, worn down by the austerity of his life, labor, and old age, there were certain unrestrained persons, even among the clergy, who exploited his infirmities to relax discipline and defiled themselves with various crimes, to the disgrace of the Church and the scandal of the faithful. Yet Hildebert, like a good shepherd, never failed in his duty: he reproved them with fitting censures in season and out of season; and, after repeated admonitions of evangelical charity and every remedy of Christian prudence had first been applied in vain, he was sometimes compelled to wield even the thunderbolt of excommunication against the obstinate and rebellious.

Some of those struck by it went so far in stubbornness that they insolently appealed to the Apostolic See and obtained absolution from their censures from the supreme pontiff himself, or from his ministers deceived by various lies and artifices, without consultation with Hildebert [Col. 0085A].

This is clear from his letter of complaint, Letter 4, Book II. In it he complains bitterly, yet most humbly and lovingly—as, he says, a son complains privately to a most dear father—that his adversaries had made him an object of mockery all day long, as though the supreme pontiff had taken from him the power, entrusted to all bishops, of correcting the enormity of his “chaplaincy”—by this humble term he means his diocese—and had restored to their offices and benefices, without satisfaction and without a hearing, clerics whom he had excommunicated only justly and canonically.

Nevertheless, Hildebert declares that he had reverently obeyed these commands of Christ’s vicar, although perhaps not altogether equitable and though burdensome to himself. Still, he beseeches him:

> “As though prostrate at the apostolic feet, not to burden the weakness of my body with anxiety of mind, but to grant me the power of disposing canonically concerning my chaplaincy.”  
> 
> [Note: [Col. 0085D] *Capellania* (“chaplaincy”) for “diocese.”]

It is probable that this was not denied him. For throughout the remainder of his life he lived, as is established, undisturbed by further tumults and so peaceably that, in the words of the author of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans*, “he always preserved alike the dignity of his age and of his order.” Despite uncertain health, he also energetically fulfilled every episcopal duty until the final period of his life [Col. 0085B].

Evidence of this episcopal energy is his journey to Redon near the end of his life for the solemn consecration of the altar in the infirmary in 1133. We learn this from the charter of Guegon of Blaigno, drawn from the cartulary of Redon, by which he gave his land at Ballac to the monastery of Redon. The reader may perhaps not object to seeing it here in full. It will also help us somewhat in determining the year of Hildebert’s death, which various authors date differently; moreover, it teaches us the solemn rite by which a promise made to sacred places was finally fulfilled in actual deed. It reads as follows:

> [Col. 0085C] “Since, with the passing away of transitory time, the memory of men also passes and slips away; and since all things rightly and praiseworthily done by man are worthy to be retained firmly and permanently, we have judged it fitting to commit to writing—things which most truthfully recall the deeds of the ancients—that Guegon of Blaigno, a most illustrious man and a man of outstanding vigor, likewise a longtime and most faithful friend of this holy church of Redon, being ever inclined willingly to assent to whatever pertained to lasting benefit, was on a certain Sunday in the church of Saint Guengar, situated in the parish of Pirriac, lovingly and reverently urged by William of Fait, monk of this sacred place, and by the hermit Hubert, who lived together in the place called Ballac, to make from the possessions which he held temporarily and fleetingly some memorable gift to the holy Saviour in the church of Redon. After all things have passed away, the Saviour grants eternal rewards for things well disposed.
>
> They also informed him that the aforesaid place Ballac, which belonged under Oliver of Pont to his own right and hereditary property, had through prolonged wars been reduced to solitude and desolation and was a thoroughfare and haunt of robbers; and that he should transform it into a place where those serving the Lord God the Saviour might dwell and live. Outwardly admonished in the ear of the body, but sensing it much more powerfully in the ear of the heart, he promised that he would do this.
>
> But lest what he had well and devoutly promised God should come to nothing through some eventuality, he at once invested the aforesaid monk and hermit with the said gift before the altar of the church of Pirriac, Daniel his provost witnessing, firmly promising that he would more fully and solemnly fulfill the same gift shortly in the church of Saint Saviour [Col. 0086A]. As a pledge for this matter, he sent a purse from his cloak to Abbot Hervaeus and the convent.
>
> Some days later it happened that Hildebert, archbishop of Tours, held a meeting at this monastery of Redon with his suffragan bishops concerning certain ecclesiastical affairs. When these had been concluded, he solemnly consecrated, together with the bishops present, the altar of the chapel of the infirmary in honor and memory of blessed Mary Magdalene. To this consecration the aforesaid Guegon came with the other barons. Led into the chapter house, in the full convent he recounted in order the gift he had made of Ballac; he received the fellowship and benefit of the church, abbot, and monks; and he promised that, if he were able to dispose of his life, he would become a monk of this holy monastery.
>
> Then he was led to the altar to offer the gift and said these words:
>
> ‘I, Guegon of Blaigno, for the purpose of eternal recompense—that is, that I may be able to escape the punishments and torments of eternal suffering—and also for the salvation of the souls of all my parents, today give upon this altar to you, Saviour of the world, my land called Ballac, in the parish of Pirriac, with all services, revenues, and customary dues owed to me from it, together with all my lordship and right: free, undisturbed, and exempt. I give it, I say, and transfer it to you, Lord Saviour, into the hand of Abbot Hervaeus, to be possessed in peace by him and by the servants of this most holy church until the end of the age.’
>
> This was done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1133, on the Nones of February [5 February], Monday, moon 21, indiction 11, epact 12, on the day when the altar of Saint Mary Magdalene was consecrated by Archbishop Hildebert. Witnesses to this gift are: Archbishop Hildebert himself; Abbot Hervaeus; Abbot Simon; and Abbot Gautier. Of the monks: Robert the physician, William of Fait, and Ralph Parta. Of the laymen: Riallon, Daniel [Col. 0086C] the provost, Cramail, and Maurice.”

In this charter of Guegon [Note: [Col. 0085D] Reported in vol. II of the *History of Brittany*, p. 285, from the Cartulary of Redon.] several matters deserve notice. First, there is the rite by which Guegon assures the abbot of Redon concerning his intended gift: as a pledge, he sends him a purse from his cloak. This appears distinctive, but it suggests that such was the practice of that age for securing promises concerning future acts.

Second, the rite by which Guegon actually fulfills his promise should also be observed: he solemnly declares his donation in person, to be offered at the altar, just as we noted above that he had solemnly declared his donation of the land at Ballac at the altar of the Holy Saviour.

That the same land was donated by different persons within a span of five years does nothing to impair the truth and genuineness of these charters. It could very well have happened that the land consisted of two portions and had two lords, each of whom, at different times and on different occasions, granted his own portion to the Church of Redon [Col. 0086D].

Finally, the year in which Guegon is said in this charter to have made his donation—namely 1133—must be noted. From it the controversy over the year of Hildebert’s death can be resolved with sufficient probability. Several learned authors differ in assigning it. Dom Robert in the *Gallia Christiana*, and the Sammarthani brothers, maintain that he died in 1136. But Dom Jean Maan and our Dom Jean Mabillon say that this occurred in 1132.

The first opinion is prevented by a charter [Note: [Col. 0086D] Reported in vol. II of the *History of Brittany*, p. 286, from the archive of the Church of Nantes.] recording Conan, duke of Brittany’s restoration of various churches to the eminent Church of Nantes, dated 4 Nones of November [2 November] 1135. Hugh, then already archbishop of Tours and Hildebert’s immediate successor, was present. On this view Hildebert had already died by then, and, as seems probable, many months earlier. For the election of Hugh was greatly disturbed by Philip, nephew of the deceased Archbishop Gislebert and then dean of Tours. With the support of Louis VI, king of the Franks, he sought with all his strength to invalidate Hugh’s election—made by the more numerous and more influential part of the electors—and to divert it to himself.

But when the matter was referred to the Apostolic See, and especially when Saint Bernard intervened, Philip lost his case. The election of Hugh, who not only did not seek it but resisted it, was approved and confirmed by the legate appointed by Pope Innocent II, together with several bishops, to settle the dispute. All this could be settled only over a period of several months. Therefore, if Hugh was present at the aforesaid restoration of 1135, his predecessor Hildebert must have died at least in the first months of the same year; therefore, not in 1136 [Col. 0087A].

On the other hand, the charter of Guegon just related forbids us to regard 1132 as the year of Hildebert’s death. It states that he officiated at the consecration of the altar of Saint Mary Magdalene in the infirmary of Redon on the Nones of February [5 February] 1133. Thus he had not died in 1132 either. Amid these perplexities, let whoever is more discerning or more fortunate than we be judge. Meanwhile, we think the middle opinion should be adopted: Hildebert died in 1134, midway between 1133 and 1135 [Col. 0087B].

But whatever year the venerable Hildebert died, it is far less important to determine than the fact that he died the pious and holy death of the righteous in a good old age. The *Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans* testify that, cheerful and eager in spirit, he gave his soul to the stars and his body to the tomb at about the eightieth year of his age. If we date his birth to 1057, because the first year of his episcopate was 1097, when, according to the same *Deeds*, he had not yet passed his fortieth year, and if we place his death in 1134, he died in his seventy-seventh year—not far from “about eighty.”

[Col. 0087C] Thus at last the venerable bishop, having passed unharmed along his path through so many thorns of anxiety; having endured repeated losses of all his possessions, so many exiles, and recurring harassments even of his own person; having washed away by patience alone and trust in God so many wrongs of calumny; and having undertaken, finally, so many labors to defend the Church of God and the dignity of his order, fell asleep in the Lord on 15 Kalends of January [18 December] 1134. He had governed the Church of Le Mans for twenty-eight years, as he himself testifies in Letter 31, Book III, and that of Tours for six years and as many months, amid the greatest vicissitudes, holily and wisely.

Yet the old necrology of the metropolitan church of Reims reads:

> “16 Kalends of January [17 December]: died Lord Audebert, formerly bishop of Le Mans, afterward archbishop of Tours.”

This would indicate not 18 but 17 December. He was buried on the right side of the altar [Col. 0087D] in his church, which he had enlarged with so many buildings and enriched with so many precious gifts. There, according to Dom Jean Maan, he shone with miracles in his metropolitan church of Tours; there he awaits the resurrection and the crown of righteousness laid up for him, which, as it is fitting to believe from God’s mercy, the just Judge will render to him.

Certainly, whether we weigh the ancient *Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans* which relate these matters concerning him and which we set forth continuously below; or consider the sentiments of piety which may be drawn from his letters, sermons, and other little works; or observe the vigilance and zeal with which he applied himself to pastoral duties, and the courage with which he resisted violators of the Church’s rights, even kings; the austerity with which, even at the height of episcopal dignity, he spent his days to extreme old age; or, finally, the contempt for temporal life with which he longed for the life to come—we shall see nothing throughout so long a course of life [Col. 0088A] that does not testify to a sublime perfection of Christian piety and episcopal holiness.

Therefore, we should not have incurred the charge of rashness and too venturesome innovation had we adorned Hildebert with the title of Saint, as was at first our intention. For the author of the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans* did so; Peter de Natalibus did so in his *Catalogue of Saints*; Cardinal Baronius himself did so under the year 1097, and often elsewhere; and the most illustrious Bishop of Toul, André du Saussay, did so in his Gallican Martyrology. The most learned editor Margarin de la Bigne had publicly bestowed this title of Saint upon him in the Paris edition of the *Library of the Fathers* of 1589; and Father Jacques Homey most recently followed him, without any objection being raised, in his *Supplement to the Fathers*. Nor did the Cologne editors, and more recently the Lyons editors, offer any reason why they withheld from him the title of Saint.

Nevertheless, however great our inclination [Col. 0088B] may have been to restore to him this honour, due to him and granted long ago, we preferred to abide by the counsel of several men eminent in Christian society and in literary piety and learning. They judged that, for this reason alone—that in the very distinguished Churches over which the venerable Hildebert presided, namely Le Mans and Tours, no public feast or office was observed for him—we ought rather to refrain from this expression of our sincere veneration for him, until the Church herself, to whom alone it belongs to crown the faithful with the title of Saint, shall by her public decree confer it upon this most devout bishop, though renowned for miracles. [Note: [Col. 0087D] Dom Jean Maan, cited above.]

We shall therefore reverently await her judgment in this matter. And we sincerely submit to her correction everything which might be found, whether in this our collection of the works of Hildebert and Marbod, in the notes, or in any of our other slight studies, to be—God forbid—at variance with the Catholic faith or unsuited to pious morals. For nothing has ever been more earnestly desired by us than to end our last day in the unity, bosom, and obedience of the Roman Catholic Church, in which, by God’s favour, we have lived hitherto; and this, trusting in His mercy, we most earnestly desire, resolve, and hope.

Moreover, in order that greater credit may be given to the matters related in this Life of the venerable Hildebert, we thought it appropriate to append immediately what the ancient author of the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans* recorded concerning Hildebert, as printed in volume III of our Mabillon’s *Analecta*, together with the notes upon him by the most distinguished M. Loyauté, a most learned advocate in the supreme court. Yet, however much trust we think should be placed in that ancient and authentic author, we do not judge that such trust should be given him that we should believe nothing concerning the venerable Hildebert except what he reported, since it is certain that he omitted many, and those most illustrious, of Hildebert’s deeds.

For example, he said nothing of the visitations of the suffragan churches undertaken by Hildebert, the Bishop of Dol alone resisting; nothing of the grave dispute with Louis the Fat, king of the Franks, concerning the deanery and archdeaconry of Tours, which brought upon Hildebert exile from the king’s dominions; nothing of the celebrated Council of Nantes, held by him in 1127 and confirmed by Honorius II; nothing of the affair of Nicholas, the mutilated canon, against Ralph the dean—of such importance that it could not be settled even by the apostolic legate appointed for that purpose. But were these and many other similar matters not deeds merely because he did not report them, though it is clear from Hildebert’s own letters, from that writer, and from many others that they occurred?
