The writer of the *Acts*, therefore, related what he had learned. We believe that those accounts ought to be followed, and we do follow them; but not so scrupulously and exclusively that we believe nothing of the deeds of the venerable Hildebert except what he narrated.

Furthermore, we judged that the title *Venerable* should be prefixed to his name, since certain manuscript codices bestowed it upon him [Col. 0089A] [Note: [Col. 0089A] M. Loyauté’s manuscript, about six hundred years old.], perhaps because Saint Bernard, in Letter 123 of Mabillon’s edition, cited here at p. 124, calls Hildebert “a man worthy of all reverence”; and because Paschal II adorned him with this title in a diploma issued at Silviniac in 1107, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March], in the case between [Col. 0090A] the abbot of Cluny and the Bishop of Chartres concerning the priory of Saint-Denis of Nogent [Note: [Col. 0090A] *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 549.]; as also did Geoffrey of Vendôme in Letters 13, 22, 23, and 24 of Book III, and many other authors of considerable reputation.

[Col. 0089]

## EXTRACT FROM THE *ACTS OF THE BISHOPS OF LE MANS*

Drawn from the treasury of the distinguished Church of Le Mans, published in 1682 by Dom Jean Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. III, where it appears thus, pp. 303 ff.:

### CHAPTER XXXV. CONCERNING BISHOP HILDEBERT

[Col. 0089B] I have resolved also to describe the deeds of the venerable Hildebert, a man of merit not inferior to that of his predecessor Hoel, lest his praiseworthy memory be covered by idle silence, and lest he who had led many into the light of truth by the brilliant exhortations of his writings should himself, through lack of a writer, remain obscure and unknown to posterity.

He was born in the castle of Lavardin, of parents indeed modest in station but honourable; he was made master of the schools and archdeacon by Lord Hoel, bishop of the Church of Le Mans, of venerable memory; and after Hoel’s death, because of the merit of his learning and upright character, he was appointed in his place by the common consent of clergy and people. He was a man gentle in manners, restrained in speech and action, and outstanding among all the clergy of that region in literary studies. Although he had diligently applied himself to learning from childhood, after assuming the episcopate he devoted himself yet more earnestly to reading the Holy Scriptures. For his mind, trained in liberal studies, could not be idle.

[Col. 0089C] According to the Prophet, he meditated day and night upon the law of the Lord; he either read the books of the divine Scriptures himself or caused them to be read before him. From them, like a most discerning bee, he gathered the little flowers of manifold thoughts and drew forth reflections sweeter than honey. From these, like a wise preparer of spices, he made a honey-sweet drink, which he offered to his hearers sometimes in writing and sometimes by living speech. He addressed exhortatory letters to persons of both sexes and of different ages, in which he argued so usefully and subtly that, imitating the ancient style, he appears to surpass all the writers of his time both in weight of thought and in elegance of expression.

When he spoke in church, the people heard his words most devoutly; but he was heard still more eagerly by the clergy, because he spoke Latin with a certain greater fluency and liveliness. His writings, most brilliantly composed both in prose and verse [Col. 0089D] and spread with great fame in various places, suffice—though we are silent—to extend his praise learnedly and eloquently to future ages. He himself, if I am not mistaken, had not yet passed his fortieth year when he was elected to the episcopal dignity.

[Col. 0090B] Fearing that the flesh, ever desiring against the spirit after its own fashion, might soften the vigour of his spirit with its enticements, he began to subdue his body by moderation in food and drink, by the hardness of his bed, and by the roughness of haircloth; to persevere in vigils and prayers; and, according to the Prophet, to wash his bed every night with a flood of tears. Whatever sins of youth he had committed, he redeemed by generous almsgiving. When he approached the altar to celebrate the most holy mysteries, he was wholly moved to tears; and thus, in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart, he offered the saving sacrifice before the divine presence.

The poor and pilgrims were always guests at his table. Every Saturday evening, following the most humble example of our Saviour, he used to wash their feet, taking great care that his good purpose should, as far as possible, be made known to no one. Although he would have chosen, had it been possible, to sit with Mary at the Lord’s feet and continually devote himself to the sweetness of contemplation, yet whenever necessity compelled him to pass to Martha’s care for the pastoral office, it cannot be said how diligently and energetically he applied himself to external ministries and strove by tireless labour to restore whatever his predecessors’ negligence had destroyed or omitted.

[Col. 0090C] At once he began, in a praiseworthy work, to build from the foundations a chapter-house, which for a long time had been wholly lacking there; he suitably adorned it and lit it throughout with windows of glass. He intended to do many other things, had he not been hindered by the onset of great troubles.

For at that time a very severe war arose between the king of England and Count Elias, because the king claimed the bishopric of Le Mans and therefore sought to oppose the bishop’s ordination. When he learned that Hildebert had been ordained, he revealed, by open incursions of war, the hostility which he had long conceived in his mind. Count Elias, though unequal in strength, attempted to resist his undertakings; but, while imprudently pursuing the enemies who had come against him, he was—alas!—seized by them, taken as far as Rouen, and cast into chains in the fortress of that city. This misfortune disturbed not only the city but the whole region of Le Mans.

[Col. 0091A] When Fulk, Count of Anjou, learned of this, he immediately came to the city with his son Geoffrey, who had already been betrothed to the daughter of Count Elias. By agreement with the citizens, he established a guard in the city’s fortifications; then, leaving his son there, he hastened away on other business. Meanwhile the king of England, seeing that the city was deprived of its lord’s protection, hurried there with the consent of certain treacherous citizens. He encamped with a large army at the episcopal village of Coulaines, burned the village itself together with the church there, and cruelly devastated all that the bishop possessed there. For, as said above, he hated Hildebert because he had accepted the bishopric against the king’s claim.

The citizens, issuing from the city equipped for war, endeavoured manfully to withstand his army. But the king, realizing that he had been deceived by the counsel of traitors, withdrew secretly with his army at evening, when the deep silence of approaching night had come on, and left the camp empty for the enemy. When the citizens rose in the morning and began to prepare themselves for battle, they discovered that the king had departed, seized his camp, found no one there, and returned home.

When Elias heard this, fearing that Count Fulk might seek to procure his proscription, he summoned the bishop and certain leading citizens to himself, with the king’s consent. He began to deal with them and humbly begged them, out of compassion for his misfortunes, to endeavour by every means to surrender the city to the king and secure his release from chains. He feared that Count Fulk, seduced by the king’s gifts, would make peace with him and, after the surrender of the city, condemn Elias to perpetual exile.

[Col. 0091B] The bishop and those who had come with him, pitying his distress, spoke with the king concerning his release and made this agreement with him: if, through their counsel and ingenuity, the city were surrendered to him, he would permit Count Elias to depart in peace and freedom. This affair was accomplished through the bishop’s skill more quickly than had been hoped; and at the same time the city was restored to the king and liberty of departure to the count. The king therefore, having recovered the city and placed in its fortifications abundant supplies of men, arms, and provisions, crossed over to England.

Meanwhile Elias stayed near the castle of Laid and in the camps round about, restoring his strength as far as he could for new conflicts, like a bull in the hiding places of the woods, fortifying his castles with rampart and ditch, and securing for himself the friendship and assistance of his neighbours. At last, in the following year, having gathered a great army of neighbours and friends, he came unexpectedly not far from the city. The king’s soldiers, together with the people, came out hostilely against him as far as Pontlieue; but, unable to sustain his attack, they were put to flight.

[Col. 0091C] Having crossed the river, he pursued them vigorously and, entering the city boldly with his army, no one resisting him, enclosed those in the fortifications under a sudden siege. But those in the citadel, at evening, kindled a huge fire and began with utmost urgency to throw blazing torches upon the houses below. The fire, strengthened by the east wind, consumed the whole city together with a great part of the suburbs. The people, stunned by the conflagration and turned to mourning, gave the count assistance that was not sufficiently steadfast. The count, setting up engines and machines against the fortifications for hurling stones, strove with every effort to storm those within. But they built engines against his engines and frustrated all his attempts.

Seeing, therefore, that he achieved nothing, that his army was gradually falling apart, and being terrified by fear of the king, who was hastening to assist his men with a very large army, he took thought for his own safety, abandoned the siege, and suddenly withdrew from the city. When this became known, it is both grievous to hear and too wearisomely lengthy to recount what great fear and astonishment seized the citizens; how great a multitude of people, with women and little children, followed him, leaving behind all that they possessed; and how cruelly and inhumanly those who remained in the city were oppressed by the enemy.

[Col. 0092A] Indeed, had not the king’s generosity restrained the rapacity of the raging plunderers, our city would certainly in those days have come to utter destruction. Finally the king, having obtained control of the city according to his own will and stationed guards in it, returned again to England.

Certain clerics, however, who had envied the bishop’s promotion from the beginning and had meditated treachery against him all day long, gravely accused him before the king. They reported that he had been privy to the betrayal when Count Elias, with the citizens’ consent, occupied the city and besieged the king’s soldiers in the fortifications. The king, therefore, holding him suspect and continually seeking occasions against him, urgently and obstinately demanded that he either order the church towers—which, he complained, had caused him harm—to be demolished, or cross over to England after him, all excuse being removed.

[Col. 0092B] Though unwilling, Hildebert was compelled by the king’s pressing command, willing or not, to undergo the perils of the sea. There the king, again urged on by Hildebert’s enemies, began vehemently to press him concerning the demolition of the towers and, for this reason, to inflict intolerable distress upon him. Moreover, in order that the king’s desire might obtain an easy and swift fulfilment, he offered the bishop a very great weight of gold and silver, from which the shrine of blessed Julian might have been made honourably—or rather, to its everlasting disgrace; for the condition was that the towers of the church should immediately be destroyed.

Hildebert wisely rejected this poisoned bargain, saying: “In our regions we lack craftsmen who know how to carry out such a work suitably. Hence so diligent a work and expenditure are fitting for the king’s provision, in whose kingdom remarkable craftsmen flourish and produce remarkable metalwork.” Yet Hildebert was hemmed in on every side by great distress, since he foresaw imminent danger from the king’s displeasure and great disgrace threatening himself and his Church from the destruction of the tower. Therefore he asked the king for a delay until he had received counsel concerning these matters. Having scarcely obtained it, and seeing that it was by no means useful for him to remain longer in those regions, he soon returned to his own church.

[Col. 0092C] He did, however, bring back two precious cymbals, a very fine cloth-of-gold cope, two silver basins, and other ornaments with which our church is adorned to this day.

Meanwhile the bishop, deeply distressed by the king’s command, the burning of the city, the destruction of the houses and all his possessions, and the expulsion of the citizens—but most sorrowful above all for the dispersal of the clerics whom the king’s violence had driven from the city—continually prayed the clemency of almighty God to deign to turn away the wrath of His indignation from the Church and people entrusted to him. The Lord, however, had pity on his affliction and tempered His indignation beyond what could have been hoped. He filled the faces of Hildebert’s enemies with shame and confusion, so that their song was turned into mourning and their organ into the voice of those who weep.

[Col. 0092D] For that king, once wealthy, who trusted in his own strength and gloried in the multitude of his army and riches, who was regarded as most terrible, like a fiercely savage lion, not only by his own subjects but by neighbouring peoples on every side, was suddenly broken and brought down to the ground; with all his glory he vanished like smoke. For when one day he had gone into the forest to hunt, he was struck by an arrow from one of the knights who had gone with him and died.

When Count Elias learned this, he came without delay to the city with the people who had followed him and again enclosed those in the fortifications under siege. They waited three months and more for help from the new king; but, deprived of every aid and with no escape open to them from any quarter, they were at last compelled to come out of the fortifications. By the count’s generosity they received immunity in life and limb and returned to their homeland.

[Col. 0093A] The city being thus pacified and its enemies driven out, Hildebert set out for Rome. Pope Paschal received him attentively into his acquaintance and friendship. Afterwards, when Hildebert proceeded to Apulia and Sicily, all honoured and revered him as though he were an angel of God. The Duke of Apulia and his uncle Roger, Count of Sicily, hearing of the fame of the bishop’s learning and integrity, received him with the greatest honour and incredible reverence.

Then Duke Roger himself prepared with his own hands three hundred pounds of precious incense and sent it through Hildebert to Saint Julian, together with a great quantity of balsam, five precious cloths, silver-gilt wine vessels, and a silver incense-box, whose workmanship surpassed its material. [Col. 0093B] Roger, Count of Sicily, likewise assigned one hundred ounces of gold for making the work of Blessed Julian, and ten pounds of the money of Le Mans for the sustenance of the canons.

In those same regions there was a certain holy and noble matron who, frequently inspired by angelic visions, had built a monastery in honour and under the name of our most gracious patron Julian. She gave the bishop’s companions, ignorant of the road and wandering through various byways in the darkness of night, the benefit of honourable hospitality; she also sent a certain cloth to our church. And blessed Julian, the Lord’s host, did not fail those who invoked him.

Moreover, Hildebert was honoured by bishops and other nobles of that province with many gifts of various kinds. At length he returned to his Church in peace and joy. A great part of what he had brought with him he distributed, by prudent administration, among the churches of the city; [Col. 0093C] the remainder he spent abundantly in restoring the church and building episcopal residences. He transferred these residences from the western side to the eastern side of the church, and built them appropriately beside the church of Saint Saviour, where the hall of Bishop Gervasius had stood in ancient times.

In an estate of his bishopric called Viriac, nearly three miles from the city, he also built a stone hall with chambers and a cellar, and increased its lands, vineyards, and tithes. By Hildebert’s counsel and earnest exhortation, the generous Count Elias adorned with gold and silver the shrine in which the blessed remains of Saint Julian rest. He also granted to our church everything which his predecessors—Count Hugh, son of Herbert; Willus [or William], king of the English; and Count Hugh, son of the marquis—had in their times conferred upon that same church: namely, *diablagium*, customs, exactions, [Col. 0093D] and whatever, justly or unjustly, it was said to possess in the cloister, in the episcopal residences, at Coulaines, and throughout the whole land of the canons contained within the Quinta, except robbery and arson.

Besides this, he granted whatever his father-in-law Gervasius of the castle of Laid had bestowed upon blessed Julian in the land of the bishop and canons beyond the River Idonea. He again established that all priests and clerics should be free and exempt from all customs and public exactions. For the building of our church he gave 147 gold coins; two marks of silver to make a daily-use thurible; and five marks to the canons. Moreover, at his death he left fifty ounces of pure gold to blessed Julian for the making of a cross; Hildebert later fashioned from it a great cross, adorned with gems and ornamental devices. From that time, therefore, he applied himself more earnestly to the construction of the church.

[Col. 0094A] About that time, while Count Rotrou of the Perche was held captive in the tower at Le Mans, the bishop visited him as he trembled before death. The count confessed his sins, asked forgiveness, bestowed his property, and confirmed by testament the dispositions he had made. He asked the bishop to visit his mother and bear witness to the testament, lest it be annulled by anyone’s contrivance. Moved by the count’s prayers, the bishop went to Nogent with Dean Hugh and Fulchard the cantor. First the count’s mother offered them the kiss of peace, and before them she devoutly confirmed the testament.

On the following day Hubert Capreolus, steward of that same count, believing that the dean had been privy to the count’s capture, seized the bishop with all his companions and committed them to prison. Whoever wishes to learn the fuller course of this affair will find it more fully in the letters of that bishop. But enough of this.

Adam, certainly a man of honourable conduct and life, a native of our diocese and then a canon of the Holy Sepulchre of the Lord, sent through R., the viscount, and G. de [Col. 0094B] Braitello a certain cross to our church. In it are set two crosses of the wood upon which the Lord Jesus suffered. Above the second cross is placed a stone from the Mount of Olives, from where the Lord ascended into heaven; at the right, a stone from Gethsemane, where the Lord was struck; beneath, a stone from the rock of Calvary, which was split at the Passion of the Redeemer and drenched with His blood. A stone from the Lord’s sepulchre is contained in the larger opening.

Hildebert received this cross amid chants and organs and a flood of tears, with clergy and people standing by; and he placed it in the mother church with fitting reverence, in the year of the Lord 117, on Easter Tuesday.

At nearly the same time, in the neighbouring regions there arose a certain hypocrite, whose own conduct, perverse morals, and detestable doctrine proclaimed him worthy of punishments for scorpions and parricides. Concealing the rabid savagery of a ravening wolf beneath the spoils of sheep, he had a countenance and darting eyes like a storm-tossed sea; his hair was bound up, his beard unshorn; he was tall in body, quick in step, walking barefoot upon the ground while winter raged; ready in speech, terrible in voice, and young in age.

[Col. 0094C] There was no finery in his clothing. His food differed openly from that of ordinary people; he lodged in burghers’ houses, stayed in porticoes, and had supper and bed in an upper room—not at all in imitation of the prophet Daniel, but in accordance with the saying: “Death has entered through your windows.” Why say more? He was famous everywhere for extraordinary holiness and learning—not in merit, but in pretence; not in truth, but in appearance; not in morals or religion, but in reputation.

Matrons and boys below puberty—for he made use of the seduction of both sexes—came to him in turn and confessed their transgressions; but they added to them by caressing his feet, buttocks, and groin with tender hands. Delighted by the lust and monstrous adultery of this great man, these women publicly declared that they had never touched a man of such austerity, humanity, and strength [Col. 0094D] that even a heart of stone could readily be moved to compunction by his speech. They maintained that monks, anchorites, and all regulars ought to imitate his religion and celibate life. They also claimed that there had been granted to him by the Lord God the ancient and authentic blessing of the prophets, and a spirit by which he could recognize and disclose the hidden sins of mortals, unknown to others, merely by seeing their faces.

When a report of this kind reached our region, the people, in their own frivolity applauding their own ruin, longed daily and all day to be deceived by his deceitful talk and for his arrival, so that they might the sooner become steadfast adherents and participants in his heresy [Note: [Col. 0093D] Thus in the original; perhaps *irremotus*, “unmoved.”]. For it often happens that the things which harm people most are more pleasing to them.

And now the passing days themselves brought this about. For he, intending to infect our fellow-countrymen with his viperous breath, sent to the bishop two of his disciples, alike to himself in life and habit, before his face after the manner of the Saviour. When they reached the suburbs of our city on Ash Wednesday, all the people, fervent in their evil purpose, received them as angels of the Lord of the universe.

[Col. 0095A] In accordance with their master’s custom, they carried staffs and a banner of the cross, at whose top an iron object had been fixed, while their colour and outward manner of life presented the appearance of penitents. The bishop, a man of the greatest piety, insufficiently fearing the snares of the Trojan horse, received them gently and devoutly and showed them a cheerful countenance and generosity. Although he had undertaken a journey to Rome, he nevertheless instructed his archdeacons, among other matters, to allow that pseudo-hermit Henry—for that was the heretic’s name—peaceful entry and permission to address the people.

When Henry entered the city walls, the mob, as we have said, applauded novelty according to its usual manner and admired the person of one unknown rather than one proven. What wonder? They thought him to surpass his reputation in uprightness, though report, which commonly employs frequent praise, had exalted him. Many clerics, blinded by his schism, factions, and private gifts, supplied material for the harangues of the common people, preparing a platform from which he might address the crowds of people obedient to him.

[Col. 0095B] While he spoke to the people, with these clerics seated at his feet and weeping, his oracle rang out as though legions of demons were uttering a murmur from his mouth with one gaping throat. Yet he was wonderfully eloquent. His speech, poured through the ears into the minds of the crowd, clung there like fresh poison that, having penetrated the inward parts, gathers all its powers around the vital organs, wages an implacable hatred against life, enters more greedily, and continually ravages.

By this heresy the people were turned in fury against the clergy, so that they threatened their servants with tortures and would neither sell them anything nor buy from them; indeed, they treated them as heathens and tax collectors. Further, they had resolved not only to tear down their houses and scatter their goods, but to stone them or hang them on the gallows, unless the prince and his nobles, recognizing their wickedness, had resisted their impious violence by force rather than reason—for a beast admits no reason.

[Col. 0095C] Some clerics living in the same city—namely Hugh of Osello, Willus Quinonbibitaquam, and Paganus Aldricus—once went to Henry for the purpose of disputation. They were violently beaten and shamefully thrown down and befouled in the face with mud and filth; scarcely, at peril of death, could they withstand the assault of the frenzied crowd. Indeed, after escaping the danger, their departure resembled flight. For, had they been seized by those men, they could by no means have escaped peril unless, under the protection of the count and his nobles, they had been able to go into hiding.

For, as has been said, the ruler of the city resisted their error and would not at all abandon the protection of the clergy. The clergy, unable to speak to that hypocrite in person, sent him a letter through a canon in the following terms:

[Col. 0095D]

> “Our Church received you and your companions with peace and honour when you came in sheep’s clothing, though inwardly you were ravening wolves plotting snares. It also showed you the intention and practical effect of brotherly charity, believing that you would faithfully warn the people concerning the salvation of their souls and sincerely sow the seed of God’s word in their hearts. But you have presumed, in a perverse order, to return anger for peace, reproach for honour, hatred and curse for charity, and to disturb the Church of God by your deceit. For you have sown discord between clergy and people, and by repeated incitement ten times over have stirred up the multitude of the seditious populace, armed with swords and clubs, against Mother Church. You offered us Judas’s kiss, and by public insult called us and all the clergy heretics. Furthermore—and this is worse—you have perniciously and faithlessly uttered many things against the Catholic faith which a faithful Christian shudders even to repeat.
>
> “Therefore, by the authority of the supreme and undivided Trinity, of the whole orthodox Church, of holy Mary the Mother of God, of Saint Peter prince of the apostles, of his vicar our reverend father Pope Paschal, and of our bishop Hildebert, we utterly forbid you and your companions, who flatter your evil and destructive error, to presume any longer, whether privately or publicly, anywhere in the bishopric of Le Mans, to preach or to spread the absurdities of perverse doctrines.
>
> [Col. 0096A] “But if, in defiance of so great an authority, you again open your impious jaws to pour forth poison, we, supported by the same authority and its privilege, excommunicate you and all your accomplices, supporters, and helpers. And may He against whose divinity you do not cease to contend cause you to be consigned to eternal curse on the day of strict judgment.”

Henry did not receive the letter; but Willus Musca recited the contents of it in his presence. Those standing by threatened him with punishment, because he openly, as seemed fit to him, boldly heaped reproaches upon Henry. Henry, changing the expression of his face at every division of the letter, repeatedly said: “You lie.” Certainly, had the count’s steward not been present—under whose escort William had undertaken that journey—he would never have returned alive to the mother church.

[Col. 0096B] After these events he was no less active in sacrilegious assemblies at Saint-Germain and Saint-Vincent, where he taught a new doctrine: women who had lived less chastely were publicly to burn their clothing together with their hair, naked before everyone; no one thereafter was to take gold, silver, possessions, or a dowry with a wife, nor give her a dowry. Instead, a naked man was to marry a naked woman, an infirm man a sick woman, a poor man a destitute woman; nor were they to care whether they contracted marriage chastely or incestuously.

While these things were being done, as he afterwards said, he examined the beauty possessed by each woman—who surpassed the others in fairness or was considered more splendid in bodily radiance. Yet the entire action and inclination of the populace depended upon his command. Such an abundance of gold and silver would have flowed to him, had he wished, that he alone would seem to possess everyone’s wealth. Though he received much, he restrained his greed, lest he seem too ambitious. Nevertheless, keeping the greater part for himself, they contributed little toward replacing the garments that, as stated, had been burned.

[Col. 0096C] At his urging many young men took hired women as wives; he bought garments for them at the price of four solidi, only to cover their nakedness. But when the heretic’s wealth had been shattered, the true Judge made known to the rest what kind of tree he was: one that puts forth leaves without fruit, occupies the ground, and destroys whatever grows around it; unable to wait for winter, it withers and dies in summer.

For the young men who, on his wicked advice, had taken wives, after a short passage of time, driven either by hunger or by the women’s sexual immorality, fled elsewhere, leaving the women wholly destitute of support. Thus those men joined themselves to other women in adultery, while the women, although their husbands were still alive, unlawfully looked for marriages with other men.

[Col. 0096D] For not one of those who had entered marriage at his exhortation—though they were many—ever showed faithfulness or respect to his wife, or she to her husband. Nor could any other woman who had renounced fornication, the luxury of clothing, and oath-taking keep herself chaste; rather, increasing her crimes from day to day, she fell into worse things.

These and many similar acts that that exacter [extortioner] was continually carrying out, when he learned of the arrival of the bishop, who, as we have mentioned, had gone to Rome, withdrew to the castle of Saint-Calais, and remained there and in the surrounding places. He did not at all desist from what he had begun, but every day renewed himself for every kind of evil. [Col. 0097A] For on the most sacred day of Pentecost, when even little faithful children are customarily devoutly present at the divine offices, this most wretched of all men, having summoned to himself a certain young cleric—by whose testimony all his wanton conduct was afterwards exposed—secretly set out in the silence of night for the house of a certain knight; and there, in the bedchamber with the mistress of the house, he remained in luxury all day until noon. Thus he would restrain his lust neither from fear of God nor from shame before men, until the enormity of his crime became known to neighbouring and distant peoples.

When these things had thus been carried on, and the aforesaid bishop, attended by a great and numerous company of his clerics, entered the suburbs of the city and with fatherly affection traced upon the people, by mouth and hand, the sign of the living God, they were stirred by the gall of heart and speech to insult the Creator, rejecting his seal and episcopal blessing: “We do not desire knowledge of your ways,” they said; “we do not desire your blessing. Bless the dung; [Col. 0097B] sanctify the dung. We have a father, we have a bishop, we have an advocate, who surpasses you in integrity and surpasses you in learning. Against this man the clergy of iniquity—your clerics—set themselves; they oppose his teaching; they abhor and reject him as though sacrilegious, fearing that by a prophetic spirit he would expose their crimes and condemn, by the privilege of learning, both their heresy and their bodily incontinence.”

But all these things will without delay recoil upon the heads of those who, trusting in some audacity unknown to us, presumed to forbid a saint of God the voice of heavenly preaching. The bishop, however, pitying their error and ignorance, meekly endured the reproaches inflicted upon him by them, continually beseeching the God of majesty to restrain the people’s error mingled with pride, lest they should be able to bring schism upon his Church. But in accordance with the voice of the Psalmist praying for the salvation of transgressors: “Fill their faces with shame, and they shall seek thy name, O Lord” (Ps. 82:17), the same Lord God permitted a sudden fire to burn the greater part of the suburbs [Col. 0097C] of the city, so that at least through temporal loss they might abandon their evil purpose and invoke the hallowed name, the name of the living God.

The bishop, reciting that saying of the Prophet, “How great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord, which thou hast hidden for those who fear thee” (Ps. 30:20), after a few days had passed approached the deceiver and restrained his impiety by divine authority. When they entered into conversation together, the bishop asked him by what merit he had obtained his profession. But he, not knowing what a profession was, fell silent. When the bishop again asked what office of what order he performed, he said, “I am a deacon.” Then the bishop said: “Tell me, therefore, whether you were present at today’s mysteries.” He answered: “No.” “Let us therefore sing morning hymns to the Lord God.” When these were begun, Henry confessed that he did not know the *dietam* [the prescribed office; reading uncertain]. Yet the bishop, wishing altogether to lay bare his ignorance, began to sing the customary psalms to the Mother of God. Of these too he knew neither the verses [Col. 0097D] nor their sequence. And so, confused with shame, he admitted his manner of life, his method of teaching doctrine, and his presumption. He was in truth a camp-follower, having acquired no learning, wholly given over to wantonness; nevertheless he had pursued the knack of speaking to the people and of throwing dice. Hence it is written: “True glory puts down roots and spreads abroad; all false things quickly pass away and fall like the flower of hay, and nothing feigned can endure long.”

Nevertheless, when the bishop had recognized Henry’s frivolity and impiety, he forbade him by apostolic authority to remain any longer in his bishopric, but ordered him, sparing our people, to direct his steps elsewhere. Convicted by the bishop’s skill, he fled secretly; and he would have disturbed the remaining regions in a similar manner and infected them with his viperous jaws, had not report been swifter. I have recorded these matters concerning Henry and inserted them into the deeds of Hildebert for the benefit [Col. 0098A] and instruction of posterity, that they may beware lest the Church of Christ should ever be disturbed by errors of this kind. Finally, Hildebert employed every means to calm, by reason together with humility, the fury of the people which Henry had seditiously stirred up against the clergy. For Henry had so enticed them to himself that scarcely even now can the memory and affection for him be erased or expelled from their hearts.

Hildebert, however, pressing on in his own time to complete the work of the Church, which had been prolonged for a long period, and hastening the dedication beyond what circumstances required, left many necessary matters there unfinished. In the year of the Lord 1120, during the octave of Easter, namely on the day of the Major Litany, he consecrated it in the honour and name of holy and glorious Mary, ever Virgin, and of the blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, and of the most pious confessor Julian. He also decreed that the anniversary of this dedication should be solemnly celebrated every year during the octave of Easter. [Col. 0098B] Several archbishops and bishops, together with abbots and many venerable persons from neighbouring churches, were present at this consecration.

Guillebert, Archbishop of Tours—a man noble by birth, distinguished in person, young in age, surpassing others in strength of character and uprightness of conduct—consecrated the high altar in the honour and name of the Lord the Saviour, of blessed Mary his mother, and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. Geoffrey, Archbishop of Rouen, who had formerly been dean of our church, and in whom learning, maturity of character, discerning justice, and well-ordered generosity shone forth, joyfully consecrated the altar of the tomb of blessed Julian in the honour and name of that same confessor. Our Hildebert himself, whose praises are contained on the present page, consecrated the altar situated in the upper and more dignified crypt, in the honour and name of holy and glorious Mary, ever Virgin, and of all the saints. Marbod, [Col. 0098C] Bishop of Rennes, worn down by old age and deprived of the sight of his eyes, but supporting the weakness of his body by strength of mind, subtlety of intellect, sound counsel, and perfected wisdom, consecrated the altar in the right-hand part of the church, in the name and honour of Saints Peter and Paul and all the apostles. Renaud, Bishop of Angers, a resourceful man who afterwards through his own efforts attained such intimacy with Louis, king of the French, that he was appointed Archbishop of Rheims by him, consecrated the altar of the Crucified One in honour of the Saviour and in commemoration of the Holy Cross. This consecration was generally celebrated, as we have said, on the same day and at the same hour.

Present at this consecration were the Count of Anjou, namely Fulk, son of Fulk, and his venerable wife, Countess Eremburga, daughter of Count Elias, to whom the county of Maine belonged by paternal right. When this Fulk and the aforesaid Eremburga [Col. 0098D] were asked by the aforementioned bishops to make some provision from their revenues for the honour of God and the salvation of their souls, so that the consecrated church might be endowed as with a dowry, they promised that they would do so in accordance with the request.

Then, after a few days had passed, the same count and countess came to Le Mans; and, entering the mother church together with many barons, before the altar of most blessed Julian, in the presence of Bishop Hildebert and the canons of the same church, they gave to blessed Julian one fair [Note: [Col. 0097D] In French, *une foire*.] in the city of Le Mans, to be held on the anniversary day of the dedication of the mother church for three consecutive days—namely Saturday, Sunday, and Monday. They also granted all revenues whatsoever, and in whatever manner the count possessed them in the city or in the boroughs, during those three days, whether from customary dues [Col. 0099A] or from fines, retaining absolutely nothing for themselves except the shedding of blood in the case of those malefactors who are subject to the court’s jurisdiction. Whatever money is found upon robbers or offenders shall belong to the church in the particular composition for that offence; but the shedding of blood shall be assigned to the officers of the court. One half of this donation shall belong to the episcopal table, while the other shall go to the use of the canons.

The countess herself made this gift together with the count, as it is written, and their son Geoffrey assented to it. Moreover, when this gift had been read aloud to both the barons and the people, and approved by all, the count took his son Geoffrey, lifted him from the ground in his arms, and placed him upon the altar of blessed Julian, offering to him both the boy himself and, through him and in him, attaching the aforesaid benefaction, while the people heard these words: “To you, Saint Julian, I entrust my son and my land; be the protector and defender of both.” He therefore left the aforesaid [Col. 0099B] boy upon the altar and, bathed in the most abundant tears, departed, intending after a short interval to set out for Jerusalem, as he had planned.

At that time there was in Apulia a certain knight named Geoffrey, son of Geoffrey of Mayenne, one of the leading men of our region, rich in silver and gold and in the wealth of great estates which he had acquired in those regions. Because of his love and remembrance of his native land, he had vowed that he would give to God and to our most holy patron Julian his chapel-treasury—that is, certain precious ornaments which he possessed in his chapel. As he was about to depart for Jerusalem, he sent letters to our bishop, containing a request that he send him some of his clerics, trustworthy and capable men, to whom those ornaments might safely be entrusted without any suspicion of fraud.

Delighted and rejoicing at this news, the bishop sent there two canons of our church: Gervasius, archdeacon of Paganellus, and Hugh of [Col. 0099C] Lavarzin, who at that time held the office of archpriest. He supplied them abundantly with the funds that appeared necessary for so great a journey. Performing their assigned business vigorously and receiving everything, as that man had directed, without difficulty, they returned by a favourable journey to our church with those ornaments, accompanied by divine grace. When the bishop learned of their arrival, he joyfully went out beyond the city to meet them with ecclesiastical splendour and a festive procession of clergy and people. Receiving gifts so holy and precious with the veneration that befitted them, he placed them, amid the great rejoicing of clergy and people, in the sacristy of the mother church.

Foremost among them was a golden panel bearing an image of the martyr Saint Demetrius, wonderfully made with marvellous craftsmanship; although its material was gold, the excellence of its wondrous workmanship surpassed it yet more wonderfully. There too an incomparable and desirable treasure is recorded: namely, a portion [*uncia*, “ounce,” as printed] [Col. 0099D] of the same martyr, together with a tooth of Saint John the Baptist and a hair of the most glorious Mother of God; likewise, an altar panel to be carried on journeys, clad on both sides with malleable sheets of gold and silver. There, indeed, one of the ribs of Stephen, the first martyr, is enclosed. Then there were two books, one of the Gospels and the other a missal, most elegantly decorated with purest gold and silver. Moreover, two silver candlesticks very finely gilded, but more finely made; a silver censer; two staffs likewise gilded; a silver cross adorned with gold and gems; a silver chalice gilded within and without; two precious chasubles adorned with the finest gold embroidery; two golden episcopal rings; two silk copes; a little pallium and a mantle; an alb; a stole; and a maniple.

When this same Geoffrey returned from Jerusalem, he came to Le Mans on pilgrimage, to show how great was his devotion and affection towards blessed Julian. When his arrival became known beforehand, [Col. 0100A] Hildebert, with the dignitaries of his church and the leading men of the city, hastened to meet him, showing joyful welcome and generosity. Meanwhile the church was adorned within with every precious thing, all the lights were kindled, and the aforesaid treasure was placed upon the high altar. Declining the procession in humility, Geoffrey arrived at the threshold of the church beloved by him and long desired. Entering the church devoutly, he completed his prayer, as we believe, and offered his patron two banners, fittingly interwoven with gold on both sides. Hildebert and his canons received him with the highest reverence and honour in the episcopal residence, cheerfully supplying him and his companions with whatever they required according to their wishes.

Encouraged by such great benefits of divine grace, Hildebert also began, according to his means, to act as a fellow-worker with divine goodness. He commendably adorned the church with books, hangings, copes, priestly and Levitical vestments, and most precious hangings [*dorsaria*] [Col. 0100B] or bench-coverings, for furnishing the choir, together with the doors before the choir. He honourably restored, as the circumstances of the time allowed, the altar panel of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius and of most blessed Julian: partly from silver which Lord Hoel, his predecessor of blessed memory, had left for this work, and partly from silver which he himself had acquired elsewhere.

He also made at his own expense two reliquaries, most beautifully covered with gold and silver, in which he carefully deposited the relics of Saints Turibius and Victor, as well as of Saint Innocent and other bishops of our church, and of Saint Tenestina, Adam, and Saint Hilary the priest. Other bodies of saints, which he had found in the church sacristy in certain caskets already decayed from age, he placed with due reverence in a stone sarcophagus behind the altar of blessed Mary, in the upper portion of the crypt.

Indeed, by a sound disposition Hildebert, prudent and [Col. 0100C] diligent both for himself and for all his canons, ascending to heaven on the wing of contemplation, cast the seed of charity—a seed which shines above and among all his works with the splendour alike of worthiness, religious devotion, and generosity. This benefaction outweighs his other extraordinary deeds; and the more it is weighed with the eye of discernment, the more closely it is found to accord with reason. For, in the chapter of the mother church, with all the canons giving their consent, he decreed that for the soul of each canon, from the day of his death until the anniversary of the prebend which he had held in life, its income should be distributed in full, in portions of five and five shillings, to the priests of the church who were not canons. These priests, two by two, were to sing honourably and according to rule the Mass, the Hours, and the Office for the Dead each day during the whole course of the year, for thirty days, for the soul of that brother, to the Lord our God in our mother church. If the income of such a prebend exceeded the alms, that surplus [Col. 0100D] was to be given to the poor and to the building of the church of Le Mans.

He also surrendered to our chapter the provostships of the church which, by grant of the bishop, were conferred upon canons from the episcopal treasury, such as archdeaconries, so that they should be turned into obediences, and no one might hold them except with the assent of the entire chapter. Furthermore, he gave the wax which the bishop receives as rent from the castle of Lid, for making eighteen candles which stand above the door of the choir. Through his assistance and watchful zeal, very many churches which the violence of laymen had formerly withdrawn from the right of our church were restored to the authority of that same church, and, by his arrangement and grant, assigned to the maintenance of the canons: namely, the church of Doreta; the church of Jublent; the church of Saint Mary of Gurzenna; the church of Saint Mary of Neuville; the church of Ponciaco; the church of Ruilliaco; the church of Troo; the chapel of Saint Quentin; the church of Saint George of the Plain; half the church of Saint John of Arches; [Col. 0101A] the church of Cergiaco; half the church of Colans; half the church of Monholdol; half the church of Novigento; half the church of Tronchet; and, in the parish of Brens, as much land as two oxen can plough.

There were, however, certain other churches in that parish which he could not restore in their entirety to the authority of the mother church. He decreed that an annual rent should be paid from them to our canons: from the church of Audoenus, five shillings; from the church of Assioco, five shillings; and from the church of Saint Vulfacius, five shillings. For his own table he retained the church of Saint Simeon of Passeio and the church of Celsiaco, which belong to the bishopric. I have inserted the names of these churches in this little work so that whoever reads these things may strive more devoutly to celebrate Hildebert’s pious memory. He also newly founded an oratory together with a vestry, for the safeguarding and protection of the church’s ornaments, and covered it with vaulted work, lest the relics of the saints or the church treasury should at any time be endangered by [Col. 0101B] a public fire or by robbery.

If from us there flowed a torrent of Tullian eloquence, we could scarcely extol Hildebert with worthy praises, although he has no need of our commendation. For his fame, through the refinement of his poetry, is known to have grown so greatly far and wide that even in the remotest and unknown regions knowledge of the servant is more widespread and more esteemed than that of the queen, and of the bishop than of the Church. Thus through [Col. 0102A] him the title of the Church’s sanctity and antiquity became known to foreign peoples—the Church which had bestowed dignity on him and entrusted its prelacy to him. For he governed it for twenty-nine years and six months, and presided over it so honourably and wisely that, by divine appointment, he deservedly was called to the summit of a higher dignity.

At that time Guillebert, metropolitan of Tours, died. Hildebert obtained the high office of that see, with the consent of Louis, king of the French, while the clergy and people of Le Mans and Tours gave their devoted assent. Yet neither the elevation of the honour conferred upon him, nor abundance of wealth, nor the enticing provocation of bodily luxury cast him down. For he always preserved alike the dignity of his age and of his order. At last, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, in a good old age, joyful and vigorous in spirit, he gave his soul to the stars and his limbs to the tomb; and he was buried at Tours, to the honour of God’s name, in the right-hand part of the church of Saint Maurice. He also happily governed that same Church of Tours for six years and six months, and his life was about [Col. 0102B] eighty years. May the merciful and compassionate Lord grant his soul rest and light without end. Amen.

Moreover, in his time the abbey of Saint George of the Wood, which had formerly been destroyed, was restored. The following were newly founded: the monastery of Carnia; the monastery of the Fountain of Saint Martin; the church of the Fountain of Gihard; the church of Saint Martin of Luccelo; and the church of Saint Mary of Beau-Lieu.

[Col. 0101]

**NOTES OF THE MOST LEARNED D. LOYAUTÉ, ADVOCATE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF THE PARLIAMENT OF PARIS, ON THE PRECEDING DEEDS OF THE BISHOPS OF LE MANS**

**NOTICE.**—Although these notes contain certain matters that may seem to contribute little or nothing to the Life of the venerable Hildebert, we nevertheless judged that nothing should be omitted from them, since even their seemingly extraneous material presents many authentic monuments of antiquity. Just as these demonstrate the author’s most complete knowledge of ancient matters, so they may provide the diligent reader with no small measure of both illumination and pleasure.

[Col. 0101C] Col. 89, line 10.—Master of the schools of the Church of Le Mans. The masters of the schools, or chancellors—titles differing only in sound—performed a threefold office and function. They taught letters to clerics; moreover, the public proclamation concerning heretics and excommunicated persons was entrusted to them. Finally, they drew up written instruments concerning the affairs of the Church. That they had schools is commonly known; hence in some places they acquired the name of grammarians. The fact itself shows that, when they laid aside the burden of teaching, they did not put off their titles; indeed, they retained responsibility for the schools.

Concerning the chancellor of Paris, see the letter of Alexander III, number XVIII among those published in volume IV of the *History of France*. In it he commands Peter the cardinal, legate of the Apostolic See, to restore and reform the discipline of learning—now growing old and fading away—into its former splendor, while first taking account of the authority of Peter, chancellor of Paris: “With regard to the government of the Parisian schools,” says the pontiff, “carefully provide and arrange whatever seems proper to you, provided that what you do in this matter does not exceed the person of the aforesaid Peter.”

What the teaching duties of the masters of the schools of the Church of Le Mans were is most plainly and fully explained by the author of the *Life of Guy*, who, after Hildebert, was bishop of Le Mans and likewise master of the schools:

“Guy therefore did not wish to refrain from instructing clerics, desiring, while he could, to benefit his pupils and subjects, according to that saying of the Apostle: ‘While we have time, let us do good to all.’ He was so attentive to the divine office that, unless an unavoidable cause hindered him, he was devoutly present at the night offices and at the daytime ones. He also taught the boys and younger youths who serve in the choir, two by two each week, to chant the responsories both for the nocturnal office and for Mass; always to minister canonically to the priests in silence, with lowered gaze and orderly dress; and to stand at the canonical hours. Thus he carefully trained them in sacred chants and the other ecclesiastical offices. The rebellious and negligent he urged, now by the rod, now by kindness, to apply their minds to worthy disciplines. For this belonged to his office. Precentors and masters of the schools are appointed in the Church for this purpose: that through their direction the canonical office may suitably be celebrated there, and that they may restrain boys and adolescents by firm discipline, [Col. 0103A] lest through their negligence or insolence contempt should flourish there, or scandal arise.”

If a more severe correction had to be publicly announced to the ears and consciences of all, it was made known by the proclamation of the chancellor and masters of the schools. This is sufficiently indicated even by chapter 9 of the Constitutions of Galon, bishop of Paris, of the year 1105: “But if perchance they will not truly amend, then let them be declared excommunicated through the chancellor who shall be in office at the time.”

This discipline, transmitted by hand, seems to have endured from the earliest times of the Church down to that age. For what else is the *apokēryxis* (ἀποκήρυξις), of which Eusebius speaks in Book V, chapter 25 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, where Victor is said to have declared by public proclamation the bishops of the East cast off and excluded from his communion: “proclaiming all the brethren there without exception to be outside communion” (Ἀκοινωνήτους ἄρδην πάντας τοὺς ἐκεῖσε ἀνακηρύττων ἀδελφούς)? Likewise in Book VI, in the chapter on Novatus: “and that it was right to make a formal public exclusion from the Catholic Church of the leader of the heresy” (Καὶ τῷ χρῆναι εὐλόγως τῆς καθολικῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἐκκήρυττον ποιήσασθαι τὸν τῆς αἱρέσεως ἀρχηγόν). And deservedly was the author of that heresy excluded from the Catholic Church by the voice of the *curio* [public herald].

[Col. 0103B] Perhaps this concerns the words found in the encyclical letter of Pope Vigilius: “Those things which, concerning the aforementioned excommunication, we had declared in words to all the members of the Church of Constantinople by public proclamation.” This appears to have been carried out by the chancellor of the Roman Church.

That the same custom prevailed in the East I infer from Metaphrastes, in his account of Alexius: “He handed them a document which they gave to Aetius, chancellor of the most holy Church, to be read.” The Greek text is indeed lacking; but the translator, unless I am mistaken, retained the word *kankellarios* (καγκελλάριος), not unknown among the barbarian Greeks.

The suspicion is strengthened by the fact that in the Acts of the councils we repeatedly read that the *primicerius* of the patriarch’s notaries—in whose jurisdiction the sacred assembly was held, and who is none other than the chancellor—had with him all the documents and records of the council, and announced whatever needed to be brought to attention or read, as though with the single voice of all. For what occurs more frequently in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, over which Cyril, patriarch of Alexandria, presided, than these formulas: “Peter, presbyter of Alexandria [Col. 0103C] and *primicerius* of the notaries, said”; “We have the documents before us for whatever may please your reverence”; and, “If your holiness commands, I shall read.”

Moreover, the chancellor also discharged the office of notary. A notable testimony to this ancient practice occurs in a certain memorandum of Ulgerius, bishop of Angers, written in support of the abbot of La Roë against the abbot of Vendôme:

“What they say—that the bishop of Angers made the charter concerning this matter as testimony to the judgment and investiture—appears more harmful than helpful to them. For it was not drawn up by him who was then master of the schools. In the Church of Angers no charter concerning matters belonging to the Church of Angers is customarily accepted unless it has been dictated and approved by the master of the schools.”

But lest anyone suppose that this was a custom peculiar to the Church of Angers, I shall establish by various examples that the practice and custom were observed everywhere. A charter of Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, dated 1094 and preserved in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, bears this clause: “I, Hugh, monk of the Church of Dijon, wrote and subscribed in the capacity of chancellor.” Likewise certain instruments of Manasses and Renaud, archbishops of Reims, copied in the same library: “Fulchrad, chancellor, examined, wrote, and subscribed.”

The author of the History of Saint-Denis produced several instruments written by the chancellors of the Church of Sens: “Girard, chancellor and archdeacon, wrote”; “Hato, chancellor, wrote.” There also one finds a charter of Gilbert, bishop of Paris, from the year 1119, with this subscription: “Theobald, chancellor, wrote.” The same author published many charters of the bishop of Laon, similarly ending: “Robert, chancellor, reread”; “I, Anselm, chancellor of St. Mary’s, reread [it]”; “I, Radulf, chancellor of St. Mary’s, reread [it] and subscribed.”

The master of the schools of the Church of Poitiers in the same fashion wrote and confirmed ecclesiastical instruments. [Col. 0104A] I saw an example in the cartulary of Preuilly, bearing the formula: “Given through the hand of Raymond, master of the schools of Poitiers.” A not dissimilar subscription is found in the same cartulary: “Through the hand of Hervé, chancellor of the Church of Tours.”

Hugh, chancellor of the Church of Tournai, also wrote a deed of donation published in Book I, chapter 45, of Aubertus Miraeus’s *Pious Donations*. One Gislebert subscribed, in place of Lord Theteridus, chancellor of the Church of Metz, to charter 54 of the same book; and similarly Raymond, in place of Aso, chancellor of that same Church, to chapter 55. The chancellor, therefore, or master of the schools, was the Church’s keeper of records or notary. Almost countless examples will present themselves to diligent students once I have made this point more certain for them.

That this was the office of the *primicerii* of notaries in the Roman Church is taught by Anastasius Bibliothecarius in his account of Julius: “He decreed that no cleric should conduct any case publicly [Col. 0104B] except in church; and that the record, which concerns all in the interest of ecclesiastical faith, should be collected through notaries, and that all documents brought into the Church through the *primicerius* of notaries should be formally promulgated.” The most ancient decrees of the pontiffs, each countersigned by the hand of the *primicerius* of notaries, confirm this.

In the East, too, there was an ecclesiastical office of notaries, and they attended bishops in all more serious business. The Acts of the Council of Ephesus testify to this, mentioning Epaphroditus, reader and notary of the most reverend Helenicus, bishop of the Rhodians, who shortly afterward is called reader and notary of the city of Rhodes; likewise Anysius, reader and notary of Bishop Firmus. Bishop Venantius of Hierapolis also subscribed to the council through his notary Therdoton. The same Acts make more than sufficiently clear the service and office which they performed in councils.

Moreover, chancellors were called into consultation if any matter came into dispute; and when documents suspected of forgery rendered litigation uncertain, they supplied authority as men learned in letters and skilled in ancient records and writings.

Here is an old judgment from the archive of St. Aubin of Angers which makes the whole matter clear. I append it in full because it marks traces of venerable antiquity that are not to be despised:

“Since our actions are quickly consigned to oblivion unless recalled to memory by some written record, it has pleased us to commit to writing a certain case between the monks of St. Aubin and the monks of St. Sergius, so that by this means it may come to the knowledge of posterity.

“Accordingly, the abbot of St. Sergius, named Delbert, and his monks laid claim against the monks of St. Aubin to the estate and church of Campiniac, and to certain other small properties. To settle this claim, Otbrannus, abbot of St. Aubin, and his entire congregation said that they were willing to go to judgment before the abbots of the provinces of Tours and Angers. Since these words greatly pleased the monks of St. Sergius, the aforesaid abbots and monks met, by equal will and consent, [Col. 0104D] at Saumur in the monastery of St. Florentius.

“The abbots who were to hear the case of their fellow abbots were five, whose names are these: Lord William, abbot of that monastery itself; Lord Bartholomew, abbot of Marmoutier; Lord Haimo, [abbot] of St. Nicholas; Lord Evanus, [abbot] of St. Melanius at Rennes; and Lord Gumbertus, [abbot] of the monastery of Milbec. All these were present, intending to hear attentively the case of their brethren and to decide it according to ecclesiastical censure. They brought with them suitable persons from their communities, whom they had found among themselves wiser and more useful for examining these matters.

“Therefore, when they had taken their seats together, they asked both abbots and their monks, whose case it was, whether each side would agree to submit to the judgment which that entire assembly should unanimously pronounce there. In answer to their question, having been asked in due order, they gave this response: ‘Know that we are prepared to follow and uphold the sentence of your judgment. This we promise you, for this is why we have come.’

“After this undertaking had been made by both parties, opportunity was given to the abbot of St. Sergius and his monks to state their case. They said: ‘We lay claim against the monks of St. Aubin to the church and estate called Campiniac, which ought to belong to the right of our monastery; and we demand of them certain other small properties, the loss of which is far less, but more recent and more evident.’

“When the monks of St. Sergius wished first to litigate the lesser matters and afterward Campiniac, the judges thought it unjust that the latter case should be examined later—the case for which the abbots had been summoned and assembled. Nevertheless, they allowed them to prosecute whichever one of the lesser claims they preferred; after its examination, they would proceed to Campiniac.

“Accordingly, when the case they had selected among the lesser matters had been concluded, the judges spoke to them thus: ‘On what ground do you assert that Campiniac belongs by right to your monastery? By witnesses, by investiture, [Col. 0105B] or by charter?’ ‘By charter,’ they replied. The judges then said: ‘Produce it for our inspection.’ And they produced two charters.

“When these had been produced, the judges withdrew from the general assembly to a private place, where they could examine more carefully the charters received from the hands of the monks. They took with them Reginald, grammarian of the city of Angers and archdeacon of St. Maurice, and Robert, dean of the same Church, men of great expertise in conducting cases. Bishop Eusebius of Angers had sent these men as his representatives to the monks’ hearing, so that, having understood what was just, they might bear witness to the truth, lest there should remain among the monks any seedbed of discord over this matter [supplied: remaining].

“The document which the monks had produced was an ordinance of King Robert, not of great antiquity. It stated that Reginald, bishop of Angers, had restored the abbey of St. Sergius—which was his own, namely by episcopal right—to the rule of the monastic order. At that time, however, the abbey had been so reduced by an ancient destruction that it was served by only a few and very poor clerics. Among the possessions said in that ordinance to have been assigned to that Church, Campiniac was mentioned in these terms: ‘The estate of Campiniac with its appurtenances.’

“After that ordinance had been read once and twice and carefully examined, the aforesaid judges returned to their former seat and spoke as follows: ‘You have shown us two charters, one recent and the other ancient. The ancient one is offered so that the recent one may be believed. But a serious ambiguity appears in them. In the earlier and more ancient charter occurs the name of one of your dependent houses, namely Campaniac, which you possess. But in the recent charter Campiniac is named, with one letter altered—*i* in place of *a*. Therefore, since we find Campaniac in the ancient charter and Campiniac in the recent one, we are compelled to believe that the recent charter contains an error, either intentional or due to the ignorance of the scribe.

[Col. 0105D] “‘There is also another point. Everything which your charter says was assigned to you comes either from the patrimony of Bishop Reginald or from the provisions of bishops and clerics. Bishop Reginald, who is said to have restored your house, could not give you what was not his. But the entire estate of Campiniac belongs by right to the counts of Anjou; and certain knights have always held, and still hold, from the counts the greater part of that estate and half the church. Among these was Alberic of Vihiers, who gave to St. Aubin and its monks, for the sake of his soul, all that he possessed in the aforesaid estate.

“‘Master Reginald bears witness to this, because Campiniac was never held by episcopal right, as he knows—he to whom nothing belonging to the bishopric of Angers is unknown. Nor does your charter name the church, which is the head of the whole estate; nor does it speak distinctly, clearly apportion, or divide. Your charter says merely: “The estate of Campaniac with its appurtenances.” If we understand these words to mean the whole estate, this will be false, because you have never laid claim, nor do you now lay claim, to those portions which knights and other persons possess. It is also plain that many persons possess extensive holdings from the properties of that estate, without claim by anyone, whether bishops, monks, or clerics.

[Col. 0106A] “‘Finally, to come briefly to an end, we judge this alone sufficient for the dismissal of the present complaint. But we see that the monks of St. Aubin offer to prove, according to the institutions of the canons, that they have held half of the church of Campiniac and some portion of the estate peaceably and without your claim for thirty years. For all these reasons now stated, most beloved brethren, we judge that you ought forever to desist from this claim and leave St. Aubin and its monks in possession without contradiction.’

“Then Lord Detbert, the abbot, and some of his monks yielded so as to acknowledge and follow the judgment. For they remembered the undertaking which they had made. Moses alone resisted, because on this account he wished to go to Rome, as he afterward did.

“Such was the hearing held at Saumur, in the monastery of St. Florentius, under the witness and judgment of men of the highest authority and holiness. None of the judges thought otherwise, whether from the order of abbots, monks, clerics, or laymen, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1074, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November [18 October].”

Ibid.—And made archdeacon. That he was archdeacon of the Church of Le Mans is established by a letter of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, which beyond doubt was written to him, whatever the very learned Juretus may think to the contrary. [Note: [Col. 0105D] See what we have said concerning this letter in the *Life of Hildebert*.] For the old manuscripts on whose authority he relies are faulty and corrupt. [Note: [Col. 0105D] This corruption of the manuscripts would have required proof.]

The inscription of a short poem by Baldric, abbot of Bourgueil, a fragment of which appears in volume IV of the *History of France*, is likewise erroneous in Hildebert’s name. [Col. 0106C] It should be written: “To Hildebert, archdeacon of Le Mans,” not “To Audebert.” Hildebert celebrated the praises of Berengar, as is clear from his elegy. Baldric therefore says of him: “Having spoken briefly about Berengar of Tours.”

Col. 89, line 12.—The merit of his moral integrity. Thus the accusation brought by his adversaries concerning a disgraceful life among women was manifest calumny. Ivo of Chartres, before whom they charged him concerning his former life, did not credit the slanders. Nor indeed does the oft-mentioned letter establish anything by assertion. He did not wish to be believed, since he openly professed that he had been influenced by empty and uncertain reports. For what else is meant by the phrases which he repeatedly presses: “For I have heard concerning you . . . if these things are true . . . for some say concerning the leading men of the Church of Le Mans . . . they add to this calumny”?

He who raised the controversy resolves it. Why say more? The most eminent author of the *Annals* dealt unjustly and unfairly with Hildebert when, with hostile and inimical spirit—such as he commonly bore toward all the great men of the Gallican Church—he misuses Ivo’s testimony under the year 1088 to depress and defile the reputation of that most holy man. No desire to reproach or malign moved me to write these things; the force of truth alone, of which I have always been a servant, compelled me. I reverence solemnly and devoutly the memory of that incomparable man, but without injury to truth.

The author of this life, who reports what occurred in his own age and could not have been ignorant of Hildebert’s character, bears witness to Hildebert’s integrity. His enemies bring fabricated accusations; it may easily be judged which testimony ought to be preferred. A judge not beholden to favor will undoubtedly approve a devout eyewitness. [Col. 0107A] Every suspicion of flattery is removed by the fact that Hildebert’s life was committed to writing only after he had departed from human affairs.

The fabricators of these slanders, which Ivo does not even report as suspicions, were certain leading men of the Church of Le Mans: namely, one of the archdeacons and a very few canons. Since they gained nothing by this course, they finally placed that excellent bishop in peril of his life. “Certain clerics,” says the author of this little book, “had envied the bishop from the beginning of his promotion; devising every kind of deceit throughout the whole day, they grievously accused him before the king and falsely said that he had been privy to treason.”

Col. 89, line 13.—With the common consent of clergy and people. Nevertheless, certain leading men of the Church of Le Mans charged his election as criminal, as Ivo testifies in the already mentioned letter of Ivo of Chartres, alleging that he had been elected neither by their counsel nor with their consent. But the rash opposition of a few was too slight a matter to endanger one elected in due form. That he was indeed attacked by false accusations may be inferred from the event:

[Note: [Col. 0107D] Other authors—and almost all of them—state that Hildebert was consecrated in 1097, on Christmas Day itself, that is, approximately six months after the death of his predecessor Hoel, whom the *Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans*, under Hoel, report to have died on the fourth day before the Kalends of August [29 July] of that same year, 1097. As to this donation to the Church of Preuilly, [Col. 0108D] made “on the day of the consecration of Lord Bishop Hildebert,” I should suspect that that day was not the very day of his consecration, but merely its anniversary, which bishops formerly used to celebrate more solemnly. It does not seem probable that Hildebert’s consecration was delayed at least eighteen months after his election.]

For Hildebert was consecrated in 1098, in the church of St. Julian at Tours, with the dean, precentor, and Geoffrey, archdeacon of the Church of Le Mans, present and favorable. The records of the cartulary of Preuilly, which I append, confirm this:

“Helias, count of Le Mans, for the remedy of the souls of my father and mother, grants, at the request of Lord Otto, abbot of the Church of Preuilly, the gift which my brother Gosbert had given to the Church of St. Peter of Preuilly from the church of Bociac and likewise from everything belonging to it. This grant I make on the day of the consecration of our lord Bishop Hildebert, in the chapter house of the church of St. Julian the martyr at Tours, to God and to St. Peter, prince of the apostles, and to Abbot Otto and the monks serving the Church. I made this grant before Lord Bishop Hildebert, Abbot Evrard of St. [Col. 0107C] Carilef, Geoffrey, dean of the Church of Le Mans, Fulchrad, precentor, Geoffrey, archdeacon, and before these my knights, William Tibulus and Richard Harengodus, and the whole assembly of St. Julian, clerics and laymen alike.

“I, Geoffrey, count of Vendôme, surnamed Jordan, wish to make known to all my present and future descendants that, just as my kinsmen Gosbert and Helias, count of Le Mans, gave the gift of the church of Bociac, so I and my son Geoffrey, surnamed Grisagonella, give and grant it for the soul of my father Geoffrey, of my mother Almoda, of myself, and of Euphronia, countess and my wife. This donation was made in the year 1098.”

Col. 89, line 27.—From these, like a wise preparer of spiced drink, [he made] a draught. In ancient Latin-Greek glossaries, *pigmentarius* is called *myropōlēs* (μυροπώλης), *pharmakopōlēs* (φαρμακοπώλης), and *myrepsos* (μυρεψός); and in Greek-Latin glossaries *pyropōlēs* (πυροπώλης) is rendered *pigmentarius, unguentarius*, “dealer in spices, dealer in unguents.” [Col. 0107D] A *pigmentarius*, then, is a druggist who sells medicated wines, blended with perfumes, honey, manna, and sugar, or with other spices of that sort.

Isidore, in his glosses: “*Tuspollen*: manna, or a kind of spice.” Peter Damian, Book VI, letter 32: “Mulled wine with honey and various kinds of spices.” Suger, Constitution 3: “Let the brethren have spiced drink from the treasury and cellar.” Since such things were expensive, they were beverages of those living delicately and luxuriously.

The author of the *Life of Guy, Bishop of Le Mans*: “Food served in succession, as artfully prepared as it is costly, spices for the belly, and the lavish variety of drinks both rouse the guest to drink and sate him.” The term is also used of a mixture of perfumes alone. Christian Druthmar, on Matthew chapter 2: “When some noble or powerful dear person had died, the body was emptied of its entrails and preserved with myrrh and aloes, or with other spices.” And an ancient author on the Song of Songs: “He first becomes a disciple and enters the cell of discipline, in which his character is compounded by his master out of various virtues, like aromas by spice-dealers from diverse ingredients.” Nor is the statement of Ekkehard, chapter 30 of the *Life of Blessed Notker*, dissimilar: “His memorial was worthily made the work of a spice-dealer in the composition of the fragrance of holy Church.”

Col. 89, line 30.—Sending letters of exhortation. Hildebert’s age produced no man whose talent was more distinguished or whose speech more polished in winning fame. During his lifetime and under his own eyes, his letters were offered in schools to young men for imitation. Peter of Blois, letter 102: “It benefited me that, as a youth, I was obliged to memorize thoroughly and reproduce from the heart the letters of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, outstanding for elegance of style and gracious refinement.” He won such glory for elegance not only for himself but also for his country that the style of Le Mans was commonly regarded as polished and highly refined.

[Col. 0108B] William of Malmesbury, Book I of the *Deeds of the Bishops of England*, speaking of Ralph, bishop of Rochester: “If you examine his learning, he drained Athens dry; if you require eloquence, speech flows from his mouth in a certain honeyed stream. To this is added the refined and, as it were, carefully groomed speech of his native soil, that is, Le Mans.”

Col. 89, line 40.—Most widely circulated. The Chronicle of Tours, under the year 1127, calls him “renowned for skill in composing verse and prose.” The Chronicle of Auxerre, under the year 1107, says more fully:

“At this time flourished Hildebert, first bishop of Le Mans and then archbishop of Tours: a man eminent in learning, who attained a special grace both in verse-writing and in prose composition. His various short works, which he published in verse, and the letters which he sent to various persons, demonstrate this. All these are wonderfully commended by their elegance of thought and by the charm and brevity of their words. Hence someone said of him:

> Illustrious alike in prose and verse, first in all things,  
> Hildebert everywhere wholly breathes the rose.

Other Italian, German, and English chroniclers report this in nearly the same words.

Col. 89, line 44.—He had not yet passed forty years. If he reckons correctly at the end of this little work, he was forty-four years old. For he says that Hildebert departed to the Lord when he had completed his eightieth year; that he spent twenty-nine years in the bishopric and six and a half years in the archbishopric. From these one can scarcely gather thirty-six years; if these are subtracted, there remain forty-four years and what is over, which he spent as canon, master of the schools, and archdeacon.

[Col. 0108D] Col. 90, line 33.—Between the king of the English. William II.
