Col. 90, line 34.—And Count Helias. He was the son of John of La Flèche. I shall revive his almost extinct memory by producing documents from the cartulary of St. Aubin of Angers, which read as follows:

“A noble man and distinguished knight, named John of La Flèche, granted something from his fief to God, St. Aubin, and his monks. Thus he gave the church of St. Ouen and his chapel, situated within his castle. His son Helias was present. Done at La Flèche, [Col. 0109A] in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1087, in the first indiction, on the second day before the Ides of February [12 February].

“Not long afterward, the aforesaid John of La Flèche, detained by the pain of illness at the castle of Gontier, tearfully seeking the monastic habit and blessing, deserved, by the grace of God, to receive them from the monks of St. Aubin. There he gave, etc. He died of his illness that same day. The monks carefully prepared his body, brought it to St. Aubin, and buried it with due care.

“His son Helias, who was present at the burial, on that same day in the chapter house willingly gave and granted, by placing a staff in the hand of Lord Girard the abbot, what his father had earlier given, and what he himself had later given, to St. Aubin. He and his brother Geoffrey received the benefice of St. Aubin.

“At the time when these things took place, Gauzbert, eldest son of John of La Flèche, was staying at Le Mans. Greatly angered against the monks, he laid claim to everything that his father had given and his brother had granted to the monks. Then, after Abbot Girard sent three monks to Le Mans, he ceased his claim, receiving from them ten pounds of Angevin denarii; he confirmed everything aforesaid and received the benefice and confraternity of the monastery of St. Aubin from the hand of Bishop Hoel, by order of the abbot.”

This is confirmed by the brief Chronicle of the Counts of Anjou in these words: “Helias, son of John of La Flèche, took as wife Sibylla, daughter of a certain count of Lombardy and niece of Herbert, formerly count of Le Mans, and received with her the county of Le Mans.”

This refutes the error of the author of the *Life of Hoel*, who writes that Helias was descended in the paternal line from the counts of Le Mans. He was bound to them only through a family connection by marriage, as is clear from this passage. These are that author’s words: “There arose a certain noble young man, named Helias, who was of the stock of the counts of Le Mans, and he began to lay claim to the county itself.”

Not long after the death of his father John, Helias undertook the war for his wife’s dowry. [Col. 0109C] After many fortunes of war, related here, he attained his desire and conferred many benefactions upon the Church of Le Mans.

Martyrology of the Church of Le Mans: “On the fifth day before the Ides of July [11 July] died the venerable Helias, count of Le Mans. At the beginning of his rule he granted to this holy mother Church everything which Count Hugh, his predecessor and son of Marchisus, had given to Bishop Hoel for damages and injuries inflicted there, and everything which Gervasius, his father-in-law, of the castle of Lit[?], [had given]. At the request also of Bishop Hildebert, he made the bed of Blessed Julian out of silver and gold.”

After becoming count, he also gave much to the monks of St. Aubin, as appears from the archive: “Count Helias of Le Mans, coming to La Flèche, increased with another portion of his land—which lies from the land of the monks to the leper-house—the gift which his father had given to the monks of St. Aubin and which he himself had granted.”

And in the same source: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1110, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November [21 October], Count Helias of Le Mans, for the remedy of his soul and those of his parents, gave half of the land of the blessed apostle Thomas, which he had established to be observed annually at the castle of La Flèche on the feast of that apostle, for whom he had built a new church there. Concerning this matter he invested Abbot Archembald on the aforesaid feast at that castle, in the monks’ house.”

Helias died in the same year. The Chronicle of St. Florentius: “1110: Count Helias died.” And the brief Chronicle of St. Aubin under 1110: “At that time, on the fifth day before the Kalends of July [27 June], Helias, count of the men of Le Mans, died, leaving his fief to his son-in-law, the younger Fulk—a man great in ability and boldness.”

All agree on this one point: Helias died in the year 1110. The month and day are disputed, for the Martyrology gives the fifth day before the Ides [11 July], while the Chronicle of St. Aubin gives the fifth day before the Kalends of July [27 June]. But the error in the charter copied above lies in the carelessness of the copyist. [Col. 0110A] For how could a man have acted and entered into such a transaction in November when he had met his last day in death in the preceding June or July?

Col. 90, lin. 34.—War between the King of the English and Count Elias. In order to make known the cause and origin of the war, and the claim which William II put forward, we must begin far back, at the source. William I had tried wrongfully and unsuccessfully to claim Maine by arms as though it were an appendage of Normandy, on the ground of proximity; but Count Herbert of Maine resisted him, with the aid and support of Geoffrey Martel, Count of Anjou, who had restored the county after it had been taken away. His military force having been broken and weakened, William turned to stratagems, very familiar to his people. He courted the count, and attained by deceit what he had been unable to gain by force: the rightful heirs were disinherited, he was named heir to the whole estate, and entered upon the inheritance while Herbert was still living and breathing.

The *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou*: [Col. 0110B]

> “In those days William, Duke of the Normans, fiercely attacked Herbert, Count of Maine; Martel was his helper and protector, and for that reason Duke William—who afterwards, having acquired England, became King of the English—suffered many evils from Martel.
>
> “In the same place: William had received Le Mans by Herbert’s consent, and was violently taking it from Elias, to whom it belonged by hereditary right.”

William of Malmesbury, Book III, echoes this:

> “He intended to restore lands formerly regarded by long custom as appendages of Normandy—I mean the county of Maine and Brittany. Maine, long before, had been burned by Martel and deprived of its lord Hugh; it had only recently recovered a little under Herbert, Hugh’s son. To be safer against the Count of Anjou, Herbert had put himself into William’s hands and sworn an oath of fealty to him. William had sought and betrothed Herbert’s daughter; but before she reached marriageable age and could be given in marriage, Herbert died of illness, declaring William his heir. He made the citizens swear [Col. 0110C] not to receive another, saying that, if they wished, they would have a gentle and upright lord; but, if they did not, they would have an excessive enforcer of his right. After Herbert’s death the people of Maine, inclining rather to Walter of Mayenne [Note: [Col. 0109] Or rather Geoffrey of Mayenne, as is clear from what follows.], whose wife was Hugh’s sister, eventually—though late—came to their senses and received William, often taught by grievous losses.”

I cannot refrain from observing in passing that Malmesbury is mistaken in making Maine an appendage of Normandy. It was always governed separately by its own counts, and only later brought under outside domination, as is clear from the Pontifical of Le Mans and the *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou*, where the following continuous succession of counts is given:

Hugh, who waged war against Bishop Segenfrid. Herbert Evigilacan, who harassed Bishop Avesgaud. Herbert Bacco, uncle of the preceding Herbert. Hugh, who, after expelling Herbert Bacco, recovered the county and, by Bertha, widow of Alan, Count of the Bretons, fathered Herbert, of whom Malmesbury speaks.

The Pontifical, in Gervase, states:

> “When Hugh had attained the height of the countship, Herbert Bacco became a monk. Bishop Gervase loved Hugh, whom he had received from the sacred font, so greatly that he sought him a wife: Bertha, namely, a most noble woman, formerly wife of Alan, Count of the Bretons. This greatly displeased Geoffrey, as the event proved. Hugh departed with his knights on account of his wife. Geoffrey burned the castle of Lît with fire. From that time, because of these actions, each bitterly hated the other: the count hated the bishop, and the bishop the count.
>
> “Seeing, therefore, that by the counsel of Lord Bishop Gervase Count Hugh had taken a very powerful wife, to Geoffrey’s ruin and detriment, Geoffrey bore Judas in his breast. By deceit he ordered Bishop Gervase to deliver Hugh to him; when Hugh had been delivered up, Geoffrey sent him to prison and held him in chains [Col. 0111A] for seven years, hoping thereby to obtain the castle of Lît. But this did him no good, because the castle-knights guarded it well.
>
> “While these things were happening, Hugh, Count of Maine, died, while Bishop Gervase was still in chains. Lord Gervase was deeply grieved by the count’s death, whereas Geoffrey, Count of Anjou, rejoiced. After Count Hugh had been buried according to Christian law, Count Geoffrey held the honour for ten years. The citizens of Le Mans threw Hugh’s wife, weeping with her children, out through one gate, and allowed the rejoicing Count Geoffrey to enter.”

The names of the children expelled with their mother, stripped of all their fortunes, are not given. From the following words of the Chronicle of Quimperlé under the year 1062, one may readily infer that Herbert III, the last of the Counts of Maine, was among them and was restored in full:

> “Herbert, Count of Maine, dies, uterine brother of Duke Conan.”

This Conan was the son of Alan and Bertha, as the same Chronicle relates [Col. 0111B] under 1066.

After Herbert III’s death William possessed the county peacefully for four years; for four years are counted from Herbert’s death to the English expedition. He crossed the sea in 1066, as the same Chronicle indicates:

> “William, Duke of the Normans, invaded the island of Britain with a great fleet.”

What happened while William was away is told by the author of the *Life of Arnald, Bishop of Le Mans*:

> “In his time William, Prince of the Normans, who had then acquired the county of Maine after its heirs had been extinguished and wholly destroyed, crossed into England with a very great army of French, Normans, and Bretons. He defeated the English in battle and, after killing their king Harold, obtained the kingdom of all England. While he was occupied for some time with the business of war, the leading men of Maine, together with the people, unanimously withdrew from the fidelity of that king. They sent to Italy for a certain marquis, Azo, with his wife and [Col. 0111C] son, who was called Hugh; these began to come thence, entirely expelling from themselves, the city, and the whole region a certain royal steward named Winfrid, whom they killed in the fortifications.”

The author further relates that the marquis, recognizing the fickleness of the people of Maine, entrusted his wife and son to the protection of Geoffrey of Mayenne—a nobleman of exceptionally shrewd intelligence, whom Malmesbury incorrectly calls Walter of Mayenne—and returned to Italy. Then, to omit much, when the common people had been stirred up against the magnates and had formed the conspiracy which they called the *communitio*, Hugh was sent away to his father. His mother Gersendis, daughter of Herbert, formerly the most illustrious Count of Maine, remained in the city; she brought into the strongest citadel of the whole city Geoffrey of Mayenne, hated by the people. He was expelled from it by Duke Fulk, Count of Anjou.

But at length, England having been pacified:

> “King William of the English”—I use the author’s words—“having assembled an innumerable army, [Col. 0111D] came into the district of Maine, besieged the castle of Fruiac, and devastated with fire and sword the fields, vineyards, and everything around it. Since the defenders could not withstand his attack, they made peace with him on the best terms they could. Having immediately received the castle and posted guards in its fortifications, he proceeded to the city and established camp by the river Sarthe, at a place called Mantula. The leading men of the city came out to that place and conferred with the king concerning peace; having received his oaths, both for immunity from their treachery and for preservation of the ancient customs and institutions of the city, they surrendered themselves and all that they possessed to his lordship and power.”

That Fulk, Count of Anjou, bore William’s victory with resentment is sufficiently shown by his refusal to allow Hoel, Arnald’s successor in the see of Tours—the city of his dominion—to be consecrated in the metropolitan church there. The same author says of Hoel:

> “Because of the dispute which had arisen between [Col. 0112A] William, King of the English, and Fulk, Count of Anjou, concerning that bishopric, Ralph, Archbishop of Tours, could not ordain him at Tours. With the assent and command of Ralph himself and of all his suffragans, he was therefore ordained with great honour at Rouen by Lord William, Archbishop of that city, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1080.”

Thus far concerning William I. What follows applies to our William II. After a few intervening matters, the author continues:

> “In those days William, the valiant King of the English, died; and his death disturbed the whole region of Maine. Among the other evils which befell at that time, a certain noble young man arose, of the lineage of the Counts of Maine, named Elias. He began to lay claim to the county; entering the castle called Ballon, he ravaged the region on every side, and especially harassed the inhabitants of the city, who resisted him courageously, by many ambushes and continual plunderings.
>
> “But since matters made little progress, and he believed that his efforts were being opposed by the counsel of the bishop, who remained inviolably faithful to Count Robert, he burst forth, by the advice of certain perverse men, into such audacity that he laid hands upon the Lord’s Christ and did not fear to confine him under guard in a castle of his patrimony called La Flèche. He removed the bishop’s clergy from his presence in such a manner that the bishop could hold neither private nor public conversation with any of them; and he assigned a rustic priest to attend him, lest the cleverness of the guards should be deceived by Latin conversation, etc.
>
> “Meanwhile Geoffrey [of Mayenne], of whom we have spoken above, judging that he had found a favourable opportunity to disturb the region anew, repeatedly sent envoys to persuade Hugh, son of Azo and now grown up, to come into the country; he obtained his consent. When Hugh was at the castle called Carcer, the leading men of the city came out to meet him, treating as nothing the oaths of fealty [Col. 0112C] which they had sworn to Count Robert.
>
> “Seeing the danger that threatened if he gave any assent to their fickleness, the bishop left the city in haste with a few companions and went to the prince, to whom he related all that had occurred. But Robert, excessively devoted to idleness and pleasure, made no rational response. Since the acts of the people of Maine seemed to him merely too burdensome for an incapable man, he showed that they displeased him little. He seemed concerned only that the bishopric should remain under his dominion. He therefore ordered the bishop to return to his church, but under no circumstances to yield the bishopric to Marquis Hugh. Meanwhile Hugh was received into the city by the common assent of all and took up residence in the bishop’s houses.”

He adds:

> “While the aforesaid count, because of his instability, was held hostile to all good men, he converted into money everything that he could possess and sold to his kinsman Elias, mentioned above, the city itself and the whole county, so far as it lay within his power. Laden with the price of this shameful bargain, he returned to his native land in great disgrace.”

I have never been able to persuade myself that Robert was so negligent and so careless of his own interests that, after losing the county of Maine, he regarded his diminished and almost ruined fortunes as utterly indifferent. It is more likely that, occupied with civil wars, he postponed vengeance to another time. Indeed, Malmesbury, in his account of William II, relates that William and Robert made peace on the condition that “the king should acquire Le Mans for the count.” He adds in the same place:

> “Both dukes were making great efforts to invade Le Mans. But the war already prepared was prevented by that which threatened from their brother Henry.”

The remaining course and development of the war is described here elegantly; therefore I add no word.

Col. 90, lin. 35.—He laid claim to the bishopric of Le Mans [Col. 0113A]. Under the pretext that he held Normandy in pledge from his brother Robert, and that Maine followed Normandy by right of accession. The Chronicle of Tours under 1098:

> “When Duke Robert of Normandy, having taken up the cross, had pledged his land to his brother William Rufus, King of England, for ten thousand marks of silver, and King William had thereby received Maine and had afterwards returned to England, word was brought to him that Le Mans was under siege. He immediately entered the stormy sea and said that he had never heard of a king perishing by shipwreck. And so, coming to Le Mans, he captured Count Elias there.”

Col. 90, lin. 35.—And therefore he contrived against the bishop’s ordination. Because it was not lawful to consecrate a bishop without consulting the count.

Col. 90, lin. 36.—But when he heard that he had been ordained. This was done with the consent of Elias’s enemies, by their authority; it could have seemed particularly grievous to him. Yet it has been observed above, from the cartulary of Prully, that Count Elias was present at the consecration of our Hildebert.

[Col. 0113B] Col. 90, lin. 43.—Captured. Elias, while fiercely pursuing his enemies, was taken in an ambush on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in 1098, by Robert of Bellême, who supported William II’s party, according to the short Chronicle of Saint-Albin of Anjou, whose words I shall presently transcribe.

Col. 90, lin. 44.—In the fortress of that city. English writers, to whom it is customary, in contempt of the majesty of history, to lapse into flattery, say that Elias was so despised and indeed scorned that they deny he was committed to custody. Malmesbury, in his account of William II:

> “A messenger from beyond the sea interrupted him while he was occupied with hunting in a certain forest, reporting that the city of Le Mans, which his brother had recently added to his power before departing, was under siege, etc. After he crossed the sea, the besiegers, hearing of his fame, scattered. A certain Elias, author of the disturbances, was captured. When he was brought before the king, the king said mockingly: ‘I have you, master.’ But Elias, whose lofty nobility did not know, even in so great a danger, how to speak humble words, replied: ‘You have caught me by chance; if I could escape, I know [Col. 0113C] what I would do.’
>
> “Then William, almost beside himself with rage and barking at Elias, said: ‘What would you do, you scoundrel? Go away—depart—flee! I grant you leave to do whatever you can; and by the face of Saint Luke, if you defeat me, I shall demand no recompense from you for this favour.’ Nothing further was said; he immediately allowed him to escape, admiring rather than pursuing the fugitive.”

And John of Salisbury, from Malmesbury’s gaps, writes in *Policraticus*, Book VI, chapter 18:

> “The King of the English surnamed Rufus was indeed valiant in arms, but little religious; by persecuting the saints, especially Saint Anselm of Canterbury, he seemed to have drawn upon himself the dart of envy by which he was destroyed. This king, I say, subdued Maine and captured its count; nor did he deign to consign him to prison custody. Mount Barbatus will bear witness to the whole deed for ever; or, if you prefer to call it by another name, let it be called Mount Barbarus, or Mount of the Barbarians.”

[Col. 0113D] Col. 91, lin. 3.—Fulk, Count of Anjou. Surnamed Rechin. He was the nephew of Geoffrey Martel I, Count of Anjou, through Martel’s sister Adela. She was married to Frerol, Count of Gâtinais, and bore Geoffrey the Bearded and this Fulk. The *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou*:

> “Geoffrey Martel, son of Fulk, having no sons, left his county—namely Anjou and Tours, which he had conquered—to his nephews Geoffrey the Bearded and Fulk Rechin. He gave Anjou and Saintonge to Fulk, and Tours with the castle of Loudun to the Bearded. These two, the Bearded and Rechin, were sons of Geoffrey Frerol, an illustrious man of Gâtinais and Loudunois, born of the sister of the aforesaid Martel.”

The author of the Chronicle of the Counts of Anjou calls their father Alberic and reveals the mother’s name in these words:

> “Geoffrey Martel, having no sons, left his property to his nephews Geoffrey the Bearded and Fulk Rechin, namely the sons of his sister Adela and Alberic, Count of Gâtinais.”

[Col. 0114A] Perhaps for this reason Fulk repeatedly declares that he held the county of Anjou by hereditary right; or perhaps he did so in order to erase the stigma of usurpation. An example is ready at hand from the cartulary of Saint-Serge:

> “I, Fulk, Count of Anjou by hereditary right, make remembrance of Geoffrey, my distinguished count and maternal uncle, and of his and my predecessors, some of whom lie buried in the cemetery of the blessed martyrs Sergius and Bacchus, awaiting the resurrection, by the counsel of my son Geoffrey and my magnates.”

In 1095 Fulk captured his elder brother Geoffrey in war, committed him to custody, and claimed for himself the counties of Anjou and Tours. For this reason, being subjected to an anathema, he paid penalties unequal to his crime. For in 1094, by the judgment of Hugh, Archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, although his brother had not been released from custody nor freed from chains, Fulk himself was absolved from the bond of anathema. The acts testify as follows:

> “Hugh, Archbishop of Lyons, legate of the Apostolic See, to his most beloved brethren in Christ—the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and all faithful members of the holy Church of God—greeting. We have judged it worthy to make known to all the orthodox how, by the command of our lord Pope Urban, we undertook the duty of coming to the borders of Anjou in the case of Fulk, Count of Anjou, in order to absolve him from the bond of anathema by which he had long been bound for the capture of his brother Geoffrey, whom he had taken in open war.
>
> “Yet the count did not evade giving an account, making satisfaction, or undergoing judgment; indeed, he was always prepared to do so. We learned also from the truthful report of reputable clerics and laymen that his aforesaid brother, when he was captured, had been excommunicated by Stephen, Roman cardinal and legate of the See, for the many injuries which he inflicted on the Church of Tours and the abbey of Saint Martin of Marmoutier. Moreover, the principality of the county of Anjou had been granted to this Fulk by that legate [Col. 0114C] on behalf of Saint Peter. We learned, moreover, by the truthful report of reputable men among his nobles, that it had been granted him by his uncle Geoffrey.
>
> “Therefore, having accepted this legation, and wishing the force of apostolic obedience to be exercised by us with greater authority, we associated with ourselves our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Bourges, in carrying out this matter. Together we approached, after consultation, the count’s brother, whom we had heard was captive. We found him so foolish—as all reported—that it seemed wholly useless and vain to entrust the rule of a country to one who had rendered himself useless to himself and to everyone by folly, so much so that he did not even wish to be freed from captivity by our hands.
>
> “We accordingly came to the monastery of Saint-Florent. On the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, in the presence of religious men, bishops, and abbots who had come at our invitation, we unanimously absolved Count Fulk, who was prepared to make satisfaction or give an account, with the approval and praise of all. We received from him assurances that, if his brother recovered soundness of mind, he would, at the command of our lord the pope or of ourselves, either make peace with him or stand ready to undergo judgment; and that he would not marry wives—the multiplicity of whom was charged against him—without our counsel.
>
> “We have judged it right to set forth for you the sequence of this transaction. The names of the religious persons present are these: Aldebert, venerable Archbishop of Bourges; Hoel, Bishop of Le Mans; William, Abbot of Saint-Florent; Bernard, Abbot of Marmoutier; Bernard, Abbot of Saints Sergius and Bacchus; Gerard, Abbot of Saint-Albin; Huald, Abbot of Saint-Nicholas; Baldric, Abbot of Bourgueil; Geoffrey, Abbot of Vendôme. Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1094, at the abbey of Saint-Florent, on the feast of Saint John the Baptist.”

I do not know whether that ambitious decree was procured by the same arts through which he broke the penalties due for his crime. The Chronicle of Tours:

> “In the eleventh year of Emperor Henry and the seventh of King Philip, Fulk Rechin, Count of Anjou, gave King Philip of France the castle of Loudun, while his brother was still alive and held in prison, on condition that the king should not compel him to release his brother from prison.”

He had many wives and children by them. The *Deeds of the Counts*:

> “Fulk took several wives: the daughter of Lancelin of Beaugency, by whom was born the Countess of Brittany, she who after her husband’s death practiced the life of a nun at Jerusalem in the church of Saint Anne. After her death he married Ermengarde, daughter of Archambald of Bourbon, by whom he begot Geoffrey Martel, an admirable man, distinguished for justice, a cultivator of every good, who was a terror to all his enemies. Lustful Fulk fell in love with the sister of Amaury of Montfort; no good man ever praised anything in her except her appearance. For her he left Martel’s mother, asserting that she was of his own kin. William of Jaligny, one of the nobler men of Auvergne, married her after she had been repudiated.”

The short Chronicle of the Counts explains this a little further:

> “Fulk took several wives: the daughter of Lancelin of Beaugency, by whom the Countess of Brittany was born. After the death of Lancelin’s daughter, he married Ermengarde, daughter of Archambald the Strong of Bourbon, by whom he begot Geoffrey Martel. Having put her away, Fulk Rechin begot Fulk by the sister of Amaury of Montfort, Count of Évreux.”

As for what kind of man and how great Fulk Rechin was thereafter, the *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou*, which, I hope, will shortly be published under the auspices of … … … the most learned son of the most learned André Duchesne, will fully instruct you. I add only that he died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, in 1109. The Chronicle of Vendôme:

> “In this year, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, Fulk, Count of Anjou, died, a man full of the bowels of piety and mercy, brother of Count Geoffrey surnamed the Bearded. In our Angevin monastery of the Holy Trinity, as he commanded, he was honourably buried.”

The Calendar of the Church of Anjou says almost the same thing [Col. 0115C]:

> “Eighteenth day before the Kalends of May: Fulk, most gentle Count of Anjou, nephew of Geoffrey Martel the Elder, died in the year of the Lord 1109.”

Col. 91, lin. 4.—With his son Geoffrey. His military achievements earned him the surname Martel II. I shall extract here a few of the many matters recounted in the *Deeds of the Counts*, because they are found in no printed manuscript, and because they cast light upon these events:

> “Geoffrey Martel II, now grown to manhood, a prudent and spirited young man, saw that the land was troubled and that the magnates of the whole county were raising their horns against his father. He resisted them bravely and restlessly considered how he might avenge his father upon his enemies. He prevailed over them all and turned them from their purpose. Eminent for justice, he was feared by all; all the men and nobles of the county obeyed him more than his father, whom they hated because of his vices.
>
> “This Fulk, having discovered a relationship, repudiated Ermengarde, Martel’s mother, while Martel was still a boy … The woman, fearing her grown stepson [Col. 0115D], whose spirit was hostile to all, could be calmed neither by rest nor waking; she sought how she might harm Martel. Often her colour was bloodless, her gait now swift, now slow; madness was plainly present in her face and expression, and she taught wicked deeds to those whom she had enticed to herself in many ways.
>
> “Geoffrey Martel, considering how to resist these things and knowing that no one attempts such a deed without allies, thought how to gain and unite to himself Hugh’s friendship, for Hugh possessed a spirit like his own; when this happens, love must arise. He joined in marriage to Hugh his sister Elizabeth, born of his mother Ermengarde and William of Jaligny. Martel granted Hugh and his wife a residence, together with whatever he possessed at Amboise, after his father’s death. Hugh, for his part, conducted his affairs prudently and pursued warfare neither too slackly nor foolishly …
>
> “Martel was killed at the castle of Candé by the plots of his own men and of his stepmother, with his father’s consent, it is said, [Col. 0116A] and was buried in the church of Saint Nicholas at Angers.”

It seems incredible to me that the father consented to the death of so great a son, since he was already old and the son, if a longer life had been granted him, would have recovered whatever his father had lost. For he was asserting a claim to the castle of Loudun against King Philip and to the county of Saintonge against William of Poitou; William, out of fear of him, built two new towers at Poitiers, one at the entrance to the city and another near the palace.

The Chronicle of Tours concerning Martel’s death:

> “1107. In the first year of Henry and the forty-seventh of King Philip, Geoffrey Martel was killed at the castle of Candé because he was a worthy man, by his stepmother, with the consent of his father Fulk, Count of Anjou; and he was buried in the church of Saint Nicholas at Angers.”

The shorter Chronicle of Saint-Albin, though mutilated at this point, narrates the whole matter more clearly:

> “At that time Geoffrey Martel the younger, Count, was preparing an army, wishing to besiege the castle called Condat. Having besieged it and already forced the enemy to surrender, the same count was summoned to a conference by those same men, as though they wished to swear fealty to him. He was killed by an arrow on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, and all his army was torn apart and scattered by slaughter and enemy ambushes. Amid the immense mourning of all the people, he was buried beside his father’s uncle in the church of Saint Nicholas at Angers.”

The Chronicle of Vendôme assigns Martel’s death to 1106:

> “In this year a star appeared, small in appearance indeed, but all marvelled that it drew behind it a great and long trail of brightness. It was seen for many days and nights to extend its course westward, foretelling great desolation. For in that very year Geoffrey Martel, the young Count of Anjou, conqueror and subduer of tyrants, protector and defender of churches, was killed in a certain siege.”

This is very good. But the Chronicle of Tours appears corrupt in postponing the event to the following year, 1107. This is likewise refuted by the authority [Col. 0116C] of the Chronicle of Saint-Florent and another Saint-Albin chronicle. Yet a scruple is raised by what is read in the subscriptions of an old charter surviving in the cartulary of Vendôme:

> “This was done in the lower chamber of the Bishop of Angers, in the year of the Incarnation 1105. A settlement was made between Lord Geoffrey, abbot, and Jeremiah, son of Fulk of La Tour, etc. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1105, in which year Geoffrey Martel, Count of Anjou, was also betrayed and killed.”

But it will be safer to agree with the concordant and unanimous authority of the chronologists than to follow the doubtful testimony of an ignorant copyist. His ignorance appears all the more clearly because the Calendar of the Church of Anjou supports the chronologists:

> “Fourteenth day before the Kalends of June: Geoffrey Martel, younger son of Fulk, killed by an arrow at the siege of Candé, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1106.”

Col. 91, lin. 4.—To whom Count Elias gave his daughter. The *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou*, under Geoffrey Martel II:

> “Count Elias betrothed to this Martel his only daughter, not yet fit for marriage, and granted him Le Mans with its dependencies. Martel often fought King Rufus and ravaged and burned many strongholds in Normandy while the king stayed in England and Count Robert, the king’s brother, remained at Jerusalem with many pilgrims. For King Rufus held Normandy in pledge.”

The shorter Chronicle of Saint-Albin also indicates this, though obscurely:

> “In 1103, when Fulk Rechin, Count of Anjou, wished, through affection for his younger son, by many great counsels and schemes to disinherit his elder son Geoffrey, the aforesaid Geoffrey surnamed Martel, perceiving his father’s intention, formed an alliance with Count Elias of Maine and took up arms against him. He immediately besieged the castle of Mazé against his father, took it at the first assault, and burned it. Then he came forth boldly to fight William, Count of Poitou, whom the aforesaid [Col. 0117A] Fulk was leading against Angers with a great army. But the Poitevins fled before battle was joined. Geoffrey then returned to Angers and, after a few days, besieged and captured the castle of Briollay.”

Col. 91, lin. 5.—He came with the consent of the citizens. This happened in 1098, the very year in which Hildebert was consecrated. The same Chronicle, under 1097:

> “In the following year Count Elias of Maine was captured by Robert of Bellême, through the defection of his own men, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, a Wednesday, and was delivered to William II, King of the English. Fulk, Count of Anjou, surnamed Rechin, received the city of Le Mans as his own on the following Saturday. Having held it for three months, and the people of Maine, after their custom, having deceived him and withdrawn from him, he surrendered it in friendship to the aforesaid King of the English, who assailed that city more by money than by military force.”

Florence of Worcester indicates that this was done in summer:

> “In the year 1098, during the summer, William the Younger, King of the English, subdued by force to his rule the city called Le Mans and a great part of that province.”

Col. 91, lin. 8.—Deprived of the protection of its prince. “Fulk received it as his own,” says the shorter Chronicle; whether by right or wrong is uncertain. Situated on the border of Anjou and Maine, Le Mans was claimed, according to opportunity, now by the Counts of Anjou, now by the Counts of Normandy; possession remained with the man stronger in arms. Here the causes may be traced back from the end.

The Counts of Anjou could call it theirs by right, since King Robert had granted it to Geoffrey Grisegonelle and his successors, as Fulk of Jerusalem writes in the *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou*, whose words are also cited in the commentary of Hugh de Clereiis [Note: [Col. 0117] It should rather be read “de Clereiis”; see *Patrologia*, vol. CLXIII, col. 1133 ff., where this short work is printed in full.] *On the Major-Domus and Seneschalship of France*:

> “David, Count of Maine, and Geoffrey, Count of Corbon, disdained to receive their fief from the aforesaid king, asserting that they could in no way be subjected to the Burgundian race. Hearing their pride and seeing no small diminution of his kingdom, the king, having taken counsel with Count Geoffrey and the leading men of the realm, fixed a time and named a day for the siege of the castle of Mortagne.
>
> “Count Geoffrey, foreknowing the arrival of the king’s army, moved his forces from Vendôme and assaulted the aforesaid castle with his customary prowess and the valour of his men. He captured Count Geoffrey and the townsmen, who had shown too little fear, and handed him over to his lord the king. David, however, disdaining to come to a conference with the king, sent word that he would in no manner submit to him and that at no time would King Robert presume to see his Le Mans. Hearing the arrogance and indignation of that count, the king gave him and his Le Mans to Geoffrey Grisegonelle, and granted it to his successors by royal gift, to be possessed by right.”

The latter words should be read thus from the manuscript. To this may be added that King Henry, at Gervase, Bishop of Le Mans’s instigation, granted the county of Maine as a benefice to Geoffrey Martel. The Pontifical of Le Mans:

> “While Lord Gervase sat in the see, Herbert Bacco began to provoke him. Seeing that he could not defend his bishopric against Bacco either through the king or by himself, the bishop asked King Henry for something which he should never have asked: namely, that he grant the bishopric to Geoffrey, Count of Anjou, only for Geoffrey’s lifetime, so that he might defend it more freely against the Count of Maine; after Geoffrey’s death it was to return into the king’s hand. This was turned to evil. When Herbert Bacco heard that the bishop had acted thus, he was moved by envy and accused him before Count Geoffrey, earnestly begging him to deprive the bishop, if possible, of his bishopric and paternal honour.”

I am not surprised that Malmesbury, by a malicious circumlocution, somehow implies [Col. 0118A] that Fulk the Elder, after deceitfully capturing Herbert, Count of Maine, had extorted the county by force. Thus he says in Book III, in his account of William I:

> “Fulk the Elder had Herbert, Count of Maine, enticed to Saintes by a promise concerning the city; in the midst of their conference he caused his attendants to seize him and bind him under whatever conditions they pleased.”

Indeed, the surviving fragment of the *History of Aquitaine*, in volume IV of the *History of France*, says nothing whatever about such conditions; it wrongly reads *Arbertus* for *Herbertus*:

> “Then Count Fulk deceitfully summoned and brought with him to Saintes Arbert, the most noble Count of Maine. On the first Sunday of Lent, after supper, in the dead of night, he seized him by treachery and took him away in chains; he held him in prison for two years. The Lord deigned to rescue him from there. In the following year, on account of that very crime, the city itself, with its episcopal see, was burned; thereafter the basilica remained deserted.”

Col. 91, lin. 48.—At the castle of Lît. Geoffrey of Vendôme, Book III, Letter 13, calls it the castle of Leda, after the not insignificant river Leda. It is likewise called so in the *Life of Segenfrid, Bishop of Le Mans*:

> “And the estate which they call Dissé, beyond the river Leda.”

And it is called *Lidus* in the *Life of Joseph*:

> “Lipidus above the river Lidus.”

Elias had chosen this most delightful retreat with the intention that, situated on the border of Anjou and Maine, it should attract many to his party. The castle of Lît was, moreover, in the dominion of Gervase, Elias’s father-in-law, as is clear from the words of the Calendar of the Church of Le Mans quoted above.

Col. 91, line 53.—Finally, in the following summer. William of Malmesbury mentions this expedition in Book I of the *Historia Novella*: “A sudden message came to him from Maine, saying that his household there was under siege . . . . Then, making for Maine, he drove out Count Elias and ordered it to be subject to his authority; and he returned to England.”

Col. 92, line 14.—But certain of the clergy. These are precisely those whom Ivo says were among the leading men of the Church of Le Mans, in Epistle 277: “Certain leading men of the Church of Le Mans say that they knew him before he entered upon his public life.” Jacques Sirmond—whom our age has produced no equal—proved by the most certain arguments, in his notes on Epistle 13 of Book III of Geoffrey of Vendôme, that Ivo wrote this letter while Hildebert was still bishop-elect.

Col. 92, line 19.—Or demolish the towers. See Hildebert’s Epistle 8, Book II, to John and Benedict, from which these words are taken almost verbatim; also Ivo’s Epistle 74, addressed to Hildebert.

Col. 92, line 23.—The perils of the sea. He describes elegantly the storm into which he was driven while being carried to an island, in verses on his exile:

> Then I board the vessel, entrusting my life to the storms;  
> The sails swell; the little boat is aided by a twofold power.  
> The harbour lay far away, when a stronger wind stirred  
> The tide, and the south wind ploughed the waters into heaps.  
> The tempest grows; the breeze drives the ship; the gaping wave rages;  
> The sail is drenched with rain; black night chooses the day.  
> Winds, sea, whirlpool, surge command despair;  
> Clouds meet us, and the very sky with its fires.  
> Almost the whole world heaps its wrath upon the frail pine-ship,  
> And everything that can harm becomes an enemy,  
> While the storm thus rages, while even the master grows pale,  
> Stands stunned, and fears that he will become food for fishes.  
> Behold, a ravening whirlwind, lifting waves to the stars,  
> Drove the now rudderless vessel to the shore.  
> Thus, miserably fortunate, with ship shattered and possessions lost,  
> I escaped winds, seas, rocks, and Jupiter.

Col. 92, line 58.—The Lord had pity. “It was judged that the man had been struck by divine vengeance, the truth of this inference being taken from the fact that he had proved an unbearable oppressor of the poor, a cruel extortioner from churches, and, whenever bishops or prelates died, a most irreverent appropriator and squanderer,” says Suger in the *Life of Louis*. John of Salisbury says the same in the place cited above.

Col. 92, line 71.—William [was at war] with his neighbours. Suger, *On the Life of Louis the Fat*:

> William, king of the English—well suited to warfare, greedy for praise, and a seeker after renown—having disinherited his elder brother Robert and happily succeeded his father William, and, after that same brother’s departure for Jerusalem, having obtained the duchy of Normandy, strove by every means in his power to attack the renowned young man, since the duchy of Normandy bordered upon the marches of the kingdom wherever it extended. Their struggle was alike and unlike: alike, because neither yielded; unlike, because one was mature and the other a youth; one wealthy, lavish with the treasures of England, a remarkable purchaser and paymaster of soldiers; the other without resources, who spared his father—the holder of the revenues of the kingdom—and by the sole resource of his good disposition raised his troops. Yet he resisted boldly.

Baldric, abbot of Bourgueil, praised the dead William in verses printed in volume IV of the *History of France*, p. 257. Hildebert speaks of his death in his poem on Hugh.

Col. 92, line 72.—When Count Elias [did this]. At last Count Elias gained possession of affairs after William II had been unexpectedly removed by death, under King Henry. Malmesbury also acknowledges this in Book I of the *Historia Novella*: “Elias, count of Maine, who held it under King Henry, was removed from life.” It is pleasant to suppose that he held and possessed it with Henry’s very willing consent; for Elias is recorded as having assisted Henry in attacking the people of Bayeux, in the short chronicle of Saint-Albin:

> 1105. In the following year the aforesaid Geoffrey Martel, at the request of Henry, king of the English, and Count Elias, went with an army into Neustria, and took and burned the city of Bayeux in one assault.

Col. 93, line 8.—Therefore, once the city had been pacified, he set out for Rome. The most eminent Baronius is therefore mistaken in supposing that Hildebert’s journey fell in the year 1107. [Note: See the *Life*.] As we shall show in connection with Epistle 19, this error produced another, more serious one.

Col. 93, line 13.—The duke of Apulia himself. Roger, duke of Apulia, and Roger, count of Sicily, are too well known for anything to need saying about them. Besides the usual writers on Sicilian affairs, one should consult Geoffrey the monk, who, at Count Roger’s request, wrote four books on the conquest of Sicily, and Abbot Alexander, who described Roger’s deeds in the same number of books.

Col. 93, line 14.—His uncle, the count of Sicily. Geoffrey the monk, Book IV, chapter 17:

> In the year 1091, Duke Roger, angered against the long-rebellious people of Cosenza, assembled an army from all Apulia; taking his brother Bohemond with him, he planned to march against and besiege them in May. He invited his uncle, the count, from Sicily, not to delay in coming there with aid. Out of love for his nephew, the latter roused many thousands of Saracens from all Sicily and also recruited forces of knights; he hastened without delay to the place to which he had been invited.

Soon afterward: “The duke gained possession of the city through his uncle’s valour”; and so repeatedly. But I do not know why Eadmer, in Book II of *The Life of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury*, calls Roger, count of Sicily, “a man of the duke of Apulia”:

> Anselm’s kindness welcomed everyone without respect of persons. And whom did it welcome? Even pagans, to say nothing of Christians. For some such persons—for many thousands of them were brought on that expedition by the man of Duke Roger, count of Sicily.

Col. 93, line 15.—Much gold and silver. The Calendar of the Church of Le Mans:

> On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August died Robert Guiscard, duke of Apulia. For the remedy of his soul, his son Roger, duke of Apulia, sent various gifts from Apulia through Bishop Hildebert.

[Col. 0120A] Moreover, Baldric, abbot of Bourgueil, extols Duke Roger of Apulia’s liberality with remarkable praises in his little poem on Duke Roger, printed in volume IV of the *History of France*, where he says:

> For your name is proclaimed throughout the whole world,  
> Whether because you lavish rich rewards upon military service,  
> Or because you wisely conduct the affairs of the commonwealth,  
> Which stand firm, not to be shaken in your days;  
> Or because you enrich churches with immense gifts,  
> Or because at this time you invite the Muses  
> By your generosity, so that Apollo cannot remain silent.

There is scarcely a celebrated church throughout the lands of Gaul which he did not enrich with royal gifts. This is attested everywhere by the calendars in which, according to custom, the days of death of those by whose wealth churches had been enriched were entered, so that the gifts of annual prayers might repay the gifts bestowed. Thus, lest even the furthest land of Armorica should have lacked a share in his generosity, the Calendar of Redon says: “On the fifth day before the Kalends of March died Roger, duke of Apulia.”

The munificence of the count of Sicily is likewise commended by Saint Bernard’s praise; see Epistle 207. Peter the Venerable, Epistle 3, Book III, considers that every hope is to be expected from him, now king. The anonymous author of the *Life of Paschal I*, in volume XII of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the year 1100, no. 18, says of the same man:

> The envoys of Count Roger come to the city, enter the curia, and, according to custom, most dutifully greet and return the greeting of the pope on the count’s behalf; then, bowing, they placed at his feet one thousand ounces of gold. This was received as devoutly as it was seasonably sent.

The Calendar of Le Mans says concerning the gifts he had sent through Hildebert to the Church of Le Mans: “On the tenth day before the Kalends of July died Roger, count of Sicily, who sent from Sicily through the hands of Bishop Hildebert one hundred ounces of gold for the work of the church of Saint Julian, and ten pounds of Le Mans currency to the canons.”

Col. 93, line 44.—The court of Lord Gervasius. Gervasius himself will act as interpreter. For he writes in the charter of donation appended to his *Life* in the pontifical of Le Mans:

> I also grant you that court of my father, situated upon the same estate, namely in the eastern corner of the city, with all the demesne plots adjoining it on every side within and without the wall, together with woodland for establishing the workshops of the cloister which I strive to build, so that there you may devote yourselves to the Lord in regular and canonical service. In it I rebuilt and adorned the most holy church of God, Saint Saviour, founded in ancient times, and I most devoutly entreat you to venerate it.

Ibid.—Of Lord Gervasius. He was bishop of Le Mans, nephew through a sister and successor of Avesgaud. The author of the *Life of Gervasius* writes:

> Lord Gervasius, a man second to none in the kingdom in wisdom and integrity, gladly received the see of his uncle Avesgaud. After receiving consecration, Count Herbert, surnamed Bacco—the uncle of Herbert who lived in the time of Bishop Avesgaud—was inflamed by the spur of envy, because many said that Gervasius was richer or better than he; and, at the same time, seeking a pretext for seizing Saint Julian’s treasury, he prevented him from entering for two years. But after two years had elapsed, Herbert Bacco, son of Haimo and Hildeburgis, received him into the see.

The Calendar of the Church of Le Mans:

> On the fourth day before the Nones of July died Gervasius, bishop of Le Mans, afterward archbishop of Reims. Besides other things which he bestowed upon his clergy, he gave them half the treasury of Saint Julian; he was the son of Haimo and Hildeburga.

Gervasius himself, in his charter of donation:

> For the remission of the great burden of my sins, for obtaining rest for my holy predecessor and uncle Avesgaud, and for the other predecessors of ours, bishops of this see, as also for my father and mother, Haimo and Hildeburga.

[Col. 0121A] Hildeburga, moreover, was Avesgaud’s eldest sister, as the author of the *Life of Avesgaud* says. Their lineage derived from the counts of Bellême. “The bishop sought Bellême, the castle of his brother William,” says the same author. Haimo, Gervasius’s father, seems to have been descended from the lords of the castle of Lede. Gervasius himself declares this in the already cited charter of donation:

> I likewise transfer to you all the customary dues which were paid to my father from your lands and which belonged to the said castle called Lit.

Geoffrey Martel, whose cause Gervasius had defended, restrained him in chains when he changed his disposition and purpose. The author of the *Life of Gervasius* says:

> Therefore, seeing that Count Hugh had, on Lord Bishop Gervasius’s advice, taken a most powerful wife to Geoffrey’s ruin and loss, Geoffrey bore Judas in his breast and deceitfully ordered Bishop Gervasius to be handed over to him. Once delivered up, he sent him to prison and kept him in chains for as much as seven years.

At last released, Gervasius rose to a higher rank through King Henry’s favour and was appointed archbishop of Reims. The same author says:

> Count Geoffrey allowed Gervasius to leave prison, on the following oath: that so long as Geoffrey lived, Gervasius should not enter the city of Le Mans. When the bishop saw that he could enter neither the city nor his own castle, he went to William, count of Normandy, and sorrowfully related to him all that Geoffrey had done to him and how he had betrayed him. When Count William heard this, he was moved by pity and gave him gold and silver, strong castles, and very great gifts. While Bishop Gervasius was staying in Normandy with the count, it happened that Guy, chief bishop of the Church of Reims, died. When King Henry heard that Guy had died, he gave the archbishopric to Bishop Gervasius, who received it joyfully, after governing the Church of Le Mans for twenty years.

The year in which he was transferred from Le Mans to Reims may be inferred from the acts of Philip I’s consecration. These establish that Philip was inaugurated in place of his father Henry in 1059, the fourth year of Gervasius’s episcopate. Subtracting four years, the translation falls in 1055.

Gervasius, however, seizing the opportunity of the seventh anniversary of the king’s consecration, made a clamour over what he believed to be the obsolete rights of the Church of Reims; and he obtained recognition that, precisely as his predecessors had done, he should be chief chancellor of France and that this dignity should belong to the archbishopric. The acts of consecration state:

> The archbishop also subscribed. For there he appointed him chief chancellor, as his predecessors had appointed their predecessors. And thus he consecrated him king.

The *Book on the Reckoning of Time*:

> With these and the others present, Gervasius spoke before the king, asserting that he ought to be chief chancellor of the king, as his predecessors had been. The king most gladly assented, and the others consented; thus the aforesaid bishop secured this for himself and his Church. That this was indeed so from ancient times is read in the attestation of a charter which King Charles made concerning the possessions of Saint Walburga, in this form: “Goslin, chancellor, wrote and subscribed in place of Heriveus, archbishop and chief chancellor.” Gervasius, moreover, was the eighth archbishop after Heriveus.

Certainly a weak and futile argument. But these matters do not belong here. There survive twenty-two letters of Stephen X, Nicholas II, and likewise Alexander II, written to Gervasius when he was already archbishop of Reims. They are included in volume IV of the *History of France*, and one may, if desired, extract from them, as from fuller memoirs, Gervasius’s acts during his archiepiscopate. He died on the fourth day before the Nones of July, as the Martyrology records.

Col. 93, line 51.—Count Elias [made] a tomb. The Martyrology of Le Mans differs slightly from that whose words I quoted above:

> On the fifth day before the Ides of July died Elias, count of the people of Le Mans. At the beginning of his rule he granted to this holy mother Church whatever Count Hugh, his predecessor, son of the marquis, had bestowed upon Bishop Hoellus of blessed memory in compensation for damages and injuries inflicted upon him: namely, the *diablagium*, customary dues, exactions, and whatever the same count of Le Mans, excepting arson and violent seizure, was said to hold, justly or unjustly, in the cloister, in the episcopal houses, at Colonies, and throughout the entire land of the canons contained within the Quinta. He also granted whatever his father-in-law Gervasius had bestowed upon Saint Julian from the castle of Lit, in the land of the bishop and canons beyond the river Idonea. During the rebuilding of this church, besides many other gifts, he gave one hundred and forty-seven gold pieces. At Hildebert’s suggestion, he made Saint Julian’s bed—wherein his most holy remains now rest—of silver and gold. Moreover, when entering upon the way of all flesh, he gave a cup of forty-eight ounces of pure gold to make one cross, two marks of silver to make a daily censer, and five marks for the canons. May his soul enjoy the joys of Paradise.

Moreover, the Martyrology calls the tomb a “bed,” as Suger does in Book *On the Consecration of the Church of Saint-Denis*: “We devoutly intended that their most sacred biers, especially those of the lords, should be adorned.”

Col. 93, line 65.—From all customary dues. The Martyrology says that he confirmed and ratified all that Count Hugh had given. What he had given is explained in the entry on Hoellus:

> Since this count had inflicted very great losses upon him, in compensation for those losses he made free and immune from every public customary due and exaction the bishop’s houses and cellars, the cloister of that Church all around, a certain estate called Colonies, and another estate of the canons called Mantula. By the counsel and assent of his nobles, he remitted the *diablagium* received from them and all the rest that seemed to belong to his fisc, and left and granted them in perpetuity to Saint Julian and to future bishops. And lest any of his successors should thereafter presume to destroy or corrupt his ordinance and that immunity, he caused the whole Church round about, together with the cloister and the buildings of the bishopric, to be marked out and enclosed by a public procession and holy water, with all the people following. Then he entered the church with that bishop and ordered the remission and immunity which he had granted to the church to be proclaimed—while the clergy of Saint Julian, the congregation beyond Saint Peter, both clerics and monks, and all the people listened, and while that bishop recited it—as is recorded in the documents of that bishop.

Col. 94, line 20.—Who were not canons. They were priests in cathedral churches who performed vicarious service for the canons. In the Church of Troyes they were called “priest-canons,” as appears from the letters of Manasses, bishop of Troyes, preserved in the collection of Trojan antiquities; in other documents of the same Manasses they are called “canon-priests.” Manasses likewise decreed that their vacant half-prebends should accrue to the canons:

> No one may be invested with any of those prebends until he has been ordained priest; but whenever one of them falls vacant, the remaining canons shall receive the revenues of the vacant prebend until a canon has been appointed in its place.

Hildebert, on the contrary, decreed that the revenues of vacant greater prebends should benefit the priests, whom I have no doubt were vicars and holders of half-prebends. Previously the bishops of Le Mans enjoyed the annates of vacancies by right, as this passage alone makes sufficiently clear.

Col. 98, line 11.—Protracted over a long time. For he was the fourth after Wulgrin, who had laid the foundations of the mother church. The pontifical in its notice on Wulgrin states:

> Although he was poorer and humbler than the bishops his predecessors, he nevertheless attempted greater works. In the fifth year of his ordination he began the foundations of the mother church, larger than they had been; but, death unexpectedly intervening, he was unable to complete it.

In the notice on Arnald:

> After he had occupied the episcopal chair for some time, the structure of the new church, which Bishop Wulgrin had begun, had been weakened by instability in the foundations and frailty in the stones; with innumerable cracks it began to threaten its own ruin terribly. While the builders tried to prop it up, it collapsed in the night with a sudden crash. Now the great arch of that structure had been built over the crypt where the body of the most blessed Julian rested, with pyramids of immense height set on either side. There the power of the most holy confessor shone forth beyond doubt: when so great an engine of construction suddenly fell, the roof of his basilica, under which the saint’s remains were covered, remained whole and unharmed, so that not even the slightest particle of that roof was damaged by the blows of so terrible a fall. Thereupon the aforesaid bishop demolished the entire structure of the work undertaken, down to its lowest foundations, and began again to build that church upon a firmer foundation and in more solid stone. Before he died, he also put a roof upon the upper part, commonly called the chancel, and laid the very solid foundations of the members called the transepts and of the towers.

And at the end:

> It demanded such great expense and such effort that it could not be completed even in the space of sixty years.

The author of the *Life* relates what Hoellus contributed according to his ability:

> At once he undertook with such zeal to complete the construction of the new Church, upon which his predecessors had laboured for a long time, that he brought the transepts and towers—whose foundations his predecessor, as has been shown above, had laid—to completion within a short time. Quickly placing their roofs upon them, he also completed all around the outer walls called the wings. He likewise adorned with flooring and ceiling the chancel that his predecessor had built, and arranged windows throughout the chancel and transepts in a praiseworthy, though excessively costly, variety of artistic workmanship.

After much intervening matter, he adds:

> The bishop, once peace had been restored, began to labour with the utmost zeal upon the construction of the new Church, which had been entirely interrupted because of its devastation. With diligent care he prepared the upper parts of the same basilica for the translation of the saints’ relics: namely, the chapel called the choir, the episcopal throne, altars laid out in suitable proportions, floors, columns and ceilings painted with the most pleasing variety, and walls whitewashed all around. He omitted absolutely nothing which he thought might be useful or ornamental, taking especial care that nothing in the entire fabric should displease the eyes of visitors. When all had thus been prepared most elegantly, he took care to summon the archbishop of Tours and the more distinguished persons of neighbouring cities to the translation of the saints, so that their presence might make the solemnity more celebrated and the people more devout. The most holy body of blessed Julian and the relics of the other saints were translated into the same basilica on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093 and the eighth year of that bishop’s ordination. On that day, if God granted him life, he had resolved to dedicate the basilica itself. So great a multitude of people is known to have assembled for this translation and solemnity, not only from our own region but also from the surrounding provinces, that no one of our age remembered ever having seen such a gathering.

Col. 98, line 15.—He consecrated [it] in the year 1120. Orderic Vitalis is greatly mistaken in thinking, in Book X of his *Ecclesiastical History*, that the mother church of the city of Le Mans was dedicated in the time of Guy, Hildebert’s successor, together with the archbishop of Tours, since Guy did not enter the episcopate until 1126. These are his words:

> He adorned in many praiseworthy ways the church of Saint Gervasius, where rests the body of Julian, the outstanding confessor of Christ; afterward, in the time of his successor, Guinmar the Breton—who was also called Guy of Étampes—he dedicated it. But, through the exigency of sins, the church which the activity of good men had richly adorned and enriched with various ornaments for the honour of God was, eight years after its dedication, disfigured and horribly ravaged by a fire which consumed a great part of the city.

This fire occurred in 1134, as Orderic himself testifies in Book XIV, and as does the author of the brief *Life of Guy*. The date of Count Fulk’s first journey to Jerusalem, likewise falling in 1120, also refutes Orderic’s error. But arguments are unnecessary, since we have Orderic admitting the error and contradicting himself. For in Book IV he says:

> When he died, Hildebert, an outstanding writer of verse, succeeded him and held the bishopric praiseworthily for nearly thirty years. He completed the cathedral church which his predecessor had begun and dedicated it reverently with the great rejoicing of the people. Not long afterward, namely in the year of the Incarnation 1125, he ascended the metropolitan see.

Col. 98, line 24.—Gislebert. He entered the archbishopric of Tours in 1119. The Chronicle of Tours, under the year 1119: “Then Ralph, archbishop of Tours, died, and Gislebert succeeded him.” When he finally died, Hildebert took his place. The same chronicle, under the year 1127: “In the first year of Lothair, Gislebert, archbishop of Tours, died, and Hildebert succeeded him.” Orderic Vitalis, Book X, without any indication of time:

> After the death of Gislebert, archbishop of Tours, Hildebert was elected by the clergy and people; and by God’s will he rose from the summit of Le Mans to the metropolitan see.

More explicitly in Book IV, concerning Hildebert:

> Not long afterward, namely in the year of the Incarnation 1125, in the fourth indiction, when Gislebert, archbishop of Tours, died at Rome with Pope Calixtus . . .

For more on him, see the *History of the Lords of Amboise* in the notes on Epistle 2, Book V of Geoffrey of Vendôme’s letters. If you wish to know the dispute arising from Gislebert’s election and the severity with which it disturbed the Church of Tours, consult that work. On Ivo, Gislebert’s nephew, see Epistle 201.

Ibid.—Archbishop of Tours. The metropolitan celebrated the consecration of the Church of Le Mans with the neighbouring bishops subject to him. It should be noted that, from the Church’s earliest youth, the festival days of dedications have customarily been celebrated with a great assembly of bishops. The numerous bishops present at the consecration of the Church of Jerusalem are attested by Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book IV, chapter 43. Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 8, likewise reports that the dedication of the Church of Antioch was adorned by the presence of ninety bishops.

In that passage Socrates observes that Julius, bishop of Rome, had been absent, and says that without his decision it was not permissible *ekklēsias kanonizein* (ἐκκλησίας κανονίζειν), “to legislate for churches”; some mistakenly interpret this as referring to the dedication of churches. But under the pretext of a dedication, Eusebius, acting under imperial auspices, had convened a council against Athanasius and against the Nicene formula of faith. Socrates declares that this had been done rashly and to no purpose, since no one may enact or abrogate ecclesiastical laws without the knowledge and concurrence of the bishop of Rome; this is what *kanonizein* (κανονίζειν) means.

There is no reason for me to deny that the supreme authority over these solemnities was formerly vested in the bishop of Rome. Certainly it was unlawful to dedicate and consecrate churches without his authority intervening. [Note: See Martène, *Treatise on Ancient Rites*, chapter 13, p. 236.] Gelasius, canon *De locorum*, *On Consecration*, distinction 1: “Without the command of the Apostolic See.” The same, canon *Praecepta*, same distinction: “A newly founded church cannot be dedicated without the authority of the supreme ruler.” And canon *Basilicas*, same distinction: “You do not seek the prescribed permissions according to custom.”

But what, finally, were these permissions? They were *formatae*, letters by which the supreme pontiff permitted bishops in their own dioceses to act in this matter at the request of donors who made an offering—thus, to use Ennodius’s expression in Oration 5. An example occurs in canon *Piae mentis*, 16, question 7. I append a model from which Roman pontiffs drew up their *formatae*, together with the formula for a petitionary offering, or *petitorium*, as Gelasius calls it in canon *Certum*, *On Consecration*, distinction 1.

*Petition for the dedication of an oratory.*

> To the most holy and most blessed Lord, Father of Fathers, Pope [name], I, your servant [name]. It pertains to the increase of the Catholic religion whenever venerable places are consecrated to divine worship in honour of the saints. On the estate [name], belonging to me by right, I declare that I have constructed at my own expense a basilica, which I desire to be consecrated in honour of the holy martyrs [name] or [name]. For lights and for the maintenance of those serving there, I offer to this basilica [property] and [property]. Therefore I ask Your Apostleship to issue your commands to the bishop of the city of [name], so that he may consecrate the aforesaid basilica with the most holy mysteries; so that, through this act in the time of your Beatitude, holy veneration may receive increase. I likewise promise that I shall claim no further right in that place, except for the sake of procession, which is due in common to all Christians. With equal prayer I request that you issue your letters to the bishop of the city of [name], so that he may solemnly entrust to me relics of the aforesaid saints.

*Reply concerning the dedication of the oratory.*

> [The petitioner] has informed us by the representation of his petition what is contained below: that, on the estate [name], belonging by right to [name], he has founded, from devotion, an oratory which he desires to be consecrated in honour of Saint [name]. Therefore, most blessed brother, if the aforesaid structure lawfully stands in your parish and it is established that no body has been buried there, then, after first receiving a lawful donation—namely [property] and [property], or [property], yielding so many solidi free from fiscal claims—and after the municipal records have been produced, you shall solemnly consecrate the aforesaid oratory without public masses. Thus neither there nor in future times shall they establish baptismal fonts there, nor shall you appoint a cardinal priest. But if perhaps he should prefer masses to be celebrated there, let him know that a priest must be requested from your loving authority, so that no such act may in any way be presumed by any other priest. You shall also place the relics received with due reverence.

The Gallican Church yielded in all things to the majesty of the Roman Church and willingly lowered its fasces; but it scarcely, if at all, allowed the power of consecrating churches—which belonged to it by right of priesthood—to be diminished or impaired. Nor could the bishops endure agents of that ancient custom and ordinance being sent in to interfere with their discipline. You have an illustrious example in Rodulfus Glaber, *Histories*, Book II, chapter 4, which the author of the *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou* inserted entire into his commentaries; it was very familiar to him.

Col. 98, line 30.—Geoffrey of Rouen. He was a Breton by birth, brother of Judicaël, bishop of Aleth; first dean of the Church of Le Mans, and Hildebert’s competitor for the bishopric. Orderic Vitalis, Book X:

> Count Elias elected Geoffrey the Breton, dean of the same church, to the episcopate; but the clergy, acting first, compelled Hildebert of Lavardin, archdeacon, to sit in the episcopal chair, and with loud voice, rejoicing in festal exultation, sang: “We praise thee, O God,” and the other things required by ecclesiastical custom in the election of a bishop. When Elias learned this, he was greatly angered and wished to resist. But when the clergy said to him, “You ought not to prefer your election to the Church’s election,” he held his peace out of reverence, because he feared God; and, lest a deadly schism should arise among the members of the Church, he consented to the canons. Geoffrey, indeed, was already confident of obtaining the bishopric, and rich feasts had already been consumed by greedy diners. But they wholly refused to have him as bishop of Le Mans. He was the brother of Judicaël, bishop of Aleth, and after the death of William, archbishop of Rouen, he presided for seventeen years.

William of Jumièges, Book VIII, chapter 17: “When William, archbishop of Rouen, died, Geoffrey, dean of Le Mans, obtained the same episcopal see.” Ivo of Chartres’s Epistle 52 survives, addressed to this Geoffrey while he was still dean of Le Mans. As we observed above from the records of the cartulary of Preuilly, he was present at Hildebert’s consecration. He died in 1125; the Calendar of Le Mans records the day of his death on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, in these words: “On the fourth day before the Kalends of December died Geoffrey, a canon of this Church, afterwards archbishop of Rouen.” I am surprised that no mention is made of his deanship, although all authors agree upon it.

Col. 98, line 40.—Marbod. More about Marbod, God willing, on another occasion, when we publish his works; for the intention has taken root in my mind of doing this service to the most ancient and most holy father of his country.

[Note: [Col. 0125C] Thus I was not the first to take an interest in the distinction of a most ancient and most holy family. Before the year 1655, about which time he died, the distinguished M. Loyauté—a man otherwise most steadfast in fairness and [Col. 0125D] truth—would never have called it so, unless he had had before him proofs of his assertion. He could rightly and deservedly call most ancient a family which is known already to have been celebrated, in the year 1130, among the foremost families of Armorica: namely, in the person of Peter Marboeuf, knight, lord of Stagnum, husband of Joanna Chabot, sister of Theobald Chabot, lord of La Rochecervière. By a charter of the year 1230, authentically produced for us from the Marbod archives, Theobald, with the consent of his brothers Gerard and Sabrehaut Chabot, grants Peter, as an addition to the dowry and marital right of his beloved sister—as the charter says—the right to cut whatsoever timber he wished in his forest of La Rochecervière.

Moreover, Hervé de Volvire, or de Fresnoy and de la Rochecervière, was asked by John Marboeuf to confirm this grant; but only after John Marboeuf had legally proved that he drew his descent in direct line, from eldest son to eldest son, from the aforesaid Peter Marboeuf: namely, through his father Theobald Marboeuf, through Richard [Col. 0126C] his grandfather, through Hubert his great-grandfather, the eldest son of the said Peter Marboeuf, his ancestor, of whom the charter of 1230 speaks. This confirmation of the grant was issued on 27 March 1304, when the aforesaid John Marboeuf flourished. From him, through grandfather and great-grandfather, descended Simon Marboeuf, who in the recently printed *New History of Brittany* (vol. II, pp. 965, 967, and 968) is named eleventh among sixty or more of the most illustrious Breton lords, dukes, or captains appointed by the duke of Brittany himself to form the honorary escort of Richard of Brittany, the duke’s brother, for the embassy planned to Charles VI, king of France, in 1419. From that year onward, descent in direct line through successive grandfathers and great-grandfathers down to the present time would not be difficult to prove.

Therefore M. Loyauté could deservedly call the Marbod family most ancient, since he knew its origin to be nearly seven hundred years old. That he also called it most holy is not likely to have been asserted without proof by a man most scrupulous in fairness and truth. Certainly, it cannot be denied that it was most holy, at least in its root. For Marbod—from whom, as often happens, since he was then more celebrated, the whole family took its name, abandoning the family name Pelliciarius—lived so holy a life in his episcopate, and, after resigning it, died so holy a monk at Saint-Albin, that he is listed among the saints of Gaul by the most illustrious bishop of Toul in his Gallican Martyrology, on the third Ides of September.

Since the civic forum itself has its own holiness, consisting in the upright administration of justice, nothing seems to prevent that family from being called most holy which, in the succession of ages from its origin onward, produced for the supreme court of Brittany at Rennes, as also for the city, so many distinguished magistrates and successive presidents conspicuous for integrity [Col. 0127D] and thereby holy in their profession. Since they often struggled or laboured for their country at peril to their fortunes and even their lives, they could not undeservedly be called parents of their country by the aforesaid M. Loyauté, himself a most upright advocate.

As to what we have here noted on the occasion of his notes on the Life of Hildebert, we declare that we were neither asked nor in any manner informed of it, whether orally or in writing. Rather, we acted of our own accord and solely from remembrance of the singular kindness with which the most illustrious president de Marboeuf then deigned to favour and honour us when we were living at Rheims in 1664, while he was lodging there on public business. From that time until now we have had no personal intercourse, nor even communication by the tip of a single letter, with anyone of that noble family. We were moved only, as we again affirm, by the desire to testify to the veneration in which we have hitherto held the memory of that most illustrious president [Col. 0128C] and in which we shall forever hold his noble family. We have also gained thereby that our conjectures regarding the most noble race of the Marbods, at Epistle 3, Book II, will perhaps appear not wholly improbable, as likewise what we stated concerning it in the preliminary notice to Marbod’s own minor works.

From the Gallican Martyrology of the most illustrious André du Saussay, bishop of Toul, in the text of the Martyrology itself:

“On the third Ides of September. At Rennes in Armorica, Saint Marbod, bishop and confessor. ‘Twelfth in succession upon this see, he bore the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb, as a living stone, by the divinely bestowed and outstanding imitation of their virtues; whence, raised up to the highest Zion, he was numbered among the precious stones with which she gleams.’”

To M. Loyauté’s note concerning the noble Marbod family we have thought it not unsuitable to append an exact transcript from the original copy preserved in the archive of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Vitré. It was copied by the Reverend Father Dom Stephen Deschamps, its prior, and sent to us after Marbod’s minor works had already been printed. From it it is clear that Marbod, then bishop of Rennes, at the request of Andrew and his sons, lords of Vitré, with the approval of Conan, duke of Brittany, and of his mother Ermengard and other nobles of the place, expelled the disorderly canons living there and established Benedictine monks in their stead, granting the church of Vitré itself to the monks of Saint-Melaine, together with several other churches and possessions. (See below, among Marbod’s charters, no. 3.)]

[Col. 0127A] Col. 98, line 47.—Raginaud. This is the same Reginald, of whom more is said at Epistle [perhaps 5, Book II; otherwise 12].
