Col. 98, line 53.—“But this consecration,” etc. The principal and most important ceremonies of a dedication were the consecrations of altars. For no church could be dedicated without the consecration of some altar, as Anselm teaches in Book III, final letter: “A church is not to be consecrated without the consecration of an altar, whether the principal altar or another altar in the same church.” And when the principal altar has been moved, Canon 5 of the Council of Meaux commands that the church be consecrated again; see it in Ivo, Epistles 73 and 80. Anselm gives this reason:

“An altar is not made for the sake of a church, but a church for the sake of an altar. Therefore, when the principal altar has been violated, it no longer seems to be a church, because that for which a church is built and consecrated is lacking. Accordingly, when that altar is new, it rightly seems that the church should be consecrated with it, through which it received its character as a church.”

By what rite churches or altars [Col. 0127B] were consecrated in those blind times of the Church, or after cruel times had yielded to milder ones, is indicated by an ancient ritual book of the Gallican Church. We have thought fit to append the words most relevant to the illustration of these matters:

“Pope Sylvester I instituted the consecrations of altars and churches according to the rite observed by the Roman Church. Yet from the very times of the apostles there were places dedicated to God, called by some oratories and by others churches, where assemblies were held on the first day of the week; and there the people gathered to hear the Christian word of God, to receive the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, to be instructed by the epistles of the holy apostles, and trained by the deeds of the holy Fathers. Although these places were exorcised with salt, they were not anointed with chrism; nor did there stand an altar of stone, raised as a memorial and anointed with chrism, in the figure of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, our altar, priest, and victim. But after Constantine, who held sole power in the empire, was granted purification by the sacrament of baptism through blessed Sylvester, then for the first time, by a law promulgated by him, all persons dwelling under the Roman Empire were allowed lawfully to build churches.”

It was customary to sprinkle the altar with holy water and then anoint it with chrism. Rabanus Maurus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, II, ch. 45:

“That the altar, after sprinkling with water, is anointed with chrism was done in imitation of the patriarch Jacob, who, after that dreadful vision, raised up a stone as a memorial, poured oil upon it, and called the place the house of God.”

Ennodius, Oration 2, compares this to baptism: “Come then, most gracious Lord, and descend in fullness for the consecration of thy work: let these temples be cleansed in the manner of the human body through baptism.” When these rites had duly been completed, “the building became a sacrament, and the earthly dwelling a heavenly assembly,” says the same author in Oration 4.

Ibid.—The greater altar. The completion of nearly the whole solemnity depends upon its consecration, as appears from Anselm, who calls it the principal altar; and from Suger, in his book *On the Consecration of the Church of Saint-Denis*, who calls it the principal altar. In the cartulary of Vendôme it is frequently called the Lord’s altar. In the same way a public Mass is called the Lord’s Mass by Gervase, bishop of Le Mans: “Let no canon presume to celebrate the Lord’s Mass or a private Mass,” etc.

Ibid.—Crypt. The word is used in a sense foreign to its proper meaning. Properly it is an underground, sacred, vaulted place, such as is almost set before our eyes by these verses of Prudentius:

> A sunken crypt lies open in its shadowy hollows.  
> A descending path, bending through winding passages,  
> teaches one to go down by steps into its hidden recess,  
> while a faint light glimmers, etc.

Gregory of Tours, *On Miracles*, ch. 33: “She entered the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter. Its altar, set upon raised platforms, stands high; its lower part, however, is enclosed by a door in the manner of a crypt, and itself has an altar containing the relics of the saints. The venerable woman devoutly descended into it, as we have said, to light a lamp.” The same author, using the term of a small shrine, ch. 38: “A crypt was built over them in marvellous workmanship; vaulted in the manner of arches, it stands with the firmest stability.” Hence in later centuries they called crypts the dependent chapels of basilicas that were somewhat lower or darker.

[Col. 0129A] Col. 98, line 57.—Fulk, son of Fulk. Fulk V, called of Jerusalem, who, upon the death of his father Fulk Rechin in 1119, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, became count of Anjou, Touraine, and Maine. The shorter chronicle of Saint-Albin, under 1108: “In the following year Fulk Rechin, count of the Angevins, died, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May.” Another: “1109: Count Fulk Rechin died; his son Fulk captured the castle of Doué and the castle of Île.” The Chronicle of Tours, under the same year: “Fulk Rechin, count of Anjou, died, and was succeeded by his son Fulk, who afterward became king of Jerusalem.” And the short chronicle of Saint-Florent: “1109: Count Fulk dies, and his son Fulk receives the countship.”

The author of the *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou* heaps praise upon this Fulk:

“After the death of Fulk Rechin, his son Fulk, abandoning the ways of his father and mother, led an upright life and governed the land wisely.”

After recording the praises of piety and war in which he abounded, he adds:

“While he was prosperously ruling the counties of Anjou, Touraine, and Maine, Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, sent envoys to France, who were to bring back with them, on the advice of prudent men, a suitable man to marry his daughter together with the kingdom of Jerusalem. By the counsel of King Louis and many expert bishops, Fulk of Anjou, who lacked a wife, was chosen. As Count Fulk was about to depart for Jerusalem, he came to Tours on the feast of Pentecost so that the archbishop, according to the custom of the holy pilgrimage, might place upon him the sign of the sacred cross.”

Later: “Crossing the sea with very great forces, he was joined in marriage to the king’s daughter and was made king of Jerusalem.” A little afterward he adds:

“After the death of King Baldwin, Fulk ruled the kingdom of Jerusalem valiantly and made the Damascenes and Ascalonites tributary to himself. Finally, before Raymond married Bohemond’s daughter, he maintained the principality of Antioch against the Turks with great labour and without any loss. By his wife he begot two sons, Baldwin and Amalric. When he had reached old age, this warlike man died and was buried with the other kings on Golgotha. The Jerusalemites appointed his son Baldwin as their king.”

He says that Fulk married Baldwin’s eldest daughter, named Melisende; but the author of the chronicle of the counts of Anjou calls her his only daughter, and believed that Fulk was summoned by the princes of the kingdom of Jerusalem, not by Baldwin. These are his words:

“The princes of the kingdom of Jerusalem sent envoys and urged Fulk, count of Anjou, to visit the places of the Lord’s Passion and to marry the daughter of King Baldwin, whom he had left as his only child and heir. The count consented, left his inheritance to his son Geoffrey Plantagenet, went to Jerusalem, and was placed upon the throne of King David in Jerusalem. He crushed Christ’s enemies. What the man began valiantly, his successors completed in their own time. Their valour, acquiring in succession the helm of the kingdom of Jerusalem, both checked the savagery of the Idumaeans, reduced rebellious Babylon to subjection, made Alexandria tributary, and in the latter part of his reign struck all the peoples of the East with amazement.”

But I do not believe him. For the short chronicle of Saint-Albin supports the *Deeds*: “1127: Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, sends word to Count Fulk that he is to become his son-in-law.” Fulk departed in the following year. The same chronicle: “1129: Count Fulk goes to Jerusalem.” And only in 1131: “Fulk is made king of Jerusalem,” says the same chronicle. So too William of Tyre, a source not of doubtful credit, whom you should consult in Book XIII, ch. 24 and the final chapter, and Book XIV, chs. 1 and 2, where he treats Fulk’s departure more fully.

John, monk of Marmoutier, adorned him with this eulogy:

“This man, abandoning the ways of his father and mother, led an upright life and wisely governed his land. He was an honourable man, valiant in arms, Catholic in faith, and kind toward the worshippers of God. Having obtained the two counties of Anjou and Touraine, he joined to them a third, Maine, through his wife. Exalting his friends and crushing the malicious and his adversaries, he soon became unequalled in glory and excellent reputation. While prosperously ruling the counties of Anjou, Touraine, and Maine, he was chosen for the kingdom of Jerusalem and joined in marriage to King Baldwin’s daughter. So long as he lived, he ruled the kingdom valiantly. He made Damascus and the Ascalonites tributary to himself. And long before Raymond married Bohemond’s daughter, he maintained the principality of Antioch against the Turks with great labour and without any loss. When he had reached old age, this warlike man died.”

Fulk died in 1142 according to William of Tyre, Book XV, final chapter; but the short chronicle of Saint-Albin places his death in 1143, and the chronicle of Saint-Florent under 1141, on the fourth Ides of November. The calendar of Saint-Serge says: “On the fourth Ides of November died Fulk, king of Jerusalem, formerly count of Anjou. Let the office be said for him as for an abbot.” This is confirmed by the Martyrology of the Church of Anjou.

Alfonso the Spaniard, a Jew converted to Christianity, speaks of him thus in a manuscript *History of Jerusalem* in my possession, Book III, ch. 93, containing a catalogue of the kings of Jerusalem:

“The noble Fulk, count of Anjou and Chartres [read: Maine], succeeded to the kingdom; the aforesaid king had given him his eldest daughter Melisende as wife. Fighting near Antioch against an innumerable host of Turks that had poured forth from the Persian Gulf, he killed three thousand, took many captive, and, while the rest escaped death by flight, won a glorious triumph over his enemies. He reigned eleven or twelve years. While hunting a hare in the territory of Acre, he fell with his horse and died by a sudden and lamentable accident, leaving two sons: Baldwin, the eldest, who succeeded him in the kingdom, and Amalric.”

This Amalric is treated by Tyre in Book XVI, ch. 1.

Ibid.—His wife Aremburgis. Her name is given in varying forms. She is called Guiburgis by Tyre, Book XIV, ch. 1; Heremburgis in the Angevin Calendar; Ermentrudis in certain manuscripts of the short chronicle of Saint-Albin; and almost everywhere Haremburgis. But the error of the author of the chronicle of the counts of Anjou, who calls her Sibylla, cannot be tolerated:

“Elias, son of John of La Flèche, married Sibylla, daughter of a certain count of Lombardy and niece of Herbert, formerly count of Maine; and with her he received the county of Maine. By Sibylla he begot Sibylla, whom Fulk, son of Fulk Rechin and afterward king of Jerusalem, married. By her he begot Geoffrey Plantagenet and Sibylla, countess of Flanders.”

Tyre states, Book XIV, ch. 1, that Fulk of Jerusalem married Aremburgis after the death of his father Fulk Rechin:

“The aforesaid Fulk, son of the elder Fulk, after his father’s death married the daughter of Elias, count of Maine, named Guiburgis, by whom he had two sons and as many daughters.”

The marriage was arranged through his mother Bertrada, as Tyre adds:

“The cause of this marriage was his mother. For when the young man was serving as cupbearer in the court of the count of Poitou, his lord, he heard of his elder brother’s death. He was seized by the same count and committed to chains because of certain castles which he tried forcibly to wrest from him. His father and brother had long possessed them by hereditary right within the territory of the aforesaid count, though as fiefs of that count. Hearing this, his mother—who had long before separated from his father and had attached herself to the lord king of France—was moved by maternal feeling, wept in supplication before the lord king, and obtained that her son should be released from chains and restored to his paternal inheritance. She further brought it about that the lord king gave to her son in marriage the only daughter of the above-mentioned Count Elias, together with all her inheritance.”

The marriage was celebrated in 1109. The Chronicle of Tours: “1109: Fulk, count of Anjou, married Haremburgis, daughter of Elias, count of Maine. By her he begot Geoffrey, who succeeded him, and Elias, afterward count of Maine, whom his brother Geoffrey later imprisoned at Tours until his death.”

It should also be remembered concerning Aremburgis that she had first been betrothed to Martel II, Fulk’s half-brother. The *Deeds of the Counts of Anjou*, under Geoffrey Martel II: “To this Martel Count Elias betrothed his only daughter, not yet fit for marriage, and granted him Maine with its appurtenances.” And under Fulk, king of Jerusalem: “He obtained from Elias, count of Maine, that his only daughter—though she had been promised to his brother Martel, whom she did not marry—be given to him together with the county of Maine. Thus the counties of Maine and Anjou are known to have been united.”

Aremburgis died in 1126. The Chronicle of Saint-Albin, under that year; and, in January, the Martyrology of the Church of Anjou: “On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February died Heremburgis, noble countess of the Angevins.” I had almost forgotten to mention that Aremburgis and Fulk jointly founded the abbey of the Oratory, as the Chronicle of Tours teaches under 1121: “The abbey of the Oratory was founded in the diocese of Anjou by Fulk, count of Anjou, and Haremburgis his wife.”

Col. 98, line 59.—By paternal right. Besides the authors cited, William of Jumièges, *Norman History*, Book VIII, ch. 34, and Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book XII: “Fulk the younger, count of Anjou, who was son-in-law and heir of Elias, count of Maine.”

Col. 98, line 60.—“The salvation of souls.” A formula customary in the West and not unknown to the Greeks.

[Col. 0131]

## Illustrious Testimonies of Eminent Men Concerning the Venerable Hildebert

### Saint Bernard

[Col. 0131B]

Besides calling the venerable Hildebert, in Epistle 44, Book II, “a great priest, exalted in the word of glory, and a great pillar of the Church,” and in Epistle 19, Book III (no. 123 in Mabillon’s edition), “a man deserving every reverence,” he addresses him thus in the same letter:

“You must see on what grounds you have chosen to write to me about me. I have an argument for your praises of me that leaves me in no doubt: your own letters praising me. In them another might perhaps delight in the distinction of learning, the sweet and pure style, the brilliant discourse, and the pleasing and praiseworthy brevity. But above all these, I prize the humility by which so great a man has taken care to anticipate so insignificant a one, both by the service of greeting, by the proclamation of praise, and by the reverence of prayer. … Nevertheless, what I am is yours; and if ever by God’s gift I shall be anything better, be assured that it will be yours, most reverend and most beloved Father.”

### Saint Anselm, Epistle 11, Book IV of Gerberon’s Edition, to Hildebert

[Col. 0131C]

“As I wish to avoid injustice, so I desire to embrace your friendship. I also confess that, if it were possible for me, I ought to love you twice as much as you love me, because you anticipated me in love, as you proved by your gift. For since you loved one undeserving, I ought to return no less. And since you indicated that what you had seen of our little works pleased you, we venture to send you some things which, I think, you have not yet seen.”

### Peter of Blois, Epistle 101, to R., Archdeacon of Nantes, on the Education of Boys

“I know that it greatly benefited me that, when I was being educated as a little boy, I drew my material not from fables but from the truth of histories. It benefited me [Col. 0132B] that, as an adolescent, I was compelled to memorize and recite word for word the letters of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, outstanding for elegance of style and gracious refinement.”

[Note: [Col. 0131C] From this the most learned M. Loyauté inferred in the notes cited above that Hildebert’s letters were set before students in his schools for imitation while he was still alive and able to see it. “For,” he says, “Hildebert’s age produced scarcely a man whose natural talent was more outstanding or whose speech more polished in winning renown.”]

### Ivo of Chartres, Epistle 167, to Hildebert

“We think well of your religious integrity, because, whenever the true and just judgment has shone upon you, you will not turn aside from the royal road.”

### Geoffrey of Vendôme, Epistle 13, Book III, to Hildebert, Concerning the Unlawful Election of Reginald to the See of Angers

“You have indeed begun well, because you have courageously risen up for the liberty of holy Church against her adversaries. Thus you have made yourself more dear to God and God’s friends, and by this have spread the fame of your name not a little.”

### The Same Geoffrey, in Epistle 11, Book III, to the Aforesaid Reginald

[Col. 0132C]

“Therefore Hildebert, a religious man who was the first bishop in the province after the metropolitan, did not keep silence. Although called by his metropolitan to your consecration, he absentented himself, and proclaimed on apostolic and evangelical authority that it was an execration rather than a consecration.”

Although a certain disagreement arose between Hildebert and Geoffrey concerning one John the Mason, a monk of Vendôme, whom Hildebert had borrowed from Geoffrey for the usefulness of his building works and retained longer than Geoffrey had hoped and wished, Geoffrey nevertheless always calls him in various letters (Epistle 15 and following) a bishop of good, blessed, and praiseworthy life. He frequently calls him venerable, dearest, his lord, and a friend dear to his heart and inmost affections. In Epistle 14 of Book III, he calls him at once a prudent and simple bishop and an excellent prelate; he promises that he will never depart from his counsel, and declares that he neither can nor ought to doubt his affection.

### Orderic Vitalis

It would be superfluous to repeat here the splendid encomia of honour with which Orderic, a contemporary of the venerable Hildebert, commended his name to posterity, since we have already reported them both in the dedicatory letter and in our preface to Hildebert’s works.

### William of Jumièges, *Norman History*, Book VI, p. 265, Concerning the Works of Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury

“The twelfth and last book was a treatise on the procession of the Holy Spirit. For at the Council of Bari he had refuted the Greeks, who denied that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. Taking his subject from this, at the request of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, he composed this book.”

This is also evident from Hildebert’s letter to Saint Anselm on this matter, namely Epistle 9, Book II, and from Saint Anselm’s Epistle 11 to Hildebert in the same book, which we have printed.

### William of Malmesbury, Book I, *On the Deeds of the Bishops of England*

“If you investigate literary learning, Hildebert drained Athens dry; if you seek eloquence, speech flows from his mouth in a certain honeyed stream, joined by the polished and, as it were, fastidious diction characteristic of his native soil—that is, Maine.”

### Marbod, Bishop of Rennes, Hildebert’s Contemporary, in Praise of Him and His Works

> When, reading your writings, I turn my eyes back to mine,  
> I seem to behold earth lying low from heaven.  
> Yours soar aloft beyond the clouds;  
> mine cling to earth, creeping with humble step.  
>
> Often reread, yours please the wise alone,  
> compressing hidden meanings into brief words,  
> as though a great gem were set in a little gold.  
> Mine lie open by an easy approach to unlearned and learned alike,  
> less carefully wrought in their maker’s preparation  
> and flowing lightly from a common vein.  
>
> Your Muse often bends itself through antithesis,  
> practising varied turns in sinuous arrangement.  
> For us it is enough to proceed along a straight path  
> and weave words, however coarse, with a thick Minerva;  
> nor do we prepare to contend with subtle Arachne.

### An Ancient Anonymous Writer on Hildebert

> Illustrious alike in prose and verse, and first in all things,  
> Hildebert breathes roses utterly everywhere.

### From Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Hildebert, archbishop of Tours, lived in the time of Pope Honorius II, to whom he wrote a letter.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] Indeed, several letters.]

Honorius began to hold the see in the year of the Lord [Col. 0133D] 1125. Hildebert wrote sermons, letters, and sacred poems, which are extant. Saint Bernard wrote one letter to him, exhorting him to acknowledge and venerate Innocent II as the true pope.

### The Most Illustrious Henry Spondanus, under 1088, no. 4

[Col. 0134A]

Following Baronius and using his words, he calls Hildebert a man of great learning and holiness alike, and a most vigorous defender of the liberty of the Church.

### From Volume I of Father Labbe’s Historical Dissertation on Bellarmine, of the Society of Jesus

Hildebert of Lavardin … whom William of Malmesbury mentions in Book III of *On the Deeds of the English*, was master of a school and, after Hoel, was elected bishop of Le Mans in 1097. Then, after the death of Archbishop Gilbert, by order of Honorius II, Roman pontiff, he was transferred in 1124 to the metropolitan see of Tours, where he died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the year 1132. The historians of Le Mans, Corvaisier and Bondonnet, disagree with one another on several points concerning him, and with Vossius, who assigns his death [Col. 0134B] to 1136, the eleventh year of Emperor Lothair. Consult them, and among earlier writers Ivo of Chartres, Geoffrey of Vendôme, and Saint Bernard in their letters; William of Malmesbury, Book V, ch. 9; Henry of Ghent, ch. 8; Bernard of Morlaix, monk of the Congregation of Cluny, in his book *On Contempt for the World*, addressed to Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny; Vincent of Beauvais, Saint Antoninus, Trithemius, and others.

### From the Gallican Martyrology of the Most Illustrious André du Saussay, Bishop of Toul, on the Third Day Before the Kalends of May

“At the monastery of Cluny, the deposition of Saint Hugh, abbot. … Chosen for the exceptional purity of his morals and excellence of mind, he discharged the arduous responsibility of so great a government with such praise for prudence and holiness that he deserved to be and to be called the archangel of monks. For truly great men flourished under his guidance and instruction and grew to that height which is near the cedars of heaven. Namely, Gregory VII and Urban II, supreme pontiffs; Alberic, bishop and cardinal of Ostia; and Hildebert, archbishop of Tours—all of whom, drawing from the fountain of his discipline and imitation the spirit of religion and saving knowledge, brought to the Church great honour and the abundant fruit of blessed assistance.”

### From the Same Martyrology, on the Fourteenth Day Before the Kalends of January

“Blessed Hildebert, archbishop of Tours, a great pillar of the Church and sounding trumpet of Christ, who defended his eternal testament upon indelible pages, having been laid to rest in the blessed sleep of death, passed to the honours of the heavenly kingdom. Of him one may indeed employ that notable eulogy which Saint Jerome long ago published concerning blessed Cyprian: ‘It is superfluous to compile a list of so great a genius, since his writings are brighter than the sun.’ Yet he was no less conspicuous and distinguished for pastoral zeal, priestly vigour, purity of life, devotion to religion, pursuit of justice, merit of patience, and the grace of every holiness.”

[Col. 0133] It is therefore not surprising that Peter de Natalibus, in his *Catalogue of Saints*, numbered Hildebert among the saints themselves; that Margarin de la Bigne in his 1589 edition of the *Library of the Fathers* adorned him with the title of saint; and that, imitating him, without objection from anyone, the Reverend Father Homey did likewise in his *Supplement to the Fathers* of 1684. John Maan, author of the *Metropolis of Tours*, also asserts that after his death Hildebert was renowned for miracles.

## [Letters and Charters]

[Col. 0135]

## Notice Concerning the Following Letters of the Venerable Hildebert

Since in our general preface to the works of the venerable Hildebert we have already spoken at sufficient length concerning the excellence and arrangement of his letters, we wish to give you, kindly reader, this one warning. Among the thirteen or more manuscript codices which we used for their recension, we found none in which they were not differently ordered from the others and indiscriminately placed. Therefore, following the example of more celebrated writers in a similar case, and on the advice of certain learned men, we judged that they should be reduced to several classes according to the diversity of their subjects. In this we especially followed the footsteps of the most learned Father Jacques Sirmond, whose memory can never be sufficiently venerated. When publishing the letters of Peter of Celle, which he had found in manuscripts placed in confusion, Sirmond distributed them into nine books for the greater convenience of the reader.

Likewise we judged it necessary to divide Hildebert’s letters into three books. Book I will therefore contain those concerning Christian devotion and the ascetic—or, as Hildebert himself more often says, contemplative—life. Book II will follow with those concerning Catholic doctrines or ecclesiastical discipline. Finally, Book III will contain those expressing simple familiarity among friends and honourable urbanity. Lest this alteration of their old order, which might cause some inconvenience to readers, be laid to our charge, we indicate in the margin of each letter the old order by such marks as “otherwise 2,” “otherwise 3,” and so forth; moreover, we here present their index, recording for each its former order and the new one lately assigned by us. We have also taken care, for public benefit, to arrange them all in chronological order, as far as we have been able to determine from the various histories, events, and conjectures of that age.

[Col. 0135]

# Letters of the Venerable Hildebert

## Book One

### Letter I

[Note: [Col. 0141C] Also numbered first. Written in the year 1100.]

### To Master William of Champeaux

[Note: [Col. 0141C] This is the same man who, having been archdeacon and teacher at Paris, became bishop of Châlons and ordained St Bernard abbot; he also attended Bernard in a severe illness. St Bernard mentions him honourably in Letter 3; see the notes of Dom Mabillon on that letter.]

[Note: [Col. 0141] + William was living outside the city of Paris, in the suburb beside the chapel dedicated to Saint Victor, in 1108.]

He congratulates him on his conversion from secular to Christian philosophy, promises him its perfection if only he neither fears nor hopes for anything, and meanwhile urges him not to cease from the office of teacher or preacher.

[Col. 0141A]

My soul rejoices and exults over your manner of life and conversion, pursuing with thanksgiving Him whose gift it is that you have at last resolved to practise philosophy. For you did not yet smell of the philosopher when, from the knowledge of philosophers that you had acquired, you drew forth no beauty of character at all.

But now, as sweetness of honey is drawn from the honeycomb,

[Note: [Col. 0141C] The Cologne and Paris editions read *lance*, “a lance”; all the manuscripts, and more correctly, read *favo*, “honeycomb.”]

so you have drawn from it a rule for right conduct. Hence, abandoning ecclesiastical dignities, you chose

[Col. 0141B]

[Note: [Col. 0141C] For, having relinquished the office of teacher, he had retired to the chapel of Saint Victor at Paris, [Col. 0142C] where he had begun a monastery, afterwards magnificently completed by Louis the Fat.]

to be lowly in the house of your God rather than dwell in the tents of sinners (Ps. 87:11). Hence you pursue ambitious possessions with inexorable hatred; hence you renounce the mercantile business of teaching; hence you judge godliness with sufficiency to be great gain (1 Tim. 6:6).

[Note: [Col. 0142C] This alludes to William’s teaching post: at Paris he publicly lectured on philosophy, perhaps gaining some profit from it, like a trader; among his hearers was Peter Abelard.]

Finally, hence you gather your whole self within the bounds of virtue; hence you do not deliberate with nature concerning your life,

[Note: [Col. 0142C] No manuscripts contain the particle *non*, “not”; nevertheless the Paris and Cologne editors judged it conducive to easier understanding.]

giving less attention to what the flesh can do than to what the spirit wills. This is truly to practise philosophy; to live thus is already to enter into a great fellowship with the heavenly beings. There is no shorter road from here to heaven. You will easily arrive there, provided you travel unburdened.

For the mind itself is a burden to itself until it ceases both to hope and to fear. No one yet lives blessedly if either the postponement of his desire torments him, or fear of falling away from his desire afflicts him.

[Col. 0141C]

Diogenes,

[Col. 0142A]

because he hoped for no one’s favour and feared no one’s power, passed a wealthy poverty in his tub, as empty of hope as he was free from fear. What the faithless Cynic so abhorred must be abhorred still more by the Christian teacher, in proportion as the profession which works through faith is more fruitful. These are obstacles to character and delay those advancing toward virtue.

Learned speech, plainer dress, and a more rigorous reconsideration of the principles of true religion make the Christian religious. Now you will display, and give expression to, the perfect philosopher if you neither hope for anything nor fear anything. This declares both true strength of mind and complete contempt for the world.

Yet report has it that some have persuaded you to abstain altogether from every kind of teaching.

[Col. 0142B]

On this matter, consider my view. Anyone who can benefit another but does not, advances without making progress. It is a virtue to provide the material of virtue even to one who will use it badly. Moreover, you have bound yourself by the evangelical counsel which the young man heard from Christ: “Go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Mark 10:21).

You therefore have a whole burnt offering to offer, not a sacrifice; for you have read in Gregory concerning their difference:

[Note: [Col. 0142C] *Homilies on Ezekiel*, Book II, Homily 9.]

> “In a sacrifice, a part of the animal is customarily offered; in a whole burnt offering, however, the whole is offered.”

And a little later:

> “When someone vows something of his own, it is a sacrifice; but when he vows to almighty God everything that he has, everything by which he lives, everything by which he understands, it is a whole burnt offering.”

Offer your whole self, then, to the Lord God,

[Col. 0142C]

because you have devoted your whole self to the Lord God; otherwise

[Col. 0143A]

you defraud Him of the whole burnt offering promised. Finally, “what use is hidden wisdom and hidden treasure in either case?” (Sirach 20:32). Gold gleams more beautifully when dispersed than when sealed. Gems differ in no respect from worthless tufa stones unless they are brought into public view. Knowledge too, when distributed, receives increase; scorning its greedy possessor, it slips away unless it is made public.

Do not therefore shut up the streams of your teaching. Rather, with Solomon: “Let your fountains flow abroad, and distribute your waters in the streets” (Prov. 5:16).

### Letter II

[Note: [Col. 0143D] Elsewhere numbered 8. Written about the year 1100.]

### To Archbishop A.

[Note: [Col. 0143D] Thus read Royal MS 4103, Victorine MS 272, and the Rouen manuscript of Saint Ouen: “to the archbishop,” namely St Anselm of Canterbury, among whose letters this is found addressed to him as Letter 50 of Book III.]

He sends a fan to his friend, ingeniously and devoutly suggesting its mystical meaning.

I have sent you a fan, an instrument well suited to driving away flies.

[Note: [Col. 0143D] On the use of the fan in the sacrifice of the Mass for driving away flies: according to James Gaetani, *Ordinarium*, ch. 53, it persisted until the fourteenth century in both the Eastern and Western Church, and even in the Roman Church itself. See Dom E. Martène, Book I, *On Ecclesiastical Rites*, ch. 4, art. 8.]

There is also something which you ought to interpret in our little gift. Consider, then, by what flies priests offering sacrifice to the Lord are more gravely harassed.

[Col. 0143B]

There are a thousand phantoms of intrusive thoughts, a thousand suggestions of the devil, a thousand temptations of mortal minds. When they insinuate themselves by an unexpected onset into the minds of those offering sacrifice,

[Note: [Col. 0143D] The editions read *inopinato*, “unexpected”; the Rouen and Évreux manuscripts read *inopino*, “unexpected.”]

when they distract them to think of other and irrelevant matters,

[Note: [Col. 0143D] The editions read *alia atque alia*, “one thing after another”; the Rouen and Évreux manuscripts read *alia atque aliena*, “other and alien matters.”]

when they attempt to introduce heretical perversity, what else do they do except harass and impede the ministers of the altar as certain flies harass those making sacrifice?

Our patriarch Abraham prefigured the driving away of such monstrous flies when he drove off the birds swooping down upon the sacrifices. For it is written: “Birds descended upon the carcasses, and Abraham drove them away” (Gen. 15:11).

[Col. 0143C]

Therefore, when with the fan sent to you, you drive away the flies descending upon the sacrifices, you ought also to disperse, with the fan of Catholic faith, the assaults of temptations which come upon the mind of the celebrant. Thus what has been accepted for practical use will furnish you with a mystical understanding.

And because the aforesaid birds are read to have descended only upon the sacrifices, not to have interrupted the rite itself, priests of Christ are thereby taught to drive away the temptations they endure in such a way that such a lapse does not compel them to abstain from the sacraments of the altar. For this failure is an infirmity which perfects strength, not one which renders the works of virtue void.

### Letter III

[Note: [Col. 0144D] Elsewhere numbered 25. Written about the year 1101.]

### To Countess A.

[Note: [Col. 0144D] This is probably Adela, wife of Stephen, count palatine of Blois, mentioned by Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book X, p. 789. He says that she was a shrewd and spirited woman, who urged her sluggish and timid husband to proceed to the holy war in the year of salvation 1101 with the other princes, and meanwhile vigorously undertook and wisely administered the government of the county of Blois in his absence.]

He praises Countess Adela for her exceptional prudence in governing the peoples entrusted to her by her absent husband, and especially commends clemency toward them.

[Col. 0144A]

The absence of your husband has imposed upon you the more laborious burden of public administration.

[Note: [Col. 0143] + Stephen, count of Blois, first crossed into Palestine in 1097 and again in 1101. In 1102, while fighting the Saracens, he was killed. From this the date at which Letter 3 was written is easily inferred.]

Yet you administer it both as a woman and alone, so that you need the assistance neither of a man nor of borrowed counsel. You possess all that the helm of government requires. Certainly such a great harmony [perhaps *concentus*, “harmony”] of good qualities in a woman belongs to grace, not nature.

God’s grace has accumulated for you titles worthy of praise, by which you might be a glory to your sex and might temper authority. For you honour womanhood while cherishing chastity in beauty; you restrain the countess

[Col. 0144B]

while preserving clemency in power. The former wins you your husband; the latter wins you your people. From one you gain renown; from the other, goodwill. Each good is, in itself, sufficiently distinguished and conspicuous, and needs no foreign tongue to plead for it.

Yet much praise accrues to clemency because it benefits more people. A beautiful and chaste woman provides for herself; but a gentle rule preserves the realm uninjured. The place of this virtue is surely among the powerful, who rule others by hereditary right, force, or the benefit of election. It is not so among the people, who possess no power to punish.

But he who is exalted detests cruelty and venerates

[Note: [Col. 0144D] Thus Victorine MS 272; Colbert MS 2662 and the Évreux manuscript read *adornat*, “adorns.”]

clemency, assigning the one to beasts and the other to human beings. It has decreed that people ought to become gentle through clemency, beasts feared through cruelty.

[Col. 0144C]

Therefore, to be cruel is to have fellowship with beasts and to deny one’s humanity. Moreover, reason is peculiar to humanity, by which it surpasses the other animals; it yields to God,

[Note: [Col. 0144D] Évreux: *credit*, “believes”; Colbert MS 2662, Victorine MS 272, and Rouen: *cedit*, “yields.”]

and reason has absolutely no fellowship with cruelty. Reason has made its divine dwelling with God and with the wise;

6

cruelty has migrated to the lowest regions and to those who delight in blood. What fellowship, then, has a human being with cruelty, when reason so loftily disdains it, leaves it so far behind, so steadfastly renounces it, and so wholly ignores it?

Reason has another companionship and is surrounded by other fellow-dwellers, among whom clemency holds no mean place. As nothing is closer to humanity than clemency, so nothing is more glorious in a ruler.

[Col. 0145A]

Clemency ought to attend reason as a handmaid attends the mistress of the household: at reason’s command it should soften stern powers, summon gentler dispositions, and spare the guilty. For reason presides over all virtues, appoints limits for all, and assigns to all the times of their proper duties.

Seneca thoughtfully composed concise maxims on clemency for rulers,

[Note: [Col. 0145D] Thus the Évreux manuscript and Colbert MS 2662. Rouen and Victorine MS 272 read: “he published the maxims of Seneca,” so that the sense is, “he provided Seneca’s brief sayings.” Hildebert himself appears to have written this in *On the Useful and the Honourable*, where he especially reports Seneca’s sayings from *On Clemency*.]

in which he chose brevity without obscurity so that those occupied with great affairs would not be weary of reading them. Receive, therefore, these maxims undertaken for you and addressed to you, and recall what you formerly learned from yourself and for yourself.

They are few:

> “It belongs to clemency to remove something from a punitive sentence. Whoever leaves no offence unpunished commits an offence. It is a fault to pursue the whole fault. He declares himself merciless whose pleasure is whatever is permitted to him.”

Likewise:

> “It is a glorious virtue in a ruler to punish less than he is permitted. It is virtue to be drawn to vengeance by necessity, not to approach it by will. It is a great thing and has something divine about it when an offended person is merciful.”

Likewise:

> “A good ruler punishes no one without penalty, proscribes no one without grief. A good ruler pursues a crime in such a way that, when he punishes, he remembers the person is human.”

Likewise:

> “A good ruler governs himself and serves the people; he despises no one’s blood—not even that of an enemy, who may become a friend; not even that of an offender, who is still a human being. Whoever the person may be, since he could not give him the crime, he thinks to take it away. Therefore, whenever blood is shed, he is ashamed.”

[Col. 0145B]

These things suffice for a mind teachable and loving discipline. From them the more diligent will readily perceive how much cruelty harms authority and how much clemency benefits it.

[Col. 0145C]

Farewell.

### Letter IV

[Note: [Col. 0145D] Elsewhere numbered 71. Written about the year 1101.]

### To a Certain Countess

This letter seems to have been addressed to Countess Adela, wife of Stephen,

[Note: [Col. 0145D] In that same year, 1101, Stephen returned to Jerusalem for the second time and, during the siege of Ramla, was captured and killed by Aropastus, satrap of the Babylonians, according to Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book X.]

count of Blois. After her husband’s death she consecrated herself to God by a monastic vow. Hildebert applauds her and offers notable counsel against temptations threatening from every side; so that she may deserve to attain the grace of perseverance in the struggle she has undertaken, he particularly commends humility to her, calling it the completion and conclusion of the other virtues.

[Note: [Col. 0145] + Adela, countess of Blois, embraced the regular life in the monastery of Marcigny in the diocese of Autun (William of Jumièges, *History of Normandy*, Book VIII, ch. 39); but the year is uncertain. Dom Beaugendre assigns Hildebert’s letter to the year 1101, incorrectly, since after Stephen’s death the countess of Blois undertook the administration of the county in the name of her son, who had not yet reached manhood.]

Whenever I hear what is happening around you,

[Note: [Col. 0146D] Thus the Évreux, Rouen, and Victorine manuscripts; Colbert MS 1168 alone reads *sunt*, “are.”]

my spirit rejoices and exults. For I hear that you are being led along the path of God’s commandments and are running with unoffending step toward the land of the living.

I hear also that, from a wealthy woman,

[Col. 0145D]

you have become poor in spirit; from a most splendid countess surrounded by throngs of attendants,

[Col. 0146A]

a humble nun, and, after the fashion of the lowliest little servant-girl, one who both provides what is necessary for the other daughters of Christ serving the Lord with you and most diligently ministers to them.

Certainly, this change is “a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.” In it you must heed the saying of the wise man: “My son, when you come to the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Sirach 2:1). I do not doubt that you have come to this service, since you came to Christ’s service through prudence.

For it was prudence that you chose

[Note: [Col. 0146D] Thus two Colbert manuscripts; Royal MS 4013 reads *quam*, “than.”]

to be lowly in the house of God rather than dwell in the tents of sinners (Ps. 83:11). But you are mistaken if, amid temptations about to emerge, you think your choice safe and think it will be brought to completion

[Note: [Col. 0146D] Thus Colbert MS 1168; Royal MS 4003 and Colbert MS 4017 read *consumendam*, “to be consumed.”]

without severe struggle. In it adversities will strike your spirit, prosperity will shake it,

[Col. 0146B]

and self-exaltation will weary it.

Against such things you must fight in such a way that enemies attacking a woman find a man. Do not think that this can happen otherwise than by retaining through fortitude in hardships the good to which you bound yourself through prudence, through temperance in prosperity, and through humility in right actions.

[Note: [Col. 0146D] Here this letter ends in the Rouen and Évreux manuscripts; but in six Colbert and two Victorine manuscripts it continues as printed here, and so in all editions.]

Israel is broken by adversities in the wilderness; under the burning thirst and failure of food it murmurs against Moses; it prefers Egyptian slavery to divine mercies. Therefore, because fortitude perished in them, they too are said to have perished from serpents.

8

The same people in the land of Midian sat down to eat and drink; then, rising to play, swollen with feasting and drunkenness, it committed fornication (Exod. 32). Consequently, twenty-three thousand of them fell in one day, devoured by swords in punishment for intemperance.

[Col. 0146C]

You see, then, O daughter of Christ Jesus, how carefully fortitude amid hardships and temperance amid prosperity must be guarded. Contempt for the world requires both; if either is lacking, whatever is chosen through prudence is emptied of worth.

But you are mistaken if, having attained these, you suppose your purpose already safe; if, sailing on this great and spacious sea, you think that you have reached port. Humility remains, and it must be joined to the other virtues if you are to receive the prize laid up for you.

By humility that course is brought to completion by which one passes from miseries to true sufficiency, ascends from houses of mud to heavenly dwellings, and returns from exile to the homeland. If you do not know what this course is, read Augustine writing these words to Macedonius:

[Col. 0146D]

[Note: [Col. 0146D] Letter 1055, vol. II of the new edition, p. 540d.]

> “Virtue in this life is nothing other than loving what ought to be loved. Not to be turned aside from it by any hardships is fortitude; not to be turned aside by any allurements is temperance; not to be turned aside by any pride is justice.”

[Col. 0147A]

In this place, humility is understood under the name of justice, as the completion and conclusion of the other virtues. Therefore the Lord also says to His disciples: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:29).

Peter and Andrew had already left their boat and nets. John had already offered the whole burnt offering of virginity. Matthew had already left the tax-office. The other apostles had already said: “Lord, behold, we have left all things and followed you; what then shall we have?” (Matt. 19:27).

Consider why those who were enemies of the flesh and the world are invited to humility. Consider what they still needed for the fullness

[Col. 0147B]

of perfection, though they had already followed Christ and left everything except Christ. A great treasure requires great protection; for the thief is eager to dig through, steal, and carry away.

The apostles possessed a precious and inestimable treasure: the very grace of redemption and Christ’s divine conversation. It was a treasure to them to be taught by Him nothing but to hate vice and embrace virtue. It was a treasure to them to progress daily, through His miracles and examples, in love of heavenly things.

Humility had to be the guardian of this treasure, and its watch had to bar pride’s approach—

9

pride, which, where it could not remain itself,

[Note: [Col. 0147C] Thus Colbert MS 1168; Colbert MS 4017 reads *sustinere*, “endure.”]

hardly endures that anyone should arrive. Born with the seal of God’s likeness, it fell from heavenly loftiness into the lower parts of the earth. Its father had a certain prerogative of blessedness: to be more expressly like the Creator.

[Col. 0147C]

But the higher he was by condition, the lower he became in power and glory. Pride lost the glory which he had through grace, by which he envies everyone; but he leaves no one in hell whom he has acquired by deserts.

[Note: [Col. 0147C] An obscure passage. It might be expressed more clearly thus: “The glory which he had by grace [the Colbert manuscript reads *habuit*, ‘had’; printed editions, *hauserat*, ‘had drawn’] pride lost, since it envies all; but he leaves no one in hell—that is, among the damned—whom he has obtained through deserts, namely those whom he has made his own under the title of evil deserts or sins.”]

For many freely follow him to hell, because he draws more people by many kinds of temptations. But against those whose face is turned toward the city from which he went out never to return, he burns with such envy that it is too little for him to have inflicted on them the death by which the body, not the soul, dies, unless he also inflicts that death by which body and soul alike

[Note: [Col. 0147D] Colbert MS 4017: “body and soul together.”]

[Col. 0148A]

die.

Hence he never ceases to oppose them, wholly intent upon making them, with Lot’s wife, look back toward Sodom’s sulphur and fire, fail to attend to Joseph’s tunic, and cease offering the tail of the victim in sacrifice.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] Colbert MS 1168: “the victim of the tail”; Colbert MS 4017, better: “the tail of the victim.”]

But above all he fights through self-exaltation, because, as he knows that he alone was defeated by it, so he believes that all can be defeated by it alone.

You, therefore, remember to embrace humility, knowing that there is nothing by which Satan is more gloriously conquered. Set the shield

[Note: [Col. 0147D] Colbert MS 1168: *scutum*, “shield”; Colbert MS 4017: *saccum*, “sack.”]

of humility against his darts. If he finds it impenetrable, he will be put to shame and cease persecuting you. Thus Bede also says on Luke: “When every temptation of Christ had been completed,

[Note: [Col. 0147D] Colbert MS 1168: *consumpta*, “consumed”; Colbert MS 4017, and more suitably to the biblical text: *consummata*, “completed.”]

the devil departed from him until a time.”

[Note: [Col. 0147D] The manuscript codices vary here and do not express an entirely clear sense. Victorine MS 272 seems clearer, reading: “You see that the devil himself is not persistent in his endeavour, that he is accustomed to yield to true virtue; and although he does not cease to envy, still he fears to press on, because he more often shrinks from being conquered.” Let the reader judge.]

You see the devil himself persistent in his endeavour, so that he does not cease to envy the offspring of the Church, true virtue;

[Col. 0148B]

yet he fears what is just, because he more often rises again

[Note: [Col. 0148D] Colbert MS 1168: *refugit*, “shrinks back.”]

to be conquered.

[Note: [Col. 0148D] Colbert MS 4017: *resurgat*, “may rise again.”]

### Letter V

[Note: [Col. 0148D] Elsewhere numbered 63. Written about the year 1112.]

### To an Illustrious Widow

[Note: [Col. 0148D] Probably Agnes, daughter of Peter, duke of Poitiers, first the widow of Alfonso the Elder, king of Galicia, and then widow of Elias, count of Le Mans, who died in 1101. After his death she consecrated herself to God in a monastery. Thus Orderic Vitalis, Book X of the *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 785. It therefore seems to have been written about 1102.]

He congratulates her because, abandoning her plan of pilgrimage to the Lord’s tomb, she preferred, renouncing all things, to take up Christ’s cross in a monastery rather than visit His tomb.

[Note: [Col. 0147] + This letter does not seem to have been written in 1101 or 1102. Dom Beaugendre states that Elias, count of Le Mans, died in 1101, but incorrectly, since he died only in 1110. Alford, who copied this letter of Hildebert in his *Annals of the English Church*, year 1125, no. 23, and Dupin, twelfth century, p. 495, hold that it was sent to Adela, countess of Blois; this opinion, however, is rejected by the learned authors of the *Literary History*.]

Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, to A., servant and daughter of Christ—formerly his beloved, but now most dearly beloved: may she deserve a good end from a good beginning.

My spirit rejoices and applauds as you depart from the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, praising and glorifying God because, resisting Egyptian slavery, you have set out upon the road to the land of promise.

[Col. 0148C]

I trust in my Lord Jesus Christ that He will make your desire prosperous, that He will perfect your steps in His paths, so that your feet may not be moved (Ps. 16:5). And indeed, I thought that the daughter of Abraham would leave Egypt by another road; but the daughter of Abraham chose a shorter way.

For I thought that you greatly desired to visit the Saviour’s tomb and to venerate in Christian devotion the workshops of our Redemption. I knew that you were offering rightly, but I doubted whether you would also divide rightly. But you have both offered rightly and divided rightly. You have offered rightly because you left all things for Christ.

[Col. 0149A]

You have also divided rightly because you preferred to follow Christ buried rather than Christ’s tomb. This division, moreover, is salutary and full of counsel. For, in order that we may become Christ’s disciples, we are commanded to carry His cross, not to seek His burial-place.

Therefore, that you may both carry this cross and follow Christ, embrace patience and embrace humility. Among the other virtues, these are found to have held primacy in human redemption. If you consider carefully, Christ’s whole life on earth was nothing other than an example and instruction

11

in these virtues.

As you proceed toward the promised Jerusalem through the serpents of this wilderness and innumerable enemies, keep the eyes of your mind fixed, so that Solomon’s saying may be fulfilled in you: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness” (Eccl. 2:14).

[Col. 0149B]

Farewell.

### Letter VI

[Note: [Col. 0149C] Otherwise 41. It appears to have been written about the year 1104.]

To Countess Adela.

[Note: [Col. 0149D] Thus the editions and several manuscripts read; but Royal MS 4103 and Victorine MS 272 give this title: “To a certain woman who, though the wife of a knight, wished to become the wife of God.” This Countess Adela may perhaps be the Countess of Blois, of whom William of Jumièges speaks thus in *History of Normandy*, book VIII, chapter 39: “When Count Stephen of Blois, husband of Adela, daughter of William, king of the English, had died, she herself governed the county for some time, because her sons were still too incapable of administering the government. When they had grown up, she adopted the habit and manner of life of a religious woman at Marcigny, during the time of Lord Peter, abbot of Cluny, and there persevered praiseworthily in God’s service until the end.”

Yet, since Hildebert calls this Countess A. so expressly “his lady,” because she was the spouse of his lord, A. may also be understood as Countess Agnes, wife of Count Elias of Le Mans, under whose jurisdiction Hildebert, as bishop of Le Mans, was subject. For after her husband had been taken from life one year after their marriage [Col. 0150C–D], she had devoted herself wholly to good works, although otherwise nothing is established concerning her becoming a nun. Nor does the fact that Hildebert addresses this Countess A. as though she were a sinner seem to oppose either opinion; for, in comparison with the more perfect monastic state, her former life amid the commotion of court and the enticements of pleasures could have given grounds for the characterization of a sinner.

Moreover, in the same William of Jumièges, book VIII, chapter 34, one of the daughters of Count Elias of Le Mans is mentioned, who, he says, married William, son of Henry, king of the English; after his death she took the religious habit at Fontevraud. Its nuns had sought and obtained from the supreme pontiff Hildebert as their patron and, as it were, director. That he fulfilled this office with the greatest zeal is shown, among other things, by his letter to Pope Honorius seeking confirmation of an alms granted to that monastery by Henry I, king of the English.]

To this widow, formerly reared amid courtly pleasures, he congratulates her on her marriage to Christ—undoubtedly through monastic profession. Hildebert very kindly urges her not to lose heart because of her perhaps somewhat freer life formerly lived in the world; for he maintains that penitents can please God as the righteous do, and widows as virgins do. He offers her various warnings from Scripture against impending temptations.

H., humble bishop of Le Mans, to A., his lady and beloved: may she earn good outcomes from a good beginning.

Know that when I call you my lady, it is because of your merit; when I call you beloved, it is because of my obligation. The spouse of my lord [Col. 0149C] is my lady. For this reason I embrace you with pure and simple [variant: “and holy”] love; for this reason I am jealous for you with God’s jealousy. I should be beaten before Christ as judge, if I did not zealously care for the spouse of Christ in Christ and for Christ.

For I say again: you are the spouse of the Lord Jesus Christ. You have been brought from the chamber of a knight to the embraces of the King. The wife of a man, you have become the wife of God. Yet I do not want you to fear repudiation, because, when you were a virgin, you preferred a man to God, a knight to the King. Our Hosea takes a prostitute as his wife (Hos. IX); Moses delights in marriage with an Ethiopian woman (Num. XII). Thus Christ quenches his thirst when the Samaritan woman offers him a cup (John IV). In streets and lanes the Gospel seeks out the poor and weak, [Col. 0150A] the blind and lame (Luke XIV:21), so that the house of the master of the household may be filled. Of creeping creatures and unclean things you have read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Kill and eat” (Acts X:13). Finally, she of whom John says in the Gospel, “Jesus loved Mary and her sister Martha and Lazarus” (John XI:5), had been a sinner.

There are innumerable examples by which Christ is represented as deigning to take even sinful women into marriage with himself. For it was said not of the righteous alone, but also of such persons: “Turn to me, and I shall turn to you” (Zech. I:3). The Evangelist says: “Some of them came from far away” (Mark VIII:3). From far away came that prodigal son, whom his father received amid music and dancing and killed the fattened calf for him (Luke XV). [Col. 0150B] Your Bridegroom zealously welcomes those who come from afar, and offers himself as husband to women who have lost count of their husbands.

Thus Christ has many wives. Agnes is his wife, and Anna, and Susanna. Agnes is wife of none but him; Anna, after another husband, is nevertheless his; Susanna is both another’s and his at once. She who loves him more bears more abundantly. She who bears more is endowed by him more exaltedly. Yet none is without a dowry, because none is barren. Among the brides of men—if the physician speaks truthfully—the fertility of all women ceases in the fiftieth year. Some receive no blessing of children at all. Among Christ’s spouses it is not so. Neither nature nor time makes any woman barren. Every age conceives by him and bears for him.

Christ’s marriage begins, indeed, at birth. All are born virgins, [Col. 0150C] a condition to which primacy in the heavenly bridal chamber belongs. A woman who bears a woman becomes God’s mother-in-law before becoming a man’s mother-in-law. What a festive—so festive—marriage! Happy is she who, scarcely born, is already married! Truly happy is she who is born for the King and law of angels! For angels neither marry nor are given in marriage (Mark XII:25), and their condition knows no sex. What need I say of Christ’s other spouses, whose fertility abounds in old age? Anna was more fruitful at eighty than she had been as a young woman (I Sam. II). Sarah bore one son to Abraham (Gen. XXIV), but bore several to the Lord. All, as Solomon says, are “with twin offspring, and none among them is barren” (Song IV:2). These are they who [Col. 0151A] say with the prophet: “Through fear of you we grew faint, and were in pain, and gave birth: we have brought forth the spirit of salvation upon the earth” (Isa. XVI:18). From him you too, my sister, my lady—from him, if I am not mistaken—have conceived. But if you have conceived, you must suffer before childbirth; and when you have suffered, you must strive to give birth. When you have given birth, then at last you will truly say: “We have brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth.”

I know, my dearest, that you have read Solomon saying: “He who fears the Lord will do good things” (Ecclus. XV:1), and in the Psalm: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX:8). But it is not the wisdom that is foolish with God, by which men are wise in doing evil; it is that wisdom which the Apostle speaks among the perfect, by which prudent virgins receive oil in their vessels [Col. 0151B] and are admitted with the bridegroom to the wedding (Luke XXV). From fear you conceived this wisdom; from conscience [variant: “from steadfastness”] you conceived fear.

Did you rejoice in plunder? You had read: “Neither thieves nor the greedy shall possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI:10). Did you lie? You had read: “The lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. I:11). Did you seek to please young men, to the injury of chastity? You had read: “Those who please men are confounded, because God has rejected them” (Ps. LII:6). Did you heed and satisfy the belly? You had read: “Food is for the belly and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (I Cor. VI:13). Had your better years passed away, while you had still done nothing good? You had read: “Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and have found none; cut it down” (Luke XIII:7).

You had done these evils, or no good at all. [Col. 0151C] You feared judgment—and rightly feared it—for you had learned that the judge will say: “Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. VIII:12). A sentence indeed to be feared and trembled at. Fear of this kind is the fear of a slave, but it is useful; for from a slave it makes a son, and, if a son, then an heir—an heir indeed of God and co-heir with Christ. By this fear you began to fear and to conceive.

Where, or what, did you begin? In the field of your mind: the spirit of a penitent. Truly a delicate conception, easily miscarried before birth. There are a thousand poisons of demons; once they have been introduced, the tender seed commonly withers away entirely and is killed, even when it has begun to gain strength. Hence Ambrose says: “I have found more easily those who have preserved innocence than those who have performed true repentance.” [Col. 0151D]

[Note: *Confessions*, book III, chapter 11, §2.]

For those who have professed repentance, remembrance of former pleasures is dangerous. The flesh longs for them most tenderly; and, forgetful of Lot’s wife, it repeatedly urges the spirit which has gone out from Sodom to look back. In this matter it is greatly and constantly intent, not so much on obtaining consent as on extorting it. Nor is it difficult for it to triumph in such a conflict, since we are all easily drawn by enticements and the inclination toward sin is more effective than the spirit’s inclination toward virtue. Therefore the inner person must suffer, since he no longer wills what he does, but does what he does not will.

I do not want you to be terrified; I do not want you to despair, if, as you begin to flee [Col. 0152A] yourself, the itch of pleasures, as though behind your back, whispers; if, in accordance with Augustine’s recollection of himself, it tugs at your garment of flesh and says: “Where are you fleeing? What have you to do with a way of life for which feminine weakness is unequal? What have you to do with a burden under which the frailty of the female sex promises collapse? Do you imagine that tender limbs, reared amid refined luxuries, can endure a long martyrdom?”

Begin—but begin in such a way that you will not repent of having begun. Let your effort be proportioned to your strength, lest you attempt what you cannot accomplish. Flesh and womanhood are a double weakness, and scarcely learn to unlearn companionship with pleasure. In neither case is religious life safe until a more mature age extinguishes the fire of both. At that time you will begin more wisely what you now profess at risk. No one repents too late whom death finds repenting. [Col. 0152B] The thief at the end of life, in gaining paradise, left an example. You have read that workers who came about the eleventh hour were made equal in reward to those who had borne the burden and heat of the day.

These and similar things oppose sacred beginnings; they extinguish the seed of virtue and choke it before birth. Such are the sirens, bitterly sweet; such are the birds of heaven, singing to the soul that is beginning. If you listen to the sirens, you will leave the harbor, drawn farther into the whirlpool of pleasures. If the birds delight you, you sow in vain, because what you sow will be eaten by birds. If you are wise, you will make yourself deaf to songs so deadly; and, lest you hear them, you will stop the ears of your mind after the example of the asp.

You have the shield of faith, by which you can receive all the darts sent by the evil one [Col. 0152C] and extinguish their fire. Weapons are also prepared for you, with which to pierce and defeat hostile enemies. If story-spinning spirits and the incanting impulses of the flesh make a noise around you, be steadfast and say: “Depart from me, you wicked ones, and I will search out the commandments of my God” (Ps. CXVIII:115). If you feel the woman within you growing warm again and wanting to fly back to her follies, be steadfast and say: “Lord, pierce my flesh with your fear; for I feared your judgments” (ibid., 120). If you begin to hate poverty and perceive a desire for riches being stirred up, return to yourself and say: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation here” (Luke VI:24). If a flatterer delights you and you grow cheerful at the praise of the little crowd, return to yourself and say: “Let not the oil of the sinner [Col. 0152D] make my head fat” (Ps. CXL:115). If it is suggested to you that you should postpone your good resolve until cooler years, answer and say: “My days will come like a thief in the night.” If raging gluttony commends more sumptuous preparations to you, answer and say: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink” (Rom. XIV:17).

By such rebukes as these enemies flee, the memory of pleasures melts away, the chatter of the flesh falls silent, and the beginnings of a holy way of life grow strong. By these means whatever the good soil of your heart has conceived from fear of the Lord your God, its cultivator, will be formed and advance toward good. Understand this fruit as the fruit of the Spirit, the fruit of which the Apostle says: “The fruit of the Spirit [Col. 0153A] is joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity; against such things there is no law” (Gal. I:22–23). In children such as these an eternal inheritance is acquired. Happy are you if such blessed offspring praise and rejoice within you; happier still if your enemy cannot triumph over you through them.

Perhaps you do not know it; but Pharaoh, still alive, rages against males of this sort, persistently practicing the envy which began before their birth and continues after it. Those whose conception caused him pain, he drowns in the river after they are born; he does not know how to be reconciled with those now born whom he hated before their birth. He therefore persecutes them to this day, nor is he ashamed to engage again after defeat, provided he hopes at last to conquer. Therefore, whether you are still giving birth or have already brought up those to whom you have given birth, fear that Pharaoh, than whom, as nothing is more perverse, so nothing is more crafty (Exod. I). Through his craftiness he triumphed over the first woman with scant equipment: with one apple he conquered; in attacking her person, he wounded human nature also. Hence the whole offspring was corrupted, and he, conqueror of the parents, found their heirs already cast down.

Therefore do not forget with what enemy you have entered into war, for what inheritance you have undertaken battle, so that you may watch over your salvation no less because of the enemy’s persistence than because of the greatness of the reward; seeking to conquer in him and through him who, dying for you, conquered, and, buried, triumphed: Jesus Christ our Lord.

### Letter VII

[Note: [Col. 0153C] Otherwise 15. Written about the year 1110.]

To M., Queen of the English.

[Note: [Col. 0153C–D] The initial M., prefixed in most manuscripts—namely, Évreux MS 19, Royal MS 4103, Colbertine MS 2131, and others—to the title “Queen of the English,” does not seem to designate any queen other than Matilda, or Maud, daughter of Malcolm, king of Scotland; sister of St Margaret; and sister of the three brothers who succeeded one another on the Scottish throne, namely Edgar, Alexander, and David. She married Henry I, king of England, after William Rufus. St Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, consecrated and crowned her. Thus says Ingulf, writer of English history, and the *Chronicle of Melrose*, p. 162.

Ethelred, abbot of Rievaulx, gives remarkable accounts of this queen’s virtues and piety, especially of her ardent charity to the poor and her heroic charity toward lepers, in his *Genealogy of the Kings of England*, near the end, or p. 368; there he calls her “most excellent and most Christian.” Henry Knyghton, canon of Leicester, likewise tells similar things about her in book II of *On the Events of England*. He states that she was reared from her earliest childhood among the nuns of Winchester; that she wore the sacred veil in order to avoid marriages repeatedly offered by her father; but that she was unable to refuse marriage with Henry I, king of England. St Anselm did not consent to this marriage until lawful witnesses had proved to him that she had assumed the veil without profession, and only as a pretext for refusing suitors.

According to Ingulf, this pious queen died in 1118, certainly full of good works. Hildebert’s salutary admonitions, full of apostolic freedom, may well be believed to have helped her persevere in those works.]

He congratulates the Princess Matilda on her marriage to the king of the English—undoubtedly Henry I—and urges her to give sincere thanks to God, the giver of all good things, and to use temporal goods with greater moderation because the righteous Judge will demand from her a stricter account of them.

[Col. 0153C]

I rejoice in your honor and in your good reputation, which becomes more favorable in my knowledge day by day. I rejoice, I say, and give thanks to the Lord God for your good, because your good is nothing other than his gift. For what do you have that you have not received? (I Cor. IV:13.) “And we all,” says the Evangelist, “have received from his fullness” [Col. 0154A] (John I:16)—from that fullness, namely, through which you have received being, have received the power to be good, and have received the power even to become better.

Consider, therefore, what you possess from so good a maker, and attend to what you owe him for so great a benefit. Consider what kind of person your craftsman has fashioned you to be, and work lest his work degenerate. I speak of temporal and passing things; but temporal and passing things too are gifts of the Lord your God. You did not earn being born noble, yet you were born of royal blood. You did not labor, yet you were made rich. You did not concern yourself about power, and behold, you have been set above the heads of the children of men. You did not entreat anyone for the glory of beauty, yet you were made beautiful even for the delights of a king. The Lord God has done these works: God is good, his works are good, because he who is supremely good made all things very good. [Col. 0154B]

Men are not good through these goods; rather, by using them well, they make themselves good. Therefore, that you too may be good before the Lord your God, use his good gift well. If you use it well, it is both his gift and your good; but if badly, it is indeed his good gift, yet by using God’s good gift badly you make your own evil. For nothing is good for a human being except the human being’s good self.

[Note: [Col. 0154D] The word *se* (“himself”) is absent in the Évreux manuscript; it is present in Colbertine 2662, Victorine 272, and Rouen.]

“And all things cooperate for good for those who are good and love God” (Rom. VIII:18). But the gifts of God are a loss to idle possessors; for in their case refusal to trade for profit is a very effective trade for punishment. Understand what I say, for the Lord has given you understanding. This our God is a great lender. I speak before him.

[Note: [Col. 0154D] Thus Colbertine, Victorine, and Rouen; but Évreux reads, “before God.”]

[Col. 0154C]

This creditor of ours urgently demands interest at an inconvenient time.

[Note: [Col. 0154D] “Creditor”: thus Victorine and Rouen. Colbertine and Victorine [apparently a conflicting report] read *creator* (“maker”).]

He is our creditor and stern; he is that man who went on a journey. He will return at the full moon.

[Note: [Col. 0154D] Colbertine 2662: “that one at the full moon”; Victorine: “that one, at the full moon”; Rouen and Évreux: “he himself at the full moon.”]

When he returns, he will demand double from you. When he has received it, he will reward you a hundredfold.

[Note: [Col. 0154D] Évreux: *centuplum* (“a hundredfold”); Colbertine 2662, Victorine 272, and Rouen read *centuplo* (“a hundredfold,” adverbially).]

O blessed exchange, in which the one demanding interest is not accused of wrongdoing, nor is the one paying burdened in any respect! O happy commerce, in which the creditor is seasonably importunate, and more than is owed is owed to the debtor! Therefore, you must fear coming to judgment without pardon if—far be it from you—you imagine that negligence in trading will go unpunished through forgetfulness. Understand what I say: [Col. 0155A] this creditor of ours has a great memory. You have forgotten yourself in a way deserving punishment if you think that he has forgotten his debt. He forgets nothing through time and nothing through preoccupation. He remembers equally what he grants today and what he granted yesterday, because both today and yesterday are his. Days upon days pass away, and years upon years; but a thousand days and a thousand years are before his eyes as yesterday’s day which has passed (Ps. LXXXIX).

Will he not then count how much he has lent you, he who alone counts the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the days of the age? (Ecclus. I:2.) Will he not divide your talents down to the smallest fractions,

[Note: [Col. 0155D] Victorine alone reads *sua* (“his”); Colbertine 2662, Victorine 272, and Rouen read *tua* (“your”).]

he who in his wisdom divided the waters from the waters? Perhaps you will summon your creditor to court when he demands from you what he entrusted to you? Understand what I say: he who will settle accounts with you is a good advocate. [Col. 0155B] Before angels he will recount the matter, yield it to truth, bring forward terrifying things, and bring in dreadful things.

But you say to me: “Though offended, he promises himself merciful; he neglects punishment, admits the penitent, withdraws threats, forgives debts, and entrusts greater things.”

[Note: [Col. 0155D] The particle *se* is absent in Rouen.]

It is so, I say. I confess it. “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. CXVIII:54). Yet many hunt after it fruitlessly. Although they have renounced the pursuit of doing good, they nevertheless hope that God—whom they deserve to have as judge—will be merciful, as though finding him propitious were the reward of wickedness, rather than, as we believe, the reward of religion. But it is not so. Evil persons do not gain God’s mercy, which even good persons promise themselves only with fear. To hope in it is a most salutary counsel; to depend wholly upon it [Col. 0155C] is a dangerous refuge. Some good things must soften the judge if we wish many evils to be judged mercifully. A cause for pardon which is close at hand is not wholly guilty. Virtue, when it comes with its beloved before the judge, intercedes. But those who are strangers to justice find the judge a stranger to mercy. Who, then, will act for you, if he—God forbid—pleads against you and turns away from you? “It is a dreadful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. X:31). Farewell; and use pleasures as a queen, not for yourself.

### Letter VIII

[Note: [Col. 0155D] Otherwise 47. Written about the year 1110.]

[Note: [Col. 0155D] Although this letter is without title in all the manuscripts I have seen, we might suppose it was sent by Hildebert to William of Champeaux at the beginning of his conversion and withdrawal to the chapel of Saint Victor, which later became a famous monastery, in order to strengthen him in the holy purpose which Hildebert had praised in the first letter of this book. The similarity of thought and wording in both letters gives room for this conjecture. In the first, he extols William because he had renounced teaching for gain, preferring piety with sufficiency to it as great profit; in this letter, he applauds him because he has offered gold and silver to God by religiously refusing them for God’s sake. In the earlier letter he urges the renunciation of temporal things, so that a mind unburdened by them may more easily be borne toward God; in this following letter, in nearly the same words, he urges the flight from desires, so that a mind coming from above, unburdened of them, may return above more freely. Accordingly, if the conjecture is sound, we should judge this letter to have been written about 1110.]

He addresses a friend, apparently recently appointed to some ecclesiastical dignity, concerning the gravity and dangers of avarice. He gracefully commends him because, by generously refusing for God’s sake the gold, silver, and other gifts offered to him, he has offered God a sacrifice most pleasing to him.

[Col. 0156A]

We rejoice at the preceding beginnings of your holy manner of life, praying their author that you may deserve to put on the ankle-length tunic and offer the tail of the victim in sacrifice (Lev. III:9). We are confident, through the cooperation of Christ Jesus, that this will come to pass. We carry good hope with us, because under his guidance you will attain the prize, since he moved you to run. In this purpose you have already learned by experience, unless we are mistaken, how many hindrances will meet you. For those advancing toward virtue find everywhere things against which they stumble. To profess it is easy enough; to persevere is difficult. Thus, although the goal toward which people run is near, many nevertheless fail on the very short road.

For we are all in Egypt, where Pharaoh, still surviving, persecutes the life of males (Exod. I).
