So many fell in the wilderness, either by swords or serpent bites, that only two entered the promised land. Finally: “Many are called, but few chosen” (Matt. XXII:14). What, however, chiefly delays priests striving in this contest, even if it does not escape your prudence, we have nevertheless resolved to write to you—not to teach you so much as to exhort you. A horse, even when running well, is greatly helped by encouraging shouts. Young oxen [Col. 0156C] move more swiftly when stirred by familiar voices.

[Note: [Col. 0156D] Évreux reads *inventis*, but Colbertine 2662, Victorine 272, and the printed editions more correctly read *juvenci* (“young oxen”).]

So virtue too seeks spurs and gains increase by exhortation. Therefore, for one laboring toward the true good, nothing is equally harmful as failing to stand firm amid riches and failing to retain freedom of mind. A mind coming from above strives upward and will scarcely reach what it aspires to unless it proceeds unburdened.

[Note: [Col. 0156D] The same thought occurs in book I, letter 1, to William of Champeaux.]

As soon as it declines toward lower goods, it degenerates and begins, through its own defect, to serve, though by nature it belongs to it to rule. It is exceedingly difficult to shake off this servitude, which is endured through will rather than necessity. For love of possession is an imperious lord, conquering minds more easily than bodies—the cruelty of Sicilian tyrants.

[Note: [Col. 0156D] Colbertine 2662 reads *singulorum immanitas* (“the cruelty of individuals”); Évreux, Victorine, and the editions read *Siculorum immanitas* (“the cruelty of Sicilians”). In all manuscripts *immanitas* is nominative, producing an incomplete sense not connected with what precedes. Perhaps it is better read *Siculorum immanitate*, in the ablative: namely, the cruelty of the two Dionysian tyrants of Sicily, each of whom, hungry for flattery, sought through punishments to subject even his subjects’ minds to himself and compelled them to think as he did. Royal MSS 4080 and 4103, Colbertine 1168 and 417, read: “the cruelty of Sicilian tyrants.”]

No master is served so long or so [Col. 0157A] devotedly. Wherever he commands, he leads his slave. One cannot escape him by flight; no violent power can remove him. For scarcely does one triumph over greed whom greed has once triumphed over. Greed effaces laws, persecutes every right, and erases divine ordinances. Greed leads a human being into the land of unlikeness, making him forget the dignity which he possesses with God and from God. Finally, as the Apostle says, “Greed is the root of all evils” (I Tim. VI:10): a root of this kind, deadly and putting forth poisoned branches.

For from it, as the prophet Hosea testifies, curse, lying, murder, and theft have overflowed, and blood has touched blood (Hos. IV:2). Under the shadow of these branches the human animal rests, taught by greed to turn aside. Such a person returns to the way with difficulty, numb and, as it were, frozen by the cold of the North Wind. [Col. 0157B] Assuredly, because of this cold, the sluggard cannot plough, and “when the sinner has come into the depth of iniquity, he despises” (Prov. XVIII:3). Pharaoh, though close to the burning plague, was hardened by this cold (Exod. XIII), because he wrongfully appropriated to himself the labor of Israel’s hands.

It cannot be said how many souls this cold has bound, whose almost completed course it has broken off, or how grievous a servitude it has imposed upon those it has held back. Many have preserved freedom of mind amid tortures; few amid wealth. Greed triumphed more miserably over Saul himself than Saul triumphed over Amalek. Balaam, captured by payment, had a mind full of cursing, though the Lord used his words to bless. Israel yielded before its enemies until, [Col. 0157C] having taken spoils from what had been devoted to destruction, Achan was punished with stones. And, to gather a rose from thorns, Atalanta, according to the poet, ran well; but when she turned aside toward gold, she was defeated and fell before Hippomenes.

We read that many even of the perfect have been assailed by this bitter dregs, and that the prophecy of many prophets has been turned into divination. For of these, as Micah says, “The priests of Jerusalem taught for payment, and her prophets divined for money; and they rested upon the Lord, saying, ‘Is not the Lord among us? Evils shall not come upon us’” (Mic. III:11). Explaining this passage, blessed Jerome says: “The priests taught for hire, not knowing that prophecy is one thing and divination another. They seemed indeed to themselves to be prophets; but because they received money, their prophecy became divination.” [Col. 0157D]

[Note: “The prophets of Jerusalem divined for money, not knowing that prophecy is one thing and divination another. They seemed indeed,” etc. Thus St Jerome, on Micah, chapter III, new edition, p. 1520.]

Those who give a price to the priceless grace of the Spirit, while paying too little attention to these things, become like the trees of the forest which, in the book of Judges, ask the olive, fig tree, and vine to rule over them, but do not obtain their request. Then they ask the bramble, and the bramble agrees.

You know, of course, that by the dry and unfruitful trees of the forest are represented false ministers of the Church, lacking fruitful grace and bearing no fruit, who wrongly seek the things of God and [Col. 0158A] do not obtain them. Of such persons the Apostle Jude says: “These are autumnal trees, uprooted, unfruitful, twice dead” (Jude 12). You also know that the anointing represented by the name of the olive is that by which the love of God is poured out into our hearts; by which God anointed the Son of God above his companions (Ps. XLIV:8); and by which Christ’s disciples are inwardly anointed, though according to the measure of Christ’s gift. Concerning this anointing God says through the prophet Joel: “I shall pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy” (Joel II:28).

Moreover, by the fig tree is indicated the old law, planted in the vineyard of the Lord—

[Note: [Col. 0158D] Colbertine and Victorine: “the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth.”]

—the vine transplanted from Egypt. The fig tree bore bad figs (Jer. XXIV:3), and it bore good ones: bad indeed, very bad; but good indeed, very good. For “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (II Cor. III:6). He alludes to this fig tree in the Gospel when he says: “A certain master of a household planted a vineyard, and planted a fig tree in the vineyard” (Luke XIII:6).

For who is more rightly signified by the vine than Christ, who says of himself to his disciples: “I am the vine; you are the branches” (John XV:1)? The wine of this vine is the new wine of the Gospel, new wine which gladdens the human heart and rejects the skins of minds which it finds made old by the dregs of antiquity. The Evangelist indicates such new wine in these words: “No one puts new wine into old skins; otherwise the skins burst, the wine is spilled, and the skins perish” (Matt. IX:17).

The bramble, however—a thorny and rough species of briar—aptly represents the man of sin, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above [Col. 0158C] everything called God or worshipped. The Psalmist indicates his thorns and stings when he says: “His mouth is full of cursing, bitterness, and deceit; beneath his tongue are toil and pain” (Ps. X:7, according to the Hebrew). And shortly afterward: “He lies in wait like a lion in his den” (ibid., 9).

Therefore, when the trees of the forest ask the aforesaid trees to rule over them and do not obtain their request, it is because people of the perversion described above do not rightly seek the things of God and hence do not receive them. For it is written: “If I regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me” (Ps. LXV:18). These persons ask for the grace of the Spirit which works within; but Peter says to Simon: “You have neither part nor lot in this word” (Acts VIII:21). They ask to be fed on the mystical understanding of the law, as though on fruits most sweet; but according to Isaiah: “The Lord blinds the heart of this people, makes their ears heavy, and closes their eyes, lest perhaps they understand, hear, see, turn, and be healed” (Isa. VI:10). They ask to cling to Christ like branches to the vine and to be imbued with evangelical teaching; but the Apostle shows that they have nothing to do with Christ: “What concord has Christ with Belial?” (II Cor. VI:15). And Solomon says: “Wisdom shall not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. I:4).

Therefore, because persons of this kind are neither governed by God’s Spirit nor subject to legal or evangelical [Col. 0159A] teaching, they ask the bramble to be their king: that is, they establish Antichrist as their ruler, already working in them the ministry of iniquity.

How great, then, is the plague of avarice; what a renunciation of virtue; how headlong a descent into hell—even the slower among us, we believe, do not fail to know. It is utterly shameful that the anointed one of God should be defiled by this ink, by which prophecy degenerates into divination, the anointing of the inward spirit is emptied out [Note: [Col. 0159D] Ebr.: “the anointing of the inward spirit,” which amounts to the same reading, “the anointing of the inward spirit.”], the mystical understanding of the Law is locked away, the savor of evangelical teaching is taken away, and those who boast that they are the kingdom of God become the kingdom of Antichrist. It is utterly shameful, I say, for a soul made like God to be subjected to this idol, to bend the knee before Baal, and by these sorceries to lose one’s humanity [Note: [Col. 0159D] Thus MSS Reg. 4080 and 4013, and Colb. 1168 and 4017: *amittere*, “to lose,” not *admittere*, “to admit,” as Vict. 272 has.], sorceries by which even the eyes of the wise are bewitched, so that they do not see heaven or remember righteous judgments. Yet we know—and give thanks to the Lord God—that in every way you flee the aforesaid storm, and are not falsely indignant that the anointed one of God should either smell the gold of gifts or seek the favor of persons. This indignation is holy and pleasing to God, and both your speech proclaims it and your conduct attests it.

We have heard, however, that there have not been lacking those who pressed you toward specious paths tending to death; who said that your resources were unequal to costly expenditures; that one ought to have at hand something which the poor may receive from one’s hand; that those who serve the altar are permitted to live from the altar; that Saul, seeking the desire of his heart through prophecy, brought some silver to Samuel the prophet. These words are the hissing of the ancient serpent, [Col. 0159C] for whom it is not enough to swallow a river unless he also attempts to make the Jordan flow into his mouth (Job 40:18). Those who say such things do not know that “better is a little for the righteous than the great riches of sinners” (Ps. 36:16).

Indeed, Saul, seeking his asses, carried a quarter of a shekel to Samuel; and Jeroboam’s wife entered to Ahijah, the man of God, with dried grapes and loaves (3 Kings 14:6). These persons, certainly, as Jerome writes (in the place cited above), because they had learned that some prophesied for payment, believed that these men too prophesied for payment. Yet neither of them is recorded as having accepted the gifts brought; rather, it is recalled that Samuel fed Saul quite hospitably, while Ahijah rebuked the aforesaid woman with rather harsh words. But let us grant that they received them: according to the same [Col. 0159D] Jerome, they should be called offerings for the Temple rather than rewards for a prophet.

Therefore, continue doing what you do; proceed as you have begun. At the voice of enchanters and of the sorcerer chanting unto death, stop the ears of your mind, [Col. 0160A] knowing that you offer to God the gold and silver which you refuse for God’s sake. For David made the water drawn, at the soldiers’ peril, from the Bethlehemite cistern into an acceptable sacrifice to God when, though thirsty, he poured it out for the Lord’s sake (2 Kings 13).

Concerning this water, blessed Gregory said to Reccared, king of the Visigoths [Note: [Col. 0159D] The manuscript codices vary greatly here. Ebroic. reads: “Concerning this water, to Rechared, king of the Visigoths,” etc. The Victorine codex 272: “Whence, to Reccared, king of the Visigoths,” etc. Colb. 2662: “Concerning this water, to Rechared,” etc. The Paris and Cologne editions: “Concerning this water, to Bertnared, king of the Visigoths,” etc. Since this passage of St Gregory is taken from Letter 122 of the *Register*, Book IX, indiction II, where St Gregory addresses Reccared himself, we judged that the passage should be restored, partly following the Ebroic., Victorine, and Colbertine manuscripts, partly the Cologne and Paris editions, as follows: “Concerning this water, to Reccared, king of the Visigoths, who had refused gold offered to him for God’s sake.” Thus blessed Gregory says: “In this matter the deed of King David comes to my mind, to whom, when … he despised.”], who had refused gold offered to him for God’s sake:

> “The deed of King David comes to my mind. When the water he had desired from the Bethlehemite cistern, which lay amid hostile troops, had been brought to him by his devoted soldiers [Note: [Col. 0160D] Colb. 2662: *illata*, “brought in”; the others: *allata*, “brought.”], he immediately said: ‘Far be it from me that I should drink the blood of these men.’ Because he poured it out and would not drink it, Scripture says: ‘He poured it out as a libation to the Lord.’ If, therefore, water refused by an armed king was turned into a sacrifice to God, let us consider [Col. 0160B] what kind of sacrifice that king offered to almighty God who, for love of Him, disdained to receive not water but gold.

> “We have written these things to your holiness like an invalid procuring an antidote for those in health. For even the hands of the sick have sometimes benefited the healthy; and we know the poet:

> To serve the whetstone’s office, which can make  
> Iron sharp, though itself has no part in cutting.  
> (Horace)

Certainly, while writing these things to you, we prayed to Him who searches hearts and reins that He would not permit your spirit to be assailed by that weakness through which you might presume to ascribe them to arrogance rather than charity. My soul does not know this imperfection, since, burdened by most grievous faults, it does not dare deny that it is lowly. Whatever has been done [Col. 0160C] [Note: [Col. 0160D] Colb. 2662: *auctum*, “increased,” rather than *actum*, “done.”] charity has taught; charity whose nature is to rejoice with those who rejoice and to be weak with those who are weak. You repay me in kind if you love me and pray for me.

## LETTER IX

[Note: [Col. 0160D] Otherwise numbered 18. Written about the year 1111.]

TO M., QUEEN OF ENGLAND.

Matilda, queen of the English—the very same woman mentioned in the preceding letter—had sent Hildebert two finely wrought golden candlesticks as a gift. He praises her generosity; and, while thanking her, ingeniously suggests both how meritorious it is for each person, according to his or her condition, to cooperate in the divine mysteries, and what spiritual benefit he himself derives from so precious a gift.

H., the humble priest of Le Mans, to M. [Note: [Col. 0160D] Hildebert to Matilda.] the venerable queen of the English, most worthy of glory and honor: greeting and the earnestness of prayers.

It is difficult always to bestow benefits with discernment and foresight. Exalted powers do not possess this prudence; for them it is beautiful to do good even to the undeserving. Having experienced such generosity in you, I follow up your blessing with thanksgiving, astonished alike by [Col. 0161A] the splendor of the gift and by the affection of its giver.

For your gift deserves very great commendation in itself, being costly in material and splendid in workmanship. Yet its value is augmented by the majesty of the sender, and what art or nature gave it is less than what it possesses from the queen. Even if it pleased neither by weight nor by the craftsman’s skill, I should nevertheless embrace it no differently than incense offered to the gods above, or the rich libations of victims. For they consider not the victim but the affection; and devotion, not expenditure, earns their favor. A pure and upright mind bends them wherever it wishes and appeases heavenly wrath no less with a penny than with a talent. Thus your mind commends your gift to me, magnifies it, and gives it brilliance. [Col. 0161B] It shines brightly indeed with its gold, but more brightly with your mind: the mind to which beneficence was pleasing; in which the will to give generously was inborn, not suggested; your mind, I say, which was willing from the heart, which gave swiftly, from which I received unexpectedly, not what I had extorted by importunity.

Moreover, from this it is also clear how devotedly you take part in the Lord’s sacraments: because, being a woman, you cannot minister them, you provide their instruments. As far as is permitted, you imitate those holy women who first approached the cross in tears and afterward the tomb with spices. Kindled, to be sure, by pious desire, they compassionately shared in the Crucified One’s suffering and served Him in burial by such attentions as they could render. You too are present when Christ is sacrificed, when He is committed to burial; neither is celebrated without your service, [Col. 0161C] when you prepare lights there, where we both believe in our hearts and confess with our mouths that the author of light is present. It makes no difference that the service is unlike, when the affection attending it is the same.

There are two things, I think, which you determined to suggest to a bishop: namely, remembrance of yourself and remembrance of his pastoral duty. Thus I understand the candlesticks sent to me as a kind of reminder: placed before me, they are to cause me both to bear the light of doctrine and to remember to pray for you. Their presence shakes and stirs my spirit, urgently exhorting me inwardly that, while I use the gift, I may profit from its example. Secretly indeed, yet quite keenly, I am commanded to consider whose light I bear, of whom the divine words say: “You are the light of the world”; and: “They do not light [Col. 0161D] [Note: [Col. 0161D] Rothom. alone has *abscondunt*, “hide,” but wrongly.] a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, that it may give light to all who are in the house” [Col. 0162A] (Matt. 10:14–15).

I embrace your exhortation, daughter of Christ. Even if this was not your intention, even if you gave simply, nevertheless I receive the service rendered by your gift so as not to despise its instruction. One may profit and be taught from any source: almost all things offer mystical meanings, and it is easy to fashion moral beauty from any object. Nothing has been created so entirely for itself, nothing is so simple, that it does not contain something from which we may learn either to avoid harmful things or to provide salutary ones.

But what shall I say of your remembrance? It has entered my breast deeply, occupied it broadly, possesses it steadfastly, and lives with me while I live. It will live with me, I say—more frequent in the future because of its very great frequency—whenever I, a sinner yet a priest, stand at the altar of the Lord. There, venerable queen, there your candlesticks will render their service for you and yours, and the bishop will render his through remembrance. Farewell.

## LETTER X

[Note: [Col. 0161D] Otherwise numbered 31. Written about the year 1112.]

TO A. [Note: [Col. 0161D] Perhaps not unreasonably you may suppose this widow—whom all manuscripts designate only by the letter A.—to be Agnes, daughter of William, duke of Poitiers, and widow of Alfonso, the elder king of Galicia. Count Elias of Le Mans, after the death of his first wife Matilda, daughter of Gervase Bochart, married her in the year 1100. But in the following year, when the said Count Elias died, he was reverently buried by our Hildebert in the basilica of St Peter of the Culture and honored with a metrical epitaph. Thus Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book X, pp. 769 and 785. Yet there is no other conjecture concerning this Agnes’s entry into a monastery than that drawn from this letter of Hildebert to her, as supposed [ [Col. 0161] + The distinguished widow designated only by the letter A. is not Agnes, whom Elias, count of Le Mans, married, as Dom Beaugendre says. For Elias had no children by his wife Agnes; whereas widow A. had borne children by her husband, as appears from the words “the offspring received from him.” This widow appears to be none other than Adela, countess of Blois, mentioned above.].]

TO A., A WIDOW.

Hildebert congratulates a certain distinguished widow on her contempt for the world. He suggests various means both for victory over temptations and for spiritual advancement, and raises her mind to perseverance by the hope of eternal rewards.

[Col. 0162B]

We trust in the Lord Jesus that He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion unto the day of Christ. For whence comes contempt for luxuries in a woman? Whence forgetfulness of extravagance? Unless from Him who said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Did not He bring you out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth, who brought forth prisoners from the pit in which there is no water (Ps. 39:3)? Or is not this change a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High (Zech. 9: [Col. 0162C] 11)?

A daughter of the world, you have become a daughter of God; nor have those things granted for use yielded to destruction. Moreover, you were lawfully married to a husband such as you yourself might have portrayed; the offspring received from him, under auspices of future virtue, softened all the burdens of marriage. To these were added ceremonial adornments and the agreeable services of attendants, by which either you acquired glory [Note: [Col. 0162D] Ebr.: *compares*, “you acquire.” Colb. 2662: *mutuavisti*, “you borrowed.” Rothom. and Vict. 272: *comparares*, “you might acquire.”] or the household was managed in order. The favor of the people also inclined so toward you that they counted among their successes whatever passed into your service. Besides, nothing was lacking to you of all that a kinder fortune could have devised as more pleasant.

These are surely the snares of death, the nets of a Christian soul. Such battering-rams shake the walls of virtues and overthrow reason’s citadel. Thus unhappy little souls are exposed to robbers, deprived of their own freedom, and exiled into Egypt under perpetual slavery. By means of these servants Pharaoh [Col. 0163A] daily kills our males, daily condemns them to mud and straw. Your soul long groaned under his yoke; but by a strong hand and an outstretched arm it was set free, and all its bonds were broken. You have gone forth into the freedom of the glory of the children of God, offering Him a sacrifice of praise and a contrite spirit, saying with the Psalmist: “You have broken, O Lord, my bonds; I will offer you a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115:17).

Certainly it was a wise and most orderly choice by which you preferred eternal things to transitory, virtues to vices, and your homeland to exile. Let us hear what Augustine says to Macedonius concerning this choice (*Letter* 155): “Virtue is nothing other than loving what ought to be loved. To choose it is prudence. To be turned away from it by no hardships is courage. By no allurements, temperance. By no pride, justice.” In a few words Christian perfection of life has been displayed to you. This is the chariot by which those who have no abiding city here seek the city to come.

Blessed indeed was that chariot by which Elijah the Tishbite, lifted up into heaven (4 Kings 2), postponed death but did not escape it; but far more blessed is this one, for whoever mounts it shall not taste death forever. Nor would the prophet have come to that fiery chariot unless he had first ascended this one. The first wheel of this most salutary vehicle has been prepared for you: it is called prudence by the witness of the holy Scriptures. Prudence was that by which you separated things to be loved from things not to be loved, useful things from harmful. Prudence, I say, was that by which you chose, according to the Psalmist, “rather to be cast aside in the house of your God than to dwell [Col. 0163C] in the tents of sinners” (Ps. 83:11).

We know, however, that many who have professed virtue have failed when adversity attacked. Israel thirsted in the wilderness, yet bore the discomfort of thirst impatiently; and therefore is recorded as having murmured against Moses (Exod. 17) and as having spoken wickedly of God: “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Ps. 77:19). The same people, amid assaults of enemies and hardships of the journey, desired the pots of meat, returned to melons, and adopted Egyptian servitude. Thus adversity breaks many; and, as you will find written, unless all things are available at their beck and call, they are cast down by every slightest thing. When poverty burns them, contempt torments them, and they see those splendid and exalted persons [Col. 0163D] whom they made heirs either by choice or by law, they fly back to riches they had disdained, complain that glory has been taken from them [Note: [Col. 0163D] Vict. 272: *adeptam*, “acquired.” Colb. 2662, Ebr., and Rothom.: *ademptam*, “taken away.”], envy their own people, and—what is a great loss to the religious life they have undertaken—while they sigh for the small things they left behind, they do not consider how great are the things they await in exchange for what they abandoned. Such people choose the goods that ought to be loved to no purpose, since, frightened by the aforesaid storms, their minds return to things not to be loved.

Courage must therefore be added to prudence, so that, when troubles arise, we may resist them most steadfastly in holding fast to what we have prudently chosen. By this virtue Paul resisted the thorn of the flesh and the angel of Satan (2 Cor. 11:23). [Col. 0164A] By it he was armed in prisons and in all the hardships which he enumerates to the Corinthians, when he said: “When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful” (2 Cor. 12:10). By it David preserved innocence amid adversity (1 Kings 26); by it he spared Saul when Saul pursued him (2 Kings 19); by it, upon hearing of his son’s death, he was consoled and ate bread.

You too must have recourse to this virtue if the sharp goad of slanderous tongues is aimed at you, if envy of your contemplation attacks you, if the hardships of voluntary poverty move you, or if insults disturb your mind’s settled state. For adversity is resisted unto victory only with difficulty unless courage is joined to prudence.

When these are joined together, temperance must necessarily be added, to preserve virtue amid prosperity—the virtue preserved by courage amid [Col. 0164B] adversity. Nothing is as harmful to virtue as the admixture of pleasure in permitted things. One guards negligently against an enemy whose entrance is expected to be peaceful. Thus a good purpose often collapses when the mind resists allurements too little, grows lax in prosperity, loves the honor bestowed upon it, and becomes arrogant through unprecedented things [Note: [Col. 0164D] Thus the Ebroic. and Rothom. MSS, not *insolutis*, as in the printed editions.].

By this luxury and fall, the beloved of God fell away from God—the beloved of whom it is said: “The beloved grew fat and kicked; he grew fat, became sleek, became bloated; he forsook God his maker and departed from God his savior” (Deut. 32:15). Of the same people you will also find this said: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. 32:6). Our Savior avoided this overthrow of virtue as an example, when the crowds wished to make Him [Col. 0164C] king and He refused the heights of the dignity offered Him (John 6).

Therefore, lest any pleasures wrest from you the fruit of religious life, fear to exceed the limits of temperance. Temperance commonly rests below what is permitted and never proceeds beyond it. If it is lacking, the other virtues either fall from their height or do not rise to it. Whatever we profess without temperance is impulse, not reason. Temperance measures one’s strength and does not depart from the mean. Thus it strengthens the relaxed at one time and moderates the arduous at another. In this way it preserves the virtues and brings them through to their reward. Certainly this construction claims for itself the third place in the aforesaid chariot, prepared against luxury and to meet the brigandage of pleasures.

[Col. 0164D] Therefore, the habit of luxuries must gradually be cut away; the assiduity of servants must be rejected; festive dress and exotic perfumes must be completely unlearned. For, while they gave evil pleasure either to you among others or to others in you, they wounded the integrity of souls. Habit is learned with difficulty; but it is especially difficult to be torn away from a habit that has held us for a long time and pleased us with much delight. Hence, unless I am mistaken, a more grievous war awaits you, and the enemy—God forbid!—is readier for victory.

If you do not know it, I call “the enemy” the luxuries frequented from the cradle, the favor of a husband, the affection of children, the diligence of attendants, and all other things [Col. 0165A] that came to you through the seductiveness of sex, the license of power, the pride of lineage, or family connections. Perhaps you will sigh for what you have left behind, recalling it all the more tenderly because it was either contemporaneous with you in time or more delightful through experience. Thus you will scarcely become accustomed to temperance, toward which it is difficult to descend because of habit and degrading because of your social condition. Yet all things are unlearned through time. Nothing clings so firmly to the human breast that it does not vanish in time. In time a mother forgets her grief, though at the death of her only son she admitted no consolation. In time a wound closes into a scar; and time has often benefited quartan fevers when medicine did not.

You too will, through time, unlearn yourself; and the remnants of desire, which cannot be conquered all at once, will more effectively be eluded one by one. Against such petty robbers and assassins, the daughter of Christ must keep watch in such a way that she neither sleeps nor slumbers; must so disregard them when they have gone that she makes them fear to return; must fight them so when they return that she does not despair of victory. For God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide the way out, that you may be able to endure it (1 Cor. 10:11). From the first day until today the Lord has regarded the prayer of the humble and has not despised their petition (Ps. 101:18). David was little, but in the Lord’s name he crushed the terrible Philistine (1 Kings 17). Judith likewise, when the priests trembled to the point of despair, delivered Bethulia through prayer and fasting (Judith 13).

[Col. 0165C] Perhaps you think the matter finished, and boast of complete victory, if neither painful nor pleasant things have wrested from you your purpose of religious life. Yet you are grievously deceived and dream of empty health if the swellings of pride have not yet subsided under the poultice of humility. Pride infects the whole body of virtue: its vital support withers, and all beautiful things are made ugly. Pride, heavenly by origin, seeks elevated minds; and, as if returning to its own source, breaks into the glory and purity of human beings, since it broke forth from the glory and purity of angels. First triumphing in heaven and then on earth, it was so native to angels that it did not depart from them; it so infected human beings that it separated them from God. And, as if it had accomplished little by casting down angel [Col. 0165D] and human, it went on to tempt God and human alike, so that it might make the one whom it saw as a companion in like nature a companion also in ruin.

This is the first and the last destruction: it surpasses all vices before all others, and is overcome after all others. For after a faithful soul emerges from the abyss of vices and ascends the saving summit of virtues, pride springs forth, as if from ambush, and rushes upon it, intending to shake to ruin the whole structure of the Lord’s house that had risen to completion. For what is more destructive to a righteous person than desiring to appear righteous? Than being delighted and exulting at greetings in the marketplace [Col. 0166A]? Than being soothed by flattering favor? Than, almost denying that one is human, measuring and falsely claiming oneself equal to the gods? Such a person, while boasting wrongly and presuming to be what he is not, is cast down into confusion and loses what he is. And he is made so much farther from God by the wall of pride as he seemed to himself nearer through the height of his virtues. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand” (Ps. 90:7).

You see, therefore, how great an impoverishment of character pride is, and how necessary humility is in good deeds. Without humility, choosing by prudence what ought to be loved is erring discernment; overcoming adversities by courage is fallen victory; resisting allurements by temperance is drunken sobriety. Therefore the fourth wheel must be joined to these [Col. 0166B], namely that which Augustine called justice, as the comprehensive completion and conclusion of all virtues [Note: [Col. 0165D] Colb. 2662 and Vict. 272 have *completionem*, “completion”; Rothom. and Ebr. have *complectionem*, “comprehension.”]. When justice is bound to the others, the whole body of our structure will rise into a chariot, then into heaven [Note: [Col. 0165D] Colb. 2662 reads “incorruption into heaven”; Rothom.: “into a chariot, you into heaven”; Vict.: “into a chariot, then into heaven”; Ebr.: “into a chariot, then into heaven,” which we judged preferable.].

This chariot is not Pharaoh’s chariot, which the Lord cast into the sea (Exod. 5), but the chariot by which, ascending Mount Zion—the great and lofty mountain, the mountain to which the God of our salvation will then grant you a prosperous journey (Ps. 67:20)—you will rise. Blessed indeed is the vehicle by which the lost sheep is returned to the flock, the found drachma is brought into the treasury, the queen of the South is brought to Solomon and transferred into David’s embrace. Truly, I say, it is blessed and worthy of every praise: by it, after labor, you will come to the denarius; after winnowing, [Col. 0166C] you will come to the barn; from exile you will return to your homeland; from slavery you will be converted to freedom.

These are those four rivers of Paradise by which the earth of the heart, soberly made drunk [Note: [Col. 0166D] *Debriata*, “made drunk”: thus all manuscripts except Victor. 292, which has *inebriata*, “intoxicated.”], sends forth the seed it has received in hope of harvest and bears fruit in patience. The house of blessed Job likewise had these four corners, into which a wind rushing in crushed the seven sons feasting there (Job 8). For, according to Gregory, our conscience is understood by Job’s house; and by its four corners are signified prudence, courage, temperance, and justice. That house stood upon four corners because the whole edifice of good will rises by the aforesaid fourfold number. But the wind rushes in and shakes the house because, when grave temptation assails us, it often drives the pure dwelling of our [Col. 0166D] conscience toward ruin. Thus, when the house is shaken, the four corners fall, because, when the abode of a good mind is disturbed, the four aforesaid virtues cannot remain standing. Moreover, when those same corners fall, they bury the seven sons feasting there, because, when those chief virtues are overwhelmed, they also suffocate the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit—the good offspring of God which feed and delight upon the pious desires of the soul as upon various dishes; grow and flourish; are strengthened and endure.

You see, therefore, my daughter, my sister, my dearest one, a wind rising and pressing upon you: a wind rushing from the north; a wind indeed that kills, but a wind that fails before the Spirit. The Spirit of the gentle breeze—the Holy Spirit, the tranquil and sweet Spirit—will overshadow your house, if only your house is founded upon firm rock (Matt. 7:25); and the rock, as the Apostle says, was Christ (1 Cor. 10). Peter stood upon this rock; for when he saw the wind coming and began to sink, he cried out: “Lord, save me” (Matt. 14:30). Because he doubted, he fell; because he was strengthened, he rose. A violent wind drove and submerged him; firm rock sustained and raised him. Let Peter therefore say: “I was pushed and overthrown, that I might fall, and the Lord upheld me” (Ps. 117:13).

[Col. 0167B] You too, driven by the wind of temptation so that you may sink, must be sustained by firm rock so that you may not be submerged: “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 120:2). Therefore presuming nothing of yourself, cast your care upon the Lord (Ps. 54:23). Distrusting nothing of God, strengthen your heart in His salvation. If you must glory, glory and exult in the Holy Spirit. This is that cord of which Wisdom says: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecclus. 4:12). For what is more certain than hoping in the Lord God, who made and formed you? What is firmer than being strengthened in His Christ, who re-formed you and will strengthen you for Himself? What is safer than glorying in the Holy Spirit who enlightened you?

To stretch out your hands toward this one and threefold cord is to rise. To cleave to it [Col. 0167C] is to be strengthened. To be drawn toward it is to run. To be bound by it is to be set free. Therefore stretch out your hands to it with Moses, so that Amalek, conquered while the prophet prayed, may also be conquered while a woman prays (Exod. 17:12–13). Cleave to it in firm faith, so that, whenever you are shaken by a storm of temptations, you may be strengthened with Peter, stand with Peter, and cry with Peter: “Lord, save me” (Matt. 14:30). Desire to be drawn by it toward it, so that, with the hope of the prize set before you, you may promise a better course, according to Solomon’s saying: “Draw me after you; we will run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3). Long to be bound to it by it, so that, having gained Sarah’s freedom and Rachel’s beauty, you may pass into the embrace of the father not of many but of all nations, saying: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 8:3).

Remember also to make a whip from the same cord, to drive from the temple of your breast the noise of worldly things and the crowd of pleasures. Before its presence, let the itch for delights flee; let the softness of purple be despised; [Col. 0168A] let the variety of dishes become tasteless [Note: [Col. 0167D] Vict.: *saeculorum*, “of ages”; Ebr. and Colb.: *ferculorum*, “of dishes.”]; let the gleam of jewels lose its brightness; let elaborate necklaces be trampled underfoot; let the secret license of marriage be abhorred [Note: [Col. 0167D] Ebr.: *abhorreant*, “let them abhor”; Colb. and Vict.: *abhorreatur*, “let it be abhorred.”]; let the pride of power fall. Prefer laws to the palace, haircloth to linen, contempt to favor, injuries to services. Delighting in such pursuits, you will enter with the wise virgins into the marriage-feast of the Lamb (Matt. 25), to receive eternal fruit from a celibate marriage.

That fruit is your God, the God in whom are all good things; that fruit is the Word of God, the Word from whom are only good things [perhaps *solo*, “from whom alone,” rather than *sola*]; that fruit is the Spirit, the Spirit of both, with whom there are nothing but good things. In this fruit is a kingdom without end, satiety without weariness, exaltation without descent, glorification without failure. Let this fruit please your taste, become sweet to you, and be loved with your whole soul [Col. 0168B] and remembered with your whole memory, so that it may one day feed and satisfy you in its everlasting glory. Farewell. Remember me in your prayers.

## LETTER XI

[Note: [Col. 0167D] Otherwise numbered 61. Written about the year 1112, or at any rate before 1115.]

TO THE MONKS [Note: [Col. 0167D] Who these monks were is uncertain. Perhaps they were monks of Vendôme, who, lest anything be detracted from the privilege of their monastery—which the supreme pontiffs wished to belong immediately to the Roman see and to be subject to its jurisdiction without any intermediary—had refused, pleading poverty, to receive the bishop of Chartres as a guest. This bishop of Chartres appears to have been none other than Ivo, who, as may reasonably be believed, had complained to Hildebert of this rebuff. This letter therefore seems to have been written about 1112, or at any rate before 1115, when, according to the Cartulary of St John, Ivo of Chartres died.]

WHO REFUSED TO RECEIVE THE BISHOP OF CHARTRES.

Hildebert first teaches them that even the stricter exercises of monastic life avail nothing without humility and mercy. He laments that they lacked these when they refused to receive the bishop of Chartres as a guest—a man whom they ought not merely to have invited but even to have drawn in at the expense of their sacred furnishings. Then, by the examples of Lot and Abraham, he magnifies the merit of hospitality, to the more diligent practice of which he exhorts those monks.

By apostolic examples we are taught to make the weakness of our neighbor our own through compassion [Note: [Col. 0168D] “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11:29).]. Therefore my soul is in bitterness, grieving that the oil of your name has been exhausted [Col. 0168C]—the oil whose fragrance of sweetness we believe the Lord once smelled; but now it is not so. For you have turned back, and according to the poet:

The slope’s beginning makes your horse pant. (OVID.)

Yet you had read: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62). But you too look back; you look back, I say—if indeed you have come to the plough, if you have found the hard and narrow way that leads to life (Matthew 7:13). Yet few find it. Outside it, many wander astray while boasting that they have set their steps upon it and run without stumbling. For there is one who, with the prophet, hides alms in the poor man’s bosom (Ecclus. 22:15); who frequents the church before dawn; who labours for the protection of the oppressed. Yet this worshipper of mercy seeks his own glory; he desires to please the people; he puts his hand out for a fee before he promises his advocacy. I am mistaken if he has found the way that leads to life.

Truth says of himself: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing” (John 8:54). And the Psalmist: “Those who please men are confounded, because God has rejected them” (Psalm 52:6). And in Proverbs: “He who pursues greed troubles his own house; but he who hates gifts shall live” (Proverbs 15:27).

Another is pleased by a loftier manner of life: he harasses his flesh with fasts, avoids more luxurious display, lives for nature, not for gluttony. If you think someone hungers and thirsts for righteousness, yet he is easily disturbed by anger; if he assigns himself a portion with hypocrites; if from his own flesh he presumes something against the honour of the flesh: I am mistaken if he has found the way that leads to life. “For the anger of man does not work the righteousness of God” (James 1:20). And concerning hypocrites the Lord says through Isaiah: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29:13). And the Apostle: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Hebrews 13).

You see a man delighting in the solitude of the desert; he accommodates himself to necessity, to roots and herbs, granting nothing to his food [Note: [Col. 0169D] Hebrew manuscript: “to his foods.”] or fire. With the Prophet, he cries out that there is death in the pot. If you see someone thus in the world that you believe him free of the world; if he thinks highly of himself beyond his true measure; if, in Pharisaic boasting, he despises the rest; if he arrogates to himself alone the primacy of righteousness: I am mistaken if he has found the way that leads to life. “For whoever exalts himself shall be humbled” (Matthew 23:12). And of those who weigh their own good or evil deeds one way and those of others another, the Wise Man says: “Weight and weight, measure and measure—both are abominable before God” (Proverbs 20:10).

Another, leaving all that he possesses, escapes to the stronghold of monastic refuge; he kisses the garment of humility, laments that he approached it too late, and bears without complaint every hardship of the struggle he has undertaken, carrying, in hope of the denarius, the burden and heat of the day. Yet this image of a monk is twisted by a more exalted rank: he cannot sleep until he has driven poor Naboth from his vineyard; he refuses to submit to duly constituted authority. I am mistaken if he has found the way that leads to life.

Certainly, in these ways the latter end of that man becomes worse than the former. To find this way, then, is exceedingly difficult; to traverse it is still more difficult. It is full of stumbling-blocks, and robbers beset it, allowing no one at all to pass without being tested. Their will is always wicked; deception is their dominion. No one has ever extracted from them a truce from doing harm. With them there is a daily and perilous encounter. From them comes an innumerable multitude of wounds, scarcely promising a scar. Under them, falls are frequent and recovery difficult [Note: [Col. 0169D] Colbert and Victorine manuscripts: “breathing-space.”]. Under them victory is rare and never secure.

Who, then, finds the way? Who traverses it uninjured once found? Who escapes the robbers, formidable with poisoned missiles, superior in cunning, trained by practice, stubborn through frequent victory, and never sated by any deaths or plunder? Who has ever triumphed over the assassins of souls?

The sound mind, inclined in every condition to virtue alone, is one to which nothing opposed presents itself as fit to embrace, and which loves nothing that it would blush to confess. Whoever lacks this is outside the way that leads to life. If a bony and bloodless countenance is to be adored in him [Note: [Col. 0169D] Thus the Hebrew and Rothomagense manuscripts; “odoured” in the others.], if a circumcised heart is to cry aloud more forcefully than cropped hair, if his speech is censorious and his attire more uncultivated, he is outside the way that leads to life. When his foot wanders about in looser shoes, when his head is shaved into a broader tonsure, when his other monastic badges proclaim him a monk, he is outside the way that leads to life. He too is outside the way and wanders abroad whose anger does not die before the sun goes down. He wanders abroad who, though unwilling to be deceived, does not fear to deceive. He wanders abroad whom you see gladly frequenting the marketplace. He wanders abroad who abounds in idle talk, who feeds upon exactions from his dependants, who regards it as gain to extort wages from a labourer by lawsuits.

You too wandered outside when you shut your doors against the bishop of Chartres; when you excluded the Christ of Jesus Christ, forgetting alike the good work and the reward of hospitality. His route compelled him to pass through your neighbourhood, and the exigency of time required him to lodge among you. Approaching night and stormy weather urgently pressed the bishop to seek lodging. There was no one in the fortress to whom the prelate could honourably turn. Surrounded by these anxieties, the man of God sat vainly before your doors and cried out in vain. He was excluded—he who, in order that he might turn in to you, ought not merely to have been invited but even dragged in. He was excluded—he who grieved more deeply that you had cast off a monk than that you had excluded a bishop; that charity had been lacking in you rather than lodging for himself. He was excluded—he in whom, if you doubt that Christ was excluded, you either have not read or have not understood Christ’s saying: “He who despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

How well it would have been for you had you deserved to have it said of you: “They constrained him, saying, ‘Stay with us, Lord, for evening is drawing near and the day has now declined’” (Luke 24:29). Perhaps you excuse your refusal by poverty; but no small quantity of gold gleamed about the altar, much silver shone there, and ornaments remained which would have been better pawned for use than that a bishop should be exposed to rain. Yet you had read: “Do not forget hospitality, for by such sacrifices God is won” [Note: [Col. 0170D] “But do not forget beneficence and sharing” (Hebrews 13:16).].

You had also read what Lot deserved through hospitality; Abraham, too, is recorded to have received him among his guests (Genesis 18 and 19). No other good deeds of Lot are recorded, except that he cherished the prerogative of hospitality, and that he preferred to expose his daughters to dishonour rather than permit any act of dishonour against the guests he had received. This was his offering; by this sacrifice he escaped the sulphur and fire of Sodom. Thus, taught of the city’s overthrow, he went out rejoicing that the reward of hospitality had reached even his household [Note: [Col. 0171C] Thus the Hebrew and Rothomagense manuscripts; others read “of the guest.”]. For the entire family was saved, and by the merit of one man provision was made for the safety of many.

We also know that angels descended to Abraham in human form, and that inhabitants of heaven were received with a countenance testifying to Abraham’s cheerful willingness. Sarah too bore witness to the same, she who, under her husband the patriarch, I believe lacked no virtue of hospitality. Consider the master of the house; observe the servants. In the house you will find devotion, in the household discipline. Indeed, in the patriarch’s house no one was found undevoted to these sacred services. He sees three men while seated at the entrance of the tent. Nor does he wait for lodging to be requested, lest, if it were obtained by prayers, it might seem to have been grudgingly bestowed. He runs to meet those who are coming and anticipates their approach with these words: “My lord, if I have found favour in your sight, do not pass by your servant” (Genesis 18:3).

See with what affection guests are invited. Those who are compelled to enter by entreaties do not extort lodging by importunity. “My lord, if I have found favour in your sight, do not pass by your servant” (ibid.). They are asked to enter, that they may receive more gladly the lodging freely offered. Their feet are washed, so that each obligation of hospitality may be discharged in its proper order. Then, at her husband’s command, the wife hastens to prepare three measures of fine flour; he himself runs to the herd; a tender calf is killed; the servant presses on with the preparations. The whole household hastens; the whole household burns with service. Nothing is done negligently in the house of the righteous. For all the members of the household, as though they had learned it from him, know that cursed is the man who performs the work of God negligently [Col. 0171C: Vulgate, “deceitfully”] (Jeremiah 48:10).

The guests had not yet departed, and behold, fertility is given to Sarah. The promise long ago made to Abraham is fulfilled through the intervention of hospitality. It is foretold that in that very year a son will be born to them, a son whom they would owe more to the promise than to marriage, more to grace than to nature. Although the Lord had predestined this for Abraham, the patriarch nevertheless attained the promised son only through preceding merits. For what is predestined for the elect is obtained through prayers and merits.

If Rebekah’s womb had remained closed, the Lord’s promise that Abraham’s seed would be multiplied in Isaac would have been in vain. Yet Rebekah is recorded to have received conception through Isaac’s prayers, so that the multiplication of offspring predestined in him might be shown to have been fulfilled through prayers. Concerning this Gregory says in the *Dialogues* [Note: [Col. 0171C] *Dialogues*, book I, chapter 8.]:

> “The very predestination of the eternal kingdom is so ordered by almighty God that the elect attain it through the labour of prayer, in order that by asking they may deserve to receive what almighty God had disposed before the ages to give them.”

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0171C] In the same place, near the end.]: “‘Isaac prayed to the Lord for his wife, because she was barren’; and He heard him and gave Rebekah conception” (Genesis 25:21). If, therefore, the multiplication of Abraham’s offspring through Isaac was predestined, why did he take a barren wife? Surely it is established that predestination is fulfilled through prayers, since he in whom God had predestined the multiplication of Abraham’s seed obtained by prayer the power to have a son.”

We do not wish to burden with more words those whom we believe burdened by the enormity and strength of their offence. Hear all together the conclusion of the matter: unless you are converted and become monks, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.

## LETTER XII

[Note: [Col. 0171C] Also numbered 56. Written in 1121.]

### TO KING HENRY

He consoles Henry—I, that is, king of the English—over the lamentable drowning of his sons [Note: [Col. 0171C] Scarcely in any histories of kingdoms can a sadder event be read than the pitiable shipwreck of two sons of a most powerful king; nearly all writers on English affairs mention it. In 1120, on the seventh day before the Kalends of December, according to Orderic Vitalis and others, Henry I, king of England, prepared to cross from Normandy to England with a great fleet. He selected one ship for himself; to another he entrusted his two sons William and Richard, together with his niece, surrounded by a numerous company of the distinguished magnates of his kingdom and young men of the first rank of the same age, under the command of a certain shipmaster named Thomas.

This man had ambitiously procured this duty for himself, even offering gold for it. More cheerful at attaining his wish, and having drunk too freely with his fellow sailors, he had scarcely put to sea before Barfleur, or the “Barbarous Wave,” in Normandy, when, unable to control himself through drunkenness, he carelessly struck a hidden and enormous rock. The unexpected impact shattered the ship; although the sea was calm and winds favourable, it sank so completely that, of nearly three hundred men—including the king’s two sons and his niece, and many of the noblest who had boarded in their company for honour’s sake—scarcely two escaped the shipwreck, clinging to a spar or mast and hanging there throughout the night. Orderic narrates and laments this more fully, *Ecclesiastical History*, book XII, p. 867 ff.

Accordingly, by this letter Hildebert seeks to console the most sorrowful father. It sufficiently suggests that, if he had ever fallen from Henry’s favour because of the dissensions at Le Mans, he had returned to it; and thereafter was so acceptable to him that he secured the king’s patronage even for his own friends, as is clear from several letters which he addressed to him.

The fable concerning the curse of Matilda, the mother, is not to be considered here. Matthew Paris asserts that she had been compelled to marry Henry against a vow of virginity and had devoted the offspring of her womb to a dreadful fate; thus, he says, the drowning of the children borne to Henry had been divinely brought about. But St Anselm established through lawful witnesses that she had never made such a vow, nor ever worn the sacred veil in her youth except as a pretext to avoid suitors, as we have already noted above. Once this was unquestionably established, the bishop, a most zealous defender of the saints and of ecclesiastical discipline, consented to Matilda’s marriage with Henry, blessed her, consecrated her queen, declared her marriage altogether lawful, and asserted this in Letter 37 of Book I. Eadmer and other contemporary writers testify to the same; the learned Fr Homey rightly preferred their judgment to the opinion of Matthew Paris, who, relying on popular rumour alone, wrote one hundred and twenty years later, to the discredit of a devout queen whom William of Malmesbury repeatedly praises as most chaste in conduct and most illustrious in piety, as do Ivo of Chartres, Letters 107, 142, 174; St Anselm, Book III, Letters 89, 93; and others.

The disastrous shipwreck of her sons, then, is not to be attributed to the falsely imputed curse of their mother, but, as many supposed, to divine justice. The sea’s whirlpools and monsters had, it was rumoured, been prepared for men guilty of even unmentionable lust, and therefore unworthy of the common burial of the faithful. Orderic further relates that several upright men withdrew from that ill-fated ship in horror at the wantonness of the young men; among them he notes two monks of Tiron—undoubtedly among those whom Symeon of Durham, Book I of *The Deeds of the English*, p. 129, says arrived in England in 1113, namely ten years before the Savignians, and established a seat there in the land of David, king of Scotland, at Selkirk for fifteen years. Indeed, the Chronicle of Melrose, concerning English affairs, vol. I, p. 168, states that the church of Tiron was founded in 1109.], and by an excellent description of the true wise man raises his mind to constancy. He elegantly demonstrates that a person’s true happiness is located not in things surrounding the person but in things within that person; to cling to these alone is to bear and honour God’s image in us.

[Col. 0172C]

When you rule well over many, you rule over no one better than yourself. For authority puts forth an example with greater praise than a sword. The former is gentle instruction and represses wrongdoing with a bloodless scourge; the latter is more often drawn in hatred than in judgment, in fury than according to law. You surely know that it belongs to a king first to rule himself, then his people; you know that a ruler triumphs obscurely over enemies until he triumphs over himself.

Hence it is that you have grown in spirit amid adversities; that your cheerful and serene countenance speaks something great concerning it. The countenance is the interpreter of the mind, and constancy declares better than speech how free the inner person is [Note: [Col. 0174D] Thus the Hebrew and Colbert manuscripts: “and what manner of his inner person he is.” The Victorine manuscript: “and because his inner person is free.” Regius: “in what manner his inner person is.”]. You have triumphed most gloriously over fortune—if, indeed, fortune is anything. It has attempted nothing so vainly or so hostilely against another. Of all the missiles that hasten its victory, it chose the sharpest, one by which I recall no one before you being wounded. And lest it should wound as though by a loosely discharged and harmless blow, it hurled it with all gathered force, trusting no less in its arm than in its weapon.

Yet fortune gained nothing by its effort, nothing by its sharpness. It marked only the skin and did not reach the inward parts. O well-defended breast, before which fortune blushes to find itself lesser! O mind, its own guardian, ignorant of having either the wise man or the king torn away from it! Neither has been taken from you; neither diminished. The one preserves the freedom of the mind, the other the security of the kingdom. It is uncertain which performs its proper office more completely in you. For no words are broken by sighs; no darkness covers your face. Your mouth has its own serenity, and a restrained smile displays the festival of your mind. Finally, the affairs of the kingdom do not hang suspended, nor do the oppressed wait in vain for help. The court is governed by the law of the court, and it has nothing to do with plunder except the punishment of plunder: a great proof of a king [Note: [Col. 0174D] Victorine manuscript: “of law.”], a great proof of a wise man [Note: [Col. 0174D] Regius: “beginning.”].

For wisdom consists in neither being carried away in prosperity nor buried in grief amid adversity. Nature prepared for a human being a certain equilibrium, by which he might always show himself the same toward either outcome. To abandon it and be altered according to the changing conditions of fortune is not nature, but a defect of nature. Every nature is good, since “God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good” (Genesis 1:31). But that nature is evil when it has fallen away from its proper condition—of this no one can doubt.

Indeed, before the Creator’s command was broken by the deadly food, human beings possessed grace assisting the good freedom of the will. Thus at that time there was nothing in the soul to offend, nothing in the flesh to cause shame. Every affection of the mind breathed and inclined toward virtue. Unlawful and unseemly impulse was wholly far from the body. Obedience claimed the whole human being for itself. All things were subject to him, so long as he himself was not subject to the woman. Once he obeyed her, he began no longer to belong to himself and to serve as many masters as he had vices. “For everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34).

The uxorious man brought this slavery upon himself when, feasting on what his Lord had forbidden, he deserved to hunger for freedom. O transgression never sufficiently punished! No descendant escaped the sentence pronounced upon the guilty parents. No one earned a reprieve from it by years or sex. We are conceived under it, to be punished even in the grave. Consider the miseries of humanity; look upon ashes: they are the tribute of sin. Sin was followed by as many punishments as disadvantages sprang from it.

The first of these punishments was that it exposed the transgressor, as if unarmed and deprived of help, to the enemy. For once a human being committed guilt, he lost grace as well. Abandoned by grace, he became like a child without a guardian, like a horse without a bridle. Thus the freedom of the will became strong for evil, cast out from grace and finding itself powerful for vices. Nor was it easy for one who had lost assistance to conquer many enticements when one enticement had conquered him even while aided. By that victory we were all defeated, and a personal offence proscribed the whole race. By it we were sold under sin, to be redeemed without silver. By it the sceptre of the taskmaster was raised and a yoke imposed upon us which could not rot away except “because of the oil” (Isaiah 10:17).

Then, for the first time, the spirit was subjected to the flesh; it still laments that lost sovereignty, of which the Apostle says: “For I do not do the good that I will; but the evil that I do not will, that I do” (Romans 7:19). Then also came the inescapable miseries of humanity and all these disadvantages, which, though imposed because of sin, were not removed together with sin. Finally, our outward person then lost the state of immutability, beginning to slip and pass away with time; had he not sinned, time would have passed while he remained. But once he had sinned, though he lived nine hundred years and more, he nevertheless immediately began, having lost stability with grace, to decline day by day and in a manner to die, as the divine [variant: “of the Lord”] threat was now at work in him: “On the day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Genesis 2:17).

Nor did he alone submit to the prescribed change; those disturbances also began to claim the inner person, disturbances which the prophet Joel thus declares under the names of caterpillar, locust, grub, and rust: “What the caterpillar left, the locust has eaten; what the locust left, the grub has eaten; and what the grub left, the rust has eaten” (Joel 1:2). The most learned of poets speaks of them in these words:

> Hence they fear and desire; they grieve and rejoice; nor do they behold the light of heaven, shut up in darkness and a blind prison.  
> (VIRGIL)

Two of these—joy and grief—are aroused by the changing course of events, though they are unable to wrest constancy of mind from the wise man. For the wise man is never found unprepared or unarmed against what you call fortune. He carries with him the means to guard against snares and to frustrate the enemy’s missiles. He seeks no equipment for battle outside himself. In every event he is safe in himself. His breast is a fertile quiver and an abundant armoury. It always overflows with arrows and abounds in defences. It cannot be exhausted [perhaps “drained dry”], since it never ceases to draw forth missiles. Armed with these, he despises all fortune’s missiles, superior alike when it favours him and when it persecutes him. When it flatters, he is ungrateful; when it thunders, he scorns it. He is moved by no turn of events, but insults them all. For there is nothing over which the conqueror of his own mind does not triumph.

Perhaps, however, you ask with what arms the wise man fights so manfully, by what method of combat he is stronger than this two-formed enemy. If you do not know, I confess that I have been deceived in believing that these arms were neither unknown to you nor lacking to you. Unhappy is he who happens to lack the aforesaid armour; most unhappy he who is even ignorant of it. In such persons Democritus found matter for laughter; Demosthenes [Note: [Col. 0175D] Thus all manuscripts, but Heraclitus is better.] for tears. But may the gamble of events never make you such a person, and may loss of a child not be followed by loss of the wise man.

You have suffered a graver shipwreck on land than at sea—of your son—if the storm of fortune has wrested the wise man from the wise man. I do not doubt this has happened if you have overlooked the instruments by which the wise man defends, not his house but himself, not his furnishings but the freedom of his mind. If knowledge of those instruments has escaped you, return to yourself, and do not delay to turn upon these present writings the eyes which you owe to the commonwealth. Though they neither sparkle with majesty of sentiment nor commend themselves by order or art, perhaps you may draw from them something by which, even from afar, you may discern the wise man’s armour. Not everything is to be despised in which many better things may be found. You will find more persons who have quenched the burning of thirst with water than with spiced wine.

First, therefore, you must observe that every age of human life is governed either by guardians brought in from without or by reason innate to it. While an heir is a little child (Galatians 4:1), a pedagogue is provided for him, to ensure that none of the capital of his inheritance slips away, that his tongue does not become accustomed to idle talk, that tender marrow does not drink in shamefulness, and that he does not remain a child until a hundred-year-old child is carried to the grave amid joyful funeral rites [Note: [Col. 0175D] Hebrew manuscript: “services,” but the other manuscripts read “funeral rites.”]. The remaining stages of life are governed by reason, unless some disturbance within its own household or some external [Note: [Col. 0175D] Thus the Hebrew and Rothomagense manuscripts; some others read “alien.”] business obstructs reason’s office.

If this happens in the commonwealth of this inner person of ours—the person whom we bear about—nothing is rightly done, nothing in order, nothing by which we may be taught what distinguishes a human being from other living creatures and unites [variant: “lives”] him to God. But when reason is at peace [Note: [Col. 0175D] Hebrew manuscript: “equal.” All others: “there is peace.”] and itself retains its freedom in administering the aforesaid commonwealth, the entire person is well governed; the mind remains the same [Note: [Col. 0175D] Hebrew manuscript: “the same mind, or.” Colbert and Victorine manuscripts: “that is, to the mind.” “The mind remains the same” is more correct.] whether adversities strike or pleasant things flatter. Then it prescribes laws of life, makes unalterable decrees, and bends itself to their administration. Then it devotes watchful attention to well-considered principles for ordering the human breast; then it creates and educates the wise man.

These principles [Note: [Col. 0175D] Here he probably means that moral philosophy, recovered from the excellent Colbert manuscript no. 2662 and the Victorine manuscript 759, which is also entitled *On the Useful and the Honourable*. It appears below.] having reached me in copied pages, I decided to set them before the public gaze, fearing the envy of posterity if I begrudged them to posterity. Thus I wrote them for those who neither use prosperity reverently nor pass through hardships unmoved.

On more carefully considering what a human being is, nothing seems more probable than that he is a divine living creature, marked as it were by a certain participation in divinity [Note: [Col. 0176D] Hebrew manuscript: “name.”]. He bears about him bones and flesh from his parent and has the savour of earth. By reason he declares himself near and akin to God. By this prerogative Moses testifies that he was divinely made in the image and likeness of God (Genesis 4). Hence human beings have also received the capacity by reason to know and love the things that are truly good. Things good merely in opinion they indeed know, but do not love as they ought or in the things in which they ought [variant: “but not as they ought”].

For reason teaches us that the things of virtue are true goods, and that these are within us; while the things we possess temporarily are goods merely in opinion, and are around us. But things around us do not belong to us; they are under another’s jurisdiction. Chance rules over them. They neither come nor remain at our own disposal. They are with us as things held by sufferance, like another person’s slave. They have nothing to do with those things in which true happiness is either possessed or lost. For no one is happy or miserable through what belongs to another. Whatever makes a human being either good or miserable is his own.

The fig tree of the Gospel obtains favour from its fruitfulness, but cutting down from its failure. As the philosopher writes [Note: [Col. 0176D] Epictetus, in Arrian.], a horse is made distinguished by its speed; one slower is destined for the mill. No contempt comes to it from humble equipment, no favour from splendid equipment. Both are foreign to it. Both are, to use a better horse rather than a better thing, attached from without. So too, anything that is not in a human being but around a human being is foreign to him.

Honours are assigned to him; a wife is joined to him, lacking nothing for the grace of marriage; in his children he kisses his own image; the abundance of the entire year is shut up in his storerooms, Croesus’ wealth in his coffers; and wherever he casts his eyes he beholds nothing but what is his. Yet their flight declares these things to be alien. All these are wandering goods, winged goods. Their nature is nowhere to remain long; their stability gives no one a more certain stability. Moreover, it is doubtful whether they stay with us more faithlessly or more hostilely.

For the matter would go on without end if I should recount the dangers of rulers, the complaints of troubled marriage, a thousand Menedemuses weeping for dissolute sons, riches unjustly amassed [Note: [Col. 0177D] Hebrew manuscript: “if amassed unjustly.” Colbert 2662: “amassed.” Victorine: “if shamefully shattered.”], or shamefully squandered; possessions seized by arms, spent on vices, taken away by fraud, transferred by prejudicial judgment, and—what is basest of all in this age—sought at the cost of one’s good name and honour. The law courts thunder with complaints of this kind; the tribunals resound. Suits are argued at crossroads; disputes take place at banquets. Laws are in people’s hands, decrees before their eyes; and there is now no time in which the Church lacks persons to expel or the court persons to condemn.

See how great is the world’s madness. It cannot rejoice until it has acquired that by which joy is turned into sorrow and the lyre into mourning. It keeps watch to acquire things which, if they come late, torment first by delay before they nourish by use; if they come quickly, they make people more certain of closer anxieties. O madmen, for whom it is a celebrated thing to be anxious lest they lack material for anxieties or cause for torments! Yet when the wise man obtains these things, he does not know how to be altered amid changing events. He is ruled by reason, which he does not doubt holds dominion in governing human actions.

The wise man sits beside reason and attends to it as a pedagogue. It teaches him to use prosperity humbly, to treat adversities with contempt, and to overcome twofold events with uniform constancy. It also teaches that its pupil should not, by an altered expression, show the things around him to be altered; that one thing is what a person ought to rejoice in and grieve over, another what it is manifest that he should desire and fear. “If the things in you are those against which there is no law,” it says, “rejoice. If they are those for which the law has been established, grieve. For the former make you blessed; the latter miserable. When the former are in you, they are both God’s and yours; but when the latter are in you, they are not God’s but yours alone” (Galatians 5).

When you know both sorts of things, then, if you love those against which there is no law, God’s image in you unfolds and performs its office. But if, knowing both, you love those for which the law has been established, God’s image is indeed in you, but, as though coated with filth or made more squalid by dust, it has fallen away from and is far from its office. For to choose and love good things rather than evil is to image God. And the more each person is conformed to one or the other in will [Note: [Col. 0177D] Printed editions: “more closely bounded.” The Rouen, Hebrew, and other manuscripts: “more conformed.”], the more like that one he is either in glory or in punishment.

## LETTER XIII

[Note: [Col. 0177D] Also numbered 57. Written about 1121.]

### TO A CERTAIN CONVERTED YOUNG WOMAN

[Note: [Col. 0177D] Some authors think this letter was addressed in 1121 to Matilda, wife of William, son of Henry I king of England, who was drowned in the shipwreck and who, after his death, consecrated herself to God in the monastery of Fontevraud. Later chosen abbess there, she died in 1150. Yet this letter seems to have been written not to a married woman but to a virgin, as the word *puella* (“young woman”) added to the title in certain manuscripts suggests, as does the term “bridegroom,” to whom he says that flight from the pomp of the world will be more acceptable than any dowry. Unless we say that William, being young, left his betrothed untouched and a virgin because the marriage had not yet been consummated. Thus, after her bridegroom’s death, she became her own mistress, bound herself by a monastic vow, and in the course of time was elected abbess. Hildebert seems to indicate this when he says that she has daughters as well as sisters, a distinction appropriate only to an abbess or superior: “Greet your daughters and sisters on our behalf.”]

He joyfully admonishes a certain nun, steadfast in her holy purpose, that she must beware of flesh and woman, as of accumulated weakness, and likewise of certain women whose neighbourhood, he declares, is a wanton enticement.

[Col. 0178B]

Joy and exultation overflow in me whenever I hear that you are safe and are following, in your purpose of holiness, the lynx, which, while pursuing its prey, does not know how to look behind its back. For you are ignorant of the false vanities and madnesses from which you fled away and remain in solitude. This is sound counsel from a provident heart. To turn away and flee from them is more celebrated than every triumph; no dowry is more acceptable to your bridegroom than such flight. This will make him a husband to you and, from a celibate marriage, will grant you immortal offspring.

Remember, therefore, to keep far from those women whose neighbourhood is an importunate and wanton enticement. It is difficult to guard virtue against this. Frequent attention to this effeminates the strength of a manly mind. You will find no one with whom it is more dangerous to travel. An enemy of this kind is overcome better by flight than by contest. [Note: [Col. 0178D] The same above, Letter 4.] For flesh and woman are accumulated weakness, and—even amid examples of virtues—easily lead to ruin. He who is granted victory over flesh and woman triumphs over every enemy at once.

Yet I trust in the Lord God that he himself will look upon the humility of his handmaid and direct your steps in his paths, so that your footsteps may not be moved. I do not doubt that this will happen if you persevere in what you have begun, if you direct the course which you have undertaken. Farewell, most beloved sister in Christ. Greet your daughters and sisters on our behalf.

## LETTER XIV

[Note: [Col. 0179D] Also numbered 62. Written about 1123.]

### TO THE QUEEN OF THE ENGLISH, THAT, BEING WITHOUT CHILDREN, SHE SHOULD MAKE CHRIST’S POOR HER HEIRS

[Note: [Col. 0179D] Thus Victorine manuscript no. 272.]

Adela—or Adelina, or, as Ingulf calls her, Aalix—who, according to his testimony, married Henry I, king of England, in 1122 as his second and childless wife, after the death of Matilda, his first wife. Hildebert had been earnestly asked by Adela, Henry I’s wife, to make her a participant in the prayers and pious works of the Church of Le Mans. He permanently granted this to her as a daughter of that Church, admonishing her to adopt Christ’s poor in place of the children she lacked and, as she had begun, not to cease supporting the monks dedicated to her at the monastery of Saint Vincent, as she had done.

[Col. 0179A]

When you receive this letter, know that your desire has been fulfilled by us. You earnestly desired to become a member and daughter of the holy Church of Le Mans, and to share in its prayers. [Note: Observe here the antiquity of associations among different churches through mutual prayers, and shortly thereafter the naming, or recitation, of the names of lay persons, even during the sacrifice of the Mass itself.
