On this subject see Dom Edmond Martène, *De antiquis Ecclesiae ritibus*, book VII, chap. 4, art. 8, where he treats it fully.]

The venerable abbot of Saint Vincent—namely William—was our messenger concerning this vow and petition of yours. Therefore, through the present page now offered to you, you shall receive what you requested, henceforth to be numbered among the sisters and daughters of that Church. We likewise have decreed that your name be regularly commemorated at the altar among those for whom we make special mention. Furthermore, from what has been told me of you, know that my spirit rejoices and rests in you. I have heard that you are wholly occupied with sacred pursuits and have found the way which leads to life. You have set your feet in the paths of the few; and your face is the face of one looking toward that city whose streets resound day by day with the praises of God. There you transfer your substance, where you will find a talent in exchange for a farthing. Happy and fruitful is such a transfer! For what you entrust to the hands of the poor you will receive back a hundredfold.

No one lays up treasure for himself unless he empties his purses into their hands. No one reaps well unless he makes his granaries suffice for their bellies. Continue, then, in what you are doing, daughter of Christ, you who are taught by God for God; proceed where you are proceeding. [Note: Another reading: “O taught by God, proceed”; but the Ebroic and Rouen manuscripts read: “O taught by God for God,” so that the sense is: taught wholly to serve God, or to belong to God [lacuna].] You proceed well if you arrive where you are proceeding. Yet we trust in the Lord Jesus that he himself will remove obstacles from his daughter’s way and direct your steps into the way of peace.

The God of Israel has, as it were, given you a pledge of his grace: he has granted you both abundance of riches and freedom from the burden of children. [Note: Thus MSS Royal 4080 and 4103; but Colbert 2662 and Victorine 272 more correctly read “her,” not “your.”] [Note: In the Lyons editions the sentence is also printed without division: “…into the way of peace, the God of Israel having a certain pledge of his grace,” etc.—entirely obscure. The Ebroic and Rouen manuscripts more correctly place a full stop after “Israel,” and then begin another sentence, as we have done here: “You have, as it were, a pledge of his grace.”] In these two things you have received a good equipment for running happily. By riches you pave for yourself the road to life; being without children, you proceed unburdened. By riches works of mercy are performed; by riches service is also rendered to him who came not to be served but to serve and to give his life for many (Matt. 20:28). Finally, by riches that Gospel saying is fulfilled: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings” (Luke 16:9).

Such friends are reliable friends; even in the day of calamity and misery, they do not know how to be unaware of their benefactor. With how great an increase will you then receive what you now entrust to them! How faithfully they will act for you when the Ancient of Days sits to search the hearts and minds of each person! In the law-courts, defendants entrust their cases to wealthy candidates for office; but in heaven no one pleads better for the accused than poor advocates. Before the supreme tribunal, the poor hold first place in repelling accusations. Hence whoever deserves the poor’s intercession may rightly hope in the Judge. He for whom their voices prevail does not fear a sentence of death.

Therefore acquire such persons for yourself; make them your advocates. Let your abundance aid their poverty. When they are in need, believe that Christ is in need. Though they have not seen you, let them see your goodwill in their blessings. Have you wool? Clothe the naked. We read that Dorcas, after Peter’s prayer, was raised up when the garments which she had made for widows were displayed (Acts 9:19). Do not neglect hospitality. Lot and Abraham, because they were accustomed to receive human beings, deserved to entertain angels (Gen. 18–19). Bury the dead, if not with your own hand, then at your expense. Tobit and Joseph live in the merits gained through burial—the one having provided burial for dead brethren, the other for Christ. Honour the memorials of the saints, and seek their aid through gifts made to them. Blessed Gregory is reported to have appeared to a certain matron who regularly attended the oratory of Processus and Martinianus, and to have promised intervention in the cause of her soul. [Note: Book II of the *Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily 32, no. 7.]

No one lacks examples of mercy; no one lacks the means to earn mercy. Peter and Andrew’s entire abandoned property, half of Zacchaeus’s goods, the widow’s two small coins, bread broken for a hungry person, and a cup of cold water are alike accepted, if the giver’s disposition is equal. For God attends not to what is offered, but to how it is offered. He is appeased when angered, not by the number of victims, but by the devotion of minds.

And he will be appeased if you persevere in what you have begun. Have you begun not to spare your riches, so that your sins may not be spared? This is good and saving counsel. The wise person never repents of it, never is ashamed of it. Indeed, Ambrose compares idle and untouched wealth to stagnant water in these words: “A well, unless you draw it out, is easily corrupted by idle inactivity and stagnant condition; when drawn, it gleams for drinking.” [Note: Ebroic: “idle”; Colbert and Victorine: merely “unmoved.”] The same author says of the same matter: “Standing water quickly breeds worms; so also abundance is pleasant when used, useless in idleness, and, as though with a muddy smell, offensive to God; it breeds worms, avengers of greed and injustice.”

But this is by no means to be feared of your wealth, since the succession of children does not press you to multiply it. In this too divine grace has thoughtfully provided for you: it preferred that you should be fruitful in spirit rather than in flesh, that you should give birth for heaven rather than for the grave. For by fruitfulness of the flesh many women move backward, anxiously considering what they may leave to heirs, what estates they may buy for them, where they may more advantageously place their grown daughters, what palaces may await grandchildren not yet born. Their sleeplessness serves these concerns; their labours store up treasure for them. They endure hunger and grow numb with cold. And what an heir, a libertine and glutton, may squander, they obtain through voluntary bodily suffering. O foolish parents, who, in dutiful service to their children, do themselves injury!

But you are fortunate, since you have none among whom to divide your mind, none for whose sake you may look toward vanities and false madness. Be wholly devoted, then, to the grace of God, without which we neither will nor work well. If you do not fail it, believe that it will in no way fail you. Farewell, dearest sister in Christ; and greet your husband on our behalf, to whom we grant the same participation that we grant to you. We give thanks to both of you because you support the monks of Saint Vincent, our sons and brothers, frequently visiting them, as I have heard, with abundant blessings. You have also done this good work, and we ask your devotion to persevere. Farewell again.

## LETTER XV

[Note: Alternative number 59. Written about the year 1123.]

**TO THE COUNT OF ANJOU**

[Note: This count is none other than Fulke Rechin. [Note: Dom Beaugendre is mistaken. The Count of Anjou to whom this letter was sent about 1123 is not Fulke Rechin, who died on 14 April 1109, or 1110 New Style. The letter appears to have been sent to the younger Fulke, son of Fulke Rechin, Count of Maine in right of his wife, named Eremburga, daughter of Count Elias.] Though he is accused by most authors of unrestrained and fickle lust, as one who repeatedly passed from marriage-bed to marriage-bed in adulterous heat, he may nevertheless, moved by some sense of repentance or piety, have bound himself by a vow to this pilgrimage to Saint James, already famous throughout the world at that time. He is the man who, in 1104, captured and burned Thouars, the most noble fortress of the dominion then belonging to the Duke of Aquitaine, as Hildebert notes here. Thus the Chronicle of Saint-Albin in Labbe.]

Hildebert does not indeed condemn sacred pilgrimages, but he places them—whatever pretext, even a vow, may have prompted them—far below the duties laid by divine providence upon each person’s station. Accordingly, he dissuades this count from his distant pilgrimage to Saint James, already very famous, maintaining that it is much more advantageous for him to set it aside and devote himself wholly to governing the peoples subject to him according to justice. To enable him to discharge this office properly, he proposes altogether excellent means.

To the memorial shrine of blessed James, most vigorous count, and man exalted by virtue worthy of praise, you have, it is reported, undertaken a journey. We do not deny that it is good; but whoever undertakes administration is bound to obedience, and unless he is summoned to greater and more useful things, he sins if he abandons it. Therefore, dearest son, inexcusable fault awaits you: you place unnecessary things before necessary ones, leisure before stewardship, and things not owed before things owed.

Among the talents which the householder distributed to his servants, no teacher and no Scripture whatever mentions wandering about the unsettled world. Blessed Hilarion, according to Jerome’s testimony, when he was near the city of Jerusalem, saw it only once, lest he seem to have despised the holy places. [Note: Jerome, *Letter* 49, to Paulinus, new edition, p. 564.] Moreover, the eye of your mind has been darkened beyond its ordinary condition if you do not see that the pilgrimage you have undertaken is full of dangerous contingencies. You will pass through the strongholds of the Duke of Aquitaine, whose hostility you provoked by prevailing in the capture of Toarcy—commonly Thouars. [Note: Thus the Rouen and Ebroic manuscripts, not “Thoari,” as in the printed editions.] With almost everyone the memory of injuries lasts longer than that of benefits. Besides, you do not know whether his father’s notorious treachery has not been reborn in the son. For more heirs of wickedness than of virtue are born today.

If you entrust yourself to a young and offended man, you will leave fear and trembling to your own people; for in him you must fear treachery from his father, fickleness from his years, and vengeance from the injury. We have also heard that the venerable King of England, your uncle, strongly disapproves of what you propose to do, bears it with distress, and steadfastly condemns it. Certainly, to scorn the counsel of such men is obstinacy bordering on madness. They can provide for your interests both by their affection and by their judgment. [Note: The printed editions read “success,” perhaps better; but the Ebroic and Rouen manuscripts, with many others, read “judgment.”]

Perhaps, however, you say: “I have vowed a vow to the Lord; I shall be charged with transgression if I make the vow void.” Recognize, prince, that you have bound yourself by a vow, but God has bound you by duty: you to the road, God to obedience; to the road by which you might see the memorials of the saints, to obedience by which you might provide for the memorials of the saints. [Note: Colbert: “merits.”]

Weigh, then, whether the fruit of the journey is so great that it can compensate for the loss incurred by interrupted obedience. If it is, make haste to lay down your shield, take the staff in place of the sword, hasten to depart, and join yourself to eloquent companions, who, according to Solomon, may serve as your carriage on the road. But if the good of administration is far greater and more fitting—which absolutely no one would dare deny—then remain in your palace; arrange relief for the afflicted, and, that all may live for you, live for all. Live for the commonwealth, giving it your nights and days. Let equity, not respect of persons, dictate the judgment of your court. Govern yourself by the laws and your subjects by love. Be the censor of your own people when you have pardoned others’ offences. Do not allow the innocent to be injured with impunity while you yourself endure injury without retaliation. Count the punishment of injustice among your more splendid triumphs. Shed blood neither without cause nor willingly. Grieve whenever you have shed the blood of one whom the law judges must be shed. Exercise power reverently in all things. Give glory to God when you do anything glorious.

Above all remember to assist the poor and the churches, for whose peace and tranquillity good princes have often purchased at the cost of their own blood. But because of such officials it is necessary to fear divine indignation: officials who do whatever they wickedly wish and unjustly act against those same poor persons and against God’s sanctuary. For such good princes with depraved officials Scripture—meaning history—now calls them Scylla, now Harpies. Scylla, indeed, is described as having a human face but encircled with dogs’ heads. The Harpies have a maiden’s face [Note: Ebroic: “a maiden face.”] but rapacious claws. Certain good princes are compared to these: they themselves abhor cruelty, complain of wrongs, and display humanity through gentleness and mercy; but their officials, in scenting prey, resemble dogs, and in rapacity the claws of Harpies.

Therefore, in fulfilment of your vow restrain the rapacity and exactions of your men, which are attended by the cry of the poor, the groans of orphans, and the tears of widows. By these things, as you may be sure, wrath is stored up for you on the day of wrath [Note: Ebroic: “if they are not restrained.”] and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works. Whoever does not correct evil when able to do so, because he shares the wrongdoer’s guilt, will also share his punishment. Therefore, as you are admonished by this present letter, use the counsel of your friends; use mine: remain at home, devote yourself to aid for the poor, do not long to behold the holy places, but strive to protect them; do not be carried about among memorials of stones, but carry about the memory of virtues.

## LETTER XVI

[Note: Alternative number 33. Perhaps written about the year 1128.]

He sharply reproaches a certain wealthy but wicked courtier for abusing riches and power, and attempts to call him back to repentance through contemplation of divine severity.

[Note: Neither the addressee nor the time of writing is known, unless perhaps it was Stephen of Garlande, one of three brothers of the same name and family. At that time he abused the favour of Louis the Fat and was immoderately increased in wealth and highest dignities. He incurred everyone’s envy at court, and finally so great the hatred of Queen Adelaide, his lord’s wife, that he was driven from court; having risen against his own lord and become a traitor, he was stripped of his chief dignities and eventually died disgracefully. This may have occurred about 1128, when Hildebert was Archbishop of Tours. Hildebert, who was not accustomed to flatter wicked men, however powerful and eminent, did not fear, with truly pontifical freedom and zeal, to reproach him for his criminal actions. It was probably to this same man, after he had been cast down from the height of his more favourable fortune, that he wrote the consolatory letter immediately following.]

I grieve, my brother, I grieve that you are so enslaved, so ungrateful to your Creator. You are the one man who has received in vain so many instruments for virtue. Perhaps you expect an invective, and pale with apprehension that a Philippic is being revived. Such anxiety certainly afflicts you, neither unusually nor unjustly. For it is customary for the guilty to fear punishments which they deserve. Hence you fear my tongue, since you furnish everyone with material for reproach. Yet this is not the writer’s purpose. I do not press you toward the noose with reproaches; rather, I labour lest your evil deeds draw you to the noose. I come to you as a physician comes to a sick person, as Menedemus came to his debauched son. My weapons pursue not your life but the shamefulness of your life. If you admit them patiently, they will draw out the corruption of vices and reconcile virtue with you.

Attend carefully, then, to the conclusion of my speech, which has enclosed its beginning. God’s grace is most serviceable to human beings, and, as though sworn to their service, grants them only those things by which they are good or can become good. For whatever it grants them is either virtue or an instrument toward virtue. From virtue itself comes their being good; from the instrument comes the immediate capacity by which they become good. Virtue is faith, moderation, self-control, chastity, gentleness, and similar qualities, by which people plainly become good and also blessed. But riches, powers, and other aids of this kind are means by which we are helped toward the good of virtue, as reeds and ink aid the art of writing.

Do you abound in wealth? It is provided for the duty of generosity. Have you become powerful? The protection of those subject to you is entrusted to you. Do you glory in intimacy with princes? You have been given an opportunity by which you alone may aid as many persons as either raging power or the unchecked retinue of the palace has resolved to harm. Thus all things are provided to mortals for virtue; and amid so many weapons of righteousness, not to be righteous is the failure of the creature, not negligence in the Creator. For God wills human beings to become good because God wills all human beings to be saved (1 Tim. 2:4); and, to remove the refuge of dangerous excuse, he prepares his grace on which we may rely, distributes aids which may support us, offers rewards by which we may be stirred, and bends his bow by which the sluggish may be frightened. Nothing is empty, nothing is useless to humankind, except the human being himself.

Although God so carefully provides all things for humanity, God, such a diligent provider, is nevertheless despised by humanity. [Note: “God” is absent in the Ebroic and Victorine manuscripts; it is present in Colbert 2662.] There is no thought of him, no concern for him, no reverence toward him. The human being rages in injuries against the neighbour, in contempt against God, and in abuse against things; guilty before the judgment of all, he gathers everything into judgment against himself. Thus we deserve a judge all the more severe, the greater our ability to do good. The more abundantly one is wicked, the more abundantly one is punished. He procures abundant punishment for himself when the means for virtue have been abundantly provided in vain.

Such a burden of condemnation is promised you by him who executes judgment and righteousness in Jacob. He has prepared many servants for your virtue—I mean riches and power, and other things of this kind, which either lie idle for harm or are employed for virtue. Your high birth invited and brought you forth to purchased estates, ancestral treasures, and ambitious palaces. You were an unformed seed, and before the material of your body had yet emerged from this earth, households of servants were becoming numerous for you and honours were being designated for you. Nature was already soothing you with certain blandishments, judging that you should be anticipated with gratuitous services, [Note: Ebroic reads “judged”; Colbert 2662 and Victorine 272, “judging.”] though it foresaw that you would be born to injure it.

Yet its accumulated services have profited it nothing, nor has costly favour. Until now, unless I am mistaken, it did not know that one person could suffice for so many crimes. Hence I suppose that it itself wonders from what folds there has emerged an image containing all the Furies. Every day Nero meets our eyes; every day Tarquin; every day Polymnestor. It is doubtful whether people more greatly disdain in you the boastfulness of Thraso or detest the cruelty of Dionysius. Indeed, whoever has offended against nature through disgraceful conduct or against laws through contempt has left you heir to his dishonour. Whatever opposes morals, honour, or sacred institutions is so familiar to you that you think yourself deserving of punishment whenever you do not commit things most deserving of punishment.

What, then, will you do when your Judge sits, and his zeal for vengeance burns against you? Will you not blush before his angels when they bear witness to your crimes and injustices? By what cunning will you escape the judgment of the apostles, whose teaching, left to you, while vainly urging innocence, has pronounced punishment? With what boldness do you promise yourself the patronage of the other saints, when, by despising their example, you forfeit their intercession? Consider the orders of the heavenly court; observe its persons. Amid so many you will find no advocate, because you will find none whom you have not offended. It is just that you should find all hostile when you have been hostile to all. Your cause there will indeed be pitiable but undeserving of pity, since both God and humankind will complain that it is full of injury to each.

Yet there still remains room for entreaty, and he who promises punishment offers himself to be appeased. But God does not have mercy on all. His mercy is not required by virtues, nor deserved by crimes. It is necessary neither for those who are very good, nor unobtainable for those who are very wicked. Between the two there is a certain mixed condition of life, not so purified as not to need a Judge appeased after death, nor so bound by crimes as not to deserve that he be appeased after death. But I do not dare promise you such a Judge until you promise yourself to be such a sinner.

## LETTER XVII

[Note: New from Colbert manuscript no. 4017, perhaps written in 1129.]

**A CONSOLATION**

To a friend.

[Note: This letter may not implausibly have been addressed to Stephen of Garlande, to whom the preceding letter was addressed. [Note: The authors of the *Histoire littéraire* do not think Letters XVI and XVII were addressed to the same man. In the former Hildebert rebukes a tyrant and attempts to draw him back from his corrupt way of life, saying, in his own words: “I labour lest your evil deeds draw you to the noose.” Could that man have been most closely joined to our Hildebert as a friend? Yet in the latter letter Hildebert calls him “my lord and friend,” and professes himself his faithful servant and true friend.] As our historians relate, about 1128, the third year of Hildebert’s archiepiscopate at Tours, Stephen, formerly Archdeacon of Paris, abused the excessive favour of Louis the Fat. He was raised to the dignity of chancellor and, after the death of his brother Anselin, to the office of seneschal or high steward of France. He burned with such frenzy of ambition and insolence that he inflicted various injuries on Queen Adela, or Adelaide, the king’s consort. Since she could not bear them with impunity, Stephen chose Amalric—who had betrothed Anselin Stephen’s brother’s daughter, and thus Stephen’s niece—as successor to his dignity. When the king wholly disapproved, Stephen dared to rise against the king himself by armed force, calling also upon the aid of Henry I, King of England, and Theobald, Count of Champagne. But when the king captured the fortress of Livry, which Stephen had occupied with auxiliary forces, and destroyed it after receiving a grave wound in the siege, he stripped Stephen of the dignity of high seneschal of France. The contents of this letter agree sufficiently with this history: Hildebert speaks with the recipient about the vanity of the world and the instability of fortune, since he had formerly been greatly loved by the king and heaped with riches but, in reverse circumstances, was hated as an enemy; hostile to the queen herself, at whose command his palaces were destroyed; and had dissipated in the costs of war the gold and silver formerly amassed. When the circumstances of the time and kingdom are considered, these details appear to fit no one more suitably than the said Stephen, to whom we have judged it probable that the preceding letter also could have been written. See Dupleix on Louis the Fat, year 1129.]

How greatly we desire and long for your good and your salvation, he alone truly knows who alone knows the secrets of hearts. But now, because I cannot speak with you face to face in person, I send these exhortatory letters to your affection. I write not because of any necessity of my own, but solely in consideration of charity. For the adversity which has befallen you, although it has taken from me bodily conversation with you, has not taken from my prayers the remembrance of you. Indeed, to confess the truth, when we celebrate the solemnities of Mass, we beseech the mercy of almighty God that he who forgets no one through ignorance may remember you through grace.

Before I begin this exhortation, I first offer a prayer, that God’s grace may go before our admonition and open the ears of your heart, so that it may gladly hear, faithfully retain, and effectively fulfil those things which concern true salvation. What, then, shall I first say to begin my exhortation? As a faithful servant and true friend, I wish to detach my lord and friend from love of the present life and raise his desire toward love of his Creator and the heavenly homeland. I must therefore say something about contempt for the world and afterward add those things which may stir his mind to love God. But because I know you are occupied with worldly concerns, I would, if I could, set forth our admonition in few words.

Let Solomon, therefore, the wisest of men, come forward first, declare to you the true judgment concerning contempt for the world, and say: “Vanity of vanities, vanity, and all is vanity” (Eccl. 1:1). O my lord, do you understand that what you hear is true? Certainly there is no reason to doubt it. Apply yourself, then, and understand the truth. Open your eyes and consider vanity. I ask you to consider diligently the course of your life, because, unless I am mistaken, in your very life you will perfectly recognize how vain all things are.

Recall how much worldly power was granted you in the time of your prosperity, how great an abundance of riches, and how great—what is greater still—your prudence in managing temporal affairs. You used to sit first among courtiers and arrange the whole kingdom of the Franks according to your pleasure. Indeed, as Solomon records having done, you became great; you made your works magnificent; you built lofty towers and beautiful palaces, planted vineyards, possessed male and female servants and a great household. You amassed silver and gold for yourself, the wealth of kings and provinces, and were filled with the delights of the children of men.

But consider briefly how much vanity and instability there are in all these things. For behold: the king himself, in whose affection you placed the greatest confidence, beside whom you used to sit because of intimacy and rank of honour, persecutes you as an enemy; and all that you had built at Paris with great labour is wholly destroyed at the queen’s command. The silver, gold, and money which you accumulated in peaceful times must now be expended in time of war; and, lest your enemies surprise you unprepared, you must think anxiously night and day. Thus, my lord, you may plainly recognize in your own life that Solomon’s judgment upon vanity is true. Solomon was exalted by royal power, incomparable in the gift of wisdom, and rich in abundance of wealth; yet though all these things were abundantly at his disposal, he ascribed no reality to them. Because he saw that they pass away, he rightly called them vanity. He should therefore be believed all the more because he learned by experience the things which he said.

If I were not pursuing brevity, I could still say things about contempt for the world which would not merely recall your mind from its desire by reason, but would strongly deter it. Such is this: “The world will pass away, and its desire” (1 John 1:17). And this: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will be made an enemy of God” (James 4:4). A fearful judgment! What could be said more terrible? For whoever becomes a friend of this world is shown to be an enemy of God. There is another reason why a rational mind ought to despise worldly things: they are acquired with the greatest labour, guarded with anxiety, and lost with grief. For it is written: “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (Wis. 6:7); and, “Those who possess riches shall with difficulty attain the kingdom of God” (Luke 18:14). What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? (Matt. 16:26.) Let this suffice concerning contempt for the world.

But if your affection wishes to raise its mind to the love of God, you ought frequently to recall the benefits God has bestowed upon you. Consider how great his grace toward you has been, how great his mercy: his grace, in that he freely bestowed his good things upon you; his mercy, in that he bore your evils patiently. Certainly, if you are willing to attend rightly, this one consideration can suffice to make you love God: by grace he gave good things in order to kindle you toward love of him, and by mercy he bore your evils in order to summon you to repentance. Finally, after he had offered repentance, he applied discipline like a loving father toward a beloved son, so that at least the man who refused to return when moved by benefits might return when chastised. For it is written: “God chastises every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6).

This war and persecution which you endure are indeed a scourge. Although your enemies persecute you from hatred, what they do is nevertheless preceded by God’s hidden and righteous ordering. Therefore do not murmur against God because of this scourge, for it would be hard for you to kick against the goad. Remember that when David fled the persecution of his son Absalom and a certain most wicked Shimei cursed him, the men who were with David grieved at the injury done to their king and wanted to kill Shimei. David, however, restrained them, saying: “Let him curse; for the Lord has commanded him to curse David, that perhaps the Lord may render me a blessing in return for this curse today” (2 Sam. 16:10).

For God’s sake, I ask you to attend carefully. Do as David did. Behold, he endured a curse; yet, although he could easily have avenged himself upon the man, he would not do so. He attributed that curse not to Shimei but to the Lord, when he said: “The Lord has commanded him to curse David.” For he was one of God’s sons and knew that he was being chastised by a loving Father. He would not attend to the wickedness of the one cursing, but to the usefulness of the curse. Therefore he said: “That perhaps the Lord may render me a blessing in return for this curse today.” I think also that he recalled his former sins. I think that he grieved deeply in his heart for adultery and homicide, and therefore endured most patiently the persecution of his son and the curse of Shimei. [Note: The printed text reads “and his”; the correction is probably “Shimei’s.” Both readings are possible.]

I have set forth this example of David so that you too may diligently consider your sins, open and hidden, small and great; and, in the persecution which you presently endure, may attend not to the utterly wicked will of your enemies but to the most merciful kindness of the Lord who admonishes you. Hear what the Lord says: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Rev. 3:19). For he strikes in order to heal; he chastises the sinner in order to cleanse him. Therefore do not reject God’s calling by closing the ears of your heart. Do not receive God’s scourges with a hardened heart. Do not cling tenaciously and obstinately in the deep mire, in love of the world. Allow God to draw you out of the pit of misery and the mud of filth.

Do not become like a cart sunk in mud: oxen pull it vigorously from the front and people push it from behind, yet neither by pulling nor pushing can they draw it from the mud. Behold, the loving God first granted you prosperity, in order to draw you; now he has applied the hand of adversity, in order to push you. Why, then, do you make the Lord, so to speak, labour so much for your conversion? Take care not to provoke him to anger. For “it is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:31). If he is moved, who can resist him? According to the judgment of the Psalm, do not trust in princes or in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation (Ps. 143:2), but in him alone who can deliver you from every distress.

But, that I may now set a limit to my exhortation, [Note: Probably: “that I may now put an end to the exhortation.”] I ask you to consult inwardly your own reason concerning what I say. For it is remarkable that your reason, which is so vigorous in providing for and arranging worldly matters, lies, as it were, dead when it comes to knowing and doing good. Yet perhaps your reason understands through discernment those things which are good, but, because pride resists, does not accomplish them. Pride rules over reason and opposes it by tyrannical law. Reason says: “If you did this or that, you would be acceptable to God.” Pride says: “If you did this or that, you would be contemptible in human sight.” O wicked and detestable slavery, when reason, which ought to rule as mistress, obeys pride as a servant-girl! I pray that reason may return to its due freedom; that pride, expelled from your heart, may depart; and that humility, which is dear to God, may take possession of its place.

## A SHORT ADMONITION
We would gladly have appended to the preceding letters two others which we found in one of the Colbert manuscripts after the last genuinely Hildebertian letter; but although their style seemed to us Hildebertian, the opening words of the first left some room for doubt. Therefore, lest on the one hand we present doubtful matters as certain, or on the other deprive readers of their edification, we judged that these letters—however outstanding in pious feeling—should be placed after all the others by way of an appendix.

## LETTER XVIII

[Note: [Col. 0189D] Otherwise 70. Written about the year 1130 [ [Col. 0189D] + Alford, in his *Annals of the English Church*, assigns this letter to the year 1125, no. 18.].] In this letter Hildebert greets Adela, wife of Henry I [Note: [Col. 0189D] Who is said to have died in 1135.], king of England, who is preparing to cross from Normandy into England. He consoles her for barrenness, asserting that no remedy is more effective for her than charity and beneficence toward the poor.

[Col. 0189C]

HILDEBERT, humble archbishop of Tours, to A. [Note: [Col. 0189D] That is, Adela; probably written about the same time as the preceding letter. Adela’s barrenness was discussed above, namely in the fourteenth letter of this book.] most excellent and most reverend queen of the English: greeting, and the earnestness of prayers.

It is reported, illustrious queen, that you must cross the sea and, by your return, restore joy and exultation to the kingdom of your crown. We do not wish you to leave Normandy without our greeting, since Christ’s poor number your welfare among their prosperities. For we have heard that you care for them and comfort them with frequent blessing. This is an excellent resolve, and one belonging to a God-fearing mind. We shall all have to plead [Note: [Col. 0190D] Thus Ebroicensis and two Colbert manuscripts, namely 4017 and 1168; the third Colbert manuscript, 2662, has *ituri sumus*, “we shall go.” Ebroicensis has *acturi sumus*, with the understood sense “we shall plead our cause.”] together before the Redeemer and Judge of all. Our advocates must necessarily go before us there, if we wish them to come to our aid.

Those advocates are the persons of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9). Such friends are trustworthy friends; even in the day of calamity and misery they do not know how to forget their benefactor. These, indeed, are understood to be the poor. Before the supreme tribunal the poor hold precedence in repelling accusations. [Note: [Col. 0190D] Colbert 1168 and 2662 read *dilationibus*, “delays”; more correctly Ebroicensis and Colbert 4017 read *delationibus*, “accusations.”] Hence whoever earns, under Christ, the intercession of the poor may rightly hope well concerning Christ the Judge. He for whom their voices prevail does not fear the sentence of death.

Therefore procure such persons for yourself; make them your advocates. Believe that Christ is needy when they are needy. Those who have not seen you perceive your affection in your blessings. If it has not been granted you from above to bear children for the king of the English, in these persons you will, without injury to chastity, bear children for the King of angels. Perhaps the Lord has therefore closed your womb, so that you might adopt an immortal offspring. If this is so, recognize that barrenness of the flesh is profit to the soul, not loss; glory, not shame; a benefit, not a scourge. For it is happier to be fruitful in spirit than in flesh, to give birth for heaven rather than for the grave.

It may even be that through assistance to the needy you will merit to obtain the offspring for which you long. Merits can indeed alter nature also; and among some persons you will find the reproach of barrenness wiped away by virtue. Abraham, because he was accustomed to receive men as guests, merited to entertain angels. Scripture likewise records that, by the prerogative of faith and obedience, he pleased the Lord. Know, queen, that by these means Sarah’s barrenness was removed and a son given to her: in him the merit of the father accomplished more [Col. 0191A] than the marital due, holiness more than nature. Although that son had been predestined for Abraham, the patriarch nevertheless attained the point of receiving him only through preceding merits. For what is predestined for the elect is obtained through prayers and merits.

Thus we also read that conception was granted to Rebecca through Isaac’s prayers, so that the multiplication of a race, which had been predestined in him, might be shown to have been fulfilled through prayers. Gregory says of this in the *Dialogues* [Note: [Col. 0191D] Book IV, chapter 8.]:

> “The very predestination of the everlasting kingdom is so arranged by almighty God that the elect attain it through the labor of prayer, in order that by asking they may deserve to receive what God had arranged before the ages to give them.”

The same author says:

> “It is clear that predestination is fulfilled by prayers, when he in whom God had predestined that Abraham’s seed should be multiplied obtained by prayer the ability to have a son.”

Farewell.

## LETTER XIX

[Note: [Col. 0191D] New, from the *Spicilegium* and the Ebroicensis and Bigotian manuscripts. Written about 1130 or 1131.] COMFORT TO A NUN: THAT IN ADVERSITIES SHE SHOULD GLORY IN HER CONSCIENCE. [Note: [Col. 0191D] Thus manuscript Victorinus, no. 272.] He consoles a nun assailed by slanders from certain persons of utterly bad character and, as appears, unjustly expelled by them even from her own monastery. He raises her spirit to endurance through the testimony of a good conscience and the example of holy women, meanwhile pledging himself as defender of her innocence before the supreme pontiff, namely Innocent II.

It is a celebrated consolation when Christ is at issue, and when one endures persecution in his cause. Therefore a daughter of Christ, whose conscience supplies glory and whose tribulation supplies a crown, should by no means be swallowed up by grief. Thus the Apostle’s conscience was his glory: strengthened inwardly by it amid hardships and persecutions, amid the torments of hunger and thirst, amid innumerable injuries from false persons, he fought the good fight, finished the course, and kept the faith (2 Tim. 4:7).

With such a conscience holy virgins and widows, trampling down sex and world, offered their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, making their service rational worship (Rom. 12:1). Hence Agnes gives thanks amid flames; Agatha praises God while her breasts are tortured; and other holy virgins seek their Bridegroom with their own blood, choosing rather to follow the Lamb wherever he goes than to follow a man wherever he goes wrongly. Such women place a pure conscience above every adversity of the world, knowing that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to be revealed in us” [Col. 0192A] (Rom. 8:18).

Take comfort from their examples, giving thanks to the Lord God because for a time you are far from the daughters of the world, whose concern is alike to diminish reverence, vows of continence, and the instruments of discipline. Yet be strengthened and be steadfast in the Lord, knowing that the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous.

We await Pope Innocent, [Note: [Col. 0191D] Thus it was written in the last years of Hildebert’s archiepiscopate at Tours. For he states here that he awaits the arrival of Pope Innocent, who was inaugurated in 1130; Hildebert himself is believed to have died in 1131 or thereabouts.] in whose hearing we shall set forth both your innocence and our complaint, and await from justice a friendly conclusion to both matters. Meanwhile, then, remember me, suggesting in my name to the other daughters of Christ who serve the Lord with you that in their prayers they make at least some mention of me before God. After the first week of Lent [Col. 0192B], moreover, send us your messenger, through whom you may learn our answer and we may learn your wishes. Farewell.

## LETTER XX

[Note: [Col. 0191D] Otherwise 12. Of uncertain date.] To the monks of Saint Cuthbert at Durham. [Note: [Col. 0191D] Thus the Ebroicensis manuscript. Durham, commonly called in English Durham, is an episcopal see in England under the archbishopric of York. It was formerly administered by Benedictines, under the invocation of Saint Cuthbert, titular and protecting patron of that church; his body too was preserved there intact and flexible, being discovered in 1069, that is, more than 418 years after his burial. See *Anglia Sacra*, in the *Chronicle of Holy Cross, Edinburgh*, at the year 1069, p. 159, and the *Chronicle of Melrose* at the year 1104, p. 163, *Anglia Sacra*, part 2.] He rejoices that their ways and pursuits are good; meanwhile he asks for their prayers and offers them his own in return at the altar, where, he says, the Son is offered to the Father.

HILDEBERT, humble servant of the people of Le Mans, to ALGAR [Note: [Col. 0192D] Thus the Ebroicensis manuscript. Algar is listed third in succession among the priors of Durham from the installation of the monks. See *Anglia Sacra*, *History of Durham*, p. 786.] the prior and to the entire convent of brothers of the monastery of Saint Cuthbert: may a good outcome follow upon a good beginning.

Since I first gained acquaintance with you, I have earnestly desired to see you again; but this has not yet pleased the Lord God, because although a man plans his way, the Lord directs his steps (Prov. 16:9). But since I hear that your ways are good, I give thanks to Jesus Christ, in whom the crown of righteousness is laid up for you. It is his gift that good is revealed to us from the North, and that, through the boiling pot, we smell the incense of your holy manner of life in the reports of those who come. My spirit is refreshed by this, giving thanks to the Lord God and rejoicing with you, whom it hears singing the Song of Ascents and setting ascents in their hearts.

Therefore we rely with so much greater confidence on the aid of your prayers, because we know that, as though from the gates [Note: [Col. 0192D] Ebroicensis reads *e floribus*, “from the flowers”; Colbert 2662, Victorinus, and Fuldensis read *e foribus*, “from the gates.”] you look within upon the heavenly Jerusalem and already see the Lord God in Zion. [Note: [Col. 0192D] The printed edition reads *interspicere*, “look between”; Fuldensis reads *respicere*, “look upon”; all the other manuscripts read *introspicere*, “look within.”] If the prayer of one who is a sinner yet a priest has any power, there we shall act for you, our brothers, where the Son is offered to the Father.

### Brief Notice

[Col. 0193]

Another letter of Hildebert is found in a manuscript codex from the Cistercian abbey of Foucarmont. It is the fifteenth among those which the Reverend Father D’Achery advised should be added to volume VI of his *Spicilegium*, at the end of volume XIII, p. 272. This letter is likewise addressed to Algar, prior of Saint Cuthbert, in exactly the same sense as this twentieth letter of the first book and in almost the same number and wording of phrases.

But since the foregoing letter in this Foucarmont manuscript is longer by several lines than in the other manuscripts and in the printed editions, and since it there commends to the men of Durham a certain monk named Robert, whom Hildebert, being himself a monk, calls his son and brother, we judged it proper to place the whole letter below, exactly as it stands, so that it might not escape the curious reader. It reads thus:

He commends a certain Robert to Algar, prior of Saint Cuthbert.

[Col. 0193A]

HILDEBERT, humble servant of Le Mans, to ALGAR, prior, and to the entire convent of blessed Cuthbert: greeting and prayers.

Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who according to his great mercy makes your ways and pursuits good. Through his grace good is revealed to us from the North, and through the boiling pot we smell the incense of your manner of life in the reports of those who come. Our spirit is refreshed by this, giving thanks to the Lord God and rejoicing with those whom it hears singing the Song of Ascents and setting ascents in their hearts.

Therefore we ask with so much greater confidence for the aid of your prayers, as [Col. 0193B] we know that, as though from the gates, you look upon the heavenly Jerusalem and already behold in Zion the Lord of saints. If the prayer of one who is a sinner yet a priest has any power, we too shall act there for you, our brothers, where the Son is offered to the Father. Finally, we humbly entreat your holiness, commending to you our brother and son Robert, that our favor may benefit him among you. Farewell.

## LETTER XXI

[Note: [Col. 0193C] Otherwise 36. Of uncertain date.] To ATHALISA [Note: [Col. 0193C] Thus the Colbert manuscripts, no. 5133.] THE RECLUSE. [Note: [Col. 0193C] Royal manuscripts no. 4103 and Ebroicensis no. 19 simply read “To A., recluse.”] He rejoices in her resolve of virginity, elegantly pursues its praise, and maintains that her state is far superior to that of married women or widows, provided that it is supported by humility.

As I considered your vow—a good vow—joy arose from your purpose, fear from the possibility of falling, and emulation from the crown. A Christian soul ought to rejoice when, having opposed [perhaps: turned away from] the mortal enticements of marriage, it seeks through virginity an everlasting offspring. Many indeed are pleased to procreate heirs and to earn marriage contracts through marital obligation. While dreaming of some comfort from offspring, these women are deceived by vain hope or tortured by waiting in delay.

Moreover, no happiness from marriage can be hoped for without cost, since it must first be acquired by a certain mingling of the flesh. She has an unhappy result who purchases the advantage of marriage at the expense of virginity. Costly is the offspring whose conception injures chastity and whose birth injures life. When it comes into the light, it is the beginning of anxiety [Col. 0194A], not material for joy. A corrupt child gives rise to hatred; but when the child is good, fear of losing it is born. What room, then, is there in the mind for joy when it is either inflamed by hatred or tortured by fear?

Perhaps it will be said that the disadvantages of the marriages described above [Note: [Col. 0193C] Victorinus 272 reads *scriptarum*, “written”; all other manuscripts read *praescriptarum*, “described above.”] are compensated by the benefit of a dowry and the acquisition of varied household goods. Yet, just as there is no restoration for this loss, so every compensation is inferior. It is an unequal bargain to purchase a brief gain by everlasting loss; whoever prefers anything to the grace of virginity provides badly for himself.

Yet wealth is preferred to virginity; but rust threatens wealth, moth destroys it, thieves lie in wait for it, and the violence of greater power is feared. To cast away the beauty of modesty in hope of these things is to persecute oneself. For the downfall of a great good is sought, a downfall at which even the rare successor to our life may begrudge us. It is exchanged for an incomparable price, which entices a thief to carry it away and the Lord to preserve it. Whoever, in order to leave heirs, lays aside the likeness of angels does not know from what an inheritance he falls.

Do you not know that those who neither marry nor are given in marriage are, according to the Gospel, like the angels of God? (Mark 12:25.) Do you not know the greatness of this good? Do you not understand that the Sabbath of virginity is a Sabbath of counsel, not of commandment: a Sabbath in which the flesh rests from the work of flesh [Note: [Col. 0194C] Ebroicensis: *carnis, quo*; Royal 4080 and 4103, Colbert 2662, Victorinus 272, and Rouen manuscripts: *carnis caro, quo*—“the flesh rests from the work of flesh, by which flesh tastes something above flesh.”], by which flesh tastes something above flesh?

Virgins do not know what feminine weakness suffers through marital license. They do not know, I say, to what wrongs a wife is subjected, how greatly anxiety wounds the fertile woman, or with what grief barrenness torments the barren. If she is beautiful, she scarcely escapes disgrace; if ugly, her husband despises her. No marriage bed is without strife—one is ashamed or weary of its married state. It follows, moreover, that the husband displeases her who does not seek to please her husband. Such a woman consults shrewd old women, resorts to sorcery, and, to gain favor, casts away innocence. [Note: [Col. 0194C] Ebroicensis, Royal 4080, and Victorinus read *innocentem*, “the innocent woman”; but Victorinus 272 and Colbert 1168 and 2662 read *innocentiam*, “innocence.”]

What rest, then, can there be for a soul to which either a husband is a punishment or conscience a scourge? Added to these are countless discomforts in the formation of seed, which announce conception and afflict nature. Pallor discolors the face, dizziness exhausts the head, pain is continual in the loins, and the stomach is frequently disturbed. Hunger is felt even amid delicacies, and with certain little clouds floating about, the eyes grow dark.

These and other are the disadvantages of marriage, which the Apostle, judging it too long to enumerate, declares thus: “Such persons will suffer tribulation” (1 Cor. 7:28). Yet I do not disparage marriage; rather, I prefer rest to labor and freedom to servitude. Virginity is a certain freedom of the flesh, owing nothing to that slavery of which the Apostle says: “The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does” (1 Cor. 7:4). Virginity, ignorant of marital business, experiences neither a woman in labor’s pains nor the uncleanness of a new birth.

Virginity is the silence of cares, peace of the flesh, redemption from vices, and primacy of virtues. Ignorant of a nurse’s vigils, virginity does not inquire what great quantity of household goods or what little draughts a foster-child needs. [Note: [Col. 0195D] Rouen manuscript reads *inquirit*, “inquires”; the others, *requirit*, “requires.”] Content with little, virginity is concerned for nature, not ambitious for the status of a matron. Breathing forth an angelic manner of life, virginity sings a new song—a blessed song, a song which no one can sing except those who have not been defiled with women (Rev. 14:4).

A virgin sings something which neither a married woman nor a widow can sing. Yet whatever a married woman or widow sings, the virgin too can sing in full. Understand, moreover, the song of all [emended: “new”] as praise of the Creator and thanksgiving. Virgins therefore praise Christ; widows praise Christ; married women praise him also. Married women praise him because from him they have the gift either of marrying without sin or of redeeming by works of mercy the fault they incur through marrying. Widows praise him because from him they have the gift that, having experienced marriage according to God, they refuse to marry again for God’s sake. Unmarried women praise him because from him they have the grace that, though they might lawfully marry men while virgins, they prefer to marry God in spirit, remaining virgins in flesh and spirit. [Note: [Col. 0195D] Ebroicensis and Rouen read *mallent*, “they might prefer”; Colbert 2662 and Victorinus 272 read *malint*, “they prefer.”]

Behold the sacred song of holy virgins: a song not old but new—not the song, that is, of Adam, in whom and through whom the integrity of mind and flesh was corrupted, but of him in whom and through whom humanity has not only been healed but even glorified above angels. The praise and exaltation of this virtue is a song unknown to widows and unknown to married women. Good widows may certainly rejoice in the other virtues and give thanks; married women also may do so, if they are good. But from the good of virginity neither married women nor widows, even good ones, can rejoice. This virtue belongs to virgins alone from Christ; the reward of this virtue belongs to them alone both from Christ and with Christ. For the virgins of Christ in some manner share a common crown with Christ, since they alone, according to John, follow the Lamb wherever he goes (ibid.).

Widowhood follows this Lamb, and marriage follows him also. [Note: [Col. 0195D] Ebroicensis, Royal 4103, Victorinus 272 and 292, and Rouen read *jugalitas*, “married life”; Royal 4080 and Colbert 1168 and 2662 read *conjugalitas*, “marriage.”] Yet neither marriage nor widowhood follows him wherever he goes. Each may follow the Lamb in the path of the other virtues, since each may imitate Christ. But neither can follow the Lamb by the path of virginity, because neither can imitate Christ in that respect. To hope for the renewed flowering of virginity is to forget nature.

Thus Christ’s virgins alone sing the new song; they alone follow the Lamb wherever he goes. Since they possessed with Christ a certain sharing in virginity, they also have a certain fellowship with him in the reward. Under this Bridegroom, integrity does not hinder fruitfulness, nor are children begotten through the service of desire. Blessed indeed is the marriage: burdened by no daily troubles, anxious about no tomorrow, and no threat to virginity. Blessed indeed is the bride whose modesty, while conceiving, is not lost; while giving birth, does not labor. But most blessed is the Bridegroom: no virgin exists unless she cleaves to him; none is chaste unless she loves him; none is free unless she serves him.

Nothing is more honorable than his love, before which not even royal majesty blushes. Nothing is more wondrous than his embrace, from which virginity gives birth and does not perish. Nothing is more living than his offspring, with whom no mortality is propagated. Nothing is more profitable than his dowry, in which eternity accompanies sufficiency. In his bride he does not seek fleeting beauty; he does not glory in gold woven into garments or in splendor of birth. Artificial beauty, and everything that enchants the eyes of those who look at it by being other than what was born, provokes hatred rather than favor, rejection rather than affection.

Indeed, he does not despise the deformed, though he is beautiful in form above the children of men (Ps. 45:2). He willingly joins himself to the poor, though rich toward all who call upon him (Rom. 10:12); he embraces the crooked and the hunchbacked, he whose single eye makes the whole body full of light (Luke 11:34). He does not regard noble names; yet who shall declare his generation? (Isa. 53:8.) He burns with love for decrepit old women, though he is the firstborn before every creature (Ecclus. 24:5). He reproaches no one for barrenness, he who “makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a joyful mother of children” (Ps. 113:9).

Yet there is one thing for which he rejects the bride and disowns her as his own. [Note: [Col. 0196D] “Rejects and disowns.” Thus Victorinus 272; but Victorinus 292, Ebroicensis, Colbert 1168, and Rouen read: “rejects and disowns her as his own.”] The sole cause of this rupture is corruption of mind. Deformity of mind offends the husband, tears apart the marriage bond, deprives her of the dowry, and casts out her who has been received. Your loving one examines the mind; from its quality he either pronounces repudiation or promises himself as husband.

Pride is suspect to him, and it cannot be reconciled with him. Their dwelling is different, and they do not inhabit the same soul, since they were not permitted to dwell together in heaven. Pride was indeed born in heaven; but, as though forgetful of the path by which it fell from there, it does not know how to return there again. Falling from the heights and celebrating funeral rites on earth, it has secured for all its own an everlasting dwelling in hell. Born from the purest and simplest substances, it still unsettles pure minds, daring to hope for victory over man when it triumphed over an angel.

Farewell; and remember to water the lily of chastity in the valley of humility with the falling drops of the divine Scriptures, lest it wither.

## LETTER XXII

[Note: [Col. 0197D] Otherwise 37. Of uncertain date.] To William, [Note: [Col. 0197D] He is the very man whom Hildebert, in his letter to the bishop of Angoulême, legate of the Holy Roman Church, calls “a man of consummate religious devotion,” sent by himself to reform the monastery of Évron.] abbot of Saint Vincent. [Note: [Col. 0197D] Namely, the monastery of Saint Vincent in the suburb of Le Mans, founded by Saint Domnolus, bishop of Le Mans, about the year 572 in the reign of King Chilperic, and now incorporated into the Congregation of Saint-Maur in France. Saint Domnolus founded it at the urging and following the example of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, as is clear from the charter of foundation, dated the day before the Nones of March, 572, which Saint Germanus subscribed. Thus Bondonnet, fol. 266.] When William was made abbot, he lamented that the best part of his contemplative life had been taken from him. Hildebert consoles him as a friend through several testimonies of Scripture, especially through the examples of Rachel and Leah, showing that it is no slight good to alternate in turn between contemplative and active pursuits; meanwhile he laments the idleness of those who strive to attend to neither—something he humbly laments concerning himself.

Experience and necessity alike have taught the wounded to flee either to friends for counsel or to physicians for healing. [Note: [Col. 0198D] Most manuscripts read *vulnerati*, “the wounded”; more correctly Royal 4080 reads *vulneratos*, “the wounded [as object].”] For this reason, dearest brother, you brought to me the contrition of your spirit and the anxieties of your mind, so that they might wholly depart through a friend’s advice or find some remedy in consolation.

You lament that the rest of contemplation which you had embraced has been taken from you, and that unwillingly you bear the burden of active care. You sat with Mary at the feet of the Lord Jesus, and behold, you are commanded to serve with Martha. The beauty of Rachel had charmed your mind, but now you are compelled to comply with Leah, who has been substituted for Rachel. Though you lie beside Leah for offspring, [Note: [Col. 0198D] Ebroicensis reads *collateres*. More correctly Rouen, Colbert 2662, Victorinus 272, and others read *collatereris*, “you lie beside.”] you nevertheless disdain her because she is bleary-eyed and unattractive.

You remember how soothing the delight was under Rachel, how harsh the service under her sister. You remember, I say, what banquets Christ supplied you when you embraced [Col. 0197C] his feet, and by what delights he drove hunger from your soul. You confess that the dishes Mary receives while sitting and listening are more savory than those Martha prepares and sets out while busily laboring. In the latter is bread for men; in the former, bread for angels. At that rich table nothing offered is loathsome, nothing undesired by the satisfied guest. There every sense of your soul reclined as a guest and was filled with a variety of spiritual dishes, tasting from them what suited each and sufficed for all.

There, by the hearing of your mind, you drank in the melody of heavenly songs, and in the streets of the heavenly Zion an angelic *alleluia* resounded for you. [Note: [Col. 0198D] Thus Rouen, Ebroicensis, and the printed editions. Perhaps *resonabat*, “resounded.”] There the fragrance “of life unto life” (2 Cor. 2:16) breathed upon your nostrils, and a breeze exhaling rose blossoms and lilies of the valleys (Song 2:1) announced eternal spring. There you also ate, as a human being, the bread of angels (Ps. 78:25), which came down from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:33).

No one understands how great a glory was displayed to the eyes of your mind except one who loves it. Before them came the most perfectly ordered law of the heavenly commonwealth, which so gathers every offense from the kingdom of God that no one envies one who is above him and no one scorns an equal. You seemed to behold virgins distinguished with the lily of chastity, martyrs with roses, confessors with violets. You judged their glory unequal in their knowledge of divinity, yet equal in eternity. In the bosom of each, however, you saw a measure so good, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing (Luke 6:38), that it seemed a gift of grace rather than a reward of virtue.

Among these things you ascended, so far as you were permitted, to the ministering spirits, considering with a more secret gaze how closely they cleave to God in love, with what humility they submit to him, and how diligently they run about, sent for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation. And because I do not doubt that you have read, “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matt. 18:10), you assigned an angel to each person, impressing upon yourself that blessed joy concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “There is joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance” (Luke 15:10).

Moreover, you returned in groaning and mourning to the wonderful workshops of torments, where “the shadow of death and no order, but everlasting horror, dwells” (Job 10:22), often recalling the prophetic saying: “Who can endure everlasting burnings?” (Isa. 33:14). The punishments of the damned now viewed, and the rewards of the blessed, increased your devotion. Thus, made a new possessor of the lower and upper watering-place, you melted wholly into tears which the consciousness of your sins had first poured out, through delay of glory. Contemplation called forth these affections in you. Through such sights you walked among the heavenly dwellings, and grieving that your soul had entered into so wearisome a lodging with the flesh, you sang with the Apostle: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23).

But now you complain that life-giving delights have been taken from you, that your passage to things above is blocked, and that the intercourse of heaven and earth has been removed—an intercourse through which you were so present to human affairs that you also shared in converse with angels. Thus you recall with greater tenderness the fruit of lost contemplation and sigh for its rest, because in caring for others you find less security and more labor. Yet if you consider carefully, the active life is material for glory, [Col. 0198D] not a descent into ruin. So that this may not pass you by as something unknown, I shall begin a little more deeply—if you do not grow weary.

You will find, dearest brother, the contemplative and active lives sometimes united in the same person and sometimes separated among different persons. To show us this through sacred and mystical histories, let Jacob be brought forward: Rachel and Leah, types, that is, [Col. 0199A] of the two lives, are shown to have been married to him together, etc. (Gen. 30:1). Christ likewise, now teaching in the plains (Matt. 16:5; Mark 6:32), now praying in the mountains (Luke 6:12; 9:10), represented both pursuits in his own practices; in them the prescribed callings harmonize so mutually that neither activity strangles contemplation nor contemplation activity.

Moses was such a person: in the tabernacle he spoke with the people; on high, he spoke with the Lord for the people. So Peter, having set aside the business of pastoral care, had ascended the watchtower of contemplation when he was told, “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13). So too Paul, helping the concerns of all the churches with the repose of a secret vision intermingled with them, was caught up into paradise and heard hidden words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter [Col. 0199B] (2 Cor. 12:4).

The other holy preachers also now come forth from the secrecy of contemplation into the public sphere of teaching, and now return from the public sphere of teaching to the secret freedom of contemplation. What they sinfully fail to do in administrative management, they lament in the sanctuary of contemplation; and what they behold in contemplation, they bring back to their subjects as need requires.

That in some persons there is action alone, while in others contemplation alone shines forth, Mary and Martha declare to us. Sacred Scripture teaches us that the two lives are figured by their pursuits. Mary, indeed, is recorded only as sitting and listening, never as helping her sister in her bustling activity, although her anxious sister, with a certain bitterness of mind, requested her assistance, saying: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me alone to serve? Tell her therefore to help me” (Luke 10:40).

Nor is Martha ever said to have mixed Mary’s part into her own service, although Truth himself bore witness that it was the best, saying: “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken from her” (ibid., v. 42). Therefore, by Mary—whose repose in sitting was interrupted by no administrative business—are represented, I think, those devoted to contemplation alone, who prefer contemplative solitude to our public life and say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Of such persons the Prophet says: “I fled far away and remained in solitude” (Ps. 55:7).

But Martha, to whom the administration of serving alone was entrusted, signifies certain priests especially of our own time, [Note: [Col. 0199D] Ebroicensis reads *operis*, “work”; Rouen and others read *temporis*, “time.”] for whom the throng of pressing business closes the sanctuary of contemplation, extinguishes the burnt offering of a contrite heart, and dries up the sacrifice of tears.

[Perhaps more clearly: “Those whom in this,” etc.] Those whom, in this great and wide sea, innumerable creeping things agitate, because they feel within their minds tumults like those of the forum, do not attain the repose of contemplation. For it cannot happen that one speaks with the Lord who, even while silent, talks with the whole world. Such a gossiping priest I, wretched man, acknowledge myself to be, [Col. 0200A] such a priest I carry about with me—a man who spends the whole day preserving living creatures, yet does not spend even a single moment preserving souls.

[Note: [Col. 0199D] Observe Hildebert’s humility. Colb. 1168 and 2662 read *conversandis* (“associating with”) instead of *conservandis* (“preserving”); Ebr., Vict. 272, Roth., and many others read *conservandis*.]

Business hostile to my spirit comes rushing upon me—business which claims me wholly for itself, which steals the secrecy of prayers, which deprives ecclesiastical offices of their proper times, and which, like a small creature, raging with daily stings, troubles me even while I sleep. And what I can scarcely confess without tears: the creeping, stealthy recollection of lawsuits follows me, miserable as I am, to the holy altars; and while I pray for its flight, I am surrounded by its assault.

You will find that such intrusive vexations were prefigured for us by those birds concerning which it is said through Moses: “Birds descended upon the carcasses, and Abraham drove them away” [Col. 0200B] (Gen. 15:11). I, unhappy man, sacrificing along with sacrificing Abraham, endure these birds too; but, since it has not yet been granted me to drive them away as he did, I have not yet been able to repel or avoid them. Woe is me: “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Yet countless losses of virtues follow the aforesaid occupations of a captive mind; and while we unhappy men lie subject to them, we do not even minister with Martha. Martha indeed ministered—but to Christ; she hurried about—but for Christ. But who could say that we hurry about with Martha, or minister with Martha, when, although we hurry about, we do so not for Christ; although we minister, we minister not for Christ? All of us, as the Apostle says, seek what is our own, not what is Jesus Christ’s (Phil. 2:21).

If, then, amid Martha’s very ministry [Col. 0200C] you desire what is your own; if you hunt after the little rumours of the common people; if you busy yourself with the seductive pleasures of the flesh, assuredly you are neither the Martha you pretend to be nor the Mary for whom you sigh. Hence, dearest brother, you have good reason to complain and good reason to weep.

But if you simply play Martha, you do well. If you move back and forth between Leah and Rachel, you do better. If you sit and listen with Mary, you do best. For action is good when, though the opportunity for contemplation is lost through its urgency, a brother who has strayed from Christ is called back. The righteous person is received in the name of a righteous person; moreover, that bread which came down from heaven and gives life to the world is distributed.

Yet it is better, taking turns in sitting, to distinguish administrative concern, [Col. 0200D] and amid Leah’s wearisome nights to take breath in Rachel’s welcome embrace. From this mixture comes a swift ascent toward heaven, when the same mind now labours for the blessedness of human beings, now shares the blessedness of angels. In the former, that is sown which is to be reaped; in the latter, what may be hoped from the seed is already seen. The former is a course toward the prize; the latter, a spur to the course.

For what shall I say of Mary’s single-minded devotion? The Saviour’s testimony alone is sufficient for her, when he says: “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42).

Martha’s concern, therefore, is good, but Mary’s part is best [Col. 0201A]. Martha’s is good, because she provides temporal assistance for her brother; Mary’s is best, because what she already embraces is eternal. Martha’s is good, because it is good to sow; Mary’s is best, because it is better to reap.

I have said this lest you suppose it no good, or only a small good, to alternate these different pursuits in such a way that one is now pleased to rest in contemplation of heavenly things, and now to labour for the benefit of one’s neighbours. It is one and the same ladder on which Jacob saw angels ascending and descending (Gen. 28:12). Since its top is described as touching heaven, it is shown that through it there is passage to heaven. By this ladder you too, brother, ascended: you saw what is done in the city of our God, upon his holy mountain.

But now you complain of descending. Once, as if looking in through doorways, [Col. 0201B] you breathed in the riches of the heavenly palace; now, cast down to these low things, you stand afar off, and though you minister abundantly to others, yet because you do not enjoy the wealth you have seen, you do not escape poverty.

[Note: [Col. 0201D] Thus above, in the twentieth letter of this book, he said to the monks of St Cuthbert: “We know that you look, as though through doorways, into the heavenly Jerusalem.”]

But let your complaint depart, I pray; let your sighs depart, for Leah too receives an inheritance in her offspring. For neither Rachel alone nor Leah alone accompanied Jacob as he returned to his homeland. Rachel accompanied her husband, the pleasing virgin because of her beauty; her sister accompanied the same man, embraced by him because of her offspring. Rachel accompanied Jacob in the son of her womb and in the sons of her maidservant. Leah accompanied the same man in the sons of her womb and in the sons [71] of her maidservant. Thus he, returning to his homeland, says: “With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and behold, I return with two companies” [Col. 0201C] (Gen. 32:10).

The same man, while returning with his wives accompanying him, sees an angel, seizes the angel, and, having prevailed in the struggle, departs limping because of the touch that withered his sinew. “All these things,” however, as the Apostle says, “happened to them figuratively” (1 Cor. 10:11). Hence likewise: “They were written for our instruction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (ibid.).

Thus, made Jacob, you embrace Leah and Rachel together, if amid the watchful cares of pastoral responsibility the brightness of the heavenly vision smiles upon you.

[Note: [Col. 0201D] Ebr.: “brotherly”; Roth., Colb. 2662, Vict. 272, and others: “heavenly.”]

Made Jacob, I say, you love Rachel for her beauty and Leah for her offspring, if you embrace the joy of contemplation in such a manner that in outward administration you seek the fruit of souls. Nor does the burden of marriage impede the journey of the laborious patriarch, [Col. 0201D] because the occupation of pastoral watchfulness does not cut off his return to his homeland.

And lest we complain that this same occupation removes the capacity for contemplation, Jacob sees the angel while returning to his parents; for the faithful and prudent servant, while seeking with devout desire the land of the living, deserves already to see God through contemplation, already to embrace him. Hence also, when the Lord was born, shepherds keeping watch over their flock see angels: for to those who keep careful and devout watch over preserving their flocks [Col. 0202A] lofty and divine things are made known.

Yet, according to the Apostle, however holy and however perfect we may be, “now we know in part, and now we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13:9). Thus Jacob, while returning, is said to have begun a struggle with the angel. For by the condition of a struggle, now the combatant prevails, now he yields. We, however, in those things concerning God which we comprehend in our minds, in some fashion prevail; but in those things which we cannot comprehend, we undoubtedly lie beneath.

Therefore, to use Gregory’s words:

[Note: [Col. 0202D] St Gregory, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, book II, homily 2, new edition, p. 1326.]

Jacob struggles, and the angel is defeated, when God is apprehended by inward understanding; he struggles and yields, because, as he strives to comprehend the unbounded light, he fails. In this struggle, when Jacob prevails, [Col. 0202B] the angel touches and withers the sinew of his thigh (Gen. 32:24), because when the mind apprehends divine delights in contemplation, the desire of the flesh withers from longing for them.

But when the sinew is withered, one foot remains sound and the other languishes: because, when the lust of the flesh is mortified in us, the foot by which we are directed toward God grows strong, while the one by which we turn away from God grows weak. Here too I think it should be noted that Jacob, struck in the thigh, stands firmly upon his sound foot; but with his weak foot he neither clings wholly to the earth nor is lifted wholly from it.

For after the allurements of this mortality which we bear about have been dried up, our inward person leans wholly and clings wholly to the foot of divine love, which prevails in him. But Jacob is partly supported by his weak foot and partly suspended from the earth, because [Col. 0202C] when love of worldly things grows weak within us, we rest upon one part of them by nature, but are suspended away from the rest for the sake of our crown. In the former, what we desire is a matter of necessity; in the latter, what we avoid is a matter of counsel. For “the creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope” (Rom. 8:20). And: “Everyone who competes in the contest restrains himself in all things” (1 Cor. 9:25).

You see, then, dearest brother, that Leah too returned to her homeland with Jacob accompanying her; that an angel met the married patriarch and did not shrink from one returning with a wife—he who confesses that a woman has been exalted above himself.

[Note: [Col. 0202D] He alludes to the Blessed Virgin, who was exalted above the choirs of angels.]

Heaven is your homeland: a homeland happy and desirable for its glory. There are your spiritual parents—blessed parents, parents who begot you for Christ, who went before you to Christ, [Col. 0202D] and who plead to Christ for you. Your return to them, even under Leah, is prepared—do not be afraid. On the way you will see the Angel of Great Counsel; and he who deigned to become the son of the Virgin Mary will not disdain to show himself to a son of the virgin Church. By the sweetness of that vision the enticements of the flesh will displease you, and the evil-persuading lust of the loins will wither. Your inward person, raised above earthly things, will grant little to nature and nothing to gluttony. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIII

[Note: [Col. 0203D] New, from volume IV of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium* and from the Ebroic and Rouen manuscripts. Of uncertain date.]

A certain archimandrite—

[Note: [Col. 0203D] Perhaps William, abbot of St Vincent, mentioned above. Since he had recognized Hildebert’s outstanding gifts in governing souls, he gladly consulted him in his difficulties.]
