—had consulted Hildebert about a most grievous temptation of the flesh, by which a demon afflicted one of his monks, particularly during prayer. In this letter Hildebert explains what he thinks about this temptation and what remedies ought to be used.

[Col. 0203A]

If what you assert about the brother entrusted to you is true, help from above must be sought for him, weapons with which he may fight must be sought, and triumph must be requested from him who “will not permit him to be tempted beyond what he is able, but will also provide an outcome with the temptation,” [73] so that he may endure it (1 Cor. 10:13).

No one should either be astonished upon hearing, or despair when experiencing it, that those professing divine service are worn down by temptations. For it is written: “My son, when you come to the service [Col. 0203B] of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1). Hence Israel, departing from Egypt, is pursued by Pharaoh with chariots and horses (Exod. 14:9); hence Satan, when about to depart from the one whom he had held in bonds from childhood, tears him more grievously and leaves him as if dead (Mark 9:25).

These are the battles which Christ’s recruits must fight. By these, as by certain tyrants, the enemy man attempts to choke the good seed, showing how great is the hatred with which he hates that whose birth and progress alike he envies. This is what the importunate tempter pursues in your brother; this is what the birds of heaven trample and devour. With new and unheard-of boldness he strives to uproot it. For, beyond the other temptations by which others also are commonly assailed, I have learned that there is something in your brother’s struggle [Col. 0203C] such that, just as I cannot hear without astonishment that a man of God is so deluded, so I can scarcely believe that the delusion is endured without harmful consent.

[Note: [Col. 0203D] Colb. 2662 and Vict. 272 do not contain the word *vix* (“scarcely”), which Ebr. has and which seems more consistent with the author’s meaning.]

For you say that, while he lies prostrate in prayer, an evil spirit attacks him, puts hands upon the praying man’s genitals, and does not cease either to touch them or to rub flesh against flesh, until it compels him, so agitated, to be defiled by an emission of semen.

[Note: [Col. 0203D] Colb. 2662 and Vict. 272 omit *sic* (“thus”), which Ebr. also has.]

Yet this delusion does not trouble him either in thought or in dreams.

[Emended reading: “this delusion troubles him.”]

It performs all this upon the man praying as though by a real human hand. When I asked you concerning the brother’s conversion, you answered that he was a virgin; moreover, that he had lived such a life that, ignorant of food prepared by fire, he bore an enemy both to his mind—

[Note: [Col. 0203D] Ebr.: “vices”; all others: “mind”—namely Colb. 4017, 1168; Reg. 4013; and others.]

—and to his flesh.

What I think on this matter, then, the present letter will disclose to you. From the character and timing of the temptation, it is easy, unless I am mistaken, to recognize what that minister [Col. 0204A] of death desires to extort from him and at which of his goods envy gnaws—namely, prayer and virginity. To overthrow these, he fights mortals with such persistence that he is not ashamed to be conquered often, provided that he can glory in a single victory.

Therefore he attacks the man praying in order either to take prayer from him altogether or to interrupt his hours of prayer. For he knows that “the Lord looks upon the prayer of the humble and does not despise their petitions” (Ps. 102:17). He knows that prayer changes the unchangeable, turns the Judge into a Father, and loosens the bonds of our wickedness. He knows that Moses, by prayer, breaks divine indignation; that Joshua arrests the course of the sun; that Elijah takes away and restores the rains; that fifteen years are added to Hezekiah; that two hundred and [Col. 0204B] seventy-six souls are spared for Paul in the ship.

You hear how great is the power of prayer: it triumphs not only over nature, but also over the Lord of nature. To wrest this from God’s servant is to take away the mediator of divine peace.

But by what reasoning can I call a man a virgin when you maintain that, through the touching of his genitals, he is defiled by an emission of semen? A person may indeed be tempted unwillingly, and may be stimulated unwillingly. But I do not know how he can be carried as far as this except willingly. If, therefore, the one tempted consents to the temptation, Satan has cause for rejoicing, and laughs at him as fallen, whom he has bent by consent toward the shameful act of fornication.

But if the brother is free from consent, let him give glory to God, because where the enemy seeks victory, there the enemy himself, conquered, falls. It is therefore for that brother [Col. 0204C] to examine his own conscience; and if he knows that he has fought manfully, let him pray—

[Note: [Col. 0204D] Ebr. reads *orare* (“to pray”) rather than *oret* (“let him pray”).]

—that he may not fall. But if he perceives consent emerging from the temptation, he must pray far more devoutly in order that he may rise again; he must persist in holy fasts, water his bed with tears every night, undertake frequent and severe discipline, chastise his body with Paul, and reduce it to slavery.

[Note: [Col. 0204D] Thus this method of voluntary scourging is not so new, since in Hildebert’s time its practice had already become established among holy men for repressing movements of the flesh.]

[Note: [Col. 0204D] Thus Colb. 2662 and Vict. 272; *lacrymis* (“with tears”) is absent in Ebr.]

The members upon which the enemy ventures beyond hearing must also be fortified with the sign of the cross and sprinkled with blessings of salt.

[Note: [Col. 0204D] So too the sprinkling of holy water is not new; Hildebert calls it “the blessing of salt” and judges it especially suitable for preserving chastity.]

A manifold armour is needed, by which the manifold blows of adversaries may be beaten back. Recognize this kind of conflict as promised to us when Joshua succeeded Moses and sought to destroy the resisting [Col. 0204D] foreigners.

[Note: [Col. 0204D] Ebr. reads *resistens* (“resisting,” singular); Colb. and Vict. more aptly read *resistentes* (“resisting,” plural), as also Reg. 4103.]

For the Lord did not will that enemies should be altogether lacking to Israel; rather, he left adversaries to them so that their children, avoiding womanish [Col. 0205A] lethargy, might learn by the practice of fighting to repel foreigners.

[Note: [Col. 0204D] Ebr., Colb., and Vict. read *eis* (“to them”); the other reading is *ejus* (“his”).] Thus, in the first book of Judges, he is found to have been unwilling to destroy certain nations or deliver them into Joshua’s hands, in these words: “These are the nations which the Lord left, that through them he might instruct Israel, and all who had not known the wars of the Canaanites, so that afterward their children might learn to fight against enemies and have experience of warfare” (Judg. 3:1).

Those wars certainly prefigured the struggle of the children of the Church, which has been left to us “against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12). For the whole life of man is as it were an arena in which continual and perilous conflict always threatens us; [Col. 0205B] in which falling is frequent and rising difficult; in which wounds are innumerable and do not readily promise a scar; in which victory is rare and never secure.

[Note: [Col. 0205C] Thus Ebr. and Colb. 2662: “where a perilous conflict is always for us.” Colb. 4017 and 1168, Reg. 4103: the same. Vict. 272: “where there is always a perilous conflict for us.”]

[Note: [Col. 0205C] Thus Colb. and Vict. read *difficile* (“difficult”); Ebr. reads *difficilis*.]

Thus, amid the slippery course—

[Note: [Col. 0205D] Ebr.: “playful”; Colb. and Vict.: “slippery.”]

—of this life, Christian religion is never safe from a fall. There is always at hand something to disturb the path—

[Note: [Col. 0205D] Ebr. reads *semitam* (“the path”); Colb. and Vict. read *quod ad vitam* (“that [leads] to life”).]

—and permit no one to pass untempted. Birds always and importunately descend upon Abraham’s sacrifice; Pharaoh always drowns our males in the river; Balak always prepares material for enticements for the people passing through; Belshazzar always carries off the sacred vessels from the temple of the Lord.

Against the snares and assaults of such beasts, let your brother multiply his diligence in prayer; let him fight with tears and sighs. In falling, let him be strengthened by hope; in victory, let him display humility, [Col. 0205C] crying with all his desire after him who says to his own in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you always, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

## LETTER XXIV

[Note: [Col. 0205D] New, from volume IV of the *Spicilegium* and several manuscripts. Of uncertain date.]

### TO A CERTAIN FRIEND, PERHAPS A BENEFACTOR OF HIS CHURCH

That even brute animals rebuke the ungrateful.

[Note: [Col. 0206C] Thus Reg. MS 4103 and Vict. 272.]

It is salutary to surpass gray hair and age alike in understanding and counsel. Even brute animals rebuke those who forget services rendered: for it is evident that they both follow their benefactors [Col. 0206A] more devotedly and, as though in thanksgiving, stand by them and show affection.

We give thanks to the Lord God that you imitate them, since by your counsel you have provided that that man’s benefits and services should not remain unrewarded with you. This I both praise and thank you for, being confident that hereafter you will provide him with still greater things. What I have done for him, [probably: the bearer of the present letter] will himself tell you more fully, since he saw, read, and understood in my letters my petitions and counsel addressed to them.

## LETTER XXV

[Note: [Col. 0206C] New, from volume IV of the *Spicilegium* and the Rouen, Évreux, and other manuscripts. Of uncertain date. In the Évreux manuscript it is placed, without any division, after the final words of Hildebert’s letter to Pope Honorius, where he treats frivolous appeals. Since it has no connection whatever with that letter, and since it is found separately in the Rouen manuscript and others, we have judged that it too should here be printed separately.]

He teaches a friend the distinction between love of God and love of the world.

Between love of this world and love of God [Col. 0206B] there is this difference: the love of this world seems sweet at its beginning but has a bitter end; the love of God begins in bitterness, but its final things are full of sweetness. The Gospel narrative shows us this by a most beautiful comparison when, singing of the wedding of our Bridegroom, it says: “Every man first sets out the good wine, and when they have become drunk, then that which is inferior. But you have kept the good wine until now” (John 2:10).

Every man—that is, the carnal man—first sets out good wine, because in his pleasure he feels a certain false sweetness. But once the frenzy of evil desire has intoxicated his mind, he offers what is inferior, because the sting—

[Note: [Col. 0206D] Absent in Évreux; present in Rouen and others.]

—of conscience, supervening, grievously torments the mind which it had previously delighted. But our Bridegroom offers good wine at the end [Col. 0206C] when he permits the mind which he intends to fill with the sweetness of his love first to be made bitter by a certain compunction of tribulation, so that, after tasting bitterness, it may drink the most sweet cup of charity.

[Note: [Col. 0206D] Ebr. reads *tergum* (“back”); Roth. reads *gustum* (“taste”).]

And this is the first sign that Jesus performs before his disciples, and they believe in him: the sinner and penitent first begins to have confidence in God’s mercy when, after long weariness of sorrow, he feels his heart raised up by the consolation of the Holy Spirit.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0207]

## LETTER I

[Note: [Col. 0207C] Otherwise numbered 17. Written about the year 1098.]

[Note: [Col. 0207C] Whom the letter G, prefixed to “archdeacon,” designates is unclear. It is probable, however, that it denotes the archdeacon of Sées, whom Hildebert seeks to instruct concerning what should be done in the case of a certain marriage. Yet that archdeacon does not seem to have complied; rather, he seems to have been prepared to permit the marriage, though unlawful. Hence Hildebert was probably compelled, as he says in the following letter, to repeat his outcry before Serlo, then bishop of Sées—as most manuscripts read, not “Sergius,” as one Colbert manuscript, no. 5133, has, since no bishop of Sées bearing that name is found in the succession of its bishops—in order that he might forbid such a marriage. Hence it is also clear that this letter, which in printed editions and some manuscripts is numbered seventh, wrongly precedes the following one, which was numbered seventeenth, as the logic of the subject proves.]

### TO G., ARCHDEACON

That no woman may marry a man whose brother she previously married, even if no carnal union intervened.

[Col. 0207A]

If faith is not denied to authority, marriage is effected by consent of the will, not by the commerce of physical union. Hence Ambrose, in his *Exhortation to Virginity*: “It is not the deflowering of virginity,” he says, “which makes a marriage, but the marital agreement.” And again: “When a girl is joined to a man, there is a marriage; it is not recognized only when she has intercourse with the man.”

Had you considered these things more carefully, as you ought, a girl surely would not enter into marriage with the man whose brother solemn wedding rites had joined her to himself and with whom she had entered into consent, although sudden death had cut short the hidden course of marriage. Those between whom such a marriage is contracted are not at all tolerated by dispensation of the Church, but are punished by the censure of justice.

Concerning such cases you will find this in chapter 10 of the Council of Tibur: “A certain man betrothed a wife with whom he was unable to have intercourse; his brother secretly corrupted her and made her pregnant. It was decreed that, although she could not be a wife to her lawful [79] husband, nevertheless the brother could not have the woman betrothed to his brother. But let the adulterer and adulteress undergo the penalty for fornication; lawful marriages, however, are not to be denied them.”

It was therefore superfluous to lead the aforesaid girl to the ordeal of hot iron, as though by that test she would prove that she had had no intercourse with her former husband. For a law is brought forward in vain when it offers no help at all in deciding the pressing case. Farewell.

## LETTER II

[Note: [Col. 0208C] Otherwise numbered 7. Written in the same year as the preceding letter.]

Hildebert urges the bishop of Sées—

[Note: [Col. 0208C] This letter must have been addressed to Serlo in the first year of Hildebert’s episcopate, since Hildebert was installed in 1097. Serlo, however, was installed in 1091 and died in 1098, if Dom Robert’s *Gallia Christiana* is to be believed. [Addition: Serlo, bishop of Sées, did not die in 1098, as Dom Robert falsely asserts, but in 1122 (Mabillon, year cited, p. 74, no. 24). Dom Bessin inserted this letter and the preceding one in the *Norman Councils*, p. 463.]]

—not to permit the completion of the marriage discussed in the preceding letter.

Continued wrong compels us to repeat our outcry. The matter is plain. Walter—

[Note: [Col. 0208C] Thus all manuscripts, not “Gautier,” as in the editions.]

—of Clinchamp [Col. 0208A] is said to have had two sons.

[Note: [Col. 0208D] Otherwise “of Dumcamp,” but Colb. 2662, Évreux, Rouen, and others better read “of Clincampo,” commonly “de Clinchamp.” This name is still known in the district of Caen in Normandy.]

The elder of them, already becoming a man, betrothed to himself a girl unequal to a husband and still immature for the business of marriage. Nevertheless, when their parents came together, the virgin was solemnly given in marriage and dowered. The remaining sacraments of marriage were celebrated; the marriage was completed by consent of the will, not by the due of physical union.

But after the man died, before they had come together, the dead man’s father prevented the aforesaid girl from returning to her parents, intending, as rumour has it, to give her as wife to his other son. Yet if authority is respected, a woman so given to a husband and united by consent was a wife, although marital intercourse did not follow. Hence Ambrose, in his *Exhortation to Virginity*: “A woman betrothed to a man,” he says, “has received the name of wife. For when marriage is initiated, then the name of marriage is assumed. It is not the deflowering of virginity that makes marriage, but the marital agreement. Finally, when a girl is joined [Col. 0208B] [to a man], there is marriage; it is not recognized only when she has intercourse with the man.”

Isidore, *Etymologies*, book IX, chapter 7: “They are more truly called spouses from the first pledge of betrothal, although marital intercourse may be unknown to them.” John Chrysostom says of the same matter: “Marriage is not made by intercourse but by will.”

Moreover, consideration must be given to the fact that it is by no means sufficiently clear whether the husband left the girl as unstained as she was uncorrupted. If the brother has defiled her by any touch whatsoever, he will succeed his brother not to marriage but to incest.

It remains, therefore, for your diligence either to prevent the marriage from being begun or to dissolve it if begun. Remember also that the girl must be returned to her parents, so that she may marry in Christ and her father’s inheritance may return to his daughter by benefit of the law. Farewell, brother, and love me as I love you.

## LETTER III

[Note: [Col. 0209B] Otherwise numbered 35. Written about the year 1098.]

### TO BISHOP M.

[Note: [Col. 0209B] It seems probable that the letter M denotes Marbod—

[Addition: Dom Beaugendre supposes that M denotes Marbod, who in 1098 had not yet been consecrated bishop of Rennes, and maintains that Raynald of Martigney was at that time bishop of Angers. Yet, as Dom Beaugendre himself testifies (p. 1389), Marbod was made bishop of Rennes in 1096 at the Council of Tours. Raynald of Martigney was designated bishop of Angers only in 1101 and was anointed with holy oil by Ralph, archbishop of Tours, in the presence of Bishop Marbod; this letter therefore seems to have been written after 1112, not to Marbod but to another, hitherto unknown, prelate.]

—who, before he later became bishop of Rennes, was only a canon and archdeacon of Angers, and wished to substitute his nephew, a man otherwise upright and learned, for himself in his canonry. For this purpose he requested Hildebert’s good offices with the bishop of Angers, then Raynald of Martigney, with whom Hildebert had been reconciled.

The letter seems, however, to have been written early in 1098, in the second year of Hildebert’s episcopate and the first of Raynald’s; for in 1099, the second year of Raynald’s episcopate, he is reported in the cartulary of the abbey of La Rota of the Order of St Augustine to have dedicated that church. The notice that it was written to Bishop M. seems to have been added by the publisher or copyist, not by Hildebert himself, who addressed it to Marbod only as a canon.

This letter also makes it clear that Marbod already came from a noble and powerful family, since the canons of Angers had already become afraid of Marbod and his relatives; the whole kinship group was suspect to them. Nor perhaps will it seem improbable that the family of the Marbods, now commonly called de Marboeuf among the people of Rennes, illustrious through ancestors and forefathers from that ancient stock, [Col. 0209D] descended from it. Even now they hold the highest offices in the Parliament of Brittany, most devoted to the king’s service and at the same time the most zealous patrons of their homeland.

As time went on, a most serious quarrel arose between Raynald and Marbod; on this see Marbod’s letter of complaint against Raynald, printed at the end of this book. For when many eminent men opposed Raynald’s election, especially Hildebert himself—who neither consented to nor wished to attend his ordination because Raynald had not reached the age required by the sacred canons for a bishop and had not yet received holy orders, as is clear from the third and fifth letters of this book—Hildebert, as Godfrey of Vendôme, who also disapproved of it, reports in letter eleven of book one and elsewhere, called that ordination not a consecration [Col. 0210B] but an execration [Col. 0210C].

But when Marbod supported Raynald’s party and promoted his election with all his strength, though it was unlawful, he was stripped of all his possessions and variously harassed by Raynald himself, unmindful of benefits received from him, when Marbod went to Rome, as may be seen from the aforesaid letter of complaint.]

A certain canon had asked Hildebert to intercede with the bishop of Angers so that he might be permitted to substitute his nephew in his canonry. Hildebert tells him what he has done for him, what obstacles he has found in the matter, and by what means he may obtain this favour from the bishop and canons opposed to him.

[Col. 0209A]

I approached the bishop of Angers on your behalf, diligent indeed but an ineffective intercessor. His advancement—

[Note: [Col. 0210C] Thus the Évreux, Rouen, and other manuscripts, not *tua* (“your”), as in the printed editions.]

—your labour, and your embarrassment were reported to him. I impressed upon him what you had conferred upon him and what you had endured for him, so that, when your merit was reconsidered, he might be instructed concerning the reward due to you.

You asked to be released from your canonry, and that your nephew should be substituted for you: a young man distinguished in character and trained beyond his peers in the disciplines of literary learning [Col. 0209B]. When the bishop, privately seeking my counsel, asked what I advised, I said: “Do not delay what you are asked to do, so that, if you love him, satisfaction may be made to a friend; if you do not love him, he may become a distant enemy. This exchange ought to be approved: by it you will either increase devotion or procure peace. If, then, he has deserved well of you, oblige him; if he is suspect, proscribe him. Learn either to avoid the name of ingrate or to remove the danger of plots.”

Moved by these words, he departed, carrying with him a favourable intention: that a successor should be appointed for you, not as the price of peace, but as an advantage of friendship. I thought the affair concluded when I learned that the bishop’s mind had changed. The canons resisted, and it is difficult to make them comply with you, whom, though you profess service, you are said to embitter by injuries [Col. 0210A].

Fear of you and yours has come upon them; and while your own person is accused of cunning, your entire family is under suspicion. They think cunning is hereditary; having experienced the craftiness of Ulysses, they fear Greeks even when bearing gifts. Thus they will scarcely receive anyone for your sake, since because of you they prejudge everyone. If, therefore, you wish to reach the end you seek, another road must be taken: whatever injuries went before must be unlearned; speech must be restrained; and you must devote yourself to the services of the great.

One must flatter power, not disparage it. In these times, offence does not obtain a favour. The favour of fortune is necessary even for those who have deserved well [Col. 0210B] to obtain favour. Most mortals are ungrateful for services, and lest they reward those who cultivate them, they complain that they have been offended. In this matter, unless I am mistaken, you will not accuse the bishop of Angers if he finds you kindly disposed and a son of peace.

82. LETTER IV

To the Archbishop of Tours

[Note: [Col. 0210C] Elsewhere numbered 9. Written about the year 1098. For Raynald of Martiniac, of whom this letter treats, is found in the cartulary of the abbey of La Roë, in the diocese of Angers, to have dedicated its church on 17 Kalends of May, 1099. Thus in *Gallia Christiana*.]

[Note: [Col. 0210C] This was Ralph II, who, according to Dom Maan, was installed in his metropolitan see of Tours in 1086 and died at the beginning of 1118.]

He advises the archbishop not to consecrate a young man

[Note: [Col. 0210C] Namely Raynald of Martiniac [ [Col. 0209] + Raynald of Martigney was elected bishop of Angers in 1101; consequently the letter is wrongly assigned to 1098.], whose election, defective in every respect, Geoffrey of Vendôme attacked in Book III, Letter II, addressed to Raynald himself. It had been carried out through the shouting of one insignificant woman—a public actress—the acclamation of the lowest rabble, the protest of the clergy, and the opposition of the greater and sounder part of the people. Accordingly Geoffrey testifies in the same place that Hildebert spoke apostolically and evangelically when, summoned by his metropolitan to attend Raynald’s consecration, he refused to go and called it not a consecration but an execration. After Hildebert, St Bernard spoke similarly in Letter 166, §1, to Pope Innocent, when he complained [Col. 0211D] that certain bishops had not consecrated but execrated the bishop-elect of Langres, who had been stealthily elected contrary to the canons. Again, in Letter 235, §2, [Col. 0212D] to Pope Celestine, he speaks against the invader of the Church of York, whom he also calls “execrated.”]

not canonically elected.

[Note: [Col. 0210D] Thus Reg. 4103 and Victor 272.]

Your request, by which we are summoned to the consecration of your bishop-elect, [Col. 0211A] would readily find our assent if reason supported it. But those who were present testify that, in the case of a young man found below the required sacred orders and age, and not elected by the clergy, the seditious shouting of a disturbed crowd extorted an episcopal election. The dean further states that the cantor, the archdeacons, and the greater part of the chapter protested as far as they could, and, for reasons of conscience, withheld their assent from such audacity, while, out of fear, they withdrew their own presence as well.

If this is so, I grieve for those who took part, because of their transgression and their contempt for justice. Who would not grieve that canonical rigor has been so trampled underfoot by such a precedent? Who would not marvel that prudent religious persons have inclined to assent to a new sacrilege? I speak with your leave. That assent, subversive of authority, would be inexcusable [Col. 0211B] if we did not think it had been extorted by necessary dispensation. For, unless I am mistaken, you yielded to fear, not to reason; and to say “I approve” meant nothing else than “I appeal to Caesar.”

No one was greater than Paul; no one was equal to Christ. Yet Paul, when he was being guarded at Damascus, was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall. Christ likewise, because the Jews had taken up stones, hid himself and went out of the Temple. Both escaped by dispensation; yet neither, when his time came, refused to die for the truth. Paul, when it was necessary, suffered for Christ; Christ suffered for the world. If the example of flight pleased you, let the example of constancy please you also. Let an assertion of truth make good the lapse caused by fear. No one falls shamefully who, after falling, fights more bravely. Let not a father’s eye be troubled by anger against his son; rather, according to Solomon, let him consider that the wounds of a friend are better than the kisses of flatterers (Prov. 27:6).

But, that more prudent counsel may be given both to you and to the young man, do not lay hands upon him hastily, lest this be reckoned either to him for judgment or to you for a fall. Whoever does not thus safeguard this matter acts from ill will. May the Father spare me, for I shall spare my own soul. In vain, I say, will you wait for me, because you will lay hands on him without me.

## LETTER V

To R. of Angers

[Note: [Col. 0211D] Elsewhere numbered 12. Written about the year 1098 [ [Col. 0211] + See the note above.—Letters IV, V, and VI concerning Raynald, bishop of Angers, were not written in 1098, but after 1101].]

[Note: [Col. 0211D] The manuscript codices vary. Évreux, no. 19, has as title “To Ratt. of Angers”; Colbert 2131, “To R. of Angers.” By the letter R. no one seems to be indicated other than [Col. 0212D] Raynald of Martiniac, mentioned in the preceding letter—a conclusion which may be inferred, indeed proved, from the context of this letter itself.]

He attempts to dissuade Raynald, elected bishop of Angers contrary to the canons, from accepting the episcopate.

[Col. 0211D]

Good brother, I have a few things against you, yet all of them are for you. Nothing in them is infected with the varnish of malice; nothing serves another’s hatred. For I am jealous for you with God’s jealousy. Therefore take up patience, and embrace this admonition for salvation, which has sprung from the root of charity.

If what is said is true, canonical ordinances reject and depose [Col. 0212A] your advancement. For the clergy did not elect you; popular threats intruded you against your resistance. You lack the orders which, as we know, must be examined in persons to be promoted. There is an age which canonical rigor, because it fears it in those consecrated, excludes from consecration. If these things are so, an endless labor lies upon you, and undertakings begun from an evil principle will not readily find a good outcome.

For in chief priests mature age is required, so that religion may fear no danger and dignity may not lose reverence. Hence it is that the heavens are opened to Ezekiel in his thirtieth year, and he sees visions of God and prophesies (Ezek. 1:1). The prophet’s age is first described, in order to show at what years preaching should be entrusted. Christ too loved John above [Col. 0212B] Peter; yet the power of binding and loosing was granted to Peter, not to John. For he who had said through Isaiah, “Remove stumbling-blocks from the way of my people” (Isa. 57:14), did not wish to place stumbling-blocks before his disciples or to set a young man above elders, although he had made him especially close to himself by the prerogative of chastity. He therefore deferred to age, not to merits; he did not prefer a married man to a virgin, but one more advanced in years to one younger.

Finally, as Luke teaches, we learn that the most blessed Virgin Mary found Christ in the Temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and questioning them (Luke 2:46). So long as completeness of years was lacking, he who was teacher of all did not exceed the bounds of a disciple. But when his full days had come, he became a teacher by right, having been a disciple by example. In all this the Church has been given a pattern to follow, and a definite boundary of age has been set, below which becoming a bishop incurs judgment by the very fact. Moreover, whoever is not found in sacred orders is forbidden by canonical ordinances to approach the high priesthood.

For what need I say concerning election, in which the people are by no means permitted to precede the clergy, but must follow the electors with their assent? Search the Scriptures, and you will find the first place in this matter reserved to the clergy. Hence Pope Celestine says to the bishops established in the province of Vienne:

> “Let no bishop be imposed upon unwilling persons. Rather, the agreement and desire of clergy, people, and order must be sought.”

Concerning the same matter, in the fifth chapter of Pope Leo’s decrees:

> “When the election [Col. 0212D] of the chief priest is under consideration, he should be set above all whom the united consent of clergy and people has jointly demanded.”

You see, therefore, my brother, how great a concourse of authorities conspires against you, how many chapters press upon you. Therefore you must fear lest, through this temporal promotion, you fall eternally with those of whom the Psalmist says: “You cast them down while they were being lifted up” (Ps. 72:18). Take counsel, therefore, for your soul; take counsel while you may. Your struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against him who was born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.

I have heard that religious abbots

[Note: [Col. 0213C] Among them Soffredus of Vendôme.]

and persons of unimpeached reputation stand against you; it is so much more dangerous to contend with them because their reputation is purer, their cause more just, and their dignity greater. Farewell; and keep this final point: to scorn counsel for salvation is to hate oneself.

## LETTER VI

[Note: [Col. 0213C] Elsewhere numbered 13. Written about the year 1098.]

He continues to deter the same Raynald, bishop-elect of Angers, now on the point of consecration, from receiving the sacred anointing.

[Col. 0213B]

It is reported that bishops have assembled for your consecration. But because authority resists it, mercy must come to its aid. This mercy, I think, will be easy to obtain if you refuse the anointing offered to you. Otherwise, to be made bishop is to increase the danger. You are a man placed under authority. You will provoke that authority more gravely if, as though through arrogance, you presume upon what you ought to await from it through mercy. A judge is readily inclined to pardon when few punishable offences are presented to him. A multitude of offences exasperates him.

## LETTER VII

To the Bishop of Sées

[Note: [Col. 0213C] Elsewhere numbered 49. Written about the year 1099.]

[Note: [Col. 0213C] Namely Serlo, who, having been abbot of Ouche, became bishop of Sées in 1091 and was consecrated by William, metropolitan of Rouen. He is mentioned in the dedication of the church of Ouche in 1099. See Orderic Vitalis, p. 777. Thus in the councils of Normandy collected by our Dom Pomeray, Serlo is recorded—not Herlo, nor Sergius, as Colbert manuscript 4017 erroneously has [ [Col. 0213] + After Robert, Dom Beaugendre in *Gallia Christiana* had asserted that Serlo, bishop of Sées, died in 1098; he now affirms that Letter VII was directed to him in 1099. Robert erred, and Beaugendre dreamed it. Serlo died in 1122].]

[Note: [Col. 0213C] Thus Reg. manuscript no. 4103.]

He praises the bishop of Sées for vigorously defending the right of sanctuary in church, and proves by St Augustine’s testimony that it must be kept inviolate.

[Col. 0213C]

We have heard, and greatly rejoiced, that your fraternity has labored most episcopally to secure the release of those violently dragged away from the Church. But “he who perseveres unto the end [Col. 0214A] shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22). We believe, moreover, that you will persevere, because you love the honor of Christ’s Church and are not ignorant of canonical sanctions. For you know that they contain this provision: “Let no one dare drag away an accused person who has fled to the Church, nor hand him over from there for punishment or death, so that the honor of the churches may be preserved.”

Augustine likewise, counting this outrage against the Church among acts contrary to faith, writes as follows to Count Boniface, who had dragged a man from a church:

[Note: [Col. 0213C] This letter, cited by Hildebert as St Augustine’s letter to Count Boniface, is one of those which recent editors of St Augustine’s works, regarding them as suspect, relegated to the Appendix of volume II. Hildebert, however, cited it as genuine, as did Gratian in Decree 16, question 4, chapter *Miror*, perhaps moved by [Col. 0213D] Boniface’s own letter to St Augustine, which immediately follows the Augustinian letter and in which Boniface humbly submits to Augustine’s rebuke and to the penance imposed by him. How fully such a rebuke by St Augustine accords with his most ardent zeal for the immunity of churches may be inferred from another famous passage of St Augustine, namely [Col. 0214C] chapter 4 of Book I of *The City of God*. There the holy doctor reproaches the pagans for the weakness of Juno herself, whose sanctuary at Troy had delivered no one from the fires and swords of the Greeks; and, conversely, recounts the reverence which Alaric, king of the Goths, showed to the basilica of the holy apostles during the very devastation of Rome, restoring its sacred vessels there in solemn procession and extending his protection to the consecrated virgin who had received them into her keeping and to the other Christians who had attached themselves to her: “Now compare,” says the holy doctor, “that sanctuary—not of some common god, or one from the crowd of lesser deities, but of Jupiter’s own sister and wife, the queen of all the gods—with the shrines of the apostles. To the former, when temples and gods had been set on fire, plundered spoils were carried—not to be restored to the conquered, but to be divided among the conquerors; to the latter, however, whatever was found elsewhere to belong to those places was brought back with honor and religious service. There liberty was lost; here [Col. 0214D] it was preserved. There captivity was enclosed; here it was forbidden. . . . . . . Finally, greed and the pride of frivolous Greeks chose that temple of Juno for themselves; mercy and humility, even in most savage barbarians, chose these basilicas of Christ. Unless perhaps the Greeks,” etc.]

> “I am astonished how suddenly the ram of the enemy has broken through the wall of faith. For I know with what reverence you have always honored the Church. By what madness were you stirred to drag a man from the church?”

The same author says shortly afterward:

> “Therefore restore unharmed to the Church him whom you irreligiously dragged away. [Col. 0214B] I have forbidden the clergy to receive the offering of your household, and I forbid you communion until, after completing the period of penance for your acts of audacity which I have prescribed, you offer to God a worthy sacrifice with a contrite and humbled heart.”

We have further been told that Gualguenus

[Note: [Col. 0214D] Thus Victor manuscript 272, Colbert 2662, Évreux 19, and Colbert 1168; Colbert 4017 alone has “Gualterius.”]

has promised, on his pledged faith, that he will by no means leave custody except with their permission. Even if this is true, neither custom nor reason allows an accused person to be dragged from a church. For he who said, “Let no one dare drag an accused person from the Church,” excluded no accused person whatsoever who might lawfully be dragged away without prejudice to justice.

We too, following a custom which does not conflict with reason or law, vindicate the full freedom of departure for even those who, in violent reverence for a pledged promise, flee to the bosom of mother Church; or else we punish their abductors by ecclesiastical discipline. If those abductors bring against the released persons an action concerning a violated pledge, ecclesiastical justice compels none of those released to answer. Farewell, and vigorously carry through what you have begun.

## LETTER VIII

To John and Benedict

[Note: [Col. 0215C] Elsewhere numbered 19. Written about the year 1100.]

[Note: [Col. 0215C] Although in certain manuscripts, such as Reg. 4103, Colbert 2131, and Évreux 19, this letter is entitled “To John Benedict,” without the conjunction *and*, it nevertheless appears from Letter 87 of Ivo of Chartres that *and* should be inserted. For the letter was written to two [Col. 0215D] distinct cardinals, as Ivo in fact writes to them: John and Benedict. According to Baronius, they were sent into Gaul as apostolic legates in the year 1100 and summoned a council at Poitiers. There, especially, the question of King Philip I of France’s illegitimate marriage with his concubine Bertrada was discussed, and various canons were enacted; these may be seen in the cited passage of Baronius. Hildebert excuses himself from attending this council because of the utter destitution to which he had been reduced by the king of England—undoubtedly William Rufus—and by his flatterers, the several *consules* of Le Mans within three years, that is, according to Du Cange, the *scabini*, or common civic governors. Since William Rufus died by an accidental arrow-shot on the second day of August 1099 [ [Col. 0215] + Incorrectly: William Rufus died in 1100 (*Hist. Litt.* XI, p. 291)], this letter seems to have been written either at the end of that year or at the beginning of the following year, 1100, when this council of Poitiers was held. [Col. 0216C] Thus harassed by so many storms, Hildebert made for Rome, almost as a beggar, as though for a harbor, to Pope Paschal II; but he did not find him there. Consult the *Life of Hildebert* on these matters. John and Benedict are mentioned in the Bernardine Chronology of Horstius and Mabillon under the year [Col. 0216D] 1100. See Du Cange, under *Consul*, *Glossary*, p. 1191, where he cites Letters 25 and 26 of our Hildebert and says: “The consuls in cities are those who elsewhere are commonly called *scabini*.” Thus the statutes of Montpellier, art. 125, on the form of the oath of consuls, that is, *scabini*, in French *échevins*.]

Before John and Benedict, cardinals of the Holy Roman Church and legates of Pope Paschal II, Hildebert excuses his failure to attend the council which they had summoned at Poitiers, oppressed as he was by excessive calamities inflicted by the consuls of Le Mans.

[Col. 0215A]

Just as the frequent concurrence of tribulations summons us to holy councils, so it also calls us back and draws us away. For the adversities that furnish us with a throng of complaints have so shattered our resources that the one consolation remaining is the very habit of suffering. They began, indeed, before the three years now completed had run their course; throughout that whole period, unfolded in continual lamentations, each new wound daily harassed wounds already received.

Thus, in so brief a time, we have endured six consuls in the city. None of them entered with peaceful intentions; each secured for himself a curtailed authority by sword and fire. The people, compelled into approval, received a tyrant from necessity, not a ruler according to law. They pretended, but did not give, affection to him whom they had received. The stronger man found loyalty in them. But the consul exercised dominion all the more harshly because he held it more briefly. His soldier, employing feigned charges, pronounced free of crimes those whom he had deprived of possessions. Because a brief reign spares no peoples, want, not will, put an end to plunder.

That devastation ranged as far as the sanctuary of the Lord. First, whatever lay outside the walls and was within our power either [Col. 0215B] vanished into ashes or was scattered as plunder. Then no few houses belonging to episcopal churches fell under like violence. In the rest, spared by the fire, both the resources of the poor and the reverence due to holy things were equally endangered. Everything was smashed, everything plundered, everything defiled. Nothing escaped the hands of men who run freely to wickedness, but not to honest conduct even for a price. The clergy, afflicted by the same injuries, judge the summit of wealth to be merely the consolation of nature; their desire is reduced to necessities, and they lack everything.

Their distress has added to the pain of our wounds; and we are more grievously ashamed because we cannot relieve their poverty than because no one wishes to relieve ours. Moreover, it would take long to recount with what unremitting tyranny the king of England has raged against us. Casting aside a king’s moderation, he resolved not to spare the bishop until he compelled the bishop to sacrilege. Since we refuse to cast down the towers of our Church, we have been forced to submit to judgments beyond the sea and to endure the injuries of the ocean—an affliction unique on earth, and a dissolution without parallel of the human fabric.

Driven, therefore, by such whirlwinds, we have resolved to set out for the thresholds of the apostles, judging it a great remedy for this new tribulation if the Roman pontiff gives us assistance both by counsel and by aid. Receive, therefore, our kindly excuse, carefully considering that our means cannot suffice both for the expenses of the journey [Col. 0216B] and for those of the council: drawn, as from a shipwreck, from the remnants of fires, they promise us failure upon the road.

## LETTER IX

To Archbishop Anselm

[Note: [Col. 0216D] Elsewhere numbered 21. Written about the year 1100.]

[Note: [Col. 0216D] At the Council of Bari in 1098, in the presence of Pope Urban II, St Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, had splendidly refuted the Greek error concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. Hildebert asks him [Note: [Col. 0216D] William of Jumièges says this of Hildebert, *History of the Normans*, Book VI, ch. 9, p. 265, where he discusses the works of St Anselm: “Anselm,” he says, “had refuted the Greeks in a council at Bari, who denied that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. Therefore, taking up the subject at the request of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, he composed this book.” The same is stated by Orderic Vitalis, *History of the Normans*, Book VI, ch. 9, and by Robert of Torigni in his addition to Sigebert.] not to begrudge committing to writing, for the benefit of the Church, the arguments which he had advanced orally in debate.]

It is characteristic of a wise man to bear with one who does not know. Therefore I was not afraid to disclose my ignorance, because [Col. 0216C] my conversation was with a wise man. Unless I am mistaken, your learning will instruct it, and your charity will bear with it. I should count myself fortunate, I say, if I had deserved either to be taught in your presence or to receive, as a familiar friend, a letter addressed to me. But place has begrudged me this, granting the service of a greeting on no other terms than that I should first travel round half the world. For one must examine the favorability of sea and air if one judges that someone in England should be greeted.

Yet charity’s bond has supplied the inconveniences of such separation; it allows no one to be absent from us, no one not to be a familiar friend. Nothing is more expansive than it. The breadth of charity and of the world is equal. Charity embraces whatever the Ocean embraces. In the sanctuary of affection charity gathers a friend into God, and an enemy for God’s sake. It does not cease to love when it ceases to be loved. It has all persons present, all as kindred. Those whom it cannot assist by service, it assists by affection.

Far be it, then, that the public benefit of charity should be taken from me by the sea’s waves, when it is written: “Many waters cannot quench charity” (Song 8:7). For charity, which has made earth and heaven one commonwealth, can easily unite inhabitants of distant shores.

[Note: [Col. 0217D] Thus also Salvian.]

Trusting in this, I have ventured to inquire and ask for what, when bestowed, [Col. 0217B] does not diminish its giver. If the sum of my requests is sought, the following page will declare it. From the reports of those who have come to us, I have learned that at the Council of Bari you delivered a discourse concerning the Holy Spirit, whom the calumnious subtlety of the Greeks fabulously asserts does not proceed from the Son. I therefore beg you to set down in a concise treatise what you proclaimed against their madness in that council. And because they do not accept the testimonies of the Latin Fathers, do not be weary of fortifying the desired work with those authorities which Greek cunning acknowledges as both its own and ours.

I ask great things, blessed Father, but things that profit alike the recipient and the giver. For knowledge is a noble possession: when distributed, it receives increase; and, scorning a miserly possessor, it slips away unless it is made public. [Col. 0217C] May the Lord preserve your holiness for us, and may my eyes see you before I die.

[Note: [Col. 0217D] At this point it is fitting to insert St Anselm’s letter to Hildebert, which is Letter 11 of Book IV of his letters in Gerberon’s edition.]

## LETTER X

To the Prior of Chartres

[Note: [Col. 0217D] Elsewhere numbered 6. Written about the year 1103.]

[Note: [Col. 0217D] Thus Reg. manuscripts 4103, Victor 272, and Colbert 2131.—Since several monasteries existed at Chartres—two of regular canons, St John’s and St Chéron’s, and two of Benedictine monks, St Peter in the Valley and Blessed Mary of Josaphat—it is not easy to determine to which prior of Chartres this commendatory letter on reform was addressed. Yet, since among them the monastery of St Peter in the Valley always held first place, it seems probable that this letter was written to the prior of St Peter, whose name is nevertheless unknown. Unless, perhaps, we say that it was directed to William, who, according to this monastery’s archives, was elected abbot from being a monk of Marmoutier in 1101 and died in 1130. The same archives show that this William, as soon as he had been appointed, diligently applied himself in speech and example to restoring regular observance, and indeed reformed the temporal estate itself for the better. From the circumstances of time and of the matter itself, therefore, it seems permissible to attribute this reform and the honor of its accomplishment rightly to him by Hildebert.]

He congratulates him on having reformed for the better monks who had declined from their first fervor of regular observance, and movingly exhorts him diligently to complete what he has rightly begun.

Your reputation could not fail to reach us, for, according to Solomon, “your name is oil poured out” (Song 1:2). Taught by its fragrance, my brother, of your devotion, we have blessed the Lord God of Israel, because your devotion is nothing other than his grace. For who could assist corrupt morals and a trampled monastic order, who could devise a remedy, unless helped [Col. 0217D] by him who said, “Without me you can do nothing” [Col. 0218A] (John 15:5)?

It is a hard thing to encourage recruits in battle; harder still to recall those in flight. Greater care is needed to restore health than to preserve it. Thus scarcely anyone doubts that, in this respect, it is easier to instruct the ignorant than to reform the perverse. Hence a more splendid glory awaits you, to whom it has been given from above both to gather what was scattered and to make firm what was broken.

Under your cultivation the barren fig tree has blossomed and returned to favor with its master, whose threats and axe it had feared. Your concern for the tree entrusted to you, therefore, will be to dig around it and spread manure about it. Such a plant easily returns to wildness; and, if you cease to cultivate it, its greenery quickly rots away. Every day the north wind blows, dangerous not only to flowers but also to fruit and leaves. The south wind must be asked to come and blow upon [Col. 0218B] its garden (Song 4:16), so that its fragrance may become like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed.

Perhaps I offend against the public good if I detain you with a long letter, if we hold with a longer page the eyes that you owe to many. Yet do not be weary of reading this one thing, nor refuse to believe what I say: you will repay me if you love me and pray for me.

## LETTER XI

St Anselm to Hildebert

[Note: [Col. 0218D] Written about the year 1102. It is found as the eleventh letter of Book IV in the Gerberon edition of St Anselm’s letters.]

Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to his lord and venerable fellow bishop Hildebert of Le Mans: temporal and eternal salvation.

The letters of your holiness make me greatly your debtor, not because they exalt me above myself, but because [Col. 0218C] they show the immense sincerity of your affection toward me. For if, in order to please God, we ought to love our enemies, much more must we love our friends lest we displease him. Therefore, if I give you either no love or less love, I judge myself unjust in my own conscience. As I wish to avoid this injustice, so I desire to embrace your friendship.

I confess also that, if it were possible, I ought to love you twice as much as you love me, because you have anticipated me in love, as you proved by your gift.

[Note: [Col. 0218D] Perhaps the fan, which Hildebert means in the second letter of Book I [ [Col. 0217] + Letter XI, Book II, would be cited more correctly after Letter II, Book I].]

For since you have loved one undeserving, I owe no lesser return; and, as you give an example, I ought to offer as much freely. Since you have indicated that what you have seen of our little works pleases you, we venture to send you certain things which, I think, you have not yet [Col. 0218D] seen.

## LETTER XII

To Roger, Bishop of Salisbury

[Note: [Col. 0219C] Elsewhere numbered 3. Written in 1102.]

[Note: [Col. 0219C] Thus Reg. manuscript 4103. Évreux manuscript 19 has *Rogerus*, not *Rogerius*, and he is so named in *Anglia Sacra*, Part I, p. 275, where it says of him: “Roger, bishop of Salisbury, called the Great; confidant of Henry I, king of England; first chancellor after the Conquest; then bishop; faithful administrator of the realm; a most zealous bishop; despiser of honors,” etc., although he was abundantly heaped with honors by the king. At the Council of London summoned by St Anselm as primate in 1102, Roger was present with the other bishops, according to Eadmer, but only invested, as was the other Roger, likewise invested, bishop of Hereford. Of the bishop of Salisbury, Haepfeld, twelfth century, ch. 28, asserts that at the same time he was a canon and master of schools at Salisbury, a canon at Lincoln, likewise a canon and archdeacon at Rouen, and schoolmaster, archpriest, [Col. 0219D] and precentor at Le Mans. “Yet,” he says, “he never appropriated to himself the collection of so great an honor.” But who could believe that Roger possessed so many benefices simultaneously, mutually incompatible even by the geographical distance of the regions? And if he truly possessed so many, who would not wonder that he did not seize so many honors for himself? Finally, who would suppose that Hildebert—a man who knew no flattery even toward supreme pontiffs or kings—would have celebrated with such praise a man weighed down and crushed by the burden of so many benefices, to the peril of his soul? Away, then, with this tale, invented to the scandal of the Church, of so many benefices held together, founded upon no other proofs and unfairly detracting from the reputation of an excellent bishop, celebrated by other authors for piety and diligent pastoral service. Let Hildebert rather be believed when in this letter he proclaims the man outstanding in virtue; nor is he flattering a powerful friend, whom he finally reminds that death is no more stages distant from a court than from a cottage. [Col. 0220C] It should also be noted that in an ancient manuscript of the library of St Victor, Paris, no. 1041, among numerous catalogues of bishops from different regions, written about five hundred years ago, there is a catalogue of the bishops of Salisbury, whose last entry reads: “Roger of Dead Valleys, great in learning and noble by birth. It is recorded of him that, when his paternal inheritance had come to him, and his friends, because of the prospect of offspring, had provided a noble girl for him to marry, and according to custom he and she were conversing alone, Great Roger, approving the girl’s beauty, advised her to accept the Son of God as spouse; he himself, however, would take no other bride besides the Virgin Mary. She reported that counsel to her friends and kept it, becoming a nun and, in due course, an abbess; he became a bishop and, loving her in God, though they were far apart, [Col. 0220D] called her his bride for the sake of holy chastity.” Thus the catalogue cited above.]

Hildebert congratulates him, apparently recently promoted to the bishopric of Salisbury, and commends to him the outstanding gifts for service to the Church of Guy, who later succeeded him in the Church of Le Mans.

[Col. 0219A]

I congratulate virtue, for I see that, under our king alone, its reward is not lacking. He knows that a royal hand shines more brightly through gifts than through a sceptre, and that it is not enough for a ruler to summon subjects to good conduct by examples unless they are also summoned by rewards. Hence your purified character has been endowed with the supreme priesthood, than which nothing is more fitting either as the reward of saints or as the material of their endeavors.

Sound indeed is the king’s disposition, which could provide Christ’s Church [Col. 0219B] with nothing better than you: by your learning those subject to you profit, and through your patronage virtue rejoices. I had resolved to ask this of you on behalf of our Guy,

[Note: [Col. 0220D] This Guy seems to be none other than Guy of Étampes—called Guido and Guiamarus by Orderic—who, as appears from this letter, was educated in the Church of Le Mans by Hildebert himself, entrusted to Roger as a friend in order to serve as schoolmaster in the Church of Salisbury, then recalled by Hildebert. After exercising the same office for some time in the Church of Le Mans, he became archpriest and precentor; finally, when Hildebert was translated to the archbishopric of Tours, he was appointed to Hildebert’s chair at Le Mans. *Analecta*, vol. III, in *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*.]

but I feared that what you were going to do of your own accord would seem to have been extorted by prayers. Benefits that arise not through another’s intervention but from spontaneous affection are more welcome. Yet I ought not to deprive this aforesaid brother and son of ours of the testimony which he has earned no less by his life than by his learning. One man has been selected from our Church in whom learning abounds for usefulness and character for example. He alone will be worth many to you, for in this one man you will find many masters. Indeed, his longer residence with you will show that I have written too little about him. [Col. 0220A] Farewell, and remember that death is no more stages distant from a court than from a cottage.

## LETTER XIII

[Note: [Col. 0220D] Elsewhere numbered 22. Written about the year 110.]

Hildebert gives thanks to St Anselm for undertaking the treatise *On the Holy Spirit*, which he had requested from him in the preceding letter.

[Note: [Col. 0220D] The ninth letter of this book.]

And a joyful day, and solemn countenances, came to me together with your treatise. I had previously received your blessing, I your servant, your servant; and my affection, made devout, gave thanks to God and to you. It was human to aid one’s neighbour through the impulse of compassion; but it was divine to defend the Catholic faith through the Holy Spirit dwelling within you. Yet it was one and the same Spirit who accomplished both, wishing the grace of virtues to abound in you, and reserving you as defender of His procession from the Son. [Note: That is, in the treatise *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son*, against the Greeks, mentioned above.] “For wisdom shall not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wisdom 1:4). Hence it was fitting that the advocate of Truth should furnish an example of religious devotion. Such a man, moreover, was well suited to pastoral watchfulness: one lacking nothing for the fullness of righteousness, nothing for the integrity of doctrine. Blessed indeed is the breast that has consecrated itself as a venerable inner sanctuary for the assembly of virtues. From it, as from hidden recesses, divine oracles proceed; and its sacred words proclaim nothing other than that it is an interpreter of the heavenly will. When I frequently recall them, amazement overwhelms me; and while I carefully consider each of them, I acknowledge that all must be ascribed to the Holy Spirit, saying with the Psalmist: “This is the Lord’s doing, and it is wonderful in our eyes” (Psalm 117:23). [Note: This letter ends here in most manuscripts: Colbert 1168, 4017, 2662; Victorine 272, 292; and Évreux 19. Yet this same letter, found twice among the letters of St Anselm, ends differently in Gerberon’s edition. The first version, on p. 386, after the words “in our eyes,” reads: “Farewell, most holy Father, knowing that my soul has greatly desired to see you, and would not begrudge winds or sea, provided that I might receive from you counsel for salvation, which I believe exists nowhere unless it is with you.” The other version, on p. 434, after the words “in our eyes,” ends as reported above, with the words, “You will repay me in return,” etc.]

You will repay me in return, most holy Father, if you make me a participant in your prayers.

## LETTER XIV

[Note: Col. 0221C. Alternatively no. 34. It appears to have been written about the year 1103.]

**TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN**

[Note: It is not difficult to guess who this Archbishop of Rouen was, designated by the letter A. in manuscript Évreux 19, and by S. in Royal manuscript 4103. During Hildebert’s episcopate only three Archbishops of Rouen are recorded. The first was William, formerly monk and abbot of Caen, installed about 1079, who held a provincial council in 1107. The second was Geoffrey, formerly dean of Le Mans, who attended the Council of Reims under Callixtus II in 1119 and died in 1128. The third was Hugh, formerly prior of Cluny and first abbot of Reading, elected in 1130. He was present at the death of King Henry I of England in 1135 and, in that same year, at Suger’s request, dedicated the oratory of St Romanus in the basilica of St Denis in France. He died in 1164. Of these three, the recipient of this letter can certainly have been none other than William. The manuscript used by M. Mauguin addresses it to Ivo, Bishop of Chartres; but it seems addressed only to an archbishop, since he calls the others his fellow-provincials, a designation proper only to archbishops.]

Hildebert denies that any marriage between blood-relations or relations by affinity can be legitimate, under whatever pretext.

As your Holiness’s letter declares, the daughter of Walter of Mayenne is said to be closely related by blood to the Count of Mortain. Before the bond of marriage joined the persons in question, this same Walter, quietly mentioning the consanguinity to me, cautiously explored what I thought [otherwise, “what I should judge”]. He said it seemed good to him that the affection produced by an intervening marriage should end the war in which the count had long raged against him. He added, moreover, that you and your fellow-provincial bishops had confirmed to him in writing that the offense of consanguinity ought to be tolerated for the sake of a swift restoration of peace and tranquillity. He therefore sought the assent of the Church of Le Mans to the intended marriage, so that, by its authority also, he might secure stability for his daughter’s marriage if ever a writ of repudiation should be drawn up against her.

But neither assent could be extorted from me nor could I be persuaded that your prudence had descended to the simplicity of those whom the Apostle reproves when they say, “Let us do evil, that good may come” (Romans 3:8). Accordingly, I took such care in this matter as belonged to me. To the man asking for assent, I communicated dissent, allowing neither blood-relations nor relations by affinity to contract unions of prohibited marriage under the pretext of any dispensation. It will be the concern of him in whose diocese the bride is known to have settled to resist this marriage until it is dissolved. May the Lord preserve you, holy Father.

## LETTER XV

[Note: Col. 0221D. Alternatively no. 64. Written about the year 1110.]

He attempts to call back a certain abbot, excessively devoted to a more elegant style, to a simpler manner of expression; and at the same time from an anciently received custom in his monastery, by which eucharistic bread was offered to communicants only after being dipped.

[Note: Some have plausibly judged that this letter was addressed to Pons, fifth abbot of Cluny from its foundation—a man who, as his deeds make clear, had already strayed far from the humility and simplicity of his predecessors, being excessively curious and inclined to worldly vanities and false extravagances. His pride was displayed at the Roman council of 1116, when, in the presence of Paschal II, he boasted that he was “abbot of abbots.” In the controversy, to the prejudice of the Abbot of Monte Cassino, he disgracefully lost his case and, by judgment of the supreme pontiff, was ordered to yield that title to the Cassinese abbot. Yet there are writers who defend him. But what defense can be made for one whom Paschal II condemned as ambitious at the aforesaid Roman council, and whom Honorius II, in a decretal letter issued from the Lateran to Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, deprived of honourable burial as obstinately unrepentant for the evils inflicted upon Cluny—unless, as he says, he had granted it out of reverence for that monastery, of which Pons had been a monk?

Nevertheless, nothing prevents us from supposing that during his rule he intermingled certain good things with so many evils. Such was his plan to commend to posterity the outstanding virtues of his predecessors, especially St Hugh, whose monk he had been. He had earnestly desired a Life of Hugh written by Hildebert; Hildebert eventually sent it to him; and this is the work which, promised and awaited so long, he calls “the page” in this letter.

Hildebert seized this occasion to disapprove the custom observed at Cluny, namely of giving the Eucharist to communicants only dipped. The Roman council under Urban II in 1095 had forbidden it, and Paschal II had prohibited it in his second decretal letter to Pons himself, Abbot of Cluny. This provides no slight ground for conjecturing that Hildebert addressed this letter to him.

It is difficult to determine how he understood this dipping. In antiquity eucharistic bread was offered dipped in two ways: either consecrated bread dipped in consecrated wine, that is, Christ’s blood; or consecrated bread dipped in ordinary wine. The first rite, as Cardinal Bona teaches in *On Liturgical Matters*, book II, chapter 19, article 3, was observed by the Greeks, and, he says, they still observe it by a custom handed down from their ancestors some centuries ago. They distribute to the people Communion under both kinds, not separately but combined with the blood, placing individual dipped particles into each person’s mouth with a small spoon. This practice also flourished in some parts of the West; but the Roman Order opposed it, as the *Micrologus*, chapter 19, states, and so did the Roman council mentioned above and the Third Council of Braga, lest the error of those who offered dipping as the completion of Communion should spread further.

There was also another form of dipping: consecrated bread in unconsecrated wine. This is still practiced among the Greeks for those near death, to whom they give sacred particles, which they call *meridae*, or, more commonly, “pearls.” See Cardinal Bona, where he treats more fully of Communion under one kind. At Cluny, however, both rites were observed, as is apparent from Ulrich, *Customs of Cluny*, book II, chapter 30. For he writes: “As many as the priest gives the sacred body itself”—that is, in the Mass—“he first dips each in the blood.” Thus this was done not only for the ministers of the altar but for all who were to communicate. Concerning the sick, especially those near death, the same *Customs*, book III, chapter 28, report: “Care is taken that the mouth of the sick person be washed before receiving the body of the Lord, which he receives dipped in wine. When this has been drunk,” etc.]

You have awaited the page promised to your Blessedness long enough and more than long enough. I confess that I promised it, but I feared that its unpolished style might displease one reading the work. This consideration imposed a long silence upon me. But when Paul was in my hands and I came upon his words to the Philippians, “Provided only that, whether in pretence or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, in this I rejoice, and will rejoice” (Philippians 1:18), I resolved to discharge my debt and to disapprove in writing, insofar as I can, the error which you approve.

Anyone is dangerously fastidious who, unless the beauty of words charms him, prejudices himself against saving doctrine. Who, burning with thirst, has thrown away water offered in earthen vessels? Or who has preferred to remain sick rather than take medicine prepared by the black and frightful hand of an Ethiopian?

First, therefore, observe that it is a culpable obstinacy to prefer custom to truth. Nor is the practice free from fault when it is known either to oppose authority or to run contrary to reason. Augustine knew this, writing in book III *On the One Baptism*: [Note: Chapter 8, p. 112, and book IV, chapter 5 of the new edition, p. 124. The same is cited at the Council of Carthage in Cyprian, article 28.] “When truth has been made manifest, custom must yield to reason. Let no one prefer custom to truth and reason, because reason and truth always exclude custom.” Again, in his book *On Baptism*: [Note: Book III, chapter 5, no. 8.] “He who, scorning truth, presumes to follow custom is envious and malicious toward brothers to whom truth is revealed, or ungrateful toward God, by whose inspiration His Church is instructed. For the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘I am the truth’ (John 14:6); He did not say, ‘I am custom.’” Again: [Note: Ibid., chapter 6, no. 9.] “Once revelation has been made, error must yield to truth. For Peter too, who circumcised, yielded to Paul preaching the truth.” Cyprian says of the same matter: [Note: “Custom without truth is the antiquity of error.” St Cyprian, Letter 74.] “Custom, however ancient or however widespread, must altogether be set below truth; and a practice contrary to truth must be abolished.”

Those furnished with these authorities incur blame if they prefer to stray after custom rather than follow truth. I have written this to you, dearest brother, so that, stirred up, you may awake and see how the tradition concerning the sacraments of the altar, celebrated in your famous monastery, agrees neither with the Gospel nor with decrees. For your custom is to give the Eucharist to no one except dipped; and this cannot be shown to derive either from the Lord’s institution or from authoritative enactments.

If you consult Matthew, Mark, and Luke, you will find bread given separately and wine separately. Hence Pope Julius says: “Those who give the Eucharist dipped to the people as the completion of Communion do not find this supported by testimony from the Gospel, where the Lord entrusted His body and blood to the Apostles. For the giving of bread is mentioned separately and the giving of the cup separately. We do not read that Christ offered dipped bread to others, except to that one disciple whom the dipped morsel marked out as the Master’s betrayer—not because it signified the institution of this sacrament.

“Moreover, if anyone should say that the aforesaid custom arose from the dipped bread which Christ handed to the traitor, as though a prescribed form had there been established by which the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world ought to be given to communicants, perhaps I should think him worthy of belief if either the Gospel or the authority of the full faith had left it clear that that bread was Christ’s body. But it is plain even to one with slight knowledge that Christ’s body was one thing and the dipped morsel of bread another; and that Judas was first fed for death by the body which he was about to betray, before the morsel of bread exposed the betrayer.

“Of this morsel Augustine writes on John: [Note: Tractate LXII on chapter XIII of the Gospel of John.] ‘Judas did not, as some careless readers suppose, receive Christ’s body at that point. Rather, we must understand that the Lord had previously distributed to them all the sacrament of His body and blood, among whom Judas also was, as Luke narrates most clearly; and afterwards they came to that point where, according to John’s account, the Lord most openly identifies His betrayer through a dipped and offered morsel. Perhaps by the dipping of the bread He signified that man’s deception (*fictio*).’”

Let this suffice for you, dearest brother, if you would prefer to follow the short path of truth rather than wander through the long detours required before abandoning custom.

## LETTER XVI

[Note: Alternatively no. 45. Written about the year 1110.]

[Note: The Royal manuscript has the letter C., by which it undoubtedly designates Cuno, or Conon, then in fact Bishop of Palestrina, cardinal, and legate of Paschal II throughout East and West. He subscribed the general Lateran council at which the concession concerning investitures, extorted by force from Paschal II for Emperor Henry V, was annulled. Several councils in various regions were held to condemn it. See Baronius under the years 1111 and 1114, who also states under 1119 that Conon refused the supreme pontificate when it was offered to him. Hildebert heartens this truly magnanimous man to carry out this affair fearlessly. Letters 266 and 267 of Ivo of Chartres, and others elsewhere, are addressed to him.]

**TO C., BISHOP OF PALESTRINA**

He congratulates the Bishop of Palestrina—namely Cardinal Conon, legate of the supreme pontiff throughout East and West—on his invincible integrity in ecclesiastical affairs, and urges him to persevere.

You possess zeal for the law, which your episcopal chair did not bestow but found already in you. The affairs of the Church committed to you demonstrate this: you have carried them out at once fearless amid threats and incorruptible amid gifts, even at risk to your life. Yet, “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matthew 10:24). Persevere, I pray; and never permit the pure silver of your conscience to be tarnished by the dross of any gift. [Note: The Paris and Cologne editors rightly supplied the word *muneris*, “gift,” although it occurs in no manuscript.] Satan will come to test you and will say: “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:9). But if I know you well, you will answer the tempter thus: “Get behind me, Satan” (ibid., verse 10).

## LETTER XVII

[Note: Alternatively no. 39. Written about the year 1110.]

Although Hildebert movingly sets before all the children of the Church the injury done to the Church through his treacherous personal detention by Count Rotrou and his steward Humbert, [Note: On Hildebert’s imprisonment, see his Life.] he nevertheless declares with apostolic force that the liberty of the Church, which he believes would be injured by a monetary ransom for himself, must be preferred to his own life. He asserts that he, once redeemed by Christ’s blood, is unworthy to be redeemed at any price.

**HILDEBERT, priest of the people of Le Mans, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, to all bishops, priests, and all the children of the Church: greeting.**

Wretched people are fortunate when it is established that they did not deserve what they suffer. For in adversity there is a certain happiness: though you may judge someone guilty, he is nevertheless innocent. Hence we glory in bonds whose cause is our consolation, not our conscience our scourge. For we glory with Paul, saying: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1:12).

But let my brothers, my fellow priests, my lords, and my friends hear what this conscience is like, and what has been the cause of my bonds. I believe they will pray for me all the more devoutly when they know that Christ suffers in me because I suffer for Christ. By the living God, and God’s Son, and the Spirit of both, I shall not lie.

Rotrou was held in chains in the tower of Le Mans. I was summoned to him when he was trembling for fear of death. He then made confession to me, made arrangements for his household, made his testament, and distributed gifts to churches. To ensure that this remained inviolate, he obtained by my entreaties that I should myself go to his mother, bear witness to the testament, forbid anyone to presume to diminish it, and forbid anyone at all to attempt its annulment.

What the count requested was done. I went—would that I had never set foot there. The count’s mother welcomed me with a kiss, applauded the testament, and gave thanks that I had come at the count’s request. Neither son nor mother denies that this happened. That same day a plan against me was formed; on the following day hands were laid upon me. You would have called it a repetition of Christ’s betrayal. On Thursday I was welcomed with a kiss. On Friday, as though I were going with Christ to the cross, I was seized with insults and placed in public custody. They even divided my garments among themselves, having already distributed my horses among those who run freely to a crime, but not to an honourable deed even for payment. [Note: Thus in the epitaph of Peter of Poitiers: “Those who freely undertake a crime—no one, even when asked, [undertakes] good deeds.”]

Now in the castle where this occurred there was the Bishop of Chartres, [Note: That is, Ivo, then Bishop of Chartres.] a man of venerable authority; but among the authors of the crime authority was without authority. In contrition of spirit he approached Humbert—for that is the name of this prince of Pharisees. At first he spoke gently to the beast, but a beast admits no reason. Then he freely accused him of sacrilege; he implored him, rebuked him in season and out of season. Finally, he delivered him to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, binding him as he should have been bound with the bond of anathema. “For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still” (Isaiah 5:25).

Religious abbots also, and hermits perfected in reputation, gathered at the stone and found a stone—not the one from which God raises up children to Abraham, but one in which there is no moisture and in which the seed of God’s word has no root. “For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.”

At last a message was sent to Count Rotrou, reporting my capture and his own shame and disgrace. [Note: Thus the Évreux, Rouen, and other manuscripts: *sua*, “his own,” not *mea*, “my,” as in the printed editions.] At first he spoke in his heart and with divided heart; finally, he ordered that I be released and that satisfaction be made to the Church.
