So that he might not appear to speak deceptively, he sent to his mother hair cut from his own head, [Note: The distinguished Du Cange cites this passage of Hildebert to establish the ancient custom of pledging faith by voluntarily cutting off one’s own hair; *Latin Glossary*, under “Capilli,” “Hair.”] adding that Humbert had inflicted upon him no less an injury in my case than if he had cut off the rest of it. “For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.”

Therefore I turn to you, my dearest brothers, my fellow priests, my lords, and my friends. I ask you to pray for me, to take care for me, to stand beside me in compassion. But I make no effort for ransom. Redeemed once by Christ’s blood, I do not seek to be redeemed again. That blood is my redemption. That blood is my price. It is unworthy that I should be redeemed for a price when my price is without price.

Moreover, infamous is the redemption by which the Church’s liberty perishes and servitude is purchased. For the members must serve if you humble the head under tribute. A cleric must be ransomed if you consider that a bishop ought to be ransomed. Those subject to him must tremble if, in the comedian’s phrase, the man whom you prepare as a defender needs a patron. Certainly I do not value life so highly that I should love it short-lived and bought back. I prefer to risk it rather than trample underfoot the common liberty for its sake. May my death benefit the Church to which I was of no benefit while I presided over it in life. It is the part of a bishop, if not to live for all, at least to die for all.

## LETTER XVIII

[Note: Alternatively no. 40. Written about the year 1110.]

He remonstrates, affectionately but movingly, with the Bishop of Sées because he leaves him without comfort in chains, and urges him to strike Humbert, steward of Count Rotrou, who variously torments him in prison, with the sword of anathema.

**HILDEBERT, prisoner of Christ Jesus, to the Bishop of Sées by God’s grace: greeting.**

[Note: As Rabodo, elected in 1106 and deceased in 1120.]

We believe that you do not know that we are held in chains near you. [Note: On Hildebert’s imprisonment, see his Life, cited above, and the preceding letter.] If you knew, your consolations would by no means be lacking to us. For you are a bishop, and you read and understand this: “I was in prison, and you came to me” (Matthew 25:36).

Know, therefore, that your fellow bishop has been consigned to prison; that Christ of God has again been handed over to soldiers; that, surrounded again by manifold guards, he is being exacted from for that which is known not to be owed. Henceforth, unless you visit him, it will be imputed not to ignorance but to fault.

Therefore let Christ of God visit the prisoner of Jesus Christ. Let Him visit him, not with bodily steps but with the affection of charity; not with the offering of material things but with prayers. You will visit us well if your soul is in bitterness on our account. You will visit us well if you pray that the Lord may not leave the rod of sinners over us. You will visit us well if, with Peter, you strike Malchus as he persecutes Christ in us.

I do not assume the role of one teaching, but of one asking. For, as Jerome says to Eustochium: “It is foolish to teach one who already knows what you would teach him.” You also read and understand that there were two swords at the supper. Peter indeed wielded one against Malchus when Malchus stretched out his hands against Christ. But we do not read that the other was drawn. Both were most fittingly found among Christ’s disciples, because both are still found among the members of Christ’s body. For the king is a member of Christ; the priest is a member of Christ. I speak to one who knows. You know the sword of the king. You know the sword of the priest. The king’s sword is the censure of the court; the priest’s sword is the severity of ecclesiastical discipline. You have read that the Evangelist prefigured these when he said: “Lord, behold, here are two swords” (Luke 22:38).

If someone wielding the sword of royal power were freeing me, the priestly sword would not be requested on my behalf. But you see that authority now bears the sword without cause. The sword has been sheathed; it has been covered in the skins of dead animals. Malchus stretches out his hands against Christ; Belshazzar against the vessels of the Temple, with impunity. There is no one consumed by zeal for the house of the Lord. There is no one who threatens with Moses and says: “I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh” (Deuteronomy 32:42). Therefore it is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in princes (Psalm 117:9). Hence: “As the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are upon the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us” (Psalm 122:2).

But God will have mercy upon us. He still “regards the prayer of the humble and does not despise their petitions” (Psalm 101:18). My hope has been placed in His angels, my anchor fixed, lest my frail little ship—my own little ship—be sunk by storms. I speak to one who knows. The angels of the Lord are His bishops; the angels of the Lord are His priests. For Malachi says: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 3:2).

If, then, you are an angel of the Lord—indeed, because you are His angel—you bear that sword which, in John, comes two-edged from the angel’s mouth. You too will bear it without cause—may that not happen—unless you cut off and hand over to Satan the son of death; unless you close and bar the paradise of the Lord your God against Adam’s remnant.

I do not say this as desiring the sinner’s death, but so that you may show the sinner his seared conscience; so that you may say to him with the Prophet: “I will rebuke you and set you before your face” (Psalm 49:21). Now that son of perdition, Humbert, is a roe-deer (*capreolus*). Humbert devised wicked counsel against me, laid hands upon me, and keeps me captive; from the count’s steward he has become the devil’s food. For the serpent that crawls on belly and breast, and to whom it was said, “You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Genesis 3:14), has eaten him, as one who knows nothing but earth. This earth has produced thorns and thistles for me; it has given me wine not to gladden my heart but to intoxicate my spirit with bitterness. For it was in bitterness that I wrote to you, asking that in it I might find you such as you would wish me to be found by you.

## LETTER XIX

[Note: Alternatively no. 44. Written about the year 1112.]

**TO R., BISHOP OF ANGERS**

[Note: Thus Royal manuscript 4103. R. designates none other than Renaud of Martigné, then Bishop of Angers.]

He sends to the Bishop of Angers—that is, the priest’s own bishop—for punishment a priest who, for want of unleavened bread, consecrated ordinary bread; this is for the scandal rather than the offense.

The priest who bears this letter, while standing at the sacred altar to perform the ministry, found no bread prepared for the host and confesses that he offered the sacrifice with ordinary bread. In this matter, although custom rather than faith is more properly impugned, [Note: Unleavened bread was introduced among the Latins by custom alone. Yet one who consecrates with leavened bread must be punished because of scandal, and also because of negligence.] we nevertheless perceive some fault in him, judging scandal and the priest’s carelessness to deserve a graver punishment than the character of the offense itself.

Since this occurred in your diocese, we place the person who sinned and the sin beneath your judgment, so that the transgression may be punished by the pastor whose flock has been disturbed by the novelty in the sacrifice. It will therefore be for your deliberation to pronounce upon the priest who “played the Greek wrongly” [Note: Thus the Évreux and Rouen manuscripts, not “consecrated,” as in the printed editions. It alludes to the Greek rite, in which the Eucharist is prepared only with leavened bread.] a sentence containing more of a father than of a judge, more mercy than severity. For it is written: “When you are angry, you shall remember mercy” (Habakkuk 3:2).

## LETTER XX

[Note: Alternatively no. 74. Written after the year 1112.]

Having repeatedly and gently urged an ecclesiastical man [Note: “Ecclesiastical man.” This letter seems to have been addressed to the then abbot of Évron. In the following letter to the Bishop of Angoulême—then Gerard, legate of the Roman Church—Hildebert says that he had often approached this abbot both personally and in letters, attempting to restore his monastery’s utterly depraved condition. Since the abbot’s wickedness and incompetence made this impossible, Hildebert was compelled to invoke the legate’s authority, relying on it to reform the monastery in head and members alike. Who that abbot was is not clear. It is, however, clear that an Abbot Daniel of St Mary of Évron subscribed in 1123 to a charter of donation made to the monastery of St Aubin by Adelard, lord of Château-Gontier, through the hands of Renaud of Martigné, Bishop of Angers. This fits the period of Hildebert’s pontificate and Gerard’s legations. Moreover, this monastery of Évron, anciently called Haurion, was formerly subject to the monastery of St Peter at Chartres, as appears from the charter of its restoration, by which Robert, Count of Blois, its restorer, subjected it to Wilbert, Abbot of St Peter, and to his monastery. There it is called a little monastery and a little community. Thus from the old Haganon of Chartres, cited in *Gallia Christiana*, under abbeys, p. 346.] to correct his conduct and carry out his office, had sung to a deaf man. By this letter he reproaches him more sharply for negligence and hardness of heart, and threatens that, unless he comes to his senses, he will deal more severely with him, lest the man accuse him of having placed a cushion beneath his elbow.

It was always necessary to send you letters repeated twice or three times, so that, at least when frequently warned, you might do what you ought to have performed of your own accord. Yet not even thus did you ever awaken, nor were you roused to fulfil the duty of your profession. You had read, however, how great is the good of obedience, which God prefers to sacrifices and vows. You had read that refusal to obey is called by Samuel [Col. 0229B] idolatry (1 Kings 15:23). Nor, I think, had this escaped you: that Saul, chosen by the Lord, through the sin of disobedience lost both His favour and the throne of the kingdom. Scripture relates that a certain one of the sons of the prophets (3 Kings 36), because, though forbidden, he ate bread and drank water in Samaria, was struck by a lion sent from the Lord. These things were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. 10:11). For the Apostle is debtor both to the wise and to the foolish, so that he may set before both the punishment of obedience violated and the reward of obedience kept. Moreover, there is no virtue whose contempt is punished more severely by the Lord. For the punishment of other offences does not extend even to the innocent. Consider Ezekiel speaking thus: “The soul [Col. 0229C] that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:4); and again: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor shall the father bear the iniquity of the son” (ibid., 20). Disobedience, however, has often involved the guiltless with the guilty, and they have become alike in punishment though unlike in fault.

The law commanded that those twenty years old and above, who could go forth to war or discharge some ministry, should be numbered. But because David commanded that all, below twenty years and above, should be numbered without distinction, the Lord was angered; and when a three-day pestilence had been sent among the people, seventy thousand men fell by the stroke of the angel (2 Kings 24). Sacred history relates that Achan, son of Charmi, presumptuously took from the accursed things of Jericho (Joshua 7). It is therefore recorded that Israel fell by the sword before the sons of the city of Ai, and that the personal offence [Col. 0229D] was followed by the ruin of the people. Finally, the whole world to this day pays the penalty for the guilt of the first-created man, and one man’s disobedience proscribed all humankind. You, brother, [Col. 0230A] ought to have considered these things, and feared judgment for contempt of obedience, if you did not care for the reward of reverence.

I know—indeed, I know—that you have abused my patience, and, as the comic poet says, that my gentleness has taught you many bad things. Yet there was a place and a time for my patience and gentleness, which ought to precede the punishment of disobedience. For we are taught by example and word that punishments should not immediately be inflicted upon transgressions. The Lord was unwilling, at the beginning of humankind’s overflowing wickedness, to destroy the human race with the waters of the flood; but, having allotted them one hundred and twenty years for repentance, He punished their iniquities all the more universally because they, following the flesh in a more carnal manner, despised the law of nature, the order of things, and the time for repentance. We have received that Jonah was sent to preach to the Ninevites, [Col. 0230B] and that, in accordance with the prophet’s word, after forty days of satisfaction divine indignation rested from them (Jonah 1). On this subject Wisdom also says: “Correct your neighbour before you threaten him” (Ecclus. 19:17).

Our Saviour likewise, instructing the apostles, said to Simon Peter: “If your brother sins against you, go and correct him between yourself and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not hear you, take with you one or two others, so that every word may stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses. And if he does not hear them, tell the Church. But if he does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican” (Matt. 18:15–17). Taught by these examples, I came to you and corrected you, but between myself and you alone. I corrected you, indeed, but did not gain [Col. 0230C] my brother. I took with me one; I took two, that my word might stand in the mouth of two or three; I took them, but not even thus did I gain my brother. What, then, remains except that, despising the Church also, you should be to me as a heathen and publican?

Far be it, however, that the Church should hear this! Far be it that I should reveal my brother’s shame! For I am ashamed whenever my neighbour does what brings him shame. Indeed, a bishop should blush at his own offence to no purpose unless he blushes also at another’s offence. It is his part to be wounded through compassion by the same darts with which he knows his neighbour to be wounded. Hence the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 1:29). Perhaps you will say to me what was said by the Corinthians: “Your letters [Col. 0230D] are weighty and strong” (2 Cor. 10:10). To this I reply: You had been wounded by the robbers into whose hands fell the man descending from Jerusalem to Jericho.

[Col. 0231A]

When therefore I found you half-dead, I first poured oil upon your wounds with the Samaritan, and then wine (Luke 10). So that the wound of disobedience might be healed by the wine of censorial correction, since it could not be healed by the oil of paternal feeling, I sent you the letters which you call severe. Woe to me, for having delayed so long to send them! Woe to me, who have nothing by which I can excuse my slowness! For I had read (Ezek. 13:18): “Woe to those who put cushions beneath every man’s elbow, and make pillows for ensnaring souls!” (Ecclus. 12:11). I had read the words of the Wise Man: “I fastened you like a nail driven on high.”

> [Note: Col. 0231D] “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven firmly home; they have been given by the counsel of teachers from one shepherd.”

But while I indulged you with flattering and gentle words, by which I might restore you to yourself, I placed, as it were, a cushion beneath your elbow; I made, as it were, a pillow by which your soul was ensnared. Eli used such a cushion and such a pillow with [Col. 0231B] his offending sons when he said: “It is not a good report, my sons, which I hear concerning you” (1 Kings 2:24). Gregory Nazianzen, in his book *On the Epiphanies*, speaks of such correction in these words:

> “Eli the priest is condemned for the iniquity of his sons because, when they profaned the divine sacrifices, he punished them with too little severity. He did restrain them, and he did rebuke them; but with the gentleness and mildness of a father, not with the severity and authority of a high priest.”

Therefore, lest I be punished for the same transgression, I have fastened this present letter with nails—nails which few fail to know, when driven deeply in, draw corruption from ulcers. For in it, laying aside the father, I have put on the bishop; I have exchanged blandishments for rebukes, and threatened harsh things instead of gentle ones, so that, if you disdain to become my neighbour, [Col. 0231C] I myself may become my own neighbour.

“Arise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” (Eph. 6:14). Rise quickly; rise today, because it is far too near to death to await tomorrow’s remedy. Rise, I say, quickly; for unless you rise quickly, unless you quickly repent, he will quickly come who will remove your candlestick from its place and another will receive your bishopric. Correction awaited too long, and never pursued, receives a merciless judge. Perhaps your soul is wearied by a longer letter, and you disdain to read what you refuse to obey. I know—indeed, I know—that a reverent mind accepts even sparing correction and desires its abundance. But whatever virtue says to the wicked turns [Col. 0231D] into punishment.

## LETTER XXI

> [Note: Col. 0231D] Written in 1111, when Paschal II—as almost all writers on ecclesiastical affairs of that age report—was unjustly seized by Emperor Henry V in St Peter’s Basilica itself, together with many cardinals and clergy; was held for more than sixty days and cruelly tortured; and was not released until he unwillingly granted him the right of investitures. He afterward annulled this grant, after holding various councils, and struck the emperor himself with an anathema. See Baronius on the year 1111 and following, where he relates these matters at length. Our D’Achery printed this lamenting letter of Hildebert, as also the following apologetic letter, in *Spicilegium*, vol. IV, p. 245, from a manuscript sent to him long before from Rouen by the most learned Lanfranc Bigot. But since both letters abounded in many errors that corrupted the very sense, and since D’Achery had examined them closely but possessed no other manuscript, he judged it improper to publish them otherwise than as they had reached him. We, having more fortunately obtained corrected copies in the Évreux manuscript, namely from the library of Perron, have judged that they should be published, corrected according to its authority, for the readers’ benefit. Both are absent, however, from Royal MSS 4080 and 4103; Colbert MSS 2131, 4017, and 5135; and Victorine MSS 272 and 292.

In this letter, addressed to a friend, he bitterly laments the injuries inflicted with the utmost violence by Henry V, Emperor of the Romans, upon Pope Paschal II and the whole Roman clergy and people, when, holding him in prison with all the clergy and cruelly tormenting him, he unjustly and violently extorted the right of investitures.

[Col. 0232A]

Let the eyes of those flow with tears, my beloved, whose charity has been wounded by the pain of the Head. I had wished again to exhort you to praises, but the common grief of all prevents particular joy. For behold: the purple of martyrs again adorns the Church in her old age, and the revived madness of faithless cruelty completes the remnants of a perishing world by the precious death of the children of God. A baleful attendant rages against Christ’s people, and the sword of the ungodly exacts penalties from piety. [Col. 0232B] The city of the Romans is given over to plunder, and the seat of apostolic eminence is profaned by the bloody ravaging of the Saxons.

> [Note: Col. 0232D] That is, the Germans.

The pope is led away captive, and the pontifical mitre is trampled beneath the feet of the wicked. The desolated chair of Holiness mourns, and Rome—whom all tribes and tongues had served—is reduced to tribute. Unclean dogs have polluted God’s Church, and the cruel barbarity of the Germans slaughters the children of the divine law and carries its ministers captive. Thus indeed is fulfilled in God’s Church the prophecy of Holy Scripture: “Her enemies have become the head” (Lam. 1:5). And again the Gospel says: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered” (Matt. 26:11). Therefore I cannot believe that it has happened without peril to the Christian religion that the ruler and teacher of the Church should be bound. [Col. 0232C] The enemy struck the stronger one, so that afterward triumph over those subject to him might be easier. Has our head been cut off, and do the remaining members not wither? Is the commander of Christ’s army bound, and will the soldier remain fearless? Good Jesus, where is the truth of your promise, if you do not remain with your Church forever? Or what does your prayer avail, if Peter’s faith fails? Strengthen, Christ, strengthen the faith of the Church, for which you prayed. Remain with us as you promised.

Moreover, be vigilant in prayer, lest we too be deceived by Satan. For behold, he whom yesterday you extolled with proclamations of praise, whom you pursued with the service of affection, shines in the world with two miracles, if one may say so. Or, if this displeases you, he is bound by two [Col. 0232D] crimes such as have not been heard even among the Gentiles. For who besides him can be found who has seized both his fathers, spiritual and carnal, by a treacherous [Col. 0233A] plot?

> [Note: Col. 0233D] This Henry V had thrown into prison both his spiritual father, Pope Paschal II, and his carnal father, Emperor Henry IV, his predecessor.

This is he who contradicts the Lord’s commandments on both tablets. For, to speak first of matters prior in deed: he did not honour the father of his flesh, but first imprisoned him, then deceitfully drove him out; afterward he rose against God and His Church, and disturbed Peter’s vicar from his see even into chains. Blessed therefore is Pope Paschal, worthy of all devoted love, who ruled the apostolic see in such a way as to deserve also to be an imitator of the Apostolic Passion. Blessed prisoner of Jesus Christ: though even his hands and feet may be bound, the word of the Lord is never bound. Whoever wishes to be a member of this head ought to reckon himself united to his head. For an injury inflicted upon fathers is seen as an insult to their children. He is not a member of this head, not a son of this father, not a subject of this prelate, who does not feel it, does not grieve with him, or mocks him. [Col. 0233B]

## LETTER XXII

> [Note: Col. 0234D] It seems to have been written in the same year as the preceding letter. *Spicilegium*, vol. IV, pp. 246, 251.

Paschal II, captured by force and deceit by Emperor Henry V, at first resisted when the emperor, employing every sort of threat and even attempting to endanger his life, sought forcefully to exact the right of investitures. But moved by the entreaties of the cardinals and leading men of the Roman people whom the emperor held and cruelly tormented, he unwillingly granted him that right. Yet as soon as he regained liberty, he annulled all that had been extorted from him by violent force. Hildebert recounts this in the present apologetic letter.

Never did the harshness of adverse fortune respond more happily to my desire than when you wrote me certain laments concerning the pope, the king, and the Romans. [Col. 0233C] For, my dear friend, your page had bound me in knots of a certain necessity, so that, if I wished to answer its first onset, I had before you the reason why I would not accuse the king of the Saxons, and, against you, the reason why I ought not to harm that affection of charity, at home and abroad. Thus, tossed amid these straits, when I judged that I ought neither to flatter your lord nor, for the sake of my honourable friend, refute what you said, I considered at length with myself what I should do. At last, finding matter in the occasion of my impending sorrow, so harassed by domestic injuries that I had no leisure to complain of crimes, I offered you silence for an answer in the meantime.

But behold, when truth is disclosed and breaks out into light, the force of the canons, the discipline of justice, the school of virtues—it is iniquity if I do not answer, and envy if I do not praise. Therefore, when the injuries of fate have fallen silent even for a little while, when amid these distresses it has been permitted to breathe, and when truth itself also pleads its cause, we comply both with justice and with God, and also please you [read perhaps: “that we may please you”], whom perhaps we have exasperated. Who has made slaughter, who has polluted holy things, who has profaned the covenant, and entered the sanctuary in pride—or, if anyone has done these things—allow me, I beg, to pass that by here. You have explained each of these matters [Col. 0234A] so copiously and clearly, and lamented them with such solemn tears of your voice, that you sprinkled me too with their streams and bore me unwillingly along with you into complaint.

Certainly, certainly, it is permissible not to keep silent with you about the praises of Pope Paschal, and not to accuse those whom I love. How blessed, as you say, is Pope Paschal, who maintained the holiness of his rank and name so that he did not fear to teach and to do, even unto blood, that which the meaning of his name marked out and the rule of his office commanded. Blessed be Jesus Christ, who does not so abandon the camp of Christian warfare amid the wedges of the enemy as not to provide it with a strong athlete and an excellent leader. His love shall not play the harlot in Israel, nor shall the hostile party rejoice in spoils from the chosen lot. [Col. 0234B] While the wakeful perseverance of our Joshua endures, the sun fixed for us in the sky shall stand at his command and shall drive away the foulness of nocturnal darkness, until the victorious troop bears back a noble trophy over vices.

But because the world lies in wickedness, and there is much bitterness and envy among the people, I think there will not be lacking someone who dares to burst out in these words: “See how you pursue with glory and honour, lift to the stars with praises, and magnify with outstanding virtues, one whom we have now seen trembling before battle, unable to endure the blast of the trumpet, contriving surrender rather than bloodshed, striking a treaty with the enemies against laws and rights, and in the end leaving the standards, declining military service, casting away his arms, fleeing and hiding: a mighty athlete indeed, who has never been accustomed either to stand in the line [Col. 0234C] of battle, to engage, or to conquer. And you call him to reward and crown! You might persuade me of this were I ignorant that brave men do not flee brave deeds. You will never make a Maccabee out of Ahab.”

> [Note: Col. 0234D] As though he said: You will never make a brave and fearless man out of one who is cowardly and afraid.

We do not doubt that Christ of the Lord will be assailed with such vexations, or far greater ones; and he himself, who has become a spectacle to the world and its angels, will endure all things bravely. But we, who profess ourselves to be his sons—for, as you say, an injury inflicted upon fathers is seen as an insult to their children—let us hasten to rise to his aid, exposing ourselves also to dangers for him. And, as though wrenching Hercules’ club from his hands, let us beat down the enemies of justice with their own assertions, so that, shattered by their own [Col. 0234D] devices [read perhaps: “contrivances”], they may be more gravely confounded and more reverently ashamed. Would that they offered us ears open to hear as patiently as they have sharpened the goads of their tongues eagerly to wound!

If Pope Paschal, for the sake of right, country, the covenant of the saints, and the commonwealth of Jesus Christ, voluntarily delivered himself into the hands of the ungodly; if he offered his neck to the axe, what could he have done, or ought he to have done, more holy or better? What more useful for his neighbour? [Col. 0235A] What more honourable for himself? Did he not so hate his life in this world as to preserve it for eternal life? Had he not observed from the canon of the Lawgiver that no greater place is given to grace toward one’s neighbour than when a man gives his life for his brothers? Who ever accused of cowardice a tribune who first cast himself into chains and afterward offered himself to be struck in place of the soldier?

But if afterward he yielded to violence and, as though fleeing, in order to draw back from the blood of saints and the slaughter of citizens the sword-edge of the right hand already on the point of flashing; if, for a time, he granted what was demanded, as though a truce had been given and a treaty concluded [read perhaps: “conferred”], until he might restore the city’s walls, set up engines of war, summon an army, forestall hardships, marshal battle-lines, and hold in the air the blows of the striking hand—what could the skill of a commander do more prudently or cautiously? Who [Col. 0235B] will condemn as imprudent one who so disarmed the enemy’s columns and so recalled them to their own lands that not even the least of those whom he had received perished at their hands?

Did not King David, that most holy and mighty warrior, flee the rage of his pursuing son, lest the walls of the Holy City should be profaned by the blood of citizens, bearing with equanimity the insults of those who reproached him, and afterward, having summoned the house of Judah and the mighty men of Israel, crush him and his accomplices more bitterly? (2 Kings 16.) An onset indeed hastens, but does not immediately attain the crown. Impatience immediately breaks forth, but, like a torrent, suddenly dries up. The more fully you draw back the engines of a ballista, the more strongly they strike.

But if, as they say, he changed, when he wished, what he had been allowed to tolerate for a time; if he made himself heard among the people and left a testament to his sons—and because that is not confirmed except by the death of the testator, renouncing home, country, possessions, and office, to be mortified in the flesh, he withdrew to the island of Pontia—[Col. 0235C] what, I beg you, what ground has malicious envy in this respect for speaking against him or gnawing at him?

But if, amid examples shared with us, a new and uncommon report [read perhaps: “and a frequent report”] prevailed in the voices of the people, and he was recalled to the chair by the tears of the cardinals and again directs the reins and exercises the functions of the apostolic summit; if he assembles a synod of saints, convenes the Church, gathers an assembly, and desires, with the consent of all, to cut away scandals from God’s house with the sickle of judgment; to establish by justice what is good and equitable; to tolerate or alter in mercy what is deferred; and to bind up what is broken with the bandages of discernment—if he has so submitted himself to the judgment of clergy and people [Col. 0235D] that it depends on their sentence whether he frames new chapters, destroys old ones, strengthens what he has established, or lets it pass unimpaired according to the circumstances of the times; whether he remains in the chair or is carried away into exile—still the tongue of the wicked will never fear to assail, persecute, and condemn this also with the stings of speech.

Do not, do not, I beseech you, whoever you are, rashly break in upon the institutions of the Fathers, examine them, find fault with their practices, or accuse their teaching. Rebuke, but only after you have first established the outcome of the matter; accuse, but only after you have weighed [Col. 0236A] that they have erred. Yet even then do so in a spirit of gentleness. Many things are done differently because of place, many because of time, many because of persons. A ruler of the Church will sometimes overlook, or do, what he condemns; when he sees the evil of schism impending, he will alter the enactments of the canons. Censure must cease when unity is being dissolved, charity wounded, and peace shaken. You have heard what is written: “They were troubled and moved like a drunken man” (Ps. 106:27). Do not accuse a bloodstained soldier of fear because he is anointed with ointments. A steward often does not know what he ought to forbid or overlook, command or permit. The faithful and prudent servant is commanded to distribute to his fellow servants a measure of wheat in its season (Luke 12:42). Wheat is given by measure when the same charity grants to the untrained what it denies to the strong; when it disciplines the devout and tolerates the wicked; when, after a little while, it relaxes by indulgence what it had now commanded by strictness. [Col. 0236B] Paul the Apostle, abolisher of the law and preacher of grace, freely proclaimed: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2). The same man afterward did what he forbade. He let his hair grow and, because of a vow, shaved his head at Cenchreae (Acts 18:18).

You do not know, brother, you do not know how diligently and carefully the Fathers do what makes you wonder, accuse, and condemn. Cease, I say, to persecute the ordinances of spiritual men, investigate secrets, and condemn decrees. We read in the canons:

> [Note: Col. 0235D] These words are from the false decretal attributed to Pope Cornelius, though Gratian reports it, *Causa* 2, question 1, canon “Oves.”

> “Let not sheep presume to accuse their shepherd.”

Whatever we do not know with what intention it is done, let us interpret favourably. The universal bishop has the power to annul all laws and rights. I turn to those who dare to aspire to [Col. 0236C] judgment.

> [Note: Col. 0236D] Thus the Évreux manuscript, but perhaps *exprobrare* (“to reproach”), or even better *asperare* (“to aggravate”).

And you, man—you, ashes, an ant in comparison with God—do you not fear to provoke a lion? Defer, defer your reproaches to another time. By the judgment of Cain, those are condemned who inflict injuries upon their fathers. Confess your offence; repent; beat your breast; wash offences with grief and tears; and, retracting your reproaches, sing, as the saying goes, a palinode—a recantation. Rebuke yourself; hasten to anticipate the Judge’s sentence yourself.

But see what I have done! While I began a letter, I wove a history. I therefore wish, at this point, to note the sum of the matter in few and brief words, so that what a reader, whether hurrying or wearied, has passed over in a digression may be grasped even by a mind occupied with reading, as though compressed [Col. 0236D] into two words. The commander of the Christian army was captured while he had gone out armed against the enemy. Whoever you are, rival of truth, blame fortune, not the tribune. The law which, while bound, he enacted, he repealed when free; what he had earlier annulled, he restored. The strong athlete rises more fiercely after wounds and bloodshed, and thereafter learns to receive blows more cautiously and return them more strongly. Renouncing all, he withdrew to retirement under laws, rights, and writings set down beforehand. This is the justice of the perfect. He is brought back to his chair by the voices of his subjects.

Men, [Col. 0237A] I beg you, let us observe his gentleness. What he taught concerning humility and obedience, he first set forth as an example in himself. The outstanding preacher bore in his hands the grace which, by the ministry of his voice, he dispensed to the children of the universal Church: whether he should depart or remain, annul what he had done or confirm it, he calls for a public and certain judgment and takes counsel concerning what is fair and good. It will therefore be better for you, deceitful tongue, to twist yourself into continual silence than to accuse the conscience of a holy man which you do not know.

But you, my heart [Note: Col. 0237C: Here he perhaps means Marbod, and urges him to praise Paschal; for he regarded him as both most dear and, as he himself was, most skilled in poetry—as his many poems testify.], and my glory, delight of kings, favour of princes, ornament among the clergy, beloved among the people, model of honour, mirror of grace, pattern of faith, and Orpheus of our age, join your person to the strings and to the sweet measures of your voice. Do what you do: [Col. 0237B] proclaim the steadfast and discerning man, who fled so as to conquer, and conquered so as to release the conquered. Thus he thrust himself into chains for his subjects, that he might draw kings bound in chains toward the palm of victory. Seek retirement; summon the Pierian Muses; amid responding instruments, modulate sweet songs of praise for his titles through the varied windings of your voice. Among the sounding pipes, let harsh flutes and shattered reeds, I beg, make their noise. Let delightful variety join in one symphony. Be David, and make me one of the accompanying singers. If I cannot follow you through every part, at least, while you breathe between cadences, I shall be able meanwhile to sound applause.

## LETTER XXIII

> [Note: Col. 0237D] Otherwise numbered 51. Written about the end of 1112 or the beginning of 1113.

In this letter he attacks a certain heretic.

> [Note: Col. 0237D] Who that heretic was is wholly uncertain. I would gladly adopt the opinion of those who think that he was none other than Henry, whom Hildebert, after returning from Rome, overthrew and drove from his diocese. For the *Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans* mention no other heretic with whom he contended. If, however, this man here attacks only the error concerning the invocation of the saints and the knowledge of blessed souls concerning what happens here, he attacks that man especially as the head and source from whom the other errors revived by the heretic Vigilantius appeared to flow. For if the blessed in glory are ignorant of what happens among us, we venerate them in vain, invoke them in vain, and pursue their images, relics, instruments of martyrdom, and so forth with veneration in vain. It is probable that he made this letter public, as he did the apologetic letter, both in order to recall to Catholic truth the faithful deceived by the heretical man and, as was fitting for a bishop, to guard his own reputation and remove from his flock the scandal caused by the slander of this utterly shameless sycophant. It seems to have been written about 1111 or 1112. On this Henry, see our Mabillon in the Preface to St Bernard, §6, and what we said concerning him in the *Life of Hildebert* under the year 1110 and following.

He attacks, as once Vigilantius did, the invocation of the saints; and he pursues this all the more fiercely because this heretic had more shamelessly dared to assert that Hildebert shared, held, and taught the same opinion as himself.

[Col. 0237C]

In a kingdom, indeed, no one seeks an associate; but in error every person seeks one. This surely happens because the agreement of a multitude lends authority to every human invention. Arian impiety would have been suffocated at its birth, had it not found guardians to rear it. Donatus’s schism would be continually oppressed by silence if it had infected a person rather than a crowd. You too, as though grieving that the perversity of Vigilantius had been suppressed by oblivion, are said to be reviving it and gathering companions for yourself, so that the planting which the heavenly Father did not plant may flourish again, long since dried up, through their cult. For these men, as they say, hold that the souls of the saints are ignorant of what occurs in this life, [Col. 0238A] and that therefore the litanies are idle by which we pray that the saints may pray for us, because they neither hear us nor know what happens among us.

> [Note: Col. 0238D] Our learned Father Sammarthanus notes in his scholia on St Gregory’s eleventh letter to Bishop John, *Register*, book V, indiction XIII, that ancient authors often call the solemn processions of clergy and people to the place appointed for a station “litanies,” because litanies, or supplications, were included in them. There he cites book XXX of the Theodosian Code, *On Heretics*, where Emperor Arcadius forbids profane assemblies to meet anywhere, by night or day, for the making of a litany. Gregory himself similarly calls a procession a litany, *Register*, book VI, letters 34 and 61. Our Hildebert uses “litany” here in the sense of solemn invocation of the saints.

My soul is wounded all the more grievously by this injury to the saints because you are said to have told certain persons that I myself think, maintain, and teach this very thing. My Judge is in heaven: I can neither deceive Him as He watches nor escape Him as He judges. I speak before Him. He knows that I have never lapsed into so great a failure as either to say or ever to think that which is foolishly thought, dangerously [Col. 0238B] believed, and taught as causing ruin.

> [Note: Col. 0238D] Thus Colbert MS 4017 and Victorine MS 292: that is, “causing disaster” or guilt. Others read *causaliter*, “causally.”

I had indeed resolved to keep silent and to pass you by as though I had not seen you. For I had read the Apostle’s saying: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). I had also read Gregory writing thus to Palladius:

> [Note: Col. 0238D] *Register*, book XI, letter 2, indiction IV.

> “Amid the words of those who praise or blame, one must always return to one’s conscience; and if the good said about us is not found there, great sorrow ought to arise.”

And again:

> “If the evil which people say about us is not found there, we ought to leap into great joy.”

Likewise:

> “If we have a witness in heaven, we have a witness in the heart.”

Let fools outside say what they please. But because it was reported to me that others too had been bespattered with the same ink, [Col. 0238C] I undertook both to show myself acquainted with this novelty and to refute its professors. He does not yet fulfil the office of bishop who, while censor of his own people, is silent concerning the vices of others. Such a profession is charged with fault whenever it does not charge the wrongdoer. For it is the priest’s task to strive not to please God alone, but together with another. Therefore he too is proved to sin unless he loves in his enemy the good which he loves in himself.

Hence, my brother, I desire that your ways and pursuits become good and are not found in the number of those whose speech spreads like a cancer, who tell fables [Col. 0239A] rather than the law of the Lord God. To such fables the perversity already mentioned is certainly added—a perversity against which the Church’s custom is known to stand, authority to protest, and reason to be lacking. For that the universal Church persists in litanies, and is accustomed in tears and contrite spirit to say, “Holy Mary, pray for us,” neither the unlearned fail to know nor the learned, when they hear it, attack.

Yet we by no means set custom before truth, knowing that nothing is owed to a custom opposed by truth. Therefore Augustine says in the third book *On the Baptism of Infants*:

> [Note: Col. 0239D] In the passages cited above on Letter 20 of this book.

> “Once truth has been made manifest, let custom yield to truth.”

Likewise:

> “Let no one set custom before reason and truth, because reason and truth always exclude custom.”

Cyprian says on the same subject: “Every custom, however old and however widespread, must be set altogether below truth; and a practice contrary to truth must be abolished.”

Yet when custom accords with truth, I hold that custom should be shown reverence and that long-established practice ought to be maintained unshaken. Augustine says of this in Book IV of *On Baptism*: “This is plainly true: reason and truth must be preferred to custom; but when truth supports custom, nothing ought to be held more firmly.”

Perhaps it has been revealed to you from above that the Church of Christ was in error until your foolish times, and that the apostolic saying has been fulfilled in you: “If in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal this also to you” (Phil. 3:15). Blessed are you, who alone have become for the Church the interpreter of heavenly secrets! I had believed that Paul alone had been caught up into paradise and heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter. But perhaps you too were caught up there and brought back from it these words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter. Yet what sign do you show us, that we may believe you? Which of the saints supports this teaching of yours? Have you an authority by which to impose silence upon me?

For I perceive—I perceive and declare—that the souls of the saints, now reigning with Christ, know what is done by us and, when it is fitting and expedient, pray for us. I do not speak from my own spirit. Anyone’s testimony on his own behalf is weak and feeble. I have with me many souls of authority, whom both their merit made shepherds of souls and the Spirit of God taught all truth.

Your vigilance has deceived me [Note: [Col. 0239D] MSS Reg. 4103, Colb. 1168, and Victorin. 272 read *mea* (“my”); many read *tua* (“your”). Better: “Your vigilance has deceived you, unless …”], unless you have read these words written in Book XII on the *Moralia* [Note: [Col. 0239D] Book 12, ch. 21 of the new edition, p. 402, where “distinct knowledge” is read in place of [Col. 0240D] “distinct thought.”]:

> “Just as those still living do not know in what place the souls of the dead are held, so the dead do not know how the life of those living after them in the flesh is ordered; for the life of the spirit is far removed from the life of the flesh. And just as corporeal and incorporeal things differ in kind, so too they differ in thought. [Col. 0240A] Yet this is not to be thought concerning the souls of the saints: since they behold inwardly the brightness of almighty God, it must by no means be believed that there is anything outside which they do not know.”

Again Gregory says in the *Moralia*:

> “The spirits of the saints are extended both inwardly and outwardly in perception, because they contemplate the very fountain of knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0240D] *Dialogues*, Book IV, ch. 33.]. “For what do those who know Him who knows all things fail to know of the things that ought to be known? Their knowledge, therefore, is indeed greatly enlarged in comparison with ours, yet narrow in comparison with divine knowledge; just as the spirits of the dead are spirits in comparison with our bodies, but bodies in comparison with the supreme and uncircumscribed Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0240D] Gregory, Book II of the *Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily 40, new edition, vol. I, p. 658.].

After this assertion of Gregory, with what rashness will you say that the spirits of the righteous [Col. 0240B] wholly do not know what is done in this life—unless with still greater madness you say that the spirits of the righteous have absolutely no life after this? To think this of them is impious, and to affirm it is heretical. For to fall into this madness empties the hope of heavenly rewards and consigns one to that misery of which the Apostle says: “If we have hoped in Christ only in this life, we are more miserable than all human beings” (1 Cor. 15:12).

Moreover, that these same souls intercede for those who call upon them, Jerome rebukes Vigilantius—whose soul you have made your follower—with these words [Note: [Col. 0240D] Vol. IV, new edition, p. 283.]:

> “You say in your little book that while we live we can pray mutually for one another; but after we have died, no prayer of anyone is to be heard for another—especially since the martyrs, [Col. 0240C] praying for vengeance for their blood, could not obtain it. If apostles and martyrs, while still in the body, are able to pray for others when they must still be concerned for themselves, how much more after crowns, victories, and triumphs? One man, Moses, obtains pardon for six hundred thousand people (Exod. 12); and Stephen, the imitator of his God and the first martyr in Christ, prays for pardon for his persecutors (Acts 7); and after they have begun to be with Christ, will they have less power? The apostle Paul says that two hundred and seventy-six souls in the ship were granted to him; and after he has been released and has begun to be with Christ, will he then close his mouth and be unable to utter a word for those throughout the whole world who have believed his Gospel? [Col. 0240D] (Acts 27).”

Furthermore, Gregory, in his homily on “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,” and so forth, refutes your ignorance in these words [Note: [Col. 0240D] St. Gregory, vol. I of the new edition, p. 1593.]:

> “The holy martyrs, our defenders, are present. They wish to be asked, and, so to speak, seek to be sought. Seek these as helpers for your prayer; find these as protectors against your guilt.”

Having considered these authorities, you cannot deny that the souls [Col. 0241A] of the good either know what is done by the living or, when it is fitting and expedient, pray for the living. Moreover, your eyes have grown far too dim if you do not see that reason itself supports the testimony of Jerome and Gregory. For no one doubts that charity excels the other virtues. Indeed, upon charity depend the whole Law and the Prophets. According to Paul, prophecies will pass away, tongues will cease, and knowledge will be abolished; charity never fails. Finally, faith fails, hope fails, but charity never fails. Hence, after the Apostle had said, “Now remain faith, hope, charity, these three” (1 Cor. 13:13), he added: “But the greatest of these is charity” (ibid.). It is greater precisely because, when faith and hope are abolished, charity remains forever.

[Col. 0241B] It remains, I say, yet not confined within the narrow measure by which one loves neighbor and God in this life, but so much greater as, after this life, one knows one’s neighbor more fully in God and God in himself. For those who reap more than they sowed will love more than they loved before, because love receives an addition beyond its due when merit is surpassed by reward.

Isaiah contemplated this increase of charity when he said: “The Lord has a fire in Zion, and his furnace in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31:9). You know, my brother, that Zion is interpreted “watchtower,” Jerusalem “vision of peace.” The souls of the saints, while they bear about the body of this mortality, are said to be in Zion: that is, gazing from afar upon the reward which they hope for and await. But they are in Jerusalem [Col. 0241C] when, laying aside the burden of flesh, they see God face to face, exchanging imperfection for fullness, hope for possession, image for truth.

The Apostle was in that Zion when he said: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13:12). He promised himself this Jerusalem when he added: “But then face to face” (ibid.). Again, the same Apostle says: “Now I know in part; but then I shall know even as I have been known” (ibid.). Therefore there is a fire in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem, because the ardor of charity is slight in this life and very great in the life to come. Here it is a little spark; there, a furnace. Here, a portion; there, fullness. For “that which is perfect” will come, and “that which is in part” will be abolished.

Yet if what you assert is true, then the souls of the saints—whom neither angels nor principalities nor powers nor things present nor things future nor height nor depth nor any creature could separate from the charity of Christ (Rom. 8:38)—put off charity together with the flesh. Those who for the Lord’s name were put to death all day long and reckoned as sheep for slaughter then cease to love God precisely when they most fully know that even an enemy must be loved for God’s sake. Since, according to Gregory’s testimony, there is nothing outside which the souls of the saints do not know, for they know Him who knows all things, who will say that they love their neighbor when they hear their neighbor’s cries and never answer; know that they are knocked upon and disdain—or cannot—open; see distresses and shut up their hearts? [Col. 0242A] What has charity to do with those from whom the groans of the afflicted draw no compassion, no tearful response—though such prayers claim precedence among all other supplications in obtaining their request?

Therefore, because love of neighbor is lacking in them, love of God is lacking also. For neither can God be loved without one’s neighbor, nor one’s neighbor without God. John bears witness to this when he writes: “He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4:20). Again: “We have this commandment from God: that he who loves God should also love his brother” (1 John 4:21). Whoever takes away one of these from holy souls leaves neither.

By now, unless I am mistaken, you sufficiently perceive where your teaching strays [Col. 0242B] and what muddy water you drink, dreaming that charity fails where charity never fails (1 Cor. 13:8); where there is joy over sinners who repent (Luke 15:10); where, just as each praises God for himself, so all praise God for all; where God is all in all. Come to your senses, therefore; and if you find no sin in yourself such that you need to ask the saints to pray for you, do not insult us who pray that the saints may pray for us.

## LETTER XXIV

[Note: [Col. 0241D] Alternatively no. 78. Written about 1112.]

Cyprian and Peter, clerics, had imprudently attached themselves to the notorious heresiarch Henry. When they came to their senses and, at Hildebert’s persuasion, returned to sounder teaching, he commends them to the entire clergy as sincere Catholics.

Hildebert, humble priest of Le Mans, to all archbishops and bishops, greetings and prayers in Christ.

Cyprian and Peter, the bearers of this letter, while they planned ascents in their hearts, descended into the pit of death by following a certain false prophet; and those who followed him persecuted themselves. This was Henry [Note: [Col. 0241D] The very same man of whom he speaks in Letter 23 [Col. 0242D] of this book; consult that letter and the *Life of Hildebert*.], a great snare of the devil and a celebrated armour-bearer of Antichrist. These aforementioned brothers adhered to him, who feigned religion by his dress and learning by his words, until the foulness of his life and the error of his doctrine became known to them.

When they recognized that his ways were not right, they first returned to themselves and then came over to us, whose diocese this pestilence had so infected that the clergy resisting it could scarcely preserve their [Col. 0242D] liberty within the walls of the church. But after many tribulations, with God’s help that serpent burst among us, his shameful life and poisonous doctrine alike being exposed. From then on these brothers, obeying our counsel, returned to the pursuit they had undertaken, abandoning the garment of deception and the angel of darkness.

We have written this, brothers, to your fraternity so that, should these young men enter your parishes, they may not be branded with any disgrace because of this change, but rather that you both may rejoice together, because each was dead and has come to life, was lost and has been found (Luke 15). Farewell.

## LETTER XXV

[Note: [Col. 0243D] Alternatively no. 38. Written about 1113.]

He describes to Gerard, legate of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Angoulême, the corrupt condition of the monastery of Évron near Le Mans, arising from its abbot’s incompetence and stupidity, and asks what should be done under Gerard’s authority for its reform.

[Note: [Col. 0243D] Gerard, or Geraud, famous for almost continuous legations in Aquitaine and other regions under Paschal II, Gelasius II, Calixtus II, and Honorius II, and for eight councils convened by him; but later guilty of defection to the antipope Anacletus because Innocent denied him the legation. Nothing further need be noted about him, lest one have to repeat to weariness what nearly all sacred writers of that age asserted. See Sirmond on Letters 19, 20, and 21 of Geoffrey of Vendôme, and Mabillon on Letter 126 of St Bernard.]

[Col. 0243A]

G. I. [Note: [Col. 0244D] I.e. Ildebertus, without *H*, as some manuscripts have it.], humble servant of the people of Le Mans, to the bishop of Angoulême by the grace of God and legate of the holy Roman Church: greetings and perfect obedience.

There is among us an abbey [Note: [Col. 0244D] The very one mentioned above in Letter 20.] called Évron, formerly exceedingly distinguished in possessions and wealth, and poorer than neighboring monasteries only in moral honor. Envying the others their rich revenues, it begs from them the beauty of morals. There is no guardianship of the rules there, no censor of violated order. The monks [Col. 0243B] persecute the monk no less than if they had made a pact with shamefulness. Whatever was granted for the brothers’ expenses through the devotion of predecessors becomes payment for iniquity, not support for religion.

Those under the cloister-rule, to whom a stricter law forbids gatherings with laypeople and idle conversation, use streets in place of cloisters and buffoonery in place of reading. They maintain a public and impregnable intimacy with women; those women, bound by promises and inducements of little gifts, are found to claim for themselves days of wickedness and nights of infamy. Amid so many injuries to their sacred profession, the commonwealth is further burdened by this prejudice: because the monks do not refrain from assailing the order, secular persons [Col. 0243C] likewise do not refrain from assailing monks. The possessions of the sanctuary are exposed to plunder and allotted to disgraceful practices; outside they are worn down by violence, within by drunkenness and licentiousness.

The negligence of the shepherd has greatly increased this deficiency alike of goods and morals. He has nothing in common with the office of abbot: neither character supports him as an example nor learning as instruction. First, owing to excessive simplicity and its kindred stupidity, he does not know what is suitable to whom. Then a stubborn and unteachable perversity prevents him from yielding to persons of maturer judgment. Thus, supported neither by his own counsel nor trusting another’s, he makes himself conform to and reproduce the slowness of an ass. Ignorant of how to inspect the workshops of conduct, he presides over the others to the detriment of holiness, not for the correction of fault. For he neither investigates hidden offenses nor [Col. 0243D] imposes discipline for manifest ones.

As seldom and uselessly as he remains in the cloister, so negligently and silently does he sit in chapter. What shall I say of the refectory? He takes no care either what is eaten in it or that anything is eaten [in it]. He has declared such implacable hatred even against the dormitory as though resting there in common were a matter of infamy, [Col. 0244A] not a form of discipline. Added to this is the disposal of ornaments and possessions, so that nothing remains for the adornment of the house of the Lord, nothing for the relief of the poor, nothing for the sustenance of the community.

It cannot be said how often I have met with him, how often I have rebuked the man before religious abbots; yet neither was reverence thereby shown to moral discipline nor correction imposed upon vices. Moreover, lest it seem that I had omitted anything necessary to his correction, I summoned and brought him before your tribunal. There, when he could not clear himself of negligence, he promised amendment and gave his pledge; but “the last state of that man became worse than the first” (Luke 11).

For, to say nothing of the order, which impunity for offenses has wholly emptied, the property of the monks has declined so far [Col. 0244B] that daily provisions are begged from the burgesses of the aforesaid place. The abbot of Saint Vincent [Note: [Col. 0244D] Namely William, mentioned above in Letter 10 of Book I.], a man of consummate religious devotion, was sent there and has informed you in the letter sent to you how ruined he found the order. Therefore, concerning these matters, instruct your son by sealed letters what seems good to you, or what ought to be decreed against the aforesaid beast. The dissipation of the revenues which the badly provident abbot is accustomed to sell in advance while still on the grass requires a swift response.

## LETTER XXXI

[Note: [Col. 0244D] Alternatively no. 42. Written about 1113.]

To R. [Note: [Col. 0244D] Raynald of Martigné.], bishop of Angers [Note: [Col. 0244D] Thus Reg. 4103; and Ebr.: “to the bishop of Angers.”].

He admonishes the bishop of Angers concerning a certain Lisiard, unjustly struck by him with an anathema for the alleged abduction of Geoffrey’s daughter. The abduction, he maintains, is not even plausible; rather, he proves that a lawful marriage took place between them, since both parties gave free consent.

[Col. 0244C]

So that we might not seem either to fail justice or, contrary to justice, to inflict upon Lisiard an undeserved sentence of anathema for the sacrilege and robbery of which you accuse him, we resolved to investigate the truth more carefully. Accordingly, from the account of the case recited to us, it is plain that the said Lisiard is neither guilty of sacrilege nor committed any violence against Geoffrey’s daughter.

For who would dare assert that a girl was taken away from a monastery of nuns when, having been placed among sacred virgins for the sake of a more mature education, her father directed her to go out to a husband, her aunt led her out, her mother wished it, and she herself consented? She consented, I say, to enter, while he lived, into marriage with no one except Lisiard, as she herself testifies. This was surely prudent counsel, more mature than her years: by this harmony her lawful marriage was so preserved that a husband was chosen who was neither inferior in lineage, [Col. 0245A] nor lower in condition, nor lesser in power.

Pope Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0245C] Namely Nicholas I.] thus shows Bishop Hincmar how primary a place consent holds in marriage: according to the laws, the consent alone of those whose union is at issue is sufficient. If that consent alone is lacking in marriage, all else, even intercourse itself, is fruitless. John Chrysostom says likewise: “Marriage is made not by intercourse, but by will.” Pope Urban also did not pass over this matter concerning the king of Aragon, who had pledged by a promise of faith that he would give his niece to a certain knight. He sets forth a canonical chapter in these terms:

> “Concerning the marriage of your niece, whom, under pressure of necessity, you have confirmed by a pledge of faith that you will give to a certain knight: equity dictates that we decree this. If she altogether refuses the man, as is said, and persists in this resolve of her will, so as utterly to deny that she will marry that man, you are in no way to compel her, unwilling and resisting, to be joined in marriage with him. For those whose bodies are one ought also to have one mind, lest perhaps, if she is joined unwillingly to another man, she incur, contrary to the command of the Lord and Apostle, either the guilt of discord or the crime of fornication. The evil of that sin, of course, is known to fall back upon the person who joined her to him in life.” [Note: [Col. 0245C] Certain errors seem to have crept into the preceding letter, whether from copyists or from Hildebert himself—if I may say so without offense to so great a man. From copyists, indeed, when they wrote *Hicmaro* in MSS Victorin. 272 and Ebroicensis, and likewise in Colbert MSS 2662 and 4017; the editors, correcting this, perhaps insufficiently attentively printed *Hincmaro*. Hildebert himself, however, cites words of Pope Nicholas found in none of Nicholas’s letters to any individual bishop. Rather, they were taken from chapter 3 of Pope Nicholas’s *Responses to the Questions of the Bulgars*, that is, to an entire people, not personally to any bishop and therefore not to Hincmar. The words of St John Chrysostom reported by Hildebert could indeed have been cited as Chrysostom’s own, since perhaps in Hildebert’s age it was not yet known that the unfinished work on Matthew from which they were taken was not the genuine offspring of the holy doctor. Finally, with respect to the king of Aragon mentioned here, nothing prevents our believing that he was Sancho himself, to whom Gratian, Causa 32, question 2, canon *De Neptis*, says that Urban II wrote, and whose words cited by Hildebert he reports. For Urban II sat at Rome from 1087 to 1099, while Sancho—or, as they say, Sánchez I, king of Aragon—reigned from 1087 to 1094. During that interval Urban II could have written to Sancho.]

## LETTER XXVII

[Note: [Col. 0245D] + Compare Alford, *Annals of the English Church*, 118, no. 8.]

To the bishop of Memoria [Note: [Col. 0246C] Among twelve manuscript codices, only Reg. no. 4103 reads thus. Who this bishop of Memoria was seems very obscure, since nowhere, as far as I know, among geographers or among geographical experts whom I have carefully consulted, is any city, province, or bishopric so designated. It seems fairly probable that this was an overseas bishop, either English or Irish, to whom the memory of the most pious queen was dear. Perhaps *Memoriensi* should be written *Momoniensi* or *Mumoniensi*. In the *Life of St Malachy* by St Bernard, ch. 4, Mumonia is mentioned as a southern part of Ireland, where Malchus, formerly a monk of Winchester, is said to have been made bishop in the city of Mumonia named Lesmor, [Col. 0246D] perhaps now Limerick; and in ch. 10 two kings are said to have ruled this Mumonia. Perhaps this Malchus himself is the bishop to whom Hildebert directed this letter, for the chronology does not oppose it. On Momonia consult the recently published *Geographical Dictionary* of the distinguished and learned Antoine Baudrand, 1700, p. 170.]

To a certain bishop, apparently English, who had commended the soul of a deceased queen [Note: [Col. 0246D] The queen, namely Matilda; see the note on Letter 4 of Book I. According to Ingulph in *Anglia Sacra*, she died in 1118. This letter was written after her death.] to Hildebert’s prayers, he promises not to fail him in the offices both of gratitude and charity. At the same time, he promises to send him the extracts from the decrees which he had begun to collect as soon as he had put the finishing touch to them.

[Col. 0245C]

[Col. 0246A] It often happens that from past events we infer what will happen in the future. Thus we hope for true friendship from you, a friendship which is not buried in you when your friend is buried. The holy and surviving affection of your heart toward the queen teaches this: it is not enough for you to intercede for her unless you obtain the intercession of others as well. You ask that prayer be made for her; but we believe that she is more able to help us by her own prayers than she needs help from our prayers.

For we must confess that she departed as a queen to whom none of the temptations of abundant delights, none of the license of power, none of the enticement of sex crept in to imperil her integrity. Apart from virtue, virtue found nothing in her. [Col. 0246B] Although we know that her manner of life does not need intercession after death, we nevertheless anticipated your exhortation, fearing judgment if we should discharge, merely when asked rather than voluntarily, the diligence in prayer which the queen had earned from us. One has cherished an ungrateful person unless one also cherishes her for her own sake. Moreover, we are not released [variant: “comforted”] from our obligation if another person secures our intercession for her. For rewarding a benefit on another’s behalf rather than for one’s own does not discharge but binds the debtor.

Indeed, we would have given thanks in the first chapter of our letter, according to the order we had set for our papers, unless the queen claimed first place for herself in writing as in our heart. For he remembers the queen too late who remembers her after something else.

The *Exceptions from the Decrees* [Note: [Col. 0246D] The *Exceptions of the Decrees*, begun but not finished by Hildebert. The Ebr., Roth., and other MSS read *Exceptiones*, not *Excerptiones* (“Excerpts”), as some wish. Since Hildebert expressly mentions here *Exceptiones*—or, as some say, *Excerptiones*—from the decrees, which he had not yet completed, they ought not easily to be denied him, since he himself testifies in this letter that he had at least begun them. Amid the disturbances which beset Hildebert, he may have been unable to finish them; and Ivo, a laborious and learned bishop, may have undertaken to bring what had been begun to completion. Otherwise it makes no sense that two authors, living far apart, should have begun the same book in the same and equally numerous words, without any mutual comparison, and continued it through many pages. Yet it should be noted that this work, or beginning of a work, is found in none of the many Hildebert manuscripts that I have seen. Nevertheless, there should be no doubt that he himself is its author, since he expressly affirms it in this letter.], [Col. 0246C] which we have decided to arrange in one volume, have not yet been brought to their end. For this work requires a heart free from cares, from which episcopal duties [Col. 0247A] [Note: [Col. 0247C] That is, episcopal care. Thus the Ebr., Roth., and other MSS, not *episcopatus* (“bishopric”), as in the printed editions; likewise here, “we shall lay aside the bishop,” which seems to have greater force (*energeia*, ἐνεργεία).] have not freed us. Nevertheless, we have already completed part of them, and in order to accomplish what remains, we shall lay aside the bishop. When finished, the work will come into your hands, and there will be no need for your envoy to weary himself by coming all the way to us to carry it. It will be our duty to have it sent to you by our own messenger. Farewell.

## LETTER XXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0247C] Alternatively no. 50. Written about 1119.]

To Bishop Gerard [Note: [Col. 0247C] Certainly the bishop of Angoulême and then apostolic legate. Thus MS Reg. 4103.]

William of Longeio, or Lonleio, had communicated with a certain Hugh whom Gerard had excommunicated; as a result, he had fallen from Gerard’s favor. Yet through Hildebert’s mediation he had been restored to it. Fearing, however, that Gerard might not forget the forgiven injury and trouble William again, Hildebert urgently asks him to confirm the pardon granted.

It redounds to the glory of power not to avenge injuries when one is able to do so. Your fraternity, considering this in a sufficiently episcopal manner, [Col. 0247B] showed indulgence to William of Longeio [Note: [Col. 0247C] The same man mentioned in Letter 20. MS Ebr. 19 reads *de Lonlegio*; others, *de Lonleyo*.]. At the council of Angoulême [Note: [Col. 0247C] Held in the time of Gelasius II in 1118, according to Labbe.], acting on behalf of Hugh—your excommunicate—he sought Hugh’s favor and lost yours. Though through our intercession he has returned to it, nevertheless, because authority offended is always an object of suspicion, he still begs through us that he may be completely forgiven.

It will be clear that he has obtained this if the person whom he offended does not obstruct his advancement. Far be it from you to fly back so to the vengeance of a forgiven injury, when the person who is to forgive an injury from the heart must anticipate the setting sun. An offended yet merciful bishop sacrifices twice to God. A priest who remembers an injury inflicted differs little from a tyrant. Moreover, one who punishes an offense he has remitted persecutes an undeserving man.

But you have forgiven it; and this is your sign: at the aforesaid council you entrusted William to us [Note: [Col. 0247C] Hildebert was therefore present at this council, but was still bishop of Le Mans, since he was not raised to the see of Tours until 1125.], ordering him to make satisfaction to God, according to our decision, for having presumed to communicate with your excommunicate. Therefore, if the prayers of a friend avail anything with a friend, let William feel that every trace of resentment has been entirely banished from your heart; for he who was able to offend is able and willing to redeem his offense by devoted services. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIX

[Note: [Col. 0247D] Alternatively no. 55. Written about 1124. Moreover, from this letter—which properly is a letter dimissory—the student of ecclesiastical antiquity may observe that in Hildebert’s day the ancient use of dimissory letters and the former stability of clerics, established by ancient canons, had not yet disappeared. During the first eleven centuries, any bishop who first laid hands upon someone so claimed him for himself and his own church that he could neither be promoted to higher orders by another bishop nor enrolled in another church except by the express permission of the bishop who ordained him. “It has been decreed by synodal sentence,” says the Council of Turin, canon 7, “that no one receive a cleric of another, according to the statutes of the canons, nor dare to ordain him for his own church, even to a different rank.” The Council of Sardica had decreed the same, and many other conciliar enactments to this effect could be cited.

Nor is this surprising. Whoever ordained a cleric acquired him for himself and his church by the best right, and ordination itself was regarded as a title of acquisition. So much was this so that it was unlawful for the cleric, without the knowledge or against the will of the bishop who had first ordained him, to do anything concerning divine matters or even to set foot outside the diocese; and for another bishop thereafter to ordain him was like usurpation of another’s possession. Whenever, therefore, a bishop granted dimissory letters to his cleric so that he might be ordained by another bishop, he in effect manumitted that cleric and transferred to the other bishop all the authority and right that he had acquired in him through ordination.

The present letter of Hildebert provides an excellent example of this discipline. Hildebert had promoted his cleric William to the subdiaconate. Aymeric, bishop of Clermont, wished William to be ceded to him, so that he might ordain him deacon and enroll him in the Church of Clermont, to serve there as archdeacon. Hildebert, acceding to the bishop of Clermont’s wishes, writes him this dimissory letter, by which he transfers every right that he had acquired in William through ordination and grants Aymeric authority to promote him to the grade of deacon and the office of archdeacon.

You will find a similar letter from Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, to Aeneas, bishop of Paris, in vol. I of the *Councils of Gaul*, pp. 669–70. Hincmar had ordained a certain Berno. “Since,” Aeneas says in his letter to Hincmar, “we do not wish him to remain in our church for a long time without your permission, we ask you to issue canonical letters concerning him to us, so that we may lawfully ordain him in our church.” Replying with a dimissory letter, Hincmar grants Berno to Aeneas and transfers his right in him to Aeneas, so that Aeneas may ordain him in the Church of Paris. Such was the form of dimissory letters in those times, very different from that of today.

For, since for some centuries wandering and absolute ordinations without an ecclesiastical title have prevailed, and ordination no longer subjects the cleric to his ordaining bishop, a cleric is not now dismissed by his own bishop to receive ordination from another in such a way that he becomes subject to the latter’s authority and jurisdiction and is withdrawn from the former’s. Rather, by virtue of dimissory letters, the foreign bishop acquires no right over those ordained; after ordaining those sent to him, he is bound to return them to their own bishop.]

He congratulates the bishop of the Church of Clermont on conferring the archdeaconry upon the distinguished William. He also expresses surprise that hereditary succession to ecclesiastical and canonical dignities has become established there, and urges the bishop to root it out completely as wholly contrary to the precepts of law and grace.

[Col. 0248B]

To his most reverend and blessed [Note: [Col. 0248D] Printed editions: “most gracious”; manuscripts: “most blessed.”] fellow bishop A., [Col. 0249A] bishop of the holy Church of Clermont [Note: [Col. 0249D] Aymeric, raised from abbot of Chaise-Dieu to the see of the Church of Clermont; a pious man and a most devoted venerator of the Blessed Virgin.], the humble servant of the people of Le Mans sends greetings and the offering of his prayers.

You have run better than I: you have attained the prize toward which I was preparing to strive. I had resolved to benefit William of Longeio [Note: Thus the manuscripts Colbert 4017 and Victorine 272; Ebr. 19 reads *de Lonlegio*, and others *de Lonleyo*. This is the same man mentioned above in Letter 17 of this book.]; but, by the providence of the Lord Jesus Christ, you enabled that same William to hear something better from yourselves: “Friend, go up higher” (Luke 14:10). Sound indeed was the counsel by which that man was appointed archdeacon in the Church of Clermont: knowledge abounds in him for usefulness, and character for grace. His birth is neither in need of legal remedy—that is, he is legitimate—nor is his family lowly. [Note: “Not in need of legal remedy” means legitimate; for a defect of birth in illegitimate or spurious persons must be remedied by law, that is, by an ecclesiastical dispensation, if they are to be admitted to orders.] No stigma has therefore clung to the young man, no embarrassment from obscurity of origin. Those who have known him more intimately in daily intercourse declare that his inward disposition is gentle and his outward conduct honourable. [Col. 0249B] This is a complete and splendid testimony. Accordingly, I caused him to be promoted to the rank of subdeacon, yielding no more to his learning than to his life. I have good hope that he will show himself a vessel for honour, prepared in the house of the Lord for every good work.
