I therefore thank your blessedness for the benefit conferred; and I yield the same William to you and to your Church, wholly free and released from the obedience he owes to his consecrator. It is more than enough to intercede with you on behalf of one whom you have voluntarily made not merely some member of the body of the Church, but an eye. Yet we have heard—and have been amazed beyond what can be believed—that canonries are held in your mother church by hereditary right. This is a pernicious and disinheriting inheritance. [Col. 0249C] A canonry is a stipend of grace, not a profit of inheritance. Grace perishes where inheritance rules. Thus to become a canon by inheritance is to depart from the Church, not to enter it. For those who say, “Let us possess the sanctuary of God by inheritance” (Psalm 82:13), are neither heirs of God nor co-heirs of Jesus Christ.

Woe to them when the Judge sits with the rulers of the earth! Woe, I say, to those whom then—not words, but blows—will teach that they lived not from the altar, but from plunder! For it is a veiled robbery when things belonging to election are claimed as inherited. Yet anyone is mistaken who says that bishops alone are to be chosen by election. Under both law and grace, election concerns every dignity of the sanctuary. God himself chose Moses; and Moses, by the Lord’s command, chose seventy men from the elders of Israel. Surely it has not escaped you that the Lord spoke thus to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men whom you know to be elders and teachers of the people; [Col. 0250A] bring them to the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant, and make them stand there with you, that I may descend and speak with you, and take from your spirit and give to them, so that they may bear the burden of the people with you and you may not be burdened alone” (Numbers 11:16).

Then, what sort of priests were to be chosen, and from which tribe; likewise Levites and all others who were to serve the tabernacle—this was a matter not of discretion but of command, not of inheritance but of law. For although the Lord deemed the tribe of Levi alone worthy of this lot (Numbers 3:17), nevertheless no one from that tribe was permitted to force his way at will or indiscriminately into whatever dignity he pleased; rather, the proper qualifications of those to be called were prescribed. Yet all these things, as the Apostle writes, happened to them as figures (1 Corinthians 10:11). The Law was both a proclamation and an example of grace.

Hence [Col. 0250B] all the dignities of the Church require their proper election. If we consider the apostles, the Lord says of them: “Have I not chosen you twelve?” (John 6:71). If the seventy-two, Luke records that they too were appointed by Christ (Luke 10:1). No one doubts that the apostles chose Stephen and the six deacons with him (Acts 6:5). In these men and in their successors the form prescribed for the Church is set forth; and failure to preserve it in the election or consecration of high and lower priests, and also of deacons, is a sign of decline brought about by accident and close to ruin. Canonical institutions likewise judge and declare that the remaining ranks, down to the lowest cleric, are to be appointed and assigned, examined and reformed, at the deliberation of bishops. [Col. 0250C]

This power, bestowed by the Lord upon bishops alone, perishes if inheritance gives anyone authority to appoint a canon or to dispose of anything in the Church. What, indeed, will be permitted to a bishop in the Church entrusted to him, if a cleric is appointed at another’s discretion? What force can sacred enactments have there, where a canon is born rather than made; where more is owed to marriage than to merit, to birth than to grace, to the forum than to heaven? Will he offer a sacrifice pleasing to God who assigns the altar to the marriage-bed; whose priesthood is promised by birth rather than character, by kinship rather than learning, by a layman begetting rather than a bishop adopting? Who would not be moved that a layman rules in the Church of Christ, when, by appointing therein a canon as heir, [Col. 0250D] he nullifies the bishop’s freedom?

That no authority has ever granted laymen any access to the disposal of ecclesiastical property, Pope and martyr Stephen shows in these words:

> “To laymen, even though they are religious, no power of disposing in any way of ecclesiastical resources is ever found to have been granted; nor do we permit this henceforth. If, therefore, any lay prince claims for himself the disposal or lordship of ecclesiastical goods or possessions, let him be judged sacrilegious. Clerics or monks who receive them through the power of such persons shall be subject to excommunication.”

[Note: This passage is extremely intricate and not easily unravelled. Hildebert cites a decretal falsely attributed to Stephen the martyr and fabricated by Isidore Mercator. Nor does Hildebert report it accurately: its opening words, “To laymen,” are found among the spurious letters of this pope, but the subsequent words, “If anyone,” are not found there. Gratian, 16, question 7, canon “If any prince,” attributes them to Callistus, although they are not found even in that pontiff’s false decretals. It thus happened that Hildebert used the collection of decretals dishonestly fabricated by Isidore—a fate shared by him, by almost all writers of that age, and even by Ivo of Chartres.]

To wish to uphold by custom that hereditary appointment of canons is either to be ignorant of, or to persecute, the tenor of the holy rules. They do not wish to abolish a harmful custom and render void a practice that has neither authority nor reason in its support. Augustine says of this in the fourth book *On Baptism* [Note: Namely chapter 5 of the new edition, p. 124.]: 

> “In vain do some, who are overcome by reason, allege custom against us, as though custom were greater than truth, or as though in spiritual matters we ought not to follow what has been revealed for the better by the Holy Spirit.”

[Col. 0251B]

The same author, in the fourth book *On the One Baptism*:

> “Once truth has been made manifest, let custom yield to truth. Surely who can doubt that custom ought to yield to manifest truth?”

[Note: The same reference.]

The same author, in *On Baptism*:

> “In the Gospel the Lord says, ‘I am the truth’ (John 14:6). He did not say, ‘I am custom.’ Therefore, once truth has been revealed, let error yield to truth; for Peter too, who practised circumcision, yielded to Paul preaching truth.”

Therefore, since Christ is truth, we ought to follow truth rather than custom; for reason and truth always exclude custom. Cyprian says on the same subject:

> “Any custom, however ancient or widespread, must altogether yield to truth; and a practice contrary to truth must be abolished.”

[Note: In St Cyprian, at the Council of Carthage concerning the baptism of heretics, the sixty-third episcopal judgment reads: “In receiving heretics without the baptism of the Church, let no one prefer custom to reason and truth; for reason and truth always exclude custom.” Oxford edition, p. 240. Hildebert here gives Cyprian’s sense rather than his exact words, drawing on the holy martyr’s letters to Pompey and Jubaianus.]

Isidore, in the second book of the *Synonyms*, says:

> “Let practice yield to authority. Let law and reason overcome a wrongful practice.”

[Note: Chapter 16, where the text reads: “Many things have been corrupted by custom; many things rashly assumed through perverse usage … Remove custom; preserve the law. Let custom yield to authority. Let law and reason overcome wrongful practice.” From this Gratian introduced into the canon, Distinction II: “Let practice yield to authority; wrongful practice,” etc.]

Since, therefore, so much authority opposes a harmful custom, it is incumbent upon you, most blessed bishop, to remove from the house of the Lord this sacrilegious hereditary abuse. A bishop’s negligence in acting against it turns to the bishop’s punishment. For it is a judicial offence in the Church of Christ either to presume something improperly or to leave uncorrected what one finds improperly presumed. Uzzah, while rendering unlawful assistance to the tottering Ark, was struck down by an angel and died [Col. 0251D] (1 Kings 15). Fire went forth from before the Lord and devoured Nadab and Abihu, sons of Aaron, because, having taken up censers, they presumed to offer strange fire (Numbers 54). Sacred history records that Uzziah, because he usurped the prerogative of the high priest, was struck with leprosy [Col. 0252A] (1 Chronicles 2). Korah and those who took up censers of schism with him are remembered as descended from the tribe of Levi; nevertheless, because they offered incense improperly, the earth swallowed them alive (Numbers 16).

Let the censers taken from the fire remain fixed in your minds, dearest brothers—censers which the Lord commanded to be attached to the altar as a memorial, lest anyone in the Church arrogate to himself what was not due. For it is no less useful to recount the punishments of wrongdoing than the rewards of virtue. Certainly punishment produces fear, which makes from a slave even a son; and, if a son, then an heir—an heir indeed of God and a co-heir of Jesus Christ. Remember, brothers, to fear with this fear: while you make the Church a possession of the secular forum, you build upon grace a structure of debt, [Col. 0252B] for which no foundation has been laid. You build upon sand, dearest brothers.

[Note: This letter was therefore written not to Aymeric alone, but to the entire clergy of the Church of Clermont.]

By the testimony of Truth, this structure of yours is promised ruin. By the testimony of Truth, “the rain will descend, the floods will come, the winds will blow and rush upon the building; and it will fall, and its fall will be great” (Luke 6:49). Do not, children, do not place your portion with those who said, “Let us possess the sanctuary of God by inheritance” (Psalm 82:13). The God of vengeance will pursue them in his tempest, and in his wrath will trouble them.

[Col. 0252C]

Your own danger also, most reverend bishop—your own, I say—is at stake, unless you labour to uproot the planting which our heavenly Father did not plant (Matthew 15), and which has not been taken from the tree whose leaf shall not fall and whatever it does shall prosper (Psalm 1:4). This planting is a deadly planting, no more destructive to its planter than to him through whose negligence, once planted, it has taken root. For no one is free from guilt who, when able, does not correct his predecessor’s wrongdoing. Pope Hilary says of this:

> “What anyone has committed unlawfully, or has found done by his predecessors, he shall condemn, if he wishes to avoid danger to himself.”

Again, the same author says:

> “We wish to exercise severity in no matter; but whoever sins in the causes of God through obstinacy or any transgression, or himself refuses to abolish what his predecessor did wrongly, will find in himself whatever he did not cut away in another.”

Moreover, should anyone attempt—by obstinacy or any audacity, which may it never be—to restrain [Col. 0252D] your uprooting hand, he himself will experience the punishment due to sacrilege. For Pope Stephen writes of such persons:

> “There are some who, either by violence or by favour, do not permit churches [Col. 0253A] to be regularly ordered. We decree that these too are to be judged sacrilegious.”

We have written these things to you, dearest brothers, more for exhortation than instruction. While writing them, we prayed to him who searches hearts and reins that he would not allow you to decline into the opinion of attributing to boasting what has been offered in charity. My soul is free from this offence, although it does not dare deny that it is liable to graver sins. You will repay me in kind if you love me and pray for me.

## LETTER XXX

[Note: Alternatively 65. Written in the year 1127. See the *Life of Hildebert*, p. 36 ff. This letter appears in Labbe’s *Councils*, vol. X, as does the following confirmation by Honorius. Apart from these two letters, nothing else concerning this Council of Nantes is found in any editions of the Councils.]

### TO HONORIUS, SUPREME PONTIFF

Shortly after his translation from the bishopric of Le Mans to the archbishopric of Tours, Hildebert, endeavouring to root out various abuses discovered in Armorica among those subject to him as metropolitan, assembled a council at Nantes in 1127 with his suffragan bishops. He earnestly requests confirmation of its statutes from Honorius, supreme pontiff.

[Col. 0253B]

To your blessedness, most reverend Father, we have resolved to write that, at the urging of the venerable Count of Brittany and with the joint counsel of the bishops of the province, we went down into Brittany. There, besides other manifold and abhorrent enormities, marriages were polluted by incest, and the sanctuary of the Lord by hereditary succession. Therefore, having summoned the same bishops and abbots, together with many religious and wise men, we sat for three days in the city of Nantes, celebrating a synod there. By the Lord’s bounty, from it there is known to have arisen both honour for the Church and great benefit for the people. [Col. 0253C]

For until the day of the said assembly, such had been the custom in the count’s land that, upon the death of a husband or wife, all the movable goods of the deceased passed into the ownership of the governing power. Moreover, whatever escaped from shipwreck was wholly claimed by the fiscal law of the land; and those who had suffered shipwreck were despoiled more miserably by the violence of the prince than by the plunder of the sea or the storm. Before the eyes of the whole council, the count renounced both exactions into our hand, asking that the sword of excommunication be extended against any who should ever attempt either to reclaim what had been relinquished or to diminish the fullness of that relinquishment. Thus he made full confession, followed the benefit with thanksgiving, and pursued with anathema anyone who diminished that benefit.

Concerning incestuous marriages, the entire assembly agreed that bishops in all their gatherings, and other priests in their churches, should publicly prohibit the contracting of such marriages; and that they should subject to excommunication all who, after the present act of the synod, knowingly entered into the bonds of incestuous wedlock.

[Note: Something similar had been established at the Council of Poitiers in 1100: namely, that sons of priests and others born in fornication should not be promoted to sacred orders unless they became monks or lived regularly in a canonical community; in no case, however, were they to hold prelacies. Chapter I, “On the Age and Qualification of Those to Be Ordained.” Baronius, under the year 1100.]

All likewise agreed, in order to strike fear into others, [Col. 0254A] that children thereafter born from such intercourse should be regarded as illegitimate, and that the paternal right should pass to legitimate heirs. Further, in celebrating ordinations we ordered canonical enactments to be carefully considered and observed without offence. With our joint consent, the synod prohibited the ordination of priests’ sons unless they first became regular canons or monks. As for those already known to have been ordained, in order to abolish succession we deprived them of the faculty of ministering in the churches where their fathers had ministered. It was prohibited, with the strictness fitting the matter, for prebends and any ecclesiastical dignities to be acquired by inheritance. Other provisions of this kind were added; the present synod both gave assent to them as proceeding from canonical institutions and decreed that they be observed. [Col. 0254B]

We therefore judged it right to report these matters to you, holy Father, so that your authority may deign to confirm what has been canonically enacted, and, by letters sent to the bishops, exhort all together that what we have decreed must be done and taught with them in Christ, they too may strive to do and teach with Christ. Moreover, do not hesitate to strengthen by apostolic confirmation the relinquishment concerning shipwrecks and the property of the dying which the count made into our hand; and forbid anyone whatever to presume to rescind it or diminish it in any respect. May the Lord preserve you for the Church, holy Father.

## LETTER XXXI

[Note: Alternatively 66. Written in 1127.]

By this letter Honorius II, supreme pontiff, confirms everything which he had learned from the preceding letter had been done at the Council of Nantes by Hildebert and his suffragans.

[Col. 0254C]

**HONORIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother suffragan bishops of the metropolitan church of Tours: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Dearest brothers, Hildebert, archbishop of Tours, watching as a good shepherd over his flock, assembled wise brethren and other religious men and, as we have learned from examination of his letter, celebrated a council in the city of Nantes according to metropolitan custom. There he dealt with incestuous marriages, the illegitimate sons of priests, and those seeking ecclesiastical benefices as though by hereditary succession; he corrected what required correction and established what required establishment. We therefore command all of you to observe without objection the things known to have been established there by him, according to the decrees of the holy Fathers, for the honour of God and the salvation of the people.

For as the members in the frame of the human body serve and obey the head as their supreme director and provider, so that the person may remain unharmed, [Col. 0255A] so the minds of the faithful, of one will [variant: of one effectual will], ought humbly to obey their prelates for the preservation of the unity of faith and the order of the Church.

Furthermore, we condemn those wicked customs which the Count of Brittany repudiated into the hand of the aforesaid archbishop in the sight of the synod: one by which, upon the death of husbands or wives, their movable goods were seized by secular authority; the other by which those who had escaped shipwreck were afterwards plundered even in harbour. By apostolic authority we forbid anyone to presume to revive them in future times. For we judge it unjust that a person whom the greatness of divine mercy has delivered from the devouring violence of the raging sea should be despoiled by the cruel rapacity of men. The authority of pious emperors has gone forth even to provide that ownership is not lost of things cast into the sea in a storm to lighten a ship. For no one casts them away with the intention of not wishing to possess them, but in order to escape danger; and whoever takes those things with the intention of gain commits theft.

Given at the Lateran, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June.

## LETTER XXXII

[Note: Alternatively 18. Written about 1127.]

Hildebert intercedes with Pope Honorius II on behalf of the canons of Saint Martin, who had incurred his displeasure while defending the rights of their church.

It is declared by no few privileges how much the Roman pontiffs have granted to the Church of Blessed Martin [Note: Indeed, by very many privileges; for several supreme pontiffs honoured that royal church, distinguished by the tomb of Saint Martin, while it was still regular and monastic observance flourished there under the Rule of Saint Benedict. But when canons succeeded the monks, they took the greatest care that they might enjoy the privileges formerly granted to the monks by supreme pontiffs and kings of the Franks. This was granted them, so that to this day they freely enjoy them without opposition. On these matters see R. P. Badier, in his French work *On the Holiness of the Monastic State*, where he treats most learnedly and fully of the privileges of the basilica of Saint Martin of Tours. The principal privilege—immunity from episcopal jurisdiction—was granted about the year 668 by Chrotbert, archbishop of Tours. It was then confirmed about 672 by Pope Adeodatus; and Ibbo, about 720, ratified and enlarged it, as our most learned Mabillon notes in his *Diplomatica*, book VI, no. 35, p. 487.], and how great a liberty they have provided. While the canons of that church were striving, with due reverence for you, to preserve it, perhaps they went too far; and, seeking to maintain their own dignity, they detracted from that of another. Their transgression, most holy Father, I neither vindicate, excuse, nor diminish; for even a slight error turns to judgment when Rome is offended. Yet charity universally requires us to plead for pardon if a brother falls into fault.

Charity therefore compelled us to knock at the door of mercy and to intercede for brothers before Peter, who is commanded to forgive seventy times seven if offended that many times (Matthew 18:22). Yet, as the aforesaid canons testify, nothing was presumed against apostolic majesty; nothing that is not defended by authentic privileges. If these have acquired stability either through the authority of those granting them or through passage of time, [Col. 0255D] we ask that the mother not withdraw from the daughter the grace she granted for peace. For freedom bestowed upon the confessor does not diminish the dignity of the apostle. Nor do we seek to honour Martin in such a way as to trample Peter underfoot.

But if the aforesaid privileges defend themselves insufficiently, let the Father spare his sons and mercifully forgive what was committed through ignorance. May the Lord preserve your holiness for us, and may your prayers prepare for us a way whereby we may be granted to come with a favourable outcome before the thresholds of the apostles.

## LETTER XXXIII

[Note: Alternatively 75. Written about 1128. See his *Life*.]

In this letter, apparently a circular because it is directed to no one by name, Hildebert complains that he has been harassed in various ways by the King of France over the rights of the Church, and abandoned by all without aid or consolation—especially by those who were bound by office to defend both him and the Church. Yet he considers that what is just should be represented to the king not harshly or stubbornly, but calmly and with the reverence due to royal dignity. He further declares that amid his afflictions he will cast his care upon the Lord, in whom, as in the cases of Joseph and David, he will never despair of help.

[Col. 0256B]

In adversity there is no small consolation in hoping for happier times. For a long time this hope has soothed me; and as a harvest still in the blade sustains the farmer, so expectation of prosperity strengthened my spirit. But now there is nothing by which I can await a clearing of stormy weather, nothing by which the ship at whose stern I sit, tossed by repeated tempests, may reach the harbour of rest. Friends are silent; priests of Jesus Christ are silent. Indeed, silent too are those through whose assistance I believed the king would be reconciled with me. I did believe it; but while they were silent, the king added to the pain of my wounds. Yet it belonged to them to oppose the burden laid upon the Church by canonical institutions. [Col. 0256C] It belonged to them, if the matter required it, to stand as a wall for the house of Israel.

But with the most serene king, exhortation is needed rather than rebuke, counsel rather than command, instruction rather than a rod. He ought to have been approached by such means and reverently instructed: not to spend his arrows upon an aged priest; not to annul canonical enactments; not to persecute the ashes of a Church already buried—ashes amid which I eat the bread of sorrow, drink the cup of mourning, and from which to be snatched away and escape, to pass from death to life. Yet amid these straits anger has never so triumphed over me that I wished to raise any outcry against the Lord’s anointed, or to seek his peace through a strong hand and the arm of the Church. Peace is suspect [Col. 0256D] when high powers come to it not by love but by force. Such peace will easily be broken, and sometimes the latter condition becomes worse than the former.

There is another way by which, with Christ leading, I may more swiftly attain it. “I will cast [Col. 0257A] my care upon the Lord, and he will grant me the petition of my heart” (Psalm 54:23). The Lord remembered Joseph, for the cupbearer of Pharaoh, when prosperity came to him, forgot and abandoned the task of interceding for Joseph. He also remembered David his servant, whom, though abandoned even by his own son, he raised with triumphs and exalted with the glory of the kingdom. Perhaps he will remember me also and bring my storm-tossed ship to rest on the desired shore. For he is the one “who regards the prayer of the humble and does not despise their prayers” (Psalm 102:8). He is the one in whose hand the hearts of kings are wax. Wherever he pleases, he alone bends and raises them into whatever form he wills. If I find grace in his eyes, I shall either readily obtain the king’s favour or usefully lose it [variant: attain it]. [Col. 0257B] For to offend a human being on account of God is to gain God’s favour.

## LETTER XXXIV

[Note: Newly published from the *Spicilegium* and manuscripts. Written about 1128. See the Preface.]

He beseeches the apostolic legate [Note: Gerard of Angoulême, then legate of Honorius II throughout Gaul.] to endeavour to reconcile him with the King of France, from whom he has suffered much for the rights of the Church.

At your arrival, most blessed bishop, my spirit rejoiced with great joy, clothing itself in gladness and exultation. For in it hope has been raised for me that the indignation of the most excellent King of the Franks against me may be softened—a king whose favour I lost while zealously maintaining the law of the Lord. When, by command of the Roman pontiff, I had moved from the bishopric of Le Mans to the metropolitan see of Tours, I found its archdeaconry and deanery vacant. [Col. 0257C] Then, after I had spent nearly a year in that metropolitan church, I received the king’s letters, stating that the king had bestowed the aforesaid offices and ordering me not to delay placing in the seats of those dignities the persons to whom he had given them.

Upon hearing this, I was unwilling, in the cause of God, to obey authority against God, knowing that it is better to obey God rather than human beings. Yet, considering that the king ought to be approached and warned to refrain from such conduct, I went to him. But I found the Lord’s anointed inexorable. I found him hardened more than befitted the Lord’s anointed. Finally, carrying back no good hope from him, I accepted a day for dealing with him. On the appointed day and at the appointed place, I appeared before those assembled, ready to answer the charges and undergo canonical judgment. Afterwards, when the cause of both sides had been heard and I was still awaiting the judgment due, the king himself forbade me either to undertake or to order anything concerning the revenues of the aforesaid dignities.

In vain I offered prayers; in vain I advanced many arguments showing that even an authority angered by manifest wrongs ought to relent. Let me be charged with falsehood unless the venerable bishop of Angers, and more than a few priests with him, bear witness for me that I was ready to carry out the judgment; that I submitted myself to the judgment of those who had no authority to judge me. [Col. 0258A] Finally, after I had departed from the king, a messenger followed me to say that the king had declared that the revenues of the possessions of the Church of Tours, so far as royal power could reach them, were not to be brought to the aforesaid church but were henceforth to be entered in the fisc and applied to royal uses. This was done. His territory too is so unsafe for me that I dare not enter it.

Yet I say this not as one raising an outcry before you against the Lord’s anointed, nor as one demanding the severity of ecclesiastical discipline. I pray that aid be given to the Church and to me through your intervention, and that the king be charitably urged [Col. 0258B] not to spend his arrows upon an aged priest, not to rise against the enactments of the holy Fathers, not to persecute the ashes of a Church already buried—ashes amid which I eat the bread of sorrow and drink the cup of mourning, and from which I earnestly desire to be summoned by the Lord, whom I implore with prayers.

I had indeed greatly desired to meet your holiness, but the king’s anger impeded my desire. Yet, as has been communicated to me, you must cross to England and carry out the legation entrusted to your prudence. If this is so, I have resolved to meet you in Normandy, if you will deign to inform me of a day and place, in order to speak with you about certain affairs entrusted to me by the Roman Church. I therefore beseech you both to specify this to me in sealed letters [Col. 0258C] and to endeavour to soften toward my innocence the king’s indignation which I incurred in defending justice.

## LETTER XXXV

[Note: Newly published from the *Spicilegium* and manuscripts. It appears to have been written about 1128. [Letter 35 is falsely stated to have been given in 1128; it was written after the death of Baldric, bishop of Dol, who died in January 1130.] See the *Life of Hildebert*.]

Hildebert petitions the supreme pontiff not to grant the pallium and its use to the bishops of Dol, his suffragans, since it had most recently been granted personally only to the now-dead Baldric by the pope, and not to the Church of Dol.

It is just that those who have repaid neither the first nor the second benefit with thanks should lose hope of further benefits. Therefore, because I have not rendered you the thanks I owed for former benefits, I have less hope for those to come. Yet your kindness gives me reason to hope, since it is your custom to do good even to the ungrateful. Moreover, your prudence is not unaware that one is pardonably ungrateful if, though unable to repay his benefactor, he has a full will to repay.

Although, therefore, I fear to be accused of ingratitude, I nevertheless still cry out after the Lord’s anointed, after my father; thus I lay before you the tears of the Church of Tours. Baldric, bishop of the Church of Dol, [Col. 0259A] has died. The Western Church is by no means ignorant that he held the pallium improperly. The catalogue of pontifical churches likewise teaches this, making no mention at all of the Church of Dol. It is therefore evident upon careful consideration that all Brittany is contained within the boundaries of the Church of Tours. Yet I do not revive any complaint to be argued on this matter, which religious persons know and testify to have long ago been decided in the Roman Church.

The venerable privilege granted by Pope Urban to the metropolitan church of Tours testifies to this very fact: it recognizes all Brittany as subject to it as its metropolitan, and declares that the pallium was granted not as a prerogative to the Church of Dol but to an individual person. Therefore I, together with the whole Church of Tours, beseech you to have regard [Col. 0259B] for what is due to the aforesaid metropolitan see and to deign to restore its dignity. We shall rightly understand ourselves to have been heard in this matter if you either wholly deny the use of the pallium to the bishop to be elected in that see or appoint a day for us and him to plead the cause.

Moreover, I have resolved to add to the foregoing prayers the request that the bishop of Angers, a man of God and an example of Christian religion, may find you gracious in his cause. We believe that he seeks not what belongs to another, but claims for the Church what is its own. Furthermore, we do not wish your holiness to be unaware that Stephen of Montsoreau has now died, but that Dean Ralph remains, to whom your sublimity had appointed a day for dealing with the aforesaid Stephen at the thresholds of the apostles—unless your mercy should decide that he must be spared and released from the labour of crossing the Alps. [Col. 0259C] Deign to make known by your letters to us and to him, as your most humble son, what pleases your holiness regarding this petition.

## LETTER XXXVI

[Note: Newly published from the *Spicilegium* and manuscripts. Written in 1128. See the *Life*.]

He informs Honorius II, supreme pontiff, of the grave affront cruelly and shamefully inflicted upon his canon; explains what he has done in the matter; and asks the supreme pontiff what he considers ought next to be done.

We do not doubt that the outrage inflicted upon our canon by the cutting off of his limbs has reached your ears. Concerning this outrage, when the mutilated man himself [Note: [Col. 0259D] Not a cutting off of the genitals, as some have thought probable; but, as M. Maan asserts in his *Metropolis of Tours*, the gouging out of the eyes—although in this and in the following letter *abscissio*, “cutting off,” is expressly and emphatically used, though it is not said which member.] lodged a complaint before us against certain persons, saying that the aforesaid injury had been inflicted upon him by their counsel and contrivance, we appointed them a day [for hearing]. Both parties appeared together, accuser and accused. But since the accuser declined to undergo judgment and sought a delaying appeal, while we were unwilling to communicate with the accused unless they first cleared themselves of the outrage done to us and to the whole Church, we received the exculpation of each under the oath of seven lawful persons. Furthermore, let your sublimity know that we are exercising the gravest justice upon those who laid hands upon the canon and presumed to mutilate him, and that we have repeatedly [a word, perhaps “resolved,” is missing] entreated the count, so that we may obtain justice concerning them. We deferred answering him until we should have your counsel on the matter. For the matter is most grave, and the greatest caution must be exercised so that others may be deterred from similar acts.

There are, however, those who say that the mutilated man himself must prove the injury against the wrongdoers. Those who think thus adhere to the judgment which the Council of Chartres [Note: [Col. 0260D] Held in 1128, according to Labbe.] pronounced, on the authority of letters of Pope Calixtus, concerning the viscount of Le Mans and Lisiard. It was there judged that the viscount himself, who complained that the men of Lisiard had dragged him from the wall of a certain church—to whose wall the viscount, after escaping from captivity, had clung while rising up toward the church—must prove by touching hot iron that he had been violently pulled away from that wall by Lisiard’s men. [Note: [Col. 0260D] Observe the right of sanctuary, so proper to churches that it extended even to places and buildings adjoining them.]

## LETTER XXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0260D] Also 68. Written in the same year as the preceding letter, concerning the same affair.]

Hildebert reports that, at the recommendation of the supreme pontiff, he restored a prebend to one Bracerius, who had lost it through the enormity of his offense, after he had done penance. At the same time he informs him what he himself has again done in the case of Radulf, dean, and Nicholas, canon, and what Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the Roman Church, has determined concerning it; and he asks him at last to set the finishing hand, by apostolic authority, to this affair, which had grievously disturbed the Church of Tours itself.

To his most holy Father and supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, HONORIUS, by the grace of God, HILDEBERT, [Col. 0260C] humble servant of Tours, the preservation of unbroken obedience.

Most blessed Father, what your graciousness requested of us has been done. For apostolic intervention restored to Bracerius the prebend which he had lost through the enormity of his offenses. Radulf also, dean of Saint Maurice, has undertaken the journey to you, secure in conscience, though not secure in the road; guided by God, not by man. If, by God’s favor, he reaches your hearing, you will know that he is troubled not by his own guilt, but rather by the hatred and accusations of certain young men—men of whom it is doubtful whether by their misdeeds they have more damaged their own reputation, or by their slanders that of others. It is for this reason that they persecute the dean’s reputation without cause: men who were unwilling, even when asked, to spare their own.

Yet the deanery was so bestowed upon that dean by us in chapter, and he was so installed in office, that no one at all opposed this promotion of his either in word or in deed. All sat peaceably at the table of the appointed meal and rose with thanksgiving. For some time, while the dean was acting, both obedience in its integrity and the power of discipline were accorded him. But the rashness of a certain Fulk, the dean’s brother, diminished this respect toward him. Nicholas was captured and mutilated by him and through him.

Concerning this mutilation—on account of which Nicholas accused the dean—and concerning the fact that the dean, with six venerable persons joined to him, [Note: [Col. 0261D] See what it means to swear “with the seventh hand” in the note to the following letter.] declared his innocence by oath, your Blessedness has already been truthfully informed by examination of our letters. You have further learned that the venerable bishop of Le Mans was present at the judgment, as were several abbots and other religious and learned men. All of these applied themselves earnestly to ensure that they should not soften the judge’s sentence through indulgence, but should follow the rigor of canonical discipline.

Although these things had thus been done, the envy of certain persons toward the dean did not rest. Since they find no matter for delay in him, they invent it themselves. Such are the people for whom it is more elegant to be condemned for lying than to earn the reward due to truth. When, moreover, it had reached your ears that, because of the outrage inflicted upon Nicholas, grave discord existed among the canons and the Church’s divine office was lacking, you ordered Lord Gerard, legate of the Roman Church, to come as far as Tours to restore peace there. When Nicholas and the friends of the dean were granted a hearing, each conducted his own case according to the accusation brought against him. Then judgment was pronounced, according to the custom of the province; and Nicholas, complaining that he was oppressed by it, appealed to the vigilance of apostolic examination. Thus the matter remained undecided between Nicholas and those against whom Nicholas had appealed.

While the bishops who had assembled to judge the case were still sitting, the legate, by authority of the apostolic see, commanded that if any canon had a complaint either against the dean or against anyone else, he should bring it forward publicly and receive, concerning his complaint, whatever justice might dictate. When the legate repeated this specifically in the case of the dean and Bido, no one whatever was found to acknowledge that he had anything against them. It therefore pleased the legate, the bishops of Le Mans and Rennes, and likewise our own humility, that none of those who, though ordered to state anything they had against the dean or Bido, had kept silent, should thereafter be admitted to accuse either of them.

Thus, now twice decided was Nicholas’s complaint against the dean and Bido. The legate carefully urged the canons to return to the unity of peace, each to show due respect to each according to his rank, and to live in the house of the Lord in such a way that equality of spirit might unite those whom distinction of rank divided. For this to be accomplished, most blessed Father, it is necessary that you set the finishing hand to the aforesaid affair. [Note: [Col. 0261D] The pontiff does not appear to have done so; for while Radulf the dean was traveling to Rome to plead his case, he was murdered—according to suspicion, by his adversaries. See the *Life*.]

## LETTER XXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0262D] Also 67. Written in the same year as the preceding letter and on the same affair.]

He again complains before the supreme pontiff that he is variously harassed by the king of the Franks, chiefly because, on account of their incapacity, he provided his Church, by episcopal right, with a different dean and a different archdeacon from those whom the king had nominated. He further relates what he did in the dispute between Radulf the dean and Nicholas the canon, who, as Nicholas alleged, had been shamefully mutilated by the dean’s brother and at the dean’s counsel.

[Col. 0262A]

To HONORIUS, his most reverend Father by the grace of God and supreme pontiff of the holy Roman see, HILDEBERT, humble archbishop of Tours, the integrity of due obedience.

I do not think, venerable Father, that your Holiness is unaware by what storms of tribulation the Church of Tours is agitated. For the king of the Franks still pursues my innocence with such zeal that he turns personal hatred into an injury to the Church. Indeed, he has taken from the aforesaid Church the court of Saint Maurice and has entered in the fisc what is clearly sanctuary property. His whole land is also suspect and closed to me and to those who are with me in the household, so that neither I nor any one of them dares set foot in it.

I am pressed by these and other straits because I have been jealous with zeal for the law of the Lord God; because I have not crossed the boundaries established by our fathers; because I have neither disposed of ecclesiastical dignities by the king’s command nor granted him the power of disposing of them. For, knowing that one must obey God rather than men, I first chose men who would bear the burden and heat of the day in carrying out the Church’s affairs. Therefore I gave the archdeaconry to one and the deanery to another. There was no one at all who objected to the man whom I promoted as dean, either when he was promoted or when he was installed in office. All had his favor, and he had that of all.

Later it happened that the dean, by virtue of his office, corrected with ecclesiastical discipline certain canons who were under the rod on account of their shameful speech and outrageous deeds requiring restraint. Taking this very badly, those same canons burned with implacable hatred against him. This hatred was greatly increased by a certain quarrel raised between the same canons and the dean’s brothers, which progressed from words to a brawl. On the occasion of this affair, and also to escape discipline, the aforesaid canons left their own church and went over to the king of the Franks, whose wrath against the dean they knew to be implacable, heaping his indignation upon him by every accusation [variant: “slander”] they could devise.

After they had left the king, one of them, named Nicholas, was captured by a brother of the dean and mutilated with the help of others, both brothers of that dean and friends. When the mutilated brother laid before me his lamentable complaint, he added that he also made an accusation against the dean, saying that he had been mutilated by the cutting off of his limbs at the dean’s instigation and counsel, and that he had been seized and mutilated by the dean’s violence. Nicholas also charged another canon, named Herbert, with having inflicted the injury upon him under like suspicion.

I assigned a suitable day to each accuser and each accused, on which, having summoned religious and competent persons, I would, with the Lord’s help, settle the case canonically. All appeared on the appointed day. All conducted their case in this manner. The man who spoke for Nicholas said that Nicholas had been mutilated at the dean’s instigation and counsel, but that Nicholas himself would by no means undergo judgment. To this the dean replied: “It was done neither at my instigation, nor by my counsel, nor even by my will that Nicholas should be mutilated. But in order that I might clear myself of the crime alleged against me and demonstrate my innocence, I have entered the present assembly at the summons of my archbishop, ready willingly to perform whatever may canonically be judged against me. Therefore, whether Nicholas postpones undergoing judgment or abandons it altogether, I nevertheless offer to the Church and to my archbishop the exculpation which the canonical sanctions prescribe.”

Having said this, the other man charged under a similar count pursued his case with a similar answer. It was then asked whether Nicholas had any witnesses against the accused. But none at all was found; none was named. Therefore it was judged that, although the dean need not undergo judgment for Nicholas, who for certain delaying reasons sought to defer judgment, he must nevertheless clear himself for the Church and declare his innocence by oath with the seventh hand of his order. [Note: [Col. 0263D] That is, with six priests beyond every exception in standing, who together with him attest his innocence by oath. On this manner in which, in former times, accused persons cleared themselves when witnesses were lacking, see Ivo of Chartres, Letter 206, to Hildebert himself, and Du Cange, *Glossarium Latinum*, under *Manus*, where he explains what it means to swear with the third, fourth, seventh, and even twelfth hand.] This was done accordingly. By the same judgment Herbert likewise furnished a similar exculpation in his own order. I have written this to you, holy Father, so that if anyone reports anything else to your Holiness concerning the aforesaid affair, you may know the truth itself.

## LETTER XXXIX

[Note: [Col. 0263D] New from the *Spicilegium* and certain manuscripts. Written about 1128.]

Hildebert earnestly commends Radulf, dean of Tours, to his friend, [Note: [Col. 0263D] This Radulf, while making for Rome to clear himself before the supreme pontiff of the accusation brought by the mutilated canon Nicholas, was murdered on the road. Suspicion of his destruction fell not without cause upon Nicholas and his followers; yet they could not be convicted, as they cast the blame, as best they could, upon highway robbers encountered on the way. This event occasioned the letter in which Hildebert dissuades the supreme pontiff from admitting appeals to the Roman court, since they were generally frivolous and, as he calls them, merely delaying.] unjustly harassed by certain wicked persons. [Note: [Col. 0263D] + See Muratori, *Analecta*, vol. III, p. 113, who printed this letter from a manuscript codex in the Ambrosian Library.]

Both use and necessity teach us to hasten to the aid of friends. Hence I am compelled to run to you not only in my own necessities but also in the distresses of my friends. Therefore, when Radulf comes to you, know that I speak to you in him and entreat you in him, that you may assist me in his case, knowing that I speak for him more devotedly than for myself. Since it is not for me to instruct you how, or with what devotion, you should assist him, I signify only this: it is my wish that you strive to help him with more earnest care than you would help me. All who have gathered against him are sons of this age, seeking rather to harm him than to advance either the Church or justice.

[Note: [Col. 0263D] + New from the manuscript of Évreux and others.]

## LETTER XL

[Note: [Col. 0264D] Written in 1129. In that year Louis the Fat arranged for his first-born son Philip, who shortly afterward died by an unhappy accident, to be anointed king at Reims; Hildebert, together with the other prelates and magnates of the realm, was summoned by the king. Concerning the king’s indignation, of which Hildebert speaks in this letter, see what we have related in his *Life*.]

Before Pope Honorius II, Hildebert excuses himself for being unable to conclude the matter concerning the marriage of Hugh of Craon, entrusted to him, because one party resisted and the king of the Franks summoned him to his son’s coronation.

[Col. 0264B]

To HONORIUS, his most reverend and most holy Father by the grace of God, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, HILDEBERT, humble servant of Tours, perseverance in unbroken obedience.

Most blessed Father, your sublimity sent us letters directing that we should endeavor to settle the case raised concerning the marriage of Hugh of Craon and his wife Agnes, after summoning both parties. When, in obedience to your command, we had given them a day for proceeding, Agnes claimed that she could not come to the case: both because of the shortness of the time, because of the place to which she could not bring her advocates, and especially because her brother Guy of Laval was at war with the count. Moreover, before the day we had appointed, the king of the Franks summoned us to crown and anoint his son king; and on the very day we had assigned to both parties, circumstances and the season compelled us to leave our see.

No one can doubt that not obeying the king, to whom we owed the requested service, whom we hoped thereby to appease, would result in injury to the Church and greater indignation against us. Since, therefore, owing both to Agnes’s excuse and to the summons by which the king had called us, we could not settle the case on the appointed day, we offered him a suitable day; but he altogether refused to accept it. We judged it necessary to report this to you, holy Father, so that if anyone represents it otherwise to you, you may know both the cause of the delay and the truth of the matter. May the Lord preserve you for His Church, holy Father.

## LETTER XLI

[Note: [Col. 0265D] Also 82. Written about 1129. The occasion of this letter was the unfortunate murder of Dean Radulf, discussed above under Letter 37.]

With truly episcopal freedom, but with the utmost reverence, Hildebert sets forth to the supreme pontiff how dangerous it is to the Church and good morals for indiscriminate appeals of every kind to be admitted at the Roman court. [Note: [Col. 0265D] + This letter is found in the *Decrees of the Gallican Church* by Bochel, book VIII, title 25.]

To his most excellent and reverend Father, HONORIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, HILDEBERT, humble servant of Tours, the integrity of due obedience.

The philosopher says: “Authority ought to be cultivated by services, not embittered by words.” Therefore, with repeated prayers I beg that this present writing may not embitter you, reverend Father, nor that you should choose to portray necessity as presumption. I have written from necessity, fearing that the safety of the Church may be wounded by the same dart by which I have been wounded. I cherish good hope in my breast that, by writing for justice, I shall not lose the Father’s favor.

That appeals of every kind should be valid or accepted in the Roman Church on this side of the Alps has neither been heard of nor handed down in sacred institutions. But if perhaps such a novelty should arise, that it please [the Church] indiscriminately to admit every appeal, episcopal censure will perish and the strength of ecclesiastical discipline will be altogether broken. For what robber will not immediately appeal at the mere threat of anathema? What cleric or priest will not rot—or even be buried—in his own filth under the refuge of a dilatory appeal? What bishop will have it in his power, I do not say to punish every act of disobedience, but even any act of it? Any appeal will shake his rod, loosen his firmness, soften his severity, bring him silence, and bring criminals impunity for their offenses.

Thus sacrileges and robberies, fornications and adulteries, will flourish with destructive growth, when the prelate has closed his mouth because of needless appeals, when he has ceased to pursue the persecutors of holy places, to punish the manifest uncleanness of priests, and to avenge the wrongs of widows and orphans. By delay of censure crimes will surely be encouraged, and those who commit offenses will descend into the depth of iniquity unpunished.

Moreover, who will fulfill that evangelical command: “Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and compel the poor and crippled and blind and lame to enter” (Luke 14:24)? Who will compel the blind and lame to enter, if the blind or lame person who is compelled appeals? Finally, no pontiff will be punished for Eli’s offense, because each man will defend his offense under the excuse of appeal. There will be no one to strike raging Saul, to imitate Moses’ punishment, to wield Phinehas’s sword, or to be able to sing to the Lord both mercy and judgment.

Examples of censure will indeed arise, but every appeal will bury its imitators alive. Truly, my learning is small and slight, like one who, in Job’s words, among eagles dwelling in steep places with their young, laps their blood (Job 39:30). It is enough: I am not ashamed either to observe or to profess my own measure. Yet, among other priests, there has come to me knowledge of which appeals the Church on this side of the Alps has hitherto accepted, and which it has refused and rejected without offense to the apostolic see.

For I have learned, and the universal Church proclaims, for whom the remedy of appeal is due: namely, those oppressed by a judgment. I have learned that those who have judges they regard as suspect or hostile, or who fear the violence of a rash mob, can and ought to be relieved by the same remedy. Thus in the second chapter of the decrees of Pope Cornelius the following was handed down to the Church: [Note: [Col. 0265D] These decretals were considered so legitimate in Hildebert’s time that Ivo of Chartres, Burchard, and later Gratian himself inserted them in their compilations. But when they were at last discovered to have entered into law from the same workshop as Pseudo-Isidore the Merchant, learned men judged them to possess no authority.] “If anyone perceives a judge to be against him, let him make use of the voice of appeal, which ought to be denied to no one.” Again, in the same source: “Let no priest commit his cause to an alien judgment unless an appeal has been made to the apostolic see; but let each have judges from his own province and known to him, unless he fears there the violence of a rash multitude or has judges hostile or suspect to him. For these causes it is permitted to appeal and have recourse to judges of greater authority and to other provinces.”

I have heard that there are other appeals, however, which are dilatory and are to be accepted from no one; concerning these we read in the sacred laws in the following words: “Whoever appeals not in confidence of a just cause but for the purpose of causing delay, lest sentence be pronounced against him; or, having confessed his act, wishes to appeal lest judgment be rendered against him—such appeals are not accepted.” Indeed, there seem to me to be many kinds of such appeals, which a prudent judge must necessarily distinguish in such a way as to preserve due fairness in all matters concerning those to be judged.

But I have briefly stated those matters which, as authority has shown [variant: “provided”] to my smallness, possess the prerogative of appeal. If they are more numerous, and if, down to the time of your chair, [Note: [Col. 0266D] Thus the manuscripts of Évreux, Rothomagus, and others; the printed editions read “his own.”] they have run under apostolic vigilance, I confess that the boundaries set by our fathers are not to be crossed. But dilatory and superfluous appeals must be entirely removed from your hearing. One must not endure the planting in the Lord’s garden of the poison of death: a poison by which relief for the afflicted will die, episcopal vigor will languish, the sparing exercise of justice will return to nothing, and the abundance of offenses will receive increase.

## LETTER XLII

[Note: [Col. 0267D] Also 69. Written about 1130.]

As patron of the monastery of Fontevraud, Hildebert asks Honorius II, the supreme pontiff, to confirm an alms granted to that monastery by Henry, king of the English, to be paid annually from England.

To HONORIUS, his most reverend Father and supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, HILDEBERT, humble servant of Tours, perseverance in due obedience. [Note: [Col. 0267D] In the dispute between Peter, bishop of Poitiers, and Hildebert of Tours concerning the tithes of the people of Condé, amicably settled through Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of Pope Honorius, Hildebert so conducted himself that Petronilla, the first abbess of Fontevraud, who was herself party to the case, asked and obtained him from the supreme pontiff as patron and defender. This letter performs that office, and also shows that he had by then long been restored to the favor of Henry, king of England.]

Both the testimony of many and our own experience have taught us that just petitions find their due effect with your vigilance, most holy Father. Therefore we ask of you, as devotedly as confidently, what befits the supreme pontiff to grant and benefits the Church when granted. The most serene Henry, king of the English [that is, Henry I], has provided for the monastery of Fontevraud a certain alms in England, to be paid to that place every year forever for the remission of his sins. With many prayers we entreat that this alms be confirmed by the authority of the apostolic see and secured by your seal.

Most blessed Father, we have undertaken this intervention with you on behalf of Christ’s virgins; for, just as their outward conduct—that is, among men—is known, so, we believe, is their purity known before God. Therefore we wish our intervention not to fail Christ’s handmaids. If the son does not deserve to be heard by the Father, may he nevertheless deserve from God some reward for his pious will. Yet good hope is laid up in our breast: that the son will be heard by the Father, since those virgins alone are sufficient for themselves to earn the favor of God’s servants.

## LETTER XLIII

[Note: [Col. 0268D] Also 60. Written about 1130.]

Hildebert judges that a priest may not kill a robber who seeks to kill him, indeed who actually attacks him with armed hand; yet he so maintains this that, in an equal case, he thinks it safer to consult the supreme pontiff.

HILDEBERT, humble bishop of Tours, to A. [Note: [Col. 0268D] That is, Aymeric, to whom Letter 29 of this second book is also addressed.] his dearest friend, the venerable bishop by God’s grace of the Church of Clermont, [Note: [Col. 0268D] Thus the manuscript of Évreux, not “Chartres,” as the Lyon edition after the Cologne edition has it; and as is read in Fleury’s *Ecclesiastical History*.] greetings.

As your letter has informed my smallness, when a certain robber attacked the priest who bears this present letter, pierced his garments with a lance, and wished to kill him, the priest struck the robber with a stone; and some think that the robber died as a result of the blow. For this offense, therefore, your prudence has now suspended that priest for seven years from the ministry of the Lord’s table. You have been pleased to seek my counsel in this matter, desiring, if I am not mistaken, that an answer be written to your inquiry as to whether the priest may return to the sacred ministry which you medicinally withheld from him.

When I consider how great an innocence is required in a priest, and especially how free from blood he ought to be, it does not seem that a priest guilty of blood should henceforth minister, even though he incurred homicide from necessity of protecting his life. For Ambrose shows in these words that a Christian man ought not seek his own life at another’s death: [Note: [Col. 0268D] *On Duties*, book III, chapter 4.] “Some ask whether a wise man, caught in a shipwreck, can—or ought to—take a plank away from an unwise shipwrecked man. To me, although it may seem preferable that a wise rather than an unwise man should escape from shipwreck for the sake of usefulness, it nevertheless does not seem that a Christian man, wise and just, ought to seek life for himself through another’s death; so that, even if he encounters an armed robber, he cannot strike back when struck, lest, while defending his safety, he stain his piety.”

Therefore, when I consider the restoration of the priest, nothing other than what has been said above seems right to me. Even if it were permissible, it would not be expedient, since it gives offense by example and creates confidence in taking revenge. If something similar had happened in the parish committed to me, I would have sent the guilty man for an apostolic hearing, so that I too might be instructed by his counsel and the sinner might receive a more certain judgment concerning restoration. Farewell.

## LETTER XLIV

[Note: [Col. 0268D] From the Mabillon edition; this is found as the one hundred and twenty-fourth among the letters of Saint Bernard, and was written about 1131.]

### SAINT BERNARD TO HILDEBERT

[Col. 0268C]

This letter of the most holy abbot demonstrates how highly Saint Bernard esteemed Hildebert and how weighty he judged his support to be in the Church’s greatest affair. In it Bernard eloquently and effectively summons him, as a great pillar of the Church, to support the cause of Innocent II against Anacletus. The reader will also see, as it were at a single glance, how amicably Saint Bernard dealt with Hildebert.

To the great priest and one exalted in the word of glory, Hildebert, by God’s grace archbishop of Tours: Bernard, called abbot of Clairvaux, wishes him to walk in the Spirit and to examine all things spiritually.

To address you in prophetic words: “Consolation is hidden from my eyes, because death divides between brothers” (Hosea 13:14). For some, according to Isaiah, seem to have “made a covenant with death and an agreement with hell” (Isaiah 28:15). For behold, this Christ of the Lord, Innocent, has been set for the fall and resurrection of many. Those who belong to God gladly unite themselves to him; but he who stands against him is either Antichrist’s or Antichrist. [Note: [Col. 0269C] Perhaps Gerard of Angoulême, who stood on Anacletus’s side.]

The abomination is seen standing in the holy place; in order to possess it, he burned God’s sanctuary. He persecutes Innocent, and with him all innocence. Innocent flees, indeed, from the face of the lion, as the prophet says: “The lion will roar: who will not fear?” (Amos 3:8). He flees in accordance with the Lord’s command: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matthew 10:13). He flees, and in this proves himself truly an apostolic man, because he has marked himself with the apostolic pattern. Paul too was not ashamed to be let down through the wall in a basket (2 Corinthians 11:13), and thus to escape the hands of those seeking his life.

Yet he withdrew not by sparing his own life, but by giving place to wrath; not to escape death, but to gain life. The Church rightly grants Innocent the office of that same man, since she sees him walking in the same footsteps.

Nor, indeed, is Innocent’s flight idle. He labors, but is honored in his labors. Driven from the City, he is received by the world. From the ends of the earth people come to meet the fugitive with bread, though the fury of Shimei—Gerard of Angoulême—has not yet ceased to curse David. Whether the sinner who sees and is angry wishes it or not, he is magnified in the sight of kings, bearing the crown of glory. Have not all princes recognized that he is God’s true chosen one? The kings of the Franks, English, Spaniards, and finally Romans receive Innocent as pope and recognize him as the unique bishop of their souls.

Achitophel alone still does not understand that his counsel has now been exposed. In vain does the wretch labor to devise a malicious plan against God’s people and to plot against the saints, who cling most firmly to the holy one and scorn to bend the knee before Baal. By no deceit will the parricide prevail in obtaining his kingdom over Israel and over the holy city, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar of faith and foundation of truth. “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecclesiastes 4:12). The choice of the better men, the approval of the greater number, and—what is more powerful than these—the testimony of his conduct commend Innocent to all and establish him as supreme pontiff.

In this matter, Father, your judgment too is awaited like rain upon the fleece, or like the late rain. We do not disapprove of a delay that savors of gravity and removes the mark of fickleness. Mary too did not immediately answer the angel’s greeting, but first considered what sort of greeting this was. And Timothy is commanded: “Lay hands suddenly on no man” (1 Timothy 5:22). Yet I speak as one known to the pontiff. I say, “Nothing in excess,” as one familiar and known: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think” (Romans 12:3).

I confess that I am ashamed that the most ancient serpent, with novel boldness, has seemed, after leaving foolish women, to attack even the strength of your breast and has dared to shake so great a pillar of the Church. Yet we trust that, although he shakes it, he does not cast it down; because the friend of the bridegroom stands and rejoices at the bridegroom’s voice: the voice of exultation and salvation, the voice of unity and peace.

## SHORT NOTICE

[Col. 0269]

I would have you warned, candid reader, that at first we intended to expunge the following letter altogether from the number of Hildebert’s letters. For when we devoted closer attention to revising them, and found it in none of the twelve manuscripts we examined for that purpose, it appeared all the more suspect to us because it seemed all the further removed from Hildebert’s style. At length, upon more careful inspection and examination, we discovered that it was nothing other than a word-for-word fragment near the end of the twenty-second letter of Saint Jerome to Demetrias.

The editors of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* failed to notice this: neither the Paris editors of 1589, nor those of Cologne in 1618, nor even the more recent Lyon editors of 1677. In good faith they placed it as a genuine letter of Hildebert, seventy-ninth in the sequence of the others.

We would therefore most gladly have passed it over in silence, had it not seemed to our learned friends and ourselves not altogether improbable that Hildebert, a most vigilant pastor, might have observed some nun excessively inclined to wander outside her monastery and determined to recall her to stricter enclosure. Perhaps he was then engaged in reading the letters of Saint Jerome—to which, as is clear from his other works, he was most devoted—and judged this fragment of the most holy doctor’s letter especially suited to his purpose. He may have considered nothing more effective for turning that virgin away from her unreflective and excessive freedom of roaming than the very words of so great a man, addressed to another virgin, and therefore sent them to her without any alteration.

Something akin to this occurs in Letter 3 of Book I, addressed to Adela, countess of Blois, where throughout almost its entire third part he quotes Seneca’s very words exactly; likewise in Letter 12 of the same book to Henry I, king of the English, and often elsewhere.

### Letter XLV  
[Note: [Col. 0270C] Otherwise 79.]  
[Note: [Col. 0269] + This letter is falsely attributed to Hildebert in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* editions of Cologne, Lyons, and Paris. See D. Liron, in the pamphlet entitled *Nouvelle littéraire aux savants de France*, 1707.]

Jerome disapproves of a virgin leaving her monastery for any destination, especially alone; most particularly on feast days, when crowds of people are generally more numerous. He sharply attacks those who seek lodging in laypeople’s houses in order to live more freely without supervisors.

[Col. 0269C]

Those who live in a monastery, and who are gathered there in large numbers, must never go out alone, never without their mother-superior. From a flock of doves a hawk often separates one, then immediately attacks and tears her apart, satisfying itself on her flesh and blood. Sick sheep leave their flock and are devoured by the jaws of wolves. I know holy virgins who, on feast days, because of the crowd of people, keep their feet at home and do not then go out, since greater vigilance is required and public exposure must be wholly avoided.

About thirty years ago I published a book on preserving virginity. In it I was obliged to proceed against vices and, for the instruction of the virgin whom I was advising, to expose the snares of the devil. That discourse offended many, because each person understood in himself what was being said, and did not willingly receive it as advice, but opposed it as though it were an accusation of his conduct. Yet what good did it do to arm an army of accusers and to reveal the wound of conscience through its pain? The book remains, but the people have perished.

I also wrote to a good many virgins, to widows, and to many others; and whatever could be said has been culled in those little works, so that either the same matters would be repeated by us superfluously, or their omission would do little harm. Certainly, just as blessed Cyprian published an outstanding work on virginity, so too many others, in Latin speech, in Greek, and in the literature and languages of every nation—especially in the churches—have praised the life of a virgin. But let this belong to those who have not yet chosen virginity and need exhortation, so that they may know what sort of thing they ought to choose.

For us, what has been chosen must be preserved. We must walk, as it were, among scorpions and snakes, with our loins girded, our feet shod, and staffs grasped in our hands, so that we may make our way through the snares and poisons of this age, reach the sweet waters of the Jordan, enter the land of promise, ascend to the Lord, and say with the Prophet: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house, and the place where your glory dwells” (Ps. 25:8). And again: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:4).

Happy is that conscience, and blessed that virginity, in whose heart, apart from the love of Christ—who is wisdom, chastity, patience, justice, and the other virtues—no other love resides; which neither ever sighs at the memory of a man nor desires to see one whom, once seen, it would not wish to dismiss, in accordance with the vocation of virgins and the glory of the heavenly and angelic household.

The reputation of virgins who behave badly brings disgrace upon the name of some. They must be told plainly: either let them marry, if they cannot remain continent; or let them remain continent, if they do not wish to marry. It is a thing worthy of laughter—indeed, of tears—that, when their mistresses walk abroad, a virgin servant precedes them more elegantly dressed, so that, because of excessive familiarity, one may take the unadorned woman one sees for the mistress. Some, separating themselves from supervision so as to live more freely, make use of baths, do what they please, and evade the watchful consciences of the many.

We see and endure these things; and if a gold coin glitters, we count it among good works. I join the end to the beginning, and I am not content to have warned you once. Love the Holy Scriptures, and wisdom will love you. Cherish her, and she will keep you; honor her, and she will embrace you. Let these ornaments cling to your breast and ears. Let your tongue know nothing but Christ; let it be able to utter nothing except what is holy. May the sweetness of your grandmother and mother always dwell upon your lips; imitation of them is a pattern of virtue.

### Letter XLVI  
[Note: [Col. 0271D] New, and from the *Spicilegium*, from manuscripts. Written about 1131. This letter shows more clearly than daylight that Hildebert not only returned to the favor of Henry I, king of the English, but also attained his friendship.]

**To Henry, King of the English.** Hildebert familiarly explains to Henry I, king of the English, the state of his health and thanks him because, at his recommendation, the king of France restored to him a certain provostship of the Church of Tours which the king had retained for four years, though at great cost.

To the most excellent king of the English, exalted by God’s grace to every honor and glory, HILDEBERT, humble archbishop of Tours, ever devoted in his services, greeting.

“I waited and waited for the mercy of the Lord Jesus Christ,” hoping that at some time he might deign to visit his servant upon the bed of sickness and so far relieve my weakness that I might see your face, find consolation in your words, and in your counsel. Yet it has not yet pleased him that his hand should rest wholly upon me; nevertheless, in his great mercy he has withdrawn it so far that I do not feel the chill that accompanies such an illness. The fever, moreover, is slight and brief, and offers hope of restoration to health.

As for those matters about which I wrote to you what I thought, since they have reached their conclusion and have been completed according to your counsel, I have refrained from writing. But I have heard from certain reports what alone, amid my illness, has brought me joy: namely, that you are well with our count, and that he has wholly entrusted himself to your counsel, so that in all matters concerning you and your daughter he will follow your will. I beg that the truth of this matter be made known to me through the present messenger or through your letters.

I do not wish your Majesty to be unaware that peace has been restored to our Church by the king; that the clergy have been reconciled with one another; that we have returned to the king’s favor at great cost; and that the provostship which he had taken from our Church and retained for four years—something which deeply afflicted my spirit—has not so much been restored to us as redeemed by us. For it could not otherwise be restored to our Church until he showed himself gracious to us in return for a fixed and stipulated service.

In this necessity, most serene king, my hope looks to you; my whole spirit cries out after you, lest your aid fail me in my present distress. Indeed, when I was not in need and sought nothing except to be loved by you and to have you deem my service worthy, you nevertheless bestowed upon your servant free and abundant blessings.  
[Note: [Col. 0272D] That is, gratuitous and magnificent benefits.]

### Letter XLVII  
[Note: [Col. 0273D] New, from the manuscript of Évreux. Written about 1131, when Hildebert, worn out by old age, expected death to be near.]

Before the supreme pontiff, Hildebert bitterly but affectionately complains that clerics whom he had justly excommunicated were absolved without consultation with him and restored to lost dignities. Meanwhile, he begs him to allow him freely to possess and exercise his episcopal jurisdiction in his diocese.

[Col. 0273A]

As a son speaks of a most dear father, so I complain of you privately among ourselves: because, in obedience to you, I have become a laughingstock to my adversaries all day long, and am exposed to their insults, so that I am put to shame as though I had altogether lost the power to govern the Church entrusted to me. This has clearly arisen because you have taken from me the canonical power, granted to all bishops, of correcting the enormities of my chapel.

To this has also been added something at which I myself am greatly astonished and at which all who hear it marvel even more: that you have commanded that those excommunicated by me should not only have restored to them the benefice of the Church which they lost through their own fault, but also be restored to communion at the altar and to the office of priesthood without satisfaction, without a hearing, and without absolution.

Although burdened by this, I have nevertheless obeyed your commands, paying too little heed to that apostolic saying: “What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what concord has the temple of God with idols?” (2 Cor. 6:15). Therefore I entreat your fatherhood with tears and prayers and, as one fallen at the apostolic feet, beg that you do not burden the infirmity of my body with anxiety of mind; rather, deign now to command that I have full authority to govern my chapel canonically.

### Letter XLVIII  
[Note: [Col. 0273D] Otherwise 14. The year in which it was written is not clear.]

**To William, Archdeacon.**  
[Note: [Col. 0273D] Namely, archdeacon of Le Mans, since in this letter Hildebert speaks as exercising his own jurisdiction, in the words: “We have judged him to be removed, and we remove him.”]

He suspends from the improperly received order, and forbids admission to the priesthood, a cleric who obtained the diaconate simoniacally.

We have learned that the brother whom you reported to have bought the diaconate for money must be removed, and we remove him, from the diaconate and above. For Peter grants no share and no portion in the order to one who, by buying it, did not receive it. Thus Simon was told: “May your money perish with you. For you have neither part nor lot in this matter” (Acts 8:20–21).

Canonical authority likewise suspends him from the priesthood, toward which he has flown, either not yet a deacon or a deacon improperly made. For how can a building stand when no foundation has been laid beneath it? Your own danger is therefore at issue if you allow the aforesaid brother to minister either in the priesthood, which he truly received improperly, or in the diaconate, which perhaps he did not receive at all.

What shall I say about his reinstatement, when no remedy whatever can be found for a disease of this kind? Thus, in the sixth chapter of the Decrees of Nicholas, you will find: “No bishop shall sell holy orders, from the greater down to the lesser, for this is simoniacal. If anyone does so, both seller and buyer shall be deprived of every ecclesiastical office.”

And in the second chapter of the Council of Chalcedon: “If any bishop, having accepted money, performs an ordination and reduces to a price the grace which cannot be bought, and ordains for money a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or any other person numbered among the clergy: whoever has undertaken this, if convicted, shall incur the loss of his rank; and the person thus ordained shall receive no benefit from such commerce and disgraceful appointment, but shall be deprived both of the dignity and of the responsibility into which he entered by money. Moreover, anyone who has acted as an intermediary in transactions so shameful and unlawful, if he is a cleric, shall lose his own rank; if he is a layman or monk, let him be anathematized.”

### Letter XLIX  
[Note: [Col. 0274D] Otherwise 54. Of uncertain date.]

To an abbot,  
[Note: [Col. 0274D] Perhaps William, abbot of Saint-Vincent.]  
that he should be merciful to brothers who asked for mercy.
