[Note: [Col. 0274D] The Évreux manuscript has: “To his canons, concerning certain persons who were outside the Church.” This does not seem to fit the “brothers” who, as he says in this letter, longed for the monastic community. We follow Royal manuscript 4103 and Victorine manuscript 272.]

He seizes upon the occasion of the approaching celebration of Easter, and upon the example of Peter and Mary Magdalene, who obtained grace from the Lord for their guilt by repentance, in order to obtain mercy for penitents.

The Lord’s Passover is here. In it both Israel departed from Egypt and the souls of the righteous came forth from darkness. This day has dawned for our use, if you use the day as an example. For, as you know, *Pascha*, “Passover,” means passage. Therefore Passover is to pass to the Father from the judge; Passover is to pass from division to unity, from discord to the kiss of peace, from the rod to mercy.

The brothers who sinned against you still sit in darkness, eating the bread of sorrow and drinking the water of sadness. Enough has been struck down in them of all that savored of Egypt. Sidon has blushed enough in its disgrace; it has paid enough punishment. They cry out after you; they cry out after us. If we do not know mercy, we have lost the surer way of human salvation.

When Peter denied him, Christ looked upon him in the very hour in which he wept. The sinner’s tears and the Savior’s pardon followed one another with no interval. Let the present feast, then, teach us to pass with the step of mercy toward brothers who long for the monastic community, heaping coals upon their heads if you are not overcome by evil but overcome evil with good.

### Letter L  
[Note: [Col. 0275C] Otherwise 23. Of uncertain date.]

**To G., Abbot.**  
[Note: [Col. 0275C] All manuscripts have the letter G elegantly written, not C, as Homeyer conjecturally restored it in his notes on Hildebert’s Letter 23, p. 491. By the letter C he intended to denote John the mason, monk of Vendôme. Concerning him Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, wrote to Hildebert Letters 16, 25, 29, and 30 of Book III, and to Paschal II the third letter of Book I. It is astonishing how little Geoffrey himself seems consistent in those letters concerning this monk of his. As he there testifies, he had granted him to Hildebert’s request for a time in Letter 25; in Letter 29 he does not deny that the monk had remained with Hildebert, by his own permission, until the time when he wrote; and in his letter to Paschal II he acknowledges that he had commended or lent him to Hildebert for the latter’s need. Yet he excommunicates him as obstinate, guilty of disobedience, forgetful of his profession, and a fugitive—as he calls him—and in Letter 30, which is almost an encyclical, announces to all the children of the Church that he is excommunicated.

This John, monk of Vendôme, was skilled in masonry. Geoffrey had amicably granted him to Hildebert as very useful for completing buildings begun by Hildebert’s predecessors or newly undertaken by himself, as the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans* report. But perhaps Hildebert retained him longer than Geoffrey wished in order to complete the work. Geoffrey took this so badly that in the third letter of Book I he complained sharply of it to Paschal II: Hildebert, despite his protests, was retaining his monk because of the usefulness of his craft.

But the context of this letter of Hildebert alone demonstrates that it has nothing to do with John the mason. Hildebert says that this G. went out into a far country and was found without a monk—that is, without monastic habit. Who could believe that he meant this of a monk who, as Geoffrey complains, had for so long been with him almost as a member of his household, indeed as his table companion? Moreover, he asserts that the man obeyed his warnings, returned first to himself and then to the monastery. Geoffrey would therefore have demanded him back in vain. Finally, in this letter Hildebert asks Geoffrey’s favor for that monk. Certainly, had he interceded for that John the mason, he would above all have sought from Geoffrey absolution from the excommunication by which Geoffrey had struck the mason so seriously that, in a quasi-encyclical letter, he announced him to all the faithful as excommunicated. Thus Homeyer’s rather slight conjecture collapses. Although the exceptionally discerning and learned Sirmond had initially leaned somewhat toward it, he at once abandoned it when he saw the first strokes of the letter G in the manuscripts.]

That a straying sheep should be restored to the fold through mercy.  
[Note: [Col. 0276C] Thus Royal manuscript 4103.]

[Col. 0275A]

Our fellow-brother and son G.  
[Note: [Col. 0276D] Thus Colbert manuscripts 2662 and 1668.]  
went out into a far country. Having found him there without monastic habit, I urged him to return to the community of monks. He believed me; first he returned to himself, and then to the monastery. Therefore you too, my son, must rejoice, because your brother was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.

Before leaving me, however, he received a letter of intercession addressed to you. When you lower your eyes to it, lower your heart also toward mercy. Mercy is a beautiful ornament of human nature; whoever lacks it degenerates badly and denies that he is human. Thus, not to know how to pity is to have fellowship with wild beasts. But far be it from you to renounce humanity and, casting aside gentleness, to sink into a wild animal. For you wholly breathe humanity and bear it both as nature’s work and as the example of learning.

Receive your son, therefore, in peace, because it belongs to your pastoral care to soften the severity of the law by the regard of compassion.

### Letter LI  
[Note: [Col. 0276D] Otherwise 46. Neither the person to whom it was written nor the year is known. It was not written to William, abbot of Saint-Vincent, as Homeyer suspected, since regular observance flourished in that monastery in his time; rather, it was probably written to a Benedictine abbot, since Hildebert sets before him the example of Saint Benedict, who did not resign the care of ill-behaved monks until he had certainly learned that none of them would heed his admonitions and amend their lives. From this a not insignificant conjecture concerning Hildebert’s Benedictine monasticism might be drawn. [Col. 0275] Neither conjecture is easily admitted, being insufficiently founded.]

He rebukes a certain regular superior because, too lightly wearied by the disorder of some subjects, he abdicated the government imposed upon him, to the prejudice of the good; and because, without consulting them, he substituted another who was less suitable, though they were unwilling.

Just as it is presumptuous to approach the governance of souls without being called, so too it is forbidden by canonical institutions for anyone, unless his own fault removes him, to lay aside a charge already undertaken. You should therefore know that a most serious scandal has arisen among the brothers who live the common life under the profession given to you, because, leaving them without consultation, you determined to appoint a steward over them against their will and resistance.

When they learned from certain reports that you had been dismissed no less readily than you had been installed, they came exhausted even to us and expressed a complaint exceedingly grave and full of groaning. For there is uncertainty whether they should more strongly accuse your departure or reject the arrival of the man whom you judged should be substituted for the people you abandoned. We believe that he will renounce the undertaking he has accepted, since he knows that one ought to be drawn into the pastoral burden, not run to it voluntarily.

But you must be severely blamed and rebuked in harsher words, since, without a cause laid down by law, you withdrew a pastor’s protection from the flock committed to you. If in that flock the perversity of one or several displeased you, your brotherhood nevertheless ought to have considered Augustine writing thus to Vincentius:  
[Note: [Col. 0276D] Thus Saint Augustine, Letter 93 to Vincentius the Rogatist, §15, new edition, p. 237.]  
“For the sake of the wicked, the good are not to be abandoned; rather, for the sake of the good, the wicked are to be tolerated.”

But if the whole flock—may it not be so!—walks crooked paths and their restless spirit finds no repose in your discourse, their case should first be laid before our ears before guardianship is laid aside. Concerning such resignation, the same Augustine says in the third book against the Donatist Parmenian:  
[Note: [Col. 0276D] Saint Augustine teaches the same in Letter 108 to Macrobius, p. 313, §16: “The true rule, demonstrated by prophetic and apostolic examples, is that the wicked should rather be tolerated, so that the good may not be abandoned, than that the good should be abandoned in order that the wicked may be separated.”]  
“He who wishes bodily to abandon those who seem plainly wicked spiritually abandons the good who are hidden; and, while he attempts to defend separation, he is compelled to accuse those whom he has not tested and does not know.”

Likewise, the venerable man in life, Benedict in grace and name, set before us an example to be embraced: he did not abandon even a few sheep until he found no one at all to whom he could be of use. Hence Gregory says concerning Ezekiel:  
[Note: [Col. 0277D] Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book II, chapter 3.]  
“Those who are guardians of souls and have undertaken the care of feeding the flock are by no means permitted to change places.”

Remember, therefore, with the utmost haste to return to the flock entrusted to you. You will be punished by the strict Judge if you delay either to obey or to correct what has been wrongly done after your departure.

### Letter LII  
[Note: [Col. 0277D] Otherwise 30. Of uncertain date.]

**To G., Priest.**

He rebukes a priest—whom he calls a *sacrifex*—because, suspecting him of theft, he tormented him under harsher interrogation in order to obtain a disclosure; this, he says, is lawful for a secular court, not for the Church.

[Col. 0277B]

To subject accused persons to tortures or to extort truth by punishments belongs to the jurisdiction of a court, not to the discipline of the Church. Therefore you ought to have refrained from punishing the man whom you suspect of having carried off your money by theft. For you are not an executioner, but a *sacrifex*—that is, a sacrificing priest—appointed to offer sacrifice for the accused, not to sacrifice the accused.  
[Note: [Col. 0277D] In place of *sacerdos*, “priest.”]

Even in cases of genuine injuries, such gentleness befitted a priest: you ought to have preferred that a guilty person should depart unpunished rather than, on an uncertain charge, rage with certain punishments. Hence Augustine says to Macedonius:  
[Note: [Col. 0277D] Augustine, Letter 103 to Macedonius, new edition, §20, p. 532.]  
“Sometimes merciful persons, even in the uncertainty itself, do not wish to inflict certain punishments upon a human being for uncertain money. It is fitting that we should also urge and exhort you toward this mercy. For it is better that you lose it, if he has it, than that you torture or kill him, if he does not have it.”

Therefore abhor handing an accused person over to torments and death—you, servant of Christ, for whom Christ was handed over to the cross and to death. But if you so carnally long for the money you have lost, Augustine shows in the same letter to Macedonius how you ought to seek its recovery:  
[Note: [Col. 0277D] Ibid., §21.]  
“Those whom we know have wickedly taken what belongs to others and have the means to return it, but are unwilling to do so, we accuse, rebuke, and condemn—some privately, others publicly, as the diversity of persons appears able to receive different medicine—yet we do not incite them to greater madness to the destruction of others.”  
[Note: [Col. 0277D] In Colbert manuscripts 1168 and 2662 alone, after the word *concitari* (“to be incited”), the following words are added: “sometimes even . . . . . we deprive [them] of communion,” which are absent from the other manuscripts, though they are in fact the following words of Saint Augustine in the same passage.]

“Sometimes also, if the matter more urgently requiring care does not prevent it, we deprive them of communion at the sacred altar.”  
[Note: [Col. 0278D] See what we have noted concerning these exceptions in Letter 27 of this book.]

### Letter LIII, or S.  
[Note: [Col. 0278D] Thus in the editions.]  
Hildebert, Archbishop of Tours: Preface to his *Selections of Ecclesiastical Rules*, concerning the manifold kinds of divine commands.  
[Note: [Col. 0278D] Thus all editions of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Juret, however, placed this as Letter 288 in the series of letters under the title: “Prologue of Ivo, by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Chartres, concerning the interpretation and dispensation of ecclesiastical discipline.”]

[Col. 0278A]

I have taken care, with no little labor, to arrange into one body selections of ecclesiastical rules: partly from the letters of Roman pontiffs, partly from the acts of councils of Catholic bishops, partly from treatises of orthodox Fathers, and partly from enactments of Catholic kings.  
[Juret: “to unite.”]  
Thus, whoever cannot have at hand the writings from which these excerpts have been taken may at least receive from here whatever he perceives to be useful for the advantage of his case.

Beginning, therefore, from the foundation of the Christian religion—that is, faith—we have gathered and classified under general headings matters concerning ecclesiastical sacraments, the instruction or correction of morals, and the examination or determination of all kinds of cases. Thus the inquirer need not unfold the entire volume, but need only identify the general heading fitting his question and read through without interruption  
[variant: “interpellation”]  
the chapters placed beneath it.

In this work we have thought it fitting to forewarn the prudent reader that, if he should not fully understand what he reads, or should think it novel or mutually contradictory, he should not immediately criticize it. Rather, he should carefully consider what is said according to strictness, what according to moderation, what according to judgment, and what according to mercy. The person who said, “I will sing to you, Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100:1), and elsewhere, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10), knew that these did not disagree with one another.

For every ecclesiastical discipline has chiefly this purpose: either to destroy every edifice raising itself against the knowledge of Christ; or to build up an edifice consisting in the power of gifts and uprightness of morals  
[Juret: “the edifice of God, by the truth of faith and uprightness of morals”]; or, if it has been defiled, to correct it by remedies of repentance  
[Juret: “cleanse it”].

The teacher of this edifice is charity. Seeking the welfare of neighbors, it commands one to do to others what each wishes others to do to himself, toward the end suited to sacred institutions. Therefore any ecclesiastical teacher who interprets or moderates ecclesiastical rules so that he refers all that he teaches or expounds to the rule of charity neither sins nor errs, since, seeking the welfare of neighbors, he intends to attain the end due to sacred institutions.

Hence blessed Augustine says, while treating ecclesiastical discipline: “Have charity, and do whatever you wish. If you rebuke, rebuke with charity; if you spare, spare with charity.” But in these matters the utmost diligence and a clear eye of the heart are necessary, so that, in punishing or sparing, sincere charity may aid in healing diseases, and no one may seek his own advantage there after the manner of venal physicians, lest he incur that prophetic rebuke: “They put to death souls that were not living, and made alive souls that were not living.”  
[Note: [Col. 0279D] The Vulgate reads differently: “When they ensnared the souls of my people, they made their souls live, and they profaned me among my people . . . in order to put to death souls that do not die, and to make alive souls that do not live” (Ezek. 13:18–19).]

For just as the practice of bodily medicine aims either to drive away diseases, cure wounds, preserve health, or increase it, and a physician does not seem inconsistent with himself when, according to the quality or extent of the illness or the patient’s condition, he applies now biting and now soothing medicines; and when he sometimes cuts with iron one whom he could not relieve by a poultice, and conversely helps with ointment one whom he did not dare cut with iron—so too spiritual physicians, namely the teachers of the holy Church, disagree neither with themselves nor with one another when they forbid unlawful things, command necessary things, recommend the highest things, and pardon venial things; when, according to the hardness of offenders’ hearts, for their correction or for the protection of others, they impose severe laws of penance; or when, according to the devotion of those who grieve and wish to rise again, taking account of the fragility of the vessel they bear, they apply the soothing remedy of pardon.

For those who pardon provide for the removal of greater diseases; those who forbid unlawful things deter from death; those who command necessary things  
[variant: “what is necessary”]  
seek to preserve salvation; and those who recommend the highest things strive to increase salvation.

A careful reader who attends to this will understand that the sacred utterances have one countenance, when he distinctly considers what exhortation is, what command is, what prohibition is, and what remission is; and that these neither fight one another nor differ from themselves, but in all things provide a remedy for health according to their moderation and dispensation  
[variant: “to dispense”].

But it must be explained somewhat more fully what weight each has, to whom they are suited, what things are remissible and what irremissible, and when or for what reasons they must be remitted. First, exhortation does not threaten punishment if someone does not follow it, but promises reward to those who comply with it. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have; give it to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:21). See how this Gospel reading places perfection in human choice: it does not compel and does not threaten.

Likewise, after praising those who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 19:12), it adds: “Let him who is able to receive this receive it” (ibid.). Yet when someone has bound himself by vow to perfection, or has ascended a rank which no one can attain without great exertion of virtue  
[Juret: “the virtue of continence”],  
then it becomes necessary and penal if what was voluntary before that ascent is not maintained. Hence the Lord says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62). Before the ascent, a person could be lower, but not worse; after descent, however, he is both lower and worse. This is said concerning exhortation.

Indulgence, however, in our judgment, since it does not choose the better course, has a remedy indeed but not a reward. Yet if anyone turns away even from this, he deserves a destructive judgment. For example, as we know from the Apostle, marriage was permitted to the human race in order to avoid fornication; and its violator deserves eternal punishment, as the same Apostle testifies: “Fornicators and adulterers God will judge” (Heb. 13:4).

This state also, as we have said concerning exhortation, compels no one except the person who has first bound himself. It is voluntary, not necessary; otherwise anyone who did not take a wife would be a transgressor. But once he has bound himself, let him hear the Apostle saying: “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release” (1 Cor. 7:27). The same Apostle, when speaking of marriage, did not say, “If a woman marries, she earns a reward”; he says only, “She does not sin if she marries” (ibid., v. 36).

Similarly, if someone invites another to daily fasts, he invites him indeed to a thing worthy of reward, if he complies and perseveres. But the person who does not comply does not become better than himself; although he remains inferior to those who perform it, he does not become worse than himself. But if he falls from his vow, he becomes both lower and worse than himself. If he restrains himself within the bounds of sobriety and a frugal table, he does not attain the rewards of the highest state; but if he falls into feasting and drunkenness, he is said to have done something deserving rebuke and shame.

These two states, therefore—one higher and the other lower—which before a vow are voluntary but after a vow necessary, have their own modes and institutions. When they are observed, as was said above, they provide a remedy for some and bring punishment upon others. When observed, they gain a reward; when not observed, they deserve eternal punishment. Therefore, before undertaking them, one must deliberate; after undertaking them, one must persevere.

Having set these matters forth beforehand, we must say something about command and prohibition.

Precepts and prohibitions, then, are of two kinds: some mutable, others immutable. Immutable are those precepts which the eternal law has ordained: when observed, they confer salvation; when not observed, they take it away. Such are: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul; and your neighbour as yourself” [Col. 0281A] (Deut. 10:12; Matt. 11:37–39); and, “Honour your father and your mother” (Exod. 20:12); and whatever similar commands there are. Mutable are those which the eternal law has not ordained, but which the diligence of later persons has devised for reasons of usefulness—not principally to obtain salvation, but to find it more safely [Jur.: “to fortify it”]. Such is the Apostle’s saying: “Avoid a heretic after a first and second admonition” (Titus 3:10). Not because conversation with such persons is in itself harmful to salvation, but because frequent association with them might indirectly corrupt the simplicity of some. You will find many things of this sort in canonical regulations.

Likewise, immutable prohibitions are those directed against vices, such as: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery,” and so forth (Exod. 20:13–14). These are those least [Col. 0281B] commandments of which the Lord says that whoever breaks them and teaches others to do so “shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19). Yet whoever observes them is not thereby immediately worthy of the kingdom of God, because they are beginnings, not perfections.

There are other interdictions which, if they had not been interdicted, neither death would work through them [Jur.: “nor would death work in them”] nor salvation be endangered. Yet the authority of the holy Fathers, to be reverenced, has decreed them in such a way that they should neither harm those now concerned nor fail, through sincere charity, to provide for the restraining of greater evils or their avoidance. An example is the rule that a cleric, after performing penance for a condemnable crime, should not remain a cleric or enter the clerical order. As blessed Augustine says, this was laid down by the strictness of discipline, not from despair of forgiveness. Otherwise there would be dispute against the [Col. 0281C] keys of the Church, concerning which it was said: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). But lest the mind should swell with hope of ecclesiastical honour and perform penance proudly, it was most strictly resolved that after penance has been performed no one should become or remain a cleric.

This ought not to be judged a superfluous diligence of later persons: while taking nothing away from salvation, they added something to humility, so that salvation might be more safely fortified, having, I think, learned from experience of some persons’ counterfeit penances through their affected pursuit [perhaps: “ambitions”] of honours. For the experience of many diseases compels the discovery of many remedies.

Such is that saying in the Gospel: “Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; no, no.’ What is more than this [Col. 0281D] is from evil” (Matt. 5:37)—not from the evil of the person swearing, but of the person compelling another to swear. It is not that swearing in human agreements from necessity is evil; rather, the person who never swears is further removed from perjury than one who swears on any occasion whatever. For it is said of the Lord: “The Lord has sworn” (Ps. 109 [110]:4). And the Apostle says: “An oath is for them the end of every controversy” (Heb. 6:16). The same Apostle also says, swearing in this manner: “The truth of Christ is in me” (2 Cor. 11:10); and elsewhere: “I die daily because of [Vulgate: “by”] your glory, brothers” (1 Cor. 15:31).

Therefore, in matters whose observance gains salvation, or whose neglect undoubtedly brings death, no dispensation may be admitted. All such commands and prohibitions must be observed exactly as [Col. 0282A] they have been ordained by the eternal law. But in those things which later discipline [Jur.: “diligence”] established for the strictness of discipline or for the safeguarding of salvation, if an honourable or useful compensation follows, a dispensation may proceed, after careful deliberation by those in authority.

For we read that many such things occurred in Gospel history, in the Acts of the Apostles, and in the proceedings of councils; and we know that they were later confirmed by the authority of apostolic men. Let us therefore take our first testimony from the Gospel. When the Lord sent the disciples to preach, he forbade them purse and bag. Yet, according to the moral discipline of our Lord Jesus Christ on earth, when the time of his Passion was at hand, he gave them back both bag and purse, first giving himself as an example that in such ordinances one must yield to the needs of the time.

Likewise Paul, when he had promised that he would pass through the Corinthians to Macedonia, and perceived that this would not at all benefit them, changed his arrangement but not his purpose. Thus he excuses himself: “When therefore I intended this, did I use levity? Or do I devise according to the flesh, so that with me there should be ‘yes’ and ‘no’?” (2 Cor. 1:17). For he did not understand himself to have changed his purpose, since whether he came to them or did not come, he sought their salvation. Thus he says subsequently: “But I call God as witness upon my soul that, sparing you, I did not come again to Corinth” (ibid., 23).

Nor could he understand that he had changed [Col. 0282C] his arrangement according to the flesh. For one who thinks according to the Lord [Jur.: “according to the flesh”] fails to carry out what he proposes when he defers to more important persons, or is overcome by profits or greater display. But the spiritual person then carries out his purpose when it was decided and confirmed by common counsel at Jerusalem, and sent through Paul and Barnabas to the brethren throughout Asia: that no one coming to the faith should be held subject to the circumcision of the Law.

The Apostle himself, writing to the Galatians, says: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2). And the same Apostle, although he withstood Peter to his face because Peter had consented to the pretence of certain Jews who considered circumcision necessary to salvation, nevertheless yielded to the need of the time and circumcised Timothy at Lystra, in order to avoid scandal among the Jews living there. By this action he showed what he says elsewhere: “I became as a Jew to the Jews, that I might gain the Jews” (1 Cor. 9:20). This must be understood as spoken not from the conduct of one acting in fear, but from the feeling of one who shares another’s suffering: wishing to help each person as he himself would wish to be helped if he were in that person’s condition.

Church leaders likewise judge many matters more strictly according to the tenor of the canons; they tolerate many because of the necessities of the times; they dispense many for the benefit of persons or to avoid the slaughter of peoples; and many things relaxed [Jur.: “changed”] by holy Fathers are confirmed by testimonies of Scripture. Thus the holy pontiff Leo of the holy Roman Church permitted neophytes [Col. 0283A] to advance to the highest priesthood, though Paul strove by public preaching to dissuade them from this matter.

[Note: Thus Nectarius, still a catechumen, was assumed to the see of Constantinople. Sozomen, Book VII, ch. 10; Baronius, under the year 381.]

Likewise, we read that Arians were received into their offices before [Jur.: “after”] they had been converted. Hence the aforesaid Pope Leo wrote to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, concerning the firmness of things not to be changed and the discernment of times:

> “Just as there are certain things which cannot be changed for any reason, so there are many things which ought to be moderated either because of the necessities of the times or because of consideration for ages, always preserving this principle: in matters doubtful or obscure, we must know that what is to be followed is that which is neither contrary to Gospel precepts nor found opposed to the decrees of the holy Fathers.”

Accordingly Augustine, in his letter to Boniface, says:

> “In causes of this kind, unless there is danger either to this or that person through the grave discord of schism, the slaughter of peoples is at stake; something must be taken away from severity, so that sincere charity may more effectively come to the aid of healing greater evils.”

The same writer says against the heretics:

> “If, they say, we must repent of having been outside the Church in order to be saved, how could we, after such penance, remain among you as clerics or even bishops? This would not occur, because indeed—what must be admitted—it ought not to occur, unless it were healed by compassion for peace itself. But let those say this to themselves, and mourn all the more humbly, who lie in so great a death of severance that they may be revived by this certain wound of their Catholic mother. For when a severed branch is grafted in, another wound is made in the tree so that the branch, which was perishing without the life of the root, may be received and live. But when the received branch has grown together with that which receives it, strength and fruit follow; if it has not grown together, that branch indeed withers, but the life of the tree remains. Such is this kind of mercy: the branch outside is grafted in without cutting off any branch that is within, though not without some, even the slightest, wound to the tree. Thus also when these persons come to the [Col. 0284B] Catholic root, neither the honour of clerical or episcopal office is taken from them, even after penance for their error; something is indeed done, as it were, in the bark of the mother-tree, against the integrity of strictness. Yet neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. 3:7).

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0283]

### 169–170. LETTER I

[Note: New, from the *Spicilegium* and the manuscripts of Foulque-Mont.]

He writes to Ranulf, bishop of Durham, on behalf of a certain Robert.

[Note: Concerning this Ranulf, or Randulf, promoted in 1099 by William Rufus, king of England, to the Church of Durham, see the *History of the Bishops of Durham*, in *Anglia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 705.]

[Col. 0283C]

To RANULF, by God’s grace bishop of Durham, to be exalted with every honour and favour, ALDEBERT, humble priest of Le Mans, sends health and prayers in Christ.

I believed that I should sin against many if I were to detain at greater length, with a longer page, those eyes which you owe to many. Therefore, that you may know all of me from these few words, consider that all which can belong to another concerning me belongs to you [supplied: “to be”]. You will in turn repay me if you love me and pray for me.

Moreover, I would humbly entreat you to receive Robert, your son and brother, the bearer of this letter, into the sanctuary of your friendship, unless I believed him already so [perhaps: “now”] well known to you and sufficiently able in his own right to merit your favour without another’s intervention. Yet I ask that, since I believe you will do good for his own sake, he may judge it better for himself to be done for my sake. Farewell.

### LETTER II

[Note: Otherwise no. 20. Written about the year 1101.]

He reminds Countess Adela of the chasuble promised him by her and asks that it be given to him.

[Col. 0284C]

Need has a worn-down brow: it is ashamed of nothing, provided it helps. Need drives one even to crime and pleads for pardon. Forgive me, then, if, compelled by it, I ask beyond my deserts. You teach me to hope for things greater than my merits, since you do not cease to bestow gifts greater than my merits. If you ask what I request, or with what confidence: I need a chasuble. You promised it to me. As I suppose, you will not abandon your promise, you who hasten to give even things not promised. Farewell.

### 171. LETTER III

[Note: Otherwise no. 53. Perhaps written about 1102, after Hildebert’s second return from England.]

He admits that he buys friendship too dearly, because he extorts from a friend only by entreaties what he should receive freely from a friend. Meanwhile, he excuses the delay in sending the history of the miracles of the Church of Exeter because its first copy had been lost.

[Note: Exeter, not Oxford; so all the manuscripts.]

[Note: This history remains unknown to this day; despite every diligence, we have been unable to discover it.]

To CLAREMBALD, most beloved brother and venerable canon of the Church of Exeter, HILDEBERT, humble [Col. 0285A] priest of Le Mans, sends abundant greeting in the Lord.

I fear, dearest brother, I fear that you will accuse me of negligence, since, though you so often asked me not to weary of recording, according to the faithfulness of the exemplar sent to me, the miracles which the Lord deigned to perform in the Church of Exeter, I delayed too long in satisfying you. You will therefore accuse me of not writing the requested work gratuitously, since you obtained it both by long waiting and by innumerable prayers. For, according to the philosopher, one did not receive gratis who, when asking, obtained.

And indeed I know that a friend sells no service: he willingly, freely, and promptly gives help. He does not know how to await entreaties, but, as though he divined the desire of one in need, he anticipates the person who is about to ask. For he doubts whether that is a service which the force of entreaties obtains—something which the considerate person does not offer, but the importunate person extorts.

But know that, in the service you asked of me, whatever diminishes the majesty [that is, the greatness] of service was far from me. From the time I learned your desire, you added entreaties in abundance. I at once resolved to comply; but the exemplar, lost by chance, held back my labouring intention. When it was absent from me for a long time, it was later found and restored to my hands, awakening my dormant desire for writing.

The work was near its end when a messenger came to me and presented a sheet in your name, containing the very matter which I had read in the first exemplar. The same messenger added that a second exemplar had also been sent to me lest, because the first had been lost, I should excuse my silence. Having received and reread the page more than once, the spirit of the reader was stirred. For it contained certain miracles found in the first copy, but presented there one way and in the first copy another way; yet I did not regard the differences as such that I should judge them contrary to each other.

In what I had published according to the first exemplar, I resolved to add nothing, remove nothing, change nothing. For a different account of the same event does not prejudice true history. I therefore left it to your judgment, my brother, whether to correct the work or suppress it altogether as faulty. You will fulfil a friend’s role if you remove from sight whatever you know tongues will fear.

I have said this beforehand to you, Clarembald—indeed, *clare valde*, “very illustrious”—lest you think that this service of my pen was dictated more by unwillingness than necessity, and that I was as weary of writing to a friend as though I regretted loving him. But since I am held on a different shore—

[Note: He was therefore writing from Gaul to England.]

—and cannot greet you unless I first have the favour of half the world, and am separated from you by many waters, yet many waters will not be able to extinguish charity. Farewell.

### LETTER IV

[Note: Otherwise Letter 76. Written about 1102, when Pope Calixtus II summoned the Lateran council at Rome, during the reign of Henry V.]

[Note: This letter was not written in 1102, for it mentions Pope Calixtus, who obtained the apostolic see in 1119.]

To the holy bishop of Séez.

[Note: So the Rouen manuscript.]

He excuses himself to the bishop for delaying, detained by necessity, to send the small gift intended for him; meanwhile, as he is about to set out for Rome for a council, he commends himself to the bishop’s prayers.

[Col. 0286A]

We know indeed, blessed bishop, that delay diminishes the worth of a benefit. For one doubts whether it is a benefit when delay torments the person awaiting it. Yet before a mind disposed to virtue, we believe that even benefits which are delayed by necessity retain their full grace. Therefore we hope that our small gift will have the favour of the person for whom it was made with labour. For we neither voluntarily delayed the benefit nor sought favour with a man who searches for grounds of ingratitude.

He lives wholly for the bishop, hating nothing that it would be better to love, loving nothing which one would be ashamed to confess. Such a man does our speech describe you, dearest brother; such a man does our spirit believe you to be, wishing you the same welfare it wishes for itself. For we desire that you may always be well in Christ, and know that you repay us in turn if you love us and pray for us.

Most of all at this time we need your prayers, since we must travel to Rome, where Pope Calixtus, having summoned bishops and abbots from this side of the mountains, will celebrate a general council in the city.

[Note: Hildebert’s acts do not show that he either undertook or ever completed this journey to the First Lateran Council.]

For us who are setting out thither, the season is dangerous through winter, the Alps through snow, the waters through their swelling, the emperor through his restraints, the city through seditions, and the palace through exactions. Certainly we believe that all these can be removed by prayers [Col. 0286C]—except exaction alone, which is tempered neither by prayer nor by fasting.

### LETTER V

[Note: Otherwise no. 29. Written about 1105.]

To Bishop R.

[Note: So the Rouen and Évreux manuscripts; perhaps Raynald of Angers.]

He asks his friend to make him a participant in the contents of the apostolic letter he has received.

Word has reached us that you have received an apostolic letter. If it has offered you a cup of grief or joy, I was the person to whom it should first have been passed after you. In every fortune one wisely hastens to a friend. Shared joy makes good fortune more welcome; adversity receives a great remedy from a friend’s consolation.

This fault of mine I can neither cast off nor blush to confess. I speak all things with a friend as securely as with myself. I am full of cracks: whatever fortune’s boldness changes, whether against or according to my desire, flows out. But I pass over these things. I want you to let me know what [Note: So Évreux and Rouen; perhaps the sense is better thus: “I want you to be willing to let me know what,” etc.] the apostolic communications have taught you. Whatever it may be, it will be more gladly heard when repeated. Redeem, then, the fault of the silence of which you stand accused, if the return of your letters shows me the things I ask.

### LETTER VI

[Note: Otherwise no. 55. Written about 1107.]

To ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury.

[Note: Thus the Évreux manuscript. Rouen has “Marbod”; but since Marbod was bishop of Rennes, such scarcity of correspondence does not seem likely between him and Hildebert. Better, therefore: “Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.”]

He urges his friend to send letters more frequently or at greater length, since they are especially welcome to him.

The rarity of travellers makes letters pass less frequently between us. It deprives us both of the service of greeting and of friendly conversation. Yet a longer letter can make up for the rarity of letters. Remember, then, to prepare something that may both console me for your absence and detain my eyes longer.

I hate words which end just as they begin to delight. But I so embrace your prolixity [Col. 0287B] that I receive longer letters even when occupied and lay them down unwillingly. They do not find me at leisure [Note: Rouen: “leisure”; but Évreux more correctly: “at leisure.”], but make me so. Farewell—and do this rather: forget me at some time, than think of me only at some time.

[Note: Perhaps clearer according to the author’s meaning: “Farewell—and do this rather: do not ever forget me, than merely think of me at some time.”]

### LETTER VII

[Note: Otherwise no. 24. Written about 1107.]

To the abbot of Cluny.

[Note: That is, Saint Hugh. During his tenure Hildebert, returning from Rome, escaped so many dangers—namely in 1106 or 1107, when, not finding Paschal II at Rome, he met him in Gaul after the council which Paschal had held at Troyes, at Souvigny, where Paschal had once been a monk. Saint Hugh died on the same day and in the same year as Saint Anselm, namely 1109. Thus Hildebert could in 1107 attribute his extraordinary escape from so many dangers during the journey to Hugh’s prayers.]

He gives thanks because, returning from Rome through the abbot’s prayers, he escaped many and most grave dangers. He declares that he would have fled to the abbot’s bosom if the Roman pontiff had allowed him to lay aside the burden of episcopal office; meanwhile he commends to him the bishop of Angers, whom he calls a novice of Saint Benedict.

I count and hold it a very great thing that you opened to me the sanctuary of your friendship. Received within it, [Col. 0287C] amid many and great dangers I have learned by experience how powerful is “the constant prayer of the righteous” (James 5:16). To it alone I owe that, returning from Rome, I passed untouched through plots laid for me; that I escaped unharmed urgent and immense storms at sea; that I did not fall among barbarian pirates, hideously misshapen in their masked appearance, denying that they were human by their bestial cruelty, and above all rejoicing that they had no fellowship with Christians.

These strangers and enemies to the Catholic religion were carried in many ships to the island of Saint Honoratus on the most holy day of Pentecost. There, having utterly overthrown the monastery from its foundation, [Col. 0288A] they struck down a great many monks with the sword; for the rest, hiding-places and a tower provided safety.

[Note: Observe that the devastation of the monastery of Lérins is reported by no writer other than Hildebert. Yet, since he supports the account here with so many circumstances and narrates it as an eyewitness, even at peril of his life, it does not seem possible rightly to doubt it. Nor did the eminent Cardinal Baronius or his most illustrious abridger Spondanus doubt it: relying even upon this letter of Hildebert alone, they assigned this massacre to the year 1107, III.]

On that same day a favourable wind had driven me away from the aforesaid island. Thus, almost snatched from the very jaws of lions, I sailed with an auspicious course to Maguelonne. I have included these details, most holy Father, lest anyone be ignorant of how great the dangers are from which I confess that your prayer rescued me.

I therefore possess and offer thanks to your religious devotion. Long ago I should have embraced your bosom as an accused man embraces an altar, if, having consulted the pope, he had permitted me to cast off the burden of a bishop. In sending me back to labour, he begrudged me glory. May God not hold it against him! Meanwhile I shall hope in the shadow of your wings, until I am brought out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth, and say: “Behold, I come to do your will, O my God” (Heb. 10:9).

As for the rest, it is superfluous to ask you concerning the bishop of Angers, that novice of blessed Benedict, [Col. 0288B] whose affection is singular toward all and wholly directed to each individual.

[Note: “Novice of blessed Benedict”: namely Geoffrey of Mayenne, who was ordained bishop of Angers in 1093 and, about 1098, renounced his episcopate and became a monk at Cluny. Raynald of Martigné afterwards succeeded him in the bishopric. See the notes to Letters 3 and 4 of Book Two.]

Farewell.

### LETTER VIII

[Note: Otherwise no. 26. Written about 1107.]

He asks Adela, countess of Blois, to provide him with travelling expenses for a journey to a council, as she had done for the bishop of Chartres.

Your husband’s absence has laid upon you the more laborious care of government. It compels you to move to various places more in mind than in body. Uncertain, therefore, in what place I should find you, but certain that I should find at every place in you the services of honour, I wrote while remaining at home to my lady. The sum of my letter was this:

> “You have, it is said, provided travelling expenses for the bishop of Chartres as he set out for a council.

[Note: In Hildebert’s time so many councils were assembled in Gaul that, from 1097, when he was elected bishop of Le Mans, to 1134, when he died archbishop of Tours, their number rose to forty-four, according to Labbe, *Councils*, vol. X. A great part of them was convened by Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, then apostolic legate. Who, then, could divine which council is meant here? I would nevertheless willingly conjecture the Second Council of Troyes, namely that of 1107, at which Paschal II was present while in Gaul and which Hildebert could have attended after returning to Gaul. Moreover, the bishop of Chartres mentioned here seems to have been none other than Ivo. Like Hildebert, he had suffered so harshly that, when both had been stripped of all possessions, each had to ask Adela for travelling expenses in order to make the journey.

[Note: This does not seem to concern the Second Council of Troyes, since Hildebert speaks in his letter to Adela, countess of Blois, of her absent husband, who died five years before the council held at Troyes in the presence of Pope Paschal II.]]

> If this is so, I beg you to share with me the benefit of the favour granted to him.”

Symmachus says: “It is customary for those who desire assistance to resort to proven supports.” Therefore I have flown to your protection, you who are wholly above womanhood, both an example and an instrument of virtue. In you live the remaining virtues of a good age; through you both your sex breathes again toward glory and your lineage retains its slipping [Col. 0289A] dignity. I should be accused of falsehood unless every person’s judgment concerning whatever is best agreed with mine on this point.

### LETTER IX

[Note: Otherwise no. 58. Written about 1107.]

To the bishop of Beauvais.

[Note: Thus the Évreux and Rouen manuscripts; perhaps Gualo or Valo, later bishop of Paris, who died in 1114 as a cardinal.]

He gives thanks for services rendered in his city to one of Hildebert’s dependants.

I confess that I have attained the fullness of my desires, since I have been granted access to the threshold of your favour. Received there, [Col. 0289B] although I do not see you yourself, I nevertheless see your affection in my young dependent: when he comes to Beauvais, whenever you consider it necessary, you extend to him the hand of protection. To seek by prayers that you not cease would be to obscure the splendour of your assistance. I do not fear that you will fail in this resolve, since both your office makes you wish to come to the oppressed and your court enables you to do so. Meanwhile, offering you heaped-up thanks, I end my letter, though I shall by no means set an end to my affection for you.

### LETTER X

[Note: Otherwise no. 28. Written about 1109.]

To S., returned from Rome.

[Note: Thus the Rouen and Évreux manuscript codices.]

Since all things ought to be common among friends, Hildebert declares that, with that friend whose return from Rome delights him, he has suffered in affection all the hardships and dangers of the journey.

[Col. 0289C]

Your return has gladdened both my face and my day. Perhaps you do not know it; but I was with you in Rome. With you I suffered the hardships of snow; with you I endured mountains, slippery with ice or made rough by rocks. I endured with you all that I grieved to see you endure. For such is the concord of minds between friends: nothing is alien to one from the other, nothing is peculiar to either. One will makes all things one commonwealth for them.

Know, then, that under these laws of friendship I returned to you in memory, was beside you in compassion, and acted for you in prayers. The Lord therefore heard and answered the cry of my heart, because you have returned safely to your friends, both with dutiful greeting to the Church and with health. Farewell.

### LETTER XI

[Note: Otherwise no. 10. Written about 1112.]

To the queen of the English, namely Matilda.

[Note: The same queen to whom he directed Letter 4 of Book One.]

He congratulates her on her good health, which he says is necessary to the observance of the laws and very useful to the welfare of the Church.

[Col. 0289D]

HILDEBERT, humble minister of Le Mans, to MATHILDA, venerable queen of the English: may you stand at the right hand of him at whose right hand stood the queen, clothed in gold and surrounded by variety.

Having heard from the bearer of this letter both of the health in which you are well and of the greeting with which you have deigned to honour me, joy arose in me from the first, while from the second there overflow to me distinction and glory. For I stand convicted of sinning against the laws and against the Church unless my spirit rejoices and exults at the welfare of her whose soundness preserves sound both reverence for the laws and the condition of the Church.

For there is nothing in which a Christian soul ought more to rejoice than in the welfare of those through whom both the integrity of the laws and the sound condition of the Church endure. I rejoice, therefore; and I shall rejoice whenever a breath of air bringing news of your safety reaches [Col. 0290B] my ears, whenever I hear that the queen lives and is well—the queen to whom authority has been entrusted for judging crime and character for providing an example of honour.

### LETTER XII

[Note: Otherwise no. 43. Written about 1115.]

To Queen M.

[Note: Thus the Rouen and Évreux codices.]

He promises Queen Matilda of the English an inviolable affection of charity and prayers, though separated by the whole expanse of seas.

Holy love knows no hindrance of place or time. Affection rules within it, being always its own master, and no outside force impairs its claim. At every time it is permitted to love, even if it is not permitted to see the person loved. Therefore, though separated from you by sea and land, I love you in Christ, carrying remembrance of you to that place where an honourable thought merits reward and an unlawful one [Col. 0290C] punishment. For at the altar of the Lord the memory of you accompanies me, and I fear that it may turn to my judgment if I deprive you of that intercession which, Queen, you have purchased by your benefits.

### LETTER XIII

[Note: Otherwise no. 32. Written at least after 1120, when Hildebert was probably restored to Henry I’s favour, as is clear from the consolatory letter he wrote to him on the drowning of his son, which occurred in 1120. The bishop of Angers mentioned here seems to have been no one other than Raynald, who did not move to the Church of Reims until after Ralph the Green, who died in 1124, according to Orderic, Book XII.]

To H., king of the English.

[Note: Thus the Rouen and Évreux codices.]

To Henry I, king of the English, whom he extols with great praise, he strongly commends the younger brother of the bishop of Angers.

Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who in your times has restored peace to the poor and ancient dignity to the Churches! We confess it as a divine gift, acclaimed by the desires of all good persons, that a judge has come to vices and a founder to morals. The throne of justice has been exalted, and under a most merciful king proper order is restored to affairs: a king who knows how to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s and to God the things that are God’s.

Moreover, whoever is said to be able to help anyone before this king has obtained the favour of a happier fortune. Even if he cannot do so, it is still a great source of glory that people suppose him able. For it is granted to no ordinary person to extort the favour of that king who judges a day badly spent in which he has no opportunity to act against ruined morals [perhaps missing: “to correct them”]. It is the mark of a great mind, glorying in virtue, to bend stern powers toward its desire.

Very many imagine that I can do this; they report that I have gained this favour in your eyes. The bishop of Angers also thinks so, a man lacking in no kind of virtue; he would not believe me to have greater power than I myself can believe I possess. He judged it right to choose your servant as his spokesman before you, in order to commend to the royal majesty his brother, to be trained in the disciplines of knighthood.

The boy indeed had access to the courts of high rank, but with a higher counsel one brother provided the other a court in which he might learn military service without unlearning honour. He was therefore sent to the summit of character, sent to the glory of soldiers, sent to the most serene king, in whose camps neither service is deprived of reward nor valour of honour. It concerns your majesty, out of regard for the bishop, to receive the boy sent to you and to win each one's favour through the other.

For my part, if my merits give me any confidence, I have resolved to make petition for him. But I know a king who pays no regard to merits, because it is his nature to surpass all persons in merits. Yet if merit is required, I deserve well of the king in that place where the Son is sacrificed to the Father. Farewell.

### LETTER XIV

[Note: Otherwise no. 73. Written about 1120.]

To M., daughter of King H.

[Note: Matilda. Concerning her Homeyer says in the *Supplement*, p. 541: “Matilda, married to Emperor Henry V, according to Matthew Paris, in 1110, and solemnly wed in 1114. After his death she was given to Geoffrey, count of Anjou, called Plantagenet, by whom she bore Henry II, king of England. She died in 1167, and the following epitaph was inscribed upon her:

> Great by birth, greater by her husband, greatest by her offspring:  
> Here lies Henry’s daughter, spouse, and parent.”]

[Note: Thus the manuscripts of Rouen and Évreux.]

He asks Matilda, daughter of Henry I, king of the English, to deign herself to inform him what is occurring in England, and especially what her father’s feeling is concerning the insult inflicted upon his daughter.

[Col. 0291C]

I speak of things known and confirmed by frequent experience. For a thirsty person it is more satisfying to extinguish the burning of thirst from a spring than from a stream. Wines taken from the first cask retain their native flavour; transferred repeatedly from one vessel to another, they deteriorate. So too, my desire is more abundantly fulfilled by learning from your letter what is happening concerning you than by another’s report. Whatever I receive from you about you will be more certain to me than if common rumour brought the same thing to my ears.

Therefore, as soon as I learned that the winds were favouring your service, I immediately sent you a letter, thinking that someone arriving from England would reveal to us the king’s will and explain what feeling a father’s heart had assumed concerning the affront offered to his daughter. That I may deserve to learn these things through you, I call after you. Yet I call as your friend in the Lord, as [Col. 0292A] your servant in Christ, as one who places your honour at the beginning of his joy. Whatever you know ought to be communicated to a friend concerning the king as well as concerning yourself, I ask that it be disclosed to me.

180. LETTER XV. [Note: New, from the manuscripts of Évreux, Rouen, and others. Already published by Dom Mabillon, *Analecta*. Written about 1122.] He thanks Reginald, monk of St Augustine, for sending him the history of the monk Malchus, written by Reginald in verse. He then promises to enter with him into a closer friendship which will never cease, and which he wishes to nourish by mutual fruits of literary talent; he also mentions certain pieces published here by himself.

HILDEBERT, humble priest of the people of Le Mans, to REGINALD, monk of Blessed Augustine: all that he himself is.

I received your *Malchus* while occupied, indeed; yet I left it reluctantly. Although hindered by ecclesiastical business, I nevertheless read it through to the end, admiring in it both the beauty of its arrangement and its power. In it, having ranged quite suitably through poetic licence, you have assisted the historical event not merely with the inventions of fable, but have also set forth, in concise speech, alike the offices of nature and of truth. The wild olive and the natural olive have so clung together in one stock that, although neither is identical with the other, each is nevertheless one in effect with the other. Thus I owe praise to your work, because I have read something most worthy; and thanks to its author, because he judged me worthy to receive what was to be read.

You shall therefore have me as another Pylades, unless you disdain to become another Orestes to me. Yet I do not dare to profess myself your companion, but I promise myself your friend. For I may not rise to the equality denoted by companionship; but I may attain to that goodwill which is the fruit of friendship, which, though begun in time, remains for eternity. Let us therefore pray for one another, that we may be saved. That it may increase daily, let us converse more frequently by writings. Let not the intervening seas hinder the office of charity; what has for a time been delayed by the distance of lands will be received more gratefully by a friendly hand.

You should know that I not only do not blame, but likewise honour and embrace, the fact that you have indicated that you inserted into your work certain offspring of my little talent, or portions of our verses. For then I begin to please myself, when I see that my writings do not displease my betters. Farewell, brother; love one who loves you; write to one who writes to you.

## LETTER XVI

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 4. Written about 1124.]

To Bishop G. [Note: Thus the royal manuscript and the Rouen manuscript. Perhaps Girard of Angoulême.] He asks a certain bishop to show favour toward a cleric named William.

For your William, holy Father, I should think it necessary to entreat you, unless he alone were sufficient to you for gaining your favour. Moreover, I judged it superfluous to stir up toward beneficence a bishop who, even before becoming bishop, was accustomed to do good even to the undeserving. Dignity did not bring this quality with it, but found it already there. Therefore I do not fear that, as bishop, you will renounce beneficence, when before you were bishop you bound yourself to it. I also believe that the aforesaid brother is not unworthy for you voluntarily to open to him the threshold of your favour.

## LETTER XVII

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 77. Written before 1125.]

To Subdean A. [Note: Namely, of Tours, named Anselm. Thus the Rouen manuscript.] After extolling the virtue of hospitality, Hildebert thanks his friend for the hospitality which he had shown, without being asked by Hildebert, to three of his clerics. He does not, however, approve the attempt to conceal or disguise this good work under the pretext of avoiding vanity.

There have been those who said that, among the six works of mercy, none is to be preferred to hospitality. I think that they observed that in hospitality there are found certain things by which the various hardships of those received are known to be repelled. For this reason [they proclaimed] most splendid the grace of hospitality, through which Lot and Abraham, because they were accustomed to entertain men, deserved also to entertain angels. Moreover, as though for a greater reward of this grace, the one escaped the overthrow of Sodom, while the other deserved to obtain a son from his barren wife.

Something from above, I think, has likewise come to you: while you practise the aforesaid beneficence, you gathered in three Christs of Christ, and made the sacrifice of hospitality—which you had rendered most welcome by its provision—even more welcome by cheerfulness. Certainly, when your dependants were passing through Tours, they plainly thanked me, declaring that a benefit had been bestowed upon them in my name. Yet I could not remember what I had done for you, or for anyone on your account, such that you ought to render service to me, or to anyone on my account. It may, however, have happened that, to avoid boasting, you said that the benefit was conferred on my behalf when you conferred it upon them for the Lord and in the Lord.

But a devout act ought by no means to have been concealed, if you yourself were not desirous of passing praise. For a grave offence attends those who despise such praise if they prefer that their good deeds remain hidden rather than be seen. Thus Gregory also says: “Whoever is now sufficiently able to trample underfoot human praise sins culpably if he conceals the good things that he does.” [Note: It is found somewhat differently in the new edition of St Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule*, chapter 35: “For whoever is now sufficiently able to trample down the desire for praise commits a fraud against edification if he conceals the good things that he does.”]

## LETTER XVIII

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 72. In Mabillon’s edition of the works of St Bernard this letter is numbered 122, where it is noted as written about 1130.]

To the Abbot of Clairvaux. [Note: Thus the Rouen and Évreux manuscripts, and others.] Moved by the fame of St Bernard’s holiness and learning, spread throughout the world, Hildebert elegantly and earnestly asks to be admitted to the sanctuary of his friendship and intimacy. Meanwhile he commends to him Gebuin, archdeacon of Troyes, as a man outstanding in character and learning.

[Note: St Bernard speaks of Gebuin in Letter 17 to Peter the Deacon, cardinal: “Certain brothers,” he says, “have taken down in their own writing some things which they heard me say in their presence … One of them is available to you: namely, the precentor of Troyes and Archdeacon Gebuin; and you may easily have, if anything pleases you, what he has excerpted.” Mabillon writes on that letter: “Hildebert calls Gebuin conspicuous for character and learning in Letter 53 [rather, number 72 in the old ordering].” Nicholas of Clairvaux praises his eloquence and wisdom in Letter 5, where he mentions his sermon on the Gospel text, “If the Son shall make you free,” etc. A volume of his sermons survives in the Victorine Library. This is the precentor of Troyes whose flowers John of Salisbury seeks in Letter 76. Compare Peter the Venerable, Book II, Letters 34 and 35.]

We believe that few are ignorant that balsam is known by its fragrance and a tree by its fruit. Thus also, dearest brother, from your reputation we have learned how fitted you are for holiness and how sound in learning. Although the distance between places separates us far from you, news nevertheless reaches us of how delightfully you spend your nights with your Rachel; what offspring from Leah abounds for you; and how wholly you show yourself both a cultivator of virtue and an enemy of the flesh. All who speak to us of you describe no other person.

Such is the fragrance of your name, like poured-out oil; such already are the rewards of your merits. Before the final harvest you gather these ears of grain from your field. For in this life there is a certain reward of virtue: conspicuous and imperishable testimony. Virtue itself gains this for itself and keeps it for itself. Its brightness is not diminished by envy, nor assisted by outward efforts. Good repute can no more be taken away by false accusations than it can be acquired by flattering favour. It lies with the persons themselves either to make it grow through abundance of virtues or to diminish it through deficiency.

Certainly, hope has been laid up in the bosom of the Church concerning your most celebrated reputation: it will not fall, because it is believed to be founded upon the firm rock. Having learned your devotion from it, we long with longing to be received into the sanctuary of your friendship, and there to be with you in remembrance, where, withdrawing yourself from the conversations of mortals, you speak with the King of Angels on behalf of mortals.

Moreover, Gebuin, archdeacon of Troyes, a man distinguished in character and learning, has greatly increased this desire of ours. We should judge him worthy of recommendation to you, unless it were certain that those whom you deign to favour need no other recommendation. If you do not know it, we have learned also from his testimony that you are in the Church one who is sufficient for the training of virtue both by example and by word. But, lest you be burdened by a longer letter, we set an end to our writing—though we shall by no means set an end to the aforesaid petition until we deserve to be heard. We ask that, by the return of your letters, we may be informed what you think of this.

## LETTER XIX

[Note: Added. Written about 1130. Among the letters of St Bernard it is numbered 123 in Mabillon’s edition.]

This is St Bernard’s reply to Hildebert’s preceding letter. He returns his praises, while claiming none of the praise offered to himself.

A good man brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart. Most reverend man, I received gladly enough the writings of your glory—or rather, of my own—finding in them grounds on which I may rightly glorify you and rightly glory myself. For this is our glory: the condescension of your eminence and your esteem for our littleness. Indeed, not to be high-minded in high station, but to associate with the lowly (Rom. 12:16), is nothing dearer to God and nothing rarer among men. Who is wise except one who submits to the counsels of Wisdom? For it says: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things all the more” (Ecclus. 3:20). You have shown this to me: greater to one lesser, elder to one younger.

Accordingly I too could extol your proven wisdom with praise not undeserved, and perhaps with praise more just than that with which it itself has deigned to honour me. For, in establishing the certainty of things, it matters what uncertain rumour proclaims and what manifest action makes indubitable. What we prove more certainly, we also proclaim more confidently. You must see, then, how you have proved what you chose to write to me about me. I hold an argument for your praises that is beyond doubt: your very letters praising me. In them another may perhaps delight in the distinction of learning, sweetness and purity of speech, luminous discourse, and a pleasing and praiseworthy conciseness. But above these, I prize that humility by which, so great a man, you took care to anticipate so small a one—by the service of greeting, the proclamation of praise, and the reverence of prayer.

Certainly, as far as I am concerned, I read in your letter about myself not what I am, but what I should like to be, and what I am ashamed not to be. Nevertheless, what I am is yours; and if ever by God’s gift I shall be anything better, be assured, most reverend and beloved Father, that it shall be yours.

## LETTER XX

[Note: New, in the *Spicilegium* and Évreux manuscript. Written about 1130. This letter makes clear that Hildebert was not only restored to the favour of Henry I, king of the English, but was made so intimate with him that he could freely intercede with him for friends. He seems to have written it as archbishop of Tours and at the end of his life, after being appointed patron of the monastery of Fontevraud by the supreme pontiff at the request of the nuns themselves. Since this order from its beginning spread widely in many directions, it seems probable that it had already reached England, and that Hildebert interceded in this letter with Henry I, already his benefactor, on behalf of some monastery of the Fontevraud order already built there. He speaks here in the first person in such a way as to attribute to himself whatever benefit King Henry might confer upon the nuns; this could be the office only of their most excellent patron.]

He entreats Henry I, king of the English, to deign to protect and honour a certain convent of nuns and its abbess.

To his benefactor and lord.

Neither speech suffices to explain how greatly we are indebted to your generosity, nor can we repay in deed the thanks that we owe for your benefits. Yet, insofar as it is granted us from above, we shall multiply prayers to God for your preservation and salvation as much as for our own. But because perhaps—something we cannot say without tears—we shall see your face no longer, we have judged it right to bring before your providence what concerns your salvation.

There is a certain dependent house in your land in which nuns of good repute and approved character are known to serve the Lord. Therefore we beseech your Highness, for the salvation of your soul and of the souls of your parents, to deign to maintain that house. May you also be willing to hear the abbess of the aforesaid place, who has earned a good name by her religious life and conduct and who, wearied in seeking protection for the said house, has come as far as you; in her, as we believe, you will receive Christ.

Finally, we have heard that you are about to cross the sea and depart far from us. But be assured of this: many waters will not be able to quench the love with which we embrace you, and in which we ask the Lord that the angel of peace may accompany your journey.

## LETTER XXI

[Note: This letter was drawn from the archive of St Vincent of Le Mans, where it bears this heading: “Concerning the dispute between us and the monks of Jumièges.” It is numbered LXXXII and is cited by Dom Bondonnet under this note: “Written in 1129,” that is, four years, as Hildebert says here, after his departure from the Church of Le Mans.]

To WILLIAM, Abbot of St Vincent. In the dispute with the monastery of Jumièges—or, as he calls it, Gemegense—over the churches of Seona and Cortegaem, Hildebert testifies that in the time of his episcopate the monks of Jumièges raised no suit or claim.

The humble archbishop of Tours, to WILLIAM, abbot of St Vincent of Le Mans: greeting and blessing.

We have recognized that it belongs to pious and holy devotion, and accords with our profession, that assent ought not to be denied to sacred desires. Hence, William, brother and abbot of St Vincent, we have judged that your requests ought to be followed with assent: you ask that the possessions of your monastery be so defended and freed from unjust attacks that you make no attempt upon what belongs to another’s right.

Accordingly, you have now requested both our assistance and our counsel concerning a certain new and irrational claim of the abbot and monks of the monastery of Jumièges, who say that the church of Seona and the church of Cortegaem, with everything belonging to them, are by right possessions of their monastery. They have at last raised this claim after four years since our departure from the Church of Le Mans, and under the summons of our venerable brother Guy, bishop, they undertook to pursue a case with us; but certain religious persons altogether affirm that they failed to appear.

What we ought and can testify concerning this matter, we both say and testify. By God’s permission, we occupied the see of Le Mans for twenty-eight years. Yet during so long a time, neither the monks of the monastery of Jumièges nor their abbot brought before us a synodal claim concerning the aforesaid churches; nor was any claim concerning them made, with us hearing it, in any council. Moreover, neither the abbot nor the monks of St Vincent, so long as we sat in the aforesaid church, were found absent when summoned to justice, or to have evaded any judgment whatsoever. I also recall that I was archdeacon for five years before becoming bishop. Yet I neither recall nor know that any synodal complaint concerning the aforesaid churches was raised.

## LETTER XXII

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 2. Written about 1131.]

To R., Archdeacon of Nantes. [Note: Thus the manuscript of St Ouen at Rouen; perhaps “of Nantes.” Royal manuscript 4103 and Victorine manuscript 292 have “Robert.” It is scarcely known who this Robert, archdeacon of Nanton or Nantes, was. Homeyus suspects—though, as he says, not without hesitation—that he was the man of whom Robert of Torigni says under 1170: “At Christmas King Henry [I of England] was in Brittany, that is, Lesser Brittany. At Nantes Robert the archdeacon, with the king’s consent, was made bishop.” And under 1184: “Robert, bishop of Nantes, a man of great integrity and our friend, died when returning from Jerusalem.” This nevertheless accords sufficiently with Hildebert’s dates: he died in 1134, when Robert, being at least twenty-five years old and archdeacon, could have died at no more than seventy years of age.]

He promises his dearest friend unending fidelity and service, especially in exile. Meanwhile he rejoices that, even in exile and amid arms, his friend devotes himself to letters, especially poetry; and he marvels that the same man is Caesar in arms and Virgil in verse.

It is right that those who share prosperity should also share adversity [perhaps, “with those in adversity”]. Hence I am pierced by the same darts by which I learned that you were wounded. Whatever it is by which you are harmed does not pursue you alone, but another as well. I endure with you all that I grieve to see you endure. You chose me as your friend while the sky was clear; you will find me so while it is cloudy. It is a shameful gain to cultivate one’s neighbour while fortune succeeds, and to ignore him when matters go badly. Therefore, whatever I have and whatever I can do, I prefer should serve an exile rather than a citizen. For as an exile you will prove a true friend whom perhaps, as a citizen, you would not have recognized.

Yet there is some remedy for this desolation of yours in the fact that, even amid arms, you continue to profess yourself wholly a poet. I judge him free from cares in whom graceful verse abounds, rich both in thought and arrangement. For it cannot be that the same breast should be both the workshop of such great anxieties and of such studies. In arms I hear that you are Caesar; in verse I marvel that you are Virgil. So long as you reproduce Virgil thus, I shall not believe that you either attend to or feel the business of Caesar or the labours of warfare. Otherwise you bear a spirit greater than that of mortals, since you remain whole amid pursuits so discordant.

## LETTER XXIII

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 27. Of uncertain date.]

To Dean F. [Note: Thus the Rouen and Évreux manuscripts.] It is the office of a true friend to anticipate by kindness the prayers of friends. He says that he has done this, and promises to do so, for the imprisoned friend of the addressee.

It is beyond one’s duty to delay aid to the oppressed until one is asked. Benefits ought to be given with such promptness that the unprepared person receives them rather than the importunate one extorts them. Therefore I have decided to anticipate the prayers for which I waited, lest, if I came to help when asked, I should be judged to have helped too late. Your prisoner will not be silent about this: I offered myself freely and gladly to him for every act of kindness. I visited him frequently with blessings, carefully pursuing every means by which either the constrictions of prison or poverty might be relieved. But lest your prayers accomplish nothing for him, I shall repeat the same actions more often. Farewell.

## LETTER XXIV

[Note: New, from the *Spicilegium* and manuscripts.]

He commends to a certain official of the Roman curia a friend named Simon, and asks him to arrange for Simon to become attached to the household of the Roman Church.

I shall confess myself successful if it be granted me to reach the threshold of your favour. I have found, I think, a short route to it, since I have resolved both to honour and to love your Simon. For custom has it that one who loves the son is loved by the father. I love the aforesaid young man, whose natural disposition and many graces of character sufficiently demand to be loved, and indeed more than loved, extolled. To achieve this, I should like acquaintance with him to be extended and for him to become attached to the Roman Church, where such character finds both favour and reward. For it has benefited many to frequent her: they obtain by their life the advancement which their condition denies them.

## LETTER XXV

[Note: New, from the *Spicilegium* and manuscripts. Of uncertain date.]

To a friend. [Note: It is not clear who this friend was, nor when this letter was written.] In response to a friend’s inquiry as to what the Lord Jesus wrote on the ground when the adulterous woman was brought before him, he explains what he has learned on the matter from St Ambrose.

You made yourself wholly known to me when you wished to be taught by me whence I had the statement that our Lord, when an adulterous woman was presented to him by the Jews for judgment, wrote with his finger upon the ground: “Earth, earth, write these men rejected.” You also asked that, if the Saviour wrote this same thing twice, or something else that had come to my knowledge, I should not consider it burdensome, sweetest brother, to write it to you.

Certainly I have learned nothing else about this except what a diligent reader can readily extract from the letters of Ambrose. I have therefore taken care briefly to set before you what became known to my smallness concerning these matters.
