It is clear that, at the accusation of the adulterous woman, the Lord bowed his head and wrote upon the ground. But the Evangelist has left us nothing certain about what he wrote, whether he wrote the same thing [perhaps “or something else” is missing], or what he wrote first or second.

But Ambrose, writing to Studius, says: [Note: See St Ambrose, Letter 25 of the first class, to Studius—or, as the manuscript of Jumièges has it, Studiosus—and Letter 26 of the same class in the latest edition. Hildebert drew from these what he reports concerning this question. Moreover, the words “Earth, earth, earth” are not found expressly except in the Septuagint. In the Vulgate, however, the equivalent is found concerning Jeconiah, Jeremiah 22:29–30: “O earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: Write this man childless, a man who shall not prosper in his days.”]

> “When the Jews had found an adulterous woman, they brought her before the Saviour, seeking to entrap him: if he acquitted her, he would seem to dissolve the law—he who had said, ‘I came not to dissolve the law, but to fulfil it’ (Matt. 5:18); if he condemned her, he would seem to have come contrary to the purpose of his own mission. Foreseeing this, therefore, the Lord Jesus, with bowed head, wrote upon the ground. What did he write, except that prophetic saying: ‘Earth, earth, write these men rejected’ (Jer. 22:29), which is read concerning Jeconiah in the prophet Jeremiah?”

Writing to Irenaeus, Ambrose says of the same woman: [Note: Letter 26, first class, to Irenaeus.]

> “A woman guilty of adultery was brought before the Lord Jesus by the Scribes and Pharisees, and was brought by this device: if he acquitted her, he would seem to dissolve the law; if he condemned her, he would alter the purpose of his coming, since he came to forgive the sins of all. For above he says: ‘I judge no one’ (John 8:15). Those bringing her said: ‘We found this woman openly committing adultery. Now it is written in the law of Moses that every adulteress is to be stoned’ (Lev. 20:10). ‘What then do you say concerning her?’ As they said this, Jesus, with bowed head, wrote upon the ground. And while they waited to hear him, he raised his head and said: ‘Let him who is without sin be the first to stone her.’ What judgment could be more divine than this: that the one who punishes sins should himself be free from sin? How can you endure one who avenges another’s offence and defends his own crime? Does he not rather condemn himself, when he condemns in another what he himself commits? He said this and wrote upon the ground. What else did he say than: ‘You see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not see the beam in your own eye’ (Luke 6:41)? For lust is like a speck: it is quickly kindled and swiftly consumed.”

Moreover, as your prudence has learned from the Evangelist’s testimony, after the first writing was finished, when Christ raised his head and the Jews were waiting for his answer, he said: “Let him among you who is without sin be the first to cast a stone at her” (John 8:7). But after the second writing, again raising his head, he is read to have said to the woman: “Woman, where are those who accused you?” When she answered, “No one, Lord,” he added: “Neither do I condemn you. Go, and sin no more” (ibid., 8:10–11).

Certainly, although John set these events in order, he omitted to write what the Lord wrote. We also have from the words of Ambrose what he wrote; but we do not have what he wrote first or what he wrote second. Farewell, brother; and if anyone else has discovered anything authoritative on these matters, I ask to be instructed through the service of your letters.

## LETTER XXVI

[Note: New, from the *Spicilegium* and manuscripts. Of uncertain date.]

To a friend. [Note: Perhaps Marbod, bishop of Rennes.] He promises inviolable constancy in friendship.

If matters go well with you, I rejoice with you; if otherwise—which may it not be!—I sympathize. For you are to be embraced both for your learning and for your manner of life, and you have earned an enduring dwelling in my heart. Thus, though far from me, you are wholly present with me in memory. Know also that since the feast of St Lawrence I have been afflicted with quartan fevers and have wholly laid aside my cares, enduring what it pleases my Lord for me to endure. Know that I am devoted to your will and service.

## LETTER XXVII

[Note: Of uncertain date.]

To a friend. [Note: Perhaps an Englishman, since he asks that his reply cross the sea to him.] He rejoices at his friend’s prosperity and safety, meanwhile offering him with all his heart whatever belongs to him.

Joy and exultation overflow in me whenever, through the service of report, I learn that you are well. For it is customary for me to honour you, embrace you, and count your advancement among my own successes. Hence the prosperity that attends you yields me fullness of joy, while your safety adds its crowning measure. Let me be charged with falsehood if you ask from me in vain what may be given to a friend and what it is expedient to bestow. Meanwhile I ask that a letter concerning your welfare may cross the sea to me, so that I may know the secret of your will.

## LETTER XXVIII

[Note: New, from the manuscript of Foucarmont and others, and the *Spicilegium*. Of uncertain date.]

Hildebert thanks a bishop who was his friend for the kindly and unsolicited assistance shown to some of his household, whom a storm had imperilled on a journey.

When stormy weather had closed the sea to our servants who were about to sail, and the favour of the winds was lacking, yours was not lacking. When they had finally boarded ship and had almost completed their voyage, treacherous weather hurled them backward from a port already near; but they found a harbour in the breast of a bishop. There was rest for the weary, there provision for expenses that had failed. Long waiting for calm weather had worn them down; but you provided them with what was necessary both for using the winds and for awaiting them.

A fair and praiseworthy benefit indeed! It was bestowed for no merits, conferred with no sorrow, and obtained by no entreaties. Nothing in it diminished the greatness of the kindness. It came at the name of a friend, not at prayers.

## LETTER XXIX

[Note: New, from the *Spicilegium*, the manuscript of Foucarmont, and others. Of uncertain date.]

Hildebert, afflicted, mourns the death of one who had become most friendly to him after having been his enemy.

Often it steals into human minds that, when people are stung by some slight agreement [perhaps “offence”], if voluntary acts do not yield to them through zeal, they fail in their duty. This is tolerable in another class of men; but among those who devote themselves to divine things it is full of grief. Your gracious letter breaks my silence. I confess that I grieve with bitter grief, having until now kept silent concerning the death of one who had clothed himself in such devotion toward the Lord and had shown such affection toward me that he now loved the man whom he had formerly persecuted, and regarded as a father the man whom he had formerly rejected as an adversary.

## LETTER XXX

[Note: New, from the *Spicilegium* and Évreux manuscript. Of uncertain date.]

To William, bishop of Winchester, he frankly acknowledges that it pleased him greatly that William had asked for his little works to be sent, and he very modestly promises to send them.

To WILLIAM, by God’s grace venerable bishop of Winchester, HILDEBERT, priest of the people of Le Mans: greeting and the earnestness of service.

I was pleased with myself, insofar as I did anything capable of pleasing your will. Thus my spirit rejoiced with great joy when I learned that your messenger was crossing the sea to me and that through him you were asking something of me. For you asked that my little works be copied out for you and, once copied, sent. On hearing this I hesitated for some time, both fearing to offend a friend and fearing to provoke laughter among readers. If I do not obey you, I commit a fault; if I presume to do what you require, I am found ridiculous. Since it was necessary to incur one or the other, I preferred [to move] readers to laughter at me rather than to offend against a friend.

The former is an inconvenience; the latter a fault. There the person is harmed; here nature is harmed. Yet I have learned from the philosopher that one who commits an injury is more wretched than one who suffers it. Therefore the wise person bears injuries calmly, but—even when offended—does not know how to inflict them. I have accordingly adopted this wisdom for your sake, most blessed bishop, so that, provided I comply with a friend, tongues that gratuitously disparage me may detract nothing from my joy. I confess that I shall count it as a favour if I gain your goodwill by these or other services. But be assured of this: you repay me in return if you love me and pray for me. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXI

[Note: New, from the *Spicilegium*, Évreux, and Rouen manuscripts. Of uncertain date.]

To a bishop. [Note: Perhaps St Anselm, to whom he had once sent a fan; on this see Hildebert, Letter 2 of Book I, and what St Anselm himself seems to mention in his Letter 11 to Hildebert in Book II: “You anticipated me in love, as you demonstrated by your gift.”] He thanks a bishop who was his closest friend for the episcopal sandals sent to him. He explains their form as observed in the Gallican Church, together with the reason why the Gospel-book is offered open to the bishop but closed to others.

Although we cannot give the thanks that we owe, we nevertheless give such thanks as we can, because you have shod your feet in readiness for the Gospel of peace. For you sent excellent sandals, in which both friendship was displayed and instruction offered. They stir our sluggishness with hidden goads and, as it were, knock with a hand that we may wake and take up the feet of those who proclaim good things.

This exhortation pleases us, and from it the sandals derive their grace, although they do not preserve the usual form of sandals. For it is both customary and rational that sandals should be pierced from above, so that the whole foot may be seen and not wholly covered. A preacher ought neither to conceal the mysteries of the Gospel from everyone nor disclose them to everyone. Hence the Lord says to the apostles: “To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the rest in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand” (Luke 8:10). And elsewhere: “Do not cast pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6).

For the same reason a hand is sent to Ezekiel in which there was a scroll rolled up; it is then read expanded before him, written within and without. From this, too, the Church has drawn the custom that the Gospel text is brought open for the bishop to kiss, but closed for others. We do not say this as though we were instructing you, but so that we may inform both a friend and a bishop what form of sandals the Gallican Church uses. [Note: Thus the *Spicilegium* from the Bigot manuscript, but erroneously. The Évreux and Rouen manuscripts are closer to the sense: “If among you they retain their complete form, we make no objection; but we explain the reason why we use pierced ones.”] But if among you [they have] not a complete … [lacuna] … may I nevertheless hope in the complete ones; that is, we explain the reason why we use them.

## BRIEF NOTICE

Although the following two letters do not appear foreign to Hildebert’s style, and although we found both in Colbert manuscript no. 4017 immediately after Hildebert’s final letter, the opening letters of each of them brought us into such doubt as to whether they were truly Hildebert’s that we judged they should almost be passed over in silence. Yet, because they contain excellent counsels for the spiritual life, and because we judged it possible that Hildebert, while still at Cluny, had composed them in the name and at the request of some archimandrite and sent them to monks established in a dependent house, we have thought fit to insert them here in smaller type, for the benefit of the devout reader, lest they perish.

[Note: Letters XXXII and XXXIII are by Odo, first abbot of St Peter of Auxerre. See d’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. II.]

## LETTER XXXII

O. to Brother R., greetings.

I beg you, dearest brother, to conduct yourself in the obedience entrusted to you in such a way that God may be praised and honoured in your life, and that through your good repute [Col. 0302D] our Church may be exalted. See that outwardly, before men, you have a good testimony, and inwardly, before God, that you rejoice in a good conscience. Now the conscience will be good if you have committed no evil deliberately, and have done, with a single-minded intention, whatever good you were able to do. [Col. 0303A] Otherwise, unless your intention is single and right, neither will the reputation that is outward be true, nor the conscience that is inward good.

The single-mindedness of intention is shown to be most upright when human praise is wholly rejected in a good work, and only the praise of God and the neighbour’s benefit are sought. Thus these two things—right action, namely, and single intention—produce two goods: for single intention gladdens the worker’s mind within through a good conscience, while right action, displayed outwardly, invites others to praise God and trains them to act well. Let us say with the Apostle—if indeed we can say it truthfully—“This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 2:12). For only that person can most justly glory whose good conscience bears testimony inwardly on his behalf.

Certainly, as it seems to me, a human being is very easily deceived; but God is never mocked. For man sees the face, but God sees the heart. Therefore let our conscience appear pure and single before God, [Col. 0303B] who sees within; and let our good work shine before men, who see the face, so that God may be glorified. Thus let our action be right and our intention single and pure, since our action proceeds in vain before the eyes if a good intention does not precede it; nor does the conscience have rest within when either a committed fault terrifies it, or human praise sought from a good work stings it with remorse.

Yet, if we wish to have a true knowledge of a good conscience, knowledge must necessarily precede conscience. For where there is no knowledge, there can be no conscience, either good or bad. But where knowledge comes first, it immediately becomes apparent whether conscience is good or bad. There are certain good people who, because of the purity of their life, do not have an evil conscience: through knowledge they diligently examine themselves. Being pure and clean, they are conscious of no evil in themselves. In these, knowledge comes first and a good conscience follows.

There are others who are indeed evil, but through knowledge recognize their own wickedness. By knowing themselves, they have an evil conscience; yet, grieving and groaning, they sometimes turn to repentance. An evil conscience speaks to their knowledge, but conscience, enlightened through knowledge, is changed for the better by repentance. There are also others, worse and far more depraved than those just mentioned, who, because of their folly, do not attend to their own wickedness. Since they either will not or cannot examine themselves through knowledge, having no light of knowledge, they sleep most dangerously amid their sins as in the blackest night. Such people return to repentance scarcely at all, or never, because they have lost repentance—that is, knowledge. For it is written: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. 1:18).

It is therefore plainly evident that one who has no knowledge cannot grieve for his sins. We see very many righteous persons weep most bitterly over the slightest faults; [Col. 0303D] and, conversely, the most wicked feel no grief for dreadful crimes, indeed even—what is greatly to be lamented—rejoice and exult. Of them it is written: “Who rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in most wicked things” (Prov. 2:14). But why is this so? Because the righteous, illumined by the light of knowledge, sternly rebuke themselves for the least things which they recognize in themselves; while evil persons, lacking the light of knowledge and utterly ignorant of themselves, do not know how to bewail in repentance even the horrible crimes they commit.

If, therefore, we desire truly to know what our consciences are like, we must apply ourselves to knowledge; and, in acquiring it, we must not rely upon our own industry, but upon God’s mercy alone and His superabundant grace. Let us therefore ask God’s mercy and implore His grace, that He may give [Col. 0304A] us knowledge and a good conscience, so that through knowledge we may truly recognize ourselves, and through a good conscience rejoice ineffably in His presence.

But woe is me, miserable man that I am, who have no good conscience and yet presume to speak of a good conscience! For how can my conscience be good, when I have committed many evils which I have not fittingly erased through repentance, and, sluggish and negligent, have refused to do the good which I ought to have done? A conscience cannot otherwise be good unless we both fittingly bewail through repentance the evils we have done and, God’s grace going before us, do the good that we can do. O good conscience, how lovable and delightful you are! O great treasure, beyond comparison with any earthly riches!

Certainly, nothing in this life is happier, nothing more delightful. But perhaps you say: “How do you know that nothing is happier, nothing more delightful? Sometimes we say that food is good because we know this by experience; [Col. 0304B] but you, as you said, do not have a good conscience. How, then, can you know that nothing is happier?” Perhaps you say this. But what am I to say? I cannot truthfully say what the Apostle says: “I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Cor. 4:4); indeed, I am conscious of much. Yet hear a comparison and understand the reasoning.

Certainly, through our eyes we see many things which we do not possess; so through reason we recognize that many things are good which we nevertheless do not do. By the same reason we discourse at length about many virtues from which we are empty. Behold: though I speak of a good conscience and discuss much by reason, I see, as it were through a good eye, what I nevertheless do not possess in myself. Hear another point: often, when we taste the bitterness of gall, we recognize the sweetness of honey. So too, one born in poverty and reared wholly amid miseries, when he considers those powerful in the world and possessed of riches, calls them happy and himself miserable, though, feeling only his own misery, he does not know by experience what their happiness is like. So, too, we who are hungry praise satiety, and we who are ill say that health is good. Thus from the unhappiness of the evil conscience which I experience, I reckon how great is the happiness of a good conscience. And because by experience I know that nothing is sadder than an evil conscience, I judge from that very sadness that nothing is more delightful than a good conscience. [Note: [Col. 0303] Saint Augustine says nearly the same thing, though more fully, in *On the Good of Widowhood*, ch. 22, vol. VI of the new edition, p. 385.]

Certainly, if a choice were offered me, I would rather endure every misery with a good conscience than possess every wealth with an evil conscience. But since those who are outside cannot see our consciences, at least our reputation, which can reach them, ought not to stink in their nostrils. “For if, trusting in our conscience, we neglect our reputation, as blessed Augustine says, we are cruel.” Indeed, in my judgment, we do not even possess a good conscience if through our negligence we incur disgrace. But if, conversely, human repute praises us while conscience within condemns us, we are like those who [Col. 0304D] are proclaimed rich in public yet are tormented in private by the straits of poverty.

You therefore, my brother, apply diligence; examine your conscience. Carefully attend to what sort of testimony it gives: attend to what it truthfully testifies to you concerning deeds, words, and even thoughts. Attend, I say, whether there is holiness in deed, truth in speech, purity in thought, and singleness of purpose in intention. If your conscience is conscious to itself of these things by their testimony, it can most rightly say that saying of the Apostle quoted above: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12).

But if by an evil deed you have ruined someone, if by your speech you have inflicted a curse or insult upon someone, if by an unlawful thought you have defiled the heart’s purity—if you have done this and have not yet made satisfaction through repentance—then I think that in these things you not only do not glory in conscience, but are tormented by inward shame. There are also certain other things by which our conscience is often put to shame: namely pride, anger, and sadness. May the merciful God take all these away from us and grant us a pure conscience. Farewell, and pray for me.

## LETTER XXXIII

To brother Fr. Fr. O., greetings.

When, dearest brother, you came to us during the feast-days of Pentecost, you called me aside and said reproachfully: “You have no care for me, but have cast me away as something worthless and useless.” When I carefully asked why you said this, you replied: “You frequently send consoling letters to the other brothers; but to me, who need them more than all the rest, who endure many temptations, you offer no consolation whatever.”

When I heard this, I accepted your rebuke gratefully and promised that, if I should have leisure hereafter, I would provide you some consolation. Yet you must know that I am frequently so entangled in such great occupations and harassed inwardly and outwardly by such great, though small, cares that I do not have leisure, as I desire, either to apply myself to reading, to write anything, or—what is better—to give myself to prayer. But because through your messenger you reminded me again, that I might remember my promise, although, as I have said, I am impeded by many things, charity compelling me, I shall briefly do what I promised.

Therefore, brother, do not be surprised if you suffer various temptations. For the life of man upon earth is temptation. Hence it is also written: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your heart for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1). Behold, in this saying you have clearly what you ought to do. You have now come to God’s service; you have now promised to serve God and live religiously. You must stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation, not for rest. [Col. 0305C] For very many, when they come to God’s service, return, with God’s permission, to their former sins because they shrink from labouring to acquire virtues.

If, then, you wish to escape the snares of temptations, you must undergo many labours both of heart and body. For who can without labour pierce his heart with compunction, cast away his own wills, and in all things fulfil the good wills of others? Who, I say, can without great labour and continual application fully recognize the devil’s manifold snares and, once known, avoid them? The labour of temptations is certainly great and not to be despised; yet for the love of God it must be borne most patiently. But lest, through temptation, you fall into despair, hear what the blessed Apostle James says: “Count it all joy, my brethren, when you fall into various temptations” (Jas. 1:2).

The usefulness of temptations, dearest brother, is great, because through temptation true humility is possessed. [Col. 0305D] For, I think, our pride would raise itself very high unless, with God’s permission, the weight of temptations pressed down that same pride. Often, when we suffer no outward temptations, we are endangered more seriously in heart by self-exaltation; and, because we neglect to consider our iniquity, we think great and incomparable things about ourselves and despise all others in comparison with ourselves.

But the merciful Lord sometimes, when He looks compassionately upon our exaltation, permits the temptation of the flesh to come upon us for our correction. He wishes the temptation of the flesh to humble the exaltation of the heart. He wishes us, conscious of our weakness, to think lowly and contemptible things of ourselves, so that through humility we may set even the least before ourselves. It is also good, when you endure any temptation, to call to mind the profession which you made. You professed chastity, community of goods, [Note: [Col. 0305D] That is, poverty, or the renunciation of private property.] and obedience. When you made this profession, you grievously offended the devil. He saw this profession and envied it. Therefore he applies distinct temptations against each particular profession. Against the profession of chastity he suggests fleshly lust; against the profession of community of goods he kindles desire for some possession; against the virtue of obedience he opposes the vice of disobedience.

But you, my brother, hold fast to your profession and carefully avoid temptation. If the devil attacks you, beware lest he conquer you; beware lest he overcome you. Resist firmly; fight manfully. If he hurls the dart of lust, oppose the shield of chastity. If he brings former actions and former pleasures back to your memory, [Col. 0306A] then, on the contrary, think of the pains of hell and its horrible punishments. For if you carefully consider the fire of Gehenna, you will quickly extinguish the fire of lust.

You must also preserve the affection of your heart within and, outwardly, [supplied: the gaze] of your eyes. For a corrupted affection of the eyes [perhaps: “of the heart”] directs the eyes’ sight toward unlawful things, and an unlawful gaze corrupts the inward affection. Therefore you must both purify the inward affection and restrain the outward gaze by discipline. Consider frequently how great the purity of chastity is, how pleasing and acceptable it is to God. Thus Truth says in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:15). For what is it to gird the loins except to restrain the flow of lust with the girdle of chastity?

O pure chastity, how high you dwell! O impure lust, how low you lie! Behold, chastity joins a human being to God and keeps God’s temple uncorrupted. Lust, on the other hand, separates a human being from God, associates him with the devil, and violates God’s temple. Therefore embrace the virtue of chastity; shudder at the vice of lust. Love the beauty of the former; flee the ugliness of the latter. Chastity is certainly a great and most beautiful virtue, provided humility is maintained together with chastity. Otherwise, we cannot please God by chastity alone unless we truly possess humility along with it. Indeed, chastity often suffers great assaults of temptations precisely because pride has not been expelled from the heart. If, therefore, you wish to be secure concerning chastity, be founded in humility.

Finally, because the devil sees that through the virtue of chastity we please God, even if he cannot take it away, he nevertheless does not cease to trouble it. Hence, while we are awake, he introduces shameful thoughts, if he can; while we are asleep, for our deception [perhaps: “by night”], he assumes the forms of various appearances. So great is his wickedness, so great his envy, that he does not consider what he makes of himself, or the forms of how base things he assumes, provided only that he may entice and deceive us. But whether waking or sleeping, as people belonging to the Lord and striving toward the Lord, let us repel shameful thoughts with good thoughts, and, fortified by the sign of the holy cross, let us not fear nocturnal illusions at all. [Col. 0306D] [Note: [Col. 0306D] Hildebert also recommends this in Letter 20 of the first book.]

It is also good for one who wishes to preserve chastity to maintain sobriety in food and drink and to persist frequently in prayer. For after the devil sees the fire of natural desire burn a little through the denial of foods, he immediately gathers within himself the spirit of wickedness and, with all his effort, emits the breath of temptation to kindle the fire of desire. Therefore it is good that the fire of desire be extinguished by the water of moderation and that the devil’s breath be repelled by the spirit of prayer.

Many things greatly assist in preserving chastity; but, dearest brother, let these suffice for you. If I still wished to discuss the profession of community of goods and obedience, the letter would now exceed due limits and its lengthier discourse would create weariness for the reader. I say only this briefly. I want you to know that whoever, after [Col. 0307A] the profession of community of goods, keeps in his private ownership either a horse, a garment, or even, what is less, an obol, cannot have any share with God or any communion with His saints unless he repents worthily. Likewise, whoever, after promising obedience, refuses with obstinate pride to obey the command of his superior can in no way be a co-heir of Jesus Christ, who became obedient unto death. [Note: [Col. 0307D] Hildebert speaks here as though he were a true monk.]

Therefore it is good that we possess absolutely no private property, lest we lose the beloved fellowship of the saints; and that we maintain obedience with the Lord Jesus Christ unto death, so that after death we may be able to receive from that same Lord the fruit of obedience. Farewell, and pray for me.

## LETTER XXXIV

[Note: [Col. 0307D] Written in the year 1099. We were unable to place this letter in its proper position because it came to our hands only when the final letter of this book was actually being sent to press. It was kindly supplied to us by our own Reverend Father Dom Theodoric Ruinart, as one of the letters addressed to Urban II which he was shortly to commit to the press. He judged it to be the work of no bishop of Le Mans other than Hildebert, since no one but Hildebert occupied the episcopal see of Le Mans from 1097 to 1099, the year in which he believed this letter was written. He had most recently received it also from the cartulary of the Abbey of Saint Vincent of Le Mans. [Note: [Col. 0307D] + See also Mabillon’s work, vol. II, p. 408.]] Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, to Urban II concerning the cemetery of Saint Vincent.

U., bishop of Le Mans, to his most holy Father.

[Col. 0307B] It is well known to all the faithful, spread far and wide throughout the spacious world, that the ancient Fathers, in order to avoid the crowds of cities, chose certain solitary places in which the bodies of the faithful might be honourably buried to God’s honour. In imitation of them, the pious and prudent concern of our holy predecessors founded, in the suburb of our city, upon possessions of the Church of Le Mans, [Note: [Col. 0308D] A Benedictine abbey still famous today, under the Congregation of Saint Maur and enjoying a regular abbot.] a certain abbey of Saint Vincent. There they themselves and their successors, the canons, and those dwelling in that part of the city known to belong to the bishop’s fief, were to be buried in succeeding times. A portion of the cemetery was separately reserved according to rule, in which [Col. 0307C] clerics were distinguished from others in the dignity of burial as they were in rank. For this reason, among other benefactions in our church, a certain prebend was granted of old to the monks of that monastery, so that those who offered sacrifices to the Lord God more particularly for our souls might be bound to us by a firm bond of charity and familiarity.

In this same cemetery, without dispute, both our bishops and canons have from ancient times down to the present obtained burial. But it recently happened, while I was absent, that one of our canons died. Consequently, while our canons were paying him in our church the service owed by brotherhood, as custom required, a few among them—always afflicted with the plague of discord—asserted that, while still living, he had commanded that he should be buried in the cemetery of Belloloco. The other faithful persons, however, who had been present at his confession and anointing, testified that he had requested burial among our brothers and fathers at Saint Vincent, although otherwise he should by no means have been interred there unless he became a monk or a regular.

But those who had stirred up the sedition committed the body of the deceased holy and religious man to burial, like sacrilegious persons, within our city but outside a cemetery, [Col. 0308B] in wholly unconsecrated ground, unlawfully appropriating the sacred rites. When the monks learned of my return, they repeatedly and humbly begged our lowliness to restore to them, according to the custom of our Church, the body of our canon. On this matter we summoned our chapter frequently and carefully, lest scandal be brought upon our Church by denying a brother his customary burial contrary to ancient custom. The greater part of the chapter likewise supported our counsel and command; but the arrogance of a few, as has been said, resisted reason and threatened punishment to all—except myself—who should carry the deceased’s body to the grave.

Indeed, the monks, finding themselves oppressed, since they could obtain their investiture neither by right nor by entreaty, appealed to the bosom of your mercy concerning those who had despoiled them. Therefore, sweetest Father, we truthfully make known to your blessedness the course of this matter, humbly entreating that you may deign to preserve its right for the poverty of the monks and crush by your authority the obstinacy of the perverse.

## BRIEF NOTICE

[Col. 0307]

Although, before committing the letters of the venerable Hildebert to the press, we omitted nothing in order to assign each of them its proper order, it could not be avoided that some of them, either not transmitted in manuscripts or omitted in editions, escaped our diligence. In the course of time, however, and long after the completion of the printing of the others, with the help of friends we recovered these few letters quite fortunately. We preferred to append them, though less orderly than the rest, rather than withhold them from the desire and benefit of scholars.

Since some of them have the style of diplomas rather than letters, we have taken care to place the genuine and proper letters first, and the diplomas or charters afterwards; to these we have appended learned notes by the distinguished M. Loyauté on certain matters.

## LETTER XXXV

[Note: [Col. 0308D] We extracted this letter from the papers of the distinguished M. Loyauté, lent to us by the distinguished M. Logé. Loyauté perhaps had extracted it from Juret’s notes on Letter 274 of Ivo of Chartres, which Juret had received from the jurist Antoine Oisel, who had found it in ancient parchments. Turstin’s name is written variously in different copies: sometimes *Turstinus*, sometimes *Turstanus*, or *Tursthannus*. With Juret, in his notes on the aforesaid letter of Ivo, we have adopted *Turstinus*.

This letter was occasioned by the serious dispute between the Churches of Canterbury and York. Ralph of Canterbury claimed that the Church of York was subject to his own Church in every respect; but Turstin of York claimed, as archbishop, that his Church was free from him. In the end, however, he lost the case in such a manner that he and his suffragan bishops, with their clergy, were compelled to render complete subjection to the archbishop of Canterbury as primate of all England. For a fuller account see Matthew Paris, in his *William the Conqueror*, and Juret at the cited place.

Nevertheless, in the Chronicle of Melrose, in Ingulph, the writer of English affairs, p. 164, it is written: “In the year 1121 Pope Calixtus, by his letters, compelled the king of England to accept Turstin as archbishop, and he was immediately received into his archbishopric without a demand for a profession.” Concerning this Turstin, Henry Knighton, book II of *The Events of England*, p. 2385, says: “Thurstan, archbishop of York, an outstanding founder of the monasteries of Hexham and Fountains and of eight others, assumed the monastic habit at Pontefract and died in a good old age; two years later his body was found fragrant and incorrupt.”]

He assures Turstin, archbishop of York, of his friendship towards him, and that he has never done, nor will ever do, anything whatsoever to oppose him in his dispute with Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury.

[Col. 0308D]

To TURSTIN, by God’s grace venerable elect of York, his dearest friend, HILDEBERT, humble priest of the people of Le Mans: never lightly to distrust a friend.

As Seneca testifies, it is a fault both to trust everyone and to trust no one. Hence you also bear some blame, if you allowed your mind to believe something adverse about a friend before proving it, and to distrust him before finding cause for distrust. For you wrote to me that it was on the lips of many that I had undertaken an embassy for the archbishop of Canterbury to the lord pope, so that one whom he himself could not bend might be bent by my authority—which is either none or slight. Your being moved, even slightly, by this report moved me not slightly. For you indicated that either I had never been the friend you believed me to be, or that I had disgracefully [Col. 0309B] ceased to be so.

But I have not yet assumed this audacity; I have not yet determined to oppose justice in such a way; I have not yet so persecuted myself as to place my shoulders under a burden which is neither easy to bear, because apostolic authority opposes it, nor honourable, because reason prevents it, nor useful, because the greatness of the danger hangs over it. Even if none of these impediments existed, I would still remember the Apostle saying: “If I rebuild the things which I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor” (Gal. 2:18).

Therefore do not believe, do not suppose, that I have changed, that I differ from what I was. I speak the truth; I speak my mind. As God lives, and the Son of God, and the Spirit of both, neither the lord of Canterbury nor anyone on his behalf has asked me either to commend his cause against the Church of York by letters or to undertake an embassy for it. There are matters which he himself disclosed to us and on which he sought our counsel, but they do not concern or hinder your cause in any way whatever. I spoke with him concerning the embassy which his predecessor [perhaps: undertook] and concerning other matters far removed from your affair; for the present I have not determined to visit the thresholds of the Apostles. You will return the favour to me if you persevere in our friendship. For I shall never endure to be forgetful of a friend, nor his deserter. Farewell. Do not delay sending me your letters.

## LETTER XXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0310C] From an old manuscript codex of Saint Albinus of Angers and from Baluze’s papers.] [Note: [Col. 0309] + See *Spicilegium*, vol. XIII. D’Achery attributes this letter to Marbod, bishop of Rennes, rather than Hildebert.] That married persons who have jointly and voluntarily vowed continence may not withdraw from their vow.

To M., [Note: [Col. 0310C] Marbod.] by God’s grace venerable bishop of Rennes, and to W., archdeacon of Angers, I., bishop of Le Mans, greetings.

Concerning the woman who, to her husband lying ill and asking for the monastic habit, not only gave consent but also, after a vow of continence had been made, herself delivered him to be tonsured, and who now, repenting of what was done, demands that he return to the marital obligation: we see nothing other than what Augustine, writing thus to Ecdicia, says: [Note: [Col. 0310D] Letter 262 in the new edition, or 199 in the old.] “What you both had vowed to the Lord by mutual consent, you ought to have fulfilled by persevering to the end. If he has fallen away from that resolution, you at least must persevere most steadfastly. I would not exhort you to this unless he himself had consented to it with you. For if you had never had his consent, no number of years would defend you.”

Indeed, the woman’s defence of her own case—that she neither gave consent to her husband through ministers of the Church nor promised chastity through them—does not, in my view, assist her in revoking the vow of continence, although, if it had been done through them, it would be called more orderly. I have written this to your blessedness, prepared to adopt without dispute the judgment of those to whom the Lord shall reveal what is better. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVII  
How it is to be understood that God sometimes punishes sin in the fourth and fifth generation.

To R., [Note: [Col. 0310D] Although we searched most diligently for this letter in more than fifteen manuscripts which we used and did not find it, we nevertheless judged it not to be omitted, because it was among the letters which the most acute investigator of antiquities, the most learned M. Loyauté, collected as Hildebertian and, like the others, copied in his own hand. This is especially so because in his theological treatise, ch. 34, p. 1190, Hildebert cites something approaching this argument from Saint Jerome, where he explains how God punishes certain sins in the third and fourth generation. Indeed, while describing the punishments of hell in *On the Order of the World*, line 358, p. 1185, he says:

> There is there a darkness which the father’s origin deserved,  
> condemning descendants through five generations.

Hence one may rightly infer that this letter is genuinely Hildebertian. We believe that the initial R. denotes no one but Ralph, bishop of Durham, to whom Letter 1 of Book III is addressed; perhaps, when Hildebert wrote this letter to him, he was not yet a bishop, a dignity which he did not obtain until 1099. Hildebert therefore calls him here simply “master.” See the notes to Letter 1 of Book III.] venerable master; I., greetings.

The interpretation which you asked for, as I have received different interpretations from different persons, I have decided to communicate to you, leaving to your judgment what is better. “Whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold” (Gen. 4:15), namely, in the seventh generation. For there were seven generations from Cain to Lamech, who killed him, and he died in the seventh generation.

There are also some who wish to read this actively, saying: “He shall be punished seventh [perhaps: sevenfold],” because someone was to kill Cain either for his seven sins or in the seventh generation, as has been said. There is another interpretation. Cain said to the Lord: “Everyone who finds me will kill me” (ibid., v. 14). To him the Lord replied: “Not so”—that is, you will not end your life so quickly, nor escape so suddenly the punishments you have deserved; but everyone who finds you will know that whoever kills Cain—that is, whoever commits fratricide, whoever perpetrates such a great crime—shall be punished sevenfold, that is, shall suffer punishment through seven generations. And the Lord set a mark on Cain so that he would not be killed; for he lived until the seventh generation. Then, as has been said, he was killed by Lamech.

It may also be understood in another way: namely, that Cain was to suffer punishments both in soul and body; for the soul is designated by three, the body by four, as is well indicated elsewhere. There is yet another explanation. Cain is said to have committed seven sins: first, that he did not divide rightly; second, that he envied his brother; third, that he acted deceitfully, saying, “Let us go into the field” (ibid., v. 8); fourth, that he killed him; fifth, that he impudently denied it, saying, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” [Col. 0311C] (ibid., v. 9); sixth, that he condemned himself when he said, “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for” (ibid., v. 13); seventh, that even after being condemned he did not repent.

Thus it was rightly said, “He shall be punished sevenfold,” as though he were to pay a penalty for each sin. For while he lived, he paid seven punishments. The first was the curse upon him over the earth; the second, that the earth did not yield him its fruits when he laboured; the third, that he was a wanderer; the fourth, that he was a fugitive; the fifth, hiding from the face of the Lord; the sixth, that he was in mourning; the seventh, that he was in fear. I have written these things to you in summary, and shall be glad if anything has pleased you. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVIII

(From Muratori’s *Anecdota*, vol. III, p. 216.) To a friend to whom Hildebert had commended both Stephen and Ralph, dean of the Church of Tours.

Greetings and devoted service.

Your affection knows that Stephen has departed, with whom Q. V. Ralph, our son indeed but your dean, was to conduct business before the apostolic tribunal. We appeal to your discretion on his behalf, [Col. 0312B] that you may obtain for him that he need not be troubled further over the cause for which he was going to Rome. [Note: [Col. 0312D] See the note to Letter 39 of Book II.]

## LETTER XXXIX

(From Muratori’s *Anecdota*, vol. III, p. 219.) To an unknown person concerning the faithful and grateful remembrance of benefits.

Greetings, and may you surpass age itself in counsel.

Even brute animals accuse those who are forgetful of services, since they are plainly seen both to follow their benefactors with greater devotion and, as if in thanksgiving, to attend upon and fawn over them. I thank the Lord God that you imitate these creatures, [Col. 0312C] for by His counsel you have provided that His benefits or services should not remain unrewarded by you. This I both praise and thank you for, trusting in your fidelity that hereafter you will provide even greater things. He himself will tell you more fully about this, since he saw, read, and understood in my letters both my prayers and my counsel addressed to them.

## DIPLOMAS GRANTED BY THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT

### I

(From the Cartulary of Saint Albinus of Angers, year 1098.) In favour of the monastery of Saint Albinus of Angers, concerning the Church of Saint Audoenus near Le Mans.

[Col. 0311D]

HILDEBERT, devoted priest of the holy Church of Le Mans, to his beloved brothers GIRARD, abbot of Saint Albinus, and the whole congregation serving Christ the Lord under his care: greetings and peace.

Because by the voice of Truth itself we are commanded to love every neighbor as ourselves [Col. 0312D], we receive the pious petitions of your affection with charitable goodwill. For when, in another year, a certain knight named Fulcoius of Mortereis chose the manner of life observed by your community, he further added that he would give you the church of Saint Audoenus, which is almost adjacent to the walls of Le Mans, and which he and his predecessors had possessed by hereditary right for innumerable years. Although in this matter all the faithful ought to rejoice for the increase of religion thereby achieved, you have nevertheless entreated and humbly begged us to strengthen that lay donation also by the authority of our consent. You do well, and do what you ought, rendering honor to God and to us, lest you appear to have entered the folds entrusted to our pastoral care with stiff necks; especially since that same church is unquestionably believed to have been founded by our predecessors, the bishops of Le Mans, and assigned to the use of monks. Therefore we rejoice that in our time a good deed has been done, since we see restored to the monastic religious life that which, through the instability of mortals, had been taken away from monks.

Accordingly, receiving the purpose of your good will with paternal feeling, we grant to you and to all your posterity in perpetuity the aforesaid church, with all tithes, offerings, and other appurtenances belonging to it, on this condition, however: that you shall pay to the canons of our mother church [Col. 0313B], whose common assent agrees with us in this matter, five solidi of annual rent as a sign of due subjection. If those solidi are not at any time paid by the appointed term, namely the Ides of December, owing to any intervening circumstance, they shall be collected without excuse within eight days. We leave this present document of our grant as a witness, that it may be an everlasting memorial for all ourselves and all our successors; and, that this instrument of our authority may retain inviolable force, we have caused it to be sealed with the seal of our church.

But if any person whatsoever, of whatever rank or authority, after becoming aware of this command of our ordinance [Col. 0313C], should attempt to act against it, and, having been admonished a second or third time, should not make amends by worthy satisfaction, let that person incur loss of his or her own honor or power, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and at the Last Judgment be subject to condemnation with the left-hand party. But upon those who defend and preserve it may there be peace and a portion with our head, Jesus Christ, to whom is honor with the Father and the Holy Spirit for everlasting ages. Amen. * ΑΜΗΝ, [Heb. אָמֵן] Amen. We have read “Amen”; we have confirmed “Amen,” saving the rights and revenues of the church, and two solidi for the synod, and eighteen denarii for the circada.

The sign of [Col. 0313D] HILDEBERT, bishop. The sign of FULCRAD, cantor. The sign of HUGH, archdeacon. The sign of GAUFRED, dean. The sign of GAUFRED, archdeacon. The sign of GRADULF, archdeacon.

Given at Le Mans by the hand of Gradulf, chancellor, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098, indiction VI, the second year of the episcopate of Lord Hildebert.

These things were copied from the cartulary of the monastery of Saint Albinus of Angers, from the cabinet of the priory of Saint Audoenus at Le Mans [Col. 0314A], and were collated with a copy drawn up by the Reverend Father and Lord Robert Hardy, then prior of the monastery of Saint Albinus of the Congregation of Saint Maur, as appeared from his original handwriting appended to this transcript.

## II. In favor of Marmoutier, concerning the church of Lupiniac

(From the archive of Marmoutier at Tours and the Baluze papers, 1118.)

We wish it to be known to all future persons and to those present that I, Hildebert, by God’s grace bishop of Le Mans, at the request of our fellow brother Lord William, abbot of Marmoutier, and the other brothers of that same monastery, have given and granted to the monks of the church of that same Marmoutier [Col. 0314B] the church of Lupiniac with all its appurtenances; likewise whatever Fulco of Marboet possessed in it and had resolved and granted to give them, so far as it appeared to belong to him; with the right of the Church of Le Mans, however, preserved.

Done in the chapter-house of the monastery of Saint Mary of Évron, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1118, in the presence and with the consent of our archdeacon Fulcher, and also of Fulco of Marboet himself. There he restored into our hand the church which he had held—or rather, the benefices of that church—and requested and consented that it be given to the monks of Marmoutier. So that this present charter of our grant might remain firm for ever, I ordered it to be marked, as may be seen, with my own seal.

## III. Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans: confirmation concerning the church of Saint Mary of Mayenne, and Robert Pavo’s gift

(From the archive of Marmoutier and the Baluze papers, 1120.)

[Col. 0314C]

Although we expend diligent effort on the many pleasures of this age and submissively procure for ourselves things useful for bodily needs, we ought not to be forgetful of the soul’s welfare. For the soul’s welfare is this: wherever power and authority avail, to assent to just petitions and to secure, by the protections of grant and confirmation, benefits bestowed for the redemption of souls upon religious places and brothers serving God.

Therefore I, Hildebert, [Col. 0314D] by God’s grace bishop of Le Mans, judged worthy of being granted the petition of a certain cleric of ours, Robert by surname Pavo, because it was just and beneficial to the soul. This Robert had and possessed the parish church of Saint Mary, situated in the borough of the castle of Mayenne. He feared danger to souls—both his own and those of his successors—if, after his death, it should return to lay control, from which, God helping and justice requiring, it had been removed. Reflecting for some time how both the danger might be avoided and that church might be assigned to religious houses and brothers, he finally resolved and vowed that it should be bestowed upon Marmoutier of Blessed Martin and the brothers there serving God [Col. 0315A], so that through the assistance of their prayers he might deserve to obtain redemption for his sins.

Recognizing, however, that such a gift ought not to be made except through episcopal grant and authority, he humbly approached us, accompanied by Hervé, chaplain of the monks. Also present with us were two officials of our church: Lord Paganus, dean, within whose archdeaconry that church lay, and Lord Fulcher, archdeacon. He asked and urgently entreated us to grant and confirm that church to the aforesaid brothers and place, together with what he possessed in the church of Parriniac. Therefore, having himself transferred it into my hand by means of a certain knife, and having relinquished it, with the other persons of Parriniac consenting and confirming—Robert himself and the aforesaid officials, F., archdeacon, and P., dean [Col. 0315B]—I, Hildebert, both out of reverence for the place and affection for the brothers, and for the salvation and welfare of the soul of that cleric Robert and of my own, gave and granted it to Marmoutier of Blessed Martin and to the brothers of that place, investing them with it by the aforesaid knife.

[Note: [Col. 0315D] Observe that in former times a donation was formally effected by the delivery of a knife.]

I placed the knife in the hand of Lord Fromund, prior, while preserving the right of our Church of Le Mans. I resolved to establish this gift by the protection of our seal, that it might remain valid for ever, forbidding under anathema that it be undone by anyone’s presumption or violence.

These acts were done in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1120, indiction XIII, epact XVIII, in the twenty-fourth year of the episcopate [Col. 0315C] of Lord Hildebert, with the following witnesses: Lord Hildebert himself, bishop; Paganus, dean; Fulcher, archdeacon; Hervé, chaplain. Of the monks: Fromund, prior; Peter Laidez; John, prior of Vivenay; William, prior of Arbenay; Walter of Compiègne; William, prior of Mayenne.

## IV. Confirmation of all rights and possessions of the monastery of Évron, granted by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans

[Note: [Col. 0315D] Several points concerning this diploma appear worthy of observation. First, from it one may infer with sufficient probability that Daniel, abbot of Évron, had returned to better conduct. In Letter 25, Book II, Hildebert had described him to Gerard, legate of the Apostolic See, as so forgetful of his office and so foolish that he did not hesitate to call him a beast. The same may be presumed of the monks of Évron, whom he had described in that same letter as so corrupt that, with no observance of the laws maintained among them, “the monks,” he says, “were pursuing a monk no less than if they had made compacts with disgrace.” While they were such, Hildebert, a good and most zealous shepherd, attempted by voice and rod to bring them back to the flock, and to themselves, when they were straying from their order, rule, and their own true selves. Later, when his care had brought them back, he embraced and cherished them as a most loving father; and by this charter of confirmation, with all his pontifical authority, he confirms their goods and possessions, as their morals had been reformed for the better—those whose ruin, even in temporal matters, he had lamented as caused by the dissolution of morals. Secondly, this charter also confirms our conjecture set out in the notes on Letter 20, Book II: that the ecclesiastical man whom Hildebert so sharply rebukes there was none other than Daniel, whom he expressly names here and, after his amendment, calls his dearest brother in Christ. Thirdly, although Hildebert declares in Letter 21, Book III, that he had held office in the Church of Le Mans for twenty-eight years, nothing prevents him from saying that he granted this charter of confirmation in the year of his pontificate that began immediately after his twenty-eighth year at Le Mans; indeed, it follows that the year in which he said he had presided there for twenty-eight years must necessarily have been the twenty-ninth year of his pontificate.]

(From the archive of the monastery of Évron, reported in a recently written history of that monastery.)

1. The bishop of Le Mans, to his beloved brother DANIEL, abbot of Évron, and to his successors to be regularly appointed for ever.

[Col. 0316A] So long as we bear pastoral care, it is fitting that we should provide more diligently for the protection and tranquillity of churches. Therefore, dearest brother Daniel in Christ, mercifully assenting to your just petitions, we grant to you and your successors, to possess quietly for ever, everything belonging by right to the monastery of Évron, built in honor of Blessed Mary, over which you preside by God’s appointment, reserving the right of the bishop and of the mother church of Le Mans; all these things are to serve in every way the support and governance of those for whom they were offered. Among them we have thought fit to specify the following by name:

First, the abbey of Saint Mary with the adjoining borough; the church of Saint Martin situated in that borough with all its appurtenances; another church of Saint Martin [Col. 0316B], called “in the Fields,” situated in the same borough; the church of Saint Peter of Torliac; the church of Saint Leodegar of Vivariis; the church of Saint Peter of Vulteriac; the church of Saint Susanna; the church of Saint Denis of Orcis; the church of Saint Martin of Castris; the church of Saint Vigor of Nael; the church of Saint Martin of Montesecurus; the church of Saint Peter of Chualon; the church of Saint Veneratus; the church of La Bazoge of Mont Pinson; the church of Champ Aion; the church of Saint Mary of Bedizium; the church of Saint Gervasius of Champ Genest; the church of Saint Nicholas of Tranlis; the chapel of Tilliac; the church of Saint Peter of Izziac; the church of Saint Martin of Curis; the church of Saint Sulpicius of Vegia; the church of Saint Leodegar; [Col. 0316C] the church of Saint Sixtus of the Chapel; the church of Saint Gervasius of Buziac; the church of Saint Paduinus of the Fields; the church of Saint Martin of Lunac; the church of Saint Gemma; the church of Saint Martin of Annon; the church of Saint George of Gesnes; the church of Saint Fronto of Megenziac; the church of Saint Christopher; the church of Saint Mary of Cambiac; the church of Saint Peter situated in that same village; the church of Saint Germanus of La Hatevalla; the chapel of Saint Audoenus; the chapel of Saint Tudisius; the chapel of Saint Gerard; the chapel of Saint Mary of Barbis; the church of Saint Cyprian of Bacondria; the church of Andoliac; the church of Intramis; the church of Valliac; the church of [Col. 0317A] Frumentriis; the church of Saint Symphorianus of Martiniac; the chapel of Saint Nicholas of Cadurcis; the church of Saint Vigor of Mengniac; the church of the Two Avalles; the church of Saint Audoenus; the church of Saint Mary of the Chapel; the chapel of Saint Mary of Lynesium; the church of Moulan; the church of Saint Peter of Chama; the church of Saint Stephen of Thorigniac; one third of the church of Nova Villula.

In the aforesaid churches, likewise, the circada dues and the episcopal share of synodal dues; in the parish of Saint George of Faschal, that part of the tithe which Ralph Rufus gave to the monastery of Évron together with his son Gerald; likewise the tithe of Masfla, which the monks of Évron possess in the parish of Lovernay; the tithe which they have in the parish of Parendius [Col. 0317B]; the tithe which they have in the parish of Ameneium; the tithe which they have in the parish of Tanneia; the tithe which they have in the parish of Courcite; the tithe which they have in the parish of Parenzis; the tithe which they have in the parish of Cyneium; and the tithe which they have in the parish of Saint John above the Arna.

We have therefore decreed that the churches named above, with all the appurtenances which the monks of Évron have lawfully possessed up to the present day, shall henceforth be possessed quietly and peacefully in perpetuity by the monastery of Évron and the brothers serving God there. Moreover, whatever possessions and estates the brothers of Évron have hitherto held by lawful possession, or may in future acquire through the canonical grant of pontiffs [Col. 0317C], we grant to the aforesaid brothers on the same terms. And we decree that these things shall remain firm and unshaken.

We also ordain that no person whatsoever may ever be permitted to disturb that monastery, harass it with reckless vexations, diminish its possessions, or retain things taken from it. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person should rashly wish to oppose this our ordinance, then, after a second or third admonition, let that person remain subject to canonical punishment and be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, until worthy satisfaction has been made for the wrongdoing committed. Upon all who preserve what is just for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen. And [Col. 0317D], that this our confirmation may be held firmer and more certain, we have caused it to be fortified by our seal.

Done at Le Mans in the year from the Incarnation 1125, the twenty-ninth year of our pontificate, while Louis was king of the Franks.

## V. For the monastery of Saint Vincent of Le Mans

(From the cartulary of the abbey of Saint Vincent of Le Mans.)

H. [Note: [Col. 0317D] Hildebert.] humble minister of Tours, to the venerable [Col. 0318A] and beloved Brother G. [Note: [Col. 0317D] Guy, who succeeded Hildebert immediately in the bishopric of Le Mans.] by God’s grace bishop of Le Mans, and to the whole chapter of that church: greeting and blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0317D] As metropolitan, he imparts blessing together with greeting to Guy, his suffragan.]

We remember that, while we presided over the Church of Le Mans [Note: [Col. 0317D] He therefore granted this charter after the year 1125, when he was transferred to the see of Tours.], Herbert Framgerius was at one time excommunicated by us on account of the first fruits and the third share belonging to priests, which he was taking in the churches of Piacé and Juillé, belonging by right to the monastery of Saint Vincent. Subsequently, compelled by illness, he restored the aforesaid revenues to the church of Blessed Vincent: namely, those first fruits and that third share. Moreover, he gave the monks of the aforesaid church two parts of the tithe from each parish, excepting those things which are known to have been bestowed by him upon the monks of Marmoutier. We [Col. 0318B] therefore remember both that restoration and the gift of tithes which Herbert made to Blessed Vincent, and we firmly retain in memory that we diligently granted the same things to those brothers. Farewell.

## VI. For the monastery of Saint Vincent of Le Mans

(From the cartulary of the abbey of Saint Vincent of Le Mans.)

200 ** Archbishop of Tours by God’s grace, to G. [Note: [Col. 0318D] To the same Guy, his successor in the Church of Le Mans, and therefore after 1125.], venerable bishop of Le Mans, and to the whole chapter of Blessed Julian: greeting and blessing.

We do not believe that it has escaped your memory that Archdeacon Josbert, at his death, gave and bequeathed certain vineyards to the church of Blessed Vincent and the monks serving God there. But after his death his brother [Col. 0318C] Drogo took those vineyards from the aforesaid church. We summoned him and the monks before us; after carefully hearing the claims of each party, we awarded those vineyards to the monks of Saint Vincent. Because Drogo refused to carry out what we had adjudged, we separated him and his entire household from the thresholds of God’s holy Church. His heirs, as we have learned, persist in the same robbery. Therefore we ask and, in asking, admonish your affection that you provide full and firm justice in this matter for the aforesaid church and brothers. Farewell.

## VII. Gift of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, concerning the church of Saint George of Nemore

[Note: [Col. 0318D] We found this diploma among the documents appended to the manuscript *History of Marmoutier near Tours*, vol. II, p. 64. (Library of the city of Tours.)]

[Col. 0318D]

No one is unaware that places dedicated to divine worship either improve through the manner of life of their inhabitants or fall from their dignity. Thus, at the urging of certain clerics professing a distinctive religious life, we gave counsel and aid to the church of Saint George of the Wood, two miles distant from Mont Auré, which had fallen from its former condition; we hoped that it would be restored to its former dignity, and we failed them in nothing [Col. 0319A] until they themselves began wholly to fail themselves. The rigor of their purpose fell so far that their superior, Matthew by name, who bore the title of abbot, violated his sacred profession, went out into the “region of unlikeness,” and abandoned both place and vow.

Since, therefore, all hope of restoring the aforesaid place under this order and with these persons has been taken from us, we grant, insofar as it belongs to us, the aforesaid church to Marmoutier; and by this charter delivered from our hand we transfer it to Abbot William, asking and earnestly beseeching him to strive and endeavor to restore there the monastic order which had formerly flourished in it. This gift I, Bishop Hildebert, made and wrote for them, with Paganus, archdeacon, and Fulcrad, cantor, giving their consent.

## VIII. Letter of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, concerning the churches of Mayenne and Saccé

(Year 1120.)

[*History of Marmoutier near Tours*, manuscript, vol. II, p. 182.]

Assent to just petitions is an inspiration of the divine gift, a venerable approval of holy authority and of all who think piously. Considering this, I, Hildebert, unworthy bishop of the mother Church of Le Mans, decreed that the petition of Juhel of Mayenne should not be refused. Summoned therefore by Juhel himself, consulted and [Col. 0319C] entreated by his mother and sister, and also begged by the barons of the castle, to grant and confirm to Marmoutier and the monks of Saint Martin his chapel in that same castle, with all its appurtenances, and likewise the chapel of Saccé with what belongs to it, I, together with those persons of our church to whom the matter appeared to pertain, decreed to assent to such just petitions.

We therefore give and grant to the aforesaid monastery the churches named above with all their appurtenances, while preserving the right of our mother Church of Le Mans, with the assent and confirmation, as stated above, of those to whom the matter appeared to pertain on our side. And lest anyone perverse or fraudulent should in future attempt to destroy or even weaken this grant—which God forbid—and prevail, we have decreed that this present charter be fortified by our authority [Col. 0319D] and seal, binding under the bond of anathema anyone who presumes this, until that person submits to suitable amendment.

These acts were done in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1120, indiction XIII, epact XVIII, in the twenty-fourth year of the episcopate of Lord Hildebert.

+ Mark of Hildebert, bishop. + Mark of Paganus, dean. + Mark of Fulcher, archdeacon. + Mark of Gervasius Paganellus, archdeacon. + Mark of Guy, precentor. + Mark of Guarnerius of Mayenne. + Mark of Gradulf, archdeacon.

## IX. In what cases only the ornaments of the church may be pledged

(From the cartulary of the distinguished Church of Le Mans called the *White Book* of the chapter, no. CCXVIII.)

[Col. 0320A]

Whoever undertakes and neglects the care of preserving the church’s goods—which are the price of sins and the patrimony of the poor—incurs, by canonical judgment, danger to his rank. Moved by consideration of this matter, I, Hildebert, humble overseer of the people of Le Mans, to remove the importunity of every suspicious petition, have by pontifical authority bound under the bond of anathema and excluded from communion with God’s holy Church all who remove, for the purpose of pledging or on any other pretext, or attempt to alienate or remove, from that church its ornaments—whether of gold, silver, or silk—bestowed or to be bestowed by the generosity of the faithful upon the Church of Le Mans [Col. 0320B] for the honor of God and the adornment of his house, unless compelled by the necessity of the chapter and the work of the church, or for feeding starving poor people when famine threatens.

## X. Instrument concerning the settlement made between the canons of Saint Julian of Le Mans and the monks of Saint Vincent

(About 1100.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 579, from the cartulary of Saint Vincent of Le Mans.]

[Col. 0320C]

Just as the condition of the whole Church is strengthened by the peaceful bond of charity, so likewise the unity of holy fellowship is dissipated by the deadly scandal of dissension. Therefore all who desire to attain the vision of eternal peace must strive with every vigilance to preserve peace with all people, if possible, and especially with brethren.

Accordingly, we, the canons of the holy Church of Le Mans, loving peace and concord and wishing utterly to cast out from our midst the evil of discord, accept from the monks of Saint Vincent, through the mediation of charity, the following settlement and concord concerning a certain claim and dispute which we long maintained against them: that they should peacefully and quietly relinquish to us, without any reservation, the tithe of Mont Rainald, which they had held for a long time despite our claim, together with burial rights and the other revenues which appear to belong to the church; that they should allow us to build a church there according to our good pleasure and possess it in perpetuity; that they should relinquish the vineyards of Rainald the cantor, which they had for some time held despite our claim; that they should promise to perform an office of thirty days for each of our deceased canons; and that they should transfer the cemetery which our predecessors had held contrary to canonical custom with laypersons [variant: “held”] on the other side of their monastery, to a more suitable and more honorable place, namely beside the monks’ cemetery [Col. 0321A].

By this agreement we established with them a lasting friendly brotherhood; and we wholly remitted to them the other matters which had existed between us and them as causes of dispute: namely, the sales of houses located in the vineyard of the spring of Saint Domnolus; six denarii of rent from a certain house in Harold’s street; and the fine concerning a serf of our church, namely Frogerius Belotus, whom they had made a monk contrary to our prohibition. Whatever the bishops of the Church of Le Mans had bestowed upon their house, we granted to them simply and without deceit. If in future they should wish to confer anything upon that house, we promised that we would grant it freely and without any payment of money, while preserving their fidelity to our church.

We also promised that for their deceased abbot [Col. 0321B] we would perform one thirty-day cycle of masses, and for each deceased monk seven masses and seven vigils; and that in their affairs we would faithfully give them our counsel and aid as to friends and brothers, insofar as circumstance and time should permit. That this concord of peace and charity might remain permanently stable, we confirmed this chirograph on the feast-day of the most blessed Julian’s departure, in the presence and with the approval of Lord Hildebert, bishop.

## XI. Diploma of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, for the monastery of Saint Victor of Le Mans: confirming churches granted to the monks by laymen

(Year 1106.)

[MARTÈNE, ibid., from the same cartulary.]

[Col. 0321D]

With what great and varied zeal the religious devotion of bishops ought to protect the peace of monasteries, venerable antiquity has transmitted to us through the holy Fathers. Unworthy as I am, Ildebert, priest of the Church of Le Mans, stirred and inspired by their examples, have decreed that provision be made for the tranquillity of the brothers serving the Lord God in the monastery of Saint Vincent, against the misconduct of certain persons [Col. 0322A].

Therefore, lest any vexation from shameless litigants should work mischief against the aforesaid monastery, we both grant and confirm in this present document, for its perpetual possession, the benefices of certain churches which faithful laymen have bestowed upon it. Yet the rights belonging to the bishop, archdeacon, and archpriest are wholly retained: namely, synodal dues, circada dues, and any other dues which, in fines, other revenues, or the protection of priests, appear to belong to the aforesaid persons.

The following list identifies the churches: the churches of Tufi, Campaniac, Ver, Avenis, Curte-lucro, Segona, Luertio, Basilgeriae, and Aceium; the chapel of Saint Audoenus of Baladon; the church of Saint Leonard; the church of Curiadoda; the church of Monasteriolum; the church of Curtismons; and the church of Ham.

This declaration of grant was made in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1106, in the episcopate of the aforesaid bishop, indiction XIV, Philip being king and Elias count. Whoever presumes to violate it, being subject to anathema, shall incur the curse of God.

## XII. Charter of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, for Marmoutier

(Year 1113.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, vol. III, Mansi folio edition, p. 63.]

[Col. 0322C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

I, Hildebert, by God’s grace bishop of the people of Le Mans, wish it to be known to all faithful of God’s holy Church, of both order and rank, that because of the affection and close relationship by which the Church of Le Mans and the Church of Marmoutier of Blessed Martin were bound to one another in a bond of love, I have given and granted to Saint Martin himself and to his brothers serving Christ for ever in Marmoutier the church commonly called Vilerx of Charlemagne by the inhabitants of that place, with all things belonging to that church, the right of the Church of Le Mans being preserved. Fulcher, archdeacon [Col. 0322D], was present and consenting, together with two other canons of our church, namely Gervasius Paganellus and Paganus.

Likewise, whatever the generosity of princes or the devotion of the faithful has already conferred upon them there, or whatever they may acquire hereafter, we establish by the present page of this our privilege, through episcopal authority, that it shall remain firm and unimpaired for them. And lest it be violated in future through the malevolently envious presumption of anyone, we confirm it for ever by the protection of our own seal.

Done in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1114, at Marmoutier, in the cloister before the chamber of the venerable abbot W[illiam?], in his presence, with William, formerly archdeacon of Redon and now prior, Peter [Col. 0323A], likewise the steward, Gervasius, my nephew, and Rainald of the Castle of Gunterius, then notary of Marmoutier.

## XIII. Confirmation by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, concerning the church of Torciac, commonly Torcé

[BALUZE, ibid.]

I, HILDEBERT, bishop of Le Mans, wish it to be known to all faithful of the holy Church, both future and present, that the monks of Marmoutier [Col. 0324A] approached us, asking that I grant and strengthen by the authority of our letters the gift of the church of Torciac, which the devotion of certain faithful persons had bestowed upon their house in our time. I received their petition with the fitting kindness, granted them that church for possession in future times, and, so that this our consent and grant might remain inviolable, ordered it to be confirmed by the present letters and the impression of the episcopal seal.

Given in the city of Le Mans, two days before the Kalends of October.

[Col. 0323]

## NOTES

### Brief notice on the notes of the distinguished M. Loyauté, most learned advocate in the supreme court of Parliament, on the eighteen letters—namely, those of the earlier collection—of the venerable Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans and later archbishop of Tours

[Col. 0323]

Since we had resolved to spare no labor in order that, so far as our ability allowed, every possible light might be cast upon Hildebert’s letters, we hoped that the very learned observations of M. Loyauté on his letters would bring them no slight benefit. Through the kindness of the distinguished M. Logé, celebrated advocate in the supreme court at Paris, we fortunately obtained these notes. Although unarranged and almost everywhere obscured by many erasures—and although they were given to us late, long after we had completed the printing of these letters—we endeavored, so far as we could, to restore them to the polished form in which their author, a man of refined critical judgment, would have presented them had he lived. We did so in accordance with his intention, lest they should lie in darkness, to the loss of the republic of letters, and perish altogether unhappily.

That these notes extend no farther than the eighteenth letter shows more clearly than light how much profit readers would have drawn from the author’s learning and erudition, if a longer life had been granted to him in which to elucidate them all, as he had intended. Yet the scantiness of the notes did not deter us from publishing them, since, as an ancient writer said, “Even gleanings are objects of divine reverence”; nor do we expect it will shame us if the notes of an author thoroughly versed in antiquity appear to eclipse our own, however modest they may be. Therefore, kindly reader, enjoy these notes, and judge our efforts fairly and favorably.

### On the First Letter—To William of Champeaux

[Col. 0323B]

“You have at last resolved to philosophize.” You have set forth a rule for acting well.
