Seneca, the most elegant of philosophers, expressed this almost word for word: “From an acquired opinion of philosophers, not at all drawing out for you an antiquated morality.” For the life of the philosopher must be in harmony with his discourse; for the philosopher’s discourse is his chosen and personal law, says Plato, the most elegant of philosophers, in *Against the Stoics*: “It is necessary that the life of the philosopher be consonant with his reason; for the reason of the philosopher is his chosen and personal law” (*τὸν βίον τοῦ φιλοσόφου τῷ λόγῳ σύμφρονον εἶναι· ὁ γὰρ λόγος τοῦ φιλοσόφου νόμος αἱρετὸς καὶ ἴδιος ἐστίν*).

“And from the ancients, ‘religious’” means chaste, most observant, and restraining oneself within fixed laws and limits. Valerius, Book 4, chapter 9; Seneca: “Let him be a rule unto himself.”

…you abandon mercantile instruction, having set aside ecclesiastical dignities. Sirmond, on Letter 11, Book II of Geoffrey of Vendôme, explains this passage: “[Col. 0323C] Literally, ‘a shipman’s blessing,’ that is, a hired one; he calls it *institoria lectio* [mercantile instruction],” as Hildebert said in Letter 1, of one “for whom base and illiberal gain is proposed as profit to a shopkeeper.” Ulger, bishop of Angers, uses the same metaphor in John of Salisbury, *Metalogicon*, Book II, chapter 20. For, as Ulger says, “…in the sale of learning, reciprocal traffic in words ought to be agreeable; for courtesy had been banished from the market-place of philosophers, and words are retailed for favour.”

“If nevertheless you proceed unburdened.” Abelard attacks William more fully and plainly in the history of his misfortunes:

> “My former master William, archdeacon of Paris, having changed his former dress, entered the order of regular clerks [Col. 0324B], with the intention, as was reported, of being promoted to a higher rank of prelacy by appearing more religious. This soon befell him, when he was made bishop of Châlons.”

“That you may shrink from being a Christian teacher.” He was called *master*. Thus Abelard repeatedly says, “our master William.” The anonymous author cited by Duchesne in his notes on Abelard calls him “Master William of Champeaux.” (Yet there was not yet a university, nor a doctorate.) “Report, however, brings that you have been persuaded by certain persons wholly to abstain from teaching.” Yet neither the habit of his conversion nor departure from the city of Paris nor his customary pursuit of philosophy called him away; rather, even in the monastery to which [Col. 0324C] he had withdrawn for the sake of religion, he at once, as was his custom, conducted public schools, as Abelard says in the *Commentaries on his Misfortunes*. Perhaps persuaded by this letter of Hildebert, William persisted in the work he had begun.

“Gems differ in nothing from common tufa-stones.” Ancient glossaries: “πῶρος, the stone: *tofus*, *tofum*; ἀσβεστώδης, *tofum* [calcareous stone].” Manuscript glossaries: “*Tofus*: a stone resembling a cauldron, soft and movable.” See Salmasius on the *Augustan History*; Virgil; Juvenal. The scholiast should be consulted.

## ON LETTER II [now 22, Book IV], to the Archdeacon of Nantes

[Col. 0325A]

[Note: [Col. 0325D] In the margin of this note, in the hand of M. Loyauté himself, appears: “But, you will say, Archdeacon of Rennes.” He perhaps stated, by conjecture rather than upon certain indications or after a thorough investigation, that Rivallon belonged to the church of Rennes; but Rivallon was most certainly archdeacon of Nantes and a contemporary (*σύνχρονον*) of Hildebert.]

It is not sufficiently clear who he was. What if he were Rivallon, whose sacred epigrams I once happened to see in an old manuscript codex belonging to the most distinguished Menard? These poems are expressly ascribed to Rivallon, archdeacon of Nantes. Sirmond, in his notes on Geoffrey, reports Marbod’s epitaph. [Note: [Col. 0326D] Rather, Sirmond on Letter 11, Book III of Geoffrey has: “The epitaph which Ulger composed in thirty verses is his work; it is carved upon the tomb of Marbod, bishop of Rennes, at Angers in Saint-Aubin.”] The man to whom Hildebert sent this letter was the foremost poet of his age. He says that he professes himself a poet amid arms; then, “In poetry he marvels at Virgil.” The same parchment leaves bear the name with the initial R.; nor is it otherwise written in almost all the manuscript codices of Hildebert which I have with me—apart from one imperfect witness of Sirmond, which gives *Rualuncus*. On its authority [Col. 0325B] we restore the heading of this letter entire even after so many centuries.

“Let him serve an exiled evil man rather than a citizen.” By what deed Rualuncus, or Rivallo, was finally driven from his country, I cannot even conjecture.

“The toils of military service.” Perhaps in some Breton or Armorican war.

## ON LETTER III [now 12, Book II], to Roger of Salisbury

See Malmesbury, p. 571; Eadmer; the author of the *Antiquities of the British Church* in Anselm. At Canterbury, on the fourth day before the Ides of August, Anselm consecrated William of Winchester and Roger of Salisbury bishops, in the presence of Gerard, archbishop of York, and the other prelates of the church of Canterbury.

[Col. 0325C] “Under your king alone.” Roger Hoveden, in the earlier part of his *Annals*, records many matters concerning Ranulf under William Rufus which will shed light on this letter:

> “Ranulf, contrary to ecclesiastical law and the order of his rank—for he was a priest—first received an abbey, and then bishoprics whose fathers had died, from the king on lease; and each year he paid him no small sum of money. This continued until that king’s death. For on the day on which he perished by being killed, he held in his hand the archbishopric of Canterbury and the bishoprics of Winchester and Salisbury. But when William had yielded to fate, Henry III, rejecting his brother’s vices, grew in virtue and did not permit churches to remain longer without prelates. He accordingly set over Salisbury Roger, a man—if Hildebert is to be believed—of the greatest stature.”

[Col. 0325D] But it is better to hear Orderic, an eyewitness and witness of unimpeachable trustworthiness. In Book IV of the *Deeds of the Kings of the English*, where he treats of William II, he says:

> “At the prompting of this man [Ranulf], the sacred offices of churches, when their pastors had died, were put up for sale. For when news came of the death of any bishop or abbot, he appointed someone to take down in writing every item found there and to convey all subsequent revenues to the royal treasury. Meanwhile an inquiry was made into who might suitably replace the deceased—not by examination of character, but of money [Col. 0326A]. The office was at last bestowed, so to speak, naked, though purchased at a high price. These practices seemed all the more disgraceful because in the father’s time, after the death of a bishop or abbot, all revenues were kept to be surrendered to the incoming pastor, and persons commendable for religion and merit were chosen.”

“He knows the royal hand.” Yet Henry, too, allowed his own treasury to profit. For after Anselm’s death he made the revenues of the archbishopric of Canterbury his own, according to ancestral custom, for a full five years. Eadmer records this in Book … And William of Malmesbury, Book I of the *Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, says:

> “After Anselm of venerable memory, escaping the bonds of the body, took leave of this life, the archbishopric lay vacant for a full five years. Throughout that period, when the king [Col. 0326B] was urged to provide for the widowhood of his mother church, he deferred with a mild answer.”

“By a gift.” Properly so in the ancient glossaries.

“To shine more brightly than by a sceptre.”

“Whose learning also.” What sort of man Guido was—whom Hildebert recommended as a friend—Orderic teaches in the passage quoted by us, so that it is clearly apparent from this that Roger did not act from his heart’s own inclination … “Terrible thoughts receive the rumours.” (*αἱ ἔννοιαι δειναὶ δέκασαι τὰς φήρους*; the Greek is materially uncertain as printed.)

“On behalf of our Guido.” The *History of the Life of Guido*, which I append from the manuscript *Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans*, will throw no little light upon this letter. The most learned and distinguished Menard possesses a portion of those manuscripts. One ought not to begrudge him the glory of preserving [Col. 0326C] such illustrious remains, the autograph of which is today found nowhere, through the injury of time …

## ON LETTER IV [now 16, Book III]

“To Bishop G.” The manuscript codex here bears only: “To a Bishop.” But who that G. may be, supplied here by other handwritten codices, is uncertain. I am inclined to believe that he is Geoffrey, bishop of Angers, to whom the other Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, wrote Letter 1, Book III. The Chronicle of Saint-Aubin of Angers says much about him, and its words were copied into the notes by its most learned editor. Yet certain documents from the archive of the church of Angers prove false the assignment of his ordination to 1093. Their subscription reads:

> “Done at Saint-Quentin in the grove beside the church on the eastern side, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August [Col. 0326D], in the year of the Lord 1095, indiction IV, epact XII, Philip king of the Franks, Fulk the Younger count of Anjou, Geoffrey of Meduana elected bishop.”

Thus he is wrongly said to have been ordained in 1093, when in 1095 he is called only elect. In the charter recording the gift of Ralph the viscount concerning the church of Saint Nicholas, the subscription of the gift of Fulk, count of Île-Colonne, to the bishop of Angers states more fully and accurately:

> “Done at Angers in the bishop’s chamber, on the ninth day before the Kalends of July [Col. 0327A], the vigil of Saint John the Baptist, in the year of the Lord 1096, indiction IV, epact …, in the second year in which Pope Urban visited Angers, Philip reigning over the Franks, Fulk the Younger ruling over the Angevins, in the twenty-ninth year of his rule, under Geoffrey of Meduana, bishop of the Angevins, in the first year of his ordination.”

Add the authority of another manuscript Chronicle of Saint-Aubin of Angers, which likewise places Geoffrey’s ordination in 1096: “1096: Geoffrey of Meduana is ordained bishop.” Perhaps he was elected in 1093, when the other Geoffrey ceased to live. The same Chronicle says: “1093: Bishop Geoffrey died, on the sixth day before the Ides of October.” The necrology of Saint-Serge of Angers confirms this in almost the same words, but postpones [Col. 0327B] the ordination to 1098. Bourdigné, the untrustworthy compiler of the *Annals of Anjou*, errs egregiously, as is his custom, by conflating these two Geoffreys, or Gauffrioles, into one and confusing their deeds.

“He conducted himself like a bishop before becoming bishop.” The anonymous author of the *Life of Guido, Bishop of Le Mans*: “Although Guido, before becoming bishop, conducted himself like a bishop in teaching, conduct, liberality, and expenditure.”

“On behalf of your William.” Several alumni of the church of Angers of this name existed at that time, so that it may be doubted which William Hildebert recommends here to Bishop G. Was it William Musca? Or William of Martigné? Documents of the greater church report that both were canons in 1103 and 1106, perhaps through Geoffrey’s benefaction. Certainly, whichever [Col. 0327C] of them he was, having gained the archdeaconry of Translière in that same church, he opposed Rainald, bishop-elect of Angers and Geoffrey’s successor, as will be discussed more fully on Letter 12. Yet, becoming better disposed and more conciliatory through Rainald’s support, he obtained, together with the archdeaconry, the deanery of Angers after Stephen’s death. The documents of the aforesaid church testify to this: in 1115 and 1116 he is called dean and archdeacon of Translière. [Note: [Col. 0327D] William Musca is mentioned in the *Life of Hildebert*; at folio 75 verso he is called a canon of Le Mans by H. in a certain letter. In that work he describes the history of H. … He is therefore not the archdeacon.] Perhaps Marbod’s complaint in his letter to Rainald refers to this.

## ON LETTER V [now 11, Book I]

Manuscripts vary in the superscription of this letter. For the … Cord. codex assigns it to the same G. to whom the preceding letter was sent, whereas Sirmond’s manuscript assigns it to Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury; Anselm’s disciple Eadmer supports this in his *History of Anselm* [Col. 0327D] … recently published in five books by the most distinguished Selden and elucidated with exceedingly learned notes. Eadmer copied it in Book III; prefatory copies of it are preserved in the library of the most noble Thou. The author of the as-yet unpublished *Life of Anselm*.

“Your prolixity indeed.” Some letters to Hildebert survive among Anselm’s correspondence.

## ON LETTER VI [now 10, Book II]

There is an old exemplar which bears the superscription: “To O., abbot of Saint …” Others acknowledge none. But what [Col. 0328A] the capital letter signifies is unclear. Odilo indeed at that time … [Note: [Col. 0328D] Odilo, perhaps, of whom Duchesne speaks in connection with Abelard? Or Osbert, of whom Gemmeticensis speaks, whose letters he adduces to Anselm and William? Or Odo, abbot of Marmoutier?]

“For who, when morals are corrupted?” Aristotle, *Ethics*, on the prodigal man. Justinian, *Novellae*, on monks.

## ON LETTER VII [now 7, Book II]

This letter has a double superscription in the manuscript books. The Cord. manuscript has: “On an incestuous marriage.” Others bear only the heading which I took care to have printed and prefixed to the letter.

“To the Bishop of Séez.”

“Walter of Clinchamp.” In the archives of the church of Jumièges there survives a judgment issued by Robert of Bellême: “Odo of Clinchamp and Walter, son of Walter.” This is Walter of Clinchamp (Clinchamp), I think, of whom mention is made here. The year 1086 sufficiently proves it [Col. 0328B]. For Walter must have lived beyond 1100, when I conjecture that Hildebert wrote this letter; he filled his household with incestuous marriages and hence with disgrace. From this passage at least it will be clear that this family was illustrious in that age, and Walter distinguished not only in the offices of peace but also in war. His name was retained by a very strongly fortified castle of the district of Séez, celebrated in Orderic Vitalis, called Mount or Mound of Walter of Clinchamp.

“Yet, with the parents’ agreement, the maiden was solemnly given.” Arnulf of Saint-Emmeram, chapter 3: “He took the woman’s hand, wrapped it in a cloth, and, as is the custom [Col. 0328C] in weddings, under witnesses gave her in marriage to the old man.”

“She was endowed.” The remaining rites of marriage were celebrated. It is not surprising that a dowry is reckoned among the rites of marriage, since, by ecclesiastical custom, it was given by men at the doors of the church. Charter of liberties of King John of England:

> “A widow shall be assigned as dower the third part of all her husband’s land which was his in his lifetime, unless she has been endowed with a smaller dower at the church door.”

Hence a dowry is said to be assigned “according to the custom of the Church” in an old charter of Louis the Younger, made public by André Duchesne, a man most distinguished by his merit, in the appendix to the genealogy of the house of Dreux. I append those words which bear on the matter and elucidate a subject [Col. 0328D] almost unknown:

> “Let all present and future know that my brother Robert has taken as wife Agnes, countess of Brienne, and has assigned her a dowry according to the custom of the Church.”

In the instrument of dowry and donation of Bertrand, count of Toulouse, at Entelle:

> “For love of you and for the honour of the children begotten by us, I give you, as a bridal gift, the city of Rodez with its county and bishopric, as … is mine; and further I give you as a dowry the city of Viviers with its county [Col. 0329A], which belongs to our Roman [estate]. I give all the things named above whole and entire to you, my wife, in the manner in which I hold them or ought to hold them, under every claim, on this condition of settlement: that, while we live, we shall have, hold, and possess them together; and if you have children begotten of me, Bertrand, and born of you, Electa, the aforesaid honour shall revert to them after our death. But if you have no children by me, and survive me, you shall have and hold it; and after your death those shall have it to whom you may wish at any time to give or leave it.”

Without a written dowry instrument, children were called only natural children. Formula 54: “Among the … of an old uncertain honour …” “This letter, which he himself … upon his aforesaid children [Col. 0329B], and whom he begot upon that very freeborn woman; yet he did not confirm to her a charter of dowry according to law … the said children were therefore called natural according to law.”

Ivo, Letter 16: Pope Evaristus calls the unions of women not marriages but cohabitations when they have not been given by their parents, endowed according to the laws, and solemnly blessed by priests. Those who [ascribe this] to Evaristus are mistaken and mislead others …

The author of the *Life of Hildebert*, concerning Henry:

> “He held sacrilegious assemblies, where he taught a new doctrine: that women who lived less chastely should remain naked before all men together with their husbands, stripped of their garments; that no one should thereafter receive gold, silver, or other possessions with a wife [Col. 0329C], nor bestow a dowry upon her; but that the naked should take the naked, and the poor the poor.”

“To his other son.” To Robert of Clinchamp, who, after 1126, subscribed the judgment of the council of Botroc together with other nobles. This will be wholly clear to you if you have leisure to see the complete copy in Book III, chapter 6, of the *History of the Perche* by the most distinguished Gilles de Bry.

“Being about to give [her] in marriage.” Letter 17 is on a similar subject. Ivo of Chartres, Letter 148 to Hildebert, discusses almost the same question. Hildebert did not hesitate to plunder his archives concerning the succession of women …; he transcribed into this letter the sayings of the Fathers—Ambrose, Chrysostom, and Isidore—cited by Ivo. This will be evident to anyone of moderate understanding. Moreover [Col. 0329D], it will not be irrelevant here to observe the Greek jurists.

“When marriage is entered upon.” The synodal collection of John Xiphilinus: *τῆς νομίμου μνηστείας τοῦ νόμου τάξιν τε καὶ κατάστασιν ἐχούσης*: “Since lawful betrothal possesses the rank and status of law.” “Since lawful betrothals hold the place and condition of marriage.” [Note: [Col. 0329] Ivo, Letter 167, holds that a betrothed woman cannot be married to another man and that the ensuing marriage must be dissolved.] This is an established proposition not only among sacred but also among secular writers, with one or two exceptions. See Balsamon, *Responses* 6, p. 365.

“Unstained, just as uncorrupted.” See Hincmar, *On the Divorce of Boso*, concerning blemishes of this kind.

[Col. 0330A] Chrysostom, Homily 16 on Matthew.

## ON LETTER VIII [now 2, Book I]

Sirmond’s manuscript codices vary. A codex of excellent authority addresses it to the same Serlo, as do several others; other manuscripts address it to Ralph the archbishop. I preferred to follow the consensus of almost all codices and assign it specifically to Ralph, concerning whom there is more on the following letter.

“I sent you a fan.” Sirmond’s handwritten glosses: “A fly-fan.”

“Priests sacrificing to the Lord are more grievously attacked.” On this matter, Iamblichus in Eusebius’ *Preparation for the Gospel*.

“They introduce [these things] unexpectedly into minds.” Another reading: “suddenly.”

“To one thing and another.” Manuscript: “to other and alien things.”

## ON LETTER IX [now 4, Book II]

[Col. 0330B]

“To Ralph.” On Ralph of Tours, the most learned and distinguished Sirmond, on Letter 30, Book I of Geoffrey of Vendôme … In his additions to Letter 108 of Ivo of Chartres he is uncertain. The *Book of the Restoration of Marmoutier*, edited by Laurent Bochelet, testifies that Ralph attended the Council of Clermont:

> “The glorious Pope Urban II, coming from the city of Rome and visiting Gaul solely out of charity, at the Council of Clermont, in the presence of almost five hundred fathers—that is, archbishops, bishops, and abbots—all of them, together with Ralph, archbishop of Tours, acclaiming and authorizing the privileges of liberty and immunity which the pope himself had sent us from Rome.”

Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, in Letter 20, Book III, calls this letter, I think, a formal [Col. 0330C] and finely formed letter.

“Rainald.” Geoffrey of Vendôme, Letter 11, Book III: “The religious man Hildebert, who after the metropolitan was the first bishop in the province, did not remain silent; though summoned by his metropolitan to your consecration, he absentented himself, and declared on apostolic and evangelical authority that it was an execration rather than a consecration.”

“Your request by which we are summoned.” Canon 61 of the universal church at Antioch. Fulbert, Letters 28 and 61.

“The seditious cry of a disturbed crowd.” On the same election, Letter 11 addressed to Rainald: “Seized sadly by the populace; and what was done there, that presumptuous and pernicious sedition accomplished.” And shortly after:

> “In that proceeding—or rather, conspiracy of the populace—which you reckon an election, law was silent amid arms; the divine voice had no place. Frivolity and vanity claimed everything for themselves, where a certain actress and public woman, shouting noisily, had more influence than the maturity of the people or the dignity of the clergy could have had.”

Hildebert, Letter 12.

“The dean also maintains it.” Stephen. Geoffrey, Letter 11: “It ought not, as I think, to be charged against me alone as a crime, when it can rather be imputed to your dean Stephen and to the persons who were present. All indeed opposed [Col. 0331A] and reproved that election which you say they made yours. Nor without reason: against their will and without their asking, you caused it to be received from the populace.” See Marbod’s letter.

“You yielded to fear, not reason.” [Note: [Col. 0331D] Here one must deal with lay investitures. Geoffrey, pp. 117 and 175: concerning the regalian rights of counts, this was violently extorted [Col. 0332D] from him. Fulbert, Letter 39. *Life of Guido*, p. 80.] Contrary to the prohibitions of the canons, the count of Anjou compelled them to this. Council of Orléans, canon 11: “Let no bishop be given to unwilling people; nor let citizens or clergy be bent by the oppression of powerful persons into giving consent.”

## ON LETTER X [now 11, Book III]

“To Matilda.” See G. [Geoffrey?] on Matilda, to whom Ivo of Chartres wrote Letters 107, 142, and 174, celebrating her generosity; Hildebert echoes him in Letter 16.

[Col. 0331B] “I should be proved to sin against the laws and against the Church of Christ, unless I rejoice at her safety and at the preservation of reverence for the laws and of the Church’s condition.”

## ON LETTER XI [now 14, Book II]

“Of Saint Cuthbert.” The Cord. codex reads “Guibert.” Cuthbert is better. It is a monastery.

“Whence every good is opened to us from the North.”

In a similar subject Hildebert seems unlike himself, and nearly contrary, in Letter 66:

> “The north wind blows daily,” he says, “dangerous not only to flowers but also to fruit and leaves; the south wind must be entreated to come and breathe over its garden.”

Yet in both passages the matter is the reform of monks and their conversion from a shameful and disgraceful life to better fruitfulness. Nevertheless he does not differ from himself at all; for here the north wind denotes the southern region [Col. 0331C] lying beneath it.

## ON LETTER XII [now 5, Book II]

“A reminder concerning salvation.” Fulbert, Letter 7: “We beg you to write him a reminder, that he may restore to the aforesaid bishop what is his and allow him to live in peace.” And Letter 63: “I think that one must wait and employ reminders, until either repentance corrects them or the sentence of the supreme Judge punishes them.” Orderic Vitalis, Book X, p. 781: “The venerable Abbot Serlo issued admonitory letters.”

“The clergy did not elect you, but popular threats thrust you in.” Rainald’s election is reproved on several grounds. First, because he is said to have been intruded by the people. The canons of the Roman bishops to the Gallic bishops teach how much weight ought to be given to popular suffrage in episcopal elections:

> “By merit and observance of the law men attain the height of such dignity; no one may arrive there through simony, money, favour, or popular patronage. For the question is not what the people wish, but what evangelical discipline requires. The people then bear witness whenever, considering [perhaps read *perpendens*, ‘weighing’] the merits of some worthy man, they bestow the breath of favour.”

The golden ages of the Church did not wish to diminish the people’s free right of suffrage in the election of bishops, as even children know; but they restrained the ambitious entreaties of the base rabble and those procured by payment. Acts of the Councils, canon 13 of the Synod of Laodicea: *περὶ τοῦ μὴ τοῖς ὄχλοις ἐπιτρέπειν τὰς ἐκλογὰς ποιεῖσθαι τῶν μελλόντων καθίστασθαι εἰς ἱερατεῖον*—“that it must not be permitted to crowds to make the elections of those who are to be appointed to the priesthood.”

“In high priests, age must be complete.” Completeness of years—that is, full days. Canon 17 of the Council of Agde: before they reach the age of a complete man, that is, before thirty. Justellus, vol. 2, on the canon. Siricius to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, chapter 9: “Longinus shall receive the priesthood, and thereafter, after ten years, may attain a bishop’s seat.” At Trullo, canon 14; at Agde, chapter 17:

> “Let no one presume to ordain a priest or bishop before his thirtieth year [Col. 0332B], that is, before he has reached the age of a complete man.”

Geoffrey, Letter 153: “Therefore let Ranulf, bishop of Durham, be expelled from the church of Luxeuil, so that digamy may not be admitted.” “Let him be expelled … that the heresy of neophytes may be rooted out,” Letter 157, “which Ranulf, surnamed Flambard, bishop of Durham, has for many years now occupied by an unheard-of kind of invasion. Having received the pastoral staff from the count of the Normans, he caused his two sons, scarcely twelve years old, to be intruded into the aforesaid church on the condition that, if the first-born died, the other should be substituted for him in the bishopric, one after another, in Jewish fashion.”

“Nor should the office lose its reverence.” Paul counts *σεμνότης*—“dignity” or “gravity”—among the virtues of bishops: Titus 2; 2 Timothy 3:8.

“He deferred to age, not merits.” At what age preaching should be entrusted. Bishops as preachers and teachers: Boniface, Letter 3 to Fulrad:

> “In God’s name I earnestly beseech the prudence of your graciousness that you cause my little son and fellow bishop Lucius, if God wills and if it so please your clemency, to be appointed and established for this ministry of peoples and churches as preacher and teacher of the peoples.”

Synesius, Letter 105: “Let a bishop, being a *νομοδιδάσκαλος* [teacher of the law] and uttering things in accord with the law, be a teacher of the law and speak what agrees with the law.” See Procopius of Gaza.

“Whoever is not found to have been in sacred orders [Col. 0332D] is forbidden by canonical ordinances to approach the highest priesthood.” The Council of Clermont, cited by Sirmond on Geoffrey, speaks to this matter as follows, canon 5: “Let no layman, cleric, or merely subdeacon be chosen as bishop.”

Bishops were originally chosen only from the household and alumni of the Church, and from those who had first enrolled in its order and, proceeding step by step, in time had reached the archdeaconry and archpriesthood. Hence Synesius, Letter 67: *ἀπὸ τροφὸς ἐκκλησίας ἀγωγὴν ἑτέραν ἠγμένος θυσιαστηρίων ἠψάμεν Θεοῦ*: “Reared outside the Church, trained in another discipline, [Col. 0333A] I should not hesitate to approach the altar of God.”

[Note: [Col. 0333D] On those promoted by a leap. Zosimus.] This displeased many, and election was therefore introduced. The author of the commentary on Paul’s Epistles to Timothy among the works of Ambrose:

> “Because those who followed in the order of presbyters were judged unworthy to hold primacies, election was devised … by the council, so that not order but merit should make a bishop, established by the judgment of many priests, lest an unworthy man rashly usurp the office and become a scandal to many.”

Celestine in the manuscript of Stella.

Zosimus, *d. d.*: “Indeed also upon his ordainers, that they should lack that order which they believed ought to be presumed without order and contrary to the prescriptions of the Fathers.” Council of Italy under Theodosius, among letters recently made public by the incomparable Sirmond: “We do not see what order his ordination had.” Geoffrey, Letter 10, Book III, to Rainald himself:

> “Afterwards you received all orders, but without order—without order, because you received them in eight days and not at fixed times—through ambition for the episcopate.”

“What shall I say of the election, in which the people may by no means precede the clergy?” Holy Roman synod.

“Pope Celestine.” Someone noted in the margin of the manuscript codex that this is not in the printed editions.

“Shall have requested unanimously.” That election is especially commended—“two hundred *…”—which is made by one and, etc. Ruricius, Letter 30, Book II:

> “You do well to ordain the man whom common consent has chosen; but warn him to pursue truth, not falsehood; peace, not disturbance,” etc.

[Col. 0333C] Eucherius, Homily *On the Ordination of a Priest*:

> “I am amazed that amid so many voices there was one voice for your most blessed bishop, and amid so many hearts one will.”

And shortly afterward:

> “But doubtless the singular privilege of merits removed hesitation of wills. Where comparison among virtues cannot enter, choice among pursuits is not troubled. The necessity of long deliberation ceases where equality does not compete; discerning judgment knows no long delays where one man, best among many, excels.”

Synesius, Letter 76, also bears on this:

> *Καὶ συνήσθην μὲν ἀνδράσιν ἐκ πολλῶν καὶ πάντων ἀγαθῶν ποιουμένοις τὴν αἵρεσιν. Πολὺ δὲ πλέον Ἀντωνίῳ συνήσθην τῆς καλοκαγαθίας, ὅτι καὶ καλῶν ἔδοξεν εἶναι καλλίων. Ἐστὶ γὰρ τούτῳ ἡ πάνδημος ψῆφος ἠνέχθη. Προστεθέντων δὲ [Col. 0333D] καὶ δυοῖν εὐλαβεστάτων ἐπισκόπων τῇ γνώμῃ τοῦ πλήθους*, etc.

> “I congratulated the people indeed that, from among many—and all good men—they made their choice; but I congratulated Antony much more upon his goodness and integrity, because he was judged better than good men. For the vote of all the people was brought to him; and when two most devout bishops had added themselves to the judgment of the multitude,” etc.

He added his vote and consented to the election. Synesius himself, Letter 67, ascribes this agreement to divine grace. The most learned Justellus expounded this more fully on canon 2 of the universal Church, Council of Nicaea. If Fathers and people, by disagreeing, were divided into opposing sides, the entire dispute was then settled by lot. Traces of this custom survive in the manuscript *Acts of Saint Euvertius, Bishop of Orléans*.

“Religious abbots.” Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, who rushed against Rainald with hostile standards and, becoming leader of a party, assailed his election in several letters—well worth consulting in Books III and IV. Also William, abbot of Saint-Florent at Saumur. Among them too was Bernard, abbot of Saint-Serge in the suburb of Angers. To them Geoffrey wrote Letter 8, Book IV; raising the signal of conspiracy from the very outset, he says:

> “If we are bound together by the bond of true charity, and if, inflamed by the fervour of the Holy Spirit, we have resolved to fight against that crooked and deceitful Rainald [Col. 0334B], whom you know, lest our souls perish with the people of God?”

He adds Bernerius, abbot of Bonneval. Sirmond, Letter 16, Book IV, to Bernerius, with whom I readily agree. Yet although he spares Rainald’s name, he nevertheless depicts and reveals him in his customary colours.

“Persons of unimpaired reputation.” Stephen the dean; Guamerius and William, archdeacons; and Hubert, archdeacon and precentor of the church of Angers—on whom see Letter 10. That they stirred up this storm will be apparent from a manuscript letter which I chose to transcribe from the cartulary of Vendôme. [Note: [Col. 0334D] Yet M. Loyauté did not reproduce it here.] It very much elucidates Geoffrey, to whom Stephen and William wrote it.

## ON LETTER XIII [now 6, Book II]

[Col. 0334C]

“You are a man set under authority.” He displays to Rainald the supreme authority of the supreme pontiff, being secure as to that of his ordinary metropolitan. For the pontiff vainly favoured the bishop-elect. Geoffrey, in the frequently cited letter written after peace had been restored, says:

> “I judged it fitting to recall to your highness these few things out of many, perhaps consigned by you to oblivion, so that you may no longer be able to be ignorant whence and how you received the name of bishop. I pass over those things which the lord pope knows and has allowed, because it is not mine to reopen what he has done. For he knew that your life was approved by no kind of religious discipline; perhaps he had heard that you were under age and had no order at all.”

Here he more modestly censures the excessive readiness [Col. 0334D] of Roman pontiffs to overturn the decrees of councils and Fathers.

## ON LETTER XIV [now 48, Book II]

“To William, archdeacon.” All manuscript codices agree on this superscription. It is not so easy to say of what church he was archdeacon. We encounter a difficulty in the formal words of deposition by which he says that he removes the simoniacal deacon from his rank: “We have recognized and do remove [him] from the diaconate and from above.” From this you may infer that Hildebert acts as censor and judge, not as adviser [perhaps *consiliarius*, “counsellor”]. No archdeacon of Le Mans bearing this name occurs. I have sometimes thought him to be [Col. 0335A] the same William, archdeacon of Angers, mentioned above; yet I decide nothing.

“Canonical authority also suspends him from the priesthood.” Improperly stated.

“Either not yet or improperly.” Tertullian says this against Marcion; Pacian likewise, concerning Novatian’s consecration, Letter 2 to Sempronianus, says of Novatian: “Made bishop without lawful consecration, and therefore not made.”

“Your danger is at stake if you tolerate the aforesaid brother.” This care especially belonged to archdeacons.

“On simony.” Comparable is the passage in John of Salisbury’s *Polycraticus*, Book V, chapter 11:

> “Equity is alienated from the seller, though it does not pass to the buyer; and purchased iniquity passes to the buyer in such a way that it by no means departs from the seller. And, unlike what occurs in other contracts, he alone sells justice who does not possess it.”

“It is better that no remedy at all be found for such a case.” A later, more lax age discovered softer extraordinary remedies, and indulgence made their use more frequent. Fuller authority, granted for the amendment of public discipline, too lenient toward crimes [perhaps *parcens*], … ruined the polity of the golden ages of old. A crime was at one time pardoned to a multitude of sinners. We learn this from a manuscript letter of Pope Zachary.

## ON LETTER XV [now 7, Book I]

“To Matilda.” The subject is the same as that of Geoffrey’s letter and the following letters.

“A judge must be softened by some good qualities.” Muret observes this Persian custom [Col. 0335C].

(The author made no note on Letter XVI.)

## ON LETTER XVII [now 1, Book II]

G. the archdeacon. This may perhaps be Gervasius Paganellus, archdeacon of the Church of Le Mans, who is mentioned in the Life of Hildebert in these words: “In those days there was in Apulia a certain knight named Geoffrey, son of Geoffrey of Meduana, one of the leading men of our region, wealthy in silver, gold, and the riches of great estates which he had acquired in those parts. Out of love for and remembrance of his native land, he had vowed to give to God and to our most holy patron Julian his chapel-treasury—that is, certain precious ornaments which he kept in his chapel. [Col. 0335D] Therefore, as he was about to set out for Jerusalem, he sent our bishop letters containing instructions that he should send him some of his clerics, trustworthy and diligent men to whom those ornaments might be entrusted without any suspicion of fraud. The bishop, delighted and joyful at this, sent there two canons of our Church: Gervasius Paganellus, archdeacon, and Hugh of Lavarzin [Note: [Col. 0335D] This man may perhaps have been Hildebert’s nephew.], who at that time held the office of archpriest. He provided them abundantly with the funds which seemed necessary for so great a journey. They carried out the business entrusted to them vigorously, received without difficulty everything which the man had commanded to be given them, and, with those ornaments, returned by a prosperous journey [Col. 0336A] to our Church, accompanied by divine grace.”

They are by no means tolerated through a dispensation of the Church, but are punished by the censure of justice. Council of Epaone, canon 30: “For incestuous unions we reserve absolutely no pardon, unless they have remedied adultery by separation. We judge that the incestuous are these persons, and that they are not to be covered by any name of marriage, apart from those whom it would be dreadful even to name.” If anyone has carnally violated the widow of his brother, who had previously been his sister, they were excommunicated and were admitted to penance only if they dissolved the marriage. “On account of humanity, he shall have penance” (Διὰ τὴν φιλαντροπίαν ἔξει τὴν μετάνοιαν), canon 20 of the Council of Neocaesarea.

[Col. 0336B] At the Council of Tribur. The same canon is cited for this matter by Ivo, Letter 22.

Yet a brother could not have his brother’s betrothed woman. Canon 54 of the Council of Elvira calls it a grave crime to feign a betrothal; Gratian corrupted this by adding a negation in *Is qui*, 31, question 3, and pronounces excommunication.

Lawful marriages, however, are not to be denied them. Second marriages were at times forbidden to persons guilty of incest. Canon 4 of the Council of Verberie. See canon *Quaedam cum fratre*, 32, question 7, and *Hi vero*, ibid. Burchard, book 17, chapter 52; the Council of Tribur deals with these persons more leniently.

To the ordeal of touching red-hot iron. Alexander II, to Rainald Cunianus, bishop: the popular law, supported by no canonical sanction—namely, the ordeal of boiling or cold [Col. 0336C] water and the touching of glowing iron.

For the law is adduced to no purpose. Hildebert rejects the forcing of a girl to prove her virginity by touching glowing iron, on the ground that not even a marriage could thereby be established with certainty. She would therefore undergo danger to no purpose in proving a virginity for which, he maintains, such a proof is of no help. That the Roman-law book *On Proofs* laid down a rule especially applicable in trials by glowing iron. The author of an old fragment inserted by Juretus in his notes on Ivo’s Letter 74: “Simoniacs are not to be admitted to trial if credible persons, even laymen or women, testify that they received money from them; nor is going to trial for matters manifest anything other than tempting the Lord. [Col. 0336D] Hence in such cases error often occurs, because God is far from those who tempt him.”

TO LETTER XVIII [now 32, book II].

“The path by which we may deserve, with a favourable outcome, to be presented at the thresholds of the Apostles.” So in the following letter: “Tossed by such storms, we resolve to set out for the thresholds of the Apostles, judging it a great remedy for this new tribulation if the Roman pontiff should assist us by counsel and aid.”

(Here end the most learned notes on Hildebert’s letters by the most distinguished and erudite jurist.)

Nevertheless, since the above-praised Monsieur Logé most kindly granted us permission to examine what the aforesaid Monsieur Loyauté had prepared concerning Hildebert’s letters, we came upon two manuscripts of Hildebert’s letter, almost contemporary with him. In the margin of one of them he himself had copied in his own hand certain brief notes, which, as one may reasonably believe, he at some time intended to publish as they stood in his mind. Judging that these would not be unwelcome to learned readers, we have added them here also, though they were written in very tiny letters, almost escaping sight.

Thus, indeed, on Hildebert’s second letter he wrote: This letter was written to Rivallon [Note: [Col. 0337D] Whence comes the word *Rival*, or, in the plural, *Rivaux*.] in the Armorican language, which is Old French. A *Rivallo* is called a rebel and an insolent man. The author of the History of Saint Turian, bishop of Dol: “A certain priest, one of the leading men of Brittany, made presumptuous use of the name assigned to him; for [Col. 0337B] he was called Rivallo (which means ‘rebel’ and ‘insolent’), and was struck by an arrow of the devil.” From this our idiom has retained *rivaux*: those who support opposing parties and stubbornly defend them.

There seem to me to have been several archdeacons of the same name, distinct persons, at the same time. Thus we read of Rivallon, archdeacon of Nantes, deprived of his rank in the Church of Nantes; and at Saint-Malo of another, a colleague of Peter.

On the third letter. Add the verses of Baudry concerning the Angevin nation, from which you will prove that learned men have always been held in great esteem among the English.

“Taken from our Church,” namely, a shoot; sons were called shoots. The abbot of Caen, Letter 5: “Though his son be one of the chief men, yet that little branch itself does not degenerate from the richness of its paternal root.” Corippus, book II: “As a shoot born from the root of its mother tree.”

On the seventh. Walter of Clincampo, commonly called de Clinchamp. “Unequal.” Husband and wife are equals.

“She was handed over.” *Acts of Abercius*: “It had been agreed between them [Marcus and Verus] that on an appointed day Lucius should come to Ephesus from the East, and Antoninus from Rome; and that Antoninus, with the goddess as witness, should hand over the girl in the temple of Diana which was there, while Lucius should receive her.”

On the eighth. “Fan.” Anselm, book III, Letter 136: “I think it safer and more careful that the chalice—lest either flies or something indecent should fall into it, as we know has often happened—be exposed to contact with unclean things whether covered or [Col. 0337D] uncovered.”

On the ninth. “Your request.” Manuscript of the Puteanus collection, in illuminated letters. In this letter he excuses himself to the people of Anjou, who had invited him to the consecration of their elect.

Glosses of Isidore. *Rogaterius*: a rival candidate.

“Religious persons”: abbots. But when they first acquired a right of vote in episcopal elections is uncertain; whether they had an equal right in elections of supreme pontiffs is likewise uncertain.

“By a necessary dispensation.” Bernaldus, priest of Constance, *On Avoiding Communion with Excommunicated Persons and on Reconciling the Fallen*. Leo the Great, writing to the bishops of Mauretania, is read to have tolerated even neophytes—men promoted from the laity to the episcopate—in the episcopate. [Col. 0338A] Yet nowhere do we read that the holy Fathers thus accommodated themselves to the times except where the Church’s leniency seemed likely to achieve more than canonical strictness.

“To judgment.” The canons of Angers appealed to the Apostolic See; hence Hildebert threatens their metropolitan.

On the twelfth. “Memorandum.” Sigefrid, Letter 6, to Gregory VII: “In your memorandum you stated that I had entrusted to your fatherhood secret counsel—indeed, counsel concerning my salvation—and added certain other matters, as though applying the file of correction, for the amendment of life and conduct.” As to the *commonitorium*, see Justellus on the African canons.

[Col. 0338B] “But the threats are popular.” Learned men disagree concerning the use of the canon of the Council of Nicaea. Sirmond denies that after the Council of Nicaea the people possessed a right of vote, and maintains that this authority belonged to bishops alone; with the sharpness of intellect in which he excels, he demonstrates this from Basil and Amphilochius.

“You fear no one.” Hincmar, bishop, to the clergy and people of Cambrai, from the decrees of Leo, chapter 35: “Let no one be ordained against his will or without requesting it, lest citizens despise or hate an unwanted bishop, and the election become less religious than is fitting [supplying: *election*]; and likewise … have one whom it did not desire.” And in the decree of the clergy of Laon concerning Hedenulf, the elect: “Because he to whom obedience must be rendered by all ought certainly to be chosen by all.”

[Col. 0338C] On the fifteenth. “You were made beautiful for the king’s delights.” *Chronicle of Tours*, year 47 of Emperor Henry and year 43 of Philip. Henry, king of England, took as wife Matilda, sister of David king of Scotland, daughter of King Melcom, or Malcolm, whom he had by Queen Saint Margaret. King Henry afterward begot by her William and two daughters, Matilda and Notha. William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Kings of the English*, p. 93 and p. 122, under William II; Henry of Huntingdon, *History*, book VI, p. 366; Edmund son of Edmund. This man was the father of Margaret, queen of the Scots. Margaret, moreover, was the mother of Matilda, queen of the English, and of David, the most cultivated king of the Scots. The same author, book VII, p. 380, places her [Col. 0338D] death in the fourteenth year, sixteenth minute. Roger of Hoveden, p. 68. Henry, the younger king of the English, assembled in London the daughter of Malcolm, king of the Scots, and of Queen Margaret—Matilda by name, sister of … Edgar, Alexander, and David—and received her in England. Anselm of Canterbury [or of Christ Church, Canterbury], archbishop, consecrated and crowned her queen on the Sunday of the feast of Saint Martin. Among the miscellaneous letters published by Gretser is a letter of Emperor Henry to Matilda, queen of the English, addressing her thus: “As we have learned from the report of some persons, we owe many thanks to your goodness and many proofs of friendship.” Perhaps it was written by him when he was seeking Adela.

[Col. 0339]

# SERMONS OF THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT (C, G)*

## 201–202 NOTICE

The sermons of the venerable Hildebert which we now bring to light from the hiding-places of ancient manuscripts—only three having previously been printed in the *Libraries of the Fathers*—the kindly reader will acknowledge with us to be his genuine offspring if he takes care to compare them attentively with the foregoing letters and sermons, and with other already published works of the same author which are beyond dispute. In both he will observe the same style, the same play upon words, similar phrases, and the same repetitions, with similar sound, of words derived from simple roots, so that it is demonstrated that the various streams can arise only from the same spring. To make this clearer, we have thought it worthwhile briefly to set out here, by way of specimen, a few examples from many, drawn from his letters and sermons.

For in both letters and sermons he plays with words, using as it were a gradation of derivatives from a simple word. Thus, for example, in Letter 7 of Book I, treating the last judgment of God: “Before the angels,” he says, “he will report, yield to truth, bring forth terrible things, inflict dreadful things.” And shortly afterward in the same place: “Though offended, he promises clemency, refrains from punishing, admits repentance, forgives offences, and commits greater things.” So in Sermon 63: “The saints rest, rest again, and come wholly to rest. First they rest in the sixth age, which is that of those living in the flesh; secondly, they rest again, and as it were rest a second time, in the seventh age, that of sleepers; thirdly, they come wholly to rest in the eighth age, that of those rising again.” And in Sermon 50: “Demons test the newly converted man more stubbornly in order to cast down God’s recruit, carry off the captive, and throw him into prison.” And there are countless examples in the sermons, as in the letters.

In Letter 2 of Book I, to Saint Anselm, he says that the birds which Abraham drove away from the victims signify distractions which come upon us even against our will, and which we too ought to drive away from prayer and especially from the holy sacrifice. He teaches this often in Sermon 20, Sermon 69, and elsewhere.

In both works, moreover, pride is often called: “Celestial by origin, always seeking higher things, so that it may return whence it fell.” This occurs in Letter 10 of Book I and elsewhere, and likewise in Sermons 27 and 68 and frequently in other places.

Likewise, in both he calls the fall and errors of sinners “the region of unlikeness, to which sinners criminally turn aside,” because through their sins they efface in themselves the image and likeness of God. Thus in Letters 4 and 8 of Book I, Sermons 12 and 13, and frequently elsewhere.

Finally, in both he employs phrases and modes of speech distinctive to himself. For example, he uses the word *exuberat*—“overflows”—for “increases and abounds,” as in Letter 13 of Book I: “Joy overflows for me.” Letter 12 of Book II: “In him knowledge overflows unto fruit, and character unto example.” And in the following letter: “Wishing to cause the grace of virtues to overflow for you.” So in Sermons 13 and 14: “The joy of the angels overflows.” Likewise he uses *sacrifex* for “priest,” as in Letter 52 of Book II, in the poem *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, and in the poem called *The Mathematician*, and frequently in the sermons and elsewhere, both in prose and verse.

We should indeed be excessive if we wished to report all the wholly similar phrases and forms of speech, and all the matching thoughts, employed by Hildebert in his letters, sermons, and other works. By these marks, as it were, drawn from the style of the indisputably Hildebertian letters, we have identified his sermons and judged that sermons assigned too uncritically to various other authors ought to be restored to Hildebert as their rightful parent.

Nor were we moved only slightly to this equitable judgment by the very collection of sermons which we discovered in various manuscripts, in whose sequence we observed sermons unquestionably Hildebertian. Thus in manuscript Saint-Victor no. 468, where several sermons are without an author’s name, the first of all is the sermon beginning *Dicite pusillanimes* [“Say to the faint-hearted”], which every editor has published under Hildebert’s name as truly his. Why then should not the others also be called his, if their style and conformity of thought support this—as we could easily prove? Thus in our Saint-Germain manuscript no. 381 is read the sermon beginning *Spiritu sancto Isaias edoctus* [“Isaiah, instructed by the Holy Spirit”], which three manuscripts of excellent authority, contemporary or nearly contemporary—namely the aforementioned Saint-Germain manuscript, Évreux no. 19, and Saint-Victor 468—unanimously attribute to Hildebert.

But we judge that we have said enough in advance on these matters, for the proof of our investigation, in our General Preface. For brevity’s sake we refer the diligent reader there. We hope that it will be more pleasing to him if we briefly indicate what benefit, or even pious delight, he may derive from the sermons of our Hildebert, and set before his eyes, as though reduced to a synopsis, those matters which concern either the doctrines of the Catholic Church, the ancient rites and discipline of the Church, or, finally, the direction of the conduct of believers in whatever state of life. From this it will also appear how rightly we have described Hildebert as at once a most pious and most learned theologian, a most zealous champion of ecclesiastical discipline as a bishop, and a most discerning teacher and safest guide of the Christian and even ascetic life. Yet it is not our purpose to include every individual matter in this notice, since it will be more than enough if we point out the sermons from which these matters may be drawn, and which the diligent reader may consult as he wishes. Let this, then, be done.

## [LIST.]

### 205–206 § I. On matters concerning theology and sacred doctrines

The immensity of God is described theologically and elegantly, Sermon 8. The immutability of God is learnedly explained, Sermon 99. The mystery of the Trinity is learnedly and subtly discussed, Sermon 53. [Col. 0341] On the eternal generation of the Word, Sermon 112. On the sending of the divine Word into the world, Sermon 8. On the sending of the Holy Spirit, Sermon 51. None of the ancients under the Old Law was saved except by faith in the Christ who was to come, Sermon 72. The mystery of the Incarnation is excellently described, Sermons 9 and 55. The same is defended against the Jews, Sermon 101. Saint Joseph never carnally knew the Blessed Mary, Sermon 60. The sacrament of the Eucharist is discussed orthodoxly, Sermon 35 and following, and frequently elsewhere. The Catholic Church’s doctrine of the reality of Christ’s body, and the word TRANSUBSTANTIATION, then first put into use by Hildebert; thereafter Peter of Celle, Stephen of Autun, and others used it, and only after him. All this has a great affinity with Hildebert’s other treatises on the Eucharist, which we shall give below. In all of them, moreover, there is teaching wholly opposed to the errors of Berengar, of whom Hildebert had been a pupil in humane letters, not in theology; Sermons 38 and 93. Christ accepted the legal observances in order to replace them with the Gospel, Sermon 57. The definition and order of predestination, Sermon 74. On the cross of Christ, see the outstanding passages in Sermons 71 and 72. On the blessedness of the saints, Sermons 9, 43, and 86. On the blessedness of angels and human beings, Sermon 43. On original sin and its transmission, Sermons 25, 111, and 112. On humanity’s miseries arising from that sin and its restoration through Christ, Sermons 2 and 100. The immaculate conception of the Blessed Virgin is suggested, Sermons 62, 70, and 101. Her assumption in body and soul is affirmed, Sermon 59.

### § II. On matters concerning ecclesiastical discipline and the various rites of the Church

Abstinence from meat during Advent and Rogationtide, Sermon 1. The ancient use in the Church of baptizing infants, Sermon 84. The feast of Epiphany more solemn than Christmas itself, Sermon 15. Penitents exiled from their own homes during the time of penance, Sermon 18. Expelled from the Church and shorn, Sermon 34. The use of haircloth imposed on penitents for mortifying the flesh, the imposition of ashes, and the practice of public penance in Hildebert’s time, Sermon 56. Penitents at times, by indulgence, reconciled for a time on Maundy Thursday, in order to prepare them to receive communion on Easter Day, though their period of penance was not completed, Sermon 34. Absolution from graver sins belongs by right only to bishops and priests; from lighter sins, however, to anyone—not by the way of authority, as with priests, but only by way of intercession—Sermon 30. A most prudent discipline of penance, Sermon 34. Confession of sins formerly preceded the Lenten fast, Sermon 18. On fast days in Hildebert’s time, refreshment was taken in the evening, Sermon 85. The origin of the Rogations at Vienne, Sermon 47. They were instituted to drive away wolves, Sermon 45; and to quell pestilence, ibid. The remarkable austerity imposed upon the faithful by the Fathers during them, the same as was publicly imposed upon penitents even for the gravest sins, Sermon 45 and following. Thursday of every week was celebrated more solemnly in the time of Pope Sylvester, in memory of the Lord’s Ascension, Sermon 49. The granting of indulgences at the dedication of a church, Sermon 87. The tract in Septuagesima, following the laying aside of Alleluia—whence it is so called—and the rite in certain churches of laying aside Alleluia, Sermon 111. The week beginning with Palm Sunday was called “Painful” in Hildebert’s time, Sermon 42; painful to the devil, Sermon 42. Invocation of the saints, Sermon 86. In the Palm procession flowers were carried and blessed together with palms. Their moral use is explained, Sermon 33. The carrying of candles in the Purification procession was sanctioned by the Fathers. This procession, however, was wholly penitential; its rite as it then was, Sermon 57. At the name of the Blessed Mary, in Hildebert’s time and also earlier, the knee was bent, Sermon 59. A proper prayer for the Assumption of Blessed Mary is noted, Sermon 59. Hildebert urged Guido, his successor in the see of Le Mans, to celebrate this feast more solemnly, Sermon 59. The general commemoration of the dead was celebrated after the feast of All Saints in Hildebert’s time, and the faithful observed a fast on it, Sermon 85. Why a candle was offered with both hands by those ordained to the pope who ordained them, Sermon 90. Tonsure and the long tunic were distinctive to clerics, Sermon 90. The obligation of sacred ministers, especially priests, to continence and celibacy, Sermon 76 and often elsewhere. In former times Mass was celebrated daily by priests, even those wearing the mitre—that is, bishops—in Hildebert’s time, Sermon 97. Condemnation of simony and lay investitures, Sermon 92. Payment must not be demanded for burials and Masses, Sermon 96. A defence of Pope Paschal II against Emperor Henry V, the violent usurper of investitures, and likewise of Innocent II against the antipope Anacletus during the schism, Sermon 98. Schools were formerly established in monasteries, especially at Cluny, Sermons 5 and 15. Monastic readings were formerly held communally in the cloister, Sermon 65. Psalms were formerly performed by monks standing, whence their various debilitating infirmities were endured for merit; laypeople too formerly observed this, Sermon 68. Hildebert’s monasticism is inferred from more than twenty sermons.

### § III. On matters concerning conduct and the ascetic life

Excellent precepts of the interior or ascetic life, especially fitting for a monk, Sermon 112 and throughout. 209–210. The praises, temptations, and defects of monastic life are vividly depicted, and abstinence from meat is there noted, Sermon 39. The Christian and interior life is continual warfare, Sermon 114. How necessary is the true and continual guarding and mortification in it of the outer and inner senses, Sermons 8, 20, and elsewhere. The two cities, of God and of the devil, continuously opposed to one another in this world, Sermons 22 and 32. An excellent description of the active and contemplative life, Sermon 64. The gifts and excellence of contemplatives, Sermon 12. Two kinds of contemplatives, according to the proper works of contemplation, Sermons 14, 64, 118, and 120. Solitude is commended to scholars as most useful for studies, Sermon 5. Noah, Daniel, and Job are figures respectively of prelates, married persons, and contemplatives or penitents, Sermon 62. [Col. 0343] The right directing of intention is necessary in all actions, Sermons 25 and 72. The birds which Abraham drove away from the victims are a figure of distractions which come upon us, even unwillingly; as Abraham drove away the birds, so we are bound to drive them from sacrifice and prayer, Sermons 69 and 116 and often elsewhere. Widespread mortality, attacks by beasts, and illnesses after Easter, already more frequent in Hildebert’s time, were generally sent as punishment for unworthy communions, Sermon 38. Pride, celestial by origin, strives to return whence it fell, Sermons 27 and 68 and often elsewhere. Through sin one departs into the region of unlikeness, because through it we lose God’s image and likeness, Sermons 12 and 13 and often elsewhere. The devil is prince of this region, Sermon 21. A diet of three days is necessary in order to return to God, Sermons 7 and 36 and elsewhere. An elegant dialogue between a worldly man wishing to turn a religious man away from his state and that man resolving to persevere in it, Sermon 73. Perseverance in the monastic order is most highly commended, Sermon 73. Christ himself is founder of the Benedictine order, Sermons 117 and 118. What the black garment and monastic crown signify, Sermon 120. Monastic silence and assiduity in common exercises are commended, Sermons 119 and 122. How exact the obedience of monks ought to be, Sermon 50. Regular or cloistral places, and the use of each for piety and moral application, Sermon 63. A moving commendation of regular observance, Sermon 70 and often elsewhere.

We refrain from adding more here, which the diligent reader may discover from the index. We have related these matters briefly in order to make known that those devoted to a genuinely Christian—indeed ascetic—life, and also inquisitive and eager students of sacred antiquity, who now seem to claim for themselves a kind of primacy among learned men, will derive no small benefit from reading these sermons.

The preachers of sacred doctrine in this age will also derive from them no small delight and profit, if they strive, as far as possible, to compose their sermons out of the very words of sacred Scripture. For they will recognize in the Venerable Hildebert, together with Saint Bernard, his friend and equal, a precursor and model of that industry which can never be praised enough. We shall not delay to indicate all these matters to the reader at the end of each sermon, as opportunity presents itself.

# SERMONS FOR THE SEASONS

## I. FIRST SERMON FOR THE ADVENT OF THE LORD  
[Note: [Col. 0343B] From printed editions and the Saint-Victor manuscript, about 600 years old, no. 468.]

### On the benefits of the Lord’s Advent

[Col. 0343A]

211 “Say to the faint-hearted: Be strengthened, and do not fear. Behold, your God will come and save you. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened and the ears of the deaf unsealed. Then the lame man shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be loosed” (Isa. 35:4–6).

Before the Lord’s coming, dearest brothers, the human race was plunged in such darkness that people neither knew God, nor wished to hear his words, nor acted rightly, nor confessed their sins. And since they were held fast by many infirmities of soul, it pleased the supreme physician to visit them and relieve them with his remedies. But the prophet Isaiah notes that they were especially afflicted by four diseases. For they were blind, deaf, mute, and lame. When he wished to heal their diseases, he wanted to announce his coming to them, lest the wretched should despair; he wanted to strengthen them by his consolations. Do you wish to hear who the messengers were? Isaiah and the other prophets. Hear what consolation he enjoined upon the messengers: “You, my ministers, say to the wretched who lie in sufferings, who despair in their infirmities: ‘O faint-hearted ones, be strengthened, for behold your God will come.’” Behold your medicine. Behold your salvation will come and save you. He will heal the infirmities to which you are subject. For then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, [Col. 0344A] and the ears of the deaf shall be unsealed; then the lame man shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be loosed.

They were blind because they did not know God; deaf because they neglected his words; lame because they did not walk uprightly through good works; mute because they kept silent about their sins. This deafness, blindness, and the other defects that follow had taken their beginning from the first man. Adam became deaf regarding the first command laid upon him by God. For when it was said to him, “On whatever day you eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall die” (Gen. 2:17), he appeared not to have heard, “you shall die,” since he did not keep the commandment. He was blind when he understood the demon’s words, saying, “And you shall be like gods.” For when he thought that he would become God, he already bore a blinded mind. This the Lord afterward reproached him for, saying: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us” (Gen. 3:22). He said this mockingly. The man who thought he would become God now found himself wretched. “He has become as one of us”—that is, like the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; that is, he has become God. This was said ironically, because he found himself otherwise than he had imagined.

Adam became lame because, when he began to walk—that is, to act—he went with a crooked step. For he was wounded by the sting of death and of the venomous serpent, and by acting wickedly became lame. The first thing he is recorded to have done was sin. A human being ought to have two feet: love [perhaps “delight”] of God and of [Col. 0345A] neighbour. Whoever lacks one of them is lame. Adam, however, became lame because he loved his wife too much but withdrew himself from the love of God. He did not love God, whose commandment he neglected. He preferred love of his wife to love of God, since he obeyed his wife’s persuasion more readily than God’s will. Thus he became lame.

Moreover, he was mute in confessing his sin, because not only did he fail to confess his sin, but he began to excuse his wrongdoing, saying: “The woman whom you gave me gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3:12). For in saying, “The woman whom you gave me,” he shifted the blame onto the woman and even wished to cast reproach upon God in the word “gave.”

You have heard, brothers, how Adam became deaf, blind, lame, and mute. Before Christ came into the world, the human race had fallen into these same vices. People were so blinded that they worshipped idols. Hence the Apostle: “They became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. And because they did not see fit to retain God in knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind” (Rom. 1:21, 28). They were deaf, according to what Isaiah says: “The heart of this people has grown gross, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and have closed their eyes, lest perhaps they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears” (Isa. 6:10; Matt. 13:15). And again: “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Rom. 10:16). And the Psalmist: “Their fury is like that of a serpent, like a deaf asp which stops up its ears” (Ps. 57:5). And again: “My people did not hear my voice, and Israel paid no heed to me” (Ps. 80:2).

They became lame through evil actions, 213 according to the words: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13:3). And again: “Foreign children have lied to me; foreign children have grown old and become lame from their paths” (Ps. 17:46). Many became mute by keeping silent about sins, according to what David says of himself: “Because I kept silence, my bones grew old” (Ps. 31:3).

All these things, dearest brothers, the heavenly physician healed. He enlightened the blind when he opened human minds to understand the Scriptures, and when he announced his Father to the world, according to what he himself says: “Father, I have made your name known to men” (John [Col. 0345D] 17:6), because he was first in the world, and the world did not know him. This is the enlightenment for which David asks, saying: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death; lest my enemy ever say, ‘I have prevailed against him’” (Ps. 12:4).

He opened ears when he cried: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 7:16). The Gentile people also had opened ears when it gladly received his preaching, as he himself says through David: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear it obeyed me” (Ps. 17:45). And these are the things the prophet promised when he said: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unsealed.” It follows:

[Col. 0346A] Then the lame man shall leap like a stag. They were lame, as we have said, because they did not walk uprightly, being not occupied in good works; but he directed the steps of human beings when he directed their hearts toward the way of the heavenly homeland. Hearts are directed when they turn aside neither to the right nor to the left. The right is God’s mercy; the left, however, is despair. Hence Isaiah says: “This is the way; walk in it, turning aside neither to the right nor to the left” (Isa. 30:21). Judas and the devil, who despaired, turned aside to the left. Origen, however, who, placing too much confidence in God’s mercy, preached that the devil would be saved—and that after a thousand years—strayed too far to the right. Therefore the middle path must be followed, so that people neither despair nor, trusting in mercy, [Col. 0346B] sin without restraint.

A figure of this is found in the ark of the covenant: when it was brought back from the kingdom of the Philistines to its place, two cows, turning aside, drew it on a cart along a straight road, so that they turned neither to the right nor to the left (2 Kings 6:10). The ark is the Church. The two cows are the preachers among Jews and Gentiles, who nourish the tall with milk and guide the Church. Therefore David says: “God takes pleasure in those who fear him, and in those who hope in his mercy” (Ps. 149:4). He sets down both hope and fear. Hope without fear is presumption; fear without hope is despair. Fear removes excessive security, lest one cling too closely to the right.

214 John rightly says of this way: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight [Col. 0346C] the paths of our God” (Isa. 40:4; Luke 3:4). But on this straight way one must leap; hence it is said: “The lame man shall leap like a stag.” When he comes to thorny and muddy [printed: mournful; perhaps *lutosa*, “muddy”] places, he will leap over them. Likewise, sinner, if love of riches meets you—riches which prick with anxiety—or if you are touched by love of lust or of any foul pleasure, leave it behind by leaping over it. The stag leaves the valleys and climbs the mountains. Leave earthly things and seek heavenly ones. Thus the Lord says through David: “He made my feet like those of stags and set me upon the heights” (Ps. 17:32).

An aging stag devours a serpent; then, burning with excessive heat, it runs to a spring. After drinking, it casts off its old skin and antlers and becomes young again. So too, sinner: kill the serpent and run to the spring—that is, to [Col. 0346D] Christ—and put off the old human being, that is, pride, so that you may say with David: “As the stag longs for fountains of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. 41:1).

It follows: “And the tongue of the mute shall be opened.” For when Christ cried, “Repent” (Matt. 3:2), those who had previously been ashamed to confess their sins then repented; by confession they uncovered their sins. Mary, who had previously been mute, cried out for pardon. The thief upon the cross, who had previously been silent, cried out for pardon. Behold, the mute woman spoke; behold, the mute man spoke.

We have shown what benefit the coming of the supreme physician brought to the world. The prophecy was fulfilled: the physician came and healed the sick. But what benefit is the salvation [Col. 0347A] of others to us unless this healing benefits us? We must fear lest anyone among us still lie in infirmity. Yet the eyes of all of us are open, because you are believers: you have known God, and the blindness of unbelief has departed. But at times you are deaf, because you avoid hearing God’s word or despise what you hear. Beware lest it be said to you: “For this reason you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 7:37). Some of you limp because you act wrongly. Some also become mute because they are ashamed to confess their sins.

But now is the time for confession and satisfaction, because the fasts are near. What is fasting except satisfaction? And what does satisfaction avail unless confession comes first? First put away your fault and acknowledge it, before seeking pardon [Col. 0347B] and undergoing the penalty of satisfaction. Therefore prepare yourselves for the Lord who is coming, and sing beforehand to the Lord in confession of sins, so that on the day of his Nativity you may sing psalms to him in a confession of praise. For the days of Advent are nothing but a preparation for doing what John cried: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight his paths,” so that we may be worthy of the coming feast and of the joy of the Nativity of 215 our King.

The ancient Fathers prepared themselves near [printed: *contra*, “against”; that is, *prope*, “near”] Christ’s Advent, that they might be worthy of the redemption to come. These days bear the figure of that time. Christ is as though about to be born. We are to represent his Nativity, so that through a new birth new joy may be brought forth for us. Therefore, “It is now the hour for us to arise from sleep. Let us therefore cast off the works [Col. 0347C] of darkness and put on the armour of light; let us walk honourably as in the day, not in revelry and drunkenness” (Rom. 13:11–12). Avoid drunkenness; abstain from flesh. Let gluttony not defile you. For the Lord whom we await is a lover of purity and sobriety. Would you not splendidly adorn your houses if an earthly emperor were about to come to you? Adorn your hearts with virtues, so that you may worthily receive the King of angels. He lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## II. SECOND SERMON FOR THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

[Note: [Col. 0347D] From a manuscript of Saint Albinus of Angers, about 600 years old.]

On the two advents of Christ.

“Who will grant me a hearer [Note: [Col. 0347D] From what follows, Hildebert seems [Col. 0348D] to have read *adiutorem*, ‘a helper,’ rather than *auditorem*, ‘a hearer.’ All biblical copies, however, have *auditorem*, not *adiutorem*.], that the Almighty may hear [Col. 0347D] my desire, and that he who judges may himself write the book, that I may carry it upon my shoulder and encircle myself with it as with a crown” (Job 31:35–36).

In this brief utterance, my brothers, if the words are carefully examined, many mysteries are found. There are, namely, four matters pertaining to Christ: his two advents and the effect of each. Likewise, there are four matters concerning humanity: the pressure of evils, the lack of goods, human merit, and reward. The last two are accomplished through Christ’s two advents and their effects; the other two—namely, [Col. 0348A] the pressure of evils and the lack of goods—are removed, so that four answer to four, as will become clearer in the course of the exposition.

The Holy Spirit, speaking through blessed Job, shows how greatly the ancient Fathers desired to see the Saviour and how eagerly they longed for his advent in the flesh, in which they awaited the liberation, redemption, and salvation of the human race. For they said: “O Wisdom! O Adonai!” and, “Do you think I shall see? When will he be born?” and things of this kind. David too said: “Awaken your power and come” (Ps. 79:3), and, “Show us, Lord, your mercy” (Ps. 84:8). Groaning over the delay, he said: “But you have rejected . . . delayed your Christ” (Ps. 88:39). And Isaiah: [Col. 0348B] “Would that you would rend 216 the heavens and come down!” (Isa. 64:1). The same, and the other Fathers, asked this in other words, seeing and feeling the misery of the human race, which is here summed up under two headings: evils were present, and goods were lacking.

To remove evils, he asks for a helper [printed: *auditorem*, “hearer”]. To grant the goods that were lacking, he asks for one who will hear his desire. Evils came from ourselves and from the devil. Thus: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others” (Ps. 18:13). And the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). What great person can do this? Not our own powers, but only God’s grace through Jesus Christ (ibid., 25). David desires the same thing, saying: “May the Lord bring him help [Col. 0348C] upon his bed of pain. You have turned all his bed in his sickness” (Ps. 44:4).

A helper is needed in the struggle against the devil, against the flesh, through which it especially disturbs us. For the just man has a bed of pain, upon which he groans while the wicked man rejoices. The bed, which before sin had been most excellently arranged, has been overturned. In reason there was keen judgment for discerning; in the will, uprightness in desiring; in sensuality, a devout strictness in obeying. What reason discerned, the will desired, and sensuality did not oppose. There was understanding without error, desire for the good without difficulty, and obedience in sensuality—as if on a bed for sweet rest. A mattress was laid beneath; [Col. 0348D] above it, a delicate linen sheet; third, a precious covering.

Now, on the contrary, through sin, there is ignorance of good in reason; desire of evil in the will; and inability in the flesh, or sluggishness in doing good. Thus a person is disturbed in many ways, and is sometimes opposed in one respect, sometimes in two. What reason itself judges good and desirable, the will rejects and carnality attacks. David bewailed this elsewhere, saying: “Have mercy on me, for I am troubled; my eye, my soul, and my belly are disturbed in anger” (Ps. 30:10): my inner eye, that is, my reason, in the present anger which I bear and the future anger which I fear; my soul, that is, my will; and my belly, that is, my flesh.

Hence Jeremiah too says: “He has made me drunk with wormwood” (Lam. 3:15), because the human race receives many bitter things and, like a drunken person, does not understand what it suffers, but rejoices in earthly things as though they were true goods, and exults in utterly evil things. Therefore Hosea says: “Ephraim is a heifer taught to love threshing” (Hos. 10:11), because even if it were permitted to be free from worldly labours, it withdraws itself through habit and does not cease from the yoke of worldly slavery. And blessed Job says: “He opened his quiver, afflicted me, and put a bridle [Col. 0349A] in my mouth” (Job 30:11). By the quiver is understood God’s hidden judgment. Therefore, when the Lord sees sins and yet does not move his hand to vengeance, he keeps his quiver shut; but when he judges by striking, he shows how much displeased him in us that he had long endured while seeing it.
