He put on the bridle when he restrained boastfulness in merits and exaltation in words.

Against the human evils that have spread, he asked for a helper, necessary for himself and for all: him who is “a helper in times of need.” Hence: “O God, attend to my help” (Ps. 69:1). He says, then, either in amazement, “Who will grant?”—as though no one’s kindness but his could confer this—or in desire, “Would that someone,” that is, someone great and powerful, namely God the Father, might grant this: that he might send the Son, so that through him, as mediator, the Almighty might hear my desire. Before God it is not words but desires that make prayers. To pray truly is to be a lover groaning in compunction, not to utter carefully composed words aloud. Hence: “My desire is before you.” One never ceases to pray who never ceases to love. Desire grows into pain while the desired thing is delayed; but God hears all the more fully as, through delay, he kindles desire more vehemently.

It follows:

“And may he write the book.” A fourfold book is found in the Scriptures. The first book is predestination; the second is the book of teaching, or hidden inspiration through Christ, who is the pattern of life for those who believe in him; the third is the bodily book of Scripture; the fourth is the book of conscience, which is easily distinguished in its proper places. Job, therefore, desires the book. But when does he ask that it be written for him, although he knew that he would not see it [Col. 0349D] in the flesh? Yet already, in the spirit of prophecy, he read in it; he asked that it be written not bodily for himself but for us. This is the book of remembrance, that is, the memorial book. Hence Isaiah: “The Lord has made a shortened word upon the earth.” This is writing not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God.

Ezekiel saw a scroll written within and without (Ezek. 2:9), concerning moral and mystical matters and the restraining of fleshly and spiritual vices; in that book were song, lamentation, and woe. Zechariah sees “a flying scroll” (Zech. 3:1), because Scripture, while speaking of things above, raises the intention of our mind toward higher things. In it the sins of all were written. In Daniel: “The court sat, and the books were opened” (Dan. 7:10).

It follows:

[Col. 0350A] “He who judges,” at the second advent. For at the first he will come veiled in the sheath of humility [printed: *humanitatis*, “humanity”]; at the second he will shine with light for the godly and terror for the wicked. At the first, he comes in weakness; at the second, in power. At the first, in our smallness; at the second, in his majesty. At the first, in gentleness; at the second, in strict judgment. Then he came to redeem; at the second advent, to reward. And he will punish more severely then, the more long-sufferingly he endures here. Here he bestows talents, which there he will demand with interest [printed: *censuris*, “assessments”; perhaps *usuris*, “interest”]. He who entrusted commandments here will require there an account of what was entrusted.

We must render an account to God on three grounds: first, because we were made human—that is, rational—according to God’s image and likeness; second, because we were redeemed—that is, made Christians; third, because we were received into the share of the saints’ lot—that is, made deacons, presbyters, and the like. The more entrusted to a person, the more is required from that person; the higher the rank, the more perilous the fall. “For, as Gregory says, we must fear lest we who are seen to have received something beyond others be judged more severely for it by the Author of the world. For as gifts increase, so too increase the accounts required for gifts.”

For what purpose, blessed Job, do you ask for the book to be written? That you may carry it on your shoulder. Therefore, at the ordination of bishops, a book is placed upon their shoulders, so that, in carrying it, they may be bound to it through ordination. This is signified by the cross made upon the shoulders of one being baptized. For the cross on the sinner’s [perhaps: breast] signifies faith in the heart; the cross on the forehead, confession in the mouth; the cross on the shoulders, the performance of works. [Col. 0350C] Hence Jacob says in the blessings of Genesis: “Issachar is a strong ass; he saw that rest was good and that the land was best, and he set his shoulder to bear” (Gen. 49:14). Whoever desires to reach the promised rest should gladly bear the burdens of the commandments.

Likewise Moses says of Benjamin in Deuteronomy: “The beloved of the Lord shall dwell confidently in him . . . and shall rest between his shoulders” (Deut. 33:12). By the shoulders are understood good works joined with patience. Christ will rest in them all the more willingly as a person bears more grievous labours for his sake. Inviting us to this, he says: “My yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11:30).

It follows:

“And may I encircle myself with it as with a crown.” David [Col. 0350D] says: “You have crowned us with the shield of your good will” (Ps. 5:13). In Exodus, the Lord’s table is commanded to have a crown made above its rim, openwork, four fingers high (Exod. 25:25). The table is divine Scripture. Hence: “You have prepared a table before me” (Ps. 22:5), and: “The little dogs eat from their masters’ table” (Matt. 15:27). The rim is made around the table because, when Holy Scripture is rightly understood, it resounds in every part of its speech with the brightness of heavenly Wisdom. It is four fingers high—that is, according to the four books of the Gospel; it is openwork because of the diversity of merits. And a second, smaller golden crown is commanded to be made above that crown: it signifies the reward of those who excel in teaching.

The crown is promised when it is said: “If you wish to enter into 219 life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:17). The smaller crown is laid above when it is said: “If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and come, follow me” (ibid., 21). Again, the first crown is the eternal rewards received with the Lord by souls departing from the body. The smaller crown exists because a higher glory is reserved in the resurrection of bodies.

This book is observed: not only in the future, but also in the present it surrounds us on every side, lest the lion who goes about seeking whom he may devour should somehow break into the city of a good conscience. Nor does he say, “a crown placed around the head,” but “around me,” because it encompasses the whole person; for the splendour of newness [printed: *vetustatis*, “oldness”] clothes the whole human being in the other age and in this one adorns and protects him. Nor does he say “may he encircle,” but “may I encircle myself.” Hence: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling” [Col. 0351B] (2 Cor. 7:15), and: “My soul is always in my hands” (Ps. 118:109). For although grace moves and protects us, something nevertheless depends upon the human person, because the kingdom of heaven belongs not to one who gives but to one who receives.

Behold, we now believe manifest what we set forth at the beginning. First, the advent is shown where the helper is desired, and the hearing of desire is its effect: the writing of the book. The second advent and its effect are shown where he is said to judge. The pressure of evils and lack of goods are sufficiently evident from what has been said. Human merit consists in carrying the book, and this belongs to the first advent. The reward—that is, the crown—is awaited in the second. Let us therefore ask the writer of the book to place it, inscribed for us, upon our shoulders, so that for carrying it well he may repay us with a crown. He lives and reigns . . . Amen.

## III. THIRD SERMON FOR THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

[Note: [Col. 0351D] From an Angers manuscript about 600 years old.]

On Christ’s various advents into the world.

“I have indeed seen the affliction of my people . . . and I have come down to deliver them” (Exod. 3:7; Acts 7:34).

The words you have just heard from my mouth are the Lord’s words, not mine. The Lord’s words are grains, not chaff; and therefore they must be chewed, then swallowed, and finally incorporated. They are chewed when the history is rightly understood; swallowed when they are understood spiritually; incorporated when they are fulfilled through faith working by love. The meaning, then, is this:

[Col. 0351D] “Seeing, I have seen the affliction of my people.” Seeing in mercy, I have seen in compassion the affliction of my people. God’s people are the souls of believers in the land of Egypt—that is, in human bodies. Egypt is the world; the land is human bodies, in which souls are daily afflicted by desires and things of this sort. To deliver them, the Lord came in the first advent in the flesh, which the Church denotes by the first Sunday. But because then he was received only by the Jews, whereas now he is gathered in that faith from both peoples, Gentile and Jew, two days of the Lord are celebrated.

Besides these, there are other advents which the Church does not celebrate. Holy Scripture, however, does not pass them over in silence. The first [Col. 0352A] was into human beings, that is, into the hearts of the prophets; another was through human beings, into the Virgin’s womb; another was into hell, below [printed: *infra*; perhaps *contra*, “against”] human beings; another was to human beings in the faith of believers; another was above human beings in the understanding of the Scriptures; another was against human beings, in the punishment of the damned.

The first advent was in shadow and smoke, with respect to the prophets, who knew Christ’s advent in a certain cloudiness and shadow. The second was in the purple of divinity and the sackcloth of humanity. Purple is a royal garment, in which divinity is understood; sackcloth is the garment of penitents, in which humanity is understood. The third was in rod and staff: in the rod, the power by which he broke the barriers of hell; in the staff, the justice by which he defeated the devil. The fourth was in wine and oil: in wine, contrition of heart; in oil, mercy, because he remits sins to penitents. [Col. 0352B] Hence in the Gospel: “When you fast, anoint your head” (Matt. 6:17), that is, your mind, with oil, that is, mercy.

In the fifth, he comes in parchment and pen, that is, in the understanding of the Old Testament, denoted by parchment because it was written on tablets, and transmitted in the understanding of the New Testament, denoted by the pen. For this reason the Holy Spirit wrote it in the hearts of believers; hence: “My tongue is the pen of a scribe writing swiftly” (Ps. 44:2). In the sixth advent, the Lord will come in fire, because fire will go before his face; and he will come with the sword of the word, by which he will strike the wicked, saying: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41).

The first advent was of mercy; the second, of patience; the third, of power; the fourth, [Col. 0352C] of grace; the fifth, of understanding; the sixth will be of justice. May he grant us to rejoice and be glad at it, he who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## IV. FOURTH SERMON FOR THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

[Note: [Col. 0351D] From the Saint-Germain-des-Prés manuscript, no. 383, about 600 years old.]

On the excellence of the God-man, or Christ.

“Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him” (Song 3:11).

Just as “no one knows,” according to the Apostle’s testimony, 221 “the things of a human being except the human spirit which is within him, so no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:11). Therefore it is the Spirit of God who speaks here through Solomon about God’s wisdom, which “none [Col. 0352D] of the rulers of this age has known.

“For if they had known it, they would never have crucified it” (1 Cor. 2:8). But who are these rulers? Certainly the enemies of the Church: philosophers, heretics, Jews, and evil spirits, who promised salvation of souls and gave precepts about blessedness and justice, which they did not confer but took away. By impostures and deceitful images of truth they deceived people, ignorant of truth, empty of [supplied: spiritual] wisdom, and full of [supplied: carnal] wisdom—or rather, folly. “For the wisdom of this world,” according to the Apostle, “is folly with God” (1 Cor. 1:18); unless a person rejects it, he does not grasp the wisdom which is from above [Col. 0353A]. For the wisdom of this world is earthly and hostile to God’s wisdom. This wisdom is “earthly, animal, and demonic,” as James says. “But that which is from above is chaste, peaceable, and modest” (Jas. 3:15, 17).

Lest anyone despair of obtaining this wisdom or consider its fruit slight, let that wisdom itself be heard: “Wisdom,” it says, “is radiant and never withers; she is easily seen by those who love her and found by those who seek her” (Wis. 6:13). Again: “To think of her is consummate understanding, and whoever keeps watch for her will quickly be free from care” (ibid., 16). With this wisdom Solomon is crowned. For with as much proclamation as this wisdom is preached as something to be sought and pursued, with so much diligence are the daughters called to enter [printed: *intrati*; perhaps *mitrati*, “crowned”] into the sight of Solomon [Col. 0353B].

But if wisdom is easily found by those who seek it and Solomon is seen by those who love him, why has no ruler of this age known wisdom and seen Solomon? Because he is neither truly loved nor truly sought: that is, they do not go forth to see him with the daughters of Jerusalem. They do not wish to go out from the darkness of blindness and ignorance into the light of faith and truth. They do not wish to leave the world in order to possess heaven; they intend to remain children of darkness, so as to be prudent in this generation. They do not wish to become children of light, so as to be wise [in] the generation to come. They do not wish [printed: *volunt*, “they wish”] to become fools in their own eyes, so as to be wiser before God. Thus the Apostle says: “If anyone among you seems wise in this age, let him become foolish”—that is, in his own eyes—“so that he may become wise”—that is, before God (1 Cor. 3:18).

Therefore they are ignorant of God’s wisdom and do not see the true Solomon in the diadem because they are unwilling to leave the darkness, where the daughters of Jerusalem are, to whom this saving exhortation is offered:

[Col. 0353C] “Go forth,” he says, “daughters of Jerusalem, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him.” This is said to us, who walk by faith, though not yet by sight, and who must strive with all our desires toward the vision of supreme peace. Therefore let us go forth, as true Hebrews, from the Egypt of darkness and the furnace of tribulations—that is, from a vain, perverse, and destructive manner of life, which closes the eyes of the mind so that it cannot fully understand the mystery of salvation. It conquers the foot of the soul [printed: *vincit*; perhaps *venit*, “comes”], lest the soul be able thereafter to return in mind and desire to the land of promise. For, surrounded [Col. 0353D] by a crowd of vices, it does not forget its own people and its father’s house—that is, the devil’s. His house is pride, on account of vices and sins. He has commanders in his army, retainers, and a populace.

There are four commanders, guarding the four sides of his army: the four corruptions of which Joel says, “What the caterpillar left the locust ate; what the locust left the grub ate; what the grub left the rust ate” (Joel 1:4). These signify the four vices that hold human nature captive: lust, vain glory, gluttony (*gastrimargia*), and anger; they go before as commanders. These are the four plagues. Whoever escapes one sometimes falls into another. Many, indeed, subdue lust but then rise up in pride; from pride they fall into gluttony, which is the greediness of the belly; from this into anger and rage.

These commanders are cruel and violent, harmful and destructive. Although they seem sweet and gentle to some, nevertheless they take them captive according to their violent custom, the law of malice, and those persons’ weakness, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “I delight in the law of God according to the inward human being, but I see another law resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin and death” (Rom. 7:12). Thus many are cut off from the Lord’s little flock through these rulers: some are dragged away unwillingly; some are drawn by enticement; some depart deceived; others withdraw voluntarily.

Behold who and how powerful are the rulers of King Assur—that is, of the devil, who exalts and casts down—for he holds whatever he can in Babylon [Col. 0354B] of confusion and presses it down into the destruction of eternal damnation. For, as we have said, he has not only commanders but also retainers. Who are these retainers? Seven corruptions of the soul. Sinners—that is, persons withdrawing from God into the region of unlikeness—are received by seven corruptions.

The first is neglect of oneself, by which they begin to depart from the way; for through the vice of negligence the straightness of the way is abandoned. Then comes curiosity about external matters and things not concerning oneself, by which a person, abandoning personal concerns, deals with or attends to others’ affairs. From the first vice one becomes sluggish toward good; from the second, restless and careless of one’s own concerns. Solomon says of the sluggish and negligent person: “The sluggard says, ‘There is a lion in the road, and a lioness in the ways.’ As a door turns on its hinge, so the sluggard turns upon his bed” (Prov. 26:13). [Col. 0354C] Of the curious person, however, he says: “The words of a whisperer are as though simple, yet they penetrate to the innermost parts of the heart” (ibid., 22).

The third retainer is desire of the flesh; the fourth, consent; the fifth, habit; the sixth, contempt; the seventh, warfare—that is, the love of sin. Negligence delays; curiosity obstructs; desire binds; consent constricts and hardens; habit drags along, because it is difficult to cast off what is customary; contempt hurls down; love of iniquity imprisons in the prison of despair.

Thus, through these seven corruptions, as though through seven precipices, the sinner descends and falls into the deep and despises. For, as Scripture testifies: “When a sinner comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3), and he despairs; confession perishes from him as from one dead [Col. 0354D]. These retainers are utterly wicked and therefore must be fled: they meet on the way those who depart into the counsel of the wicked and lead them into the abyss of perdition.

It is most difficult to escape these four aforementioned commanders and these seven retainers, but much more difficult to conquer them and wholly erase them from the land of the human mind. But what shall we say of the infinite crowd of common people who follow King Assur after his commanders and retainers? Joel says of this: “A nation has come up over my land, mighty and innumerable; its teeth are like the teeth of a lion” (Joel 1:6). The innumerable nation of King Assur is the infinite multitude of vices. For there are creeping things without number that come up over God’s land—that is, over the human [Col. 0355A] soul, because every soul belongs to God, according to the saying: “As the soul of the father, so the soul of the son is mine.” It has teeth like a lion’s, because our adversary, the devil, who goes around like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour, is the suggester and instigator [printed: *incensor*; perhaps *incentor*, “instigator”] of all evils. Of him the Prophet says: “Indeed Assur has come with them; they have become a help to the children of Lot” (Ps. 82:9).

The children of kings are children of turning aside. For *Lot* is interpreted “turning aside”: that is, angels from their power, because by turning away from the truth, in which they did not stand, they departed into the devil’s retinue. Thus Assur also comes with those spiritual wickednesses which he suggests and kindles; they are a help to him and to his own followers, because he uses them as weapons for our conquest. This is the king of Babylon, as Isaiah reads: “Demons meet one another, and owls and shaggy creatures dance there” [Note: [Col. 0355D] The Vulgate: “Shaggy creatures shall dance there, and owls shall answer there.”] (Isa. 13:21–22).

Behold, you have heard how great are the hindrances and what obstacles the daughters of Jerusalem must pass through in order to see King Solomon. Unless they have gone forth from these difficulties, unless they have been freed from this body of 224 death, they do not see Solomon crowned, nor understand him speaking. Thus the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Rise, go out into the plain, and there I shall speak with you. And I rose and went out into the plain, and behold, the glory of the Lord stood there for you” (Ezek. 3:22). The man full of God could not see the glory of the Lord unless he went out from the narrow confines of vices, by which the wicked are cramped within themselves, into the plain—that is, into the expansiveness of charity and virtue. For charity [Col. 0355C] produces an expansion of joys. But every wicked person suffers constriction, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Tribulation and distress upon every soul that does evil; but glory and peace for everyone who does good” (Rom. 2:9).

But for captive and miserable souls, who will grant a going forth, that they may breathe from this death into life? Hear the Apostle: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (Rom. 1:7). This is King Solomon, who frees by grace, not by merits. For just as that wicked king prepares nets by which to catch sinners and kill those caught, so the peaceable king arranges the instruments of virtues and orders distributions of graces, by which he weakens that king’s strength and overturns his machinations.

Now, against [printed: *cur*, “why”; perhaps *contra*, “against”] the four aforesaid commanders of vices—the caterpillar, locust, grub, and rust, [Col. 0355D] that is, lust, vain glory, gluttony, and anger—he has set four principal and, as it were, cardinal virtues: justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance. By these are defended and held fast those whom the previously mentioned commanders of vices seek to cut off from the body of Christ. For those dragged unwillingly need fortitude; those enticed, temperance; those deceived, prudence; those who depart voluntarily, justice [printed: *prudentia*, “prudence”; perhaps *justitia*, “justice”].

These commanders are eminent and unconquered: they put adversaries to flight and crown their own. They are ministers of the peaceable King and fight against the retainers of King Assur by means of seven women, as though seven maidservants. Isaiah speaks of them: “Seven women shall seize one man, saying: ‘We shall eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be invoked over us: take away our reproach’” (Isa. 4:1). As if to say: We have sufficient power and ability to defeat the retainers of King Assur and bring away the crown of triumph, if you are our helper.

The same Isaiah explains who these women are, saying: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11:2). These seven sanctifications are rightly called women because, just as bodily generation does not take place except through a woman, so spiritual generation occurs only through the sevenfold Spirit. Thus through these seven women those seven 225 spiritual wickednesses are conquered. These are [Col. 0356B] the seven columns upon which Wisdom built her house (Prov. 9:1). To these gifts [printed: *muneribus*; perhaps *mulieribus*, “women”], and to the four aforementioned commanders, is added the great multitude of charisms, of which the Apostle says: “There are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit; there are diversities of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are diversities of workings, but the same God who works all things in all” (1 Cor. 12:4).

Behold the battle-line of the peaceful king, prepared to meet the daughters of Jerusalem, so that they may have free passage to go out and see him. This king is good and wise: he makes the road peaceful and renders it safe for those who come to him. Let us therefore go out confidently to him, even if we see the Egyptians in pursuit. For he who delivered the Israelites from the destroyer by blood, and from the Egyptians by water, will himself deliver those who go out to him from the angels of wrath and from spiritual wickedness, by the blood of the covenant and the water of baptism. For, as John says, he came through water and blood to deliver us (1 John 5:6): through the blood, namely, of redemption, and through the water of washing. By blood we are redeemed from punishments; by water we are washed from sins. The deliverance is perfect, because the deliverer is incomprehensible. For this is he who says in the Gospel: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

There is a threefold freedom: that of nature, of grace, and of glory. Natural freedom is freedom from necessity, because before sin no necessity and no difficulty pressed upon man. The freedom of grace is called freedom from sin, because through it we obtain remission of sins, beneath whose yoke we were held as slaves. The freedom of glory is that which frees from all corruption, and which will be possessed in heavenly blessedness. Natural freedom ennobles human nature; the freedom of grace reconciles it; the freedom of glory exalts it.

You have heard sufficiently how King Solomon makes our going forth easy, and what freedom he offers for beholding God’s glory. The freedom of grace restores the freedom of nature and gains the freedom of glory. In this way God of our salvation makes our journey prosperous: namely, the true Solomon, king of peace, who made both one; who does not utterly destroy us, but often passes among us. Of him the Shunammite woman says to her husband:

[Col. 0357A] “This man who frequently passes by us is good. Let us therefore make for him a little upper room, and put in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a lampstand” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 4:9–10).

And what did she thereby deserve? Though barren, she conceived and gave birth. By this woman and her husband we understand flesh and spirit, confidently joined together for good, according to the saying: “My heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God” (Ps. 83 [84]:3). Or by the husband is understood the higher part of reason, which is the image and glory of God. The woman, however, is the lower part, the glory of the man; it is called knowledge, and attends to the action and ordering of temporal matters, just as the higher part, called wisdom, watches over the contemplation of heavenly things.

[Col. 0357B] Wisdom takes counsel with truth; in its apprehension it delights, and in its embrace it glories. Knowledge, like Martha, administers temporal matters and diligently considers how temporal things should rightly be done. It governs them rightly indeed when it humbly submits itself to be governed by its husband. Therefore this humble and devout woman refers counsel and judgment to her husband as to her head, saying: “This man is good,” and so forth. For the Lord is our spirit; the soul is as mistress, the body as servant. These three work together in one house; and if they agree in good, they recognize the good man. The Apostle prays that they may preserve unity in the bond of peace, saying: “May the God of peace sanctify you wholly, so that your spirit, soul, and body may be kept sound and blameless on the day of Christ” (cf. 1 Thess. 5:23).

[Col. 0357C] If, therefore, they are preserved in wholeness and sincerity, the good man is recognized—namely, the spiritual Elisha, that is, Christ—whose goodness has no end, and who says in the Gospel: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone” (Luke 18:19). He does not refuse the testimony of goodness, but does not accept the title of teacher without confession of his divinity; and he challenges the erring doctor of the law to understand the truth, because he confesses him good but not God, although to be good and to be God are one and the same for him, whose goodness is not a quality but nature, not an accident but substance; who existed without beginning both good and God, but not teacher. He began to be teacher, but did not begin to be good or God.

This is the man of whom Zechariah says: “Behold the man, Rising is his name” (Zech. 6:12). He himself is the Rising, because he is begotten without beginning, ineffably begotten. This one frequently passes by us. For he approaches and withdraws; he takes up and ceases, because “he has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9:18). He approaches, therefore, by adding grace; he withdraws by taking it away. He approached Judas by calling him and giving grace; but because he did not find a steadfast mind, he abandoned him, so that he might be wholly and completely the devil’s.

Blessed, however, is he to whom he comes intending to remain: that is, whom he does not abandon, but with whom he makes his dwelling together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Therefore, that he may remain with us without ceasing, let us make him an upper room. An upper room is prepared for him when the height of religious devotion is built in the mind for God’s honor.

[Col. 0358A] For the upper room is on high. Jesus celebrated the Passover with his disciples in an upper room, because he rests and is refreshed upon the lofty throne of the mind, amid the abundant variety of virtues, as though amid the harmonious assembly of spiritual guests. Many prepare the Passover for the Lord below, because they do not raise their minds to the things above, but in damnable desire bend toward the things that are upon the earth. “Pure and undefiled religion,” however, “is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from this world” (James 1:27).

True religion, therefore, consists of two things: compassion and innocence—so that by compassion we may help others, and by innocent living may harm neither ourselves nor others. The good man gladly enters and dwells in such a lodging,

[Col. 0358B] provided, however, that it contains the bed of peace: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. 5:9). Wisdom is justified by her children, in whom she rests as on a bed, because “his place has been made in peace.” But because pride disturbs peace, the chair of humility must be added, since his spirit rests only upon one who is humble and quiet and trembles at his words. The good man especially commends this virtue to us, saying: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

This chair is contrary to the chair of Eli the priest, who, falling backward, died with his neck broken (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 4), because he did not correct his sons. Therefore his seat became a chair of iniquity. But because no one does anything perfectly unless he knows how it ought to be done,

[Col. 0358C] a table must be added—that is, understanding of Scripture—so that we may sing praise to the Lord wisely and discerningly, according to the saying: “Sing wisely” (Ps. 48 [49]:8), and “that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we may have hope” (Rom. 15:4). On this table are found many spiritual dishes necessary for refreshing the inward person. But because a lamp is not brought to be put under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house of the Church (Matt. 5:15), a lampstand is brought in. “What benefit is there in hidden wisdom and concealed treasure?” (Ecclus. 41:17). None.

The slothful servant who hides the talent entrusted to him in a cloth and does not put it out at interest, so as to return a profit to the Lord, is rebuked and condemned.

[Col. 0358D] At the table we learn what, how, and when we ought to speak. From the lampstand we pour forth for others what we have drawn from the table. At the table we are taught; at the lampstand we teach. Let a lampstand therefore be added to the table, so that the word of preaching may be set on high.

When these things have thus been accomplished, the soul that was formerly barren conceives and gives birth. It conceives by willing; it gives birth by acting. Great and truly good is this man—indeed, Solomon—whom the daughters of Jerusalem are invited with such proclamation to go out and see.

This is that most mighty Samson, who laid low bands of enemies with the jawbone of an ass, and in whose figure Issachar was called a strong ass for bearing burdens. For Christ bore our sins with wonderful strength

[Col. 0359A] in his body upon the wood. At his voice those pursuing fell. For when they came to seize him and he asked them, “Whom do you seek?” and they answered, “Jesus of Nazareth,” he immediately replied, “I am he” (John 18:4). And they fell backward through the power of the voice of which it is said: “He gives to his voice a voice of power” (Ps. 67 [68]:34). As with the jawbone of an ass, he struck down the crowd holding swords and clubs.

Of him it is read in the book of Judges that, when he had entered Gaza, the city of the Philistines, they learned of it, surrounded the city in siege, and rejoiced that they had captured the mighty Samson (Judg. 16:1). But what did he do? In the night he removed the gates of the city and climbed to the top of the mountain.

In the Philistines the Jews are signified,

[Col. 0359B] because “Philistines” is interpreted “falling through drink”; and the Jews, made drunk with the drink of worldly desire and envy, and with the cup of diabolical suggestion, fell into eternal condemnation. In Gaza hell is signified; in Samson, Christ. For Samson is interpreted “their sun,” and Christ is the Sun of righteousness—a sun not of all, but of those upon whom he shines. For he does not enlighten every human being simply, but every human being coming into this world—not into this lower world, which lies in wickedness, but into that higher world in which John was when he said this.

Therefore, when the Jews saw him dead and his body placed in the tomb, they immediately assigned guards; and they rejoiced that he who had shone forth as the author of life was held fast within hell’s enclosures, like Samson in Gaza.

[Col. 0359C] But as Samson went out by night and carried away the gates, so Christ, rising before dawn, not only went freely out of hell but also destroyed hell’s very barriers, carried away its gates, and ascended the mountain’s summit. For by rising he removed the gates of hell, and by ascending he entered the realms of heaven.

[Col. 0360A] Of him Isaiah speaks in the person of angels marveling and rejoicing: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63:1). Who is this, “beautiful in his robe,” that is, in the garb of humanity, “marching in the greatness of his strength,” that is, of his divinity? While the angels are silent, he himself answers: “I am he who speaks righteousness,” rendering to each according to merits, “and am a champion” against demons, “to save the human race” (ibid.).

Again the angels ask: If you are such, “why is your garment red,” that is, your body, “and your garments,” that is, your limbs, “like those of one treading in the winepress?” (ibid., 2). Christ answered them so fully that there is no need to inquire further: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me” (ibid., 3), when I endured the pressures of the cross alone, without sin. He does not say, “I endured,” but, “I trod,” because in enduring the cross he trod down—that is, destroyed—death.

This one, therefore, comes from Edom and Bozrah with dyed garments. Edom, interpreted “earthly and bloody,” signifies the world. Bozrah, interpreted “fortified” or “strong,” signifies hell, where souls were held fast as though beneath many guards. Christ therefore comes with dyed garments, that is, with bodily limbs, from Edom, that is, from the “earthly and bloody world.” He also comes from Bozrah, because, having despoiled hell, he ascended victorious with his faithful ones, appearing splendid and beautiful, though formerly reckoned by the wicked as without form or comeliness.

[Col. 0360C] Let us, therefore, who are called daughters of Zion, imitate Christ’s footsteps and, as it were, carry the cross after him. Let us go out from Edom, that is, from the earthly and bloody world, loving neither it nor the things that are in the world.

> **Note:**  
> [Col. 0359C] Concerning the preceding note and other similar notes, repeatedly scattered through these sermons, which seem to imply or establish Hildebert’s monastic profession—see what we have said in the *Life of Hildebert*, where we presented arguments on both sides and left the reader entirely free to decide what opinion to hold.
>
> Yet, granted that freedom, we trust that the fair-minded reader will not disapprove if we in turn use that same freedom, and do not conceal our inclination to maintain Hildebert’s monastic profession, at least as probable.
>
> [Col. 0359D] This conviction has indeed grown stronger in us because, after the publication even of the index to Hildebert and Marbod, material from the writings of our own Mabillon came to our attention, from which we believed we ought to adhere more firmly to the opinion of Quercetanus, who maintained Hildebert’s monastic profession and whose view we reported at the beginning of his *Life*.
>
> Mabillon himself—for whose recent death, in a pious old age, alas, all good people and all men of letters mourn with us—relates in the preface to volume III of the *Analecta* that, when he was engaged in publishing the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans* there reported, the *Acts* of nine bishops from Aldric onward were missing; this, he says, made his edition incomplete. When Baluze, in his kindness, learned of this, he voluntarily communicated to us the Chesnian copy from the famous Colbertine Library, of which he was superintendent, a copy transcribed from a more abbreviated *History of the Bishops of Le Mans*, so that we might fill the gap in our edition from it.
>
> He repeats this in volume III of the *Analecta*, p. 275, where he notes that those *Acts*, copied in the manuscript by Chesne’s own hand, begin from the beginning of the bishops and end with Guy, who immediately succeeded Hildebert in the episcopate of Le Mans, and who alone among the bishops of Le Mans is counted by that name.
>
> From this it is more certain than certain that Chesne, or Quercetanus, knew the history of the bishops of Le Mans exceedingly well, since he himself had transcribed it, and among other things knew very well those matters concerning Hildebert as Guy’s immediate predecessor in the see of Le Mans. Yet he could not have acquired this knowledge except chiefly through reading the more extensive *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, which, as Mabillon says, he had copied in his own hand and abridged into a more compact form—where not even a syllable is read concerning Hildebert’s monastic profession.
>
> Yet that great man, whom all scholars until now have revered as a most learned and clear-sighted investigator of antiquity, and whom Mabillon in the passage cited above calls, as it were, a second father of our history, nevertheless did not cease to maintain that Hildebert was a Cluniac monk and a disciple of St Hugh, while he endeavored to elucidate the Cluniac Chronicle with his notes. That distinguished man would certainly not have devoted such serious attention to this task unless he had recognized that the work—compiled by Dom Francis de Rivo, grand prior of the monastery of Cluny and doctor of the Sorbonne, at the command of Dom James de Ambasia, then abbot of Cluny—was supported by the weightiest reasons and authentic monuments.
>
> We are therefore not ashamed to erase the mark of suspicion with which, before reading this dissertation of Mabillon, we somewhat too readily, yielding to another’s counsel, though friendly, had stained Dom Francis de Rivo. At the very beginning of the *Life of Hildebert*, we had said too rashly that he might have asserted Hildebert’s monastic profession only from conjecture and opinion.
>
> For the exceedingly shrewd Quercetanus did not judge the silence of the writer of those *Acts* concerning Hildebert’s monastic profession to be so important that he ought to refrain from affirming it, when he saw that the writer had omitted far more notable deeds of Hildebert—deeds that were not thereby untrue because that writer had passed them over. Did that writer, for instance, mention Hildebert’s well-known discipleship under Berengar, from which Baronius nevertheless took occasion to attack him as if he had led a more dissolute life? Did he mention Hildebert’s very serious dispute with the most powerful King Louis the Fat over the deanery and archdeaconry of Tours—a dispute that brought upon him banishment from the whole dominion of a man otherwise a most vigorous defender of the Church’s rights?
>
> Did he mention that very celebrated lawsuit involving the dismembered Canon Nicholas, which not even Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and apostolic legate for this purpose, could settle; which gave occasion for the treacherous murder of Ralph, dean of Tours, unjustly accused, as he made his way to Rome; and which led Hildebert to most humble, yet very weighty, complaints before the supreme pontiff against the Roman curia’s too ready reception of frivolous—or, as he calls them, dilatory—appeals? Finally, did that writer recount the celebrated Council of Nantes, so necessary to the Breton Church, indeed so timely for the whole province, later approved and confirmed by Honorius II?

> We would be excessive if we wished to enumerate the even more notable deeds of Hildebert that he omitted, but which are nevertheless proved beyond doubt from his letters, other works, and most trustworthy authentic documents. That author reported, as commonly happens, what he had learned; and concerning those things we judge that he deserves credence, and we give it in good faith. But we do not believe that matters which he did not report are false, or altogether doubtful merely because he did not report them, if they can be established from other certain, or at least probable, arguments.
>
> The very fair-minded Quercetanus judged likewise; and therefore concerning Hildebert he did not believe or assert only what that author wrote, but also what he learned from authentic monuments. Since he recognized Hildebert’s monastic profession as sufficiently proved by arguments and authorities in the Cluniac Chronicle, he did not hesitate to affirm it, although that writer omitted it.
>
> We therefore judged that we should follow in the footsteps of this illustrious leader in maintaining, at least probably, Hildebert’s monastic profession—with all the greater right because, whether from his letters and sermons or from his other writings, we observed, if not invincible proofs, at least indications suggesting it, which we have not neglected to note in their proper places as occasion arose. We considered these to have, as it were, the force of positive argument and to deserve more credence than the simple conjectures of negative argument, on which alone those rely who, with insufficient modesty—to say nothing stronger and more fitting—do not shrink from calling Hildebert’s monastic profession a chimera,

> [Col. 0362D] and, relying only on the silence of certain writers, do not hesitate to strip from the sacred Cluniac, indeed from the whole Benedictine, order a prelate conspicuous among the foremost men of his age in holiness and learning.
>
> We say this on the occasion of the notes repeatedly appended by us to the sermons, in which Hildebert’s monastic profession seemed to us to be indicated—a profession maintained before us, together with Quercetanus, by Dom Robert and the brothers Sammarthani.
>
> [Col. 0361D] *Gallia Christiana*, under the bishops of Le Mans, at Hildebert: they testify in express words that he was brought forth from the cloister of Cluny to the office of schoolmaster at Le Mans—as does recently even one who thinks otherwise, if he pleases.

Let us therefore go out from this, that we may deserve to behold King Solomon in his diadem—that is,

[Col. 0361A] Christ. There is a threefold vision by which he is seen. The first is in exile; the second will be at judgment; the third will be in the kingdom. Of the first it is said to Thomas: “Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:29). Of the second it is said: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6). Of the third: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:20); and again: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:10).

In the first he appeared gentle; in the second, just; in the third, glorious. In the first, he loosed; in the second, he will acquit; in the third, he will perfect. In the first he appeared lovable; in the second he will appear terrible; in the third, wonderful, because even angels desire to look into him. In the first he sowed faith; in the second he will instill terror; in the third he will enlarge love.

[Col. 0361B] In accordance with these three visions, he received three names.

> **Note:**  
> [Col. 0362D] Hildebert took this from St Jerome’s commentary on Ecclesiastes, chapter 1, on the words: “The words of Ecclesiastes, son of David, king of Jerusalem,” vol. II of the new edition, p. 715.

Solomon, Ecclesiastes, Jedidiah (4 Kings [2 Samuel] 22:1). Solomon means “peaceful,” as he truly was in the first vision, when he was peaceful with those who hated him. Ecclesiastes means “preacher,” when he shall be seen in the second vision, because “he will summon heaven above and earth, to judge his people” (Ps.

[Col. 0362A] 49 [50]:4). Jedidiah means “beloved.”

> **Note:**  
> [Col. 0362D] *Jedidiah*: “beloved of the Lord.” So Jerome in the passage cited below.

This will be in the third vision, when he will be loved not in part but wholly, because he will be seen wholly; for he will be loved as much as he is seen. In the first vision, good and evil persons saw him, but not all. In the second, both evil and good persons will see him, and all will. In the third, good persons alone will see him, and all will.

The daughters of Zion urge us toward this threefold vision, but especially toward the third. The vision of exile is signified by the vision in which he appeared to the two disciples travelling on the road to the village of Emmaus in the form of a traveler. He seemed a traveler to them because what he was was not revealed to them. Thus here we behold through a mirror in an image; in the future we shall see truth face to face. There the contemplative life reigns in vision. Here the second [life] labors by faith, not yet possessing what it desires.

[Col. 0362B] Let us therefore see him in this mirror-like vision, so that we may be able to know him in the vision of his actual appearance.

And as the vision is threefold, so too is the diadem threefold: that of the stepmother, the mother, and the father. For his stepmother crowned him, his mother crowned him, and his father crowned him; but his stepmother with a crown of misery, his mother with a crown of justice, his Father with a crown of glory. His

[Col. 0363A] stepmother is the unbelieving Synagogue, which crowned him with a thorny diadem and enclosed him both within and without. Without, with the bodily thorn; within, with the spiritual thorn. Without, with the thorn of suffering; within, with the thorn of compassion and contrition. For he suffered with us and was pierced with compunction for us; and, so that he might consume the thorns of our vices like blazing fire, he received the crown of thorns. For vices and sins are signified by thorns. Hence it was said to the human being in the curse: “The earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3:18); and elsewhere: “Thorns and thistles grow in the hands of the drunkard” (Prov. 26:9).

He was willing to be wounded with thorns for us, so that we too, for his sake, might likewise be pierced by the sting of penitence on account of our inward thorns. Solomon’s mother is

[Col. 0363B] the Blessed Virgin, who crowned him with the crown of justice. This crown consists, as it were, of four precious stones: namely, the four affections of the mind, which are joy, love, sorrow, and fear.

Christ received these affections from his mother and possessed them in ordered form. Thus the Lord says: “She crowned me with the crown of justice,” because justice is ordered affection. He had joy, according to the saying: “My heart has rejoiced, and my tongue exulted” (Ps. 15 [16]:9). He had love, because, having loved his own, he loved them to the end. He had fear, because he began to be afraid and distressed. He had sorrow, because his soul was sorrowful unto death.

In this sorrow three wills are considered: the will of the Father, the will of the Spirit, and the will of the flesh. The Father’s will was to fulfill the dispensation—namely,

[Col. 0363C] to redeem the human race through Christ’s death; the Spirit’s will was to obey the Father; the flesh’s will was to avoid death, because flesh naturally recoils from death. The Father’s will honored him; the Spirit’s will crowned him; the will of the flesh loved him. Therefore, when Christ said, “Let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39), expressing the human will, he immediately corrects and lovingly adds: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (ibid.).

Behold the crown of justice with which the mother crowned Solomon. But the Father crowned him with the crown of glory: not only with the glory of immortal and impassible flesh and spirit, but with that glory which he had with the Father before the world existed. With that glory, indeed, he crowned him—though he had received it in being eternally begotten [variant: “which, however, he had received in being eternally begotten”]—when he so glorified him upon earth “that every tongue may confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:11).

In the first diadem, therefore, he was contemptible; in the second, wonderful; in the third, ineffable. We who are of Zion, who are daughters of Jerusalem, are therefore admonished to behold him in the diadem of his mother by imitation, directing the affections of our minds after his example, so that we may be able to attain the Father’s diadem. May he deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## V. FIFTH SERMON FOR THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

> **Note:**  
> [Col. 0363D] From a manuscript of Angers.

On the incarnation of the Word.

[Col. 0364A]

> “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and behold King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him” (Song 3:11).

Glorious things have often been said concerning the glorious Mother of God. And I perhaps, even if I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels, shall nevertheless labor in vain, because “the well is deep, and I have nothing with which to draw” (John 4:11). Yet I cannot be silent about that of which the whole earth speaks. Would that my speech may be pleasing to her; then it will not be fruitless.

What is more glorious among us than to see a king proceeding in his splendor, clothed in purple and crowned with a diadem?

[Col. 0364B] Far more gloriously was our King crowned today in the bridal chamber of his mother. For today that saying of Jeremiah was fulfilled: “The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31:22). After the angel’s announcement, “You shall conceive and bear” (Luke 1:31), and the Virgin’s modest consent, “Let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid., 38), the Son of God was conceived—or rather, to speak more truly, was begun.

For he was not conceived from diverse seeds, similarly brought together, but formed from the flesh of the Virgin alone; not gradually over intervals of time like others, but immediately a man in all his members, immediately endowed with a soul, of the same knowledge and the same power that he possessed when, at thirty years old, he preached. Hence he is designated by the prophet with the title of “man.”

[Col. 0364C] Solomon urges us to behold how he was crowned there today, saying: “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and behold.” The discourse is directed especially to us—to the learned, I mean, to whom it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, while to others they are given in parables—and especially to those who devote themselves to ecclesiastical discipline; who, having set aside the eloquence and fruitless verbosity of philosophers, come to draw waters from the springs of the Savior; and who are not without reason understood by the daughters of Zion.

For Jerusalem and Zion signify the Church. The daughters of Jerusalem and the daughters of Zion, therefore, are daughters of the Church. Jerusalem is literally interpreted “vision of peace”; it is situated near Zion, whose municipality, called Mello, was located in Zion. By the daughters of Jerusalem we understand laypeople, as less

[Col. 0364D] learned and needing the protection of a municipality. By the daughters of Zion we understand the learned: both because of their eminence in knowledge, because of their guardianship and instruction of others, and because Zion is interpreted “watchtower” or “contemplation.” For it was prophetically said—and said to us in the prophet—“Son of man, I have appointed you a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. 3:17).

For they are like dwarfs upon giants’ shoulders, like little ibises [variant: *ibiciones*, or *ibiculi*, “small ibises”] upon eagles’ wings—that is, interpreters of Holy Scripture. To them, I say, it is said: “Daughters of Zion,” to whom the Lord opened the mind so that they understood the Scriptures. “Go forth.”

[Col. 0365A] The same was said to Abraham, the man of God: “Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Gen. 12:1). There are three things that compel us to sin: the prompting of our own flesh, the prompting of one’s neighbor, and the prompting of the devil or of the world.

Let us therefore go out from our land—that is, restrain our Eve; and from our kindred—that is, close our ears to the neighbor who counsels evil, “like one who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth” (Ps. 37 [38]:15); and let us flee from our father’s house—that is, from the world and its prince, the devil, who entices us with his pleasures—taking refuge with the Most High, that he may overshadow us with his shoulders and that we may hope beneath his wings.

Even if Scripture did not exhort us to go forth, the unpleasantness of the place itself compels us to leave. Which of us, if lying in mud, would not prefer to go out rather than remain? What is this world and its desire but mud and its filth? Hear what is said of lovers of the world: “They have rotted like beasts in their dung” (Joel 1:17). Hear the Apostle, who reckons such things as dung. How great are the filths amassed in this dungheap is plain.

[Col. 0365B] Adam, the first and greatest giant of all, vomited over us the filth of disobedience; and so great was its stain that it miserably defiled all his posterity. Next Cain added the dung of fratricide; Lamech poured over it the stench of bigamy; before the Flood, women exceeding men, and men submitting their own bodies to womanly acts,

[Col. 0365C] heaped filth upon filth. Let whoever can consider how many defilements have filled this foul valley down to the present day, even to an intolerable stench.

Therefore, go forth, daughters of Zion, so that you who embraced dung in place of saffron may remember that you are human beings, not swine. You, indeed, who have come to study, leaving your land

> **Note:**  
> [Col. 0365D] Perhaps he addresses the learned men—of whom he spoke above—who, like himself, had come to Cluny in order to devote themselves to sacred letters under St Hugh, the abbot; they admired his wisdom and learning joined with piety, as the queen of Sheba admired Solomon’s wisdom.

and your kindred, coming with the queen of Sheba to hear Solomon’s wisdom. But one must go out rather by the disposition of the mind than by a bodily journey. It is especially expedient for you also to depart, because he who eats a sour grape has his teeth set on edge and cannot break bread.

But what is the cause? Have the teeth, losing their former strength, become softened? Has bread, sweeter than other foods, been deprived of its pleasantness?

[Col. 0365D] By no means. Numbness is the cause. Thus, one who serves the pursuit of learning, if he entangles himself in worldly affairs, becomes numbed by habit. Nature is sufficient for our studies; instruction is sweet; he recoils from breaking bread through the numbness of habit.

Go forth, therefore, and behold King Solomon. Solomon had three names: he was called Jedidiah, Solomon,

[Col. 0366A] and Ecclesiastes. Jedidiah means “blessed of the Lord” or “beloved by the Lord.” This is Christ. Christ indeed is in the beginning with the Father, one distinct person with another, and is *homoousion* [ὁμοούσιον, “of the same substance”] with the Father; but no human being shall see him and live. You may believe; you may not see.

Nor do I say, “Behold Ecclesiastes,” that is, the preacher; for this is still to come, when all flesh shall see the salvation of God, and, with the sermon changed, he will thunder harsh words at some, saying: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). To others he will smile with gentle speech, saying: “Come, blessed ones; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid., 25:34).

Understand Jedidiah, therefore, because he is incomprehensible; await Ecclesiastes, because he will be terrible.

[Col. 0366B] Now behold Solomon, because now he is gracious and desirable to see. For Solomon means “peaceful.” This is Christ the man, who is our peace, who “made both one, dissolving the wall of enmity between us and God” (Eph. 2:14). Behold him; he has been seen by us all. Our eyes have seen God’s salvation. And although rejected and filled with reproaches, still behold the king, because he is at once rich and poor.

Today behold him in his diadem. A diadem is one thing and a crown another. A crown is a simple golden circle, used by kings at lesser solemnities. A diadem is, as it were, a double crown, when another circlet, set with gems, is added above the crown itself.

[Col. 0366C] Indeed, by interpretation of the Greek name, it signifies doubleness. The crowns of the soul, therefore, are natural goods; but the gems laid over them to form a diadem are gratuitous goods. When the natural affections of the soul are ordered within it, they crown and adorn it; when disordered, they become its mockery. Hence Solomon says: “A beautiful but foolish woman is a golden ring in her nostrils” (Prov. 11:22).

There are, indeed, four natural affections: fear, hope, joy, and sorrow. Hence the poet:

> Hence they desire, fear, rejoice, and grieve.

> **Note:**  
> [Col. 0365D] He cites the same verse, in the same sense, in letter 12 of the first book, to King Henry. We note this in order that we may infer from it that this sermon is a genuine work of Hildebert. This may also be confirmed by what Hildebert immediately says here concerning the manner in which he asserts that the Blessed Mary crowned Christ her Son, which he had set forth in the preceding fourth sermon, universally considered without doubt to be Hildebert’s.

(*Aeneid* 6.733.)

These, then, must be so arranged as to adorn the head of the soul. Fear is on the forehead, for “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” [Col. 0366D]. Hope is at the back of the head, because it concerns only future things and things not seen. Joy is on the right, so that all joy may be in the Lord, who will place us at his right hand. Sorrow is on the left, for we ought to grieve over our transgressions, which are the reason why the goats are placed on the left. But when the four virtues are rightly placed over these, the soul’s diadem is made [Col. 0367A]. These virtues are justice, prudence, temperance, and fortitude.

Justice must be placed over fear, because one who fears God will do good and will render to God and to one’s neighbour what belongs to each. “Justice is the constant and perpetual will to render to each his due.” Prudence must be placed over hope. For hope has beside it two things greatly to be feared: namely, the abyss of despair and “the Ceraunian mountains of presumption.”

> [Note: [Col. 0367D] Mountains of Epirus exposed to lightning, concerning which Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, II, elegy 6:
>
> “As I could, I passed the Ceraunian mountains with a straight sail.
>
> I had to be warned to avoid the savage rocks.”
>
> [Col. 0368D]]

Therefore one must hope prudently, lest anyone, attending too greatly to God’s justice, say with Cain: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for” (Gen. IV, 13); or, attending too greatly to God’s mercy, presumptuously say: “Even if a mother should forget her son, God nevertheless will not forget us” (Isa. XLIX, 15) [Col. 0367B].

Temperance must be placed over joy; for one must always exult in fear. The Apostle clearly indicates this: when he has said, “Rejoice in the Lord always,” he immediately adds, “Let your moderation be known to all men” (Phil. IV, 5). Fortitude must be placed over sorrow, lest the depth of sorrow swallow us up, lest the pit press its mouth over us. Thus the soul is adorned by the weapons of justice on the right and on the left.

Therefore, on this day of the Lord’s conception, Christ the man was crowned in his Mother’s womb with this diadem, because both natural and gratuitous goods were most perfectly ordered in him. But by the statement that his mother crowned him, it is understood that another and yet another crowned him. For his stepmother, the Synagogue, crowned him when he bore upon his head—terrible to angels—a thorny and shameful crown. Yet on the day of his resurrection his Father crowned him with the crown of immortality and glory. On the day of the final winnowing his household will crown him. For he will come with the senators of the earth, because the Lord will come, and all his saints with him.

In the meantime God will judge in his mother’s crown, the crown of mercy; for solely through the compassion of his own will he was made man. The stepmother’s crown was a crown of misery. The Father’s crown was a crown of glory. The last will be a crown of power, or of justice. Hence the Apostle says: “There is laid up for me a crown of justice” (II Tim. IV, 8). For he will come “like a mighty man roused from wine” (Ps. LXXVII, 65).

In his mother’s crown, he is changeable; in his stepmother’s crown, contemptible; in his Father’s crown, admirable; in his household’s crown, terrible. Therefore let the daughters of Zion see him in the crown of mercy, and be pierced with compunction, or imitate him. The wicked, then, will see him in the crown of power and will perish. The just will see him in the crown of glory and will rejoice.

Let us act, therefore, lest we too perish with those who perish. Let us hasten likewise to the coming of the Judge who beholds all things. For if he finds us unprepared, who will be able to excuse us? Will repentance excuse us? Yet we scorn to perform [supp. *agere*, “to do”] it in the flesh. Will good works excuse us? Yet we do not do them at the time when they should be done [Col. 0368A]. Will the frailty of the flesh excuse us? Yet opposite us will stand virgins who, in the flesh, conquered the flesh’s frailty. Rightly he will say to us: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV, 41), where the fire is not extinguished and the worm does not die; where there is continual groaning, where the sensation of penal pain is everlasting.

Let us set before our eyes how great an evil it is to be made exiles from the heavenly homeland, to be deprived of the crowns of the saints, to die to the blessed life, and to live unto eternal death. From this may Jesus Christ our Lord deliver us, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## VI. SIXTH SERMON FOR THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

> [Note: [Col. 0368D] Also in the manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.]

On the Incarnation.

“Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon [Col. 0368B] in the diadem with which his mother crowned him, on the day of his espousal and on the day of his heart’s joy” (Song III, 11).

“Whoever pursues words alone, Solomon testifies, will find nothing; but the keeper of prudence will find good things” (Prov. XIX, 8). In these words, dearest brethren, we see that whoever thinks only carnal thoughts will find nothing but death. For he seeks words alone, and therefore finds nothing but the killing letter. Let us then, brethren, understand something spiritual above the letter in these words—indeed, the Spirit himself who gives life, who elsewhere says through Solomon: “He who presses the breasts firmly expresses butter” (Prov. XXX, 33).

The breasts are the two Testaments. Whoever expresses them, rather than childishly following the letter, will find rich butter and delightful food. To express such butter, let us direct our understandings toward comprehending these words of Solomon. It is said: “Go forth, daughters of Zion,” and so forth.

There is a good going forth, and there is an evil one. Evil was the going forth of Judas, of whom it is said: “He went out . . . and it was night” (John XIII, 30). Of an evil going forth it is likewise said: “He went out and spoke the same thing” (Ps. XL, 7). Evil too was Dinah’s going forth: she went out to see the women of that land; Shechem son of Hamor loved her and violated her. Thus there came to be grief for her father, disgrace for the nation, and insult to her brothers (Gen. XXXIV, 1).

This is the soul corrupted by the vice of curiosity. It goes out and sees the women of Hamor’s country [Col. 0368D], namely, the wicked delights suggested by the devil; and, leaving the guide of its youth, it joins itself to the devil, dwelling in the land of pilgrimage—that is, in a foreign land—where it cannot sing the Lord’s song.

The good going forth to be sought is that by which Moses wishes to go out from Egypt with God’s people, where God’s people are afflicted by Pharaoh in mud and brickmaking and serve under harsh labours. Bricks made from mud are afterward hardened by fire. Thus sins, at first easy to dissolve, grow hard, as it were, through habit; for it is difficult to reject what has become customary.

But see how Moses wishes to lead the people out. He says: “We will go a three-days’ journey, that we may sacrifice to our God” (Exod. V, 3). For God wishes you to withdraw from the darkness of sins through three days—that is, in thought, speech, and deed. By the same triad those who draw us into Pharaoh’s slavery furnish us a threefold path of evil-doing, and by the same threefold path draw us back into Pharaoh’s service [perhaps *retrahant*, “draw back,” rather than the printed *recurrant*].

Isaac too went forth well, that he might meditate in the field; for whoever wishes to meditate in the heavenly field goes forth from worldly things. Solomon exhorts us to this good going forth when he says: “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see.”

Christ is seen in three ways: he is seen in the world, he will be seen at judgment, and he will be seen in the kingdom. The first vision is of grace [Col. 0369B], the second of justice, the third of glory. Of the first it is said: “He was seen upon earth and conversed with men” (Baruch III, 38). Of the second it is said: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke III, 6). Of the third it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8). In the first vision he was seen by both good and evil persons; in the third, by the good alone.

Accordingly, Solomon was fittingly called by three names as a figure of these three visions: Edila [or Idida], Ecclesiastes, and Solomon. The name Edila accords with the first vision, for by this he deserved to be loved by us. Ecclesiastes, that is, “preacher,” accords with the second, when he will sit in judgment. The name Solomon, meaning “peaceful,” accords with the third, because then he will give peace.

Therefore the daughters of Zion—that is, holy souls contemplating him through faith—go forth to see him [Col. 0369C]. That city too was called by three names: first Jebus, then Salem, thirdly Jerusalem. For the Church now ruled by Solomon, the true Solomon, is Jebus while it tramples down vices; afterward Salem, when vices have in part been purged; finally Jerusalem, that is, “vision of perfect peace.”

> [Note: [Col. 0369D] “Jebus, which is Jerusalem” (Josh. XVIII, 28).]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0369D] “And he passed into Salem, the city of the Shechemites” (Gen. XXXIII, 18).]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0369D; Col. 0370D] “And he went up through the valley of the son of Hinnom, beside the Jebusite on the south: this is Jerusalem” (Josh. XV, 8).]

The Lord enters only this city, not Cain’s city. Hence: “I am the Lord, and I do not enter the city” (Gen. XXXIII, 18). One must therefore go forth, if one wishes to see King Solomon, outside the camp and outside the devil’s city. Forget therefore your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty. Hence: “Go out from the midst of Babylon, my people” (Isa. XLVIII, 20) [Col. 0369D].

“From the midst” is said fittingly and with moderation. Every middle is enclosed by two extremes. Babylon’s first extreme is original sin, through which we enter Babylon. Its last extreme is venial sin, without which we do not live. The middle is mortal sin, through which we lose life. Therefore, if you cannot flee Babylon’s two extremes altogether, you can at least avoid its middle.

It follows in what they ought to see him: “In the diadem with which his mother crowned him.” Christ’s flesh is signified by many names [Col. 0370A]: it is called tabernacle, ark, table, and here diadem. Yet it is not said that his mother clothed him with this diadem, but crowned him with it, because God, from the pure bodily substance of the sacred Virgin—that is, without male seed—by the operation [the text reads *comparatione*; perhaps *operatione*] of the Holy Spirit provided most pure flesh for the Word of God.

This is the new thing of which the prophet says: “The Lord has made a new thing upon the earth: a woman will encompass a man in the enclosure of her womb” (Jer. XXXI, 22). This is the gate of which Ezekiel says: “No man shall pass through it” (Ezek. XLIV). Christ, indeed, is the mountain [or stone] cut out from the mountain without hands.

It is rightly said that he was crowned with this flesh, because in the flesh he triumphed over the devil. Had he not possessed flesh, the devil would not have attacked him. But he concealed his divinity, exposing his humanity to the devil; and while the devil sought the food of humanity, he was pierced by the sting of divinity [Col. 0370B].

He was crowned on the day of his heart’s espousal and on the day of his heart’s joy. The day of espousal and joy is the day of the Incarnation, when human nature was joined to the Word of God; when the Virgin rejoiced that she had conceived the Son of God while remaining untouched, and that the Holy Spirit had overshadowed her—the Spirit who is the common joy and shared gladness of us all.

Let us therefore depart from worldly cares and contemplate through faith the true Solomon, so that in the future we may see him face to face. For this is eternal life: to see the Father and Jesus Christ whom he sent. May he himself deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## VII. SEVENTH SERMON FOR THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

> [Note: [Col. 0370D] From manuscript no. 381 of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.]

On the mystery of the Incarnation.

“I looked in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a Son of Man was coming with the clouds of heaven; he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him. And he gave him power and honour and a kingdom . . . . His power is an eternal power that shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Dan. VII, 13–14).

Daniel burned with heavenly desires—and thus deserved to be called by the angel, the minister of his understanding, “a man of desires.” Having received understanding from God through an angel, he poured out his soul so that he might pass into the wondrous secret of contemplation [Col. 0370D] and perceive the inestimable riches of the mystery hidden from ages in God.

This is the mystery of the Incarnation of the Word, who was in the beginning with the Father. Of it Jeremiah says: “The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman will encompass a man” (Jer. XXXI, 22), namely, in the enclosure of her womb. This is the holy Virgin who, through the working of the Holy Spirit and without a man’s approach, conceived and bore a Son consubstantial (*homousion*) with the Father from her own substance: so that he who was the Son of God in divinity might weep as the son of a man [perhaps “of the Virgin”] in humanity [Col. 0371A]—not two sons, but the one man Christ Jesus. This is unheard-of and ineffable.

Therefore the man of desires rightly says not simply “Son of Man,” since he is not only the Son of Man but also the Son of God. For with the truth and property of each nature preserved, the vessel of human weakness was joined to the light of divinity, so that there might be light in the vessel, the Word in flesh, God in man.

This is that little stone cut from the mountain without hands which, Daniel testifies, grew into a great mountain and filled the face of the whole earth. This is the stone of help upon which Moses is said and read to have prayed with raised hands. Of it Zechariah says: “The Lord will bring forth the chief stone, and will make its grace equal to grace” (Zech. IV, 7) [Col. 0371B].

For he, the mediator between God and men, is called a stone because of his firmness and solidity. He is the foundation which has been laid, as the Apostle says, and which no one can change. Of him the Lord says through Isaiah: “I will lay in the foundation of Zion a precious, tested cornerstone” (Isa. XXXVIII, 16). Elsewhere: “I will place in Zion a stone of stumbling and of scandal” (Isa. VIII, 14).

But to some he is a stone of stumbling and scandal, and to others a stone of help. For to some the sun of justice shines forth, prevenient grace and assisting grace going before; others he seems to overshadow, not delivering them from the darkness of blindness. Hence he himself says: “I came into this world for judgment, that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind” (John IX, 39).

He is therefore rightly called both the stone of help and of stumbling: in him some are warmed and enlightened, while others strike against him and are blinded [Col. 0371C]. “For he is set,” as Simeon says, “for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel” (Luke II, 34).

This chief stone, making grace equal to grace, is truly chief because he is the Firstborn among many brethren, endowed with the honour of the firstborn among the many whom he is not ashamed to call brethren. For brethren are those “whom God foreknew to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. VIII, 29): that is, those who are conformed to the Son, who is the Father’s begetting, not a creature.

This conformity consists in a twofold sharing, because he shares with us and we ourselves share with him. For he took from what is ours and gave to us from what is his. From us, indeed, he took nature and weakness; from himself he gave grace and glory [Col. 0371D].

By this exchange the brotherhood of adoption was contracted, not an equality of forms—that is, of natures—made (Rom. VIII, 39). He is therefore rightly called the Firstborn among many brethren, possessing pre-eminence of honour and power over the others and distributing to the others according to his will. He is also called “the Firstborn of every creature” (Col. I, 15), because he was begotten of the Father before every creature.

He is therefore rightly called the chief stone, to whom the Spirit was given without measure and in whom “all the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” (Col. II, 9)—and “from his fullness we all received grace for grace” (John I, 16) [Col. 0372A]. Namely, we received the grace of glorification for the grace of justification; the grace of the homeland for the grace of the way. The one is made equal to the other, because whoever is granted greater grace in the present will shine with greater glory in the future.

This stone, therefore, is precious and tested, upon whom, as Zechariah says, “are seven eyes” (Zech. IV, 10), because the fullness of sevenfold grace rested upon him, according to Isaiah’s words: “And upon him shall rest the spirit of wisdom and understanding” (Isa. XI, 2). These are the seven women who take hold of one man, namely Christ: the seven gifts, which bear the likeness of women because through their infusion children of adoption are begotten for God. They are said to take hold of Christ in order that they may hold him firmly and not let him go.

They pass over all others, as it were, until they come to Christ, and take hold of none of the patriarchs and prophets. For there is no other man who does not sin. In all the others the spirit of tribulation has lodging, not a dwelling-place of rest. It was indeed in the prophets and other just persons; but because they were mere human beings and sinners, it was in them but did not remain. It dwelt in them but did not fill them. Therefore the Gospel says of Christ alone: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John I, 33) [Col. 0372B].

He is the cornerstone who, though rejected by the builders—that is, the scribes and Pharisees who wished to establish their own justice—was nevertheless made the head of the corner, joining in himself, as the corner-stone, the two walls, namely Jews and Gentiles [Col. 0372C]. He was well able to do this because he was cut from the mountain without hands: that is, born from the Jewish people, not by desire but solely by God’s gift.

For from ancient times the Jewish people, by the prerogative of adoption, were called a special people and firstborn, and were compared to a mountain. This little stone grew into a great mountain and filled the face of the earth. Of this Isaiah says: “In the last days the mountain of the Lord’s house shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills, and all nations shall flow to it” (Isa. II, 1).

For just as Christ is called King of kings and Holy of holies, so he is mountain of mountains, surpassing in wisdom and power all those who share in his grace.
