He came to lead people out of Egypt’s iron furnace, where they were afflicted with tribulation and pain, into the holy wilderness [Col. 0372D].

> [Note: [Col. 0371D] Perhaps the following should be added: “Thus Moses said to Pharaoh.”]

“The God of the Hebrews has called us, that we may go a three-days’ journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the Lord our God, lest perhaps plague or sword befall us” (Exod. V, 3).

The Son of Man is the God of the Hebrews, who himself wished to become a Hebrew—that is, a passer-over—for our sake; for he rejoiced like a giant to run his course. Thus he is rightly the God of the Hebrews, that is, the passer-over of those who do not cling to the way but, forgetting what lies behind, stretch themselves forward with the Apostle. He called us out of the Egypt of this world so that we might go a three-days’ journey into the wilderness.

We depart from Egypt by a three-days’ journey if, cleansing words, deeds, and thoughts [Col. 0373A], we become pure in heart, so that we may see God. But the prince of Egypt, seeing himself pressed to let God’s people go, wishes at least to obtain this: that they should not go far away, saying, “Do not go far away.”

> [Note: [Col. 0373D] “Go and sacrifice to your God in this land” (Exod. VIII, 25). “Nevertheless, do not go farther away” (v. 28).]

For he wishes to possess us, if not in deed, then in speech; if not in speech, then in thought. He does not wish us to depart from him through the complete three days. He wishes to have at least one day in us. In others he possesses the whole three days. But blessed are those who withdraw from him through all three days.

The three-days’ journey is also faith in the Trinity; or Christ himself, dying, buried, and rising again. He called us to go by this road into the wilderness and to sacrifice to our God. The Son of God does not wish us to remain in deeds of flesh and darkness, but to go out into the desert: that is, to a place empty of the disturbances and waves of the age [Col. 0373B], and to the rest of silence. For the words of wisdom are learned in quiet and silence. Here we can offer sacrifice to God and render our vows to the Most High.

Therefore, lest the plague of sin or the sword of eternal death befall us, let us obey God who calls us. Let us go out from the waves of business, the tumult of vices, and Egypt—that is, the darkness of ignorance—into the wilderness of virtues, so that in this way we may receive the light of knowledge.

The man of desires, therefore, without turning his gaze in different directions, directed the gaze of his mind upon this one like a Son of Man, admiring and desiring with all his heart his coming into the world. But he looked in a vision of the night, not of day or light. There is a threefold vision: vision of night, vision of day, and vision of light.

The night vision is before grace [Col. 0373C]; the day vision under grace; the light vision in glory. In a vision of night, or a nocturnal vision, the patriarchs and prophets beheld him. Of this the Prophet says: “You spoke in a vision to your saints and said: I have placed help in one who is mighty” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 19). For the holy prophets and patriarchs saw the help of human beings placed in the Mighty One—that is, in the arm of the Lord—of whom it is said: “To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII, 1).

But they saw in a vision of night: that is, in an enigmatic and clouded understanding of the mind. To the Apostles, however, a vision of God was granted, but not a vision of light, because truth appeared to them, yet shod; divinity appeared, yet covered with a cloud. With burning speech he sounded in their hearts, and with his finger inscribed the new law in their minds. Emmanuel was seen upon earth by them and conversed with them: that is, “God with us”—with us in intercourse, with us in conformity, with us by sharing flesh in the likeness of sin [Col. 0373D].

He says through Ezekiel:

> [Note: [Col. 0373D] Thus it is cited by St Paul, II Cor. VI, 16.]

“I will dwell in them and walk among them; I will be their God, and they will be my people” (Zech. XIV, 7).

But in the future there will be the vision of light; and, as though the shoe-latchet were loosed, truth will be seen in its own form. Then, Zechariah testifies, “there will be one day, known to the Lord, neither day nor night; and at evening time there will be light.” For when Christ has delivered the kingdom to God the Father, and evening comes—that is, the end and consummation of all things—there will be neither day nor night (Rev. XXI, 25), but light alone [Col. 0374A]. Just as there will be neither alternation of day and night but a continuation of light, so nocturnal and diurnal vision will cease. Prophetic vision will cease, knowledge will be destroyed, and the vision of light will succeed.

Truth distinguishes this difference between nocturnal and diurnal vision in the Gospel: “Abraham,” he says, “rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John VIII, 56). Elsewhere he says: “For many prophets and kings wished to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke X, 25). It is as though he plainly said: Abraham and the prophets did indeed see with the eye of faith the day of my birth, but they did not see as you see; they desired to see, but it was not granted them. They saw in the night; you, in the day.

For this mystery, as the Apostle says, was not made known to other generations as it was revealed to the holy Apostles. Thus in Numbers (I Tim. III, 16): “The hearer of God’s words said . . . : ‘I shall see him, but not now; I shall behold him, but not near. A star shall rise from Jacob and a rod shall arise from Israel, and the Lord shall strike Moab’” (Num. XXIV, 16–17).

You who hear God’s words, attend carefully, that you may grasp the mystery of faith in your minds and carry it out in worthy works. “For every hearer of the word and not a doer,” as James says, “will be compared to a man considering the face of his birth in a mirror: he considered himself, went away, and immediately forgot [Col. 0374C] what he was like” (Isa. I, 13). Such persons are swift to hear and slow to act: they wish to know but not to do.

Our mirror is the instruction of the sacred page, in which are made known the dignity of our original creation, the misery of the ruin that followed, the goodness of restoration brought about by grace, and the certainty of future glorification. Yet some, considering these things, forget to humble themselves amid evils and to give thanks amid goods. Nor do they deserve wisdom, because “wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul” (Wis. I, 4), which says: “The wicked shall seek me and shall not find me.” For they hate wisdom, because one does not come to the wisdom [perhaps “knowledge”] of hidden things except through obedience to the commandments. Hence: “Have you desired wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will give it to you” (Sirach I, 35) [Col. 0374D].

At another time it is said to you: “Do not seek things higher than yourself, nor examine things stronger than yourself; but always think upon those things which the Lord commands you” (Sirach III, 22)—both before his wisdom is received and after it has been received. Nor was that hearer of God’s word without it, who said: “I shall see him, but not now; I shall behold him, but not near” (Num. XXIV, 27), as though saying: I shall see him in light, but not now. The one whom I see in the night I shall behold in the day, but not near.

Hence Isaiah says: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar; his anger burns like fire and is grievous to bear” (Isa. XXX, 29) [Col. 0375A]. If the name of the Lord—that is, the Son—comes from afar and not from near, in the name of the Father who is God, then by his coming he made known that he is God.

He is the star and rod arisen from Jacob and rising from Israel: a star because he enlightens; a rod because he strikes, directs, and heals. He enlightens the blind, directs the lame, heals the deaf and mute, and strikes the leaders of Moab—that is, the princes and powers of darkness. Hence Isaiah says: “Behold, the eyes of the blind and the ears of the deaf shall be opened. Then the lame shall leap like a stag, and the tongues of the mute shall be opened” (Isa. XXXV, 6).

The human race was burdened by many maladies, which the heavenly physician deigned to relieve by coming to us. Those were blind who lacked two eyes [Col. 0375B], the moral and the mystical. The moral is sweeter; the mystical more acute. Hence the bridegroom says to the bride: “You have wounded my heart with one of your eyes,” because God is more apprehended by the mystical eye than by the moral.

> [Note: [Col. 0375D] “You have wounded my heart with one of your eyes” (Song IV, 9).]

They were deaf because they did not have ears to hear, according to Isaiah: “I spoke, and you did not hear; you did evil in my eyes and chose what I did not wish” (Isa. LXV, 12). Elsewhere: “You will hear with your ear and will not understand” (Acts XXVIII, 26). They were lame because they lacked the steps of faith and good work, or lacked the teaching of both Testaments. Before the Saviour’s coming the world limped with the staggering gait of faith and doctrine. For that woman in the Gospel had spent all her substance on physicians who had not helped her (Luke VIII, 43).

Then, because he had no cloven hoof and did not chew the cud, he was unclean [Col. 0375C]. He was also mute, whose mouth Satan had closed so that it did not resound in praise of God. It was not nourished by love and remembrance of God; and therefore the world’s burning tongue was unable to sing a new song, namely a song to our God. For he is mute toward God who does not remember him. Why does he cry out? Why does he speak, who does not sound the song of Zion—that is, the new song? He did not sing the new song, but the song of the world, when he was ignorant of the song of heaven.

But when Emmanuel came, scattering like ashes the cloud of sin and ignorance which covered the whole earth, he opened both the eyes of the blind and the ears of the deaf; he directed the lame into a spiritual leap, so that they might leap from vices to virtues and from the world to heaven [Col. 0375D]; and he loosed the tongues of the mute to sound forth God’s praises.

He came with the clouds of heaven, came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him. The cloud of heaven is heavenly flesh, which he did not bring with him from heaven but assumed in the Virgin’s womb without the contagion of sin. For the Holy Spirit preceded the Virgin, sanctifying her wholly and filling her with the fire of love, so that the supreme priest might receive a tenth part from a sanctified tenth. For he received the firstfruits of our flesh.

Hence Isaiah says: “The Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt, and Egypt’s idols will be shaken” (Isa. XIX, 1) [Col. 0376A]. The light cloud is the flesh in which he appeared: a cloud because it gives us refreshment against the heat of vices; light because it was without the corruption of iniquity, which in Zechariah is said to “sit upon a talent of lead” (Zech. V, 7).

In this cloud he entered the Egypt of this world, and its idols fell: that is, the chief vices of this world’s vices failed in the hearts of believers. He came even to the Ancient of Days because, although in the cloud he was known as less than the Father, in divinity he was known as equal to him. By the Father’s will, just as he was born in the Virgin’s womb, so he was presented on the cross by the Jews.

The Father gave him power, kingdom, and honour, when he made known to the world that he had begotten him omnipotent and king, and therefore to be honoured as the Father. “For whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him” (John V, 29) [Col. 0376B]. “His power is an eternal power, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed.” His kingdom will have no end, because his kingdom is not of this world. May he deign to grant this to us, he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## VIII. EIGHTH SERMON FOR THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

> [Note: [Col. 0375D] From Saint-Germain manuscript 381.]

On the mystery of the Incarnation.

“The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10).

Jacob, about to give blessings to his sons, foreknowing in the Spirit that from his seed would be born him in whom the blessing of all nations would be accomplished, called his sons and said to them:

> “Gather together, sons of Jacob, that I may declare to you what shall happen in the last days; gather together and hear Israel your father” (Gen. 49:1).

Then he added: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations.”

The patriarch Israel, by the change of his name, attained an enlargement of power. His own name, hateful and rejected, having been set aside, he was chosen by God and beloved by his mother. With his mind captivated by him whose name is “the Living One and the Seeing One,” he became, with Jeremiah, like a child who does not know how to speak; and, with Moses, slow and impeded of tongue. Sounding but faintly because of the slenderness of his speech, he embraces the feet of that humility whose majesty’s head he cannot reach. For the head of Christ is God, and he is indeed the hidden God. Ineffable is his majesty, by whose silent proclamation humanity is exalted.

Leaving aside, therefore, the heights of divinity—which know neither past nor future—he uttered, beneath a certain covering of words, that which was [to be], declaring to his sons, as he blessed them, that he would come—the one whom the crowds, going out to meet him, cried:

> “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 23:39).

“The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations.”

The tribe of Judah deserved to possess the privilege of royal rule when, while the other tribes trembled and despaired, it alone, by God’s command, confidently entered the Red Sea with the holy and faithful Moses and Aaron. Hence Hosea says:

> “But Judah came down as a witness with God, and is faithful with the saints” (Hos. 11:12).

Rightly, then, the sceptre is understood as the administration of royal dignity. It was not taken away, nor did a ruler fail from Judah’s thigh, until he came who was to be sent: that is, Christ. He was to be sent because he was promised; promised because he had been chosen for this before the world’s beginning. Although kings from Judah failed in Zedekiah or Gedaliah, priests or leaders administering the royal office nevertheless did not fail until Christ came.

But from where did Christ come, for what did he come, and whither did he come?

> “I,” he says, “went forth from the Father and came into this world” (John 16:28).

Behold from where and whither he came. Hence the prophet says:

> “His going forth is from the height of heaven” (Ps. 18:7),

that is, he proceeds eternally from equality with the Father, from whom he was brought into the circle of the earth in time. For the Evangelist says of him:

> “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1:10).

And he adds:

> “He came unto his own, and his own did not receive him” (ibid., v. 11).

But if he came into this world and was in the world, then he came there where he was; he was sent there where he was not absent. For he is absent neither from east nor west nor from the desert mountains, since he is God. And if he is God, he is not enclosed by place nor bounded by local extent, but he who says, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24), is everywhere and always, essentially and wholly present.

For he is Wisdom,

> “reaching mightily from end to end, and ordering all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1).

From the beginning [of the world] to the time of the Incarnation, he powerfully accomplished wondrous works and instructive testimonies through the Old Testament; from the Incarnation to the end of the world, he sets forth the sweetness of the Gospel. He reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly because, remaining unchangeably from eternity unto eternity, he acts and orders all things everywhere in perfection.

Of him it is said:

> “Wisdom is more mobile than all moving things, and reaches everywhere because of her purity” (Wis. 7:24).

She is not called more mobile than moving things because she moves in herself—for it is written in the prophet, “I am the Lord, and I do not change” (Mal. 3:6)—but because she moves, governs, and orders all else; because, though one, she can do all things, and, remaining, renews all things, as is read in the Book of Wisdom (Wis. 7:27).

By a will always unchangeable and by the same eternity, Wisdom moves spiritual creation through time; she also moves bodily creation through time and place, so that by that motion she may govern the natures she created. When, therefore, she does such things, we ought not suppose that her substance, which is God, is more mobile in bodily or local respects. For she is more inward than every thing, because all things are in her; more outward than every thing, because she is above all things; more ancient than all things, because she is before all things; and more new than all things, because she is after all things. Therefore we understand her as eternal without time, wholly everywhere without place, and as making all mutable things without any change in herself.

Yet this Wisdom is said in the prophets to be sent and to be future, while in the Gospel she is read to have come. How, then, is this mission of Wisdom, which contains all things—that is, Christ—to be understood? How shall we understand him to have been sent into the world, or to have come? We must [speak] soberly concerning him, because we are [not] adequate to conceive anything worthy of him. For, from the incomprehensible and ineffable secret of divine majesty, he gave himself to be comprehended and seen by human beings when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Hence:

> “He was seen upon earth and conversed with men” (Bar. 3:38).

He did not, therefore, come into the world by changing place, since he was in the world, but by putting on flesh, so that he might fittingly appear to fleshly persons without change in himself. Thus the Word of the Father came from the royal seats into the world, clothed in the form of a servant.

But for what did he come? To heal wounds, raise the dead, and cure the half-living. He is that Samaritan who appeared to the wounded man who, descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers and had his wounds bound up. The priest and Levite passed him by, offering no help: that is, the old law and priesthood, which could not free the man wounded by robbers—that is, struck down by demons. Therefore the Samaritan, descending by the same road, approached him in order to heal him, the one whom, while half alive, he had heard was to be awaited.

The Samaritan—that is, the guardian—is Christ, who, neither slumbering nor sleeping, guards Israel. Through Isaiah he says:

> “One cries to me from Seir: ‘Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?’ The watchman said: ‘Morning comes, and also night. If you seek, seek; turn back and come’” (Isa. 21:11).

Seir is interpreted “rough” and “hairy.” By it is signified the misery of human infirmity: the man wounded by robbers was distressed. Having obtained no remedy through priest and Levite, he cried from Seir—that is, from a place of horror and vast desolation, where, bristling with punishments and hairy with vices, he lay—to the Samaritan, as though saying with the Apostle:

> “Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24).

For there is none who delivers except the Samaritan, the true guardian. Therefore he cries to this one, who descends by the same road—that is, was “tempted in all things according to our likeness, yet without sin”—saying: “Watchman, what of the night?” namely, the night of vices and ignorance. You are able to free the poor man from the night of punishments and misery, he who has no helper. Look upon the hosts rising against me by night [the reading after “night” is uncertain; perhaps “against me rising”]. Rescue me, captured by robbers and left half alive. For I have lost the life of grace, but not the life of nature. The best life has been lost, by which the soul lives in praise of God. The good life has been corrupted, by which nature lived in integrity. The life of sin has been introduced. For life is threefold: that of nature, of grace, and of vice. Restore the lost life, renew the corrupted one, remove the introduced one.

It is now the time called a time for acting, no longer for commanding, because the commandments of the laws could not help. For

> “there is a time to keep silence and a time to speak” (Eccl. 3:7).

The time for speaking was in the law, where there was the voice of words without the working of grace, and a multitude of promises without the bestowal of their realities. But now is the time to keep silence concerning those legal matters and to fulfil spiritual ones: namely, that you may come to free us, ascend the palm-tree of the cross, eat its fruit, take away sin and death, and restore life.

And the watchman said: “Morning comes, and night.” This is said with the Apostle:

> “The night has gone before, but the day has drawn near. Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (Rom. 13:12; 2 Cor. 6:2),

in which I shall hear and help you, unless you receive grace in vain. Rise, therefore, from the sleep of torpor and ignorance; cast off the works of darkness, that is, evil deeds that come from darkness and lead to the outer darkness; and put on the armour of light. Adorn and arm yourselves with virtues against the fiery darts of the enemy, that you may be worthy to receive the Saviour for whom you wait. Put on Jesus Christ, who shall refashion the body of your lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory. His way is undefiled and his dwelling uncontaminated: he does not dwell in a body subject to sins, nor rest except upon the humble, quiet person who trembles at his words.

Cast away the stones from the streets of your hearts; shatter the idols of your minds; return to your hearts, you transgressors; call upon him in truth, and you shall find him.

This, then, is what the Samaritan says: “Morning comes, and night”—the night, namely, of unbelief and ignorance. The night of blindness and vices came long ago, but now it is no more, because morning has come, when light rose upon those sitting in the region of the shadow of death. Therefore, if you seek me, seek with your whole heart—not in word and tongue, but in deed and truth. Turn away from evils and come to me by doing good; for now your salvation is nearer than when you believed, that is, when you began to believe.

You have received the oracles of answers, as he says through Isaiah:

> “My Righteous One is near; my Saviour has gone forth” (Isa. 51:5).

And again:

> “It shall not be far off, and my salvation shall not delay; I shall give salvation in Zion, and my glory in Jerusalem” (Isa. 46:13).

How sweet and lovable a promise! How sweet and gracious a saying, worthy of all acceptance! For Jesus Christ is the Righteous One and Saviour of the Father—that is, sent by the Father—not, of course, one who justifies or saves the Father. He has from the Father the power to justify and save, he who came in the Father’s name into this world to save sinners: sinners, indeed, who confess their sins, not the righteous, that is, those presuming upon their own righteousness, according to the saying:

> “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke 5:32).

This too greatly raises the minds of believers. For what is there with God to compare with the gift of health, or with the prolongation of salvation? [Suggested reading: “For what with God is comparable to the gift of health or to the proclamation of salvation?”] Hence the Father says:

> “My salvation shall not be far off, and shall not delay,”

that is, beyond the hour eternally appointed; rather:

> “I shall give salvation in Zion, and my glory in Jerusalem” (Isa. 46:13).

Zion is interpreted “watching,” Jerusalem “vision of peace.” Zion, therefore, is the present Church, which guards beforehand against assaults of enemies from afar, gazes in the mirror of Scripture upon the face of her birth, keeps her heart with every vigilance, sets a door of self-restraint upon her lips, and guards her garments lest she walk naked on the road, according to Habakkuk:

> “I will stand upon my watch, and set my step upon the fortification; and I will look to see what may be said to me, and what I may answer to one who rebukes me” (Hab. 2:1).

Jerusalem is the heavenly Church, which enjoys the vision of peace, where there is full and perfect peace without the disturbance of unrest, according to the saying:

> “He has made peace your borders” (Ps. 147:15).

And elsewhere:

> “I will give peace in your borders” (Lev. 26:6).

Thus the Samaritan, that is, our guardian, is salvation in Zion and glory in Jerusalem: here he saves by justifying; there he glorifies by placing at his right hand.

He is that Elisha who sent his staff to raise the son of the Shunammite. When the boy could not rise by itself, Elisha himself finally came, contracted himself, and fitted himself to the dead child; and the dead child rose. Elisha was mocked as bald by boys when he went up to Bethel, while they cried, “Take him away, take him away; crucify him” (John 19:15). He sent the staff to raise the son of the Shunammite when, through Moses, he gave a law which chastised but did not help, admonished but did not heal.

For by a great and profound judgment God gave the law before sending his Son, so that he might humble human pride and convict human insufficiency, lest humanity claim righteousness for itself and judge that Christ had come in vain. Therefore, when the staff had been sent through the servant—that is, when the law had been given through Moses—the dead person was not justified, because transgression dwelt when the law entered in. Through the law came knowledge, not the destruction, of sin.

Therefore Elisha himself contracted himself, because

> “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.”

He was not emptied by an emptying or alteration of his divine form; rather, the assumption of the servant’s form was added, and the form of God did not depart. He seems, as it were, to have divested himself of dignity when, being in the form of God, he clothed himself with the form of a human being. And he fitted himself to the dead child because he was

> “made in the likeness of men, and found in habit as a man” (Phil. 2:7).

Here “likeness” expresses reality. He was made in the likeness of a human being because, in the unity of person, a rational soul and flesh were joined to the Word. Although he was the only Son of God, Son not by grace but by nature, so that he might also be full of grace, he became the Son of Man: God and man; not two Sons of God without beginning, but man, having received a beginning, less than the Father in the form [of man], equal to the Father in the form of God. In his outward condition—that is, in his manner of life—he was found by those who wished to test him as another human being: he drank, ate, sat, and performed the other offices of humanity.

By this union and fitting together, therefore, the dead person rose. Likewise, it is read in the Gospel that, when the angel of the Lord descended once a year into the pool called Probatica, the water was stirred, and the one who first descended into the pool was healed (John 5:1–4). This is the Angel of Great Counsel,

> “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2:3),

who descended into the Probatica pool—that is, the penal pool—when he came to the carnal synagogue, which loved earthly things and offered carnal things. It had five porticoes, in which lay a multitude of sick persons awaiting the movement of the water (ibid., vv. 2–3): that is, the five books of Moses, by which sicknesses were exposed but not healed. This is the child carrying the five barley loaves, by which he was burdened, not fed.

But when the Angel came, the water was stirred—that is, the people were stirred up to crucify him, raising their voice against him like a lion in the forest—and thus one person was healed through one person. No one was found able to open the book and loose its seals except the Lion from the tribe of Judah. Through him none is healed except one, because no one deserves healing unless he is joined to Christ by charity, as a member to its head.

Nor did Jacob’s sons deserve to hear this mystery except when gathered together in the Lord’s name, he who says:

> “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:20).

For when they had gathered, he foretold to them what would happen in the last days—that is, in the last age. We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. 10:11); as the apostle John says:

> “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18).

[Note: This allusion would not appear admissible if referred to the Vulgate, since at 3 Kings 17:6 the text reads: “The ravens also brought him”—that is, Elijah—“bread and flesh in the morning, and likewise bread and flesh in the evening, and he drank from the torrent.” But it accords very well with the version of the Seventy Interpreters, which some were still using in Hildebert’s time, where the text reads: “The ravens brought him loaves in the morning and flesh in the evening, and he drank water from the torrent.” From this it is inferred that, when Hildebert cites Scripture differently from its wording in the Vulgate, this happened because he very frequently used the version of the Seventy Interpreters as though it were familiar to him.]

And in the evening the raven brought flesh to Elijah, and in the morning loaves (3 Kings 17:6), because at the evening of the world the incarnate Saviour is present for righteousness; and on the morning of the third day the heavenly bread, which gives life to the world, baked in the furnace of the Passion, rose in glory. Hence Moses said to the children of Israel:

> “In the evening you shall eat flesh, and in the morning you shall be filled with loaves” (Exod. 16:12).

At this hour, therefore, the Angel of Great Counsel descended from the Father’s assembly to heal the one. The Samaritan descended to bind up the wounded man. Elisha approached to raise the dead. He came who restored the one made alive to his mother, the Church. To him be honour and glory through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## IX. First Sermon on the Nativity of the Lord

[Note: E. Sangerman. 381.]

Concerning the Lord’s nativity.

> “The Lord is our exaltation, the Holy One of Israel our king” (Ps. 89:19).

The Lord of lords, King of kings, whose name is Almighty, did not disdain or reject fellowship with human weakness, but, as the Apostle says, “he took hold of Abraham’s seed, not angels” (Heb. 2:16). For this dignity was not granted to angelic nature, that God should be joined to it in one person; rather, he took flesh from Abraham in order to save Abraham’s children.

Hence Isaiah says:

> “I shall bring forth seed from Jacob, and from Judah one possessing the highest mountains; and my chosen ones shall inherit my inheritance; there my servants shall dwell” (Isa. 65:9).

This is Abraham’s promised seed, to whom the Lord said:

> “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18).

Christ is called Abraham’s seed because he took hold of Abraham’s seed. He did not bring flesh with himself from heaven, nor did he form new flesh anew from elsewhere. Rather, from the mingled mass of humanity he assumed the cloud of sanctification, that he might be a giant of two substances and a two-formed nature. In him are shown the dignity of human nature, God’s mercy and grace by which he deigned to do this, and the care he had for us. For he pursued and seized human nature as it fled before him—fled far away indeed, at a great distance, because salvation is far from sinners. Since this is great, wondrous, and full of astonishment, he so exalted the weakness of our flesh that it was joined to the Word of the Father in unity of person.

This is the woman who, as the Gospel parable relates, lights a lamp and, after overturning the house, finds the drachma which had been lost. For when humanity was lost in the first-formed man, who was the source of loss—while we are the offspring of our father—Wisdom, in order to find the lost drachma, that is, to find the human being inscribed with the king’s name and image, lit a lamp. That is, she placed light in a clay vessel, because with the light of divinity she kindled the clay vessel of human weakness. And after the house had been overturned—that is, after the world lying in wickedness was changed for the better by the right hand of the Most High—the drachma was found; and that prodigal son who had perished, returning to his father from a distant exile, was found.

The laws of nature are dissolved where God becomes human; and here [the reading has “and man”] man is made divine, where he who is born in a mother is begotten without a father. Therefore let the heavens rejoice and the earth exult, because our nature has been joined to the Word; things in heaven and things on earth have been restored; peace has been given to human beings on earth; and glory has been made to God in the highest, as the losses caused by the angels’ fall are repaired. Hence the angels sing:

> “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2:14).

For they glorify God for the repair of their own diminution. They praise God for the reconciliation of nature, through which all things have been accomplished, because the kindness and humanity of God our Saviour have appeared—that is, the kind God, made human, has appeared when he came to seek and save that which had perished.

The Son of the Father alone—not the Father himself, nor the Holy Spirit—assumed flesh, so that God, who had created the world in his wisdom, according to the saying,

> “Lord, you made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 104:24),

might save by that same Son the things in heaven and on earth. The Son—not the Father or the Holy Spirit—was sent into that [world], so that he who was Son in divinity might be [not another, but] the Son in humanity. And lest the Father himself should be the Son, if God the Father were born from a human being, in God’s great counsel and ineffable wisdom neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit assumed flesh, but the Son alone: so that he who was the Son of God in divinity might himself become the Son of Man in humanity; born for truth, he might be born from a human being as a human son, so that, as the truth of one begotten, he might possess the name of Son in both births by being born—not by adoption or designation.

Isaiah, marvelling at both his births, struck by the horror of a depth beyond [what can be spoken] and astonished beyond the abyss’s height, says:

> “Before she travailed, she gave birth; before her labour came, she bore a male. Who has ever heard such a thing, and who has ever seen anything like this?” (Isa. 66:7–8)

The mind fails; the voice falls silent. Elsewhere he says:

> “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8)

This must be understood not only of the eternal generation, but also of the temporal. For John too, sanctified from the womb—than whom none greater arose among those born of women—showed himself weak before the explanation of this incomparable generation, saying:

> “One stronger than I shall come after me, whose sandal-thong I am not worthy to loose” (John 1:17),

that is, “I am insufficient to open the bond [variant: “knot”] of the mystery of the Incarnation, the manner of the secret.” Flesh is rightly called a sandal, because divinity came to us, as it were, shod with it.

But concerning the words, “Before she travailed, she gave birth,” and so forth, the interpreter of truth, as though shaking out this covering, says: Before the Virgin travailed, God the Father gave birth—that is, he begot the Son; before her labour came, namely Mary’s, God the Father bore a male, that is, a mighty Son, through whom all things were made and subsist. He is called male not because of sexual distinction, but because of the greatness of his power, just as he is called the arm, of whom it is said:

> “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Ps. 63:1 [as cited]).

Who, however, has ever seen the like: that the same one should be born here, first from the Father without a mother, and secondly from a mother without a father? Therefore do not marvel that we confess that the Father has given birth, when he himself says:

> “Shall I, who cause others to give birth, not myself give birth?” (Isa. 66:9)

God the Father therefore gave birth, and the Virgin travailed—not two, but one and the same Son of God, of whom it is said:

> “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6).

Great and exalted is this child, whose birth is ineffable. Ecclesiasticus says of him:

> “A poor and wise child is better than an old and foolish king, who does not know to provide for the future; though one comes forth from prison and chains to a kingdom, and another, born in a kingdom, is consumed in poverty” (Ecclus. 4:13–14).

He is the child chosen from among thousands, of whom the Father says:

> “Behold my child whom I have chosen” (Isa. 42:1; Matt. 12:18).

Though poor, this child has many children obedient to him, for whose sake he himself became a child. For though he was rich, God with God the Father, through whom all things were made, he became poor for our sakes, so that by assuming our poverty he might share his riches with us. As he made himself poor, he enriched his members with heavenly gifts. For, insofar as he was human, he was filled with the Holy Spirit, which was given to him without measure; and from his fullness we have all received.

As he became humble in order to exalt us, and poor in order to give the kingdom of heaven to us who are poor in spirit, so he became a child in order to make his own children, concerning whom Isaiah says:

> “Behold, I and my children whom the Lord has given me” (Isa. 8:18).

Indeed, in the prophets he is often called a child because of the privilege of purity: he “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth”; he “did not walk in the way of sinners, nor stand in the counsel of the ungodly, nor sit in the seat of pestilence” (Ps. 1:1). Hence all who wish to be his disciples must become children, because, taking a child, he placed him in their midst and said:

> “Whoever does not humble himself as this little child shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 9:35).

This is also why the firstfruits of the innocent children were consecrated: they confessed him not by speaking but by dying, so that all who wish to offer a sacrifice to God may strive to be conformed to them in purity of life. For the sake of such children, in order to free them from the hand of the destroyer, he became a child, sharing soul and flesh, like them in punishment but not in guilt. Hence the Apostle says:

> “Since the children shared in flesh and blood, he likewise participated in the same, that through his death he might destroy him who had the dominion of death,”

that is, the devil,

> “and might free those who through fear of death were subject to slavery” (Heb. 2:14–15).

God certainly had another possible means of our deliverance, but none was more fitting to heal our misery: that the human being who had fallen through pride should rise through humility, and that the one who had subjugated humanity to himself through cunning and deceit should be conquered by a human being through wisdom and justice; so that, just as a human being destroyed humanity, so a human being might free humanity from the devil’s hand.

For unless the one who conquered the devil were human, humanity, having voluntarily subjected itself to him, would seem to be exalted not justly but violently. But if a human being conquered, then once again the devil would destroy a human being; and, for a human being to conquer, it is necessary that God be human, lest he be able to sin. For if he were merely human [variant: “purely” human], or an angel, he would easily sin in humanity, since it is certain that each nature fell by itself.

Therefore, because the children shared in flesh and blood—that is, they were corruptible human beings composed of body and soul, the latter being signified by blood—Christ participated in the same, that is, in flesh and soul. He likewise did so because he was passible and mortal, “tempted in all things according to our likeness, yet without sin” (Heb. 4:15), so that through his death he might destroy the devil and free those subject to him, their sins being blotted out, through which we had been captives under him.

For we had fallen into the power of the prince of this world, who led Adam out [suggested correction: “deceived”], made him his own, and began to possess us almost as household-born slaves. But the Redeemer came, and the deceiver was conquered. What did the Redeemer do to our captor? He stretched out a mousetrap for him and placed in it, as bait, his own blood. The devil shed innocent blood and was then commanded to withdraw from the guilty. For, because he stretched out his hand against one in whom he had no right at all, he deservedly lost those in whom he seemed to have some right. He held us only by the chains of our sins. These were the captives’ fetters.

But the poor and wise child came and bound the strong man with the chains of his Passion. He entered his house—that is, the hearts in which he dwelt—and plundered his vessels, which he had filled with his bitterness. But the child, taking them away and making them his own, poured out the bitterness and filled them with sweetness.

The child born, therefore, is wise and good. He is surely better than an old and foolish king. He is truly good, whose goodness has no number, for whom being good is not one thing and being God another: his goodness is divine nature, and his wisdom is divine essence. For he is the Wisdom that came forth from the mouth of the Most High; a certain firstborn emanation of the sincere brightness of the Almighty; the radiance of eternal light, the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness.

He is the child who [reveals] not his face but his back parts. His face, shining with excessive brightness, is invisible to a mortal eye, but his back parts can be seen. Hence, when Moses asked to see his face, he answered:

> “No human being shall see my face and live,”

and added:

> “Stand in the cleft of the rock, and you shall see my back parts when I pass by” (Exod. 33:20 ff.).

Therefore, whoever cannot see the face of the true child should at least see his back parts—but in his passing. The face is the brightness of divinity; the back parts are the humility of the assumed humanity. The face is:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1:1).

The back parts are:

> “The Word was made flesh” (ibid.).

No one living amid these senses of mortal flesh, however advanced—even like Moses—can see the face of this child: that is, penetrate by the mind’s sight the mystery of unity and Trinity. This is reserved for the saints in the future as glory, according to the saying:

> “This is eternal life: that they may know you, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3),

as the one only and true God. This is the great abundance of God’s sweetness which he has hidden for those who fear him.

But if you cannot see the face, see the back parts, standing in the cleft of the rock when he has passed: that is, understand the Incarnation of the Word in such a way that you believe that he afterwards rose in glory. For by death he passed to life, from earth to heaven, from the world to the Father. It is not enough to believe that he died; the wicked also acknowledge that. Rather, they must be answered along the way of truth: one must believe that he rose in power. This is done by the person who stands fixed in the cleft of the rock, that is, in faith in Christ’s Passion.

> “For the rock was Christ,”

as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 10:4).

Thus one stands in the cleft of the rock who believes that the God who suffered was human. For believers’ faith in the Passion did not consist in believing that a human being suffered, as he appeared to do, but in believing that the one who died was God and human. Nor did Thomas, to whom it was said,

> “Because you have seen me, you have believed” (John 20:28),

believe what he saw. He saw a human being and confessed God, saying:

> “My Lord and my God” (ibid., v. 29).

Thus he beheld the humanity and believed the divinity. Whoever so believes stands in the cleft of the rock and sees the child’s back parts in his passing; from them that person ascends to contemplation of the face. For although the face preceded the back parts, one comes not from the face to the back parts but from the back parts to the face, so that the progress may be from lower things to higher.

[Col. 0386B] These are the most ancient things and the new, which are to be eaten when the old things have been cast away, as Moses says: “You shall eat the most ancient of the old things, and you shall cast away the old when the new arrives” (Lev. 26:10). Here there are three things: most ancient, old, and new. This Child has always possessed the most ancient things; He began the new things; He received the old things—that is, He sent beforehand the signs of the new. The most ancient things are immutable, not made but to be made; He made the new things, He spoke the old things. Therefore the most ancient things are the equality, co-eternity, and consubstantiality of the Begotten with Him who begets; the new things are His temporal birth from the Virgin; the old things are the signs and proclamations in the Law and Prophets of the coming Emmanuel.

The most ancient things, therefore, are to be eaten, because those who hunger and thirst for righteousness will be satisfied by understanding them, [Col. 0386C] according to that saying: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16:15), or your mercy. The new things also are to be eaten, so that while we are little children here, we may be nourished with the bread of angels—that is, with milk transformed for infants [perhaps read *in lac*, “into milk”]. For man ate the bread of angels, though not in the pure clarity of the form in which angels enjoy it, yet in the cloud in which He willed to be seen.

When the new things arrive, therefore, the old things are to be cast away, because, when the light of truth shines forth, its tokens are to be removed. Those tokens were, as it were, words promising; God remains for us a promiser until He becomes a fulfiller. When He fulfilled what was promised, He changed the wording and removed the timber. He does not say, “I shall give,” but “I have given.” Nor is it said, “The light will shine,” but “A Child is born to us.” The promise ceases, because the manifestation of truth takes place. [Col. 0386D] The old things pass away because the new succeed them, according to the Apostle: “Therefore, if anyone is a new creation in Christ, the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new for him” (2 Cor. 5:17).

For the old error departed because truth sprang up from the earth; for the earth gave its fruit when Mary bore the good Word. This Child is good, poor, and wise, and certainly better than “an old and foolish king, who does not know how to provide for himself in the future” (Eccl. 4:13). Who is this old and foolish king? It is surely he who, on account of his perversity, is called the prince of this world, concerning whom the wise Child says: “The prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John 15:30). And again: “Now is the judgment of the world; now the prince of [Col. 0387A] this world shall be cast out” (John 12:31). He is called prince of the world not because he was the Lord and creator of the worldly creation, but because he is the prince and leader of those who love the world.

257 Thus this old king is foolish. He is king because he was created in a kingdom, namely in the empyrean heaven, that is, the fiery heaven. Rabanus says that heaven takes its name from brightness, not from heat, because, set apart from the world’s revolving motion, as soon as it was created it was filled with holy angels, among whom Lucifer was present and pre-eminent. Hence the Lord says: “Where were you when the morning stars praised me, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?” (Job 38:7). He calls the angels “morning stars” at the beginning of the human condition.

He is rightly called both king and old: king, because, [Col. 0387B] as Ezekiel says, “he was full of perfection and beautiful amid God’s delights, and the seal of His likeness” (Ezek. 28:13); old, because, as Job testifies, he himself was the beginning of the ways of God (Job 40:14), since he was created among the first works of God; but foolish, because he did not provide for himself in the future. Created in the eminence and loftiness of true knowledge, he swelled with such pride that he presumed himself able to be equal to the Most High. For he said in his heart, as Isaiah says: “I shall ascend into heaven,” that is, to equality with God; “above the stars of heaven I shall exalt my throne,” that is, above the other angels; “and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 16:13–14). But the more he presumed, the more grievously he fell.

Hence Isaiah says: “How have you fallen from [Col. 0387C] heaven, Lucifer, you who arose in the morning? You have fallen to earth, and you shall be dragged down even to hell, into the depth of the pit” (ibid., 22:15). Truth says in the Gospel: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). Therefore this foolish king, though old, not providing for himself in the future, was not content with what was his and dared to usurp what belonged to another. Hence he was stripped even of what was his: created more splendid than the other angels, and for that reason called Lucifer, he fell through his own fault and became Hesperus, the evening star.

Cast down from the empyrean into the darkness of this air, he is mocked by the poor and wise Child, who came forth from prison and chains to a kingdom, while that one, born in a kingdom, is consumed by want. Marvel at the wisdom of the poor Child and the folly of the old king. For he, born in a kingdom, is consumed by want; [Col. 0387D] he wanders through waterless and arid places seeking rest and does not find it (Luke 11:24), because he abandoned true rest. “He sleeps beneath the shadow of the reed and in moist places” (Job 40:16), as Job testifies. He once flourished gloriously among the cedars of Paradise; but the poor and wise Child came from prison and chains to rest and a kingdom. For He was unjustly seized by the Jews, seized and bound; yet, patiently enduring all these things according to the Father’s will, He was fastened to the cross with nails, and by this obedience He obtained the kingdom. “For His dominion has been made upon His shoulder” (Isa. 9:6). Therefore “God exalted Him and gave Him the name that is above every name” [Col. 0388A] (Phil. 2:9). He who in suffering appeared weak, in rising again was made known as God.

Let us therefore rejoice and sing psalms wisely, because such a Child has been born to us, of whom the angel said to the shepherds: “Behold, I proclaim to you great joy, which shall be for all the people, because today a Savior has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke 2:10)—that is, Bethlehem, which is interpreted “house of bread,” because there was born the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world. There He was laid in a manger, where the ox fed with the ass, because for this reason He deigned to be born: that He might reconcile two peoples to God and refresh them with heavenly bread.

Therefore rejoice knowingly and sing psalms wisely. Blessed indeed is the people who know jubilation—that is, who understand the rationale and manner [Col. 0388B] of jubilation and psalmody. For jubilation is inexpressible joy, which can neither be explained in words nor kept silent. A psalm is a good work. Let us therefore rejoice in mind and sing psalms in deed, preparing dwelling places of the breast for our King and washing our hands among the innocent, because “our exaltation belongs to the Lord, and to the Holy One of Israel, our King” (Ps. 88:19). That is, the Lord and our King assumed our nature; He sanctifies us here, that in the future He may make us Israel, that is, those who see God. He swiftly stripped spoils from our robber; He bestowed health upon the weak, liberty upon captives, inheritance upon exiles, and, after destroying our enemies, gave us peace. To Him be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## X. SECOND SERMON ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Note: [Col. 0387D] From a manuscript of Saint-Victor, Paris, and from Lyra.]

Concerning the Nativity of the Lord.

[Col. 0388C]

Most dearly beloved brethren, as we are about to observe with most faithful devotion the holy and venerable, glorious and singular solemnity—that is, the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ—we ought, with His help, to prepare ourselves with all our strength and diligently examine every hidden recess of our soul, lest perhaps some sin lie concealed which may both shame our conscience and offend the eyes of the divine majesty.

For although Christ our Lord rose after His Passion and ascended into heaven, nevertheless, as we believe, He observes and carefully considers how each one of His servants endeavors to prepare and order himself for celebrating His Nativity without avarice [Col. 0388D] and anger, without pride and lust. For according as He sees each person endowed with good character, so He will dispense to that person the grace of His mercy. If He sees him clothed in the light of charity, adorned with the pearls of righteousness or mercy, chaste, humble, merciful, kind, and sober; if He recognizes him as such, He will dispense His body and blood to him through the ministry of His priests, not for judgment but for healing.

But if He sees someone drunken, covetous, suspicious, I fear that to him may be said what the Lord declares in the Gospel: “Friend, how did you enter here without [Col. 0389A] a wedding garment?” (Matt. 22:12). And—may the Lord avert it!—what follows may happen to him: “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid., 13). Behold what sentence, on the day of judgment, he will receive who approaches the Lord’s feast stained with the filth of vices and without the remedy of repentance.

For at the Nativity of the Lord, as at spiritual nuptials, Christ was joined to His bride, that is, the Church. Then “truth sprang up from the earth; then righteousness looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84:12); then the bridegroom came forth from his bridal chamber—that is, the Word of God the Father came forth from the virginal womb. For He came forth with His bride, that is, the Church, when He assumed human flesh. Therefore, invited to these most holy nuptials and [Col. 0389B] about to enter the banquet of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, see with what garments we ought to be adorned. As far as we can, therefore, with God’s assistance we ought to prepare both our hearts and bodies, so that the heavenly inviter may find in us nothing unclean, nothing foul, nothing dark, nothing unworthy of His eyes.

This, then, most dearly beloved brethren, we must consider not superficially but with great trembling. For we have been invited to the Lord’s nuptials, that we ourselves, if we act well, may cleave to the Bridegroom. Let us consider to what nuptials, to what Bridegroom, to what marriage we have been invited. For we have been invited to a table where the food of men is not found, but the bread of angels. Let us therefore take care lest perhaps, in the soul, where we ought to be adorned with the pearls of good works, we [Col. 0389C] should appear wrapped in old rags; and lest lust at some point make filthy those who are evil—the transmitted wording is internally corrupt, referring also to those who are good in God’s eyes and whom chastity has made white.

Therefore, whenever the days of the Lord’s Nativity or the other coming festivals occur, as I have frequently urged, we ought to abstain not only from the unhappy company of concubines but even from our wives, and we ought to keep ourselves free from every anger, so that former sins may be redeemed through almsgiving and repentance. Let no hatred of any person be kept in the heart. What vanity used to expend through gluttony [perhaps read *superbiam*, “pride”], let righteousness begin to distribute to the poor through mercy; what lust or gluttony spent [perhaps read *dissipavit*, “squandered”] in the world, [Col. 0389D] let piety lay up in heaven.

And although it is fitting that we should always give alms, yet especially on holy solemnities we ought, according to our means, to give more abundantly; above all, let us invite the poor more frequently to our feast. For it is not just that at a holy solemnity, among a Christian people belonging to one God, some should become drunk while others are tormented by hunger and danger to life. For we and all the people are servants of one God; and if we act well, we shall attain one blessedness together.

Therefore, brethren, as we are about to receive the Lord’s Nativity, let us be cleansed from every defilement of conscience. Let us meet Him, not in silken garments, but in precious works. [Col. 0390A] Garments can cover naked limbs; they cannot adorn the conscience. Indeed, it is a greater shame to go about with the limbs splendidly clothed and the mind polluted.

Let us therefore first adorn the disposition of the inner person, so that the clothing of the outer person may be more beautiful. Let us wash away spiritual stains, so that not carnal garments may shine in us. But let those things which we have urged cling to the renewed understanding of your charity—things spoken briefly and now repeated more briefly. For we give these exhortations, most dearly beloved brethren, because the Lord’s Nativity is at hand. Therefore, as for a nuptial and heavenly union, let us, through Christ’s assistance, prepare ourselves free from every lust and adorned with good works. Let us distribute alms to the poor; let us reject anger or hatred from our hearts as poison; let us faithfully preserve chastity.

Let us invite the poor more frequently to our table. Rise for the morning vigils; standing in church, worship or sing psalms. Utter no idle or worldly words yourselves, and correct those who wish to utter them. Preserve peace with all, and call back to concord those whom you know to be in discord. If, with Christ’s help, you faithfully desire to fulfill these things, you will be able to approach the Lord’s altar in this [Col. 0390B] world with a secure conscience and faithfully attain eternal blessedness in the world to come, through the granting of our Lord Jesus Christ.

## XI. THIRD SERMON ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Note: [Col. 0389D] From a Saint-Victor manuscript.]

Concerning the Nativity of the Lord.

[Col. 0390C]

> “The kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared, not because of works of righteousness which we had done, but according to His mercy He saved us” (Titus 3:5).

Brethren, the human race had been acquired by the cunning of diabolical fraud. Through the sin of the first parent, the devil had subjected it to his dominion [the printed text has *dilectioni*, “affection,” perhaps for *ditioni*]. But the Lord, the just Judge, who does not wish to inflict anything unjust even upon His adversary, but does all things either through mercy or through justice, willed to redeem the human race by grace in such a way that He should not seem to inflict injury upon the devil.

Therefore, since Satan had acted cunningly against man by deceit, the Lord willed [Col. 0390D] to act prudently against Satan for man’s sake through wisdom. Thus the Lord employed this plan for human restoration. It was necessary that one sent to fight against the devil should be such as neither to succumb nor to act irrationally, but to manage all things with wisdom. Adam was a mere man, and thus through human frailty he succumbed to diabolical temptations. Therefore a mere man could not be sent for redemption, since he might have sinned either of himself or when tempted. Yet an angel could not be sent in this warfare, since he could sin—he who had previously sinned through pride. Therefore one who could not sin had necessarily to be sent.

But [Col. 0391A] no rational creature exists that cannot sin, except God alone. Why, then, was not the Father sent, nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone? Because, as was said above, the cunning enemy had to be dealt with through wisdom. Now the Son is the wisdom and prudence of the Father, through whom all things were made and foreseen. Because He is prudence, He acted rationally; because He is wisdom, He acted wisely; and because He was God, He could not sin. Therefore the Son was sent: being prudence, He did all things rationally; being wisdom, He handled all things wisely; being God, He could not sin.

Yet it accorded with reason that, just as man had been overcome and made captive, so man, by overcoming the demon, should free human nature. [Col. 0391B] Therefore not a mere man was sent, but God and man: man, to fight; God, to sustain the fighter. There is another reason as well. Through the old man there was great discord between God and human beings; through the new Mediator concord was made. But since He was mediator, it was fitting that He should have kinship with both parties. Thus, since He was to reconcile man to God, He who stood between both had to be God and man.

Therefore the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared—that is, God and man. Yet it was not by works of righteousness which we had done, but according to His mercy that He saved us. And He appeared fittingly. For the birth of God [perhaps read “of Christ”] was revealed in many ways: it was revealed to shepherds through angels; [Col. 0391C] it was revealed to kings through a star.

For we heard in the Gospel that “there were shepherds in the same region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them, and they feared with great fear. And the angel said to them: Do not fear. For behold, I proclaim to you great joy, which shall be for all the people, because today a Savior has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord” (Luke 2:8 ff.). And where was He born? “In the city of David,” that is, Bethlehem. “And this shall be a sign to you: You shall find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger. And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (ibid.).

Hearing this, [Col. 0391D] the shepherds came as far as Bethlehem and saw what had been told them by the angel. Rightly did the angel announce this, because the King of angels had been born. And it was fitting that the angel should appear with great light, because he declared that the Sun of righteousness, light in darkness, had risen. It was announced to shepherds because He was born who said: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11).

He appeared to kings through a star because a King and a star had arisen: a King, as it is written, “But I have been appointed King by Him” (Ps. 2:6); a star, as it is written, “A star shall arise from Jacob” (Num. 24:17). He rightly appeared, then, to shepherds and kings, because He was born both king and priest, of royal and priestly lineage. Of royal [Col. 0392A] seed, because He was of David’s seed; of priestly seed, because Mary was related to Elizabeth. The messenger was highly commendable because he was an angel, and with a great voice, concerning which we read in the Gospel: “And the wife of Zachariah was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth” (Luke 1:5).

But hear what he brought: “Behold, I proclaim to you great joy, because today a Savior has been born to you.” Truly, great joy. We were captives in prison; we lay sick. The physician has been born. Behold, great joy. Joy was far greater for human beings because the angels rejoiced and said: “Glory to God in the highest.” There was joy among the angels over restoration of their diminished order. They praised the Lord for the restoration of humanity, for the restoration of angels.

And there is peace for human beings because we had discord with [Col. 0392B] God and with the angels; but through the Mediator we have been reconciled. Because by sinning we were strangers, the angels also reckoned us strangers to their fellowship. Indeed, angels held human beings in such contempt that they allowed themselves to be worshipped by them. This is why Lot and Abraham worshipped angels, and they were not forbidden before Christ’s coming. But after the Lord was born, when John wished to worship an angel in the Apocalypse, that same angel restrained him from worshipping him, saying: “See that you do not do it; I am your fellow-servant and that of your brethren” (Rev. 19:10).

Formerly angels despised human nature as inferior; but after they see it assumed above themselves, they fear to see it prostrate before them. Nor do they disdain man as a companion, when above themselves they worship the man who is God. [Col. 0392C] Peace is proclaimed to human beings—but not to all, rather to people of good will. As though they were saying: Those shall be reconciled who have a good will to be reconciled. And those have a will to be reconciled who devote themselves to the Creator and do not act contrary to His will.

It should be noted why he said “of good will” and not “of good action”: because good will is sufficient when the ability to act is lacking. Thus good will sometimes avails without good action, but action never avails without good will. He therefore preferred to say “of good will,” which is common to all who are saved.

We have shown, most dearly beloved brethren, how the kindness and humanity of the Savior appeared, but the order of His glorious birth must not be passed over in silence. His advent was foretold and prefigured long beforehand by the prophets and also by many figures. For Isaiah says: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon Him” (Isa. 2:1). This was also previously shown in the figure of Aaron. The Lord commanded rods to be brought from each tribe. Twelve rods were brought, including one that had belonged to Aaron the priest; Moses placed them in the tabernacle of testimony. But Aaron’s rod, on the following day, was found to have put forth flowers and leaves and borne nuts (Num. 17:2–8). [Col. 0392D] Behold prophecy and figure.

Jesse was David’s father; the root of Jesse is the Jewish family. The rod is Mary; the flower is her Son, upon whom the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove. Likewise, Aaron’s rod, which produced nuts without seed [the Vulgate reads “almonds”], signifies Mary, who bore Christ without seed. In the nut, which signifies the Lord’s body, there are three parts: husk, shell, and kernel. The bitter husk signifies the flesh, which experienced the bitterness of the Passion. The shell signifies the bones. The inner kernel signifies the soul, white with virtues.

Since this Nativity of the Lord had been foretold and foreshown by these and similar things, the Lord willed to fulfill the promises. Therefore the angel Gabriel was sent to Mary in Nazareth and announced the Lord’s descent into her womb [Col. 0393A] (Luke 1:26). It was fitting that Gabriel, whose name is interpreted “strength of God,” should announce the Lord who was to be born, since He would fight with a strong hand against the prince of this world. And it was very appropriate that Christ, who had been prefigured by the flower mentioned above, should be conceived in Nazareth, which is interpreted “flower” or “shrub.”

The eminent emperor had an eminent forerunner, John the Baptist, who recognized the Lord from his mother’s womb. John too was announced by the same Gabriel and, contrary to the order of nature, was born from the barren Elizabeth, who was Mary’s kinswoman. Christ was conceived in the sixth month after John’s conception. Once Christ was conceived, Mary went hastily into the hill country, entered Zachariah’s house, and greeted Elizabeth. On hearing the greeting, the infant leapt exultantly in Elizabeth’s womb (Luke 1:39 ff.). [Col. 0393B] John began to be a prophet before he was born, and the servant recognized the Lord—the conceived one recognizing the Conceived One. Through the grace of the Child, the mother was filled with a prophetic spirit and said: “Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” And Mary remained there three months and returned to her own house (ibid., 43, 56).

Afterward Joseph happened to go to Bethlehem with his pregnant wife. When the days for her delivery were fulfilled, they turned aside into a stable; she gave birth without pain and wrapped Him in swaddling clothes (Luke 2:7). Thus, through the working of divine power, Christ was born from a Virgin without the Virgin’s gate being opened: virgin before birth, virgin in birth, virgin after birth. Concerning this virginal gate the Lord said to Ezekiel: “This gate which you see shall be closed; it shall not be opened, and a man shall not enter through it” (Ezek. 44:2). [Col. 0393C] The Lord God of Israel entered through it, and it shall always remain closed.

Great merit, great gift, great grace! A handmaid bore the Lord; a creature, the Creator; a daughter, her father; daughter of divinity, mother of humanity. We have received two births of the Lord: one divine, the other human; the former without a mother, the latter without a father. Today, most dearly beloved brethren, we celebrate the temporal birth undertaken for our sake. Let us rejoice over our restoration. Today the sick man received health; today the captive, liberty; today the exile recovered his inheritance. Let us therefore receive today the coming King. Let us prepare dwelling places in our breasts for such an emperor, that He may deign to receive us [Col. 0394A] into the heavenly Jerusalem—He who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## XII. SOLE SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF THE LORD’S CIRCUMCISION

[Note: [Col. 0393D] From Saint-Germain manuscript no. 381.]

> “On Mount Zion there shall be salvation, and there shall be a Holy One; and the house of Jacob shall possess those who had possessed them; and the house of Jacob shall be fire, and the house of Joseph a flame” (Obad. 1:17).

The trumpet of a sweet and gentle promise sounded in the hearts of the faithful through the prophet Obadiah, that he might enlarge the minds of believers with spiritual exultation and perfect love, like the Savior’s music and heavenly harmony. “There shall be,” he says, “salvation on Mount Zion, and there shall be a Holy One.” Salvation will exist precisely because there is a Holy One. [Col. 0394B] For this is the Holy of Holies; at His coming the anointing of the Jews ceases. Before He was conceived, He was called Jesus—that is, Savior. Thus the evangelist teaches: “For He Himself shall save His people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21). He is rightly, therefore, divinely called Jesus, since by His work He fulfills the meaning of His name.

Concerning Him John says: “I saw a mighty angel coming down from heaven, clothed with a cloud, with a rainbow upon His head; His face was like the sun, and His feet like pillars of fire, and He held in His hand an open little book” (Rev. 10:1–2). The storehouse of grace—that is, sacred Scripture—heaps together many things which the two eyes of the bride, the mystical and the moral, can marvel at but cannot fully investigate. For behold: He whom above it calls holy, elsewhere a child, and elsewhere a prophet, here it calls a mighty angel. Thus He is a child by the prerogative of innocence and purity; holy by the grace of sanctification; a prophet by foretelling future things; and an angel by announcing present things.

For *angelus* means “messenger”; and who has been a truer messenger of the Father’s will than the Angel of Great Counsel? [Col. 0394C] He is rightly called the Angel of Great Counsel, because He alone was the Father’s counsellor from eternity in the ordering of things, and announced to us the counsel kept silent from eternal times; in Him, too, all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. For He is Wisdom, who says:

> “The Lord possessed me from the beginning of His ways, before He made anything from the beginning. I was ordained from eternity, before the earth was made. The abysses did not yet exist, and I was already conceived; the springs of waters had not yet burst forth; the mountains had not yet stood in their heavy mass; before the hills I was brought forth . . . When He prepared the heavens, I was present, arranging all things with Him . . . . . And I delighted day by day, playing before Him at every time” (Prov. 8:22 ff.).

Therefore this Angel knows the Father’s secrets; He is also mighty, though a Child, because He bound the strong man and conquered the powers of the air. For this reason He came down, not by changing place, certainly, but by assuming the garb of a servant’s form. Hence He is said to be clothed with a cloud, because, clothed with flesh, He appeared to the world; He says through the prophet: “He made me like [Col. 0395A] a chosen arrow; He hid me in His quiver” (Isa. 49:2). This quiver is the cloud of flesh in which the power of divinity lay hidden.

Christ’s flesh is rightly compared to a cloud because it gives us refreshment against the burning of vices and the heat of sins, from which the prophetic man asks to be refreshed and delivered [the printed text has *verberari*, “be struck,” perhaps for *liberari*], saying: “Forgive me, that I may be refreshed before I depart and am no more” (Ps. 38:14). For when You forgive me, so that I may be refreshed from the heat of varied desire and the fervor of worldly allurement, I shall indeed depart from this life but shall no longer be—in true being.

Thus this angelic cloud carries across consciences, or darkens understandings, but gives the refreshment of absolution to our souls and the light of true knowledge. For it extinguishes the poisons of vices and drives away the darkness [Col. 0395B] of ignorance. This is that Angel who went before the children of Israel as they journeyed, in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night; when He went before, they followed, and when He stood still, they remained in camp (Exod. 13:21).

What are these pillars except the Angel’s two forms: one of God, the other of man; one of Lord, the other of servant? For the pillar of cloud which went before by day is the form of His human assumption, which by day—that is, in the time of grace—goes before us, leading us into the land of promise. The Mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, went before us as it were by day when in Himself He gave us an example, that we might follow His footsteps. All His action is our instruction. As our Prince, by deed and word He prescribed for us the law of going and of running to our homeland, lest we depart from His signs by turning to the right or left, but that we may run after Him in the fragrance of His ointments. Like a bridegroom proceeding from his bridal chamber, He rejoiced as a giant to run His course.

He is rightly called the Bridegroom, because He was frequently promised by the prophets; and because He has a bride, He is Bridegroom. Therefore, as He is called Bridegroom from the prophetic betrothal, so also His bride is called the Church, frequently promised to Him, as in: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2:8). [Col. 0395C] The bridal chamber of both Bridegroom and bride was the virginal womb, where the Angel of Great Counsel was joined to human nature as bridegroom to bride, while the integrity of virginal incorruption was preserved.

He indeed came down like rain upon fleece: the comparison is plain and the likeness fitting. For wool, whether receiving or giving off water, is not torn but remains whole. Thus integrity was preserved in the Virgin before birth, in birth, and after birth.

[Note: [Col. 0395] What is enclosed in brackets is printed word for word also in Peter Lombard, *Commentary on Psalm 71*, part III, verse 6.—Editors of the *Patrologia*.]

For this is the gate facing east which Ezekiel records as having been shut, the Lord saying to him: “This gate shall be shut and shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it. For the Prince shall enter by the way of the gate and shall go out by its way” (Ezek. 44:2–3). This is the Prince of whom [Col. 0396A] Isaiah says: “A prince shall devise things worthy of a prince, and he himself shall stand over leaders” (Isa. 32:8).

This Prince, whom no one could endure if He wished to be known in manifest power, willed to descend with utmost gentleness into the Virgin’s womb without any disturbance, like rain upon fleece. Therefore “He rejoiced as a giant to run His course” (Ps. 18:6). He is rightly called a giant because, unshaken and irrevocable, surpassing all human beings in incomparable power, He Himself ran the course. He did not dwell or stand in it because the world’s allurement did not hold Him. What course? Behold: “His going forth is from the summit of heaven, and His course reaches unto its summit” (ibid., 7).

This, then, is the way that the mighty giant of twofold substance and dual nature ran: because, proceeding eternally from equality with the Father, he came into the world clothed in the cloud of flesh and was made visible, knowable by human beings; and again, leaving the world, he ascended to the Father—not as though he had ceased to be in the world. Nor did he ascend to the Father as though he had not always been with him. Rather, just as before he was clothed in the cloud he was in the world, and the world was made through him, and, when he is said to have come into the world in the cloud of flesh, he appeared visibly to the world; so he is said to have left the world, not because of his absence but because his visibility was withdrawn, and to have ascended to the Father because, by ascending into heaven, he was shown to be equal to the Father.
