Thus the mighty angel went before us in a pillar of cloud, because in the time of grace, as though in the cloud of flesh, he instructed us, [Col. 0396C] so that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we might live soberly with respect to ourselves, justly with respect to our neighbor, and piously with respect to God in this world, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ (Tit. 2:12). But by night he went before us in a pillar of fire. The pillar of fire is an image of divinity. “For our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24), because, as fire consumes wood, hay, and straw, so he consumes these things in us; he tests the elect in the furnace of tribulation as a potter tests vessels. Of him Malachi says: “He is like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ soap; he will sit refining and cleansing as silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and strain them as gold” (Mal. 3:2–3).

For our God is like a refining fire [Col. 0396D] to those who commit grave sins, visiting their transgressions with the blows of graver punishments. But to those who admit light sins and minor offenses he is like fullers’ herb, so that, once washed, he may restore their cleanliness and wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion. By the sons of Levi, however, priestly rank is understood. But if the priests of the Lord must be tested and purified, what is to be said of the rest, when judgment begins with the house of God? “Begin,” the Lord says through Ezekiel to the angels who administer vengeance, “with my holy ones” (Ezek. 9:6). If, then, judgment begins here with the sons, what will the most wicked servants do? If the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and sinner appear? (1 Pet. 4:18).

[Col. 0397A] Rightly, then, he who so refines and strains sinners is said to go before us in a pillar of fire, and this in the night of sins and vices. For as the rising of the day signifies grace, so the darkening of night signifies sins—a night which especially enveloped the world before the Savior’s coming, because light had not yet arisen for those sitting in the region of the shadow of death. The second death is understood here: that which will be in hell, of which vices and sins are the shadow. Thus the region of the shadow of death is understood as the kingdom of sin, the region of dissimilarity. Therefore those who rise from sins, who put their souls to death, do not fall into the second death. Hence John says: “Blessed are those who have a share in the first resurrection; over these the second death has no power” (Rev. 20:6). The first resurrection is that of the soul from vices; [Col. 0397B] the second will be that of the body rising from death. Of the first the Apostle says: “Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14). And Solomon: “How long, sluggard, will you sleep? When will you rise from sleep?” (Prov. 6:9)—from this sleep, that is, from the body’s carnal pleasures? No one rises from the night of vices and ignorance unless the Lord awakens and enlightens him through his grace. For of the way of iniquity it is said: “Many will enter through it, and they will not return.” They indeed enter by themselves, but do not return by themselves; rather, by God’s grace going before them and leading them back.

Rightly, therefore, the mighty Angel is said to have gone before the children of Israel in a pillar of fire, because by the power of divinity he breaks the bonds of sins in the elect. [Col. 0397C] “There was a rainbow upon his head” (Rev. 10:1), that is, divinity in humanity. For God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, and “his face was like the sun, and his feet like pillars of fire.” The angel’s face is understood to be those in whom the image and likeness of God shines forth, as in contemplatives. They are like the sun, because their meditation is in heaven; they shine amid this crooked and perverse generation like fixed lights in the firmament of heaven. Pouring themselves out over their own souls, they pass through the place of the wonderful tabernacle unto the house of God, with the sound of exultation and confession, the cry of one feasting.

But his feet are said to be those firm in faith, ministering to the needs of others and providing the hay of their pleasantness and kindness; those who, with Martha, are anxious about ministry [Col. 0397D] and troubled about many things, wishing for what they cannot accomplish, and therefore their will, though ability is lacking, is reckoned to them as a deed. These are like pillars of fire because, kindled by the Holy Spirit, they relieve others’ need and by their example kindle others to the same end.

The angel also had an open book in his hand, because by his deeds he fulfilled Holy Scripture: partly by preaching, partly by accomplishing what had been said concerning himself, and finally by opening its meaning. He is the almighty Word of the Father who, while all things held their midmost silence and night had reached the middle of its course, came from the royal thrones.

There are three silences. The first was [Col. 0398A] before the Law; the second under the Law; the third will be in glory. The first was ignorance of sickness; the second, despair of reason; the third, the attainment of health. Before the Law, humankind did not recognize its disease and therefore was silent, not seeking a remedy. But when the Law entered, through which comes knowledge of sin, and showed the sick their wounds, silence was immediately broken, because the sick began to seek a remedy for health; but they sought it through the works of the Law, where there is no salvation. Wishing to be healed, they could not find what they sought.

At last, therefore, when a human being considered that no one could be justified through the Law, as though exhausted by daily cries, he again ceased to speak, despairing of salvation; and the second silence followed. Then the almighty Word of the Father, coming in the flesh, [Col. 0398B] broke the silence: he spoke peace, gave grace, set forth mercy, promised pardon, and the sick began to hasten to the physician and, with purity of faith and confession of truth, to demand the remedy as though with mighty cries. Thus, invited by this presence [variant: “Thus, having been invited by this presence”], a human being acts so as to receive health through God’s grace. But when full health comes and the blessedness of coming immortality is given, there will be nothing further to request, according to the saying: “On that day you will ask the Father nothing” (John 16:23). Then there will be the third, unending silence of consummation.

Between the first and third silences sounded the many words of the Law given through Moses, in which, as the Apostle says, there was a night of words. Between the middle and the last [Col. 0398C] there sounds one word, one grace: namely, the kindness and humanity of the Savior. Moses, servant of God, uttered many words and many sayings. God the Father sent one Word, one utterance. Moses’ many sayings were powerless, because they could not bring about what they said. But the Father’s one Word was almighty: he not only spoke, but did whatever he willed. Of him the Father says through Isaiah: “My word which goes forth from my mouth shall not return to me empty, but shall accomplish whatever I have willed and shall prosper in the things for which I sent it” (Isa. 55:11). This Word still speaks while he gradually works his promises in his own people. But when all promises have been fulfilled in him, because nothing further will be lacking, there will be happy silence forever.

[Col. 0398D] “While, therefore, all things held their midmost silence.”  
[Note: [Col. 0397D] The Vulgate has: “While a peaceful silence encompassed all things, and night in its course had reached the middle of its way.” [Col. 0398D] (Wis. 9:14).]

He rightly says “all things,” because not only those under the Law despaired, but the things that had been promised were failing. “And while night in its course held the middle of its way, it came from the royal thrones.”  
[Note: [Col. 0398D] Ibid.]

A threefold night is understood: the devil, the present life, and sin. Night, then—that is, the devil—had reached the middle of its course, its way, because he was drawing almost the entire human race after him like a flock into the abyss of destruction. The present life is night; the future life, day. This night has evening; that day has dawn. The evening of this day began when Adam sinned. The dawn [Col. 0399A] of that day began when Christ rose, according to the saying: “Weeping will lodge at evening, and joy in the morning” (Ps. 19:6).

This life, then, is night; but what is the course of this night? Mortal life runs downward, just as immortal life runs upward. The latter’s way is upward in heaven; the former’s way is downward in hell. The middle way is the course of the present life, which we enter by being born, run through by living, and leave by dying. Thus this night has the middle of its course when death has dragged into hell all whom it found on the course of the present life. For no mortal person could yet ascend to immortal life.

The third night is that of sin, which, beginning from original sin, ran on through actual sins. Therefore, when, after the original [Col. 0399B] guilt, there had followed the threatened prohibition and the transgression of natural and written law, sin had come to its highest growth; then night had, as it were, reached the middle of its course. Hence the Apostle says: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Rom. 5:14). But this night was manifold. When the light appeared, it immediately began to slope toward its setting and diminish.

See, therefore, the most orderly plan of divine dispensation. When every hope of recovered salvation had perished and night was carrying everything away with itself, then the almighty Word was sent to deliver humankind, so that the gift of divine grace might be commended all the more. He came, he says—but from where, and to where? [Col. 0399C] The Word of the Most High, the only Son of the Father and King, came from the royal thrones: that is, from the Father’s council, from equality of majesty, from the royal seat to flesh, to the cross, to death; from heaven’s light even to hell’s darkness. At this heaven is astonished, earth marvels, humanity trembles, and the angelic height reveres. For this is a work without precedent, humility without measure, grace without merit, gift without price. He whose greatness has no end deigned to humble himself so greatly for us that he not only was made of a woman for us, but was also made under the Law, receiving the mark of circumcision, so that he might accomplish spiritual circumcision in us and free us from the burden of the Law as from other punishments.

[Col. 0399D] Hence the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the Law, that he might redeem those who were under the Law and that we might receive adoption as sons” (Gal. 4:5).

On the eighth day from birth every Hebrew infant was circumcised according to the Law; and the child Jesus, who came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, received from his parents according to the flesh the carnal sacrament of circumcision on the eighth day of his Nativity, which we celebrate today. Thus he who was circumcised on the eighth day was made under the Law, and on the fortieth day the legal offering was made for him. He received those legal rites not in order to be expiated by them, but in order to free us from them, who were held in servitude by them—just as he endured death in order to free us from it, according to the saying: “I will be your death, [Col. 0400A] O death; I will be your sting, O hell!” (Hos. 13:14).

He therefore received the sacrament of circumcision in order to bring carnal circumcision to an end and bring spiritual circumcision to perfection for us [variant: “commend it to us”], and in order to appear as the son of Abraham, who first received the command of circumcision. Circumcision was performed on the eighth day after birth and with a stone knife, signifying Christ the rock, of whom it is said: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4), who rose on the third day. In the present time we are circumcised from vices; and in the eighth age, which will belong to those perfectly raised, we shall be circumcised from every corruption of punishment and guilt, when our youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s.

That general circumcision of the future age is prefigured by spiritual and inward circumcision, which must be kept not only in the outward but also in the inward [Col. 0400B] person, and must be offered not only in one part of the body, as was carnal circumcision, but in every member, so that we may present our members not as instruments of iniquity to sin but as instruments of righteousness to God. Let us therefore circumcise our hearts, lest we think harmful and malicious things; our eyes, lest we behold vanity; our ears, lest we hear voices of blood; our nostrils, lest we delight in the filth of impurity; our tongue and lips, lest we burst forth in words of malice or set mouth and tongue against the earth. Let us also circumcise our feet, lest they be swift to shed blood, and our hands, lest they be stretched out to touch forbidden things.

This is the true and saving circumcision by which the inward person is made alive: by it we do not cut off the skin of the flesh with stone knives, but put off the old [Col. 0400C] person with his deeds and put on the new, who has been created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth. The Apostle commends it, saying: “For it is not circumcision which is outward, in the flesh; but the one who is a Jew inwardly, and circumcision of the heart in spirit, not in letter” (Rom. 2:28–29). The figure therefore ceases, fulfilled in truth through Christ, who was made under the Law in order to redeem those pressed down and liable under the Law. From what? From the devil, from sins, from destruction, from the unbearable Law. Hence Peter says: “This is a burden which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear” (Acts 15:10).

He was also made of a woman in order that we might receive adoption as sons: that is, the goods of grace, through which people become children of God. For we receive adoption because the only Son of God did not disdain participation in our nature: made of a woman, so that he might not only be the only-begotten and have brothers, but might also become the firstborn among many brothers. God has one only Son, whom he begot from his own substance; but he did not beget us from his own substance. For we are a creature, which he did not beget but made; and therefore, in order to make us Christ’s brothers according to our own mode, he adopted us. He is Son by nature, whom the Father begot. But we are children of God by favor and condescension.

This, therefore, is the manner in which God—when we were not born from him but had already been created and established by his word, and when he made us his children—adopts us. Hence, “He gave them power to become children of God, [Col. 0401A] to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12). Therefore he who is uncreated according to divinity “was made of a woman according to the flesh, in order that through him we might receive adoption as sons” (Gal. 4:5). He does not say “that we might receive,” but “that we might receive again,” in order to signify that we sinned in Adam, from whom we are mortal.

This is therefore the one who was made, through whom salvation was to come on Mount Zion: that is, in those established in the eminence of virtues, who, with unveiled face, behold the glory of the Lord. For Zion is interpreted “contemplation” or “watchtower.” And through this the house of Jacob shall possess those who possessed it. For just as in the days of Joshua the children of Israel entered the land of promise and cast seven peoples from the holy land, so, when the Word of God came and provided them guidance, the house of Jacob—that is, faithful overthrowers of vices—possessed [Col. 0401B] those who had possessed them, after they had become Christians. Following the sign of the heavenly King, receiving and bearing in their hands the sword of the Spirit, they conquered the world, according to the saying: “This is the victory that conquers the world: our faith” (1 John 3:4). For as miracles multiplied, they rescued [variant: “terrified”] those sitting in darkness, and summoned them from darkness to light, from the coldness of vices to the warmth of faith and the fire of charity, which the Lord came to cast upon the earth.

Hence it follows: “And the house of Jacob shall be fire, and the house of Joseph flame.” The house of Jacob and Joseph is one and the same: that is, the one holy Church, one part of which fights on earth and the other [part] triumphs in heaven. But it is called the house of Jacob according to the part that fights and overthrows vices; [Col. 0401C] the house of Joseph according to the part that triumphs and rests in blessedness. For Jacob means “supplanter,” Joseph “increase.” Therefore here it will be fire, there flame: here charity burns fervently, but there it will blaze, where God shall be loved with the whole heart and the whole mind, according to Isaiah’s saying: “The Lord lives, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31:9). For in Zion—that is, in the contemplation of the present Church—charity is like fire. But in the eternal [variant: “fraternal”] Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of peace—it will be like a furnace and flame.

“For now we know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect comes, that which is in part will be done away. Now we see through a mirror [Col. 0401D] and in an enigma; but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:10), when, raised to the royal thrones and the heavenly court through the Angel of Great Counsel, we shall perfectly cleave to the peace of God, which surpasses every understanding, adorned with glory and honor together with King Solomon. May he who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## XIII. FIRST SERMON FOR THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

[Note: [Col. 0401D] From Saint-Germain, no. 381.]

“Then the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and shall appoint for themselves one head, and shall ascend from the earth, because great is the day of Jezreel” (Hos. 1:11).

The solemnity of this day, foreseen by the prophets in the Spirit and distinguished by prophetic attention, brings a special increase of exultation and faith to the hearts of believers. For on this day the wall of the Gentiles ran to meet the wall of the Jews. Sheep from another fold came together to the Shepherd, so that the stone rejected might become the head of the corner, joining in himself the two walls of Jews and Gentiles; and, as sheep from opposite sides came to the sheep, there might be one fold and one Shepherd. Therefore the solitude of the Gentiles exults and rejoices, which today has become like a lily among thorns and a beloved among daughters.

For today the Church of the Gentiles, once barren, began to bear many children, when it sent its firstfruits in the three Magi to adore the King of kings; and she who had more children—the Synagogue—began to grow weak. Though taught by the prophetic utterance [Col. 0402B] of Law and prophets that he whom the Magi adore, born in Bethlehem, is the Christ, it planned, for its part, not to render him royal honor but to exercise hostile cruelty against him. “For when Herod” the king “heard” that a new king had been born, “he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him” (Matt. 2:3). Nevertheless, from that people too the Lord, measuring out the valley of the tabernacles, saved a remnant, according to the saying: “A remnant shall be saved” (Rom. 9:27).

Today, therefore, the Son of Man was glorified and manifested. Hence this day is called Epiphany, that is, manifestation or appearance, because the Son of God was manifested and revealed to the Gentiles in the star; in the waters of baptism he was declared by the Father’s voice and the opening of heaven; and at the wedding, by the changing of water into wine. The holy Fathers decreed that this day should be solemnly observed because it shines with these proclamations of powers. Yet the first cause of its celebration and veneration was that, as a new star announced the rising of the true light, three Magi came by one journey, guided by that same star, to adore Christ and offer mystical gifts—gold, incense, and myrrh—so that Isaiah’s saying might be fulfilled: “All shall come from Sheba, bringing gold and incense and announcing praise to the Lord” (Isa. 60:6). And the prophet David says: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of the Arabs and Sheba shall bring presents” (Ps. 71:10). Each of these words breathes heavenly mysteries.

Attend carefully, therefore, brothers, and bring together the words of the prophetic and evangelical oracle. Attend carefully to who came, how many, under what guide, from where and to where they came, and what they offered. Kings came, Magi came, and three came, though they had many in their company. The Magi were certainly not necromancers or sorcerers, as some say, but Chaldean philosophers, who philosophized about individual things and had learned to discern the things signified from them and to recognize future events from the circumstances of things. They are said to have been of Balaam’s lineage and successors of his teaching, he who had foretold: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a rod shall rise from Israel, and it shall strike [the] leaders of Moab” (Num. 24:17). They came from the land of the Persians, where the river Saba is, from which the region [Col. 0403A] takes its name. All these things serve allegorical signification and demand a spiritual meaning.

Thus in them are signified spiritual kings, such as they themselves were: those who govern themselves and others in virtues; who guard their heart with every vigilance; who dispose their hearts in virtue—that is, in charity—so that they may have not merely the appearance of virtue but virtue itself. Of such Scripture says: “The heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord, and wherever he wills he will turn it” (Prov. 21:1). For, as Jeremiah says: “A person’s way is not his own, nor does it belong to a man as he walks to direct his own steps” (Jer. 10:23). Those are rightly called heavenly and spiritual kings who cleave to the King of kings whom the star reveals. To them the Prophet says: “And now, kings, understand; be instructed, you who [Col. 0403B] judge the earth” (Ps. 2:10). As if to say: Heavenly people, who already reign in hope and will reign in the future reality, when you shine like the sun in the kingdom of the Father—you who judge the earth, that is, accuse and condemn earthly things in yourselves—understand him whom the star declares, you who are Magi and philosophers: not, certainly, according to the earthly philosophy that deceives, of which the Apostle says, “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit” (Col. 2:8), but according to the heavenly theology by which you know the mystery of the kingdom of God.

Therefore let those who are kings govern well and judge rightly; and let those who are Magi—that is, theologians—understand how they come, from where they come to the new King, and how many come. For, as has been said, kings and Magi come, and three come, because in [Col. 0403C] Christ they were to adore that supreme Trinity, and because in them the Gentiles dispersed from Noah’s three sons were foreshadowed as coming to Christ. But how do they come? With the star as guide. This star is the illumination of faith, which is the substance of things hoped for [Note: [Col. 0403D] “The substance of things hoped for” (Heb. 11:1).], “and the proof of things not seen,” as the Apostle says; it is the beginning of good things, through which God exists in us, through which we are made divine by participation in the divine substance [variant: “unto participation in the divine substance”]. This is the foundation laid in the hearts of believers, which no one can alter: faith working through love, laid in the foundation, which permits no one to perish. The star does not shine or lead unless faith works through love. “For faith without works is dead” [Col. 0403D] (Jas. 2:26). Therefore a star without light is faith without activity.

But the new star, herald of the new birth, shone among the others with marvelous brilliance, because faith which does good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith, drives away the darkness of vices and illuminates the minds of believers with wondrous brightness, showing them both the way by which and the homeland to which they go: Christ, who is the way by which one goes, and the truth and life to which one goes. This is the royal way concerning which the children of Israel were commanded to walk by the king’s highway, turning neither to the right nor to the left. For those to whom it has been given to know God must follow Christ, so that neither the right hand of prosperity nor the left [Col. 0404A] hand of adversity may move them from the path of righteousness, but that they may pass through the fire of burning tribulation and through the water of dissolving love into refreshment.

This way which the star indicates is most excellent. It is the way of which Jeremiah says: “Stand in the ways, ask for the eternal ways of the Lord, and seek which is the good way” (Jer. 6:1). There are many ways through which the good way is sought and found. There are many pearls by which one comes to the one precious pearl. The eternal ways, therefore, are the apostles and prophets, in whose pattern and teaching the good way and the precious pearl are found: namely, Christ, who is way in example, truth in promise, and life in reward; way according to the humility of his humanity, truth and life according to the height of his divinity.

That star revealed these mysteries to the Magi; illuminated by it, they understood where they were going [Col. 0404B] and to what end. Hence Isaiah, speaking to the spiritual Jerusalem, says: “The nations shall walk in your light, and kings in the brightness of your rising” (Isa. 60:3). Behold the star that went before the kings; behold the lamp which did not come to be put under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, to shine for all who are in the house: namely faith, in whose light the nations walk toward Christ, possessing the two feet of charity and keeping the teaching of the two Testaments, between which truth is known, according to the saying: “In the midst of two living creatures you shall be known.” Faith produces these feet among the nations, makes them advance by the double foot of love, and brings forth understanding of the two Testaments. For through faith knowledge of the commandments is acquired. Hence Isaiah says: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand.” Through faith, moreover, hearts are purified and inner eyes preserved.

This is the lamp which shines as light in the earthen vessel of the human mind. It must not be placed beneath the bushel of human fear, but upon the lampstand of holy confession, because, just as one believes with the heart unto righteousness, so confession is made with the mouth unto salvation. This is the brightness of the rising in which the kings walked, because it declared to them the ineffable birth of the new King; it showed them both generations of the Word, of which Isaiah says: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). This is the brightness of which the Prophet says: “May the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us” (Ps. 89:17), and elsewhere: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us” (Ps. 4:7). For it declares the face—that is, the appearance—[Col. 0404D] of him whose rising it reveals, because, just as his face is invisible, so his birth is ineffable.

In this light, therefore, in this brightness, the kings of Tarshish and the islands—that is, the Churches of the Gentiles, situated upon the sea of this world and battered by waves of tribulation but not broken—walk toward Christ. Coming from Sheba, they bring gold, incense, and myrrh to God and the Son of God. Sheba is interpreted “captivity” or “way of life.” Thus by Sheba is understood spiritual captivity, because the world was held captive under the devil, and the old way of vain living in which the prodigal son, in the region of dissimilarity, squandered [Col. 0405A] his substance by living luxuriously. Wishing to be filled with the leavings of the swine, he attached himself to one of the citizens of that land—that is, to the devil—and fed swine, because he delighted in unclean and filthy deeds.

But when the morning star shone, recalling the Father of spirits whom he had left, he began to depart from Sheba—that is, from the misery of devilish captivity and vain conduct—and hasten to the Father whom he had left, that is, to Christ (Luke 15:15 ff.). This prodigal son is the Church of the Gentiles, daughter of the highest King. Forgetting her former disgrace, she migrated from Babylon of confusions to Jerusalem—that is, to the vision of peace—to which the Prophet says: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people, and the King will desire your beauty [Col. 0405B] and your loveliness” (Ps. 44:11). Likewise Isaiah: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, because your light has come and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you” (Isa. 60:1).

As if to say: O Church, you who fell among the Jews, arise among the Gentiles; you who fell through denial and vices, arise through confession and virtues; you who fell through unbelief, arise through faith. You, therefore, who are silent, who sleep, arise and keep watch, and thus be enlightened, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead”—that is, from sins—“and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14). For he is the light which enlightens every person coming into this world. “Arise, therefore, and be enlightened, because your light has come”: that is, the Son of God has appeared in this world; “and the glory of the Lord has risen [Col. 0405C] upon you” (Isa. 60:1): that is, the heralding star of the glorious King and sign of faith. As it shines, the kings of Tarshish—that is, explorers [variant: “imitators”] of true joy—rise from Sheba with holy Jerusalem; coming with gifts to adore the Lord, king of heaven, they offer mystical gifts by which they profess their faith: gold, incense, and myrrh. By their mystical offering, these signify that the one to whom they are offered is king, God, and mortal.

For in gold, which is customarily given to kings as tribute, the royal power of the newborn child is signified. In incense, which is burned in sacrifice to God, his divine essence is shown. In myrrh, with which the bodies of the dead are embalmed, his mortal nature is signified. These gifts are fitting to the mystery. For by these three are indicated royal power, divine majesty, and human mortality, which the Catholic mother Church believes and proclaims to have existed in Christ’s person. She honors and adores him, now reigning in heaven, not with mystical or figurative gifts, nor with empty presents offered, but with gold, incense, and myrrh brought forth from the storehouse of our heart.

For we offer gold to God when we shine with the light of wisdom and, when driven by tribulations, do not fail through patience. Just as gold excels among metals, so wisdom excels among gifts. Gold, too, is drawn out by the striking of the hammer; thus the faithful soul is advanced to [Col. 0406A] better things by patience in tribulation. Tribulation is the striking; progress is the drawing out. Hence the Apostle says: “Tribulation works patience; patience, testing; testing, hope; and hope does not put to shame, because the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts” (Rom. 5:3).

We also offer incense to Christ when, burning with love for him, we strive to please him through the practice of devout and sincere prayer. Of this it is said: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. 140:2). But we bring myrrh forth from the secret place of the heart when, through love of Christ, mortifying our body from vices and desires, we sternly restrain the wantonness of the flesh. This is the myrrh of which the bride says in the Song of Songs: “My fingers distilled first myrrh” [Col. 0406B] (Song 5:13). First myrrh is indeed the chastisement of the flesh for heavenly glory.

There is also a myrrh that is neither first nor true: mortification of the flesh for empty glory. For the person who afflicts the flesh while hunting temporal praise carries the cross under compulsion. Driven by the desire for empty glory, he is forced to bear the cross, retaining the appearance of myrrh but not its power. Therefore he will be numbered among the foolish virgins, and his lamps will be extinguished because he lacks oil—that is, the Spirit. He indeed has his loins girded, but does not bear burning lamps in his hands; and therefore he will be cast into the outer darkness.

Let us therefore offer first myrrh with the Apostle, who says: “I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be found reprobate” (1 Cor. 9:27). [Col. 0406C] Let us also offer the incense of holy prayer and gold—once the treasuries of our hearts, of wisdom and confession, have been opened. For these gifts, stored in the treasure-house of the mind, are brought forth when one believes with the heart unto righteousness and confession is made with the mouth unto salvation.

279. Let us therefore come with these gifts: with the myrrh of mortifying vices, the incense of prayer, the gold of heavenly contemplation, and faith’s guiding star; and, with the kings of Arabia and Saba, let us worship the Savior in Bethlehem of Judah. Behold: they come to Bethlehem and find the newborn King. It was anciently called Ephratha. Ephratha means “mirror”; Bethlehem is interpreted “house of bread.” Rightly is it the house of bread, in which the heavenly bread, the bread of angels, deigned to be born—the bread that refreshes the angelic powers; he who was not merely born of [Col. 0406D] David in Bethlehem, since “his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity.” For he went forth from the Father who is without beginning, yet not in an initial manner, but indeed eternally, because a, p, e, u, and u, e, a, d, etc. [Note: [Col. 0405] So in the manuscript. Perhaps *i* should have been written instead of *a*, and thus explained: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.”]

Bethlehem therefore is not least, although, when compared with the cities of Judah, where there are many thousands of people, it may seem a small village; for the prerogative of the Lord’s birth surpasses all. He who rightly bears the type of the Church, in which truth is found if it is worthily sought, exalted this mirror of the Lord’s glory with marvelous proclamation. Rightly, therefore, Christ chose to be born in that place which bears the type of the whole Church and, by its name, indicates Christ as the food of life for all the faithful. [Col. 0407A] For it is itself the city of the Lord of hosts, in which, as we have heard the truth, so we see it—a truth which outside her no one sees or hears, no one truly believes or praises. For there is no place of true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church, nor is praise beautiful in the mouth of a sinner; indeed, as Solomon says, “A gold ring in her nostrils: a beautiful but foolish woman” (Prov. X, 22).

Therefore, that praise may be pleasing and comely, let us ascend with the Magi from Saba to Bethlehem, bearing gifts and thus worthily proclaiming the Lord’s praise. For whoever offers the Lord these mystical gifts is already able to offer the sacrifice of praise, of which the Lord says through the Prophet: “The sacrifice of praise shall honor me” (Ps. XLIX, 15). [Col. 0407B] There is the way by which one who ascends merits to see the salvation of God. Therefore the holy Magi, bringing gifts and proclaiming praise to the Lord, deserved to find him, so that the saying of Hosea, set forth above, might be fulfilled: “The children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, etc.” (Hos. I, 11).

By the children of Judah the Jews are signified; by the children of Israel, the Gentiles: together, because they have one Lord, one faith, one baptism. They have been made one body because the Spirit whom they received was one; they have been made one body because of the fellowship effected by the Spirit—namely, with the Father and the Son—which, although the Trinity effects it, is understood to belong to the Holy Spirit. For he is the Spirit of the adoption of sons. He is the love and bond of Father and Son. To him, therefore, belongs the fellowship [Col. 0407C] by which the children of Judah and the children of Israel are gathered together, that the one body of the only-begotten Son of God may come to be.

For just as the one human body consists of many members, and one soul animates all the members, making the eye see, the ear hear, and so with the rest, so the Holy Spirit contains and gives life to the members of Christ’s body, which is the Church. And just as a severed member of the human body retains the form by which it is recognized, but does not thereby follow life, since the Spirit does not aid apart from unity, so whoever is divided from the unity of the aforesaid peace retains the sacrament as it were a form, but does not live by the Spirit apart from unity. In vain, therefore, does one glory outwardly in the form unless the Spirit gives life inwardly, [Col. 0407D] the Spirit who is poured out in hearts. He is the anointing by which brothers truly dwell as one; without this anointing they do not wish to be one, and, though not in body, nevertheless in mind they are one. And [f. “But others”] are like a yoked but restless beast, which does not draw but carries. Of them it is said in the book of Jesus son of Sirach: “The heart of a fool is a cart-wheel; it carries hay and continually murmurs” (Ecclus. XXXIII, 5). Such persons are not gathered in the name of Jesus, but those are who have an anointing from the Spirit. Of them Truth says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII, 20).

Great is what is granted them when the Most High dwells in their midst, [Col. 0408A] because they are gathered in his name. Nor ought we merely to gather in his name, but also to walk in it, according to Amos: “Will two walk together unless they have agreed?” (Amos III, 3). Yet they will not agree except in the name of him through whom the Spirit of peace is given; without that Spirit there is not a joining, but a tearing apart of hearts.

Thus in his name we are gathered together at the beginning, and we walk together by making progress, until we arrive at mutual embrace. In this way the children of Judah and the children of Israel are gathered: not merely in body, but in faith and mind. Hence the Lord says through Micah: “Gathering, I will gather you wholly, O Jacob; I will bring together the remnant of Israel; I will place him together like a flock in a fold, like sheep in the midst of pens” (Mic. II, 12). He does not simply say, “I will gather,” but, “Gathering, I will gather,” so that the doubling of the expression may show the joining of heart and deed. But by what they are joined is declared when he adds: “And they shall appoint for themselves one head.” That is, all shall appoint Christ as their head. Hence the Lord says through Ezekiel: “And one prince in their midst.” [Note: [Col. 0407D] The Vulgate has: “But the prince in the midst,” not “one prince.”] “My servant David,” that is, Christ according to the flesh, born of David. For he, as the Apostle says, is “the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, holding the primacy in all things,” namely, of “the body,” which is “the Church” (Col. I, 18).

He is head of the Church in both respects, because the Church is united to him as a body to its head by grace and by nature. Since, therefore, he stands in relation to the Church as head to body, he provides for the Church [Col. 0408C] and governs it; and in him are all the Church’s spiritual senses, just as all the bodily senses are in the head. For just as the soul animates and vivifies our entire body, while in the head it perceives with all its senses—and therefore all things are subject to the head for action, whereas the head is set above to deliberate, because it in some manner performs the role of that part of the soul which deliberates for the body, and in it every sense appears—so Christ the man is head of the entire people of the saints as though of one body. The wisdom of God enlightens them all down to the last righteous person, and this wisdom was more fully in Christ.

Other human beings are wise in one way; Christ the man is wise in another. For he does not merely possess the benefit of that Wisdom by which all human beings are made wise, [Col. 0408D] but himself bears its very character, full of truth and grace. Therefore he is the head of all who receive from his fullness.

Accordingly, the children of Judah and the children of Israel, appointing this one head for themselves, shall ascend from the earth—that is, from earthly and carnal desires—ordering ascents in their hearts, namely the steps of the virtues, by which they ascend in progress from virtue to virtue until they see the God of gods in Zion. And all these things occurred through Jezreel, whose day is great. “Great,” he says, “is the day of Jezreel,” that is, of the seed of God; for Jezreel is interpreted “seed of God.” This is the Son of God, *homoousios* (“of one substance”) with the Father, [Col. 0409A] who eternally went forth from the Father and, by assuming flesh, became the seed of Abraham, in whom all nations shall be blessed, and whose expectation he was. Therefore his day is rightly called great: not only that day on which he deigned to be born of the Virgin, but also that on which, led by a star, he willed to reveal himself to the Gentiles on the thirteenth day after his birth.

Great, therefore, is this day of Jezreel, on which the Gentiles came to worship the Lord. This day, thus marked by so many mysteries, is therefore to be celebrated with the highest devotion. For, as we have said, it was sanctified by a threefold prerogative of mighty acts. Thus on the thirteenth day after his birth he became known to the Magi through the star; thus also, in the thirtieth year of his age, to fulfill all righteousness, he deigned to be baptized by John in the Jordan; and on the same day, when the year had come round, invited to the wedding [Col. 0409B] at which the steward of the feast was present, he changed water into wine. Mystically, he thereby signified the wedding of bridegroom and bride, and, in changing water into wine, indicated the transformation of legal observance into the spiritual understanding of the Gospel.

For he came to John’s baptism, not as one needing his sins cleansed, but imparting regenerating power to the waters; not as a servant needing purification, although the Lord did not disdain to be baptized by a servant. The Master received baptism from the disciple, a baptism through which there was no remission of sins, but by which people were accustomed and prepared for Christ’s baptism. There the heavens were opened above him, and the Father’s voice thundered: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. III, 17; XVII, 5). There [Col. 0409C] the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove, because to those baptized in the Spirit the gate of heaven is opened. There the mystery of the Trinity was indicated: the Father in the voice, the Son in the man, the Spirit in the dove. For whoever pursues by worthy works the faith in the Trinity which he professes in baptism shall deserve in the future to contemplate that same Trinity face to face. May the Lord bring us to that vision—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## XIV. SECOND SERMON FOR THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

[Note: [Col. 0409D] From an Angers manuscript.]

“Thou who sittest upon the cherubim, appear before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh” [Vulgate: “make manifest”] (Ps. LXXIX, 2).

[Col. 0409D]

The prophets had often written to us promises concerning the Savior’s coming, as though with the pen of a swiftly writing scribe, as if saying: “Wait; wait again.” Many heralds had come, but each was rich only in promises. One indeed said: “Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let thy heart be strengthened, and endure the Lord” (Ps. XXVI, 14). Another said thus: “If he delays, wait for him, for he will surely come” (Hab. II, 3). Both had departed with one purpose from God’s secret chamber, yet had brought back nothing from it except a promise.

Even our Harpist, [Col. 0410A] as though already wearied by waiting, by a certain indirect reproach attributed fault to God, saying: “But thou hast rejected and despised; thou hast delayed thy Christ” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 39). Isaiah, a man of noble and urbane eloquence, said, as though indignantly: “Would that thou wouldst rend the heavens and come down” (Isa. LXIV, 1). David had already passed from longing to command, saying: “Bow thy heavens and descend” (Ps. CXLIII, 5). In this manner that whole assembly of prophets, as though wearied by too long a waiting, varied their utterances: now longing, now commanding, now complaining, now indignant. At last the Expected One came and closed the prophets’ mouths. The promise was given, and silence was imposed upon those who had promised.

Let the lawgiver, then, be silent, [Col. 0410B] because he is more impeded of tongue before God. Let Isaiah be silent, because he confesses that he has unclean lips. Let Jeremiah be silent, because he is a child and does not know how to speak. Let Ezekiel be silent, because he eats defiled bread. Let Daniel be silent, because after the vision he was grievously weakened. Let Hosea be silent, because he took a harlot as wife. Let Amos be silent, because he is not a prophet but a shepherd who plucks sycamore figs. Let the voice of the Church burst forth and say: The humanity and the divinity of our Savior have appeared; for he came not only with wine and oil, but also with purple and sackcloth. Christ, both God and man, at one time did certain things in which he appeared true man; at another, certain things in which he appeared true God—because, like an actor playing a part, he successively transformed himself into diverse forms. Of this play Wisdom says: “I delighted day by day, playing before him in the world’s circle” (Prov. VIII, 30). For on the day of his birth, God appeared as man.

Therefore let the Church say: Lord Jesus, at thy Nativity thou wast found in the appearance of a man, made a little lower than the angels. But today thou who sittest upon the cherubim, Lord of angels and men, appear before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. As if she said: Lord Jesus, we have already seen thee laid in a manger, wrapped in swaddling clothes, crying among animals. Mary saw thee, Joseph saw thee, the shepherds saw thee; and now it is the thirteenth day since these things happened. Therefore appear today according to thy sitting also upon the cherubim. And so it came to pass.

[Col. 0410D] Therefore he appeared as God in three ways, though not in the same form except through the cycle of time. On the thirteenth day after his birth he appeared to the kings of the Gentiles, the star standing over the place where the child was. For they too, by offering incense to the Lord, confessed him to be God by their gift. In his thirtieth year, on the same day, he appeared to John the Baptist and to the crowds gathered around him, by the Father’s testimony. In the following year, on the same day, he appeared as God before his mother, his disciples, and the wedding guests through the changing of water into wine.

These three manifestations are indicated by the following three names: Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. But if they are spoken in reverse order, they will follow the order of the narrative. Let us therefore say: “Appear before Manasseh, Benjamin, and Ephraim.” Manasseh means “forgetfulness”; these are the Gentiles, who forgot the one God. Concerning them, as those who forgot, it is said: “All the families of the Gentiles [Vulgate: all the ends of the earth] shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. XXI, 28). And elsewhere: “Understand, you who forget God” (Ps. XLIX, 22). He appeared before them through the star.

Benjamin is “son of the right hand.” He was first called Benoni [f. Benjamin], 284 that is, “son of sorrow,” because his mother died in the travail of his birth. This is John the Baptist, son of the Synagogue or of the Law, which died when he had recently been born, because “the Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke XVI, 16). But his father called him Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand,” namely of divine power. For his birth from aged and barren parents was not the work of human power, but the divine power appeared before him in baptism. Ephraim means “fruitfulness.” These are the disciples, to whom he himself said: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV, 16). He appeared before them at the banquet.

These words may also fittingly be applied to the triumphant Church, that is, the spirits of the blessed, who cry beneath the throne of God: Lord Jesus Christ, thou who art just and wast unjustly judged before an unjust judge; who, as a sheep before its shearer, didst not open thy mouth; who wast seen as lowly and without beauty, like a leprous man—now at last manifest thyself [f. “manifest thyself,” as another reading has it] before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh; and so he will come. For God will come manifestly and will not be silent (Ps. XLIX, 3), powerful [Col. 0411C] like one roused from wine (Ps. LXXVII, 65), like a judge without mercy.

Certainly, at the judgment there will be three orders of human beings: those to be judged, those judging, and those already judged. The intermediate sort will be judged; their fruits, that is, their works, will be examined, while the angels say, “Behold the man, and his works with him.” These are signified by Ephraim, because they will be judged by their fruits. Those who have left all things and followed David [f. Christ] will judge; to them it was said: “You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” [Matt. XIX, 18]. These are understood through Benjamin, because the right hand—that is, the power of judging—has been granted them. The unbelievers have already been judged, and their judgment is now known to the Church. Since they are, as it were, manifest enemies, sentence is not now [f. “now”] pronounced upon them. These are understood through Manasseh, to whom God has been given over to forgetfulness, as one dead to their heart.

Therefore the souls of the blessed, desiring the day of the Lord in order that they may receive double recompense, say: Lord, manifest thyself [f. “manifest thyself,” or “make manifest”] before Ephraim, that is, those to be judged; Benjamin, that is, those judging; and Manasseh, that is, those already judged.

Nevertheless, these words may belong to the Church militant, as though she said: Lord Jesus, Word of the [Col. 0412A] Father, before the Law thou didst indeed become known in time, but to few and only slightly. “For the invisible things of God have been understood from the creation of the world through the things that have been made” (Rom. I, 20). Under the Law thou wast known beneath the veil of figures, beneath the shadow of the watery, killing letter, which became abundant in leaves but not in fruit, according to the saying: “Israel was a luxuriant vine, or one whose branches covered the cedars of God.” [Note: [Col. 0411D] The Vulgate has: “Israel was a luxuriant vine, bearing fruit equal to itself; according to the multitude of his fruit, he multiplied altars” (Hos. X, 1).] Now, however, at the fitting time, make thyself manifest before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh.

Under the Law thou wast only announced, but to us made manifest—that is, uttered forth. For the Father’s heart “uttered forth a good word” (Ps. XLIV, 1), and thus it was uttered from the Father’s heart into the Virgin’s womb, and from Mary’s womb into the bosom of the Church. It is called “uttered forth” [Col. 0412B] as made manifest because what is uttered brings its flavor with it: namely, the grace of his mercy, as something more inward and secret than other things. For the Lord’s mercies are over all his works, and the mercy-seat was set above the ark, because mercy is above lives. For the Samaritan came to the wounded man with the wine of rebuke and the oil of compassion.

Therefore thou who sittest upon the cherubim—that is, upon the fullness of knowledge—make thyself manifest to us by giving to individuals and to all alike from that fullness of knowledge; make thyself manifest to us by giving [supplied: oil] upon the beard, and from the beard down to the hem of the garment. Appear, therefore, before the tribe. These are the three men whom Ezekiel sees saved: “Noah, Daniel, and Job” (Ezek. XIV, 14). The married, that is, the active, are understood through Ephraim, [Col. 0412C] who produce fruits, that is, works of mercy; prelates through Benjamin, for it is divine, not human, power not merely to extinguish vices in oneself but to uproot them from others; contemplatives through Manasseh, who sometimes forget even themselves, that is, what their nature requires of them, because at the sound of a singing girl a flock forgets to eat.

But note that the tribe of Manasseh was divided (Josh. XIV). One part, because it abounded in cattle, chose to remain in grazing land around the Jordan. These are those who place their hope in the uncertainty of riches and, having forgotten that they are in exile, seek a permanent city as though they dwelt there. The other part quickly crossed the Jordan in order to receive the lot of sanctification under the measuring-line of allotment. [Col. 0412D] These are contemplatives who, with the Apostle, forgetting what lies behind, stretch themselves toward what lies ahead. Therefore he says: “Appear before Ephraim,” that is, the active; “and Benjamin,” that is, prelates; “and Manasseh,” that is, contemplatives.

But according to the two outward works of contemplation, there are two kinds of contemplatives. For its outward works are two; inward meditation alone is interior. The outward works are prayer and reading; and so contemplatives are cloistered persons and scholars. [Note: [Col. 0411D] Observe here that scholars are joined with cloistered persons, or monks: namely, those who, with him—who, as is fitting to believe, studied at Cluny under the discipline and instruction of Saint Hugh the Abbot—devoted themselves to sacred letters with much labor and austerity nearly approaching monastic life, though they were not monks.]

Therefore cloistered persons, who, living without private possessions—that is, without what is their own—choose the common life, should say: [Col. 0413A] “Lord, teach us to pray.” Scholars, however, living a lean life amid hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, should say: “Lord, teach us to devote ourselves to reading, because wisdom is sweet.” Yet it is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly, but in the land of the living [f. “of those who labor”]. Nor do I suppose that you have come here in order to abound in delights, overflow in pleasures, and be utterly dissolved in wantonness [f. “dissolution”]; but that, stirred up, you may apply yourselves to labor and hardship. The reward of labor in the present is illumination of the heart; in the future, the glorification of the whole human person. May the righteous Judge grant this to us when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire. Amen.

## XV. THIRD SERMON FOR THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

[Note: [Col. 0413D] From a Victorine manuscript.]

[Col. 0413B] “When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: ‘Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the East, and have come to worship him’” (Matt. II, 1–2).

When the Creator of all, dearest brothers, taking the form of a servant for servants, had come secretly into the world, he wished to make himself known to human beings by three signs. For today he was worshipped by the Magi in Bethlehem; today he was baptized by John in the Jordan; today he was glorified at the wedding by the changing of water into wine. [Note: [Col. 0413D] He had said the same thing in the first sermon on the Epiphany.] The first manifestation occurred in the first year of his birth; the second, in the thirtieth; [Col. 0413C] the third, in the year following his thirtieth. Yet by divine dispensation these three manifestations occurred on the same day in different years.

But let us now speak of the first. The Lord wished to reveal his birth to three Magi dwelling in Chaldaea by the appearance of a new star. Since they were skilled in astronomy and saw a new star appear, they understood from their art’s experience that a new king had come. But because a prophet among them, namely Balaam, had foretold many ages before: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a rod shall rise from Israel” (Num. XXIV, 17), when they beheld a marvelous star, incomparable to any other, they believed that the one of whom Balaam had foretold had been born.

Thus they came by divine inspiration to Jerusalem, the metropolis of Judaea. [Col. 0413D] They turned aside to King Herod and inquired concerning the child; and when they turned aside to him, the star disappeared from them. Herod summoned the scribes and asked where the Messiah promised in the Law was to be born. They said, “In Bethlehem.” Since Herod was a foreigner and held the kingdom of the Jews unjustly, to the injury of the Romans, he considered how he might kill the child, fearing that he would lose the kingdom. He therefore did not dare to go with the Magi to seek the child, lest the parents conceal the child when they heard of his coming. He accordingly ordered the Magi to search carefully for the child and report back to him, saying that he wished to worship him.

The Magi departed; seeing the star again, [Col. 0414A] they rejoiced, and with it as their guide they came to Bethlehem. The star was not fixed in heaven but hung in the air, and clearly showed the house in which the child was. In the Persian manner they offered gifts, though gifts fitting to the mystery: gold, incense, and myrrh—signifying by gold a king, by incense God and priest, and by myrrh one subject to death. Behold the first manifestation.

In his thirtieth year, however, he came to John, who baptized, not for the remission of sins but for the restoration of Christ’s baptism [read: “in preparation for Christ’s baptism”]. Although water had previously washed bodies, he wished nevertheless to sanctify it so that it might have power to cleanse souls. He came free from sin and sought baptism in order to sanctify the waters and to give an example of humility to all. Once he had been baptized, [Col. 0414B] the heavens were opened, he saw the Spirit descending upon him in the form of a dove, and the Father’s voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17). Behold the second manifestation.

In the following year he was invited to a wedding. When the wine failed, he had six jars filled with water and changed it into wine; and this was the beginning of signs.

By these three signs, dearest brothers, Christ manifested himself to the world, and in all of them appeared to be God. In the first he is worshipped as God by the Magi; in the second he is declared to be the Father’s Son; in the third divine power is made evident by the first miracle. It is also called Theophany, which means “divine manifestation,” [Col. 0414C] because in all these things he appeared to be God. You have heard the truth of the history and have also learned the reason for this festival’s name. Let us further see whether some mystery lies hidden in the things mentioned above.

The star appeared, brothers, because it signified that a light had arisen for peoples in darkness. Of him it is said: “He was the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I, 9). It appeared to the Gentiles because it foretold that the Gentiles would receive the light of faith, according to the saying: “The people who walked in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. IX, 2). He wished to be born in Bethlehem because Bethlehem means “house of bread,” and there he was born. But he underwent death in Jerusalem, which was populous, because he did not seek worldly glory. Rather, as the teacher of humility, [Col. 0414D] he deigned to be born of poor parents, in a humble place and a lowly manger. When about to die, he chose a populous city, so that before the eyes of so many people gathered for the festival he might undergo death for us with greater public disgrace.

When they turned aside to Herod, they lost the star that went before them, because Herod is the devil: whoever turns aside to him, having lost the light, is blinded; but when one leaves him, one immediately receives again the true light one had lost. The house in which the child was signifies the Church. Whoever seeks Christ finds him in the Church. There they worship, believe in, and serve him. Having found Christ, we learn from the gifts what we ought to offer: [Col. 0415A] namely, myrrh, which is suitable for the dead. For dead bodies are customarily anointed with it lest worms arise there, because its bitterness kills the worms. But a person who comes to the Church must mortify the flesh with its vices and desires, lest the worms of sins arise.

Once vices have been extinguished, prayer is necessary, signified by incense, which obtains forgiveness, and of which it is said: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight” (Ps. CXL, 2). Works of charity commonly follow, signified by gold. For just as gold excels other metals, so charity surpasses all other virtues. For it is the fullness of the Law. These three, therefore, are necessary: repentance, signified by myrrh; prayer, [Col. 0415B] signified by incense; and charity, signified by gold.

In the second manifestation, moreover, the sacraments of our salvation were displayed. For he wished to show in himself what is bestowed upon those baptized. When anyone is regenerated in baptism, the whole Trinity works there. Therefore the whole Trinity was shown where Christ was baptized: the Son in Christ, the Holy Spirit in the dove, and the Father revealed himself in the voice. The Spirit appeared in a dove because the dove is the bird of simplicity [supplied: “symbol”]; through this bird he wished to signify the innocence which he grants to those regenerated. The Father’s words, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,” signify that the baptized are sons of God and that those who had previously displeased him begin to [Col. 0415C] please him. The opened heavens signify that what had formerly been shut through sin is opened for the baptized.

The wedding, however, at which he manifested himself for the third time, signifies the union of Christ and the Church. There water is changed into wine because the old Law has been transformed into the Gospel. The ancient Law is compared to water because it did not inflame those subject to it with love for God. The Gospel is wine because, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, it makes believers fervent in God’s love.

This day, dearest brothers, has been consecrated by mysteries so great and such as these. And in some manner this festival is greater than the solemnity of the Nativity. For, as Augustine says, the second birth is greater than the first. [Col. 0415D] In this second birth baptism, which is the regeneration of souls, had its beginning. In this, water [Church] was made the mother of many peoples. The first birth is carnal, but this one spiritual. Therefore, just as the soul is worthier than the flesh, so the birth of the soul is worthier than that of the flesh. In the first he entered the world; in the second he entered heaven.

How fittingly these three things came together on one day: the star leading to Christ, the sacrament of baptism, and the changing of water into wine. In this order the formation of our life appears. When a person is converted to faith, the star—that is, the light of faith—leads him to Christ; then, after being instructed in faith, he approaches the sacrament of baptism; afterward he drinks and is perfected by the cup of Gospel teaching, since, lest he fail from thirst on the way, the drink of preaching is prepared daily for the traveler.

Therefore, beloved, this solemnity, full of so many mysteries, is to be celebrated with the highest devotion, because today you rejoice in your own birth, which today took its beginning in Christ’s baptism. [Col. 0416A] Today you rejoice in the conversion of the Gentiles, whose firstfruits today came to Christ. Receive Christ at your tables, who today received the Gentiles coming to him. In the poor, Christ is received; in the poor, Christ is fed; in the poor, Christ is clothed. For he himself says: “What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me” (Matt. XXV, 40). If you receive them in this world, they will receive you in heaven. Hence the Lord says: “Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke XVI, 9).

For he was poor in the world, loves the poor, and gives his kingdom to the poor. Hence: “Blessed are the poor [in spirit], for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 3). May the Lord Jesus Christ, who for us willed to descend from heaven, grant us through growth to ascend to the heavenly court. He lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## XVI. ONE SERMON ON THE GOSPEL FOR THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY

[Note: [Col. 0415D] From a Victorine manuscript.]

“When Jesus had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. And behold, a leper came and worshipped [Col. 0416C] him, saying: ‘Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst cleanse me.’ And Jesus, stretching out his hand, touched him and said: ‘I will; be cleansed.’ And immediately his leprosy was cleansed” (Matt. VIII, 3).

When Christ wished to dwell among human beings, he both showed through miracles the power of his might and, in his deeds, instructed our faith through mysteries. The Lord preached on the mountain to a few disciples, and at that time great crowds had not yet ascended to him. Jesus came down from the mountain, and great crowds followed him. And behold, a leper came and worshipped him, saying: “Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst cleanse me.” O how great was this leper’s faith! He had heard what was said of God: “All things whatsoever he willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (Ps. CXXXIV, 6). He had heard that God, through the prophet Elisha, had cleansed Naaman, commander of Syria, from leprosy by immersing him in the Jordan (IV Kings V); and that God made all things by his will alone.

He said: “Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst cleanse me.” Thou needest not command, but only will, because power follows thy will. Therefore, if thou wilt, thou canst cleanse me. Seeing the faith of the one invoking him and the wish of the supplicant, he said: Since you ask and pray for my will, I will; I command; I lay on my hand. When he says, “I will,” he shows that he wills; when he says, “Be cleansed,” he commands. When it is read, “Stretching out his hand, he touched him,” it shows that he laid on his hand. But why did he touch the leper, although he was unclean [Col. 0417A] and could have cleansed him by his word alone?

For he wished to humble our pride. Therefore he did not shrink from touching the leper’s flesh in order to help him. Any rich or proud person who recoils from touching someone sick and horrible in the foulness of corrupting decay, who disdains even to look upon him and does not wish to approach him in compassion—this person the Lord rebukes both in word and deed. Behold, the Creator of heaven, King of angels, came down into the world in order to touch a leper, as though he said: “Behold, I came to touch in humility what seems foul to you through pride. Let not what the emperor does be contemptible to the servant.” For Solomon says: “He who despises the poor reproaches his Maker” (Prov. XIV, 31), because “he made us, and not we ourselves” (Ps. XCIX, 3).

By such a saying he rebukes us, and he will rebuke the proud [Col. 0417B] when he says: “I was sick, and you did not visit me” (Matt. XXV, 36). And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.

He also performed another miracle in the same Gospel, in which a great sign of humility appears. After the cleansing of the leper, a centurion came to him, beseeching him and saying: “Lord, my servant lies at home paralyzed.” And Jesus said: “I will come and heal him” (Matt. 8:7). And the centurion answered and said: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (ibid.). This centurion was a Gentile; he had many soldiers under his authority. He had no law commanding him to show compassion to his neighbor; yet he grieves, not for a son, not for a soldier, but for a slave. Christian rulers, if they see their slaves [Col. 0417C] become ill, despise them, think them worthless, and take no care for them. But this Gentile, taking great care for his slave, sent the elders of the Jews to the heavenly Physician, asking him to come and heal his slave. Since he was a Gentile and a foreigner, he did not dare, as Luke says, to approach him bodily; but he sent the elders of the Jews as though they were members of the household (Luke 7:3), as natives who might ask more confidently. Though he did not dare to appear in person, he nevertheless drew near in faith; and therefore it is said in this Gospel: “The centurion came to him”—if not in body, at least in faith—making his request through intermediaries.

Jesus, however, was going with them; and when he was no longer far away, the centurion sent friends to him, saying: “Do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” He had asked him to come, but [Col. 0417D] he did not say this of a bodily coming, but of the approach of compassion. He was separated from the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0417D] Rather, from the Jews.] by idolatry. He asks him to draw near, not through justice, but through mercy. The envoys, however, understood him to mean a bodily coming: “Therefore the Jews asked him to come, saying: ‘He is worthy that you should grant him this, for he loves our nation, and he himself built us a synagogue’” (Luke 7:3–5). To them the Lord said: “I will come and heal him” (ibid., 6). Thus he went with them. But when the centurion heard that he was coming, he again sent friends, saying: “Do not trouble yourself, because I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.”

[Col. 0418A]

Observe the words of this faithful Gentile. He reports three sufferings of his slave: that he lies prostrate, that he is paralyzed, and that he is grievously tormented, in order to show the anguish of his own soul and move the Lord to mercy. “My servant,” he says, “lies at home.” If someone asks, “Why did you not bring him here, as those others did who brought the paralytic on a bed?” he replies: because there is no need to bring before the sight of one who sees him whose power is everywhere present. Thus he tells him: “The servant lies at home.” As though he said: “There is no need for me to bring him before you.” Why then does the Lord say, “I will come and heal him,” when he had not requested his coming? “There was a certain royal official whose son was ill at Capernaum; he asked him to come down and heal his son” (John 4:46). To him [Col. 0418B] the Lord Jesus said: “Go; your son lives.” He wished to come to the slave of one who did not ask, and he refused to go down to the son of a king who urged him. Why, brothers? Because “with God there is no respect of persons” (Eph. 6:9).

We pray for [perhaps: care for] wealth, and run to rich persons when they are sick; but we shrink from going to the poor. Behold, the King of kings does not delay to go to a slave, and disdains to go to the son of a king. Christ was poor because he loved the poor, in order to enrich the poor with his riches. Therefore the Lord wished to go to the slave, but the centurion tells him: “I am not worthy, because I am a foreigner. I am a soldier girded with a sword, shedding blood. I am not worthy of your presence.” This is what that Gentile reveres, dearest brothers, which no Christian today reveres, although unclean. [Col. 0418C] None of us, when approaching the body of the Lord, says: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” Rather, he prepares for him a filthy lodging and receives him within it. But this man says: “I am not worthy; only speak the word, and I believe that my servant will be healed.”

Let us compare together the leper and the centurion. Let us see, since the faith of each was great, whose was greater. The leper says: “If you will, you can cleanse me.” The centurion says: “Only speak the word.” The former asks for a will; the latter, for a command. Yet he who believes that divine power is present in will alone considers the divine power more subtly. He has the greater faith who trusts not only in a command but in will alone. Nevertheless, the centurion’s faith is great and wonderful. For he says: “Therefore I believe that by your word [Col. 0418D] you can heal. For I am only a man, and you are God. I have soldiers under my authority; but you have angels, who work wonders. If, therefore, I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes—that is, if even men obey me, a man—then much more will angels and all nature obey you, God, because you can do all things.”

Christ so marveled at his faith that he said to those following him: “I have not found such faith in Israel” (Luke 7:9). For the Jewish people, although they had prophets, did not recognize him; rather, they said that he performed all miracles through Beelzebub. A lay ruler of the Israelites, asking the Lord for his daughter, did not say, “Speak the word,” but “Come quickly [Col. 0419A] before my daughter dies.” Nicodemus, a teacher of Israel, hearing of the mystery of faith, said: “How can this happen?” (John 3:3). Mary and Martha said: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died” (John 11:21), as though, being absent, he could not have saved him. Thus: “I have not found such faith in Israel.” Therefore he says: “As you have believed, let it be done to you. And the servant was healed in that hour” (Matt. 8:13).

Learn, my brothers, from these things some example for our life. Christ came down from the mountain because he came down from heaven; and after he chose to live among humankind, many crowds followed him, because they imitate his footsteps. Therefore, if anyone is leprous, let him come to meet him. Leprosy, brothers, is grave [Col. 0419B] sin, by which the soul is defiled. If, therefore, any among you is ensnared in such sins, let him run to the true physician and say: “If you will, you can cleanse me.” For it was commanded in the old Law that, if anyone were leprous, he should be expelled outside the camp and, when made well, show himself to the priest. Similarly, one guilty of grave sins ought to be outside the Church, and through the priest, restored to health, received again into the Church.

The Lord invites us to humility when he desires to visit a slave. Therefore let not the poor person be despised, because the Lord is honored in the poor. Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of iniquity, that in the future they may receive you into eternal dwellings, through the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## XVII. ONE SERMON FOR SEPTUAGESIMA

[Note: [Col. 0419D] From the Saint-Germain manuscript, II. 383.]

[Col. 0419C]

“Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all indeed run, but one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it” (1 Cor. 9:24).

Called today to the racecourse of the spiritual stadium, dearest brothers, we must thoughtfully consider how we ought to run and from what we ought to abstain. A stadium, literally speaking, is said to be a quarter of a mile; Hercules is reported first to have run it in one breath. At its end, in ancient times, a pole was set up bearing a crown woven of flowers; and for the sake of obtaining this, a fleet company of young men was accustomed to run, so that one of them, if he could run more swiftly, might be first to seize the prize—which we call a crown—and thereby receive the praise of the king and spectators, and then especially many rewards of gifts. [Col. 0419D] Many aimed at this with a common purpose, but all were surpassed by one, who, because he was swifter in running, seemed more worthy than the rest of an accumulation of goods. And as much as the victor, enriched with royal gifts, rejoiced, so much did the defeated grieve, deprived not only of gifts but dishonored by the shame of their slowness. They did indeed abstain from foods harmful to running, but not equally; for his abstinence had been greater who was swifter in the race.

Do not be surprised, brothers, that the Apostle furnished an example to be imitated for the safeguarding of souls from pagan custom, lest any of you should suppose that pagan observances are to be followed in nothing at all—those from which Christian religion, under Christ’s compulsion, has made us strangers. First, let your charity recognize that from their rite the Church has appropriated certain sacred things for herself, to be carried out not carnally but spiritually. Among these is this most useful example which today’s [supplemented: reading] has set before us. The course of the stadium, measured out for their running, signifies the limit of the present life, given to us for the race of our salvation; as the Lord says and warns: “Run, wretch, run; hasten while you have time, lest you fall into death.” For they ran to obtain a temporal and perishable prize, so as to receive earthly gifts from a mortal king. [Col. 0420B] Let us run better, to obtain a spiritual and imperishable prize, so that from the King of kings, eternal and immortal, we may receive eternal and unfailing gifts, hearing his desirable voice saying: “Come, you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. 11:18). They abstained from rich foods, so that they might be more nimble in running. Let us abstain more nobly, not so much from foods as from vices, so that we may be swift to run.

But the fact that out of a great multitude of young men one received the prize while the rest ran in vain ought, as far as we are concerned, dearest brothers, to cause great fear: namely, lest we all be surpassed by one, although we have resolved to run for the crown.
