Therefore the Apostle warns: “So run that you may obtain it.” And how shall we obtain it, if we refuse to run? And if at some time we begin to run, alas, wearied by the grossness of vices, we disgracefully fail in the race. For although the whole Church is divided into clerical and lay ranks, there is no one among them who runs for the crown of glory. Some, anxious with insatiable greed; some, polluted by unbridled pleasure; some, swollen with the pride of worldly display—not only refuse to run, but do not even know how to open their eyes to receive the crown. Hence the Psalmist: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless” (Ps. 52:4). And the Prophet: “Like people, like priest” (Isa. 14:2). For we have been so blinded and cast down into a kind of pit of forgetfulness that, thinking nothing of the future, we suppose there is no life besides this one, [Col. 0420D] in which we carry out our desires.

To say more: many, in their madness, while feeding greedy souls with pleasurable desires and raging like wolves against those subject to them, say that they never wish to have another life. Such persons destroy the nature of humanity and follow the nature of beasts, which irrationally and shamelessly are ever bent upon sexual desire and lust. For the Creator of all things placed humankind over earthly creatures on this condition: that by using temporal things well, after death we might enjoy eternal things. What, then, must be done, brothers? All of us are lost unless we are raised up by divine mercy. It itself summons us to run, saying: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John 12:35).

If, when it calls, you wish to resume the race, it will be permitted not only to one but to very many to attain the crown. And just as the same person did not always win in every race, but the person defeated at one time became victorious at another when his strength had been renewed, so let us, if hitherto defeated, take care henceforth to be victors. The path of running is set before our eyes; on it, the slower we have been, the swifter we can be—if we will. For how can we remain inactive and sluggish in the race, when we have not only the Apostle exhorting us to receive the crown, but also our Savior exhorting us to receive the denarius? For he, the supreme householder, who planted the vineyard—that is, the holy Church—promises that he will give the denarius of heavenly recompense to us who entered the vineyard to labor late, that is, at the end of the world; treating us as equal to the first laborers, who bore the burden and heat of the day from morning until evening.

You have indeed heard him, in the true and fitting parable of the Gospel, inviting laborers into the cultivation of his vineyard in the morning, at the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours, and giving all an equal denarius when the work was done. If you desire the meanings of the hours which you have heard, learn that morning was from Adam to Noah; the third hour, from Noah to Abraham; the sixth, from Abraham to Moses; the ninth, from Moses to the coming of our Lord and Savior; [Col. 0421C] and the eleventh was from the Lord’s coming until the end of the world. In this hour we, the last laborers, entered the vineyard; but because we are lazy and slow in work, we cannot be certain of the denarius.

Let us therefore strive to work more swiftly, so that we may be secure concerning the denarius. And since today we are called by the supreme householder, let us not despise his call but endeavor to enter the vineyard to labor. For he suitably instituted the present fast for this purpose: that we may be able, in this season, through penitence and the mortification of the flesh, to wipe away our countless sins which we have committed through delight in the flesh on the other days of the year. Moreover, this day, which is as it were the gateway of the fasts, withdraws from us throughout the entire continuation of its office the song of joy, Alleluia, [Note: [Col. 0421D] Concerning this manner of laying aside the Lord’s song, Alleluia: the ancients seem to have laid it aside only with reluctance. Hence, indeed, in the final periods of the divine office on the Sunday preceding Septuagesima, there is the remarkable repetition of Alleluia in certain principal churches. In some of these, it was sung not only at every verse of each psalm, but even at the middle of every verse. Our learned Martène observed this in certain more notable churches, such as Rheims and Senlis, from their Ordinaries, in his treatise *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 16, “On Septuagesima”; and, particularly and suitably to our purpose, in that of Le Mans, over which Hildebert presided as bishop. Its Ordinary reads: “In the middle of every verse Alleluia is said once, and at the end of every verse Alleluia three times; and at the end of the psalm Alleluia is said; and thus Alleluia is enclosed.”] and expresses penitents and mourners, teaching us that we ought to cease from excessive joy and remain in weeping and tears of penitence.

[Col. 0422A]

Thus, by frequently repeating its name, we addressed Alleluia itself, in a manner desiring to keep it with us as a guest, saying to it: “Remain with us today,” and so forth. We also bade it a final farewell, saying: “May the good angel of the Lord accompany you, so that you may return to us again.” Thus we may know that we shall not rejoice perfectly before the time when, renewed by the body and blood of our Redeemer, we joyfully receive that same song. The antiphon of the Mass, commonly called the Introit, laments with the penitents, saying: “The pains of death surrounded me” (Ps. 17:5). The collect likewise, with the responsory, resounds with the affliction of penitence. Finally, the chant which we substitute for Alleluia, called the Tract [Note: [Col. 0423D] What he says here of the Tract—namely, that it is so called because it has long chants—seems all the more probable because, during the week of Septuagesima, the readings at Matins were drawn out so that in many churches the entire Pentateuch was read in choir during that week. The aforementioned Martène cites many examples of this custom in the place cited above.], because it has lengthy melodies, teaches penitents to cry to the Lord with deep groaning; and likewise the remaining words of the office, arranged in order, seem to express not the joy of rejoicing persons but the grief and sorrow of sinners.

If you ask concerning the name of the day called Septuagesima, know that it derives its name not so much from the number of days, as those suppose who count so many days from it to the Paschal feast, as from the perfection of the number from which that same number begins. This number consists of ten multiplied seven times. The seven pertains to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the ten to the ten commandments of the Law. These are joined in such a way that neither the gifts of the Holy Spirit can be preserved without the commandment of the Law, nor the commandments of the Law without the gift of the Holy Spirit; and whoever keeps one will undoubtedly possess the other. This number fittingly suits penitents, so that by especially keeping the ten commandments of the Law in this season they may recover the grace of the Holy Spirit which they lost by sinning.

Alternatively, according to some, Septuagesima is so called literally because the Israelite people were held captive in Babylon for so many years; when, after that long time, they returned, they consecrated to God a fast of the same number in commemoration of that liberation. But since it is suitable to penitents both according to history and according to allegory, let us strive in this season to bewail our sins, so that after this life, which revolves through seven days, our souls may be freed from Babylon—that is, from infernal captivity—[Col. 0422D] enriched with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and may joyfully receive from the King of kings the unfading crown for the race and the denarius for the day’s labor in the vineyard. Amen.

## XXVIII. ONE SERMON FOR THE BEGINNING OF LENT

[Note: [Col. 0423D] From the Victorine manuscript.]

### On Penitence

[Col. 0423A]

[Note: [Col. 0423D] These are not the words of Scripture itself, but a summary narrative taken from chapter 12, verse 1 and following of the book of Numbers.]

“Mary, [Note: [Col. 0423D] From the very context of this sermon it is clear that Hildebert delivered it, at the beginning of Lent, to penitents while he expelled them from the church by the solemn rite. This was properly the bishop’s office, and belonged to archdeacons only by their mandate or permission. This rite still continues in various churches. On this expulsion see our Dom Edmond Martène, who discusses it at length in his treatise *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 17, ‘On Tuesday at the Beginning of the Fast,’ p. 130 [Col. 0424D] and following. Yet several matters concerning discipline may be observed from this. First, penitents not only were expelled from the Church, but, as exiles from their own homes, fulfilled the penitence imposed upon them—although this appears to have been done only from voluntary zeal. Second, the practice of penitence extending over several years was common in Hildebert’s age. Third, confession of sins preceded the Lenten fast. This rebukes the lukewarmness of many faithful persons in the present age, who scarcely—or not even scarcely—approach penitence except in the final days of Lent, or even when Easter is ending.] Moses’ sister sinned by murmuring against him and was struck with leprosy. Therefore Moses cried to the Lord, saying: ‘God, I beseech you, heal her.’ The Lord answered him: ‘Let her be separated outside the camp for seven days, and afterwards she shall be recalled.’ Thus Mary was excluded outside the camp for seven days; when these had passed, she was recalled.”

The punishments of the Old Testament, dearest brothers, were inflicted for the correction of people in that time, but were written for our chastening. Let us therefore see, beyond the historical narrative, what benefit the Church of God takes for itself in Moses’ sister, [Col. 0423B] and what instruction for life she provides us. That Mary who sinned by murmuring against Moses, her brother and leader, signifies the soul of anyone who murmurs against a superior, disdains to obey him, and refuses to receive the commands of salvation; but when these appear too burdensome, he murmurs and consequently refuses to perform them. Thus, by abandoning the Lord’s commandments, he is defiled with the leprosy of sins, and this is made manifest when his fault is made public.

But a good superior, seeking the salvation of his neighbor, has compassion upon the sinner, requests through prayer the aid of divine medicine for the sick person, and daily cries to the Lord: “God, I beseech you, heal her.” The prayers of the faithful in the Church are very powerful, because, moved by them, the Lord recalls the sinner from his evil way. The Lord heard Stephen’s prayer and converted the persecutor Saul to penitence. The Lord answers, therefore, when he does what is requested, when he moves inwardly the mind of the sinner, when he makes the sinner approach the remedy of confession. And Mary’s being expelled outside the camp for seven days means that, while the sinner is doing penance, he is expelled from his own house and humbly asks pardon for sins; and when the assigned penitence has been completed, he is cleansed from the leprosy of crimes, reconciled, and recalled. The seven days signify the time of penitence. Seven is fitting for the penitent, because he awaits forgiveness from the sevenfold Spirit. Hence seven years are also often imposed in penitence.

Therefore, dearest brothers, you have fulfilled what this signifies. You sinned by refusing obedience to the Lord’s commands. You murmured, and you were struck with leprosy [Col. 0424A] and uncleanness. You deserved to be expelled from the house of the Lord. But we, whose duty it is, prayed for you; and the Lord commanded us to expel you outside the camp—that is, outside the communion of the Church. Yet this expulsion is for salvation, not destruction; for correction, not perdition. In this manner Adam was expelled from Paradise, so that he might be corrected in this exile of misery and, through this temporal punishment, avoid eternal punishment. Although the man had sinned, God did not abandon him, for he always invites him to penitence.

After Adam had sinned and hidden himself out of shame—which was already a great sign and hope of penitence, when a sinner begins to be ashamed of his fault—the Lord deigned to visit him, appearing to him after midday, and called him: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9). That is: “In what misery are you placed?” By calling him by name, he gives a sign that he calls him back to penitence. By asking, “Where are you?” he shows that he does not know the sinner’s way. For God’s “not knowing” is his reproving. By appearing at midday, the Lord shows that he grows cold toward the sinner’s love: when in a human being [perhaps missing: “the light of grace”] is extinguished, the fervor of charity grows cold. Adam answered him: “I heard your voice in Paradise, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.” Therefore he expelled Adam from Paradise, made tunics of skins for him and his wife, and clothed them.

All these things, dearest brothers, are fulfilled today in you. [Col. 0424C] You were in Paradise, because you were in the Church of God. He gave you commandments, and you transgressed them. You heard his voice when you understood the preaching of his vicar. He cries daily to you, “Adam, where are you?” when he says: “Return to me with all your heart, in fasting, weeping, and mourning” (Joel 2:12). You are ashamed in his sight when you heard the correcting voice in preaching. The Lord visits you when he moves your hearts to penitence. And each one of us, while doing penance, should say: “Lord, I heard your voice”—that is, your preaching—“in Paradise”—that is, in the Church—and I heard your threats, that is, the judgment by which you threaten sinners, saying: “Let the wicked be ashamed and be led down [Col. 0424D] into hell” (Ps. 30:18); and again: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:18). Therefore “I was afraid, because I was naked” of virtues, “and I hid myself”; that is, I was ashamed, not daring to appear in [Col. 0425A] your sight, in accordance with the words of the penitent son, who says: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (Luke 15:18).

Sinners, therefore, are expelled from Paradise when the Church is temporarily withdrawn from them. They are clothed with tunics of skins, that is, with sins [perhaps: hair-shirts], because they are represented as forgetful of sins [perhaps: burdened with sins]; for the skins of dead animals signify the dead works of sinners. Therefore do not grieve over this expulsion, but receive it with humility. It is better that you be expelled from this present house for your correction than from the heavenly kingdom for everlasting damnation. O how terrible is the sentence when sinners hear: “I do not know you; depart from me, all you who work iniquity. [Col. 0425B] Go, you cursed, into eternal fire!” (Matt. 25:41.) He will come in wrath, for the Lord will come openly and will not keep silence. Hear what he threatens when he sees human sins: “Are not these things stored up with me and sealed in my treasuries? Vengeance is mine, and I will repay in due time. I will render vengeance to my enemies and repay those who hate me” (Deut. 32:34 ff.).

Because the Judge’s severity is so great, he must be appeased before he comes. The Psalm tells how he is to be appeased: “Let us go before him in confession” (Ps. 94:2). This means: before his face appears in judgment, let us anticipate him by condemning what we have done, so that when he comes he may not find something to condemn. For either he will judge our sins, or we will. It is better, therefore, [Col. 0425C] that we judge them, because “it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:3). Our judgment grants a brief punishment; his judgment, an eternal one. “Enter,” therefore, “his gates in confession” (Ps. 99:4). “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; for his mercy endures forever” (Ps. 105:1).

He wishes us to confess, not because he himself is ignorant of our sins, but so that the devil may hear that we have repented and thus have nothing with which to accuse us. The devil, therefore, wishes us to be silent; God wishes us to confess. This is the order: the first human being was prohibited before sinning, lest he sin, and was told: “Confess your sin,” because beforehand he had nothing to confess. To the second human being, namely Cain, who sinned against his brother, it was said: “You have sinned; be still.” And through Isaiah it is said to us: “Cease to do perversely” (Isa. 1:16). Nor is it enough to cease from evil unless we confess past sins. Therefore David exhorts us: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.” He set an example and said: “I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the ungodliness of my sin” (Ps. 31:5).

When all these things have been done, the final remedy, satisfaction, is necessary, lest our sin remain unpunished. John the Baptist, who was truly a model of penitence, instructs us in this when he says: “Produce fruits worthy of penitence” (Luke 3:8). The devil knows all this and knows that confession is humiliation. Since he himself fell through pride, he wants us not to humble ourselves, because he desires to hinder our return. Thus, as he labored to make the first human being fail to keep what had been enjoined upon him—that is, not to sin—so he strives by every means to prevent a person from keeping what is commanded him.

Hence David repents of not confessing, saying: “Because I kept silent so long, my bones grew old” (Ps. 31:3), because silence in such matters corrupts a person more and more. The devil wants you not to say: “I have sinned.” When a person tries to do this, he tries and labors to shut the person’s mouth. Or, if he discloses the sin, the devil makes him confess it with a greater sin; for he makes the sinner excuse himself. Thus the sin is doubled: he sinned, and he excused the sin. For when some are rebuked and asked, “Why did you do this?” they answer: [Col. 0426B] “Because the devil did it.” But did he compel you? He could persuade; he could not compel. If the devil alone offered counsel and God were silent, a person might have something with which to excuse himself. But God cries through reason, through the Scriptures, through preachers: “Do not sin.” God is on the right, the devil on the left; the human being is set in the middle. God persuades him to do good; the adversary dissuades him; but the human being consents to the devil. This is what the devil accomplished in the first human being. For when Adam was accused by the Lord, he excused himself through the woman, and the woman through the serpent.

Avoiding this danger, David says: “I said: Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40:5). You have heard the manner and order of doing penance; hear the time. Solomon says: “Do not delay to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day; for the wrath of God will suddenly come in the time of vengeance, and it will destroy you [Vulgate: ‘destroy you utterly’]” (Ecclus. 5:8–9).

Behold, dearest brothers, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. What you have sinned on other days, expiate in the time of penitence. Therefore do not delay, but repent as soon as you can. Do so now, because you do not know the day or the hour when he will come. Do so now, because you ought not to fast before confession. What order is it to punish sins before confessing them? First the sins must be confessed, afterwards punished. Whoever postpones confession until the last day of Lent gives a sign that he does it under compulsion, because he delights in sin. God has promised forgiveness to the penitent, [Col. 0426D] but he has not promised tomorrow’s day to the person who delays.

When you come to confession, do not laugh, but come humbly acknowledging that you have sinned. If you can, let the eye weep; if not, at least let the mind grieve. For an outward tear is the sign of inward sorrow and washes the stain of sin. God wished the whole body to work in penitence because the whole body had been subject to guilt. He commanded the heart, eye, mouth, and whole body to expiate sin. For the Prophet says: “Return to me with all your heart, in fasting, weeping, and mourning” (Joel 2:12). When he puts “with all your heart” first, he teaches that there is the fountain of penitence. Weeping refers to the eye; mourning, to the mouth or mind; fasting, to the whole body. The eye saw vanity; the mouth spoke falsehood; the ears heard vain things; the hands committed murders; the feet were swift to shed blood; the heart thought evil. Therefore let the heart repent, the eye weep, the mouth pray, the ear hear preaching, the hand give alms, and the feet come to church. Thus the Apostle says: “As you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. 6:19).

The Creator gave human beings their members to serve him, and you made them serve his enemy. Alas for sorrow! People labor to possess a good vineyard, yet do not labor to lead a good life; they labor that their possessions may be good, but do not labor that they themselves [Col. 0427B] may be good. Thus they love their possessions more than themselves, although they possess things for their own sake, and their vineyard is worth more to them than their soul. Yet they will lose the vineyard but not lose the soul. Cultivate that soul, therefore; root out the thorns of vices, so that the shoots of virtues may bear fruit in you. For the Lord of the vineyard will come to render to its cultivators according to their merits. Then the good “shall come with rejoicing, bearing their sheaves” (Ps. 125:6). And who are those who shall come with rejoicing? “Those who sow in tears shall reap in rejoicing” (ibid., 5). Therefore sow [perhaps: “sow,” for printed *sumite*, “take”] in tears as penitents, that you may deserve to enter the house of the Lord rejoicing, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. [Col. 0427C] Amen.

## XIX. ONE SERMON FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY OF LENT

[Note: [Col. 0427D] From Saint-Germain manuscript 383.]

Or rather, the beginning of an incomplete sermon.

The devil tempted Christ in three ways: through gluttony, when he said, “Command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matt. 4:3); through avarice, when, showing him all the kingdoms of the world, he said, “All these I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me” (ibid., 9); through vainglory, when he said, “If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down” (ibid., 6). By these three ways he had conquered the first man; and therefore he attacked Christ by these same three, wondering that he was without sin, and contriving to catch him by one of these means.

For other vices arise from these, and whoever is caught in them is easily led into worse things. Whoever delights in the pleasantness of food and drink sometimes eats and drinks to excess. From excess the flesh is inflamed to lust. But whoever is stirred by the goads of lust easily falls into fornication and adultery. And whoever is an adulterer envies and hates the adulteress’s husband; he kills him, if he can, or feigns a false friendship; and while he presents himself as a friend in face and words, in heart and deed he is an enemy. See how many sins and evils proceed from the intemperance of gluttony. Seeing this, the crafty enemy first tempted Christ through gluttony, thinking that, if he caught him in the appetite for food, he would easily lead him on to graver sins.

The same is true of vainglory and avarice. Thus, in order that they may be exalted, as has been said, men do not refuse to commit sacrilege, murder, perjury, fraud, betrayal, and false witness; they practise thefts and robberies also, and submit to every kind of disgrace, so that they may accomplish what they desire. Therefore the faithful must watch carefully against the snares of the crafty enemy, so that those who are Christians may repel the tempter in Christ’s manner. When he offers worldly honours or human praise, let the fall of him who fell through pride be considered. But when he tempts through avarice, under the pretext of acquiring necessities, let reason answer: nature is satisfied with little; avarice with nothing.

For if these three entrances are closed to the devil, we shall easily escape his other snares. “Whoever despises small things,” Solomon testifies, “will gradually fall into greater ones” (Ecclus. 19:1). Every sin, moreover, is committed in three ways: in thought, word, and deed. Some vices exist only in the soul; some are first conceived in the soul and afterwards practised through the body. In the soul are unbelief, envy, hatred, anger, indignation, credulity or wrongful suspicion, arrogance, ambition, and avarice. These are held in the mind and move within thought, but sometimes appear outwardly through certain signs: envy through detraction, anger through insult. Thus also the rest, though inwardly corrupting the soul, break forth outwardly through some sign.

Sin is committed in word through perjuries, lies, false testimony, deceits, curses, mockery, insults, lustful speech, buffoonery, every discourse tending to persuade men toward evil or dissuade them from good, flattery, obscene speech, and every idle word. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “For every idle word that men have spoken, they shall render an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12:36). Sin is committed in deed through thefts, robberies, murders, drunkenness, revelries, fornication, adultery, oppression of the poor, excessive acquisition of temporal goods, things done for the pleasure of the flesh, things done to harm others, and everything undertaken with a wicked intention. By all these means the soul dies in sin. [lacuna]

Here this sermon ends in the manuscript.

## XX. FIRST SERMON IN LENT

> **[Note: From the Angers manuscript.]**

### On repentance

> “Set your house in order [Vulgate: Give orders concerning your house], for you shall die and shall not live” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 20:1).

When Hezekiah, after incredible triumphs, had been lifted up in pride and had not given fitting thanks to the Lord, he fell sick unto death. Isaiah came in the Spirit and said, “Set your house in order”; that is, provide who is to succeed you as king. For unless you repent of your pride, you shall surely die.

This admonition was personal, uttered once by the Spirit to Hezekiah, who reigned over Judah and Jerusalem. It is also general and daily, addressed to every faithful soul. For day by day the Holy Spirit cries generally to each one of us: “Set your house in order”; for unless you set it in order, you shall die the death of the soul, and afterwards eternal death. And do not believe Origen, who teaches that the Lord will not be angry for ever, indeed that he will even have mercy upon demons; for “you shall not live,” that is, you shall never thereafter be restored to life.

It is also a spiritual and annual admonition in this Lenten season, in which a fixed and brief period has been appointed for us to correct the negligences of other times.

> **[Note: Rule of St Benedict, chapter 49, “On the Observance of Lent.” From these terms of the Rule of St Benedict, no slight conjecture may be drawn concerning Hildebert’s monasticism, and indeed his Benedictine monasticism; he cites them for his own institution as though they were natural to him.]**

But we must see to which master of a household the Holy Spirit speaks, and concerning what house he commands an ordering to be made. Certainly four houses are read of in theology: the devil’s house, where are the children of unbelief and vessels of iniquity, of which he himself says: “I will return to my house, from which I came out” (Luke 12:24). But because that master of the household is hardened like a stone, this admonition is not directed to him. We must therefore consider the other three.

The house of man, then, is made by hands and visible; the house of the soul is created and rational; the house of the Lord is spiritual and destined to reign. A man inhabits his own house; the soul administers its house; the Lord illumines his. Man does so by necessity, the soul by nature, the Lord by grace.

Of the house of man the unjust steward said: “That, when I am removed from my stewardship, they may receive me into their houses” (Luke 16:4). The present admonition cannot be thought to concern the ordering of this house, since it is commanded rather to be despised than loved. For Abraham was told: “Go out from your land and from your kindred” (Gen. 12:1); and the bride was commanded: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. 44 [45]:11).

Indeed, the house of the soul is the man himself; and by “soul” he means reason, to which, as to a master of the household, has been entrusted the guardianship and commanded governance of our flesh and soul.

Of this house it is written: “Three things drive a man from his house: smoke, dripping water, and a bad wife”—that is, the sin of ignorance, the sin of suggestion, and the sin of one’s own concupiscence. These not only do not allow reason to rule in its own house, but even force it into servitude. But the house of the Lord is the soul itself; and thus, in a wonderful manner, the soul is both the lord of man and the house of God. Hence the Apostle: “The head of the woman is the man; the head of the man is Christ; and the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3).

Of this house it is written: “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9:1). And since it would be absurd and vain to admonish so great a master of the household concerning the ordering of his own house—“For who has helped the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” (Isa. 40:13)—it is clear that the words “Set your house in order” were spoken to the soul.

This ordering, however, is exceedingly difficult and requires much diligence. For those through whom it is carried out themselves need ordering. Just as it is difficult to find a guard if the guards themselves must be guarded, so it is difficult to order if those who order must themselves be ordered. The virtues, certainly, are those through which the soul orders its house, lest it grow wild beyond measure.

This master of the household is powerful; he has a very large retinue. He has servants who are external and run about outward things; and he has interior servants who always stand before his countenance. The exterior servants are the five bodily senses and the members assigned to the senses; their ordering is frequently and readily found in Scripture. For it is written: “Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity” (Ps. 118 [119]:17). “Restrain your tongue from evil, and let not your lips speak deceit” (Ps. 33 [34]:14). Stop up your ears, lest they receive reproach against your neighbour. Restrain your nostrils, lest they seek delight in foreign scents. Close your hand, lest it receive gifts against the innocent. Put your feet in the fetters of wisdom, lest they run to shed blood. And there are many such things concerning their ordering.

The interior servants, moreover, are chiefly the four affections of the soul, of which Virgil speaks, saying:

> “Hence they desire, fear, rejoice, and grieve in turn.”  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, book 6, line 733.)

> **[Note: From the verse of Virgil cited by him in this sermon, it may no less plausibly be conjectured that this sermon is truly Hildebert’s, since he often cites this same verse, and in the same sense, in other sermons, and especially in the twelfth letter of the first book, addressed to Henry I, king of England. Note also the birds driven away from Abraham’s sacrifice, concerning which he also speaks in the second letter of the first book.]**

These, I say, are joy and sorrow, hope and fear. For just as the master of a household cannot lack a doorkeeper, steward, cupbearer, and chamberlain, so these stand by us as serving in their likeness. Fear is the doorkeeper, sorrow the steward, joy the cupbearer, and hope the chamberlain.

For it is written of fear: “Fear of punishment is the gate of the kingdom.” And elsewhere: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110 [111]:10). This doorkeeper has gates and a small door in the midst of the folding doors, which he ought to set in the way and close if perverse thoughts should attempt to rush upon the soul. These must be cast out like dead flies, lest they spoil the sweetness of the ointment (Eccles. 10:1), just as Abraham drove away the birds (Gen. 15:11).

One of the gates is deprivation of the vision of God; the other is the fire that shall not be extinguished; the small door likewise is the worm of conscience that shall not die. Therefore, when enemies rush in, let fear set these before them and say: “You shall by no means enter, lest through you my lord be deprived of the vision of God, tortured by eternal fire, and perish while his own conscience bears witness against and accuses him.”

Zephaniah mentions the two gates: “There shall be a cry,” he says, “from the first gate, and a howling from the second” (Zeph. 1:10). For the wicked will cry out when their conscience accuses them; they will howl when they hear the harsh word: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). Therefore let the soul tell its doorkeeper to keep watch, lest, like Ish-bosheth, while the maidservant who kept the door slept, it be struck in the groin by robbers (2 Kings [2 Sam.] 4:5 ff.).

When the doorkeeper is watchful, let fear, seated and tranquil, call the steward and say: “Set the table, gird yourself, and serve me.” Let sorrow hasten and first set out loaves—that is, tears for sins. This is the daily bread that we ought to eat for our daily transgressions. He fed on this bread who said: “My tears were my bread day and night” (Ps. 41 [42]:4); and again: “You will feed us with the bread of tears” (Ps. 79 [80]:6).

But let the soul say to sorrow: “Child, have you any relish?” (John 21:5). “Man does not live by bread alone” (Matt. 4:4); serve cooked food, otherwise my soul will sit dry. Let sorrow therefore set out three dishes of cooked food: first, remembrance of our miseries; second, recollection of exile and the delay of our homeland; third, the difficulty of returning.

As he sets out the first, let him say: “Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3:19); and: “My son, remember your last things, and you shall never sin” (Ecclus. 7:40). As he sets out the second, let him say: “Woe to you, because your sojourning has been prolonged; for you dwell among the inhabitants of Kedar; your soul has been long a sojourner” (Ps. 119 [120]:5). And again: “By the rivers of Babylon you sit there, and you ought to weep while you remember Zion” (Ps. 136 [137]:1). Let the third be set out, and let him say: “The righteous man shall scarcely be saved; and you, wretch, where will you appear?” (1 Pet. 4:18). What will the desert shrub do where the cedar of Lebanon is shaken?

This steward is harsh and unbridled, yet faithful. His food is rough but healthful; bitter in taste, but, when swallowed, it becomes sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Its seasoning is humility, for humility is the first-born daughter of the highest King, the salt and seasoning of the other virtues.

Refreshed by such food, let the soul call the cupbearer and say: “I thirst” (John 19:28). Mix a drink that may gladden my countenance, since food has strengthened my heart; for it is written: “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous” (Ps. 32 [33]:1). Let joy therefore hasten and offer three kinds of drink. The first is the infusion of operative grace; the second, cooperation with grace that follows; the third, final perseverance.

Setting out the first, let it say: “The light of the Lord’s countenance is marked upon you, and therefore he has given joy in your heart” (Ps. 4:7). Setting out the second, let it say: “Your justifications are songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage” (Ps. 118 [119]:54). Setting out [printed: *apparens*, perhaps *apponens*, “setting out”] the third, let it say: “Have charity, and do what you will.” All things are difficult—indeed, easy—for one who loves. A drop hollows a stone. “Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. 26 [27]:14).

This cupbearer is cheerful and should be embraced. Happy is this drunkenness, which makes men sober. The golden cup of Babylon is suspect; I prefer to thirst.

Let the fourth servant come forward—namely hope—to prepare the bedchamber and say: “You have eaten and drunk enough; come, lie down, rest. I too have prepared three bed-coverings for you: confidently hope for the resurrection of the flesh, the communion of saints, and eternal life, for this mortal shall put on immortality, and this corruptible shall put on incorruption. Besides this, there will be the joy of each individual; you will rejoice no less in another’s good than in your own. Beyond these things, you shall live a blessed and unchangeable life.”

This chamberlain should be heeded, because the bed [printed: *stanter*, perhaps *stratum*, “bed”] which man had turned about in his infirmity, he restores to due order. Blessed is the soul if it thus sets its house in order. Let us therefore labour, each and all, that from the table of sorrow we may pass to the table of communion, and that afterwards from both we may be transferred to the table of the Father, made heirs of God and co-heirs of Christ, who is God blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## XXI. SECOND SERMON IN LENT

> **[Note: From the Angers manuscript.]**

### On the true conversion of the sinner, and Christian unity

> “Return, you returning children, says the Lord, for I am your husband; and I will take you, one from a city and two from a kindred, and I will bring you into Zion” (Jer. 3:14).

This is not the counsel of a man but of the Holy Spirit, who through the prophet Jeremiah exhorts us to conversion, promising us acceptance and introduction into Zion. Yet what he proposes is very difficult; what he urges is burdensome—namely, that we should return to the Lord by turning back. For many things hinder our conversion; very many obstacles confront us and do not allow a mind bound by sins to breathe freely in liberty.

But all difficulties are broken if we have the Spirit as guide, who by his sevenfold grace repels seven obstacles that dissuade the mind from conversion. To emerge from these and escape their occupations is not the work of human power, but of heavenly grace. These are the seven more wicked spirits whom the unclean spirit, having gone out of a man, takes with him when he walks through dry and waterless places and finds no rest, so that by their help he may claim for himself again the house from which he had gone out (Luke 11:26). These are the seven demons cast out by the Lord from Mary Magdalene (Luke 8:2), and the seven peoples occupying the land promised to the Israelites.

For the unclean spirit has many offspring. His first offspring are the seven principal vices, more wicked than the rest: vainglory, anger, envy, acedia, love of money (*philargyria*), gluttony (*gastrimargia*), and lust. Vainglory puffs up; anger disturbs; envy scatters; acedia casts down; love of money pricks and troubles; gluttony bends and dishonours; lust discolours and defiles. These seven passions, these seven wicked spirits, claim human beings—that is, souls—as their dwelling places. Virtues cannot dwell with them, “for what fellowship has light with darkness?” (2 Cor. 6:14).

A soul occupied by so many vices cannot withdraw from the unclean spirit and be rescued from those seven spirits more wicked than the rest, unless the good Spirit of the Lord helps it toward spiritual liberation by his sevenfold grace: so that, when the seven spiritual wickednesses—like seven hostile peoples—have been put to flight, conquered, and cast out of the land of the human mind by seven virtues, like the true Israelites, the holy virtues may occupy their places.

Therefore let us not lose confidence or despair, for the Spirit helps our weakness. For he speaks to us through the prophets because we are now sons and friends, regenerated by his grace and not slaves; for, as the Apostle testifies, we are now no longer slaves but sons (Eph. 2:19). Christ says: “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends, because the servant does not know what his lord does; but I have called you friends, because all things which I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15)—all things, that is, which were to be made known to us. For they could not themselves receive all things.

We are sons, not servants, if we are led by the Spirit of God. “For those who are led by the Spirit of God,” as the Apostle says, “are sons of God” (Rom. 8:14). Nor is it a small thing to be sons of God, for “if sons, then heirs: heirs indeed of God, and co-heirs of Christ” (Rom. 8:27). But we do not attain these things unless we turn and return to the Lord.

Let us turn in heart and return in deed. Let us turn by declining from evil; let us return by doing good. But from what does he urge us to return, and to what? Certainly, from dissimilarity to likeness; from migration to honour.

Man migrated unhappily. Hence Jeremiah: “Hearing, I heard Ephraim migrating. Ephraim is an honoured son to me, a cherished child” (Jer. 31:18). This migration must be carefully considered, which the prophet commends with such earnestness when he says: “Hearing, I heard Ephraim migrating.” The prophet heard with ears capable of hearing. He heard inwardly from Truth and understood, and therefore repeats himself: “Hearing, I heard.” He heard of Ephraim’s migration, and perceived its cause, which he indicates from the very name.

For *Ephraim* is interpreted “fruitfulness.” Man, created in fruitfulness, migrated; that is, placed amid delights, he kicked back, according to Moses’ saying: “The beloved grew fat, became thick, was enlarged, and kicked back” (Deut. 31:15). He grew fat because of the pleasantness of the place [corrected from *amoenitatis locum*]; he became thick through the benefit of his created condition; he was enlarged through the gift of grace. Therefore he kicked back through the vice of disobedience.

Speaking in his person, the Prophet says: “I said in my abundance: I shall never be moved” (Ps. 29 [30]:7). Ephraim said this—that is, man abounding in every gift and perfect donation descending from the Father of lights, with which man was endowed in paradise. But though abundance was his, the fullness of his fatness overflowing upon the earth, he said: “I shall never be moved from this good.” Instead, he believed the devil who said: “You shall by no means die; but you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:4–5).

Man therefore believed the devil and migrated from good to evil. From what good? To what evil? From righteousness to iniquity, from rest to misery, from blessedness to death. Having received the portion of substance that fell to him, he went into a far country, namely that of dissimilarity, in which he is made distant from God—not by place, since God is wholly everywhere and eternally—but by attaching himself to one of the citizens of that country, namely the devil, who is prince of the region of dissimilarity in which man is made distant from God.

He began to feed swine, that is, to delight in deeds of defilement, not casting off hidden shame. Nor did he merely go away; he also stood and sat. He went by consenting, stood by defending, and sat by teaching. In going away is fickleness; in standing, obstinacy; in sitting, pride.

He abandoned piety, which is the worship of God and consists of three things—faith, hope, and charity. Impiety attacks it through three things: vanity, curiosity, and will. These are the three impious powers through whom it attacks: the devil, the flesh, and the spirit. There are three weapons of impiety, and three of its servants. Gathering together as one against the Lord and against his Christ, they say: “Come, let us oppress the righteous man, for even the sight of him is burdensome to us” (Wis. 2:15). As it were, they make a pact and prepare a potion of death, each contributing something: the devil suggestion, the flesh delight, and the spirit consent. Thus man migrated, changed from blessed to miserable.

Unhappy migration! Most evil and abominable Galilee! This is not that Galilee in which Jesus went before the apostles: “He will go before you into Galilee,” he says; “there you shall see him” (Matt. 28:7). In this Galilee God is seen; in that one the vision of God is lost, for there are darkness and gloom, but here light and brightness. Into that one men migrate from good to evil; into this one, from evil to good.

He who was born in truth willed to migrate, so that in him we might migrate to life; for he migrated when he was made in the likeness in which we had died. “Ephraim has become like a deceived dove, without a heart,” as Hosea says (Hos. 7:11), when, by grace, he took up him whom the appearance of a dove declared to be our husband—that is, our head and Lord.

He who says through the prophet, “I am your husband, and I will take you, one from a city and two from a kindred,” is our husband because he is our head. And he is our head because, as members to a head, we are joined to him by grace and nature. From his fullness we have received grace, and from our weakness he received nature. In him are all our spiritual senses, as bodily senses are in the head.

He therefore took us up by grace in order to restore the honour which we lost and the glory which we forfeited. For man abandoned his honour and became inglorious, because “when he was in honour, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48 [49]:13, 21).

But what is that honour, and what that glory? God made man in his own image and likeness. Behold the greatness of man’s honour and dignity. God’s work is precious; earth shows him to be lowly, but virtue shows him glorious; the image makes him precious, and while he possesses it he is rightly called man. But when, neglecting it, he falls into vices, he loses the name of man and is compared with senseless beasts, according to the saying: “Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31 [32]:9).

For, stripped of the adornment of the heavenly image, he also loses the name of man, because he did not preserve the grace of man. Therefore in Ezekiel the name is repeated: “Man, man” (Ezek. 14:4), so that one who outwardly bears the form of a man may also retain inwardly the image—that is, [grace], which is the image of God in man and in the rational mind. In this mind are memory, understanding, and love; according to these man was made in the image of God—not of the Father alone, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, but of all three together. Hence: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). He did not say, “I will make,” and “my”; but, “Let us make,” and “our,” thereby declaring fellowship and removing an understanding of singularity.

According to these three, then, man is the image of the Three. “For there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” (1 John 5:8). There are three hypostases, distinguished by their properties, but they are one because they are of one essence. There are three realities, always most blessed and always living, which are to be enjoyed; and they are one highest reality, shared by all who enjoy them, in which there is primary likeness as there is primary equality. So also in the mind there are three properties—memory, understanding, and love—and these three are in one substance, to which they belong substantially, that is, in the mind.

> **[Note: Peter Lombard speaks in this way at the beginning of Book I of the *Sentences*.]**

Man is therefore rightly said to have been created in the image and likeness of the ineffable Trinity: in the image, namely memory, understanding, and love; in the likeness, namely immortality and innocence of soul. Man, then, created in honour, adhered to the Father by memory, to the Son by understanding, and to the Holy Spirit by love.

For the uncreated Trinity implanted in man a created trinity. But by migrating from the blessed and supreme Trinity, man fell into a dreadful and foul trinity, made not by the ineffable Trinity but by the deceitful Satan: the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life. To this trinity every evil is subject, as every good is subject to the supreme Trinity. This trinity [lacuna] is the region of dissimilarity, where memory is scattered, understanding blinded, and will defiled.

Yet from this monstrous trinity we rise again through another trinity promised to us by the supreme Trinity. For the uncreated Trinity raises up the trinity of creation by infusing the trinity of sanctification: faith, hope, and charity. “These three remain, but the greatest of them is charity” (1 Cor. 13:13). Therefore the prophet urges us to return through the Trinity to that supreme Trinity which liberates trinity from trinity, saying: “Return, you returning children.”

For, with understanding enlightened through faith, we begin to return to the Father; with memory made firm through hope, to Wisdom, that is, the Son; and with will made peaceful through charity, to the Spirit. “Return,” he says, and adds the reason: “For I am your husband, and I will take you, one from a city and two from a kindred, and will bring you into Zion.”

Behold: the Trinity takes three—one and two—but one from a city and two from a kindred. There is a good city and an evil city. The evil city is the world set in wickedness, concerning which the Lord says through Hosea: “I am the Lord, and I will not enter the city” (Hos. 11:9). And through Jeremiah: “Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death” (Jer. 21:8–9). Everyone who dwells in this city shall surely die; whoever goes out shall live.

The good city is the holy Church. This is the city of the righteous, the faithful city, the city set upon a mountain which cannot be hidden. From the evil city no one is taken; indeed, all who dwell there die. From the faithful city someone is taken, but only one: namely, one who belongs to the unity of this city, whose God is one, whose faith is one, and whose baptism is one (Eph. 4:5).

God is one, I say, because though there are many called gods and many lords, yet for us, if we belong to this unity, there is one God, blessed for ever (2 Cor. 11:33). So likewise, though “there are three who bear witness in heaven”—the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit—yet these three, although they are three realities to be enjoyed, do not extend our faith toward a triple God, but toward one God (1 John 5:7). There are indeed three coeternal and co-blessed hypostases, distinct in their properties; and these are one, or one God, in kind of essence.

But Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not “one” in our faith in the sense which Hilary attests: “They are three in substance, but one in harmony”; nor are they a triplicity, but a Trinity.

> **[Note: These words are found in St Hilary, *On Synods*, sections 29 and 31, in this form: “That they may indeed be three in substance, but truly one in harmony.” Yet they are not Hilary’s own words, but those of the Council of Antioch at the Dedication [*in Encaeniis*]. Hilary is only their translator. Indeed, because of these very words, he acknowledges in section 31 that the faith of this council may deservedly be held suspect, although in section 32 he subsequently excuses it charitably.]**

Faith is likewise called one, not in number and kind. For the faith in me, in you, or in another person is numerically distinct; but it is one by likeness, because it is jointly present in all, just as the will of two persons who understand the same thing is called one, or the faces of two very similar persons one. It is called the Catholic faith—that is, universal—because all are commanded to believe the same thing and to act in the same manner. Baptism also is called one because it cannot be repeated and because it is equally good whoever may administer it.

Therefore, whoever preserves this unity is not undeservedly one; and, as one, is not rejected by the One, but is accepted. Nor is only one from a city taken up, but also two from a kindred; and thus three are taken up, because he who takes them up is threefold.

This kindred is not carnal but spiritual, by which hearts, not bodies, are joined; and the union of hearts is much holier and worthier than that of bodies. By this intelligible and heavenly kindred, the faithful not only have mutual fellowship and the bond of charity among themselves, but the members are also joined to the head, so that Christ may be one in all and through all.

For just as the Prophet says of the union of brothers which comes about through this kindred: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one” (Ps. 131 [133]:1), so the Lord says of the union of head and members: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that person is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12:50). And concerning both together it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and all things were common to them” (Acts 4:32).

This holy kinship, therefore, brings about a twofold union: for it joins the members to the head by an indissoluble bond, and associates them with one another in devout charity, so as to preserve unity in the bond of peace. Divine is this kinship, by which Christ’s kingdom, which is not of this world, is framed together and held fast [Col. 0437C], so that nothing can separate it from the love of God. From this kinship two are taken, because to those who truly belong to it is given to fulfil the two commandments of charity, and to bear others’ burdens as their own, that they may fulfil God’s law. Rightly, therefore, they are also called two, because they seek not only what is their own, but also what belongs to others, dispensing goods that come to them for use, not as possessions proper to themselves, but as things held in common for all, and especially for the household of faith.

These are they who build with silver, gold, and precious stones; the same persons who think on the things of God, how they may please God, not the world. As those who build with wood, hay, and stubble are signified in one person, so likewise are those who think on the things of the world [Col. 0437D], how they may please the world: those who seek not to leave their possessions but to multiply them; who attend not to eternal things but devote themselves to earthly pursuits. Yet, because they do not prefer earthly foundations—or rather, if the alternative were set before them, would rather lack these things than Christ—they shall be saved on account of the foundation, but as through fire. These, therefore, are rightly signified in one, because whatever comes to them for use they retain as though it were their own—that is, as belonging to themselves, their wives, and their children. Nevertheless, because the Most High has not despised our imperfection, but His eyes have seen it, they too are taken and shall not be left behind.

Therefore three are taken; they are taken by the Threefold One, and offer threefold things to the Threefold One. For these are the three of whom Samuel said to Saul: “When you come to the oak of Tabor, there three men going up [Col. 0438A] to God at Bethel will find you: one carrying three kids, another carrying three loaves of bread, and another a flask of wine. And this shall be the sign that the Lord has anointed you as prince over the people” (1 Kingdoms [1 Samuel] 10:3).

The anointed prince, whom the three ascending to Bethel find, is Christ, “anointed with oil above his companions” (Ps. 44[45]:8); he “to whom the Spirit was not given by measure” (John 3:34); and “in whom all the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” (Col. 2:9). He is found, then, but only by three, who indeed go up to Bethel, and only beside the oak of Tabor. Most worthy and spiritual is this oak, beside which so great a Prince is found. It is not lofty in stature, but immeasurable in strength. It is a lowly tree, yet exalted in anointed might.

This is that sycamore into which Zacchaeus, short of stature, climbed [Col. 0438B] in order to see Jesus as he passed by; for unless someone climbs this tree, he cannot rightly behold Jesus in his passing. Hence he himself said to Moses: “Stand in the cleft of the rock” (Exod. 33:22)—the rock which is Christ: “and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:1). This is what it means to climb the sycamore tree. For the cleft of the rock is Christ’s Passion. The sycamore is the tree of the cross; for *sycomorus* is interpreted “foolish fig.” It is rightly called a fig, because it provides us with delightful food, heavenly bread, for inward refreshment; but “foolish” in the estimation of all unbelievers, whether Jews or Greeks. Hence the Apostle: “We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling-block indeed to the Jews, but to the Gentiles [Col. 0438C] foolishness” (1 Cor. 1:23).

For what is preached concerning Christ’s cross and Passion is a stumbling-block to the Jews, because of the shame of their own crime. And it is foolishness to the Gentiles, puffed up with human reason and the wisdom of the flesh, who consider nothing possible except what they observe in natures; among them the course of nature has greater force than the power of divine might. Yet through “this foolishness it pleased God to save believers,” as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 1:21). For it is not truly foolishness, as it appears to unbelievers, but great power and wisdom, revealed to believers. Hence the same Apostle says: “But to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, we preach Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (ibid., 1:23), that is, Christ’s Passion, in which God’s power and wisdom appear to them, because they have been called to life by that calling with which they were called, which is without repentance [Col. 0438D] (Rom. 11:29), that is, without any change in the divine counsel; according to the purpose: “For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance,” as the Apostle says (Rom. 11:29).

To them, therefore, the sycamore is neither foolish nor weak, but wise and most strong: strong indeed, because it defeated the devil, triumphed over death, and scattered the Jews; wise, because it set humility against pride, so that the righteousness of humility conquered that which could call itself the strength of power.

Therefore what appears to be God’s foolishness and weakness is stronger and wiser than men [315], that is, beyond what human beings can be or understand. Thus this sycamore is not folly or foolishness, as it appears to the ungodly [Col. 0439A], but power and glory. Hence the Apostle: “The word of the cross is indeed foolishness to those who perish, but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God” (1 Cor. 1:18). This tree, therefore, is strong, although lowly.

This is the dwelling of the coot [or: *silica*] of which the prophet says: “The dwelling of the coot is their leader” (Ps. 103[104]:17). [Note: [Col. 0439D] The Vulgate has: “The dwelling of the heron is their leader.”] For the coot is a bird of marsh or sea; it nests upon a rock set in the sea. This rock is lowly but strong: beaten by the waves, it is not touched [read: broken], but breaks them. So too Christ’s cross, struck by the questionings of torments and the contradictions of arguments, was not moved or bent, but was raised all the higher. Unless someone climbs upon it by the steps of faith and humility, he cannot see truth. For unless one believes, one shall not understand; and [Col. 0439B] he who does not humble himself as a little child does not enter the kingdom of heaven.

Hence that oak of Tabor is rightly named: *Thabor* is interpreted “coming light,” because it is the oak of the light that comes. For from it light comes to believers. By this apparent folly and foolishness we are illuminated with wisdom and prudence; we are adorned with power and grace. Let us therefore climb this sycamore with Zacchaeus, that we may be able to behold Jesus. Let us come to this oak of Tabor with the three men ascending to Bethel, that we may be able to find the King of kings, who is found by none except those who ascend to Bethel.

For Bethel is interpreted “house of God,” and signifies the Church, in which God truly dwells, who says: “Behold, I am with you until the end of the age” (Matt. 28:20) [Col. 0439C]. This is the house, the place of which Jacob, waking, said: “Truly the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it! This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28:16), that is, the gate by which one ascends to heaven. There Jacob sets up a stone as a pillar, pouring oil upon it. And here it is said: “This shall be the sign for you, that God has anointed you as prince of the people.” Therefore the stone raised as a pillar and smeared with oil, and the man anointed as prince of the people, are the same.

But why does he say that the finding of him by the three men at the oak of Tabor is a sign of anointing and princely rule? For through the cross God became known, who had already been God but was hidden. Through the cross he merited exaltation, and the name of God was made manifest in him, because “the Lord reigned from the wood,” and “dominion was made upon his shoulder”; he who said of himself: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32) [Col. 0439D]. And again: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. 140[141]:10). Therefore before the Passion he was alone, and thus did not appear as prince of the people; but after passing through the Passion, in the resurrection the glory of immortality blossomed.

Therefore, with mourning changed into joy, him who went out from Jericho—that is, from the changeableness and failures of this misery—[Note: [Col. 0439D] Here the sermon ends in the manuscript codex, which is mutilated here.]

## XXII. THIRD SERMON IN LENT

[Note: [Col. 0440D] From the Victorine codex.]

On repentance.

[Col. 0440A]

“Hear, O Israel, the commandments of life; receive them with your ears, that you may know prudence . . . You have grown old in a foreign land, you have been defiled with the dead, you have been reckoned with those who are in hell [Note: [Col. 0440D] The Vulgate has: ‘With those descending into the underworld’; you have forsaken the fountain of wisdom.] You have forsaken the fountain of living water” (Baruch 3:9–11).

The Lord, dearest brethren, admonishes you through the prophet Baruch to hear his commandments. He rebukes you because you are dead in your sins, because you have forsaken him; yet he calls you by an honorable name, in order to recall to your memory what you ought to be, saying: “O Israel! O my nation, Church!” You ought to be Israel—that is, one who sees God and understands [Col. 0440B] his mysteries—because you are his peculiar people. You who until now have heard commandments of death, now hear commandments of life, namely, those which lead you to life; and you who were learning the righteousness of this world, receive with your ears, that you may know prudence.

See what you are, and to what misery you have been reduced, though once you were blessed. You have miserably grown old, though formerly you were renewed in baptism through the new man, namely, through Christ. For two men are said to exist. The first Adam is called old because he was corrupted by sin. Of him the Apostle says: “Put off the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error” (Eph. 4:22). The second Adam, namely Christ, is called new because he is without sin and also renews others through virtues. Of him the Apostle says: “Put on the new [Col. 0440C] man, who according to God was created in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. 4:24; the printed citation reads v. 15). But whoever sins is said to grow old; that is, to imitate the old man.

Accordingly it is said: “You have grown old in sins, in the land,” that is, in earthly things, by following earthly things; for the first man is of the earth, earthly, and desires what is earthly. The second man is heavenly, from heaven, disposing heavenly things. I say, in a foreign land. For this is not our homeland, but the heavenly Jerusalem is our city, from which we are exiled through the sin of our first parent.

It next explains more clearly how you have grown old: “You have been defiled with the dead,” that is, with sinners, who are dead in relation to God—that is, who tend toward eternal death. Of them it is said: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. 8:22). “You have been reckoned with those who are in hell” [317]. There are two cities, that of the devil and that of God—namely hell and paradise—and two households, the righteous and the unrighteous. The soldiers of God are written in the book of the living. The soldiers of the devil are reckoned with those who are in hell. Of them it is said: “Let them be blotted from the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous” (Ps. 68[69]:29). And why? You have been defiled and reckoned with the dead, because you have forsaken the fountain of living water, that is, Christ [Col. 0441A], who is the fountain of eternal good. Whoever drinks of him shall never thirst; he washes away the sins of the world, and from him flows living water, that is, an abundance of eternal life.

You have heard, dearest brethren, how dreadful a sentence has been pronounced over us. Because you have sinned, you have been reckoned in hell. Alas, what an evil desert, what a grievous reward! From an evil work comes evil fruit; from shameful military service, a shameful crown. “For the wages of sin,” as the Apostle says, “is death” (Rom. 6:23; the printed citation reads 7:23)—not inherited, not passing, but eternal. What then, wretches, will you do? Where will you flee, blind nation? You forsake life and go into death. In hell there is no redemption; in hell there is no confession that is of use. Hence David: “For in death there is none who remembers you; but in hell who shall confess to you?” (Ps. 6:6).

We ought to understand this in a profitable sense. For the rich man [Col. 0441B] in hell confessed his sin to Abraham, but uselessly, because repentance has a place only where confession has a place. Hence the Apostle: “Let us do good while we have time” (Gal. 6:10). For the Lord says through Isaiah: “In an acceptable time I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. 49:8). But how suitable is that time of hearing? “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2): that is, the present is the acceptable time for repenting, confessing, praying, and doing good works, in which the Lord will hear you and in which you can merit salvation.

There are two days: the day of human beings and the day of the Lord. The day of human beings lasts as long as life lasts, because then people are in their own power, so that, if they wish, they may tend toward life or hurl themselves into death. [Col. 0441C] These are human days because people are in human hands—that is, in the hands of priests—so that now they may loose them, now bind them. Beyond this their power does not extend. Hence it is said that God alone has the power to administer remedy after death. Thus after death comes their day of the Lord, because then people are in his hand, so that all things are done not according to their own will, whether they are led toward death or life, but according to the Lord’s grace or justice.

It is the day of the Lord because then the Lord appears as he is. He is not seen in a riddle through a mirror, or in obscurity, as at present. Hence it is said: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief” (2 Pet. 3:10). What then are we waiting for here, where we have been placed [Col. 0441D] in order to work, so that we may deserve to be co-heirs in Christ’s homeland? In the present, military service is performed; in the future, the reward is rendered. In the present, seed is sown; in the future, it is gathered. But the time is short, as the Apostle says, for the form of this world is passing away (1 Cor. 7:31).

The Lord awaits us, who says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live” (Ezek. 18:33). He waits for us to repent. But unless we repent, that waiting produces wrath for us, as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that the goodness of God leads you to repentance? But according to the hardness of your heart and your impenitent heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and judgment” (Rom. 2:4–5). “Therefore awake, you who sleep,” as the Apostle says, “and arise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14).

We sleep because we have forgotten the heavenly homeland. There [perhaps: Here] we seem in sleep to have found true riches, but when awakened in death we shall find nothing, because we shall depart naked, as the Psalmist says: “When the rich man dies, he shall take none of all things, nor shall his glory descend with him” (Ps. 48[49]:18). Let us therefore awaken in the present, discovering that true riches are not here, because it is now time for us to rise from sleep, namely from the sleep of forgetfulness.

But there are some so occupied with so many and such great vices that they despair of being able to obtain forgiveness. They resemble the devil, who in the arrogance of pride deigns not to repent. They are like Judas the traitor, who, despairing because of the greatness of his crime, hanged himself with a noose. Against these the Apostle says: “The wrath of God has come upon those who despair” (Eph. 5:6). He who despairs [Col. 0442B] is said to sin against the Holy Spirit. Therefore it shall not be forgiven him, neither in the present nor in the future (Mark 3:29).

Let him, therefore, who despairs come to his senses and hear what the Lord says through Ezekiel: “If the wicked man repents of all his sins which he has committed, and keeps all my commandments, he shall surely live and shall not die. I will remember none of all his iniquities. Is it my will that the wicked should die, and not rather that he be converted from his ways and live?” (Ezek. 33:14 ff.). I offer the example of the Ninevites. Hence it is written: “Turn the wicked, and they shall be no more” (Prov. 12:7). The thief on the cross did not despair; rather, repenting at the very moment of death, he changed the punishment deserved by his deeds into martyrdom. O thing worthy of wonder! Repentance makes one disinherited [Col. 0442C] from the kingdom reign in the kingdom; and he who had been far away through sin draws near through repentance.

But, brethren, not every repentance saves; only worthy repentance justifies. What, then, is worthy repentance? To repent worthily is to bewail evil deeds already done and not to commit deeds that ought to be bewailed. It is not worthy repentance to repent of past sins unless one ceases from other sins. Hence it is written: “You have sinned; be still” (Ecclus. 21:1). And the prophet: “Cease to act perversely” (Isa. 1:16; the printed citation reads v. 18).

But you, dearest brethren, are negligent in repentance, because when you come to confession you do not bewail your sins. Yet tears in repentance avail more than many fasts over a long time accompanied by joy and laughter. Peter, having denied the Lord three times, wept bitterly. [Col. 0442D] Hence someone said: “I have read of Peter’s tears; I have not read of his satisfaction.” Mary, the sinful woman, came to Christ and wet his feet with tears; and the merciful physician healed her wounds.

The Lord prescribes this manner of repentance through the prophet Joel, saying: “Turn to me with your whole heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning, and rend your hearts” (Joel 2:12). For David, repenting, says: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall drench my couch” (Ps. 6:7). And elsewhere: “The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping” (ibid., v. 9). This is the second washing; the first preceded it in baptism. Even present life was prolonged in return for tears, as when it was said to Hezekiah: “You shall die and not live,” and, turning to the wall, he wept (4 Kings [2 Kings] 20; the printed citation reads XIII), and fifteen years were added to him [Col. 0443A]. If weeping grants present life, much more does it bestow heavenly life.

Therefore weep voluntarily for your sins in the present, lest you weep under compulsion in the future. Hence it is written: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 8:12); and there is where sins are punished. But here they are punished for salvation, there for punishment. Yet fasting must be added to tears, so that, when the soul which shared in the sin is afflicted, the flesh which sinned may be punished through abstinence. But fasting without almsgiving avails no more than almsgiving without fasting. Fasting with almsgiving is a double good. Fasting without almsgiving is no good. And again, it avails nothing to abstain from foods unless one abstains from sins. “Break [Col. 0443B] your bread for the hungry, and . . . do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. 58:7).

When the Lord forbids sinning during fasts, he then shows what we should do instead: namely, that we should undo sins by repenting, confessing, weeping, fasting, and giving alms, so that, purified from sins in these holy fasts, we may deserve to receive the Lord with a pure heart on the day of resurrection and to rejoice with him through all ages of ages. Amen.

## XXIII. FOURTH SERMON IN LENT

[Note: [Col. 0443D] From Saint-Germain manuscript 381.]

On repentance.

“Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God, because you have fallen through your iniquity. Take words with you, and return to the Lord; and say to him: [Col. 0443C] Take away all iniquity, receive what is good, and we shall render the calves of our lips” (Hos. 14:3).

This is the heavenly and salutary counsel which the Spirit of truth, speaking through the prophet Hosea, conveys when he says: “Return, O Israel, to the Lord,” and so forth. In these words the Holy Spirit makes clear from what and to what Israel ought to return: namely, from iniquity to the Lord God.

There are four departures by which the unhappy and miserable soul removes itself from God, exiled into a region of darkness and the shadow of death. The first is worldly joy arising from the prosperity of this age, when all things come according to one’s wish in riches, honors, and other similar things [Col. 0443D]. In these lies happiness not of the right hand but of the left: transient and mortal happiness. Those things are indeed good and are from God, and many saints are found to have abounded in them. Possessors of mortal things are blamed, not because of any fault in the things themselves, but because of an excessive desire to enjoy them, and because they have called blessed the people to whom such things belong. They are not accused because they possess them, but because inwardly they subject their affections to things that pass away and fix their minds upon them. For elsewhere the Prophet says: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61[62]:11). The Prophet condemns not riches or their masters, but their slaves, who set their hearts upon them, hoarding rather than spending [Col. 0444A], rejoicing in such things and exulting when they have done evil. The end of this joy will be occupied by mourning, and this laughter will be mingled with sorrow, because the heart is lifted up before ruin.

Worldly joy, then, which is perceived in two ways—either when abundance of temporal things smiles upon one, or when desires for most evil things are fulfilled—is one and the chief way of departing from God. The second is immoderate sorrow, which likewise arises in two ways: from the lack of temporal things, and from the increase of sins and an excessive accumulation of vices. It occurs when someone is deeply distressed and grieves because temporal things do not prosper for him, while he sees others abound in them. Hence the Prophet, speaking in the person of a certain weak man, says: “My feet were almost moved; my steps were almost poured out, because I was zealous against the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. 72[73]:2)—that is, temporal, carnal, animal, not spiritual peace.

Seeing sinners possess such peace, he became so jealous—that is, [supplied: fell into such sorrow] and grieved so greatly—that the feet of his mind were almost moved from uprightness, and the steps of his conduct from equality [read: from inequality] [Col. 0444B]. But the sorrow arising from the totality of sin occurs when someone considers his sins, imagines that the multitude of divine pity and mercy is overcome and exceeded by the greatness of his sin, and is thereby swallowed up in the abyss of despair. This is the unforgivable sin and blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, of which John says: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John 5:16). [Col. 0444C] Behold the second cause of departure.

The third is hypocrisy, which displays one thing outwardly and holds another inwardly. By it a person does not wish to be or become [that is, to be considered] what he desires to seem: he presents a pallid and bloodless countenance, displays a pale and covered face; he hides a wolf beneath a sheep and conceals a serpent beneath a dove. Hypocrites are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly shine before people, but inwardly are full of filth and dead men’s bones, exhaling a deathly stench (Matt. 23:27; the printed citation reads v. 17). They are like a dish washed on the outside but inwardly unclean with the filth of vices.

Hypocrisy is like a whitewashed wall, concerning which it is said: In a wall not joined to others but erected separately, if you make a door, whoever enters is outside. The hypocrite is a wall shining on the surface but muddy within: he is not joined to others by the glue of charity, but stands apart—that is, exalts himself—seeking his own glory, not that of Jesus Christ; if, indeed, he makes a door by imitation, he is outside charity. For of such persons the Apostle says: “Having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3:5) [Col. 0444D].

He is the reed beneath whose shadow the unclean spirit rests. For, as blessed Job says, “The unclean spirit rests beneath the shadow of the reed and in moist places” (Job 40:16). The reed, hollow within and shining [Col. 0445A] without, is the hypocrite, who outwardly glitters in the appearance of holiness but is inwardly empty of virtues; its shadow is deceitful pretence.
