Hence the Prophet: “The sons of men are liars in the scales, that they may deceive in vanity together” (Ps. 61[62]:10), that is, in the balance of righteousness, because by false testimony they deceive the eyes of those who look upon them, when they display themselves as ministers of righteousness though they are deceitful workers.

The moist places are the hearts of carnal people, fluid with the stain of lusts. Therefore beneath the shadow of the reed—that is, in a mind darkened by the appearance of pretence and seared by the vice of hypocrisy—and in the hearts of carnal people, moistened by the flow of enticements, rests the unclean spirit. He finds no rest in waterless and dry places, that is, in the hearts of saints chastened from every stain of harmful pleasure [Col. 0445B]. Behold the third stain of departure, namely hypocrisy.

The fourth, more difficult than the others, is pride, likewise considered in two ways: in the exaltation of the mind and in outward boasting. It is one thing to swell inwardly, another to vaunt oneself vainly outwardly. Pride is love of one’s own excellence. It strikes the human mind in three ways: when someone attributes the good he possesses not to God but to himself; or, if he says that he received it from God, boasts that he obtained it by his own merits; or, if he acknowledges that he received it freely, exalts himself above others and insults those who do not possess it.

Pride, celestial in origin, always seeks what is high, hiding beneath ashes and sackcloth. This is the beginning of sin; it rages through every vice; it is conquered last; it also creeps into good works. This is the little beast that consumed more of Absalom’s army than the sword [Col. 0445C]. Therefore it must be destroyed together with the foregoing plagues, coming from itself and presuming upon itself, desiring [read: seeking] to seem more than it is, lest it arrogate to itself what belongs to God or attribute to its own merits what God’s grace bestows.

You have understood briefly the incentives of our turning away and distancing ourselves, and how by these four ways one enters the region of unlikeness. In four other ways one returns to the likeness of God and arrives in the land of the living. Hence in the Song of Songs it is said to the Synagogue, which strayed in Christ’s Passion: “Under the apple tree corrupted” (Song 8:5), that is, blinded beneath the tree of the cross; from the Bridegroom’s voice it is said: “Return, return, Shulamite; return, return [Col. 0445D], that we may behold you” (ibid., 6:13; the printed citation reads v. 12). *Sunamitis* is interpreted “discordant,” or *anema* (“wind” [?]), or “captive”; and therefore by her is understood the sinful and unhappy soul, alienated from God through discordant religion and caught in the snares of hunters.

Hence Wisdom exhorts her to return in almost the same words in which the prophet urges Israel to turn to God. For Wisdom says through Solomon, “Return, Shulamite,” and the Holy Spirit says through the Prophet, “Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God,” as though the voice of both were saying: “O unhappy soul, captured by the devil, despised by man, and forsaken by God: after so many and such great departures and violations, by which, forgetful of your Savior, you have cast his words behind you [Col. 0446A], return and come back, I say, from unhappy and harmful joy; and turn to spiritual and heavenly joy, so that you may rejoice in the Lord, as the Apostle exhorts us, saying: ‘Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice’” (Phil. 4:4).

“In the Lord,” he says, not in the world. For no one can rejoice in the Lord and in the age, just as no one can serve two masters. “For the friend of this world,” as James says, “is made an enemy of God” (Jas. 4:4). These two joys differ greatly and are altogether contrary; they cannot be in the same person at the same time. Let joy in the Lord therefore prevail; let joy in the world end. Let the former always increase; let the latter always diminish, until it ends.

What is worldly joy? [Col. 0446B] “Unpunished wickedness: namely, to indulge in luxury, to gorge oneself with drunkenness, to stink with filthiness, and to suffer no evil; to commit evils of this kind and not be chastised by any adversity, but to do all things amid the peace of the flesh and the security of an evil mind—this is worldly joy.” [Note: [Col. 0445D] From Augustine, Sermon 171, *On the Words of the Apostle*, on Phil. 4.]

Therefore it is a great mercy of God not to leave wickedness unpunished, lest there be joy in the world. It is good for us that he comes to our aid by chastising and scourging us, lest he condemn us in the future to the fire of Gehenna. Let Israel, therefore, turn from destructive joy to salutary gladness, which is the oil of a good conscience and the glory of the King’s daughter, which is within; concerning it the Apostle says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our good conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12) [Col. 0446C].

Return also, Shulamite, from condemnable sorrow, and turn to fruitful compunction, so that you may be pierced in the chamber of your mind over your own sins and those of others, and over the delay of the heavenly homeland. Blessed indeed are those who so mourn, for they shall be comforted. Return also from the pretence of superstition, from the fabrication of hypocrisy, and turn to the truth of piety, so that you may place not merely your mouth but also your heart in the power of charity; so that you may not seek human praise or popular favor, but may glory with the Apostle in Christ’s cross (Gal. 6:14). Return likewise from windy pride, from the swelling of self-exaltation, and turn to the fullness of humility, because “Upon whom does the Spirit of the Lord rest, except upon the humble, quiet, and trembling at his words?” (Isa. 66:2).

Behold: in these four ways there is a turning back from evil and a turning to God. Or perhaps it says “return, return” four times because of the four principal virtues, so that the soul which strayed through four vices may turn to the Lord through the four virtues opposed to them—justice, temperance, fortitude, and prudence [Col. 0446D]. Something else may also be indicated by these words. The pattern of holy life is expressed in two words by the Prophet: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36[37]:27). One turns away from evil in two ways, by will and by deed; and likewise good is performed by will and by deed. Therefore he separately doubles twice the words, “Return, return.”

[Col. 0447A]

Therefore the Holy Spirit cries out together in the prophet, “Return, O Israel”; and the Wisdom of the Father in the king, “Return, Shulamite,” so that you who were unworthy of divine regard while you were in exile may now, having worthily returned, be looked upon as pleasing to us. He then shows how one ought to turn, adding: “Because you have fallen through your iniquity.” Brethren, we fall through iniquities because we were conceived in iniquities. Indeed, we were conceived in original iniquities through a fault inherited from our parents; but we fall through actual sins by our own fault.

But that we may be loosed from these, let us do what follows: “Take words with you, and return to the Lord; and say to him: Take away all iniquity, receive what is good, and we shall render the calves of our lips.” The manner of our absolution is expressed in these words, granted to us for the perfection of repentance. [Col. 0447B]

Perfect repentance consists in three things: compunction of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction by works. Concerning the groaning of the heart the Prophet says: “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50[51]:19). Concerning confession of the mouth the Prophet elsewhere says: “I said: I will confess to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. 31[32]:5). Concerning satisfaction by works, he himself says elsewhere: “I labored in my groaning” (Ps. 6:7). For, by mentioning groaning and the fullness of labor expressed through groaning, he signified satisfaction by works under the name of labor.

Satisfaction consists chiefly in three things: fasting, prayer, and almsgiving. Fasting is twofold, bodily and spiritual. Bodily fasting is that by which we restrain ourselves [Col. 0447C] from food; spiritual fasting is that by which we abstain from vices. It is neither sufficient nor effective to afflict the flesh by bodily restraint unless one inwardly chastens the mind by spiritual abstinence, by which we avoid vices and shun sins. Likewise there is prayer of the mouth and prayer of the heart. The cry of the lips avails nothing without the labor of the soul. But the cry of the heart, even while the bodily voice is outwardly silent, is always heard by God.

Concerning this cry the Lord said to Moses, though he was silent: “Why do you cry to me from the earth?” (Exod. 14:15). Moses lay prostrate, as is there related, and the Lord said, “You cry.” But he was silent with his mouth; he cried with his heart. In the same way Susanna, accused by the elders of a false charge, cried to the Lord.

[Col. 0447D] Let us not, then, pray to the Lord merely in words; rather, from the inmost affection of the heart, as from a holy altar, let our prayer be directed like incense before the Lord. For concerning those who pray only with their lips, Truth says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII). And through Isaiah: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX, 13; Matt. XV, 8). Therefore let the affection of the heart accord with the cry of the mouth, so that we may offer him rich whole burnt offerings. Almsgiving likewise is twofold, bodily and spiritual. Bodily almsgiving opens the hand and assists the needy; spiritual almsgiving [Col. 0448A] corrects the erring and forgives the offender. For it is spiritual almsgiving to bring back an erring brother. Whoever turns a brother who has sinned from the error of his way, as James says, will save both his soul and his own (Jas. V, 20). But whoever forgives his brother when he sins against him—not merely seven times but seventy times seven—earns forgiveness for himself from the Lord. Otherwise the heavenly Father will not forgive us our sins unless we forgive others; by this bond [perhaps “safeguard” or “condition”] we are bound in the Lord’s Prayer when we say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12). Thus every almsgiving is fulfilled in two ways: by giving others our goods and by forgiving them their wrongs. Hence Truth says in the Gospel:

[Col. 0448B] “Give, and it shall be given to you; forgive, and it shall be forgiven you” (Luke VI, 38).

For these are the two offices of mercy: to pardon wrongs and to dispense benefits. In nothing is the enemy so defeated as by mercy, which exalts itself above judgment; for wherever a work of mercy is found at the judgment, even if it bears something fit for burning, the whole shall be blotted out as by a wave of mercy. Those who act thus sanctify their fast, as the Lord says through Joel: “Sanctify a fast” (Joel II, 15)—that is, make your fast holy, if we refrain not only from food but from vices, forgive those who sin against us, and bestow goods upon those in need. The Lord indicates this manner of fasting through Isaiah, saying:

“On the day of your fast your own will is found, [Col. 0448C] and you exact payment from all your debtors. Behold, you fast for lawsuits and quarrels, and strike with a wicked fist. Do not fast as you have done until this day. Is such a fast as this what I have chosen? Is this what I have called a fast? Is not this rather the fast that I have chosen? Loosen the bonds of impiety; undo the bundles that weigh down; set free those who are broken; and break every burden. Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and homeless into your house . . . Then your light shall break forth like the morning, and your healing shall arise swiftly; your righteousness shall go before your face, and the glory of the Lord shall gather you” (Isa. LVIII, 3).

This teaching is sacred and salutary. It includes three kinds [Col. 0448D] of sins, which it commands to be dissolved. By “bonds of impiety” are understood the interwoven structures of wicked thoughts and wills, which bind one another together when further evils are joined to a perverse thought. The “bundles that weigh down” are the flow of useless words, by which we are weighed down as by a heavy burden, since death and life are in the power of the tongue.

> [Note: [Col. 0447D] Something seems to be missing here to designate the third kind of sin. It may perhaps be referred to the words, “Break every burden,” by which [Col. 0448D] the sin of deed may be understood, concerning which he says: “By it every sin of deed is understood.”]

By “every burden” every sin of deed is understood. This is the threefold way of sinning: in heart, mouth, and deed. These are the three dead persons whom the Lord raised, because, oppressed by these three kinds of sin, we lie as though dead. Therefore, that we may rise again to life, let us by repentance [Col. 0449A] and fasting loosen and break the bonds of wicked thoughts, the bundles of malignant words, and the burden of perverse deeds; and let us set free those who are broken—that is, those who sin against us—by pardoning them from the heart. Let us break our bread for the hungry: our own bread, not another’s, not bread obtained by robbery. For whoever offers God a sacrifice from robbery does the same as if he sacrificed a son in his father’s sight. Let us bring the needy and homeless into our house, that we may be hospitable toward one another, as the Apostle says: “Do not forget hospitality and beneficence” (Heb. XIII, 1). Let us then be beneficent by breaking bread and hospitable by providing shelter, that we may receive heaven.

Nor are the three words set down without reason: “undo,” “loosen,” “break.” [Col. 0449B] By these three he indicates the prescribed form of perfect repentance, which is carried out by groaning of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction in deed. These three are also denoted by Hosea’s words: “Take away all iniquity, and receive what is good, and we shall render the calves of our lips.” They are truly penitent who ought to say to God: “Take away all iniquity,” so that you leave nothing of sickness, nothing of the former ruin, lest a revived planting of evil seed sprout again. This is done through contrition and lamentation of heart, which first lays, as it were, a foundation upon the rock; and, when through it evil has been removed—that is, the guilt of sin has been loosed—we shall be able to offer what is good. Hence he adds: “And receive what is good,” namely confession of sins, besides thanksgiving; “and we shall render the calves of our lips”: that is, through confession [Col. 0449C] we shall offer you good works, works of the new life, and through the sacrifice of contrition and the mortification of confession.

Let us offer a sacrifice of righteousness by fasting, giving alms, and praying. For works are signified by “calves” and mouths by “lips,” because fasting without almsgiving is of no avail, nor does prayer penetrate heaven unless it has two wings—fasting and almsgiving. By fasting the desires of the flesh are mortified in us; by almsgiving we relieve the needs of others. For what profit is there in depriving yourself of something through fasting unless you give to another who lacks it what you have deprived yourself of? Otherwise, you fast in order to increase your purse, to make a greater heap of money, not to refresh the hungry poor person. In vain do you spread out your hands to God in prayer, as Wisdom testifies, if [Col. 0449D] you do not, according to your means, stretch them out to the poor person who asks.

There are, moreover, others who in their fasts do not avoid an abundance of food and drink; unable to restrain for longer than usual the impulse of their gluttony, they merely alter the hour of dining, being accustomed to rise early in order to satisfy drunkenness. Isaiah reproaches them thus: “Woe to you who rise early to pursue drunkenness, and continue drinking until evening, so that you burn with wine” (Isa. V, 11). Such persons therefore change the time during the fast but do not change the vice; they change the hour but do not avoid the fault, for they reserve their stomach for a luxurious supper. Isaiah elsewhere rebukes this vice of theirs, saying: “Woe to you who are mighty in drinking wine, and strong men in mixing [Col. 0450A] drunkenness” (Isa. V, 12). Above, he rebukes two things in them: that they anticipate the time by rising in the morning, and that they pursue drunkenness. Here, however, he accuses them not of anticipating the time but of the vice of revelry and drunkenness, because, not avoiding the extravagance of feasting during the time of fasting, they maintain a difference in time, not in sin. Such fasting belongs not to continence but to luxury.

Let us therefore make two wings for prayer, by which it may fly to the Lord: fasting and almsgiving; for as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin. It ought to sweat in your hand until you find a poor person to whom you may give it. For although we ought to do good to all, as the Apostle exhorts, especially should we do so to the members of the household of faith—that is, to those [Col. 0450B] who are our brothers in faith—and most particularly to oxen treading out the grain, that is, preachers and teachers of truth. For one must act differently toward the ox treading grain and toward the passing beggar. To the latter—the beggar—you give because it is written: “Give to everyone who asks of you” (Luke VI, 30). But to the former, namely the ox treading grain, you ought to give even when he does not ask, because it is written: “Blessed is he who considers the needy and poor” (Ps. XL, 1). And elsewhere: “Blessed is he who anticipates the voice of the petitioner” (Wis. VI, 14).

Let us therefore bestow mercy upon all in common, but especially upon those who share our profession, and among them above all upon preachers, who for Christ’s sake have become servants of men, instructing others by the word of truth and by the example of holy conduct. For it is written in the Law:

[Col. 0450C] “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain” (II Cor. IX, 9);

and in the Gospel: “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke X, 7). Armed with both swords, the Apostle says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” (I Cor. IX, 11). Behold, the caution concerning almsgiving and the order of mercy have been indicated. Therefore let our prayer [perhaps: “almsgiving”] be fortified by prayer and fasting, and let fasting itself be sanctified by prayer and mercy, so that worthy repentance may thus be performed.

What is worthy repentance? That which abolishes sin, that which corrects crime. And that repentance corrects crime which brings hatred both of the sin committed and of committing it, together with the desire to make satisfaction. For repentance is to lament evils committed and no longer to wish to commit what must be lamented. [Col. 0450D] Repentance is not worthy if one grieves for sins but does not guard against future sins. Hence in Genesis: “Have you sinned? Be still.” And Isaiah says: “Cease to do perversely; learn to do good” (Isa. I, 16). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Go, and sin no more” (John VIII, 11). He does not say, “Do not sin,” but “Do not wish”—that is, let there be no will in you to sin.

Let us therefore bring forth fruits worthy of repentance, as evangelical Truth exhorts us, so that according to the quality and quantity of what has been committed, there may be a corresponding quality and quantity of repentance and satisfaction; and for all these things what you are to hope for will be made clear. See what follows: “Then your light shall break forth like the morning” (Isa. LVIII, 8). For as the light of morning dispels darkness, so for those who fear [Col. 0451A] the name of the Lord and truly repent, the sun of righteousness rises, driving away the darkness of errors and illuminating the mind through the infusion of grace. “And your healing shall arise swiftly” (Isa. LIII), namely the washing away of all sins and perseverance in a good life until the end. Finally, “the glory of the Lord shall gather you” (ibid.): that is, Christ, who is the glory of the Father, according to the words, “Awake, my glory” (Ps. LVI, 9), shall receive you to himself, according to the words, “Where I am, there also my servant shall be” (John XII, 26), so that you may see him face to face. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## XXIV. FIFTH SERMON IN LENT

> [Note: [Col. 0451] St. Germain MS no. 381. Hildebert also seems to have preached this sermon on the beginning of the fast, when he expelled penitents from the church according to the solemn rite.]

On repentance.

[Col. 0451B]

> “How long, sluggard, will you sleep? When will you rise from your sleep? You will sleep a little, you will doze a little, you will fold your hands a little in order to sleep; and poverty will come upon you like a traveler, and want like an armed man” (Prov. VI, 9–11).

As the kingdom is promised to those who are watchful, so Wisdom threatens eternal destruction to those who sleep. This slumber is perverse and therefore, brothers, must be vigorously avoided. It is not a sleep of the body but of the mind; it does not grant the mind rest, but imposes oppression upon it. Elsewhere Wisdom warns us against this sleep, saying: “Do not give sleep to your eyes, nor let your eyelids slumber” (Prov. VI, 4). He gives sleep to his eyes who negligently neglects care for himself or for others [Col. 0451C]; and he slumbers who indeed recognizes blameworthy matters in himself or in others but, through weariness of mind, does not correct them with the rebuke they deserve. Such sleep is negligence, and this slumber is not inappropriately called sluggishness or acedia. May God avert from our eyes such sleep and such slumber.

This sleep and slumber arise from night, not from day, and therefore darken rather than illuminate the eyes of the mind. Hence the Apostle: “Those who sleep sleep at night, and those who are drunk are drunk at night” (I Thess. V, 7). Detestable is this night, which produces such offspring. It is not the night of confession, in which the saint rises to confess the Lord, but the night of confusion, in which the beasts [Col. 0451D] of the forest and the young lions pass through roaring in order to seize prey. Judas was in this night when he betrayed the Lord. We must flee from this night as from Babylon, because this night truly is Babylon—that is, the confusion of vices and sins. Therefore those who sleep, namely those who become numb and rest in temporal things, forgetful of eternal life, sleep in the night: the confusion of sins and vices has drawn them in. And those who are drunk, using these temporal things without moderation, do so from the night of sin. Let us therefore flee this night that produces such slumber; this is to flee from the midst of Babylon. Thus, as Jeremiah exhorts us, saying, “Flee from the midst of Babylon” (Jer. L, 8), [Col. 0452A] so that each may save his own soul, the Apostle also warns us to avoid this slumber, saying: “Let us not sleep as the others do, but let us watch and be sober” (I Thess. V, 6). Let us watch, despising these fleeting and transitory things; let us be sober, using them moderately and rightly.

Moreover, just as there is bad sleep, so there is good sleep; and just as there is good wakefulness, so there is bad. To sleep to the world is good, and to watch for God is good. Hence the bride said: “I sleep, but my heart watches” (Cant. V, 2). For she slept to the world, not in the world, and watched for God, not for the world. The opposite is to watch for the world and sleep to God. For whoever sleeps to God sleeps in the world; and he does not watch in the world, but for the world. For it is one thing to watch for the world and another to watch in the world. To watch [Col. 0452B] for the world is the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God; to watch in the world is the prudence of the spirit, which is from above. To sleep to the world is continence, because we separate ourselves from its tumults and works in order to keep a spiritual Sabbath in the heart. But to sleep in the world is negligence and bodily sluggishness, whence comes the curse; for, as Scripture says, “Cursed is everyone who performs the work of God negligently” [Vulgate: “deceitfully”] (Jer. XLVIII, 10).

But if cursed is the person who performs it negligently, neither is free from a curse the person who does not perform it: like the sluggard who is to be stoned with ox-dung (Ecclus. XXII, 2), that is, because he despises and rejects preaching. By its teaching and example he is not stirred to avoid evil nor moved to do good, [Col. 0452C] but, cast down upon the ground, being earthly he savors and seeks earthly things, not the things above, which awaken from sleep. And because he does not penetrate the height of eternity, Wisdom sets before him the example of the ant, so that he may be roused at least in this way, saying: “Go to the ant, sluggard, consider her way, and learn wisdom. Though she has no leader, she prepares her food in summer and gathers at harvest what she may eat” (Prov. VI, 6–8). It is as though he said: If the words of a teacher do not move you, learn from the ant the wisdom of working. For if so small an animal, without a ruler, lacking reason, provides for its future with nature as its guide, how much more ought you—made in the image of God, called to behold his glory, assisted by the teaching of doctors, and having the Creator himself as your guide—[Col. 0452D] to gather in the present the fruits of good works by which you may live eternally in the future.

The present life is compared to harvest and summer, because amid the heat of temptations this is the time to gather merits for future rewards. The day of judgment, however, is compared to winter, because no opportunity remains for laboring for life; each person will only be compelled to bring forth from the storehouse of past action what he has stored there. Rise, therefore, sluggard, from the sleep of torpor. Be watchful, you negligent person, and keep your heart with every guard, because from it proceed life and death. There are some who perform works that appear good but do not keep their hearts with all diligence, spoiling those works through negligence or perverse intention. [Col. 0453A] They sleep badly in the world, but watch still worse for the world. As Wisdom rebukes their sleep, so also their wakefulness, saying: “Do not delight in the paths of the ungodly, nor let the way of evil men please you . . . for they do not sleep unless they have done evil, and sleep is taken from them unless they have caused someone to fall” (Prov. IV, 14–16). Oh, what detestable wakefulness! They remain awake in order to harm others. Do not watch thus, brothers; rather, watch for God, and love [or pray to] him, lest you enter into temptation. Shake sleep also from your eyes, rubbing the brows of your hearts with the hands of good works. Rise, you who lie down, as the Apostle says: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall illuminate you” (Eph. V, 14).

Thus far, brothers, [Col. 0453B] you have slept enough; thus far you have given yourselves to sloth; thus far you have been occupied with the pleasures of vices. Hence the Apostle calls each one of us, saying:

> [Note: [Col. 0453D] These words are not found in the Apostle except as an interpretative paraphrase.]

“You who sleep in the bed of vices, wrapped in negligence and confounded by forgetfulness of God, rise through repentance, [331] so that, extending yourself into the inward parts, you may despise earthly things and hate vices; and arise through confession with the mouth and the performance of works, so that you may slay the old man within yourself and put on the new,” as the Apostle exhorts, saying: “Put off the old man with his deeds, and put on the new, who was created according to God” (Col. III, 9). That is, put off the form of the earthly and old man, and put on the new man—the image of the heavenly man—so that, as hitherto you have been earthly after the likeness of the earthly one [Col. 0453C] and have led an earthly life, walking according to the flesh, so henceforth you may strive, through the heavenly one, to become heavenly. For through him now is the hour for you—that is, the opportunity and power to rise from sleep. Cast off, therefore, the works of darkness, that is, the works of the old man, which are done in darkness and lead to eternal darkness; and make no provision for the flesh in its desires. For if you have put on the form of Christ, you will not be compelled to serve the flesh in its desires, though you must serve it in its necessities. Rise, therefore, from the dead—that is, from sins—you who lie as if dead among the dead; and Christ shall illuminate you, so that you may see him now through a mirror and in an enigma, but in the future face to face.

These temporal felicities are like the dreams of sleepers. [Col. 0453D] The friends of this world are like people dreaming that they have found treasure. Some in dreams think that they possess riches, and upon waking find themselves deceived by a false image. So lovers of the world, embracing temporal goods, suppose that they have received true goods; but when awakened by death, they understand that these were false goods, as the things previously held vanish away. Hence the Prophet: “They slept their sleep, and the men of wealth found nothing in their hands” (Ps. LXXV, 6). And elsewhere: “Like the dream of those who awake, Lord, in your city you shall reduce their image to nothing” (Ps. LXXII, 20). That these things vanish is most clearly explained [Col. 0454A] by the same Prophet, who says: “When a man dies, he shall take none of all things, nor shall his glory descend with him” (Ps. XLVIII, 19).

Rise, therefore, brothers, from so dangerous and deadly a sleep. “Return to the heart, you transgressors,” and follow the counsel of the prophet Ezekiel—indeed, of the Holy Spirit—by which he exhorts us, saying: “Turn and do repentance from all your iniquities; make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit, and you shall not die, says the Lord, because I do not will the death of one who dies,” that is, of the sinner (Ezek. XVIII, 30–32). Return, therefore, and live. Consider, brothers, how great the mercy and patience of our Redeemer are: every day, when we fall, he unceasingly urges us to rise; when we go astray, he recalls us [Col. 0454B] to the way [perhaps “life”]. We abandon him, but he does not abandon us, whom he redeemed. He made us his soldiers and, as a mark of military service, gave us a name from his own name. But what have we done? Even if we wished to be silent, Moses cries out: “The beloved people grew fat and kicked; grown fat, enlarged, it abandoned God its maker and departed from God its savior” (Deut. XXXII, 15). For when he had given it every good thing, made fat by God’s blessings and becoming wanton, it kicked against God, abandoned him who had made and saved it. It violated the covenant made with its Creator, to whom in baptism it had promised to renounce Satan and all his pomps. But behold, you have performed Satan’s works and clung to him, abandoning God.

Therefore mother Church today [Col. 0454C] rebukes us and her other children in whom she recognizes that she has suffered loss, with paternal severity, so that, after reforming them through medicinal austerity, she may gather them with maternal compassion. She invites the wounded to show their wounds, lest wounds not shown and untreated fester. For those who show them, she prescribes different kinds of treatments, so that appropriate medicinal poultices may be applied according to the quality and quantity of the wounds. For this reason mother Church temporarily separates from her bosom those wounded by deadly wounds and entangled in grave crimes, yet humbly imploring the medicine of repentance, clothed in haircloth and with their heads sprinkled with ashes. Ashes signify the humility of repentance; haircloth, the harshness of a conscience pricked by sin.

[Col. 0454D] Evidence for this practice is found in testimonies of the Old Testament, established for ever. From these, then, the Church learned at the beginning what she now does sacramentally. For Genesis relates that, because of the sin of transgression and apostasy, God expelled Adam from the paradise of delight, to work the ground from which he had been taken (Gen. III, 19). Numbers likewise relates that Miriam, Moses’ sister, sinned by murmuring against him and was struck with leprosy. Moses also cried out to God: “O God, I beseech you, heal her.” The Lord replied: “Let her be separated outside the camp for seven days, and afterward she shall be recalled.” Thus she was excluded for seven days (Num. [Col. 0455A] XII, 10 ff.); when these were completed, she was recalled. But these and other things happened to them in figures.

This Miriam, who sinned by murmuring against Moses, her brother and leader of the people, signifies the soul which murmurs against God or against the teacher given it by God; it scorns to obey him and receive from him the precepts of salvation, which, because they seem burdensome to it, it complains of and refuses to perform. Thus it is defiled by the leprosy of vices and appears leprous when its fault is made public. But the devout shepherd, seeking its salvation, showing compassion for the sinner, and requesting the aid of medicine for the sick, cries daily to the Lord, [333] saying: “I beseech you, heal her.”

Therefore the prayers of the faithful have great power with God, as James says: “The continual supplication [Col. 0455B] of a righteous person has great power with God” (Jas. V, 16). Indeed, God heard Stephen’s prayer and converted Saul the persecutor to repentance. Therefore, answering the petitioner, the Lord commanded that she be separated outside the camp for seven days and then recalled. The Lord answers one who prays when he pierces the sinful soul with repentance, but commands that it be cast outside the camp for seven days. Being cast outside the camp pertains to confession. Therefore he is cast outside the camp who is admonished to confess sins, according to the words: “Pour out your hearts before the Lord,” so that you may cast out through confession the poisons of sins which you had kept shut up within, and, emptied of the bitterness of vices, may be filled with the sweetness of graces. This happens through seven days. For the number seven [Col. 0455C] of days signifies the sevenfold grace granted to those who truly repent. Hence seven years of repentance are also given. Peter likewise went out and wept bitterly, but only after the Lord had looked upon him.

God, then, patient and abundant in mercy, wishing to heal those broken in heart and bind up their wounds through his shepherds, to whom he gave the power of binding and loosing among the nations, decreed that those defiled by sins, like lepers, be cast out for a time from the camps of the Church. Thus, soothed as it were by the medicines of the shame of separation and the harshness of satisfaction, they may be reconciled to their Head and glorified through him and in him. Therefore, brothers, do not consider unworthy what the Church does concerning you; rather, embrace with the arms of humility and love the medicine of your salvation. For as a sick person patiently endures when a physician burns or cuts his putrid flesh, so you too must endure these remedies of repentance, by which, even when placed outside the Church in ashes and haircloth, you may worthily make satisfaction to God, so that your spirit may be saved on the day of resurrection.

Rise, then, sluggard, and awaken from sleep; for, whether you wish it or not, you will sleep a little and doze a little. Suddenly the Judge comes, who weighs your deeds, and sudden destruction shall come upon you. Therefore do not delay from day to day, nor be slow to turn to the Lord, who says: “Turn and do repentance, [Col. 0456A] and make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Return and live.” For if repentance and renewal of spirit come first, life follows. The Lord indicates the manner of true confession and repentance through the prophet Joel, saying: “Turn to me with your whole heart, in fasting, weeping, and mourning; and rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel II, 12). In these words the three things are distinguished: compunction of mind, confession, and performance of work; through them confession is made perfect and true repentance fulfilled.

Isaiah indicates how the renewal of spirit occurs, saying: “Wash yourselves; be clean; put away the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes; cease to do perversely; learn to do good” (Isa. I, 16). For it is not enough to be washed [Col. 0456B] unless we persevere in cleanness until the end. But if you do this, consider what you shall obtain from it: “If your sins are as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and if they are red like crimson, they shall become like white wool” (Isa. I, 18). Scarlet and crimson signify graver sins, such as murder, adultery, and the like. Therefore not only lesser sins, but even graver and more detestable crimes—for which penitents are today also expelled from the Church—shall be blotted out through confession and repentance. Thus you who yesterday were stained and defiled shall now be found cleansed and whitened like snow and white wool, from which Christ’s garment without spot or wrinkle may be made.

But he himself said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5). [Therefore pray] that [Col. 0456C] he may work in you both the willing and the accomplishing of good, and strengthen you in every good work, so that you may be reconciled to him and may reign with him, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for everlasting ages. Amen.

## XXV. SIXTH SERMON IN LENT

> [Note: [Col. 0455D] From St. Germain MS no. 381.]

On good works.

> “Sow righteousness for yourselves in truth, and reap in the mouth of mercy. Renew for yourselves your fallow ground, for it is time to seek the Lord.”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0455D] Hosea X, 12. The Vulgate reads: “Sow for yourselves in righteousness, and reap in the mouth of mercy; renew [Col. 0458D] for yourselves your fallow ground; but it is time to seek the Lord.”]

Because these are days which we ought to observe with the greatest diligence, so that we may worthily arrive at the Lord’s coming Pascha with minds purified, God profitably admonishes us through the prophet Hosea to sow righteousness in [Col. 0456D] truth, reap in the mouth of mercy, and thus renew our fallow ground; and he gives the reason: because it is time to return to the Lord. He promises us two things, and the Spirit of God commends them spiritually [perhaps “particularly”]: namely, truth and mercy, which are all the ways of the Lord. “All the ways of the Lord,” as the Prophet testifies, “are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10).

For he made the journey to us twice—that is, came into the world twice. At his first coming he openly displayed mercy by granting grace; at his second he will show truth by examining merits and repaying each according to them. He is the evangelical [Col. 0457A] man who, going on a journey, called his servants and delivered his goods to them: to one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one. He who received five gained another five, and he who received two gained another two; but he who received one dug into the ground and hid it. On his return, having settled accounts with them, he rewarded with most abundant glory those whom he found to have increased their gain, admitting them into the joy of their Lord; but from the wicked and slothful servant he took the talent and commanded him to be cast into outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. XXV, 14 ff.).

Take heed, brothers: this concerns you, for it was written for your sake. For whatever has been entrusted to us by God that can avail toward attaining God’s kingdom is reckoned to us as a talent. Consider therefore God’s mercy [Col. 0457B] and truth. Understand God’s goodness and severity in the bestowal of the talent. Weigh his mercy in the demand for profit. Behold his justice. He went on a journey through the flesh which he took for us. For the proper place of flesh is earth, because it is from earth, according to the words: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III). What a lowly thing man is by reason of flesh: he is earthly and not heavenly. Yet he is precious by reason of the soul, in which is God’s image and likeness. The earth—that is, the flesh—shows him to be lowly and contemptible; the seal of the image declares him great and exalted. Nevertheless, unhappy, dull, and foolish man sets flesh before spirit. What abuse! What perversity! What dullness! It is as though he preferred earth to heaven.

For in each of us there are two things: flesh and spirit. And the flesh, as the Apostle testifies, has desired against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. Flesh is said to desire because the soul acts according to it, just as the ear is said to hear and the eye to see, whereas the soul properly hears through the ear and sees through the eye. For flesh desires nothing except through the soul; nevertheless it is said to desire when the soul, through fleshly desire, resists the spirit. Therefore by “the flesh desiring” he means fleshly pleasure, which the spirit has from and through the flesh, opposed to the pleasure which it has by itself.

When, therefore, these oppose one another, almost everyone consents in this struggle to the inferior, that is, to the flesh [Col. 0457D]—a cause for grief and lamentation. We ought rather to consent to the worthier, that is, to the spirit. For, as the Apostle says, we are debtors to the spirit, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh, although we ought to supply it with what it needs (Rom. 8:12). “For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes it with food and cherishes it with clothing” (Eph. 5:19). For the flesh is a good thing: it is a creature of God, as is the soul; neither this nor that is a part of God. Yet the flesh is a lesser good, while the spirit is a greater good; the supreme good, however, is God. Thus, for the living soul placed between the supreme and the lesser good—that is, between God and the flesh—we are debtors to the spirit, because, although it is inferior to God, it is superior to the flesh.

Attend, then, to the works of the flesh and of the spirit which the Apostle enumerates, and you will see that you ought to obey the spirit, not the flesh [Col. 0458A]. For the works of the flesh are fornication, uncleanness, impurity, and things of that sort. . . . But the fruit of the spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, and things of that sort (Gal. 5:18). Just as these are to be loved and sought for their own sake, because in them lies the preservation of what is right, so the works of the flesh are to be fled and hated for their own sake, because in them lie disgrace and the suffering of evil, according to the Apostle’s saying: “God delivered them over to passions of dishonour” (Rom. 1:36).

According to this flesh, then, Christ went into a far country, as we have said: just as he led our flesh, as it were, into foreign lands when he raised it into heaven. He, therefore, going into a far country—that is, ascending into heaven—entrusted his goods to his servants when he gave gifts to men. To one he gave five talents [Col. 0458B], that is, these five temporal and external things subject to the senses, and knowledge of them; to another two, namely, understanding of mysteries and the practice of virtues; to another one, namely, understanding.

And he who had received five worked with them and gained another five, while, guarding himself against the pleasure of visible things, he also restrained others from them by warning them. He who had received two gained another two, while by preaching and performing wonders he instructed such persons as thereby flourish in knowledge and in the practice of virtues. But he who received one hid it in the earth because, entangling himself in earthly affairs, he did not seek spiritual gain.

After a long time—that is, from the Lord’s Ascension until his second coming—the lord of those servants came and settled accounts [Col. 0458C] with them. Examining each person’s actions, he brought forth each one’s innocence, each person’s conscience either accusing or defending him; and, establishing many who had used their gifts well [or: had deserved well] over many things, he rewarded them with the crown of ineffable joys, while he consigned those who had deserved badly to darkness and mourning.

Consider therefore, brothers, the ways of the Lord by which he deigned to come to us: first, in mercy, granting us the gifts of grace; second, in justice, requiring from us what is due. By this learn to fear him as Lord and to love him as Father. For he is to us as a father, mercifully providing for us. Hence the Apostle says: “The Father of mercies and God of all consolation” (1 Cor. [Col. 0458D] 1:3). And he is to us as Lord, avenging all our devices. Hence the Prophet says: “He is merciful and avenges all their devices” (Ps. 148:8 [printed: LXLVIII]). Therefore he is to be loved because he is Father, and feared because he is Lord, as he says through Malachi: “A son honours his father, and a servant his master. If then I am Father, where is my love? And if I am Lord, where is my fear?” (Mal. 7:6 [printed citation]).

Let us therefore fear him as Lord and love him as Father. But love is proved by observance of the commandments. Hence the wise man counsels us, saying: “Fear God and observe his commandments, for this is the whole of man” (Eccles. 12:13), that is, every human being ought to direct himself to this. For in these two things the perfection of righteousness consists. This is the wholesome and heavenly counsel [Col. 0459A] of a wise man: namely, that we should fear God and love him from the heart. For this is the ladder by which one ascends to life.

Yet he did not say, “Fear God and love him,” but, “Observe his commandments,” knowing that the proof of love is the performance of a work. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word.” True love, therefore, is proved in keeping the commandments. Thus Peter, in a threefold love of confession [variant: confession of love], is three times entrusted with the care of the flock. For when the Lord asked a third time, “Simon son of John, do you love me more than these?” and he for a third time *sedente* (“sat”) [variant: *reddente* (“answered”), or *respondente* (“replied”)], “You know that I love you,” pastoral care was entrusted to him a third time, when the Lord said: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17).

Thus it is plainly shown [Col. 0459B] that, just as no one ought to undertake pastoral care except out of love for God, so the diligent performance of the task reveals the truth and holiness of love. For John testifies in the Catholic Epistle: “He who says that he loves God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4). But no one can love God unless he also loves his neighbour. Hence Saint John says: “He who does not love the neighbour whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4:20). And again: “If anyone sees his neighbour in need and closes his heart against him, how does the charity of God remain in him?” (1 John 3:17).

Let no one, then, deceive himself by saying that he loves God if he does not also love his neighbour; nor let him profess that he loves his neighbour [Col. 0459C], whom he ought to love as himself, unless, according to the apostolic counsel, he “does good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith” (Gal. 6:10), that is, to those who belong to our household through faith—that is, Christians.

Indeed, eternal life is to be wished for all through love, although the same offices of love cannot be rendered to all; these should be bestowed especially on the brethren, because we ought to be more ready and more disposed toward some good work on behalf of our brethren, since we are members of one another. For if the reins of freedom [variant: generosity] are loosened toward all, they ought especially to be loosened toward members of the household—that is, Christians—who have the same Father and are designated by the name of the same Master.

Let us therefore do good while we have time [Col. 0459D]. The present life which we behold is the time for sowing. In it we are permitted to sow whatever we will; but when the time for sowing has passed, it will be taken away. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “Work while it is day; night is coming, when no one will be able to work” (John 9:4).

But what is the reward of this work? What is the true recompense of love? Hear and see: “He who sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit, just as he who sows in the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh” (Gal. 6:8). And again: “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; he who sows in blessings will also reap from blessings” (2 Cor. 9:4).

You have heard the reward of spiritual sowing; but the recompense of love is indicated in John’s Catholic Epistle [Col. 0460A]: “God is charity, and he who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:16). And how great a thing it is to remain in God and to have God abiding in oneself, Truth likewise says in the Gospel: “He who loves me will be loved by my Father, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

Behold the ineffable good and the sublime reward: “We will come to him and make our dwelling with him.” But of whom does he say, “We will come”? He does not speak of one person alone; otherwise he would have said, “I will come.” Rather, he speaks of three. “For there are three,” as John says in the Catholic Epistle, “who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit” (1 John 5:7).

These three, therefore, come to him not as guests who soon depart from him, but make their dwelling with him. They come to some persons with whom they do not make their dwelling, because they later abandon them. For there are some who receive the grace of God in vain. Hence the Apostle says: “We exhort you, brothers, not to receive the grace of God in vain” (2 Cor. 6:1). Explaining elsewhere who they are that receive God’s grace in vain, he says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Eph. 4:30).

This does not mean that the Spirit, who is God in the Trinity, can be affected by any sadness or distress, since he is unchangeable; rather, he speaks under the metaphor of a guest [Col. 0460B]. For one who drives an inhabitant from his house grieves him. By this comparison those are said to grieve the Spirit of God who drive him from his temple—which we are—by the uncleanness of their life and the enormity of their morals.

For when we act well, the Holy Spirit given to us rejoices in us, seeing that his admonitions advance to our benefit. Therefore, if we advance through him, he rejoices—that is, he remains in us as an inhabitant. Otherwise he is grieved—that is, he abandons us. For, as was said, he is not grieved in such a way as to suffer. Since he is impassible, he is said, in figurative speech, to be grieved when he withdraws from us. Just as a man is grieved when he is expelled from his own house which he built for himself, so the Holy Spirit is said to be grieved when he is driven by evil works from the person whom he cleansed for himself in baptism [Col. 0460C].

It was not without reason, then, that, when Truth said, “We will come,” he added, “And we will make our dwelling with him,” so that he might signify a dwelling not temporary but everlasting. In the present life the whole Trinity dwells in us through faith; in the future, through sight [Col. 0460D]. For now we walk by faith in things unseen—that is, we press toward God—and not by sight, that is, by the present reality of vision, because “while we are in this body, we are away from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:6).

But how are we away from him, when he is wholly and present everywhere, and when it is written elsewhere: “In him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28)? Without doubt he is everywhere and all things are in him; yet we are said here to be away from him because, although God is everywhere, he is not seen here as he is in heaven. Therefore we are away here, not by faith but by sight.

And it should be understood that one person is a traveller on the road, another is a traveller outside the road. He who journeys and walks by faith [Col. 0461A] is not yet in his homeland, but is already on the road. But he who does not believe is neither in the homeland nor on the road. Let us therefore walk as being on the road, because the King of the homeland has made himself the road. Christ, the King of the homeland, is also truth itself. Here, however, he is the road for us, because we go to Christ and because we go through Christ. For he says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

The way is illumination through faith; there is illumination through sight. At present we are illuminated only through faith, not through sight. For it cannot happen to a person living mortal life that, once the cloud of all bodily imaginings has been removed and dispelled, he should possess the most serene light of unchangeable truth and, with his mind wholly estranged from the habit of this life, cling to it steadily and without deviation.

[Col. 0461B] Therefore, having set forth, though only in part, the rewards of sincere love and of spiritual sowing, love, brothers, God with your whole heart—not the world—and your neighbours as yourselves. Sow not in the flesh but in the spirit; not sparingly but in blessings; not failing but persevering, so that in due time you may reap from blessings the surpassing greatness of glory.

But hear what is to be sown and how: “Sow righteousness for yourselves in truth.” “For yourselves,” says the Lord, not for me, because I have no need of your goods. Hence, when we have done everything well, let us say: “We are unprofitable servants, because we have done what we ought to have done” (Luke 17:10). We are unprofitable, indeed, not to ourselves, since we advance by doing good, but to God, to whom we have contributed nothing; he does not profit from our goods [Col. 0461C], nor become better or more blessed from our progress.

[Col. 0461C] Therefore sow righteousness for yourselves, not for him; sow not iniquity. For Isaiah says: “Woe to you who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as with a cart-rope” (Isa. 5:18). They draw iniquity with cords of vanity who, adding sins to sins, cast, as it were, a long rope, so that with their hands and feet bound they may be thrown into the net of which it is said: “The cords of sinners have surrounded me” (Ps. 118:61). And again: “Each person is bound by the cords of his own sins” (Prov. 5:22).

Thus Ahithophel and Judas, one of whom betrayed David and the other Christ, deservedly perished by hanging: as though drawing their sins with a long rope. But the red heifer, which signified the flesh of the Saviour and from whose ashes water for sprinkling was made, was chosen such that it had never drawn a yoke nor been bound with cords (Num. 19:1), because iniquity is compared to cords, and righteousness is its opposite. Thus he fittingly says: “Sow righteousness.”

This is spiritual sowing, which is always done in tears. Hence: “Blessed are those who mourn” (Matt. 5:5). But the harvest will be in joy, according to the saying: “Those who sow in tears will reap in exultation” (Ps. 125:5). Those who sow in the flesh sow in gladness, but mourning follows afterward—the mourning which, as Solomon says, “occupies the end of joy,” and “laughter will be mingled with sorrow” (Prov. 14:13).

This is evil sowing; but salutary is that by which righteousness is sown, not robbery, so that you may offer God an oblation from your own righteousness [variant: substance], not from another’s injury. For, Scripture says, the offering of the wicked is abominable to God (Prov. 15:8); and one who offers God a sacrifice from robbery acts like one who sacrifices a son in the sight of his father, and like one who offers flesh [variant: swine’s flesh] to God in sacrifice [Col. 0462A].

Therefore sow not robbery, not iniquity, but righteousness: that is, good works, works of charity, works of peace. Give to the needy, assist the oppressed, judge for orphans, defend widows, forgive those who sin against you, so that the saying may be fulfilled: “Give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:38). Let the will make sacrifice in these matters, if resources are lacking. Do not therefore be sad if you have a good will, from which peace is reaped. For peace is not given on earth to the rich, but to persons of good will.

Zacchaeus had this good will. He sowed in it no less than in deed: receiving the Lord joyfully into his home, he gave half his estate to the poor and restored fourfold from the rest to those whom he had defrauded. His great will gave much [Col. 0462B], sowed much. In this same will, too, the poor widow who placed two small coins in the treasury sowed not a little—indeed, as much as Zacchaeus. She put in a smaller amount of wealth, but she had an equal will.

There is also another, more trifling thing from whose sowing an eternal harvest is reaped: namely, a cup of cold water. Hence the Lord says: “Whoever gives a cup of cold water will not lose his reward” (Matt. 10:42).

If, then, one who possesses gives to one who does not possess, he has given as much—if he gave from full charity—as that widow gave in two small coins and Zacchaeus in half his estate. But if someone has not even this, let him be at peace provided that he has the will alone; let him fear this: that he may possess and not give. For if he has and does not give, he has frozen within, because his will has grown cold.

Such a person neither sows in truth nor in the mouth of mercy. For many sow, but not in truth, because they perform works, but not with a right intention. Charity directs intention, and the intention [variant: action] that follows gives form to the work. But just as there are some who preach not from truth but from an earthly motive, so there are those who sow works that appear righteous, not in truth but in pretence. Truth warns about them [Col. 0462D]: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7:15).

And through Isaiah: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13; Matt. 15:8). And elsewhere: “God is near to their mouth and far from their inward parts” (Jer. 12:3), because in their words they display the simplicity of the dove, while beneath their lips they have serpentine bitterness and wolfish ferocity. They are among the good in name, not in gift; in body, not in mind; in number, not in merit; in appearance, not in affection. In many things they are with us, but not in the one thing—that is, charity.

For this reason, whatever they do profits them nothing, because, as the Apostle says: “If I distribute my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3).

Therefore sow righteousness in truth—that is, in unfeigned charity and in love of mercy—so that, out of mercy, you may invite others to the same end; so that the virtue of righteousness may be planted in the root of the mind and be proclaimed by the voice of one speaking righteousness. Thus may the hidden observer be pleased by the secrets of your intention, and may the offices of speech help your neighbours; and thus, through mercy and truth, may we ascend to the Lord as by certain paths. He willed to descend to us by these same paths, as was said above, so that we might sing to him of mercy and judgment and, formed after his pattern, render these same things to him.

To accomplish this worthily, “Renew for yourselves fallow ground”: that is [Col. 0463B], make a new heart for yourselves, cutting down the shrubs of crimes with the ploughshare of compunction and tearing up the thorns and briars of stinging vexations. For now is the time to seek the Lord. Certainly he is not to be sought by word and tongue alone, because “not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven,” but by deed and truth; for everyone who seeks finds, everyone who asks receives, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. Therefore seek the face of the Lord. Renew fallow ground for yourselves. Abstain from every appearance of evil.

Sow righteousness in truth and in the mouth of mercy, and thus you shall reap when you come, coming with exultation and carrying your sheaves: that is, the fruits of seed, namely, the crown of rewards and exultation. May the merciful Lord grant this to us. Amen.

## XXVI. IN LENT. SEVENTH SERMON

> [Note: From the Victorine manuscript.]  
> On repentance.

[Col. 0463C]

> “Shake yourself from the dust; arise, sit down, Jerusalem; loose the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion. For thus says the Lord: You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without silver” (Isa. 52:2–3).

Hear, dearest brothers, how sweetly, how affectionately, the heavenly bridegroom desires to reconcile the Church to himself. The loving Father exhorts his daughter to salvation. She lay in the dust and long kept watch while bound in captivity. Now he admonishes her to rise from the dust, loosen her bonds, and leave captivity.

Dust is human carnality: fragile, established in no solid virtue. Of it David says [Col. 0463D]: “My soul has been humbled into the dust; my belly has clung to the earth” (Ps. 43:25). Dust also means temporal riches, which pass lightly and flee as though before the wind. In this dust people seek blessedness and do not find it; they blow upon it in their labour, and the dust takes away [variant: defiles] their eyes, because desire for temporal things blinds minds.

The Apostle rebukes this when he says: “Seek the things that are above, not those that are upon the earth” (Col. 3:1), as though saying: Why do you wretches seek in dust? What you seek is above, not on earth; you stir up dust, and it leaps into your eyes. The things upon the earth are “vanity of vanities,” as Solomon says, and all is vanity (Ecclus. 1:1). David rebukes such persons when he says: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4:3).

Therefore the Lord says through Isaiah: “Shake yourself, Jerusalem”—that is, vision of peace, my Church—“from the dust,” that is, from the hearts [variant: impurities] of your carnality [Col. 0464A], from the carnality of temporal things. “Those who are in the flesh,” says the Apostle, “cannot please God” (Rom. 8:8). And the Lord says of riches: “You cannot serve God and mammon” (Matt. 6:24), that is, riches.

Shake from yourself, therefore, the dust of worldly vanities, and afterward arise. It is as though he said: You cannot first arise while you are weighed down in dust. For sins weigh down the soul, and temporal things weigh it down as well. What is weighed down sinks; while it is burdened, it strives in vain to rise. Let it cast off its burden so that it may rise.

Thus sinners are called stone and lead, because while they live in this sea they tend toward the depths as lead and as stone. Hence the prophet Zechariah says: “Iniquity sits upon a talent of lead” (Zech. 5:7–8). Moses says of sinners: “The depths covered them; they descended into the deep like a stone” (Exod. 15:5). And again: “They were submerged like lead in mighty waters” (ibid., 10). Hence David, a sinner, says: “My iniquities have passed over my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me” (Ps. 37:5).

Peter had some lead in himself when the Lord summoned him to himself upon the waters [Col. 0464C]. He began to sink because the weight of doubt was in his faith. Hence he heard from the Lord: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14:31). Likewise the Lord says in the Gospel: “Come to me, all who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:18).

Therefore in this passage the Lord says: “Shake yourself, Jerusalem, from the burden of dust”; and afterwards: “Arise and sit.” We ought to sit, not in pride, nor lying down, according to that song: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept” (Ps. 136:1). That is, above the temporal things of this world—for Babylon is called “confusion”—we ought to sit, not mingled with them but treading them underfoot, repenting and weeping for our sins.

It follows: “Loose the bonds from your neck.” In the first creation humankind was made free, but afterward it sold itself to the devil. And for how much did it sell itself? Hear for how much. The Lord afterwards says through Isaiah: “You were sold for nothing.” The devil’s currency is sins, by which he buys human beings [when they sin]. Humanity handed itself over to him for such currency. Hence the Apostle, speaking in the person of a sinner, says: “I am carnal, sold under sin” (Rom. 7:14).

But the devil deceived humankind by promising what he did not fulfil, saying: “You will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:5). Humanity obeyed and ate the fruit, yet received no other reward than sin.

Thus it was sold for nothing. But after humanity handed itself over to the devil, the devil as purchaser placed bonds upon its neck [Col. 0465A]. Do you wish to know what these bonds are? Let us speak, then, about the bonds. When a person sins, he adds one sin to another, and in the same act another and another; like a person who, in order to commit theft, kills someone by night. Then, if someone knows of the crime and he fears him, he sometimes kills him with poison. From the stolen money, moreover, he pursues feasts, drunkennesses, and lusts. Once the mind becomes evilly conscious of such great crimes, it is made readier thereafter for every crime; and thus, by chaining sins to other sins, it makes for itself a very great rope and drags behind it a great tail of crimes.

Hence Isaiah says: “Woe to you who draw iniquities with cords of vanity, and sin as with a cart-rope” (Isa. 5:18). David says of these cords: “The cords of sinners have surrounded me” (Ps. 118:51). These are the cords with which people will be bound at the end of the age. Hence the Gospel says of the man who entered the wedding without a wedding garment: “The king commanded the servants to bind his hands and feet and cast him into outer darkness” (Matt. 22:13).

For the Lord will use no other cords to bind human beings than those which they themselves have made. They themselves have prepared bonds and chains for themselves. Hence it is written: “Each person is bound by the cords of his own sins” (Prov. 5:22). With these cords the devils make snares to catch people, according to the Psalmist, who says: “They stretched cords into a snare; beside the path they set a stumbling-block for me” (Ps. 139:6).

There is indeed a road for us to the heavenly homeland, but evil hunters set snares beside the road, so that they may draw back from the way of life those whom they can and lead them into the error of death [Col. 0465C]. Therefore the Lord drove sinners from the temple with a cord (John 2:15), in order to show that the cord of sinners is their condemnation.

These are the bonds placed upon the neck of Jerusalem, and by which she is bound in captivity. But the Lord who redeemed her, who gave the price for her, has freed her from captivity if she wishes to depart. Thus he cries to her: “Loose the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion.” Loose them through repentance; break them through satisfaction; shake your neck free from the devil’s yoke and submit it to Christ’s yoke, whose yoke is light and whose burden is sweet to bear. Leave the prison, leave the stench; and you can indeed leave well. For the price has been given. Your enemy can no longer retain you if you wish to leave.

Break the rope that follows you, lest the devil have something by which to drag you. See the cart laden with sins; see what it is that you now drag, miserable woman, what it is that weighs you down and prevents your ascent to the heights. The righteous have wings by which they fly to heaven and can say, “I shall fly and rest”; but the wicked drag a cart and descend to the depths. Hence it was said above: “Woe to you who draw, as with the bond of death, the cart of sin.”

It follows:

“Thus says the Lord: You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without price.” It is as though the Lord said: You [Col. 0466A] did not deserve that I should redeem you, because you sold yourselves for nothing, and yet you shall be redeemed. But how? By your silver? No: rather, without silver. The silver of the whole world could not redeem you; rather, the price is my blood.

Peter states this more openly in explaining it: “You were not redeemed from your vain manner of life”—that is, from vain glory—“with corruptible gold and silver, but with the blood of the immaculate Lamb” (1 Pet. 1:18).

You have heard, dearest brothers, how the Lord invites his bride to salvation. You are that redeemed bride; you are those lying in the dust. To you it is said: Arise. You are the captives commanded to depart. “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2). You are bound by the bonds of sins; you are blinded by the dust of riches. Turn to the Lord, because the Lord loosens those in fetters; the Lord enlightens the blind.

Behold the time of penitents: come to the physician, because the medicine has been prepared. Do you wish to know what the medicine is? “Cease to do perversely; learn to do good” (Isa. 1:16). These two things suffice for salvation. Whoever wishes to be healed should take these two draughts. The true physician has assigned this time as the time for treatment. For forty days belong to penitents.

This is the period which the Lord appointed for the sinful Ninevites to repent. For he said: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah 3:4), as though saying: I wish to overthrow them because their merits demand it; yet I shall grant a reprieve of forty days, and unless they repent through fasting, it shall be overthrown [Col. 0466C]. This number of days was appointed for fasting and prayer. Elijah fasted forty days; Moses fasted the same number of days. Christ also consecrated this number by his fasting.

When he himself, who is the true Jonah, was proclaiming to us the destruction to come—which truly would have come unless we repented—the loving Father wished, in order to restrain our pride, to give an example of satisfaction. The loving Father said, as it were: Do not, children, disdain to make satisfaction for your sins, because I, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found, was the first to fast for sins and made satisfaction for forty days.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since you slept during other times, behold, awaken in this one; you have lain long enough in your vices. Behold, it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep. Your sleep is the darkness of vices. So long as we are in vices, we remain in darkness and do not see our own shamefulness. Let us now come to the light; let us now blush for our shamefulness.

For what are lust, drunkenness, buffoonery, lying, perjury, homicide, betraying a companion, betraying the Lord, usury, false judgments, slanders, jealousies, except shamefulness and cruelty? Hence the Apostle says: “What fruit did you have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 13:12). “Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light; let us walk honourably as in the day” (Rom. 15:13) [Col. 0467A].

We are in the day because we have believed, because we have received Christ. But one who is in the day and walks naked goes dishonourably. Therefore put on the garments of virtues, lest you appear naked in the sight of the Lord. “For the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thess. 5:2). Therefore be ready, because at an hour when you do not expect it, the Son of Man will come.

For the day of the Lord is the death of each person. This day is called both the day of salvation and the day of perdition, according to the difference of merits. Know that both days draw near. For the Apostle says: “Our salvation is now nearer than when we believed” (Rom. 11:13). And Moses says: “The day of perdition is near, and the times hasten to be present” (Deut. 32:15). It is as though he said: Do not trust in life, because the day of perdition is near. And even if someone lives a long time, let him not trust in length of days, because all times, however long, hasten to be present—that is, they exist in order to pass away. Hence David says: “Man has become like vanity; his days pass like a shadow” (Ps. 143:2).

Hear therefore what God threatens on that day: “I shall render vengeance to my enemies, and repay those who hate me.” Seek God while he can be found; call upon him, because he is swift to forgive. In the future he is ready to judge. Learn by example how swift he is to forgive, and I shall give an example.

> [Note: [Col. 0467D] From this it is clear that some of these sermons were not copied altogether exactly as they were delivered, since the context suggests that an example of God’s readiness, [Col. 0468D] or swiftness, to forgive those who quickly repent ought to be supplied and narrated in the sermon itself.]

Learn from this example, dearest brothers, to be stirred to swift repentance and to turn to the Lord. Wash evil consciences with tears; redeem sins by alms. Shake off the dust of vices; arise; break the bonds of evils [variant: vices], so that you may deserve to see the Lord in the land of the living, he who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## XXVII. IN LENT. EIGHTH SERMON

> [Note: [Col. 0468D] From the Victorine manuscript.]  
> On repentance.

> “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world . . . . . . for everything that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. . . . And the world passes away, and its lust; but he who does the will of God remains for ever” (1 John 2:16).

[Col. 0467D]

There is a certain spiritual enemy, dearest brothers, which blinds the human race, entices it with false goods, and draws it back from love of the heavenly kingdom by its pleasures. It is called the world, and it is wrongly called *mundus* (“clean”), because it does not make people clean but unclean. For it disfigures blessed souls upon whom God’s image has been impressed; it captivates the children of unbelief over whom it rules; and it condemns the miserable to eternal death, because those over whom it rules become enemies of God. James says: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (Jas. 4:4).

It is the reason why people serve the devil. For no one serves the devil unless he loves the world; he does so because he loves the world, of which the devil is prince [Col. 0468A]. For just as, if someone ardently loved the maidservant of an evil ruler but could not possess her unless he were willing to subject himself to that evil master, he would rather endure that master’s dominion than avoid the maidservant’s company, so lovers of the world subject themselves to its prince—not because they love him, but because they love the world.

For if someone asked a lover of the world, “Do you love the devil?” he would immediately reply, even though he served him: “I do not love him.” Therefore it is the world that they love, and for the world’s sake they serve the devil. Hence, when the Lord said in the Gospel: “No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate one and love the other, or he will endure one and despise the other” (Matt. 6:24), it is as though he said: Either he will hate the devil and love God, or he will endure the devil and despise God.

For he says that the devil is endured, not loved, and that God is despised, not hated. A person endures the devil’s dominion for the world’s sake; he does not love it. And God is not hated but despised. Since the world makes people enemies of God and subjects them to the devil’s dominion, John the Evangelist therefore recalls us, dearest brothers, from love of the world in his Epistle and says: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world.” John himself then sets out the ways in which the world entices people and plunges them into the depths: “For everything that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life.” Let us therefore treat each in turn.

[Col. 0468C] The pleasures of the flesh are those which the flesh seeks through unlawful impulse: gluttony, drunkenness, lust, excessive sleep, empty laughter, and so forth. Since the flesh is nearer to us, the world first attacks us through its vices. The more familiar the enemy, the more destructive he is; and many have fallen through its vices: Adam through gluttony, Lot through drunkenness, Solomon through lust. We must always oppose gluttony with abstinence, because it was the beginning of our captivity. It is the fuel of other pleasures, since from it come lust and drowsiness. It is very often the cause of great indulgences. It is the consumption of great sums of money. It produces disgrace in the mind.

What shall I say about drunkenness? Drunkenness takes away reason and weakens the body. Of it it is written: “Wine produces much provocation, anger, and many ruins” (Ecclus. 31:38). And elsewhere: “A drunkard shall not become rich; wine and women make the wise apostatize” (Ecclus. 19:1). And the Apostle says of it: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is dissipation” (Eph. 5:19). But no vice of the flesh is baser or more destructive than lust. The lustful are compared to beasts rotting in their own dung. Hence the prophet says: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1:17). And Solomon: “A harlot woman shall be trampled down like dung” (Ecclus. 9:10). Lust defiles and destroys body and soul. Hence Solomon says: “Do not give your soul to harlots in anything, lest you destroy yourself and your inheritance” (Ecclus. 9:6). The fornicator loses not money alone, but the soul, which is dearer than money.

Sloth and sleep are likewise pleasures of the flesh, which Solomon rebukes, saying: “How long, sluggard, will you sleep? How long will you not rise from sleep? You will sleep a little, slumber a little, and poverty will come upon you like a traveller, and want like an armed man” (Prov. 6:10). Of laughter he says: “I accounted laughter an error, and said to joy: Why are you vainly deceived?” (Eccles. 2:2). And again: “Laughter shall be mingled with sorrow, and mourning shall seize the end of joy” (Prov. 14:13). And the Lord says: “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall weep!” (Luke 6:25).
