The Lord is not recorded to have laughed; but he is found to have wept over Lazarus and over the city of Jerusalem. We are amid miseries, and amid miseries we ought rather to weep than to laugh. When a child is born, what does it do? It weeps. And why does it weep? Because it confesses that it has been born into misery; for the children of Adam are born for pain and labour, as it is written: “A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day of their coming forth from their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40:1). We have treated well, brothers, of the concupiscence of the flesh, which is the first snare of the world. 349

The second snare, named by John, is the concupiscence of the eyes. Let us therefore say what the concupiscence of the eyes is: namely, desire for outward things—gold and silver, or any possession whatsoever. It is called the concupiscence of the eyes because, through the eyes, desire for those things is communicated inwardly to the soul. There are many whom the devil does not assail through the desire [perhaps: greed] of the flesh, yet allures their eyes through greed for external things.

Money is God’s creature. God therefore is not angered because a creature is loved, but because it is preferred to him. Do you admire the beauty of a creature? The Creator is more beautiful. If you love the creature because it is beautiful, you ought to love the Creator more, because he is more beautiful. The creature is precious; the Creator is more precious. He is indignant because what is less precious is loved more than he himself, who is more precious and who made the creature. “Riches,” as Solomon says, “shall not profit on the day of vengeance; righteousness shall deliver from death” (Prov. 11:4).

[Col. 0469D] He calls it the day of vengeance when, at the end, God will avenge the contempt shown him—namely, that he was esteemed by men as less worthy than his own creature—when, as David says, “the righteous shall see the rich man, and fear, and laugh at him, and say: Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but trusted in the multitude of his riches” (Ps. 51:9). They will not say that he possessed riches, but that he hoped in them and not in the Lord. For what is more vain than to hope more in the world than in God?

The third snare is the pride of life. When the devil has been unable to subdue a righteous man either by the ordinary concupiscence of the flesh or by desire for outward things, after every perfection of religious life he strikes him with the dart of pride. That vice is the devil’s own: for pride fell from heaven. For that alone the devil is to be punished. Adultery will not be imputed to him, nor drunkenness [perhaps: violence], nor fornication, nor robbery. Yet envy is pride’s companion. Therefore he envies the upright man, desires to deceive him, and employs every effort to do so through pride, which was his first vice, as it is written: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10:15).

We have expounded, brothers, the three snares of the world. The Lord willed to be tempted by these three, so that by conquering he might teach us to conquer. Therefore we must fast against gluttony, which is the beginning of our captivity and the fuel of the other fleshly pleasures. The fast was forty days long, and this span signifies the present life, in order to signify that throughout all the time of our life we must abstain so as to subdue the flesh.

[Col. 0470B] Christ fasted in the wilderness in order to teach those who wish to abstain to flee the turmoil of the world. Hence David says: “Behold, I fled afar off, and remained in the wilderness” (Ps. 54:8). Yet David did not seek a wilderness in a literal place; rather, being free from love of the world, he made a wilderness for himself among men. Therefore, when he had fasted forty days and forty nights and was hungry, the tempter approached him. He could have cast him away [or: driven him away], had he wished; but he wished to be tempted and to conquer, in order to teach us to overcome temptations.

The devil first attacked him through the concupiscence of the flesh, beginning with gluttony, when he said: “Command that these stones become loaves” (Matt. 4:1). Against the enemy’s dart he set the shield of authority, saying: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (ibid.). Afterwards, as Luke relates (Luke 4:4 ff.), he tempted him through the desire for external things, showing him all the kingdoms of the world upon a mountain and saying: “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me.” With the sword of God’s word he shattered the enemy’s weapon, when he said: “For it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.”

At last he assailed him through pride, when he set him upon the pinnacle of the Temple and urged him to cast himself down. Scripture met him with the answer: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God.” Thus, once the enemy had been conquered, angels came and ministered to him. By this he teaches, dearest brothers, that this season of abstinence has been appointed for us so that you may fight after the Lord’s example and conquer by the authorities of Scripture.

[Col. 0470D] At no time does the enemy tempt more persistently than in the time of abstinence. Then gluttony acts more strongly when it is subdued. Then lust burns when it is resisted. Then greed urges more fiercely when it is opposed. Hence the prophet Isaiah says: “Behold, on the day of your fast your own desires are found, and you exact payment from your debtors” (Isa. 57:3). Therefore, in this season, let him who is healthy beware lest he be wounded; let him who is wounded strive to be healed.

You who are a sinner, hear the prophet: Turn to the Lord and abandon your sins; and when he adds, “while you are alive and well” [perhaps: “while it is still possible, while you are alive and well”], make confession. For one who repents only in sickness and then dies does not depart this life securely, as Scripture says: “When a man has finished, then he begins” (Ecclus. 18:6). Labour, therefore, while you have time. Punish your sins, lest Christ punish them, lest your adversary have something in you of which to accuse you. But may the Lord, who came to call sinners to repentance and does not will the sinner’s death but that he should turn and live, inspire in us the grace of repentance—he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## XXVIII. IN LENT. NINTH SERMON

> [Note: [Col. 0471D] From the Victorine manuscript. This sermon, however, is perhaps one of those in which, in view of the repeated citation of passages of Holy Scripture—so numerous that scarcely enough margin would have existed to mark them—it seems that unarranged material for composing a sermon more systematically has been supplied, rather than the sermon itself as it was actually delivered. A discerning reader may notice several such examples in this series of sermons.]

### On Repentance

351 “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. He who does not love me does not keep my words” (John 14:23–24).

Hence the Psalm says: “Their fury is according to the likeness of a serpent, like that of a deaf asp, stopping its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers or of the enchanter charming wisely” (Ps. 57:5). And behold his words spoken through Isaiah in the person of the Father: “A vineyard was made for my beloved, and he fenced it about. He selected stones out of it, planted it with a choice vine, built a tower in its midst, and dug a winepress in it; and he waited for it to bear grapes, but it did not bear them [and it bore wild grapes] . . . Men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard. Behold, I shall show my vineyard what I shall do to it. I shall take away its hedge, and it shall be for condemnation [perhaps: plundering]; I shall make it desolate; [Col. 0471C] it shall not be pruned or dug, and briers and thorns shall grow upon it; and I shall command the clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. 5:1 ff.).

The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel. These are the words of the Father concerning the Church. The Church was made a vineyard for the Beloved—that is, for the honour of his Son, who was the Beloved. Hence the Father himself says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5). He fenced it about—that is, he set angelic defences around it. He removed from it the stones, that is, those who had hearts of stone, namely unbelievers; and by faith he planted it apart from the mass of the lost. He set a tower in its midst, namely Christ, who is also the refuge of all. He dug a winepress in it, namely repentance, which, by pressing through the mortification of the flesh, purifies the wine—that is, the faithful, who intoxicate others by preaching and by causing them to forget earthly things through their deeds.

[Col. 0472A] Thus the Beloved says in the Song of Songs: “I drank my wine with my milk” (Song 5:1). For the good works of the faithful delight and give drink to God. Or the winepress signifies the martyrs, who by suffering give examples to others; or it denotes Christ’s passion. Hence it is written: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and among the nations there was no man with me” (Isa. 63:3). By grapes are meant good works; by wild grapes, deadly and evil works. It shall be for plundering by men and demons, and they shall plunder it. By the wall he understands the protection of the Scriptures, made out of diverse sentences and strengthened by the cement of one and the same faith. Superfluous riches shall not be pruned away, nor shall it be dug by casting out the thorns of vices. The clouds are the apostles and other prelates, who defend against the heat of vices and rain divine grace upon sinners. Hence Isaiah says: “Who are these that fly like clouds to heavenly things?” (Isa. 60:8).

[Col. 0472B] God rightly complains of the vineyard, because they have become corrupt and abominable in their pursuits; there is none who does good, not even one. And, as Isaiah says: “As the people, so the priest; as the servant, so the master; as the maidservant, so the mistress” (Isa. 14:2). Even among monks there is no perfect religious life; rather, they are like Simon of Cyrene, whom they compelled to carry the Lord’s Cross. He carries the cross and does not die, but lives for the world; he carries the cross, but under compulsion. Thus monks mortify their bodies, but sometimes under compulsion, and therefore without fruit.

Hence Gregory says: “Simon carries Christ’s Cross under compulsion, when a sinner performs the deed of a righteous person without fruit, because he is not led to a good work by good will.”

> [Note: [Col. 0471D] Hildebert does not indeed quote Saint Gregory’s very words, although he does not seem greatly to depart from Gregory’s meaning when he says that the person who is not led to a good work by good will carries Christ’s Cross under compulsion, like Simon, and that the sinner performs the righteous person’s deed without fruit. The holy pontiff, reproving hypocrites who seek men’s empty praise through an affected and excessive mortification of the body, compares them to Simon of Cyrene carrying Christ’s Cross under compulsion. Simon does not therefore die upon it, but does not cease to live; and thus he carries the Cross without fruit. He says as follows, *Morals*, book VIII, chapter 44, on the eighth chapter of blessed Job: “Therefore, to carry Jesus’ Cross under compulsion is to endure the affliction of abstinence for an intention other than that which is necessary. Does not he carry Jesus’ Cross under compulsion who, as though at the Lord’s command, subdues the flesh, but nevertheless does not love the spiritual homeland? Thus Simon indeed carries the Cross, but by no means dies, because every hypocrite afflicts [perhaps: torments] the body by abstinence, yet lives for the world through love of glory.”]

What of priests? “They say and do not do; therefore do not act according to their works” (Matt. 23:3). Of them and other rulers Isaiah says in the person of the Lord: “My princes are ungodly and companions of thieves; all love gifts and pursue rewards.” Everywhere the Lord is sold. What of false judges? Of them the Lord says through Isaiah: “Woe to those who call evil good, and good evil, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter! . . . Woe to those who justify the ungodly for gifts and take away from the righteous the justice due to him” (Isa. 5:20). They are like Judas, who sell 353 truth; and truth is God. Hence he says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

[Col. 0472D] What of the rich? Of them the Lord says through Isaiah: “Woe to you who join house to house and add field to field” (Isa. 5:8). And David says: “He heaps up treasure and does not know for whom he shall gather it” (Ps. 38:13). Or: “Do not fear when a man has become rich and the glory of his house has increased; for when he dies, he shall take none of it with him, nor shall his glory descend with him” (Ps. 48:17–18). Again: “A little is better for the righteous than the many riches of sinners.” But, as the Apostle says: “The time is short; it remains that . . . . . . those who buy should be as though not possessing, and those who use this world as though not using it; for the fashion of this world passes away” (1 Cor. 7:29, 37).

What of kings and princes? David says: “A king is not saved by great strength, nor shall a giant be saved by the abundance of his power” (Ps. 32:16). Again: “I saw the wicked highly exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was no more, and his place was found no more” (Ps. 36:35). What of robbers? They are like the rod by which the Lord corrects his servant and which afterwards is thrown into the fire. They trust in their own strength, but “the horse is deceitful for safety; in the abundance of its strength it shall not be saved” (Ps. 32:17). Elsewhere: “Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days” (Ps. 54:24).

But what does the Lord say concerning those who harbour hatred? “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you . . . For if you love those who love you, what reward shall you have?” (Matt. 5:44, 46). Again the Lord says: “If you do not forgive men, neither will my Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:14). Again: “If you offer your gift before the altar, first go and be reconciled to your brother; first go, acknowledge your brother, and then, when you come, you shall offer your gift” (Matt. 5:23–24).

[Col. 0473C] But, as Gregory says, arrogance makes us objects of hatred. For he says: “If perhaps a quarrel occurs with a neighbour, we are ashamed to make satisfaction first; but humble God first invited us, his enemies, to reconciliation through himself, and by sending us ambassadors, such as Paul, who says: ‘I beseech you through Christ: be reconciled to God.’” But against such people the Lord says: “Whoever is ashamed of me and my words, of him shall the Son of Man be ashamed in his majesty” (Luke 9:26). John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15)—“Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (3 John 3:10). Hatred is contrary to charity, upon which all virtues ought to be founded.

What does Paul say of fornicators? “Do you not know that he who cleaves to a prostitute becomes one body with her? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Far be it!” (1 Cor. 6:15–16). Again: “Neither a fornicator nor a covetous person shall possess Christ’s inheritance” (1 Cor. 5:11). What does the Apostle Paul say of adulterers? 354 “Husbands, love your wives” (Eph. 5:25). For whoever commits fornication sins against his own body; “the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24), he says, and therefore “he who loves his wife loves himself” (Eph. 5:28).

[Col. 0474A] What of traitors? “They speak peace to their neighbour, but evil is in their hearts” (Ps. 27:3). Of them Solomon says: “An unjust man deceives his friend and leads him by a way that is not good” (Prov. 16:29). And what need is there to go through each case? “All have turned aside; all have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13:3). All gape after earthly things. David fittingly says of them: “Our years shall be meditated upon like a spider” (Ps. 89:10), which, in making webs, consumes its entrails in order to catch worthless prey, namely flies. Thus people consume themselves in labour in order to obtain temporal things. Hence Solomon says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Ecclus. 1:1). And, what is the final and worse crime, you cannot endure correction. “A pestilent man does not love one who corrects him” (Prov. 15:12). But open correction is better than concealed love, and: “The wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who hates” (Prov. 27:6).

For if anyone preaches, they do not listen. Therefore David compares them to the asp-serpent, saying: “Their fury is according to the likeness of a serpent, like that of a deaf asp stopping its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers and of the enchanter charming wisely” (Ps. 57:5–6).

For these and similar reasons God complains of his vineyard. But “every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire. Already the axe is laid to the root” (Matt. 3:10). There are three kinds of bad trees: dry trees; leafy trees without fruit; and leafy trees with bitter fruit. Dry trees signify those dried up from all God’s grace and openly wicked. Leafy trees signify hypocrites, of whom the Lord says: “Woe to you, hypocrites! You are like whitened tombs of the dead, which outwardly appear beautiful to men, but inwardly are full of dead men’s bones” (Matt. 23:27). The third kind signifies false prophets and heretics, of whom the Lord says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7:15).

[Col. 0474C] The axe is Christ, who cuts by his divinity and spares by his humanity. Cease, therefore, to act perversely; learn to do good; and follow God, who says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matt. 16:24; Luke 9:23). But Gregory explains how one may deny oneself:

> [Note: [Col. 0473D] Homily 32 on Luke, chapter 9.]

“Let us abandon ourselves as sinning has made us, and remain what grace has made us.” We are indeed ourselves by nature, but not ourselves by wickedness. Hence the Apostle says: “Let him who stole steal no longer.” For elsewhere it is written: “Overthrow the wicked, and they shall be no more” (Prov. 12:7).

Gregory says:

> [Note: [Col. 0474D] In the same place.]

“The cross is taken up in two ways: either when the body is afflicted [perhaps: tormented] by abstinence, or when the mind is afflicted by compassion for a neighbour. The Apostle foreshadows these two ways when he says: ‘I chastise my body and bring it into subjection’ (1 Cor. 9:17); and again: ‘Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?’” (2 Cor. 11:29).

[Col. 0475A] We must understand the meaning of the Cross. Hence the Apostle says: “That you may be able to comprehend what is the length, breadth, height, and depth of the Cross” (Eph. 3:16). If we deny ourselves, we ought much more to deny what is ours. “For the malignant spirit,” as Gregory says,

> [Note: [Col. 0475D] Homily 32 on the Gospels.]

“possesses nothing in this world as his own. We must therefore wrestle naked with the naked one. For if a clothed man wrestles with a naked man, he is more quickly thrown to the ground, because he has something by which he may be held.”

And if you cannot mortify the body so greatly and entirely renounce what is yours, at least cleave to the poor, because: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). There are three kinds of poor persons. Some are poor under compulsion, who would wish to possess much. Others leave everything, as Peter says: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Matt. 19:27). Others are voluntarily poor, as David says: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61:11); and theirs is the kingdom of heaven, because they are poor in spirit.

Hence David says: “He shall spare the poor and needy, and shall save the souls of the poor” (Ps. 71:13). Of such persons the Lord says: “Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person shall receive a righteous person’s reward. And whoever gives even a cup of cold water only to one of these least ones in the name of a disciple—amen, I say to you—shall not lose his reward” (Matt. 10:41–42). And Solomon says: “He lends to the Lord who has mercy on the poor” (Ecclus. 29:2). And Christ says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9). For nothing is cheaper [than alms given to the poor], nothing dearer than the kingdom of heaven once it is possessed. It costs only as much as you possess. “Lay up therefore for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves neither dig through nor steal” (Matt. 6:19).

[Col. 0475D] But do not give alms for human favour. “When you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matt. 6:3). Let human favour not know what the performance of divine commands does. And do not despise poverty, because the Lord says: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). And Solomon says: “Whoever despises the poor reproaches their Maker” (Prov. 17:5).

Consider, brothers, that life is short and men die [swiftly]. Who is the man who shall not see death? But the death of the soul must be feared more than the death of the body. There are three deaths of the soul: in thought, in deed, and in persistence; these are signified by the three dead persons raised by Christ. David speaks of thought: “O wretched daughter of Babylon . . . blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock” (Ps. 136:8). But blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly.

[Col. 0476A] In this Lent, therefore, especially prepare the way for the Lord who comes to you, so that you may worthily receive him, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages.

## XXIX. ON PALM SUNDAY, FIRST SERMON

> [Note: [Col. 0476D] From the manuscript of Angers.]

“On that day seven women shall take hold of one man, saying: We shall eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be invoked over us.”

In the literal sense, the prophet threatened in the Spirit the desolation of Judaea and the future scarcity of men; but this is not read to have been fulfilled. For nowhere do we read that the men of Israel were reduced to such a scarcity, while women survived, that seven women married one man. For she who did not produce offspring in Israel was accursed, and it was not permissible to do so without a husband, since there was no prostitute in Israel. The meaning, therefore, is that there were so few men that seven women necessarily belonged to one man. Since husbands ought to provide their wives with clothing and food, lest the husband flee from their expenses, they say to him: “Keep what is yours for yourself; we shall eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be invoked over us; let us be named after your name,” just as Sarah is called Abraham’s and Marcia Cato’s.

But this prophecy has been fulfilled in us. For not only the things done among them, but also the things said among them, happened to them as figures of us. Now, indeed, in the Church seven men take hold of one man, and on that day they will still take hold of him.

[Col. 0476C] But on this day one man—namely Christ—takes hold of a human being. Hence it is said: “A woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31:22): namely, the one God, who is unchangeable. For in all other things, to be and that which is are different. But you, O Lord, are always the same and remain in the same condition. Hence: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4). For this reason God loves unity, namely peace and concord, especially between flesh and spirit; but dissensions, schisms, and heresies his soul has hated. And there is none who does good, none, until he comes to one; because “one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4:5), and “all indeed run, but one receives the prize” (1 Cor. 9:14). For as the bridegroom is one, so too is the single bride of the one bridegroom; and whoever does not gather many things into one with him scatters them. It belongs to him indeed to gather what is scattered. “For our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24).

Fire, however, is defined by the philosopher as a gathering of homogeneous things. Hence [perhaps: therefore] we cannot properly grasp this unless we proceed through the unities. For there are eight unities which Holy Scripture distinguishes, seven of which lay hold of the one. Hence the Psalmist said watchfully: “One thing I have asked from the Lord” (Ps. 26:4); and he did not say “one [masculine thing],” because seven unities hasten toward the one. There are eight unities: the first, carnal; the second, natural; the third, moral; the fourth, virtuous; the fifth, personal; the sixth, social; the seventh, spiritual; the highest, substantial or super-substantial. The first is in marriage; the second in the womb; the third in the household; the fourth in the world; the fifth in Christ; the sixth in heaven; the seventh in the soul; the eighth in the kingdom.

[Col. 0477A] From the first we descend; in the second, we begin; in the third, we are companions; in the fourth, brothers; in the fifth, believers; in the sixth, citizens; in the seventh, heavenly beings; in the last, heirs. Of the first it is said: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24), from which we draw our origin. The second is when the soul is infused into the body, and is called natural because then one is first born in the womb and secondly is to be born from the womb; of it we read: “Soul and flesh are one human being.” The third is when we are gathered together to live together by the law of custom [and friendship]; of it we read: “Who makes those of one manner to dwell in a house” (Ps. 67:7). The fourth is when we are united in charity for God’s sake; of it we read: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one” (Ps. 132:1). And in the Apostle: “Keeping the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:3). It is called virtuous, not because charity is a virtue, but because it is the form of the virtues.

The fifth is in Christ, of which we read: “God and man are one Christ; without this faith it is impossible to please God.” The sixth Christ made; for he made both one. Before Christ’s coming, angels did not know us but loathed us as citizens of Babylon. Yet Christ, our peace, destroyed the wall of enmity between us and them, and thus now our citizenship is in heaven (Phil. 3:20). The angel no longer allows us to worship him, because we are his fellow-citizens and fellow-servants of Christ. The seventh is when, with the whole mind and according to the measure of our life, we cleave to God. Of it we read: “He who cleaves to God is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 6:17). The eighth is the unity of three persons in one essence, which whoever passes through the aforesaid unities in exile shall grasp in the kingdom.

Thus also the children of Israel first departed from Rameses, which is interpreted “commotion,” corresponding to carnal unity. Then they set out for Socoth, which is interpreted “tabernacles,” when, namely, the soul is enclosed within the body’s tabernacle. The seventh was at Assur, which is interpreted “cypress,” which is upright and without . . . and corresponds to the seventh unity.

[Col. 0477D] These seven unities were signified by seven elevations attached to the single shaft in the lampstand. For in the lampstand there were four sets of seven about one shaft: namely, seven tops, seven lamps placed above, seven pouring-vessels, and seven reeds proceeding from the shaft, together with the seventh foot supporting the shaft itself. By the seven tops, as we have said, are signified the seven aforesaid unities, upon which are placed the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, like lamps shining in God’s house.

Opposite the first unity is placed the first gift, namely the spirit of fear. For the lust of the first parents transmitted sin to the little child, and from it sin dwells in our mortal flesh. We fear only because of sin; if sin were absent, neither would fear exist. Upon the second unity is placed the spirit of piety. Piety is the worship of God, which in Greek is called *theosebeia* (θεοσέβεια), as though it were then said to the human being: “To the other living creatures are given lesser souls without reason; but to you is given a soul in the image and likeness of God. Therefore it is your duty to know God, to love him when known, and to worship him when loved.” And this is piety, that is, divine worship, which is laid upon him.

[Col. 0478A] The spirit of knowledge is placed upon moral unity. Knowledge is the lower part of reason, through which a person rightly manages and administers earthly things and the affairs of the world, so as to live rightly in the midst of this crooked nation—where no one excuses being mortal.

[Col. 0478B] Thus far proceeded the philosophers of the Gentiles, whose intellects were exhausted in these three matters even to sweat; but because they stopped there, although more remained, they did not live out half their days. The faithful person, however, proceeds until the fountain of unity is shown to him and he hears: “Here worship God.” Let us therefore proceed too, we who have understood more than those elders.

Upon virtuous unity is placed the spirit of fortitude. “For love is strong as death” (Song 8:6). What is stronger than to hate father and mother, wives and children—indeed, even one’s own soul—for God’s sake? This is that most fervent glue with which Noah’s ark was coated inside and outside. Upon spiritual unity is placed the spirit of counsel. For by lofty counsel the Word was made flesh. This is the mystery hidden from the ages. In its own time it became known to men and angels. For in this matter no one was his counsellor, nor did anyone teach him prudence.

[Col. 0478C] Upon spiritual unity is placed the spirit of understanding. Understanding is the power of the soul by which it perceives invisible things. Neither sense, nor imagination, nor reason perceives how our free mother, who is above, bore us to make good the loss of the angels. Upon spiritual unity is placed the spirit of wisdom—namely, that wisdom which is said to derive from *sapor*, “taste,” of which it is said: “Wisdom shall not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wis. 1:4). The wisdom said to derive from *sapere*, “to be wise,” makes even wicked men wise. For if there is delight in carnal love, there is a far more ineffable savour and sweetness in spiritual love, when the created spirit is joined to the uncreated Spirit.

There follows concerning the seven pouring-vessels. This is the Septuagesima of weeks, which the Church represents in order to signify the aforesaid seven unities, so that their remembrance may be poured into our minds through it. For the sake of those who do not read or do not understand the Scriptures, the Church visibly administers certain things in its offices, through which the mind is led onward to the knowledge of invisible things. There is a Septuagesima of days, extending from *Circumdederunt me* (“They surrounded me”) until the Saturday in White, which represents the captivity of the children of Israel under the Chaldeans. There is also a Septuagesima of weeks; that is, there are seven weeks, the first of which is *Circumdederunt me*, the last *Laetare*, according to which the first Sunday is entitled Septuagesima, [Col. 0479A] the second Sexagesima, the third Quinquagesima, and the fourth Quadragesima, which agrees with the number of days. These seven unities are signified in the Church. Thus the first bewails the miseries of carnal unity, saying, “The groans of death surrounded me”; while the last joyfully marvels at the delight of spiritual unity, saying, “Rejoice, Jerusalem.” Our pope likewise represents this by carrying about the golden rose. The intervening ones may also be adapted to their respective unities. But let us hasten to what follows.

Thus it is clear that already seven women have taken hold of one man: for, since these seven weeks represent the condition of this life—even in the things we read and sing—in the two that follow, up to Easter, the Church treats of Christ alone, and the tearful remembrance of his sufferings [perhaps *mysteries*] is heard. Nevertheless, the first seven lamps belonged to the shaft—that is, to Christ—as women taking hold of one man. For he was anointed above his companions, not having the Spirit by measure.

But on that day of which it is said, “That day, a day of wrath,” those who share in the seven unities will take hold of one man; that is, they will know that that one man is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Yet today, in the solemn procession, seven women take hold of one man. For in the Lord’s procession, which we represent today, some went before and some followed, and both cried out: “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matt. 21:9). There was also there an animal bearing the Lord; and here this is the number seven in the lampstand, of the branches together with its base.

For those going before signified that they belonged to him, because there are three branches on the left: that is, the perishing members of the Old Testament, which proceeded from the head toward the east. Those following signified the same thing, because there are three branches on the right: that is, the Fathers of the New Testament apart from the apostles. Both these and those cried: “Hosanna to the Son of David.” For the faith is the same, although the times have changed.

Both these and those are the three men whom Ezekiel saw being saved: Noah, Daniel, and Job. Noah—that is, prelates—cut branches from trees: that is, they expound to the peoples the teaching of both Testaments. Job—that is, active persons—spread their garments upon the way: that is, from their own resources they support the poor, like Job, who warmed the sides of the poor with the fleeces of his sheep. Daniel—that is, contemplatives—cry: “Hosanna to the Son of David.” But the apostles and disciples who were with the Lord are compared to the beast of burden, glorifying God and bearing him in their hearts from sea to sea and to the ends of the whole earth. The Church today represents these persons surrounding Christ, as though on this day seven women were taking hold of one man.

But when we take hold on that day, we shall say: “We shall eat our own bread.” For now we eat another’s bread. In a foreign land we obtain foreign breads for ourselves; but in our own land we shall eat our own bread. Foreign bread is the bread of sorrow. For in the valley of weeping God feeds us with the bread of tears, so that one day it may be said to us: “Rise up after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Ps. 126:5).

There are four such breads, corresponding to the four causes of weeping, on account of which it was said: “Blessed are you who now weep.” For we ought to weep for our own sins, as David wept, saying: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall drench my couch” (Ps. 6:7). We ought also to weep for the sins of others, as the Lord also wept for Lazarus; and when he saw the city, he wept over it, saying: “If you too had recognized your sins, you too would weep, just as I do.” We must also weep for the exile in which we are, as David wept, saying: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged! I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar; my soul has long been a sojourner” (Ps. 119:5). The Apostle too laments, saying: “Who shall deliver me from this body of death?” Fourth, we must weep from longing for the heavenly homeland. So too wept the man who said: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered you, Zion” (Ps. 136:1).

These are the four breads of sorrow which were offered under the Law: bread baked on a griddle, bread baked in a frying-pan, bread cooked in water, and bread baked in an oven. A griddle has many perforated openings, like a net, through which the fire supplied beneath burns what is set above it. In this manner sorrow for our transgressions, insofar as it remembers sins, burns and cauterizes the conscience with as many openings as it pricks.

But bread broken in a frying-pan is not burned by flames rising upward. Thus, when we grieve for our neighbours’ sins, there is made the frying-pan of the saints. Indeed, sorrow at the delay of exile is bread cooked in water, because, through love of flowing water, all mortal things perish in the abyss of this exile. But the upper irrigation, for longing for the homeland, is bread baked in an oven: that is, in the heat of that fire which the Lord came to cast upon the earth, which, coming from heaven, set ablaze the offerings of righteous Abel.

Feeding upon these breads, we shall eat our bread above. “Man shall eat the bread of angels.” And we shall cover ourselves with our own garments. There are two parts of a human being: soul and flesh. God clothes each with its proper garment. Immortality is the garment of the body; innocence, the garment of the soul. After—and because of—sin, the human being was stripped of both. On that day they shall be restored to us; but because our Father is provident, perhaps because when we wore them they had become somewhat sooty, he will restore them washed and whiter. It was a white garment to be able not to die; it was a white garment to be able not to sin. Far whiter will it be not to be able to sin; and thus clothed, we shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of our Father.

Only let the name of Christ be invoked upon us. His first name is “Christ,” and his denominative name is “Christian.” This name, taken in that latter sense, is invoked upon us on the way; but in the homeland we shall be called by the first name. For whoever ascends will be called Christ. “No one has ascended into heaven except him who descended from heaven”; but Christ alone descended. Therefore no one but Christ will ascend. For the members must follow where the head has already gone before, so that in all his members Christ may thus be whole there.

“You shall not break a bone of him” (John 19:36). While he alone dwelt in a human being, he was Christ among human beings—that is, anointed in fullness; and from the ointment of the head, certain drops trickled down upon the beard and even to the hem of his garment. For “of his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16); but when we receive fullness then, we shall truly be Christs. “They shall render into our bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing” (Luke 6:38).

May the Lord Jesus, our Anointed One, pour this highest and complete anointing upon us on that day: that day, I say, when seven women shall take hold of one man; on that day when heaven and earth are to be shaken, when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire. Amen.

## XXX. SECOND SERMON FOR PALM SUNDAY

[Note: From the Victorine manuscript.]

> “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field, which the Lord has blessed. May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, abundance of grain and wine.”

The heavenly Father congratulates you, dearest brothers, because you have come to meet him as most beloved children, with such joy, with so many flowers, with so many palms, with such fragrance of virtue. Sensing the force of the sweet fragrance of his people, he cried out in excessive rejoicing: “Behold, the smell of my son”—

[Note: “[Col. 0481D] We judge that this most intricate passage, scarcely intelligible as it stands, may be restored as follows: ‘Behold, the smell of my son. I perceive his works as a most sweet fragrance.’ Hence the Apostle: ‘We are the good fragrance of Christ to God’ (2 Cor. 2:15). And afterward he sets forth what fragrance this smell may be compared with: ‘Like the smell of a full field,’ where there are many flowers, etc.”]

—because, as the Apostle says, he truly is my son. I perceive his works as a most sweet fragrance; and he afterward sets forth what fragrance this may be compared with: “Like the smell of a full field,” where there are many and various flowers.

Rightly did he compare it with the smell of a field. For the field is the world, in which God scattered his seeds, and in which the varied flowers of virtues shine. But some flowers choose the most spotless integrity of the flesh: these are lilies in God’s field. There are those who have shed their blood for Christ: these are roses in the Lord’s field. For the thorn too flowers in the Lord’s field. One who had formerly been dreadful with the thorns of sins flowers through works of charity while feeding, clothing, lodging, visiting, and consoling the poor. He covers his thorns because, according to the Apostle, “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

Therefore the Lord rightly says in congratulating his people: “Behold, the smell of my son, like the smell of a full field.” But lest anyone presume to say that he possesses those virtues of himself, he adds: “Which the Lord has blessed.”

This congratulation concerning you, dearest brothers, was prefigured in ancient times in Isaac and his sons. Although many know the history, it must nevertheless be touched upon briefly, so that, when you have found its mystery, that which pertains to you may be explained. Isaac is read to have had two sons by Rebecca: Esau, the firstborn, and Jacob (Gen. 25:25). When Isaac was full of years and his eyes had grown dim, he called Esau and said to him: “Bring me some of your hunting, and prepare food from it, that I may eat and bless you” (Gen. 27:4).

When he had said this, their mother persuaded Jacob to bring her two kids, so that she might prepare food from them for his father and Jacob himself might present it to his father in Esau’s guise and steal his brother’s blessing. When the food had been prepared, his mother dressed Jacob in Esau’s garments, which she kept at home, so that Jacob himself might present it to his father and steal his brother’s blessing. But because Esau was hairy, she covered his bare hands and neck with the skins of kids.

When he had offered the food to his father, the latter said in wonder: “How were you able to find it so quickly, my son?” Jacob answered: “It was God’s will that what I wanted should quickly meet me” (ibid., v. 20). His father therefore felt him and found hairy hands, and thought that he was Esau. He ate the food offered to him and drank wine. Then, being satisfied, he kissed him; and, sensing the fragrance of his garments, said: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field, which the Lord has blessed. May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, abundance.”

In this history, dearest brothers, our great rejoicing is figured. God, who is represented by Isaac, has from the beginning of the world begotten only two peoples in his faith: the Jewish and the gentile. The Jewish people was the firstborn son, because it first possessed the worship of the one God. God is ancient because he is eternal; his eyes had grown dim because knowledge of faith in him had greatly perished in the world. He desired to be satisfied by the hunting of his elder son when he desired to be fed by the good works of the Jewish people.

But while that people was negligent and occupied with external goods and the figures of the Law, as though in hunting, Rebecca—that is, spiritual grace—our mother, who bore and instructed us, commanded us, who had been gentiles and afterward became sons, to offer food of good works to our God and to steal the blessing of the elder brother. She commanded us to kill two kids: that is, to mortify our sins, both original and actual.

We put on the garments of the elder son because, after mortifying vices and fulfilling the precepts of the Law which had been given to the ancient people, we have been adorned with good works. The skins of the kids, with which the hands and neck were covered, are the remembrance of sins: though sins have been cleansed in us, yet in humility we acknowledge that we submitted our necks to sins and directed our hands toward evils.

That Isaac did not recognize him and nevertheless blessed him is what the Psalmist says: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. 17:45). He did not see him, because he “was not sent except to the sheep which had perished of the house of Israel.” The Father wondered that his son had found hunting so quickly because the sudden conversion of the gentiles was wonderful. It was God’s will that the son should find hunting so quickly: that is, that the faith of Christ should so quickly fill the world.

The Father ate the food offered to him and was refreshed by wine, because God was delighted by the mortification of our vices and the fervour of good works. The Father kissed the Son when God reconciled the gentile people to himself. Hence in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1). Sensing the fragrance of the garments—that is, the good works with which the soul is adorned—the Father congratulated the Son in these words: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field, which the Lord has blessed.”

This congratulation, brothers, must be fulfilled in us. The Father rejoices in our good works. For in this Lent you have, as it were, slain your kids, your sins; and, offering to your Father the food of virtues, you stand before him, and through the fragrance of virtues which you bore in your minds you have manifested the smell of sons. Therefore he cries: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field.”

But hear what blessing your Father grants you for these gifts: “May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, abundance.” He wishes for you diverse things, and two things, because you are diverse and two kinds of people in the Church of God.

[Note: “From these words of this sermon a not slight conjecture may be drawn that Hildebert delivered it at Cluny, while he was living there before his appointment to the office of schoolmaster at Le Mans. For there truly were there two classes of people: laymen, flocking there from every side, and monks, who under Saint Abbot Hugh devoted themselves alike to a more solid piety and to sacred letters. Among them Hildebert so distinguished himself by piety and by sermons, delivered before them at the command of the most holy abbot, that, as his fame spread abroad, Hoellus, the most devout and zealous bishop of Le Mans, summoned him thence to be schoolmaster of his church; a few years later, as we related in his Life, he promoted him to the archdeaconry.”]

Some possess temporal things; others despise the world for God’s sake; and both are gathered here. Here are God’s poor, that is, monks; there are the rich of the world, that is, laymen. For contemplatives he prays that the dew of heaven be given; for secular persons, the fatness of the earth. The dew of heaven, sweet and subtle, is spiritual grace, which instils into minds the sweetness and subtlety of heavenly contemplation. The fatness of the earth is the fruitfulness of good grace, which abounds in earthly goods. Hence David: “Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness of the earth” (Ps. 62:6). The Lord desires this blessing for his field, that is, his people, which has delighted him with its flowers.

But beware, dearest brothers, lest in the Lord’s field a bare thorn be found without flowers. If the Lord finds it in his field, it will be cut down with his sickle and cast into the fire. A thorn bare of flowers is a sinner bare of good works. Alas! There are now more thorns than roses in the Church of God. One rose, many thorns; and the rose among thorns is injured by the thorns. Hence in the Song of Songs: “As a rose among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters.”

[Note: “The Vulgate has: ‘As a lily among thorns’ (Song 2:2).”]

Behold: souls which ought to be daughters of God are called thorns. They harass, prick, and tear good souls. For when evil people see good persons, they speak against them; they neither wish to be good themselves nor love the good. Although they speak peaceably in their presence, they speak against them when absent. Of such David says: “They surrounded me like bees” (Ps. 117:12). Bees have honey in the mouth and a wound in the sting of the tail. So too all who flatter with their tongue but secretly, out of malice, serve [perhaps: strike] are bees: in speaking, they offer the sweetness of honey, but in secretly striking, they inflict a wound.

There are other people who openly afflict the good, such as those who seize the goods of the Church by plundering. Of them the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: “You have consumed my vineyard, and the plunder of the poor is in your house” (Isa. 3:14). Those consume the vineyard who devour the goods of the Church. The thorns also harm the Lord’s roses in another way. If evil persons see a poor person or a stranger, a widow or an orphan, they oppress them in judgment in favour of a rich man and accept gifts against the innocent. But David says: “I know that the Lord will execute judgment for the needy and vengeance for the poor” (Ps. 19:13). “The Lord guards strangers; he will uphold the orphan and widow, and he will destroy the ways of sinners” (Ps. 145:9).

What shall we say of fornications, murders, usuries, perjuries, hatreds, and those who consent to them? Of these David says: “If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Ps. 49:18). One runs with them and places one’s portion with them who consents to them. The Lord’s field is full of many thorns.

For these thorns the Lord wore a crown of thorns, because, as Isaiah says, “He himself was wounded for our sins and bruised for our crimes” (Isa. 53:5). Our thorns pierced him, because he accepted the punishment for our sins, which he had not committed, according to that saying: “Then I paid what I did not steal” (Ps. 65:8). Brothers, rightly pay for what the Lord paid for without deserving it. Turn your thorn into a rose. The redness of a rose signifies shame. Be ashamed because of your sins, and you will become God’s roses.

There are two kinds of shame, of which it is written: “There is shame that brings sin, and there is shame that brings glory” (Ecclus. 5:25). Hence the Lord rebukes the sinner through the Prophet: “The forehead of a harlot has become yours; you refused to be ashamed” (Jer. 3:3). Therefore be ashamed of your sins and confess them to a priest. Some say that they can repent without a minister of the Church; but no one ought to presume this. The power of loosing has not been given to everyone, but only to the apostles and their vicars, to whom it was said: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 18:18). And: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20:23).

When the Lord had raised Lazarus, he said to his disciples: “Go and loose him” (John 11:24). Lazarus bears the person of all penitents; the apostles, the person of ministers. Although Lazarus was alive, he could not walk until he was loosed. Likewise, unless compelled by the necessity of death, a penitent is not to be loosed except by a minister of the Church. Therefore, in the old Law, healed lepers were commanded: “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” The Apostle James says: “Confess your sins to one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. 5:16). And David: “For I shall declare my iniquity, and I shall confess [variant: *I shall consider*] concerning my sin” (Ps. 37:19).

For this reason the Lord willed that one person should be loosed by another: so that one should need another, and thus the unity of charity might be preserved; and so that a person might not trust in himself and spare himself. For this reason he willed to entrust us to human beings to be healed, not to angels, so that the frail might condescend to the frail, according to the Apostle: “If a person be overtaken in any offence, you who are spiritual, support such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. 6:1).

Therefore approach your prelates confidently; confess your sins to your physicians, so that you may flower in the Lord’s field and render to God your Father a sweet fragrance, so that he may say to you: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field.” May God, who came to call sinners to repentance and does not will the death of the sinner but that he should be converted and live, deign to grant you this grace. He lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## XXXI. THIRD SERMON FOR PALM SUNDAY

[Note: From the Victorine manuscript.]

> “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your King comes to you, gentle, sitting upon an ass and a colt, the foal of a beast under the yoke” (Matt. 21:5).

The heavenly King commands us, dearest brothers, through the prophet Zechariah to rejoice at his coming. The Lord comes for reconciliation. He who had been estranged through the sin of the first parent, before he came sent beforehand as envoys the prophets and patriarchs, saying to them: “Say to the daughter of Zion,” that is, announce it to my Church. He calls her the daughter of Zion because she ought to be a daughter of watchfulness and love. For Zion is interpreted “watchfulness,” because she ought to guard herself against spiritual enemies.

And he adds what they are to say: “Behold, your King will come to you.” Through sin the Lord had withdrawn from humankind, to whom he had been near while it lived rationally. For the Lord appears to have been angry with Adam when, after the first man’s sin, the Lord is read to have walked in paradise in the breeze after midday—unless by this act he signified to miserable humanity that he who had been kind and gracious toward it was now, by the estrangement of guilt, removed from it, walking in grief and saying: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 2:12). That is: In how great a misery are you placed?

The breeze in which he walks signified that charity in the human mind had cooled, and that he himself was cooled from love for humankind. This cooling was after midday—that is, after the heat of charity had departed from the human mind. But he who had withdrawn through justice came through mercy, namely through “the bowels of the mercy of our God, by which the dawn from on high has visited us”: “He bowed the heavens and came down, and darkness was under his feet” (Ps. 17:10).

He bowed the heavens—that is, the heavenly things, even the Godhead and the angels themselves—through the compassion which he had for the restoration of humankind; and he himself came down, uniting human nature to himself. The angels were bowed when, descending to the Lord, they ministered to him (Matt. 4:7). But though humble, though a participant in our frailty, nevertheless the darkness and blindness of worldly persons were under his feet: that is, the world was wholly subject to him.

And when the mighty warrior came to battle, “he placed his tent in the sun” (Ps. 18:6). The tent of Christ is understood to be that in which he campaigned for God the Father. He placed it—that is, established it—in the sun, that is, in the Virgin, who was “beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun” (Song 6:9): moon, because she illuminates the darkness of night; sun, because beyond others she alone burned with the heat of the Holy Spirit.

When his tent had thus been prepared, advancing as a bridegroom, he became the bridegroom of the Church through union of the flesh, coming forth as though from his bridal chamber—that is, from the Virgin’s womb. “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (ibid.): that is, as mighty and unconquerable, to run the course of his warfare. He came to battle against the prince of this world, saying: “Now the prince of this world shall be cast out” (John 12:31), namely from the minds of human beings, in which he had previously ruled.

He chose a few poor people with him, as the Apostle says: “He chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1:17). For what were Peter and Andrew but unlearned and low-born men? Yet among those few one fell, namely Judas, who betrayed him. This Judas was covetous and a thief; holding the money-box, he carried the things that were put into it. Seeing Mary pour precious ointment upon the Lord’s head, he said: “Why this waste? For it could have been sold for much and given to the poor” (Mark 14:5). Therefore he went to the chief priests to betray him to them.

Unhappy Judas! He wished the loss which he believed had arisen from the pouring out [perhaps *effusion*] of the ointment to be made good by the price of his master. And when the merciful master wished to correct his erring disciple, he said: “He who dips his hand with me in the dish, this one is about to betray me” (Matt. 16:23), so that, knowing that he knew his thoughts, he might repent. But while the others withdrew their hands, Judas, in the shamelessness with which he was to betray him, put his hand with his master’s into the dish, that by his boldness he might feign a good conscience.

When he said, “One of you will betray me” (John 13:21), and the others said, “Is it I, Lord? Is it I, Rabbi?” (Matt. 26:22), they called him Lord, but Judas called him Master, by which he wished to diminish the sin he had conceived. For it seemed less serious to betray a master than the Lord. But the Lord overcame even him by the patience with which he endured him; and although he knew him to be the betrayer, he nevertheless did not refuse to wash his feet.

The Lord was therefore handed over to the Jews; this betrayal was prefigured in Joseph. Jacob had twelve sons, but loved one above the rest, namely Joseph, whom all the others envied. When their father sent him to visit his brothers and the flocks, and he came to Dothan, the others, inflamed against him, said to one another: “Behold, the dreamer comes. Come, let us kill him and see what good his dreams will do him” (Gen. 37:19–20). For he had dreamed that he was in a field and that the sheaves of his brothers were worshipping his sheaf; and again, that the sun, moon, and eleven stars had worshipped him. By Judah’s counsel, therefore, he was sold to the Ishmaelites, who carried him into Egypt.

All these things, dearest brothers, are understood mystically of Christ. Jacob signified God, who sent his Son, Christ, into Dothan—that is, into the world—to visit his brothers, that is, the Jews, to see what they themselves and the flocks entrusted to them were doing. Joseph is interpreted “increase,” and Dothan, “deficiency.” Thus the Lord can be signified by Joseph, who daily causes the Church to increase in virtues. And rightly is the world compared with Dothan, because through the failure of virtues it daily diminishes.

Joseph’s brothers were in Dothan and pastured their flocks there. The Jews were intent on worldly matters and instructed others in worldly matters. They called him a dreamer because, when he preached invisible and unheard things, these appeared to be dreams, though such dreams have some figure. Joseph’s sheaf signifies Christ, who said: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone” (John 12:24). The sheaves of the others signify all faithful persons who bear fruit and worship God.

Again, the sun worships Christ, and the moon and stars and the brightness of angels, because they tremble before him; and the Church—that is, the faithful—supplicates and venerates him. He was sold to the Ishmaelites—that is, to the Jews—by Judas the betrayer. The type and the one typified were called by the same name. Ishmaelites are interpreted “hearers.” But the Jews were hearers of the Law, not doers, against whom the Apostle says: “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only” (Jas. 1:22). They led him into Egypt, that is, into the darkness of death. For Egypt is interpreted “darkness,” as David says: “They placed me in the lowest pit, in dark places and in the shadow of death” (Ps. 106:10).

He afterward indicated that death more expressly through Joseph. We read that, when Joseph’s mistress loved him and wished to entice him to consent to her, he fled, leaving the cloak by which she wished to hold him. She accused him before her husband of wishing to force and violate her. For this reason he was sent into a dark prison with two others, namely the king’s cupbearer and baker. Of these, one, namely the cupbearer, was saved and released from prison, as Joseph foretold; but the other, namely the baker, was hanged on wood. Joseph too was at last released from prison and deserved to become lord of Egypt.

Under this figure the Lord’s death and resurrection are more clearly shown. That mistress who wished to entice Joseph to herself is understood as the Synagogue, which wished to entice Christ to itself by striving to make him like itself in its understanding of the Law. For the Jews would have loved him if Christ had wished to live carnally and understand the Law carnally. But, casting away the veil—that is, the carnal and literal understanding of the Law—he fled from consenting to the synagogue.

But she accused him before her lord, that is, Pilate, as one wishing to abolish the Law, and caused him to be condemned with two thieves. One of these was saved, saying: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 24:42); and Christ himself foretold and promised: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (ibid., v. 43). But the other, persisting in wickedness, died upon the wood unsaved.

O how different the merits which Christ distinguishes in the midst! Both signify the future judgment, in which through the cross he will condemn some and save others. O how different are the paths! One ascends into heaven; another descends into hell. The punishment is similar, but the reward different. The one is an example for sinners, lest they despair: at the very point of death he deserved paradise by a single word. The other is a terror for the despairing and impenitent, who, unwilling to repent, died in their sins. Then Christ’s death will be equally near to both and equally beneficial to both, if they would be willing; for Christ’s death compels no one.

In this hour Adam went out of paradise, in which the thief sought paradise. Joseph’s release from prison signifies the liberation of the risen Christ from death. The Lord afterward became lord of Egypt because, after the resurrection, he enlightened and converted the gentile people who were in darkness. Hence it is written: “The people of the gentiles who walked in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. 9:2). Nor did he become Lord of the gentiles only, but also of the Jews. For there are two walls in the Church: one of Jews, the other of gentiles.

Here therefore, dearest brethren, are contained in the aforesaid announcement the coming of Christ and this salvation of both peoples. For it says: “Behold, your king comes to you, gentle, upon a colt of an ass, the foal of a beast under the yoke.” For the King of heaven comes—not as a stranger, but as yours—through the humanity which, as we have said, he assumed. And he comes to you, that is, [Col. 0488D] for your salvation; for he comes not for himself, who has no need of a servant, but [supp. he is] he whom the servant needs; he comes to you, who were needy and exiled: “Raising the needy from the earth, and lifting the poor from the dung-hill” (Ps. 112:1). That is, he raises those asleep in sins from the earth, namely from earthly pleasures, needy of true riches; and he lifts from the dung of vices those poor in virtues. Hence it is written: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1:17), that is, fools in the dung of vices. He comes not angry, not terrifying, but gentle and humble. He humbled himself unto death, even death upon the cross. Indeed, he was so humbled that he said: “But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men, 371 and the outcast of the people” (Ps. 21:7).

[Col. 0489A] Hence he said: “My God, my God, look upon me: why have you forsaken me? The words of my offenses are far from my salvation” (Ps. 21:2). And again: “My God, I shall cry by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and it is not folly in me” (Ps. 21:3). But we must consider how the Son of God says that he has been forsaken by the Father, to whom he is coequal and consubstantial. God granted the ancient Fathers only temporal things: abundance of grain and oil, and victory over enemies. But when God came into the world, preaching and promising other goods which the human race had lost through its own fault, and in order to show by word and example that temporal things are not true goods, he chose to be so poor in the world that the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head, and that he asked water from [Col. 0489B] a girl beside a well. Behold, this man seemed so forsaken by men that he suffered want and tribulation; and therefore he says: “My God, my God, look upon me.” Strengthen me, lest I fail in this wicked tribulation, forsaken by you. Therefore look upon me. And “why have you forsaken me?” means: Why have you appeared to forsake me? As though he said: Others do not know, but I have understood. You have therefore forsaken me in temporal matters in order to give eternal things. They do not know why you have forsaken me, but I shall explain it. Namely, you have forsaken me because the sins of my people, whom I came to redeem, required this; and this is meant by “because of the words of my offenses”—that is, the offenses of human beings—“far from my salvation,” because their sins grant [that is, require] that I be slain for them. “I am a worm and not a man,” that is, trampled and worthless like [Col. 0489C] a worm, and not regarded as a man, but as a madman possessed by a demon; “the reproach of men,” upon whom people cast reproaches; and “the outcast of the people,” of whom it was said: “This world will never be free unless this man is cast out.”

The other of these says: “My God, I shall cry by day, and you will not hear.” This must be understood as follows. There is a twofold will, one natural and the other spiritual. The natural will is to love the present life, to shrink from death, and to love prosperity; yet this will is not sinful if it agrees with the spiritual will. The spiritual will is to love heavenly things and not to fear death or adversity. Christ chose to have both wills, in order to teach how both ought to be possessed. For he feared [Col. 0489D] by the nature of the flesh when he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38); but he overcame the natural by the spiritual. When the former prayed for prosperity, it was not heard. When the latter prayed for adversity, that is, for the redemption of the world, it was heard. This is the meaning of: “My God, I shall cry by day, and you will not hear.” “By day,” 372 that is, for prosperity, “and you will not hear.” He cried for prosperity when he fed five thousand people with five loaves and two fishes, and the people therefore wished to make him king. The flesh would have wished this; but the will of the soul prevailed, since, when the Lord saw the people’s intention, he withdrew alone to the mountain, away from the people. Thus it willed this, and was not heard.

Again: [Col. 0490A] “I shall cry by night, and you will not hear.” He cried in the night, that is, amid the adversity of the Passion, when he said: “Father, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39), that is, this Passion. The flesh, shrinking from death, prayed this, and was not heard. Again he cried; but what did the spirit pray? “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (ibid.). Behold, the flesh struggled with the spirit, but the will of God was preferred to the human will and was heard. The head of the martyrs therefore feared, lest martyrs despair when, by nature, they feared sufferings. For if the head had not feared, the members would say: “I am not of the head [better: of the body]. The one head did not fear.” Behold, the head fears and teaches the members that to fear is not a sin; yet fear is overcome. But let us see what follows.

[Col. 0490B] “Sitting upon an ass and a colt, the foal of a beast under the yoke.” All this is said mystically. For it could not literally be fulfilled that he sat upon both. Yet as the Lord approached his Passion and came to Jerusalem, he sent two disciples to a village, where, outside at the crossroads before the gate, an ass was tied with her colt; and he said to them: “Untie them and bring them to me” (Matt. 18:18). The beast under the yoke signifies the Jews, who were under the yoke of the Law, bound by many transgressions and many sins. The colt of the ass signifies the Gentile people: young, because newly converted to the faith; and the ass’s colt, because through the primitive Church Jews and peoples were converted. The two were before the gate, at a crossroads, because Christ is the gate, as he himself says: “I am the door” (John 10:7). Outside [Col. 0490C] this gate each was, while each remained bound by sins. They were placed at a crossroads because they followed many paths of error. Two disciples were sent because there are two kinds of preachers who were sent to the two peoples: Paul and Barnabas were sent to the Gentiles; Peter and the others preached in Judaea. He untied them. The Lord sits upon those whom he has untied, because through indwelling grace he found rest in their hearts.

Likewise, brethren, every day the Lord, sitting upon the ass and upon the colt, goes toward Jerusalem when, governing the soul of each faithful person—his own beast of burden—he leads it to the vision of peace. He sits upon the beast of burden when he presides over the universal holy Church and kindles it with desire for the peace above. Let us therefore go out to meet him 373 [Col. 0490D] with palms, that is, with victories won over the devil and his works, and with the flowers of virtues. Let one offer the flower of love, which is the chief root of all virtues. Of it Gregory says:

> “As many branches spring from one root, so many virtues are born from charity alone.”

[Note: [Col. 0489D] Homily 27 on the Gospels.]

Let another offer the flower of virginity and the lily of chastity. This is that virtue which Jesus commended in John, whom he loved, and which John himself praises in the Apocalypse: “These are those who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins” (Rev. 14:4). Let another be endowed with the flower of humility and imitate him who says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble [Col. 0491A] in heart” (Matt. 11:29). Let another be adorned with the flower of mercy, because “blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7). Let another hold the branch of penitence [read: patience], because “blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:10). Let another burn incense, that is, prayers, saying: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. 140:1). Let another receive Christ in the poor, remembering the saying of the Gospel: “What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40). And so let no one approach the Lord empty-handed, that we may all deserve to be ridden by the Lord, and that, sitting upon us, he may deign to lead and govern us into the highest Jerusalem. He who lives and reigns unto ages of ages. [Col. 0491B] Amen.

## XXXII. FOURTH SERMON FOR PALM SUNDAY

[Note: [Col. 0491D] From manuscript E of Saint-Germain, no. 381.]

> “Raise a standard in Zion . . . Gather yourselves [Vulgate: take courage] . . . A lion has come up from his lair; the plunderer of the nations has raised himself . . . to make the land . . . a wilderness . . . For this, gird yourselves with sackcloth, mourn and howl” (Jer. 4:6 ff.).

These words, by which through Jeremiah the Lord exhorts us to gather together and raise a standard against the lion coming up from his lair, are spirit and life, because when spiritually understood they give life to hearts, strengthen weakened knees, and raise slack hands. They must therefore be understood spiritually, because the lion is spiritual, not bodily; the standard is spiritual, and Zion is spiritual. This [Col. 0491C] is the lion of whom Peter says: “Your adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). He goes about because he encircles by snares and seduces through manifold deceit. Hence Habakkuk: “He spreads his net, and never ceases to slay the nations” (Hab. 1:17). This is not the apostolic net, woven with the double texture of the New and Old Testaments, which, cast by evangelical fishers—that is, the apostles—into the sea of this world gathers fish of every kind, that is, human beings; rather, Christ’s fishers cast the evil out, while retaining and feeding the good. But the devil’s net does not gather but scatters, as Truth himself says of him in the Gospel: “He who does not gather with me [Col. 0491D] scatters” (Luke 11:23); it does not feed but suffocates; it does not give life but kills.

This is Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who killed the male Hebrews and kept the females alive (Exod. 1:16), because the devil, king of darkness and author of tribulation, strives to suffocate and extinguish the virtues of the saints and their manly deeds—those who, like true Hebrews, pass and go beyond the way of this world without clinging to carnal allurements, running toward their homeland. But he increases and preserves the females, that is, the works of the weak and carnal. This net is woven not from straight but crooked threads, that is, from varied and manifold deceits, because he himself is a liar and the father of it, that is, the author of falsehood. [Col. 0492A] He first devised falsehood when, swelling with pride, he said: “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14). And again, to the first parents: “In whatever hour you eat, you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:5). He spread this net when he exercised every deceitful snare to seduce and capture man—something he began by this net in Paradise, when he seduced him by a deceptive suggestion—and thereafter he does not cease to kill.

For as beasts of the forest, once they have tasted human blood, always thirst for it, so this roaring lion and plunderer of nations, enticed by choice food and rich fare, strives with all his power always to slaughter and consume more. Hence Habakkuk: “His portion is fat, and his food choice” (Hab. 1:16). For this lion seeks precious and choice foods, [Col. 0492B] whose arrogance is greater than his power and whose rage is greater than his strength; he raised himself so high that he stretched out his hand even against the head of the human race, that is, against Christ. During Christ’s Passion he also tempted the disciples, according to the saying: “Behold, Satan has demanded you, that he may sift you like wheat” (Luke 22:3); and he brought down some who seemed great. He drew Judas, who carried the money-box, into the crime of perdition; Judas went out into the abyss of despair, and thus he slaughtered and consumed him, stored him in the net, and kept him shut in, with the mouth of the pit pressing down upon him. He also cast Peter, prince of the apostles, into the guilt of denial, and thus slaughtered him but did not consume him, because he did not swallow him into the abyss. For the Lord looked upon [Col. 0492C] him, who had said to him: “And I will pray for you, that your faith may not fail” (ibid., 32)—and “going outside, he wept bitterly” (Matt. 26:75). Then, by the confession of threefold love, he utterly rooted out [read: expiated] the guilt of his threefold denial.

But carefully observe the power and order of grace in Peter’s restoration. Though he was the first of the apostles, God permitted him to fall, so that through his own fault he might learn how he ought to have mercy on the faults of others; and he raised him from his fall, so that sinners might learn from him the ground and order of their own rising again from a fall. For confession followed weeping, weeping followed going out, and going out followed the Lord’s look; for he would not have gone out unless he had wept, nor wept unless the Lord had looked upon him—[Col. 0492D] him who could truly say with the Prophet: “Driven,” namely by the lion, “I was overthrown” from the height of virtues [read: from the summit of virtues], “but the Lord received me” (Ps. 117:19), receiving me by looking upon me.

Good is this look, by which the sinner is helped, not crushed; illuminated, not blinded; healed, not condemned. This look is help and light: not that of one hostile, but of one gracious; not of one angry, but of one merciful. The Lord did not look upon the sin of the Sodomites and Gomorrites in this manner. “I will go down,” he says, “and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry that has come to me, or not” (Gen. 18:21). God speaks after the manner of one angry and threatening, not of one doubting; his wrath is without [Col. 0493A] disturbance, because he is unchangeable, but God adapts himself to human speech in order to instruct humankind. To restrain people from rash judgment, he chose first to examine Sodom’s evils before judging them. Thus God sees those sinners, but as it were from afar, not near at hand; angrily, not graciously; for destruction, not for warning. Hence the Prophet: “The Lord is exalted, and he looks upon lowly things; and he knows lofty things from afar” (Ps. 137:6).

But he looked upon Peter from near at hand and made him fear, according to the saying: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble” (Ps. 103:32). The earth is the human mind; when he looks upon it—that is, touches and illumines it by his grace—he makes it tremble with the dread [read: fear] of sins, while, being looked upon, it is disturbed and afraid. [Col. 0493B] Therefore he looked upon Peter so that Peter might look upon his own guilt, recoil at the sight of it, blush from horror, and by blushing amend. Health-giving is this look, by which the sinner is set before his own face, so that what, in negligence, he had cast behind his back, he may carefully bring before his face. He certainly would not do this unless the Lord looked upon him—that is, unless grace preceded and aided him. For it is written in Proverbs concerning the way of wickedness: “All who enter by it shall not return, nor attain the paths of life” (Prov. 2:19). This is not said because many do not rise after a fall, return from wickedness, and hold to the paths of life; rather, they do not do this of themselves.
