Of themselves, indeed, they can enter into wickedness and can fall, but they cannot return and walk in the straight way. [Col. 0493C] Hence Jeremiah: “I know, Lord, that a person’s way is not his own, nor is it a man’s to walk and direct my steps” (Jer. 10:23). Hence also the Apostle says: “It is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy” (Rom. 9:16).

Let us therefore implore, brethren, to be looked upon by the Lord in such a way that, illumined by his grace, we may go outside with Peter. But what is it to go outside? To uncover the wound of hidden sin, reveal the concealed disease, accuse oneself rather than defend oneself. Hence the Prophet: “I made my offense known to you, and did not hide my injustice” (Ps. 31:5). And elsewhere: “Pour out your hearts before him” (Ps. 61:9). And what is it to go outside? To put off the old human being with its deeds [Col. 0493D] and put on the new human being, so that one may be able to say with the Apostle: “I live—yet no longer I; rather, Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). For unless each person repents of the old life, he cannot begin the new, because a new patch is not sewn onto an old garment, lest the tear become greater; nor is new wine put into old wineskins, lest they burst (Matt. 9:17); nor does a variegated garment please the bridegroom.

But again, I ask, what is it to go outside? It is to be free from the turbulent commotions of evil thoughts, by which the sinner, while wakeful [read: negligent], cannot hear the word of God or behold the vision. For in the quiet of the mind and amid the anxiety [read: solitude] of worldly tumults [Col. 0494A] Moses heard the voice of the Lord and saw the vision. While mingled with the Egyptians, he did not hear the Lord’s voice; but after killing the Egyptian, when he fled into the desert and remained there forty years, he became, as it were, asleep to the restless tumults of earthly desires. Thus he deserved to receive the divine voice, because through heavenly grace, the more one dies to the desire of earthly things, the more truly one awakens to the knowledge of inward realities. The mind then penetrates the words of God more truly when it separates itself from external actions and tumults. But a person is wakeful badly when the heat of worldly cares insolently disturbs him. For the crowd of clamorous thoughts closes the ear of the heart; the more their sound is restrained, the less the voice of the presiding Judge is heard. A person cannot perfectly suffice for both things while divided, because, while entangled outwardly, he grows hard inwardly.

[Col. 0494B] Therefore let the sinner go outside from oldness by putting on the new human being; from silence by confessing sin; from noisy tumult by giving himself to the quiet of solitude. Thus he shall weep bitterly for his own sins and those of others, as from the lower spring, and for desire of the heavenly homeland, as from the upper spring; 377 and then the threefold confession of love will follow, so that, since God is triune, he may profess three times that he loves him—not them—for although God is triune, he is nevertheless but one God. This is also a confession of praise, by which we eagerly praise God, just as the former is a confession made in leaving sin, by which we humbly bewail our sins.

From the examples set forth it is now clear what splendid [Col. 0494C] feasts the strong lion seeks. Like a two-edged enemy he lies in wait, setting snares and traps to capture people. Some he slaughters and consumes: that is, after their fall he constrains them, as though by cart-ropes, lest they rise again. Others he slaughters but does not consume: he sifts them like wheat and casts them down by crushing them, but grace comes to their aid and raises them up. Hence in the Song of Songs: “I shall say to the north wind: Give; and to the south wind: Do not hinder.” The north wind is the unclean spirit, harsh and cold. The south wind is the gentle and mild Spirit, warming cold minds with the fire of love. Hence: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; breathe upon the bride’s garden, that its spices may flow.”

[Note: [Col. 0493] The Vulgate reads: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; breathe upon my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song 4:16).]

As though he said: Depart, unclean spirit; and you, Holy Spirit, restore us. [Col. 0494D] Therefore I shall say to the north wind: “Give,” because I restrain the devil lest he be able to retain those whom he has captured; and to the south wind, that is, the Holy Spirit: “Do not hinder,” that is, do not withdraw grace, without which they cannot return. Thus I shall restrain the former so that he may desist; I shall send the latter so that he may assist and lead them back. Others he neither slaughters nor consumes, because he does not shake their purity [read: holiness] by a deadly stain; they can say with the Prophet: “Those who surrounded me surrounded me like fire among thorns, and in the name of the Lord, because I took vengeance on them” (Ps. 117:12), because I did not fear the hostile camp rising against me; rather, they themselves were weakened and fell. These sing a song; those, a lament; [Col. 0495A] and others, woe. For Ezekiel saw a scroll, upon which these three things were written inside and outside: “A song, a lament, and woe” (Ezek. 2:9). And it was said to him: “Take the scroll and devour it” (Ezek. 3:1). This scroll is Sacred Scripture, which, to those who understand spiritually, depicts within and without—that is, before Christ’s coming and after it—the threefold life of humankind. For one part contains song, another lament, and another woe. They sing the song who, from the first hour, prevenient grace having acted, avoided the condemnable corruptions of crimes, unpolluted by any dregs of mortal sins and not buried beneath heaps of sand, such as John the Baptist and the Mother of the Lord. Others sing the lament who, although they have sinned mortally, have nevertheless been revived when stirred up by grace, such as Peter. [Col. 0495B] Others sing woe: those who did not wash away crimes with tears, but, reaching the abyss, despised, according to the saying: “When a sinner comes into the abyss, he despises” (Prov. 18:3). 378 And: “The dead shall not praise you, Lord, nor all who descend into hell” (Ps. 113:17).

How horrible and dreadful these things are, brethren. Horrible indeed is the fall into the abyss where woe is sung. This is to perish in Egypt. For among the children of Israel some also perished in Egypt: namely, those who sing woe. Others died in the wilderness: namely, those who sing lament. Others are in the holy land: namely, those who sing the song. Therefore, that you may not perish in Egypt and may escape everlasting woe, gird yourselves with sackcloth and howl: that is, in vehement contrition of heart produce [Col. 0495C] fruits worthy of penitence. Ashes and sackcloth are indeed the arms of penitents. Therefore gird yourselves, because the plunderer of nations has raised himself in order to make the territory a wilderness.

This is the holy land, the city of the righteous, the faithful city, which the plunderer of nations attempts to defile and reduce to a wilderness; but he cannot do so. Hence Ecclesiastes: “There was a small city, and few men in it; a great king came against it, surrounded it, and built a fortification around it, and the siege was complete. But a poor and wise man was found in it, who delivered the city by his wisdom” (Eccl. 9:14–15). The small city is the holy Church, small in number, not in merit, in comparison with [Col. 0495D] the larger number of the reprobate. Hence the Gospel says: “Do not fear, little flock” (Luke 12:32). And elsewhere: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22:14). It is small because of the fewness of the elect, not because of the multitude of the called. Although it is small, it is nevertheless unconquerable and invincible, because it is fortified by strong supports. For its foundation is upon the rock, that is, upon Christ: “For the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). Hence the Lord says to Peter: “And I say to you that you are Peter” (Matt. 10:18), so named from me, the rock; “and upon this rock,” from which you are called Peter, “and upon me, not upon you, I shall build my Church.”

This is that small city [Col. 0496A]—small because it has few men in it. There are indeed many carnal and unlearned persons in it, so that at times the moon, that is, the Church, seems dark; yet there are few men in it who act manfully. Hence Isaiah: “The Lord saw that there was no man, and he was astonished because there was none to meet him” (Isa. 59:16), namely, none intervening for others, as Moses did in the wilderness, saying for his brothers: “Either forgive them this sin, or blot me out from the book of life” (Exod. 32:31). Few such men are in this city, who set themselves as a wall for the house of Israel. Yet there are some within it. For this is the city Jerusalem, to which the Lord says: “Your kings shall be your foster-fathers” (Isa. 49:13), namely, the apostles and apostolic men, whose hearts are in God’s hand, who govern themselves and others spiritually. Hence King Abimelech says to Abraham: [Col. 0496B] “You are to us as God” (Gen. 20).

Of such men Isaiah says elsewhere: “Those who hope in the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall take up wings like eagles; they shall run and not grow weary; they shall walk and not fail” (Isa. 40:31). He rightly says, “Those who hope in the Lord,” not in themselves, because, as Jeremiah says, “Cursed is he who makes flesh his arm” (Jer. 17:5). They shall renew their strength: weak in the world, they shall become strong in God; foolish in the world’s eyes, they shall become wise before God, according to the Apostle: “If anyone among you seems wise in this age, let him become foolish that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God” (1 Cor. 3:19). Therefore these shall renew their strength, both here according to the quality of their conduct [Col. 0496C] and after death, when they become immortal; and they shall take the wings of virtues, by which they may fly to God and rest. Hence the Prophet: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, that I may fly and rest?” (Ps. 54:7). They will take these wings like eagles, that is, renewed. For the eagle, as the story goes, renews itself when its beak, overly hooked with age, is struck against a rock. Thus those who put to death the oldness of sin through the rock, Christ, being renewed, die to the world and are renewed for God. Hence: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102:5).

Such people run to God on the feet of twofold love, and they shall not grow weary, because all things are easy to one who loves. They walk by advancing from virtue to virtue. [Col. 0496D] And they shall not fail until they see the God of gods in Zion. Such are the men of this city, though they are few. They have invincible warriors, who may be killed but cannot be bent, because they have an unconquered leader, namely the house of the coot. Hence the Prophet: “The house of the coots is their leader.”

[Note: [Col. 0495D] Vulgate: “The house of the heron is their leader” (Ps. 103).]

The house of the coot, a sea-bird or marsh-bird, is a rock in the water which, battered by waves, breaks them but is not broken. This house is strong, though it is not on high. This is our rock, namely Christ, who, though he suffered so much from the Jews, remained whole—than whom nothing is stronger, nothing humbler. The Jews were dashed against him and were broken; he remained whole. He is therefore deservedly the leader of the citizens of this [Col. 0497A] city. Most worthy is this city, ruled by such a leader and inhabited by such citizens, whose foundation is upon a rock, humble indeed but invincible.

It has four sides: it is square, namely by the four principal virtues—justice, courage, prudence, and temperance. Hence in the Apocalypse: “The city lies foursquare; its length is as great as its breadth” (Rev. 21:16), because wherever the virtues are present, they are equal. It has four gates, the four Evangelists, and twelve towers, the twelve Apostles, concerning whom it says: “Proclaim” to the Lord “in its towers” (Ps. 47:13), that is, preach in the concord of the apostles. Above, it has the covering of the Holy Spirit. For the roofs of the houses of this [Col. 0497B] city are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, according to the saying: “Who covers its upper parts with waters” (Ps. 103). These are the waters of which Truth himself says: “He who believes in me, from his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7:38). Explaining this, the Evangelist adds: “He said this of the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive.” They too are houses of this city, in which God is known, according to the saying: “God shall be known in her houses, when he receives her” (Ps. 47:4). But by what is he known in those houses? By the covering, namely by the grace of the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness” (1 Cor. 12:7), that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, through which God appears in a person.

[Col. 0497C] Therefore this city is glorious. Hence David: “Glorious things are said of you, city of God” (Ps. 86:3). Though earthly, it is unconquerable, against which a great king comes. This is the king of Babylon, that is, of confusion; not his own power but our weakness has made him great and strong. Surrounded by many spiritual wickednesses, he comes against the city of God in order to make it a wilderness. But whence does he come? From Babylon, of which he is king. Hence Truth says: “For the prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John 14:30). It is as though there are two cities, Jerusalem and Babylon, mingled in body but divided in mind. One is of the good—our Jerusalem—whose ruler is Christ and which begins from the first righteous person; the other is of the evil, whose ruler is the devil and from which every unjustly shed blood is required. This is called Babylon. Its citizens afflict and persecute the citizens of Jerusalem. These two kingdoms are contrary and greatly opposed. These two households, of the righteous and the unjust, are very much disunited and discordant. One tends toward life, the other toward death. The citizens of Jerusalem are written in the book of the living. The citizens of Babylon are assigned with those who are in hell, of whom it is said: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous” (Ps. 68:19).

Therefore, my brethren, heed Jeremiah’s counsel: “Flee from the midst of Babylon,” that is, from vices and confusion, so that each may save his own soul. For whoever does not depart from its midst [Col. 0498A] shall die. For there is no life in this city, because God does not dwell in it, but in Jerusalem, that is, in the city of the righteous, as he says through the prophet Hosea: “I am God and not man, the Holy One in your midst, and I shall not enter the city” (Hos. 11:9), namely, the city of the evil, or Babylon. Therefore in the midst of Jerusalem, that is, the city of the saints, God is holy and strong; but he does not enter the city of the evil, because he hates the assembly of evildoers. That, then, is the city of those who die; this is the city of those who live.

Hence the Lord says through Jeremiah: “Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death: whoever remains in this city shall die, but whoever goes out shall live” (Jer. 21:9). For that is the city upon which neither dew nor rain falls, but upon [Col. 0498B] Jerusalem, the city of faith, it does. Yet even Jerusalem itself is not wholly rained upon, because within it are citizens of Babylon whom the rain of grace does not moisten. Hence the Lord says through the prophet Amos: “I rained upon one city, and upon another city I did not rain; one part was rained upon, and the part upon which I did not rain dried up” (Amos 4:7). Babylon is the city not watered by divine rain, because the city of the righteous, Jerusalem, is irrigated—but only in respect of the grain, not of the chaff. This is the city of which Amos says: “Two or three cities came to one city to drink water, and they were not satisfied” (ibid., 8). These are the faithful from the Gentiles and the Jews, or descended from Noah’s three sons, who come to the one city, namely the holy Church, to drink the living water [Col. 0498C] springing into eternal life, and are not satisfied here; for those who hunger and thirst for righteousness shall be satisfied not here but in the future. For the more one drinks here, the more eagerly one thirsts; the more perfectly one tastes, the more vehemently one desires.

Against this city comes the great king, namely the devil, the plunderer of nations; he has laid siege round about it, surrounding it with the walls of seven vices, opposed to the seven spirits of the Lord, and constructing fortifications of flattering prosperity and raging adversity.

These fortifications are the gates of hell, concerning which the Lord, entrusting this city to Peter, says: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16:18). The gates are sins, threats, and the blandishments [Col. 0498D] of heresy, through which the weak fall into death: those who built the house of their profession not upon the rock but upon sand, because they do not follow Christ with simple and true intention. But whoever has received faith with the inward love of the heart easily overcomes every assault [read: every thing that presses upon him]. Such a person becomes far from the gates of death and is placed in the gates of life, that he may proclaim God’s praises. Hence the Prophet: “You raise me from the gates of death, that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. 9:15). Behold gates against gates: the gates of Zion against the gates of Babylon; the gates of Paradise against the gates of hell. For these gates are virtues and every excellent practice through which one comes to the vision of peace. The Prophet desires that these be opened to him, saying: “Open to me the gates [Col. 0499A] of righteousness” (Ps. 119:19). For what purpose? “Having entered them, I shall confess to the Lord,” that is, I shall proclaim the Lord’s praise.

Stand firm, therefore, brethren, in these gates, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against you, nor shall the great King seize you—that is, the lion coming up from his lair. Rather, from the lions’ lairs you shall obtain crowns for yourselves. Hence the Bridegroom says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Come from Lebanon, my bride, come, you shall be crowned—from the lions’ lairs, from the mountains of leopards” (Cant. 4:8). Thus the lion was mentioned above. Here now not only lions but also leopards are named in the plural, by which the multitude of demons is signified. They are likened to lions because of pride or violence, and to leopards because of cruelty or the changing character of their snares. [Col. 0499B]

Lucifer is compared, individually, to a lion: more glorious than the others through the privilege of his creation, but more deformed from the beginning of his falling away [the text reads *electionis*, “choice”; perhaps *defectionis*, “defection”]. Of him Isaiah says: “How have you fallen, Lucifer, who rose in the morning?” (Isa. 14:12). “Every precious stone was your covering” (Ezek. 28:13). And Job: “He is the beginning of the ways of the Lord” (Job 40:14). And concerning the same one: “This dragon, which you formed to be played with” (Ps. 103:26). For this is that dragon who, falling from heaven, drew with him, as John says, a third part of the stars (Apoc. 8:12), that is, of the angels.

The mountains—that is, the proud hearts of human beings—are the lairs of such lions and leopards. But the bride is crowned from their lairs when, by her preaching and industry, those in whom the devil formerly reigned are converted to Christ, so that, after he has been expelled and overcome from their hearts and Christ the true King has entered, they may obtain the crown of victory. Hence the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers and powers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12). The Apostle does not exhort us to fight against a human being, but rather for him: against the devil, who works with him and within him. Let us pray and do whatever we can, that the devil may be expelled with his angels and that human beings may be set free. For the demons themselves fight as riders upon horses—that is, upon human beings. Let us therefore kill the riders and take possession of the horses, so that we may be the cavalry of salvation. Hence, “his cavalry is salvation.” And elsewhere: “You ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. 3:8). [Col. 0499C–D]

Therefore, having Christ as rider and as the one who mounts us, leader and guide, let us stand in battle-line. Let us not yield, because Wisdom says to you: “If the spirit of one in authority rises against you, do not leave your place” (Eccl. 10:4); nor should you abandon it. You can indeed do this, if the poor man aids you—the one who delivered the city from the hand of the strong man, of whom Scripture continues: “A poor and wise man was found in it, and he delivered the city by his wisdom” (Eccl. 9:15).

But who is this man? He is the one of whom Zechariah says: “Behold the man: East [*Oriens*, ‘Rising’] is his name” (Zech. 6:12). For he is the only-begotten Son of the Father, ineffably begotten from him before the ages. Though he was rich—God with God the Father, through whom [Col. 0500A] all things were made—he deigned to become human for us, so poor that he had nowhere to lay his head. Yet though poor, he was wise—indeed, Wisdom itself, which came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the Firstborn, “reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1).

This is the poor man of whom Zechariah says: “Rejoice greatly, daughter Zion; shout for joy, daughter Jerusalem. Behold, your King comes to you, just and a Savior, himself poor, riding upon an ass and the colt of an ass. He shall speak peace to the nations, and his power shall be from sea to sea” (Zech. 9:9). The daughter Zion and Jerusalem is the Church, which now beholds and sees peace through faith, and shall see it in the future. In its literal sense, rejoicing and jubilation are spoken for the mystery of this solemnity, because our Savior, [Col. 0500B] riding upon an ass and coming to Jerusalem, was received by the crowds with immense joy and glory as one poor and meek. For after the disciples sent into the village had untied the ass, brought it to the Lord, and laid their garments upon it, he sat upon it. A very great crowd came out to meet him and spread their garments in the road. Others cut branches from the trees and spread them in the road. Those going before and those following cried out: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest” (Matt. 21:9).

Christ’s words and the deeds he performed in bodily presence must be received reverently and with the highest veneration. Whoever hears them with a hearing ear, not negligently, is born of God. But whoever despises them is not of God, [Col. 0500C] but of the devil as father. Hence Truth, speaking to the Jews, says: “He who is of God hears the words of God”—that is, by understanding the works that he does. “Therefore you did not hear, because you are not of God” (John 7:37).

Therefore our Lord and Savior spiritually approached Jerusalem, which is “the vision of peace,” and came to Bethphage, which is interpreted “house of the mouth,” when, having become incarnate, he visited the holy Church, in which is the vision of peace, and reconciled her to himself through confession. And he sent two disciples, that is, two orders of preachers: one to the Gentiles, the other to the circumcision. They were sent two by two for knowledge of the truth and purity of deed, or in the sacrament of the twofold love, by which teachers of the Church ought rightly to shine. And he said to them: “Go into the village that is opposite you” (Matt. 21:2), that is, penetrate the barbarous and unlearned regions of the world, as though they were the walls of a fortress set against you. For the world was armed against Christ with philosophical reasoning [the text reads *prophetica*, “prophetic”; perhaps *philosophica*] and Pharisaic tradition. “And you shall find an ass and a colt with her.”

The ass signifies [Col. 0500D] the Jews, subdued beneath the yoke of the Law, yet entangled in sins. The colt signifies the Gentile people, free and unruly, upon whom no teacher endowed with reason had imposed the bridle of instruction and correction. Therefore it was entangled in the bonds of sins. But the apostles untied it, scattering the bonds of sins, according to the saying: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). And they brought it to Jesus and laid their garments upon it, that he might sit upon it: because by divine precepts and spiritual grace they first adorned the hearts of both peoples, formerly bare of virtues and rough with the filth of vices, so that they might receive Christ [the text adds: *susciperent*]. . . .

But the lesser crowd lays garments in the road. These are those who subdue their bodies, mortifying the flesh with its vices and desires, so as to prepare a way for Christ to the mind; for Wisdom does not dwell in a land of those who live pleasantly, nor in a body subject to sins. Others cut branches from trees and spread them in the road. These are those who take good examples from the holy Fathers and also set before others a rule for living well. “All, both those who went before and those who followed, cried out: [Col. 0501B] Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matt. 21:9). *Hosanna* means “salvation”; and thus both the Fathers who went before and those of the present who faithfully believe proclaim salvation granted to all in the Son of David. For no one could be saved without faith in the Mediator of God and human beings, whether before or after the incarnation. He is the Blessed One, uniquely free from sin and full of grace and truth, who comes in the name of the Lord—that is, of the Father—because he sought not his own individual glory but that of the Father. Therefore all say to him: “Hosanna”—that is, “Save, I beseech you, in the highest”—namely, that he may lead us from the lower regions to the heavenly ones and repair the loss caused by the fall of the angels, joining earthly things to heavenly.

Let the daughter Zion therefore rejoice, and let the minds of the faithful exult, because we have such a King: at whose [Col. 0501C] name every knee bends, of things heavenly, earthly, and infernal; who comes to us, girded with humility, poor but wise, who by wisdom delivered the city. For he is that stronger one in the Gospel who bound the strong armed man—that is, the devil—restraining him from seduction, and plundered his goods. For, leading captivity captive in triumph, he stripped him of his spoils, according to the saying: “I shall rejoice as one who finds abundant spoil” (Ps. 118:162). Yet for this he made more use of wisdom and justice than of power. Though by the most equitable right and by strength he was able to bind and conquer the devil, he set aside what he could do in order to do what he ought to do. He restrained power and displayed justice through his wisdom.

[Col. 0501D] Therefore Wisdom brought it about that the great King was conquered by justice, not by power. For the devil, through the vice of his perversity, is a lover of power and a deserter and assailant [Col. 0502A] of justice; and powerful human beings imitate him in this. Therefore Christ willed to conquer not by power but by justice, so that in this a human being might learn to imitate him.

But by what justice did he conquer the proud one? Behold: Christ appeared weak and humble. Though the proud one found in him nothing deserving death, he nevertheless killed him. Therefore he justly lost the debtors whom he held, and released those who believed in Christ, whom he killed though he had no debt at all. Thus wisely and shrewdly he overthrew the tyrant and robber of the nations and liberated humankind. Hence, by a prophetic spirit, nursing infants—that is, the simple and innocent—going with palms to meet the conqueror of the devil and death and giver of life as he came to the place of his Passion, sang royal praises, saying: “Blessed is he who comes [Col. 0502B] in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel” (Matt. 21:9).

Today the holy Church, recalling the glory of this triumph, celebrates a solemn procession under the sign and banner of the cross, carrying in its hands green branches of trees and flowers with palms behind the banner of the holy cross, so that it may spiritually fulfill in a second action what it represents figuratively. Therefore let us possess the greenness of unfading faith, the flowers of shining virtues, and the foliage [perhaps *fructus*, “fruits”] of good works. Thus, in simplicity and innocence like children, recalling with effectual remembrance Christ’s triumphant Passion, let us raise the sign in Zion, imitating the traces of Christ’s Passion.

This is the sign which Ezekiel mentions, saying: “Mark the sign Tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the abominations” (Ezek. 9:4). *Tau* is interpreted “he consummated,” and it has the form of a cross. Therefore the sign of the cross is understood by *tau*, in which our consummation lies. Let this sign, then, be raised and not hidden, because “a lamp does not come to be placed under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, that it may shine for all who are in the house” (Mark 4:11). Let it be raised, I say, in Zion—that is, in the soul contemplating God—which [Col. 0502C] groans and grieves over its own abominations and those of others. Thus, as the sign of the cross is outwardly impressed upon foreheads, so faith in the Passion and zeal for imitation may be instilled within the soul; and by this it shall be consummated and perfected: here in justice, and in the future in eternal glory, which may the King of glory grant us. Amen.

### XXXIII. FIFTH SERMON ON PALM SUNDAY

> **Note:** [Col. 0501D] In manuscript Sangerm. 383. Whatever Hildebert discusses in this sermon concerning the various names of Palm Sunday and the different rites observed on it appears to have been taken wholly from Alcuin, *On the Divine Offices*, where he treats Palm Sunday. The same material was copied by an unknown author and published by Wolfgang Lazius at Antwerp in 1560 under the title: *Fragment of an Unknown Author, On the Rites and Ceremonies of the Roman Church, Found in an Ancient Codex*. In the same volume this fragment is appended to another fragment, which he attributes to Charlemagne, as a supplement to the matters lacking in that Carolingian work concerning the same rites; it is also found among Alcuin’s works. Moreover, our Martène has treated all these matters at length and very learnedly in the treatise *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 20, “On Palm Sunday,” p. 188. There, unless I am mistaken, a printer’s error slipped in when he wrote that this Easter was called *capitularium*, whereas perhaps it should be *capitilavium*, a word closer to *capitalavantium*, which Alcuin uses here and Hildebert after him. This day was also called *Pascha petitum*, “the requested Easter,” and “of the Competents,” that is, requested by those petitioning together, because catechumens then jointly requested instruction through the Creed in the articles of faith, and it was granted them, so that, as Hildebert says here, those hastening to receive God’s grace in the Paschal feast might learn the faith which they ought to confess.

[Col. 0502D]

By the choice of this present day, dearest brethren, you ought to recognize the mysteries [Col. 0503A] with which it shines, taking care that the instructed mind may inwardly examine the source from which arise the joyful gladnesses that we celebrate outwardly. But lest an excess of words produce weariness in your minds—especially since the office of this day is prolonged in very long chants and most pleasing jubilations concerning our God—I shall first endeavor to offer you a few words concerning its name, which is distinguished by various titles.

For it is called the Day of Palms, or of Flowers and Branches; likewise *Hosanna*, the Requested Easter, or Easter of the Competents, and *Capitalavantium*. Although these are so named according to popular custom, all nevertheless retain a definite and fitting meaning. It is called the Day of Palms because on it our Lord, seated upon an ass and about to suffer for the salvation of humankind, went to Jerusalem. A very great crowd of rejoicing people met him with branches of palms and various trees, crying: “Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21:9).

It is also called the Day of Flowers because holy mother Church, in commemoration of such great joy, wished on this day above others, at the yearly recurrence, to carry blessed and consecrated flowers while singing, so that she might joyfully meet her Redeemer. It is also called the Day of Branches because, for the same reason, not only palms but also green branches are borne today by the children of the Church. It is called *Hosanna* today because the Hebrew people [Col. 0503B] going before and following the Lord appeared to sing to the same Lord, “Hosanna,” which is interpreted “save.”

It is called the Requested Easter, or Easter of the Competents, because today the Creed, or the belief of the holy faith, was delivered to the candidate neophytes, so that those hastening to receive the grace of God in the Paschal solemnity might learn the faith which they ought to confess. They are called *competentes*, “those seeking together,” as though jointly petitioning—that is, petitioning for the grace of God. The people call this day *Capitalavantium*, because it was customary today to wash the heads of infants who were to be anointed on Holy Saturday, “lest perhaps, dirtied by the observance of Lent, they should approach the anointing.” This week is called “greater” either because greater sobriety is observed in it, or because a greater office than in other weeks is celebrated.

[Col. 0503D] Let these brief remarks about the names of this day suffice. Some of them remain as they are understood literally; others signify something else allegorically. For throughout all the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, the palm always signifies victory. By the palm branches, therefore, is signified that victory by which our Lord through his death destroyed the death of our soul, and through the trophy of the cross overcame the devil, prince of death. By flowers is expressed the fragrance of virtue, captivated by which faithful souls accompany their King as he advances toward Jerusalem—that is, the holy Church—so that, celebrating Pascha, that is, the passing-over, with him, they may deserve to rise with him to the heavenly places.

By the branches of trees are signified the sayings of the ancient prophets, which the person who instructs the simple [Col. 0504A] and less learned hearts of brethren by examples gathers and spreads in the road, lest they stray upon the way of truth. The *Hosanna* repeated and reiterated so often by the people signifies the unity of faith by which we ought to live. For although among the people of the faithful there is diversity of rank, sex, and age, we nevertheless ought with one voice and one confession of praise to cry out to our Savior, saying: “Hosanna,” that is, “Save.” Indeed, the Hebrew word, rendered in Latin, means “Save,” or “Make your people safe,” or “the whole world.” Since such names are fitted to this day through the suitable significations of our ministers [the text reads *ministrorum*; perhaps *magistrorum*, “teachers”], it should be briefly shown to you by what works of our Savior it is illustrated.

For, as the holy Evangelist relates, six days before the old Passover, counted from yesterday, Jesus came to Bethany, to the house of Simon the leper, where he had raised Lazarus. There they made him a supper, and Mary also, taking a pound of ointment, [Col. 0504B] anointed the Lord’s feet and wiped them with her hair. When Judas the traitor indignantly objected to this, Jesus answered in praise of the woman: “She has done a good work toward me” (Matt. 26:10), and so forth, as the narratives concerning this matter continue in the Lord’s Passion.

Following the custom of this good work, the holy man Gregory occupied himself wholly on this very day—namely, yesterday—in giving alms and washing the feet of the poor, so that what the most devout woman did for the head, that is, Christ, he might do for Christ’s members, that is, the poor. Therefore the same day, having no proper office, is thus titled in the Sacramentary: “Saturday is free from the public station, when the lord pope gives alms.”

If you wish to take the flower of allegory from this action, know that ointment signifies justice, and this is why it is said to have been a pound. Whoever perfectly observes justice undoubtedly washes the Lord’s feet; whoever loves mercy by living well anoints his feet with ointment; and those who give abundantly to the poor wipe the Lord’s feet with their hair. Therefore the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment—that is, the whole world with the renown of that most devout woman and with the virtue of the faithful who imitate her in such matters.

For the fact that the Lord came to Bethany six days before Passover signifies that he hastened, on the same sixth day, to redeem by his own blood the human being whom the serpent’s fraud had destroyed on the sixth day of creation, passing through Bethany, that is, “the house of obedience.” [Col. 0504C–D] Leaving the aforesaid city of Bethany on the next day, namely the fifth day before Passover, which is today, “he sent two disciples into Jerusalem, saying to them: ‘Go into the village that is opposite you, and you shall find an ass and a colt; untie them and bring them to me.’ Having untied them, they brought them to Jesus and placed their garments upon them, and made him sit upon them. When the crowd that had come for the feast day heard that Jesus was going to Jerusalem, they took branches of palms and came out to meet him, and cried: ‘Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’” (Matt. 21:2–9).

[Col. 0505A] But because these deeds of the Lord, recounted in the Evangelist’s words, are sufficiently clear in their literal sense—since they happened as they are described—the mystical meaning should be opened briefly. The two disciples signify the two orders of preachers, one among the circumcision and the other among the Gentiles; or Peter and Philip, whom Jesus sent into Jerusalem, that is, into the holy Church. One of them, namely Philip, brought Samaria, like an ass, to faith in Christ; the other, namely Peter, brought Cornelius from among the Gentiles, like a colt, to faith in Christ.

Likewise, by the two animals are figured the two peoples, Jewish [Col. 0505B] and Gentile. At the coming of the disciples they were bound, because each people was constrained by the bonds of its own sins. The apostles’ garments are either teachings of virtues or works of justice. Hence the Psalmist says: “Let your priests be clothed with justice” (Ps. 131:9). The very great crowd which spread its garments in the road signifies the innumerable multitude of martyrs, who, stripping themselves of their own garment, make a way for the simpler people by which they may be able to arrive at the vision of peace.

By the little ass upon which the Lord sat are figured the simple hearts of the Gentiles. Like an untamed animal, they had remained unbound by any reins of discipline, proceeding toward mute idols wherever they were led. By presiding over and governing them, the Lord was leading them to the vision of eternal peace.

Finally, it is believed not to have occurred without the reason of a great mystery that, on this day in particular, as the Lord made his way toward Jerusalem, he employed the service of beasts of burden, caused varied ornaments of palms, branches, and flowers to be carried about him, and wished to be called King and Lord—things which, though he had often come to Jerusalem before, he had previously refused to allow. For this reason he entered with such great glory: because he knew that the time of his Passion was now at hand, and he compelled the hearts of the Jews to be stirred up against him, so that through the death of his body he might destroy the death of our souls.

Therefore, most beloved brethren, because we recall his Passion, even if we cannot die for him—because, with the persecutors of the Church pacified, we do not have war against them—let us nevertheless take care to mortify the vices of our members, so that after the mourning of the Passion, receiving the joys of the Resurrection, we may be able to rise with him from vices to the heights of virtues. Amen.

### XXXIV. FIRST SERMON ON THE LORD’S SUPPER

> **Note:** [Col. 0505D] From the Victorine manuscript.

[Col. 0505D]

“Come, children, listen to me; I shall teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 33:12).

You have heard, dearest brethren, with what sweet voice and with what affection the most gentle Father calls you back. He does not estrange you or terrify you, but invites you to amendment in a fatherly voice. While he promises hope of pardon, he gives place for repentance. You have acted as enemies [that is, by sinning you have behaved as his enemies], yet he calls you children, saying: “Come, children, listen to me.” By calling you children, he wishes you to acknowledge him as Father. For the sweet Lord speaks humbly even to those hostile to him. To Judas the traitor, when he came against the Lord with a crowd, he said: “Friend, for what have you come?” (Matt. 26:50). [Col. 0506A]

In like manner he says to us: “Children, you who until now have withdrawn from me through sinning, come through doing good.” For the sinner departs while sinning, just as he himself will say at the end of the world: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12)—“Depart from me, all you who work iniquity” (Matt. 7:23). And as the Psalmist says: “The wicked shall not dwell beside you, nor shall the unjust remain before your eyes” (Ps. 5:6). And if you do not know the way, listen to me, because I am the way and the truth, and I shall teach you the fear of the Lord. How? Namely, if you fear the Lord; for, as Solomon says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; and he who fears the Lord will do good” (Sir. [Col. 0506B] 15:1).

The Psalmist invites us to this fear when he says: “Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for there is no lack to those who fear him” (Ps. 33:10). “Come,” he says, and then adds why one must come: “Who is the person who desires life, who loves to see good days?” (Ps. 33:13). He promises life if you come; you shall see good days if you fear him. There is none among you who would not spend all his money if he knew that his life could be prolonged by a few years. If, then, you are willing to spend what is yours for this present life, so frail and so wretched, why will you not give yourselves and what is yours for eternal life?

He calls his uninterrupted brightness “good days,” to which no darkness succeeds. Of it the Psalmist says: “One day”—that is, an uninterrupted day—“in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11) of present days. For how can night exist where the righteous will see God in the land of the living? The land of the living is the heavenly homeland. There are three lands: the land of the living is paradise; the land of the dead, where death is everlasting, is hell; and the land both of the dead and of the living is this world, where good and evil people are intermingled. [Col. 0506C]

He teaches how you may come to that life, or to that land, when he says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 33:15). Two things are necessary for the perfection of salvation: the uprooting of vices and the building up of virtues. For it is not enough to be clean of vices unless the merit of good action is added. The Psalmist set forth both when he asks: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest on your holy mountain? The one who walks without stain and works justice” (Ps. 14:1–2).

Hence Gregory says: “Good things are not acceptable to God when, before the eyes of God, they are stained by the mixture of evils.” And through Solomon it is said: “Whoever offends in one thing shall lose many good things” (Eccl. 9:18). James testifies to the same point, saying: “Whoever keeps the whole law, yet offends in one point, has become guilty of all” (Jas. 2:10). Paul says: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5:6). [Col. 0506D]

Turn away, therefore, from evils, lest you commit them hereafter. [Col. 0507A] Turn away from evils by sighing and groaning over those of the past, and washing them away by confession and repentance. But some rise more readily according to the variety of their faults; others scarcely, or never, wish to rise. Among their number are those who acquiesce in flatterers. For the tongues of flatterers, as Augustine says,

> **Note:** [Col. 0507D] Vol. IV, on Psalm 9; new edition.

bind souls in sins. Hence Solomon rightly says: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” (Prov. 1:10). Sinners entice either when they offer future [the text reads *perpetrata*, “committed”; perhaps *perpetranda*, “to be committed”] evils by blandishments, or when they extol evils already committed by their favor, as the Psalmist says: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked person is blessed” (Ps. 10:3).

Therefore the Lord, who raised three dead persons, when one of the disciples said to him, “Lord, allow me first to go and bury my father” (Matt. 8:21), answered: “Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead” (ibid., 22). The Lord raised three dead persons; he learned of a fourth from the disciples who reported him, but did not undertake to raise him. This dead person signifies those who are brought down into the practice of evil habit through flattering tongues. His not raising him signifies that such persons can scarcely rise from their vices. Hence it is well said: “Leave the dead to bury their own dead.” The dead bury the dead when sinners extol a sinner through their favor. But those who pursue a sinner with praises hide one already dead beneath the mound of their words.

Other persons, however, were raised in different places. For the Redeemer raised the girl in the house, the young man [Col. 0507B] outside the city gate, and Lazarus in the tomb. Likewise, one lies dead in the house who is hidden in sin—whose sin, that is, has not become known. The dead person is carried outside the gate whose wickedness has been disclosed even to the shame of public commission. The one who is burdened beneath the mound of burial is weighed down by the repetition [the text reads *interpretationem*; perhaps *increpationem*, “rebuke”] of his habit. But the merciful man calls the dead back to life when, by divine grace, he illumines with the regard of his light those dead not only in hidden but also in open wickedness, and those weighed down by the mass of habit.

And here it is plainly given to understand that whoever sins secretly must be raised secretly by private confession, as the girl was raised in the house; while whoever has publicized a sin must do public penance, just as the young man was restored to life in public. At the resurrection of the girl, the crowd is ordered to leave, except for a few witnesses—namely, father and mother—who are commanded not to reveal it to anyone. Likewise, for lighter hidden sins private penance should be imposed, and the fault should be kept silent. Because her resurrection was easier, he compared her death to sleep, saying: “The girl is not dead, but sleeps” (Matt. 9:24). And she was raised by an easy word when he said: “Girl, arise” (ibid., 25).

But the young man was raised in public, [Col. 0507C] with a great crowd accompanying him.

> **Note:** [Col. 0507D] Something appears to be missing here, which might perhaps be supplied as follows: “The young man, raised in public with a great crowd accompanying him, signifies a public sinner. For his resurrection Christ, before everyone, touches the bier—that is, he draws back from the bier of iniquity one struck by salutary shame. Lazarus, etc.” [Col. 0508D]

Lazarus, dead four days and lying in the tomb, is wept for by the Lord; the stone is removed, and he is called with a loud voice: “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11:43). For one held by so long a death was not to be called with an easy voice. The Lord teaches us to grieve at the gravity of sin when we see our neighbor dead already, fetid in evil habit and corrupting others with the stench of his example. He must be called with a loud voice, because he must be rebuked publicly before the Church if he cannot be recalled from an evil habit by the correction of a private voice. Hence the Lord says: “If your brother sins against you, correct him between yourself and him alone. If he does not listen to you, take with you one or two witnesses. But if he does not listen, tell the Church” (Matt. 8:15, 17).

[Col. 0508B] These are those lepers who must be cast out beyond the camp until they are cleansed. Leprosy is a disease that spreads and is conspicuous [the text reads *videns*, “seeing”; perhaps *nitens*, “shining”]; public sin is likened to it because it corrupts others and becomes known to all. Hence in the Gospel the Lord commanded the lepers: “Go, show yourselves to the priests” (Luke 17:14). This showing signifies public disclosure before the whole Church. Therefore those sinning publicly ought to do public penance, so that those who have contaminated others by an example of sin may by their own public penitence invite those same people to repentance. Therefore, brethren, let none of you be ashamed to do penance outside the Church. This is done as a dispensation [so that they may rise again]. The Lord willed it to be done, providing for your benefit and that of others. Therefore, acknowledging their sins, let them seek pardon with groaning.

[Col. 0508C] For it is the law of iniquity to sin and to excuse sins, as Adam did. Not only did he sin, but, transferring his sin to another, he wished to excuse himself, saying: “The woman whom you gave me gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3:12). Therefore he wished either to twist or to shift the blame onto the woman, and also onto God. When he says, “The woman gave me from the tree,” he wishes to cast back the blame upon the woman; when he adds, “whom you gave me,” he seems to wish to defame God. The woman, however, turns the blame back upon the serpent, saying: “The serpent deceived me” (ibid., 13). You put forward this excuse when you say, “The devil forced me.” For what else is “the devil forced me” than “the serpent deceived me”? Behold, she who plunged us into sin [Col. 0508D] and left us the stain of death along with her excuse.

Therefore you do not humbly acknowledge your iniquity when you lift it somewhat off yourselves by the pride of excuse. You do not say with the Psalmist: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50:5). Rather, rend your hearts and not your garments; humbled, cast yourselves daily upon the ground; fall upon your faces.

There are two kinds of falling: forward and backward. To fall backward belongs to the wicked, while to fall upon one’s face belongs to the elect [Col. 0509A]—that is, to blush for evils committed. Whoever falls backward falls where he does not see; thus the wicked plunge into eternal damnation and do not foresee their fall. Thus the Jews, wishing to seize Christ, fell backward, according to the Psalmist: “Let all who hate Zion be turned backward” (Ps. 24:5). But whoever falls upon his face sees where he falls. Thus Job, upon hearing of his many adversities, fell upon his face and worshiped the Lord.

Think, therefore, dearest brothers, of expiating your sins simply [perhaps: humbly], because every sin will be punished either in the present life or in the life to come. It is better, therefore, to be punished here temporarily than to be tormented eternally hereafter. It is better to be outside the Church here for a time than to be exiled outside the heavenly Jerusalem [Col. 0509B] without end. Repentance is the medicine of the soul, by which sins are punished; and it is therefore called *poenitentia* (“repentance”) as though *punitiva* (“punitive”), because a person punishes in himself what he committed wickedly.

For this reason those doing penance let their hair and beard grow, so that they may show the abundance of crimes by which the head—that is, the mind or soul—of the sinner is burdened. For although the Apostle says, “If a man lets his hair grow, it is a disgrace to him” (I Cor. 11:14), penitents accept that disgrace because of the deserts of their sins. They afflict themselves in sackcloth, which is made from goats, so that they may remember sins, which are signified by goats. They are sprinkled with ashes, that they may remember that they are ashes and shall return to ashes.

Today, dearest brothers, penitents are reconciled, so that they may be prepared to receive [Col. 0509C] the Lord’s body on the Sunday of the Resurrection. The holy Fathers therefore established reconciliation of penitents on this day, because today, at the supper, the Lord first bestows the sacrament of his body and handed it to his disciples to receive. Since reception of the Lord’s sacrament is deferred until Easter Day because of the joy of the Lord’s resurrection, it seemed fitting that sinners who are reconciled unto redemption should be prepared for its reception on the day on which the body of the Lord was first consecrated and delivered to the Jews.

Therefore, just as you are prepared outwardly, so prepare the dwelling-place of your mind, cleansed to receive your Lord, so that you, the members, [Col. 0509D] may be joined to Christ the head and may become with him participants in eternal life in the heavenly hall.

> [Note: Since this final period, apparently through the copyist’s carelessness, is very intricate and scarcely intelligible, yet the author’s meaning seems to become apparent upon closer investigation, and it may also be inferred from it that, through the Church’s indulgence for a time, out of reverence for Easter, persons who had not yet completed their penance were sometimes admitted to communion. We therefore judged that the period could be arranged and restored with a more satisfactory connection as follows: “But because, among those who are reconciled, some, having completed their penance, [Col. 0510D] are prepared to receive the body of the Lord, while others are not worthy because they have not yet completed their penance: nevertheless, in order that the joy of so great a festival may be complete and that the faithful may rejoice that the body of the Church is whole, these latter are received, through indulgence, to communicate in the Church for a time, so that, rising from sins, they may deserve to come from the joys of this festival to the joys above, through the grant of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father,” etc.]

But among those who are reconciled, some, having completed their penance, are prepared to receive the body of the Lord; others are not yet worthy of the sacrament because they have not completed their penance. Yet, for the joy of so great a festival, they are received through indulgence to communicate in the Church for a time [Col. 0510A], that they may rejoice that it is a whole body and, by rising from sins through the resurrection celebrated in this festival, may attain the joys above, through the grant of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## XXXV. SECOND SERMON ON THE LORD’S SUPPER

> [Note: [Col. 0510D] E., manuscript of Saint Albinus of Angers.]

“Set the table; behold from the watchtower those eating and drinking. Rise up, rulers; take the shield” (Isa. 21:5).

Both pages of the Testament testify that the sacrament of this day must be celebrated with great devotion of heart and moderation of body. For Isaiah, foreseeing in [Col. 0510B] the spirit of wisdom the mystery of the Lord’s Supper, urges us with the most exact diligence to observe it; and he likewise indicates the manner in which one should approach, when he says: “Set the table; behold from the watchtower those eating and drinking. Rise up, rulers; take the shield.”

This is a holy and saving exhortation, by which four things to be observed are indicated to us, so that we may be found worthy to partake in such great sacraments: namely, the setting of the table, contemplation from the watchtower, rising up, and taking the shield. Thus equipped, we may eat and drink not unto judgment but unto life. In this order a wonderful arrangement, full of instruction and grace, shines forth. We are first commanded to set the table; then to behold from the watchtower; next to rise and take the sword; and finally to eat and drink.

But what is this [Col. 0510C] table, and how is it set? This table is not carnal but spiritual; intellectual rather than visible. It is the table of faith, not yet of hope; not figurative or shadowy, but life-giving and sanctifying. Scripture commends to us a threefold table: one in the Law, the second in the Gospel, the third in heaven; the first is Moses’ table, the second Christ’s, the third God’s. The first was in figure, the second in truth, the third will be in glory. The first teaches; the second perfects; the third glorifies. The first is in the letter, the second in the Spirit, the third will be in rest.

Of the first table Moses wrote, when the Lord said to him: “You shall make a table of acacia wood, and overlay it with pure gold” (Exod. 25:23). Of the second the Apostle says: “You cannot partake [Col. 0510D] of the table of Christ and of demons” (I Cor. 10:21). Of the third, Truth speaks in the Gospel, saying: “That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22:30), or, the table of God.

The table, then, which the prophet here mentions is the Lord’s Supper. Schismatics, whisperers, slanderers, and all who serve the tabernacle of the flesh may not approach it. Of this the Apostle says: “We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat, but whose bodies are burned outside the camp” (Heb. 13:10).

Here the Apostle touches upon a practice of the old Law and discloses the mystery of its sacred meaning. According to the Law, on the feast of propitiation or expiation, a calf and a goat were sacrificed within the camp of Jerusalem; their flesh was burned outside the camp, and none serving the tabernacle was permitted to eat from them (Lev. 16:27 ff.). Behold the shadow; behold the figure of truth. For Christ is the calf and the goat. He is the calf because, teaching in power and authority, he gave forth the lowing of preaching to the whole world [Col. 0511B], drove back the obstacles of vices by the twofold horn of the cross and charity, and, by the summits of the two Testaments—as though by the double fork of reason—crushed heretical importunities and every blasphemy of knowledge exalting itself against Catholic truth.

He is also the goat “in the likeness of sinful flesh.” For he did not assume sinful flesh, but its likeness. Therefore, in the mystery, the calf and goat were sacrificed within the camp of Jerusalem through the cries and judgment of the Jews demanding his death. Thus Mark says that he was crucified at the third hour (Mark 15:25), whereas the other Evangelists report that he suffered at the sixth hour (Luke 23:44): at the third hour, that is, by the tongues of the Jews within Jerusalem; at the sixth hour, by the hands of Gentile soldiers, [Col. 0511C] outside the camp, at the place of Calvary. Accordingly, his flesh was burned by the fire of passion outside the camp, on the cross. The altar where the flesh was burned is the altar of the Church, where Christ’s body and blood are consecrated daily.

We therefore have a heavenly altar: namely, the sacrifice of the body and blood consecrated on the altar. Those who serve the tabernacle—that is, bodily pleasures and delights—have no authority, that is, no permission, to eat from it. Such are those who fully indulge the flesh even in its desires, as fornicators, adulterers, drunkards, and all who serve the lusts of the flesh and earthly opinions hostile to God. “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” But those whose bodies are burned outside the camp may eat from this altar: that is, those who, outside the mode of life [perhaps: association] of worldly and carnal people, [Col. 0511D] set aflame by the fervor of the Holy Spirit, consume whatever is carnal, fleeting, and lustful in themselves, mortifying the flesh and putting their members to death, fighting against vices and desires.

For Jesus too, in order to instruct us by the pattern of his own example, suffered outside the camp—that is, outside the will and desires of the body—and indeed outside the gate. For the gate of the city is the bodily sense, in which Christ sinned in nothing. Therefore let us too, after his example, with the door of the senses shut within, suffer outside the desires of the flesh, going out to imitate him [Col. 0512A] outside the camp of our bodies and patiently bearing the reproach of his cross—that is, his passion—which is a reproach and mockery to unbelievers, but sanctification and redemption to us.

Let us therefore shut the doors of the senses against outward enticements, going outside the camp—that is, outside bodily delights. These are the windows down to which the earth descends, and through which death descends unless a guard is placed at them to repel what is harmful. Thus the prophetic man prays: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth—or, according to the letter, over my heart—and a door of enclosure, or continence, upon my lips” (Ps. 140:3). For if doors—that is, the guard and barrier of restraint—are set over the lips, eyes, and other senses, the human heart does not fly away from itself while beholding vanity amid tumultuous desires. [Col. 0512B] Rather, it is gathered into one, so that it may be found in prayer to God and, when found within itself, may find God’s truth within itself.

Thus David says: “I found my heart in order to pray to you, O Lord.”

> [Note: Vulgate: “Your servant found his heart to pray to you” (II Kings [II Samuel] 7:27).]

For a person can scarcely ever find his own heart when it flies away in various directions and ranges, pleased by all things vain, borne toward many things by insatiable desire and troubled over many things, finding no rest—the true rest which is not in the land of the dying but in the region of the living.

Therefore let us place upon the windows of the body the door of continence and steadfastness, so that through God’s guard we may preserve our hearts. For because the gatekeeper did not guard the door properly, Ish-bosheth was killed by enemies (II Kings [II Samuel] 4:5–6). Dinah also, Jacob’s daughter, went out [Col. 0512C] to see the women of the land of the Canaanites; she was violated by Shechem, son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of that land, and he soothed her sorrow with blandishments (Gen. 34:1 ff.).

Dinah goes out to see the women of a foreign land when the human mind neglects the pursuits of honorable conduct and divine contemplation, concerns itself with vain affairs, entangles itself in curious activities, and wanders outside the rectitude of order. Shechem, prince of the land, oppresses her because the devil corrupts the mind when he finds it amid outward cares and wandering occupations, and joins it to himself through wickedness. And because the mind, recovering its senses after fault, is afflicted by grief and tries to lament the sin it has committed, the corrupter and deceiver [perhaps: corrupter and instigator] the devil strives [Col. 0512D] to soothe its grief with blandishments. He repeatedly sets before its eyes empty hope and false security, in order to remove the benefit of grief. Now he brings forward others’ graver deeds; now he persuades it that what has been done is nothing. Now he speaks of God as merciful and promises time for repentance, so that while the mind is led astray by these means, repentance may be delayed: thus it receives no good things in the future because no evil things grieve it now, and is then swallowed up more fully by punishments because it now exults in the worst deeds.

Let us beware, brothers, lest we be seduced through these gates and windows, by which we are led outward and suffer plunder in our inward parts [perhaps: are exposed as prey]. This is what Saint Jeremiah laments, saying: “My eye has plundered [Col. 0513A] my soul” (Lam. 3:51). There are eyes of the flesh, which are opened toward evil; there are other eyes of the mind, which pass into unity, so that one mind may rejoice in the one God. But this eye which plunders the soul is the eye of the flesh, whose office is to report within what it has seen outside: it is the eye of temptation, because through it we are tempted. Thus: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). It is the eye of death, because evil progeny comes from it. This eye therefore plunders the soul when, through it, the soul goes out from love of inward and heavenly things to desire the things we see outwardly.

Let our Dinah—that is, the soul—therefore remain at home with her father. Let her not go out curiously, drawn from the house [Col. 0513B] of the mind to see the women of another land, so as, abandoning virtues and good pursuits, to serve worldly allurements. Jacob is commended in Scripture because he lived at home, while his brother Esau was occupied with hunting. “Esau,” it says, “became a man skilled in hunting, a man of the field; but Jacob was a simple man, dwelling in tents” (Gen. 25:27). What is signified in Esau’s hunting except the vices of those who, given over to outward pleasures, follow the flesh? He is also called a man of the field because lovers of this age dwell in outward things all the more as they leave their inward parts uncultivated. But Jacob is called simple and said to live at home because all who refuse to be scattered among outward cares remain simple in thought and in the dwelling-place of conscience.

To dwell at home is to confine oneself within the barriers of the mind and not disperse oneself outwardly through desires, lest, while one longs after many things outside, one depart from oneself through alienated thoughts. Therefore let us go outside the camp of the flesh and be consumed by the fire of the Spirit, so that we may not depart from the barriers of the heart—that is, the secret places of the mind—and there, examining ourselves, set the table. But how is this heavenly table to be set, and where? It must certainly be placed in the heart. How? By faith: that we may believe in our heart that it is other than it appears. Bread and wine indeed appear, but it is the flesh of Christ, who hung for us upon the cross, and blood which was poured out for us for the remission of sins. For Truth openly says: “Take; this is my body, which will be given [Col. 0513D] for you” (Matt. 26:26). And again: “This is the blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many” (ibid., 28).

As though I had entrusted [perhaps: commended] to you a certain sacrament, in which one thing appears, another is signified and contained. Therefore, “the words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6:63): that is, understood spiritually, they give life. For he does not give the sacrament of his body and blood as food in such a way as to suffer a division of his own nature, to be torn into pieces by bites like meat sold in a market. This was the opinion of carnal people and of those ignorant disciples who, hearing Truth say, “Unless you eat the flesh [Col. 0514A] and drink the blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:53), said, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat? Who can listen to him? This saying is hard” (ibid., 60–61). And they went back.

The teaching about so ineffable a sacrament is indeed hard, but for the faithless and unbelieving, who could not set the Lord’s table in the inner chambers of their hearts. They say with Jeremiah: “Let us put wood into his bread” (Jer. 11:19). For he is the bread that came down from heaven, which gives life to the world. They put wood into him who do not obey his truth and sweetness with the hearing of faith, but resist with obstinate hardness of mind. To such people the good saying is hard, because for them it is “an odor of death unto death”; [Col. 0514B] but to believers and those who yield to it, it is “an odor of life unto life.” Likewise, to those who do not discern the Lord’s body and approach it without self-examination, it is judgment and death. For the Apostle says: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (I Cor. 11:29).

One is unworthy who is in sin, who remains in the will to sin, who handles it irreverently and approaches with an undevout mind. Such a person, the Apostle testifies, is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, because by taking a good thing badly he incurs a stain; for even holy things harm the wicked. To the good they are for salvation; to the wicked, for judgment. What we receive at this table is holy. The recipient is not guilty because the thing received is evil, but because, in receiving [Col. 0514C] it badly, an evil person receives badly what he receives. Therefore, at the meal one must beware of receiving a good thing badly.

> [Note: A Hildebertine expression. See Letter 7, Book I.]

For a good thing badly received harms the wicked, just as, conversely, evils patiently borne benefit the good. Let each person therefore set the table—that is, examine himself—loving the uprightness of faith and cleansing himself by the lament of repentance, so that, if there are daily sins, they may at least not be mortal sins. And when he approaches the altar, let him forgive his brother, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). Otherwise he eats judgment of condemnation—namely, for himself, not for you, if you are good. Therefore, being good, endure the evil person securely, so that you may come to the reward of the good; for the evil person cannot defile you.

Judas could indeed associate with Peter, but could not defile him; and both approached the Lord’s Supper. Yet Peter approached unto life, and Judas unto death—the death deserved by everyone who does not discern the Lord’s body from other foods. Some receive it with singular veneration and the prerogative of devotion, but without discernment and negligently. Therefore set the table, approaching with faith and the twofold foot of charity, that you may be enlightened. For the Prophet says: “Approach him and be enlightened” (Ps. 33:6). And after the table he adds: “Behold from the watchtower.” For unless someone has set the table in his heart through faith, he does not deserve to behold from the watchtower—that is, in Scripture. Isaiah says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand [Col. 0515A].”

> [Note: “If you do not believe, you will not remain” (Isa. 7:9).]

For faith in invisible and hidden things opens the understanding of mysteries. Thus the prophetic man says: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, because I have believed your commandments” (Ps. 118:66). And elsewhere: “From your commandments I have gained understanding” (ibid., 104). He does not say “the commandments,” but “from the commandments,” because keeping the commandments brings forth understanding of hidden things. Thus: “Do you desire wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will give it to you” (Ecclus. 1:33). Otherwise it will be said to you: “Do not seek what is higher than yourself, and do not search into what is stronger than yourself; but always consider what the Lord commands you” (Ecclus. 3:22)—that is, before wisdom has been received and after it has been received: before, that you may receive it; after, that you may receive it more fully.

Scriptures are compared to watchtowers [Col. 0515B] because, as from a watchtower we see far off and foresee the incursions and assaults of enemies, so through the understanding of Scripture we see future things far in advance, and still view, as from a distance, the hidden obscurities of mysteries and allegories. For we see through a mirror and in an enigma, not by revelation face to face. By examination of Scripture, we also avoid the snares of enemies that forestall our vigilance. The same Scripture is also called a mirror, in which an image is seen, because through the instruction of sacred Scripture the image of our entire condition is set, as it were, before our eyes: how great was humanity’s dignity in its first creation; how great humanity’s calamity in transgression; how great the honor in the giving of the Law; how great the splendor of grace’s glory; what God gave [Col. 0515C] and permitted; what the devil took away; what the Decalogue showed; what Christ restored. [Supply: Who could explain these things in words?]

Therefore Saint James, teaching through the mirror of Scriptures, says: “Every hearer of the word who is not a doer will be compared to a man considering the face of his birth in a mirror; for he considered himself, went away, and immediately forgot what sort of man he was” (Jas. 1:23–24).

Therefore, that we may behold in this watchtower, let us stand continually upon it, so that we may not be like the unintelligent person who hears but does not do, but like the diligent person who hears and does; for, according to the Apostle, “the doers of the Law, not the hearers, will be justified before God” (Rom. 2:13). Isaiah indicates how one must stand upon this watchtower in order to contemplate its depths, saying: “Upon the Lord’s watchtower I stand, standing continually by day; and at my guard-post I stand all the nights” (Isa. 21:8).

This watchtower is most worthy, upon which the prophet stands continually, because in keeping it there is great recompense. It deserved to be called not only a watchtower, but also a guard-post and a table: a watchtower, because it teaches and enlightens; a guard-post, because it guards and protects those who guard themselves; a table, because it refreshes and strengthens. Habakkuk says of it: “I will stand at my guard-post, fix my step upon the fortification, and behold what may be said to me and what I may answer to one reproving me” (Hab. 2:1).

Therefore we must stand upon it [Col. 0516A] with the prophet, through the day of contemplation and the night of action, or through the day of prosperity and the night of adversity, so that we may thus be able to contemplate the things set before us on the table. For that heavenly table is not empty or void, but is filled with most precious dishes. On it are festive and restorative courses, by which, aided against the hunger of spiritual famine, we are freed lest the eyes of the mind languish through want. Hence Solomon says: “When you sit at the table of a rich man, observe what is set before you, and know that you ought to prepare similar things for him” (Prov. 23:1). For this is what the giver of the eternal banquet requires.

In these words the spirit of counsel truly spoke with a voice sweet and terrible: sweet to the obedient, terrible to those who despise it. Those who receive will live; those who reject will perish. To those who receive, rewards will be given; to those who reject, eternal punishments. The obedient will be enrolled; the disobedient will be proscribed.

But who is this great rich man? He is the poor and wise child, who, though he is rich as God with God the Father, wished to become poor for us, so that by his poverty he might heap heavenly riches upon us. Thus he is poor in our weakness, rich in his divinity: the Lord of hosts, the King of glory, who takes away the spirit of princes, terrible among the kings of the earth.

When, therefore, you approach the table of one so rich, do so not with the steps of your feet but with the dispositions of faith and charity. Carefully consider the excellence of the table and the grace of what is set upon it. This table is understood in three ways: as the sacrament of the Eucharist, [Col. 0516C] the mystery of the Incarnation, and the teaching of sacred Scripture. In these the inward person is filled with rich and heavenly refreshment, according to the saying: “We shall be filled with the good things of your house” (Ps. 64:5). This is the storehouse of grace, the cellar of the Holy Spirit, the paradise of every fruit, where each soul finds what is expedient for it.

At this table, then, that rich man whose immeasurable riches the Apostle proclaims has set before us royal and delicate dishes, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to the palates of the faithful: humility, peace, love, obedience, and perseverance. The first course of the good banquet is humility, woven with three cords [perhaps: courses]. The first form is that by which one is subject to a superior and does not prefer oneself to an equal; it is called sufficient. The second [Col. 0516D] is that by which one is subject to an equal and does not prefer oneself to an inferior; it is called abundant. The third is that by which one is subject to an inferior; it is called complete and perfect.

This the rich man fulfilled, who came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. By word and example he summons us to the virtue of humility, as its chief teacher, when he says: “Learn from me,” not that I am the Son of God, or that I am King of kings, or that I am coeternal and co-working with the Father, but “because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). He appropriately added “of heart,” because the perfection and truth of humility do not consist in outward dress or speech, but [Col. 0517A] in the disposition of the heart and the practice of holy action.

The rich man fulfilled this humility not only when he emptied himself, but also when he girded himself with a towel and washed his disciples’ feet, saying: “Do you know what I have done to you? I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet; you too should wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14). It was as if he were saying that servants should not disdain to render to fellow servants what the Teacher gave to disciples, what the Lord bestowed on servants. “For the disciple is not above the teacher, nor the servant above the lord. It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher, and the servant like his lord.”

Let us thus eat this heavenly course at the rich man’s table: casting off the exaltation of heart and eyes, let us preserve Christ’s pattern in the stature of humility, returning to the rich man what we have received from his table.
