True humility is fulfilled in two ways: by contempt for outward things and by the rejection, or renunciation, of one’s own will. Unless a person despises outward things, recognizing that true happiness is not in them; unless he also rejects himself, considering his own work rather than another’s, attending more to the beam in his own eye than to the speck in another’s, not presuming to walk amid wonders above himself—as Simon Magus did, seeking apostolic power rather than its life, seeking glory rather than grace; unless he also renounces his own will, doing violence to his own destruction [perhaps: making a path toward it]—he lacks the virtue of humility.

The second course is peace, which the rich man commended to us on earth in two ways: by the word of teaching and the pattern of example. By word, when he says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, [Col. 0517C] for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9). And elsewhere: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:50). The Apostle also says: “Have peace with all people, if it is possible, as far as it depends on you” (Rom. 12:18). By example, because he himself reconciled things in heaven and on earth. Thus the Apostle says: “Making peace through his blood, whether things in heaven or things on earth” (Col. 1:20). He also joined the two peoples in himself, preaching peace to those far off—that is, the Gentiles—and to those near—that is, the Jews. Thus the Apostle says: “He himself is our peace” (Eph. 2:14), because he reconciled things in heaven and on earth. Therefore the Apostle says: “He is the one who made both one” (ibid.).

Accordingly, at his birth the angels are first recorded as singing the song of peace: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14)—namely, through the restoration of heavenly and earthly things. Glory is to God in the highest, where he is praised by angels, because the fall among angels is repaired from humankind. And in the third [clause], peace was made for human beings—not for others, but for those who are of good will. Or: “Glory to God in the highest and on earth,” that is, glory from the angels, whose number he restored, [Col. 0517D] and from the human beings whom he redeemed; and peace was made for people of good will. Or again: through God, glory is in the highest; and on earth peace is for human beings—that is, angels glory in heaven and human beings have peace on earth, but only when they are of good will.

Thus the Prophet says: “In his days righteousness and an abundance of peace shall arise” (Ps. 71:7). And elsewhere Isaiah says: “You will give peace upon peace” (Isa. 26:3). Again: “He will make peace for us”: namely, the peace of immortality and glorification, which follows the peace of reconciliation, as Christ says to the apostles: “I give you my peace; I leave you peace” (John 14:27). “I give” to those who arrive; “I leave” to pilgrims—that is, I shall give to those who triumph; I leave to those who fight. He showed such peace even to his traitorous disciple that at the meal, in the kiss, and in other matters he did not avoid him, but called him friend, saying: “Friend, for what [Col. 0518B] have you come?” (Matt. 26:50).

Those today are unlike him who offer peace to others only in words, having the venom of asps beneath their lips and causing harm especially under the pretext of peace. Satan then entered Judas so that he might betray his Teacher, and daily fills many like him, who betray the brothers whom they encounter and deceive their neighbor, devoted to fraud rather than assistance; they do not sleep unless they have done evil and exult in the worst deeds (Prov. 2:14).

Therefore, avoiding their most malicious evasiveness, let us feed on the course of peace from the table of the rich Peacemaker, who, when he was cursed, did not curse in return. Let us preserve peace in three ways: toward ourselves, toward God, and toward our neighbor. For the virtue of peace is fulfilled in us if we have peace toward ourselves, being merciful to our own soul. For one who is evil to himself—to whom is he good? One who is his own enemy—to whom is he a friend? Let peace, then, begin with ourselves. Let us restrain our inward enemies—that is, the movements of the flesh, and the flesh itself as it rebels and grows wanton—under the dominion of reason, so that in the ark of our heart clean animals may rest with unclean and Daniel may lie fearless among lions.

Let us also have peace toward God. We have sinned through stumbling-blocks.

> [Note: [Col. 0517D] Something seems to require supplying here, perhaps in this way: “We have sinned; therefore let us repent. Let us regard that very nature [Col. 0518D] not as sweet but as embittering even in repentance.”]

And toward our neighbor, let us not do to others what we do not wish done to ourselves; rather, whatever we wish people to do for us, let us do likewise to them. And when we have done everything well, let us say [Col. 0518D]: “We are useless servants; we have done what we ought to have done” (Luke 17:10).

The third course follows: love, which the rich man set before his guests, commending it to us through the work of virtue and the grace of teaching. For, as the Apostle says, “God commends his love in us [Rom. 5:8], because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom. 5:8). He could show us nothing greater or more excellent than this. For this is grace without merit, a work without precedent. For, as Truth testifies, “No one has greater love than this: that someone should lay down his life [Col. 0519A] for his friends” (John 15:13). Truth says, “for friends,” meaning disciples of truth; Paul says, “for enemies,” because Christ laid down his life for enemies in order to make them friends.

Therefore he laid down his life not only for those who were then friends, but also for enemies, so that he might turn enemies into friends, and so that so great an example of love might direct our steps in his paths. Thus Peter says: “Since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same thought” (I Pet. 4:1). And elsewhere: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you may follow his footsteps” (I Pet. 2:21): so that the choir of believers, as it were, may answer Christ the teacher in harmonious imitation or thanksgiving.

This mystery is indicated by the title of that psalm which says: “For Maheleth, for responding: an instruction of Heman the Israelite.”

> [Note: [Col. 0519D] Psalm 87 reads “the Ezrahite,” not “the Israelite.”]

*Maheleth* is interpreted “choir,” by which the harmony of love is understood; *Heman* is interpreted “his brother,” namely Christ. His brothers are those who, with the Apostle, glory in the cross of the Lord; they are true Israelites, that is, those who see God. They therefore understand the mystery of the passion celebrated by the rich man and set before us “for responding”—that is, so that we may answer him by imitation and thanksgiving. But this cannot avail unless it is done in *Maheleth*, that is, in a choir or harmony of love, according to the Apostle’s saying: “If I deliver my body so that I may be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. 13:3).

Thus let us answer the rich man, whose fragrance awakens and delights us like the scent of a full field. Of him Wisdom says: “Have you seen a man swift in his works? He shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before the ignoble” (Prov. 22:29). How great is this man! What kind of rich man is he, who is swift in work and stands only before kings, not before the ignoble, because he is seen only by the wise person, whose eyes are in his head? For wisdom shall be justified by her children.

If, then, you are a child of wisdom, you have seen the man of whom Zechariah says: “Behold the man; *Oriens* [‘the Rising One’] is his name” (Zech. 6:12). That is, you have understood the wisdom that came forth from the Father, the firstborn, against which there is no wisdom, prudence, or counsel. This is the man swift in his work. Others are swifter [Col. 0519D] in speech than in work: they say and do not do. But this man—that is, Christ—first showed swiftness in deed rather than word, because he began first to do and then to teach.

Thus he is swift and vigorous in good work: like a giant he exulted untroubled and irrevocably to run his course; he stood before kings, not before the base-born—that is, before the apostles and the other faithful, of whom Scripture says: “The heart of the king is in God’s hand, and he will turn [Vulgate: incline] it wherever he wills” (Prov. XXI.1). And elsewhere: “And now, kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth” [Col. 0520A] (Ps. II.10). And Isaiah: “Kings shall be your foster-fathers, and their queens your nurses” (Isa. XLIX.23). And in Hebrew it is said: “O king, you are to us [as] your God.” He stood before such persons because he opened their ear and gave them a learned tongue, that they might know how to support the fallen by a word. And again: “[Note: At [Col. 0519D], Isaiah (IV.5) reads thus: ‘The Lord gave [Col. 0520D] me a learned tongue, that I may know how to raise up by a word him who is weary; morning by morning he raises, he lifts up my ear, that I may hear as a teacher.’] He opened my ear, that I might hear.” He is rightly said to have stood before them “as a teacher,” since he granted them to know the mystery of the kingdom and to perform deeds worthy of a prince. But he did not stand before the base-born: that is, those made degenerate by the uncleanness of vices, who are not born of God but of the devil as father—those to whom Christ says: “You are from your father the devil, and you desire to do the desires of your father” (John VIII.44). Great, therefore, is the swift man who stood before kings, not before the base-born: for [Col. 0520B] through him the eyes of kings are enlightened, and those of the base-born are darkened. Kings rise, and the base-born fall. “For this one is set for the fall and resurrection of many” (Luke II.34). Of him Isaiah says: “A prince will devise things worthy of a prince, and he himself will stand above rulers” (Isa. XXXII.8).

Therefore this prince of princes and leader of leaders, just as he commended to us the excellence of charity by his deed, so also, as though repeating the same dish in words, set it before us at table, saying: “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you” (John XIII.34). How health-giving and full of piety is this command, by which he orders us to love one another as he loved us—that is, unto the end for which he loved us: namely, that we may be children and may have life! Every human being, indeed, is to be loved in [Col. 0520C] God or for God: either because he is righteous, or that he may become righteous. Insofar as he is a sinner, he is not to be loved but opposed; insofar as he is human, he is to be loved for God’s sake.

Catholic teaching commends four objects to us for love: first, that which is above us, namely God; second, that which we are, namely ourselves; third, that which is beside us, namely our neighbors; fourth, that which is below us, namely our body. Yet we ought to love our neighbor’s soul more than our own body, because the mind is capable of the highest and supreme blessedness, whereas the body is not. “For eternal life,” as Truth says, “is to know the Father and Jesus Christ whom he sent as the one and only true [Col. 0520D] God” (John XVII.3).

But because carnal and vicious love—the love by which [people] wrongly love one another—is detestable and infernal, Truth, distinguishing it from true love, did not simply say, “Love”; but added, “as I have loved you,” indicating the manner in which we are to love. When he calls the commandment of charity new, this newness is not to be referred to its time of appearance, but to charity’s effect. For the same commandment is contained even in the old law. Thus we read in Deuteronomy: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your mind, and with all your strength” (Deut. VI.5). And in [Col. 0521A] Leviticus: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. XIX.18).

Therefore it is called new, not by the condition of novelty, but by the consuming of oldness and the restoration [perhaps: renewal] of God’s image—an image which makes children of wrath into children of grace, children of the devil into children of Christ, and children of darkness into children of light. Hence Wisdom says: “Let there be for you a fountain of living water, first one in which no stranger shares.” [Note: The text reads: “Let your springs flow forth, and in the streets distribute your waters. Have them for yourself alone, and let no strangers share in them” (Prov. V.16–17).] This is the fountain of charity, which no one can possess and be evil. A person steeped in the gall of malice may indeed possess faith, knowledge, prophecy, and other gifts and sacraments, but not charity. This is the wedding garment, in which the guests recline securely; lacking it, one is cast outside. This is the seamless garment, woven from above throughout [Col. 0521B], which the soldiers did not tear but allotted by lot to one person. By this garment the cold is driven away—the cold in which Peter shivered while warming himself at Caiaphas’s coals.

Of this Solomon says: “Love is strong as death; jealousy is hard as hell” (Song VIII.6). For just as death separates the soul from the body, so the love of God separates it from the love of temporal things; and just as in hell [perhaps: in the suffering of hell] no torment of the wretched is lessened or turned aside from the severity of punishment, so charity cannot be recalled from concern for our salvation by the assaults of any hostility. Commending it with special praise and preferring it to all else, the Apostle says: “The greatest of these is charity” (I Cor. XIII.13). And again: “I show you a still more excellent way: if I speak with the tongues of men and angels but do not have [Col. 0521C] charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (I Cor. XII.31; XIII.1). And Truth says: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you love me and keep my word” (John XIII.35). For the proof of love is the performance of a deed.

Consider, brothers, how precious and necessary is the dish of charity. If it is absent, all else is possessed in vain; if it is present, all things are possessed. It alone distinguishes the children of the kingdom from the children of perdition; and as a body without a soul is dead, so a soul without charity is reckoned dead. This, then, is the new dish on the Gospel table. When it is placed upon the old table of the Law, dishes are set forth [Col. 0521D] which do not refresh, but generate an incentive to hunger. Hence the people of the Law sang an old song—“eye for eye, tooth for tooth.” But Christ’s Church exults in a new song, saying: “He has put a new song in my mouth, a hymn to our God” (Ps. XXXIX.4): namely, a song of peace, love, redemption, and glorification.

Let us therefore take from the rich man’s table this dish of newness, which, like bread, strengthens the human heart. In its strength Elijah traveled for forty days without suffering any weariness. The fifth [Col. 0522A] dish follows: obedience, which he commends to us through the Apostle, saying: “Obey your rulers” (Heb. XIII.17). Again: “Let every soul be subject to authority” (Rom. XIII.2). And through Samuel: “To resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse to keep and to obey is like the crime of idolatry” (I Sam. XV.23).

From the evil opposite of disobedience we understand the good of obedience. To show us more earnestly that it must be kept, “Christ became obedient for us unto death”—not just any death, “but death on a cross” (Phil. II.8), which is more shameful. Great is the evil of disobedience, and great the good of obedience. Through disobedience an angel fell from heaven and a human being departed from paradise. Through obedience [a human being] rises to fellowship [Col. 0522B] with angels, according to the words: “Raising the needy from the earth . . . that he may set him among the princes of his people” (Ps. CXII.7–8), that is, among angels. Conversely it is said: “He who practices pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house” (Ps. C.7).

There remains the final dish in the enumeration, placed at the end because it leads to the end: perseverance. The rich man set it before us by deed, because “having loved his own, he loved them to the end” (John XIII.1); and by the word of Christ himself: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. XXIV.13). And elsewhere: “To the victor I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Rev. II.7). Whoever has competed lawfully shall be crowned. This is the many-colored, long garment [Col. 0522C] which Jacob made for his especially beloved son Joseph (Gen. XXXVII.3). Joseph means “increasing”: that is, any believer increasing in the gifts of grace. Yet he shall not be crowned on that account without the long garment—that is, perseverance—which belongs to everyone who begins good and does not desist.

You have heard what dishes [are set before you] on the rich man’s threefold table. Therefore, when you sit at it, humble yourself in order to believe, that you may be exalted to understand. For there is a sitting of humility and of exaltation. “Look out from the watchtower” (Isa. XXI.5). That is, continually ponder, faithfully store up, and sweetly embrace in faith “what is set before you, so that you may prepare similar things. Put a knife to your throat” (Prov. XXIII.2), as Wisdom teaches you, saying: [Col. 0522D] “When you sit down with a prince to eat, carefully consider what is placed before you, and put a knife to your throat” (ibid.). He uses “throat” for speech, because the voice is in the throat; “knife” for discernment, because with it we cut. Thus one who sits at Scripture’s table to eat puts a knife to his throat when, while diligently meditating the sayings of Wisdom, he draws forth from his mouth discriminating words and turns over upon his tongue no words more often than the words of the heavenly oracle. [Note: [Col. 0521D] Alternatively: When he meditates upon the sayings of those who have uttered Wisdom’s words, [Col. 0522D] he draws forth discriminating words from his own mouth, and turns over upon his tongue no words more often than the words of the heavenly oracle.]

This is done by one who has power over [Col. 0523A] his own soul: that is, one who chooses and preserves the noble state of a wise mind amid the errors of deceivers and the suggestions of harmful persons. If, therefore, you sit with Christ the prince in order to be refreshed by the bread of the heavenly word, carefully attend to what is written; and preserve before God the discernment of sacred reading in your speech—provided, however, that you are such a person and so learned that you have power over your own soul.

But, in order that you may do this worthily, arise, princes; seize the shield, you who eat and drink. Princes are chosen spiritual men who fear God. They first arise and then take up the shield, in order thus to eat and drink. They arise from darkness and the shadow of death, laying aside the image of the earthly man and assuming the image of the heavenly, according to the Apostle’s words: “As we have borne the image of the earthly, [Col. 0523B] let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (I Cor. XV.49). Therefore, having arisen, let us take up the shield of apostolic armor, by which we may extinguish the fiery darts of the devil. Hence he says: “Take up the armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day and stand perfect in all things” (Eph. VI.13).

He then explains what that armor is and what sort it is, describing Christ’s soldiers as equipped and armed in advance by six virtues: the belt of continence, by which we restrain the lust of the loins, where the devil’s power lies; the breastplate of justice, by which we render to each person what is his own; and the footwear of twofold love, by which the feet of our affections are protected, lest they touch the earth and be torn by the thorns of vices and the briars of heretical doctrines, so that we may walk confidently upon scorpions. He also adds [Col. 0523C] faith as a shield: resting on it as the single foundation and defense of the other virtues, we may stand firm in this battle and repel the missiles of assaults, lest they pierce the vital parts within us. He also gives hope of salvation as a helmet. This wraps around the head of our mind; by it our mind is raised upward, lifted toward invisible things, awaiting the Lord and Savior as its reward.

Armed with such splendid and invincible weapons, we do not yield to the enemy. To strike and drive him away, the sword of the Spirit is added—that is, the sword given by the Spirit: the word of God. This is the two-edged sword, teaching about temporal things and eternal things, promising in the Old Testament their consolation in the former and in the New [Testament] their perfection [perhaps: possession] in the latter. The promise [Col. 0523D] of temporal things belongs to one edge of the sword; the promise of everlasting things, to the other. Of this sword the Lord says: “I came not to send peace, but a sword” (Matt. X.34).

Therefore, when we have arisen and taken up the armor of David’s tower, let us eat and drink. For to such people the food, drink, and Savior are sweet and life-giving. Hence in the Song: “Your throat is like the finest wine, worthy for my beloved to drink, and for his lips and teeth to chew over” (Song VII.9). By the throat the eating of the Lord’s flesh is signified; by the wine, the drinking of his precious blood. This peace of life and understanding, this cup of salvation, [Col. 0524A] is worthy to be given to the Beloved for drinking and for chewing over with lips and teeth. So sacred a thing is neither worthy nor able to be given except to the Beloved, concerning whom the Father says: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. III.17), from whom alone comes its preparation.

At his word—namely, “This is my body,” and “This is my blood”—the kinds of nature are changed; nor is it worthily received by any except by his lips and teeth: that is, by those who gaze from the watchtower, confessing with lips of heart and mouth, and who, as faithful investigators, convey the truth they have discovered into the stomach of memory. To such persons the bridegroom says: “Eat, friends; drink and be intoxicated, dearly beloved” (Song V.1). The joyful and generous Lord invites his guests to feast.

Take heed to yourself, you [Col. 0524B] who hear these things, and consider whom he invites to the feast: he who, hungry and thirsty, desires to be fed by you. “When he had fasted,” says the Evangelist, “he was hungry” (Matt. IV.1); and he said to the Samaritan woman: “Give me a drink” (John IV.7); and while hanging on the cross he said: “I thirst” (John XIX.28). For a long time we have shamelessly left the Lord—our salvation—hungry, thirsty, and fasting. We denied him the food he desires, because, obstinate and stubborn in evils, we neglected to correct our errors by the remedy of repentance. It is now time for us to rise from sleep, for our salvation is nearer now than when we believed. The day of our redemption is now at hand. The release from our captivity is now beginning.

Now is the time for us, transforming Jacob’s likeness in ourselves, to refresh our Isaac—that is, Christ—with [Col. 0524C] homely and savory foods. At Christ’s birth God made Sarah laugh. Let us do so, lest—far be it!—we be judged guilty of ingratitude. Therefore let us offer to the great householder, whose guests we are, the food of faith and justice, the fare of humility and generosity; for he does not eat with a proud eye and an insatiable heart. Those who thus eat and drink at the rich man’s table are friends already in the present, but will be dearly beloved in the future, where they shall become from Jacob Israel: that is, from wrestlers, those who see God; from faith they shall attain knowledge, from the way their homeland, from running rest. There they shall be intoxicated by the abundance of God’s house and shall drink from the torrent of divine delight. May he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages grant this to us. Amen.

### XXXVI. THIRD SERMON FOR THE LORD’S SUPPER

[Note: From the Angers manuscript.]

[Col. 0524D]

“Turn back and do penance from all your defilements, and iniquity shall not be your ruin. Cast away from yourselves all your transgressions, and make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. And why will you die, house of Israel? I do not desire the death of the sinner [the Vulgate has: ‘of the one dying’], says the Lord. Turn back and live” (Ezek. XVIII.30–32).

Consider, brothers, with what sweet voice and what fatherly affection the most gentle Father calls us back: the Father of mercies, the God of all consolation, who [Col. 0525A] elsewhere says through the Prophet: “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. XXXIII.3). This faithful and divine word must be received with eager devotion. He does not estrange or terrify you, but invites you with a fatherly voice to amendment; he gives room for repentance while promising hope of pardon. You were enemies through sin, yet he calls you children, saying: “Come, children.” In calling you children, he wills you to acknowledge him as Father. You were [children] of Belial, a dwelling-place of Satan; yet he calls you the house of Israel, saying: “Why will you die, house of Israel?” You ought, that is, to be children of Israel, Abraham, and Jacob, of whom it is said: “He is not God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. XXII.32).

You have grown old in a foreign land, being reckoned among the dead; and the most merciful Father urges [Col. 0525B] newness, saying: “Make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit.” See by how many titles of his love for us he consoles and raises us up. For the Lord is gracious to all who call upon him—but to those who call upon him in truth, that is, for his own sake, he who is Truth. For those do not call upon him in truth who seek him for another reason and not for his own sake. Such people are lying, inconstant [perhaps: importunate], and vain; yet to these persons sitting in the region of the shadow of death he promises life, saying: “Turn back and come.” This happens through repentance, just as you became dead through sin. Repentance is the second plank after shipwreck.

Therefore you, children, who until now have withdrawn by sinning, return by repenting and doing good. For one who sins descends [Col. 0525C] from God and distances himself from God—not by place, since God is wholly everywhere, but by dissimilarity. Hence at the end he will say to such persons: “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Matt. XXV.41). And the Prophet says: “The wicked shall not dwell beside you, nor shall the unjust remain before your eyes” (Ps. V.6). Come, therefore, children; and if you do not know the way and manner of ascending, hear me, who am the way, and I shall teach you the fear of the Lord—the useful matter, namely, how you should fear God. For Solomon says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. Fools despise wisdom and instruction” (Prov. I.7), that is, the uprightness of divine teaching and the purity of holy conduct.

Therefore whoever desires to ascend to wisdom, the mother of spiritual delights, should establish in his heart the foundation of divine fear, since the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. Understanding is good, certainly, but only if it is understood and possessed intelligently: namely, if it is seasoned with the salt of wisdom and the fire of love, so that we may become a sacrifice worthy of God’s altars. “Every sacrifice,” says Truth, “shall be salted with fire, and every sacrifice shall be salted with salt” (Mark IX.48). As a worm is kept away from flesh by salt, so the salt of wisdom and the seasoning of continence restrain in us the incitements of vices. And just as the burnt offering was consumed by fire upon the altar, so the flame of charity consumes whatever is harmful in us.

For love is strong as death, because just as nothing resists death when [Col. 0526A] it comes, but it changes even what existed before into another state, so nothing can stand against charity when it comes: it too changes what existed before and renews what was old. Of it Truth says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth”—that is, charity into human hearts—“and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke XII.14), inwardly in affection and outwardly in effect. For the fire of love burns in these two ways. Hence the bridegroom says to the bride: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (Song VIII.6). For thought is indicated in the heart, action in the arm. We therefore place Christ as a seal upon our heart when we retain an unceasing remembrance of him, as though our heart were sealed by love for his name, lest [Col. 0526B] the phantom of a wicked suggestion creep in—just as a mark is customarily worn, tied to finger or arm, for more frequent remembrance of something. We set him as a seal upon the arm when we strive to fulfill in deed what he did and taught, as though they were true examples of virtue.

The fear of the Lord is, as it were, the gate to doing this. For the gate of conversion is fear of vengeance. “Fear the Lord, therefore, for those who fear him lack nothing” (Ps. XXXIII.10): first, that is, no spiritual good, because to those who seek first the kingdom of God all things are added, according to Truth’s testimony. Thus the bride also says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song II.6). The right hand signifies eternal life; the left, the supports of [Col. 0526C] the present life. Thus his left hand is under the head when the hearts of the faithful are strengthened through participation in the sacraments, through the pledge of the Spirit, and through the consolations of Scripture. His right hand will embrace them when heavenly rewards are received after this life.

Fear the Lord, therefore, for those who fear him lack nothing. Turn back by fearing, not the world, and turn not merely from some but from all your iniquities. For, as James says: “If anyone keeps the whole Law but fails in one point, he has become guilty of all” (Jas. II.10), because the other things he has kept do not profit him unto salvation. Do penance, therefore—which is truly to turn away from all iniquities—and iniquity shall not be your ruin. For when the sinner groans with all [Col. 0526D] his heart, God remembers none of his iniquities for eternal punishment. Therefore, by repentance and confession cast away from yourselves all your transgressions in which you have transgressed by deed, word, or thought, so that you may rise from the threefold disease.

For the Lord is recorded to have raised three dead persons in three different places and to have employed different means in their resuscitation, so that, according to the manner of their fall, the naming (nominatio) of sinners might be shown to be easier or more difficult [perhaps: resurrection, or even their summons]. He raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue in the house; the widow’s only son outside the gate; and Lazarus in the tomb. By these three are signified all kinds of those who sin mortally. Everyone who sins damnably [Col. 0527A] lies dead either in the house, at the gate, or in the tomb. He dies in the house who is killed by the sin of hidden pleasure; he lies at the gate who is burdened by public sin through a transgression of speech or deed. But one is pressed beneath the mound of burial [Note: [Col. 0527D] He said the same thing in Sermon 31.] when he is burdened by the practice of a harmful habit, and by the stench of his exposed scars corrupts those around him.

Yet the merciful and compassionate Lord recalls these persons to life, because by the light of his regard divine grace illumines not only those dead in hidden iniquities but also those dead in open ones and those crushed beneath the weight of a perverse habit.

From this it is clearly understood that a public offense requires a public remedy, whereas a slight and secret offense can be erased by easy and hidden repentance. For the girl lying in the house rises with few witnesses, and they are commanded [Col. 0527B] to tell no one. The young man is raised outside the gate while a great crowd accompanies and sees. Lazarus was called out from the monument with such a thunderous voice that, because of this, many of the Jews went away and believed in him [Jesus], and crowds came to meet the Lord with palms.

And because one who sins less gravely is raised more easily, he addresses the girl before a few people, declaring that she is not dead but sleeping; in this he shows that a soul like hers is quickly raised. He strengthens the young man with more witnesses, saying: “I say to you, arise” (Luke VII.14), because such souls sometimes return to life with greater difficulty. At Lazarus’s tomb he groans, is troubled, weeps, and cries with a loud voice: “Lazarus, come out” (John XI.43). Likewise one weighed down by a long habit of sinning is raised only with difficulty and, as it were, great labor.

The Lord learned from a disciple of a fourth dead man, yet did not wish to raise him. By this are signified those who willingly yield to wicked lips and deceitful tongues; they rise from vices rarely or never, because, their heads made fat with the oil of sinners, they despise Wisdom’s counsel: “Turn at my correction; behold, I will pour out my spirit to you and make my words known to you” (Prov. I.23). Against the vice of flattery and deceit Wisdom sets forth a remedy, saying: “I will pour out my spirit to you and make my words known to you.” For the anointing of the Holy Spirit, which teaches us concerning all things, and God’s words as a remedy against deceitful tongues, had been experienced by the prophetic man when he said: [Col. 0527D] “What shall be given you, or what shall be added for your deceitful tongue? Sharp arrows of the Mighty One, with desolating coals” (Ps. CXIX.3).

The arrows of the Mighty One are Solomon’s words, which, fixed in the human heart, make in it a wound not of envy but of love. By their native power of virtue, they overcome the tongues of flatterers, if desolating coals are added: that is, examples of saints converted from iniquity. These are rightly called coals and desolating, for as coals come to life again from dead coals and, with other coals applied, set others ablaze, so saints who were previously dead returned to life when warmed by the fire of charity. When their examples are set before others, these others too are inflamed; and [Col. 0528A] sin’s kingdom in them is destroyed and laid waste.

Therefore let us set the arrows of heavenly words and the examples of saints against wicked lips and deceitful tongues, so that the Spirit’s anointing may abound in us and dry up the sinner’s oil, lest, with the fourth dead man, we be buried while held by the bonds of death. Of him Truth thus answers: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. VIII.22). Dead persons bury the dead when sinners soothe a sinner with unworthy and false praises and, as though hiding one who is dead beneath the mound of their words, flatter him.

Against them Wisdom, counseling you, says: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them. If they say, ‘Come with us,’ do not walk with [Col. 0528B] them, for their feet run to evil” (Prov. I.10–11). See with what maternal affection Wisdom addresses us, warning us not to consent to evil people if they entice us by flattery, urge us to do what should not be done, or magnify offenses already committed with unworthy favor. Flee such people, whose perverse conversations corrupt good morals. Wisdom rebukes those who act otherwise as little children and fools, saying: “How long, little children, will you love childishness, and fools desire harmful things?” (Prov. I.22). He rebukes you who have hitherto loved childishness.

Wisdom corrects you, and the righteous man rebukes you in mercy—that is, Christ, who rebukes and chastens those whom he loves; who has mercy after anger and crowns after scourges; heals after suffering and receives after casting out. He cast us [Col. 0528C] outside the camp of the Church, as though stained by leprosy of sin, exercising fatherly severity; today he receives us, today he brings us back inside the camp, into the tabernacle. He receives us as persons cured from the contagion of leprosy. For he himself works in his ministers, and in them he speaks: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X.20). And the Apostle says: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (II Cor. XIII.3). Therefore what his ministers do is not unfittingly said to be done by him, who works in them.

Thus, just as formerly in the Old Testament he distinguished by Levitical priests those contaminated with leprosy and separated them from the tabernacle and camp until, cleansed, they showed themselves [Col. 0528D] to the priests, so that by them they might be introduced into the tabernacle, offering the gift prescribed by the Law; so now through evangelical ministers he has decreed that those corrupted by the leprosy of sin, and sent outside the Church by those ministers in order to do penance, should through those same ministers be introduced into the Church once cleansed by repentance. They are to show themselves to his vicars, offering for cleansing not a gift of goats or calves but the sacrifice of righteousness: a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to God. Thus may those who possessed the old spirit make for themselves a new heart and a new spirit, and may those who bore the image of the earthly man bear the image of the new man, so that they may be reconciled to the Most High.

To this [Col. 0529A] the Vessel of Election exhorts us, saying: “As we have borne the image of the earthly, so let us bear the image of the heavenly” (I Cor. XV.49). This is the devout and saving exhortation, this useful counsel and health-giving remedy which the Apostle—or rather the Holy Spirit in him—sets before us. The first Adam was earthly because he was from earth, heavenly [perhaps: earthly]; the second Adam, that is Christ, because he came from above, according to the words: “He who comes from above is above all” (John III.31). The image of the earthly is oldness; the image of the heavenly is newness.

Oldness is threefold: that of heart, speech, and deed. The oldness of the heart is twofold, consisting in carnal and worldly desires. Carnal desires are those by which people do things pertaining to the pleasures of the flesh, such as sexual excess, feasting, [Col. 0529B] and the like. Worldly desires are those by which we seek things that foster the pomp and pride of the world, such as dignities, powers, and similar things. Concerning carnal desires Peter says: “Cast away fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul” (I Pet. II.11). And Paul: “Walk in the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh” (Gal. III.16). Concerning worldly desires the same Apostle also says: “The grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and piously in this age” (Tit. II.12): soberly in relation to ourselves, justly toward our neighbor, and piously toward God.

The prophetic man had consumed this oldness of heart in himself when he said: “I have become like a wineskin in the frost, yet I have not forgotten your statutes” (Ps. CXVIII.80). A wineskin is made from the skin of a dead animal and has no sense of cold or heat. Frost means vices and sins, by which charity grows cold and iniquity is kindled. This is the pot kindled from the face of the north. Therefore one becomes like a wineskin in frost when, having mortified in oneself the desire of flesh and world, one does not grow cold in charity amid the chill of vices, but is kindled more and more by fiery coals.

The oldness of speech is likewise twofold. It consists in self-assertion and disparagement—that is, arrogance and malicious detraction. By self-assertion we sin against ourselves; by disparagement we sin against our neighbor. For by self-assertion we exalt ourselves and speak boastfully about ourselves; by disparagement we malign brothers and distort their good deeds. By self-assertion some become whisperers, that is, sowers of discord among brothers. By disparagement some become detractors, who deny or distort other persons’ good qualities. The Apostle calls these people hateful to God, and the Prophet condemning them says: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue” (Ps. XI.4). He refers deceitful lips to disparagement, and the boastful tongue to self-assertion. Thus in Hannah’s song [Col. 0529D] we read: “Let old things depart from your mouth” (I Sam. II.3). And again: “Do not multiply lofty speech in boasting” (ibid.). “Old things” refer to disparagement; “lofty things,” to self-assertion.

The oldness of deed is also twofold: shameful acts and crimes. Shameful acts are those a person commits in his own body, such as sexual excess and the like; crimes are evils [Col. 0530A] inflicted upon one’s neighbor. Shameful acts, then, defile us; crimes torment our neighbors. Behold the threefold oldness which is the image of the earthly man. This is the three days’ journey by which Moses wished to withdraw the children of Israel from Pharaoh and lead them into the wilderness to sacrifice to our God, signifying that we ought to depart in three ways—as though by three stages—from the spiritual Pharaoh, that is, the devil, so that he may not keep us even for one day.

And just as oldness, the image of the earthly man, is threefold, so newness, the image of the heavenly man, is threefold: that of heart, speech, and deed. Newness of heart is twofold love, namely love of God and of neighbor. It eliminates the oldness of the heart because it empties carnal and worldly desires. For where there is love of God and neighbor, the dominion of carnal, empty, and worldly love is excluded [Col. 0530B]. Newness of speech likewise is twofold: confession of sins and confession of praise. Confession of sins accuses us; confession of praise glorifies God. Confession of sin eliminates self-assertion; confession of praise destroys disparagement. Newness of deed likewise is twofold: continence and justice. Continence stands against shameful acts; justice against crimes. The former makes one turn away from evil; the latter, do good.

The Apostle exhorts us to both, saying: “Do not be conformed to this age,” which pertains to continence, but “be reformed in the newness of your mind” [Vulgate: “of your understanding”] (Rom. XII.1), which pertains to justice. By continence we are stripped of oldness; by justice we are clothed with newness.

Thus therefore make for yourselves, O house of Israel, a new heart [Col. 0530C] and a new spirit, and you shall not die—that is, the second death, says the Lord—for I do not will the death of the sinner, but reconciliation. Hear, brothers, how great are the mercy and patience of our Redeemer, who does not wish us to fall into sin; and, if we have fallen, urgently exhorts us to rise. We abandon him, but he does not abandon us; indeed, he calls those who stray back to the way, and promises life to those who return, saying: “Return, and live.” From what do we return, and to what? From death to life, from vices to virtues, from earth to heaven, from the destroyer to the Saviour. For this is the day of reconciliation appointed by the holy Fathers for penitents, that they may be prepared to receive the mystery of the sacred body on the Sunday of the Resurrection. This day, moreover, has been assigned for the reconciliation of penitents [Col. 0530D], because on this day the Lord first consecrated, at supper, the mystery of his sacred body and blood, and handed it over to his disciples to receive.

Since, therefore, reception of the Lord’s sacrament is deferred until Easter Day, because of the joy of the Resurrection, it was fittingly ordained and handed down by the apostles that sinners should be prepared for spiritual reception and reconciled to blessed redemption. Therefore, you who seem to be preparing yourselves outwardly, adorn the inner dwelling-place of your minds, so that you may deserve worthily to receive the King of kings and to reign with him forever in the heavenly court. May he himself deign to grant this to you. Amen.

### XXXVII. FOURTH SERMON ON THE LORD’S SUPPER

[Note: From the Victorine codex; Col. 0531D.]

[Col. 0531A]

> “When the Lord Jesus had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot; and after the morsel Satan entered into him. And Jesus said to him: ‘What you are doing, do quickly.’ Therefore, when he had received the morsel, he went out immediately. Now it was night. When therefore he had gone out, the Lord Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Little children, I am still with you a little while. I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you’” (John 13:27–34).

Your charity knows well enough, dearest brothers, that the whole perfection of our life and edification is derived from the Gospel. Its words, given to us by the supreme teacher, are precious and daily exhort and edify you abundantly [Col. 0531B]. We now set them before you, not because you do not understand them well, but that you may recall to memory what you understand; not in order to teach, but to offer you the admonitions of our Lord and to move ourselves together with you.

In the Gospel appropriate to the present day, we are instructed concerning patience, love, and humility, and are taught how great a condemnation is incurred by one who refuses correction. For when Judas had been invited to correction by many kinds of indications, threats, sacraments, examples, and lamentation, at last the Lord exposed him, and, as it were by commanding, brought upon him the condemnation and ruin for which he was prepared.

For when Judas thought that his wicked intention was known to no one, the Lord repeatedly identified him without naming him before the Passion. Thus when he said: [Col. 0531C] “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:70). And at supper, when he said: “He who dips his hand with me in the dish, he will betray me” (Matt. 26:23). And after supper he said: “You are clean, but not all” (John 13:10). He said this so that, on hearing that his thought had been disclosed, Judas might come to his senses and turn from his wicked purpose.

He also frightened him with threats when he said: “Woe to that man through whom the Son of Man will be betrayed. It would have been good for that man had he not been born” (Matt. 26:14). He invited him to love through sacraments when he gave his own flesh and blood even to the betrayer. For that sacrament is given to men so that the body of the Church may be joined to its head, and so that unity may be visibly marked in the very form of the sacrament [Col. 0531D]. For just as many grains make one bread, and just as wine is pressed from many clusters, so the body of Christ is built from many human beings. The Lord therefore offered Judas the sacrament of unity, in order to invite him to the humility [perhaps “unity”] of love.

He also exhorts to humility by an example. Although he furnished that example of humility for the sake of the other disciples, nevertheless it is said that he made such a condescension particularly in order to call back his enemy from wickedness. This is indicated at the very beginning. For the Evangelist says: “And when supper had been prepared, although the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot to betray him, Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and was going to God, rose from supper, laid aside his garments, and, having taken a linen cloth, girded himself. Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the feet of his disciples” (John 13:2–5) [Col. 0532A].

Accordingly, when supper had been prepared, he mentioned the betrayer’s wicked intention in order to indicate that it was on Judas’s account that he washed the disciples’ feet. In this deed the Lord displayed a great example of humility, at which good Peter recoiled. For he was terrified to see so great a majesty bending before his feet; he did not wish to see Christ humbled at his feet and could not endure it. Therefore he said: “You shall never wash my feet” (John 13:8).

But we must note why it says, “when supper had been prepared,” although we read that after the washing of the feet the Lord offered Judas a morsel of bread [Col. 0532B]. We should not understand the supper to have been ended while bread was still upon the table; for they were still dining when the Lord rose. “When supper had been prepared,” therefore, means that it had already been made ready and brought forth for use at the common table.

John wished to show how great Christ’s humility was in washing the disciples’ feet. For he first wished to commend Christ’s exalted majesty when he said: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and was going to God.” His great power is expressed when the Father is affirmed to have given all things to him. His great exaltation is proclaimed when he is declared to have come forth from God. Knowing this, he who said, “You are Christ, the Son of the living God,” was terrified at having his feet washed by him.

And what wonder is it that he laid aside his garments for his disciples, when he stripped off flesh for his enemies? What wonder is it that he girded himself with a towel in the manner of a servant, when, taking the form of a servant, he was found in appearance as a man? What wonder is it that he poured water into a basin to wash his disciples’ feet, when he poured out his blood for the uncleanness of sins? [Col. 0532C]

But one asks why, after saying that he “began to wash the feet of the disciples,” he later adds: “He came, therefore, to Simon Peter” (ibid., 6). This seems to imply that he had first washed the other disciples’ feet. Yet it should be understood thus: having first briefly stated the substance of the matter by saying, “He began to wash their feet and wipe them with the towel,” he afterwards returned to narrate the sequence of the event, saying: “He came, therefore, to Simon Peter.”

We should also inquire into what he later says: “He who has been washed does not need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean” (ibid., 10) [Col. 0532D]. For if he is wholly clean, why is it necessary for him to wash his feet? Here baptism is plainly being mentioned. Whoever has been washed in baptism has been wholly washed through baptism. Yet, because one must pass through this world and dust clings to one’s feet—that is, one commits venial sins, concerning which the apostle John says, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8)—each person needs to cleanse his feet, that is, his passage through this world, from venial sins, or to cleanse the dispositions of the mind.

Hence it was customary to wash the feet of saints received as guests, so that if they had contracted any defilement on the road, the fellowship of the brothers’ love might cleanse it [Col. 0533A].

After completing this office of humility, Christ taught why he had done it. “Do you know,” he said, “what I have done for you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for I am. Therefore, if I, Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, how much more ought you also to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:12–14). This means: If I am Teacher, learn from the Teacher; if I am Lord, let not the servant be ashamed to do what his Lord does. “The servant is not greater than his master” (Matt. 10:24).

You have heard, dearest brothers, how the Lord wished to call back an evil disciple by indications, threats, sacraments, and examples. It remains for you to hear how he grieved over him. For the passage continues below: “When he had said this, Jesus was troubled in spirit and testified, saying: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me’” (John 13:21) [Col. 0533B]. He grieved because he could not correct his disciple; he grieved because he was about to expose the obstinate man to the others and pronounce sentence upon him.

Therefore, when all asked who he was, he said: “It is he to whom I shall offer the dipped bread.” And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot (ibid., 26). Judas did not, as some think, then receive Christ’s body. Rather, we must understand that the Lord had already given the sacrament of his body and blood to all, including Judas himself, as Luke clearly shows. He wished to offer dipped bread in order to signify a dipped—or steeped—heart; and after the morsel, Satan then entered into him.

Why, when he had said above, “the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to betray him” (John 13:2), does he now say, after the morsel, that Satan entered into him? (ibid., 27) Above he put in the inclination; now he introduced the effect [Col. 0533C].

Note also that good things harm, and that evils sometimes benefit. For the Lord’s body, which is good, harms if received unworthily; the thorn of Satan given to Paul, which is evil, benefited him. Likewise this bread offered by Christ and received unworthily by Judas brought it about, by his deserving, that the devil should have greater license over him and inflict severe vengeance upon him. For grace having been withdrawn, he left him free to act wickedly, in accordance with what the Lord says through David: “He let them go according to the desires of their hearts; they shall walk in their own contrivances” (Ps. 80:13).

Likewise, by permitting, he says: “What you are doing, do quickly.” That is: Since I cannot call you back from evil, I give you power to accomplish evil. “You could have no power over me unless it had been given you from above.” Therefore, when he had received the morsel, he went out immediately. He went out because he departed from God and from the fellowship of the good. “Now it was night.” This time was fittingly assigned to him, because blindness had darkened his mind [Col. 0533D].

After efforts to reclaim the wicked disciple had been made in vain, and after the remaining company had been purified from fellowship with the impious man, the Lord strengthened his chosen ones for the purification of the righteous. First he formed them by love, saying: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.” It was new because human beings are generated in four ways: either without a mother, as Eve; or without father and mother, as Adam; or from father and mother, as other human beings; or, in a fourth way, Christ alone was begotten from a mother without a father. The man created according to God was new because he is God and man.

He had come to preach a new kingdom, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 4:17), concerning which he said: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36) [Col. 0534A]. And among all fellow citizens he sought those who, in their conduct in the world, would despise temporal things and long for heavenly ones. To them it is said: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man” (Eph. 4:23). To such persons he gave a new commandment.

But why is love of neighbour called a new commandment, when the old law said: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself”? (Matt. 22:39). It is new because it has been extended even to enemies; for in the old law it was said: “You shall hate your enemy” (Matt. 5:43). And why did he admonish them concerning love alone, and then add: “By this all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another”? (John 13:35). For the other virtues—faith, prayer, almsgiving, virginity, and the rest—may be common to good and evil people. Love alone belongs only to the good; and therefore the Lord’s sheep have been branded with this sign [Col. 0534B], because by this sign alone it will be known whether they belong to the flock of the Lord Jesus Christ.

Let us therefore love one another, because charity is from God; and whoever loves his brother has been born from God and sees God. Let no one be ashamed to seek another’s peace first, since Christ was not ashamed to call us, his enemies, back to reconciliation. Shall a Christian then be ashamed to do what Christ did for Christians? Therefore be reconciled, brothers, if there is any disagreement among you.

May God, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house, who is true peace, who made both one, bring you to peace and to its preservation, and cause you to persevere in it until the end. He lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

### XXXVIII. FIFTH SERMON ON THE LORD’S SUPPER

[Note: From the Victorine and Lyran manuscripts; Col. 0533D.]

[Col. 0534D]

> “Our Lord Jesus Christ, on the night on which he was betrayed, took bread, and, giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘Take and eat: this is my body, which shall be given up for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.’ For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes” (1 Cor. 11:23–26).

[Col. 0535A] With the moment of the Lord’s Passion drawing near, dearest brothers, when the Lord was now almost at the point of betrayal, he who had previously observed the legal observances and sacrifices—all of which were figures of Christ’s incarnation and Passion—willed, when the truth came, to set aside the shadow. The spotless lamb in the ancient Law and the other victims prefigured the true Lamb to be sacrificed on the cross. He therefore wished to eat and sacrifice the figurative lamb, and to preserve the shadow of the thing figured until the sacrifice of the true Lamb should take place.

Thus, before the time of his Passion, he wished to celebrate the old Passover with his disciples and eat the lamb, and then to put an end to the old figures. Therefore, after the supper of the lamb, he substituted the new Passover for the old now ended, and distributed his body and blood to the disciples [Col. 0535B]. For if he had first given his body and then the lamb, he would not seem to have ended the old Passover by the new. He therefore took bread and blessed it, and afterward gave them the cup.

It must be understood that the whole of human nature, in soul and body, had been corrupted. Therefore the Lord, who came to free both, had to be united to both, so that the soul might be freed through a soul and the body through a body. Therefore at the altar we set forth bread and wine to represent both, so that through the bread made into his body and worthily received by us, we may believe that our body will at some time be conformed to Christ’s body in immortality and impassibility; and likewise, through the wine changed into blood and received by us, that our souls will be conformed to Christ’s soul in this world while we live and in glory when we rise again [Col. 0535C].

And because the soul, like the body through bread, had to be represented by something bodily, among all creatures nothing was found by which it could be represented more closely than blood, which is called the seat of the soul. But because receiving blood seemed horrible to human nature, wine was set in place of blood, to signify the consolation or sustenance of the soul [the reading is uncertain].

Yet we must not understand that in receiving the blood we receive the soul alone and not the body, or that in receiving the body we receive the body alone and not the soul. Rather, in receiving the blood we receive the whole Christ, true God and man; and likewise, in receiving the body, we receive the whole Christ [Col. 0535D]. And although the body and blood are received separately, we do not receive Christ twice, but once.

This custom of receiving separately became established in the Church because Christ gave separately to his disciples at supper, so that they might understand that they must be conformed to Christ’s soul and body. Moreover, water is placed with wine in the sacrament in order to represent the water which flowed with blood from Christ’s side. That water signifies either the people or baptism, in which the people are cleansed through the shedding of Christ’s blood.

Nor should we doubt that, through the sacred words of a priest’s blessing, bread is changed into the true body of the Lord, so that the substance of bread does not remain. Yet Christ willed the colour and taste of bread to remain, and the true substance of Christ’s body to lie hidden beneath that appearance [Col. 0536A], lest, if it appeared in the quality in which it truly is, the human mind should recoil from receiving a true man.

Thus, when the Lord said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6:34), some who heard this turned back in abhorrence, thinking that he commanded his flesh to be eaten under the appearance which they saw. But a Christian must necessarily believe that, through the words possessing the power of blessing, the Lord’s body can equally be consecrated by the hands of any priest who possesses priestly order, whether good or evil, and that the Holy Spirit is then present in that consecration.

Christ willed to show his body under the appearance of bread because he himself is the living bread who came down from heaven, and he willed under the appearance of bread to signify the union of the body with the head, as the Apostle says: “We who partake of one bread, though many, are one bread, one body” (1 Cor. 10:17) [Col. 0536B]. For just as bread is made from diverse grains, so from diverse members we are made one body of Christ in the union of hope, faith, and charity.

Therefore, whoever wishes to be united to Christ’s body as a member should partake with others of the bread of heaven. For the Lord broke the bread and gave it to all [supplied]; because he willed that what is one should be shared by all, saying: “Take, through conformity, and eat this sacrament.” “Do this in remembrance of me,” so that by receiving the body and blood we may have remembrance of his Passion; and, in receiving the body, that just as he died for us, so we may die for him if necessary [Col. 0536C].

Likewise concerning the cup, which he called the New Testament—that is, the new promise—because through that blood he promised not temporal things but eternal ones. This commemoration must be made until he comes, that is, until the end of the age, when he will come for judgment.

But see what follows: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person prove himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup” (1 Cor. 11:27–28). Therefore he is unworthy who is entangled in mortal sin, that is, who remains in the will to commit mortal sins. A person proves himself not by comparison with others but by considering by himself what manner of person he has been; because “he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment”—that is, condemnation—“to himself. Therefore among you many are weak and sickly” (ibid., 29–30) [Col. 0536D].

God punishes in this life with fevers and other illnesses those who have received his body unworthily; and, what is worse, many sleep unto death, as we still see that mortality often happens after Easter. Therefore, dearest brothers, since the Lord willed his body to be received and shared by us for the preservation of unity, if anyone departs from unity through anger, discord, or hatred, he receives the Lord’s body unworthily and cannot be united with Christ through participation in it.

For just as the bond of charity unites many [Col. 0537A], so discord and hatred, which are one, divide. Take care, therefore, brothers, that the poison of discord does not generate hatred among you and corrupt within you the love of charity. Look to your head; look to the cause of your redemption. For Christ saved us from love alone, as the Apostle says: “God, who is rich in mercy, because of the exceeding charity with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together in Christ, by whose grace you have been saved. Therefore, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Eph. 2:4–5).

“No one has greater love than this, that one lay down his life for his friends.” Christ, however, had greater love, because, as the Apostle says: “While we were still ungodly [Vulgate: weak; Col. 0537B], he died for the ungodly” (Rom. 5:6). No one else had this love, to die for enemies. Hence the Apostle says: “Who would dare to die for a good man?” (ibid., 7).

Therefore, before he preached love, he showed love. He often invited the disciples to love; but in his final discourse, strengthening love in the disciples’ hearts, he sowed it—or rather confirmed it—by example and words. For John says, as you have just heard: “Before the feast day of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them unto the end” (John 13:1) [Col. 0537B].

Since he was about to depart for a time from the disciples who were in the world, lest they be troubled or divided from unity, at the end he showed them a sign of love, lest they abandon him because of fear. He changed and *coerozavit* them [Note: Col. 0537D: that is, joined them, strengthened them, or united them heartily] into concord, lest discord tear them apart. Behold the sign of love: “He rose from supper, laid aside his garments, and, having taken a linen cloth, girded himself. Then he put water into a basin and began to wash the feet of his disciples and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded” (ibid., 4–5) [Col. 0537C].

When Peter recoiled at this humanity, he said to him: “What I do, you do not know now; but you shall know afterward” (ibid., 7). Thus he preached by his deeds; but afterward he explained what he wished to be understood in those deeds. For after washing their feet, he took his garments, reclined again, and said: “Do you know what I have done for you? You call me Teacher, and you speak rightly, for I am. Therefore, if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you also should do” (ibid., 13–15) [Col. 0537D].

Behold, by his deeds he invited them to love and humility, so that no one should thereafter be ashamed to do what the Lord did. Thus, if it seems degrading to a powerful person to wash someone’s filthy feet, it is now authoritative and fitting to do what the Lord did. Therefore, having strengthened them by his example, and seeing in them the mystical figure of his Passion fulfilled [Col. 0538A], he began to console them in these words and exhort them to the bond of love:

> “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now. I give you a new commandment, that you love one another. By this all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (ibid., 33–35).

As though he said: “I am about to leave you for a time and go to my Father. Until I have destroyed the wall that is between God and man, you cannot come. I am going to another country; for the present I leave my household; and therefore I ask that there be no further disagreement among you. Nor do I only ask: I also make it a commandment, so that no one may dare transgress it. And I call it new, so that it may not grow old for you, but may always be renewed within you.

“I impose this commandment upon you especially because by this all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” [Col. 0538B]. Other virtues can be common to good and evil alike; but true love belongs only to true Christians. I have placed my sign in them, by which they may be distinguished from others. By this sign all shall know that you are my disciples.

He himself explains what love they ought to have, by which they differ from the rest, when he says: “As I have loved you.” Not, that is, the love by which people love iniquity. But whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul. People love because of their iniquity, but they do not love as God loved; for God loved us not for his own advantage but for ours. Therefore a friend must be loved in God, and an enemy for God’s sake—he who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen [Col. 0538C].

### XXXIX. SIXTH SERMON ON THE LORD’S SUPPER

[Note: From an Angers manuscript; Col. 0537D.]

> “Having loved his own who were in the world, Jesus loved them unto the end” (John 13:1).

One may question whom John the Evangelist calls Christ’s own, since the world is his, and all who dwell in it. Yet Sacred Scripture customarily calls Christ’s own, in a spiritual sense, those whom he chose with the Father from eternal days to be made conformable to his glory. Hence it is written: “The Lord knows who are his” [Note: “In the morning,” he says, “the Lord will make known who belong to him” (Num. 16:5); Col. 0537D–0538D]. And elsewhere: “The master of the household knows the number of his cattle” [Note: Vulgate: “The righteous man knows the lives of his cattle” (Prov. 12:10); Col. 0538D].

Sometimes he calls Christ’s own, in a singular sense, those whom he chose beforehand from among the elect during the days of his flesh under the Father, so that they might be his witnesses in all Judea, Jerusalem, and Samaria, and so forth. Of them he himself says: “Holy Father, keep those whom you gave me; they were yours, and you gave them to me” (John 17:11). In a third way, he calls Christ’s own all who have been marked in baptism with the idiom of his character—that is, with the sign of the holy cross—and named after him, that is, called Christians from Christ; to them he says: “Hear, my people, and I will speak to you” (Ps. 49:7). Yet they are still together in the threshing floor, grain with chaff, and in the winepress, oil with dregs [Col. 0539A].

Certainly, of these three groups—namely, the elect, the pre-elected, and Christians—the foregoing phrase may fittingly be expounded of the elect thus: “Having loved his own,” from eternity, “who were in the world,” while many of them were still of the world, “he loved them unto the end,” that is, unto the end of time, and especially at the end, that is, in this time of grace, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

But consider the greatness of love thus: hear who loved, and how, and whom, and how greatly. Who? God. Hence the Prophet says: “You are my God” (Ps. 15:2). How? Freely. Hence he adds: “For you have no need of my goods” (ibid.). Whom? Enemies. Hence the Apostle: “When we were enemies, he loved us” (Rom. 5:16). How greatly? Even unto death. Hence: “Christ became obedient for us even unto death” (Phil. 2:8) [Col. 0539B].

But it may be expounded of the disciples thus: “Having loved his own”—that is, those joined to him in a certain domestic familiarity of social affection—“who were in the world,” but no longer of the world, as he himself testifies when he says: “Therefore the world hates you, because you are not of the world” (John 15:19), “he loved them unto the end,” unto the end of his life, and especially at its end.

But consider who, how, whom, and how greatly. O who? The Lord and Teacher. How? As brothers. Hence, stretching out his hands toward his disciples, he said: “These are my brothers” (Matt. 12:50). Whom? Fishermen, unlearned men, the weak and ignoble things of the world, and, as it were, the world’s refuse—men of whom the world was not worthy. How greatly? He came to minister to them [Col. 0539C], and especially loved them today.

For Jesus knew that he would pass from the world to the Father, and that they would go after him, as he himself had said: “Where I am, there also shall my servant be” (John 12:26). Departing from them, he showed them the way of following and left them food on which to feed during the journey: that is, he gave them a way and provisions for the road. Under the form of bread and wine he gave his body and blood to be eaten and left them to be consecrated. Thus he himself says: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 12:19). Christ was the price on the cross; he is provisions in the wilderness; he will be the reward in heaven.

This is the food of the mature, which fortifies against adversities, bestows benefits, and preserves benefits bestowed. This is Elijah’s food, concerning which it was said: “Arise, eat; for a great journey remains for you” (3 Kings 19:7) [Col. 0539D]. Whoever, while asleep, eats this food eats and drinks judgment to himself. If he eats while awake, he shall walk in the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights, that is, throughout the whole time of this life, even to the mountain of God. Of this it is written: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” and so forth (Ps. 23:3).

He showed them the way in the washing of the feet: this way is humility. The first parents, who sinned through pride, unequal in sex but equal in arrogance, went away into the region of unlikeness; but we must return to our own country by another way, that is, the opposite way. Hear that this way is humility. When Abbot Antony saw in the spirit all the snares of the enemy cast before him as though plainly present, he groaned and said: “Who will pass through these?” And a voice was heard: “Humility” [Col. 0540A].

Certainly, in the washing of the feet Jesus, Lord of Sabaoth, to whom angels minister, expressed humility: girded with a towel and wholly equipped in the manner of servants, he bent himself down, his knees fixed to the ground, to wash the feet of men; the hands that created the stars were drawn in to wipe the soles of the poor. This washing benefited them in three respects. It was an example, a sacrament, and an argument. An example of humility, a sacrament of the remission of venial sins, and an argument for mutual love.

Concerning Jesus’ example he says: “If I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet; for I have given you an example, that you also should do likewise” (John 13:14–15) [Col. 0540B]. Understand thus that it was a sacrament. When Peter saw his maker, the craftsman of his clay-made form, bending to his feet, he was terrified; and, refusing to be washed, he heard: “Unless I wash you, you shall have no part with me” (ibid., 8). This cannot at all be understood of the outward washing of feet, but its meaning is: Unless I first wash hands and head—that is, mortal sins—and then feet, that is, venial sins, you shall not reign. For one must enter without even a venial stain.

That it was an argument of love is clear. For it is a sign of great love to serve a person even to the point of washing his feet, so that what is done outwardly by the hand may more truly be accomplished inwardly in affection. Hence the Lord, when the washing was ended, said: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (ibid., 34) [Col. 0540C], as though saying: “I committed this commandment to writing through Moses and often repeated it in words, but now I give it to you—that is, I represent it by manual action.”

It remains for it to be expounded concerning Christians. Yet we shall find the words thus: When Jesus loves his own, he loves them especially unto the end. The proof of love is the performance of a deed. Let us see in how many ways our God loves us, in how many ways he deals mercifully with us. For his mercies are over all his works. As many mercies as he shows, so many proofs of love there are. He knew this who said: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy” (Ps. 50:1).

Consider the great mercy; consider the mercies as though they were the number of daughters of great mercy [Col. 0540D]. “For the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. 118:64). Great mercy is aptly so called, because there is also a small mercy. Small mercy is the blessing of the left hand; great mercy, the blessing of the right: small mercy is the left hand under the head; great mercy, the right hand embracing the whole person. Small mercy consists in the necessities that are added; great mercy, in the kingdom that is sought. The flesh thirsts for the small mercy; the spirit for the great. Hence: “My soul thirsted for you; in how many ways has my flesh also thirsted for you” (Ps. 62:2).

Let the flesh therefore cry and say: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your small mercy.” Let the spirit cry and say: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.” For that which is called small is great in itself. It is a great thing to grant benefits to the undeserving, to give freely to the ungrateful, and to repay evil with good; but it is called small in comparison with the great mercy. It is also small in relation to that for which it is given, namely necessity [Col. 0541A].

Hear how little is sufficient for necessity: “Having food and covering, let us be content with these” [Note: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6:8); Col. 0541D]. And elsewhere: “Give me neither riches nor poverty, but provide only what is necessary for my sustenance” (Prov. 30:8). The philosopher also says: “For necessity, a remedy is enough; for superfluity, nothing is enough.”

Yet these small mercies produce great works of great merit. For the daughters of this mercy are the seven works of mercy, six of which are read in the Gospel and the seventh in Tobit. For by its benefit we feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, receive the stranger, clothe the naked, visit the sick, console the prisoner, and bury the dead [Col. 0541B].

But the daughters of great mercy are far more numerous, indeed almost innumerable; nevertheless, let us take a few from many. Certainly, there is mercy that is great, greater, and greatest. Patience is great; discipline is greater; justification is greatest.

See how great is God’s patience. He did not wait for the angel who sinned to repent; he cast him down from the region of the living into the region of the shadow of death. Hence: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). He did not wait for our first parents either, though he knew their frailty; rather, he struck them with a sentence of curse, whose force was transmitted, as if by hereditary right, to all their posterity [Col. 0541C]. But us he not only waits for through day, month, and year: his patience waits even into old age and senility for repentance; discipline tests us for righteousness; justification enlightens us for life. The first is like an outstretched and threatening hand; the second, like a hand laid upon one and striking with the fist; the third, like a hand placed beneath, lifting upward. The first is for warning, the second for healing, the third for protection.
