The priests implored the first between the porch and the altar, crying: “Spare, O Lord, spare your people.” The Prophet implored the second, saying: “Test me, O God, and try me; burn my reins and my flesh [Vulgate: my heart],” etc. (Ps. 25:2). The same man implored the third elsewhere, saying: “Wash me yet more from my iniquity” (Ps. 50:3).

The first has, as it were, three daughters. For while God bears with us, he admonishes us by benefits, by sayings, and by examples: by benefits, that we may love the giver; by sayings, that we may fear the avenger; by examples, that we may imitate good fathers [Col. 0542A]. Therefore let us love, but without presumption; let us fear, but without despair; let us imitate, but without hypocrisy.

The second, called the greater, likewise has three daughters. For when a father chastises the son whom he loves, he chastises either for correction, preservation, or completion: beginners for correction, those making progress for preservation, and those who have arrived for completion. In the first manner he corrected Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, covering her with leprosy. In the second, he preserved Paul through the thorn of his flesh, lest the greatness of his revelations exalt him. In the third, he brought to completion the whole company of martyrs.

The third, called the greatest, is divided into two. There is a first and a second justification: the first makes a person righteous; the second is performed by the righteous person. For we are not like a dead instrument in the hand of God who justifies us, as a sword is to a soldier or an adze to a craftsman. The first has, as it were, three daughters: first, the infusion of grace; second, the cooperation of free choice; third, the blotting out of sin [Col. 0542B]. The infusion is gratuitous, cooperation voluntary, and deletion divine. Infusion drives away darkness; cooperation uproots thorns; deletion smooths wrinkles.

Moreover, the second justification itself bears three daughters. The first is continuance in what is good; the second, advancement into what is better; the third, completion in what is best. Jerome says in his commentary on the Twelve Prophets that, as the reprobate person is taken from life amid a heap of vices, so the elect person is taken amid a heap of merits—that is, at such a point that, if it were possible for them to live longer, the former would nevertheless become no worse thereafter, and the latter no better. This is the end to which God especially loves his own, when throughout the course of life he loves them in the matters already mentioned [Col. 0542C].

Among these are certain intimate friends [f. *familiares*] of his, like his secretaries, whom he loves as the apple of his eye.

> [Note: From this eloquent praise of the monastic state, together with the equally impassioned attack on monastic defects, a not insignificant conjecture may be drawn that Hildebert delivered this sermon while he was still residing at Cluny, in the early period of Pons, the ambitious pseudo-abbot, when regular observance began to be endangered. It might perhaps have wholly perished had not Peter the Venerable—by the favour of divine grace—Pons’s successor after Hugh II [Col. 0542D] (who presided over Cluny for only three months) restored to its former condition the primitive fervour of so many holy abbots and monks. From this it may also be inferred that Hildebert truly was a monk, indeed a Benedictine, since he so strongly commends the monastic abstinence imposed by the Rule of Saint Benedict and so zealously urges the careful avoidance of defects arising within it.]

These are cloistered men, who have despised the life of the world; who have chosen to be lowly in the house of the Lord rather than dwell in the tents of sinners; who have become the outcast of the people and the reproach of humankind. For them God reserves judicial authority over others, as he himself says: “You who have left all things and followed me … when the Son of Man shall sit upon the throne of his majesty, you too shall sit upon thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:27) [Col. 0542D].

These are that elder son who is in the field, to whom the father said: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.” Yet let this son take utmost care not to wish to take a kid for private feasting with his friends. The kid is a wanton and foul-smelling animal, offered under the Law for the [f. *deletione*] turning away [Col. 0543A] of sin. To eat a kid with friends, therefore, is to sin with a certain pleasure.

The cloistered man eats the kid sometimes with friends, sometimes in friends, sometimes for friends. With friends: if in his mind he returns to their common habitation and way of life, whom he has left; or—God forbid—if he even returns in deed, like a dog to its vomit or a sow to its mire. In friends: if he defends their known evils, if he encourages them by praising them, or if he does not weep and intercede for them. For friends: if he even lends them a helping hand; if he spends on his dear ones what he ought to give to the poor; if he despoils his cell in order to clothe his nephew, because he is his flesh and blood.

Yet even on account of friends the solitary person can eat the kid amid the very cheapness of vegetables, the dryness of legumes, and the scantiness of fish. He may find pots of meat if, beyond the means of his place, he wishes the same things to be served to him [supply: that he would have had in the world]; if, beyond the custom of those among whom he lives, he seasons these foods with exotic condiments and compels them to degenerate from native austerity into adulterated sweetness; if he anticipates the common hour without cause; if he takes more than is proper. In short, he eats goat’s flesh in the cloister who, as though a privileged monk among others, wishes to use more luxurious food, more refined clothing, softer beds, and to attend shorter and less frequent vigils.

> [Note: A Hildebertine phrase.]

I fear that such a man will be excluded from eating the fattened calf which the father granted to the repentant son. But that we too may be found worthy [Col. 0543C] to be brought to the feast of that calf, who offered himself for us, let us love Jesus who loves us. Let us love him because he is good to us, but especially because he is good in himself, so that he too may love us to the end—and especially at the end—when he comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## XL. Seventh Sermon for the Lord’s Supper

> [Note: From Victorinus and Lyra.]

“Be imitators of God, as most dear children; and walk in love, as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savour” (Eph. 5:1–2).

The Apostle exhorts you, dearest brothers, that, since you are children of God, you should not degenerate from so great a Father [Col. 0543D]. For that son is worthy of his father who resembles a good father. Whence, moreover, shall anyone recognize himself as a Christian [as a son], unless he shows himself to be a Christian and a son of Christ, from whom Christians also take their name? But if he is Christ’s son, he is also God’s son. Therefore, since you are all Christians and sons of God: “Be imitators of God,” as those who are his children.

> [Note: Lyra has: “Each person recognizes himself as a Christian and a son of God. For Christians are so called from Christ [Col. 0544D]. But if he is Christ’s son, he is also God’s son. Therefore, since you are all Christians and sons of God, be imitators,” etc.]

Thus John says: “See what manner of love the Father has given us, that we should be called, and should be, children of God” (1 John 3:1). He then adds wherein you ought to imitate him [Col. 0544A]. Thus John says: “He who says that he abides in him ought himself also to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6). Christ never ceased in the world; he was always walking; no carnal pleasure detained him. He never slept in vices.

He does not command us to imitate the Father in divinity, because indeed you cannot be gods either by nature or by participation in deity. He does not command imitation in miracles, but commands us merely to proceed by walking. But with what feet? Not with feet, but with hands; not with the steps of the body, but with the steps of the mind. You are to ascend a high mountain rising to heaven. You know how long each person spends in the ascent of that mountain: one a hundred years, namely as long as he lives; another sixty; another forty; another twenty; another ten; another a single day [Col. 0544B]. But because perhaps you do not know the way, the Apostle teaches the way when he adds: “Walk in love.” Have love, and you will ascend to heaven.

For love itself has two wings by which people are borne: love God and your neighbour. Behold, the two wings that carry us to heaven. By these two wings our Father ascended. For he loved God and his neighbour. He loved God as Father. Whatever he did in the world, he attributed not to himself but to his Father. For he said: “The word which you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me” (John 14:24). And in the prayer of his Passion, when he prayed that the cup might pass from him, he said: “Your will be done” (Luke 22:42). Thus he placed the Father’s will before his own will.

What shall I say of his love of neighbour? It is wonderful [Col. 0544C], because, as the Apostle says, “Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savour” (Eph. 5:2). O how great a love! The immortal God was sacrificed for us like a lamb, like a ram. “No one has greater love than this: that one lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

At least, dearest brothers, let us imitate the Father, who first loved us, first showed us the way, leaving us an example that we might follow in his footsteps. Let us love one another, because charity is from God; and whoever loves his brother is born of God and sees God. For charity is the queen of virtues. All serve charity. If there is any virtue which is not subject to charity, it ceases to be a virtue. “Charity,” as the Apostle says, “covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8). And because charity is higher than all virtues, it alone will remain in the future when the others perish. Charity never fails. This virtue alone will exist among angels and human beings in the future, because with exceeding ardour they will love both God and one another as fellow citizens and children of the same Father (Rom. 13:8) [Col. 0544D].

Therefore the devil labours more to mingle hatred among brothers than any other vice. For the more he sees them bound and allied together for battle, the less he can do against them; but if he introduces internal wars while the enemy is outside, he conquers more easily within. For when discord arises, detraction, envy, contention, and other evils follow from it [Col. 0545A].

> [Note: Lyra: “For when that root arises, there follows…”]

Thus John says: “He who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he goes, because darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2:11). We have explained, dearest brothers, the road by which one ascends to heaven; now we must see how we walk upon it. For he says: “Walk, while you have the light, in love.”

The first step of a person approaching God is repentance, and through it the asking of pardon.

> [Note: Lyra: “for a person approaching.”]

But you cannot ask pardon unless you have love of neighbour; and, just as you ask pardon from your neighbour for sins against you, you must first grant pardon to your neighbour who sins against you [Col. 0545B].

> [Note: Victorinus: “Just as you ask pardon from your neighbour for sins against you.” Lyra: “And just as you ask pardon, grant pardon first to your neighbour for sins against you.”]

For the Lord says: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:14–15). Behold, love of your enemy is necessary if you wish your sins to be forgiven. But you will say: “He takes away my possessions; he has inflicted insults on me.” Behold, brothers, through sin you have lost your heavenly inheritance. Do you wish to recover it? Lose your temporal possession, so that you may recover the heavenly one. Do you wish to have both? You indulge yourself too much. Forgive insults. Imitate Christ—

> [Note: Lyra: “Imitate Peter.”]

—who said while he was being killed: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). And again: “Be merciful, as your Father also is merciful” (Luke 6:36).

After repentance, it is necessary to avoid vices. In this love is greatly useful. For love does not work evil. “Charity does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, does not rejoice in iniquity” (1 Cor. 15:4) [Col. 0545C]. One who loves his brother cannot commit murder, adultery, theft, perjury, false witness, or robbery; he cannot envy, quarrel, or do any evil to his neighbour.

After the removal of vices follows the practice of virtue. There it is quite clear how much love can accomplish. For the good life is one kind contemplative and another active. The contemplative person dwells and studies in thinking of and loving God; but he cannot exist without love of God and neighbour, according to John, who says: “If anyone says that he loves God and hates his brother, he is a liar” (1 John 2:4) [Col. 0545D]. The active life, however, consists wholly in love of neighbour: feeding the poor, clothing them, receiving them as guests, and visiting them in sickness or prison.

Therefore, dearest brothers, every good life is founded in love. But there is a vice among people which very greatly extinguishes love: namely, detraction. This vice must be abhorred among brothers; such persons are sowers—

> [Note: Lyra: “this is a seedbed.”]

—of discord. This is the sword—

> [Note: Lyra: “flame.”]

—of the devil: the conflagration of hatred, death, and the cruel ruin of the soul [Col. 0546A]. Of such people David says: “They speak peace with their neighbour, but evils are in their hearts” (Ps. 27:3). Solomon also says: “The whisperer and the double-tongued are accursed, for they have disturbed those who live in peace; a third tongue has stirred many” (Ecclus. 28:15–16).

For the “third” is one who, secretly speaking to his neighbour, accuses another before him and invents many things which he has not heard, informing him that that person said this and that evil about him. By stirring him with the poison of his tongue, he makes an enemy out of one whom he had previously loved; yet when he sees the person whom he has just accused, he smiles at him—

> [Note: Lyra: “he rises for him, smiles at him.”]

—and embraces him as though he loved him greatly. The tongue sins easily, and because it is in moisture—

> [Note: Lyra: “in dampness.”]

—it slips easily [Col. 0546B]. James speaks of it, saying: “The tongue is a small member and boasts great things” (Jas. 3:5). Again he says: “See how small a fire kindles so great a forest; and the tongue is a fire, the whole world of iniquity. The tongue is set among our members and defiles the whole body … No human being can restrain the tongue—

> [Note: Lyra and the Vulgate: “tame.”]

—it is a restless evil, full of deadly poison” (ibid., 5–8). “If anyone thinks himself religious, while not restraining his tongue but deceiving his heart, that person’s religion is vain” (Jas. 1:26). James says all these things about the tongue.

Therefore, dearest brothers, a bridle must be put upon the tongue, lest it detract, accuse, or speak evil, according to David: “I have set a guard upon my mouth” (Ps. 140:3). Nor must the mouth merely keep silence: the ears must also be stopped, lest they hear an accusation. Thus Solomon says: “Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue; make doors and bolts for your mouth” (Ecclus. 28:28) [Col. 0546C], especially since lying is a great evil. Thus David says: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood; may the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue” (Ps. 11:4). Fear, brothers, the Apostle’s sentence: “Neither robbers nor revilers shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10). Look to your Father, who, when he was cursed, did not curse in return. Therefore it benefits us—

> [Note: Lyra: “it also benefits us.”]

—even when provoked, not to curse. “Therefore,” as James says, “do not speak evil of one another” (Jas. 4:11). Does not love and reciprocal service avail more than hidden gnawing?

What, then, does David say? “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1) [Col. 0546D]. It is good because it is useful to serve one another.

> [Note: Lyra: “each other.”]

It is pleasant because nothing is sweeter than love. Inviting us to it, Christ gave an example of humility because he wished to serve, not to be served, when he washed the feet of his disciples and said: “Do you know what I have done to you?” (John 13:12). That is to say: I have given an example of humility; for “if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, how much more ought you to wash one another’s feet?” (John 13:13) [Col. 0547A].

Rise, therefore, dearest brothers; follow the example of so great a Father, removing evil from your thoughts and forgiving one another from your whole heart, if hidden hatred lies in your hearts. May the God of peace and love remain with you all and give you true peace, so that through it you may attain eternal life.

> [Note: Lyra: “and life eternal.”]

Amen.

## XLI. First Sermon on the Passion of the Lord

> [Note: From a Victorinus manuscript.]

“Our Lord Jesus Christ, dearest brothers, suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people by his own blood. Therefore let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb. 13:12–13) [Col. 0547B].

You have heard sufficiently, dearest brothers, the order of our redemption; yet it is fitting to commemorate this benefit many times. For the more frequently a benefit is remembered, the more the mind is inflamed in love for the benefactor. Therefore we must recall how great a reproach the Lord suffered for us: namely, that when he was led to a shameful death, he was cast out of the city as vile and contemptible; he carried his cross; he was crucified between thieves at Calvary; and he was killed where the condemned were beheaded. He appeared, as David says, “the reproach of men” and “the outcast of the people” (Ps. 21:7) [Col. 0547C].

But though the Jews did these things with a perverse intention, the merciful Lord willed them to occur in a great dispensation. For he wished not only to grant humankind redemption by this kind of death, but also to shape our life. He did not without reason wish to be crucified rather than stoned or punished by another kind of death. Rather, the Apostle teaches that something must be understood in his being cast out and crucified when he says: “Let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach.”

Let us therefore see how we ought to go out, from what camps, and how to bear reproach. So long as we live in this mortal body, we are away from the Lord. In this body we are like soldiers in a camp, fighting against the spiritual enemy. But we must not delight in this camp, because, as the Apostle says: “We are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you shall die” (Rom. 8:12) [Col. 0547D]. Therefore we must go out from this camp, so that we are not subject to the flesh as to a lord. It ought to serve, not rule. Hence the Apostle says: “I chastise my body and reduce it to servitude” (1 Cor. 9:27), that is, that it may serve the soul.

This going out is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matt. 16:24). We must deny, indeed, not what the Lord did there, but what we ourselves have done. Whatever good we have is from God; whatever evil, from man. Therefore, let the one who stole steal no longer [Col. 0548A]. You have heard what it is to go out from the camp.

Now let us see what it is to bear the reproach of Christ. This is the same as what is said in another saying of the Lord: “And let him take up his cross” (ibid.). The Lord wished to choose this kind of torment so that we might take from it a pattern of life. Just as a crucified person cannot direct his limbs toward any actions, so we ought to crucify the old man with his vices and desires, so that neither foot nor hand nor any other limb may be able to perform or even to devise any wickedness. Hence the Apostle says: “Through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). Therefore let us take up the cross and crucify vices within ourselves.

The cross is taken up in two ways: either when the flesh is mortified because of vices, or when one shares the suffering of one’s neighbour. But it is not enough to take up the cross unless we follow him. Therefore he added afterward in the Gospel: “And let him follow me” (Matt. 16:25) [Col. 0548B]. Not everyone who carries a cross follows the Lord. He carries the cross in following the Lord who mortifies himself by voluntary choice and dies to vices.

Christ and Simon of Cyrene were not bearers of the cross in the same way. Christ carried it willingly and died upon it; Simon did so under compulsion and did not die upon it. Simon signifies those who neither fast voluntarily nor voluntarily mortify their flesh, but do so under compulsion and do not die to vices. Christ, by contrast, does both. You have heard of Christ’s reproach undertaken for your sake. It was prefigured by many Fathers.

For we read of the prophet Elisha that, when he went up a mountain, certain ill-speaking boys followed him and cried, “Go up, baldhead!” (2 Kings 2:23) [Col. 0548C]. At the prayer of the righteous man, two bears came from the forest and devoured forty-two boys. Elisha signifies Christ, who was bald, that is, free from superfluous vices. Hair, because it lacks feeling, signifies superfluities; the boys signify the Jews who mocked Christ lifted up on the cross. The two bears from the forest signify Titus and Vespasian, coming from the Gentiles, who scattered the Jews, who had been nourished [supply: in the wilderness] for forty-two years. For this was the period from the Lord’s Passion to the destruction of Jerusalem.

But though it is called the reproach of Christ, it must be so called not in relation to us but in relation to the Jews. They thought Christ’s death the greatest weakness. But we say it is Christ’s greatest strength and the greatest example of patience [Col. 0548D], humility, and mercy. Hence the Apostle says: “The word of the cross is foolishness to those who perish, but to believers it is the power of God” (1 Cor. 1:18). Let us believe that this is the power of God, lest we incur a curse.

We read that Noah had three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. He planted a vineyard, became drunk from its wine, and fell asleep in his tent with his private parts uncovered. Ham his son, seeing his father thus uncovered, mocked him and reported it to his brothers [Col. 0549A]. But the two brothers, hearing this, covered their father with a cloak without looking upon his nakedness. When Noah learned this, he cursed not Ham but his son Canaan, saying: “Cursed be Canaan; let him be the servant of Shem and his brothers” (Gen. 9:25).

Noah, whose name means “rest,” signifies Christ; the vineyard signifies the Jews, who gave him the wine of his Passion, by which he slept upon the cross and his human nature appeared naked and, as it were, powerless. Ham signifies the Jews, who mocked Christ naked and dead upon the cross. The two brothers are believers from both peoples, who excuse Christ’s weakness. The Lord took vengeance not only upon the fathers but also upon the sons, now making them our servants [Col. 0549B].

We have spoken with you, dearest brothers, concerning Christ’s reproach. We have also spoken of leaving the camp and bearing the cross. In this feast we enact a certain representation of this mystery. For we go out from the city, bearing a material cross.

> [Note: It seems probable that Hildebert delivered this sermon while bishop of Le Mans, on the Friday preceding Palm Sunday. On that day, as our Martène noted in his *Treatise on the Divine Offices*, ch. 19, no. 26, the canons of Le Mans solemnly and devoutly carry to the monastery of Saint Vincent the image of the Crucified One which clergy and people customarily adore on Good Friday, to be brought back with procession to the mother church on the following Sunday. The ordinary of the same church, as the aforementioned Martène reports, describes it thus:
>
> “[On the Friday before Palm Sunday, when the image of the Crucified is carried to Saint Vincent, covered with a cloth, there must be four priests in albs and stoles, going barefoot with others vested as far as Saint Vincent, so that the chaplain of our church is at the head, the chaplain of Gordana at the feet, the chaplain of Saint Michael at the right arm, and the chaplain of Saint Ouen at the left; and four boys with the subdeacon, likewise barefoot. When they have arrived at the said church, let the responsory of Saint Vincent be sung; when it is finished, with prayer and petitions, let them leave the Crucified there until Palm Sunday.”]
>
> It therefore seems that Hildebert most fittingly adapted the Apostle’s words, “Let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach”—that is, Christ’s reproach—to the theme of his sermon in accordance with this rite [Col. 0550C], in order to stir the devotion of his hearers more vividly, while explaining to them the mystery of the rite: “We go out from the city,” he says, “bearing a material cross. Therefore, as we enact the figure, let us also fulfil the reality in deed,” etc.]

Therefore, as we enact the figure, let us fulfil the reality in deed. But some of us linger too idly in the camp, because we delight in carnal things. Some are anxious about riches, some devote themselves to lust, some to gluttony, some to vain glory, and others to other vices. But now let us speak of the rich.

The rich of this age are those who are proud, who exalt themselves, and think themselves happy. But, as Augustine says, “nothing is more unhappy than the happiness of sinners.” While rejoicing in excessive prosperity and not foreseeing their everlasting downfall, they are blinded [Col. 0549C]. Hear how they are blind. David says of such blinded persons: “The senseless man shall not know, nor shall the fool understand these things: when sinners have sprung up like grass, and all workers of iniquity have appeared” (Ps. 91:7–8)—namely, so that they may perish for ever and ever.

Sinners are said to spring up when they are advanced to great riches [Col. 0550A] or are said to seek power, when they shine in distinguished garments; yet these things are like grass, which now flourishes and immediately withers. As he says elsewhere: “Man—his days are like grass; like a flower of the field, so shall he pass away” [Vulgate: “so shall he bloom”]. They are like people seeking silver who, having found lead, return to their homeland. They are like one dreaming that he has found and possesses riches, who, when he wakes, finds himself deceived, as David says: “They slept their sleep, and the men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75:6).

O brothers, be afraid, because time is short, and you cannot possess both forms of blessedness. Hear what was said to the rich man burning in flame: “Remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted, while you are tormented” (Luke 16:25) [Col. 0550B], because the kingdom of heaven has been given to the poor. Thus the Lord says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). And David: “He will spare the poor and needy, and save the souls of the poor” (Ps. 71:13). Therefore “make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 6:20).

There is another kind of people who, though not rich, desire to be rich and envy the goods of others, such as plunderers. They are always miserable and will be more miserable in the future, because they lose both goods. But what does the Lord promise them?

> [Note: That, near the end of this sermon, he attacks the despoilers of churches so sharply may perhaps apply to the consuls, or—as they are called—the *scabini* of Le Mans [Col. 0550D]. At the time when William Rufus, king of England, and afterward his successor Henry I were trying to compel Hildebert to allow the towers of his cathedral church to be demolished, because they thought them threatening to their fortress, they could never obtain this from him. Therefore the said consuls, wicked flatterers of royal power, inflicted such violence upon the Lord’s sanctuary itself—as Hildebert says in the eighth letter of the first book—that, when all the city’s churches had been violated and plundered, whatever episcopal power there was, he says, was either dissipated in robberies or vanished into ashes. Hildebert was consequently reduced to such utter poverty that, after even his episcopal mitres had been plundered, he could not attend the Council of Troyes because of extreme want; and he was compelled to take refuge with the supreme Pontiff at Rome only by almost begging his way there. See above, *Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans*, and what we have related on this matter in the *Life of Hildebert*.]

“Woe to you who plunder, for you yourself shall be plundered!” (Isa. 33:1). He who has become a wolf in the present will be food for the wolf in the future [Col. 0550C]. These wolves attack not only people but also God and the Lord’s possessions. They violate and burn the house consecrated to the Lord, where the Lord’s body and blood are offered and prayers are poured forth. But, as the Apostle says: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3:17).

They seize ecclesiastical goods dedicated to God for the redemption of sins [Col. 0551A], and eat the sins of the people. Shepherds ought to cast those sacrilegious plunderers, those wolves, out of the Church, because wolves ought not to be among sheep. If the Lord will condemn in the future those who do not give what is their own, what then will he do to those who seize what belongs to others? What more should I say? They are instruments of the devil, through which the devil attacks [f. *affligit*, “afflicts”] the Church and oppresses the innocent. They are like a lion seeking someone to devour: he rises in the morning, desiring to satisfy his hunger, and has nothing to eat unless he plunders.

What of lust? It contaminates everything; it confounds everything. It made David both an adulterer and a murderer; it corrupted Solomon; it killed Samson. It defiles body and soul. Other crimes are horrible, but this one is foul-smelling. It turns people over to a reprobate mind [Col. 0551B]. This lust produces adulteries and bears incest. People do not guard themselves from their relatives, from those connected by marriage, from a godmother, or from a spiritual daughter—which, as Gregory says, is a great sin.

## XLII. Second Sermon on the Passion of the Lord

> [Note: From Colbert manuscript no. 1017.]

“They pierced my hands and my feet; they numbered all my bones” (Ps. 21:17).

This present week, dearest brethren, deriving its name from its character, is called laborious, or, as people commonly say, from *poena* (“punishment”), in rustic speech *paenosa* (“painful”). If you ask the reason for this designation, remember the Lord’s Passion. For in this week the sufferings of the Lord are recited, and the punishments which he endured, not for his own sins but for those of others, are proclaimed to the people. If you wish to know what punishment Christ suffered, look upon him hanging on the cross, and listen to him uttering from that very cross such complaints as these: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they numbered all my bones” (Ps. 21:17).

Yet these complaints are not those of impatience, but rather of mercy. For he who suffered did not grieve for himself. But who could adequately consider, or adequately recount, the Lord’s Passion and punishment? Let him himself declare what he endured; let him himself bear testimony concerning his punishment—he who suffered it. “They pierced,” he says, “my hands and my feet; they numbered all my bones” (Ps. 68:12). And again: “They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (ibid., 22).

Consider, I beg you, what a punishment it was: for hands and feet to be fastened with nails, and thus to be stretched out upon the very cross, so that all the bones, extended by excessive stretching, could be counted. Do not, brethren, turn your eyes away from Christ’s cross; do not turn your ears aside from his words. Behold, he speaks from the cross, and he speaks to you. He speaks to those for whom he suffers. Therefore I entreat you: show the affection of compassion and the affection [read: effect] of imitation. For this is what he thirsts for; this is what he hungers for. Remove from yourselves the gall of wickedness and the vinegar of most evil thought. Let your conduct be righteous; let your thought be pure.

Behold, you have heard in part—but only a very small part—what punishment Christ suffered. Consider next by whom, how, and how patiently he suffered. Hear the Psalmist speaking in Christ’s person: “My friends and my neighbours drew near and stood against me; and those who were close to me stood far off” (Ps. 37:12). O Lord Jesus Christ, what will your enemies do to you, when even your friends oppose you? He whose friend is hostile can scarcely place trust in an enemy. Yet you, Lord Jesus, are certainly not powerless, but altogether almighty. You who suffer at the hands of such people—what do you do to them? What do you say to them? I know, Lord, I know what you answer me: “I do absolutely nothing; I say absolutely nothing. I willingly endure the Passion, and exact no vengeance at all, either in word or in deed. ‘For I was like a deaf man and did not hear, and like a dumb man not opening his mouth’” (Ps. 37:14).

“I am that patient and gentle sheep, of whom it is written: ‘Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he did not open his mouth’” (Isa. 53:7). O example of patience, worthy of imitation and admiration—indeed worthy of admiration and love, worthy of imitation! Let the impatient and powerless contemplate this example and blush: those who through impatience refuse to suffer, yet, when they do suffer, cannot avenge themselves because of their powerlessness. Truly wretched are those who cannot patiently carry out the vengeance they wish for [read: those who cannot carry out, in the impatient manner they desire, the vengeance they desire]. By contrast, blessed is Christ, who willingly endured punishment and did not choose to inflict upon his persecutors the vengeance that he was able to inflict.

Therefore the punishment endured by the Lord gave this week, as has been said, the name *paenosa*, “painful.” But anyone who investigates carefully will find other punishments for which this designation may fittingly and justly belong to this week. For there are two kinds of people who are grievously afflicted at this season and undergo very great punishment. They labour greatly because they bear an immense burden; and they sometimes wish to lay down that burden, yet cannot.

O burden to be abhorred and never placed upon one’s neck! Whoever places it upon himself is compelled to carry it; and, when he wishes to lay it down, he is prevented by some hindering circumstance. These burdens, dearest brethren, are sins. The man who said in the Psalm laboured beneath this burden: “For my iniquities have risen above my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed me down” (Ps. 37:5). Consider, therefore, the two kinds of people who wish to lay down these burdens but are unable to do so.

What is it to lay down a burden except to abandon sin? Yet whoever wishes to abandon sin must reveal it by confessing it to a priest, as it is written: “Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him” (Ps. 36:5). But often, when the sinner considers the greatness and multitude of his guilt, he is ashamed to confess what he has done; and although he grieves deeply for his sins, he nevertheless foolishly conceals them within the bosom of his conscience and, through excessive shame, does not reveal them to the one to whom he ought.

O fool! Why are you ashamed to tell a human being what you were not ashamed to do in the sight of the Lord? Put shame away from you; run to the priest; disclose the secret and confess the sin. Otherwise contrition of heart will profit you nothing if, when you are able, confession by the mouth does not follow. “I cannot do this,” he says. “I would gladly abandon sin and impose the greatest punishment upon myself for it, if I could usefully do so without confession. But because this cannot be done, I prefer to conceal my sin and end my life in sin rather than endure shame for so great a guilt.” And it often happens just as he says: when some occasion of illness comes upon him, he dies without confession.

Such a sinner, who does not confess sin out of shame, therefore often dies without the fruit of repentance. He is in some measure represented by the son of the patriarch Judah named Er. For Er, as Scripture relates, took Tamar as his wife; but because he was wicked in the sight of the Lord, he died childless (Gen. 38:3 ff.). Now *Er* is interpreted “clothed in skins” [read: “hairy”], and *Tamar*, “bitterness.” What, then, does “clothed in skins” signify except the sinner? What does Tamar signify except the bitterness of sin?

That sin is signified by skin is plainly shown in Genesis, where we read that after their sin the Lord made garments of skins for Adam and Eve (Gen. 3:7), as though, after they had sinned, the Lord had plainly said to them: “See, clothed in skins, how hairy you are outwardly; and by this diligently consider what you have become inwardly through sinning.” For just as hair arises from superfluous humours, so sin arises not from nature itself, which is good, but from the defect of a perverse will.

Thus Er, whose name means “clothed in skins” [“hairy”], takes Tamar as wife when the sinner, considering the guilt of his iniquity and judging himself, receives in his heart the greatest bitterness for that guilt. But because he does not confess the sin through shame, he is like Er who, having taken Tamar, dies childless. Although he receives great bitterness for his sin, still from that bitterness—because he does not confess the sin—he produces no fruit of repentance, as it were no son.

There is another kind of person whose heart is consumed with great bitterness when considering his own guilt, yet who is restrained from confession of it not so much by shame as by love of sin. But perhaps someone will ask how bitterness can coexist with pleasure. We answer briefly that there are diverse affections and diverse perspectives within the sinner’s heart. For sometimes even one who loves sin, compelled by reason, looks toward God; and when he considers God’s dreadful judgment, what delights him immediately causes him horror. That horror instils fear; fear produces bitterness; and so the same mind is now made by penal bitterness [read: “affected”], now infected by the wickedly alluring pleasure of sin.

Those, therefore, who feel such great delight in sin regard it as useless to go to confession. For they say to themselves: “What profit is there for me in confessing sins which I know I cannot abandon because of excessive love?” The second son of Judah, namely Onan, figuratively represents the man who does not go to confession because of love of sin. After the death of his brother, Onan took Tamar as wife; but because he spilled his seed upon the ground, he died childless.

For what is it to spill seed upon the ground except to fix one’s delight upon earthly and carnal desires? The seed from which a son could be begotten is spilled upon the ground when the heart’s affection, from which good works could arise, is scattered amid earthly desires. But although a sinner of this kind is sometimes pierced with compunction over sin and, as if by contracting marriage, is joined to Tamar—that is, to bitterness—he nevertheless dies childless. For, abandoning confession through love of sin, he obtains no fruit of good work.

Behold, we have distinguished two kinds of sinners for whom the present week is exceedingly painful, because they carry a great burden of sins and nevertheless refuse to relieve themselves: some do not confess out of shame for sin; others do not confess out of love of sin. There remains a third kind of sinner, worse than those mentioned above: those who consent to sins and yet feel no bitterness for their sins. Such sinners have been so blinded by the very habit of sinning that they commit grave sins without knowing that they sin. They are like a numb limb in the body: although it is very sick, it loses the faculty of sensation through excessive weakness and does not feel the pain of its illness.

Concerning those who do not grieve for their sins, but—what is worse—rejoice when they have done evil, it is written: “Those who rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in most wicked things” (Prov. 2:14). This third class of sinners is fittingly represented by Judah’s third son, Shelah, who did not take Tamar in marriage. *Shelah* is interpreted “forsaken.” Therefore Shelah—that is, the forsaken man—does not take Tamar, that is, bitterness, as wife when the sinner, blinded because God has forsaken him and left to himself, is in no way made bitter in his heart over sins which he does not understand.

Of such people, whom God forsakes, the Psalm says: “He gave them over according to the desires of their heart” (Ps. 80:13). And again: “Of whom you remember no more, and they themselves have been cast away from your hand” (Ps. 87:5). These sinners, who do not know themselves, must be wept for because they do not weep; they must be lamented because they do not groan.

You should know that sinners of this kind are worse than those already mentioned. For even if the others do not abandon sin for some reason, they nevertheless understand that they are sinners and sometimes groan deeply over their sins; and they draw nearer to salvation in proportion as they do not ignore the greatness of their weakness. It would therefore be more beneficial for these people to know themselves and, knowing themselves, to weep, than to remain ignorant of themselves and rejoice and exult as though they possessed a good conscience.

Because of these three kinds of people—those who, blinded in heart, do not know their sins; or who, if they know them, neither confess nor abandon them, whether through human shame or through delight in sin—three miracles occurred in the Lord’s Passion. For thus we read: “The earth shook, the rocks were split, the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose” (Matt. 27:51–52).

The earth is shaken when the heart of the sinner, to whom it was said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19), is shaken by consideration of its guilt. The rock is split and the tomb opened when, through God’s grace, hardness of heart is dissolved and the mouth formerly closed in concealment of sin is afterwards opened for confession of that same sin. But what good does it do if the tomb has been opened and the dead person does not rise? Notice that one who rises passes from death to life. What is death except sin? And what is life except good work? For by sin the soul dies, and by good work it is made alive. It is therefore necessary that, once the tomb has been opened, the dead person should rise and pass from death to life. That is, after confession the sinner must abandon the sin he has confessed and apply himself watchfully to good works.

Behold, we have examined three classes of sinners and have described, in some measure, the punishment of two of them. Now let us say something briefly about the punishment which the devil himself suffers in this week.

What punishment, dearest brethren, do you suppose torments that devil? What envy tortures him when Christ’s mercy leads those whom he has until now possessed as his own slaves from the bondage of sin to the freedom of righteousness? It is indeed a great punishment for him when he sees the sinner recognize his sin, groan in recognizing it, weep in groaning, disclose it in weeping, and after disclosure abandon it altogether. He is also tortured by great envy when he sees Christ, lifted up upon the cross, drawing all things to himself. He is afflicted by immeasurable punishment when he, the armed strong man, is defeated by the stronger Judge who comes upon him, Christ; when all his weapons are broken; and when even his spoils are forcibly snatched from his hand by Christ himself.

Behold, we have made mention of the Lord’s punishment, of the punishment of certain sinners, and of the devil’s punishment, in order to show why the present week is called painful. Therefore, dearest brethren, judging the punishment of sinners, of which we have spoken above, to be fruitless, and abhorring the devil’s punishment as is fitting, let us consider the Lord’s punishment and his power. Let us see not only how patiently he endured punishment, but also how great was the love he displayed in his Passion, and that his love was not merely patient but also kind.

For he both endured and loved his persecutors who crucified him; and, hanging on the cross, he prayed for them, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23:34). Therefore, dearest brethren, let us imitate Christ’s patience, and let neither tribulation nor distress separate us from his great love. May he himself deign to grant this, whose kingdom and dominion remain without end through ages of ages. Amen.

## XLIII. ON THE HOLY DAY OF EASTER. FIRST SERMON

[Note: From Saint-Germain manuscript 381.]

“A growing son is Joseph, a growing son and fair in appearance; the daughters ran upon the wall” (Gen. 49:22).

When Israel blessed his assembled sons and foretold what would happen in the last times, he celebrated Joseph among the others, both with exceptional love and with a solemn, mystical blessing, in praise of the Saviour, saying: “A growing son is Joseph,” and so forth.

For Joseph, both in the meaning of his name and in his actions, prefigured the person of the Saviour. Sold by his brothers to the Ishmaelites for the price of thirty pieces of silver, he was exalted in Egypt on account of righteousness. So too Christ was sold by his brothers—namely Judas and the other Jews—for the same price to the spiritual Ishmaelites, that is, the Jews, who bear the name of the Ishmaelites in mystical interpretation. For Ishmaelites are interpreted “obedient to themselves,” as though not to God, because they follow their own perverse thoughts and do not walk in God’s good ways.

But by this sale, which proceeded from the countenance of God, his name was not extinguished through God’s judgment; rather, his glory was magnified over all the earth. Thus was fulfilled the petition which he himself plainly addresses to the Father through the prophet: “Let my judgment come forth from your countenance; let your eyes behold equity” (Ps. 16:2).

For our Saviour, dealing with the Jews by the principle of equity rather than by a display of power, as it were placed himself under the Father’s judgment; and, pleading on his own behalf and setting out his case, he speaks against the people through Micah: “My people, what have I done to you, or how have I wearied you? Answer me. For I brought you out of the land of Egypt and freed you from the house of bondage” (Mic. 6:3).

For a long time the Lord had endured the malice of the Jews; for a long time he had awaited their conversion, as he himself says through the prophet: “I have laboured in enduring” (Jer. 6:11). But, seeing them incorrigible, and lest it should appear that their failure to turn to an understanding of truth proceeded from him, he showed instead that he had bestowed benefits deserving every love and obedience: he had not been burdensome to them and had inflicted no evil upon them, except perhaps for correction, not destruction. It is as though he said: “I have done you no evil, but many good things; for I brought you out of the land of Egypt and from the house of bondage.”

What is said to them according to the letter is spiritually applied to us. For we are spiritual Jews if we confess Christ. He brought us out of the land of Egypt, that is, from darkness and tribulation, and from the house of bondage to the devil or to sin. “For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 3:34). Therefore let them not flatter us [read: “let us not flatter ourselves”], as though the things said specifically about the Jews do not concern us; for, as the Apostle says, they were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. 10:11).

Therefore he rebukes us in them, and, as though pleading a case against us, indicates that he has conferred many benefits without merit on our part. It is as though he says: “What more ought I to have done for my vineyard that I did not do? Why do you not follow me? Why have you not obeyed me?” When they fail to answer, he turns his words toward God the Judge, saying: “Let my judgment come forth from your countenance; let your eyes behold equity” (Ps. 16:2).

It is as though he says: “May the judgment by which I was unjustly condemned by Pilate and by the Jews, and by which I am daily judged by blasphemers, proceed not from their wickedness but from your countenance—that is, from your gaze, namely the purity with which you behold us. Let that judgment not result in my destruction, as they intend, but in my glorification, as my innocence deserves and its devout appeal has obtained.”

He, despised and rejected by the Jews, passed in the apostles to the Gentiles, where, as Joseph in Egypt (Gen. 37), his magnificence was exalted above the heavens. Behold Joseph: sold by his brothers, exalted in the Egypt of this world, afterwards despised and rejected [read: “despised and rejected, afterwards exalted”]. Hence he truly says: “A growing son”—growing, certainly, in himself and growing in his own people.

This is Joseph, whom Israel loved above all his sons because he had begotten him in old age. Israel is God the Father, who has many sons by grace but one only by nature. Him he loves above all as natural, as only-begotten; the others he loves as adopted sons. He loves the others for the sake of this one, and this one for his own sake. According to the Apostle, he is “the firstborn among many brethren” (Rom. 8:29), because he was begotten before all things, although born in old age. Possessing the paternal inheritance, he rules in his own dominion after the manner of a firstborn and apportions to others according to his will, because the Father begot him in old age and caused him to be incarnate at the end of the ages.

He who was begotten of the Father before the world was born of the Virgin in the old age of the world. The Father loves him above all others, as he himself says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5). This, therefore, is the Father’s beloved Son, and the growing son. The word “growing” is doubled, a word of increase, in order to indicate manifold increase. Now Joseph is interpreted “increase”; hence, playing upon the meaning of the name, he calls him Joseph and adds “growing,” and, to indicate the perfection of increase, doubles it: “A growing son is Joseph, a growing son.”

He repeats the name “son” just as he repeats the term “growing.” For as he was born twice according to two births—one from the Father and the other from the mother—so he increased in two ways: in himself and in his members; and in himself in two ways, namely in soul and in flesh. He increased in the good of the soul because sorrow was turned into joy, as he says through the Prophet: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness” (Ps. 39:11).

God turned the mourning—that is, the sorrow of the Passion, concerning which Christ said, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38)—into the joy of blessed resurrection. Likewise, when the sackcloth was torn, he was girded with gladness, that is, with the glory of immortality. For previously he bore sackcloth and was clothed in haircloth, according to the saying: “When they troubled me, I clothed myself in haircloth” (Ps. 34:13).

Therefore he possessed a sackcloth garment, but not the guilt deserving sackcloth. Sackcloth signifies mortality, passibility, and human frailty. The misery of this sackcloth is the consequence of sin, from which he was wholly free: in him there was no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. This is the rock upon which it is impossible to find the tracks of the serpent. “And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:1), as the Apostle says.

Upon this rock, from which Peter is named just as the Christian is named from Christ, it is impossible to find the tracks of the serpent—that is, the weapons of the devil, the marks of the devil’s warfare: namely, vices and sins, which our enemy uses as weapons to deceive and overcome the faithful. Christ did not possess these; rather, the spiritual Joseph destroyed them in those who did possess them. Of him the Father says through Isaiah: “By his knowledge my righteous servant shall justify many, and he himself shall bear their iniquities” (Isa. 53:11).

Behold, he is called righteous and servant. He is righteous not only because, as man, he is without sin and full of grace, but because, as God, he makes others righteous. Therefore he is righteous because he is full of righteousness and truth; he is the one who justifies, not one who is justified, because he is not cleansed from sins but cleanses others. He is servant according to his humanity, because he was obedient to the Father unto death.

Thus he shall justify many, not all, because “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22:14), by his knowledge—that is, by the teaching of truth, which dispelled the darkness of ignorance, illuminated the elect with rays of divine light, and reconciled to the Father those who had been far off through his instruction. Thus Isaiah says: “The discipline of our peace was upon him” (Isa. 53:5). Truly his instruction is one of peace, because he is our mediator; and a mediator is not mediator of one person but of two, since a mediator restores the discordant to peace.

Now we were at variance with ourselves, with our neighbour, and with God. We were at variance with ourselves because we did what we did not wish to do, according to the saying: “What I do not wish, I do, and I hate what I do” (Rom. 7:19). We also acted with hostility toward our neighbours, because we sought to draw them not into the way of salvation but into the abyss of destruction, blind people leading the blind. We were also at variance with God because we did not glorify him as Lord, serving the creature rather than the Creator (Rom. 1:25). But, having heard the instruction of peace through him who is our peace, we return, like wandering sheep, to the learned shepherd, who says through Isaiah: “The Lord has given me a learned tongue, that I may know how to sustain with a word one who has fallen” (Isa. 50:4).

This righteous and learned one, therefore, justified many by his knowledge, and by his strength multiplied strength in the weak who have no strength, when, after the sackcloth of mortality was torn, he received the diadem of everlasting joy and glorious immortality; when what the whole sackcloth had formerly concealed shone forth [read: “flashed forth”]; when the disfigured flesh blossomed again, as the Lord says through the prophet: “And my flesh blossomed again” (Ps. 17:7).

He did not say simply, “It blossomed,” but “It blossomed again.” For the human flesh which the Son of God assumed lost, in the first parent, the flower of its condition—namely freedom from guilt and punishment. The first condition of humanity shone brightly [read: “of man when created”]; that flower fell in the fall of transgression, but was restored in the resurrection of the Saviour. He was anticipated with blessings of sweetness in his conception; he was free from every stain and guilt; and, rising from the dead, with death swallowed up in victory and death’s sting crushed, our flesh blossomed again in its head, so that where our weakness had appeared, our glory might shine forth.

Through him, therefore, the flower of the grass was restored. “For all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass has withered and the flower has fallen” (Isa. 40:8). He clothed himself with grass in order to consume in us wood, hay, and stubble, and to clothe us with garments of salvation and glory, so that through him our deformity might bloom again.

This is Aaron’s rod that put forth leaves, and the almond tree that blossomed, concerning which Ecclesiastes says: “The almond tree shall blossom, the locust shall grow fat, the caper-bush shall be scattered, because man shall go to the house of his eternity” (Ecclus. 12:5). What is this almond tree that blossomed, and when did it blossom? This almond tree is the growing son—namely Joseph, that is, Christ.

For the almond has three things: a husk, a shell, and a kernel; and Christ truly subsists in three substances. In him is the husk of flesh, the shell of mind [that is, soul], and the kernel of divinity. The husk has bitterness, the shell strength, and the kernel sweetness. From weak flesh he feels bitterness, as he says through the prophet: “My reins rebuked me” (Ps. 15:7). In the affection of the flesh he shrank from carrying out the Father’s dispensation as he willed; but in spirit he did not hesitate or refuse, but promptly accomplished the Father’s will. Hence he himself said: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 16:41).

Rightly, therefore, Christ’s soul is represented by the shell, since it could in no way be recalled or drawn back from the purpose of human redemption. The kernel, however, sweet to the taste, driving away hunger and providing refreshment, rightly signifies Christ’s divinity. It is of infinite sweetness to those who thirst, and satisfies them in such a way that it fulfils their desire to taste—the one into whom angels desire to look, and what they always do, they desire to do without ceasing. There is there satiety without disgust and desire without sighing. Neither satiety brings weariness nor desire brings torment, because there is sweetness without measure, according to the saying: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 35:9). And elsewhere: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16:15). Behold satiety; behold sweetness.

This kernel is good, but hidden, because according to Isaiah he is God (Isa. 44:14). Yet he is found by those who seek, received by those who ask, and opened to those who knock, provided that they do this piously and perseveringly [read: “provided, however”]. But this kernel, this God, did not stand forth or shine out unless the husk was broken and removed from the shell. Honey was not found in the mouth of a living lion, but of a dead one.

[Note: This is scarcely intelligible. Perhaps rather: “Therefore the husk was removed from the shell—that is, the body from the soul—but neither was removed from the kernel, that is, from the Deity or Word.” This will be clear from what follows.]

Therefore the husk was removed from the shell, not from the kernel; or the shell from the husk. Thus, when the lion was dead, honey was found in his mouth, because the soul departed from the body, but neither departed from the Word of God. The lion truly died; but after the sword had been poured out in hell and captives had been led forth from there, on the third day, when the husk was healed, the lion poured forth honey.

And when Joseph, wishing to be recognized by his brothers, said: “I am Joseph your brother, whom you sold. Is my father still alive?” (Gen. 45:5), it was as though he said: “He does not yet live in you, because I have not yet ascended in your heart to my Father after being sold, after being handed over. But recognize me: I am the true Joseph, equal to the Father, though sold and slain.” Behold the honey: namely, the abundance of sweetness, the disclosure of truth. Thus the kernel formerly hidden shone forth, and the almond tree, as though dry and withered, blossomed.

The flower of grass which had fallen sprouted again; and, when the almond tree blossomed, the locust grew fat and the caper-bush was scattered. In the locust the Gentiles are understood; in the caper-bush, the Jewish people. For the locust moves by leaps and does not walk except by leaping, and it is carried along without order. Such was paganism, which formerly was borne through vices not step by step but as if by leaps, and was carried with extreme disorder, because it “changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man” (Rom. 1:23).

Behold its great and thoughtless leap; and, with still greater dullness, it leapt into worse precipices: afterwards into the likeness of birds, then of four-footed creatures, and finally of serpents (ibid.). Behold the locust’s leaps. How bitter these leaps were—deadly to itself! The locust wounded itself with these lethal weapons, until the young hart, that is, the Son of the Father, “leaping upon the mountains and skipping over the hills,” made leaps from heaven into the Virgin’s womb, from the womb into prison, from prison [read: “into flesh, from flesh”] into hell, and from hell into the palm, according to the saying: “I will climb into the palm tree and eat [variant: seize] its fruits” (Song 7:8).

These are leaps of salvation, not destruction. He chose to leap by the leaps of life in order to draw the locust back from the leaps of Gehenna. He leapt by the leaps of man in order to draw the locust back from perverse leaps. He himself leapt so that the locust might leap—that is, so that it might set in its heart ascents and steps of virtues by which it may ascend to behold the young hart of the deer, namely Christ, proclaimed beforehand by the patriarchs and prophets, who were deer longing for the fountains of living waters, namely Christ.

Thus this locust, when formerly lifeless and lean, firm [read: foolish] and barren, was fattened when the almond-tree blossomed, because after Christ’s resurrection [Col. 0561A] it was visited by the apostles. Among them our Samson—that is, Christ—went to take a wife from among foreigners. He mounted the apostolic horses and directed the four-horsed chariots of the four evangelists toward the nations. Hence Habakkuk: “For you ascend upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. L, 8). As these chariots came, the locust was fattened. Having received the spirit of life and recovered fertility, she who had formerly been barren became fruitful in children; she who had previously lain beneath seven demons was enlarged by the gifts of sevenfold grace; instead of a curse she received grace, instead of *Uri* [read: vengeance], forgiveness. But when the locust was fattened, the caper-plant was destroyed, because while the barren woman bore many children, she who had many children was weakened—that is, the Synagogue, which [Col. 0561B] is rightly signified by the caper-plant.

For the caper-plant is said to cling to rock and to benefit the kidneys [that is, perhaps, to heal them]. By it Israel is understood, which of old clung to God, to whom it was joined in friendship. Therefore the caper-plant was destroyed and the locust fattened, because blindness has happened in part to Israel, so that the fullness of the nations might enter. Hence the Lord says to the Jews: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXI, 43). And again: “I came into this world for judgment, that those who do not see may see”—that is, the nations—“and that those who see may become blind” (John IX, 39)—that is, the Jews. When the barren branches were broken off and the barren [read: fruitful] wild olive was grafted in, the locust was fattened and the caper-plant destroyed, because, the sons and members of the household having been excluded, strangers are received.

Hence [Col. 0561C] the Lord, addressing the Church through Isaiah, says: “I shall bring your sons from afar, and the sons of foreigners shall build your walls, and their kings shall minister to you” (Isa. VI, 10). We see this both literally and spiritually. For princes of the nations throughout the world built churches, such as Constantine, who constructed twelve churches at Rome in honor of the twelve apostles, and many others, who built many churches and supplied them with what was necessary. Allegorically, the sons of foreigners are the martyrs and teachers of the nations, by whose faith and virtues the holy Church is founded.

On account of this abundance and this fattening of a people rich in virtues, the locust is summoned to joy by Isaiah, who says: “Rejoice [Vulgate: praise], O barren woman who does not bear; exult and praise, [Col. 0561D] you who did not give birth, for the children of the deserted woman are many, more than of her who has a husband” (Isa. LIV, 1): that is, of the Gentile people rather than of the Synagogue; of the locust rather than of the caper-plant. Isaiah himself, signifying the fruitfulness of the locust’s people, says: “Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles” (Isa. LIV, 2).

Greatly, then, was the locust fattened: she enlarged throughout the whole world the place of the tent—that is, of the Church, signified by Moses’ tabernacle—and spread over the whole world the crimson and hyacinth-blue skins of the tabernacles, that is, the preachers, lofty through the power of martyrdom and the grace of contemplation. But all this comes from the fact that “man has gone to the house of his eternity” (Eccl. XII, 5). This man is Christ, concerning whom [Col. 0562A] Isaiah says: “Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is accounted exalted” (Isa. II, 22). And Jeremiah: “He is a man, and who shall know him?” (Jer. XVII, 16, according to the LXX). One is scarcely found who knows him, because, although he breathes and lives as a man, he is nevertheless exalted.

Therefore he went into the house of eternity, because he passed from this world to the Father—that is, to the invisible realities of the Father’s majesty. This passing-over is called *Pascha* in Hebrew. Hence in Exodus, concerning the Paschal Lamb: “You shall eat in haste. For it is the Pascha, that is, the passing-over of the Lord” (Exod. XII, 11). See the shadow; attend to the figure of the truth which we taste. There the Pascha—that is, the lamb—was sacrificed in the evening; here our Pascha, Christ, was to be offered in the evening of the world. There the Lord passed [Col. 0562B] through Egypt in a subjected creature; here Christ passed into heaven in his own form. He passed over first, that we might pass over. Where? To Bethlehem with the shepherds. And for what purpose? “That we may see the word which has happened, which the Lord has shown us” (Luke II, 15).

This passing-over, from which Pascha receives its name, is good and health-giving. For this reason Christ was sacrificed: that he himself might go into the house of eternity and that we might pass over into Bethlehem, that is, into the house of bread. For the house of bread and the house of eternity are the same. He who is eaten here as the flesh of the lamb is received there as the bread of angels. There man eats the bread of angels; here he eats flesh roasted by fire, because that bread was baked in the furnace of the Passion. Hence the Savior’s flesh, under the appearance of bread, is today received by all the faithful, so that we who [Col. 0562C] cannot attain, together with the angels, the truth [better reading: the truth itself] of this bread may at least retain its appearance and taste the sacrament, to which none should approach except worthily. For whoever approaches unworthily eats and drinks death for himself.

Let us therefore gird our loins with the belt of continence—that is, the pleasures of the flesh; let us have sandals—that is, the examples of the holy Fathers—upon our feet, that is, in our works; and let us hold in our hands the staffs of spiritual watchfulness, so that our soul may always be in our hands. Thus let us eat in haste. For we do not know how long it is permitted. We do not know what the coming day will bring forth. Therefore let us not delay, lest we be among those of whom the Lord says through Haggai: “This people says: The time has not yet come [Col. 0562D] for the house of the Lord to be built” (Hag. XVIII, 2).

Therefore whoever desires worthily to celebrate the feast of the resurrection should strive swiftly to fulfill the commandments of life and should not neglect to imitate Christ’s Passion. Let no one grow sluggish on this journey of life, lest he lose his place in the homeland. For this is the day holding primacy among other days, concerning which the prophet says: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” (Ps. CXVII, 14). Let us exult in mind and rejoice in work, because we have been anointed with the blood of the spotless Lamb on both doorposts.

This is the third day on which we are raised and live, as the prophet Hosea says: “Come, and let us return to the Lord, because he himself has begun, and he will heal us. [lacuna] He has made us alive after two days; on the [Col. 0563A] third day he will raise us, and we shall live in his presence; we shall know and follow on that we may know the Lord” (Hos. VI, 1, etc.). This third day is celebrated by us, on which resurrection and life are promised us. But what is the first day? What the second? The first is the day of the Passion; the second, of burial; the third, of resurrection. On the first we are redeemed [read: *redimimur*]; on the second we are healed; on the third we are consummated.

This was the three-day journey toward which Moses and Aaron hastened, saying to Pharaoh: “The God of the Hebrews has called us, that we may go a three days’ journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to our God” (Exod. V, III). And Pharaoh opposed them, saying: “Do not go farther.” Pharaoh—that is, the devil—did not wish them to reach the mysteries of the third day and of the third stopping-place, which was at Ethan, which [Col. 0563B] is interpreted “signs for them,” because there they heard that God would go before them by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire. This did not occur at Rameses, which was the first stopping-place, nor at Socchoth, which was the second, but at the third—that is, at Ethan.

Rameses is interpreted “the agitation of the moth”; Socchoth, “tabernacles.” Therefore, if you desire to depart from Egypt—that is, to leave behind the dark deeds of the world and the shadows of errors—depart at once from Rameses, lest you store up treasure where the moth destroys and thieves break through and steal. Depart also from Socchoth, that is, from the tabernacle of the body, desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ; and come to Ethan, that is, to the place of signs, where you may enjoy the mysteries of the third day, where the pillar of cloud will go before you according to his humanity, and that of fire according to his divinity.

[Col. 0563C] He appeared in cloud in the day of this present life; he will appear in fire in the night of the future judgment, when there will be light for the godly and the blaze of assumption [read: destruction] for the ungodly. Now through the cloud of flesh he refreshes believers; then through the fire of divinity he will enlighten the good and burn the ungodly.

The Lord mentions these three days in the Gospel, saying: “Behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow; and on the third day I am consummated” (Luke XIII, 32). On the first day he casts out demons, because on the day of the Passion he cast out the prince of this world. On the second day he performs healings, when, descending into hell, he brought out the righteous who were dwelling there and opened to them the entrance to eternal blessedness. On the third day he is consummated, because on the day of resurrection the final [Col. 0563D] enemy, death, is destroyed, and the glory of blessed immortality, granted by God, is most certainly hoped for and awaited by all the faithful.

“This,” therefore, is the true “day which the Lord has made” (Ps. CXVII, 24). Yet he also created all days, but adorned this one with outstanding titles of grace and praise. Come then, brothers, on the two feet of charity, and let us return to the Lord in heart, speech, and deed, because he took hold of Abraham’s seed, not angels, and healed us from the wounds of sins. He made us alive after the two days of Passion and burial, because, rising from the dead on the third day, he raised us with himself already in hope, and some in actual fact; and we shall live both now and in the [Col. 0564A] future in his presence.

How delightful it is to live in his presence! For he is beautiful in appearance, more comely in form than the children of men; the sun and moon marvel at his beauty—that is, the heavenly and earthly beings reverence him—and in love and desire of beholding him, the daughters ran about upon the wall. Hear that they ran about, and that they did so upon the wall. Whatever you do is of no avail unless your feet stand upon the wall. For the wall is faith, without which it is impossible for anyone to please God. It is the foundation of all good things which has been laid, and no one can alter it.

Let each person walk upon this wall, not at a slow pace or with lagging foot; and let him not run crookedly, but straight ahead with the Apostle, who says: “Thus I run, not as though toward uncertainty; thus I fight, not as beating [Col. 0564B] the air” (I Cor. IX, 26). For he runs toward uncertainty who does such things that from some of them he can hope, and from others despair. He beats the air in combat who contends with words rather than deeds, who justifies himself with his tongue while his life condemns him.

Let us therefore run upon this wall with the daughters of Zion. Let us not cling to the world; let worldly enticement not capture us; let worldly vanity not please us. Rather, let us be with those who pass by, concerning whom the prophet says: “Those passing by did not say: ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you’” (Ps. CXXVIII, 8). Let us pass through the way of this world, following him who “rejoiced as a giant to run his course.” Let us add works to faith, because faith without works is dead, so that we may fulfill what follows in the prophet: “We shall know and follow on, that we may know the Lord” (Hos. [Col. 0564C] VI, 3). For we must first know the Lord by faith and follow him by imitation in deed, so that at last we may be able to know him in visible presence—that is, face to face. May he himself deign to grant this to us, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## XLIV. ON THE HOLY DAY OF PASCHA. SECOND SERMON.

[Note: [Col. 0563D] From the Victorinus manuscript.]

“Christ our Pascha has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V, 7). Thus the apostle Paul.

Therefore, if Christ is Pascha, we must consider what the Law says concerning Pascha, that we may perceive more subtly what was previously said concerning Christ. For Moses says: “They shall take of the blood of the lamb and put it upon [Col. 0564D] both doorposts and upon the lintels of the houses in which they shall eat it; and they shall eat the flesh that night roasted with fire, and unleavened bread with wild lettuces. You shall not eat any of it raw, nor boiled in water, but roasted with fire. You shall devour its head with its feet and entrails; nor shall anything of it remain until morning; and if anything remains, you shall burn it with fire” (Exod. XII, 7, etc.). There is added: “And thus you shall eat it: you shall gird your loins, have sandals on your feet, hold staffs in your hands, and eat in haste” (ibid.).

All these things, clearly, produce great edification if they are examined through mystical interpretation [Col. 0565A]. For who the blood of the lamb is, you have learned not merely by hearing, but by drinking. This blood is put upon both doorposts when it is drawn not only with the mouth of the body but with the mouth of the heart. For the lamb’s blood is put on both doorposts when the sacrament of his Passion is received with the mouth for redemption and is also, in the whole mind, prepared for imitation.

For one who receives his Redeemer’s blood in such a way [that] he does not yet wish to imitate his Passion drinks the blood at one doorpost only, although it ought also to be put upon the lintels of the houses. For what do we understand spiritually by houses except our minds, in which we dwell through knowledge? Therefore, one who directs the intention of his thought to the imitation of the Lord’s Passion puts the lamb’s blood on the lintel of the house.

[Col. 0565B] Or certainly our houses are our very bodies, in which we dwell while we live; and we put the lamb’s blood upon the lintel of the house because we bear the cross of his Passion on our forehead. It is further said of this lamb: “And they shall eat the flesh that night roasted with fire.” We eat the lamb at night when we now receive the Lord’s body in the sacrament, while we do not yet see one another’s consciences. Yet this flesh must be roasted with fire, because water makes excessively soft the flesh it has cooked, whereas fire now bakes it; for when the very force of his Passion makes it stronger for resurrection and capable of bringing incorruption into the mind, his flesh has, that is, been hardened.

Hence the Psalmist also says: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. XXI, 16). For what is a potsherd before fire but soft clay? Yet fire makes it solid. Therefore the power of his humanity dried up like a potsherd, because through the fire of the Passion it grew into the power of incorruption.

[Col. 0565C] But receiving the sacraments of our Redeemer alone does not suffice for the true solemnity of the mind unless good works are also joined to them. For what benefit is there in receiving his body and blood with the mouth while opposing them by wicked conduct? Therefore it is rightly further added concerning eating: “And unleavened bread with wild lettuces.” He eats bread without leaven who performs upright works without the corruption of vainglory, who offers the commandments of mercy without an admixture of sin, lest he perversely plunder what he seems to distribute rightly.

They too mixed the leaven of sin into their good action to whom the Lord said reprovingly through the prophet: “Come to Bethel and act impiously” (Amos IV, 4); and shortly afterward: “And sacrifice praise from what is leavened” (ibid. 5). For one offers praise from what is leavened who prepares a sacrifice for God from robbery.
