[Col. 0565D] Wild lettuces, however, are very bitter. The lamb’s flesh must be eaten with wild lettuces, so that when we receive the body of the Lord, we may afflict ourselves in tears for our sins. May the very bitterness of repentance wipe away from the stomach of the mind the foul moisture of a perverse life. It is then added:

“You shall not eat any of it raw, nor boiled in water.” Behold, these words of the history itself now draw us away from a historical understanding. For did that Israelite people, dwelling in Egypt, ordinarily eat the lamb raw, that the Law should say to them, “You shall not eat any of it raw,” and add, “nor boiled in water”? But what does water signify except human knowledge, according to what is said in the voice of heretics: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. IX, 17)?

[Col. 0566A] What is the raw flesh of the lamb except thoughtless and irreverent reflection? Whatever we think, we in some manner cook carefully in the mind. But the lamb’s flesh must be eaten neither raw nor cooked in water, because our Redeemer is neither to be judged a mere man nor is it to be considered by human wisdom how God could become incarnate. For everyone who believes the Redeemer to be a mere man—what does he [read: “except that he”] seek to cook in water through an understanding of divinity? Everyone who attempts to examine his incarnation according to human wisdom wishes to cook the lamb’s flesh in water—that is, to penetrate the mystery of his dispensation through knowledge alone [read: *per solam scientiam*].

[Col. 0566B] Therefore whoever desires to celebrate Pascha, that is, the solemnity of joy, should neither cook the lamb in water nor eat it raw, so that he may neither seek to penetrate the depth of that incarnation through human wisdom nor believe in him as though he were a mere man; but he should know that all things are dispensed through the power of the Holy Spirit.

It is then rightly added: “You shall devour the head with the feet and entrails,” because our Redeemer is Alpha and Omega: God before the ages, and man at the end of the ages. To devour the lamb’s head, therefore, is to receive his divinity by faith; but to devour the lamb’s feet is to seek out the footsteps of his humanity through love and imitation. What are the entrails, however, except his hidden and mystical commands expressed in words? We devour them when we eagerly receive the words of life.

In this word “devouring,” what else is reproved but our sluggishness, because we do not investigate his words and mysteries for ourselves and unwillingly hear what others have said? “Nothing of it shall remain until morning,” because his sayings must be examined with great diligence, so that before the day of resurrection appears, in this night of the present life, we may penetrate all his commandments through understanding and action. But because it is difficult for every sacred utterance to be understood and every mystery to be penetrated, [Col. 0566D] it is rightly added: “If anything remains, you shall burn it with fire.” We burn with fire what remains of the lamb when we humbly commit to the power of the Holy Spirit what we cannot understand and penetrate concerning the mystery of his Incarnation. For how could anyone proudly dare either to contend with power or to declare what he does not understand [the text reads: “what he understands”]? Yet he delivers it to fire when he entrusts it to the Holy Spirit.

Since, therefore, we have learned how Pascha must be eaten, let us now see by whom it ought to be eaten. It follows:

“Thus you shall eat it: you shall gird your loins.” What is understood by the loins except the flesh? Hence the Psalmist prays, saying: “Burn my loins and my heart” (Ps. XXV, 7). For if he did not know that the desire [read: pleasure] of lust lies in the loins, he would never have asked that they be burned. Hence, because the devil’s power has prevailed most strongly over the human race through lust, it is said of that creature in the Lord’s speech: “His power [Vulgate: strength] is in his loins” (Job XL, 11).

[Col. 0567A] Therefore the one who eats Pascha must have his loins girded, so that one who celebrates the solemnity of resurrection and incorruption may no longer be subject to corruption through any vices, may subdue pleasure, and restrain the flesh from lust. For he has not recognized what the solemnity of incorruption is who is still subject to corruption through incontinence. These things are hard for some, but narrow is the way that leads to life. We now have many examples of those who practice continence. Therefore it is rightly further added: “You shall have sandals on your feet.”

For what are our feet except our works? And what are sandals, made from the skins of dead animals, by which our feet are protected, except the ancient Fathers who invited us to the eternal homeland? When we behold their example, we protect the feet of our body. To have sandals upon the feet, therefore, is to behold the life of the dead and preserve our footsteps from the wound of sin.

“Holding staffs in your hands.” What does the Law signify by the staff except pastoral guardianship? It should be noted that we are first commanded to gird our loins and afterward to hold staffs, because those who undertake pastoral care ought already to know how to master the surges of lust in the body, lest, while preaching strong things to others, they themselves succumb to soft desires.

[Col. 0567C] It is rightly added: “And you shall eat in haste.” Know with haste the commandments of God, the mysteries of the Redeemer, and the joys of the heavenly homeland; and take care to fulfill the commandments of life with haste, because we know that today it is still permitted to do good, but whether it will be permitted tomorrow we do not know. Therefore eat Pascha in haste—that is, either walk or pant toward the solemnity of the heavenly homeland. Let no one grow sluggish on this journey of life, lest he lose his place in the homeland. Let no one weave delay around pursuits to be undertaken, but let him complete what he has begun. Let no one be permitted to complete what he began badly; but may our most loving Lord Jesus Christ himself help us not to be sluggish in the love of God—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## XLV. ON THE ROGATION DAYS. FIRST SERMON.

[Note: [Col. 0567D] From an Angers manuscript.]

[Col. 0567D] “The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him. It is good to await silently the salvation of God” (Lam. III, 5, 6).

Although we ought always to seek the face of our God, according to that saying of the prophet, “Seek his face always” (Ps. CIV, 4), yet certain days are specially appointed for us to seek God. These are called the days of the Litanies, that is, of the Rogations, on which we ought especially to confess sins and persist in fasting and almsgiving, so that our prayer may be able to penetrate heaven without obstruction. For Jeremiah says: “You have set a cloud in opposition, lest prayer pass through” [Col. 0568A] (Lam. III, 44).

This is not a bright cloud by which prayer is impeded, but a dark one; not a light cloud, but a heavy one: “a talent of lead” (Zech. V, 7), upon which oppressed iniquity sits. Therefore, that the face of iniquity may be dissolved, let us act according to the counsel of James, who says: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be saved. But if any among you has wandered from the truth, and someone has converted him from the error of his way, he should know that he will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (Jas. V, 16, etc.).

Prayer, therefore, is necessary, but confession must come first. Here a distinction must be observed. There is confession of venial sins, and there is confession of mortal sins. There are hidden sins, and there are manifest ones. Greater sins or offences [Col. 0568B] we must confess to those who have received the keys, to whom it was said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them; whose sins you retain are retained” (John XX, 23). These are the prelates and teachers of the holy Church, to whom graver offences must be disclosed, just as in the old Law leprosy was shown to the priests, according to whose judgment its cleansing was treated. For it belonged to them to deliberate concerning cleansing from leprosy or to judge one already cleansed.

But there are certain light and venial sins which it is permitted to confess to one’s equals, concerning which James says: “Confess your sins to one another.” After confession he adds concerning prayer: “And pray for one another, that you may be saved.” For prayer is not pure without confession of heart or, if there is opportunity, of mouth.

[Col. 0568C] Hence the Bridegroom joins myrrh and incense, saying: “I shall go to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of incense, and there I shall speak to my beloved: You are altogether beautiful, my friend, and there is no stain in you” (Cant. VI, 7). The Bridegroom does not go to the bride or speak to his beloved except upon the mountain of myrrh and incense; there he commends her beauty.

The Bridegroom had indeed a bride as his wife, who was beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun. Foreigners desired her and, having violently carried her away, held her long. At last, after a long succession of messengers whom he had sent beforehand, he himself came and freed her from the hand of enemies. This is Christ, of whom John says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John III, 19). And the Apostle says: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI, 2).

Christ is the Bridegroom; the Church is the bride, whom he betrothed to himself three times, as he says through Hosea: “I shall betroth you to myself forever, and I shall betroth you to myself in justice and mercy, and I shall betroth you to myself in faith” (Hos. II, 20). [Col. 0568D] He says three times, “I shall betroth,” because he betrothed her three times: first in the patriarchs, who kept his ring undefiled and received the dowry of the natural law and certain heavenly commandments—as Noah concerning the ark, Abraham concerning circumcision; second, in the time of the prophets, giving them as betrothal gifts the justifications and judgments of the Mosaic law, to which he added mercy, exhorting them to repentance so that they might escape the misery of captivity; [Col. 0569A] third, he betrothed her at the advent of the Son, when through the Gospel he declared the faith of the Trinity, where she received as dowry evangelical commandments and sacraments. Then he freed her from the hand of enemies—that is, demons—who had wholly defiled her, that is, polluted her by the guilt of idolatry.

But he, coming and betrothing her for the third time, cleansed her of the blood of sins and presented her unstained, as he says through Ezekiel: “I washed you with water and cleansed your blood from you; I anointed you with oil, shod you with *anthinum* [as printed], girded you with fine linen, adorned you with ornament, gave a crown upon your head, and you became my wife” (Ezek. XVI, 9, 10).

Behold with what ornaments the bride, formerly polluted by many lovers, is adorned, so that she may please the one true Bridegroom, who now desires her beauty and formerly abhorred her stench. But water comes first, by which her blood is cleansed. This is the water of baptism, the water of compunction, by which blood—that is, sins—is washed away, so that the oil—that is, the anointing of spiritual grace—may then be poured in.

[Col. 0569B] Thus the bride is washed with life-giving water, that the error of ancient transgression may be abolished; she is anointed with oil, that the brightness of virtues may be poured in; she is shod with hyacinth-blue, that is, with hope of heavenly things, because hyacinth has an appearance like God’s throne; she is girded with fine linen, that is, chastity, restraining the loins with the bond of continence; she is adorned with the ornament of charity; she is crowned with the diadem of eternal beauty; and thus she is made beloved by the Bridegroom.

These ornaments the Bridegroom bestowed upon his beloved in the third betrothal, when he spoke to her heart; and this was on [Col. 0569C] the mountain of myrrh and incense. Myrrh signifies the bitterness of repentance; incense, prayer, according to the saying: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL, 23). And thus our prayer is directed to God like incense if the myrrh of bitterness—that is, repentance—is added to it; repentance is not true without fasting and almsgiving.

Let fasting and almsgiving, therefore, be added to prayer. For this is a person’s righteousness in this life: fasting, almsgiving, and prayer. “This kind of demons is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. XVII, 20), as Truth says in the Gospel; nor are sins conquered except through almsgiving, because as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin. Do you wish your prayer to fly to heaven and to the Lord? Make it two wings, fasting and almsgiving, by which it may fly to God. Fasting chastises [the flesh]; almsgiving refreshes one’s neighbor. Therefore give to others what you denied yourself by fasting, lest your fasting enlarge your purse rather than refresh your brother.

Fast in such a way that you rejoice when another eats what you would have eaten for your midday meal; for “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX, 7). If you give bread sadly, you have then lost even the merit. Therefore act from the heart; give cheerfully, and persist in prayers, because God swiftly hears the prayers of those who act well. While they are still speaking, he says: “Behold, I am here.” How great is the joy and exultation in our good Lord God, who is present to hear before the voice is completed in prayer!

“For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and [Col. 0570A] his ears are toward their prayers” (Ps. XXXIII, 16), so that he may grant what they ask: namely grace for grace, the grace of glorification for the grace of justification—not merely “to prayers,” but “into prayers,” so that the swiftness of hearing may be marked.

Truly, therefore, the Lord is good to those who hope in him and to the soul that seeks him. But we must consider whom they seek, when they ought to seek, with what righteousness, and whom they ought to ask. Those who worship seek; to worship is to seek. Thus they seek when they worship as they ought to worship. Truth teaches: “True worshipers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John IV, 23). And David says: “He is near to all who call upon him”; and, defining this, adds: “To all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. CXLIV, 18).

Therefore the Lord is near to true worshipers who [Col. 0570B] worship him in spirit—that is, with pure affection and a clean intention—and in truth, because they seek the true good, that is, the eternal good, not what is temporal and passing away. They seek the heavenly kingdom and the things which lead to it, as Truth says in the Gospel: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Luke XII, 11). He does not say, “And afterward seek these things,” but “they shall be added,” plainly showing that these things are not to be sought as our goods, although they are necessary on the way. The kingdom, however, must be sought, and our end must be placed in it.

“Seek first,” therefore, “the kingdom of God”: that is, seek the kingdom of God alone, since it is more precious than all else; and seek his righteousness, that is, those things which lead to the kingdom. The Lord indicates three of these by a threefold likeness in the Gospel: bread, fish, and egg, saying: “Which of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? Or if he asks for an egg, will offer him a scorpion?” (Luke II, 11).

[Col. 0570C] He sets forth three things which the heavenly Father gives his children and opposes to them three other things which he does not know how to give. Bread is Christ, because as a table is poor without bread, so without charity all else is nothing. Its opposite is the stone, that is, hardness of heart, namely the rigor of hatreds. The fish is faith in invisible things: just as a fish is born and nourished beneath the covering of waters and is not broken when struck by the waves of the sea, so faith is drawn from invisible places and, struck by the waves of this world, is not overcome. Its contrary is the serpent, that is, the venom of unbelief.

In the egg, hope is understood, because a completed offspring is not seen in it but is hoped for through brooding. The scorpion, whose sting must be feared behind one, is opposed to hope. To hope, therefore, looking backward is contrary, since hope ought to stretch itself toward what is before.

[Col. 0570D] You have heard sufficiently who seek God—namely, true worshipers—and what they ought to ask—namely, the kingdom of God and his righteousness, that is, bread, fish, and egg—and how: namely, in spirit and truth. For God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth, so that spiritual people may worship Spirit spiritually, and true people may worship Truth truly.

But with what persistence? The Apostle teaches: “Pray without ceasing” (I Thess. V, 17). And James: “The continual prayer of a righteous person has great power” (Jas. V, [Col. 0571A] 16). The Lord also openly teaches in the parable of the unjust judge and the widow that “one ought always to pray and not grow weary” (Luke XVIII, 1). Likewise in that parable where a friend lends three loaves to a friend, if not because of friendship, at least because of his importunity.

Here three loaves are expressly given; above, one, because the one is divided into three when charity, which is one, is extended toward God, friend, and enemy. Let us pray, therefore, assiduously and without ceasing, inwardly or outwardly, by word or by work. For there is prayer of the heart, prayer of the mouth, and prayer of work.

Moses, though silent, is read in Exodus to have cried out to God (Exod. XIV, 13), because although he was silent with his mouth, he nevertheless cried out in his heart. So too Susanna, while she was accused by the two wicked elders (Dan. XIII, 42). This cry of the heart, [Col. 0571B] even while the bodily voice is silent, is heard by him. This cry is a great intensity of thought, produced by the elevation of thought and the harmony of virtues.

But the cry of the voice is not always heard, because “not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII, 21). For it is not a great thing to love in word and tongue, but in deed and truth. Moses prayed by work when, with Hur and Aaron supporting them, he lifted his heavy hands to God (Exod. XVII, 12). The lifting up of hearts and hands makes a voice audible before God. Therefore Jeremiah admonishes us to lift hearts together with hands, saying: “Let us search out our ways and seek, and let us return to the Lord; and let us lift our hearts with our hands to God in heaven” (Lam. III, 40, 41). Therefore whoever wishes to be heard by God, whose seat is heaven, should strive more to raise to God the intention of the heart and the working of the hands than the cry of the voice.

Therefore let us cry out to the Lord in these three ways, because he to whom we cry is threefold, and the things sought are threefold. Again, for most urgent petition he exhorts us a third time, saying: “Ask and you shall receive; seek and you shall find; knock and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7). For everyone who asks in this manner receives, because he asks in the name of Jesus. Of him Truth also says: “Whatever you ask in my name shall be done for you” (John 16:23). But in this we are weak and often go astray, unless the Spirit assists our weakness; for, as the Apostle testifies, we do not even know “what we should pray [Col. 0571D] for, unless the Spirit helps us, who intercedes for us with unutterable groanings” (Rom. 8:26). Therefore, with him interceding for us—that is, making us intercede—let us pray without ceasing. For one does not cease praying who does not cease doing good and being righteous; and especially when a general scourge of mortality, or some other evil, or the sword of enemies attacks, let us take refuge in the aid of prayer, as Hezekiah and the other holy Fathers are recorded to have done.

Accordingly, these Litanies were instituted by the Fathers when, because sins demanded it, the people of God were cruelly destroyed by the rage of wolves, so that through this three-day fast and [Col. 0572A] the three days of Rogations, both those then living might be delivered from the bites of visible wolves—that is, demons—and we might be rescued from the teeth of spiritual wolves, that is, demons. Hence these days came into the customary observance of the festival. Therefore let us also keep these days according to the ordinances of the Fathers, with reverence and devotion, in abstinence of the flesh and humility of heart, so that we may be able to overcome the temptations of spiritual wolves and find the saving help of God for which we wait. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages.

[Note: [Col. 0571D] See what we noted concerning the Litanies on the twenty-third Epistle of the second book; and here note the abstinence from flesh already instituted at that time on the days of Rogation.]

## XLVI. ON THE ROGATION DAYS. SECOND SERMON

[Note: [Col. 0572D] From Victorinus and Lyra.]

Divine Scripture, dearest brethren, sometimes invites [Col. 0572B] us to tears, sometimes to joy. For Christ says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5). At the end he likewise added: “Rejoice and exult, for your reward is great in heaven” (ibid., 12). But an order must be observed in these two matters: first one must grieve, afterward rejoice. First he said, “Blessed are those who mourn”; afterward, “Rejoice and exult.” Therefore the Lord says to his disciples: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice; you indeed shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John 16:20). Thus he said that weeping comes first and joy follows afterward.

For a sinner must first cleanse his conscience with tears, make satisfaction to the Lord in fasting, weeping, and lamentation, in order to deserve forgiveness, [Col. 0572C] and after forgiveness rejoice in the household of the Lord. Therefore when the conscience has become clean, when the faithful servant has worthily served God, then afterward let him rejoice also in his conscience, according to the Apostle: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12); and in the hope of recompense, according to the Lord: “Rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven.”

According to these two things, brethren, two seasons have been apportioned to us: one of sorrow, the other of joy. During the fasts of Lent we weep; on the day of the Resurrection we rejoice. The Lord displayed this division of seasons in himself. For forty days before the Resurrection he abstained from food; for forty days after the Resurrection he strengthened his disciples [Col. 0572D] in many ways. And he who in the first forty-day period touched no food, in the second sometimes ate with the disciples. Therefore the sinner, dead in vices and not yet come through virtues to the resurrection of the soul, should grieve and abstain from unlawful things [perhaps also from lawful things]; but after he has risen from dead works, he may rejoice and afterward return to lawful things.

Yet in a time of joy let no one presume to be secure; rather, let him who stands take heed lest he fall. For when the devil sees a person secure, and made unwatchful by security, he attacks him and hurls unexpected darts; and the one who had previously risen dies, and does not imitate the risen Christ, of whom it is written: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more” (Rom. 6:9). For just as Christ rose once and dies no more, so the faithful soul, after once rising from vices, must not return to the death of vices, lest it rightly be called a dog returning to its vomit.

Therefore, lest people should grow proud in a time of joy and presume upon security, the Lord scourged our mother, the Roman Church, with a plague of mortality, so that her members might fear at these times. Thus the Greater Litany was fittingly instituted at these times throughout all the Churches, so that people should not wander abroad in joy but always remain in humility. Thus, deservedly, a day of sorrow [Col. 0573B] has been mingled with seasons of gladness, to invite us to fear.

There is another reason as well. At times mortality occurs among people on these days because they receive the body of the Lord unworthily. Hence the Apostle: “Therefore among you many are weak and infirm, and many sleep” (1 Cor. 10:30). For he especially provokes the wrath of God who receives the Lord’s body in a filthy lodging. He offends the King more grievously who presumes to lodge him in an unclean house than does one who says irreverently: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” Both are dangerous: both not to receive, and to receive unworthily. He who does not receive hears: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you” (John 6:54). He who receives unworthily hears: “He who eats the body of the Lord unworthily [Col. 0573C] and drinks his blood shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, and eats and drinks judgment to himself” (1 Cor. 11:27, 29). He incurs the judgment of condemnation in the future, and sometimes temporal or bodily punishment in the present. Hence the Apostle: “Therefore among you many are weak and infirm, and many sleep.”

Fasts and prayers should accordingly be undertaken at these times, that the Lord, offended by his people, may spare them. For prayers are greatly necessary. The wrath of God is appeased by prayer. The Jewish people had worshipped a molten calf, and the Lord said to Moses: “Let me be, that my fury may be angry against them.” Moses replied: “We beseech you, Lord, let your anger cease, and be merciful concerning the wickedness of your people”; and [Col. 0573D] the Lord was appeased (Exod. 32:10 ff.). Enemies are conquered by prayer. When Moses prayed on the mountain, Joshua overcame Amalek. Salvation is obtained by prayer, according to the Apostle. Hence: “Pray for one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. 5:16). By prayer Hezekiah deserved both healing and an extension of life. Peace is given by prayer: “Pray for those things which belong to the peace of Jerusalem” (Ps. 121:6).

There are four kinds of prayer, which the Apostle notes when he says: “I entreat first of all that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made” (1 Tim. 2:1). Supplications are made when we ask to be delivered from evils through adjurations. Prayers are made when we pray that some good things may be given to us, as when [Col. 0574A] we say: “That you may grant us peace, we beseech you, hear us.” Petitions are made when we pray for others, as: “That you may deign to grant eternal rest to all the faithful departed.” Thanksgivings are for benefits bestowed. Therefore pray, brethren, for peace, for unity, for kings, for crops, for prelates, for the departed. For this reason they are called Rogations: because in them the Lord must be asked, who says: “Ask and you shall receive; seek and you shall find; give, and it shall be given to you” (John 16:24). May he himself hear your prayers and defend you from every adversity—he who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0573D] See what we noted concerning the Litanies at Epistle 23, book II.]

## XLVII. ON THE ROGATION DAYS. THIRD SERMON

[Note: [Col. 0574D] From the Victorinus manuscript.]

[Col. 0574B] “Which of you shall have a friend, and shall go to him at midnight and say to him: ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him?’ And he, answering from within, shall say: ‘Do not trouble me; the door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give you anything.’ And if he persists in knocking, I say to you, even if he will not rise and give him because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needs. And I say to you: Ask and it shall be given to you; seek and you shall find; knock and it shall be opened to you” (Luke 11:5 ff.).

Now, dearest brethren, these are days of Rogation [Col. 0574C] and prayer; therefore we judge it fitting to proclaim something to you concerning prayer. We see, dearest brethren, that prayer is exceedingly necessary in every adversity and need. The Gospel teaches through a certain parable that no aid is so useful and none so powerful for our help as continual prayer. Hence James says in his Epistle: “For the continual supplication of a righteous person has great power” (Jas. 5:16). Therefore the Lord, speaking to people so that they may come more readily through things known to things unknown, sets forth a parable concerning a friend who prays importunately, saying: “Which of you shall have a friend and shall go to him,” and so forth.

All these things, although understood simply, can be beneficial by imitating constant prayer; [Col. 0574D] yet, received in a more spiritual sense, they can nourish the soul. The friend who comes from a journey is our mind, which departs from us as often as it wanders outside in seeking temporal things. It therefore returns from its journey and desires to be refreshed with heavenly nourishment when, returning into itself, it begins to meditate upon things above and spiritual things. But one whose mind always wanders among outward things [the text reads “inward things”] has nothing to set before his friend who desires refreshment, because until then he had not studied divine utterances greatly. Therefore in the night of its ignorance he goes to his friend—that is, to the Lord, who is our friend, as he himself says: “I shall no longer call you servants, but [Col. 0575A] my friends” (John 15:15).

He asks, moreover, that three loaves be lent to him: that is, an understanding of faith in the Holy Trinity, by meditating upon which the soul is refreshed and through which it is comforted amid the toil of the present life. Friend asks friend, but the latter will not rise, because God wishes to await the earnestness of the praying soul. He therefore answers: “Do not trouble me; the door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give you anything.” The door of the friend is understanding of the divine word; this door seems shut when preaching ceases. His children are the apostles and other preachers, whom he nourished with the bread of his preaching. They gathered that bread while they lived, but now they have died and rest with God in the bed of heavenly repose.

[Col. 0575B] Therefore, when a preacher is lacking, there is no one to open to the seeking soul an understanding of the divine mysteries. This is what the Lord seems to say when he declares: “The door is shut, and the children”—that is, the preachers of the soul—“are with me and rest in bed with God.” Yet if that person perseveres in prayer, the Lord, moved by prayers made without ceasing, will arise, open the mind of the ignorant person, and grant him as many loaves of the heavenly word as are necessary for salvation.

But observe what he concludes from the parable: “Ask,” he says, “and it shall be given to you; seek and you shall find; knock and it shall be opened to you.” In this petition, dearest brethren, you must note three things without which you cannot come to salvation: you must ask [Col. 0575C] by praying, seek by living rightly, and knock by persevering. For it is not enough merely to ask the Lord with words, unless we also seek diligently how we should live, so that we may be worthy to obtain what we ask; as he himself testifies when he says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven shall enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21). Nor does it avail anyone to begin good things unless he carries what he has begun through to the end; hence it is said: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

But the statement “Ask and it shall be given to you” requires examination, because not everyone who [Col. 0575D] asks receives. Many ask and do not receive. Yet elsewhere he teaches how this petition ought to be made: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John 16:23). He promises, therefore, that if something is sought in the name of Jesus, who is Savior, it will be given. For that person asks in the name of the Savior who asks for what pertains to true salvation. Hence the Lord says to the apostles, while they are still weak: “Until now you have not asked anything in my name” (ibid., 24), as though he plainly said: You cannot ask in the name of the Savior, since you do not know how to seek eternal salvation.

But, dearest brethren, there are many things we ask in the name of the Savior. We ask for temporal goods and earthly prosperity, not in order to serve God longer, but in order that we may more freely be at leisure for fleshly pleasures. One asks for a wife, another for an estate, another for clothing, another for food. These indeed may be sought, but not sought excessively. Heavenly things, however, we must seek continually and even importunately. Temporal things must be sought in necessity, but not continually. Hence the Lord in the Gospel: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. 6:11).

But something still graver occurs when someone asks for an enemy’s death and persecutes by prayer one whom he cannot pursue with the sword. Another pronounces a curse unto death and so is held guilty of the death of the one he curses. God commands that an enemy be loved, yet God is asked to kill the enemy. Another prays for [Col. 0576B] his own sins, while he himself by no means forgives those of another. Of such persons the Lord says through Isaiah: “When you stretch out your hands, I shall turn away my eyes from you; and when you multiply prayer, I shall not hear. For your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1:15). Thus those who speak well but live badly do not ask in Christ’s name [the text has *pereunt*, “perish”; perhaps *non petunt*, “do not ask”]. To them God says: “Why do you call me Master and Lord, and do not do what I say?” Of such persons Solomon says in Proverbs: “He who turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer shall be an abomination” (Prov. 28:9). Likewise, if someone has anything against his neighbor, unless he forgives it when he prays, he asks wrongly. Hence the Lord commands in the Gospel: “When you stand to pray, forgive if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father [Col. 0576C] who is in heaven may forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:12 ff.).

Therefore it must be understood that not everyone who seems to pray before people is found to make petition before the sight of the eternal Judge so as to be heard. For the prophet would not say, “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth,” unless he knew that we sometimes do not call upon the Lord in truth. But if the Lord exercises discernment in giving gifts, what wonder is it when people know how to give good things to their children? Hence he says: “Which of you, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent instead of a fish? Or if he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?” [Col. 0576D] (Luke 11:11 ff.).

Similarly, when someone prays for things that ought not to be prayed for, God does not grant things that ought not to be granted. Bread signifies charity, because just as it is the principal food, so that a table without it seems poor, so charity is the principal virtue, in whose root the other virtues are implanted. If, therefore, someone asks God for bread—that is, the virtue of love—will he give him a stone, that is, the hardness of hatred? A fish signifies faith, because just as a fish is beaten by frequent waves and yet is not destroyed, so faith remains firm amid tribulations. If someone asks God for a fish, that is, faith, he will not offer him the venomous serpent of unbelief. An egg is compared with hope, because in an egg the offspring is not yet seen, but the offspring of the future bird is hoped for; and the faithful, in [Col. 0577A] present hope, do not yet behold eternal glory, but await it as future through hope. The scorpion is compared with desire for, and return to, earthly things, because it carries venom in its tail, which is behind. Whoever was tending toward heavenly things and afterward returns to earthly things [imitates a scorpion]. Therefore, one who seeks from God the egg—that is, hope of heavenly things—will not receive a scorpion returning to earthly things.

Therefore, dearest brethren, do not ask from God for things that ought not to be asked for, but seek earthly things [only in passing] in necessity and heavenly things continually. For when necessity of mortality or some plague presses upon us, the help of God must be sought, as in these Rogations, which were devised for the greatest necessity. For when, because sins demanded it, the peoples of Gaul [Col. 0577B] were being destroyed by the rage of wolves and no remedy for this scourge [the text reads “crime”] could be found, bishops assembled in the city of Vienne and jointly decreed that they should keep a three-day fast. When the Lord had mercifully removed the plague [the text reads “brought it upon them”], these days came into the custom of annual observance, to be celebrated in the provinces of Gaul before the Lord’s Ascension.

Therefore let us also keep these days as has been decreed in councils, with utmost reverence and devotion, with abstinence of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0577D] Note here the same discomfort in dress and austerity in food prescribed for the faithful in celebrating the Rogations as was publicly imposed upon penitents even for more serious sins; with this distinction, however: it was imposed upon penitents as a necessity, but was only commended to the other faithful from devotion.], and humility of heart, so that we may escape the rage of visible wolves and be able to overcome the temptations [the text reads *testamenta*, “testaments”] of invisible wolves, that is, unclean spirits. Let no one put on costly garments during these days; rather, the Fathers decreed that people should mourn in sackcloth and [Col. 0577C] ashes. Drunkenness and feasting are forbidden. Let no one presume to ride there; but let all proceed barefoot and, with contrition of heart, entreat mercy for their sins, for the preservation of crops, and for other necessities, so that God’s compassion may be moved by our tears and prayers. He lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## XLVIII. ON THE ROGATION DAYS. FOURTH SERMON

[Note: [Col. 0578D] From Victorinus and Lyra.]

“Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved. [lacuna] If any of you has wandered from the truth and someone converts him, he should know that whoever has caused a sinner to be converted [Col. 0577D] from the error of his way shall save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (Jas. 5:16, 19–20).

Although on other days, dearest brethren, you ought to be invited to confession and repentance, in fasts especially—which were devised for the cleansing [perhaps *remedy*] of sins—we are admonished to confess our faults. Thus James the apostle, who was called the brother of the Lord because he was his relative (for the mother of the Lord and his [Note: [Col. 0578D] That is, James’s.] mother were sisters of Mary), says: “Confess [Col. 0578A] your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved.” But discernment must be exercised as to what sins they are and to whom they are to be confessed. For they are not to be confessed to just anyone, because authority to forgive sins has not been given to just anyone, but only to those to whom it was said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20:22)—namely, the apostles and those who hold their office, that is, bishops and priests.

Nevertheless, if there are light sins which we commit daily, we may confess them reciprocally to our equals, because they are cleansed by the prayers of our neighbors. Hence clerics daily say the *Confiteor* among themselves in church, and after making confession offer prayers for one another. The Apostle James speaks of this confession when he says: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved.” But if the sins are graver, they must be disclosed to priests and, according to their judgment, punished and cleansed by fasts, prayers, and almsgiving. These graver sins, which were signified by leprosy in the old Law, were commanded to be shown to priests. [Col. 0578B] Hence the Lord commanded the lepers in the Gospel: “Go, show yourselves to the priests” (Luke 17:14).

Nor, dearest brethren, should you merely confess light sins among yourselves and graver sins to priests. If someone is unwilling to confess and be converted from error, you should also bring one another back from his evil way, because whoever causes a sinner to be converted from the error of his way shall save his soul—indeed, also his own. For if it is a great thing to rescue flesh—that is, one’s neighbor—from temporal death, much more is it to free his soul from the death of Gehenna. Therefore each person can be a preacher to his neighbor; each ought to admonish his brother on the road, in church, at home, whether by word or by example. For one admonishes his brother to be converted when he acts rightly in his sight. He urges him to give alms when he gives something to a poor person while his neighbor sees it. When he receives a guest, he invites another to hospitality. Let no one wish to be saved alone, lest he seem to envy the salvation of others. Let one draw another with him while he hastens from this dung-heap to the things above.

For just as each of you, wishing to travel to Jerusalem, diligently [Col. 0578D] invites and urges his brother to come with him, so you ought all the more earnestly to lead [the text reads *consepelire*, “bury with”] your brethren with you to the heavenly Jerusalem, where there is no narrowness and no fear, but true peace and glory. For the road to that Jerusalem has been made ready through him who says: “I go to prepare a place for you” (John 14:3). For formerly there was no place for humankind in heaven; but Jesus our Redeemer prepared a place there by his precious blood. The wall of sins stood between God and humanity, and [Col. 0579A] therefore humanity could not pass to God. Hence before the Passion he said to his disciples: “Where I go, you cannot come now” (John 13:36); meaning: I say “now” because, when the wall has been broken down, you will be able to come where I go. This was foreseen by the Spirit [perhaps “David”], when he says: “In my God I shall pass over the wall” (Ps. 17:30).

He destroyed the wall when by his single death he abolished our two deaths. For he extinguished both the death of sin, which was in the soul, and the death of hell, which was sin’s punishment, by his single bodily death. Hence Gregory says: “He brought to us his one death and loosed our two deaths which he found.” He set his single death against our double death, and by dying subdued our double death. Thus he lay in the tomb for one day and two nights, that is, he extinguished the darkness of our double death. And when, after the two nights and one day during which he had been dead, he returned to life by rising again, he showed the effect of his death: by destroying our two deaths, it restored the life we had lost; and thus the bitterness [Col. 0579B] of his death was changed into the joy of life.

[Note: [Col. 0579D] Gregory, *Morals on Job*, book IV, chapter 17.]

This he foretold to the apostles when he said: “Sorrow has filled your heart, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John 16:6), because a fruitful sorrow repaid the exchange with greater joy, recompensing life for death and a day for an hour. For he lay dead for forty hours: he gave up his spirit at the ninth hour on the sixth day, and resumed his body at the first hour of Sunday. Thus he was dead for four hours on Friday, twelve [Col. 0579C] hours of the following night, twelve hours of the Sabbath, and twelve hours of the second night, all of which make forty.

But let us see how great a recompense of joy the Lord gave for this period of sorrow. He who by dying made his disciples sorrow for forty hours, by rising made those same disciples rejoice for forty days, repaying a day for an hour. Because he remained in the world during these forty days, he gladdened the apostles with the joy of his Resurrection. Therefore the Catholic Church ordained that these days should still be celebrated with great joy and with abstinence set aside. During those forty days in which he is recorded to have associated with his disciples, one ought neither to fast nor mourn, because it is a time of joy, not abstinence. For this observance received testimony from Christ, of whom it is read in the Gospel that, when the Jews asked why the disciples did not fast, he replied: “Can the children of the bridegroom mourn while the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then they shall fast” (Mark 2:19).

Therefore the holy Fathers did not wish to prescribe abstinence from fasting before the Ascension; but, compelled by certain causes, the Greater Litany was instituted in the Roman Church. At that time a very great plague afflicted people because the magnitude of sins demanded it. [Col. 0580A] Therefore, in order to obtain God’s mercy, a fast was established at this holy time, and the holy Fathers decreed that it should be observed by the individual Churches throughout the world: “not riding, but proceeding barefoot; not wearing costly garments on that day, but putting on hair-shirts and sprinkling ashes upon the head.”

This Litany is interpreted as *Rogatio*, “petition,” from the Greek name [Note: [Col. 0579D] He said the same in the preceding sermon.], because on that day we ought to implore the mercy of God and the intercessions of the saints: that divine compassion may free us from eternal death, while we pray for peace, against plague, for the preservation of crops, and for other necessities; and that the Lord, who sometimes lays his scourges upon us either for vengeance or for correction, may not repay us according to our sins [Col. 0580B] but may spare us according to his mercy.

We ought also to take the Ninevites as an example in fasting (Jonah 3:5), because when the overthrow of that city was imminent according to the divine decree [the text reads “knowledge”], they set aside abundant feasts and turned to fasting, making even livestock and children fast with them. When animals fasted—though nature had denied them prayers—they nevertheless aided the tears of the penitents by their lowing. Children were separated from their mothers’ breasts, so that they might become partners in repentance even though they had not been participants in sin. Therefore Christians ought, for their salvation, to do what livestock are recorded to have done for human salvation.

But it is of no avail for the flesh to abstain from food unless the soul abstains from sins; nor is abstinence of any avail unless almsgiving is given. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Is not this the greater fast which I have chosen: Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and wandering into your house” (Isa. 58:7). Therefore give the poor person from your substance, so that you may render thanks to God for benefits bestowed upon you and have hope for the preservation of crops. For whoever sows in blessings shall also reap from blessings, by the grant of the Lord, who lives and reigns through ages of ages.

## XLIX. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD. FIRST SERMON

[Note: [Col. 0579D] From Victorinus and Lyra.]

“The sun was raised up, and the moon stood in its order.”

[Note: [Col. 0580D] Thus according to the Septuagint translators; but according to the Vulgate: “The sun and moon stood in their dwelling-place” (Hab. 3:11).]

Today, dearest brethren, is the joyful [Col. 0580D] feast of the Lord’s Ascension; today the captivity of the human race has been destroyed. Foreseeing this Ascension, the prophet Habakkuk said: “The sun was raised up, and the moon stood in its order.” For while the Lord remained in the world with the apostles, the apostles, confident in the presence of their Lord, did not look to heavenly things. But after the Lord withdrew himself from their sight and ascended to heaven, the soldiers longingly desire to ascend where their Lord has ascended. For it is our custom that the household desires to follow the king who goes before it. Hence the Church says in the Song of Songs: “Draw me after you” (Song 1:31). [Col. 0581A] For she desired to be drawn after the ascending King once she lacked his present consolation.

Therefore the sun of righteousness, who enlightens every person coming into this world, was raised up to heavenly things by his Ascension. The Church, however, is called the moon. But just as the moon receives its light from the sun, so the Church is enlightened by Christ; and just as the moon sometimes suffers eclipses, so the Church sometimes endures failures among her own. But after the Ascension this moon stood in its order, because then it grew through preaching and went forth into tribulation. Then Peter, who had yielded to the voice of a doorkeeper, did not withdraw before the opposing voice of Nero.

This ascent is one of the leaps of which Solomon speaks in the Song of Songs: “Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains” [Col. 0581B] (Cant. I.8). He comes leaping, because, in coming for our redemption, he made certain leaps. For he came from heaven into the Virgin’s womb; from the womb into the manger; from the manger he came to the cross; from the cross into the tomb; from the tomb to hell; from hell he returned to heaven. Hence the Psalmist says: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the height of heaven” (Ps. XVIII.6). Elsewhere the same writer indicated this rejoicing when he said: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Ps. CIX.7).

In the world there was a torrent of death, flowing from the sin of the first parent. He drank from this on the way, because he tasted death in passing; and therefore he rejoiced, because in dying he laid his body in the tomb, which in rising again he raised above the angels. By the resurrection he raised above the angels [Col. 0581C] human nature, which had previously been lower than the angels. Hence it is written: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. VIII.6). For as long as he was capable of suffering and mortal, he was lower than the angelic nature, which is immortal; but after God the Father crowned with the glory of resurrection and the honour of immortality him who had formerly been lower, he was made higher than the angels.

Therefore, when the angels saw human nature set above themselves—though they had previously seen themselves set above it, and had formerly allowed themselves to be worshipped by human beings—they feared to be worshipped by the human race thus exalted. Abraham worshipped an angel. He saw three and worshipped one, and the angel did not forbid the worship. John wished to worship an angel after the resurrection, [Col. 0581D] but the angel did not permit him. They looked upon humankind, exalted [by grace], whom they had formerly seen humbled by its own fault. They honoured human nature, which they saw raised above themselves. They knew indeed that before sin humanity had been made to restore the angelic legion that had fallen, but they did not know of its redemption through the Son of God.

[Note: [Col. 0581D] In this sermon, while treating the creation of the angels, Hildebert seems to hold that among the angels a certain angel was first created and was set above the other orders by a more excellent perfection, so that he constituted, as it were, an order peculiar to himself, surpassing the other orders. His nature, indeed, was more subtle and the image of God more like; every precious stone was his covering, since he was placed above all the companies of angels, so that by comparison with them he appeared more glorious. Hence, turned to pride by excessive brightness, he said: “I will ascend into heaven; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV.14). Thus he himself fell, and many from each order who agreed with him fell and were condemned.

This opinion appears wholly consistent with the assertion put forward by Hildebert in his theological treatise, recently discovered by us in a manuscript from Lyre and to be appended below [Col. 0582D]. There, in chapter 20, discussing Lucifer’s excellence before his fall, he says: “Before those who fell, there was one more excellent than all the others; and authority seems to intend that he was more excellent not only than those who fell, but than all.” To prove this, he employs the same words of Holy Scripture that he used in this sermon, namely, “Every precious stone,” etc.; and he further cites St Gregory and Isidore. From this a reciprocal proof may seem to be drawn: that this sermon, which we extracted from the Victorine manuscript and also from the same manuscript of Lyre, in which we found the aforesaid theological treatise, is truly Hildebert’s; and that the author of that treatise was truly Hildebert. We therefore judged it fitting to bring it to public light as his legitimate offspring.]

At the beginning of the world God made a certain angel surpassing the others, very beautiful and wise, of whom it is said through the prophet: “You are the seal of the likeness of God, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of God’s paradise” (Ezek. XXVIII.12–13). For he possessed a more subtle nature; in him a more similar image of God is indicated, when it is afterwards said through the prophet: “Every precious stone was your covering” (ibid.). Since that first angel was set over the nine [Col. 0582B] orders, he was therefore adorned and covered, since he was placed above all the companies of angels and was more splendid by comparison with them. But, turned to pride by excessive brilliance, he said: “I will ascend into heaven; I will place my seat in the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV.14).

Many of the other angels agreed with him; while wishing to become like God, they were made lower than angels [perhaps: human beings]. That first angel and his companions fell from heaven, while the other good spirits remained. It is believed that a part of each of the nine orders fell; to fill their places, humanity was made. Unless human beings had sinned, they would have been saved [perhaps: made] like the angels and immortal. [Col. 0582C] For if Adam had not sinned, he would have lived in paradise upon the fruits of the trees and would have begotten children without concupiscence. Yet each person would have remained on earth until the appointed end; then, having received and tasted the fruit of the tree of life, which was in the midst of paradise, he would have been translated alive into heaven.

But when humanity sinned, death entered the world; immortality perished, and ascent into heaven perished. Yet God, in his highest mercy, became man and redeemed humankind; by his death he destroyed our death; by his resurrection he restored immortality; by his ascension the Lord made for us an entrance into heaven. The Lord-Man himself filled the place of the highest angel. Other, lower human beings restored the fall of the lower orders.

[Col. 0582D] Thus Christ, according to his humanity, is above [Col. 0583A] all creatures. Hence the Psalmist says: “You have subjected all things under his feet” (Ps. VIII.8). Yet God is greater and higher than that man—namely, the Father and the Son himself according to divinity, as also the Holy Spirit. Hence the Apostle says: Then the Son himself “will be subject to him who subjected all things to him” (I Cor. XV.28).

Of those human beings, some, according to their merits, are placed higher, together with the angels. Hence in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John XIV.2). And elsewhere it is said: “Human beings shall be equal to angels” (Luke XX.38). If you ask how many will be saved, hear Gregory saying:

[Note: [Col. 0583D] Homily 34 on the Gospels.]

“There is believed to ascend thither as great a multitude of human beings as the multitude of angels that remained in heaven,” as it is written through the prophet: “He established the boundaries [Col. 0583B] of the nations according to the number of the children of Israel” (Deut. XXXII.8).

This, therefore, dearest brothers, is that day on which the angelic host rejoiced in fellowship with humanity. This is that feast which is the end of all other feasts, without which the benefit to humankind would perish. For unless he was to ascend into heaven, the Passion would be empty and the resurrection useless. It is so great that in the time of Pope Sylvester, in honour of the Ascension, Thursday was celebrated every week just as Sunday is celebrated in remembrance of the resurrection.

Let us therefore rejoice with the angels, who on this day, meeting with great joy the royal Son ascending to the Father, ask: “Who is this King of glory?” And others, inviting him, said: “The Lord strong and mighty; the Lord mighty in [Col. 0583C] battle” (Ps. XXIII.6). And truly he proved mighty in battle, because, ascending on high, he led captivity captive. For the liberation of the soldier was the victory of the king. But what does the liberation of our companions avail us unless we become their companions? Let us therefore labour, dearest brothers, so that, as we have been redeemed by the same blood, we may likewise be rewarded with the same prize of ascension, through the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## L. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD. SECOND SERMON

[Note: [Col. 0583D] From an Angers manuscript.—From this sermon also the reciprocal proof may be confirmed: both that this sermon is truly Hildebert’s and that the theological treatise discussed in connection with the preceding sermon is his. For in both, in almost the same words and with the same testimonies of Holy Scripture, he assigns the gloomy air as a prison to the transgressing angels. Here he says: “For the first apostate, having been made a devil from an angel, fell from the empyrean heaven into this gloomy air, which was assigned to him as a prison until,” etc., as above in this sermon. But in the aforesaid twentieth chapter of the theological treatise he says: “Because he was so proud against his Creator, he was cast down into this gloomy air [Col. 0584D] with all those who had agreed with him. . . . For they were not permitted to dwell in heaven, which is the bright homeland; nor on earth, lest they afflict human beings too greatly; but in the gloomy air, which is like a prison to them, until the time of judgment. Then they will be thrust down into the abyss of hell, according to that saying: ‘Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels’” (Matt. XXV). Who would not perceive the complete conformity both of the thoughts and of the very words in this sermon and in that theological treatise, and from this at least suspect that both had the same author?]

“Come, let us ascend to the mountain of the Lord” (Isa. II.3).

[Col. 0583D] Jeroboam set up golden calves in Dan and Bethel, raised altars for them, installed priests there, and offered sacrifices, in order thereby to turn back the children of [Col. 0584A] Israel—that is, the ten tribes—so that they should not go up to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the Lord (III Kings XII.8). Yet the prophets, consumed by zeal for the house of the Lord, continually called them back, saying: “Come, let us ascend to the mountain of the Lord,” and so forth. This voice is not merely an exhortation but also a dissuasion, as if it said: Do not ascend to Dan and Bethel, but come with us to the mountain of the Lord. For it belongs to those who are perishing to say: “Come even to the disgrace of the place.” They called Bethel Bethaven.

[Note: [Col. 0584D] Thus the manuscript. Perhaps better in sense: “to the disgrace of the place, Bethel, which they called Bethaven.”]

But the mountain of the Lord is Mount Moriah, upon which the temple and altar of the Lord were built, which Abraham saw from afar when he lifted up his eyes, in order to sacrifice his son there (Gen. XXII). There also he saw the angel in the threshing-floor of Ornan the Jebusite returning his sword to its sheath, after the plague made by the Lord [Col. 0584B] in Israel.

Nevertheless, although the aforementioned exhortation properly belonged to that time, it is no less necessary every day, and more necessary in our own days. More people now follow the ways of Jeroboam (I Par. XXI) than in his own days. Almost all of us, having abandoned—or rather neglected—Jerusalem, go up into Dan or Bethaven; nor is this error recent: the kingdom of Israel has been divided. It was begun at the beginning of the world’s birth: namely, when that noble creature was created, when the morning stars made cloudy [perhaps: rejoiced]—I mean, the angels. Lucifer, who rose in the morning, whose covering was every precious stone, swelled in the abundance of his power, and his iniquity came forth from his fatness; 477 and he said: “I will ascend into heaven; I will place my seat [Col. 0584C] in the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV.14).

He ascended into Bethaven, which means “house of an idol,” or “useless house,” or “vanity,” by the way of pride onto the mountain of power and dominion [perhaps: condemnation]. Likewise Adam, our father, the apostolic root, ascended into Dan, which means “judgment,” that is, discernment. Believing the other apostate, who said, “You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III.5), he ascended by the way of avarice onto the mountain of knowledge now at hand. But because it is written, “Before ruin the heart shall be exalted” (Prov. XVI.18), the fall of each followed upon the exaltation.

For the first apostate was made a devil from an angel. From the empyrean heaven he fell into this [Col. 0584D] gloomy air, which was assigned to him as a prison until the end of time, when he will be sent into the eternal fire prepared for him and his angels. [Col. 0585A] Of his fall it is written: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke X.18). The second apostate, “when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. XLVIII.13). He was cast out from the garden of delights into the dung-heap of our mortality, as into a dark place full of rocks; he was broken in natural gifts, blinded in gratuitous gifts, and wrapped in the filth of sins.

In this manner, those who are inflamed by the lust of ruling ascend after Satan into Bethaven. Whoever seek knowledge that puffs up follow Adam into Dan. Therefore, because the multitude of chaff in the Church follows such leaders, the grains groan among them and cry out: “Come, let us ascend to the mountain of the Lord”; as if [Col. 0585B] they said: “We do not follow you, Satan: you ascend to the North, which is cold and evil, though named for the right hand,

[Note: [Col. 0585D] The words “though named for the right hand” appear superfluous to the sense.]

from which every evil is opened, and from whose face Jeremiah saw a boiling pot” (Jer. I.13). “Nor do we follow you, Adam: for we do not wish to be wise beyond what it is fitting to be wise, nor, if you burst open, shall you bear children for him. But we shall ascend to the mountain of the Lord. And you transgressors, return to your heart and come with us.”

If perhaps the chaff say, “How shall we go with you? You neither know whither we should go nor the way” [perhaps: “we do not know”]. For who has come to announce to us what eye has not seen and ear has not heard? Hence the Prophet seems to have spoken out of despair: “Who shall ascend to the mountain of the Lord?” (Ps. XXIII.3).

[Col. 0585C] But we must not despair, brothers. We have as our guide on the way Jesus Christ, who, having rejoiced as a giant to run his course, today ascended to the mountain of the Lord and sat at the right hand of the power of God, leaving us an example that we might follow in his footsteps. But because he ascended, leaping upon mountains and passing over hills, let us also ascend step by step, by the way of the hills, to the mountain. For if in our heart we arrange ascents from the valley of tears, we shall go into the house of the Lord, proceeding from strength to strength, until the God of gods is seen in Zion.

The way of the Lord is indeed hidden; but, Lord, show us your ways and teach us your paths. Let us therefore first consider the ascents of Christ Jesus, that through those same ascents we may know how to imitate him. From the sequence of the Gospel we perceive [Col. 0585D] that there were seven ascents of the Lord. This is sufficient, because the number seven is the number of universality; thus all his ascents can be understood through seven. He ascended from the water into the wilderness; he ascended Mount Tabor and was transfigured; he ascended the mountain alone to pray; he ascended the mountain when he chose the apostles and gave them the law of the Gospel in a sermon; he ascended upon a she-ass; he ascended the cross; he ascended into heaven.

We do not much concern ourselves with whether he ascended in this order; rather, let us order our own ascent. First, then, he ascended in order to be tempted by [Col. 0586A] the devil; second, to be transfigured; third, to be glorified—for he prayed to be glorified by the Father; fourth, to be understood; fifth, to be known as a gentle King. Hence: “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, gentle,” etc. (Matt. XXI.5). Sixth, to be exalted. Hence he himself says: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John XII.32). Seventh, to be raised. Hence: “While they looked on, he was raised up” (Acts I.9).

In the first he conquered; in the second he shone forth; in the third he prayed; in the fourth he taught; in the fifth he set matters in order; in the sixth he redeemed; in the seventh he intercedes. He did all these things for us; for they concerned not his own need, but ours. His first ascent was an example for us; the second, consolation; the third, refuge; the fourth, instruction; [Col. 0586B] the fifth, aid; the sixth, the price; the seventh, the reward.

In this way the Christian must ascend after Christ: that is, ascend through hills to the mountain of the Lord. The hills are so called because they can be cultivated (*coli*); for while we ascend, it is the time of cultivation, that is, of earning merit.

[Note: [Col. 0586D] Here something is missing, which may be supplied, not far from the author’s sense, thus: “but the time of resting is when we shall have been received upon the mountain.”]

It remains to consider the hills that lead to the mountain. The first hill is that of testing; the second, of hope; the third, of prayer; the fourth, of truth; the fifth, of mortification; the sixth, of perfection; the seventh, of glorification. These seven ascents have their own ways and distinct hills, of which Jeremiah says: “Stand in your ways” (Jer. VI.16); and elsewhere: “The ways of the Lord,” that is, [Col. 0586C] “straight ways to the Lord, gladdening the heart” (Ps. XVIII.9).

By the way of patience we ascend to the first hill; by the way of fear, to the second; by the way of devotion, to the third; by the way of meditation, to the fourth; by the way of temperance, to the fifth; by the way of obedience, to the sixth; by the way of perseverance, to the highest mountain. But one ascending through these ascents should be fortified by the Lord’s Prayer as by a companion. Prayer is a sweet vehicle on the way, a faithful forerunner to the Lord, announcing to him beforehand the coming of one who ascends. One may adapt a proper petition to each ascent, so that, as it were, seven songs may be reckoned to the seven steps.

Therefore, the faithful person ascending after Christ from the water of baptism must prepare to endure temptations, [Col. 0586D] because Amalekites—that is, demons—will immediately meet him in the wilderness; immediately fiery serpents—that is, incentives of the flesh; immediately Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan—that is, occasions of the world—in order to cast out God’s recruit, carry him off defeated, and throw him into prison. But let the Christian consider Christ’s first ascent, set before him as an example, entering the way of patience, according to that saying: “Son, when you ascend [elsewhere: come] to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare yourself for temptation” (Prov. II.1). Christ conquered, and through him the Christian will conquer; thus [Col. 0587A] he will escape to the first hill, that is, to testing. For tribulation works patience, and patience testing. What the furnace does for gold, the moth for iron, and the flail for grain, tribulation accomplishes for the righteous.

Therefore on this ascent let him say: “Father, may your name be sanctified in me.” In baptism the name was received from your name: from Christ I received the lot of being a Christian. May this name be made holy in me without wavering, and established in me, so that I may always share in the reality as I always do in the name.

But lest he think the struggle endless or useless, let him consider Christ’s Transfiguration, which was accomplished for our consolation, that we may await the same glory with sure hope. For, conformed to the brightness of his body, we shall be heirs of God and co-heirs of Christ. For he himself says: “Father, I will [Col. 0587B] that where I am, there also my servant may be” (John XII.28). But because this hope produces a multitude of joys—the ambulatory places, as it were, of priests, by which it is enlarged in tribulation—lest joy be self-assured and sluggish, let him ascend by the way of fear. For one must rejoice in the Lord with trembling, according to that saying: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Prov. XVIII.14). Hope and fear are joined as millstones between which the Christian is continually ground; Moses is reported to call them a pledge received in security.

But, standing on the hill of hope, let him pray that what he hopes may be done for him, and say: “May your kingdom come,” when you have delivered the kingdom to God and the Father, so that kingdom may be within kingdom. Draw me from the servitude of exile to the freedom of the kingdom. But lest, wearied by long expectation, he become drowsy or fall asleep, let him flee to prayer. [Col. 0587C] Hence those who were sleeping were told: “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation” (Matt. XXVI.41). For if he prays for wine, grain, oil, and his household, there are as many persons for whom he prays as there are companions in prayer. But one must ascend to this hill by the way of devotion. For the undevout person, if he asks, asks judgment for himself, and his prayer will become sin.

And when he has prayed, let him say: “May your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth” (Matt. VI.10). This is the gathering together (*synaxis*) of all our prayers; for we cannot piously will anything that God does not will. But because our will is to have, as it were, God’s will, so that it may be directed according to it, when the Christian has prayed and poured out his soul and heart before God, let him submit himself as Christ submitted himself: “Nevertheless, [Col. 0587D] not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. XXVI.39). As your will shall be done by me in heaven, so meanwhile let it be done on earth.

But since one must pray in spirit and truth, it remains to ascend the hill of truth, which Christ also taught in his fourth ascent, so that the Christian may know to seek the truth of the New Testament, hidden beneath the shadow of the Old. But one must ascend [Col. 0588A] by the way of meditation. Hence also: “His will is in the law of the Lord, and he shall meditate day and night” (Ps. I.2); elsewhere: “Blessed are those who search his testimonies” (Ps. CXVIII.2); and again: “The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom” (Ps. XXXVI.30). Then let him say: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matt. VI.11). For Sacred Scripture is bread by which the soul is satisfied.

Once truth is known, the Lord’s talent must be put out at interest; and, that abyss may call to abyss, our springs must be led abroad, so that curtain may draw curtain. But where a person’s life is despised, his speech too remains to be despised. It follows, therefore, that the Christian must mortify his flesh. Thus the Apostle ascended, who says: “I chastise my body and reduce it to servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become rejected” (I Cor. IX.27).

One must ascend by the way of temperance, so that as our members served uncleanness unto iniquity, so they may be restrained to serve purity unto righteousness. This temperance is clearly taught when the Christian is told: “Turn away your eyes, that they may not see vanity” (Ps. CXVIII.37); and elsewhere: “Restrain your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit” (Ps. XXXIII.14). In this manner are performed the things that pertain to the restraint of the members, for which the Prophet prayed when he said: “Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (Ps. CXVIII.120). Thus the free spirit, pressing down its flesh like a yoked [Col. 0588C] she-ass and setting its household in order through God’s aid, so that it may rightly rule over the woman, should say: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI.12). Debts are sins, but especially those which arise from the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0587D] This entire period enclosed in brackets has been transcribed exactly as it stands in the Angers manuscript; but through the copyist’s fault it is so corrupt that it can scarcely be understood. We have restored it, as closely as possible to the author’s sense, as follows; let the reader judge whether suitably. “For because, while we live in the flesh, we are bound by a certain tribute of nature and are compelled, even unwillingly, to follow the first movements of the flesh, which are not in our power, we ought nevertheless to ask forgiveness for those debts, as belonging to corrupt nature. The Apostle paid this debt when he said: ‘What I do not wish, that I do.’ And: ‘Creation was subjected to vanity unwillingly.’ One who kills them in the morning as sinners of the earth, and dashes their little ones against the rock, may safely pray for the forgiveness of such things. Certainly these are sufficient,” etc.]

[“For because we are bound by a certain tribute of nature, while we live in the flesh, to follow the movements of the flesh—the first impulses, which are in our power, wholly owe themselves to the flesh—even unwillingly. The Apostle paid this debt unwillingly when he said: ‘What I do not wish, that I do’ (Rom. VII.19). Hence: ‘Nature was subjected to vanity unwillingly’ (Rom. VIII.20). He may safely pray for the remission of such things who, in the morning, kills them as sinners of the earth, who kills their little ones against the rock.”]

Certainly these ascents suffice for ascending the mountain of the Lord. Yet some wish to perform works beyond obligation: they wish not merely to reign, but also to judge with the Lord. These are those who, leaving all things, follow the Lord; to whom the world is crucified, and they to the world. These are the senators of the earth, with whom he will come to judgment; and he will sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. Because they heard from the Lord: [Col. 0589A] “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor” (Matt. XIX.21), they ascend by the hill of obedience to the mountain of perfection.

This way of obedience is easier and shorter; apart from it, scarcely or rarely are people made perfect. For obedience, like the beam of a cross, fixes all a person’s members immovably. A person cannot walk when he wishes, and a guard has been set over his mouth. Thus the members are constrained so that they may not be allowed to fulfil their due [perhaps: undue] obligations. Food, clothing, walking, taste, speech, prayer, exhortation, and reading are placed not under one’s own decision but another’s. Then, standing upon this hill, let him say without ceasing: “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. VI.13), that is, do not allow us to be led into temptation.

[Col. 0589B] For against such persons the adversary pours himself out wholly in temptation; he tries every device of his art and leaves untouched nothing by which he can tempt. Those whom he possesses quietly in the world, who are carried away like dust from the face of the earth, he does not labour greatly to push into a fall. For they run headlong into the precipice of themselves. But he always strives toward what is forbidden, and persecutes certain of the best, that he may consume the good things of the earth, and according to that saying:

[Note: [Col. 0589D] “His portion has become fat, and his food is choice” (Hab. I.16).]

And elsewhere: “He will eat grass like an ox”—even the finest grass. If he cannot do otherwise, he at least does not allow him to climb to the summit of virtues without hindrance. He magnifies the glory of his name among the people, so that he may at least delight in the good fragrance of his own name.

Having passed beyond these hills, let him enter [Col. 0589C] the way of perseverance and ascend to the mountain of the Lord. This is the way: the righteous walk in it; the uncircumcised and unclean do not walk thus. But Abraham’s children come by it with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves. There the God of gods is seen in Zion, not through a mirror but face to eye; not in an enigma but face to face. May our Judge and Advocate receive us into that vision: he who is God, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## LI. ON THE DAY OF PENTECOST. FIRST SERMON

[Note: [Col. 0590D] From a Victorine manuscript.]

“The heavens were established by the word of the Lord, and all their power by the spirit of his mouth” (Ps. XXXI.6).

You ought to know, dearest brothers, what and how great this solemnity is, and why it is universally celebrated throughout all the Churches. Today the Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples. Today, by inflaming their hearts, he strengthened them.
