We know what kind of teachers of the holy Church they were before the coming of the Holy Spirit; and after his coming we have learned what strength they acquired. Certainly that shepherd of the Church, to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted, to whom the guardianship of the sheep was committed, to whom primacy among the apostles was granted—we know from Christ’s Passion how great was his weakness, or how great his strength, before the coming of the Holy Spirit. For when the maidservant who kept the door said [Col. 0590A] to Peter, “Are you not one of the disciples of this man?” he said, “I am not” (Matt. XXVI.69). Behold: struck by one woman’s voice, because he feared to die, he denied life. Then Peter denied on earth him whom, in that same Passion, the thief confessed upon the cross. Thus the thief was stronger than the standard-bearer; the insurgent stronger than the Apostle.

But after the resurrection, as the Psalmist says: “The heavens were established by the word of the Lord, and all their power by the spirit of his mouth.” The Word of the Lord is the Son of the Father, as it is written: “In the beginning was the Word, 483 and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I.1). He is called the Word because, as a word is the manifestation of a hidden understanding, so Christ, coming into the world, was the revelation of the Father, whom he made known to people [Col. 0590B] who did not know him. Thus he himself says to the Father through the Psalmist: “I shall declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. XXI.13); and again in the Gospel: “I have made known your name to the people whom you gave me from the world” (John XVII.6).

The apostles are called heavens because, as the heavens rain upon the earth so that it may bear fruit, the apostles watered the dry minds of unbelievers with the dew of preaching. And as God is said to dwell in the heavens, so he is said—or believed—to dwell by spiritual grace in the minds of the apostles, as it is written: “The minds of the righteous are the seat of wisdom”; but Christ is the Father’s wisdom. And elsewhere: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII.20).

Such heavens were established—that is, strengthened—by the Word of the Lord after the resurrection, since earlier they had been weak in faith. [Col. 0590C] He strengthened them by rebuking and by helping: by rebuking, as it is written in the Gospel, “At last, as the eleven disciples were reclining, Jesus appeared to them and reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him risen” (Mark XVI.14). He strengthened them by helping, because he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John XX.23). He also strengthened them by promising assistance, when he said: “I shall not leave you orphans; I shall come to you” (John XIV.18). “But the Paraclete, the Holy [Col. 0590D] Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and will bring to your remembrance all things whatsoever I have said to you. Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid” (ibid. 26).

You have heard, dearest brethren, how the heavens were established by the Word of the Lord. Let it also please you to hear how all their power came from the Spirit of his mouth. Christ is again called the Father’s mouth, because through him incarnate the Father spoke to the world, as he himself says in the Gospel: “And the word which you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me” (ibid., 24). The Holy Spirit is said to be of the Father and of the Son, because he proceeds from both [Col. 0591A], and both send him. The Father sends him, as it is written: “The Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things” (John XIV, 26). And the Son sends him, as he himself says: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John XVI, 5).

This Paraclete—that is, Consoler—coming today, according to the Son’s promise, in the form of fire, set the hearts of those disciples aflame, so that, whereas before they had not dared to oppose the powers of this world, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit they sternly resisted everyone. And this is all their power—that is, the apostles’ strength—through the Spirit of his mouth, that is, through the Spirit of the Son and of the Father. See Peter’s courage after he was filled with the Holy Spirit, when the apostles were preaching [Col. 0591B] the word of God in Jerusalem. After the coming of the Holy Spirit, the chief priest and all who were with him were filled with jealousy; they laid hands on the apostles and put them in prison. But the angel of the Lord opened the doors by night and brought them out. On leaving, the disciples again preached in the Temple. The chief priest, having summoned the council, sent to the prison for them to be brought. But the messengers returned and said: “We found the prison carefully locked and guards standing at the doors; but, on looking inside, we found no one.” Others reported that they were preaching in the Temple. They were then brought without force, because the authorities feared the people whom the apostles had already converted. Then the magistrate [Col. 0591C] ordered them not to preach any longer in Christ’s name. But Peter answered: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts V, 29). Behold Peter: before the coming of the Holy Spirit he was frightened by the voice of a serving-woman; after its coming he did not fear to resist the chief priest himself.

But consider, dearest brethren, that the Spirit appeared over Christ in the form of a dove, and descended upon the apostles in the form of fire. He appeared in the form of a dove [over Christ] because, although he is the judge of the human race, nevertheless, coming into the world, he did not wish to show himself severe but gentle to all. He did not wish first to strike sinners, but to draw them by gentleness, because gentleness is signified by the dove’s simplicity. He came in fire in all persons [perhaps: “in human beings”] [Col. 0591D], because our sins, which the Lord first endured through gentleness, we ought through zeal for righteousness to burn away with the ardour of repentance.

There is another reason why he showed himself at one time in a dove and at another in fire: because he makes those whom he fills simple and ardent—simple in malice, ardent in virtue and teaching. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. X, 16). For the serpent is a shrewd animal, as is read concerning the asp: being wise and seeing the enchanter approaching, it presses [Col. 0592A] one ear to the ground and blocks the other with its tail, so as not to hear the enchanter’s voice. Therefore neither serpent without dove nor dove without serpent ought to exist in human beings, so that the serpent’s shrewdness may attend to the dove’s simplicity, and the dove’s simplicity may correct the serpent’s shrewdness.

Seven virtues are also said to be present in the dove, which the Spirit produces in the faithful. The dove lives beside streams, so that, on seeing a hawk, it may plunge in and escape; it chooses the better grains; in another’s nest [printed: *in vico*, perhaps *in nido*] it feeds foreign chicks; it does not tear with its beak; it lacks gall; it nests in caves; it has a groan instead of song. Thus holy men dwell in the streams of divine Scripture, by which their hearts are watered, so that by their memorials [or: admonitions] they may escape the assaults of the devil. They choose the better grains—that is, better opinions, not heretical ones—on which to feed [Col. 0592B]. They nourish as sons, by their teaching and example, foreign chicks—that is, persons formerly estranged from God. They do not tear with their beak: that is, they do not corrupt good statements [of Scripture] by tearing them apart through the error of heretics. They nest in the clefts of the rock—that is, in the wounds of Christ, who is the firm rock; there they place their nest, that is, faith and refuge. They have groaning instead of song, because, just as others delight in song, so the saints delight in groaning and tribulation.

Therefore let us prepare the lodgings of our hearts for such a Consoler; let us cleanse them of vices and adorn them with virtues, so that we may be worthy to receive him who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

LII. SECOND SERMON ON THE DAY OF PENTECOST

[Note: [Col. 0591D] From the E. Victorinus manuscript. This sermon appears to have been delivered by Hildebert, as bishop, to subordinate pastors or curates, perhaps assembled for a synod, who are generally summoned by bishops about these days [Col. 0592D]. For throughout it he commends to the fellow-priests whom he addresses their pastoral duties.]

[Col. 0592C]

“When the days of Pentecost were being fulfilled, all the disciples were together in the same place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent rushing spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting; and divided tongues as of fire appeared to them, and the Holy Spirit rested upon each one of them” (Acts II, 1).

It is entirely fitting, dearest brethren, that throughout these days you should assemble in the house of God, since in them the holy disciples assembled in the same house at Jerusalem and received the Holy Spirit, with many graces pertaining to our office. Let us therefore see what was given to them, so that in [Col. 0592D] them you may learn what has been given to us. The Lord had given the apostles power to cast out demons and heal infirmities; he had also given them power to forgive sins when he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John XX, 22). But because they were to go to all nations and preach amid many persecutions, in accordance with what had been commanded: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI, 15), they first had to be instructed and strengthened [Col. 0593A], and the languages of all peoples had to be bestowed upon them. They had to be instructed, so that they might know what to preach; strengthened, so that they might dare to preach; and languages had to be given them, so that they might be able to preach to different nations in their respective tongues. For these three things were necessary for preaching to the whole world: knowledge, boldness, and language. If they had possessed knowledge but were afraid, they would have failed. If they had possessed knowledge and boldness but lacked the gift [printed: *genere*; perhaps *gratia*] of speech, they would again have failed.

Therefore the Holy Spirit was given to them in the form of fiery tongues. Fire possesses light and heat: in its light is signified the illumination of teaching, and in its heat the fervour of boldness; while in the form of fire bestowed upon the apostles is signified the Spirit’s gift of languages. In this illumination, they were given a perfect knowledge of the Gospel, which [Col. 0593B] they could not perfectly learn before the Spirit’s coming, according to what the Lord said to them: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John XVI, 12). Elsewhere he says: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things” (John XIV, 26). Thus the new law was formed and inscribed in the apostles’ minds at the coming of the Holy Spirit. The apostles were inflamed to boldness: Peter, who had previously feared at a woman’s voice, after the coming of the Holy Spirit did not fear Nero’s voice, because “the heavens were established by the Word of the Lord, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth” (Ps. XXXI, 6).

It should be noted, dearest brethren, that the Spirit came with a sound; this signifies that he would transform them through the sound of preaching [Col. 0593C]. It should also be noted that they were to be gathered in the upper room. Sitting belongs to teachers and judges, and they themselves were to become teachers and judges of the Church. The height of the upper room indicates the sublimity of the commandments and heavenly gifts; their being gathered together signifies the unity of the Church. You have heard, dearest brethren, what was given to the apostles in these days and why it was given to them. Now these things have been given for our edification—to us, who, though unworthy, are their vicars.

[Note: [Col. 0593D] The author was therefore a bishop.]

But since these matters were for the most part prefigured in the Old Testament, let us first add something concerning the old law, so that the same matter may be confirmed from both Testaments and then better understood by us. We read in Exodus that, on the fiftieth day after the departure from Egypt, after the sacrifice of the lamb in Egypt, the law was given on Mount Sinai, in this manner: the Lord descended amid smoking fire upon Sinai; thunder and trumpet-blast began to be heard; lightning flashed; clouds covered the mountain; and the people were forbidden to approach the mountain, lest they see the Lord and cross the appointed boundaries. But Moses and Aaron ascended the mountain, and all the commandments of the law were given by the Lord (Exod. XIX). See how closely the Old and New Testaments agree. After the sacrifice of the lamb and the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, the law was given on the fiftieth [Col. 0594A] day. Likewise, after Christ’s Passion and the deliverance of God’s children from hell, perfect knowledge of the new law was given to the apostles on the fiftieth day. As there the Lord descended in fire, so here the Spirit appeared to the apostles in the form of fire; as there was a noise, so here there was a sound. The trumpet signifies preaching; the thunders, warning [printed: *communicationem*, perhaps *comminationem*]; the lightning flashes, the radiance of miracles; the clouds, the obscurity of the law. For the apostles preached the truth and threatened the punishment of Gehenna. Both laws were given on high: the former on a mountain, the latter in an upper room. Moses and Aaron are on the mountain, while the people are below, separated from it: the teachers of the Church ascend to the sublimity of mysteries, but the people are forbidden to investigate higher things.

All these things, dearest brethren, drawn from both Testaments, although they do not befit us because of our fault, nevertheless ought to befit us by reason of our office. We priests are placed in the upper room [Note: [Col. 0593D] He speaks as a bishop to fellow-priests and subordinate pastors.]; we are placed on the mountain, because we have been raised to the height of so great an order, so that, like watchmen, we may provide for God’s flock against the cunning of the crafty enemy. We sit in the upper room of God’s house because we are teachers and judges in God’s house. We must therefore teach those subject to us; but one who ought to teach must possess the knowledge that he teaches. Thus the person who undertakes the office of teaching must necessarily be enlightened by the fire of doctrine. It is therefore great rashness to receive the priesthood without possessing the gift of knowledge. Those who ought to sit in the upper room in place of the apostles are those who have not deserved [Col. 0594C] to be deprived of the light of knowledge. If we are judges, we must judge justly and boldly: justly, lest we oppress the poor; boldly, lest we fear power. Therefore whoever sits in God’s upper room should receive the fire and fervour of boldness against rebels, obeying him who says: “Do not fear those who kill the body, etc.” (Matt. X, 28). Thus the fire of the Holy Spirit will be in us, so that we may be found filled with the light of knowledge and the fervour of boldness.

Moses was filled with zeal for justice when he rose up against God’s people who had sinned. For we read in Exodus that, after he had delayed many days, receiving from the Lord on the mountain [printed: “in the mountains”] the commandments of the law and the pattern, the people sinned and worshipped a molten calf. The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Go and descend; my people have sinned, and they have worshipped a molten calf” (Exod. XXXII, 7). Moses came and destroyed the molten calf, and ground it [printed: *tribuitque*; perhaps *contrivitque*] to powder; he scattered it, gave the children of Israel a drink made from it, and, standing there, said: “Whoever belongs to the Lord, let him join me” (ibid., 26). The sons of Levi joined him, and he said: “Let every man put his sword on his thigh. Go through the midst of the camp, and let each kill his brother, friend, and neighbour” (ibid., 27). And they did so.

This man is to be imitated in his fervour for justice, dearest brethren [Col. 0595A]. If the Lord’s people sin, let priests take up the swords of correction. And first a priest most powerfully puts the sword upon his own thigh when he first cuts away from himself the enticements of desires; then let him go through the midst of the camp. He walks through the midst of the camp who judges in such a way as never to be bent by affection. With this sword neither brother nor friend is to be spared. The preacher must also break the body of the idol and reduce it to powder, put it into water, and give it to the children of Israel to drink. The body of the idol means that of the devil or of the wicked person. These must be broken from pride and reduced to the dust of humility by the word of preaching; washed in the water of baptism; and incorporated into the body of the faithful through confirmation.

You have heard how you may possess the fire of [Col. 0595B] the Holy Spirit, and how the way must be adapted through the gift [printed: *genere*; perhaps *gratia*] of tongues. When we preach, we must not employ only one mode of preaching; when we correct, we must not correct in a single manner. For simple things must be preached to some, moderate things to others. Likewise, one person must be rebuked more sharply, another drawn more strongly by gentleness. These are, as it were, different languages. The person has the grace of language who has learned to observe appropriate modes of speech. Therefore, dearest brethren, you will be worthy to sit in God’s upper room if you have knowledge and fervour in your heart, and the discernment of moderation in your mouth. Whoever wishes to rule the Lord’s people without knowledge is like a blind person leading a blind person. Consider, brethren, how great a burden you have undertaken, for which you must render an account. Two talents have been entrusted to you: one [Col. 0595C] of understanding and the other of action. Keep what you have and multiply what you keep. For it is not enough to preserve what has been entrusted unless you strive to multiply what you have preserved. May God, who has entrusted his treasure to us, preserve in us what he has entrusted and multiply what he has preserved, so that he may reward us in his eternal kingdom for our labour—he who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

489 LIII. SOLE SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF THE MOST HOLY TRINITY

[Note: [Col. 0595D] From an Angers manuscript.]

“A river went out from the place of delight to water the whole surface of the earth, and from there it was divided into four heads” (Gen. II, 10).

The word of the Lord is what you have heard through my mouth [Col. 0595D]. This word is food for the mature: solid food, and it must be broken and chewed in order to be swallowed [printed: *transigatur*; perhaps *transglutiatur*]. Through Moses the Lord made this word, a word shortened upon the earth—that is, in respect to the surface of the letter; but it is weighty and fruitful in respect to the marrow of its meaning. For here the subject is the principal Trinity, the primal Trinity, the general Trinity, and the Trinity which the Lord made upon the earth—how weighty these are, you may judge from the mere hearing of them.

Certainly, we cannot speak worthily about the principal Trinity, because we lack words akin to the matters of which we speak, even common ones. It is also utter madness for a human being to wish to speak of the ineffable; for, as Solomon says, just as one who eats too much honey vomits it, so one who investigates majesty will be overwhelmed by glory (Prov. XXV, 57). We should not be ashamed of this ignorance, but regret it. For I know that flesh and blood cannot reveal it; but the Son can, because no one knows the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him (Matt. XI, 27). Therefore let us ask the Son to reveal to us the Father, himself, and the Holy Spirit; and let us say to him: “Rabbi, where do you dwell?” “Come,” he says, “and see.” Do you not know that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? This is elsewhere expressed more plainly: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30). For the consubstantiality of both consists in one being in the other.

But concerning the Trinity of persons, hear what the beloved disciple above the others says: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” (I John V, 7). In the Old Testament he also revealed to our fathers the same two articles concerning the Trinity, although to few people and in a manner far different from that used with us. For he openly indicated the article concerning unity of essence; but he set forth the other, concerning the Trinity of persons, under a veil of things and words, more concealing than unveiling [Col. 0596B]. Therefore we give thanks to you, Lord Jesus, because you have hidden these things from the prudent and wise and revealed them to little ones. Yet the reason for that veiling was this: the Jews alone lived amid nations given over to the error of many gods while worshipping one God. If, therefore, those nations had heard or read of three persons in the Godhead, they would have mocked the Jews because of the number of gods. Indeed, many stiff-necked Jews would easily have been swallowed by the same Charybdis. This is why the Seventy, who translated their canon of the Old Testament for a Gentile king, where an authority concerning the Trinity occurred, either obscured it in an inextricable fashion, altered it by inserting something else, or omitted it altogether, lest the Egyptians suppose that the Hebrews worshipped several gods. Hence their lawgiver openly said of the unity of the Godhead: “Hear, Israel: your God is one God” (Deut. VI, 4). But he veiled the Trinity when he said: “A river went out from the place of delight.”

Thus Plato—the teacher of the Academy, I mean—who directed the whole sublimity of his philosophy toward the investigation [Col. 0596D] of the Godhead, after rereading the books of Moses more attentively, boasted that he had found especially in this passage one being who did all things and another through whom that one acted; but he did not deny that he could not find the third. But by the same Spirit by whom it was written, the mystery of the Trinity has been revealed to me. For the river going out is the begotten Son, of whom the Prophet says: “Our God is a glorious river, leaping forth into the thirsty land”; and he is also called a fountain by Solomon: “The fountain of wisdom is the word of God in the highest” (Ecclus. I, 5). Of him the Psalmist also says: “The rushing of the river”—that is, of the Son’s Spirit—“makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV, 5). And again: “Lord,” namely the Father, [Col. 0597A] “with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. XXXV, 10): that is, life is with life, one with another. This river goes forth from a place—that is, from its principle, that is, from the Father, who is its principle. For we call the principles of things “places”; hence, figuratively, we call the principles of arguments “commonplaces.” But the Father himself is the place—that is, the principle—of delight, that is, of love, namely the Holy Spirit. For, as Augustine says, the Father is the principle of the whole Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 0597D] *On the Trinity*, book II, chapter 17, no. 4.]

And this is the sense: the river goes out from the place which is also the place of delight; that is, the Son is from the Father, who is his principle and also the principle of the Holy Spirit. In this respect Plato stumbled somewhat, since he understood the place of delight as the earth below—by the action of the Holy Spirit, who first wished to be poured out before he was also revealed.

[Col. 0597B]

Behold, these words treat of the principal Trinity; the following words explain the other Trinities. This river waters the whole surface of the earth. I do not mean merely the eminence of the earth—which would scarcely be understood plainly even literally of the river of Paradise—but this is the sense: it waters the whole earth, including everything upon the face of the earth. For we sometimes call that which is above the “surface,” as in a twofold division of a house when we say that one part of the house is the surface and the other the foundation. Therefore, by “earth” in this place understand the world with all its appurtenances—that is, heaven, earth, sea, and everything in them; by “surface,” the angels, who in the empyrean heaven have received a place of dwelling above [Col. 0597C] the face of the perceptible world. In these two every creature is included. Therefore the river—that is, the Son—waters, governs, and makes fruitful the vast world and the angels.

For angels are the primal Trinity. But in the world the general Trinity is considered; and, that this may become clearer, we must begin higher up. “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I, 1). In this way God willed there to be two Trinities: for there is a Trinity in heaven and also a Trinity on earth; but each of these Trinities is threefold—that is, a Trinity of Trinities. For there are three Trinities in heaven and three on earth. In heaven there is the principal, or operative, Trinity—namely, God the Trinity—which is called operative because it is creative [printed: *crealis*; corrected *creatrix*], and principal because it is before every creature. There is another Trinity [Col. 0597D] in heaven, called the wrought Trinity—that is, created—or primal, because it began with time: namely, the angelic nature. There is there a third Trinity, called the Trinity of works, namely of those things which God works from age to age; it is called general because it is mingled with all generations. Likewise, there is on earth a threefold Trinity, which will be explained below. But although, as has been said, there are three Trinities in heaven, nevertheless each individual Trinity is threefold—that is, in unity—because there are three Trinities of them.

Certainly, in the principal Trinity there is Trinity in unity, Trinity of unity, Trinity of Trinity, and unity of Trinity. Since these terms are not commonly used, they require a hearer who is not only sound but devout. “Trinity in unity” is the Trinity of persons in unity of essence. “Trinity of unity” is the threefold consideration of the respects in which three are one. “Trinity of Trinity” is the threefold consideration of the respects in which one is three. For the theologians’ whole consideration of the Trinity turns upon these two points: to explain in what respects three are one, and in what respects that one is three. Seeing that the philosophical consideration was insufficient, which says that things identical in being are identical in number, species, or genus, they considered more profoundly, saying that the unity of the three persons is considered in three respects: identity of essence, co-equality, and co-eternity. Hence the statement concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: “One is the Godhead, equal the glory, coeternal the majesty.”

For although certain things are of the same nature, as any father and his son, they are nevertheless neither coeval nor coequal. Likewise, though certain things are coeval, as fire and brightness, they are nevertheless neither of the same nature nor coequal [Col. 0598B]. Therefore that unity, considered in the three respects stated, is above every creature; and this is the Trinity of unity: that is, the consideration of the three—so to speak—of nature, equality, and eternity, in which the three persons are one. Under equality we understand wisdom, power, justice, and the rest.

To this Trinity, as though corresponding from the opposite side, there responds a threefold “Trinity making three”: the consideration in which one essence is three. The theologians similarly considered that this can be assigned in three respects: otherness, property, and attribution. For one person is not another; rather, the person of the Father is other than that of the Son, and that of the Son other than that of the Holy Spirit. Likewise, the property of the Father is other than that of the Son, and that of the Son other than that of the Holy Spirit. Likewise, the name of the Father is other than the name of the Son; and the attribution—that is, the predication—of the Father is other than that of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. This is the “Trinity making three”: the consideration that the one is three in the three respects that can be assigned.

Next comes the primal Trinity, that is, the angels; but this Trinity is likewise threefold. For there are three orders of angels—the higher, the middle, and the lower—each of which again contains three orders within itself, as may be found fully and clearly in Dionysius’s *Celestial Hierarchy*.

Next comes the Trinity of God’s works. There are three works of God: creation, re-formation, and confirmation, ordered in their respective times. For this world is like a garden, and God himself is like a gardener. As there are three times for gardening—the time of planting, the time of watering, and the time of ripeness and gathering—so in the world there was first the time of creation, of which it is written: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth, etc.” (Gen. I, 1). There followed the time of re-formation, of which it is written: “When the fullness of time had come, etc.” (Gal. IV, 4). The time of confirmation follows, of which it is said: “Behold, I shall create a new heaven and a new earth” (Isa. LXV, 17).

But the Trinity of works [Col. 0599A] is threefold. Every work is completed in three stages. In the work of creation, indeed, he created, arranged, and adorned. He created on the first day, arranged on the second and third, and adorned on the remaining three days; because this is clear in Genesis, we pass it over. Likewise, in re-forming he did three things: he washed us, strengthened us, and illuminated us. For through sin humanity fell into a pit of filth, as though upon a heap of stones; thus it was defiled, broken, and also placed in darkness. But Christ washed us from sins in his blood; he strengthened us when he gave us power to fight and resist the tyrant of our flesh. For he set our feet upon a rock and rescued us from the darkness of unbelief; because whoever follows him does not walk in darkness but will have the light of life (John VIII, 12).

[Col. 0599B]

Likewise, in confirming us he grants us three things: nothing will be lacking, nothing will be hidden, nothing will terrify. Nothing will be lacking from the fullness of blessedness; nothing will be hidden from the mutual knowledge of consciences; nothing will terrify us concerning the end of blessedness. This is the Trinity of works made threefold.

Next comes the Trinity that is on earth, which is nevertheless threefold. For within this Trinity there is a Trinity: the Trinity of union, the Trinity of testimony, and the Trinity of office. Indeed, God had made humanity in his own likeness; but when he saw his image in us deformed by us, he himself was made in the image and likeness of ours. He did not disdain to assume our nature, though we did not fear to despise his. He therefore assumed ours, so that image might repair image and likeness likeness.

The river, therefore [Col. 0599C], going out from the place of delight, was divided into four heads: that is, made visible from invisible, it was distributed through the four regions of the world. “For into all the earth has gone out the sound of the apostles, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 5). That is: coming to us, the Apostle accomplished what he had seen, what he had been accustomed to do as though in heaven. For it is difficult to abandon what one is accustomed to. Therefore, because he had known there the Trinity of Trinities, he likewise accomplished three Trinities on earth. These are the loaves which the friend lends us; these were the three measures of flour which the woman mixes until the whole is leavened: namely, the Trinity of union, corresponding as though from the opposite side to the principal Trinity. For whereas in that Trinity there are three persons and one essence, in the union of Word and human being there are three essences and one person: God, soul, and flesh; yet Christ is one. This is the Trinity of union.

Next comes the Trinity of testimony, concerning which John says: “There are three who bear witness on earth: spirit, water, and blood” (John V, 8)—that is, charity, baptism, and martyrdom. For we shall all stand before the tribunal of the Judge: there every human being and all his works will appear with him. But woe to one who is alone, because the word of one mouth will not be believed; rather, every word will stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses. Blessed is the one who brings with him the witnesses mentioned above: whose charity, having been possessed, will bear witness; whose faith will allege that it was nourished in the waters of baptism; and for whom the voice of blood will cry [Col. 0600A] from the earth to the Judge. Nevertheless, blessed is the one for whom two of these bear witness, provided one of the two is the Spirit. For spirit and water suffice; spirit and blood suffice, if the water was not excluded through contempt for religion but through a circumstance of necessity. The Spirit alone also suffices, because its testimony has sufficient weight.

There remains the Trinity of office. Our priest according to the order of Melchizedek established in his Church three orders of those to be saved: married people, the continent, and prelates. These are the three men whom Ezekiel sees in the Spirit as saved—Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. XIV, 14)—who nevertheless preceded the head before it came forth into birth. For three branches proceeded on this side from the shaft [Col. 0600B] of the lampstand, and three on that side (Exod. XXV, 31); and these three are in the house of the highest householder, serving according to the order of their turn: the first at the mill, the second in bed, the third in the field.

See how God orders all things through Trinities in heaven and on earth, so that it has been said no less truly than elegantly: “God delights in an odd number”; and “first” must be understood. For the first odd number is three, on account of these six Trinities embracing all things. Six is called the first perfect number, so that it may appear that Genesis truly said not that six is perfect because God completed his works in it, but rather that his works are perfect because God completed them in a perfect number.

[Col. 0600C]

But what concern are so many Trinities to us? Certainly, all are necessary for us, and without all of them there is salvation for no one. We are indeed in the lowest Trinity, that of office; for there is no believer who, if he wishes to be saved, is not either in the ark with Noah, in continence with Daniel, or in marriage with Job. But from the last Trinity we must pass to the highest and principal Trinity, the knowledge of which is eternal life. We must ascend through the four middle Trinities as by certain steps, more eminently from practical philosophy at the threshold [printed: *marginali in vestibus*; perhaps *in vestibulo*] to the higher theoretical philosophy.

For we pass through the wilderness of this present life in the manner of a good traveller. When such a traveller goes from place [Col. 0600D] to place, he travels with something—with some provision, that is; he is not delayed by fair or foul weather; and he travels by some road. Thus we too depart from the first Trinity and proceed with the second. For unless someone brings with him some of the witnesses, he will not reach the destination toward which he is travelling. We enter through the third, for Christ is the way; and one who walks without faith in the incarnate Word walks in a trackless place, not on the way. But we pass beneath the fourth. For whatever may happen in the works of God—whether prosperity favours us [printed: *foveant*; perhaps *faveant*] or adversities test us—we must pass with head humbled beneath the hand of God, lest a blaspheming tongue pass upon the earth. We walk beside the fifth: “Make,” the Lord says to Moses, “everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Exod. XXV, 40). For we must lead an angelic life on earth if we desire to reign with them in heaven [Col. 0601A]. But we hasten to the sixth and final Trinity. Therefore we proceed from the first with the second, through the third, beneath the fourth, beside the fifth, to the sixth: namely, by this one, with this one, through this one, beneath this one, beside this one, to this one. These are the Lord’s beautiful ways and his peaceful paths; for them let us pray individually and let us pray all together, and say: “Show me your ways, Lord, and teach me your paths” (Ps. XXIV, 4). May God the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—hear us as we pray, he who is God blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

LIV. SOLE SERMON ON THE MOST HOLY SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST

[Note: [Col. 0601D] From Évreux manuscript no. 19.]

[Col. 0601B]

The flesh of Christ set before us to eat, and his blood to drink, are not a provision of man but of God; not of wrongdoing but of mystery; not of temporal nourishment but of eternal. For on the day before he suffered, the Son of God prescribed to his disciples the form of this sacrament, explained its efficacy, and commanded that the same be done. The fullness of time had come, in which, according to the dispensation of the divine counsel, the Law yields to the Gospel, shadow to body, figure to truth. The day was already declining toward evening, about to present to the faithful both the end of legal observance and the beginning of grace. Behold, our Redeemer, when he had already celebrated the mystical Passover, took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take [Col. 0601C] and eat of this, all of you; for this is my body, which shall be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Cor. 11:24). Then, taking also the cup, he blessed it in like manner, gave it to his disciples, and said: “Take and drink from it, all of you; for this is the cup of my blood of the new and eternal covenant, which shall be poured out for you. Do this in remembrance of me” (ibid., 25).

Behold, my brethren, the handing down of the Christian sacrifice. Behold its form. Bread is taken from the table and blessed—but it is ordinary bread, refreshment for the flesh, temporal sustenance. Yet through the hands and words of Christ, the bread becomes Christ’s flesh; it becomes food for the soul; it becomes the restoration of eternal salvation. Certainly, this change [Col. 0601D] is the work of blessing, not of origin; the service of grace, not the debt of nature; power, not ordinary usage.

Do not, brethren, do not ask how this happens; do not doubt whether it happens. Do not approach irreverently, lest it become death to you. For he through whom bread is mystically changed into flesh is God; he who testifies that bread truly becomes his flesh is both God and man. The Vessel of Election is the one who threatens judgment upon anyone who does not discern so holy a flesh. O Christian, think the same concerning wine; give wine the same honor. He is the Creator of wine who advances wine into Christ’s blood; Christ himself is he at whose testimony the person drinking this wine drinks Christ’s blood. The Doctor of the Gentiles is he by whose assertion one who drinks Christ’s blood unworthily drinks death. [Col. 0602A]

To say more on these matters, consider, brethren, in what order Christ delivered this sacrament to his disciples; what is owed by one who approaches worthily and by one who approaches unworthily. Our Savior, as the Evangelist testifies, “did not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfil it” (Matt. 5:17). Therefore, in order that he might himself celebrate the Passover and eat the lamb of the Law, the Lamb of the Gospel reclined at the prepared supper. Without delay, while supper was still being eaten, he rose from the table and, Lord of all, washed his disciples’ feet. Then the Lord returned to the table and instituted the sacrament of his body and blood, giving bread separately and wine separately, and while giving them commanding that the same be done in remembrance of himself.

Certainly, in the divine page feet are frequently found to signify the dispositions of the mind. The prophet, jealous over the wicked and seeing the peace of sinners, cries: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps had almost slipped” (Ps. 72:2). And again: “Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you; because he has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from falling” (Ps. 114:7). The Church also, replying in the Song of Songs to her bridegroom, who desires her to open to him and says, “Open to me, my sister, my bride, my near one, my dove, for my head is full of dew and my locks with the drops of the night” (Song 5:2), says: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed [Col. 0602C] my feet; how shall I defile them?” (ibid., 3.)

Thus feet signify the dispositions of the mind, because by them we either approach the Lord or are made distant from God. Therefore the disciples’ feet are washed first, because they ought first to eat the bread of life and then drink the wine of immortality. For the mind had first to be cleansed before it presumed to partake of that food of which they had already heard the Lord say: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:56). Even those who were already cleansed from dead works, who already glorified Christ in their bodies and bore Christ, were nevertheless made foul within by the dust stirred up from their thoughts and needed washing. Therefore the Lord said to Peter: “He who has been washed needs only to wash his feet, but is wholly clean” (John 13:[Col. 0602D] 10). The feet, therefore, are washed beforehand, so that those about to receive this sacrament might be taught that their thoughts too must be washed beforehand.

And this also is that in which our righteousness must abound beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees. It must abound, I say, not only toward one’s neighbor but also toward God. Their righteousness toward their neighbor commands one to love one’s neighbor but permits one to hate one’s enemy. For thus the Law says: “You shall love your neighbor, but you shall also hate your enemy” (Matt. 5:43). But ours abounds, which he himself showed must be extended even to loving enemies, in these words: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (ibid., 44).

Likewise, in their righteousness toward God, the person sacrificing the lamb of the Law girds his loins; but ours abounds, which, eating the lamb of the cross, girds both loins and breast. Attend to the Truth speaking to the disciples: “Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35). John also saw the Son of Man “clothed in a long robe, and girded at the breasts with a golden belt” (Rev. 1:13). They are commanded to gird their loins so that they may learn to restrain the wantonness of the flesh. The Son of Man is shown to the disciple girded at the breasts with a golden belt, so that we may understand that wandering thoughts must be restrained.

According to this righteousness, then, the justified disciples return with Christ to Christ’s supper. Such as they are, they return; such as they are, they receive [Col. 0603B] Christ’s body and blood. They return with washed feet and recline unto salvation. They receive the sacrament reverently and feast upon life. They eat in time, but advance unto everlasting strength. They are fed with the body, but their souls are satisfied. They crush it with their teeth, yet it reaches the mind whole.

Therefore you also, to whom it was said in them, “Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Cor. 11:24), wash yourselves in mind, if there is nothing to be washed except the feet. If your bodies have already been washed outwardly, let your hearts be washed. The Apostle says: “He who eats the flesh of the Lord and drinks his blood unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (ibid., 29).—“This saying is hard” [Col. 0603C] (John 6:61). He who eats and drinks eats and drinks judgment upon himself. This saying, I say, is hard: hard to hear, but harder in experience. It is indeed hard—but for one who eats unworthily, for one who drinks unworthily.

Who eats and drinks unworthily, however, the same Apostle shows when he adds: “Not discerning the body of the Lord.” Therefore, lest you eat unworthily, discern; lest you drink unworthily, discern. You discern if you recognize that this sacrament differs from ordinary foods in dignity, fruit, and reverence. Its dignity is the reality of Christ’s own flesh; its fruit is eternal life; its reverence consists in this: it is sinful to be separated from it. These things must be apprehended by the senses of the mind, not weighed by human reasoning. Therefore Moses says in Leviticus: “Whoever eats of the sanctified things [Col. 0603D] through ignorance shall add a fifth part to it and offer it to the priest” (Lev. 22:14).

Moreover, as the Catholic Fathers understood it, to eat the sanctified things through ignorance means not to attend to the dignity of the sacrament, to be ignorant of its fruit, and to deprive it of due reverence.

> [Note: Col. 0603D. “Sanctified things,” that is, the body and blood of Christ.]

Therefore whoever handles this with outward senses must necessarily add inward senses also. For it is fitting that such food be prepared upon the altar for the guests at the banquet. Some of them eat bodily, others spiritually. Some experience what nature preserves in bread and wine; others what grace supplies in both.

[Col. 0604A] At this table the five senses of the body recline as external guests and handle the appearance of bread. They pronounce upon the appearance and are occupied with it in time. They distinguish the qualities of things; sensing transient things, they can do nothing further. They feed upon what remains of nature and leave to the five senses of the mind what belongs to grace. For it belongs to grace that the substance of bread is changed into flesh; that hidden effects are brought about; that provision for the journey to the homeland is prepared; that a human being feasts with angels; that enduring strength is gained; that creature is united to Creator; that the Advocate enters into covenant, so that, pleading now for those who eat worthily, we may deserve to be found among the lambs, chosen with the good fish, and stored with the grain in the Lord’s barn.

These are spiritual things, and the spirit alone claims their experience for itself.

> [Note: Col. 0603D. That is, the spiritual person alone attains them.]

The spirit alone contemplates these things by a certain vision; it hears without the sound of a voice, smells from afar, touches gently, tastes eagerly. The Law commands that this fivefold capacity be added to the sanctified things which are eaten through ignorance. It commands, I say, that it be added, that it be brought to attention, so that while the outward person is occupied with the appearance of bread, the inward person may attend to the reality of flesh and be satisfied with the fruit of the earth.

Then what is added is commanded to be offered to the priest. But to which priest? To him of whom it is said in the Psalm: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4). To him we must offer, to him attribute, whatever in the sacrament tastes of divinity, whatever is saving, whatever is reverent.

You hear that bread is changed into wine.

> [Note: Col. 0604D. Here there is a manifest error of the copyist, who writes “wine” in place of “the body of Christ.”]

The highest priest performs these things. [Col. 0604C] You hear that the one who eats remains in Christ, and Christ in the one who eats. Who testifies to this? Truth does not know how to lie. You hear that eternal life also comes from this. Who testifies to this? Truth does not know how to lie. You hear this and believe it, yet approach it irreverently: you depart judged.

For when you are about to come to the altar, it is necessary that you be judged either by yourself or by Christ. Therefore the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Let a man prove himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup” (1 Cor. 11:28). And shortly afterward: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (ibid.). Woe to you if you are anticipated by Christ’s judgment! Woe to you if you touch Christ when he says, “Do not touch me” (John 20:17)! This presumption adds sin to sin and pronounces punishment.

Judas was guilty and a murderer in intention; he approached with the disciples and was still tolerated among the apostles as Christ’s familiar companion and table guest. But when, receiving a good thing evilly, he did not give glory to God, the guilt of his intention was increased by the execution of the deed. Then that betrayer was handed over to the devil; then he was exposed; then he was forsaken. Then the chain of sins increased: its first cause was the crime of theft; its second, the intention of parricide; its third, contempt for sacred food; its fourth, trafficking in blood; its fifth, the kiss; its sixth, despair; its last, hanging. [Col. 0605A] By such a chain the wretched man was dragged to death; suspended by it, he burst open in the middle.

Eli likewise, the priest, rebuking his sons for the sin against sacrifice, said: “The report that I hear of you, my sons, is not good. If a man sins against a man, God may be appeased for him; but if he sins against God, who shall pray for him?” (1 Sam. 2:24). He did indeed rebuke his sons, but, as authority testifies, with the gentleness of a father rather than the severity of a high priest. Hence it came to pass that Hophni and Phinehas died struck by the sword, the ark of God was captured, Israel fled before the Philistines, and the whole people paid for the crime of a few. Eli also fell from his chair and died, showing how severe a punishment contempt for sacrifice receives.

Other examples remain by which we are plainly taught that, in the sacrament of the Lord’s table, wicked persons have nothing that brings salvation. But lest too long a discourse burden any of you, we shall defer them until tomorrow. Perhaps some have brought delicate ears; since we cannot hold them by a useful discourse, we must hold them by a brief one.

## Sermons on the Saints

[Col. 0605]

## LV. On the Feast of the Annunciation of Blessed Mary. One Sermon

> [Note: Col. 0605D. From the Sangermanensis and Victorine manuscripts.]

On the Incarnation.

[Col. 0605B]

> “I have made you hear new things, and they are sealed things which you do not know” (Isa. 48:6).

> [Note: Col. 0605D. “I have made you hear new things from that time, and preserved things which you do not know.”]

These are the words of the Holy Spirit speaking thus in a vision to Saint Isaiah and revealing a mystery hidden from the age. Of it Jeremiah says: “The Lord has created a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man in the embrace of her womb” (Jer. 31:22). This woman is the Virgin Mary, of whom Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isa. 7:14). For since the Virgin’s son [Col. 0605C] is true God, born of the Father before time, he is also with us by the assumption of nature and by true dwelling with human beings upon earth, according to Baruch: “He was seen upon earth and conversed with human beings” (Bar. 3:38). And the Apostle says: “He was found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:7).

This, therefore, is the new thing which the Lord has made upon earth: namely, that a virgin conceived and gave birth without the intercourse of male seed. For she “encompassed a man in the embrace of her womb” (Jer. 31:22), because from the sanctified flesh of the virgin alone, by the operation of the Holy Spirit, the Son of God was conceived in the Virgin’s womb. Therefore the Son of God became the Son of Man in the virginal chamber; united as bridegroom to bride, the Son of God according to the truth of nature born God from God, and the Son of Man according to the truth of nature born man from man, so that by being born he might possess the name “Son” truly in both births, not by adoption or title, and might be one Son, one Christ, true God and true man. Thus we confess not two Christs or two sons, but God and man as one Son. For that reason we call the Only-Begotten remaining in two natures or substances, neither confused [Col. 0606B] nor mingled; and we confess the Blessed Virgin to be Mother not only of man but also of God, because she brought forth in time the very one whom the Father generated from eternity.

We venerate his two births: one from the Father before the world, above flesh, time, and nature; and one made in the last times for our sake [variant: “above us,” as is clear from what follows] and according to us—“for our sake,” because for our salvation; “according to us,” because he was born as a man from a woman, the time of conception being preserved; “above us,” because he was conceived not from seed but from the Holy Spirit and the holy Virgin, above the law of conception. Therefore one and the same is the Son of God born before the ages and born in the age; and both births belong to one, namely the Son of God, the one divine and the other human. Marveling at the ineffability of both, Isaiah says: “Before she travailed”—namely, the Virgin Mary—“she gave birth. Who has ever heard such a thing, and who has seen anything like it?” (Isa. 66:7).

These are the new things, sealed in the hidden places of God’s mysteries, which the Spirit of God revealed to the prophet and through the prophet, and which he further announced to the holy Virgin by the angel Gabriel in an open revelation, as evangelical Truth says: “The angel Gabriel was sent to the Virgin Mary” (Luke 1:26), descended from David’s tribe; and, announcing good news, he said: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you” (ibid., 28). Troubled at his words, she was addressed by the angel: “Do not fear, Mary, for you have found grace before the Lord. Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name [Col. 0606D] Jesus” (ibid., 31). But when she doubted how this would happen, since she did not know a man, the angel again said to her: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore also that holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God.” Mary said to the angel: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid., 35).

[Col. 0607A] After the holy Virgin’s consent [variant: *concessum*, “granting,” for *consensum*, “consent”], the Holy Spirit came upon her according to the angel’s word, purifying her and preparing the power of the Word’s divinity, and likewise, perhaps, the generative power of his humanity [the text is defective], and then the wisdom and ever-existing power of God Most High overshadowed her—that is, the Son of God, *homoousios*, that is, consubstantial with the Father. He joined to himself flesh, endowed with a rational and intellectual soul, from the most holy and pure blood of the Virgin—not by sowing seed, but by creating it himself.

Thus today the Virgin’s womb becomes the gate of heaven, through which God descends to humankind in order to provide them ascent to heaven. The most blessed Virgin hears and marvels that she, who knows no union with a man’s embrace, is to bear a son; but she is strengthened [Col. 0607B] and instructed by the angel by what power there can be fulfilled in her that which nature does not allow to happen in other women. “Do not fear, Mary,” he says, “you have found grace before the Lord” (Luke 1:31), as though he said: What I announce to you has no power of nature, but is the gift of incomparable grace. Therefore he adds: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (ibid., 35).

It must not be supposed, as certain heretics maintain, that the Holy Spirit supplied in the Virgin the place of seed; rather, he so cleansed her mind from the filth of vices and filled it with the sweetness of divine love that she became worthy of a heavenly birth, and the power of the Most High made for itself from her immaculate flesh a heavenly dwelling in the virginal chamber. Hence it is added: “For that which shall be born [Col. 0607C] from you, holy, shall be called the Son of God” (ibid.). He who was to be offered for the sanctification of sinners had to be holy. It was fitting that his origin be free from fault, since through him the faulty generation of Eve’s children was to be cleansed.

For Eve inflicted three evils upon those who follow her: the dominion of man over woman, conception in sin, and childbirth in pain. But in the Virgin’s conception no carnal desire intruded; no sorrow attended her conception; no difficulty attended her childbirth. He who came to gladden the world ought not to sadden the dwelling of the womb. Therefore, just as this conception lacks every corruption, so, although heretics chatter otherwise, the Virgin’s womb remained whole and undefiled in conception and childbirth.

For this is the closed gate which Ezekiel, the Son of Man, saw: “The Lord turned me to the way of the gate that looked toward the east, and it was closed; and he said to me: Son of Man, this gate shall remain closed and shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it; and it shall remain closed” (Ezek. 44:1). Hear, brethren, and rejoice. This is a magnificent prophecy [Col. 0608A] concerning the incorruption of the most holy Virgin, who was a virgin before childbirth, in childbirth, and after childbirth. This is the unburned bush in which God appeared speaking to Moses, because the Virgin, having borne the speaking King, appeared to many who thought carnally to have married Joseph; but she was truly free and untouched by every man’s embrace.

Therefore the closed gate is the immaculate Virgin, who was seen to have neither an equal nor a successor. The way of the gate is the Holy Spirit, who closed this gate and revealed it to us. The East toward which it looks is Christ, whom the Virgin knew that she had conceived; and therefore he is called the way of the gate, because he leads to it. For the Holy Spirit is that prophetess whom Isaiah approached—that is, he made himself worthy to approach her—saying: “I approached the prophetess, [Col. 0608B] and she conceived and bore a son; and the Lord said to me: Call his name: ‘Hasten, strip away the spoils; hurry to plunder’” (Isa. 8:3).

> [Note: Col. 0607D. The Victorine manuscript has: “Hasten to strip away the spoils; hurry to plunder.”]

This prophetess, then, is the Holy Spirit, from whom comes every prophecy, who among the Greeks is called *Pneuma* (πνεῦμα), a neuter word; among the Hebrews *Ruha*, a feminine designation; among the Latins *Spiritus sanctus*, masculine. Isaiah approached this prophetess in mind, and she conceived and gave birth; that is, she caused the Virgin to conceive and bear a son, according to the saying: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power,” etc. (Luke 1:35). And elsewhere:

> [Note: Col. 0607D. In the Creed.]

> “Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.”

And his name was called “Church” [the text has *Ecclesia*, perhaps an error for *Accelera*, “Hasten”], because the word of God runs with speed; and “Strip away the spoils,” because “Christ, ascending on high, led captivity captive” (Eph. 4:8); and “Hurry to plunder,” because, triumphing over principalities and powers in himself, he despoiled hell.

Therefore wonderful and worthy of adoration is the Virgin’s conception and generation, which God’s wisdom commends, saying: “O how beautiful and chaste is a generation with glory; for its memory is immortal, because it is known both to God and to human beings!” (Wis. 4:1). Therefore chaste, and for that reason most beautiful, is the Virgin’s generation and conception, celebrated without the union of seeds and accomplished without the experience of corruption. This will not seem impossible or improbable—though the wisdom of this world, which God has made foolish, judges otherwise—if someone reasons concerning [Col. 0608D] God’s power or works not by human sense, but beholds with the understanding of the mind God’s invisible things as to be understood through the things that have been made.

For consider: if the sun’s ray, penetrating crystal,

> [Note: Col. 0607D. Hildebert himself expressed this comparison of the sun penetrating crystal without breaking it in the verses to be given below:
>
> Sun, crystal, and water provide some image  
> of a virginal birth and build up faith.  
> If the stone is dipped in water and exposed to the sun,  
> it remains whole and gives forth sparks.  
> If you observe well anointed water, sun, crystal, and fire,  
> they are the Spirit, the Word, the Virgin, and God the child, etc.]

neither pierces it by entering nor shatters it by departing, how much more did the Virgin’s womb remain whole and closed at the entrance of the true and eternal Sun. As a sign foretelling this, that burning and unconsumed bush which we mentioned above is read to have been shown to holy Moses; and Aaron’s rod, that of the high priest, though neither alive at the root nor nourished by moisture, produced the fruit and flowers proper to its nature. [Col. 0609A]

Why, then, does unbelief deny that God can make a man from a woman without a man, when he made the first man neither from man nor from woman? Certainly, the conception and birth demonstrate the true humanity of the one born; their novelty and incorruption attest his true divinity. In this conception is a great and wonderful sacrament: namely, the union of Christ and the Church, or of the Word and the soul. For the Virgin Mary became the Church, or any faithful soul that is a virgin through incorruptness of will and purity of faith. Hence the Apostle says: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin [Col. 0609B] to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2).

Likewise, the angel announcing that Mary conceived is the preacher of truth: through his preaching, the faithful mind conceives the Word of God and then gives birth. It conceives by believing; it gives birth by bringing forth into the light a good work. For faith without works is dead. And just as the Virgin, after the angel’s message and the Savior’s conception, went with haste into the hill country, so the faithful soul, having conceived God’s Word, forgets what lies behind and stretches itself toward what lies before, so that it may attain the prize of the heavenly calling.

Rejoice, therefore, most beloved; again I say, rejoice, because today’s feast commends to us the new conception of the Virgin, in which the beginning of our restoration is celebrated and an evidence of divine mercy and power is set before us. For if the Lord of all things, seeking runaway servants, came to exercise judgment rather than show mercy, he would not put on the frailty of the earthen vessel, by which he might have compassion upon us and suffer for us. And although this appears foolish and weak to the Gentiles, who rely on the subtleties of earthly and empty philosophy and judge the Creator according to the laws of the creature, [Col. 0609C] what is nevertheless more powerful than to grant conception to a virgin contrary to the laws of nature, and through the death of assumed flesh to restore mortals to the immortality of glory? Hence the Apostle says: “What is weak in God is stronger than men, and what is foolish in God is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1:25).

[Col. 0609D] Physicians of bodily sufferings are indeed called wise, because they know, according to the character of diseases, to apply like things to like and eagerly set opposites against opposites. Thus the medicine of heavenly wisdom has been adapted to the wounds of our flesh and spirit: by certain opposites and by certain likenesses it has healed us.

For the Savior came in the likeness of sinful flesh, tempted in every respect according to likeness, without sin, so that in the very thing in which he was tempted and conquered, temptation might henceforth grant the grace of conquering. He also set his newness against our oldness, his righteousness against our unrighteousness, his humility against pride, so that we who had fallen by pride from the flower-bearing seat [Col. 0610A] of the blessed might be renewed through his humility and return to the joys of paradise. We were deceived by the serpent’s wisdom—that is, cunning—and are delivered by God’s wisdom. And as that wisdom was called wisdom when it was folly, so this thing called folly is wisdom so great and incomprehensible that it became for us the medicine that restores lost life. These are the opposites.

The likenesses, however, are these: he who was born of a woman freed those deceived through a woman; man freed human beings; mortal freed mortals. Divine wisdom could indeed have aided human falls in another way. But no mode was more fitting for healing our misery. For thus he most greatly stirred up our love toward himself and commended his love to us. Consider, brethren, and ask your hearts: if, when you had been deprived of an earthly inheritance and placed in a dark prison, a king or some other mighty person, laying aside royal splendor, descended to be with you, so that like one of you he might endure the miseries of your captivity and, when opportunity was found, free you from that captivity, how could he better make known to you his love for you and stir up yours toward him? For Truth says: “No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

Therefore, as our Lord—our physician and liberator—descended to his servants, his sick, his captives, humble and exalted: humble in having compassion, exalted in freeing us from the slavery of the devil, he became through the humility of our humanity as it were milk for little children, [Col. 0610C] though in the exaltation of his divinity he is the bread of angels. For through flesh we have suckled majesty. He wished in the region of unlikeness to nourish us with the milk of his Incarnation, by which he might make us grow toward the sweetest and inestimable taste of his divinity. Yet, so long as we walk by faith and not by sight, this taste is never granted fully to anyone, however pure in heart; it is reserved for perfect satisfaction in the reward of the righteous, when the Lord’s glory shall be manifested. For none of those on the journey can possess in pilgrimage what is promised upon arrival.

Therefore, all who have been called in Christ, let us with all our heart venerate and with due observances honor the wondrous announcement of our deliverance, recalled to our memory by this present feast. Let us consider how great are the things promised us in heaven, lest things that seem desirable to blind and covetous minds upon earth turn our course back from the rampart of the heavenly calling. Let us love the mercy by which we have been redeemed; let us preserve chastity, of which he showed himself a lover when he formed for himself an immaculate body from the blood of the Holy Virgin. Let us be conformed to him who set his life on earth as the rule of Christian conduct; who at his first coming reformed his image in us and will reform in himself the body of our humility, made conformable to the body of his glory: Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns for endless ages. Amen.

## LVI. On the Feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary. First Sermon

> [Note: Col. 0611D. From a Victorine manuscript.]

[Col. 0611A]

> “After the days of Mary’s purification were fulfilled according to the Law of Moses, they took Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord … and to offer a sacrifice, according to what is said in the Law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” (Luke 2:22).

It was customary, dearest brethren, in the old Law that if a woman bore a male child, she herself should refrain from entering the temple for forty days; afterward, coming to the temple, she offered her son with sacrifices (Lev. 12:2). The Lord had commanded in the Law that, if she could afford it, she should offer a lamb for her son together with a turtledove [Col. 0611B] or a dove. But anyone who could not afford to offer a lamb was to offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons.

Therefore the Lord, who had not come to abolish the Law but to fulfil it, and who in all his actions in some way formed our life, wished to be circumcised on the eighth day and presented in the temple with offerings on the fortieth. But because he was going to instruct us in poverty, he everywhere set forth an example of poverty. Therefore he preferred that for himself there should be offered a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, the offering of the poor, rather than a lamb, which was the offering of the rich.

For the Son of the Virgin was poor: born in a humble place, wrapped in cheap cloths, laid in a lowly manger, having nowhere in the world to lay his head, enduring many reproaches, and killed by a shameful death in a notorious place. In every respect he supplied an example of poverty and humility and of contempt for all present things.

And there was a certain blessed old man who, desiring to see the Lord’s day, “had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death unless he saw the Christ of the Lord” (Luke 2:25). Therefore, coming today into the temple in the Spirit to receive the fulfillment of the promise, he saw the one he had desired; he received him, bore him, and said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace” (ibid., 29)—you who had kept him alive so that he might see you. According to your word, that is, according to your promise, you dismiss me in peace, because I see peace. Why then do you dismiss me in peace? Because [Col. 0611D] “my eyes have seen your salvation” (ibid., 30).

This is the festival, dearest brethren, which you celebrate today with such joy—if not in reality, at least in outward form. The light in the candle signifies Christ, born of the Virgin; for Christ has arisen as a light for the upright in heart. The wax signifies Mary’s virginity. The virgin is a little bee, which produces wax and brought forth without intercourse; for bees are born from honey. Wax has the same emblem of virginity; but just as you carry it outwardly [that is, the candle], so carry it also in your mind. Yet if you wish to carry it thus, offer also the turtledove and the dove. For the dove signifies simplicity; the turtledove indicates chastity. The turtledove is so devoted a lover of chastity that, if it loses its mate by chance, it takes no care thereafter to seek another.

[Col. 0612A] Therefore, that person offers a dove who keeps himself innocent, harms no one, and bears in his mind none of the gall of hatred toward anyone. But the person offers a turtledove who, living chastely with his wife, keeps and abstains himself from another woman in his mind [perhaps: “keeps himself abstinent from another woman, both in mind and body”]. Or, if he has no wife, he withdraws himself from every defilement of lust. Nor does the righteous person alone offer the turtledove or dove: the sinner does so as well. Both birds, accustomed to utter groaning rather than song, signify in this world the weeping of penitents. Thus the sinner is compared to the dove or turtledove when, acknowledging himself a sinner, he laments for his wicked deeds.

But there are two kinds of penitents. Some do penance publicly, others secretly, according to the differing character of their crimes.

[Col. 0612B] Those who sin publicly and corrupt others by their bad example ought to repent publicly; and, just as they were an example of corruption, so should they become an example of amendment. The rest, however, are punished privately. These two birds signify both kinds of penitents. For the turtledove, wandering alone, is accustomed to groan; whereas the dove utters its groans among a flock of others. Thus the turtledove signifies those who repent secretly, and the dove those who repent publicly.

These little birds, dearest brethren, are for us a pattern of life. You who do not know books, read in them what you ought to do. For God’s creatures exist not only for your food, but also for your example. The heavenly Teacher daily intimates this through created things. In these birds the righteous person finds what

[Col. 0612C] he ought to imitate; these birds teach the sinner what he ought to do.

But, considered spiritually, the dove, which instructs us, is an example of seven virtues. It lacks gall; it does not live on carrion or worms; it feeds upon seed; it chooses the better shoots; it has groaning instead of song; it often nourishes the young of others; it sits upon waters so that, when it sees the shadow of an approaching hawk, it may avoid it; it nests in a crevice of rock or in a cave.

In all these respects, brethren, this bird is worthy of wonder. Every bitterness of gall ought to be absent from our hearts. No vice is so utterly evil as hatred. No martyrdom avails if hatred dwells in the heart, according to the Apostle: “If I should deliver my body so that I might be burned, but have not charity,

[Col. 0612D] it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3). No offering is accepted by God if hatred is held in the heart, according to that saying: “If you offer your gift before the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then, when you come, you shall offer your gift” (Matt. 5:23). No remission of sins is given if hatred is not expelled from the heart, according to the Lord’s sentence: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:14). Hatred drives God out of the mind, according to the saying: “Wisdom shall not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wis. 1:4).

[Col. 0613A] Therefore you ought in this respect to imitate the dove, so that you may be free from every gall of hatred. Again, the dove eats neither carrion nor worms. So a human being ought not to delight in dead works; he should take care to avoid worms—that is, evil consciences—which gnaw at the soul. Carrion is sin; the worm is an evil conscience arising from sins, which continually condemns and accuses a person. A person would not dare appear in the sight of others if people said to him what his conscience daily reproaches him with. Sins must therefore be avoided, lest they punish together with an evil conscience. Sins must be avoided because a person is the servant of as many masters as he has vices. Sins must be avoided because “the wages of sin is death” (Rom. 6:23)—eternal death, as the Apostle says; and, as David says,

[Col. 0613B] “Salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. 118:155).

Sins must be avoided because they are a stench and produce shame. They are a stench, according to the saying: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1:7). They produce shame, according to David’s saying: “Let the wicked be ashamed and be led down into hell” (Ps. 30:18).

Likewise, the dove feeds on seed and chooses the better grains. Thus the righteous person ought to be satisfied by the Lord’s words. For Christ says: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4). For just as there are two substances in a human being, namely body and soul, so two foods are necessary: bodily food, which nourishes the body, and the word of God, which refreshes the soul. We are on pilgrimage and therefore need provision for the journey. We ask for this bread in the Lord’s Prayer,

[Col. 0613C] when we say: “Give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:11)—that is, in the present life. The Lord gives this bread to all, saying: “I do not wish to send them away fasting, lest they fail on the way” (Matt. 15). A person fails on the way if the food of preaching is withheld from the sinner, or if the time offered for God’s service is regarded with distaste. For one who rejects God’s word is not of God. “He who is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 7:37). You must also choose the better grains, because the mind must always be directed toward the higher commandments.

There is another virtue of doves which is greatly to be imitated.

[Col. 0613D] For it nourishes the young of others. In this is signified the virtue of mercy, by which we are commanded to love even strangers, as it is said: “Give yourself to everyone who asks you” [variant: “Give to one who asks you”] (Luke 6:30). And elsewhere: “Be merciful, as your Father also is merciful” (ibid. 36). And elsewhere: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have?” (Matt. 5:46). Therefore strangers too must be loved for the Lord’s sake. Parents also must be loved, but they are to be loved for their own benefit; for he who said, “Love your enemies” (ibid. 44), also said: “Honor

[Col. 0614A] your father and your mother” (Exod. 20:12).

In every person a person ought to recognize his own nature; and when he sees another suffer, he ought to sigh in compassion. Hence the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 2:19). And again the prophet: “When you see one naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. 58:7). A person ought to consider that he is a fellow servant of the same Lord, who is no respecter of persons. And if the sufferer himself is not a reason for you to do him good, let the Lord who promises and commands be the reason why you extend your hand to him. “For he who gives to the poor lends to the Lord” (Prov. 19:17).

The fifth admirable virtue of the dove is that it lives beside streams, so that, seeing the shadow of an approaching hawk, it may avoid it. This is especially to be followed in the dove.

[Col. 0614B] For we have a certain spiritual enemy flying through the air, who continually goes about seeking whom he may devour.

[Note: Hildebert makes the same assertion in his first Sermon on the Ascension and in his Theological Treatise, chapter 20.
