In both, he says that the gloomy air is assigned to demons as a prison, where they are detained until the end of time—or, as he explains it, until the Day of Judgment—when they will be cast into the eternal fire which, as Christ himself says, has been prepared for the devil and his angels.]

He neither dwells altogether among us nor is very far removed from us. If he always lived on earth, scarcely anyone could avoid his snares; nevertheless, no one ought to be secure, because he wages war from nearby. Hence demons are called “powers of the air.” And the more invisible he is, the more fearful he is. But we see his shadow in the water because in Scripture we learn the likeness of his cunning devices. Therefore let us flee to Scripture whenever we sense his crafty temptation. If he says to us, “Commit adultery,” Scripture is ready and teaches: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:14). If he says, “Commit theft,” Scripture presents itself and forbids:

[Col. 0614C] “You shall not steal” (ibid. 15). When he tells us to be angry, Scripture threatens: “Whoever is angry with his brother is liable to judgment” (Matt. 5:22). When he urges us to lie, Scripture threatens: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. 5:7). Scripture exhorts and threatens punishment. Let the faithful soul sit beside such streams, so that it may notice the approach of the enemy who lays snares.

The dove has groaning instead of song. In this the sinner ought to imitate the little bird. Let him turn joy into tears. “Blessed,” says the Lord, “are you who now weep, because you shall laugh” (Luke 6:21). And conversely: “Woe to you who laugh, because you shall weep” (John 16:20). Mary washed sins with tears. Peter, after sinning, wept bitterly and deserved forgiveness; tears wash

[Col. 0614D] sins in the second place after baptism. Tears must be shed not only for ourselves but also for wretched neighbors. When Christ had nothing for which to weep on his own account, he wept for Lazarus: “For he groaned within himself and wept” (John 11:3). Jesus wept for Jerusalem. If, then, the Lord grieved for all, why do you not suffer with others? Why do you not mourn for yourselves? As the Prophet says: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall drench my couch” (Ps. 6:7)—“A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise”

[Col. 0615A] (Ps. 50:19). He calls sins “nights” and the conscience “bed,” in which a person rests if it is good; if it is bad, he is tormented. A bed is rest for the healthy and labor for the sick.

The final virtue follows. It nests in crevices of rock or in cavities of a wall. The rock is Christ, upon whom the Church ought to nest. It profits no one to act well if he ascribes it to himself rather than to God’s grace—that is, if he glories in himself and not in the Lord. “For it is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man” (Ps. 117:8). Therefore, since we have salvation through the mediator, let us give thanks to the mediator, by whose bloody wounds we have been redeemed. The crevices of the rock are Christ’s wounds, from which flowed the blood, the price of our redemption. The cavity

[Col. 0615B] is the opened side, from which came the sacraments of our salvation, namely blood and water: the one for redemption, the other for regeneration.

In all these things, dearest brethren, let us imitate the dove. Thus let us offer the dove in the temple. What was done figuratively in ancient times, let us now fulfill spiritually. Let us follow the footsteps of the blessed Virgin Mary, who showed herself in mind to be such as she was in the presentation of the figure. Let us ask the most blessed Queen, who is the medicine of the world and gate of heaven, the hope of the wretched and consolation of sinners, that she may make favorable to us the Son whom she presented today in the temple, and grant us that peace which the blessed old man understood when he said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace”

[Col. 0615C] (Luke 2:29), so that we may deserve to see God’s salvation, of which the same man said: “And my eyes have seen your salvation” (ibid. 30): our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## LVII. SECOND SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF THE PURIFICATION OF THE BLESSED MARY

[Note: From the Saint-Germain manuscript.]

“The Lord came from Sinai and rose for us from Seir. He appeared from Mount Paran, and with him were thousands of saints. In his right hand was a fiery law” (Deut. 33:2).

Moses, God’s most loving servant, who deserved to speak with God face to face as a man with his friend,

[Col. 0615D] understanding through the revelation of the Spirit the mystery of this solemnity, announced it to us as though in a certain riddle of words, saying: “The Lord came from Sinai,” and so forth. Sinai is interpreted “command” or “temptation”; Seir, “rough” or “hairy”; Paran, “fruitful.” Thus by Sinai is signified the Mosaic law; by Seir, prophecy; and by Paran, the Gospel.

In the law there was indeed a voice of words by which the children of Israel were tested by the Lord. For those who had previously said, “Whatever the Lord tells us, we will do and obey,” when they heard the voice of words at Sinai were terrified, unable to bear what was said. Hence the Apostle, preferring evangelical sweetness

[Col. 0616A] to legal harshness, says: “You have not approached darkness and a voice of words, which those who heard excused themselves from hearing further speech. For they could not bear what was said; and therefore they said to Moses: Speak to us and we shall hear; let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die” (Heb. 12:18).

For just as they were terrified in the literal sense on hearing the Lord’s voice speaking through an angel, unable through fear to endure the angel’s voice, so, having experienced the severity of the law, even all the greater and more perfect were stunned, because there was command and precept without assisting grace; there was knowledge of sin but not its removal. Through it a person recognized his disease, but did not receive its remedy from it. Hence the Apostle says: “The law entered in so that the offense might abound” (Rom. 5:28). For the oldness of the letter, if the newness of the Spirit is absent, makes people guilty by knowledge of sin rather than frees them from sin. Hence Solomon says: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. 1:18). This is not because the law itself is evil, but because the commandment possesses goodness only in the letter that shows, not in the Spirit that helps.

Nevertheless, from this law—that is, from Sinai—the Lord came, because it not only announced the Savior’s coming by heralding testimony, saying: “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren like me; him you shall hear” (Deut. 18:15); but also foreshadowed the coming Christ through many signs and sacraments, and in a manner directed people, through its own insufficiency, toward the giver of grace. For, since it is the power of sin and does not justify the ungodly—commanding what cannot be fulfilled without grace—it sufficiently reveals to a person his weakness, so that, recognizing it, he may seek justifying grace. Therefore, when it cannot heal one made weak and convicted of transgression [supplied: “heal”], it sends him to Christ who justifies, and thus bears witness to the Lord Savior: by commanding and threatening, while justifying and helping no one, it introduces the grace of Christ and indicates that a person cannot otherwise be justified [variant: “indicates that a person needs the grace of Christ”].

[Note: Here it is excellently explained throughout how the new law succeeded the old.]

Therefore it is rightly said that the Lord came from Sinai—that is, from the law—because he did not refuse to receive even the legal sacraments, so that, ending the oldness of the letter, he might bring forth into light the newness of the Spirit. For behold: after the Lord’s Circumcision had been celebrated

[Col. 0616D] on the eighth day according to the rite of the law, on the fortieth day from that same Nativity he was offered by his parents in the temple with sacrifices, as the Gospel reading relates: “After,” it says, “the days of her purification were fulfilled”—namely, Mary’s, or Christ’s—“according to the law of Moses, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord and to offer a sacrifice, according to what is said in the law of the Lord: a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” (Luke 2:21).

It was written in the law that a woman who, having received seed, had borne a male child should abstain from entering the temple for forty days; afterwards, coming to the temple, she offered her son together with sacrifices (Lev. 12:6).

[Col. 0617A] If she could, she offered a lamb together with a turtledove and a dove. But one who was unable to offer a lamb offered two turtledoves or two young pigeons. Therefore Christ, who came not to destroy the law but to fulfill it, as he wished to be circumcised on the eighth day, so also wished on the fortieth day to be offered in the temple with sacrifices—not because of any need of his own or his mother’s, since neither mother nor son needed to be purified by sacrifices, but for our benefit. Just as he came to John’s baptism not in order to receive something from it but to confer it upon us, not in order to advance himself but to provide for us, so, when he was presented in the temple with sacrifices, he gave form to our life.

For, setting before us at once a pattern of humility and poverty, he wished the offering of the poor, not of the rich, to be made for him—namely, a pair of turtledoves

[Col. 0617B] or two young pigeons—in our figure. For the Son of the highest King, rich, God with God the Father, through whom all things were made, born of poor parents, taught in every way both a lesson in humility and contempt for the world. Accordingly, both birds, the turtledove and the dove, were wisely offered for him, so that they might indicate the character and manner of our conduct. The turtledove, which does not seek another after losing its companion, signifies chastity. The dove signifies simplicity, because the conduct of the righteous must be chaste and simple if they are to offer a sacrifice pleasing to God. For that person offers a dove who preserves innocence unto the end, so as to harm neither himself nor others. That person offers a turtledove who makes no provision for the flesh in its desires. And because both birds have groaning

[Col. 0617C] rather than song, tearful compunction is rightly signified.

There are also two kinds of compunction: the higher and the lower watering, namely when, recalling the punishments of evils, we fear; or when, burning with desire for heavenly things, we groan at delay. Therefore two young birds are commanded to be offered: one as a whole burnt offering, when we are inflamed with love for heavenly things; the other for sin, when we groan over evils committed.

Thus it was not without cause, nor without the reason of a celebrated mystery, that the Lord wished to come from Sinai—that is, from the law—from which he has above been shown to have come in many ways. For the law foretold his coming in speech, prefigured it in sacrament, and sent people to him through its own weakness. He, receiving the legal observances into himself, fulfilled the law and established our life by mystical figures.

[Col. 0617D] He also rose for us from Seir—that is, from prophecy, which is rightly understood by Seir, interpreted “rough” or “hairy”—because the prophets rebuked the offending people with harsh reproof and foretold future events as though in a riddle. For they announced the sacraments of Christ and the Church under a veil, according to the saying: “Dark waters [supplied: “waters”] in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17:12), that is, obscure teaching in the prophets. And again: “His shadow covered the mountains” (Ps. 79:11), that is, darkness and obscurity covered the prophets—the teachers of the Old Testament, first illuminated by the light of teaching—because their prophecies were wrapped in clouds of figures and coverings of words, according to Moses’ saying:

[Col. 0618A] “The heavens shall be dark with dew” (Deut. 33:28). For heat is in dew; that is, there is obscurity in the teaching of the prophets. And from the darkness of this dew—that is, from Seir—the Lord rose for us from prophetic utterance, because the prophets bore witness to the Lord, foretelling what Christ’s coming fulfilled. They foretold to us Christ, “who was made for us wisdom from God, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30).

They also proclaimed the sacrament of this solemnity—namely, the Lord’s presentation in the temple—not as in a riddle, but by plain and explicit testimony. Thus Malachi, through whom God the Father speaks concerning the light and lamp—that is, his heralding Word, namely Christ and John—says: “Behold, I send my angel, and

[Col. 0618B] he shall prepare the way before my face; and immediately the Lord whom you seek and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire shall come to his holy temple” (Mal. 3:1).

The Son is the Father’s face, because the Son is the image of the Father, the first likeness and the first equality. Thus he himself says: “He who sees me sees my Father also” (John 14:9). Therefore before this face—that is, before the manifestation of the Son—the Lord sent an angel to prepare the way of the face: John the Baptist. He is called an angel, not by sharing in angelic nature, as some have thought, but by participation in office. For angel in Greek means “messenger.” John is therefore rightly called an angel, since he not only foretold Christ, saying: “One stronger than I will come after me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie”

[Col. 0618C] (Mark 1:7), but also pointed him out when present, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). And again: “One stands among you whom you do not know” (ibid. 26).

Hence it is consequently said: “And immediately the Lord whom you seek shall come to his temple” (Mal. 3:1). For the bridegroom’s friend ran before him only for a short time; the voice—that is, John—went a little before the Word, Christ. John is the voice of the Word crying in the wilderness: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (Mark 1:3).

The Lord whom you desire came immediately to the temple, namely Christ the Savior, who is the Creator of all things. And just as on this day he was presented in the holy temple according to the law, so daily he comes spiritually

[Col. 0618D] into the spiritual temple, of which the Apostle says: “For the temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3:16), giving or increasing grace. He says to his faithful: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:10). And elsewhere: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:20).

Therefore let us cleanse the temple of our mind, where we may receive our Lord and Master when he comes. Let us prepare the way of the Lord by repenting, believing, and rejecting crooked things; and let us make his paths straight by doing good to all—and doing so for eternal, not earthly, things—so that we may raise our hands in holiness rather than bend them down toward earthly things.

[Col. 0619A] For when Moses raised his hands over the stone of help, God’s people overcame Amalek; but when he lowered them, they were overcome (Exod. 17:11). Let us therefore raise our hearts, with our hands, to the Lord in heaven, and we shall overcome Amalek—that is, the demons thirsty for the blood of our death.

Let us prepare ourselves as a temple and house for the Lord, lest there be said to us what the Lord reproaches the offending people through the prophet Haggai: “This people says: ‘The time has not yet come to build the house of the Lord’” (Hag. 1:6). And what the Lord threatens them through the same prophet: “You looked for much, and behold, it became little; and you brought it into the house, and I blew it away. For what reason? says the Lord: because my house is deserted, while each of you hastens to his own house” (ibid. 9).

[Col. 0619B] Attend carefully, brethren, to how severely those are struck by the Lord who make his house deserted while hurrying to their own houses. They build their own houses who, swollen with pride of mind, presume upon their own merits and reject grace; by this they become strangers to God’s house. For their mind and conscience will be deserted by God, so that it may now be called not God’s temple or a house of prayer, but a den of robbers. There the Lord and Master has no place, he who says through Isaiah: “To whom shall I look, except to the poor little one, the contrite in spirit, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:1).

For God looks upon the lowly and dwells among the humble; but he knows the high—that is, the proud—from afar: he sees them by knowledge, but does not look upon them by grace. Therefore the proud and arrogant,

[Col. 0619C] who have not deserved that grace, look toward what is greater, walking in things great and wonderful beyond themselves; but when God blows upon it, it becomes little, and what they rashly promised themselves they by no means attain.

Let us therefore beware lest, in the likeness of such people, we make God’s house deserted in ourselves, grieving the Holy Spirit of God. As the indweller of the true temple, the Apostle says that he is grieved when, because of the foulness of our conscience and conduct, he withdraws from us. Instead, let us adorn the bridal chamber of the mind with curtains of devout thoughts and coverings of holy deeds that shine before people, so that they may glorify our Father who is in heaven; so that in the chamber of our mind, as in the beauty of a house and the dwelling-place

[Col. 0619D] of God’s glory, the Lord and Master may make his dwelling, together with the Angel of great counsel, of whom John says: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, having great authority,

[Col. 0620A] and the earth was illuminated by his glory; and he cried out mightily, saying: ‘Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great’” (Rev. 18:1).

This is the Angel, the author [variant: “actor”] of both Testaments, who descended from the equality and invisibility of the Father’s majesty, emptying himself by assuming the form of a servant. Yet he did not lose on earth the great authority which he possessed as equal to the Father—on earth, that is, in the Church, which, having received seed, produces fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold. It was illuminated, when the darkness of vices and ignorance had been driven out, by his glory—that is, by his teaching, grace, and example.

For this is the Lord whom Isaiah saw sitting and reigning, exalted and lifted up not only in all things but also above himself—namely, in

[Col. 0620B] the angels, in whom he sits and through whom he decrees his judgments. These are much higher than human beings, elevated above them by the eminence of their dignity. And his house—that is, the Church—was full. This is the house which the wise woman builds; the foolish woman scatters it from his majesty—that is, from the light of his grace.

For he is the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world. Of him that aged Simeon said: “A light for the revelation of the Gentiles and for the glory of your people Israel” (Luke 2:32). Simeon was that righteous and God-fearing man who, desiring to see the Lord’s day, “had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Christ of the Lord” (ibid. 26). Therefore, coming in the Spirit into the temple to receive what had been promised, he saw what he desired, took him into

[Col. 0620C] his arms, and carried the one he loved, saying: “Now”—that is, having seen the Redeemer—“you dismiss your servant, Lord” (ibid. 29), to bodily death, whom you had kept alive so that I might see you. And you dismiss me “according to your word” (ibid.), that is, according to your promise, so that I may not see eternal death, because I see eternal life. “Therefore you dismiss me in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples, a light for the revelation of the Gentiles” (ibid. 32).

Behold the Angel of counsel—that is, Christ—and he is both salvation and light: for he is the Lord who saves and the light who illumines. That aged Simeon carried this light in his arms. Hence the holy Fathers established this custom: that at

[Col. 0620D] today’s feast the holy Church should carry light in its hands,

[Note: It would be possible to demonstrate from many sources that the carrying of candles in the hands is extremely ancient; this is affirmed here by Hildebert, who lived in the eleventh century and says that the practice had already been established by the Fathers while he explains its mystery. This procession, which Emperor Justinian decreed should first be held at Constantinople—not that he was the first to introduce it into the Church, as some have thought—although it contains something of the devout joy with which blessed Simeon was moved in his sacred embrace of the child Jesus, nevertheless appears to have been in some measure penitential.

For that devout emperor decreed that it be celebrated in order to allay the plague or mortality devastating the city; and this favor seemed able to be obtained from God only through the works of humble penitence. This is also suggested by the rite by which this supplication was formerly celebrated at Rome: the supreme pontiffs themselves, cardinals and prelates, indeed the clergy and people alike, proceeded only barefoot.

This barefoot rite did not escape the notice of Martène, who reports and approves it in his treatise *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 15, where he treats the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Mary, drawing upon the *Roman Order*, chapter 5, by Cencius, and Jacobus Gaetanus, chapter 78. The same conclusion may be drawn from the manner in which this procession was formerly celebrated in the distinguished Church of Arles. For from a manuscript pontifical of that church, about five hundred years old, it is clear that there, except for two boys clad in silk copes proceeding before the cross, all the clergy, including the archbishop himself with his senior assisting ministers, were ordered to wear only woolen copes. They did not remove these until returning to the church, when the archbishop put on pontifical vestments and the others more precious vestments for the principal Mass.

Finally, the violet color which the Church generally employs for this procession, and especially during Lent, indicates that this procession ought to be performed in a spirit of compunction and penitence.]

signifying in the wax that true light “which God prepared for the revelation

[Col. 0621A] of the Gentiles and for the glory of his people Israel”: that is, so that that Spirit, the raiser-up at the Lord’s coming, may be revealed to the blind eyes of the Gentiles, and so that Israel may glory in receiving its promised and desired one.

Therefore, imitating righteous Simeon, let us receive light from light and carry it in our arms—namely, in the two arms of charity: loving God for his own sake and our neighbor for God’s sake—so that what that holy and God-fearing man did as a sign and performed as a figure, we too may fulfill in spirit.

Let us carry in the hands of faith and charity the candle, namely light in wax: the Word in flesh, God in man. In the simplicity of his divinity, in the form of God, he is light; but in human appearance he is a lamp or candle—that is, light in an earthen vessel

[Col. 0621B] or in wax, that is, in the form of a servant—according to the saying: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Ps. 118:105).

Wax, when fire is applied, produces light and drives away darkness. So too human nature, united to the Word of God, who is a consuming fire—“For our God,” as the Apostle says, “is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24; Heb. 12:23)—drove away the darkness of our blindness and vices and poured into our hearts the light of true knowledge. Hence: “A light has arisen in darkness for the upright in heart” (Ps. 111:4). For Christ, the true light, arose for this purpose: to remove darkness and make our steps straight.

Therefore let us carry this light with uplifted hands, because a lamp does not come to be placed under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may shine upon

[Col. 0621C] all who are in the house. Let us who are under him fill with virtues, deeds, examples, and miracles the temple of him who sits upon the throne, so that everything within us may bless him who sits on the high throne; and so that those who burst forth into his praises may encourage others, that in ourselves and in others we may make a house of the wondrous tabernacle. This we can indeed do because the house of the Church is full of his majesty, and “the earth was illuminated by the glory of the angel crying mightily: ‘Babylon has fallen’” (Rev. 18:1). For in his power he overthrew the city of confusion when he entered the house of the strong man—that is, the devil, whom not his own strength but our sins had made strong—and bound him, restraining him from

[Col. 0621D] deceiving the faithful. He plundered his vessels because he joined to himself, having turned them back, those whom that wicked one possessed, so that those who had formerly been vessels of iniquity, children of wrath, children of unbelief, became vessels of righteousness unto sanctification of life, children of grace, children of God.

The names were changed because their merits were changed, according to the saying: “Nor will I remember their names upon my lips” (Ps. 15:4). But who did this? The Lord strong and mighty in battle, at whom the trembling prince of this world marvels, saying:

[Col. 0622A] “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. 23:8.)

Thus the Lord Ruler accomplished all these things: he who came from Sinai, rose for us from Seir, and appeared from Mount Paran. For Paran is interpreted “fruit-bearing”; rightly, by Mount Paran is understood the grace of evangelical teaching, which the Lord delivered to his disciples upon the mountain when, opening his mouth like a desirable treasure, like a well of living waters, like a paradise of every fruit, he said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” etc. (Matt. 5:3).

Such excellent teaching was fittingly delivered upon a mountain, for it contains the height of righteousness, the eminence of grace, and the perfection of glory; there is the life-giving Spirit, not the letter that kills, so that it may bear manifold fruit in the hearts of the faithful. This is that word concerning which the Lord says through Isaiah: “My word which shall go forth from my mouth shall not be empty, but shall prosper; for through it you shall go forth in joy and be led forth in peace” (Isa. 55:11). From this word of truth, therefore, the Lord appeared as from Mount Paran—he who had been veiled for them in the Law and the Prophets.

For he was revealed in the Gospel: appearing in majesty with Moses and Elijah upon the mountain, he showed to three disciples the glory of his own and our resurrection. He too, while the disciples were at supper, was lifted up in a bright cloud into heaven, according to Habakkuk: “The sun was lifted up into heaven, and the moon stood in its order” (Hab. 3:11 [Col. 0622C]). From these things it is evident what the glory of the Lord is that was revealed in the Gospel through manifest and wondrous signs. It nullified the glory of Moses’ face, as the Apostle says: “For that which was glorious in Moses is now without glory because of the surpassing glory” (2 Cor. 3:10)—that is, in comparison with the surpassing glory which is in the New Testament, where the glory of God is seen purely and clearly, where the Lord who ascends above the setting is known truly to possess the Name.

Therefore he is not without reason said to have appeared from Mount Paran, and with him thousands of saints; for once truth had been proclaimed through the Gospel, the authority of the apostles was strengthened, and the seed of Abraham was multiplied like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea. So great a multitude of peoples entered through the narrow gate when the seed of the Gospel was cast forth, that Isaiah, marveling at their number and rapid increase, says in the Spirit: “Shall the earth bring forth in one day, or shall an entire nation be born at once? For Zion travailed and brought forth her children” (Isa. 66:8 [Col. 0622D]).

Thus with him are thousands of saints—that is, an innumerable multitude. Hence Daniel: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7:10). And through Isaiah the Lord says to the primitive Church: “The children of your barrenness shall yet say in your ears: ‘The place is too narrow for me; make room for me that I may dwell.’ And you shall say in your heart: ‘Who has begotten these for me? I was barren and did not bear, exiled and captive; and who has reared these? I was left desolate and alone; where then were these?’” (Isa. 49:20 [Col. 0623A]). In these words the Church, formerly subject to the reproach of barrenness, marvels how she brought forth, so quickly, such children and so many, who appeared with the Lord.

“In whose right hand was a fiery law”: he who came from Sinai, rose for us from Seir, and has a fiery law in his right hand. He himself has a right hand and a left. The right hand signifies spiritual and earthly [perhaps “eternal”] goods; the left, temporal goods. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 8:3 [Col. 0623B]). Elsewhere: “In his right hand are years of life; in his left, riches and honor” (Prov. 3:15). But many reverse these, putting the right for the left and the left for the right, like those who said: “Blessed is the people to whom these things belong.”

On the left, therefore, is the law of death, the law of the flesh, the law of the members; on the right, the law of the Spirit, the law of life, the law of birth. On the left will stand the sinful goats and the reprobate at the division of the future judgment. On the right, the sheep and lambs—that is, the simple and the good, who according to the purpose are called saints—where they shall praise God without end, that is, love him with their whole heart. May the merciful God grant that we sit there. Amen.

## LVIII. Third Sermon on the Feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary

[Note: From the Saint-Germain manuscript. (Col. 0623D)]

[Col. 0623C]

> “The Lord brought me into the land of Israel and set me upon a very high mountain, upon which there was, as it were, the structure of a city facing south. And he brought me there; and behold, a man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze, with a linen cord in his hand and a measuring reed in his hand; and he stood in the gate” (Ezek. 40:2).

Just as the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear with hearing, so our mind cannot be satisfied in marveling at the unsearchable riches of God’s wisdom and the inscrutable sacraments of the mystery hidden from eternal ages, which the Lord, though secretly, nevertheless expressed through his prophets by certain sacraments.

Hence the Son of Man—namely, the prophet Ezekiel—is led onto a very high mountain, upon which was, as it were, the structure of a city, and so forth. He is rightly said to be led to the mountain, which he could not reach by himself, because no one comes to the Son unless the Father draws him to him (John 6). For this mountain, so high and exceedingly lofty, is the little stone cut from the mountain without hands, which grew into a great mountain and occupied the surface of the earth. This is the mountain set upon the summit of the mountains. This mountain alone is the one from which we await our coming help.

For there are many mountains to which we lift up our eyes, saying with the Prophet: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains” (Ps. 120:1 [Col. 0624A]), while nevertheless looking toward the one “from which help may come to us” (ibid.). But the Prophet raises his eyes especially to this mountain, saying: “To you I lift up my eyes, you who dwell in heaven” (Ps. 122:1). Many have held various opinions about this mountain: some thought that he was Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets. But Peter truly confessed him to be the Son of God.

Therefore this mountain is not like the other mountains, in which the Spirit is present by measure. For in none, as in this one, did the fullness of divinity dwell bodily. Rightly, therefore, is this mountain called exceedingly high, because he dwells in heaven. Thus David, rebuking the various errors concerning this mountain, reproves those who err, saying: “Why do you suppose other mountains to exist besides this mountain, in which it pleased God to dwell?” (Ps. 67:17 [Col. 0624B]).

We shall be able, in whatever way, to ascend this mountain if we do not press our hands down to earthly works, but raise them to heaven with Moses. Yet we cannot do this unless Hur and Aaron raise those hands—that is, Christ through the Holy Spirit. For by Hur the Holy Spirit is understood, because Hur is interpreted “fire”; by Aaron, Christ, who is called “the dwelling-place of strength.” Therefore, if you wish to ascend this mountain, “set your hearts upon your ways,” as the prophet says (Hag. 1:7). “Go up to the mountain, carry timber, build the house” (ibid., v. 8).

Some ways are those from which we turn aside; some, those to which we go; some, those by which we go. For the Prophet says: “I considered my ways and turned my feet to your testimonies” (Ps. 118). The ways from which we turn aside are sins, namely perverse ways, which are on the left. For Solomon says: “The perverse ways are those on the left” (Prov. 4:27). The ways to which we go are the ways of righteousness, which are on the right and which the Lord knows. The ways by which we go are the ways of innocence. First we must leave evil, so that we may thus arrive at works of righteousness. Hence it is said: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:11).

Therefore, if we wish to ascend this mountain, we must ascend by only eight steps, which the Lord distinguished in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit; blessed are the meek; blessed are those who mourn; blessed are the merciful; blessed are the pure in heart; blessed are the peacemakers; blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness; blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5:3 [Col. 0624D]). This is called the eighth virtue.

By these steps, then, we can ascend the very high mountain; but not unless we carry the wood from which the house of the Lord, or city, may be built. This wood is the cross of Christ, whose breadth and length, depth and height, we ought to imitate. Its breadth: in the expansiveness of charity, so that, as he placed upon the cross prayed for his enemies, saying, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34), so we too, imitating him, may love our neighbor [Col. 0625A]. For all his action was instruction for us. Its length: in the long-suffering of charity, so that unto death we may love God with our whole heart and our neighbors as ourselves. Its height: so that, in the hope of all we do, we may meditate only upon heavenly things. Its depth: so that we may establish all our good upon Christ’s foundation. For he is the foundation which no one can change.

We must therefore carry this wood if we wish to ascend this mountain and build a tabernacle for the Lord, according to that which was shown to Moses on the mountain. Those wishing to build a house for the Lord must act in likeness to this mountain, so that we may suffer in likeness to it. For the Lord says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16:24 [Col. 0625B]).

Thus by this wood we shall be able to ascend the mountain upon which is, as it were, the structure of a city—that is, the Church, which is not called a city but “as it were a city.” This is “Jerusalem, which is built as a city” (Ps. 181:3). David said “as a city,” as Ezekiel says “the structure as it were of a city,” because the Church is not a city but resembles a city, just as neither is it a house, although it is called a house. For the Church is called both house and city: city because of the multitude of those called; house because of the small number of the elect.

“This city is small, and there are few men in it,” as Solomon says, “against which a great king came, besieged it, and built fortifications around it; and the siege was completed. And a poor and wise man was found in it, and he delivered it by his wisdom” (Ecclus. 9:14 [Col. 0625C]). That great king who came to besiege the little city is the devil, who boasts himself great and strong; it was not his own strength but our sins that made him strong. With his princes and an innumerable multitude of wicked persons and vices, he attacked the Church.

Understand by the princes the greater vices, namely those dispositions which the prophet Joel describes metaphorically: “What the caterpillar left, the locust consumed; what the locust left, the grasshopper consumed; what the grasshopper left, the mildew devoured” (Joel 1:4). These are the four vices opposed to the highest virtues; and with them come creeping things without number, to attack the little city. But there is found in it a man—indeed strong and poor—of whom the prophet says: “I looked, and a man entered; I considered, and there was none to meet him” (Isa. 59:16 [Col. 0625D]).

This man is strong. For he bound the strong man and plundered his goods. And he is poor, because, though rich with God, for our sake he became needy and poor, so that he did not even have where to lay his head. When he was offered for us in the temple today, he willed that no offering should be offered for himself except the offering of the poor: namely, a pair of turtle-doves or two young pigeons. He was also wise, because Wisdom founded the earth and established the heavens by her prudence. This poor man delivered the city not by power; for he did not violently overpower the devil, but by wisdom, because, when the devil dared to attack him over whom he had no right at all, he lost the power which, though unjustly, he exercised over all.

This is he whose appearance was like bronze, and who had a measuring reed in his hand: namely, the power by which, from his immeasurable grace, he distributes measured gifts to his elect, fittingly dividing the spoils according to the form of the house [Col. 0626A].

“And he stood in the gate.” He who stands in the gate is partly seen and partly not seen: so Christ was seen in his humanity while remaining invisible in his divinity. As a sign of this reality, the Church has established that, in the present solemnity, she represents the purification of this child and his mother by candles. In the wax, which is visible, humanity is understood; in the fire, whose nature is invisible, divinity.

Therefore he stood in the gate of the city facing south. This gate is the blessed Virgin Mary, who faces—that is, looks and leads—toward the south, where the light of righteousness is full, namely toward the grace of the Holy Spirit. This gate, as the Prophet says, shall always be shut, and no man shall pass through it, because she was a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth.

Therefore Christ entered through this gate, which faces south. Hence: through the more hidden birth [perhaps, “through the upper gate”], which faces north, by the way of which gate the prophet Ezekiel saw six men coming, each with an instrument of destruction in his hand; and one man clothed in linen, with a writer’s ink-horn at his loins. And the Lord said to him: “Pass through the midst of the city, and mark Tau upon the foreheads of those who groan and mourn” (Ezek. 9:2 [Col. 0626B]).

These six men are any human beings. For six is the number of universality and generality, because God made all things in six days and rested on the seventh. These men, then, descending through the upper—that is, the earlier or prior—gate, namely through Eve, who faces north, whence evils burn forth—that is, those who consent to the devil—each have an instrument of destruction in his hand, because each drew from that gate the cause for which they deserve death.

But the man who stood in their midst—Christ, namely, of whom it is said, “One stands in your midst whom you do not know” (John 1:26)—delivered these six men through the mystery of the letter Tau, that is, through the passion of his cross. This man was clothed in linen and had the appearance of bronze. The same thing is signified by bronze and linen garments: namely, the humanity with which the Word was clothed, though according to different states. For he is said to have been clothed in linen before the Passion because of his immunity from sin and the labors of the Passion; but he is said to have had the appearance of bronze because of the glory of immortality. For no metal is more enduring than bronze, and Christ, having died—or rather, having risen—now dies no more [Col. 0626D].

By the command given to him by the Lord Father, this man marks Tau only on the faces of those who mourn and grieve; but in the morning of the general resurrection he will slay all the others, according to the Prophet: “In the morning I slew all the sinners of the earth” (Ps. 100:8).

“A writer’s ink-horn at his loins.” The loins are the firmer parts of the body, situated behind as though following the face that goes before. Thus the more perfect saints follow Christ, their face [perhaps “they follow,” not “imitate”], and do not go before him, lest they hear what was said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan, for you do not savor the things that are of God” (Matt. 16:23 [Col. 0627A]). All the saints, therefore, follow Christ and do not stubbornly go before him; and for this reason the Savior’s loins are not irrationally mentioned.

At these loins is the writer’s ink-horn, because these are the mourners and groaners whose foreheads Christ marked with the letter Tau, and through whom he distinguishes the rest of the faithful by the same sign from the others. Passing through the midst of the city, this man—the man who had also stood in the gate—scattered from the Lord’s city all workers of iniquity.

The reed also in his hand is the Holy Spirit, who writes and dictates the unseen, unknown, and unheard rewards of the saints, according to the saying: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9 [Col. 0627B]). May he himself deign to grant this to us, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## LIX. First Sermon on the Feast of the Assumption of Blessed Mary and on Her Praises

[Note: From the Angers manuscript.—It is probable that Hildebert delivered this sermon not simply to the people, but to men distinguished by exceptional piety, whose “conversation was in heaven,” as he says: such as were the monks of Cluny who lived with him under Saint Hugh, before whom he frequently preached by Hugh’s command. He states here that they had heard so many sermons from him, so often aired, and, in comparison with whom, Hildebert humbly professed himself dust and ashes.

From this sermon it is clear, first, that he believed in the assumption of blessed Mary into heaven in body and soul, which he here endeavors to prove. Secondly, that the Church then used a collect other than the one now used. Thirdly, that such reverence and devotion toward the most blessed Virgin already prevailed that, upon hearing her name, the faithful would press their knees to the earth.

Yet it is remarkable that, after Hildebert was promoted to the bishopric of Le Mans, although the feast of the Assumption was celebrated in his church, as the ancient *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, edited by our Mabillon in vol. III of the *Analecta*, testify, it was nevertheless observed less solemnly. As the same acts report, the canons used only one double [office] and incense at Lauds. Hildebert is not recorded as having changed this rite, perhaps because of the many and grave burdens of his church that stood in the way. He left this to be done, and perhaps urged it upon his successor Guy when he was transferred to the see of Tours.

For, as the same *Acts* relate, Guy decreed in his chapter, with all the canons present and assenting, that the Assumption of blessed Mary—which from ancient times until his own day had been observed among them less solemnly than it ought—should henceforth be celebrated in the same manner and with the same honor, but more magnificently, as the summer solemnity of Saint Gervasius is observed in their church; and that the octave of the Assumption should be observed like the feast of Saint Lawrence. The same bishop granted from his own revenues that double offices might be celebrated and incense prepared at Nocturns for the same Assumption.

For the institution of this feast, consult what our Martène has learnedly noted on the matter in his recently published treatise *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 33, [lacuna] 25; we do not repeat it here for the sake of brevity. (Cols. 0627C–0628D)]

I am dust and ashes, who speak to you. Therefore I blush and fear to speak God’s word to you. I blush, I say, because your conversation is in heaven; but I, like a beast, have rotted in my dung. I fear, moreover, lest you perhaps expect from me, a mute and tongue-tied man, the fragrance of discourse—you who have heard sermons so numerous and so often aired [Col. 0627C]. Yet I fear even more lest the Lord say to me: “Why do you recount my righteous acts and take my covenant upon your mouth?” (Ps. 49:16).

Nevertheless, because a painter often depicts a beautiful person while himself ugly, I shall speak to you under a figure, because perhaps it will turn to wisdom for you, though to folly for me. But you, Lord Sabaoth, open my mouth, that you may fill it.

The present solemnity, moreover, concerning the praise of the blessed Virgin Mary offers us matter for speech. Although I am unable adequately to expound her inexpressible praise, even if I spoke with the tongues of men and angels, yet with Isaiah we can say something in this manner: “The glory of Lebanon, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon, has been given to her” (Isa. 35:2 [Col. 0628A]). With due respect to the prophet, let us add something to his words. What he foretold was to be fulfilled, we shall state as fulfilled. Therefore let us say: Today the glory of Lebanon, the beauty of Carmel, and Sharon’s beauty have been given to her.

In the literal sense Lebanon, Carmel, and Sharon are mountains which Sacred Scripture often commends for their excellence in pastures, trees, and wild animals. Figuratively, however, they signify the excellence of virtues that is in the saints. Here they may be applied to indicate the threefold crown which was stored up for the blessed Virgin while she was on earth and was rendered to her today in heaven.

For the blessed Virgin possessed three things, each as worthy of wonder as it is of a special recompense. She was Virgin, Mother, and Mother of God. It is indeed great and praiseworthy to have been a virgin; but it is greater in every way, and more marvelous, to have been fruitful in virginity and, after the emptying of the womb, to have the womb sealed. It is great and ineffable to have been the Mother of God.

In memory of these three things, Greek wisdom established that the three names should be inscribed in this manner on icons of the blessed Virgin painted in her image: “Virgin, Mother of God.” Among them, however, this is one word, *Theotokos* (“God-bearer”); among us, two. Therefore, because she was Virgin, the glory of Lebanon was given to her; because she was Mother, the beauty of Carmel was given to her; because she was Mother of God, the beauty of Sharon was given to her.

Lebanon is interpreted “whitening.” There is as much difference between whiteness and whitening as between genus and species [Col. 0628C]. For *candor* properly means whiteness, whether the natural whiteness of a white thing that endures while the thing itself endures—as in snow and the lily—or whiteness that comes accidentally or by artifice. But *candidatio* properly means only native and enduring whiteness. By “whitening” we understand the whiteness of birth, that is, eternal birth. Therefore, by whiteness and whitening, the purity of our flesh is signified.

But there is one purity of our flesh after a fall: when someone, paying to corrupt flesh what is almost its due tribute, even after lawful embraces begins to restrain and contain his flesh, and thereafter to preserve the purity of flesh which he had defiled. This purity is rightly called continence, because it labors to restrain the reins which it had loosened for the flesh.

There is another purity, as it were natural and enduring, with integrity of flesh. He who possesses it by the benefit of age preserves it always unharmed by the benefit of virtue. This is properly called virginity, as though *viror genitus*, “begotten greenness.” Sacred Scripture suggests this distinction to us: it compares virginity to the lily, whose whiteness of birth is enduring; but it compares continence to fine linen. For fine linen springs from green earth and is grass-colored; but raw, it is dried, beaten, boiled, twisted, and through great and lengthy labor brought to a white color. For the fine linens are the justifications of the saints. Those who first fell are called not properly righteous, but justified; not properly holy, but sanctified [Col. 0629B].

Therefore there was given to the blessed Virgin not the glory of whiteness, but of whitening—that is, of virginity. Certainly, so far as we infer from different places of Sacred Scripture, the glory of virgins consists in three things, by which, as by certain prerogatives, they are distinguished among others. This is not to say that the glory of other virgins is not surpassing and exalted. For some married persons are preferred even to virgins in glory and merit; but because in the Virgin it is of greater glory, because they are, as it were, the insignia of a triumph, they are proclaimed in a special way.

For virgins are assigned a hundredfold fruit. Virgins alone are also said to sing the new song. Finally, because they are virgins, they follow the Lamb wherever he goes. Thus the excellence of virgins consists in three things: in the number of sheaves, in the new song, and in the journey with the Lamb [Col. 0629C].

For Truth in the Gospel enumerates three fruits of good soil according to the number of those to be saved: the thirtieth in Job, the sixtieth in Noah, the hundredth in Daniel. Why the higher fruit is assigned to the virgin must not be neglected as a subject of inquiry, because it is useful to know. According to Bede’s natural method of reckoning, all numbers below one hundred are found on the left hand; whenever you wish to designate any one of them, you must place a finger on the left hand as a counter. But when you count one hundred and beyond, you pass from the left to the right. Therefore the thirtieth and sixtieth fruits belong to the left, but the hundredth to the right; and thus virgins have the fruit of the right hand.

The left hand is naturally slower in us and is not fitted for bearing every burden; indeed, when blows and strikes threaten, it is naturally put before the other parts of the body, as more suited to receiving and enduring blows. But the right hand is more agile and therefore more suited to inflicting blows. Hence the state of virgins is not without reason compared to the right hand, as more capable of serving God; but the state of the rest is compared to the left, as more burdensome for earning merit [Col. 0629D].

There follows the beauty of Carmel and Sharon. Carmel is interpreted “true circumcision”; it is called true, that is, complete. This is the circumcision of the eighth [age] that we await, when spirit and flesh will be circumcised from every fault and punishment. Thus complete circumcision exists in each of the two sabbaths, which the two Carmels suitably represent. One, in which foolish Nabal lived, was in the middle of Judaea; the other, in which Hebal built an altar to the Lord and received fire from above, was in the borders of Israel.

In this way, the sabbath-rest of the soul is given even now, in the midst of this age—that is, in the seventh age now underway—to the spirits of the blessed. But we await the sabbath-rest of the body at the end of the ages. Today, however, the blessed Virgin has attained both blessedness of soul and glorification of body. Let us establish this so that no one may doubt it, by authorities.

Today’s collect proclaims: “Yet she could not be held down by the bonds of death,” etc. Likewise [it is proclaimed] by the invitation of the angels at the Lord’s Ascension: “Who is this who comes up from Edom?” etc. (Isa. 63:1 [Col. 0630B]). Her ascent too was prophetically foretold: “Who is she that comes up like the shining dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun?” (Song 6:9). In Scripture the beauty of the sun and moon is not usually applied properly except to bodies. Hence also it is written: “The presence of the fruitful Virgin embraces heaven [variant *praesentiam*: ‘heaven embraces the presence of the fruitful Virgin’], when the mother of the mediator comes” [corrupt text: *cum mater me. ve.*; proposed reading: *cum mater mediatoris venit*]. And: “The sun was raised up, and the moon stood in its order” (Hab. 3:11).

How, moreover, will that Davidic saying be fulfilled, “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her” (Ps. 44:15), if her being brought is postponed until the common resurrection? And when could they be brought earlier, if not today? We cannot discover it.

This same point may further be proved by a plausible argument from analogy. Husband and wife are two in one flesh; more expressly, mother and son are one flesh. Certainly, the holy Fathers, promulgating decrees under the Holy Spirit’s dictation, established this rule for spouses: if one leaves the world and cleaves to God, the other is not to remain in the world. For it did not seem lawful to them for the flesh of one person to be torn apart so violently. So likewise in other cases it ought to seem improper if one part of virginal flesh is in heaven while the other is returned to the soil; if it is granted to one part not to see corruption, while the other dissolves into ashes.

For as the blessed Virgin was made immune from the woman’s curse, to whom it was said, “You shall give birth in pain” (Gen. 3:16), because she gave birth without pain, so she was made immune from the common curse of man and woman, to whom it was said, “You shall go into ashes.” Hence she is said to have been blessed by the angel because she was freed from the primordial curse. Thus the beauty of Carmel—that is, of complete circumcision—was given to the Virgin today [Col. 0630D].

No less was the beauty of Sharon given to her. Sharon means “the sound of principality.” Therefore the beauty of Sharon is the beauty of principalities—that is, of angels. For she was not merely joined to the angels; today, confident in her Son, she was exalted in her own beauty above the choirs of angels. For if Solomon, when his mother came to him concerning Adonijah’s petition, placed beside himself a throne for her, it is more plausible that Christ placed his mother at his right hand, according to the saying: “The Queen stood at your right hand” (Ps. 44:10 [Col. 0631A]). And, as on the day of the Lord’s Ascension: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1). Isaiah’s saying was also fulfilled: “The young man shall stand with the virgin” (Isa. 62:5).

Nor is it without reason that the Church is accustomed to implore the intercession of the blessed Virgin more ardently than that of the others, so that, on hearing her name, she presses her knees to the earth; indeed, from reverence for her name, the vows of peoples resound like a stormy sea. Why this happens has been explained in another sermon; here we pass it over.

Therefore let each of us prostrate ourselves; let us all prostrate ourselves at the feet of the blessed Virgin, who today has become brighter than the stars and loftier than the angels, so that through her intercession we may see the mother with her offspring, the Son and the Father, who is blessed for ages. Amen.

## LX. Second Sermon on the Feast of the Assumption of Blessed Mary and on Her Praises

[Note: From the Angers manuscript. (Col. 0631D)]

[Col. 0631B]

> “I turned to the way of the outer gate of the sanctuary, which faced east, and it was shut. And the Lord said to me: ‘This gate shall be shut; it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it; and it shall be shut for the prince. The prince himself shall sit in it, to eat bread before the Lord’” (Ezek. 44:1).

Here Ezekiel bears the person of the human race, desiring to escape from the lake of misery and the mire of filth; as though he said: “I, an exile from the homeland of blessedness and cast down in this valley of tears, looking about through all former ages, sought the way of salvation and did not find it [Col. 0631C]. Heaven could not free me, nor earth, nor the world with all its equipment, nor man. For we are all afflicted together and sick together. [And I found no one] who [did not] rather disdain than relieve my weakness.

“But at last I turned to the way of the outer gate of the sanctuary, to the childbirth of the blessed Virgin.”

Now no wise person is ignorant that the Lord Jesus exists from two natures and in two natures. The divine nature is the inner sanctuary. Those who are within behold it—I mean the angels and spirits of the blessed, who already rest in their homeland, in their palace, indeed in their chamber, while he gives them drink from the torrent of his delight. The human nature is the outer sanctuary, because Christ refreshes the Church militant, which still has its tabernacle in the sun, by the participation of his body and blood. Or rather, that nature had an inner sanctuary because it is hidden, and an outer sanctuary because it is manifest.

For we do not see the Trinity of persons in unity of essence; but the trinity of substances in persons we know, speak of, and expound. For when God came to us, he made upon earth a new Trinity, namely a temporal one, which might correspond, as it were by contrast, to the eternal Trinity. Therefore the inner sanctuary is the Word in the beginning with the Father, bearing all things by the word of his power. The outer sanctuary is the Word made flesh in time, making purification for our weakness [Col. 0632A].

The gate of the inner sanctuary is God the Father, the Son saying: “I went forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16:28); hence the Psalmist: “His going forth is from the highest heaven” (Ps. 18:7). The gate of the outer sanctuary was the blessed Virgin, through whom God, made human, entered into our city, of which he himself says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:14). Its foundations are in the holy mountains, and the rushing river of the Holy Spirit makes it glad. This is the holy Church, city of the great King, and it faces east.

All those conceived from sexual union, not without concupiscence, although they bring their offspring into the light of birth, nevertheless, because they themselves carry with them the sackcloth and the merit of sackcloth, are darkened by the soot of sin and sit in darkness and in the region of the shadow of death. The Son of the Virgin alone was brought forth into the light in such a way that he is not only light himself, but also enlightens every person coming into this world [Col. 0632B].

And this gate was shut. Although no one can doubt the Virgin’s integrity, nevertheless, so that the matter may be made certain—indeed more certain than certain—the prophet adds the Lord’s authority in confirmation, saying: “And the Lord said to me: This gate shall be shut; no man shall enter through it.” That is what is reiterated a third time. Here, to be sure, “man” is understood not as denoting sex but as husband, so as to signify the matter more explicitly—as if he said: not even her husband, that is, Joseph, shall know her. Fittingly, moreover, it is said three times that it was shut, since she is beyond doubt Virgin before childbirth, in childbirth, and after childbirth.

It follows: [Col. 0632C] “And it shall be shut for the prince”—namely, for him of whom the Lord says: “Now the prince of this world shall be cast out” (John XXII [read: XII], 31); and again: “For the prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John XIV, 10 [read: 30]). But just as by the words, “No man shall pass through it,” the integrity of the flesh is denoted, so by the words, “It shall not be opened to the prince,” the integrity of the mind is denoted: she banished from her mind every consent to evil suggestion.

But what is added above—“The prince shall sit in it”—is not to be understood of the prince just mentioned. For how could he who is not even permitted to enter be said to sit in it? [perhaps: “is proclaimed”] This prince, rather, is he of whom it is said: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Son of God, Prince of Peace.” Sitting is used to signify humility, as in: “You have known my sitting down and my rising up” (Ps. CXXXVIII [139], 1); and again: “Rise up after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Ps. CXXVI [127], 8)—that is, after humility, hope for exaltation. No slight humiliation of the Word, indeed, was the assumption of the form of a servant.

It follows: “That he may eat bread before the Lord.” For he himself says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John IV, 34). Obedient, therefore, to the Father, he reconciled us to God. In this manner he ate bread before the Lord, restoring freedom to us by his will. You have heard these things expounded concerning the Virgin’s childbirth, her integrity, and the fruit of our salvation. Yet they may also be fittingly applied to us who devote ourselves to the reading and study of Holy Scripture. 531

[Note: [Col. 0633D] From these words of Hildebert in this sermon, two inferences seem possible. First, that he possessed this sermon, like several others included in this collection, while at Cluny, where together with many men of the same order he devoted himself to reading and the study of Holy Scripture, having now, as he says here, for the most part set aside the fictions of the poets, whom he compares to talkative frogs. Second, when he says that he had sailed through the pallid arguments of sophists hateful to God and had taken leave of the pompous opinions of philosophers, who, “while they were still among us,” he says in the first person, “attempted to raise their eyes above the heavens,” and whose more learned members—the Academics, he means—confessed that truth lay hidden as though in the well of the abyss: nothing prevents this from being understood of Berengar. Hildebert had formerly been his constant hearer in humane letters and philosophy, but renounced his teaching as soon as he perceived him setting his mouth against heaven, when, concerning the sacred Eucharist, he dared to prefer his own views to the Church’s general and orthodox judgment and attempted to instil his heresy into the minds of the faithful with grandiloquent and empty speech and with his sophisms. We have rightly judged this worthy of notice in Hildebert’s favor: his judgment on the sacred Eucharist was always orthodox and remote from Berengar’s erroneous opinion, as his many sermons, special treatises, and shorter works testify; and he is said to have been the first to employ the word “Transubstantiation,” later adopted and, as it were, consecrated by the Church. Let the reader judge our conjecture.]

For we have now for the most part set aside the fictions of poets, who are compared to talkative frogs. Moreover, we have sailed through the pallid arguments of sophists, who are called hateful to God. We have taken leave of the pompous opinions of philosophers who, while they were still among us, attempted to raise their eyes above the heavens; their wiser members—I mean the Academics—confessed that truth lay hidden as though in the well of the abyss. We have abandoned grandiloquent speech, following truth-speaking speech. For we sought wisdom; but behold, it was not in the land of those who speak pleasantly, or who live pleasantly. We heard of it [Col. 0633B] hidden in Ephrathah—that is, in a mirror or watchtower, that is, in an image—but behold, we found it in the fields of the wood, that is, in the manifestation and obscurity of the New and Old Testaments.

Each one of us, I say, can now truly say: “I turned myself to the way of the gate of the outer sanctuary, which faces east.” As there are two parts of the Church, militant and triumphant—the former on the way, the latter in the homeland—so the holiness of the one differs from that of the other. The outer sanctuary, therefore, that is, the holiness of the present Church which is still outside, is justification through faith and good works. Its gate is Holy Scripture, which teaches us to live rightly in the midst of this crooked nation; through it, whoever enters and goes out shall find pasture. [Col. 0633C] The way of this gate is charity. A man placed at the crossroads of this world, and standing, as it were, at the earth’s navel, can turn himself east, west, south, or north.

For there are four ways of man: the way of weakness, the way of necessity, the way of vanity, and the way of truth. The way of human weakness—the way of Adam—is Jericho: the way by which man, made in the image of God, passes like flowing water through the succession of times until he returns to his dust. This inclines southward, which is hot. For we live by a certain solar [perhaps: “warmth”] heat; when it is extinguished, it is necessary to enter another way, 532 namely the way of necessity. This is the way of all flesh, by which “the spirit passes, going and not returning.” This inclines toward the west.

But the way of vanity [Col. 0633D] is the way of sins, more suitably called a precipice, by which we plunge from blood into blood, [Col. 0634A] drawing a long rope behind us. This is the broad way leading to death, when we riot through the fields of license; of it it is said: “Their way is darkness and slipperiness” (Ps. XXXIV [35], 6); and again: “Their way is a stumbling-block to them” (Ps. XLVIII [49], 14). This inclines northward, toward him who said: “I will set my throne in the north” (Isa. XIV, 13). Of him Solomon says: “The north wind is cold and hard” (Ecclus. XLIII, 22): right-handed only in name, binding up the waters—that is, freezing the streams of grace.

The way of truth is charity, of which the Apostle says: “I show you a still more excellent way” (I Cor. XII, 31). This inclines eastward, because this way is the narrow way that leads to life; therefore one must strive to enter through it. By this way one must go to Holy Scripture. Yet [Col. 0634B] we cannot conceal that many of us proceed by another way: some, by knowing much, may despise others; some, that they may be praised; some, that they may gain profit; some, that they may build themselves up; others, that they may also build up their neighbors. But hear what one man said of these matters: “To wish to know in order to be known is pride; to wish to know in order to make gain is simony; to wish to know in order to be built up is prudence; to wish to know in order to build up is charity.”

Holy Scripture, moreover, is aptly compared to a gate. For there are four things in a gate: the threshold upon which we walk; two doorposts, one on either side, set above it; and the upper lintel, resting upon both doorposts. In the same way, there are four things in Holy Scripture, just as there are four feet [Col. 0634C] on the Lord’s table: history, allegory, morality, and anagogy.

History is the threshold, because the others are laid upon it. It consists, as it were, of three stones, being contained in three works of God: the work of creation, the work of reconciliation, and the work of confirmation. The Father created; the Son reconciled; the Holy Spirit confirmed—each in its own time. Of the time of creation it is written: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth, etc.” (Gen. I, 1). Of the time of reconciliation it is said: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Gal. IV, 4): namely, when the heavens dropped dew from above and the clouds rained down the Just One, the earth was opened and brought forth the Savior. “He is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II, 14), making peace through his blood for things in heaven and [Col. 0634D] things on earth (Col. I).

The time of confirmation is future, when God will make a new heaven and [Col. 0635A] a new earth, and the good will be gathered from the midst of the evil. Once they have been separated, “God, wonderful in his saints,” will appear (Ps. LXVII [68]). For now dregs still mingle with oil, tares with wheat, the grape with wine, chaff with grain. In the time of reconciliation, the Son says: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John V, 17). In the time of confirmation, the Holy Spirit could truly say: “The Father works until now, and from this point I myself now work”—when he makes our bodies spiritual, and flesh cleaves to spirit, and spirit to God.

Morality likewise consists, as it were, of three stones. For our morals are formed in three schools: the school of discipline, the school of nature, and the school of grace. In the first we learn to be inferior; in the second, [Col. 0635B] equal; in the third, superior. That is: to be under another, with another, over another; or to be subject, to coexist, to preside—that is, disciples, companions, teachers. In the first are those who humbly submit to prelates; in the second, those accustomed patiently to bear the disorderly habits of their companions; in the third, those known to preside wisely over those subject to them by word and deed.

Although the school of nature is naturally prior, nevertheless, according to the order of moral formation, the school of discipline comes first. For nature gave birth to all human beings equal; but that one is put over or under another is from the Lord God, from whom is all authority, who “placed men over our heads.” Yet people, made for good and not corrupted through pride, have become impatient of equality, [Col. 0635C] striving to be set over one another and desiring to surpass one another, provoking one another. Therefore, before all else, the insolence of character must be subdued, until the stiff-necked will, worn down by stern and divine laws, is humbled.

We rightly call the third school, that of grace, the foremost. It claims for itself the name “spiritual,” though this name is common to the others, because it abounds in delights and in the gifts [perhaps: “endowments”] of charity. For you see very many living peacefully under a teacher; many too living blamelessly among equals 534 and content with a good moderation. But if you release them from the yoke of discipline and fellowship, you see very few—rare exceptions—presiding humbly and profitably: men who forget themselves, do not seek their own interests, and do not wish to lord it [Col. 0635D] over the clergy.

Allegory is the other lintel, likewise considered in three classes of saints: those before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. For the deeds of these times, by reciprocal signification, mystically prefigure one another; thus the expulsion of penitents at the beginning of Lent signifies the expulsion of the first human beings from paradise, and so forth.

Anagogy, which is the upper stone, is as one whole and undivided stone, for it treats of God and heavenly realities. This gate, moreover, faces God. “Whoever [Col. 0636A] gives of his seed to the idol Moloch shall die the death, and the people of the land shall stone him” (Lev. XX, 2). The seed is the word of God; the idol Moloch is the devil, who rules in the world not truly but only as if he did. Whoever, therefore, learns or teaches the word of God for some worldly advantage gives of his seed to the idol Moloch, and such a person shall die the death of the soul. For as the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul; when he departs, the soul dies. For there is no fellowship between God and an idol. The bed is narrow and the covering short: it cannot cover both. The majesty of God and the love of the world neither agree well nor dwell in one seat. For whoever is a friend of this world becomes an enemy of God.

What the Lord commands is hard and difficult to fulfil; [Col. 0636B] but reckon that this was spoken to you: “Issachar is a strong ass, lying down between the boundaries”—that is, the teaching of the two Testaments—“he saw that rest was good, and that the land was excellent, and he bent his shoulder to bear” (Gen. XLIX, 12). Therefore, since you are already on the way, seek and you shall find; and since you have already approached the gate, knock and it shall be opened to you. May he who opened the eyes of the man born blind, Jesus Christ our Lord and Teacher, open our understanding to comprehend the Scriptures: he who is God, blessed for ages. Amen.

## LXI. ON THE FEAST OF THE ASSUMPTION OF BLESSED MARY, AND ON HER PRAISES: THIRD SERMON

[Note: [Col. 0635D] From the Angers manuscript.—This sermon has a close affinity with the sixth sermon On the Incarnation, which begins with the same words: “Go forth.” It is, however, distinct from that sixth sermon and longer; this should be noted. That sermon is from a Saint-Germain manuscript; [Col. 0636D] this one, however, is from the Angers manuscript.]

“Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon [Col. 0636C] in the diadem with which his mother crowned him” (Song III, 11).

535 Whoever follows words alone will find nothing, Solomon himself testifying that the keeper of prudence will find good things; and “he who presses the udders hard to find milk will bring forth butter” (Prov. XXX, 33). The words by which our infancy is nourished are the two Testaments. We press them hard when we search in them for the spiritual understanding that springs up and enriches. We say this because we know that Jews, wise according to the flesh, refer the proposed words to Solomon; but we seek, on the authority of Scripture, one better than Solomon, prefigured in him.

The discourse, then, is directed to the daughters of Zion, that is, souls contemplating God, that they may go forth to see King Solomon. There is a twofold going forth: evil and good. Judas went out from truth and perished. Hence, “He went out immediately; and it was night” [Note: [Col. 0636D] John the Evangelist says this of Judas, chapter XIII, verse 30: “Therefore, when he had received the morsel, he went out immediately. And it was night.”], etc. Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, went out to see the women of the region, and she was defiled and violated by Hamor. For when the soul goes out to the desires [perhaps: “pleasures”] and lusts of the world, it lies exposed to be corrupted by the devil. Behold the evil going forth.

But the good going forth [is that] by which the children of Israel went out of Egypt, led by Moses—indeed, by God—where they were oppressed by grievous slavery. [Col. 0637A] Hence, at the third station they receive the cloud, that is, the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Abraham too went out of his land and from his kindred that he might receive an inheritance and offspring like the stars of heaven. Very many testimonies of Scripture occur concerning such a departure.

Jeremiah shows whence one must go out, saying: “Go out from the midst of Babylon” (Jer. L, 8). Babylon is the confusion of the world, having beginning, middle, and end. The first extremity is that with which we are born, namely original sin; the second is that without which we do not live, namely the middle term, venial sin; the final extremity is mortal sin, with which we live wickedly—or rather, lose life, that is, God. For to depart from him who is life is not to be. Without him, indeed, there is no true being. Hence: “I passed by, and behold, he was not” (Ps. XXXVI [37], [Col. 0637B] 16). Certainly it would have been better for that man not to be than to be thus. Let us therefore go out from the midst of Babylon. We have escaped original sin by baptism; in many small matters we all offend; let us at least avoid mortal sins.

Zechariah also says: “Ho, ho, flee from the land of the north” (Zech. II, 5), that is, from the kingdom of the devil, who rules over the cold—that is, the wicked. For the Lord’s song is not sung in a foreign land. And in the Song of Songs: “If you do not know yourself, go out and follow the tracks of your flocks” (Song I, 7), that is, of fools, “and feed your kids,” that is, illicit and unclean impulses. He does not command this; rather, he foretells what will happen to one who goes out. For one who does not know himself, in going out is drawn into conceiving 536 and fulfilling perverse desires. This is the confusion of which the Psalm says: “From Bashan”—that is, confusion—“I will bring back” (Ps. LXVII [68], 23), those who are in the deep sea, in the midst of Babylon.

To show this departure, the Lord suffered outside the gate. Let us also go out to him outside the camp. Isaac too went out to meditate in the heavenly field, namely through contemplation, at the decline of day—that is, when the heat of sin had waned. Having thus gone out, we shall be able to see King Solomon.

His vision is threefold. He was seen in the world; he will be seen in judgment; thirdly, in the kingdom. The first is a vision of grace; the second, of justice; the third [addition required: “of glory”], by all the good, from whom the wicked person shall be taken away. In the first, he is Jedidiah, that is, Beloved, made like [perhaps: “similar to”] us through the flesh; in the second, the Preacher, that is, one who will speak in the assembly of all; [Col. 0637D] in the third, Solomon, Prince of Peace and shepherd of true peace. He is seen here by us through faith; in judgment, through the flesh; in the kingdom, through hope [perhaps: “sight”]. Whoever sees through faith shall not fear in the assembly of judgment, but shall rejoice in the kingdom. “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 9). This third vision is eternal life.

Those see him as king who are willing to be ruled by him and do not presume to depart from his governance, saying: “The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing” (Ps. XXII [23], 1). He himself rules them with an iron rod—that is, with inflexible justice—that they may resist the impulses of the flesh and advance by the steps of virtues as by stations. Thus, having here reconciliation through Solomon and tranquility of mind, they shall hereafter possess complete [Col. 0638A] rest—a rest that cannot exist as long as the righteous person struggles with the flesh.
