But there he shall enjoy a pacified kingdom, which the daughters of Zion await: faithful souls contemplating the Lord’s glory.

We see through a mirror in an enigma, as daughters by the grace of adoption, that we may beget spiritual offspring for God, “whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. XXXI, 9), where Solomon reigns. Yet first [there is] Salem, after penitence has trampled down [sin], through justice; then Jerusalem, through the crown. It is a fine correspondence: the three visions accord with Solomon’s three names and the city’s three conditions. The connection is likewise good. The daughters of Zion go forth to see King Solomon. It has been said who are to see—namely, the daughters of Zion—by what means, if they go forth, and whom they are to see. Now [Col. 0638B] it remains to say in what, and what kind of one, he is to be seen. See, I say, in the diadem: believe in the incarnation and attend to its benefit.

In Holy Scripture Christ’s flesh is expressed by different likenesses: sometimes by the ark, containing manna, the rod, and the tablets, because in the flesh [was] a soul conscious of the Father’s secrets; sometimes by the tabernacle in which he serves in warfare: “He set his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. XVIII [19], 6). Again, by a cloud; hence the prophet says: “The Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud” (Isa. XIX, 1). Here, however, it is expressed by the diadem with which his mother Mary crowned him. And she is rightly said to have crowned him, because she “did not conceive from the tree of lust, nor, like other women, disfigure or dishonor him by original sin; but immaculate, untouched, and free from every [Col. 0638C] sin, she brought forth the Holy of Holies,” the flower of purity, the Redeemer of all.

For truth sprang up from untilled earth. Therefore the flower of the field and lily of the valleys—that is, of the humble—crowned and, as it were, encircled him, according to the saying: “A woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. XXXI, 22). From no other source, but from her own most pure flesh, she will supply the material, without the hands of those embracing. Behold Ezekiel’s gate in the house of the Lord: “shut, and no man shall enter through it” (Ezek. XLIV, 2). Here is the bread in Leviticus “enclosed” [perhaps: “baked”] in an oven (Lev. XXIV, 5): that is, the bread of life, formed in the virginal womb and baked by the fire and work of the Holy Spirit.

This flesh is also a diadem, because it is the cause of victory. For unless the Word had become incarnate, [Col. 0638D] the devil would not have attacked him. But when he desired in it the food of flesh which he saw, he was pierced by the sting of divinity which he had not foreseen. Hence the Lord says to Job: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook?” (Job XL, 20). Leviathan is called “their addition,” that is, [the addition] of human beings, to whom he once brought the fault of transgression and extends it daily, even to death, by most wicked suggestions; and he introduced the fault of suggestion in order to draw them to the consent of delight. But the Lord, made man, drew him out, because he made a hook from the devil’s own seed by assuming a body in which the devil would desire his food, the death of the flesh; but divinity was there, to pierce the face of the ravager.

It follows: “On the day of his betrothal.” A twofold betrothal is understood here, either that of Solomon’s mother or that of his son: namely, actively or passively. On the day of conception—that is, on the day on which she conceived—the mother was betrothed to God. Hence it is written in a certain sermon: “I was betrothed to a man in God, and I pleased the highest God.” For she was made fruitful by divine power, not made pregnant in the human manner. Hence: “Therefore also the holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke I, 35).

On that same day our Solomon, Jesus Christ, betrothed the Church, joining her to himself through nature and grace. For God was joined to human nature in the virginal womb, whence he came forth [as a bridegroom] from his chamber (Ps. XVIII [19]). His mother also crowned him, that is, honored him on the day of her heart’s joy, namely his birth, just as on the day of conception. For she who conceived without lust and [Col. 0639B] without a man’s act also brought forth what she had conceived without labor and pain: a virgin in conceiving, a virgin in giving birth. This joy is called not of the flesh but of the heart—that is, of discernment.

What, and how great, was the joy for the mother to bring into the light the light of all: the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world, for her salvation and that of all; her own and all people’s Creator, Begetter, and Savior! If the Magi rejoiced with exceedingly great joy when they found him, should not she rejoice far more, seeing in herself and through herself the prophecies fulfilled which she had long known to have been foretold? Hence she says: “My spirit has exulted in God my Savior” (Luke I, 47).

All of us ought to share in this betrothal, because faithful souls have Christ as their lawful bridegroom, according to the saying: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI, 2); and [we ought to be] partakers of joy, because “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II, 14).

We have heard of the diadem bestowed by the mother; there is another bestowed by the Father: “You crowned him with glory and honor” (Ps. VIII). As he is united in nature with his mother, so he is of one majesty with the Father and from the Father. Let us therefore go forth so that we may be able to see King Solomon in beauty, through his own gift, who lives and reigns, etc.

## LXII. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT GENOVEFA: ONLY SERMON

[Note: [Col. 0639D] From the Angers manuscript.—Hildebert seems to have delivered this sermon in the royal monastery of Saint Geneviève in Paris itself, before the regular canons of that very celebrated church. For scarcely any others could more properly be designated “heirs of the blessed virgin Geneviève,” as he calls his hearers, than men consecrated to God under the patronage of that sacred virgin—men perhaps then troubled, as he says, by temporal tribulation and the loss of friends. On what occasion or at what time Hildebert came to Paris is not openly clear. Nevertheless, nothing prevents us from supposing that, while he lived at Cluny for several years, he came at some point to Paris, where, in the royal monastery of Saint Martin of the Fields, a most noble ascetical house of the sacred Cluniac order, he himself now a monk and celebrated for preaching, may have been invited by the most devout canons to deliver this sermon. We do not consider it unreasonable to conjecture the same regarding the two following sermons on Saints James, Christopher, and Germanus the Elder, bishop of Paris. Let the kindly reader receive our conjectures fairly and favorably.]

[Col. 0639D] “When Elisha passed through the city of Shunem, a Shunammite woman detained him, that he might eat bread with her; and she prepared a table, a chair, a bed, and a chamber for him” (III Kings [II Kings] IV, 8).

[Col. 0640A] 539 From the surface of the words, or of the history, three things are commended in this woman: the virtue of hospitality, the work of virtue, and the reward of the work. The virtue of hospitality is commended when she compelled him to sit with her. The work of virtue, when she prepared for Elisha the things mentioned above—a table, and so forth. The reward of the work, when he raised her son. The virtue of hospitality is praiseworthy when anyone is received as a guest; but it is more praiseworthy and more gracious when the guest is compelled to be received.

The virtue of hospitality is commended in Lot, of whom we read that he compelled the angels, in the town, to accept hospitality (Gen. XIX). It is also commended in the disciples who, as they went to Emmaus, compelled the Lord to remain with them (Luke XXIV). Why, then, should hospitality not be commended in the great Shunammite woman? She is called great either because of the virtue of hospitality or by way of distinction. For there is a lesser Shunammite as well as a great Shunammite.

We read (III Kings [I Kings] I) that when David had grown old and could not be warmed, a Shunammite woman was sought for him, a young girl of twelve years, and she was found and brought into his bed to warm him. He received her, yet did not know her. Thus, literally speaking, we find two Shunammite women: this lesser one who warmed David, and that great one who received Elisha. A third is read of by Solomon in the Song, where it says: “Return, return, Shunammite [Vulgate: Shulammite], return, return, that we may look upon you” (Song VI, 12). But this one is only figurative and is not a Shunammite. Thus we read of three Shunammite women: [Col. 0640C] the first lesser, the second great, the third figurative.

This third signifies the Gentile world, which our peace-making Solomon calls to faith. It is therefore lawful and possible for us to take the other two Shunammite women figuratively. For all things happened to the Jews as figures. The first Shunammite, then, is the glorious Virgin; the second, the virgin Geneviève; the third, converted Gentiledom, which is also called a virgin according to the Apostle: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI, 2). From these three, therefore, we shall compose our sermon.

For by the hidden dispensation of the Holy Spirit, the passing of the virgin Geneviève [perhaps: “followed”] the childbirth of the blessed Virgin Mother of God; [Note: [Col. 0640D] It is celebrated on the third day of January, that is, the tenth day after Christ’s sacred Nativity and three days before Epiphany.] and the calling of the Gentiles at Epiphany necessarily follows. We observe these solemnities in this order.

But why is the departure of the virgin Geneviève inserted while the child is still crying in the cradle? [Col. 0641A] Why, while the tender flesh of the Savior is still pierced by the harsh knife of circumcision, do we nevertheless celebrate in honor of the virgin Geneviève? The blood still flows from the wounds, and on the third day we celebrate the virgin’s feast. Those who treat of the natures of things report that a medicine should be applied on the third day to lessen the pain of wounds. But does our Lord, who is the supreme physician, need the medicine of mortals? He had pains; he did not have causes of pain [supplied]. Certainly I read that Christ suffered pain, but never that he laughed. For he was a man of sorrows, not one given to laughter. Do you wish to hear how full of sorrows he was? The cause of his sorrow is our sins. Therefore, one who removes the cause of his sorrow ministers medicine to him.

[Col. 0641B] Blessed Geneviève diminished this cause. But what is this that you say? I do not read of her sins; I read of her fasting, her tears, her prayers. Therefore, since sins are the cause of sorrow, and this virgin did not have them, and diminished that cause in herself and in others, she applied remedies to those wounds.

The first Shunammite, then, is a singular virgin; the second, a general virgin; the third, a spiritual virgin. The first was mother and daughter of God; the second, prostitute and bride; the third, poor woman and handmaid. The first warmed David; the second returned to God; the third received Elisha. David did not know the first as she warmed him; the second returned to Solomon who called her; the third received Elisha as a guest in her home. The first was sought; the second was found; the third was brought into David the king’s bed to warm him.

[Col. 0641C] This was the Virgin Mary, who was a lesser Shunammite—that is, humble. For we read that she possessed humility above all others. Hence she commended herself by humility, not by another virtue, saying: “For he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke I, 48). But who sought her? Certainly, as many sought her as desired her. Hear Isaiah say: “Rise, poor little woman of Anathoth” (Isa. X, 30). And elsewhere: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. XI, 2). Jeremiah says: “The Lord shall make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. XXXI, 22). And David: “My substance is with you” (Ps. XXXVIII [39], 8).

By whom was she found? By the angel Gabriel in Nazareth, by whom she was found, as beyond the ordinary course of women, so also greeted beyond the ordinary course: “Hail,” he says, “full of grace” (Luke I, 28). And “she was found by Joseph to have conceived in her womb of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. I, 18). She was brought to David, [Col. 0641D] who could not be warmed because of old age, though he was covered with the skins of dead animals.

David means “strong of hand.” This is the Son of God. But it can never be said that he grew old, since he is eternal and unchangeable, the disposer of times, and is never altered through time. 541 He is said to have grown old because, just as there are six ages of human beings, so there are six ages of time, and in the sixth our salvation visited us [perhaps: “visited us for salvation”], recalling to himself a people growing old in wickedness. Or he is said to have grown old because for five ages he had grown old in human hearts and had fallen from their remembrance: people who worshipped idols never remembered the one God.

But what does it mean that he was said to be covered with skins yet could not be warmed? The skins are the legal sacraments. Just as flesh is covered by skin, so the truth of the incarnation was covered by them. And the sacraments of the Law are rightly called skins, because skins come from dead animals. Similarly, those sacraments belonged to what was mortal—that is, to the Law—which conferred death rather than life, because the Law threatened death. While the sacraments of the Law covered the truth of the flesh, Christ our David could not be warmed—that is, he could not set us aflame with love for himself. For his being warmed is nothing other than our, who are his members, being stirred to love him.

Therefore the virgin Shunammite was sought and found, who lay in the same bed with him, because the Son of God—“my king is in the Holy One”—was united in the unity of person from the nature of his mother [perhaps: “from the nature of his mother and divinity”], and not of divinity; she warmed him. But with what fire? With the fire of charity, of which he himself says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it should burn?” (Luke XII, 49). And elsewhere: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. IV, 24). With this fire the Virgin warmed him.

Before the incarnation he had forgotten humankind, because he was not then exercising works of mercy. But after he slept in the same bed with the Virgin, he exercised works of mercy. Great indeed was the Lord’s mercy then: the Creator of human beings descended for the salvation of human beings from the Father’s bosom into the dung-heap, from the heavenly throne into the Virgin’s womb, into the valley of tears, where he became a lowly and despised man, and so poor [that he had nowhere] to lay his head.

Who can speak adequately of his humility? How great was the humility by which the head feared by kings humbled itself to wash the disciples’ feet! It is wonderful and astonishing that he humbled himself even unto death, becoming obedient to the Father in all things. Thus he was warmed in the blessed Virgin: that is, he set us, grown old in sin, aflame with divine love. But because he had come for this purpose, he did not yet rest, lest he be charged with what is commonly charged against a man, [Col. 0642D] that he did not complete the work he began. So that he might be warmed still more, he did certain other things by which he might stir us more strongly to the fervor of charity: he preached, suffered death, and did many things of this sort. 542 And he called the Church the mystical Shunammite.

For our David, Christ strong of hand, whom the Virgin Mary warmed, is himself the true peace-making Solomon, who calls the figurative Shunammite—that is, the Church—saying: “Return, return, Shunammite, return, return, that we may look upon you” (Song VI, 12). Note that Solomon calls the Shunammite four times, saying: “Return, return, Shunammite, return, return”; and not without reason. For the Gentile world had departed from God in the four ways by which every believer ought to cleave to God, and by which Scripture commands that whoever loves God should love God more than himself, and should love himself, his own flesh, and his neighbor as himself.

The Gentile world had withdrawn from God in these four ways: for the Gentiles venerated creatures more than the Creator; they served the creature and not the Creator. They hated themselves, because “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul.” They did not love their neighbour, because they transgressed the commandment: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. 4:16). They held their own flesh in hatred, because they killed themselves. Therefore Solomon, that is, Christ, called four times when he said: “Return to the love of your neighbour; return to the love of your own flesh.” But the third Shunammite, that is, “great,” received Elisha. [Col. 0643B] She is the blessed Mother of God, or someone like her, who received Elisha, that is, Christ, because Elisha and Solomon are one and the same. And David is like Christ, who was crucified on Calvary, or who was prefigured in bald Elisha.

But how did that Shunammite receive Elisha? In the upper chamber she prepared a table, a chair, and a bed, and, moreover, a lampstand (4 Kings 4). By the table, chair, and bed are understood the three orders of men in the Church: namely, prelates, active persons, and contemplatives. These are the men whom the priest Ezekiel saw: Noah, Daniel, and Job. By the table, therefore, prelates are understood, who refresh and feed others with the nourishment of Holy Scripture, who open God’s treasuries. By the chair, active persons are understood: they sit in part, rest in part, and [Col. 0643C] work in part. Such are married people, who partly labour for the world—that is, they care for children, wife, and so forth—and rest in these things, while aspiring but little to heavenly matters. Hence the Apostle says: “He who has a wife and children is divided” (1 Cor. 7:33). By the bed, however, contemplatives are understood, who already enjoy the Sabbath of the mind and direct their whole attention toward heavenly things.

Blessed Geneviève, therefore, and anyone like her, thus prepared for Elisha a table, chair, and bed; for she refreshed others with the bread of divine teaching. She prepared him a chair because she supported the poor by the labour of [Col. 0644A] her own hands and did not neglect the care of divine things. She prepared him a bed because, although she sometimes occupied herself with temporal matters in order to feed the poor, her soul nevertheless did not depart from contemplation of God, but always enjoyed the Sabbath of the mind. Moreover, she prepared him a lampstand: that is, the power and authority of miracles, by which she became known and shone in the world. Hence it is said: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:14).

These things, then, blessed Geneviève—or one like her—did for Elisha. But what did Elisha, that is, Jesus Christ, do for her? He raised her son, that is, her spirit, when, after the separation of its mortal members, he received it into eternal life. It is well said, “after the separation of mortal [Col. 0644B] members,” because before death our members can be called mortal, but after death only dead.

Note, however, that Elisha had sent the Shunammite a staff to raise her son; for the blessed Mother of God, or one like her, was “staffed” and purified by the Lord—that is, tested through tribulation—before her spirit was raised. But you are heirs of the blessed virgin Geneviève, because she left you as imitators of herself. Take care, therefore, lest you fall away from imitating her. Let each imitate her as far as he can. Whoever can but is unwilling, let him concern himself with temporal matters so as to support the poor from them. Whoever can and will, let him devote himself to psalmody and prayers. Do not be disturbed by temporal tribulation or by the loss of friends. Rather, imitate the virgin [Col. 0644C] who offered herself as an example of right living. May Christ our Lord help us toward this: he who governs us, refreshes us, and rests in us; who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## LXIII. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT JAMES THE APOSTLE, SAINT CHRISTOPHER THE MARTYR, AND SAINT GERMANUS “THE ELDER,” BISHOP OF PARIS: FIRST SERMON

> **[Note: Col. 0643C]** From the Angers manuscript.—Certain matters in this sermon, as also in the following one, seemed worthy of notice. First, it appears not improbable that these sermons were delivered by Hildebert in the very monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, before the monks there serving God under the Rule of Saint Benedict, perhaps on the same occasion on which he had treated the preceding sermon on Saint Geneviève in her monastery—namely, whenever he repeatedly came from Cluny to Paris.  
>
> Secondly, it should be observed that Hildebert, as truly a monk, addressed monks. This is clear because, addressing them and praising Saint Benedict by name, he says in the first person: “Not without reason our superiors are called abbots by blessed Benedict . . . They are indeed our fathers, for they provide for us not only through the administration of temporal things, but daily beget us through the teaching of spiritual things,” etc. These words, and many which follow, and similar expressions, seem fitting to no one other than a monk, and indeed a Benedictine. This is further demonstrated by his very exact description of monastic exercises, offices, and cloistered places, and also by his moral application of them. Yet here a manifest error of the copyist appears: he wrote *cancellare* in place of *cellerarie* (“cellarer”). This is clearer than daylight from what precedes and follows. For what purpose would a monastery have not a *cancellarius* but a *cancellarus*? As our most keen investigator of antiquity, Montfaucon, very learnedly observed and proved from a very ancient plan in chapter 8, p. 114, of his *Italian Diary*, this was the person charged with enclosing by railings the place set aside for games (such as formerly were the games of the Campus Boarius). Yet, since the word *cancellare*, “to cancel” or “to erase,” is beautifully written in the manuscript, we have scrupled to alter it; nevertheless, any sensible reader will not hesitate to substitute the name *cellerarius*, “cellarer.”  
>
> Nor do we think the special designation here applied to Saint Germanus, “the elder,” wholly negligible; nowhere else have we read of his being adorned with this epithet. Yet perhaps some trace of it may be suspected in the parish church at Paris where some believe Saint Germanus first lived, and which the populace calls in French *Saint-Germain-le-Vieil* (“Saint-Germain the Old”). Finally, it should be noted that already in Hildebert’s time, that is, at the end of the eleventh century, Saint Germanus’s feast was celebrated so that, as he says, people “kept Sabbath” from servile work. Although this was perhaps observed as obligatory in honour of Saint James, whose feast fell on the same day, it was probably adorned with more solemn worship because of reverence for Saint Germanus, patron of the city itself as well as of its suburb, in memory of the miraculous translation of his body, which Hildebert expressly mentions near the end of the following sermon.].

> “The calf, the lion, and the lamb shall remain together, and a little child shall lead them” (Isa. 2:6).

[Col. 0645A] “As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God: the Most High himself founded and established it.” Noah gathered clean and unclean, untamed and countless animals into the ark, to preserve them in the cataclysm of waters (Gen. 7). Isaiah prophesied that calf, lion, and lamb would dwell together under the leadership of a child. Peter too saw creeping things on a sheet, things not fit for human food, and heard: “Rise, Peter, kill and eat” (Acts 10:13). What Noah therefore prefigured in deed, Isaiah prophesied in speech, and Peter apprehended in vision, we see fulfilled in the fullness of time. The Church of God has been gathered from the ends of the earth, from every tribe, tongue, and nation under heaven. Calf, lion, and lamb remain together, and a little child leads [Col. 0645B] them.

Yet these three may have a mystical meaning [the text reads *sirtica*, perhaps for *mystica*]. They may be explained with reference to the general gathering of the faithful into the Church, the personal gathering of three saints into one feast, and the spiritual dwelling together of cloistered men [perhaps “their dwelling together as one”]. Thus a fitting term is assigned to each: first, “they shall remain”; second, “they shall rest”; third, “they shall dwell.”

Concerning the general gathering: calf, lion, and lamb—that is, Jew, Gentile, and Christ Jesus, mediator of both—shall remain together. That is, the wall coming from circumcision and the other coming from uncircumcision are united in the cornerstone, who makes both one. Certainly the Jew is compared to a calf by reason of resemblance, both because of the exercise of labour and because of the wantonness [Col. 0645C] of youth. For the calf is a rustic animal accustomed to the yoke; and of the Jew it is said: “Ephraim is a trained heifer, loving to thresh; I passed over the beauty of her neck; Judah shall plough, and Jacob shall break his furrows” (Hos. 10:11). From his youth—that is, from Israel’s departure out of Egypt—he bore the yoke of the Law. Yet he too, sometimes running wild like a young calf, putting forth horns and hoofs, went after strange gods, as it is written: “They turned back, so as to be without a yoke; they became like a deceitful bow” (Hos. 7:16). And elsewhere: “The beloved grew fat, became sleek, grew broad, and kicked” (Deut. 32:15).

The Gentile is compared to a lion: *leōn* (λέων) in Greek denotes a king.

> **[Note: Col. 0646D]** Two scribal errors have crept in here. The first is that λήων was written in place of βασιλεύς, where the author maintains that λέων means “king” in Greek. The second occurs below: seven lion cubs and seven steps are placed on Solomon’s throne, whereas the explicit scriptural text mentions only six.

Among the Gentiles, however, and not among the Jews, monarchy always existed. They were also bloodthirsty, thirsting for human blood. Hence: “Will a lion roar in the forest if he has not found prey?” (Amos 3:4). And it is written of the king of Babylon: “The lion caught enough for his cubs and killed for his lionesses; he filled his dens with prey and his lair with plunder” (Nah. 2:12). But so far as this passage is concerned, the explicit likeness between lion and Gentile may be stated thus: the lion is the strongest of animals and fears no encounter with anyone, yet it fears fire and a cock, especially a white one. The Gentile did not know that sins would be punished eternally, nor that God would come as judge and avenger of wickedness. He heard the cock—that is, the evangelist, who rouses those lying down and rebukes the sleepy—saying: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3:10), and he was terrified. Hence: “The mountains were shaken by him; the earth and the world trembled before his face” (Nah. 1:5). And elsewhere: “All the foundations of the earth were troubled and moved” (Ps. 81:5). And: “Terrible is he who takes away the spirit of princes, terrible among the kings of the earth” [Col. 0646B] (Ps. 75:13). The cock whom he feared was white—that is, bringing good news. Thus the ancients counted their days by white pebbles in prosperity and black ones in adversity; and at its admonition “the lion, like an ox, eats straw” (Isa. 11:7). This is the lion that killed the prophet sent to Jeroboam at Bethel (3 Kings 13).

Christ is compared to the lamb, but only by reason of his Passion. Hence: “The Lamb slain from the foundation of the world” (Rev. 13:8); and elsewhere: “Like a lamb before its shearer, he was silent and did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7). And when John said, “Behold the Lamb of God,” he added, “who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). For through his Passion he removed and blotted them out from us. Therefore, in his Passion he was a lamb, [Col. 0646C] especially according to the Latin derivation. For *agnus* (“lamb”) is said to derive from *agnoscere* (“to recognize”). Those who treat of natural history report that, however great the multitude of sheep, a lamb recognizes its mother by her bleating alone. Consider, therefore, that at Christ’s crucifixion no small crowd stood around the Crucified One. Some mocked him, shaking their heads and saying: “Ah, you who destroy the temple of God!” (Matt. 27:40). Others wept over the innocent man condemned. Others beat their breasts, marvelling at the signs they saw. Yet in so great a crowd he recognized his mother, whom he, a virgin, entrusted to a virgin.

These, I say, remain together. “For we do not have here an abiding city, but seek one to come”; and we are pilgrims, like all our fathers. To an eager mind every delay seems a lingering. Therefore we linger on the road, we who long for our homeland. To delay is to remain somewhere beyond what is due. Therefore delay carries danger with it, or it is to remain beyond the will of the one who waits. Hence: “Lord, do not delay”; and elsewhere: “Though he delay, wait for him” (Hab. 2:3); and: “While the bridegroom delayed” (Matt. [Col. 0647A] 25:3). He seemed to himself to linger who said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23); and: “Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24).

There follows the personal gathering of saints into a single feast. Certainly, on this day the feast of three saints is observed: James the apostle, Christopher the martyr, and Germanus the Elder, confessor. Although we have assembled especially in honour of blessed Germanus, I think he would not wish his own memory to be celebrated while the others are passed over in silence. Today, therefore, lion, lamb, and calf rest together: that is, apostle, martyr, and confessor.

By the lion we understand the apostle. For just as the apostles are called mountains from Christ the mountain, foundations from Christ the foundation, so also they are lions from the Lion of the tribe of Judah, according to the text: “The remnant of Jacob shall be in the midst of peoples like a lion among the beasts of the forest and like a lion’s cub among flocks of sheep” [Col. 0647B] (Mic. 5:8); and: “The lion, strongest of beasts, fears no encounter with anyone” (Prov. 30:30). They themselves endured the first assaults of the world. These are the seven lion cubs on Solomon’s throne: “Solomon also made a great throne of ivory. No work like it existed in all kingdoms” (3 Kings 20:18); it was ascended by seven steps, and on their summits, on either side, seven lion cubs stood guard, skilfully fashioned as protectors of the steps. In this manner we must pass through the midst of the apostles if we wish to ascend from strength to strength, to see the God of gods in Zion: that is, through their teaching, imitation, and intercession. [Col. 0647C] Indeed it is written: “Waters shall pass through the midst of the mountains” (Ps. 103:10).

Yet the apostles are compared to lions on another ground of resemblance. When a lion grows weak, it devours a monkey and regains strength. Great was the weakness of the apostles when they went to the Gentiles, among whom they found the monstrous gods of every sort being worshipped. For the sins of neighbours are a griddle [*frixorium*, perhaps “a cause of burning pain”] to the righteous. Hence: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11:29). Idols—or rather idolaters themselves—are compared to monkeys. For although a monkey is not a human being, it nevertheless mimics the likeness of many human beings. Likewise idols possess only the outlines of living beings, not perception. Hence: “They have mouths and do not speak; they have eyes and do not see. Those who worship them become like them” [Col. 0647D] (Ps. 113:5). For that which does not sound forth the praises of God is mute. Thus the idols of living creatures are as monkeys, and idolaters are as monkeys; the apostles incorporated such monkeys of idols into themselves and regained strength.

The martyr is denoted by the calf. For the calf was the principal sacrifice under the Law, offered by the priest and the ruler of the Synagogue for the avowal of his sin. Certainly every faithful person offers himself as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God. More glorious, however, is the sacrifice consummated through the cup of Passion. Of these it is written: “They shall lay calves upon your altar” (Ps. 50:21). There is another basis for the calf’s likeness to the martyr. A calf is useful not only in ploughing while alive, but also after death, [Col. 0648A] because its flesh is edible and its hide is useful for many things; these three may suffice. From it are made shoes, and skins by which liquids are carried through dry and waterless places to refresh the souls of the thirsty. Certain water-vessels are also made among the Ethiopians. When these have been filled with water, they descend into the caverns of dragons hidden in the very bowels of the earth; striking hydraulic instruments [the text has *hydraulia*, perhaps *hydraulica*] with coral rods, they produce a terrible sound. Aroused by it, the dragons ascend and carry them through the air into Egypt, so that they may eat their flesh. For it is shameful to them for royal weddings to be celebrated without dragon flesh.

Certainly the usefulness of martyrs while they lived is sufficiently set out in the reading of their acts. But when they suffered, they gave their flesh, as it were, to those present [Col. 0648B] to eat, since they offered them an example of suffering for Christ. To posterity, moreover, they left, as it were, a beneficial feast: the memory of themselves and their interceding relics. Shod by their examples, we tread unharmed upon serpents and scorpions; from them we offer the thirsty the example of a life-giving life; by their merits and prayers, we summon demons out of possessed bodies, as dragons from their hiding places.

By the lamb the confessor is understood, according to the Greek derivation: ἅγνος (*hagnos*) in Greek means “pious” [or “chaste”]. Confessors are men of God who stand before the Lord of the whole earth. First taking pity on themselves, they also showed mercy to us in word and example. Pleasing God, in the time [Col. 0648C] of wrath they became reconciliation. There is also another reason why the confessor is compared with a lamb. Under the Law a continual sacrifice was made from a lamb (Num. 28), and it could not be made from another animal, although other offerings could vary according to what the hand of the offerer could find. That sacrifice prefigured the Church’s confession. Now there is confession of sin, according to which a person is called one “confessing”; and there is confession of praise, according to which one is called a “confessor.” This latter the confessors continually offered on the way and in their homeland, confessing God as it were morning and evening.

These three rest together today: that is, they have left us the memorial of their rest. “For when today we keep Sabbath from servile work,” we represent their unending rest. Beautifully, moreover, it is said: “They shall rest.” For the saints rest, rest again, and rest together. First they rest in the sixth age, while living in the flesh; second, they rest again, as if resting a second time, in the seventh age of those asleep; third, they rest together in the eighth age of those rising again. For the saints, rejoicing in hope amid tribulations, possess the Sabbath of the heart amid afflictions and rest in these very works, rejoicing that they have been accounted worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus. But when they fly from the prisons of their bodies, they rest from their works, according to the saying: “From henceforth the Spirit says that they may rest from their labours” (Rev. 14:13). But when this mortal shall put on immortality, they rest together in both sabbath-rests, clothed in the double garment of glorification.

[Col. 0649A] There follows the third gathering, that of cloistered persons into one common dwelling. In monasteries lion, calf, and lamb dwell together; hence: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one” (Ps. 132:1). Namely: the shepherd, called in Hebrew *abbot* and in Latin *father*; the steward, who may be called the apothecary, who collects and stores only the brothers’ particular goods, in order to distribute necessities to them at the fitting time; and the one who, watchful in matters pertaining to God, devotes himself to meditation, reading, and prayer.

By the lion the shepherd is understood, according to the saying: “Noble is the anger of the lion.” For it is, as it were, proper to an abbot

> To spare the submissive and to subdue the proud.  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid*

[Col. 0649B] The steward is compared to the calf, by whose labour provisions are procured for the community. There is another reason, if we are unwilling to conceal it, why the steward is compared to the calf. For when the calf gathers grain and straw by its labour, it is content with straw alone, leaving the grain to its master. In this manner the good steward, assigning himself only modest and cheap things, supplies the community with whatever is better, according to Gregory’s saying: “The best steward is one who reserves nothing for himself.” But if—may it never be!—he wishes to heap up for himself a private store from goods entrusted to him, he cannot do this without great sin; and from a calf he has become a hedgehog. For when the hedgehog finds apples fallen upon the ground, it rolls itself over them and, laden by the benefit of its spines, returns to its den. A person’s thorns are [Col. 0649C] sins, according to the saying: “Your land shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3:18). Therefore a steward cannot hide the brothers’ goods away in his den without thorns of this sort, so that it may truly be said of him: “Beware of false ministers, who come to you in calves’ clothing [perhaps *sheep’s* clothing], but inwardly are ravenous hedgehogs.”

The community is not inappropriately signified by the sheep, which, having despised the world and put off wool as it were, is a naked flock of shorn sheep following naked Christ.

Moreover, there are four kinds of sheep: weak, pregnant, strong, and wandering. Observe the corresponding kinds in a community: beginners, those making progress, those who have attained, and those who stray. The first need instruction; the second encouragement; [Col. 0649D] the third congratulation; the fourth recall—so that beginners may progress, those progressing may attain, those attaining may persevere, and those straying may return. Hence in the cloisters of communities four places are assigned, as it were, to their proper offices. On the western side of the cloister is the submission of the pupil; in the part adjoining the church, moral reading; in the church itself, spiritual meditation; and toward the east, in the chapter-house, material correction. By submission humility is acquired; by reading truth is maintained; by meditation God’s sweetness is tasted; by correction integrity is restored. From this it is sufficiently clear how these four places correspond to the four distinctions among the brothers.

[Col. 0650A] Thus the faithful dwell together, at present in churches and cloistered persons in monasteries; and a little child leads them: namely, he of whom it is written, “A child is born to us” (Isa. 9:6), who may be called a child from purity or from the office of obedience. Hence the Father says of him: “Behold my chosen servant [*puer*]” (Matt. 12). He is called little because of humility, for Christ was humbler than anyone humble. But now he will be a little child; he will come as the greatest Judge, like a mighty man made drunk with wine, sparing no one. He will come to separate those now dwelling together, because “then two shall be in the field: one shall be taken and the other left,” etc. (Luke 17:34). Then he will come full of days, whose hair is like white wool, “and whose feet are like bronze” (Rev. 2:18); he will hold the winnowing fan in his hand and [Col. 0650B] separate grain from straw, large fish from small, sheep from goats. In that winnowing, may Jesus Christ, our Lord and our Judge, place us with the sheep at his right hand, when he comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## LXIV. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT JAMES THE APOSTLE, SAINT CHRISTOPHER THE MARTYR, AND SAINT GERMANUS “THE ELDER,” BISHOP OF PARIS: SECOND SERMON

> **[Note: Col. 0649D]** From the Angers manuscript.

> “My son, you have sat at the table of a rich man: consider what is set before you, and know that you ought to prepare like things.”
>
> **[Note: Col. 0649D]** The Vulgate: “When you sit to eat with a ruler, carefully consider what is placed before you” (Prov. 23:1).

The surface of these words plainly shows that a father speaks to his son. There are two fathers: carnal and spiritual. For just as sons are “contracted” [perhaps *procreati*, “begotten”] by a carnal father through carnal [Col. 0650C] generation, so through the Holy Spirit they are renewed as sons by the regeneration of baptism. Which father, then, speaks here—the carnal or the spiritual? Certainly the carnal father does not address his son in this manner; rather, he would say: “My son, if you sit at the table of a rich man, see that you put cushions beneath his elbow; flatter him; laugh when he laughs; praise him when he does evil, so that he may reward you.” Therefore such a father does not speak here, but the spiritual father does, as may be inferred from what follows.

This father—Christ, I mean—has two sons, one younger and the other older. The younger is active; the older contemplative. The younger wanders, running here and there; he is divided into parts; he [Col. 0650D] thinks partly of God’s concerns and partly of worldly concerns. Now he provides for children, now for a brother, now for a wife. See, this one is divided and wandering. But the other is steadfast: he is devoted only to divine contemplation; he plants his foot firmly; he does not move. The first is troubled and anxious; the older is fed and rests. The younger is Martha, troubled and occupied with many things. The older is Mary, who, sitting at the Lord’s feet, is fed by divine reading and rests in supreme contemplation.

To the younger it is said: “Because you shall eat the labours of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. 127:2). But the older dares to say: “Who will give me wings like a dove? And I shall fly [Col. 0651A] and rest” (Ps. 54:7). Again, the first says: “You have held my right hand, guided me according to your will, and received me with glory” (Ps. 72:24). But the older says: “You have made my feet like those of deer, and you will set me upon the heights” (Hab. 3:19; Ps. 17:34). Although both are sons of the father, it is the contemplative son who speaks here.

I therefore speak to you, brothers; for you are not divided into separate concerns, but are content with contemplation alone. He says, therefore: “My son, you have sat at the table of a rich man,” and so forth. Truly you sit at a rich man’s table, because you are in obedience.

> **[Note: Col. 0651D]** Here Hildebert speaks only as a true monk, as also in what follows, but especially near the end.

Brothers, not without reason are our superiors called abbots by blessed Benedict—a term interpreted as “fathers”; hence we cry: “Abba, Father” (Mark 14:36). They are indeed our fathers: [Col. 0651B] they provide for us not only in the administration of temporal matters, but daily beget us through the teaching of spiritual matters and moral instruction. Therefore, upon hearing the name “abbot,” you should immediately remember the name “son,” that you may be his sons—that is, truly obedient. Rightly then, because you are sons, your father speaks to you. But what is signified here by the table, holy doctors explain to us; we cannot alter their interpretation.

This table, then, is the Eucharist set before us on the altar-table: that is, the Lord’s body and blood, poured out for us on the cross. You ought therefore to sit at this table—that is, you ought to be prepared worthily to receive what is set before you on the altar-table—and you ought to prepare like things for him, so that, just as [Col. 0651C] he poured out his blood for you, so you too may be ready to pour out yours for his name. Even if there is no occasion to pour it out for God, yet be ready in heart and mind to undergo this.

> **[Note: Col. 0651D]** An altogether difficult passage, which might be restored as follows: “But even if there is no occasion for pouring it out, nevertheless be ready in heart and mind to pour it out for God.” “How hard,” etc.

How hard this saying is! Truly hard. For which of you is so perfect that, if an executioner came with sword drawn above his neck and said—not, I say, “Deny God,” which would be unheard of, but “Commit a grave sin,” which certainly amounts to the same thing; or “Go in to this woman”; or “Utter a lie”—which of you, I ask, would answer him and say: “Strike, executioner. ‘I will never make a member of Christ a member of a prostitute, because he who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her’ [Col. 0651D] (1 Cor. 6:15); I will never defile my mouth by uttering a lie”? Who, I ask, would say this? No one. Therefore no one prepares like things for him. Therefore no one seems to sit at the table of the rich man, since no one seems prepared to undergo martyrdom for Christ’s name.

What, then, shall we say to this? Do not be afraid, brothers. For your Father first made a remedy for you. Although blood and water are said to have come from his side for many reasons, this was nevertheless one reason: that those who could not suffer and shed blood for his name might at least have water—the water signified by the water which came forth with blood from his [Col. 0652A] side—which might be equivalent to martyrdom. There are three kinds of water: water of tears, water of sweat, and water of a fountain. The first is of contrition; the second of mortification or labour; the third of refreshment. Of the first it is said: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall water my couch” (Ps. 6:7). And elsewhere: “My tears became my bread day and night” (Ps. 41:4). Of the second it is said: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3:19). Of the third it is said: “You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Saviour” (Isa. 12:3).

You can possess the water of tears; if it comes from contrition, it avails as the martyrdom which you cannot undergo. This may also be inferred from the words the Lord speaks in the Gospel. When the mother of the sons [Col. 0652B] of Zebedee asked the Lord that one of her sons might sit at his right hand and the other at his left, the Lord said to them: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” They answered: “We can.” And he said: “You shall indeed drink my cup” (Matt. 20:21). This was true of James, who was killed by Herod; but John ended his life in peace. What then does the Lord’s saying to them, “You shall indeed drink my cup,” mean, except that John’s water of tears and will were equivalent to—or counted as—martyrdom?

For this reason too, since the Lord does not permit even one iota to occur in the Church without reason, when the feast of James and Christopher is celebrated, the feast of the confessor, blessed Germanus, is not undeservedly celebrated as well. It is as though James were saying to him: “Do not fear, Germanus. Although your blood was not poured out in martyrdom, you nevertheless had some disposition of will by which you are equivalent to martyrdom. This is clear because he wished your feast to be celebrated with ours.” Therefore, brothers, even though you cannot undergo martyrdom, you can at least possess the water of tears, so that you may sit at the rich man’s table and prepare like things for him through water of contrition: that is, just as he poured out water [from his side] for you, so you too may have water of tears for him.

But nevertheless, brothers, although this passage is so interpreted, without prejudice to that exposition and without detracting from the authorities of the saints, we venture to explain it otherwise. Yet it will not cease [Col. 0652D] to be a father’s speech to his son; rather, we shall explain what follows differently.

So far as we can discern from the sacred passages of Holy Scripture, “table” is understood in five ways. The first table is that of the poor; the second, of the world; the third, of the devil; the fourth, of the rich man; the fifth, of the father. Again: the first is of necessity; the second of vanity; the third of iniquity; the fourth of truth; the fifth of consummation. Observe their differences. Nature provides the first; avarice, the second; faithlessness, the third; grace, the fourth; life, the fifth. Again: the first refreshes, the second inflames, the third suffocates, [Col. 0653A] the fourth satisfies, the fifth consummates. Again: beasts sit at the first; serpents at the second; dogs at the third; birds at the fourth; heirs at the fifth.

Of the first you have in the Gospel: “Do not the little dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table?” (Mark 7:28). Of the second, in Isaiah:

> **[Note: Col. 0653D]** This is not found in Isaiah, but in Jeremiah, chapter 51:7: “Babylon was a golden cup in the Lord’s hand, making the whole earth drunk.”

“The table of Babylon—there is a cup upon it.” Of the third you have in the Apostle: “You cannot partake of the table of demons” (1 Cor. 10:21). Of the fourth you have here: “My son, you have sat at the table of a rich man.” Of the fifth, in the Gospel: “When you sit at the table of the Father” (Luke 22:39).

The poor whose table is the first are the human race, because it is poor and needy, because it does not suffice for itself and requires another’s help. Upon that table three dishes are set: bread, salt, and water—or bread, a relish, and drink. For by the name “salt” we understand a relish, and by the name “water,” drink. That a relish is understood by “salt” may be seen in Ezra, where it is read that, when the leaders of the Israelites were rebuilding the walls of the city of Jerusalem, the neighbouring peoples reported to Artaxerxes, king of the Persians and Medes, that the children of Israel were rebuilding the walls; and they add: “Do you suppose that we are forgetful of the salt which we eat in your court?” [Note: Thus in the Septuagint, 1 Esdras 4:14. But the Vulgate reads: “Now we are mindful of the salt which we eat in your palace.”] Behold: a relish is denoted by the name “salt.” That drink is denoted by water may be seen where Abraham placed upon Hagar a vessel of water (Gen. 21). And Moses says: “When we passed through the wilderness, we bought water with gold and silver” (Deut. 2:6).

These three things, then, are for refreshment, because they are natural; and these three fittingly belong to the first table. For “table” (*mensa*) is so called from “measure” (*mensura*). Daedalus was the inventor of the table and chair. He made a three-legged table proportioned to the measure of one person. For he saw among men some weak and some sound; and those who were weak could not dine with the others, and for this reason he made a three-legged table proportioned to one person, so that one unable to dine in the manner of others might thus be refreshed. But what was made only for necessity has first been extended into excess, and is supported by more than three legs. Certainly, now the three aforesaid dishes do not suffice for some. Now the baker is asked to employ all his skill and attention in making unheard-of bread; the fish of the sea and the birds of heaven do not suffice together with the beasts of the earth. Wine mixed with diverse kinds changes its original colour. Where such things are set forth, it is rather an immeasurable table than a table; a table of excess rather than necessity; of gluttony rather than nature.

At the first table, as was said, sit beasts—that is, men like beasts in sensuality, insatiable according to the flesh as beasts are, not according to the spirit, whose food is [perhaps: “not so those who walk according to the spirit, whose food, etc.”] [Col. 0654A] divine contemplation. But you make this table more slender: for you take less than is placed there, so that it may be distributed to the poor.

At the second table, which is that of vanity and of the world, five things are served, which always urge vain things; serpents sit at it. Boethius enumerates them in his book *On the Consolation*. They are human favour, riches, honours, glory, and power. But these irritate rather than satisfy; indeed, they provoke hunger. This will be evident from a comparison. Let there be five men. Let one be placed upon a pinnacle, holding a fan, and, in order to refresh himself, drawing in the breeze: what would you say of him? Surely he is hungrier than before. Such a man, therefore, is to be ridiculed.

Likewise, let another be placed upon sand, and, to quench his hunger, let him chew and spit out sand: he irritates hunger rather than [Col. 0654B] refreshes it. Let a third be placed in a blazing furnace and desire to swallow sparks: he burns inwardly. Let a fourth lick jewels, imagining that he will draw moisture from them: he will not drive hunger away; it harms rather than helps. Let the fifth lick individual limbs: he is not thereby satisfied [printed: “constrained”]. By the breeze, therefore, is understood human favour; by the sand, the desire for riches; by sparks, the desire [printed: “choice”] for powers, for which those who oppress others burn; by jewels, the glory of riches; by limbs, the pleasure of luxury and vices. See, then, whether these satisfy. Indeed [supplied: if not], they irritate. Serpents sit at these things—that is, those who creep, who strive to ascend to a higher rank, to abound in riches, and so forth.

At the third table, which is the devil’s table and suffocates, three things are set forth: *seneciae*, husks, and refuse. A *sene* is an unclean animal; hence *seneciae*, any unclean foods. Nor should you be troubled that in the prologue to Ezekiel some correctors say that *sinantiae*, not *seneciae*, ought to stand there; for *sinantia* and *senecia* are different things. *Sinantia* is a certain membrane in the mouth, which the Indians are accustomed continually to chew. But *senecia* means any unclean food, such as food sacrificed to idols. Husks are a sort of legume having broad pods but empty within. Refuse is the waste of hemp and flax. *Seneciae*, then, are the foods of pagans who eat things sacrificed to idols. Husks are those of Jews who cling to the bark of the letter and possess no spiritual sense. Refuse is that of heretics, [Col. 0654D] who abandon true meanings—which are the true light of souls—and choose refuse, that is, perverse meanings, for their error. Thus *seneciae* are [and] husks are the surface of the letter [of the Jews]. Refuse is the errors of heretics. [Note: Here there seems to be a gap in the sense, which, in view of the foregoing, may perhaps be supplied thus: “*Seneciae* are the ravings of idol-worshippers. Husks, etc.”] At this table sit unclean dogs—that is, pagans, Jews, and heretics—who are suffocated, and who on account of these things deservedly go to hell.

At the fifth table, which is the rich man’s table, three things are set forth: the fatted calf, the good things of the earth, and the marrow of wheat. The fatted calf is the Lord’s body and blood. This is that fatted calf which the father killed for the son returning from a far country. The good things of the earth are reading. Hence Moses says: “You shall eat the very oldest of old stores, and when new ones come, you shall cast away the old” (Lev. 26:10). “The very oldest of old stores” are the natural and moral precepts, which we eat by observing them. “The old,” that is, the legal ordinances, you shall cast away when the new things arrive, that is, the grace of the Gospel. Behold the good things of the earth. The marrow of wheat is that most purified flour which was placed in sacrifices. This is prayer. The Lord sets these three before us against the other three: against the flesh, against the world, and against the devil.

Against the incitements of the flesh the Lord gives the fatted calf, that is, the body and blood of the Lord. We ought therefore [Col. 0655B] to be prepared to receive the divine body at every time. If you are priests, you ought so to tame your flesh that nothing prevents you from receiving worthily always and at every time. Likewise for those of lower rank. Otherwise you will not sit at the rich man’s table.

Next he sets reading against the world. For the world often says to us: “Ah! You are in the cloister all day, where the air is confined. It would be good for you to go out and undertake some obedience, where you would have clear [printed: “secret”] air,” and such things. Answer, brother: “Get behind me, Satan. I shall not go out; for it is better to read in the cloister than to go outside.”

Set reason against the devil. For the devil often attacks us with temptations when he cannot draw us away from [Col. 0655C] prayer, especially a superior and others who have care of the brethren. When the devil sees them praying, he prods them: “What are you doing here, and why are you praying? What will the brothers eat today? Rise, go, you superior, and you cellarer; it is entrusted to you—procure what they are to eat.” No: “Get behind me, Satan. There is a time for praying and a time for administering.”

Likewise, he attacks the simple cloistered monk. When he sees him praying at length, he suggests: “What use is this rumination upon psalms? You chew over psalms all day. A brief prayer pierces the heavens. Should you not pray as the Lord taught in that brief and concise prayer?” “Certainly I shall not leave,” you say, “because you are always lying in wait for me and tempting me; and therefore, because you do not desist from temptation, I shall not cease from [Col. 0655D] prayer.”

At this rich man’s table sit birds—that is, holy men hoping to fly from this fourth table to the fifth. This rich man is Christ, rich and poor together in one: rich because God, poor because man. You are those who sit at this table, who make the first [perhaps: “first table through your fasts”] more slender, tame your own flesh, renounce the world, and fight with the devil.

At the last table, which is the Father’s table and at which heirs sit, only one thing is set forth—nothing more—the vision of God. Thus Martha was told: “But one thing is necessary” (Luke 10:42), nothing more; and David: “One thing have I asked from the Lord” [Col. 0656A] (Ps. 26:4), nothing more. Therefore, you who are commonly with us at the first table, and especially sit at the fourth, awaiting your place as heirs at the fifth, pray that, by the merits of blessed Germanus, whose translation we celebrate today, you may deserve to sit as heirs at the Father’s table, whose are kingdom and dominion for ages of ages.

## LXV. A SINGLE SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF THE NATIVITY OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

[Note: From Lyranus and Victorinus.]

“When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law, in order that he might redeem those who were under the law” [Vulgate: “made”].

Dearest brothers, by a great dispensation the Lord willed [Col. 0656B] to redeem the human race, and by a certain wondrous example of humility he provided to send his Son for our deliverance. This mission was fittingly planned, once men had been convinced that they could obtain no salvation of themselves, neither through natural law nor through written law. For he allowed two periods to pass: namely, before the Law and under the Law. In the time before the written Law there was the law of nature and the guidance of reason, by which the human race could in no way be saved, because, owing to human frailty, it began to be darkened and to turn to idolatry. But the written Law, afterwards given, itself began rather to harm than to help. For by forbidding sins—“You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:13), [etc.]—it set men’s minds more aflame toward those sins.

But when the fullness of time came, or the completion of the time which God had foreseen, he sent his Son, so that the grace of Christ might supply what neither law could accomplish—that is, might liberate the human race. And though he had been awaited and foretold through many ages, when he was at last to come, John was sent ahead, the forerunner appointed to announce the coming of so great an emperor. Hear the order; hear the arrangement.

The Son of God was coming to fight against the devil and the world [printed: “to fight in himself”]. He sent before him a strong soldier, who might invade the world and, by announcing his coming, terrify the king’s enemies and draw into his lordship whomever he could. A strong prince, a strong soldier—and by a strong soldier both were [Col. 0656D] foretold. For the angel Gabriel, whose name is interpreted “strength of God,” foretold the advent of both (Luke 1). They were strong and came to do strong deeds, and they had Gabriel, the strength of God, as their messenger. The soldier was born, and many rejoiced at his birth. But how great would be the joy at the birth of the emperor, when so much was sent beforehand at the birth of the forerunner! You have heard the joy at his birth; hear the joy of his running before.

John came into the wilderness of Judea, preaching and saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2). He is said to come into the wilderness because those whom he exhorts had been deserted by God. When he commands them to repent, he does not frighten them, but draws them to his Lord; moreover, he draws them by promising the means of reconciliation when he says, “For the kingdom of heaven has drawn near,” as if to say: “The kingdom of life has drawn near.” Thus he drew some. Hear how he frightened enemies. Seeing the Pharisees, he said to them: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (ibid., v. 7). Behold how he prepared the way for his Lord, frightening some and attracting others. Of him it was said through the prophet: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Isa. 40:2). A road is broad; a path is narrow. The road signifies the broader precepts of knowledge, [Col. 0657B] in which secular persons may lawfully use counsel or marriage and worldly possessions; the path signifies the stricter way, such as that of monks and hermits. He commands both road and path to be prepared for the Lord, because one goes to the Lord both by the active and by the contemplative life.

Already he exhorted men by preaching, and adorned his preaching with good works and life. Behold what works he had: “A garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his loins” (Matt. 3:4). The leather belt was from the skin of a dead animal. “And his food was locusts and wild honey” (ibid.). He clothed himself in rough garments because he tamed the flesh by harsh means and rebuked [or refuted] the impious with harsh corrections. He girded his loins because he broke the lust dwelling in the loins by the restraint of chastity. Locusts are mute creatures, silent in the fields, whose flight is lively and soon falls. He ate honey because his preaching tasted sweet to his hearers; he ate locusts because, while he preached, he was thought to be Christ. For they asked: “Are you the Christ?” (John 1:20). Behold, he was lifted up in flight like a locust; but, replying, “I am not the Christ” (ibid.), he quickly fell from that exaltation like a locust, which quickly falls when flying.

Thus in so great a preacher we may find an example for our own life. When he clothes himself in rough things, he instructs us to tame the flesh by labours. When he girds his loins with a belt, he invites us to chastity. When he does not acknowledge himself to be Christ and proclaims himself inferior, [Col. 0657D] saying, “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (Mark 1:7), he teaches us to humble ourselves. When he labours by preaching to others, he invites us to win the salvation of the brethren. When he flees to the wilderness, he invites us thereby to strip off the world. And who [Col. 0658A] is more perfect than John, according to the Lord’s testimony: “Among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen” (Matt. 11:11). Christ, however, was not born of a woman but of a virgin. Therefore Christ is not asserted to have been less than or equal to John, but greater. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “He who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he” (ibid.). For Christ was in the present Church, which is the kingdom of heaven, because God reigns in him through humility, since he came not to be served but to serve. Yet he was greater than John in power and in the dignity of God’s might.

Let us therefore rejoice in the birth of so great a forerunner, as it was said: “Many will rejoice at his birth” (Luke 1:14), so that John, whose name is interpreted “grace of God,” may by his merits confer God’s grace upon us, drive away diseases, remove storms, and grant abundance of fruits, with the help of the Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

## LXVI. FIRST SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF SAINTS PETER AND PAUL

[Note: From the Angers manuscript.—This sermon appears to be one of those in which the material of a sermon rather than the sermon itself as delivered by its author is preserved. Although perhaps Hildebert himself wrote it in no other fashion, it may be that, being most eloquent whether by nature or art, he reserved for more exact extempore exposition the material of the discourse which he had prepared beforehand. Moreover, no one can fail to conclude from the end of the sermon itself that it was delivered to Benedictine monks by a Benedictine monk; and, as seems probable, at Cluny, whose most celebrated monastery and basilica of astonishing workmanship had from the beginning been dedicated under the invocation and patronage of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. Hence he says that the Cluniacs whom he addresses glory in those from whom they received the seed and origin, as well as the progress, of their sacred order—a progress so great from its very beginning that under its first five abbots this tree of life extended its branches through nearly all the provinces of Europe, beneath which innumerable monks either received the primitive observance of the Benedictine Rule or restored it when it had declined.]

“I saw, and behold, a lampstand wholly of gold, and two olive trees were above it, one on the right and the other on the left. And the angel who spoke with me said to me: ‘Do you know what these are?’ And I said: ‘I do not know.’ And he said: ‘These are the two sons of oil, standing before the Lord of all the earth’” (Zech. 4:1 ff.).

The prophet Zechariah saw this vision, part of which the angel explained. He saw the Lord. Great, therefore, was he who saw; greater, he who showed; greatest, [Col. 0658C] he whom he saw—namely Christ as man. Therefore do not expound what the angel expounded. In the parables which the Lord expounded, and in the commands which the angel explained, none of the holy Fathers dared otherwise to expound, add, alter, or diminish. What remains untouched is reserved for prelates to expound.

The angel therefore said: “The wholly golden lampstand is the Lord of all the earth. The two olive trees are the two men, or sons of oil, standing before him: namely Peter and Paul.” For Christ is the Lord of all the earth. After he rose, appearing to the disciples, he said: “Do not fear; I have conquered the world. All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (John 16:33). He is rightly called a lampstand. For a lampstand has two things in itself: material and form—gold, namely, and the shape impressed upon it. Thus Christ too is in two natures. By gold divinity is signified; by form human nature is denoted, under which [Col. 0659A] divinity lay hidden. For divinity came to us shod, and was found in appearance as a man. This lampstand is wholly golden.

Gold signifies three things: divinity, wisdom, and charity. If divinity is understood by gold, it is wholly golden; for the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily in him (Col. 2). If also you understand wisdom by gold, it is wholly golden; for he is full of wisdom, upon whom rested the Spirit of wisdom and understanding. He himself is the wisdom of the Father. Finally, if by gold you signify wisdom, even thus he is wholly golden, because he was full of charity. For through charity alone he came forth from the secret place of divinity, from the Father’s bosom, into the world and redeemed the human race.

The angel said that two sons of oil stood before this Lord. Because the angel did not teach the reason for this, we may wonder why he said that these stand before him, while he passed over in silence the hundreds of thousands standing before him. This must be examined first, since it too was left untouched by the angel. Peter and Paul are called sons of oil, or men of mercy, to denote fullness—namely, fullness of mercy—as we are accustomed to say “an alabaster jar of ointment,” “bottles of wine,” “a cask of oil.” To understand this, one should know that, in a general sense, the name “oil” denotes the unity of graces, as in: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8). “I have found,” says the Father, “David my servant” (Ps. 88:23)—that is, Christ, obedient unto death—“I have anointed him with my oil,” that is, with the Holy Spirit proceeding from me; for the Holy Spirit rested upon him. He possessed in himself the fullness of gifts.

More particularly, however, the name “oil,” as far as can be gathered from sacred Scripture, denotes six graces: two according to its nature, and four according to its effect and use. Oil naturally has lightness and richness. By lightness we understand mercy; by richness charity is signified. That mercy is understood by oil is found in the parable of the innkeeper, who applied wine and oil to the wounded man (Luke 10). The innkeeper, that is Christ, healed the wounded human race with [supplied: oil], that is mercy, [Col. 0659D] and with wine, that is truth. For truth sprang from the earth, that is, Christ from the Virgin Mary; and mercy and truth met together. That charity is signified by richness is found here: “I have found David my servant; I have anointed him with my holy oil” (Ps. 88:21). And it is commanded: “All fat shall belong to the Lord” (Lev. 3:18).

There are three kinds of fat: the fat of the entrails, of the liver, and of the kidneys. According to the twofold charity, there is charity toward God, charity toward ourselves, and [p. 561] charity toward one’s neighbour. Therefore all fat belongs to the Lord alone, because no almsgiving and no fruitful work exists without charity. We must see why these men are called full of mercy. Is it not because mercy was shown to them? This indeed is true. For the Apostle says: “I was a blasphemer and persecutor, but now I have obtained mercy” (1 Tim. 1:13). Likewise mercy was shown to Peter, who, although he denied the faith, nevertheless obtained forgiveness. Yet they are especially men of mercy because they acted mercifully toward us, instructing, preaching, and drawing us to faith.

Let us inquire, then, whether they were full of charity. Let us bring forward the Apostle; he is of age, let him speak for himself. He says of himself that “neither death nor life shall separate me from the charity of Christ” (Rom. 7:35). But because he often brought forward particular statements that are less useful, such as: “Lord, even if I must die with you, I shall not deny you” (Matt. 26:35), let us hear Christ bearing witness to him: “Simon, do you love me more than these?” (John 21:15).

According to its effect, four kinds [printed: “offices”] are denoted in oil. Oil is useful to sailors when they wish to investigate something in the deep; it is useful also for seasoning foods; it is useful for a lamp and for medicine. The first is in waters, the second in a flask, the third in a lamp, the fourth in medicine. The first is poured out, the second stored, the third lit, the fourth prepared. The first leaps forth, the second refreshes, the third illuminates, the fourth provides healing. The first is of confession, the second of preaching, the third of virtue, the fourth of intercession.

Of the oil of confession Solomon says: “Let not oil fail from [Col. 0660C] your head” (Eccl. 9:8), that is, let confession not be absent from your heart. If you are good, confess praises; if you are evil, confess sins. This oil is contrary to the oil of flattery, of which it is said: “Let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat” (Ps. 140:5). Of the oil of preaching it is said in the Song of Songs: “Your name is poured-out oil” (Song 1:2). “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. 18:15). Of the oil of virtue, that is, the working of miracles, it is read in the Old Testament: “The hands of the priest were anointed with oil upon the right thumb, together with the blood of the ram of consecration” (Lev. 18:14). In the hands, however, are understood works of miracles. Of the oil of intercession it is said in the Gospel: “Give us of your oil, because our lamps are going out” (Matt. 25:8), that is, intercede for us.

Let us see whether Peter and Paul had the oil of confession. Hear then the Apostle confessing when the Lord appeared to him on the road and saying: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” (Acts 9:6). Behold, he who formerly had marked Christ with blasphemies and persecuted him now calls him [p. 562] Lord; he promises no longer to live according to his own will, saying: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” Hear Peter too confessing and saying: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 29:27).

We should not pass hastily over the confession of Peter and Paul and of the Church. If Peter, through the fervour of love insufficiently circumspect, was accustomed [Col. 0661A] to say, “Behold, we have left all things,” what are these “all things” which he says he left? We read that “charity believes all things” (1 Cor. 13:7). Without the things believed, salvation cannot exist; he did not leave these. We read also of other things: “In all things let us show ourselves as ministers of God” (2 Cor. 6:4). Did he leave those? There are also all things of which it is said: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. 6:35). But human life cannot subsist without these. Yet now let us find what “all things” he left: namely, those of which Ecclesiastes says, “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. 1:2). He had left all these things: the love of the world and the desires of the age.

Again, when Peter alone was speaking, why did he say: “Behold, we have left all things” (Matt. 29:27)? Because there are two things in a human being: flesh and soul. Sometimes the flesh says, “I leave all things,” but not the soul. But according to Gregory: “Such renunciation is not sufficient.” Therefore he says: “We have left all things,” the inner and outer human being, as though one of them were speaking: “I, the outer, together with the inner, have left all things.”

That they were full of the oil of preaching is manifest. Does not Paul say: “I travelled from Jerusalem to the Illyrian sea, preaching; and truly I laboured more than all” (1 Cor. 15:10)? Of Peter it is read in the Acts of the Apostles that, through his preaching, in one day “three thousand fell [read: believed], and on another day five thousand” (Acts 2:42).

What need is there to speak of the oil of virtue, that is, the working of miracles in which [Col. 0661C] they excelled? Is it not read that the sick were healed by Peter’s shadow? (Acts 5.) This is not read of Christ. With due reverence to Christ, Peter did greater things than Christ. In Peter was fulfilled what Christ said: “You shall do the work that I do, and you shall do greater works than these” (John 14). Concerning Paul, to omit now the other things in which he shone, we know certainly from the Scriptures that whomever he excommunicated, the devil immediately tormented.

That the grace of intercession was especially attributed to them is wonderful in our eyes, although our mediator between God and men is there as our advocate, and the glorious Virgin, and also blessed John, than whom none greater has arisen among those born of women, as it is written, intercede for us. [Col. 0661D] Yet Peter and Paul entreat more tenderly and closely for us, because they too sinned very grievously. Was Paul not a blasphemer and an open persecutor of the Church? Peter likewise became before the Lord [our intercessor], but denied his faith. Therefore no one sinned more grievously. The more strongly they experienced our offences, the more earnestly they implore the Lord for us. As Dido is read to have said to Aeneas among other things:

> Not unacquainted with misfortune, I learn to bring aid to the wretched.  
> *(Virgil, Aeneid)*

For this reason they are said here especially to stand before him, although many thousands of angels and holy spirits [Col. 0662A] stand before him. For Christ, as an emperor, has one judge, namely Peter, and another teacher, namely Paul. To Peter indeed were entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Peter opens them and closes them. Christ’s judgment follows Peter’s judgment. For it was said to him: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). It was not said: “Whatever Christ binds,” but: “Whatever Peter binds.” Therefore he has these as assessors; we have them as most faithful intercessors.

But although they pour out prayers to the Lord for all, they intercede more earnestly for cloistered persons, religious men, and for you to whom I speak. You indeed glory in Benedict and others, from whom you received the religious life of your order. But you can and ought especially to glory and trust in these, from whom [Col. 0662B] you received the seed and order of your order. For there are three things in your order: origin, progress, and end. Its origin is contempt of the world; its progress, obedience; its end, presence with the Lord unto the end. You have progress from Paul, where it is said: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” (Acts 9:6).
