From Peter you have origin, where it is said: “Behold, we have left all things”; and the end, where it is said: “And we have followed you” (Matt. 19:27)—that is, we have had perseverance unto the end. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## LXVII. SECOND SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF SAINTS PETER AND PAUL

[Note: From the Angers manuscript.]

[Col. 0662C] “Make for yourself two beaten silver trumpets for summoning the people” (Num. 10:2).

Great, my lords and brothers, is the solemnity of this day; great is today’s celebration, in which the Church commemorates the passion of Peter and Paul. After the solemnity of our Lord and of the blessed Virgin, this solemnity is rightly preferred to others: it is made for us by the stretching out upon the cross of Peter, prince of the apostles, and by the beheading of Paul, who is the vessel of election. To the one were entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and because of the constancy of his faith he deserved to hear from the Lord: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18). And again: “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). To the other, after the Lord’s glorious ascension, the glory [Col. 0662D] of the Lord was revealed, which so wholly illumined him that it appointed him a vigorous watchman of the Lord’s house. He himself says: “Last of all, as to one untimely born, the Lord appeared also to me” (1 Cor. 15:8).

To Peter was entrusted the Gospel of the circumcision; to Paul, that of the uncircumcision. Peter became the preacher to the Jews; Paul became the merciful restorer to life of erring gentile peoples. They are the foundation of our faith and the support of the holy Church. The Church stands firm in its solid structure by their teachings. Their sound, like the blast of trumpets, has gone out into all the earth; through their doctrine the Church shines as the moon through the sun. Faith grew under Peter’s teaching. Judea too in part came to know Christ; [Col. 0663A] under Paul’s teaching, gentile peoples came forth from the filth of unbelief into the light of truth. Hence he himself says: “He who worked in Peter for the apostleship worked also in me among the gentiles” (Gal. 2:8).

The saying in the Book of Numbers fittingly applies to them: “Make for yourself two beaten silver trumpets for summoning the people.” We must therefore consider by whom these trumpets were made, how they were made, and for what use: namely, for summoning God’s people. These trumpets signify holy preachers, namely those whose feast is today; and they were chosen for preaching not by their own merits but, clothed with power from on high, were appointed preachers by Moses—that is, by the Lord Jesus. Hence it is fittingly said: “Make for yourself two trumpets.” Moses, that is Christ, makes those trumpets for himself—that is, for his own honour—so that, as they sound far and wide, he may have heirs to whom he grants the blessing of eternal joy.

And although Moses in many respects signifies the Lord, he may spiritually signify him through the interpretation of his name itself; for Moses is interpreted “drawn from water.” And our Moses, that is Christ, is drawn from water when a human being is raised from the understanding of sacred Scripture to knowledge of him. Nor do we compare Scripture incongruously to water, which, like water, washes, refreshes, and cools us. It washes when it continually puts before us those things by which the stains of the soul are wiped away. It also washes us when, lest any stain remain in us, it cries: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 3:2). And again: [Col. 0663C] “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 3:33).

It refreshes us by not allowing us to forget the reward which we await in heaven. It sustains us on the way by impressing upon [p. 565] our minds the gifts with which we are to be gifted in our homeland, as in: “The righteous shall shine, and shall run to and fro like sparks among reeds” (Wis. 3:7). It cools us by exhorting us, through the examples of the saints, to extinguish within ourselves the incitements of vices.

Moses, taken from the waters, was nourished by Pharaoh’s daughter. So too Jesus Christ, when he is received by a faithful soul, nourishes that soul and is nourished within it. Formerly subject to unbelief, when it has received such an inhabitant it rejoices, entering into faith and casting unbelief away. In it God grows, while day by day every soul burns ever more ardently in love for him. For he who is immeasurable and wholly everywhere cannot grow in himself, but can become greater in us.

At the sounding of trumpets the walls of Jericho fell. Jericho is interpreted “moon,” and signifies this world, which is always waning and never remains in the same state: “For the form of this world passes away” (1 Cor. VII, 51). In some things it rises, and in others it dies. The seven walls of Jericho [Col. 0664A] are the seven principal vices, which have in many cases been extinguished by the sounding trumpets—that is, by holy preachers. At the seventh sounding these walls will fall utterly. For at the end of the world, or at the last judgment, vices will be removed in such a way that thereafter they will stir no one.

We also read concerning these trumpets that Gideon, about to attack the Midianites, took trumpets; with the trumpets, jars; and in the jars, lamps. A marvellous way of fighting enemies! Battle is declared, and, with weapons of war set aside, trumpets, jars, and lamps are taken up. Marvellous is this battle; more marvellous still is the victory that follows it. No weapons flash, yet the enemies are put to flight; men armed without arms subdue their foes unarmed; Gideon crushed the Midianites.

Gideon is interpreted “encircling fortification,” and signifies Christ, [Col. 0664B] who, remaining in the virginal womb, encompassed heaven and earth. Thus he was in the Virgin without being absent from heaven. “Midianite” is interpreted “encircling fortification,” and signifies Christ, who, remaining in the virginal womb, fall into despair, and, while despairing of salvation, rush from evil to worse evil.

> [Note: [Col. 0663D] The passage has plainly been corrupted by the copyist and might be restored as follows: “Midian” is interpreted “judgment,” or “one who disputes.” It signifies those accused of crimes, who, while despairing of the last judgment and of their salvation, rush from evil to worse and fall into despair.]

Such persons Gideon—that is, God—pursues and conquers by the sounding of trumpets, the breaking of jars, and the display of lamps. For holy preachers, when they break the jars—that is, when they expose their bodies to torments—bring forth lamps by which they conquer those who resist them. For the glorious wonders that follow in their suffering cause many to be converted, call them to faith, and strengthen them so that they may be steadfast in faith.

These are the hammered silver trumpets which, through the repeated blows of the world and the many [Col. 0664C] bitternesses of sufferings, are extended all the more in the love of God the more they are struck. These trumpets are silver, for teachers ought to be instructed in the divine sayings, lest, when they wish to teach, they be found unlearned. Hence: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire” (Ps. II, 7). Such hammered and silver trumpets serve to summon the people of God. Holy preachers ought therefore to devote themselves to gathering the scattered into the unity of faith.

And it should be noted that under the old Law those trumpets, which were figures of spiritual trumpets, were appointed for these four purposes: to summon the people to war, to advance, to a feast, and to a festival. Likewise our trumpets [Col. 0664D] call us to war, while they urge us to advance in virtues; they call us to a feast when they teach by word, and show by example, with what religious devotion and purity of mind one ought to approach the Lord’s table. They call us to a festival when they teach us how we ought to take part in temporal feasts: we ought to participate in them so devoutly that we may deserve to be present at the festivals of angels.

> [Note: [Col. 0664D] Something seems to be missing here, which may be supplied thus: “They call us to war when they kindle us for battle against temptations. They call us to advance when they urge us to advance in virtues. They call us to a feast,” etc.]

May he deign to grant this to us, he who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## LXVIII. THIRD SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF ST PETER THE APOSTLE

> [Note: [Col. 0665D] From the Angers manuscript.—This sermon seems rather to have been a familiar exhortation delivered within the cloister before regular canons, whom it expressly names, or before monks, whose austere manner of life it notes, than a public sermon delivered before the Christian populace. For why should Christian laypeople receive such an exact description, down to minute details, of deficiencies in cloistered life? Since, moreover, it explicitly calls its hearer a regular canon [Col. 0666D], it is more probable that Hildebert delivered this before regular canons. Their former life was no less strictly bound by vows of obedience and renunciation of private property, and was scarcely less austere in food and labour, than that of monks.]

[Col. 0665A]

> “Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all the expectation of the Jewish people” (Acts XII, 11).

We read in the annals:

> [Note: [Col. 0666D] Josephus, *Antiquities* XVIII, 9.]

that Gaius Caesar exiled to Lyons Herod the Tetrarch, who beheaded John, together with his wife Herodias; but Herod Agrippa, the brother of Herodias, he not only endowed with the tetrarchy of Galilee, but even made king of the Jerusalemites. Wishing to win the favour of the Jews, Agrippa killed James the son of Zebedee and, during the days of unleavened bread, sent Peter to prison, intending after Passover to put an end to his life by punishments at the people’s pleasure.

But Peter, freed by an angel, [Col. 0665B] burst forth into thanksgiving, saying: “Now I know truly,” and so forth. This story is often repeated in the Church because it edifies us in two ways. First, it instructs us by the outward surface of the letter; second, it feeds us with spiritual understanding as with the kernel of wheat. Again, according to the letter, it forms us in two ways: first, that, placing all hope in the Lord, we may attribute our blessings to him; second, that, in accordance with the Wise Man, each person may be his own accuser at the beginning of his speech.

Peter hoped in the Lord and was delivered; yet he was not exalted, but pursued God with thanksgiving. In the same way, when we are troubled, let us cry to him; he will hear us and deliver us in our trouble. “When the children of Israel were troubled, they cried to the Lord from their distresses, and he healed [Col. 0665C] them” (Ps. CVI, 15). Jonah cried from the belly of the whale and was vomited forth (Jonah II). Daniel cried, and the mouths of the lions were shut (Dan. XIV). The children cried, and the fire was removed from the furnace. Peter cried from prison, and the chains fell from his hands (Acts XII).

But how Peter accused himself in this thanksgiving is not evident, unless perhaps he silently accused himself at the beginning of his speech when he said, “Now I know truly,” as though pressing the point. Each word carries weight, as if he said: “When I seemed wise in my own eyes, I was discovered in my folly; I asserted certain things as true and was found a liar. But now I truly know what I say; here my Lord and Master will find nothing to reproach in me.”

But why should I dare to declare that the keeper of the keys of heaven, the judge of the world, Christ’s vicar, the prince of the apostolic company, was foolish and a liar? I dare say it confidently, for these things are written of him. Let no one despair because of the enormity of sin. This Peter spoke rashly when he said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke V, 8). He differs no more from the madman who says, “Depart from me, physician, [Col. 0666A] because I am a sick man.” He spoke foolishly when he said: “It is good for us to be here,” and so forth (Luke IX, 33). Hence the Evangelist says: “For he did not know what he was saying” (Luke XII). He spoke from faint-heartedness when he said: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen”; hence, rebuked by the Lord, he heard: “Get behind me, Satan” (Mark VIII, 33). He spoke from the habit common to human beings: “Lord, behold, we have left all things and followed you; what then shall we have?” (Matt. XIX, 27). For it is characteristic of Adam’s children to seek their own advantages. What need is there to say how presumptuously he spoke when he said: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. XXVI, 35)?

See how the bark of the letter instructs us. Its spiritual kernel, however, gives us a fuller understanding; for beneath one bark there is a threefold kernel. Let us therefore search the wall of the letter and find the desirable treasure of understanding. Here lies a general, a particular, and a final meaning: namely, concerning the Church, the contemplative man, and the human spirit.

Certainly, when the Church has been washed in the laver of regeneration and sprinkled from the font of baptism, she stands as it were upon the shore of the sea. There she sees Pharaoh and the Egyptians drowned; and, as Moses broke forth into their song, so she too breaks forth into praise of God, saying: “Now I know truly that the Lord has sent,” and so forth. “Now” is customarily used for the time of grace, as in: “Behold, now is the acceptable time.” Let us consider the angel whom the Lord sent.

Theology speaks of four kinds of angels. There is the angel of Satan, the angel of peace, the angel [Col. 0666C] of mystery, and the angel of counsel. The first strikes with the fist, the second builds up, the third strengthens, and the fourth liberates: that is, demons, human beings, heavenly powers, and Emmanuel. Of the first the Apostle says: “There was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me” (2 Cor. XII, 7). Of the second: “The angels of peace shall weep bitterly” (Isa. XXXIII, 7). Of the third: “Who makes his angels spirits” (Ps. CIII, 4); and: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent for service?” (Heb. I, 14). Of the fourth: “And he shall be called the Angel of great counsel” (Isa. IX, 7). He alone delivers; hence the Gospel says: “If the Son sets you free, you shall truly be free” (John VIII, 36).

Of him the Church says: “The Lord the Father sent [Col. 0666D] his Angel,” that is, one consubstantial with himself, “and rescued me from the hand of Herod.” Herod is interpreted *pellicius*, “deceiver,” from *pellicio*, “I deceive.” He is Leviathan, who sits in ambush to kill the innocent; the serpent more cunning than all living creatures; the hammer of the whole earth; the mighty wind in which Peter had begun to sink. We plainly indicate this rescue when, in catechizing [that is, for baptism], we say: “Come out of him, unclean spirit”; [Col. 0667A] and we indicate the manner of liberation when we say: “Do you renounce Satan and his works?”

But note that the Church says she was rescued from the hand, not from the hands. The devil has a left hand and a right. And just as a victor draws a captive enemy with his left hand, while striking him with his right so that he may go more readily, so before Christ’s coming the devil drew the human race captive and scourged it at his pleasure, since he is even said to have snatched some persons alive into hell. Christ rescued us from the hand that draws, not from the hand that scourges. For they still build upon the Church’s back, or scourge sinners; the righteous person still inwardly feels hammer and anvil; demons still attack the Church, just as they have attacked it from its youth. But this hand is right-handed not for the devil, but for us: for he scourges the son whom he wishes to receive, and works in us patience, tested character, and hope.

It follows: “And from all the expectation of the Jewish people.” Do the Jews acknowledge Herod as king? They are called not a senate, not a people, not citizens, but a mob, according to the saying: “The little hare is a feeble people” (Prov. XXX, 26).

> [Note: [Col. 0667D] Something seems to be missing here. For the crimes are not identified, though the author says that they are all the crimes which, as he says, the canonical epistle includes under three heads. I should readily judge that the following belongs here: what John the Evangelist enumerates in the First Epistle, chapter II, verse 16—namely, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life—by which the feeble mob is infected. Once these have been identified, the author rightly adds what the inattentive copyist probably omitted: “These are all the crimes,” etc. This seems to be clarified and proven from what follows.]

These are all the crimes, although the canonical epistle includes them under three heads. It is dangerous to be with this mob. Mud defiles, slime binds, and the deep devours. The lust of the eyes carries with it, as it were, a writer’s arsenal [perhaps “inkstand”], full of vanities; for by as many vanities as it afflicts a person, it infects him with as many blackening stains. The lust [Col. 0667C] of the flesh is slime, that is, sticky mud; whoever it seizes, it sticks to itself, as if inseparably. Hence flesh is said to have been made from slime rather than from mud or earth, to suggest by this its burning adhesiveness. For our flesh is so adhesive that our spirit, made in the image of God in the highest purity, is glued to it and, if it were possible, would never wish to be separated from it, but to be clothed over it.

The pride of life, however, is the abyss into which Lucifer drew with him a third part of the angels, or stars. The Prophet rejoiced that he had been rescued from mud, saying: “He drew me out of the pit of misery and the mire of dregs” (Ps. XXXIX, 3). The Prophet still complained that he was in the slime of the flesh, saying: “I am stuck in the mire of the deep, and there is no footing” (Ps. LXVIII, 3). And lest he be swallowed by the abyss of pride, he cried: “Let not the storm of water overwhelm me, nor let the deep swallow me” (ibid., 16). Thus the Church has been rescued from mud, slime, and the deep; she has been rescued from all the expectation of the Jewish mob.

This is also, as we have said, the voice of the contemplative man in the cloister, who, having taken the wings of a dove, flees into solitude—[Col. 0668A] solitude of mind rather than of desert. He lives among men above men, for he lives as an angel on earth. Yet this is not the voice of just anyone in a cloister; for it was not always Peter’s voice. But when he had become three-named—named Simon, surnamed Barjona, that is, son of John, and additionally named Peter—and until he had passed the first and second guard and the iron gate, he did not exalt himself.

In this way he spiritually passes the first guard if he is Simon, that is, obedient; the second if he is Barjona, that is, son of the dove; and the iron gate if he is Peter, that is, firm. The first guard is the bond of habit; the second, the iron gate, the appearance of vanity. The first binds, the second torments, the third kills. The first must be driven away, for:

> Though you drive Nature out with a pitchfork, she will still return.

The second must be endured; the third fled. How difficult the passage through the first guard is, that person knows who says in the book of experience: “Let us also [reading uncertain], since it is difficult to repel what is customary.” This passage is hard; it takes some virtue to pass from banquets to fasts, from meat to vegetables, from silks to hair-shirts, from cushions to straw bedding, from impunity to beatings, and, to say it all in brief, from one’s own will to the yoke of obedience. Truly, this is “the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.” For what is more marvellous, what worthier, than this transformation? A person is changed from olive lees into oil, from dregs into wine, from chaff into grain, and, to use a more familiar expression, from a log into a calf. For one who was formerly a log—that is, useless wood—becomes a young calf, [Col. 0668C] producing horns and hoofs, placed upon the altar of the Lord as a burnt offering of sweetest odour.

The cloistered man passes this guard with obedience as guide and companion. Against every assault of habit he sets the vow of religious life and says: “I shall not follow you, habit; I have vowed a vow to the Lord. I shall follow him wherever he goes.” Once habit has been subdued, the assault of temptation follows: the torrent, that is, the flooding lion in the onset of its wrath. Unusual illnesses attack him: frequent pain in the eyes from vigils; coughing from cold; trembling of the legs from prolonged standing in choir; swellings of the knees from frequent bending of the knees; constriction of the arteries from dry food; and so forth.

> [Note: [Col. 0668D] Perhaps *tubera*: in French, swellings or lumps.]

But more difficult still is the slander of brethren. When they see a man praying longer, keeping vigils more frequently, eating more strictly and less often, they say: “This brother of ours [Col. 0668D] dreamed of the abbot’s death; therefore he disfigures his face in order to deceive the eyes of those looking at him.” And when he passes before them, they mock him and say: “Behold, the dreamer comes” (Gen. XXXVII, 19): “He will be our abbot.” Or perhaps he will envy others or emulate their perfection, and will attempt [perhaps “be burdened”] beyond his strength.

The passage through this guard is more difficult, for it trips the steps of a person once he has been set on the way. It shakes every foundation that the person has laid, and often overturns it. This is the wind that crushed the house upon Job’s children while they were feasting. No one will pass through it unless he is a patient and humble Barjona. Hence we read of Anthony that, when he saw in the spirit all the snares of the devil’s temptations, he cried in great astonishment and lamentation: “Who will pass through these?” A voice came to him from heaven, saying: “Humility.”

Certainly there still remains the iron gate; passage through this third thing is irremediable: namely, the appearance of truth. For when the devil sees that he has achieved nothing through the two things previously mentioned, he attacks under the appearance of rectitude, like a counsellor [Col. 0669B] of salvation and a faithful confidant. He surrounds the man as if with four watches of soldiers, placing one at his head, one at his feet, one before him, and another behind him.

The lower watch is concern for the flesh; the upper, pride arising from virtues; the rear, remembrance of what was left behind; the front, the pressure of tribulations. The first binds, the second puffs up, the third exalts, and the fourth chokes. The first approaches, then, with modest step and lowered head, and says: “Peace be with you” (John XX, 21). The other asks: “Is your coming peaceful?” “It is peaceful,” he says. We must especially beware of this one; for an enemy is not easily guarded against when a peaceful entrance is expected.

At last he begins thus: “You ought to take care of the flesh, for no one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. V, 29). This is the fourth thing that you ought to love out of charity. This beast of burden has been entrusted to you; and as a burden and a rod, so fodder is owed to a beast of burden. Your flesh is like a string in a lyre. Those who sing in choir are like a lyre giving forth sweet melody in the singer’s ear. You ought therefore to stretch your string, not break it; for if you break it, will you not injure the lyre of the brethren and him for whom you play? We also read: ‘Let the citizen be fed so that the enemy may be expelled.’ And: ‘Behold, I have given you foods, the herb of the earth, and every living creature upon the earth.’ The regular foods that you use overwhelm you rather than nourish you. The cheese provided is wretched; eggs contemptible; legumes cause swelling; water constricts the stomach. I would speak of fish, but let meat be put before you.”

Beware, and see how crafty this worldling is. Therefore be Peter, and answer firmly: “Get behind me, Satan. Man does not live by bread alone” [Col. 0669D] (Matt. IV, 4). “I have food to eat that you do not know. I do not live in order to eat; rather, I eat in order to live. Only so much fodder is put before my beast of burden that it can be satisfied even by the leftovers. Bread and water are a blessed life. ‘In the strength of this food Elijah walked forty days to Horeb, the mount of God’” (3 Kings XIX, 8). And when you have said these things, pray to the Lord: “Pierce my flesh, O Lord, with your fear” (Ps. CXVIII, 120).

When this adversary has been put to flight, the upper watch approaches, no less deceitful, and says: “You are noble and learned; long study has made you know all the rules of your order. You are something of a scholar in outward matters. Why then do you sit here idle all day? Why do you hide the Lord’s talent in a napkin? Would you not preserve the strictness of the order more soundly than any of your prelates? You would have easier access [perhaps “ascent”] to princes through your friends; you would obtain things more easily. Go, make friends for yourself among the brethren; diligently search out the abbot’s secrets, so that you may accuse and expel him. Run about among those dear to you, so that they may run about for you. Make yourself all things to all people, that you may acquire the staff—the pastoral crozier—for yourself.”

Beware, good man. See how wicked this one is. He does not wish you to be the disciple of Christ, who says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29), but of him who says: “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, [Col. 0670B] 14). This is the force that, attacking an imprudent man, killed one of the ten virtues. This is the tower that fell upon the eighteen men who were building it. This is pride, heavenly by origin, which dwells in the minds of the exalted; and, flying back toward its own beginnings, bursts forth into human rank, in order that it may break forth into the rank of angels.

Be Peter here too, and say: “Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant” (Luke XIX, 22). You promise to make me exalted, but in a position of authority I would make myself contemptible. Hence the Apostle: “If you have secular judgments, choose those who are contemptible among you” (1 Cor. VI, 4). Yes, I know the rule; therefore, according to the rule, the higher I am, the more I ought [Col. 0670C] to humble myself in all things. “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song V, 3). And when you have said this, pray to the Lord: “Lord, let not the foot of pride come upon me; let not my heart be exalted, nor my eyes lifted up.”

When this one too has been put to flight, the rear watch approaches and says: “You madman, you left the world at an untimely moment [the reading perhaps ought, in the author’s sense, to be ‘timely’], having learned the vanities that are under the sun. You would be safer in religious life after having learned them, for things known are more easily avoided. You should also know what is happening among those dear to you. ‘For whoever,’ as the Apostle says, ‘does not care for his own is worse than an unbeliever’ (2 Tim. V, 8). Go back to your own people, and from your property you will generously give alms, which you cannot do here. If you fear popular rumours, you may even, while remaining in your habit, [Col. 0670D] go to Jerusalem, visit the holy places where the Lord’s feet stood, and visit the supreme thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul.

“In the days of your old age, you will return to the cloister; for the end, not the battle, crowns, and the Lord judges the ends of the earth.”

Beware, good man: he wants to make you a wanderer, not a regular canon. He wants to change you into a pillar of salt. He wants you to be a reproach of men and an outcast of the people, so that it may be said of you: “This man began to build and could not finish” (Luke XIV, 30). Be Peter and say to him: “I am not a dog that I should return to vomit” (2 Pet. II); “forgetting what is behind, with the Apostle I stretch forward toward what lies ahead.” My Lord Jesus Christ did not come down [Col. 0671A] from the cross when he was told, “Come down, and we will believe you” (Matt. XXVII). He died on the cross for me, and I shall die on the cross of obedience for him and for myself. And when you have said these things, pray to the Lord: “Confirm, O God, what you have wrought in me” (Ps. LXVII, 29).

When this has been done, the front watch approaches and says: “Behold, nearly all the goods of this monastery have perished. The vineyards have been struck with hail, the crop has belied hope, the ox has been killed while ploughing. On what will you live? With what will you clothe yourself? The Lord’s promise, ‘Seek first the kingdom of God, and these things shall be added to you’ (Luke XII, 31), amounts to nothing. Events have turned out contrary to it. You cannot dig; you are ashamed to beg. If you are wise, take care of yourself.”

Certainly, good man, be Peter and say: “I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed [Col. 0671B] seeking bread” (Ps. XXXVI, 25). And: “Those who fear God lack nothing. God, the physician to whom I have entrusted myself, knows when these things should be given and when withdrawn: ‘The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord’” (Job I, 21). A father will not deny travelling provisions to his son, he who gives their food to beasts of burden and to the young ravens that call upon him. And when you have said this, pray: “Give me neither riches nor poverty, but grant me only what is necessary for my sustenance” (Prov. XXX, 8).

Therefore, when you have passed through this iron gate, you may cry out: “Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his Angel and rescued me from the hand of the *pellicius*”—that is, the world—

> [Note: [Col. 0671D] Herod, who is interpreted *pellicius*.]

“and from all the expectation of the Jewish mob.” The “expectation of the mob” is spoken by analogy: just as one besieging a fortress does many things to no purpose and says, “I shall add one more thing and wait to see whether it succeeds,” so these are, as it were, after the first and second guards, Herod’s final expectations. When these are frustrated, he ceases the siege.

This is also, as I have said, the voice of the human spirit on the day of its death, when it flies from the body of this death as one freed from prison and cries: “Now I know truly,” and so forth, “and he rescued me from the hand of Herod,” that is, of the *pellicius*, that is, the body; for *pellicius* is said to derive from *pellis*, “skin”; “and from all the expectation of the Jewish mob,” that is, of the members [Col. 0671C] through whose service the flesh wars against me. For he rescued my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling, my ears from tales, my tongue from lying, and my hands from robbery.

Certainly, we undergo the first rescue from sins of this kind in baptism; the second, gradually from temptations in the desert; and the third, from every corruption, we await in heaven. Therefore, may Jesus Christ, our Lord and our Angel, who first rescued, rescue a second time and rescue a third time, when he comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## LXIX. SOLE SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF SAINT MARY MAGDALENE

> [Note: [Col. 0672D] From the Angers manuscript.]

> “For three crimes of Moab, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he burned the bones of the king of Edom unto ashes” (Amos II, 1).

Amos the Tekoaite was a prophet, but one of obscure speech. He himself testifies that he was not a prophet—that is, neither by lineage nor by office and training was he among the prophets. But, while he was a shepherd plucking sycamore figs, the Lord sent him into Israel as a man tongue-tied and unable to manage his own speech, to prophesy against the fat cows of Samaria. Hence the truth that he received from the Spirit he set forth in words so unarranged and apparently unwilling to be understood, as though he had not expressed in his words what we have previously set out according to the letter: he prophesied the irrevocable vengeance of the Lord against Moab, because Moab did not cease to persecute in death the king of Edom whom it had persecuted alive, but overthrew his tomb, burned his bones, and scattered his ashes.

Yet this prophetic threat may be applied to the consequence of the prohibition which God gave Mary Magdalene, and to the consequence of the exhortation which the teacher of the Gentiles left us in writing: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think soberly” (Rom. XII, 3). For when the Lord had risen from the dead and appeared to Magdalene, she wished, according to custom, to kiss and touch his feet; but he forbade her in these words: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John XX, 17).

This prohibition may move us to ask why a woman so beloved and so loving was forbidden to touch him whom she loved and who loved her. For we may speak with the Lord who forbids her in this way: “Remember, Lord Jesus, that this woman whom you loved was she whom, when you saw her weeping, you yourself also wept. She is [Col. 0672C] she to whom you gave testimony of discerning attention, saying: ‘Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her’ (Luke X, 42). She is she who, when Peter had denied you—he who had said, ‘Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you’ (Matt. XXVI, 35)—and when Thomas was far away—he who had said, ‘Let us go and die with him’—did not fear the threats of the Jews in womanly fashion, but pursued your Passion all the way to the tomb with open lament and pitiable groaning. She is she who, when your body was not found, wasted away in such grief that, bending and bending again, she watered the tomb with more abundant tears than she had watered your feet.

“What is this, Lord Jesus: you compel disciples foolish and slow of heart to believe to touch your hands [Col. 0672D] and side, but keep this woman, who seeks you with such love, far from touch? If you were going to say, ‘Do not touch me’ (John XX, 17), why did you say, ‘Mary, do not weep’ (Luke VII, 13)? Why, I ask, was she forbidden to weep if she was to be forbidden to touch? What happened to you in the underworld, that you, the fountain of mercy, should dry up on returning to us? Whence comes such a sudden change? You who, amid blows, scourges, nails, and the spear, did not forget to have mercy on your enemies but prayed the Father to forgive them because they did not know what they did—now risen and impassible, do you reject one who seeks you? Or, in a new judgment, do you decide that the Pharisees ought to be obeyed, and begin to abhor the touch of a sinful woman? What is this, [Col. 0673A] Lord Jesus? Reveal it to us.”

To our not unwarranted hesitation the Lord replies: “For three crimes of Moab, and for four, I will not turn her back”; as if to say: “I will turn her back from three and four crimes, but I will revoke the sentence of pardon that I had given; I will remember none of the mercies [the text perhaps reads ‘miseries’] that I had shown her, if I do not ascend in her heart to the Father, if she burns the bones of the king of Edom unto ashes.”

Moab, indeed, is interpreted “from the father,” and suits the person who sins openly, who not only is not ashamed to sin but even rejoices when he has done evil and glories in the most shameful things.

This expression was agreed upon for use in legal instruments, which call some sons “without a father,” others “from a father.” A son of a prostitute is called “without a father,” because his father is uncertain; and even if he is certain, the law nevertheless does not recognize him, and he is therefore not called to an inheritance. But a legitimate son is “from a father,” because he surely expects his father’s inheritance. In this way Magdalene was “from a father,” carrying her father’s name in everyone’s mouth, because she publicly did his works—her father, I mean, of whom the Lord also said to the Jews: “You are of your father the devil” (John VIII, 44).

For she is that woman in the city who was a sinner: so publicly prostituted that, content with a cheap price, she endured the soft handling of her body. From her the Lord cast out seven demons—that is, the four and the three crimes. Demons occupied the sanctuary of the Lord; and the temple destined for the Son of the Virgin had already become a temple [Col. 0673C] of Venus, so that the Prophet might complain concerning her: “All the demons have entered into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made corpses a guard for the fruits” (Ps. LXXVIII, 1).

Let us not be ashamed to tell of her disgrace, nor let you be ashamed to hear it, because this disgrace is for her glory and for our instruction. For she so covered the blackness of her crimes with the beauty of her virtues that she may answer the angels: “I am black, but beautiful” (Song I, 4). Thus he cast her father out from her when she forgot her people, that is, the seven vices which the Prophet distinguishes by the three and the four. For three kinds of crimes come first, under which every sin is included; and afterward there are sometimes four, as it were accompanying and added to these.

These three are evil thought, perverse speech, and wicked action. Their enumeration is easy and, as it were, reduced to one. But it matters greatly to us if we distinguish how many ways we sin in heart and how many ways we are turned from the crime of the heart; and likewise concerning the other two modes.

Thus we sin in heart by rejecting thoughts that descend and receiving those that ascend. Since we are not sufficient of ourselves, as though from ourselves, to think anything good, good thoughts descend to us from God, because “Every best gift and every perfect gift descends from the Father of lights” (James I, 17). Evil thoughts, however, rise from ourselves. Hence the Lord said to those going to Emmaus: “Why do thoughts arise [Col. 0674A] in your hearts?” (Luke XXIV, 38).

It would be superfluous to describe how manifold and wicked they are. Each of us knows, and has learned in the book of experience, what poisonous draughts the evil spirit pours into the channel of our mind; what varied and useless images of things it paints in the bedchamber of our heart. Like tiny gnats, these fly [the printed reading is perhaps *involvant*] into the very eyes of the mind and pursue God’s ministers up to the altar of the Lord of hosts, in order to snatch away or disturb there the brief remembrance of Christ hanging on the cross. These are the dying flies that spoil the sweetness of ointment; these are “the birds which Abraham drove away until sunset” (Gen. XV, 11).

Elijah also, who shut heaven by his word, did not shut his mind against these thoughts when he thought himself to be left alone. Therefore he was rebuked by the Lord, and found it easier to shut heaven than his mind against these thoughts which rise evilly from us.

By three means God turns us away from this sin of the heart. The first conversion is to return to the heart; the second, to ascend in the heart; the third, namely, to go beyond the heart. In the first there is a humble heart; in the second, a moderate heart; in the third, a lofty heart. Of the first the prophet says: “Return, transgressors, to the heart” (Isa. 46:8); nor is this saying to be despised, since it descended from heaven: “Know yourself, O man.” This is when a man recognizes what he owes to himself, to his Creator, to his neighbor, and to his own body. Secondly, he ascends spiritually from virtue to virtue, until “the God of gods is seen in Zion” (Ps. 83:8), that is, in the watchtower of contemplation [Col. 0674C]. Of this the Prophet says: “He has arranged ascents in his heart” (ibid., 6). In the third, we sometimes go beyond ourselves to see God; hence the Apostle: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God” (2 Cor. 5:13), and the Psalmist: “Man shall approach a lofty heart” (Ps. 63:7).

The servant is drawn to the first by the spirit of fear; the hired servant is called to the second by the spirit of counsel; the son is raised to the third by the spirit of wisdom. Thus he deserves at times to ascend above the heart, that is, to that “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has ascended into the heart” (1 Cor. 2:9).

Likewise, we sin with the mouth in two ways: by speaking evils and by keeping silent about goods. We speak evils in six ways. There is false speech, concerning which it is said: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7). There is idle speech, concerning which it is written: “Each has spoken vain things to his neighbor” (Ps. 11:3). There is also shameful speech, concerning which it has been said: “Let no foul speech proceed from your mouth” (Eph. 4:19). There is excusatory speech, of which the Psalmist says: “Let not my heart incline to words of wickedness, to make excuses for excuses in sins” (Ps. 140:4). There is deceitful speech, of which the same writer says: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips” (Ps. 11:4). There is useless speech, concerning which the Lord himself says: “For every idle word that men have spoken, they shall render account on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12:36). And there are whatever other kinds of this sin may exist.

The tongue is a restless, deadly member [Col. 0675A]: ready for speaking, inclined to speak against others. We are converted away from it if we set a guard upon our mouth, if we restrain our lips from the things just mentioned. We speak good things, however, in three ways. We speak about ourselves, about our neighbor, and about God. Let speech about ourselves be accusatory; about our neighbor, edifying; about God, laudatory. For the wise person, at the beginning of his speech, is his own accuser. Hence the Lord says through Isaiah: “Do you declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26). Thus David spoke of himself: “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me; against you alone have I sinned, and done evil before you” (Ps. 50:6). Let speech toward one’s neighbor be edifying and unceasing; hence the Apostle says: “Insist in season and out of season; rebuke, entreat” (2 Tim. 4:2).

[Col. 0675B] Let speech concerning God be in praise, to which the Prophet exhorts his soul: “Praise the Lord, O my soul; I will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing to my God as long as I exist” (Ps. 145:1).

Likewise, we sin in deed in two ways: by turning away from good and by doing evil. Evil is done in three ways: by insult, blasphemy, and injustice. There is insult when we sin against ourselves, treating our bodies dishonorably through shameful passions. There is blasphemy when we sin against God himself, or against the religion of faith; hence it is said: “The name of God is blasphemed among the nations because of you” (Isa. 52:5). Injustice is against one’s neighbor, for equity is owed to one’s neighbor. Therefore sin against him is injustice—that is, non-equity, or action contrary to equity.

[Col. 0675C] We are converted from this sin if, with Martha, we take pains to be solicitous about frequent service; or if, sitting with Mary, we taste and see that the Lord is sweet. With Martha we work, performing works of mercy, six of which the Lord numbers in the Gospel (Matt. 25); seven are read in Tobit (Tob. 21). These are: to feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, receive the stranger, visit the sick, console one placed in prison, and bury the dead. With Mary we rest, devoting ourselves to the works of contemplation, which are four: meditation, reading, prayer, and thanksgiving—of which there will be a clearer account later.

Magdalene was converted from these sins, as was shown by signs and confirmed by the Lord’s testimony [Col. 0675D]. The sign of her conversion from a perverse heart was the abundance of her tears; from the mouth, her frequent kissing of the feet; from deed, the anointing of the feet and head.

It remains to discuss the four sins which follow. The first is the minimizing of sin; the second, exultation after sin; the third, its spreading by example; the fourth, persistence through contempt. For some minimize or defend their sins by fate, by the stars, or by the constitution of their temperament. Let us consider how detestable this is. For it is as though they were making war upon the Lord. What God detests and hates, such a person approves and loves [Col. 0676A]; he receives God’s enemy and furnishes him with a fortress. Indeed, he casts back the accusation, under a certain obligation, upon the very author of fate and of the stars and of human constitution. Nor does he heed Isaiah’s threatening saying: “Woe to those who call good evil, bitter sweet, and light darkness” (Isa. 5:20).

There are also those who rejoice when they have done evil; hence it is said: Nothing offends God so much as a neck raised high after sins. For there are four kinds of exultation which Sacred Scripture detests: exultation in the world, in one’s own body, in an evil spirit, and in the human spirit. In the world, when prosperity smiles upon us; in the body, when the desires of the flesh are gladly fulfilled; in our own spirit, when knowledge without charity inflates us; in an evil spirit, when we applaud ourselves [Col. 0676B] because we have fulfilled the will of the devil, or when we rejoice in the evils of our neighbors. But there is one praiseworthy exultation: in the Holy Spirit, of which it is said: “Rejoice, righteous ones, in the Lord” (Ps. 32:1).

There are also those who draw others into sin by word or example. This is indeed the chair of pestilence, unknown to the one who teaches a human being knowledge; against them the prophet threatens: “Woe to those who draw sins as though with a long rope.”

> [Note: [Col. 0675] Vulgate: “Woe to you who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as though with the rope of a cart” (Isa. 5:18).]

These are those who mingle blood with blood. It is not enough for them to perish for ever and ever unless they also draw others with them into eternal destruction. There are likewise those who persevere in all these things. Such a sinner has been swallowed up, and the pit has closed its mouth over him. He does not lift his eyes to heaven; he does not remember the judgments of God [Col. 0676C]; he is bound in the tomb, and therefore confession perishes as though from one dead. “For when he has come into the depths, he despises” (Prov. 18:3).

Behold how the Lord turns Moab away from three and four sins. But this happened when, seeing the Lord dying and dead, this woman, regarding him as a mere man, ceased to believe that he was God; or perhaps she loved him so humanly that she did not wish to be deprived of his presence, and preferred to minister to a man on earth rather than adore God in heaven. Of this even to the apostles it was said: “It is expedient for you that I go” (John 16:7). And so this woman, having all her affection toward the man Christ, reduced the bones of the king of Idumea to ashes. For Idumea is interpreted as “earthly.”

[Col. 0676D] Therefore Christ is the king of Idumea, who ruled over all the ends of the earth and far out at sea. Idumea is also said to mean “bloody,” which equally suits Christ, because he reigned from the wood; his garment on the cross was made like a garment in a winepress, and thus, like the king of Idumea, he ascended from Edom with dyed garments. His bones are his divinity; for as bones are the strength of flesh, so divinity is the strength of humanity. What else, then, is it to reduce his bones to ashes except to confuse the divine nature with the human—to regard him who is God as merely a man? Therefore she would not cease to believe him a mere man unless Christ ascended in her heart to equality with the Father [Col. 0677A]; nor would the conversion granted to her benefit her.

> [Note: [Col. 0677D] Here Hildebert seems to have held that Magdalene loved Christ as a man, not as God.]

And this is the meaning of “I will not turn her back after her sins”: that is, my conversion will not benefit her, because she burned the bones of the king of Idumea to ashes—that is, while burning with love for my humanity, she was forgetful of my divinity.

It remains for us to explain how this applies also to us who devote ourselves to reading Sacred Scripture. The prophet exhorts us not to dispute impudently concerning the articles of faith. For certain persons, seeking a kind of useless subtlety—or uselessness—in philosophical disciplines, employ petty verbal distinctions in contentious argument; to use these in disputation is to reduce Christ’s bones to ashes. [Col. 0677B] Lest this happen, the Apostle warns us, saying: “Do not be wise beyond what it is fitting to be wise, but be wise unto sobriety” (Rom. 12:3). Even if God permits [variant: “agrees that”] us to employ the phantoms of the liberal arts, if we should wish to proceed in this Scripture in the same sophistical fashion, we shall be hateful to God, attempting to bring the croaking of Egypt’s frogs into the land of Goshen.

Therefore let us ask that blessed penitent, whose solemn feast and sweet remembrance are observed today—a remembrance rightly recalled by human beings because she has passed into the joy of angels—that she may intercede for us with the Lord, that he may grant us rightly to understand in the Holy Spirit. Nor should the patronage of this penitent be regarded lightly; for, as she shares a name with the Blessed Virgin, so in some manner she is compared with her in example. The Lady does not disdain to share her name with the handmaid, the Queen with the young woman, the Mother of God with her who had been a sinner.

[Col. 0677C] For both are called Mary, a name which means “star of the sea,” and which suits them because of their examples. In this great and wide sea, each offers us the guidance of a preceding light. The one is for us an example of chastity, the other of penitence; the one of an unstained life, the other of a life whitened after its stain. Although the former is the greater light and the latter the lesser, yet—speaking with due reverence for the Virgin—the latter’s example is more difficult than the former’s. For there are more in the Church who have corrected their errors than who have never known how to err: more, I say, who have been justified than who are righteous. More, therefore, make progress by this woman’s example.

But shall I speak, or be silent, concerning the aid of each? It is beyond doubt true that the aid of the Blessed Virgin is unique, since more than all others a mother can prevail with her son. Yet, because she did not know sin, did not experience within herself the extinguishing of the tinder of sin, did not know by experience how intolerable is the contest in which a person arms himself against himself, or how difficult is the victory in which the same person conquers and is conquered, she intercedes for us, as it were, from a certain lofty height [Col. 0678A]. But this woman, who knows our formation, pours out her whole self in prayers; she wholly casts herself at the Lord’s feet, and is not ashamed even to ask importunately until she obtains her request.

May she therefore intercede for us with the Lord, that he may give us help in tribulation, understanding in reading, and reward for labor: Jesus Christ, our Lord and Master, who is God, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## LXX. A SINGLE SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF SAINT PETER IN CHAINS

> [Note: [Col. 0677D] From the manuscript of Angers.—And this sermon seems to have been delivered before monks, and Benedictines, by a Benedictine monk. For in his description of monastic exercises he employs chapter 35 of the Rule of Saint Benedict [Col. 0678D], when he speaks of the weekly kitchen-server. From this it may also be inferred that abbots were then permanent, since he asserts that their occupation is continuous and genuinely distinct from the others, which he declares to be only temporary and subject to change at the abbot’s discretion.]

“Peter indeed was kept in prison; but prayer was made without ceasing by the Church to God for him” (Acts 12:5).

Herod Agrippa, who in the seventh year of his reign [Col. 0678B] was miserably struck down by an angel, after killing James, the brother of John, with the sword, saw that this pleased the Jews. He proceeded to seize Peter during the days of Unleavened Bread and put him in prison, handing him over, bound with two chains, to four squads of soldiers. An angel, striking his side, set him free.

Whatever things have been written were written for our instruction. Instruction is the bread of readers—bread because it strengthens the human heart. Thus the writing concerning Peter’s chains is our bread; and it is no ordinary bread. It is not a little cake, which is only crust; nor a wafer, which is only crumb; but solid bread, having crust and crumb—that is, the surface of history and spiritual understanding [Col. 0678C]. It feeds us with both crusts, refreshing us in two respects: in zeal for intercession and in certainty of hope.

For two comparisons are presented. The first is Peter and the Church: Peter in prison, and the Church in unceasing prayer. The second is the Jewish people and the angel: the Jewish people awaiting blood, and the angel laboring for his liberation. Therefore, if it should happen that the Church suffers, and especially that her shepherd is bound, let us strive in every way for their liberation, particularly by praying specifically for him. We ought not to be like a dead instrument of God, doing nothing and only imploring divine aid when human aid is not lacking, since it is written: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:16).

Nevertheless, all hope of liberation is placed in God [Col. 0678D], not in man, because the angel liberated him; and because, according to Jeremiah: “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man, and makes flesh his arm” (Jer. 17:5).

After being refreshed by the crust, let us see in what way the crumb also refreshes us; this is not to be passed over hastily. For the crumb is sweeter and fuller. Hence the Bridegroom says to the Bride: “You have wounded me with one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck” (Song 4:9). The surface of history penetrates and moves the hearts of hearers [Col. 0679A], but spiritual understanding penetrates far more deeply; it moves more powerfully and descends to every particular. For then speech is living and effective, and more penetrating than every sword.

Let us therefore seek the spiritual prison, the spiritual squads and chains, and the spiritual side of Peter which, when struck, brings liberation. Certainly there are three prisons: the legal, the natural, and the regular. The first is public custody, in which accused persons are confined according to the institutions of law. The second is the human body, which weighs down the soul and depresses the mind in its many thoughts. The third is the cloister, in which the contemplative man, fleeing the paths of hedges [uncertain reading], fastens his feet in its fetters. The first is for punishment; the second for exercise; the third for leisure. Through punishment we are restrained from evil; through exercise we advance in good; through leisure we rest in the best good.

[Col. 0679B] Of the first it is written: “Evilmerodach raised Joachim from prison” (Jer. 52:31). Joseph too is read to have been placed in prison (Gen. 39), and to have found favor with the lord of the prison. Of the second it is said: These are those who have flown out of their bodies as though from prisons. Elsewhere: “Let the groaning of those in chains enter into your sight” (Ps. 78:11). Of the third it is said to one imprisoned: “Sit; rest. You have opened your mouth: do not pass beyond.” And the prisoner himself says: “Pierce my flesh with your fear, O Lord, for I have feared your judgments” (Ps. 118:120).

Let us speak of these prisons. And because Peter is read to have been called by the Lord in different ways—five times, that is, Peter in Greek or Latin; five times Cephas in Hebrew and Syriac; five paraphrastic forms, Simon son of John—let us also use these names in this manner: Peter was kept in prison; Cephas was humbled in prison; Simon son of John pursued philosophy in prison.

The custody of Peter in the legal prison has been discussed above. Let us consider the natural prison. Cephas means Peter, that is, “firm.” This is the human spirit, which, being immortal and indissoluble, is called firm in comparison with the flesh, so that it may truly be said: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41). Or, by an allusion to the Greek word *kephalon* (*κεφαλή*, “head”), Cephas is called “head” [Col. 0679D], because the spirit is and is called the head of the flesh, according to the saying: “The head of the woman is the man” (Eph. 5:23).

This Cephas is humbled in prison; hence it is said: “My spirit, my soul, and my belly have been humbled upon the earth” (Ps. 30:10). He was humbled there by the Lord, who says: “I made every breath; because of his iniquity I grieved him a little” (Isa. 57:16). But what are the four squads which guard the human spirit, and what are the two chains binding it?

A *quaternio* is said to be a soldier who has four soldiers under him, just as a centurion has one hundred and a decurion ten. Thus, while the four elements in the human body remain on guard—that is, while their proportionate and physical, or natural, bonds remain strong—they preserve the deposited spirit as faithful guards [Col. 0680A], each having, as it were, four soldiers under it. For, as those troubled by the labor of the world teach, there are four ages of man, four humors belonging to him, and four qualities of those humors. Each element has its own quality, its own humor, its own age, and its own season.

Certainly the two chains are natural love and the Creator’s command. Of love it is said: “No one has ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 6:29). And the Apostle says of the same: although “we are burdened by the body, we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over” (2 Cor. 5:4), if that can be. The spirit is also held there by the command of him who created it. For since there are four things which a man is commanded to love, the fourth and last is the flesh. [Col. 0680B] Earlier he also said: The command given to man is, “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20:13), whereby he is also commanded not to lay hands upon himself.

For he would wrong the lord of the prison if he departed against the will of the one who confined him. When Peter’s side is struck and the guards fall asleep, the spirit flies out. The side commonly signifies union; indeed, the companions of powerful persons are called either good or bad “sides.” The woman too was made from the man’s side, signifying the union that was to come: “And the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24). Therefore the human side is the union of soul to flesh. When it is dissolved, the guards sleep—that is, they return by their own weight to their own origin, according to the saying: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). But the spirit, as is read in Wisdom, returns to him who created it.

The chains fall from his hands: he is free from the command, and the dwelling of the body no longer pleases him as life. This is proved by the reply of a head found by a hermit. When the hermit had learned many things from the dead man about infernal punishments, he added whether the dead man wished him to obtain from the Lord by prayers that he should rise again, be baptized, and be able to be saved. But he replied: “Must I die again?” The saint answered, “Certainly.” “I do not wish,” he said, “to be raised.”

Yet it must not be denied that triumphant spirits still love their flesh. Hence beneath God’s throne they are said to cry: “Judge, O Lord, the blood of your saints that has been shed” (Rev. 6:10). But they do not wish to receive it such as they left it [Col. 0680D]. Yet prayer is made for it, as though they said: “The little lodging which I had on earth showed mercy to me; would that the Lord repay it on my behalf.” Thus Cephas is freed from prison. For this liberation the Church prays daily to God for him. Finally, in the Lord’s Prayer we cry: “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13), that is, from the corruption and weight of the body. For this also the Apostle cried: “Who shall deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24).

It remains to speak of the regular prison. Simon son of John pursues philosophy in this prison. Simon means “obedient”; John, “God’s grace,” or “one in whom there is grace.” Truly, although we are all bound to obey God, because “obedience is better than sacrifices” (1 Sam. 15:22), nevertheless, by antonomasia [Col. 0681A], the cloistered man is called obedient, because he opened his mouth in a vow and said: “The Lord is my portion; I have said that I will keep your law” (Ps. 118:57). And: “I have sworn and established that I will keep the judgments of your righteousness” (ibid., 106).

He pursues philosophy through contemplation, in accordance with what is said of Moses: that he philosophized with the Lord for forty days and forty nights. The squads are the four occupations in which he ought continually to be occupied. For he is not permitted to wander about, lest, like Dinah, he be found wandering and violated. These occupations are reading, prayer, meditation, and regular exercise.

Observe, moreover, the fourfold character of each. Sacred reading is like a four-legged table in the house of the Lord. It has history, allegory [Col. 0681B], tropology, and anagogy. Of Jerusalem, historically, we read: “Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you” (Matt. 23:37). Allegorically: “Arise and shine, O Jerusalem, because your light has come and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you” (Isa. 60:1). Tropologically: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in unity itself” (Ps. 121:3). Anagogically: “The Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother” (Gal. 4:26).

Prayer likewise has four qualities. It ought to be modest, like that of the man who, not daring to lift his eyes to God, said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13). It should be pure—that is, only for those things which pertain to the name of the Lord Jesus, namely eternal things. Hence: “Seek first the kingdom of God” (Matt. 6:33); and seek it alone, because all these things shall be added to you. Since God is spirit, prayer must be in spirit and truth—that is, for spiritual and eternal goods. Hence the Apostle says: “Lifting pure hands” (1 Tim. 2:8) in prayer.

[Col. 0681C] It should also be expansive, because it must extend even to enemies. Hence: “Pray for those who persecute you” (Matt. 5:44). Thus Christ prayed on the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23:34). And the chief martyr, bending his knees, prayed: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:60). It should also be devout; otherwise it is a sacrifice without fat and is not offered to the Lord as a most sweet-smelling odor. For it is written: “I will offer you fat holocausts with the incense of rams” (Ps. 65:15).

Meditation is likewise fourfold: one should meditate on what was, what is, what will be, and what would have been. On what was, in order to hope; on what is, in order to grieve; on what will be [Col. 0681D], in order to rejoice; on what would have been, in order to fear. Of the first it is written: “I thought upon the ancient days, and had the eternal years in my mind” (Ps. 76:6). Of the second: “I will recall all my years in the bitterness of my soul” (Isa. 38:15). Of the third: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered you, O Zion” (Ps. 136:1). Of the fourth: “Unless the Lord had been with us—let Israel now say—unless the Lord had been with us when their fury was enraged against us, perhaps the water would have swallowed us up” (Ps. 123:1).

Regular exercise is also fourfold: one kind is daily, that is, diurnal; another weekly; another intermittent; another continuous. By daily I mean that by which the Rule assigns him to some manual labor at fixed days and hours. Weekly exercise makes one the weekly kitchen-server—

> [Note: [Col. 0681D] On weekly kitchen-servers, Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 35.]

—or reader at table, and the like. Intermittent exercise is the office of sacristan, apothecary, and the like: the abbot binds whom he wishes and when he wishes to these, or, releasing them, shows them mercy. Continuous exercise is that held by the leader of the flock—I mean the abbot—and to him it is said: “You shall eat the labors of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” [Col. 0682B].

Moreover, he is bound by two chains. The first is the profession of obedience; the second, love of his order. He opened his mouth in a vow and bound himself. Animals are bound by ropes; human beings by words. But if he does not love his order, he is no longer Simon son of John. Simon is the Cyrenian who was compelled to carry Jesus’ cross. He is the wheel of the cart that carries hay and always murmurs.

Indeed, his side is every habit of living according to one’s own will; and this is a very great bond. For in life it is difficult to abandon what has become habitual. If these habits are struck—that is, if the numbness of the teeth resulting from the eating of sour grapes is removed—the chains fall from his hands. I do not say that they cease to exist, but that they no longer weigh upon him [Col. 0682C]; now the bonds have become ornaments. Hence it is said of Wisdom: “Put your feet into her fetters” (Ecclus. 6:25), “and they shall become ornaments for you.” Now his prison has become a house in which he may say: “This is my rest for ever and ever; here will I dwell, because I have chosen it” (Ps. 132:14). If anyone calls him out, he will say: “I will not follow you; ‘I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?’” (Song 5:3).

He prefers to sit in the cloister rather than walk in the marketplace; to read in silence rather than chatter amid laughter; to pray or meditate in church rather than go to watch a spectacle in the street. Thus, in some way, he has been released from prison and chains. Yet he is still in the natural prison. For while we are away from the Lord, we endure exile, and besides this, bonds and prisons. The spirit must wait, act manfully, and be strengthened until he comes who confined it, who, standing at the door of the prison, knocks and says: “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11:43); “Friend, go up higher” (Luke 14:10).

[Col. 0682D] When he has entered, he will hear from the Lord: “Well done, good and faithful servant: because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21). May Jesus Christ our Lord bring us with you into that joy when he comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## LXXI. A SINGLE SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF THE EXALTATION OF THE HOLY CROSS

> [Note: [Col. 0683D] From Victorinus.]

[Col. 0683A]

“The word of the cross is indeed foolishness to those who are perishing; but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God” (1 Cor. 1:18).

Since, dearest brothers, we are about to speak to believers concerning the mystery of the cross, we do not believe that you will judge it foolishness for us to preach to you a crucified God. But to unbelievers, to whom God has not revealed the hidden things of his counsel—to those who are perishing, as the Apostle says—it is foolishness to preach that God, the creator and immortal ruler of all things, died and was hung upon so vile a punishment as the cross was at that time.

But to those who are being saved—that is, believers, to whom God through the Holy Spirit has granted knowledge of the majesty of his mercy—the word of the cross appears not merely not a disgrace, but even the greatest power of God [Col. 0683B]. Hear again the Apostle saying that the Lord’s cross appeared a disgrace, scandal, and foolishness to unbelievers: “We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. 1:23). It was a stumbling block to the Jews because they were said to have crucified their Lord when they were mocked by the Gentiles. To the Gentiles it was reckoned folly because it seemed impossible to them that God should die.

Let us hear how great a power of God it was that he so humbled himself for us, and how necessary it was. A certain change had taken place between God and human beings through the sin of the first man. For whereas man had first been like God by beholding innocently, he was made unlike him through guilt. Since the old man thereafter was evil, he was made like the beasts, as the Psalmist says: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. 48:13). Man was in honor when he was like God. He did not understand when he sinned. Therefore he was made like the beasts when sin made him irrational.

Two creatures had sinned: the devil and man. But the one sinned by himself, the other through another. Since, therefore, the devil sinned by himself, he did not deserve restoration, especially because he remained of such subtle and spiritual essence. But man [Col. 0683D], since he was made from mud and was deceived by so crafty a tempter, did not lose hope of pardon.

Therefore, when God and man stood thus opposed, and yet hope of pardon and redemption ought not to be denied by so just a judge, divine providence considered the most equitable means of reconciliation. Reason requires that one who wishes to unite two opposites should set between them such a mediator as has affinity with both. Since on the one side was so great a God, and on the other so small a human being, they had to be reconciled through such a mediator as would be both God and man. Therefore, by a just judgment, God, wishing to reconcile the human race, became man. Had he wished to redeem angels, he would have assumed an angelic nature; but because he judged human beings alone worthy of redemption, he reasonably assumed human nature and the person of a servant.

[Col. 0684A] He ordered these things by divine dispensation. For beforehand he prefigured his coming by many symbols and foretold it in many prophecies, so that he might be authoritative, having been signified beforehand over so many ages. But let us speak of many other things and increase our faith through the things of old.

When the children of Israel, because of their sins, were afflicted and slain in the wilderness by fiery serpents, the Lord commanded that a bronze serpent be made and raised on a pole before the children of Israel. Those wounded by the other serpents, when they looked upon it, were restored to health through its aid (Num. 21). The Lord himself makes clear that he intended to be understood through this figure, when he says in the Gospel: “As Moses raised up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be raised up” (John 3:14).

The serpent contains a twofold signification. It is a venomous and a shrewd animal. When struck, it hides its head; and lest it hear the enchanter’s voice, it presses one ear to the ground and stops the other with its tail. It is taken in a good sense when it is said: “Be prudent as serpents” (Matt. 10:16); and in a bad sense when it is said to the Jews: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?” (Luke 3:7). Thus the serpent signifies the Lord insofar as it is prudent, because he himself is the wisdom of the Father; it signifies the devil insofar as it is venomous [Col. 0684C]. For the Lord wished to be denoted by a serpent because he was about to fight against spiritual serpents. Through the material of bronze, Christ’s strength is described. The serpent was of bronze, because two things are necessary in war: strength and prudence. Therefore, since he was the true David—that is, “strong of hand”—who was to fight against Goliath, that is, the devil, he is rightly described as bronze, as strong; rightly, too, as a serpent, as prudent. It is set upon the summit of a rod—that is, it is suspended upon the height of the cross. Those wounded by other serpents, that is, by demons, through sinning, look upon the true serpent, that is, the prudent one; through believing and doing good they are saved, freed from the poisons of sins.

Hear also a figure more plainly denoting the mystery of the Incarnation [Col. 0684D]. Abraham had an only son, namely Isaac, whom the Lord, testing him, commanded him to sacrifice upon a mountain that he would show him. Abraham saddled his ass, taking two young men with him; Isaac gathered the wood; and at last, on the third day, he reached the place. Then he said to his servants: “Wait here with the ass; and after we have worshipped, we shall return to you. Therefore he took the wood and placed it upon his son, while he himself carried the fire and the sword” (Gen. 22:5). And when he had prepared his son, he placed him upon the pile of wood; and, as he was willing to sacrifice his son, the Angel said to him: “Do not stretch out your hand over the boy” (ibid., v. 12). [Col. 0685A] Then Abraham, looking back, saw a ram caught by its horns among the brambles, and sacrificed it in place of his son.

Abraham signifies God the Father, who sacrificed his Son by sending and delivering him. Hence the Apostle: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up to death” (Rom. 8:32). Abraham is interpreted “father of many nations.” Isaac signifies Christ, whose name is interpreted “joy.” Christ indeed is the joy of human beings and angels. The two young men who went with him are the Jewish people. They are said to be two because, after Solomon’s death, they were divided into two kingdoms: the ten tribes of Israel, over which Jeroboam ruled; and the two other tribes, Benjamin and Judah, over which Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, reigned. The ass, moreover, denotes the folly [Col. 0685B] of the Jews; the wood, the cross; the third day, his coming to the place, because Christ was sacrificed in the third age of the world, under grace. Isaac carried the wood, and Christ carried his cross. The Jews still wait with the ass, because, remaining in their folly, they could not attain to the understanding of the holy Trinity.

Nor was Isaac sacrificed, because the divinity—that is, the Son of God, or eternal Word—was not sacrificed; but the ram, that is, Christ’s flesh, which was caught in the brambles, that is, in tribulations, by its horns, that is, by arms outstretched on the cross. This cross, prefigured by so many temporal figures, finally became the salvation of the world. There is a reason why the Lord chose this kind of suffering rather than another: in one respect it is fourfold [Col. 0685C], as though embracing the four quarters of the world; and in another respect a further signification is contained in its parts. Its height signifies the hope of salvation that we have in heaven; its breadth, charity extended even to enemies; its length, perseverance in good works; its depth—that is, the part which lies hidden—the profound mysteries of God’s judgments. Hence the Apostle: “Your judgments, O Lord, are incomprehensible” (Rom. 11:33). The Apostle alludes to this mystery when he says: “That you may be able to understand with all the saints what is the length and breadth and height and depth” (Eph. 3:18).

Therefore we must all venerate this cross, upon which hung the price of the world. The price was given for all of us, if we are willing to depart from vices. Today it was exalted [Col. 0685D] in Jerusalem. Let us likewise exalt it in each church, so that it may commonly be salvation to us, through the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit unto ages of ages. Amen.

## LXXII. A SINGLE SERMON ON THE PRAISES OF THE HOLY CROSS

> [Note: [Col. 0685D] From the Angers manuscript.]

> “If I am lifted up, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

Humble and meek David, strong of hand and desirable in appearance, and despised by his brothers before his exaltation—namely Christ the Lord, rejected by the Jews—says this, signifying by what death he was to die [Col. 0686A], namely the death of the cross. Elsewhere he says: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14). Touching upon the shadow of the legal history, he discloses its mystery and spiritual meaning.

For Moses relates in Numbers (ch. 21) that, when the children of Israel were struck by fiery serpents in the wilderness, the Lord provided for them by commanding that a bronze serpent be raised upon a piece of wood; those who looked upon it were healed of the bites of serpents. The serpent suspended upon the wood is Christ: a serpent because mortal; bronze because immortal—mortal according to his humanity, immortal according to his divinity. For through the serpent’s persuasion humanity fell into the condemnation of death [read: *fell*]. Accordingly, a serpent was fittingly lifted up upon the wood as a sign of that very death [Col. 0686B]. What, then, hung there except the Lord’s death?

This is Moses’ serpent, which devoured the serpents of Pharaoh’s magicians (Exod. 4). This is the serpent at which Moses was terrified and fled. For, at the Lord’s command, he threw his rod upon the ground; when it was changed into a serpent, he fled. But again, at the Lord’s command, he took hold of its tail, and it returned to a rod. The rod is the power of divinity; the serpent, Christ’s mortality. Since death entered through a serpent, mortality is rightly signified by it. Thus, the rod in the serpent is Christ in death. Moses was terrified and fled because, when Christ died, the disciples were terrified and withdrew from the hope in which they had stood, according to the words: “My eyes failed while hoping in my God” (Ps. 68:4, LXX). Again: “I looked to the right [Col. 0686C] and saw, and there was none who knew me” (Ps. 141:5). And Isaiah says: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me” (Isa. 63:3).

But when the tail was seized, the serpent returned to a rod, because he who was first slain later, when all things had been accomplished, returned by resurrection to what he had been before. For through the resurrection God was made known: when death had been consumed by life, nothing serpent-like appeared in him. Hence after the resurrection he says: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 18:28).
