And the Apostle, saying that he was exalted because of the humility of his Passion, says: “And he gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. 2:9). “The name” does not mean that he had not previously had a name and all power [Col. 0686D]; rather, what he had previously possessed in hiddenness was, after the resurrection, set forth openly. And so the serpent returned to a rod, because God was made known in death.

Therefore he was a serpent by mortality, and bronze—or a rod—by the unchangeableness of divinity. This rod cast upon the earth and made into a serpent devoured the serpents of the Egyptian magicians, because the Son of God, made flesh, after the dignity of glory had become obedient unto death; through the very death of his flesh he destroyed the serpent’s dreadful wound [variant reading: “he rendered void the dreadful wound of the serpent”], and consumed death and death’s sting, according to the words: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell!” (Hos. 13:14).

Moses’ rod, by which Egypt is subdued and Pharaoh overcome, may also be understood as the cross [Col. 0687A] of Christ, by which the world is conquered and the ruler of this world, together with the principalities and powers, is defeated. For the serpent is customarily used for wisdom and prudence. Hence: “Be prudent as serpents” (Matt. 10:16). And elsewhere: “The serpent was more prudent [Vulgate: *crafty*] than all animals” (Gen. 3:1). Thus the cast-down rod becomes a serpent and devours the serpents of the Egyptian magicians, because the cross of Christ—whose preaching seemed foolish, and which Moses, that is, the Law, contains, according to the words, “For he wrote of me” (John 5:46)—is transformed into wisdom so great that it devours all the wisdom of Egypt, that is, of this world.

Look upon it: God made the wisdom of this world foolish after he made manifest Christ crucified, the power of God and [Col. 0687B] the wisdom of God, who said: “I shall catch the wise in their craftiness. [Note: [Col. 0687D] This gives the Apostle’s sense, not his words.] Where is the learned man? Where is he who weighs the words of the law? Where is the teacher of little children?” (1 Cor. 1:19). The princes of Zoan became foolish; Pharaoh’s counselors were made senseless. Good was such a transformation, by which the rod passed into a serpent and the serpent returned to a rod. Yet the faithless, not understanding it, broke out into reproaches, according to the words: “Your enemies reproached, O Lord; they reproached the transformation of Christ” (Ps. 88:52). They reproached, that is, the fact that Christ died; yet this is not to be reproached but venerated. For this is to be changed from temporal life to eternal life, from earth to heaven, from the Jews to [Col. 0687C] the Gentiles. This is the change of the right hand of the Most High.

Therefore life [read: *rod*] had to be changed into a serpent and afterward return to a rod, because Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead: to suffer for the blotting out of our sins and to rise for the completion of our justification. As Isaiah says: “He was wounded for our iniquities; he was bruised for our crimes” (Isa. 53:5). And again: “By his bruise we have been healed” (ibid.).

Behold the true Isaac with the wood, and Abraham with the ram caught among brambles. For Isaac is divinity; Abraham, God the Father; the ram, humanity; the wood, the cross; the rod, the brambles of Jewish malice; the thorns of which the Prophet says: “They flamed up like fire among thorns” (Ps. 117:12), because, kindled by the torches of envy and blinded by the error of malice, they raged against Christ [Col. 0687D]. The ram, however, was caught among brambles in Isaac’s stead. Isaac was not offered because it was not divinity but humanity, laboring among the brambles of Jewish malice, that was offered by God’s will.

Therefore Christ is serpent and ram according to the flesh: serpent because mortal; ram because offered, and because with the horns of the cross he defeated the aerial powers, concerning whom it is said: “Horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden” (Hab. 3:4). Indeed, in the horns of the cross his strength did not fail but was hidden. For he conquered secretly, though outwardly he appeared conquered. Hence Ambrose says: “The flesh about to perish cries out at the separation [Col. 0688A] of divinity.” For death could not be there unless life departed. Yet the divinity is not said to have been separated from him with respect to the natural union that existed between God and man, but with respect to the manifestation of divine power. For there he did not display divine power, but hid it, because, as Isaiah testifies: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he was silent and did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7). He did not exercise strength there, but concealed it, setting before them flesh, mortal flesh, upon which they might rage. “For if they had known,” as the Apostle says, “they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

Yet some of the Jews knew something of him, just as certain demons were not ignorant of some things concerning him. Both the demons and the wise among the Jews knew him to be the Messiah foretold in the Law and the Prophets; but they did not know that he was God, or the Son of God. The demons did not foresee that by his death they would lose their power, nor did the Jews foresee that they would lose their place and nation [Col. 0688B]. They did not perceive that they were being conquered where they supposed themselves to conquer. But the lesser people did not even know him to be the Messiah. All were blinded because they hated the truth; nor did they understand truth itself, so as to foresee the last things.

They deserved this through the pride of their will, whose will was so proud that they denied their need of divine help. Yet some were enlightened out of that blindness; some were freed out of that mass of Gentile perdition and mercifully regarded by the Lord—namely those for whom he prayed upon the cross, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23:34). These were the lesser people among that people, who persecuted the Lord not from envy but from zeal, having zeal for God, though not according to knowledge. They thought that they were rendering service to God. Of them Peter says: “I know, brothers, that you did this through ignorance” (Acts 3:17) [Col. 0688C]. They, therefore, were distinguished from that utterly evil body when the Lord deigned to pray for them, fulfilling what he had taught: “Pray,” he says, “for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. 5:44).

Behold great charity, immense compassion: returning good for evil, blessing for cursing. There are six distinctions in the rendering of good and evil, and among all the others two excel, and one excels among all. The first two are to return good for good and evil for evil. Another two are not to return good for good and to return evil for good. Another two are not to return evil for evil and to return good for evil; these excel among the others. But among all, that excels by which good is returned for evil—the thing Christ did. Upon the cross he prayed for his persecutors: reckoned among criminals, crucified for sinners. As he says through the Prophet: “In return for their loving me, my enemies slandered me; but I prayed” (Ps. 107:4).

Thus divinity is not without reason said to have been separated, because there [Col. 0689A] he did not reveal the arm of his strength or the light of his divinity. There appeared what he had taken from his mother, and there was hidden what he had taken from the Father. As a figure of this, it was commanded in Leviticus (ch. 16) that the high priest take two goats: one for sacrifice and the other *apopompeios*, that is, the goat sent away. He was to set the latter alive before the Lord and, after prayer had been made over it, send it into the wilderness. In the two goats, both natures of Christ are indicated. In the sacrificial goat, the human nature; in the sent-away goat, the divine. That goat is sacrificed; this one, with the sins of the people and prayers poured out over it, is sent into the wilderness, because Christ is crucified according to one nature and, according to the other, is invoked by prayers to be merciful toward our iniquities; and he proceeds into solitude [Col. 0689B]—that is, into the bosom of the Father, to which no one comes except he himself and the Holy Spirit.

He went, therefore, into solitude: that is, he restrained and concealed the power of working, and bore our iniquities, not in order to possess them but to consume them. “For our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24). Thus at the time of the Passion the divinity is said to have gone into solitude, that is, into heaven, not by changing place but by in some manner restraining its power, so that the ungodly might complete the Passion. The Jews therefore appeared temporarily to prevail, but in truth they were conquered. “For they entered into the lower parts of the earth,” as the Prophet says, “and became portions of foxes” (Ps. 62:11): because inwardly they were blinded and outwardly were led captive; inwardly they were swallowed by the abyss of earthly desire; outwardly they were reduced to miserable slavery beneath the rulers of the world [Col. 0689C], who are compared to foxes, according to the words: “Tell that fox” (Luke 13:32).

Thus the Jews who rejoiced that they had conquered were struck by the cross’s hidden strength, just as Jacob, wrestling with the angel (Gen. 32), prevailed against him but was struck by him in the thigh and limped. For the sinew of his thigh withered, because the Jewish people descended from Jacob seemed physically to prevail against Christ; but, their sinew struck, they limped, because, their minds blinded, they lost the straight steps of faith and truth. The Jews, therefore, were conquered in the horns of the cross; for there death was destroyed and the devil defeated. Hence the same canticle continues: “Death shall go before his face” (Hab. 3:4). And likewise: “The devil shall go forth before his feet” (ibid.) [Col. 0689D].

Consider the Redeemer’s victory, which he accomplished [variant: *procured*] through the cross’s hidden power. In one encounter he defeated three kinds of enemies, according to the words: “You struck the head from the house of the ungodly” (ibid., 3:13). He destroyed death, according to the words: “I shall be your death, O death!” (Hos. 13:14). He was about to fight against proud Goliath, that is, the devil, but was not afraid. Rather, hastening joyfully, as though to combat, and advancing as though setting an army in motion against the strong one, he came forth from the highest heaven and “set his tent in the sun” (Ps. 18:6). For he came forth ineffably before the ages from equality with the Father and entered the world. Going forth from the Father to fight the strong one, he came into the world without abandoning him and without changing place [Col. 0690A]. Thus he says: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16:28). He came where he already was, because he was in the world and the world was made through him; but he appeared visibly where he had not previously appeared.

Coming, moreover, he prepared for himself a suitable place to fight. For he “set his tent in the sun” (Ps. 18:6), namely the dispensation of the flesh, in which he came to overthrow this world’s errors and wage war against the ruler of the world. A tent is a military dwelling; and the Son of God, fighting in flesh against the ruler of darkness, set his tent not in darkness but “in the sun.” The sun does three things: it burns, gives light, and distinguishes times. In burning, toil—that is, the anguish of the Passion—is suggested; in light, manifestation; in the distinction of times, temporal change [Col. 0690B]. Therefore Christ set the tent of his flesh in the sun: that is, in labor, openly, and under temporal change, according to the words: “I have labored, enduring” (Jer. 6:11); and again, “I have labored, crying aloud” (Ps. 68:4). Openly, because a lamp does not come to be hidden under a bushel, but to be placed upon a lampstand, that it may give light to all who are in the house. Under temporal variation, because he advanced through the successive stages of age, according to the words: “Jesus advanced in age and wisdom” (Luke 2:52).

Thus he “set his tent in the sun” in order to fight proud Goliath, that is, the devil. He entered the contest with him in order to free the poor from the powerful, and the poor person who had no helper—that is, to rescue the human race from the devil’s hand. It was not his own power but our sins that had made him strong [Col. 0690C]. He usurped dominion over us not through his own strength but through our weakness—that is, through the perversity of our desire—according to the words: “Do not hand me over, O Lord, to the sinner according to my desire” (Ps. 139:9). Upon the cross he freed from that powerful one the poor person who had no helper, because neither angel nor patriarch nor any human being was able to free the poor from the powerful one, except the one chosen from thousands: namely the lion from the tribe of Judah. On the altar of the cross he fulfilled at once the office of king and priest: of king, because he fought and conquered; of priest, because he offered and made propitiation. He offered no victim other than himself, and made propitiation to no God other than himself. In offering, he fought; in fighting, he offered himself. By offering himself, he rescued the needy, destitute, and poor person from the hand of those stronger than he [Col. 0690D], that is, from the demonic powers—namely the human race, which is like one needy person: needy morally, because in labor and sweat it seeks its bread; poor, because, cast out from the purity of wisdom, it possessed an empty and shadowy wisdom.

Therefore the Son of Man had to be lifted up upon the wood, not only to conquer the devil but also to draw all things to himself: to himself, that they might love him, imitate him, and reign with him. They are to love him because he first loved us, so that we might love him. Before the foundation of the world he loved us with the sweetness of his charity, and in time he displayed the supreme affection of charity, laying down his life for the redemption of many. “For no one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13) [Col. 0691A]. Thus, by laying down his life as the most health-giving pattern of example, he drew us into love for himself.

He also instructed us to imitate him through the manner of his death. For he who died because he willed it, and when he willed it, also died as he willed it. The Savior did not choose this manner of death in vain, although he was able to depart this life in another way. Since it was within his power to die or not die, and to die in this way or that, he did not choose the cross in vain: he chose it in order to crucify us to this world, he who said, “Take up your cross and follow me.” For as long as the body of sin is being destroyed, the outward person is decaying so that the inward person may be renewed; for us it is the time of the cross.

Therefore in this life a Christian ought always to hang upon the cross [Col. 0691B], not in body but in spirit; not in flesh but in mind. By the spiritual nails of God’s commandments, we must have our limbs fastened, so that they may not be moved toward evils, from which we ought so perfectly to rest that neither their sight nor their remembrance touches our minds. Whatever was done upon the cross was likewise done in the burial, so that the Christian life may be conformed to these things. Christ’s eyes grew dim upon the cross, so that our eyes may turn away from seeing vanity; his ears were opened to blasphemies and insults, so that our ears may be opened to the cries of the poor. Christ tasted vinegar and gall upon the cross so that we may be strong to bear the bitterness of suffering and patiently endure evil people with us, without conforming ourselves to them. For Christ too, having tasted it, would not drink, signifying that such people—old and evil people—are to be endured but not imitated. In this also he signified that strength [variant: *fearfulness*] in tribulation must not silence the word of preaching.

Christ’s hands were stretched out on the cross, so that our contracted hands might learn to give what is theirs to the needy and to enemies [variant: “so that our hands might learn to give what is theirs to the needy, and never be closed to them, or even to enemies”] [Col. 0691C]. His feet were fastened to the cross with nails, so that our wandering feet might be directed in God’s way. Thus he wished to be lifted up upon the cross not in vain, but so that, according to the four divisions of the cross, by which the four regions of the world are signified, he might draw all things to himself for love, imitation, and reigning together with him. “All things” means not stones and wood, but every kind of human being, peoples of every age. For all, both those who came before and those who followed, cried: “Hosanna in the highest” (Mark 11:10), because none before or after the Incarnation could be saved without faith in the mediator between God and human beings.

For he is the man in Ezekiel who marks *tau* upon the foreheads of all persons who are saved. “There came,” he says, “six men from the way of the upper gate, which faces north, and each had an instrument of destruction in his hand. There was also one man among them clothed in linen, with a writer’s inkhorn at his loins [Col. 0692A], to whom the Lord said: ‘Pass through the middle of the city and mark *tau* upon the foreheads of those who groan and mourn over all the abominations.’ And he said to those who followed: ‘Pass through the middle of the city and strike. But do not kill anyone upon whom you see *tau*’” (Ezek. 9:2).

Consider carefully, brothers, how great this man is who marks the others, and who the six men are who come to him. The six men are the peoples of the six ages, who come from the way of the upper gate. The gate is the Law of the Lord, by which a person is directed and taught the paths of justice in order to enter life. Hence the Prophet: “Open to me the gates of justice; this is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Ps. 117:19). There is, however, a lower gate and an upper gate. The upper—that is, earlier—gate is the natural law; the lower—that is, later—gate is the written law, which faces north and does not deliver from the north. The first parent was the first transgressor of the natural law [Col. 0692B]. The written law, moreover, enclosed all under a curse.

When the first parent, by first sinning, harmed all people in himself through disobedience and transgression, he also condemned all his posterity and subjected it to death until the coming [of Christ]: “For death reigned,” as the Apostle says, “from Adam to Moses” (Rom. 5:14)—that is, until the Law, and even under the Law—because neither natural law nor written law was able to take away death’s dominion. Thus the six men came from the way of the upper gate—that is, the peoples of the six ages—from the way of the natural law, not merely of the written law, seeking the salvation they had found in neither law. Each had in his hand an instrument of destruction—that is, of grief—because the entrance to heaven lay open to none; and of sin, because they had not only been corrupted in the apostate root but had also added their own offenses [Col. 0692C]. “For all have sinned,” as the Apostle says, “and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:13). Hence Jacob mourns that his gray hairs are to be brought down with sorrow to the underworld.

But one man came among them, clothed in linen down to the ankles: namely Christ, who came in the sixth age for the redemption of the world. He is distinguished from the rest by a certain unique power. Of him the Prophet says: “Will not Zion say: ‘A man, and a man, was born in her; and the Most High himself founded her’?” (Ps. 86:5). No human being can say—that is, persuade—Zion, namely the Synagogue, that a man has been born in her and that the Most High himself founded her. The faithless Synagogue does not receive this. Yet this is the one of whom Moses says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord God, God is one” (Deut. 6:4); and the Apostle: “One God, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4:5). This one was clothed in linen down to the ankles, in whom the purity and perfection of humanity are signified. For the ankle is the extreme part of the human being, the body’s end. Therefore Christ’s ankle-length linen garment is perfect humanity [Col. 0692D], immune from every vice and full of truth and grace, and a sacrifice sufficient for human redemption. Hence the Prophet says: “But you have prepared a body for me.”

This is the red heifer [or cow] (Num. 19), in which there was no blemish and which had not drawn a yoke. It was burned outside the camp; from its ashes was made water for sprinkling, for the cleansing of the unclean [Col. 0693A]. The red heifer is Christ’s weak flesh, reddened by the blood of the Passion. Hence: “Why is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread the winepress?” (Isa. 63:2). To the angels who ask thus, Christ replies: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me” (Isa. 63:3). The winepress is the pressure of the Passion, which the Son of Man is said not merely to have endured but to have trodden. In the word “treading,” he suggests two things: endurance and victory. For he so endured death that, by enduring it, he conquered and destroyed it. Hence in Lamentations: “The Lord trod the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah” (Lam. 1:15).

Rightly, therefore, was the heifer red, because it was dyed with the blood of the Passion. Hence Jacob, in blessing Judah, says in a figure of Christ: “He will wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of grapes” (Gen. 49:11) [Col. 0693B]. It was burned outside the camp because Christ was crucified outside the city gate at the place of Calvary. From its ashes was made water for sprinkling, by which baptism was signified. Through it people were cleansed from contact with the dead, because through Christ’s baptism we are cleansed from the iniquity and deathliness of this dying life. That water was sprinkled with hyssop, which signified the humility of Christ’s Passion, because our redemption is completed through faith in the Passion and the water of washing. Hence John says in his Catholic Epistle: “Jesus Christ is he who came through water and blood” (1 John 5:6).

For just as the Israelites were delivered from the destroying angel through the blood of the lamb and the passage of the Red Sea, so the Church is saved especially by these sacraments of blood and water [Col. 0693C]. Thus, in the Passion, blood and water flowed from Christ’s side as he slept on the cross: the blood of redemption and the water of washing, which are the mysteries of our salvation. Therefore the water of sprinkling, which derives its power from the blood of redemption, cleanses defilement. This is the stream of water which, in Ezekiel, heals the waters of the Dead Sea and gives life to all that it reaches. For he says: “The waters were descending along the right side of the Temple, to the south of the altar” (Ezek. 47:1). These waters entered the Dead Sea and went out; the waters were healed, and all things to which the stream comes shall live, and there shall be many fish, because these waters came there. In a wondrous manner, dead and unbearable waters [Col. 0693D]—waters without substance, in which nothing can live because they do not know him who says, “I am life” (John 14:6)—are healed by the living waters of the Gospel. Through his stream the created and dead waters have many fish, and everything they reach lives, because that stream springs up into eternal life. Of it Zechariah says: “On that day water shall go out from Jerusalem, and half of it into the first sea, that is, the Dead Sea.”

> [Note: [Col. 0693D] In Zechariah, chapter 14, verse 8, the text reads: “And it shall be on that day: living waters shall go out from Jerusalem, half of them toward the Eastern Sea, [Col. 0694D] and half of them toward the western sea.”]

And Ezekiel says: “Its waters shall go out from the sanctuary, and its fruit shall be for food and its leaves for healing” (Ezek. 47:12). Wondrous in power is the water of sprinkling that heals, feeds, and gives life [Col. 0694A], because it is made from the ashes of the red heifer—that is, the Lord’s flesh, reddened with precious blood.

Behold the ankle-length garment in which that one man was clothed, he who had a writer’s inkhorn at his loins. The loins are the people who come after, who seem as it were to follow. Therefore they rightly signify the followers of truth whom God chose from eternity, foreknowing that they would be conformed to the image of his Son. The writer’s inkhorn, therefore, is the teaching of God the Father, which Christ bore at his loins because he displayed it in the service of his humanity to the whole people, to whom it is said through the Prophet: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one” (Ps. 44:4). And he himself says in the Gospel: “I did not come to send peace but a sword” (Matt. 10:14). Thus the teaching of truth is called a sword [Col. 0694B] because it separates what is carnal from what is spiritual; and an inkhorn because it is spiritually written in the hearts of believers; and a writer’s inkhorn, that is, God the Father’s. Hence he himself says: “My teaching is not mine, but belongs to the Father who sent me” (John 7:16). And elsewhere: “I do not speak from myself” (John 14:10). For he who is not from himself does not act from himself, but speaks from him from whom he is.

When the Lord said to him, “Pass through the city and mark *tau* upon the foreheads of those who groan and mourn over all abominations,” he himself did all things according to the Father’s will. Therefore, when the Father said, “Pass through the city: ‘Mark *tau* upon the foreheads of those who groan and mourn over all abominations’” (Ezek. 9:4), he who was marked [Col. 0694C] by the Father marked others, according to the words: “For him God the Father has marked” (John 6:17), so that he might mark others. He marked *tau*, which has the form of a cross; hence in *tau* the saving sign of the cross is understood.

That he places a sign upon the foreheads of the men who groan, etc.—upon the foreheads, that is, both of body and heart—so that the sign of the cross may shine upon the foreheads both of body and mind: outwardly appearing in the performance of works, and inwardly resplendent in the truth of faith. These are the two doorposts which in Exodus are smeared with the blood of the paschal lamb, so that they may be saved from the destroying angel. “They shall take,” he says, “of the blood of the lamb, and put it upon both doorposts and upon the lintels of the houses” (Exod. XII, 7). The blood is placed upon both doorposts when it is received not only by the mouth of the body but also by the mouth of the mind, and is pondered with an attentive mind for instruction [or imitation]. For whoever so receives the Redeemer’s blood that he is not yet willing to imitate His passion places the blood on one doorpost only, though it must also be placed upon the lintels of the houses. The houses are our minds, in which we dwell through thought. The lintel is intention, which presides over thought and action. Therefore whoever directs the intention of his thought to the imitation of the Passion places the lamb’s blood upon the lintel of the house.

The blood of the lamb placed upon the doorposts of the Israelites thus bears the same mystery [Col. 0695A] as the Tau marked upon the foreheads of the groaning men; and as those were saved by the blood from the destroyer, so these were saved by the Tau from the slaughter of those passing through. For He says: “Do not kill any one upon whom you see the Tau” (Ezek. IX, 6). Those who do not receive this sign perish in eternal death. But those who receive it, set free from the destroyer, merit to live forever. This is the sign of which the Prophet says: “The light of Thy countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us” (Ps. IV, 7).

But who are marked by this light? Those who receive the testimony of the One who marks them, who mark—that is, stamp—their hearts with faith in Him, according to the saying: “He who comes from above is above all; he who receives His testimony has set his seal that God is true” (John III, 31). For he has placed in his heart [Col. 0695B] as it were a special sign—namely, the true God, who came from above for the salvation of humankind. Therefore, those whom He who came from heaven marks, mark their own minds with His character so that they may put their enemies to flight. These are the twelve thousand from each tribe marked in the Apocalypse. The bronze serpent, raised upon the wood, drew these to itself. This is the wood upon which the cluster from the holy land is carried by two men (Num. XIII, 15). This is the wood which Elisha cast into the water in seeking the axe from its handle [variant: “from the table”], and by which it floated (IV Kings VI, 5). This is the tree of life, the sweet wood, which dried up [variant: “cut”] the tree of death.

Therefore upon this wood God-Man was exalted, so that He who is above all might draw all things to Himself: that He might be loved, imitated, and seen—not as He appeared [Col. 0695C] in the form of a servant, but as He is in the form of God. He granted this vision to the confessing thief, saying: “Today thou shalt be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43): by sight, when I shall reveal myself to thee; which is to be in paradise.

[Note: [Col. 0695D] Variant, that is: “And thou whom thou now seest only by sight, today I shall reveal myself face to face [Col. 0696D] to thee”; which is, etc.]

For to be with Him who is life is truly to be in paradise. Hence He promises His own, as a great gift, that they shall be with Him, saying: “Father, those whom Thou hast given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII, 24). He does not simply say, “Where I am, they also may be,” because He Himself is everywhere; but He added “with me,” because even the wretched may be where He is who is absent nowhere, yet not be with Him, because they do not enjoy Him. For only those are blessed who enjoy Him alone; they see Him as He is, because [Col. 0695D] they are not blessed except through Him who is blessedness and eternal life. May He deign to grant this to us. Amen.

LXXIII. FIRST SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS.  
[Note: [Col. 0696D] From the Angers manuscript.]

“I lifted up my eyes unto the mountains, whence help shall come to me” (Ps. CXX, 1).

He who lifts up his eyes does not sleep; he who awaits help labours. Therefore this is the voice of one wakeful and labouring, which you have heard through my mouth. For it is a Song of Degrees, that is, a song of one ascending. But who is it that ascends, and whence does he ascend? Why does he ascend, and whither does he ascend? He ascends from the valley of tears, from the place which the Lord has appointed for him. He ascends from strength unto strength (Ps. LXXXIII); for he has arranged these ascents in his heart. He shall ascend to the triumphant Church, the [militant] daughter to the free mother which is in heaven, until with her he sees the God of gods in Sion (ibid.).

For by the name “degrees” an ascent is signified. Whoever ascends to Him who made all things in weight, number, and measure, and by whose ordinance the day endures, must necessarily ascend step by step and in order. But whoever descends from Him finds ruin and a precipice, not steps. Thus the legion of demons sent into the swine rushed headlong into the sea (Matt. VIII). Indeed, the lament of one descending might be: “I bent my eyes down to dung, whence judgment shall come to me.” Dung denotes the superfluities of temporal things. [Col. 0696B] For the necessary things are the blessings of the Lord’s right hand, by which He feeds human beings and beasts. These are “His left hand under my head.” But of superfluities the Apostle says: “I have judged them to be as dung” (Phil. III, 8). And the Prophet: “Why do you embrace dung instead of saffron?” (Lam. IV, 5). For these defile and burden even when you take food to restore the body naturally: if you pour in anything superfluous, it will be either unpleasant or harmful. Of superfluities the Wise Man says: “They are acquired with labour, possessed with trembling, and lost with sorrow.”

But we promised a song of one ascending, which may properly belong to today’s solemnity, as though the Church were saying: “Throughout the whole course of the year, on fixed and appointed days, [Col. 0696C] I lift my eyes to one, or to some, of the mountains, whence the refuge of intercession shall come to me. Today I lifted my eyes to all the mountains, whence at last help shall come to me.” Sweet indeed is help in tribulation. Therefore, when that day comes—the day of wrath, the day of calamity and misery—they will deliver me from evil tidings and harsh speech. Those whom the heir of the heavenly world now rejoices to have as fathers, at the end he expects as judges, that they may judge the orphan and the humble, lest man continue to exalt himself upon the earth.

It should be noted that many mountains surround the ascending Church: some are good, some evil. To some one must flee, and from others one must flee. To make this clearer, among the many mountains mentioned in Sacred Scripture we select only four, which, as it were, surround the Church militant from east and west, south and north. And because what is carnal comes first and afterward what is spiritual, let us begin from the north. Let Mount Gilboa be in the north; Mount Samaria in the west; Mount Armenia in the south; Mount Israel in the east. Mount Gilboa is the aerial powers; Mount Samaria, the sorrowful hypocrites; Mount Armenia, the true shepherds; Mount Israel, the holy intercessors. The first is a cold world; the second lukewarm; the third hot; the fourth luminous. The first [Col. 0697A] is a wolf; the second a hireling; the third a good shepherd; the fourth a merciful judge. The first seizes in order to kill; the second leads in order to devour; the third strives to guard; the fourth intercedes in order to draw to himself. Therefore the first must be fled; the second endured; the third heard; the fourth implored.

The first must be fled, because Zechariah says: “Ho, ho! Flee from the land of the north, says the Lord” (Zech. II, 6). The second must be endured, because Truth says: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII, 3). The third must be heard, because Moses says: “Ask thy fathers, and they will tell thee; thy elders, and they will declare it to thee” (Deut. XXXII, 7). The fourth must be implored, because the Prophet says: “Praise God in His saints” (Ps. CL, 1).

But because the angel of Satan very often transforms himself into an angel of light, just as a whitewashed wall deceives the eyes of those who look upon it, great diligence must be applied in recognizing them. Yet we have heard Truth teaching and saying to us: “By their fruits you shall know them” (Matt. VII, 20), that is, from past events and daily works. Of events we read in histories; but of works we read in the book of experience. We read that on Mount Gilboa the Philistines prevailed against the people of God, and Saul and Jonathan, greatly beloved, fell there, and the mighty and renowned of Israel [Col. 0697C] were slain together (I Kings XXXI). This is the labour of demons: to cast down God’s people. While the first parents could still say, “We two are a multitude,” terror invaded them from the north, so that they were compelled to make themselves loin-cloths (Gen. III). The demons especially seek the blood of kings and priests, so that, when the shepherd is struck, they may easily scatter the sheep. For, having drained the fountain, they hope that the Jordan may flow into his mouth: “His food is choice food; he eats fine grass like an ox” (Job XL, 10).

Of the mountains of Samaria it is written that the fat cattle of Samaria pastured upon them (Hos. X); they who made golden calves in Dan and Bethel, who turned the people’s heart away to follow foreign gods. These are they who sat upon Moses’ seat, binding unbearable burdens upon the people while themselves unwilling to move them with one finger; who seek milk and wool from the Lord’s flock, but in their breast have less concern for the salvation of souls. [Col. 0697D] What is weak they do not visit; what is broken they do not bind up; what has strayed they do not bring back. But if anything is strong, they slaughter it. Of them the Lord says through the prophet Amos: “Woe to you who are wealthy in Sion, who trust in Mount Samaria, nobles, heads of the peoples, entering the house of Israel in pomp” (Amos VI, 1).

Upon the mountains of Armenia Noah’s ark rested while the waters of the flood still overflowed the earth. These are the true shepherds, ready to lay down their lives for their sheep; who set themselves as a wall for the house of Israel; who bear Noah’s ark—in which clean and unclean are still mingled together—in the midst of the waves, until, when every flood has ceased, the eight souls who are saved with it go forth: that is, all those who are foreordained to the eighth blessing. [Col. 0698A]

On the summit of the mountains of Israel is Mount Moriah, upon which the Temple was built: where are the altar, the sanctuary, and the sanctuary of the sanctuary [variant: “holy of holies”], the ark of the covenant, the mercy-seat and cherubim, king and priest, ephod and diadem, and every temporal sacred thing. These are the blessed spirits who reign with the Lord: namely, that wondrous temple made by Him who made the dawn and the sun, after whose pattern and shadow the Levites and priests served.

Having considered the ancient events of the mountains, we may also behold their daily works, which become known when their riders are seen. For upon the first mountain sit four dangerous smiths; [Col. 0698B] upon the second, four ridiculous men; upon the third, four glorious men; upon the fourth, the King of glory—not now with feet and face veiled, as Isaiah saw Him, but with unveiled face seen by those who believed in Him. Zechariah indeed saw (chap. I) four horns that had come to scatter Judah and Jerusalem, and four smiths to crush the horns. But we, with due respect to the Prophet, interpret the smiths as scattering Judah and Jerusalem—the men of whom the Church says: “Sinners have built upon my back; they have prolonged their iniquity” (Ps. CXXVIII, 3). For from the beginning of the hidden Church, she has been placed between hammer and anvil; and from the blood of righteous Abel to the end of the world, iniquity pressing down and justice suffering have not been, and will not be, lacking.

How dangerous these smiths are we judge from their blasts. The first emits a spirit of fire; the second, a spirit of sulphur; the third, a spirit of darkness; the fourth, a spirit of storms. Although they have never ceased to blow, nevertheless in the age of the martyrs the spirit of fire especially harmed land and sea, when faithful men were proscribed in exile, afflicted with tortures, and slain by elaborate deaths. In the time of heretics the spirit of sulphur raged, because heretics with their most evil exhalations infected almost the whole air, of whom it is written: “Their throat is an open grave; they dealt deceitfully with their tongues; the poison of asps is under their lips” (Ps. V, 11).

But in the time [Col. 0698D] of false brethren, which is now in progress, the spirit of darkness rules, while the brood of vipers barks within the bowels and shakes the sides of its mother. They have indeed an appearance of godliness, but devote themselves to works of ungodliness; they confess, or profess, the Christian name, yet, so far as lies in them, break the unity of Christianity. They are rotten members in the Church, and because of their decay one must fear lest the sound part be drawn away. But in the days of Antichrist the spirit of storms will blow: that is, a persecution compounded of all these, in which, if it were possible, even the elect would be shaken.

A certain Father saw in the spirit four men sitting upon the mountains of Samaria. “I saw,” he says, “a spirit with swollen cheeks chewing the sand of the sea-shore. The second, lying upon a blazing furnace, swallowed into his throat the sparks flying out from it. The third, sitting upon the pinnacle of the Temple, joyfully received with open mouth the breath of a gentle breeze, and, to make it flow in more abundantly, stirred the air with his hand and a fan. The fourth laughed at each of them, though he himself was no less laughable than the others; for he laboured to suck the flesh of his own limbs, now applying his hand, now his arm, now his foot, now his shin to his mouth.” Drawing nearer, I considered their faces, terrible to behold because of their incomparable leanness, and asked why they did this. I learned that they suffered from an unspeakable hunger, and that saying of the Prophet occurred to me: “My strength is dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. XXI, 16), “because I forgot to eat my bread.”

The unspeakable hunger [Col. 0699B] of these men is a fourfold cupidity: of wealth, goods, vain glory, and pleasures. Natural hunger may be greatly refreshed by food, though not extinguished. But this hunger always opens new gulfs. The greedy lover of wealth never says, “Enough.” He is the one who chews sand. The powerful tyrant, like a leech, thirsts insatiably for blood; and this one greedily draws sparks into himself through desire for vain glory, so as to swallow the whole air, and he would endure no remedy. Even a philosopher among the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0699D] Perhaps Seneca.] declared the man given to pleasure contemptible and comparable to swine. Lovers of such things are found on the mountains of Samaria even beneath ashes and haircloth.

There are chariots which rest upon the mountains of Armenia: namely, Elijah’s chariot [variant: “Helpe”], the chariot of Amminadab, [Col. 0699C] and the new cart upon which the ark of the Lord was brought back from the land of the Philistines: “The chariot of God is manifold by ten thousands, thousands of rejoicing ones; the Lord is among them, in Sinai, in the sanctuary” (Ps. LXVII, 18). These are virgins; those continent after a fall; prelates; and married persons. For the virginal chariot is fiery and carries one upward, because it bears the fiery—that is, the star-like; indeed, it is angelic—to live in the flesh above the flesh; to be in the flesh and not do the things of the flesh, where a man does violence to himself and nature suffers refusal.

But the chariot of Amminadab, whose name means “spontaneous of the Lord,” consists of those who after a fall bind themselves by a vow of continence. Of these the bride says that her soul is disturbed by fear; but concerning them one must first fear lest they return [variant: “be recalled, or fly back”] to their accustomed ways. For it is hard to abandon what is customary, and it is almost impossible to triumph over the flesh if it has first triumphed over us.

The new cart, drawn by lowing cows as far as the field of Joshua the Bethlehemite (I Kings VI), signifies ecclesiastical teachers, who fill the ends of the earth with their lowings until they bring the Church which they bear, turning neither to the right nor to the left, into Joshua’s field: namely, until the faithful become heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, as He Himself says: “Father, I will that where I am, there also my servant may be” (John XII, 26).

But the chariot of God, manifold by ten thousands, signifies married persons, [Col. 0700A] whose multitude is abundant in the Church of God, and who also pursue the multiplication of humankind, according to what was said in the beginning: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. I, 22).

Upon the mountains of Israel sits our [Saviour, or fountain], watering them from His heights and sending from them certain drops that drip upon the earth. The ascending Church, as though lightly bedewed by these, cries out among the surrounding mountains, declaring what it thinks of them: “I turned my eyes away from the mountains of Gilboa, whence shipwreck comes to me. I bent my eyes toward the mountains of Armenia, whence help sometimes comes to me. I fixed my eyes upon the mountains of Armenia, whence consolation comes to me. I lifted my eyes to the mountains [Col. 0700B] of Israel, whence help shall come to me.”

This song may also be understood spiritually: it is the response of a contemplative and cloistered man against the mockery of someone living in the world, who insults him for his lowliness, because he chose to be in the house of the Lord rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.

“I, placing my hope in the uncertainty of riches, whose god is the belly and whose glory is in shame, assail the poor monk with intolerable taunts, saying: ‘Why do you despise the riches of this world? Do you not know that Job, abundant in flocks and herds, was singularly commended by the Lord in these words: “Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth?”’ (Job I, 8). Has David, king and prophet, escaped your memory—he who surpassed all men of his time in wealth, and of whom the Lord said: ‘I have found a man according to my heart’? Are you unaware that riches are the material for alms, which the Lord, desiring obedience to His commands, mentions when He says: ‘Give alms, and behold, all things are clean to you’ (Luke II, 41)? Hear the Lord’s forerunner: when a multitude of sinners flocked to him as he baptized, asking what they needed to do, he did not say, “Fast, keep vigil, pray, flee far away, and remain in solitude”; but he said: “He who has two tunics, let him give to him who has none” (Luke III, 11), and let him do likewise with food.

“Furthermore, brother, what do you condemn in marriage? Why do you shrink from marriage, commended to Adam, newly made, as the first-fruits of all sacraments? Satan seems, as though stealthily, to have introduced [Col. 0700D] continence in order to restore his entrails to Pentapolis. Abraham, an old man faithful in person, pleased God in marriage, so much so that he received a son against hope, in hope of the coming blessing. Through Jacob he is commended for the multiplication of children, entering Egypt with seventy souls. Christ Himself was unwilling to be born of a virgin unless she were married. Why do you flee from this common cohabitation of humankind? If you serve God as a soldier, let your good works shine before men, that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

Against these things, cloistered man, do not contend with words; but modestly, as is fitting, [Col. 0701A] add: “Brother, you speak truly. There are many paths to God, but some are safer for some than others. There are valleys and hills through which you teach that one must travel by a long road; I seek shortcuts, and therefore I lifted up my eyes unto the mountains, whence help shall come to me. For my chief captain, Christ, showed me two mountains more eminent than the rest: humility and obedience. Hear the eminence of humility: ‘Whoever wishes to be greatest among you, let him be the servant of all’ (Matt. XX, 26). And elsewhere the Lord says: ‘The smaller thou art in thine own eyes, the greater thou shalt be in mine.’ Consider obedience: ‘The Lord became obedient unto death, even death on the cross; wherefore God also exalted Him and gave Him a name which is above every name’ (Phil. II, 8).

“By these most lofty mountains Christ leaped forth to run the way; I wish to follow Him as He runs, with greater ease. Riches are good, but burdensome. Alexander of Macedon, to pursue the enemy more swiftly, cast down his burdensome riches in the desert. Indeed, in marriage, as also in little Zoar, I can be saved; but I observe that Lot rather ascended the mountains in order to save his soul.”

Yet I still taunt the cloistered man: “What you say is good, except that you place your hope only in the future when you say, ‘Whence help shall come to me.’ ‘Shall come’ is a delaying phrase, a raven’s cry. It is also good to rejoice in the enjoyment of present things, because God provides them for our use.”

And you, cloistered man, answer this: “I do not wish to rejoice in these things, when I hear: ‘Woe to you who laugh; blessed are you who now weep’ (Luke VI, 21). The Christ [Col. 0701C] whom I now follow, I read that He wept; I never read that He laughed. Delay increases desire, for as it increases, merit also increases. Hence: ‘Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let thy heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord’ (Ps. XXVI, 14). If I am not now burdened with wealth alongside you, carried in horses and chariots, covered with skins, fattened with rich foods, warmed by embraces, delighted with conversations: I know whom I have believed; a crown of righteousness is laid up for me. I shall be clothed with double garments when the glory of the Lord appears. If you speak thus to me, good man, you will stop my mouth, and I shall put my finger upon my mouth; and according to my measure I shall try with you to lift my eyes to the mountains.

“Nevertheless, because narrow is the way that leads to life, let each of us, let all of us, lift our eyes unto the mountains, whence help shall come to us; and through their merits and prayers may Jesus Christ our Lord, our Judge, raise us from lowly things to the right hand of the Father, when He comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire. Amen.”

LXXIV. SECOND SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS.  
[Note: [Col. 0701D] From manuscript E of Angers.]

“All the vessels which Hiram made for King Solomon were of bronze. The king cast them in the clayey ground of the plain of the Jordan” (III Kings VII, 45).

Taught by the Holy Spirit through Solomon, my brothers, [Col. 0702A] we have learned that “golden apples in silver settings are one who speaks a word in its season” (Prov. XXV, 11). We have proposed to speak a word of God at a fitting time in honour of all the saints. We see present silver settings—that is, hearers instructed in and capable of receiving the divine utterances—in whom, as in silver settings, the teaching of truth may rest and joyfully find welcome in the spirit of fruitful action. The time is fitting, capacity is not lacking, and the place is appropriate. We confess that golden apples—that is, perfect sayings of wisdom—are lacking to us; but would that we might be able to offer something, however small, not unworthy of your hearing and suited to the occasion.

If the words which we have proposed are examined more closely in their brevity, the present and future excellence of the saints is shown, and their manifold grace is made known by their progress and reward. For the literal sense says that Hiram made for King Solomon vessels of the purest bronze [or brass] for the adornment of the Lord’s house. Solomon is interpreted “peaceful,” and signifies our Peace—that is, the Lord Jesus—who, breaking down the wall of enmity, made peace for those who were near and those who were far off, that is, Jews and Gentiles; and who, beyond the peace of reconciliation, will give the peace of immortality. He is also called Jedidiah, that is, “beloved,” of God the Father. Hence: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. XII, 18).

And He is Ecclesiastes—that is, the preacher—who from love and grace gathers together and addresses the assembly of the faithful; and, appearing visibly to the world through assuming our flesh, strove through Himself and through His ministers to build for the Lord a house from the congregation of believers, which in the future He will illuminate through the presence of His vision and dwelling. The faithful are aptly called vessels for honour, not dishonour, strong rather than earthenware, and are therefore said to have been made of the purest bronze. Bronze is an exceedingly strong and durable metal, consumed by no rust and very resonant. The saints, too, here sound forth the confession of sins or praise, as in the future they will sing heavenly hymns more fully; and then in body they will be most strong, consumed by no rust of age. They also strive, according to their strength, to be cleansed in flesh and spirit, and no storm of tribulation can separate them from the love of God. [Col. 0702D] They can be killed, but cannot be bent. Hence the Apostle: “Neither death, nor life, nor anything else shall separate us from the love of Christ” (Rom. VIII, 39).

Hiram, an outstanding and wondrous craftsman, cast these vessels to aid King Solomon. Hiram is interpreted “living on high,” and figures the Holy Spirit, who, just as He asks—that is, makes people ask—so makes them live on high, namely those whose citizenship is in heaven. Thus He makes vessels from bronze; indeed, “casts” is the more elegant expression, because our God is a consuming fire. “Stone melted by heat,” says Job, “is changed into bronze” (Job XXVIII, 2): when one who was cold through unbelief and hard through insensibility, melted by the fire [Col. 0703A] of God, is changed into true strength; and one who was formerly strong in evil becomes unconquerable in good.

Behold a precious vessel set apart among God’s gifts. Such was Paul, called a vessel of election. This wondrous craftsman fills a boy who plays the lyre and makes him a Psalmist; He fills a continent boy, Daniel, and makes him judge of incontinent elders. He fills a shepherd plucking sycomore fruit, Amos, and directs him to prophesy. This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High—that is, of the One living on high, namely Hiram.

He casts in the furnace of earth—that is, in the labour of tribulation. Hence: “Give us help from tribulation” (Ps. LIX, 13), that is, He turns tribulation into perfection [variant: “progress”], because “the furnace tests the potter’s vessel, [Col. 0703B] and the temptation of tribulation tests righteous persons” (Ecclus. XXVII, 6). “Tribulation works patience; patience, testing; and testing, hope; and hope does not confound” (Rom. V, 5), because patience is exercised through tribulation and proved through exercise, so that hope of one’s neighbour may be increased.

A vessel thus fashioned gives forth, like bright bronze, a clearer sound, which blessed Job, struck by the loss of his children and possessions, uttered to God when he burst forth not into blasphemies but into a profession of divine praise: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I, 21).

These vessels are formed through the skill of our craftsman in clayey ground, from which the moulds for casting vessels were made; but Hiram Himself makes the moulds. By these moulds is signified Holy Scripture, containing examples of saints, who according to their bodies were earth—and fruitful earth, producing thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit. Hence Job says: “The earth from which bread came forth [Vulgate: ‘arose’]” (Job XXVIII, 5), that is, the doctrine of refreshment.

This ground is called clayey, for clay is soft and suited to receiving or making every sort of impression and mould. By this is shown the prompt obedience of the saints in carrying out the divine commands. From their examples a mould—that is, a rule of good living—is prepared for us, until Christ be formed in us. Therefore Hiram, that is, the Holy Spirit, is said to have made the earth clayey, and from it a mould for forming other vessels, [Col. 0703D] because from the beginning of the world He established earlier saints of such a kind that later ones might by His grace be formed in their likeness.

The moulds themselves, among which the vessels are formed, were afterwards hardened by fire, because the holy Fathers stood invincible amid tribulations. But bronze melted by fire enters the clay moulds so that a vessel fit for heavenly ministries may be made, when they themselves, beneficially humbled and softened by the flame of divine love or human adversity, enter by good works upon the path of the Fathers, that by running well they may attain their rewards. For just as vessels were not always kept enclosed in clay moulds, so saints need not always be confined within rules for good works; once good work has been completed, the palm of blessed recompense ought to be awarded [variant: “separated”]. Just as, after vessels have reached perfection, they are brought into the light when the restraints of the moulds are broken, so, hidden, secret, and effective grace is fittingly shown in work: the wisdom of the craftsman is recognized as working inwardly in the flowing metal almost without assistance, so that [variant: “as though”] a beautiful vessel suddenly appears in the midst from hidden workmanship.

Hence: “The Spirit breathes where He wills, and thou hearest His voice, but knowest not whence He comes or whither He goes; so is everyone born of the Spirit” (John III, 8). He breathes, teaches, fills, and instructs when He wills, where He wills, and as He wills. Being invisible, He works invisibly. “For God is Spirit, and those who worship Him must worship in spirit and [Col. 0704B] truth” (John IV, 14). This is the fire which the Lord sent upon earth and wished vehemently to be kindled, for forming vessels of the Lord’s house. Hence some are appointed apostles, others shepherds and teachers, deacons, presbyters, bishops, and the rest, whom the Holy Spirit distinguishes for the form of the house, distributing to each as He wills.

These works of the saints, like broken moulds, come to an end insofar as labour is concerned, because once they have received the crown of righteousness, the offices of laborious activity will cease. Nevertheless—indeed, more perfectly—the Holy Spirit will reign through charity in the elect. Nor should it be left unmentioned that more solid vessels, namely bronzes, are formed even in less clayey moulds, according to the saying: “My strength is dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. XXI, 16). And although the saints of the New Testament were more perfect than the saints of the Old Testament, according to the sayings: “We, having the first-fruits of the Spirit” (Rom. VIII, 23); and, “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke X, 24), yet because the saints’ solidity in the future will be much greater than in the present—as bronze is admittedly much more solid than earth—all these things are formed in the region of Jordan.

Jordan is interpreted “descent,” and baptism was celebrated in it. Those who are baptized ought to be humbled from the swelling of pride; and the ancients believed in the baptism to come. We have seen it bestowed and being bestowed. In them there went before the figure [of those] who were baptized in Moses and in the sea; but to us has been given the saving reality. Therefore they remain, as it were, beyond the Jordan, [Col. 0704D] but we on this side of the Jordan. This is well signified by the two and a half tribes which received their portion of land beyond the Jordan, and the rest which had their inheritance on this side. And those had much cattle, these little: because those gave greater attention to temporal things, while these, leaving all things, naked follow naked Christ.

It is also called a plain region because the faithful people is gathered from the Gentiles converted throughout the breadth of the world, not from Jews alone. Hence: “We heard of it in Ephrata; we found it in the fields of the forest” (Ps. CXXXI, 8).

Nor is it without mystery that, in the construction of Solomon’s Temple, David, Solomon’s father, is said to have prepared an abundance of gold and silver for the costs and expenses; and Hiram to have supplied the same Solomon with assistance in craftsmanship and certain other matters. David in this place bears the figure of God the Father, who is the Father of our Solomon; and he is “strong of hand,” because He works powerfully through the hand—that is, the Son. From eternity He prepared everything necessary for the building of the Church, and by eternal disposition and election anticipated both the number and merit of the elect, so that in time it might come to pass just as it had been in His will before times.

As has been said, Hiram signifies the Holy Spirit; Solomon, Christ. These three are one and work together, because the operations of the Trinity are indivisible. Whatever the Father does, the Son also does, and so does the Holy Spirit. Hence: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of His mouth all their host” [Col. 0705B] (Ps. XXXI, 6). David is said to have prepared what Solomon needed; Hiram to have cast vessels for Solomon. For all things pertain to the honour of Christ, who appeared glorious in the flesh and united to Himself His bride—that is, the Church—by nature and grace. Hence Isaiah: “With all these thou shalt clothe thyself as with a garment” (Isa. XLIX, 18).

Likewise, Hiram came forth as the friend of David and Solomon, because the Holy Spirit is the love of the Father and Son, their bond and connection. Likewise King David is mentioned, and Solomon and Hiram similarly. These three are not three kings but one King, who governs us here unto righteousness and will lead us in the future unto glory. Hence: “The Lord governs me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture He has placed me” (Ps. XXII, 1).

Behold, we have heard how, and through whom, so great glory has been granted to the saints whose solemnities we celebrate today. May He who lives and reigns for ages of ages bring us to their fellowship, aided by the merits of those same saints. Amen.

611. LXXV. THIRD SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS.  
[Note: [Col. 0705D] From the Angers manuscript.]

“**I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valleys, and to observe whether the vine had flowered and the pomegranates had budded**” (Song of Songs 6:10).

It is most fitting, my brothers, that on the feast of All Saints we should, according to our small ability, say something to their glory and our own edification. For it is right that we should exalt with praises, insofar as we can, those whose aid we continually ask to sustain us; [Col. 0705D] and if it be proper for us to render due honour to any individual saint, what worthy thing can we offer when all are gathered under one celebration? For the more benefits are heaped upon us through them, the more ardent should be our affection toward them. Their remembrance will at last become noble if our own good things are increased by their examples and merits. Nor should it be doubted that this solemnity was established by divine inspiration, so that, if through the yearly cycle we honour the feast-days of individual saints less fully—whether through negligence, ignorance, occupation with secular affairs, or other causes—we may strive on this occasion to compensate, according to our ability, for whatever was done insufficiently or poorly in their particular celebrations.

[Col. 0706A] Just as in the Old Testament suitable sacrifices from various fruits, crops, or animals were offered on different feasts—for example, at Passover, a lamb with wild lettuces and roasted ears of grain; at Pentecost, loaves of firstfruits; and thus at the other festivals certain proper things were taken and offered to God according to the decree of the Law—while at the Feast of Tabernacles offerings were made from all the fruits of the earth or of the year: so at other feasts we commemorate now the virtues of one apostle, martyr, confessor, virgin, or several such persons; but at this feast we commemorate the feast of all together.

Therefore, if the number or cloud of sins does not hinder us, it is certain that not only a multitude of angels but also the divine Majesty is present at our devotion, as the Holy Spirit testifies through Solomon [Col. 0706B] in the Song of Songs, saying, “I went down into the garden of nuts.” But how does he descend who is everywhere, or whither does he ascend who is absent nowhere, according to that saying: “If I ascend into heaven, thou art there; if I descend into hell, thou art present” (Ps. 138:8)? And: “Neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains?” (Ps. 74:7).

Yet descent is spoken of in four ways. There is a descent of judgment, as in the punishment of Sodom. There is also a descent of protection, as in delivering the Hebrews from the land of Egypt. There is likewise a descent of the Incarnation. Hence: “He bowed the heavens and came down” (Ps. 17:20). Finally, there is a descent of visitation, as here. This last kind of descent also occurs in four ways. He descends by correcting those who stray, supporting the weak, strengthening those who do good, [Col. 0706C] and placing the mature in rest.

Thus he descends into the garden, that is, the Church. Though elsewhere it is represented under other figures—as in a citadel [perhaps “threshing-floor”], a house, a tabernacle, or a temple—the beauty of the whole universe is understood much more elegantly in a garden. In it four things are especially considered: a watering fountain, that is, baptism or saving doctrine; then herbs from which ointments are prepared, that is, gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are the first incentives to virtues; then trees, that is, believers advancing upward; afterwards fruits, that is, manna by which the spirit is refreshed. These four things suitably correspond to the four preceding acts: the fountain, that is, doctrine, is given for correction; by ointments the weak are supported; trees, that is, those advancing, are strengthened [the text has *conformantur*, perhaps *confortantur*]; fruits are placed in rest.

This garden is especially one of nuts [the text reads *unicum*, perhaps *nucum*]. A nut has four parts: three shells and a kernel, which either is not eaten with them or is eaten less sweetly. There is an outer, native, earthly, bitter shell, with which the kernel is not eaten: namely, sin, with which no one is saved or incorporated into Christ. The second shell is woody and hard, with which the same kernel is not eaten: that is, mortal sin, which, unless removed, allows no one to be admitted to salvation. The third, inner, thin shell is venial sin; unless it is taken away, the kernel is eaten less pleasantly. Therefore, that [Col. 0707A] the kernel may be eaten in its sweetness, it must be carefully cleansed from these three.

It follows: “That I might see the fruits of the valleys.” The twofold valley signifies twofold humility, namely that of heart and body. The fruits signify confessors, pleasing to God through the fragrance of faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues. For whoever gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind.

“And that I might observe whether the vine had flowered.” Through the whiteness, purity, and fragrance of the flower, the beauty of virginity is fittingly expressed. For among the flowers of the Church neither roses nor lilies are lacking. This flower belongs to the vineyard or vine: that is, it proceeds from Christ’s grace and imitation of him. By pomegranates martyrs are denoted, because of their red rind enclosing many seeds within. [Col. 0707B] For no one reaches the palm of martyrdom without the merit of many virtues.

The propriety of the words should also be noted. Fruits are “seen”; flowers and pomegranates are, as it were, inspected more carefully. These are the scarlet and hyacinth-blue skins placed beneath [perhaps “above”] the tabernacle (Exod. 25). The goat-hair coverings and curtains, and other things of that kind, touch the earth or are close to it; these two do not. For the martyr, placed amid torments, leaves all worldly things and desires to attain the sight of the Lord of the world, that is, Christ, who is the flower of virgins, the crown of martyrs, the grace of the continent. Virgins, however, while they transcend carnal union in view of a greater reward, choose for themselves a seat higher than that of other faithful people. Certainly, as [Col. 0707C] Jerome says: “To live in the flesh beyond the flesh is not an earthly life but a heavenly one.” — “These follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. 14:4).

See how great and what kind of solemnity belongs to the present day, honoured by patrons so great and such as these. And just as it seems formerly prefigured by the Feast of Tabernacles, so it depicts more fully than the other festivals the state of the life to come. For saints gathered from every part of the world will be present—every one who has been or will be—and they will come rejoicing, bearing their sheaves, when God has wiped every tear from the saints’ eyes, removed the filth of the daughters of Zion, and bestowed upon them “what eye has not seen nor ear heard” (1 Cor. 2:9). Those who meanwhile [perhaps “formerly”] had been scattered and assailed by miseries will then be gathered into one and [Col. 0707D] recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.

How great the glory, what loveliness, what beauty, when each person’s face shall shine like the sun! Yet this is a small glory in comparison with divinity, which is eternal life. Each nature will possess its own delight: bodily eyes, for seeing the glorified flesh of Christ and of all the saints; inner eyes, for enjoying the fatness of wheat—that is, divinity itself. Since no tongue suffices to speak of this, nor can the meditation of the human heart fully understand it before seeing it, we shall rather leave it to the divine counsel, lest we be charged with presumption.

But because it does not profit us to be present at human festivals if it should happen that we are absent [Col. 0708A] from the festivals of angels, let us turn our vows and prayers toward them, that we may deserve to reach those of whom we speak, through the favour of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## LXXVI. ONE SERMON ON THE FEAST OF SAINT NICHOLAS

[Note: From the Angers manuscript, Col. 0707D.] On continence.

“**Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands**” (Luke 12:35).

Everything that is said, my brothers, must be considered not only from the discourse which is spoken, but also from the person speaking. For example: if a child speaks, we prepare our minds to hear childish speech. But if a man speaks, we weigh whether what is said is worthy of a man. [Col. 0708B] Likewise, if an unlearned person or an educated person speaks, we make a distinction. But these words which we have set before you were spoken not by any merely wise being—that is, angel, prophet, or priest—but by the very Wisdom of God, begotten of the Father and dwelling among us in the flesh. His words must be weighed all the more diligently because they cannot be despised without danger.

Whoever despises the word of Moses is stoned. Whoever tramples underfoot the word of God deserves worse punishments, especially because in these words are contained both the form and order of holiness. For to know what ought to be done but not in what order is not perfect knowledge, since even good things, if done out of order, are not free from blame. Hence in the Song of Songs: “He ordered charity within me” (Song 2:4). [Col. 0708C] And: “Sing wisely” (Ps. 46:8).

Therefore the Saviour first sets forth purity of flesh and mind, that is, chastity, so that useful perseverance in works may afterwards accompany it. Hence Paul: “Pursue peace and holiness”—that is, continence—“without which no one shall see God” (Heb. 12:14). Let us therefore attend to Truth saying, “Let your loins be girded.” Secular and divine Scriptures alike testify that men’s organs of lust are in the loins, women’s in the navel. Thus Job says: “His strength”—that is, Behemoth’s—“is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job 40:11). He had first said: “He shall eat grass like an ox” (ibid., v. 10), that is, carnal persons, since all flesh is grass, and especially those who appear clean; for he does not much concern himself with filth.

Thus an ox more greedily consumes unclean grass. It is made known how he prevails over such people, so that, the more plainly the enemy is recognized, the more easily he may be overcome. Both sexes indeed are greatly laid low by the weakness of lust [the text has *substruitur*, perhaps *substernitur*], and are especially overcome by the devil through this sin. Yet the Lord signified both sexes through the more worthy sex. Behemoth is correctly interpreted as “animal.” For in this manner he rules over bestial and brutish people as though they were cattle. Sexual intercourse is common to us and cattle; hence the fifth commandment: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:14). The fifth plague, namely the death of cattle, is prepared for such people; and whoever, after the manner of cattle, loosens the reins to lust will without doubt incur eternal death.

Do you hold back—or contain—yourself, man, in what a beast cannot; and do you hope for what a beast cannot. You labour in restraining yourself; a beast does not. You shall rejoice eternally; a beast shall not. If the work exhausts you, the reward consoles you. But perhaps you choose to wander in free lust, restrained by no law. Do you not fear guilt? Beware the plague: if you are a beast, fear death. Hence: “Do not become like horse and mule, in which there is no understanding” (Ps. 31:9).

Those about to eat the Passover are told: “You shall gird your loins” (Exod. 12:11). In the loins is the pleasure of the flesh. Hence: “Burn my loins and my heart” (Ps. 25:7). Accordingly Gregory says: “Whoever celebrates the Passover should gird his loins, so that he who celebrates the solemnity of incorruption may by no means be subject to the corruption of lust.”

But, conversely, Job says: “The eye of the adulterer watches for darkness, saying, ‘No eye shall see me’; and he covers his face” (Job 24:15). He commits an unlawful deed all the more securely because he did not fear being seen. Again: “He loosens the belt of kings”—that is, the Lord permits the continence of the proud to be loosened—“and girds their loins with a cord” (Job 12:18), that is, with the bond of sin; hence they are cast into outer darkness with hands and feet bound.

For this reason in Exodus (chapter 28) linen breeches are first prescribed for the priest. They are imposed on no unwilling person, but must be voluntarily offered to God; for not all receive this saying, except perhaps one who has freely made a vow, and who may at times be compelled to fulfil it. To receive holy orders, to which this obligation belongs, is in a sense to make a vow; without it no one is worthy to approach priesthood or ministry at the altar. They are rightly called linen. For linen, only after much labour and rubbing, scarcely at last puts off its earthly and native colour and receives whiteness.

[Note: On the same point Hildebert, in his treatise *On the Sacred Vestments*, speaks of the priest’s alb or long garment, Col. 0709.]

For the same reason the tunic is of linen, signifying continence of the whole body, that is, general continence, just as the breeches signify particularly the repression of the generative parts. They are attached to a belt made of four colours, and so forth (Exod. 39); the *tunica poderis* [perhaps *pedalis*], that is, the ankle-length garment, descends to the feet, that is, it endures unto the end.

We who are established in holy orders have been placed under the necessity of continence. There is no middle ground: we shall be either on the mountain [Col. 0709D] or in Sodom. The angels wished to lead Lot, after he had left Sodom, to the mountain. They fittingly invited him to the angelic life, saying: “Save yourself on the mountain” (Gen. 19:17). But he said: “I cannot be saved on the mountain. There is, however, a small city, Zoar” (ibid., v. 19), that is, married life, which is permitted to laypeople.

To be in Sodom is to perish in the fire of lust. To be on the mountain is to preserve the height of continence. To flee burning Sodom is to avoid criminal passions. Fornication must be fled along with the other vices. It is difficult to be in fire and not be burned. But whoever commits fornication sins against his own body, because he also defiles the body. Conversely, Paul says: [Col. 0710A] “Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit?” (1 Cor. 6:19). We owe service to him whose temple it is, and it is dangerous to drive so great a guest from his own temple. If you do not wish to spare yourself, you ought to spare him.

Therefore, in the punishment of the Sodomites God showed the stain of their crime for the instruction of others, when he caused them to perish by sulphur and fire. Sulphur stinks and fire burns, so that those who burned with the stench of perverse desires of the flesh might suffer sulphur and fire, and from this punishment learn what they had done through unjust desire.

Likewise, a hem with a trailing edge is assigned to the priest, so that chastity may be strengthened to the end. Blessed Job, wishing to deter people from the crime of lust and specifically defining it for this purpose, says: “It is a fire devouring unto destruction and rooting out all growths” (Job 31:12), that is, the good operations of the soul; for if this evil is not resisted, even those things which seemed good perish.

It should also be noted that Truth says not “loin” but “loins,” in the plural, in order to indicate purity of mind and body. The serpent is told: “You shall crawl on breast and belly.” It crawls on its belly when it exercises lust in deed through human members; on its breast when it defiles by thought. And because thought leads to deed, “breast” is placed first. Thus, because Job fortified his thought, he overcame breast and belly with one guard, saying: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I should not even think of a virgin” (Job 31:1). In order to preserve his thought chastely, he made a covenant with his eyes, lest he first carelessly look upon what [Col. 0710C] he would afterward unwillingly love; for death enters through the windows of the senses. He guards them outwardly lest through them the soul desire external things.

One ought not look upon what it is unlawful to desire. Thus he says: “If my eye has followed my heart” (ibid., v. 7). For just as temptation is drawn in through the eyes, so sometimes an inwardly conceived desire compels the eyes externally to serve it. It is as if he said: I was unwilling either to see what I might desire, or, by seeing, to follow the things I desired. “For what portion would God have from above in me?” (ibid., v. 2), because other good works do not please him without purity.

Hence: “All the beasts of the field play there, and he sleeps under the shade in the shelter of the reed, in moist places” (Job 40:15). He cannot sleep in the hearts of saints, because if at any time he lodges there for a brief moment, he is wearied by the heat of heavenly desires and, as it were, pricked to depart as often as they sigh toward eternal things with inward love.
