Moist places are the generative members through which lust is committed. By the reed is meant the glory of pride. These two rule too strongly in man: one belongs to the spirit, the other to the flesh. There he sleeps as though at rest. Thus he swallows a river and is not amazed—that is, the multitude of the human race. Among laypeople he reckons this as little; but he trusts that Jordan may flow into his mouth. Jordan means “descent”: namely, that one who professes the ways of truth through the habit of humility and knowledge [Col. 0711A] of letters may flow into his mouth.

The devil is an animal when he tempts through lust; a serpent when through malice; a bird when through pride. Hence God says to Job: “Will you play with him as with a bird?” (Job 40:24). For the commendation of this continence Ezekiel sees a man girded at the loins; John, girded about the breasts, because in the Old Testament the deed, and in the New also the mind, is made chaste. Hence: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28).

The priestly vestments are made of twisted byssus. Byssus is twisted when chastity is doubled. And the king of Sodom says to Abraham: “Give me the souls; take the rest for yourself” (Gen. 14:21). For demons especially seek to capture souls. A person whose conscience is unclean is not clean. If the devil can ensnare a person with a threefold cord—thought, speech, and deed—he rejoices. But if not, he strives at least to hold him with one.

Evil thoughts proceed from the heart and defile a person. For when the enemy is shut out from the effect of the deed, he attempts to pollute the secret realm of thought; but one must withdraw from him during the whole three-day period. Many have perished because of the appearance of women. David saw Bathsheba washing herself and desired her. Solomon, because he inclined his sides toward foreign women, fell through this into idolatry.

Abstinence is of very great value for preserving this chastity. Hence the Apostle: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is lust” (Eph. 5:19). And Solomon: “Wine and women make wise men apostatize” (Ecclus. 19:2). The same writer says: “Wakefulness, suffering, and anger attend the undisciplined man; healthy sleep belongs to a temperate man” (Ecclus. 31:23). And: “A prostitute scarcely costs one loaf of bread” (Prov. 6:27). Bread drives away hunger for a day; repeated indulgence rather inflames lust.

Noah, through drunkenness, uncovered his thighs. Lot, through drunkenness, committed incest. The sin of the Sodomites was abundance of bread. And: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. 32:6). For, as Jerome says, “the belly and the genitals are neighbours; a belly boiling with wine overflows into lusts.” Balaam knew this, and at his counsel adorned women were sent among the Israelites. Lust conquered those whom weapons could not conquer. The beauty of women captured the iron of men. The people had previously conquered, not through their own strength, but by preserving chastity. They were conquered, not by the strength of soldiers, but by the beauty of women.

Phinehas deserved praise and reward because he pierced the copulating pair with a spear through their genital parts. Therefore, as Solomon says, let each man’s sword be upon his thigh, that is, let him restrain the wantonness of the flesh. Likewise in the Song: “Turn away your eyes”—those of wantonness and licentiousness—“for they have made me fly away” (Song 6:4). And Jeremiah: “My eye has plundered my soul” (Lam. 3:51). For one who conceals the pleasure of the flesh in secret easily strays into the fault of wicked action.

Whoever, instructed by these examples and warnings, lives continually in continence offers God a perpetual sacrifice. This sacrifice is not offered by those who serve marriage, but by those devoted to perpetual chastity. God delights in this first and daily feast according to the Law, that is, the continual sacrifice. Once this foundation has been laid, “let lamps be burning in your hands.” Lamps, that is, good works, ought to shine before one’s neighbour, so that those who see them may glorify the Father who is in heaven, who gives us both the good will and its accomplishment. And this was to be in the hands, that is, in the exercise of continual work.

Blessed Nicholas shone gloriously through this purity of flesh and mind, which we have sufficiently commended, and through holiness of works, as the deeds of his life relate; he pleased both human beings and God, the searcher of hearts. May the Lord Jesus Christ direct our desire toward conformity with him and participation in his glory.

## LXXVII. ONE SERMON ON THE FEAST OF SAINT ANDREW THE APOSTLE

[Note: From the Angers manuscript, Col. 0711D.]

“**Make for yourself two beaten silver trumpets, by which you may summon the multitude when the camp is to move**” (Num. 10:2).

The Lord says in Deuteronomy: “If, while walking along the way, you find in a tree or on the ground a bird’s nest, and a mother sitting upon the chicks or eggs, you shall not take her with the young, but shall allow her to go, keeping the young captive” (Deut. 22:6). We walk along the way when we run through divine Scripture, which is the way of salvation. We find a nest, that is, some saying: on the ground, that is, one pertaining to the active life; in a tree, one pertaining to the contemplative life. By the mother he means history; by the eggs, the hidden sense; by the chick or offspring, the manifest sense, from which we are able to be refreshed. Therefore let us cast away the mother, that is, history, and hold fast the spiritual and moral sense, so that by carrying it out we may live eternally.

According to the letter, Moses is commanded in the book of Numbers to make two silver trumpets for summoning the people. Let the Jews keep the letter for themselves; let us seek the spiritual understanding. Moses here therefore bears the person of Christ. Pharaoh’s daughter—that is, the Church, or the faithful soul, formerly the devil’s daughter—receives him in the waters or from the waters of baptism or spiritual doctrine, and nourishes him in the court, that is, in the breadth of the heart. Christ grows not in himself but in us. Faith in Christ is Christ in the heart; he ought always to grow. This one delivers the people from Egypt, that is, the faithful from the devil and the world.

To accomplish this, by the Father’s command and eternal counsel he makes trumpets, that is, preachers, whom he sends two by two, so that they may preach the two commandments of charity. They are silver, so that the words of preachers may shine with the brightness of eloquence and not confuse the minds of hearers with any obscurity of their own. They are beaten, because those who preach the wrath to come must grow through the blows of tribulations, and render a sound to God all the sweeter as they endure harsher things beneath the hammer of the whole earth. Hence: “The apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were judged worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Christ” (Acts 5:41). Likewise, when they were forbidden in Acts of the Apostles to preach in Jesus’ name, hear what they say: “We must obey God rather than men” (ibid., v. 29). And Paul says: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12:10). And: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5:10).

For, as the Apostle testifies: “This light and momentary tribulation works an eternal weight of glory” (2 Cor. 4:17). Here timbers are hewn; here stones are polished, to be placed in God’s building. There will be no need of a file with a smooth iron. Thus saints are shaped by blows; the wicked, like the devil, are drawn tighter. Hence in Job: “His heart shall be hardened like a stone and drawn tight like a smith’s anvil” (Job 41:15). Again, of the same: “He shall stiffen his tail like a cedar” (Job 40:12).

Such trumpets—bright with divine eloquence, proved by life and holiness—are able to summon the people. By their blast they can destroy the walls of Jericho. Through them our truer Joshua destroys the seven principal vices, namely pride and the rest, on the seventh day: that is, when the cycle of seven days has been completed, they will fall altogether. These trumpets were used at the Jubilee, because the saints do all things worthy of the promise and eternal rest [supplied: *digna*].

Gideon also, whose name is interpreted “a surrounding fortification” [the text has *mutatio*, “change”], that is, the Lord Jesus, armed with such trumpets and jars containing lamps, put the Midianites to flight (Judg. 7). The trumpets sounded; the jars, that is, the bodies, were broken for truth, and therefore the lamps, that is, miracles, shone forth. “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15). For through death they pass to life.

Hence Solomon says in Proverbs: “Bad, bad, says every buyer; but when he has gone away, he boasts” (Prov. 20:14): namely, the one who desires to purchase eternal rewards in heaven. What he had to endure in the present seemed bad and bitter, so that when through death he has departed from the world he may boast, seeing openly that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us. By this hope he endures hardships. “For discipline, when it is bitter,” as the Apostle says, “in the present has in the end a most peaceful fruit; for all discipline seems not to be of joy but of sorrow” (Heb. 12:11). Again: “If you refuse the discipline of the Father, you are illegitimate children.”

Such trumpets summon the people now to battle against enemies, now to a feast or banquet, now to a festival. They summon them to battle against the devil and against spiritual wickedness. Thus: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (Jas. 4:7). And at the end they will summon them to judge demons: hence, “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” And: “The saints shall run to and fro like sparks among reeds” (Wis. 3:7).

They also summon them to battle against the domestic enemy, that is, the flesh, which desires against the spirit, in this way: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14). And: “Flee fornication, that you may resist its desires” (1 Cor. 6:18). These trumpets likewise invite the people to the banquet of divine reading, that in the present we may be nourished from the word of God and the bread of angels. Blessed is the one who hears God’s words and does them, so that through this banquet we may be raised to eternal fullness, where we shall drink from the torrent of delight.

They likewise summon us to the present feast, so that the remnant of thought may keep a feast-day for God, and then we shall come and make our dwelling with him. It is a great feast to have God as guest in the lodging of the heart. He fittingly celebrates the Sabbath who gives attention to good works. Hence in Exodus: “Observe the Sabbath day,” and the other feasts which must be observed by us, not carnally but spiritually. Through these we shall come to the eternal solemnity, where “in the voice of exultation and confession is the sound of one feasting” (Ps. 41:5). There will be eternal solemnity, assemblies and gatherings, where we may praise God for ages of ages and celebrate a truer jubilee.

Moreover, they summon us to move the camp and make stopping-places, which signify the stages and advances of the righteous, such as Paul shows when he says: “Forgetting the things behind, I stretch forth to the things ahead” (Phil. 3:13). And the Psalmist: “He has arranged ascents in his heart” (Ps. 83:13), where grace may be heaped upon grace.

The harmony of the mysteries should be noted. Moses, drawn from the waters, makes silver trumpets to summon the people. The Lord, walking beside the Sea of Galilee, makes two brothers fishers of men, so that with the nets of the Gospel they may draw people out from the sea of this world to the harbour of salvation. Yet first this trumpet of ours, blessed Andrew, whose feast we celebrate today, calls his brother Simon, saying: “We have found the Messiah” (John 1:41). See the well-sounding trumpet: deep calls unto deep. One curtain draws another; and whoever hears says, “Come.”

In Andrew there is true brotherhood, true charity: he shows the treasure he has found to his brother. In Simon there is true humility: he does not disdain to follow one younger and later [perhaps *posterius*, “afterward”]. They follow with the steps both of body and mind, leaving nets and boat behind. But how much did either leave, who had almost nothing? He left much who abandoned wholly the little that he had, who first abandoned the will to possess. As much was left by the follower as could previously have been desired by one who did not follow [the text has *a sequente*, perhaps *a non sequente*]. For God does not weigh how much you offer, but from how much you offer it; in his sacrifice the purse is more easily despised than the will. He left much who, with love of the world, cast away care for the body.

Hence: “Whoever does not hate father and mother, and even his own soul, is not worthy of me” (John 12:25). They followed not only like others by drinking the Lord’s cup—that is, by dying for him—but also by enduring the same manner of death, namely the cross. True is the kinship of those whom the same faith and passion truly made brothers.

Hence in the Song: “A man brings for its fruit”—that is, for the vine—“a thousand pieces of silver” (Song 8:11), that is, the perfect price, whatever that may be. The kingdom of heaven is worth as much as you have. It is bought with the smallest thing as with the greatest, because what is least in quantity is greatest in devotion—even a cup of cold water. Let no one excuse himself on account of the price. It is worth as much as you are worth: give yourself, and receive it. Whatever else you may give, if you withhold yourself, you have accomplished nothing. Hence: “Your vows are upon me” (Ps. 55:12).

Cain offered rightly, but did not divide rightly, because he withheld what was dearer. Why, O man, do you plead poverty? Will alone is reckoned perfection. Let the poor see and rejoice. And: “We shall render the calves of our lips” (Hos. 14:3). The widow offered more than all others in two small coins.

But if we do not yet wish or are able, after the example of these apostles, to give our life for the Lord, let us at least learn to relinquish our possessions. If not yet everything, then at least something, or our superfluities, we ought to distribute to the poor. But how will one give himself who will not give a coin? Yet “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12). Therefore let us do violence to ourselves.

Andrew, whose name is interpreted “manly,” did violence manfully to his own soul through preaching; and therefore he received a hundredfold here and eternal life in the age to come. May he also grant this to us through Andrew’s intercession—he who lives and reigns as God for ages of ages. Amen.

## LXXVIII. FIRST SERMON ON THE FEAST OF SAINT STEPHEN THE PROTOMARTYR

[Note: From Saint-Germain, Col. 0715D.]

“**We have heard a report from the Lord, and he has sent an envoy among the nations: ‘Rise, and let us rise against Edom in battle’**” (Obad. 1:1).

[Col. 0715C] 622 Just as the eye is not sated with seeing, nor the ear with hearing, so neither can we be sated by hearing what is written concerning the Lord and considering by what means he edifies and instructs us and raises us up against harmful things. For you have heard here the words of the Holy Spirit speaking in the prophet Obadiah concerning our leader and king. So that greater faith may be given to his words and reverence shown to them, he joins himself to the other prophets who drew from the hidden counsels of God and says that he heard a report from the Lord—the Lord who opens the inner eyes and unseals the ears to perceive the secrets of his counsel, and who also opens the mouth to speak a good word. Hence the Apostle says: “That utterance may be given to me when I open my mouth” (Eph. 6:19).

Elisha likewise asks the Lord in the Book of Kings for an opening of the eyes, saying: “Open, Lord, the eyes of your servant, that he may see that more are with us than with them” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 6:17). Likewise, in the same book, the opening of ears and eyes is said to be given by the Lord, as we read: “The Lord will open my ears”; and “he opened Hagar’s eyes, and she saw a well of living water” (Gen. 21:19). It is therefore clear that neither ears are opened to hear good things, nor to understand what is salutary, nor the mouth to speak heavenly things, except by God. For the Prophet also says: “Incline my heart, O God, to your testimonies, and not to avarice” (Ps. 118:36 [119:36]).

But the devil loosens the eyes, ears, and mouths [Col. 0716A] of those who think and speak wicked things, just as Satan opened Judas’s eyes and ears when he entered into him and put it into his heart to betray the Lord. He also opened his mouth, so that, having received money, he might speak with the Pharisees about how to betray him. Therefore God opens the mouth of those who speak God’s words. But the devil opens the mouth of those who speak not God’s words but jesting and obscenities. Likewise, the devil opens the ears of those who receive vain reports when they hear them, contrary to the law which says, “You shall not receive a vain report,” and of those who turn their hearing away from truth and turn instead to fables. Such people cannot be heard by the Lord, according to the saying: “For this reason you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 8:47).

Isaiah says of such people: “The heart of this people has grown gross, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have closed their eyes, lest at any time they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears” (Isa. 6:9; Matt. 13:14). And the Psalmist says: “Their fury is like that of a serpent, like that of a deaf asp which stops its ears” (Ps. 57:5 [58:4–5]). And again: “My people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not heed me” (Ps. 80:12 [81:11]). He opens the ears of those who turn their ears away lest they hear the voice of blood, and of those who hear the mysteries of God with the Apostle who was caught up even to the third pole [read: heaven] and heard secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter. Thus he opened the ears of his servant Obadiah 623, so that he heard a report from the Lord and could say with David: “I will hear what the Lord God says within me” [Col. 0716C] (Ps. 84:9 [85:8]).

What he heard from the Lord he next discloses. He heard, indeed, a great matter: that the Lord “sent an envoy to the nations.” This is the envoy who says through Jeremiah: “I heard a report from the Lord, and I was sent as an envoy. Assemble, and come against Idumaea, and let us rise for battle” (Jer. 43:14 [49:14]). Behold, this envoy himself heard a report from the Lord; otherwise he would not have come unless he had known that this was so appointed in the will of the Father, whose will with his is one, just as the majesty and power are one. He says that he heard from him because the Father is not from the Son, but the Son is from the Father, and has from him whatever he has. Therefore he heard the report from the Father, whose counsellor he is: “For no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him; and no one knows the Son except the Father, and anyone to whom the Father wills to reveal him” (Luke 10:22).

For the Son reveals both himself and the Father. Hence he is called the splendour of glory, because, having become human, he made the Father known, as a ray makes known the sun, according to the saying: “Father, I have made your name known to humankind” (John 17:6). And again: “I have glorified you upon the earth” (ibid., v. 4). This envoy is most worthy and wondrous; for he surpasses all in beauty, excels in wisdom, and exceeds all in strength. For he is “more beautiful than the children of men” (Ps. 44:3 [45:2]), because he is free from sin [supplied] and singularly distinguished by the gracefulness of graces. But since beauty is not sufficient for perfection without wisdom and eloquence, it is written of him that “grace is poured out upon his lips” (ibid.); for through his speech he received the grace of reconciliation.

But again, since beauty and eloquence do not make a perfect envoy without vigour in warfare, he is also shown to be most skilled in war, when it is added: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one” [Col. 0717A] (ibid., v. 4). And again: “Your arrows are sharp; peoples shall fall beneath you in the hearts of the king’s enemies” (ibid., v. 6 [45:5]). This envoy has a sword and arrows, so that he may strike enemies both near and far. He shoots arrows from afar against adversaries; with the sword he cuts them down at close range. For thence come sword and arrow. This is the two-edged sword, cutting with both Testaments; on one side it cuts away carnal vices, on the other spiritual ones.

This most mighty envoy is the man Christ Jesus, who was sent by the Father to the nations. By his own presence he first came to the lost sheep of the house of Israel; then, in the apostles, he passed over to the nations. But there he experienced the water of contradiction, since he exhorts his soldiers to battle, saying: “Rise, assemble, and come against Idumaea, and let us rise in battle against her” (Jer. 49:14). Wise and mighty, he addresses his envoys and exhorts the leaders of his cavalry on its march. 624 For he has cavalry and horses; hence: “Your cavalry is salvation.” And again: “You will mount upon your horses” (Hab. 3:8).

He therefore exhorts his own, seeing that struggle threatens them: Rise, as though you sleep in peace. Rise for afflictions; do not fear to enter a grievous battle, and do not be anxious: you will have me first in the battle-line. I, who appeared to Joshua holding a sword, and said to him, “I will not abandon you nor forsake you”; and who overcame Amalek beneath the banner of my cross while Moses fought—I shall be with you; I shall fight for you.

Behold the strong and invincible Samson, who laid low companies of men with an ass’s jawbone: that is, with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, he struck the hearts of the apostles so that, humbled, they might fall beneath him. For Samson is interpreted as “their sun.” This is Christ, the Sun of righteousness, with healing in his wings, of whom the wicked say in the Book of Wisdom: “We have strayed from the way of truth, and the sun of righteousness has not shone upon us” (Wis. 5:6).

This is that Samson who, when he went to take a wife from among foreigners, was met by an oncoming lion; but he tore it apart like a kid of the goats. When he returned, he found a honeycomb in the mouth of the dead lion and spoke, as it were, a proverb: “Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness” (Judg. 14:5 [14:14]). Our Samson, that is, Christ, went to take a wife from among foreigners when, leaving his own house and abandoning his inheritance, he passed over in the apostles to the nations, as he says through Jeremiah: “I have left my house; I have abandoned my inheritance” (Jer. 12:7). A roaring lion met him, that is, the people of the nations opposing him and mockingly saying: Who are these proclaimers of new demons? What are these wonders they commend to us? They preach to us some unknown dead god.

But our Samson tore him apart like a kid of the goats: that is, insofar as he was a kid of the goats, a feeble sinner. For the kid, because under the law it was offered for sin, signifies the people of the nations, enfeebled by pleasures. Therefore the lion was torn apart like a kid: with the foulness of vices and the savagery of opposition cast off, that sinful people was justified, according to the saying: “Convert the wicked man, and he shall not be.” And in the mouth of that lion, now dead to sin but living to God, sweetness or a honeycomb is found—that is, the sweetness of divine utterances, which are, to the palate of faith, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

Such an envoy befitted the highest King: one of wondrous appearance, immeasurable power, and ineffable wisdom, who does not proceed to battle heedlessly and in disorder, but gathers his own together so that he may more readily break the wedges of the enemy, saying to his followers: “Assemble and come against Idumaea in battle” (Jer. 49:14). With his followers gathered, he goes to battle; of them he says in the Gospel: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst” (Matt. 18:20). For if God is for us, who can stand against us? Thus the head hastens to the contest with the members.

The whole Christ fights like the leader of an army; the members follow, imitating his footsteps. A person—or army—knowing that it cannot endure in battle without his aid cries: “Take hold of weapons and shield, and rise to help me” [Col. 0718C] (Ps. 34:2 [35:2]). In the shield is understood the protection of his good will; but we are his weapons, because just as we are armed by him, so he arms himself from us, using us as weapons to fight [J.: to subdue] enemies. Grave, therefore, is the conflict which the whole Christ enters with such deliberation and careful provision.

For he rises in battle against Edom. It had three names: Esau, Seir, and Edom, which is interpreted “bloody” or “earthly”; by it is understood every conspiracy of those who oppose. For there is rebellion against us from the flesh, from the visible and invisible enemy. Hence the Apostle says: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood only” (Eph. 6:12), that is, not merely against human beings, who are visible and frail, or against vices arising from the flesh, but against principalities and powers, the rulers of this darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness. Against such beings is our struggle, against whom we have perpetual enmity; for even those troublesome human beings whom we suffer—the Apostle calls them such—are made so by those powers. For they incite and inflame them, move them as their vessels, and touch them as instruments. Just as Christ governs and rules those who are light, so the devil drives and incites those who are darkness toward every evil.

Therefore we should pray not against the wicked person but, indeed, for him—against the devil who works with and in him—and do whatever we can, that the devil and his angels may be expelled, and human beings liberated from them. For the demons themselves fight, as riders upon horses, and [in] human beings [Col. 0719A]. Let us therefore kill the riders, that we may possess the horses.

Let us not omit the Davidic armour when we are about to fight, so that, just as David attained triumphant glory after overcoming proud Goliath, we too, having conquered these principalities and powers, may, as those who contend lawfully, attain with the boy David—that is, Christ, who is strong of hand and lovely to behold, into whom even angels desire to look—the glory of victory. For David, in the Book of Kings (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 17), humble and small in stature, fought against the great and proud Goliath. He rejected Saul’s armour because it was too heavy. But he took five stones from the torrent and put them in the shepherd’s pouch, where he was accustomed to milk; he took a sling in his hand, and thus armed advanced against the Philistine. He threw three stones against him, struck and felled him with one, and then ran over him and cut off his head with his own sword.

This David is the whole Christ; proud Goliath is the devil, proud because he is great in his own eyes. Against him the holy martyrs, about to contend, cast away Saul’s armour when they despise all carnal and earthly things, and deliver even the flesh itself, as though a sling, into the hands of the impious. They do not fear “those who kill the body, but him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28). They take the sling in hand, that is, faith in action, because “faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:26); and they put the five stones from the torrent into the pouch and the shepherd’s vessel, where milk was drawn.

The five stones are the Law, for it is set forth in the five books of Moses. The torrent signifies those who pursue and love the slipping and passing world; to them the Law is useless and superfluous because they lack the grace by which the Law is fulfilled. The fullness of the Law, therefore, is charity, understood in the shepherd’s vessel, by which we love God with all our heart and our neighbour as ourselves. He threw three stones and felled him with one, because enemies are overcome by faith in the Trinity and the Unity. He struck him in the forehead, because he did not have in his forehead the sign of Christ, that is, Tau; those marked “upon the foreheads of the men,” as Ezekiel says (9), “who groan and mourn” are delivered from the angel, minister of vengeance, by whom those lacking this [Col. 0719D] sign are slain.

Armed with such weapons, the saints of God contend against their enemies and conquer them, as did this protomartyr Stephen, whose feast of triumphant passion is celebrated today. He had the sling in his hand, that is, faith working through love, for with the other seven deacons he was chosen by the apostles to serve tables. He had the shepherd’s pouch, that is, love of God and neighbour, for in his very passion he prayed for his persecutors, saying: “Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge” (Acts 7:59 [7:60]). He therefore had the breadth of charity, which he extended even to loving enemies. He also had height, because he asked God as his reward, saying: “Lord, receive my spirit” [Col. 0720A] (ibid., 58 [7:59]). He also had length in charity, because he persevered in it to the end. Thus he deserved to see the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God’s power.

That Christ is elsewhere read as sitting at the right hand of the Father does not, through this difference of words, indicate a variation of local position. Rather, when he is read as sitting, his rest and kingship are signified; when he is read as standing, his aid is commended. Stephen therefore saw him standing because in his passion he had him as his helper. If, then, we wish to conquer enemies, if we wish to see the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God’s power, let us retain the armour described above: having the sling in hand, that is, faith in works, and the five stones in the shepherd’s pouch, referring all things to the kingdom of charity; doing nothing for worldly glory or with regard to earthly advantage; extending charity even to enemies, grieving more over their crimes than over our own blows, wasting away more over their impiety than over our own suffering and death. Thus let us advance against the rulers of darkness as lawful contenders.

This is one battle; each person has another within himself, where he fights against the flesh. This is a grievous and more troublesome war. Whoever prevails in it will separate the invisible enemies, that is, the rulers of the world; once they are conquered, we shall then be able easily to overcome those who are the rulers of wickedness, namely, all their ministers. For once the commander is overcome, the army easily takes flight. We read that, once Holofernes, commander of the army, had been slain, the multitude of the forces was put to flight and overcome by the Jews (Judith 15).

Following the example of this combatant, this strong athlete of God, let us, with the mighty envoy leading us, rise in battle against Edom: that is, against the flesh and against the princes of darkness. Let us cast the three stones from the shepherd’s pouch against the rage of those who stone us, together with the good protomartyr, so that, with Jeremiah, we may scatter, uproot, plant, and build up the assembly of evil people, from whom will be required all righteous blood shed from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah slain between the temple and the altar. Thus, when the planting which the heavenly Father did not plant has been uprooted, may the generation of the righteous be built up, through which we may deserve to reach, with God, the heavenly house in which there are riches and glory, everlasting [read: eternal]. May God grant this to us, he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

LXXXIX. SECOND SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF SAINT STEPHEN THE PROTOMARTYR  
[Note: From Victorinus, Col. 0719D.]

“Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:44).

Our Lord and Redeemer, dearest brothers, came into the world solely out of love; and therefore he wished to establish his own in love. In the Old Testament, because of the weakness of an untaught people, it was commanded: “You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy” (ibid., v. 43). Behold, that command is now enlarged. Enemies are now included under love. Nor did he merely command this: he fulfilled what he commanded. He was led to the Passion; he was mocked and scourged. Yet in that very Passion he prayed for his persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

But someone may say: It is a great labour to love enemies and to pray for persecutors. Nor do we deny it. It is no small labour in this world; but there is a great reward in the world to come. Hear how great the reward is. Stephen, whose feast is celebrated today, one of the seven deacons ordained by the apostles, entered [Col. 0721B] the synagogue and began to dispute with the Jews; and no one could resist the Spirit who spoke. But they drove him outside the city and stoned him. Yet he, looking up to heaven, said: “I see the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:55). And whence came this reward? Because, kneeling down, he cried out: “Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge” (ibid., 59 [7:60]).

He saw the heavens opened because the way was prepared, and Christ was ready to receive and to help; hence he rose for him, because Stephen saw him standing. Sitting belongs to one judging and reigning; standing, to one helping. Therefore, although we cry daily, “You who sit at the right hand of the Father, have mercy upon us,” Stephen now sees him standing, because he wished to show honour to his martyr and to show himself ready to help him.

Stephen was the first martyr after Christ’s Ascension, and the first to follow him in imitation by praying for enemies. The Lord prayed in his Passion for his persecutors; Stephen prayed for those who stoned him. Amid that downfall of stones, when another person might have forgotten his dearest ones, he commended his enemies to the Lord. The Lord wished to open the heavens manifestly to the first martyr, so that his followers might be secure concerning their recompense. He wished to be seen standing, so that all later people might believe that they too would be helped by the Lord in the same way. Nor was Stephen’s prayer unheard, for some of his persecutors were converted to the Lord.

For Saul, who is now also called Paul, a most wicked persecutor, guarded everyone’s garments [Col. 0721D] so that he might share in the crimes of all who struck Stephen. Afterwards he was converted and, from a wolf, became a lamb; from an enemy, a friend; from a most wicked persecutor, a most faithful preacher. Behold, Paul enjoys Christ’s brightness with Stephen; he rejoices with Stephen and reigns with him. Stephen gives an example of prayer for persecutors; Paul gives an example of pardon for converts.

The solemnity of this saint, dearest brothers, which we must celebrate, excels in merits, in the martyr’s great devotion, because it excels in examples. To what saint do we read that it was ever granted to raise six dead persons after his death? For blessed Stephen, after his death, raised six dead persons in Africa, as we have learned from the account of blessed Augustine: first a certain priest, then a boy, afterwards a certain religious woman, then a certain girl, afterwards a young man, and finally a certain little child.

[Note: Col. 0721. Saint Augustine himself recounts these same events, but more fully, in *The City of God*, book XXII, chapter 28, new edition, p. 668.]

Eucharius, too, a priest, suffered from the long-standing illness of kidney stones; but he was healed through the memorial shrine of this martyr. Later, however, when another illness became severe, he died. But after this priest’s tunic had been brought to and brought back from the memorial shrine of the same martyr, and laid upon the body where the dead man lay, he was restored to life through the merits of the blessed martyr.

We read concerning a boy that, while he was playing on a threshing floor, oxen drawing a vehicle ran out of their course, crushed him under the wheels, and he immediately expired while convulsing. His mother took him up and placed him at the same memorial shrine; and not only did he come back to life, but he appeared unharmed. A religious woman, however, was ill, and the tunic of a religious woman was brought to that memorial shrine; but before the tunic could be brought back, she died. Nevertheless her parents covered her corpse with this tunic, and, her spirit returning, she was made well.

On a certain day, when a Syrian *banus* [a title of uncertain rank] was praying at the memorial shrine of the same martyr for his sick daughter and had brought the girl’s garment there, behold, two boys ran to him from the house and announced that she was dead. But his friends who were with him prevented the boys from telling him, lest he should weep in public. When he returned home, deeply moved by grief, he threw the garment he was carrying over the dead body of his daughter, and she was restored to life.

Again, the son of a certain man had died; the friends anointed his body with the martyr’s oil, and he immediately returned to life. The sixth remaining person was raised in this way: Eleusius, a man of tribunician rank, having a little child dead from illness, placed him upon the martyr’s memorial shrine, and after much prayer poured forth with tears, raised him up alive. These and other like things the Lord wrought through the martyr. But we read these examples out of many because they seem greater.

Therefore, brothers, let us rejoice on the feast of so great a patron. Let us pray to him that, just as he prayed for enemies, so he may pray for us, his friends. Let us imitate his charity, that we may be companions in virtue and sharers in reward. Let us imitate him, who grieved more over the sins of his persecutors than over his own wounds, more over their impiety [Col. 0722D] than over his own death. And rightly more: for in their wickedness there were many things that could be mourned; in his death there was nothing that ought to have been grieved over. Eternal death followed their impiety; perpetual life followed his death.

Let us therefore imitate, at least in some measure, the love of so illustrious a teacher. Let us love our brothers in the Church with the same disposition with which he then loved his enemies. For you know that without love no virtue has worth. John says: “Everyone who does not love his brother remains in death” (1 John 3:14). And it is true: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (ibid., v. 15). Charity is the root of all virtues. Therefore, when the root perishes, the branches perish also [lacuna]. Martyrdom has no value without love; almsgiving has no value without it. Hence the Apostle says: “If I hand over my body so that I may burn, and if I distribute my possessions as food for the poor, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3). But may God, who first loved us, himself inspire it in our hearts. Amen.

LXXX. FIRST SERMON FOR THE FEAST OF SAINT JOHN THE EVANGELIST  
[Note: From the Saint-Germain manuscript, Col. 0723D.]

“The days of my people shall be like the days of a tree . . . because they are the seed of those blessed by the Lord, and their descendants are with them; and it shall be that before they call, I will hear” (Isa. 65:22).

By these words the Holy Spirit, through Isaiah, raises the hearts of the humble, stops the mouths of the proud, offers great hope to the poor in spirit, and checks the presumption of the friends of this world, when he promises the likeness of the tree of life and the granting of desire before the voice of calling, saying: “The days of my people shall be like the days of a tree, and before they call, I will hear.” O how welcome, sweet, and great is this promise, by which the likeness of a tree is promised to the seed of the blessed and to their descendants! This is not the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, in which we fell, but the tree of life planted in the midst of paradise.

The tree of the knowledge of good and evil was, as it were, the devil’s instrument for casting down humankind (Gen. 3), when he rashly advised the human being to do what had been forbidden, adding a false promise. For, taking occasion through the tree, the crafty serpent worked the vice of concupiscence in the human being. He sent out hook, dragnet, and net, and captured the entire human race, though it was established radically in one human being. Hence in Habakkuk: “He lifted up everything with his hook, drew him into his dragnet, and gathered him into his net; over this he shall rejoice and exult. But he who is coming shall come and shall not delay; and the soul of the unbeliever shall not be upright within itself” (Hab. 1:15; 2:3).

Observe carefully [Col. 0723C] with how much craft and cunning the devil deceived the human being. For he sent out, as it were, a hook when, approaching the woman deceitfully, he asked: “Why did the Lord command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” The woman replied: “We eat from the fruit of the trees of paradise; but concerning the tree which is in the midst of paradise, he commanded us not to eat, lest perhaps we die” (Gen. 3:1). Having thus discovered, through the hook of his crafty question, what the woman feared, he removed it by the dragnet of false denial, adding: “You shall by no means die” (ibid., v. 4). And so as more easily to persuade her of what he intended, he added the net of fraudulent promise, saying: “On whatever day you eat, your eyes shall be opened and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil.” The woman therefore took of its fruit and ate (ibid., v. 5).

It is sufficiently clear how the contriver of deceit cast down humankind through the tree, and therefore rejoiced and exulted. But he who conquered humankind on the occasion of a tree was overcome by the power of a tree; and the human being who fell through the tree of exaltation rose again through the tree of humility. Of this he adds: “He who is coming shall come and shall not delay; and the soul of the unbeliever shall not be upright within itself” (Hab. 2:3). Who is this one whose coming the prophet announces with such proclamation and exultation? This is the tree of life. For, as Solomon says, “Wisdom” [of the Father] “is a tree of life to all who embrace her, and whoever holds her fast is blessed” (Prov. 3:18).

By this tree the savagery of the crafty enemy was broken; by this same tree good things were restored to us and the devil’s deception exposed. This tree was exalted through humility; the tree of death was humbled through pride. This tree first withered in barrenness, but afterwards marvelously put forth leaves in abundant fruit, when the green tree was dried up. Hence the Lord says through Ezekiel: “I, the Lord, have humbled the lofty tree, dried up the green tree, and made the dry tree put forth leaves” [Col. 0724B] (Ezek. 17:24).

This is the tree which Elisha cast into the water to seek the axe, and the iron floated to the tree. For while the sons of the prophets were cutting wood by the water, the iron of an axe fell from its handle into the water. They therefore called Elisha, who came, extended the handle over the water, and immediately the iron sprang from the water back to the handle (4 Kings [2 Kings] 6). The iron which fell from the handle into the water signifies the human race, which, withdrawing from God through the offence of the first transgression, fell into the flow and current of this misery and instability.

This is the river Chebar, beside which Ezekiel sat grieving [read: laments] among the captives. This is the water of Babylon’s rivers, of which the Prophet says: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept” (Ps. 136:1 [137:1]). This is the Dead Sea, from which no living water flows for eternal life of salvation—the water of which, if one drinks, one shall never thirst. That water produces thirst; this extinguishes it. Into that turbulent and bitter water, the iron of the human race fell through the sin of the first human being. And our Elisha came, that is, Christ, summoned by the prayers of the prophets, and cast the tree into the water, to which the iron returned. For, presenting himself to the world, who is the tree, in the likeness of sinful flesh [Col. 0724D], he drank from the torrent on the way, because he tasted the bitterness of passion and death, when the Jews gave him vinegar mingled with gall to drink. Thus the iron floated to the tree: that is, the human being returned to God, the servant to the master, the sheep to the shepherd, the prodigal son to the father. Thus the humble tree put forth leaves when the lofty tree was dried up: that is, “when the head was struck from the house of the wicked, and its sceptres were cursed” (Hab. 3:13).

The house of the wicked—that is, of wickedness—has its head, namely the devil; and its sceptres are those who are worse in malice and who “come like a whirlwind to scatter God’s house” (ibid., v. 14). But it cannot be moved, because it has its foundation upon the rock and its head in heaven, which is the head of every principality and power. This, therefore, is the head [Christ] struck from the house of the wicked when he took away the ill-assembled company from him and brought it back to himself.

Hence Habakkuk says: “Woe to him who gathers what is not his own, and suddenly the one who bites him shall rise up.”

[Note: Col. 0725D. “Woe to him who gathers wicked avarice for his house, that his nest may be on high, and thinks himself delivered from the hand of evil.” Thus the Vulgate has it: Habakkuk, chapter II, verse 9.]

And Jeremiah cries: “The partridge [Vulgate: has brooded] gathered what it did not bear; it made riches, not with justice, and in the middle of its days it shall leave them, and at its end it shall be found foolish” (Jer. 17:11). The devil is compared to the foolish little bird, the partridge, which made riches without justice when it subjected another’s servant to itself through deception. But it was abandoned in the middle of its days when, its head having been struck, the wicked are weakened; and, having left it, it returned to the head from the house of God. But at its end it shall be found foolish when, its dominion emptied, it shall be cast into the fire prepared for it and its own.

Therefore the Lord dried up the lofty tree and made it wither when the humble tree put forth leaves, namely when Aaron’s rod put forth leaves and bore almonds. When the tree planted beside the courses of waters gave its fruit in its season (Ps. 1). This is the tree of life, namely the Wisdom of the Father, which is planted beside the courses of waters and planted in the midst of paradise: beside the courses of waters because the Son of God was made human through the operation of the Holy Spirit, whose grace quenches the heat of sin as water does thirst; and in the midst of paradise because Christ is in the midst of the Church as head and prince.

This is the shaft of the lampstand in the tabernacle of the Lord, having three branches on this side [Col. 0725C] and three on that. For in Christ, as branches in a vine, are the three orders of the faithful who existed before grace and who were then founded under grace. These are the three men whom Ezekiel saw as to be saved: Noah, Daniel, and Job; that is, married persons, the continent, and rulers, or prelates. Therefore the tree of life brought forth this fruit in its season when it gave the twelve fruits of grace, namely the apostles: “the blessed, and the seed of the blessed, and their descendants” (Isa. 65:23).

Tripartite here is the distinction: namely, “the blessed,” “their offspring,” and “their descendants.” Behold the fruit of the tree of life, of which holy Job says: “If a tree is cut down, it grows green again, and its branches shoot forth” [Col. 0725D] (Job 14:7). This tree of life is Christ the Lord: when it was cut down by death, its branches shot forth, as he says in the Gospel: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 8:28). And again: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). And through the Prophet: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. 140:10).

For Christ the Lord was, as it were, alone when through death he passed from earth to heaven, from the world to the Father. But as he passed by and went down from Jericho [Col. 0726A], twelve followed him crying out: that is, the two peoples, Jews and Gentiles, cried to the Lord in faith and followed in his footsteps by living soberly, devoutly, and justly. Then the woman suffering from a flow of blood, standing behind him, touched the hem of his garment. Finally, so great a multitude believed that Isaiah, as though filled with astonishment, marvels and says: “Can a land give birth in one day, or shall a nation such as this be born?” (Isa. 66:8). And Hosea: “Israel shall put forth shoots like the lily; his root shall break out like that of Lebanon; his branches shall spread, and his glory shall be like the olive tree” (Hos. 14:6).

Precious, therefore, is this tree, whose cutting caused branches to shoot forth with such abundant spreading, and whose fruit is so great and such as this, as he says through Hosea: “I am like a thick juniper tree; from me fruit is found” [Col. 0726B] (ibid., 9). The Lord shows in the preceding words of Isaiah what that fruit is: “According to the days of the tree, so shall be the days of my people.” Then he distinguishes that people itself into the aforesaid three orders: the blessed, their offspring, and their descendants: “Before they cry out, I shall hear them.”

The blessed, therefore, are rightly understood as the apostles, who received the first fruits of blessing and grace. Their offspring are those whom they begot in the faith. Their descendants are those begotten in the faith by their children. Hence in the Proverbs: “The good man leaves heirs, children and grandchildren; and the substance of the sinner is kept for the just” (Prov. 13:22). This good man is he who is also understood as the tree of life, namely Christ, in comparison with whom no one is good. He has heirs, children, and grandchildren. For those begotten by him or by the apostles shall be heirs indeed of God and fellow-heirs of Christ [Col. 0726C]. These are those “whom God foreknew to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. 8:29).

Among the children—that is, among those blessed by the Lord—stands out the most holy Evangelist John, whose feast is celebrated today, through the grace of virginity, the singular privilege of love, and the gift of immeasurable wisdom. For he is that disciple whom the Lord called away from the storm-tossed sea of marriage, so that a virgin might follow the Virgin; and to him from the cross he entrusted his Virgin Mother, saying to the mother concerning the disciple, “Behold your son,” and to the disciple concerning the mother, “Behold your mother” (John 19:26).

> [Note: Col. 0726D. Hildebert here appears to have held that John was the bridegroom at the wedding of Cana.]

He is that disciple whom [Col. 0726D] Jesus loved greatly—not perhaps more fervently than the others, but more intimately, because he was near to him both by kinship and by bodily purity. When the day of his departure was at hand, he gathered the brethren, descended into the place dug for his burial, bade them farewell, and fell asleep in the Lord. He was as free from the pain of death as he was untouched by bodily corruption.

He is that disciple who reclined upon the Lord’s breast at supper, who drank the fullness of spiritual wisdom from the fountain of the Lord’s breast; intoxicated by it, he burst forth into a theological utterance so weighty that he thundered more loftily than Paul himself, and the whole world could not contain him [Col. 0727A] when he said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1:1). Thus he is deservedly compared with the soaring eagle, which gazes upon the sun’s brightness with eyes undazzled. So John, with the unwavering gaze of his mind, contemplated the true light—namely Christ’s divinity, eternity, and equality with the Father. As though he were a sounding trumpet, the womb of the heretics was made childless and their words became barren.

For while John—that is, the grace of God—was proclaiming truth, the mouths of those clamouring against truth were stopped, and the malice of teachers who falsely shoot at the upright in heart was disclosed [variant: “who, with darkened heart, shoot at the upright”]. They do not sleep unless they have done evil, and they exult in the worst deeds. Concerning them [Col. 0727B] Hosea says: “Give them, Lord: what will you give them? A womb without children, and dry breasts” (Hos. 9:14).

The fulfillment of this imprecation came about in the Apostle John, who, raising his voice like a trumpet, terrified the minds of sinners, cast down and scattered the tongues of those who desire the wars of heretics, stopped the tongues of the wicked, and freed the lost. Of this multitude Isaiah says: “The great trumpet shall sound, and those who had been lost shall come from the land of the Assyrians and from the land of Egypt, and they shall worship the Lord on the holy mountain in Jerusalem” (Isa. 27:13).

This trumpet is excellent: not merely of horn, but of silver and gold. It is of horn because, as horn rises above and surpasses flesh, so the disciple beloved by the Lord overcame carnal affections and lusts [Col. 0727C], setting his mind on things above, not on things upon the earth; walking in the flesh, but not warring according to the flesh. Thus horn adheres to the flesh and rises above it. This trumpet is also silver and gold because it shone in the beauty of eloquence and excelled in profundity of meaning [variant: “in the profundity of meanings”]. For gold signifies wisdom, and silver eloquence.

This trumpet is also ductile, because it is not broken by hammering but drawn out. Tested by the hammers of tribulations, it did not fail but advanced; when cast into a cauldron of boiling oil, it came forth unharmed alike in body and mind. Therefore, as this trumpet sounded, those who had been lost came from the land of Assyria and the land of Egypt: that is, from the pride of heretics, from the affliction [Col. 0727D] and sorrow of evils. For “Assyrian” is interpreted “directing,” and “Egypt” “affliction” or “darkness.”

Such fruits does the tree of life bear: through it those triumph over their adversaries who, before they cry out with their mouths, are heard as they cry in their hearts; their days shall be like the days of the tree of life. For just as Christ now dies no more and death shall have no further dominion over him, but he reigns eternally with the Father, so “the blessed of the Lord, and their offspring, and their descendants with them, shall rejoice forever” (Isa. 65:23), shining like the sun in the kingdom of the Father. May he who lives and reigns for ages of ages deign to grant this to us. Amen.

LXXXI. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT JOHN THE EVANGELIST. SECOND SERMON.

> [Note: Col. 0727D. From Victorinus.]

[Col. 0728A]

“Foxes have dens, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8:20).

Our Lord and Redeemer, brothers, lamenting the impiety of humankind, seeks to lodge with us and finds no dwelling-place. People will not receive him as a guest; they prefer to receive God’s adversaries. And who are God’s adversaries? Foxes and birds of the air. For he says: “Foxes have dens, and birds of the air have nests.” The fox is a deceitful animal and therefore signifies deceit; birds signify pride and self-exaltation [Col. 0728B]. For the proud person flies upward to the stars, lifting himself on the wings of boastfulness.

He calls human breasts “dens,” because in them perverse thoughts prepare a precipice for others. Likewise, the nests of birds are in their minds, because there their young—that is, works of pride and self-exaltation—are nourished. Pride is one thing, self-exaltation another. Pride is when someone desires to be above everyone else; self-exaltation is when someone strives to make himself equal to his superiors. Pompey was proud, because he would tolerate no one before him.

Thus deceit and pride find dwellings in us. But the Son of Man—that is, the Son of the Virgin—has nowhere, that is, finds nowhere to lay his head, who is our head. For “the Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there was one who understood or sought God. All have turned aside; together they have become useless” [Col. 0728C] (Ps. 13:2).

Let us now consider deceit and see whether it can be found to have a place in any human being. Deceit exists when one thing is done and another pretended. Hence people act deceitfully, of whom the Psalmist says: “They speak peace with their neighbour, but evils are in their hearts” (Ps. 27:3). And again: “Each has spoken vain things to his neighbour; with deceitful lips, with heart and heart they have spoken” (Ps. 11:3). Those who promise one thing and do another seem to have double hearts. Again he says: “There is no truth in their mouth; their heart is vain” (Ps. 5:10).

Is not this kind of hatred, dearest brothers, common among people [Col. 0728D]: the more one hates a brother, the more eagerly one hastens to reconciliation—not in order to love him, but in order more cunningly to crush him by deceit? For one can harm him more abundantly once one has become privy to his counsels. There is another kind of deceit. People readily swear that they will keep faith with friends, and then harm them more effectively and more foully when they are unsuspecting. Under oath they deny possessing what they received; nor is it enough to commit perjury once, but they become perjurers twice over the same matter. They willingly do everything for those whom they wish to deceive, so that a lord may not beware of his own man, and a man may more easily inflict injury upon his lord. Thus faith perishes; reverence perishes. Neither son keeps faith with father [Col. 0729A] nor father with son; and when friends have brought every evil upon friends, they stand ready to assert under oath that they are innocent. Thus “they related things in order to hide snares; they said, ‘Who will see them?’” (Ps. 63:6).

There is again another kind of deceit, called hypocrisy. Some fast and afflict themselves before people in order to be seen as good, and rejoice in that reputation although they wholly deviate from it. We have briefly touched upon deceit. Let us now turn to pride.

Pride is the root of all vices. It cast an angel down from heaven when he wished to make himself equal to God. It makes a person forget his own frailty. It makes him stretch himself out presumptuously. It causes all things to be done for praise. It wants everything to be seen. It lays its hand upon everything [Col. 0729B]. If someone is wise, he boasts—against such people the prophet says: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isa. 5:21)—yet they glory in having the power to do evil. Against them the Psalmist says: “Why do you glory in malice, you who are mighty in iniquity?” (Ps. 51:3). These boast in their evil deeds and utter greater things concerning great matters; Scripture rebukes them, saying: “Do not multiply lofty, boastful speech” (1 Sam. 2:3).

Pride also dares to rise against God and his servants. Such people neglect to enter church and make little of the divine office. They regard the Lord’s priests as contemptible. Every observance of religion is trampled underfoot by the proud; and, as the Apostle says, “we have become like the refuse of this world” (1 Cor. 4). But God comforts us [Col. 0729C], who said: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me first. If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also” (John 15:18). But know that “whoever despises you despises me also” (Luke 10:16).

This contempt should not trouble those who suffer it, but those who inflict it, because the Lord will take vengeance for the insult done to himself and his own. Luke relates that the Lord spoke a certain parable concerning the vindication of his own. He says: “There was a judge in a certain city who did not fear God and did not respect man. There was a widow in that city, and she came to him saying, ‘Vindicate me against my adversary.’ And for a long time he would not. But afterward the judge said within himself, ‘Although I do not fear God or respect man [Col. 0729D], nevertheless, because this widow is violent [variant: troublesome] toward me, I shall vindicate her.’ This the judge of iniquity did; and will God not vindicate his elect? I tell you that he will swiftly vindicate his own” (Luke 18:2).

This is the parable which the Lord spoke about the avenging of his own. For he himself will cast down the powerful from their throne and exalt the humble (Luke 1). He exalted humble David and cast down proud Saul. No vice is so hateful to God and to human beings as pride. For God breaks every proud person.

There is another vice that greatly occupies and defiles all Christians: namely lust. It assaults both sexes and takes away that flower of virginity by which every soul pleases God, and by which this John, whose feast is celebrated today, was loved by God. For because he was a virgin, the Lord held him more intimately than the others. In a certain intimacy he reclined upon the Lord’s breast at supper. The Lord also entrusted his mother to him, as a Virgin to a virgin. So greatly did he love him and hold dear the incorrupt disciple [Col. 0730A] that, while all the other apostles died in martyrdom, John alone passed gently to the Lord and without bloodshed, as the Lord had promised him in the Gospel.

For when he said to Peter, “Follow me” (John 21:19), that is, imitate me by dying on the cross, Peter turned and saw that disciple following him, and said: “Lord, what about this man?” (ibid., 21)—that is, what will he do, by what death will he die? Jesus said to him: “Thus I will that he remain until I come” (ibid., 22): I will that he remain alive and whole until I appear to him with the other brethren.

For the history relates that when John was ninety-seven years old, the Lord appeared to him with his disciples and said: “Come to me, for now it is time for you to feast with me at the banquet with your brethren.” John rose and began to go. But the Lord said to him: “On the Lord’s Day, seven days from now, you shall thus come to me.” Having said this, he was received into heaven.

When the Lord’s Day came, therefore [Col. 0730C], the whole multitude assembled in the church. From the first cockcrow he celebrated the mysteries of the Lord, addressed all the people until the third hour, strengthened and instructed them. When he had ended his sermon, he prayed for his people; and when he had completed all things, he had bread brought to him. Looking up to heaven, he blessed it, broke it, and distributed it to all, saying: “May my portion be with you, and yours with me.” Then he had the pit of his tomb prepared and spread his garments there.

Then so great a light appeared over the people for almost an hour that no one could endure it. Making the sign of the cross over his whole body, he stood and said: “You alone are with me, Lord Jesus.” He threw himself upon the tomb; blessing them all, he laid himself down in his sepulchre, commanded that he be covered, and immediately gave up his spirit. And immediately manna appeared, coming forth from the tomb, which that place still *glunit* to this day.

> [Note: Cols. 0729D, 0730D. We have been unable to find this word, as obsolete, in any author we have seen or in any dictionary. Nothing else occurs to us by way of conjecture as to its meaning except that the place of which Hildebert speaks, where the tomb of St John the Evangelist stood, still preserved this manna issuing from his tomb; or perhaps that this precious manna was still flowing from that place. Let the reader decide.]

Therefore, brothers, strive to imitate him, so that with the other virgins you may sing the new song and follow the Lamb wherever he goes. He is the one whose flesh was stained by no defilement. When, in his youth, he wished to marry, the Lord said to him: “John, you are necessary to me; I require your service.” Again, when on another occasion he wished to marry, the Lord brought upon him an illness by which he recalled him. Therefore have him as your patron, that with him you may reign in heaven, through the help of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

639. LXXXII. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH. FIRST SERMON.

> [Note: Cols. 0731D, 0732D. From Victorinus and Lyra. This sermon appears not to have been completed, or at least not to have been copied in full by the scribe. I infer, however, that it was delivered by Hildebert himself after he had become bishop, since here he professes himself Christ’s vicar. This was at that celebrated dedication of the Church of Le Mans which he magnificently completed through his own care and expense, in the presence of the more distinguished prelates of the province of Tours; see his Life under the year 1120. He may also have delivered this sermon on the anniversary of the same dedication, as he did the subsequent ones.]

“It was the Feast of Dedication at Jerusalem, and it was winter; and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s portico; and the Jews surrounded him . . . and he said to them: ‘You do not believe, because you are not of my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life’” (John 10:22).

Dearest brothers, Solomon built the Lord’s temple in Jerusalem, richly adorned it with much goldwork and many precious gems, dedicated it when it had been constructed with great solemnity, and celebrated each year its dedications—called *encaenia* in Greek—commanding that they be celebrated successively thereafter. When these *encaenia* were once being observed in Jerusalem, Christ wished to honour that feast by his presence and wished also to speak to the people.

If, then, that temple, in which only the blood of animals was poured out, was worthy of such great reverence, the present Church, where the true sacrifice is consecrated daily, demands far greater veneration. If the divine presence wished to attend that feast, there can be no doubt that the dedication of his Church is visited by divine grace. And because on the day of dedication the Lord wished to address the people, it seemed fitting that we, his vicars [Col. 0731B], should follow the example of our head and consider what we ought to understand from the Lord’s words.

> [Note: Col. 0732D. This is the title proper to bishops.]

But observe what the Lord said in his preaching, so that our life may be shaped by the teaching of his words. He apprehended [variant: “rebuked”] his adversaries and praised his disciples. To his adversaries he said: “You do not believe me, because you are not of my sheep.” But concerning his own he said: “My sheep hear my voice; I know them; they follow me; and I give them eternal life.” Behold, dearest brothers, you have gathered for the dedication of the church. Consider whether you are among the adversaries or among the Lord’s sheep. For the Lord knows his own, as he says there: “I know them.”

He therefore taught us to recognize the sheep by this distinction—whether they hear his voice—when he says: “My sheep [Col. 0731D] hear my voice.” But because hearing his voice is not enough unless the hearer wishes to fulfill it in deed, according to the Apostle James, who says: “Be doers of the word and not hearers only” (Jas. 1:22), he adds: “And they follow me.” The person who follows the Lord walks as the Lord himself walked. The Lord did not command us to go ahead, but to follow. He was the first to test the ford, the first to show the way beforehand, the first to be baptized, the first to fast [Col. 0732A], the first to be poor, the first to preach, the first to receive insults, the first to pray for enemies, the first to lay down his life for his sheep.

For he invited us to despise the world, saying: “Everyone who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33). Already while fasting in the wilderness, he had despised all the kingdoms of the world when the devil said to him: “All these things I shall give you, if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:9). The Lord said to him: “Go away and flee, Satan”—that is, “you are an adversary, who teach people to love earthly things.” Likewise, when the Lord had fed people with five loaves and two fishes, they wanted “to seize him and make him king”; but he “fled alone to the mountain” (John 6:15).

He was so poor that the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head. Of him the Apostle says: “You know that the Lord became poor for our sake, so that, though he was rich, you might become rich through his poverty” (2 Cor. 8:9). Wearied from the journey and thirsty, he asked water from the Samaritan woman. Sometimes he also ate on the road. For there, at the well, the disciples offered him food which they had bought in the city. For it is written: “His disciples had gone into the city to buy food” (John 4:8); and later in the same Gospel it is said: “The disciples urged him, saying, ‘Rabbi, eat’” (ibid., 31). Behold, the Lord did not seek wine to quench his thirst, nor did he always seek a house in which to eat food.

The Lord’s disciples were also so poor that from hunger they plucked ears of grain from the fields and ate them. For it is written: “His disciples, being hungry, began to pluck ears of grain and eat” (Matt. 12:1). The Lord did not wish to have riches in this present life, nor to possess anything here, lest he invite others to love riches. He willed that riches should be merely provisions for the journey, because we are in exile and journey toward our homeland; because we have no enduring city here; and because, while we live, we are away from God.

Let us therefore not carry the burden of riches upon our backs, lest the weight crush us on the way. There remains a narrow road through which a camel cannot enter. The camel is the hunchbacked rich man, whose back is swollen by the burden of money. Unburden yourselves [Col. 0732D] by giving to the poor, because the tenacity of avarice will not go unpunished. A heap of money does not grant eternal life. Hence the Lord says: “See to it and beware of every kind of avarice, because a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses” (Luke 12:15).

After the Lord had thus rebuked them for avarice, he spoke the parable of a certain rich man, [who said]: “What shall I do, because I have nowhere to gather my fruits? And he said: This is what I shall do: I shall tear down my barns [Col. 0733A] and build larger ones; and there I shall gather all that has grown for me and my goods, and I shall say to my soul: Soul, you have many goods stored up for many years. Rest, eat, drink, feast. But God said to him: Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and whose will be the things you have prepared?” (ibid., 17). This man was condemned not for robbery, but for graspingness . . .

LXXXIII. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH. SECOND SERMON.

> [Note: Col. 0733D. From Victorinus.]

On the heavenly building, and those who are fit for it.

“Her foundations are upon the holy mountains. The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the tabernacles of Jacob; glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 86:1).

[Col. 0733B] From the beginning of the world, dearest brothers, the Lord began to build the city glorious beyond all the tabernacles of Jacob, but it has not yet been completed. For he wished to have a dwelling in which he might abide; he wished also to have a household to serve him—not because he himself needed it, but so that he might find occasion to do good to those who serve him.

But because he was a king richer and more exalted than all rulers—for he himself says through Wisdom, “Through me kings reign” (Prov. 8:15)—he wished to have a more wondrous and exalted house, so that he who was eternal might build for himself an eternal city. In order that it might be eternal, he wished its structure to be stable; therefore its foundations are upon the holy mountains. The gates of that city are also better than all the tabernacles of the Jews, because Solomon’s temple cannot be compared to this house [Col. 0733C].

Many glorious things have been said and are said concerning this city of God, things spoken by many prophets and apostles. This is the city called by many names: Zion, Jerusalem, the kingdom of heaven, the Church, and others. It is built in heaven, but its stones are squared on earth and afterward raised to heaven. All the angels labour at its building, because this ministry has been assigned to them until the end of the age: once it is completed, they will glorify God there forever.

Many masons and workers of this sort have spoken [variant: “are placed”] in the world. Those who work well acquire for themselves not money but a kingdom; those who work badly are bound in an eternal prison. Archbishops, bishops, and priests have been appointed craftsmen of this building [Col. 0733D]. They are visited daily by angels, who carry to the high commandments the stones they prepare. The Lord has set them upon earth, that the workers may be instructed. Whoever works otherwise is rebuked by the supreme Judge in the present life or condemned in the future.

The agreement with the workers was not that they should labour for one literal day, but for the span of the one present day. For the whole life is one day. The tool by which the work is done never breaks, but the worker is often wearied by sloth. Yet the supreme King, who has so many workers, who causes so many angels to labour, who instructs his craftsmen by so many commandments, has many adversaries [Col. 0734A] who try to destroy that building and strive in every way to hinder those preparing it. Often they carry off even the chief craftsmen captive and destroy the stones they were preparing.

Yet the adversary cannot seize anyone outright, but lies in wait to snatch the poor person while drawing him in. He alluringly promises false goods; thus he removes the wretch from God’s work, leads him away with himself, and kills the deceived person in everlasting death. Daily there is conflict between the craftsmen and God’s adversaries; sometimes the adversaries flee, sometimes the craftsmen succumb. Yet they do not therefore cease to prepare some stones, and so the building grows daily.

This city, dearest brothers, of which we have spoken, is nothing other than the assembly of the blessed, called Jerusalem because there in heaven they contemplate true peace, namely God. Of this city David says: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose sharing is in the same thing” [Col. 0734B] (Ps. 121:3). The city is built as blessed souls are transferred to heaven and the number of the blessed increases.

Its foundations are called the holy mountains because the apostles and prophets are the foundations of the Church: the whole Church is founded upon their faith, preaching, and Scriptures. Hence the Apostle: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. 2:20). The gates of that city are faith and baptism; for those who fall back after baptism have repentance, confession, and satisfaction. These are better than all the tabernacles of Jacob—that is, than all the legal institutions of the Jewish people [Col. 0734C].

The stones of this city are individual believers, prepared here through good works so that afterward they may be placed beyond the heavens in the assembly of the saints. The craftsmen are preachers, who, as if with the tool of preaching, soften human minds by cutting away excesses. As the Apostle Paul says: “We are God’s fellow-workers; you are God’s building. According to the grace of God given to me, as a wise architect I laid a foundation” (1 Cor. 3:9).

The angels are ministers of this city because they have been assigned to guard us and carry the souls of the blessed to heaven. Hence the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent into service for those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation?” [Col. 0734D] (Heb. 1:14). The adversaries are demons, who hinder the prelates of the Church from preparing people for the kingdom of heaven; they also lead the prelates captive and destroy those very stones, lest they be placed in the building. But let us first discuss the hindrance caused by adversaries, and afterward return to the city of God with which we began.

You know, beloved, that when you approached the Lord and received his faith, you were asked: “Do you renounce Satan and all his works?” And your answer was: “I renounce him.” What was this promise? Did you not promise to avoid every sin [Col. 0735A]? Did you not renounce the devil and promise henceforth to cling to Christ? But the devil, expelled from heaven, envies those who are returning to heaven. He tries to violate your promise or make you forget it.

When he sees himself driven from your hearts and God reigning there, according to the one who says, “Arise, O God, at the boundaries of my enemies” (Ps. 7:7)—that is, in the hearts of the ungodly, which had been the boundaries and dwellings of demons—he says: “I shall return to my house from which I came out”; and coming, “he finds it empty, swept, and adorned” (Matt. 12:14), that is, cleansed of vices and adorned with virtues. Then he takes seven spirits more wicked than himself—that is, the capital vices opposed to the seven principal virtues [Col. 0735B]—and, coming, they dwell there; and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first.

For it is better not to know the truth than, after knowing it, to turn back; because then he causes a person to fall into one sin, then into another, and so turns it into a habit. Thus what Solomon says comes to pass: “When the sinner comes into the depth of vices, he despises” (Prov. 18:3). For then he is not ashamed of his sins, does not tolerate correction, and his heart is hardened so that he does not care to repent but turns to despair. This stone cannot be polished or placed in the Lord’s building.
