There is another kind of people, so tightly held by the love of worldly things that, although they are softened by hearing preaching, the smoke [variant: “rope”] of habit [Col. 0735C] draws them back, and they cannot disregard the money they have accumulated. Hence the Lord says: “It is difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:23), and for this reason he is compared to a camel: just as a camel cannot lay aside its natural hump, so a rich person can scarcely leave behind the love of accumulated money; just as the camel cannot pass through the eye of a needle, neither can the rich pass along the narrow track of the way. Of this it is said: “Narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matt. 7:14).

A person leaves much behind who leaves the love of money. Hence Peter says: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19:27). He has left much who has kept nothing for himself. The Apostle does not condemn those who are rich, but those who wish to be rich—that is, who love riches [Col. 0735D]. Hence he says: “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation, and into many harmful desires that plunge a person into ruin” (1 Tim. 6:9) and destruction, because covetousness is the root of all evils.

For perjuries, usuries, flatteries, deceptions, simonies, thefts, murders, pride, sacrileges, and adulteries are committed for money. Therefore David says: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61:11). Such persons can scarcely be polished so as to be placed in the temple of God.

There are others whom some pleasure of the flesh holds fast. They care nothing for money, but are so weak that they can scarcely resist the temptation of gluttony and lust; indeed all day long they either delight in revelries and drunkenness, linger in brothels with prostitutes, or make their own home a brothel [Col. 0736A]. They often repent, yet return to the same things; thus they increase their sin when they return to their vomit. They are compared to beasts of burden, because like beasts they rot in their own dung. Of them the Apostle says: “Not in revelling and indecencies” (Rom. 13:13). Again: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is lust” (Eph. 5:18). Of prostitutes he says: “Whoever clings to a prostitute becomes one body with her” (1 Cor. 6:16). From this come incest, adultery, and abominable kinds of lust.

There are people who are neither rich nor given over to lust, yet are full of wickedness and, as if under a spirit of probity, devote themselves to murder. Of them David says: “Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days” [Col. 0736B] (Ps. 54:24). Their food is the shedding of blood. Of them David says: “Why do you glory in malice, you who are mighty in iniquity?” (Ps. 51:1). Such people can scarcely be drawn back from murders.

There are other people who cannot openly do harm and cannot become rich, but envy and disparage the rich. They accuse them secretly and always devise evils against them, though they speak well of them publicly. Of them David says: “They speak peace with their neighbour, but evils are in their hearts” (Ps. 27:3).

645. LXXXIV. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH. THIRD SERMON.

> [Note: Col. 0735D. From Victorinus.]

On the reverence to be shown to churches.

[Col. 0736C]

The Apostle Paul says: “Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, in order that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word of life; so that he himself might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind, but that she might be holy and without blemish” (Eph. 5:25).

Listen, dearest brethren, to Paul the Apostle, the herald of your exaltation, the proclaimer of your dignity. Hear with how great, or of what kind, a love Christ has been joined to the Church; hear how great a grace his mercy displays. For the Apostle says: Christ loved the Church out of gratuitous goodness, not because merits had preceded, since he loved us first. And how much did he love? Hear how much. He gave himself up for us, that is, for our redemption. He did not send a prophet, an angel, or an archangel; but, as the good shepherd, he laid down his life for his sheep (John 10), so that by humbling himself he might invite his own to humility. For he humbled himself unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2), that is, the death of a thief.

For this reason he first gave himself up, so that afterward he might sanctify [the Church] by the washing, namely by the water of baptism. For the wave of baptism can receive nothing unless, through the shedding [variant: “confusion”] of blood, the water is sanctified for the office of cleansing. Thus the Church is said to have been born from Christ’s side. This mystery was prefigured in Adam from the beginning of the world. “For the Lord cast a sleep upon Adam, took one of his ribs, and made a woman” (Gen. 2:21). Adam’s sleep signified Christ’s death on the cross, while he hung upon which blood and water flowed from his side. These two are the sacraments from which the Church arose.

When Noah made the ark at the time of the Flood, he constructed a door in its side, because the ark—that is, the Church—received from Christ’s side the door of faith and salvation. Hence the Lord says to the Church in the Song of Songs: “Arise, my beloved, and come, my dove, into the clefts of the rock” (Cant. 2:14). Arise from the body of vices, and come through good works, trusting in the clefts. The clefts of the rock are Christ’s wounds; he is the rock, that is, the firmness of the Church. Hence the Apostle says: “And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4).

Therefore the Apostle first stated that the Lord gave himself up, and then added: “that he might sanctify [her] by the washing,” namely the water of baptism. It follows: “in the word of life,” because, once we have been redeemed by baptism, the word of life—that is, the Lord’s commandments—is necessary for us. These are life, because “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matt. 4:4).

For this reason the table of the presentation-bread was placed at the entrance of the tabernacle, and seven loaves lay upon it: because sacred teaching and the table of the divine [variant: “rich”] Scriptures were necessary for those entering the church. In them are contained the teachings of the twelve Apostles, signified by the twelve loaves. And therefore he signified [variant: “added”]: “that he might present to himself a glorious Church,” through immortality, “not having a spot,” of grave sin, “or wrinkle,” of some lighter sin, “but that she might be holy” in virtues “and without blemish” from vices.

For the Lord wishes to dwell in a clean hall, adorned with the beauty of virtues. Hence the Psalmist says: “I have loved the beauty of your house” (Ps. 25:8). And elsewhere David says to the Church: “And the king shall desire your beauty” (Ps. 44:12). The beloved Church, then, received this: that, as the Lord betrothed her, God established for her a bridal chamber and a house in which his bride might delight through the teaching of preaching, and, having fallen, might be reconciled through confession and repentance.

This is the place, dearest brethren, in which you have now assembled, which is called *ecclesia*, or basilica. *Ecclesia* means “convocation,” because all are summoned here, signifying that, united in one faith and love, all are one body. A basilica is so called because it is a royal house; for *basileus* in Greek means “king.” This, moreover, is the dwelling-place of the true King.

The very arrangement of the building should remind your minds, for your instruction, of what must be remembered. For in the structure of this material house, the church, there are diverse members which seem to denote something in us. In this church there is a tower with bells, supporting columns [variant: “columns which support”], windows, a door, two walls, and individual stones joined with mortar; all these mystically signify something in us.

The head signifies Christ, because, as the Apostle says, “he is the head of the Church” (Eph. 5:23), and in him the treasury of divine mysteries is stored. The head is lower than the body because Christ humbled himself by taking the flesh of a servant (Phil. 2), so much so that, in his humanity, he was made lower than the angels as long as he remained capable of suffering. But after the resurrection he was raised above all angels. David indicates both points when he says: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6), because human nature—passible, corruptible, and mortal—was lower than angelic nature. But after the resurrection, “you crowned him with the glory and honour of immortality, and set him over all the works of your hands” (ibid., v. 7), that is, over the angels and over all those who are properly called [variant: “are made”] the works of God because of their dignity, since they are rational—as though God had created them with his own hands.

The tower is confession and repentance, to which captives have recourse. The bells are the priests, the heralds of the Church, who invite people to confession. Thus the Lord admonishes through Isaiah: “Cry aloud; do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1). And again: “You shall hear my words from them.”

The columns of the Church are the pastors, who by their preaching and correction uphold the house of God. Hence in the Song of Songs: “He made its columns of silver” (Cant. 3:10). Silver is a bright and resonant metal; thus pastors sustain [variant: “hold fast”] the house of God by the sound of preaching. David says: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire” (Ps. 11:7).

The windows are understood to be the divine Scriptures, through which the Sun of righteousness, that is Christ, shines upon us; yet in the present life we do not see openly. Hence the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13:12), that is, in obscurity. Thus the Church says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved looks upon me through the windows” (Cant. 2:9), that is, through plain [note: perhaps “not plain,” if attention is given to the words immediately preceding] meanings.

The door is faith, because through it people enter the Church. The two walls are the two peoples, Jewish and Gentile, from whose converts the Church was established. Hence the Apostle says: “preserving the unity of faith in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:1).

Thus this place is not only effective for performing sacred rites, but useful for edification; moreover, it is especially venerable because the Lord’s body and blood are sanctified there for our salvation. There children are baptized. There sinners are reconciled. There souls are fed. There prayers are poured forth; hence it is written: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. 21:13). David declared beforehand what ought to be done in it, saying: “I shall enter into your house; I shall worship toward your holy temple, and confess your name, O Lord” (Ps. 5:8).

Indeed, it is so venerable that the Lord, whenever he entered Jerusalem, always turned aside to the Temple, giving us an example that, when we enter a city, the church ought to be sought first. Therefore the Gospel says: when Jesus had entered Jerusalem, he entered the Temple and vindicated his house for the service of prayer; and he cast out from the Temple those selling and buying, saying: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. 21:13). On that account he was seized and crucified by the Jews. For when the Jews saw that he had such power over them all that he drove them from the Temple with a cord, they conspired against him. Hence David says: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68:10), namely: love for my Church, which I defended, consumed me—that is, became the cause of my death.

So the devil, through his children and his members, attacks the Church in every way. He even incites against their mother the children whom the Church herself bore and nourished. Thus the mother complains in the Song of Songs: “The sons of my mother fought against me” (Cant. 1:5). Elsewhere it is written: “I have nourished and raised children, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1:2). What contempt is greater? What violation greater? What rashness greater than to plot against the ministers of the Church in a holy place and in God’s hall—that is, in God’s Church, the temple of the Holy Spirit? The Apostle cries out to them: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3:17). Amen.

## LXXXV. FOURTH SERMON FOR THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

[Note: From an Angers manuscript.—It is probable that Hildebert delivered this sermon to monks of the Order of Saint Benedict, whose name he expressly mentions here and whose particular glory he commends to them. He also seems to address the Cluniacs of Cluny itself, enriched to such a degree by the liberality of the wealthy of the earth that they possessed even kings of nations as though tributary to them. Such was the parent of Alfonso, king of Spain, who assigned an annual payment to the sacred monastery of Cluny; Alfonso himself, mindful of the notable service rendered him by Saint Hugh the abbot in a most serious affair, ordered that payment doubled. From this Hildebert takes occasion to commend benefactors to the monks, maintaining that, since through their exceptional beneficence the monks were indebted to the wealthy of the earth, they ought to earn merit not only for themselves but also for their benefactors, by ensuring that their own spiritual goods should benefit unto salvation those supported by temporal goods.

Many things worthy of notice also occur in this sermon. For example, even in Hildebert’s time, as also for many years afterward, fasts were continued until evening. Here he rebukes those who fasted through the day in order that they might feast more lavishly at the evening meal—a practice now very common among the heterodox of our own time. Hildebert also uses the compound word *cenophagizare*, “to dine together,” when he describes the superabundance of joy in which the blessed will jointly share in the future life: there, he says, they will dine together with the Lord. That is, as the blessed John the Evangelist says in Revelation 19:17, they will be gathered to the great supper of God, where he promises that he will dine with them and they with him (Rev. 3:20). Finally, he seems to indicate a fast observed by the faithful on the day of the Commemoration of the Dead, in aid of souls to be purified by purgatorial fire. Saint Odo had recently instituted this commemoration in his monasteries; afterward the universal Church received and devoutly celebrated it.]

“Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in the selfsame thing” (Ps. 121:3).

In Sacred Scripture, “Jerusalem” is named in three senses. Jerusalem is called that bloodthirsty city of which it was said: “A prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke 13:33). And the Lord says to it: “Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets sent to you” (Matt. 23:37).

Jerusalem is also sometimes called the Church militant, which still has its tent beneath the sun, which now serves under the Lord on earth in order one day to reign with the Lord on high; as in: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you” (Isa. 66:1).

Jerusalem is also called the Church triumphant, consisting of angels and the spirits of the blessed. Of it the Apostle says: “Jerusalem which is above is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. 4:26). And the Prophet says to her: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion” (Ps. 147:1). For her sole and entire office is to praise the Lord. Hence elsewhere: “Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5).

Now the Prophet here speaks of the Church triumphant, as can be understood from the two words which follow. For he added: “as a city.” It is not a city in the strict sense of the name, but it is like a city by likeness. Properly speaking, a city is an assembly of people living under law [note: that is, living under one law and the same right]. But that Jerusalem is an assembly not merely of human beings, but of human beings and angels. What “whose participation shall be into the same thing” means belongs to her alone. For the participation—that is, the dwelling—of the Church militant and of every individual city is in that which is “the same,” that is, unchangeable and abiding in the same state.

It remains to see in what respect it is built as a city by likeness.

Three things occur in the construction of a city. First, stones are forcibly extracted from the quarry by hammers and iron levers, amid much human labour and sweat. Second, they are polished, rough-hewn, and squared with chisel, axe, and rule. Third, by the craftsman’s hands they are arranged in their proper places.

In this manner, three things are considered in the building of the heavenly Jerusalem: separation, polishing, and placement. Separation is violent; polishing is purgatorial; placement is eternal. The first occurs in distress and affliction; the second in patience and expectation; the third in glory and exultation. By the first, a person is sifted [variant: “is known”] like wheat; in the second, a person is tested like silver; in the third, placed in the treasury.

For the living stones of which it is built are the spirits of those whom God foresaw would be conformed to the image of his glory. While they remain in their bodies, they are still in the quarry. For the mass of the body presses and confines them most tightly. Hence it is said: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15). He desired to be drawn out from this when he said: “Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24).

We must be shaken by many blows in order to be drawn from it in a fit condition. “For through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.” Believe one who had experienced such things when he says: “In many watchings, in labours beyond measure, in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, and so forth” (2 Cor. 11:27). Hear the Prophet concerning the distress of separation: “The groans of death surrounded me; the pains of hell encompassed me” (Ps. 17:5).

How intolerable, too, is that separation when the final [note: perhaps *ficeles*; likely *finales*, “those knots of body and soul which are finally dissolved through death”] bonds are undone and the corresponding relations are broken. Let them read in the book of experience about the man who did not wish to be raised again by Antony, lest he should have to die once more.

After this separation, those who are found immediately fit—which is rare—are raised up, as was Lord Benedict, whose path was seen by certain persons to stretch toward heaven. But we speak according to the greater [variant: “lesser”] number, who pass with wood, hay, and stubble, and are polished in purgatory. Of this the Apostle says: “If anyone’s work is burned, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:15).

After polishing, they are raised and fitted to their proper places by the craftsman’s hand, arranged to remain in the sacred building. The Church indeed represents these three things each year: separation on the vigil of All Saints; placement on their feast; and polishing on the Commemoration of the Dead. For a day of fasting is a day of affliction. Hence the Lord says: “On the first day of the seventh month you shall afflict your souls” [note: the Vulgate reads: “In the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, you shall afflict your souls”] (Lev. 16:29).

For that person does not truly fast who reserves his stomach for a luxurious supper, who does not eat more sparingly and more dryly than usual, and who does not make almsgiving and prayers the wings of fasting. But the feast-day signifies a superabundance of joy, in which the saints dine together with the Lord. Thirdly, the Commemoration of the Dead is observed so that those being polished in purgatory may obtain full absolution, or a mitigation of punishment. Thus the Church represents these three things concerning the spirits of the blessed: whence they pass, whither they pass, [and by what route they pass].

Yet in this exposition I seem to do an injury to the angels, who hold the first rank in the spiritual building. Therefore we may explain this construction otherwise, lest we seem unmindful of the angels.

In Sacred Scripture, the frequently used name “city” simply signifies, by antonomasia, earthly Jerusalem; as in: “When the Lord saw the city, he wept over it” (Luke 19:41), and in Micah (6), “The Lord cries out to the city.” Heavenly Jerusalem, therefore, is built as the rebuilt Jerusalem was built.

After the Babylonian destruction it began to be rebuilt under Jesus the high priest, with Zerubbabel as leader; and under Nehemiah it was rebuilt in this manner. First seven gates were set in place; then stretches of wall were extended from gate to gate. Let it not trouble us that more gates than these are found in Ezra (2 Esdras 4). For in cities smaller gates are found beneath the principal ones.

The names of the gates are these: the Old Gate, the Fountain Gate, the Horse Gate, the Sheep Gate, the Dung Gate, the Fish Gate, and the Valley Gate. In the same way, that Craftsman who made the dawn and the sun has already founded in his spiritual city seven gates, which Matthew recounts when he says: “Blessed are the poor; blessed are the meek,” and so forth (Matt. 5:3). The eighth is like a stretch of wall between the gates, when he adds: “Blessed are you when people curse you and persecute you,” and so forth (ibid., v. 11).

In their order, certain matters are explained more fully where the text speaks of the heavenly powers, the blessed fathers, prophets, apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins. What follows—“all the elect”—belongs to the stretch of wall. Thus the first gate is the angels; the second, the patriarchs; the third, the prophets; the fourth, the apostles; the fifth, the martyrs; the sixth, the confessors; the seventh, the virgins. The first is heavenly; the second faithful; the third shadowy; the fourth judicial; the fifth terrible; the sixth exemplary; the seventh admirable.

Literally, the Old Gate was so called because it was founded at the beginning of Jerusalem’s birth, when Jerusalem was still called Salem or Solyma, in the days of Abraham or of Melchizedek, king for ever (Gen. 14). Likewise, God the Father through the Son “in the beginning created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), that is, the angels and all bodily matter. Since angels are the primordial creature, they are rightly called the old and heavenly gate. Hence, when Jacob awoke after seeing the angels, he said: “This is the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28:19).

The city was also called Salem, which means “peace.” For, after Lucifer was cast down with his followers, peace was perfected among those remaining when the accuser of their brethren was expelled.

Literally, the Fountain Gate was that through which there was passage to the fountain of Gihon, above which Solomon was anointed king. By it are signified the patriarchs; for from them faith and the worship of God had their origin, and were conveyed to us as from a fountain through streams. Abraham was the first publicly to proclaim the name of the one God; of him it was said: “The faithful elder is the first way of believing.” In his time the Lord, through circumcision as through a certain mark, separated his flock from the other nations.

Literally, the Sheep Gate was beside the Temple; through it animals destined for sacrifice were brought in. Above it stood the Tower of Opher, that is, “cloudy,” so called because of its height. By it the prophets were prefigured. For Samuel first caused people of one manner of life to dwell in a house, where all things were held in common after the manner of coenobites, who watched day and night over hymns and divine songs. Samuel called this company of prophets, as it were, the Lord’s flock.

This gate is called shadowy, because they prophesied beneath figures of deeds and coverings of words. Literally, the Horse Gate was so called because they released there the horses that had ascended toward the Temple, beyond which it was not permitted to proceed on horseback. By it are prefigured the Apostles.

In Sacred Scripture, however, a horse is often taken in a bad sense, as a sign [variant: “in indignation”] of pride because it walks with raised neck. Hence it was said: “A horse is deceitful for salvation” (Ps. 32:17). For this reason too the children of Israel were forbidden to multiply horses for themselves. Yet a horse is sometimes taken in a good sense, as where it says: “Your riding is salvation.” Thus Zechariah (6) is read to have seen chariots coming out from between mountains, with red and black horses, and likewise white ones.

The Apostles, therefore, are not unsuitably compared to horses because of their swiftness. For the Lord said to them: “Go into the whole world”; and they, going forth, preached everywhere, and with immeasurable speed “their sound went forth into all the earth” (Ps. 18:5), so that, like horses, they might swiftly bear Christ their rider around the world. This gate is called judicial because they were appointed judges by the Lord when he said: “You shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). Therefore the Church congratulates them, saying: “You righteous judges of the world, and true lights of the world.”

Literally, the Dung Gate was that through which the filth collected from every part of the city flowed out. By it the martyrs were prefigured, whose bodies were reckoned as dung and whose blood was poured out as cheaply and abundantly as water. Hence it is written: “They poured out the blood of your servants like water around Jerusalem. They made the mortal remains of your servants food for the birds of heaven, the flesh of your saints for the beasts of the earth” (Ps. 78:3).

This gate is called terrible. They were stoned, sawn apart, and killed by the sword; for Christ they were burned in flames, stretched upon racks, hung on gallows, and torn apart [variant: “cut apart”] by claws. This whole array [variant: “unanimity”] of tortures was not only terrible to see, but even the remembrance of it is horrible to hear.

The Fish Gate faced the Mediterranean Sea, and through it fish merchandise was brought into the city. By it are prefigured the confessors, who live amid the whirlpool of vices, are carried against the assaults of waves, and are struck by surrounding storms, yet are not cast down. This gate is called exemplary because, together with the word of doctrine, they provide us with an example of life.

The Valley Gate led to the Valley of Jehoshaphat. By it virgins are prefigured. For humility is signified by the valley. Virginity and humility are sister virtues; hence the Blessed Virgin mentioned humility alone, saying: “Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:48). This gate is called admirable. For what is more admirable than to lead an angelic life on earth: not merely to live in the flesh apart from the flesh, but even against the flesh?

Moreover, when I hear virgins called the Gate of Jehoshaphat, I tremble throughout with horror. For Jehoshaphat, by interpretation, means “judgment.” I fear that men may perhaps be judged by virgins—not by authority, but by comparison—because through two things, namely the frailty of the flesh and the ignorance of the mind, I thought that we found some consolation of excuse before the Judge’s tribunal. But I fear that he may set before us virgins whose sex is frailer and whose minds are naturally less endowed with understanding, so that in the two matters already named we may have no refuge of excuse.

These seven gates which we have named have already been immovably founded in the heavenly Jerusalem; from them the stretches of wall will be built until the consummation of the age. The fabric of the walls, however, is made from two kinds of material. On both faces of a wall squared, projecting stones are placed; but in the middle, cheap and irregular fragments of stones are concealed. By these two kinds are signified the active and contemplative persons.

For the active, as Ambrose says, do not possess merits sufficient in themselves for life. Therefore they must make spiritual friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that these may receive them with themselves into eternal dwellings, just as the side [variant: “literal”] stones carry the central mass upward with them.

Consider therefore, you to whom I speak, how great an obligation rests upon you. It is not enough for you to have merits merely sufficient for your own life, unless you also possess an abundance of merits for those who have made you indebted to them. For kings of nations and wealthy people of the earth have bestowed upon this coenobium, as upon others, their estates and possessions, so that the poor of Christ who are devoted to divine service might be sustained by them. A double obligation therefore rests upon you: a sufficiency of merits for yourselves, and an abundance for them.

May God, who gives seed to the sower and bread in abundance to the eater, grant to you and to us this sufficiency and abundance; and may Jesus Christ our Lord receive into eternal dwellings both us and those whom you draw with you, when he comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire. Amen.

## LXXXVI. FIFTH SERMON FOR THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

[Note: From an Angers manuscript.]

“Truly the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it” (Gen. 28:16).

At the dedication of a church, my brethren, the Church customarily sets forth this text for frequent consideration. Its meaning must therefore be examined more carefully, so that your devotion may inwardly be refreshed from it. We must see, then, who said these words, where, when, and why.

Who? Jacob the patriarch is recorded in Genesis (ibid.) to have spoken these words. Where? At Bethel. When? When he was departing from Beersheba and making his way to Aram [Vulgate: Haran]. Why? Because an angelic vision was shown to him.

For, departing from Beersheba and making his way to Aram, he wished to rest at night in a certain place. He placed a stone beneath his head, and in a dream saw a ladder, angels ascending and descending, and the Lord standing upon the ladder. When he awoke, he said: “Truly the Lord is in this place.”

Therefore, if anyone is to enter the fellowship of angels, he must first go out from the pleasures of the body and the affections of corruptible flesh, according to the Lord’s saying to Abraham: “Go out from your land and from your kindred” (Gen. 12:1). Moses also says in Exodus: “I shall pass over, and see [Vulgate: ‘I shall go, and see,’ etc.] this great vision” (Exod. 3:3). One must indeed pass over in order to be able to see the great vision. And David says: “I poured out my soul; I shall enter [Vulgate: ‘I shall pass over’] into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God” (Ps. 41:3).

Jacob means “supplanter”; Beersheba, “well.” In this journey of Jacob the life of the Christian is expressed: namely, whence one should begin, how one should advance, and where one ought to arrive. There are displayed in it the beginning, progress, and end of the faithful.

Now there is a good well and a bad well. The good well is of satisfaction, depth, and abundance: from it waters spring up into eternal life, and this is the deep well from whose water one who drinks shall not thirst again. This is the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, or Scripture issued by the sevenfold Spirit. The princes dug this well, and the leaders prepared it [Vulgate: “prepared it”], as is read in the book of Numbers (ch. 21).

There is also the devil’s well: the well of the abyss, of iniquity, and of despair. Of it the righteous person prays: “Let not the well press its mouth over me” (Ps. 68:16). There is also the well of covetousness, from which whoever drinks shall thirst again. For covetousness is not satisfied by possession, but rather hungers more eagerly to seek. Through this well one comes to the well of destruction; and this well is contrary to the preceding one: well against well—that is, seven more wicked spirits assaulting the seven virtues given by God.

Whoever resolves to enter the spiritual way by the steps of virtues goes out from and withdraws from this well. Thus Abraham, the ancestor of our Mediator, went out from Ur of the Chaldeans—that is, from the power of demons and the burning of vices.

Having departed from Beersheba, therefore, Jacob journeyed toward Aram, which means “lofty” and signifies the heavenly life to which the good traveller desires to arrive. But, wearied on his way, he pauses and sleeps in a place called Bethel, that is, “house of God,” which signifies the present Church, namely the Church militant, through which one comes to the future Church, namely the Church triumphant.

To sleep on the journey is, during the passage of this present life, to rest from the love of temporal things; and, in the course of passing days, to close the eyes of the mind to the desire for visible things—eyes which, before sin, innocence had kept properly closed, but which the seducer opened in our first parents. For the fault of concupiscence opened eyes which innocence had kept closed.

To behold angels ascending and descending is to contemplate the citizens of the heavenly homeland: how closely they cling to their Creator in love, and with what compassion of charity they stoop down to our infirmities. [Col. 0746A] From their example we ought to [take] our pattern and, insofar as we can, relieve the misery of [our neighbours]. It should be noted, however, that the sleeper sees angels when he lays his head upon the stone: for one who withdraws from outward things penetrates inward realities when, with attentive mind, he observes the imitation of the Redeemer. He lays his head upon the stone who cleaves to Christ in mind. For those who have withdrawn from the activities of this present life and yet do not direct their attention to things above may sleep, but they cannot see angels, because they have laid their head not upon the stone but upon the earth. Often indeed, the more securely they cease from outward things, the more broadly they heap up within themselves the clamour of unclean thoughts [variant: *tumulant*, “they disturb,” or *comprimunt*, “they repress”]. [Col. 0746B] Hence it is truly said of the Synagogue: “Her enemies saw her and mocked at her Sabbaths” (Lam. 1:7). The enemies—that is, demons—mock certain persons’ Sabbaths when they draw their very periods of rest into unlawful pursuits. The saints, however, labour more arduously while sleeping than while awake, because, in overcoming by abandoning worldly activities, they fight daily against themselves: lest the mind grow numb through negligence; lest under constricted leisure it grow cold toward heavenly desires; lest it give itself more than is fitting to such rest; lest, sparing itself under the appearance of discretion, it languish away from perfection. Hence in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2). And: “If I give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids” (Ps. 131:4).

He also sees the Lord leaning upon the ladder, because every contemplation tends toward error [Col. 0746C] 656 unless the Lord moderates and governs it. This journey also signifies the departure of the Hebrew people from Egypt. For “Hebrew” is interpreted “one who passes over,” and Egypt, “darkness.” From Egypt he comes into the desert, where the tabernacle is made. The good traveller, having shaken off the darkness of error and sin and seeking heaven with his mind, considers this world a desert for himself—not a bridal chamber but a lodging-place—since he has no abiding city here, but seeks the city to come. Here he has a tabernacle which he frequents, namely the Church, where he serves God; outside it there is no place of true sacrifice; there the Trinity is worshipped worthily and purely, and seen with a heart cleansed through faith. This is the desert of Idumea, as is read in the title of the psalm—that is, of the earthly [Col. 0746D] world—where one thirsts and hungers, but passes through under the protection and shade of the tabernacle.

The tabernacle is made of acacia wood, resembling white thorn, hewn and smoothed: that is, from saints cleansed in the present life from every roughness and deformity of sin; with upright boards interwoven by bars and other means, with curtains, coverings, and skins laid beneath [variant: *superpositis*, “laid over”]. Besides signifying diversity and the beauty of virtues, it was movable and portable. For we are strangers and pilgrims, where the sound of hammer and axe is heard, while the various desires of peoples resound like a storm-tossed sea. Thereafter, under Joshua, they came into the land of promise, where the Temple was built of squared and polished stones joined by nails and cement, where neither axe nor hammer was heard [Col. 0747A]; and this building was immovable. For when the saints have been fully cleansed in the resurrection and are to live forever, without labour and without misery, all things will be peaceful and tranquil, no longer to be disturbed by any unrest. Both structures are the house of God, and both are consecrated and anointed.

These two things were literally accomplished by the ancient people. Material churches are also made today by the Christian [people], and are consecrated and dedicated, that God may be served in them as in those former ones, although in a more excellent way. In the dedication itself many things are mystically performed: inscriptions of letters, sprinklings, and many other acts. Yet both these and those former things were made for human beings. “For human beings were not made for the Sabbath, but the Sabbath for human beings” (Mark 2:27); and therefore those were destroyed [Col. 0747B], and these will be destroyed, so that others—that is, spiritual structures—may be built. Of these the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy” (1 Cor. 3:17). And elsewhere: “It is God’s building” (ibid., 9). And: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” This is truly the house of God and the place of God, in which the Lord truly is. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord is in his holy temple” (Ps. 47:1). And: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, in the city of our God, in 657 his holy place [Vulgate: ‘mountain’]” (Ps. 144:3).

But since he who is everywhere is present essentially and truly, why is he said to be truly here? Here he is by grace; here he is for salvation; here he is enduringly, according to the saying: “We shall make our dwelling with him” (John 14:13)—which is not so in those who believe for a time and fall away in the time of temptation. Therefore to these persons the Lord is truly Lord; for he is truly lord who is his servant; the others are not. Hence in Malachi (1:6): “If I am Lord, where is my fear?” And therefore: “Blessed is the nation whose Lord is its God” (Ps. 31:12). Blessed is the people because of his lordship; no less blessed because of his service, for to serve him is to reign.

Nor should it be passed over that this traveller is changed from Jacob into Israel. By what means? Because he prevailed over the angel in wrestling. The angel is the angelic—that is, divine—word, namely the law of God, which opposes the pleasures of the flesh. He prevails over it in wrestling because he grows strong to fulfil the commandments, so that, having set all else aside for their sake, he fears no punishment. The angel also blesses the victor, because it obtains for him eternal blessing. But, touched in the thigh, he limps, because [Col. 0747D] while he eagerly longs toward the right—that is, toward heavenly things—he gives less care to the left, that is, temporal things. He also becomes Israel hereafter, that is, one who sees God face to face, because here he beheld through faith. Israel is in Aram or Jerusalem—the one who was Jacob here while he wrestled—so that there he may say, “Truly the Lord is in this place,” when God shall be all in all, hidden in the shelter of his face from the opposition or disturbance of human beings. It may fittingly be added that, awakening, he says this, because one who in this life slept amid the clamour of the world, when he awakens in resurrection or death, fully knows how delightful it is to see God and to be indwelt by him. Hence: “I shall be satisfied when [Col. 0748A] your glory appears” (Ps. 16:15).

May the Lord, builder, consecrator, and inhabitant of his temple—without whom we are and can do nothing—make of us and within us in the present life such a house for himself as he may bring to the glory of his vision and everlasting dwelling: he who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## LXXXVII. ON THE DEDICATION OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT NICHOLAS. SIXTH SERMON.

[Note: [Col. 0747D] From Victorinus.]

[Note: [Col. 0748D] He does not expound the text itself, but the history drawn from the text.]

“Solomon built the house of the Lord in Jerusalem in seven years, and in the eighth the king and the children of Israel dedicated it. Therefore Solomon held a solemn feast on that day, and all Israel stood as a great assembled multitude; and the king prayed to the Lord, saying: ‘Hear, O Lord, the voice of the prayer which your servant [Col. 0748B] prays to you in this place, that you may hear the prayer 658 of your people Israel, whatever they pray in this place. And when you hear, you will be merciful. But if they sin against you—for there is no human being who does not sin—and repent and worship you, you will be merciful to your people who have sinned against you.’ And the Lord said to him: ‘I have heard your prayer which you have entreated before me’” (2 Chron. 6:7).

All the deeds, dearest brethren, of the ancient law are figures of the new law and were entrusted to memory for our sake. The Temple of the Lord made in ancient times was a figure of the Church, and its dedication an example of our dedication. If the place where sacrifices and victims were offered was called the house of the Lord, much more ought the [house] of prayer [Col. 0748C], in which the sacraments of his flesh and blood are celebrated, to be called the house of the Lord. And if the Lord promised there to hear the prayer of his people, how much more will our prayers be received in this place, where there are true worshippers [variant: “orators”] of the Lord’s passion? And if a festival was celebrated at the dedication of that Temple, which was shadowy and figurative, how great rejoicing ought to be undertaken at the consecration of our mother, the [Church]?

That it is said to have been built in seven years and its dedication celebrated in the eighth is not to be believed without symbolic significance. For during seven years—that is, through the whole time of this life, which is measured by seven days—the building up of the Church, that is, of the faithful who are the Temple of the Lord, does not cease [“to rise” supplied by the printed text], as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that you are the temple of the Lord and the dwelling of the Holy Spirit?” (1 Cor. 3:16). And it is written again: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” But the festival was held in the eighth year because it signifies the joy of our dedication on the day of the Resurrection, called the eighth day, which follows the time of this life signified by seven years. Let us hold fast in our minds the remembrance of the resurrection to come, of so great a festival [variant: “solemn celebration”]; and in the joy of our mother all her children ought to assemble, rejoice, and congratulate their mother upon her sanctification.

But because children come from many regions and reach their mother with much labour [Col. 0749A], they ought not to depart from so great a festival unrewarded. The holy Fathers therefore established that at the dedication of a holy church remission of sins should take place, so that, although the washing away [variant: *abolitio*, “abolition”] of crimes occurs there at other times, they may experience their mother’s help especially at her festival. The Lord himself shows that this festival is venerable, since he deigned to be present at the feast of dedication, as it is written in the Gospel: “The Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem, and Jesus walked in Solomon’s portico” (John 10:22). The solemnities of dedication are called *encaenia*.

This dedication was also prefigured in Jacob’s time. For when Jacob, having left his father and fled from his brother Esau, was going to Laban to seek a wife, on the road he took stones [Col. 0749B] lying on the ground, placed one beneath his head, and slept in that same place. In a dream he saw a ladder set up to heaven, with angels ascending and descending; rising, he took the stone, set it up as a pillar, poured oil upon it, and made an altar to the Lord, saying: “This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28:17). Behold: this man of old, without law and without Scripture, sanctified an altar to the Lord and called it the house of God, because through the Holy Spirit he foreknew that the tabernacle of God would be there. All these things were only figures.

Jacob signifies Christ, who, as though leaving the Father when he assumed flesh, left heaven; leaving his parents, that is, the Jews from whom he had assumed flesh; and leaving his homeland, that is, Judaea, went to the Gentiles to take a bride. Jacob’s sleep on the journey signifies Christ’s death upon the cross. The stone which he placed under his head signifies Christ’s humanity united to divinity. Divinity is Christ’s head, as the Apostle says: “God is the head of Christ.” The ladder set up to heaven is the way and ascent through the steps of virtues. For one ascends to heaven—that is, to the heavenly life—by the steps of diverse virtues.

The descending and ascending angels are preachers who announce to us the kingdom of God. They ascend and descend when they preach at one time more sublime things, at another more humble things. John ascends when he says: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). Paul descends when he says: “We preach Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:1). And the same person [Col. 0749D] who descends sometimes ascends, and he who ascends sometimes descends. John descends, saying: “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14); Paul ascends when he says: “We preach Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24).

[Jacob] calls the stone the house of God because Christ, in a spiritual sense, was the dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit; whence it is written: “Full of the Holy Spirit, he returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4:1). It is also said that Jacob poured oil upon the stone because Christ was anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit as king and priest: as king, as it is written, “But I have been established king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. 2:6); as priest, as it is written, “You are a priest [Col. 0750A] forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4). David testified to his anointing, saying: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8). He is the gate of heaven because Christ is the door of paradise, as he himself says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10:7).

But although, dearest brethren, remission because of your labour and rejoicing at this festival are due to you, you ought nevertheless to know that not every sin is remitted to you here, but those sins for which you have repented and which you have confessed. For if a sinner wishes his sin to be remitted to him, if he wishes his [own] wounds to be healed, he must not conceal them from the physician. The sinner must first acknowledge his fault, then disclose it, and then ask for medicine. First let him say: [Col. 0750B] “For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50:5); then let him add: “I made my offence known to you, and I did not conceal my injustice” (Ps. 31:5); finally let him say: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak” (Ps. 6:2).

As different herbs suit many infirmities, so different remedies suit the diseases of sins. One person is saved in marriage, another in virginity, another in widowhood. One fights against the world and the devil amid the turmoil of the world. Another, fleeing the world’s clamour, defeats the spiritual enemy; but above the others is the contemplative life, that is, the monastic life, the eremitic life. These have put off the world; by clothing themselves in humble garments, they have despised it; by pursuing obedience, they have displayed love. Three virtues especially reign [variant: “fight”] in it [the world]: charity, humility, and obedience; in their dwelling, brotherhood is manifested. As the Psalmist says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together as one” (Ps. 132:1). Humility is shown beforehand in the lowliness of garments. Obedience is displayed in willing service, while they submit to the will of their brethren.

These are those who despoil Egypt. When the Lord wished to lead the children of Israel out of Egypt (Exod. 12), he commanded them all to borrow from their neighbours vessels of gold and silver and everything they could, secretly to flee away [variant: *auferre*, “to carry away”], and thus to despoil Egypt. The children of Israel are monks who flee Egypt, that is, the darkness of this world. For Egypt is interpreted “darkness.” [Col. 0750D] They steal vessels from their neighbours when they draw some of the worldly persons among whom they live along with them, and despoil Egypt—that is, the world. And because they always desire to despoil Egypt for God, they build their monastery among worldly people, providing not for their own benefit but for the public good. They prefer to place their house beside the sea, so as to draw out some fish from places of slavery—that is, sinners from the depths of the sea—and save others, rather than to live in the mountains and save no one with them.

But, dearest brethren, although every church ought to be venerated because it is a mother, those churches ought especially to be frequented where pledges of the saints, where the relics of saints, are kept. Therefore this church ought to be venerated by all the faithful [Col. 0751A], since it preserves the memory of so precious a confessor, namely the blessed and venerable Saint Nicholas.

[Note: [Col. 0751A] It is probable that the church of Saint Nicholas at Angers is intended here. It is reported to have been consecrated by Urban II, while he was then active in Gaul, namely in 1096, as appears in Dom Robert’s *Gallia Christiana*, under the bishops of Angers, p. 229, at the entry for the younger Geoffrey; and this sermon seems to have been delivered at its dedication.]

He began to serve God from infancy; even at the breast, resisting the law of nature, he observed fasts. Moreover, this church possesses a certain prerogative for which you ought especially to render it reverence and honour and serve it: blessed Peter, through his vicar, the pope of the Roman Church, visited it, [Col. 0752A] sanctified it, dedicated it, and decreed [variant: “granted”] a perpetual remission, year by year, to those celebrating the festival of this blessing. Consider, dearest brethren; consider, faithful people, that you have holy intercessors of God, and especially the precious confessor Nicholas, so that through his merits you may be found worthy of the eternal homeland, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMONS ON VARIOUS SUBJECTS

[Col. 0751]

## LXXXVIII [Various Subjects I].

[Note: [Col. 0751D] From the printed editions, but collated with and corrected from the manuscript of Évreux. We find this sermon in all editions, but we almost presented it among the letters, because we discovered it in the excellent manuscript codex of Évreux, or Péronne, in the very sequence of letters; and the text of the sermon itself, even in the printed editions, seems to urge this upon us, since it there calls itself “the present page” [Col. 0752D]. Yet, since it was published as a synodal sermon, it could be that Hildebert actually delivered it in a synod and afterwards had it copied for the benefit of absentees and sent to them as a kind of encyclical letter. We publish it from the aforesaid manuscript, corrected in more than thirty places.]

## SYNODAL ADDRESS TO PASTORS ON LUKE 12: “TO WHOM MUCH HAS BEEN GIVEN, MUCH WILL BE REQUIRED OF HIM.”

[Col. 0751B]

The Gospel declaration teaches you how great a watchfulness you owe to the sheep entrusted to you, saying: “The more that is entrusted to someone, the more is required of him.” Now three things have been entrusted to you by him “from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift” (Jas. 1:17). “For what do you have that you did not receive?” (Rom. 4:7.) And: “We all, as the Evangelist says, received from his fullness” (John 1:16). From his fullness, I say—from him from whom you have that you are Christians, that you are priests, that you are pastors. That you are Christians is for your own sake; that you are priests is for God’s sake; that you are pastors [Col. 0751C] is for the sheep’s sake. For because you profess Christ, you ought to preserve faith; because of the office of priest, to propitiate God; because of the care of pastor, to feed the flock. Thus from the first you bear Christ’s name; from the second and third you act in Christ’s stead. Let us examine each point more fully, so that, with the Lord’s help, we may draw something from them for our instruction.

You ought to remember, brethren, the promise you made in baptism, and to whom and under what witness you bound yourselves. Your promise is the Catholic faith; the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are those to whom you pledged faith; the Church is witness to the covenant. The Apostle testifies “that faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:26): dead because the vitality of action does not live in it; dead because it does not move or direct the soul toward the joys of the heavenly homeland. The demons possess faith of this kind and yet are separated from fellowship with the good spirits. They believe, and nevertheless eternal fire is prepared for them. Indeed, faith without works is a flower without fruit, a sheaf without grain, coinage without silver. Nothing can be threshed from such a sheaf to feed the soul. With such coinage one cannot buy the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world. Though there are many dwellings in the Lord’s house, none at all is purchased with coinage of this kind.

There is, certainly, another coinage held in value in the city of our Lord. Through it mortals have a certain commerce with the heavenly beings; through it the assembly of human beings and the assembly of angels become one commonwealth. In this coinage the king delights in his own image; in exchange for it he offers the kingdom of heaven for sale to anyone. Do you wish to be refreshed by that bread after which no one hungers? Produce this coinage, and it will satisfy you. [Col. 0752C] Do you wish to find the judge favourable when he sits with the senators of the earth? Produce this coinage, and he will place you at his right hand. Do you wish to be received at the wedding supper of the Lamb? Produce this coinage, and he will admit you. Do you wish to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living? Produce this coinage, and they will not be hidden from you.

Now this coinage, so acceptable and so shining, is Christian faith; but not the faith devoid of works, rather that upon which the structure of works has been built. The Lord desires and requires such faith from us, just as a seller requires pure, precious coinage from a buyer. You promised him this faith, if you remember well; by this faith you made a covenant with him; you made yourselves debtors to the Trinity for this faith. For when you were asked, “Do you believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth?” and answered, “I believe,” you bound yourselves to the Father. When you were asked, “Do you also believe in Jesus Christ, [Col. 0752D] his only Son, [Col. 0753A] our Lord?” and replied, “I believe,” you bound yourselves to the Son. When you were told, “Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit?” and added, “I believe,” you bound yourselves to the Holy Spirit. It is exceedingly serious to recoil from a covenant of this kind. For if you lie to the Father, the inheritance promised to the children will not profit you; if to the Son, the humanity assumed for you will not profit you; if to the Holy Spirit, the charity poured into your hearts will be extinguished.

Since, therefore, this promise of faith has been made and the foundation laid, build upon it gleaming stones, precious stones. Their construction will suffer no danger when “God shall openly come” (Ps. 49:3); no burning, when “a fire shall blaze in his sight” (ibid.); no shaking, when “a mighty tempest around him” (ibid.) rages.

Having thus set forth what your fraternity owes by reason of Christian faith, the following page will teach you what you owe as priests. God, first offended by original transgression, is frequently offended by actual sin. The former, committed once, was removed by Christ suffering once upon the cross. The latter, when committed, is removed daily by Christ daily offered upon the altar. To remove the former, Christ was sent into the world—God and man, victim and priest. To remove the latter, a minister of the altar is appointed in the Church—not God but man, not victim but priest. Therefore it belongs to your calling to appease heavenly wrath by sacrifices; it belongs to your ministry through the mystery of the Lord’s body to recall sinners to divine grace.

Yet not everyone who intercedes for others obtains a hearing with God; nor does everyone who offers sacrifice to God appease him. A criminal offers sacrifice; but the Lord says through Isaiah (66:3): “The criminal who sacrifices to me is like one who kills a dog.”

[Note: [Col. 0753D] “He who slaughters an animal is like one who brains a dog.”]

The wicked person offers sacrifice; but, according to Wisdom, “The Most High does not regard the offerings of the wicked, nor will he be propitiated for their sins by a multitude of sacrifices” (Ecclus. 34:23). And the Prophet says: “If I have looked upon iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me” (Ps. 65:18). Believe me, believe, brethren, believe, fellow priests: God is not appeased by such prayers. I speak with his own testimony; I say something more. God is provoked by the offerings of the impious. If you do not believe me, believe a greater authority. Gregory says: “When one who is displeasing is sent to intercede, the judge’s mind is provoked to anger.” Therefore your sacrifices provoke the Lord if your life displeases him. But he himself will be appeased by others on your behalf if you have first made a journey of three days, so that sacrifice may be offered to him by you. This is the journey Moses, speaking to Pharaoh, indicated in these words: “We shall go a three days’ journey into the wilderness, [Col. 0754A] that we may sacrifice to the Lord our God” (Exod. 8:27).

What is this journey, dearest brethren, which the people of the Lord are commanded to travel before sacrificing? What are these three stages, after which a sacrifice pleasing to God is offered? The first stage is to turn away from evil; the second, to do good; the third, to order ascents in one’s heart. Of the first the Apostle says: “Let him who stole steal no longer” (Eph. 4:28). Of the second he says: “Put on the *armamenta* (‘arms’) of God, that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil” (Eph. 6:11) [variant: *armaturam*, ‘armour’]. Solomon, marvelling at the third in the Song of Songs, says: “Who is she that comes forth like the rising dawn?” (Song 6:9). Therefore, if according to the Apostle you renounce the works of the flesh, you have made the first stage. If, according to that same Apostle, you put on the new human being, created according to God in true righteousness and holiness, you have made the second stage. If, following the Prophet, you have ordered ascents in your heart, you have made the third stage. Once these are completed, your sacrifices will please the Lord. In these the Lord of hosts will hear your prayers. For in these Judah becomes his sanctification; in these Israel becomes his dominion. This threefold stage, because it especially belongs to you, is especially required of you.

Hence priests sacrificing to the Lord make mention of such stages, saying: “Therefore we, your servants, and also your holy people, mindful of the blessed passion of the same our Lord Jesus Christ, and likewise of his resurrection from the dead and glorious ascension into heaven, offer to your most excellent majesty from your own gifts and grants a pure and certain victim.” For they ought so to remember the death and cross of Jesus Christ that by his grace they mortify and crucify their flesh with its vices and desires; so to recall the renewal of the resurrection that by its example they aspire to the resurrection of the soul; so to remember the glorious ascension to heaven that, imitating him, they strive to climb the ladder Jacob saw.

These, certainly, are the things belonging to the profession of priests. But because you are pastors, you ought to feed the sheep. Hence the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, prophesy concerning the shepherds of Israel: do not shepherds feed the sheep?” (Ezek. 34:2). Behold: by the Lord’s testimony pastors do not feed themselves but the sheep. For it is a pastor’s duty to seek not what is [Col. 0754D] his own, but what belongs to Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 13); not the advantages of temporal things, but the salvation of souls. Let us hear what the Holy Spirit says through the same prophet concerning those who feed themselves and neglect the sheep: “You consume milk,” he says, “and clothe yourselves with wool; you have not strengthened what was weak, you have not restored what was sick, you have not sought what was lost; you have broken what was strong, and my sheep have been scattered because there was no shepherd” (Ezek. 34:3). By these words pastors are rebuked who feed themselves and not the sheep.

Who are those who feed themselves? Those of whom the Apostle says: “All seek what is their own, not what is Jesus Christ’s” [Col. 0755A] (Phil. 2:21). Who are those who seek their own things? Those who consume the sheep’s milk and clothe themselves in their wool. Who are those who do not seek what belongs to Jesus Christ? Those who do not strengthen what is weak, do not restore what is sick, do not seek what is perishing, and break what is strong and fat. The milk of all the sheep is everything that subjects offer their prelates to sustain temporal need. They offer tithes and first-fruits: tithes and first-fruits are the sheep’s milk. They offer altar-offerings and alms for the dead: offerings and alms are the sheep’s milk. Having said what the sheep’s milk is, let us say also what their wool is. One who gives milk gives drink; one who gives wool gives honour, for wool is an honour to the body. Its nakedness is covered by it; its weakness and shame are covered by it. Thus wool is every honour bestowed by subjects upon prelates.

Therefore, when the first reclining places at banquets are offered, and the first seats in synagogues, wool is provided. When they are greeted in the marketplace and addressed, “Hail, Rabbi” (Matt. 26:49), wool is provided. These are what pastors seek who feed themselves and neglect the sheep: namely, the advantage of supplying their needs and the breath of favour and praise. But perhaps you say in reply: “Do not those who serve the altar live from the altar? ‘Who plants a vineyard and does not eat from its fruit? Who muzzles the ox while it treads the grain?’” (1 Cor. 9:7.) “Yes,” you say, “the worker is worthy of his wage” (Luke 10:7). It is permitted you to eat the sheep’s milk, to drink their milk, and to be clothed in their wool—although it is neither lawful nor expedient to seek it.

But this is permitted only to those who, while sustaining their temporal need with milk and wool, do not neglect the sheep’s infirmity. For if you do not strengthen the weak sheep, do not restore the sick, and do not seek the straying, you consume the sheep’s milk ruinously, because you feed yourselves and despise the sheep. What then are the sheep that are sick, straying, or weak? If you do not know, learn; if you know, show by your works that you know. Those are sheep, but weak sheep, who believe for a time and fall away in the time of temptation. Those are sheep, but weak sheep, who, although they understand the needy and poor, although they make their ways and pursuits good, nevertheless yield to threatening adversities: they yield to the loss of children [Col. 0755D]; they yield to damage to temporal property. Peter was a weak sheep when in Caiaphas’s courtyard he denied Christ at the voice of the doorkeeper.

[Note: [Col. 0755D] Peter in denying was a weak sheep; likewise Pope Marcellinus.]

When, then, a pastor perceives that a sheep is weak and fears scourges, he should apply the consolation owed by his duty of strengthening, and say: “My son, prepare your soul for temptations” (Ecclus. 2:1). When temporal tribulation comes, let him bring forth: “The father loves the son whom he corrects.” He also has this to add: “You must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations.” And this: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear; but with the temptation he will provide the outcome, so that you may be able to endure” [Col. 0756A] (1 Cor. 10:13). To say these and similar things to a weak sheep is to strengthen the weak sheep. Therefore let the prescribed help of consolation be at hand for weak sheep.

Let strengthening also be available for sick sheep. Sick sheep are “men of blood and deceit, whose mouth speaks vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity” (Ps. 143:8). Sick sheep are children of darkness, entangled in fleshly desires which wage war against the soul. In short, they suffer the pitiable disease of whom the Apostle says: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked; neither adulterers, nor fornicators, nor men who lie with males, nor the greedy, nor the rapacious shall possess the kingdom of God” (Gal. 6:7). All such lie like sick persons, languishing as though numb with a kind of paralysis. Accordingly, that paralytic who was carried to Christ and lowered before Christ through an opened roof is read as having prefigured souls paralysed in this manner. For what else is a soul weighed down by diverse vices, which has lost the strength to strive toward better things, than a paralytic badly numbed and altogether deprived of bodily strength?

It is your task to carry such a paralytic, as it were, upon certain shoulders, to open for him the roof of the house, and to present him to the physician. For it is fitting that you place the shoulder of compassion beneath a soul lying prostrate in such sickness; that you become weak when it is weak, and burn when it is scandalized, so that with the Apostle you may say: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:19.)

[Col. 0756C] But perhaps the sick man despairs so greatly; perhaps he does not know his physician; he does not know by whose hand he may rise; he does not know by whose treatment he may recover. The roof of the house must be opened for him: unless the roof is opened, the paralytic will not be lowered before Christ. The roof of the house is the understanding of the Scriptures. There lie hidden the physician’s grace, kindness, and power. Therefore, when the sick sheep despairs, open the prophet saying: “Hope in the Lord, and do good; and you shall dwell in the land and be nourished by its riches” (Ps. 36:3). When it distrusts the physician’s kindness, let it learn what the physician says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should be converted and live” (Ezek. 33:11). When it does not know the physician’s power, let it hear from the shepherd: “Whatever the Lord willed, [Col. 0756D] 668 he has done in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses” (Ps. 134:6). To say these things and others like them is to open the roof. By the opening of the roof the paralytic will be lowered [perhaps: “let down”] before the physician—the sinner before Christ. If you bestow this care upon all the sick, you strengthen sick sheep.

It is also your duty to seek the sheep that are perishing. The sheep that goes astray and perishes is the one deceived by the perversities of heretics, the one separated from the unity of the Church. In recalling these from error, be diligent shepherds; be insistent. Hear the Apostle saying: “Preach the word; press the matter in season and out of season” (1 Tim. 4:2). To whom in season, and to whom out of season? In season, certainly, to those willing; out of season to those unwilling. For there are sheep which, once recalled, return; and there are those that refuse to return, who love to perish. These the good shepherd especially seeks. The good shepherd lays down his life for them when, in searching, the briars of injuries prick him; when the thorns of persecutions weary him; when the madness of rulers frightens him; when the diversity of tortures lacerates him. Then the shepherd is good: he recalls the straying sheep and seeks the perishing sheep; thus he recalls the straying and seeks the perishing.

If, after Arius, a sheep strays—if with Arius it separates the Son from the Father—the sheep hears from the shepherd that saying of the Son: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). If a deceived sheep babbles with Eutyches of two persons in Christ, it is restrained by the authority of Athanasius, who says of Christ:

> [Note: Col. 0757D. In the Creed.] “Although he is God and man, nevertheless Christ is not two, but one.”

Likewise: “He is altogether one: one not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person.”

If a sheep bears the mark of Sabellius, the brand of Donatus, or the cauterizing scar of other heretics, let the shepherd bring forward the prophets, rely upon the Gospel, and fight with the Apostle. By these and other authoritative pages let him recall the straying sheep and seek the perishing one. There is also this reason why he should recall the straying and seek the perishing: lest, through fear or negligence, he fail to recall the straying or seek the perishing. He thereby breaks what is strong and kills what is fat. For what follows is: “And you have broken what was strong.” A sheep is strong when it remains in the catholic faith, does not depart from the unity of faith, and does not break Peter’s nets. Yet [Col. 0757C] the shepherd breaks and kills this sheep if he does not recall the straying or seek the perishing. For one who is not strong believes that there is no danger in straying and none in perishing when he sees the shepherd silent, negligent, lax regarding those who stray and perish. Consequently, it comes about that the sheep itself does not fear to stray or perish. For it says to itself: “If it were evil to fall into heresy, to follow Arius, or to imitate Donatus, the shepherds would speak against it: they would recall the straying and seek the perishing. Since, therefore, they are silent, they teach me by their own silence to go after those men and to believe with them.” Thus, when the shepherd is silent—neither recalling the straying nor seeking the perishing—by the shepherd’s negligence the sheep that was strong is broken, because [Col. 0757D] one who is catholic is joined to the faithlessness of heretics.

Behold, dearest brothers, it is clear that the fault is that of silence alone, not of example: hence the weak sheep is not strengthened, the sick one is not made strong, the straying one is not recalled, and the strong one is broken. But perhaps the shepherd tries to excuse such harmful silence; perhaps he will bring to the Lord the skin of a dead sheep. Rebuked because he was silent concerning a straying sheep, because by his silence he broke the strong sheep and killed it, he will offer the master of the household, as an excuse for the sheep’s death, something like its skin: “I warned it not to stray, but it did not hear my voice; I taught it not to commit fornication away from you, but it despised my teaching; I was burned by frost [Col. 0758A] and heat, and sleep did not come to my eyes.”

If the matter stands thus, shepherd, you have rendered a good account concerning the dead sheep. If you admonished and rebuked, you have redeemed your soul. But if you lie, the Searcher of hearts cannot be deceived; the skin of excuse cannot free you. If, I say, you lie, woe to you, because you were silent; because you did not recall what had strayed, nor seek what had perished. Hear what the Spirit speaks through Ezekiel: “If, when I say to the wicked, ‘Wicked man, you shall surely die,’ you have not spoken so that the wicked man may guard himself from his way, that wicked man will die in his wickedness, but I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. 33:8). If silence therefore deserves so grave a condemnation, what does example deserve? If your silence is punished thus, with what indignation [Col. 0758B] must your public iniquity be punished?

Brothers, forestall this indignation by confession and repentance. Let the pattern of the future judgment dwell in your hearts. Let the storm and terror of that dreadful day cling there. The master of the household will come, to separate the sheep from the goats, to draw his net to the shore, and to cleanse his threshing-floor of chaff. Woe then to shepherds of sheep who are to be numbered among the goats! Woe to fishers of souls who are then to be cast out among the bad fish! Woe to laborers in the Lord’s harvest who are then to be consumed without being consumed, with the chaff, in everlasting fire! Pray, brothers, pray to the Lord of the harvest that, on the day of winnowing, he may in mercy gather you into his granaries. We believe that no one attains this by his own merit. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign [Col. 0758C] to show you this mercy. May he deign to acknowledge and embrace you as his household when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

670  
## LXXXIX [On Various Matters II]. Synodal Address to Shepherds

> [Note: Col. 0758D. From the Saint-Germain manuscript, no. 383.]

### On the duties of good shepherds

“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep; but the hired shepherd, and he who is not a shepherd, whose sheep are not his own, . . . flees, etc.” (John 10:11).

The Lord Jesus Christ, the good and true shepherd, showed by example what he had taught by word. He laid down his life for his sheep; he himself endured death in order to free his sheep from death. He gave an example of humility in order to condemn pride. He patiently bore the injuries inflicted upon him—cross, nails, lance, spittle, blows, mockery, and insults—in order to commend the virtue of patience. He showed shepherds how humbly and diligently they ought to care for their flocks.

He condemned hired shepherds, who seek earthly gain from the pastoral office; who pretend to be shepherds but are exposed in the needs of the sheep. They seize the rule of churches as though they were to guard the Lord’s sheep; but when they see the wolf coming, they abandon the sheep and flee, because they do not care for the sheep’s salvation, seeking “their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2:21). They wish to preside, [Col. 0759A] not because they wish to be useful, but in order to gain worldly glory and profit. Where the need is greater and pastoral care is most required, they forget that they are shepherds. When wolves rush in, they withhold assistance; they do not set themselves in opposition for the sheep’s defense; they do not stand in the breach for the house of Israel; they are not inflamed with zeal for uprightness; they do not exercise the rigor of severity. They fear the threats of rulers, dread the enmities of tyrants, fear losing temporal advantages, shrink from hearing insulting words, avoid losses, and shudder at reproaches. They know nothing of suffering anything for righteousness, nor do they follow the footsteps of Christ, who suffered for his sheep, leaving shepherds examples of suffering.

Keep in mind, brothers, what the Lord says through Isaiah the prophet: “Listen to me, you who know what is just. . . . Do not fear the reproaches of men, nor be afraid of their blasphemies; for as a garment the worm shall consume them, and as wool the moth shall consume them; but my salvation shall be for ever” (Isa. 51:7). By these words the Lord strengthens us to bear with equanimity the reproaches inflicted for righteousness, so that we may not care about the insults of the reprobate, but may constantly proclaim the truth and bravely [Col. 0759B] defend justice, whoever rebukes us and whoever inflicts insults or mockery.

The Psalmist gloried in the insults brought upon him, saying to the Lord: “You have made me a reproach to the foolish” (Ps. 18:9). And it is said of the apostles: “They went away from the presence of the council rejoicing because they were considered worthy [Col. 0759C] to suffer insult for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41).

You ought to observe, brothers, that just as the moon is sometimes bright and sometimes dark, so the holy Church, which bears the likeness of the moon and, illuminated by the sun of righteousness, illumines the night of this age, is sometimes bright and shines with the tranquility and light of prosperity, and sometimes is darkened by the storms of adversity. Yet, darkened by adversities, it is no less precious and no less beautiful in the sight of those who live rightly or look rightly. It itself says: “I am black, but beautiful; daughters of Jerusalem, do not look upon me because I am dark” (Song 4:5).

Likewise, good shepherds and good prelates of churches are in no way diminished before God, or before those who judge rightly, when they are despised by wicked [Col. 0759D] people for righteousness’ sake, or even trampled underfoot and treated unworthily. Rather, this ought to be as pleasing to them as if they were honored and praised. So much steadfastness and strength ought to be present in good shepherds that they are neither turned from the truth by human praise and flattery, nor disturbed by abuse. The Lord showed this in saying to the prophet: “I have made your face like a diamond and like flint” (Ezek. 3:9). Both stones, diamond and flint, are very hard; but one, the diamond, is valued highly, while the other, flint, is often trampled underfoot.

Thus a good shepherd of the Church is like a diamond when he is honored and praised by people, yet is not turned aside by human praise or flattery.
