The face of the good shepherd is also like the hardness of flint when, for righteousness’ sake, he is despised by the wicked, or even trampled underfoot and treated unworthily; nevertheless, he does not grow weary or lose heart [perhaps: “fail”], but resists with unconquered strength and perseveres immovably in the defense of justice. Hired shepherds possess none of these qualities: they know how to suffer nothing for Christ’s name, sometimes contending and growing angry, not because the Lord’s sheep are endangered, but because temporal advantages are being lost.

See to it, brothers, that you are not in God’s Church like hired shepherds while serving the Lord. See to it that you do not serve him like hired shepherds while exercising ecclesiastical offices. See to it that earthly reward is not your aim. Let temporal recompense not be your desire, but eternal recompense; nor despair concerning life’s necessities, because if in pure simplicity you seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, [Col. 0760B] without doubt the other things you need will be added to you.

Watch confidently over your flocks. Resist bravely both visible and invisible wolves. Defend your subjects, as far as you can, both from temporal losses and from spiritual injuries. Visible wolves are robbers who inflict temporal losses upon people. Invisible wolves are demons, who devise spiritual injuries for souls by suggesting adulteries, fornications, murders, thefts, robberies, frauds, usuries, perjuries, buffoonery, pimping, and the like. Good shepherds vigilantly resist both kinds of wolves; hired shepherds set no defense against either. But you, brothers, strive to resist both. Remove temporal losses [Col. 0760C] as far as you can, but especially beware of spiritual injuries. For it is more grievous to lose eternal things than transitory ones, heavenly things than earthly.

Defend your sheep from the violence of visible wolves, from the malice and cruelty of tyrants. Do not be timid and sluggish in doing justice and exercising ecclesiastical severity, so that you may rescue your sheep from the bites of invisible wolves. Devote yourselves to preaching, exhortation, and correction. Rebuke offenders, that they may desist from evil; exhort those doing well, that they may advance in good things, extend themselves from good to better, and always ascend from virtue to virtue. Order your conduct so that all who see and hear you may receive from you an example of holiness and a model of good behavior. If you show in deed what you teach in speech, [Col. 0760D] your preaching will be useful, welcome, and sweet to hearers. Ezekiel the prophet shows this when he says: “And I ate, and it became in my mouth as sweet honey” (Ezek. 3:3). Their preaching is sweet from whose mouth life does not contradict preaching; for, as blessed Gregory said: “His speech has no sweetness whose conscience reproaches him for a wicked life.”

Therefore blessed Paul too, the outstanding preacher, instructing preachers and showing what is fitting for good preachers, said: “But I chastise my body and reduce it to slavery, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 16:19). And you also, brothers, chastise your bodies and reduce them to slavery. Strive that your works may shine before the Lord and before people, so that your preaching may be useful, welcome, and sweet; so that your sheep may gladly hear your voice and, as you lead the way on the path of righteousness, may follow more eagerly. Watch, attend, and labor for this purpose, brothers, that for the labor of the pastoral office you may receive [Col. 0761A] the eternal reward, bestowed by the eternal shepherd, our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and glory through all ages of ages. Amen.

## XC [On Various Matters III]. Synodal Address to Shepherds

> [Note: Col. 0761D. From Victorinus and the Angers manuscript.]

“You did not choose me, but I chose you, that you may go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain” [Col. 0761B] (John 15:16).

You know by whom this was said, and you know to whom it was said. It was said by the Lord, and said to his disciples. Yet it was not said only to them, but also to you, whom he has called to share their authority and care. For just as he willed us to share in their authority, so he willed us to share in their exhortation. It is right that one who delights in the dignity of authority should not evade the labor of office. He is delicate who wishes to use authority but declines to be exercised in administering that authority. Indeed, one deservedly deprives himself of honor who seeks honor without burden.

For to you, who are shepherds of souls, the good Shepherd and Lord of shepherds speaks, saying: “You did not choose me, but I chose you, that you may go and bear fruit, and that your fruit [Col. 0761C] may remain.” In these words he left you four matters to consider: your dignity, your office, caution, and constancy. Your dignity, where he says, “I chose you”; your office, where he says, “that you may go”; caution, when he adds, “and bear fruit”; and constancy, when he adds, “and that your fruit may remain.” Dignity lies in election; office, in service; caution, in fruit-bearing; constancy, in continuance.

For it is great that he chose you, he who is not deceived when he chooses. Greater is the work to which he chose those who were chosen; greatest, because he chose you in preference to others. The meaning is this: “You did not choose me”—that is, you did not choose me by any kind of choosing—but I chose you by every mode of choosing. For there are three modes of choosing: election, sub-election, and pre-election. Election is when, from a multitude of good and bad, the good are chosen; when grain is separated from a heap, oil from a press. Sub-election is when, from the good who have been chosen, the better are chosen. Pre-election is when, from the better, the best are chosen.

In this order Aaron and his sons were chosen to exercise the priesthood before the Lord. First, from every nation under heaven, the Lord chose the children of Israel as a people especially his own. From them he then chose the children of Levi, who, as spiritual ministers, serve the Lord in the tabernacle by a perpetual rite. From these, moreover, he chose in preference Aaron and his sons as priests, [Col. 0762A] to appease by their prayers and offerings the Lord’s indignation against the people.

In this manner, certainly, he chose us when through water and the Holy Spirit he separated us from the breasts of unbelief. He made a sub-election when he called us into the lot of the saints and, advancing us to the order of the clergy, set us apart from the common flock of believers by a distinctive tonsure of the head. He made a pre-election when he placed you over the heads of people as stewards of his household, so that you might give it food at the proper time. Great indeed is his election; greater, his sub-election; greatest, his pre-election.

How great it is that, at the lifting of our hands, the heads of kings bow down. And if kings and kingdoms of men, being beneficent and greater among men, offer you gifts—indeed, the whole Church acknowledges you as Fathers and awaits you as intercessors. As the reward of privileged love, it was given and said to Peter: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). As a singularity of authority, it was given and said to the apostles: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). Consider how great this is, even if it amounts to human ascent to the embassy [perhaps: “binding”] of angels. How great, then, if the ascent of angels is inclined at the discretion of human beings?

But woe to those—may God avert it—who, though they have been at the head, relapse into the tail; though first, become last; though stones of the sanctuary, are scattered [Col. 0762C] at the head of every street. Woe, I say, to fishers of souls if they are to be cast into the sea among bad fish! Woe to shepherds of sheep if they are to be numbered among goats! Woe to workers in the divine harvest if they are to burn like chaff!

What follows concerns office: “I have placed you that you may go.” By this placement I wish you to be active spiritually, just as by walking. There are, I say, four postures of human beings: reclining, sitting, standing, and walking. Every person is so positioned in a place that he either lies down, sits, stands, or walks. These differ from one another in this way. When a person lies down, all parts of his body rest. But when he sits, the lower parts rest while the upper parts labor in holding themselves upright. When he stands, the whole person labors in raising himself, because by natural weight he is borne downward [perhaps: “carried downward”]. When he walks, arduous labor from motion and fatigue are added.

In the same way, there are four states of people in the Church of God. Some of the faithful are good, others evil. We do not distinguish the number of the evil, because they have multiplied beyond number, and their confusion admits no distinction. The state of the good, however, admits distinction just as it does order. Certainly, among the good some are active, some contemplative, and some are prelates over both; thus there is one kind of evil faithful person and three kinds of good faithful persons.

The evil, therefore, are those lying down, [Col. 0763A] resting in the world, who place all their hope and delight in the world’s riches; whose god is their belly, and who have not made God their helper; who say: “Soul, you have goods laid up for many years; feast, drink, rest” (Luke 12:19).

He guards a good fortress who guards himself. Such persons lie cast down; they sleep at night and are drunk at night. Among the good, however, are good married people, who make good use of lawful things. But such people are divided: in part they serve the world, in part God, as the Apostle says. They honor God from their substance, devote themselves to works of mercy, and make friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity. Yet they are concerned for wives and children, fields, vineyards, olive groves, and things of this kind. Meanwhile, even amid this concern, they sometimes pass through while carrying with them wood, hay, and straw. And because they are in part delighted by the world and in part exercised in good works, they are said to sit: they labor in higher things and rest in lower things.

Others are contemplatives, whose citizenship is in heaven, because they place their peace in God. In the world, however, they have tribulations, so that to live in the world is death and to die is gain; and they say with the Apostle: “Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). These are said to stand. For they serve as soldiers and labor upon the earth, resting, so to speak, upon the very joints of their feet and refreshed as though by the lightness [perhaps: “gentleness”] of the higher air.

Others, however, are prelates. Their duty is to walk—that is, to range among the aforesaid [Col. 0763C] classes of people, now to these, now to those, now to others, dispensing rebuke, exhortation, and consolation as the provisions of God’s word. “For Jesus, walking by the Sea of Galilee, called disciples” (Matt. 4:18), to whom he afterwards said: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15). Therefore you have been chosen to go; thus it is dangerous merely to stand and ruinous to sit.

Go, then; rouse those who lie down, and say: “Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14). It is now time for you to rise from sleep, lest the thief come, assault, and break into your house. But if, oppressed by heavy slumber, he does not awake at the voice of the one who touches him, “cry aloud, do not cease” (Isa. 58:1); raise [Col. 0763D] your voice, because the Lord cried with a loud voice when he raised the man dead four days. Add threats also, and the terrors of judgment, by whose cleansing force the lethargy may be roused. It is a harsh piercing to say how they will pass from waters into fire, that their fire shall not be extinguished and their worm shall not die. “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 22:13).

Pass from these to those who sit, exhorting them to advance to better things, and say: “By the rivers of Babylon sit [perhaps: ‘sitting’] and weep while you remember Zion” (Ps. 136:1); extend your hand to the poor, so that your right hand may be forgotten. For in vain does the person stretch hands to the Lord who, according to his ability, does not stretch them out to the poor. But if one who sits should at some time wish to stand, place a hand under the one leaning upon it, and say: “Rise after you have sat, you who have eaten the bread of sorrow” (Ps. 126:2). For those who stand are promised that they shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

From these one must pass to those who stand. They need consolation in their labor. To them it must be said: “Stand in your ways, act manfully, let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” (Ps. 30). For in a little while you shall see him. And this: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize [Vulgate: ‘snatch’] it” (Matt. 11:12).

This is the labor of your office. For not without reason is the Church of God, which you govern under its very Author, compared to a little ship that is tossed by waves but not submerged. This world is the great and wide sea. There are creeping things without number. There are many ways of crossing the water. Some cross by a ford, some by a vessel, some by a bridge; others lie hidden, drowned in the waves. These are the four states noted above. Those lying down, not finding the city’s way, are overwhelmed by the whirlpool of waves. Married people cross by the ford: they are amid the waves; their clothes are made wet by conspiring knots [the reading is uncertain; perhaps “treacherous knots, or waves”], while their feet are cut by stones and entangled in mud. [Col. 0764C] When they have crossed, whatever is wet in them will be dried by purgatorial fire, and they will be saved as through fire.

Contemplatives cross by the bridge, choosing a narrower and more elevated way. To them the world is dead, and they to the world. From afar they await the world’s storm; they cross dry-shod amid hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, many vigils, and many labors. But you cross by ship, remaining dry amid the waves. It is therefore your duty to help the others: lest anyone fall from the bridge, but that you may raise him; lest anyone stumble or go astray at the ford, but that you may extend the right hand of help; and that you may draw out those submerged by stronger waves.

What follows concerns caution: “See, therefore, how you walk.” One must walk cautiously, namely in order that you may bear fruit. Three fruits are mentioned in the Gospel (Matt. 13): the thirtyfold, the sixtyfold, and the hundredfold. The hundredfold belongs to virgins, of which we have spoken elsewhere.

> [Note: Col. 0763D.] Hildebert seems here to allude to his book *On Virginity*, which he asserts that he published among several other small works, Epistle 45, Book II. Despite every diligence, we have nowhere been able to find it. See our notes on that epistle. What he notes here near the end concerning the sacred vestments with which a priest clothes himself when about to minister at the altar, he explains in almost the same words in the *Treatise on Sacred Vestments*, which we shall place below among the shorter works. From this we infer reciprocal confirmation that both this sermon and that treatise are genuinely Hildebertian.

The thirtyfold belongs to subjects, for thirty arises from ten multiplied by three. Subjects are saved in faith in the Trinity and observance of the Decalogue. The sixtyfold is [supplied: that of prelates], that is, doubled fruit. It is not enough for a prelate to keep himself unstained from this world unless [Col. 0765A] he also instructs his subjects to avoid it. It is not enough for him to be good in himself unless he also makes others good, so far as lies in him. For garlands increased threefold by tens crown others, but doubled garlands crown prelates. Nor, I think, is it without reason that it is said: “Let lamps be burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35). A lamp in the hand suffices for subjects, because they will render account only for themselves to the Judge who sees all things. But this does not suffice for prelates unless they bear one in each hand. Hence, when the lord pope ordains someone priest, the ordinand offers a burning candle in each hand to his ordainer, signifying that he will present to the supreme shepherd care for himself and for his own people.

Paul bore a sheaf in one hand when he said: “I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Cor. 4:4); and a sheaf in the other when he said: [Col. 0765B] “I traveled round from the Illyrian Sea as far as Jerusalem.”

> [Note: Col. 0765D. Rom. 15:19. The Vulgate has: “So that from Jerusalem, and round about as far as Illyricum, I have filled up the Gospel of Christ.”]

What follows concerns constancy. For the end crowns the struggle, and the Lord judges the ends of the earth. Therefore let your fruit remain—that is, endure. You have been commanded to offer your Lord the tail of the victim as a sweet-smelling offering. To signify this, you have been given the ankle-length tunic, that you may persevere in the command [perhaps: “purpose”], lest it be said of you: “This man began to build and was unable to finish” (Luke 14:13).

Behold: the greater your eminence above others in honor, the greater is the difficulty of the burden of administration, because by as many steps as you ascend in rank, by so many bonds of accountability you are bound. For who is bound by as many bonds as the priest who is clothed in vestments to minister? First he is bound by the enveloping amice; then he binds his breast with bands passed around under the armpits; thirdly, he tightens his loins with the girdle, as though it were said to him: “Constrain your jaws, and set a guard upon your mouth; constrain”—that is, crucify—“your flesh with its vices and desires.” Do this, and you shall live; you shall be blessed, and it shall be well with you. Yet pray to him without whom you can do nothing, that, as he has chosen you, so he may help you to go and bear fruit: Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ever. Amen.

678  
## XCI [On Various Matters IV]. Synodal Address to Priests

> [Note: Col. 0766D. From Victorinus.]

> [Note: Col. 0766D. It is phrased somewhat differently in the Vulgate, but nevertheless has the same meaning.]

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: A priest who has a blemish shall not offer [Col. 0765D] sacrifices to God, nor approach his ministry. If he is blind, if lame, if of a small, large, or crooked nose, if of a broken foot . . . If he is hunchbacked, if bleary-eyed, if he has a white spot in his eye, if a scab on his nail . . . Every one who has a blemish shall not approach to offer sacrifices to the Lord . . . A man who is leprous shall not eat of those things which have been sanctified to the Lord” (Lev. 21:17; 22:4).

All things, dearest brothers, which are commanded in the old Law concerning the priesthood seem, when understood spiritually, to pertain to our priesthood. There bodily defect in the priest is condemned; here defect of mind, indicated through vices, is shown. Let us consider one by one how the Lord, by his command, compels the defectiveness of the mind to be removed from the priesthood.

First, he commands that a blind priest shall not offer sacrifices to the Lord. A blind priest is one who does not understand knowledge of Scripture and, through ignorance, does not know in what direction to extend the steps of doctrine or conduct. Of such persons it is written through Isaiah: “The watchmen of Jerusalem are all blind” (Isa. 56:10): namely, those who ought to provide for God’s Church and lead others are blind—that is, ignorant of the Lord’s commands. How rightly are those removed from the priesthood who do not know how to govern God’s people, nor know what they ought to teach! For the Lord says: “If the blind lead the blind, both fall into a pit” (Matt. 15:14). Both fall into the precipice [Col. 0766B] of sin, because both are ignorant of the way of truth. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel concerning shepherds: “You are blind and leaders of the blind” (ibid.).

God’s priests ought to be prudent in the Scriptures, that they may find there the means to feed the Lord’s flock and defend themselves against the spiritual wolf. Hence Solomon, praising the eyes of the Church in the Song of Songs, says: “Her eyes are like doves beside streams of water” (Song 5:12). The eyes are the shepherds, who ought to keep watch around the Lord’s flock. They ought to be doves, because they should be innocent and simple in their consideration of the Scriptures, lest some heretical opinion corrupt sound understanding. They are described as being beside streams of water. By the streams of water is understood the overflowing knowledge of the Scriptures. The different streams are different senses [or interpretations]. [Col. 0766C] It is the nature of the dove to dwell near flowing water, so that, when the hawk comes, it may escape its snares by plunging itself into the wave. In the same way, shepherds ought to flee for refuge to the fortification of the Scriptures against the snares of the devil.

What follows is: “If he is lame, he shall not offer sacrifices to God.” A lame man has one sound foot and limps with the other. To this lame man are compared those shepherds who partly understand the Scriptures rightly, and partly proceed rightly in their understanding, but in one respect preach wrongly and limp by holding some erroneous belief in the faith. Jacob, lame in body, prefigured this lameness of mind, because the people Israel, when Christ came into the world, limped in mind. [Col. 0766D] For they thought rightly concerning Christ when they considered him human, but wrongly when they did not understand him to be God. Those who limp in faith must be removed from the priesthood, lest they cause those whom they ought to govern to limp in the same fault.

It follows: If they have a small nose, let them not offer sacrifices to God. In the divine page, the nose signifies discernment. For by the nose a good and a bad smell are distinguished. Hence Solomon, describing the Church in the Song of Songs: “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus” (Cant. VII, 4). The nose of the Church is the holy teachers, who know how to distinguish the fragrant teaching of the Catholic faith [Col. 0767A] from the stench of heretical perversity. Like the tower of Lebanon. Lebanon is a mountain whose name is interpreted “whitening.” Lebanon signifies the Church, because she is made bright in virtues. The tower of Lebanon signifies the teachers of the Church, because they are a defense and refuge for the faithful. Which looks toward Damascus. Damascus is interpreted “drinking of blood.” Blood denotes the desires of the body. Damascus, therefore, denotes or represents the world, which delights in blood—that is, in bodily pleasures; but that tower, namely the holy teachers, stands opposed to the world, and therefore is said to look toward Damascus.

But let us return to the matter at hand. If anyone has a small nose—that is, slight discernment, so that he does not properly distinguish in ministry what ought and ought not to be done, and [Col. 0767B] does not rightly distinguish by what spirit each thing is done, whether good or evil—he is not worthy of the priesthood. He will suppose certain things to be good which are evil, if he lacks true discernment. Of this discernment the Apostle says: “To another is given discernment of spirits” (I Cor. XII, 10). If he has a large and crooked nose, let him not offer sacrifices to God. He has a large nose who ranges abroad with unrestrained discernment. For there are some who investigate every matter beyond measure; to them the Apostle says: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think soberly” (Rom. XII, 3). For when someone searches out the divine mysteries beyond measure, he falls into error, since he cannot attain by understanding what he was investigating. But, as the Lord says: “If anything remains over, it shall be burned with fire” (Exod. XII, 10); [Col. 0767C] that is, whatever cannot be known shall be entrusted to the Holy Spirit.

If he has a broken foot or hand, let him not offer sacrifices to God. The faithful person is said to walk on two feet and to travel in the way of the Lord when he strives to accomplish in deed what he teaches with his mouth. But he has a broken hand who either preaches and does not fulfill it in deed, or fulfills it in deed and does not preach it to others. Each is to be removed from the priesthood whose life is at variance with his words: those who preach well and live badly. The Lord marks them in the Gospel when he says: “They say and do not do.” But to the priest who ceases to preach the Lord thus threatens through Ezekiel: “Son of man, I have appointed you a watchman for the house of Israel. You shall hear my words from my mouth and announce them to them on my behalf. If, when I say to the wicked man, ‘You shall surely die,’ [Col. 0767D] you do not announce it to him so that he may turn from his most evil way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but I shall require his blood from your hand. But if, when you have announced to the wicked man that he should turn from his ways, he does not turn from his way, he shall die in his iniquity. But you have delivered your own soul” (Ezek. XXXIII, 7). Hand signifies the same thing as foot. For the hand denotes working, the foot walking. To walk and to work are the same thing in the divine page.

It follows: If he is hunchbacked, let him not offer sacrifices. A hunchbacked priest is one whom the weight of earthly covetousness presses down, and who directs himself more sluggishly toward the things above. For while, bent over, he longs after the lowest things, he bears the burden of anxious care as though it were a weight. And because the rich man who longs after earthly things is hunchbacked, he compared the rich man to gold [perhaps “a camel”], saying: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Mark X, 25). That all priests devote themselves to avarice, Jeremiah says: “From the least even to the greatest, all devote themselves to avarice; and from prophet to priest, all deal deceitfully” (Jer. VI, 13).

It follows: If he is bleary-eyed, let him not offer sacrifices to God. Bleary-eyed is an intellect which indeed flashes forth toward knowledge of truth, but is obscured by carnal living. For there are some who could study the divine page well and understand it well [Col. 0768B] if they wished; but, intent upon pleasures, they obscure their intellect and, living in filth, defile its light—that is, their intellect. He has a white film on his eye who, though wise, places before the eye of his intellect a cloud of arrogant wisdom or righteousness, and reckons himself to appear blind and foolish by ascribing to himself what he does not yet know. Or he has a blemish in his eye who is intent on earthly wisdom rather than divine wisdom, and thinks himself wise when he is foolish. Hence it is written: “The wisdom of this world is folly with God” (I Cor. III, 19). He has a continual itch who does not repent of grave sins and is thereby defiled. The Lord commands that all these men, dearest brothers, be removed from the office of priesthood; but you who bear the name of priesthood, beware lest you be found unworthy of all these dignities and offices [Col. 0768C].

XCII [On Various Matters V]. ADDRESSED TO THE CLERGY, PERHAPS DELIVERED IN A SYNOD  
[Note: [Col. 0767D] From Victorinus.]

“In all things, dearest brothers, let us present ourselves as ministers of God: in much patience, in tribulation, in necessity, in chastity, in knowledge, in gentleness, in unfeigned charity, in the word of truth; giving no offense to anyone, lest our ministry be blamed” (II Cor. VI, 4).

Our Lord and Redeemer, through his grace, dearest and most beloved brothers, chose his ministers in his palace, in his house; for he himself says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV, 16). Hence you are also called clerics—that is, those chosen by a divine lot [Col. 0768D]. For *clerus* is interpreted in Greek as “lot,” because you have been set apart from others by lot, that is, by divine election. For this reason Matthias was chosen by lot. From this the name had its origin. Thus, by his mercy, the Lord willed us to be chosen as his ministers. As the Apostle says: “Let a man regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God” (I Cor. IV, 1). Since, then, we are ministers, we ought to minister. But since we are ministers, in all things we ought to present ourselves as ministers of God. For Christ himself was our minister, as he says: “I came not to be ministered to, but to minister” (Matt. XX, 28) [Col. 0769A]. Much more ought we, who are servants, to serve.

Those are called servants of the Lord who do not serve merely for appearance, but faithfully obey the will of the Lord in all things; and then they are advanced into such intimacy with God—

[Note: [Col. 0769D] Here there is an evident break in the sense, which we judge may be supplied thus: “They are advanced, so that they do nothing except for his sake. Others, however, are not faithful servants, [Col. 0770D] but hirelings: they labor for earthly gain, not for the salvation of men; and when,” etc.]

—advanced for earthly gain rather than for the salvation of men; and, when they are judged especially to serve God, they serve money. These have already received their reward, 682 because we cannot serve two masters, God and Mammon (Matt. VI). But perhaps some object to us: “We have not received freely, nor therefore ought we to give freely,” because some purchase orders for a price and enter into prelacies and promotions in the Church through money. An evil entrance, an evil excuse; [Col. 0769B] because they enter badly and sell badly, they incur a double condemnation. He who buys is condemned with Simon Magus, to whom Peter said: “May your money perish with you” (Acts VIII, 20). He who demands a price is a Gehazi and receives the leprosy of Gehazi. For when Elisha had cleansed Naaman, commander of Syria, of leprosy in the Jordan (IV Kings V), Naaman returned and offered the prophet many gifts. But he refused to receive them. When Naaman had departed, Gehazi, his disciple, followed him, demanding gifts from him; when he had received them, the prophet, seeing everything through the Spirit, rebuked him, and leprosy struck him. Thus he is both a Simonian and a Gehazi who buys the gifts of the Holy Spirit and afterward sells them. And since he has entered the house of the Lord like a thief, he must be driven from the house of the Lord like a thief [Col. 0769C]. “For he who does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs up another way, is a thief and a robber” (John XVI, 1). But he enters another way who makes not Christ but money his door. He must be driven out, because the Lord drove buyers and sellers from the temple. He must be driven out, because lepers are commanded to be expelled from the camp. All Gehazis have been struck with Gehazi’s leprosy.

Again, he does not enter through the door who enters through a lay hand. For spiritual things have not been entrusted to laypeople, but to the vicars of the Lord. The vicars of the Lord are those who hold the place of the apostles. Let laypeople administer their castles and villages, not the strongholds of the Lord; temporal matters, not ecclesiastical ones. Therefore he who enters through another than the vicar [Col. 0769D] of the Lord does not enter through the door. Canonical clergy, therefore, should neither buy nor sell benefices, nor the admission of priests into churches; nor should they receive from a lay hand, nor permit a layperson to share in the altar. For the Apostle says: “Those who serve the altar share in the altar” (I Cor. IX, 13). But let us return to the matter at hand.

As has been said, the Apostle commands us to present ourselves in all things as ministers of God. It follows: In much patience, in tribulation, in necessity, in chastity, in gentleness, in unfeigned charity, in the word of truth. The Apostle teaches us how [Col. 0770A] we may present ourselves as ministers of God. If persecutions come, let us not fail but endure. If the necessities of poverty occur, let us not despair but trust in the Lord. For he says to his ministers: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you; the servant is not greater than his master” (John XV, 20); but “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. V, 10). Hear, then, how the Lord consoles one who endures want, saying: “Do not be anxious, saying: What shall we eat? What shall we drink? Or with what shall we be clothed? For your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first, therefore, the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. VI, 31).

It follows: Let us present ourselves in chastity. This [Col. 0770B] is that virtue, dearest brothers, which is exceedingly necessary in our order. This is what commends us; when it is destroyed, it makes us contemptible before the world. We are the vessel of election; we are “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (I Pet. II, 9). We bear the vessels of the Lord; Scripture cries to us: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. LII, 11). The Apostle corrects us, saying: “Fornication and all uncleanness must not even be named among you” (Eph. V, 3). He does not say, “Let it not exist,” but, “Let it not even be named.” Not only fornication and uncleanness must be removed from you, but also every false suspicion of either. For we ought not dwell with women unless they are joined to us by close ties of blood [Col. 0770C]. Nor ought we speak with them except before lawful witnesses, so that all *suspectio* (“suspicion”)—perhaps *suspicio*—may be removed. “You are the light of the world; let your light shine before men” (Matt. V, 14).

The Apostle names two things: fornication and uncleanness. But first he speaks of fornication, afterward of uncleanness. Fornication is natural intercourse, but illicit. Fornication is with a prostitute; moreover a woman, whether adulteress or concubine, is called a prostitute. Fornication, dearest brothers, is forbidden us because, since we are ministers of the Lord, we are his members: “But he who,” as the Apostle says, “is joined to a prostitute becomes one body. Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Far be it!” (I Cor. VI, 15). How shameful that a cleric should be led captive by a prostitute [Col. 0770D], so as to become a member of a prostitute. For if marriage is forbidden us, how great a crime will fornication be judged among us. Since married laypeople are commanded to abstain for a time in order that they may devote themselves to prayer, and continence is commanded of the lower orders, how much more must purity be preserved by priests, who handle and consecrate the body of the Lord. To them the Apostle commands “that each should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification” (I Thess. IV, 4).

One day David came hungry to Abimelech the priest and said: Give me some food. But he said: “I do not have ordinary bread at hand, [Col. 0771A] but only holy bread. Tell me, are your young men clean from women?” “They are,” David said, “from yesterday and the day before, and the vessels of the young men have been clean and holy.” Therefore the priest gave him consecrated bread (I Kings XXI, 4). If, then, the priest asked whether they were clean from women on that day in order to receive the bread of presentation, what ought priests to do continually in order to receive the body of Christ? You have heard concerning fornication how great a sin it is; now hear concerning uncleanness.

Uncleanness is that shameful act which males commit with males. It is rightly called uncleanness because it is extreme filthiness of mind and body; and this uncleanness is not only a sin but also [Col. 0771B] a punishment for sin. For when the Lord sees them mutually despising him and trampling his commandments underfoot, he turns them over to a reprobate mind, so that they may practice that abominable shamefulness and understand and perceive it [perhaps: “and neither understand nor perceive it”]. For the Apostle says: “Since they did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge, he gave them over to a reprobate mind, and gave them over to dishonorable passions. For males, abandoning the natural use of the female, burned in their desires for one another, males committing shameful acts with males” (Rom. I, 4). O how abominable that a member of Christ should not merely commit fornication, but should himself become a prostitute! This is the uncleanness which the Lord severely punished in two cities. For Scripture says: “The men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked and sinners before the Lord” (Gen. XIII, 13). He is called a sinner before the Lord whose sin God does not leave unpunished; and yet, delaying punishment for a long time, he at last says: “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grievous” (Gen. XVIII, 20). Sin is called an outcry when it is not only conceived and carried into act, but multiplied by habit. Then fire and sulphur rained from heaven, and the cities were burned and overthrown. They were rightly destroyed by sulphurous fire because they burned with fervent lust. Likewise, all Sodomites who follow them, if not in the present life, at least in the future will perish by fire [Col. 0771D], because of the disgrace which they suffer in the present.

It follows: Let us present ourselves in knowledge and gentleness, so that we may be diligent in the Scriptures and gentle—that is, approachable and mild; hence it is said: “Blessed are the meek” (Matt. V, 5). In unfeigned charity. This is the virtue which is the completion and perfection of virtues. For if you were of one mind in love, the members would never suffer. As hatred scatters the Church, so the bond of love builds it. Hatred generates detraction and envy, which are the plague and ruin of the Church. Through hatred is lost that benefit and delight of which David says: “Behold how good 685 and delightful it is for brothers to dwell together in [Col. 0772A] unity” (Ps. CXXXII, 1). Through it Christ, who is true Wisdom, is driven out, because the Spirit—or Wisdom—will not enter an ill-disposed soul. Mark what he says: In unfeigned charity. This is said because of those who have [alternatively, “speak”] peace with their neighbor but evil in their hearts.

It follows: In the word of truth. Love the word of truth, brothers; for this reason the Apostle says: “Putting away malice and falsehood, speak the truth” (Eph. IV, 25). For the children of the devil are all children of falsehood, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and its father” (John VIII, 44). And: “The Lord shall destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. V, 7). In all these things, dearest brothers, present yourselves as ministers of God [Col. 0772B], so that our ministry may not be blamed. “For through us,” as the Apostle says, “the Word of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles” (Titus II, 5; Rom. II, 24). For laypeople take their example from us; and we who ought to be for them an aroma of life are an aroma of death. Henceforth, dearest brothers, amend your way: let your speech be modest, your bearing honorable, your countenance humble, your tongue gracious, your mind full of love, and your hands full of good works. With the help of the Lord Jesus Christ, without whom you can do nothing. He lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

XCIII [On Various Matters VI]. SYNODAL ADDRESS TO PRIESTS  
[Note: [Col. 0771D] From Victorinus and Angers.]

“I was made like [*assimilatus*] in the hands [V: hand] of the prophets, says the Lord” (Hos. XII, 10) [Col. 0772C].

Which Lord? The Lord of the prophets—as if he said: “I was made like in the hands of my prophets.” Whom do you think is the Lord of the prophets? Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. They are his prophets in relation to the Father, because they were sent by him, according to the text: “Who spoke beforehand through his prophets concerning his Son” (Rom. I, 2). They are his in relation to the Son, because they spoke of him, according to the text: “That the things written in the law, the prophets, and the psalms concerning me may be fulfilled” (Luke XXIV, 44). They are his in relation to the Holy Spirit, because they spoke by his inspiration—indeed, he himself spoke in them—according to the text: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 19).

Nevertheless [Col. 0772D], there the Lord of the prophets is spiritually called the Son, for they are his according to each of his two natures. According to his divinity they are his as creatures of their Creator, servants of their master. According to his humanity they are his as his fellow-tribesmen and neighbors. For he was made for God the Father from the seed of David according to the flesh. And if the tradition of the Hebrews is true—that Manasseh took Isaiah’s daughter as wife and begot Amon by her—Christ came forth from Isaiah’s thigh. Thus Christ was made like in the hands of his prophets because he was not only foretold by their words but was also prefigured, by a certain kind of likeness, in the deeds of their times [perhaps: “in their own deeds”] [Col. 0773A].

To select a few examples from many: when David hid among the Ziphites (I Kings XXIII), he foreshadowed Christ’s coming hidden in the flesh to the lost sheep of the house of Israel; when he played the drum at the gates of the city, he foreshadowed Christ’s extension upon the cross, where his bones were numbered beyond number; when he hid in a cave, he foreshadowed the repose of burial, because after the second anointing he had no enemies—that is, “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him” (Rom. VI, 9).

Evangelical prophets, however, are priests, whose lips preserve wisdom and from whose mouth others seek knowledge; whose eyes are in their head, that is, in Christ, and see the hidden things of Scripture; who, digging out the wells [Col. 0773B] of their fathers, find water springing up to eternal life; who see the realities of the sacraments hidden beneath the veil of images. Do you think that he does not have lynx-like eyes who sees fruit beneath a leaf, a kernel beneath a shell, marrow beneath bark, treasure beyond a wall—that is, the life-giving spirit beneath the killing letter, a wheel within a wheel, angels ascending [and descending] by the ladder? Therefore, since they see so many and such great things, they may fittingly be called prophets, that is, foreseers. Hence, after the Gospel is read, the Gospel-book is handed open to the priest to be kissed, but to the others closed. It is as though at that moment it were said to him: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the rest, in parables” (Luke VIII).

Moreover, Christ is made like in the hands of priests. He is made like [Col. 0773C] in two ways: in the sacrament and in the pattern of his works. For when, at the altar, through the words of priests, the flesh and blood of the Creator are made from created things, handled by their hands, received by the mouth, and distributed to others, he is made like in their hands—that is, he is handled under the likeness of bread and wine. But he ought no less to be made like in their hands, that is, in their works. The vicars of Christ ought to bear about the likeness of Christ. For not only the apostles, but the princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali, are to be called vicars of Christ; indeed, as arrows in the hand of the mighty man, so are the sons of those cast forth; as the Almighty sent the disciples into the whole world, so sons born in place of fathers are sent forth, wherever they may image Christ in themselves [Col. 0773D]. Hence: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (Phil. I, 17).

Certainly he is represented in them in many ways. If Christ is a mountain, they too are mountains. If Christ is a foundation, they too are foundations. If Christ is a shepherd, they too are shepherds. Truly, no one has denied that he himself is the door. Yet (for brevity’s sake, I shall say) we can define four works of Christ, from whose pattern the priest is not permitted to depart. Christ preached, as he himself says: “I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, preaching his commandment” (Ps. II, 5). [Hence] he also preached tirelessly; therefore: “My throat has become hoarse” (Ps. LXVIII, 4).

In this manner it is the priest’s office to preach, because it has been said to him: “Cry out; do not cease” (Isa. [Col. 0774A] LVIII, 1). And elsewhere: “Let your springs flow abroad, and distribute your waters in the streets” (Prov. V, 16). Moreover, Christ interceded for sinners, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke XXIII, 34). Likewise, it is the priest’s task to appease God’s indignation by prayers. For this reason they eat the sins of the people; hence it is written: “If a soul from among the people sins, let it offer for the turning away of sin, and the priest shall pray for it, and the Lord shall be merciful to it” (Lev. IV, 14). For this purpose Christ gave his body and blood to the disciples and commanded priests to distribute them, saying: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke XXII, 19). Finally, Christ left us an example, that you might follow his footsteps. In this manner the priest ought to go before [Col. 0774B] others as a leader by example, because it is written: “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16).

Observe, then, the four likenesses of Christ in the priest’s hands: preaching, intercession, sacred communion, and exemplary conduct. And from these he is designated by the name priest, because in each of these he gives what is sacred. In preaching, he gives us what is sacred from God. In interceding, he gives God what is sacred for us. In communicating, he gives what is sacred when he causes God to dwell in us. In going before and drawing others after him, he gives God sacrifice from us. On account of these four things Peter was told three times: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI, 17): feed by word, feed by communicating [Col. 0774C], feed by example. For “word” includes preaching and intercession.

Moreover, because the Levitical priest did not offer without his libations, the evangelical priest must preserve his own libations for each of these sacrifices. He offered preaching with wine and oil; intercession with rose and lily; sacred communion with fire and sword; exemplary conduct with weight, measure, and number. Preaching has something of wine in the threatening of punishments, and the mildness of oil in the promise of rewards; sternness in rebuke, mildness in charity. For the hoe of correction ought to proceed from the root of charity. Hear of wine in the Apostle: “Rebuke the unruly” (I Thess. V, 14). Hear also what follows concerning oil: “In a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. VI, 1), and of meekness.

Intercession has a rose in compassion. For not only the shedding of blood for Christ is the work of the rose, but also the mortification of the flesh and compassion for one’s neighbor. The Apostle offered a rose when he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (II Cor. XI, 29.) Intercession has a lily in the purity of the intercessor; the hand must be clean if it desires to cleanse a filthy vessel. He who appeals to the judge on behalf of offenses must live without offense, lest, if one who is offended [perhaps “gives offense”] intercedes, he provoke anger rather than restrain it; lest, when he has said, “Hail, King of the Jews” (Matt. XXVII, 29), he strike his head with a reed.

In communicating [Col. 0775A], fire and sword are necessary: the sword in the flesh, fire in the spirit. Let the priest circumcise every foreskin of his flesh from each of his members; let him cut away the reproaches of Egypt; turn away his eyes lest they see vanity; his ears lest they hear a judgment of blood (Ps. CXVIII). Let him restrain his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit. Let him shake his hands free from every gift; nor, at the brief contact of another’s skin, let his unhappy soul grow cheerful. Let his feet not run with a thief when he sees one, nor let him place his portion with adulterers. Beyond these things fire is necessary—but not just any fire: rather fire from heaven, fire unto heaven, fire for heaven; namely, the Lord as fire, the Lord’s fire, fire offered to the Lord: that is, the illumination of the Holy Spirit, the sending upward of the sacrifice, and the humiliation of a contrite heart [Col. 0775B].

The Spirit indeed is fire, according to the saying: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. IV, 24); and it is from heaven, according to the saying: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Matt. XII, 49). But the ministry of sending the sacrifice by the hand of an angel to the high altar of the Lord is the Lord’s fire, according to the saying: “Who makes his ministers a flame of fire” (Ps. CIII, 4), that is, looking toward heaven. For it is the nature of fire to be carried upward and to carry upward with itself what it burns. In this manner the priest sends the sacrifice upward, and when he has sent it, says: “Go, it is the dismissal.” Fire offered to the Lord here is that of which it is written: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. L, 19).

Moreover, the priest’s deeds that are an example to others must be done with the weight of dispensation, so that [Col. 0775C] whenever he makes a dispensation, at least an equal recompense may correspond to it; with the measure of his own capacity, because it is right for each person to measure himself by his own rule; and with the number of watchful discernment. By these libations God is appeased concerning the sacrifice of the Eucharist. 689 Without them, the sacrifice offered does not open the door but makes an enemy.

But to this it will be said: Why do you preach an almost unbearable yoke, when the Lord said that his burden is light and his yoke sweet? To this one may say that all difficult things are most easy to one who loves. Let us consider what was imposed upon the Levitical priest during the days of his service: bodily purity; abstaining from wine and strong drink, and every drink that can intoxicate; and not going out to public conversations among men. The first is enjoined upon the evangelical priest; the other [Col. 0775D] two are permitted. But perhaps they will say to me: “Physician, heal yourself. You lay heavy and unbearable burdens on us, yet you are unwilling to move them with your finger.” To this I say: “What I say indeed seems grievous, but it is true, and it must not be concealed.” When I enter before the altar of God, I have become a spectacle to God, angels, and men; if I stand polluted in flesh and spirit, how abominable I am! Let us consider.

Antiochus Epiphanes placed an idol in the temple of the Lord, and because of that abomination it was not lawful to sacrifice in the temple until it had been consecrated. In this manner, if I am a vessel of incontinence and lust, at the altar, beside the Son of the Virgin, I set the son of Venus. When I utter the words of the Canon and the word of transubstantiation [Note: [Col. 0775D] Note the word “transubstantiation”], and my mouth is full of contradiction, bitterness, and deceit, although I honor him with my lips, nevertheless I spit in the Savior’s face. When I presume to receive my Lord, into my mouth so polluted, it would be lighter if I threw him into the mud of the streets. Therefore be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord; be cleansed, you who bear the words of the Lord; be cleansed, you who offer the sacrifice of the Lord; be cleansed, you who bear the body of the Lord to others, so that, being cleansed, you may one day grasp in the truth of reality what you now bear in likeness. Through Christ our Lord—that is, our Judge—who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

XCIV [On Various Matters VII]. SYNODAL ADDRESS TO PRIESTS OR PASTORS  
[Note: [Col. 0776D] From Victorinus.]

[Col. 0776B]

“Moses placed in the tabernacle a bronze basin in which Aaron and his sons might wash when they entered the Holy of Holies; he made it from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle” (Exod. XXXVIII, 8).

The figure of this matter, O priests, concerns you, teaching how you ought to be cleansed in the house of the Lord. For whatever was done in the temple under the ancient law foreshadowed something future, which lay concealed under a figure in the Church of God. Moses, 690 as has been said, placed in the tabernacle of the Lord a basin—according to some, made of bronze—in which Aaron, who was high priest, washed himself, and his sons [Col. 0776C], who were of lower rank; he made it from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle. For women did not enter the tabernacle, but stood before the entrance of the tabernacle.

Aaron, that high priest, prefigured the chief priests of the Church, and his sons prefigured the other, lesser priests. By the bronze basin is understood the law of Christ, in which both priests and bishops, by study and reading and the completion of works, ought through compunction to be cleansed unto purity of heart, so that through purification they may be found worthy to penetrate the Holy of Holies—that is, the secrets of God. But the mirrors of the women are the commandments of God; the women are the souls of the saints. The commandments of the Lord are compared to mirrors because, just as women discover by a mirror the beauty and [Col. 0776D] ugliness of the face, so holy souls understand in God’s commandments whether there is anything blameworthy in their deeds, or whether they have done anything worthy of praise. They cannot enter the eternal tabernacle—that is, eternal glory—but the women nevertheless keep watch at the doors of the tabernacle, because holy souls, while they are still weighed down with the frailty of flesh, continually watch in longing for entrance into the eternal tabernacle.

Behold, dearest brothers, you have a vessel prepared in which you ought to wash away the ugliness of the mind and, by casting off vices, temper the purity and brightness of the soul [perhaps “attain”]. For the law [Col. 0777A] of the Lord is set forth for all, to teach you to be cleansed from vices and adorned with virtues. Read the Scriptures, devote yourselves to reading, so that you may find edification for yourselves and provide abundant pastures for your flock: “For whatever things,” as the Apostle says, “were written, were written for our instruction” (Rom. XV, 4). The ancient Fathers would not have wished so earnestly to commend past events to memory in writing unless they had labored to build up posterity by example.

Otherwise, as the Lord says, you will be blind guides of the blind (Matt. XV, 4), unless you know the way by which the flock is to be guided. “And it is very dangerous,” as Gregory says, “that he who does not know how to hold the reins of his own life should become a judge of another’s.” For through blindness on the roads [perhaps “of one man”] a multitude of blind persons will perish. For “if the blind [Col. 0777B] lead the blind, both fall into the pit” (ibid.). Behold the pit; behold the precipice before your face. Behold, the spiritual enemy daily devises your ruin, and you do not care to drive away the darkness of your error by study and reading. Alas for sorrow! When you ought to be examples of goodness, you are examples of error. For if the priest falls, how much more will the people perish? Hence in Job it is read: “If God finds perversity in his angels, how much more those who dwell in houses of clay, who have an earthly foundation, shall be consumed as by a moth?” (Job IV, 19).

Here by the angels of God are understood priests, who announce salvation to human beings; for *angelus* is interpreted “messenger.” Hear Malachi saying that a priest is called an angel: “The lips of the priest [Col. 0777C] preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II, 7). Secular people, however, are said to dwell in houses of clay because their bodies are wholly defiled by the mud of vices; and if the Lord finds perversity in his angels, how much more will those who dwell in houses of clay—namely secular people—be consumed as by the moth of vices.

A moth is born from a garment, and by gnawing it corrupts that very garment from which it is born. In the same way, the flesh is the garment of the soul. But this garment has its moth, because from the flesh itself is born the vice by which the flesh is continually torn. Priests therefore ought, by living well, to guard themselves lest by living badly they harm both themselves and others. [Col. 0777D] For if, through their negligent oversight or evil exhortation, the Lord’s sheep perish, it is fitting that they lose “eye for eye,” as is commanded in the Law (Lev. 24:20).

You ought to understand how, in the Church, an eye is given for an eye. A priest is the eye and overseer of the Church entrusted to him, lest the wolf tear apart the Lord’s sheep by sudden bites. But when, whether by preaching falsehood or by living badly, he corrupts [or: perverts] the eye of understanding of some simple and unlearned person, he too must lose his own eye—that is, the office of oversight—and is no longer permitted to be the eye of the Church. Therefore, let him cease to be the eye of others who has extinguished the eyes of those subject to him. For if anyone is ignorant and unlearned, he ought not to be troubled by false preaching, but should be turned toward better things or [Col. 0778A] instructed.

Hence it is written in the Law: “You shall not curse the deaf, nor place a stumbling-block before the blind” (Lev. 19:14). He curses the deaf who slanders one who is absent; he places a stumbling-block before the blind who, by preaching falsehood, causes a person who is ignorant and uninstructed to stumble. Hence elsewhere Moses says: “You shall not sow your field with diverse seed” (ibid., 19). The field is the Church of God, which preachers nourish with the seed of the word, as the Apostle says, for God’s subjects. He sows God’s field with diverse seed who mingles falsehood with truth in preaching.

Solomon describes in his Songs what kind of priests ought to be—how strong and how courageous in guarding the Lord’s field—when he says: “Sixty valiant men surround Solomon’s bed, of the bravest of Israel; all hold swords and are most skilled in [Col. 0778B] war. Each man’s sword is upon his thigh, on account of the terrors of the night” (Song 3:7).

The true Solomon is understood to be Christ, because he is indeed peaceable, he who reconciled his Father with all [men supplied], as the Apostle says: “While we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Rom. 5:10). Moreover, Solomon is interpreted “peaceable.” Solomon’s bed is the assembly of the faithful, in which the Lord dwells and rests. Sixty valiant men surround the bed—namely, the prelates and priests of the Church—who go about defending the city of the Lord and strive against vices and spiritual enemies. They are said to be sixty because they attain perfection in observing the Lord’s commandments.

Sixty is made up of six and [Col. 0778C] ten. Six signifies perfection, because God completed his works in six days and rested on the seventh. Ten signifies the ten commandments of the Law. Thus by the number sixty are understood those who are perfect in the present life. They are chosen from the bravest of Israel. All the faithful are called Israel, as those who see God; for Israel is interpreted “a man seeing God.” The bravest of Israel guard the Church by preaching and know how to defend it from the assault of demons and the attack of heretics.

It follows: “All holding swords,” that is, the spiritual word of God. God’s word is called a sword because, as a sword attacks enemies and cuts on both [Col. 0778D] sides, so too the word of God is set against spiritual enemies and at once cuts the vices of preacher and hearer. They are most valiant for wars because those who are to fight against spiritual enemies must be trained in the art of spiritual battle. It follows: “Each man’s sword is upon his thigh.” By the thigh are understood fleshly pleasures. Priests hold swords upon the thigh because they must not only defend those subject to them by the word of God, but likewise suppress the pleasures that rule within them. And all this is “on account of the terrors of the night,” that is, on account of the hidden snares of the malignant spirit, who lies in wait during the night of this age for the saints, especially those eminent in the Church, so that, when they have been deceived, he may defile [Col. 0779A] Solomon’s bed—that is, the repose of the saints.

## XCV [On Various Matters VIII]. A Synodal Address to Diocesan Pastors

[Note: [Col. 0779D] From Victorinus and Lyra. Perhaps from a synod.]

> “A certain man, going abroad, called his servants and entrusted his goods to them. To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one. Now he who had received five talents gained another five; and he who had received two, another two. But he who had received one went away, dug into the earth, and hid his master’s money” (Matt. 25:14).

This parable, dearest brothers, spoken by the Lord to his disciples, pertains not only to those who came before, but also to those who came after. For that man who went abroad [Col. 0779B] is our Redeemer, who, having assumed flesh in the world and left his servants here—that is, the apostles—went abroad when he ascended to the Father. Heaven was, as it were, foreign to him with respect to the flesh, whose native country is naturally earth. But in departing he did not wish his servants to remain idle; rather, he entrusted to them a treasure which they were to multiply through gain.

That treasure is spiritual gifts, of which the Apostle says: “We have a hidden treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7). And he entrusted to them five talents. The five talents signify knowledge of outward things, because external things are apprehended through the five senses. This gift particularly belongs to the active life, and the man multiplied what he had received. For there are some who, although they cannot understand [Col. 0779C] mystical things, nevertheless acquire what they can through outward knowledge and, by making progress both themselves and others, double the amount of the money entrusted [reading: “promised”]. Two, however, signify understanding and action. Some understand the subtle meaning of the Scriptures, and what they comprehend they communicate to others by word and example; thus they gain a doubled return from their undertaking. It is called doubled either because they benefit both themselves and others, or because they turn both servants to the Lord.

But the one who hides the single talent in the earth and does not double it by gaining represents the person who expends and entangles in earthly matters the ability received from God, seeks no spiritual profit, and does not lift his heart from earthly thoughts [Col. 0779D]. Of such persons it is said through the prophet: “They are wise to do evil, but they do not know how to do good” (Jer. 4:22).

You, dearest brothers, are those servants of the Lord to whom, entrusting the treasure of wisdom, he says: “Trade until I come” (Luke 19:13), so that you may render the interest on the money entrusted to you. Behold, the Lord’s sheep and the treasure of preaching have been entrusted to you, that you may multiply it among them. For the Lord did not wish his sheep to be in the desert of this world without pasture, lest they fail on the way. Hence he says in the Gospel: “I do not wish to send them away fasting, lest they fail on the way” (Mark 8:3). For people fail on this way of the present life unless they are refreshed with heavenly bread.

[Col. 0780A] Therefore the Church rejoices, saying: “The Lord guides me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me in a place of pasture” (Ps. 22:1). “In a place of pasture”—that is, in the holy Scriptures, which contain food for the soul—“he has placed me.” The Lord entrusted these pastures to you, that you might pasture his sheep from them.

But hear how the Lord complains through the prophet about the contemptible learning of shepherds: “When you shepherds drank the purest water, you troubled the rest with your feet; and my sheep fed on what had been trampled by your feet, and drank what your feet had troubled” (Ezek. 34:18). They drink the purest water when they draw the streams of truth through right understanding; but to disturb the water with their feet is to corrupt, by evil living, the pursuits of holy meditation [Col. 0780B]. The sheep drink water troubled by their feet when subjects do not follow the words they hear, but imitate only those examples of perversity that they desire. When they do not do what they say, the things which are perverted by their deeds, as though the fountains had been corrupted, become mud beneath their feet.

A shepherd ought to preach first by deed and then by voice. Hence it is said to him through the prophet: “Go up onto a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion” (Isa. 40:9). Ascend to the eminence of virtues before you proclaim anything to Zion—that is, to the Church.

The Lord willed that some should be set over others, although they were of one nature. For although he had begotten all human beings equal by nature, the fault of humanity, through the varying order of merits, placed some [Col. 0780C] above others. Yet that inequality [variant: diversity] which arose from vice is ordered by divine judgment, so that, because no one can stand equally with everyone else, one person may be ruled by another. Hence all who preside ought not to weigh within themselves the authority of their rank; remembering the equality of their condition, they should not rejoice in presiding but in being of service.

For our ancient Fathers are remembered not as kings of human beings but as shepherds of flocks. And when the Lord said to Noah and his sons, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth,” he immediately added: “Let your terror and dread be upon the animals of the earth” (Gen. 9:1). Yet rulers must necessarily be feared by their subjects when they discover that God is not feared by them, so that those who do not dread divine judgments may at least fear to sin [Col. 0780D] through human fear. Therefore those who exact fear from those living perversely rule, as it were, not human beings but animals.

When, therefore, a person is good, be his equal; when he sins, be willing to rule him. Thus Peter, prince of the Church, refused to be excessively venerated by Cornelius when he acted rightly, and acknowledged himself to be like him, saying: “Rise; do not do this, for I too am a human being” (Acts 10:16). But when he repeated [variant: rebuked] the crime of Ananias and Sapphira, he showed with what great power he stood above others.

Hence, as Truth teaches, the half-dead man is brought by the Samaritan’s care into an inn, and wine and oil are applied to his wounds, so that the wounds may be bitten by the wine and soothed by the oil [Col. 0781A]. For it is necessary for a shepherd sometimes to apply, through wine, the bite of pain, and through oil, the gentleness of compassion.

But I fear that what is said of you is this: that not only do you not rebuke vices, but even applaud them with your adulterous tongue; and you do not consider what is said through the prophet: “Woe to those who sew cushions beneath every elbow of the hand, and make pillows beneath the head of every age, to catch souls” (Ezek. 13:18). To sew cushions beneath every elbow of the hand is, by soft flattery, to cherish souls falling from their uprightness and reclining into love of this world. For an elbow is received, as it were, by a cushion, and the head by pillows, when the severity of correction is withheld from the sinner.

Paul says, “Insist seasonably”; he first set before it “unseasonably” (1 Tim. 4:2), because correction destroys itself in the hearer’s mind by its own worthlessness when the importunate person does not know how to find an occasion.

[Note: [Col. 0781D] Perhaps more clearly: “Insist seasonably, unseasonably.” He placed “seasonably” first and added “unseasonably,” because correction destroys itself in the hearer’s mind by its own severity when the importunate person does not know how to have or apply an occasion.]

Against those unwilling to rebuke, the prophet says: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56:10). They are dogs because they ought to keep watch around the Lord’s flock; but they cannot bark because, when the wolf comes, they flee or fall silent. Therefore he says: “You have not gone up against the enemy, nor set a wall for the house of Israel, that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezek. 13:5). To go up against the enemy is to oppose the powers of this world freely in voice for the flock’s defense; and to stand in battle on the Lord’s day is to resist those fighting wickedly out of love for [Col. 0781C] justice.

Therefore, although you ought to incorporate the wicked person into yourself, he instead makes you conform to his life. The common cry of all is: “The world is corrupt where it is wealthy.” Against such people the Psalmist says: “Do not envy evildoers, nor be jealous of those who commit iniquity, for they will quickly wither like hay and speedily fall like the green plants of herbs” (Ps. 36:1). Hear also what more grievous thing he threatens them: “For evildoers shall be destroyed, but those who wait for the Lord shall inherit the earth” (ibid., 9). And: “Yet a little while, and the sinner shall not be” (ibid., 10). You complain of riches; but hear what he says: “Better is a little to the just man than the many riches [Col. 0781D] of sinners” (ibid., 16). And Paul says: “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2:4).

For how much more intolerable it is if the leader of others falls than if a weak sheep strays [reading: “errs”]! Consider how great is the nobility to which you belong, of whom Peter says: “But you are an elect race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:9). If you are royal, you ought to rule. If priests, you ought to make yourselves pleasing offerings to the Lord and pray for the people’s sins, not increase those sins.

You indeed have been given two talents, as we have said; but hear what the master says to his servants [Col. 0782A] when he returns from his journey. He says alike to the servant returning five talents doubled and to the one returning two doubled: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your master” (Matt. 25:23). But the servant who was unwilling to work with his talent returns to the Lord with words of excuse, saying: “Lord, I know that you are hard: you reap where you have not sown, and gather where you have not scattered; and, being afraid, I went away and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours” (Matt. 15:24).

It should be noted that the useless servant calls his master hard, though he neglects to serve him for profit; and he says he feared to employ the talent for gain, though he ought only to have feared returning it to his master [Col. 0782B] without profit. There are many among the ministers of holy Church whom this servant represents: they fear to undertake the paths of a better life, yet do not fear to lie idle in the slothfulness of their body.

The master therefore says: “Wicked and slothful servant, you knew that I reap where I have not sown and gather where I have not scattered. You ought therefore to have given my money to the bankers, and, when I came, I should certainly have received what was mine with interest” (Matt. 25:26). The Lord is hard because he commands hard things. He reaps where he does not sow, because he exacts vengeance from the nations among whom God did not sow the Law. He also gathers some from those nations, where he did not scatter the seeds of the Law; they are constrained by his words, as though he were saying: If, in your judgment, I demand what [Col. 0782C] I did not give, how much more, he says, do I demand what I gave for distribution.

To give money to bankers is to expend the knowledge of preaching upon those who are able to put it into practice by works. The Lord therefore exacted this punishment from that servant, for he says: “Take the talent from him and give it to him who has ten talents” (ibid., 28). It seems more fitting that the talent taken away should be given to him who had less rather than to [the one] who had more—that is, to the one having two, not to the one having ten. But upon subtle consideration, it is more to have two—that is, understanding and action—than five, or knowledge of outward things. It is therefore fitting that he who has one talent—that is, understanding of the Scriptures—and neglects it while he is foolish in secular matters, should lose it by divine punishment [Col. 0782D]. And it often happens that one who serves faithfully in knowledge of outward things merits understanding of mystical matters.

It follows: “For to everyone who has, shall be given, and he shall abound; but from him who does not have, even what he seems to have shall be taken from him” (ibid., 29). Other spiritual gifts are given to one who has charity; but one who does not have charity loses even what he seemed to have received. For many who are wise and naturally keen, if they are slothful, lose nature’s good gift and the reward promised them. But it seems to pass to those who possess less by nature and acquire through industry [Col. 0783A]. Or, to one who has faith and good will, if he has little in deed, it will be given by the good Judge. But he who does not have faith, without which there are no virtues, loses even the virtues which he has naturally. Or, one who has love for the word is given understanding; but one who does not have charity loses every good thing he has.

A more grievous sentence follows: “And cast the useless servant into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 25:30). Therefore consider, dearest brothers, whether any of you buries the talent entrusted to him in the earth. Fear the coming Judge, who will settle accounts with you concerning the entrusted money. See that the slothful servant is condemnable, because he is condemned in the present and in the future is cast [variant: destroyed] into outer darkness. [Col. 0783B] Before his coming, let us keep watch concerning the account to be rendered, so that our Lord Jesus Christ may reward us in heaven with the other [variant: angels] as servants faithful in the money entrusted to us—he who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## XCVI [On Various Matters IX]. Against Simoniacs

[Note: [Col. 0783D] From Victorinus.]

> “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Any man of the seed of Aaron who is leprous … shall not eat of those things which have been sanctified” (Lev. 22:4). “Whoever is defiled with leprosy and is separated at the judgment of the priest shall have torn garments, an uncovered head, and a mouth covered with a garment; he shall cry out that he is polluted and unclean. Throughout the time during which he is leprous and unclean, he shall dwell alone [Col. 0783C] outside the camp” (Lev. 13:44).

I fear, dearest brothers, that this judgment may touch some of us. I fear that this leprosy may contaminate one of us. Lepers are commanded to keep themselves from things sanctified to the Lord; they are commanded to leave the camp. Who, then, are those whom leprosy contaminates, unless heretics, marked by the various colors of heretical perversity? There are also some in the Church whom simoniacal leprosy has seized.

All such persons are called simoniacs after Simon Magus, who attempted to purchase the gifts of the Holy Spirit with money (Acts 8). That Simon Magus has not yet died, because he still has many accomplices and imitators in the Church of God. Some purchase grades of ordination; others, by money, purchase the care [Col. 0783D] of souls and become shepherds of churches; others purchase fellowship among the canons. This kind of people must altogether be removed from those sanctified to the Lord—that is, from the body and blood of the Lord—and also outside the camp, that is, outside the Church. If, then, they must be removed from the sacraments, how dare they celebrate the sacraments? If they ought to leave the camp, how dare they dwell within the camp?

Yet there are some presumptuous persons conscious of this crime who display what they are not, because they wish to appear to be priests. But Gregory says: “Though not before human eyes, they are deprived of the priesthood before the eyes of God.” Behold, brothers, you are not priests if inwardly you are foul with this leprosy [Col. 0784A]. Nor are only those who buy to be cast out of the Church; much more those prelates who sell, to whom the Lord said: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. 10:8). Those who buy do not buy of their own desire, but because they cannot obtain it otherwise. Those who sell make simoniacal purchasers by refusing to give freely.

The Lord taught that all must be cast out of the Church not in word but in deed. For having entered the Temple, he made a whip of cords and drove out those selling doves, first overturning their seats (Matt. 21:12). Who are those who sell doves except those who receive money for the laying on of hands, and who sell the gifts of the Holy Spirit, signified by doves? First he overturns their seats, and afterwards [Col. 0784B] drives them from the Temple, because he commands that they first be deposed from the seat of their honor and then separated from the number of Catholics. Nor did he merely drive them out, but also scourged them, because the Lord not only condemns them in the present, by removing them from fellowship with others, but also torments them in the future, condemning them to eternal punishment.

But note what is said: “He shall have torn garments, an uncovered head, and a mouth covered with a garment.” His tunics ought to be torn, because everyone should know the plans concerning his error; all should know why they are expelled, and, seeing the punishment, should be afraid. His head is his mind and will, which rules the person as the head rules the body; it should be laid bare to all.
