But his mouth should be covered, lest he teach impieties further and lead others into the same error.

There is another kind of simony [Col. 0784C]: many sell sacraments and, abandoning baptisteries, confessions, and preaching, demand a price for burials. But those who sell the Mass make the body of the Lord a thing for sale and make themselves comparable to Judas. He betrayed [Christ] for thirty coins; these sell him for one. “A nation without counsel,” as Moses says, “and without prudence; would that they were wise and understood and foresaw their last things!” (Deut. 32:28). See clearly your last things in the end, because those whom the same fault binds, the same fault also constrains.

Because they demand a price for baptism and confession, they are comparable to Gehazi, Elisha’s disciple. For when Elisha had cleansed Naaman, prince of Syria, of leprosy by dipping him seven times in the river Jordan [Col. 0784D] (4 Kings 5), and the prince offered him gifts, the prophet refused them. But Gehazi, his disciple, ran after the departing prince without his master’s knowledge and sought a gift from him as if in his master’s name. When he returned and was convicted of the crime he had committed, the prophet said: “Because you have received silver from Naaman, Naaman’s leprosy shall cling to you and your seed.” And he went out from him leprous (4 Kings 5:26).

Naaman, cleansed of leprosy in the Jordan through sevenfold immersion, signifies the sinner baptized and cleansed from the leprosy of heretical perversity through sevenfold grace. Gehazi, however, signifies heretical priests who demand gifts for the sacrament of baptism [Col. 0785A] and are therefore condemned to leprosy, because Gehazi and his seed—that is, his followers, who are called Gehaziites—were condemned.

From this you may learn [variant: “you can say”] how grave a matter it is to demand a price for the sacrament of baptism. Concerning confession, however, there must be no doubt that payment is not to be sought. For the Lord commanded in the Law: “If your brother has become impoverished and weak of hand, and you receive him as a stranger and sojourner and he lives with you, do not take interest from him” (Lev. 25:35). That is: if some sinner has grown weak in good work and weak of hand—that is, in acting, through sin—and you receive him into your house—that is, into your protection—by preaching, exhorting, and giving penance, do not [Col. 0785B] demand monetary interest as payment.

“Whoever,” says Gregory, “preaches for the purpose of receiving here the reward either of praise or of a gift undoubtedly deprives himself of eternal reward.” Such a false preacher is called the Lord’s “dove-like woman” [variant: “concubine”] in the Songs, where it is said: “Solomon has sixty queens and eighty concubines” (Song 6:7).

The queens are teachers of the Church, who through the merit of faith and knowledge approach the bed of the eternal King and bear spiritual children to God. They are sixty because this number is formed from ten and six multiplied, signifying those who are perfect in the commandments of the Law. For six signifies perfection, because the Lord completed all things in six days. The concubines, however, are false preachers, who do not [Col. 0785C] preach him sincerely but for temporal gain. They are not wives because, although through their preaching they sometimes bear children to God, they do so not from will but for the advantage of earthly profit. They are rightly eighty, because the number eighty consists of ten multiplied by eight. The first four of the octad signify the four elements from which all earthly things are made; the second four, the four seasons of the year. Thus temporal earthly things are understood through eight.

Now, from Scripture: when Sarah, Abraham’s wife, had died, [Note: [Col. 0785D] This is taken from St Jerome’s *Book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, chapter 23, verse 16. It reads as follows: “And Abraham heard Ephron, and Abraham weighed out to Ephron the silver which he had spoken in the hearing of the sons of Heth.” In the Hebrew, as we have set it down here, his first name is written *Ephron*, the second *Ephran*. For after he had been overcome by the price, so as to sell the burial place for silver—although Abraham compelled him—the letter *vau*, which among them is read as *o*, was removed from his name; and instead of *Ephron* he was called *Ephran*. Scripture signifies that he was not a man of complete and perfect virtue, since he was able to sell memorial places for the dead. Therefore let those who sell graves, and are not compelled to receive a price but extort it even from unwilling persons, know that their name is changed and that something of their merit perishes, since even he who accepted against his will is secretly reproved. Thus St Jerome, *Book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis*. At this passage our Martianay observes that the readings are now likewise *Ephron*, [Hebrew uncertain in the source], and *Ephran*, [Hebrew uncertain in the source], without the letter *vav*, as they stood in the Hebrew exemplars of St Jerome.]

Abraham asked Ephron to sell him, for money received, a place of burial in which to bury his dead wife (Gen. 23). Ephron, however, did not wish to receive money for it, but to give the land freely. Yet, being compelled, he received it; and afterward he was called Ephran, though he had previously been called Ephron. Ephron is interpreted “strengthened” or “perfect”; Ephran, “weak” or “imperfect.” If, therefore, he who, although unwilling, could nevertheless in some way be induced [Col. 0786A] to accept payment for a burial was condemned by a change of name and called Ephran—that is, “imperfect”—what will be said of these persons, who are not compelled but freely demand it themselves? Will they not be condemned still more and numbered [variant: “announced”] among the imperfect?

All these things, dearest brothers, admonish you to refrain from this leprosy, lest, like those mentioned above, you incur the same condemnation. May he deign to avert this, he who lives and reigns as God for ages of ages. Amen.

## XCVII [On Various Matters X]. On the Excellence of the Church and the Christian Priesthood

[Note: [Col. 0786D] From manuscript Ebr. Peronianus 19, Victor. 272, Germ. 381.]

Isaiah, instructed by the Holy Spirit, says: “In the year [Col. 0786B] in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne; and the whole earth was full of his majesty, and those things which were beneath him filled the temple” (Isa. 6:1).

The sacred history teaches that Uzziah, king of Judah (2 Chron. 26:19), was struck with leprosy upon his forehead because, presumptuously assuming the priesthood, he offered unlawful incense. By nullifying the ceremonies of the Law, he defiled the Lord’s temple with the contagion of crimes, increasing the iniquity of evildoers by his example rather than condemning it by the Law. Therefore, while that leprous king lived, the Lord is said to have sat upon a high throne, because the Lord withdraws himself from those in whom sin reigns. “For what fellowship has Christ with Belial? Or what agreement has the temple of God with idols?” (2 Cor. 6:15). Truth [Col. 0786C] also says: “You cannot serve God and mammon” (Matt. 6:24).

Hence, too, when Judaea rejects the word of life, the disciples turn to the nations, knowing that Christ is not among those who were already carrying about Antichrist. But when the wicked king has died, the Lord sits upon the throne, because once sin dies in us, the Lord reigns in us and exercises rule in us. Hence, when Pharaoh had died and the people had departed from Egypt, “Judah became his sanctification” and “Israel his dominion” (Ps. 113:2).

Moreover, the throne upon which the Lord is shown sitting through the prophet is the Church of Christ Jesus our Savior; it is the hearts of the faithful. For the seat of the Lord is the soul of the just person. [Col. 0786D] In the soul of the just person the Lord dwells, rests, and reigns. Consider the Prophet speaking thus: “The Lord chose Zion; he chose it as a dwelling for himself” (Ps. 131:3). And the Lord himself: “Upon whom,” he says, “shall my Spirit rest, except upon the quiet and humble person, who trembles at my words?” (Ps. 66:2).

That seat King Uzziah indeed occupied for many days. For a long time he sat upon it in great pride. By Uzziah, whose name is interpreted “the strength of the Lord,” the prince of darkness is fittingly understood and the devil is aptly figured. For he is strong to assail unhappy souls; it is difficult for a human being to conquer him by human power. But the fact that he is strong belongs not to himself but to the Lord. For he has no power from himself, since even the fact that he is a spirit is from God, not from himself.

Of his strength the Gospel says: “When a strong man armed guards [Col. 0787A] his courtyard, all that he possesses is in peace” (Luke 11:21). This strong man armed therefore deceitfully ascended the Lord’s throne [Col. 0787B], sat proudly, and ruled as an extortioner. He deceived our first parents by cunning and conquered them by trickery, not by force—pretending counsel rather than bringing forth weapons. Those whom he could not subdue by violence he subjected to himself by fraud, reckoning it a glorious triumph to overcome children in their parents by whatever means.

He sat in great pride because he became so much more puffed up through victory in that he triumphed not over just any creature, but over the image and likeness of the Creator. He held dominion as an extortioner because, when he had subjected only two persons to himself, he extorted freedom from all their children. He reigned from tree to tree: from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil to the tree of the Cross; from the taste of the fruit, beautiful to look upon and sweet to eat, [Col. 0787C] to the bitterness of the Passion.

But when the fullness of time came, in which God sent his Son—by whom the Dayspring from on high visited us—the leprous Uzziah died: his strength was crushed and his power weakened. Then the head of the ancient serpent was crushed; then the hammer of the whole earth was broken; then the strong man armed, who guarded his courtyard, was conquered by the coming of one stronger than he. Then his weapons were taken from him. Then his spoils were distributed.

The Redeemer himself testifies to this, when, as the moment of his Passion drew near, he said: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John 12:31). Therefore, when this prince had been cast out and the extortioner of the world expelled from the Lord’s throne, the prophet sees the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne; he sees [Col. 0787D] the whole earth full of his majesty, and sees the temple filled by those things which were beneath him.

Pay close attention, brothers, to the fact that the Church of God is called a throne. Yet it is not called simply a throne, but, with an addition, a lofty throne; nor merely a lofty throne, but also an exalted throne. In this, so far as it appears to our smallness, the Church’s threefold height is declared. For the whole Church is a throne—that is, sublime and eminent—by the dignity of its foundation. The same Church is a lofty throne by the anointing of its priests; it is an exalted throne by the prerogative of its merits. Hear Paul saying: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11). Therefore the Church has no other foundation [Col. 0788A] than Christ Jesus. To be placed upon this foundation is to be baptized with Christ’s baptism. But when we are baptized with Christ’s baptism, we rise upon Christ’s throne; and not only upon Christ’s throne, but also into Christ’s temple. For then Christ begins both to preside over us [read: “and in us”] and to make his dwelling among us. We shall say something further. Then, together with Abraham, we receive three angels as guests, who promise our spirit that, from the subdued old flesh, formerly barren, Isaac shall be born—that is, laughter: not laughter mingled with pain, but that of which the Apostle says, “The fruit of the Spirit is joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, and the rest, against which there is no law” (Gal. 3:22). O truly splendid, truly sublime Church, which the foundation of faith [Col. 0788B] so raises up that it becomes both the Lord’s throne and his temple! Nor is it simply a throne, but, as we have recalled, a lofty throne also. This kind of loftiness belongs to priestly anointing. It shines forth in Christ’s Church—the light and sun of the Church—by Christ’s own testimony. It shines forth, I say, both in the administration of the sacraments and in watchfulness over souls. O new and divine power, through whose ministry the bread of angels is daily prepared for mortals! O rank to be professed with fear and trembling, whose pastoral charge over his sheep is deemed worthy not by a son of men, but by the Son of Man! O most lofty and distinguished throne, on which the prophet, as upon an exalted throne, sees seated the man whom the multitude of angels worships! He sees a man seated, I say, because he sees Christ seated; he sees [Col. 0788C] Christ ruling; he sees Christ now bearing the appearance of one reigning, now performing the office of one judging. For in these ministers of his Church Christ judges before the Judgment; before the final winnowing he winnows; before the net is filled, he gathers the good fish and casts the bad outside. He judges, not with the judgment of a civil court but of the Church; not earthly cases but heavenly ones; not bodies but souls. Likewise he winnows—he winnows, I say—because through these same ministers he casts the chaff of the wicked from the threshing-floor [read: *area*, not *aera*] of the Church by the winnowing-fan of discipline. He gathers the good fish and casts the bad outside. No one but Christ gathers fish; no one casts fish outside. Peter’s net is not yet full. It has not yet been drawn to shore. It will be filled and drawn to shore. But when these things shall happen, [Col. 0788D] the Son of Man confesses that he does not know; whence he himself says: “But of that day and hour no one knows, neither angel nor Son of Man, but the Father alone” (Mark 13:32). Yet meanwhile he gathers the good fish and casts the bad outside. But he does neither of these things by himself; through the ministers of the altar he does both every day. For from this great and wide sea, where creeping things without number dwell, he draws out good fish to be gathered and kept. He also draws out bad fish, to be thrown away and trampled by beasts. For he calls the just and gathers them to glory; he calls the unjust and appoints them to Gehenna.

O most exalted dignity, higher than every secular power, through which the Lord already accomplishes all these things! To what [Col. 0789A] kings does the Lord say: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14)? To whom, I say, does he say: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. 2:8)?

Not the tongues of emperors but those of priests have been made the keys of heaven. Priests alone, with Christ, open and no one shuts; they shut and no one opens. By the counsel of priests weak souls are helped, fetters are broken, the way to the heights lies open, earthly things are joined to heavenly, human beings to angels, and creation to the Creator. Great, therefore, is the honor—the honor of the priesthood. But grave is the danger attached to this honor. For this rank is a rank of hazard [read: *casualis*, “hazardous,” not *causalis*], unless the dignity of anointing is illumined by merits. A priest is then an effective intercessor when, acting officially for the guilty, he so acts as to move the Judge’s grace both by the merit of his life and [Col. 0789B] by the word of his teaching. These three things [read: “these two things”] make a priest perfect. From these three [and from these two] the priest receives both authority and grace. From anointing, indeed, the person receives authority to consecrate substances to be consecrated, and efficacy to bless substances to be blessed. But from life and teaching the priest earns the favor of his Lord and obtains the love of Christ his Savior. For on account of the example of living soberly, justly, and devoutly, and on account of the zeal to sow the seed of God’s word, the Lord says to the good and faithful servant: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I shall set you over much; enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. 25:22).

Now, most beloved brothers, it has now, unless we are mistaken, [Col. 0789C] become known to you why the throne of the Lord, which the prophet called lofty, he subsequently calls exalted also: namely, because of life and because of teaching—life, which holiness adorns; teaching, which charity embellishes. These are what raise a priest to heaven, by which he moves from mud-built houses to heavenly dwellings. These are to be preferred to all vows. These are more pleasing to the Lord than all sacrifices. If, perhaps, these are lacking, the priest’s throne is indeed lofty, but it is not yet an exalted throne. For God does not acknowledge a priest without holiness; the Law kills a priest without teaching. According to the Apostle’s testimony: “Without holiness no one shall ever see God” (Heb. 12:14). By the Law’s ordinance, the priest dies [Col. 0789D] who approaches the Holy of Holies without bells. Holiness does violence to God; it is more effective than every sacrifice in breaking heavenly indignation. At the sound of priestly trumpets the walls of Jericho fell, to show that at the Church’s preaching the height of secular pride must be brought low. Further, we believe that the priest is called by the prophet to the eminence of holiness when he says: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion” (Ps. 40:9). “Go up upon a mountain,” he says. Moses went up the mountain to receive the Lord’s Law. Luke records that Mary, having conceived God’s Son, immediately went into the hill-country. Christ is found both to have made a practice of praying in the mountains and to have been transfigured on a mountain. [Col. 0790A] Likewise, when he came to redeem humankind, though, as Pope Leo testifies, many means were available to him, he nevertheless chose, for our restoration, the ascent of the cross. These things surely show that the life of a priest ought to be lofty: he has become lawgiver to the Lord’s people; he preaches that what Mary bore in imitation must be borne; he undertakes to offer prayer for the guilty; he is to be transfigured in all people, for all people, so as to become all things to all; he declares that those who do not carry Christ’s cross cannot become Christ’s disciples. It is unworthy for a professor of so great an office to cling to earthly things. For the Lord wills that the minister of the altar resemble his profession and display lofty merit, consecrated to lofty offices. He wills him to walk in the Spirit, since he himself has subjected even [Col. 0790B] unclean spirits to him. Finally, he wills him to become a pure vessel, a clean vessel, because it is said of priests through the prophet: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52:11). Priests are those who bear the Lord’s vessels: that is, by carrying out priestly ministry, they bring faithful souls into the heavenly treasury. Hence those who carry the Lord’s vessels must themselves become vessels of the Lord—not clay vessels, but golden ones; not vessels for dishonor, but for honor; not vessels from which Belshazzar drinks with his concubines, but those from which the Redeemer drinks of the fruit of the vine with his disciples in his Father’s kingdom. That is, they must not be vessels in which the devil takes delight with those whom he has subjected to every shameful act and employs for every iniquity; [Col. 0790C] but vessels in which he who said to his disciples, “I am the vine; you are the branches” (John 15:5), may drink with them from the fruit of the vine—that is, rejoice and exult in the shedding of his blood, by which he has acquired for himself such precious vessels and brought the devil’s claims over them into his own power.

But sacred history teaches that priests advance into such vessels by observing three days. For Moses, speaking to Pharaoh at the Lord’s command, says: “We shall go a three days’ journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the Lord our God” (Exod. 5:3). Moses cannot sacrifice to the Lord in the wilderness, nor can the people, unless the journey of three days is first completed. That journey is faith, by which [Col. 0790D] one believes in the heart unto righteousness; confession, by which believers make profession unto salvation. This faith alone is the way by which one goes from earth to heaven, passes from Egypt into the land of promise, and by which the queen of the south comes from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom. Yet three stages must be made on this way; when these have been completed, a sacrifice pleasing to God will be offered. To cease from evil is the first stage; to do good is the second stage; to set the ascents in one’s heart is the third stage. Therefore whoever, believing in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, puts on God’s armor in order to stand against the devil’s snares, is on the way and makes the second stage. Whoever, believing in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, follows that blessed soul [Col. 0791A] of whom Solomon says in the Song of Songs, “Who is this who goes up through the wilderness like a column of smoke, from the spices of myrrh and frankincense?” (Song 3:6), is on the way and makes the third stage. A priest surely makes mention daily of such stages whenever, sacrificing to the Lord, he says:

> Therefore we, your servants, and also your holy people, mindful of the same Lord our Jesus Christ—of so blessed a Passion, likewise of his resurrection from the dead, and also of his glorious ascension into heaven—offer to your most excellent majesty, from your gifts and grants, a pure sacrifice, etc.

No one doubts that in the present passage the mitred priest recalls Christ’s death, resurrection, and ascension [Note: [Col. 0791D] That is, the bishop.]. This recollection is a saving recollection if, as Christ dies, the priest also dies to sin, crucifying his flesh with its vices and lusts; this is to make the first stage in the Catholic [Church supplied]. It is truly a saving recollection if, as Christ rises from the death of the flesh, the priest rises from the death of the spirit, putting on the new human being, who is created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth; this is to make the second stage in the Catholic Church. It is, I say, a saving recollection if, as Christ ascends to the Father, the priest ascends by Jacob’s ladder and sings with the prophet the song of ascents; this is to make the third stage in the Catholic Church. Behold, brothers, behold the way; to be outside it is to wander far from one’s homeland. Yet to be on it is not immediately to journey toward the homeland. “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:26). Therefore in a priest faith without work is a way without stages. Our adversary the devil often so delays those who have entered this way that they fail even at the first stage. For this enemy is he whom not even the Son of the Virgin passed by without being attacked. He is that enemy whose quiver is never exhausted [read: *exhauritur*], since he never ceases to draw missiles from it. He is that enemy who, although he cannot always injure, always wishes to do so. He is that enemy over whom victory is rare and never secure. If we engage him relying on our own strength, we yield to him [read: *cedimus*, not *credimus*], because a lion is stronger than sheep. If we hope to escape by flight, he easily overtakes us, because he is swifter than eagles. If we seek to deceive him, we are deceived, because he is craftier than serpents. Indeed, he is that serpent [Col. 0791D] which crawls on belly and breast, eats earth all the days of its life, and never ceases to lie in wait for the woman’s heel. He is that serpent which has infected all with its venom, except him who saw all beneath the fig tree. But we have as our advocate in heaven our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom victory over the serpent is promised us, rest from his assaults, and healing for our wounds. Let us therefore hasten to him with the whole intentness of our minds, for he is our refuge and strength; he is our helper in tribulations that have found us exceedingly. Let us humble our souls before him, because he has regarded the prayer of the humble [Col. 0792A] and has not despised their petition. Let us implore him with tears and groaning, that he may crush Satan beneath our feet; that he may not prevail against us on the way; that he may not oppose our saving stages until victory; that the minister of ancient uncleanness may not encrust vessels made for honor; and that leprous Uzziah may not again creep up onto the Lord’s throne. May Christ deign, in him, to hear his anointed ones and, in him, to administer the help of his grace. He lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## XCVIII [On Various Matters XI]. ON MAINTAINING PEACE IN THE CHURCH UNDER THE SUPREME PONTIFF, STEADFASTLY IN PERSECUTION

[Note: [Col. 0791D] From Victorinus and Lyra.]

> “There is no authority except from God; and those that are from God have been ordained. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13:1).

[Col. 0792B] Hear, dearest brothers, what the Apostle of the Lord cries out to us. Authorities, he says, whether of the world or of the Church, are not to be despised, because all are ordained by God; and whoever contradicts and resists those ordained by God insults the one who ordained them. Therefore we must visit our prelate, the lord pope, our counsellor, because he is a counsellor; we must venerate him because he is a shepherd. For the bishops of the Church must be venerated as teachers and as the Lord’s vicars. The Lord wished his priests to be so venerated and feared that in Deuteronomy he threatened, saying: “Any man who acts presumptuously, refusing to obey the priest or judge, shall die.” [Note: [Col. 0792D] Deut. 17:12. These are not the words but the sense.] Likewise, when Samuel was rejected by the Jews, God says: “They have not rejected you, [Col. 0792C] but me.” And the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Whoever hears you hears me, and him who sent me; and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). When he had cleansed the leper, he said: “Go, show yourself to the priest” (Matt. 8:4). And later, at the time of his Passion, when he had received a blow from the servant of the high priest, and the servant said to him, “Do you answer the high priest in this way?”, the Lord spoke nothing contemptuous and took nothing from the priest’s honor. Rather, maintaining and showing his innocence, he said: “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness concerning the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23). Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles, when the blessed Apostle Paul was told, “Do you revile God’s high priest?”—although in their time the Jewish priesthood had been destroyed when the Lord was crucified, and afterward had passed over to Christians alone—Paul nevertheless, reverencing even that empty title, said: “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest; for it is written: ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people’” (Acts 23:4).

Since, therefore, the old priesthood of the old Law was held in such authority that the Lord threatened death to those resisting it, what do you suppose are those who are enemies of the priesthood of the new Law and rebels against God’s Church, and are frightened neither by the threatening of the pre-eminent Lord nor by the vengeance of the coming Judgment [read: “neither by the threatening of the present Lord, nor by the vengeance of the coming Judgment”]? Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, who, contrary to the Law, Moses, and the priest, attempted to claim for themselves the right of offering sacrifice, immediately paid the penalty for their undertaking. For the earth opened a deep bosom as its joints parted, and the gap of the receding ground swallowed them alive as they stood. Yet the wrath of the indignant God did not strike those who had been the instigators; rather, fire coming forth from the Lord consumed the remaining two hundred [Note: [Col. 0793D] Num. 16:32 has two hundred and fifty.] participants in that crime [read: *sceleris*, “crime”], thereby proving the vengeance. Thus God warned and showed that their attempt, by human will, to overthrow [read: *evertendam*, not *eruendam*] an ordering established by God was an act against God. But King Uzziah too, when he carried a censer and violently usurped the offering of sacrifice against God’s Law, refused to obey the Church despite the resistance of the priest Zechariah; confounded by divine indignation, he was marked on his forehead by the discoloration of leprosy, branded in that part at which those who win God’s favor are marked.

Therefore, dearest brothers, care must be taken that no one dare rise up against God’s priests, lest the Lord choose severely to avenge those who act in his place. These men have been set [Col. 0793B] in the Church for our benefit [read: *utilitatem*, not *humilitatem*], that they may provide for us, render account to God for our salvation, and preserve the unity of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0793D] I would suspect this sermon to have been delivered by Hildebert when he was already Archbishop of Tours, on the occasion of the schism then dividing the Church into various parties because of the defective election of Peter Leo, or Anacletus. Gerard, that wicked Bishop of Angoulême—prominent through so many legations and councils held in Gaul, and at last punished by a miserable kind of death through divine retribution—was especially favorable to Anacletus. Indeed, Hildebert himself had initially adhered to Anacletus’s party, because he had learned that the greater number of votes favored him; but, amicably warned of the matter by St Bernard, he immediately passed over to Innocent II. To Innocent’s party Hildebert, as metropolitan of Tours, successfully drew the whole of Armorica with his suffragans and friendly primates. Yet this sermon could not implausibly be referred to about the year 1111, when Hildebert was still Bishop of Le Mans. About that year he wrote to a certain friend of his—perhaps Marbod, Bishop of Rennes—Letter XXII, Book II, in which he laments the extreme violence cruelly inflicted by Emperor Henry V upon the supreme pontiff Paschal II and the whole Roman clergy, in order to extort the right of lay investitures. In the following letter—also XXII of the same Book II—he excuses whatever Paschal himself, pressed by the entreaties of that Roman clergy, so shamefully imprisoned and harassed, had done in those straits. I ask that you consult those letters with the notes on pages 107 and 109. See also Baronius under the year 1111, where he narrates all these matters at length, including the revocation of that coerced concession by Paschal at the council convened shortly afterward for this purpose, where he also struck Henry himself with an anathema.]

God wished us to be concerned for this unity, lest, departing from the way or making schisms, we should be divided from the unity of faith by various [Col. 0793C] errors. For as there is one Lord and one shepherd, so he willed there to be one household and one flock. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “There shall be one flock and one Lord” (John 10:16). And in the old Law he said to Israel: “The Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4). That God is one he shows more plainly in the Gospel, saying: “I and the Father are one” (John 17:22). And again it is written concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: “And these three are one” (1 John 5:7). Therefore the Lord willed his own to be like himself: as he was one, so the Church should be one. Hence the Lord says to the Church in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one; my perfect one is one” (Song 6:8). The seamless tunic of the Lord figures this mystery of unity. Of it it is written [Col. 0793D] in the Gospel [Col. 0794A] that the soldiers who crucified him, because it was seamless from the upper part and woven throughout, said to one another: “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it, to see whose it shall be” (John 19:24). Christ’s garment was whole from its upper part because Christ’s Church receives from heaven—that is, from the Father and the Son—the unity and solid firmness of faith inseparably. The Lord did not wish his seamless garment to be torn, because he does not permit the unity of the Church to be violated. Paul therefore commanded concerning this unity: “I beseech you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing, and that there be no schisms among you” (1 Cor. 1:10). And again: “Preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond [Col. 0794B] of peace” (Eph. 4:3).

For just as the sun has many rays but one light; a tree many branches but one strength, established by a tenacious root; and though many streams flow from the same spring, and their number seems diffused by the abundance of overflowing plenty, unity is nevertheless preserved in the source: sever a ray from the sun, and unity does not admit a division of its light; break off a branch from a tree, and once broken it cannot bud; cut a stream off from its spring, and when cut off it dries up. So the Church of God, suffused with light, spreads its rays throughout the whole world; yet it is one light, diffused everywhere, and the unity of the body is not divided. It displays the branches of its fruitfulness throughout the earth, and broadly extends its plentifully flowing streams. There is one head and one source, and, through the harmonious increase of deity [possibly corrupt: *deitatis successibus*], it is abundant for the preservation of this unity.

Let us now consider the old Law. He who is slain as a figure of Christ is eaten in one house. The Lord commanded in the old Law, saying: “It shall be eaten in one house; none of its flesh shall be carried outside” (Exod. 13:46). You cannot cast Christ’s flesh and the Holy One of the Lord outside; nor is there any house for believers other than the one Church. The Holy Spirit designates and proclaims this house, this lodging-place of unity, in the Psalms, saying: “God, who makes those of one manner dwell in a house” (Ps. 67:7)—that is, those of one mind dwell in a house. In God’s house, that is, in the Church, those dwell unanimously who persevere in concord and simplicity.

Therefore, dearest brothers, to preserve this unity the Lord willed to build [Col. 0794D] his Church upon one person [Col. 0795A]—namely, upon him of whom he said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church; and to you I shall give the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven. And you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Matt. 16:18). Peter, therefore, is the foundation to which the Church is joined; for all the Church’s members adhere through his faith. For he became both teacher and prince of the apostles, and shepherd of the faithful, because he was pre-eminent in faith. When the Lord examined his followers about their faith, saying, “But who do you say that I am?”, Peter answered, as the stronger in faith: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid., v. 15). And, hearing the strength of his faith, the Lord granted him to be the foundation of his [Church supplied], [Col. 0795B] able to aspire to heaven. Therefore, when we are in danger, he must, once converted, strengthen us. For the Lord prayed for him that his faith might not fail.

Since, therefore, brothers, Peter is our teacher and his vicar is our lord, we ought to approach the shrines [read: *adire limina*, not *audire luminaria*] of the apostles, visit our lord the pope, and seek counsel from him, so that we may know how to steer the Lord’s Church safely amid the many and great waves of this world. For storms arise daily in God’s Church, because some wish to dissipate its unity and, by sowing discords, extinguish the union of peace. They attack the Church’s shepherds so that, once the head has been struck, the members may be shaken with terror. [Note: [Col. 0795D] Perhaps this refers to the disturbances stirred up by Emperors Henry IV and Henry V against Paschal II.] For the Church suffers not only from outsiders but also from its own household and brothers; and civil wars, against which one does not guard, are worse than foreign wars, which are foreseen. At the beginning [read: *initia*, not *invía*] of the world, a brother killed righteous Abel; his brother Esau pursued Jacob as he fled. Joseph was sold by his brothers, and the Lord was betrayed by a disciple. But it is no disgrace for us to suffer from brothers what Christ suffered; nor is it glory for them to do what Judas did. We do not fear their insults, by which they daily tear apart both themselves and his life [Note: [Col. 0795D] That is, Paschal II and his life. Note Hildebert’s zeal for ecclesiastical discipline.]; we do not dread the clubs, stones, and swords which they hurl with parricidal words. What shall we say of them? They are murderers before God; yet they cannot kill unless the Lord permits them to kill. And although we must die once, still they destroy us daily through their hatred, words, and sins. Yet we shall not for that reason be moved from the purpose of righteousness, because ecclesiastical discipline must not be abandoned through fear, nor priestly censure relaxed.

They are like their father, who, immediately after he had been created, rose up against [read: *erectus*, not *creatus*] his Creator and said: “I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I shall set my throne; I shall sit upon the mountain of the covenant, in the sides of the north; I shall ascend above the height of the clouds and shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 13:14). For those who trouble God’s priests ascend into heaven; they wish to rise above God’s stars and set their throne upon the mountain of the Covenant, because they wish to reign above bishops. Bishops, indeed, are the heavens, God’s stars, the mountain of the covenant, clouds, and the sides of the north. They are heavens because they contain God’s mysteries; hence David says: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:2). They are stars because the Lord says of them: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14). They are clouds because they moisten the minds [read: *mentes*, not *nubes*] of the faithful with the dew of preaching; of them it is said: “Who are these that fly like clouds?” (Isa. 60:8). They are [Col. 0796B] the sides of the north because they are neighbors to sinners who persist cold in sins; or because they offer their sides to endure the North Wind—that is, the devil—who brings the coldness of sin upon human beings. Of him it is said in the Song of Songs: “Arise, north wind; blow through my garden” (Song 4:16)—that is, test my Church, that through victory won over you it may receive glory. They are the mountain of the covenant because in them is the height of the knowledge of both Testaments.

But you who are children of the Church, defend the Church. Let no one deceive you with empty words. Christ’s Church cannot be made adulterous. She is incorrupt and chaste. He will not attain [read: *perveniet*, not *pertinet*] Christ’s rewards who abandons Christ’s bride. He can no longer have God as Father who does not have the Church as mother. Whoever wishes to divide the Church wishes to tear Christ’s garment. No good person abandons God’s Church or departs from God’s household. The true sheep, as the Lord says, know him, and he cries to all: “Whoever is not [Col. 0796C] with me is against me; and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11:13). The wind does not carry off wheat, nor does a storm overthrow a tree founded with a secure root. Empty chaff is tossed by the tempest; weak trees are overthrown by the attack of the whirlwind. May the children of God appear, so that their heavenly Father may reward them as they stand in faith, and so that in heaven, where there is one Lord, they may become one Church [Note: [Col. 0796D] Lyra: “one Church”; “that we may become one body.”] for ages of ages. Amen.

## XCIX [On Various Matters XII]. ON CHRIST’S SPLENDID BENEFITS TOWARD US

[Note: [Col. 0796D] From the Angevin source.]

> “Christ the Lord, the breath of our mouth, was taken in our sins; to him we said: ‘In your shadow we shall live among the nations’” (Lam. 4:20).

These are Jeremiah’s words in the Lamentations—or rather, the words of the Holy Spirit speaking in the prophet. In them the truth of both natures in Christ is expressed, and the surpassing greatness of divine charity toward us is commended. For when our Lord and Savior is called spirit, he is undoubtedly shown to be God. For God is spirit, as is truth [read: *veritas*, not *charitas*], “and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24): in spirit, that they may worship him with sincere affection and an unstained mind; and in truth, that they may ask from him not vain and passing but true and unfailing goods. But when “Christ” is added, he is shown to be true man; and when it is further said, “He was taken for our sins,” his extraordinary and ineffable love toward us is declared.

For Christ is called “anointed”: *Messias* in Hebrew, *Christos* in Greek, and in Latin *unctus*, “anointed,” from *chrisma*, the word for which Christ is called *Christus*—that is, “anointed from anointing.” For Greek *chrisma* is called *unctio*, “anointing,” in Latin. In the Old Testament kings and priests were anointed as a sign of this Anointed One, that is, Christ. By them was prefigured the true and spiritual [King and priest], who was anointed not with visible or bodily oil, but with the spiritual and intelligible fullness of the Holy Spirit, which was given to him without measure. To others it is indeed given by measure; but to him it was not given by measure: “in him the whole fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” (Col. 2:9), [Col. 0797B] that is, solidly and perfectly, not in shadow but truly, according to the saying: “Full of grace and truth, from whose fullness we have all received”—that is, “grace for grace” (John 1:14): certainly the grace of justification, and in exchange for it the grace of glorification; the grace of reconciliation, and in exchange for it the grace of eternal vision. For God crowns his own gifts in us and turns his grace into our merit. Hence eternal life is not only a reward for righteousness but is also called grace for grace. And therefore from that Anointed One, without measure, grace of anointing flowed out upon the members as from the head, according to the saying: “Like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard, Aaron’s beard, down to the hem of his garment” (Ps. 132:2).

Aaron, whose name is interpreted “dwelling of strength,” is Christ the Lord, who by the arm of his strength defeated the proud one and conquered the prince of the world, using power against him—not brazen weapons to extinguish the enemy’s darts. Above all, with the dagger of humility he pierced the vital parts of the proud enemy. In order to fulfill all humility, he loved us so greatly that he not only assumed for us a temporal birth, but also tasted the vinegar of the Passion and the salt of death. “For though he was in the form of God,” as the Apostle says, “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death upon a cross” (Phil. 2:8). O what a proof of love! What an experience of charity! [Col. 0797D] For through this, “God commends his charity toward us,” as the Apostle says, “because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us; justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him” (Rom. 5:8). The preceding prophetic utterance contains this.

He was taken, he says, in our sins—that is, on account of sins: not because our sins deserved his death, for even our good deeds do not suffice for that; but our sins and transgressions demanded his most holy death, our curse his blessing, so that the death of the Blessed One might undo the death of the cursed, according to Hosea: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your sting, O hell” (Hos. 13:14). And by his grace he might take away our offenses, [Col. 0798A] he who paid what he did not seize.

For Adam seized it, usurping the forbidden tree, transgressing the commandment, turning aside to the counsel of the ungodly, aspiring to become lord. But Christ alone offered himself as restoration for the Fall, as the price for the offender’s justification. Hence the Apostle says: “And you, when you were dead in transgressions, he made alive with Christ, granting you, that is, all your offenses; blotting out the bond of the decree which was against us; fastening it to the cross; stripping principalities and powers, he made a public display of them confidently, triumphing over them in himself” (Col. 2:14).

See how great is the fruit for us of Christ’s death: he forgave our sins and made us alive together with him; justifying us by faith, directing us by hope, kindling us by charity, lest any stain of vices defile our [Col. 0798B] hearts, so that we may now walk in newness of life. He removed the bond of the decree. The decree was the law imposed upon man in Paradise: namely, that he should not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. God gave this decree to man so that his obedience might be tested and, once shown, rewarded with the crown of eternity.

But man, though he was amid an abundance of riches, overflowing with the well-weighed riches of free choice [MS: *libertatis*, “of freedom”], yielding in proud exaltation to the devil’s persuasion, departed from God into the region of unlikeness; turning away from the good, he adhered to evil. The bond of that violated decree was the remembrance of that transgression, by which our consciousness [MS: *scientia*, “knowledge”] and the ancient enemy rose up for our accusation and condemnation. But Christ erased this through the cross and removed it from our midst, so that now neither our conscience [Col. 0798C] may fear nor the devil find anything to allege.

For our old man, according to the Apostle, was crucified with him: that is, the sin by which we were old was erased through his cross, so that the body of sin—that is, the mass of sins—might be destroyed, and sin might no longer rule in our mortal body. Though it is there, it has nevertheless lost its dominion through the mystery of the cross, lest through the consent of free choice it return to its own rule. Therefore let us beware lest we restore strength to the disarmed enemy, conquered in the trophy of the cross, by voluntarily turning aside from evil [MS: *ad malum*, “toward evil”].

Christ himself also stripped the infernal principalities and powers, when the stronger one descended into the house of the strong man, [Col. 0798D] bound him, and plundered his goods: Christ, that is, who is strong and mighty above all, entered the devil’s house—that is, hell, where stands the dwelling of the prince of darkness. It was not his own strength but human sins that made him strong; yet one stronger, becoming man, came upon him and bound him, diminishing his power, confidently and publicly triumphing over him in himself—that is, in the presence of his majesty—and plundered his goods. That is, he brought forth from there the righteous, who by God’s sentence descended to the lower regions until the debt was discharged; he overthrew the house and stripped hell. Feeling the might and power of him who descended to hell with angelic legions, the princes of darkness cried out: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. 23:8).

The powers going before [Col. 0799A] Christ answered them: “The Lord, strong in deeds, and mighty in all that he wills, mighty in battle” (Ps. 23:8), where he fought against your prince, conquering him under the banner of the cross. For when blood without fault was shed, the bonds of all faults were erased—those by which debtors who believe in him had formerly been held by the devil. Hence the Gospel says: “Which shall be poured out for many” (Matt. 26:28). Therefore, stripping the infernal principalities and powers, he brought away others whom he had formerly held—namely, he led his own far from that kingdom to another, that is, to heaven: “Ascending on high,” as the Prophet says, “he led captivity captive” (Ps. 67:19), so that those whom the devil had miserably captured and made captives of hell, Christ might happily capture.

[Col. 0799B] These are the spoils of triumph which Christ the victor, having subdued them, took from the princes of darkness. Hence he says through the Prophet: “I shall rejoice like one who finds great spoil” (Ps. 118:62). See how God’s charity is commended to us in these things: he valued us so highly that for us he gave his only-begotten Son over to death. Though he was “in the form of God,” that is, in full essence and in equality with the Father, “he emptied himself.” How? Not by emptying out his substance or changing the form of God, but by “taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2). The form of a servant was added; the form of God did not depart.

To commend humility more greatly, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father for the sake of others—not only enduring insults and reproaches, blows and spittle, but [Col. 0799C] even unto death. How great a humility! The God of glory humbled himself unto incarnation, unto participation in mortality, unto the people’s mockery, unto spittle and bonds and blows and scourges, unto death. And, if this is too little, the kind of death must be added: not just any death, but death on a cross, which is more ignominious.

See, we have an example of humility, a remedy for pride. See perfect obedience, supreme charity, great humility. The Most High chose to undertake these things by lofty counsel for our benefit, not from any necessity of his own. Two things are wondrous: namely, the manner of his emptying and its fruit, which was not simple or slight but manifold and supreme. The manner [Col. 0799D] of emptying was threefold: the Son of God descended to flesh, to the cross, and to death. At this heaven is astounded, earth marvels, man trembles, and the angelic height reveres. A work without example; humility without measure; a gift without price; grace without merit.

And the Most High wished to be joined to us, that we might be enriched; to be humbled, that we might be exalted. His every action is our instruction [MS: *locutio*, “speech”]; Christ’s life is for us a rule of living; Christ’s death is our redemption and deliverance from death. Christ’s life instructed ours; Christ’s death destroyed ours. For our sake Christ deigned to be water thirsting, [Col. 0800A] bread who for us became way, truth, and life. The way is in the example, truth in the promise, life in the reward.

Therefore you who hear, attend diligently; embrace sweetly; faithfully lay up what is set before you concerning the heir [MS: *haerili*, perhaps “of the heir”], the only-begotten Son of the highest Father. For in such an account there is no lack of things to move hearts, penetrate minds, soothe souls, and kindle them to love the Savior. For it was not without reason that he chose to redeem us with such great difficulty, though he who sustains all things by the word of his power could have delivered us by command alone. But the Lord saw the greatness of human malice and considered humanity’s ingratitude. Therefore, lest the human being who had proved ungrateful for the first condition should also make little of Redemption, Wisdom procured it amid much difficulty [Col. 0800B] and bitterness [MS: *procreavit*, “brought forth”].

For he who is the Father’s Wisdom, the blessedness and life of heavenly spirits, did not disdain, in response to our defect and the increase of wickedness, to assume the role of one at a loss (*aporians*), as Isaiah says: “The Lord saw, and evil appeared in his eyes; and he saw that there was no man, and he was at a loss because there was none to meet him” (Ps. 59:15).

Attend, brothers, to the manner of this seeing and the reason for this being at a loss. For he is said to have seen our evil, though all things are naked and open to his eyes; he is said to have been at a loss, though no motion of change can occur in him, with whom, as James testifies, “there is no change nor shadow of turning.” In that ineffable [Col. 0800C] simplicity of his unbounded [Note: He says the same in the *Prose*.] and wholly ubiquitous essence, there is no local change, because “he reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8); enclosed by none of all things, excluded from none of all things. Nor is there alteration by temporal change.

For just as he is not varied by local motion, so neither is he altered by a succession of affections, as though sadness succeeded joy in him, or tranquility anger, and the like. Through the prophet Hosea he says: “I am God and do not change, and I shall not enter into the city.” [Note: “I am God and not man; the Holy One in your midst, and I shall not enter into the city” (Hos. 11:9).] Or there is no change in him in essence, nor any shadow of alternation in his works, as though he did some things well and others badly. For as he himself is always good and never evil, so he always performs good works [Col. 0800D] and never evil ones.

Nevertheless, the prophet says that he was at a loss and saw evil. For all our things are open to him, of whom the Apostle says: “The word of God is living and effective, and more penetrating than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit; and no creature is invisible in his sight” (Heb. 4:12). This Word is not vocal but substantial, abiding rather than passing. This is the Word who was in the beginning with God the Father, the splendor of his glory and the image of his substance; coeternal with the Father, as brightness is with fire, and coequal [MS: *coaequus*], glorifying and [Col. 0801A] making the Father known, as a ray does the sun—yet distinct from him in person, just as an image differs from, or is distinguished from, that of which it is the image.

This Word, then, is truly living, because he is life itself and gives life to all things. He is life, in whom being, living, and living well are not different things; rather, what is his essence is his life, and that same thing is his blessedness. Everything in him is one: it is life; it is light. Therefore he who is, is life giving life to all, because through him all things were made, and everything made through him was life in him.

Thus this Word is living and effective, that is, able to do what he wills; and therefore he can condemn or save if he wills. And, being powerful, he is also wise, because he is more penetrating, sharper, and more discerning than every two-edged sword—that is, than every carnal [Col. 0801B] or spiritual intelligence. For the mind of a human being is a two-edged sword, of which the prophet says: “The human heart is deep [Vulgate: perverse] and unsearchable; who shall know it?” (Jer. 17:9).

And he reaches, by ineffable knowledge, even to the division of soul and spirit—that is, of sensuality and reason. For he knows how sensuality is divided from reason, and how it is divided within itself, when, devoted to many things, it is lower and given to lower realities, or, recalled from these, is more worthy. He sees also how reason itself is divided within itself: when it longs for God, when below it contemplates heavenly things, or when on earth it considers how worldly matters ought rightly to be conducted. He sees also how it is distinguished from sensuality, when it surpasses what is lower than itself, that which is higher in it [Col. 0801C] [Note: Something appears to be missing here, e.g. “looks up,” or “marvels.”] [lacuna]

Therefore the Word of God sees where sensuality ends in the soul and where reason begins; and, to speak generally, no creature is invisible to him. For he sees all things because he created all things. Hence he says through Jeremiah: “Do you suppose that I am a God at hand and not a God afar off? If a man hides himself in secret places, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth, says the Lord?” (Jer. 23:23–24).

This is the well of living waters, bearing the name “of the Seeing and Living One.” Hence in Genesis: “Isaac was walking along the way leading to the well whose name is that of the Seeing and Living One; for he dwelt in the southern land” (Gen. 24:62). To one who is granted to dwell in this land, in which the hot wind—that is, the Spirit of truth—blows, belongs a loftier way, [Col. 0801D] leading to the well whose name is sight—that is, charity—which leads to the vision of the Seeing and Living One.

Of this he says through Jeremiah: “This people has committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves old cisterns which cannot contain living waters” (Isa. 2:13). Therefore the Lord, living and seeing, sees all things, and evil appeared in his eyes.

God is said to see in many ways. He sees by knowing, as he sees all things; he sees by approving, as he looks upon the humble; he sees in order to punish, as he looked upon Sodom; he sees in order to have mercy, as he looked upon the affliction of his people in Egypt. Thus he sees [Col. 0802A] our evil, not approving it or newly coming to know it, but in order to punish or have mercy. For he who strikes also heals, as he himself says: “I shall kill and I shall make alive; I shall strike and I shall heal” (Deut. 32:39).

He first struck in justice; then he healed by mercy. The justice of the avenger came first; the compassion of the merciful one followed, according to the saying: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” (Hab. 3:2). Therefore he mercifully saw our evil, not to condemn us but to cleanse us from it; and he saw that there was no man, namely, one who did not need his glory. “For all have sinned,” says the Apostle, “and need the glory of God” (Rom. 1:23)—that is, the mercy through which God appears glorious.

Thus he sees that there is no man sufficient to himself, [Col. 0802B] either for righteousness or for salvation, because no one can give satisfaction for himself or another except Christ. Hence the Prophet: “A brother does not redeem; shall a man redeem?” (Ps. 48:8). For if the brother—that is, Christ, who is the firstborn among many brethren—does not redeem, then another man will redeem [MS: *non redimet alius homo*, “no other man will redeem”], because another “will not give his own ransom and the price of redemption for his soul” (ibid.).

For the sin of the human race was so great that it could not be forgiven through another victim, unless the only-begotten Son of God died for us who were debtors to death. Therefore the Word of God was at a loss—that is, he was grieved—because there was none to meet him. That is, he assumed sadness, not in his divinity but in his humanity; not from a necessity [Col. 0802C] of his condition but by the will of his mercy. For there was no angel or human being to meet God the Father by giving satisfaction, that is, by offering the price of redemption.

Therefore the Lion from the tribe of Judah was at a loss; for he assumed our sadness as he assumed our flesh. For he was sad who says in the Gospel: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38). He who assumed true human nature did not disdain to assume its proper attributes.

Therefore he was truly at a loss [that is, made weak], according to human nature, to whom Jeremiah says: “He shall be like a settler in the land, and like a traveler turning aside to lodge” (Jer. 14:8). For he was seen on earth and conversed [Col. 0802D] with men; yet he did not dwell there as a citizen, but passed through as a traveler tending toward the city of his dwelling. For he did not stand in the way of sinners, but “rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6). He turned away from prosperity, exposed himself to adversity, fled even the kingdom of this world, and went to meet death, because his kingdom is not of this world.

He became like a wandering man who cannot save, as though he had no certainty of place or word. He seemed unstable in local dwelling, for he had nowhere to lay his head; he was also thought inconstant in word, since he seemed to teach contrary things. For he who had said, “Unless you eat my flesh [Col. 0803A] and drink my blood, you shall not have life in you” (John 6:54), himself also said: “You will not eat this body which you see, nor drink that blood which those who crucify me will shed.” [Note: Perhaps the Catholic reader will hesitate at these words and wonder that Hildebert, so Catholic and so learned in Sacred Scripture, reports as Christ’s own words statements which do not in fact appear to be his in the Gospel text, and from which recent heterodox thinkers might at first sight seem able to derive an occasion for defending their errors concerning the holy Eucharist.

Yet if they are considered more attentively, as St Augustine himself reported these very words and explained them [Col. 0803C] in Psalm 98, they in no way appear to derogate from the wholly orthodox doctrine of the real presence of Christ’s body and blood in the holy Eucharist—a doctrine which Hildebert always held, asserted, and defended with all his strength, as though for altars and hearths. This may indeed be proved from almost countless passages in his sermons and other smaller works.

For example, in Sermon 35, the second sermon for the Lord’s Supper, he says: “Bread and wine are indeed seen, but it is the flesh of Christ who hung for us upon the cross, and the blood which was shed for us for the remission of sins.” There also he rebukes the stupidity and unbelief of the Capharnaite people, who, imagining that Christ would cut off certain pieces from his body and give them to them, went back, saying: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?”

He likewise affirms this in Sermon 38, the fifth sermon for the Lord’s Supper, p. 422, where, setting forth his doctrine at length concerning the holy Eucharist, he concludes thus: “We ought not to doubt [Col. 0803D] that through the sacred words of the priest’s blessing bread is changed into the TRUE body of the Lord, so that the SUBSTANCE of bread does not remain; but Christ willed the color and taste of bread to remain, and under that appearance the TRUE SUBSTANCE OF HIS BODY to be hidden, lest, if it appeared in the quality IN WHICH IT TRULY IS, the human mind should shrink from receiving the TRUE man.”

Likewise, in Sermon 54, on the Feast of the Most Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist, p. 495: “Between Christ’s hands and words bread becomes Christ’s flesh; it becomes the food of the soul . . . Do not, brothers, do not ask how this happens; do not doubt whether it happens . . . He who bears witness that bread truly becomes his flesh is God and man . . . Christian, understand the same concerning wine; honor the same in wine. The Creator of wine is he who transforms wine into blood.”

We offer a few testimonies from among many—indeed, very few from among Hildebert’s almost innumerable testimonies concerning the real existence of Christ’s body and blood—so as to remove from the reader’s mind even the slightest [Col. 0804B] stain of heterodoxy from this most learned man. To assert this doctrine he published whole treatises, in prose and verse, which the fair-minded reader will find below; and he was the first to use the word TRANSUBSTANTIATION to establish that divine and real transformation of bread and wine into Christ’s true body and blood. Only after him, being almost a century later, did Peter of Blois (Sermon 84 and elsewhere) and Stephen of Autun use it—men whom some learned scholars regarded as its first authors.

Moreover, whoever reads more attentively the outstanding treatise which he expressly published on the sacrament of the altar will surely agree with us that nothing more forceful, explicit, or learned can be read among the works of orthodox writers for excluding the fiction of a mere figure from the holy Eucharist and establishing there the reality of Christ’s body and blood. For throughout he uses words proving this, such as: “Not only in his spirit, but also in his flesh.” Again: “The body which is with us and in heaven is also with us in different places, upon different altars, not at different times.” Again: “Nor is it a phantom body, but a true one—not only in the sacrament, but also in itself.” Again: “Therefore it is there bodily, because of the true nature of the body.”

So, when in the same treatise he discusses the presence of Christ’s body in different places, he says that beneath each particle the body remains whole and immeasurable; and [Col. 0804D] therefore, although the sacrament is divided into parts, the body is nevertheless not cut into parts. Finally, in this treatise he expounds so clearly everything concerning the circumstances of the reality of Christ’s body that, even if he had published this alone, it would be more than sufficient to remove from him the stain of any error whatsoever.

Far then from the fair reader’s mind be even the lightest suspicion concerning Hildebert’s faith. He reported the foregoing words in order to raise an objection against himself, which he immediately resolves in an Augustinian sense and almost in the very words of the holy doctor. Nor should our modern innovators derive anything more from those words in defense of their error than they can from St Augustine’s own doctrine, which they have always hitherto sought in vain to misuse.]

Yet, rightly understood, these statements in no way contradict one another. For when he says, “Unless you eat the flesh,” and so forth, he speaks of spiritual flesh, which no one receives unjustly, no one receives unto death, and no one eats unless he is good. Of this he says: “Why do you prepare tooth and belly? Believe, and you have eaten.” [Note: The very words of St Augustine, *Tractate XXV on John*, v. 57.]

Therefore to eat this flesh spiritually is to remain in him and believe in him, as he himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (ibid., 36). For he eats spiritually who remains in the unity of [Col. 0803B] Christ and of the Church, which the sacrament itself signifies. But one who is at discord with Christ does not eat Christ’s mystical flesh or drink his blood, even though he daily receives the sacrament of so great a thing unto judgment.

But where he says, “You will not eat this body which you see,” and so forth, he speaks of sacramental eating, because both the good and the evil receive Christ’s body and blood; [Col. 0804A] but the former well, the latter badly: the good unto life, the evil unto judgment. For one who receives the Lord’s body unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, because he does not discern the Lord’s body (1 Cor. 11); that is, he does not distinguish it from other foods, but receives it indiscriminately and negligently, failing to show the singular veneration due to it, though one must approach its communion with the greatest devotion.

For this is the heavenly manna, the bread of angels, on which angels feed with great nourishment, archangels are satisfied, and into which the exalted powers desire to look. Therefore, with minds purified and judging ourselves, let us eat of that bread and drink of the cup. For if we presume to approach without judging ourselves, we shall be judged by the Lord.

For whoever receives unworthily shall be guilty of the body and [Col. 0804B] blood of the Lord. A terrible sentence! For he shall pay the penalties of Christ’s death, because he shall be punished as though he himself had slain him who for our sake became like “a wandering man who cannot save” (Jer. 14). Since he was not rescued from the cross, the faithless considered him unable to save. Hence they said in mockery: “He saved others; himself he cannot save” [Col. 0805A] (Matt. 27:42).

Thus they deemed him the lowest of men and like a leper—that is, defiled by sins and struck by God for his own sins. But he was wounded because of our iniquities; he was bruised because of our crimes; for us he became a curse, that he might free us from the curse. The Lord laid upon him the iniquities of us all—that is, the penalties of our iniquities—and he bore the sins of many, as Isaiah says (ch. 53), and prayed for transgressors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). At this utterance, according to the Gospel of the Nazarenes, [Note: Observe the Gospel of the Nazarenes.] many thousands of Jews standing around the cross believed.

For he who saved others was not powerless to save himself. Nor was it folly or shame for him that he himself was not heard when he was heard for others. But do not be disturbed if we say that he was not heard for himself, since he himself said through the Prophet: “I shall cry by day and by night, and you will not hear” (Ps. 21:2). Christ cried by day—that is, in the light of virtues, since no darkness of vices [Col. 0805B] was in him—and by night, that is, in the distress of his Passion, saying: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:35). That is: if there is another victim through whom redemption can be accomplished, let the Passion pass from me, which is called a cup because a pleasing victim is a drink-offering.

“For he was offered,” as Isaiah says, “because he himself willed it” (John [sic], 53:7). But if there is no other victim through whom man can be redeemed, let your will be done, not mine: that is, let the will [Col. 0805C] of our divinity be fulfilled, not the will of my humanity; let the will of my reason be done, not the will of my sensuality.

When he had thus prayed, he was not heard, namely as regards bodily salvation. For he himself says: “And you will not hear” (Hab. 1); but the Apostle says that “he was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5:7). Does the disciple then contradict the Master? The one says, “You will not hear”; the other, “He was heard.” But Truth speaks truth, and the disciple of Truth does not lie. He was not heard so that he might not die, but he was heard so that he might rise. In this he was heard, and not in that; and the fact that he was not heard in that is no folly in him.

Indeed it appears folly; it appears altogether foreign to God. It is accounted foolishness by Gentiles and a stumbling block to Jews. Hence Isaiah: “His work is foreign, that he may perform his work; his work is strange to him” (Isa. 28:21). For it appears foreign that God should suffer, and exceedingly strange that God should die. He came indeed to do his work—that is, to redeem the human race—but the work is foreign to him, because it does not befit divinity to be scourged, spat upon, and crucified.

That he was not heard, but was crucified and buried, was no folly in him; rather, it was wisdom, so that he might thus wisely redeem the human race. Thus the crafty and proud enemy was conquered, and the world was delivered. The price having been given, the captives were redeemed: Jews and Gentiles. [Col. 0806A] The price was immense, but the acquisition great. Hence Isaiah: “He shall give the ungodly for his burial, and the rich for his death” (Isa. 53:9). The ungodly, that is, the Gentiles, who were without *theosebia*—that is, without the piety of divine worship—and the rich, that is, the Jews who gloried in the riches of the Law and the Prophets, he shall give to his Father for his death and burial—that is, through death and burial.

See what a manner of being at a loss—that is, of examination—and how great a fruit: namely, the release of captives and the preparation of the kingdom, that is, grace and glory prepared by God for humanity amid great distress and difficulty, so that the unprecedented difficulty of restoration might render beholden the person whom the ease of the first condition had made ungrateful.

For Christ the Lord, the spirit of your mouth, was taken in sins. He is called both Spirit and Christ, and the truth of both natures is shown in him. For he is the giant of double substance and of twofold nature, from eternal generation. Spirit from temporal spirit. Christ indeed is simply called Spirit, but “of our mouth” is added because we must believe in him and confess him. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. To him we said: “In your shadow [Col. 0806B] we shall live.”

The shadow of Christ is grace, through which he becomes for us shade and refreshment: inwardly, against the law of the members; outwardly, against the heat of tribulations, according to the saying: “You overshadowed my head in the day of battle” (Ps. 139:8). And elsewhere: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Ps. 16:8). This is the shadow of the juniper, [Col. 0806C] under which the bridegroom rests with the bride. Concerning it the angel says to Mary: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

The prophetic man desired to be refreshed by this shadow, saying: “Forgive me, that I may be refreshed before I depart and be no more” (Ps. 38:14). It is as though he said: “I suffer heat; I burn with the incentives of sins. But by forgiving me, refresh me before I depart from this life, because if you do not forgive me, I shall indeed depart, but shall no longer be in true being.” This shadow is good and salutary, because, driving away harmful things, it grants true being.

Therefore, refreshed and restored by this shadow, we shall live—not with mortal or temporal life, but with immortal and everlasting life. May the merciful Lord grant this to us. Amen.

C [Various Matters XIII]. ON CHRIST AS THE RESTORER OF HUMAN SALVATION AFTER ADAM’S FALL. [Note: E, Eberbach manuscript 19.]

[Col. 0806D]

“Sing to the Lord a new song, because he has done wondrous things” (Ps. 97:1).

The Prophet urges us to sing to the Lord a song of praise, not an old song but a new one: not that by which Israel was told through Moses, “You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy” (Matt. 5:43), but that by which Christ instructs us in these words: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (ibid. 5:44). Such a song he demands from us—he who has wrought wonders for us.

[Col. 0807A] God is wonderful in his saints, because he is wonderful in all his works. Yet he is more wonderful in himself, because he has wrought more wonderful things concerning himself. For he, though God, became man. By the death of the Lord the slave was made alive; the prince of this world was cast out. Behold the wonders of the Lord God. Behold the benefits of his salvation. All his other wonders yield place to these, since his mercies are above all his works.

That we may speak somewhat more fully concerning these matters, let each of you speak to the Lord in prayer; let all speak together. Perhaps it will be granted us to speak about the Lord and in the Lord, so that someone may profit, even if not all profit. Therefore let every person attend: God was made man for us. O great and ineffable mystery!

[Col. 0807B] O grace by which, as Leo testifies, [Note: [Col. 0807D] St Leo, Sermon I, On the Nativity of the Lord.] the saint draws near to the palm of victory, the sinner is invited to pardon, and the Gentile is called to life! By this earthly things are united to heavenly, temporal things to eternal, human things to divine.

By this grace the woman lit a lamp and sought the drachma which she had lost; having sought it, she found it; and, having found it, she summoned her friends and neighbours, saying to them: “Rejoice with me, all of you, because I have found the drachma which I had lost” (Luke 15:9). For from the grace of righteousness the sun shone forth from the lantern of our flesh, so that the Wisdom which created all things might diligently seek, as with a lamp kindled, its drachma: our nature, brought by him and with him into destruction, to which it had consented in sin.

At its discovery the powers of heaven and the angelic authorities rejoiced together, according to what is said by the mouth of Truth: “There is joy in heaven before the angels of God over one sinner doing penance” (Luke 7:10).

[Col. 0807C] O the one advancement of humankind, to which God did not begrudge God! O supremely happy being, at whose formation the joy of angels overflows! Let man therefore rejoice with the angels—indeed, even above the angels. For when God was made a little lower than the angels, man was exalted above the angels. Let him rejoice, I say, and sing the new song, having advanced from the old man to the new man.

Behold, brothers, the first division of our subject has been briefly set forth: the unmixed and undivided union of God and man. Unless I am mistaken, you await the second part of the proposition we have undertaken.

[Col. 0807D] From your silence we discern your desire. This, surely, if you recall it well, is as follows. A certain householder had one only slave, but a stubborn and wicked slave. He fell into illness; he sought a physician and did not find one. In his parents there was a cause which, as though by hereditary right, had left sickness to the son. The sickness was coeval with the slave, born with the slave, and growing with the slave. Consequently it was all the more difficult to cure, the nearer to him it was in origin, the longer in time, and the more numerous in kind.

Indeed, the bed of the sick man itself showed how great this illness was.

[Col. 0808A] The bed was so foul and filthy that even the slave himself recoiled from seeing it; it was so decayed with excretions that it could scarcely support the one lying upon it. For when necessity pressed, it was impossible for him to leave it; yet to lie longer among filth and worms was unbearable. Harsh was the condition of the bed, which avenged its own injuries with injuries of its own! Miserable were the straits of the man lying there, whose life, without funeral rites, was itself a funeral!

Days upon days and years upon years passed, and there was no one to care for him; no physician sat beside him who could help him. O wonderful love of the Lord for his slave! His Lord remembered mercy. He entered the house, but in the whole house no corner free from stench was found. The slave was rotting in filth, yet not even so did the Lord despise him.

[Col. 0808B] In order to speak more familiarly with his slave, he did not shrink from entering the bed; then, gently embracing him, he asked to be recognized. Alas for sorrow! The slave did not recognize the Lord when he came nearer; he did not understand when he saw him lying in the same bed. When he said, “I am your Lord,” the slave spat in his face. When he added, “I know the remedy,” he laughed at him. He turned away his hearing when the Lord prescribed [variant: “set forth beforehand”] a healing regimen for him; he recoiled from service when the Lord uncovered the flowing discharge.
