Finally, he gave no thanks when the Lord promised to make him whole from sick, sound from infirm, a co-heir from a stranger, and free from a slave. Yet the Lord neither grew angry at the insults nor turned away from one who turned from him. The bed was indeed burdensome to him, but without complaint he bore what was burdensome in the bed.

[Col. 0808C] Its squalor was grievous and its stench severe, yet willingly and freely he endured both. These and the other discomforts of the bed were, however, so hard that their severity caused the Lord to breathe out his spirit. But the breath that attended the departing spirit was so sweet and pleasant that its fragrance restored health to the sick man.

O wondrous kind of illness, O wondrous kind of medicine! The Lord suffers compassionately through love and dies; the slave is bathed in the breath of the dying one and is healed. To the fullness of the benefit was added not only the freedom of the slave, confirmed by the Lord’s death, but also the sharing of the inheritance with the sons.

Attend, brothers, attend to what mystical meaning this our illustration bears. Know, then, that the entire posterity of the first-created man is designated by the name “slave.” “For everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34).—“But if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

[Col. 0808D] Since every human being is with sin, every human being is a slave of sin. Such a slave fell into hereditary sickness because the first parent inflicted the wound of death upon his descendants. That wound is the wound of the soul: the wound by which its soundness was shaken off, mortality imposed, and freedom taken away. This soul, dying, does not die; diminished, it is not diminished; consumed, it is not consumed. It lay hidden in the fig tree, came down from the fig tree, and passed into all, except him who saw all beneath the fig tree.

[Col. 0809A] Hear the Apostle saying: “Through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death” (Rom. 5:12). That one man was Adam, who transmitted death to all through sin. If you ask what sin was, it was a transgression of obedience; if death, it was the loss of grace. Man had received the command not to touch the tree entrusted to him; he touched it and remained a transgressor of the command; he ate, and was deprived of God’s grace. For the Creator, finding him a despiser of the command, judged him unworthy of grace. But for grace to be absent from the soul is for life also to be absent.

This is the illness through which every soul lay prostrate for so long, by which it drenched its bed with manifold filth. Its bed is the dwelling-place of its flesh. Concerning this bed John, speaking figuratively of Jezebel in the Apocalypse, says: “Behold, I will cast her upon a bed, and those who commit adultery with her” (Rev. 2:22).

[Col. 0809B] O unhappy bed, upon which the punishment of transgression still rages! For both the consenting spirit and the flesh that ate lost grace alike. Accordingly, a sentence was pronounced against it to which not even the end sets an end. Under this sentence we are all born, to be punished even in the grave.

Consider the miseries of the flesh; attend to the ashes: they are the tribute of sin. The tribute of sin is that we fail from hunger and thirst, that we fall into the affliction of diseases, that by countless deaths we come to death. I speak of small things: filth also infects the bed, and its stench spreads farther and wider.

[Col. 0809C] The filth of the bed is the sins of the flesh; and the sins of the flesh are fornication and impurity, gluttony and drunkenness, and other things of this kind. Of these it is said through the prophet: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1:17). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “For from the heart proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies” (Matt. 15:19).

The stench of such things is spread far and wide, because the whole world lies in the evil one. The whole world reeks with examples of wickedness; with Lazarus it is wholly four days dead. Certainly all these things followed the transgression of the first man. For all the sins that we commit are filth derived from filth. But from what filth, except that of which Scripture says: “No one is clean from filth, not even an infant whose life upon the earth is one day” [Note: [Col. 0809D] Job 14:4. It is cited in nearly this form by St Cyprian, *Testimonies*, Book III, no. 54.]?

[Col. 0809D] The human race, infected by this filth, found no one to wash it. Neither human merits, nor angelic administration, nor the sacrifices of the Law extinguished the Creator’s indignation kindled by it. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “No one was able, neither in heaven nor on earth nor beneath the earth, to open the book or to look upon it” (Rev. 5:3). And through Isaiah the Lord speaks these words: “What is the multitude of your victims to me? I am full. The burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fatlings, and the blood of calves and goats I have not desired” (Isa. 1:11).

Through the Psalmist, too, the Son says to the Father: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire”; and then he adds:

[Col. 0810A] “Burnt offering and sin offering you did not require. Then I said: Behold, I come, to do your will, my God; I have desired it,” etc. (Ps. 39:7–8). Now his will was that his Son should die for the slave. Therefore the Lord stooped into the house of the slave, because the Maker of the world descended into the world; because the salvation of our God came to save that which had perished.

The Lord stooped, I say, because he who committed no sin was made sin for us—that Holy One of holy ones. He stooped, because the Creator of angels was made a little lower than the angels. This was fitting for the remedies to be applied: the physician had to appear visible to the sick person in order to be seen by the sick person. It was fitting that he who was to have compassion on the sick should show himself capable of suffering to the sick.

[Col. 0810B] Therefore the Lord entered the bed of the slave, because the King of kings and Lord of lords clothed himself with true human flesh. For, that the invisible God might be seen by us and that the immortal one might die at our hands [for us], “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

This Word, veiled by the flesh which he assumed from us, bore in that assumed flesh our hardships, carrying our sins in the flesh without the sinfulness of flesh. In it rest laboured, sufficiency lacked, light grew dark, soundness was weakened, morals were punished, loftiness was bowed down. Finally, in it was fulfilled what Isaiah said concerning this Word: “God sent the Word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel” (Isa. 9:8).

[Col. 0810C] The Word was sent into Jacob because the Word was incarnate from the house of Jacob for the house of Jacob [variant: “for the house of Israel”]. Hence Truth itself says: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). And Paul, reproving the blindness of the Jews, says: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be preached to you; but since you have rejected it, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

For they rejected it. Indeed, the Word sent into Jacob fell upon Israel because it was held cheap and reckoned by Israel as nothing and emptiness. When I say Israel, I mean the Pharisees and scribes; I have in view the teachers of the Law and the chief priests. They boasted that they possessed knowledge of the Law, were accustomed to converse with angels, were true Israelites, and saw the God of gods in Zion.

[Col. 0810D] Yet denser darkness covered them than covered Egypt on their account. “For they did not believe in God, nor did they hope in his salvation” (Ps. 77:22). Their own wickedness blinded them: they groped at noon and alienated the Holy One of Israel, who strove to draw them from the pit of misery and the mire of dregs.

The price of the whole world was held cheap among them. The creature rebelled against the Creator; the disciple was ashamed of the teacher; the sick man detested the physician; the accused assailed the advocate; the vessel rebuked the potter; the hungry person disdained bread; the muddy person recoiled from the fountain; the abject person rejected glory; the buried person rejected resurrection.

He healed the sick, and concerning one doing good works it was said: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John 9:16).

[Col. 0811A] He commanded demons, and to blaspheme him they cried: “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Luke 11:15). He raised the dead, and amid these very tokens of divinity the cross was prepared [variant: “carried out”] for him: “Let us put wood into his bread, and let us root him out from the land of the living” (Jer. 11:19).

Then, covered [variant: “overwhelmed”] with spittle and sentenced to the spectacle of the cross, he expired amid the insults which he endured for the slave. But from the condition of the dying one such a gentle fragrance breathed upon the languishing slave that, when he was bathed in it, health was restored to him.

O blessed and healing breath, by whose drawing the slave’s life [variant: “way”] was restored, freedom bestowed, and the inheritance shared with the sons! By this breath understand the divinity of Christ to be signified. Hence Job says: “My wife recoiled from my breath” (Job 19:17).

[Col. 0811B] For Judaea recoiled from the divinity in Christ, detesting peace [variant: “prayer”] with God in Christ. For this reason she slandered her benefactor; for this reason she hurled stones at him; for this reason she also cried: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19:7).

By this divinity it came about that the Son’s sacrifice was acceptable to God the Father, lest the mediator between God and humankind should plead in vain for guilt—he in whom the nature of God and of man was without guilt. By these two natures your transgression, O man, received a writ of pardon; from glory, shame; from freedom, slavery; banishment from a homeland; death from life.

By their personal union was made the eye-salve that wiped away the darkness of the man born blind. By them arose that oil, at whose presence the yoke of the oppressor decayed. By them Jacob’s ladder was set up, by which you may now ascend to the fellowship of angels.

[Col. 0811C] By them the sword was removed from paradise, so that you may return—even late—to paradise, eat, and live forever. Finally, by them the prince of this world was cast out, thereafter to exercise no authority over the children of adoption, unless someone voluntarily subjects himself to him.

Therefore let man give thanks to the Man-God, because he is the one who endowed him with participation in divinity, who broke the yoke of his slavery, who opened his closed eyes: Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## CI [On Various Matters XIV]. Against the Jews: On the Incarnation

[Note: [Col. 0811D] From the Évreux manuscript, no. 19.]

[Col. 0811D]

I perceive, dearest brothers, I perceive with that Wise Man who says: “More pleasant is the fruit which longer hope brings forth.” Therefore the fruit of divine converse with humankind ought to be all the more delightful to us, the longer its expectation was, the more wonderful its manifestation, the sweeter its experience, and the greater its benefit.

Messengers were sent beforehand, to proclaim the most holy converse, invite people to it, promise rewards to those who would come, and eternal punishment to those unwilling to come. These were the prophets, who are known not only to have taught that converse beforehand in words, but also to have prefigured it in deeds.

[Col. 0812A] Thus Moses says: “The Lord will raise up a prophet from among you, like me; listen to him” (Deut. 18:15). And Isaiah: “Behold,” he says, “a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:34).

Scripture records that the prophecy of this aforesaid converse occurred in the actions of certain persons. Thus Jeremiah prophesies when stripped naked; David when he bears himself in his own hands; Daniel when cast into the lions’ den; Hosea when he takes a prostitute as wife; Jonah when he is held for three days and three nights in the belly of the whale.

The Apostle, both briefly noting that these prophecies had come beforehand and showing that the converse had been fulfilled in Christ, writes to the Hebrews:

[Col. 0812B] “God, who in many portions and in many ways formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us in the Son” (Heb. 1:1).

“He has spoken to us in the Son,” he says, because he has spoken to us in Christ. How did God speak to us, being invisible and unknown to us? That he might be seen and known by us, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The Word of God, the Son of God, was seen by us in flesh; in flesh he spoke with us about us.

He spoke concerning the reconciliation of man with angels, his placement among angels, and his advancement above angels. He spoke, I say, concerning the change of our dissimilarity into his likeness, our shame into his glory, and our death into his life.

[Col. 0812C] Concerning all these things the Creator of all had, before all ages, counsel with himself, and in time he held converse with man. To reveal that secret counsel, two angels were sent into the world: one to disclose the counsel, the other to fulfil what had been disclosed. One was to announce to the Virgin Mary that our mediator would be born from Mary a virgin; the other, in flesh taken from the Virgin, was to declare our advocate.

Moreover, that mediator and advocate of ours was born for us today, as Isaiah promised us: “A child [little child],” he says, “is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6). A child, he says, is born; and this child is God and man. God and man carried out the business of the aforesaid counsel.

Let no one lack faith when virginity in the mother is proclaimed. Both events indeed occurred against nature, but for nature; both are works of grace, yet a service to nature. Both are new, yet promised by oracle. Both are benefits, yet of differing use.

[Col. 0812D] For modesty in the Mother is the glory of the person; the divinity of the Son is the advancement of nature. Modesty was preserved in the Mother, to testify that her Son is Man-God. Divinity was united to man, to unite to God those who believe in the Man-God.

Let the unhappy Jew blush; let the more unhappy Helvidius be confounded. The Jew detracts from Christ’s divinity; both detract from the perpetual virginity of Christ’s mother. The Jew rages when it is said: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

[Col. 0813A] He likewise turns away his ear when he hears: “Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14); and in Ezekiel: “This gate which you see shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, but it shall remain shut forever” (Ezek. 44:2).

This gate is our Virgin, yet a gate closed forever. She is a gate because through her Christ entered the world, yet through one closed forever. Well closed forever, because closed before childbirth, closed in childbirth, and closed after childbirth. Away with the unbelief of the Jew, who fables that Christ was conceived by Joseph. Away with the filth of Helvidius, who prates that children were born to the Virgin after Christ’s birth.

But our discourse is still with you, O Jew. For the face of Moses is still veiled among you; the radiance of your own Law has not yet shone upon you, nor the mysteries of the prophets. Denser darkness covers you than covered the Egyptians on your account. Riches abound for you, yet you are tortured by want. A more nourishing meal is set before you, yet you waste away from hunger.

[Col. 0813B] You carry grain in the ear, yet you have not tasted, nor known, how sweet it is. David’s young men, passing through the fields, rubbed ears of grain and ate; the priests of the temple broke and ate the loaves of the presentation. Rub, then, the ear of the Law; break the barley of the Law, and you will find the fine wheat of the Law. For beneath choking chaff you will find satisfying marrow; beneath the killing letter, the life-giving Spirit.

Open the cisterns, the wells of the prophets, O Jew, and David’s spring, leaping up with water unto eternal life, will meet you. But you, wretch, stop up the veins of clearest water; with the Philistines you fill in the wells dug by Isaac’s children. For you oppose smoke when the brightness of the Law is made clear to you. You mock the grace of God when it is declared that the Virgin Mary conceived as a virgin and gave birth as a virgin.

[Col. 0813C] In the patriarchs and their children you hear of works of grace and believe, reverence, and extol them; but in the Creator of the prophets, why do you embrace nature in such a way as to persecute grace? Sarah bore a son to Abraham when sterility and old age had taken from them all hope of offspring (Gen. 17). You cannot deny, O Jew, that Sarah owed Isaac more to promise than to marriage, and more to grace than to nature.

Before Moses, the bush that was seen burning suffered no harm from the fire (Exod. 3). You cannot deny, O Jew, that this work belonged more to the sign than to the bush, and more to grace than to nature. Israel thirsted in the wilderness and impatiently endured the distress of thirst; Moses came to the rock, struck it twice, and abundant waters came forth, so that the people and their beasts drank. You cannot deny, O Jew, that this work belonged more to the sign than to the stone, and more to grace than to nature.

I shall speak of something plain. I think few are ignorant of the stone called crystal. This stone is of a most brilliant and white colour.

[Col. 0813D] It is commonly said that, when it is sprinkled with water and then placed beneath the burning sun, it emits sparks. Yet these sparks leave no fissure in the stone, no traces of something issuing from it. In the crystal the same integrity and the same brightness remain. Something comes forth from it useful for human needs, so that it surpasses the stone’s brightness; yet, if sun or water be lacking, it is not found capable of emitting fire.

But when both come together, something is produced from both at once in the crystal which fittingly images the Virgin’s conception and birth. For to what can the most holy Virgin more rightly be compared than to crystal, in whom, as though to crown the fullness of her other virtues, the brightness of perpetual virginity shone forth?

[Col. 0814A] She, being prepared for the divine mysteries, is, as it were, sprinkled with water, about to receive a greater grace: that she might wonderfully receive the Son of God as God, and yet more wonderfully bring forth that same one as Man-God. For it seems less alien to nature that a Virgin should be filled with heavenly power than that true human substance should proceed from a virgin.

But perhaps, O Jew, you wonder by what water I have said that the Virgin was sprinkled. By water understand the Holy Spirit. Concerning such water the Lord spoke through Joel: “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Joel 2:28). And through Ezekiel: “I will pour,” he says, “clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” (Ezek. 26:25).

[Col. 0814B] When the Virgin is sprinkled with this water, she is invisibly prepared to receive the Sun of righteousness. She is prepared, I say, because the Holy Spirit protected her by overshadowing her from every heat of fleshly desire. Hence this was added to the increase and fullness of grace in our Virgin: that the Son of God, about to enter her, might find her “purified from another’s guilt” and free from her own.

For Wisdom could not enter a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins (Wis. 1:4).

## CII [On Various Matters XV]. On the Book of Life

[Note: [Col. 0813D] From the Angers and Saint-Victor manuscripts.]

“Hear, Israel, the commandments of life, and write them in your heart, and I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey” (Deut. 4:1).

Brothers, you ought to attend carefully to these words. What I have set before you are not my words but the Lord’s. I offer them to you not as their inventor, but [Col. 0814D] relate them as a messenger. In their sequence three things are proposed to us by the Lord: first, by what name we are called; second, what we are bound to do; third, what we obtain first [variant: what reward we obtain].

First, therefore, we ought to consider the honour of the name we have received. We are called Christians. What could be fairer or more honourable for a human being than to be distinguished by the name of his Creator? If we share in his name, let us also share in the reality. For one who says that he is a Christian ought to walk as Christ walked; and thus we shall be truly Israel.

[Col. 0815A] Israel is interpreted “one who sees God,” which without doubt will be attained by those who imitate Christ. But how can this be, that we may deserve to see God, when we cannot perceive even souls or angels, and when Scripture says: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18), and the Lord says to Moses: “Man shall not see me and live” (Exod. 33:20)?

For this reason it should be known that a human being has outward eyes, which are those of the body, and inward eyes, which are those of the mind. With these spiritual eyes it belongs to the true Christian to see God: here, while we are on the way, through faith; but in the homeland, face to face. Here he is contemplated from afar in a riddle; there he will be known as he is in reality, and this is eternal life. “For this is eternal life: that they may know you, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

[Col. 0815B] How we ought to follow him he himself declares to us, saying: “Hear, Israel, the commandments of life.” It is as if he said: “O Christian, who sees God through faith, hear the commandments of life, by observing which you are preserved for eternity.” But because the human mind easily forgets what it hears, whereas things committed to writing are retained longer because Scripture calls them back to memory, the Lord adds: “And write them.”

Perhaps you will say in reply: “We, who have not learned letters and do not know how to write, how can we write?” Open your ears [variant: “turn your ears”]; I shall explain both how you may know how to write a book and how to read in it—a book which you can always have with you without any burden, and by whose teaching you will be wise as soon as you can possess it. It is more precious than gold, and you can have it without a penny or an obol.

[Col. 0815C] You know what a scribe commonly does. First, with a scraper he begins to cleanse parchment of grease and remove large stains; then with pumice he rubs away completely its hairs and sinews. If he did not do this, lettering placed upon it would neither take nor endure long. Afterwards he applies a ruling-line, so that he can preserve order in writing.

You too must do all these things if you wish to possess the book which I have set before you. The parchment of this book will be your heart, as you have from the Lord’s words, if you consider what follows. For after he said, “Write them,” he added, “in your heart,” thereby plainly declaring that our heart is to be the parchment for receiving God’s commandments. It must first be cleansed, and its stains removed with the sharp edge of a cutting scraper.

[Col. 0815D] Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). The Prophet likewise asks: “Create a clean heart in me, O God” (Ps. 50:12). The scraper of the heart is repentance, through which crimes are removed. It consists in three things: contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction in deed. It is indeed burdensome and laborious to beginners, but sweet and not burdensome to those who love. Hence: “My yoke is sweet, and my burden light” (Matt. 11:30).

But some of you, because you do not desire a clean heart, always wish to plead an excuse when some act of satisfaction is imposed upon you. You say, “How can I fast when others are eating?”

[Col. 0816A] Yet perhaps you can sin while others abstain. Or, if someone is commanded in satisfaction to give to the poor, they say that their resources do not suffice for so many alms—though nothing seems lacking to them for doing evil. For such people the Lord’s yoke is not light, because they neither love nor desire to have a clean heart. Therefore no good can endure long in such people.

After this cleansing, with the pumice of prayers and alms, the hairs—that is, venial sins—must be removed: sins consisting in excessive laughter, excess of food, delight in stories or gossip. All of these, if turned to habitual use, are grave sins. Beyond this, a ruling-line must be applied to our heart, and thus we can preserve order in writing.

Some of us have a crooked heart.

[Col. 0816B] When they prosper, they praise God; of such it is said: “He will praise you when you have done him good” (Ps. 48:19). But when some adversity occurs, they blaspheme, saying that God is not just, that the Lord’s way is not just, and that he is not kind—though, on the contrary, he appears exceedingly good to the upright. Hence the Prophet says: “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright of heart!” (Ps. 72:1).

Therefore, in order that God may always be just to us, whether in adversity or prosperity, we must apply to our heart the ruling-line—that is, the lives of the holy Fathers—by which we may govern ourselves, imitating them: the life of that athlete, the good Job, and of many others, such as Paul, Martin, and Lawrence. Let us consider that a father corrects the son whom he loves.

Have, then, an upright heart, blessing the Lord in all things. Know that, if he has sent you adversity, it is for correction on account of sin; if prosperity, it is so that you may give to others [and perform works of mercy].

[Col. 0816C] Therefore always say with the Prophet: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth.—Rejoice in the Lord and exult, O righteous, and glory, all you upright in heart” (Ps. 33:1; 31:11).

When, therefore, you have your heart prepared, nothing remains but for me to teach you what to write. On the first leaf and the first line write: “Your God, God is one” (Deut. 6:4); that is, believe in the almighty Father and love him. On the second line of the same leaf write: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (Exod. 20:7); that is, believe that the Son is in no respect less than the Father in divinity, but equal to the Father, and love him.

[Col. 0816D] For whoever believes that the Father has a Son less than himself dishonours the Father, as though he begrudged, or lacked the power, to beget a Son equal to himself. Thus he also forbids us to believe concerning the Son what ought not to be believed concerning himself, and to swear falsely or swear idly, which is a great sin.

On the third line of the same leaf write: “Keep the Sabbath day”; that is, believe in the Holy Spirit, because he is our rest and consolation, both in the present, as on the way, and in the future, as in the homeland. For Sabbath is interpreted “rest,” by which we understand the Holy Spirit. He is said to be observed by the person who does not offend him.

Behold, on this first leaf are written matters which properly belong to love of God, and the Trinity is expressed here. On the second leaf write matters which belong to love of neighbour. The first of these is: “Honour your father and mother” (Exod. 20:12), not merely by showing them respect in words, but by providing them with necessities or ministering to them.

[Col. 0817A] But we do not show the reverence we ought or provide necessities; instead, we strip them of their possessions, while

> The son, before his father’s day, inquires into his years.

Yet the reward is appended when it is said: “That you may be long-lived upon the earth” (ibid.): not only in the land of the dying, where we plainly see many good things bestowed upon those who love their parents, but also in the land of the living, where no end is awaited and they shall be rewarded with eternal goods.

This is called the land of the dying, because no one comes into it who will not die or is not already dead.

[Col. 0817B] But how can those love strangers who despise their own, who, to omit other considerations, are their flesh and blood? It follows: “You shall not kill” (ibid., 13), by which homicide both of body and soul is forbidden. For there can be killings of a person by deed and by will, even while he lives and walks with me; and killing of the soul by the corruption of example alone, when we lead our neighbour into the error of evil.

The sixth commandment of God is: “You shall not commit adultery” (ibid., 14), where every unlawful sexual union is forbidden. For every sexual union other than that with a lawful wife is unlawful and a grave sin, although even in that union there can be excess and sin.

The seventh is: “You shall not steal” (ibid., 15), in which every robbery, every theft, and every kind of usury is forbidden. For who ought more rightly to be called thief and robber than one who, while I sleep and while I wake, secretly takes and carries off what is mine—not merely now, but continually?

[Col. 0817C] The eighth is: “You shall not bear false testimony” (ibid., 16). Here lying and perjury are forbidden. The ninth is: “You shall not desire your neighbour’s wife” (ibid., 17), where desire for another’s wife is forbidden.

But had he not said this above when the Lord prohibited adultery? Yes; but there the act is forbidden, whereas here the will is forbidden: “For if anyone sees a woman in order to desire her, he has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:18).

The tenth commandment follows: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property—neither slave nor maidservant, [Col. 0817D] nor anything that belongs to him” (ibid.); by it are forbidden not only robbery and theft, but also greed and the desire to possess what belongs to another. See what God commands you to write; once all these things have been written in your heart, it is necessary to keep this book secure, lest any enemy be allowed to inspect it, or to erase it by casting filth upon it, or to inscribe in their place other things contrary to them [variant: “write over them”]. For our adversary the devil always lies in wait for us; and, so far as he can, he erases these things and writes their opposites—namely, criminal sins. For each of these commandments has a different contrary.

The contrary to the first commandment is stealthy insinuation: the mind is insinuated away by vain thoughts [Col. 0818A] so that it abandons truth and adheres to falsehood, following the falsehood of idols; to the second, error; to the third, love of the world; to the fourth, impiety; to the fifth, cruelty; to the sixth, fornication; to the seventh, rapacity; to the eighth, falsehood; to the ninth, adultery; to the tenth, covetousness. These are the devil’s things. Therefore know for certain: if you find any of these in your heart, it is not God’s commandment but rather the devil’s.

We ought therefore to fit this book with a lock—namely, God’s grace against the enemy’s cunning—736 grace which is at hand for all who hope in Him [variant: “prepare themselves for Him”]. Once this has been acquired, deception, about to establish itself, flees far away; it at once forces its way in when grace departs. You will possess this book and be able to read in it everywhere, even with closed eyes.

If you seek the reward with which [Col. 0818B] those who write this book in their heart and obey these commandments of the Lord will be rewarded, hear the Lord, who deceives no one and never will, and whose every utterance is true: “I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey.” That land is excellent, in which you will find streams flowing with milk and honey. But what is meant by the phrase “flowing with milk and honey”? By milk, which comes from an animal’s flesh and blood and is white and nourishing to the body, is understood the brightness and glorification of our flesh. For then our bodies will shine like the sun. By honey, however, which is sweet to those who taste it and is made from dew sent down from heaven and flowers, is understood the blessedness of our heavenly souls. Thus that land is the heavenly homeland, where we shall be wholly blessed, in body and soul alike, receiving [Col. 0818C] the twofold robe: namely, agility, immortality, radiance, and impassibility of the body, and the full knowledge of God [supplied: “in the soul”], which God has promised to those who love Him. May our Lord Jesus Christ Himself deign to lead us to it, He who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## CIII [On Various Matters XVI]. TO PASTORS: ON PREACHING THE DIVINE WORD

[Note: [Col. 0817D] From the manuscript of Saint-Germain, no. 383.]

> “Let ravens from the torrents gouge out the eye that mocks its father and despises its mother’s bearing, and let the young of the eagle devour it” (Prov. 30:17).

You will find, [most beloved brothers, in the holy Scriptures,] varied and wondrous flowers by which the Lord’s sheep may be fed, [Col. 0818D] and faithful souls refreshed with delightful, spiritual nourishment. You will have an abundant supply both for healing sick sheep and satisfying hungry ones. From them you will learn the plain sense of the narratives and understand the mysteries of allegories; from them you will receive the sweetness of moral teaching, from which you will gather precepts of moderation, instructions in true and pure religion, and examples of holy and devout conduct. You will see how to teach the truth of the catholic faith, how to commend integrity of morals, and how to show the order of right living. You will weigh what is suited to different persons, places, 737 and times, so that, according to the diversity of persons, the needs of times, and the suitability of places, [Col. 0819A] you may profit everyone and supply each individual with what is useful and necessary—threshing on the Lord’s floor like oxen that chew the cud and divide the hoof.

For you ought to practise rumination, that is, continual meditation upon Holy Scripture, together with the cleft hoof—that is, with discernment—so that you carefully distinguish what ought to be said to whom in preaching. For not everything is to be said to everyone. And, as Moses says, an ox and an ass are not to plough together (Deut. 22:10); so one and the same sermon is not to be delivered to the learned and the unlearned. Rather, the discourse of rulers must be adapted and altered in accordance with the diversity of persons and the capacity of hearers.

Thus also, among the four rivers that signify [Col. 0819B] the four virtues of the Church, the fourth is called Phison, interpreted as “a change of speech”; for one of the four chief virtues, namely prudence, causes the mouths of pastors to change according to the capacity of their hearers, so that in the food of the divine word each may receive what he most needs. Let the less learned receive edification in faith and morals; the sorrowful, the joy of consolation; the negligent, rebuke; the lukewarm, exhortation; the discordant, unity of mind and brotherly love; let the erring be recalled, sinners reproved, penitents and suppliants obtain mercy, those persisting in evil be sharply refuted; and those who rise against Christ’s teaching and the authority of mother Church, displaying as it were the eye of their own subtlety, be put to shame [Col. 0819C] and pierced through, as the Prophet admonishes when he says: “Let ravens from the torrents gouge out the eye that mocks its father and despises its mother’s bearing.”

The ravens coming from the torrents are good pastors and good priests, steeped in the streams of the holy Scriptures. They are called ravens, that is, black and contemptible in the sight of human beings, though they are beautiful and venerable in the sight of God, as is said in the Song of Songs in the person of the Church: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 1:5).

Ravens from the torrents ought to gouge out the eye that mocks its father and despises its mother’s birth-pangs, because good priests and good prelates ought, with the authorities [Col. 0819D] of the holy Scriptures as javelins—that is, as arrows of authoritative sayings—to pierce, convict, and refute not only Jews and unbelievers, but also schismatics [Note: [Col. 0819D] This sermon does not appear to have been delivered except by a bishop, and that in a synod.] and false Christians. Confident in their own cleverness and glorying in the eye of their own subtlety, they mock 738 their father by deriding the simplicity of Christ’s commandments—Christ, who begot them in faith—and they despise their mother’s bearing by scorning the authority and fruitfulness of mother Church, who daily conceives new children in the catechumenate and gives them birth in baptism.

For observing all these things, those entrusted with the teaching office over souls need great learning, great diligence, and great caution, because [Col. 0820A] it is exceedingly difficult not to offend in a word of teaching. As blessed James says: “If anyone does not offend in word, he is a perfect man” (Jas. 3:2). One sins in speech not only when shameful, harmful, malicious, or insulting things are said, but also whenever idle and empty words are uttered. One sins in speech when what is holy is given to dogs and pearls are cast before swine. One sins in speech when the talent of God’s word, which ought to be distributed to the poor, is hidden in the earth and the measure of spiritual wheat is withheld from Christ’s household.

Thus the Psalmist, in the person of Idithun—that is, “the one who leaps over,” who, by striving toward heavenly things, had already leapt over worldly things—yet feared to offend both in speaking and in keeping silence. As though placed in anxiety and seeing danger on every side, [Col. 0820B] he guarded his mouth, saying: “I said: I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue. I set a guard upon my mouth, while the sinner stood against me. I was dumb and silent, even from good things, and my sorrow was renewed” (Ps. 38:1). Seeing the sinner standing against him and seeking grounds for accusation in his words, so that he might rebuke and insult him, he was silent and dumb, lest he give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine. But again, seeing that by speaking God’s word he might have profited some, he grieved that he had kept silent from proclaiming good things.

See then, brothers, how great a perfection it is not to offend in speech: one offends both when things are said that ought not to be said, and when [Col. 0820C] things are not said that ought to be said. For one to whom the treasure of God’s word is entrusted must neither be prodigal, so as to expend it rashly, nor miserly, so as to hide it when he can be of benefit.

But if teachers of churches must take such great care not to offend in speech, how much more diligently must they provide that they do not offend by the example of their conduct. If any priest or prelate offends his subjects by living badly, furnishing them an example of greed, pride, luxury, wantonness, buffoonery, gluttony, excess, ambition, arrogance, contention, detraction, discord, 739 anger, or idleness—if, I say, by the example of his evil conduct he corrupts his subjects in these or other vices—what good is it to feed with the word those whom he kills by example?

Therefore the Lord said to the scribes and Pharisees: “Woe to you, who neither enter yourselves nor permit others to enter” (Matt. 23:13), because, by living wickedly, they made their own teaching contemptible. Those whom they ought to have led into life by good teaching, they drew back by evil living. Blessed James the apostle therefore warned that not many should become teachers, because it is most difficult not to offend, and dangerous to offend—especially for teachers, whose offenses are judged more severely.

Consider, brothers, your office. Consider that you have become teachers of souls. Consider how grave a danger [Col. 0821A] it is to have undertaken an office and not attend to it, reflect upon it, or labor to fulfil it. Wake up and do not grow dull. Carry out the care entrusted to you. Apply yourselves and labor, so that you may fulfil your office; so that learning, diligence, caution, circumspection, chastity, humility, self-restraint, moderation, and every temperance may be in you. Thus, by living well, teaching well, and offending in neither respect, may you bring the flocks entrusted to you to the upper sheepfold, to the folds of the heavenly kingdom, where the rage of wolves exercises no cruelty, where there is fullness of joy and secure tranquility. May the good Shepherd, Jesus Christ our Lord, deign to lead us there—He who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## CIV [On Various Matters XVII]. ON HEARING THE WORD OF GOD DILIGENTLY

[Note: [Col. 0821D] From Victorinus.]

[Col. 0821B]

> “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28).

Hear, most beloved brothers, how great an affection of love the Lord shows us: He calls us back, as a shepherd calls back lost sheep, while we toil in worldly affairs and are burdened by the weight of many sins; and He promises to refresh you, thirsty and hungry in the wilderness of this world. He says: You who labor amid the turmoil of secular affairs, come to me through faith and good works, and I will set you in eternal rest. And you who are burdened by the weight of sins, come to me, and I will lighten you by forgiving sins; and beyond this I will refresh you with virtues [Col. 0821C] and sound preaching, according to the saying: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matt. 4:4).

God provides this refreshment through His preachers. For when they preach, God refreshes the hearers. Hence the Gospel says: “Whoever receives one whom I send receives me” (John 13:20). And again: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). See, most beloved brothers, I bring you that refreshment; receive it, then, with your whole heart.

The Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever is from God hears the words of God” (John 7:17). But to His enemies He says: “Therefore you do not hear, because you are not from God” (Luke 8:47). Again: “Whoever hears my commandments [variant: “Whoever has the commandments, etc.”] and keeps them is the one [Col. 0821D] who loves me; and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John 14:21). See, brothers, how good it is to hear God’s commandments and keep them, because God reveals Himself to us through observance of His commandments. For you cannot attain knowledge of God unless you hear His commandments frequently. Yet hearing does not suffice unless we keep them. Therefore the apostle James says: “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves” (Jas. 1:22).

But I know well enough that your enemy the devil always lies in wait for you, so as to take the word of God out of your heart, lest you be able to fulfil in deed what you have heard. Perhaps you are those of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Other seed fell beside the road; it was trampled down, and the birds of heaven devoured it” (Luke 8:5). The seed is God’s word; what falls beside the road signifies those who hear God’s word; then the devil comes, signified by the birds of heaven—that is, of the air—and takes the word out of their hearts, lest they believe and be saved.

Therefore arms must be taken up against such an enemy in ambush, as the Apostle says: “Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light” (Rom. 13:12). The works of darkness are criminal sins, which lead people “into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 8:12): where there is unquenchable fire, an immortal worm, perpetual thirst, insatiable hunger; where there is [incurable] pain; where [Col. 0822B] the creature of God, made in God’s image and likeness, for whom the Creator deigned to become a creature and to endure such insult that, as the Apostle says, “he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8), loses its Creator and is cast into eternal punishment. Therefore do not be deceived. Know that “neither fornicators, nor adulterers, nor the greedy, nor thieves, nor robbers, nor revilers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10).

[Note: [Col. 0821D] This sermon appears to be incomplete.]

## CV [On Various Matters XVIII]. ALLEGORIES CONCERNING ISAAC AND REBECCA AS A FIGURE OF CHRIST AND THE CHURCH

[Note: [Col. 0822D] From the Remigian manuscript, in which it is entitled: “To Aldebert, bishop of Le Mans.”]

While the mystery of the sacrament concerning Abraham’s servant and the seeking of a wife for his son Isaac was being discussed [Col. 0822C] (Gen. 24), there is added: “Put your hand under my thigh, that I may bind you by oath through the Lord God of heaven and earth, that you do not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I dwell, but that you go to my land and to my kindred, and from there take a wife for my son Isaac.”

I wish briefly to bring forward certain matters from the history of Abraham and Isaac, so that we may more fittingly demonstrate in them those things which belong to allegory. Abraham calls his servant and commands him to put his hand under his thigh and, as the old translation has it, to swear by the Lord God of heaven. He immediately commands that no wife be taken for his son Isaac from the daughters of the Canaanites, but that the servant go to his kindred and bring back a wife for him from there.

The servant did as commanded: he put his hand under Abraham’s thigh and swore; he took from all his master’s goods and went to Mesopotamia. Standing beside a spring of water, he proposed in prayer that the girl to whom he should say, “Lower your water-jar, that I may drink,” and who should answer, “Drink; indeed, I will also give your camels water,” should be the wife of his master Isaac. At once Rebecca came out and replied to the servant asking for water: “Drink, my lord.” Swiftly she lowered her jar upon her arm, gave him drink, and also drew and offered water for the camels.

The servant brought out gold earrings weighing two shekels and bracelets weighing ten shekels. When asked, she stated her lineage; she also said that there was ample room in her father’s house for lodging and that they had an abundance of straw and hay. Rebecca had a brother named Laban. He came out eagerly, and, seeing his sister’s earrings and bracelets, invited the servant indoors; he gave him straw and hay, provided water to wash the feet of the camels and the men with him, and set bread before him. But the servant refused to eat unless he first secured the marriage arrangement for his master’s son. As soon as he obtained it, he brought out vessels of gold and silver and garments, and increased Rebecca’s gifts; he also offered presents to her brothers and mother. Rebecca and her maidens mounted camels and followed the man. [Col. 0823B] He returned quickly to his own house.

At that time Isaac was walking along the road that leads to the well whose name is “the Living and Seeing One”; he lived in the southern land, and had gone out to meditate in the field as the day was already declining. But as soon as Rebecca saw Isaac, she descended from the camel and asked the servant who that man was who was coming through the field. He replied: “He is my master.” Then she quickly took a veil and covered herself. Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother Sarah and took her as his wife; and he loved her so greatly that it softened the grief which had come upon him through his mother’s death.

What does it mean that Abraham commands his servant to put his hand under his thigh and swear by the Lord of heaven, except that through that member was to descend the flesh of Him who would be Abraham’s son in His humanity and Lord in His divinity? Thus the servant is told, “Put your hand under my thigh and swear by the God of heaven,” as though it were plainly said: “Touch my son and swear by my God.” Hence he is commanded to place his hand not upon the thigh, but under the thigh, because from that thigh was to descend One who, though truly human, would come above all human beings. It was therefore not fitting that he put his hand upon the thigh, because no flesh is above that flesh which the Father’s Only-begotten united to Himself for our redemption.

What does it mean that a wife is forbidden to be brought for beloved Isaac from the daughters of the Canaanites, except that no reprobate souls are joined to Him of whom it is written: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17)? But the servant is commanded to bring a wife for the son from Abraham’s kindred because the holy Church of the elect alone was to be joined to the Only-begotten Son; and, by predestination and foreknowledge, the Only-begotten Himself did not regard her as a stranger.

Who, then, is the servant sent to bring the wife, except the order of prophets and apostles and of all teachers? When they impart the word of preaching to good minds, they become, as it were, agents who unite each soul with the Only-begotten Son. The servant went, taking with him all his master’s goods, because, in the things they say about the Lord, they display in themselves the riches of virtues, so that they may draw people all the more swiftly to follow God because they show their hearers in themselves [Col. 0824A] what they proclaim.

The same servant stood beside the spring and, according to his fixed purpose, set forth which girl should be chosen, because holy preachers examine the streams of sacred discourse and from them discern both what words of their preaching they should entrust and to whom, and from which hearers they should derive the confidence of certainty. He asks for a drink because every preacher thirsts for the soul of his hearer. But Rebecca supplied a drink because the holy Church of the elect, through the strength of her faith, satisfied her preachers’ desire. For she who confessed the God whom she heard offered her preacher the water of refreshment and cooled his spirit.

It should be noted that she set the water-jar down from her shoulder upon her arms, because that confession is pleasing which proceeds from good [Col. 0824B] work. Or rather, she gave water because she did not remain idle in what she believed: she at once undertook to preach what she had heard, and by teaching many produced preachers from herself. For water in a jar is the knowledge of preaching in due measure, because the holy Church strives “not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sobriety” (Rom. 12:3). The water-jar upon the arms is the doctrine of preaching expressed in work.

She offered drink not only to the servant’s companions but also to the camels, because the Church preaches the word of life not only to the prudent but also to the foolish, in accordance with Paul’s saying: “I am debtor both to the wise and to the foolish” (Rom. 1:14). Or again, water is given even to beasts of burden when instruction is given regarding how bodily care should be regulated: it ought not to be lavished in accordance with desire, yet it should not be withheld in necessities, as it is written: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14). For He who forbids such provision in desires undoubtedly permits it in necessity, according to the further saying: “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Eph. 5:29).

The servant gave Rebecca earrings and bracelets, because every preacher adorns both the hearing of [the] holy Church through obedience and her hands through the merit of good works. The earrings weigh two shekels and the bracelets ten shekels, because the first virtue of obedience is in charity; and charity is distinguished in two commandments, that God and neighbor may be loved. Right action, meanwhile, is made perfect through fulfilment of the Decalogue, so that, when good actions have begun, [Col. 0824D] no evil deeds may any longer be committed.

Rebecca reported that in her father’s house there was a spacious place to lodge, because the holy Church showed that she had already known the law of nature from the former people and received the words of preaching in the wide bosom of charity. For a spacious lodging-place for a teacher is breadth of goodness in the hearer’s heart. Hence some are told: “Make room for us: we have wronged no one, corrupted no one” (2 Cor. 7:2)—“You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections” (2 Cor. 6:12). It is as if they were openly told: Make a spacious place in your minds for receiving doctrine, but remain narrow toward thoughts of the flesh.

She declared that she had an abundance of straw and hay because [Col. 0825A] the holy Church, hearing the words of life, rendered earthly provisions to preachers. Paul, considering these provisions as almost nothing, said: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (1 Cor. 9:11).

Rebecca’s brother was Laban. When he hurried out and saw his sister’s earrings and bracelets, he invited the servant inside, because there are certain carnal persons [variant: “who”], joined to the faithful, who, when they observe gifts of the Spirit, are held in wondering admiration. Though they do not advance as far as works, they nevertheless admit into their soul the word of preaching so as to receive faith. For they often observe good persons shining [variant: “to shine”] by miracles and do not reject the things they hear [variant: “hear”] concerning eternity, although, because they do not follow the holy Church of the elect in morals, they remain in carnal conduct.

Laban offered straw, hay, water, and bread; but the servant refused to accept them unless he first secured the cause of his master’s son’s marriage, because many people are ready to support their teachers with temporal provisions, but holy preachers do not wish to receive temporal things unless they first obtain eternal ones. If they find no fruit in souls, they disdain to take bodily provisions. Nor do they wash their feet with water, because no consolation relieves the labor of their desire.

But as soon as the servant secured the marriage arrangement of his master, he brought out vessels of gold and silver and garments, which he gave Rebecca, because the teachers of the holy Church furnish her with as many ornaments as the goods of virtues they teach. She who first received earrings and bracelets now received vessels of gold and silver and garments; later, increasing in strength toward spiritual gifts, she became rich through enlarged gifts, filled with the spirit of prophecy and the grace of virtues.

The servant offered gifts to her mother and brothers because, from the time the Church came to faith, the Gentile world grew strong in temporal glory after her conversion. We see this even now: Christians everywhere suffer affliction, while pagans of every sort glory in earthly power. Her brothers too receive gifts, because those who retain faith in her only verbally but do not follow their profession in their conduct, living carnally, are customarily treated kindly by the faithful because they appear to be believers. Therefore the mother and brothers receive gifts, yet remain excluded from the portion of inheritance: because whether unbelievers or carnal persons who remain within the profession of faith, they do not attain the portion of the eternal inheritance, but for a time obtain the glory of heavenly generosity.

Rebecca followed the man with her maidens, because the holy Church has with her as companions souls of lesser merit, though they do not share in certain ascents of the mind upon the bed of contemplation. Such souls are, as it were, Rebecca’s maidens: they follow in conduct, but do not ascend at all to the bed of contemplation. 745 The same servant also had certain persons in his company, because among the holy prophets there were some who lived well but did not have the spirit of prophecy; and among the blessed apostles and teachers there were many [Col. 0826A] who maintained a good life in their conduct but did not bring forth words of preaching.

The servant returns quickly to his house because, when holy preachers obtain the life of their hearers by preaching, they immediately give thanks to Him from whose gift they have received [variant: “commanded”], so that they attribute nothing to themselves in that work, but to its Author.

At that time Isaac was walking along the road that leads to the well whose name is “the Living and Seeing One.” Who is the Living and Seeing One but almighty God? Of Him it is written: “As I live for ever, says the Lord” (Deut. 32:40). And again it is said of Him: “All things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. 4:13). The well of the Living and Seeing One is the depth of Holy Scripture, which almighty God has given us to water the mind.

What, then, is the road that leads to the well of the Living and Seeing One, except the humility of the Only-begotten’s Passion, through which that which the streams of Holy Scripture previously spoke in concealment has been opened to us? For unless the Only-begotten Son of God had been incarnate, tempted, seized, struck with blows, smeared with spittle, crucified, and killed, the depth of this faith—that is, of Holy Scripture—would not lie open to us. What, then, has the humility of His Passion become for believers except the key of opening, through which we find the well of God’s mysteries [variant: “ministries”] and draw the water of knowledge from its depth? The sacred page speaks of His incarnation, Passion, death, resurrection, and ascension; because we have come to know that these things occurred, we now understand what we have heard. [Col. 0826C] They could indeed previously be read, but because they had not yet happened, they could not be understood. Therefore John says: “The Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered, to open the book and loosen its seals” (Rev. 5:5). He loosed its seals who, by being born, dying, rising again, and ascending to heaven, opened the hidden things of Holy Scripture to us.

It should be noted that the text says not “he walked along the road leading to the well,” but “he walked back and forth.” For one walks back and forth along a road when he treads it by going and returning. The Lord walked back and forth in the humility of His Passion because at one time He endured verbal insults from the Jews, at another false testimony against Himself, at another slaps, at another spittle, at another a crown of thorns, and at another the cross. Thus to have walked back and forth in the humility of the Passion is repeatedly to have endured so many adversities and reproaches in different ways.

When Rebecca comes, Isaac dwells in the southern land because the only-begotten Lord and our Redeemer remained, when the Church came to Him, in the minds of those people. From that people came the prophetess Anna, and from it Simeon, who received the Lord in his arms. He had gone out to meditate in the field. The Lord Himself explains that the field signifies the world, saying: “The field is the world” (Matt. 13:38). He went out into it in that He deigned to appear visibly, as it is written: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones.”

Young men trained [variants: “chosen” or “to be trained”] for the use of arms customarily practise in arms. Thus Isaac went out into the field to meditate, because our Redeemer, giving His followers a model of humility, showed in Himself through the exercise [variant: “army”] of His long-suffering Passion an example of patience. The practice of arms is the repeated experience of sufferings. He who endured blows [variant: “words”], the hand, the spear, and the cross allowed His Passion to be repeatedly inflicted upon Him even unto death. We have learned the arms of the Passion because through them we are secretly freed from the adversary, as the Lord Himself says: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

He went out to meditate in the field when the day was already declining because He undertook the exercises of suffering near the end of the world, as the Psalmist speaks concerning the exposition of His crucifixion: “The lifting up of my hands is the evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140:2).

But what does it mean that Rebecca is brought to Isaac on the back of a camel, except that, as we have said, Rebecca signifies the Church, while the camel—bent in its habits and burdened with idolatrous worship—signifies the Gentile people, over which she rides? For those who found gods for themselves to worship had, as it were, caused a burden to grow upon their backs from themselves, which they bore. Rebecca, therefore, coming to Isaac is brought upon a camel’s back because the Church, hastening to Christ from the Gentiles, is found amid the distorted and vicious practices of the old life. When she saw Isaac, she descended from the camel because the more subtly the holy Church recognizes her Redeemer, [Col. 0827C] the more humbly she abandons the pursuits of carnal life and opposes in herself vicious crookedness. Thus, on seeing Isaac, she descends: having known the Lord, the Gentile world forsook its vices and, leaving the heights of pride, sought the low places of humility.

What does it mean that Rebecca saw Isaac while seated upon the camel, except that the Church coming from the Gentiles looked upon her Redeemer while she still rested upon vices and had not yet adhered to spiritual conduct? Nor should it trouble us that the servant too had come with camels on which he carried his master’s wealth, because even holy preachers, although they now excel in both understanding and life for comprehending and expressing higher things, still experience in themselves the contradiction [Col. 0827D] of the flesh. For they see another law in their members resisting the law of their mind and taking them captive under the law of sin (Rom. 7:23). They carry riches on camels because, lest the greatness of revelations exalt them, a thorn of their flesh is given them (2 Cor. 12:7). For they possess this treasure in earthen vessels (2 Cor. 4:7), so that the surpassing greatness may be God’s power and not come from themselves.

Who, then, speak lofty things through the flesh, yet still feel in the flesh the contradiction arising from vice—what else do they do but carry riches upon the crooked backs of camels? But Rebecca, when she sees Isaac, learns from the servant, whom she asks who that man is, because every day the holy Church still understands, through the sayings of the prophets and apostles, what it ought to believe concerning its Redeemer. [Col. 0828A] She immediately covered herself with a cloak, because the more subtly she penetrates the mysteries of her Savior, the more deeply she is ashamed of her former life; and she is ashamed because she acted perversely. She took care to cover herself with a cloak because, having seen the Lord, she blushed at the weakness of her conduct; and she who had formerly been carried freely upon the camel is afterwards, having descended, covered by shame. Hence the same Church, converted from its former exaltation, is addressed through the apostolic voice, as though to Rebecca descending from the camel and drawing a cloak over herself: “What fruit, then, did you have at that time in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21).

Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother and took her as his wife, because in place of the Synagogue, from which the Lord was born according to the flesh, he loves the holy Church and joins her to himself in love and contemplation. Thus she who was formerly near through kinship—that is, related through predestination—afterwards, once joined in love, immediately becomes his wife. He loved her so greatly that he tempered the sorrow which had come from his mother’s death, because by the gain of the holy Church our Redeemer wiped away the sadness that might have arisen from the loss of the Synagogue. For when Rebecca is joined to Isaac, grief over his mother’s death is removed; because when the holy Church, coming from the Gentile world, is brought as far as the bed of contemplation, Judaea is counted as nothing.

If we take care to interpret the names themselves, Isaac means “laughter,” while Rebecca means “patience.” Laughter belongs to joy, but patience to tribulation. And although the holy Church is already held aloft in the contemplation of heavenly joy, it nevertheless still has something sorrowful to endure from the burden of mortal flesh. Isaac and Rebecca are joined—that is, laughter and patience are mingled—because in the holy Church there comes about what is written: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12:12), so that prosperity arising from contemplation may gladden her, while adversities arising from tribulation may still disturb her.

## CVI [On Various Subjects XIX]. ON GRATITUDE TOWARD GOD AND TRUE CONVERSION TO HIM

[Note: [Col. 0827D] From Victorinus and Lyranus.]

[Col. 0828D] “My people, what have I done to you? Or in what have I been burdensome to you? Answer me. For I brought you out of the land of Egypt and delivered you from the house of bondage” (Mic. 6:3).

“Bring me to remembrance, that we may not be judged together. Tell, if you have anything, that you may be justified. Your first father sinned, and your interpreters long transgressed against me.”

For a long time, dearest brethren, the Lord endured us; for a long time he postponed punishment, inviting us to repentance. But when he sees that he waits in vain and that his own people are unwilling to be corrected, he calls us to a hearing, asking through the prophet Micah: “My people, what have I done to you? Why do you abandon me? Why do you not obey me? [Col. 0829A] Answer: what reason have you for neglecting obedience to me? I have done you no evil, nor have I been burdensome to you. And if I have done anything, I have done it for correction, not for destruction. No evils, but many goods, have I done for you. For I brought you out of the land of Egypt”—that is, out of the land of darkness; “I delivered you from the land of slavery,” from the devil, who had taken you captive from your homeland.

Bring to remembrance, if you have anything that you can rightly answer. I shall gladly allow us to be judged together, and let you charge me with not having done what I ought to have done. “Tell, then, if you have anything, that you may be justified.” This means: I do not speak first against you, lest you say that you are overwhelmed by a multitude of words. But if you have anything for yourself, speak yourself. For if I previously did you any good, I did it not because of your merit, nor because of that of your parents; [Col. 0829B] for your first father sinned, and your interpreters—that is, your teachers—also transgressed against me.

You have heard, dearest brethren, what the Lord has justly said in anger against you. Yet, although the Lord is great, although almighty, he nevertheless moderates his anger; and lest we complain of him when he exacts vengeance from us, he first wished us to answer, if we had anything to say. Let each, therefore, consider how he may answer. But I do not see what we can answer to so great a benefactor. If it please you, let us hear of his benefits—sparingly at least, since we cannot remember them all. “Is he not,” says Moses, “your Father, who possessed you, made you, and created you?” (Deut. 32:6). David likewise says: “He made us, and not we ourselves” (Ps. 99:3). Behold first how he gave us our being.

What shall I say of the temporal benefits which he bestows daily? “He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:45). “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and those who dwell in it” (Ps. 23:1). He gives us food in due season. But since these are temporal things, let us consider another, remarkable and spiritual benefit. “For you know,” as the Apostle says, “the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: that for your sakes he became poor, though he was rich, that by his poverty you might become rich” (2 Cor. 8:9).

The shepherd came through the wilderness of this world to seek the lost sheep, carried off by wolves. Having found it, he bore it back to the flock on his own shoulders and delivered it through many tribulations. For, on behalf of the sheep, as Isaiah says, “he was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7). For when the Jews stripped away the fleece of his flesh in order to kill him, he did not rebel before them or cry out; upon the mountain he prayed for them: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23:34). And when they struck him, saying, “Prophesy: who is it that struck you?” (Luke 22:64), he himself remained silent. Therefore, as Isaiah says: “He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7); he did not resist, but endured patiently.

And when he cried upon the cross, “I thirst” (John 17:28), [Col. 0830A] he sought not so much bodily drink as their salvation, as Christ himself says through David: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68:22). For when he sought from them, as it were, food, they offered him bitter foods like gall, and stale foods, sour through the age of vices, like vinegar. But for what cause, for what crime, did he suffer this? Hear what Isaiah says: “He was wounded for our sins; he was bruised for our iniquities; he laid upon him all the iniquities of us all, and by his bruise we have been healed” (Isa. 53:5). David says again concerning him: “Then I paid what I had not taken” (Ps. 68:5). For he paid for what he had not committed. Thus he bore the punishment of sin, he “who did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. 53:9; 1 Pet. 2:22). Indeed, he himself bore our sorrows. For, as Moses says, he spread out his wings, took them up, and bore them upon his shoulders (Deut. 32).

Through all these tribulations, though he was the only [natural—supplied] Son of God, he wished us also to become adopted sons of God, so that we might be his brothers. Hence John says: “But to as many as received him, he gave power to become sons of God—to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12). And the Lord says through the Prophet: “I will declare your name to my brethren” (Ps. 21:23). And Paul says: “That we might be heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8:17). Christ himself says in the Gospel: “Where I am, there my servant also shall be” (John 12:26). And wishing to ennoble us with angelic honor, he says: “Men shall be like angels.” [Col. 0830C]

Behold, dearest brethren, we have related, as though only a marked portion, one small part of God’s so many benefits—though they are innumerable. Let each, therefore, say with David: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. 115:12). You know well enough that, being obliged to him for such great benefits, you ought to be obedient. If you do not pay what is due, hear what the Lord says: “I have nourished sons and exalted them, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1:2). And again through David: “My people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not attend to me. And I dismissed them according to the desires of their heart; they shall go in their own devices” (Ps. 86:13).

For it is a great and grievous punishment when the Lord withdraws grace and allows the wretched person to rush headlong into life [perhaps: into vices]. Hence the Lord says through Moses: “I will hide my face from them, and I will consider their latter end” (Deut. 32:20). This means: I shall see, and withdraw my presence from them, and announce to them their latter end—that is, the end to which their works will lead them. Behold, the Lord calls us his despisers. Yet truly, do you not despise him when you reject the words you have heard? “The servant who knows,” as the Lord says in the Gospel, “his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 12:47).

We see many commandments of the Lord; let us see whether we fulfill them. God commands us not to kill. But how many among us, while they kill in their mind those whom they hate, have hands full of blood, whose feet are swift to shed blood! For, as the apostle John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:17). [Col. 0831A] It is commanded: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:14). And the Apostle says: “Husbands, love your wives” (Eph. 5:25). But do not some among you love other men’s wives more than your own? Thus they sin doubly: against their neighbor and against their own wife.

The Lord commands through David: “Do not covet plunder” (Ps. 61:31). But that you act contrary to this commandment, the Lord himself says through Isaiah [to the rulers of his people]: “You have devoured the vineyard, and the plunder of the poor is in your house. Why do you crush my people and grind the faces of the poor?” (Isa. 3:14–15). In this authority there is a twofold nature, a single sacrilege [perhaps: a single nature, a twofold sacrilege]. When he says, “You have devoured the vineyard,” that is, my Church, he touches those who abuse the Church’s resources for bodily pleasures—resources given for the support of the poor—either reserving them for themselves or distributing them to relatives, and making the poverty of others into the wealth of themselves and their own people; and this is sacrilege. When he says, “The plunder of the poor is in your house,” he marks that plundering by which those who are commanded to give what is theirs take what belongs to others; [and this is another sacrilege]. What follows—“Why do you crush my people?”—refers to rulers who unjustly crush and oppress the property of the common people.

As for usury, false judgments, flattery, [Col. 0831C] deceits, perjuries, breaches of faith, and other sins: all these are the returns which you render to God for his benefits. Therefore let Moses rebuke you when he says: “A crooked and perverse generation—is this what you return to the Lord, foolish and senseless people?” (Deut. 32:6). Since, then, the Lord has bestowed so many benefits on you, dearest brethren, and you have been so ungrateful and have returned evil for good, what will you say? Will you come to a hearing with him? Certainly this is not fitting, because the Apostle says: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9:20).

Since, then, you do not dare to come to judgment, receive counsel concerning what you should do. For Moses says [in God’s person]: “I will lift up my hand to heaven and say: I live for ever. If I sharpen my sword like lightning, [Col. 0831D] and my hand grasps judgment, I will render vengeance to my enemies; and to those who hate me I will repay” (Deut. 32:40). This is said by comparison. Being about to swear, he says: “I will lift up my hand to heaven and say: As surely as I live for ever, so surely shall this be true: if I sharpen, as I truly shall do, my sword, which until now has seemed an enemy [perhaps: blunt], while I delayed vengeance.”

He then explains what it means for him to take up the sword: “If my hand,” or my Son, “grasps judgment,” signified by the sword, “I will render vengeance to my enemies.” Mystically, to lift the hand to heaven is for the Son of Man to be exalted on the day of the Ascension, so that he may at last come to judgment and execute vengeance.

Therefore, dearest brethren, I shall give you sound counsel, by which you may escape these threats and not compel him to summon you to a hearing. Yet this counsel is not mine, but that of the prophet David, who experienced it. He says: “Enter his gates in confession” (Ps. 99:4), as though saying: You who, by your sins, are outside the house of God, do not remain outside, where evil spirits are and where the wolf lies in wait; but accuse yourselves [the text reads *excusate*, perhaps for *accusate*], and enter to the Lord. Do you know how? In confession. Confess and do penance, and the Lord will forgive you your sins. Do not doubt it; for David says: Take an example from me: “I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my sin. For this every saint shall pray to you at the fitting time” (Ps. 31:5). [Col. 0832B]

You know how commendable confession is. No one is so holy that he does not sin, and therefore all seek confession. Even the saints in this world need it. This is the final medicine, the last remedy for sinners. This is the tower to which all the oppressed flee, in which wounded fugitives are healed. Through this Mary Magdalene was saved. Through this Peter, after his denial, recovered the apostolate. Through this the thief, at the very point of death upon the cross, deserved to hear: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

From where comes this benefit? From God’s goodness alone, as David says: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is for ever” (Ps. 105:1). We may therefore safely ask pardon, because he is patient and greatly merciful. The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works. Hence the Prophet says: “Confess, returning children, and I will heal your wounds” (Hos. 14:5). And David says: “Will one who falls not add to rising again?” (Ps. 40:9). Therefore sing to the Lord in confession, because “the Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. 144:18). He is the one who has mercy on the truly repentant.

This is the counsel of which I spoke to you. [Col. 0832D] You cannot otherwise be reconciled to God; and therefore repentance must not be delayed, since this present life is not promised for long. Let each one run to his prelate and make peace with God—not tomorrow, but today; for, as John the Baptist says, the axe has already been laid to the root of the tree, to strike you unless you hasten to amend yourselves. Let no one despair because of a most shameful life, when he may obtain pardon.

[Note: [Col. 0831] Observe that certain sermons are not copied in full, but only their undigested subject matter.]

[Give now an example of some sinner converted to the faith and saved; and give examples for this purpose also of many others who, though despairing, nevertheless returned to the way of salvation and were converted to the Lord.]

And likewise, dearest brethren, let no horrible sin lead you into [Col. 0833A] despair, because there is no fault so grave that it does not have forgiveness. Consider, therefore, dearest brethren, consider the final day of life. Prepare yourselves, for it will come and will not delay. What will you say when you stand before the judgment-seat of Christ?
