The righteous man will scarcely be saved, and only through many tribulations and temptations—that is, with great difficulty—because on this side demons, on that side flesh, on another side the world assault him; and yet he must resist so many enemies. Where will the ungodly appear, who love prosperity, avoid these labors, and do not resist vices? You are blind, you are drunk, you sleep, if you do not recognize these things. O wretches, wretches! The riches of this age blind you. This shows that you are sinners: you love riches. David says: “Behold, these are sinners; and abounding in the age, they have obtained riches” (Ps. 71:12). But “they shall leave their riches to strangers, and their tombs, their houses, for ever” (Ps. 48:11).

Therefore, brethren, store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, where you may flourish for ever, where you may rejoice for ever, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## CVII [On Various Subjects XX]. ON LOVE OF NEIGHBOR

[Note: [Col. 0833D] From Victorinus.]

“Jesus, knowing that his hour had come for him to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them unto the end” (John 13:1).

But you, dearest brethren, by God’s grace understand the things commanded us by the Lord, because they are read daily in your hearing. You do not need to be taught, but reminded. Yet it is our office to call to your remembrance what you understand. You know how great was the discord caused by our sin between ourselves and God; but the gracious and merciful Lord wished to reconcile the human race to his Father. He loved his creature not because of its merit, but through his mercy. Sent by the Father, therefore, he fulfilled obedience unto death; and as he approached death, he wished to invite us to love. For his death was the reconciliation of God and human beings. [Col. 0833D] But human beings could not be reconciled to God unless they were first reconciled among themselves.

Therefore, on the day before he suffered, he bound his own together in love by word and deed. Let us now consider the deed and afterwards the word. The Lord saw that service and humility are the fuel and form of love. Therefore he wished first, by example, to invite us to serve, so that after the seed [the text has *fomitem*, “fuel”; perhaps *sementem*, “seed”] of the word, he might more easily sow in them the love of charity. This was the service of humility by which the Lord assumed the role of one serving. For the Evangelist says of the Lord: “He rises from supper and lays aside his garments; and having taken a towel, he girded himself. Then he poured water into a basin, [Col. 0834A] and began to wash the feet of his disciples and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded” (John 13:4).

After completing the washing of the feet, he showed why he had done this. “Do you know,” he says, “what I have done to you? You call me Master and Lord, and you say well, for so I am. If, therefore, I, the Lord and Master, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you also should do” (ibid., 12). Clearly, therefore, he did not wash for his own sake, but invited others by this example of humility, so that they might not be ashamed to do what the Lord had wished to show in himself.

Having first provided the fuel of love, he proceeds, saying: “Where I go you cannot come now; and therefore I say ‘now,’ because I give you a new commandment” (ibid., 33). The Lord was about to depart and prepare a place, as he says elsewhere: “I go to prepare a place for you” (John 14:2). The way had not yet been opened, nor had the wall been broken down, of which it is written: “In my God I shall pass over the wall” (Ps. 17:32). But after he destroyed death by his death and, leading captivity captive, despoiled hell—as it was written concerning him, “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O hell!” (Hos. 13:14)—then was fulfilled what had been foretold concerning him before his death: “I will come again and receive you to myself, that where I am, you also may be” (John 14:3).

But when the Lord departed again, he wished to establish peace and concord in his household, so that those who would long be desolate through his absence might comfort one another in love. He shows why he specially imposes this commandment on them: “By this,” he says, [Col. 0834C] “all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (ibid.). It is as though he said: My sheep are now mingled with the sheep of the devil. I set a sign; I set a brand, by which the one may be distinguished from the other. Other virtues are common to both good and evil people, but true love belongs only to the good.

True love indeed has two branches: the love of God and of neighbor. This virtue is the root of all virtues. Other virtues without love are worth nothing, as the Apostle says: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I deliver my body so that I may be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3). Whoever has love has the other virtues, because on this depend the law and the prophets. This is the virtue that extends its branches even to enemies; hence the command: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5:44). Therefore it is called a broad commandment. David says: “I have seen an end of all perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118:96), because love is the culmination of all perfection.

For in the old law it was commanded that enemies be held in hatred: “You shall love,” he says, “your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:39). Many benefits arise from love: for example, remission of sins, preeminence in the Church, and eternal life. For it was said of Mary: “Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47). It was said to Peter: “Peter, do you love me? Yes, Lord. Feed my sheep; feed my lambs” (John 21:16). It was said of the disciple whom Jesus loved: “Come, my beloved, to me, for it is time that you feast at my banquet with your brethren.”

Therefore, dearest brethren, embrace love, love concord, preserve peace, if you wish to have peace with God; [Col. 0835A] for peace is called the guardian of every virtue. The angel announced peace when he said: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). The Apostle also announced peace when he said: “As far as lies within you, have peace with all” (Rom. 12:18). Christ announced it when he said: “I leave peace to you; I give you my peace” (John 14:17). When he entered among the disciples, he said: “Peace to you” (Luke 24:36). And he commanded the apostles: “Into whatever house you enter, first say: Peace to this house” (Luke 10:5).

Since peace is imposed upon us by angelic, apostolic, and divine preaching, we must obey such authoritative commands. For it is no small presumption to transgress so commendable a command. Yet we know that for some among us it is difficult to love enemies; but it is necessary to amend this one element of love, which is not common to the wicked. And you will receive no reward from love unless you love your enemies; for, as the Lord says: “If you love your friends, what reward will you have? Do not even the Gentiles and tax collectors do the same?” (Matt. 5:46).

Therefore apply yourselves to grant forgiveness to enemies, because, as the Lord says: “If you do not forgive human beings their sins, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:15). It may therefore be concluded that you expect pardon from the Lord in vain unless you forgive your neighbor. Thus you cannot repent of any sins, because no forgiveness would be given you for any unless you granted forgiveness to your enemies. Consider, therefore, dearest brethren, and keep this unavoidable commandment. Cast from yourselves, if it is in you, the poison of hatred. Have peace among yourselves, because you are brethren, because you seek pardon from the Lord.

Recall that today the Lord kissed Judas, his enemy, and called the betrayer “friend,” saying: “Friend, for what have you come?” (Matt. 26:50). [Col. 0835D] Therefore give the kiss of reconciliation, not the counterfeit of betrayal. Whoever falsely kisses an enemy will be Judas’s companion. May the God of peace and love grant you peace, he who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## CVIII [On Various Subjects XXI]. ON WORKS OF MERCY

[Note: [Col. 0835D] From Victorinus.]

“Do not emulate evildoers, nor be jealous of those who work iniquity; for they shall quickly wither like grass and swiftly fall like the green herbs” (Ps. 36:1).

There are many in the world, dearest brethren, who, when they see people of this age flourishing and abounding in every temporal good, however sinful and however wicked they may be, while they see good people despised by the world and subjected to every evil, are indignant and believe the wicked to be happy and the good miserable. Thus many themselves become wicked and imitate the wicked, in order that they may prosper with the wicked in this world. Of such people David the Psalmist speaks and consoles them, saying: O faithful person, who sees the unworthy prosper, do not emulate—that is, do not be indignant at—evildoers, that is, those who act badly, if they prosper. Nor be jealous—that is, do not love or imitate—those who do iniquity on that account, as if by committing iniquity you could prosper.

Do not be concerned if you see them flourishing, powerful, despising others, glorious, famous, more venerated than others, and honored by all; for they shall certainly wither like grass. Grass flourishes today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace. Likewise the powerful person who now flourishes withers in a moment, because either he loses everything or death deprives him of his goods; and he falls swiftly like the green herbs. The green herbs are lowly and have no deep root: they are green in winter and wither in summer. Winter is the present age, in which the human race grows cold through sins. Summer is the day of judgment, when the righteous shall shine like the sun.

When you see temporal things quickly passing away, and those who possess them quickly perishing, do not hope in present goods, but “hope in the Lord, do good, dwell in the land, and you shall be fed upon its riches” (Ps. 36:3). What does he mean by “Hope in the Lord”? That he will give true goods. And in order that you may hope for them, do good, for one hopes in vain who does not act rightly. And that you may act rightly, dwell in the land. The land of a person which you ought to cultivate is the body. We are pilgrims in this mortal body, yet while we are in it we ought to cultivate it. While time permits, let us make our pilgrimage in this mortal body by plucking out the thorns of vices, so that afterwards we may sow the goodness of God. And thus, that you may act rightly and uproot vices, “you shall be fed upon its riches,” that is, upon his Scriptures, where the treasure of wisdom is.

Moreover, perseverance is necessary; and in order to have it, “delight in the Lord” (ibid., 4). Despising the pleasure of the world, love him alone and embrace him. Then at last “he will give you the petitions” (ibid.) not of the flesh, which loves present things, but of your heart, which loves eternal things. But if you are a sinner, I shall now give you good counsel: “Reveal your way to the Lord” (ibid., 5), that is, your crooked way, and hope in him, and he himself will do it. It is as though he said: Judge your sins through repentance, and hope that God will forgive them; and he will indeed do so.

Someone might say at the same point: “They will soon die, because perhaps in the future they will prosper likewise.” To this he answers: “Those who do evil shall be cut off from the kingdom of God; but those who wait shall inherit in the land of the living” (Ps. 36:9). Therefore, “Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened; and wait for the Lord” (Ps. 26:14). He who now despises you will last only a little while, because “yet a little while, and the sinner shall not be; you shall seek his place and shall not find it” (Ps. 36:10). Now he has a place in the present age, to cleanse the righteous by scourges and reproaches; but then he will have no use, after he has been removed from this world.

Therefore do not look upon the greatness of his wealth, because “a little is better for the righteous than the many riches of sinners” (Ps. 36:16). Is he strong? Do not care, because “the arms of sinners shall be broken” (ibid., 17). Do they carry a sword? Do not fear, because “their sword shall enter their own hearts, and their bows shall be broken” (ibid., 15). Do the righteous suffer disgrace and reproach? Do not care, because “they shall not be confounded in the evil time, and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied, because sinners shall perish” (ibid., 19).

But sinners shall be confounded and ashamed when it is said to them: “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:4); whereas “the righteous shall not fear an evil report” (Ps. 111:7), because he will not hear that curse. Yet fools, who do not understand true goods, judge those people blessed “whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity; whose sons” are so beautiful and tender “like young plants in their youth; whose daughters are adorned like the likeness of a temple,” because they are adorned with garments like some temple; “whose storehouses are full, pouring forth from one vessel into another; whose sheep are fruitful, abundant in their offspring; whose oxen are fat.” For when they go out from their folds, their dumb young follow them. “There is no breach in the wall,” because their houses are strong and made of marble, “nor passage, nor outcry in their streets” when they sleep. Such are their riches; and therefore fools “called happy the people to whom these things belong.” But certainly they are not happy; rather, “Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God” (Ps. 143:11–15).

In these ways, dearest brethren, David reasons about the riches of this age, proving them vain and unable to make people happy. They are not prohibited so that they may be unable to help him, but so that people may not make them rule over themselves.

[Note: [Col. 0837] This period appears to require restoration as follows: “They are not prohibited in such a way that they cannot be loved; but in such a way that people may not allow them to rule them.”]

Hence avarice is called “the service of idols” (Eph. 5:5). For the person who makes gold or silver his highest good, who is proud because of them and places his hope in them, worships an idol. Hence Paul says to Timothy: “Command the rich of this age not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the true God, who provides all things abundantly for enjoyment” (2 Tim. 6:17). There are many people who love riches so greatly that they might be called their guardians [perhaps: worshippers] rather than God’s. They delight in looking at coins in a chest.

Therefore the Lord wished to be poor in the world, in order to make riches contemptible and to teach that other riches must be sought. Hence he says: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). And he says to his disciples: “You are not of this world; if you were of this world, the world would love what was its own” (John 15:19); and therefore do not wonder if the world hates you. To show that costly garments do not please him, he says: “Those who wear soft garments are in the houses of kings” (Matt. 11:8), as though saying: Those clothed in soft garments belong not to the court of the supreme King, but to the courts of earthly kings.

To show that the poor, rather than the rich, are blessed, he says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). That is, I have opened my kingdom to them; I have made them my household counselors. Yet, lest the rich should despair, he gave them counsel: though the kingdom of heaven was not theirs, he commanded them to make friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that those friends might receive them into eternal tabernacles. Again: “Whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person shall receive a righteous person’s reward” (Matt. 10:41). For whoever supports a righteous person shall share in the righteous person’s reward.

Again Isaiah says: “Blessed is he who has his seed in Zion and his household in Jerusalem.” Therefore sow, dearest brethren, in Zion—that is, in heaven—where a hundredfold return is promised for all that you sow there. Multiply your money there. Place it in the Lord’s hands; for whoever gives to the poor gives to the Lord, who said: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40). [Col. 0838C] For if you place your treasure there, your heart will dwell there. “For where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Matt. 6:26).

Do not hesitate to entrust your property to such a Lord, who neither knows nor can deceive, since he is true in his promises. Learn from Martin how good it is to clothe a poor person. For when he had divided his cloak in half with a needy man, Christ appeared to him at night, clothed in that same garment, saying: “Martin, still a catechumen, has clothed me with this garment.” A certain householder too, accustomed to receive poor people as guests every day, once received Christ among the others [Col. 0838D]. For the Lord wished to show him that what he did for his members, he did for himself. When someone wished to pour water over his hands among the others, he disappeared. But that night Christ appeared to him and said: “On other days you received me in my members; today you received me in my own person.”

Therefore receive Christ into your homes, 759 brothers; set Christ at your tables. Clothe Christ; and this is the fast the Lord has chosen: “Break your bread for the hungry, bring the needy and wandering into your house; when you see one naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. 58:7). Behold, brothers, the flesh of the poor person is our flesh [Col. 0839A]. For the nature is the same. How, then, can you see it naked without compassion? Do you wish to receive mercy from God? Show mercy to this person. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7).—“Be merciful, as your Father also is merciful” (Luke 6:36).

Do not neglect the fire of sin. Do you wish to extinguish this fire? You possess water with which to extinguish it. Almsgiving is water: for just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin. Do you wish to cleanse your heart? Give alms. Hear what the Lord says to the Pharisees: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11:41). Daniel gave this counsel to King Nebuchadnezzar: “Redeem, O king, your sins by alms” [Col. 0839B] (Dan. 4:24).

Therefore, dearest brothers, if you truly desire to be rich, love true riches. Through money you lost God; through money be reconciled to him, so that he may prepare for you a place among his poor. And may the God of peace, who redeemed us from death, fit you for every good work, that you may do his will—to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## CIX [On Various Matters XXII]. ON THE WORKS OF MERCY  
[Note: [Col. 0839D] From Victorinus.]

Our Lord, not wishing any one of us to perish, and seeking fruit from his trees in his Church, as in his field, does not cease to admonish us, before the time of pruning comes, when he must cut down the fruitless trees, that while there is time [Col. 0839C], and while, with God’s help, the matter lies in our power, we should do good works. For when the time for doing good has passed, nothing remains but repentance.

No one will then say to you, “Clothe the naked,” where immortality will be everyone’s garment. No one will say to you, “Receive the stranger,” where all live in their own homeland; for now we are strangers in this same world. No one will say, “Visit the sick,” where everlasting health exists; no one will say, “Bury the dead,” where death does not exist. All these offices of mercy will not be necessary in eternal life, where there will be peace alone and everlasting joy.

At this present time we do not sufficiently consider [that is, know] how greatly God commends works of mercy to us, and makes even his saints love [that is, help the poor] [Col. 0839D], so that we may make friends for ourselves here from the mammon of iniquity, that when we fail they may receive us into eternal dwellings. For when the servants of God, while continually calling upon God, sometimes need those who possess the riches of the world and distribute alms, these people act as princes do with earthly substance, so that they may deserve to have a share with them in the reward.

I said this because of the joy of kingdoms, of which we heard earlier. Did not God make his servant [perhaps “raven”] feed Elijah? (3 Kings 17). Did not birds minister to him when people were lacking? Did not a raven bring him bread in the morning and meat in the evening? [Col. 0840A] God therefore showed that he can feed his servants from whatever source and in whatever way he wishes; and yet, in order that a devout widow might be able to feed him, he caused him to be in need.

Thus Elijah’s need became abundance for the devout woman’s soul; and what Elijah could not give the widow from his own resources, he gave her abundantly from God’s mercy. Hence it is evident that God’s servants sometimes do not have, so that those who do have may be tested. That widow had nothing; what her husband had left her was exhausted, and she was about to die with her children. So she went out to gather two pieces of wood in order to make bread for herself, and then Elijah saw her: the man of God saw her when she was seeking those two pieces of wood.

That woman bore the figure of the Church. Two pieces of wood make a cross; she sought, though about to die, the means by which she might live forever. [Col. 0840B] Thus, with the mystery foreshadowed, Elijah runs to her whom he had heard to be needy. She tells him her intention and says that she will die when she has used up what remains.

Where, then, is what the Lord said to Elijah: “Go to Zarephath of the Sidonians; for there I have commanded a widow to feed you”? (3 Kings 17:9). You see how God commands, not in the ear, but in the heart. Do we read that some prophet was sent to that woman and told her, “Behold, the Lord says: my hungry servant is coming to you; minister to him from what you have. Do not fear want: I shall supply what you give”? We do not read that this was said to her. Nor do we read that an angel was sent to her in a dream and foretold Elijah’s coming, or that anyone admonished the woman concerning feeding him. [Col. 0840C]

But God commands in wonderful ways. Those to whom the Lord speaks in their thoughts are said to have been commanded by his speaking, by his inward suggestion in the heart, of what was needed for the widow’s soul. Thus also in the prophecy [of Jonah, chapter VII] we read that the Lord commanded the worm to gnaw the root of the gourd. What does “he commanded” mean, except that he prepared its heart? By God’s inspiration, therefore, that widow had a heart prepared to obey. Such was the one who had come; such was the one called with Elijah: he who was in Elijah to command was himself in the widow to obey.

“Go,” he says, “make for me first out of your poverty; your riches shall not fail.” For the widow’s estate was a little flour and a little oil, and it did not fail. Who has such an estate? Secretly the widow fed the servant [Col. 0840D] of God, whose entire estate hung upon a nail. What poverty could be happier than this? She received for herself such things as she hoped for at the end.

I have said this so that we may not hope for the reward of our sowing in the very time when we have sown. Here we sow the harvest of good works with labor, but in the future we shall gather its fruit, according to what was said: “They went forth and wept as they scattered their seed; but they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125:6).

For this was done as a sign, not as a household provision. That widow who fed the man of God received this: what she sowed was not great, nor did she reap [perhaps “and”] a great harvest. [Col. 0841A] The fact that the flour did not fail and the oil was not diminished until the Lord gave rain upon the face of the earth was temporary; yet then she began to be more needy, when the Lord deigned to send rain. Then she would have to labor, not wait, but gather the fruits of the field; whereas when it did not rain, her sustenance did not come easily.

[Note: [Col. 0841D] Perhaps the particle *non* does not appear superfluous for the proper sense.]

This sign, which God had granted her not merely for a few days, was a sign of the future life, where our reward cannot fail. God is our flour. Just as it had not failed through those years, so he will not fail for eternity. Let us hope for such a reward when we give alms. Nor should anyone perhaps delay because of such a thought and say: “I shall feed some hungry servant of God, and my jar will not fail; I shall always find the oil in my vessel [Col. 0841B] full.” Do not seek this. Sow securely; your harvest, whether sooner or later, will come; but when it comes, it will have no end.

## CX [On Various Matters XXIII]. ON THE MORTIFICATION OF THE FIVE SENSES  
[Note: [Col. 0842D] From Victorinus.]

“Know, dearest brothers, that our old man has been crucified, so that the body of sin may be destroyed and we may no longer serve sin” (Rom. 6:6).

The Apostle brings us joyful news, beloved; and because it is a common good, he invites everyone together to hear it. You had a most evil enemy of the soul: she overthrew the whole world and, although she was a handmaid, nevertheless compelled her mistress to serve her. [Col. 0841C] And who was that handmaid? The flesh, of course, concerning which the Apostle says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, but the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17). For these two oppose each other; indeed, they corrupt all so thoroughly that scarcely anyone could resist its will—rather, it had sold everyone to Satan.

Thus the Apostle speaks in the person of the fleshly human being: “But I am fleshly, sold under sin” (Rom. 7:14). No struggle is more grievous than that in which one feeds one’s own enemy, when the one who attacks is from one’s own household, when one does every good thing for him and he repays evil. Such is the flesh: the more it is nourished, the more it exults, and the more it rises up against the soul.

It has five servants, namely the five senses of the body, through which it led the soul captive [Col. 0841D]. For when anyone sins, he is either deceived through seeing, drawn through hearing, enticed by unlawful smells, delighted through eating, or performs evil by his hands. By these five powers the flesh overcame the first human being, and the human being yielded, though placed in Paradise. But it first attacked the woman, as the weaker part.

Hear how the woman sinned by the five senses of the body. Through her ears she received and assented to the devil’s persuasion, when he communicated such things, saying: “On whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:5). Behold how the woman yielded through hearing. Now observe how she was deceived by smell and sight, as Scripture says: “The woman saw that the tree was good, sweet for eating, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful in appearance” (ibid., 6). When it says “sweet,” she was captured by smell; when it says “beautiful to the eyes,” she was captured by sight. Two servants still remain, which perpetrated the whole crime: touch and taste. See, then, how through them the flesh completed what it had begun. For it is written: “And she took of its fruit and ate” (ibid.). Touch therefore served; taste completed the sin.

Thus, when the origin of all human beings had been overthrown, those servants afterward subjected the world. Seeing, therefore, that the flesh so conquered the world [Col. 0842B], because the handmaid had subjected her mistress to herself, the Lord and our Redeemer devised, together with his mercy, a plan by which he might free the world from this captivity. He put on our enemy in order to conquer and restrain her and weaken her servants, so that thereafter his own people could resist her and the mistress might govern her own household.

He therefore chose a fitting punishment, namely the cross, upon which he would crucify our enemy and punish our senses. The eyes saw the shamefulness of punishment and those who mocked, and experienced the darkness of death; the ears heard the foulest reproaches; the mouth said, “I thirst” (John 17:28), 763 and tasted the bitterness of gall and vinegar; the hands were crucified, and the entire flesh suffered there, so that it might wholly be subject to us and thereafter obey the soul.

This is the message which the Apostle declares, saying: Know, dearest brothers, that our old man has been crucified—that is, the flesh was weakened on the cross. Therefore you no longer have an excuse for struggling with it. Behold, it lies defeated; behold, the handmaid has been scourged. Do not nourish her any longer, lest she again grow proud and again entice you into sins; for this is why the Lord crucified her: that the body of sin might be destroyed and that we might no longer serve sin.

This is the victory, this is the crucifixion, prefigured through Joshua. For we read in the Old Testament that when Moses had died, Joshua brought the people of Israel into the promised land and routed [perhaps “disturbed”] some peoples of that region, while turning others away from himself by fear. It happened that the lord of a certain great city [Col. 0842D], called Gibeon, had made an alliance with Joshua (Josh. 9). When the five kings of that region heard that the Gibeonites had made an alliance with Joshua, they went up to fight against Gibeon. The Gibeonites therefore sent to Joshua, that he might bring them help.

Joshua accordingly attacked the five kings and threw them into confusion before Israel; and he sent great stones upon them from heaven, and more died from the stones of hail. Joshua prayed to the Lord that the sun should stand still opposite Gibeon, and the moon likewise, and that they should not move until the children of Israel had fully avenged themselves upon their enemies. Thus the sun stood in the midst of heaven [Col. 0843A] and did not hasten to set for the space of one day. Never before or afterward was there such a long day, the Lord obeying the voice of a man.

The five kings fled and hid themselves in a cave. Joshua was informed that they had hidden in the cave. Therefore, after the other fugitives had been defeated, he ordered the kings to be brought out of the cave and said to the leaders of his army: “Go and put your feet upon the necks of these kings” (Josh. 10:24). When this was done, he hanged them upon five stakes and killed them; and they hung until evening. When the sun was setting, he ordered his companions to take them down from the gibbets and throw them into the cave in which they had hidden; and they placed enormous stones over them.

This, dearest brothers, is the figure of our conflict [Col. 0843B]. Joshua is Christ, because Joshua himself is called Jesus, so that the one who signified him might also share his name. Our Jesus brought the people of Israel—that is, the faithful—into the land of the living when he came into the world to call us, defeat our enemies, and lead us, once freed, back to the kingdom of heaven.

The Gibeonites signify 764 sinners who are joined to Christ through faith and good works. The five kings are the five bodily senses, which endeavor to subject faithful souls who are reconciled to Christ through faith and good works. They experience battle and, as faithful persons, flee to Christ’s aid. Christ and his preachers attacked the five kings: Christ by resisting and giving help, teachers by admonishing. The stones which came [Col. 0843C] from heaven are the scourges by which he corrects people, subdues the flesh, and weakens the pleasures of the senses by restraining them.

The sun and moon stood still for the space of one day because, before Christ came into the world, the moon—that is, the Church—was waning and tending toward its setting, since there were few faithful people of Christ. The sun, that is, Christ, was passing away, because they had sinned and was setting in almost all. But in the time of grace he stood still, while he set human minds aflame with the ardor of his faith; and that standing will last for one day, that is, throughout the whole time of grace.

The five kings hid in a cave because the five senses are always sunk in earthly matters and rely upon the acts of the body rather than service to God. But God draws them out from earthly matters when he compels them to serve the soul and apply themselves to good work. [Col. 0843D] He commanded the leaders to place the necks of the kings beneath their feet when he enjoins preachers and teachers to restrain fleshly pleasures both in themselves and in others, so that the flesh may no longer exercise such power in us. He hung the kings on stakes because he crucified the old man with himself. Toward evening the kings were taken down from the gibbets and shut up in the cave, because in the evening Christ’s members were taken down and laid in the tomb, and the entrance of the monument was closed by a stone.

You have heard, dearest brothers, how the power of our enemies was weakened by the cross. Hence the Apostle: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world!” (Gal. 6:14).

Therefore prepare yourselves for spoil, confident of victory, to which Solomon invites us when he says: “My son, when you come to the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1). Close the doors of the body if you wish to be delivered from the snare of temptation. Hear what the Lord says in the Gospel: “When you pray, enter into your chamber” (Matt. 6:6). The person enters the chamber who ceases to delight in external things, flees inwardly to the mind, and closes the doors of the five senses.

If you wish to despise the desires of the flesh, remember ashes; remember what you will become and where you are going. Recall what was said to the human being: “You are ashes, and to ashes you shall return.” Keep in memory what Job says: “I am to be consumed like rottenness [Col. 0844B], and like a garment eaten by moths” (Job 13:28). This Job 765 excellently describes the misery of the human being and the brevity [of his life] when he says: “A human being born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries” (Job 14:1).

For one who fears death must always fear evil action. Hence Solomon: “Remember your last things, and you shall never sin” (Ecclus. 7:40). What do you expect in this warfare? For human life upon earth is warfare. Expect eternal, not hourly, goods. Expect to rise with Christ in glory. Say with blessed Job: “All the days in which I now serve as a soldier, I wait until my change comes; you will call me, and I shall answer you” (Job 14:14).

When eye, ear, hand, or nostril persuades you toward something [forbidden] [Col. 0844C], do not yield to them. Rather, consider that they will be food for worms and be reduced to dust; that they are from ashes and shall return to ashes. If a sinner ought at some time to repent in ashes, according to Job, who says: “I reproach myself and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:6), it is fitting that ashes should repent in ashes. Therefore, if the human being is ashes, if he is rottenness, “why does earth and ashes grow proud?” (Ecclus. 10:9).—“Why do you glory in wickedness, you who are powerful in iniquity?” (Ps. 51:1).

Wretches flourish in riches. Behold, sinners themselves, abounding in the age, have acquired riches. But when Christ’s poor see this, they laugh at them. As David says: “The righteous shall see him and laugh at him, and shall say: Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and prevailed in his vanity” [Col. 0844D] (ibid., 6). But because their storehouses are full, overflowing from this into that, they called blessed the people for whom these things exist. But this is false, David says: it is not for that reason that they are blessed; rather, “Blessed is the people whose God is the Lord” (Ps. 143:15).

We have taught you, brothers, how you should resist the flesh and its members, remembering from what they come and into what they will be reduced. But above all there is a certain spiritual key by which all things must be kept: namely, the banner of the cross, the remembrance of Christ’s Passion. Whenever temptations of the world come upon you, make the sign of the cross upon your members [Col. 0845A], so that those which were weakened through it may still be restrained by its sign.

In this matter Moses commanded in Egypt that the two doorposts and the lintel should be smeared with blood, so that the destroying angel might not enter (Exod. 11). The two doorposts are body and soul, which must be fortified with Christ’s blood: the body through receiving the sacrament, the soul through conformity. The lintel, brothers, is that which must always be fortified by the sign of the cross. But if the doors of the body are guarded [perhaps “closed”], the destroying angel will not be admitted.

To this cross, brothers—to embracing the Passion—because in this way he triumphed over our enemies and guards us with his banner, the Lord comes today into Jerusalem. Let us therefore go out and crucify our flesh with its vices and desires [Col. 0845B]; let us receive his reproach; let us die to sins for him, so that as he accepted death for us, so we may accept death for him. For otherwise we shall not be joined to the Church [perhaps: “which must be rightly administered”] unless we first die to sins.

Hence Peter was commanded in a vision, when a vessel full of unclean animals was offered to him: “Slay and eat what they are, and make them like yourself.” But the Apostle exhorts us to slay ourselves, saying: “I beseech you through the mercy of God to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God” (Rom. 12:1). Let us therefore sacrifice ourselves to God by groaning and weeping. “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50:19).

There are two kinds of sacrifice [Col. 0845C], one hidden and the other manifest. Hence it was said to the sons of Zebedee, James and John: “You will indeed drink my cup” (Matt. 20:23). Yet James [the word *alone* is missing] died by the sword, which is manifest martyrdom; while the other ended his life without the shedding of blood, but suffered hidden martyrdom, now by fasting, now by laboring.

Thus the Lord commanded us to carry the cross when he said: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16:24). This is the cup of suffering, concerning which David says: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I shall take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115:13): namely, the cup of suffering.

May Christ, who died for us while we were sinners, through his grace make us dead to sin, so that our soul may rise in virtues. He lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## CXI [On Various Matters XXIV]. ON ADAM’S SIN AND OUR CAPTIVITY ARISING FROM IT  
[Note: [Col. 0845D] From Saint-Germain.]

“My people went down into Egypt at the beginning, to dwell there as a settler, and Assyria oppressed him without cause . . . . . My people were taken away for nothing; their rulers act unjustly, says the Lord” (Isa. 52:4).

The Father of mercies and God of all consolation, in a prophetic lament, reveals the fall of the first human being and the ruin of all posterity in him, grieving and complaining as he says: “My people went down into Egypt,” and so forth. This is said by him who, “seeing the city, wept over it, saying: If only you too had known the things that belong to your peace; but now they are hidden from your eyes” [Col. 0846A] (Luke 19:41).—“Jerusalem, Jerusalem . . . . . how often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling!” (Matt. 23:37).

What an abundance of the most merciful Father’s tenderness is conveyed in these words, by which the Almighty’s good and perfect will is declared not to be empty or unfulfilled. For when he says, “I wished to gather your children, and you were unwilling,” he by no means indicates that what the Almighty willed would remain undone—he who did whatever he willed in heaven and on earth—but shows that it is brought to effect, although earthly Jerusalem is unwilling and resists. “I wished,” therefore, he says, “to gather your children, and you were unwilling”; that is, all whom I gathered I caused, by your will, always to be obstinately disposed.

For this is that fleshly city from which is required all righteous blood, shed from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of the son of Barachiah. This is the water of contradiction—that is, the contradicting people—which went down into Egypt in the beginning, because in the first parents it fell into the depths, because it did not recognize. What did it not recognize? It did not perceive the deceiver’s fraud; it did not foresee the fall of the one tempted. For if it had known the enemy’s deceit and its own ruin [Col. 0846C], it would never have delayed over what was forbidden. It had no foreknowledge of its own fall and no discernment of hostile snares; and therefore it went down from Jerusalem into Jericho, from Paradise into Egypt, from the life of contemplation into the death of transgression, from the blessedness of angelic glory into the misery of Gehenna.

It went down in three ways. The first descent was the touching of the forbidden tree, by scornfully violating the prescribed law. The second occurred when it was cast out of Paradise into the place it had assigned itself by sinning—that is, into this valley of tears and lamentation. The third was when, after death, it descended to the lower regions. The first descent, therefore, is from justice to iniquity; the second [Col. 0846D] from rest to misery; the third from misery to the infernal prison. In the first the soul was bound; in the second the flesh was loosed; in the third both are punished.

In these three ways the people of God went down into Egypt in the beginning—that is, in the first parents: created by God without any vice, placed in the abundance of good and the fullness of riches. For God took the human being whom he had formed and placed him in the Paradise of delight, to work and keep it. The human being was placed amid delights, but in order to work and keep: namely, to advance [perhaps *proficeret*, “make progress”] and not fail. The one who advances works; the one who does not fail keeps. The one works who performs the good that is commanded; the one keeps who avoids the evil that is forbidden.

Since, then, the good things commanded cannot benefit unless the evil things prohibited are avoided, it was said with great providence that he should work and keep. For everything done perishes unless it is carefully guarded. He does not keep the good that he does unless the forbidden evil steals in. A multicolored garment does not please the heavenly bridegroom. Therefore we must always do good and carefully guard ourselves in the very good works, because evils creep into good works when those same good things that we do so lift the mind up that they serve not the doer [perhaps “the action”] but self-exaltation.

This is signified in the book of Maccabees, where we read (1 Macc. 6:46) that Eleazar, striking the elephant in battle, brought it down, but fell dead beneath it [Col. 0847B]. Such are some people who do good things indeed but fail through pride in those very things, because pride creeps into beneficent acts as well. This is the little beast that consumed more of Absalom’s army than the sword. This is the greatest sin, that is, the heavenly vice: first among those departing and last among those returning [variant: “first among those beginning, and last among those ending”].

Thus the first human being, while placed in the delights of Paradise, migrated from good, to which he had been lifted up, into evil. Jeremiah speaks of him: “Hearing, I heard Ephraim migrating: Ephraim, a son honorable to me, a delicate child” (Jer. 31:8). Ephraim is interpreted “fruitfulness” or “abundance.” This is the first human being, created without sin; for by the condition of nature all human beings existed in him, just as all sinned in him [Col. 0847C].

He is rightly Ephraim because he excelled in the abundance and fullness of knowledge, power, and grace; and therefore he was an honorable son and a delicate child. For endowed with the honor of God’s likeness and the seal of his image, he was nourished in the delights of Paradise, and therefore is called a delicate child. But, though he was in honor and abundance, he did not understand. For he said: “I shall never be moved” (Ps. 29:7); and therefore “he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. 48:13).

Therefore Ephraim, the honorable son, the delicate child, migrated from the image and likeness of God in which he was created into the region of unlikeness: as it were from Jerusalem, which is “vision of peace,” into Babylon of confusion [Col. 0847D], and into Egypt of darkness and tribulation. For Babylon is interpreted “confusion,” but Egypt “darkness” or “tribulation.”

Therefore iniquity came forth from the fatness of the first-formed human, as though the richness of the earth had burst out upon the earth. For just as thick earth, luxuriant because of the abundance of its fertility, produces thorns and thistles, so Adam, endowed with free choice and abundance of good, produced the thorns of transgression and the thistles of curse, by which he bound all his posterity. For a heavy burden lies upon the children of Adam, and through this he became like a divining 769 idolater. For Samuel bears witness that resisting is like the sin of divination, and refusing to obey is like the crime of idolatry [Col. 0848A].

Adam contradicted and did not obey God saying: “From every tree of Paradise eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat” (Gen. 2:16). He commanded two things: one concerning action, the other concerning keeping. It belonged to action that he should eat from all the other trees; to keeping, that he should not touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. But because he neglected and failed to attain that for which he was placed in Paradise—that is, because he forgot to eat his bread—he migrated from there and became captive.

This migration is evil and dreadful. This migration is not revelation, but darkening. It is not Galilee, to which Christ went before his disciples, saying, “I shall go before you into Galilee” (Matt. 26:32); but it is Galilee [Col. 0848B], that is, a place of rolling or wallowing, to which Adam went before his descendants. For he is the origin; we are the offspring of misery.

The Lord expresses through Isaiah the manner of this harmful migration, saying: “My people went down into Egypt, to dwell there as a settler.” For by this migration he became a settler in Egypt, an inhabitant of the world, a citizen of Babylon—he who had been an inhabitant of Paradise, a companion of angels, a beholder of God.

The cause of this migration was the word spoken to the first parents in Paradise: “On whatever day you eat, you shall know good and evil” (Gen. 3:5), just as the word spoken in Nebuchadnezzar’s court was the cause of the Jews’ destruction, when it was said that all nations ought to be subject to him, and added that the Jews alone were rebelling. Therefore Assur [or the Assyrian], stirred up [Col. 0848C], gathered an army, came against Jerusalem, destroyed it, and carried the people of God captive.

As the cause of that figurative captivity was the aforementioned word uttered in Nebuchadnezzar’s court, so the cause of our spiritual captivity was the serpent’s word spoken to the first parents in Paradise: namely, “At whatever hour you eat, you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil.” The human being assented to this seductive promise, and so perished in descending into Egypt.

The serpent deceived the human being by a threefold deception, bound him as it were with a threefold cord, and deceitfully promised him all that is in the world. Enticed by these things, the human being put earthly things before heavenly. For there are three things in the world that must not be loved, as John says: “Little children, do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world; for there is nothing in the world except the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” [Col. 0848D] (John 2:16). These are three principal and, as it were, capital vices: pleasure, covetousness [variant: “avarice”], and vain glory.

By these three the devil drew the human being into the region of unlikeness, though he retained the likeness of God, in which he had been created, through three others: memory, understanding, and love. The tempter therefore set forth three things in order to remove from God by three things the human being who adhered to God through three virtues: so that he who was like the Trinity through a trinity might become unlike it through a trinity.

This is the trinity of vices denoted by those three words: “you shall eat, you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” [Col. 0849A]. For he tempted them by gluttony, saying, “On whatever day you eat”; by pride, “you shall be like gods”; by avarice, or concupiscence, “knowing good and evil.” By this lying, deceitful promise, as by a threefold dart, he wounded the human race in the first-created man, in whom, as the Apostle says, all sinned. The prophet Habakkuk marks this threefold snare of the venomous serpent not without grief and groaning, when he says: “He raised up the whole with a hook; he drew it in his dragnet and gathered it into his net; over this he shall rejoice and exult” (Hab. 1:15).

For the devil, the cruel enemy and roaring lion who prowls about seeking someone to devour, rejoices and exults when he has seized a human being and tramples his life into the earth [Col. 0849B]. Therefore he exulted with immense joy when, in the apostate root, he corrupted all the branches and bound humanity to himself at the paltry price of harmful pleasure. By Adam’s transgression, ruinous bargaining, and deceitful eating, we were sold; that one man, deceived by the serpent’s persuasion and unlawful taking, consigned all his offspring to perpetual slavery.

Such is the custom observed between sellers and buyers: one who gives himself over to another’s ownership first receives from the buyer a price for the loss of his own freedom and the addition of perpetual servitude. This certainly took place between Adam and the serpent. For he received from the death-dealing serpent the harmful price of freedom; departing from natural freedom, he gave himself to the service of him from whom he received the deadly price of the fruit [Col. 0849C]. Hence he subjected all his offspring to the service of the power whose slave he became.

He was created upright, without guilt, without vice; but he did not keep himself upright, because he deserted his ruler and turned aside to the deserter. Falling from the potter’s hand, he became a broken earthen vessel. God permitted this so that, through his misery, he might learn that without God he can do no good. For he could sell himself, but he could not redeem himself. By free choice he sold himself beneath iniquity’s dominion, received as his price a slight pleasure from the forbidden tree, and thus, made captive, says: “But I am carnal, sold under sin” (Rom. 7:14).

Recalling and lamenting this, the corrupted stock says through the Prophet: “I considered the days of old, and I kept eternal years in mind” [Col. 0849D] (Ps. 76:6). For by unlawfully taking the tree of good and evil, he gained the discernment of misery and the distinction of blessedness; and by experience man came to know evil, which he had previously known neither through prudence nor through experience of good. For these two are known differently: good is known through the prudence of good, evil through the experience of evil. Through the prudence of good, good is known and evil is perceived; through the experience of evil, evil is known and good is perceived—known and lost. For he feels what he has lost, since, when the good is lost, it will go ill with him.

Thus fallen man considered the days of old and kept eternal years in mind, because through experience he discovered how far apart were the goods he had lost and the evils he had found: how far the ancient—that is, aged—and old, measurable days, imposed upon him because of sin, differed from the eternal years. As it is said: “You have made my days old and measurable,” compared with the eternal years, whose sweetness he had already tasted and would have enjoyed more fully had he remained standing, when he was to be transferred from animal life to spiritual life [Col. 0850A].

Thus that tree was rightly called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, because by touching what was forbidden man was to distinguish good from evil through experience. Contraries are known from contraries: emptiness from fullness, and hearing from silence. So, from the life which the first parents possessed, the deprivation of that life could be known—the deprivation now called death. That life was sweet, and they feared to lose it. Therefore its sin would not have been persuaded upon them unless they had been told that they would not die from it [Col. 0850B], and would not lose what they loved.

But the devil deceived them through the commandment and killed them by it, when he cast out the hook of pleasure, the dragnet of pride, and the net of greed. Entangled by these, man descended into Egypt; there he grew old, becoming a resident there, according to Baruch: “Hear, O Israel, the commandments of life; receive prudence with your ears. You have grown old in a foreign land; you have been defiled among the dead; you have been counted with those who are in hell; you have forsaken the fountain of living water” (Bar. 3:9).

By these words the Lord admonishes and rebukes us through the prophet Baruch: we are to hear the commandments—the commandments of life—with ears capable of hearing, by which we may hear what the Spirit says. Hence John in the Apocalypse: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” [Col. 0850C] (Rev. 2:7). With these inward ears the Prophet heard, who says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Ps. 84:9).

With these ears are heard the words of life. Those who hear them live inwardly; but those who do not hear them, or hear them only with the bodily ear, have grown old in a foreign land. This is the land of the curse, which the Lord cursed because of Adam’s sin, saying: “Cursed is the earth in your work; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3:18). This is the land of human flesh, which before sin neither hindered the spirit from good nor impelled it toward evil. But after sin the condition of weakened humanity was changed: the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that we do not do whatever we wish [Col. 0850D].

Therefore the prophetic Spirit calls back to prudence, by an honorable name, the human being who had departed into a foreign land—that is, into the region of unlikeness—saying: “O Israel”: namely, my creation and the gift of grace; that is, my Church, which ought to be Israel, “one who sees God.” You who until now have heard words of death, now hear the commandments of life, those which lead you to life, because now are days of life, days of salvation, “giving no offense to anyone.” You, then, who had wandered like a lost sheep, return from the foreign land which the Lord cursed to the land of blessing, concerning which it is said: “You have blessed your land, O Lord” (Ps. 84:2).

This is the holy land in which no one stands “unless, with Moses, he removes the sandals from his feet” [Col. 0851A] (Exod. 3:5), that is, the examples of dead works from his affections. And you who once looked upon false follies, now receive prudence, so that you may know whence you fell and into what: from how great a good to how great a misery you have been reduced.

For you, formerly created in good and placed in blessedness, have grown old in misery and in guilt, becoming a member of the old man; and afterwards, restored and reconciled by the grace of the new man, you fall daily, yet even so assisting grace does not abandon you. You have grown old, then, in a foreign land: in sins and earthly things, loving earthly things which pass away. This is a foreign land, for our homeland is not here among these things, but in heaven, from which we were expelled through the first man’s sin.

How you grew old in the foreign land is shown by what is said: “You have been defiled among the dead,” that is, among sinners, who are dead in soul through sin [Col. 0851B]. For as the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul; without God the soul is like a corpse. Faith, as the hope of immortal life, is the life of mortal life; conversely, unbelief and every harmful superstition are death. Hence Christ says: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. 8:22); and elsewhere: “He who believes in me shall pass from death to life” (John 5), from the death of unbelief, that is, to the life of faith.

Therefore one who is defiled among the dead is counted with those who are in hell, of whom the Prophet says: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous” [Col. 0851C] (Ps. 68:29). A terrible and dreadful sentence is pronounced against sinners: unless they rise through repentance, they are counted in hell. Behold the end of evil work; behold the reward of temporal service: “For the wages of sin,” as the Apostle testifies, “is death” (Rom. 6:23)—not temporal or transitory death, but eternal death. For in hell there is no redemption and no profitable confession, according to the words: “In death there is none who remembers you; but in hell who will confess you?” (Ps. 6:6).

This threat is dreadful. There is no place there for repentance or useful confession, but only for recompense according to merits. After this life we receive what we earn here, because no one earns merit except while in the body. Hence the Apostle says: “We must all be made manifest before the judgment-seat of Christ, that each may receive the things proper to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” [Col. 0851D] (2 Cor. 5:10). He will be judged according to those things in which he is found at the end, according to the saying: “The Lord shall judge the ends of the earth” (1 Sam. 2:10). For as each departs from this life, so shall he be judged in judgment.

Therefore the serpent lies in wait for the heel, that is, for the end, so that at the end of iniquities he may cast a person into eternal destruction. But why have you been defiled and counted among the dead? Because you have forsaken the fountain of living water: namely, Christ, who is the fountain of living waters springing up into eternal life. Whoever drinks from these shall never thirst. By this fountain filth is washed away, mountains are watered, enemies slip and fall.

What then are you doing, wretches? Where are you fleeing, blind ones? You abandon life [Col. 0852A] and hasten toward death; you forsake the living fountain and dig old cisterns that cannot hold living waters. Therefore my people grew old in a foreign land when it went down into Egypt to reside there; and Asshur oppressed it without any cause.

For *Asshur* is interpreted “directing” or “exalted.” This is the devil, who wished to exalt his throne above the stars of heaven, that he might become like the Most High. He oppressed God’s people in Adam when he seduced him by a deceitful promise, but without any cause, since humanity had done him no harm for which he should draw it into sin. Therefore my people was taken away for nothing, since it did not deserve the fraud of seduction. Thus its rulers act unjustly, when they pervert one who is simple and innocent, draw him into the slavery of sin [Col. 0852B], and lead him from the homeland of paradise to inhabit this pilgrimage throughout the whole period of the present life, which proceeds by the recurrence of seven days; they make him live in exile, as it were, for seventy years.

Hence Solomon says: “A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam, from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb until the day they return to the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40:1). Thus the king of the Assyrians led the children of Israel captive to Babylon, oppressing them. Their actual—rather, bodily—captivity was a figure of our spiritual captivity and represents both forms of our Septuagesima, which is observed for seventy days: namely, from the Sunday “The pangs of death surrounded me” (2 Sam. 22:5) until the Saturday in albis. For the children of Israel too were held seventy years in Babylonian captivity [Col. 0852C].

And we are held captive in the exile of this age, as though in a foreign land, throughout the whole sevenfold course of this life, sitting and weeping by the rivers of Babylon and not singing there the new song. Hence in this Septuagesima, which the Church observes, songs of joy and exultation are silenced, as are *Alleluia* and “Glory to God in the highest.” And because God granted the children of Israel permission to return before the seventy years were complete, from which time they began to return, but when the seventy years were finished they returned fully from Babylon to Jerusalem under Jesus the high priest: so, before the end of our Septuagesima—that is, this sevenfold course—through Jesus Christ, the high priest who comes in the last age, the means has been prepared for us to return from the Babylon of this world to the heavenly Jerusalem [Col. 0852D].

For our priest redeemed us from the Assyrian’s power at the price of spotless blood. Hence Habakkuk: “He who comes shall come, and shall not delay”; and “the soul of him who is unbelieving shall not be upright in him” (Hab. 2:3). And Isaiah: “Shall prey be taken from the strong man, or can what has been taken captive by the mighty be saved? For thus says the Lord: Indeed, captivity shall be taken from the strong” (Isa. 47:24).

For Christ, the stronger one, came upon and bound the strong devil; and through the shedding of his blood for the remission of sins, captivity has been delivered from the hand of the mighty. Yet in the mind, not in the flesh, we await the redemption of our body; nor has liberation been wholly accomplished in the soul, because sin exists, though not in us. We have therefore already begun to return under Jesus our leader, because we have begun to love him. For one begins to depart from Babylon when one begins to love God.

This return will be consummated when the sevenfold course of this life has been completed. The Church fittingly signifies this in Septuagesima: near its end, that is, on the Paschal Sabbath, where the sacraments of our redemption are performed, she sings *Alleluia*, because she is redeemed in part and is therefore glad; yet because a long way still remains, a long stretch of labor lies before her. But why is the Tract—that is, “Praise”—and *Alleluia* sung with the Gradual throughout the following week? Because we are travelling on the way of this life [Col. 0853A], and therefore laboring and fearing various perils; redeemed in part and still to be redeemed in part, we rejoice in part and grieve in part. We rejoice in hope; we groan in actuality. “For every creature,” as the Apostle says, “groans and labors in birth until now” (Rom. 8:22).

But on the Saturday in albis, when this Septuagesima concludes, a double *Alleluia* is sung, expressing the joy of our twofold glorification. For when the sevenfold course of this exile has been completed—during which, as long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord—our twofold nature, glorified, will possess, as it were, a twofold sabbath-rest. We shall be placed at God’s right hand and, rejoicing without end in the twofold robe, shall praise him. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## CXII [On Various Matters XXV]. ON THE VARIOUS DEPARTURES OF THE SOUL, THAT IT MAY REACH GOD

[Note: From the Saint-Germain manuscript.]

[Col. 0853C]

“Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land which I shall show you . . . and you shall be blessed” (Gen. 12:1).

Great indeed and difficult is that to which the Lord exhorts us under the figure of Abraham; yet it is beneficial and healthful for those who observe it. For what is said historically to the father of many nations, that is, Abraham, is preached mystically to his children—that is, to us, who are his children not by flesh but by faith. For those who are of the flesh are not counted in Abraham’s seed, but those who are of faith.

Each one of us, therefore, brothers, is admonished in Abraham to depart from spiritual Egypt, hunger after the hidden manna, and seek it with all earnestness; for everyone who seeks finds, and whoever asks receives—provided that he seeks and asks in the name of Jesus, like the Gospel merchant who, seeking fine pearls and finding one precious pearl, sold all that he had and bought it.

Behold, you all profess to seek it. For what human being does not desire life and love to see good days? All indeed confess that they wish for life and love to see good days; but they do not truly love, and do not find the precious pearl and hidden manna, because they do not seek as those who find seek. They seek and desire the best thing, but they do not seek it in its own land; therefore they neither find nor receive it.

For that precious pearl itself—that is, wisdom, which dwells in the heights, not in the land of those who live pleasantly—says of itself: “The wicked shall seek me and shall not find me,” because they seek by words, not deeds [Col. 0854A]. Many, as the Apostle says, “profess that they know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Titus 2:16). How, then, is that precious pearl, that hidden manna, to be sought? Wisdom herself teaches you, saying: “Do you desire wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will give it to you.”

[Note: “My son, desiring wisdom, preserve righteousness, and God will give it to you” (Ecclus. 1:33).]

Elsewhere, however, it is said: “Do not seek things higher than yourself, nor search into things stronger than yourself; but always think upon those things which the Lord has commanded” [Col. 0854B] (Ecclus. 3:22).

Seek, therefore, brothers, the precious pearl as she herself teaches: namely, by keeping the commandments, and you shall find it. For Truth also says in the Gospel: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23)—that is, I with the Father and the Holy Spirit. As though he said: He will find the precious pearl and receive the hidden manna if he loves me and keeps my words.

Love the Lord, therefore, brothers, and keep his words, so that you may thus arrive at the one Word which is the hidden manna: namely, the Word which was in the beginning with God, whom God spoke once—that is, he eternally and unchangeably begot from himself his own Word, equal, coeternal, and consubstantial with himself [Col. 0854C]. The begetter does not precede the begotten in eternity, surpass him in greatness, or excel him in power; he begot a Son whom he did not precede. For the Father was not before the Son. Yet by being born, the Son received from the Father not only that he should be Son, but also that he should exist and be God.

But perhaps this objection slips into your mind: if by being born he received that he should be Son and should exist in his birth, then he was not, nor was he Son. But the Father who begot was; therefore the Father was without the Son, or before the Son. Devout faith rejects this. For in that generation, as in the procession of the Holy Spirit, no temporal intervals are to be imagined; there is no before or after there. No alteration of past and future is to be sought there, nor the shadow of succession; rather, the truth of primordial equality and likeness is to be believed [Col. 0854D].

For the Son, in being born, received from the Father to exist and to be Son; and the Holy Spirit, by proceeding, received this from both. Yet neither did the Son begin to exist by being born, nor the Holy Spirit by proceeding; but the Son is always Son, and the Holy Spirit always Holy Spirit. As the generation of the Son is unutterable, so the procession of the Holy Spirit is ineffable.

This, then, is the hidden manna and precious pearl “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2), which, as has been said, very many profess to seek and love, yet do not find [Col. 0855A]. For if they found and bought it, it would not seem too costly, nor would any price be withheld for acquiring it. Oh, how little progress that person has made who, distracted by manifold labor, has not yet found what he seeks, does not yet know what he professes, and does not yet possess what is desired, because it is sought where it cannot be found! Where? In outward things, when the Lord says: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21).

Why, then, do you seek outside yourselves what you cannot find outside yourselves? Since what you seek is within you, it is near you. But how near, the Apostle teaches: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Rom. 10:8). Have you heard where the pearl you seek is? Come then and buy it. Come, buy and eat the hidden manna, as Isaiah says: “All who thirst, come to the waters”—the living waters, that is, of the Old and New Law—“and you who have no silver” [Col. 0855B] (Isa. 55:1): no Ciceronian eloquence or philosophical industry. Hasten by faith, without the silver of earthly philosophy and empty deceit.

“Why do you spend silver, and not on breads, and your labor, and not on satisfaction?” (ibid., 2). Why do you expend the industry of your intellect and the effort of your study not on spiritual bread, where refreshment and life are found, but on the leaves of words and the subtleties of empty questions, which fly over the mind and do not satisfy the soul? How long do you love—that is, embrace in desire—and laboriously seek vanity and falsehood: happiness in these temporal things, which are vain and false, pass away, and do not accomplish what they promise?

Rather seek and buy the hidden manna at the price of faith and good work. For through faith what is not seen is believed, and through patience what is not possessed is awaited. “For now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face” [Col. 0855C] (1 Cor. 13:12). Thus that hidden manna is in us in some manner, and in another manner is not in us. It is surely in us through faith and hope, because “faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not appearing” (Heb. 11:1); but it is not in us by sight.

“For we walk by faith,” says the Apostle, “and not by sight, because while we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:6), although he himself is wholly everywhere and present. For though he is present, we do not grasp his presence nor behold his form. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel of the disciples and other elect: “That where I am, they also may be with me” (John 14). He did not simply say, “Where I am, they also may be,” because even the wicked are where he who never departs is present; but the wicked are not where he is, because they do not cleave to him.

The good, however, are not there where he is and with him [Note: This negation seems superfluous and contrary to the sense.], because they cleave to him in present faith and in the false appearances of life [or: likeness of life]; but in the future they will cleave to him by sight, when the truth of faith and the reality of hope succeed [Col. 0855D]. There the hidden manna shall be revealed, and it will be in the land of the living, the desirable land, to which the Spirit of God calls us, saying: “Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house.”

For we are spiritual Hebrews, to whom a threefold departure from the land of the curse is enjoined, just as it was to the children of Israel from Egypt, when Moses said: “The Lord, God of the Hebrews, has called us from Egypt, that we may go a three days’ journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to our God” (Exod. 3:18).

The three days’ journey is understood as Christ, who through the mysteries of three days—his passion, burial, and resurrection—procured the salvation of his people [Col. 0856A]. The three days’ journey is also understood as faith in the Trinity, through which we depart from the Egypt of vices. It is also understood as a threefold way of declining and a threefold form of progressing.

For just as one departs from God into the region of unlikeness in three ways—by evil thought, word, and deed—so, when these are turned to their opposites, one advances in three ways and returns to God’s likeness: by thinking, speaking, and doing good. Thus, just as there is a threefold difference in the bad ground upon which the seed falls—some falls by the way, some upon rocky ground, and some among thorns—so there is a threefold distinction in the fruit of good ground: seed falling into the ground produced some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, and some a hundredfold [Col. 0856B].

Let us therefore go the three days’ journey in the wilderness: that is, in faith in Christ’s passion, burial, and resurrection; in faith in the Holy Trinity; and marked by a threefold form. Called inwardly by God, let us go out of Egypt—that is, the darkness of vices and ignorance—into the wilderness, where we serve not two masters but one; where the left hand does not know what the right does; where dying flies do not destroy the sweetness of ointment, that is, of pure prayer.

Good is this wilderness, in which the sacrifice of righteousness and praise is offered to God. For praise is not becoming in the mouth of a sinner whose acts are corrupt in many ways. Wicked and destructive is that wilderness of which it is said: “Woe to one who is alone” (Ecclus. 4:10), that is, to one who lacks charity. For one abandoned by God is alone.

Let us therefore travel by this way and reach the desirable land, where we shall eat the hidden manna. Let us go out, then, from our land, our kindred, and our father’s house. These three things must be fled, so that through three others we may arrive at the pearl of the Trinity and, as it were, return with the Magi to our own country by another way [Col. 0856D].

First, then, “go out from your land.” A human being’s land is the will of the flesh, because he comes from earth and returns to earth when he is subject to earthly pleasures and serves carnal desires. Let a person therefore put off fleshly pleasures and, walking in the Spirit, cut away carnal desires, if he wishes to attain the desirable land. Hence the Apostle: “Walk in the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh” (Gal. 5:16). And Peter: “Cast away fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul” (1 Pet. 2:11).

This is an evil land, which brings forth such shoots. Of it it is said: “Cursed is the earth in your work; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” [Col. 0857A] (Gen. 3:18). This is the pleasure of the flesh, inflicted through the curse of the first transgression: an incentive to vices, producing for the soul the shameful passions as thorns and thistles. This land does not nourish, but dissolves. This is water without substance. Hence the Prophet: “Perhaps our soul would have passed through intolerable water” (Ps. 123:5).

Water without substance is the sweetness of this life, infected with vices and sins. It has poverty, not substance; want, not subsistence, because the things which generate such sweetness do not truly exist but all pass away without fruit. For example, consider those who gain gold and such things by sinning. It is without substance because one loses faith here and, descending into hell, does not carry these things with him. “For when a man dies, he shall not take all things, nor shall his glory descend with him” [Col. 0857B] (Ps. 48:13).

He therefore lost the greater in order to gain the lesser; he increased his money and diminished, or extinguished, his faith. Something—I know not what—abounds in the chest, but something much greater has diminished in the heart. You rejoice over the chest and do not lament over the heart.

In this water without substance, that prodigal son lost his substance (Luke 15), which he had received from the Father. He attached himself to one of the citizens of that country—that is, the region of unlikeness, namely the devil—feeding swine, that is, delighting in earthly and unclean acts, and desiring the husks of the swine, which fill the belly but do not satisfy. So the sweetness of carnal pleasure, though it delights for an hour, nevertheless provides no satiety, but brings upon one a lack of every good.

This water also led astray the hundredth sheep, for which the loving shepherd in the Gospel rejoices to have searched, leaving the ninety-nine in the wilderness [Col. 0857C]. But before restoring it, he threatened it, as though from afar, with the staff of Mosaic law and the rod of prophetic utterance, so that the little sheep, recognizing that it had gone out—rather, had strayed—might be terrified, and thus, wishing to return but unable by itself, might humbly seek the one who would restore it. Washed in the life-giving water of baptism, he would return it to the angelic fellowship from which it had fallen and reconcile to the Father the prodigal son, worn out by long want and long an exile and stranger.

That land, then, is cursed and therefore to be fled, since it is watered with such water. This is not “the living water which the Lord promised to the Samaritan woman, from which whoever drinks shall never thirst” [Col. 0857D] (John 4:10). That water is from rivers of water springing up into eternal life; this, however, is from the rivers of Babylon, beside which holy men sit and weep. They do not have here an abiding city, but seek the city to come and await the redemption of the body.

Therefore the saints sit beside those rivers and do not immerse themselves in them, because, forgetting what lies behind, which they count as dung, they stretch themselves toward what lies ahead.
