They have their dwelling or citizenship in heaven (*conversantes*; perhaps *habitantes*, “dwelling”), while living in the flesh, but they do not walk according to the flesh. Go out, then, from the land of curse [Col. 0858A], that you may attain the land of blessing, which the Lord has blessed. Go out from the land of the dying, which is desert because no saint dwells there; pathless because Christ, who is the way, truth, and life, is not there; and waterless because the rushing river does not gladden it—so that you may reach the land of the living.

Go forth from your kindred. A person’s kindred is curiosity, which is rightly placed after pleasure; for whoever devotes himself to pleasures of the flesh and serves fleshly desires must necessarily be subjected in many ways to curiosity. For example, if someone gives himself to lust, is he not anxiously concerned to discover how he may please a woman and how he may entice her? If to gluttony, does he not seize and extort from every side in order to satisfy his appetite? This vice of curiosity is near and akin to human weakness [Col. 0858B], against which the Lord warns us to keep watch in the Gospel, saying: “Do not be anxious for your life, what you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall put on” (Luke XI, 22). And elsewhere: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow, for each day’s own evil is sufficient for it” (Matt. VI, 34).

Such kindred, then, is evil: it offers no consolation, but begets sorrow. Moreover, the sorrow of the world works death. This kindred disperses the soul among many things, so that it is not directed, with the Prophet, toward seeking the one thing: [Note: [Col. 0857D] “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this will I seek.”] Rather, it is divided by many loves of worldly things and faithlessly occupied by manifold concern for worldly affairs. For nothing is more laborious than to be inflamed by earthly desires. Nothing brings greater anxiety and [Col. 0858C] misery than, abandoning higher things, to be carried away toward outward things by desire for earthly possessions. But nothing is more peaceful, nothing more divine, than to desire nothing in the world.

Therefore the people of Israel receive the observance of the Sabbath as a gift. Egypt, however, was struck by a multitude of flies. For one who follows God receives the Sabbath—that is, repose of mind—so that he may not be wearied by the appetite of fleshly desire. Egypt, that is, the world, is struck by flies—that is, by the importunate cares of desires. Hence Solomon says: “Dying flies spoil the sweetness of ointment” (Ecclus. X, 1); for superfluous thoughts, which arise in a mind thinking carnally, fall short of [read: “destroy”] the sweetness by which one is inwardly anointed through the Spirit. They spoil it because they do not permit him to enjoy its integrity.

Hence we read in the Gospel [Col. 0858D] that, when the crowd had been put out of the house of the ruler of the synagogue, Jesus entered the house, took the girl’s hand, and she arose (Mark V). Therefore the crowd is driven outside so that the girl may be raised up: first the multitude of cares and anxieties is expelled from the hidden places of the heart, and then the soul which lies dead within rises again, brought to life. For while a person disperses himself through innumerable thoughts of desire, he by no means gathers himself back to thoughts of himself, nor does he fully receive Wisdom, who is God—as does the one who wholly withdraws himself from every fluctuation of fleshly thoughts.

Hence Solomon says: [Note: [Col. 0857D] In the original Sangermanensis manuscript this was written, through a copyist’s error: “But the wisdom [Col. 0858D] of the scribe is interpreted as leisure, and he who is diminished in action will perceive it by action.” We have restored the reading as in the Vulgate.] “The wisdom of a scribe comes in a time [Col. 0859A] of leisure; and he who is less occupied with action will gain wisdom” (Ecclus. XXXVIII, 25). And elsewhere: “Let your activities not be many” (Ecclus. XI, 12). And through the Prophet the Lord says: “Be still, and see that I am God” (Ps. XLV, 11). For unless a person withdraws from the tumults of the world and shakes off from the eye of the mind, as it were, the dust of earthly love, he is not able to behold the unbounded simplicity of the Godhead.

Thus this utterly evil kindred of curiosity must be fled, lest the most sweet embrace of the Spirit be lost. “For,” as Solomon says, “wisdom is better than all the most precious riches, and nothing desirable can be compared with it”; wisdom says: “I, wisdom, dwell in counsel and am present among learned thoughts. By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just. [Col. 0859B] By me princes rule, and the mighty decree justice” (Prov. VIII, 11).

The kings are the apostles and other saints, who know how first to govern themselves well, and then the Church subject to them. The lawgivers are the authors [variant: “teachers”] of both Testaments and subsequent writers of the Church; the princes and mighty are the other teachers and rulers of the faithful, who surely possess no good thing except through wisdom. For Wisdom herself says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5). And the Apostle says: “It is not of one who wills, nor of one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX, 16).

Let us therefore depart from that most evil kindred, where wisdom does not dwell or give her voice, whose fruit is better than gold and precious stone and whose offspring are better than choice silver. Receive, [Col. 0859C] therefore, brothers, as Solomon teaches, the discipline of wisdom rather than money; choose instruction rather than treasure. In order to do this, go forth from your kindred—that is, withdraw yourself from the occupations and entanglements of the world—for “no one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs” (II Tim. II, 4).

Go forth also from your father’s house. The father of evils is the devil, according to the saying: “You are from your father the devil, and you do the desires of your father” (John VIII, 44). The devil is called the father of evils not by nature—for God did not create nature evil, as Manichaeus believed—but by imitation; for God made nature good in all things. Indeed, Truth plainly declares this in the preceding words: “And you do the desires [Col. 0859D] of your father”; as though he said: I call you children of the devil because you perform his desires.

Now people become children of the devil in two ways: by the law of conception and by the law of imitation. For they are conceived in sins and iniquities. Hence the Prophet says: “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. L, 7). Since the intercourse of parents is not without lust, the conception of children born from their flesh cannot occur without sin. It is not descent that transmits sin to little children, but lust; nor does the fruitfulness of human nature cause people to be born with sin, but the foulness of lust which human beings possess from the most just condemnation of the first sin.

Therefore David, although born of lawful and just marriage—in which, that is, neither the fault of unfaithfulness [Col. 0860A] nor a stain could be found—nevertheless, because of original sin, by which children are naturally bound over to wrath, not only the children of the ungodly but also all who are born from the sanctified flesh of the righteous, cries out: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. L, 7).

Saint Job also says that no human being is clean from defilement, “not even if his life upon the earth is but one day.” Therefore the Apostle says: “We too were by nature children of wrath” (Eph. II, 13), because, on account of original sin, having been handed down from our fathers through the corrupt law of our conception, we are born debtors to eternal life [read: “punishment”] and children of the devil. Some also become children of the devil by imitation—namely, children of unbelief, who carry out his desires. Hence in the Book of Wisdom: “Through the envy [Col. 0860B] of the devil death entered into the world” (Wis. II, 24); and, because it wishes us to understand that this happened by imitation rather than propagation, it adds: “But those who belong to his party imitate him” (ibid., 25).

But people become children of God in four ways: by predestination, calling, justification, and magnification. Hence the Apostle: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. And those whom he predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, those he also magnified” [printed: “glorifieavit”] (Rom. VIII, 29). Predestination concerns those not yet existing; calling, those who have turned away; justification, sinners; magnification, those who have arrived.

Though four things are mentioned here, [Col. 0860C] one is in God and three are in us. For our predestination is not in us, but lies hidden with God. The other three are in us—calling, justification, and magnification—which are effects of predestination, not its cause. Predestination is the preparation of grace; its effect is the bestowal of grace. It is a great thing to become the child of so great and so benevolent a Father, who gives all things freely, who gave the power to become children of God to those who believe in his name.

But the extreme of misery is to become a child of iniquity—that is, of the devil. For just as one born of God is born unto righteousness and life, so one born of the devil is born unto iniquity and death. Hear the Apostle considering both: “Just as,” he says, “you presented your members for iniquity, [Col. 0860D] so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. VI, 19).

Children of the devil are begotten from the devil as father and Babylon as mother, just as children of God are begotten from Christ as father and Jerusalem—that is, the Church—as mother. But “daughter Babylon, unhappy,” as the Prophet says: what can an unhappy woman offer except misery? Miserable, therefore, are her children who love and follow her. But blessed is he who repays her with the recompense which she herself has repaid. For she tears away from his mother a child of the Church, born of God, whom the Church as a woman in sorrow bears, and sets him at her own breasts as though he were her own; with the seductions of her pleasures she nurses him for the devil’s work. But blessed is he who repays her her recompense: who seizes her little ones before they grow strong in malice, [Col. 0861A] weans them, and dashes them against Christ the Rock. Blessed is the one who migrates from such a house into the house of the Lord.

To this the Prophet exhorts the human soul, saying: “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear; forget your people and the house of your father” (Ps. XLIV, 11); put aside the customs [variant: “laughter”] of Babylon and flee the devil’s house. For the devil has, as it were, his own house: pride. In it he dwells. In it he chose his seat, when swollen with pride of mind he said: “I will exalt my throne beside the regions of the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14).

Pride began from an injury done to God; it inhabits the minds of the exalted by celestial origin, lurking beneath ashes and sackcloth. This is rightly called the devil’s house because [Col. 0861B], just as the Spirit of the Lord rests upon the humble and quiet person, so the evil spirit rests upon the obstinate and proud. If, therefore, you wish to reach the desirable land, if you wish to attain the hidden manna, go forth from the land of pleasure, from the kindred of restless curiosity, and from the ungodly house of the proud father.

But perhaps you say: “This is a hard saying; and who can hear it?” (John VI, 60). Truth answers you: “Take my yoke upon you … for my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. XI, 29)—but it is so for those who love and taste it. For love and experience of sweetness make things that are heavy and unbearable easy and almost nothing. It may seem hard to you, then, because you have not yet tasted the sweetness of God’s word, which he has hidden [Col. 0861C] for those who fear him. Taste, therefore, and see that the Lord is sweet, who says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 28).

Refreshment is not exhaustion but consolation and progress. Return, transgressor, to your heart. Even reason teaches you what I say; natural reason convinces you. See: you delight in the flesh of a prostitute, but is not the flesh of Christ more delightful? You pursue gluttony as a sweet thing, but is sobriety not far sweeter? Pride lifts you up, but humility is far more powerful. Far be it from you to judge the devil’s garment, clotted with blood, better than Christ’s garment, which is without spot or wrinkle.

But in order to lay aside the devil’s garment, avoid the three things mentioned above. For in those three, as in their heads, all vices are joined and allied. Hence John says: “Little children, do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world; for there is nothing in the world except the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life; and the world and its desire pass away” (I John II, 16). That is: the desire of the flesh, namely pleasure; the desire of the eyes, namely curiosity.

Therefore let us turn away from the passing world and its desires, lest we fall together with what is falling. And as those three things must be renounced and avoided, so three things are proposed to the one who departs from them, through which he is led to the desirable land: namely, a garden, a wine-cellar, and a chamber. For the Lord leads us first into [Col. 0862A] the garden, then into the wine-cellar, and finally into the chamber, where, resting, we shall be satisfied with the fruit of the desirable land.

These three are mentioned in the Song of Songs. Of the garden the bride says: “My beloved went down into his garden, to the bed of spices, to feed in the gardens and gather lilies” (Cant. VI, 1). Of the wine-cellar the bride says: “The king brought me into his wine-cellars; he set love in order within me” (Cant. I, 3). And of the bed she says: “Our bed is flowering” (ibid., 15).

The garden is understood as the Church, which is “an enclosed garden, a sealed fountain” (Cant. IV, 12): namely, the active life, where, as in a garden, the flowers of virtues are fragrant and shoots of good works spring forth, so that those who see them may glorify the Father who is in heaven. Hence the Apostle: “We are the sweet fragrance of Christ to God [Col. 0862B] among those who are saved and among those who perish” (II Cor. II, 15). This is the fragrance of which Isaac says: “Behold the fragrance of my son, like the fragrance of a field full of blessing from the Lord” (Gen. XXVII, 27).

The flowers of the trees in this garden therefore give forth a most sweet fragrance and bear precious fruit: confidence in the present and life in the future. We who have been led into the garden on the first day’s journey must now be led, on the second day, into the wine-cellar. The wine-cellar is understood as divine Scripture, or divine contemplation, where we are refreshed by the sweetness of grace, intoxicated as if by the fragrance of unmixed wine and filled with its cup. We are transferred from love of earthly things to contemplation of heavenly and supernal things. Such intoxication is pleasing: it intoxicates so as to make sober; it does not weigh down but lifts up, [Col. 0862C] and raises us even to the house of God—“with the sound of rejoicing and confession, the cry of one feasting” (Ps. XLI, 5).

For from the heavenly house there resounds for the soul contemplating heavenly things a certain song and sweet melody, by which it is soothed; and, like a deer, it longs for fountains of water—that is, for God himself, who is the fountain of living waters springing up into eternal life. Scripture itself is also rightly compared to a wine-cellar, where we are refreshed and sustained by the taste of manifold understanding. If we seek moral teaching, understanding of allegories, the truth of histories, or the revelation of anagogy, we find all of it there. Scripture is the storehouse of the Holy Spirit, the paradise of every fruit, where each soul finds what benefits it.

It remains now that, on the third day’s journey, our King should bring us into the chamber. But up to this point we have spoken, as it were, soberly and in human terms because of your weakness. Concerning the bed, however, we can speak only with an ecstasy of mind that comes from God. Hence the Apostle: “Whether we are carried beyond ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you” (II Cor. V, 13). It is a great and inscrutable mystery, to which the sharpness of your mind cannot in any way rise.

For this bed has its place between God’s left hand and his right; for God has a right hand and a left, according to Solomon’s saying: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Cant. VII, 6). And elsewhere: “In his right hand are years of life, and in his left riches and honor.” [Note: [Col. 0861D] “Length of days is in his right hand, and in his left riches and glory.”] [Col. 0863A] These are the two ranks between which the dove’s feathers sleep—that is, the teachers of the Church—according to the prophetic saying: “If you sleep between the two ranks, the dove’s feathers are silvered” (Ps. LXVII, 14).

The Church is called a dove because of simplicity, according to the saying: “My dove is one, my beloved is one” (Cant. VI, 8). It is called silvered because it is instructed by divine utterances. The dove’s feathers are the teachers and prelates of the Church, whose preaching is borne heavenward. The ranks are the glorious allotted portions of the Church. For *clerus* in Greek is called *sors* in Latin, “a lot”; hence *cleronomia*, that is, “inheritance,” which is also called a lot because it is given by lot—that is, by divine election.

Therefore the dove’s feathers sleep between the two ranks: that is, they rest amid the inheritances, namely [Col. 0863B] between God’s left hand and his right. The left hand signifies Christ’s humility; the right hand, his divinity. In the present life, the humility of his humanity is placed beneath our head; by it we are consoled, raised by hope, and given an ascent to him. But in the future his divinity will embrace us. This is our twofold refreshment: on earth we are sustained by the fruit of the virginal womb, and in heaven we shall be satisfied by the fruit of the Father’s womb, where the vision and enjoyment of both forms—divine and human—will gladden and glorify us.

For he is the one “into whom angels desire to look” (I Pet. I, 12). They indeed look into him, and do so with desire, because they desire what they possess and possess what they desire. For if they desired and did not obtain it, there would be anxiety in desire, and thus punishment. But if they possessed and did not desire, satiety would seem to be followed by disgust. Therefore, lest there be anxiety in desire or disgust in satiety, those who desire are satisfied and those who are satisfied desire. They desire without labor, because desire is accompanied by satisfaction; and they are satisfied without disgust, because satisfaction is always in desire.

This bed, placed between the two ranks, is most sweet, delightful, and greatly desirable, where we shall be satisfied with the vision of twofold glory. For what is more desirable, more secure, or sweeter than to rest between God’s left hand and his right? Behold: three things from which one must depart have been set forth, and three others by which one must ascend to the desirable land. Let each be compared with its counterpart, so that nail [Col. 0863D] may drive out nail. For the Lord’s garden empties your land. Likewise the Lord’s wine-cellar banishes every earthly kindred—that is, the curiosity that distresses you. Nor does the bed placed between God’s right hand and left overthrow any less the house of the ungodly.

Therefore, with fitting attention, the devil and the Spirit of God call out: “Go forth from your land, from your kindred, and from the house of your father; and come, with the steps of the mind and the feet of twofold love, into the land that I shall show you.” For no one can see, unless the Holy Spirit reveals, what neither carnal eye has seen nor ear heard: what God has prepared for those who love him (I Cor. II), that is, the land of the living. There I shall bless you in a glorified soul, [Col. 0864A] and you shall be blessed in a glorified body. Again, I shall bless you by contemplation of divinity, and you shall be blessed by the vision of humanity. May almighty God bring us to that blessing. Amen.

## CXIII [On Various Subjects XXVI]. ON THE TWO CITIES OF GOD AND THE DEVIL

[Note: [Col. 0863D] From Victorinus.]

787 “Go out, my people, from Babylon, lest you share in her sins and receive of her plagues; for her sins have reached unto heaven, and the Lord has remembered her iniquities” (Rev. XVIII, 4).

There are, therefore, dearest brothers, in the world two kingdoms, two rulers, and two households. One kingdom is God’s; the other is the devil’s. The households of the two kingdoms have always opposed one another from the beginning of the world. [Col. 0864B] The devil’s kingdom is called Babylon; God’s kingdom is called Jerusalem. Babylon means “confusion”; Jerusalem, “vision of peace.”

But let us speak first of the city of God. In this city is a strong wall, of which the Prophet says: “Zion, the city of our strength: the Savior shall be placed in it as a wall” (Isa. XXVI, 1). It has twelve gates, as John was shown in a vision. He says: “The angel showed me the holy city Jerusalem, which had a great wall and twelve gates” (Rev. XXI, 12). This city is founded upon mountains. Hence David: “Its foundations are upon the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI, 1). There is there a very great tower to which all have refuge. Solomon says of it: “The tower of David was built with battlements; a thousand shields [Col. 0864C] hang upon it” (Cant. IV, 4). That tower touches heaven.

There are also many other towers, but lower ones, of which David says: “May peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers, Jerusalem” (Ps. CXXI, 7). There is never night there, but always day. John says: “There shall be no night in it” (Rev. XXI, 25). There are always watchmen and guards there, of whom the Church says in the Song of Songs: “The watchmen who guard the city found me” (Cant. III, 3). The Lord himself also makes the city and keeps watch, for “unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain” (Ps. CXXVI, 2).

There is no filth in it. All things are clean and bright; all things flower, all things are fragrant. There is no anger, no discord, no reproach, but a certain communion of love. The citizens of that city care for others’ concerns as well as their own. They provide for one another and admonish one another. Others’ losses are their own; they feel and relieve others’ pain. There are constant heralds there, who continually urge them to care for themselves. They refuse no one who flees to them, but protect him. They draw to themselves all whom they can. They do not know how either to take or to covet another’s goods, but generously give away their own. They suffer nothing except from citizens of Babylon, [with whom] there is always warfare. With those among whom they dwell there is always God’s peace.

Their food is to obey the will of their Lord and to seek what his will is. Their dishes are the Lord’s commands, [Col. 0865A] more desirable to them than gold and topaz; and they remember his commandments in order to do them. They burn with love for those who are absent, and love them. They desire to imitate the virtue of the good, not to envy it. No one remains in this city unless he is a soldier, for “the life of man upon earth is warfare.” All are always armed, because they must always fight: their enemies do not know how to cease, but always either lie in ambush or fight.

You have heard, brothers, the description of the city; you have heard the character of its citizens. But the description must be interpreted for a fuller understanding. The city’s wall is the guardianship of angels, assigned to us for protection. The city itself is the Church. The twelve gates are the twelve apostles, who through preaching or writing gave believers access to God. It is founded upon mountains because it is founded upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets. The tower of refuge is [God himself,] of whom David says: “Be to me a protecting God and a house of refuge, a fortified place” (Ps. XXX, III). The other towers are any saints eminent in virtues and moving others by word and example.

There is no night there of unbelief, of which the Apostle says: “The night has passed; the day has drawn near” (Rom. XIII, 12). The watchmen are bishops, priests, and other prelates who keep watch over the Lord’s sheep. The heralds are preachers, to whom it is said: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their crimes” (Ps. LVIII, 1).

Babylon, however, has a wall: namely, a legion of angels, that is, evil spirits; and five gates, namely [Col. 0865C] the five bodily senses, through which one enters into confusion. David says of these: “You lift me up from the gates of death” (Ps. IX, 15). It has no tower, but a dark pit, which is despair. From it the citizens of Jerusalem cannot rescue anyone; and of it it is written: “When the sinner comes into the depth of sins, he despises” (Prov. XVIII, 3). Into this depth fell the first devil. Into it fell Judas and the Jews, who are altogether blinded and hardened.

In Babylon there is always night—that is, blindness of heart. The character of its citizens is as follows. They love and acquire this world’s riches by every means: theft, robbery, usury, bloodshed, and deceit. They devote themselves to revelries, drunkenness, and lust. There is no faith [Col. 0865D] among them. They delight in deceiving not only citizens of Jerusalem, but also their own people and themselves. They envy everyone richer than themselves. They rejoice in others’ losses; they do not know how to show mercy. They speak peace to their neighbor, but evil is in their hearts. The sinner borrows and does not repay. There is no truth in their mouth; their heart is vain. They swear evil against their neighbor and deceive him; they receive gifts against the innocent. “These trust in chariots and these in horses.” All have turned aside; together they have become useless. There is none who does good, not even one.

All the ungodly dwell in this Babylon. They always labor to capture citizens of Jerusalem, and they drag many people to themselves. To these the Lord cries, saying: “Go out, my people, from Babylon.” But since the two households are intermingled in it, because good [Col. 0866A] and evil people live bodily together in the world, the determined [read: “undetermined, or doubtful”] [remain] as to how they shall go out—not in body, but by the difference of their minds. This is what he says: “Lest you share in her sins”; for if you avoid sins, you will also avoid sinners’ torments. And this is: “And receive not of her plagues,” because the sinner has many scourges, if not in the present, then in the future. But some are for correction and others for punishment.

Bodily illnesses and losses of possessions are for correction. Eternal death is for punishment. “For the wages of sin,” as the Apostle says, “is” eternal “death” (Rom. VI, 23). When he says, “You shall not receive of her plagues,” this must be understood of the punishments of hell, because temporal afflictions are common to all. But Babylon truly receives plagues because her sins have reached unto heaven—that is, to God’s knowledge. God is said to be ignorant of sins when he does not punish them; he is said to remember when punishment is given for faults. Therefore he says: “God has remembered her iniquities.”

You therefore, dearest brothers, who have been deceived by the rulers and citizens of Babylon and led captive there, go forth through repentance. “Break the bonds of your neck, captive daughter Zion”; and why, house of Israel, will you die? The price of your redemption has been given; Christ’s blood has been poured out, and yet you remain in prison! The Babylonians show you false riches so that [Col. 0866B] you may love them and forsake your Creator. Hear how Moses rebukes you: “You have forsaken the God who begot you, and forgotten the Lord your Creator” (Deut. XXXII, 18). Let the ungodly man forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him.

Remember that “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field” (Isa. XL, 6). David explains how flesh is grass when he says: “In the morning it flowers and passes away; in the evening it falls, hardens, and withers” (Ps. LXXXIX, 6). This means: a human being flowers in the morning, that is, in childhood and youth; but in the evening he falls. He hardens in the corpse and clings [read: “withers”] in the dust; for after a human being comes a corpse, after a corpse a worm, and after a worm ashes. This is said concerning the human being.

But what of the labor [Col. 0866D] we expend upon temporal things? “Our years shall be spent like a spider” (Ps. LXXXIX, 10): that is, we living in years are compared to spiders. What does a spider do? It consumes its own entrails in making a web, and labors over it solely to catch a worthless prey—flies. Likewise, people of this world wear out their bodies by laboring, passing through many dangers, and gaining a worthless reward, namely transitory things. O wretched people! They will leave their riches to strangers, and their tombs will be their houses forever; for when the rich man dies, he shall take nothing away, nor shall his glory descend with him.

We have shown, brothers, that human beings and human things are transitory. Therefore do not be deceived by the Babylonians through false riches, but go out from them through repentance. Do not repent of one sin only, but of all. Whoever has many sins, unless he gives up all but one, is like someone bound with many chains who breaks all but one, yet that single chain is enough to keep him bound. He is also like a sailor whose ship has many holes: unless he stops all but one, water comes in through that one and carries it to the depths. He is like someone with many arrows in his heart: though the rest are pulled out, if one remains, that one alone will cause death. So one who has many mortal sins, unless he abandons all except one, that one alone is the cause of damnation.

It is indeed beneficial to abandon some sins, so as to receive a lighter punishment in hell; but it does not suffice for attaining salvation. Thus one who gives up some but not all does not leave Babylon, though he is, as it were, near its gate and [better prepared] to depart. [Col. 0867B] Mary had sinned much, wept much, and many sins were forgiven her because she loved much (Luke VII). Peter sinned in one matter, because he denied the Lord, and he wept over one matter. Therefore weep as much as you have sinned: if one sin, one; if many, many.

Do you wish to be freed? Break your chains. Then redeem yourself by alms. For the Lord willed that some should be rich and others poor. If all were rich, people would have no one through whom to redeem their sins. Lazarus was placed before the rich man’s gate, that the rich man might see by whom he could redeem his sins. Thus he remains without excuse when he gives nothing to the poor. Wash yourself in the river of mercy, so that, departing Babylon, you may deserve to be received into Jerusalem.

May the Lord who dwells in Jerusalem send us help from the sanctuary [Col. 0867C] and protect us from Zion—he who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## CXIV [On Various Subjects XXVII]. ON CHRISTIAN WARFARE

[Note: [Col. 0867D] From an Angers manuscript.]

“Human life upon earth is warfare” (Job VII, 1).

It is necessary, dearest brothers, that the vigorous soldier of Christ overthrow within himself the most strongly fortified city of Nineveh, and conquer its proud king—that is, the devil—who is exceedingly strong. Therefore he must press against him with great toil and great effort, so that the devil himself may be cast down and his city overthrown. For relentless labour conquers all things, and courage climbs to the heights.

Blessed Job displayed and taught in himself the pattern of this warfare [Col. 0867D]. He experienced the grave temptations and assaults of this enemy through the loss of his possessions, bereavement of his children, and affliction of his own flesh. We must therefore believe one who has experienced it, for he fought against the enemy both outwardly and inwardly. The devil indeed stirred up against him an inward and domestic enemy, namely his wife, who by her words sought to lead him into despair when she said: “Bless God and die”—whereas she ought rather to have offered words of consolation to relieve her husband’s pain. But Christ’s soldier is not moved by the harshness of her words [Col. 0868A], nor drawn into despair, as is apparent from his answer: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?” (Job 2:10). “Since he gave, and since he has taken away, blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

Again, when the devil could not overcome him through his wife, he stirred up other inward and familiar enemies—namely, Job’s friends. Coming to console him, they burst out into reproach. Hence that same man said to them: “You compose words for reproach, and you strive to overthrow your friend” (Job 6:26). And what plague is more effective than a false friend? Yet although he endured so many conflicts within and without, none could move him from his purpose of holiness, because “in all these things Job did not sin with his lips” [Col. 0868B] (Job 1:22).

Whoever wishes to be trained as such a soldier in Christ’s warfare should strive to imitate him. In order to serve more freely, he should not be burdened by the weight of earthly business; for, according to the Apostle: “He who competes in the contest abstains from all things” (1 Cor. 9:15). And elsewhere: “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2:4). But for perfect victory he must have four things: an enemy against whom he may contend; weapons by which he may fortify himself and strike down his enemy; provisions by which he may sustain himself; and rewards for which he may fight.

One enemy is inward, such as the flesh itself; another is outward, namely the devil. This enemy, as Peter says, “goes about like a roaring lion, seeking [Col. 0868C] whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). This enemy is ancient and long practised in this sort of conflict. From the beginning he has attacked us; from the beginning he seeks to kill us. Thus it is written: “He was a murderer from the beginning” (John 8:44). Since, as has been said, he is ancient and therefore more practised, greater vigilance is truly needed in resisting him.

Again, he is invisible and concealed from us, because he is spiritual. Hence Paul: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12). Again, this enemy attacks us from nearby; he is not far removed from us. We always have him at our heel, at our side; indeed, he dwells in this dark air.

[Note: [Col. 0867D] Observe that Hildebert here asserts that demons dwell in this dark air. He also maintains this in his theological treatise, chapter 2; in the second sermon on the Ascension [Col. 0868D]; in the first sermon on the Nativity of the Lord; and elsewhere. From this a reciprocal proof may be drawn both that these sermons and that treatise are genuine works of Hildebert.]

Thus, when Paul had said, “against spiritual forces of wickedness,” he added, “in the heavenly places,” that is, in the air, and therefore near us [Col. 0868D]. And because, as has been said, this enemy is ancient, he is the more experienced; and because he is hidden, his combat is the more difficult, and he must therefore be guarded against more carefully.

The soldier also has an inward enemy, namely his own flesh, which lusts against the spirit. Of it it is said in Hosea: “Guard the doors of your mouth from her who sleeps in your bosom” (Mic. 7:5). We always have this enemy with us, since this contest is continual and unceasing. Hence Gregory: “Born from the defect of the flesh, we carry within ourselves that by which we may have conflicts” [Col. 0869A].

Therefore he must have weapons by which he may fortify himself and strike down the enemy. First, he must have the shield of faith, by which he may quench all the fiery darts of the most wicked one—that is, the incitements of vices. For, as Prudentius says:

> First Faith enters the field,  
> To fight amid the doubtful chance of battle. . . .

Of this shield of faith David says: “You have crowned us with the shield of your good will” (Ps. 5:15). Since the length and severity of the struggle, and even the delay of the kingdom, might lead him into despair, he must have “the helmet of salvation” (Eph. 6:17), that is, of the spirit, which covers and protects the whole head—that is, the mind—lest he be drawn into despair by the dangers already mentioned [Col. 0869B].

Again, he must have “the breastplate of righteousness” (ibid., v. 14), that is, charity, which covers and fortifies the whole body on either side. Hence Paul: “Through the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left” (ibid., 11). Charity is called the breastplate of righteousness because through charity we render to each person what is his due. The hooks of this breastplate are works of mercy: clothing the naked, feeding the needy, and the like. This breastplate ought to be about the loins and the reins, so that the mind’s faith or hope may not waver in anything. Let our vital parts, wrapped and fortified by the breastplate of charity, be kept unharmed, lest a place be given to the enemy breaking in through it. The hooks of this breastplate are intertwined and continuous when works of charity are intertwined and connected.

Thus Christ’s soldier has these weapons for his protection [Col. 0869C]: the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation—that is, hope—and the breastplate of righteousness—that is, charity.

To cast down the enemy, moreover, he must have a sword with which to strike at close quarters, and a spear with which to strike from afar. The sword is the word of the Gospel, of which the Apostle says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (ibid., v. 17). Let him have a spear by which to strike from afar, namely the testimony of the Law. For a spear has wood and iron: wood by which it is held, iron by which it cuts. Similarly, the Law has the letter, by which it is held; it has spiritual understanding, by which it cuts and divides.

Some have this sword in their mouth, but do not wish to gird themselves with it. They strive to restrain the sins of others, but refuse to slay their own—indeed, they cherish them [Col. 0869D]. Yet each person ought first to set forth in himself the example of a good work and afterwards teach others, lest, as Paul says, after preaching to others they themselves become reprobate. Therefore let Christ’s soldier gird himself with such a sword by restraining evil [impulses] within himself. Hence David: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one” (Ps. 44:4). And in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35). And the Law commands: “You shall gird your loins” (Exod. 12:11). And David: “Test my reins and my heart” (Ps. 25:7). By the reins are understood fleshly vices, such as lust, drunkenness, and the like; by the heart, spiritual vices [Col. 0870A], such as envy and pride.

Again, this soldier must have footwear—that is, something with which to protect his feet—lest he be harmed by the thorns of sins and the scorpions which he is to tread upon. Hence the Apostle: “Feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. 6:16). Footwear is made from the skins of dead animals. Just as from one skin footwear may be made for many rather than for one only, so many persons may be fortified and instructed by the example of one father. These shoes should be covered beneath, toward the ground, and open above, such as are said to have been those of the apostles.

[Note: [Col. 0869] The apostle’s footwear was covered underneath and open above. Hildebert also observes this, in the same sense, in Letter 31, Book I.]

By these shoes it is signified that our preaching should not touch the earth—that is, it should not be undertaken for any earthly consideration—but [that] God alone should be appointed the end both of the work and of the preaching [Col. 0870B].

The horse of this soldier is our body, because the soldier whom we portray is spiritual. This horse must be tamed, lest it become too wanton and proud and so throw its master. That good soldier tamed his horse who said: “I chastise my body and reduce it to servitude” (1 Cor. 9:27), that is, I drive it back lest it exalt itself, so that it may obey the will of the Lord who commands. David taught that this horse should be checked and reproved with the bit of continence, saying: “Constrain their jaws with bit and bridle” (Ps. 31:9).

But lest this horse go backward or stand still—for standing still is in a manner to go backward—it needs spurs: that is, the admonitions of the Fathers, by which the horse is urged on and, advancing by the steps of good works, stretches itself toward what lies ahead [Col. 0870C]. For, as Solomon says: “The words of the wise are like goads, fixed deeply upward” (Eccl. 12:11).

Behold the weapons by which this soldier fortifies himself and strikes down the enemy. He must also have provisions to sustain him in this warfare; but he ought to have them not for excess, but for necessity, according to the saying: “Having food and clothing, with these we are content” (1 Tim. 6:8). Hence John, when soldiers asked, “What shall we do?” answered: “Be content with your pay” (Luke 3:14). Nor should Christ’s soldier be anxious even in seeking necessities, since he knows that his Lord knows that he needs all these things. Hence the Lord says: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat [Col. 0870D], or what shall we drink?’” (Matt. 6:31). He who serves for the kingdom should not be anxious about food. We do not, however, abolish prudence; we remove anxiety.

Again, this soldier must be certain of the reward for which he fights. For certainty of the reward contemplated lightens the labour of warfare, since whoever hopes for exalted things willingly endures hardships. No one clearly knows in the course of this life how great this reward is, but he will know in his homeland. For, upon arriving, he will find more than he could estimate while on the way. This gift, to put it briefly, is perfect knowledge of God, which we shall have when we see God as he is. Hence: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” [Col. 0871A] (Ps. 16:15).

To obtain this, “the warfare of man’s life is upon the earth”; and as “man” is understood temporally, so also is “life.” Now “man” is spoken of according to nature, as here: “What is man, that you are mindful of him?” (Ps. 8:5). Man is spoken of according to guilt, as in: “Man born of woman lives for a short time.” Man is spoken of according to grace, as in: “He enlightens every man coming into this world.” The life of nature is that by which a human being breathes. The life of guilt is that by which sin lives in us. The life of grace is that by which Christ lives in the heart. Two are from God; the third is from man. Of all these David says: “O God, I have declared my life to you” (Ps. 55:9). For he declares even those lives which belong to nature or grace to God, because he confesses that he has them from God. The Apostle confesses the third, which is the life of sin, in some measure [perhaps: humbly] [Col. 0871B], when he says: “I was a blasphemer” (1 Tim. 1:12).

The life of grace is above the earth; the life of nature is on the earth; the life of guilt is beneath the earth. Hence Paul, concerning the life of grace: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). The life of nature is on earth, where man is born for labour. Hence Job: “Man is born for labour, and the bird for flight” (Job 5:7). The life of guilt is beneath the earth; and the one whose life was in guilt will deservedly have death in punishment in the future. Therefore we must be soldiers of Christ so that we may live with him in glory, because his cavalry is our salvation, and his whole life was a warfare upon the earth. Hence: “I was troubled in my exercise” (Ps. 54:3). His life ought to be our discipline; for he suffered for us [Col. 0871C], leaving us an example so that we may follow in his footsteps. He who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## CXV [On Various Matters XXVIII]. ON CHRISTIAN WATCHFULNESS

[Note: [Col. 0871D] From Sangermanensis manuscript 381.]

“Set up for yourself a watchtower, place before yourself bitter things, direct your heart upon the straight way” (Jer. 31:21).

This is a devout and salutary exhortation, by which the Spirit of God admonishes us through Jeremiah the prophet to set up a watchtower for ourselves, to place bitter things before ourselves, and to direct our heart upon the straight way. For as long as we are in the body, according to the Apostle, we are away from the Lord, walking by faith and not yet by sight. We are in exile and in combat. For the life of man upon earth is warfare [Col. 0871D] and temptation, as Scripture says. Hence Wisdom says: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1). For those preparing to submit themselves to divine power are met by manifold temptation. They are tempted by pleasant things; they are tempted by harsh things. Thus Pharaoh once pursued the children of Israel as they departed from Egypt, together with the Egyptians (Exod. 15). So, when the devil is forsaken, he sends temptations harsher than usual, he who goes about roaring, seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5).

Therefore we need a watchtower, from which we may avoid the enemy’s snares. On a watchtower we stand higher, and from it we see the enemies’ approaches farther off and foresee the coming help of friends [Col. 0872A]. From a watchtower crops are guarded and words are directed to others. This watchtower is good, and therefore it must be set up in the inner chamber of the mind, for it serves so many purposes. It is the watchtower of contemplation and discernment. Contemplation fortifies us; discernment guards us. This watchtower, then, is twofold: namely, a guard and a fortification.

Hence Habakkuk: “I will stand upon my watch, and set my foot upon the fortification, and I will contemplate, that I may see what is said to me and what I may answer to the one rebuking me” (Hab. 2:1). Unless he were trained in the discernment that guards and fortified by the art of contemplation, he could neither contemplate what is said to him by the Lord nor answer the reprover. His understanding would be blunted [Col. 0872B] by the ray of contemplation; his speech would fail. When making his reply, his mind would be stupefied and his lips would tremble.

Moses, that lawgiver, as soon as he began to hear God’s words, knew himself burdened by human weakness, so that he professed himself unable not merely to answer the Lord but even to speak with him. “I beseech you, Lord,” he says, “I am not eloquent, neither yesterday nor the day before; and since you spoke to your servant, I am more slow and impeded in tongue” (Exod. 4:10). Though he had been trained in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, when he heard the Lord’s voice and received his utterances, he felt his own voice to be thin and feeble, his tongue slow and impeded; and he declares himself mute when he considers the Word who was in the beginning with God [Col. 0872C].

Worthy, then, is the watchtower which, when a person sets it up for himself, both guards and is guarded, both fortifies and is fortified, and contemplates both what is said to it and what it should answer. It does not fail to know what God says to it, what man urges, or what the devil advises. God speaks holy things; man, double things—hence, “They spoke with heart and heart”; the flesh, pleasant things; the devil, boastful things. Therefore let us believe God alone and place hope in him alone; let us yield neither to man, nor to the flesh, nor to the devil.

Hence Micah: “Do not believe a friend; do not trust a leader. Guard the doors of your mouth from her who sleeps in your bosom, for the son dishonours the father” (Mic. 7:5), and a man’s enemies are those of his own household. Therefore let us stand upon the watchtower of discernment and contemplation, guarding the fruits of good works [Col. 0872D] and the garments of virtues, lest we walk naked and empty upon the way. Let us beware the cunning of spiritual enemies, who anticipate our watches and place stumbling-blocks upon our path. Let us consider with what intention those approach us who put forward the appearance of brothers and display the face of friends.

For even now false brothers enter secretly under the guise of peace and religion, wishing to spy out the liberty which we have in Christ Jesus: beneath a sheep’s skin they bear a wolfish spirit, carrying honey in their mouth and a sting upon their back.

[Note: [Col. 0871D] Perhaps he said this against the crafty heretic Henry [Col. 0872D], whom he expelled from the diocese of Le Mans.]

Therefore let us always be on the watchtower. Let us look about ourselves on every side, for on every side are stumbling-blocks, on every side snares. Beasts of the forest also pass by, roaring, and lion cubs, that they may seize prey and seek food for themselves [Col. 0873A]. Their food is earth—that is, the life of livestock—for it was said to the serpent in the curse: “You shall crawl upon your belly and breast, and all the days you shall eat earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0873D] “You shall go upon your breast, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. 3:14).]

Let us therefore beware lest the beasts and lion cubs—that is, demons—find food in us: namely, an evil life, the life of a sinner, in which they delight and upon which they feed. Some of them are compared to lions, namely the greater ones; others to cubs, namely the lesser. For among them are principalities, powers, and virtues, against whom we have a struggle, not only against the flesh. Hence the Apostle: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood” only, “but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this darkness [Col. 0873B], against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12).

Therefore the watchtower is very necessary to us, upon whom so difficult and manifold a struggle threatens. For when we came to serve God, we undertook a contest against our flesh and against blood—that is, human beings who are our neighbours but do not keep the law, because they labour not to benefit their neighbour but to harm him—and against spiritual forces of wickedness: invisible and evil demons, who must therefore be greatly feared and guarded against. Beyond all these kinds of enemies, there is a certain spiritual enemy who blinds peoples, lures them with false goods, and by his pleasures and delights draws them away from love of the heavenly kingdom. [lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Thus this sermon ends here, and for that reason seems to be incomplete.]

## CXVI [On Various Matters XXIX]. TO MONKS

[Note: [Col. 0874D] From Victorine and Lyran manuscripts. Perhaps delivered while he was staying at Cluny.]

[Col. 0873C]

“Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1).

Thus, dearest ones, David congratulates your brotherhood—

[Note: [Col. 0874D] Lyranus: That is, he congratulates the monks and his own people.]

—and in this way he praises with great exultation our assemblies, which he foresaw from afar in the spirit, saying: “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity.” He sets forth two things: good and pleasant. For not everything pleasant is good, nor is everything good pleasant. Martyrdom is good, but it is not pleasant. Will [perhaps: one’s own will, or pleasure] is pleasant, but it is not good. But the fellowship of brothers is good [Col. 0873D] and affords delight.

But whose shared dwelling does he praise? That of spiritual brothers, not carnal ones. Jacob and Esau were carnal brothers, and therefore their common dwelling was not pleasant. But the shared dwelling of spiritual brothers is pleasant because it tends toward unity. They have one purpose, one mind, one food; they seek one supreme good. Each seeks one thing: namely, to dwell eternally in the heavenly Jerusalem with the rest of the faithful and with the angels [Col. 0874A], saying with the Prophet: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:4)—that is, the days of eternity, which alone ought properly to be called life.

For the present life is death: it is full of miseries; it is not in the homeland but in exile. Hence the Prophet sighs, saying: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has long been a sojourner” (Ps. 119:5). Kedar means “darkness”: that is, my soul has long been a sojourner among the impious. The Apostle also says: “All creation groans and travails” (Rom. 8:22); yet amid groaning it bears the fruit of good work.

But what consolation is there amid groaning? Let us first see the causes of groaning, and then return to consolation [Col. 0874B]. There are four causes of our grief. We weep because of sins, because of the miseries of this age, because of compassion for our neighbour, and because of love for [perhaps: the delay of] the reward. He wept because of sins who said: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall water my couch” (Ps. 6:7). The same man groaned over miseries when he said: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged; my soul has long been a sojourner” (Ps. 119:5). The Apostle, who commands us to weep with those who weep and rejoice with those who rejoice, grieved out of compassion, saying: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:29). The Lord also wept over Lazarus and, seeing the city, wept over it [Col. 0874C].

The righteous weep because the reward is delayed, saying: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered you, Zion” (Ps. 136:1). As though they said: We are now amid rivers—that is, amid the flow of confusion—but above them, because we have overcome everything in the world or belonging to the world. There we sat, because we are neither raised up through pride nor lying down through ruin; and we wept. But why? Because we are not in our homeland; and this is what is meant by “when we remembered you, heavenly Zion.” Behold the causes of groaning.

What, then, is the consolation? What we said above: “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity.” For spiritual brothers are citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem and share the same exile. They console one another [Col. 0874D], speaking of their homeland and rejoicing together in hope of recovering their inheritance, according to the saying: “Rejoice, righteous ones, in the Lord; praise befits the upright” (Ps. 32:1).

It is good for brothers to dwell together in unity because Christ loved unity. Thus he says in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one, my undefiled one is one” (Song 6:8). Again, in the Gospel: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in their midst” (John 17:11). He prayed to the Father for the unity of his own: “I ask not for these only, but [Col. 0875A] for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may be one, as we also are one” (John 19:24).

He signified this unity in his body by his tunic. For when the soldiers had broken the legs of the thieves, they came to Jesus and did not break his legs, so that what had been written might be fulfilled: “You shall not break a bone of him” (ibid., 36).

Christ’s body signifies the Church. He wished the body’s integrity to be preserved in order to signify the unity of the Church. In the same way, his tunic was seamless, woven from the top throughout. It was not divided, but allotted by lot. He did not wish it to be divided because the tunic is the Church, with which Christ is clothed as with an ornament; it is whole and allotted by lot—that is, chosen by the divine lot.

Immediately after the Ascension the primitive Church preserved this unity [Col. 0875B]. For we read in the Acts of the Apostles that “the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). This unity, dearest brothers, can be maintained only by love and the bond of peace. Love is the spiritual and proper virtue of the saints. Hence the Lord: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another; I leave peace to you; I give you my peace” (John 13:35). And the Apostle: “Pursue peace with all, without which no one shall see God” (Heb. 12:14). And the Lord: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:9).

The righteous ought to be as David says of himself: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord” (Ps. 51:10). The olive is the tree of peace, green in winter and summer. Therefore, if the righteous person wishes to stand in the house of the Lord, let him be an olive tree: peaceful and fruitful in prosperity and adversity, lest he begin to be a wild olive [Col. 0875C].

No wars are more grievous than civil wars. There the danger is serious, where battles are both outside and within. But whoever is righteous, let him persevere strongly, lest he be scattered through scandals. The simple are indeed troubled; but sowers of discord are condemned. Hence the Lord: “Woe to him through whom scandal comes” (Matt. 18:7). But that the perfect are not scattered through scandal, the Lord says through Solomon: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” (Song 2:2). For the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, the faithful—often do not wish to trouble the Church; that is, they persevere in the perfect whiteness of virtues [Col. 0875D] amid its tribulations.

This was prefigured in Abraham’s sacrifice. The Lord commanded Abraham: “Take a heifer, a she-goat, and a ram, each three years old; also a turtledove and a dove.” Taking all these, he divided the four-footed animals through the middle and placed the parts opposite one another; but he did not divide the birds. Then birds descended upon the carcasses, and Abraham drove them away. When the sun had set, thick darkness came, and a lamp of fire appeared, passing between those divisions (Gen. 15:29).

By the four-footed animals are signified carnal persons [Col. 0876A].

[Note: [Col. 0875D] We judge that this very tangled passage, corrupted by the copyist, may be restored to the author’s meaning as follows: “Whether they are secular rulers, signified by the ram; or prelates, signified by the heifer, when they feed others with the milk of holy preaching [Col. 0876D]; or priests, signified by the she-goat, since they surpass others in virtues and, by their example, nourish them as it were with their own flesh.”]

Whether they are secular rulers, signified by the ram, or prelates of the Church, who feed others with holy preaching, or those whom the she-goat signifies: all are three years old, because all must remain in faith in the holy Trinity. The turtledove and dove are birds which express perfect righteous persons through chastity and simplicity. Carnal persons, then, are divided through quarrels and scandals, and rise one against another; but the righteous remain uncorrupted and steadfast, and are not divided. The birds descending upon the carcasses are demons, whose food is the discord of carnal persons. Abraham’s driving away the birds signifies a certain correction by which the righteous person drives demons away from them with the hand of holy rebuke.

The setting of the sun signifies that, for those engaged in quarrelling [Col. 0876B], the sun of righteousness sets. Hence the Apostle: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4:26). When the sun departs, darkness follows—blindness of mind in the present life. For the mind’s eye is disturbed by rage; and in the future comes the fire of Gehenna. You have heard, brothers, of the steadfastness of the good and of the punishment of the discordant. Blindness of mind is to be feared; the punishment of Gehenna is to be feared. Nothing is more shameful than strife among religious people, who ought to shine as lights in the world.

These contentions commonly arise from envy and detraction. But if there is detraction in the cloister, where is regular silence? What does the Apostle say? “If anyone thinks himself religious and does not restrain his tongue, that person’s religion is vain” (James 1:26). “Therefore,” as David says, “keep your tongue [Col. 0876C] from evil and your lips from speaking deceit” (Ps. 33:14).

See from where you have come and to what you have come. You have gone out from the world and fled to the camp of God. You possessed [perhaps: left behind] temporal riches, having come to obtain heavenly ones; and therefore you have chosen poverty, so that each of you may say: “I chose to be abject in the house of the Lord rather than dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. 88:11).

Lot and his wife went out from Sodom. Lot did not look back; his wife, neglectfully looking back, was changed [into a pillar of salt (Gen. 26)]. These two signify two kinds of people fleeing the world. The manly-minded person does not look back to what is behind. The effeminate person, like a dog returning to its vomit, returns, and his spirit hardens [Col. 0876D]. Therefore what you have forsaken must be handed over to oblivion, and you ought to be intoxicated by hope and desire for heavenly things.

There is an intoxicating drink in the Church; but how splendid it is! For people contemplating the abundance of the heavenly Jerusalem “shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house.” They are intoxicated—that is, from desire for it they forget parents, children, wives, lands, riches, and honours. Do not prefer yourselves one to another; rather, let whoever is greater among you become your servant. Abandon gatherings for conspiracy and detraction. Hear [Col. 0877A] what the perfect man says in the Psalm: “I have not sat with the council of vanity, nor will I enter with those who work iniquity. I have hated the assembly of the malicious, and I will not sit with the impious” (Ps. 25:4).

Nevertheless, if there is something in the Church which gives you scandal or disturbs the peace of the Church, you are not forbidden to have it examined by the lord—that is, the prelate—and corrected as is fitting. And may the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## CXVII [On Various Matters XXX]. TO BENEDICTINE MONKS

[Note: [Col. 0877D] From an Angers manuscript.]

“Open your gates, Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars” (Zech. 11:1).

[Col. 0877B] Zechariah, the eleventh of the prophets, after the destruction of the holy city had already occurred, predicts another destruction to come through the Romans. Amid the very beginnings of the rebuilding of the Temple, by the spirit of prophecy he foretells the vengeance for the Lord’s Passion: the destruction of the people, the overthrow of the city, and the demolition of the Temple. The same prophet also says that the Lord would visit that very city in humility: “Rejoice greatly, daughter Zion; behold, your king comes to you, righteous and a saviour, seated upon a young ass, the foal of a she-ass” (Zech. 9:9).

The testimony from Zechariah which we set before you may also be understood of the sending of the Holy Spirit, who descended on the disciples gathered in the upper room on the day of Pentecost, kindling their hearts with the ardour of his fire. This saying of Zechariah is suitable for a fourfold interpretation [*tetrasyrticon*, perhaps *tetrasticon*]: [Col. 0877C] historically, as referring to the destruction of the Temple; as referring to the sending of the Holy Spirit on Pentecost; as referring to the daily inspiration of that same Holy Spirit; and as referring to the perfect infusion of heavenly grace which shines forth in the more perfect. The first interpretation concerns a threat; the second, an exhortation; the third, congratulation; the fourth, perfection. The first exposition is singular; the second particular; the third general; the fourth special.

Thus, threatening according to the literal surface of the history, the prophet says: “Open your gates, Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars” [802] (Zech. 11:1). Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia in Judaea, loftier than all others and rich in the tallest cedars. It is therefore rightly understood as the Temple, lofty in its structure and dazzling to human eyes in its ornament; hence Micah calls it a cloudy tower:

> “And you, the cloudy tower of the flock, daughter Zion” (Mic. 4:8).

Or it may be so called because everything wooden found in the Temple—its panelling, beams, and the like—was made from cedarwood. Thus the Temple is rightly understood by Lebanon. Addressing his voice to the Temple, then, the prophet says: “Open your gates, Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars”—that is, the fire of the Romans, through which you will be cast down to the ground in vengeance for the Saviour.

The Roman army, surrounding the city, gained victory with the Lord’s permission. Following the custom of victors, it violently seized everything upon which its abundance had set its eyes. [Col. 0878A] After its enemies had been slain or taken into captivity, they stripped off the silver and gold which had been attached to the panels with gold and silver nails as thick as a finger. They burned the panels themselves, as Josephus relates, so that, once the wood had been reduced to ashes, streams of silver might flow out as the nails melted into liquid.

This is, as you have heard, the historical exposition of what we set before you. Let us now see how it may be applied to the primitive Church: “Open your gates, Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars.” Lebanon is used both in a good and in a bad sense, because it has two interpretations. For *Lebanon* means “whiteness” or “whitewashing.” Whiteness is natural; whitewashing is sometimes falsely applied over hidden ugliness, so that what is foul within may seem fair without. [Col. 0878B] Thus the Lord in the Gospel compares certain people to whitewashed tombs, outwardly white but inwardly full of every impurity (Matt. 23).

Lebanon signifies Christ because of the beauty of his virtues and the incomparable perfection of his life. Hence David says: “More beautiful in form than the children of men” (Ps. 44:3 [45:2]). And in the Song of Love: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands” (Song 5:10). He is the one “walking in his robe,” whose “eyes are more beautiful than wine and whose teeth are whiter than milk” (Gen. 49:12). Speaking to him, the prophet says: “Open your gates, Lebanon.” By the gates are understood the apostles, whose hearts God opened when he drenched them with the dew of his grace. These are the gates of which we read in the Psalm: “Enter [‘Open’] his gates with confession, his courts with hymns; give thanks to him” (Ps. 99:4 [100:4]).

John, in his Apocalypse (ch. 21), says of these gates: There were twelve gates: three to the east, three to the west, three to the south, and three to the north. Or, if we attend to the etymology of the name, the apostles are fittingly understood by “gates.” For a gate (*porta*) is said to derive from carrying (*portando*): carried by apostolic teaching on the way, we are sustained on the way and raised up to [803] our homeland. It was the custom of the ancients to mark out with the furrow of a plough the site for a city to be built; and, when they reached the place where gates were to be made, they lifted the plough. Hence it was called a *porta*.

It follows: “And let fire burn your cedars.” By cedars the same thing is to be understood as by gates—namely, [Col. 0878D] the apostles—of whom it may be said that the Lord consumed them when he incorporated them through the Holy Spirit. Hence Peter was told: “Kill and eat” (Acts 11:7). We say that the Lord adorned these cedars, that is, certain persons among them. For at first they had ignorance and fear. When the Paraclete was given, fear yielded to steadfastness; knowledge dispelled the darkness of ignorance. Their hearts were opened to understand the Scriptures. Their timidity was animated for preaching. They were afraid because they had heard the saying: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves” (Matt. 10:16). Nor is it surprising that a few feared the countless multitude, the unarmed feared the armed, the simple feared the cunning, the unlearned feared the learned, and commoners [Col. 0879A] feared tyrants.

This may also be expounded so as to apply to the universal Church gathered, from circumcision and uncircumcision, into one cornerstone. The Church is not inappropriately called Lebanon, concerning whose beauty the bridegroom says in the Song of Love: “You are wholly beautiful, my friend, and there is no stain in you” (Song 4:7). Therefore the Lord says through the prophet: “Open your gates, Lebanon,” and so forth.

There are three gates through which one opens to the Lord and by which one goes to him. To signify this, there were three courts around the Temple. These three gates are three fears: servile fear, initial fear, and filial fear. Through the first gate goes the servant; through the second, the disciple; through the third, the son. The servant is drawn by fear of punishment; the disciple follows through love for the teacher; the son hastens forward through desire for his father. The Church opens these gates [Col. 0879B] according to the diversity of her children, stirring some toward a humble heart, some toward a moderate heart, and some toward a lofty heart: toward a humble heart, as where it says, “Return to your heart, transgressors” (Isa. 46:8); toward a moderate heart, as here: “Fear the Lord, all you his saints” (Ps. 33:8 [34:9]); and, “He has set ascents in his heart in the valley of tears” (Ps. 83:6 [84:5]); toward a lofty heart, as where it says: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5:48); and, “Man shall approach the lofty heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63:7 [64:6]).

“And fire shall consume your cedars”: that is, the Holy Spirit shall raise the perfect to higher things through the greater dwelling of his grace. Those whom distinctive obedience commends are raised high by the privileged grace of gifts.

The fourth exposition concerns the perfect—namely, cloistered prelates—who are found in proportion as they are more perfect to be fewer. But someone will say: How can you fittingly designate a cloistered man by the name Lebanon, when his clothes show him unkempt, his fasts emaciated, and his vigils pale? [804] To one asking thus, the answer may be this: You do not know how to look; you cannot perceive [perhaps *you do not look into*] what inward delight lies hidden, or what and how great a fruitfulness of spiritual gifts cheers the mind. You notice the manure placed around the fig tree; you do not observe the fig tree’s fruitfulness. You cannot judge inward beauty by the outward eye.

The souls of such persons are fattened with God’s good things on the way and shall be satisfied in their homeland. Such, we read, were the Macarii, Pauls, and Anthonys, [Col. 0879D] whose way of life was in heaven, so much nearer to God as it was farther removed from the tumult of the world. To signify this perfection of holiness [perhaps *of the holy*], the high priest wears a red mantle, so that in him and through him an example of perfection may shine forth.

Thus to the perfect, and to every one of the perfect, it is said: “Open your gates, Lebanon,” for the Church still hidden and tender. God established three things through which, brothers, the summit of perfection consists among you. Do not suppose that the blessed Benedict laid the foundation of your way of life. When the Lord Jesus founded the Church, he ordained the holiness of your life in three things: brotherly love, common possessions, [Col. 0880A] and humble obedience.

Of brotherly love it is written: “The believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). Of common possessions we find it said: “None of them said that anything was his own, but all things were common to them” (ibid.). Of the humility of those who obey it is said: “Whoever is greater among you shall be your servant” (Mark 10:43). It is true that blessed Benedict did not first discover the principle of blessed life, but added certain accessories: dryness of food, roughness of clothing, divisions of fasts, and hours of prayer.

At the first gate Judas perished, becoming an apostate and falling away from brotherly love. At the second, Ananias and Sapphira perished, because they wished to keep something as their own. At the third, Simon Magus perished, because he refused to obey and therefore [Col. 0880B] died under the guilt of death.

“And fire shall consume your cedars.” In this reading, cedars are understood in a bad sense. Evil cedars are set against the gates of man: envy against brotherly love; private ownership against common possessions; and improper disobedience against obedience. Open your gates to the Lord, brothers, by loving one another and possessing nothing as your own; and the fire—that is, the Holy Spirit—will consume your cedars, that is, wipe away every tear of the mind.

Behold: we have carried out, according to our measure, the promised fourfold exposition of Zechariah’s saying. Let each of us therefore pray that the Holy Spirit may cleanse in us what is muddy, illumine what is dark, and bring to completion what is imperfect. And since it is the nature of fire to be carried upward and to draw with it what it has set aflame, [Col. 0880C] let us pray that it may snatch us up to meet [805] our Lord, our Judge, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

CXVIII [Various Subjects XXXI]. ON MONASTIC PERFECTION

[Note: [Col. 0879D] From Victorinus.]

“When Lot was going out from Sodom, the angels spoke to him, saying: ‘Save your life; do not look back.’ Lot said to them: ‘There is a small city to which I can flee, called Zoar.’ The angels said to him: ‘Save yourself on the mountain’” (Gen. 19:17).

You know, dearest brothers, that Lot, Abraham’s nephew [or brother], lived among the worst people in Sodom and Gomorrah. When the Lord wished to overthrow those cities, [Col. 0880D] he sent angels to cause Lot, his wife, and his daughters to leave the places of the wicked, lest they perish with the wicked. As they were going out, the angels said to him: “Save your life; do not look behind you, and do not stop anywhere in the whole surrounding region.” But his wife was changed into a pillar of salt because she looked back behind her.

In Lot and his wife are represented two kinds of people who leave the world: one kind abandons the world; the other, by looking back, comes to death. By Sodom and Gomorrah the world is understood, because *Sodom* means “mute blindness,” and *Gomorrah*, “harshness.” For the world is mute, that is, irrational and comparable to dumb animals. [Col. 0881A] Hence the Psalmist says: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13 [49:12]). Human beings are harsh and fierce because they persecute themselves and the righteous.

Therefore angels—that is, messengers, namely preachers—are often sent to draw some people out of the world. They command them to save their souls and flee the fire of Gomorrah: that is, to renounce lust and the desires of the age. They are commanded not to look behind them, because all who have received grace and entered the paths of life ought not return to what they have abandoned. For it is better not to have known the truth than, after knowing it, to turn back.

Some look back and are changed; others neither look back nor are changed. [Col. 0881B] The woman looks back and is changed into a pillar of salt, because it is womanish and unmanly in spirit to return to the stench of the world; and those who return become salt, teaching others not to do such things and not to suffer such things, as a seasoning [for them].

But the angels command Lot to save himself on the mountain. This mountain is the contemplative life, which one is commanded to approach by leaving the world and abandoning all worldly cares. This is that contemplative life of which [806] we read in the Gospel. A certain young man said to the Lord: “Teacher, what good thing shall I do to have eternal life?” He said: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” The man said to him: “Which ones?” Jesus said: “You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; honour your father [Col. 0881C] and your mother; and love your neighbour as yourself.” All these things belong to the active life.

Afterwards the young man said: “I have kept all these; what do I still lack?” Jesus said to him: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have and give to the poor; and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me” (Matt. 19:16). But Lot, seeing that he could not climb this mountain, said: “There is a small city to which I can go up; it is Zoar.” That small city signifies the active life, to which one flees who cannot ascend the mountain. For *Zoar* means “little one.” It is better for him to be content in Zoar—that is, in the lesser life—with lay conversion [perhaps *way of life*] and marriage, than, after taking hold of the mountain of virtues, to return to low things—that is, to worldly matters.

Yet we read later: “Lot went up from Zoar and dwelt on the mountain” (Gen. 19:30). [Col. 0881D] There is, indeed, for him a suitable ascent: from this life [perhaps “from the active life”] he should ascend to the contemplative life. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever leaves father or mother or wife or children or fields for my name’s sake shall receive a hundredfold” (Matt. 19:29).

Dearest brothers, whatever was written was written for our instruction. You have abandoned Sodom and Gomorrah; you have fled the fire of lust and concern for worldly pleasures; you have already ascended the mountain.
