Take care, beloved, that you do not [Col. 0882A] look back. Let the things you have set aside become worthless to you: they are deceptive and transient goods. Love the heavenly things, which are true and everlasting goods.

You are truly poor, because you have stripped yourselves of everything in order to share in true blessedness. Of you it was said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). It says “in spirit,” because those who are poor by compulsion, not in mind, are by no means blessed. You have followed Christ, saying: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Matt. 19:27).

You have bought the Lord’s treasure, of which it is written: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man who finds it hides; and for joy over it goes and sells all that he has and buys that field” (Matt. 13:44). [Col. 0882B] This treasure is the kingdom of heaven; that field is divine discipline, that is, evangelical and divine knowledge. The treasure is hidden because the kingdom of heaven is learned and acquired through divine teaching. The man who finds it hides it. The good man hides it in order that it may be kept from wicked spirits and from human praises. For when he boasts of being good—because whoever publicly displays a treasure wishes it to be plundered—he goes and sells what he has.

He begins to go when he begins to love; he sells all that he has when he sets aside what he retains; he buys that field when he comes to zeal for heavenly discipline. The kingdom of heaven is offered for sale to all, because, Gregory says, nothing is cheaper when it is bought; nothing is more precious when it is possessed, [Col. 0882C] because it costs as much as you have. Therefore, you who have sold everything for it, labour to possess what you desire. For no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully. “Whoever perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

In the world you were under your own free power. Behold, for God’s sake you have submitted yourselves to God’s yoke, so that, with the knowledge of sin removed, you may be held in a good purpose by the chain of obedience. But since it profits nothing to do good under compulsion, do nothing except willingly. For those who do good under compulsion are compared to Simon of Cyrene, whom the Jews compelled to carry Jesus’ cross. The Cyrenian carries the cross and does not die: he is compelled, but without fruit. Likewise monks torment their bodies with vigils, fasts, and labours, but often under compulsion. Hence Gregory says: [Col. 0882D] “He carries Christ’s cross under compulsion who, not led voluntarily to a good work, performs the work of the righteous as a sinner and without fruit.” He carries the cross and does not die who emaciates his body while living for the world.

Therefore be subject willingly; obey your masters in the Lord. Nothing is greater than obedience. For as disobedience harms, so obedience has power. Adam perished because he was disobedient. Christ rose because he obeyed the Father unto death. Hence the Apostle says: “As through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one many shall be made righteous” (Rom. 5:19). Jonah was disobedient and was swallowed by a sea-monster. Saul was disobedient and was seized by a demon.

We read in the Lives of the Fathers that one of the Fathers, placed in ecstasy, saw four orders before God. [Col. 0883A] The first order consisted of persons suffering illness and giving thanks to God. The second consisted of those who practise hospitality and minister in this work. The third consisted of those who pursue solitude. The fourth consisted of those who, for God’s sake, are subject to the Fathers in obedience. This order, then, which rendered obedience was above those three orders; it wore a golden necklace and possessed greater glory than the rest.

The elder said to the one in ecstasy to whom this was shown: “Because all the others had some freedom to fulfil their own wills, whereas those who practise obedience abandon all their wills. This whole order depends upon the will of the commanding Father, [Col. 0883B] and therefore has received a greater glory than the others.”

CXIX [Various Subjects XXXII]. TO BENEDICTINE MONKS

[Note: [Col. 0883D] From an Angers manuscript.]

“Jesse took an ass full of loaves . . . and a kid from the goats, and sent them by the hand of his son David to Saul” (1 Sam. 16:20).

When Saul was troubled by an evil spirit, David, who knew how to play the harp, was found and summoned by his father [perhaps “by King Saul”]. His father sent him with gifts to appease the king’s anger. The history is well known; but since all these things happened to them as figures, I believe that beneath the veil of these words [Col. 0883C] the Saviour’s conception was prophesied by Samuel, though it was quite plainly foretold by others as well. Yet it was not fully known from what persons, or in what persons, it would take place.

It had been very fully prophesied by Isaiah, who said: “Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a Son,” and so forth (Isa. 7:14); and by Jeremiah: “The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31:22); and by Isaiah: “Before she travailed, she gave birth to a male child” (Isa. 66:7). The ancients also cried: “Send forth the Lamb, O Lord, ruler of the earth” (Isa. 16:1). Yet they did not foretell from what elements that conception would be made. Samuel supplied something by the words cited above.

For he shows quite fully the elements from which the Saviour’s conception was to exist, and directs us to their interpretation when he says, [Col. 0883D] “an ass full of loaves,” rather than “loaded.” For if he understood nothing mystical, he would seem ridiculous in saying this. Therefore he predicts the Saviour’s conception; for as his generation is ineffable [perhaps “his generation cannot be narrated”], so his conception is ineffable—indeed, contrary to nature. Since he predicts his conception, while leaving intact the peace of the historical narrative, we may today add and say: “Today Jesse took an ass full of loaves, which he sent by the hand of his son to Saul.”

This conception of the Saviour is far different from human conception. Human conception has existence from only two things. The Saviour’s conception, however, is from three. The former occurs from two bloods in flesh, namely soul and body. Afterwards, in a human being, through the course of forty days, flesh comes to exist without a soul and takes on the features of a body. This conception takes place without male seed, from three things: soul, flesh, and Word. [Col. 0884A] Since it was new and unheard of, it was foretold by a new and unheard-of kind of words. For who had ever heard that anyone’s conception took place from an ass, a kid, and a word? No one.

This conception took place in a wondrous and ineffable manner. For as a little stream passes through a pipe-like channel, so the Son of God descended into the Virgin’s womb, in order to take from her a channelled little stream. Therefore understand the ass as Christ’s soul. For an ass is a harmless and gentle beast. Hence, because of its gentleness, it is the first beast that a human being is recorded to have ridden; whence *asinus* (“ass”) is said to derive from *sedendo* (“sitting”). This beast, I say, is humble in comparison with the others: it does not devour with teeth, toss with horns, tear with claws, or trample with feet.

This is Christ’s humble spirit, upon which the fullness of divinity bodily—that is, solidly—sat. It was humble and gentle, because, like a sheep before its shearer, it was silent and was humbled even unto death. Such a spirit is worthy of God’s full indwelling. For upon whom does God dwell, if not upon the humble, quiet person who trembles at his words?

This ass was full of loaves. A remarkable matter! I can scarcely understand of what loaves he speaks. Had he said simply “full of bread,” the interpretation would be easy enough. For the bread which came down from heaven fully refreshes Christ’s soul, which it fully inhabits and to which it has united itself ineffably. But [Col. 0884C] he says, in the plural, “loaves.” He therefore removes us from an understanding of the divine bread. A remarkable matter!

I have read that Pharaoh ate loaves made by the baker’s art, which are sins inflicted through ingenious deceptions. But God’s ass was never full of those loaves. There are also the offering loaves, some of which were baked in an oven, others in a frying-pan, others on a griddle, and others in water. These loaves are the memory and recollection of sins, which are cooked in the oven of our mind. But did he have a recollection of sins? Far be it! For he is the one “who committed no sin” (1 Pet. 2:22), “nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Matt. 15:36).

We also read of the seven Gospel loaves with which he himself satisfied and filled seven thousand people: they are the sevenfold graces of the Holy Spirit. The Lord wished Christ’s soul to be filled with these loaves, because he gave him fullness of knowledge. But he had this knowledge before he assumed a soul, as is known to everyone. We must therefore seek the fullness of other loaves. For just as, insofar as he is God, he had the fullness of uncreated knowledge, so, insofar as he is human, he had the fullness of created knowledge; [Col. 0884D] he is one thing insofar as he is God, and another insofar as he appeared incarnate. Hence his soul was full of loaves other than the Gospel loaves.

These are the loaves of labour, the loaves of sorrow, the loaves of presentation, and the loaves of strength. For we read that he laboured in preaching. Hence it is said: “I laboured enduring [alternatively, crying out]; my throat became hoarse” (Ps. 68:4 [69:3]). We read that he grieved: for he wept over Lazarus, wept over the city, and over the women. Isaiah also says: “We saw him full of sorrows, having neither beauty nor comeliness.” Concerning the loaves of presentation, we read in Leviticus that no one was permitted to eat them except priests alone. Concerning the fourth, we read that Elijah, in the strength of one loaf, fasted for forty days.

Therefore he laboured in preaching, grieved in compassion, gave an example in action, and suffered in strength. He preached in order to instruct; he had compassion in order to benefit; [Col. 0885B] he acted in order to give an example; he suffered in order to redeem. But he was fuller of the fourth loaf, namely that of passion, than of the others, and it was more beneficial to us. For the bread of passion was not only redemption for us, but perfection. For upon the altar of the cross it was the price; upon the altar it was food or drink; in death it was provision for the journey; in heaven it was reward.

Behold the loaves with which our holy Ass was full. Likewise, there was “a kid from the goats.” Christ’s body is customarily compared to a kid, because sin is customarily signified by a kid, and he assumed flesh resembling sinful flesh. And just as there are two things in us, guilt and punishment, and he is made like us in one of them but not in the other—namely in punishment, not in guilt—so there are certain things in a kid in which he is like it, but not in others. For a kid is a foul-smelling, wanton, and rough animal; and through these three kinds are indicated habitual vice, licentiousness, and instability. The stench is in habit, wantonness in instability, and roughness in corruption.

Of stench it is said: “My wounds have rotted, or become putrid” (Ps. 37:6 [38:5]). Elsewhere: “They have utterly decayed like beasts in their dung” (Joel 1:17). Of instability it is said: “Not so the wicked, not so; but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1:4). “The plains rise and descend to the place which you founded for them.” Of barrenness [perhaps “roughness”] it is said: “The earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3:18).

[Col. 0885D] In these respects Christ’s flesh is not like a kid, but it is like it in others. A kid feeds on bitter things; by feeding, it raises itself on high. It crosses lofty and trackless places. And Christ was fed on bitter things. For he was seized in the garden, then dragged before Caiaphas, experienced scourges, was sated with reproaches, died on the cross, and after death was pierced with a lance.

Christ raised himself on high. Although, by the nature of his sentience, he recoiled from death, nevertheless, with reason as guide, he subjected his own will to the divine will, saying: “Not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. 26:39). He crossed low and high places when a bright cloud lifted him into heaven as the disciples watched. Hence it is said: “As they watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes” (Acts 1:9).

Likewise, he was from the goats—that is, from the midst of the perversity [811] of the Jews, which is customarily represented by goats. There were good Jews among the patriarchs and prophets; [Col. 0886A] bad ones among the scribes and Pharisees. There were good ones in the primitive Church, that is, among the apostles. There will be good ones at the end of the world, when the hearts of the children shall be turned to the fathers.

Christ was born from goats, because he was incarnate in the time of the perverse. Therefore Jesse—that is, God the Father—took the ass and the kid, that is, Christ’s soul and flesh, and created them through the hand of his Son, that is, through his Son, who is called his hand. Hence: “And the hands of God strengthen me.” For as he made all things through the Son, so through Christ he created the soul and flesh and, in creating them, united them to himself.

But, you will say, it is strange that you say Christ’s soul is signified by the ass. For in the conception of a human being, the body ordinarily precedes the soul. Therefore, if the prophet wished to follow this order, the kid ought to have been placed before the ass. But by God’s wondrous ordering and lofty counsel, the prophet arranged it thus, lest you should understand Christ’s conception to be like that of others. For in his conception neither did the body precede the soul nor the soul the body.

His Father therefore sent this Son, thus conceived, to Saul—that is, to death. For by Saul we customarily understand death. Yet what you say is strange: he was conceived for life, not for death; nevertheless, on the very day on which he was conceived, after a cycle of thirty-two and a half years, he died. Hence, when he was sent into the flesh, he was said to be sent into death. Foreseeing this, Moses said: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” (Exod. 34:26), that is, you shall not kill Christ on the same day on which he was conceived, [Col. 0886C] a command whose transgressors the Jews are held to be.

Although these matters may be expounded concerning the conception of the Savior as we have said before, yet, if we wish to attend more keenly and subtly to those words, they are set forth concerning you, to whom I speak. It is therefore said of you: Jesse took, through the hand of his son, the ass, because he also handed you over to death. “By the son of Benedict I mean his arrangement—that is, the counsel or deliberation by which he devised the Rule and the order of your manner of life.” For the hand of the son is his writing, in which he handed down to you what he had conceived in mind; and it was written by the hand of the son, through whom he delivered you to death.

For if you are observers of that Rule, you will be dead to the world. As a dead person does not see [Col. 0886D] what is done in the world or hear people when they chatter, so he leaves behind everything that promises itself to him. And you have left the world; you neither see people nor ought to hear their chatter. For as a dead person is buried lest he be exposed to human sight, so you too are, as it were, buried within the boundaries of the cloister, lest you appear to the sight of people, 812 whose conversations you ought to avoid. And as a dead person is wrapped in a winding-sheet, bound with bands, and thus buried, “so you too, wrapped in a tunic and bound with a belt, ought even to sleep.”

You may observe this in three brothers: one had been rich in the world, another poor in the wilderness, and another had departed from the world. The one who had been rich came to the poor man so that he might help him. The latter said: “Go to my brother, so that he may help you.” And he [Col. 0887A] said: “Why do you mock me? Is he not dead? How then can he help me?”—“Likewise,” he said, “I too am dead and cannot help you.” So you too are dead to the world.

“You are the ass and kid of Benedict. But do not be troubled because I call you an ass”; for the Lord especially rides upon you, is always with you, and you are with him. Hence the Prophet: “I became like a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you” (Ps. 72:13). You are that ass of whom Jacob said: “Issachar is a strong ass, lying down between the boundaries” (Gen. 49:14), bearing burdens upon his shoulders. “For your father imposed boundaries upon you, which you must not transgress” in eating, reading, sleeping, or speaking.

“Even if you are disgusted, you are not permitted not to go with the others to the table.” If you wish to keep vigil, nevertheless you must enter the dormitory with the others; and if you wish to sleep, you must keep watch with the others; if you wish to speak, you must be silent with the others; if you wish to read, you must cease with the others and at times exchange words. Thus you lie down within the boundaries and have submitted your shoulders to bear burdens.

But how good these things are, each of you knows in the book of experience; and therefore each knows better what, as we know, burdens your shoulders above all else: namely, the vow. For you said: “I have sworn and resolved to keep the judgments of your righteousness.” But with what loaves is such an ass filled? Namely, lamentations alone befit a monk. If he is a monk, he ought to be wholly occupied with prayers and tears, not rejoicing and laughter. A monk, indeed, is said to be the keeper of one. Whoever keeps himself [Col. 0887C] is filled with loaves. What are these loaves? Tears for one’s own sins. Hence: “Rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Ps. 126:2). And again: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall drench my couch” (Ps. 6:7). And again: “My tears were my bread day and night” (Ps. 41:4).

They are also tears for neighbors’ sins, as the Lord wept over Lazarus and over the city: “If only you had known, you also, etc.” (Luke 19:42). For the sins of one’s neighbors are the frying-pans of the righteous. They are tears over the length of exile, as David says: “Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged” (Ps. 119:5); and tears from desire for the kingdom. Hence it is said: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept” (Ps. 136:1). You ought to be filled with these loaves.

You are [Col. 0887D] a kid taken from the goats—that is, from the house of this wicked 813 and perverse generation. For the kid has roughness in its hair. So you ought to have roughness, that is, lowliness, in your clothing. Your garment ought to be of goat hair, or monastic—that is, you ought to have dirty, cheap, and rough garments, signified by the hair of kids, which is rough and cheap.

Do you wish briefly to hear what a monk’s conduct ought to be? His face should be thoroughly washed with tears; his breast hoarse with sighs; his food scanty; his bed hard; his sleep brief; his prayer continual; his reading moral; his gait humble. These are the “filth” which a monk ought to possess. Whoever neglects this filth will not have fruitfulness. These are the dung and filth which your father Benedict applied as manure to the fig tree in order to make it fruitful. Elsewhere it is said of the same matter: “The slothful man shall be stoned with ox-dung” (Ecclus. 22), that is, whoever is sluggish in these matters will not obtain fruit.

Behold, you are an ass full of loaves and a kid taken from the goats, whom Jesse—that is, your father Benedict—took and sent to Saul, that is, to death, through the hand of his son. His son is his counselor and deliberator. For first he devised the Rule and the rigor of your order, and [Col. 0888B] afterward committed it to writing. What is written is the hand of the son; and through this hand of his son he sent you to Saul—that is, to death—because you are not permitted to transgress what he left in writing. Therefore, you who are now dead to the world, die also with Christ, whom the Father sent to die for the people,

> [Note: [Col. 0887D] It seems that no contemptible—indeed, an almost unquestionable—proof of Hildebert’s monasticism can be drawn from this sermon, in which he so often mentions either Saint Benedict, his holy Rule, or monastic exercises. For although he exhorts, in the second person, the monks to whom he spoke to monastic virtues, he applies what he says to himself when he concludes in the first person and in his own voice: “That at last we may meet him in the air, to receive from him eternal blessing,” etc.]

that at last we may meet him in the air, to receive eternal blessing from him, when he himself, our Lord Jesus Christ, comes as judge to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire. Amen.

## CXX [On Various Matters XXXIII]. TO BENEDICTINE MONKS. ON PERFECTION

> [Note: [Col. 0888D] From Victorinus.]

We read, dearest brothers, that Jacob had two wives (Gen. 29), namely Leah and Rachel: one dim-sighted, the other seeing clearly; one fruitful in children, the other scarcely having two sons. And he served seven years for Leah and seven for Rachel. These are figures of the Old Testament. The New Testament loves the truth, though veiled, which it obtained while hidden under its shadow; and when that truth is presented to us, the mind of the understanding person, searching its inner meanings, is satisfied by the spiritual savor of understanding.

This Jacob of whom you have heard figures God the heavenly Father, who daily begets children for himself by adoption. The two wives signify the two ways of life by which human beings live: the active and the contemplative. Leah signifies the active life, Rachel the contemplative. Leah is interpreted “laboring,” because the active life, though serving God, [Col. 0888D] sweats amid the labor of this world. It serves God when it receives, visits, consoles, and buries the poor, and renders them the other works of mercy. It toils when it procures for itself, its children, and its wife the means of life and the means by which Christ’s poor may be fed.

Leah is dim-sighted because, as long as we are involved in worldly affairs, we cannot clearly see God. Yet she is fruitful in children, because more active persons than contemplatives are found. Rachel, however, is interpreted either “sheep” or “seeing the beginning,” because contemplatives [Col. 0889A] are simple and innocent like sheep and, freed from the tumult of the world, are devoted solely to divine contemplation, so that they may more clearly see him who says: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8:25). Hence she is described as not dim-sighted, but beautiful and seeing clearly.

She has two sons because there are two kinds of contemplatives. Some live in community; others are solitary, separated from human beings. Hence one of the two is called Joseph and the other Benjamin. Joseph, interpreted “increase,” represents those who live together; Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand,” signifies one who has God alone as his living companion and the consolation of God’s right hand, not that of a human being.

The seven years signify the seven lives that run through the seven days, during which a person acquires the active or contemplative life; but the contemplative life is more properly that of the blessed and perfect than is the active. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor” (Matt. 19:21). And he says of Mary: “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42). But observe that he says: “Which shall not be taken away from her.” The active life will be taken away, but the contemplative endures forever. The active exists only in the present; contemplation begins here but will be perfected in heaven, because there we shall see God face to face. Him whom we behold here through a mirror and in an enigma, there we shall praise unceasingly, according to the Psalmist: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5).

But [Col. 0889C] 815 what is that house? The house of the heavenly kingdom. When the plan of our redemption had been revealed to David, he rejoiced and said: “I rejoiced at the things said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord’” (Ps. 121:1). As though disclosing to us the divine counsel—what he had heard and what had been revealed to him—he says: “We shall go into the house of the Lord.” He then describes what the house of God is, saying: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is into the same thing” (ibid., 3). For the heavenly Jerusalem is not a city, but is built as though it were a city, while the faithful—living stones bound together with the cement of love—are set into its building; and it will continue to increase until the last righteous person.

But the active life does not extend [there] so far, because there works of mercy are not performed [variant: “are not impeded”]. For how can mercy be shown where no miserable person is found? How will one feed a poor person where no one is hungry, where the bread within [variant: “of life”] satisfies everyone? To whom will one give drink where no one thirsts, but outside an eternal living [variant: “stream”] quenches the thirst of all?

But you, dearest brothers, have chosen the better part, since you resolved to despise the world. You preferred to disdain earthly things rather than lose heavenly things for brief and fleeting glory. Since, as we have said, there is a twofold life for those devoted to God, you have, by sounder counsel, undertaken the safer life, understanding the delight of that fellowship concerning which the humble Prophet [Col. 0890A] says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 131:1).

This life is indeed safer and sweeter, where one guards another lest he fall, or raises him if he has fallen; where one encourages another; where each is kindled by the other’s example. This was not unknown to wisest Solomon, who said: “Woe to one who is alone, because if he falls, he has no one to lift him up” (Eccl. 4:10). Hence it is the life of penitents, the life of those fighting against the world, the life of those fleeing to God, the life of sons who had gone astray and return to their father.

This is the house in which the son who had despised his share of the property through luxurious living is reconciled to his father. In that son, as your charity knows, a fitting parable of the sinner is contained. For as that son went abroad into a far country [Col. 0890B] (Luke 15), and there squandered his substance in luxurious living, so the sinner, while he loves carnal pleasures, lives as an exile from the Lord; and the more unlike God he becomes by sinning, the farther he is removed from the Lord.

A person’s substance is everything that, while alive, he thinks, understands, and says; God distributes this substance equally to all. The sinner consumes it when he expends his knowledge, life, thoughts, and words upon temporal pursuits. It is said of the son that 816 he began to be in want, attached himself to one of the citizens of that country, and that the man sent him to his farm to feed swine. He desired to fill his belly with the husks which the swine ate, and no one gave him any.

For the sinner lacks the good word [variant: “the true good”] and the food of virtues. Hence David says: “The rich have lacked and hungered, but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Ps. 33:11), that is, no true good, which is every good. He attached himself to one of the citizens because he attached himself to one of the princes of this world, that is, the devil, according to the Apostle: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers and against the rulers of the world” (Eph. 9:1). And the Lord calls them princes of this world, saying: “Now the prince of this world shall be cast out” (John 12:31).

The pig is an unclean animal that delights in filth, and therefore demons are compared to pigs, because they are filled with the filth of sins. The sinner feeds them with the filth of his crimes, and he himself becomes their food. [Col. 0890D] Husks are food for pigs; fornication, drunkenness, gluttony, and such things are the food of demons. The sinner wishes to be filled with husks, and no one gives enough to satisfy him, because desire [variant: “pleasure”] always hungers for itself; and the devil often does not grant a person the object or the power of his desire once he makes him already his own dead possession.

But the repentant sinner, turning to God the Father, says: “I shall arise [better: ‘But the repentant sinner, turning to God the Father, says: I shall arise,’ etc.], and go to my father, and say to him: ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son’” (Luke 15:18). He who lay in sins rises when he recognizes his sins and says: “I have made my offense known to you, and I have not hidden my injustice” (Ps. 39:11).

But what did the Father do? Moved by mercy toward him, [Col. 0891A] he met him, fell upon his neck, and kissed him. He said to his servants: “Quickly bring out the first robe and clothe him; put a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet; bring the fattened calf and kill it, that we may eat; for this son of mine was dead and has come to life, was lost and has been found” (Ps. 39:22).

Then the heavenly Father sees the wanderer when he moves him to repentance. Hence the Gospel says that, after Peter had denied the Lord three times, the Lord turned and looked at Peter; Peter remembered the Lord’s word and “went out and wept bitterly” (Matt. 26:75). When he looked at him, he visited his mind, and at once he wept bitterly. He runs to meet him because the sinner cannot approach God by himself unless God helps him. Hence it is said: “And your mercy shall follow me” (Ps. 22:6). And again: “Return to me, and I shall return to you” (Zech. 1:3).

He threw himself upon his neck because he imposes his burden upon him, of which he says: “Take my yoke upon yourselves … for my yoke is sweet and 817 my burden light” (Matt. 11:29–30). He kisses him when he delights the sinner with fuller sweetness of his own, according to that word of the Church: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1). This is the house, dearest brothers, where the Lord imposed his burden upon the sinner when he makes him live according to the Rule of the holy Fathers. Here he kisses him when daily, through us, he refreshes him by the words of preaching. You are [Col. 0891C] those servants to whom the Lord commands: “Bring out the first robe and clothe him” (Luke 15:22).

There are two robes. One is when, in the present, the soul is clothed with the garment of virtues. The other is the robe of immortality, when the body is raised at the end of the age. These two robes are two resurrections. One is that of the soul, when it is raised from the vices in which it lay dead. The other is that of the body, when our body, conformed to the body of Christ’s glory, will be renewed on the day of judgment.

The first robe is to put on Christ through conformity and transformation. Hence the Apostle: “Put on the new human being, who was created according to God” (Eph. 4:24). And again: “Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed [Col. 0891D] in the spirit [variant: ‘newness’] of your mind” (Rom. 12:2). You clothe the sinner with this garment when, by admonitions and example, you make him conformed to Christ.

Or, alternatively, that the garment may be distinguished from the ring, let us understand the robe as the Holy Spirit, by whose overshadowing the sinner is governed; and that new garment is called the purity bestowed through the Spirit. The ring, however, is conformity to Christ. You place Christ’s ring on his hand when you imprint [variant: “press”] upon his works the seal of Christ’s likeness. For on the ring is a royal image, signifying the likeness of Christ which we ought to bear in our works, signified by the hand. Therefore, the person who bears the ring [Col. 0892A] on his hand is one who departs from Christ in no work.

Again, you give shoes to his feet because, by the examples of the holy Fathers who have departed from the world, you lessen its [vicious] affections. For shoes, made from the skins of dead animals, signify the examples of the holy Fathers, who are already dead; the feet signify the affections through which one goes either to good or to evil. The feet of the affections must therefore be put into these shoes, lest they feel the earth or lest the serpent lying in ambush beside the way find them somehow bare.

Again you are commanded to bring the fattened calf and kill it. Who is this calf but Christ, who was sacrificed for us upon the altar of the cross? He is fattened because he is filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0892B] You bring him and again sacrifice him when daily, in the sacrament of the altar, you represent his Passion. For the repentant sinner, clothed in the robe of virtues, ought to approach the altar and, refreshed by his body and blood, unite himself [variant: “make himself fitting”] to his head.

It follows: “And let us eat.” God eats with you when he delights in your works. For his food is that you do the will of his Father. The feast for the sinner is the joy that is held in heaven over his conversion. Of this joy he says in the Gospel: “There is greater joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need repentance” (Luke 7:10).

Every day, dearest brothers, such a feast is celebrated among us. Every day there is present a multitude of angels, rejoicing over the conversion of sinners. Consider, therefore, the dignity of our order. Consider for what you have come. A place does not make one holy, but one’s conduct. An angel sinned in heaven; Adam sinned in paradise. Yet no holy place profited them. If places could protect their inhabitants, neither man nor angel would have fallen from his dignity.

Consider what the black garment and the tonsure urge upon you. The lowliness of the garment declares contempt for the world; hair shorn from the crown of the head signifies the removal from the mind of the excess of sins. O how astonishing, blameworthy, and worthy of grief it is if pride lies concealed beneath such a habit; if one lowly person envies another; [Col. 0892D] if, after despising secular things, the mind returns again to covetousness; if it loses the future life together with the present!

Humility, therefore, signified by the garment, is necessary for us; and charity, signified by common use,

> [Note: [Col. 0891] That is, common use of temporal goods.]

and obedience, understood through subjection; and discipline, understood through the sharpening of the staff. May God, who causes those of one manner to dwell in a house, establish [variant: “build”] and strengthen you in every good work, that he may deign to place you with himself in heaven. He who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## CXXI [On Various Matters XXXIV]. TO MONKS

> [Note: [Col. 0893D] From the Angers manuscript.]

[Col. 0893A]

“Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and its spices shall flow” (Song 4:16).—“A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” (ibid., 12).

We must see who is speaking, to whom he is speaking, and concerning what he speaks. Who speaks? Christ. To whom? To the north wind and the south wind. Concerning what? The garden. For what purpose? That spices may flow. He who speaks here, then, is a gardener. For he is the one who planted from the beginning the garden of delight, that is, paradise. Hence the woman was not far from the truth when she called him a gardener, saying: “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have laid him” (John 20:15). And he is truly a gardener, because he was born in a garden, [Col. 0893B] detained in a garden, and buried in a garden. He planted the garden, orders the garden, and governs the garden.

Such a one speaks here to the north wind and the south wind. The north wind is the northern wind; the south wind, the southern. The north wind is called “right” in name only; for it encounters clouds so that they may not rain and obstructs them, whence *aquilo* is said to be as though “binding waters.” The south wind, however, is a warm wind, suited to nourish the shoots of gardens, and therefore it is called a gardener. “Arise, north wind,” that is, withdraw; “and come, south wind, and blow through the garden, and its spices shall flow.”

Behold, four things are set forth here. First, a command; second, conversation; third, cooperation; fourth, completion. For he commands the north wind to withdraw; with the south wind—that is, the Holy Spirit—he converses, as though exhorting and persuading him to come into the garden and cooperate with him, so that it may bear fruit.

Besides this, it should be observed that five gardens are read of in sacred Scripture. The first is principal; the second particular; the third general; the fourth individual; the fifth spiritual. Again, the first is for grafting; the second for witnessing; the third for knowing; the fourth for resting; the fifth for walking about.

The principal garden, then, is the womb of the Blessed Virgin, from which that royal flower came forth. Hence Isaiah: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 2:1). The Lord chose this garden for grafting; for from the root of the garden a trunk came forth, into which the Lord grafted a shoot of nobler stock—that is, in the womb [Col. 0893D] of the Virgin he assumed flesh.

The second garden, which we have called particular and which the Lord chose for witnessing, is the primitive Church of the Lord’s disciples, upon whom the Holy Spirit descended in tongue and fire. It was particular because the other wall of the Gentiles had not yet been raised; it was raised through their preaching. Of this you have in the Gospel: “My Father is the husbandman, and you are the branches” (John 15:1), who invites you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain. He chose them for witnessing, as he himself says: “You shall be my witnesses in Judea and Jerusalem” (Acts 1:8).

The third, called general and intended for knowing, is the universal Church gathered from both peoples. Of it Isaiah says: You know what I have done. I made for myself a garden among Jews and Gentiles, and I made this garden for knowing, where we shall know him himself, the Father, and the Holy Spirit as one God.

The fourth garden, which is individual, is the soul of every righteous person; the Lord made it individual for resting. Hence it is said: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person, who trembles before God?” (Isa. 66:2). The fifth, which is spiritual and made for walking about, consists of cenobites, whom God chose especially for himself and among whom he walks and strolls, as is signified in the saying: “God walked in paradise” (Gen. 3:8).

The Lord makes, cultivates, and governs these gardens. Therefore he says: “Arise, [Col. 0894B] north wind,” that is, let the obstacle withdraw from the gardens; “and come, south wind,” that is, Holy Spirit, whose grace is sweeter even than southern sweetness; “and blow through the garden,” so that, just as chaff is shaken from grain by a great blast of wind, so every obstacle may depart from these gardens when the grace of the Holy Spirit comes.

The number of these persons [variant: “righteous persons”] corresponds to their respective impediments. For every garden has its own impediment. The first garden has its impediment, namely original sin. To it the Lord says: “Arise, north wind,” that is, “O concupiscence, depart from this garden.” “For the flesh of the Virgin was cleansed by God, so that it did not even experience the first movements.” “And come, south wind,” that is, Holy Spirit. This is not a command, but a conversation; for the Son does not command the Holy Spirit, but they customarily converse with one another in this way. Hence in Genesis: “Let us make man in our likeness” (Gen. 1:26); and here: “Come, south wind, and blow through the garden,” so that it may not even experience the first movements and its spices may flow.

The particular garden likewise has its north wind, namely ignorance and fear. For unlearned persons were chosen as preachers. Hence it is said: “God chose the weak things of the world” (1 Cor. 1:27). They also had fear. For the Lord had said to them: “Behold, I send you into the midst of wolves” (Matt. 10:16). They therefore had great cause for fear, since they were to be sent to preach before kings and rulers, as though saying: How then shall we go, since we are unskilled [Col. 0894D] and unlearned before those who hear us? Therefore the Lord says: “Arise, north wind,” that is, let all ignorance and fear depart; “and come, south wind,” that is, Holy Spirit, “and blow through the garden,” giving full knowledge and perfect charity, which drives away fear; “and its spices shall flow.”

The third garden has its north wind, namely the devil, who says: “I shall place my seat in the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14). This north wind was an impediment to the primitive Church before his death. To this north wind, therefore, the Lord says: “Arise, north wind,” that is, “Depart, devil, lest you impede my garden and its perfection; and come, south wind,” that is, Holy Spirit, [Col. 0895A] “and blow through the garden,” that is, fill it with your grace.

The impediment of the fourth garden is imperfection. For no one is so perfect as to know God except through a mirror and in an enigma. But in the future we shall see face to face, so that, although here it may be said, “Arise, north wind,” yet in the future it will be said more truly, because “when that which is perfect has come, that which is partial shall be abolished” (1 Cor. 13:10).

The fifth impediment is temptation. Cenobites experience temptations more than others; for the more someone dissents from temptation, the more he feels temptation, when he so prepares himself that he does not consent to it. Indeed, before it comes, he does that for which it ought to have come. Therefore we who have left everything—

> [Note: [Col. 0895D] He speaks thus as a monk.]

father and mother and the world, indeed who have hated even our own flesh—the devil attacks [Col. 0895B] us in order to tempt us. To him the Lord says: “Arise, north wind,” that is, “Withdraw, tempter, and do not tempt one who is at peace, lest my garden succumb to you; and therefore come, south wind, and blow through the garden,” that is, make it not succumb to temptations.

When these have withdrawn and the Holy Spirit has come, distinct spices flow [variant: “blow”] from each of the gardens. An aroma is called, as it were, *aerioma*, from fragrant air; hence a spice is called an *aroma*. From the first garden, therefore, an aroma flows: Christ, whose fragrance fills us all. Isaac perceived this fragrance when he blessed Jacob and said: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field” (Gen. 27:27). The second aroma is preaching. For the Lord commanded his apostles: “Go, preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15). The aroma of the third garden [Col. 0895C] consists in virtues, by which holy Church, fragrant with them, is acceptable to God. The fourth aroma is the future perfection of both parts. The fifth is the ministries, devotions, and sacred prayers of those under a rule.

Besides this, every garden is “a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” (Song 4:12). The first is enclosed, therefore, because entrance into it was open to no human being. This is that gate which Ezekiel saw, which was always closed and no one opened; its fountain is sealed with the seal of the cross. The third was enclosed by the covering of angels and sealed in faith. The fourth is sealed in the body with God’s image. Hence the Prophet: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been sealed upon us” (Ps. 4:7). The fifth is enclosed by dwellings and wall, rule and vow; one fountain is sealed with Saint Benedict’s seal, the other with blessed Augustine’s seal.

Let us therefore cry with one voice and say: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind, and blow through the garden, and its spices shall flow.” May he deign to do this, who is to come in holiness to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire. Amen.

## CXXII [On Various Matters XXXV]. TO MONKS

> [Note: [Col. 0896D] From the Angers manuscript.]

“Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16:24).

This is the voice of one who goes before and exhorts; for unless he went before, he would say to no purpose: “Whoever wishes to come after me,” etc. For one who follows says, “Wait for me”; one who goes with others says, “Let us go”; one who goes before others says, “Follow.” But we must see who this is who says, “Whoever wishes to come after me”; to whom he says it; where he goes; and by what way he goes.

It is Christ, indeed, who said this. And to whom? To those willing persons who devoutly embrace the way of salvation. For he does not love compelled service but voluntary service. Where does he go? To Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life. By what way? By charity, through which each person can follow Christ the Lord. For no other road is to be traveled.

It should be noted, moreover, that there are four roads by which a human being travels: one toward the south, another toward the west, another toward the north, another toward the east. For there are four regions of the world. The road that goes south is the weakness of human nature. For the south wind is warm, and our weakness comes from heat, namely from blood. The road toward the west is the necessity of death, of which it is said: “Remember, man, that you are ash and shall return to ash” (Gen. 3:19). And the Psalmist says: “Man is a spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. 77:37).

Another road is toward the north. The north wind is cold and signifies the devil, the instigator of sin. For sin is the road of going north, that is, to the devil, to Gehenna, where death is without end and pain unceasing. Hence: In hell there is no redemption.

The road toward the east is charity, by which one goes to God. Every Christian ought [Col. 0896C] to travel this road. To signify it, when we pray we turn our hands and faces toward the east, indicating that we wish to go and direct ourselves there. Likewise, when we bury the dead, we bury them so that their feet are toward the east and their head toward the west, thereby indicating that the head turn thence toward the east [perhaps with “ought to” omitted in the source].

Note that there are two things which burden and hinder those who are advancing toward Christ: namely, sins and riches. Of sins the Prophet says: “My iniquities have multiplied; they have risen above my head,” that is, above my mind, “and like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me” (Ps. 37:5). Of riches the Lord says: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28). Indeed, philosophers despised these riches [Col. 0896D], and regarded them as 823 unbearable burdens. For a certain philosopher sold all his inheritance, and, having received the money, went out to sea; and when he was in the depths of the sea, he threw the money, or riches, into the sea, saying: “Sink, most ruinous riches! I drown you, lest you drown me.”

Likewise, in the words, “Whoever wishes to come after me,” you ought to observe two things: namely, that some follow Christ from afar, while others follow him closely. Those follow from afar who have not yet wholly abandoned temporal things. But those follow closely who have renounced the world in mind and body and have denied themselves, [Col. 0897A] to whom the Lord’s saying applies: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and follow me.” One who is on a cross has his limbs so fastened to the cross that he cannot use them for unlawful things. Likewise, one who has fastened himself to the cross does not stretch them out toward unlawful and shameful acts; indeed, he does not have power over himself. This is especially fitting for you religious men, who have even your tongue fastened to the cross—a restraint which Christ did not have. For, placed and raised upon the cross, he spoke and prayed, which a monk does not dare to do.

Note that four bore the cross: Christ, the two thieves, and Simon of Cyrene, whom the Jews compelled to carry Jesus’ cross. But they bore it differently. Christ bore the cross of obedience, for he was obedient to the Father unto death. Another bore the cross of penitence: namely, the thief [Col. 0897B] who repented of his sins, saying, “Remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). Another bore the cross of compulsion: namely, the thief who would not be converted but remained in faithlessness. Another bore the cross of pretence, like Simon of Cyrene.

Likewise, in cloisters and religious houses, some bear the cross of obedience, after Christ’s example, obeying God and their prelates. Others bear the cross of penitence: they repent of their sins like the thief, asking the Lord for pardon. Others bear the cross unwillingly. For it happens that they are beaten, scourged, and defamed, and are not permitted to be irreligious [perhaps: “so that they are not allowed to be irreligious”]. Others bear the cross hypocritically. For they pretend to be religious so that they may thereby be promoted to abbacies and such offices. [Col. 0897C] These latter two do not bear the cross well; the other two bear it well.

But note that the Jews say to Christ: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matt. 27:40). Likewise, the devil says to religious men: “Come down from the cross, young man! Do the will of the flesh; you will fast enough,” and other such things. But to others, who are of mature age, he says: “Gather money, so that when you are old you may have the means to provide for yourself; thus you will not be burdensome to the abbot.” And in many other ways he says: 824 “Come down.” Against him you ought to say: “I will not come down. Here I shall remain upon the cross until Christ comes and says to your spirit: ‘Come forth; come to me; I shall reward you.’” May he himself deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. [Col. 0897D] Amen.

## CXXIII [On Various Matters XXXVI]. TO MONKS

[Note: [Col. 0897D] From Victorinus.]

“I sought my beloved and did not find him; the watchmen who went about the city found me, struck me, and wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took my cloak from me” (Song 5:6).

These words, dearest brothers, are those of the contemplative Church [variant: “soul”], stripped of earthly things. By God’s grace assisting, you have followed her footsteps; therefore you ought to hear her words, so that she who instructed you by example may also teach you by speech. Hear how, and by what aid, she arrived at the contemplative [Col. 0898A] life, so that you too may arrive there by the same work.

She says in the Song of Songs that, while she was among worldly things, seeking her friend—that is, Christ—she could not find him, being entangled in secular [cares]; she could not devote herself to longing for him. But perhaps she heard the doctors of the Church preaching contempt for the world, since “no one can serve two masters, God and mammon” (Matt. 6:24), that is, riches. She was not seeking them; but when perhaps she had heard them or read their writings—that is, those of Augustine, Gregory, Jerome, and the rest—they found her; she did not find them. And when they preached such things, they struck her with fear lest, on account of the world, she lose her heavenly bridegroom; and they wounded her heart with love and desire for her friend, that is, Christ. Thus [Col. 0898B] the watchmen of the walls—that is, the teachers who defend the walls of the Church and supply them with fortifications by their preaching, lest it be shaken by spiritual [rather, carnal] people or heretics—took, that is, removed from her, her cloak: that is, the adornment of earthly things in which she had been entangled. For she set aside all secular things and, stripped naked of earthly concerns, gave herself solely to divine contemplation.

You, dearest brothers, have chosen this way beforehand and have stripped off your cloak, so that with Peter you may say to the heavenly bridegroom: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19:17). If many of you have not abandoned great riches because you did not possess useless riches, nevertheless you have left much, because you have set aside love for all secular things. Peter was a fisherman and obtained food by his craft, and yet [Col. 0898C] he says: “We have left all things.” He leaves much who retains nothing for himself. But because Socrates and Diogenes, and other philosophers, did the same, despising earthly things, he adds: “And we have followed you,” by imitating you according to our ability.

[Note: [Col. 0897D] Here he speaks in the first person as a true monk.]

If we can attain anything, we cannot be made equal to him. Yet when we follow, some are nearer and others farther away; Mary was nearer than Martha. The latter ministered; the former devoted herself to divine words. Yet neither [variant: “neither of them, however”] acted wrongly—indeed, Martha acted well—but Mary acted better; for it is written: “Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken from her” (Luke 10:43). When he says “the best part,” he shows that Martha’s part too is good. It is best because it makes one perfect, [Col. 0898D] as the Lord says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor” (Matt. 19:21). And again: “Everyone who has left father or mother or wife or children or fields for my name’s sake shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life” (ibid., 29).

You have fulfilled, both in will and in deed, what the Lord said: “Every one of you who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33). Some renounce in will, as David says: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61:11). But you have renounced the things themselves. Therefore, being stripped and freed from the burden, you are more ready to complete the course, [Col. 0899A] as the Apostle says: “Everyone who strives in the contest abstains from all things” (1 Cor. 9:25). You, however, are in a contest. Certainly, no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully.

For believers have a manifold struggle in this world. The believer fights against the flesh, as it is said: “The flesh desires against the spirit” (Gal. 3:17). And again: “I see a law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin” (Rom. 7:13). Likewise, the believer fights against the ungodly, of whom the Lord says: “You shall be hated by all people for my name’s sake. If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also” (Matt. 10:12). And David says: “The sinner watches the righteous and seeks to put him to death” (Ps. 36:32).

He has a third enemy, harsher and more cunning, of whom the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of these present darknesses, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12), [Col. 0899B] that is, against spiritual wickednesses dwelling in heaven, that is, moving about in the air.

[Note: [Col. 0899D] Hildebert affirms the same opinion concerning the dwelling of demons in the air in his first sermon on the Ascension of the Lord, his sermon on the Purification of Blessed [Col. 0900D] Mary, his sermon on Christian Warfare, and below in the Theological Treatise, chapter twenty.]

The first enemy, the flesh, harms by inciting unlawful impulses. The second, the tyrant [supplied: the world], harms by bringing tribulation. The third, that is, the devil, harms by suggesting temptations. The first must be conquered by taming it through fasts, vigils, and labours, as the Apostle says of himself: “I chastise my body and reduce it to servitude” (1 Cor. 9:27). And elsewhere: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth” (Col. 3:15), 826 because we are debtors not [Col. 0899C] to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom. 8:8). And if you live according to the flesh, you shall die.

The second must be conquered through suffering. Hence the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:8). And elsewhere: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5:44). And the Apostle: “Do not defend yourselves, beloved; for it is written: ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,’ says the Lord” (Rom. 12:19). If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink. And the Lord says: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. 5:39).

The third must be repelled by not consenting to [his] suggestions. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not give place to the devil” (Eph. 4:19); rather, with the sword of the Holy Spirit, that is, the word of God, and with the authorities of Scripture, destroy his darts. For when the enemy says, “Commit adultery,” answer contrariwise: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal,” etc. (Exod. 20:14). Thus oppose to each vice its particular commandment by the authority [of Scripture]. This the Lord also taught us in his own temptation, setting something from scriptural authority against each admonition of the devil. For when the devil commanded him to make bread from stones, [Col. 0900A] he said: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4). Again, when the devil urged him to cast himself down from the pinnacle of the temple, he replied: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (ibid., 7). Again, when he urged him to fall prostrate and worship him, he answered: “It is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’” (ibid., 10).

With these arms, therefore, the Lord equips us, so that whenever temptations press upon us we may seek defenses in divine sayings; and when a diabolical temptation begins to arise in the mind, we may immediately crush it, lest it turn into delight. For if it turns into delight, it is sin; if it is immediately overwhelmed, it is victory. Hence it was said to the serpent: “The woman shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. 3:15). [Col. 0900B] The serpent’s head is called the devil’s suggestion, because it is the beginning of sin. The heel signifies the end, because it is the final part of a human being. The woman crushes the serpent’s head when the faithful soul extinguishes an arising suggestion. The serpent lies in wait for the heel when it lays snares for the end of human beings; and if at the end it can deceive a person, it leads that person to destruction.

Nor is Christ to be followed only in resistance to and removal of vices, but also in the practice of virtues. For there is no virtue which he did not first display. Thus he says: 827 “Blessed are the poor” (Matt. 5:3); yet he became poor though he was rich. He says: “Blessed are the meek” (ibid., 4); and he is meek, who says of himself: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).—“Blessed are those who mourn” [Col. 0900C] (Matt. 5:5); yet he wept over Jerusalem and over Lazarus. He says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (ibid., 6); yet he says of himself: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34).—“Blessed are the merciful” (Matt. 5:7); yet he was moved by mercy for the thief and Mary the sinner. He says: “Blessed are the pure in heart” (ibid., 8); yet he is the one “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22). He says: “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Matt. 5:9); yet he prayed for his persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23:34); and he was led like a sheep to slaughter. He says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5:10); yet he suffered [Col. 0900D] for us, “leaving us an example, that we may follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21).

Thus the seven beatitudes were fulfilled in him. In all these things you can follow him, so that you may say: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19:27). But above all, four virtues are necessary for this order: charity, humility, obedience, and discipline. Sharing food signifies charity. Humbleness of clothing signifies humility. Your mutual obedience to prelates signifies obedience. Your having a master signifies discipline.

Charity is the root of all virtues: the bond of all brothers. [Col. 0901A] Where charity and love are, there is the gathering of the saints. “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one” (Ps. 132:1). Whence comes that pleasantness, unless from charity? This is the virtue that gives Christ as a fellow-dweller, as he himself says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in their midst” (Matt. 18:20). Christ always loves the unity of his own; hence he prayed to the Father: “Father, preserve in my name those whom you have given me, that they may be one, as we also are” (John 17:11).

Humility is the servant of all virtues; pride their destroyer. This is the virtue which the Lord showed by example and continually preached in word: by example, when he washed feet; by word, when he said, “Learn from me” (Matt. 11:29)—not [Col. 0901B] to make the world or raise the dead, but “because I am meek and humble of heart” (ibid.). O saving teaching! O faithful master! He did not wish to command what he himself did not do. Death was administered from the cup of pride; life sprang from humility. The exalted Lord looks upon humble things by loving them; he knows lofty things from afar by rejecting them, because “whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11). The humble tax-collector was exalted; the proud Pharisee was humbled.

This is the virtue which commended 828 the centurion when he said: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter beneath my roof” (Matt. 8:8). Obedience is the inciter to virtue. For reciprocal service kindles the ardour of love; serving through humility produces obedience. As the disobedience [Col. 0901C] of the first human being produced death, so the obedience of the second Adam produced life; for he was obedient to the Father unto death. Of this Samuel says: “Obedience is better than sacrifices” (1 Sam. 15:22).

Discipline is a corrective and must not be despised. David says: “Embrace discipline, lest at some time the Lord be angry and you perish from the righteous way” (Ps. 2:12). Again it is written: “He who rejects discipline is unhappy” (Wis. 3:11). And Solomon says: “My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord; do not fail when you are rebuked by him; for God corrects the one whom he loves” (Prov. 3:11). Therefore these four virtues are necessary: charity, the root; humility, the servant; obedience, the inciter; discipline, the corrector. [Col. 0901D] May God, who makes those of one disposition dwell in a house, strengthen and confirm you in every virtue and patience, so that, your course completed, you may rejoice forever with him who lives and reigns unto ages of ages. Amen.

## CXXIV [On Various Matters XXXVII]. TO NUNS

[Note: [Col. 0901D] From Victorinus and Lyra.]

[Note: [Col. 0901D] Perhaps to the nuns of Fontevraud, of whom Hildebert was patron and director, appointed by the supreme pontiff.]

“All the glory of the king’s daughter is within; she is clothed round about in golden fringes of varied work. Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be brought to you” (Ps. 44:14).

[Col. 0902A] In this prophetic verse, most beloved daughters, the glory of our Lord is described, and your merit also is not passed over in silence. This daughter of the king is also a mother: mother in her humanity and daughter in her divinity. For the King of heaven was born from his daughter. He created for himself the mother in whom he would be conceived and from whom he would be born. For just as he founded for himself the city of which it is said: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86:5)—that is, in her he was born as man, and he founded her as the most high God—so he created the mother from whom he would be born as man, and he created her as God.

David therefore calls her the king’s daughter, whose glory he describes thus: other women and royal daughters glory in outward beauty, but this daughter’s glory is within. Of this the Apostle says: “This is our [Col. 0902B] glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). For she preferred to possess in her conscience the beauty of the mind rather than the fragile, passing, and empty [variant: “lowest”] bodily form which is a temptation to the eyes. And her 829 glory was in golden fringes: in perseverance in good works. For fringes, which are at the end of a garment, signify perseverance; gold signifies good works, adorned with the brightness of radiance. And although the glory of innocence lay hidden in secret, she herself was clothed round about in the variety of many virtues. What she bore in her heart, she showed in her bodily conduct.

The Lord indeed commanded: “Take care not to perform your righteousness before people so that, seeing your works, they may glorify you” (Matt. 6:1). [Col. 0902C] It is not the appearance of works that is forbidden, but the intention of vain glory. Whose mind was purer, face humbler, speech sweeter [supplied: than Mary’s]? What virgin was more chaste? She was the pattern of all goodness. She always called herself a handmaid: “Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). And again: “Because he has looked upon the humility of his handmaid” (ibid., 48). She was beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun. Why enumerate each quality? She was seen to have no equal before her and none to follow her.

She was brought first to the Lord because he chose her before others, and the Holy Spirit overshadowed her, so that she might feel no fire of any evil will. “Virgins shall be brought to the king [Note: [Col. 0902D] Here there is a gap, which may be supplied thus: ‘Virgins after her, because she holds the first place, because no one,’ etc.],” holds it, because no one can be made equal to her [Col. 0902D]. Certainly, they can follow her, but cannot attain her; they can be followers, not companions. Therefore virgins shall be brought after her. But what virgins? Not any whatsoever, but those who will be near to her—her kinswomen, that is, her distinctive imitators.

For there are certain virgins chaste in body but corrupt in mind. These are not near her; these do not follow; these shall not be brought to you, O Lord. For integrity of flesh is of no value without integrity of mind. There are other virgins who do not seek the glory of continence but human praise; they desire the reward of their virginity. But because their glory is not within, they too shall not be brought in this manner. They follow the daughters described above. These are the foolish virgins who have no oil in their vessels. Lamps in the hands are works; vessels, however, are each person’s conscience; oil is the glory of works. Wise virgins have oil in their vessels and glory in their consciences; the foolish seek glory from human favour and therefore do not have with themselves what they seek elsewhere. But when the bridegroom comes, these will have shining lamps; theirs, however, will be extinguished, because it will then appear that works done for vain glory were not bright. There are also virgins who, though chaste and free from unclean desire [variant: “pleasure”], are occupied with other vices.

[Col. 0903B] Pride lifts up the minds of some, whether because they are more learned, nobler, or more prudent. These do not imitate her, who calls herself a handmaid rather than a mistress. But those who do not imitate her shall not be brought [to the king] after her. For although the Queen of heaven bore the King of heaven, although she carried her Creator, she nevertheless always pondered Solomon’s saying: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3:20). The humble Son, who “came not to be served but to serve” (Matt. 20:28), said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). He wished to have a humble mother, and he wishes to have humble daughters. Whoever is not humble is not a child of the Father who is in heaven. She herself also says in her song: [Col. 0903C] “He has put down the mighty from their seat and has exalted the humble” (Luke 1:12).

There are virgins who gladly wander and linger outside; and even if the body remains in the cloister, the mind nevertheless wanders outside. These are unlike her who went with haste into the hill-country, not lingering there, not curious about what she saw, not detained by conversations. But by what was she detained? By the mysteries which she saw and heard. For Scripture says: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2:19). There are other virgins who delight in idle chatter, detraction, and laughter, and do not apply themselves to divine praises. These are not her companions. When she spoke with her kinswoman, [Col. 0903D] she was not occupied with empty matters, but praising and magnifying God concerning the secrets of heaven, she burst forth in these words: “My soul magnifies the Lord” (Luke 1:12).

Therefore, dearest daughters, if your Queen, your Lady—indeed not yours alone, but ours and the angels’—the example and pattern for us all, fled the world in order that she might devote herself to God alone, [strive to imitate her.] Those who love things in the world have the world’s anxiety. The Apostle cries to you: “The form of this world is passing away. I wish you to be without anxiety. She who is without a husband is concerned how she may please God. The unmarried woman and virgin considers the things of the Lord, that she may be holy [Col. 0904A] in body and spirit; but she who is married considers the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (1 Cor. 7:31).

You have the highest King as bridegroom, whose beauty sun and moon admire. Take care lest the spiritual adulterer suggest something in the ear of your heart that may move your bridegroom to anger against you. Hear his threat through his Prophet: “You have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you” (Ps. 72:27). He himself therefore teaches what each of you ought to confess: “For me it is good to adhere to God; to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. 72:28). Therefore adhere to him, placing all your hope not in relatives, 831 but in him alone.

Consider what his will is. A good bride searches out her husband’s will, in order that she may serve [Col. 0904B] his will. This, then, is his will: that you be chaste both in mind and body; that you be humble and recollected [variant: “joined to him”] handmaids according to your profession, in which you said at your consecration: “I am a handmaid of Christ; therefore I present myself in the condition of a servant.”

[Note: [Col. 0903D] Roman Pontifical, “On the Consecration of Virgins.”]

It is God’s will that you avoid wicked conversations. “For, according to the Apostle, evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33). Unjust speakers are the envoys, advocates, and messengers of the spiritual adulterer, namely the devil, who wishes through them to violate the temple of the Holy Spirit—which you are. Therefore you are in a cloister, so that you may be enclosed and no messenger of the devil may enter to tempt and deceive you. Close, therefore, not only the cloister but also your hearts. Beware the temptation of the eyes, David saying: [Col. 0904C] “Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity” (Ps. 118:37).

Again, this is your bridegroom’s will: that if any woman behaves improperly, she should not resent being subjected to discipline. For David says: “Embrace discipline, lest at any time the Lord be angry” (Ps. 2:12). For “we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with this world” (1 Cor. 11:32). It is better for you to be scourged in the present by the hand of the presiding abbess than to be condemned in the future by the voice of God the judge.

It is God’s will that, if poverty constrains you, you should endure it together. For he who became poor did not call you amid riches, but in poverty; for the poor bridegroom wished in the present to have a poor bride, because he dwells [Col. 0904D] with you in the future, [where] in that true good, which is every good, those who eat shall be satisfied. This is the good of which David says: “Those who fear the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Ps. 33:11). This is God’s will: that there be no envy and no detraction among you, but love alone. Then God will be in your midst.

Do not be saddened if you are lowly, for you shall reign as queens with your King. Therefore let the daughters of Zion rejoice in their King. Hear what David says: “I have chosen to be lowly in the house of my God rather than dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. 83:11). The blackness of your garment signifies lowliness and humility. How shameful [Col. 0905A] and abominable it is if pride lies hidden beneath that garment. Consider, therefore, what bridegroom you serve: he knows every conscience and condemns every sin. Love him as merciful; fear him as judge. Let the mind be modest, the countenance humble, the speech gentle, the walk honourable, and life in every respect irreproachable, so that you may reign in heaven with your bridegroom, through the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns unto ages of ages. Amen.

## CXXV [On Various Matters XXXVIII]. TO NUNS

[Note: [Col. 0905D] From an Angers manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0905D] Perhaps to the nuns of Fontevraud. This sermon appears rather to be a premeditated outline for a sermon than a sermon actually delivered as it stands here. This is demonstrated by the many divisions and subdivisions of which nearly the whole text consists; it is not probable that a preacher would have delivered them in a single mass without more extensive explanation. Yet it seems quite probable that this sermon, like the preceding one, was delivered by Hildebert before the nuns of Fontevraud, at the time when they obtained him from the supreme pontiff as their patron and director.]

### ON HEARING THE WORD OF GOD PROPERLY

“Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, forget your people and your father’s house, and the king shall desire your beauty” (Ps. 44:12).

[Col. 0905B] We read of three kinds of hearers of the divine word: the sluggish, the active, and the contemplative. The sluggish hear and despise what they have heard. The active hear and obey what they have heard. The contemplative hear and fall asleep in an embrace. The sluggish are torpid; the active labour; the contemplative rest. Of the sluggish it is written: “The sluggard hides his hand under his armpit” (Prov. 26:15). To the active it is said: “Because you shall eat the labours of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall go well with you” (Ps. 127:2). Of the contemplative one reads: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s? I shall fly and be at rest” (Ps. 54:7).

The sluggish are weak; the active strong; the contemplative at leisure. The sluggish have a threefold weakness: they are blind in their eyes; contracted in their hands, because they gather and do not distribute; lame in their feet, because [Col. 0905C] they turn aside toward the neighbouring paths of error and do not take up the straight way of salvation. The sluggish are torpid toward God, but not toward the world. For in many labours they store up for themselves the riches of the world and God’s wrath for the day of wrath. The active, however, are torpid toward the world, not toward God. These store up for themselves the riches of the world and God’s mercy. The contemplative are torpid toward the world but not toward God. These store up for themselves the riches of the eternal world and the blessedness of the eternal God, remembering what Truth commands: “Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys” (Matt. 6:19).

Therefore hear, daughter, and see: hear in such a way that you see, because hearts are dark where life does not follow teaching. For it is better not to know the truth than, having known it, [Col. 0905D] to turn back; for those who do not hear have both a lesser guilt and a more tolerable punishment. Those who hear and do not do have both greater guilt and a severe punishment. Those who hear and do have their guilt remitted and rejoice in glory. Woe, then, to those who hear and do not do: hearing in doctrine, 833 destroying in life. “For they are compared to a foolish man who considers the face of his birth in a mirror” (Jas. 1:23). He considers who recalls to mind how and for what he was born.

The mirror in which he considers is the mind, by which one discerns what has been contracted; for as an image is in a mirror, so knowledge is in the mind; and as a mirror represents the form of all things, so in the mind of one thinking every image of what is thought is reflected. The form passes from the mirror when there is no representation of the thing; and the image perishes in the mind when there is no recollection of the thing. He therefore considers in a mirror the face of his birth who remembers in his mind how and for what he was born. And then he sees himself to be nothing but earth borne by earth, and thus raises his mind to eternal things, because he perceives by reason that earthly things are nothing; and for a time he is pierced with compunction so long as he remembers his misery. But the foolish man, when he has passed on, forgets what he was like.

[Col. 0906B] The foolish man passes on when he foolishly returns to transitory things, and forgets what he was like when he is immersed in earthly cares or ensnared by earthly pleasures. Such is everyone who hears the divine word and does not do it. For when he hears the teaching of the word, he recognizes himself to be nothing and so begins to produce [variant: “despise”] earthly things. But when the teacher’s voice has passed, the compunction of the weeping mind perishes, and thus the shoot does not reach the ripeness of fruit.
