This is the seed that fell among thorns, and the growing thorns choked it. Thorns are the pricks, or pleasures, of the world, which often prevent the seed of the heavenly word from bearing fruit in the hearer’s mind.

But why are we drawn apart in different directions? “One thing is necessary.” Hence it is said: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious” [Col. 0906C] (Luke 10:42). Martha’s name is repeated so that she may be recalled more attentively from anxiety. Yet one thing is necessary for her. In many things there is anxiety; in one there is fulfillment. Thus many things were forgiven the sinful woman because she loved much. She did not love many things much, but loved one thing much. Had she loved many things much, nothing would have been forgiven her. Therefore, daughter—that is, faithful soul—hear many things so that through many things you may preserve the one thing.

He calls her daughter, recalling that he is her father. There are, indeed, three states of the faithful soul. In the first she is captive, in the second free, in the third blessed. Captive, she is oppressed under the slavery of sin; free, she fights under the leader Justice; blessed, she glories in the fullness of joy. To the captive it is said: “Return, [Col. 0906D] return, Shulammite” (Song 6:12), so that from captive you may become free. To the free it is said: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. 26:14), so that from free you may become blessed. To the blessed it is said: “Sound the trumpet to God in Zion” (Joel 2:1)—“make joyful noise to God with the voice of exultation” (Ps. 46:2).

In the first 834 state she is a handmaid; in the second, a daughter; in the third, a friend. The handmaid fears, the daughter loves, the friend embraces. To the handmaid it is said: “Return to your mistress and humble yourself [Col. 0907A] beneath her hand” (Gen. 16:9), so that from handmaid you may become a daughter. To the daughter it is said, “My free daughter: ‘Blessed is he who repays you’” (Ps. 36:8), so that from daughter you may become a friend. To the friend it is said: “How beautiful you are, my friend, how beautiful you are! Your eyes are those of doves” (Song 1:14).

You therefore, daughter, if you desire the embrace of the highest King, must first hear; and so that afterward you may see your friend, forget your people. These are the words which the father desires the [daughter] to hear and which the daughter ought to keep. Yet we find it difficult to forget this people, which the more it is repelled, the more stubbornly it strives to resist; and the more frequently it thrusts itself upon us, the more sharply it wounds us within. There are three peoples that threaten the faithful soul: the first worldly, the second fleshly, the third spiritual. The first people are evil human beings, who draw one away from good; the second, desires of the flesh, which suggest evil things; the third, thoughts of the mind, which compel one to sin. Of the first people it is written: “If d. m. t. s. t. a. esse pro [lacuna].” Of the second: “Abstain from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul” (1 Pet. 2:11). Of the third we read: “My days have passed away; my thoughts have been scattered, tormenting my heart” (Job 17:11).

The first people are the friend of the world and are made the enemy of God. The second are the friend of the flesh and the enemy of man, according to the saying: “And a man’s enemies shall be those of his own household” (Matt. 10:36). The third are the friend of the mind and the enemy of peace, according to the saying: “Dying flies spoil the sweetness of ointment” (Eccl. 10:11). [Col. 0907C] The first people are evil; the second are evil itself; the third are sin. There is, moreover, a fourth, hostile to sins, whom the daughter is commanded to forget; hence it adds: “And forget your father’s house.” Far different is this father, whom she is commanded to avoid, from Him who commands that he be avoided. For a human being has three fathers. The first begets a human being; the second captures him; the third claims him. The first begets unto the life of the flesh; the second seizes him for the punishment of the mind; the third claims him for eternal joy. The first father is a man; the second is the devil; the third is God. The first is indicated there: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28). The second there: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44). The third there: “Our Father who art in heaven” [Col. 0907D] (Matt. 6:9). Under the first we are; under the second we are badly; under the third we are blessedly. Under the first we live carnally; under the second we sin mortally; under the third we reign happily. Therefore the third Father remains, so that the first may be forsaken and the second not imitated. So that the daughter may fulfil all that she hears, let her forget her people and her father’s house; thus she overcomes four things: the world, the flesh, the mind, and the devil.

The wars of the world are external; the wars of the flesh are domestic; the wars of the mind are deceptive. Victory is difficult to gain where the throng of opponents is so great, where a person does not conquer unless first he conquers himself. It is a domestic war, and therefore [the reading may be corrupt: “and not the more”] [f. “and therefore the more”] [Col. 0908A] to be feared. Let the handmaid therefore trust in the Lord, the daughter in her Father, the friend in her Beloved, who is able to raise up children of Abraham from these stones. And though the contests of wars terrify, let the rewards of the conqueror attract.

A grave war is indeed declared, but glorious is that which is promised to the victor: “And the King shall desire your beauty.” And beauty is threefold. There is beauty in the voice, beauty in the face, beauty in the heart. Beauty is in the voice because she speaks beautifully; beauty is in the face because she does good works; beauty is in the heart because she meditates holy things. Hence the Beloved, so greatly compassionate toward the labour of his beloved and touched by love, no longer able to endure it, bursts forth into words of love: “You have wounded my heart, my sister; you have wounded my heart” (Song 4:9).—“For you are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (ibid., v. 7). Arise [Col. 0908B] from labour to rest; from misery to glory; from victory to the crown; and come into the bridal chamber, where the Friend will be without end in the embrace, and with the friend in the bed. May He grant us rest there—He who lives and reigns as God without end, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## CXXVI [On Various Matters XXXIX]

> [Note: [Col. 0907D] From Victorinus.]

### ON DEVOUTLY HEARING THE WORD OF GOD, AND HAVING CONFIDENCE IN GOD

> “No one puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the new wine will burst the wineskins, and it will be spilled, and the wineskins will perish. But new wine ought to be put into new wineskins” (Luke 5:37).

The Lord Jesus Christ, dearest brethren, while speaking to human beings, sometimes sowed the word of life by a comparison, sometimes [Col. 0908C] by figures, sometimes openly. He set forth this comparison against those who receive the word of preaching in unclean vessels and pour out the sweetness of heavenly grace. You, therefore, beloved, when you hear the spiritual word, ought to receive it with a clean heart.

Hear what the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one puts”—that is, ought to put—“new wine,” that is, the grace of the new law, “into old wineskins,” that is, into vessels of sin; for if they have become old through corruption, the new wine is spilled. For “he who is of God hears the words of God” (John 8:37); and the Apostle says: “The evil man” [Vulgate: “the natural man”] “does not receive the things that are of God” (1 Cor. 2:14).

But hear what ruin, what [Col. 0908D] punishment belongs to those who do not receive the word of God. For it continues: “And the wineskins will perish.” For to those who neglect the word of preaching, that very word becomes a word of condemnation. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15:22). But, as the Apostle says: “For those who do not submit to the truth, wrath and indignation—and upon every soul that does evil” (Rom. 2:8).

Why then, brethren, does no seedbed of correction appear among you? Rather, the crowd of worldly thoughts prevents you from coming to Christ. You are like the paralytic of whom the Gospel says: [Col. 0909A] “They came to Jesus carrying a paralytic, who was borne by four men; and, because of the crowd, they could not bring him before Jesus. They uncovered the roof where he was, and, having opened it, they lowered the bed on which the paralytic lay. And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: ‘Son, your sins are forgiven you.’” Then he added: “Take up your bed and walk” (Mark 2:3–5).

This healing of the paralytic signifies the salvation of the soul which, after the long enticements of carnal sluggishness, longs for Christ. The ministers who carried him are the teachers of the Church, who by preaching, correcting, and praying offer and draw the sinner to God. They are rightly read to have been four, because all the strength and teaching of preaching is established by the four books of the Gospel.

Or there are four virtues by which [Col. 0909B] the confidence of the mind is raised to obtain salvation: prudence, temperance, justice, [fortitude]. These desire to offer the paralytic to Christ; but the crowd of thoughts, obstructing the mind’s sight, prevents Christ from being seen, for the perverse custom of the world holds one back. Yet while the ministers labour to lead a person to salvation, worldly affairs try to hinder them.

But what do those who carry him do? They do not remain outside in the lower places, where the crowd is in tumult; rather, they climb upon the roof of the house in which Christ teaches. That roof signifies the sublimity of Scripture. Teachers open it to the sick person when, by expounding, they remove the veil of obscurity. No one can be corrected except through [f. “No one, however, except through”] the teachings of the Scriptures. Hence the Psalmist asks: [Col. 0909C] “By what does a younger man correct his way?” and adds, “By keeping your words” (Ps. 118:9).

Thus, when the roof has been opened, the sick person is lowered before Jesus, because one comes to the knowledge of Christ in humility through the revelation of Scripture. That the sick man is lowered with his bed signifies that Christ ought to be known by a person still established in this flesh. But after one has arrived at the knowledge of God, Christ first loosens the bonds of sins, in order to show that the soul cannot be saved, healed, and cleansed from the paralysis of sins unless God, through the grace of His mercy, forgives a person’s sins.

Indeed, we should observe how much each person’s own faith avails before God, when another’s faith availed so greatly. Therefore, when the Lord was about to heal the man of paralysis, He first [Col. 0909D] forgave his sins before healing his body, in order to show that, because of the bond of sin, he was condemned to such infirmity.

There are sometimes reasons why the Lord brings afflictions upon human beings. Sometimes the Lord permits His own people to be afflicted so that, through patience, they may gain a greater crown, as Job did. Sometimes it is for the preservation of virtues, lest good people be lifted up in pride, as the Apostle says concerning himself: “Lest I should be exalted by the greatness of the revelations, there was given me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me” (2 Cor. 12:7). Sometimes people suffer evils because of their sins, for correction, as did this paralytic, or as David, who suffered persecution from his son because of Uriah’s wife. Sometimes [Col. 0910A] illness is given to someone so that through his healing—whether granted by God or by His servants—God may be glorified, as with the man born blind, of whom the Gospel says: “Neither he sinned nor his parents, but that the works of God might be made manifest in him” (John 9:3). Sometimes it is the beginning of eternal condemnation: they receive evils in this life so that their punishment may begin already in the present life [f. “so that those who committed evils in this life may already in the present…”] and endure in the future. Herod underwent this: all his limbs were dissolved, and thus he died.

It continues: “Rise, take up your bed, and walk, and go into your house.” To rise from the bed is to raise the soul from carnal desires. To take up the bed [Col. 0910B] is to lift up the flesh itself from the earth—that is, from earthly things—by the reins of continence. To go home is to enter, or return, to paradise.

Therefore, beloved, I began this discourse so that you might know that the crowd of worldly vanities and hindering thoughts stands in your way, lest you be able to come to the Lord. And just as this paralytic suffered a loosening of his limbs from the infirmity of vices, so adversities come upon you because of your sins. You desire peace, yet do not keep peace, because inner discord produces outward wars for you. Minds disturbed by vices heap disturbances upon the earth. But as the Lord says through the Psalmist: “If my people had heard me, if Israel had walked in my ways, perhaps I would have humbled their enemies for nothing” (Ps. 80:14). For true [Col. 0910C] peace cannot be possessed except from Him who said: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14:27).

Pray therefore to the Lord that He may send help from the Holy Place, because He defends from enemies the person who takes refuge in Him. Hear how great a mercy the Lord bestowed upon the children of Israel when Samaria was besieged, in the time of Elisha and Joram king of Israel.

Ben-hadad, king of Syria, gathered an army against Joram king of Israel and besieged him in Samaria. There was such a famine in Samaria that an ass’s tail [Vulgate: “head”] was sold for eighty pieces of silver. And when the king was passing one day along the wall, a certain woman cried out, saying: “Save me, my lord king.” He said: “If the Lord does not save you, from where can I save you—from the threshing-floor or from the winepress? What do you want?” She answered: [Col. 0910D] “Another woman and I made an agreement that today we should eat my son and tomorrow hers. Therefore we ate mine, but she hid hers.”

The king therefore tore his garments and, angry with Elisha the prophet because he was not asking the Lord to save them, threatened and plotted to kill him, sending a messenger ahead. But Elisha was sitting in his house with other elders and, knowing as a prophet the king’s plot, caused the door to be barred. When the king came, he said to the prophet: “Behold, so great an evil is from the Lord; why should I wait any longer for the Lord?” But Elisha said: “Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: At this time tomorrow, a measure of fine flour shall be sold for one shekel, and two measures of barley for one shekel [Col. 0911A] at the gate of Samaria.”

Then one of the captains, on whose hand the king leaned, answered: “Even if the Lord should make floodgates in heaven, could what you say happen?” Elisha said: “You shall see it with your own eyes, but you shall not eat of it.”

After this prediction, four lepers of Samaria, dying of hunger, who were near the entrance of the city, said: “Why do we stand here? Let us go into the enemy’s camp. If they spare us, we shall live; if they kill us, what does it matter, since we are going to die here?” Therefore, rising at night, they came to the camp of Syria and, as the Lord willed, found no evil [m. “nothing”], because the Lord had made a sound to be heard in the Syrian camp: the noise of the advance of horses and of innumerable people. They supposed that the king of Israel had summoned [f. “had brought”] Egyptians [Col. 0911B] and other hired forces.

They therefore left asses, horses, and riches in the camp and [supplied: fled], desiring only to save their lives. The lepers accordingly entered the camp; they ate and drank, and stole and hid away many riches. Then they came joyfully and reported to their fellow citizens [Col. 0912A] what they had found. The gatekeepers ran to the king and reported what they had heard. But the king, fearing deceit—that, while pretending flight, the Syrians might be lying hidden in pits—sent five men on the five remaining horses to investigate. When the report was confirmed, they plundered the Syrian camp, finding countless riches and such abundance of provisions that a measure of fine flour cost one shekel, and likewise two measures of barley, in accordance with the prophet’s word.

Moreover, the king appointed at the gate the captain concerning whom Elisha had prophesied, and the crowd trampled him. Thus was fulfilled what the prophet had said: “Your eye shall see it, but you shall not eat of it” (4 Kings 6–7). Behold, dearest brethren, how great confidence and hope ought to be placed in the Lord. “For it is good to trust [Col. 0912B] in the Lord” (Ps. 117:8). And again: “Blessed are those who fear the Lord” (Ps. 127:1). Hope therefore in the Lord, so that you may say with the Psalmist: “O Lord my God, in you have I hoped; save me from all who persecute me, and deliver me” (Ps. 7:2). To Him be honour unto ages of ages. Amen.

## A BRIEF NOTICE

[Col. 0911]

[Col. 0911B] Do not be surprised, kindly reader, if certain of the sermons that follow have not been placed in their proper order. For they happened to come into our hands only after the preceding ones had already been printed. Yet we judged that they ought not for that reason to be omitted, since they are genuinely Hildebertine, and in them we found some matters concerning the ancient rites of that age, and other matters likely to be of benefit to readers.

## CXXVII [On Various Matters XL]

### ON THE PASCHAL SOLEMNITY

> [Note: [Col. 0911D] From Lyranus.]

[Col. 0911C]

The Apostle Paul says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7). Therefore, if Christ is the Passover, we must consider what the Law says about the Passover, so that we may see more closely whether the things spoken by Moses appear to have been said concerning Christ. For Moses says: “They shall take of the blood of the lamb and place it upon both doorposts and upon the lintels of the houses in which they shall eat it; and they shall eat the flesh that night roasted by fire, with unleavened bread and wild lettuces. You shall eat none of it raw, nor boiled in water, but only roasted by fire. You shall devour the head with its feet and entrails, and nothing of it shall remain until morning; whatever remains shall be burned with fire” [Col. 0911D] (Exod. 12:7). And it adds: “Thus shall you eat it: you shall gird your loins, have shoes on your feet, hold staffs in your hands, and eat in haste” (ibid., v. 11).

All these things plainly produce great edification for us if they are examined by mystical interpretation. For who the blood of the lamb is, you have learned not now by hearing but by drinking. That blood is placed upon both doorposts when it is drawn not only with the mouth of the body, but also with the mouth of the heart. For the lamb’s blood is set upon both doorposts because the sacrament of His Passion is received with the mouth for redemption and also considered with the whole mind for imitation. Whoever receives the blood of his Redeemer in such a way that he does not yet wish to imitate His Passion has placed the blood on only one doorpost. It must also be placed upon the lintels of the houses.

For what are houses spiritually, except our minds, in which we dwell by thought? The lintel of this house is intention itself, which stands above action. Therefore, whoever directs the intention of his thought toward imitating the Lord’s Passion places the lamb’s blood upon the lintel of the house. Or indeed our houses are our very bodies, in which we dwell as long as we live; and we place the lamb’s blood upon the lintel of the house because we bear the cross of His Passion upon our forehead.

It adds concerning the lamb: “And they shall eat that flesh roasted by fire.” We eat the lamb at night—we who now receive the Lord’s body in the sacrament—while we do not yet see one another’s consciences. Yet the lamb’s flesh must be roasted, for fire [supplied: “fire”] indeed dissolves flesh which water has boiled; but fire without water cooks and strengthens it. Therefore fire cooked the flesh of our Lamb, because the very force of His Passion [“the man,” perhaps an intrusive reading] made Him stronger for resurrection; and from death He gained strength unto incorruption, namely when His flesh was hardened by fire. Hence the Psalmist also says: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21:16). For what is a potsherd before the fire except soft clay? Yet it is subjected to fire in order to be hardened. Therefore the strength of His humanity dried up like a potsherd because, through the fire of Passion, it grew into the strength of incorruption. [Col. 0913A]

But receiving the sacraments of our Redeemer alone does not suffice for true firmness of mind unless good works are also joined to them. For what benefit is it to receive His body and blood with the mouth and to oppose Him by perverse conduct? Hence it is fittingly added concerning eating: “And unleavened bread with wild lettuces.” A person eats bread without leaven who performs right works without the corruption of vain glory, who offers works of mercy without an admixture of sin, lest he perversely seize what he apparently distributes rightly.

They too had mixed this leaven of sin into their good action, whom the Lord rebuked through the prophet’s voice: “Come to Bethel, and act impiously” (Amos 4:3); and shortly afterward: “And sacrifice praise from leavened bread” (ibid., [Col. 0913B] v. 6). For a person offers praise from leavened bread who prepares a sacrifice to God out of robbery.

Wild lettuces, however, are very bitter. Therefore the lamb’s flesh is to be eaten with wild lettuces, so that when we receive the Redeemer’s body, we may afflict ourselves with tears for our sins, in order that the very bitterness of penitence may wipe away from our stomach the moisture of a perverse life. It adds: “You shall eat none of it raw, nor boiled in water.” Behold, now the very words of the history lead us away from the historical sense. But what, dearest brethren—was that Israelite people, while still in Egypt, accustomed to eat the lamb raw, such that the Law should say to it, “You shall eat none of it raw,” and add, “nor boiled in water”?

But what does water signify except human knowledge, according to what is said through Solomon in the voice of heretics: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. 9:17)? What are the lamb’s raw flesh, except unconsidered and irreverent thoughts, with His humility set aside? For whatever we think through subtly, we as it were cook in the mind. But the lamb’s flesh is to be eaten neither raw nor boiled in water, because our Redeemer is neither to be judged a mere man nor to be considered through human wisdom in respect to how God could become incarnate.

For everyone who believes that our Redeemer is a mere human being—what else does he do but eat the lamb’s flesh raw, since he refused to cook it through the understanding of divinity? But everyone who tries to examine the mysteries of the Incarnation according to human wisdom wishes to boil the lamb’s flesh in water; that is, he wishes to penetrate the mystery of His dispensation through undisciplined knowledge. Therefore, whoever desires to celebrate the solemnity of Paschal joy should neither boil the lamb in water nor eat it raw: he should neither seek to penetrate the depth of that Incarnation through human wisdom nor believe in Him as a mere human being. Let him eat the flesh roasted by fire, so that he may know that all things are administered by the power of the Holy Spirit.

It is then rightly added concerning Him: “You shall devour the head with the feet and entrails,” because our Redeemer is Alpha and Omega: God before the ages and human being at the end of the ages. To devour the lamb’s head, therefore, is to receive His divinity in faith. To devour the lamb’s feet is to seek out the footsteps of His humanity through love and imitation. But what are the entrails except His hidden and mystical commands, which we devour when we receive the words of life eagerly? In this word “devour,” what else is reproved but the sluggishness of our own laziness, because we do not seek out His words and mysteries for ourselves, and unwillingly hear sayings from others? [Col. 0914A]

“Nothing of it shall remain until morning,” because His sayings must be examined with great diligence, so that before the day of resurrection appears, all His commands may be penetrated through understanding and practice in this night of the present life. But because it is very difficult for every sacred utterance to be understood and every mystery of it penetrated, it is rightly added: “If anything remains, [Col. 0914B] you shall burn it with fire.” For we burn with fire what remains of the lamb when we humbly reserve to the power of the Holy Spirit that which we cannot understand and penetrate concerning the mystery of His Incarnation. Thus no one should presumptuously dare either to despise or to pronounce upon what he understands [f. “what he does not understand”]; rather, he should commit it to the fire when he reserves it to the Holy Spirit.

Since, therefore, we have learned how the Passover is to be eaten, let us now understand in what manner it ought to be eaten.

It continues: “Thus shall you eat it: you shall gird your loins.” What is understood by the loins except the pleasure of the flesh? Hence the Psalmist asks, saying: “Burn my loins” (Ps. 25:7). For if he had not known that the pleasure of lust is in the loins, he would by no means have asked that they be burned. And because the devil’s power has prevailed most strongly over humankind through sexual vice, it is said of that voice of the Lord: “His power” [Vulgate: “strength”] “is in his loins” (Job 40:11).

Therefore, whoever eats the Passover must have his loins girded, so that one who celebrates the solemnity of resurrection and incorruption may no longer be subject to corruption through any vices: let him tame pleasures and restrain the flesh from lust. For one who is still subject to corruption through incontinence has not known what the solemnity of incorruption is. These things are harsh for some; but “narrow is the gate that leads to life” (Matt. 7:14). And there are already many examples of the continent.

Thus it is fittingly added: “You shall have shoes [Col. 0914D] on your feet.” For what are our feet except good works? And what are shoes except the skins of dead animals? Shoes protect the feet. What are the dead animals from whose skins our feet are protected except the ancient Fathers who have gone before us to the eternal homeland? When we look upon their examples, we protect the feet of our own work. To have shoes on one’s feet, therefore, is to look upon the life of the dead and to keep one’s own footsteps from the wound of sin.

“Holding staffs in your hands.” What does the Law signify by a staff except pastoral guardianship? And it should be noted that we are first commanded to gird our loins and afterward to hold staffs, because only those ought to undertake pastoral care who already know how to tame in their own body the fluidity of lust, lest, while they preach strength to others, they themselves be weakened and overcome by soft desires. [Col. 0915A]

It is fittingly added: “And you shall eat in haste.” Observe, brethren, observe what is said: “in haste.” Learn with haste the commandments of God, the mysteries of the Redeemer, and the joys of the heavenly homeland; and take care to fulfil the precepts of life with haste. For we know that today, while it is still permitted, we may do good; whether it will be permitted tomorrow, we do not know. Eat the Passover in haste, therefore: that is, long for the solemnity of the heavenly homeland. Let no one grow sluggish on the journey of this life, lest he lose his place in the homeland. Let no one weave delays around pursuits that ought to be sought; rather, let him complete what he has begun, lest he be unable to fulfil what he has badly begun.

If we are not sluggish in love for God, Jesus Christ our Lord Himself, whom we love, helps us—He who lives and reigns unto ages of ages. Amen.

## CXXVIII [On Various Matters XLI]

### SYNOD ADDRESSED TO PASTORS

> [Note: [Col. 0915D] From Lyranus.]

> “The word of the Lord came to Ezekiel, saying: ‘Son of man, prophesy concerning the shepherds of Israel, and say to them: Woe to the shepherds who fed themselves. Are not flocks fed by shepherds? You ate the milk and clothed yourselves with the wool; you killed what was fat, but you did not feed my flock; you did not strengthen what was weak,’ etc. ‘But you ruled them with severity and with power, and my sheep were scattered. But I will require my flock from the shepherds’ hand’” [Col. 0915C] (Ezek. 34:1).

You, brethren, are shepherds of Israel, and you ought to feed the faithful in the Church of Christ. The Lord complains of you through His prophet and threatens the greatest woe—that is, destruction and ruin—because, though you are shepherds, you are unwilling to feed His flock by word or example; indeed, you feed yourselves. But, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “You shut the kingdom of heaven before men; you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those entering to enter” (Matt. 23:13).

You are not like Job, who said: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame” (Job 29:15). He is an eye to the blind who removes the darkness of ignorance and imparts the preaching of virtue. He is a foot to the lame who strengthens those not wholly ignorant of the ways, and confirms the doubtful by authorities. But how do you strengthen the faith of others when you do not know how to strengthen your own faith?

Hear what the Psalmist says: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly … but meditates in the law of the Lord day and night” (Ps. 1:1). Behold how David describes the blessed man. First he shows goodness in the man’s own person; afterward, his devotion to the divine Scriptures, so that he may teach others. He identifies three blessednesses in the blessed man, corresponding to the three deaths in the miserable person. The miserable person sins in thought, action, and habit; but blessed is the one who has not walked in counsel, because he does not think evil; who has not stood in the way of sinners, because he does not remain in action; and who has not sat in the chair of pestilence, [Col. 0916A] nor teaches others to sin.

Thus, those of you who are not such do not feed the Lord’s sheep. They are hirelings, not shepherds, who seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ; who love the glory of this world, not that above; who love the first places at feasts, the chief seats in synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men. Do you not turn humility into pride? The Lord says through Isaiah: “My princes are impious and companions of thieves; all love gifts and pursue rewards” (Isa. 1:23).

He goes on to explain how they feed themselves: “You ate the milk and clothed yourselves with the wool; and you killed what was fat.” By milk he understands food, and by wool clothing. Thus they receive food and [Col. 0916B] clothing from the sheep, yet do not do what they ought. But worse is what follows: “And you killed what was fat.” Here he calls the rich person “fat.” You indeed kill the rich person when you receive money for forgiving his sins.

“You did not strengthen what was weak”: that is, you did not heal what was sick. He calls weak the person of whom the Apostle says: “Receive” [Vulgate: “take to yourselves”] “the weak in faith” (Rom. 14:1), and strengthen his faith with love. There is no one among you who has not many times heard the belief held by many laypeople: that the Lord, descending into hell, brought out [f. “led out”] everyone, both believers and unbelievers, and emptied hell. This heresy long ago flourished greatly among heretics and still produces error among many.

Heretics have been led into this error by what is said in the Gospel: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 8:28). Hence Gregory says: There are heretics who say that the Lord descended into hell and, after death, announced Himself to all and converted them; and that those who confessed were saved. Yet this is contrary to the words of the prophet David: “For who shall confess to you in hell?” (Ps. 6:6); and of the Apostle: “As many as have sinned without the law shall perish without the law” (Rom. 12:2); and of the prophet: “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. 13:14). If He was a bite, He took a part and left more behind. But what is written, “I shall draw all things,” must be understood of the elect [f. “from among the elect”], as Gregory says. [Col. 0916D]

Moreover, many are weakened in faith regarding other matters, yet are not strengthened by your preaching. You are not like our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom it is written through Isaiah: “He shall not break a bruised reed, and he shall not quench smoking flax” (Matt. 12:20). He breaks a bruised reed who does not extend a hand to the sinner or bear his brother’s burden; and he quenches smoking flax who despises in little ones the spark of faith that is already smoking, already showing a sign of growing and hidden fire within itself.

“And you did not heal what was sick.” He does not heal the sick who does not care for his neighbour’s health. Against such persons Job says concerning himself: “The eye that saw me bore witness [Col. 0917A] for me that I had delivered the crying poor man and the orphan who had no helper. The blessing of the perishing came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow … I broke the jaws of the wicked man and snatched the prey from his teeth” (Job 29:11).

How will they heal the sick who kill the living? As the prophet says: “They killed souls that do not die and made alive souls that do not live” (Ezek. 13:19). He kills one who is not to die who condemns the just person; and he tries to make alive one who is not to live who seeks to absolve the guilty from punishment. One must consider what the fault is, and what penitence follows the fault. For it often happens that a priest condemns the undeserving, or unworthily looses those who ought rightly to be bound. Hence Gregory says: “He deprives himself of the power of loosing and binding who exercises it according to his own wishes, not according to the conduct of those subject to him.” [Col. 0917B]

“But you ruled them with severity and with power.” Against these severe people the Apostle says: “If a person has been overtaken in some offence, you who are spiritual, instruct him in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. 6:1). Disciples ought to follow the Master, who said: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). Sinners are not to be tested [f. “frightened”] with severity, but called and drawn by seeking opportunities, as the Apostle says: “Redeeming the time” (Col. 4:5).

To redeem the time is, when someone seeks a suitable opportunity to rebuke and appropriately admonish a sinner—whether by eating with him, going with him, or visiting him—he breaks some resolution of his own, whether [f. “not”] to fast or to sing Mass, and afterward makes up for it by prayers and alms. The Apostle says: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke, in all patience and teaching” (2 Tim. 4:2). Reprove rebels publicly; entreat the obedient; rebuke the less obedient. “Entreat the elders as fathers, the young men as brothers, old women as mothers, young women as sisters; honour widows” (1 Tim. 5:2). Sinners should be invited to tears with sweet words. [Col. 0917C]

There are two kinds of compunction: one by which a person fears eternal punishments; another which is inspired by heavenly rewards. For the soul, sensing God, is first pierced by fear and afterward by love. Thus it weeps from fear of punishment and weeps because the reward is delayed. These two kinds are signified in a certain history. For it is read that Achsah, the daughter of Caleb, sat upon an ass, sighing. Her father said to her: “What is the matter?” She answered: “Give me a blessing. You have given me a southern and dry land; add a watered land.” And her father gave her an upper watering-place and a lower watering-place (Job 15:18).

Achsah therefore signifies the soul sitting upon an ass—that is, upon the irrational motions of its flesh—which, sighing, asks its Father for watered land because the grace [Col. 0918A] of tears must be sought from our Creator. For there are some who already freely receive the gift of speaking for justice, defending the oppressed, giving their own goods to the needy, and possessing ardour of faith, but who still do not have the grace of tears. Therefore they must strive to weep daily for the sins without which we cannot live, whether out of love for the heavenly kingdom or fear of punishment.

The soul receives the upper watering-place when it weeps from love for the higher kingdom; it possesses the lower one when it mourns from fear of hell. They lose so great a grace through the severity of teachers. For this reason they are even turned to despair by the excessive harshness of rulers, while those rulers do not know how to moderate their learning; and thus those who ought to be drawn are lost.

This is indicated in the sons of Jacob. Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, having gone out from her father’s house, was loved and seized by Shechem the prince; he lay with her and forcibly violated her (Gen. 34). When they heard this, Jacob’s sons were intensely angry. Shechem and Jacob’s sons made peace, agreeing to give the sister if he and all the males were circumcised. But when all the males had been circumcised, that did not satisfy Jacob’s sons. Rather, Simeon and Levi, taking swords, entered the city; after killing all the males, they killed Shechem and carried off their sister.

Dina, Jacob’s daughter, signifies the soul, the daughter of Christ. When she wanders among outward things—that is, among vices—she is corrupted by Shechem, that is, the devil, prince of this world, or by some tyrant. Against him rage the teachers of the Church, signified by Jacob’s sons, so that they do not let him, nor his helpers, go until they are circumcised—that is, until they cut away their guilt from themselves [Col. 0918C] and turn the will of the flesh into sorrow. But the ministers of the Church, when they do not know how to moderate their zeal, continue to rage even after vices have been cut away, and become harsher; and while they persist too much in the severity of discipline, turning wretches to despair, they kill them with the sword of justice more intolerably.

To these and others like them the Lord says: “My sheep have been scattered, but I will require them from the hand of the shepherds.” Consider therefore, dearest brothers, with what diligence the people of the Lord must be guarded and governed, and how great your danger is. For the Lord will require at your hands the death of those who thus perish, and you will perish not only for your own sins but for the sins of all [perhaps: sheep]. But may the Lord, who is the true Shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep, himself grant you [Col. 0918D] strength and courage against spiritual wolves, and prudence in guarding his people, so that you may offer them to him pure on the day of judgment: he who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

847. CXXIX [On Various Matters XLII]. ON DESIRING AND SEEKING THE KINGDOM OF GOD  
[Note: [Col. 0917] From St-Germain MS no. 383. In this sermon the monk himself appears to address monks.]

“Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness” (Matt. 6:35).

Great and difficult, brothers, is our undertaking. For we wish to show the hidden manna, which is at hand but cannot be seen except by the eyes of the mind. This is that precious pearl which the Gospel merchant found and, having sold [Col. 0919A] all that he possessed, bought. Behold, you all profess to seek it, but you have not yet found it; for if you had found it, you would buy it, nor would it seem too costly, nor would any price be withheld for purchasing it. Oh, how little has that great, that long-lasting, that manifold labor of yours yet accomplished: you have not found what you seek; you do not yet know what you profess; you do not yet possess what you desire!

It is hidden—not, I say, from everyone, but from those who seek it where they cannot find it. Where? In outward things, although the Lord says: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21). If therefore it is within you, why do you seek outside what you cannot find outside? You are wandering. He acknowledged this who said: “I have wandered like a lost sheep” (Ps. [Col. 0919B] 118:176). A human being wanders—yes, wanders—but, good Jesus, seek your servant lest he perish.

Since, therefore, what you seek is within you, it is near you; but it is near because you yourselves are near yourselves. Hence the Apostle says: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Rom. 10:8). For we are not speaking of that “which eye has not seen, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2), but of that which can be possessed in this life. Have you heard where the pearl you seek is? Come then and buy it. “Bad, bad, says every buyer; but when he has gone away, then he boasts” (Prov. 20:14).

Yet this transaction cannot be made without the price of faith. And faith comes by hearing. You hear; what remains except that you obey? If you do so, the wisdom you seek will meet you like an honored mother [Col. 0919C]. For she is honored when, in hearing, the ear obeys her; because faith is not [of] that which is seen, and faith has no merit where human reason furnishes proof. The person who begins to believe does not merely, I say, desire, but desires to desire with the Prophet, who says: “My soul has desired to desire your justifications” (Ps. 118:20).

Who then is the one who believes? Who is the man who desires life, who loves to see good days—not only of the life to come, but also of the present life? 848 For there are tents of the Lord, and there are also dwelling places of the Lord. The tents are those of soldiers: “The life of man is warfare upon earth” (Job 7). Hence: “How beloved are your tents, O Lord of hosts” (Ps. 83:1). For not only the eternal house of the Lord, but also the tents [Col. 0919D] of the present life are to be loved and desired. Hence the Prophet says: “My spirit desires and fails for your courts” (ibid., 3). He says “courts,” not “house.” For in the present we are in the courts; in the future we shall enter the hall.

But he who said, “My spirit fails for your courts,” was languishing with a certain love and desire. Hence in the Song of Songs: “Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Song 2:5). Nor is it surprising that the courts of the Lord are desired, because “one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11).

But if you seek the way to those courts, hear what the Lord says to Abraham: “Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land which I will show you” [Col. 0920A] (Gen. 12:1). A person’s land is the pleasure of his flesh. Let a person therefore depart from the pleasures of his flesh, if he wishes to come to the desirable land.

It follows: “And from your kindred.” That kindred is curiosity. For whoever gives himself to the pleasures of the flesh must necessarily be curious about many things. For example: if someone serves lust, is he not curious how he may please a woman and how he may entice her? If he serves gluttony, does he not extort from every side in order to satisfy his appetite?

It is added: “And from your father’s house.” The father of evils is the devil; hence in the Gospel: “You are of your father the devil, and you do the works of your father” (John 8:44). For just as the one born of God is born to righteousness and life, so the one born of the devil [Col. 0920B] is born to iniquity and death.

But miserable is the daughter of Babylon. What can the wretched woman bestow except wretchedness? Wretched, therefore, are those who follow her; but blessed is he who repays her the recompense which she herself gave. For she takes from his mother the son of mother Church, whom she herself bore to God, places him at her own breasts as though he were her own, and nurses him for the devil’s work. Babylon has rendered this to our mother, the holy Church, not once or twice but very often. But blessed is he who repays her the recompense which she herself rendered: that is, he who seizes her little ones before they grow into the strength of wickedness, weans them, and dashes them against the rock—that is, against Christ.

The devil, father of this city, has a house of his own: namely, pleasure. In this house [Col. 0920C] the devil dwells. In it he has chosen a seat for himself; in it he finds what belongs to him. For whoever, setting aside God’s will, follows his own 849 will thereby falls into self-confidence; self-confidence produces pride, and this is vanity. Whoever, therefore, wishes to come into the land to which he [calls] us must leave the will of the flesh, leave curiosity, and leave birth [perhaps: vanity].

But you say: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (John 6:61). It seems hard to you because you have not yet tasted its sweetness, which the Lord has hidden for those who fear him. “Taste therefore and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9). Is not the Lord faithful in all his words, he who says: “My yoke is sweet, and my burden light” (Matt. 11:[Col. 0920D] 30)? Is he not the same faithful one in all his promises, who says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (ibid., 28)?

For it is refreshment, not exhaustion—not I who say it, but the Lord. Yet I say this to one who has not tasted and does not savor what I say. What then shall I do? Where shall I turn? How shall I show him the hidden manna, so that at least in this way I may convince you? I see that you delight in the flesh of a harlot; but is not the flesh of Christ more delightful? You pursue gluttony as though it were a sweet thing; but is not sobriety far sweeter? You are exalted by pride as though it were some good; but is not humility far better? Far be it that the devil’s garment should be better than Christ’s garment! Reason itself does not suggest this.

I argue from opposites, because by opposites I know better. Return therefore to your heart; return, you who have wandered. We shall go a journey of three days, so that the desirable land may be shown to us. For there are three things which bring us into the desirable land. The Lord brings us into his garden, then into his wine-cellar, and at last into his chamber; when we have rested there, we shall see the desirable land, eat its fruit, and possess it.

Our first day’s stage, therefore, is to enter the garden—that is, to love the virtues. For the Lord’s garden is the love of virtues; and it is fittingly called a garden. For as in a garden there are diverse fruit-bearing trees and fragrant herbs, so here diverse virtues bring forth their own fruit and most pleasant fragrance. What fruit is greater than that which arises [Col. 0921B] from virtues: security in the present and eternal life in the future? What fragrance is sweeter? Hence: “We are a good fragrance to God” (2 Cor. 2:15).

Since therefore we are to enter the garden on the journey of the first day, it remains that on the second day we be led into the wine-cellar. A wine-cellar is the place where the best things produced in the field are stored. The Lord’s wine-cellar is divine Scripture; for there you will find stored for your use whatever has grown in the garden of virtues, but . . .  
[Note: [Col. 0921D] Here the sermon ends mutilated.]

CXXX [On Various Matters XLIII]. TO THE PEOPLE  
[Note: [Col. 0922D] From St-Germain MS no. 383.]

850. “Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel; you shall hear the word from my mouth and announce it to them from me” (Ezek. 33:7).

[Col. 0921C] You see, brothers, that such was the will of our Lord: that he established me, an unworthy sinner, to govern this Church, not through my merits but through his mercy, and entrusted to me the care of you and of others belonging to this see. For every bishop or archbishop ought attentively to guard the peoples committed to him, instruct them in the Lord’s commandments, carefully inspect and know, as far as possible, the conduct of each person, so that he may approve and strengthen those who act well, and call back those who act badly to the way of truth and righteousness.

For this reason the Lord says through the Prophet: “I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel”; as though he said: You who have received a position higher than others are set as though in a watchtower, so that, placed in a loftier station, [Col. 0921D] you may observe the lives of those below, provide for their salvation, rebuke the evils they have committed, and show the path of equity and the lamp of truth to those who are ignorant. “You shall hear the word from my mouth and announce it to them from me,” because you will read my laws and discern my will in the Scriptures; and you will speak to them not your own commands but mine.

Thus the Lord commands bishops to guard their subjects. But if a bishop neglects the care of those subject to him, he will pay the penalties both for his own sins and for the sins of others, according to the Lord’s declaration through the same prophet: “If, when I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ you do not announce it [Col. 0922A] to him nor speak, so that he may turn from his wicked way, he indeed shall die in his iniquity; but I will require his soul from your hand.” But if you “announce it to the wicked man and he has not turned from his iniquity, he indeed shall die in his iniquity; but you have delivered your own soul” (ibid., 8).

Behold, you can understand how great a sin threatens us unless we labor and keep watch for your [supplied] salvation, unless we admonish and instruct you to live well. Yet condemnation will be yours if you do not keep what we tell you. It is ours to announce God’s commandments; it is fitting for you to fulfill what is announced. It is ours to provide what is necessary and salutary for you; it is fitting for you to obey our commands—indeed, the Lord’s commands.

We must fear what the Apostle says: “Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel” (1 Cor. 9:16), and what is read in the Old Testament: “Let the sound be heard 851 when the priest enters the sanctuary in the Lord’s presence, lest he die” (Exod. 28:33). For the priest dies if no sound is heard from him, because he provokes God’s wrath against himself if he ceases from preaching through negligence.

You ought to heed what the Lord said: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat; therefore keep and do whatever they tell you” (Matt. 23:2)—whatever I say that pertains to the chair. For if they command you contrary to justice, you ought not to comply. Again the Lord says: “He who despises you despises me, and he who [Col. 0922C] receives you receives me” (Luke 10:16). You ought carefully to consider with how much honor and joy you should receive the teaching of bishops or priests, since in them you either receive or despise the Lord himself.

Christian teaching consists chiefly in faith and life. In faith: that you may know what you must believe, for “without faith it is impossible for anyone to please God” (Heb. 11:6). In life: that you may know how you ought to live according to the Christian faith. Concerning faith, you all truly know that one must believe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons, one almighty God, without beginning and without end, creator of all creatures, ruler of all powers, seeing all things, judging all things.

Moreover, you believe—and must believe—that the Son of God assumed our flesh from the Virgin; that he lived in this world for thirty-three years; that meanwhile he gathered disciples and taught them what they were to preach and how they were to teach the peoples; and that, having finally instructed his disciples in heavenly teaching through the preaching of the divine word and the example of good living, he allowed himself to be seized by the Jews and crucified. Buried, he rose on the third day and ascended into heaven, in the sight of the disciples, on the fortieth day after the resurrection. On the day of Pentecost he sent the Holy Spirit; strengthened by him, the apostles did not fear kings and tyrants, [Col. 0923A] but steadfastly preached Christ’s name everywhere and established churches throughout the world.

Likewise one must believe that in baptism all sins are forgiven; that at the altar the true body and blood of Christ are offered by priests; likewise, that our Lord Jesus Christ will come a second time for judgment; and that all human beings will rise again in the same flesh in which they formerly lived, so that the righteous may be made blessed in body and soul, and the wicked tormented in body and soul. These are the first teachings of Christian faith. This is elementary teaching, which even little children can grasp. Priests ought to instruct their parishioners in this faith, and fathers their children. This faith suffices for salvation for those who do not have opportunity to do good works.

852. But whoever has opportunity [Col. 0923B] must lead a pure and upright life together with sound faith; for “faith without works is dead” (James 2:26). Therefore we said that believers must be instructed both to believe rightly and to live well. The person who keeps God’s commandments lives well.

The commandments of God are: to love God as Father; to fear him as Lord; not to do to another what one does not wish done to oneself; to preserve chastity of mind and body, whether in virginity, marriage, or widowhood. So that chastity may be preserved, moderation in food and drink must be practiced. For a stomach inflamed by wine readily produces lust; therefore Scripture says: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down by excess and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34).

What is not spent in food and drink through moderation should not be greedily stored up; rather alms should be distributed [from it], guests received, the naked clothed, and the sick visited. In all these persons Christ himself is received. Hence it is said: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7). For judgment without mercy shall be given to one who does not show mercy. If those who do not give their own goods for Christ are judged and condemned, what will happen to those who plunder the goods of others?

Therefore, brothers, flee avarice: do not heap up superfluities; do not acquire even necessities unjustly, namely through fraud, theft, usury, falsehood, or robbery. “For greed is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10). Through greed wars are waged, murders committed, brigandage practiced, [Col. 0923D] frauds and perjuries committed, plunder coveted, and peace violated. But peace pleases God, so that lovers of peace are reckoned children of God. Hence it was said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. 5:9). Hence also the Apostle: “If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Rom. 12:18).

For the prophet says concerning plunder: “He who offers to God from the plunder of the poor is like one who slays a son in his father’s sight” (Ecclus. 34:24). Love therefore peace and gentleness. For if you were perfect, you would not take vengeance even upon enemies, since the Lord says: “Love your enemies. Do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5:[Col. 0924A] 44). And the Apostle says: “Do not give place to the devil” (Eph. 4:27)—“but give place to wrath” (Rom. 12:19). The one who, stirred to anger, takes vengeance gives place to the devil within himself. Therefore we ought to give place to wrath—that is, to endure those who are angry against us. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good” (Rom. 12:21). The person who, injured, is moved to harm another is conquered by evil; the one who patiently endures and does not follow the devil provoking him to anger conquers evil with good.

But if you possess the virtues mentioned above, you must avoid pride, lest your mind be exalted because of some virtue, lest you prefer yourselves to others, 853 and lest you attribute your goods to yourselves rather than to the Lord. For pride is the first vice of those departing from God, but the last of those returning to the Lord. [Col. 0924B] If you are proud of good works, you lose whatever had been acquired. Hence the Apostle: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5:6). And the prophet: “He who gathered wages put them into a bag with holes” (Hag. 1:6). For from a pierced bag that which is poured in at one place goes out at another: indiscreet minds do not consider how the reward gained from a good work may be lost through an evil work.

Keep these things, brothers, and turn them over in your hearts. For this is the way that leads to eternal life, through him who grants strength, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

CXXXI [On Various Matters XLIV]. SYNODAL ADDRESS TO PASTORS  
[Note: [Col. 0923D] From Lyranus.]

[Col. 0924C] “God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night; and the stars. And he set them in the firmament of heaven, that they might shine upon the earth, and rule the day and the night, and divide light from darkness . . . . . God also said: ‘Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing of living soul, and the bird over the earth, beneath the firmament of heaven’” (Gen. 1:16 ff.).

Thus, dearest brothers, God willed to make the creatures of the world in such a way that, in the manner of their creation, he might signify to us something of a mystery. Let us see what is prefigured for us in the lights, in day and night, in the firmament, and in the earth; and let us imitate whatever in them ought to be imitated. For this figure concerns us, brothers, because we are those lights of the firmament.

What is the firmament except Scripture, upon which the Church is established? What are the lights of the firmament except the pastors of the Church, who illuminate it by expounding it to others? When you expound God’s Gospel, what else do you do but make clear the firmament of heaven—that is, Scripture? There are two lights, the greater and the lesser: the day signifies the wise [perhaps supplied], and the night the unlearned. The greater light may be so called because wise teachers instruct those more [perhaps: less] capable. What is Augustine but a sun in the Church? And to whom does he speak except the wise?

But you priests of lesser learning are the lesser light; you rule the night—that is, the laity, who do not know [Col. 0925A] the Scriptures. Yet whatever kind of light you are, you are nevertheless light; to you it is said: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14). You shine in the midst of a crooked nation like lights. The other clerics, who have no preeminence over God’s people, are called stars, because, although they do not govern, they shine upon the earth—that is, the Church—by teaching and conduct. Thus the lights divide [perhaps supplied: day and night], because they discern the capacity of each person, preaching humble things to the carnal and profound things to the spiritual.

God also said: “Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing of living soul, and the bird over the earth.” Having prefigured the pastors of the Church, on the following day he showed their office. For he created fish and birds from the waters. By the waters he understands baptism. By fish and birds he designated two classes [Col. 0925B] of believers reborn through baptism. Some love worldly things and follow the broad paths of this world; these are called fish, of whom David says: “The birds of heaven and the fish of the sea, which pass through the paths of the sea” (Ps. 8:9). The sea is the world; the paths of the sea are the broad ways of this world. Others are birds—that is, those flying toward heavenly things on the wings of virtues.

In both classes are found persons regenerated by baptism; therefore the office of regeneration has been entrusted to you. You beget children of God. In this generation the Holy Spirit is father and water mother. Hence the Lord says to Nicodemus: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). The first generation, from a carnal father, makes persons carnal; the second, from the Spirit, makes them spiritual. Hence he says to Nicodemus: “What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of spirit is spirit” (ibid., 6). As people are born carnally into the world, so they are born spiritually in order to enter heaven. You, however, are ministers of this entrance; you make children of the devil into children of God.

Behold, the gate of heaven has been entrusted to you. But beware lest you resemble baptismal water. Water washes sins away and afterward descends into foul places. Likewise, a wicked priest absolves people by his office, yet by his wickedness deserves to fall into hell. To you is said what is said to the apostles: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matt. 18:18). [Col. 0925D] There are two keys, one for closing and the other for opening. One opens to penitents; the other repels the unrepentant. Office does not arise from merit, nor merit from office. Many enter who do not have the keys, and many have the keys who do not enter. The sheep enter and the pastors are cast out.

But when the Lord had cast the sellers and buyers from the temple, blind and lame persons approached him, and he healed them. Thus he casts unworthy priests out of his house and receives in the temple, through repentance, the blind in knowledge and lame in action—that is, sinners, many of them ignorant of the law—while he has inspired the lay people and blinded learned scholars.

Pastors are compared with doves, [Col. 0926A] 855 because they ought to provide for others simply and innocently. They ought to fly toward heavenly things, so as to show the way by example. The Scriptures are windows through which they see God and provide for others. “Let your light shine before people” (Matt. 5:16). You are salt, so that by your preaching you may season and extinguish worms—that is, sinners. These three things are necessary for you: the light of good conduct, the eye of discernment, and the salt of preaching. Those who preach well and live badly are indeed salt, but they are not light.

The Lord says through Ezekiel: “The priests have despised my law and defiled my sanctuaries; they made no distinction between holy and profane, and did not understand the difference between polluted and unclean” (Ezek. 22:26). There are others who do not know how to preach, to whom it is said: “Mute dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56:10). If one does not have the eye of discernment, he absolves and binds unworthily. If he is not salt, he is a dog about the Lord’s flock, but does not drive the wolf away by the bark of preaching. If he is not light, he brings others in but does not enter himself. Therefore these three are necessary for you. If one of them is lacking, you guard the people of God dangerously.

Consider therefore your burden. The prophet Hosea cries to you: “Hear this, priests, and attend, house of Israel, for judgment is for you” (Hos. 5:1). He adds why they should expect judgment: “For you have become a snare to Zion” (ibid.), and an outspread net. This means: you who ought to free others entangle them by your evil example. Consider then what you are. God [Col. 0926C] entrusted his money to you, saying: “Conduct business until I come” (Luke 19:13). May the Lord, who said, “I am the good shepherd” (John 11:14), preserve his pastors and flocks, and lead them into the heavenly Jerusalem, where there is peace, joy, and life—he who lives and reigns, etc.

CXXXII [On Various Matters XLV]. AT THE ORDINATION OF CLERICS  
[Note: [Col. 0925D] From Lyranus.]

“The Lord Jesus appointed seventy-two others also, and sent them ahead of him into every city and place where he himself was about to come. And he said to them: ‘The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the workers are few’” (Luke 10:1).

In the primitive Church, dearest brothers, he chose twelve apostles, to convert some and govern others. But [Col. 0926D] 856 when the Church began to multiply, he willed that pastors too should increase, and added another seventy-two. Bishops and archbishops today hold in the Church the place of the twelve apostles. Other priests perform the role of the seventy-two.

Likewise, in the old law there were different ranks of priests: some higher and others lower. The order of presbyters took its beginning from the sons of Aaron. Those called priests in the Old Testament (Lev. 8) are those now called presbyters; and the one then called chief of priests is now called bishop. For *presbyter* is called “elder” in Greek, not on account of age, but because of honor, dignity, and the teaching of wisdom; those who receive these are called presbyters. They are called priests because they administer sacred things in the consecration of the divine body, in baptism, and in the office of preaching.

Aaron held the highest place of priesthood in the old [law]. His sons held a lower rank of priesthood. In the same way bishops are above priests, and although all share in priesthood, bishops possess greater sacraments than presbyters. Bishops mark the forehead with chrism, dedicate churches, ordain, and consecrate ecclesiastical vessels and altars. Others only consecrate the body and blood [of Christ], baptize, absolve, and bless marriage. But now we shall say something about the dignity of [Col. 0927B] your order, so that you may know what power you receive and how you ought to enter it.

[Note: [Col. 0927D] This proves what our Martène asserted in book I of *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, chapter VIII, article 3, no. 4: namely, that the decrees of councils establishing that a presbyter, even if, as Hildebert says here, very worthy, should not be ordained before his thirtieth year, were still in force in the eleventh century. He gives a notable example in Saint Benno, later bishop of Meissen, who is said to have received the Levitical blessing only in his twenty-fifth year, and the presbyteral blessing only in his thirtieth, in his Life in Surius, 16 June. The aforesaid Martène also discusses many decrees on this matter at length in the place cited above.]

It was decreed in the holy canons that no presbyter should be ordained before his thirtieth year, even though he be very worthy. For our Lord was baptized in his thirtieth year and then began to preach. No layman, no man married twice, no husband of a widow is to be ordained; rather, he must be irreproachable, as the Apostle says: “A bishop must be irreproachable, the husband of one wife, sober, prudent, well ordered, chaste, hospitable, a teacher, not given to wine, not violent, but gentle, not quarrelsome, not covetous, ruling his own household well. Moreover, he must have a good testimony from those who are outside” (1 Tim. 3:2).

[Col. 0927C] It is the Apostle’s custom to call a presbyter a bishop, as Paul writes in the Epistle to the Philippians to the bishops at Philippi and to the deacons. By “bishops” he intended presbyters, since there could not be several bishops in one city. He prohibited bigamists when he says, “the husband of one wife” (1 Tim. 3:2). The husband of a widow is excluded from this order, because it was commanded in the law that “the priest shall take a virgin as wife” (Lev. 21:13). Further, care must be taken that he knows letters, that he lacks no bodily part, nor should he be among public penitents on account of the unworthiness of the ministry [perhaps: “on account of the dignity of those ministering”]; and legal precepts enacted that nothing at all defective be offered to God.

In the ancient [Col. 0927D] priesthood it was permitted for a priest to have one virgin wife, for the succession of offspring, because the priest was not taken from another tribe. In the new priesthood it is not so, but [pure lineage?] . . . rather, a pure election is required, and marriage is forbidden. For the ancient priests abstained from their wives during the week of their service and did not depart from the temple, as we read of Zechariah (Luke 1). If, then, the ancients abstained from their wives while they performed priestly service, [Col. 0928A] how much more should these priests and Levites preserve chastity by the obligation of their ordination? For if Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying: “Abstain for a time, that you may have leisure for prayer” (1 Cor. 7:5), and this is addressed to lay persons, much more does it apply to priests, whose office of prayer and sacrifice is continual.

Therefore such great diligence and purity befit this ministry. The Lord commanded, saying: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). Thus power is given to the priest to make Christ’s body. Baptism is first pure water; but through blessing it is changed into a sacrament. And whereas water previously could cleanse the body alone, now through the priest’s blessing it can wash the soul also. The priest’s blessing also joins in marriage the two persons who are marrying.

There is also afterward given by the Lord to priests a certain divine authority, proper to God alone. For he said: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven” (John 20:23). What merit! What a gift! A human being can absolve human beings. A human being can remit human sins. And because he receives a power of special prerogative over others, he has a consecration more worthy than others.

Holy anointing is poured upon their hands, so that the Holy Spirit, signified by the oil, descends into the works of their consecration. Their alb, with which they are clothed, is of linen and signifies the purity of continence. It must be girded, because the priest must hold his purpose firmly. Hence the Lord says: “Let your loins [Col. 0928C] be girded” (Luke 12:35). He wears the towel because he is shown to be one of the Lord’s guests at table, as was said above, and the principal guest. He wears the *orarium*, that is, the stole, because he receives the yoke of prayer and preaching. The *orarium* touches the neck and breast, because the yoke of prayer and preaching must be exercised from reason [perhaps: “from the inmost breast”], so that he may hold in his mind what he utters with his mouth, as the Apostle says: “I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the mind. I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (1 Cor. 14:15).

The chasuble signifies charity, because as the chasuble rises above and contains the other garments, so all virtues are contained in charity. Great, brothers, is your ministry; great the gift; great [Col. 0928D] the grace. Therefore the vessels in which such things are placed must be clean. Therefore you must shine like lampstands in the house of the Lord. For to you it is said: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14). You must therefore shine in the world and drive errors away. Again it is said to you: “You are the salt of the earth” (ibid., 13). You must season with the salt of teaching. And the Lord says to you: “Conduct business until I come” (Luke 19:13).

CXXXIII [On Various Matters XLVI]. TO PASTORS  
[Note: [Col. 0929D] From St-Germain.]

[Col. 0929A]

“Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 33:12).

The fear of the Lord, as the Prophet testifies, is the beginning and first step by which one comes to wisdom. Fear and hope accompany one another; there ought to be no fear in anyone without hope, nor hope without fear. For these are the two millstones between which the Christian is ground in this present life, so that he may become the bread of Christ. In this matter Christ’s priests and the other prelates to whom care of souls is entrusted must take great heed, lest they teach one without the other. For concerning this it is written in the Law: “You shall not take the upper or the lower millstone from anyone as a pledge” [Col. 0929B] (Deut. 24:6). He takes the upper millstone who so preaches God as a strict judge that he makes him—that is, the sinner—despair of pardon. But he takes the lower millstone who so preaches God as merciful that he removes fear of the just Judge. Of such people it is said: “They put to death souls that do not die, and give life to souls that do not live” (Ezek. 13:19). Yet they ought rather to imitate Elisha, fitting themselves upon the dead man—that is, upon the sinner—in order to raise him again.

For every prelate ought to fit himself to the flock entrusted to him: namely, to place mouth upon mouth, eyes upon eyes, ears upon ears, and the other members upon the corresponding members of the flock committed to him, so that by his preaching and the testimony of good works he may be able to guard that flock. Paul [Col. 0929C] the apostle, an outstanding preacher, placed mouth upon the mouth of the flock entrusted to him when he said: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (2 Cor. 6:11). The Prophet placed eyes upon the eyes of his flock when he said: “Our eyes are ever toward the Lord” (Ps. 122:2). He placed hands upon hands when by his preaching and example he restrained the hands of those subject to him, lest they be given over to the shedding of blood.

Therefore, brothers, that you may be able to fit yourselves upon the dead boy—that is, upon someone entangled in sins—hear the Prophet saying: “Sound the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of your feast” (Ps. 80:4). That is: announce much, and with resounding preaching, not only to yourselves but also to others; and sound the trumpet at the new moon—that is, in the new moon, by which the new life is signified, in which and unto which the trumpet must be sounded for God. But how will those priests sound the trumpet who do not know how to expound the Gospels and Epistles, the Creed, and the Lord’s Prayer? Therefore, as the Apostle commanded Timothy, saying, “Attend to reading, exhortation, and teaching” (1 Tim. 4:13), so we ask your charity also to devote yourselves to Holy Scripture, so that the divine word may abound in you, from which you may build up others.

For we know, brothers, that by teaching, admonishing, rebuking—at one time gently, at another severely—a good shepherd and diligent priest nourishes and gives milk to the tender, calls back the estranged, waits for [variant: rouses] the sluggish, and chastens the headlong [Col. 0930A] so that they may return, lest the devil find some wanderer outside the camp. You know, moreover, brothers, that it was commanded to the priest in the Law (Exod. 29) that he should have clean garments, and that upon those same garments he should have bells with pomegranates; and, so arrayed, should bring blood into the Holy of Holies. If he presumptuously acts otherwise, he shall die.

By the bells we ought to understand the sound and voice of prayer, which God requires from the priest’s soul, saying: “Make me hear your voice,” and: “Let your voice sound sweet in my ears” (Song 2:14). For, as the Apostle says (Heb. 5), the priest who is surrounded by infirmity must first pray for himself, and then for the people. For this is the chief thing, and the purpose for which the priest is appointed. But because a voice which good devotion does not accompany is useless, pomegranates are fittingly interspersed with the bells, since God more willingly hears that voice which piety, brotherly love, and compassion for Christ’s cross accompany. To those who pray in this way the Lord says through Isaiah: “While you are still speaking, I shall say: Behold, I am here” (Isa. 58:9).

Let us therefore, brothers, ascend to the house of wisdom, which is supported by seven columns, beginning with fear, which is the beginning of wisdom: so that through the spirit of fear we may be poor in spirit; through the spirit of piety, meek; through the spirit of knowledge, mournful for our sins; through the spirit of fortitude, hungry for righteousness; through the spirit of counsel, merciful; through the spirit of understanding, pure; through the spirit of wisdom, peaceful. And thus wisdom shall overcome malice, “and the peace of God, which surpasses all [Col. 0930C] understanding, shall guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 4:7), our Lord, who lives, etc.

## CXXXIV [On Various Subjects XLVII]. TO PASTORS. AGAINST SIMONIACS  
[Note: From Saint-Germain; Col. 0930D.]

“Hear this, priests; attend, house of Israel; listen, house of the king, because the judgment is the Lord’s; for you have become a snare to those who observe you, and a net spread over Tabor, and you have turned sacrifices aside into the deep” (Hos. 5:1).

In these words the prophet Hosea, while rebuking all who live wickedly, most especially reproves the house of the king—that is, the household of Christ: namely, clerics, priests, and monks, who are Christ’s special household and who [Col. 0930D] ought to serve Christ the King in a more particular way in the holy Church, because they are appointed to ecclesiastical offices. The Prophet chiefly threatens these with the Lord’s judgment, adding the cause of their judgment and condemnation when he says: “For you have become a snare to those who observe you, and a net spread over Tabor, and you have turned sacrifices aside into the deep.”

Priests who live wickedly and darken the splendor of the priestly order—indeed, who turn their glory and dignity into disgrace and reproach—have become a snare to those who observe them, because, although they have been given as watchmen to the house of Israel and as guardians of the holy Church, they themselves invite and ensnare their subjects in sin: those for whose salvation they ought to provide, and whom they ought to draw back from sins by word and example. By giving examples of sin, and by living wickedly before their eyes, they cause them to fall into the filth of shameful acts and the cruelty of evil deeds, and thus to enter the devil’s snares.

For how will any layperson or unlearned person revere God’s commandments when he sees them despised by a priest? How will he shudder at sins which he knows are irreverently committed by priests and clerics? How will laypeople abhor fleshly uncleanness when they hear that certain clerics or priests are stained by the infamy of fornication?
