How will laypeople preserve humility of mind, or show signs of humility in their dress, when they have observed in clerics and priests signs of arrogance and pride—in their garments, shoes, tonsure, [Col. 0931B] oaths, games of dice, buffooneries, excesses, wanton and jesting speech, face, gesture, gait, dress, and appetite for vainglory?

How will laypeople avoid avarice or despise earthly things when they see clerics, priests, monks, and abbots longing for earthly advantages, pursuing temporal gain, and, as though neglecting heavenly things to which they ought to attend, applying themselves in every way to the coveting of earthly goods? By these and similar practices, certain clerics, monks, and priests who live wickedly have become a snare to those who observe them—that is, to the laity. As the laity observe their lives, they are corrupted by their example, caught in the enticements of vices, and receive, as it were, exhortation and instruction to live wickedly from those by whom they should have been formed in right living through words and deeds. Those who ought to open by their prayers the gates of the kingdom of heaven shut them both against themselves and against others, since neither do they enter themselves nor permit others to enter, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who neither enter nor allow others to enter” [Col. 0931C] (Matt. 23:13).

The Prophet adds the second cause of judgment and condemnation when he says: “And a net spread over Tabor.” Tabor is a mountain of Galilee, where hunting is frequently practiced and nets are spread to catch birds. Tabor means “coming light.” By Tabor is understood the Church, which is illuminated by the sun of righteousness and illumines the night of this age. Hence in the Psalm: “Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in your name; your arm is with power” (Ps. 88:13).

A net is spread over Tabor—that is, over the holy Church—when those who preside in the holy Church devise schemes for deceiving the simple and oppressing the poor; compose deceitful words, contrive frauds, weave deceits by which they steal the rights of others; or even feign holiness in order to rise to ecclesiastical dignities. All these things, brothers, you see abound in the holy Church—whence there is the greatest cause for grief. Now nearly all, like hunters and bird-catchers, set snares of deception for one another.

The third cause added by the Prophet is this: “And you have turned sacrifices aside into the deep.” The sacrifices are the sacred solemnities of Masses [Col. 0932A], or sacred prayers, or any ecclesiastical offices; likewise almsgiving, fasts, vigils, and whatever is offered to the Lord in the holy Church. Those turn all these things aside into the deep who perform them not for the heavenly things which are above, but for those which are in the depths—namely, on earth, which is the lowest of the elements. They turn sacrifices aside into the deep who seek temporal advantages, human praise, or favor from spiritual offices; or who, because of grace bestowed upon them by God, desire to please human beings rather than God. Their bones—that is, their virtues, which ought to be the bones of the soul—are scattered, because they cannot withstand the assaults of vices, and lose whatever good they appear to possess. And while they seek to please [Col. 0932B] people, they become contemptible to God, as the Psalm says: “The Lord scattered the bones of those who please people; they were put to shame because God despised them” (Ps. 52:6).

God must be worshipped with pure intention. God must be served for his own sake. God himself is the great and incomparable reward of his service [variant: “of service to him”]. Therefore, brothers, serve him for his own sake, not for temporal profit or worldly glory. This was the intention of Simon Magus, who wished to buy the gift of the Holy Spirit so as thereby to obtain worldly profit and glory. It would have been good had he desired the Holy Spirit in order to be sanctified by him; but he sought the Holy Spirit from the apostles not out of love for the Holy Spirit, nor from zeal for sanctification, but so that, by laying hands upon the sick, he might gain greater money and thus obtain profit and glory.

Accordingly, you see, brothers, that those who receive holy orders, or who perform ecclesiastical offices in order to obtain profit and glory, follow Simon’s example and are not altogether free from the roots of the Simonian perversity. For these are the roots of simony: to desire temporal profit and to desire to be glorified by people. Simon Magus sought to acquire these two things through spiritual gifts, and therefore was not worthy to receive the spiritual grace which he believed saleable. Rather, he was rejected with the gifts he offered and eternally condemned, as Peter said: “May your money be with you unto destruction” (Acts 8:20).

[Col. 0932D] Consider, then, how detestable simony is, how shameful and abominable it is to be simoniacal and to be counted among heretics. Remember that the Lord cast sellers and buyers out of the Temple (John 2), those, namely, who made the house of prayer a house of commerce. Today, brothers, they make God’s house a house of commerce not only who give or receive gifts for holy orders, but everyone who performs ecclesiastical offices entrusted to him for temporal ends, and whoever in God’s Church “seeks his own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2:21). All such persons are condemned by the Lord and cast out of the Temple.

We do not say, however, that you ought to refuse temporal benefits if they are offered; but we say that you ought not to celebrate divine [Col. 0933A] offices with the intention of seeking temporal things, because God must be served for God’s own sake. Divine service must be performed not for temporal advantages but in expectation of heavenly rewards, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. 6:33).

Therefore, brothers, despise earthly things; lift your minds to heavenly ones. Abstain from buffoonery and vanities, wantonness and deceit, uncleanness and vainglory. Take care to do good before God and people. Show your subjects examples of light; provide an example of continence and chastity, patience and humility, mercy and gentleness, lest you become a snare to the watchtower by giving evil examples; lest you spread a net over Tabor by entrapping the less cautious; lest you turn sacrifices aside into the deep by seeking temporal things from spiritual ones; and lest you incur the judgment threatened by the Prophet. Rather, by living well and rightly instructing your subjects, may you receive at the highest judgment an eternal reward for your own merits and theirs, so that you may receive the unfading crown. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns, God three and one, for ages of ages. Amen.

## CXXXV [On Various Subjects XLVIII]. TO PASTORS. AGAINST SIMONIACS  
[Note: From Saint-Germain; Col. 0933D.]

Yesterday, brothers, we said a little about the roots of the Simonian heresy. To uproot it and tear it from the field which the Lord has blessed, the holy Fathers labored with much zeal, cutting down its sprouting branches by severe rebukes, threats of Gehenna, and deposition of the guilty, as with sickles and hoes; and pursuing the roots themselves with the subtlety of doctrine and the authority of Holy Scripture, as with living fires.

But although this pest arose at the beginning of the primitive Church and began with Simon Magus (Acts 8), and was immediately condemned and execrated by Simon Peter; although it did not greatly increase in the time of the apostles or martyrs, nor in the time of the confessors Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, Gregory, Eusebius, Hilary, and other learned men who flourished as outstanding doctors in the holy Church and zealously [Col. 0933C] and vigorously fought against the attacks of heretics in defense of Catholic truth; and although simony could not in their age greatly extend its branches—yet roots always remained. From these, in the present times, many branches now proceed and shoots spread far and wide, occupying almost the whole vineyard of the Lord and crushing the fruit of good vine-shoots.

You see that almost everywhere the intention is earthly gain and worldly glory; almost all delight in human favor and in the honor paid to them. Therefore clerics who are rich or powerful seek ecclesiastical honors either by [Col. 0934A] money or seize them by violence. Those in poverty desire advancement to holy orders, not from a desire to serve God, but with the intention of becoming rich through sacred offices and rising through acquired riches to power and high estate.

Some, aware that they are unworthy of ordination, or lacking honorable birth, or not adorned with good conduct or learning, or even stained by infamy, nevertheless thrust themselves forward shamelessly and are admitted to the clergy, or even advanced to holy orders, through money, private friendship, some temporal service, or undue favor. Some, having received canonical ordination, perform divine offices by a money bargain.

[Note: “Canonical,” perhaps “of canonical dignity,” as Hildebert speaks below and elsewhere.]

[Note: Thus now, in almost all cathedrals and wealthy collegiate churches, a fee is shamelessly demanded for burials and ecclesiastical offices.]

Some expel from the churches to which they have been assigned and attached, through money and usurpation, priests canonically ordained [Col. 0934B] and living honorably. Some, disdaining ordination, usurp for themselves the benefices of chapels, which belong only to priests. Others shamelessly demand and violently extort a price for burial or other ecclesiastical offices. Others, despising the smaller churches in which they were ordained, transfer themselves to greater and richer churches, not by canonical calling but through simoniacal ambition.

Others purchase, by a concluded bargain, the prebends of churches called canonical, or provostships; and they say that they purchase not spiritual benefices but temporal ones alone. Yet in the present Church temporal and spiritual benefices are joined, as body and soul are joined in a human being; and whoever buys one does not leave the other unbought, as is plainly shown in the canonical Decrees in these words: “If anyone should object that not the consecrations themselves are bought, but the things which arise from consecration, he is proved plainly to be talking nonsense.”

For a bodily Church, or a bishop, or an abbot, or anything of the sort, can in no way function without bodily and external goods, just as the soul does not live bodily without the body. Whoever sells the one without which the other cannot arise does not refrain from selling either. And what follows shortly afterward is most terrible: “Who does not see that the Masses or prayers of priests or clerics of this kind provoke to anger the God whom they suppose they are appeasing by such means?”

[Col. 0934D] Consider, then, brothers, how dreadful is the scourge of simony, how horrible a crime, how detestable an evil, which corrupts faith and is counted among heresies. Beware of the branches mentioned above, which proceed from that iniquity. Uproot the roots themselves by despising worldly gain and glory. Guard yourselves lest you be infected with this poison. Guard the churches entrusted to you lest they be corrupted by this plague. Uproot other vices also, so that through sincerity and purity worthy service may be rendered to God.

You have been appointed cultivators of the Lord’s vineyard: see that it does not remain uncultivated. See that through [Col. 0935A] your negligence it does not produce wild grapes instead of grapes, bitterness instead of sweetness, and the harshness of torments instead of the delight of heavenly rewards. Devote yourselves to preaching, correction, and admonition. Correct the evils that abound. Everywhere are frauds and perjuries; everywhere robberies and thefts; everywhere usury and covetousness; everywhere lust and drunkenness; everywhere murders and adulteries; everywhere fornications; everywhere envy and detraction.

Say to your subjects with the prophet Hosea: “For the Lord has a judgment against the inhabitants of the land: for there is no truth, no knowledge of God, no mercy in the land. Cursing, lying, theft, adultery, and murder have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4:2). Declare their crimes to the people [Col. 0935B], lest God require their sins from your hands because of your silence. Admonish them to do good with a good intention, to perform just things justly: namely, not for human praise or earthly reward, but for heavenly recompense. May he deign to grant this to you, who lives and reigns, God three and one, for ages of ages. Amen.

## CXXXVI [On Various Subjects XLIX]. ON THE FIRST SUNDAY OF LENT  
[Note: From Saint-Germain; Col. 0935C.]

Strive, dearest brothers, you who desire to cleanse your souls from sin, not to depart by any byway of shamefulness from this path of fasting and amendment which you have undertaken.

[Note: Several matters in this sermon seem worth observing. First, Hildebert’s zeal to turn the people entrusted to him away from those profane festivities with which they began the very sacred season of Lent, on the holy day itself of the first Sunday of Lent. However diligently the shepherds of the Church have labored against this evil, its roots do not seem wholly uprooted. Even now, in many regions of the Christian world, that first Sunday in Lent is disfigured by buffooneries; because of the festive torches which they light, it is commonly called *le Dimanche des brandons*—“Brandons Sunday.” Although the use of meat is not permitted on that day, as it formerly was, it is so marked by profane merriment [Col. 0935D] that in ancient civil contracts it is even designated as a formal date for payments; and in certain places the common people prolong this abuse until the third Sunday of Lent.

It should also be noted from this sermon that the Lenten fast was formerly observed for no more than thirty-six days. The faithful offered this number of days, as a tenth part of the year, to God as though in tithe. Hildebert probably derived the discussion of this observance here reported from Homily 16 on the Gospels by Saint Gregory the Pope. For that most holy pontiff says there: “From the present day—that is, from the first Sunday of Lent—until the joys of the Paschal feast, six weeks occur, which make forty-two days. Since six Sundays are subtracted from abstinence, no more than thirty-six days remain in abstinence. But since the year consists of three hundred and sixty days, while we afflict ourselves for thirty-six days, we give, as it were, the tithe of our year to God; so that we who have lived for ourselves throughout the received year may mortify ourselves for our Creator, through abstinence, in its tithes.”

It should also be observed that the four days preceding the first Sunday of Lent, so that the forty-day number consecrated by Christ’s fasting might be completed in addition to the other thirty-six days, were added only long after Saint Gregory—according to most learned authorities, only about the eighth or ninth century. Nor was this observed universally in all churches, since the Church of Milan has not even now adopted this addition of four days. It still begins Lent on the sixth Sunday before Easter, content with fasting only thirty-six days, with Saint Charles approving this in the First Provincial Council.

It is also clear from this sermon that abstinence was enjoined during Lent not only from meat, but also from the marital debt and every kind of luxury—such as wine, vehicles, hunting, lawsuits, and even arms. These were prohibited so strictly that among the grounds for the deposition of Emperor Louis the Pious, he was especially reproached because, “contrary to the Christian religion and his vow, deceived by the counsel of evil men, without any public advantage or certain necessity,” as the Acts of his deposition, chapter 3, state, “he had ordered an expedition to be undertaken during the days of Lent.” Our Martène has discussed all these matters fully and very learnedly in his recently published treatise *On the Ancient Discipline of the Church in Divine Offices*, chapter VIII.]

For some of you, through the deception of the ancient [Col. 0935C] enemy, have adopted on this day a custom which ought not so much to be followed as despised: because meat alone is not forbidden you today, you think that [Col. 0936A] you may more freely indulge every bodily pleasure and every shameful act. You have found this occasion: because it is permitted you to eat meat, it may also be permitted to use fleshly pleasures. These are not the works of Christians but of pagans.

For pagans, also called Gentiles, celebrating the feast of their gods—that is, Jupiter, Saturn, Minerva, and Venus—after immense gluttony of food and drink and shameful banquets, would gather outside the city at the theatre, which is also called a brothel. There they first exhausted themselves in every kind of jest and finally, with prostitutes who hid in the caverns of that theatre, in licentiousness. Therefore, as Paul Orosius relates, the devil whom they worshipped incited them to this foul uncleanness so that, to him to whom they paid sacrifice from animal victims, they might also pay sacrifice from the strength of their own bodies. For the devil is polluted and unclean, and he requires for himself a polluted and unclean sacrifice. Hence he is interpreted as *pollens*, that is, “glory of skin,” because he greatly delights in lust, which is aroused by the beauty of the skin.

But as far as the service of God differs from that of the devil, so far does the life of those called Christians from Christ differ from the life of those subject to the devil and serving him in all things. Therefore, brothers, you must desist today from this and every evil custom, because this day is not only the head of fasts but also the head of the ages. It must therefore be venerated with great worship and religion [Col. 0936C], not polluted by lustful pleasures, because both in name and in mystery it seems consecrated beyond the other days.

It is called especially the Lord’s Day because he placed it first in the order of days, and because, having overcome death—which he unworthily accepted for us—and having conquered the enemy from whose power he snatched us, he rose mightily from the dead on that day and established it for us to observe in honor of his resurrection. [Col. 0937A] How, then, do we wish to rise from the death of the soul if we are unwilling to honor the day of resurrection? And on what ground do we think to cleanse our minds by fasting if we wish to enter polluted through the gate of fasting?

Perhaps someone unrestrained, more obedient to bodily pleasures than to God’s law, will answer me as I censure mortal people and reprove my own sins together with the iniquities of others: “You who preach that the natural union of male and female and the bond of love established from the beginning ought to be cherished, how do you ask impossible and useless things—that I should, during some fast, abstain from the woman who is my flesh, as from food?”

To him I, though a sinner, shall readily reply: God did not give the good things of the world for people to abuse them, but for them to use justly. Marriage, indeed, like the other riches of the world, is good when it is rightly maintained; but if wrongly used, it turns into sin. Hence Gregory [Note: Book XXVI on Job, chapter XIX]: “Whatever we receive for the use of life, we turn back to the use of vices.” Nor do I preach the separation of so sacred a union; rather, I prescribe abstinence for the brief period of thirty-six days. For what profit is there in abstaining from meat while not laying aside fleshly works? Whoever has lived throughout the year in these and other pleasures ought at least to refrain for God during [Col. 0937C] this short span.

Why are you called *vir* (“man”), from bodily strength, if you do not possess this strength in your soul, so that for God, who gave you all things and from whom you daily ask greater things, you cannot reckon a tenth part [variant: “cannot forego a tenth part, or cannot do without a tenth part”]? For whoever considers carefully will find no more than thirty-six days, which are the tithe of the year, in this abstinence. For since a full year consists of three hundred and sixty-six days, if from three hundred and thirty and from sixty-six there are subtracted the same number of days which I mentioned, these days are consecrated to fasting.

Of these six days, which together with their nights comprise one hundred and fifty hours, a tenth part is fifteen hours. But because we cannot make up from these a whole day together with the following [Col. 0937D] night, to add to the aforesaid number and devote to fasting, ecclesiastical usage has established that what is not rendered in this respect should be supplied by fasting on the Sundays of the same season from meat and fleshly pleasures. For on these days, because they are consecrated to the very name of God, refreshment of food is granted and license to sin withdrawn. What brings life—and is better—is given to us; what brings death—and is worse—is withdrawn from us. If we did not defile ourselves with vices and fleshly pollutions, we would surely render from these the full tithes of the year.

But because it has been said to us, regenerated by the sacred font and now tasting not the flesh of figures but of the true Lamb, by the Lord himself: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 0938A] (Matt. 5:20), the Christian religion has established that it should change into fasting not only thirty-six days, on account of the tithes of the year, but also, with them, the four days beginning from the head of the fast, on account of the perfection of so great a mystery: forty days.

For this Lenten fast has great authority from the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel. Moses the lawgiver fasted forty days in order to receive the Law. Elijah, greatest of the prophets, who deserved to be carried into heaven in a fiery chariot, when Jezebel pursued him, was first fed by angelic food and afterward [Col. 0938B] abstained from all food for the same number of days. [Lacuna.]

[Note: This sermon ends in no other way; it therefore appears mutilated.]

## CXXXVII [On Various Subjects L]. ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST  
[Note: The same as no. 65, but differently; Col. 0937D.]

“But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the Law, that he might redeem those who were under the Law” (Gal. 4:4).

By a great dispensation, dearest brethren, God willed to redeem humankind and, by a wondrous example of humility, to send his own Son for our deliverance. By careful counsel he had provided a fitting time for this mission, in which people might be convinced that they could possess no salvation from themselves, neither through the natural law nor through the written law. For he allowed two periods to pass—namely, before the law and under the law—so that he might come in the time of grace. Before the written law [Col. 0938C] there was the natural law, that is, the guidance of reason, which did not bring salvation. The written law, however, given later, began rather to harm than to help. By prohibiting sins—“You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:13)—it inflamed human minds more toward those very sins. But when the fullness of the time foreseen by God came, he sent his Son, so that the grace of Christ might supply what neither law was able to accomplish.

And although he had been awaited and foretold for many ages, at last John the Forerunner was sent ahead of the one who was to come, to announce the arrival of so great an emperor. Hear the order: the Son was coming against the devil; he sent before him a mighty soldier, to invade the world, terrify the king’s enemies, and draw to his Lord whomever he could. A mighty prince, a mighty soldier—and both were announced through a mighty soldier [supplied]. For the angel Gabriel, whose name is interpreted “Strength of God,” foretold the coming of each. They were mighty, and came to do mighty deeds. The soldier was born, and many rejoiced at his birth. O what great joy was to be at the birth of the emperor, when such joy was sent beforehand at the birth of the forerunner!

You have heard the joy at his birth; hear the office of him who ran before. John came into the wilderness, preaching and saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2). [Col. 0939A] He is said to have come into the wilderness because those whom he exhorted had been deserted by God. For he commanded them to repent. He did not frighten them, but drew them to his Lord by promising fruit, when he said, “For the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” Thus he attracted some. Hear how he frightened the enemies. Seeing the Pharisees, he said to them: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?” (ibid., v. 7). See how he prepared the way of the Lord: drawing some and frightening others. Of these things the prophet said: “A voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Isa. 40:3).

The way is broad; the path narrow. The way signifies the broader precepts, such as the lawful use of marriage and of worldly things. The path signifies a stricter life, that is, that of monks [Col. 0939B] and hermits. Both are seen to be prepared for the Lord. Therefore he exhorted people by preaching, and adorned his preaching with the works of his life. Behold the works. His clothing was of camel’s hair, and a leather belt was around his loins. His food, moreover, was locusts and wild honey. He clothed himself in rough things, and with harsh rebukes broke the ungodly. He girded his loins because he restrained lust. Locusts are small creatures leaping through the fields, whose flight is lively but quickly falls. He ate honey because his preaching tasted sweet to his hearers. He ate locusts because, while he preached, he was thought to be Christ. For they asked: “Are you the Christ?” (John 1:20). See: he was lifted up in flight like a locust; but, answering, “I am not the Christ” (ibid.), he quickly fell from that exaltation, like a locust which quickly falls while flying.

Thus in so great a preacher we can find an example for our life. When he is clothed in rough garments, he instructs us to tame the flesh by labours. When he girds his loins with a belt, he invites us to chastity. When he does not acknowledge himself to be Christ, but proclaims himself inferior, saying, “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (Luke 3:26), he teaches us humility. When he labours by preaching to others, he invites us to win the salvation of our brethren. When he flees into the wilderness, he urges us to strip ourselves of worldly things. And who was more perfect than John? The Lord testifies: “Among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen” (Matt. 11:11). For Christ was not born of a woman, but of a virgin; John is not said to be less than Christ [Col. 0939C–D], lest he be thought [supplied] Christ’s equal, but Christ is [held to be] greater [supplied: than the angels]. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “He who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he” (ibid.). For Christ was in the present Church, which is the kingdom of heaven, and in it God reigns; he was lesser according to his humanity, because “he came not to be served but to serve” (Matt. 20:28). Yet he was greater than John in power and in the dignity of virtue.

Therefore let us rejoice at the birth of so great a forerunner, of whom it was said: “At his birth many will rejoice” (Luke 1:14), so that John, whose name is interpreted “grace of God,” may by his merits obtain God’s grace for us, drive away diseases, remove storms [Col. 0940A], and grant abundance of crops, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## CXXXVIII [On Various Subjects, LI]. ON THE PERFECT CONVERSION OF THE SOUL

[Note: Col. 0939D. From St-Germain.]

“Then the Lord brought the children of Israel out of Egypt; they crossed the Red Sea; and, journeying through the wilderness, they ate manna. After long labours, at last they came to the Jordan; and when they had crossed the river, they circumcised themselves a second time, and it was said to them: ‘Today the Lord has taken away from you the reproach of Egypt.’ They remained in the camp until they were healed; and the name of that place was called Gilgal. At last, having gone out from the camp, they ate of the fruits of the land, and manna failed them [Col. 0940B]” (Joshua 5:8).

This event, dearest brethren, conveys the great mystery of our progress. Egypt, from which the Lord brings forth his people, is sin, which is fittingly interpreted as “darkness.” For sins are inward darknesses, which lead to the outward darkness, namely hell. Nor do we read that the Lord led the children of Israel into Egypt, but that he led them out. It is yours to be led into sin; it is God’s to set free. God’s people, leaving Egypt, cross the sea. In the sea there are two things: water and bitterness. By the water we understand tears of repentance; by the bitterness, contrition of heart. For it is not enough to abandon sin unless we have a contrite heart and bring forth worthy fruits of repentance. Yet we must not remain in the sea, [Col. 0940C] but cross it and come into the wilderness. For we are not always to mourn for our sins; rather, once repentance has been accomplished, we must come to the holy and religious life which belongs to Christians. This is fittingly signified by the wilderness. For it is abandoned by many. Hence the Lord said: “Narrow is the way that leads to life, and few enter through it” (Matt. 7:14).

That way is narrow and solitary; dry, because it is trodden by the dry; and truly solitary, because in Egypt it has great crowds of companions, but in the wilderness it will have few companions, or none. Hence the Psalmist: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. 140:10), because once he has crossed over, he will have many companions: namely, the angelic companies and all the saints. Egypt too [Col. 0940D] is a flat land, fair in appearance but full of marshes. So also the way that leads to death is not steep but delightful, and full of marshes—that is, uncleannesses.

In the wilderness the children of Israel were fed with manna, which rained upon them from heaven; and the Christian people, while pressing toward their promised inheritance, are sustained by the word of God. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, of which the Lord says: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4). This bread nourishes God’s people in three ways. It frightens them away from vices by threatening the punishments of hell; it delights them with promises; and, while those promises are delayed, it discloses certain mysteries, lest they fail upon the way. But because [Col. 0941A] the word of God—that is, sacred Scripture—does not seek support from Tully’s rhetorical ornament, being sufficiently strong in its own truth, there are people disgusted with this bread who say: “Let us return to Egypt, to the fleshpots” (Exod. 16:3), that is, let us apply our study to secular writings. But those who do not fail make progress and at last come to the Jordan, which is near the promised land.

You have heard, dearest brethren, that the children of Israel crossed the sea as they left Egypt. As they draw near to the promised land, these same people come to the Jordan, which they also cross. For that wilderness through which those journey who are striving toward the promised land is the field which Caleb’s daughter asked of her father, having an upper and a lower spring. He [Col. 0941B] who presses toward the joys of eternal life promised to him is pricked with compunction at the beginning of his journey and weeps for the sins gathered from these lower things. But after repentance has been fulfilled, he lives justly and piously in this world—which is to cross the wilderness with much labour. And, wearied by many labours, reflecting also upon the perishable and transitory things of this world, he desires to lack them and to possess eternal things. Hence the Apostle: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23); but because these things are delayed, he bursts into tears.

The position of the places also accords with this mystery: in Egypt’s situation the Red Sea is lower down, while the Jordan, in relation to the land, is higher up. Having crossed the Jordan, they circumcised themselves a second time. Circumcision, which was performed on the eighth day with a stone knife, signified that the putting away of defilements is accomplished through Christ, for the sake of the eternal blessedness which we shall attain on the eighth day of the resurrection. But the putting away of defilements requires an order. No one becomes most beautiful all at once. First, therefore—that is, at our departure from Egypt—we put away shameful acts. Yet unlawful impulses still flourish in our fragile flesh. Saints, even if they restrain themselves from them, are accustomed to be stirred by the sight of women, the pleasure of foods, and worldly glory, until they have advanced so far that, captivated by the sweetness of heavenly things, they care for nothing earthly and are not stirred by the sight or touch of worldly things. Rather, they remain in the camp until they are healed.

For while saints feel those impulses, they refrain from the sight [Col. 0941C–D] of women, from eating pleasant foods, and from soft clothing. At length, accustomed to abstinence through long practice, they go out: they see women, eat sweet foods, put on whatever clothing they choose, and are not captivated by pleasure in these things. When they have done this, the Lord has removed from them the reproach of Egypt. For in Egypt was incurred the reproach which accompanies saints through the wilderness of this life—namely, concupiscence, the mother of all evils. But he who, having overcome the enticements of the flesh, desires only heavenly things, is visited by God and receives understanding from him; the mysteries of heaven are revealed to him, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “I will sing and understand in the blameless way: when will you come to me?” (Ps. 100:2). Therefore the place of the second circumcision was called Gilgal, that is, “revelation.”

Then one eats from the fruits of the land. Whoever has attained so great a perfection that for love of heavenly things he values earthly things as nothing may, in regard to the condition of the present life, eat from the fruit of the land—that is, of the Church—because he may safely partake of Christ’s body and blood. Nor did they eat only of the fruit of palm trees [Col. 0942A–B], but of the fruits of other trees. This indicates that we shall receive from the Lord not only what we deserve, but much more. For “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18).

That manna failed after they had eaten from the fruits of the land signifies that the Scriptures, which are our refreshment on the way, will cease when we are in our homeland. Hence elsewhere: “The heaven will be folded up like a book.” [Note: Col. 0941D. “The heavens shall be folded up like a book” (Isa. 34:4).] This heaven—that is, divine Scripture—is made from the skins of dead animals, which are now spread out and later will be folded up. These dead animals are the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments, whose faith and righteousness are set before us in the Scriptures, so that they may be for us, as it were, models of faith and good works. Hence it was said [Col. 0942C]: “You shall be known in the midst of two animals.”

## CXXXIX [On Various Subjects, LII]. ON THE TRUE FREEDOM OF THE CHRISTIAN SOUL

[Note: Col. 0941D. From St-Germain.]

“If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

[Note: Col. 0941D. Observe that Hildebert also discussed, in the same sense, the threefold freedom of nature, grace, and glory in Sermon 4, “On the Advent of the Lord,” p. 225, and in almost the same words. Since that sermon is undoubtedly Hildebert’s, we judge this one also to be by the same author. This also seems capable of proof from the allegory of Jacob’s struggle with the angel, here applied to contemplatives, which Hildebert presented in the same manner and sense in Book I, Letter 22, to William, abbot of St Vincent of Le Mans, and which he frequently employs in sermons when speaking of contemplation. If, therefore, it may be concluded from this that this sermon is truly Hildebertine, why not also the others collected in the same manuscript?]

Three freedoms are found in sacred Scripture: one of nature, another of grace, a third of glory. The first frees from necessity; the second from sin; the third from every punishment and misery. Creation conferred the first, by which we were made free from every necessity, a noble creature in God. In the second we are regenerated by grace and baptism, a new creature in Christ; in the third we shall be crowned unto salvation, a glorious creature in the spirit. We began in the first; through the second [Col. 0942D] we advance; in the third we shall be consummated. Through the first we are subject to God by the law of creation; through the second we have subjected the flesh to ourselves by the law of re-creation; through the third we shall overcome death by the power of glorification.

After the first, the second was necessary for righteousness, since the first had already become obsolete through sin; nor could we attain the third except through the second, [Col. 0943A] because no one comes to the Father except through the Son. Of this second and third liberation Truth says: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free.”

But how was this liberation accomplished through the Son? “The Son emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7), and made the first step of humility into flesh, the second onto the cross, the third into death. His whole life is our teaching, and every action of his is our lesson. Nor do only his sayings and deeds, but each of his members—his feet, hands, breast, and head, as it were—speak to us and show us the way of our salvation and liberation.

The feet are mercy and judgment, because one has no force without the other. For mercy by itself would make people negligent; judgment by itself would make them despair. If someone considers mercy alone—because God is gracious and very merciful, and the earth is full of the Lord’s mercy—and not justice, by which rewards answer merits in due exchange, he thereafter sins securely, promising himself impunity for all his sins. But if he considers justice alone, saying: “Terrible among all the kings of the earth, who takes away the spirit of princes, who touches the mountains and they smoke” (Ps. 71:13), he will easily fall into the danger of despair. Now these two are joined, so that mercy may strengthen hope and judgment instil fear.

At these feet penitents fall down in humility with Mary the sinner; with tears of repentance they wipe away their sins and seek pardon through due satisfaction. Then, after the sickness of sins is cured, it is fitting that nature be strengthened by food and drink. [Col. 0943B–C] The sick person has nothing with which to refresh himself if he has accumulated nothing for himself except sins. Therefore he hungers for virtues, by which he may both guard himself better henceforth and pursue good works more freely. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:6). It is necessary that the hungry people, whom the Lord fed in the wilderness, approach the Lord’s hands as beggars, as though about to receive alms, saying: “Your hands, O Lord, made me and fashioned me” (Ps. 118:73); do not despise the works of your hands.

These two hands are generosity and benevolence; either without the other would not suffice. One person is generous but not benevolent, and another the reverse. But God, who possesses everything that exists and wills everything that is good, refreshes us with a generous and kindly hand when he communicates his own body and blood to us. Christ gave his blood for us: on the cross, as the price; on the altar, as the cup; in pilgrimage, as provision for the journey; in the departure from Egypt, as escort; in the homeland, as advocate. This blood flowed with water from the Lord’s side; from these sacraments was prepared the eye-salve that wiped the eyes of the man born blind; the cleansing wash that cleansed the stain of sins; and the most holy oil pressed out through which the yoke of the devil’s power might wholly decay.

This hand protected captive Esther as she entered [Col. 0944A] before the king with a golden sceptre, received her when she entered into an embrace, and made her queen on the royal throne. Esther is the righteous soul, journeying away from its homeland; it is captive, surrounded on every side by enemies, the vices. With these weapons we defeat vices and acquire virtues. Thus armed, we are made fit to recline with John upon the Lord’s breast, so that there may be poured out to us what we may pour out to others. This is the treasury of the heavenly armoury, in which all treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. Whoever has nothing from this fullness has absolutely nothing.

From there, with Mary justified, we ascend by contemplation to the Lord’s head, when the mind, winged with virtues, raises itself above itself and, hating—or wholly forgetting—its earthly dwelling, says with Moses: “Lord, if I have found grace [Col. 0944B] in your sight, show me yourself” (Exod. 33:13). This soul too ascends the mountain of contemplation with Abraham and the boy, leaving the servants with the ass in the valley (Gen. 22). Abraham is reason; the boy is understanding, or innocence, which ascends the mountain of contemplation with reason, leaving the servants—that is, the cares and desires of the flesh—in this valley of misery and mortality, together with the ass, that is, the sluggish flesh. This is the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell, in which the Lord took counsel with Moses and Elijah.

Then we shall say with Peter: “It is good for us to be here” (Mark 9:5); then with Paul we shall hear secret words, and with Isaiah we shall say: “My secret is for me; my secret is for me” (Isa. 24:16). Then we shall receive the blessing with Jacob, having become victorious in the struggle; our name will no longer be Jacob, but we shall be called Israel, after we have been struck in the thigh, where the excess of carnal lust is denoted. We shall walk with one foot only: that is, with one affection we shall set aside carnal things, and with one foot pursue heavenly things, where our immense desire, devout devotion, and most sweet affection reject earthly things and say: “It is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. 72:28).

One clings to God in three ways: through imitation, through contemplation, and through enjoyment. The first attachment is laborious; the second affectionate; the third delightful. The first and second belong to this life: here is the labour of action and the affection of contemplation; the third will be in the life to come. There we shall see face to face what we now see in a mirror and in an enigma. May he himself deign to grant this to us, etc.

## CXL [On Various Subjects, LIII]. ON PASSION SUNDAY

[Note: Col. 0943D. From St-Germain.]

Now that the season of Lent is passing away and the joys of the most holy resurrection are drawing near, the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion, dearest brethren, comes before us each year, striking the whole Church today with its tearful account. Although many days still remain from this day until that which especially merited to see its own author crucified, nevertheless the holy Fathers have appointed that this same Passion be read to us during the days that follow, [Col. 0945A] especially blessed Gregory, who in all ecclesiastical offices, both daily and nightly, introduces from this point until the Paschal feast the words and sorrow of the Passion, teaching that we ought to weep for him without whom we can possess no complete joy.

Therefore, whoever are confident that we are to be members of our Redeemer, let us feel the pain and injury of so great a head. Hence the Prophet: “Every head is sick, and every heart sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in it” (Isa. 1:5). And the Apostle: “If one member suffers, let all the other members suffer with it” (1 Cor. 12:26). Since we acknowledge that Christ—who is our head and crown, a member higher and more honourable than all—suffered, let us, the lower members, suffer with him. [Col. 0945B]

Especially since he willed to suffer not for any sin of his own, but for our redemption, that he might redeem us from the ancient slavery of the devil and make us perpetual inhabitants of the heavenly homeland from which we were excluded as captives. For he, ineffably merciful, willed to cleanse our sins and iniquities not with gold, or any kind of metal, or ornaments of beautiful variety, nor even with victims of slain animals, but with his own body sacrificed upon the altar of the cross and his most precious blood poured out. “Truly he bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (Isa. 53:4); and he himself, our mediator with the Father, said: “You did not ask for a holocaust or a sin-offering; then I said: Behold, I come” (Ps. 49:7).

The meaning is: O God the Father, since for [Col. 0945C] the redemption of the human race I saw that you did not desire [reading uncertain; perhaps *captare*, “seek”] a holocaust of animals, I immediately said, “Behold, I come,” that I may be sacrificed for the salvation of my people. Behold, dearest brethren, we have heard that Christ was sacrificed for us. We should therefore greatly rejoice and grieve: rejoice because it was a happy fault which merited to have such a Redeemer; grieve because we see no imitator of so great a Passion.

Though he died bodily, he requires from us a sacrifice not only of the death of our body, if necessary, but of amendment of life and humbling of spirit: namely, that our spirit, in astonished awe at such great and ineffable humility of its Creator, may tremble, and, overcoming the enticements of the flesh, have with him who suffered a certain compassion. Hence: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” (Ps. 50:19). And although it is impossible for our bodily frailty to follow his immeasurable divinity, nevertheless we follow him well according to the measure of our humanity if we sacrifice the vices of the body by fasting and vigils, and rejoice to remain clean and spotless before his eyes. Hence the prophet: “Wash yourselves; be clean,” etc. (Isa. 1:16).

But how, when the fury of persecution threatens, shall we lay down our lives for him, when for his Passion we cannot even fast from vices and from every kind of food for a short time? In what way, then, do we imitate his Passion, when we forbid our bodies none of their defilements? Indeed, what is worse, in boldly resisting his commands, we are opposed to him as though he were an enemy. [Col. 0946A] For while he cries in the Old Testament, “You shall not kill; you shall not steal” (Exod. 20:14), and gives the other commands of the law, we, as though provoking his wrath against ourselves, mad and senseless, commit adultery, kill, and steal. Moreover, the more all vices are forbidden us, the more eagerly we take care to pursue and love them.

Likewise, while he threatens in the New Testament of the Gospel: “Everyone who says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ and whoever says, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 5:22), we, on the contrary, touched by the zeal of envy, proudly and contumaciously heap every abusive insult upon our brethren. We must therefore restrain our minds from such things and from similar ones if we hope to share in his redemption.

For he is the true priest and high priest of future [Col. 0946B] goods, who offered to God his Father not the blood of goats and bulls, but himself, namely an unblemished lamb, cleansing our conscience from dead works—that is, sins—and through this entered once into the holy places, that he might appear before the face of God for us. Other priests, after slaughtering the flesh of animals according to the custom of the old law, entered the Holy Place once every year. This priest is eternal; he came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it. Not in each year, but in the final year of his life, after sacrificing himself once upon the altar of the cross, he entered the holy places—that is, heaven—that he might disclose the Father’s mysteries to servants who followed him through faith, and grant them these mysteries to possess after the end.

Other priests, when the time of sacrifice had been completed, made haste to return to their own homes, intending to return to the Temple the following year. But this one, when the mystery of his Passion and Resurrection had been accomplished, ascended to the palaces of heaven, his proper home. He will return not the following year but at the end of the age, to examine in righteous judgment the merits of the good and the evil, and render rewards to the good and punishments to the evil. [Col. 0946C]

What shall we do on that day, brethren, when we must render an account not only of evil deeds but also of idle words? If we dread all the faults of the tongue, which are counted as nothing, what must be feared concerning the other members—our hands and feet and the rest—which we know without doubt to have committed many unlawful acts? For if we pay the penalties for all the sins that we have committed, we are eternally condemned and lost. Therefore now, each of us, in proportion as he loves his soul, should erase past sins through repentance, take care not to repeat them, and not kindle again what he once extinguished through God’s grace. For whoever repeats what he has already lamented provokes God to anger against himself, so that, when called, God may not hear him. Hence he says through Solomon: “I called and you refused; you despised all my counsel and neglected my rebukes; but I shall laugh at your destruction and mock when what you feared comes upon you” (Prov. 1:24).

How fearful a voice, dearest brethren, by which our Redeemer threatens that he will laugh at our destruction. Therefore let us continually open the ears of our mind to his commands, so that we may see him not terrifying but [Col. 0947A] gentle. And how could we endure him as terrifying and angry against us, when in this present life we can scarcely bear his lightning or thunder for fear? If we are temporarily terrified by the movement of a single creature, with what courage shall we await the Creator coming with fire to judge, shaking not only the earth but also the heavens? For, as the Psalmist says: “Fire shall blaze before him, and a mighty tempest round about him” (Ps. 42:3). And the Judge himself says through the prophet: “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also heaven.” [Note: Col. 0947D. Vulgate: “Yet one little while, and I will move heaven and earth” (Hag. 2:8).]

Fear, brethren, the coming of that Judge, at whose fixed [Col. 0947B] judgment there will be no opportunity for redemption. Cease from wicked conduct and the evil habit of the present life, and strive to suffer with your Redeemer, so that with him you may happily rise, after judgment, from the tombs of vices to the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

## CXLI. 880 * SERMON FOR PALM SUNDAY

On the weakness of the law of Moses for the restoration of humankind, and the power of Christ’s law to accomplish it.

David, foreseeing in the Spirit, says: “The Lord has delivered the poor man from the mighty one, and the poor man who had no helper” (Ps. 71:12).

Not everyone possesses knowledge: some do not know this poor man, others do not know that poor man. We exhort those who know; we instruct those who do not know. That poor man is our first parent and his posterity; that powerful one is the devil [Col. 0947C]. Our first parent was rich in Paradise, poor outside Paradise; free before sin, a slave after sin. Great were his riches, because he abounded in all that he desired so long as he desired what God commanded; true was his freedom, because he was subject to God’s dominion alone so long as he made good use of free choice. But when he desired what God did not desire, the rich man became needy and the free man enslaved: he needed a physician and served sin. From that time he received shame instead of glory, anxiety instead of tranquillity, and the muttering and tumult of vices instead of converse with angels. From that time the prince of this world made him his kingdom; the strong armed man made him his court; the father of darkness made him his blinded possession.

Against such a powerful adversary, our poor man had no help from himself, none from reason, none from the Law [Col. 0947D]. Since he was born corrupt from one corrupt, conquered from one conquered, debtor from a debtor, sinner from a sinner, he could not suffice to liberate himself. Reason could indeed enable Adam’s sons not to sin unto death; but it could not heal the death which they had already contracted in part. It gave them a safeguard against what was future, not a remedy for what was past. The Law was supplied—not to heal the wound, but to prepare those who kept the Law for grace. Nor does “the Law bring our imperfect state to perfection” (Heb. 7:19); nor does it restore our expelled one to Paradise; nor return our dead one to life [Col. 0948A].

When Gehazi went before Elisha to raise the son of the Shunammite (4 Kings 4), he carried the staff, entered the house, and laid the staff upon the child; but the child had neither voice nor consciousness. Rightly, therefore, did the child’s mother hold Elisha’s feet; rightly did she not depart from Elisha; rightly did she hope in Elisha, saying: “As the Lord lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you” (1 Kings 1:26). Elisha heard and granted the petitioner’s plea: he went down and entered, stretched his whole body over the dead child, and raised the dead one.

Attend to the figure in the story, you who do not know; let the negligent be reproved. Our first parent, abandoned by God’s grace: hence came the failure of the soul, hence the death of the soul. Flesh dies when it is deprived of the soul; the soul dies when it is separated from God [Col. 0948B]. This death was threatened to humankind before sin, inflicted because of sin, and removed by him who had no sin. For you have read that it was said to man: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2:17).

Therefore, for the human race dead by such a death, a pious mother pleaded—a holy mother, the mother of whom the Apostle says: “But that Jerusalem which is above is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. 4:26). She is a mother, certainly, not through the act of the flesh but through the demonstration of love; a mother because she precedes us in time and intercedes for us in prayer; a mother, I say, because she bears a mother’s affection toward us, since our progress is most welcome to her. He knew this who said: “There is joy in heaven before the angels of God over one sinner doing penance” (Luke 15:10). She requested our manumission; she requested our life—not with a movement of the lips but with the affection of charity [Col. 0948C]. Our mother was heard, and provision was made for our life.

For, that man might be trained to merit the riches of God’s glory and prepared to receive God’s healing grace, Gehazi went before the prophet with the staff, because Moses ran ahead with the legal covenant. The unbearable staff was the burden of the Law: that Law which teaches sin but does not justify; which punishes but does not crown; which possesses more severity than mercy. Have you killed? You are commanded to be killed. Have you cut off? You are commanded to be cut off. Do you gather wood on the Sabbath? You are commanded to be stoned. Our sick man was laid beneath this staff; our dead man was weighed down. Our death was not made void, nor our wound healed [Col. 0948D].

For the dead to be raised, Elisha himself had to come; because it was necessary for the God-man to prepare for man the antidote of life. He spread himself upon the bed over the dead man; this man was stretched upon the gibbet for the dead man. The spirit of life was restored by Elisha’s breathing, because grace was restored to humankind by the dying of the God-man. The revived child returned to his mother’s bosom; justified man ascended to fellowship in the heavenly city.

Let the pure person, therefore, recall and revere what is commemorated today: what the God-man did for humankind. For today our Elisha entered the house in which the staff had been laid upon the dead man [Col. 0949A], because the salvation of our God was sent today into the city of Jerusalem, in which the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel were weighed down by the burden of the Law; he ascended humbly.

Let man, I say, consider with what humility the true prophet entered upon the office of our redemption; with what patience he endured; with what wondrous charity he drew us to himself. If you do not know his humility: the Lord of the universe clothed himself in the form of a servant, was born from a poor virgin, and was placed in a manger. Although free from the Law, he was circumcised according to the Law and lived under the Law without complaint. Moreover, he ate with sinners and tax collectors; as he approached the place of suffering, he rode upon an ass; he washed the feet of the disciples whom he had chosen from among the common people. From his birth to the end of his life he strove to ensure that, just as there was a special and unparalleled integrity in his mother [Col. 0949B], so there might also be a singular and unique humility in the Son.

If patience is in question: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter” (Isa. 53:7); he was delivered over to the spectacle of the cross, wounded for our iniquities, and reckoned among the wicked. Yet, lest you attribute these indignities to inability to resist rather than patience, “more than twelve legions of angels” (Matt. 26:53) were available to him, by whose aid he could have escaped even the hands of sacrilegious attendants. But he endured the aforesaid wrongs patiently because, as Pope Leo testifies, the one who had come to die for the salvation of all would save no one if he remained unharmed.

And what shall I say of charity, when this alone sufficiently testifies to it: while the Jew crucified him, he prayed that God might forgive the Jew? This charity—this wondrous charity! While nails were applied by enemies to his hands, a lance to his side, and gall to his mouth, his hands, side, and mouth acted for his enemies [Col. 0949C]. By his blood was washed away the offence which the crucifier had previously contracted; by his prayer, that which the crucifier was then committing.

There were displayed no powerful weapons, no victorious weapons, no weapons by which one fights “against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world’s darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavens” (Eph. 6:12). Girded with these weapons, your advocate entered the field today to fight. On Friday he fought bravely; on the first day of the Sabbath he triumphed. Under these weapons action was taken for your cause, battle was waged for your liberty, triumph achieved for your glory [Col. 0949D].

What then will you render to this advocate of yours for so great a matter concerning you? The price he expended for you is indeed great; yet what he asks of you is attainable and lies to hand. For he asks that you not take away his right; he asks that you not assign his servant to an alien master. Your soul is his right; your body is his servant. He made your soul his right when he laid down his soul for it; he made your body his servant when he gave his body over to death for it. He purchased your whole self with his whole self.

Consider, then, what he demands from your spirit and what from your body, both his servants. “Love him with your whole heart” (Deut. 6:5): this fulfils what he demands from your spirit. Give your entire self to his members, and you fulfil what he demands from your bodily members [Col. 0950A]. His eyes grew dim in death, so that your wandering eyes, your eyes that turn aside to behold vanity, might turn away. His ears were opened to insults and blasphemies, so that your ears might not be closed to the cry of the poor. His mouth was given gall and vinegar to drink, so that your lying mouth might speak truth and judgment. His hands were stretched out upon the cross, so that your contracted hands might be stretched out to the needy. His feet were nailed to the cross, so that your crooked feet might be directed into straight paths. His body bore the straits of death, so that your decayed body might become a member of his body.

Behold what pleases the Lord God in you, for which he bought you, and what he asks of you. Your Lord has placed it in your own choice whether you deserve punishment or reward from him [Col. 0950B]. He does not know how to spare if you are a wicked servant; he does not know how to reward sparingly if you are a good servant. If he finds you a wicked servant, you will encounter his indignation with evil spirits; if faithful, you will enter with angels and the elect into his heavenly city, Jerusalem.

Moreover, that blessed entrance is signified by the Hebrew children; by them is signified the resurrection of blessed sleepers. For when the Lord entered the holy city of the Hebrews, the children, proclaiming the resurrection of life, cried with palm branches: “Hosanna in the highest” (Matt. 21:9). What else, dearest brothers, what else is sung in the present responsory than the nature, the scope, and the everlasting blessedness of the members in the future resurrection? What do the children coming out from their houses announce, except that the faithful will come forth from their graves? What is declared by their meeting him, except what the Apostle says: “We who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up with Christ into the air, and thus we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:16) [Col. 0950C]?

We shall indeed be with the Lord—but only if the Lord finds us children, not in spirit but in malice; if he sees palms in our hands and flowers. Palm branches are signs of victory; in flowers is displayed the delightfulness of virtues. The patriarch Jacob perceived this fragrance from afar when he said: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27:27). Thus the children are remembered as having met the coming Saviour with branches of palms, because the faithful, emerging from the graves of vices, are foretold to appear when Christ comes for judgment [Col. 0950D]. But because it is necessary that they so lack what the Judge condemns that he may find what he crowns, these same children carry flowers in their hands: the faithful are described as pleasing only in the beauty of virtues. Hence it was also said: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27).

You therefore, dearest brothers, considering the humility of our Saviour, imitating his patience, and embracing his charity, rise steadfastly against the power of vices. Strive to meet him at judgment with the fragrance of virtues, so that you may be able to praise him and reign with him, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

[SERMONS.]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING SERMONS

(*Anecdota drawn for the first time from the manuscripts of the Ambrosian Library by Ludovico Antonio Muratori, librarian to the most serene Rinaldo I, Duke of Modena, etc. Volume III, p. 214. Padua: Seminary Press, 1713, quarto.*)

[Col. 0951]

There follow in an Ambrosian manuscript, written in characters appropriate to Hildebert’s age, two sermons. One of these was delivered at the Council of Chartres and afterwards set forth by its author; I do not think it should be disregarded. I cannot readily affirm when that Synod of Chartres mentioned here was held. Yet we may conjecture that it took place in the year of Christ 1124, since the Chronicle of Maillezais, according to Labbe’s testimony, *Collection of Councils*, vol. X, p. 906, records: “In the year 1124 there was a council at Chartres.”

Moreover, there will not be wanting persons who, thoughtfully and with anxious consideration, observe that in this same sermon only three sacraments are enumerated: first marriage, second baptism, and third the sacred libation of the Lord’s table. Since the other sacraments of the Church are there passed over in silence, suspicion will at once arise that the sermon’s author may furnish weapons to innovators of our own times and approve only these three sacraments.

But it must be observed that the ancient ecclesiastical writers were not so scrupulous that, whenever they treated of sacraments, they always mentioned seven. The Catholic Church has indeed always possessed and recognized neither more nor fewer than seven. The Fathers treated of them severally, as is evident from the expositors of dogmatic theology; but you will perhaps rarely, or never, find among them one who formally undertook a discussion of all—that is, the seven—sacraments of the Church. Above all, we owe to Peter Lombard, the so-called Master of the Sentences, in addition to other theological arguments assembled into one body, a complete treatise on the seven sacraments, arranged according to the method later maintained by the theologians of the schools.

And in fact the author of this sermon speaks of the three sacraments in such a manner as not to exclude the rest; indeed, he sufficiently indicates that other sacraments are held in the Church when he writes: “There are three sacraments in the city of our God which both preceded the rest in time and are known to hold primacy in the restoration of the children of God.” From these words we understand that he regarded only these three as earlier than the other sacraments in their origin and institution. Finally, since this writer promises at the outset to speak about marriage, baptism, and the Eucharist, but subsequently pursues the subject of marriage alone, we must conclude that the sermon itself has reached us incomplete and mutilated at the end.

## CXLII. 880 * SERMON FOR THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

[Col. 0951A]

I perceive, dearest brothers—I perceive with that wise man who says:

> Sweeter is the fruit which longer expectation brings forth.

Therefore the fruit of the divine converse with humankind ought to be so much the more pleasing to you as its expectation was longer, its manifestation more wonderful, its experience sweeter, and its benefit greater. Messengers were sent beforehand, to announce the most holy converse, invite human beings to it, promise rewards to those who came and eternal punishment to those unwilling. These were the prophets, who are known not only to have foretaught that converse in words but also to have prefigured it in deeds [Col. 0951B].

Thus Moses says: “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among you; listen to him as to myself” (Deut. 18:15). And Isaiah: “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14). There were also persons whose actions Scripture records as having been prophecy of the aforesaid converse. Thus Jeremiah, when he is stripped, prophesies; David, when he bears himself in his own hands; Daniel, when he is cast into the lions’ den; Hosea, when he takes a prostitute as wife; Jonah, when he is held three days and nights in the belly of the whale.

The Apostle, briefly encompassing both the fact that these prophecies had preceded and that the converse was fulfilled in Christ, writes to the Hebrews: “God, who in many portions and in many ways formerly spoke to the fathers and prophets, has in these last days spoken to us in the Son” (Heb. 1:1) [Col. 0951C]. “He spoke to us in the Son,” that is, he spoke to us in Christ. How did God, invisible and unknown to us, speak to us? So that he might be seen and known by us [Col. 0952A].

> “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

The Word of God, the Son, was seen by us in flesh; in flesh he spoke with us about us. He spoke about reconciling man with angels, placing man among angels, and raising man above angels. He spoke, I say, about changing our dissimilarity into his likeness, our death into his life, our shame into his glory. Concerning all these things, before all times, the Creator of all had with himself a plan: converse with humankind in time.

But so that that secret counsel might be disclosed, two angels were sent into the world: one to reveal the plan, the other to accomplish what had been revealed. One was sent to announce to the Virgin Mary that our mediator would be born from the Virgin Mary; the other to declare in the flesh assumed from the virgin that he was our advocate [Col. 0952B]. Now this mediator and advocate of ours was born for us today. Therefore Isaiah promised us thus: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6). “A child is born,” he says; yet this child is God and man. God and man carried out the business of the aforesaid plan.

Let no one lack faith when virginity in the mother is proclaimed; let no one lack hope when divinity in the offspring is preached. Each event occurred contrary to nature; each was the work of grace, though an office of nature; each was new, though promised by oracles; each was a benefit, though different in operation. For the mother’s chastity is the glory of her person, while the Son’s divinity is the advancement of nature [Col. 0952C]. Chastity preserved in the mother bears witness that her Son is God-man. Divinity was united to man so as to unite to God the human beings who believe in God.

Let the unhappy Jew blush; let the still more unhappy Helvidius be confounded. The Jew detracts from Christ’s divinity; both detract from the perpetual virginity of Christ’s mother. The Jew rages and burns when it is said: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). He likewise turns away his ear and perverts Isaiah when he observes what is written: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14); and in Ezekiel: “This gate which you see shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, but it shall remain shut for ever” (Ezek. 44:2) [Col. 0953A]. It is a gate because Christ entered the world through it, yet through one closed for ever: rightly closed for ever, because closed before childbirth, closed in childbirth, and closed after childbirth.

Let the perfidy of the Jew, who falsely claims that Christ was conceived by Joseph, perish. Let Helvidius’s filthiness, babbling that children were born to the Virgin after Christ’s birth, perish. But still, O Jew, our speech is addressed to you; for the face of Moses is still veiled among you. The splendour of your Law has not yet shone upon you, nor have the mysteries of the prophets. Denser darkness covers you than covered the Egyptians because of you. Riches abound to you, yet you are tortured by want. A most nourishing feast is laid before you, yet you fail from hunger. You carry grain in the ear, yet have neither tasted nor perceived how sweet it is.

David’s youths, passing through the fields, rubbed the ears of grain and ate. You too, rub the ear of the Law; break the barley of the Law, and you will find the fine wheat of the Law. For beneath the suffocating chaff you will find nourishing marrow; beneath the killing letter, the life-giving Spirit. Open the cisterns of the prophets; clear out the wells, and you will encounter David’s fountain, a fountain of water springing up into eternal life [Col. 0953C].

But you, wretch, stop the channels of the clearest water; with the Philistines you fill in the wells that Isaac’s servants dug. For you set stubborn resistance against the Law’s brightness when it is revealed to you; you insult God’s grace when it is reported that the Virgin Mary conceived as a virgin and gave birth as a virgin. In the patriarchs and their children you hear, believe, revere, and extol the works of grace; but in the Creator of the prophets why do you embrace nature in such a manner as to persecute grace?

Sarah bore a son to Abraham when barrenness and old age had taken from them hope of offspring. You cannot deny, Jew, that in Isaac Sarah owed more to divine permission than to marriage, more to grace than to nature. Before Moses, the bush seen burning suffered no loss from the fire [Col. 0953D]. You cannot deny, Jew, that this was more the work of a sign than of a bush, of grace than of nature. Israel thirsted in the wilderness and endured the distress of thirst impatiently. Moses came to the rock, struck it twice, and waters flowed out in greatest abundance, so that the people and their beasts drank. You cannot deny, Jew, that this was more the work of a sign than of a stone, of grace than of nature.

I shall speak of an evident matter: I believe few people do not know the crystal stone. This stone is of a most brilliant and white colour; when water is poured over it and it is then exposed to the hot sun, it is famously said to emit little sparks. Yet the sparks leave neither any fissure in the stone nor any traces of their own departure. In the crystal the same integrity and the same brightness remain. What comes forth from it benefits human use, yet does not mar the brightness of the stone. But if either sun or water is lacking, it is not found fit for emitting fire [Col. 0954A]. When both come together, what is produced in the crystal from both may fittingly image both the Virgin’s conception and her childbirth.

For to what may the most sacred Virgin be more fittingly compared than crystal, in whom, as though to crown the fullness of all other virtues, the brilliance of perpetual virginity shone forth? Being prepared for divine mysteries, she is, as it were, drenched with water to receive more abundant grace: by it she would wonderfully receive the Son of God as God, and yet more wonderfully bring forth that same one as God-man. Indeed, it appears less alien to nature that a Virgin should be filled by heavenly power than that true human substance should issue from a Virgin [Col. 0954B].

Perhaps, however, O Jew, you wonder by what water I have described the Virgin as drenched. Understand the Holy Spirit by the name “water.” Speaking through Joel of such water, the Lord says: “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy” (Joel 2:28). And through Ezekiel: “I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” (Ezek. 36:25). As the Virgin is drenched with this water, she is invisibly prepared to receive the sun of righteousness. She is prepared, I say, because the Holy Spirit protected her by overshadowing her from every heat of carnal desire. Hence there accrued to our Virgin an increase and fullness of grace, so that the Son of God entering her might find her both cleansed from inherited guilt and free from guilt of her own [Col. 0954C]. For wisdom could not enter a malicious soul or dwell in a body subject to sins.

## CXLIII. 880 ** SERMON AT THE COUNCIL OF CHARTRES

The cause that intervened prevented the completion in writing of the sermon delivered at the Council of Chartres. I remember that some of those presiding requested that I should not think it burdensome to write it out for the instruction of the less learned. You too, dearest brothers, in making the same request, added many inducements by which you thought the drowsiness of my pen might be awakened. Indeed, a bishop ought so to live that even when buried he lives for all either by example or by word [Col. 0954D]; a priest is inferior to the people before God if neither his teaching nor his life is a blessing.

Moreover, brothers, you added this, knowing that I had pledged myself to honour you, love you in Christ, and comply in all these matters which it is fitting for a friend to ask or which I can do when asked. Therefore I promised to be present to your wishes—though I wish I had not made the promise. For I shall be accused of falsehood unless I perform what I pledged; if I indulge my pen, I shall be found a ridiculous writer. Thus there is fault in silence and embarrassment on the page. Yet I preferred that my talent should be charged with deficiency rather than that I, a priest, should be charged with falsehood. Hence I set my hand to the work, asking that it may be kept far from human eyes if you find that it fears human tongues. If perhaps you discover that I have added or removed something, or have not maintained the same order, know that I resolved to write, not to preach, and to correct in writing whatever fault there was in the sermon [Col. 0955A].

Unless I am mistaken, the present text began: “The wise man’s eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness” (Eccl. 2:14). On the surface of this letter nothing is found that instructs faith or benefits morals; for, whether a man is wise or foolish, his eyes are nowhere but in his head. A deeper meaning must therefore be sought. Fruit lies hidden in leaves; the mouth of the well is closed. Remove the leaves and you will find fruit more precious than all works, and all things that are desired cannot be compared with it. Dig out the well and you will encounter a fountain of water springing up into eternal life [Col. 0955B].

The Apostle says: “The head of the woman is the man, and the head of the man is Christ” (1 Cor. 11:3). This head is the head from which oil descends upon the beard, Aaron’s beard. From this head the whole body of the Church subsists, feels, is enlivened, and is governed. Christ, therefore, is the head of the Church. Scripture declares that the wise man’s eyes are in such a head. But this is not the wisdom of the wise according to this world, which is foolishness with God; for men “are wise to do evil, but they do not know how to do good.” There is another wisdom, truly and far different: that by which we store up treasures in heaven; by which, in having compassion on the poor, we lend to God; by which we make friends for ourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when we fail, they may receive us into eternal dwellings.

Let the wise person fix attentive eyes upon this wisdom in Christ, his head. Let him read in Christ that salvation comes from no one apart from him. He follows Christ for Christ’s sake if he measures out the steep and narrow way, saying with the Psalmist: “For the words of your lips I have kept hard ways” (Ps. 16:4) [Col. 0955C]. This likewise rests upon you, whose profession is the priesthood—upon you, I say, before others—for Christ himself is also your head.
