To turn the lights of the mind away from Christ is to walk in darkness. Therefore, lest darkness overtake you, let the lights of your heart be in him. For Christ is light from light.

Christ is the book of life, but a book written without and within. If your lights are directed toward this light, your ways and pursuits will become good. If your eyes cling to this book, outwardly you will see in him: with Mary, Christ adored in the gifts of the Magi; with Anna, received in the Temple; with the disciples, betrayed to the Jews by a disciple; with John, pierced by nails and lance. Outwardly, I say, you will behold him committed to the tomb by Joseph’s service, guarded in the tomb by soldiers, and raised from the tomb with angels as witnesses [Col. 0955D]. Inwardly you will adore the only-begotten Son of God, daily hearing from the Father: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). Inwardly you will contemplate the wisdom by which the deeps burst forth and the clouds thicken with dew. Inwardly you will embrace your restoration [Col. 0956A].

> “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

Moreover, through all these things you will be taught that a priest owes glory to God, discipline to himself, hatred to vices, alliance with good morals, instruction to the people, and reverence to the sacraments—contempt for which sacraments is judgment.* Therefore, having been asked to write concerning these matters because I obey priests, I ask for the help of priests’ prayers, that perhaps the door of mercy may be opened to those who knock and that by their intercessions I may be able to do what I do not trust myself able to do either by talent or merits.

There are therefore three sacraments in the city of our God which both preceded the others in time and are known to hold primacy in the restoration of God’s children. The first is marriage, the second baptism [Col. 0956B], and the third the sacred libation of the Lord’s table. In the youth of the world, God impressed their form and assigned fixed boundaries which authority does not permit to be exceeded, because it is not expedient to exceed them. The marriage of the first parents set forth the pattern of Christian marriage. The washing of the Flood prefigured baptism. In Melchizedek’s sacrifice was prefigured the sacrament of Christ’s altar. Since, with the Lord’s help, we intend to say something further about these, it is necessary that we review each in turn.

In the marriage of the first parents, the common consent of male and female bound them together. Both were of an age suitable for raising offspring. One wife was under one husband. By the more private liberty of the marriage bed, the man knew his wife. Marriage was undivided until death. Behold the pattern; behold the first limits of marriage [Col. 0956C].

Yet necessity, offspring, and hardness taught us to exceed these limits and to use the flesh more carnally. For it is agreed that necessity caused brother to unite with sister for the work of marriage, and the names of kinship to be joined to the names of marriage. Then, through desire for offspring, one man entered into several wives. Divorce, however, arose from the hardness of husbands.

Let us hear what the Lord said concerning Jacob: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1:3). Yet he was chosen before birth, loved before merit; a patriarch descended from patriarchs; from Jacob, Israel; from a keeper of sheep, a beholder of the heavenly host. He moved between Leah and Rachel, doubtless paying the due of marriage. Elkanah, though Peninnah bore him children, received Samuel from Hannah. There were other holy men who entered not only into free women but also at the same time into maidservants, seeking the blessing of children through flesh beyond flesh [Col. 0956D].

If the unions of such men with such women incurred divine indignation, Augustine would not commend Abraham’s marriage in these words: “Just as the merit of patience is not unequal in Peter, who suffered, and in John, who did not suffer, so the merit of continence is not unequal in John, who experienced no marriage, and in Abraham, who begot two sons. For John’s celibacy and Abraham’s marriage served the Lord according to their time.”

Moreover, the Saviour showed, when speaking to the Jews, that the hardness of men dictated the bill of divorce: “Moses permitted you to put away your wives because of the hardness of your hearts. But from the beginning it was not so” (Matt. 19:8) [Col. 0957A]. Thus, within the bounds of the first marriage, consanguinity was admitted because of necessity; multiple wives because of desire for offspring; and separation because of men’s hardness.

“But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son into the world, made of a woman, made under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law, that we might receive the adoption of sons” (Gal. 4:4). His coming restored the sacrament of marriage to its earlier form. From that time consanguinity together with affinity was excluded from marriage, the number of wives was removed, and divorce was forbidden by the Law of the Gospel. For because “a new man came into the world, he gave new commands to the world: ‘I give you a new commandment,’ he says, ‘that you love one another as I have loved you’” (John 13:35). And again: “By this all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (ibid., 35).

Holy and without parallel were both the life and teaching of this new man. Since he came to human beings in charity, he enlarged charity among human beings by both teaching and life. Under him we learn that even enemies must be loved, so that charity may be enlarged. We learn that good must be returned for evil, so that charity may be enlarged. We learn that marriages must be contracted only among strangers, so that charity may be enlarged [Col. 0957B]. This is also a great and renowned good of marriage: those born enemies become friends through it. Thus husband and wife are united in flesh, while their entire kinship is united in spirit.

Under grace, moreover, multiple wives were excluded from Christian marriage because, after the Saviour’s birth, spiritual children rather than carnal ones ought to be sought. Jacob begetting those who would beget Christ is not so much to be imitated as John refusing to beget for Christ’s sake. Thus the Apostle says: “I wish all men to be as I also am” (1 Cor. 7:7). And so that man should not become “like horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Tob. 6:17), the licence of competing spouses was abolished. So that he might not burn with the fire of fornication, one woman was granted to one man. The Apostle also speaks of this in these words: “Let each man have his own wife because of fornication, and let each woman have her own husband. But I say this by way of concession, not command” (1 Cor. 7:6) [Col. 0957C].

Furthermore, it was God who, in order to propagate the human race, joined one flesh to one woman; but Lamech was a man and a sinner, who first divided one flesh between two wives. In this, already then, one good of marriage was annulled: namely faithfulness, by which, just as a wife is forbidden to enter another union while her husband lives, so also a husband is forbidden to enter another while his wife survives. Therefore, lest Christian marriage should be deprived even of such a good, plurality yielded to unity. Divorce also yielded to stability, in which Augustine shows that there is a sacrament of marriage:

> “Every good of marriage was fulfilled in Christ’s parents: offspring, fidelity, sacrament. We plainly recognize the Lord himself as the offspring; fidelity, because there was no adultery; sacrament, because there was no divorce.”

Now “no divorce” means nothing other than that marriage remains stable and firm until the death of one spouse [Col. 0958A]. Certainly, one might reasonably say that Augustine’s assigning the sacrament, while omitting all the other things required in lawful marriage, especially to its stability, was said rather by way of prerogative than exclusively. For authoritative teaching has handed down that a sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing. That marriages are to be celebrated at marriageable age is a sign of a sacred thing. That they are celebrated by the consent of both man and woman is a sign of a sacred thing. That one man is joined to one woman only is a sign of a sacred thing. That mutual marital intercourse is permitted and honourable is a sign of a sacred thing. That those joined in the Lord cannot be separated is a sign of a sacred thing [Col. 0958B]. Therefore, when the Apostle spoke of marriage, he said: “This is a great sacrament; but I speak in Christ and in the Church” (Eph. 5:32). Clearly, Christ is the bridegroom of the Church, and the Church is Christ’s bride.

When the Fountain sat upon the fountain, it was the time of the wedding; and that hour was about the sixth hour. The Evangelist shows this when he says: “Jesus, wearied from the journey, sat upon the fountain; it was about the sixth hour” (John 4:6). If authority is to be trusted, the sixth hour is the sixth age. In that age the wedding had to be celebrated; for that age is the fullness of time, in which the Church became marriageable and more ready for her husband. Before that time she was little, and did not yet have breasts. When this time had arrived, she was found to have breasts [Col. 0958C] and to be more ready for her husband. Augustine shows this in these words in his book *On the Time of the Christian Religion*:

> “We say that Christ then wished to appear to men and his teaching to be preached among them, when and where he knew that there were people who would believe in him. For he foresaw that, in those times and places where the Gospel was not preached, all people would have been such at his preaching as—not indeed all, but many—were in his bodily presence: people who would not believe in him even when he raised the dead. Such also we now see in many people: although the proclamations of the prophets concerning him are fulfilled with so great a manifestation, they still refuse to believe, and prefer to resist by human cleverness rather than believe such clear and evident, such lofty and so sublimely proclaimed, divine authority, so long as the human understanding is little and weak in believing divine truth. What wonder, then, if Christ knew that the earth was filled with such unbelievers in earlier ages, that he rightly did not wish to appear to them or be preached to them, since he foresaw that they would believe neither his words nor his miracles?”

These points having thus been set forth, provision was made for the weakness of mortals, both by a fitting remedy and at an opportune time. Jesus sat beside the well at the sixth hour because he knew that at the sixth hour the Samaritan woman would come to the fountain. Thus she too came to the fountain and found the living Fountain. The Fountain was thirsty and freely asked that drink be given to him. The Samaritan woman complied: she gave from the fountain to the Fountain, herself about to receive the Fountain of water springing up into eternal [Col. 0959A] life. Therefore Christ asks for a drink at the sixth hour; at the sixth hour the thirsty Samaritan woman ministered to him.

This was the opportune time: the time in which the master of the household would make a wedding for his Son; in which Christ would kiss the Church with the kiss of his mouth; in which the Bridegroom, himself a Virgin, would delight to dwell and rest between the breasts of his Virgin Bride. It was, I say, the opportune time in which he would beget children of adoption; in which he would nourish little ones with milk, but strengthen the robust with the bread of doctrine. Therefore that fullness of time, divinely ordained and long awaited for the celebration of spiritual nuptials, is mystically signified by the concurrence of years required in contracting a carnal marriage. Hence it too is a sacrament, because it is a sign of a sacred reality.

## CXLIV. ON MUTUAL CONSENT

[Col. 0959B]

**880.** It is worth not passing over in silence that willing and mutual consent established the union between Christ himself and the Church. Christ chose the Church; having chosen her, he loved her unto the end, and will remain with her whom he loved even after the end. Speaking to his disciples about this election, he said: “I chose you out of the world, that you may go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain” (John 15:19). “The Lord,” it says, “has chosen Zion; he has chosen her as his dwelling-place” (Psalm 131:13). Revealing his love to these same disciples, he says: “I will no longer call you servants, because the servant does not know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, because I have made known to you all things whatsoever I heard from my Father” (John 15:15). The Evangelist, briefly describing the greatness of this love, says: “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them unto the end” (John 13:1). That is, he loved them so greatly that he ended his temporal life for their sake. O love truly blessed and worthy of imitation! It began before the cross, led to the cross, and will remain after the cross. For when the Lord sends his disciples out to preach, as lambs among wolves, he says: “Do not fear; behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

He therefore who chose the Church in this way, who loved her after choosing her unto death, undoubtedly gave consent to her marriage. That this Bride consented to her choosing and loving Bridegroom is made clear by wise testimonies. “Jesus, walking by the Sea of Galilee, saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting nets into the sea; for they were fishermen” (Matthew 4:18). Therefore “he said to them: ‘Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men.’ They immediately left their nets and boat and followed him. And going on from there he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he said to them: ‘Come after me.’ They immediately left their nets and father and followed him” (ibid., 19). He also saw Matthew sitting at the tax office, and said to him: “Follow me”; and he immediately followed him (Matthew 9:9). Others followed as well, whom Scripture records as having said: “Lord, behold, we have left everything and followed you. What then will there be for us?” (Matthew 19:27).

These are called, and with a scant outfit abandon the whole world for Christ. They come to the wedding, about to pass from wedding-guests into the Bride. They lay down nets, to catch men more fruitfully than fish. They reject the enticements of carnal marriage, to beget children more happily for heaven than for the grave. They renounce legal business, preferring true riches to deceptive ones. It cannot be doubted that these firstfruits of the Church gave their consent to him who called them, since they immediately followed the caller.

Every day the devil’s concubine is also called: when her menstrual uncleanness is washed in Christ’s fountain, she too becomes Christ’s Bride. Every day the daughter of the Canaanite woman is freed from the demon by the mother’s faith. Every day the queen of the south comes from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom. Every day our Hosea takes a prostitute as his wife. Let us hear, moreover, with what love such a Bride burns.

In the Acts of the Apostles the disciples are flogged; after they have been beaten, they are ordered not to speak in Jesus’ name. Yet they give thanks and rejoice “because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41). They do the same outside the synagogue as they confess Christ. They are placed in public custody, saying that “there is salvation in no one else” (Acts 4:12). Yet they give thanks and rejoice “because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus.” Stephen is led outside the city to be stoned by the Jews. Herod sends men to afflict certain members of the Church, and hands [Col. 0960C] Peter over to prison, intending after Passover to bring him before the people. Yet they give thanks and rejoice “because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus.”

Paul is beaten with rods three times for Christ, stoned once for Christ, shipwrecked three times for Christ. Yet amid very many labours, more imprisonments, and excessive beatings, he cries: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” (Romans 8:35). Others endure mockeries and beatings; they accept no deliverance; they are excluded from common benefits; they wander about in sheepskins and goatskins, a spectacle to men, and become as though the refuse of the world. Yet amid flames and the teeth of raging beasts, they say with Paul: “Who shall separate us [Col. 0960D] from the love of Christ?” Finally, for Christ the Church is put to death all day long; for Christ she is reckoned as a sheep for slaughter, having experienced what the Lord says to his own: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will suppose that he is offering service to God” (John 16:2). Yet amid a thousand deaths she exults with Paul and cries with Paul: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” She burned with this love when she said through Solomon: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I am sick with love” (Song of Songs 2:5).

Behold the sacred consent full of grace. By this consent the marriage between Christ and the Church was contracted: a marriage in which virginity gives birth and is not destroyed. Children are begotten, to whom the grave does not promise hereditary mortality. [Col. 0961A] Therefore that mystical consent is signified by the consent required in contracting carnal marriages. Hence it too is a sacrament, because it is a sign of a sacred reality.

Nor is what we have said—that one is to be joined to one—devoid of mystery. For Christ’s Bride is one, because the Church of Jesus Christ is one. From differing members comes one body under Christ the head. From two flocks comes one fold under Christ the shepherd. Therefore the Lord himself speaks through Solomon: “My dove, my perfect one, is one; she is the one of her mother, the one of her who bore her” (Song of Songs 6:8).

Cyprian, against Novatian, says on the same matter:

> “The Church is one, though through the increase of her fruitfulness she expands more broadly into a multitude, just as there are many rays of the sun, but one light; and many branches of a tree, but one strength founded in its clinging root.”

And again:

> “This sacrament of unity, this bond of inseparably adhering concord, is shown when in the Gospel the Lord’s tunic is not divided at all or torn; but, as they cast lots for Christ’s garment to determine who should put on Christ, the garment is received whole.”

Therefore God speaks to Moses, saying: “It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not carry the flesh outside the house” (Exodus 12:46). The flesh of Christ and the Lord’s seed cannot be cast outside; nor is there any house for believers except the one Church. The Synagogue departed from this unity, and, forestalled by Christ’s betrothal, degenerated into the adulteress of Antichrist. Already then she opposed her lawful Bridegroom, when she prostituted herself on the high places with stone and wood. [Col. 0961C] Her husband sent those who said to her: “Return”; and she did not return (Jeremiah 3:7). At last he himself came—he came, I say, he came to her—and found her in her menstruation. He offered her a ring for her hand, golden ornaments, and silver-studded ornaments for her ears. Finally, promising her his favour if she returned, he said: “Return”; and she did not return.

Alas! She was then left in her filth because she abandoned David’s fountain, open for washing away her disgrace. She was then left upon the bed of prostitution because she did not know the time of her visitation. She then deserved the writ of divorce because she rejected the true Bridegroom, reviling the man born blind and saying: “You are one of his disciples; but we are disciples of Moses” [Col. 0961D] (John 9:28). She then received it because she rejected his sweet yoke and light burden, when she cried: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15).

Yet there will be—there will be, I say—a time when she returns from rejection to grace, when from repudiated she is changed into beloved, when from prostitute she advances into a virgin. Then she too will become Christ’s Bride: not indeed another, but the same one and the one dove of Jesus Christ. But as Christ’s Bride is one Bride, so the Church’s Bridegroom is one Bridegroom. She has one Bridegroom; one she loves, one she knows, for one she bears children, one she nurses. That one is the Holy of holies. He is both God and man.

Many chosen ones preceded this Holy of holies, and many also followed him. As sacred history relates, when Jacob was born from Rebecca, a hand and arm came out first. Then, after the head had emerged, the remaining members finally came into the light. The hand that came forth first held the sole of Esau’s foot, who had gone ahead of him; thus it preceded the head that was to be born, yet it was itself a member of that head-to-be-born. The remaining parts followed the head once born, yet those parts were members of the head now born. As both the former and the latter members are one body, so the head of this body is one head.

Thus the prophets preceded Christ; thus Elijah and Elisha; thus most of the champions of the Old Testament. To prevent the stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart, from going after foreign gods or following the broad and spacious way which leads to death, they are known to have bound and restrained its feet with the Pentateuch of Moses, as though with the bonds of five fingers. But [Col. 0962B] when Truth sprang from the earth, the apostles followed Truth; the martyrs followed; and those followed whom Matthew records as having come into the householder’s vineyard at the eleventh hour. Those indeed preceded Christ in time under the Law, but through faith they became members of the Christ who had been born. As both those and these members are one body and the Church is one, so Christ is the one head of the one body and the one Bridegroom of the one Church.

Consider Moses: he was the Bridegroom’s herald, not the Bridegroom. Consider him who was more than a prophet: he confesses himself unworthy to untie the strap of the Bridegroom’s sandal. Look upon Paul: the Bridegroom said that he must suffer many things for the Bridegroom’s name. Look at Peter and Andrew; run through the disciples. They were indeed members of the Bridegroom’s household, but none was the Bridegroom. You see, then, that the one Bride of Christ is the Church, and that the one Bridegroom of the Church is Christ. The sign of both unities is the unity of the persons required individually in contracting a carnal marriage. Hence this too is a sacrament, because it is a sign of a sacred reality.

Although nuptial intercourse, permitted in view of offspring, is necessary for raising up seed, it also contains a great sacrament. For Truth declares that there are two generations in these words: “That which is born of flesh is flesh” (John 3:6); therefore that which is born of Spirit is spirit. Now carnal generation is carried out wholly carnally, whereas spiritual generation is wholly accomplished spiritually. You see water; you see [Col. 0962D] the catechumen; you see the minister. But you do not see what is done in the water, what is done in the catechumen, or what is done through the minister. You see a pure element, but by the sign of the cross and the power of words it acquires a hidden efficacy. A child bound to the devil descends into the font, but emerges free, belonging to himself and to Christ. The minister utters the words, but the Lamb baptizes—the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. This generation creates a new offspring from old material, not borrowing a substance but removing guilt. For it cleanses the person from the old contagion, incorporates that person into Christ’s body, and makes the earthly heavenly. In the first generation the first Adam is begotten; in this generation the second Adam is reborn. From the former the devil is begotten; through the latter he makes good the loss of angels. Hence that which begets in [Col. 0963A] flesh is a sacrament, because it is the sacred sign of that which begets in spirit.

We read that the Lord said concerning those who mutually agreed to marriage: “What God has joined together, let no man separate” (Matthew 14:6). Hence the marital bond cannot be dissolved except at the death of one spouse. On this matter the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: “A woman is bound for as long as her husband lives. But if her husband falls asleep, she is freed from the law of her husband. Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39). Therefore, while both survive, the law of marriage also survives, unshaken. So too the spiritual marriage of Christ and the Church is never dissolved, never broken, because neither Christ nor Christ’s Bride ever dies. [Col. 0963B] “For Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall have no further dominion over him” (Romans 6:9). And the Apostle says: “If our earthly house is dissolved, we have a house not made with hands, but eternal in heaven” (2 Corinthians 5:5).

Therefore both live in heaven; in heaven each rejoices with the other. The Bridegroom lives in heaven, perfected in soul and body together. The Bride lives in heaven, by no means happier because of her glorified spirit, but more secure because of her flesh yet to be glorified. The Bridegroom rejoices with the Bride, because God has wiped every tear from her eyes and has brought her into his bridal chamber. The Bride rejoices with the Bridegroom, because he sits at the right hand of Majesty on high, and his kingdom is a kingdom of all ages. Charity has taught and moved this mutual rejoicing—charity, that inextinguishable charity which does not know how to pass away with time.

[Col. 0964A] Isaiah says of this charity: “The Lord has said, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isaiah 31:9). You know, dearest brethren, that Zion is interpreted as “watchtower,” while Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.” Therefore the souls of the saints, while they bear about the body of this mortality, are said to be in Zion: that is, watching from afar, hoping and awaiting their reward. But these same souls will be in Jerusalem when, having received the twofold robe, they see God face to face, exchanging imperfection for fullness, hope for possession, image for truth.

The Apostle was in that Zion when he said: “Now we see through a glass, in an enigma” (1 Corinthians 13:12). He promised himself this Jerusalem when he added: “But then face to face” (ibid.). Again he says: “Now I know in part; but then I shall know even as I am known” (ibid.). Thus there is fire in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem, because the fervour of charity is small in this life and very great in the life to come. Here it is a little spark; there, a furnace. Here, a portion; there, fullness. “For that which is perfect will come, and that which is in part will be done away” (ibid.). But just as Christ never dies and the Church never dies, so this blessed charity between them is never extinguished and never will be extinguished; their most blessed spiritual marriage is never dissolved and never will be dissolved. Yet the permanence of the consecrated union is signified by the stability of carnal marriage: the stability allotted to a living husband and wife not by man or by the lawcourt, but by God and by heaven. Hence this stability too is a sacrament, [Col. 0964C] because it is a sign of a sacred reality.

## SHORTER WORKS OF THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT

[Col. 0963]

## NOTICE

It would be superfluous to repeat here what we noted in our general preface concerning the various shorter works of the venerable Hildebert. We wish only to inform you, kindly reader, that Hildebert speaks so frequently in his letters about his own shorter works that no doubt remains that he wrote far more than those writings which have hitherto been made public, or which, newly assembled through our efforts, are here presented to him.

Thus, in Letter 2 of Book III, to Clarembald, canon of the Church of Exeter, he expressly states that he wrote a *History of the Miracles* of that same church, and promises that he will revise it in another style from a second copy sent to him by that canon. In the present disturbances we have not been permitted to discover that *History* in England. Moreover, at the end of Letter 15 of the same Book III, he addresses Reginald, monk of Saint Augustine, as follows: “You should know that I honour and welcome the fact that, as you have observed, you have inserted into your work certain propositions, daughters of my small talent, or portions of our verses. For then I begin to please myself, when I see that my writings do not displease greater men.” This indicates that even then Hildebert’s nocturnal studies were held in no small esteem among learned people. In Letter 30 of the same Book III, to William, bishop of Winchester, he says to him: “For you asked that my shorter works be copied out for you and, once copied, sent.” On hearing this, I hesitated for a long time, fearing either to offend a friend or to provoke readers’ laughter. Thus the most humble author disparages his own works—works which more learned men valued so highly that they did not hesitate to adorn their writings with fragments of them.

Whether the legal *Exceptions* or *Extracts* which all editors of the *Library of the Fathers* have until now attributed to our Hildebert, and which we give here as Letter 53 of Book II, are the very same text that begins Ivo’s preface to his *Decree* in exactly the same words, let the more discerning reader judge. Meanwhile, from Letter 27 of Book II by the same Hildebert, we know that he began *Extracts from the Decrees*, which, as he says, he had intended to arrange in one volume and of which he had already completed a part. Episcopal duties did not permit him to finish them; but once those duties had been cast off, he promises in that same letter to bring them to completion as soon as possible.

The shorter works which we present here have been brought to light, with all the discernment and diligence we could command, from manuscript codices of the best standing, most of them nearly contemporary; we have taken care to identify these at the head of each work. Enjoy them, kindly reader; and if perhaps you find anything not distinguished with complete precision, then—since whatever it may be offers nothing except what is orthodox and consistent with good morals—may your kindness, I pray, excuse at least our efforts.

[Col. 0965]

## PROLOGUE TO THE LIFE OF SAINT RADEGUND, QUEEN OF THE FRANKS

[Note: [Col. 0965A] This *Life of Saint Radegund*, formerly sent to our Reverend Father Mabillon by the Reverend Father Dom Claude Stephanot, a most zealous student of antiquities, Mabillon himself had proposed to publish when a suitable opportunity arose. But, occupied with more serious studies, he inserted only the Prologue of the Venerable Hildebert into volume I of his *Analecta*, and kindly left the work itself to us for publication as we searched everywhere for Hildebert’s writings. The aforementioned Stephanot had recovered this *Life* of the holy Queen from two manuscripts of the best standing belonging to the royal collegiate church of Saint Radegund at Poitiers. In the older manuscript, on the first page, one sees a bishop depicted in sacred vestments, offering a book on bended knees to crowned Saint Radegund, dressed in black and in the habit of a nun, who is seated and places a crown upon his mitred head. Above it, in ancient lettering, is written this designation: “Bishop Hildebert.” Around the head of the blessed Queen is written: “Saint Radegund, Queen.” Two nuns likewise dressed in black stand beside her, with these inscriptions: “Saint Agnes”; “Saint Disciola.” Below, in the margin of the illustration, these two verses are read:

> Christ pardons the sins of the shepherd through the reward of so great a labour,  
> and the Queen crowns him.

Who the nuns standing beside Saint Radegund were, we learn from Gregory of Tours: concerning Saint Disciola, in *History of the Franks*, Book VI, no. 9, where her precious death is narrated; and concerning Saint Agnes, in Book IX, no. 42, where Saint Radegund, in the diploma there reported, asserts that Agnes had been blessed as abbess by Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris. Our Ruinart notes in his annotations on Gregory of Tours [Col. 0966B] that both are honoured as saints in the Church of Poitiers on 13 May, and that they are invoked as saints in the litanies of Poitiers published by Henri-Louis Chasteigner, bishop of Poitiers. We judged that this image, an outstanding monument of antiquity, should be presented to the reader at the head of the preceding page, faithfully drawn from the original and, so far as possible, engraved by our direction.]

[Note: [Col. 0965] + Added to this latest edition of the Life of Blessed Radegund: (1) a division into chapters with summaries; (2) notes from the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, vol. III, August.]

[Col. 0965A] **881–886. 1.** It belongs to the wise man to measure his strength and not undertake anything beyond it. Your affection, dearest Seimane, has driven me to this resolve: I preferred to be found a laughable writer rather than disobedient to you. At your exhortations I have ventured to write the *Life* of the most blessed Radegund, although not so much slowness of talent as the occupation of episcopal administration prevented me from devoting attention to study.

[Note: [Col. 0966B] Mabillon, in volume I of the *Veteres Analectae*, p. 296, calls this same man “Seimarus” instead of “Seimanus,” and in the index of that volume surnames him “of Poitiers.” We do not know whether Mabillon gave him this surname from his birthplace or from an office which he held in the city of Poitiers. At least, among the bishops of Poitiers we find no prelate of this name or period. But it is clear from this prologue that he was a man of great authority, since Bishop Hildebert so readily obeyed him and entrusted to him the correction or suppression of his work. BOLL.]

[Col. 0966A] Trusting, however, in the grace of him who makes the tongues of infants eloquent, I had recourse to the writings of Fortunatus and of the nun Baudonivia.

[Note: [Col. 0967B] From this it is confirmed that the Acts which we published under the names of Fortunatus and Baudonivia are authentic, since both works guided the venerable Hildebert. BOLL.]

Each of them pursued the aforesaid life, and made, as it seems to you, only meagre dishes from a precious store.

[Note: [Col. 0967B] Here Hildebert calls the works of Fortunatus and Baudonivia “meagre precious dishes” because they were composed in a dark and difficult style. Although Hildebert at times polished the rough style of both writers, he nevertheless left some matters equally obscure, as Mabillon complains in volume I of the *Veteres Analectae*, p. 298, in these words: “I hoped that by the help of this little book certain most obscure words occurring in Fortunatus’s *Life* of this same Radegund would be clarified; but, after comparing Hildebert’s and Fortunatus’s writings, I found that Hildebert either passed over the rough passages or repeated the same obscure words, and that nothing beyond elegance of style is to be found in Hildebert which is not present in the books of Fortunatus and Baudonivia.” + Some barbarous words about which the learned J. Mabillon complains are explained in the notes to the *Acts of the Saints*, *Life of Blessed Radegund* by Fortunatus and Baudonivia, vol. III, August, pp. 67–83. BOLL.]

Having carefully examined their writings, I resolved to follow Fortunatus, to whom very great authority accrues no less from his life than from the rank of bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0968B] This also refutes the opinion of those who denied Saint Fortunatus episcopal rank. BOLL.]

Yet I resolved to add certain miracles which Fortunatus did not touch upon at all, but which the nun is found to have commended to memory [Col. 0968A]; not, however, all of them, but only those more worthy of narration, which make known both the merit and reward of that most blessed woman. Anyone wishing to know the rest will not regret consulting Baudonivia’s volumes. Therefore consider the little work to be the result of labour undertaken for you. It shall not fall into other hands before, upon your examination, it is either judged worthy to be suppressed and rejected, or, if approved, offered to public view. You will repay me a great reward if you withdraw from human eyes whatever you judge liable to fear their tongues. It shall therefore be in the discretion not only of yourself, but also of those whom you decide to admit, either to publish it corrected or to conceal it entirely as defective.

[Col. 0967]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT RADEGUND, QUEEN, COMPOSED BY LORD HILDEBERT, BISHOP OF LE MANS, BEGINS

## CHAPTER I. The Saint’s homeland, royal lineage, captivity, upbringing in Gaul, and pious works which she practised until marriageable age

[Col. 0967C]

**2.** As the sacred authority of the Gospel testifies: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matthew 5:4)—that earth, namely, for which the Prophet longs: “May my portion, O Lord, be in the land of the living” (Psalm 118:57). By the hope of this land, the glorious and venerable Queen, blessed Radegund, consoled the hardships of her exile; in abandoning her temporal inheritance, she earned the everlasting one. She is said to have been of the Thuringian people, beautiful in countenance, distinguished in birth, and still more distinguished in character. No newly acquired nobility made her illustrious; rather, she derived it from ancient parents. [Col. 0967D] Her grandfather, named Bessinus, and her father Berectarius each attained royal rank.

[Note: [Col. 0967D] This king of Thuringia is called Bisinus by Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book II, chapter 12, and Basinus by others. BOLL.]

[Note: [Col. 0968D] The father of our Saint is called Beretharius by some, as is evident from the text of Gregory of Tours. BOLL.]

The blessed virgin, deriving lofty descent from them, shone far more brightly through the torches of her virtues than through the fasces of dignities.

**3.** When she had already outgrown the cradle and the Thuringian land was devastated by invading Franks, she too was carried away captive with the rest. By the lot of captives [perhaps “captivity”], she fell to King Chlothar as spoil—not so much to serve his marriage-bed by marriage as to benefit him by her character and example. Through this event the girl left her homeland and, by the king’s command, was taken to an estate in Vermandois named Athies, to be brought up there for some time. Guardians of most honourable life and illustrious reputation were appointed for her, under whom she might learn letters without unlearning virtue. Nor was it difficult for her to be formed in liberal rudiments, since the sharpness of her mind and the marks of her chastity surpassed her age and sex no less than did her talents. Already in the virgin a certain grave old age was beginning to show itself; and as she set the ascents [Psalm 83:6] in her heart, only the weakness of age opposed her. Yet amid the goads of time and sex, [Col. 0968D] she inexorably abhorred losses of chastity, longing only for the beauty of good character. Thus, among the other advances in virtue in which her tender childhood burned with zeal, she was eager to help the poor, frequent churches, and attend the divine offices.

[Col. 0969A]

**4.** She also had the practice of always withholding something for herself from her daily food and providing the poor with more abundant leftovers. Having carefully collected these, the girl, casting aside royal pride, distributed them among gathered poor people. Her service was commended by humility, and her reward was increased by devotion: after first washing each person’s head, the freeborn virgin poured water over their hands, herself served the food, and went round with lights lest anyone lack anything. Then, with her companions of the same age, she entered the church in the reverence of old age; there she rendered a hymn and commended her chastity to God. And lest forgetfulness of that Gospel saying should ever steal upon her—“Whoever does not carry his cross and follow me cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:27)—she ordered a cross to be carried before her, which her cleric was accustomed to make from wood for this purpose and carry himself.

[Col. 0969B]

[Note: [Col. 0969D] From this construction, at least, we understand the meaning of Fortunatus, who relates the same matter in a loose and obscure phrase. BOLL.]

After prayer, she cleaned the pavement with a garment; with a cloth, she reverently swept away the dust lying about the sanctuaries, removing whatever dirt or dust the carelessness of those dwelling there had left behind.

**5.** These were the virgin’s amusements; such were the habits her tender childhood assumed: kindly affection toward the poor and remarkable compassion toward the afflicted. Far from her was the fickleness of an unstable woman; far from her borrowed adornment. Nothing artificial was in her face, nothing vain in her speech. Her walk was nature’s work, not art’s. Rarely did anything beyond necessity attend her table or dress; and if it happened sometimes, it was yielded to her rank [Col. 0969C], not granted to pleasure. Thus, amid luxury and ignorant of luxuries, there was nothing suspect to virtue, nothing that threatened moral ruin.

**6.** Indeed, before she had yet reached marriageable years, she already judged virginity’s reward small unless the glory of martyrdom increased it. While this most tender virgin desired to attain it, she is remembered to have endured much from her household, both beyond and for the sake of righteousness. But when the time approached at which the aforesaid King Chlothar intended to unite her to himself in marriage, she fled by night from Athies with a few companions, avoiding by a lofty design that succession of the race whose conception is an assault upon chastity and whose birth is an assault upon life. At last the virgin was found and taken to Soissons: there she was indeed to marry a mortal king, but not to lose the grace of the eternal King.

## CHAPTER II. Her marriage to King Chlothar and the pious life which she led at court during marriage

**7.** Thus, joined only in outward appearance to an earthly prince, the noble queen began to become more than earthly—heavenly. For although the marriage was celebrated in the Lord, her mind was neither exalted by human glory, broken by pleasure, nor bent by enticements. The same contempt for the world and the same humility remained in the queen. Nothing in her character was claimed for itself by the secrets of marriage, by sovereignty, or by wealth. The queen took less pleasure in the use of these things than she was permitted to do.

[Note: [Col. 0969D] Hildebert seems here to use the adverb *citra* in the sense of “less,” as far as we can infer from the meaning—unless *licuit* should be read in place of *libuit*, so that the sense would be: the queen was permitted to make use of these things less—i.e., further or more—than she wished. BOLL.]

In short, she turned these three things into instruments of virtue: by the example of her chastity she moderated her husband’s impatience; by her power she aided the accused; and by her wealth she assisted the poor. Thus, passing without offence through the occasions of moral failure, she lived not for herself but for the realm, not for pleasure but for virtue.

8. From her virginity onward, her first resolve was that whatever accrued to her from revenues, whatever came to her by legal donation, should all serve the needs of the poor. Of what remained, she assigned one part to the Church and another to the care of her own body. [Col. 0970B] Even this latter, considering her rank as queen, served necessity rather than adornment. She carefully investigated where the sick lay, what was lacking to the monks, and what solitude the hermits inhabited. Those whom she could not visit in person she visited with gifts of many kinds. [Note: [Col. 0970D] “Blessings” here means gifts or small presents, elsewhere called *eulogiae*. BOLL.] For some she herself sewed clothing; to others she sent more generous provisions. To what afflicted persons was the queen not present? Who shivered with cold and was not warmed by the queen’s woollens? Who cried out after the queen and departed unheard? What did a poor person ever seek from the queen that was not more willingly offered? What day did she not judge lost if she had done nothing for those ruined in their morals? When was she so occupied with bodily attire that she could not attend to the cases of orphans? [Col. 0970C] And because she had read, “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7), she strove to be present for the teaching of priests and to commend herself to their prayers. None of them was burdened by exaction; none by the arbitrary power of royal authority; none was needy unless the merciful queen had failed to know of that need. Indeed, she believed it would count against her at judgment if, while the queen was rich, the angels of the Lord should beg.

9. Moreover, amid so many proofs of virtue, she established a house at Atteia and dedicated it as a lodging for poor women. She also appointed attendants whose diligence should ensure that the poor lacked nothing. There were there countless changes of clothing and suitable provision both for the living and for the dead. The queen believed that the resources of mercy were lacking in something unless she served in burial those whose life she served. [Col. 0970D] Frequently entering the aforesaid house, she was accustomed to minister to those reclining, sit beside those lying down, wipe with cloths the pus flowing from the ulcers of the sick, and wash the ulcers herself. She also bent down to wash the heads of the weak with healing decoctions, soothing with ointments things which one would judge dreadful to see and fearful to touch. For those requiring more attentive service, the queen, acting as a handmaid, prepared baths, patiently enduring many unpleasant things from the sick that would have aroused nausea in any little servant-girl. When they came out, she customarily offered them cups of drink, so that a draught might strengthen those loosened by the baths.

10. Diligently performing these services, the queen preferred to serve the poor in a neglected house rather than to rule in a palace. If you wish to know how she conducted herself in matters concerning her husband, [Note: [Col. 0971D] We have retained this sense in the text as we found it; but in place of *quae cura maritum gerebant*, we think one should read *quae circa maritum gerebat* (“how she conducted herself toward her husband”). With this slight alteration the meaning is rightly understood, as will be evident to the reader; and we have noted it for the reader’s convenience. BOLL.] she was so accommodating to her husband that the chamber of her Creator might not displease him: a workshop of modesty and a dwelling ignorant of shameful and disgraceful conduct. There were no gatherings of young men there, no conversations hostile to virtue. The maidservants were taught chastity more by examples than by lashes. Their life was as though the queen had borne her own character in her womb. [Col. 0971B] The psalter grew damp in the queen’s hand, and until she had sung it through in tears and groaning, she deferred taking food. When she came to table, she was accustomed to heed nature, not pleasure. For, knowing that the experience of luxuries borders upon sins, she preferred water to wine and vegetables to royal delicacies. A faithful servant brought her vegetables more secretly; after taking them, she seemed rather to break her fast than to drive away hunger. It cannot be said how often she rose fasting from the table, believing that an injury was done to Christ if the queen presumed to dine while Christ’s poor had not yet eaten. Taking an opportunity as well, after a morsel of bread she often left the table, intending either to sing a hymn to God or to render the service owed to the poor. [Col. 0971C]

11. For what shall I say about sharing the marriage-bed? She always approached it for this reason: to gain her husband, not to satisfy seductive pleasure. Indeed, lest Satan tempt her husband, she rendered what was owed to her husband; she did not exact it. [Note: [Col. 0972D] This clear phrase of Hildebert wholly conflicts with the virginity which some writers say the holy queen preserved in marriage. BOLL.] If anything sinful occurred in this matter, whether through his favor or through an admixture of pleasure, she hastened at once to blot it out not only with tears but also with severe bodily suffering. Pretending some reason for rising, she spread a rough hair-shirt upon the floor, to which she clung naked until the cold had pierced her marrow and she almost gave up her breath. Thus the queen both showed regard for marriage and preserved modesty: she neither deprived her husband of due reverence nor diminished by lust the good of marriage. There were those who said that the king had taken to himself a monk rather than a laywoman as wife. The king himself, bitterly resenting her purpose of piety, accused his wife of feigned religion, adding that such severity was entirely unsuitable to marriage, and that a wife might more gently accommodate herself to her husband, and a husband to his wife. But Christ’s daughter, not in the least withdrawn from her holy purpose by these words, sweetened the king’s bitterness with gentle speech. [Col. 0971D]

12. During Lent, moreover, persevering more long in holy vigils, she heaped torments upon torments, so that the flesh, disciplined by them, might be compelled to serve the spirit. Her face grew pale with fasting, and her limbs, wounded by the rough hair-shirt, knew no rest amid their torments. She had a nun familiar to her, alike in devotion and in name, Pia, who secretly used to send her the aforesaid garment, which always clung to her beneath, while above it Christ’s daughter was covered with royal clothing. [Col. 0972A] It was her custom, especially at that time, to go round the nearby shrines of the saints, carefully seeing that neither the ornaments of the church nor the ministers of the churches lacked resources. She also strove to provide lights for every altar, which she was said to trim with her own hands. But at the hour when the priest offered the sacrifices, she passed through the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion with a certain suffering of mind, and burned for God the pleasing holocaust of a contrite spirit. [Col. 0972B] For she beat upon heaven with such sighs and was drenched by such a torrent of tears as though Christ were again being seized by Jewish hands and again seen to be crucified.

13. When the saving service had been completed, she did not return to the palace before, accompanied by a few people, she had visited with pious attentiveness the sick lying all around. She did not know how to plead the inconvenience of the time, nor was she detained by rain or snow. She was moved by no discomforts whatever, provided that she might serve the welfare of the poor. The queen, yet humble, washed the heads of some and prepared baths for others. For those who had either no bed or a harsher one, a softer bed was prepared by adding straw [Col. 0972C] or feathers. She ended the day in such occupations, returning late at night.

While she was thus occupied with these most blessed affairs and prolonged her stay, the king sent messengers to urge her to return more promptly: the king was seated at table, the nobles were waiting. She preferred service to the poor to the royal command, unwilling to return before completing what she had begun. Hearing this, the king is recorded to have taken it grievously and to have rebuked the queen, who returned late, more sharply than was fitting. Yet afterwards, repenting, he humbly begged pardon, steadily accusing himself because he had grieved the Holy Spirit and had presumed to grieve His temple. He added more generous gifts to his entreaties, so that his faithful and devout wife might distribute them to the poor [Col. 0972D] as though in redemption for her husband’s offense. When this was done, the king’s anger so subsided that he himself both gave thanks to God for his wife’s great devotion and ordered more generous funds to be provided for her, that she might relieve the need of the poor more abundantly.

14. When priests of Christ came to the palace and, as an urgent matter required, sought royal help, she rejoiced with such exultation as though Christ Himself were certainly present. [Col. 0973A] She received them with the honor she had been taught to show, heard them speaking with deeper devotion, and humbly ministered to them as they reclined. It could not readily be discerned whether she displayed Martha rather than Mary. She attended to the concerns of all and complained that she herself was weighed down by all their burdens; no one lacked her blessing, no one the help requested. She declared that only what passed into their service had been allotted to her own use. Neither the administration of her household nor the affairs of the kingdom diminished her diligence toward them. As they departed, she accompanied them in tears and prayed that they would deign to remember her there where the Son is offered to the Father. [Note: [Col. 0973D] A phrase familiar to Hildebert.]

15. Nor was her concern less for criminals dragged either to prison or to punishment because of their own crimes. For their salvation she ran about; for all of them, one by one, she pleaded, frequently reminding people that one ought to have mercy on a guilty person’s blood, since even the Redeemer’s blood was shed for the guilty. [Col. 0973B] And lest her effort of compassion be in vain, she did not cease to soothe the prince’s mind with entreaties until the one who had pronounced a sentence of justice pronounced one of mercy. In freeing the condemned, Christ bestowed such grace upon her that at her name locked prisons stood open, iron chains were loosed, and those whom the court’s judgment had sentenced to death or tortures went out unharmed.

16. For when, in a country estate called Perona, she was walking about in peaceful leisure, prisoners held under sentence in a nearby jail began to cry out that the queen might deign to assist them. Hearing this, Christ’s daughter carefully asked what was happening and why there was shouting. [Col. 0973C] The guards lied that there was a crowd of poor people present, asking for food. The queen believed the servants, and alms, which they pretended were being asked for, were sent to those crying out. Having received them, the prisoners fell silent, restrained by the guards’ threats and blows lest they cry out further. Yet they deserved to be heard, crying more devoutly in heart than in speech. For on the following night, while the queen continued her customary prayers, by divine will the unlocked prison opened, the chains were broken, and those who had been kept for punishments and death came out unharmed. [Col. 0973D] And, lest they seem ungrateful for so great a benefit, they threw themselves at the knees of the blessed woman, gave thanks, and publicly declared that they had been delivered from their chains by her holy merits.

17. Once the miracle had been spread abroad, Christ’s daughter was not lifted up by such glory; rather, at its report, her face suffused with blushes, she declared herself unworthy, she for whom the Lord had deigned to grant the aforesaid benefit to His servants. Persisting therefore in humility, she wore down her tender limbs with multiplied disciplines, [Note: [Col. 0973D] “Disciplines” here does not mean voluntary bodily flagellations, whose use became widespread only in the eleventh century. Among ecclesiastical writers of an earlier age, *disciplina* is used for any bodily affliction, as may be seen in Du Cange’s *Glossary*, under “Disciplina.” BOLL.] becoming more abundant in her acts toward the poor and Christ’s churches the more secure she now was concerning her reward. [Col. 0974A] Thus, when on feast-days she wore gilded garments, as befitted a queen’s rank, and the girls around her praised her, she sighed from the depths and lamented herself unworthy of such clothing; immediately taking it off, she dedicated it to the adornment and honor of some church. Moreover, whatever gems, purple cloth, or costly adornment came to her, she assigned wholly to holy altars or ecclesiastical ornaments.

## CHAPTER III. The holy woman’s monastic profession; her generosity toward churches; the foundation of the convent at Poitiers; the king’s vain attempt to draw her back into marriage.

18. The queen’s resolve rose to such a point that, casting aside the insignia of power and trampling worldly glory underfoot, she ardently desired, herself poor, to follow the poor Christ. To be worthy to fulfill this desire, she went to blessed Medard [Col. 0974B] and requested from him both the religious garment and his blessing. The bishop did not at all accede to her request. “The sacred law of marriage,” he said, “does not permit the lawful bonds of marriage to be dissolved while both wife and husband are alive.” [Note: [Col. 0974D] Thus Hildebert too judged the holy woman’s marriage with King Clothar to have been valid and lawful. BOLL.] The blessed woman persisted, and, flooding her modest face with abundant tears, begged to be veiled. There was an uproar in the church: clergy and people alike resisted the queen’s vows with a united judgment. The nobles pulled her away as she threw herself upon the holy altars, firmly forbidding the bishop to presume to lay hands upon the queen. Seeing both leaders and people oppose her plan, she entered the sanctuary and, her mind strengthened for a new resolve, placed upon her own head the habit of religion. Then she returned to the bishop and said: “May the Lord God require my soul from your hand if you fear the king of men more than the King of angels.” [Col. 0974C] When he heard this, he laid hands upon her, overcome not so much by her entreaty as by her constancy.

19. Thus blessed Radegund, entering upon the arduous way, distributed with a lavish hand among the poor and churches the wealth and royal equipment that remained to her after her fortunate emergence from this great and wide sea. As soon as she wholly put off the queen, she laid upon the Lord’s table the garments in which she had been crowned—an offering acceptable to God and full of grace. She is also said to have broken up and distributed to the poor her golden girdle, bracelets, and earrings, all adorned with precious pearls. [Col. 0974D] Then, proceeding and entering the cell of a certain saint, she loaded and honored the holy altars with tapestries, bands, clasps, and sleeves heavy with woven gold. Next she distributed no lesser gifts to various monasteries, whose reputation under the venerable fathers—namely venerable Dado and holy Gundulf—was held to be complete and distinguished.

Then, carried to Tours by a fortunate voyage, how devotedly she showed herself at the tomb of blessed Martin, how great a holocaust of tears she offered, and with what sighs she beat upon heaven, the mind can scarcely grasp and the tongue scarcely explain. [Col. 0975A] Her devotion was testified not so much by the ornaments offered to the several altars as by her deep groans and the pavement wet with tears.

20. Having prayed, she arrived at Caudata (Cande). There too she offered rich furnishings for the Lord’s table, where the most glorious confessor of Christ and bishop Martin had rendered his blessed spirit to heaven. Not far away was an estate called Suedas (commonly Saiz), which had come to her by deed of gift. When the blessed religious woman turned aside to it and remained there for several days, word was brought to her that the king wished to recall her to the palace and complained bitterly that the majesty of the kingdom was deprived of the counsel and wisdom of so great a woman. [Col. 0975B] Hearing this, the woman devoted to God trembled; wholly turned to God, she poured herself out in tears by night and day, praying that He would not permit her again to be entangled in worldly allurements. She also resolved that her tender limbs should be worn down with harsher punishments, so that, if prayer accomplished too little, she might at least obtain the fulfillment of her vows through suffering.

21. At that time there was in the fortress of Caino (Chinon) a just and God-fearing man named John. [Note: [Col. 0975D] He was a priest, a Breton by nation, says Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, book I, ch. 23, living in the highest religious devotion. He had shut himself up more strictly in a certain cell near an oratory or chapel, later erected under the title of Saint Radegund. In it is still seen the tomb of the aforesaid John, distinguished by holiness even after death and by miracles, but empty since 1565, when Calvinists consumed his exhumed body in a profane fire. So our Ruinart in his notes on this chapter.] His religion had made him notable and famous, enclosed as he was in a most severe prison-cell. Blessed Radegund sent him by faithful messengers a costly golden cloth, marvellously adorned with gems and pearls, containing one thousand gold solidi—the remaining part of her royal ornaments. [Col. 0975C] She asked him both to pray for her and to pray on her behalf; and, if he should learn by certain report or foresee in spirit anything concerning the king’s aforesaid intention, to reveal it to her without delay.

Having heard this, the man of God spent the following night in vigils and prayers. At dawn he promptly informed her of what divine mercy had made known to him: namely, that the king would by no means be permitted to assign her again to his marriage, although he might strive to accomplish this by many efforts. He also sent to Christ’s daughter, as she had asked, a hair-shirt with which her rebellious flesh might be subdued by harsher discipline.

22. Receiving both gift and message, the blessed religious woman gave thanks to God and departed joyfully for Poitiers. Without delay, she sent letters to the king and asked that an oratory be built for her near the walls of the aforesaid city. [Col. 0975D] Her wish was granted; at the king’s command, Pientius, then bishop of Poitiers, and Duke Ostrapius completed the monastery in a short time. [Note: [Col. 0975D] His feast as a holy bishop is celebrated at Poitiers on 13 May. On him and on Ostropius, or Austropic, the duke, see Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, IV.18.] A multitude of virgins was received there and attained, through the teachings and examples of the most blessed religious woman, the reward of the hundredfold fruit. [Col. 0976A] Under the abbess of that place, who had received the governance of souls by Radegund’s choice, she strove to live in such a manner as to be considered humbler than all and more abject than all. [Note: [Col. 0976D] Namely Saint Agnes, mentioned above, whom Saint Radegund herself had chosen and arranged to have appointed, as is clear from her letter to the bishops, reported by Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks* IX.42; to her Radegund submitted herself as to her superior and humbly obeyed.] She struggled to be beneath all in service, but above all in holiness.

23. But because those who desire to live piously must suffer persecution, the blessed woman was not permitted peacefully to reach the desired harbor of the voyage she had undertaken. For the king, prompted by certain counselors, resolved to do what she had long feared: to draw her away from sacred service and renew the bond of marriage. Thus, in order to carry out what he had conceived in sacrilegious intent, he decided to go to Poitiers with his son Sigebert and Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris. When he had arrived at Tours and this report had spread through the whole province, the religious woman sent the aforesaid bishop a letter full of … [Col. 0976B] [Note: [Col. 0976D] A word is missing here, but may easily be supplied from the phrase of Baudonivia, who above called those letters “full of firm purpose” or “fearless constancy,” sacramental letters; we explained the meaning of that epithet there in the notes.] She begged him not to allow the repose of the contemplation she had undertaken to be troubled by any vexations, for it was impossible that she should prefer the king of men to the King of angels.

24. After reading the letter, the bishop threw himself at the king’s feet and implored him to abandon his purpose, to keep his hands from one consecrated to Christ, and to show reverence to the Holy Spirit, who had made His own dwelling in a fragile vessel. The bishop’s intercession was heard; and because the king had feared violence, he was not ashamed to confess his offense. [Col. 0976C] The ruler begged forgiveness and asked to be aided by the prayers of her whose marriage he had not been worthy to possess. Moreover, lest anyone thereafter incite the king to the same attempt by similar counsel, a severe punishment devastated those by whose persuasion the king had resolved to recall her to the debt of marriage. For just as the blasphemous and unhappy Arius found the end of his own madness, so they experienced divine indignation by disgorging their entrails.

## CHAPTER IV. The holy woman’s austere abstinence, cruel affliction of the body, and other monastic virtues, by which she then shone most gloriously at Poitiers.

25. Thereafter the most holy woman, casting off all fear, happily completed her course, kept the faith, and awaited from the Lord God the crown of righteousness laid up for her. [Col. 0976D] Her aim was steadily to afflict herself, tirelessly to serve the poor, and without offense to observe the rule of the community. Though one woman was divided among so many concerns, she was so wholly present in each that she seemed to give each person individual care. From the day when she wholly renounced the glory of the palace, she strove to deprive herself of a good portion even of the very scanty food by which she was sustained. [Col. 0977A] From then on, she knew no cook’s skill and no stimulus of gluttony. From then on, disdaining ordinary luxuries, she met necessity with legumes and herbs; no seasoning of oil or salt was added to such fare. She had bread as well, but barley bread, which she herself baked. Taken once daily, it broke the fast but did not remove hunger. The thirst kindled by the excessive dryness of the bread she relieved by a draught either of honeyed water or of pear-wine. [Col. 0977B] She made no mention whatever of wine or beer. Her breast, hardened with ashes and covered over with a hair-shirt, promised a cross rather than rest.

26. Indeed, although the tender limbs of a woman could scarcely suffice for so many and such grievous sufferings, during the days of Lent the woman nevertheless added to her punishment and the Lord to her crown. Throughout that whole season, except on Sunday, she abstained utterly from all bread. Throughout that season, she was sustained by a meager refreshment of roots and herbs. No addition of salt or oil tempered their harshness. During the same period she mitigated the burning of thirst by a touch of plain water. This too was taken only on the days of the aforesaid refreshment, and so sparingly that, with her lips torn by dryness, she lost her former ability to sing psalms. [Col. 0977C] Yet, yielding to no inconvenience, she never ceased from their chanting, but continued, as she could, to complete the office. Amid these injuries to the flesh and torturing pains, she often passed the night sleepless in continual prayer. Her companions in vigils were abundant weeping and meditation on the joys of heaven. Rising toward these in a certain flight of mind, she was so present to the affairs of human beings that she was also present to the affairs of angels; she tasted and saw how sweet the Lord is, sighed, and said: “There is no number to His mercies [Vulgate: wisdom]” (Ps. 147:5).

27. And because she was also taught by the Spirit that whoever labors more receives more reward, she added a new torment of the flesh to the labors of fasting and vigils. [Col. 0977D] Ingenious in devising punishments, she ordered a plate of *aurichalcum*—a copper-like metal—to be made for her. [Note: [Col. 0977D] Others write *orichalcum* or *aurichalcum*, a well-known kind of metal. BOLL.] Heated in fire, she was accustomed to press it deeply into her tender limbs, lest [perhaps: “so that”], if she had sinned in any way through pleasure, she might be purified by the ensuing pain. She repeatedly fastened this torment upon her flesh, persecuting herself as an enemy because, perhaps without wishing it, she had been pleasing in a way conducive to fault.

During one Lent, when the aforementioned labors seemed insufficient to her for winning the Lord’s grace, she bound both arms and neck in iron rings, encircling the rest of her body with a triple chain. [Col. 0978A] The weight of iron alone was a heavy punishment, but more grievous was the deeper cutting into the flesh. Covered by the iron, she bore a hidden martyrdom without a witness. The Lenten observance had already passed when utmost necessity compelled the deeply embedded iron to be removed. It was scarcely removed, when so much blood flowed from her torn body that, her vital strength drained from her breast, she almost gave up her spirit. Thus, persecuting herself day by day, she lived for her own punishment and as an example for others.

28. In another Lent, she devised another kind of torment against limbs so often wearied. She ordered a bronze vessel full of burning coals to be set beside her, commanded her attendants to leave, locked her cell, took off her hair-shirt, and—woman strong above woman—armed herself for punishment. [Col. 0978B] It seemed too little to her to offer God each day a contrite heart unless she also burned her flesh as a voluntary holocaust. With her mind therefore prepared for the cross, she threw herself into the fire. A more glowing coal was sought; turning her limbs over upon it, she let the fire, deliberately sought, tear and penetrate skin and flesh. A longer delay in the fire pursued her tender body with a deeper wound. Glowing bronze was rolled against her limbs; her inmost parts were consumed by heat. Everything was done lest anything remain unburned, as though she begrudged her own unburned parts. To the torment was added, as though another torment, her very disregard for the burned flesh. She thought a woman’s glorious victory could remain hidden, but decaying flesh disclosed the secret martyrdom by its stench; and blood flowing over her whole body made known what [Col. 0978C] her tongue had kept silent.

29. Who would dare deny Radegund the reward of martyrdom? Who would claim that she lacked a sword or an executioner? Who would deny martyrdom there, where the torturer is a woman, the instrument flame, and Christ the cause? If you seek an executioner, none is more cruel to another than she was to herself. If a sword, you will find as many swords as coals. If a cause, she strove to gain Christ. Let others think what they wish; I shall not hesitate to affirm that Radegund, wounded by a rough hair-shirt, afflicted by continuous fasts, emaciated by the weight of iron, and burned by coals and glowing bronze, both earned the reward of a martyr on earth and possesses it in heaven. [Note: [Col. 0977D] Perhaps for this or a similar line of reasoning Boninus Mombritius prefixed the title “martyr” to the Acts of Saint Radegund. BOLL.]

30. Perhaps someone will think that this remarkable woman, wearied by so many tortures, approached works of mercy more slowly. But whoever wishes to know her devotion in this virtue should read the following page. [Col. 0978D] From the time she put off the queen and put on the humble nun, every Thursday and Saturday she gathered poor people and prepared both baths and a common meal. Receiving them in the guest-house, she herself washed their heads with her own hands, scraped off scabies with her nails, wiped away corrupt matter, drew worms from ulcers, and applied oil. More humble than any little servant-girl, she was ashamed to serve none of their needs. [Col. 0979A] She also took sick women, whom she knew to require such care, into the baths, scrubbed their filthy shoulders, and diligently rendered suitable service to every limb.

31. She carefully investigated what each person needed, giving everyone cloths and shoes according to need. [Note: [Col. 0979D] In medieval writers *sotulares* are also called *subtalares* and mean shoes, as may be seen in Du Cange’s *Glossary*. BOLL.] She did not regard it as burdensome to set out seats for them, bring napkins, or offer water for washing their hands. She set out dishes too, providing and distributing more nourishing foods for the sick. If anyone was oppressed by more serious illness, she herself cut bread and meat for that person. Some she herself fed with her own hands. A cloth hung from her shoulder, with which she wiped what fell either from the mouths of the weak or from their spoons. [Col. 0979B] Young women attendants were present, but none of them took over the office of serving. Radegund performed whatever care the occasion required; as necessity arose, she hurried about. Radegund bent down before those lying down, stood before those sitting, and fasted before those eating. There was no disorder there, Radegund in a manner imposing monastic silence. Finally, when the meal was over, she hurried to her cell, praying that all her work might always begin from God and bring to completion through God what it had begun.

Every Sunday likewise, as on the aforementioned days, she provided a meal for the poor. But because on that day the more solemn celebration of the Masses was at hand, after the first dishes had been distributed, after [printed *per*, read *post*] a cup had been offered once to all, she returned more quickly to the monastery, leaving young women with the poor to carry out carefully the service begun. [Col. 0979C]

32. She had a devotion toward lepers as intense as though she did not doubt that Christ Himself was present. When they were kindly received, she immediately washed their hands with water and did not shrink from touching and tending their torn skin. She was not afraid to embrace women whose faces had been horribly wounded by the aforesaid disease, nor to kiss them closely. Then a table was set, and care was taken with softer coverings and footstools lest they should sit too harshly or with their feet dangling. Who can deny that Radegund ministered to the lepers she received? Who would dare say that a work full of abundant reward was entrusted to another? Would she have shrunk from offering a cup, when she did not disdain to give a kiss? [Col. 0979D] Let no one believe that Radegund loved the crown so lukewarmly that she feared to earn it when it was offered. She would have been imperfectly concerned for the reward if she begrudged its service—and its reward—to others. Yet she begrudged it while, girded for action, she performed without disgust a service others found repellent.

When they had eaten and were about to rise, she gave them the necessary clothing, extending to their departing hands both a kiss and money. Wherever she knew people lay afflicted by fevers or any illnesses, she carefully inquired what remedies would benefit them, what they would prefer to eat, and what delicacies they desired. [Col. 0980A] She failed none in their wishes, provided these agreed with their condition. It often happened that those known to have been ill for a long time recovered lost health through her *eulogiae*, that is, gifts. [Note: [Col. 0979D] Above Hildebert used *benedictiones* for *eulogiae*; both words among medieval authors are used for gifts or small presents. BOLL.] All were astonished at her generosity and wondered where so much wealth came from, not knowing that the Lord’s promise was now being fulfilled: “Give, and it shall be given unto you” (Luke 6:38).

33. Thus rich toward the poor, she restrained herself under severe poverty. She pursued soft clothing with unrelenting hatred; beneath the hair-shirt with which she was covered, she wore rougher garments. Although she could have had an abundance of costly things, she often lacked even these, knowing that among the virtues is a poverty brought about not by necessity but by will. [Col. 0980B] Thus, when at one time she lacked sleeves, she divided one of her stockings to make coverings for her arms. Blessed woman, who did not wish to abound in such a way as to feel no want. She did not yet seem to herself truly poor unless, together with poverty of spirit, she also bore material lack.

34. Amid these cares for the poor and daily mortifications of the flesh, she was the first to rise for Matins; the first to be present at the appointed hours; and the first to hurry to fulfill whatever might be commanded. If she had begun later than the others or had performed some good work later, she immediately accused herself of negligence, as though she had sinned in a punishable manner, and did not delay to ask pardon. In carrying out those duties which the rules of the order impose upon each person, she often took the place of others. She believed that no day had been spent not idly [text: *non*] unless by her own labor she relieved the labor of the others. [Col. 0980C] When she was to work in the kitchen, she alleged no inconvenience and put forward no excuse. Entering it, she was not ashamed to throw out filth which any servant-girl would have recoiled from even seeing. Then she herself drew water from the well, carried it herself, lit the fire herself, cleaned the bowls, cut the vegetables, attended to the legumes, and took care both to cook sufficiently and to distribute suitably. Thus obeying the monastic rules, she completed without complaint the week’s duty she had undertaken.

Moreover, she customarily cleaned the entire floor of the monastery, its workrooms, and even its inner chambers, so humbly that she refused neither to carry out baskets full of filth nor to endure the stench. [Col. 0980D] Provided that she suffered for Christ, poverty seemed wealth to her, labor rest, and reproach glory.

35. At the common table the same things as for the others were set before her, but she did not take the same things. For she would put fine flour upon coarse “second bread,” [Note: [Col. 0980D] The Latins call “second bread” bread to which some bran has been added. BOLL.] as though she were going to bring it to her lips to eat, while she recoiled from allowing its flavor to touch her palate at all. Yet lest she fail entirely, she took from the barley bread a refreshment nearly equivalent to fasting.
