Rising from the table, she devoted the remaining time either to a hymn to God, to reading, or to psalms. [Col. 0981A] When she ceased from chanting psalms, one of the nuns was present to recite the divine utterances of Scripture. Listening to these with great earnestness, she urged the others to attend carefully to the reader and to consult the mirror of souls concerning their inward disposition. Whenever she encountered an obscure passage, she explained it to those who did not know and rebuked the negligent.

36. When, therefore, the day had been spent in such blessed occupations, and the others were already asleep, she herself wiped and anointed each sister’s slippers, carefully observing which needed renewal. Then she went to bed, which was as humble as anything could be and as little suited to pleasure. At that time too a reader was present, so that the blessed nun, even waking from sleep, might be nourished by spiritual delights. If the reader happened to fall silent, supposing that the weary woman was resting and sleeping, she immediately heard: “Why are you silent? Read; do not stop.” Moreover, lest there be any doubt that her heart remained awake while her limbs rested in a brief sleep, she sang psalms even while sleeping, truly able to say with the Prophet: “The meditation of my heart is always before you” (Ps. XVIII, 15).

37. She rose at midnight, and until the community came to the monastery, she devoted herself amid tears and groaning to psalms and contemplation. Contemplation so claimed her mind that, although absent in body, in spirit she nevertheless continually frequented that city whose streets resound with praises from day to day. She was wholly possessed by its delights, and her heart could utter nothing other than the nectar of heaven and the grace of its joys. Hence, when one day she wished to call the *posticiaria*, who was passing near her, and assign her some task, she spoke “Alleluia” in place of her name. This happy error occurred more than once. Where her treasure was, there also was her heart.

38. What shall I say of the sick nuns, whom Radegund visited every day and for whom, while fasting herself, she prepared more delicate foods? Shrinking from none of the discomforts either of illness or of sex, she lifted and washed the sick, carried them out, and brought them back. She herself provided them with little broths and decoctions, omitting none of the things their bedridden condition required. Nor was there less diligence or devotion in receiving guests. Having received them in Christ, she herself washed their feet and offered water to those about to dine. In short, she herself supplied everything by which the needs of guests are relieved. If a religious person happened to be received, she privately inquired into his character, pursuits, and life. If she learned that he lived under stricter disciplines, she subjected herself to the same observances and used his example to increase in virtue. She believed herself to have advanced less than perfectly unless, in her own deeds, the deeds of all the perfect shone forth. Her works spoke of such persons; she commended them to Christ’s virgins and preached that they should be imitated. Yet she suggested nothing to others that she did not teach more by example than by word.

[Col. 0982A]

39. Her whole life spoke holiness. Her whole being breathed Christ. Apart from hatred, she had nothing to do with vices. Zeal for the law and continual meditation upon the law introduced a company of virtues. Neither adverse nor favorable events diminished any of these. In every condition righteousness was secure with this woman. She made no mention of the splendor of her birth or the glory of her marriage. She grieved more at having entered the embraces of a king—by which not even a captive was captured—than at having left them. Having experienced these things, she made good the loss to modesty by the prerogative of her merits. Consider her character; consider her deeds; observe her unceasing penitence: you must confess that no virtue was lacking to this nun. For unless she had prudence, she would not have preferred salutary things to harmful ones, nor things to be desired to things to be avoided. By fortitude and temperance, moreover, she was always steadfast and consistent with herself.

40. Amid these things, humility, preserved until the end, held a certain primacy. Nor can anyone say that humility was lacking to this poor woman, who, while holding a sceptre, knew nothing of pride. If one asks concerning abstinence, she indulged nature little and appetite not at all. No one was gentler than she: though a queen and wronged, she sought no revenge. In every action and word she imposed measure through discernment; she attended to circumstances and observed the limits of things. In her own concerns she gave thanks; for the injuries of others she wept. When injured, she was readier to offer pardon than the offender was to ask for it. She feared to anger Christ if, being angry, she should see the sun go down. Before her no one maliciously disparaged another with impunity. I must fail if I attempt to unfold her individual virtues.

She was shut up in her cell until she rendered her spirit to God. She was the pious executioner and priest of her own body. There, pressing on with long fasts to the injury of nature, wounded by haircloth and afflicted by secret torments, she interceded with God for every rank of the Church. By her most holy prayers and letters, sent among discordant princes on behalf of concord, rest was won for the churches and peace restored to the land.

## CHAPTER V. Various miracles that God wrought through the intercession of this saint

41. Moreover, she obtained such grace from God that at her name the sick were healed, the seas were calmed, and life was restored to the dead. It often happened that those laid low by a long-standing illness, after receiving her blessed gifts (*eulogiæ*), recovered their former health. Some also escaped quartan fevers and other illnesses after tasting leaves from trees to which she had applied her holy hands.

42. At that time there was a certain matron in Francia whose eyes had been darkened by prolonged blindness. Having heard of the holy woman’s renown, she was led by the hands of her servants to Poitiers. Asked to make the sign of the cross upon the woman’s eyes, the nun declared herself unworthy that remedies for diseases should be expected from her touch. At last those who devoutly pleaded for the unhappy woman were heard. But because she preferred that no one rather than a crowd should witness the grace that God worked through her, the woman was ordered to be brought late at night. When brought, she fell at the nun’s knees; the sign of the cross was made upon her eyes; and, her blindness driven away, her sight was restored.

43. A girl named Fraiflidis was wonderfully tormented by a demon. Among the blessed hands of the woman devoted to God, she deserved both liberation and rest.

Another woman was grievously afflicted by an illness: a worm was eating away the inside of her shoulders. While Christ’s daughter devoutly prayed to Christ for her, the skin burst and the worm sprang out; within a few days her health was wholly restored.

[Col. 0983B]

One of the nuns was so violently held by fevers that, now consumed by fire, now by cold, she entirely despaired of life. Christ’s bride ordered that this woman, who had lain bedridden for six months, be brought before her; she also ordered water to be heated and carried, once heated, into the cell. What the blessed nun commanded was done without delay. Then, all others dismissed, she placed the fevered woman in the bath, touched her limbs in compassionate service, and assailed heaven with groaning and tears. Behold: health followed where it had been despaired of; and as though the illness feared her touch, it departed at that very moment beneath her blessed hands. But the woman, restored to her former health, declared the merit of her healer by receiving the remedy.

44. The wife of a certain Inderedi had obtained a barren fecundity: she was accustomed to give birth for the tomb, not for her husband. The offspring conceived in her womb invited the parents to funeral rites rather than to a cradle. Thus from that time that ill-fertile womb was a mother only as the procurer of funerals: though it promised a human being, it did not produce one. What more? The time of birth came, and behold, the mother brought into the light, without life, an infant dead before it had been born. The father, accusing nature, turned to grace. Full of faith, and placing his hope for an heir in Radegund alone, he wrapped the lifeless corpse in her haircloth. His blessed confidence obtained a happy outcome: touched by the garment, the boy opened his eyes, cast off the color of death, and, restored to life, was returned to his mother’s breast—he who had come forth from that breast for the tomb. The received infant alleviated both the anguish of childbirth and the sorrow of death.

45. A servant of the nuns, named Floreius, had boarded a boat by the command of blessed Radegund in order to fish. As he was being carried out into deep water, a storm arose and he began to be in danger. Wind and waves rose on every side, lifting their crests higher, and seemed to have sworn his shipwreck. Terrified by this, Floreius repeatedly had recourse to Radegund’s name. He invoked Radegund, often repeating: “Help us, most holy one, while we obey your command.” At her name the force of the winds subsided, the seas became calm, and Floreius reached harbor, having obtained what he prayed for.

46. Great are the things that precede, but by no means lesser are those that follow. Christ’s daughter had ordered a beautiful laurel tree to be uprooted and planted before her cell. Once this was done, its root, refusing the alien soil, immediately withered after transplantation. When the abbess learned this, she said jokingly to the blessed woman: “Until you obtain from God that the dry laurel adhere to the earth, I suspend you from food.” Although the abbess said this playfully, Radegund nevertheless gave her complete obedience as though she had spoken seriously. Having prayed, she immediately saw the laurel put on green foliage, become covered with new leaves, and, its roots striking more deeply, gain by grace the fruitfulness it had lost through violence.

47. Concerning the wife of a certain Carpenter, whom an evil spirit had possessed, the abbess spoke to blessed Radegund more jokingly than seriously: “Mother, I excommunicate you unless the poor woman possessed by the demon is set free and finds rest within three days.” Yet this too was not said in vain: a *fraelex* outcome followed without delay.

[Note: We do not know what the word *fraelex* properly means, and have sought it in vain in various lexicons. What if it is a printer’s or copyist’s error, and *felix* was intended in place of *fraelex*? Certainly no few errors have entered this work of Hildebert; but we can correct such corruptions only by conjecture, since we possess these Acts of St Radegund only in this single edition. —Bollandists.]

The next day, while the nun prayed at greater length through her intercession for the unhappy woman, the demon departed through her ear and left free the little vessel which it had long harassed with its customary presumption.

[Col. 0984C]

Another most miserable woman was also brought to her. Through a similar affliction, a wicked spirit had wrested from her both peace of mind and bodily rest. You would have thought that the enemy feared the presence of the blessed woman, before whom the afflicted woman could not be presented except by the greatest force. Once presented, however, the poor woman was ordered to be thrown upon the floor and not removed from it until both health had been restored to her and she herself restored to her friends. For the holy prayers had such power that, when the most holy woman placed her foot upon the possessed woman’s neck, the unclean spirit departed by unclean passages and left the woman unharmed.

48. Moreover, one of the nuns, a woman familiar to the blessed one, lamented the loss of sight because the surface of her eye had covered it. Yet she too obtained healing: she placed upon the eye wormwood which the holy woman had held to her own breast so that it might become milder. Once the herb had been applied, it immediately drove away both pain and blood, restoring to the woman joy together with sight.

One day, while the nun was praying in her cell, she heard what sounded like the voices of people in distress. On asking what had happened, she was told that one of the nuns had died and that the others were performing for her funeral the offices prompted by human affection. On hearing this, she ordered the lifeless body to be carried in and presented to her in the cell. There was no delay; and behold, when the corpse was brought, those who had carried in the dead woman were compelled to withdraw some distance. Then, with witnesses removed, the woman who was to pray shut the cell. She cast herself upon the ground, on her knees (*genita*), assailed heaven with prayers and groaning, invited life with tears, and presumed by grace what she did not hope for from nature.

[Note: Hildebert appears to have derived or coined this word *genita* from the noun *genu*, “knee,” as the sense makes clear: it plainly indicates that the saint then prayed prostrate or on her knees. —Bollandists.]

True religion is a commanding thing, changing the laws and fixed order of nature. Religion obtained that Christ’s daughter should ask nothing from Christ in vain. Nor was she disappointed even in this pious desire, but found such great favor with God that, by her merits, the woman destined for burial was restored to life. To the amazement of those who had brought in the corpse, the nun emerged unharmed; she accompanied to the assembly her sisters who had been preceding her to the tomb.

49. A nun named Animia was swollen with fatal dropsy, and physicians were summoned in vain; they promised nothing but imminent funeral rites.

[Note: Certainly something is disordered in this sentence. For the syntax to work, *lethalis hydrops* should be read as *lethali hydrope* or *hydropisi*, “with fatal dropsy.” If, perhaps, Hildebert used *tumuerat* actively in the sense of *tumefecerat*, “had swollen,” then *quamdam* should be substituted for *quaedam*, so that the sense would be: “Fatal dropsy had swollen one of the nuns,” etc. —Bollandists.]

As she was almost breathing her last, she seemed in a dream to see blessed Radegund visit her as she lay ill, together with her abbess; after visiting her, they placed her in a bath, anointed her limbs with oil, and finally clothed her in white garments. On waking, the nun felt her illness alleviated. Then, when full daylight had dawned, as the fatal waters dried up, her swollen abdomen subsided and returned that same day to its proper measure, so that no trace at all of the disease remained.

[Note: Here *modulus* is used in the sense of “measure”; Hildebert means that the abdomen, previously swollen with dropsy, returned to its former shape or dimensions on that very day. —Bollandists.]

50. Great was Radegund’s merit, since she obtained even this from the Lord: that the works of her hands should receive a certain dignity beyond those of others. A ball of yarn spun by her blessed fingers was being gnawed by a shrew (*sorex*); the shrew suffocated and died. No one doubts that this happened through the woman’s merits: when a worm (*vermis*) sought to consume her labors, grace preserved them.

[Note: It is remarkable that Hildebert here calls this animal *vermis*, “worm,” though above he himself called it *sorex*, “shrew.” —Bollandists.]

Furthermore, a girl named Goda was so pressed by the burning of fever that prolonged distress promised her nothing but death. After her resources had been wasted in vain upon physicians, she deserved neither healing from any of them nor to be heard by any saint. Compelled, therefore, to have recourse to tested help, she ordered a candle made to the size of her own body to be lit in honor and in the name of the blessed woman. When this was done, as though the fire had consumed the material of her illness, the illness was consumed at the same time as the candle. The woman rose whole; and, owing her recovery to the most holy woman, she did not escape the storms of this world before, having professed herself a nun, she changed her conduct for the better.

51. Moreover, among the other manifestations of grace by which blessed Radegund adorned Christ’s Church, she embraced true poverty with pure affection, so that from the goods she herself had assigned to the monastery she regarded nothing as her own and gave away absolutely nothing belonging to another without the permission of her abbess. Therefore the abbess assigned for her use a wine-vessel of about eight *modii*, from which, as a generous dispenser, she might supply whomever she wished. Into this vessel the Lord infused such abundance that, when emptied, it was not diminished, and, when distributed, it did not fail. The woman, by emptying it, and grace, by replenishing it, seemed to have entered into a contest.

52. My undertaking is a vain undertaking if I strive to commit to memory every single thing which the Lord deigned to work through her. For very many things remain, by which she is remembered to have shone more widely not only while living, but also while sleeping in Christ. Yet while she drew out long sighs because of the delay of her reward and wasted away wholly with longing for heavenly joys, a young man appeared to her, tall in stature and bearing in his face a divine beauty. When the most holy woman feared him as he approached more closely and was apprehensive of his caress, he said: “Why do you disturb me with such groanings? Why do you waste away so with longing for me? Do you not know what rewards are laid up for you with me? Know that you are the foremost gem in the diadem upon my head.” With these words the young man vanished, leaving the blessed woman in ecstasy and joy alike. She revealed this vision only to two women close to her, making them swear not to presume to disclose the secret of the Lord her God while she remained subject to the laws of the frail world.

55. But when the long-sighed-for, long-awaited moment of her calling approached, the blessed woman passed unharmed through the storms of this great and spacious sea, and committed her weary limbs and nature confessing its mortality to ash and haircloth. The multitude of virgins, suddenly disturbed by the event, filled the cell with plaintive groanings and beat it with lamentations. Tears flowed, finding no comfort at all. At last the most blessed woman, lifting her eyes to heaven, exchanged the exile of this world for her homeland and labor for rest by a happy passage. She died on the Ides of August, leaving the sacred flock to benefit from the patronage of her who had ruled it by teaching and example. Nor is it right to believe that Christ’s daughter pleads in vain before Christ for her own, she through whose merits it is established that the dead were raised, demons expelled, troubled seas calmed, and those oppressed by various ailments restored to their former health—her Bridegroom, the Lord Jesus Christ, working through her, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: Here occur several unusual words which may perhaps delay a less learned reader. We have therefore judged it proper to transcribe here their explanation, taken from our Mabillon’s *Life of St Radegund*, vol. I of the *Acta Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*: for example, *felte*, *posticaria*, and *piratium*.

*Felte*, or *feltrum*, *filtrum*, is cloth or a garment made from wool and hair pressed together, not woven; a garment covered with gold and gems appears to be called *felis* by analogy with it. Mabillon, after the most learned Du Cange.

*Posticaria*, or *posticiaria*, derives from *posticum*, which, Papeas says in his *Vocabulary*, is a hidden door, so called because it is removed from public view. A *posticiaria* is a woman responsible for receiving things brought into the monastery and dispatching things sent out; among nuns she is commonly called *la tourière*, as our Menard demonstrates in *Concordia Regularum*, ch. 61, §14.

*Piratium* is a drink pressed from pears, commonly called by the Normans *du poiré*. Thus Du Cange.

When Hildebert says that this holy queen wore down her flesh by multiplied “disciplines,” one must not infer that voluntary self-flagellation by disciplinary scourging—certainly not introduced until the eleventh century by Dominic Loricatus and Peter Damian—was already in use in St Radegund’s time. He uses the word to suggest that the blessed queen omitted no means of wearing down rebellious flesh, including the discipline which he himself, in Book I, Letter 23, recommends frequently and severely for restraining the unbridled motions of desire.]

[Col. 0987]

## NOTICE

Since this little work on the Life of St Radegund was taken from one of the Poitevin manuscripts, we judged that it would not be out of place to append to it the preface found in another manuscript, kindly sent to us by Dom Leonard Senemaud, a monk of the monastery of St Cyprian at Poitiers, of our congregation. From him we also received the image of St Radegund placed at the beginning, graphically drawn under his care; and, after Stephanotius, he again collated the aforementioned manuscripts with the utmost accuracy. This preface appears to support the celebrated Poitevin tradition concerning the miracle of the oats: as they relate, and as is narrated here, the oats grew so suddenly and miraculously that St Radegund was hidden among them while fleeing King Chlothar, or Clothar, who wished to recall her from the monastery to the palace and her former marriage. Yet neither Gregory of Tours, nor Fortunatus—the holy queen’s closest friend—nor Baudonivia, her contemporary and intimate, a nun who described her life in minute detail, mentions this circumstance; nor does our Hildebert after them. Let the reader judge what is to be thought of such a tradition. The preface is as follows.

[Col. 0987A]

Because the miracles of the saints are to be recalled for the edification of the faithful, their recital ought not to be burdensome, since their imitation brings release from sins. Nor should it be imputed to rashness or presumption if deeds neglected or omitted through indolence are committed to writing, provided this is done in obedience. Therefore it is quite worthwhile not to pass over in silence how the most blessed Queen Radegund, having received the veil from blessed Medard, bishop of Noyon, made her way to Tours with her dearest and most intimate companions, Agnes and Disciola. There she visited with utmost devotion the thresholds of blessed Martin, archbishop of Tours, and went around them in what remained of her royal garments, which she had formerly worn at the palace. Then she came to Candes, eagerly desiring with all her effort to see the place in which Christ’s confessor Martin was raised from the *modius*.

At last, when she came to the estate of Suedas, situated in the Poitevin territory, she was told that the king wished to recall her to his marriage. As has been learned from the report of the ancients, the blessed woman immediately set out and met a certain farmer carrying oats. She addressed him in these words: “If anyone asks you whether you have seen someone passing through here the day before yesterday, firmly reply that no one has passed along this route since the hour when you were sowing these oats.” By divine providence the oats immediately grew so that the aforesaid queen could hide herself among them. Soon afterward the aforementioned king came to the said place and questioned the farmer, who shrewdly recounted in due order all that he had heard from the blessed queen. Then the king, having received the farmer’s answer and considered the course of the miracle, turned back, preferring to abandon his own wife rather than offend God’s mercy. For not many days later the blessed queen entered Poitiers. Her life, it is agreed, was such that no one acquainted with the deeds composed concerning her should hesitate to believe that, when she departed this life, entrance into the heavenly homeland stood open to her.

All the rest exactly as in the other manuscript.

[Col. 0987]

# LIFE OF SAINT HUGH, ABBOT OF CLUNY, WRITTEN BY HILDEBERT

(This Life has already been published from the Bollandists’ *Acta Sanctorum*. *Patrologia*, vol. CLIX, col. 857, under St Hugh of Cluny.)

[Col. 0989]

# THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT’S BOOK ON THE COMPLAINT AND CONFLICT OF FLESH AND SPIRIT, OR SOUL

## NOTICE

The first person, so far as I know, to publish this book on the complaint and conflict of flesh and spirit, or soul, was the Reverend Father Jacques Homey, an Augustinian of the community, as it is called, of Bourges, in 1684. He had brought it forth from Royal manuscript no. 223, which we were not permitted to inspect. We were, however, permitted to inspect another manuscript from the same Royal Library, no. 4103. We carefully collated it with the Saint-Victor manuscript no. 272 and the Peronne manuscript, in the library of the monastery of St Taurin at Évreux, no. 19, and report its variant readings below.

No one who has read even moderately in Hildebert’s other works, whether letters or sermons, can doubt that this book is genuinely Hildebert’s. The phrases, turns of expression, and almost everywhere identical thought, all savoring the same eloquence of Hildebert, prove it beyond doubt. Nevertheless, the most learned Dupin listed it among the doubtful minor works of Hugh Dufoliet in his *Index of Ecclesiastical Authors of the Twelfth Century*, Part II of his *History*, p. 951. That most discerning man would certainly not have done so had he possessed our rather large Corbie manuscript, in folio, at least six hundred years old, which contains the works of that Hugh. Among them there is found absolutely nothing which even by title approaches this conflict of flesh and spirit.

Moreover, Hugh was so far from being a monk of Corbie that his own minor works proclaim neither that he was ever a monk nor that he was Benedictine; rather, they everywhere identify him as a regular canon of St Augustine. In the chapter “On Temperance,” he declares that he and his followers must observe Augustine’s rule. As for this book, Homey assigned it first place among fragments of Hildebert’s minor works; and he published in his *Supplement to the Fathers* no work ascribed to Hildebert which we have not found in Hildebert manuscripts—and indeed in many and excellent ones. We have judged it preferable to publish it under the title *Conflict of Flesh and Soul* rather than *Spirit*, since he always introduces her—not him—as speaking in the feminine gender.

Perhaps Hildebert published this small work after the devastation inflicted by the consuls of Le Mans, flatterers of William Rufus, upon the church of Le Mans and the episcopal houses and estates, by sword and fire, as he says; and while, by order of the aforesaid king, he was kept in a most foul prison with feet and hands bound in iron. He composed this book, partly in prose and partly in verse, for his own consolation, just as Boethius, placed in hardship, once produced his book *On the Consolation of Philosophy*. Hence Hildebert begins this book as follows.

[Note: + Among the manuscript codices of the Royal English Library is codex no. 32, p. 239, entitled: “Dialogue of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, on the conflict of spirit and flesh, partly metrical and partly prose.” It is plainly the same work as that entitled “On the dissension of the inner and outer man, by Hildebert, archbishop of Tours,” among the manuscript works which Philip, bishop of Bayeux, gave to the abbey of Bec.]

[Col. 0989A]

My house had collapsed in a fire, and I was anxiously intent upon rebuilding it. I had ordered timber to be cut and squared, and expenses supplied for the work. I was wholly occupied with this; neglecting episcopal affairs, I measured now by sight, now by reed, where I should lay the foundations and how far I should extend the halls. While I thus labored as a curious surveyor, there appeared before my eyes a certain woman wearing the bearing of one mourning, as though something had happened contrary to her desire, and like one making complaint.

Her form was beyond description, her stature unknown, her vitality remarkable, and such as you would think promised immortality. Her expression was not always the same: sadly she looked toward earth; more cheerfully she looked toward heaven. She seemed to gaze more tenderly upon heaven, to long for heaven, and to remain with me unwillingly. At first she appeared whiter than snow and fit for royal embraces, displaying an inestimable beauty—but one that was precarious, obtained, I think, from elsewhere. Then she seemed stained by a certain squalor, such that you would not doubt water was needed to wash it away. In her hand was a little book; and in the book I remember that this poetic line was written:

> Whether you rejoice or grieve, desire or fear—what does it matter?

I was astonished, I confess, and silently resolved to wait and see what she would say and do. Then she said: “I wonder that you have so forgotten me, so forgotten our long-standing companionship, as to provide no dwelling for me. Yet you knew that I was a guest,

[Note: “Yet you knew that I was a guest.” Variant: “You knew that I was a guest.”]

and that, as you had learned from apostolic testimony,

[Note: “And that, as you had learned from apostolic testimony.” Variant: “And which, as you had learned from apostolic testimony.”]

‘we have here no lasting city’ (Heb. XIII, 14). This house, in which I suffer wearying and prison-like confinement, I know must be dissolved;

[Note: “Must be dissolved.” Variant: “That it is.”]

but when, I do not know. It is built from mud and, by the privilege of its material, declares its ruin. Everything constructed from such material hangs upon an uncertain hazard. Entering this tent of clay, I did not immediately understand its laws or heed its impending ruin. For I did not know under what servile condition the mistress was oppressed,

[Note: “Under what servile condition.” Variant: “Under what condition of a slave.”]

she who endured the continual attacks of those enemies whom to escape is to triumph gloriously.

“At length, however, as prolonged association teaches a guest the master’s secrets,

[Note: “As prolonged association teaches a guest the master’s secrets.” Variant: “Whom the master’s secrets …”]

more and more all things became apparent: I disliked everything, and observed there confused laws and inverted sovereignties—namely, that the mistress of the household was enslaved and the maidservant ruled. The maidservant, powerful to evil, had bewitched my freedom by such imperious charms

[Note: “Had bewitched my freedom.” Variant: “Bewitched my freedom.”]

that I obeyed whatever she commanded and followed her in every direction she went before me. She, indeed, insolent and mistrustful of the sincere governor,

[Note: “And mistrustful of the sincere governor.” Variant: “And mistrustful of the governor.”]

admitted for me [that is, apart from me], through her enticements, infamous lovers; and while I was subjected to the shame she suggested, she herself did not escape the shame either. From the time that this disgraceful alliance became known to me, I began to be ashamed of the deception and weary of the lodging. Yet it was not lawful to leave, and to escape the corruptors whom I had admitted. I grieved, I confess; hating that most sorrowful dominion, I rehearsed to you—who have no one equally intimate with me—the harsh stories of my confusion.

[Note: “I rehearsed the harsh stories of my confusion.” Variant: “I chose the harsh stories of my confusion.”]

“Do you not remember with what tearful complaint I once appealed to you? With what anxious groans I bewailed my freedom, wickedly lost? Perhaps your own sighs too have escaped you, and you do not remember with how abundant a flood of tears you lost buried cheerfulness, whenever, amid the other secrets of your chamber, I recalled to you my pitiable servitude. Consider, I beg you, what you promised me as I pleaded; with what hope you dried up the abundance of my tears. When witnesses had been sent far away, I told you by such complaints what I suffered and what I feared for the future:

> A guest in a narrow, fragile house, now, now about to fall,  
> I am oppressed under a servile condition.
>
> And as though imprisoned in heavy chains or shut in a jail,  
> I can scarcely hope that freedom remains.
>
> A grievous yoke I wear upon my neck, and in heavy fetters—  
> Alas for sorrow!—I am dragged toward death, though I shall not die.
>
> I remember that I was once accustomed to hope for great things,  
> While, O Christ, you were not another lover, but the one alone.
>
> Integrity, beauty, and fresh raiment were worthy  
> Of a lofty Bridegroom’s dowry, favor, and marriage-bed.
>
> A renowned dowry, eternal favor, an undefiled marriage-bed:  
> In these were fruit and honor and unending peace.
>
> Entirely pleasing, because wholly fresh, because white in dress,  
> Having won God by chastity, I hoped for heaven.
>
> I took the road to the heights; a broad way lay open,  
> And there was one to accompany me and to go before me.
>
> Alas for me! How teachable I was in being deceived; how ready  
> To undergo disgrace; how swift to my own ruin!
>
> My Bridegroom had fashioned the lodging with wondrous art,  
> And, received into it, I was chaste for a short time.
>
> For a crafty adulterer, though noble in origin, deceived me,  
> While the maidservant secretly unbarred the doors.
>
> I weep that through her enticement modesty perished  
> And that, guilty of shameful deeds, I succumbed.
>
> If I sigh for the Bridegroom’s favor, wrongly despised,  
> And in mind return with groaning to my first husband,
>
> She murmurs, contradicts me, commands that I use  
> Present delights, and seduces her mistress with wealth and reputation.
>
> By these perverse means she overturns a noble beginning  
> And, imperious, drags the wretched woman wherever she wills.
>
> This is the law of my lodging: as an exile, for the present  
> I am bound by these things; bitter day will dissolve this pact.
>
> I shall depart—but I know not where, I know not when;  
> And perhaps that day will be my last.
>
> A house, therefore, must be established in which, free from the sad  
> Prison, I may remain by a perpetual right.

I remember that you answered me, as I lamented these things, your voice impeded by sobbing:

> Dear companion, lay aside fear; cease your complaints.  
> Behold: I shall do what you desire and request.
>
> What stones, then, do you square? What timber  
> Do you order cut? What is that rod doing in your hands?
>
> The house for which I sigh does not rise in carved marble,  
> Nor is its structure bound with lime mixed with sand.
>
> No fir is fit for its beams; no stones for its columns;  
> It has absolutely nothing that can grow old.
>
> For everything … [lacuna] … but I sing vain things; winds carry  
> Empty words and prayers: the stone lives in that dwelling.

As I see myself reproved, my mind, full of cares, replies:

[Note: “My mind, full of cares.” Printed reading: *mens curis pletia*; variant: *mens circum plena*.]

> This time is not sufficient; it does not serve my wishes.

Having lamented these things [Note: [Col. 0991] “Lamenting these things.” [Col. 0992D] “Lamenting these things, she…”], she fell silent, intending, as I think, to say something further, had she not perceived from the cast of my eyes [Note: [Col. 0991] “had perceived from the cast [of my eyes].” [Col. 0992D] “had perceived from the movements [of my eyes].”] that I was occupied with matters I had undertaken. For I was occupied, nor did her accusatory speech wholly recall my feeling from the present enterprises. Yet I began silently to wonder who this might be—she who boasted of intimacy with me, who disdained a prison, who dreamed of palaces. At last, turning my eyes back to her, I addressed her sadness thus:

“Your bearing offers me many things worthy of inquiry, and the sadness of your countenance many more; none of these, I think, should be passed over carelessly—provided, however, that you first show me who you are, or what your name is. Desiring to learn this from you, I promise to be a most attentive hearer: my alert ears and fixed gaze upon you will show that my mind has undertaken instruction; and, lest any signs of a distracted mind remain [Note: [Col. 0993] “signs of a distracted mind.” [Col. 0994D] “by the judgment of the mind.”], I throw away this rod, collect my scattered spirit, and give my clients a holiday for the day [Note: [Col. 0993] “a holiday for the day.” [Col. 0994D] “a day’s holiday.”]. Whatever it was that held me anxiously occupied is deferred until tomorrow. Come then: while there is leisure, do not delay to explain first who you are, and then whatever is troubling you.”

At this she, as though indignant because I had not immediately recognized her, rebuked my slowness in both look and voice:

“I was indeed complaining that you were preparing no dwelling whatever for me, a guest and one now about to leave the tent of this pilgrimage, and providing no refuge. But a graver and more just complaint remained: that the memory of our companionship, born with you, had thus slipped from you, as though, in accordance with the ravings of poets, an infernal Lethe had wrested from you the remembrance of heavenly things. You even ask who I am, as though forgetfulness of my services seemed too slight an injury to you unless you also confessed that you did not know your own worshipper.

[Col. 0993C] “Alas for me! Where have the services born with you gone? Where has that companionship turned aside which is neither begun nor dissolved by human choice? To what end has the covenant vanished which nature dictated, which a most secret law ordained, which we struck before birth, which was known to the mother before her children? Who among fickle friends, who test fortune, has experienced a faith so treacherous? Finally, not to know me, who have never existed without you—what else is this than to live like a beast and deny that one is a human being? Show, if you can, what you have done without me, what you have determined without my knowledge. I know the thoughts of your heart; I know the secrets of your chamber. If you write, I move your fingers; if you speak, I open your mouth. The ordinances and expenditures of the household, and likewise the laws concerning delinquent servants, are found with me and are promulgated through me.

“If your household obeys you more carefully, know that this is due to my authority, not to the loyalty of your dependants. Their loyalty will depart when I depart; and when you are to be buried, the friendship you now imagine genuine and not feigned will prove false when you are buried. None of those hands which now flatter you and now sit beside you when you are sick will escape this fate. Yet, lest you expect no service from them at all, they will bury you, in order also to display their contempt for an empty corpse; memory will withdraw from your breast and the burial-place from their sight alike.

[Col. 0994A] “Perhaps, however, they will weep—not because I have left you so soon, but because I have left you so late. They will indeed weep; yet not so much on your account as because they will find nothing about you to plunder. They will weep, I say, but only if the people look at them, if he whom they think will be your successor sees them. Nor should you wonder that those to whom you may have been a harsh master will discharge your funeral rites with languid and listless concern [Note: [Col. 0993] “will discharge the funeral rites.” [Col. 0994D] “will render services.”]. From the moment I depart, you will bring weariness even to true friends and become food for worms. No one is so close to you that the sight of your corpse will not weary him after three days. To behold the remains of so unfortunate a friend is matter for revulsion.

[Col. 0994B] “Do you then recognize me, without whom you never enter house or chamber? Do you recognize, I say, a companion so constantly present to you, so friendly, so united with you? Do you recognize her who fills, rules, and possesses your whole self? Pray, recognize me; it is mine that you have not yet wasted away in hunger [Note: [Col. 0993] “that you have not yet wasted away in hunger.” [Col. 0994D] “that you have not yet wasted away in disgrace.”]. You are inhuman if you deny services so many and so great; you are more witless than a beast if you do not know one so near, your nearest neighbor. But if reason has been so extinguished in you, if kindness has been so strangled, what remains except that we should attend the funeral of virtue also with its due obsequies?”

> Alas! What a shameful crime, what must be restrained,  
> How discordant with the soul, how shameful!  
> Worldly care, stirring the agitation of the heart,  
> Teaches one to assail right and honour.
>
> [Col. 0994C] Virtue is a thing far too abject, a disgrace to a man;  
> Crime is an honour [Note: [Col. 0993] “Virtue is a disgrace to a man; crime an honour.” [Col. 0994D] “This verse is lacking through a lacuna in the Évreux manuscript.—Virtue is a crime against every honour.” Codex Victorinus, 272.],  
> Virtue is a cheap pinnacle, a dowry without fruit:  
> You scarcely please with impunity, scarcely without grief.
>
> You are saleable goodness, useless, burdensome  
> Merchandise, courting only the great;  
> Easily cast off, hard to resume,  
> You vanish like a wisp of smoke.
>
> There is none whom you please with a simple wish,  
> None who grieves when you are injured, no witness being present,  
> None who loves or protects you freely,  
> None who promises patronage.
>
> High praise is wealth; poverty is crime;  
> Wickedness prevails, honourableness is despised.
>
> [Col. 0994D] Ah! Now laws threaten the innocent;  
> Those who dare crime win sceptres;  
> Ah! With what anxious labour each person  
> Hastens to a physician, from love of the flesh.
>
> Of the soul’s diseases there is no complaint;  
> Slow healing follows the sick woman [Note: [Col. 0993] “follows the sick woman.” [Col. 0994D] “follows the woman who has gone forth.”].
>
> Whither shall I return, I who am so faithful a companion,  
> What bitter cup shall I then drink,
>
> [Col. 0995A] You do not consider, O man; and what you admit,  
> You neither know as your companion nor revere.  
> Thus now, thus even now [Note: [Col. 0995] “Thus now, thus even now.” [Col. 0996D] “If not thus even now.”], so many vows of its own  
> Are known to you, yet do not help the soul.
>
> Be forewarned: after this dwelling [Note: [Col. 0995] “this dwelling.” [Col. 0996D] “this abode.”]  
> A sad habitation will swiftly succeed.

“And excellently, I say, I know you; and I am ashamed of my slowness, since I had to be prompted by familiar signs to recognize my one and only [or “beloved”] companion. From them I have also learned what has driven the serenity from your countenance: the dwelling that you desire [Note: [Col. 0995] “which you desire.” [Col. 0996D] “which it desires.”]. For I know that our inward person is in bitterness and, as the Apostle says, ‘groaning, labours in birth until it is delivered from the slavery of corruption and passes into the freedom of the glory of the children of God’ (Rom. 8:21).

[Col. 0995B] “Likewise, because this earthly house is perishing, it seeks an incorruptible house, ‘a house not made with hands but eternal in the heavens’ (2 Cor. 5:1). How blessed it is, indeed, and with what festal joy it resounds, it belongs neither to the present time nor to our capacity to unfold. But I should like you to explain why you accuse so harshly this little man whom you carry about, and by whose attendant’s seductions you lament that you have been deceived and corrupted. Nor do I ask merely why this old and ruinous workhouse displeases you, or why you wish to be released from these straits. For I know—know well—that you hope for a most spacious dwelling, that there has been promised to you a city most spacious

[Col. 0995C] and most beautiful, most broad and most joyful, most holy and most secluded, most orderly and most peaceful, most firm and most secure, most rich and most radiant. Suspended in desire for it, you despise the workshops of the flesh; at last you sigh for the day, murmuring to me: ‘I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ’ (Phil. 1:23); to be with Christ is far better.

“But I am particularly moved by this: you ascribe the whole cause of your corruption to the outward man, appearing to complain and grieve over intimacy with the flesh as Hercules did over his stepmother’s poisoned garment. Yet he received death through a bodily covering in one way, and you received corruption through a fleshly covering in another [Note: [Col. 0995] “Yet he received death in one way, and you corruption through a fleshly covering in another.” [Col. 0996D] “Yet he in one way—indeed you in another—received it through an incarnate covering.”]. He, plainly, furnished his garment with no means of harm, no source of poison; that which overthrew Alcides [Hercules]

[Col. 0995D] came from elsewhere, not from Alcides. But you use your body as the instrument of those things that harm you, as a master uses a servant, as an artisan an implement. Did you not yourself confess that this follower of yours is given life by you, moved to all things through you, and is pus and ashes without you? Is it not yours, by reason, to choose what is better; to will and not will, to love and hate; and, through these affections, to move and carry about your faithful servant toward things good or evil?

“Who raves so desperately as to accuse the doors of a house of crime or wickedness because their master goes through them to commit sacrilege or theft? Why then do you stain another’s innocence with the paint of your own crime [Note: [Col. 0995] “with the paint of your crime.” [Col. 0996D] “with the juice of your crime.”]? Why do you speak so ill of my present evil, while so indulgently overlooking your own; why do you recount it so mournfully and excuse it so compassionately?

“Yet you have read Solomon, who says of those who weigh their own goods and evils differently from those of others: ‘Weight and weight,

[Col. 0996B] scale and scale [Vulgate: “measure and measure”], both are abominable before God’ (Prov. 20:10). What then is your complaint against me, or how does this fleshly lodging defile spiritual purity? I am eager to hear. Many things concerning me are better known to you; whatever they may be, I prefer to learn and correct them rather than flatter and applaud myself with false righteousness. I willingly hear my error, though not gladly from the one who recounts it; that man is a friend who seeks to remove the fault, not to insult the faulty person. If, therefore, some argument supports you, let it come forth; do not torment one who waits by delay, for every delay by which instruction in goodness is deferred is long.”

Then she, as if summoning me to patience, soothed my anxiety with this song:

> Many leaders of Latium endured much for freedom:  
> They exposed children to exile and their own heads to the sword.  
> Happy they would be, if thus the grievous yoke were shaken off  
> And nothing more miserable followed the miserable.
>
> But harsh slavery oppressed ill-freed necks,  
> And each bore a hundred masters in his own crimes.  
> If it pleased them to live under true freedom [Note: [Col. 0995] “If it pleased them to live under true freedom.” [Col. 0996D] “If it pleased them to live for true freedom.”],  
> They would be ashamed to serve not a human being but sin.
>
> For that slavery passes away and is relieved at least by death;  
> This is eternal and gains no end through its end.  
> What then will you say is not to be borne with an even mind [Note: [Col. 0995] “with an uneven mind.” [Col. 0996D] “with an unequal mind.”],  
> Provided that you cast off the master and the dreadful yoke [Note: [Col. 0995] “Provided that you cast off the master and the yoke.” [Col. 0996D] “Provided that you spurn both master and yoke.”]?
>
> [Col. 0996D] Lest you ever bear this master, remember to bear me;  
> Let Peter’s patience be an example to you.
>
> The Rock had entrusted Peter with the highest pontificate,
>
> [Col. 0997A] The watch over the flock, and the keys of heaven.  
> Peter, now exalted by apostolic honour,  
> Shone deservedly in signs, powers, and speech:  
> The lame had received back their steps; Tabitha, life;  
> Sapphira had already paid for her crime by the loss of life;  
> Garment and shadow had already put diseases to flight [Note: [Col. 0997] “shadow had put diseases to flight.” [Col. 0998D] “garment and shadow had put diseases to flight.”],  
> And sacred prayer had raised paralytics.
>
> Yet Paul’s correction pleased this—this Peter;  
> Nor did Peter cast Saul’s crimes in Paul’s teeth [Note: [Col. 0997] “Saul’s crimes.” [Col. 0998D] “Paul’s crimes.”].
>
> Therefore, while I teach what corruption is drawn forth,  
> What death comes to me from you, bear both patiently.  
> He mocks good character who does not patiently endure a teacher;  
> To despise him enriches the mind with guilt.

“As I see, you have endured my sung complaint with less displeasure; but it has drawn a wrinkle upon you that I ascribed all my calamities to this fleshly lodging, accused it of shameful pleasures, and wept over the freedom smeared with its ink. You are angry and astonished to be called the author of these things because it seems to you that I use the body as an instrument for them in no other way than a master uses a servant or an artisan an implement.

[Col. 0997B] “But the most illustrious founders of the Christian faith thought and decreed far otherwise. From consideration of their testimonies you will readily learn who is first at fault, how much guilt is to be charged especially to one party and how much to both together. And lest the beginnings of such calamities escape you as unknown, I shall begin a little further back, if you are not weary [Note: [Col. 0997] “a little further back, if you are not weary.” [Col. 0998D] “a little further back, nor let it weary you.”].

“Before the life-giving ordinance of fasting was broken by deadly food [Note: [Col. 0997] “the life-giving ordinance of fasting.” [Col. 0998D] “the life-giving ordinance.”], the inhabitants of Paradise suffered no distress in Paradise,

[Col. 0997C] and there was nothing from the flesh to assail the soul, nothing from the soul to offend the Creator—nothing, I say, nothing whatever, by which either their delights might be diminished or their innocence broken. Of their prosperity and glory, and likewise their righteousness, Augustine says in *The City of God* [Note: [Col. 0997D] Book XIV, ch. 26, and elsewhere at length.]:

> “Man lived in Paradise as he wished, so long as he wished what God commanded. He lived enjoying God, by whose goodness he was good. He lived without any want, having it in his power always to live thus.”

Likewise, against Julian: “Far be it,” he says, “that we should believe there was anything which could sting our sense, inwardly or outwardly, with pain; weary it with labour; confound it with shame; burn it with heat;

[Col. 0997D] bind it with cold; or offend it with horror!”

“Behold, you see that nothing innate within, nothing presented from without,

[Col. 0998A] caused those inhabitants of Paradise to depart either from the glory of the creature or from reverence toward the Creator. Yet against this harmony of flesh and spirit, against blessings flowing together from every side, certain external enticements rose up: namely, the serpent more cunning than all living creatures, and the fruit beautiful to behold and pleasant for food.

“By these enemies a nature more fragile was tempted, and a sex weaker to resist [Note: [Col. 0997] “weaker to resist.” [Col. 0998D] “more fragile to resist.”]. For our flesh was tempted, woman was tempted, and in the same person the condition was tested which might yield to hunger or be deceived by simplicity. It was difficult [Note: [Col. 0997] “It was difficult.” [Col. 0998D] “Nor was it difficult.”] for one woman to be surrounded by so many persuasions, when both food acted against her and cunning pleaded its case.

“Thus the flesh, pleased and stirred by new counsels,

[Col. 0998B] adopted a new audacity for itself. Being itself now provoked to eat, it provoked the spirit to consent. Hence, Catholic authority testifies, from the subduing flesh and the subdued spirit, as though from husband and wife, was generated that first sin through which no infant is declared clean, even one whose life upon earth is but a day old. From that time onward fleshly enticements made a perpetual compact with familiarity with the flesh. This old fellowship, begun in Paradise [Note: [Col. 0997] “This old [thing] and in Paradise.” [Col. 0998D] “The old man and in Paradise.”], adhered firmly and so securely that all posterity is still held bound in its chains.

“One scarcely triumphs over pleasure when pleasure has once triumphed over him; it is difficult to resist it because it became superior in the first conflict. For enemies are emboldened by successes, and having been victorious brings another victory in its train.

[Col. 0998C] Moreover, if anything is pleasant through use, we naturally incline to it without compulsion [Note: [Col. 0997] “we naturally incline to it without compulsion.” [Col. 0998D] “we incline naturally to it as a gratuity.”]. Hence the flesh sighs for fleshly delights, and the more gratifying experience of them is, the more intemperate its appetite.

“This law of the members neither baptism effaces, nor time destroys, nor will erases. It is written in indissoluble ink [Note: [Col. 0997D] Homeyer in his notes: “He alludes,” he says, “to Job 13:26: ‘For you write bitter things against me.’ On these words St Gregory, *Moralia*, ch. 23: ‘What we say passes away; what we write remains.’”], and children unwillingly bear its decree, to which their parents willingly subjected themselves. Sacred washing remedies its guilt indeed; but that it itself remains, the groans and complaints of holy souls attest. He who was ‘caught up to the third heaven and heard secret words which it is not permitted a man to speak’ (2 Cor. 12:4) nevertheless complains that he feels

[Col. 0998D] this law in his members, resisting the law of his mind and leading him captive under the law of sin (Rom. 7:23).

[Col. 0999A] “Of this same law, that Augustine who is familiar to you [Note: [Col. 0999D] Thus Hildebert congratulates himself that St Augustine was familiar to him; this is chiefly demonstrated by his very frequent citations of Augustine in the theological treatise to be set below, by which he is eager to support almost his entire teaching.], speaks against the heretic Julian as follows: ‘This law of sin, which is in the members of this body of death, is both remitted through spiritual regeneration and remains in mortal flesh: remitted, certainly, because its guilt is dissolved by the sacrament through which unbelievers are reborn; but it remains because its desires work, against which even believers contend.’

“Therefore, though you surpass Aristotle in sophistries, Ulysses in cunning, and Simon in deceits [Note: [Col. 1000D] Homeyer conjectures that Simon the Sophist is mentioned here, concerning whom Aristophanes says: “When they have escaped Simon, the wolves immediately go ravening.”], you will nevertheless try in vain to persuade this [body] that it is free from seduction, whose lusts are both sustained by nature’s debt and restrained by the help of grace. Yet I have no complaint against you concerning its guilt. To complain of a sickness for which a complete remedy has been provided in the sacred font is to disparage the saving medicine.

[Col. 0999B] “But if I denied that I grieve over your daily assaults and your unrestrained shamelessness, my secret groans and the sighs that draw forth tears—of which no witness is better than the people—would proclaim me a liar [Note: [Col. 0999] “of which no witness is better than the people.” [Col. 1000D] “of which there is no better witness to proclaim me a liar.”]. For I complain; burdened heavily by you, doing not what I wish but doing the thing I do not wish, I lament daily with Paul: ‘Unhappy man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?’ (Rom. 7:24).

“At that age I was wholly ignorant of this, because both the sting of sin and the use of reason lay hidden together. A virgin bride, I gloried in a virgin bridegroom, who might call me whenever he wished to those weddings where the choir of apostles sits as best man, where David is the singer, where the instruments of angels resound. That quiet bridal chamber, guardian of chastity, was prepared and

[Col. 0999C] hoped for me: there is chaste offspring [Note: [Col. 0999] “where there is chaste offspring.” [Col. 1000D] “where there is a chaste concubine.”], no multitude of flames steals the husband’s favour, no bill of divorce exists, and the bridegroom binds the bride to himself so chastely that he knows neither the lust of embraces nor the corruption of touch.

“Wretched me! While I was girding myself for the solemnities of such a marriage, you—you, I say—became to me ‘a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence’ (1 Pet. 2:8); you ‘became a serpent in the way and a horned viper in the path’ (Gen. 49:17). For when the slumbering faculty of choice awoke, contempt for lusts presented itself to you and enfolded itself around you as pigs offer themselves to a wallow [Note: [Col. 0999] “presented itself.” [Col. 1000D] “obliterated itself.”]. You made yourself too hospitable, too obliging toward them; you wholly rejoiced

[Col. 0999D] at their arrival, lavishly accommodating that ancient friendship which you had made with them beneath the fig tree and confirmed by an unshaken decree.

“Mindful of this covenant of yours, they learned to run together from every side, like dripping water to a bilge,

[Col. 1000A] toward this lowest and weakest wantonness of the flesh. Some indeed made an irresistible assault upon you through bodily senses, others through the images of thoughts that came before you. Hence this fleshly and muddy lodging, disturbed, breathed out into me, shame upon shame, a stench of stirred-up mud; nor could I avoid sensing the pestilential air of an agitated wallow while sharing a dwelling with filthy swine.

“Moreover, this prison is compacted from matter to which the flame of nearby pleasures readily clings. Who, then, doubts that one imprisoned in it is heated when a neighbouring blaze casts ashes and sparks upon him? You see, therefore, by what lust the flesh is moved as though male, by what wickedness such a husband extorts the spirit’s consent,

[Col. 1000B] and what offspring is generated by them both. You see, I say, how an alien stench blows upon me and what fumes I endure from the fire brought near. You see this and are angry if I complain of the frying-pan of flesh, in which the strength of my fat has been dried up and ‘my bones have dried up like fuel for the fire’ (Ps. 101:4, LXX).

“What wonder if, on account of your wantonness [Note: [Col. 0999] “if on account of your wantonness.” [Col. 1000D] “if on account of your lacuna.”], in which I fear to enter with muddy swine, I wish to leave? ‘For I wish and desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ’ (Phil. 1:23); for to be with Christ is far better. You will find that better souls have desired this also, and that they have borne witness to my assertions both by experience and in speech.

“For what else did David seek when he said,

[Col. 1000C] ‘The tribulations of my heart have multiplied; deliver me from my necessities’ (Ps. 24:12), except that grace should restrain the flesh, which naturally lusts against the spirit, since will could not restrain it? What is clearer than the Apostle’s statement: ‘The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh’ (Gal. 5:19)? I shall not be weary of adding to what has been said how many and how great blessed actions this conflict of yours against me nullifies, or what joys it interrupts with frequent troubles. And lest, being overfond of delights, you should disdain a longer prose account, I shall discharge my promises in metrical brevity.

“But what you say—that it is mine by reason to choose what is better, to will and not will, to love and hate, and through my own affections [Note: [Col. 0999] “through my own affections.” [Col. 1000D] “through these affections.”] to move and carry about my faithful servant toward things good

[Col. 1000D] or evil—if you attend more carefully, it convicts you of ingratitude and impatience. For all this serves and works for your salvation no otherwise than the stern and morose correction of a husband serves a wife who either takes correction badly

[Col. 1001A] [Note: [Col. 1001] “who takes correction badly.” [Col. 1002D] “who is addressed fairly.”] or is proud. For commands come before you against the poisons of pleasures that meet you: harmful things are described and wholesome things proclaimed. Therefore, if within the bounds of this life [Note: [Col. 1001] “the bounds of this life.” [Col. 1002D] “the bounds of this diet.”] you restrain desire, sound health, capable of change [Note: [Col. 1001] “health capable of change.” [Col. 1002D] “unchangeable.”], promises and pledges to remain with you forever. But if you reject even what is permitted or set your hand to forbidden things, this corruptible will not ‘put on incorruption, nor this mortal immortality’ (1 Cor. 15:53). If this has not yet satisfied you, I shall answer you more fully another time when you inquire.”

> The power of the human soul claims seven operations for you:  
> It gives life, senses, embraces diverse arts,  
> Corrects excesses, pursues virtues, directs  
> [Col. 1001B] Its gaze toward Deity itself, and rejoices in it.
>
> The first is also present in seeds; brute animals  
> Share another; two, three, belong to our own nature,  
> And [perhaps: “toward”] the heavenly realm; yet heavenly things [Note: [Col. 1001] “yet heavenly things.” [Col. 1002D] “not heavenly things.”] come first.
>
> From the first operation bodies are nourished and grow;  
> From it come vigour, union, combination, motion,  
> Rest, form, and a certain harmony.
>
> From the next it touches, sees, hears, tastes, smells,  
> Hates, loves, seeks what suits it, avoids what is contrary,  
> Dissolves into sleep, wanders in dreams with the mind,  
> Remembers the past, attends to what is to come, and performs  
> Many things that are performed not by sense but by reason [Note: [Col. 1001] “many things that are performed not by sense but by reason.” [Col. 1002D] “many things that sense does, but not reason.”].
>
> The third traverses liberal and other arts,  
> Whatever talent or instruction supplies,
>
> [Col. 1001C] Gathers them, and clings to minds through varied advancement.
>
> The fourth teaches one to renounce forbidden things, and every guilt [Note: [Col. 1001] “forbidden things, and every guilt.” [Col. 1002D] “recalls [one] from forbidden things and sluggish guilt.”];  
> Then one begins to know oneself,  
> To strive toward and pass into a new beauty.
>
> From the fifth we learn to be held by nature’s law,  
> To shun things not permitted through love of virtue,  
> And to abstain from some permitted things, even unwitnessed [Note: [Col. 1001] “some [permitted things], even unwitnessed.” [Col. 1002D] “some, even without a witness.”].
>
> The sixth carries the unstained soul, almost equal to the heavenly beings,  
> Into sight of the sun and the highest light.
>
> The seventh binds it and constrains it with a steadfast love;
>
> Given in marriage to God [Note: [Col. 1001] “given to God.” [Col. 1002D] “placed beside God.”], it considers what dowry it now beholds,  
> What bridal chambers, what adornments, what festivals make it radiant.
>
> Who may say, “Come, beautiful one” [Note: [Col. 1001] “Who may say, ‘Come, beautiful one.’” [Col. 1002D] “Who may say, ‘Come, bride.’”]? Blessed and greater souls have said it;
>
> [Col. 1001D] Yet they possessed neither such virtue  
> Nor such speech as might enable them to disclose it:  
> The hidden reward exceeds understanding and merit.

“If you deny that these operations are impeded by the desires of the flesh,

[Col. 1002A] then either you have fallen wholly below humanity or advanced above humanity—you alone are so freely blessed that you do not know the lust which wages war against the aforesaid operations with a numerous army and triumphs through diverse impulse [Note: [Col. 1001] “triumphs through impulse.” [Col. 1002D] “triumphs through effect.”]. For it does not have equal licence in every soul; rather, each soul preserves or loses its freedom according as it resists or favours the enticements that encounter it.

“Nor are all the operations assaulted by the same trouble at the same time [Note: [Col. 1001] “all at the same time, nor every…” [Col. 1002D] “all at the same time, nor all…”]. Some are choked at their birth like grain in the blade; others, already advanced, wither like ears of grain burned by excessive heat [Note: [Col. 1001] “burned, wither.” [Col. 1002D] “burned, are emptied.”]. There is also that which attacks them inwardly and that which destroys them outwardly. That these things may become clearer to you, I shall not be weary of explaining, as it is granted me from above, the assaults and ruin

[Col. 1002B] of each operation.

“Our first operation, then, is giving life; the second, sensation; the third, art; the fourth, correction; the fifth, virtue; the sixth, contemplation; the seventh, rest. Antiquity, having carefully investigated the force of each, gave them these names. The first of them, the more pleasing it is to the flesh, is the safer from the flesh’s unrest. For the flesh loves the office of giving life and has made so great a peace with it that, if it knows anything contrary to it, it both recoils from it with implacable hatred and opposes it with anxious concern.

“Hence even those who cry with Paul, ‘I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ’ (Phil. 1:23), nevertheless fear death because the flesh naturally rejoices in this office of the soul. Christ had come to die,

[Col. 1002C] and nevertheless said: ‘Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me’ (Matt. 26:38). Likewise, when he had withdrawn from his disciples to pray at greater length, he stirred himself by the anxiety of the Passion even to a sweat of blood [Note: [Col. 1001] “stirred himself by the anxiety of the Passion.” [Col. 1002D] “was disturbed by the anxiety of the Passion.”]. In this statement, certainly, venerable authority handed down that nothing else is to be understood except a certain sharing in the life of the flesh: this was so present by natural law that it did not impede the good of obedience.

“This being so, sudden troubles often break into your great love and close covenant; the flesh, stirred to hatred of life, solicits the spirit’s consent. For, just as it is ruinously moved by desire for enticements, so by the anxiety of cares,

[Col. 1002D] through which that huntress after pleasures, fearing to be long subject to them and long wearied, gradually begins to be weary of life and is pleased to renounce the grace of giving life, whose services become bitter through mingled inconveniences.

[Col. 1003A] Thus, fired by hatred of life, it breathes out certain, as it were, torches against its guest, the soul, so that the soul too may grow warm and burn in the same fire. The pilot of a ship scarcely, or never, escapes the stench of its bilge; it is less difficult for the disposition with which the little ship of the body is utterly filled [Note: [Col. 1003] “it is less difficult for the disposition.” [Col. 1004A] “it is less difficult for the disposition.”] not to reach the upright spirit, when he, drenched in it, so carnally complies with the commands of the flesh that he thinks it a great service to oppose that giving of life for which he considers living a great punishment.

“From this is born a shameful and ridiculous appetite for death, an evil offspring which, in the manner of the viper, commonly chokes and destroys its parents. Your own times have had some whom grief at lost money drove either into the waters or to the noose. Why should I speak of the ancients, whose similar madness provoked poets not at all to be silent in their truthful assertions [Note: [Col. 1003] “whose similar madness…” [Col. 1004A] “whose deaths, provoked by a similar madness…”; [Col. 1003] “madness, truthful assertions.” [Col. 1004A] “madness, avenging assertions.”]? Do you not recall that you yourself testified to this when you sang the following verses concerning the origin of an intended death?”

> Though the flesh is pleased by what is given life and loves  
> This service of the soul, yet it happens that, broken  
> By long evils, it disdains life, renounces its years,  
> Prefers to die once rather than many times,  
> And to be snatched away by final death rather than survive so many deaths.
>
> But though flesh presses for these things, the will is not a murderer  
> Until the spirit—like a wife—turns and favours it [Note: [Col. 1003] “and the wifely [spirit] favours it.” [Col. 1004A] “and [the spirit] favours its wives.”].  
> Subdued by these goads and by flattering strife,  
> Transgression is generated; for while the flesh cries out  
> And the spirit hears it, guilt is created by consent;  
> And in creating this wickedness, flesh becomes husband, spirit wife.

[Col. 1003]

# The Moral Philosophy of the Venerable Hildebert, Bishop of Le Mans, on the Honourable and the Useful

Much enlarged and corrected beyond the earlier edition, published from a manuscript codex of the Library of the Seminary at Padua and illustrated with notes. (G)*

## To the Most Distinguished Man

Joseph Valentinelli,  
Prefect of the Library of St Mark at Venice

This little work  
of the Venerable Hildebert,  
recovered from the parchment leaves  
of the Library of the Seminary at Padua,  
is most willingly dedicated, given, and offered  
by Vincenzo De Vit.

## Preface to the Reader

What I had intended, having at last found a suitable opportunity, I now fulfil as promised and present entire before your eyes, kindly Reader: the little work of the Venerable Hildebert entitled *Moral Philosophy on the Honourable and the Useful*. Eleven years ago I had already given a specimen of it, copied almost word for word from this same codex, from which certain sayings of Varro had been drawn and published by me in print long ago [Note: [Col. 1003] See *Sayings of M. Terentius Varro, for the most part unpublished, edited from the manuscript codex of the Library of the Seminary at Padua and illustrated with commentary*, etc., Padua, 1843, Seminary Press, octavo. There, pp. 82–94, after a few preliminary remarks, you will find this specimen taken from the chapter on fortitude and security and collated with the edition.].

What I had there prefaced concerning both this codex and this little work of Hildebert, I shall briefly repeat here, and shall explain the merits of this edition of ours in comparison with the others.

Formerly this codex belonged, as I learned later, to a certain Conrad Celtis, a learned man, from whom it passed into the possession of Antonio Querengo. In Querengo’s house it had already been seen and consulted by the celebrated copyist John of Rhodes [Col. 1005] [Note: See Thomasinus, *De bibliothecis Patavinis manuscriptis*, p. 87; Valentinelli, *Della biblioteca del seminario di Padova*, p. 32; and also Varro’s *Sentences*, cited below, which are prefaced by a fuller description of this codex, pp. 12–15.]. Finally, together with many other books, it passed into the library of the Seminary of Padua, where it is still preserved under no. CI. Its date, as we there likewise stated, is assigned to the thirteenth century. The form of the script comes very close to rounded Roman minuscule; the initial letters of chapters, headings, and marks placed at the ends of these chapters are painted in red and blue. In the same colours, according to preference, are likewise written the names of the authors whose words are quoted.

This codex contains several works, partly excerpted and partly copied almost entire, from various Latin writers. We have likewise listed their sequence there. At the very beginning, among them, the foremost place is occupied by a work entitled: *Introduction to Moral Philosophy*. Although it is presented here under that title and without its author’s name, that it is the work which others—as reported above—call *Moral Philosophy, On the Honourable and the Useful*, and that it is by the same author, namely the venerable bishop Hildebert, of whom we possess several other works, has been shown with sufficiently strong arguments by the distinguished editor of his works [Note: Here is the title of that edition, which we have adopted in our own: *The Works, Both Published and Unpublished, of the Venerable Hildebert, First Bishop of Le Mans and Then Archbishop of Tours. To Which Have Been Added the Minor Works of Marbod, Bishop of Rennes, Hildebert’s Contemporary*, etc., edited by Dom Antoine Beaugendre, priest and monk of the Congregation of Saint-Maur. Paris, 1708, large folio. The work in question appears in this edition—which alone we shall cite—from p. 959 onward.]. We have thought it proper to reproduce here also his prefatory notice, so that the merits of our codex may subsequently appear more clearly.

## Notice Prefixed to This Work by Its First Editor

“959–960 We recovered this treatise from an excellent Colbert manuscript, no. 2662, about six hundred years old. It contained the letters of the Venerable Hildebert; immediately after the last of these followed, in the same hand and script, this work, which, considering its style and the turns of expression that Hildebert frequently employs in his letters, we judged to be his genuine composition. We further judged it to be precisely the work of which Hildebert speaks in Letter 12 of Book I, addressed to Henry I, King of England, in which he tries to console him for the unhappy drowning of his sons. Having there urged him to steadfastness, he gives a full and elegant description of the principles of the true sage:

> ‘When these principles, that is, had come into my hands in copied pages, I resolved to set them forth before the public gaze, fearing the envy of posterity if I begrudged them to posterity. I therefore wrote them out for those who neither use prosperity with reverence nor endure adversity unmoved.’

This agrees with what he writes in Letter 3 of the same Book I to Adela, wife of Stephen, Count Palatine of Blois. There he urges her, while she holds the helm of the county of Blois during her husband’s absence, to clemency, which human reason alone recommends. He asserts that Reason itself has published for princes concise chapters on clemency taken from Seneca, and that it loved a brevity not obscure, so that those occupied with great affairs might not tire of reading them. Now, in this treatise, Hildebert employs, above all other authors, Seneca’s sayings, chiefly drawn from the book *On Clemency*. We believe that he compiled it from several pagan books while still a young man devoted to humane letters and with those books at hand; this can be demonstrated from his frequent citations of poets. We collated this treatise with another manuscript from the celebrated Parisian library of Saint-Victor, no. 759. We found that it differs from the Colbert manuscript only in being somewhat fuller, and in that at certain, though very few, places we rejoiced to find some sayings of pagan writers supported and, as it were, consecrated by testimonies of Holy Scripture. We adhered to it all the more willingly because we judged that it had a closer affinity with the metrical treatise, *On the Four Virtues of an Honourable Life*, which we found among Hildebert’s minor poetical works in the very ancient Colbert manuscript no. 6327, and which we considered should immediately be appended to that book *On the Honourable and the Useful*.

“Who is denoted by the letter R, by which he marks the excellent and exalted man to whom he sends this treatise, I would not venture to decide. Yet not without probability I would conjecture that he is Reginald, a monk of Saint Augustine, to whom Hildebert addressed Letter 15 of Book III, thanking him because he had kindly received certain propositions—the daughters, as he calls them, of his little talent—and had even inserted them among his own works.

“Moreover, there is no doubt that through frequent reading of Seneca, Cicero, Sallust, and the other masters of ancient eloquence, whom Hildebert had diligently studied in his youth, and from whose chief sayings—as also from celebrated poets—he had compiled this treatise, he formed for himself that concise and elegant style, saying much in few words and scattering fine wit everywhere, which all learned men hitherto have admired in his works, but especially in his letters.”

So far the distinguished editor. Let us now turn to our codex.

What he had conjectured—namely, that Hildebert compiled this treatise from a great many pagan books—is made wholly clear by a simple inspection of our codex. There one may see that the author’s own words are very few, and that the whole work has been elaborated from the sayings or maxims of ancient authors [Note: Hildebert himself plainly acknowledges this at the very outset. See nos. 1 and 2.], namely Cicero, Sallust, Seneca, Boethius from the books *On the Consolation [of Philosophy]*, Isidore, and the poets Horace, Terence, Juvenal, Persius, and Lucan. He also cites Plato, though not from the Greek text but from Cicero’s translation, whose wording he uses. From the Holy Bible he cites the Epistles of Saint Paul, and Solomon from the books of Proverbs, Ecclesiasticus, and Wisdom. Further, as we said, these authors’ names are displayed in the manuscript in a distinct colour of script; and wherever Hildebert inserts his own words, he prefixes to them the word **AUTHOR**, likewise in a distinct script.

It must nevertheless be noted that these authors’ names do not always correspond to the words quoted in the codex, and that some things are at times attributed to one author which belong to another. Thus several maxims are attributed to Seneca that are found in the collection of Publilius Syrus, as it is commonly transmitted, although we do not doubt that these too were for the most part compiled from Seneca’s books. Likewise, several things belonging to one of the cited writers are ascribed to the author himself. [Col. 1007] Hence we infer that the designation of authors’ names in our codex originated from some copyist of this work—a learned man indeed, and somewhat trained in reading classical authors—but not from the author himself, who surely would never have fallen into this error.
