Therefore, retaining these authors’ names wherever the sequence of the discourse seemed to demand or at least permit it, we have nevertheless often omitted them and relegated them to the notes below; there, having sought out the passages quoted in the text itself, we have identified them by the author’s name.

The passages from poets which, both in our codex and in the edition, are copied in a continuous sequence of lines—with the sole exception of a passage from Horace describing the differing pursuits of ages—we have presented, as in editions of the poets themselves, distinguishing verse from verse. In the notes we have indicated variant readings, some of which are by no means negligible, especially those found in certain Horatian passages, which might be of value to new editors of Horace. We intend the same to be said of a few readings from the other authors.

As for passages from those who wrote prose, our manuscript transmits them so that you will find them in printed editions only slightly altered. We have likewise collated these with the texts of those authors and noted the results below, except for a few passages whose source still remains unknown to us.

Moreover, this is not the sole merit of our codex when compared with the edition. For the text itself in it—to omit the many notes found in the margin—differs astonishingly from the printed text, not only in words but also in substance. It is much fuller and at times more correct, as appeared from the specimen we presented, and will appear still more clearly from this complete edition which we have prepared [Note: In the printed edition the work ends with the words: “It requires practice. Here ends the book of moral matters.” In ours this formula is absent, and after *requires* a passage from Boethius is added, bringing the treatise to an end.].

It remains for us now to discuss briefly the man to whom this work was dedicated by Hildebert. The distinguished editor, as we saw above, from the letter R which he had found in the Colbert manuscript, conjectured that this work had been dedicated to a certain Reginald, monk of Saint Augustine. By contrast, our codex reports it dedicated to a certain Henry, a most distinguished man, in these very clear words: “At your urging, O most excellent and generous man, Henry, I was endeavouring to gather together the teaching of moral philosophers, scattered through many volumes.”

When I saw this, Henry I, King of England and Duke of Normandy, immediately came to mind: a man cultivated in good letters from childhood and renowned in warfare. As early as 1106 he subdued by war Normandy, which through the negligence of his brother William II had been divided among many lords; and he is in fact praised by very many ancient writers both for wisdom and for piety [Note: See Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, on the eleventh and twelfth centuries, ch. 12, art. 6.], Hildebert himself not excepted. Although Hildebert is said at one time to have been less welcome to him [Note: In the *Life of the Venerable Hildebert*, prefixed to his works.], he nevertheless later so won his favour that, as an intimate, he could intercede with him on behalf of his friends, as Hildebert’s letters written to him between 1120 and 1130 testify [Note: See Letter 12 of Book I, and Letters 13 and 20 of Book III.]. To these should be added the encomium found at the beginning of this very treatise:

> “I think that you devote no small diligence to this form of honourableness; for you cling to what is honourable by so close and indissoluble a bond that not even the violent upheaval of this most destructive rebellion shakes from you concern for honourableness. Though the necessity of the times may draw you toward crimes, your mind nevertheless opposes and protests.”

All this led me to conclude that Hildebert addressed this work to that Henry. Although this conclusion cannot be established by arguments so unanswerable that every other possibility must be entirely excluded, it nevertheless seems sufficiently probable on the authority of our codex.

These, kind reader, are the matters of greater importance which I have taken care to mention beforehand; I leave the rest, of less weight, for your examination. Meanwhile, farewell; and I ask you again and again to receive this work of mine, whatever its worth, kindly and favourably.

# MORAL PHILOSOPHY: ON THE HONOURABLE AND THE USEFUL

[Note: [Col. 1007A] Our codex reads: “Here begin the *Introductions to Moral Philosophy*.”]

## PREFACE

[Col. 1007A] 961–962

1. At your urging, O most excellent and generous man, Henry, I had been intending to gather together the teaching of moral philosophers, scattered through many volumes [Note: [Col. 1007A] The codex has *conabar*, “I was endeavouring.”]. While, in the silence of the first watch of the night [Note: [Col. 1007A] The edition incorrectly has *canticinium*. The word is *conticinium* [Col. 1008A], from *conticescere*, “to fall silent,” and denotes the first part of the night. See Forcellini’s lexicon, under this word.], I was searching my memory concerning this matter, sleep suddenly stole over me. And behold: a man commendable for a sober dignity was preceding certain figures no less reverend for their mature gravity. At once, as happens, an inward intuition told me that the first of them was Tully, the founder of Latin eloquence; after him came that most elegant teacher of morality, Seneca, with certain others, whom their words, which I shall report to you in due course, will make known [Note: [Col. 1008A] The codex has *declarabunt*, “will make plain.”].

2. As they conferred together, I thought that by definitions [Col. 1009A] and distinctions they were gathering moral philosophy, as it were, into a systematic art; and that I too might rightly insert maxims which I had heard from others or from these men. [Note: [Col. 1009C] The edition has *nos*, “us”; but *eos*, “them,” is more correct, as in our codex, for immediately afterwards the author speaks of himself: “and I too,” etc.] Therefore, when I awoke, setting down what I had heard by the service of my pen [Note: [Col. 1009D] Thus Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* I, prose 1, says that he “sets down his complaint by the service of his pen.”], I resolved to pursue brevity. First, because, as Seneca says, “memory is frail in dealing with individual matters and insufficient for a crowd of things; moreover, lest memory let what it has received escape, and recent matters overwhelm the old” [Note: [Col. 1009D] Seneca, *Benefits* VII.28, with slight changes.]. Hence Horace:

> Whatever you teach, be brief, so that receptive minds  
> May quickly grasp your words and faithfully retain them.  
> Every superfluous thing flows from a full breast.

[Note: [Col. 1009D] Horace, *Ars Poetica* 335 ff. In the edition, instead of “Hence Horace,” there appears: “Therefore he seems admirably to describe the writer who says: ‘Whatever,’ etc.”]

Furthermore, your diligent insistence was urgently and repeatedly demanding from me the completion of the work I had promised; for I discovered that, for a mind that longs, [Col. 1009B] nothing is hastened enough, and speed is delay to desire. Moreover, the fruit of this work, to be stored in the little chamber of memory, did not permit itself to be treated at greater length [Note: [Col. 1009D] The edition reads: “to be carefully stored, would in no way permit itself to be treated at greater length.”]. Tully says: “No part of life, whether in public affairs, private affairs, law-court matters, or domestic concerns, can be without moral philosophy. In cultivating it lies all the honourableness of life; in neglecting it lies disgrace” [Note: [Col. 1009D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.2, where *duty* appears in place of “moral philosophy.” In the rest the texts agree.]. Receive, then, a concise portion of it, as though someone were offering you [Col. 1010A] a cup to sip from a great river [Note: [Col. 1009D] A Terentian expression, *Adelphoe* IV.2, at the end.]. I think that you devote no small diligence to this pattern of honourableness. For you cleave to what is honourable by an indissoluble bond [Note: [Col. 1009D] The edition has “by a close and indissoluble embrace.”] so that not even the violent commotion of this most destructive rebellion shakes from you your concern for honourableness. Although the necessity of the times may drag you toward crimes, your mind nevertheless resists and protests.

3. Tully: [Note: [Col. 1009D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.3. In this whole chapter the author follows Cicero not in wording but in ideas. This further shows that he reduced Cicero’s doctrine of duties to an epitome, preserving the division proposed by Cicero himself.] Deliberation in forming a resolution is threefold. The first concerns the honourable alone, the second the useful alone, and the third their conflict. The first is subdivided into two, for we doubt whether the matter in question is honourable or shameful [Note: [Col. 1009D] “For we doubt whether the act was honourable or timely.” So the edition, with a marginal supplement: “perhaps *at an appropriate time*.” This false reading is refuted by Cicero, who in the cited passage says: “For deliberation usually concerns not only whether something is honourable or shameful, but also, when two honourable courses are proposed, which is more honourable.”], and, when two honourable courses are proposed, which of them is more honourable. The second likewise is divided into two; for one deliberates whether [Col. 1010B] something is useful or not, and, of two useful courses, [Note: [Col. 1010D] “For inquiry is made, when two useful courses are proposed, which of them is more useful.” So the edition.] which is more useful. The third remains undivided. Thus there are five deliberations: first, what is honourable; second, the comparison of honourable courses; third, what is useful; fourth, the comparison of useful courses; fifth, when what appears honourable appears to conflict with what appears useful [Note: [Col. 1010D] “The fifth deliberation is when the useful and the honourable appear opposed to one another.” So the edition.]. We shall discuss each of these most fully in the order stated, beginning with the honourable.

# QUESTION I: ON THE HONOURABLE

[Col. 1009]

[Col. 1009C]

4. Tully: “The honourable is that which draws us by its own power and attracts us by its own dignity. … Virtue is a disposition of the mind suited to a human being in the manner of nature” [Note: [Col. 1010D] Cicero, *On Invention* II.53 has: “There is something which by its own power attracts us to itself … drawing us by its dignity.” And ch. 54: “For virtue is a disposition in accord with nature’s manner.” Moreover, this second sentence is lacking in the edition.]. Virtue, therefore, and the honourable are different names, but the thing denoted is altogether the same. Seneca: “Virtue is so attractive that even the wicked have an inborn inclination to approve the better course. For who is there who does not, even amid crimes, desire the reputation of goodness? … You will find no one who would not prefer to enjoy the rewards of wickedness without wickedness” [Note: [Col. 1010D] Seneca, *Benefits* IV.17.].

The honourable, therefore, arises from four sources: prudence, justice, courage, [Col. 1010C] and temperance. Prudence is the discernment of good and evil, with an appetite for good and abhorrence of evil; or the discernment of good things, bad things, and things indifferent from one another. Justice is the virtue that renders to each person what is his due. Courage is the even endurance of dangers, labours, and either fortune. Temperance is the virtue that restrains unlawful motions of the mind when, by the persuasion of prosperity, they rush upon us [Note: [Col. 1010D] Here too he follows Cicero in the sources of the honourable, but differs somewhat in the definitions. For Cicero in the cited passage defines prudence as knowledge of good things, bad things, and things indifferent—or of things neither good nor bad, as he has in III, no. 15—or finally as knowledge of things to be sought and avoided, as in *On Duties*, no. 3. The same may be said of the remaining virtues in his cited and other passages. In the edition, however, only the second definition of prudence given by our author appears; the first is omitted.].

## ON PRUDENCE

5. Prudence goes before all these like a lamp, as though showing the way to the others; for it is prudence’s function [Col. 1011A] to deliberate, and that of the rest to act. Deliberation, however, ought to precede action. Sallust: “Before you begin, deliberate; and after you have deliberated, action must be prompt” [Note: [Col. 1011D] Sallust, *Catiline* I. In place of this author’s name the edition reads: “Hence the poet says: ‘Before you begin,’ etc.” This certainly displays the editor’s incompetence in reading ancient writers. So elsewhere, as will be seen in the following notes.]. Solomon: “Let your eyelids go before your steps” [Note: [Col. 1011D] In the Vulgate translation, Proverbs IV.25: “Let your eyelids go before your steps.” The words following appear to have been added by way of explanation; compare Ecclesiasticus XXXVII.20: “Before every act let settled counsel go before.” In fact, in the edition, after Solomon’s words one finds: “That is, let counsels go before your acts—prudence, namely, before justice.”]. Let your counsels precede your actions.

Justice follows prudence, but two passions—namely fear and love, or desire—and two fortunes, namely adversity and prosperity, obstruct justice’s office. Suppose, for example, that wisdom makes someone worthy of your favour, but someone tells you that, if you associate yourself with the said wise man, you will incur the hatred of a powerful person: behold, fear will make you desist from the duty of justice. Again, suppose there is someone toward whom you ought to be generous. Then, if you wish to keep what you possess because it seems useful to you and is not easily recovered, [Col. 1011B] desire opposes justice. For this reason justice must be supported by two pillars: courage against fear and temperance against desire. In the case of fortunes, it is clear why temperance must be opposed to prosperity and courage to adversity: the former would raise us up, the latter cast us down.

6. Prudence, therefore, distinguishes evils from goods, and goods and evils from one another. Since this virtue draws us by its own power, it is included under the honourable. Tully: “For we are all drawn and led by a desire for knowledge, in which we think it noble to excel. But to stumble, err, be deceived, or be ignorant we think evil and shameful” [Note: [Col. 1011D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.6. Yet in *On Invention* II.54 he gives the parts of prudence differently: memory, intelligence, and foresight; he defines the last as follows: “Foresight is that through which one sees something future before it has happened.”]. Its parts are foresight, circumspection, caution, and teachableness.

### On Foresight

[Col. 1011C]

7. Foresight is present knowledge testing [Note: [Col. 1012D] The edition reads *pertractans*, “thoroughly examining”; *tentans*, “testing,” is more correct.] the outcome of future events. Its office is to make provision for the future through present circumstances and to forestall impending calamity by counsel. Boethius: “It is not enough to look upon what lies before one’s eyes. Prudence measures the outcome of things” [Note: [Col. 1012D] Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* II, prose 1.]. Tully: “It is a mark of great ability to foresee future events in thought, to determine beforehand what may happen in either direction and what must be done when anything occurs, and never to omit provision, lest one ever have to say: ‘I had not thought of it’” [Note: [Col. 1012D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.23.]. Seneca: “It is the counsellor’s duty to prevent a man from trusting in his good fortune, to dispel his foolish confidence in a power that will always remain his, and to teach him that all things given by chance are unstable and flee [Col. 1012A] with a swifter course than they arrive” [Note: [Col. 1012D] Seneca, *Benefits* VI.33.]. Boethius: “Fortune will never make yours what the nature of things has made alien to you” [Note: [Col. 1012D] Boethius, cited passage, prose 5.]. Seneca: “One does not return by the same steps by which one came to the summit; between the highest and the lowest fortune there is no interval” [Note: [Col. 1012D] Seneca, cited passage.]. “False friends, however, offer flattery instead of counsel, and their one contest is who can deceive most pleasingly” [Note: [Col. 1012D] Same author, ibid., ch. 30.]. Tully: “For then we think ourselves such persons as we are rightly praised for being; from this countless faults arise, when men puffed up by their own opinions are shamefully ridiculed and fall into the gravest errors” [Note: [Col. 1012D] Cicero, cited passage, ch. 26.]. Juvenal:

> … There is nothing which a person cannot believe of himself  
> When he is praised as possessing power equal to the gods.

[Note: [Col. 1012D] Juvenal, no. 70. The edition reads, in place of Juvenal: “Hence the poet,” etc.] Seneca: “Therefore most people, ignorant of their own strength, [Col. 1012B] because they believe themselves as great as they hear themselves called, undertake wars that will end in disaster” [Note: [Col. 1012D] Seneca, *Benefits* VI.20 and 31. The example offered by the author is likewise taken almost word for word from this book of Seneca.].

Let this example suffice concerning flatterers, who readily deceive, and the true counsellor. Xerxes, king of the Medes, declared war on the Greeks. One of his intimates said that the Greeks would not await a messenger, but would turn their backs at the first report of his arrival. Another said that Greece could not be conquered, but would be overwhelmed by the mass of the army. Another said that they should fear finding cities deserted and empty, and that the king would have nowhere to employ such vast forces. Another said that even the nature of things could scarcely suffice for him: the seas were too narrow for his fleets, the camps for his soldiers, and the plains for deploying his cavalry forces; the sky could scarcely contain his arrows. While in this manner they incited the king, burning with excessive self-esteem, [Col. 1012C] Demaratus said: “The multitude which pleases you is a thing to be feared by you; for it is true that an immoderate multitude can never be governed, and what cannot be governed cannot last long. Nothing is so great that it cannot also perish.” What Demaratus had said came to pass [Note: [Col. 1012D] The edition has “Democritus,” here and shortly above; but our codex, and Seneca, have “Demaratus.”]. Thus true counsellors plainly possess more foresight than flatterers.

### On Circumspection

8. Circumspection is caution against opposing vices. Its office is to preserve frugality without, in fleeing avarice, falling into wastefulness; and to withdraw from rashness without falling into fear. Solomon encouraged this office when he said: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” [Note: [Col. 1012D] In the Vulgate translation, Proverbs II.23.]. For, in saying “with all vigilance,” he prefixed [Col. 1013A] “all,” lest you shut the door against enemies on one side while opening an entrance on the other. Horace:

> The flight from a fault leads into a vice, if it lacks skill;  
> While fools avoid vices, they run into their opposites.

[Note: [Col. 1013D] Horace, *Ars Poetica* 31.]

### On Caution

9. Caution is the discernment from virtues of vices which bear the appearance of virtue. Isidore leads us toward its duties when he says: “Certain vices wear the appearance of virtues, and thereby deceive their followers more perniciously, because they cover themselves with the veil of virtue. For under the pretext of justice, credulity is practised; and lax sloth is believed to be gentleness” [Note: [Col. 1013D] Isidore of Seville, *Sentences* II.35.]. Cicero: “There are no traps worse than those hidden in the likeness of duty” [Note: [Col. 1013D] This passage of Cicero is unknown to me. The edition reads: “There are no more hidden traps, says Cicero,” etc. The codex notes that the following sentence belongs to our author.]. For the horse deceived the Trojans precisely because it falsely assumed the form of Minerva.

### On Teachableness

[Col. 1013B]

10. Teachableness is the prudence of teaching the unlearned. Its office is that a person should first instruct himself and then others, in accordance with Solomon’s saying: “My son, drink water from your own cistern and scatter your springs abroad” [Note: [Col. 1013D] In the Vulgate translation, Proverbs V.15–16. The edition gives the entire passage thus: “My son, drink water from your own cistern and streams from your own well. Let your springs flow abroad”—where our codex has “scatter your springs abroad,” perhaps from the very ancient Old Latin translation—and “scatter waters in the streets,” where the Vulgate has “divide.”]. To drink water from one’s cistern is to draw wisdom from one’s own mind. Terence:

> Such is the constitution of all human nature:  
> People see and judge others’ affairs better  
> Than their own. This is because in our own concerns we are hindered  
> Either by excessive joy or by distress.

[Note: [Col. 1014D] Terence, *Heauton Timorumenos* III.1, at the end.]

To scatter springs is to teach others [Note: [Col. 1014D] The edition adds: “To lead springs abroad is to pour knowledge into others.”]. Tully: “In relation to this virtue two things must be avoided: first, that we should take unknown things for known and rashly assent to them [Col. 1013C] [this is presumption]. Whoever wishes to avoid this fault—and everyone ought to wish to do so—will devote time to study and diligent reflection. The second is to bestow excessive study and much labour upon obscure, difficult, and unnecessary matters” [Note: [Col. 1014D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.6. The words in square brackets are not Cicero’s, but our author’s.].

This fault is called curiosity, because excessive labour is expended for little usefulness; as happens if, abandoning moral philosophy, you apply yourself too intently to astrology, geometry, and even to certain vanities of dialectic. Seneca: “It is better to retain a few precepts of wisdom in memory, and to have them in use and ready at hand, than to have learned many things which are not ready at hand. The great wrestler is not the one who has learned every hold, whose use is rare, but one who has diligently trained himself in a few; for it does not matter how much he knows if he knows as much as is sufficient for victory. So in studies many things delight, but few [Col. 1013D] help. Though you do not know what cause makes the ocean overflow, or what separates the conception of twins yet joins their birth, or why those [Col. 1014A] born at the same time have different destinies, no great harm will come from passing over matters which it is neither possible nor useful to know” [Note: [Col. 1014D] Seneca, *Benefits* VII.1.].

## ON JUSTICE

11. Justice is the virtue that preserves human society and the common good. It preserves for you the coexistence of all people, so that one person may hold lands and resources which another needs. Envy and sedition would therefore be stirred up, unless justice were present to render to each person his due. It also maintains the intercourse of life [that is, business dealings] in the following way: while several people pursue the same mode of livelihood, such as trade or military service, one person’s gain diminishes another’s profit. This would provoke jealousy unless justice, guardian of equity, were present. This virtue also rises above every hardship.

“For no one can be just who fears [Col. 1014B] death, exile, pain, or poverty, or who puts their opposites before equity. Thus, in my opinion, the whole ordering of life requires the assistance of other people, which is provided through justice. Above all, a person needs relatives with whom he can converse; and justice is necessary to those who sell, buy, hire, let, and are occupied in the making of contracts. Its power is so great that even those who live by wrongdoing and crime cannot live without some share of justice. For one who steals or snatches something from any one of those who rob together leaves no place for himself even in robbery. If the chief pirate does not distribute the booty equally, he is either killed by his companions or abandoned by them” [Note: [Col. 1014D] Cicero, *On Duties* II.11.].

### On Severity

[Col. 1014C]

12. Justice is divided into severity and liberality. Severity is the virtue that restrains injury by the punishment it deserves. “The first duty of severity, then, is that no one should harm another unless first provoked by an injury. The second is to use common things as common, private things as private. There is, however, no private property by nature; rather, it arises either from long-standing occupation, as in the case of those who formerly came into unoccupied places; or from victory, as in the case of those who gained possession in war; or from law, as in the case of those who became heirs through their fathers’ wills. Private property also arises through agreement, stipulation, or lot. Hence it follows that each person holds as his own whatever share of things by nature common has fallen to him. Further, if anyone seeks more, [Col. 1014D] he will violate the law of human society” [Note: [Col. 1014D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.7. Moreover, this passage is incomplete in the edition.].

From this all sedition arises: because you try to transfer my private possessions to your own use. Seneca: “People would live most peacefully if there were not two words, namely ‘mine’ and ‘yours’” [Note: [Col. 1014D] This is among the maxims of Publilius, no. 763, where “if they were removed” occurs instead of “if there were not.” The word “namely,” however, was, I think, added by Hildebert.]. “The third duty of severity is [Col. 1015A] to expel from human society the destructive kind of people. For just as certain limbs are amputated if they begin to lack blood and life, lest they harm the rest, so this likeness of a human being—this beast of savagery and brutality—must be separated from common life; for such persons are human beings in name, not in reality” [Note: [Col. 1015D] Cicero, *On Duties* III.6, near the end; the final words, however, are from I.30.].

For what difference does it make whether someone changes himself from a human being into a beast, or bears a beast’s brutality under the form of a human being? Seneca: Thus such persons must not be spared, for “the judge is condemned when the guilty person is acquitted” [Note: [Col. 1015D] This too is among the maxims of Publilius, no. 388.]. “Yet anger must especially be avoided in punishment, for with it no one will maintain that mean which lies between too much and too little” [Note: [Col. 1015D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.25.].

### On Liberality
[Col. 1015B] **13.** Liberality is the virtue of the mind that dispenses benefits; considered in its disposition we call it kindness, and in its effect beneficence. [Note: [Col. 1015D] Cf. Cicero, ibid., 7.] This virtue consists wholly in giving [and repaying]. In giving, take care not to be harsh. SENECA: “For what person has been content to be asked either mildly or only once? Who, when he foresaw that something would be requested from him, did not draw down his brow, turn away his face, or pretend to be occupied? A benefit ought to be owed in the same spirit in which it is bestowed.” [Note: [Col. 1015D] Seneca, *On Benefits*, I.1.] For God loves a cheerful giver. [Note: [Col. 1015D] St Paul, II Corinthians 9:7.] “Therefore a benefit ought not to be given carelessly. No one owes what he has not received but has extorted.” [Note: [Col. 1015D] Seneca, loc. cit.]

Second, beware of delay: “When an honourable opportunity for doing good is given, seize it immediately; for delay drives glory away and forfeits the right. He is mistaken who hopes that the person whom he has wearied by delay and forced by waiting will answer him favourably.” [Note: [Col. 1015D] Same author, loc. cit. In the edition the entire period between *beware of delay* and *he is mistaken* is omitted.]—“For a benefit that has long clung to the giver’s hands is unwelcome. He who delays long is next door to refusing; he who acts late has long been unwilling. You subtract as much from gratitude as you add to delay, when shame is poured over me as I make my request. Whoever remits this shame multiplies his gift. It is best to anticipate each person’s desire; next best, to follow it. He did not receive freely who received only after asking. Nothing is bought more dearly than that which is extorted by entreaties: for one must utter the troublesome and burdensome word, with lowered countenance, ‘I beg.’ Every benefit that comes unasked will endure. What is immediately and readily taken is more welcome than what is received late from a full hand; for whoever must be asked after another detracts from the giver. Nothing is so bitter as to hang in suspense for a long time. Some bear the cutting off of their hope more calmly than its long prolongation.” [Note: [Col. 1015D–1016A] Seneca, *On Benefits*, II.1–5, where he has *praescidi* and *trahi* in place of *praescindi* and *protrahi*.]

Third, beware lest a benefit harm those to whom it is given, or others. “For those who give something to a person in order to harm him must be judged not beneficent or liberal, but ruinous flatterers. . . . Many, moreover, are so desirous of glory that they take more away from some people than they bestow upon others. Nothing is further from the duty of liberality, nor more opposed to it.” [Note: [Col. 1016D] Cicero, *On Duties*, I.14.] SENECA: Such a man gave to ambition, not to me. TULLY: “Let us therefore use that liberality which benefits those to whom it is given and harms no one.” [Note: [Col. 1016D] Cicero, ibid.]

Fourth, beware lest the benefit exceed your means. “For in such liberality there is often a desire to seize money in order that resources for generosity may be available. Moreover, an injury is done to children or relatives, for whom it is fairer that means should be provided and left, rather than transferred to others.” [Note: [Col. 1016D] Cicero, ibid. The second period is absent from the edition.]

Fifth, beware of reproaching the recipient. “Between two persons is the law of a benefit: one ought immediately to forget that he gave, the other to remember that he received. A good man never thinks of what he has given unless reminded by one repaying him. He has bound himself tightly who, while giving, thought that he was receiving; he gave as if receiving, and received as if he had not given. Reproaches are grievous, and light-minded are those who shortly afterwards repent of their benefit. Those spoil all gratitude to whom one says: ‘O arrogance! I have no wish to receive anything from you; whatever you give, you spoil.’” [Note: [Col. 1016D] Seneca, *On Benefits*, II.10–13; our author has collected small passages into one. It should be noted, however, that in the previously cited chapter the reading is *inter quos lex est* (“among whom is the law”), which everyone sees is an error; with our text one must read *inter duos* (“between two”), as the sense requires.]

Sixth, beware of the malicious cleverness of refusing. “Antigonus told a Cynic who requested a talent that it was more than a Cynic ought to ask for. But when he requested a coin, he said that it was less than a king ought to give. See how maliciously he refused. For he could have given a talent, because he was king; he could have given a coin, because that man was a Cynic.—Alexander acted better: when he gave a city to someone who said that a city did not suit his humble fortune, he replied: ‘I do not ask what it is fitting for you to receive, but what it is fitting for me to give.’” [Note: [Col. 1016D] Seneca, *On Benefits*, II.18 and II.16.]

Seventh, beware of complaining about an ungrateful person. “You will make the ungrateful man better by enduring him, worse by complaining of him. The louder voice of the reproacher overcomes his uncertain shame. No one fears what already seems to be the case. Shame, once exposed, is lost. . . . He is not such as we hoped; let us be such as we were—unlike him.” [Note: [Col. 1016D] Same author, *On Benefits*, VII.28–29.]—“He is ungrateful for one benefit; he will not be so for a second. He has forgotten two; a third will restore the memory of what had slipped from memory.” [Col. 1016D] [Note: [Col. 1016D] Same author, *On Benefits*, I.3.] What reason is there to exasperate one upon whom you have conferred many benefits, so that from a friend he becomes an enemy? [Note: [Col. 1016D] Same author, *On Benefits*, VII.30.] Be generous in giving, not harsh in exacting. [Note: [Col. 1016D] Cicero, *On Duties*, II.18.] For, since injuries sink deeper than services, what should a person expect who offends [while obliging]?

The duty of liberality, therefore, is to give to every powerful person, and to imitate the gods. “If you imitate the gods, then give even to the ungrateful; for the sun rises also for criminals, and the seas lie open to pirates. . . . The gods,” says Seneca, “the most excellent authors of all things, begin to give benefits to those who do not know it and persist in giving them to the ungrateful. The gods do not cease to heap up benefits, having one settled purpose: to wish to help. Let us imitate them. Let us give, therefore, though many gifts have been bestowed in vain. The ungrateful man has not wronged me, but himself. For a benefit always delights the grateful person, but the ungrateful only once. It is not the mark of a great spirit to give a benefit and lose it; but to lose it and nevertheless give is the mark of a great spirit.” [Note: [Col. 1017D] Seneca, *On Benefits*, IV.26 and VII, at the end.]

—“Virtue is to give benefits that are not necessarily to return. I would rather not receive than not give; whoever fails to give what he promises is beforehand guilty of ingratitude.” [Note: [Col. 1017D] Same author, *On Benefits*, I.1.] For to give in order to receive is to sell one’s freedom. Therefore, if you promise an unworthy person, give—not so as to benefit him, but so as to redeem your word. Although you ought to give to every petitioner, “in conferring a benefit, however, regard must be had to worthiness: one must consider the character of him to whom it is given, his grateful disposition toward us, shared life and fellowship, and benefits previously conferred in our interest. . . . And although we do not live with perfect persons but with those who possess likenesses of virtue, I think that no one should be disregarded in whom signs of virtue appear. One ought especially to honour anyone in proportion as he is more adorned with the gentler virtues—temperance and modesty. For a brave and great spirit in a person who is not perfect or wise is usually more ardent than it should be. Above all, let us give most to the one by whom we are most loved; and we must weigh the degree of zeal and goodwill that each has shown toward us. For many do many things through a certain rashness without judgment, or from illness, or driven by a sudden impulse of the mind as though by a gust of wind; such actions ought not to be reckoned benefits as great as those bestowed deliberately, thoughtfully, and consistently.” [Note: [Col. 1017D] Cicero, *On Duties*, I.14–15. The final period is absent from the edition.]

—“Likewise, the case of a person oppressed by misfortune differs from that of one who seeks to improve his circumstances while none of his own affairs are adverse. A readier kindness is owed to the unfortunate, unless perhaps they deserve their misfortune. Yet in the case of those who wish to rise to a higher station, we ought by no means to be too restrictive.” [Note: [Col. 1017D] Cicero, *On Duties*, II.18.] Likewise, benefits are better placed among good poor persons than among the rich. [Col. 1017D] For wealthy persons do not wish to be bound by a benefit [Note: [Col. 1017D] The edition incorrectly reads *volunt* (“they wish”) instead of *nolunt* (“they do not wish”).] but, when they receive even a very great benefit, think that they themselves have given it, or suspect that something is expected from them. . . . Likewise, if you confer a benefit on a wicked rich person, the gratitude remains with that one man, or perhaps with his household; but if you confer a benefit on a good poor person, all good poor people see provision made for their protection and think that they themselves, not their fortune, are being regarded [when you benefit the good poor person]. Therefore, if the matter comes to a choice, follow Themistocles, who said: “I prefer a man who needs money to money that needs a man.” [Note: [Col. 1017D] Cicero, *On Duties*, II.20. The words in brackets are wholly redundant from the preceding material.]

We shall give gifts that are not superfluous. You will not give military weapons to a woman, nor wine to a drunkard; rather, to whomever you give gifts, give gifts that will drive out that person’s particular ailment. [Note: [Col. 1018D] The edition reads: “We shall give gifts not reproaching each person with his own ailment.”] Let us seek no gifts so costly as rare gifts intended to endure, because we ought never to give reminders. So far concerning these matters.

## On Repayment, Which Is Contained Under Justice

**14.** “No duty is more necessary than returning gratitude. For if Hesiod bids us return in a larger measure than we have received, what ought we to do when challenged by a benefit? We should imitate fertile fields, which return more than they received. But if we do not hesitate to confer benefits on those whom we hope will be useful to us, what ought we to be toward those who have already been useful? For whether we give or do not give is in our power; a good man may be permitted not to repay, if he cannot do so without injury.” [Note: [Col. 1018D] Cicero, *On Duties*, I.15.] Therefore, first beware lest you forget the benefit. “For all hate a person who forgets a benefit, and think that this injury is done even to themselves, since it discourages liberality.” [Note: [Col. 1018D] Cicero, *On Duties*, II.18.]

“For he is ungrateful who denies that he has received a benefit; ungrateful who conceals it; ungrateful who does not return it; most ungrateful of all who has forgotten it. A person cannot ever become grateful if the entire benefit has slipped from his memory. It is evident that he has not often thought about returning it if forgetfulness has crept in. He never wished to be grateful who threw the benefit so far away and placed it beyond his sight. Memory loses nothing except what it does not often look back upon. Therefore I say: do not forget a past benefit. Few turn their thoughts toward past benefits. For no one values what lies in the past, but treats it as though it were lost. If he summons you before a judge, it begins to be not a benefit but a loan; and although returning gratitude is a most honourable thing, it ceases to be honourable if it is necessary.” [Note: [Col. 1018D] Seneca, *On Benefits*, III.1–7. The author has combined an equal number of maxims into one; they are presented less correctly in the edition.]

Second, beware lest you approach a benefit through an injury. “For some people are insufficiently grateful. They are accustomed to wish some misfortune upon those to whom they are indebted, in order to demonstrate that their affection remembers the benefit. Their disposition resembles that of people inflamed by perverse love: they wish exile upon their beloved so that they may accompany the fugitive; they wish poverty so that they may give more to one in greater need; they wish illness so that they may sit beside the sufferer. In short, lovers vow whatever an enemy would wish. The outcome of hatred and insane love is almost the same. But it is unjust to sink someone in order to draw him out, to overthrow him in order to raise him up, to shut him in in order to release him. For injury is not the end of a benefit; nor is it a service to take away what the one who takes it away had bestowed.”

Third, beware lest you hurry too much to show yourself grateful. “He who anticipates the time of repayment sins just as much as he who does not follow it. What you do not wish to remain with you, you regard as a burden, not a gift. It is a sign of rejecting a gift to send something back in return and to overcome one gift by another. He who is annoyed that he has not repaid it regrets having received the benefit.” [Note: [Col. 1019D] In these two articles also there are maxims perhaps taken from the same author, but the places are unknown to me.]

Fourth, beware lest you repay a benefit secretly. “Ungrateful is the person who gives thanks with witnesses removed. Above all preserve this: receive kindly; for if you receive kindly, you have returned gratitude—not so that you may consider the account settled, but so that you may repay with greater assurance. For we shall satisfy goodwill with goodwill, and deed with deed.” [Note: [Col. 1019D] Seneca, *On Benefits*, II.23 and 35. In the edition these final words occur here less correctly.]

[Col. 1019B] ## On Beneficence

**15.** “Again, one kind of beneficence consists in service, another in money. The latter is easier, especially for a wealthy person; the former more splendid and more worthy of a good man” [Note: [Col. 1019D] Cicero, *On Duties*, II.15.] and is closed to no one. Of the former it is written: SENECA: “Virtue lies open to all; it does not seek a house or a property, but is content with the bare human being.” [Note: [Col. 1019D] I have not discovered from what passage of Seneca this maxim was drawn.]

“Although each form of virtue makes a person grateful, one is drawn from the money-box, the other from virtue. Likewise, that which consists in money exhausts its own material. Thus beneficence [in giving] is diminished by beneficence. The more people toward whom you exercise it, the less able you are to exercise it toward many. The other, by the habit of doing good, makes people readier and more practiced in doing good. While Alexander was seeking to win Macedonian favour with money, his father Philip wrote these words to him: ‘What error has carried you into this hope—that you think those faithful to you whom you have corrupted with money? You are acting so that the Macedonians regard you not as their king but as their servant and supplier.’ The recipient indeed becomes worse and more ready to expect further gifts.

“This kind of generosity, nevertheless, is not to be rejected altogether; for suitable needy persons ought often to receive a share of one’s family property, but carefully and moderately. For many have squandered their estates by giving thoughtlessly. Nothing is more foolish than to arrange matters so that you cannot continue for long to do what you gladly do. Lavish giving is also followed by plunder; once people begin to be in need because of giving, they are compelled openly to lay hands upon others’ property, and incur greater hatred from those from whom they have taken than favour from those upon whom they have bestowed. Accordingly, one’s household resources should not be so shut up that beneficence cannot open them, nor so unbarred that they stand open to everyone. The measure of giving must therefore be referred to one’s means; for generosity has no bottom, since those accustomed to receive always desire more.” [Note: [Col. 1019D] Cicero, *On Duties*, II.15, with a few changes or omissions. [Col. 1020D] The final words, however, are absent from the edition.]

[Col. 1020A] ## On Lavish Giving

**16.** “There are two kinds of lavish givers: some are squanderers, others liberal. Squanderers are those who pour out their wealth upon banquets and gifts for actors and pimps—things of which they will leave behind either brief memory or none at all. Liberal persons are those who use their resources either to ransom captives from pirates, to assume another’s debt for the sake of a poor friend, to assist friends with dowries for their daughters, or to help in acquiring or increasing some other possession.” [Note: [Col. 1020D] Cicero, ibid., II.16.] We have just spoken of beneficence in money.

## On Beneficence in Service

**17.** “Beneficence in service is exercised by helping with advice and defending in legal cases through eloquence. But persons must be warned, when they wish to help some, not to offend others. For they often either harm those whom they ought not to harm, or harm those whom it is not expedient to harm. If this is done unwittingly, it is negligence; if knowingly, rashness. You must also employ whatever apology you can toward those whom you have unwillingly offended when you could not act otherwise, and the offence committed must be recompensed by definite services.” [Note: [Col. 1020D] Cicero, ibid., II.19.]

TULLY: “But although a legal case consists in accusation and defence, defence is the more praiseworthy. Yet accusation is quite often to be approved, although we ought to undertake it only once and not often. . . . For it belongs to a harsh person—or rather, scarcely seems to belong to a human being—to bring capital danger upon many, and, for the sake of reputation, to undertake to be called an accuser. . . . Care must also be taken not to accuse an innocent person in a capital trial, since this cannot be done without crime. Nothing is more inhuman than to turn eloquence, given for the salvation of human beings, to the ruin of the good. . . . It is the judge’s duty always to follow the truth; but the advocate’s sometimes to defend what is probable, although it is less true.” [Note: [Col. 1020D] Cicero, ibid., II.14.]

SALLUST: “All persons who deliberate about doubtful matters ought to be free from hatred, anger, friendship, and pity. The mind does not readily discern the truth where these impede it.” [Note: [Col. 1020D] Sallust, *Catiline*, 51, beginning.] TULLY: For judges, because of envy, take away from the rich; because of pity, they add to the poor. Each person lays aside the role of friend when he assumes that of judge. The judge must also take care lest his speech reveal a defect in character, when something is said, either in jest or maliciously, for the purpose of assiduously disparaging those who are absent. [Note: [Col. 1020D] What is cited here and below under Tully’s name may perhaps be Seneca; the passages, however, are unknown to me. In the edition several words are absent.]

TULLY: Care must likewise be taken that we seem to respect and love those with whom we have exchanged conversation. Rebukes sometimes prove necessary; in them one must employ both a raised voice and a sharper gravity of words. Care must also be taken that we not seem to do these things in anger; rather, as we come to burning and cutting, so we shall come rarely and reluctantly to this kind of correction. Yet anger must be far removed, since with it nothing can be done rightly or thoughtfully. It must also be made clear that whatever bitterness a rebuke has is undertaken for the sake of the person rebuked. Even in disputes with enemies, if we hear things unworthy of us, it is right to preserve dignity and banish anger. For actions done in agitation cannot be performed steadily, nor approved by those present. It is also unbecoming to praise oneself, especially falsely, and, to the ridicule of one’s hearers, to imitate the boastful soldier. “In all these matters one must follow people’s character, not their fortune. But who is there who would not prefer the favour of a fortunate and powerful person to the case of a poor but good person? For toward the one from whom a more ready recompense seems likely, our inclination is more favourable.” [Note: [Col. 1021D] Cicero, *On Duties*, II.20.]

[Col. 1021B] ## On Kindness

**18.** There is another division of kindness: whatever virtues render what is due to good persons are parts of that same kindness. Religion renders to God his due; filial devotion to parents; innocence to inferiors; friendship to equals; concord to fellow citizens; reverence to superiors; mercy to the needy.

## On Religion

**19.** Religion is the virtue that offers care and ceremonial observance to the Divinity. [Note: [Col. 1021D] Cicero, *On Invention*, II.53 has: “Religion is that which brings care and ceremonial observance to some higher nature, which they call divine.” Our manuscript reads *afferunt* (“they bring”).—What follows is less sound, and I have not found the passage of Tully cited here.] Its first duty is [TULLY]: to repent of a crime committed. [If one properly repents of crimes, the first elements of wrongful desire must be rooted out, and minds too tender must be trained by harsher disciplines.]—The second [because it is a duty of religion] is to regard the mutability of temporal things as of little account. HORACE:

> Day is driven on by day,  
> And new moons hasten to their death. . . .  
>
> The year, and the hour that snatches away the kindly day,  
> Warn you not to hope for immortal things.  
>
> Yet the swiftly moving heavenly moons repair their losses;  
> When we have fallen  
>
> Where pious Aeneas, rich Tullus, and Ancus have fallen,  
> We are dust and shadow. . . .  
>
> We and all that is ours are owed to death.

[Note: [Col. 1021D] Horace, *Odes*, II.18; IV.7; *Ars Poetica*, 63.]

The third duty is to commit our life wholly to God, according to the saying of the poet JUVENAL:

[Col. 1021D]

> If you want advice,  
> Allow the gods themselves to weigh what suits us  
> And what is useful for our affairs.  
> For the gods will give everything best suited to our welfare;  
> A human being is dearer to them than to himself. . . .  
>
> One should pray for a sound mind in a sound body.

[Note: [Col. 1021D] Juvenal, *Satires*, X.346–350, 356.]

“Yet the help of the gods is not won by womanish prayers; rather, by watchfulness, action, and good deliberation all things prosper. When you have surrendered yourself to sloth and idleness, do not call upon the gods at all; for then they are angry and hostile.” [Note: [Col. 1021D] Sallust, *Catiline*, 52.]—“Know that you have then become free from all desires when you have reached the point of asking God for nothing that you could not ask openly. What madness there is now among human beings! They whisper their most shameful prayers to the gods, and if anyone puts an ear near, they fall silent; they ask God for what they do not wish human beings to know. But live with human beings as though God sees you; speak with God as though human beings hear you.” [Note: [Col. 1021D] Seneca, *Letters*, 10.]

The fourth duty [of religion] is to observe truth. SENECA: “Truth separates the role of free person and slave; falsehood joins them.” [Note: [Col. 1022D] I do not know where this maxim occurs.] TULLY: “Therefore [the Stoics] think that this virtue is called *fides* (‘good faith’) because through it what has been said is done. But not every promise is to be kept—namely, those which are useless to the persons to whom you have promised them, or which will harm you more than they benefit those to whom you have promised. For it is contrary to duty to set a greater loss before a smaller one. Thus, if you have promised to come as an advocate in someone’s case and meanwhile your son begins to be seriously ill, in this circumstance it is not contrary to duty not to do what you said. Nor are deposits always to be returned. If someone in sound mind has deposited a sword with you but demands it back while insane, it is contrary to duty to return it. If someone has deposited money with you in order to make war upon his country, do not return the deposit in this case, because you would act against the commonwealth, which ought to be dearest to you. Thus things that seem honourable by nature become dishonourable in particular circumstances.” [Note: [Col. 1022D] Cicero, *On Duties*, I.7 and 10, compared with III.25.]

## On Filial Devotion

**20.** “Filial devotion is that through which dutiful service and diligent reverence are rendered to those united by blood and to those who cherish their country.” [Note: [Col. 1022D] This is Cicero’s definition, *On Invention*, II.54.] Nature herself leads us to its duties. SENECA: “Just as no one needs to be stirred up to self-love, so neither does the law command us to love our parents or indulge our children. It is superfluous to urge us toward that to which our mind itself moves us.” [Note: [Col. 1022D] Seneca, *On Benefits*, IV.17.] Accordingly, we must take greater care not to inflict any injury upon our own people. SALLUST: “Whom will you find faithful to you among strangers, if you have been an enemy to your own people?” [Note: [Col. 1022D] Sallust, *Jugurtha*, 10.] TERENCE: “What sort of person will he be toward others who dares to deceive his father?” [Note: [Col. 1022D] Terence, *Adelphoe*, I.i.30, where the text reads:

> For one who has become accustomed to lie to or deceive his father,  
> Or has dared to do so, will dare it much more toward others.]

[Col. 1022D] ## On Innocence

**21.** Innocence is purity of soul, abhorring every infliction of injury. By this virtue the gods are appeased. HORACE:

> If a hand free from guilt touches the altar,  
> No costly victim  
> Will more sweetly soften hostile household gods.

[Note: [Col. 1022D] Horace, *Odes*, III.23.] Whoever wishes to preserve this virtue will regard all crimes, however small, as great. HORACE:

> For no one is born without faults; the best person is he  
> Who is troubled by the fewest.

[Note: [Col. 1023D] Horace, *Satires*, I.3.6, 8.] JUVENAL:

> No one believes himself to sin as much as you permit him to;  
> So widely does everyone indulge himself.

[Note: [Col. 1023D] Juvenal, *Satires*, XIV.2, 33, where *ipsi* (“they themselves”) is read in place of *omnes* (“everyone”). The variant is not to be despised.]

Its duty is to attract many people without harming anyone. SENECA: “He threatens many who offends one.” [Note: [Col. 1023D] Seneca or Publilius Syrus, *Mimes*, no. 485, where instead of *qui unum offendit* is read: *qui uni facit injuriam* (“who does injury to one person”).] Another duty is not to seek vengeance. SENECA: “It is ridiculous to lose one’s innocence through hatred of a wrongdoer.” [Note: [Col. 1023D] Same author, ibid., no. 834.] Nor should crime be avenged by crime. SALLUST: “Many have been ruined because they wished to avenge their own injuries too bitterly.” [Note: [Col. 1023D] Sallust, *Jugurtha*, 42.]

## On Friendship

[Col. 1023B] **22.** “Friendship is goodwill toward the person loved for that person’s own sake.” [Note: [Col. 1023D] Cicero, *On Invention*, II.55, where: “Friendship is goodwill toward someone in good things, for the sake of the person himself whom one loves, together with his corresponding goodwill.”] Its duty is to will and not to will the same things in honourable matters. Another duty is to admonish a friend privately and praise him publicly. TULLY: This indeed is the law of friendship: that we neither ask disgraceful things nor do them when asked. SENECA: Another law is, “that you should deliberate about everything with a friend, but first about the friend himself.” [Note: [Col. 1023D] Seneca, *Letters*, 3.] A third duty is not to strive to know what he himself wishes to conceal. For it is more humane to dissemble than to make an effort to discover that by which a friend will hate us. A fourth is that harshness should not break friendship, according to the poet LUCAN:

> One ought not fail a friend in adversity;  
> But no loyalty has ever chosen unhappy friends after following the prosperous.

[Note: [Col. 1023D] Lucan, VIII.534–535.]

SENECA: “If you wish to be loved, love.” [Note: [Col. 1023D] Seneca, *Letters*, 9.]

[Col. 1023C] ## On Reverence

**23.** Reverence is the observance that renders due honour to persons of weight or exalted by some prerogative. [Note: [Col. 1023D] Cf. Cicero, *On Invention*, II.53, where *observantia* is defined in entirely different words as that through which persons surpassing others in some dignity are deemed worthy of a certain observance and honour.] Its duty is to imitate one’s elders. “For it is best to imitate the footsteps of one’s elders, if they have gone before rightly.” [Note: [Col. 1023D] Seneca or Publilius Syrus, *Mimes*, no. 613, where: “It is best to follow the footsteps of one’s elders if they have gone before rightly.”]—“We ought to choose a good man and always keep him before our eyes, so that we may live as though he were watching and do everything as though he saw it. . . . For the greater part of sins is removed if a witness stands by those about to sin.” [Note: [Col. 1024D] Seneca, *Letters*, 11, where *peccaturis* (“those about to sin”) is read in place of *peccatis* (“sins”).]—“Therefore do not think that any place is without a witness.” [Note: [Col. 1024D] Same author, or Publilius Syrus, *Mimes*, no. 574.]

## On Concord

**24.** Concord is the virtue that spontaneously unites fellow citizens, compatriots, and persons living together under the same law. Its duties are these, as PLATO has excellently written:

> “We are not born for ourselves alone; our country claims a part of our birth, our friends another part. And, as the Stoics hold, all things are created for human use, and human beings are created for the sake of human beings, so that they may mutually help one another. Therefore we must follow nature as our guide in this matter: bring common advantages into the public sphere, bind human society more firmly among human beings through the exchange of services—by giving, receiving, by actions, resources, and service.”

[Note: [Col. 1024D] Plato, that is, as reported by Cicero, *On Duties*, I.7.]

—“And by yielding to many persons in many matters from one’s own right. For it is not only liberal but sometimes even advantageous to yield a little of one’s own right.” [Note: [Col. 1024D] Same author, *On Duties*, II.18.]—“For through concord small things increase; through discord the greatest things collapse.” [Note: [Col. 1024D] Sallust, *Jugurtha*, 10.]

## On Mercy

[Col. 1024B] **25.** Mercy is the virtue by which the mind is moved by the misfortune of the afflicted. “This virtue considers nothing human foreign to itself.” [Note: [Col. 1024D] Cicero, *On Duties*, I.9 has: “Care for others’ affairs is difficult, although that Terentian Chremes considers nothing human foreign to himself.” Further, Terence, *Heauton Timorumenos*, I.i.25, said:

> I am human: I consider nothing human foreign to me.]

This accords with the saying of the Apostle Paul: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” [Note: [Col. 1024D] Paul, II Corinthians 11:29.] Mercy regards others’ inconveniences or losses as its own. “Whoever is merciful toward one in misfortune remembers himself.” [Note: [Col. 1024D] These words might have a place among the maxims of Publilius Syrus. Their source is unknown.]—“Care for others’ affairs is nevertheless difficult.” [Note: [Col. 1024D] From the recently cited passage of Cicero.]

## On Cruelty and Negligence

**26.** Against the two aforementioned kinds of justice, namely severity and liberality, one must guard against two opposing kinds of injustice, namely cruelty and negligence. Cruelty is the infliction of unmerited injury; negligence is failure to repel injury when one can and ought to do so. Negligence is opposed to severity, for to defend and to disregard a defence are opposites. Likewise cruelty is contrary to liberality, for to bestow a benefit and to inflict an injury are opposites.

The causes of cruelty are fear, avarice, and ambition. Fear arises when one who intends to harm another fears that, unless he does so, he himself will suffer some disadvantage. Avarice arises when people undertake an injury so as to obtain what they desire. SALLUST: “Ambition also [that is, love of preferment] has compelled many mortals to become false: to keep one thing hidden in the breast and another ready upon the tongue; to judge friendships and enmities not by their reality but by advantage; and to maintain a fair appearance rather than a good character.” [Note: [Col. 1024D] Sallust, *Catiline*, 10, where *subegit* (“subdued/compelled”) is read instead of *coegit* (“compelled”), as in our manuscript. The edition incorrectly reads *nullum* (“no”) instead of *vultum* (“appearance”).]

What is troublesome in this class is that the desire for power occurs more often in magnanimous and generous persons. Magnanimity makes men readier for attack, and munificence supplies it with greater resources; hence greater wickedness comes from their ambition than from that of the poor. Therefore the saying of LUCAN is true:

> There is no loyalty among partners in rule, and every power  
> Will be impatient of a sharer.  
>
> Alas—blind and mad  
> Fury of ambition!  
>
> There is no loyalty or filial devotion among men who follow camps,  
> And whose hands are for sale: there is justice where the reward is greatest.

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Lucan, I.92; X.147, 407.]

Cruelty is divided into force and fraud. Fraud seems fox-like, force leonine; both are wholly alien to humanity, but fraud deserves greater hatred. For there is no more deadly pest of all injustice than that of persons who, especially when they deceive, make it their business to appear good men. Therefore HORACE:

> Let spirits lurking beneath a fox never deceive you.

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Horace, *Ars Poetica*, 437.]

And JUVENAL:

> Shaggy limbs indeed, and hard bristles upon the body,  
> Promise a savage spirit.  
>
> No trust should be placed in the face. For what district does not abound  
> In gloomy, obscene men?

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Juvenal, *Satires*, II.11, where the first verse is:
>
> > Shaggy limbs indeed, and hard bristles over the arms.
>
> This is also the reading in the edition.—And ibid., a little above.]

The causes of omitting defence—that is, of negligence—are these: persons either do not wish to incur enmities, labour, or expense; or are so held fast by their own affairs; or are so alienated by hatred that they allow those whom they ought to protect to be abandoned. Yet it is safer to neglect a good person than a bad: the good merely becomes more sluggish when neglected, the bad more wicked. It is likewise safer to neglect a wealthy person than one in misfortune. TERENCE:

> All whose circumstances are less prosperous are, somehow,  
> More suspicious; they take everything more as an insult,  
> And because of their helplessness always think themselves neglected.

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Terence, *Adelphoe*, IV.iii.14–16.]

In every injustice it matters greatly whether the injury is done from disturbance of mind or deliberately. Disturbance is generally brief and temporary; therefore actions that arise from a sudden impulse are lighter than those inflicted after premeditation.

[Col. 1025D] ## ON FORTITUDE

**27.** Fortitude is the virtue that beats back the assaults of fortune. Its parts are magnanimity, confidence, security, magnificence, constancy, and patience. Magnanimity is the spontaneous and rational undertaking of difficult things; confidence is the mind’s certain hope of bringing an undertaking to completion; security is not fearing impending disadvantages or the failure of an undertaking already begun; magnificence is the completion of difficult and splendid things; constancy is a firm stability of mind persevering in its purpose; patience is the even-minded endurance of insults and every adversity. [Note: [Col. 1025D] These definitions should be compared with those given by Cicero, *On Invention*, II.54. The edition varies in several points. Thus at the end it reads: “Patience is the virtue that bears evenly the assaults of insults and every adversity.”]

## On Magnanimity

**28.** The poet encourages us toward the duties of magnanimity when he says:

> . . . prepare your minds  
> For the great work of virtue and the highest labours.

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Lucan, IX.380.]

And another poet:

> Virtue, opening heaven to those unworthy to die,  
> Attempts a path by a forbidden way,  
>
> And with fleeing wing scorns  
> Common crowds and the damp earth.

[Note: [Col. 1026D] Horace, *Odes*, III.2.21 ff.]

TULLY: “When this virtue makes someone ready to undertake hardships, it attends to the common advantage rather than his own. For just as knowledge separated from justice ought rather to be called cunning than wisdom, so a spirit prepared for dangers, if driven by its own desire rather than by the common good, bears the name of rashness rather than fortitude.” [Note: [Col. 1026D] Cicero, *On Duties*, I.19, with slight alterations.]

This virtue thus rouses lethargy. LUCAN:

> Cast off delay: delay has always harmed those ready for action.

[Note: [Col. 1026D] Lucan, I.281. This passage is absent from the edition, as are also the following four passages in sequence.]

HORACE:

> Begin. The rustic who postpones the hour of right living  
> Waits for the river to run away; but it—
[Col. 1026C] It slips and will keep slipping through all the rolling ages. [Note: [Col. 1026D] Horace, *Epistles* I.2.41–43, where it has: *qui recte vivendi* (“who [—] of living rightly”).]

PERSIUS:

“It will happen tomorrow. The same thing will happen tomorrow—what? Surely you are granting a great day; but when another light comes, we are already consuming yesterday’s tomorrow. Behold: another tomorrow will carry off these years, and there will always be a little further on. [Note: [Col. 1026D] Persius V.66–69.]

The philosopher TULLIUS defines the duty of this virtue: “Those are to be considered magnanimous not who commit injustice, but who repel it.” [Note: [Col. 1026D] Cicero, same passage, where *non* is lacking in the second place.] In this virtue the first precaution is against avarice. “For it is not consistent that one who is not broken by fear should be broken by desire; nor that one who has shown himself unconquered by toil should be conquered by pleasure or desire.” [Note: [Col. 1026D] Same author, same passage, ch. 20.] The second precaution is against ambition; for distinction is sought through hardships. “The more difficult something is, the more glorious it is; [Col. 1026D] for scarcely is anyone found who, having undertaken labours, does not desire glory as though it were his reward.” [Note: [Col. 1026D] Same author, same passage, ch. 19.]

The wise person places the fruit of virtue in conscience; the fool, in glory. For through glory they suppose that they will rise to positions of pre-eminence. “True greatness prefers to be a leader rather than to seem one. But whoever depends upon [Col. 1027A] the mistaken opinion of an ignorant multitude is not to be counted among great men.” [Note: [Col. 1027D] Cicero, cited passage. The edition reads: “prefers himself to be a leader rather than to seem one.” In a marginal note, however, it emends *errore* to *ore*, which is not to be rejected.]

Therefore honours must not be sought through glory. For the poet’s saying is true:

Virtue, ignorant of disgraceful rejection,  
Shines with unstained honours,  
And neither takes up nor lays down the axes  
At the pleasure of the popular breeze.  
[Note: [Col. 1027D] Horace, *Odes* III.2.]

The third precaution is against rashness. “To behave rashly in battle and engage the enemy hand-to-hand is something monstrous and like the behaviour of beasts. Yet if necessity requires it, one must fight, and death must be preferred to disgrace . . . . . . For one must never incur the danger of flight, lest we seem weak and cowardly.” [Note: [Col. 1027D] Same author, same passage, chs. 23 and beginning of 24.] Hence Lucan’s saying is true:

[Col. 1027B] Flight alone is a cowardly crime. [Note: [Col. 1027D] Lucan IX.283.]

TULLIUS: “Yet one must avoid offering oneself to death or danger without cause; nothing is more foolish than this. Therefore, in confronting dangers, let us imitate the practice of physicians: they treat slight illnesses lightly, but are compelled to apply hazardous remedies to more serious diseases. Thus, to wish for adverse weather in calm conditions is madness; but to remedy a storm by whatever means is wisdom—especially if, once the matter is settled, you will gain more good than the evil you feared.” [Note: [Col. 1027D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.24, where various readings must be weighed. The reading is *in advertendis periculis*, “in attending to dangers,” in place of *in adeundis*, “in confronting.”]

For what is written in the poet is true:

Strength without counsel falls by its own weight.  
Even the gods advance restrained strength  
[Col. 1027C] To greater things; the same gods hate forces  
Setting every crime in motion within the mind.  
[Note: [Col. 1027D] Horace, *Odes* III.4.]

## On Confidence

29. The duty of confidence is to hasten toward the completion of a task.

Believing nothing done while anything remained to be done.  
[Note: [Col. 1027D] Lucan II.657.]

For nothing is less becoming to those who have made progress than not to advance further.

## On Security

30. The duty of security is to provide consolation against the harshness of fortune. Accordingly Horace says:

In adversity it hopes; in prosperity  
A well-prepared breast fears another lot.  
Jupiter brings back shapeless winters,  
And likewise  
[Col. 1027D] Drives them away; it will not be so  
If it is ill now, and formerly was so. . . . . .

The welcome hour which is not hoped for will come unexpectedly.  
[Note: [Col. 1027D] Horace, *Odes* II.10; *Epistles* I.4.14.]

[Col. 1028A] Against this virtue fear thus contends.

## DIALOGUE BETWEEN SECURITY AND FEAR

[Note: [Col. 1027D] Among the excerpts attributed to Seneca, entitled *Book on Remedies for the Blows of Fortune*, which others attribute to Martin of Braga, this dialogue is likewise found, but is presented as occurring between Sense and Reason. Most deny that this work belongs to Seneca, although all loudly proclaim it to be his, since it has plainly been patched together from various passages taken from his books, as will be seen if the individual items are actually examined. Yet it must be admitted that certain material from other authors has also entered it, especially in our text, as will be evident from comparison. Moreover, in our manuscript the speakers are distinctly indicated, and there is also more material which is absent from the printed editions. [Col. 1028D]]

31. FEAR says: You will die.

SECURITY: That is human nature, not punishment. I entered under this condition: that I should depart.

FEAR: You will die.

SECURITY: It is the law of nations to return what one has received.

FEAR: You will die.

SECURITY: Human life is a journey: when you have walked far, at last you must return.

FEAR: You will die.

SECURITY: It is foolish to fear what I cannot avoid.

FEAR: You will die.

SECURITY: I thought you were bringing something new. I came to this end, I am moving toward it, every day leads me there. At my birth Nature set before me this limit in the world. What do I have to resent?

FEAR: You will die.

SECURITY: LUCAN:

. . . . . death, the final penalty,  
Is not to be feared by men.  
[Note: [Col. 1028D] Lucan VIII.355. It is lacking in the printed editions of the Senecan excerpts.]

FEAR: You will die.

SECURITY: Even the person who postpones death does not escape it.

FEAR: You will die.

SECURITY: I am neither the first nor the last; many have gone before me, and many will follow.

FEAR: You will die.

SECURITY: This is the end of human service.

[Col. 1028C] FEAR: You will die.

SECURITY: I know that I am a rational and mortal animal.

FEAR: You will die.

SECURITY: Nothing is burdensome when it happens only once.

FEAR: You will die.

SECURITY: Under this condition all things are brought forth: whatever has begun must end.

FEAR: You will die.

SECURITY: No mortal can threaten me with that.

FEAR: You will die; you will be beheaded.

SECURITY: It makes no difference whether I die by cutting or by stabbing.

FEAR: You will often be struck, and many swords will be turned against you.

SECURITY: It does not matter how many wounds there are; only one is fatal.

[Col. 1028D] FEAR: You will die abroad.

SECURITY: There is one road to heaven for everyone. [Note: [Col. 1028D] In the printed editions of Seneca: “From wherever one starts, there is one road to the underworld.” In our edition, however, another reply follows the question “You will die abroad,” namely: “Sleep is no heavier outdoors than at home.” The rest is omitted down to the passage from Juvenal.]

[Col. 1029A] FEAR: You will die abroad.

SECURITY: I am ready to pay wherever the moneylender calls upon me.

FEAR: You will die abroad.

SECURITY: No land is foreign to death.

FEAR: You will die young.

SECURITY: This one thing makes the young person equal to the old.

FEAR: You will die young.

SECURITY: It is best to die when living is still pleasant.

FEAR: You will die young.

SECURITY: It is best to die before you wish for death, as JUVENAL says:

This punishment is given to the long-lived: that, with renewed  
Disaster always in their house, amid many griefs and in  
Perpetual sorrow and black clothing, they grow old.  
[Note: [Col. 1029D] Juvenal X.243.]

[Col. 1029B] AND LUCAN:

Only the last day, together with the end of blessings,  
Has arrived; and by swift death it forestalled sorrowful things.  
Fortune comes before disgrace. Does anyone  
Dare surrender himself to favourable destinies unless death is ready?  
[Note: [Col. 1029D] Lucan VIII.29. The first verse is read thus: “Unless the last day comes with the end of empire and blessings.”]

FEAR: You will die young. 977

SECURITY: Perhaps fortune is withdrawing me from one misfortune so that I may certainly not be subject to another, or to old age.

Luxury fears neither untimely ashes nor a bitter funeral;  
Rather, old age is more to be feared than death.  
[Note: [Col. 1029D] Juvenal XI.44.]

FEAR: You will die young.

SECURITY: It does not matter how many years I have, but how many I have received. If I cannot live longer, this is our old age: whoever comes to the end of his destiny dies old.

[Col. 1029C] FEAR: You will lie unburied.

SECURITY: . . . . an easy loss, a tomb. [Note: [Col. 1029D] Virgil, *Aeneid* II.646.]

. . . . . Whether decay dissolves corpses  
Or a pyre does so makes no difference: Nature receives  
All things into her peaceful bosom, and bodies owe their end to themselves . . . .

Death is free from Fortune: the earth receives all  
That it has generated; he who has no urn is covered by heaven.  
[Note: [Col. 1029D] Lucan VII.909–911 and 918–919. In the edition, only these words from the passage are read: “He who has no urn is covered by heaven.”]

FEAR: You will lie unburied.

SECURITY: If I feel nothing, the loss of an unburied body does not concern me. If I feel anything, every burial is a torment.

FEAR: You will lie unburied.

SECURITY: It makes no difference whether fire, a beast, or the earth [Note: [Col. 1030D] The manuscript more correctly reads *time*, “time.” Moreover, the following five lines are lacking in the edition.] consumes me. This is the final burial of all.

[Col. 1029D] FEAR: You will lie unburied.

SECURITY: Why do you tremble at something which by right is most safe? [Note: [Col. 1030D] Security answers this to himself.]

FEAR: You will lie unburied.

SECURITY: Burial was invented not for the sake of the dead but of the living, so that bodies offensive to sight and smell might be removed—wherein consideration is shown to our eyes.

FEAR: You will fall ill.

SECURITY: The time comes when I shall make trial of myself. [Col. 1030A] A brave man appears not only at sea or in battle; virtue is displayed even in bed.

FEAR: You will fall ill.

SECURITY: Either I shall leave the fever, or it will leave me; my business is with the disease: it will either conquer or be conquered; I cannot remain forever.

FEAR: People will speak ill of you.

SECURITY: I would be moved if they did so from judgment; now they do it from sickness. For those who do not know how to speak well do so not because I deserve it, but because it is their habit. The insults of the ignorant must be heard with equanimity, and one proceeding toward honourable things must despise such contempt.

FEAR: You will go into exile. [Note: [Col. 1030D] The following eight lines are lacking in the edition.]

SECURITY: You are mistaken: whatever I may do, I cannot leave my fatherland; [Col. 1030B] there is one fatherland for all, beyond which no one can go.

FEAR: You will go into exile.

SECURITY: Into whatever land I come, I come into my own. No land is exile, but another fatherland.

FEAR: You will not be in your fatherland.

SECURITY: I am in my fatherland wherever I am well. But that through which one is well lies in the human being, not in a place.

FEAR: Pain threatens.

SECURITY: If it is slight, let us endure it, because endurance is easy; if severe, let us endure it, because glory is not slight.

FEAR: Pain is a harsh thing.

SECURITY: It is immovable, if endurance is present. [Note: [Col. 1030D] In the edition, in place of *immobilis*, “immovable,” one reads: “Indeed, you are weak.”]

[Col. 1030C] FEAR: Few can endure pain.

SECURITY: Let us be among those few.

FEAR: We are of weak nature.

SECURITY: Do not slander Nature. She brought us forth strong.

FEAR: Poverty is pleasant to me.

SECURITY: On the contrary, you are pleasant to poverty. The fault is not in poverty but in the poor person.

FEAR: I am poor.

SECURITY: You are not poor, but you appear so. Birds lack nothing; cattle live from day to day. Great wealth, great pride.

FEAR: I am not powerful.

SECURITY: Rejoice: you will not be powerless.

[Col. 1030D] FEAR: That man has great wealth.

SECURITY: Do you judge that he is a human being? The chest is full; the man whom you think master of the money is a cash-box.

FEAR: That man has much.

SECURITY: If he is avaricious, he does not possess it; if prodigal, he will not possess it. The man whom you think happy often grieves, often sighs.

[Col. 1031A] FEAR: Many accompany him.

SECURITY: Flies follow honey, wolves follow corpses, ants follow grain; that crowd follows prey, not the man.

FEAR: I have lost my money.

SECURITY: Perhaps it would have lost you.

FEAR: I have lost my money.

SECURITY: You will have the benefit of losing it.

FEAR: I have lost my money.

SECURITY: O fortunate you! If you lost greed together with it . . . . . But if greed remains with you, nevertheless you are happier, since the material for your evil has been removed.

FEAR: I have lost my money.

SECURITY: Another lost it so that you might have it.

FEAR: I have lost my money.

[Col. 1031B] SECURITY: You will be less encumbered on the road, safer at home.

FEAR: I have lost my eyes.

SECURITY: But does it not also have its own pleasures? 978

FEAR: I have lost my eyes.

SECURITY: The mind has eyes of its own, through which there is a costly path to many desires. You will lack many things which would have had to be torn out so that you might not see them. Blindness is a part of innocence. Eyes show one person adultery, another a house to covet, another a city.

FEAR: I have lost my children.
