SECURITY: Foolish is the person who bewails the death of mortals. They have perished though destined to perish; God received them, he did not take them away. In this manner Fear, which was never going to give faithful counsel, ended its war with Virtue.

32. What is read in HORACE is true:

[Col. 1031C] The man who is just and firm in his purpose  
Is not shaken from his steadfast mind  
Either by the passion of citizens commanding what is wrong  
Or by the face of a threatening tyrant.  
[Note: [Col. 1031D] Horace, *Odes* III.3.]

LUCAN:

. . . . . Fear itself of coming evil has sent many  
Into the greatest dangers; bravest is he  
Who is ready to suffer what must be feared.  
[Note: [Col. 1031D] Lucan VII.104.]

“It belongs to a strong and steadfast mind not to be disturbed in adverse circumstances, nor to be cast down from its position by turmoil, but to use present judgment and not depart from reason.” [Note: [Col. 1031D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.23.] For there are more things that frighten us than oppress us, and more often we suffer from opinion than from reality. Therefore do not be miserable before the time: those things which you have feared as though impending may perhaps never [Col. 1031D] come.

## On Magnificence

33. The duties of magnificence are partly peaceful and partly military. In peaceful matters, two precepts of Plato must be observed by rulers: “First, that they should guard the welfare of citizens in such a way that whatever they do they refer it to that end, forgetting their own advantage; second, that they should care for the whole [Col. 1032A] body of the state, lest, while protecting some part, they abandon the rest. . . . For those who provide for one part and abandon another introduce ruinous faction into the state. . . . They must also beware of rivalry. Plato says that those who compete with each other over which of them should govern the state best act as if sailors disputed which of them ought chiefly to steer the ship.” [Note: [Col. 1031D] Same author, same passage, I.25.]

In military duties, the first point is “to undertake war with the intention that one may live in peace without injustice.” [Note: [Col. 1031D] Same author, same work, I.11.] The second is “before undertaking an action, to employ careful preparation.” [Note: [Col. 1031D] Same author, same work, I.21, at the end.] For a long preparation for war brings a swift victory. This preparation is seen in four things: dependants, municipalities, expenditures, and words.

[Col. 1032B] TERENCE:

A wise person ought to try everything first by words rather than arms.  
I prefer that we look out for ourselves rather than avenge this man’s injury.  
[Note: [Col. 1031D] Terence, *Eunuchus* IV.viii.19; IV.vi.25.]

The third duty is “not to despair through cowardice, or to be overconfident through desire.” [Note: [Col. 1031D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.21.] For an immoderate love of possession leads into dangers. Accordingly Horace says:

Gold delights in passing through guards  
And breaking through rocks more powerfully  
Than a thunderbolt’s blow . . .

Gifts . . .  
Entangle savage leaders.  
[Note: [Col. 1032D] Horace, *Odes* III.16.]

The fourth is to dread disgrace more than death; to look more to honour than to safety or [Col. 1032C] other advantages. The fifth is to exercise one’s body through frequent labours.

Idleness always gives a foolish mind. [Note: [Col. 1032D] Lucan IV.704. Where the variant is *variam*, “fickle”; but others, as does our text, read *vanam*, “foolish.”]

The sixth is, once battle has begun, to raise good natural disposition by encouragement: now to exalt the spirit by praise, now to dispel indolence by warnings. The seventh is, in the clash, to rush to meet the first attacks, to bring help to those who are giving way, and to support those who are wavering. The eighth is “after victory has been won, to spare those who were neither cruel nor savage.” [Note: [Col. 1032D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.11.]

The ninth is to keep treaties and promises, and one must not agree with those who say: “It makes no difference whether one conquers enemies by deceit or by courage.” [Note: [Col. 1032D] The edition reads: “For one must not agree with those who say: ‘Who asks whether there is deceit or courage in an enemy?’]

“Regulus demonstrates this: captured by the Carthaginians and sent [Col. 1032D] to Rome concerning an exchange of prisoners, he swore that he would return. When he came to Rome, he did not judge that the prisoners ought to be returned; then, though his friends tried to detain him, he preferred to return to punishment rather than break his pledged word.” [Note: [Col. 1032D] Same work, I.13 ff.]

“But since many judge military affairs greater than civic ones, this opinion must be diminished; for many have sought wars from the desire for glory. . . . But if we wish to judge truly . . . weapons abroad are of little account [Col. 1033A] if there is no counsel at home.” [Note: [Col. 1033D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.22.]

Against such people, SALLUST:

“All people who strive to excel other animals ought to exert themselves with the utmost effort, lest they pass through life in silence like cattle. But all the power of our nature lies in mind and body; we use the mind more for command, the body for service. It seems more right to seek glory by the resources of intellect than by those of strength.” [Note: [Col. 1033D] Sallust, *Catiline*, opening. The edition reads: “Hear the poet speaking of such persons: ‘All people,’ etc.”]

“For indeed whatever honourable end we seek with a lofty spirit is accomplished by the mind, not by bodily strength; yet the body must be exercised so that it can obey counsel and reason.” [Note: [Col. 1033D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.23.]

## On Constancy

34. The duty of constancy is to maintain seriousness in either fortune. “For the same expression and the same face throughout life are admirable; for it is the mark [Col. 1033B] of a well-ordered mind to be able to stand firm and remain with itself.” [Note: [Col. 1033D] Seneca, *Letters* 2. The preceding period is not found here, however; perhaps the author transferred it here from another letter of Seneca or another book.]

Hence HORACE:

Remember to preserve an even mind in difficult circumstances,  
And likewise, in prosperity, one restrained  
From insolent  
Joy.

Likewise:

In straitened circumstances he appears spirited and brave;  
The same man, wiser, will draw in  
His swollen sails beneath  
An all-too-favourable wind.  
[Note: [Col. 1033D] Horace, *Odes* II.3; II.10.]

This indeed is the law of constancy: that we be neither obstinate in evils nor fickle in prosperity. For there is a constancy in evils which is not a virtue.

Hence HORACE:

One part of humankind steadfastly delights in vices and presses on  
[Col. 1033C] With its course; a large part swims about, now pursuing what is right,  
At times enslaved to what is wrong.  
[Note: [Col. 1033D] Same author, *Satires* II.7.6.]

And JUVENAL:

The nature of the wicked is always mobile and variable:  
when they commit a crime, constancy remains. What is lawful  
And unlawful they begin at last to perceive after  
Their crimes have been committed; nevertheless nature returns  
To condemned habits, fixed and unable to change. For who  
Has set a limit to sinning once he has recovered  
The shame driven from his brow, worn away by use?  
Is there any human being whom you have seen despised for one  
Disgraceful act?  
[Note: [Col. 1033D] Juvenal XIII.13, 236–244. Where *ferme*, “nearly,” is read in place of *semper*, “always.”] . . . .

980 Inconstancy is opposed to this virtue: a movement of the mind among various pursuits. Some labour under this vice so unceasingly that their constancy is said to be unstable. “There are [Col. 1033D] those who are insufficiently consistent with themselves in opposite circumstances: they despise pleasure most sternly, but are weaker in pain; they disregard glory, but are broken by disgrace.” [Col. 1034A] [Note: [Col. 1033D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.21.]

The poet HORACE rebukes this vice:

. . . Why does my judgment fight against itself?  
What it sought, it despises; what it lately abandoned, it seeks again.  
It boils over, and disagrees with the whole order of life:  
It destroys, builds, changes squares into circles.  
[Note: [Col. 1033D] Horace, *Epistles* I.1.97–100.]

THE SAME AUTHOR:

Fickle, I love Tibur at Rome, and Rome at Tibur. . . .  
The fault lies in the mind, which never escapes itself. . . . . .

Those who run across the sea change their sky, not their mind. . . .

With what knot am I to hold Proteus, who changes his shapes?  
[Note: [Col. 1033D] Same author, *Epistles* I.8.11; I.14.13; I.11.27; I.1.90. Where the reading is: “With what knot am I to hold Proteus changing his shapes?”]

From this one thing arises the fact that no one lives content with his own lot, but praises those pursuing different things. Hence HORACE:

The sluggish ox desires trappings; the horse desires to plough.  
Let each willingly practise the craft which he knows, I shall judge.  
It is right for everyone to measure himself by his own measure and foot.  
[Note: [Col. 1034D] Horace, *Epistles* I.14.43; I.7.98.]

[Col. 1034B] ## On Patience

35. Lucan shows the duty of patience when he says:

Patience rejoices in hardships.

What is honourable gives greater pleasure whenever it costs one dearly.  
[Note: [Col. 1034D] Lucan IX.403.]

This virtue is a remedy for injuries. For:

Whatever it is unlawful to correct  
Becomes lighter through patience.  
[Note: [Col. 1034D] Horace, *Odes* I.24, at the end.]

Just as, conversely, through impatience you make your lot harsher when you cannot change it. TERENCE likewise says:

What chance brings, we shall bear with an even mind.

. . . It is ignorance  
To kick against the goad.  
[Note: [Col. 1034D] Terence, *Phormio* I.ii.88; same work, v. 27. The edition has: “For it is ignorance to kick against the goad.” The following two sayings are from excerpts of Seneca, passages unknown to the editor.]

SENECA: “An intemperate sick man makes the middle course harsh.” Add this: “No thing is so easy that it does not become difficult if you do it unwillingly.”

[Col. 1034C] ## ON TEMPERANCE

36. “Temperance is the dominion of reason over desire and other unruly impulses.” [Note: [Col. 1034D] Cicero, *On Invention* II.54, where he nevertheless posits only three parts of it: self-control, clemency, and modesty. Our author has added others.] This virtue is the adornment of the whole life and the calming of all disturbances. Horace recommends it:

Unless the vessel is clean, whatever you pour into it turns sour.  
Despise pleasures: pleasure bought with pain harms.  
The greedy person is always in want; seek a fixed end for your desire.  
The envious person wastes away at another’s prosperity.

. . . . . . . . . . Whoever will not govern anger  
Will wish undone what pain and passion have urged.  
Anger is a brief madness. Rule your mind: unless it obeys,  
It commands. Restrain it with reins; restrain it with a chain.  
[Note: [Col. 1034D] Horace, *Epistles* I.2.54–63.]

Its parts are those virtues which govern shameful impulses: namely modesty, reserve, abstinence, honourableness, moderation, frugality, sobriety, [Col. 1034D] chastity.

## On Modesty

37. Modesty is the virtue that preserves one’s bearing, every [Col. 1035A] movement, and our occupation beyond deficiency and short of excess. 981 Horace says of it:

There is a measure in things; in short, there are fixed limits  
Beyond and short of which the right cannot stand.  
[Note: [Col. 1035D] Horace, *Satires* I.1.109.]

TULLIUS: “In dress it must be observed that every adornment unworthy of a man be removed from the human form.” [Note: [Col. 1035D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.36.]

SENECA: “Bad outward adornment is the messenger of a badly ordered mind.”

TULLIUS: “Cleanliness must be practised, not offensive nor too elaborate, but only such as avoids rustic and uncivil negligence. Movements are of one kind in the body, another in the mind. In bodily movement care must be taken that we do not use a gait so slow and soft that we appear like bearers in processions, nor, when hurrying, adopt excessive rapidity. For when this happens, breathing becomes laboured, faces change, mouths are contorted; and these signs show that constancy is absent. Movements of the mind are twofold: rational thought and appetite. The activity of reason is exercised in seeking truth; appetite impels to action. Therefore care must be taken that reason presides and appetite obeys. For if appetites do not obey reason, to which they are subject by the law of nature, not only minds but bodies also are disturbed. One may observe the very faces of angry persons, or of those stirred by fear, or exulting in pleasure: all their faces, voices, movements, and postures are altered.” [Note: [Col. 1035D] Same author, same work; I.29.]

For when the heart is inflamed by the flames of anger, it throbs; the body rages, the tongue thrusts itself out, the face burns, the eyes grow fierce and familiar persons are no longer recognized. [Col. 1035C] Hence JUVENAL:

You may discern the torments of a hidden mind in the sick  
Body; you may discern its joys as well: the face takes its expression  
From both.  
[Note: [Col. 1035D] Juvenal IX.18.]

From these things it is understood that all appetites must be restrained and quieted.

38. Occupations differ according to the diversity of characters, ages, and affairs. For just as there are many dissimilarities among bodies—for you may see some more swift in practical activity, others strong for wrestling—so there are greater varieties of character in minds. Some possess wit and urbanity in speech; these, cheerfulness; those, freedom from care. Others you may see as shrewd in pretence and concealment; [Col. 1035D] others are simple and open, thinking that nothing should be done secretly or by intrigues: cultivators of truth, enemies of deceit. Why should I mention every instance? PERSIUS:

A thousand types of people, and a variegated practice of life:  
Each person has his own will, and no one lives by a single desire.  
[Note: [Col. 1035D] Persius V.52.]

TERENCE:

As many people as there are, so many opinions; each has his own way.  
[Note: [Col. 1035D] Terence, *Phormio* II.iv.14.]

[Col. 1036A] TULLIUS: “Accordingly, let us chiefly devote ourselves to those pursuits for which we shall be better fitted. . . . And although other pursuits may be better and more serious, nevertheless let us measure our studies by the rule of nature. . . .”

For example, if you are weak in body but talented and endowed with a lively memory, you will pursue not military service but literary studies. 982 But if you are strong and dull-witted, military service rather than literary study. . . .

“For it is not fitting to follow that aspect of nature which you cannot attain. . . . But if necessity draws us to pursuits unsuited to our ability, every care must be taken to perform them, if not honourably, at least not too dishonourably; and we must strive not so much to pursue goods not granted to us as to flee vices.” [Note: [Col. 1035D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.21, though neither in the same order [Col. 1036D] nor in exactly the same words. The material in brackets was added by our author for explanatory purposes.]

[Col. 1036B] 39. Horace briefly explains what belongs to the different ages:

The boy, who now knows how to form words  
And marks the ground with firm foot, delights in playing with equals;  
He quickly gathers and lays aside anger, and changes from hour to hour.

The beardless youth, once at last free from his guardian,  
Delights in horses and dogs and the grass of the sunny field;  
Wax to be bent toward vice, harsh toward advisers,  
Slow to provide what is useful, prodigal of money,  
Lofty in spirit, desirous, and swift to abandon those he loves.

With changed interests, the age and spirit of manhood  
Seek wealth and friendships, serve honour,  
And fear committing what they may soon labour to alter.

Many inconveniences surround the old man: either because  
He seeks wealth, then miserably withholds what he has found and fears to use it;  
Or because he handles all matters coldly and timidly—  
A procrastinator, long in hope, inactive and avid for the future,  
Difficult, complaining, a praiser of the time passed  
[Col. 1036C] In his boyhood, a critic and chastiser of the younger.  
[Note: [Col. 1036D] Horace, *Art of Poetry* 158–174.]

Therefore he truly

Praises past years and despises the present,

because in our life there is continual deterioration, as the same poet elsewhere shows:

What does destructive time fail to diminish?  
The age of our parents, worse than that of our grandfathers, produced  
Us, more wicked still, soon to produce  
An offspring yet more vicious.  
[Note: [Col. 1036D] Same author, *Odes* III.6, at the end.]

40. Since this is so, “the duty of an adolescent is to respect those older than himself and to choose from among them the most approved persons, whose counsel he may use; for the inexperience of early age must be guided by the prudence of old men.” [Note: [Col. 1036D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.34.] For the young man, as TERENCE says:

While the mind is uncertain, it is driven this way and that by the slightest impulse.  
[Note: [Col. 1036D] Terence, *Andria* I.vi.32.]

[Col. 1036D] TULLIUS: “For at the beginning of adolescence there is the greatest weakness of judgment when each person establishes for himself the kind of life he has most loved. Thus he becomes involved in some course of life before he has been able to judge which would be best.” [Note: [Col. 1036D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.32.]

Therefore the young man’s duty is, according to TERENCE:

To look, as into a mirror, upon the lives of all,  
[Col. 1037A] . . . . and draw an example for himself from others.  
[Note: [Col. 1037D] Terence, *Adelphoe* III.iii.62.]

SENECA: “For it is good to observe, in another’s misfortune, what one must avoid.” [Note: [Col. 1037D] Seneca, in the *Proverbs*, or in the mimes of Publilius, see under letter B.]

TULLIUS: “This age especially must be kept away from lusts,” [Note: [Col. 1037D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.34.] in accordance with JUVENAL:

. . . . Let what you dare shamefully be brief,  
Though certain first crimes are consumed with the first beard.  
[Note: [Col. 1037D] Juvenal VIII.165.]

HORACE:

For play produces trembling rivalry and anger,  
Anger produces fierce enmities and deadly war.  
[Note: [Col. 1037D] Horace, *Epistles* I.19.48.]

TULLIUS: “The age of adolescents must be exercised in labours of mind and body, so that its energy may be effective in military and civic duties.” [Note: [Col. 1037D] Cicero, cited passage.] 983 Hence HORACE:

[Col. 1037B] Let the boy, robust through harsh military service, learn, my friends,  
To endure narrow poverty.

And elsewhere:

. . . . . . . Now give yourself to better things.  
What the fresh jar has once been steeped in will preserve its scent  
For a long time.  
[Note: [Col. 1037D] Horace, *Odes* III.2; *Epistles* I.2.68.]

PERSIUS:

“Despise it!” The jar, struck, rings out and spitefully  
Answers from its unbaked, green clay.  
You are moist and soft clay; now, now you must hurry and be  
Fashioned without end upon the swift wheel.  
[Note: [Col. 1037D] Persius III.21 ff.]

TULLIUS: “And even when they wish to relax their minds and yield to pleasure, let them beware of intemperance and remember modesty. This will be easier if they wish older people to be present at their games. One may indeed use play and jest, but as one uses sleep and rest: that is, once we have satisfied the claims of serious duties. For we were not made for play but for seriousness.” [Note: [Col. 1037D] Cicero, cited passage; and I.29, though not word for word.]

Hence HORACE:

Certainly it is useful wisdom, after trifles have been cast aside,  
To grant children play at the fitting time.  
[Note: [Col. 1037D] Horace, *Epistles* II.2.141. Here the manuscript contains two verses by the same author from *Epistles* I.19, which, as they appeared in the edition, we cited above.]

TULLIUS: “There are altogether two kinds of jesting: one ungentlemanly, wanton, shameful, obscene; the other elegant, urbane, witty, and amusing.” [Note: [Col. 1038D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.29.]

41. The duties of mature men are those which the poet listed above, in which nothing requires correction by any rule. TULLIUS: “For old men bodily labours seem to require diminution, but exercises of the mind [Col. 1037D] increase.” [Note: [Col. 1038D] Same author, same work, I.34.]

TERENCE:

No one has ever ordered his life by such sound calculation  
[Col. 1038A] That circumstances, age, and experience do not always bring something new,  
Something that warns him; so that what you think you know, you do not know,  
And what you thought foremost you reject when you experience it.  
[Note: [Col. 1038D] Terence, *Adelphoe* V.iv.1 ff.]

TULLIUS: “Old people must therefore make an effort to assist friends and the young by counsel. But an old man must especially beware of surrendering himself to weakness and idleness.” [Note: [Col. 1038D] Cicero, cited passage.] Otherwise one will say to him:

Do you prepare to appease envy after abandoning virtue?  
[Note: [Col. 1038D] Horace, *Satires* II.3.13.]

TULLIUS: “Although luxury is shameful at every age, it is most disgraceful in old age. For if intemperance in desires is added, the evil is twofold: old age itself incurs disgrace, and it makes the intemperance of the young more shameless.” [Note: [Col. 1038D] Cicero, cited passage.]

JUVENAL:

[Col. 1038B] . . . . . . . Domestic examples of vices corrupt us  
More swiftly and more readily . . .

. . . We are all readily taught  
To imitate shameful and wicked things.  
[Note: [Col. 1038D] Juvenal XIV.31–32 and 40–41.]

42. The duties of public officials are likewise different. The duty of a ruler, TULLIUS says, is to reckon “that he bears the person of the state, preserves its dignity, safeguards its laws, and remembers that they have been entrusted to his good faith. The duty of a private citizen is to live with fellow citizens under equal law—not exalting himself too much, not too submissive, not too abject—and to desire in the commonwealth things that are peaceful and honourable.” [Note: [Col. 1038D] Cicero, cited passage.]

Let him beware lest Sallust’s statement apply to him: “There are always some in a state who possess no resources, envy the good, exalt the wicked, and strive to change everything.” [Note: [Col. 1038D] Sallust, *Catiline* 37.]

[Col. 1038C] TULLIUS: “The duty of a foreigner is to do nothing beyond his own business, to inquire into nothing belonging to another, and not to be curious about another state. The occupation of those who buy from merchants what they immediately sell is base. For they gain nothing unless they lie excessively, and nothing is more disgraceful than such empty pretence. . . . Therefore a household estate should be 984 acquired by occupations free from disgrace, and preserved by frugality.” [Note: [Col. 1038D] Cicero, cited passage and ch. 42; and II.24.]

OVID:

It is no lesser virtue to preserve what has been acquired than to acquire it.  
[Note: [Col. 1038D] Ovid, *Art of Love* II.13.]

SENECA: “For no profit is as great as sparing what one possesses.” [Note: [Col. 1038D] Seneca, or Publilius, *Mimes*, no. 577.]

Yet wealth should be acquired in such a way that we imitate the man of whom it is written: “Our Demetrius lives not as though he has despised all things, but as though he has [Col. 1038D] allowed others to possess them.” [Note: [Col. 1038D] Same author, *Letters* 62.]

TULLIUS: “Medicine and architecture are honourable professions for those suited to them. Trade, however, if small-scale, must be considered base; if large and extensive, importing much from every region and distributing to many without ostentation, it is not greatly to be blamed. Agriculture is nothing better, nothing more productive, nothing more worthy of a free person.” [Note: [Col. 1039A] Cicero, *On Duties* I.42.]

The poet HORACE praises this in the words:

Blessed is the man who, far from business  
(Like the ancient race of mortals),  
Cultivates his ancestral fields with his own oxen,  
Free from every debt.  
[Note: [Col. 1039D] Horace, *Epodes* II, opening.]

## On Reserve
43. Modesty consists in preserving propriety in bearing, speech, and expression. TULLY: “In the composition of the body, nature seems to have exercised great care. For she placed our form, in which there is a comely appearance, openly; but she concealed those parts given for nature’s necessities [Col. 1039B], because they would have had an unsightly appearance. Human modesty has imitated this careful workmanship of nature. Whatever nature concealed, all persons of sound mind remove from sight; they even take pains to meet necessity as secretly as possible, and use those necessary parts sparingly, neither calling the parts nor their functions by their proper names. It is likewise faulty to introduce delicate language in a serious matter. When Pericles and Sophocles, colleagues in the praetorship, had met concerning their common duty, and by chance a handsome boy passed by, Sophocles said: ‘O Pericles, what a beautiful boy!’ Pericles replied: ‘It befits a praetor to keep not only his hands but also his eyes [Col. 1039C] restrained.’ Had Sophocles said this at a banquet, he would rightly have escaped censure.” [Note: [Col. 1039D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.35 and 40.]

Concerning this modesty of speech HORACE says:

> Sad words befit the sorrowful face;  
> Threat-filled words the angry; wanton words the playful;  
> Serious words the grave to utter.  
> For nature first forms us inwardly for every  
> Condition of fortune; she delights us or drives us to anger,  
> Or bows us to the ground and oppresses us with heavy grief;  
> Then she expresses the emotions of the mind through the tongue, its interpreter.  
> If a speaker’s words are discordant with his condition,  
> Roman knights and foot-soldiers alike will raise a laugh.  
> It will matter greatly whether it is Davus who speaks, or bold  
> Pythias, who has gained a talent from sharp-witted Simon;  
> Whether it is a mature old man or one still ardent in blooming youth;  
> A powerful matron or a diligent nurse;  
> A wandering merchant or the cultivator of a green little field.  
> [Note: [Col. 1039D] Horace, *Art of Poetry* 105 ff.; the verse concerning Pythias “who has gained a talent from sharp-witted Simon” has been transferred here from verse 238 of the same work. Moreover, this much-disputed passage of Horace may perhaps receive some light from this source.]

[Col. 1039D] He sets forth a fourth duty when HORACE says:

> Never will you pry into his secret.  
> [Note: [Col. 1039D] Horace, *Epistles* I.18.37.]

[985] He adds a fifth:

> And you will conceal what has been entrusted to you, even when tortured by wine and anger …  
> Often consider what you say concerning each man, and to whom.  
>   
> [Col. 1040A] Avoid the questioner, for he is likewise a chatterer.  
> Open ears do not faithfully keep things entrusted to them:  
> A word once released flies forth irrevocably.  
> [Note: [Col. 1039D] Id., ibid., v. 381—and 18.71. The final verse appears thus in editions of Horace: “And once released, it flies forth irrevocably.” Yet our reading too should not be despised.]

Therefore you should by no means disclose a secret to a chatterer; for you cannot demand silence of another if you have not supplied it yourself. If you accuse a chatterer, TERENCE replies:

> I am full of cracks; I leak this way and that.  
> [Note: [Col. 1040D] Terence, *Eunuch* I.2.25.]

Therefore devote yourself to hearing more willingly than speaking. Above all, avoid quarrels. For to contend with an equal is hazardous, with a superior mad, and with an inferior—or a fool—base. “He harms the absent man who quarrels with a drunkard.” [Note: [Col. 1040D] Among the sayings of Publilius, no. 6; to these, I think, the preceding sayings should likewise be referred, although I have not hitherto found them.]

## On abstinence

44. Abstinence and propriety, moderation and frugality, restrain the inducements of food. The first of these is to anticipate the appointed time of the meal; the second, to seek more luxurious foods. JUVENAL rebukes the first:

> Marius, an exile, drinks from the eighth hour onward and enjoys  
> The gods’ anger.  
> [Note: [Col. 1040D] Juvenal I.49.]

The second he rebukes when he says:

> … You must know the measure of your own mouth, and observe it  
> In matters both greatest and least, even when fish is being bought;  
> Do not crave a red mullet when you have only a gudgeon  
> In your purse.  
> [Note: [Col. 1040D] Idem III.34.]

A third vice is to devote attention to elaborate presentation, which JUVENAL rebukes:

> … And truly it matters by no slight distinction  
> With what gesture a hare or a hen is carved.  
> [Note: [Col. 1040D] Idem V.123.]

[Col. 1040C] And LUCAN:

> O prodigal luxury of resources, never content with a modest provision;  
> O ambitious hunger for foods sought on land and sea,  
> And glory in so great a table—  
> Learn how little is enough to sustain life,  
> And how little nature requires …  
>   
> … For peoples, a river and Ceres are enough.  
> [Note: [Col. 1040D] Lucan IV.373 and 381.]

The fourth is to gape with excessive appetite. The fifth is to exceed the measure of refreshment, as HORACE understands when he says:

> … Every corrupted judge judges truth badly.  
>   
> Indeed, feasts sought without end turn bitter.  
> [Note: [Col. 1040D] Horace, *Satires* II.2.8; ibid. VII.107.]

Therefore abstinence is not to anticipate the appointed time for eating. This pleasure makes use more agreeable. [Col. 1040D] JUVENAL:

> Rarer use commends pleasures.  
> [Note: [Col. 1040D] Juvenal, II, end.]

SENECA: “Nothing is pleasant unless variety refreshes it.” [Note: [Col. 1040D] Seneca, or rather P. Lysus, in the *Mimes*, no. 387.] Hence HORACE:

> A hungry stomach rarely despises common food.  
> [Note: [Col. 1040D] Horace, *Satires* II.2.38.]

[Col. 1041A]

## On propriety

45. Propriety is neither to seek more luxurious food nor to labour over excessive elaboration of its presentation. This virtue is commended by HORACE:

> Often the welcome changes, and the clean suppers  
> Of poor men beneath a humble roof,  
> Without tapestries or purple,  
> Have smoothed the anxious brow of the rich.  
> [Note: [Col. 1041D] Horace, *Odes* III.29.13 ff.]

## On moderation

46. Moderation is to recall excessive appetite for food under the rule of reason.

## On frugality

47. Frugality is not to exceed the measure of refreshment, in accordance with LUCAN:

> His feast was, nevertheless, to have conquered hunger.  
> [Note: [Col. 1041D] Lucan II.384, concerning Cato’s character and manner of life. This passage is also cited below.]

[Col. 1041B]

## On sobriety

48. Sobriety is to restrain excess in drinking. Its duty is to check the evils of drunkenness. [986] HORACE makes this clear in these words:

> What does drunkenness not reveal? It uncovers what was hidden;  
> It commands hopes to be deemed certain; it drives the unarmed into battle.  
> It removes the burden from anxious minds; it teaches arts.  
> Whom have fruitful cups not made eloquent?  
> [Note: [Col. 1041D] Horace, *Epistles* I.5.16 ff.]

## On chastity

49. Chastity is to tame licentiousness by the restraint of strength. SALLUST: “If desire possesses and rules the mind, the mind has no power. For no one has ever at the same time obeyed desire and expediency.” [Note: [Col. 1041D] Sallust, *Catiline* 54, with a few changes.]

SENECA: “Pleasure [Col. 1042A] is fragile, brief, and degrading; it produces disgust. The more eagerly it is drained, the more swiftly it rebounds into its opposite; one must continually either repent of it or be ashamed of it. There is nothing magnificent in it, nor anything suited to the nature of a human being who is close to the gods. It is a low thing, arising through the service of shameful and worthless limbs, foul in its outcome.” [Note: [Col. 1041D] Seneca, *On Benefits* VII.2.]

It is indeed abominable, for the sake of a foul prostitute and a dishonourable part of the body, to bend the freedom of the soul into slavery and to make one’s own labour serve another’s pleasures. TULLY: “Therefore a brave man should always keep ready to hand how far human nature surpasses brute animals. They feel nothing but pleasure and rush toward it with all their force; but the human mind is nourished by learning and reflection. Accordingly, if anyone is more inclined to pleasure, let him beware of belonging to the race of beasts. [Col. 1042B] Hence it is understood that bodily pleasure is unworthy of human excellence, since it seeks hiding places. For if anyone is raised a little higher, although he is captivated by pleasure, he conceals his appetite for it out of modesty.” [Note: [Col. 1041D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.30.]

Therefore let us flee the dominion of flattering pleasure. “For pleasures, most seductive mistresses, for the most part turn men away from virtue.” [Note: [Col. 1041D] Id., *On Duties* II.10. What follows is absent from the edition.] OVID:

> Venus and wine have broken lofty hearts.  
> [Note: [Col. 1041D] Ovid, *Fasti* I.301. But here *non* is read in place of *nam*, as the context requires.]

Likewise: “Wine and women make wise men apostatize.” [Note: [Col. 1042D] Vulgate translation, Ecclesiasticus XIX.2.]

# QUESTION II. ON THE COMPARISON OF HONOURABLE THINGS

[Col. 1041]

[Col. 1041C] 50. It remains to treat the second question, that concerning the comparison of honourable things. Prudence belongs to knowledge; the other three—namely justice, courage, and temperance—belong to action. Action must be preferred to knowledge. This may be proved. TULLY: “Suppose someone is passionately eager to understand the nature of things. While he is contemplating matters most worthy of knowledge, someone announces that danger threatens his country, which he himself can assist: would he not cast aside all his study, even if he thought himself able to count the stars and measure the magnitude of the world?” [Note: [Col. 1042D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.43, with a few changes.]

Prudence, therefore, comes after the other three; but among these temperance is to be preferred to the other two. For by temperance a human being governs himself, but by courage [Col. 1041D] and justice his household and city; yet a person’s own dominion is better than an external one [987], as HORACE says:

> You will rule more widely by taming your greedy  
> Spirit than if you joined Libya to far-off  
> Territories and made each Carthaginian  
> Serve one man.  
> [Note: [Col. 1042D] Horace, *Odes* II.2.]

Hence SENECA: “If you wish to subject all things to yourself, subject yourself to reason.” And TULLY: “If reason rules you, you will rule many kings.” [Note: [Col. 1042D] These sayings are from sources still unknown to me.]

For where is a human being’s good without his being good himself? Yet one must never act against temperance out of love for the other virtues. “For some things are so foul and shameful that a wise man would not do them even for the preservation of his country; and some are obscene even to name,” [Note: [Col. 1042D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.45.] such as killing one’s son and renouncing the faith.

Justice, however, is better than courage. “Greatness of spirit, if it is separated from common advantage, will be a kind of savagery and barbarity.” [Note: [Col. 1042D] Id., ibid. I.44.] Within justice itself there are ranks of duties. “The first duties are owed to the immortal gods, [Col. 1042D] the second to one’s country, the third to parents, and the rest thereafter in successive degrees.” [Note: [Col. 1042D] Id., ibid. I.45.]

Thus far the section on honourableness has been completed; what we now undertake concerns that which is called useful.

# QUESTION III. ON THE USEFUL

[Col. 1043]

[Col. 1043A] 51. The useful is that which ought to be sought on account of its benefit. Some divide it into goods of the soul, goods of the body, and goods of fortune. Goods of the soul are divided into branches of knowledge and virtues, of which we spoke in treating honourableness. Goods of the body are beauty, noble birth, speed, strength, size, and health; these often bring more disadvantage than benefit, because they take away good morals, according to JUVENAL:

> So rare indeed is harmony between beauty  
> And chastity.  
> [Note: [Col. 1043D] Juvenal, Satire X.297.]

OVID:

> She is chaste whom no one has solicited.  
> [Note: [Col. 1043D] Ovid, *Amores* I.8.43. This passage is lacking in the edition.]

Noble birth too commonly brings the degenerate more disgrace than praise. SALLUST: “The more splendid the life of one’s ancestors, the more shameful [Col. 1043B] is the sloth of their descendants. And indeed the matter stands thus. For ancestral glory is like a certain light for descendants, which allows neither good nor evil to remain hidden. … But those who live lowly lives in obscurity—if they commit some offence in anger—are known by few, whose fortune and reputation are equal.” [Note: [Col. 1043D] Sallust, *Jugurtha* 85, from the middle; and *Catiline* 51, after the beginning.]

To this JUVENAL adds:

> Every vice of the soul bears a crime more conspicuous in itself  
> The greater the man who sins is thought to be.  
> [Note: [Col. 1043D] Juvenal, Satire VIII.140, where the text has *quanto maior*.]

But if you seek true nobility, hear the poet JUVENAL:

> Nobility of soul is virtue alone and unique.  
> [Note: [Col. 1043D] Id., ibid., v. 19.]

For nobility alone adorns the soul with morals; hence the same poet:

> You owe me first the goods of the soul …  
>   
> … For who would call this man well-born, who,  
> [Col. 1043C] Unworthy of his lineage, is distinguished only  
> By a famous name? …  
>   
> It is wretched to rest upon another’s fame …  
>   
> I would rather that Thersites were your father, provided you yourself were  
> Like Achilles’ son and took up Vulcan’s arms,  
> Than that Achilles should beget you resembling Thersites.  
> [Note: [Col. 1043D] Id., ibid., vv. 20–30, 32, 76, and 268–270.]

If there is any benefit in such nobility, it is surely that which TULLY indicates in these words: “The best inheritance transmitted from fathers to children, surpassing every patrimony, is the glory of virtue and of deeds performed, to bring dishonour upon which must be judged a sin.” [Note: [Col. 1043D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.33.]

But in the other [988] bodily advantages, what benefit is there for a human being, when beasts surpass him in those very things? BOETHIUS: “For you do not surpass elephants in bulk, bulls in strength, or tigers in swiftness.” [Note: [Col. 1044D] Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* III, prose 8.] As JUVENAL testifies:

> Death alone declares  
> How tiny are the little bodies of human beings.  
> [Note: [Col. 1044D] Juvenal X.173.]

[Col. 1044A]

## On the goods of fortune

52. The goods of fortune are wealth, pre-eminence, and glory. Estates, dependants, private property, treasure, and adornment are referred to wealth. Among estates, buildings and lands are counted. TULLY: “Care must be taken, if you build, that expense does not exceed measure; moderation must be observed in building.” [Note: [Col. 1044D] Cicero, *On Duties* 39, though not word for word.] Hence HORACE:

> Whoever loves the golden mean,  
> Safe from the squalor of a decaying roof,  
> Soberly lacks the enviable  
> Palace.  
> [Note: [Col. 1044D] Horace, *Odes* II.10.5.]

Hence TULLY: “One’s rank should be adorned by one’s house, not sought wholly from one’s house; nor should the master be honoured by the house, but the house by its master. A spacious house, if it is solitary, disgraces its master—especially if it was built by a former master and is accustomed to be thronged. For it is hateful when passers-by say: ‘O ancient house, alas, how unlike is the master who rules you!’” [Note: [Col. 1044D] Cicero, cited passage.]

Therefore hear the poet HORACE:

> Whom prosperity has delighted beyond measure,  
> Changed fortune will shake. If you admire anything, you will surrender it  
> Unwillingly. Flee greatness: beneath a poor roof  
> You may outstrip the life of kings and the friends of kings.  
> [Note: [Col. 1044D] Horace, *Epistles* I.10.30 ff.]

And LUCAN:

> … O secure means of the poor man’s life,  
> And narrow homes! O gifts of gods  
> Not yet understood!  
> [Note: [Col. 1044D] Lucan V.527.]

Therefore in building let us follow Cato’s temperance, of whom LUCAN writes:

> His feast was, nevertheless, to have conquered hunger, and his great household gods  
> To have driven winter away with a roof.  
> [Note: [Col. 1044D] Idem II.384. See also above.]

[Col. 1044C] For scant furnishings beneath a small roof are praiseworthy. HORACE accordingly says:

> A house is meagre where there are not also many things left over  
> To deceive their owner and profit thieves.  
> [Note: [Col. 1044D] Horace, *Epistles* I.6.45.]

For the size of a house does not expel anxieties. HORACE:

> Richer than untouched treasures  
> Of Arabia and wealthy India,  
> Though you occupy with your buildings  
> All the Tyrrhenian and Black Sea,  
> If divine Necessity fixes  
> Her adamantine nails in your lofty roof,  
> You will not free your spirit from fear  
> Nor your head from the noose of death …  
>   
> Whether you are rich, descended from ancient Inachus,  
> Or poor and of the lowest  
> Stock, living beneath the open sky,  
> You are a victim of pitiless Orcus.  
> We are all driven to the same place; for all,  
> [Col. 1044D] The lot is shaken in the urn, sooner or later  
> To come forth …  
>   
> [Col. 1045A] Neither house nor estate, neither a heap of bronze nor gold,  
> Has removed fevers from the sick body of its owner  
> Or cares from his mind. The possessor must be well  
> If he is to think of using accumulated things well.  
> A house or possessions help the man who desires or fears  
> As painted pictures help the bleary-eyed, or hot compresses the gouty.  
>   
> [lacuna]  
>   
> Pale death knocks with equal foot at the cottages of the poor  
> And the towers of kings.  
> [Note: [Col. 1045D] Horace, *Odes* III.24; II.3; *Epistles* I.2.47 ff.; *Odes* I.4.]

53. With dependants, the first duty is that the master should provide necessities; the second, that he should require service. SENECA: “A master is mistaken if he thinks slavery descends to the whole human being; its better part, the soul, is excepted. [989] Bodies are subject to masters, but the mind is its own master, so free and wandering that not even in the prison in which it is enclosed can it be kept from using its impulse, acting greatly, and going forth [Col. 1045B] as companion into the infinite. Therefore live with your inferior as you would wish your superior to live with you; and whenever it comes into your mind how much authority you have over a slave, let it likewise come into your mind that your master has just as much authority over you.” [Note: [Col. 1045D] Seneca, *On Benefits* I.20; *Letters* 47, from the middle, with a few changes or omissions.]

54. The first duty of a member of a household is to conform his own conduct to that of his master. HORACE suggests this in these words:

> The service of a powerful friend is pleasant to the inexperienced;  
> The experienced man fears it. While your ship is on the open sea,  
> Attend to this: do not let a changed wind carry you backward.  
> Sad men hate the cheerful, and merry men the sad;  
> The quick-tempered hate the calm, the sluggish the active and diligent.  
> Drunken drinkers of Falernian wine, in the middle of the night,  
> Hate the man who refuses proffered cups, even though  
> You swear that you fear night vapours.  
> Remove the cloud from your brow; often the modest man  
> [Col. 1045C] Takes on the appearance of the obscure, the silent man that of the bitter …  
>   
> Whoever persuades them that you agree with their pursuits  
> Will praise your game as its patron with both thumbs.  
> [Note: [Col. 1045D] Horace, *Epistles* I.18.86–95; ibid., vv. 65–66.]

The second duty is to recommend worthy persons to one’s master; hence HORACE:

> Examine again and again the person whom you recommend, lest later  
> Another’s faults bring shame upon you.  
> We are deceived, and sometimes entrust a man unworthy of trust; therefore  
> Do not go on defending one whom his own fault oppresses, once you have been deceived.  
> Yet preserve one thoroughly known, if charges test him,  
> And protect him when he trusts your patronage …  
>   
> For your own affair is at stake when your neighbour’s wall is ablaze;  
> Fires neglected are accustomed to gather strength.  
> [Note: [Col. 1045D] Idem, ibid., vv. 76–85.]

The third is to restrain greed and lust; hence the same HORACE:

> Let needy desire not always drive and torment you …  
>   
> [Col. 1045D] Let no maidservant or boy wound your heart  
> Within the marble threshold of your venerable friend.  
> [Note: [Col. 1045D] Idem, ibid., v. 98; ibid., vv. 72–73.]

The fourth is to cast aside arrogance, in accordance with HORACE:

> Neither praise your own pursuits nor criticize another’s …  
>   
> … Yield to the gentle commands  
> Of your powerful friend.  
> [Note: [Col. 1045D] Idem, ibid., v. 39 and vv. 44–45.]

[Col. 1046A] The fifth is to refrain from complaints; hence the same HORACE:

> Those who keep silence before their king about poverty  
> Will endure him asking for more; there is a difference whether you take modestly  
> Or seize …  
>   
> For if a raven could be fed in silence, it would have  
> More food and much less quarrelling and envy.  
> [Note: [Col. 1045D] Idem, ibid. 17.43–45 and vv. 50–51.]

Why these things should be carefully observed, the same HORACE teaches:

> To have pleased leading men is no least praise.  
> [Note: [Col. 1046D] Idem, ibid., v. 35.]

The sixth duty is to fulfil whatever the master demands and not be burdened by any want. LUCAN:

> The poverty that serves is burdensome not to itself but to its master.  
> [Note: [Col. 1046D] Lucan III.152.]

Above all, he should beware of chattering. JUVENAL:

> The tongue is the worst part of a bad slave.  
> [Note: [Col. 1046B] Juvenal IX.120.]

If possible, moreover, he should choose such a master that serving him is no disgrace; for the services of slaves are made honourable by the rank of their masters.

55. Concerning private property, treasure, [990] and adornment—collectively called riches—the philosopher’s saying is quite elegant. TULLY: “Nothing, I say, shows a mind so narrow and petty as the love of riches.” [Note: [Col. 1046D] Cicero, *On Duties* I.20.] Therefore great is the person who uses gold as if it were earthenware; nor is that person less great who uses earthenware as if it were gold. TULLY: “Nothing is more honourable or magnificent [991] than to despise money if you do not possess it, and, if you do possess it, to apply it to generosity.” [Note: [Col. 1046D] Id., cited passage.]

For he seems excessively generous who said, TERENCE:

> [Col. 1046C] I do not buy hope at a price.  
> [Note: [Col. 1046D] Terence, *Adelphoe* II.2.11. This is a proverb concerning those who seek an uncertain thing by a certain loss.]

56. We ought to be recalled from the desire for wealth for these reasons. The first is that human life is brief. HORACE:

> The short span of life forbids us to entertain a long hope.  
> Who knows whether the gods above will add tomorrow’s time  
> To today’s total?  
>   
> Avoid asking what tomorrow will bring;  
> God buries the outcome of future time  
> In a cloudy night;  
> And laughs if mortal man anxiously goes beyond  
> What is permitted. Remember with equanimity  
> To order what is present …  
>   
> … That man is master of himself  
> And will live gladly who is able, day by day,  
> To say: “I have lived.” Tomorrow perhaps the Father  
> Will cover the sky with a black cloud,  
> Or with clear sunshine.  
>   
> [Col. 1046D] A mind glad in the present  
> Will hate to concern itself with what lies beyond, and with a happy  
> Smile temper what is bitter. Nothing is blessed  
> In every respect.  
>   
> Swift death took away bright Achilles;  
> Long old age wore down Tithonus;  
> And perhaps the hour will grant to me  
> What it has denied to you.  
> [Note: [Col. 1046D] Horace, *Odes* I.4.15; IV.7.18; I.9.13; III.29; II.16.]

[Col. 1047A] SENECA: “In this indeed we are all deceived, because we do not look ahead to death. A great part of it has already passed; whatever portion of life lies behind us, death holds.” [Note: [Col. 1047D] Seneca, *Letters* 1, after the beginning.] Therefore fix in your mind that without any interruption you die daily.

57. The second reason is that the love of possession besieges virtues. HORACE:

> He has lost his arms and abandoned virtue’s post  
> Who always hastens to increase his wealth and is buried by it …  
>   
> For joys do not fall to the rich alone,  
> Nor has he lived badly who passed unnoticed in birth and death.  
> [Note: [Col. 1047D] Horace, *Epistles* I.16.67 and ibid. 17.9.]

As the miser says. JUVENAL:

> No one asks where you got it; but you must have it.  
> [Note: [Col. 1047D] Juvenal XIV.206.]

HORACE:

> Birth and virtue, unless accompanied by wealth, are cheaper than seaweed.  
> [Note: [Col. 1047D] Horace, *Satires* II.5.8.]

Nothing is enough when you are worth only as much as you have, says JUVENAL:

> As much faith as each man keeps in his money-chest,  
> So much does he possess …  
>   
> Unhappy poverty has nothing harsher in it  
> Than that it makes people ridiculous.  
> [Note: [Col. 1047D] Juvenal III.143 and 152.]

HORACE:

> The great reproach of poverty commands one both to do and suffer anything.  
>   
> Queen Money bestows both birth and beauty;  
> Virtue, fame, honour, things divine and human obey fair  
> Riches. Whoever has amassed them will be  
> Famous, brave, just, wise, and even a king.  
> [Note: [Col. 1047D] Horace, *Odes* III.24; *Epistles* I.6.36; *Satires* II.3.95.]

58. Yet wealth gives him the opposite of all this: in place of virtues, money brings vice and disgrace. This is the third reason for despising it; hear the poet JUVENAL:

> Money first introduced foreign customs,  
> And soft riches broke the ages with shameful luxury.  
> [Note: [Col. 1047D] Juvenal VI.298.]

LUCAN:

> … Poverty, once second among men, is shunned.  
> [Note: [Col. 1047D] Lucan I.165.]

HORACE:

> Ages fruitful in sin first polluted marriages, lineage, and homes.  
> [Note: [Col. 1047D] Horace, *Odes* III.6.]

HORACE shows that money confers no nobility when he says:

> Though you walk more proudly because of money,  
> Fortune does not change your birth.  
> [Note: [Col. 1047D] Idem, *Epodes* IV.5.]

59. The fourth reason is that no gain satisfies the love of possession; for, as HORACE says:

> … Proud riches grow; yet  
> Something is always lacking from the curtailed estate.  
> Care follows growing money,  
> And a greater hunger …  
>   
> The more each person has denied himself,  
> The more he will receive from the gods. With those who desire nothing,  
> [Col. 1048A] I seek the camp naked, and rejoice to desert  
> The party of the rich …  
>   
> … He is well to whom a god has offered  
> With sparing hand what is sufficient.  
>   
> For he is not poor who has the use of things;  
> If your belly, side, and feet fare well,  
> Royal riches will be unable to add anything greater.  
> [Note: [Col. 1047D] Idem, *Odes* III.24; III.16; *Epistles* I.12, beginning.]

JUVENAL:

> The love of money grows as money itself grows,  
> And he who has none desires it less …  
>   
> … For the man who wishes to become rich  
> Also wishes to become rich quickly.  
> [Note: [Col. 1047D] Juvenal XIV.138 and 175.]

60. The fifth reason is the fear that money implants. JUVENAL:

> Though you carry only a few small vessels of pure silver,  
> Once you set out by night you will fear sword and club  
> And tremble at the shadow of a reed stirred in moonlight.  
> The traveller who carries nothing will sing before the robber …  
>   
> [Col. 1048B] … Miserable is the guarding of a great fortune.  
> [Note: [Col. 1048D] Idem X.19 ff.; XIV.303.]

61. The sixth reason is that it desires the slavery of its seeker. Hence HORACE:

> Accumulated money commands or serves every man;  
> It ought rather to follow the rope entirely than lead it.  
> [Note: [Col. 1048D] Horace, *Epistles* I.10.46.]

Therefore I agree with the speaker who says:

> I strive to subject possessions to myself, not myself to possessions.  
> [Note: [Col. 1048D] Idem, ibid. I.19, where the text has *submittere*, “to subject.”]

Since this is so:

> You would not rightly call a man blessed because he possesses much;  
> More rightly does he take the name of blessed who knows  
> How wisely to use the gifts of the gods,  
> To endure harsh poverty,  
> And to fear disgrace worse than death.  
> [Note: [Col. 1048D] Idem, *Odes* IV.9.]

SENECA: “Cheerful poverty is an honourable thing; indeed, if it is cheerful, it is not poverty. He who gets on well with poverty is rich. The poor man is not he who has little, but he who desires more.” If you wish to become rich, money is not to be added, but desire is to be subtracted. “For the shortest road to riches is contempt for riches.” For a person can despise all things, but cannot possess all things. “Therefore Diogenes, empty-handed, was richer than Alexander, who possessed everything. For there was more that Diogenes did not wish to receive than Alexander could give. What does it matter how much lies in a man’s chest or granaries, if he covets another’s goods, if he counts not things acquired but things yet to be acquired? You ask what is the measure of riches? The first measure is to have what is necessary; the next, what is sufficient. … What nature desires is obtainable and at hand; we toil for superfluities … What is sufficient is within reach.” [Note: [Col. 1048D] Seneca, *Letters* 2, near the end; Letter 62; *On Benefits* V.4; Letter 2 cited; Letter 4 at the end, where *expositum*, “set forth,” appears in place of *appositum*, “at hand.” The middle passage seems to be by Seneca, although it has not been identified by me. Compare, however, Varro’s saying, no. 108: “Do you wish to be rich? Add nothing to yourself by thinking, but take away from others.” Compare also the excerpts from Seneca entitled *Book on Poverty*.]

BOETHIUS: “For nature is content with very little and the smallest things.” [Note: [Col. 1048D] Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* II, prose 5, about the middle.]

[Col. 1049A]

## On pre-eminences

62. The appetite for pre-eminence must be moderated; for the fall from a height is more grievous. The truth of this [992] is recorded concerning them. JUVENAL:

> Great power, subject to great envy, hurls some men down;  
> A long and distinguished roll of honours overwhelms them.  
> [Note: [Col. 1049D] Juvenal X.56.]

LUCAN:

> Envious violence of fate, denying those at the summit  
> Long endurance; falls grievous beneath excessive weight …  
> Great things collapse upon themselves; the gods have set  
> A limit to growth even amid prosperity …  
>   
> O gods, easy in giving the highest things,  
> Difficult in preserving the same!  
> [Note: [Col. 1049D] Lucan I.70, ibid. 81 and 510.]

SENECA: “For you recover fortune more swiftly than you retain it.” [Note: [Col. 1049D] Seneca, or Publilius Syrus, *Mimes*, no. 252, where the text has *reperias*, “you find,” rather than *recipias*, “you recover.”] Hence HORACE:

> A great pine is more often shaken by winds, and lofty  
> Towers fall with a heavier crash; lightning strikes  
> The highest mountains …  
>   
> Fortune, delighting in a cruel task  
> And stubbornly playing her insolent game,  
> Changes uncertain honours,  
> Kindly now to me, now to another.  
>   
> I praise her when she remains; if she shakes her swift  
> Wings, I resign what she gave, and carry myself forward  
> With my own virtue, seeking honourable  
> Poverty without a dowry.  
> [Note: [Col. 1049D] Horace, *Odes* II.2 and III.29.]

TERENCE:

> O Fortune, how you are never perpetually good!  
> [Note: [Col. 1049D] Terence, *Hecyra* III.3.46.]

The second cause of the question is that it seeks pretence. SALLUST: “For it is difficult for those in power to obey, when they have feigned goodness through ambition.” [Note: [Col. 1049D] Sallust, *Jugurtha* 85, after the beginning.] For many are humble not in heart but only through fortune, and become proud when elevated. TERENCE:

> [Col. 1049C] … Certainly it is as I think:  
> As circumstances offer themselves to us, so we are all great or humble.  
> [Note: [Col. 1049D] Terence, *Hecyra* III.3.20.]

Therefore the duty of those set above others is to draw the interests of the multitude toward their own advantage. TULLY: “Of all things, nothing is better suited to retaining pre-eminence than to be loved, and nothing more alien to it than to be feared.” [Note: [Col. 1049D] Cicero, *On Duties* II.7, where the text has *opes*, “power,” in place of *praelationes*, “pre-eminences.”] SALLUST: “It is safer to rule willing people than unwilling ones.” [Note: [Col. 1049D] Sallust, *Jugurtha* 102.] TULLY: “Subjects hate the man whom they fear, and everyone whom a man hates he desires to perish … Fear is a poor guardian of permanence.” [Note: [Col. 1049D] Cicero, cited passage; but more correctly Ennius, quoted by Cicero in the cited passage.] Hence JUVENAL:

> Few kings ascend to Ceres’ grain without slaughter and bloodshed,  
> And few tyrants die a bloodless death.  
> [Note: [Col. 1049D] Juvenal X.112, where the text has *vulnere*, “wound,” in place of *sanguine*, “blood.”]

TULLY: “On the contrary, goodwill is a faithful guardian [Col. 1049D] even for permanence; [for it makes enduring by the proclamation of praise one who has died.] Those who wish to be feared by [Col. 1050A] those whom they themselves fear must necessarily fear those same persons.” [Note: [Col. 1049D] Cicero, cited passage. The words in square brackets are not Cicero’s.]

Hence BOETHIUS: “Do you consider powerful the man whose side a bodyguard surrounds, who fears more greatly those whom he terrifies?” [Note: [Col. 1049D] Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy* III, prose 5.] TULLY: “Dionysius, fearing barbers’ razors, had his hair singed by glowing coal; Alexander of Pherae, when he came from dinner to his bedroom, sent his guards ahead to his wife to search women’s chests, lest some weapon should be concealed in their clothing.” [Note: [Col. 1049D] Cicero, cited passage.]

Let one set above others remember that he is a private person; for those who unexpectedly attain what they had not hoped for often embrace the most wicked hopes. TERENCE:

> We all become worse through licence.  
> [Note: [Col. 1050D] Terence, *Heauton Timorumenos* III.1.74.]

Those set above others are tortured, as HORACE says:

> … Why, unhappy tumults  
> Of the mind, flying around panelled  
> [Col. 1050B] Ceilings?  
> [Note: [Col. 1050D] Horace, *Odes* II.16.10.]

And no heavier care is added to mortals than when long hope arrives.

## On glory

63. Glory is the widely spread proclamation of some great deed or good art. Human effort therefore aims at it, because without it our virtue becomes known to few. HORACE:

> Virtue concealed differs little from buried sloth.  
> [Note: [Col. 1050D] Id., *Odes* IV.9.29.]

Moreover, as those who speak of great men report still greater things, glory gives a second life, as the poet HORACE says:

> The Muse forbids a man worthy of praise to die.  
> [Note: [Col. 1050D] Id., ibid., Ode 8.28.]

To show that he had not said this seriously, he says elsewhere:

> [Col. 1050C] Though Agrippa’s portico and Appius’ way  
> Have seen you well known, you must nevertheless go where Numa and Ancus went.  
> [Note: [Col. 1050D] Id., *Epistles* I.6.25–27.]

BOETHIUS:

> Death scorns lofty glory;  
> It enfolds alike the lowly and the high head,  
> And levels the lowest with the highest.  
> [Note: [Col. 1050D] Boethius, cited work II, metre 7.]

We seek glory with immoderate desire because good people wish rather to appear good than to be so, while bad people wish rather to be bad than to appear so. [993] For true is the saying of the poet HORACE:

> False honour delights, and lying infamy terrifies,  
> Whom but the faulty and deceitful man?  
> [Note: [Col. 1050D] Horace, *Epistles* I.16.39.]

BOETHIUS: “The fruit of glory, moreover, has very often been pride; hence the Greek tragedian cries: ‘Glory [Col. 1050D] among thousands of mortals makes them nothing else than a great swelling of the ears.’” [Note: [Col. 1050D] Boethius, cited work III, prose 6, which reads: “But how often glory is deceptive, how often attended by tumults!” Hence not without reason the tragedian cries:

> Ὦ δόξα, δόξα, μυρίοισι δὴ βροτῶν  
> Οὐδὲν γεγῶσι, βίοτον ὤγκωσας μέγαν.

That is: “O glory, glory, you make the spirit swollen in ten thousand people when they are nothing!” Moreover, these are two verses of Euripides’ *Andromache*.]

That glory has no benefit if it lacks other goods is shown by JUVENAL’s saying:

> However great glory may be, what will it be if it is glory alone?  
> [Note: [Col. 1051D] Juvenal VII.81.]

TULLY: “If anyone labours to attain glory, let him make himself such as he wishes to be considered. [Col. 1052A] But if he thinks that he can obtain lasting glory through empty display and feigned speech or expression, he is gravely mistaken. True glory strikes roots; but all counterfeit things quickly fall like straw, nor can anything simulated be lasting.” [Note: [Col. 1051D] Cicero, *On Duties* II.12, almost entirely word for word.]

# QUESTION IV. ON THE COMPARISON OF USEFUL THINGS

[Col. 1051]

64. The fourth question concerns the comparison of useful things, and is treated as follows: “The advantages of the body are compared with external goods in this way: it is preferable to be healthy rather than rich. Conversely, external goods are preferred to bodily goods: it is preferable to be rich rather than to possess the greatest bodily strength. Those things also which are bodily goods are compared with one another: good health is better than size, and strength than speed. External goods likewise are compared with one another: glory is better than riches, and urban revenues than rural.” [Note: Id., ibid., end.]

## QUESTION V. ON THE CONFLICT OF UTILITY AND HONOUR

65. We have said that the fifth inquiry in forming a plan is the question concerning the conflict between utility and honour. For if it is useful to draw things to oneself, but honourable to distribute them to others, our mind very often has, in deliberation, an anxious and divided concern: namely, whether, despising utility, it should adhere to honour, or the reverse. Pothinus sought to impress the opposition of these two upon King Ptolemy when, in Lucan, he argued thus:

> Law and right, Ptolemy, make many men guilty;  
> Praised loyalty pays the penalty when it supports  
> Those whom Fortune crushes. Join the Fates and gods;  
> Follow the fortunate, flee the wretched. As the stars  
> Are distant from the earth, as fire from the sea, so utility from right.  
> The whole power of sceptres perishes if it begins  
> To spare the just; regard for honour overturns citadels.  
> The freedom of crimes, and every restraint removed from swords,  
> Preserves hated kingdoms. Savage man, you cannot do everything  
> With impunity unless you continue doing it. Let him leave the court  
> Who wishes to be devout. Virtue and supreme power  
> Do not coexist: he whom cruel deeds shame will always fear.

[Note: Lucan, *Pharsalia*, VIII.484–495. These are the words of Pothinus, highly influential at the court of the Egyptian king, by which he urges Ptolemy to kill Pompey.]

66. Yet, by the highest authority of the philosopher Cicero, these three—namely the good, the honourable, and the useful—are so intermingled that whatever is good is also judged useful, and whatever is honourable is likewise declared useful; hence it follows that everything honourable is useful. [Note: These matters are drawn from Cicero, *On Duties*, II.3.]

Hold, therefore, most firmly and do not waver at all: the honourable is useful in such a way that nothing is useful unless it is honourable. Nor do I say that these two differ merely in number, but in their entire proper character. For example, “this man” and “this animal” do not differ, because this man is this animal and this animal is nothing other than this man. Yet, for something to be an animal, nothing is required except substance together with life and sensation; whereas for it to be this man, rationality together with morality is required—properties which are said to differ. The useful and the honourable stand in a similar relation. For, although they are the same in number, something must yield benefit in order to be useful; but in order to be honourable, it must attract us by its own dignity. Since, therefore, they are one and the same thing, it follows that no use of anything is useful if it differs from the virtues. For this reason, there is absolutely no opposition between utility and honour.

67. But because the common people believe every temporal advantage to be useful, while what is unlawful conflicts with what is honourable, the question of the controversy between utility and honour has been proposed. CICERO:

> “It seems useful to a man to increase his own advantage at another’s disadvantage and to take something away from another. But this is more contrary to nature than poverty, death, or pain. For it destroys from the outset the fellowship of humankind. If this disposition were implanted in us—that each person, for his own gain, should despoil or wrong another—the fellowship of the human race, which is according to nature, must necessarily be broken apart. If every limb thought itself better off by drawing into itself the health of the neighbouring limb, the whole body would necessarily be weakened and perish. So too in human society. For, just as it is permitted for each person to prefer acquiring for himself rather than for another what pertains to the use of his own life—and nature does not oppose this—so nature does not permit us to increase our resources by despoiling others. But as it is more contrary to nature to rob another for one’s own advantage than death or pain, so it is more in accordance with nature, if it were possible, to undertake labours and hardships for all than to live without hardship amid great pleasures. Furthermore, when someone wrongs another in order to gain some advantage for himself, either he thinks that he is doing nothing contrary to nature, or he judges poverty to be more to be avoided than committing an unjust injury. If he thinks that he is acting against nature, he is inhuman; if he judges that committing an injury is evil but that poverty or death is worse to suffer, he is mistaken. For a defect of the mind is more grievous than death and poverty.”  
> [Note: This whole chapter is abridged, in almost the same words, from Cicero, *On Duties*, III.5.]

68. Perhaps someone will say: “Then would not the wise person, if he himself were perishing from hunger, take food from another person who was useful for nothing?” “By no means,” I reply. “For my life is not more useful to me than such a disposition of mind—namely, that I should violate no one for the sake of my own advantage.”

[While life is lost, the corruption of the body—that is, death—is incurred; but if I cast aside this disposition, I incur a defect of the mind. And just as a defect of the mind is more grievous than one of the body, so the good of the mind—namely virtue—is better than life, the good of the body.]

“Furthermore, it is not fitting for a good man to lie, accuse, rebuke, or deceive for the sake of his own gain. Therefore nothing is of such value, and no advantage is so desirable, that you should lose the name of a good man. What benefit, said to be gained from these things, can bring as much as it takes away if it strips one of the name of a good man and removes trust and justice? Why, then, do people see the gains of things but not the punishment—not only of the laws, but of dishonour, which is most bitter? Therefore this deliberation itself bears witness that it is between alternatives: they deliberate whether to follow what they see to be honourable or knowingly to pollute themselves with crime. In the very hesitation, indeed, there is wrongdoing, even if they do not proceed to it. Therefore matters in which deliberation itself is shameful ought not to be deliberated at all; and, in every deliberation, the hope of concealment must be removed. For we ought to be sufficiently persuaded that, even if we could conceal ourselves from all the gods, nevertheless nothing ought to be done greedily, lustfully, or improperly. For an act stained with so many vices cannot be useful. Even if a wise man possessed a ring with the power to render him invisible, he should not think himself permitted to do more than if he did not possess it; for good men seek honourable things, not merely many things.” [Note: This chapter also, apart from what is enclosed in brackets, is drawn, as a more explicit explanation of the preceding matters, from Cicero, *On Duties*, III.6, 20; III.8, at the end; and III.9. In the last-mentioned place Cicero refers to the ring of Gyges, concerning which the ancients told many tales.]

Nor will a good man dare to will anything which he would not dare to proclaim. But if you refrain from disgraceful conduct because people would not fail to notice it, you do not love goodness but fear punishment; and in this you imitate the nature of beasts. HORACE:

> The cautious wolf fears the pit, the hawk  
> Suspected snares, and the kite the baited hook.  
> The wicked hate to sin through fear of punishment;  
> The good hate to sin through love of virtue.

[Note: Horace, *Epistles*, I.16.50–52. Our manuscript here presents several readings by no means negligible, and perhaps even an unpublished verse, namely the third:

> The wicked hate to sin through fear of punishment,

unless one wishes to regard it as arising from Horace’s own following line:

> You will admit nothing into yourself through fear of punishment.

Moreover, Hildebert’s edition reads the second verse thus:

> He avoids suspended snares and the covered hook.

Let learned men decide.]

69. Since it is clear from the foregoing that the honourable alone is useful: “If some appearance of utility should present itself to you and, when you fix your attention upon it, you perceive dishonour attached to it, you should not say that such utility is then to be abandoned; rather, you should understand that where dishonour is, utility cannot exist.” [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, III.8.]

Indeed, if we wish to judge rightly, whenever dishonour carries before it an appearance of utility, the outcome of the very matter usually refutes it. For we see that when what is honourable seems useless, it is nevertheless brought to such an end that unexpected advantage arises from it. Thus Damon and Pythias, “who, it is related, were so disposed toward one another that, when Dionysius the tyrant had fixed the day of execution for one of them, and the man condemned to death had requested a few days in order to arrange his affairs, the other became surety in the meantime for his appearance, on the condition that, if he did not return, he himself must die. But when the former returned on the appointed day, the tyrant, admiring their loyalty, asked them to admit him as a third witness to their friendship.” [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, III.10.]

See how it was useful both for one to remain for his friend and for the other to return for his friend, although at first each course was thought dangerous; thus, beyond the limit of calculation, honourableness has a useful and unexpected outcome. Dishonour, on the other hand, has an action as ruinous as it is shameful. “Therefore, whenever what seems useful is compared with what is honourable, let the appearance of utility fall, and the strength of honour prevail.” [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, III.11.]

70. One who observes these precepts may live in the tranquillity of honourableness and pass life according to the rule of reason. CICERO:

> “For just as in lyres or pipes, although they differ only slightly, the difference is nevertheless usually perceived by the craftsman, so we must conduct our lives lest anything be out of harmony—and much more so, inasmuch as the harmony of actions is better than that of sounds. Therefore, just as the ears of musicians perceive the slightest differences in lyres, so, if we wish to be keen observers of character, we shall often understand much from little. From the expression of the eyes; from relaxed or drawn brows; from sadness, cheerfulness, appearance, speech, forcefulness or lowering of the voice, and other such things, we shall easily judge what is fittingly done and what deviates from duty. In this respect it is not disadvantageous to judge from others what each such thing is like: when something is unbecoming in others, we may avoid it ourselves. For, I know not how, we see faults more readily in others than in ourselves.”  
> [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, I.40–41. There are several variant readings by no means negligible.]

Hence the poet HORACE:

> Though with bleared eyes, anointed with ointment, you clearly see your own faults,  
> Why do you discern so sharply the faults of your friends?  
> [Note: Horace, *Satires*, I.3.25–26.]

71. Therefore the man who loves honourableness should make frequent and constant use of these precepts. For this small section contains the choicer sayings of nearly all teachers of morals; hence you may look upon them here more easily than if you gathered them scattered through wandering among many volumes. SENECA:

> “The reading of many authors and books of every kind contains something wandering and unstable. For it is true that he who is everywhere is nowhere. Those who spend life in travel come to have many lodgings but few friendships. The same must happen to those who attach themselves familiarly to no individual minds, but run through everything hurriedly and in haste. Food does no good and does not become part of the body if it is expelled immediately after being taken. Nothing impedes health as much as frequent changes of medicines. A wound in which remedies are tried does not come to a scar. A plant which is transferred too often does not grow strong; and nothing is so useful that it helps in passing. A multitude of books distracts. Therefore, since you cannot read as much as you possess, it is enough to possess as much as you read. It is the mark of a fastidious stomach to taste many things which, being diverse and different, defile rather than nourish. Therefore always read approved authors; and if at times you wish to turn aside to others, return to the former ones. When you have gone through many things, select one thing to digest that day.”  
> [Note: Seneca, *Letters*, 2, with a few changes or omissions.]

For that good must be cultivated which is improved by delight.

72. Besides this, strive unceasingly to fulfil in reality and action the moral precepts which you see. CICERO:

> “For just as physicians and orators, although they have received instructions, cannot achieve anything worthy of praise without practice, so the precepts of duty are indeed handed down in order that we ourselves may act; but the magnitude of the matter also demands use and exercise.”  
> [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, I.18.]

“Oppose vice,” says BOETHIUS in the book *On the Consolation*; “cultivate virtues; raise your minds by hope toward things above; offer humble prayers to the Most High. If these are upright, they cannot be ineffective. For a great necessity of uprightness has been imposed upon you—if you do not wish to deceive yourselves—since you stand before the eyes of the Judge who sees all things.” [Note: The end of the chapter, with a few changes. Among these we note *oppose vice* in place of “oppose vices,” and “raise your minds by hope toward things above” in place of “raise the mind toward right hopes.” This passage of Boethius is absent from the edition, where, after “demands,” there is added at the end: “Here ends the book of Moral Teachings.”]

## THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT’S LITTLE BOOK ON THE FOUR VIRTUES OF THE HONOURABLE LIFE

(From the Colbert manuscript, no. 6327. Not previously published.)

## NOTICE

It sufficiently requires a diligent reader to have read through the preceding *Moral Philosophy on the Honourable and the Useful* of the venerable philosopher Hildebert, in order to discover that the following poem *On the Four Virtues of the Honourable Life* is nothing other than a synopsis of the moral judgments and precepts which he himself collected in the preceding treatise, either for his own benefit or for the instruction of young men to whom his studies were imparted for the formation of character. Peter of Blois gives this testimony of himself in Letter 102, to R., archdeacon of Nantes, on the instruction of boys:

> “It benefited me that, as a youth, I was obliged to make the letters of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans—pre-eminent for elegance of style and pleasant refinement—firmly my own and to render them from the heart.”

Why, then, should not his poems also have been composed to assist boys’ memory? According to Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, book X, p. 770, they were disseminated not only throughout Gaul but even “carried to Rome, and, as he says, were admired in the schools of the witty and among the teachers of the Romans”; perhaps they were imposed upon those boys for memorization as well. We have drawn this poem from Colbert manuscript no. 6327, about five hundred years old, which, because of the similarity of its subject, we considered should be placed immediately after the preceding book. We have added nothing in the margin here, since there are almost as many maxims as verses.

> Many learned men have set forth  
> Four eminent qualities of the virtues;  
> If the human mind conforms itself to their forms,  
> An upright life will make a perfect man.  
>
> Therefore we have described them by their proper offices,  
> So that man, obedient to these, may be rightly ordered.

## ON PRUDENCE

> Therefore, you who desire that prudence may govern your conduct,  
> And wish to follow wherever this companion leads you,  
> You will then be able to order your life according to reason,  
> If you weigh every matter by its proper merits.  
>
> Let not the opinion of many deceive you, but value things  
> As their own nature contains their worth.  
> For some things are believed to be good and are not;  
> Others are believed so, and are indeed good.  
>
> Do not marvel at riches which you will lose;  
> Do not value highly anything that can depart.  
> Do not preserve your own possessions as a guardian keeps another’s,  
> But, as their master, use what is yours rightly.  
>
> If you are wise, you will always possess yourself unchanged;  
> And though circumstances change, you yourself remain.  
> As the varied order of events or seasons remains,  
> So do not change yourself; rather, adapt yourself.  
>
> The closed hand makes a fist, the open hand a palm;
