> Though it bears different forms, it is still the same hand.  
> So the wise person adapts himself to differing circumstances,  
> Yet does not thereby alter his own character.  
>
> Be a subtle discerner of counsels;  
> Do not quickly approve falsehood through light credulity.  
> Guard against rashly deciding doubtful matters too soon,  
> Lest a hasty judgment brand you.  
>
> Affirm nothing, because things very like the truth  
> Are not thereby at once proved clearly true.  
> Conversely, what at first you judged false  
> Often proves afterwards to have been true.  
>
> Falsehoods often take on the appearance of truth;  
> Truth often lies hidden beneath a covering of falsehood.  
> A smooth brow conceals a flatterer; a harsh one, a friend;  
> Thus we are deceived by the ambiguous forms of things.  
>
> But one who is prudent, amid so many clouds of things,  
> Will cautiously hold the road upon an unobstructed path.  
> If you are prudent, look ahead to events that are coming,  
> Setting before your eyes all things to come.  
>
> Let nothing be sudden to you; let all things which may happen  
> Be premeditated in your mind.  
> The prudent person does not say, “I did not think these things would happen,”  
> But is present as one expecting and prepared.  
>
> For he waits—not fearing them as uncertain,  
> As though he doubted, but guarding against them as certain.  
> Hence events that were anticipated in advance by watchful care  
> Cannot harm the mind when they arrive.  
>
> When you are about to begin a work, remember to look to its end.  
> Begin—but accomplish it with a joyful hand.  
> [Note: Perhaps: “accomplish it with a slow hand.”]
>
> Let the last things accord with the first; for some things  
> Have such an evil end that they ought never to have been begun.  
> The wise man can neither be deceived nor seek to deceive:  
> In the one case he would be called foolish, in the other wickedly crafty.  
>
> Let opinion differ from the judgments of a wise man in this:  
> What he thinks ought to have the force of law.  
> Scorn to have your senses play with you like dreams;  
> Let not the thoughts of your mind be vain.  
>
> If you delight in their foolish sport,  
> Though arranging everything, you will reap only weariness.  
> But let the efforts of your mind be fixed and sure,  
> And press themselves upon some object with solid seriousness.  
>
> Whether your mind inquires, deliberates, or contemplates,  
> Let it never turn aside from the path of truth.  
> Nor let your speech drip forth in empty flow;  
> Let what you say carry useful weight.  
>
> Whether it persuades, advises, consoles, or commands,  
> Let nothing be empty, nothing lacking usefulness.  
> Be sparing in praise and still more sparing in blame;  
> Error is committed if moderation is absent in either.  
>
> Let your praise grant merit to no one through favour;  
> Let not the person but the vice lack your praise.  
> It is fitting that you be a witness to causes, not partisanships:  
> Look not at who the person is, but what the cause is.  
>
> Do not be thought hasty in making promises;  
> Let the deed be more generous than the promise.  
> Be more restrained in words, more abundant in deeds,  
> And do nothing unless counsel leads the way.  
>
> The wise person’s mind distributes itself across three times,  
> Attending to the past, present, and future.  
> Recall the past, behold what is to come,  
> And manage present matters with reason.  
>
> He who neglects what went before ruins his life;  
> He who neglects the future rushes headlong—each is taken captive.  
> Prudent diligence will set before itself  
> On one side the goods of future time, on the other its evils,  
>
> So that evils may become lighter in view of goods,  
> And goods moderated by consideration of evils.  
> Do not always remain indiscriminately occupied in action,  
> But sometimes give rest to your mind.  
>
> Yet let that rest not grow dull in idle sloth,  
> But let your leisure be full of honourable pursuits.  
> For the wise person never knows how to remain inactive in leisure;  
> He relaxes, but does not release, his heart from its discipline.  
>
> He hastens what is slow, calms what is disturbed, and loosens what is bound;  
> He levels what is steep and makes rough things gentle.  
> For he knows what ought suitably to be attempted, and by what path,  
> And what final result will follow from his undertakings.  
>
> With swift mind he sees all the contrivances of foolish counsels  
> And easily defeats them by skill.  
> From the part he grasps the whole; from what is near, what is distant;  
> From what is open, what is hidden; from small things, great things.  
>
> Let not the great rank of the speaker move you;  
> Consider not so much who speaks as what he proclaims.  
> Consider not how many you please, but whom:  
> The favour of the few is often more fitting.  
>
> Seek what you may find; learn what you can learn;  
> Desire what it befits good men to desire.  
> Never place yourself upon so lofty a summit  
> That you tremble standing there and fall by stepping back.  
>
> High places are always suspect through fear of a fall;  
> The road is more safely kept upon level ground.  
> When prosperity in every circumstance smiles upon you,  
> Then greater caution is required of you.  
>
> Then, as though hemmed in everywhere by hostile ambushes,  
> Take care to use good counsels,  
> That you may govern the movements of the mind with a tight rein  
> And not give free rein to your impulse.  
>
> And, like one who walks with trembling step over slippery ground,  
> Set down your foot with careful pressure,  
> So that, looking round to see whence and whither you proceed,  
> You may escape the many dangers of your life.

## ON FORTITUDE

> If anyone truly possesses the steadfastness of a strong mind,  
> He lives confidently, free, and fearless.  
> Freedom makes him cheerful, confidence firm,  
> And a mind conscious of good does not permit trembling.  
>
> It is a great good of the firm mind, well constant to itself,  
> To endure life’s end without fear.  
> If you are magnanimous, you will deny that you can be harmed,  
> You who press down every adversity with a strong heart.  
>
> You will mock with laughter when the enemy serves you. [Note: Perhaps *desaeviet*, “rages fiercely.”]  
> You will say, “He has not harmed me; he only wished to harm me.”  
> And when he has been delivered into your hands  
> And you seem to have an opportunity for revenge,  
>
> It will be revenge enough to have been able to take revenge;  
> For it is enough to be able to spare your enemy.  
> To forgive the defeated is a noble kind of vengeance;  
> If you grant pardon, you will have taken revenge sufficiently.  
>
> Undermine no one; gnaw at no one in whispers.  
> Hate treachery; come out openly.  
> Do not make war unless you have declared it beforehand;  
> For stealth and deceit become the weak.  
>
> It is not magnanimous rashly to enter dangers,  
> Nor, conversely, to be terrified by cowardly fear.  
> For unless the mind is conscious of a corrupted life,  
> There is nothing from which fear can arise within it.

## ON TEMPERANCE

> Now we shall give you the precepts of the moderate virtue  
> Which restrains and checks the movements of the mind.  
> If you pursue it, cut off all that fluctuates,  
> And put reins upon your desires.  
>
> Consider what nature seeks and what greedy desire craves;  
> Yield to the former; the latter ought to be restrained.  
> If you are moderate, you will advance so far  
> That you can be sufficient even to yourself.  
>
> He who is sufficient to himself was born rich;  
> At his birth he brought his own riches with him.  
> Neither robber nor thief will be able to take them away from him;  
> He will enjoy them as long as he lives.  
>
> Let there be a measure in wishing and a rule in desiring;  
> Let added reins restrain wandering appetites.  
> Let flatteries be absent, by which pleasure, having ensnared the mind,  
> Draws it on through hidden allurements.  
>
> Let want never creep upon one who eats;  
> Let drunkenness not mingle with one who drinks.  
> Remember to observe this among fellow diners:  
> Do not perhaps burden anyone by your sobriety.  
>
> Do not appear, as though holier than they, to condemn them,  
> While you fail to imitate them in a similar way of life.  
> Do not cling too much to present delights,  
> Nor covetously pursue those which are absent.  
>
> Let your table be furnished at little expense; pleasure  
> Is not to be sought there, but hunger to be checked.  
> It is not flavour but hunger that ought to strike the palate;  
> The stomach does not wish to be stretched, but to be nourished.  
>
> Let dreadful desire be bought off as cheaply as possible—  
> The effort required is rather that it should not exist.  
> And, as one conformed to the divine likeness,  
> So far as is permitted, put off the burden of the flesh.  
>
> If you are rightly sober, let your house not be splendid in adornment,  
> But excellent through thrifty convenience.  
> [Note: Thus in the preceding treatise *On the Honourable and the Useful*: “It is not the master who ought to be made honourable by the house, but the house by its master,” chapter “On Temperance.”]
>
> Sobriety neither wishes nor does it become a house  
> To add reputation to its master, but the master to his house.  
> Do not make it your aim to seem other than you are,  
> Nor fashion yourself into more than you are.  
>
> Take care that your frugality is not sordid,  
> That your poverty is not filthy and insufficiently clean,  
> That simplicity is not dull through foolish stupidity,  
> Or gentleness slack through feebleness.  
>
> Let your resources not be cramped, though they be small.  
> Cheerful poverty is worth wealthy kingdoms.  
> Do not let what is yours seem small to you, nor what belongs to another seem great;  
> Let what you possess be pleasing and sufficient to you.  
>
> You will avoid shameful things before they can occur,  
> And no one will be more to you than yourself whom you must fear.  
> Believe that all things must be endured except what is shameful.  
> Shameful things are those by which modesty is wounded.  
>
> I warn you not only to avoid shameful deeds:  
> Shameful words also must be avoided.  
> If perverse licence loosens their reins,  
> Life will gradually flow away once modesty is broken.  
>
> Seek not ornaments in speech, but usefulness;  
> Let plain things be more pleasing to you than honeyed ones.  
> Some jokes, after serious matters, are to be set aside  
> [Note: Perhaps: “mingled in” or “received.”]  
> Yet even these must be conducted in fitting ways.  
>
> Let majesty or reverence not feel itself injured,  
> Nor modesty suffer loss thereby.  
> For laughter is blameworthy if it is excessive,  
> Childishly gushing, or womanishly sounding.  
>
> There are also laughs not accompanied by graciousness  
> And by which a person becomes disliked:  
> Namely, one conspicuous, proudly displaying signs of merit,  
> [Note: Perhaps: “signs of a proud mind.”]  
> Or one secretly made, marking malicious hearts;  
>
> Or one drawn from the unjust stream of pleasures,  
> Which another’s pain often produces.  
> Therefore, if you see jokes appropriate to the occasion,  
> Be cautious even in these and comport yourself reverently.  
>
> So that no one may mark you as excessively harsh,  
> Nor be entitled to despise you as base.  
> Be urbane, not a buffoon, and of moderate wit;  
> Let witticisms lack the tooth, jokes vulgar buffoonery.  
>
> Let speech avoid shouting, laughter guffawing,  
> One’s gait noise: do everything modestly.  
> If the time advises relaxing your cares by rest,  
> That rest will certainly not be sloth for you.  
>
> And when others relax themselves in jokes and games,  
> Do something holy or pious.  
> If you are rightly sober, avoid the flatterer entirely:  
> When he says “hail” to you, beware of him as of an enemy.  
>
> Great is the effort needed to avoid flattering whispers  
> And not to be captured by the art of soft song.  
> Hardly anyone is so sober, so hard and stern,  
> As to be able to overcome their blandishments,  
>
> Which, by a certain art of modulation, powerfully  
> Press strong hearts as do the Sirens.  
> Let being approved by anyone base be as shameful to you  
> As though everyone approved you on account of shameful things.  
>
> Let no one earn your affection by flattery;  
> Earn no one’s affection in a like manner yourself.  
> Let neither rash boldness nor boasting accuse you;  
> These go beyond the boundary of sobriety.  
>
> Be willing to be advised; endure correction patiently;  
> Love whatever usefulness may be available.  
> If someone reproves you deservedly because you have sinned,  
> You should know that he has benefited you.  
>
> But if he reproves you undeservedly when you have not sinned,  
> Still consider that he wished to improve you.  
> A bitter accuser brings harsh words over slight faults;  
> Always fear slight words more than harsh ones.  
>
> Rejoice whenever you are hated by the wicked,  
> Who do not spare to tear apart your reputation.  
> Let it be your greatest praise to be blamed by the wicked;  
> It is a great sign of goodness to have displeased bad people.  
>
> You yourself should strive to be free from every vice  
> And to be a watchful guardian of your life.  
> But be neither a curious investigator of another’s conduct  
> Nor a harsh censor if he sins.  
>
> Rather, correct wrongdoing without reproaching it,  
> Always preceding harshness with kindness.  
> Let not the mercy of one who corrects be difficult—  
> Let him be willing to open a way of pardon to the corrected person.  
>
> Let the sober person desire only what it is useful to possess,  
> And learn only what benefits him to know.  
> It will be beneficial to have learned some things;  
> There are things that do no good, indeed often cause harm.  
>
> Do not raise anyone too high or press anyone down too low;  
> It is sounder to place each in the rank he deserves.  
> When others speak, strive to listen willingly;  
> When you have been advised, be ready to speak.  
>
> Do not be reluctant to answer one who asks,  
> Nor reluctant to yield to one who disputes.  
> It is sometimes useful to yield even to wrong statements,  
> Lest quarrelling arise with a worse evil.  
>
> Let no unworthy movements of body or mind occur;  
> Let vigilant care attend you.  
> Nor, because no other witness sits beside you,  
> Let your care and shame therefore be less.  
>
> I do not know why you should fear another more than yourself:  
> It makes no difference whether you or the people see you.  
> Be yourself your people, your court, and your theatre:  
> Be ashamed before yourself to will shameful things.  
>
> Let your heart be noble, not frivolous; your mind steadfast, not stony;  
> Let good qualities not be corrupted by related vices.  
> The twig and leaf are akin to one another,  
> Yet the latter is mobile, while the former is void of motion.  
>
> Thus immobility is not constancy in a stone;  
> The two nevertheless borrow each other’s appearance.  
> Therefore let the steadfast person avoid immobility,  
> And let the mobile person take care not to flow away in lightness.  
>
> Let mobility be steadfast and constancy mobile;  
> Thus each will be suited to the good of the other.  
> Be fair toward all, neither despising those beneath you  
> Nor fearing those above you, but acting rightly.  
>
> Flatter no one, but be kindly toward all;  
> Reserved with a few, you will be equitable toward all.  
> Take care not to demand back a gift you have bestowed;  
> Beware of being negligent in returning one received.  
>
> Let your judgment be sterner than your speech,  
> Let the severity of your life be greater than that of your expression.  
> Be gentle in vengeance, detesting impiety,  
> Slow to anger and prompt to spare.  
>
> Do not seek to spread your own praise,  
> Nor let another’s praise be a punishment to you.  
> Give no credence at all to accusations, rumours,  
> Biting remarks, or suspicions.  
>
> Above all despise those who, in feigned simplicity,  
> Carry concealed poisons in order to harm others.  
> In adversity be firm; in prosperity humble and cautious;  
> Do not change your purpose.  
>
> Be a concealer of virtues, as some are of vices;  
> Let empty glory have no great power over you.  
> Despise no one’s lack of knowledge, and patiently endure speakers;  
> [Note: Perhaps: “patient in speaking.”]  
> Learn to speak less often yourself, and to be silent more.  
>
> Do not despise cheerful persons, although you yourself are more serious;  
> Show yourself teachable; always love to learn.  
> Do not readily disclose, through boasting, what you know:  
> Let modesty forbid this, lest things unknown to you be learned. [The syntax is uncertain.]

## ON JUSTICE

> What but reflection upon nature’s silent covenant  
> Teaches us the name and principle of justice?  
> By this covenant rational communities, joined together,  
> May preserve themselves through reciprocal aid.  
>
> Therefore that covenant by which nature has bound us,  
> By which the stability and order of human peace endure,  
> By which God is worshipped and man reverently loved—  
> This alone ought rightly to be called justice.  
>
> Here there is no need for anyone to decide whether it is expedient:  
> Whatever justice commands to be done will be expedient.  
> Therefore, whoever wishes to attain justice by pursuing it,  
> I urge him first to fear and love God.  
>
> Burning with love for Him, from this you will imitate Him:  
> You will harm no one, indeed you will wish to help.  
> Then you will be called a just man by every people;  
> Then you will be dear and venerable to all.  
>
> For, to be just, it is not enough merely to harm no one;  
> Rather, strive yourself to help those who harm you.  
> It is not yet the glory of justice merely not to be harmful;  
> Yet from this a step is made toward better things:  
>
> Namely, that, once you cease to harm, you should wish to benefit,  
> Restraining plunderers and commanding stolen goods to be restored.  
> Do not care to weave a dispute from words spoken ambiguously;  
> Rather look more closely to the speaker’s intention.  
>
> Let nothing be more binding for you than a sworn undertaking;  
> Fidelity ought to have the force of an oath.  
> Whenever a matter of truth is dealt with before you,  
> Let faithfulness and religious scruple be preserved.  
>
> Though you may not wish to invoke God by swearing,  
> Yet the truthful witness is present to your words.  
> Even if this too were not the case, it would nevertheless be just  
> To act in accord with truth and justice.  
>
> If you cannot preserve faith except by speaking falsely,  
> We say that faith must be preserved even in this way.  
> [Note: Perhaps read: “Understand cautiously: and thus [faith] is not to be preserved.”]
>
> You ought rather to be excused than said to have deceived,  
> Since faith is admittedly redeemed by speaking falsely.  
> When a cause exists which worthily demands silence,  
> The just person takes care not to uncover a secret.  
>
> He is silent about what ought to be concealed and says what ought to be said:  
> Thus peace suited to him and secure repose  
> Reign in the solid citadel of his mind, while some conquer others  
> And others are conquered by justice.  
>
> Pursuing these things with wakeful diligence,  
> You will be able joyfully to approach your final day—  
> Cheerful while seeing the world’s sorrows, firm amid things that collapse,  
> Tranquil amid turmoil, unafraid of the end.

## ON THE MEASURES OF THE INDIVIDUAL VIRTUES

> Therefore, these described forms of virtue can clearly make a man perfect  
> If he strives to retain, for a definite end of life,  
> The measure which each virtue ought to have.

## ON PRUDENCE

> Now, if prudence oversteps its proper bounds,  
> You will become a man of suspect cunning.  
> You will then be called an eager prier into secrets,  
> One who desires too greatly to learn every harm.  
>
> Astonished, ever brooding and suspicious,  
> You will be seen marked with a sign hateful to all;  
> Your excessively deep craftiness will be so suspicious  
> That it dares to discover every possible offence.  
>
> With finger outstretched, you will be pointed out as full of guile,  
> A deceiver powerful in duplicity;  
> Perverting truth, warring against simplicity,  
> Inventing accusations with contriving fraud.  
>
> At last you will acquire so detestable a name  
> That all the people will call you a bad man.  
> Prudence is therefore rightly marked by these stains  
> If it does not know how to keep its lawful measure.  
>
> But this is its measure: a balance considered on both sides,  
> So that there is in it neither craftiness nor stupidity.

## ON MAGNANIMITY

> If excessive confidence lifts you up beyond measure as magnanimous,  
> You become puffed up, turbulent, and threatening.  
> Disregarding the measure by which honourableness composes itself,  
> You raise yourself too high in voice and gesture.  
>
> Under upright brows, fierce in action,  
> You disturb peace, striking here and driving away there.  
> But although you attack everything with reckless audacity,  
> You are nevertheless not permitted to conquer all things.  
>
> You will encounter some things whose excessively harsh mass  
> Will press down your strength with a heavier weight;  
> And, pitiable, a hard end.
died,
Or a mournful reputation will survive him.

Therefore the measure of a high-minded heart is maintained. [Note: Col. 1064C: perhaps *magnanimi*, “of a high-minded [heart]”.]

Neither by daring too much, nor by fearing too much.

## ON MODERATION

But moderation must take care not to be too sparing,

Nor draw in the timid hand with a clenched nail.

As when a mirror is applied to the limbs themselves, excessive mutilation makes wholeness foul.

Moderation therefore, restraining itself along the middle path,

Must avoid luxury and avoid avarice.

Lest either prodigal luxury dissolve someone,

Or a sordid life mark him through avarice.

## ON JUSTICE

The virtue of justice, besieged by two vices,

[Col. 1064C] sits between softness and cruelty.

Let watchful care therefore ensure that, by fearing to be harsh,

You do not permit what is wrong through excessive indulgence.

Or, while with fervent zeal you cut away offences,

Let no one love a person who cares to spare no one.

But then justice’s censure will appear fitting,

And its rule will thus be made straight,

If neither lax remission makes discipline contemptible,

Nor savage severity makes it hateful.

Therefore whoever wishes worthily to order his own life,

So that he may be useful both to himself and to many,

Should hold in his heart this rule of the virtues set forth above,

To be observed by him with discerning judgment:

So that, weighing persons, causes, places, and times,

He may take care to adapt himself to these by suitable means.

## [THEOLOGICAL TREATISE.]

[Col. 1065]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING TREATISE  
1005–1006

[Col. 1065] Although we found this Treatise in an excellent manuscript, about six hundred years old, of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Lyre in the province of Normandy, marked E, placed amid several indubitable works of the Venerable Hildebert and written, apparently, in the same hand, and could therefore judge it to be a genuine little work of his, yet one single line prefixed to it in that manuscript delayed us somewhat from giving it to the public light. It is precisely the line which, at the beginning of St Anselm’s *Elucidarium*, among his works published many years ago by our Gerberon, reads thus: “Having often been asked by my fellow disciples to resolve certain little questions, I did not have the means to meet their importunity. . . .”

But since in the Lyre manuscript that line has been deleted by another line drawn over it, we judged that it had perhaps been added by some copyist preparing to transcribe St Anselm’s *Elucidarium*, and immediately changing his plan had erased it himself, so that he might commit to the same parchment this Treatise of Hildebert which he had at hand. We therefore willingly shook off our scruple concerning it as less legitimate, and judged that it ought not to prevent us from regarding this excellent treatise as Hildebert’s, or from committing it to the press for the public benefit, provided this could be demonstrated from other evidence.

We thought that we had achieved this with no little success on several grounds. First, from a comparison of this theological Treatise with that *Elucidarium* of St Anselm which the aforementioned Gerberon—who had drawn it from two English manuscripts, one from a roll in the Morton Library at Oxford and the other from the College of St Benedict at Cambridge—relegated to the Appendix as unworthy of St Anselm and, as he himself says, full of trivialities. By contrast, our Treatise of Hildebert contains everywhere excellent, sound, and orthodox doctrine.

Secondly, we established it from the conformity between the doctrine contained in this theological Treatise and that which is found scattered through many sermons of the same Hildebert, indeed expressed so similarly that it is often set forth in both almost in precisely the same words and supported by the same arguments and authorities. Thus, for example, in chapter 20 of this Treatise, when speaking of demons, he says:

> Because he grew proud against his Creator to such an extent, he was cast down into this dark air. . . . He was not permitted to dwell in heaven, which is the bright homeland; nor on earth, lest he trouble humankind too much, but in the dark air, which is his prison until the time of judgment. For then he will be thrust down into the abyss of hell, according to that saying: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.”

He asserts the same thing in almost exactly the same words in the second sermon on the Ascension of the Lord, which we drew not only from the Victorine manuscript but also from the Lyre manuscript, from which we likewise obtained this Treatise. There it reads:

> From the empyrean heaven he fell into this dark air, which has been assigned to him as a prison until the end of time, when he shall be sent into the eternal fire prepared for him and his angels.

He also teaches the same doctrine concerning demons, explains it in nearly the same words, and proves it by authorities in Sermon 1 on the Nativity of the Lord, Sermon 1 on the Purification of Blessed Mary, the sermon on Christian warfare addressed to monks, and elsewhere throughout his writings.

Likewise, when chapter 3 of this Treatise treats of God’s immensity, it says that God “is truly everywhere without place, just as he is everlasting without time.” Thus in Sermon 8, on the mystery of the Incarnation, he says that the divine substance, which is God, is everlasting without time, wholly everywhere without place, and makes all mutable things without any change in itself. He repeats this in the same words in the sermon on Christ’s benefits toward us and in many others.

We could say the same, unless we seemed excessive, concerning God’s immutability and his other attributes, of which Hildebert speaks in his sermons in the same way and, for the most part, in the same terms as in this Treatise. Hence we thought we might infer that this little work is a true and genuine composition of his.

Nor, therefore, could we altogether rashly infer from this that the authors of scholastic theology in that age could have drawn no small assistance from this Treatise, whether one considers the substance of their doctrine or even its order. This applies even to the very standard-bearer, as it were, of scholastic theology—Peter Lombard, deservedly honored with the title Master of the Sentences. He lived many years after Hildebert, dying only in 1164, whereas Hildebert departed this life about the year 1132, that is, more than thirty years before the said Lombard.

1007–1008 Since Peter Lombard himself asserts, as a kind of foundation for his entire theology, that there are certain things to be enjoyed and others to be used, and adduces to prove this the same authority of Blessed Augustine, from Book I, chapter 4 of *On Christian Doctrine*, which Hildebert cites in this Treatise in precisely the same words, it may reasonably be inferred that Lombard derived this from Hildebert’s Treatise.

Nor would I doubt that Cardinal Robert Pullus himself, to whom some also assign primacy in scholastic theology, benefited in some degree from the studies of our Hildebert, if the chronology is taken into account. Hildebert himself was appointed headmaster at Le Mans about the year 1087, after spending some eight years at Cluny under St Hugh. Hildebert could have composed this Treatise at Cluny about the year 1084, at which time Pullus—who is said not to have restored the University of Oxford until 1133—had scarcely reached adolescence, since he died only in 1150. Peter Lombard himself, who did not leave this life until 1164, was then passing only his childhood, or at least his earliest adolescent years.

If therefore we consider chronology, it is probable that both Pullus and Lombard benefited rather from the studies of Hildebert, their elder, than that Hildebert derived anything from the writings of those younger than himself. Just as he himself could have learned much from St Anselm, his elder, as he indeed testifies in Letter 13 of Book II, formerly numbered 22, where he gives Anselm thanks for kindly sending him his book on the procession of the Holy Spirit. That Hildebert published this Treatise while still a young man—that is, in or after about his twenty-fifth year—may be inferred from the terms he uses at its beginning, when he says that he will give an account of his faith and hope only with modesty and fear. This was especially fitting not for a teacher instructing as though from a chair, but for an ingenuous young man addressing fellow disciples with whom he was engaged.

What we have said concerning Peter Lombard, Master of the Sentences, is very far from intending to detract in any way from the honor rightly due to the sacred labors of that most celebrated bishop. Rather, his memory has always been held by us in the highest reverence, and his diligence deserves commendation. For he took care, with such zeal and clarity, to gather from every source whatever could contribute to the elucidation of sacred theology and arrange it for public benefit; nor perhaps did he consider it unworthy of his learning and celebrated reputation to draw much, for his own studies and those of his disciples, from Hildebert, his elder and a theologian already very renowned among learned people.

Meanwhile, let the diligent reader observe that the scholastic theologians of that age observed in their assertions no method other than that found in this theological Treatise of Hildebert, although they generally used different terms. For just as Hildebert, in setting forth his doctrine and proving his propositions, employs the testimonies of Holy Scripture and the authorities of the holy Fathers and doctors of the Church; then himself presents, under the words “It is asked,” “It is commonly asked,” “An objection is raised,” and the like, whatever objections might be made to him in each article or chapter; and thereafter does not fail to resolve them very learnedly and soundly: so scholastic theologians, after setting forth and proving their assertions, raise objections against themselves for fuller discussion and understanding under the heading “You will object,” and afterward reduce and dissolve them according to their principles.

Moreover, since Hildebert chiefly supports his doctrine by the authorities of the holy Fathers, though he has not always quoted them exactly word for word, we have, for the reader’s greater convenience, sought out and noted the greater part of them with all the diligence we could. Since he relies especially on the authorities of Blessed Augustine, who, as Hildebert himself says in *On the Conflict of Flesh and Soul*, was more familiar to him, we applied ourselves to tracing these particularly, not without tedious labor. Yet where the very words proved more difficult to find, we supplied in the margin other passages of the same most holy Doctor presenting the same meaning.

Since he cites the opinions of the other Fathers more rarely, we left the investigation of these to the diligence of the curious reader. We judged Hildebert worthy of unquestioning trust in other matters, since we observed him to be so faithful in almost innumerable citations from St Augustine that in no judgment whatsoever did he depart from the thought of that most holy Doctor—except in his opinion, in chapter 20 of this Treatise, that angels were created without virtue and vice. We did not fail to note in its place that this is alien to St Augustine’s teaching.

Furthermore, although we could have adduced other and more numerous arguments than those mentioned to attribute this Treatise to Hildebert, we are not people who wish to compel the judgment of the learned reader to accept our view. We have regarded it not as absolutely certain, but as highly probable from the conjectures reported. Meanwhile, we hope it will not be unwelcome to him that we have dedicated to public use this excellent and ancient monument of theology, found amid other unquestioned little works of the Venerable Hildebert and rescued from bookworms and moths by no small labor.

[Col. 1067]

# THE THEOLOGICAL TREATISE OF THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT, BISHOP OF LE MANS

(From the Lyre manuscript, about 600 years old. Not previously published.) (G)\*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1067A]

1009–1010 We must be prepared, as Peter says in his epistle, to give an account with modesty and fear to everyone who asks concerning the faith and hope that are in us (II Peter III, 15). Therefore, in order that modesty may be preserved together with fear, and fear together with assertion, let us avoid, as the Apostle commands, profane novelties of speech (I Tim. VI, 20), and let us not incline in any direction through rash assertion.

For it is better not to speak grandly, so that one does not err dangerously, than to define contrary things. But insofar as we can, let us rest upon the traces of authorities [manuscript: *vestigiis*, “upon the traces”]; and where certain authority is lacking, let us especially endeavor to agree with those who come closest to the authorities. Let us not presume upon our own opinion, but interpret the Scriptures devoutly.

For Scripture, as Blessed Augustine says [note: Col. 1067D, Book V of *On Genesis according to the Letter*, ch. 3, no. 8], “mocks the proud by its height, holds the attentive by its depth, nourishes the great by truth, and instructs the little by affability.” If, therefore, any obscure matters occur to us, let it be our purpose to have recourse to authorities; then to present what the wise people of our own time think about them, why it pleases us to follow these rather than those, and, where reason and authority concur, to bring this into the light according to our ability.

## CHAPTER I. On Faith

And since all things must be regulated by faith as by a measure [Col. 1068A], lest anything overflow as superfluous, as the Apostle says, “To each according as God has apportioned a measure of faith” (Rom. XII, 5), we must first consider what faith is and what parts it has.

“Faith,” as the Apostle says, “is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. XI, 1). It is the substance of things hoped for because they subsist in us. He calls “things hoped for” those eternal goods which we desire, such as immortality and the like, which already subsist in us through faith and which in the future we shall possess through experience [manuscript addition: *possidebimus*]. It is the evidence of things not seen—that is, proof—because if someone doubts that such matters can ever be proved by human reason, as if one asks, “How do you know of the Virgin’s childbirth, or of the future condition of the elect?” I have no other evidence than this: I believe without doubt [Col. 1068B] what the prophets and others who spoke through the Holy Spirit said concerning these things; that God would in no way deceive them when he spoke and worked miracles in them; and, since I see that what they said has for the most part been fulfilled, I do not doubt that the rest will be fulfilled.

Faith, therefore, is the substance of things hoped for in relation to us; it is evidence of things not seen in relation to others. But this definition shows more the effect of faith than what faith itself is, nor does it encompass every part of faith, since it includes not things past but only things future.

Faith can therefore be defined thus: it is a voluntary certainty concerning absent things, situated above opinion and below knowledge. It is voluntary because it is not compelled; it concerns absent things, that is, matters not subject to bodily senses; it is above opinion because believing is more than opining; it is below knowledge because believing is less than knowing. For we believe in order that we may someday know.

Hope arises from faith and may be defined thus: hope is confidence in future goods arising from God’s grace and a good conscience. According to some, charity arises from faith and hope; charity is love of God for his own sake and of one’s neighbor for God’s sake. Hope and charity arise from faith as from the foundation of all goods [supplied: *oriuntur*], because nothing can be hoped for, nor can what is hoped for be loved, unless it is first believed. Yet something may be believed which is not hoped for or loved. Although faith, hope, and charity exist simultaneously in time [Col. 1069B], and faith has no prior merit to hope and charity, faith nevertheless precedes hope and charity in causation, because we hope and love for this reason: that we believe. Likewise charity arises from hope, because we love future goods because we hope for them. What we hope to obtain, we love.

But because, as authority says, hope is a certainty arising from preceding merits; likewise, to hope for anything without merits should be called not hope but presumption; and without charity there is no merit—some persons think that hope arises from faith and charity. For, as Augustine says in *On Faith and Works*, chapter 16 [supplied, perhaps: *spei*, “of hope”], it is faith working through love that is the foundation, not the faith of demons, by which they themselves believe and tremble. And if hope proceeds from faith working through love, then hope arises from faith and charity [manuscript: *spes oritur*].

For authors frequently give this order: faith, hope, charity (I Cor. XIII, 13). This, it is said, is because charity is greater. Yet that opinion, as it seems to me, may be resolved thus. Hope is certainty arising from preceding merits; this must not be understood of merits preceding hope itself, because no merit precedes hope, but of merits preceding that which is hoped for.

This is the difference between faith and hope: faith concerns past things, such as Christ’s birth and passion; present things, such as the true body of Christ on the altar; and future things, such as immortality and the like. Hope, however, concerns future things only. Again, faith concerns both good and evil things; hope concerns only goods to be obtained. For hope of some misfortune ought rather to be called despair of goods than hope [Col. 1069D].

It must also be known that faith concerns only those things which are not seen. Gregory says in a homily [note: Col. 1069D, Homily 16 on the Gospels]: “Things apparent do not have faith, but recognition.” Again, in the same place: “Since Paul says, ‘Faith is the substance of things hoped for,’ that is, of things not seen (Heb. XI, 1), what cannot be seen is truly said to be believed; for what can be seen can no longer be believed.”

Thomas saw one thing and believed another: he saw the man and confessed God, saying, “My Lord and my God” (Ps. XXXIV [Col. 1070A], 23). Augustine says [note: Col. 1069D, *On the Gospel of John*, ch. VIII, Tractate 40]: “We believe in order that we may know; we do not know in order that we may believe. For what is faith except believing what you do not see? Faith, therefore, is believing what you do not see; truth is seeing what you did not believe.”

Certain authorities appear to hold that faith may exist even concerning things which are seen, as in John: “Now I tell you before it happens, so that, when it has happened, you may believe” (John XIV, 29). Hence Augustine says [note: Col. 1070D, Tractate LXXIX on John]: “What does this mean, ‘so that, when it has happened, you may believe’? For even he to whom it was said, ‘Because you have seen, you have believed’ (John XX, 29), did not believe what he saw. He saw flesh; he believed God hidden in flesh.”

But we say that things which are seen are believed in the sense in which each person says that he has believed his own eyes. Yet this is not the faith built up in us; rather, from the things which we see [Col. 1070B], there is brought about in us a belief in things not seen. Augustine says in the book *Questions on the Gospels* [note: Col. 1070D; something similar in Sermon 242, at the end of the Psalm]:

> There is also a faith when belief is given not to words but to things themselves present, when the Wisdom of God itself will offer itself to the saints for contemplation through open sight.

Perhaps Paul speaks of that faith, the presence of the things themselves and of the light itself, when he says: “For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith” (Rom. I, 17).

But it may be said that Augustine [manuscript: *Apostolus*, “the Apostle”] says this not of the sacrament of faith but of the thing believed. For the faith itself by which we now behold God in a riddle through a mirror is a sacrament of that future vision in which we shall behold God face to face, as we now do not see [manuscript: *non, sicuti nunc, videmus*].

[Col. 1070C] It may be asked: Did Peter have faith in Christ’s passion, which he saw with his own eyes, when faith is not—or rather, according to the manuscript, when faith is of—things not apparent? To this one may answer: he had not faith but recognition, except in the customary improper expression, “I believe my eyes.” Yet in what he saw he had no merit if he believed it; rather, his merit lay in believing that he whom he saw hanging upon the wood was God. Faith, therefore, which serves edification, is not concerned with things apparent.

It is commonly asked whether faith is a virtue. Prosper, from Augustine’s sayings: “There are three highest virtues: faith, hope, charity.” The Apostle also says: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. IV, 3). Again, faith has merit; but nothing has merit [Col. 1070D] except virtue.

Some nevertheless say that faith is not a virtue, on the basis of the Apostle’s words: “If I have all faith but do not have charity, I am nothing” (I Cor. XIII, 2). Here he implies that faith can exist without charity, whereas no virtue can exist without charity. Yet faith working through love can rightly be called virtue; thus virtue without love is not virtue.

If you object, “Then there are two faiths,” there are nevertheless not two, but the same faith increased. Hence: “Increase our faith” (Luke XVII, 5). For, as Jerome says, to the extent that we believe, we love, and conversely.

## CHAPTER II. On the Faith of the Ancients

[Col. 1071A]

To what has been said must be added an account of the knowledge of faith possessed by the ancients, and how it was increased through the law of Moses and through the law of the Gospel. Faith is at times accompanied by little knowledge and great constancy and devotion, as in the woman to whom it was said, “O woman, great is your faith” (Matt. XV, 28); at other times by great knowledge and little constancy, as in Peter, who denied Christ; and likewise in us, which is not so pleasing to God.

Since faith cannot exist altogether without knowledge, even though the knowledge is not perfect, God from the beginning so moderated the knowledge of himself that, just as he could never be wholly comprehended, so he could never be wholly unknown. He did not wish to be wholly comprehended, so that [Col. 1071B] faith might possess merit; nor wholly concealed, so that unbelief might not be excused by ignorance.

There is a certain knowledge of faith without which salvation could never exist at any time: namely, knowledge that God exists and that he rewards those hoping in him, according to the Apostle’s saying: “One who approaches God must believe that he is and that he is a rewarder of those who hope in him” [note: Col. 1071D: Heb. XI, 6; the Vulgate reads, “of those who seek him”].

But since God is invisible, according to the Evangelist John: “No one has ever seen God” (I John V, 12), how could he be made known? Partly through human reason and partly through divine revelation, both methods of which the Apostle shows. For he says: “What is known of God is manifest in them” (Rom. I, 19). By saying “manifest in them,” he plainly shows that there was in them that by which they could know God. But when he adds, “God manifested it to them” (ibid.), he shows that human reason by itself would be insufficient unless divine revelation [manuscript: *ratio*, “reason”] came to its aid.

Divine revelation takes place in two ways: by inward aspiration [manuscript: *inspiratione*, “inspiration”], and by instruction in doctrine, which occurs outwardly through deeds or words. By human reason they could know that God exists. Since the human mind cannot be ignorant of itself, it knows that it at some time began to be. Nor can it be ignorant that, when it did not exist, it could not give itself the substance by which it might exist. Therefore, in order to exist, it was made by another, who consequently is known not to have begun; for if he had begun through another, he could not be the first author of existence for all things.

They could also discern divine wisdom and goodness from the ordering [Col. 1071D] and government of visible things. It is therefore apparent that even before the Law, from the things that were made, God’s invisible things could be perceived from the creation of the world.

Through the written Law, knowledge of faith began to increase. For then he through whom deliverance would occur—that is, the Messiah—began to be promised, although the manner of redemption was not fully known. Yet both before the Law and during the time of the Law there were always some to whom faith in the Incarnation was revealed, who, like pillars of the Church, believed.

It is asked concerning those simple persons to whom revelation had not been made [Col. 1072A], though they nevertheless believed that God exists and rewards those who hope in him, whether they were saved. Some say that they were not saved, on the basis of these authorities.

Augustine, to Optatus:

> Only that faith saves by which we believe that no human being is freed from the contagion of death contracted through the first birth except through the one Mediator. By the most saving faith in him, who is both man and God, those too were saved who, before he came in the flesh, believed that he would come in the flesh. For their faith and ours are the same: they believed that what we believe has happened would happen.

The same author, in *On Rebuke and Grace*: “No one is delivered from the condemnation brought about through Adam except through faith in Jesus Christ.”

Gregory, on Ezekiel: “And those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying, ‘Hosanna to the Son of David,’” etc. [note: Col. 1072D: The same is implied in Job II, 24]. For all the elect who could be in Judaea, and those who are now in the Church, believed and believe in the Mediator of God and humankind.

Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book II, chapter 12:

> The same faith in the Mediator made the ancient righteous people—small and great alike—safe; for just as we believe that Christ came in the flesh, so they believed that he would come; as we believe that he died, so they that he would die; as we believe that he rose, so they that he would rise; and both we and they believe that he will come to judge the dead.

Accordingly, these persons say that none of the ancients could be saved unless they believed at least these four things: that Christ would come, die, rise again, and judge. But those to whom revelation had not been given were wholly ignorant of these things [Col. 1072C]. How, then, did they believe them?

Others, with whom we agree more, say that they possessed faith in Christ veiled in mystery: what those to whom revelation had been given knew and believed, these others believed, although they did not know it. For they had entrusted their faith to those others. Hence in Job: “The oxen were ploughing, and the she-asses were feeding beside them” (Job I, 14). Those were the she-asses feeding beside the oxen: like the many simple people in the Church today who, though they do not know how to set forth the Trinity so distinctly, nevertheless believe because in faith and humility they adhere to those who both know and believe it.

An objection is raised: if to possess faith in Christ veiled in mystery meant believing that God exists and rewards those who hope in him [Col. 1072D], and philosophers too believed this, then they possessed faith in Christ veiled in mystery. But authority says that they could not by human reason have possessed faith in the Incarnation.

Yet, as we have already said, to believe that God exists and rewards those who hope in him by humbly adhering to the ploughing oxen, who both knew and believed this, was to possess faith in Christ veiled in mystery. We judge that certain Gentiles were of this kind, such as the widow of Zarephath. Job too was a Gentile. Thus we say that the simple persons of that time believed everything that we believe because they believed those who knew and believed everything.

But in the time of grace it is no longer enough, as it was then, to believe that God exists and rewards those hoping in him [Col. 1073A], because the manifestation of truth has now been made. For the degree and measure of faith corresponded to the times. Cornelius had faith, but not faith sufficient for salvation. Hence Augustine says [note: Col. 1073D, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, ch. 7, no. 12]:

> The angel said to Cornelius, “Your alms and prayers have been accepted,” before he believed in Christ; yet he did not give alms and pray without some faith. For how did he call upon one in whom he had not believed? But if he could have been saved without faith in Christ, Peter, the architect of the Church, would not have been sent to him.

From this authority it is evident that, although Cornelius believed what those simple ancients believed, this no longer sufficed because of the character of the time.

## CHAPTER III. On the Parts of Faith, or on the Unity of God and His Existence in All Things

[Col. 1073B]

After what has been said, let us pursue the parts of faith. There are two matters in which faith chiefly consists: the mystery of divinity and the sacrament of the Incarnation. First, then, concerning that part of faith which pertains to the unity of the divine substance.

Just as reason has demonstrated that God exists, so it has demonstrated that he is one, in order that the beginning and end of all things might be one. For if there were two, either both would be insufficient or one superfluous. If something were lacking in one which the other possessed, it would not be supremely perfect. But if nothing were lacking in one which the other possessed, since all things would be in the one, the other would be superfluous.

There is therefore one principle, one author of all visible things [manuscript: *quae videntur*, “which are seen”], as reason and many authorities prove. Thus in prophecy: “Hear, Israel: your God, God is one” (Deut. VI, 4). He is truly one because he is unchangeable and invariable. For with him there is no alteration or shadow of turning, because being is not one thing for him and being wise another, nor being immense, eternal, good, or just.

When, however, he is called just, wise, and so forth, we do not indicate a diversity of properties, for there is none in God, but diverse effects which God works in creatures. When he is called just, we understand that he judges justly; wise, that he makes and governs all things wisely; merciful, that he mercifully spares sinners.

Augustine, against Arius [note: Col. 1074D, Letter 120, to Consentius, no. 13]:

> Let us understand God, insofar as we can: good without quality, great without quantity, creator without need, present without position, wholly everywhere without place, everlasting without time, making mutable things without change, suffering nothing. Whoever thinks of God and cannot yet wholly find what he is, nevertheless devoutly takes care, insofar as possible, to think nothing of him which he is not.

This divine substance is wholly everywhere, and all things are in it, because all things are in it, as John testifies: “All things were life in him” (John I, 4), that is, immutably, because their disposition and order were in him [Col. 1074A] from eternity. For things which have origin and mutability in actuality did not begin to be in God.

God is everywhere and in every creature, as he himself says through the prophet: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII, 24). Elsewhere: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 8). Again: “Wisdom reaches from end to end” (Wis. VIII, 1), that is, from the least creature to the greatest, from one extremity to the other.

But all things are in God in one way, and God is in all things in another. All things are in God not by essence, because, as Augustine says, whatever is in God is God; but, as we have said, by disposition. For, as Augustine says concerning John, just as an ark exists in the mind of its maker before it is made, so all things have existed in God from eternity [Col. 1074B]. It does not follow that they have therefore existed from eternity because they have existed in God from eternity. For if they had begun in God, there would already be change in God.

An objection is commonly raised: if creatures are in God because they are known by God before they are made, then evils are in God because they are known by him before they are done. But, as we have said, creatures are in God because their disposition is in him, and so forth; God is not the author of evils.

We have shown that creatures are not in God by essence; God, however, is in every creature by essence. Certain slanderers of truth say that he is everywhere by power, not by essence, as though the pollutions of filth could touch him if he were essentially everywhere. This is so frivolous that it is not even worthy of an answer [Col. 1074C], since even a created spirit cannot be polluted by the filth of a body, even one leprous or however defiled.

Finally, let them be asked what must rather be granted concerning God: that he is nowhere by essence, or everywhere, or somewhere in such a way that he is not everywhere. If anyone dares to say that the divine essence is nowhere, what does it mean that it is somewhere and not everywhere? For if the divine substance is somewhere in this way, why is it not everywhere? Is it therefore local? Let them therefore grant that he is everywhere essentially.

For the authority which they commonly introduce destroys rather than aids their error—namely, “God is everywhere, not by places but by actions.” In order to foster their error, they falsify the truth [manuscript: *fucos veritati officiunt*, perhaps “they do injury to truth through disguises”]. For that authority reads as follows: “God is everywhere; we approach him not by places but by actions.”

It must therefore be confessed that God is truly and essentially in every place, yet he is not contained by any place, because he is uncircumscribable. Augustine, to Dardanus:

> We must not suppose that God is spread through all things by a spatial magnitude, like smoke or this light which is diffused; but rather as wisdom is in two persons, neither of whom is wiser if he is physically larger. One wisdom is in both: no greater in the greater, no smaller in the smaller; in one person, the same as in two. So too God, without labor governing and without burden sustaining [manuscript: *continens*, “containing”] the world, is wholly in heaven, wholly on earth, and absent from neither.

He is whole because he does not present one part of himself to one part and another part to another. He is in himself because he is not contained by those things in which he is present, as though he could not exist without them. For take bodily spaces away from bodies, and bodies will not exist. Take bodies themselves away from their qualities, and they will not be where they are; and therefore they must necessarily not exist.

Objection: Today a new creature comes to be, as does a soul. Previously it was nothing, because it was made from nothing; God was not in it when it was nothing; now he is in it. Therefore he is where he was not before; consequently he is mutable. But just as, when a cloud is set against a ray of the sun, the ray is nevertheless not elsewhere than it was before, while the cloud is [Col. 1075B] where it was not; and the ray did not begin to be there because the cloud began to be where the ray was: so God, when, before that creature existed, he was everywhere, was in the very place where it was made. Therefore he is not now elsewhere than before.

Thus we also say concerning the world and all creatures that, although they have not always existed, nevertheless authority says that God is in each individual thing; yet he is not where he was not, because he is truly everywhere without place, just as he is everlasting without time. As Augustine says: “Although we are not yet able fully to investigate this, nevertheless we believe without doubt that God is essentially everywhere. Nothing whatsoever that he has made can subsist—even for a moment—without him, because he contains and penetrates all things and is contained by none; for, by reason of his [Col. 1075C] immensity, he cannot be comprehended; by reason of his purity, he cannot be defiled; and by reason of his simplicity, he cannot be divided.”

Augustine, *To Dardanus*: “He is present wholly and equally not only to the whole creation but also to each part of it.” In the same work: “We must confess that God is everywhere through the presence of his divinity, but not everywhere through the grace of indwelling. For because of this indwelling—where the grace of his love is without doubt recognized—we do not say, ‘Our Father, who art everywhere,’ although this too is true, but, ‘who art in heaven.’”

Let us therefore say that God is in all creatures, and equally so through the presence of deity, or through essence; but through indwelling grace he is not in all, but only in the good, nor equally in them, because the better they are, the more abundantly he dwells in them—that is, the more perfectly he is [Col. 1075D] known and loved by them. Just as the soul, as Augustine says in his letter to Jerome on the origin of the soul, is wholly and simultaneously present in every particle of the body, neither less in the smaller parts nor greater in the larger; yet it exercises its effects more intensely in some and more weakly in others, although it is essentially present in every part of the body.

God is not in the wicked through indwelling grace, because they are not illuminated by him. Hence: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5), just as the light of the sun floods the eyes of a blind person but is not apprehended by him. This light illuminates the good, however, not equally. Augustine, *To Dardanus*: “Although God, who is everywhere, does not dwell in all things, even in those in which he dwells [Col. 1076A] he does not dwell equally. For whence comes that which Elisha requested (4 Kings 2), that the Spirit of God who was in Elijah might rest upon him doubly? And why are some saints holier than others, unless they possess God as indweller more abundantly?” Those are said to be far from him because, by sinning, they have become most unlike him; and those approach him who, by living well, receive his likeness. God, therefore, is everywhere by presence, or by essence, and equally in every place; yet he is not in a place—that is, he is not local.

It is asked concerning a created spirit whether it is in a place, or is non-local. Some say that it is not local, or in a place, adhering too closely to Augustine’s authority on Genesis: “A bodily creature is moved [Col. 1076B] through times and places; a spiritual creature is moved only through times: it is moved by affections, as from sadness to joy, and also by learning what it does not know, as in angels; for in this there is a before and an after. God is moved neither through times nor through places.”

But where Augustine says that a spiritual creature is not moved through places, he means this: it does not have local circumscription. Things which have dimensions are circumscribed by place, because a beginning, middle, and end are assigned to them according to place. But a created spirit has no dimension; nevertheless, because it has a limit—because it is so there that it is not elsewhere [variant: “that it is elsewhere”]—it is local, although it does not produce spatial extension in a place. For even if many spirits were here, they would not make the place narrower [Col. 1076C] so that it held fewer bodies.

God alone, therefore, because he contains all things within himself, according to the saying: “In him we live, move, and are” (Acts 17:28), has no limit and is not contained in a place. But whatever has a limit is, in some respect, local. Ambrose, in the book *On the Faith* addressed to Emperor Gratian: “Thus Isaiah said: ‘For one of the seraphim was sent to me’ (Isa. 6). A spirit indeed is said to be sent, but the seraph to one person, the Spirit to all. The seraph is sent for ministry; the seraph performs ministry. The seraph passes from place to place, for it does not fill all things, but is itself filled by the Spirit.” Here Ambrose plainly says that angels are local.

## Chapter IV. On the Trinity

[Col. 1076D]

Having considered these matters, it remains to consider those which concern the distinction of the Trinity. First let us adduce the testimonies of authority. In Genesis: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). By the plural he shows the Trinity. The Psalmist: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). In the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1:1).

Reason also has certain exemplars of this inquiry and consideration in the things that have been made. For God, who cannot be seen in himself, has been made manifest in his work. [Col. 1077A] For just as a human being’s wisdom is not seen except by that person himself, unless it is made manifest through speech, so God’s wisdom could not be known until it was manifested through his work. That work is as it were an outward word, in some manner revealing God’s wisdom, just as the word of the heart—that is, the thought of the mind—is made manifest through the word of the mouth.

And because among all creatures the rational creature comes nearest to the likeness of God—for it alone was made in God’s image and likeness—the human mind could discover within itself a clearer trace of the Trinity than in other creatures. For it saw that wisdom, which is itself, is born within it; and that it loves its own wisdom. Thus wisdom proceeds from mind, and from mind and wisdom proceeds love, by which [Col. 1077B] the mind itself loves the wisdom begotten from itself. These three—mind, love, and wisdom—exist together. They are three, yet one substance in which these three, namely mind, love, and wisdom, are distinct from one another, since mind is neither wisdom nor love, and wisdom is neither mind nor love; yet the unity of substance does not depart.

The mind then ascends from these to its Creator and considers that he possesses wisdom, and how he has never been without wisdom. It also considers that he has always loved his wisdom and has always had love toward it; and this love is coeternal with the Eternal One and with his coeternal wisdom. Again it considers that in God nothing can be different from God; and thus the wisdom of God is God, and the love of God is God. Therefore unity remains in the Trinity. This [Col. 1077C] Trinity is the Father, who is from no one; the wisdom of the Father, which is begotten from the Father; and the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and is very frequently called in Holy Scripture the love of the Father and the Son. These three persons are distinct, because the Father is neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit, nor is the Son the Father or the Holy Spirit; yet these three persons are one substance, one God.

Augustine, *On the Trinity*: “We say three persons of one and the same essence, or three persons, one essence; we do not say three persons from the same essence, as though essence were one thing and person another.”

Here we must consider why, in the holy Trinity, that person who is from no one is called Father. Clearly, because he begot the Son from his own substance—the Son who is [Col. 1077D] called the wisdom of the Father, or the Word, because he is begotten from the Father himself. Hence in the Psalm: “My heart has uttered a Word” (Ps. 94:1 [as cited]).

He who proceeds from the Father and the Son is called the Holy Spirit, because he is breathed forth by the Father and the Son for sanctification. Yet he does not come without the Father and the Son, because the Trinity is undivided. But for him to be breathed forth by the Father and the Son is for him to be from the Father and the Son; and this is eternal for him, though he is given and received in time. Thus the Holy Spirit is the gift of the Father and the Son; and when he is given, he is given in time. For him, to be given by the Father and the Son is nothing other than, when he is given, to be from the Father and the Son—something eternal and timeless for him, though he is given in time. Just as the Spirit’s being of the Father and the Son is eternal for him, so he is [Col. 1078A] breathed forth by the Father and the Son in time.

Bede, in the homily for the first Sunday after the Ascension: “When the grace of the Spirit is given to human beings, the Spirit is certainly sent by the Father and also sent by the Son; he proceeds from the Father and also proceeds from the Son, because his mission is his very procession, since he proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

Augustine, Book V of *The City of God*, says: “He proceeds not in the manner in which he is given. But what is given is referred both to him who gave it and to those to whom he gave it. Again, if he does not proceed except when he is given, then certainly he would not have proceeded before there were persons to whom he might be given. For a gift can exist even before it is given; but it cannot in any way be called a bestowed gift unless it has been given.” [Variant: *donum* (“gift”) for *donatum* (“bestowed gift”).]

Here a major question arises: why are the three things in the soul not called three persons, whereas the things found in the Godhead in likeness to them [Col. 1078B] are called and are three persons? It may be said in reply that they are not persons because they are mutable affections of the soul. For sometimes the soul is without knowledge and love. Nor can it be said, “A human being’s knowledge is a human being; a human being’s love is a human being.” But God’s wisdom is God and God’s love is God, because in God nothing is other than himself.

Therefore the three persons are one God, one substance, one nature: these three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Father is from no one. Hence Augustine says (*On the Trinity*, Book IV, no. 29): “The Father is the principle of the Trinity—that is, within the Trinity—because he is not the principle of himself, but the Son and the Holy Spirit are from him, while he is from no one.”

We have many authorities that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. The Apostle says: “The Lord sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying: Abba, Father” (Gal. 4:6). And in the Gospel: “The power of God went forth from him” (Luke 6:19). The Greeks, however, say that the Holy Spirit proceeds only from the Father and not from the Son. They say this because no mention of it is made in the Apostles’ Creed—that is, the shorter Creed—nor in the Creed given at the Nicene synod, at the end of which is found the manner in which it said: “Let him be anathema,” which we interpret as though it meant otherwise, that is, contrary to this. But since this was neither affirmed nor denied there, we do not say anything contrary to that Creed.

## Chapter V. On the various names distinguishing the persons of the Trinity by their properties

[Col. 1078D]

From what has preceded, we must observe that in the holy Trinity there are certain names that distinguish the persons. There are also others that signify the unity of nature or substance, such as: God, omnipotent, eternal, immense. These are said according to substance. For it is no different to be by nature than to be God, omnipotent, eternal, immense, wise, just, and the like. Therefore, just as there is one essence and not three, so there is one God and not three: one God, omnipotent, eternal, immense, wise, and so forth.

Augustine, Book VII of *On the Trinity* (ch. 1, no. 1): “Because for him to be God is the same as to be, it is not permissible to speak of either three essences [Col. 1079A] or three gods.”

There are other names by which the Trinity is distinguished: Father, unbegotten, begetter. These belong only to the Father. To the Son alone belong these other names: Son, begotten, born, Word, and others like them. To the Holy Spirit belong these other names: Holy Spirit, gift, proceeding from the Father and the Son. These names signify the properties by which the persons are distinguished. For it belongs to the Father alone to be a principle [supplying: “to be”], to be Father, and to be unbegotten, because he is from no one. It is proper to the Son to be begotten from the Father. It is proper to the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and the Son. But in being God, omnipotent, wise, just, and so forth, the Father is not distinguished from the Son and Holy Spirit, because the Son too is God and omnipotent and the like; and the Holy Spirit [Col. 1079B] likewise.

It is asked, since it does not belong to the Holy Spirit to be begotten, whether he may be called unbegotten. Augustine, *To Orosius* [Note: [Col. 1079D] See the *Commonitorium* of Orosius and Augustine’s book addressed to him, vol. VIII, p. 605 ff.]: “The certain faith declares the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten. For if we call him unbegotten, we shall seem to affirm two Fathers; but if begotten, we are charged with believing two Sons.”

Likewise Orosius to Augustine: “Did the Father beget the Son by will or by necessity?” Augustine: “Neither by will nor by necessity, because there is no necessity in God; will cannot bring forth wisdom. For it is reported that when a heretic asked one of our number whether the Father begot the Son willingly or unwillingly, he gave this admirable reply: ‘Then tell me, heretic: is God the Father God by necessity or by will?’ [Col. 1079C] If he had said ‘by necessity,’ a great absurdity followed; if ‘by will,’ he was answered: ‘Therefore he is God by will, not by nature.’ Thus, just as the Father is God by nature, he begot the Son by nature; and this begetting is eternal and ineffable.” Hence the prophet: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8).

Some customarily object as follows: “For the Son to be begotten by the Father is nothing other than to be from the Father; this [variant: ‘but this’] belongs to the Holy Spirit also, namely to be from the Father; therefore it belongs to him to be begotten by the Father.” To this we say that although the Son and the Holy Spirit are from the Father, the Son is from the Father in one way and the Holy Spirit in another.

Augustine [Note: [Col. 1080D] Book II against Maximinus the Arian, II.1, vol. VIII.]: “The Spirit too is from the [Col. 1079D] Father, but not as born—rather, as given.” The Son too proceeds from the Father, as he himself shows in John, saying: “I proceeded from God and came” (John 8:42). The Son is from the Father by proceeding and by being born. The Spirit is from the Father not by being born, but by proceeding. Both proceed from the Father, but in an ineffable and dissimilar manner.

The Holy Spirit, therefore, is not begotten; for, although he is from the Father and the Son, if he were begotten, he would then have two fathers, and thus there would be confusion in the Trinity, in which there would be both two fathers and two sons. What begetting is and what proceeding is cannot be known in this life. Nevertheless Augustine says in Book II of *On the Trinity* concerning this [Col. 1080A] begetting (ch. 1, no. 3): “For him, to be from the Father—that is, to be born from the Father—is no different from seeing the Father; nor is seeing the Father at work something different from working equally. But who understands this?”

Ambrose, *On the Trinity*: “How the Son is begotten from the Father is impossible to know: the mind fails, speech falls silent—not only human speech but that of angels also. It is above angels, above cherubim, above every understanding. We are commanded to believe; we are not permitted to investigate. Set arguments aside where faith is sought. For it is permissible to know that the Son was born; but it is not permissible to know and investigate how he was born.”

Some, however, presuming upon their own intelligence, say that they do not fail to know these matters and others of this kind, adhering to Jerome’s authority on Ecclesiastes, where “who” is very often used in the Scriptures not for what is impossible but for what is difficult, as there: “Who shall declare his generation?” But Jerome understood this of the generation according to the flesh, which can in some measure be declared.

It is commonly asked, since the Son’s generation from the Father has neither beginning nor end because it is eternal, whether he ought to be called always begetting [the Father], or always begotten [the Son]. Gregory, on Job: “The Lord God Jesus Christ, in that he is the power and wisdom of God, was born from the Father before times; or rather, since he neither began to be born nor ceased, let us speak more truly: he is always born. But we cannot say, ‘He is always being born,’ lest he seem imperfect. [Col. 1080C] Rather, in order that he may be designated both eternal and perfect, let him be said always to have been born, so that ‘born’ may pertain to perfection and ‘always’ to eternity. Although, even in saying ‘perfect,’ we stray far from expressing that truth, because what has not been made cannot be called perfect. Yet the Lord, condescending to the words of our weakness, says: ‘Be perfect, as your Father in heaven is perfect’” (Matt. 5:48).

Likewise it is said in the Psalm: “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). He said “today” because that generation does not pass away; “I have begotten,” because it lacks a beginning.

## Chapter VI. On the equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit

To what has been said above must be added that, although the Son [Col. 1080D] is from the Father, he is nevertheless neither later nor inferior, but coeternal, co-omnipotent, consubstantial, and coequal with the Father; and the Holy Spirit is likewise with the Father and Son. Augustine, *On the Trinity* (Book II, ch. 14, nos. 6 ff.): “The Son is coeternal with the Father just as brightness is coeval with fire; it would be eternal if fire were eternal.”

It should be noted that the Son is equal to the Father according to substance, not according to the property by which he is distinguished from the Father. In that he is Son, he is one God with the Father, one nature, one substance, and equal to the Father. If, insofar as he is begotten from the Father, he is not equal, then he is unequal; but this is not true. For insofar as the Father is unbegotten and the Son begotten, neither equality [variant: “nor inequality”] is considered; the same holds for the Holy Spirit.

Augustine, *On the Trinity*: “That the Son is said relatively to the Father: the Son is not equal to the Father insofar as he is said to be Son in relation to the Father, but insofar as he is said with reference to himself, the Son is equal to the Father. Whatever is said with reference to itself is said according to substance. It follows, then, that he is equal to the Father according to substance: therefore the substance of both is the same.”

One of the three persons should not be called a part of this holy Trinity. For the whole Trinity is one simple and indivisible substance. Nor are two persons something greater than one, or three than two. Since each is the divine substance and the three are that same [Col. 1081B] substance, two or three are not something greater than one.

Augustine: “In the Trinity, which is God, the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God, and these three are one God. Nor is one a third part of this Trinity, nor are all of them something greater than the individual persons, because its greatness is spiritual, not bodily.” Again: “Because God is Trinity, he is not therefore to be thought threefold; otherwise he would be less in each than in all three.”

This too must be considered: nothing is said of the holy Trinity according to accident. For whatever is said according to accident is mutable, but in God there is nothing mutable.

Yet not everything said of God is said according to substance, because certain things are said according to relation [Col. 1081C] or property, such as Father and Son. Augustine, Book V of *On the Trinity* (ch. 4, no. 5): “An accident is not usually said to be anything except what can be lost through some change in the thing to which it occurs. But in God nothing is said according to accident, because nothing happens to him. Yet not everything said according to substance is said as subsisting, because it is said without any relational reference, or because it expresses the unity of the divine substance, such as God, omnipotent, and the like.”

And all these, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1081D] In the Conference with Maximinus the Arian, no. 11.], are said of the individual persons, and are said not plurally but singly of the three together. For as the Father is God, omnipotent, wise, just, and the like, so too are the Son God, omnipotent, and so forth, and likewise the Holy Spirit; and these three are [Col. 1081D] one God, omnipotent, one wise God, and so forth. This applies to everything said according to substance, except the name “person.”
