For although the name “person” is said according to substance, it may be predicated of the individual persons: “The Father is a person, the Son a person, the Holy Spirit a person.” Yet one cannot say: “These three are one person.” Augustine: “Person is said with reference to itself, just as God and the like. This alone is the name which, though said of each individually and with reference to itself, is received in the plural, not in the singular.”

In short, as Augustine says, the name “person” was devised so that, when the question was asked, “What three?” or “What three things?” one might answer with one term: “Three persons.” Augustine: “Therefore we say three persons, not so that any diversity of essence may be understood, but so that it may be possible to answer in one term when it is asked, ‘What three?’ or ‘What three things?’ The answer is: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. ‘Three persons’ was said, by which term he did not intend diversity but intended distinctness, so that not only unity but Trinity might be understood there. For in unity there is no diversity, since such as the Father is, such is the Son; but there is distinction. Nor is he singular, when one says, ‘God is,’ for then there would no longer be a person.”

Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Law*: “He is one indeed, but not singular; in the mystery he has another outside himself, one who is with the other.” Ambrose, *On the Faith* addressed to Emperor Gratian: “What is of one substance cannot be separated, even if it is not of singularity [Col. 1082B] but of unity.” Singularity pertains to person; unity to nature.

Here a considerable question arises: since, according to Augustine’s testimony, the name “person” is said according to substance, and since this is the definition of person—“a person is an individual nature of rational substance”—how are we to understand “The Son is another person than the Father”? This may rightly be said: “The Father is a person,” that is, a rational substance. But when it is said, “He is another person,” we do not dare to say, “He is another rational substance.” Likewise, when we say, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons,” can we not say, “three rational substances”?

It may be answered: when it is said simply, “The Father is [Col. 1082C] a person,” or “The Son is a person,” this means “a rational substance.” But by addition its signification is restricted: “The Son is another person,” that is, distinct through another property; “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons,” that is, distinct through three properties. For just as, when it is said, “The Son is God,” he is not distinguished from the Father, but when “The Son is God from God” is added, distinction then arises; so, when it is said, “The Father is a person; the Son is a person,” distinction has not yet arisen. But when “another person” is added, or, in the plural, “there are three persons,” distinction is indicated. If anyone can solve this question more suitably, however, I prejudge no one.

Moreover, there is one name, namely “Trinity,” which is not said individually of any person but of all together. It is not substantial, but signifies the plurality of persons. Thus some names in the holy Trinity are said individually and not commonly—for example Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, which refer to property—while others are said jointly and not individually—for example God, omnipotent, and the like [supplying: “which refer to nature”].

## Chapter VII. On the distinction of the persons of the most holy Trinity by particular determinations

After what has been said, this must be considered: the names pertaining to the unity of the divine substance are also used, with qualifications—indeed, even without a qualification—in distinguishing the persons [Col. 1083A]. Thus wisdom and goodness refer to substance, because the three persons are one wisdom and one goodness. Yet when “the wisdom of the Father” is said, it refers only to the Son; and when “the goodness of the Father and Son” is said, it refers to the Holy Spirit; similarly with charity.

For the whole Trinity is one spirit and one charity. But when “Holy Spirit” is added, or when “charity of the Father and Son” is said, it refers only to the Holy Spirit. For the Father is spirit and the Father is holy, but he is not the Holy Spirit. These names too often signify persons without appended determinations: through “wisdom” the Son is understood, as is very frequently found in Solomon’s Proverbs; through “goodness,” the Holy Spirit.

Jerome also often used this name in signifying the persons, saying: “In the psalm of confession [Note: [Col. 1083D] That is, in the penitential Psalm 50, namely *Miserere*.] David asks for three spirits, saying: ‘Confirm me with a ruling spirit; renew a right spirit within my inward parts; do not take your Holy Spirit from me.’ Who are these three spirits? The ruling Spirit is the Father; the right one is Christ; the holy one is the Holy Spirit.” Thus Jerome says three spirits, that is, three persons.

Augustine likewise, Book I of *On Christian Doctrine* (ch. 4, nos. 4–5), spoke of three things, having regard to the plurality of persons. For he says: [Note: [Col. 1083D] From this it seems possible to conjecture that Peter Lombard took the opening of the first book of his *Sentences*. There, indeed, he asserts, almost as the foundation of his theology, that some things are to be enjoyed and others used; and in proof of his view he adopts the very words of blessed Augustine which Hildebert uses here [Col. 1084D].] “Some things are to be enjoyed; others are to be used. Those which are to be enjoyed make us happy; by those which are to be used we are helped, as we tend toward happiness, if we wish to return to our homeland. [Col. 1083C] We are to use, not enjoy, the latter; for to enjoy is to cleave to something for its own sake. The things to be enjoyed, therefore, are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and this same Trinity is one certain thing, common to all who enjoy it.”

It is therefore evident that the same names are sometimes used to signify unity of substance and sometimes plurality of persons. Similarly, the names power, wisdom, and goodness are names of substance and belong equally to each person. Yet in Sacred Scripture the Father is very often understood through power, the Son through wisdom, and the Holy Spirit through goodness. It is not useless either to ask or to answer one who asks why this occurs.

Since the names Father, Son, and Spirit have been transferred from creatures to the Creator himself, lest they seem to signify in God what they signify in us, power is attributed to the Father and wisdom to the Son. For among human beings the father is earlier than the son and the son later; in the father, diminution may be marked by age, and in the son, imperfection of understanding by lesser age. Therefore power is attributed to the Father, lest he seem earlier than the Son and nevertheless less powerful; [Col. 1084A] and wisdom to the Son, lest he seem later and less wise than, or inferior to, the Father.

Nor is the Son called wisdom as though he alone were wise, since the whole Trinity is one wisdom; nor the Father power as though he alone were powerful, since the whole Trinity is one omnipotence. But this should especially be said where doubt might have been greater. Hence the Creed says: “I believe in God the Father almighty.” Spirit also commonly signifies rigor and is usually taken to denote cruelty [Note: [Col. 1084D] Rather, it signifies love and is not usually taken to denote cruelty; therefore, etc. This is plainly a scribal error.]; and therefore he is more frequently called goodness and kindness.

Here a most difficult question arises. If three persons are said to exist in God because he is wise, powerful, and kind, why not rather four or five, or far more, since he is strong, just, merciful, [Col. 1084B] devout, and so forth? It may be answered that whatever is truly said and believed of God is referred to these three. If he is called strong, incorruptible, immutable, and the like, all this belongs to power. If provident, watchful, intelligent, all belongs to wisdom. If devout, gentle, merciful, this belongs to goodness. In these three is supreme perfection. For wherever these three occur—to be able, to know, and to will, which is kindness—nothing is lacking. If any one of them is removed, there is no supreme perfection. The Trinity, therefore, is perfect: it can neither be diminished nor increased.

Signs of this holy and indivisible Trinity also appear in creatures. The sign of power is the immensity of things; of wisdom, their beauty; of goodness, their usefulness. Through these outward things, invisible realities are known by the rational creature.

[Col. 1084C] Just as the substantial names of which we spoke before are said of the individual persons, so likewise are those names that belong to God temporally in relation to creation, such as God, creator, merciful. For, as Augustine says in *On the Trinity* (Book V, ch. 6, no. 17), he was not Lord before there was a servant. Thus he began temporally to be Lord when the creature began in time to serve him [Note: [Col. 1084D] “God … is therefore the true Lord: he does not need a servant, whereas the servant needs him.” Augustine, Letter 138, to Marcellinus, no. 6.].

Likewise, God began in time to be Creator when he made the creature; for he did not create creatures from eternity, nor are they coeternal with the Creator. And although the Father is God the Creator, and likewise the Son and Holy Spirit, there are not three Lords but one, nor [are there] three creators but one.

Augustine shows through the analogy of a thing which begins to be called a price without changing itself that certain things are said of God temporally without any diminution in him. In Book IV of *On the Trinity*: “When a coin is called a price, it is called so relatively; yet it has not changed when it began to be a price, nor when it is called a pledge, or anything similar.” Therefore, if a coin can be called a price relatively without changing itself, [Col. 1085A] how much more should this be understood of the immutable substance of God: although he begins to be called something temporally, nothing has thereby happened to, or is to be understood as having happened to, God’s substance, but only to the creature in relation to which he is so called.

It is evident, then, that what begins to be said temporally, having not been said before, is said relatively—not according to an accident that has happened to God, but according to the accident of that thing in relation to which he is called so. Thus God is Creator and Lord in time; yet it is true that he is Lord of all from eternity and Creator from eternity, but Lord from eternity, not Creator from eternity.

## Chapter VIII. Whether the properties of the persons are the persons themselves

After the foregoing, it seems necessary to inquire whether those properties [Col. 1085B] by which the persons are distinguished are the persons themselves. That the persons are distinguished by properties is found in the saying, “In essence there is unity; in persons, property,” and in many other authorities.

Some wished to say that those properties were not the persons themselves, objecting thus: if the persons are distinguished by them, how are they the persons themselves? Authority and reason refute them. For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1085D] This occurs everywhere, and frequently, in *On the Trinity*.]: “Whatever is in God is God.” Therefore the property of the Father is God. Just as the Father is God, so the Father’s property is God, because the property of the Father is the Father himself. Nevertheless, one does not say simply, “Property is God,” or “Property is Father,” but “the property of the Father.” Just as one does not say absolutely, “Will is God,” but “the will of God is God.”

For what are the property of the Father, the property of the Son, and the property of the Holy Spirit, except the persons themselves, mutually distinct and differentiated? Jerome, in the letter *On the Explanation of the Faith* to Pope Damasus: “In confuting Arius, we say that the Trinity is one and the same substance. In identifying the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons by their properties.” Again: “For we confess not merely names, but also the properties of the names—that is, persons, or, as the Greeks express it, hypostases.”

Thus Jerome calls the properties persons. Isidore says: “God is called simple either because he does not lose what he has, or because he is not one thing and that which is in him another.” Reason too may answer the objection as follows: if there are three properties or relations in God which are not [Col. 1085D] the divine substance itself, then the divine essence—which is the Trinity—would not have been the divine essence alone from eternity. But the Trinity alone is what exists from eternity, and it is also one God.

Let us therefore confess that the three persons, or the three properties of those persons, are one God, one substance; and that those three persons are properties. Although they are far beyond our senses and human reason, nevertheless they must be believed without doubt. For as blessed Gregory says: “Faith has no merit where human reason supplies proof.” For faith is not contrary to reason but above reason. Therefore, one who is unwilling to believe anything except what he comprehends by reason, as philosophers do, has no merit in his faith; but merit belongs to one who believes what is not contrary to reason and yet is above reason. Hence the Apostle: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart; that is, the word of faith” (Rom. 10:8). It is therefore not contrary to reason, but above it.

What was assigned above as the Father’s proper characteristic is to be unbegotten; and this is to be Father. Nor should Augustine’s statement trouble us:

> [Col. 1085D] *Epistle* 238, to Pascentius. “To say ‘unbegotten’ is not the same [read: the same thing] as to say ‘Father,’ since ‘Father’ is said in relation to the Son, whereas ‘unbegotten’ indicates no relation.”

Thus, to say that the Father is unbegotten is not the same as to say that He is Father; yet, in the holy Trinity, to be unbegotten and to be Father are the same thing, just as [Col. 1086B] to be the Father’s Wisdom, to be His Son, and to be the Father’s Word are the same thing. Nevertheless, the name “Son” signifies a relation, whereas “Word” and “Wisdom” do not.

Augustine, in *On the Trinity*: “To say ‘unbegotten’ is not the same as to say ‘Father’; for, even if He had not begotten a Son, nothing would prevent His being called unbegotten. For no one is a father because he is unbegotten, nor unbegotten because he is a father. Therefore ‘unbegotten’ is not said in relation to something else, but in relation to itself; whereas ‘begotten’ cannot be said except in relation to something else. Indeed, He is Son because He is begotten, and, because He is Son, He is certainly begotten. As Son is related to Father, so begotten is related to begetter. As Father is related to Son, so begetter is related to begotten.”

At this point it must be noted that, since the Son is [Col. 1086C] Wisdom begotten from the Father, and the Father is wise by His own Wisdom, the question arises whether the Father is wise by Wisdom begotten from Himself. Augustine says that this must not be granted. For if He were wise by Wisdom begotten from Himself, then, since for Him to be is to be wise, the Father would already have being from the Son, rather than the Son from the Father. Therefore the Father is not wise by wisdom begotten from Himself, but by the unbegotten Wisdom which He Himself is. For the Father is unbegotten Wisdom.

If it is objected: “Since the Father is wise either by begotten Wisdom or by another wisdom,” this is not true, because the whole Trinity is one Wisdom—

> [Col. 1086D] Read: “the Father is wise by begotten Wisdom, or by another wisdom,” which is not true, because there is one Wisdom, etc.

—in the Father unbegotten, in the Son begotten; as it is said: “The Son is God from God, light from light, source from source.” The Father is not God from God; therefore He is other. He is not [Col. 1086D] source from source; therefore He is other. This is not true, because He is one God with the Son and one source of all creatures. For the Father is the source of the Son, because the Son is from God; and the Father and the Son are the source of the Holy Spirit. Yet the whole Trinity is one source of creatures.

Likewise, although the Father is not wise by Wisdom begotten from Himself, He is not wise by another wisdom. Augustine, in *On the Trinity* (Book VII, chapter 2, section 3): “If the Son alone understands for Himself, the Father, and the Holy Spirit, it follows that the Father is not wise from Himself, [Col. 1087A] but from the Son; nor did Wisdom beget Wisdom, if the Father is said to be wise by that Wisdom which He begot. For where there is no understanding, wisdom cannot exist either. Accordingly, if the Father does not Himself understand for Himself, and the Son understands for the Father, then surely the Son makes the Father wise. And if, for God, to be is to be wise, and if His essence is that Wisdom, then the Son does not have essence from the Father—which is true—but rather the Father has essence from the Son—which is false. Therefore God the Father is wise by that Wisdom which He Himself is, His own Wisdom; and the Son is the Father’s Wisdom.”

Some commonly raise the following question: God the Father begot God the Son, and thus God begot God. This may certainly be granted; for it is read concerning the Son: “God from God, light from light.” If God begot [Col. 1087B] God, He begot either Himself or another; neither of these should be granted. That He did not beget another God is manifest, because there is only one God. Augustine shows in *On the Trinity* that it must not be granted that God begot Himself, saying: “Whoever thinks that it belongs to divine power for God to beget Himself errs all the more, because this is not so not only of God but of no spiritual or bodily creature: for there is absolutely no thing which begets itself.” Therefore one ought not to say, “God begot Himself”; for the divine substance did not beget itself, nor another divine substance, but the person of the Father begot the person of the Son.

Moreover, it must be known that, just as the Trinity is inseparable, so it acts inseparably: whatever the Father does, the Son and the Holy Spirit do likewise. [Col. 1087C] An objection is made: Only the Son assumed flesh; but this is an operation. Therefore the Son does something which the Father and the Holy Spirit do not do. The answer is that, although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit act inseparably, something nevertheless belongs to one which does not belong to another. The saints illustrate this by an analogy.

For in a ray of sunlight brightness and heat are inseparably joined. Brightness illuminates; heat dries. Heat does not illuminate, nor does brightness dry. Likewise, in the holy Trinity the whole Trinity effected the Son’s Incarnation: the whole Trinity effected both that that man should exist and that He should be united to the Word, but not that He should be united to the whole Trinity. Therefore that operation belongs no more to the Son than to the Father; but the union belongs to the Son, not to the Father. [Col. 1087D] So too the voice from the cloud was heard from the Father alone: “This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5). For if it were the voice of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, “This is my Son,” etc., would be false. The Son is not His own Son, nor is He the Son of the Holy Spirit. Yet the whole Trinity effected that voice; but it belongs to the Father alone, because the Father alone was signified by that voice. Likewise the Holy Spirit alone appeared in the dove, although the whole Trinity effected it; but the Holy Spirit alone appeared in it, because the Holy Spirit alone is signified by it.

It is commonly asked whether the Spirit was present in that dove otherwise than in other creatures. Not otherwise with respect to the presence [Col. 1088A] or essence of the Godhead—as we have already said, since He is equally present to all creatures—but otherwise with respect to signification.

## CHAPTER IX. On Foreknowledge and Predestination

Since the Trinity’s foreknowledge, ordering, and will precede the act of everything it does, there arises here an inquiry concerning God’s foreknowledge, providence, predestination, will, and power. It must be known that God’s wisdom, because of its diverse effects, is called by several names: knowledge, providence, predestination, and ordering. Knowledge concerns things existing; foreknowledge, things future; providence, things to be governed; ordering, things to be done; predestination, those to be saved.

[Col. 1088B] It is commonly asked concerning foreknowledge whether it is the cause of things, or whether things are the cause of foreknowledge. But, as Boethius shows in *The Consolation of Philosophy*, neither is to be granted. For if things exist because they are foreknown by God, then, since evils too are foreknown, foreknowledge would be the cause of evils, which is wholly irrational. Again, if things are foreknown by God because they are to be, then what is temporal would be the cause of what is eternal.

Origen, however, says in his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans: “A thing will not occur because God knows that it will occur; rather, because it is going to occur, it is known [1033] by God before it happens.” This may be explained thus: “Because it is going to occur,” that is, “that which is going to occur,” so that no cause is indicated there. For Isaiah foretold that the Jews’ blindness would come, saying: [Col. 1088C] “God gave them eyes that they might not see,” etc. (Isa. 6:10); yet it did not occur because he foretold it, but he foretold what would occur. Thus God eternally foreknew that blindness; yet it did not occur because He foreknew it, but He foreknew it because it would occur—He from whom nothing can be hidden.

Foreknowledge, however, is improperly spoken of in God. With Him nothing is future and nothing past. In Him there is neither earlier nor later; but in relation to things future for us, we say that He foreknows the future, although, in relation to Him, this is to know them as present. Authority says that His knowledge can neither increase nor diminish. One who knows all things cannot know more, nor can one who cannot [Col. 1088D] forget know less.

An objection is raised from Jerome’s statement on Habakkuk: “It is absurd to reduce God’s majesty to this: that He should know, moment by moment, how many gnats are born or die, what is the number of fleas and flies, how many fish are born [read: *natent*, “swim”] in the waters, and similar matters. We are not such clever—or false—flatterers of God [read: *faceti*, “clever,” or *falsi*, “false”] as, while we drag down God’s power to the lowest things, to insult ourselves by saying that rational and irrational beings are subject to the same providence.”

Some explain this thus: “It is absurd to reduce God’s majesty,” etc. He does indeed know, since nothing can be hidden from Him, but not moment by moment as we do, for we cannot know all things simultaneously. Others explain it thus: “It is absurd,” etc., that He should know about gnats and such things in the sense that He should have concern for them. For, as the Apostle says, “God does not care for oxen” (1 Cor. 9:9). God has concern for human beings because He appoints angels for their protection; hence: “Their angels always see the face of the Father” (Matt. 18:10).

A further dissimilar objection may be made here [read: *non dissimilis*, “not dissimilar”]. There is someone who will never read, though it could be that he reads. It is asked whether God knows that this man will read or does not know it. We cannot say that He knows him to be going to read, because it is false that he is going to read. Augustine, in *To Renatus*: “What of foreknowledge itself, which is altogether thought to be foreknowledge? If something is foreknown and will not occur, how can that which is not future correctly be said to be foreknown?”

> [Col. 1089D] Something similar in *City of God*, Book V, chapter 10, section 2.

If we say, “He does not know that he will read,” the objection is made: It could be that he reads; and if [Col. 1089B] this occurred, it would certainly be known by God, and this could occur. Therefore it could be known by God; therefore He can know more than He knows—which is altogether false.

We leave the solution of this question to the judgment of others. Yet it seems to me that neither alternative should be granted. If anyone asks, “Does He know that this man will read?” I shall not say, “He knows that he will read,” or “He does not know that he will read,” or “He knows that he will not read.” For He never does not know this, nor does He not know that, since nothing is hidden from Him.

It must be said that this is the difference between foreknowledge and predestination: foreknowledge concerns both those to be saved and those to be damned; predestination concerns only those to be saved. Of the predestined, none can be damned; of the reprobate, none can be saved. The reprobate are foreknown for death; the predestined are foreseen for life.

Augustine, in [Col. 1089C] *On Rebuke and Grace* (chapter 13, section 39): In Revelation it is said, “Hold fast what you have, lest another take your crown” (Rev. 3:11). For if another cannot receive it unless this man loses it, the number of the elect is fixed—that is, the predestined number of the elect—and can neither increase nor decrease.

It is objected that it could decrease, because all could be damned. For everyone who is saved is saved by grace, and what is given freely can fail to be given. Likewise it is argued that it could increase, because all could be saved; for unless they could be saved, they could not be blamed for being damned. But it is true that the number of the predestined cannot increase because it cannot occur that someone should be saved who is not predestined; and it cannot decrease because it cannot occur that someone should be predestined and damned.

For it is true in itself that “this man can be damned,” because it is true that he could fail to be predestined. But “this predestined man can be damned” is not true, because both cannot occur: that he be predestined and that he be damned. Likewise, “this man can be saved” is true; but “this reprobate man can be saved” is not true, because it cannot occur that he be reprobate and be saved.

The following objection concerning foreknowledge is commonly made: God foreknew that this man would read, or something of that kind; but [Col. 1090A] it can occur that he does not read. Therefore what God foreknew can fail to be; consequently God’s foreknowledge can be mistaken. But, as we say of some future thing, if it is future—namely, if this man is going to read—it cannot fail to be. For it cannot occur that it be future and yet not happen; and yet what is future can fail to happen, because it is future in such a way that it could fail to be future.

Likewise, if something is foreknown, it cannot fail to happen, because it cannot occur that it be foreknown and not happen; and yet what is foreknown can fail to happen. This is true because it could fail to be foreknown. Nor does it follow: “Therefore God’s foreknowledge can be mistaken,” since it would then be mistaken if both were the case: namely, that what is foreknown should happen and yet should not happen.

[Col. 1090B] Since predestination is divine election, according to the Apostle’s words, “Whom He chose before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1:4), it is commonly asked why God chose this person rather than that one, as in the case of Jacob and Esau. Some say: He chose this man because He foreknew that he would be the sort of person who would believe in Him and serve Him. But Augustine retracts this in the *Retractations* (Book I, chapter 32, section 2), clearly showing that if one were chosen on account of future works, election would no longer be by grace. For if it is by works, as the Apostle says, it is no longer by grace.

The same author, in *On Predestination*: “He chose us not because He foreknew that we would be such persons in the future, but in order that we might become such through that election of His grace, by which He made us gracious in His beloved Son.” Therefore, when He predestined us, He foreknew [Col. 1090C] His own work.

> [Col. 1089D] Augustine likewise affirms this in *On Free Will*, Book III, chapter 24, section 9.

Yet Augustine himself, commenting on the prophet Malachi’s passage, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1:3), says: “He has mercy on whom He wills, and hardens whom He wills” (Rom. 9:18).

> [Col. 1090D] And this in the same place, *On Free Will*.

But this will of God cannot be unjust, for it arises from hidden merits. Although sinners have become one mass through the universal sin, there is nevertheless some difference among them. Therefore something precedes in sinners by which, though they are not yet justified, they are made worthy of justification; and something likewise precedes in other sinners by which they are worthy of dullness [read: hardening]. But what he meant we do not know, unless perhaps we say that he meant what we said above: namely, that [Col. 1090D] blessed Augustine retracted it.

## CHAPTER X. On the Will of God

It remains now to consider the will of God. God’s will is the first cause of all things, and therefore is unchangeable. Other causes are changeable because they are not first, and therefore often fail; but this will, because it has no cause before it, can neither fail nor change. And because God’s will is the first cause of all things, when it is said, “This is so because God willed it,” one must not ask why God willed it. For the first cause has no cause.

Although God’s will is one, and is God Himself, nevertheless, because of diverse effects, His wills are spoken of in the plural. Hence the Prophet: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all His wills” (Ps. 110:2). As the same Prophet, on account of the effects of mercy and justice, speaks in the plural: [Col. 1091A] “I shall sing forever of the mercies of the Lord” (Ps. 88:2); and elsewhere, “The just judgments of the Lord are right, rejoicing hearts” (Ps. 18:9). Yet, in respect of God Himself, there is one mercy and one justice, which are what He Himself is; so it is also with the will.

For in sacred Scripture the will of God is sometimes understood as that which is identical with God and coeternal with Him; and this will is always fulfilled. Of this the Apostle says: “Who resists His will?” (Rom. 9:19). And elsewhere: “That we may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” [Col. 1091B] (Rom. 12:2). This will may be called God’s good pleasure or His ordering. Hence the Prophet: “Whatever He willed, He did” (Ps. 113:3), that is, whatever He determined that He would do.

At other times command or prohibition is called the will of God because they are signs of God’s will, just as signs of anger are called anger, and signs of love, love. God is said to be angry, although there is no anger in Him; but only the outward sign by which God is shown to be angry is called anger, as in the drowning of the Egyptians. So command or prohibition, because they show us what God wills, are called the will of God. Of this the Lord says in the Gospel: “May Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth” (Matt. 6:19). And elsewhere: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven [Col. 1091C] is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. 7:20). Many things are done contrary to this will. Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter* (chapter 33, section 58): “Unbelievers indeed do many things contrary to God’s will when they do not believe His Gospel.”

Just as command and prohibition are signs of the divine will, so too are action and permission; and therefore they are often called the will [of God] in sacred Scripture. Hence the Apostle’s saying: “He wills all to be saved” (1 Tim. 2:4), that is, He causes us to will. See how that which He works in us is called God’s will. Likewise promise is also called God’s will; hence again the Apostle’s saying: “He hardens whom He wills” (Rom. 9:18).

And Augustine in the *Enchiridion*: “Nothing occurs unless the Omnipotent wills it to occur, either by permitting it to occur or by doing it Himself.” [Col. 1091D] Nor should it be doubted that God does well even when permitting things which are manifestly done badly. For these occur only by a just judgment; and certainly everything just is good.

Thus we have four signs of the divine will: command, prohibition, action, and permission, while God’s will is one and unchangeable. Therefore one must carefully observe where Scripture speaks of God’s good pleasure itself, and where it speaks of a sign of good pleasure.

When it is found that “God wills good” and “does not will evil,” this is understood of God’s good pleasure. He wills good—that is, He approves it and judges it to accord with Himself. He does not will evil: He does not approve it or judge it to be like Himself [read: “and similar expressions”]. [Col. 1092A] Although He does not will evils, He nevertheless wills evils to exist.

To understand this, some things are good in themselves and for another end; some are good for another end but not in themselves; some also are good in themselves but not for another end. Things good in themselves and for another end God wills—that is, He both wills and approves their existence—because they are good for another end. So too He wills things good in themselves but not for another end, such as goods which can occur but do not occur: He wills every good, that is, He approves it; yet He does not will them to exist, that is, He does not approve their existence, because they are not good for another end.

Evils which occur, evil in themselves but good for another end, God does not will—that is, He does not approve them—yet He wills them to exist. For unless He willed evils to exist, they could in no way exist. If He willed them not to exist and could not bring that about, He would be powerless, as [Col. 1092B] we are, who sometimes cannot do what we will. Therefore evils could not exist unless He willed them to exist; for, if He were unwilling, how could anything occur, when Scripture says: “Who resists His will?” (Rom. 9:19).

Therefore, since God eternally foresaw in His wisdom all things, both good and evil, among them all He saw some which, if they existed, would be good in themselves and also for another end; and these He not only willed but also willed to exist. He saw others which, if they existed, though good in themselves, would not be good for another end; and therefore, though He approves them—for He wills nothing to exist without cause—He did not will them to exist. Likewise, when He saw other things evil in themselves but good for another end, He willed them to exist. For which is better to exist: things good only in themselves, or things which, though not good in themselves, are nevertheless [Col. 1092C] good for another end? Surely those good for another end. Yet we shall not grant, “If He wills them to exist, then He wills them”; nor, “If they are good for another end, then they are good.”

Therefore, when someone sins, he acts contrary to God’s will, because he acts against God’s command and because God does not will what he does; yet he does what God wills to exist. For example, the Jews then did God’s will in killing Christ, and yet God willed that evil to exist because it was good for another end.

Some commonly object: God the Father willed Christ to suffer and die; therefore He willed the Jews to scourge and kill Him, and thus they did what God willed. This must not be granted, because, since their act was evil, it did not please God, who wills no evil, although it pleased God that that act should exist. For these words are commonly understood thus: “This man does what God wills,” that is, what he does God rewards and accepts gratefully. It is therefore clear that God wills evil to exist, yet does not will evil; nor does He will anyone to do evil, since He does not reward this but rather punishes it. But He wills good to exist and men to do it, because He accepts and rewards it. This is what Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*: God’s will is always fulfilled, either concerning us, by us, or in us concerning us; [Col. 1092D] yet we do not fulfill it when we sin. It is fulfilled by us when we do good, for we do it because we know that it pleases God.

> [Col. 1091] All this is taken word for word from chapter 100, section 26, of the *Enchiridion*.

“These are the great works of God, sought out according to all His wills, [Col. 1093A] and so wisely sought out that, when angelic and human creatures had sinned—that is, when they had done what they themselves willed, not what He willed—even through the very will of the creature, by which what the Creator did not will was done, what He did will should be fulfilled: He making good use even of evils, as though they were supreme goods, for the damnation of those whom He justly predestined to punishment and for the salvation of those whom He mercifully predestined to grace.

“For, insofar as they themselves are concerned, they did what God willed. But insofar as God’s omnipotence is concerned, they in no way willed to bring this about. For by the very fact that they acted against His will, His will was done concerning them. Therefore the works of the Lord are sought out according to all His wills (Ps. 110:2): so that, in a wonderful and ineffable way, [Col. 1093B] even what is contrary to His will does not occur apart from His will. For it would not occur unless He permitted it; and He permits it not unwillingly but willingly. Nor, being good, would He permit evil to be done unless, being omnipotent, He could make good even from evil.”

Many carry out God’s will while striving to alter it, and, while resisting His counsel, serve it, because that which results from human effort serves His ordering.

An objection may be made thus: It is good that evil should exist; but God is the author of every good; therefore He causes evil to exist. This must not be granted, because evils are not made with Him as their author. But it may be said that He causes evil to exist as something good; for He Himself works evil toward good.

The following objection is commonly made about command and prohibition. [Col. 1093C] God commands what He does not will to exist, because good things are commanded to many persons who do not do them. Thus He very often commanded the Jews what they did not do; yet it was not God’s good pleasure that they should do those things, or that those things should exist, because, as we have already said, whatever God wills to exist, since He can do all things, is wholly done; otherwise He would be powerless if He willed something to exist and it did not exist.

Likewise, He forbids someone to do evil—often to those same Jews—and, when he does it, God wills that it should exist, because nothing can exist unless God wills it to exist. Hence it appears that He commands someone what He wills to exist, and forbids what He wills to exist [read: what He wills not to exist]. But if He wills it to exist, why does He forbid it? And if He does not will it to exist, why does He command it?

The answer may be that He commands it because it is good [Col. 1093D] in itself, and it belongs to a lord to command his servant what is good in itself and good for the one whom he commands. If it pleases Him to help the servant to do it, this is mercy; if it does not please Him to help, it is justice. Likewise He forbids evil to His servant because it is evil in itself and evil for the person forbidden; and it belongs to a lord to forbid his servant evil, so that he may have no excuse on that account.

Here too it must be considered that, although what is commanded is good for this person, it is not necessarily good [for] the whole; and what is forbidden him, though evil for him, is good for the whole. The good of the whole is greater than that of a part; and the evil of one part is less than the evil of the whole. [Col. 1094A] Therefore, what is good for one person but not for the whole, God does not will to exist; and what is evil for one but good for the whole, He wills to exist, lest the good of the whole be impeded. For He does nothing or permits nothing which is not good for the whole, although God’s judgments are hidden from us; as it is said in Job: “Not even a leaf falls from a tree without cause” (Job 5:6).

## CHAPTER XI. On God’s Omnipotence

We must now speak of God’s power. Many authorities say that God can do all things. Augustine, in *Questions on the Old and New Law*:

> [Col. 1093D] In the Appendix to volume III, part II.

“God can indeed do all things, but He does nothing except what accords with His truth and justice.” In the same work: “God could have made all things at once, but reason forbade it. Therefore it must be confessed that God can do all things.”

But Augustine says in *On the Spirit and the Letter*: God is not called omnipotent because He can do everything, but because He can accomplish whatever He wills, so that nothing can resist His will so as to prevent its fulfillment or impede it in any way. The answer may be that Augustine, when he says that God is not called omnipotent because He can do all things, takes “all things” in an excessively broad sense, so as to include evils, which God neither wills nor can do.

The same author, in *On the Creed*: “God Almighty cannot die, cannot be deceived, cannot become miserable, cannot be conquered. Therefore, that He cannot do these and similar things not only shows that He is omnipotent, [Col. 1094C] but truth also compels us to confess that one who could do this would not be omnipotent.” Thus it is clear that He is omnipotent because He can do everything He wills. Absolutely speaking, it may also be said that He can do all things; nevertheless He cannot sin, because this is not one of the “all things.” But if human actions, such as walking and so forth, are objected, it may be said that they belong to His power, although He cannot possess them in Himself. For He cannot walk, yet He can bring it about that walking occurs.

I think we should consider whether God can do more things than He wills to do or does do. Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*: “The will of the Omnipotent can do many things which it neither wills nor does.” For He could have caused twelve legions of angels to fight against those [Col. 1094D] who seized Him. In Matthew’s Gospel: “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and He will at once provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. 26:53). In the same work: “Then, in the clearest light of wisdom, what the faith of the godly now holds will be seen: how unchangeable and effective God’s will is; how many things it can do and does not will; yet that it wills nothing which it cannot do.” These authorities show that God can do many things which He does not will.

This can also be proved by reason. God does not will to justify all, yet who doubts that He can? Augustine, in *On Nature and Grace*: “The Lord raised Lazarus in body; must it be said that He could not [Col. 1095A] raise Judas in mind? He could indeed, but He did not will it.”

The saying of Augustine in *On the Creed* is objected against our saying that God can do some things which He does not will to do: “God can do only what He wills,” and so it seems that He cannot do something which He does not will. But the saying must be explained thus: “He can do only what He wills,” that is, He can do nothing unwillingly. For it cannot occur that He should do anything unwillingly, since He cannot be compelled.

Again it is objected: Whatever God can do, He can will. But He can do something which He does not will; therefore He can will what He does not will. And if He can will what He does not will, His will is changeable and not eternal, but begins to will something which it did not previously will.

Augustine, addressing God in the *Confessions* (Book VII, chapter 4), says: “You are not compelled unwillingly to anything, because Your will is not greater than Your power. Yet it would be greater if You were greater than Yourself.” Hence it seems that God cannot do something which He wills to do. The answer may be that “God’s will” is understood in many ways, as was indicated above: sometimes for the effect of the divine will, sometimes for that which is in God and is God Himself. Therefore, when Augustine says, “God can do many things which He does not will,” he has regard to the effect—that is, He can do what He does not effect. He does not refrain through inability. In this sense it may be said: “God can will what He does not will.”

But if we speak of God’s very will, which is what He Himself is, He can do nothing except what [Col. 1095C] He wills, and can will nothing except what He wills. For to will is the same as to be, and to will is also the same as to be able; therefore Augustine says, “Will is not greater than power.” In this or another suitable way the foregoing contradiction can be resolved.

It must not be omitted here that some, puffed up by knowledge, say that God cannot do anything other than what He does, or omit anything among the things which He does. They try to establish this as follows: Whatever God does, it is good and just to be done; for He can do only what is just and what ought to be done. Therefore God ought not to refrain from doing the things He has done; but what ought not to be cannot be. Therefore He cannot refrain from doing the things He does.

Likewise, they prove that He ought not to do anything other than what He does thus: What He does not do ought not to be done, because, if it ought to be done, He would do it. But what ought not to be done by God cannot be done by Him. Therefore He cannot do the things which He omits to do.

But, as it seems to me, every poison lies hidden beneath the word “ought.” For if we say, “God ought not to do those things,” it follows, “Therefore He cannot do them”; if we say, “He ought to do them,” then, “Therefore He cannot refrain from doing them.” But neither proposition should be granted concerning God. For, as Augustine says, there was another manner [Col. 1096A] possible to God, but none more suitable for healing our misery. Yet we shall not say, “He ought to have redeemed the world in another way,” or “He ought not,” because He does nothing from obligation but solely from goodness. Human beings act from obligation, because they become better by acting, or worse if they do not act.

Some say that God cannot make the things He makes better, because, if He could, He would make them better; and if He could not, He would be envious. Augustine, in *Eighty-Three Questions*: “The God whom He begot, because He could not beget one better than Himself—for nothing is better than God—He begot equal. For if He could and would not, He would be envious.” From this they wish to say that if God could make a thing better and did not do so, He would be envious. But the analogy does not hold, because He begot the Son from His own substance.

> [Col. 1095D] This exceedingly tangled period, due to the copyist’s carelessness, might perhaps be more successfully reconstructed as follows: “The analogy does not hold, because He begot the Son from His own substance; if He could have made Him equal to Himself—as He could, and as this was essentially necessary to Him—and had not done so, [Col. 1096D] He would have been envious, especially since He could not make one better from His own substance.”

[Col. 1096B] He begot the Son from His own substance; if He could make that same Son equal to Himself and did not do so, He would be envious. But He could make other things, which He did not make from His own substance, better.

Augustine, commenting on Genesis: “God could have made a human being such that he could neither sin nor wish to sin; and if He had made such a person, who doubts that he would have been better?” We should ask in what sense they understand that a thing cannot be better. If it cannot be better because it cannot receive the greater good which it lacks, then it can be better if it is made capable of a greater good—which He who made it can do.

That expression, however, is ambiguous: “God can make better, better.” If it is explained thus, “He can make something better,” that is, “by a better wisdom,” it is false, because His [Col. 1096C] wisdom cannot be increased. But it is true in this sense: “He can make better,” that is, He can make a better thing.

## CHAPTER XII. On Faith in the Incarnation

We must now deal with that part of faith which pertains to the sacrament of the Incarnation. As the Apostle says: “God sent His Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that through sin He might condemn sin” (Rom. 8:3). By these words he partly discloses the mystery of the Incarnation. For He came into the world in order to condemn the devil and free humankind. But since the Son of God, who is everywhere, was in the world, how did He come into the world? He came because He who was invisible appeared visible.

> [Col. 1096D] That is, He who was formerly invisible appeared visibly.

[Col. 1096D] It is customary to ask why neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit assumed flesh, but the Son alone. To this one may say: it was not fitting for the Father, because it does not belong to him to be sent, since he is not from another; nor for the Holy Spirit, lest there should be one Son in humanity and another in divinity, and thus two Sons in the Trinity. Therefore the person of the Son was incarnate, so that he who was Son in divinity might be Son in humanity as well. It was also fitting that, just as the Father made the world through his Wisdom, so he should redeem it through that same Wisdom; and [Col. 1097A] because both natures in man were corrupted, namely soul and body, he assumed both in order to liberate both. Yet he did not assume a human person; for he assumed a nature, not a person.

Augustine, in the book *On Faith to Peter*: “For God the Word did not take up the person of a man, but nature. For in Christ there are two natures, divine and human, and three substances—flesh, soul, Word—but not two persons. For God is one nature and man another; yet God is not one person and that man another.” As Augustine says to Felicianus: “The Son of God is one thing, the son of man another, but not another [person].” Likewise, the Son of God is one thing from the Father, another from his mother, but not another [person].

Against the statement that he did not assume a person, the following objection is made: he assumed soul and body, [Col. 1097B] but these make one person [perhaps: “a single person”]; therefore 1043 he assumed a person. Some resolve it thus: those two, joined together, are one person; but before they were assumed by the Word, they were not joined together, for by assuming them he united them, and by uniting them [perhaps: “uniting”] he assumed them. Yet one may again object that the soul is an individual substance of rational nature, which is the definition of a person; therefore he assumed both nature and person. This would indeed follow if that soul existed before it was assumed; for a soul is a person, just as an angel is. For what is a human being except a human soul and a body? But he did not assume a person because what he assumed was not a person: he assumed the soul by creating it, and created it by assuming it.

The same objection [Col. 1097C] might be made thus: the Son of God assumed a man; but no man exists who is not a person. We readily grant this; but, as we have said, that man did not exist before he was assumed. For although the body existed beforehand, the soul did not; and thus he did not assume a man who already existed, but one whom he created by assuming him. Hence it does not seem that one should grant, “He assumed some particular man,” but simply, “He assumed man.” Yet this seems capable of being proved as follows: he assumed the man who hung on the cross, who was conceived of the Holy Spirit; therefore, some particular man. But this seems sophistical, like the following: “Last year I saw him who is bishop; therefore, I saw some particular bishop.” But whatever may be granted in a controversy of this kind, let us hold this without doubt: he did not assume a person. For, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1097D] Epistle 238, §4], “When the facts are agreed upon, no dispute should be maintained over words.”

To the foregoing question the following may again be added: if no person was assumed because that man did not exist before he was assumed by the Word, then, from the time he was assumed, that man was a person; and if the man assumed by the Word is a person, since that man is united to the Word, a person is united to the Word, and thus person is united to person. This must not be granted. For the man assumed by the Word is not another person, but is one person with the Word. For it is written: “The assumed man is assumed into a union [Col. 1098A] of person, not of nature,” because he is not one nature with the Word, but one person with it. For as soul and flesh are one human being, so God and man are one Christ, although the union between God and man is far greater than that between soul and flesh. For a greater union can exist between spiritual nature and spiritual [Note: [Col. 1098D] Thus the manuscript.] [perhaps: “spirit”] than between the spiritual and the bodily. God, however, is spiritual nature, and man is spiritual nature; hence the union between God and man is so great that man is called God, and God man. Yet the soul is not called flesh, nor flesh soul.

Likewise, concerning that person one may say: “Christ is true God, true man”; but one cannot say: “Man is flesh; man is soul; man is God.” This is explained as follows: that is, God and man united to God; thus God united [Col. 1098B] to man is man. I do not reject this explanation; nevertheless, it seems to me that those words contain more. For if the words “Man is God” say nothing other than “man is united to God,” why can one not say, “Flesh is soul,” since flesh is united to soul; or “soul is God,” since it is united to God? Therefore it is said: “Man is God; God is man; and he who is man is also God.” Hence in the Prophet: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86:5). And in John: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven” (John 3:13). For, as Gregory says: “He is temporal from his mother; he is eternal from the Father; he who made is he who was made.”

Concerning this it is customary to ask whether it should be granted that [Col. 1098C] the assumed man is God. But since Augustine says, “The assumed man is the only-begotten Son of God,” I do not see with what face this can be denied. Some, however, grant the negative statement: “The assumed man is not God,” that is, human nature is not divine; and they prove that this is their meaning by the authority of Jerome, who says: “The Word is God, not the assumed flesh.” This authority does nothing against us. For no one grants the statements, “The assumed flesh is God,” or “Human nature is God.” Although the assumed man and human nature are the same thing, they nevertheless distinguish the mode of speaking, just as God is nothing other than divinity, and yet, though one says, “Man is God,” one does not say, “Man is divinity.” For [Col. 1098D] that would be to say, “Man is the divine nature.” As Ambrose says: “Not by a changeability of nature, but by the union of person, man is God and God is man.”

## Chapter XIII. Concerning those things that pertain to Christ as dwelling among human beings

Accordingly, it must be granted without doubt that he did not, as some have said, first assume flesh and then soul; rather, the Word of God united flesh and soul to himself simultaneously. Here, however, differences of opinion are found. Certain learned men say that the flesh which he took from Mary was formed over forty days, and that once it had been formed—that is, once it possessed the features of a human being—[Col. 1099A] 1045 the Word of God simultaneously united flesh and soul to himself. They intend to establish this from Augustine’s authority in his commentary on John, where it is said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). On this passage Augustine says: “This number accords with the perfection of the Lord’s body, because, as physicians say, the form of the human body is completed in so many days.”

Others wish to say that, as soon as that flesh was set apart by the Holy Spirit, it had some differentiation of members, but so slight that it was not perceptible to the eyes; whereas during the forty days of which Augustine speaks, it became complete and recognizable. At the very moment of its being set apart, he simultaneously assumed flesh and soul. The authorities agree more with these latter. Gregory the Younger: “When the angel announces and the Spirit comes, immediately the Word is in the womb; immediately within the womb the Word is flesh.” Augustine, in the book *On the Trinity*: “He would not be the mediator of God and men unless the same one were God and man, the same in both, one and true; and the whole Trinity, whose will and operation are one, made that servant-form which the Son alone assumed. Flesh was not first conceived in the Virgin’s womb and then divinity came into the flesh; but as soon as the Word came into the womb, while the truth of his proper nature was preserved, he was made flesh and perfect man—that is, he was born in the truth of flesh and soul from that flesh to which the Word was united.”

It is asked whether [Note: [Col. 1099] Here there is a lacuna in the manuscript. Perhaps: “whether Christ’s flesh was free from sin.”] [lacuna] Augustine says that this was so; but through that very setting apart it was cleansed by the Holy Spirit, both from sin [Col. 1099C] and from the tinder of sin. He freed Mary wholly from sin, though not from the tinder of sin; yet he so weakened it that she is believed not to have sinned afterward.

Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*: “With the exception of the holy Virgin Mary, concerning whom, on account of the honor of the Lord, I wish no question at all to be raised when sins are being discussed. For from this we know that more grace was bestowed upon her for overcoming sin in every respect, because she deserved to conceive and bear him whom we know certainly had no sin. Therefore, with this Virgin excepted, if all the holy men and women could be gathered together, what would they answer except what John says: ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves’” (1 John 1:8).

But if Christ’s flesh was subject to sin in Mary and in the others from whom he descended, how will this be reconciled with the statement: “Levi was tithed in Abraham” (Heb. 7:9)? For Christ was tithed in Abraham. Augustine resolves it thus: Levi was tithed in Abraham because he descended from him through concupiscence; Christ was not tithed in him because Christ’s flesh did not descend from him through concupiscence. But did not the same flesh descend through concupiscence in David [Col. 1099D] and in Mary? Yet it was not Christ’s flesh, because that would be to say that it descended into Christ through concupiscence, which is altogether false.

Some wish to say that just as, in Adam before [Col. 1100A] sin, there was a certain clean and holy particle, so after sin it was preserved, both in Adam himself and in all his successors in a direct line down to Mary; and they say that they derive this from Gregory.

Many authorities testify that this man was full of grace and truth from his very conception, and that he possessed such wisdom as could not increase. Jeremiah: “The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man in the womb of her womb” (Jer. 32:22). What is meant by “a woman shall encompass a man,” except that he was a perfect man in wisdom from his very conception, though not in bodily size? For some held that he was as great in the womb as on the cross. For from his very conception God anointed him [Col. 1100B] with the oil of gladness above his companions.

But this seems opposed by what is said in the Gospel: “Jesus advanced in age and wisdom before God and men” (Luke 2:52). Yet one may say that, even if he did not advance in wisdom in himself, he nevertheless advanced in human beings—that is, they advanced through his wisdom and became better. Thus it is customary to say, “This man advances in his episcopate,” not because he himself at some time becomes wiser, but because he instructs others well; “before God,” that is, for God’s honor and for human advancement. Bede, on Luke: “He is rightly said to be full of wisdom, not advancing in wisdom through intervals of time, wisdom with which he was always full from the hour of conception, since ‘in him,’ as the Apostle says, ‘the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily’” (Col. 2:9).

[Col. 1100C] Some customarily ask whether Christ’s soul had, or has, wisdom [perhaps: “knowledge”] of all things. Some say that it had [perhaps: “did not have”] all knowledge, and did not know all that God knows. They wish to prove this as follows. That soul was created; but in no respect is a creature equal to the Creator; therefore it did not know what God knows. Again, if that soul has wisdom equal to God’s, it will be false that God possesses in every good a greater sufficiency than his creature. Again, the Apostle says: “The Spirit of God alone searches all the depths of God” (1 Cor. 2:10); therefore that soul cannot know all things.

To this it may be said that, although that soul, joined to the Word of God, knows whatever the Word himself knows, [Col. 1100D] it is not equal to him in knowledge, because that knowledge belongs to the Word by nature, but to that soul by grace. Again, as to their objection that God has greater sufficiency than his creature in every good: understand that this was said where a creature’s good is found to be other than the Creator’s good. But since the wisdom of that soul is nothing other than divine wisdom, how can a comparison be made there?

For it must unquestionably be said that there was no wisdom in Christ’s soul besides the divine wisdom. For if it were other than divine wisdom, it would be lesser; and if that soul’s wisdom were lesser, how could it comprehend the whole? Therefore that man would know less [Col. 1101A] than God. Accordingly, in order firmly to maintain the truth that that soul was ignorant of nothing but knew all things, one must say that it was not by another wisdom that the soul was wise, but by wisdom that is in God by nature and in that soul by grace.

Their statement, “The Spirit of God alone searches all things,” makes more against them; for the Apostle immediately adds: “But we have the Spirit of Christ” (1 Cor. 2:16). But that soul possessed the Spirit of God [perhaps: “of Christ”] above all others. Against their perversity John the Evangelist says: “The Spirit is given to others by measure, but to Christ it was not given by measure” (John 3:34). But since there are two natures in Christ, let us see to which the Spirit was given, divine or human. To the divine nature it does not belong to receive, but to give. Therefore it was given without measure to the human nature; [Col. 1101B] but where there is no measure, there is no limit. Therefore that soul knew all things. For if it knew some things and not others, it knew by measure, and its knowledge had a limit.

Fulgentius also raises many arguments against that error, maintaining by the authority of the Apostle that that soul had knowledge of all things, where he says: “In whom are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God” (Col. 2:3). It may likewise be proved by reason thus: no one knows anything which his soul does not know; but all concede that Christ knew all things; therefore his soul knew all things. Yet although they cannot answer the foregoing arguments, they still object to us: if that soul knows all things because it is joined to one who knows all things, then it ought to be called omnipotent because it is joined to the Omnipotent.

[Col. 1101C] To this it may be said that the soul is naturally capable of knowledge, and that which it is naturally capable of was bestowed upon it without measure. But since being God is identical with being omnipotent, this could not be bestowed upon a creature.

## Chapter XIV. What defects of human nature Christ assumed in assuming human nature

After the foregoing, it must be considered that, as Pope Leo says, our Lord Jesus Christ assumed every one of our infirmities except sin. To demonstrate that he had a true body, he assumed bodily defects—hunger, thirst, and the rest; to demonstrate that he had a true soul, he assumed defects of the soul, [Col. 1101D] sadness, fear, and such things.

Here it may be objected that he did not have ignorance, yet ignorance is not sin; therefore he did not assume all our infirmities. To this it may be said that, just as concupiscence is sin and yet, after the remedy of the sacrament, is not imputed unless one consents to that motion, so ignorance is sin and yet is not imputed unless it arises from negligence, concerning which the Apostle says: “Whoever is ignorant shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14:38). Invincible ignorance, however, is not imputed; nevertheless, as we maintain, it is sin. For everything that separates us from God is called sin; and through these things we are unlike God and recede from him, and therefore it is called sin.

If it is objected that he did not have repentance, repentance is not one of all our infirmities. That he had sadness and fear is established from the Gospel: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38). And elsewhere: “Jesus began to be afraid and distressed” (Mark 14:33). Augustine: “He assumed sadness as he assumed flesh. For if he did not have it, why does the Gospel say: ‘My soul is sorrowful even unto death’? Then, when the Gospel says, ‘He slept,’ did he not sleep? Therefore Jesus was sorrowful, but by will, not necessity, he assumed real sadness.” Ambrose: “He assumed my sadness; he assumed my will. I confidently name sadness, I who proclaim the cross.”

[Col. 1102B] Yet other authorities are found which seem to remove sadness and fear from the Savior. Jerome: “Lest his passion should rule his mind, he began to be sorrowful at the prospect of suffering,” and [the printed text is uncertain; perhaps: “he began to be sorrowful for another reason”]. Likewise: “Let those be ashamed who think that the Savior feared death and, from dread of the Passion, said: ‘Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me’” (Matt. 26:39). Augustine: “Prefiguring the weak in himself, he said, ‘Let this cup pass from me.’ For Christ, who was to rise on the third day, did not truly fear suffering, when Paul added: ‘I desire to depart and be with Christ’” (Phil. 1:23).

To this it must be said that there is a kind of sadness and fear which so rules the mind and subjugates reason, contrary to the Lord’s command once conceived, that it leads into sin—as Peter, through fear, denied him. It is of such fear that the authors speak when they say that Christ did not fear. But there is a moderated fear, naturally present in man and without sin, just as hunger and thirst are; and this was in Christ. For he recoiled from death.

It should be noted that there were two wills in Christ. Augustine says: “The will of the Father is not other than that of the Son”; and according to that will Christ willed to suffer and die, just as the Father willed it. But there is another will, which may be called natural appetite, [Col. 1102C] whose function is not to will death; and according to this will it was said: “Not my will, but yours be done” (Luke 22:42). And elsewhere: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 5:50). Yet in him the will of reason always prevailed, by which he willed the same as the Father. That there were two wills in Christ we have from the metropolitan synod [Note: [Col. 1101D] Namely, the Third Council of Constantinople, A.D. 680], at which Bishop Macarius was condemned for maintaining that there were not two wills in Christ.

It is also customary to ask whether he prayed for or desired anything that he did not obtain. Some wish to say that the prayer in which he prayed, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39), was not heard, because he prayed it out of weakness. Likewise, they wish to say that according to human affection he willed the salvation of all; hence [Col. 1103A] the verse: “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68:22), that is, when I desired their faith. But since he says in John, “I do not pray for those who are of the world,” it does not seem that he prayed except for those who were to be saved. For it does not seem fitting either that his prayer should not have been heard, or that he should have prayed for something which he knew would not please the Father, since he knew all things.

Some ask whether it should be granted: “Christ is a creature.” It does not seem that this should be granted without qualification. For if he is a creature, he has a beginning; but Christ is from eternity. Therefore this would follow: if he is a creature, he has a beginning; if he has a beginning, he has not always existed. Yet it may be granted with a qualification: Christ is a creature insofar as he is man, [Col. 1103B] because insofar as he is man he has a beginning. Nevertheless, one should not grant without qualification: “Christ has a beginning.”

Ambrose also proves by many arguments against Arius that Christ is not a creature or an adopted son. For though, insofar as he is man, he is not Son of God by nature, because insofar as he is man he is not of one substance with the Father, nevertheless he is not adopted. For an adopted son is one who, having previously not been a son, is afterward adopted as a son; but that man did not exist before he was the Son of God. Therefore, if I am asked, “Is Christ Son of God by nature?” I grant it, but with qualification. I grant neither that Christ, insofar as he is man, is Son of God by nature nor that he is Son by adoption, but rather by union. Hence the Apostle: “Who was predestined [Col. 1103C] Son of God in power,” etc. (Rom. 4:1). For predestination belongs to him not insofar as he is God, 1050 but insofar as he is man.

Against Ambrose’s statement, “Whatever the Son of God has by nature, the Son of Man has by grace,” the following is customarily objected: God is immeasurable, eternal, immortal; therefore that man is eternal, and so on. But that man is temporal, mortal, and passible. To this it may be said that, just as God is said to have suffered, died, and been crucified—hence the Apostle: “They crucified the God [Vulgate: ‘Lord’] of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8)—although God in his own nature cannot die or suffer, and although all these things are said of God through the union with the Word, so likewise the things that belong to God are said of that man through union with the Word. Hence in the Prophet: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86:5). And in John: “No one has ascended into heaven except the Son of Man, who descended from heaven” (John 3:13).

But it is objected: if that man is eternal, then he lacks a beginning, which is false, for he has a temporal beginning. But it does not follow that, if the man [Col. 1103D] is eternal, he lacks a beginning, because the first statement is figurative speech; just as it would not follow: “God is crucified and dies; therefore he ceases to live.” For, as Augustine says, one must see in what respect a thing is said.

It is also asked whether Christ had faith, hope, and charity. Concerning charity there is certainty: for out of charity he laid down his life for his brothers. That he had hope is established from the Psalm, where he says: “Preserve me, O Lord, for I have hoped in you” (Ps. 15:2); and in another: “In you, O Lord, I have hoped” (Ps. 30:1). The authors interpret these psalms as referring to Christ. But the Apostle says: “Hope that is seen is not hope; for what a man sees, why does he hope for?” (Rom. 8:24). Christ, however, saw all things. But the Apostle says this in accordance with what pertains to us. That Christ had faith should not be granted.

It is also asked whether he merited anything for himself. For it is certain that he merited for his members. The Apostle says that he also merited for himself: “Therefore God also exalted him” (Phil. 2:9). And in the Psalm: [Col. 1104B] “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Ps. 109:7). For he merited immortality and impassibility for his body. But since he was innocent, all this was owed to him, and thus he did not have it by merit. Yet someone may merit what is owed to him, as a son, to whom his father’s inheritance is due, merits it by serving his father.

Many say that Christ merited nothing for his soul and that nothing was added to his soul; for, as they say, it was perfectly blessed. John says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). Gregory likewise says that Christ’s soul had nothing in which it could advance. Yet it can be proved that he merited even for his soul, and that something was added to his soul after [Col. 1104C] the Passion. For before it he had fear and justice; but after the Passion he could neither grieve nor be troubled. Therefore impassibility was added to his soul, so that it could no longer suffer. Hence he merited glorification, impassibility, and so forth not only for his body but also for his soul.

But Gregory’s statement, “Christ’s soul had nothing in which it could advance,” must be understood of knowledge and love. For his knowledge and love could not increase. It should likewise be known that God is not one part of that person who is Christ, and man another. For if they were integral parts of that person [Note: [Col. 1103] The Apollinarians asserted three parts in Christ, which St. Augustine declares vain and heretical in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, ch. 24, §67], that person would have been increased by the assumed man. Augustine: “Christ is one person of twofold [Col. 1104D] substance”; yet God cannot be called a part of this person. Otherwise, before the Son of God assumed the form of God, he was not whole, and he grew when man was added to his divinity.

## Chapter XV. Whether Christ could sin

It is customary to ask whether Christ could sin. Some wish to prove this by the authority: “He could transgress, and did not transgress; do evil, and did not do it” (Ecclus. 31:10). But we do not think this is said of Christ, but of holy men. Again, they object: Christ had free choice; therefore he could be turned in either direction. But this is invalid, since angels too have free choice and yet are so confirmed by grace that they cannot sin. Much more, therefore, do we believe that that man, united to God through grace, was confirmed from his very conception.

Again, it is objected: that man could have been not united to the Word; and if he had not been united to the Word, he would have sinned like other men; therefore that man could sin. But we do not deny that he could sin—for he would have sinned if he had not been united to the Word—but after he had been united to the Word, he could not sin. And he could be damned, because damnation follows sin. But what could be more absurd than that the Son [of God], who was that man, could be damned?

Here it must be noted that there are three states of man, and that the Son of God assumed something from each. The first state [Col. 1105B] was before sin, in which man was created. The second state is that into which he fell by sin. The third state is that into which he is to be transferred after the resurrection. The first state possessed the possibility of dying, not the necessity: for he could die and could refrain from dying. The second 1052 state has the necessity of dying, for he dies necessarily. The third state [perhaps: “state”] has neither the necessity of dying, as the second does, nor the possibility of dying or sinning, as the first does.

From the first state Christ had the capacity to die and the capacity not to die; for he died by will alone. Hence he is also called by some “mortal by will, immortal by nature,” because, being without sin, which is the cause of death, he would never have died unless he willed [perhaps: “if he had not willed”]. From the second state [Col. 1105C] he had such defects as hunger, thirst, and so forth. From the third state he had the inability to sin.

One may ask: since Christ could have died a death not inflicted by others and thereby redeemed the human race, why did he choose to die such a death, in which the condemnation of many, such as Judas and others, occurred? [One may answer:] in order to draw us to love of himself. For the more grievous the death he endured for us, the more we ought to love him.

## Chapter XVI. Whether, in Christ’s death, divinity was separated from humanity

Moreover, it is customary to ask whether, in his death, divinity was separated from humanity. Some wish to say that [Col. 1105D] divinity was separated from the flesh, but not from the soul. They should not be believed, since Pope Leo says: “From the time he assumed man, he did not lay him aside.” All orthodox believers hold this: after that ineffable union, divinity was separated neither from the soul nor from the flesh. For divinity was not incarnate twice, nor did it assume flesh twice.

Therefore we say without doubt: from the time the Son of God became man, God is always man and man God. For the soul was separated from the flesh, but divinity from neither. Augustine explains the words, “I have power to lay down my life and to take it up again” (John 10:18), in this way: divinity did not lay down the soul; rather, the flesh laid down the soul in [Col. 1106A] death and took up the soul again in the resurrection.

Augustine says in the same book addressed to Felicianus [Note: [Col. 1105D] St. Augustine teaches the same in Tractate 47 on John, in Psalm 4, §2, and frequently elsewhere]: “Thus, in dying, he did not abandon his flesh in the tomb, just as in being born with it he formed it in the Virgin’s womb. Thus, without life departing, he died, as he suffered without power perishing in him. At one and the same time he was wholly in hell and wholly in heaven. Among the dead resurrection was more powerful; above the heavens was the life of the living [perhaps: ‘more vital’]. Truly dead, truly living: in him the assumption of mortality underwent death, and divinity, preserved, did not lose life.”

It is objected: if the Son of God was not separated from the man in death itself, then he did not then cease to be man; but a dead man is not a man; therefore he was not then man. How frivolous this is is evident to everyone. For one could equally say: a man is not a man because he is not a rational mortal animal, which is utterly false.
