For when they say, “A dead man is not a man,” or “is not a rational mortal animal,” they speak of man according to this state. Again, it is objected: if he was man, he was either mortal or immortal; not mortal, because he was dead; not yet immortal, because that came only after the resurrection. This we readily grant. Yet they object that he was neither mortal nor immortal on the authority of Anastasius: “Accursed be whoever does not confess that this whole man—namely, both soul and body—which he assumed, was again assumed, or liberated from the dead and raised after the third day: Amen, amen.”

[Col. 1106C] To this we say that Anastasius spoke then against those who denied his resurrection and thought that he who alone among the dead is free [perhaps: “was free”] was held in death; and therefore he said “the man again assumed,” that is, liberated from death. Again, Ambrose on Luke: “‘Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying: My God, my God, look upon me, why have you forsaken me?’” (Matt. 27:46). “The man cries, dead by the separation of divinity. For since divinity is free from death, death could not exist unless life departed, because life is divinity.” But Ambrose understood divinity to be separated from that man insofar as it exposed that man to death, as in the Psalm: “Why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 21:1), that is, “Why have you exposed me to death?”—not because he was forsaken or divinity was separated from him by abandoning him. For he seemed to be forsaken by God, or divinity seemed to depart from him, when he did not display his power.

## Chapter XVII. On the angels: when they were created

Having treated the parts of faith, it seems proper to add something concerning the first creation of things. Although Plato said that there are three principles—matter, form, and maker—Catholic faith believes that God is the one principle of all things, whose goodness was the cause of all things. For since he was eternally supremely good and perfectly blessed, he willed that others should share in his blessedness. And because his blessedness cannot be shared except through intellect, and is possessed in proportion as it is understood, [Col. 1107A] he made rational creatures, in order that they might understand, understand and love, love and possess, possess and enjoy. He distinguished them in this manner: one part remained in its own purity, namely the angels; another part was joined to a body, namely souls.

It is asked why this was done, since the soul would have been of greater dignity had it remained in its own purity. To this it may be said that, although the soul was more excellent than its body, God nevertheless willed to associate it with a body, in order to show in the human condition a new example of the eternal union between spirit and God. For it seemed that a creature could not be united with its Creator. But when a spirit, which is the more excellent creature, is united in such great love to so lowly a creature as the body that it cannot be constrained to will to leave it, it is evident that a created spirit can likewise be united to the supreme good. He caused souls to be associated with bodies, so that in them [Note: [Col. 1107D] Perhaps read: “He willed that a created spirit should in this manner be united to the supreme good, so as to possess it; and he caused souls to be associated with bodies, so that in them,” etc.] they might serve God and merit the true and supreme good.

Therefore, since rational creation is divided into angels and human beings, it seems fitting to speak first of the angels. Concerning them one must consider when they were created, where they were made, and what sort of beings they were made.

Certain authorities seem to maintain that the angels were made before every creature, as in the saying: “Wisdom was created first of all” (Ecclus. 1:4), which was spoken of the angels. This seems to accord with what is said in Genesis: “In the beginning God created heaven [Col. 1107C] and earth” (Gen. 1:1). For if these were made in the beginning, nothing was made before heaven and earth. And in the Psalm: “In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands” (Ps. 101:26).

It therefore seems that angelic and corporeal nature were created at the same time. Hence that saying of Solomon: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18:1). “All things,” that is, spiritual and corporeal nature; and thus the angels were not created earlier in time than that matter of the four elements. Yet “wisdom was created first of all,” because, though not preceding in time, it precedes in dignity.

Jerome, however, in his Epistle to Titus seems to think otherwise, saying: “Not yet are six thousand years of our time completed; and how many eternities of ages must we suppose [Col. 1107D] to have existed in which angels, thrones, and dominations served God and subsisted, at God’s command, without the changes and measures of times?” Adhering to this authority, some say that time began with the world, since there was no changeability before the world; yet they maintain that angels existed before the world [Col. 1108A] immutably and timelessly.

We, however, approve more highly the earlier opinion. What Jerome says derives from the statements of Origen; he did not state it as an assertion, but said it in doubt and inquiry: “How many eternities,” and so forth, “must be supposed to have existed before,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER XVIII. In what place the angels were created

The question is asked where the angels were made. Authorities seem to maintain that they were made in heaven. Hence in the Gospel: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). Here we do not call “heaven” the firmament, which was made on the second day, but the splendid empyrean heaven, which was immediately filled with angels: namely, that upper region as far as [Col. 1108B] the still undifferentiated structure of the elements extended.

For, as we have said, the angels and that corporeal matter were created together. Thus Augustine expounds that passage as follows [Note: [Col. 1107D] *On Genesis according to the Letter*, §7.]: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”: “heaven,” that is, the angels; “earth,” the whole corporeal structure, in whose upper part the angels were made.

But if they were in heaven, how could Lucifer say, as we read in Isaiah: “I will ascend into heaven; I will set my throne in the north; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13)? There he calls the sublimity of the Godhead “heaven.” “I will ascend into heaven,” that is, to equality with the Godhead.

## CHAPTER XIX. What the angels were like when created

It remains to say what the angels were like when made. [Col. 1108C] In their first condition three things seem to have been attributed to them: an indivisible and immaterial essence, and therefore one naturally imperishable through the reason implanted in it; spiritual intelligence; and likewise free choice, by which they could, without compulsion, incline by their own will to either alternative.

Some customarily ask whether they were created good or evil, just or unjust, free or miserable. [Note: [Col. 1107D] Hildebert seems at this point to have departed from St Augustine, to whom he adheres so firmly in all other respects. For St Augustine, *City of God*, XII.11.2, expressly affirms that God created the angels with a good will—that is, with the chaste love by which they might cleave to him—at once creating their nature and granting grace. Hence, he says, it must never be believed that the holy angels existed without a good will, that is, love of God. Likewise, in *On Genesis according to the Letter*, II.8, he declares that from the time they were created they enjoyed, in holy and devout contemplation, the eternity of the Word itself. And in *Against Julian*, II.8.43: “Catholic faith,” he says, “holds that evil did not proceed except from good, nor injustice except from justice; because the angel and the human being, of whom these things are said, were certainly first good and just.”]

It ought to be clear that they were good at the first beginning of creation, that is, without fault. For the supremely good Creator could not be the author of evil. But at that time they were neither just nor unjust, nor did they then possess any virtue. For every virtue is merit, and all merit arises from free choice; but free choice always concerns the future, [Col. 1108D] not the present or the past. What is cannot then not be, and what is not cannot then be; and therefore it is not within the power of free choice.

Thus it was not within their free choice that they should then be good, which was from creation, or evil, which was not; but only in the future. Just as someone sitting has it in his power to stand, but not then: he cannot [Col. 1109A] stand at that very moment, but only in the future. Accordingly, we say that at the beginning of their creation they possessed no virtue, justice, or anything else of that kind, unless we understand some natural capacity as a virtue, such as reason, intelligence, and the like.

Nor can we say that they were unjust, because they were without fault; and since they were without fault, they were not miserable, because punishment does not precede guilt. Yet neither were they blessed, because they were not created in blessedness but for blessedness. If, however, any authority says that they were just or blessed in creation itself, it calls that state—without misery and without fault—“blessedness” or “justice.”

Some object as follows: if at the beginning of their creation they did not possess virtues or blessedness, then God made them imperfect. But it was unfitting for him who is supremely powerful and perfectly good to make anything imperfect. It may be said, however, that they were perfect because they possessed everything which they ought then to possess.

For “perfect” is said in three ways: according to time, according to nature, and universally. Perfect according to time [is that] which has whatever time requires and what it is fitting to possess at that time; and in this way the angels were perfect. Perfect according to nature [is that] which has whatever is due or expedient to its nature for glorification; and in this way the angels were perfect after confirmation [in grace], and the saints after the resurrection. Universally and supremely perfect is that to which nothing is lacking; and this belongs to God alone.

[Col. 1109C] This is what we have said concerning what the angels were like in creation. Immediately after creation, however, some turned toward their Creator and some turned away. To turn toward God was to love; to turn away was to hate. In those who turned, the wisdom of God began, as it were, to shine out in a mirror, and by it they were illumined. Those who turned away were blinded, and divine wisdom did not shine in them, because they had turned from the light, like a mirror turned from the face of the beholder.

When the former stood and the latter fell, God divided the light from the darkness. He made the light and divided it, because their goodness was his gift. He did not make the darkness, but divided the light from them. Thus the angels were first created; hence it was said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), [Col. 1109D] that is, the angels. Then they were formed, namely when they turned toward their Creator. Hence it was said: “Let there be light” (ibid., v. 3).

But one may ask whether something was bestowed on them after creation by which they might love. It was: namely, cooperating grace, without which a rational creature cannot make progress. For it can fall, but [Col. 1110A] cannot advance without cooperating grace. Hence nothing can be imputed to those who fell. For without cooperating grace [Note: [Col. 1109D] Perhaps more intelligibly, in view of what follows: “Hence there is nothing that can be imputed to those who fell; for without cooperating grace,” etc.] they could not make progress; but that grace was not given to them, nor was it their fault that it was not given, because no fault had yet preceded in them.

It may be answered that, for those to whom that grace was given, it was not given by merit, because there was as yet no merit. But that it was not given to the others was their fault—not because their fault preceded in time, but causally. For just as grace in the former is the cause of merit and does not precede merit itself in time, so in the latter fault was the cause why, by God’s just judgment, grace would not be given. Yet even in time this did not precede that; for, since all things are present to God and he needs no one’s testimony, as [Col. 1110B] soon as anyone sins he can justly judge him—not afterward, but simultaneously. If he chooses to delay, that is mercy.

Their fault can be considered in this respect: although without cooperating grace, which they had not yet received, they could not make progress, yet through what had been bestowed on them by creative grace they could refrain from falling. For there was nothing in them that could compel them to do so; and if they had not turned aside by their own will, what was given to the others would also have been given to them.

The question is asked whether there was any interval between their creation and their fall. It may be said that there was no interval, although one thing was prior and the other subsequent, yet without an intervening period. For they were not always evil, as some wish to say on the authority: “He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44). But it does not say “a murderer in the beginning,” but “from the beginning,” that is, immediately after the beginning; and “he did not stand in the truth” means that he did not remain in it, not that he had never been in it.

He may be called the murderer of himself, because he too is called a human being, as in: “An enemy, a man, did this” (Matt. 13:28). Or, as Augustine explains [Note: [Col. 1109D] Tractate 42 on John, §11.], “from the beginning,” that is, from the time when humanity existed, he was a murderer, because through envy he hurled humanity into death.

Again, Augustine says on Genesis: “It may not without reason be thought that the devil fell through pride at the beginning of time, and that there was no time when he lived peaceably and blessedly with the holy angels; but that from the very beginning of creation he apostatized, because, as the Lord says, [Col. 1110D] he did not stand—and this from the beginning, from the time he himself was created, who would have stood if he had wished to stand.” This authority may be explained in the manner stated above.

## CHAPTER XX. On Lucifer’s excellence before the fall, and his ruin after it

Before those who fell there was one [Note: [Col. 1109D] Hildebert asserts the same in Sermon 2, *On the Ascension of the Lord*, which we have recovered not only from the Victorine manuscript but also from the Lyra manuscript, from which we also drew this theological treatise. In that sermon and in this treatise he uses, in support of his position, the same Gospel testimonies and explains them in the same way. We therefore judged both that sermon and this treatise to be genuine works of Hildebert. This may also be confirmed by what Hildebert says about evil angels: in almost the very words of this chapter, he declares the murky air to be the prison of demons until they are cast down into that eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. The same is found in Sermon 1, *On the Purification of Blessed Mary*, and in the sermon *On Christian Warfare*, and elsewhere frequently. This accords with the teaching of St Augustine, who in *Enchiridion*, ch. 28, §9, maintains that certain angels were cast down by impious pride and thrust from their heavenly dwelling into the lowest darkness of this air; and in Epistle 102 to Deogratias, §20: “They dwell,” he says, “in this nearby and murky heaven, as in their aerial prison.”] more excellent [Col. 1111A] than all the others. Authorities seem to mean that he was superior not only to those who fell, but to all others, as Job says: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40:14). And in Ezekiel: “You are the seal of likeness, full of knowledge and beautiful in perfection; you were in the delights of paradise” (Ezek. 28:12).

Gregory explains this thus [Note: [Col. 1112D] Homily 34 on the Gospels.]: “The more sublime his nature is, the more sublimely is the image of God shown forth as expressed in him.” Again, in Ezekiel: “Every precious stone was his covering” (Ezek. 28:13). “Every precious stone,” that is, all the angels, was his covering, because, as Gregory says, he was brighter than all of them in comparison with them. Hence he was called Lucifer, who is to be understood not as an order but as one spirit.

As Isidore says, immediately after he was created, without any interval, [Col. 1111B] considering the profundity of his own knowledge, he became proud against his Creator; and, as is said in Isaiah, he wished to be equal to God: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13). He wished to be like him not by imitation but by equality. Indeed, the following authority seems to mean that he wished not merely to be equal but superior: “He exalts himself above every being called god or worshipped as god” (2 Thess. 2:4).

Because he was so greatly proud against his Creator, he was cast down with all those who consented to him into this murky air, for our testing, that they might be an aid to our [Col. 1111C] exercise. They were not granted to dwell in heaven, the bright homeland, nor on earth, lest they should infest human beings too greatly; but they are “in the murky air, which is as a prison for them,” until the time of judgment. Then they will be cast down into the abyss of hell, according to the saying: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:42).

And just as they possess greater or lesser knowledge, so they hold greater or lesser dominions: some over one province, some over one vice. Thus one speaks of the spirit of pride and the spirit of lust. Yet there is doubt concerning this: whether all are now in this air until judgment, or whether some are already in the lower hell. We have no very certain authority on the matter.

Some nevertheless wish to say [Col. 1111D] that Lucifer, who sinned more than the rest, was immediately plunged there, together with some of the others. Origen also says that those overcome by saints and by persons living justly and devoutly no longer have power to tempt others, but are immediately plunged there. This is quite likely. Origen says: “I think indeed that the saints, resisting these instigators and conquering them, diminish their army [of demons], or destroy as many of them as possible; nor is it thereafter permitted for that spirit [Col. 1112A] which has been conquered by a saint living chastely and modestly to attack another human being again.”

It should also be known that good angels are so confirmed by grace [in good] that they cannot sin, while evil angels are so hardened by malice that they cannot do good. It is objected that they have free choice; therefore they can incline in either direction. But they are not said to be free on that account, as we shall show in this place: if “free” means voluntary, then good angels refrain from evil not under coercive necessity but by free will, and evil angels likewise refrain from good.

Again, Jerome says: “God alone is one in whom sin cannot occur. All others, since they are free, can incline their will in either direction.” But how this ought to be understood may be inferred [Col. 1112B] from these words of Isidore: “Angels are mutable by nature and immutable by grace.” Thus it seems we must grant that good angels can sin according to their nature—that is, their nature does not resist this. Yet it must not be granted that good angels can sin; rather, they cannot sin—that is, the grace by which they have been confirmed resists it.

And although evil angels are hardened by malice, they have not lost their keen intelligence. For, as Isidore says, they flourish in a threefold sharpness of knowledge: subtlety of nature, experience of times, and revelation from higher powers. Augustine [Note: [Col. 1112D] *On the Divination of Demons*, ch. 4, §§8 ff.]: “Evil spirits are permitted to know certain things about temporal affairs, partly through subtlety of perception, partly through a more cunning experience of times [Col. 1112C] because of their very great length of life, and partly because holy angels report to them what they themselves learn from almighty God, at his command. Sometimes, moreover, wicked spirits foretell, as if by divination, even what they themselves are going to do.”

The question is asked whether they foreknew their own fall. For if they foreknew it, either they were unwilling to avoid it, and thus before the fall they were foolish and malicious; or they wished to avoid it but could not, and thus they were miserable before they fell. Because of these difficulties Augustine says in his work on Genesis that they did not foreknow their fall.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the distinction of the orders

[Col. 1112D] After the foregoing, it must be considered that Scripture testifies in many places that there are nine orders of angels. In these orders there are found three triads, and in each triad three orders, so that the likeness of the Trinity may be shown as impressed in them above other creatures. There are three higher, three lower, and three middle orders. The higher are seraphim, cherubim, and thrones; the middle, dominations, principalities, and powers; the lower, virtues, archangels, and angels.

[Col. 1113A] Here we must consider what we call an order, and whether this distinction of orders existed from creation. An order of angels is called a multitude of spirits who resemble one another more than others do. Thus the seraphim burn with charity more than the rest: *seraphim* means “burning.” Cherubim excel the others in knowledge: *cherubim* means “fullness of knowledge.” *Throne* means “seat.” Thrones are, as Gregory says, those who are filled with such grace from God that God sits in them and through them determines his judgments.

Powers are those who have surpassed the powers of principalities. Principalities are those who, while arranging what must be done for those subject to them, preside over them for the fulfillment of divine ministries. Powers are those who have received more power than the rest in their order, [Col. 1113B] so that hostile powers are restrained under their authority and cannot tempt human beings as much as they desire. Virtues are those through whom signs and miracles more frequently occur. Archangels announce greater matters; angels, lesser. Since charity is a greater gift than knowledge, the highest order takes its name from the more worthy gift. Again, to know is greater than to judge, for knowledge informs judgment. The same applies to the others; and so the excellence of the orders is assigned according to the excellence of gifts.

Nevertheless, as Gregory says, these gifts are common to all; for all burn with charity and are full of knowledge, but the higher they are, the more excellently they possess these gifts above the others. Gregory says: “In that highest city, each order is designated by the name of that thing which it has received more fully [Col. 1113C] in gift.”

Here the following question arises. If an order possesses more fully the gift from which it is named, then cherubim surpass all in knowledge. But those who love more know more, for God is known only to the degree that he is loved. Therefore seraphim surpass others not only in charity but also in knowledge. Hence some explain the authority in this way: “Each order is designated by the name of that thing which it has received more fully in gift”—that is, more fully than all beneath it.

Or we may say that the comparison is not made with angels but with other gifts. Just as among human beings, when the same person has several virtues, he nevertheless possesses one more fully [Col. 1113D] than the others—as Job patience and David humility—so also among angels. Thus that authority can be explained: “It is designated by the name of that thing which it has received more fully in gift,” not more fully than all other angels, but more fully than its other gifts.

It remains to ask whether these orders existed from the first creation. It is clear that they did, since authority says that some fell from each individual order. But it cannot be said, with respect to that fallen part, that they then burned with charity; therefore they do not seem then to have been seraphim. It may be said that, although at the beginning of creation they did not burn with charity, that order was nevertheless distinguished from the others because it was more capable than the rest of loving.

For just as we see in bodily things that some, by their nature, are more solid and firm than others, and likewise cleaner and brighter, so in those spiritual natures there could, from the very beginning of their creation, be degrees of difference suited to their purity and excellence, both in essence and in form; whereby some were higher and some lower. The higher were created more subtle in nature and more penetrating in wisdom; the lower, less subtle in nature and less penetrating in wisdom. But only he who made all things in number, weight, and measure could weigh these invisible distinctions among invisible things.

[Col. 1114B] The question is asked whether all in the same order are peers and equals. This has seemed true to some. But it cannot stand, since Scripture says that Lucifer was more excellent than all the others. He was evidently of the higher order, yet more excellent within that order. For just as among all virgins of one order one surpasses another in virginity, so it can also be among angels.

We read that a tenth order must be completed from human beings. For evil angels, when they fell from each of the orders, made one order, because they were alike in malice—though “order” is improperly said of them—and that order is restored from human beings. Hence Scripture indicates that the tenth order is to be completed from human beings.

But since Gregory says that human beings are to be assumed [Col. 1114C] into the orders of angels—some into the higher order, namely those who burn more with charity, and some into the lower order, namely those less perfect—it does not seem that a tenth order is made from human beings, but that only nine remain. It may be said that they are said to be assumed into angelic orders according to the correspondence of the gifts they have with angels [Note: [Col. 1113D] Perhaps: “They are said to be assumed not according to the correspondence of gifts which they have with angels,” etc.]; but according to the nature they possess, which differs from angels, they are said to constitute another order.

And although what fell among angels is restored from human beings, on account of which the Apostle says: “To restore all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth” (Eph. 1:10), it must not be understood that humanity was made only for those who fell. Even if angels had not fallen, human beings would no less have been made. Hence Gregory says that human beings are chosen not according to the number of those who fell, but according to the number of those who remained. Gregory says: “For that heavenly city consists of angels and human beings, and as many of the human race ascend to it as angels remained there, as it is written: ‘He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels’” (Deut. 32:8, according to the Septuagint) [Note: [Col. 1114D] Where the Vulgate has: “He established the boundaries of peoples according to the number of the children of Israel.”].

## CHAPTER XXII. On the sending of angels

[Col. 1115A]

Certain authorities seem to mean that not all angels are sent, as in Daniel: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7:10). Again, Dionysius says in the *Hierarchy*: “Those higher hosts never depart from the innermost realities, because those who remain never perform an external office.” *Hierarchy* means “episcopacy,” because it treats there of the preeminence of angels. From these authorities some say that only the lower orders are sent.

But Isaiah says in opposition: “One of the seraphim flew to me” (Isa. 6:6). Dionysius resolves this as follows: those spirits who are sent receive the name of those whose office [Col. 1115B] they perform. Hence they say that the angel sent to Isaiah to cleanse the prophet’s lips was of the lower order; but he is called a seraph because he came to burn up and consume the prophet’s sins.

Again, the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent for service?” (Heb. 1:14). Hence it seems to some that all are sent, and that the one sent to announce the Holy of Holies was of the higher order. But it is objected: why, then, are not all called angels, but only the two lower orders? The answer is that these two orders do this more frequently and almost by an office specifically imposed upon them. Nor should it appear unworthy if even the higher orders are sent, since he who is the Creator of all descended to these lower things.

Thus Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael seem to belong to the higher order; and these are not names of orders but of spirits [Note: [Col. 1115D] On these matters see especially St Gregory, Homily 34 on the Gospels.]. Michael means “Who is like God?” Gabriel, “Strength of God”; Raphael, “Medicine of God.”

Scripture says that angels are appointed for the guardianship of human beings, as in the Gospel: “Their angels always see the face of the Father” (Matt. 18:20). Gregory also says that each person has one good angel appointed to guard him, and one evil angel appointed to exercise him. Although good angels desire our good and labor generally for the salvation of all, the one appointed to guard a particular person especially exhorts that person to good. This we read concerning Tobit’s angel and concerning Peter’s angel [Col. 1115D] in the Acts of the Apostles.

Likewise, although evil angels desire the evil of all, the evil angel permitted to tempt a particular person attacks that person more intensely. But we are uncertain of this, and Scripture has not determined [Note: [Col. 1115D] See St Gregory, *Moralia on Job*, IV.25 and XXXIX.15.] whether one angel has been assigned to guard many persons, or individual angels to individual persons. Yet, since the elect are as numerous as the good angels, and it is clear that there are more people among both the good and the evil than there are good angels, how can every human being, good and evil alike, have individual good and evil angels assigned for guardianship?

Moreover, it must be known that the knowledge of angels [Col. 1116A] can increase up to the judgment. Hence, when the Lord ascends, the angels ask in Isaiah: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63:1); and in the Psalm: “Who is this king of glory?” (Ps. 13:10). Thus it may be said that their knowledge does not diminish, because they forget nothing, being confirmed by grace; but it can increase until the future consummation, when they will be fixed and immovable in what they know, so that they can know neither more nor less.

Against our assertion that angelic knowledge can increase seems to stand what Isidore says: “Angels know all things in the Word of God before they happen.” Gregory says in the *Dialogues* [Note: [Col. 1116D] Gregory says the same in *Moralia on Job*, II.2.]: “What is it that they do not know there, where they know him who knows all things?” But it may be said that, even if they see—indeed, possess—him in whom all the treasures of wisdom are, still they know in him only as much as [he himself] wishes to reveal to them. Yet they are said to know all things, that is, to be ignorant of nothing. For one is ignorant of nothing who knows whatever he ought to know, and whatever at that time he wishes to know. In all things their will agrees with the divine will, nor do they wish to know anything except what they know God wills.

The merit of angels is said to consist in this: that they desire our good and labor for our advancement. Hence the Apostle says: “And the angels are yours.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the works of the six days

As we have said: at the beginning of creatures God created heaven, that is, the angels; and earth, namely, [Col. 1116C] that still-confused matter of the four elements, which was called chaos. This was before every day. It remains, therefore, to see how he distinguished that matter through six days.

As Genesis says, light was made on the first day (Gen. 1 throughout). Some interpreters say that this light was a certain shining body, like a luminous cloud, which was carried around, like the sun now, by rising and setting, making night and day. Others say that the light made on the first day was angelic nature turned toward its Creator, as we have already said.

“On the second day the firmament was made, to divide [the] waters from [the] waters.” Bede says that the firmament consists of waters consolidated like crystal stone; [Col. 1116D] this is quite likely, since its color also indicates it. Some interpreters, however, seem to maintain that it is of a fiery nature. That waters were above the firmament is found both in Genesis and in the Prophet: “Waters that are above the heavens bless God” (Ps. 148:4). What sort of waters these are is not certain to us; but, as interpreters say, they are either solidified like ice or suspended in vaporous form, like vapour—that is, smoke—which is more likely.

On the third day the waters were gathered into one place and dry land appeared. On the fourth day luminaries were made to serve as signs and times, that is, so that through them [Col. 1117A] a distinction of times might arise. For from the moment creation existed, time also existed, because creation could not exist without changeability; and wherever there is movement, there are before and after. Nor is time anything other than the interval from what is before to what is after. But before the luminaries there was not this distinction of time such as exists through the sun, moon, and other stars.

On the fifth day water brought forth fish and birds; hence the saying: “Some you send back to the deep, some you raise into the air.” On the sixth day earth brought forth animals of diverse kinds; and on that day, after all things, humanity was made in the image and likeness of God. Rightly was humanity made after all things, since humanity was to be preferred above all.

The sequence itself, as we have set it out, and many interpreters seem to mean that matter was made before every day, as [Col. 1117B] we have said, together with the angels; afterward the kinds of things were distinguished from that matter during six days. Some, however, think that these distinctions of things were made not through temporal intervals but simultaneously. But since Moses spoke to a rude and carnal people, he had to speak of God as of a human being, who forms and completes works through intervals of time.

Hence Augustine says: “What could be made by God at once could not be spoken by man [at once].” Nor do we deny that God could have made it so if he had wished [Note: [Col. 1117D] “What that light is, and by what alternating motion . . . is remote from our senses and cannot be understood by us as it is; nevertheless, it must be believed without any hesitation.” Thus St Augustine, *City of God*, II.7.]. Nor does Augustine assert this; he says: “It could have been made simultaneously.”

Again, Augustine says: “Because that from which something is made, although not earlier in time, is nevertheless earlier in origin than that which is made from it, Scripture could divide by times what God did not divide by times of making.” Those who adhere to these authorities call the six days six distinctions of works, which were made simultaneously according to God, but had to be narrated in order. The first opinion, however, is much more probable.

On the seventh day, “God rested from all his work which he had accomplished” (Gen. 2:2), because after making every kind of thing he made nothing further. But the saying in the Gospel is objected: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5:17). For he works daily, creating new souls and also propagating one thing from another. But this is not making new kinds of things; although a new soul is now created, it adds nothing new, since soul already existed before.

Another reading in Genesis says: “God rested on the [Col. 1117D] sixth day,” and so forth. But both are true: he is said to have rested on the sixth because, once the sixth day had been completed and the seventh begun, he ceased from distinguishing the kinds of things.

Here one may ask: if he completed all works in six days and added nothing new after those six days, why do we continue counting days to the seventh? If it is said, “Because the seventh is other than those,” then the eighth is likewise other than them, and the ninth, and so on. Yet these are not other in the distinction of things. Likewise the seventh was not other in the distinction of things, because no distinction of any work was made on it as [Col. 1118A] on the other six days. For making the seventh day was not making another kind of thing, because day had already preceded it.

It may be said that, although no work was made on the seventh day, there was another state of things there, namely the completion of all things; therefore we proceed as far as it, and afterward immediately begin again.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the creation of humanity
Having dealt with these matters, it remains to discuss the creation of man, his fall, and his restoration. In Genesis it is said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). Man was made in the image of God according to the soul. For as an image is seen in a mirror, so the soul can know God in its reason [Col. 1118B]. Hence the saying: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us” (Ps. 4:7). For as a man is recognized by his face, so God is recognized in reason itself, as it were in his image. Man, therefore, is God’s image by reason. Hence the Apostle says: “Man is the image and glory of God” (1 Cor. 11:7). And he is *to* the image, because he is not altogether like him. The Son is the image of the Father, and not *to* the image, because whatever the Father has, the Son has wholly by nature. But man is so God’s image that he is *to* the image, because this is not by nature but by participation or imitation. For he possesses those things which belong to deity. God is justice itself, wisdom itself, goodness itself; man is not wisdom, justice, or goodness itself, but can be wise, just, good, and the like. [Col. 1118C] Augustine, *On the Trinity* (Book XII, ch. 7): “Man is the image of God, and to the image, because he is not equal to the Father but approaches by a certain likeness. The Son is the image, and not to the image, because he is equal to the Father.”

It should be noted that man was made not only in the image of the Father, but of the whole Trinity, since it is written: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). “Our,” that is, of the whole Trinity. It should also be noted that both the image impressed upon some thing and the thing in which it is impressed are called an image. Thus reason itself is called an image, because it has been impressed upon the soul as a seal; and man is called the image of God. Augustine, in *The City of God* [Col. 1118D] (Book XI, chs. 26, 28): The Trinity itself is one thing; the image of the Trinity in some thing is another. Because of that image, the thing in which it is impressed is likewise called an image. Thus both a panel and what is painted upon it are called an image—not because of the panel itself, but because of the painting upon it. Man was made in God’s likeness because he was made innocent and without fault.

Concerning angels, it is commonly asked whether they were made in God’s image, since this is nowhere read. Yet although it is not written, it ought not to be doubted; what God said concerning man, he intended to be understood also of angels.

Man is also said in another sense to be in God’s image because, just as all things come from God, so all human beings come from Adam [Col. 1119A]. But being in God’s image in this sense belongs only to the first man. In this respect the soul can be said to be in God’s likeness, because it is immortal and indissoluble. Augustine, *On the Greatness of the Soul* (ch. 2, no. 3): “The soul was made like God because God made it immortal and indissoluble.” God did not make it from his own substance, as certain heretics wished, but from nothing. Augustine: “What is from God must necessarily be of the same nature as he is, and thereby immutable; but the soul is mutable; therefore it is not from him. But if it was made from no other thing, beyond doubt it was made from nothing, though by God himself.” He formed the body from the mud of the earth and breathed a soul into it. Hence Genesis says: “He breathed [Vulgate: *inspired*] into his face the breath of life” [Col. 1119B] (Gen. 2:7), that is, he breathed a soul into him. But whether the soul was created within the body or outside the body, we have no very certain authoritative teaching. Augustine, however, says on Genesis: “It seems that the soul of the first man was made outside the body and entered it by its own will.” But, as he himself says, he spoke this while investigating Genesis rather than asserting it.

> [Note: The same, Book IX of *On Free Choice*, ch. 21, no. 59, Col. 1119D.]

But whatever may be said concerning the soul of the first man, it is more probable concerning other souls that they are created in the body. If it is asked at what age man was made, Augustine says: Adam was immediately made, without any gradual development of limbs, at the age of maturity, just as Moses’ staff was immediately turned from a staff in his hand into a serpent.

## Chapter XXV. On the Formation of Woman

[Col. 1119C]

As Genesis says: “God cast a sleep upon Adam and took one of his ribs” (Gen. 2:21), and from it formed woman. Here one may ask why God did not create all human beings at once, as he did the angels. The reason is that he wished there to be one beginning of the human race, in order to curb the devil’s pride. For, to confound his arrogance, man received what the devil had sought through pride, namely, to be a beginning: so that, as God is the beginning of creation for all things, man might be the beginning of generation for all human beings. There is another reason why God wished all to come from one: that, recognizing themselves to be from one, they might love themselves as though they were one. [Col. 1119D] In this event the mystery of Christ and the Church was signified. For as woman was formed from the side of the sleeping man, so the sacraments of the Church [variant: “so the Church’s sacraments”] flowed from the side of Christ sleeping on the cross—namely blood and water. By blood he redeemed the faithful; by water he washed away sins in baptism.

It is commonly asked whether woman was made from that rib with the addition of some substance taken from outside, as some commonly say. But if God added external increase in order to complete the woman’s body from that rib, then, since what was added was greater than [Col. 1120A] that rib, one ought rather to say that woman was made from that added substance, from which she received more parts of her substance. It remains, therefore, for us to say that the rib was multiplied within itself and that woman was formed from it, with no addition taken from outside. For it was greater to make something from nothing than to multiply a small substance within itself. We say the same concerning the five Gospel loaves.

It is asked whether it belonged to the nature of that rib that woman should be made from it. To see this, one must understand that the causes of all things that come to be existed eternally in God. For that man, horse, and the like should come to be in this manner was eternally in God’s disposition; and these are called in Scripture the primordial causes, because no others precede them. Although the cause of all things is one—namely the divine disposition, which is nothing other than God himself—yet because the effects are many, Augustine speaks in the plural [Col. 1120B] of the primordial causes of all things existing in God.

> [Note: Book III of *On the Trinity*, ch. 9, no. 16. See also, on these matters, St Augustine, Book VI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, ch. 15, nos. 26 and 29, Col. 1120D.]

He also introduces the comparison of an artisan, in whose design lies what sort of chest is to be made, square or oblong; and this design proceeds eternally. In creatures, however, causes of some things—but not of all—proceed. As Augustine says, God implanted certain causes in things, according to which some things arise from them: such a shoot from this seed, such fruit from this tree; that one who is now young grows old at such a time; and the like. These too are called primordial causes, though the term is not altogether proper, for they have prior causes which existed eternally in God [Col. 1120C]. The causes which are in creatures are not first universally, but they are first in their own kind, because they are first in relation to subsequent things. Therefore they too are called primordial, because God implanted them in things in the first establishment of things, which was made in six days. And as creatures are mutable, so these causes are mutable. Although it belongs to the nature of a young person eventually to grow old, this can nevertheless be changed; but the causes which are in God, uncreated, are immutable. For God’s disposition cannot change, because God is immutable.

It is clear from this that the causes of all things are in God; and the causes of some things are also in the nature of things, as we have shown concerning seed and tree. Such things are said to occur according to nature, that is, according to the customary course of things. But the causes of other things exist in God alone and not in the natures of things: for example, that a dry rod blossomed, that a donkey spoke, and the like. These are said to occur by miracle, because they occur contrary to the nature of those things—that is, not according to the causes implanted in those things by God. Augustine includes among such things the fact that woman was made from a rib [Col. 1120D]. For it was not causally present in the rib that woman should be made from it, but it was in God’s power, who did not bind his power to the natures [variant: “numbers”] of things. Augustine on Genesis:

“Therefore, one mode is that by which this herb sprouts in this way, this age brings forth in this way and that one does not; man speaks, cattle cannot. The reasons for these and similar modes are not only in God, but have also been placed by him in things re-created [variant: “equally as in created things”] and created. But that dry wood should blossom [Col. 1121A] and bear fruit; that a woman barren in youth should give birth in old age; that a donkey should speak; and the like: he indeed gave to the natures which he created the capacity for these things also to happen from them, but not so that they should have them in their natural motion. The Lord, therefore, has hidden in himself the causes of certain deeds which he did not implant in created things; and he fulfils them, not by that work of providence by which he established natures that they might exist, but by that by which he governs them as he wills—the natures which he established as he willed. One of these was that woman was thus made from the side of the sleeping man.”

The first establishment of things had from this the possibility that woman might altogether be made in this way; but it had this only in the sense that she could be made so.

Just as the woman’s body was derived from the man’s body, some wished Eve’s soul likewise to have been propagated from the man’s soul, and all souls after the first to be derived by propagation, as bodies are. But Jerome forbids this under anathema, adducing the Prophet’s authority: “He who formed their hearts one by one” [Col. 1121B] (Ps. 31:15). In this he sufficiently indicates that God does not create soul from soul, but makes them individually from nothing. Augustine, however, asserts nothing on this matter, but inquiringly reports differing opinions about the soul: some wished all souls to have been created at once; others, not at once but by propagation; others, neither at once nor by propagation—the opinion Jerome affirms.

## Chapter XXVI. On the State of Man before Sin

“God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight” (Gen. 2:15). By these words Moses plainly shows that man was created outside paradise and afterwards placed in paradise. This is said to have been done because he was not to remain there, or lest he should attribute God’s benefit to nature rather than grace. The saints report that Paradise was a most elevated place in the eastern region, such that even the waters of the Flood could not reach it. In it were trees of diverse kinds: the tree of life, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and many others. The tree of life was so called because its fruit was of such a nature [Col. 1121D] that it protected against the failing of death and every trouble of infirmity. The other was the tree of knowledge, which received its name not from a nature that conferred knowledge, but from what followed from the prohibition: whoever hastily ate its fruit would know by experience of evil the difference between the good he had left and the evil he had found. For he had beforehand knowledge of good and evil: of good, through experience and not merely knowledge; of evil, through knowledge alone and not through experience.

Here one must consider [supplement: what was the state of man before sin, etc.] the condition of man before sin. As the Apostle says: “The first Adam was made into a living soul” [Col. 1122A] (1 Cor. 15:45), that is, into a body endowed with sensation, which was still animal. For it needed the nourishment of food. He also had a mortal body: he could die and could not die; he could sin and could not sin. But when the fixed number of years had been completed, he was to be transferred to that state [supplement: “when a certain number of years had been completed, he was to be transferred to that state,” etc.] in which he could neither die nor sin. Before sin, therefore, he was immortal in the sense that he could avoid dying, not immortal in the sense that he could not die. And if Adam and Eve had not sinned, as Augustine says, there would have been in Paradise an unstained marriage-bed: conception without lust and childbirth without pain.

What their children would have been like if they had not sinned—whether they would immediately have been able to walk, speak, and do other things—we have no certain authoritative teaching. Augustine, however, seems to hold that they could have done these things as soon as they were born, saying:

> [Note: On this see St Augustine, *Unfinished Work against Julian*, Book III, no. 198, Col. 1121D.]

“It raises the question whether, if the first human beings had not sinned, they would have had children who used neither tongue nor hands. For because of the necessity of the womb, perhaps it was necessary for infants to be born; although a rib is a small part of the body, God did not on that account make the man’s wife small. Thus the Creator’s omnipotence could have made her children fully grown as soon as they were born. But, leaving that aside, he certainly could have done so because he granted it to many animals, whose young, although small, nevertheless run and follow their mothers as soon as they are born. By contrast, for a human being at birth, the feet are not fit even for walking [Col. 1122C], nor are the hands capable even of grasping; and, with the breasts lying beside them, they can do more to weep hungrily than to suckle [variant: “rise”]. Thus this infirmity of flesh wholly accords with infirmity of mind.”

But since Augustine says this without asserting anything definite, some reasonably think that even then an age would have been awaited for performing these acts and the like—not because of a defect, since they would not have sinned, but because of the condition of nature. Similarly, they could not wholly abstain from food, yet this was not due to defect but to the condition of nature [variant: “the natural condition”].

An objection may be raised: If they had not sinned—

> [Note: *Peccarent* for *peccassent*, and similar forms, are a manner of speaking often used by Hildebert; this should also be observed in what follows, Col. 1122D.]

—they would never have died. Therefore, even if they did not eat, provided they did not sin, they would never die. They could therefore live without nourishment. To this we say that they would sin not only if they ate from the forbidden tree, but also if they did not use the things granted, since they naturally desired them. For in this they would act against natural reason, which had been given them so that they might use lawful things. Another objection is made: Since hunger is a consequence of sin, if they had not sinned they would not suffer hunger; but, without hunger, eating seems superfluous. The answer is that, even if they had not sinned, they would have had an appetite for eating; having this appetite, they would use the things granted in order to prevent hunger. That appetite is natural and moderate; hunger, however, is an immoderate appetite for eating [Col. 1123A].

From the state which we have described, man with all his offspring was to be transferred, without the pain of death, to that highest good which had been prepared for him. For as there are two natures in man, bodily and spiritual, so God had prepared two goods for him, temporal and eternal. And because that which is animal comes first and afterwards that which is spiritual, the temporal good was first given; the other, namely the eternal, was not then given but was set before him. To preserve what he had given, God added the precept of nature. The natural precept was discernment, through which he was inspired to know what was necessary to his nature and what was harmful. In order to merit what he had set before him, he gave the precept of obedience, saying: “Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat,” etc. [Col. 1123B] (Gen. 2:17).

Seeing, then, that man would ascend through obedience to the place from which he himself had fallen through pride, the devil envied him. He who had first become a devil—that is, one flowing downward—through pride, became Satan, that is, adversary, through envy. Therefore he tempted the woman, in whom he knew reason to be less vigorous than in the man. But, lest the temptation become less hidden and thereby not be able to be guarded against, he was permitted to tempt only through the serpent, so that through the outward covering she might perceive the cunning. Augustine on Genesis:

> [Note: Book XI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, ch. 12, no. 16, Col. 1123D.]

“When the devil approached to tempt, and could not do so unless permitted, he could not act except through that by which he was sent.”

Why did the woman not recoil from the serpent? The answer is that, since it had been newly created, it is thought to have received from God the function of speech [Col. 1123C]. The temptation proceeded thus. First he approached her with a question, in order to gather from her reply how he ought thereafter to address her: “Why do you not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil?” (Gen. 3:3). The woman replied: “Lest perhaps we die,” etc. (ibid.). In these words she gave an opening for temptation when she said, “Lest perhaps,” etc. Therefore the devil immediately said: “Eat, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (ibid., v. 5). He tempted her through three things: through gluttony, when he said, “Eat”; through vainglory, when he said, “You will be like gods”; through avarice, when he said, “Knowing good and evil.” Gluttony is an immoderate desire for eating; vainglory, love of one’s own praise; avarice, [Col. 1123D] an immoderate love of possessing.

Since one kind of temptation is interior and another exterior, man was tempted by exterior temptation. Exterior temptation takes place outwardly by sign or word, in order that the person tempted may be inclined to consent to sin. Interior temptation is a movement of perverse delight through which the mind is driven toward sin, and it is much more difficult to conquer. Thus man, struck by exterior temptation, fell, and deserved to be punished all the more severely because he was overthrown by a lighter impulse.

## Chapter XXVII. On the Sin of the First Man

At this point it seems necessary to inquire into the origin and root of that sin. Augustine, on Genesis [Col. 1124A] (Book XI, ch. 5, no. 7), says: “The tempter would not have cast man down unless pride had previously arisen in his mind.”

> [Note: “Ah, pride! Did he say: ‘I have sinned’? It has the ugliness of shame, but it does not have the humility of confession.” *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book XI, ch. 35, no. 47, Col. 1123D–1124D.]

Some therefore hold that before yielding to the temptation he had that pride. But, since pride is a vice, it would follow that he sinned before yielding to the temptation [variant: “pride”]. Therefore he did not first sin through suggestion, since authority says that the devil’s sin is inexcusable because he fell not through suggestion but through his own pride; whereas man, who fell not by himself but through another, could rise through a mediator. This authority can therefore be explained thus: the tempter would not have cast man down, namely into these miseries, unless pride had previously arisen in his mind. For if we said, “He would not have cast man down into sin unless pride had first arisen,” then man would have had pride before he sinned. It can also be said that the tempter would not have cast man down into the act [variant: “increase”] of that sin—namely, that he should eat the forbidden fruit—unless pride had first arisen. For pride is the root or cause of every sin.

When the woman heard, “You will be like gods,” etc. (Gen. 3:5), she was lifted up into pride; and that pride was to be repressed by the punishments which followed that sin. But, since human nature was without fault, it is commonly asked from where that consent to evil proceeded. To see this, one must understand that God placed two appetites in the first man: the appetite for what is just and the appetite for what is advantageous. He placed the appetite for what is just in the will, so that man might merit through it, either by retaining good when he could abandon it, or by retaining evil when he could abandon it [Col. 1124C]. He placed the appetite for what is advantageous according to necessity; for man cannot fail to desire his own advantage. God therefore placed this in man necessarily, so that man might be rewarded in it. Hence this will be the greatest punishment of the impious in hell: they will always desire their own advantage and will never attain it. So too it will increase the glory of the good, who cannot grow lukewarm in love for the advantage they possess.

God placed a measure within this appetite for advantage, so that man might desire what ought to be desired, when it ought to be desired, and in the manner in which it ought to be desired. But because he desired advantage beyond measure—namely, to be like God—he abandoned the appetite for what is just; and in this he sinned, because he abandoned justice. He sinned not because he desired advantage, [Col. 1124D] but because in desiring it he abandoned justice; and this was to desire advantage beyond measure. For justice is the measure in the appetite for advantage. The sin of the first man, therefore, was abandonment of justice, which the Apostle calls “disobedience” (Rom. 5:10).

It is asked whether the will preceded that sin. It does not seem that he willed or deliberated to abandon justice. Yet he did will to desire that thing for which he abandoned justice; and he did not will to abandon justice, but willed the thing on account of which he abandoned justice. He abandoned justice by will, not in the sense that the will preceded it in time. For it is not true that every sin is temporally preceded by will, since the will to evil is itself a sin. Rather, this is said of an act: every evil proceeds from will, as did that act, namely the eating of the fruit, which some call the first sin of man; and this may readily be granted. For in one sin there are both guilt and act, yet they are not called two sins but one. Thus one who has the will to commit homicide and later commits it does not then commit another sin, but carries out in deed what he previously had in will [Col. 1125A].

It is asked which of them sinned more, Adam or Eve. But, as the Apostle says: “Adam was not deceived, but the woman” (1 Tim. 2:14). Thus in Genesis, when questioned, the woman says: “The serpent deceived me.” But the man, when questioned, does not say, “He deceived me,” but: “She gave me from the tree, and I ate.” The woman is said to have been deceived in that, having heard the words “You will be like gods,” etc., she became so puffed up that she believed what was said to be true. Adam, however, was not deceived because, as Augustine says:

> [Note: “They believed more readily that God could forgive sinners than they patiently endured not knowing what it was, or why he had forbidden them to take food from it.” *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book XI, ch. 31, no. 41, Col. 1125D.]

he did not believe this to be true, but thought both possible: both to comply with his wife and to make satisfaction to God through repentance. Therefore he sinned less, since he thought of forgiveness. From these words it appears that there was greater pride in the woman than in the man, and therefore a greater sin. The woman also sinned against God and neighbour; the man only against God. Further [Col. 1125C], the woman was punished more severely, being told: “In pain you shall bear your children,” etc. Hence it appears that she sinned more.

An objection is made from what Isidore says: “Sin is committed in three ways: through ignorance, weakness, or deliberate intent. Eve sinned through ignorance because, as the Apostle says, she was deceived. Adam sinned through deliberate intent because, not deceived, he sinned knowingly and prudently. Peter sinned through weakness. It is more serious to sin through weakness than through ignorance, and more serious to sin through deliberate intent than through weakness.” One sins through deliberate intent when one commits evil by purpose and deliberation; through weakness when one sins by accident or disturbance. These words seem to assert that the man sinned more than the woman. The answer may be that he sinned more in one respect: namely, his deliberation seems to have been greater than the woman’s [Col. 1125D], and he possessed greater knowledge; and from one to whom more is entrusted, more is required. Yet we shall not say simply that he sinned more, as we would say of a priest or a layman if they committed homicide. If a layman acted from long-standing hatred and a priest from sudden anger, it could not simply be said that the ordained man sinned more; yet he sinned more in one respect, namely because he acted against his order.

[Col. 1126A] It is commonly asked why God permitted man to be tempted, when he foreknew that he would yield to the tempter. Augustine says:

> [Note: “Why should God not permit man to be tempted, to be tested, convicted, and punished by that temptation, when proud desire for his own power brought forth what it had conceived?” etc. *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book XI, ch. 11, no. 15, Col. 1125D–1126D.]

“It does not seem to me that man would deserve great praise if he could live well merely because no one urged him to live badly, when he had it both in his nature to be able and in his power to will not to consent to the persuader, with God’s help.”

It is likewise commonly asked why God created man, whom he foreknew would fall, since he is supremely merciful.

> [Note: “Foreseeing that evil persons would come to be, God nevertheless created them for the benefit of the saints.” *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book XI, ch. 22, no. 29. He repeats the same point many times in that book, Col. 1126D.]

The same question applies to the angels who fell. Augustine on Genesis: “Since the just make progress through the unjust, and the godly through the ungodly, it is said in vain that God ought not to have created those whom he foreknew would be evil and beneficial to the good. For why should he not create those whom he foresaw would benefit the good, when, just as he foresaw that they would be evil, so he also foresaw what good they would do from their evil deeds?” [Col. 1126B]

## Chapter XXVIII. On the Grace Possessed before Sin

It remains to inquire what grace man possessed before the fall: whether he could stand through it or not. One must understand that he could not make progress without superadded grace, as we said concerning angels; but he could refrain from departing from what he had received through the grace bestowed upon him in creation. For it is one thing to do good, another to turn aside from evil. Through that aid of grace which he had received in creation, he could turn aside from evil; but without superadded grace he could not do good. Augustine, *On Rebuke and Grace* [Col. 1126C] (ch. 11, no. 32 and following):

“If this aid had been lacking to an angel or a human being when they were first made, since their nature was not made such that it could remain without divine aid if it willed, then it certainly would not have fallen through its own fault; for the aid without which it could not remain would have been lacking.”

In the same work: “God had given man a good will. For he had made him upright in it; he had given him aid without which he could not remain in it if he willed, and through which he could [supplement: if he willed]. But that he should will, God left to his free choice.” Again: “He had received the ability, if he willed, but he did not have the willing by which he could do so. For if he had had it, he would have persevered.”

From these authorities it is evident that man could, through what he received in creation, refrain from yielding to the tempter. For unless he had been made such that he could avoid falling and resist the tempter, as Augustine says, he would not have fallen by his own fault [Col. 1126D]. An objection is made: what he could accomplish without cooperating grace, he could thus accomplish by the aid of creative grace, namely not to consent to the persuader. But this would be merit, and every merit is progress; therefore he could make progress through it. We answer that not consenting to evil is not merit; rather, merit lies in loving good while turning aside from evil [Col. 1127A]. There is no merit in turning aside from evil, but in becoming good through turning aside from evil; yet one cannot exist without the other. Thus we say that if man or angel had turned aside from evil, he would indeed have had merit and would have made progress; but not in turning aside from evil, rather in loving good while turning aside from evil. For this he needed cooperating grace. For the former alone, the aid of creative grace sufficed.

Before sin, therefore, man had from free choice and from that aid of grace the ability not to sin—that is, to avoid evil. But, as we have said, he needed cooperating grace to do good. After the fall, however, he needs not only cooperating grace but also operating grace. Operating grace makes a person rise from sins and also makes him will the good. Cooperating grace works with one who wills, so that he may do good [Col. 1127B]. Before the fall, however, he needed only cooperating grace. For he had not yet fallen and therefore did not need grace through which he might rise, but only that through which he might make progress. After the fall, operating grace comes first, moving and stirring the heart. Of this the Prophet says: “And his grace will go before me” [Vulgate: “His mercy will go before me”] (Ps. 58:11). This grace goes before by inspiring; the other follows by helping. Grace first works without us, and there man merits nothing because he then receives the good will. But afterwards he employs the will received and cooperates with grace; in this lies human merit. For human merit does not lie in receiving a good will, since there he does nothing, but in using the will received. Hence the Apostle says: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not empty” [Col. 1127C] (1 Cor. 15:10).

This can also be seen by an analogy. A tool is first made so that through it a person may do something which it does not cut by itself, but only when guided by the craftsman’s hand. Thus the will is first raised up by operating grace; and, once raised up, it is aided and guided to work well by cooperating grace. Hence the Apostle says: “To will is present with me, but I do not find the ability to carry it out” (Rom. 7:18). Yet grace effects both willing and doing, and cooperates with willing: effecting willing belongs to operating grace; bringing to completion belongs to cooperating grace.

It is commonly asked whether man possessed the virtues before the fall. Some say that he did not, and attempt to show it thus. He did not have fortitude, because [Col. 1127D] he yielded to an evil suggestion; nor justice, because he despised God’s command; nor prudence, because he did not guard himself; nor temperance, because he desired what belonged to another [variant: “he improperly desired forbidden food”]. We readily grant that he did not possess them then, namely when he sinned; but it must not be granted that he did not possess them beforehand. Augustine says in a homily: “Adam was found evil when he had lost charity.” Again: “The prince of vices, when he overcame Adam, made from the clay of the earth in God’s image, armed [variant: “adorned”] with chastity, ordered by temperance, radiant with charity, stripped and at the same time destroyed our first parents of those gifts and such great goods” [Col. 1128A]. Ambrose, to Sabinus: “When Adam was alone, he did not transgress, because his mind adhered to God.”

Some, asserting that whoever has charity cannot lose it, object as follows to what we have said. Augustine, to Count Julian: “Charity which can be abandoned was never true.” We answer that it was true in two senses: both with respect to permanence and with respect to subsistence. It was not true—that is, permanent and steadfast. Again: “Let your own spring be for you, and let no stranger share it,” etc. But it does not say “one who will become a stranger,” that is, evil, but “one who is then a stranger.” For one who is evil toward God cannot possess charity; nevertheless, one who will become evil can possess it now, or one who is now evil can possess charity at another time [Col. 1128B]. For it seems foolish to say that anyone in this life is so confirmed that he cannot become evil, when this is promised only in the other life. We therefore admit that Adam possessed charity and afterwards lost it. Yet no one should suppose that we say he possessed it in the very beginning of his creation, as we said above concerning the angels. Rather, he was in Paradise for some interval, since Scripture says that he was put to sleep and that the animals were brought before him, to which he gave names.

It is asked whether he foreknew his own fall. We say that he did not, as we said of the angel [Col. 1128C], and for the same reason that we advanced there. Augustine on Genesis says: “As punishment for this sin Adam was expelled from Paradise into this place of miseries, as it says there: ‘He cast him out from the paradise of delight, lest perhaps he eat from the tree of life and live forever.’”

> [Note: On this expulsion see Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book XI, ch. 40, no. 54, where he also maintains that Adam was, as it were, excommunicated, Col. 1127D–1128D.]

These words seem to mean that if they had eaten afterward, they would never have died. But on the other hand, because of sin he was made mortal; how then would he not die while sin remained? The answer is: if he were not punished with this punishment of death, he would be punished with a graver one, because his miseries would never end as they now end—

> [Note: Namely, through death, Col. 1128D.]

—as the devil’s miseries will never end. But because we have no certain authoritative teaching on this, some wish to say that, even if he had afterwards eaten, it would not have conferred immortality upon him. They expound the words, “Lest he eat from the tree of life” [Col. 1128D] (Gen. 3:22), in this sense: he is unworthy to eat from that tree which formerly conferred immortality. Therefore, so that he could not approach it, a certain fiery guard was placed before Paradise—namely a turning flaming sword, because it was moved before Paradise in the ministry of the cherubim. That sword signified the tribulations of this present life, which are temporary and passing. *Cherubim* means “fullness of knowledge” and signifies charity. Thus, after sin, it was necessary to return to the eating of the tree of life through tribulations and through charity, which is the fullness of knowledge [Col. 1129A]. For since the cherubim with the flaming sword stands before the gate of Paradise (Gen. 3), no one can enter there unless he has passed through the flaming sword.

It is commonly asked whether he had previously eaten from the tree of life. Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*: “It is certainly rightly understood that, before the malignant persuasion of the devil, they had abstained from the forbidden food and had made use of what was permitted, especially of the tree of life.” But this does not seem to be something that should be asserted on authority.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On free choice

Beyond the other penalties, for that sin man incurred the penalty of suffering [read: loss] of free choice. For, as Augustine says in the *Enchiridion* [Col. 1129B] (ch. 30, no. 9): “By misusing free choice, man lost both himself and it.” We must therefore see what free choice is; what it was like before sin; and how it was depressed through sin.

It may be defined thus: Free choice is the capacity of the rational will by which good is chosen through cooperating grace, or evil when that grace abandons it. It consists in two things, namely will and reason. It is called “free” with respect to the will, and “choice” (*arbitrium*) with respect to reason. It belongs to reason to see what ought, or ought not, to be chosen; to the will belongs the act of desiring. Thus reason, like an attendant, shows the way: it advises what it sees ought to be done, and dissuades from its opposite. The will, like a mistress, leads reason with it toward whatever it has been inclined [Col. 1129C] to. For the will is not drawn by reason; reason merely shows the will what it ought to desire. Reason, however, is drawn by the will and is led even toward things done contrary to reason. For reason naturally resists—that is, it judges that something ought not to be done—yet it is overcome and consents.

Since free choice consists in these two things, it has been given to the rational creature alone. It alone among creatures has will and reason. Brute animals have sensation and appetite, namely sensual appetite, but lack will and reason; and therefore they do not have free choice. Although we share sensation and appetite with beasts, free choice distinguishes us from them, and [Col. 1129D] all merit rests upon it. For since it is compelled by no force and no necessity, it deservedly earns either blessedness or misery. Sensation and appetite, however, make neither blessed nor miserable. Otherwise brute animals could partake of blessedness or misery.

Likewise, natural intelligence, memory, and all similar things make no one either just or unjust; nor, accordingly, is either great intelligence or feeble memory alone imputed. Therefore will alone, which is always free and can never be compelled, is judged by God according to merit; it is always free from necessity. For where necessity exists, there is no freedom; where there is no freedom, there is no will, and consequently no merit.

[Col. 1130A] Moreover, it should be known that free choice concerns only future things. What is present is not within our power as to whether it exists or does not exist; but whether it is disposed in this way or not is within the power of free choice. Nor does it concern every future thing, but only those things which can both happen and not happen.

We must now see what it was like before sin. Four states of free choice may be considered in man. Before sin, nothing hindered him toward good and nothing compelled him toward evil. Then reason judged without error, and the will desired good without difficulty. After sin, however, before it has been restored through grace, it is pressed and overcome by concupiscence. After restoration, before the confirmation that will occur in the future, it is pressed but not overcome. [Col. 1130B] After confirmation, it can neither be pressed nor overcome.

There is a threefold freedom: from necessity, from sin, and from misery. It is equally free from necessity both before and after sin. As it could not then be compelled, so it cannot be compelled now. This freedom is equal in all, no less in the wicked than in the good; it is as complete after sin as before sin.

There is another freedom, namely freedom from sin, of which the Apostle says: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17). And elsewhere: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free in relation to righteousness . . . But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification” (Rom. 6:20). Man lost this freedom by sinning; and this is what Augustine means when he says: [Col. 1130C] “By misusing free choice, man lost both himself and it.” Freedom from necessity was not lost, but freedom from sin. “For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34). Only those who are restored through grace possess this freedom from sin—not because they are wholly without sin, but because sin does not rule them. This is what is properly called freedom.

In doing evil, free choice is not properly so called, because reason there disagrees with the will. Reason judges that what the will desires ought not to be done. In good, reason agrees with the will and serves it without contradiction. Hence Augustine says in the *Enchiridion* [Note: Col. 1129D: Ch. 30, no. 9; our newer editors think the reading should be *recti facti*, vol. VI, p. 207.]:

> This is true freedom because of the liberty of acting rightly, and pious servitude because of obedience to the command.
