Thus it is clear that in both good and evil the will is free from necessity, but only in good is it free from sin. Hence Augustine, in *On Grace and Free Choice* (ch. 15, no. 31): “The will is always free in us, but it is not always good. Either it is free from righteousness [read: free from righteousness], when it serves sin, and then it is evil; or it is free from sin when it serves righteousness, and then it is good.”

There is again freedom from misery, of which the Apostle says: “The creation itself will be freed from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:21). No one possesses this freedom in the present life. [Col. 1131A] One can indeed be free from sin in the present life, because, as we said above, although no one is without sin, yet once sin no longer reigns in a person, that person is free from sin. But no one in the present life will be freed from the penalty of sin.

## CHAPTER XXX. In what respect free choice was diminished through sin

From what has been said it is clear in what respect free choice was diminished through sin: then there was no difficulty in living rightly [read: willing rightly], no impediment from the law of the members to making progress. But before it has been freed from sin through grace, it can neither will nor accomplish good. It is as if we should say of someone in chains: “This person cannot [Col. 1131B] walk”—that is, he does not have this within his own power—and yet we grant: “It is possible for this person to walk,” because it may happen that he is released and walks.

The Apostle mentions this defect of ours when he says: “Willing lies close at hand for me, but I do not find the accomplishing of it” (Rom. 7:18). Unless it is freed through grace working within and awakening the heart, free choice itself cannot be raised toward good. Hence: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36). Even after he has set it free, unless it is helped by cooperating grace, it cannot accomplish good. Thus it now needs operative grace, by which it is freed, and cooperating grace, by which it is helped to merit; whereas before sin, as we said above, it needed cooperating grace alone. Before it fell, it did not need [Col. 1131C] a liberator, but a helper.

But the following objection is made. Before someone has restored free choice—that is, while he remains in sins—he has free choice. If he has free choice, he can be bent in either direction. Therefore free choice is not free; or, if it is free, then while he still remains in sins he [the person] can will good. Thus it seems that before grace is given he can will good.

But the matter is as with the person in chains: he cannot walk before being released; yet it is true in itself that “it is possible for him to walk,” or “he can walk,” in the same sense. Similarly, we do not deny of that sinner, pagan, or anyone else that it is possible for him to will good, [Col. 1131D] or that he can will good—but only in this sense: namely, if grace is given by which he is freed and which cooperates with him.

To will simply is one thing; to will good as good is another. To fear simply is one thing; to fear God is another. To love is one thing; to love God is another. Fear and love, stated simply, are affections; with the addition, they are virtues. To will belongs to us by nature; to will good, by grace. For simple affections are naturally in us, as from ourselves; the additions are from grace.

Hence Augustine, in *On Rebuke and Grace* [Col. 1132A]: “Some goods are great, some intermediate, some least. The virtues by which one lives rightly are great goods. The forms of all bodies, without which one can live rightly, are least goods.” [Note: Col. 1131D: “The virtues by which one lives rightly are great goods; the forms of all bodies, without which one can live rightly, are intermediate goods; but the powers of the mind, without which one cannot live rightly, are least goods.” Thus St Augustine, *On Free Choice*, bk. III, ch. 19, no. 50.]

The powers of the mind, without which one cannot live rightly, are intermediate goods. No one uses virtues badly; but everyone can use the other goods—that is, intermediate and least goods—not only well but badly. Therefore no one uses virtue badly, because the work of virtue is the good use of those things which we can also use badly. Free choice is found among intermediate goods, because we can also use it badly; but it is such that we cannot live rightly without it. Its good use, however, is already virtue, which is found among great goods, and no one can use these badly.

From this authority [Col. 1132B] it is clear that will is among intermediate goods, while good will is among great goods. Good will is not present in us by nature but by grace. Yet it may be said that even the wicked naturally will good, and thus it seems that before receiving grace someone has willing of good. But naturally willing good is nothing other than judging by reason that something is good—for example, when a tyrant says: “I would like to be a good monk, to leave the world,” and the like. He naturally desires good, but good does not delight him. Therefore one cannot properly say, “He wills good”; nor is such willing meritorious. Rather, it is willing accompanied by delight in good, when good pleases him and he has it in his intention.

Hence the Apostle says: “God is the one who works in us both willing and accomplishing [Col. 1132C] according to good will” (Phil. 2:13). Good will first exists by nature, but has no merit; afterward it becomes good through grace, and then it has merit.

Furthermore, it should be known that free choice is not so called because it is equally disposed toward both alternatives, namely good and evil. For of himself anyone can fall; but he cannot rise of himself unless he is helped by God’s grace. Free choice is sufficient of itself for evil, but not sufficient of itself for good. Even good angels are not without free choice, yet they are so confirmed that they cannot be evil. Likewise evil angels are not without free choice, although they are so obstinate that they cannot be good. Free choice is therefore called free [Col. 1132D] because it is voluntary.

That good angels cannot be evil is caused not by necessity but by a will confirmed through grace. That evil angels cannot be good is caused not by any compulsion, 1083 but by a will obstinate in evil. Yet both the one and the other are mutable. Hence Jerome: “God alone is one in whom sin cannot occur. All others, since they possess free choice, can be bent in either direction.”

It is also written of God that he has free choice. Ambrose, *To Gratian*: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3:8). The Apostle likewise [Col. 1133A] says: “The one and the same Spirit works all things, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11). “As he wills,” he says—that is, according to the choice of free will, not in obedience to necessity. In God there is no choice other than the divine will, which does all things not by necessity but by goodness. For goodness is his nature.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Why the sin of the first human being is imputed to his descendants

Having set forth the sin of the first human being and the penalty that he thereby incurred, we must see why it is imputed to his posterity. For all who descend from him through concupiscence are subject to that sin and are guilty, on its account, of original sin.

It may be said in answer that it is imputed to all because [Col. 1133B] all committed it. Hence the Apostle says: “In whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). This may be explained thus: “In him all sinned,” that is, they are held guilty in his sin. For, as the Apostle says: “Through the disobedience of one man many are made sinners” (ibid., 19). This is because they descend from him through the law of sin. It is not imputed to them because they were then originally in him, since Christ too, according to the flesh, was then in him. But because they descend through concupiscence arising from that sin, it may be said that sin is imputed to the whole posterity because they are conceived in the effect of this sin—that is, in the law of sin arising from it: namely, into concupiscence, theft, homicide, and so forth. These are not imputed to posterity because [Col. 1133C] generation itself does not take place according to their effects, that is, according to the motion proceeding from them.

The preceding question is commonly resolved by some as follows. That sin, and no other, is imputed to all descendants because the sin committed in paradise was most grave. Ignorance did not lead him into sin, nor weakness of the flesh, since before sin neither was in him. Therefore that sin was so great that it even changed nature. The whole nature of humankind was corrupted by that sin.

Augustine, *On the Greatness of God* [Note: Col. 1133D: What treatise this *On the Greatness of God* may be is not clear either from Possidius’s index or from any other catalogue of St Augustine’s works. I would have suspected a copyist’s error, by which he carelessly wrote *Dei* (“of God”) instead of *animae* (“of the soul”); but since the whole of *On the Greatness of the Soul* contains nothing relating to Adam’s sin, I judged that the reader would be sufficiently served if I noted that Augustine asserts in many places what Hildebert here says about the gravity of Adam’s sin, arising from the ease with which he could have resisted temptation. Thus in *On Rebuke and Grace*, ch. 12, no. 35: “Adam, with no one frightening him, and indeed against the command of God who warned him, used free choice and did not stand firm amid so great a happiness, [Col. 1134D] amid such ease in not sinning.” Likewise in bk. II of the *Unfinished Work against Julian*, no. 17: “It was very much within Adam’s freedom to abstain from that which he had wrongly desired, because there was not yet a vice by which the flesh might desire against the spirit . . . Not yet placed in the flesh of sin, he had need of no necessary aid from the likeness of sinful flesh.” Many similar passages could be brought forward; but these suffice to show the reader that Hildebert has asserted nothing except what he learned from St Augustine himself.]:

> That command was violated with so much the greater injustice as it could have been kept with easier observance. Desire did not yet resist the will, as afterward followed from the penalty of transgression.

Yet it does not seem that we should grant without qualification [Col. 1133D] that this sin was more grave than all others, since it is written: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age [Col. 1134A] nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32). But that sin is known to have been forgiven to the first parents, as authorities say. [Note: Col. 1134D: “Death is due to the flesh of sin.” St Augustine, *Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans*, no. 48.]

Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*: “Just as those first human beings, by afterward living rightly—whence they are deservedly believed to have been freed by the Lord’s blood from final punishment—nevertheless did not merit in that life to be restored to paradise; so also the flesh of sin, even if, after sins have been forgiven, a person lives rightly in it, does not immediately deserve not to suffer the death which it has drawn from the propagation of sin.”

The claim that all were in Adam is commonly opposed as follows. If all who descended from Ham were in Adam through the substance Ham received from the first parents, they existed there. But [Col. 1134B] in the small portion propagated in Cain [read: Ham], there were not as many atoms as there were human beings descended from him. Therefore it does not seem true that each person’s substance existed in the first parent.

One may answer that, although that portion was at first very small, it increased and became great—namely, as great as it will be at the resurrection—without any external substance passing into it. For it has leaven from foods, but foods do not pass into human substance itself. This can be proved as follows. A child who dies on the day of his birth will rise in the stature he would have possessed had he lived to full age, with no illness or bodily defect preventing him. Thus it is apparent that even if he had lived, the parts of that substance would not have been taken from elsewhere but would have increased within themselves, as did the rib from which the woman was made and the five evangelical loaves.

Yet we do not deny that foods pass both into humours and into flesh, whence some persons are stouter than they ought to be. But this excess will not be present at the resurrection, because it does not belong to the truth of human nature. [Col. 1134C] The “truth of human substance” [read: nature] means what existed in the first parents; that alone will be present at the resurrection. But those parts made from foods, into which food passes, will be cast off as superfluous.

## CHAPTER XXXII. What original sin is

Next we must inquire what original sin is [Col. 1134D] and why it is called original. Some say that original sin is the debt by which all are bound on account of the sin of the first human being, because eternal punishment is due for it unless they are freed through grace. They say that original sin is not sin; but if Scripture at times calls it sin, they maintain that sin there is put for the punishment of sin. And just as children sometimes go into exile for a parent’s sin according to secular justice, so all are held guilty for that sin according to God’s justice.

Thus, according to them, there is no sin in the soul of a child, because they say: “If it has never sinned, there is no sin in it.” Yet they grant that original sin is in it, because it is bound by the debt of sin. But they plainly speak against the Apostle, when he says: “Through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners” (Rom. 5:19). Behold: the Apostle calls them sinners before they are regenerated. [Col. 1135B] But if, as they say, there were only the punishment of sin in these persons before guilt, they would not be sinners. Again the Apostle says: “Through one human being death entered into the world, and death through sin” (ibid., 12). The Apostle’s words indicate one sin that entered and another thing, namely punishment itself.

Others say that original sin is disobedience, and that this disobedience is in all before they are reborn. But it does not seem that a child is disobedient, since it has never been commanded anything. How can one who cannot yet use reason be called either obedient or disobedient? For disobedience belongs to the will; and just as obedience is voluntary, so too is disobedience. But original sin is not voluntary.

Leaving these views aside, original [Col. 1135C] sin may be called desire for evil and ignorance of good. Hence Augustine, in *On Rebuke and Grace*: “There are two penal things in every human being: ignorance and difficulty. From ignorance comes error, so that one may approve false things as true; from difficulty comes torment.” [Note: Col. 1135D: “There are indeed these two penal things in every sinning soul: ignorance and difficulty. From ignorance error brings disgrace; from difficulty torment afflicts.” St Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*, ch. 67, no. 81.] Thus, through the resistance and torment of the pain of carnal bondage, persons cannot refrain from lust.

But an objection may be raised: since the soul of a child does not yet will or refuse anything, how does it have desire for evil? Yet just as the defect of blindness exists in the eye of a blind person at night but does not appear, and one cannot distinguish between a sighted and a blind person until daylight comes, so there is a defect in the child but it does not appear. When the time arrives at which it ought to desire good and be ignorant of evil, it is ignorant of [Col. 1135D] good and desires evil.

Again it is objected: original sin is remitted in baptism; but after baptism the desire for evil remains, and so on. Therefore it does not seem that original sin is remitted by baptism. But, as Augustine says [Note: Col. 1135D: “So long as the law of concupiscence remains in the members, its guilt is dissolved, though it itself remains; but it is dissolved for the one who has received the sacrament of regeneration.” Thus St Augustine, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, bk. II, ch. 28, no. 45; likewise repeatedly elsewhere.], although concupiscence remains after baptism, it does not remain as to guilt, because it is not imputed to those who have been reborn. This is the remission of original sin: that it is not imputed. Although concupiscence of the flesh is in the baptized person, it is not imputed unless the person follows after the concupiscences. If that occurs, it is no longer original but actual sin.

Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence* [Col. 1136A]: “From this concupiscence, which, though it is no longer reckoned as sin in the regenerate, every offspring is born bound by original sin.” And shortly afterward: “Concupiscence of the flesh is forgiven in baptism, not so that it does not exist, but so that it is not imputed as sin. For this is not to have sin: not to be guilty of sin.” Again: “Just as other sins have passed away in act but remain in guilt, such as homicide and the like, so conversely it can occur that concupiscence has passed away in guilt and remains in act.”

From these authorities it is clear that desire for evil is original sin, under which ignorance of good is included. Hence original sin is sometimes found in the plural in Holy Scripture, because, as we said, one of these things comes from the other [Col. 1136B] and is therefore contained under and within it.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Why it is called original

After this we must see why that sin is called original. It is so called because it is contracted from the origin, that is, from parents. For when someone is generated, that sin itself is transmitted. Hence David: “My mother conceived me in sins” (Ps. 50:6).

The following objection may be made. When [a human being] is generated, only flesh is drawn from the parents through propagation; for, as we showed above, souls do not come through propagation. Moreover, through the propagation of flesh the soul is not yet infused, as natural philosophers say, but only when the body has already been formed. Moses clearly shows this in Exodus: “If someone strikes a woman [Col. 1136C] and causes a miscarriage, if it is still unformed, he shall be fined money; but if it has been formed, he shall render life for life” (Exod. 21:22). “Formed” is understood as ensouled.

And if sin is transmitted from parents in the very propagation, Gregory says, it seems that original sin belongs to that which is propagated. But it is still without a soul, and every sin belongs to the soul. How, then, can sin exist in that seed? For just as every virtue is in the soul, so too every sin.

One may answer that not only the soul is subject to the bond of sin. Gregory: “But the flesh also”—not because that sin is in the flesh, but because the soul contracts it from the corruption of the flesh. Unless flesh were propagated in [Col. 1136D] concupiscence, the soul would not be bound by that sin. Hence Christ is said not to have had sinful flesh, but flesh like sinful flesh, because that flesh was propagated from his mother not through a man’s concupiscence but through the operation of the Holy Spirit. All others have sinful flesh, not because sin is in the flesh but because it is the cause of sin.

Augustine, *On Faith to Peter*: “When husband and wife unite with one another in order to beget children, the parents’ intercourse is not without lust.” [Note: Col. 1136D: “When spouses do not abstain, they demand from one another the debt of the flesh, not from a will for offspring but from pleasure in lust; nevertheless, this pleasure does not fall into guilt because of marriage, but receives pardon because of marriage.” Bk. I, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, ch. 14, no. 16.] “For this reason the conception of children born from the same flesh cannot be without sin, [Col. 1137A] in which it is not propagation but lust that transmits sin to infants.”

It is therefore clear that original sin is transmitted in conception itself, because unless conception occurred in flesh in this manner, the soul would not contract concupiscence from the union of flesh.

If it is asked what that corruption is, which we said exists in the flesh—whether it is sin or not—it may be called sin, that is, the punishment of sin. But if we take “sin” in its usual sense, namely guilt, that corruption in the flesh will not itself be called sin. That it is a corruption of sin may be known from its effect, just as a defect is known to be in a vessel because it makes wine sour.

Again it is commonly asked: since someone’s parents have been cleansed of original sin through baptism, how can a child contract that sin from them? [Note: Col. 1138D: This was Julian the Pelagian’s objection against the transmission of original sin; Augustine answers it at length in various places.] Augustine [Col. 1137B] shows this in *On the Baptism of Infants* by the following comparisons. How does the foreskin which is removed by circumcision remain in one begotten by circumcised persons? How does chaff, which is separated by human labor with such force, nevertheless remain in the grain born from purified wheat? So sin, which is cleansed through baptism, remains in those begotten by the baptized. Again, in the same work: “For what begets is that which still contracts oldness, not that by which it has advanced in newness among the children of God. Parents do not generate children according to that generation by which they have been born anew, but rather according to that by which they themselves were first carnally generated.”

Furthermore, it is commonly asked by what justice an innocent soul [Col. 1137C] created by God is held bound by that sin, when it is not within its power to avoid it. For it is not within the power of free choice to avoid it or not, since the soul does not yet use free choice and is not in that body before it is subject to the sin.

Some resolve this as follows: that soul, although it does not come by propagation but is newly created clean by God, becomes guilty of the sin because, when it is infused into the body, it finds that body suited and disposed to sin; it delights in this, and from such delight contracts the sin. But if this were so, it ought to be called actual, not original, sin. For if this sin arises from delight, it is not another’s but belongs to one’s own will, whereas Augustine and others call [Col. 1137D] it another’s.

Augustine, in *On the Baptism of Infants*: “It is clear that some sins are proper to each individual, in which only those whose sins they are commit sin; but there is that one other sin in which all sinned.” Therefore we think it must be said that God’s justice is hidden, by which the soul is held guilty of that sin which it cannot avoid and which it has not committed by its own will. For, as the Apostle says: “The judgments of God are incomprehensible, and his ways unsearchable” (Rom. 11:13).

It is also commonly asked whether that sin is voluntary or necessary [Col. 1138A]. That it is not voluntary is clear from what has been said above. Again, if it is called necessary, it ought not to be imputed. Therefore some wish to say that it is neither voluntary nor necessary. Yet the Prophet says: “Deliver me from my necessities” (Ps. 24:17). Hence it seems absurd that it should not be called necessary [read: that it should be called necessary].

For if someone asks: since God, who made the soul immaculate, knows that it will contract the stain of sin from the body and, before death separates it from the body, be damned—why does he join it to the body? We give the same answer as above: namely, that God’s justice is hidden.

Some commonly object as follows. When the soul is created in the body, and is not in the body before it is held by that sin, then as soon as it exists it has the stain of sin. Therefore it is never such as it is created by God to be. For it is created innocent by God but is never innocent, since it is stained as soon as it exists. But there is no contradiction: God creates it clean—that is, it has no stain from its creation—and thus, as regards creation, it is such as God creates it. It is always good and clean as regards creation. [Col. 1138B]

Furthermore, it is commonly asked whether all souls are equal by creation, or whether some are more excellent than others, as was the case among angels. It seems probable to many that, from creation itself, no soul is more capable than another of understanding or retaining things in memory. The following objection is made: if they depart from the body before baptism, they have equal punishment; if immediately after baptism, equal crowns. Thus it appears that in their creation they are indifferent. But, as we have already said in the treatise *On Free Choice*, things arising from the first creation, such as intelligence and memory, make one neither less blessed nor worthy of punishment. [Col. 1138C]

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On actual sins

Having spoken of original sin, it seems proper to speak of actual sins. First, we must observe that they are not imputed to descendants, according to Ezekiel: “This proverb shall no longer be in Israel: ‘The fathers ate sour grapes and the children’s teeth were set on edge.’ The soul that sins shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. 18:2).

The statement in Exodus seems contrary: “I will repay the iniquity of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me” (Exod. 20:5). But, as Jerome says, this refers to children who imitate their fathers’ evils, as the conclusion of the authority indicates: “of those who hate me.” If the son does not imitate the sins of his father, he is not punished for them.

An objection is raised: if this is to be understood of imitators, why is it said only [Col. 1139A] to the third and fourth generation, when all who imitate their fathers’ sins, in however remote a generation, are liable for them? The saints resolve this thus: it was said “to the third and fourth” because it is more usual for children to imitate their fathers’ deeds up to the fourth generation, when these deeds are still known to them and, as it were, present.

Augustine interprets this as temporal punishment, because children are often punished temporally in vengeance upon their parents for their parents’ sins: they may be born blind, become blind or lame after birth, or suffer any other punishment. But in the future, as the Apostle says: “Each person shall bear his own burden” (Gal. 6:5).

Jerome, commenting on Ezekiel, says that in us the prompting of the flesh is like a father; the first son is like [Col. 1139B] the first movement of awareness toward sin, and this is the first offspring. The grandson comes if one decides to act, or completes the act in deed; the great-grandson, if one not only does evil but also glories in one’s crime. This is the fourth generation—not because three generations precede it, but it is called four because it occupies fourth place after the first motion, which is posited as a kind of father.

Therefore God does not punish the first and second impulse—that is, the initial awarenesses, without which sin cannot occur—with damnation. But he punishes the third and fourth generation, because these are sins unto death. To prove that the first motion is not punished: when Ham sinned by mocking his father’s nakedness, it was not he who laughed but his son who received the sentence. “Cursed,” he says, “be Canaan; he shall be a slave [Vulgate: ‘a slave of slaves’—Col. 1139C] to his brothers” (Gen. 9:25). For what justice would there be in the father’s sin and the pronouncement of sentence against the son, unless this occurred as such a signification?

## CHAPTER XXXV. What is the cause of sin?

We have set forth the difference between original and actual sin. Now we must discuss sin generally. Four questions must be examined: what is the cause of sin; what is called sin and in what thing it exists; and in what ways it is said to occur. The cause of every sin is a will turning away from God.

Augustine [Note: Col. 1139D: *Enchiridion*, ch. 23, no. 8]: “The cause of all good things is God’s goodness; but the cause of evil things is the mutable will turning away from God”—first that of the angel, then that of the human being [Col. 1139D].

## CHAPTER XXXVI. What sin is
If it is asked what sin and evil are, one may answer: Nothing, according to the saying: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). For, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1139D] *Confessions*, book III, ch. 7, §12]: Evil is nothing other than the privation 1091 of good. Therefore evil is not something, but the privation of something [Note: [Col. 1139D] “Everything called evil is nothing other than corruption.” St Augustine, *Against the Letter of Manichaeus*, ch. 35, §39.].

For whatever exists is either a work of God or a work of a human being imitating [Col. 1140A] God. Now a human being does nothing when, through sin, he withdraws from God. That may be called the work of a human being imitating God in which, by acting, the human being does not withdraw from God—for example, building a house and the like. But if we wish to weigh this matter more subtly, it may be said that whatever exists is a work of God. For God works in two ways: some things directly, such as natural things; some through his servants, such as artificial things. Therefore, since he makes those things through his servants, it is clear that he himself makes them. Hence it may be said that whatever exists is God’s work; but evil is not God’s work, and therefore is not anything.

But if evil is not anything, how can it corrupt good? Abstaining from food is not a substance, yet the substance of the body, if it altogether abstains from food, languishes and is broken down. Thus sin [Col. 1140B] is not a substance; but God is substance and the true food of the rational creature.

But since evil is called the privation of good, it must be considered of what good it is the privation. To see this, one must note that “good” is said in different ways. God is the highest good, and every good, whose essence is goodness. For him, being good is the same as existing. Therefore, just as he cannot fail to exist, since he lacks beginning and end, so he cannot fail to be good, since his essence is goodness; and consequently there can be no privation of this good.

Creatures are called good by participation, and therefore can be deprived of their good. And just as there are two kinds of creature, spiritual and bodily, so the creature’s good is twofold. The good of the spiritual creature is one thing; that of the bodily creature another.

[Col. 1140C] The good of the spiritual creature consists in two things: knowledge of truth and love of virtue. The good of the bodily creature is either within it or outside it. Its good within itself is the soundness of its senses and faculties, according to the five senses. Its good outside itself is the ordered distribution among creatures. For what is corrupted or improved exists for the sake of human beings; and whatever is good or evil is good or evil for human beings. Therefore the good of human beings is threefold. One good is outside them, namely that which exists in creatures; another is within them—and of that, one part is in the soul and another in the body. Thus evils too are threefold.

For, universally, the privation of any good is called evil, whether it be the good that is in the body or the good that is in creatures. But although each of these is an evil, one is fault, another punishment and not fault, and another is neither fault nor punishment but tends toward punishment. For corruption of that good which is in the soul is both sin and fault. For by the incorruption of this 1092 good we are united to God; by its corruption we are removed from God. As we have said, the soul’s good consists principally in two things: knowledge of truth and love of virtue. The corruption of knowledge may be called ignorance. Of this the Apostle says: “If anyone is ignorant, he shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14:38). The corruption of love is covetousness, which “is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10). And the more [Col. 1141A] this ignorance and covetousness increase, the more the soul’s good is corrupted, and in this respect the soul is said to be corrupted. For, since the soul is an incorporeal substance, it cannot be corrupted in its substance, but only in the good in which it participates.

Here one may ask in what further respect the soul can be corrupted once it lacks those two things, namely knowledge of truth and love of virtue. For when the substance itself and vice are present there, as in demons and wicked human beings, if it sins again, the corruption of what good will that sin be said to be? For there is no other good there except nature itself, which has been deformed; but this cannot be corrupted in its essence, because it is simple and incorporeal. Nor is there in it [Col. 1141B] a virtue capable of being corrupted. From what, then, can it be deprived? For after an eye has once been deprived of sight, it cannot be deprived of that sight again.

One may answer that the more it loves injustice, the more it is deprived of justice—not by losing justice, which it does not possess, but by losing its capacity to recover it, which is certainly a good. For the more unjust a person is, the further he departs from justice. The same applies in other cases. Just as a sick person, the more severely he falls ill, is the more deprived of health—not by losing health, which he does not have, but because he is further removed from it. Those natural goods which the soul still possesses—reason, intelligence, memory, and so forth—are likewise more worn away and darkened the more the soul is deformed by sins.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. In What Nature Sin Exists

[Col. 1141C]

It now seems necessary to say in what nature sin is said to exist: whether in the spiritual, the bodily, or both. But, as we have already said, not every corruption of good is sin, but only the corruption of that good which belongs to the spiritual nature. It is therefore clear that fault or sin can exist only in spiritual nature. Nor do we deny that there is evil in bodily nature. Thus the prophet says: “Is there evil in a city which the Lord has not done?” (Amos 3:6). But he calls punishment, 1093 not fault, evil—such as infirmities and things of that kind.

And since every nature, whether bodily or spiritual, is good, it is evident that evil cannot exist [Col. 1141D] except where good exists. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1141D] He states the same point in the passage cited above, *Against the Letter of Manichaeus*, ch. 35, §39. See *On the Grace of Christ*, 18, [Col. 1142D] §19]: Nothing called evil is not at the same time good; nor can evil exist unless something good exists. Again Augustine: What is a wicked human being but an evil nature? But if a human being is a nature, and thus is in some respect good because he is a nature, what is a wicked human being but an evil good? Good insofar as he is human; evil insofar as he is unjust. Therefore whoever says that it is evil to be human, or good to be unjust, falls into the assertion: “Good is evil, and evil is good” (Isa. 5:20).

Here one must consider whether evil acts ought to be called sins or not. Some say that all acts [Col. 1142A] are indifferent, so that in themselves they are called neither good nor evil; but an act is called good because it is done with a good intention, evil because with an evil intention. Thus to kill a person out of zeal for justice is good, but out of hatred evil; in itself it is neither good nor evil. Hence Ambrose: “Let your disposition give its name to your work.”

Some oppose this opinion thus: if every act is indifferent, then adultery and perjury are also indifferent; but these acts cannot be anything but evil. Therefore not every act is indifferent. They explain this as follows. “To commit adultery” and “to commit perjury” denote not only the act but also the vice; therefore, although these are not indifferent, the acts themselves—namely, intercourse with a woman and swearing—are nevertheless indifferent. Accordingly, on this view acts are not sins. Nor is killing a person called an evil act because it is sin, but because it proceeds from an evil intention. The same applies in other cases.

Yet it may properly be said that an evil action is sin, in this sense: to kill a person is sin, that is, an act of sin. For, as Augustine says, two things are considered in sin: act and liability. The act lies in the deed; liability in the will. Thus in the sin which is homicide, the liability is the very injustice or vice of the will. So long as that remains, the person is guilty whether the act occurs, has not yet occurred, or has already passed. By customary usage and the language of Scripture, both are called homicide; they are not two sins or two homicides, but one and the same thing, though in different modes—namely, in will and in act.

For evil is spoken of in two ways: substantively [Col. 1142C] and actively [perhaps: adjectivally]. The corruption or privation of good occurring in the soul is not only evil, but is evil itself, that is, wickedness, such as injustice and the like. An action is called evil, not because it is evil itself, but because it displays evil.

## 1094 CHAPTER XXXVIII. What Are the Modes of Sinning, or the Ways in Which Sin Is Committed

Sin is committed in two ways, as Isidore says: by covetousness and by fear—when a person either wishes to obtain what he desires or fears that he may incur what he dreads. Again, a human being sins against himself, against God, and against his neighbour. What is done against God is called an offence (*delictum*), for example perjury and unworthy participation in the sacraments. These sins are said to be committed against God because in them contempt of God is greater. Other sins committed against ourselves or our neighbours are called not offences but sins.

An offence is also so called when we fail to do what we are commanded; a sin, when we do what is forbidden. The two are not used interchangeably, one for the other.

Again, as Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1142D] Book XXIII on Job, ch. 17], there are seven capital vices, from which all other evils arise. For there is none that has not arisen from one of them. Pride is the love of one’s own excellence. It is not a vice that we love excellence, but that we strive to arrogate to ourselves [Col. 1143A] by participation that good thing, namely excellence, as though it were our own exclusive possession.

There are four kinds of pride, as Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1143D] Book XXIII on Job, ch. 4]. The first is when a person attributes to himself the good which he possesses. The second, when he believes it has been given by God, yet regards it as given on account of his own merits. The third is when he boasts of possessing what he does not possess. The fourth is when, despising others, he wishes to appear singularly distinguished. This final kind comes closer to the devil, who wished to be above the angels.

From pride, in the first place, arises envy, which is hatred of another’s happiness. For when the proud person sees his neighbour either equal to him in the same good or exalted above him, he begins to envy him; and from a slight injury he is stirred to anger against his neighbour. Anger is impatience under inward pain. These three strip a person of every inward good. For three things are to be loved: God, [Col. 1143B] one’s neighbour, and oneself. Pride takes away God; envy, one’s neighbour; anger, oneself.

Then follows sloth (*acedia*), which is confusion of mind or inward sadness. Since the human mind cannot live without some joy, after losing inward joy it wanders out to external things. This gives rise to avarice, which is an immoderate love of possessing. And when it already delights in external things, it first delights in the vice closest to nature, namely gluttony, which is an immoderate love of eating; and then in lust, which is the appetite for libidinous pleasure.

1095 The remaining vices are placed under pride, not because they are predicated of it, but because they are set after it as the mother of the others. For pride is the root of all evils. But again it is read: “Covetousness is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 4:10); therefore it is also the root of pride, and pride is consequently not the root of all evils. One may answer that pride and avarice become one thing when pride is love of one’s own excellence. For, as Augustine says: “What person is more avaricious than one for whom God is not enough?” Or it may be said that pride is the root of all evils, that is, of evil dispositions; covetousness is the root of all evils, that is, of evil actions.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. What the Difference Is among the Virtues

Seven virtues, produced by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, are set against those seven vices. The difference between gifts and virtues is this: gifts are the first movements in the heart, like certain seeds of virtues cast upon the soil of our heart; virtues [Col. 1143D] are like the crop that rises from them. For they are effects of gifts and certain good habits now established; and the seven gifts are called the seven spirits. Hence in the Apocalypse (ch. 5) John saw seven spirits moving before the throne of God. The “spirits” are called the inspirations that precede virtues; they are gifts only, not merits. Virtues, however, are both gifts and merits. For in the former God works without us; in the latter he works with us.

From fear, which is the beginning of wisdom, humility is born; from the spirit [Col. 1144A] of piety, gentleness is born; and so through each of those things enumerated there: “Blessed are the poor” (Matt. 5:3), etc.

Here it should be observed that, as Augustine says, there are four kinds of fear: servile, worldly, initial, and filial. Servile fear causes one to refrain from evil because of punishment threatened by a human being, while retaining the will to do evil. Worldly fear is refraining from good because of punishment feared from a human being, as occurred in Peter. There is also divine fear: fearing God because of present or hellish punishment, yet fearing God without love of good. It contains anguish and the torment of punishment, which belong to the wicked; and this fear is servile.

But if a person fears with an accompanying delight in good, fear is initial; and this fear is the beginning of wisdom, when a person begins to have wisdom and to taste God, where fear and [Col. 1144B] hope accompany one another [Note: [Col. 1143D] “Unless a person begins to worship God in fear, he will not attain love.” St Augustine, on Psalm 149; and shortly afterward: “You have begun from fear; you will be brought to completion in wisdom.”]. Hence it is read: Fear 1096 is not without hope. The more good will—that is, charity—increases, the more fear of punishment decreases. But if love alone is present, fear becomes filial and chaste, and remains for ever and ever.

It is therefore clear that initial fear is not in charity—not, I mean, in perfect charity—but in incipient charity. Hence John says in his Epistle: “Perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4:18), namely initial fear; thereby he indicates that, although charity in initial fear is not yet perfect, it is nevertheless charity. Christ prohibits servile and worldly fear when he says: “Do not fear those who kill only the body and have nothing they can do to the soul” (Matt. 10:28). Afterwards he adds concerning initial [Col. 1144C] fear: “But fear him who can cast body and soul into hell” (ibid.). He would not command this unless charity, though not yet perfect, were present in it.

It should be noted that this fear is sometimes called servile in divine Scripture, because its disposition is servile, and because in both it and the other fear there is fear of punishment. But that fear makes one cease from an evil deed, not from the will to commit it; this one makes one cease both in deed and will. Bede, commenting on the parables, says that both fears will cease in the future. This seems contrary to the Psalmist’s statement: “The holy fear of the Lord, enduring for ever and ever” (Ps. 18:10). But Bede’s statement may be explained thus: both fears will cease—that is, both fearful dispositions: the disposition of initial fear, namely fear of being punished. The disposition of filial [Col. 1144D] fear is fear of being separated.

Augustine: Chaste fear loves freely, fearing not punishment but separation [Note: [Col. 1143D] “Chaste fear is that by which one fears offending the person loved. For an adulteress fears her husband differently from a chaste wife: the adulteress fears that he may come; the chaste wife, that he may leave.” Augustine, on Psalm 118, sermon 12, §4.]. For the perfect do not fear punishment by the punishment of hell, but separation in the present through some punishment. In the future, however, they will fear neither punishment nor separation; yet there will be fear there, but reverence [perhaps: “but reverence itself”]. For they will attend to two things in God himself: majesty and mercy. From majesty comes reverence; from mercy, love. Thus they will fear his majesty—that is, they will be subject to him with reverence [Note: [Col. 1144D] Here there appears to be a gap, which might perhaps be supplied in the author’s sense as follows: “They will experience his mercy and love him.”].

[Col. 1145A] It is customary to ask whether both fears existed in Christ. That filial fear existed in him is clear: according to his humanity, he showed reverence to God. Initial fear, as some say, did not exist in him. For John says concerning him in his Epistle: “Perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). But who doubts that Christ possessed charity in the highest perfection? Again, initial fear is fear of hell; but Christ did not fear hell, for he was exempt from every sin. Hence he was certain that those punishments could in no way overtake him.

But it is objected that Isaiah enumerates the seven gifts as having existed in him, saying: “The spirit of 1097 wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him … and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11:3). But, as they say, [Col. 1145B] what belongs to the members is attributed to Christ. For Christ did not possess that gift in himself, but in his body. Again, they object that in Christ there was the fullness of all gifts; therefore this gift also. They answer this as follows: Christ did not possess every individual gift, since he did not possess repentance for sins, which nevertheless is a gift of God. Yet he possessed the fullness of all gifts because nothing necessary to perfection was lacking to him. But if he had possessed initial fear, or repentance, or similar things—which, although gifts, belong to the imperfect—they would undoubtedly not have conferred perfection but would have provided the beginning of a perfect life.

Others hold that the gift which is initial fear was in Christ, though one should not therefore believe that initial fear was in Christ. For fear of the Lord is one of the seven gifts, not two; but it has two effects. According to one it is called initial; according to the other it is called chaste and filial. According to this latter effect it was in Christ. Therefore the gift which is initial fear in others was in him, yet initial fear was not in Christ, because Christ did not have fear according to that effect. So there are two people, one of whom has imperfect faith and the other perfect and steadfast faith: we say they have one faith, one virtue. It does not follow that, if they have the same faith and one has it imperfectly, the other also has it imperfectly. And this seems more probable than what we said previously.

Nevertheless, some concede these statements: Christ possessed [Col. 1145D] initial fear and feared hell, yet was certain that it could not overtake him—just as someone placed in a high tower fears a precipice with a certain horror, though he is certain that he will not fall.

## CHAPTER XL. On the Sacraments

Against sins, both original and actual, of which we have now spoken, remedies of the sacraments have been devised. Three points concerning them must be considered: what a sacrament is, why it was instituted, and in what it consists.

Augustine: A sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing; that is, a sacrament is a visible form of invisible grace. Thus in the sacrament of baptism the washing away of vices is signified through that visible outward washing. [Col. 1146A] For every sacrament ought to have a 1098 likeness of the thing of which it is a sacrament. Hence Augustine: “If sacraments did not possess some likeness of the things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all.”

An objection is made that the foregoing definition does not apply only to sacraments, since before any signification it belongs to water to be a visible form of invisible grace: just as bodily stains are removed by water, so stains of the soul are removed by grace. But if it is to belong to sacraments alone, it must be understood in this way: a sacrament is a visible form of invisible grace bestowed in it—that is, grace which the sacrament itself confers. For it is not only the sign of a sacred thing but also an efficacious cause. This is the difference between a sign [Col. 1146B] and a sacrament: for a thing to be a sign, it requires nothing except that it signify that of which it is asserted to be a sign; it need not confer it. A sacrament, however, not only signifies but also confers that of which it is the sign.

Again, this is the difference: a sign may exist only for signification, even though it lacks likeness, such as a circle indicating wine [for sale]. But a sacrament signifies by institution and also represents by likeness. For, as we have already said, a sacrament must always have some likeness to the thing of which it is called the sacrament. It should also be known that in Sacred Scripture *sacrament* is sometimes called a sacred and mystical reality, such as the sacrament of the Incarnation.

Next, one must consider why sacraments were instituted. [Col. 1146C] They were instituted for three reasons: instruction, humiliation, and exercise. For instruction: because before sin a human being possessed knowledge of truth and could then see God without a mediator, but was blinded by pride. In order to return to knowledge, these visible things are necessary, by which the mind is instructed to understand invisible things.

For humiliation: because the rational creature was of such dignity that its good was not itself but only that which is the highest good, whereas for other things their own being is their good, as for a stone or wood. Before sin, in order to attain that good, nothing else was necessary except to desire it. For if a person desired it, he would know it to be his good; and if he knew it to be his good, he would know it to be better than himself, because whatever is the good of another and lies outside that other is better than it. And if he knew it to be better than himself, he would subject himself to it and possess it through this desire, because rational nature has such freedom that it can never possess that good unless it wills it. Hence it alone comes into judgment.

But through pride a human being lost that good; through humility he must recover it. Yet it is not enough 1099 in this one respect to be humbled by being subjected to God, because that too was required before sin; after sin one must do more. Therefore sacraments were instituted, so that we may be subject not only to God but also to an inferior nature: in these things a human being seeks salvation, though not from these things. For it is a great display of humility to seek salvation in visible things much inferior to the human being [Col. 1147A].

They were instituted for exercise because a human being cannot be without exercise. Thus, being removed from evil and superfluous exercise, one might be exercised in good; God instituted sacraments and their appointed places, so that Mass may be heard in church, confession made there to a priest, and the like.

There are three kinds of exercise. One pertains to the building up of the soul, the second to the body, the third to the destruction of the soul. God enjoined the first, permitted the second, and prohibited the third. A sacrament consists in three things: things, actions, and words—things such as water and oil; actions such as submersion or immersion and breathing upon; words such as invocation [Col. 1147B] of the Trinity.

Here one may ask: since human salvation consists especially in these sacraments, why were they not instituted from the beginning—so that from the beginning there might have been the sacrament of baptism, confirmation, and so on? One may answer that, just as the knowledge of faith gradually increased over intervals of time, so it was fitting then that the sacraments should be obscure; now, because it has come into the light, they are manifest. For although circumcision and baptism are signs of the same grace, inwardly freeing from sin, this is more clearly signified in baptism, “which washes the whole body [Note: [Col. 1147D] For various rites of baptism, see our Martène, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, book I, ch. 1, art. 14, §5 and following. There he treats at length of the various immersions, their rite and number, which he considers to have been everywhere in use until approximately the thirteenth century; before that, he believes that infusion or affusion was neither permitted nor customary except in cases of extreme necessity. This passage from Hildebert [Col. 1148D] supports his view that candidates for baptism were immersed naked in the baptistery with their whole bodies. How, and with what care, propriety for both sexes was then observed in administering this sacrament of baptism, he discusses there at length and with complete learning from the best authorities; to transcribe them here might perhaps have wearied the reader.],” than in circumcision, which removed only a small portion of one member.

Therefore from the beginning of the world, both in the period of natural law and in the period of written law, remedies of the sacraments existed against original and actual sins [Col. 1147C]. First there were sacrifices, such as the offerings of Abel, Noah, and the other faithful. Afterwards there were not only sacrifices but also circumcision, which was commanded in Abraham’s time.

Gregory the Younger: What baptismal water accomplishes among us, that among the ancients was accomplished either, for infants, by faith alone; for adults, by faith in sacrifice; or, for those descended from Abraham’s stock, by the ministry of circumcision.

But since sacrifices were also offered for infants, 1100 how can Gregory’s statement, “For infants, faith alone,” be true? One may answer that by “alone” sacrifices are not excluded; rather, “faith alone” means bare faith, though veiling mysteries, among infants—that is, among those to whom no revelation had been made [Col. 1147D] of the future Incarnation. For adults there was the efficacy of sacrifice, because the perfect, to whom the mystery of the Incarnation had been revealed, understood the efficacy of sacrifices—that is, what those sacrifices signified.

Circumcision was commanded for Abraham. It was performed on the eighth day, and the foreskin was [Col. 1148A] perhaps removed with stone knives. It was commanded because it was instituted as a remedy against original sin, which we contract from our parents, being begotten in concupiscence, which rules more strongly in that member. Circumcision of the flesh signified circumcision of the mind, by which the soul is cleansed from vices. It was performed on the eighth day because the eighth signifies the resurrection that shall be after this life, which revolves through seven days. There will be perfect circumcision, because the flesh will be freed from the servitude of corrupt humanity.

Therefore that sacrament had a twofold circumcision: circumcision from sins, which is in the soul; and circumcision from both sins and every punishment of sins, which will occur in the resurrection, in both soul and body. Thus there are three circumcisions: the first is the sacrament, and two are [Col. 1148B] realities of that sacrament. The stone knives signified Christ, of whom the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10), who “takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

It is asked concerning women what remedy they possessed against sin. Answer: faith, sacraments, and offerings. It is also customary to ask concerning infants who died before the eighth day what remedy they possessed, or whether they were damned. Bede seems to say that they were damned, when he says: He who now cries out terribly and savingly through the Gospel, “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5), formerly cried out through his law: “The male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised, that soul shall perish [Col. 1148C] from his people, because he has made void my covenant” (Gen. 17:14). But it seems better to leave this to God’s judgment than rashly to define anything.

It is asked what difference exists between circumcision and baptism with respect to efficacy. 1101 Bede: Circumcision under the law rendered the same aid of saving healing against the wound of original sin which baptism now customarily renders in the time of revealed grace, except that they could not yet enter the gate of the kingdom. After death they were consoled only by blessed rest in Abraham’s bosom, and awaited in happy hope their entrance into heavenly peace.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the Ten Commandments, or the Written Law

[Col. 1148D]

Having stated what remedies against sins existed before the law, it remains to see what was added by the law itself. On this matter the following must be considered: why it was given, to whom, when, and where. The written law was given in order to restore the natural law and cause it to live again, since through sin it had become obsolete [Col. 1149A], and in order to prepare a rude people by legal figures for future truth. It accomplished the first through the natural Ten Commandments; the second through figurative matters, such as the Paschal lamb and the like.

To whom was it given? To Abraham’s seed in the twelve tribes which descended from Israel’s twelve sons.

Here one may ask why it was given only to these. One may answer that it was given to that people and not another because it was set forth as a figure. Hence the Apostle says: “All things happened to them in a figure” (1 Cor. 10:11). It was sufficient to show in one people what God proposed for the sake of figure and example. But the new law is commanded to all, because it was not a figure but the reality itself that had been prefigured.

Since among that people some were perfect, some middling, and some utterly wicked, the law was given to the perfect as a sign; [Col. 1149B] to the middling as a pedagogue, to teach what ought to be done, forbid what ought to be avoided, and correct errors by punishing them; to the wicked it was given by the angry Judge as vengeance, so that whoever is filthy might become filthier still. Conversely, it was provided for the good by a loving Father, so that whoever is just might be justified still further.

When was it given? On the fiftieth day after the departure from Egypt and the immolation of the Paschal lamb. Likewise the new law was given 1102 to the apostles—that is, the Spirit writing upon the heart—on the fiftieth day after the immolation of the true Lamb, Christ. Where? On Mount Sinai, just as Christ delivered on a mountain the discourse containing the perfection of the New Testament.

In the Old Testament, as in the New, three things are contained: promises, sacraments, and commandments. The promises of the Old Testament were temporal goods—whence it is called “Old”—in which, nevertheless, the eternal promises of the New and eternal blessedness were prefigured, though obscurely. Its sacraments included circumcision, which was also before the law; the observance of the Sabbath; many sacrifices prefiguring the true Paschal Lamb; and similar things. These latter, since they had not existed previously, were added in the law, through which future truth was shown more plainly than before, although it was still hidden. The sacraments of the New [Testament] are baptism, and so forth.

God wished brute animals to be sacrificed to him in order to exercise the people in his worship and remove them from idolatry, lest they sacrifice such animals to demons. It remains to speak of the commandments. The commandments include natural and figurative ones. [Col. 1150B] The natural commandments are the ten which flow from natural law. They were not begun in the written law but renewed, because they had been erased through sins. These are the Ten Commandments, also called moral commandments. They were not brought to an end in the new law; rather, they were fulfilled more perfectly. The figurative commandments were given for a time, provided by God to foreshadow future truth; once truth had fulfilled them, they came to an end.

In those Ten Commandments, love of God and of neighbour is commanded: the three on the first tablet refer to the love of God; the other seven on the second tablet refer to the love of neighbour [Note: [Col. 1149B] At these words the Lyran manuscript codex ends, with a line added beneath the final line of its last page, as though referring to the immediately following page, which is missing. Other pages probably followed [Col. 1150B] to complete this treatise—as, from what precedes, may be conjectured. This loss has occurred, not without great detriment to readers and even to Catholic doctrine itself.].

[Col. 1149]

## THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT’S SHORT TREATISE ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE ALTAR

(From the Colbert manuscript, no. 2262. Never published
[Col. 1149C] 1103 Who can grasp in understanding how Christ’s flesh comes down daily from heaven to us upon the altar, and from the altar into us, and yet does not leave the heaven from which it comes? For just as Christ’s divinity first came to us from heaven, so now his humanity comes to us from there; and as his divinity came from heaven without departing from it, so now his humanity comes from heaven, although it always remains there. And as divinity came through humanity, so humanity comes from there through divinity. Then God was manifest through his humanity; now man is hidden through his divinity. Then God sensibly; now man insensibly. Then God humanly; now man divinely. Nor is [Col. 1150C] man present only in his spirit, but also in his flesh; nor without his divinity, but with it, in it, and from it; and therefore the whole thing is effected divinely.

For what is more divine than that Christ’s body, although it is flesh and not spirit, is nevertheless food not for flesh and body but for spirit and mind? It is indeed food for the inner person, yet not human but divine: spiritually and divinely entering into the spirit—not changing itself into spirit, but spiritually and divinely feeding the spirit, entering spiritually, working spiritually. It comes from heaven by a spiritual way and returns to heaven by a spiritual way. This body, while it is with us, is also in heaven; it is likewise with us in diverse [Col. 1151A] places, upon different altars, at no different time. It is not divided into parts, but is whole and entire upon each altar; not one thing here and another there, but one in number. It is not imaginary but true, and not merely in the sacrament but in itself.

It is in one place only according to a natural mode, but in many places according to a mode of power. In one place by nature; in many by divine grace and power. In one place bodily; in many spiritually. For it is not characteristic of a body to be able to exist simultaneously in many places, but of a spirit—perhaps of no spirit except the divine, that is, uncreated and uncircumscribed, and not of a created and therefore circumscribed spirit.

Yet something similar, though in the opposite direction, 1104 occurs in the divine Spirit—or rather, if it is better said, in God the Spirit. For just as this body, assumed by God and made God’s body, and therefore in a certain manner deified and divine, subsists bodily and naturally in one place, but is spiritually and virtually in many places, so conversely God himself, although he is spiritually and essentially in many places—indeed, in all places—nevertheless, according to a certain mode of existing, that is, personally, is in one place only: namely, in the assumed man, through the grace of the fullness of divinity, as the Apostle says (Col. 2:9), dwelling bodily. He assumes what belongs to a body and gives to the body what is his own, not by changing it but by joining it to himself.

For one must not understand the supreme Spirit as dwelling bodily somewhere, or his [perhaps “supreme”] body as existing spiritually somewhere, as though either spirit became body somewhere or body became spirit somewhere. Rather, the uncircumscribed Spirit dwells somewhere, according to a certain mode of existing—that is, through the union of person—circumscribedly: namely, so as to be there that he is nowhere else. This pertains to the body, whose natural condition is to be circumscribed. But this body is simultaneously whole in many places, according to the manner of spirit. Thus “bodily” and “spiritually” do not signify the natures of the things subsisting, but their modes of subsisting. The Apostle says that the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ (ibid.), not because of the nature of the indwelling God, but because of the mode of indwelling.

Christ’s body, moreover, is not only whole at once in different places according to the manner of spirit—that is, upon many altars—but even upon each individual altar it has, to some extent, a spiritual mode of existing. For although everywhere, according to the condition of a body, it is sensible in itself, it is nevertheless present to us on the altar, according to its own appearance, insensibly. Hence it may be said to be there both sensibly and insensibly: sensibly, indeed, because of the true sensibility of the body and because of the sacramental form subject to the senses; insensibly, however, with respect 1105 to its appearance and our senses’ perception. Therefore in one respect it is there bodily, because of the true nature of the body, the form of the sacrament as stated, and a certain mode of existing; in another respect it is there incorporeally, namely with respect to the act of sensing and a certain mode of existing.

For insofar as it is on the altar such that one may truly say, “It is in this part of the altar and not in that part,” it is in the part where its sacrament is, and it is not in that part where its sacrament is not; in this respect it is circumscribed in place according to the manner of a body. But insofar as it is not so present on this altar that it is not, at the same time and in the same manner, wholly elsewhere—that is, on any other altar—it exists there uncircumscribedly, and far transcends the common nature and mode of subsisting of bodies. Perhaps in this respect the Creator surpasses not only the nature and mode of subsisting of bodies but also that of spirits, and overcomes their power.

Therefore do not investigate the nature of this body’s mode of subsisting—which it has not from nature or according to nature—by nature; attend rather to the divine power. Do not ask what created and less powerful nature is accustomed or able to do; consider instead what divine grace and power can do [not “after itself”]. This is an uncreated and omnipotent nature, an innate nature, from which come all nature and all power.

[Note: Col. 1151D. These words appear to have been inserted uselessly by the copyist.]

Therefore let human reason, accustomed to follow accustomed nature, not introduce or entertain its customary little questions concerning this unusual and divine matter. For inquiries concerning those things which accompany natural, not virtual, modes of existing in place [perhaps: “naturally, but not virtually”] have no place here. For virtual modes greatly exceed and are far removed from natural ones. Therefore sense should not presume here to ask what it otherwise asks: namely, since the Lord’s body is on the altar, in what place or in what part of that altar it is not; what part of the body is beneath what part of the sacrament; or how the parts are arranged—which are above, below, to the right, to the left, before, and behind; and whether a larger part of the body occupies a larger space and a smaller part a smaller space. For beneath the individual parts of the sacrament there are not individual parts of the body; rather, beneath each part equally, as beneath all parts, are all the parts—that is, not one limb beneath one part and another beneath another, but beneath every individual part the whole and immeasurable body.

Therefore, even when the sacrament is divided into parts, the body is not divided into parts, so that it may itself be received divided and part by part; 1106 rather, beneath the divided parts, and in every individual part, it is received by each recipient as whole and undivided. Nor should reason infer that, if this whole body is somewhere, it is not whole elsewhere; or that, if a place is smaller than this body, it cannot contain this body, which is larger than it. These things are indeed true not only of other bodies but also of this body according to the mode of existing that accompanies nature—not according to that which follows divine power.

It is likewise true that, if a woman has given birth, she has lain with a man; yet this is true concerning the mode of giving birth or conceiving known to nature, not concerning a mode which the Author and Founder of nature holds in his own power above nature and not implanted in nature. But as God’s power immensely surpasses the common mode of nature, so it surpasses sense, especially human sense, corrupt and weak. In no effect of divine power does human rational capacity seem to fail as completely as in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. In other matters perhaps it can accomplish something; but here, what can it do?

Can it comprehend how the substance of bread and wine is changed into the substance of the Lord’s body and blood, while the accidents of bread and wine remain unchanged, without the substance either of bread or of wine? How can accidents exist without a subject, or these accidents in that in which they naturally exist, without a subject? The way in these matters is unknown to reason, but not wholly unknown to faith. Here reason is ignorant of everything, but faith presumes what reason cannot comprehend. Faith advances through reason’s deficiency. By grace faith knows what reason can know through no experience. And the weaker reason is here, [Col. 1154A] the stronger faith is; the less—or not at all—reason works here, the more faith, working more or altogether, merits.

Let reason therefore gladly yield here, that the merit of faith may increase. Let it not begrudge faith its merit, because what faith merits, it merits not for itself but rather for reason. Faith will be abolished [perhaps “charity” or “reason” is to be supplied], but reason will remain and be advanced through the merit of faith. Faith exists only on the way; reason will exist also in the homeland, and there in fullness. Faith sows, but reason will reap. Reason will be rewarded for faith’s merit, because it in some manner cooperates toward that merit and itself merits something—indeed, much. For it is reason’s merit that it does not prefer itself to faith’s simplicity; it does not strive to go before, but to follow. If it cannot do this, it nevertheless does not contradict; it relies not upon its own power, [Col. 1154B] but upon God’s grace. It yields to grace, concedes the palm to faith, and gives glory to God, confessing that he can do [perhaps: “can do better”] what it cannot comprehend.

Most especially, however, in this sacrament reason experiences and fully recognizes its deficiency—except that even this it sees to be reasonable: that, in God’s mysteries handed down to man for belief, what cannot be penetrated by reason should nevertheless not fall away from faith.

## [ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE MASS]

[Col. 1153]

## A SHORT NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK

We have drawn this book, *On the Exposition of the Mass*, from Colbert manuscript no. 6101, of excellent quality and, as we have been able to judge, about six hundred years old. It is evident that the beginning of the *Exposition of the Mass* published at Cologne in 1568 by Melchior Hittorp was taken from this manuscript, or from ancient codices which he does not identify: the wording is precisely the same as far as the Introit of the Mass, from which point everything is wholly different.

We have judged it all the more probable that this work should be attributed to Hildebert because it more strongly savours of allegories familiar to Hildebert and seems to have a greater affinity with his other poems on the holy Eucharist. In the aforesaid Colbert manuscript 6101, it was immediately followed by his principal poem on that subject—which we accordingly append to this *Exposition*—a poem attributed beyond doubt to Hildebert in all editions, and also by Hittorp himself in his collection of authors on the divine offices. We have also judged that this method of preparation, placed at the end of the manuscript, ought more suitably to be placed at the beginning.

[Col. 1153]

## THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT’S BOOK ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE MASS

*(From Colbert manuscript no. 6101. Not previously published.)*

### How priests who approach to effect the body and blood of the Lord ought to prepare themselves

[Col. 1153C]

Priests who approach to effect the body and blood of the Lord must flee pride, envy, detraction, murmuring, hatred, covetousness, and avarice. Hence the Apostle says that those who do such things “shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10). Even slight and venial sins must be avoided, insofar as human nature can do so and divine grace grants it. They must embrace chastity with the greatest earnestness and devote themselves to continence.

If a layman—indeed, any believer—cannot pray unless he abstains from the marital act, for the Apostle says, “Do not defraud one another, except for a time, that you may be free for prayer” (1 Cor. 7:5), then the priest, for whom sacrifices must always be offered on behalf of the people, must always pray; therefore even the layman must always abstain from marriage.

“For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body” (1 Cor. 11:29).

Augustine:

> Judas was such a man, and yet he came in and went out with Christ’s holy apostles. He came with them alike to the Lord’s supper. He could associate with them; he could not defile them. Peter and Judas both received from the one bread; yet what share has the faithful with the unbelieving? Peter received unto life; Judas unto death. Thus, as with a good fragrance, so also with good food: it gives life to the good and death to the wicked. For Judas, to whom the Lord handed the morsel, made room in himself for the devil not by receiving an evil thing, but by receiving a good thing badly.

[Note: Col. 1155D. St Augustine, on chapter 6 of the Gospel of St John, Tractate 36; and on chapter 13, Tractate 71.]

[Note: Col. 1155D. *Expositions of the Psalms*, on Psalm 3.]

Thus anyone who receives the Lord’s sacrament unworthily does not make it evil because he himself is evil; nor, because he has not received it unto salvation, has he received nothing. [Col. 1155B] For the Lord’s body and blood were no less truly present even with those to whom the Apostle said: “Whoever eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29). Whoever lives well in this Church is not judged [perhaps: “prejudiced”] by another’s sins, because each person in it shall bear his own burden. And whoever in it eats Christ’s body unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.

### 1109 The order concerning sacred vestments, and first concerning the amice

The amice is the first vestment with which we encircle the neck on every side. For the voice is in the neck; therefore, by the neck the use of speech is expressed. By the amice we understand the guarding of speech, concerning which the Psalmist says: “I said: I will guard my ways” (Ps. 38:1); and: “I have set a guard upon my mouth” (ibid., v. 2). In this first vestment restraint of speech is enjoined.

[Note: Col. 1156D. Thus the Roman Pontifical, in the ordination of a subdeacon.]

### On the alb

Afterwards we put on the linen tunic, which we call the alb. It ought to restrain the priest’s hands and arms, so that he does nothing except what is useful; his breast, so that he thinks nothing vain; his belly, so that in seeking delights beyond measure he does not presume to make himself gluttonous; the members beneath the belly, so that by wantonness he does not spoil all the beauty of the priestly dress; his knees, so that they do not become sluggish in perseverance in prayer; his shins and feet, so that they do not run toward evil. Therefore priests should be so clothed that they restrain both their body from wicked deeds and their mind from perverse thoughts.

### On the girdle

[Col. 1155D]

The linen tunic is bound with the girdle of continence, as the Lord commands: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35), so that every pleasure may be restrained by two virtues: obedience to God and the mortification of natural impulses [the printed text has *naturalem disputationem*, “natural discussion”].

### On the stole

The stole signifies the light and sweet burden of which the Lord says: “Take my yoke upon you” (Matt. 11:29); and: “For my yoke is sweet” (ibid., v. 30). In that the stole extends to the knees, which are accustomed to bend, we understand the cause of humility, concerning which the Lord says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29).

### On the chasuble

The chasuble pertains generally to all clerics. It signifies the works that pertain to all: hunger, thirst, vigils, nakedness, reading, psalmody, prayer, manual labour, teaching, silence, and the like. Whoever is clothed in these works is clothed in the chasuble.

### On the cloth, or maniple

The cloth which we call the maniple 1110 signifies the cultivation of pure thought, by which we strive to restrain our natural and, as it were, inborn pleasures. It is carried in the left hand, to show [Col. 1156B] that in temporal life we endure the weariness of superfluous moisture—that is, of carnal pleasure. The mind also at times feels weariness, as the Psalmist says: “My soul has slumbered because of weariness” (Ps. 118:28). By the cloth we understand pure thoughts with which we wipe away the troubles of the mind and weaknesses of the body.
