### On the Mass

Mass is celebrated for many reasons. First, that we may ask God; second, that God may receive our prayers and offerings; third, for those making offerings and for the dead; fourth, for the kiss of peace; fifth, that the offering may be sanctified; sixth, that the offering of Christ’s body and blood may be confirmed through the Holy Spirit; seventh, that the *Our Father* may be sung (Matt. 6:12), [Col. 1156C] in which seven petitions are contained—three spiritual and four temporal.

The Lord first taught this prayer to his disciples and apostles. Of it the prophet says: “Whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Joel 2:32). They are seven in number on account of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, or the seven grades of the Church. Why is this offering repeated daily, when Christ saved the world through his passion and death no longer has dominion over him? There are many reasons. First, because we sin daily; second, because after sins the body of Christ is commanded to be offered to penitents, so that they may find salvation through Christ’s body and depart after penance; third, so that the great benefit of the Lord’s passion may not be consigned to forgetfulness; fourth, so that it may resemble the Day of Judgment in the Church, on which the righteous shall be separated from the unrighteous.

### On the Introit

The Introit of the Mass is so called because through it entry is made into the office of that Mass. The verse is sung because through it one returns to the Introit. The *Gloria* is sung to show that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have equal glory and coeternal majesty: “In the beginning, and now, and always, and unto ages of ages. Amen”—that is, in past, present, and future time.

### On *Kyrie eleison*

[Col. 1157A]

*Kyrie eleison* is celebrated so that the Father, who handed over his only Son for us, may rescue us from the punishments of hell. *Christe eleison* is said so that the Son also, our Lord Jesus Christ, may, together with the Father, free us from everlasting punishments and grant us eternal life, as he himself says: “Father, I will that where I am, there also may my minister be” (John 12:26). *Kyrie* means “Lord”; *eleison* means “have mercy.”

### On the *Gloria*

“Glory to God in the highest” is sung to show that, at Christ’s birth, glory in the highest belongs to the angels, who never sinned nor had discord with God; and that peace was made by Christ Jesus among all people of good will, who until Christ’s birth, [Col. 1157B] because of their sins, had discord with God and with the angels.

### On the prayer

Prayer is called from praying, because through it good things are prayed for the people. It is called the Collect because the people are gathered into one for prayer.

### On the Epistle

The Epistle is read in order to show, through the Gospel, that Christ is about to come near. The Epistle is called “sent over” because it was sent by the apostles concerning the law of Moses and the prophets. It signifies the prophecy of John, who announced that Christ was near.

### On the Gradual

The responsory is so called from responding, because it begins with one person [Col. 1157C] in order that all the people may return praise. It is called the Gradual, in distinction from other responsories, because they chant this one upon the steps, and, when one person ceases, the others answer the same thing. The verse follows. In the verse the singer must draw his thoughts to himself and consider with himself how, or what, he has learned from his master.

### On the Tract

[Note: Col. 1157D. For the Tract and *Alleluia*, see above Sermon 111, near the end.]

The Tract sometimes expresses tribulation, as in “Out of the depths” and “You have moved”; sometimes joy, as in “Sing joyfully” and “Praise.”

### On *Alleluia*

*Alleluia* expresses joy, or praise to the Lord, in remembrance of eternal glory. The verse moves the singer [Col. 1157D] to consider inwardly wherein he has cause to praise God or to rejoice. *Alleluia* is said: “Praise to you, eternal [God].” *Lu*: “Praise to you, author of light.” “Praise to you, illumination of light.” That jubilation which we call the Sequence signifies that state before our Lord God when speech in words will not be necessary, but the sole thought of the inward mind will show what it contains within itself.

### On the Gospel

The Gospel is called “good news,” because it announces to us Christ’s birth, reproaches, passion, burial, resurrection, ascension into heaven, and coming at the end of the world for judgment. [Col. 1158A] It also announces to us in the future life after death, rest after labour, and a kingdom after service. The Gospel is read after the Epistle so that its preaching may be announced thereby to the people.

### On the Creed

“I believe in one God” is sung so that, because the people have heard Christ preaching from the ambo, they may show with what faith they receive his teaching.

### On the Offertory

When people make their offerings, chant is performed in order to show that people ought to return thanks and praises to God while they strive and labour with their hands and other members in such works as may please him.

### On the office of the Mass

Some simple people are accustomed to ask from what point the Mass begins in the whole office, so that if perhaps they have not arrived for the entire office, they may know at what offices they ought to present themselves without retracing anything. The Mass, therefore, is called from the point where the priest begins to offer sacrifice to God until “Go, it is the dismissal.” The celebration of this office proceeds so as to show what was done at that time concerning the Lord’s passion and burial, and how we ought by our service to recall to memory what was done for us.

Concerning the Offertory it is written in the book of Paralipomenon: “The priests went in to King Hezekiah and said to him: We have sanctified the altar, and the whole house of the Lord, and the burnt offering” (2 Chr. 29:18). And a little later: “King Hezekiah arose [Col. 1158C] and gathered all the princes of the city, and went up to the house of the Lord; and together they offered seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven he-goats for sin, for the kingdom, for the sanctuary, and for the people. And he commanded the priests, the sons of 1113 Aaron, to offer them upon the altar to the Lord. He also stationed the Levites in the house of the Lord with cymbals, psalteries, and harps, according to David’s arrangement. And when the burnt offering was offered, they began to sing praises to the Lord and sound trumpets, while the various instruments which King David had commanded resounded. And while all the multitude worshipped, the singers who held the trumpets continued in their office until the burnt offering was completed. When the offering had ended, the king bowed down, and all who were with him, [Col. 1158D] and they worshipped” (ibid., vv. 20 ff.).

Likewise now in the Church, when the Gospel has been read, the people offer, the choir sings, the priest receives, represents before God with heart, mouth, and hands, bows down, and prays. Therefore the office that we call the Offertory begins at the point where, after the Gospel, the priest says, “The Lord be with you,” and ends at the point where he says aloud, “For ever and ever.” Therefore its final words are uttered aloud so that they may be heard by the people and the prayer may be confirmed by the people’s response.

For Christ deigned to come to Jerusalem on Palm Sunday and there to await the day of his immolation. He came down from the Mount of Olives, with a great crowd coming to meet him, and was greeted according to the good custom of the ancient tradition in Judaism. Therefore the priest greets the people, saying, “The Lord be with you.” Afterwards he says, “Let us pray,” thereby warning them that each of those making an offering should return to his own conscience. If anyone has something to immolate, let him immolate it; that is, if anyone is conscious of his own fault, let him pray that he may now die by an invisible blade. If anyone has a voluntary sacrifice, let him seek it for whatever matter before it leaves his hand, that it may be acceptable to the Lord and not despised, as Cain was despised because he did not offer rightly.

### On the corporal

Meanwhile, a linen cloth (*syndo*, or *syndon*) is placed upon the altar, which we customarily call the corporal. All are admonished—people, ministers, and the priest himself—that as that linen has been cleansed of all natural greenness and moisture, so may the mind of those making offerings be free from every carnal desire. While the priest receives the offerings, the singers sing, because while the crowd sang, “Hosanna in the highest,” Christ received their vows. The purity of the linen signifies the purity of the minds of those who sang to the Lord.

### Again, on the office

The priest, having received the offerings of those 1114 who are permitted to offer, returns to the altar in order to arrange upon it before the Lord the offerings which he will sacrifice to him in the ensuing parts of the Mass. For Christ, after receiving the vows of those singing, entered Jerusalem and the temple of the Lord, where the altar was, and there presented [Col. 1159C] himself for the future sacrifice. While the choir sings, the priest goes to the altar and prays—something he warns the others to do when he says, “Let us pray,” and does himself. For he first prays for his own offenses, so that he may be worthy to approach the altar and touch it, lest what happened to the Beth-shemites happen to him, who dared to look upon the ark of the Lord. Of this it is written in the book of Samuel: “Because he struck from the people seventy men, and fifty thousand of the common people” (1 Sam. 6:19).

### On the censer

By the censer which the priest presents over it after the prayer is signified the one through whom the Lord may deign to be propitiated to him, namely, our Lord Jesus Christ. The censer signifies his body, concerning which it is written in Exodus: “That incense may be offered in it to the Lord, lest perhaps he die” (Exod. 30:20).

Then the priest, turned toward the people, says: “Pray for me, brethren,” etc.

### The secret prayer is said

It is called the Secret because it is said secretly, and it belongs to the priest alone to offer sacrifice to God alone. Since we speak to God by thoughts, a resounding voice is unnecessary; words alone are needed, so that by them the priest may be reminded what he ought to think. The priest also says the Secret so that Christ’s hidden things, which were being done at that time, may be brought back to our memory. For the Paschal Lamb lay hidden in Christ, who was to be sacrificed. This was hidden from the apostles. [Col. 1160A] It was hidden from the other faithful who were with him until the day of the Supper, when he deigned, by opening it, to make his passion known. It was hidden from the Jewish people and evil spirits, concerning whom the Apostle says: “For if they had known God, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

“For ever and ever.” The people respond, confirming his prayer: “Amen.” And the priest says: “The Lord be with you.” The priest greets the people, praying that the Lord may be with them. The people in turn pray for the priest, that the Lord may be with his spirit as well: “And with your spirit.” And the priest says: “Lift up your hearts.”  
R\. “We have them to the Lord.”

Hence blessed Augustine says: “We are still turned toward the earth, but when we consider 1115 [Col. 1160B] how God is praised in heaven, let us have our heart there; and not without reason do we hear: ‘Lift up your hearts.’ Let us raise our heart upward, lest it rot upon the earth.” The priest confirms his hearers: “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God” for such great gifts.  
R\. “It is fitting and just.”

Here the voice is necessarily raised. The priest cries out to the people, I say, so that they too may have what he already has: namely, hearts lifted up; and then, so that they may give thanks to God for serenity of mind. What all may do together—namely, give thanks to God—is acclaimed aloud. What pertains only to the priest—namely, the sacrifice of bread and wine—is done secretly.

This office is called the Preface, or Preparation, because it prepares the minds of the brethren for seemly conduct in the venerable assembly of the holy angels, who are accustomed to be present [Col. 1160C] at the consecration of Christ’s body; and therefore it is sung aloud. It begins with the greeting before “Lift up your hearts” and ends with the hymn “Holy, holy, holy,” etc.

Here the celebrant recalls to us that office which Christ performed when he went up into the great furnished upper room, spoke much there with his disciples, and rendered a hymn to God the Father, as John relates, until he went out to the Mount of Olives, where he gave thanks to God the Father. There he sang the hymn in which he prayed the Father to deliver his disciples from evil, and the matters that follow in the same Gospel. The altar, therefore, is the Lord’s table at which he dined with the disciples; the corporal is the linen with which he was girded; the cloth is the labour caused by Judas the betrayer. Thus he ascends into the upper room in Christ’s stead when “Lift up your hearts” is said. The hearers respond: “We have them to the Lord,” etc.

There follows: “It is truly fitting and just, right and salutary, that we should always and everywhere give thanks to you, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, through Christ our Lord.” The Apostle Paul says (Eph. 1) that all things in Christ are restored, those that are in heaven—that is, what fell from there among the angels is made whole again from human beings. Those things on earth are restored when human beings themselves, who are predestined to eternal life, are renewed from the oldness of corruption. Therefore the priest says: “Through whom the angels praise your majesty.” Here too the order of archangels is understood. “The dominions adore”: here also are included the principalities of holy spirits. “The powers tremble; the heavens and the virtues of the heavens.” By “heavens,” which are God’s seats, are understood the thrones, upon which Almighty God always presides to exercise his judgment. “And the blessed seraphim celebrate together in exultant fellowship.” By the seraphim and cherubim likewise is understood the order nearest and closest to him.

Blessed Pope Gregory [Note: Col. 1161D. Homily 34 on the Gospels.] has sufficiently discussed these nine orders in a certain homily on the Gospel; whoever wishes will find it in his own books. The continual divine praises of these nine orders of angels are understood as an acceptable sacrifice to God. To these aforesaid orders, the tenth order of the human condition is joined; and in its voice the priest says: “With whom we beseech you to command that our [Col. 1161B] voices also be admitted, saying in humble confession: Holy, holy, holy.”

The hymn follows, and it is called a hymn because it is filled with thanksgiving and the praises of angels. This hymn was added by Pope Sixtus. The choir says in unison: “Hosanna in the highest! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest!”

Hence Isidore says: “*Hosanna* cannot be wholly transferred into the interpretation of another language. For *osi* means ‘saving’; *anna* is an interjection, signifying a movement of the mind under the emotion of one beseeching. The complete form is *Osianna*, which we pronounce *Osanna* by shortening the vowel *i*.”

[Note: Col. 1161D. See the Sermon on Palm Sunday. From this it can also be proved that this Treatise is Hildebertine.]

It means “save,” with “your people” or “the whole world” understood. This part of the hymn was sung by the crowd [Col. 1161C] preceding the Lord Jesus on Palm Sunday. The deacons, subdeacons, and other ministers who surround the priest represent those who were with Christ in the great furnished upper room and attended upon him in bodily service. The women are also represented, who, when the disciples fled, remained steadfast during the Lord’s passion.

After the hymn “Holy, holy, holy” has ended, those standing around bow themselves, venerating the divine majesty with the angels and the Lord’s incarnation with the crowds. They remain bowed until the whole present prayer is finished, that is, until after the Lord’s Prayer the words “but deliver us from evil” are said. Thus here are represented those to whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “You are they who have remained with me in my trials” (Luke 22:28).

“You therefore, most merciful Father, through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, we humbly ask through devout thought toward you, and we petition through the performance of good works, that you may receive—by preceding our good will—and bless—by following it in good actions—these gifts of bread, in which there are flour and water; these offerings, 1117 in which there are wine and water: by them may we be endowed with eternal blessedness and fortified in this present life against the devil’s persecution; these holy, unblemished sacrifices—that is, those through which we may be sanctified—and through the representation of these visible things may we sacrifice to you before you upon your high altar, with a contrite heart and a humbled spirit, being through these unblemished—that is, uncontaminated by the stains of this life.”

[Col. 1162A]

Here priests offer three prayers, as the Lord did after going out to the Mount of Olives before his betrayal (Matt. 26). The first is for the universal Church and its rulers; the second for particular brethren whose alms or gift they have received, for those whose sponsors they have become, or whose presence they uphold in the office of the Mass—their sacrifice being praise; the third for the priests and ministers themselves, who share with holy Mary and the apostles in one Lord, that is, following the example of those who offer sacrifice visibly and invisibly, so that in all things they may be protected by the Lord’s defense.

We are taught in the Old Testament for whom we ought to offer sacrifices: namely, for vows, for freewill offerings, for sin, for the kingdom, for the sanctuary, and for Judah [that is, perhaps, for enemies]. When we fulfil what we promised in tribulation, we offer for vows. When we give thanks for benefits received, for freewill offerings. When we are contrite for sins committed, for sin. When, with hearts uplifted, we make petition for the kingdom, for kings. When we pray for the stability of the sacred orders, for the sanctuary. When we pray for the peace and unity of the people, for Judah. Where sacrifice is made for the pope, for the king, for the bishop, and for the other [Col. 1162C] rulers, this is done according to Paul’s ordinance, who instructed Timothy about this, saying: “I urge, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people,” etc. (1 Tim. 2:1).

First, we offer to you for your holy Catholic Church, which you may deign to pacify, protect, unite, and govern throughout the whole world, restraining visible enemies and giving strength against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places; that she may have conduct proper toward you and mutual charity among her members; and govern her so that we may not turn aside from the way of truth, nor believe merely for a time and [the text is defective] in time of temptation; together with our Pope N., our bishop N., and all orthodox believers [Col. 1162D] and worshippers of the Catholic and apostolic faith.

“Remember, O Lord, your servants and handmaids, and all who stand around.” Where “all who stand around” is said, the authority of the canons commands that a priest must by no means celebrate Mass alone; nor should anyone, at this time of prayer, sit down, unless bodily weakness prevents it; rather, all should stand around and pray.

> [Note: Col. 1162D. A scribe’s error: read “unless bodily weakness prevents it.”]

“Whose faith is known to you”: they believe in your sight; and their devotion is known, as they carry out pious works. “For whom we offer to you”: that is, those through whose charity and request we approach [Col. 1163A] this altar with an offering; or those who offer you this sacrifice of praise—that is, those who offer through us, who sustain bodily poverty and need, and give temporal things to your ministers so that they may reap spiritual things—for themselves and all who belong to them. The following words explain with what intention they do these things: not for temporal gain or for the splendours of this world, but for the redemption of their souls—that is, in hope of receiving salvation with the saints—and for their bodily welfare, so that bodily health may lead to the salvation of their souls. And they pay you their vows: what they have vowed in heart, they fulfil in deed, to you, the eternal, living, and true God; for apart from you there is no God, and those who are called gods are false and without life, benefiting neither themselves nor others.

“Communicating”: that is, we offer these things to you, desiring [Col. 1163B] and seeking through them—which surpass all our acts—that we may have communion and a share in everlasting blessedness with those who offered themselves and what was theirs to you in heart, word, and deed for their salvation, and who are the example and confirmation of this sacrifice. “And venerating their memory.” We therefore venerate their memory: following their example, we sacrifice to you daily, lest the effect of so great a salvation slip from our frail memory; rendering thanksgivings to you, God, and to them, because you are the institutor of so great a sacrament and the giver of every good thing, while they have gone before us by their deeds and assist us by their intercession.

First, of the glorious and ever-Virgin Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and also of your blessed apostles and martyrs Peter and [Col. 1163C] Paul, Andrew, James, John, Thomas, James, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon and Thaddaeus; Linus, Cletus, Clement, Sixtus, Cornelius, Cyprian, Lawrence, Chrysogonus, John and Paul, Cosmas and Damian; “and also of those whose solemnity is celebrated today in the sight of your majesty,” and of all your saints: by whose merits and prayers grant that we may in all things be fortified by the help of your protection, through the same [Christ].... Through him we approach you, God the Father: as Mediator, he stands before your countenance while we direct our prayers to you through him. Hence Paul says: “Approaching God through himself, ever living to intercede for us” (Heb. 7:15).

> [Note: Col. 1163D. The words “and also of those ... is celebrated” are not found in the Canon now used by us in the Mass. Our Martène notes, however, that in former times the names of those whose feast was celebrated on that day were commonly mentioned after the names of the saints in various books of Canons. Thus, in a very ancient manuscript of the Royal Library, about nine hundred years old, after the names of Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius; Hilary, Martin, Augustine, Gregory, Jerome, and Benedict, there is added: “And also of those whose glorious triumph is celebrated today in the sight of your glory.” These words, says Berno, abbot of Reichenau, in his little work *On the Rites of the Mass*, were added by Pope Gregory III, of whom the *Liber Pontificalis* also says: “In the Canon of the Mass he added that this should be spoken by the priest: ‘Whose solemnity is celebrated today in the sight of your majesty.’” In the ancient Gallican sacramentary the following is added: “And of all your saints [Col. 1164D] who throughout the whole world have suffered for your name, Lord, and of your confessors, by whose merits,” etc. See Martène himself, book I of *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, chapter 4, article 8. This passage of Hildebert, moreover, gives no small support to his assertion.]

“This offering of our service, and also of all [Col. 1164A] your household, we beseech you, Lord, graciously to accept.” Here prayer is made to God that he may deign to receive the vows of his elect; and therefore the offering is presented to him by a demonstrative expression: “This offering, therefore,” etc. What follows was added by St Gregory: “And order our days in your peace, deliver us from eternal damnation, and command that we be numbered among the flock of your elect.” It shows that no one in the present world can be secure concerning his own steadfastness, however perfect he may appear; and therefore one must continually pray that one’s days in this present world may be ordered in peace, visible and invisible enemies having been removed, so that one may thus be counted among the flock of the elect.

From “You therefore, most merciful Father” to this point is celebrated [Col. 1164B] the sacrifice of the elect, who have nothing in the flesh that resists them, nor anything in conscience that disturbs them. For just as there were two altars in the tabernacle of Moses, or in the temple of Solomon—one for incense, the other for burnt offering—so there are two sacrifices of the holy Church. One is that in which all carnal impulses have been stilled. It is celebrated from the beginning of the prayer until the offering, “You, God,” where those already reigning with God are commemorated, and with whom the Church, if not in all, at least in many of her members, is united and incorporated. The other is that in which carnal impulses must daily be slain. This the priest performs as he descends to the universal sacrifice and the immolation of Christ, celebrated from this point, “Which offering,” through “To us also, sinners.”

“You, God, we beseech, in all things make this offering [Col. 1164C] blessed,” through which we may be blessed here and eternally; “enrolled,” through which all may be inscribed in the fellowship of the saints; “ratified,” that is, distinguished from all offerings that are falsely immolated to false and vain idols, where nothing is valid; “reasonable,” through which we are aroused from brutish understanding and perceive on what ground, or with what regard for salvation, we act; “acceptable,” so that we who are displeasing in ourselves may through this become acceptable and pleasing to you. Deign to make it for us the bod+ y and blo+ od of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

> [Note: Col. 1164D. From the same manuscript—On the two crosses. The priest makes two crosses over the offerings, beside the chalice, to teach that Christ was taken down from the cross, because he was crucified for two peoples.
>
> On the cross made over the chalice. The cross formed over the chalice and the offered particle sets before our eyes Christ’s very body, because it was crucified for us. Therefore the priest touches the four sides of the chalice with the body, because through it the human race came from the four quarters of the earth into the unity of the body and returned to the peace of the Catholic Church.]

Who, on the day before he suffered, took bread into his holy and venerable hands, and, raising his eyes to heaven, to you, God his almighty Father [Col. 1164D], gave you thanks, blessed it, and broke it. [Col. 1165A] He himself broke the bread which he was to give to his disciples, to show that the breaking and passion of his body would not come about apart from his will, as he had previously foretold: “I have power to lay down my life” (John 10:18).

He gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and eat of this, all of you: THIS IS MY BODY.” For just as the flesh of Christ which he assumed in the virginal womb is his true body and was slain for our salvation, so the bread which Christ delivered to his disciples, and which priests consecrate daily in the Church, is, by the power of the divinity that fills it, the true body of Christ. Nor are they two bodies, that flesh which he assumed and this bread: they are the one true body of Christ, so that while it is broken and eaten here, [Col. 1165B] Christ is immolated and eaten, and yet remains whole and living.

Likewise, after supper, taking also this [Note: Col. 1165D. These notes are taken from the margin of the same manuscript.

> On the presence of angels at the time of sacrifice. Just as angels are recorded to have stood by when the Saviour’s body had been laid in the tomb, so they ought also to be believed to stand by at the time of consecration when the mysteries of that same most holy body are celebrated.]

excellent chalice into his holy and venerable hands, again giving you thanks, he blessed it and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and drink from it, all of you: FOR THIS IS THE CHALICE OF MY BLOOD, of the new and eternal Testament.” Supply: “confirming.” It is called the new Testament in distinction from the old, which was confirmed by the blood of goats and bulls, as is found in Exodus (29:8), when Moses gathered this blood and sprinkled the people, saying: “This is the blood of the Testament which God has commanded for you.” Likewise, the new Testament—that is, the Gospel, [Col. 1165C] in which the promises of eternal life and the heavenly homeland are contained—was confirmed by the blood of Christ’s passion, which is daily celebrated in the Church. For every testament is confirmed by the death of the testator.

It is called the eternal Testament because the Testament which Moses wrote, sprinkled with the blood of different animals, and confirmed, was imposed only until the time of correction, as Paul says to the Hebrews (9); and it was set aside at Christ’s coming. For what was then done with diverse cattle has, since Christ’s coming, been done in the offering of bread and wine and in holy and upright morals; it was confirmed in the death of Christ and is eternal, according to the Psalmist’s words: “You are a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4). For from the passion [Col. 1165D] of our Lord Jesus Christ until the consummation of the age, bread and wine are offered upon the altar according to the rite of Melchizedek; and what is there seen, believed, and understood [Col. 1166A] will never be changed.

“The mystery of faith.” Bread and wine are a mystery, that is, a sacrament or signification of this same faith, this same hope, and this same charity of ours. For just as one bread is made from many grains and one wine from diverse clusters, so through integral faith, perfect hope, and intimate love of God and neighbour, we ought to become one in Christ, according to the Gospel: “Father, I will ... that all may be one” (John 17:21). And elsewhere: “They had one heart,” etc. (Acts 4:32).

“Which shall be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins”: certainly for the elect and for those who, in the fervour of charity, desire to follow the footsteps of my passion [Col. 1166B].

> [Note: Col. 1165D. On the elevation of the chalice. The priest’s and deacon’s elevation represents Christ’s taking down from the cross. The deacon who raises the chalice from the altar and wraps it in a cloth from the rim [perhaps *ora*] of the chalice to its rim represents Joseph, who boldly entered before Pilate, requested Jesus’ body, and, having bought a linen cloth, wrapped it in it.
>
> On those who carry the Lord’s vessels. The acolyte holds the paten wrapped in a linen cloth; the subdeacon holds it uncovered. From this it plainly appears that consecrated vessels ought properly to be touched only by consecrated clerics, as Ezra formerly ordained and the decrees command.
>
> On the raising of the subdeacon. When the subdeacons, standing upright, look toward the priest’s work, they represent the friends and neighbours of whom, after recounting the course of his passion, Christ complains to the Father: “You have put friend and neighbour far from me” (Ps. 87:19). When they present themselves with the paten, they recall the affection of the holy women at the Lord’s tomb.]

“Whenever you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance of me.” In leaving us this saving sacrament so that he might imprint it upon our hearts and minds, the Lord acted as a person near death who leaves some precious gift to a friend, saying: “Keep this with all diligence in remembrance of me, so that as often as you see it, you may remember me.” The friend who receives this gift that has been left cannot fail to grieve and mourn for his friend’s death whenever he looks upon it, if he has loved him with his whole soul. Likewise, whenever we approach to celebrate [perhaps *conficiendum*] or receive the sacrament of the eternal gift [Col. 1166C] which the Lord left us to keep in remembrance of himself, we ought to approach with fear, contrition of heart, and every reverence, recalling how greatly he loved us, he who offered himself for us in order to redeem us.

“Wherefore, O Lord, we your servants and also your holy people, remembering the same most blessed passion of this your Son, our Lord, and also his resurrection from the dead and glorious ascension into heaven, offer to your excellent majesty from your own gifts and grants.” Gifts are divine graces when, through the invisible immolation of a contrite heart, the faithful offer themselves to Christ. “And grants”: these are given in temporal action when they perform these visible things through pious observance. “A pure victim,” that it may purify consciences; “a holy victim,” [Col. 1166D] that it may sanctify and strengthen us in good works as an example to others; “an immaculate victim,” that we may not fall into deadly ruin and that it may preserve us undefiled; [Col. 1167A] “the holy bread of eternal life,” which, by making us already abide in God amid this frail body, causes us to contemplate, meditate upon, and desire eternal life; “and the chalice of everlasting salvation,” by which the infirmity of our souls, faithfully and healthfully refreshed, is saved not temporarily but forever.

From “Which offering” to “everlasting salvation” is commemorated the order of the Lord’s incarnation and passion: the manner in which he acted and instituted this sacrament for us. What is outwardly performed is the sign of what lies hidden within, according to the Apostle’s words: “Put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit” (1 Pet. 3:18). It follows:

“Upon which deign to look with a propitious and serene countenance, and to accept them, as you deigned to accept the gifts [Col. 1167B] of your just servant Abel.” This happened when the Lord, rejecting the gift of Abel’s brother Cain, looked upon Abel’s gifts (Gen. 4); and, as blessed Augustine says, to show that Abel’s victim was acceptable to him, he sent fire from heaven which kindled and consumed it entirely. By this means Cain knew that his own offering had been rejected, while Abel’s sacrifice was pleasing to the Lord.

“And the sacrifice of our patriarch Abraham” (Gen. 15). Augustine, from the *Tractate on Psalm 103*: A sufficiently mystical saying was made concerning that sacrifice, when Abraham received from the Lord’s answer three animals: a three-year-old ram, a three-year-old heifer, and a turtledove and a pigeon. He divided the ram, divided the goat, divided the heifer; but he did not divide the birds. [Col. 1167C] Thus it is here. That is, as long as people are animal and carnal, they are divisible: they are easily led into schisms, sects, and heresies. But the birds—that is, spiritual persons who fly upward to heavenly things on the wings of virtues—do not admit division and do not devise schisms. Peace is in them, and they preserve it in others as far as they can. Where it fails in others, they retain it in themselves, fulfilling the Apostle’s command: “So far as it depends upon you, live peaceably with all” (Rom. 12:18).

“And that which your high priest Melchizedek offered you: a holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim.” Melchizedek is read to have offered bread and wine to Abraham as he returned from the slaughter of his enemies (Gen. 14), but he is not read to have offered them to the Lord. Nevertheless, it must be believed that he first offered this bread and wine to the Lord, since he is called the high [Col. 1167D] priest of the Lord. In this preceding prayer, however, the people are understood, who give their offering—that is, bread and wine—according to the order of Melchizedek; and this expresses the pious desires hidden within, whether they are for thanksgiving, according to the altar of incense, or for sin, according to the altar of burnt offering. For visible sacrifice is the sacrament, that is, the sacred sign, of invisible sacrifice. Hence Augustine: “Praying and praising, we direct to him the voices which we sacrifice, to whom we offer in the heart the very things which we sacrifice; and thus, in sacrificing, we know that visible sacrifice is to be offered to no other than him of whose invisible sacrifice we ourselves ought to be in our hearts” [Col. 1168A]. In this sacrifice also, instituted by Christ with his own hands, Abel, Abraham, and Melchizedek are commemorated, whereby the Lord’s sacrament is confirmed as prefigured long before, and the merits and intercessions of such great men are understood. The Church’s wondrous faith is also introduced when it adds:

“We humbly beseech you, almighty God, command these things to be borne by the hands of your holy angel to your altar on high.” Christ’s body is made such not by the merit of the consecrator but by the Creator’s word and the power of the Holy Spirit. For just as it is God who baptizes, so it is God himself who, through the Holy Spirit, makes this bread his flesh and this wine his blood. [Col. 1168B] Why indeed did the priest set them forth to be borne in the sight of the divine majesty, unless it might be understood that these things are accomplished in that priesthood?

“That as many of us as shall receive the most holy body and blood of your Son from this participation at the altar may be filled with heavenly blessing and grace.” With spiritual eyes the priest sees what mortal eyes cannot. For he sees and believes that the present sacrifice is borne by angels’ hands; he perceives that the Lord’s body must be eaten by the human mouth and his blood drunk, and that the souls of those receiving them are filled with heavenly blessing and grace. Nor does the wondrous faith and pious devotion of those ministering bring it about that the nature of bread and wine is changed into the rational nature of Christ’s body and blood; rather, sins are blotted out there for those who act and take part with contrite [Col. 1168C] heart and humbled spirit. A commemoration for all the dead is also inserted when it is said:

“Remember also, O Lord, your servants and handmaids N. and all who have gone before us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace. To them, O Lord, and to all who rest in Christ,” etc. For it is unlawful to pray for unbelieving and impious dead persons, just as it is for evil spirits. “Grant them a place of refreshment, light, and peace,” we beseech you, through Christ our Lord. “A place ...”: according to blessed Augustine, when sacrifices either of the altar or of any alms are offered for all baptized dead persons, they are thanksgivings for the very good, propitiations for those not very bad, and, [Col. 1168D] for the very bad, though they give no assistance to the dead, they are nevertheless some consolation to the living. To those whom they benefit, they benefit either so that remission may be complete or at least so that condemnation itself may become more tolerable. It follows:

“To us also, your sinful servants, who hope in the multitude of your mercies, deign to grant some share and fellowship with your holy apostles and martyrs: with John, Stephen, Matthias, Barnabas, Ignatius, Alexander, Marcellinus, Peter, Felicity, Perpetua, Agatha, Lucy, Agnes, Cecilia, Anastasia, and all your saints.”

> [Note: Col. 1167D. From the same manuscript—On raising the voice. When [Col. 1168D] the priest raises his voice, saying, “To us also, [Col. 1169D] sinners,” the centurion is represented, who said from the deep affection of his heart: “Truly this man was righteous.” For the Gentiles, fearing God at Christ’s death, glorify God by their open-voiced confession; the Jews, merely striking their breasts, return in silence.]

The sacrifice having been completed, as it were, upon the altar of burnt offering [Col. 1169A], and the pious disposition of penitents having been anticipated, the ministers and those standing around consider the multitude of their sins and the multitude of God’s mercies. Since the impulses of the flesh are not yet stilled, as in the former sacrifice—the sacrifice of incense, that is, of praise—they humbly ask, conscious of their weakness, that they may have some share with the saints who have preceded them in the faith of this sacrament; and, by imitating their life, have fellowship with them in reigning in eternal blessedness. This is explained by the following words: “Into whose company, we beseech you, admit us, not weighing our merit but granting pardon, through Christ.” For the power of you, the supreme physician, is greater than the weakness of any sick person.

“Through whom you always create, sanctify, make alive, and bless all these good things”: you create bread and wine, so that the earth may conceive [Col. 1169B] and bring them forth; you sanctify, changing the simple nature of this bread and wine into the nature of your body and blood; you make alive, because you make your body living and true, thereby causing our inward person to live; and as you sanctify and make alive, you bless. For first the bread is consecrated and blessed by priests and by the Holy Spirit; then, although it appears to be bread, it nevertheless truly becomes Christ’s body. Hence blessed Augustine says: “Not every bread, but bread receiving Christ’s blessing, becomes Christ’s body.” “And you bestow them upon us,” so that we may enjoy these things. For the Lord and our Redeemer, having regard for our frailty, because he knew us to be prone to sin, delivered this sacrament to us, so that, since he can no longer die and we sin daily, [Col. 1169C] we may have a true sacrifice by which we can be expiated through him. For Christ, according to his perfect divinity, is with the Father the giver of every good; and with him, because Christ, the faithful witness, has gone before into heaven and draws human beings to be with himself; and in him, because, without the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, outside him there is no place for a true sacrifice. To you, God the almighty Father, who bestow these things in the unity of the Holy Spirit, belongs all honour from us—that is, the rendering of divine worship—and glory—that is, the purity of a clean conscience glorifying you—through all ages of ages. Amen. It follows:

“Let us pray. Instructed by saving precepts.” The saving precepts consist in evangelical teaching; “and formed by divine institution.” The institution is understood as the tradition which he deigned to hand down and institute in perfecting [perhaps *in perficiendo*] the sacrament of his body and blood. Here it should be noted that one should not enter upon it presumptuously, but with reverence and a tranquil heart we dare to say: “Our Father, who art in heaven.” We find the Father in heaven; let us therefore attend to how we live upon earth. For one who has found such a Father ought to live in such a way as to be worthy of coming to his inheritance. Let them therefore understand that they are brothers when they have one Father; and let a master not disdain to have his servant as an equal, whom the Lord Christ willed to have as his brother.

[Col. 1170A] “Hallowed be thy name.” The hallowing of God’s name is that by which we are made holy; for his name is always holy. “Thy kingdom come.” We also desire that his kingdom may come. It will come even if we do not wish it; but to desire and pray that his kingdom may come is nothing other than to desire that he make us worthy of his kingdom. Therefore, when we pray and say, “Thy kingdom come,” we desire that it may come to us. “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” Angels serve you in heaven; may we serve you on earth. Angels do not offend you in heaven; may we not offend you on earth.

Another interpretation: our spirit is compared to heaven, and our flesh to earth. Thus, “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth” means that, just as your command pleases our mind, so too may our flesh consent to it.

Another interpretation: let heaven signify the Church, which bears God, and earth unbelievers, to whom it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3). When, therefore, we pray [Col. 1170B] for the enemies of the Church, we pray that his will may be done as in heaven, so on earth: that is, just as in your faithful people, so also in those who blaspheme you, so that they may become heaven.

“Give us this day our daily bread.” This prayer may simply be understood to be offered for daily food, that it may abound for us; and if it does not abound, that it may not be lacking. Another interpretation: “our bread,” that is, your Eucharist—your body—give us as daily food. What, then, is “our daily bread”? It means: let us so live that we are not separated from your altar. Thus we ask both simply for this, [Col. 1170C] and for whatever is necessary to our soul and flesh in this life; all is included under daily bread: “But let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of the chalice” (1 Cor. 11). Hence blessed Augustine says:

> [Note: Col. 1170D. *Tractate 26 on John*: “See therefore, brothers: eat the heavenly bread spiritually; bring innocence to the altar. Though sins are daily, let them not be deadly. Before you approach the altar, consider what you say: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.’ You forgive, and you shall be forgiven. Approach securely: it is bread, not poison. But see whether you forgive; for if you do not forgive, you lie, and you lie to him whom you do not deceive. You can lie to God; you cannot deceive God. He sees you within, examines you within, and within either condemns or rewards you.”]

“And lead us not into temptation.” There are two temptations: one of testing and the other of seduction. That no faithful person may be led into the latter, he entreats his Father, saying, “And lead us not into temptation”—that is, do not permit us to be led in by him who tempts us, the author of wickedness. “But deliver us from evil.” Whoever wishes to be delivered from evil testifies that he is in evil. Therefore “turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. 36:47), so that what you prayed may be fulfilled: “Deliver us from evil.” Amen.

Thus our Master has summarized all our prayer in this brief saving utterance [Col. 1171A]. The following prayer, “Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord,” is an exposition of this final petition: “from all evils ...” From what evils? Namely, past, present, and future. With every disturbance of evils removed, repose of peace is sought from God when it is said: “And by the intercession of the blessed and glorious ever-Virgin Mary, and the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and Andrew, and all the saints, graciously grant peace in our days.” No peace is safer than obedience to the Lord’s commands: to turn from evil and do good. Since nothing can be attributed to human merits, it adds: “Aided by the help of your mercy”; and then more aptly, “may we always be free from sin”; and, because we pray for peace, it joins: “and secure from every disturbance.” Through [Col. 1171B] our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, through all ages of ages. R. Amen. It follows: “The peace of the Lord be always with you.” R. “And with your spirit.”

By the peace it is established that the people have given their assent to all that is done in the mysteries and celebrated in the Church; and these are shown to be completed by the seal of concluding peace. That Christ’s body remains on the altar until three prayers are completed—namely, “Instructed by saving precepts,” the Lord’s Prayer itself, and “Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord”—signifies that Christ’s body rested in the tomb for three days. After the three prayers, Christ’s body is removed from the altar, which in this signification is taken for the tomb, because after three days Christ’s body rose from the tomb [Col. 1171C].

> [Note: Col. 1171D. From the same manuscript—On the Lord’s body in three parts. By the particle of the offered Mass placed in the chalice is shown Christ’s body, which has already risen from the dead; by that eaten by the priest or by the people, his body still walking on earth; by that left on the altar, his body lying in the tomb.]

“Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy upon us,” twice; but at the end, “grant us peace.” It is a prayer for the people who are to receive Christ’s body, that by the mercy of the innocent Lamb sudden and rushing sins—namely, sins of thoughts and words—may be taken away. As by his passion he bore the sins of the whole world, so now he bears those of the Church which is about to receive him through the Eucharist.

On Communion [perhaps: On the Post-Communion]. The following antiphon—that is, a responsive chant—preserves the rights of brotherhood, in which each person seeks the other’s benefit and strives to provoke others to the joys of the resurrection. This type was borne by the two who recognized the Lord in the breaking of bread and immediately went to [Col. 1171D] Jerusalem, where they found the eleven assembled, etc. Those men, indeed, sang the antiphon which we customarily call the Post-Communion.

On the collect after Communion. The priest gives the final blessing, which we call the prayer, because before his ascension into heaven the Lord led his disciples to Bethany and blessed them there. The priest observes this custom when, after [Col. 1172A] the sacraments have been completed, he gives the solemn blessing.

On *Ite, missa est*. Only then does the deacon say: “Go, the dismissal is made,” that is, “Go in peace to your homes.” Yet prayer has been sent for you to God and has been borne before the sight of the divine majesty by angels, who are called messengers. The people reply: “Thanks be to God.” For after the Ascension the apostles worshipped the Lord, returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple, praising God and blessing the Lord.

The other blessing, or Collect over the People, in Lent. This is regularly used in Lent. Immediately after it is placed that [prayer] in which spiritual refreshment is commended; here the battles of Christ’s soldiers against the ancient enemy are commended. The holy fathers of old gave their blessing to the saints at the end. And when we have familiar intercourse with God’s servants, “according to the custom of our religion,” before we part from them, we ask for a blessing at the end.

> [Note: Col. 1172D. Observe the ancient custom of blessing, which even now many monks customarily receive from their superiors when entering or leaving the monastery; from this Hildebert’s monastic status could also probably be inferred.]

On the order of the crosses.

There are six orders of crosses in the Canon. The first is where it is said, “And bless these gifts,” signifying the natural law: namely, “Do not do to another what you do not wish done to yourself.” This law lasted from Adam to Moses, because although the holy fathers of that time did not see the Lord’s cross, they nevertheless endured suffering of the flesh for love of him.

The second is where [Col. 1172C] it says, “You, God, make this offering blessed,” signifying the law given through Moses. Under it the holy fathers endured Christ’s suffering out of desire for him.

The third is where it says, “And taking bread into his holy and venerable hands,” signifying the proclamations of the prophets, which extended from the prophet Samuel to John the Baptist, who, while Christ was still alive, also touched him with his hands.

The fourth is where it says, “a pure victim,” signifying the Gospel which Christ preached in his own time; because in those days the saints who bore Christ’s suffering united his body.

The fifth is where it says, “you sanctify, you make alive,” touching the churches of the Gentiles, because, while burying Christ’s body, they endured his suffering.

“Through him and with him” signifies the salvation of Gentiles and Israel at the end of the age. Together completing Christ’s body, they will especially endure [Col. 1172D] Christ’s cross—that is, his suffering. For the number six, reckoned by its parts, is first [perhaps: “less”] perfect without another. The five orders of crosses made before the sixth, when the chalice is touched with the offering, are the five ages of the world up to Christ’s coming. The sixth order is the sixth age, from Christ’s coming to the end of the age.

On the diversity of the crosses.

[Col. 1173A]

These things which are customarily done in different ways over the bread and wine—there is no statement from any authority of Scripture as to why they are so represented and in such a place, or why some make more of them and others fewer. If the priest made the sign of the cross once over the bread and wine, that could suffice, because the Lord was crucified once. But, as the Apostle says, let each abound in his own understanding; and what is done from devout devotion and looks to some mystery should not be thought idle. For when the priest makes five crosses over the bread and wine and around the chalice, he directs us to the reconciliation, or remembrance, of the five wounds which Jesus Christ suffered for us. But when he makes three, he suggests to us faith in the holy Trinity. [Col. 1173B] And by all these we must be fortified above and below, around and within. Then, from the words of Saint Augustine in *On Christian Doctrine*: “Whatever can be suitably applied from the testimony of the Scriptures, provided it is not absurd, is not to be rejected by a Catholic understanding.” When the Lord blessed bread and wine, if he made the sign of the cross, those who were present knew it, especially since the banner of the holy cross had not yet been raised. But after the Lord’s passion, as Blessed Augustine says in his exposition of the Gospel of John, if this sign is not applied either to the foreheads of believers, or to chrism, or to the sacrifice, or to the water of baptism, none of these is rightly accomplished; and what is done more frequently from devout devotion, or repeated in the consecration of that mystery, accumulates for us the power of so great a sacrament. Blessed Ambrose indeed says: “Whichever church you enter, follow its custom, if you do not wish either to suffer or to cause scandal.”

## Why the canon is said secretly and the Lord’s Prayer aloud

It should be noted why the canon is said secretly and the Lord’s Prayer aloud. Clearly, Christ says in the Gospel: “But when you pray, enter into your chamber,” etc. (Matt. 6:6). And the prophet Jeremiah says: “God ought to be worshipped in the mind [variant: in spirit].” [Note: This is not found in Jeremiah, unless perhaps equivalently.] And elsewhere: “If a man is hidden in hiding places, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?” (Jer. 23:24.) [Col. 1173D] For this reason the canon is pronounced in secret words; and also for another reason: namely, that when silence has been established all around, the ministers and those standing by may recollect themselves during the canon itself and attend to the force and meaning of so great a sacrament, so that it may profit them. But the Lord’s Prayer, concluded in brief words, is sung in a loud voice, so that through its utterance and efficacy all present may be stirred to faith in so great a mystery, both by what precedes in the canon and by what follows after the said prayer. Finally, the Apostles are read to have said nothing more in the breaking of bread than the Lord’s Prayer.

## That the seven petitions of the sacred canon correspond to the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer

[Col. 1174A]

The order of the aforesaid canon should be observed. For there are seven petitions in the canon, just as in the Lord’s Prayer. There are three from the beginning down to *Quam oblationem* (“Which offering”). The first is for the universal Church; the second for particular brethren; the third for priests, ministers, or those standing by. The fourth extends from *Quam oblationem* to *Nobis quoque peccatoribus* (“To us also, sinners”). Namely, first comes the order of the Lord’s passion, then the remembrance of his resurrection and ascension. Secondly, Abel, Abraham, and Melchizedek are inserted, together with their offerings, in confirmation of the Lord’s sacrament. Thirdly, the wondrous faith of the Church in bringing about the body and blood of the Lord is manifested. Fourthly, [Col. 1174B] remembrance is made for all the dead.

The first petition in the Lord’s Prayer reads, “Hallowed be thy name”; it corresponds to the universal Church, which knows no other name under heaven except the name of the Lord. The second, “Thy kingdom come,” answers to particular brethren, who render vows and make offerings, so that God may reign in them. The third, “Thy will be done, as in heaven so on earth,” is fitting for priests and ministers, who wish and desire to be joined and incorporated with blessed Mary, the apostles, and the other saints. The fourth, “Give us this day our daily bread,” is applied to the order of the passion, resurrection, and ascension, because he himself is the living bread who came down from heaven. The fifth, “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors,” is joined [Col. 1174C] to the holy men Abel, Abraham, and Melchizedek, who, most ready for acknowledgment and prefigurers of the Lord’s sacrament, obtained God’s grace through faith and gentleness. The sixth, “And lead us not into temptation,” is added to the wondrous faith of the holy Church, which prays that they may not be led into the temptations of heretics. The seventh, “But deliver us from evil,” accords with the remembrance of all the dead, where the living pray that, together with all the faithful departed, they may be delivered from evil.

## That they ought to receive the Lord’s body only while fasting

It is plainly evident that when the disciples first received the body and blood of the Lord, they did not receive them fasting. For the Gospel says that while [Col. 1174D] they were eating, Jesus took bread and blessed it; and it had also said above: “When evening had come, he reclined with the twelve; and while they were eating he said: One of you will betray me” (Matt. 26); and afterward he handed over the sacrament. Yet is the institution of the universal Church to be criticized on that account, whereby it is always received by those fasting? For it pleased the Holy Spirit that, in honor of so great a sacrament, the Lord’s body should enter the Christian’s mouth before other foods. Therefore this custom is observed throughout the world. Nor, because the Lord gave it after food, ought brethren who have dined, or after [Col. 1175A] supper, to assemble to receive it; nor did those whom the Apostle rebukes and corrects act thus, by mixing these sacred things with ordinary meals. For the Savior, in order to commend more forcefully the greatness of that mystery, wished to impress this last thing upon the hearts and memory of the disciples from whom he was about to depart for his passion. He did not command it; and therefore, as to the order in which they should henceforth receive it, he left the apostles—through whom he was to order the Churches—to preserve this custom [variant: rite].

## Whether the Eucharist should be received daily

Someone may say that the Eucharist should not be received daily. You ask why. “Because,” he says, “days ought to be chosen on which a person lives more purely and more continently, in order to approach so great a sacrament more worthily.” [Col. 1175B] “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29). Another says the contrary: “Indeed, if the wound of sin and the onset of disease are so great that such medicines must be deferred, each person should by the authority of the bishop be removed from the altar to do penance, and by that same authority be reconciled. For this is to receive unworthily: to receive at the time when one ought to be doing penance; not to withdraw oneself from communion, or restore oneself to it, at one’s own discretion whenever one pleases. But if the sins are not so great that each person should be judged worthy of excommunication, he ought not [Col. 1176A] to separate himself from the daily medicine of the Lord’s body.”

Perhaps the person who best resolves the dispute between them is the one who advises them especially to remain in Christ’s peace; but let each do what, according to his faith, he devoutly believes ought to be done. For neither of them shrinks from the body and blood of the Lord; rather, each believes that he is eagerly honoring the most health-giving sacrament. Zacchaeus and that centurion did not quarrel with each other, nor did either prefer himself to the other, when one joyfully received the Lord into his house and the other said: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Matt. 8:8). Both honored the Savior in a different and seemingly contrary way; both were wretched because of sins; 1134 both received mercy. This comparison is also supported by the fact that, among the first people, manna tasted in each person’s mouth according to his own desire. So also does that sacrament by which the world has been subdued in the mouth of every Christian. For one, in honoring it, does not dare to receive daily; the other, in honoring it, does not dare to omit it on any day. This food desires only not to be despised, just as manna did not tolerate disgust. For this is why the Apostle says that it was received unworthily by those who did not distinguish it from other foods with the singular reverence due to it.

*The book of exposition of the Mass ends.*

# [On the Mystery of the Mass]

[Col. 1175]

## Brief notice on the following poem

This poem has acquired various titles in various manuscript codices and editions. The Paris edition of 1548 has: *On the Harmony of the Old and New Sacrifice*. The Antwerp edition of 1560 by Wolfgang Lazius, and certain manuscripts: *Verses on the Mystery of the Mass*. The Évreux codex: *Here begins Hildebert’s book on the Mass*. The Cologne edition and the new Lyons edition of 1677: *Verses of Hildebert, Archbishop of Tours, on the Mystery of the Mass*. This title indeed seems to imply that Hildebert did not publish this poem until he presided over the see of Tours, that is, after the seventieth year of his life and the year of Christ 1125. Yet, considering his old age and the very weighty business which he was compelled to undertake immediately after his installation in the see of Tours, this seems less probable.

It is more probable that he composed it either while he was still living at Cluny under Saint Hugh, or when he became schoolmaster at Le Mans; at that time it greatly concerned him to show himself entirely free from the errors of Berengar, whose pupil he had been in the liberal arts, and to prove this also by public writing. This he accomplished in the two preceding treatises and in the present and following poem. But since neither the variety of those titles nor the period when he published them is of great importance to the matter, we shall not delay the reader with this discussion. We merely observe that we give this poem collated and corrected from six manuscripts of the best quality, enlarged by fifty verses from the Colbert manuscript 6101; and that we have thought proper to insert here the summaries omitted in many editions, including the new Lyons edition, and marked in the Paris edition as in the manuscript codex of Évreux.

Moreover, manuscript no. 103 of Marmoutier has the following title: “A little work composed in metre by Lord Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, on the harmony of the old and new divine sacrifice. It begins.” Then follows:

### An elegiac poem by Brother Peter Paillardi of Le Mans on the Harmony of the Old and New Divine Sacrifice

[Note: He was Peter Paillardi, monk of Marmoutier, Hildebert’s contemporary.]

Hildebert of Le Mans is here: read, O reader,  
This work, distinguished in genius and in morals.

A work distinguished in morals; he ought not to have forgotten the little book  
In which are the holy mystical laws of Christ’s supper.

The holy mystical laws—the Mass, the solemn vows—  
Here believe that the true God is always present.

That God is always present is supreme mercy:  
The sacred victim grants heaven to his Christians.

1135–36 The sacred victim can grant his own eternal life;  
For this pardon we ask before God.

We ask before God that the dreadful corruption may be driven away  
By which the human race slips and falls.

The sinner slips and falls; everywhere the righteous man’s spirit  
Seeks the bright stars of heaven.

May the spirit that seeks the stars receive the joys of the blessed life;  
May the holy grace of the eternal God grant them.

[Col. 1177] These matters concerning the office of the Mass, by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans.

In another manuscript of the same monastery, no. 121, the title is absent, but these verses stand in its place:

## Apology

When an old error, reader, and a new one entangle you,  
I beg you, granting pardon to the writer, discern the cause.

I left behind many falsehoods which I could not remove.  
While I labor to pass cursorily through a barren task,

No page can contain how many evils the hand has increased,  
While I speak, either the eye is occupied with trifles or the ear is open.

Perhaps it will help toward pardon to know the fault.  
Beyond counting are those whose correction escaped notice,

And even now they remain hidden, although they had been sought.  
Therefore I beg you, spare the wretched writer who was compelled,

Who, wishing to do better, unwillingly made such ruinous things.  
If, having heard these things, you do not wish to yield,

And are uncertain whether to bless me, first hear this:  
In short, I am Davus; you, if you can, be Oedipus.

[Col. 1177]

# Verses of the Venerable Hildebert on the Mystery of the Mass

[Col. 1177A]

I have undertaken to write what the mystical sacred rite  
Of the Mass represents from the ancients, and what the minister does.

In place of the many sacrifices, in place of those repeated daily,  
The one true victim—God—was offered once. [Note: Heb. 9.]

Christ disclosed the covering of the Law, and the true Lamb  
Removed the lamb that merely signified.

The priest offers this Lamb, and testifies that in it  
The figures cease and the reality of the figures is enacted.

Thus he represents both the altar of the temple and that of the cross:  
That he may commemorate the sacred things of the one and enact those of the other.

Therefore I shall sing briefly what is enacted or commemorated in the Mass,  
And to what each thing is to be compared.

## On the entrance of the Mass

The company of prophets, heralding Christ who was to come,  
Is said to have foretold the mystery of the cross.

[Col. 1177B] With longings, praises, and many prayers  
It sighed beforehand for him, exalted him, and sought him.

The entrance of the Mass, which the choir sings before,  
Recalls these three and sets them in a like order.

First sighs are recounted, then praises,  
Then prayers: here you have what is denoted by each.

The office represents sighs; the *Gloria*, praises;  
The *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) repeated three times, prayers.

## On the priest’s coming to the altar

Meanwhile the priest comes in sacred vestments  
To the right side of the altar, to offer gifts.

The seasons in which, O Judea, your Emmanuel returns  
To visit you, are marked by that coming.

For the minister proceeds from a secret chamber;  
[Col. 1178A] God comes from a hidden birth [variant: “Having arisen secretly,” other manuscripts].

He is covered in sacred garments; flesh covered the Word,  
Wholly free from stain, wholly consecrated to God.

He stands at the right, because the people who sought vain  
And accursed gods were, as it were, the right hand.

## On the *Gloria in excelsis*

After this the priest begins the angelic hymn to the Father,  
And the choir completes what he has begun with a loud voice.

Beginning it, he recalls the joys  
Which the angel taught the shepherds at the Savior’s birth.

He recites the songs which the heavenly beings sang afterward:  
“Glory,” which the choir completes with a loud voice.

## On the Prayer

Then [Note: Reg. 4103: “Then the praying priest”; others differ.] he who is about to pray urges the others to pray;  
Christ commanded the disciples and did the same himself:

[Col. 1178B] For while teaching the crowds on the mountain, he prayed,  
And established for those brethren a form of prayer. [Note: Matt. 6.]

## On the Epistle

The reading which follows signifies the teaching of those  
Seventy-two who had been sent before. [Note: Luke 20.]

## On the Gradual

While the choir sings responses to their teachings,  
It teaches that it has given its assent.

## On the Alleluia

The following *Alleluia* recalls what glory of mind  
Accompanies faith, and what devout praise of mouth.

## On the Gospel

Then the Lord’s sacred words are read on the left.  
The people [Note: This seems to allude to the ancient custom of the faithful: even laypersons attended divine offices only standing, but were permitted to carry staffs, so that, while present at longer solemnities, they might be less tired by leaning on them. As the modern author of the *Life of the Most Devout Lord de Chasteuil* noted, the Marcnites still observe this rite: at the entrance of their churches there are bundles of staffs, from which every person entering takes one, so that, standing through the office in accordance with their custom, he may be less fatigued. Yet they lay them down for the Gospel and for the elevation of the sacred host. For, as Tertullian notes in *On Prayer*, ch. 12, to sit in the sight of the living God while the angel of prayer still stands by is most irreligious—unless, as he says, we reproach God because prayer has wearied us. Hildebert himself further suggests that this standing rite belonged particularly to monks when, in Sermon 3 for the feast of Saint Peter, among the hardships which he urges them to bear for merit, he counts illnesses arising from prolonged standing in choir. On this standing in choir, imposed also upon clerics, see our Martène, *On Divine Offices*, ch. 3, no. 12, where this is discussed fully and learnedly.] sets aside staffs, stands, and uncovers its head.

[Col. 1179A]

And lest the enemy coming upon them sow tares, [Note: Matt. 13.]  
The mystical form of the cross is impressed upon their foreheads.

Judea rejecting the faith, Christ’s grace  
Passed over to the nations; Israel still wanders. [Note: Acts 13.]

Whenever the Gospel is recited,  
This passing-over comes to mind and is represented by the place.

It is read on the left because the people to whom it passed over  
Had gone astray and were, as it were, idolaters on the left.

That you may be attentive, patient, and upright against the enemy,  
Your head, your staff, and your very posture teach you.

By uncovering your head, you are instructed to listen attentively;  
When you reject the staff, you are instructed to spare.

[Note: Two verses are absent here in the editions and other manuscripts, but are read in Royal MS 4103, Victorine MS 27, and Colbert MS 6101.]

You imitate pressing the teaching of the Word upon your heart  
When you clasp your breast above with both hands.

Standing, you learn that we are accustomed to fight while standing,  
[Col. 1179B] Because grievous combat awaits you beneath a watchful enemy.

## On the Creed

Behold, the choir takes up the compendium of our faith,  
Teaching that it has given its assent to the Word.

For here it shows how much the person has profited  
In whom he has believed, what faith is, and what it will give.

The order is good: the soldier and disciple answer,  
“I follow,” where the king and master call.

And the sheep testifies that it has been marked  
With the mark which its shepherd knows and acknowledges as his own. [Note: John 10.]

The craftsman, the standard-bearer, and the head himself approve these things;  
By these the work, the chiefs, and their own members are sustained.

## On the Offertory

[Col. 1179C]

Having thus confessed faith, the devout people are urged to pray  
That they may be steadfast in it and, moreover, fit their work to it.

The choir singing the offertory promises the effect,  
As though it said: “I believe, I shall confess, I shall act.”

Hence after this the minister offers the gifts to be consecrated,  
And afterward the people offer what the law permits them.

The order is fitting: you see the Gospel precede,  
Faith then disclosed, and gifts then given.

You hear in order to believe; and you believe in order to become a victim.  
Thus we begin to be, and are, God’s.

Furthermore, the gifts which the more devout people offer  
May recall the gifts of the house of Judea.

When Solomon consecrated the temple and the altar of Solomon,  
A great multitude of victims was offered by the people. [Note: 2 Chron. 4.]

[Col. 1180A] Using your example, O Judea, the faithful people  
Give themselves and their goods to the altar; you give neither.

## On the offering of bread, wine, and water

Not without mystery, nor without reality, is either bread brought to the altar  
[Note: “Nor without reality, either bread”; Royal MS 4103: “not without reality for you, bread.”]  
Or wine, to which you add water.

Figures foretold that both were to be given to God;  
Tradition taught it; holier usage maintains it.

They say that under a typical rite and as a figure of what was to come,  
Melchizedek sacrificed both to the Lord. [Note: Gen. 14.]

The Redeemer himself gave both to his disciples at supper,  
Both transformed into his body. [Note: Matt. 26; Mark 14; Luke 12.]

The practice itself is fitting, by which he is so sacrificed below  
That his flesh remains inviolate above.

You wonder at water mixed with wine; but it is  
A great sacrament and not devoid of reason.

[Col. 1180B] Flowing water is passing humanity: humanity, mingled with the wine,  
Is joined to Christ, to Christ’s blood.

The minister who separates either water or wine  
Separates the head himself from his members.

Furthermore, no spring is without blood, nor blood without a spring;  
Both together save; both together consecrate.

1139 When the lance searched the entrails of Christ hanging on the cross,  
Blood and water flowed out together. [Note: John 19.]

As both flowed together, offer both together:  
Remove one, and you do not imitate the work of the cross.

[Note: Ten verses lacking here in the editions and most manuscripts have been supplied from Colbert MS 6101, where the following heading was found in the margin.]

### How the chalice and host are to be placed upon the altar

These sacraments are arranged on the altar in a varying manner;  
The right hand of the offered bread holds the chalice.

For the right side of the Almighty hanging on the cross  
Poured out bloody water through its wound.

Thus the priest sacrifices at the altar in remembrance of this,  
And thus the continual victim washes away our sins.

It is not to be blamed if the bread is placed at the front  
And the chalice behind it:

The former arrangement maintains the insight of reason;  
The latter accords with the Church’s usages.

## On the Secret Prayer

After these things have thus been set forth, the priest prays secretly,  
Recalling and imitating the secret prayers

Which Christ made when, O Judah, you had already been dismissed,  
He withdrew a little and prayed three times, saying:

[Col. 1181A] In an exemplar manuscript [Note: It is not indicated which manuscript codex this was; perhaps it was Colbert MS 6327, where these words are indeed written in red.] these words were inserted, written in red: [Note: In the Évreux manuscript these words are written in red: “Then the priest bows before the altar, praying: ‘In a spirit of humility.’ Then he secretly urges the people to pray for him, saying: ‘Pray for me, brethren.’”] [Note: These words are absent from Royal MS 4103, but are present in the Victorine manuscript.] “Father, if it is possible, let this chalice pass from me.” (The same could be rendered in metre thus:

With your will preserved, he may fittingly pray thus:  
“Kind Father, let this chalice pass from me.” [Note: Matt. 26; Mark 14; Luke 22.])

By these prayers, as though by a certain sacrifice of the lips,  
An offering is made which itself bears the type of the Law.

The high priest gave mystical gifts to the Lord  
For himself, for the people, and for the chief priests.

For the ram, goat, and calf bore  
His own sins, those of the people, and those of the high priests.

The calf bore the sins of the high priests, the goat the evils of the people;  
The leader of the flock himself expiated his own transgression. [Note: Lev. 16.]

The Savior recalled these three things in a threefold prayer,  
Already then acting alone for us all. [Note: After this verse Colbert MS 6101 alone has:

He prayed; he asked for himself because he had glorified,  
And for his own, whom the Father himself had given him;

[Col. 1182D] And, seeking pardon for his enemies, he asks it for the ruler;  
For the ruler of the people commanded that he be killed.

Thrice prostrate upon the ground, contrition of heart, and that  
Bloody sweat were a cross before the cross.

The anxiety he endured, as the shadows promised their end,  
Was a victim pleasing to the supreme Father.]

[Col. 1181B]

For when he had thrice lain prostrate on the ground, contrition of heart  
And that bloody sweat [Note: Luke 22.] were a cross before the cross.

Already then his anxiety, as the shadows promised their end,  
Was more pleasing than the old rite [variant: “than the old rite alone”].

## On the Preface

When these things are done, the priest greets the people in a lofty voice  
And bids them lift their hearts on high.

Then he declares that thanks must always be given to the Father through Christ,  
And afterward consecrates the gifts which are to be consecrated.

If you carefully note everything, the Son did all this:  
After praying, he asked the disciples for the cross.

1140 First he commanded them to watch and immediately to pray;  
Then to sleep; afterward the Lamb and altar endured.  
[Note: This is the reading of the editions. Évreux: “and the altar of God”; Royal MS 4103, Colbert MSS 6327 and 6101, and Victorine: “the altar was”; Évreux: “the altar of God.”]

[Col. 1181C]

Surely when he says to them, “Watch,” [Note: Matt. 26; Mark 14; Luke 22.] he greets them;  
For the soul’s salvation is present if we keep watch.

When he commands prayer, he advises them to have their heart on high,  
For prayer alone commands what is heavenly.

When at last he calls them to rest, he teaches them to give thanks;  
For by repose of mind we give thanks to him.
