For to give thanks is to render ourselves pleasing to the Lord—  
What a mind, hand, and mouth free from vices accomplish.

May everyone who sacrifices under Christ the judge become such a one—  
He under whom even the righteous man trembles.

With the song of the heavenly beings, whom it is certain stand by the altar,  
He asks that his own prayers may afterward be admitted.

“With whom [he asks] that our voices also may be admitted,” etc.

He asks that his own voice may agree with their praise,  
Whom many a page teaches stand by the sacred rites.

[Col. 1182A]

If you wish to give credit to the words of the man  
Who is manifestly known everywhere to have poured forth heavenly nectar:

At the time when the priest stands as suppliant at the altars  
And the Son himself, remaining, is sacrificed to the Father,

The heavens lie open; the heavenly choir is present; the lower world  
Is joined to the higher; author [variant: actor] and act become one.

When the minister’s mind, voice, and life  
Agree with these companies, he undoubtedly gives thanks.

### Holy, Holy, Holy

Then fittingly [Note: Victorine manuscript: “for the people.”] with the people he sings “Holy” three times, and what follows,  
Before consecrating the mystical gifts.

We believe these praises were taken from Isaiah, [Note: Isa. 6.]  
In which the Three and the One Supreme are indicated.

[Col. 1182B]

“Holy” set three times signifies that he is threefold; but  
“Lord and God of Sabaoth” proclaims him one.

To these Three and this One the priest sacrifices, the angel offers;  
The clergy ascribe [praise], and the people alike venerate.

And because some receive him in the sacred gift,  
They glorify the Lord for the sacred gift.

They venerate him with those praises by which heaven resounds,  
Which two of the seraphim sing night and day.

For what they have received, they fittingly render these as thanks,  
Lest they seek in vain what they are to receive.

[Note: Thus it stands in the Évreux manuscript in place of the summary.]

## How the old sacrifice agrees with the established new one

Thus far I have explained what is represented in the office  
Of the Mass itself and what the minister does.

[Col. 1182C]

From this, all that is commanded to be offered  
In the former sanctuary may fittingly be recalled.

1141 For whatever is done in the Church, provided it benefits  
Morals or faith, is a victim pleasing to God.

We offer calves of the tongue, sacrifice goats,  
Reduce incense and the male of sheep [that is, the ram] to ashes.  
[Note: Lev. 9.]

When we sing or read what restrains evil  
And calls the people and us to better things,

Then also a calf and goat are sacrificed,  
When you tread down pride and suppress luxury.

The lamb comes from the innocent, the dove from the simple,  
The turtle-dove from those who weep, far from the highest joys. [Note: Lev. 5.]

You offer loaves baked in an oven upon the altars  
[Col. 1183A] If no scourges shake the strength of your mind.

You offer them mixed with oil if piety moderates justice  
And strikes the guilty less than [Note: Royal MS 4103 and Victorine: “than it may lawfully strike”; the others: “than it may please [one to strike].”] it lawfully may.

You offer unleavened bread if a purer mind approaches you  
And heavenly love bakes away the unstable things of the flesh.

You also offer fine flour if you gather together those whom error had divided,  
Join them to the faith, and do the same yourself.

Teaching this gently in catechesis, immersing them in baptism,  
And training them to bear hardships, you bake them.

Thus these things teach morals and figure Christ;  
Thus the remaining things of the Law have a twofold use.

But the rest of the Mass so recounts the sacred things of the Law  
That it presents, under the cross, the sacred mysteries of the cross.

For all that the Law, herald of what was to come,  
[Col. 1183B] commanded to be done within the Holy of Holies is recounted.

It is difficult to disclose these things, because I am constrained  
By metre, names unknown to metre, and the subject matter.

Grant pardon, reader; for my verses it is enough  
To disclose the matter and its use, not its outward appearance.

Yet do not expect that I shall undertake to explain to you  
Every single word or action.

My style will run to the sum of things, and I shall sing how the altar  
Represents the shadow of the Law and the work of the cross.

Once a year, and to the high priest alone, the Holy of Holies lay open,  
While the people remained outside in prayer. [Note: Lev. 16; Heb. 9.]

That corner was separated by a veil from the former sanctuary  
And was sacred through the presence and converse of heavenly beings.

[Col. 1183C]

It was distinguished by a censer, an altar of incense,  
And the covenant of the testament.

It was also distinguished by the notable table which stands above the ark,  
Over which each cherub bends down to overshadow it.

The high priest approached it once in the year,  
Bearing mystical gifts for himself and for the people:

Namely, the blood of the goat and calf  
Which Aaron’s offspring sacrifice before the doors,

And likewise coals, which sacred Scripture teaches  
Are to be taken from above the outer altar.

The priest places these in the censer,  
And burns so much incense that abundant smoke overshadows him.

He sprinkles the table, and afterward sprinkles  
The sacred outer altar with blood that makes peace.

[Col. 1183D]

Then he returns to the people and washes his garment; yet he was not  
Clean until late in the evening.

This place, this priest, these gifts were signs;  
The signs have passed away; the things signified remain.

The former sanctuary represents the Church, the latter heaven;  
The high priest, Christ; the blood, the bitterness of the cross;

The coals, O Christ, the summit of your virtues;  
The censer, flesh; the burning incense, prayers.

[Col. 1184A]

The supreme table represents the Father; the altar, the heavenly hosts;  
By the garment humanity is denoted; by evening, human death.

These brief explanations disclose the veils of the things to you;  
By them you see those things, but as though half unveiled.

1142 From these, the matter becomes accessible to you no otherwise than if  
You were to look at the interior of a house from its doors.

The inner realities of the sacred mystery will be opened, Christ, by your teaching—  
You by whose death the inner parts of heaven lie open.

Therefore I have explained the same parts which I endeavor to sketch,  
In the order in which the canon sets them forth.

Thus you will more easily learn what work and what words of the minister  
Recall or enact the Law of the cross.

### “You therefore, most merciful Father,” through “unimpaired”

The high priest entered the sanctuary with the blood of calves;  
Christ himself entered heaven with his own [blood].

[Col. 1184B]

The priest always approaches the altar with blood,  
Ever mindful of blood poured out.

For as often as he reconsiders the blood shed—in word, cross, and mind—  
So often he bears it in sacred form.

For remembering blood is, as it were, a kind of blood;  
The repeated cross makes us mindful of this.

The remembrance of death is present wherever the anointed hand  
Impresses mystical signs of the cross upon the everlasting foods.

Thus the priest, following Aaron and Christ, frequents the altar;  
He bears this draught of blood.

For in the first verse he marks the banners of salvation  
Three times over the gifts placed before him.

There, already mindful of death—and gently and devoutly so—  
He calls the same gift by a threefold name.

First he calls the foods “gifts,” then names them “offerings,”  
[Col. 1184C] And afterward designates them by the name of “sacrifice.”

He calls them gifts because God gave them, so that by them  
Flesh might be sustained by law and custom.

They are offerings because God is presented with them, and thereby  
Rewards the giver, to whom the giver gave them.

[Note: Thus the editions and Colbert MSS 6102 and 6327 and the Victorine manuscript; Évreux: “Now because”; Royal MS 4103: “For indeed.”]

But their being reckoned by the name of sacrifice shows  
Why he first calls them offerings.

Namely, because they are sacrificed and fittingly reward  
The author who returns what was given to him.

Thus the same things which he calls gifts, when they are sacrificed,  
Are offerings because by them they reward God.

By these names also the threefold victim, already recounted in my writing,  
Is quite beautifully indicated.

For all that was promised in those victims  
They say is fulfilled and bear under a visible form.

[Col. 1184D]

For what the priest formerly hoped for in the ram, the people in the goat,  
And the leaders in the calf, [Note: Lev. 4.]

The cross bestowed it; the food tastes of it; the whole rite proclaims that the offering has been rendered,  
Marking these three sacred things by three names.

### “First, which we offer to you,” through “our bishop.” “Remember, Lord, your servants,” through “the living and true God”

The Levitical priest, entering the Holy of Holies, prays  
[Col. 1185A] For himself, for his ruler, his people, and his household. [Note: Lev. 16; Heb. 9.]

Before the cross Christ prays both that he himself may be glorified  
[Note: John 17.] And that those whom God gave him may be preserved.

In heaven too the priest always acts for the people,  
The lord for the servant, and the shepherd for the flock.

Our priest, following Aaron and Christ in this,  
First makes supplication for the whole Church,

Then also for the health of the pontiff and king,  
And afterward for the rest as is fitting.

### “Communicating and keeping memory,” through “may we be fortified by their aid”

The Law commanded that live coals taken from the altar’s fire  
Be carried into the Holy of Holies. [Note: Lev. 16.]

The Law commanded that Aaron, hastening, should burn incense to God  
[Col. 1185B] When the same coals had been placed in the censer.

Christ carried to heaven the censer of flesh, as though filled with coals  
By the abundance of virtues.

He took these from God’s fire, by which the weak things of the mind are burned  
And the slippery impulses of lax flesh are consumed.

As though among coals, the priest carries the names of the saints  
[Note: Colbert MSS 6101 and 6327: “among the Holy of Holies”; Royal MS 4103 and Victorine: “among the holy”; Évreux: “among sacred holy things.”] by commemorating them.

For we compare these to living coals,  
Which shine in action and glow with love of righteousness.

Finally, the thing that follows figures the shadow commanded by the Law:  
While he sacrifices, the minister has this fire in his mind.

For when the priest entered the Holy of Holies, [Note: Lev. 16.]  
He bore on his breast the written names of the fathers.

Namely, implying the examples and faith of the ancients  
[Col. 1185C] Which are to be imitated by those to whom the mystical table is open.

Nor is it enough for God to remember the good in words  
Unless you yourself display good deeds in your conduct.

Thus the priest, warm within and shining without,  
Himself become a coal, bears coals.

Thus he fittingly intertwines the names of many fathers;  
Thus he himself represents many fathers by his merits.

### “This offering therefore,” through “to be numbered.” Through Christ. “Who on the day before he suffered,” through “For this is my body.” “Likewise, after supper,” through “you shall do this in remembrance.” “Therefore, remembering, Lord,” through “an unspotted victim”

The Levitical priest at prayer is veiled by this cloud of smoke,  
So that while he burns incense no one may see him. [Note: Lev. 16.]

By this prayer for us, by this diligent service, he prays
[Col. 1185D] Christ, so that he may pass beyond angelic sight. [Note: [Col. 1185] Luke 22.]

No one knows how much the presence of the flesh received  
Can avail before the Father, or what prayers accomplish without speech.

Before these prayers yields whatever the Levite offers,  
In whatever manner, at whatever time, or in whatever rank.

By these prayers the Father is made to unlearn the judge’s wrath,  
And is certainly bent and made mindful of the Father. [Note: [Col. 1185D] Colb. 6101 and Ebr. 19 read thus. Colb. 6327 has “wrath”; Reg. 4103 and Victorinus, “to depart, the judge’s wrath.”]

As beneath a cloud, he who performs Christ’s office,  
Christ himself also, repeatedly handles and offers the sacred gifts.  
[Col. 1186A] [Note: [Col. 1186D] Ebr.: “Christ the bishop”; the others: “Christ.”]

For this is the power, this the efficacy, of the Word  
And of the cross: that mind and tongue give place to them.

Man does not know—and it is hidden even from the heavenly beings—how the grace of the words and the mystery of the cross  
Advance the food.

[Note: [Col. 1186D] Here in Colb. 6101 are found these four verses, absent from the printed editions and from most other manuscripts.]

While the sacrificing priest, extended over the offerings, overshadows them,  
He signifies the winged cherubim and seraphim.  
When he covers the sacred altar of incense,  
To which the high priest may enter once only.

The priest then begins insistently to pray these words,  
Which, while their outward appearance remains, renew both gifts.

1144 He begins, contrite with all his heart, and burning  
The bright incense of prayers in the censer of his mind.

“We beseech [thee], being appeased …”

[Col. 1186B]

He prays that God, appeased, may receive the gifts  
And order our times in peace.

He prays that from the mass of perdition  
God may choose to number us among the elect.

He prays that this same God may bless the food he has given;  
He prays that he may make it enrolled and ratified.

He prays that this work of the altar may be performed fittingly,  
And that it may be such as God himself accepts and approves.

When he asks the Lord to bless what he has created,  
He asks that he renew it for the better and advance it.

When he asks that the food be enrolled,  
He asks that God allot it to himself and call it his own by sanctifying it.

[Col. 1186C] When he asks that it be ratified, he asks that he may not hope in it in vain,  
But that it may profit him, and that his petitions may be confirmed.

When he asks that this be performed fittingly—he who rightly  
Offers the gifts—he asks that he may rightly distribute them.

Therefore the blessing of this food is greater grace,  
More abundant fruit, and enduring strength.

All this, indeed, is conveyed in those words  
Which the priest adds—not his own, but the Lord’s.

For he is about to recount what Christ uttered or did  
When he dined and the blessed supper took place. [Note: [Col. 1185] Matthew 26.]

“Who, the day before he suffered, took bread.”

At this word “bread,” bread still common is taken from the altar,  
And, having been taken, is raised with both hands.

Then, when the priest comes to “he blessed,”  
He impresses upon it the mystical signs of the cross with raised hand. [Note: [Col. 1185] Matthew 26; Mark 14; Luke 22.]

[Col. 1186D] Nor does he set it down upon the altar before, O Christ,  
He has represented your words and spoken these over it:

“Take and eat of this, all of you.”

Then he raises and signs the chalice, and does not set it down  
Until he has repeated the author’s words over it thus:

“Take and drink from it, all of you,” as far as “for the remission of sins.”

If there is any faith in the fathers whom blessed life makes everlasting,  
[Col. 1187A] This food, once flesh, becomes food for the soul.

By these words both are taught, on proven authority,  
To acquire new powers greater than their own.

Under the cross and under the word nature is renewed:  
Bread honours the altar with flesh, the chalice with blood.

Therefore, when the priest comes to those words  
By which so great a grace is bestowed upon the altar,

He raises both, indicating that both bear something higher  
Than common foods, and something greater. [Note: [Col. 1187D] Colb. 6101 reads *gerit*, “bears”; Colb. 6327, *gerat*, “may bear.” So also Reg. 4103 and Victor.; Ebr., *ferat*, “may carry.”]

Whatever has prepared sustenance for the soul has prepared nourishment for the flesh,  
All inferior to the consecrated foods.

And whenever the priest has offered these,  
Christ commands him to be mindful of himself.

By this sacrament we confess in remembrance  
That the Creator of all things, as man, underwent death.

[Col. 1187B] 1145 That, rising, he ascended into heaven: these three things indeed  
Indicate what kind of sacrificer that food requires:

Namely, that he die in the flesh, rise in mind,  
And seek the heavenly temple by fifteen steps. [Note: [Col. 1187D] Thus the printed editions, Reg. 4103, and Victor. 272; but Colb. 6101, 6327, and Ebr. read *carni*, “to the flesh,” which is preferable.]

Thus, mindful of him who suffered, rose, flew to the stars, and went there,  
Both we and likewise your people, great God. [Note: [Col. 1187] Matthew 28.]

From your own gifts and gifts given to you we offer pure gifts,  
Holy gifts, and also immaculate gifts.

They are gifts given to us by the Lord; for what he gives as food,  
We ourselves offer by sacrificing it.

We offer them pure, because no oldness is mingled with them,  
[Col. 1187C] Nor do they need the aid of the Law in order to save.

We offer them holy, because one who discerns the sacred foods  
Profits and is sanctified by offering them.

We offer them immaculate, because what was an immaculate victim,  
And what he gave, becomes ours and is given by him.

The priest, standing in attendance, begs that God, serene and merciful,  
May look upon and bless [or: approve] those gifts.

May they please him no less than what the boy Abel offered,  
[Note: [Col. 1187] Genesis 4.] than what Abraham offered, than what the king and priest of Salem offered.

In these three is indicated the form of the several sacred rites:  
What the law of nature, the delivered Law, and the sacred supper gave—  
[Note: [Col. 1187D] The editions, including the new Lyons edition, also read—incorrectly—“what law delivered, abbreviated law”; all manuscripts without exception read “what the sacred supper gave,” as printed here.]

[Col. 1187D] The law of nature, the delivered Law, and the abbreviated Law—  
Each pleased God by its own offering.

Yet unequally: for in the latter, salvation is said  
To have been complete through supreme hope and faith.

[Col. 1188A] This is sufficient in itself, perfect, and needs no future things;  
Nor does it possess anything from the past by which it may be helped.

“We humbly beseech thee.” “Remember also, O Lord.” “To us also, thy sinful servants,” as far as “all honour and glory.”

The Law commanded the table, the shadow, and the altar to be sprinkled  
Outwardly with peace-making blood. [Note: [Col. 1187] Leviticus 4.]

The Son is said as often to sprinkle the Father  
As, by the sprinkled blood, he appeases him.

[Note: [Col. 1187D] Within the Canon itself we have found no mention, nor even a trace, of this sprinkling, although we have examined the writers on liturgies for this purpose with all diligence possible. No explanation occurs to us except conjecturally: perhaps it was a particular rite of the Church of Le Mans; yet not even Martène himself, the indefatigable investigator of ecclesiastical rites, reports it. It is therefore mere allegory.]

He always sprinkles the heavenly beings, because he continually  
Repairs and restores their flock once sprinkled. [Note: [Col. 1188D] The printed editions and most manuscripts read *superos*, “the heavenly beings”; Ebr. reads *solus, servos*, perhaps preferable.]

He always sprinkles human beings too, because he continually renews them once sprinkled  
And reconciles them to the Father.

[Col. 1188B] Standing at the altars, the priest himself sprinkles them,  
When, mindful of the blood sprinkled, he unites them.

He unites them by appeasing God, replenishing the ruin  
Of the spirits, and restoring life to the guilty.

God, Life itself, dying, bestowed all this upon the world;  
The mention of his death still bestows it through him. [Note: [Col. 1188D] Ebr. adds “thereafter.”]

Therefore the sacrificer sprinkles the Father with blood  
When remembrance of the one sprinkling appeases him.

He sprinkles the assembly of heavenly dwellers  
When remembrance of the one sprinkled one replenishes them. [Note: [Col. 1188D] Reg. reads “purifies.”]

He sprinkles those also whom the water of salvation washed,  
When remembrance of the one sprinkled blood purifies them.

1146 The priest, doing this, having assumed the posture of a suppliant,  
Prays that the mystical gifts may be borne on high.

[Col. 1188C] Standing upright, he adds that participation in the table  
May profit and inwardly nourish all who receive it.

“Remember also, O Lord, thy servants,” etc.

And lest pious remembrance of the buried be omitted,  
He asks the same both for the departed and for himself.

He asks it for himself when he prays to be joined to the saints,  
Whom he himself names by their names.

That angel, by whose hands that sacred minister  
Prays for both gifts to be carried on high,

Is his angel; or they are those whom reverent antiquity  
Says are sent down from above to attend the sacred rites.

The heavenly altar is the sight of God; for sacred gifts to be borne there  
Is for them also to please God through their merits.

For angelic hands to carry them is for the heavenly beings to rejoice  
[Col. 1188D] In our devotion and in the sacred mysteries.

What are borne on high by so secret a rejoicing  
Appease and pacify God.

Therefore the pious sacrificer sprinkles the Father with blood,  
[Col. 1189A] When remembrance of the one sprinkled thus appeases him.

When he obtains pardon for the living and refreshment for the dead,  
And the portion that he asks for himself,

He is said to sprinkle both heavenly and mortal beings;  
For the remembrance that cleanses us replenishes them.

Moreover, when the priest names the lofty altar,  
To which he humbly prays the consecrated gifts to be borne,

He clearly recalls the inner part of the veil,  
Into which the high priest entered once. [Note: [Col. 1189] Leviticus 16.]

When he asks that the sacred gifts be carried upwards, he signifies the goat  
Which the Law commands to enter the desert wastes.

For the Law places two goats at the doors of the Temple:  
One it assigns to the desert; the other dies.

Christ is each goat in different respects:  
For he suffered upon the wood and lives in the height of heaven.

[Col. 1189B] Here he lives humbled; there he reigns in the wilderness,  
Whither he himself carried back the sheep upon his own shoulders. [Note: [Col. 1189D] Ebr. 19, Colb. 6101, and Colb. 6327: “carried back the sheep.”] [Note: [Col. 1189] Luke 15.]

Thus the priest remembers the Law and remembers the cross,  
Asking that both gifts be carried on high.

“To us also, thy sinful servants.”

While he recalls the saints, he recounts the shoulder-piece,  
[Note: [Col. 1189] Exodus 39.] which bore the written names of the twelve fathers.

For the *logion* covered the breast, and the shoulder-piece the shoulders  
Of the high priest entering the sacred inner place.

Bearing in each of these the names of the forefathers engraved upon gems,  
He was a herald and type of what was to come.

For we bear the *logion* when we name the fathers  
Near the beginning of the Canon;

We bear the burden of the shoulder-piece when we insert the fathers’ names  
In this part of the sacred Canon.

[Col. 1189C] Then too the minister bears the *logion* and shoulder-piece  
When the fathers’ character and the labour itself please God.

1147 “Through him, O Lord, thou dost ever create all these good things,” etc.

Behold, it is next added that through Christ,  
Good Creator of the world, you always create all these good things.

You sanctify and give life; you likewise bless,  
Glorifying the work of the first creation.

For because God the Word so cleaves to humanity, and because creating and created man  
Are one person,

Whatever God orders or works through the Word  
[Note: [Col. 1189] John 1.] is said to be done through Christ.

Therefore through Christ the nature of things is renewed,  
And common food becomes a special good.

Through Christ also the one God sanctifies both,  
[Col. 1189D] Gives life alike to both, and likewise blesses them.

He sanctifies because this grace is also given to things:  
That one who rightly receives them may be sanctified by them.

[Note: [Col. 1189D] These two verses are absent from the Colbert manuscripts but occur in the Évreux manuscript.]

He gives life because this quickening is given to things,  
That one dying inwardly may be quickened by them.

Then he blesses them likewise, because from this it follows  
[Col. 1190A] That one who rightly receives them is blessed.

Through Christ there is honour and also glory to the Father,  
Through whom the Father causes all things to be glorified.

It is also with Christ, because he too is glorified,  
With whom the Father causes all things to be glorified.

It is at once in Christ, because each is the one God;  
And what is in this one is in both alike.

“Let us pray.” “By the precepts.” “Our Father.” “Deliver us, we beseech thee,” etc.

The mystical ordinances of the Law require the high priest  
To return to the people and wash his garments. [Note: [Col. 1189] Leviticus 16.]

Yet he was unclean—such was the warning of those same ordinances—  
Until the sun had already set.

Christ returns to the Church, which he did not leave by departing,  
Coming to its aid by sharing its suffering.

[Col. 1190B] He washes its garments in the living waters—  
The fountain that continually heals our wounds. [Note: [Col. 1189D] Colb. 6101 and 6327 read *menstrua*, “monthly” or “recurring.”]

Yet that fountain itself, while it washes, will be unclean and in need of washing  
So long as the sun serves the world.

For while this sun performs its task,  
Stains will cling to Christ’s members, and there will be something to wash.

The priest is said, as it were, to return to the people,  
By again multiplying prayers for the people.

And now, as though outside, he changes his voice; and praying,  
He exhorts the choir also to pray together.

He recalls the lofty form of prayer,  
[Note: [Col. 1189] Matthew 6.] which Christ established and taught his own. [Note: [Col. 1189] Luke 11.]

“Our Father, who art in heaven.”

By such services and by the intervention of sacred rites,  
[Col. 1190C] And together with the dipping in sanctifying water,

He who washes the people is said to wash his own garments  
[Note: [Col. 1189] Leviticus 16.] and restore them to God by the fountain of prayers.

Yet he remains unclean until the sun sets;  
For while he lives, every human being has something to wash.

Thus the returning sacrificer becomes fit to receive  
And receives both together unto life.

1148 Now, as it were together with the people, he asks for himself seven gifts,  
Which Christ willed and established to be asked for.

The first three of these will indeed remain without end,  
But the loving Day promises an end to the rest.

For the Father’s holy name will always be such  
That it is blessedly feared, loved, and revered. [Note: [Col. 1190D] Colb. 6101 reads “is worthy.”]

[Col. 1190D] And his good kingdom will always exist: therefore every scandal,  
And everything that resists, will be far away.

As in heaven, so on earth the will shall always be done,  
And in neither place will there be anything to be rejected.

The Father’s will is accomplished equally in both  
When what the angel loves and wills, the human being also loves and wills.

[Col. 1191A] Moreover, as some of the ancients understood it,  
The body is taken as earth, the spirit as heaven.

The divine will is accomplished in these together  
When the body is subject to, and supports, the spirit.

These three now attend the righteous amid diverse circumstances;  
After the world’s end they will be without end.

The remaining four will cease: none will need to be fed,  
And there will be none whose debts require forgiveness.

No one will be able to be tempted; thereafter no evils will exist  
From which the Creator must deliver the elect.

For by the daily bread I understand the Word of life,  
Or the sacrament by which a person lives inwardly.

Then the righteous person will need neither teaching nor that food,  
[Note: [Col. 1191D] Better: Colb. 6101, Reg. 4103, Victor. 272, and Ebr. read “who”; Colb. 6327, “to whom.”] who will know every good, for whom God himself is food.

“Deliver us, we beseech thee, O Lord.”

[Col. 1191B] Because he remembers the past, he is burdened by the present;  
The priest himself fears future evil.

He asks that God, through the prayer of the saints, may deliver him from it,  
And that the peace given may make our times tranquil.

Turmoil harms the Church when it rages;  
Peace nourishes the seeds of fruit sown in hope.

Next follows the breaking of bread handed down to us  
By the Lord, itself also bearing something of the Law.

By the Law’s command, fine flour is ordered to be diminished,  
[Note: [Col. 1191D] Leviticus 28.] to be sacrificed to God only in fragments.

Thus the Redeemer is said, while dining, to have broken the sacred bread  
And to have distributed it broken among his own.

We too, not without purpose following the Law and Christ,  
[Col. 1191C] Properly divide the gifts consecrated to God.

For there are three parts of the Church: one labours  
On earth; high rest already cherishes another part.

A merciful fire refines the part that remains,  
And passage to rest lies open to it once refined.

Different in merits and in the lot of their places,  
The broken victim signifies these three parts.

The portion dipped in wine is suited to the living;  
The flesh itself expiates by the work of blood and flesh.

For the blessedly departed, one of whom, being purer,  
Does not need this intercession, while another does.

Reason commands [or: teaches], and custom maintains, that the remaining portions be offered;  
Yet the same fruit is not given to both.

For while the minister stands at the sacred altars for the righteous,  
He gives thanks on behalf of the righteous.

[Col. 1191D] Whereas for those whose punishment is to be remitted, the avenger now tempers punishment,  
And now hastens their full rest. [Note: [Col. 1191D] Colb. 6101 and 6327: “for those to be saved.”]

By these foods we receive the food of that Lamb  
Whom the Law foretold, the cross bore, and the altar signifies.

1149 [Note: [Col. 1191D] These ten verses occur only in manuscript Colb. 1601 and are absent from both the editions and the other manuscripts.]

Not raw, nor boiled in water, but roasted by fire:  
Thus the Lamb should be eaten by peoples and tribe.

By the raw Lamb, pure from earth, and by the Lamb boiled in waters,  
Schism is signified: Emmanuel himself is divided.

The flesh roasted upon coals is cooked and clings to the bones:  
Thus our flesh is bound to God from heaven.

Nor should anyone who performs the suppliant work of the sacrificer  
Use this without wild lettuces.

Wild lettuces are the humble compunction of the heart,  
By which one piously washes away sins through weeping and groaning.

The priest, about to receive this in mystery from Christ himself,  
Asks three gifts both for himself and for the people.

First, he asks that he be numbered among those  
Who are ashamed to be driven in the flesh by the storm of flesh.

Then he asks that he be glorified in that kingdom  
To which the head draws its members to be glorified.

Finally, because the flesh sluggishly resists the spirit,  
[Col. 1192B] And the unhappy spirit yields to the flesh itself,

He begs for peace, by which each may become what the other is,  
And they may will and follow the same things in concord.

For unless it is well ordered through you, a human being is not justified  
Now, nor shall be justified eternally.

Ancient tradition distinguishes in this sense  
That the clergy pray in a threefold voice thus.

Judaea, to return to Christ’s faith, is signified  
When the Father moves to the right and completes the work. [Note: [Col. 1191D] Thus Ebr. and Colb. 6327; the printed Colb. 6110 reads: “When he moves a portion to the right.”]

[Note: [Col. 1192D] These six verses occur only in Colb. 6101.]

Meanwhile the united people partake of these foods,  
Whence the choir returns songs worthy of God.

Then the sacrificer, turning, salutes clergy and people,  
And asks that these holy things assist the suppliants.

“Ite” is added, because our devotion is sent  
[Col. 1192C] By angelic hands to the heavenly dwelling places.

[Note: [Col. 1192D] These five hexameter verses occur in Colb. 1168, Reg. 4103, and Victorin. 272, under this title: “What each side of the altar signifies.”]

There is a reason why the right side of the altar holds  
The beginning and end of the Mass, and the left the middle.

The right signifies the Jews, the left the Gentiles.  
Our faith began from the former, was brought to the latter, and will return to the former;  
And at the end of the world they will be faithful.

[Note: [Col. 1192D] These eleven verses occur only in Colb. 1168, absent from all others, and immediately follow the line, “Completes the work.”]

They believe that the Church has three parts of the faithful:

The angelic assembly always attending the Lord,  
And holy persons now half-blessed by merit;  
The third part is tormented, but through affliction is purified.

From this comes the mystical breaking of the heavenly bread.

The larger portion rightly signifies the part already completed;  
Another portion of the bread, which is commanded to be kept dry,  
Signifies those whom I have called half-blessed.

The third portion, customarily taken when placed with the blood,  
[Col. 1192D] Signifies those stationed in the struggle of the present life,  
Whom it still holds until judgment purifies them.

All of us are taken from the midst when the fates press on,  
And are drawn where our completed life calls us.

These are never punished; those are punished always; others for a time;  
And the purified are granted passage into rest.

For these, the sacred altar—or a life free of crime,  
Or friendship purchased by acts of service—obtains this.

[Col. 1193A] Perfect persons and utterly wicked persons are helped by no prayers of their people,  
No expenditure of prayers, no burnt offerings.

For the righteous needs none of these, nor does the utterly wicked deserve them;  
The person for whom the sacred table prepares pardon is in the middle.

1150 Yet it often helps the living who wander from the path of life,  
That they may return, even if late.

Hence, whenever the sacred altars are attended,  
The broken victim is allotted to three portions.

The portion dipped in wine prays for the living,  
And the flesh itself expiates by the work of blood and flesh.

For the blessedly departed, one of whom, being purer,  
Does not need this intercession, while another does.

To you, Supreme One, we offer two portions; yet for these same persons  
The portions offered together do not operate alike.

For one portion is for the saints, another for those to be sanctified;  
[Col. 1193B] [Note: [Col. 1193D] Several of the following verses are variously placed or omitted in the manuscripts. In Colb. 6101 they are read as printed here. In Ebr. and the printed editions, after “those to be sanctified,” appears: “Remembrance for the rest sets forth the reason for the other,” which also occurs in Colb. 6327.] the former gives thanks, the latter entreats God.

The victim is praise for the righteous; for those to be justified it is  
The vows of prayers that rest may sooner be granted them.

But this forgiveness does not assist the rest,  
Whose evil death and wicked life  
[Col. 1194A] Have earned punishment.

This food becomes flesh from bread, God from an element:  
Simple in mystery, threefold in usefulness.

This food becomes a sheep upon the wood, a strong lion in the tomb,  
A bird flying to the stars, a king seated above the stars.

And lest you think that tomb or cross is lacking to it,  
The chalice signifies the tomb, the altar the cross.

[Note: [Col. 1194D] These two verses stood in the margins of the printed editions. Since they express the same sense, we judged that they should be inserted among the others, although we have found them in no manuscripts.]

The altar performs the office of the cross, the chalice of the tomb, the paten of the stone,  
And the white linen cloth the office of the shroud.

That faith may be present, and terror and dread withdraw,  
The food itself becomes flesh, while the appearance of bread remains.

+ On the change of places in the Mass.

There is a reason why the right side of the altar holds  
The beginning and end of the Mass, and the left the middle.

[Col. 1194B] The right signifies the Jews, the left the Gentiles.  
Our faith began from the former, is transferred to the latter, and returns to the former;  
And at the end of the world they will be faithful.

[Col. 1193] After these verses, the 1548 Paris edition of Claude Chevallon immediately gives the following hexameters, absent from the other editions. They occur only in the manuscript of Marmoutier, no. 103, and there are attributed to Hildebert.

Other verses on the sacrament of the altar.

[Col. 1193B]

Bread, consecrated on the altar by the power of the Word,  
Becomes divine flesh, the medicine of our guilt. [Note: [Col. 1194D] These two verses are taken from the immediately following book, *On the Eucharist.*]

No other celebrates, although another appears to do so;  
God the Word performs this sacred mystery.

For the Word made flesh teaches the sacred words,  
And through the sacrificer ministers flesh from bread. [Note: [Col. 1194D] Note a word familiar to Hildebert.]

Here God is both work and worker: he consecrates and is consecrated;  
[Col. 1193C] He becomes a creature, through whom all things are created.

For the thing whose substance was formerly bread  
Passes by the gift of divinity into Christ’s flesh.

Man does not know—does not know; the angel marvels that this has happened,  
And fears the inscrutable ordinance of the hidden mystery.

He does not know by what measure or by what demonstration of power  
The king who creates the elements, God, comes forth from an element.

But such a change belongs to the right hand of the Lord,  
By whom all that is exists, and whom the world and heaven obey.

Therefore these things are removed from our eyes,  
Known to us only by the light of the mind,

1151 So that our faith may thus be taught unto righteousness,  
And the reward of faith may consequently be greater.

The same author, on the new sacrifice abolishing the old.

(From manuscript Colb. 6327, Reg. 4103, Ebr. 19, and others. Not previously printed.)

[Col. 1193D]

Melchizedek offered bread and wine to the Lord;  
[Col. 1194B] Christ, establishing the same, annulled the old covenant.

For a long time between the two there was another manner  
Of sacrifice, which possessed some power of expiation.

For the lamb of the Law expiates fleshly acts,  
Signifying the Lamb who washes us, made a victim.

When this was offered once, that former rite ran its course;  
The present reality drove away what had been a sign.

What place is there for dawn after the sun has risen?  
What place is there for vows when the sailor has reached port?

[Col. 1194C] The Law was dawn; ox and goat were vows;  
The cross is sun, the cross is harbour; these and the rest have passed away.

Beneath the cross the ephod ceases, and the king’s anointing fails.

1152 The cross closed the Temple; the cross solved the Law’s riddles.

Goat, sheep, sparrow, ram, and fat of calves  
Proclaim nothing: God, the victim, is their end.

Let the Hebrew spare the sheep; the cross removed flesh from the altar.  
After Christ, to sacrifice beasts is the work of beasts.

Though he died once and can die no more,  
The same one is sacrificed daily without a wound.

Bread on the altar is God on the cross: let there be no doubt.  
Life itself declares that it is made by this Word of life,

Which quickens the mind; nor did Christ establish empty things.

[Col. 1194D] The substance of bread passes into Christ’s flesh;  
In this flesh there is nothing fleshly and nothing bloody.

The Spirit touches, sees, and receives this in remembrance:  
Sacred order, devout tradition, the devout victim of bread,

By which the horrible blood of the old rite is shown empty.

A blessed secret, a new power, a useful sacrament,  
[Col. 1195A] By which the liquid, made blood, is a life-giving washing.

For because, when sinning, we always need medicine,  
We always have this medicine for sins.

This is given unto life—but if, guilty one, you revere it—  
[Col. 1196A] He who sits at the Father’s right hand and is sacrificed on altars.

Behold, you see the types and signs in the Law have perished,  
And the three sacraments have returned to their proper head.

[ON THE HOLY EUCHARIST.]

[Col. 1195]

A BRIEF NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING BOOK.

[Col. 1195] That this book *On the Holy Eucharist*, recovered from manuscript Colb. 6327, is truly Hildebert’s is suggested by its allegories, phrases, and expressions familiar to Hildebert, as well as by complete verses interspersed in it which are unquestionably Hildebert’s: for example, “At the sacred Nativity,” etc., which all manuscripts attribute to him; and “Bread on the altar,” etc., which are the first of those immediately appended in the Paris edition of 1548 to his poem *On the Sacrifice of the Mass*. Nor should it be surprising that Hildebert treated the Holy Eucharist in verse twice, or even more often, since he perhaps did so at different times; nor is it unusual for the same author, for diverse occasions or opportunities, to treat the same subject more than once.

[Col. 1195]

THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT’S BOOK ON THE HOLY EUCHARIST.

(From the Colbert manuscript, no. 6327. Not previously printed. All the summaries are painted in red in the manuscript.) (G)*

§ ONLY SECTION. Why bread and wine are offered in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, and why water is mixed in.

[Col. 1195B]

If God has chosen three things to be sacrificed to himself,  
I do not wish God’s sacred rites therefore to be thought diverse.

For God is one, and that which is sacrificed is one,  
Though it appears different according to the times.

No reasoning teaches, since God is truly one,  
That he desires a varied or changeable offering.

He himself, never changing his will,  
Provided for us merely by changing the rite.

For only the rite changes; the reality does not change.  
For with these very things sacrifice was formerly offered to the Lord,

Abel first offered a lamb, the Law a calf,  
And grace, which surpasses them, offered bread and wine.

[Col. 1195C] These three alone are believed to have been pleasing to God;  
Those who worshipped God are said to have worshipped him in these.

Before the given Law came the law of reason;  
A third law came, that of perfect religion.

1153 Therefore the two laws which preceded ours  
Taught by prefiguration what takes place in the Church.

The former is believed to have had holy fathers;  
The latter had those circumcised in flesh who pleased God.

The former performed, under those same fathers,  
The sacrament which Christ performed more truly—our altar’s sacrament.

This is said to have prevailed under Abel, Melchizedek, and Abram,  
And they are said to have held the figure of the new sacred rite.

Melchizedek, although no genealogy is read for him,  
[Col. 1195D] Is nevertheless counted no lower than these.

The Law in which circumcised flesh pleased the Lord  
[Col. 1196B] Had anointed high priests of a single lineage.

Such was the anointing that signified Christ,  
The true sacrificer who expiated the sins of the world.

But that tribe of Levi, because it supplied the high priests,  
Alone possessed the right and office of priests.

Both for sins and for peace-offerings,  
Sacrifice was accepted only from their hands.

None among them attained the summit of the high priesthood  
Unless he had been born from the family line of Aaron.

He alone entered once into the Holy of Holies,  
Entering with the blood of goats or calves.

He bore two stones on his shoulders, one on each side,  
Upon which he bore the inscribed names of the fathers. [Note: [Col. 1195D] “For twelve.”] [Note: [Col. 1195D] Exodus 28.]

Thus he bore all the tribes upon each shoulder,  
Sacrificing and praying to God for himself and the people.

[Col. 1196C] I have spoken briefly of the old manner of offering sacrifice,  
So that there may be a fuller abundance of speech concerning the new.

Before the Lord made the world, he foresaw  
How he would annul the sin of the first father.

Adam had not sinned, yet the Lord had foreseen beforehand  
That he would be redeemed by the holocaust that he willed beforehand.

But thereafter it pleased the Lord to show it by figures,  
So that faith might be more beyond doubt for those to come.

Abel, the first son of Adam, slaughtered a lamb;  
And the Lamb of God himself washed away Adam’s sin.

For the same one, made God, priest, and victim,  
Washed away both the deeds of transgressing Adam and ours.

Abel’s lamb signified Christ, the Father’s Lamb;  
His brother killed him, and Judaea likewise killed the Lord.

Therefore you can see that Abel and the figure of the lamb  
[Col. 1196D] Signified the sacred realities of the Christ to come.

Melchizedek is read to have given bread and wine,  
[Col. 1197A] But nowhere is he read to have set water beside them.

Why did Melchizedek cut off a portion from a portion?  
Did he not foresee that three gifts would afterwards be consecrated to God?

Therefore, if they were then a figure of the new sacred rites,  
Why did they not have the water which we offer together with them?

And the Lord Jesus, who washed away the world’s crimes,  
Before the cross sacrificed bread with wine.

But nowhere is it read that he himself drank water with it  
Or gave his disciples anything but wine.

What then is this: that we join water to wine,  
And consecrate neither wine nor water by itself, but both?

When it is written that Melchizedek neither prefigured water  
Nor that God established it at the supper.

If you see what water and wine signify,  
[Col. 1197B] The question now seeming obscure will become clear.

Nothing other than the Son himself is offered to the Father,  
Through whom our nature is reconciled to God.

For the bread now sanctified upon the altar  
Is undoubtedly the substance of his body.

It is that same body which we believe was born for us from the Virgin  
And now raised above the heavens.

And the wine of the chalice sanctified upon the altar  
Is the blood poured out for us on the altar of the cross.

For he said that the bread was the body he had taken,  
And the cup the drink of blood to be poured out.

We mix in water, which runs and flows: by it  
1154 The human being is signified, a fleeting thing and ash.

Therefore the remaining body is joined to its head  
When my substance is sanctified together with Christ.

For, made human, he is our true mediator,  
[Col. 1197C] The reconciler of our nature as though it were his own.

If you separate the water, you have separated us from Christ;  
If you remove the wine, there is nothing that you have sacrificed.

But why did Melchizedek, offering bread and unmixed wine,  
Omit water and not prefigure both?

It was a time when Christ had not been born from the Virgin  
And sinful humanity had not been restored through him.

Nor had we then deserved to be united with Christ,  
From whom the sin of the first father had cast us out.

For neither Melchizedek nor all who sacrificed  
Stripped us of the sin of the first father.

Therefore he could not join us to Christ  
Whom he plainly could not reconcile to him.

That most true sacrificer was awaited,  
[Col. 1197D] By whom the old despoiler would lose his ancient right,

Who wondrously redeemed mortals by death  
And, justly righteous, took away what the wicked one held.

Perhaps you wonder that he himself consecrated  
Bread with wine but did not join water to wine,

Although, in the same institution, they began what we  
Observe by perpetual religious practice.

Especially since the Law and shadow had already passed away,  
And, with the new victim entering, the old victim wholly fell;

Since God was human, redeeming us humans,  
And establishing what Melchizedek had prefigured.

[Col. 1198A] But observe how ordered an arrangement is made,  
How each thing is distributed in its own time.

For we know that the night in which God established these things  
Preceded the day on which he was to suffer.

Therefore, mortal, capable of suffering, and about to die,  
He established these sacred rites, soon himself to become the true victim.

And you believe, human being, that you could not be redeemed  
And were not to be restored except by Christ’s blood poured out.

But the blood had not been poured out, nor had you been restored.  
For that reason you were not joined to Christ at the supper.

Thus at the supper God consecrated bread and wine,  
But did not join the water which signifies you.

For all that Law and Prophet sang concerning the death of the cross  
Had first to be fulfilled.

Therefore, after Christ’s death had accomplished the sacrament,  
[Col. 1198B] And the prince of sin had been subdued by a wondrous law,

We, whom Christ had stripped from the ancient robber,  
He lawfully joined to himself as his own.

What neither Abel nor Melchizedek nor the victim of the Law  
Had done, the victory of our King did.

For the same one, made God, priest, and victim,  
Released and expiated the deeds of transgressing Adam.

The cross was the altar on which Christ is sacrificed;  
Blood and water flow, and humanity is joined to Christ.

Here too the bond recording our death is annulled;  
[Note: [Col. 1197D] Colossians 2.] the faithless one falls, and humankind is restored.

Thus, when God himself had provided for our salvation,  
And we had been released from the miserable law of sin,

Following at once his command and example,  
We resolved to use the sequence of this holocaust.

[Col. 1198C] For whenever we consecrate bread and wine upon the altar,  
We mix in the water that he mixed upon the altar of the cross.

Thus let no one separate in himself  
What God joined at the supper and at the cross.

Therefore, faithful person, believe that the consecrated bread  
Which you receive is God sacrificed for us.

Although he was once made a victim to God the Father,  
Whenever he is received he daily expiates our deeds.

May he always be our mediator before the Father  
And present us as our truest helper.

1155 The shepherd bears the sheep in order to restore them to the fold.

Here he intercedes with the Father, he who gives with the Father.

Therefore let us joyfully receive this holy thing,  
That God may remain in us, and we in him;  
For what we have on earth as a kind of pledge  
We shall receive more perfectly in his kingdom.

### Why Three Masses Are Celebrated at the Nativity of the Lord

[Note: [Col. 1197] The manuscript attributes all these verses entirely to Hildebert, and they are found here in this manuscript.]

Learn what the holy solemnities of the Mass at the Nativity signify, and why three are celebrated.  
The first in the night, the next beneath the dawn, the last in fullest daylight,  
They denote the times under Noah, under David, and beneath the holy cross.  
Holy rites existed under Noah, under David, and under Christ;  
Night, dawn, day; shadow, figure, God.

### The Prologue of the Following Work Begins

Whoever you are, clothed in the image of our Redeemer,  
And delighting in the sacraments of the divine page,  
Read our little book, in which I have briefly written  
What must rightly be held concerning Christ’s body.

Since this writing is very necessary for all,  
It must especially be observed by those who serve the altars:  
So that they may learn and not be ignorant what is owed to the man  
Who, with Judas, wickedly gnaws at the sacraments of the Lord.

Therefore let the inward understanding of a man taste  
The food and drink of everlasting sweetness,  
So that, in reading, the palate of a good mind may discern  
How greatly this saving food advances one toward life.

### § 1. That the true and same flesh now consecrated upon the altar is that which was born of the Virgin and is believed to have suffered on the cross

[[Note: [Col. 1199D] The same two [verses] as at col. 1193.] Bread consecrated on the altar by the power of the Word  
[Col. 1199B] Becomes divine flesh, the medicine of our guilt.]

It becomes no flesh other than that of Christ who redeemed us,  
Full of sacrament, food and sustenance of the mind.  
This flesh is daily sacrificed for the world, although it is not seen as flesh,  
But has the appearance of bread.

The nature of things stands aghast; the order of things marvels at the consecrated one,  
Who was once born of the Virgin and is [now] from a little bread.  
It is dreadful that the Word made flesh becomes flesh again;  
That a swiftly occurring reality changes the natural course.  
Yet it is the same flesh that was then born of the Virgin,  
And is now consecrated from bread by the Word of life.

Then, for us human beings, he deigned to be born a human being;  
Now in his mercy he desires to feed us with his body.  
He became human in order to raise us who had fallen;  
For this reason the bread of life was given, that it might satisfy us.

[Col. 1199C] What use would the bread of life, given from heaven, have been,  
If the human being to be redeemed had perished through hunger while suffering?  
Therefore Christ’s being born from a body is not enough,  
Unless the hungry human being incorporates that one into himself.

### § 2. That Christ, the bread of angels, made himself known to the world endangered by hunger for the Word

A dreadful hunger for the Word once oppressed humankind,  
And hungry humanity had nothing to eat.  
The bread of angels came down from heaven to the depths,  
When the final file was already about to cut down the world;  
Veiling his divinity beneath the chaff of our flesh,  
He made himself known to the world by revealing signs of deity.

Therefore the merciful Creator did not wish his creature to perish,  
Descending as a human being so that his own [creature] might return to the stars.

[Col. 1199D] The whole human being had collapsed; all was shaken.  
The Lord came to meet the perishing one, made a sacrifice—  
A sacrifice, however, holy, living, and immaculate;  
A sacrifice which, itself sanctified, drives away stains;  
A sacrifice greater than which none could be offered,  
And which was sufficient to make satisfaction for us.

### § III. That no one other than Christ could make satisfaction for Adam’s sin; and that, although immortal according to divinity, he always [reading uncertain: *sewel*] willingly died for us according to the nature of his humanity

No sacrifice could have been worthy or sufficiently adequate  
[Col. 1200A] To wipe out Adam’s guilt, if Christ were absent;  
For Adam owed [the debt], and Adam, so poor, did not possess  
The means to make satisfaction, being hindered by grave guilt.

God himself could do it, yet ought not [to do it alone]; therefore it was necessary  
That the God-man should do this, without whom it could not be done.  
Thus, because God can do all things, and because man owes [the debt],  
Each nature provides the material for such a deed.  
From two natures there comes to be one and the same person,  
Healing our bodies and also our souls.  
Nor are God and man here two, because Christ is one—  
One not wrongly mingled in the nature of the other.

Although he was immortal in each nature,  
His majesty and justice being preserved,  
He willingly underwent the cross—he who would not have died unless he willed—  
Destined by his own lot to give us life without end.

And what the true God ought not to endure by virtue of deity,  
This blessed man endured for the truth of justice,  
So that at last the divine will might be accomplished—  
That will which orders all things by everlasting power.

Christ is believed to be the living sacrificial victim on the wood of the cross,  
Through whom mortal substance became divine;  
A sacrifice by which the blessed, the world, and heaven are filled,  
And those who eat of it shall not die eternally.

This is the true food; this is the true refreshment of bread.  
Whoever does not know it, his hope will become empty.  
This is the true flesh by which we are fed, of the true Lamb,  
Through whom the violence of the sulphurous pool grew cool.

### § IV. That the lamb slain under the Law, roasted and eaten by the people of Israel, bore the type of Christ; but, when grace succeeded and the true sacrifice appeared, the legal ceremonies ceased

[Col. 1200C]

No longer is a roasted lamb given to the people through Moses;  
Christ the Lamb is present, having suffered for us on the cross.  
That former lamb was the figure of the one to come;  
The shadow has withdrawn, the light is present, God becomes a pure sacrifice.

Christ is now sacrificed as the solemn sacrifice;  
Yet death no longer has dominion over him who suffered once.  
Grace has succeeded; that old Law has disappeared;  
And for the world a new Law, new light, and a new king have shone forth.

No sheep now propitiates; the blood of calves accomplishes nothing;  
Nor do the burnt offerings of oxen: the old order of sacred rites has perished.  
Now the minister ceases to slaughter beasts,  
Since the merciful Master himself came to be slain.

[Col. 1200D] Therefore Law drove away law, God the Lamb drove away the lamb;  
And what the old [order] prefigured, the new one himself accomplished.  
When bitter suffering roasted him as with sacred fire,  
He was offered to the Father as a living sacrifice on the altar of the cross.

We mark both doorposts of the house with his blood,  
And drive the enemy far from our borders,  
While with lips and heart we commemorate the sacred things of the cross  
And partake of his body together with his blood.

### § V. That the Lamb, though sacrificed in diverse places, remains whole, and is wholly received as food by the people of the faithful

Though he is sacrificed throughout the whole world,  
[Col. 1201A] He remains whole in the kingdom and is always one;  
And though he seems to be distributed in portions,  
Here he is received whole, and in heaven he is worshipped whole.

Filling stars and earth, he remains one everywhere,  
Never failing: food for all things and all things for each person.  
This, indeed, is the food which the ancient food signified,  
With which God fed Israel through the pathless wilderness.

Manna was every food for every people in the mouth, [Note: [Col. 1201D] Exod. XVI.]  
Having varied flavour for their diverse dispositions;  
Of it, one taking little was as though taking more,  
And was satisfied, because it was sufficient for all.

At last, in our time, a great mystery  
Has shone forth, and the mystical reality produces a great cause.  
The Lord is indeed manna, created from the Virgin Mother,  
Whose body is consecrated from bread upon the altar.

[Col. 1201B] But how unlike are this food and that food!  
For this food is God; the other food was shadow and ashes.  
That food perished, and those eating it perished,  
Who did not hunger for Christ, the bread of life.

O holy bread, praiseworthy gift of faith!  
He is all things to all; one, and sufficient for all.

### § VI. That Christ’s flesh is consecrated not by the merit of the consecrator but by the word of the Creator; and that it is not received more by the good nor less by the wicked

The angel thirsts for this bread, hungers for it, and is refreshed by it;  
By it the pilgrim human being is sustained while still living.  
How blessed the bread, blessed the flesh, rich the sacrifice—  
Feeding human beings on earth, and citizens in heaven!

From it the good person does not desire more, nor the wicked person less;  
[Col. 1201C] For Christ makes his own portion equal for all.  
But his own fault draws one who receives wrongly to death;  
Glory exalts to heaven one who receives worthily. [Note: [Col. 1201D] That is, “glory.”]

When this bread is blessed by the mouth of the priest,  
It cannot be less in a humble priest or more in a greater one.  
Though the one presiding over the holy altar be unclean,  
No defilement can stain this sacred thing.  
The power is equal, though the consecrator’s life is unequal;  
For a human being does not create this work, but the power of the Creator does all.

### § VII. That, while standing at the altar, the priest bears Christ’s likeness and offers Christ; and that he himself is also called Christ, living and crucified

The priest standing at the altar prays over the sacred rites;  
Here God fills him with heavenly manna; grace distils dew,  
When divine power rains down from above upon all  
[Col. 1201D] That the priest’s wondrous prayer consecrates.

The sacrificer is nothing other than Christ’s image,  
While he handles the sacred body of Christ together with the blood;  
And while he fixes his eyes and heart upon heaven,  
He crucifies himself by stretching out hands and arms;  
And while weeping he recounts Christ’s death,  
He slays the deeds of his flesh for the Lord, as though upon the cross.

Thus the human being, made a sacrificial victim, offers Christ to Christ;  
Thus he suffers the cross while commemorating the acts of the cross,  
[Col. 1202A] And is rightly Christ, because crucified and anointed,  
Joined by the member of faith [variant: “by faith”] to Christ’s body.

### § VIII. That the Almighty alone is sanctifier and administrator of the sacrifice, while the priest is only a minister; and that the flesh is on the altar by the same Word by which it was created in the Virgin’s womb

No other celebrates, though another appears to do so:  
God the Word performs this holy mystery.  
For the Word made flesh administers the sacred words,  
And through the sacrificer instructs [or rules] bread by the Word.

Here God is both work and worker: he consecrates and is consecrated;  
And he through whom all things are created becomes a creature.  
For the thing whose substance remained bread by that same [Word]  
Passes into Christ’s flesh by the gift of deity.

Humankind does not know; the angel does not know; both marvel that this is done,  
[Col. 1202B] And stand in awe at the unsearchable covenant of the hidden sacred rite.  
They do not know by what measure or evidence of power  
The King who creates the elements comes forth as God from an element.  
But such a change belongs to the right hand of the Most High,  
Through whom everything that exists has vigour, and whom world and heaven obey.

### § IX. That the potter of heavenly vessels can change a small portion of bread for the better, that is, into the glory of his flesh, since he was able to refashion from death into life the vessel of our humanity which he assumed and baked in the fire of his passion

It is possible for him who knows how to create all things  
To call forth again one thing from another.  
When and how he wills, the potter turns soft clay,  
And, creating new vessels, shapes and adorns them more fittingly.

The work obeys the Lord, whose power rules over it,  
[Col. 1202C] So that he can restore the vessels he wishes to break.  
Therefore the power of that God, manifest power of the Father,  
Came down to us, whom the vessel of flesh enclosed.

This vessel dried out, well baked in the kiln of the cross,  
Taught by the craft of its potter to rise from death.  
It was soundly baked, and no changing water softens it;  
It removes the world’s stains and our excesses.

A very hard vessel: it shattered mighty hell,  
And, redeeming humanity on the cross, subdued death by death.  
From this vessel flows the oil of highest goodness,  
Which drives away every harmful thing in the washing of baptism.

A blessed vessel indeed, filled with the fountain of life,  
Which nourishes our bodies and also calms souls in peace.  
In this same vessel the divine lamp shines forth,  
Whence blessing attends the banquets of the holy table.

[Col. 1202D] And because our faith judges it utterly empty  
To receive bread without wine in the holy supper,  
Let us seek wine from the Lord after receiving bread  
And perceive what sacrament is in it.

It does no good first to have eaten if we thirst,  
For we can in no way allay our thirst:  
Drinks of great desire follow food,  
Especially when we have received the roasted flesh of the Lamb.  
Roasted flesh makes our mouths thirstier  
[Col. 1203A] Than tender flesh which soft water boils.

Therefore, with God’s favour, from the fountain of the mind I shall set forth  
Whatever mystery I perceive concerning the sacred wine.

### § X. That wine is offered with bread in the sacrifice because flesh is not rightly communicated without blood, nor blood without flesh

Wine is brought to the altar; it is offered together with bread.  
Both gifts are offered to God when the new Passover is celebrated.  
God delights in both, receives both with approval and praise,  
Through which Christ is plainly shown to be mortal and God:

God, because Christ forms himself under both kinds;  
Mortal, because from them he reproduces the death of the cross.  
Earth and vine respectively produce these two things from themselves,  
And by the priest’s hand the Son offers [them] to the Father.

This was once signified through Melchizedek,  
Who offered to the Lord consecrated bread and wine.  
[Col. 1203B] In the histories concerning him we cannot find alike  
The name either of his father or of his forefathers.  
Whom does he signify but Christ, a man without a father,  
Born eternally of God the Father without a mother?

I rightly affirm this high priest—and God—[Note: [Col. 1203D] Heb. IV.]  
Who penetrates the heavens and gives law from heaven. [Note: [Col. 1203D] Perhaps “and king,” so that it may rhyme with the end of the following verse.]

He is the strengthening bread and the abundant vine,  
Making souls glad and cleansing them from sin.  
The flower of virginity, consecrating this bread and vine,  
Brought forth for this world a fruit full of deity [variant: “the fruit full of deity”].

From the bread comes flesh; from the vine comes sacred blood,  
Which Wisdom conceals so that people may not see wrongly.  
[Col. 1203C] The Lord hides the mystery of heaven for a time,  
And reveals it, when faith calls for it, to whom he wills and when.

### § XI. That the Lord willed the depths of the heavenly sacraments to be hidden, so that they might be concealed from unbelievers and the merit of faith might grow among believers

These things have therefore been removed from our eyes [variant: *ex*, “out of”],  
And are not fully known to us except by the light of the mind,  
So that our faith may thus be trained unto righteousness,  
And a greater reward of faith may consequently follow.

Or God willed these mysteries to remain hidden  
So that Judaea might not make mockery of this,  
If we ate the raw flesh of a slain human being  
And drank a cup of raw blood.

Therefore let us enjoy the reason of sacred food and drink;  
And through faith, not through appearance, let us ascend on high.  
[Col. 1203D] Since by bodily sight and taste we cannot  
Discern in the mind what kind of things these are,  
Let the mind, satisfied by God, prove by inward taste  
What sight [corrected from *jus*, “right”] and the tongue cannot [perceive] by outward sense.

Neither the form nor appearance of bread is to be examined;  
Rather, the power of the sacrament must be held in the heart.  
Nor should anyone expect anything but good from wine;  
For the blood belongs to the mind, wine to the eyes.

[Col. 1204A] Though it seems to have the flavour of wine,  
With faith coming to aid, it is plainly sacred blood.  
This is that blood which was poured out from Christ’s wound  
And passes through the priest’s mouth to benefit souls.

And lest anything be lacking to the sacrament,  
A living fountain must be present in the wine upon the altar.

### § XII. Water is mixed with the blood because both flowed together from the Saviour’s side on the cross: the blood of redemption, namely, and the water of baptism, by which the Church is signified

Water is mixed with wine, and by it we are signified—  
We who are made alive by saving nourishment.  
The peoples fortified by grace are signified by water,  
Whom Christ’s blood joins to its head as members.

Moreover, if wine is offered to the Lord without the fountain,  
It denies that Christ’s passion was for the people.  
[Col. 1204B] For if the creature needing redemption were absent,  
Why would God have become human, or why would he have died?

Conversely, if the fountain should be without wine mixed with it,  
It shows that the people remain alone without Christ.  
Wine without the holy fountain accomplishes nothing here,  
Nor is the saving fountain propitiated without blood.

As both flowed from Christ’s sacred wound,  
So both ought to be placed together in the offering.  
God is the true vine; Christ is held to be the fountain of life;  
A fountain seems to come from a fountain, blood from a vine.

Therefore one is not sacrificed without the other,  
Since in this way the sacred passion is fully commemorated.

### § XIII. We do not read that water was mixed with wine in the consecration of the Lord’s cup; but, so that nothing might be lacking in this sacrament for the commemoration of the passion, the apostles later decreed that this should be done

[Col. 1204C]

This was not performed at the birth of the cup,  
When the new Passover was consecrated after the old Passover:  
For the Lord, changing bread alone and the liquid of wine  
Into his own flesh and sacred blood,  
Is read to have given them to the disciples while they were dining,  
And to have taught that we should do the same in remembrance of him.

Wondrous power of God who dines! He himself becomes the meal,  
Dining daily with us just as then.  
And because blood and water flowed together  
From the wound in his side, our second washing,  
The moderate judgment of the ancient fathers decreed  
That those two should be together at the paschal feast,

[Col. 1204D] So that what appears to have been done on the altar of the cross  
May now be repeated by us in honour of the cross.  
Three things complete the holy mystery: fountain, flesh, blood.  
These three redeem us, and by these three the serpent perishes.

Whoever removes wine from these three things at the holy altar  
Will not be able worthily to sacrifice without a tail.  
[Note: [Col. 1203D] He alludes to the rite of the ancient sacrificer, in which the victim was commanded to be offered with its tail. “From the sacrifice of peace-offerings they shall offer to the Lord the fat and the entire tail” (Levit. III.9).]

### § XIV. That although wine and water are typically mixed before consecration, after it only blood is drunk, because the water is changed into blood, so that the people signified by water may understand themselves to be brought to perfection in something better

[Col. 1205A]

Although three gifts are set upon the Lord’s table,  
After they are sacrificed there are only two.  
Water is first mixed with wine, but when it is consecrated,  
There will be nothing but blood, by which the spirit is inwardly nourished.

A mystical thing is given: Christ’s blood drinks it up;  
For God transfers our ashes into his own members.  
He transfers them when we are joined to him through his body,  
And through faith are created as new members of so great a head.

He also transferred [us] long ago, when the anointing of holy chrism  
Made us peoples new in the fountain of washing.  
[Col. 1205B] Yet the fountain of washing signifies the fountain of the wound,  
And through each God heals the wounds of souls.  
He first makes their hearts clean in baptism;  
After the washing, he cleanses those who have fallen by the water of blood.

Therefore only two things are received, blood and flesh;  
The third thing is a type of the peoples who are redeemed.  
One substance satisfies; the other intoxicates the mind.  
Both bind the Catholic people in covenant with God.

By these twins our twofold substance is restored,  
Which the sentence of death inflicted through old Adam;  
Life glows in the blood; flesh rejoices, refreshed by flesh;  
The aged world rejoices to be renewed by both goods.

By these the human being, grown old in sins, is renewed;  
By these, reborn through the power of faith, he comes to life again;  
By these human nature regains its own honour;  
[Col. 1205C] By these it rejoices to have conquered the serpent’s fury.

### § XV. That through reception of this sacrament and the power of the saving cross, paradise is opened to humankind and the devil is overcome

Now the ancient inhabitant returns to the seat of paradise;  
Now redeemed humanity claims heaven as its dwelling.  
The cross accomplishes this: its gleaming splendour above all things  
Strikes down the enemies of humankind in Endor.  
[Note: [Col. 1205] He alludes to Joshua’s victories, of which the Psalmist says: “They perished at Endor; they became as dung of the earth” (Ps. LXXXII.11).]

The Lord’s cross is heaven’s throne and hell’s chain;  
The cross is heaven’s key, the way of life, death’s restraint.  
The cross penetrates heaven, fills the world, cleaves the abyss;  
On our foreheads the cross has impressed the Crucified One.

Now we see the letter Tau written on no one’s forehead,  
[Col. 1205D] Since we bear the sign of the cross impressed upon us.  
That sacred character bore the mystical signs of the cross  
And kept away the sword of death and deadly plague.

Now, because the life-giving grace of the wood redeems us,  
The letter under the sign of the typical sign is erased.  
The cross opened the path for those tending toward paradise;  
For the fateful right that obstructed it has been cut away.

That sword-bearing cherub of God, the entrance having been opened,  
Now permits Christ’s worshippers to enter, its sword withdrawn.  
That flame-spewing, turning sword is at rest,  
[Col. 1206A] And paradise’s joyful gate lies open to Christ’s worshippers.

All who love enter; for since the time of John  
The Baptist, this holy gate, closed for so many years, stands open.  
Heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it, [Note: [Col. 1205D] Matt. XI.]  
Since grace succeeded the Law for the people.

The King of heaven rejoices to be proclaimed above the stars,  
And gives weapons to the robber, so that with them he may approach his camps;  
He no longer threatens losses to one fighting for the kingdom,  
But rather gives prizes to one who conquers, though he is conquered.

A profitable contest! Such violence is blessed!  
When a robber’s own robbery becomes pardonable,  
And when the conquered one grants honour to the conqueror,  
Then the victor calls himself inferior to the defeated.

### § XVI. That the gate of the kingdom was closed to the holy fathers before the Law and under the Law, but after grace was given it lies open to the penitent thief and to sinners

[Col. 1206B]

At first the gate of rest, shut against patriarchs and prophets,  
Has now been made open to the thief.  
To him virtue gave a shield, death life, hope a good weapon;  
Faith furnished arms, Christ’s confession furnished heaven.

This thief flies past the heat and burden of the day  
Before the others, to the seat of rest, through the truly open gate.  
Many former ages did not bring them into the kingdom,  
But a brief hour brought this man in.

Long labour harassed Moses under the Law;  
Now the daily denarius nonetheless makes this man equal to him.  
And where formerly the fathers and mothers of the prophets  
[Col. 1206C] Could not enter, thieves and prostitutes now enter.

Behold: the thief, fastening his foot behind Christ’s footsteps,  
Enters the kingdom, crucified with the Crucified One.  
The Canaanite woman, once called a dog, enters by believing.  
You, Hebrew people, called God’s vineyard—do you turn back?  
Faithless one, you flee from entering and bark backward,  
Nor cease to fasten a bite upon the work of mercy.

And since God’s mercy receives these people weeping for their evils,  
You sharpen your teeth against him, lacking compassion.  
Set aside your rage, for the former times have passed;  
Through Christ more prosperous times succeed.

Those whom your Law is accustomed to stone and kill with the sword,  
The grace of Christ now strives to call back to life.  
Grace is now better than the letter that killed,  
Under which righteousness, like the sun, lay hidden beneath a cloud.

[Col. 1206D] Grace proclaims that the Messiah has now come,  
Grace which removes the harsh yokes of the Law and gives us rest.  
Yet you await another; but learn and search  
The writings of the prophets: here you can find Christ,  
Whom Law, angel, and prophet foretold.  
Christ is present; all things are filled with Christ’s praise.

The elements together acclaim that God has come;  
Yet you do not heed the testimony of the elements.  
For a new star shows the King of heaven born.  
[Col. 1207A] And water, yielding new wine, now bears witness that he is God.

Life blessed the dead and the sick with health;  
Under his feet the sea lay spread out to be trodden.  
Finally, when he dies, sun and moon were darkened;  
The trembling earth shook, and the buried rose.  
Those too whom hell had long wickedly held captive  
He restored to those above, when that heavenly King returned.

The sacrifice of the cross tears apart the veil of the temple and the stones;  
Yet the stone that you have in your heart is not yet split.  
Do you not, Judaea, move at the sight of so many signs?  
You are still, to your harm, held blind in the darkness of unbelief.

Behold what you await: all mystical things have been uncovered.  
See the true Messiah even through miracles.  
And because the interior things, stripped of their veil, lie open,  
[Col. 1207B] Enter with us and worship the divinity of the Crucified One.  
Remove the dense veil of your Moses from your face;  
Learn new worship, now that the former worship has ceased.

### § XVII. That Christ is the true Moses, who, having rescued us from the devil’s servitude, was sacrificed as the paschal lamb and leads us through this world’s wilderness to the promised kingdom

You who seek Moses, now behold Christ as Moses:  
No burden of Pharaoh will harm you if you worship him.  
That Moses was typical; this true one redeemed us  
And destroyed the people of Pharaoh by the sword of the cross.

Thus the true Moses led us through the Red Sea,  
Destroying the old serpent in the washing of faith.  
He established a better celebration of the sacred Passover:  
[Col. 1207C] The Lamb suffered, sacrificed for us.

Your Passover was once shadow and figure of the true one;  
God the sun has shone forth and commands the darkness to depart.  
He feeds us through the region of the world’s wilderness  
And leads us to the station of milk and honey.

He feeds in the Church whenever the words  
Of the Gospels are recounted to us; the power of sacred things
