Feeds at the altar with bountiful nourishment,  
When it mercifully refreshes the hungry entrails of the mind.

Indeed, he feeds at home when, after spiritual [food],  
He abundantly gives us grain foods;  
He feeds also in heaven, when the mind caught up above the sky  
Clings wholly to God, captivated by heavenly sweetness.

Thus Christ, the bread of life, feeds us everywhere,  
Providing food both to angelic citizens and to human beings.

[Col. 1207D] Therefore, faithless people, darkened by your fathers’ blindness,  
Cease to be a wild vine, that you may become a fruitful grape.  
May Christ’s grace soften you with sacred rain, so that at last  
You may produce a rich cluster in the vineyard of life.

Because the digression concerning Judaea detained me for a little,  
Now, pen, return to the former matters.  
As it is effective [variant: *vacat*, “is futile”] to scatter a grain of wheat upon a rock,  
So I judge it futile that Christ is [preached] late to Judaea;  
And the seed signifies Christ, the rock Judaea,  
Barren in fertility, which always remains stony.

### § XVIII. That our Lord Jesus Christ himself is the grain of wheat which, falling dead into the earth and rising again, was multiplied in the sacrament of life; and from this grain many grains of the faithful sprang, which now make one bread with him in the Church

[Col. 1208A]

This is the grain of wheat which faithful earth  
Continually brings forth, returning its seeds to heaven.  
By this grain heaven’s granaries have been multiplied;  
The holy city Jerusalem grows rich, satisfied by it.

This is the grain of wheat which came from heaven,  
Whose fat enriches our souls and bodies.  
It willingly fell into the earth in order first to die,  
And through this rose again to be multiplied.

From one grain abundance flows into many grains,  
From which one bread is now made in heaven.  
[Col. 1208B] For whenever we are begotten through faith increasing in Christ,  
From one grain we are created like countless grains.  
While we taste his flesh and the draught of his blood,  
One bread comes to be, and this wine becomes the sacrifice.

Thus two are read to be together in one flesh:  
Christ and the Church thus constitute one.  
Thus God dwells in us and we in him,  
While here he prepares himself as our head, and we as his members.

### § XIX. That no one who has become a member of the devil should presume, in the manner of Judas, to approach Christ’s body; Judas was condemned not so much by consciousness of his prior guilt as because, still sinful and unclean, he presumptuously approached the sacred table

Whatever member cleaves to so great a head  
Should always hope to live in Christ’s body.  
[Col. 1208C] Nor, once cleaving to it, should it relapse into shameful pollution,  
Or be cut off from Christ’s member by the sickle of a prostitute.

That cannot be called a member of Christ’s body  
Which serves Satan and is subjected to a prostitute.  
The immaculate bridegroom loves an immaculate bride,  
United to himself from heaven by a virginal covenant.

Therefore, whoever you are who do not belong to Christ’s body,  
While you are still defiled and have not repented,  
You must not hasten toward the Lord’s table,  
Lest, if you presume, you appear like Judas.

Judas knew in every way that he had sinned,  
Yet did not withdraw himself from the sacred feast.  
He was guilty in two ways: both of the crime of betrayal  
And of contempt for violated religion.

Therefore, when the Lord’s judgment and such great punishment followed,  
[Col. 1208D] Satan suddenly entered into him together with the bread.  
Thus a twofold sentence and punishment punishes him  
Whom the Lord’s gentle [variant: “simple”] correction did not benefit.

Judas furnishes examples in the Church for those to come,  
That they may not handle the Lord’s body except with pure minds.  
For one who receives wickedly with Judas will be excluded;  
One who receives well with Peter will be counted among Christ’s people.

### § XX. No believer may be ignorant of the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, which is celebrated daily in the Church, lest perhaps, because of what he does not know, he be judged unworthy to receive it

Many receive it, but wholly do not know what it is that they receive,  
[Col. 1209A] And divine vengeance threatens them.  
Everyone ignorant of it is unknown, because he does not know  
Whence salvation arises and whence the fountain of pardon is opened.

He is unknown: a person eating of consecrated things,  
As Moses says, shall bear the penalty of ignorance.  
Solomon is added here, framing a sacred example, [Note: [Col. 1209D] Prov. XXIII.]  
In which shines forth an enigma of the sacred mystery:

“When you sit,” he says, “at the lofty banquet of a ruler,  
Consider with discerning mind what foods you eat.”  
For reason, the lover of virtue, must first know  
What benefit life-giving flesh brings to the mind.

The psalm of king and prophet alike moves us here:  
“For the Lord is sweet; taste and see.” [Note: [Col. 1209D] Ps. XXXIII.]  
Hence it is clear that none of the priests  
May be ignorant of the power of the mysteries.

[Col. 1209B] If a person rightly knew what power is active in the sacred things,  
He would never approach the heavenly table except clean.  
Because he has not learned this, he receives sacred things irreverently,  
And openly takes judgment and death to himself.  
Thus Christ’s flesh, given as medicine,  
Immediately prepares for him a snare and ruin of death.

For although someone may be of religious life,  
If he does not know what he is doing, he lives to his own destruction.  
How can one defend the honour of the sacred mystery  
Who has not yet tasted its savour in the mind?

Therefore let one ignorant of sacred things learn and revere them,  
Lest he someday be burdened with the many [penalties] of a despiser.

### § XXI. Every priest ought to know the Lord’s sacraments, by which he may instruct the people subject to him and form them in faith; without them he cannot worthily perform the priesthood

[Col. 1209C]

Let him first wish to know what the general sacrifice is,  
What the tree of life is, what spiritual bread is;  
What the altar and cup are, what water is poured into them, and wine;  
And how those two are one after each has been consecrated.

Let him wish to know what the water of the Flood brought and took away—  
Deep water indeed, but itself also a profound figure.  
Finally, why the cross marks the cup, why the cross adorns the altar,  
Made bright by the blood of the Lamb slain for us;  
Why chrismal anointing is performed at the baptismal font,  
And what the cross applied to the foreheads of the reborn confers.

But why do we penetrate the abyss of the Lord’s sacred things?  
Let the sacrificer wish to know everything by which one goes to him.

[Col. 1209D] One who does not know such things, after every burden of guilt,  
Cannot bring medicine either to himself or to the people.  
Indeed, he turns out badly as a blind leader of the blind,  
Whom grave ignorance harms together with the rest.  
But whoever has learned all that he ought to know  
Is rightly a priest and fittingly provides the path of light.

### § XXII. The priest who follows Christ’s footsteps and announces the word of life to the people is called both the Lord’s Christ and his angel; and, while he kindles his neighbour to knowledge of God and love of heavenly things, he receives a seraphic dignity

He is rightly a priest whose holy pattern of life  
[Col. 1210A] Becomes a devout model of living for the people subject to him;  
Whose life, warm with love of true virtue,  
While it rightly imitates Christ in deeds and speech,  
Is an angel of the Lord and is also called his Christ—  
One who seems to bear the cross and represent Christ.

Yet Christ God himself, as Isaiah makes clear,  
Is the highest angel, born of mother Mary.  
That angel is good enough through himself;  
This angel, made by him, is good from another source.

This messenger ought, sent from the Lord,  
To carry heaven’s faithful commands to the faithful people;  
And then, returning, as our herald to report to the Lord  
The burdens of the mourning people upon earth.

Standing in the temple as a mirror and lamp of faith,  
Contemplating God and meditating on heavenly things,  
He calls back to the heights the cold hearts of the flock, blackened  
[Col. 1210B] By the dark soot of sin, formerly sluggish toward life’s joys;  
He makes them burn with the fire of faith  
And, kindled by God, shine with the brightness of life.

Such a one deservedly shines with a seraphic countenance,  
Whence his neighbour grows warm as the frost of sin flees.

### § XXIII. That the shining coal is the same as the seraph. For when holy rulers in the Church rekindle God’s people, extinguished by the darkness of sins, toward heavenly things by the word of salvation and the example of good action, they are truly said to kindle other coals

This shining coal, leading the peoples of faith in his footsteps,  
Makes them living coals.  
But what must be done with coals in the Church?  
The incense of works, the incense of prayers, and the heart must be burned upon them;  
[Col. 1210C] Let both be burned in the censer of flesh and mind—  
A twofold sacrifice pleasing to God and humanity.

Now, weary, let my tongue speak immediately of two  
Out of the rich mass of many coals.  
Lawrence was a burning coal, fire within fire,  
To whom death worthily granted the palm of victory in heaven.

Nicholas, the worthy bishop of the Lord, was a coal,  
Whose splendour of virtues is manifest from afar.  
The former was a coal reddened with blood, roasted amid coals;  
The latter was a coal burning with merits, rich in the fatness of oil.

God willed that those long born black through ancestral error  
Should be kindled by fire from the heavenly fire.  
Whom would not the manly struggle of the one kindle?  
Whom would not the childlike compassion of the other move?

[Col. 1210D] By his example may we deserve the laurel through blood;  
By this man’s purified life may we give gold to the Lord.  
Each was a soldier of God and a faithful steward,  
And by speech and hand strove to lay up treasures in heaven.

I set forward these exemplary teachers of faith  
To teach through them every minister of the altar  
To be devout, generous, brave, chaste, wise,  
Patient for righteousness amid adverse circumstances.

Such persons are worthy to receive from the tree of life;  
The sentence of ancestral death does not exclude them.  
Such persons deserve to bear offerings to God,  
[Col. 1211A] And are not forbidden to stand at the Lord’s sacred rites.

### § XXIV. That it is exceedingly terrible to approach the sacraments of the altar, where, amid the assembly of angels and human beings, Christ himself, the highest pontiff and priest, offers himself to each person as food of life or death, and subtly discerns each person’s merits

Therefore, prudent person, learn the sacrament of life;  
And when you receive those things—the judgment of God—tremble.

Terrible is the matter, and one greatly to be feared,

that you partake of Christ’s body, with Christ present.

For if perhaps you are willing to give credence to the Scriptures,

which often teach us true things concerning Christ,

at the time when Christ, a sacrifice dear to the Father,

is offered upon the lofty altar by the hands of the priest,

the whole choir of saints is present, heaven here stands open,

and the host of angels attends the God who is present.

[Col. 1211B] Here Christ is truly present, the author of the sacred rites,

discerning the minds alike of the righteous and the great.

For he knows and clearly sees who ought to partake

of the saving bread, whether they have pursued vain things or fitting ones.

And though a fleshly priest stands at the altar,

the supreme pontiff is said to celebrate the sacred mysteries here.

He breaks the bread, he presents it, he blesses it,

and says that what he gives with the blood is his body.

1167 Come then [variant: “And you”], sinful man, do you presume, though unworthy,

to approach the Lord’s table and the pledge of life?

Learn as soon as possible what you are, what Christ’s flesh is,

and in what vessel you wish to place the divine gifts.

Unless the vessel in which they are received is pure,

[Col. 1211C] they become destruction to the one who receives them wrongly.

Therefore Paul counsels that each person first examine himself,

and then hasten to the bread and sacred cup.

For whoever discerns the Lord’s body beforehand—

what it is that he receives [Note: [Col. 1211D] 1 Cor. 11.], and how great it is when God reveals it—

let him eat it without fear, yet only after he has been tested,

when no capital charge of guilt accuses him.

For although lesser sins may blame someone,

since not even one hour of life is lived without sin,

yet I do not think such a one should be excluded from the sacred feast;

rather, that which continually harms him must be healed.

And because daily we are weighed down by the burden of sin,

we are continually relieved by such remedies.

The dispensation of the wisdom of the Almighty

[Col. 1211D] provides the means by which the wounds of the mind may be healed.

### § XXV. That, according to diversity of merits, Christ is sacrificed in the Church as lamb and goat, as was prefigured in the Law; so that, as Jerome says, the more perfect feed upon the flesh of the Lamb, while sinners and those acting impiously feed entirely upon the goat.

Therefore let every faithful person prepare his heart for God,

so that it may become his dwelling-place in pure heavens.

[Col. 1212A] The Lord flees sluggish hearts, hearts full of filth;

his grace is always present in the pure heart.

And let the soul which is still compelled to suffer want,

and cannot satisfy its good hunger with the flesh of the Lamb [variant: “cannot”],

at least eat of the flesh of the sacred goat,

which is customarily slain as an offering for the people’s sin.

The ancient order of sacred things does not teach that human beings are equal;

neither reason nor the diversity of merits requires this.

Thus Moses commands that a goat be sacrificed with the death of a lamb,

because under both types he wishes Christ to be signified.

Yet he is not a goat who condemns and hates goats.

1168 But what each person displays through this distinction of the sacred rite is as follows:

we sacrifice the lamb when we maintain righteousness;

[Col. 1212B] the goat when, asking pardon, we weep for our crimes.

Nor do I think it absurd that Christ is signified by the goat,

since he is often sacrificed as a he-goat or a buck [Note: [Col. 1211D] Lev. 16.].

For the Law offers twin goats at the altars,

because it declares that Christ has a twofold substance.

Before the temple doors the people sacrificed one,

and laid their many sins upon the head of the other.

This one, bearing the sins of his people,

they then sent away to seek the wilderness wastes.

Christ is both goats: for he is slain while hanging upon the cross,

and seeks the wilderness when he rises, ascending toward heaven—

he who bore our evils while suspended from the wood, and brought back

the sheep that had been found to the ninety-nine.

He who, mighty at the Father’s right hand in the honour of divinity,

[Col. 1212C] reigns and fills the altars in the world with flesh and blood—

though once slain and no longer able to die,

his death is nevertheless renewed for us unto life.

The devotion of priests daily sacrifices Christ

upon the altar through the lawful celebration of the sacred rites;

for what is consecrated upon the altar as bread and wine

is reckoned as the Saviour suspended on the cross.

The altar is the wood of the cross, and the chalice signifies the tomb;

here he dies, here he sleeps: each sacred memorial indicates this.

On this [Note: [Col. 1211D] That is, on the altar.] he is the Lamb; from this [Note: [Col. 1212D] That is, from the tomb.] the mighty Lion arose; and as an eagle,

flying toward the stars, he draws spiritual persons to himself.

[Col. 1212D] **CONCLUSION. That the priest and every faithful person ought to conform to his head, which is Christ, and follow him spiritually into heaven.**

Therefore, whenever the priest recites these sacred rites,

let him consider the cross of the flesh, that he may conform himself to Christ.

Let the flesh, crucified together with its vices, first die,

and let the mind, made alive to God, rise and follow him.

Thus, by dying well, it rises; thus it also lives to him.

Thus redeemed, a person goes where his maker has gone.

## ON THE WORKS OF THE SIX DAYS

[Col. 1213]

### A BRIEF NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING POEMS

We have brought forth this poem, along with several others following it which we shall indicate in appropriate places, from a manuscript codex about five hundred years old. This codex was transferred from the library of the celebrated abbey of Saint-Amand in Pabula, or Elnone, to the Royal Library, where it now exists as no. 247. Since it expressly bears Hildebert’s name, there seems to be no room for doubt that it is his genuine composition. We have committed these poems to print all the more willingly because, in his customary manner, he draws and adapts, with particular subtlety and ingenuity, the creation of all things—even temporal and inanimate things—to spiritual and moral meanings for the edification of the faithful.

[Col. 1213]

[Note: [Col. 1213C] Thus the aforementioned codex, without the initial “H.”] **ILDEBERT OF LE MANS, ON THE WORKS OF THE SIX DAYS.** (Gen. 1–2.) (G)*

1169 **THE FIRST DAY**

[Col. 1213A]

The Almighty made heaven and earth in the beginning;

his Son was the Beginning.

In this he made heaven for those who seek heavenly things in their minds,

and earth for those who desire earthly things too greatly.

Scripture reports that the earth was empty and void;

thus those who desire earthly things become empty.

The abyss is described as covered with thick darkness:

it signifies hearts clouded by the darkness of sin.

The gracious Spirit moved over the waters;

for he strengthens minds and gives life to wandering souls.

By these words baptism was indicated,

which he himself was to consecrate in the times of faith.

And the Lord said, “Let there be light,” and light was made;

for the sacred light of faith follows baptism.

[Col. 1213B] Rightly the first light signifies faith; for it is the first

virtue of everyone who comes to the Lord.

After this the Creator divided darkness and light,

and darkness was called night, while light was called day.

Understand the wicked by darkness, the righteous by light:

God’s foreknowledge divided them according to their merits.

### THE SECOND DAY

Then the firmament, created after the following light,

Scripture says signifies sacred Scripture,

which strengthens those striving to shine after the baptism of faith

and fortifies them against the snares of the enemy.

Then God divided the waters from the waters,

placing this firmament between them.

By these waters are signified the human and angelic races,

[Col. 1213C] divided by merits, condition, and places.

Sacred Scripture, placed in their midst,

is set before us, but lies beneath the spirits.

For the Law was not written for the divine ministers—that is, the angels—

who fully see what the letter has touched upon.

[Col. 1214A] The Law was given to humanity, by which it separates spiritual things

from carnal vices, as waters from waters.

### THE THIRD DAY

The third light was present when the waters flowed together into one:

the sea came to be, and the dry land that had been hidden appeared.

The stormy sea signifies the wicked, and dry land the righteous,

who, as long as they live, thirst for righteousness.

Then the green herb and fruit-bearing trees signify teachers,

whom hardships cannot break.

The earth is commanded to produce these with their seeds—

that is, the words of God and works of righteousness.

Those who hold these in mind and minister them to their brothers

produce this seed according to its kind.

What was first called dry land is afterwards called earth;

[Col. 1214B] so, when the waters are removed, we are called earth.

For if we are separated from the vices signified by the flowing waters,

we shall be fruitful earth.

And we shall render multiplied fruit to the Lord:

a shining work of righteousness and devotion.

1170 **THE FOURTH DAY**

On the fourth day God made two great lights,

by which Christ and the Church are signified.

Shining in the firmament of Scripture,

they give the greatest lights to the believing people.

And just as the sun illumines the moon with its own light,

so Christ fills the Church with his light.

And as the moon drives away the darkness of night with its light,

so the Church banishes our darkness.

[Col. 1214C] Understand the stars in the firmament as the righteous [or saints],

who cling to Scripture and drive away our blackness.

And fittingly the earth first produced herbs with trees,

and afterwards the bright lights shone in heaven;

for then every faithful person shines with the light of virtues,

when he has first performed some praiseworthy work.

[Col. 1215A] God is said to have created, on the fifth day,

things that crawl in the waters and fly through the air on wings.

Having received Christ’s light, our mind is commanded

to cast out harmful things in the sea of the heart.

Those things which creep, as it were, and are covered by the abyss’s darkness,

it must immediately drive away by applying judgment.

Those which seek the heights, as it were, and become near to heaven,

let it preserve and nourish in its mind.

That God is affirmed to have seen both to be good,

those who grasp the mysteries give this reason:

there are evils which creep secretly in the hearts of the good,

for they strive to draw them to evil.

But when they are driven out and the saints are tested through them,

they become good because they increase the merits of the saints.

[Col. 1215B] Thus God is said to have seen these to be good, but not to have made them,

seeing that they can assist the good.

### THE SIXTH DAY

At God’s command, on the sixth day the earth brought forth

creeping thing, beast of burden, and wild animal.

These signify the outward movements of a person,

which seek earthly things in the manner already described.

What the sea produced signifies the inner

senses of a person, which, like fish, the depths conceal.

But the earth’s offspring signify the outward movements of a person;

both, plainly, lie open.

Note also this: wherever the letter signifies carnal

movements, you will find that what you choose is produced.

For our flesh is heavy, and nature always draws us downward;

thus it seeks earth as though born for it.

[Col. 1215C] Thus, when all those things had now been completed

which gave the world adornment and beauty,

and which could indicate what might adorn

the figurative, lesser world, the Creator of the world said:

“Let us make man, whom our image

and likeness may adorn.” What great gifts he gave,

creating all things for humanity—if humanity had kept the giver’s commands

and had not, by sinning, become equal to the beasts!

1171 Yet do not think these gifts were given to the outward person:

the inward person alone possesses these gifts.

Thus, created invisible and immortal,

he is rational, and so like God.

Reason within us is a certain image of divinity,

and that part of us alone sees God.

By this alone we are set above dumb animals,

[Col. 1215D] and by its aid seek him who rules heaven.

The likeness of divinity consists in our imitating God

through righteousness and nobility of character.

Human creation has another dignity,

which God’s mystical words fittingly signify.

In the other works God had said, “Let there be”; here he said, “Let us make”:

the matter seemed worthy of deliberation.

And rightly the triune Divinity together made the one

whom it alone made in its own image.

And God added: “Let him rule over the earth and over those things

which the sea, the land, and the light air contain.”

This creature, shining with the image of divinity and more worthy,

is set above the rest by the Creator’s word—humanity;

not by force, in which many animals are stronger,

[Col. 1216A] but by reason, which retains God’s image.

While a person uses it well, he is deservedly placed above them;

when he uses it badly, he becomes like the beasts.

Thus Divinity, with a certain weight of judgment

and deliberation, made humanity in its own image.

When it says “our,” the Trinity of Divinity must be recognized;

for one alone could not say “our.”

By saying, “He made him in the image of God,” repeatedly using “God,”

it indicates that three are not to be believed to be gods.

It is then added that male and female were made,

though one human being was first said to have been made;

for the male retained the seed of the female sex,

and woman was made from the rib of the man.

Therefore, wishing to bless humanity’s posterity,

which could not proceed from one alone,

[Col. 1216B] the Lord’s voice rightly blessed two persons in one,

as God is read to have done with Melchizedek:

in Abraham’s loins he then blessed Aaron,

when Abraham, returning victorious from the enemy, gave tithes.

Thus the first man was two persons, though he prophesied one flesh,

when he received as his companion the woman made from himself.

And in blessing two persons thus in one, God also wishes

to commend the bonds of marriage.

Then follows God’s blessing, given to everyone

who diligently performs what it commands:

“Increase, fill the earth with a numerous offspring,

and subject it to yourselves.” Note these words.

“Rule also over the creatures of the sea and the birds,

and likewise over those of every kind which earth produces.”

He wishes us to increase and multiply in righteousness,

[Col. 1216C] and that human hearts be filled with the good things of doctrine.

1172 He commands us, by mortifying the earth of our body, to subject it

to the rule of the soul,

and to rule over the unlawful movements

of our heart and body, as he taught above.

That God gives all herbs and fruit-bearing trees,

you may understand as food for these persons.

Understand the little and the great—the herbs and trees—as the faithful,

who provide sacred nourishment to the fathers;

and they provide it not only to the fathers, but also to the good and bad,

whom cattle and birds signify.

For Christ’s mercy commands that one be able to give to everyone

who asks, but especially to the holy fathers.

God saw all that he had made, and it was very good

(as is immediately added); look back at the preceding words.

[Col. 1216D] In the other cases it is said separately that he saw it to be good,

but this is not said when man was formed.

The mystical expression does not say “he saw man to be good,” but “they were good,”

not praising man by himself, except together with the rest.

That Spirit of God by whom these things are related

knew that man would sin.

Therefore he did not wish to praise by himself the one

who alone would set aside the Creator’s command;

and his praise is spoken among the praises of beasts,

he who by sinning deserved to become equal to a beast.

Therefore on the sixth day the world and all its adornment

were formed, through God’s working.

The world’s perfection was made in a perfect number,

by the ordering of so good an artisan.

[Col. 1217A] And on the seventh day the Creator completed

the work that he had done; consider these words more carefully.

The Lord is said to have made nothing on this day,

yet he says that on this day he finished his work.

If, however, you look attentively, you will see two things made:

for he made the day and blessed it.

And fittingly God completed all things in this number,

through which the cycles of time always run.

On this day God rested from all those things

which he had accomplished; note this too.

God did not rest, weary in the human manner,

[Col. 1218A] nor because, being true rest, he was overcome by labour.

Not so: the Lord’s rest means ceasing,

for then he ceased to create new works.

But if you perceive these things more subtly in your mind,

you will find a higher meaning that may be expressed.

We work so that, assisted by the reward of works,

we may rest; but divinity is otherwise.

Indeed, God created the world from goodness alone,

yet he did not need the world’s goods.

And he rested not in these things, but from them, needing none of them;

giving rest, not receiving it.

[Col. 1217]

## THE PHYSIOLOGUS OF HILDEBERT, BISHOP OF LE MANS, BEGINS

(From Royal manuscript 274, formerly Elnonensis. Not yet published.) (G)*

1173 **ON THE LION**

[Col. 1217B]

The lion has three natures and thus three figures,

which, O Christ, I have written of you in twelve verses.

Other animals are mentioned in the divine books,

concerning which I have added the mystical things I learned in turn,

trying whether I could write in different metres.

Nor do the added verses merely complete our number.

For the strong lion, standing upon the high peak of a mountain,

whenever he descends by whatever path to the valley below,

if he senses a hunter through a familiar smell,

smooths over with his tail every track impressed by his feet,

so that the hunter cannot seek out his lair from these.

When born, he does not wake until the sun has made its third circuit,

but his father, uttering a roar, awakens him.

[Col. 1217C] Then he comes, as it were, to life; then he acquires his five senses,

and whenever he sleeps he never closes his eyes.

Thus you, who dwell upon the summit of highest heaven,

when at length it pleased you to visit the earthly realm

in order to raise the human race fallen through sin,

were not wholly known to any demon:

that Mary’s womb was your chamber, O Christ;

and he who begot you caused you to rise after three days,

when, avenger of death, you yourself underwent the death of the cross.

You guard us; you never sleep at any time,

lest the wolf snatch away anyone from your own flock.

### ON THE EAGLE

They say that the eagle is foremost above every flying creature,

and that it renews itself thus when weighed down by old age.

It seeks out a spring whose running never fails,

and above it it comes near to God in heaven.

[Col. 1218B] Then the blazing sun sets both its wings ablaze for it,

and diminishes what is large and lightens what is heavy.

Then too the mist close by is consumed by fire,

which its old life has gathered over its eyes.

Soon it plunges and immerses itself in the clear waters of the spring,

and, as it falls from its nest, it suddenly becomes new.

Its beak, by which it tears food, is curved,

and it can scarcely take even a little food from any source.

But striking a rock, or biting food as it is accustomed to do,

it wears down the crooked part; thus it takes food thereafter.

A person burdened with sins from his mother’s origin

is like this eagle, but is renewed thus:

he rises above the cloud and feels the burning of the sun

when he despises the world with its pomp.

He becomes new in Christ, immersed three times in the living flood [Note: [Col. 1217D] Note baptism by immersion.].

[Col. 1218C] Of himself that gracious one says: “I am the living spring.”

He wears down his crooked mouth through words that pray to Christ,

because Scripture frequently declares that Christ is the rock.

1174 Now the new bread is sweeter than all honey;

that bread is Christ, food made without death.

### ON THE SERPENT

Now the old serpent rejoices to become new,

and, fasting, shudders with emaciation.

Its worn-out skin trembles; its bones alone remain,

not its strength.

It seeks a narrow opening in a rock,

scarcely moving itself; and when at last it comes there,

it passes through and strips off the flesh

of its old skin.

[Col. 1218D] Returning to whatever streams of water it chooses,

it casts out its poison beforehand in order to lose its thirst:

[Col. 1219A] therefore I shall fear it less in water,

when it is without venom.

If it sees a man without clothing,

the serpent withdraws far away as from fire;

but when it sees one wearing a garment,

it rises against him.

When a man overcomes it and it pursues him persistently,

he disregards his body and makes it a shield;

yet it takes care of its head

lest it die.

Whoever is renewed once in the sacred font,

if you sin again, you are hard as flint;

therefore, whenever you grow old,

always imitate the serpent.

Let your food be scant, and your limbs be reduced;

[Col. 1219B] out of what you do not eat, aid the wretched.

Weep in penitence, and often say to the Lord:

“Have mercy.”

The rock’s opening signifies this path,

and the rock also signifies Christ; for through him

anyone becomes new and receives life

without end.

When you come to his lofty temple

in order to drink the holy and blessed word,

first vomit out the venom you have,

which harms the heart.

Within the heart are angers blacker than a serpent,

and hatreds which, like mothers, give birth to hatred;

within the heart are unfriendly quarrels,

[Col. 1219C] and envies.

Within the heart are proud furies conceived,

for you despise your equals and those above you.

Hearts are full of these

and many other poisons.

Being pure of these, as if naked of clothing,

you will drive away demons—the serpent’s symbolic counterpart—

as the sun’s orbit suppresses

the blind darkness of night.

1175 Yet you will endure many struggles,

and while you live you will be in the contest.

Therefore wisely imitate the serpent,

the guardian of its head.

Do you wish to be worthy of new life without end?

Your head must always be kept unharmed:

[Col. 1219D] by this head I mean that which you have

in Christ himself, the Prince.

### ON THE ANT

The ant offers us an example of labour

when it carries its customary food in its mouth.

And in its actions it shows spiritual matters,

which the Jew does not love, and is thereby guilty.

So that it may be secure against the coming winter,

while it is warm it does not rest.

Let us also labour, brothers, while we have time,

that we may be secure at the time of judgment.

It gathers wheat if it finds it; it rejects barley:

I myself gather the New Law, not the Old.

[Col. 1220A] But lest it sprout when moistened by rainy showers,

or perish because it can no longer be useful,

the prudent ant splits every grain it gathers in two;

this means that the Law has two paths.

It speaks earthly things and at the same time reveals heavenly things;

now it feeds the mind, and now nourishes the body.

May either feed us, so that fear of hunger may depart

at the time of judgment, which resembles winter.

### ON THE FOX

The crafty fox is called full of many deceits;

the farmer loves it [Note: [Col. 1219D] Rather, hates it.] because it steals poultry.

But when it is hungry because food is lacking, it finds a trick

by which it may catch cawing birds.

It stretches itself out upon the ground, lying on its back,

and, as though dead, draws no breath.

[Col. 1220B] A crow or black raven thinks it a corpse

and alights in order to eat it and tear it with bites.

The fox leaps up lightly and suddenly seizes the bird,

repaying its sad service by consuming it with its teeth.

The fox therefore bears a double figure, which it is useful to know:

at one time like the devil, at another like deceitful people.

He is truly dead who caused death to exist;

this means that he pretends not to do evil.

Whoever eats his flesh by presenting an empty thing as real—

that is, any sin or evil—

is as though swallowed by him, when the demon, fox-like in his snares,

draws him down with himself to Tartarus.

Thus deceitful people deserve the name of fox,

and many people in this age are such.

[Col. 1220C] Herod too was one who commanded that Christ be sought [Note: [Col. 1219D] Luke 13.]:

pretending to believe, while concealing his intent to destroy.

### ON THE STAG

The stag is said by the *Physiologus*—when it teaches this account (*logos*)—to have

two natures and two figures.

For it draws out great serpents with its nostrils

from the caves of earth or the hiding places of rock.

It devours them; then, as the foul venom grows hot,

it burns with thirst to seek the clear waters of a spring.

When it drinks these, full as it is, it overcomes the poison [variant: “that is, vomits it out”],

and makes itself young when it sheds its antlers.

We also, caught by the deceit of the evil serpent,

contract poison and burn with its flames.

This is lust, or hatred, or anger,

[Col. 1220D] or even excessive greed for money.

We ought to run to Christ, the living fountain;

when he moistens us, he drives out the poison we have taken in.

1176 When these have been removed, we are young, and our proud things are broken—

those which, like antlers, strike the wretched.

Antlers are a burden borne upon the stag’s head,

yet they do not thereby seem a disgrace to their master.

When they cross rivers together and travel together,

and go far in seeking pasture,

they proceed in a line, bearing their heads suspended,

each resting upon the haunches of another.

They retain this practice even if they are a hundred in line;

[Col. 1221A] but when the one in front is weary, it falls back.

Thus all take turns and bear one another,

never failing, and thus they complete their journey.

By such conduct they urge us with devotion to bear

the burdens of others and teach us to help them.

Thus the law of Christ our master must be fulfilled;

whoever does this will find pasture.

### ON THE SPIDER

The spider, a worm, busily strives to weave many threads

into skillfully fashioned nets for you, fly,

that, flying, you may be caught there: you are sweet and useful food to it.

The delicate work is pleasing, yet because it is fragile it profits it nothing.

Any breeze draws away the spread web; it breaks and falls into nothing.

[Col. 1221B] A person follows these little worms by despising his enemies,

whom he devours by making them wretched; and he is greatly pleased

when he can harm another. Yet what he does is evil.

When he dies, the web wrought by the spider just described falls.

### ON THE WHALE

Above every creature living in the sea is the whale,

a monster great enough to rise above the waters.

Whoever looks upon it thinks it a mountain in the sea,

or an island standing in the midst of Ocean.

Whenever it wishes to relieve the very great hunger

which it frequently bears, it cleverly opens its mouth.

Then a breath of scent comes forth like a hook,

[Col. 1221C] to draw little fishes to itself.

Only little ones: for it cannot seize anything great

or perfect, nor hold it in its mouth.

The fish swallows and shuts up the little fishes within;

yet it did not swallow Jonah in that way.

If there is a storm when summer is going or coming,

and it stirs the sea to its depths,

the whale immediately rises to the surface waters:

it is a considerable headland to behold.

Then sailors hasten to tie their swift ship to it

because of the storm, and to leap ashore.

They kindle the ever-burning fire carried by the ship,

to warm themselves or cook food.

The whale feels the fire and then plunges down in flight

[Col. 1221C] whence it had first risen, and the ship thus perishes.

The devil is mighty and great in body like a whale,

as the great magicians whom he makes demonstrate.

He hungers and thirsts for the minds of all people everywhere,

and destroys those whom he can.

But he draws the little ones in faith by sweetness of speech,

for he does not draw people steadfast in faith.

Whatever anyone trusts in, or casts his hope upon,

is immediately dragged to Styx, and thus also deceived.

## ON THE SIRENS AND THE HOMOCENTAUR

[Col. 1222A]

Sirens are sea-monsters resounding with loud

1177 voices and producing songs in many melodies.

Unwary sailors very often approach them.

They make sound with excessive sweetness of voice

and bring either shipwreck or deadly danger.

Those who escaped them have reported that they are such:

from the navel upward is a most beautiful maiden;

below this, birds make up the monster.

The homocentaur likewise is a creature of double form,

in which an ass is mixed with a human body.

Very many people are now similarly double in speech:

saying one thing, then immediately doing another;

what they profess outwardly, they do not likewise work inwardly.

[Col. 1222B] For there are many who speak of virtue

but indulge in riches. O, how their pulpits shine! [Note: [Col. 1221D] “Here certain matters must be corrected,” according to a note in vol. XI of the new edition of *Histoire littéraire*. Read *humano* (“human”), in place of *in humano* (“in a human [body]”), and *turpibus* (“shameful things”), in place of *opibus* (“riches”). It is less correct to say *homocentauris* than *onocentauris*, French *l’onocentaure*. This restoration of the words will not be doubtful to anyone who attends to the text of St Jerome [Col. 1222D] on Isaiah 6:13, 22: “Moreover,” he says, “the name *onocentaur* is compounded from asses and centaurs,” etc. The prophet himself speaks of the onocentaur in chapter 34, verse 14. The onocentaur is likewise named by Aelian, *On the Nature of Animals* XVII.9; by Isidore, *Etymologies* XI.3; and by Manuel Philes, *On the Properties of Animals*, chapter 40.]

### ON THE ELEPHANT

Among the Indians elephants are so great in body

that one might well judge them equal to mountains.

They go together as sheep seek pasture;

they mate face-to-face when they come together.

They give birth only once, though they live so many years—

three hundred, that is—and do not bear twins.

But the female bears one offspring, carrying it for two years,

and when she gives birth she stands in deep water lest it fall.

It cannot rise, because it never bends its legs:

if it happens to fall, this is what the mother fears.

When it wishes to rest or restore itself by sleep,

[Col. 1222C] it leans against the trunk of a small tree.

The hunter marks and cuts this tree, conceals the cut by a support,

and sits hidden, watching until the elephant seeks rest.

When the elephant, secure as before, comes to the tree’s shade,

it leans upon it and falls as the tree falls.

If no human is present, it groans and at last trumpets;

then an old elephant runs up, wishing to raise it,

but cannot, though it strives. Then this one too trumpets while weeping,

and many others, even large ones, come.

When all are unable, they strive to send forth calls,

at which a small and very young elephant quickly appears.

Its trunk—marvellous though it is—raises the fallen elephant,

and thus it escapes the snares described above.

[Col. 1222C] Smoke from this animal’s hairs, placed beneath a roof,

drives away serpents and all creatures carrying venom.

Thus the first man Adam has now fallen through the tree;

Moses wished to raise him, but could not.

After him the prophets wished to do so, but could not;

at their prayers the Lord came for this purpose.

Though he is small, because God became human,

he thus raised Adam, guilty for eating.

Whoever comes rightly to his fragrance, full, that is, of his words,

[Col. 1223A] will thereby be blessed.

1178 Through him every vice will indeed flee from the heart;

after that no cause of death will harm that person.

### ON THE TURTLE-DOVE

The turtle-dove does not know an empty sea;

once wed to one husband,

she remains joined to him night and day.

No one will see her without her husband;

but if she is deprived of him by widowhood,

she will nevertheless never marry another mate.

She will fly alone and sit alone,

and will always keep him as though he were living;

waiting, she remains chaste.

Thus is every faithful soul,

[Col. 1223B] made blessed by a covenant with her husband.

For Christ is her husband

when he fills her heart from himself.

Living well, she always clings to him

and seeks no alien friend.

Though Orcus has taken him,

whom she believes remains in heaven,

she looks for him to come thence again,

to judge the whole microcosm.

### ON THE PANTHER

The panther is a four-footed creature, than which none is more beautiful,

[Col. 1224A] black, marked with rounded spots of white.

Having fed upon varied prey and been satisfied,

it withdraws and sleeps, stretched out in a hollow cave.

But after three days it rises, and then at last it roars.

Such a sweet fragrance comes from its throat

that in its power it surpasses every spice.

Every beast which hears its voice immediately hastens to it,

following the breath full of sweetness.

All do this; only dragons, when the panther sounds,

either flee or become sluggish in body;

they lie hidden in their caves and do not appear at that time.

The panther is allegorically called Christ,

who surpasses all people in beauty of form.

He was satisfied because he takes as many to himself as he wishes;

and he slept when by dying he redeemed us.

[Col. 1224B] He uttered his roar after he rose from death.

Ascending into heaven, where he reigns present with the Father,

all nations thus followed him in belief.

The ancient serpent, our enemy,

flees and hides and does not appear at that time.

For, though it dares openly to deceive none, it deceives many.

May he who reigns through all ages defend us from this.

The poem finished, let praise and glory be to Christ.

If these verses please no one else, let them please Tibaldus.

[Col. 1223]

1179 **HIS AFORESAID POEM ON THE ORDER OF THE WORLD.** (G)*

[Note: [Col. 1223] Thus the manuscript codex formerly Elnonensis, now Royal, no. 274, about 500 years old.]

### NOTICE

The following poem is all the more rightly attributed to Hildebert because even from its title it seems to have a greater affinity with his preceding poem *On the Work of the Six Days*. Indeed, one might call it almost a continuation of that work, since it begins where the preceding poem ended. That poem ends with the formation of man on the sixth day and goes no further; this one begins with Adam’s sin and, through the eras first of the law of nature and then of the written Law, prepares the minds of readers, as it were, for the New Law and the Gospel, for the Incarnation of the divine Word, and finally carries forward the sacred history to the preaching of the apostles and the very foundation of the Roman Church through blessed Peter.

### PROLOGUE, OR INVOCATION

[Col. 1223C]

O greatest one, for whose coming the vows of the saints and the longings of the devout thirst,

whose advent the dregs of this age require,

fulfil what the holy prophets sang concerning you;

by coming, put an end to the world raging against you.

You see how every good person groans beneath afflictions;

therefore everyone who loves you cries to you with all his heart.

Hear those who cry out, who call upon the kingdom of heaven;

come when entreated, giver of the pleasant kingdom.

Send down to earth the sickle of judgment to come;

send here the reaper, hastened for the harvest,

for the dry harvest falls with exhausted stalks.

[Col. 1224C] Deign to be present for the harvest laid low:

the grasses of earth do not know how to yield you pleasing return.

What the soil now produces are tares and brambles.

Therefore, recompense of all merits,

bring yourself here without delay, for the time and hour demand it.

Formerly I composed in verse the cause of birth—once condemned, born of the holy Virgin—

a matter of faith not previously enclosed; with your guidance, I shall unfold it anew.

You make the mouth of the mute employ speech when you will.

Beneath a certain tree the first-created Adam fell [Note: [Col. 1223C] Gen. 3.];

the law concerning the fruit having been given, he wantonly violated it.

By the serpent’s persuasion he himself incurred the punishment of the guilty one,

[Col. 1225A] passing the punishment of sin to all his posterity,

by which every later offspring pays the burden of death.

For when the father fell, he was cast out of paradise.

He lost his native dwelling and his homeland’s house.

Every human being is exiled after tasting the fruit with the father.

After this first Ceres became heir to his crime;

and through the father’s gift she became first in every evil.

Alas for sorrow! His stock always flowed downward into worse things.

The ages bore this as though it were a common rope,

by which death dragged all people into the infernal caverns.

This is the eclipse which happened to the fathers themselves,

from whose blood the race of peoples flowed forth.

When their offspring increased, a vicious stone grew hard;

and the devouring torches of envy in the human mind,

kindled within it, urged it to use the sword.

[Col. 1225B] It used it, burned with rage, and was soaked in a brother’s blood [Note: [Col. 1225] Gen. 4.].

What a frenzied hand! How profane was he

who first grasped the hilt by which he performed such deeds!

And every arm was cruelly extended,

by whose stroke a brother’s flesh fell, smitten bitterly.

1180 This first blood, as we know from Genesis as an index,

widely diffused, produced a similar practice,

a deadly example for mortals.

Neither brother spares brother, nor children spare father,

nor father his children, nor mother her children.

Enslaved right hands suffer the throats of their masters.

If any anger arises, anger immediately suggests striking.

If one person bitterly provokes another by words,

the latter draws the avenging sword and sheds blood.

[Col. 1225C] Every blade is wet with blood for worthless gain.

Therefore, while the first world raved with these diseases,

ever piling sins upon sins already accumulated,

mingling heavenly things with human, sacred places with profane,

the offended one whom no feeling knows how to restrain

compelled unclean flesh to enter the avenging waters.

The righteous Noah, skilled in shipbuilding, saved eight [Note: [Col. 1225] Gen. 6.].

A formula of baptism, in which was the water of the flood.

By these few the losses of the second world are repaired,
and time began again to roll back into its own course.

They now became fathers in their turn: that is, those begotten begot;
and men were born, remarkable for their great bodily stature,
whose speech of lips was diversified at the tower.

Polluted crowds are nourished at the breast in the twin city  
[Note: [Col. 1225D] Sodom and Gomorrah.],
at the breast of luxury, whom the heavenly flame consumed;

[Col. 1225D] but by their merits it preserved righteous Lot unburned  
[Note: [Col. 1225] Gen. XIX].

Phoebus shone in those same days—
not heaven’s Phoebus, but Abraham, who with faithful mind
gave the earth the brightness and warmth of faith.

For he cultivates one faith in three Persons,
not delaying to worship Three in an equal Godhead.
He is made foremost through the gifts of divine religion,
which nourish the elder recipients of tithes;
before the Law he was first a *Apella* [circumcised man]  
[Note: [Col. 1225D] That is, circumcised.].

Now he believes the typological meaning, in obeying through loss of flesh:

[Col. 1226A] therefore, illustrious in faith and in every way dear to the Lord,
having subdued nature’s right for faith’s covenant,
he received a son begotten by his wrinkled mother  
[Note: [Col. 1225] Gen. XXI].

Though this son was his sole hope of offspring,
he was commanded almost to sacrifice him, but was spared by a recall  
[Note: [Col. 1225] Gen. XXII].

By one deed he was seen as both pious and criminal;
yet love raises no charge of crime.
A wool-bearing victim, taken from thorns, is slain
for the bound boy, who is in no way stained with blood.
The prudent man likewise fashioned this type within his breast:
what he conceals in words he reveals by right action.
O what great merit that father possessed before the Thunderer!

1181 From him come nations, coming after him and from him,
likened to stars or numbered with the sands,
and, as though depicted, blessed in him.

[Col. 1226B] From this plant so great a race is sown,
which Habakkuk cannot clearly match with numbers.

Jacob, mighty in wrestling, belonged to this lot;
by guile the blessing gives glory to us.
Hence God is seen upon the ladder with the heavenly host  
[Note: [Col. 1225] Gen. XXVIII.],
changing his name as an omen of the coming stock;
therefore they were quite aptly called Israelites.

Then twelve sons were born to the aged patriarch:
the youngest in age became great in piety.
The sun and moon worship him in one night,
together with an equal number of stars, as likewise happened among his brothers.
The region of Memphis received him from the Ishmaelites.
When Joseph fled illicit intercourse  
[Note: [Col. 1225] Gen. XXXIX.], he prepared this gain for himself:
that he should govern Egypt  
[Note: [Col. 1225] Gen. XLI.], as is written in the book.

And, appointed steward over Pharaoh’s goods,

[Col. 1226C] he interprets dreams, which he unravels with a wise mind.
He declares that a harsh season of famine is to come;
a grievous season lasted through seven harvests.
Supplies fail in aged Jacob’s land  
[Note: [Col. 1225] Gen. XLII.];
to escape destruction, he leaves that same homeland.
The Majesty of Heaven commands this, and necessity compels it.

With a small band he soon enters the fields of Memphis:
the son is worshipped; thus the vision is fulfilled.
A spacious land is granted  
[Note: [Col. 1225] Gen. XLVII.], yet this little people is not content;
but at last, begetting offspring, they filled it.
Like camp-servants and despised ash-bearers  
[Note: [Col. 1225] Exod. I.],
they are compelled for many years to serve tyrants  
[Note: [Col. 1226D] For “obey tyrants.”].

God, pitying their sorrow and toil,
chose two men, through whom he removed the burden from them.

[Col. 1226D] He gave signs by which the two brothers might contend:
eloquent Aaron, and Moses, second in signs  
[Note: [Col. 1225] Exod. III.];
the one polished in speech, the other ready for miracles.

Thus the good advocates stand before Pharaoh,
leaders of the people and bearers of commandments.
The king, when the word has been spoken, mocks with proud heart,
scorning God  
[Note: [Col. 1225] Exod. V.], who demands the Hebrew people.
Lest he seem dull, he refuses to dismiss the populace.
At the first encounter magical art is fought with magical art.
Here, surely, beneficent faith is openly mighty through the displayed signs!

[Col. 1227A] For, because you do not yield, a wooden serpent turns into serpents,
multiplying the sign; the serpent becomes wood again  
[Note: [Col. 1227] Exod. VII et seqq.].
Since you do not know how to yield, king, you provoke worse things.

For the conquered land is all the more tortured by plagues.
Blood, through foulness, deprives rivers and springs of drink  
[manuscript: “fills”].
Every kind of fish perishes in an alien death.
Since you do not know how to yield, king, you provoke worse things.

Then the uncultivated marshes, commanded to do so, produced frogs;
everything is filled with them; only the Hebrews are left free—
their houses and ovens, even the king’s ivory bed;
the frogs’ swelling boils in pots with cooked food.
Since you do not know how to yield, king, you provoke worse things.

At the touch of the rod many gnats from the dust
afflict both cattle and the people inhabiting that land.

[Col. 1227B] Since you do not know how to yield, king, you provoke worse things.

Flies, you have arrived and inflicted many torments.
Since you do not know how to yield, king, you provoke worse things.

Behold, the fifth affliction rages outside and within;
the diseased life of cattle falls in sudden death.
All livestock is struck down, yet the king remains blind in heart.
Since you do not know how to yield, king, you provoke worse things.

At the divine command, when the furnace supplies ashes,
that standard-bearer scatters them in a thousand wounds:
blisters swell, scorching men and beasts.
Since you do not know how to yield, king, you provoke worse things.

As you yourself command, God, clouds thicken in the air;
thunder gives forth a sound unknown to that country’s custom;
1182 suddenly rain pours down in many streams;
hail becomes fiery, and in pitiable destruction perishes

[Col. 1227C] whatever remained in the fields beneath the hail-storms;
grass also perishes, and that from which woman makes thread.
Since you do not know how to yield, king, you provoke worse things.

Behold the heavy locust, which wind and gentle breeze,
according to Moses’ word, carry through the region,
to complete the heap of grief; it gnaws fruit from the tree,
and whatever is green could not perish more completely by fire.
Since you do not know how to yield, king, you provoke worse things.

With the lamp removed, excessive darkness having come,
the people are enwrapped and oppressed by a three-day night.
Bereft of sun, as though their eyes were gouged out,
they seek one another’s touch and guidance;
shut indoors, none uses his steps.
Night envelops them, but does not envelop the Hebrews:
for the worshipper of the true God cannot be held beneath night.

[Col. 1227D] Since you do not know how to yield, king, you provoke worse things.

Let Scripture testify what the final plague was like:
wonders follow greater wonders, dreadful things more dreadful things;
the hand of the Almighty fills all with lamentation,
striking down the bodies of all firstborn.
Death reigns in the cattle-stalls; it reigns in palaces;
every cottage, full of nocturnal biers, mourns.
Great is the divine vengeance, and great the ruin.
Death envelops them, but does not envelop the Hebrews;
for the blood of the great lamb is upon the doorposts as a type.

[Col. 1228A] Egypt laments, presses and harasses the Jews
to take quickly the path so often demanded by signs.
After many winters they are granted leave to depart.
They rise, not slowly, rich in diverse goods;
they are enriched, while the natives are despoiled;
the people long captive depart as fugitives.

Recurring terror, produced by error, presses him;
the king of dreadful barbarism fiercely pursues them.
He brings up forces that you may return beneath cruel yokes.
But be confident: no dangers are at hand for you;
he whose worshipper you are will be a wondrous avenger.

Why do you deceive yourself, king? Spare your horses, since you will perish.
It is wiser indeed to restrain the reins with moderation,
lest, if you do not turn back, you be swallowed by the grim whirlpool.
You who drive peoples onward—the whirlpool will drive you onward too.

[Col. 1228B] Everything has its time: what now flowers presently withers.
Now the sea, opened by the rod, displays a broad gap
at the divine nod  
[Note: [Col. 1227] Exod. XIV et seqq.], [lacuna].

Here he heaps punishments upon them; here he lays dry sands beneath them.
Here horseman, here great chariot, here tyrant swims.
Israel passes through this, but the impious host remains behind.
Israel is saved; the Saviour is glorified.

For this people journeying through the desert
he promised provisions and preserved their clothing;
manna flowed before the camp like rain from the stars.
When it thirsts, it drinks from a rock with a flowing stream.
Through the covenant it receives instruction for life.

The Law teaches it to live wisely and reverently:
not to bow the heart before sacred images;
to keep Sabbaths by resting and doing nothing;

[Col. 1228C] to obtain life if it wishes to honour its parents.
It also distinguishes this, lest an impious hand strike anyone down;
the Law’s knife threatens him lest he become an adulterer  
[Note: [Col. 1227] Exod. XX.];
it forbids men to be thieves, because many hang upon a cross;
it commands that nothing be proved by a false witness;
for right living, nothing belonging to one’s neighbours should be coveted  
[Note: [Col. 1227D] That is, neighbours.].

These and what remains, Israel, secure earthly goods for you.
Thus you will live among them, so that you may be rich in due season.
When they are not observed, you soon come to punishments.
If anyone injures another, he soon exchanges eye for eye;
God takes tooth for tooth: thus the letter mitigates wrath.
Whoever is held under the Law will be imperfect;
for the Law’s strict curse condemns you,
since transgression of one iota makes the whole transgression.

[Col. 1228D] 1183 Therefore it binds all whom it wearies by commanding.
Bound, as it were, by a certain rope of this command,
none of the saints ascended to the kingdoms of the heavens.

Some became a mockery after being struck with lashes  
[Note: [Col. 1227] Heb. XI.];
some, confessing righteousness, endured chains;
some, daring to speak what was right, were shut in prison;
some were cut with saws, their backs sliced;
some were tested; others too were stoned;
they paid in blood for the blows of the executioner.
They hide in caves and winding recesses;

[Col. 1229A] [Note: [Col. 1229D] [ [Col. 1229] This note appears at the foot of column 1229, but the callout number (69) has not been printed in the text.] Judith I.]
solitary woodland places and every high mountain please them.
They are covered not in woven cloth, but in cheap covering,
which the poverty of a lowly goat has woven for them.
Naked of possessions, they are harsh toward adversity,
desiring nothing, summoning in their hearts what is to come.
By hope they believed what they saw inwardly as future;
not darkened by crime, they shone in the light of signs:
healing lepers, recalling the dead to life,
and curing the blind and mute, the deaf and those unhinged in mind.

As you have heard, what did the world produce worthier than these?
Yet not even for this were they safe when freed from the flesh.
I prove by the witness of Scripture that glory was not yet won;
because of the first man’s crime, the gate loved the threshold
of the side drawn forth, as the enemy persuaded it.

We leave untouched the mighty heroes,
never broken in combat,

[Col. 1229B] many companies fighting for the Law,
who, protected by shields, overthrew men armed with strong weapons.

I pass over David, whose bold hand struck down
the giant who loudly condemned Israel  
[Note: [Col. 1229D] I Reg. XVII.],
and who won a thousand trophies among the Philistines.
This warrior also earned the name Psalmist;
psalms sing to him, and instruments of the holy Spirit are granted him,
that in a certain metre he might weave a song concerning Christ.

He was found a herald to whom the world answers in echo;
for the psalm-singing order makes especial use of this ten-stringed instrument,
so that the mysteries of the threefold faith,
like a lamp, may shine upon all who bear Christ’s name,
and it can frame prayers and banish the dregs of the soul.

I shall include the Maccabees among praises—but Judas especially,
who, following his father’s example, is always occupied with the Temple.

[Col. 1229C] For his fathers’ Law he gains the consolation of brothers;
with a giant sword he fights for the Hebrew ordinance.
A steadfast doorpost, whom no enemy terrifies,
he goes about sleeplessly, until every deserter falls,
having ravaged the camps of those attacking his people.

When the uncircumcised appear in force,
bearing the martial standards in a kingly hand,
he gives the signal with a harsh trumpet, though he has few soldiers.
Such thirst for battle on behalf of ancestral laws presses him on:
he drives against the sword as anger drives the lion,
and like a conspicuous fire feeds upon brushwood.
Thus raging in battle, as fire consuming torches,
tossed by sea as the sailor seeks a harbour,
he stands more renowned than Achilles for a thousand causes.

[Col. 1229D] Therefore he preferred to die rather than let the Law be robbed of honour.

Now, as though she contests it, the very famous woman Judith
wishes to be counted among the titles of blessed men.
Knowing what is hers, she demands in common song
that the right hand of valour should be the cause of salvation.
Among those whose right hand is present, she refuses to be absent from praise.
The honourable heroine, the investigation of song, will enclose you:
she will adorn our poem as purple adorns a garment,
if rich eloquence grants the service of her tongue,
so that polished praise may briefly contain much.

Greater than truth itself was the understanding of this woman,
who becomes a warrior and a prudent counsellor.
At the time when, Bethulia, you spurn Holofernes’ law,

[Col. 1230A] by a certain decree made under no happy omen,
when the people had either to submit or to die:
for above the mountains there were neither wells nor springs.

1184 Stirred by better prayers, she prudently frustrates the priest’s vow, and saves the people’s thousands.
Soon she lays aside widow’s dress; soon the diligent woman changes her appearance.
For adornment she takes whatever she considers splendid:
a tunic whose price proves anything but cheap;
as befits her sex, she confines her combed hair in a head-dress;
she takes a saffron-coloured band, an ornament for the head;
a precious jeweled necklace also encloses her breast;
she binds her arms with a linen garment,
which, when crumpled, can scarcely be gathered in the fingernails.
Silk gleams beneath, a trailing outer garment hangs down;
bracelets form glittering circles with their splendour;

[Col. 1230B] and one ring and then another gives its gift to her fingers.
Her gait sweeps its train of precious fabric;
nor do I omit the pendant hanging from her neck.
Her maidservants, witnesses, arrange these garments everywhere,
lest they be wrinkled or offensive through unevenness.
Her face is not painted with cosmetics in place of the beam of light;
for, with her unadorned face, none can be her equal.
Clever observer and guide of equal beauty,
if you had known her carried off, you could say nothing.

In character and manner of life she had not thus adorned herself
when she flourished beside the person of her destined husband;
nor did lust or shrewd thought give her this rule or this appearance,
but she wishes to employ her powers thus:
that alone she may engage the prince in single combat,
and the prince may perish, lest he renew the war thereafter,

[Col. 1230C] when desire will fix its darts in the nest of his heart.
No arrow is more certain than a woman’s ribbon.
Thus we conceal bread so that the hook may draw fish;
when you charm a bird, the pipe gives sweet sounds.

The new maiden had descended from the mountain’s tower;
through the hollow valley the woman took her path;
soon, having completed the journey, she came to the fixed tents.
The Assyrians hurry forward to ask in order who or what she is;
the nearer they come, the more and more they are astonished.
And marvelling at the ray of the maiden, as though she were a new star,
each attendant thinks: “O, if only you would have me!”
Thus she holds all husbands unheard-of [in her power].

Judith, sound in mind, encircled by the crowd of people,
speaks thus with the leader and reverences him, herself lower, at his knees.

[Col. 1230D] Best of the great, bright glory of the Assyrians,
whose glory flourishes, whom the submissive world adores,
whom wild beasts of the woods and creatures of the fields obey,
whom every beast fears, gentle among the fierce,
and every winged creature, or whatever the water gives the power to swim:
hear, if it please you, matters worthy of your praise.

This foolish people, which has not your merciful favour,
has no hope in wings or shields;
it does not trust in mountains or walls that will collapse,
nor is it secure through a deceptive rampart surrounding it.
It has another hope, for great and small alike:
its defence is to commit no crime.
If none sins, none will fall through you.

[Col. 1231A] Their Saviour is he who is lawgiver and creator.
You may spend many five-year periods fighting in vain,
trying vainly to make one who fights grow weary.
But it will come true within five days,
as he who created all created things showed me.
They are now learning sins; for they are exhausted by thirst  
[printed: *satis*; perhaps *sitis*, “thirst”].
Because of the burning thirst, they now fail to distinguish
the blood condemned by the Law, and therefore slaughter animals;
if they should perhaps drink it, they will offend and perish.
Like an ox beneath the knife, the entire people will fall of itself.
He who protects the righteous punishes those who commit crimes.
Thus they will be straw for you to thresh, as in threshing;
nor will your army suffer the slightest loss.
The handmaid’s speech, best commander, is not false.

[Col. 1231B] He who sits above the stars recently sent me to you;
I bear the message sent, and seek only what is salutary:
in this matter he wishes your handmaid to remain with you.

1185 When the barbarian hears such things, he immediately delights inwardly;
impatient of delay, he is suddenly blinded by love.
Turning the whole desire of fornication in his breast,
he becomes joyful, with a rich table spread more freely;
and he ceases not to pour Bacchus into the pit of his stomach.
More full than usual was he; Judith was serene in spirit.
Night draws the entire household, with all the soldiery, into sleep.

The woman, eminently worthy to give a pattern of virginity,
stands before the leader’s bed, his limbs breathing the sleep of two [sleep and death].
With victorious right hand striking the enemy’s throat,
she gave him, from the sleep of flesh, the sleep of death:

[Col. 1231C] the head, cut by the sword, stained the bed with blood.
Having inflicted such death, Judith returns undefiled,
and praises God, bearing a trophy from the enemy.

The ancient age once produced such athletes,
through whom enemies were uprooted and repelled,
whom praise makes eternal and glory now makes flourish.
For, illustrious in hope and desirous of the heavenly kingdom,
they regarded the world’s torment as a great talent.
Yet not even for this were they safe when freed from flesh:
because of the fathers’ offence, heavenly glory was delayed;
because of the fathers’ children, the ages lacked kingdoms;
because of the fathers’ root, the abyss swallowed the ages.
Both impious and holy uttered this lament beneath that prison,
mighty men in arms, whom it drew into the courts of death.

[Col. 1231D] There are mournings, tears, and pains there,
gnashing of teeth and everlasting stench.
There is darkness there, deserved through the father’s origin,
condemning posterity through five ages;
but the final age of time set limits to death.

Removing this burden, he gave sight of the true sun:
the Sun from the star, Christ from the maiden-mother.
Yet modesty remains whole when the Virgin’s womb gives birth,
surpassing nature’s order for the honour of the Godhead.
There is one conceived who has received seed from heaven,
at the angelic servant’s command by the word of the heavenly one;
she conceives from heaven when she receives Gabriel’s “Hail”  
[Note: [Col. 1231D] Luke I].

This is that faith which you, faithless man, falsely mock:

[Col. 1232A] that a pure woman should give birth contrary to nature.
Ask the ancient signs revered by the Synagogue:
you will be compelled to believe what you, faithless one, now reject.
For the bush burned but remained green in the honour of its foliage;
it endured the burning and did not lose its greenness.
Though the root gives nothing, the dry shoot nevertheless puts forth leaves,
adding the beauty of virginity with its supplied foliage.
The fleece is wet with rain while the dry ground is not wet;
the earth is wet with the drop while that fleece is not wet.
For a mother worthy of God, these are signs concerning the Virgin:
God here shows repeated what he once gave as unprecedented.

While virgin childbirth bears divine limbs,
it gives a flower of offspring not furrowed by any plough.
The shut gate of heaven becomes a passage before the Lord alone;
Mary’s closed womb bears the flower of purity,

[Col. 1232B] whole in giving birth, as whole in conceiving.
How richly endowed, therefore, is the Virgin’s bed!
The shepherds were taught by heaven’s heralds.
Then the new star, like a faithful little servant,
summons the Magi’s hearts there with an offering of gifts.

From this, by wondrous means, Herod’s madness rages,
and he kills two-year-olds whom their mothers nurse.
By slaughtering this flock he wishes to destroy the child-king;
but his own guardian preserves Jesus unharmed,
fleeing diligently with holy Mary his mother.
The child sucked milk flowing from his mother’s breast,
and the Creator of all drank breasts as though a sinner—
breasts full of heaven and delightful in the enclosure of modesty.
He presents the foreskin of flesh owed to the Law:

[Col. 1232C] he is purified by a turtledove, by whom the guilt of the world is washed away.
He is clothed in swaddling-clothes, nourished by food and years;
1186 and, as though learning and opening the first elements,
he hears teachers and questions elders.
At six lustrums [thirty years] of age he was skilled in the Law, written in chalk, which the world had received from him.

For our losses the Jordanian river washes him,
that it may cleanse the stain which Eve planted through the age.
The demon tempts him  
[Note: [Col. 1231D] Matt. IV.], but he himself endures as a wrestler.
Threatening impious rocks flee, becoming watery within themselves.
He hungers and sleeps, and turns sad matters beneath his breast;
he serves his disciple at the feet in the manner of one who washes.

Yet all this was remote from the Godhead;

[Col. 1232D] for he showed both natures in their fullness:
when signs were performed, the radiance of the Godhead flashed forth.
At the beginning he commands a great vessel to produce wine,
and causes wonder that wine is created without a vine  
[Note: [Col. 1231D] John II].

He restored the sight of people whom night had condemned;
to cleanse leprosy he presses it with gentle touches,
and restores the decayed vessels of bodies to their souls.
He makes limbs deprived of action firm;
he checks the flow by which the body wastes away, the flow of blood  
[printed: *semen*, “seed”; corrected to *sanguinis*, “blood”].
He gave increase of loaves among mouths eating;
he who consecrated us fed five thousand.
He calmed winds and traversed swelling waves.

[Col. 1233A] He restores tongues whose capacity had failed to speech;
deaf ears were open furrows for sounds.
He removed fever and chills—fever and burning heat.

After this, seized, he was stretched upon the cross with nails;
he climbed the palm which he made fruitful:
on its branch, with the hook of Godhead,
he pierces Leviathan’s jaws and cuts short death’s wings.
The exalted serpent confronts the lowly serpents,
a dread fighter, so that the traveller may draw them thence.
Life undergoes death; sweetness drinks vinegar;
not a man but a worm, unarmed, conquers the armed man;
the Lamb conquers the robber, the calf, by dying, the lion.
The Virgin’s Lamb washes the sheep—the world—of every crime.
The illustrious victim, Christ, becomes *starioc* upon the altar  
[Note: [Col. 1233D] A scribal error: he wrote *starioc* instead of Greek *σταυρῷ*, “of the cross.”].

[Col. 1233B] The opening of his side then gave the libation of life,
making the Father appeased and the world reconciled.
Water, flesh, blood: the pious serpent expiates the wicked one.
These three are our salvation, through which the former evil tree withers  
[Note: [Col. 1233D] Or “tree,” namely the forbidden one.]:
this is the coin of the price by which the Highest redeems earthly things,
and by which the spoil of the abyss is restored to God the Father.

The ancient exile, whom the wicked persuader ensnares, returns free to his kingdoms after his deceit has been swallowed up  
[Note: [Col. 1234D] Perhaps *techna*, “by fraud.”].
Endowed by this wood, all the blessed returned.
Crucified, he fulfils the promise by despoiling the abyss.
The closed tomb holds the bones of the precious body;
therefore on the third day, when flesh has been reclaimed from the grave,
he rises, restoring the ashes of many righteous persons.

[Col. 1233C] Afterwards he offers himself to be touched and seen;
and now, not to a prostitute, he is seen by a woman in the garden,
appearing free from death’s miseries to his disciples.
He gives words and eats; to Didymus he displays his wounds,
his palms and side, that he might be the more indubitable.

Having strengthened their minds with these proofs,
he gave them the right to loose and bind sins,
and, according to merit, to untie the woven knot.
Sending them to teach the world a second birth
and to cleanse it in the divine font under the threefold Name,
he commands them by living voice to drive away all harmful things.

When all was fulfilled, as you have in the book,
victorious with the palm, he returned to heaven’s glory.
The flesh which had hung crucified ascends to heaven;
Christ joyfully climbs back whence he had descended,

[Col. 1233D] to be both merciful and stern judge at the end.

His majesty is equal with the Father, and his power equal;
equal are honour, strength, and shared supremacy.
God is one and unconquered with the reigning Person;
the Spirit of both shines with equality of honours;
for the Godhead of Father and Son is always equal.
These three persons, in the worship of the Godhead,

[Col. 1234A] 1187 are not separated, but are rightly worshipped as one.
The inspiration of the Church teaches belief in one divinity.

Hence, foul ruler of sin, you forge diverse heresies
and a new schism by twisting sophistry.
You displayed idols and established them in the seats of shrines,
which foolish nations worshipped, bringing sacrifices.
Thus Thetis is a goddess with Neptune, Juno with Jupiter—
divinities fit for mud; likewise Proserpina and Pluto;
Apollo, unshorn at the neck, is a false god.
What shall I say of woodland Diana and Diana of the crossroads?
What of Latona fleeing the great Python?
Scylla’s dogs are not empty of divinity.
What prevents the Erythraean harlot from being a goddess?
Pan is not mortal, nor Scylla’s winged creature.

[Col. 1234B] Is it not lawful to seek Nymphs around waters?
The gods, who are in a river’s whirlpool, are often drenched:
you would better call them adulterers or prostitutes.
The first fears created those errors.
The deeds of tyrants seized the names of gods.
At kings’ nod the world sacrifices and pays tribute.

But when the order of days required it, the Maker of things,
putting an end to these matters, removed this Fury of error,
sending twice six servants—namely, apostles  
[Note: [Col. 1234D] That is, apostles.]—
to bring lamps to human minds, which empty night had condemned.
Refined from heaven and taught by the sacred Spirit,
1188 they go to plough the carnal fallow fields with the word.

Peter soon spread the fragrance of faith in Rome,

[Col. 1234C] driving the sacrilegious rite from the City of Romulus.
At his words fierce men bow their necks.
The queen city rejoices to submit her lofty neck,
mistress of so many kingdoms, to an old man’s reins—
she whom the crafty African rival had not conquered in war,
nor the Punic enemy filled with Roman blood,
nor all Carthage, once a great abyss to herself,
which boldly compelled the kings of earth to bear her tribute
while it subdued the world’s regions:
she is conquered by Peter and casts her idols behind her.

Cephas, supreme head over head, destroys every impiety.
Flaming altars cease to devour entrails;
the dry idol-sacrifice no longer belches according to ritual;
nor does the fat of goat entrails trouble the fates;
men do not seek things to come from the underworld by ox or pig;
