[Col. 1234D] the augur does not consult Fortune’s lot by means of a paunch.
Nor does the diviner obtain oracles from a winged bird.
Rome does not sing the Salii’s song, given by Numa,
nor of the Ancile, since the tale is now base to her.
The applause of the theatre is now shut down through disuse;
she disdains to watch the games of the gymnasium  
[printed: *ludos*; perhaps *nudos*, “naked” games].
No one wishes to be anointed for wrestling with rich oil.

[ON THE ORNAMENT OF THE WORLD. THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT, BISHOP OF LE MANS.]

[Col. 1235]

NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK.

How greatly Hildebert excelled in poetic art is clear even from this poem alone. For although in it he has at times transgressed the rules of metre somewhat freely, this very slight defect is more than compensated by the nobility of its ideas, its play upon words, and those pleasures of expression permitted to poets; yet, in his usual manner, by these he strives to raise his readers’ minds from earthly to heavenly things. We drew this work from the Colbert manuscript no. 3019, where it was said to have been copied under Hildebert’s name from manuscript codex no. 4 of the monastery of Brenne, in the diocese of Soissons, of the Premonstratensian Order.

[Col. 1235]

ON THE ORNAMENT OF THE WORLD. It depicts the world’s adornment, shows that it will perish, and accordingly invites the reader to the unfading delights of heaven. (G)*

[Col. 1235A] Raise your polished style, Clio, to the breeze of speech;
sprinkle my mouth with the shower of your nectar.

I imitate the bee, whose skill does not allow her wax
to remain barren of honey.
Unless you give honey, my wax thirsts for a honeycomb;
therefore let dew drip upon me from your honey-flowing mouth.

There is a grove of which I speak, a grove daring to touch the clouds;
this place, O Paradise, rivals yours.
Here Nature has tested what her art could do
and, with all the honour she could, painted the place.
For a certain glory of things has dripped into these regions,
but wealth’s abundance flowed as though with a cloud.

Nard breathes there, spices grow, nectar
is prepared, balsams sweat, honey flows.

[Col. 1235B] The bramble bears apples; the laurel berries; the wild olive, olives;
the thorn produces roses; cattle milk; the grape, wine.
Every tree there receives a double honour:
the branches bear offspring, the shade clothes the ground.
The multitude of branches delights in both fruit and shade;
hunger is driven away there, and heat removed.

Here you may see the elm, which the vine does not allow to remain chaste,
but solicits its assistance toward fruit.
In a kind of marriage vine and elm wed each other:
the vine indeed conceives wine; the elm nourishes it.

Cedar, palm, and cypress rise, bloom, and breathe fragrance there:
the cedar stands, the palm blooms, the cypress smells sweet.
Apple, olive, and pear-tree are red here, green there, swelling elsewhere—
the first with apples, the second with leaves, the third with pears.

[Col. 1235C] Not to mention the common multitude of trees,
the remaining trees nevertheless exceed number.
The wood is proud of honey or grape, incense or herb:
honey flows, grapes drip, incense smells, grass is green.
Taste commends these two, vigour the other two;
1189 the guest enjoys the former, the latter prevail against fevers.
One flavour or another drives thirst from the mouth;
one strength or another takes fever from the body.

The backs of rocks swell where, wounded by small clefts,
they have in the midst of the cleft something like a whirlpool.
A little spring, bursting out, murmurs at the opening;

[Col. 1236A] there you may see the water of the spring play like a torrent.
The last portion of the rock feigns the shape of a beak
and, a host, receives waters flowing from the rock.
Nature bored two openings in this beak,
so that each may blow out the water of the sea.

O how playful the spring, how sweet its playfulness!
Here water plays, here babbles, and there leaps.
Sweet in scent, flowing in moisture, dark in colour,
cassia, myrrh, and pepper are fragrant on the bank.
The voices of birds, the sweetness of spices, the purple of flowers
sing pleasantly, entice the nostrils, and adorn the ground.
Zephyr blows there, not Eurus; spices sweat,
not ice; there it is spring—winter does not rule there.
Nard, flower, and bird breathe, smile, and sing:
hence comes scent, hence beauty, thence melody.

[Col. 1236B] For nard burns with fragrance, the rose blooms, the bird sings:
the first pleases the nostrils, the second the eyes, the third the ears.
The stream invites, the swan delights, the peacock casts shade:
the bank [invites] to sleep, the waters with murmur, the peacock with its wheel.
The stream babbles, the swan plays the lyre, the peacock displays pride:
the stream with murmur, the swan with throat, the peacock with wheel.

The playful kid, wandering bird, and joyous fish among grass
leap on the wet ground [printed: *in nudo*; corrected to *in udo*], sing, and swim in the stream.
The stag frolics, the lion rejoices, the doe plays:
the stag with antlers, the lion with strength, the doe with foot.
Here the calf runs about, the fawn leaps, the ox lies down here.
The hare plays, seeks vegetables, goes and returns.
Here the one fears no burden, this one no snares, that one no fall;
this one fears no traps, that one no dog.

[Col. 1236C] Amid so many splendid jewels of things,
a meadow, your mirror, rises here—a playful woodland.
From so many delights, from so many distinctions,
this place claims for itself a great bundle of praise.

This ground blooms, abounds, and smells sweet with some Arguses,
many Narcissuses, and countless Orpheuses.
There Argus is star-bearing, Narcissus flower-bearing, Orpheus lyre-bearing;
the first gleams, the second adorns, the third sings.
The peacock bears Argus, the flower Narcissus, the swan Orpheus;
the beauty of eyes adorns the former, its own lyre the latter.
The peacock’s tail sparkles with stars in its beauty;

[Col. 1237A] the flower bears [its beauty] in leaf, the swan the lyre in its mouth.

Despising the lowly crowd with royal head,
the cedar there dares to hide its top among the stars.
Among the rest it receives the title of honour;
it does not deign that anything at all be its equal.
No arrows conspire there to harm the cedar,
nor rain, the numbness of cold, or the wrath of the south wind.
A new fuller, with green tunic or verdant foliage,
has clothed it against the force of winter.

Dense and shining, the branch is green with bark and foliage;
dense in branches, shining in bark and foliage, it is green.
The branch beneath its leaves shelters birds, the trunk beneath its bark nourishes bees, and the root beneath the ground gives water.
The branch shelters birds under its canopy; the trunk beneath bark
nourishes bees; the root beneath the ground sweats water.

[Col. 1237B] As though certain playful things sport with the trunk’s fissures:
the trunk gapes; a crowd of bees frequents the cleft.
A double knot there puts forth two breasts;
honey-flowing nectar drips from each breast without.
Nature forms a lathe-turned cup with fingers around both knots,
and prepares it to drink the honey.
The stream that babbles beneath the cedar’s foot waits
until the amphora overflows with honey for it.

The full vessel pours honey into the water, and together
these two, mingled, make something like electrum.
The honeyed liquid draws one by drinking; the nectar by murmur:
the drink tastes sweet in the mouth; the murmur is melody in the mouth.
Then, as though joined dances played in the valley,
a lovely pageant sports when the rose paints the ground.

[Col. 1237C] Here winter takes precedence and departs; here spring assumes precedence and arrives;
the others conclude; therefore the chorus answers.
The playful nightingale, the weeping swan, the gentle *ormella*, and light lark
perform celebrated praises.
Their names play upon the birds themselves:
their voice will taste like honey to you, if you note the words well.

You sound this, Philomela: that you are the lovely daughter of light;
the swan shows by its name that it bears a lyre in its mouth.
Because it sings melody with its mouth, it is called *ormella*;
the lark can prove that it is a bird worthy of praise.
O playful troop of birds! O delightful spectacle!
O sweet measures! O paradise of God!

A wall, embracing every part between its two arms,

[Col. 1237D] gathers the whole grove, resembling a belt.
A river unfastens this belt at the entrance,
releasing the arms joined by its knot.
A bridge woven over with timber and marble repairs
the breach in the rampart, becoming its clasp.
Each end of the bridge was a rampart on one side and the other,
although it knots the work with its joined stream.

A gate stands in the middle with lofty summit;
its top escapes from our eyes toward the stars.

[Col. 1238A] If anyone wishes to know the gate’s fabric, Mulciber
wove that work of pine and cedar.
If anyone investigates what beauty gilds it,
these four things variegate it with their drops:
the milky beauty of silver, the fiery blaze of gold,
the flaming light of gems, and ivory of elephant.

A ray of silver distinguishes the posts there;
through the places a golden flame sparkles and glides.
Each threshold shines with the light of gems; ivory whitens
the openings which the sculptor has carved there.
Look upon each thing: silver gleams, gold flashes,
gems sparkle, noble ivory smiles.
Mulciber sweated over the whole work;
the nobility of craftsmanship shone there in highest praise.
Lest Vulcan perhaps fail in anything, the entire

[Col. 1238B] legion of Cyclopes came to that work.
A certain majesty of gold clothes the timber
and enriches *nedem* (sic), an uncertain reading, with its honour.
There an arch gleams with twice six gem-stars,
and circles the doors like the zodiacal sphere.
As far as art can counterfeit, a bird flies in gold,
fish swim, stars gleam, a human being lives.
At the gate saffron shines; the pyrope’s flame burns:
the one makes flowers purple; the other makes the work bright.

Disdaining to yield to Iris’s starry beams, that colour strives to imitate the sky.

This heavenly rainbow (if I may speak without offence to its title) is brighter than that one and has more brilliance.

That one can gleam through Phoebus’ aid and the gift of a cloud;

[Col. 1238C] this one gleams without sun and without the cloud’s aid.

That one indeed deceives the eyes; this one delights them. That one shines for a time; this one endures long.

This, unless I am mistaken, is royal Nature, flourishing with so many titles, so full of riches, so abundant in goods.

Here [perhaps: in these things] I devote myself; I am wholly in these things. Beauty delights the eyes, song the ears, fragrance the nostrils, flavour the mouth.

If you ask what the description you are reading accomplishes, our writing will portray this briefly for you.

Although this grove, like a kind of rose of the world, flourishes throughout the whole earth, yet this beauty will pass away.

And because the flower of the world swiftly passes and withers, run, I pray, to that rose which never fades.

There is a rose which says, “I am the flower of the field”; certainly a golden rose,

[Col. 1238D] knowing no beginning and having no end.

That holy rose, remaining what it was, was made a vegetable for us, so that weak humanity might taste the vegetable.

It blossomed in heaven and withered in the world: there always fragrant, here made somewhat pale.

Paradise possesses this flower; the seraphim behold it; the world cannot contain it; hell does not know it; humanity worships it.

[Col. 1239]

**1191–92. THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT’S POEM ON THE BOOKS OF KINGS.**

(From a manuscript at least five hundred years old, from the monastery of St. Marianus at Auxerre, of the Premonstratensian Order.)

**ON THE FIRST BOOK.**

[Col. 1239A]

Elkanah of Ramathaim, husband of Peninnah and Hannah, had come to Shiloh to perform sacred rites for God.  
[Note: [Col. 1239C] 1 Kings.]

Peninnah receives portions of the feast, and so do her children; Hannah, though barren, receives one portion of food.

Hannah is thought drunk by the priest Eli, while she is silent in the temple and, weeping, moves her lips.

Because sorrowful Hannah did not change her countenance, she deserved soon afterward to conceive.

Hannah asks for a son, and God gives her Samuel, who as a boy becomes Eli’s pupil at Shiloh.

Those begotten by Eli are called Phinehas and Hophni; with them he himself perishes, because he restrained them too little.

They eat the fat which the Law ordered to be burned, and they sleep with prostitutes before the house of the Lord.

[Col. 1239B] While Samuel sleeps, he is called three times by the Lord; Samuel promptly comes to Eli three times, thinking that Eli is calling him.

“I do not call,” said Eli. “Thereafter, when someone calls you, do not come to me, but say, ‘Speak, Lord; I hear.’”

The Lord comes and instructs Samuel, called a fourth time, concerning the evil which He Himself foresees for Eli.

The enemies attack; Israel brings the ark forward to meet them and believes itself destined to conquer through it.

Israel flees; Phinehas and Hophni are killed; and by Philistine force the ark of God is taken.

It is reported at Shiloh that the ark is being carried off by the enemies, and Eli, falling backward from his seat, dies.

The enemy sets the ark beside Dagon at Ashdod; in the morning Dagon lies as though worshipping it.

[Col. 1239C] Dagon is set upright; at dawn he lies a mutilated trunk, his head and hands cut off upon the threshold.

All the people of Ashdod suffer from putrefying hemorrhoids, and sudden mice ravage their crops.

The ark is sent from Ekron to Gaza, from Gath to Ashkelon, and likewise the foul tumor comes forth among them.

Golden offerings—mice and hemorrhoids—are sent to God, and the ark of God is placed upon a cart.

Each untrained cow lows though her calf remains behind; yoked together, they carry the ark to Beth-shemesh without a driver.

Samuel has sons, Joel and also Abijah, whom the people accuse of selling judgments.

The people ask Samuel to give them a king; the Lord disapproves, though He commands that it be done.

Saul seeks in Zuph the lost she-asses of his father Kish;

[Col. 1240A] Samuel gives him the kingdom and anoints him.

Nahash refuses to grant the men of Jabesh-gilead any treaty of peace unless he deprives them of their right eyes.

When Saul hears this, coming from the field with oxen and pitying Jabesh, he slaughters both oxen.

Sending out pieces of the oxen, Saul summons the companies: “Thus,” he says, “will I do to the oxen of anyone who does not come.”

Saul leads the forces of Israel and Judah to Bezek; Nahash is slain, and the king wins the people’s approval.

The sun shines, and Samuel by prayer brings thunder and rain; the people acknowledge that they sinned in asking for a king.

Leading innumerable bands across Israel’s fields, the Philistine stations his camp at Michmash.

King Saul and his son Jonathan possess a sword, but the people have neither spear nor sword.

[Col. 1240B] In the space which a pair of oxen plough in one day, Jonathan lays low twenty Philistines.

Because one armour-bearer kills those whom Jonathan strikes down, the people proclaim this the work of the Lord.

While Saul pursues the Philistines, he forbids anyone to take food, laying a curse upon the people.

Hungry Jonathan eats honey taken from a tree; by pleading, the people prevent Saul from killing him.

Samuel imposes a task upon Saul, to be carried out promptly: by destroying Amalek, he is to wipe out everything belonging to it.

From Amalek perish the things deemed worthless; the fat livestock remains, and likewise fat King Agag.

[Col. 1240C] **1193.** “God prefers obedience to every burnt offering”: declaring this, Samuel yields Agag to the sword.

When Samuel seeks the house of Jesse of Bethlehem, he takes a calf there, so that he may feign a sacrifice.

Jesse has a son, a shepherd named David; Samuel anoints him king of Israel.

King Saul offers a burnt offering in priestly fashion; and, wishing to appease [perhaps: please], he thereby provokes God.

A sling casts a stone; Goliath falls, struck in the forehead. And you, David, cut his throat with his own sword.

A thousand are ascribed to Saul, but ten thousands to David. The woman’s song displeases Saul.

The song is potent in effect, because when David plays the lyre, the spirit that torments Saul departs.

[Col. 1241A] King Saul wishes to pin David, who stands before him, with a spear; but it falls in vain while David leaps away.

When Saul asks David for a hundred foreskins, David, killing enemies, doubles this number for Michal.

To bring David out in the morning to be killed by Saul, guards keep watch within and before the house.

Michal, covering a statue with a skin, says that David is present; through the window she causes him to flee.

Ahimelech prepares bread and a sword for David; when Doeg reports it, the king kills Ahimelech.

When fleeing David, foaming, strikes the gateposts, Achish does not kill him, for he thinks him mad.

While Saul relieves himself in a cave, David, hidden there, cuts short his cloak.

When Nabal had denied provisions to David’s men,

[Col. 1241B] Abigail, who was Nabal’s wife, does not know it.

As David comes angrily to kill Nabal, Abigail, carrying gifts, appeases him.

When Nabal hears that his wife has given gifts, he is stricken with grief because his own possessions have been lost.

Samuel dies, while the multitude of peoples weeps; he is buried with his fathers at Ramah.

When Saul sleeps, David carries away the cup and spear: he could have killed him, but grants him mercy.

Achish was king of Gath; to David fleeing there he assigned Ziklag, where he might rest.

Achish wishes to lead David into battle against Saul, but the nobles refuse and make him return.

Enemies arrive and enter the land of Israel; King Saul and all his people are terrified.

[Col. 1241C] King Saul seeks the dwelling of an oracle-woman and asks her to raise up a dead man for him.

“Woman, you compel the dead Samuel to rise”; and Samuel says: “Tomorrow, Saul, you will be with me.”

Gilboa ought not to be watered by rain or dew, for Saul and Jonathan are killed there.

Bands of Amalekites burn captured Ziklag with its contents and return with David’s two wives.

When hastening David defeats the bands of Amalek, he joyfully comes to his own wives, both of them.

Alas, grief! The wall at Beth-shan has the suspended bodies of Saul and Jonathan, mutilated and headless.

The band of Jabesh proceeds to Beth-shan by night; reaching the wall, it carries away Saul and Jonathan.

**ON THE SECOND BOOK.**

[Col. 1241D]

Because the Amalekite claims that he himself killed Saul, David immediately kills him at Ziklag.

David is anointed king by Judah at Hebron, and Joab, commander of the horsemen, is under his authority.

Israel anoints Saul’s son Ish-bosheth as king, and renowned Abner leads his troops.

Joab, Abner, and the two forces come to Gibeon and sit on opposite sides near the pool.

When twice twelve young men, commanded to play, engage in their contest, they kill one another by reciprocal wounds in the side.

**1194.** The armies clash and a most grievous slaughter occurs on both sides;

[Col. 1242A] Abner flees, along with his companions.

Asahel is swift in running, the equal of gazelles; pursuing Abner, he runs and presses him.

Abner says: “Asahel, I do not wish you to strike down the fleeing young men for their spoils, for you are Joab’s brother.”

Impatient Asahel presses Abner; but Abner, striking his pursuer in the groin, casts him down dead.

Abner sleeps with Rizpah, Saul’s concubine; Ish-bosheth reproaches him for it. Threateningly, Abner therefore deserts him.

Saul had first united David with Michal as wife; later, taking her from him, he gave her to Phaltiel.

As Phaltiel leads away Michal, whom he has lost, Abner restores her to David at Hebron as a token of peace.

David and Abner dine; Abner departs in peace; then Joab deceitfully recalls and kills him.

[Col. 1242B] Ish-bosheth sleeps, and his doors are not secure; secretly Rechab and Baanah kill him with swords.

David, receiving Ish-bosheth’s head from Rechab and Baanah, kills both men, who thought they were bringing rewards.

David, anointed king of all Israel by every tribe, as an outstanding warrior crushes the Philistines.

Capturing Jerusalem, he drives out the Jebusites and establishes it as the head of his kingdom.

The enemy comes through the Valley of Rephaim and devastates everything; at Baal-perazim David defeats him.

Instructed by the Lord, David does not confront the enemy: he circles round and destroys him from the rear.

The ark, which had long ago come from Kiriath-jearim, is with Amminadab, who lives in Gibeah.

David commands the ark to be put upon a cart and drawn by yoked oxen;

[Col. 1242C] and they begin to convey it.

When the sons of Amminadab drive the cart, Uzzah follows the ark and Ahio drives before it.

The ark of God is carried; the king and all Israel play; drums and sistra sound, and lyres with citharas.

The ark of God seems about to slip when an ox kicks; Uzzah grasps it with his hand and immediately falls dead.

David fears thereafter to take the ark with him, and the Gittite Obed-edom keeps it.

God, increasing his wealth, blesses Obed-edom, in whose house the ark remained three months.

David comes playing the lyre to Obed-edom’s dwelling, and from there returns to Jerusalem carrying the ark.

When Michal sees David leaping before God,

[Col. 1242D] she despises him; therefore she bears no offspring.

While David dwells in Hebron, Ahinoam of Jezreel first bears him Amnon.

David has a son, the boy Absalom, who is more beautiful than the handsome young men of Israel and Judah.

Tamar, Absalom’s full sister, is exceedingly beautiful, born to the king by Maacah, daughter of Talmai.

David had intimated to Nathan that he would build a temple; Nathan, returning in the morning, forbids him to build it.

Machir is from Lo-debar, and Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s lame son, lives in his house.

Brought from Lo-debar and receiving his father’s possessions, Mephibosheth eats with David’s sons.

King David was bound in peace with Nahash of Ammon;

[Col. 1243A] he dies, and his son Hanun reigns.

David sends servants to Hanun to offer consolation; the enraged king says that they have come to spy upon him.

At once every garment is cut by Hanun up to the buttocks, and the beards of the envoys are shaved halfway.

The famous city of King Hanun was named Rabbah; Joab hastens to ravage it.

To defend Hanun, four kings come with their peoples: King Rehob, King of Ish-tob, King of Zobah, and King Maacah.

Before the gates of Rabbah, Joab and Abishai fight, and the native peoples flee when their kings are defeated.

While Uriah remains at the siege near Rabbah,

**1195.** his wife Bathsheba is in Jerusalem.

David compels Bathsheba to sleep with him; she soon returns home, but pregnant.

[Col. 1243B] Uriah brings Joab’s news of the war to the king; the king orders him to go home and gives him a feast.

Uriah wishes to lie down only with the servants; neither his home nor lovely Bathsheba attracts him.

The king asks Uriah why he did not rest with his wife after his return; the stern man replies:

“Far be it that any pleasure should charm Uriah while Joab bears the harsh burden of war.”

The king says to Uriah: “You shall dine with me late; tomorrow I shall give you little letters to show Joab.”

As David’s finger marks the words of the letter, Uriah’s hand carries the tokens of his own death.

Uriah is slain where he fights thick among the enemy, when Joab gives the signal for his companions to retreat.

Since Joab does not wish to take for himself the victory from Rabbah,

[Col. 1243C] he has David come, who quickly takes it.

David kills Hanun, takes his diadem, and returns to Jerusalem carrying much plunder.

To feed the sick man, his sister Tamar enters Amnon; while she prepares food, she is compelled to have intercourse with him.

Absalom has brought Amnon to dine at Baal-hazor, and has him killed while Amnon believes he is being refreshed.

Absalom lives as an exile in Geshur for three years; King Talmai, his grandfather, is powerful there.

Joab prompts a woman of Tekoa, who approaches David with these words:

“One son was ploughing, and this son killed him. They wish to stone him; thus none will remain for me.”

King David says to the woman of Tekoa: “This son shall live,

[Col. 1243D] and I shall not allow grief to befall you twice.”

“The dead man was Amnon,” says the woman of Tekoa to the king; “if you destroy Absalom, you cannot restore him.”

David, admonished by the prudent speech of the woman of Tekoa, soon causes Absalom to return from Geshur.

Absalom remains sorrowful in Jerusalem for two years, unable ever to come before his father’s face.

Absalom sends messengers and entreats Joab to come and grant him an interview.

Angered, Absalom burns Joab’s fields with fire; Joab, who had formerly refused to go, then visits him.

By Joab’s intervention the king gives Absalom kisses and commands him to appear before him as often as he wishes.

Absalom is at Hebron, accompanied by many soldiers; there he is made king by Ahithophel and by the people.

[Col. 1244A] David leaves Jerusalem barefoot and weeping, but Hushai, David’s friend, remains there.

Ahithophel wishes to go with twelve thousand men and swiftly strike down David in flight.

Servants hasten after Ahimaaz and Jonathan and seek to capture them at Bahurim.

A woman spreads groats over the mouth of the well, as though she were drying them; Jonathan and Ahimaaz hide in the well.

Jonathan and Ahimaaz leap from the well at Bahurim and warn David to flee farther away.

Because credulous Absalom acts on Hushai’s advice, Ahithophel deservedly kills himself with a noose.

On the hill at Bahurim, Shimei reproaches fleeing King David and throws stones at him.

David entrusts the forces to three commanders,

[Col. 1244B] and instructs them to spare Absalom in Gilead.

Ittai, Joab, and Abishai attack Absalom, and a great slaughter of the people occurs in the forest.

Absalom rides on a mule; his head catches in a branch, his mule goes on, and he remains hanging.

Joab’s threefold spear is thrust into Absalom’s heart; he still struggles, and ten armour-bearers kill him.

Sheba prepares war against David’s rule in Israel; but Judah restores David to the kingdom.

**1196.** David, intending that Amasa command the great host, wishes Amasa to be leader in place of Joab.

While you feign kisses for Amasa, Joab, your right hand holds his chin and your left gives the sword to his side.

As Joab attacks Abel in order to capture Sheba,

[Col. 1244C] a woman of wise counsel persuades him.

The wise woman of Abel throws out Sheba’s head, which Joab receives from the wall and then withdraws.

There is famine for three years in David’s time because Saul had killed the people of Gibeah.

Seven young men of Saul’s line are crucified by the Gibeonites, and thus God’s wrath departs.

While Armoni and Mephibosheth hang on crosses, their mother Rizpah guards their bodies night and day.

By day Rizpah drives away the birds, and by night the wild beasts; the king orders it, and then buries Rizpah’s sons.

Jishbi-benob, fighting, wishes to kill exhausted David; immediately Abishai kills Jishbi-benob.

The Philistine places a camp near the gate of Bethlehem, whence David, thirsty, wishes water brought to him.

[Col. 1244D] Bethlehem’s gate is reached through the midst of the enemies by three brave men, and water is drawn and brought.

“Far be it that I should relieve my thirst with your blood,” says the king; pouring it out, he offers the water to the Lord.

David numbers the peoples of Israel and Judah, and Gad, God’s prophet, suitably says:

“Three days of plague; or seven years of famine; or three months of flight must be endured by you.”

“I prefer,” David replies, “that the Lord’s right hand strike me rather than that an enemy hand make me a fugitive.”

Three days pass, during which the angelic hand gives seventy thousand of the people to death.

Near Jerusalem was the threshing floor where David sees the angel who is killing the people.

[Col. 1245A] The threshing floor, oxen, cart, and yokes belong to Araunah, and Araunah wishes to give these freely to the king.

The threshing floor is delivered to the king at a price, together with the oxen, which the king there burns; and the people are saved.

**ON THE THIRD BOOK.**

David is cold because sluggish old age has overcome him; he cannot be warmed by any clothing.

The beautiful virgin Abishag the Shunammite lies with the aged king, feeds him, and warms him.

The people, Joab, and Abiathar make Adonijah king; when David learns it, he forbids this to happen.

He orders Solomon to be established as king in his place. Solomon is led to Gihon and made king there.

[Col. 1245B] While terrified Adonijah holds the horn of the altar, Solomon commands him: “Behave rightly; do not fear.”

At the end, David commands Solomon to give Joab and Shimei to the sword.

David dies; Judah and Israel mourn him; King Solomon buries him in his own city.

Because you ask Solomon to take Abishag the Shunammite as wife, Adonijah, you immediately perish.

When ordered to leave the altar, Joab refuses; Benaiah kills him there by the king’s command.

The king forbids Shimei to leave Jerusalem; Shimei goes to Gath, and the king orders him killed.

At Gibeon God appears to Solomon in a dream: “Ask, and whatever you ask I shall give you,” He says.

When Solomon asks that wisdom be given to him,

[Col. 1245C] he is given this, riches also, and the highest glory.

“While you sleep, woman, another woman steals your living child and secretly brings you her own dead child.”

Two women claim the child; Solomon orders it killed and adjudges half to each.

One urges this to be done; the other forbids it. “She,” says the king, “who forbade it is the child’s mother.”

**1197.** Solomon made the house of the Lord such that no work like it could be made.

The Lord’s house is built of stone material, and no sound of iron is heard there.

It was forty cubits broad and thirty cubits high; the structure of the house was sixty cubits long.

Firwood covers the floor; cedar covers the interior wall,

[Col. 1245D] and the ceiling is made of cedarwork.

No one sees the wood; rather, pure gold is visible, with which the ceiling, wall, and entire floor are overlaid.

Each of the two cherubim is ten cubits high and spreads two wings, each ten cubits in extent.

The two cherubim within are made of olive wood and are outwardly golden in all their parts.

The wing of each cherub touches the wall so that their wings meet each other in the middle of the temple.

So great is the sacrifice offered to the Lord when Solomon dedicates the altar, that I cannot count it.

Solomon offers twenty-two thousand oxen and one hundred and twenty thousand sheep.

No fewer than a hundred rams are for your table, Solomon, with thirty oxen each day as well.

[Col. 1246A] No one can count the birds, fish, stags, roe deer, or other wild animals which Solomon eats.

Every day King Solomon feeds twelve thousand quadrupeds suitable for his soldiers.

Solomon has forty thousand quadrupeds, which he continually feeds, fit for his chariots.

Those to whom Solomon supplies weapons, clothing, and food are twelve thousand horsemen each day.

Woman conquers everything, because she conquers you, Wisdom, when Solomon, overcome by love, worships gods.

Solomon himself worships the Sidonian Astarte, Chemosh of Moab, and Moloch of Ammon, the gods of his wife.

When Ahijah made twelve pieces from a cloak, he ordered Jeroboam to take ten of them.

[Col. 1246B] King Solomon dies; his son, called Rehoboam, buries him and bears his diadem.

Israel goes with Jeroboam and asks Rehoboam himself to lighten the yoke which Solomon imposed.

The advice of the elders, sought by Rehoboam, urges him to please the people and lighten the harsh yokes.

The young men advise that the yoke should not be lightened, and Rehoboam trusts the young men’s counsels.

“My father,” Rehoboam declares, “struck you with whips; but for me, in place of whips, there will be many scorpions.”

Only the tribe of Judah serves King Rehoboam; ten tribes follow King Jeroboam.

Rehoboam sends Adoram to exact tribute, but all Israel stones him when he arrives.

[Col. 1246C] One hundred and eighty thousand men hasten with Rehoboam to destroy Jeroboam.

There was a prophet named Shemaiah; seeing so great a host depart, he speaks to them thus:

The integrity of the kingdom belonged to Solomon for David’s sake, but Rehoboam receives an honour less than Solomon’s.

Let Judah return; let Israel not be destroyed, but let Jeroboam sit upon his own throne.

As soon as Judah hears this, it returns and rests; yet afterward Jeroboam becomes wicked.

Many of Israel’s people come to the Lord’s temple which gleams with gold at Jerusalem.

Jeroboam fears that he will be deprived of his kingdom if his people gather to Rehoboam.

He makes calves, works of wondrous art, and commands the peoples to go

[Col. 1246D] to worship the calves.

A golden calf is at Bethel and its counterpart at Dan: this work and these gods are yours, Jeroboam.

A feast day is celebrated, on which Jeroboam compels a great multitude to go with him to Bethel.

**1198.** King Jeroboam burns incense to the calf upon the altar. Behold, a man from Judah cries out against it:

“A man named Josiah will arise from David’s house, who will kill priests upon this altar.

“This shall be the sign: the altar will immediately split apart, and the ash upon it will fall to the ground.”

The king then raises his hand and quickly orders him seized; immediately his hand becomes withered and cannot be drawn back.

The altar quickly splits, as that man had said,

[Col. 1247A] and the people see the ash fall.

Jeroboam asks the man to seek help for him; he seeks the Lord and restores the hand.

Then the man from Judah goes on, and a certain prophet follows him and asks him to eat with him on his return.

The man of God says: “When the Lord commanded me to go to Bethel, He forbade me to eat at Bethel.”

That prophet replies: “Behold, an angel spoke, and through him I have been instructed to give you food.”

The man returns and eats; but while they sit, the man who deceived him cries out prophetically to him:

“You did not obey, and now you cannot be buried with your own fathers: thus speaks the Lord.”

The man rides upon an ass; a lion soon kills him, eating nothing and not killing the ass.

[Col. 1247B] The corpse is seen thrown in the middle of the road; the ass stands there, and the lion likewise stands.

When he learns this, the prophet seeks the slain man and, weeping, carries him to his own tomb at Bethel.

Jeroboam’s son, called Abijah, lies sick, and both parents mourn without rest.

The king orders his wife to go and consult Ahijah, whether their son Abijah will soon meet death.

Old age has made Ahijah see nothing with his eyes; he remains at Shiloh, seeing the truth in his mind.

The queen comes to him disguised as another woman, but he says: “Wife of Jeroboam, enter.”

Jeroboam sins, worshipping the calves which he made; and I have been sent to bring you harsh news.

The sick Abijah, whom Jeroboam begot,

[Col. 1247C] will be dead when you come home.

From now on no member of Jeroboam’s family will be buried; only your Abijah will be given burial.

If any of Jeroboam’s family dies in the fields, birds will eat him; if anyone dies in the city, dogs will eat him.

When the queen came and entered her home at Tirzah, her son Abijah immediately gave up his life.

For three years the tribe of Judah keeps God’s law and Rehoboam’s; no enemy prevails against them meanwhile.

Shishak, king of Egypt, plunders Jerusalem when Rehoboam and Judah desert God.

Yet afterward Rehoboam and Judah entreat God, and God makes Shishak withdraw.

Rehoboam dies; buried with Solomon,

[Col. 1247D] his son Abijah assumes the rule.

Jeroboam comes, invades Abijah’s lands, and strives wholly to crush Judah.

When King Abijah cries to the Lord and fights, Jeroboam barely escapes back to his own territory.

Jeroboam dies; his son Nadab is raised by the people of Israel to wield the sceptre.

The city of Gibbethon is inhabited by Philistines; while Nadab besieges it, Baasha kills him.

The troops flee and birds tear Nadab apart, and Baasha is established king at Tirzah.

By Baasha’s sword all Jeroboam’s line perishes; Ahijah, your prophecy is known to have proved true.

After Abijah is buried by Judah’s people, his son Asa becomes sceptre-bearing king.

[Col. 1248A] There is continual war between Asa and Baasha. Asa’s God is the true God; Baasha’s is a calf.

The prophet Jehu often foretells evils for Baasha; afterward Baasha is delivered to death by a blow.

**1199.** In order to harm Asa and dominate the regions of Judah, Baasha determines to build Ramah.

King Asa, giving gifts, asks aid from Ben-hadad, the sceptre-bearing king wearing the Syrian diadem.

With Ben-hadad’s aid many evils befall Baasha; thus Ramah is not built by him.

After Baasha is buried, Israel makes Elah king, who resembles his father Baasha in character.

Omri, commander of the army, besieges Gibbethon; Elah ordered his bands to remain there.

While Elah, king of Israel, drinks drunkenly in Tirzah,

[Col. 1248B] his servant Zimri delivers him to death by the sword.

Zimri obtains Tirzah and becomes king of Israel; by his sword the entire house of Baasha falls.

Omri, made king of Israel, attacks Tirzah in order to punish the servant who rules there.

Israel arrives and surrounds Tirzah’s walls, wishing with all its strength to destroy them.

When Zimri sees that he will be captured by Omri, he enters the palace and burns himself and it.

Shemer was the nobleman who sold the hill to Omri; there the king built the new walls of Samaria.

Omri dies; when he is buried at Samaria, his son Ahab is placed on the throne.

King Ahab takes the wicked Jezebel as wife and follows Baal, whom his wife worships.

[Col. 1248C] The Sidonian king is called Mechbaal; he is Jezebel’s father and follows Baal.

Elijah declares that unless he himself commands it, neither dew nor rain will come to the people.

Near the Jordan is a stream called Cherith; Elijah sits there and drinks from it.

By God’s gift, ravens provide bread and meat; thus they restore Elijah twice each day.

When it is too long without rain, the stream diminishes and dries up; then Father Elijah seeks other water.

There is a Sidonian place which the ancients called Zarephath; Elijah comes there, and a widow receives him.

The widow’s vessel is seen to contain a small amount of flour; only a little vessel of oil remains to her.

[Col. 1248D] The oil is not diminished, nor is the flour reduced; yet Elijah and the widow make use of them.

The widow’s son dies; Elijah lies upon him and, after prayers are poured forth, restores the boy to life.

Three years and six months pass, and no rain is seen anywhere in all the lands.

King Ahab seeks Elijah but does not find him; Obadiah finds him and reports this to him:

“King Ahab commands that you be sought through various regions and wishes to have speech with you.”

Elijah immediately orders Obadiah to go. He calls the king, and the king comes in haste.

Near Jezreel is a mountain named Carmel; Elijah, King Ahab, and the people go there.

Behold, four hundred and fifty prophets

[Col. 1249A] are there, who declare themselves worshippers of Baal.

Elijah sees so many priests of idols and does not hesitate to lay down this proposal for them:

“Let there be one altar of Baal, and let one ox be set upon it; let there be an altar of the Lord, and an ox set upon it.

“Wood having been placed, let no fire be applied beneath. Thus let Baal and my God prove themselves by fire.

“Let the priests cry out: if Baal is God, let him send fire and consume his ox with fire.

“If the Lord is God, I shall cry out to Him, and the Lord shall consume His ox with fire.”

Then an ox is placed upon each of the two altars, and sufficient wood is supplied, but no fire is there.

The priests cry out and cut their bodies with knives; Baal neither hears them nor gives them fire.

[Col. 1249B] Then Elijah asks the Lord God to give fire; without delay the heavenly flame consumes the ox.

**1200.** Elijah commands all the prophets to be seized, leads them to the Kishon, and kills them with the sword.

Elijah warns the king to go quickly to Jezreel, lest rain impede his return journey.

Elijah prays prostrate upon Carmel’s summit, and soon the Lord gives clouds and rain.

Coming to Jezebel at Jezreel, Ahab tells her everything, how Elijah had done these things.

Through a servant Jezebel sends word to Elijah: “Since you have destroyed the prophets, so shall I do to you tomorrow.”

As Elijah flees, coming beneath a juniper tree, he desires death for himself and falls asleep.

[Col. 1249C] An angel calls him to eat. He rises, and behold, unleavened bread and a vessel of water appear.

He eats and sleeps; the angel calls him to eat, and he eats the bread which he sees set out.

For forty days and as many nights he goes without eating, and Elijah comes to Horeb.

A certain cave is seen on Mount Horeb; while Elijah remains inside it, the Lord says to him:

“Go out and stand before the Lord who is coming; then such terrifying things will come first.”

There is a great and strong wind, but God is not there. A wondrous shaking follows, but God is not here.

There is a very great fire; God is near, but He is not here;

[Col. 1249D] a gentle breeze whispers: God is here as He comes.

While Elijah covers his face with his little cloak, a heavenly voice says to him: “What are you doing here?”

He replies: “I have been zealous with zeal, because the people go after Baal and refuse to follow you.

Israel [perhaps: Jezebel] has struck down each of your prophets with the sword; grieving that I survive, she seeks my death.”

The Lord says to him: “You will go, Elijah, and King Hazael of Syria will be overcome through your action.

“Anoint Jehu king over Israel; and Elisha shall be anointed in your place and be my prophet.”

King Ben-hadad of Syria wishes, having brought thirty-two kings with him,

[Col. 1250A] to capture Samaria.

Ahab is king of Israel; shut within the walls, he and Samaria’s people fail and tremble.

King Ben-hadad commands this: whatever silver and gold he has there, and his wives and children, he must give to him.

Terrified, Ahab replies: “I am yours, and all that is mine is yours, my lord, as you have commanded me.”

Ben-hadad commands him: “Tomorrow I shall send servants to you, and they shall take from Samaria whatever pleases them.”

Ahab sends word to Ben-hadad, whom he sees laying snares for him: “This is too harsh; I shall not allow it to happen.”

Ahab and Ben-hadad fight upon a mountain summit; the Syrians turn their backs, and Israel presses after them.

When fleeing Ben-hadad sees himself defeated, he says that Ahab is king of a mountain God.

[Col. 1250B] A year passes; Ben-hadad restores his chariots and horsemen and returns, hoping to crush Israel.

Ben-hadad is seen defeated by Ahab in the plains, and the Lord is known to be strong everywhere.

There is a city called Aphek; enclosed in the city, Ben-hadad hides as though he thinks he can never escape.

The nobles sent by Ben-hadad cover their limbs with sackcloth and, coming thus to Ahab, bring these words:

“Ben-hadad will be your servant and will perform whatever you command, if you give him his life.”

Ahab says: “I will. Let Ben-hadad be joined to me by treaty and remain my brother for all time.”

Then humble Ben-hadad comes with lowered head, and King Ahab places him in his own chariot.

[Col. 1250C] Behold, a prophet says to his companion: “Strike me.” But his companion refuses to be the striker.

He tells his companion that a lion would destroy him.

**1201.** The companion goes away, and a lion comes and immediately destroys him.

Another man comes; to him he says, “Strike me,” and the man strikes him, and blood flows from his head.

Then the prophet covers his whole face with dust and, coming to Ahab, delivers this speech:

“While the battle was under way, a certain man captured a fugitive and entrusted him to me under this law:

“Unless you restore him, pay a talent of silver, or give me your own head in place of the captive.

“But the one entrusted to me escaped as a fugitive, and he who entrusted him to me therefore demands a severe penalty.

“You will either return the man or give him money,”

[Col. 1250D] says the king, “or you deserve to be put to death by your own judgment.”

When, with his face wiped clean, he was recognized as a prophet, Ahab plainly declares a like judgment:

“King Ben-hadad was rightly a man destined for death; but you have given him life and are therefore worthy to die.”

Naboth had a vineyard in the city of Jezreel; King Ahab covets it and wishes to buy it for himself.

“This vineyard,” Naboth says, “was my fathers’; let it belong to my descendants. I will not take a price.”

When Ahab hears this, he gives his sorrowing limbs to his bed; he eats no bread and wishes to die of grief.

Jezebel prepares letters and affixes a seal; sending them to Jezreel, she gives a grim command.

At Jezebel’s command two men testify to a crime,

[Col. 1251A] by which Naboth is to be killed.

Naboth is said to have declared, “Blessed be the king and God”; then, seeing the witnesses, the people stone him.

When Ahab learns this, rejoicing, he enters Jezreel; Elijah meets him and speaks thus:

“You are the destroyer of the man whose goods you have plundered; avenging God’s wrath will thereafter give you to death.

“Your blood will be poured out, and a dog will lick it where Naboth’s blood was licked from the dogs’ mouths.

“And dogs will eat Jezebel; thus both your line and hers will perish, as the entire house of Baasha perished.”

He puts on sackcloth, fasts, mourns, lies upon the ground, and walks with bent head.

God says to Elijah: “Do you see this, how King Ahab laments and seeks forgiveness night and day?

[Col. 1251B] Tell Ahab that I do not wish to bring evils in his days; afterward evils must be given to all his house.”

King Asa dies; his son, named Jehoshaphat, buries him and receives the rule.

King Ahab and Jehoshaphat, joined by a strong alliance, come to Samaria and speak there.

“Ramoth-gilead ought to be mine,” says King Ahab. Jehoshaphat immediately seeks to go there with him.

“I shall go,” Jehoshaphat replies, “but consult the prophets, I pray, whether prosperity can attend us.”

Behold, four hundred come, and each prophesies that God wishes the kings to go to Ramoth-gilead.

Zedekiah puts iron horns upon his own forehead and, coming to Ahab, says to him:

“Go to Ramoth-gilead; you will swiftly capture it,

[Col. 1251C] and, pursuing them, destroy Syria with these horns.”

“Is there another prophet left in Israel?” King Jehoshaphat asks. Then Ahab says this:

“There is nearby Micaiah, who never prophesies prosperous things but always harsh ones.” Jehoshaphat demands him.

A eunuch is sent; going, he summons him, and Micaiah is quickly brought into the midst.

Do you wish us to go to Ramoth-gilead? King Ahab says:

“Go,” Micaiah says, “and it will go well.”

King Ahab adjures Micaiah in the Lord’s name to speak the truth. Then he says to him:

“I saw Israel scattered, as sheep without a shepherd are accustomed to roam over mountain ridges.

1202 “God I saw seated upon a lofty throne, and a great multitude of spirits stood by.

“‘Who,’ God says to them all, ‘will command [better: deceive] your Ahab?’  
‘I will deceive him,’ says one spirit.

“By the Lord’s command, through whom you are to be deceived: a lying spirit is to be in your prophets.”  
[Note: [Col. 1251D] Perhaps: “And I will be a lying spirit in your prophets.”]

As soon as Zedekiah struck Micaiah sharply on the cheek with his hand, the man who struck him said:

“Did God, passing me by, speak these words to you?”

But, enduring the blow, he answered fearlessly:

“When, seeking hiding places, you enter an inner chamber within an inner chamber, you will be compelled to know whether I spoke truly.”

Micaiah is ordered shut in a grim prison; and King Ahab and Jehoshaphat go to Ramoth-gilead.

[Col. 1252A] When King Ahab sees the king of Syria approaching, he instructs Jehoshaphat how he should proceed:

“You shall go conspicuous in royal garments, a chariot, and royal arms, and you will be visible to my people.”

Then Ahab entirely conceals that he is king and goes off in a small chariot, like a common soldier.

The king of Syria exhorts the squadrons which he sees to be strong: disregarding the rest, let King Ahab perish.

The foremost Syrian squadron, believing Jehoshaphat to be Ahab, attacks him and seeks to overthrow him.

When Jehoshaphat, crying out, made known that he was not Ahab, the whole squadron passed him by; thus Jehoshaphat survived.

Israel and Syria fight in harsh conflict, and for a long time it is uncertain which can prevail.

An arrow went at random and flew by chance; [Col. 1252B] Ahab, pierced near the lung, perished.

When it became known that the Syrian arms were victorious, fleeing Jehoshaphat returned to Jerusalem.

Ahaziah, whom King Ahab begot, is king of Israel; he is like his father and worships images.

## ON THE FOURTH BOOK

Ahaziah, having fallen through the latticework in your house, cannot move your limbs and fears death.

You send servants to Ekron, Ahaziah, and command them to inquire of Beelzebub whether your death is near.

An angel ordered Elijah to meet the servants and taught him what word he should say to them.

Elijah, meeting the servants, says: “There is one God, [Col. 1252C] the God of Israel; nor is there another God.

“Because Ahaziah believes Beelzebub to be God, and because he has now sent you to consult him, say that Beelzebub cannot help him, but that by the Lord’s command death will soon come upon him.”

When the servants report Elijah’s word to Ahaziah, the king sends men—perhaps soldiers—and asks him to come.

When their captain hurried with fifty men and summons Elijah to speak with the king, the captain [‘Ammovet’; better: ‘Admonet,’ ‘addresses’] Elijah as though he were a worthless boy, despising him and calling him a man of God.

Elijah caused flames to descend from heaven, [Col. 1252D] by which the captain and his companions perished.

Another captain comes with as many men, whom fire burns; the third is spared, for he was humble.

He says to Elijah: “Father, I beg you, do not destroy me,” and, bowing, says to him: “The king asks that you come.”

When Elijah comes, he declares: “Ahaziah, you shall perish; henceforth you will not be able to rise from your bed.”

The citizens of Samaria bury King Ahaziah and give the sceptre to his brother Joram.

With a certain cloak he strikes the Jordan’s wave. Thus Elijah divides its waters.

Then Father Elijah crosses the river dryshod, and Elisha follows him.

1203 Elijah says: “Ask what you wish, Elisha; before I am taken up, I want to do whatever you desire.”

You ask, Elisha, that a double portion of Elijah’s spirit be granted you; an excellent thing is requested.

Then Elijah says: “Although this is a difficult matter, if you see me as I am carried away, you shall receive it.”

Marvelous things come, by which the two are separated: namely, a chariot and horses of fire appear.

While God takes Elijah up into the air in a whirlwind, Elisha, seeing him, repeats: “My father!”

Elijah’s cloak falls, but Elisha strikes the waters with it and the river is not divided.

He calls upon the God of Elijah and strikes the Jordan’s waves; and quickly the waters part.

While all the springs of Jericho were being drunk from, the people sought your aid, Elisha.

[Col. 1253B] You cast salt into the springs and call upon the Lord, Elisha; thereafter the waters of Jericho are drunk sweet.

A boy cuts wood; the iron slips into the waters of the Jordan, and the boy had borrowed it.

The man of God places a cut piece of wood in the waters; immediately the iron floats, which you draw out, boy.

There is distress among the company; death is cried out in the pot, because colocynth, which was wrongly put in, is there.

You, Elisha, moderating the herb, mix in flour; thereafter the pot provided health-giving food.

While the boys of Bethel say, “Go up, bald man,” you judge this mockery, Elisha, grave.

You curse them. Two bears, which they encountered, kill forty-two of them.

A creditor wishes to take the widow’s sons as slaves; [Col. 1253C] but she possesses only a little oil.

Therefore, Elisha, you order it to be poured into very many vessels. Thus the widow fills the vessels with drops of oil.

A man carries twenty small loaves in a bag; you order them distributed to the crowd, Elisha.

And while the attendant boy doubts this among one hundred men, he soon sees all satisfied and food left over.

A woman of Shunem, seeing Elisha, gives him bread and offers him hospitality.

She grieves deeply because she has no son, and her husband is already very old.

The prophet assures her that she will bear a child after a year; and the year passes, and she bears a son.

He grows and comes to his father at harvest; pain arises in the tender child’s head.

[Col. 1253D] He is sent to his mother, who holds him on her knees; and suddenly he dies at midday.

The Shunammite goes swiftly to Carmel. Elisha is there; she sees him and asks him.

Weeping, she falls down, embracing Elisha’s feet; his servant Gehazi wishes to remove her.

The man of God says: “Do not, for bitter grief weighs upon her, and the Lord has not disclosed this to me.”

Then he gives his staff to Gehazi, instructing him as he hastens: “Put this upon the child’s face.”

The grieving Shunammite does not let the man of God go, and does not consider Gehazi, sent out, sufficient.

The staff is placed, but there is neither voice nor perception. Gehazi reports this, and the man of God comes.

Looking at the child, Elisha, you lie upon him, [Col. 1254A] and do not hesitate to press the dead limbs with your own.

Mouth is joined to lips, eyes to eyes, and hands to hands; and the child becomes warm.

After praying as he restored him, Elisha, you walk once through the house, return to the child, and lie upon him.

Then the child yawns seven times, and the joyful Shunammite receives her son, alive and well.

Naaman, a Syrian commander, comes and asks Elisha to heal him of the wound of leprosy.

And as the prophet commands, Naaman is washed seven times in the waters of the Jordan, and his leprosy departs.

1204 After running after Naaman, Gehazi takes from him two talents of silver, which he conceals as his own.

Elisha does not wish a gift of greed to be accepted. He commands it, and Naaman’s leprosy is given to Gehazi.

[Col. 1254B] So that the inhabitants of Samaria may be ensnared, the Syrians lay ambushes in many places.

Elisha reports these places to the king of Samaria. Thus the people of Syria are continually thwarted.

The king of Syria asks which of his servants is a traitor. Then a certain servant says to him:

“The prophet Elisha tells the king of Samaria whatever counsel we devise in the bedchamber.”

The king of Syria commands troops to hurry by night and capture the man of God who is at Dothan.

In the morning the servant rises and sees troops near the walls; weeping, he says to the man of God: “What shall we do?”

The holy man sees the mountain full of an angelic host; God causes this to stand ready for his help.

[Col. 1254C] The fiery company cannot be seen by the servant’s eyes; immediately, at the man’s prayer, it is seen by the servant.

Looking at the enemies, Elisha curses them and asks the Lord to take sight from them.

Then coming to them, he gives them these words:

“This is not the city of Dothan, nor is this your road. I will be your guide; hasten after me. With me as guide you will see the one whom you seek to see.”

The enemies hasten; Elisha the guide goes before them until he shut them within the gates of Samaria.

The king of Samaria sees the enemies enclosed within the walls and prepares to kill so many fighting men.

Elisha gives them ample food and orders them afterward to return to the king of Syria.

The land of Moab ought to provide annually to the people of Samaria two hundred thousand sheep.

Sesa, king of Moab, refuses to send the tribute. Therefore Joram brings Jehoshaphat to his aid.

The king of Edom accompanies them; thus the three kings go out and wish to overthrow the king of Moab.

On the seventh day light finds them in the deserts of Idumea; there is no river, spring, pool, or rain.

Men and beasts spread out in different directions; it is reported that a little water is found far away.

The three kings come and ask the prophet Elisha that the Lord may grant them water through him.

The man of God has a psalmist play near him, and the hand of the Lord comes upon the prophet.

Then Elisha commands trenches to be made through the fields, and says to the people: “Thus says the Lord:

[Col. 1255A] ‘No wind will be seen by the people, nor will there be rain; yet every trench and field will have water.’

When all three kings’ armies rise in the morning, waters flow over the fields like a river.

A river swells from so much water and wets the land; and the stream was red like blood.

Moab thinks the three kings have fought one another, and, supposing the river runs with blood, says:

“Go, Moab, to the plunder, since your enemy has been slain; now you will be rich from his spoils.”

Moab goes; but Israel puts him to flight and attacks a city of Moab, more famous than the others.

Seeing that the three kings have prevailed, the king of Moab is so afraid that he commits a dreadful deed.

The king of Moab has one son, exceedingly dear, [Col. 1255B] who is to possess the glory of his father’s kingdom.

The kings look on, and the king of Moab, bringing a grievous burnt offering, sacrifices this child upon the wall.

There is great indignation among the nations against the kings; they spare Moab and return to their own lands.

King Benhadad of Syria, having stationed a very great camp, surrounds the walls of Samaria with a strong enemy.

Shut up in the city, Joram cannot fight the enemy, and the people of Samaria perish from famine.

1205 The people could scarcely pay the price for donkey flesh, and could scarcely buy dove’s dung.

A poor little woman comes to the king of Samaria and, seeking judgment, sets forth these words:

[Col. 1255C] “This woman consumed my son with me; behold, she hides her own son, whom she had agreed we should eat.”

The king, deeply grieved, swears that Elisha shall now die, and hastens on his way to kill him.

When Joram, grinding his teeth, comes to Elisha’s threshold, Elisha sees him and says:

“Tomorrow there will be a great abundance of flour in Samaria, so that a measure of fine flour will cost a stater.”

A prince is present, upon whom the king leans; he says this to the man of God:

“If the Lord were to open for us the floodgates of heaven, what you foretell could not happen.”

The man of God says: “You will see the flour of which I speak, but you will not taste it.”

By night angelic legions come to the camp, and [Col. 1255D] make terrible sounds of arms everywhere.

Benhadad thinks that the king of Egypt or the Hittite king has brought aid to the besieged citizens.

Benhadad immediately flees, leaving everything in the camp, and seeks to save their lives.

Four lepers enter the camp by night; wealth is found, and no one is seen there.

They report to the citizens that the enemy has departed, and the camp is seen to be full of every good thing.

The citizens of Samaria hurry to the Syrian camp, and riches beyond number are taken.

Moreover, such an abundance of flour is brought by the people that your word, Elisha, is shown true.

[Col. 1256A] That wicked prince who rejected Elisha is, by the king’s command, made guardian of Samaria.

The wretch, crushed by the crowd carrying flour, dies in the gateway beneath the people’s feet.

Jehoshaphat dies and is borne to his father’s tomb; his son Joram receives the diadem.

He worshipped images; his mother was Athaliah, daughter of King Omri.

Through Baal’s rites and the slaughter of his own brothers, he deserved to lose the service of the king of Edom.

Yet attacking the rebelling Edomites, fighting in Seir by night, he routed them.

Judah buries Joram. After him his son Ahaziah [Ochozias] is king, a thoroughly wicked man.

[Col. 1256B] He is a worshipper of Baal; his mother Athaliah teaches him this—she follows the Baals and is the daughter of King Ahab.

The man of God comes while Benhadad is ill at Damascus. Then Hazael, the commander, says to him:

“Benhadad has sent me to ask whether his death is near.”

The man of God answers: “Say that he will recover. Yet I want you to know that Benhadad will suddenly die, and that the Lord gives his diadem to you.”

On the following day Benhadad is dead, and Hazael is placed upon his throne as king.

Then, Elisha, you command a certain servant to go quickly and make him take a flask of oil.

When you make the servant hasten to Ramoth-gilead, you tell him what you want him to do:

[Col. 1256C] “When, seeing Jehu, you lead him into an inner chamber . . . . . [perhaps: “you will lead him.”]

And do not report to others what you do to him.

“Anoint Jehu king; he himself, being king of Israel, shall strike Jezebel and all Ahab’s house.

“He shall destroy Baal; whoever worships Baal shall perish by Jehu’s sword. Thus says the Lord.”

Immediately he hurries; the servant anoints King Jehu, tells him what he is to do, and goes away in flight.  
[Note: [Col. 1255D] II Kings I.]

The servants ask: “What did that young man do to you?” Jehu tells them all fearlessly:

“I have been anointed king of Israel by him. Elisha 1206 has approved this, and the Lord wishes me to be king.”

The people then venerate Jehu as king and place garments under him as the appearance of a throne.

[Col. 1256D] King Joram of Samaria had wounds, received while fighting the people of Syria.

He lies at Jezreel; and you, King Ahaziah of Judah, are coming to visit him at Jezreel.

When King Jehu hears that the kings are at Jezreel, he leads his force there and seeks to seize them.

The two kings go out to Jezreel in two chariots, and, thinking Jehu peaceful, meet him.

Jehu orders the arrayed troop to advance, himself leading his squadron in front.

“Is there peace for me?” Joram asks. Jehu answers: “There is no peace while Jezebel is a prostitute and sorceress.”

[Col. 1257A] As Joram turns his chariot and flees, Jehu pursues him in a field of Naboth.

Then Jehu, bearing a bow, swiftly shoots an arrow, which the Lord willed to pierce Joram’s heart.

Immediately the commander Badacer throws him from the chariot, and Joram stains Naboth’s field with blood.

When Ahaziah [Ochozias] sees the plot, he runs away; wounded, he returns, but soon dies.

Entering Jezreel, Jehu strikes with the sword those whom he sees of all King Ahab’s family.

The king sees wicked Jezebel in the citadel and orders his eunuchs to throw her down through the window.

The horses’ hoofs trample Jezebel’s lifeless body, so that almost nothing of her limbs remains.

[Col. 1257B] Of her there is seen only the skull of her head, the upper part of the hands, and the upper part of the feet.

Those whom the Samaritans maintain in splendid state are the seventy sons of King Ahab.

The citizens of Samaria bring the severed heads of those seventy before Jehu at Jezreel.

When King Jehu sees the two heaps of heads, he leaves Jezreel and goes to Samaria.

There he sees your brothers, Ahaziah, coming, and strikes forty-two of them down.

Coming to Samaria, Jehu orders all servants of Baal and worshippers of Baal to hurry.

And declaring that Ahab had served Baal only a little, [Col. 1257C] he says that he himself will serve him more.

Jehu pretends that he wishes to sacrifice to Baal, and the entire house is filled with sacrilegious people.

Entering the house, he has garments brought to him and orders Baal’s priests to put them on.

When he sees Baal’s servants serving the Baals, he has them all killed with swords.

Then he burns Baal’s image, shrine, and altar; the place where the altar had been becomes a latrine.

King Jehu kills in Israel all men of King Ahaz’s line whom he sees.

A prophet comes to Samaria, sent by the Lord, and speaks these words to the king:

“You have done well in crushing the Baals [Col. 1257D] and in being the destroyer of King Ahab’s house.

“But because the people offer burnt offerings to calves, your good deeds are little pleasing to the Lord.

“Four kings of Samaria shall be born from you; afterward others shall arise from another family.”

The people of Samaria, after burying Jehu’s body, establish Jehoahaz as sceptre-bearing king in his father’s place.

Athaliah, desiring the kingdom of Jerusalem, kills as many of the royal seed as she can.

She would have destroyed Joash, son of Ahaziah [Ochozias], but Jehosheba secretly steals him away and strives to rear him.

Jehoiada was high priest, and Jehosheba was his wife, but, 1207 King Ahaziah [Ochozias], she was your sister on your father’s side.

Athaliah holds Judah’s rule for six years, [Col. 1258A] and serves Baal, whom Jezebel worshipped.

When the boy Joash has entered his seventh year, the high priest Jehoiada gives arms to the soldiers.

The high priest asks them to guard the Lord’s Temple and instructs them to be guardians of Jerusalem.

Calling the nobles and binding them all to himself by covenant, he does not hesitate to reveal the entire plan.

For he says that Joash, son of Ahaziah [Ochozias], survives, and that he wishes to give him his father’s diadem.

The nobles approve the plan, greatly rejoicing, and command Joash to be made king.

Then Jehoiada brings Joash into the Temple, crowns him, and makes him sceptre-bearer.

A song rises in the Temple; applause resounds everywhere, [Col. 1258B] and the people cry, “Hail, King Joash!”

Athaliah enters and declares that a conspiracy has been prepared; Jehoiada drives her out and has her killed.

Then he destroys the priest named Mattan and demolishes Baal’s shrine and image.

Then Joash, sceptre-bearer, is led into the royal palace, and abundant feasts are given everywhere to the people.

The king often offers great gifts in the Temple, and the people often give their own gifts to the altar.

The king sees that the priests bring all these things and maintain the Lord’s Temple, which is old.

Immediately the king orders a chest placed in the Temple, and the people fill it with continual offerings.

By the high priest’s direction, all this is entrusted to craftsmen, [Col. 1258C] who repair the Temple with excellent work.

King Joash feared the Lord while High Priest Jehoiada lived; when the high priest died, the king worshipped images.

Zechariah, whom Jehoiada begot, reproves the crime; at Joash’s command the people stone him.

Servants kill Joash with the sword; then his son Amaziah is made king of Jerusalem.

He overcomes the Amalekite peoples and the king of Edom, and, having despoiled the Amalekites’ gods, worships them.

Hazael, king of Syria, leads armies against Israel; he puts the people of Jehoahaz to flight and kills them.

Only ten chariots remain to Jehoahaz, and only ten thousand foot soldiers.

Suffering this violence, Jehoahaz begins to worship the Lord [Col. 1258D] and humbly seeks the Lord’s help.

With God’s aid the king of Israel then has rest, and King Hazael does not harm Jehoahaz’s kingdom.

King Jehoahaz dies and is buried in Samaria; Joash is placed upon his father’s throne.

When King Joash visits the sick Elisha, he calls himself wretched if this father should die.

Then, at his father’s command, the king takes a bow in his hands, and the father places both his hands over them.

When Joash’s arrow passes through the window, Elisha says: “With this you will strike Syria.”

“Strike the ground with the arrow,” Elisha says; the king then strikes the ground three times.

He replies: “If you had struck the ground six times, you would have crushed warlike Syria six times.

[Col. 1259A] But because, striking three times, you ceased to strike the ground, henceforth you will strike Syria only so many times.”

While Elisha is being buried by the people of Israel, a robber had been killed and is thrown upon him.

When the dead man touches Elisha’s holy bones, the limbs of the man of God restore him to life.

King Benhadad of Syria goes through the lands of Israel, but, overcome by Joash, he goes away fleeing three times.

Then, foolish Amaziah, you challenge King Joash; angered, he sends you these words:

“The thistle in Lebanon presumed to send to the cedar: ‘Make the daughter of your son my wife.’

“1208 Immediately a great beast came upon it, and the thistle fell beneath the weight of its feet.”

Having spoken these warnings, Amaziah does not desist [Col. 1259B] and does not fear to lead Judah against Joash.

When Joash engages him, Amaziah is taken while fleeing; Joash binds him and goes to Jerusalem.

When Joash prepares to cut off Amaziah’s head with the sword, he makes the citizens of Jerusalem see this.

Amaziah then orders the citizens to open the gates, and Joash remains king and lord of Jerusalem.

Joash takes all Jerusalem’s gold as he wishes and breaks down four hundred cubits of it.

Having taken hostages, he loosens Amaziah’s bonds; then glorious Joash returns to Samaria.

Servants hasten to kill Amaziah with swords, and the diadem of your father is given to you, Uzziah.

Uzziah repairs Jerusalem’s old walls, even those which King Joash had formerly destroyed.

[Col. 1259C] He subdues the Philistines and Ammonites and establishes that they shall pay him tribute.

The king has three hundred and seven thousand men, who surpass every armed battle line.

Utterly destroying Gath, Uzziah breaks down Jamnia and gives all its inhabitants to death.

Exalted by excessive wealth, Uzziah, you were; and the more numerous your goods, the more they harmed you.

Uzziah, you presume, in the manner of a priest, to offer incense, and sudden leprosy is given upon your forehead.

After the people of Jerusalem bury Uzziah, they appoint Jotham, sceptre-bearer, in his father’s place.

King Jotham kindly loves the people of Jerusalem and is a stern conqueror of tyrants.

He builds the gate of the Lord’s house so that [Col. 1259D] this is higher than all the gates.

After King Joash’s limbs are borne to the tomb, Jeroboam is made sceptre-bearer in his father’s place.

Jeroboam overcomes Benhadad, king of Syria, and restores the lost places of Samaria.

The Samaritans bury King Jeroboam and give you, Zechariah, your father’s rule.

Shallum attacks and kills Zechariah with the sword and holds Samaria as king for a short time.

Menahem comes to Samaria and kills Shallum, and the people appoint Menahem king.

After the people of Samaria bury Menahem, they set Pekahiah as sceptre-bearing king in his father’s place.

Pekah, plotting, destroys Pekahiah, and [Col. 1260A] the people of Samaria obey him as sceptre-bearing king.

Jotham dies, and the people bear him to the tomb; his wicked son Achaz reigns.

He strives to burn his own son in the flames and sacrifices him to his carved images.

Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah, king of Israel, come to Jerusalem intending to plunder it.

King Ahaz gives gold to Tiglath-pileser the Assyrian and asks help against the two kings.

The Assyrian king comes and strikes Rezin with the sword, killing many of Pekah’s people.

Fighting, the Assyrian takes and enters Damascus; King Ahaz comes there and brings him gifts.

Seeing how beautiful the altar of Damascus is, King Ahaz orders one like it made at Jerusalem.

[Col. 1260B] Ahaz sacrifices calves and sheep upon this altar, and thus follows the gods whom Canaan worshipped.

He orders the doors of the Lord’s house everywhere shut, lest the people offer burnt offerings to the true God.

Hoshea attacks Pekah and kills him with the sword; the people establish him as king of Samaria.

Shalmaneser, king of Assyria, goes against Israel and, seeking Samaria, gains and takes it.

Imprisoning Hoshea, he binds the Samaritans and brings them away into Assyria.

1209 The nobles cause King Ahaz’s body to be buried, and give you, Hezekiah, your father’s kingdom.

Moses had raised a bronze serpent; the foolish people, burning incense to it, worship it.

[Col. 1260C] King Hezekiah breaks the serpent after taking it down, and, burning the shrines, crushes the images.

Throughout the lands of Judah he destroys groves and high places and commands sacrifice to the Lord alone.

Sennacherib, king of Assyria, stations troops at Lachish and thus prepares war against the people of Jerusalem.

Rabshakeh is the envoy’s name; near the wall he gives this speech to Jerusalem’s people:

“Citizens of Jerusalem, let not Hezekiah deceive you, who thinks that the Lord’s piety will save him.

“Your king will not be able to bring you safety, nor will the Lord be able to bring aid to the king.

“This people will either drink its urine and eat excrement, or subject itself beneath Sennacherib’s feet.”

Hezekiah reports through messengers to Isaiah [Col. 1260D] Rabshakeh’s words concerning the Lord, and his threats.

Isaiah says: “Hezekiah has nothing to fear, for the Lord will grant you help.”

Hoping now to overthrow Jerusalem, Sennacherib has led the Assyrian people near Libnah.

There are one hundred and eighty thousand men together; when night comes, an angel kills them.

When Sennacherib sees so many people slain in the morning, he returns to Nineveh lest he likewise perish.

Sennacherib bows in worship in the temple of Nefrat [Nesroch], and his son Adrammelech kills him with the sword.

The rejoicing Hezekiah pays vows to God, and the people of Jerusalem burn incense to God.

[Col. 1261A] When Father Isaiah visits the sick Hezekiah, he orders him to set his affairs in order, prophesying his death.

Isaiah then leaves; but Hezekiah, weeping, asks that the Lord defer the time of his death.

The prophet returns and immediately says to the king that the Lord has heard his prayers.

He also says that the king will live fifteen years and, after three days, will go forth in health.

The king says to Isaiah: “By what shall I believe that I shall be well? I ask you, let the Lord provide a sign.”

Isaiah says: “A miraculous sign will occur: the sun will send its rays backward or forward.”

The hesitant king says: “The sun quickly approaches the ocean’s wave; but, I ask, make the sun take its course backward.”

The people hasten to see the great sundial, [Col. 1261B] and the sun retraces its course by ten steps.

After three days Hezekiah walks forth safely, offering incense and sacrifice to the Lord in the Temple.

Thereafter the happy king lives fifteen years, and the people of Judah remain at peace.

King Merodach [Berodach]-baladan sends nobles of Babylon, with letters, to go to Jerusalem.

They enter the palace of King Hezekiah and convey their own king’s friendship.

Hezekiah receives them with splendid expense and enriches them with many gifts.

Unwittingly, the king displays to the nobles’ eyes everything precious in the Temple or treasuries.

Isaiah groans and, coming to Hezekiah, [Col. 1261C] wishes to utter this prophetic judgment:

“The king of Babylon shall arise, lead armies, and take Jerusalem in grievous war.

“Plundering the Temple, he will carry away its gems and gold and transfer Jerusalem’s people into slavery.”

When the grieving people carry Hezekiah to the tomb, wicked Manasseh, you receive your father’s sceptre.

Manasseh burns incense to the host of heaven and, favoring diviners, seeks out soothsayers.

1210 Manasseh kills all the righteous and prophets in Jerusalem and sets up images in the Lord’s house.

He burns his own son and sacrifices him, and worships Metabaal like the Baals.

He offers burnt offerings in groves and high places [Col. 1261D] and leads Judah’s people into these crimes.

Manasseh is believed to have been carried off by the people of Judah into a cave.  
[Note: [Col. 1261D] Perhaps, and better: “by the people of Syria,” since II Chronicles, chapter 33, has: “Therefore he brought upon them the commanders of the army of the king of Assyria, [Col. 1262D] and they captured Manasseh and, bound with chains and fetters, led him into Babylon.”]

They establish Ammon in his father’s kingdom.

When King Ammon is betrayed by his servants and buried, Josiah is made sceptre-bearer after his father.

Seeing that the Temple is now nearly ruined, Josiah commands that skilled craftsmen be present; and, seeking gold to give those renewing the sanctuary, he orders the priest Hilkiah to look for it.

While Father Hilkiah gathers gold in the treasuries, it happens that he takes up the book of Moses from there.

Josiah orders it opened in the Temple [Col. 1262A] and has it read while the people listen.

There is read the sacred law, which pronounces death upon those who make carved images and burn incense to statues.

The king tears his own garment, compelled by grief that the people of Jerusalem worshipped images.

The king also makes a covenant before the Lord that he will keep the law which Moses taught; and the people swear that they will not transgress the law, but will do as is written in this book.

Immediately Josiah destroys the altars of images which his father and which his grandfather had worshipped.

He burns Astaroth, Melchon, Chemosh, and Baal with fire, and crushes all the vessels devoted to the gods.  
[Note: [Col. 1262D] Perhaps “vows” or “vessels dedicated to the gods.”]

He removes the horses of the sun which he sees before the house of God and puts diviners and soothsayers to death.

[Col. 1262B] Whatever the people of Jerusalem had built on high places or in groves, he destroys and burns.

Josiah’s right hand strikes down with the sword there all who make idols and worship gods.

Immediately Josiah hastens to Bethel and destroys every image which he finds there.

King Josiah kills the priests upon the altar where Jeroboam formerly gave incense.

He orders the bones of graves burned upon the altar and has it wholly reduced to ashes.

Seeing a tomb, he asks whose it was; and one old man says to the king:

“Here lies that good prophet who was from Judah and foretold what your right hand is doing.”

The king then forbids that man’s bones to be moved, and also the bones of the man who buried him.

Josiah admonishes all the citizens of Samaria to reject images and remember God.

Josiah destroys every carved image which he sees and has inquiry made lest statues lie hidden.

Returning to Jerusalem, Josiah celebrates the Passover; no Passover was more celebrated than this since Samuel.

When Pharaoh Neco seeks the lands of the Assyrians, he wishes to lead his people through Josiah’s territory.

Josiah arrays his forces against Neco and wishes to drive the army from his own borders.

But when a certain boy shoots, an arrow flies and suddenly wounds Josiah.

Josiah is carried to Jerusalem and buried, [Col. 1262D] and Joad [Jehoahaz] exercises his father’s rule.

King Neco comes, captures Joad [Jehoahaz], carries him off bound, and Pharaoh shuts him in prison.
