Then he wishes Joad’s brother to be king of Judah. This was Eliakim, but he calls him Joachim.

The people of Jerusalem have Joachim buried and give the diadem to his son Joachim.

There is a king of Babylon called Nebuchadnezzar; as a warrior he attacks the people of Judah.

King Nebuchadnezzar captures Joachim, binds him, and gives the kingdom to Joachim’s uncle.

[Col. 1263A] 1211 The people of Judah previously called this man Mattaniah, but Nebuchadnezzar now calls him Zedekiah.

Zedekiah then revolts from Nebuchadnezzar. Jerusalem is captured, and he himself is captured.

The king orders Zedekiah’s sons slaughtered by servants, then commands his eyes to be put out.

King Nebuchadnezzar shuts Zedekiah in prison, and thus Jerusalem’s royal glory perishes.

[Col. 1264A] 1212 Nabuzardan, a commander, is sent from Babylon, coming to Jerusalem to plunder it.

Burning the Lord’s Temple, he destroys the citadels which Jerusalem’s nobles had formerly held.

Then he carries away the gems, gold, and everything splendid in material or workmanship.

He removes two such bronze columns, such as the world possesses no two equals.

[Col. 1263]

# THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT, BISHOP OF LE MANS: MORAL APPLICATION OF VARIOUS PASSAGES OF SACRED SCRIPTURE (G)*

DEVISED BY HIMSELF FROM THE OLD TESTAMENT AND RENDERED IN VERSE.

(From a manuscript codex of the monastery of St. Marianus at Auxerre, of the Premonstratensian Order.)

## § I. “And God called the firmament heaven” (Gen. 1:8)

(It is also found in Colbert MS no. 1367.)

[Col. 1263B]

The firmament made heaven is a mystical matter: for heaven is the good angel who was afterward made a firmament, made firm so that he could no longer fall, because he stood fast while the other fell away.  
[Colbert: “here the other falls away” (hic dilabitur alter).]

## § II. The likeness of Paradise and the Church

(From the two Gemmeticum manuscripts, 77 and 98.)

Paradise denotes the Church; and in Paradise is the tree of life, Christ in the Church.

The other trees are righteous men; their fruit, a good deed. Four rivers flow from one fountain.

Thus there are four books of the Gospel; their teaching waters us and makes us fruitful.

[Col. 1263C] The tree through which Adam knew what things are good and what evil is called the freedom of our will.

## § III. God looks upon the heart, not the gift itself (Gen. 4:4)

(In the Gemmeticum manuscript.)

God looked upon Abel; he looked upon his gifts. The giver’s disposition pleases more than the gifts.

Therefore he first looked upon the giver and afterward upon the gift; for through the gift Abel is pleasing, and through Abel the gifts are pleasing.

## § IV. What the different storeys of Noah’s Ark signify (Gen. 6:14)

(It is found in the above-mentioned Colbert MS 1367.)

Noah’s ark was narrow above but broad below, completed in a cubit. Below, brute beasts are placed; [Col. 1264B] above them, human beings; above these, birds. The ark represents the Church. We know that many within it are irrational [Colbert: “unreasoning”]; thus it is broad among them.

There are human beings in it, but few who seek what is their own and avoid sin; thus it is narrowed among these.

There are rare persons in it who have the power to despise the world and, with the wings of virtues, are raised like birds to the stars. These dwell near the cubit in the upper part.

For their places are rightly distinguished according to their merits.

The cubit signifies Christ; the Church’s hope reaches toward him, and, having attained him, desires nothing further.

## § V. “I will set my bow,” etc. (Gen. 9:13)

Judgment has passed through water and will be through fire.

The blue and red color in the bow signify this: [Col. 1264C] blue is in water, reddish in fire.

## § VI. What Abraham’s leaving his country signifies (Gen. 12:1)

Abraham is told: “Leave your land and your kindred; you shall be established as leader of a great nation.”

The land is the flesh; our kindred is the race of vices.

He leaves both who has mortified the flesh with its vices; to him a greatest nation is given—abundant virtue.

1213 ## § VII. On the Same Passage (Gen. 12:1)

(From the Gemmeticum manuscript.)

The land is the flesh; our kindred is the race of vices.

He leaves this land who has mortified the flesh with its vices; to him a greatest nation is given—abundant virtue.

§ VIII. Why the Sodomites could not enter Lot’s house (Gen. 19:1)

[Col. 1265A]

The savage people of Sodom wish to enter Lot’s house, but cannot.  
The wicked desire to criticize the life of the righteous,  
but find no entrance, no way by which they may get within:  
a most firm wall, the holy guest, bars them.

§ IX. Lot fleeing Sodom: the chaste man (Gen. 19:4)

Lot flees burning Sodom and seeks the mountains;  
the man who flees Venus seeks the heights of a pure life.

§ X. The sacrifice of Isaac, a figure of Christ’s sacrifice (Gen. 22:5)

(Also from the Gemmetic manuscripts 77 and 98.)

Abraham is the Father; Isaac is Christ; the two servants are  
the people divided under the lot of the two kingdoms.  
The ass is folly. Isaac is led to sacrifice;  
the servants wait and hold back the beast of burden.  
Thus they remain with folly, nor do they deserve to be present  
at the sacred mystery, nor to believe that Christ suffered.  
Rather, they await his coming, until he himself  
returns to them at the last times of the world:  
then they will receive the Word and become believers.

The boy Isaac—and Christ—are said to have carried the wood of the cross;  
yet it was the ram, not the child, that was sacrificed.  
Thus Christ’s flesh, not his Godhead, suffered upon the cross.

+ Otherwise, Turin manuscript 117.

Abraham signifies the Father; Christ, his own victim;  
Israel and Judah, the two servants; the brute beast,  
folly. The boy is led away, while the attendants remain behind  
and hold the ass. The foolish people refuse to be companions of Christ,  
remaining under the law, which has been made void.

“The boy [carried] the wood,” etc.

§ XI. Rebekah, a figure of the Church (Gen. 24:15)

When Rebekah, riding upon a camel, saw the bridegroom,  
she descended; and, reddening with shame,  
covered her face. The bridegroom signifies Christ; Rebekah,  
the Church from among the nations. This Church had been in corrupt  
and crooked ways; when she came to know Christ, she moved toward him,  
descended from worldly pride, and, recalling her former  
deeds, suffered the shame of confusion.

§ XII. Sarah buried in the double cave: a type of the contemplative and active life (Gen. 25:19)

Her husband is said to have buried Sarah in a double cave.

[Col. 1265D]

The double grave signifies the twofold life,  
active and contemplative. The husband signifies the teacher  
of the Church; the wife, the soul, which, dead to the world,  
must be buried in the twofold way, so that here it may be both

1214 contemplative and active, and buried as regards vices.

§ XIII. The meaning of “the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field” (Gen. 27:21)

(In the Gemmetic manuscript.)

The field full of flowers signifies the world full of virtues;  
cups, doctrine; the creeping violet flower low to the ground,  
those who avoid the summit of honour.  
Thus the examples of the good give fragrance like flowers.  
The son is the Gentile people; and when, now scattered throughout  
the world, it believes, its scent is the scent of a field.

§ XIV. Occasions of sin must be avoided (Gen. 34:1)

[Col. 1266A]

Dinah went out to see unfamiliar women;  
Shechem, ruler of the land, violates her, then soothes her  
with flatteries. She signifies the soul wandering in many [reading uncertain: *digna*, perhaps *multa*]  
directions beyond its resolution. Immediately the unclean spirit,  
called the prince of this world, corrupts it.  
If, coming to its senses, it wishes to weep for its sins,  
the corrupter soothes it with flatteries, setting worldly  
pleasures before it and striving in many ways to hold it back.

§ XV. The meaning of Joseph’s story (Gen. 37:2)

(From the Gemmetic manuscript.)

In Jacob see the Father; in Joseph, Christ;  
in his brothers, the Jews. Joseph was sent by his Father  
to his brothers; Christ by the Father to the Jews.

[Col. 1266B]

They are in Dothain: for each, Dothain means “defection.”  
They are in defection. The brothers plot  
their brother’s death; the Jews, Christ’s. Both are stripped:  
Joseph of his garment, Christ of his bodily covering.  
Joseph enters the cistern; Christ, hell.  
This one is sold to the Ishmaelites, and that one to the Gentiles  
through the commerce of holy faith. Joseph was led  
into Egypt, and Christ’s faith is made known throughout the world.  
Joseph rules there; Christ rules in the world.

§ XVI. The meaning figured by Moses’ rod changed into a serpent (Exod. 4:3)

(In the Gemmetic manuscript.)

Moses is Israel, and the rod is heavenly power;  
the serpent is the mortal nature of humankind. Through it

[Col. 1266C]

death came. Moses holds the rod: Israel of old  
felt the Lord’s power, protected by it.  
He cast it onto the ground; and the prophets foretold  
that the Lord would be incarnate. The rod becomes a serpent:  
God became man. Moses flees; the impious people flee Christ  
and deny him. Later, this one holds the serpent’s tail—the Church,  
which is held to be Christ’s body.  
Believing, Judaea will hold its final part.  
The serpent is changed into a rod: God, who came as mortal,  
will appear condemning sins.

§ XVII. The meaning of Israel’s departure from Egypt (Exod. 14:11)

(From the Gemmetic manuscript.)

The Israelites are ourselves; Pharaoh, Satan; the world, Egypt;

[Col. 1266D]

baptism, the Red Sea. The king is drowned beneath the waters,  
and Satan’s kingdom perishes in baptism. The people journey toward  
Jerusalem, but wander through the desert.

1215 We too, wandering through the desert of this world as we live,  
make for the heavenly homeland. Many carnal battles remain  
for them; spiritual ones, for us.

§ XVIII. The meaning of Moses’ standing afar off, while the Lord spoke upon the smoking mountain, and Moses’ approaching the darkness in which God was (Exod. 20:21)

The mountain smokes; here God speaks; the crowd stands below.  
Moses approaches: the crowd signifies the unlearned;  
the leader of the people, teachers; smoke, an obscure parable.  
When God sets forth mysteries in Holy Scripture,

[Col. 1267A]

the dull stand far off, desiring outward things;  
the learned approach and investigate inward things as well.

§ XIX. The worshippers of the calf are struck down by the Levites (Exod. 32:27)

“Girded with the sword, he commands [them] to go from gate to gate.”  
Moses commands that brothers be killed at the gate. This matter  
is mystical: for the sword is the word, and the gate is sin.  
Through this sin enters into us. When a teacher  
pursues crimes by the word, he goes through each one  
girded with the sword, going from gate  
to gate. He kills his brother when he extinguishes  
the sin within him; he dies to the vice by which he had formerly lived.

§ XX. The meaning of Moses’ seeing God’s back parts (Exod. 33:23)

[Col. 1267B]

When Moses stood upon the rock, he saw the back  
of God as he passed by, not his face. The rock is Christ; on it  
Moses stands when a very great people believes in him.  
It does not see God’s face: this people refused to know Christ  
when present. It sees his back parts: after his death,  
the greater part came to know him by believing.

§ XXI. Mystical explanation of the temple vessels (Exod. 37:16)

On the Lord’s table bowls and cups are prepared.  
By the table are signified the nourishment of doctrine;  
by the bowls, the great eloquence of the sacred word.  
A cup is a smaller measure; therefore by cups  
is meant a lesser measure of the word. Let the teacher give both:  
bowls to the perfected, cups to the lesser, so that those  
who can receive more may drink more from them, and the lesser less.

On the base are cherubim, and an ox and a lion carved.  
This base is the order of priests, which bears the weight of the temple—  
here, the burden of the Church; and the cherubim is full knowledge.  
Thus in a presbyter there ought to be perfect knowledge,  
the gentleness of an ox, and the fierceness of a lion.  
Let him plant virtues through doctrine, nourish them  
with gentleness, and drive sin away with fierceness.

1216 § XXII. Mystical explanation of the priestly vestments (Exod. 39:1)

Golden little bells and pomegranates  
hung upon the high priest’s garment: this is a mystical matter.  
The garment signifies conduct; the bells, the word;  
the pomegranates, faith, which joins many seeds  
under one rind. Thus one faith binds together  
the many hearts of the good. Every priest

[Col. 1267D]

ought to possess these three together: faith, doctrine, and religious devotion.

§ XXIII. Cedar and hyssop in the sacrifice (Lev. 14, according to the Septuagint)

Cedar, hyssop, and scarlet twice-dyed  
accompany the slaughtered heifer. When we mortify the flesh,  
we slaughter the heifer. Hyssop signifies  
true faith in Christ. “The rock was Christ,” says the Apostle.  
The cedar, knowing no corruption, signifies to me hope of eternal life; red scarlet, the flame  
of love by which the devout mind burns—twice dyed,  
by the love through which both God and neighbour are loved.  
When the flesh is slaughtered, let this threefold virtue follow.

§ XXIV. Distrust must be avoided (Num. 13:1)

[Col. 1268A]

The spies are said to have delayed forty days  
at Jericho. When they returned to camp,  
they praised to the Jews the land’s fertility.  
They did not believe; God rebukes them for unbelief.  
For as many days as their embassy had lasted, so many years, justly,  
the fertile kingdom is delayed to the doubting people.

§ XXV. Avarice punished (Num. 32:1)

Because they had many cattle, Reuben, Gad,  
and half-Manasseh sought pastures beyond the Jordan  
and did not love the dwellings of the promised land.  
Thus those avaricious persons who are excessively intent on earthly  
things deserve to remain outside the heavenly homeland.

§ XXVI. “You shall not wear a garment woven of wool and linen” (Deut. 22:11)

[Col. 1268B]

Reject a garment woven of wool and linen.  
Linen is covered within under a covering of wool.  
Understand wool, because of the sheep, as simplicity  
which one displays outwardly while retaining deceit in the heart.  
Whoever wears wool and linen in a garment is marked as double-minded—  
one who meditates deceits in his heart before speaking.

§ XXVII. The meaning of the upper and lower springs (Josh. 15:19)

Caleb’s daughter signifies for us the soul; the little ass,  
irrational impulses. Achsah controls the ass:  
she controls it, while it is controlled; the power of the soul is worthier than it.  
Her father gave the lower spring and the upper spring.

1217 Thus God gives the sighing soul tears from fear of hell  
and tears from love of the heavenly homeland.

§ XXVIII. The meaning of Achsah, sitting weeping and sighing upon the ass, asking Caleb (Judg. 1:15)

(In the Gemmetic manuscript.)

As the Fathers relate, Achsah signifies the soul; the beast of burden,  
irrational impulses. Achsah governs the beast,  
and the power of the soul, worthier than they, governs these impulses.  
Her father gave the lower spring and the upper spring.  
Thus God gives the sighing soul tears from fear of hell  
and tears from love of the heavenly homeland.

§ XXIX. The meaning of Samson’s overthrowing the temple by shaking its columns (Judg. 16:27)

Samson signifies Christ; the overthrow of the temple  
signifies the death of the body. Samson killed many  
in death; after Christ’s death, as religion grows throughout  
the world, all believers die to their vices.

§ XXX. On Samuel’s threefold calling by God (1 Sam. 3:4)

[Col. 1268D]

Why did the divine voice call Samuel three times,  
although he heard the caller at the first voice?  
That threefold calling signifies a threefold office,  
for he was to be prophet, priest, and leader.  
Thus it calls him leader, high priest, and prophet.

§ XXXI. Gentleness of speech calms the angry (1 Sam. 16:23)

David was able by the lyre to soothe the king’s rage;  
we may soothe the anger of the powerful with gentle speech.

§ XXXII. The meaning of Abner struck by Joab in the groin (2 Sam. 3:27)

Abner, in the Latin word, signifies presbyters.

[Col. 1269A]

Abner means “light of the father.” God is the Father, and he gives them  
to the world as light through both doctrine and life.  
Joab struck him in the groin. Joab is called “enemy” among us,  
and signifies the enemy of the human race.  
When the enemy casts down priests by the crafty  
weapon of lust, Joab strikes Abner in the groin.

§ XXXIII. The meaning of Bathsheba, David, and Uriah (2 Sam. 11:3)

(In the Gemmetic manuscript.)

Bathsheba is the Law; King David, Christ; Uriah,  
the Jews. The naked maiden pleases the king.  
The Law, naked and not clothed in figures, pleases Christ;  
he takes her from the Jews and joins her to himself.  
The husband is unwilling to enter the house: nor does the people of Israel  
enter into spiritual understanding.

[Col. 1269B]

Uriah bears writings; deceived through writings, he perishes.  
So too the Jew perishes by following writings.

1218 § XXXIV. Apparent injustice sometimes becomes justice (2 Sam. 16:4)

David unjustly divided Mephibosheth’s land  
between him and his servant Ziba. God repaid him this  
as he deserved when power was restored to him.  
Between Jeroboam the servant and Rehoboam, David’s descendant,  
God divided the kingdom: a fitting vengeance.

§ XXXV. The meaning of the boy raised by Elisha (2 Kgs. 4:29)

(Also from two Gemmetic manuscripts.)

The prophet is said to have sent his rod  
through a servant to the dead boy; it did no good.  
But [the reading is *sic*, perhaps *sed*, “but”] he came and measured himself to the boy’s form, and restored him

[Col. 1269C]

to life. This signifies something else.  
The rod is the Law; the servant, Moses; the prophet, the Lord.  
The dead boy can signify all of us.  
The Law given through Moses cannot bring to life  
the human race buried in the death of sin.  
God contracted himself to the form of a servant and came  
to us; thereby he raises the human race.

§ XXXVI. The meaning of the arrows shot by Joash at Elisha’s command (2 Kgs. 13:14)

(Also from two Gemmetic manuscripts.)

Elisha commanded the king to bring a bow  
and arrows. The king brought them. He ordered him  
to open the window; the king opened it. “Shoot,” he said; and the king shot

[Col. 1269D]

an arrow. This is a mystical matter and signifies something else.  
The horn of the bow is the Old Law; the New is the string.  
The string bends the stiff horn, the rigor  
of the old Law, from history toward allegory.  
Words are arrows; the king, the teacher; the open window,  
the light of doctrine. Let this first respond within him;  
then let the teacher instruct and, by teaching, shoot the arrow.

§ XXXVII. Nebuzaradan, a type of Satan encouraging gluttony (2 Kgs. 25:8)

Through Nebuzaradan, the king of Babylon destroyed  
Jerusalem’s walls; he was chief of the cooks.  
The king of Babylon is Satan; the chief of cooks is  
the belly; the walls of heavenly Jerusalem are the righteous.

[Col. 1270A]

Hence Peter says: “You are built up as living stones.”  
The unclean spirit has often deceived through the belly.

§ XXXVIII. Job scraping his sores with a potsherd: repentance (Job 2:8)

(From the Gemmetic manuscript.)

Sin is pus. This pus flows outward  
when confession sends sin from the heart outside.  
The harshness of life is signified by the potsherd.  
Job scrapes the pus with the potsherd when anyone,  
having confessed his sins, wipes away guilt by living austerely.

1219 § XXXIX. The meaning of Behemoth swallowing a river (Job 40:18)

(From Gemmet.)

Behemoth swallows the river and hopes that the Jordan  
will flow into his mouth. These are mystical words.  
Behemoth formerly swallowed up the human race before

[Col. 1270B]

baptism; now he tries to possess the baptized.

§ XL. The meaning of the words spoken to Job: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook?” (Job 40:20)

The Father is the fisherman; the world, the sea; the Son, the hook;  
the flesh, the bait; the Godhead, the iron;  
Christ’s generation, the line. When Leviathan the fish devours the bait,  
killing the flesh, he is caught and held by the Godhead.

§ XLI. The meaning of “a fire in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31:9)

There is fire in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem.  
Jerusalem means “vision of peace”; Zion, “contemplation of peace.”  
Zion signifies the present Church: with its mind as though from afar  
it contemplates the one Lord. In it is a fire  
of love, but not full; but in that Jerusalem it is full,  
where peace and God are seen.

[Col. 1270C]

Hence the prophet says: here is fire, and there a furnace.

§ XLII. The meaning in Ezekiel of the wheel standing, lofty, and terrible (Ezek. 1:18)

(From Gemmet.)

The wheel is Scripture: standing, because it directs morals;  
lofty, because it promises heaven; terrible, because it threatens.

§ XLIII. The meaning of mourning, song, and woe (Ezek. 2:9)

A book was given to Ezekiel in an ecstasy of mind.  
In the book he saw mourning, song, and woe written.  
Holy Scripture is the book that proclaims these three things to us:  
mourning upon earth for the contrite;  
a song of joy in paradise; evils and the woe of hell for the reprobate.

§ XLIV. The meaning of dark water in the clouds of the air (Ps. 17:12)

[Col. 1270D]

Understand water as doctrine and clouds as the prophets.  
As the Psalmist says, this water is dark in the clouds,  
for the prophets write many things obscurely.

1220 § XLV. The instruments hung upon the willows by God’s people (Ps. 136:2)

Willows, it is said, are in the midst of Babylon.  
This barren tree signifies barren persons whose action  
bears no fruit, but is the confusion of the world.  
Such people avoid doctrine; therefore teachers  
hang their instruments upon them and prefer to be silent  
rather than give what is holy to dogs or pearls to swine.

§ XLVI. Praising God with timbrel and choir (Ps. 150:4)

[Col. 1271A]

The timbrel signifies mortification of the flesh;  
in song, the choir is concord. When a religious person  
mortifies the flesh, being unlike in conduct to those  
among whom he lives, he praises the Lord by the timbrel, but not  
with the voice of the choir. He is commanded to offer praises in both ways,  
so that, mortifying himself, he may be in concord with his brethren.

§ XLVII. “A net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures” (Prov. 1:17)

Nets are spread in vain before winged creatures.  
Understand virtues as wings and the winged as the righteous.  
The nets are snares of sin constructed by the devil;  
they are set before these in vain, because such persons avoid them.

§ XLVIII. “A golden ring in the snout of a swine: a beautiful and foolish woman” (Prov. 11:22)

[Col. 1271B]

A woman both foolish and fair is like a ring of gold  
in the snout of a swine that rolls in mire. Gold  
in mire is beauty in a foolish body; mire  
stains gold, and folly stains beauty.

§ XLIX. Solomon crowned by his mother (Song 3:11)

[Col. 1272A]

How Solomon received a crown from his mother:  
Solomon is Christ; his mother, the Synagogue.  
She gave Christ a crown of thorns, a crown made from thorns.

+ § L. The meaning of the feast of Easter being celebrated for forty days

Festivals are customarily celebrated for no more than eight days;  
Easter for four times ten. Hear why this is so.  
Christ gave himself over to death for forty hours,  
both on the cross and in the tomb; and for an equal number of days  
we celebrate the feast of his resurrection in his honour.

+ § LI. The meaning of the people’s receiving grain freely for food, but becoming servants when they received it for seed

[Col. 1272B]

In Egypt the people received grain for seed as servants,  
but for food as free persons. The point deserves notice.  
Free is the person to whom many things are permitted and whose rule is lax.  
If he is fed with the sacred word, he receives grain freely for food;  
if he seeks the seeds of the word  
and becomes a teacher, he must be the Lord’s servant.

[Note: [Col. 1271D] Thus in the manuscript itself.] OF ST HILDEBERT, BISHOP OF LE MANS, ON THE FIRST CHAPTER OF ECCLESIASTES.

(From a manuscript formerly at Elnon, now Royal manuscript no. 274, of approximately the year 500.)

[Col. 1271]

1221 § I. “Vanity of vanities,” said Ecclesiastes, “and all is vanity” (v. 2)

[Col. 1271C]

King Solomon, renowned and ever eager for wisdom,  
having investigated highest and lowest things with the file of intellect,  
when he observed that every created thing changed its condition  
whether through increase or through any hindrance [reading perhaps *interimentum*, “destruction”],  
declared in a thoroughly sound utterance that all things are vain.  
What he called vain, he meant mutable:  
this rule of the word contains everything enclosed within places.  
And whatever through age receives alteration—  
to speak expressly, whatever comes to be that previously was not—  
is judged vain, because it is bounded by some end.  
There is also a final order, sometimes local,  
of heavenly beings, which increases by ranks of honour.

[Col. 1271D]

And then it changes when it serves us.  
But I judge the human race far more vain:  
it is plainly vain because it comes to be through an empty body,  
which its own decay consumes as a woodworm does wood.

§ II. “What profit has a man from all his labour which he labours under the sun?” (v. 3)

Therefore, since human nature is such,  
why should he amass a treasury of many riches?

[Col. 1272C]

Why seek the flowers of the world? Why seek false honours?  
What he has guarded badly, or accumulated foolishly,  
his heir will scatter; death will plunge him beneath Tartarus.  
He takes nothing with him except a heart blinded by sin.

§ III. “A generation passes away, and a generation comes; but the earth stands for ever” (v. 4)

Every race of a people, like a flowing wave,  
now succeeds itself by being born, now by dying.  
One people thrusts out another, which its own generation has produced:  
those whom you see present now, you soon see vanish.  
At last the King of heaven will give fire, when, at the end,  
as the Fathers write, the four elements will perish—  
not so that they may no longer exist, but that they may be better.  
After the world has been cleansed from the diseases of calamities,  
then the purified earth will truly begin to endure.

§ IV. “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place” (v. 5)

[Col. 1272D]

God wished this to be demonstrated by the sun’s course,  
and by the law of the greater to show that of the lesser.  
At its rising the sun always returns, both another and the same:  
now it presses upon dawn; now it holds the western region.  
Now it emerges, then, inclining toward its descent,

1222 hastens again to behold the *zinzivas* [perhaps *zinzavos*; the editor conjectures that this authorial coinage denotes the sun’s circular course].

[Col. 1273A]

Its setting as it were persuades a certain person  
to reflect upon the perishable natures of things.

§ V. “Being born again there, it circles through the south and bends toward the north,” etc. (v. 6)

He calls the sun *pneuma* [“breath” or “spirit”], because in springtime,  
giving life to the mass of the earth, it warms it to bring forth shoots.  
Now it remains oblique, lest it be unequal to things;  
for in so doing it moderates both zones,  
so that there may not be excessive cold or excessive heat.  
When it lifts itself up, it softens northern cold.  
After gloomy winters, summer then renews all things.  
When, on its wintry wagon, it is diverted southward,  
it gains this advantage: it tempers the heat for things.  
Otherwise the womb of wearied earth, as though its delivery  
were ceasing, would fail, if it bore all things with the same burden.

§ VI. “All rivers enter the sea, and the sea does not overflow. To the place from which …” (v. 7)

[Col. 1273B]

Although the descending course of all waters  
pours into the sea, they nevertheless never overflow from it.  
All natural philosophers say that they have, from the ages,  
been dried by the sea’s saltiness and swallowed by its heat;  
we do not affirm this, nor prove it by any certain witness.  
For if they were exhausted, they would have to be renewed again.  
But after the Creator, as Ecclesiastes later proves,  
consecrated the sabbaths, he created nothing new for the world.  
From that time no new thing has arisen in the age.  
The stock of things given by the order of six days endures;  
the old origin endures, and the Maker himself remains at rest.

[Col. 1273C]

Therefore the streams flow, and return again renewed;  
the same waters are recalled to the place of their source.  
They have flowed into the sea; they go, and return revived.  
A course given by the Creator lies open in the earth,  
called the “land of the sea.” By waters you are signified, O human being:  
you flow away into the earth, yet do not fill its granary.  
The earth receives bodies formed from the first mud  
at the end of the age, yet is never filled.  
But it restores the absorbed race to a better arising,  
when this corruptible thing rises again renewed.

§ VII. “All things are difficult; man cannot explain them in speech. The eye is not satisfied …” (v. 8)

There is no ability to set forth the hidden laws of things,

1223 either by the effort of speech or by sight’s perception;  
the ear does not hear, nor does any person comprehend them in the heart.

[Col. 1273D]

To no mortal in this present life  
is it granted to disclose nature’s concealed causes.  
For now we learn all things through riddle or example;  
now we know the arts of things only in parts.

[Col. 1274A]

But when the gracious face of your God appears face to face in reality,  
then everything will be open to us.  
Then humankind will truly be able to see what is concealed.

§ VIII. “What is it that has been? It is that which shall be: nothing new under the sun,” etc. (vv. 9–10)

What has already passed away in perishing is restored to this world,  
and the same will be born that former ages possessed.  
For things removed are renewed by seed;  
indeed, through age they preserve posterity:  
for every thing there is an established line of descent.  
Thus I learn that what is present existed in former time;  
a brief question, by expounding its mode, will clear up the knot.  
Death has laid man low, but genus and species repair him—  
different in number, but truly the same in name;  
for the definition of things gives the true name.

[Col. 1274B]

Here material reality identifies what is distinct.  
By its gift, many humans would be as one  
single thing, if circumstances differentiated by places  
and the passion of a departing word were absent.  
This one is a mortal animal endowed with reason;  
another, born for this purpose, an animate being endowed with reason.  
Yet he is not the same, because he is an individual reality.  
If a definition is given, one thing will be recognized;  
a univocal name receives the designation of reason.  
Therefore they are one. If I proceed to the remaining things,  
every substance governed by the same law will follow.  
The species of a woody plant is a tree which existed before;  
the tree passes away, but the succession of the genus remains.  
Herbs wither, but grow green again through seed.  
The devouring gulf of the age cherishes through time, like a mother,

[Col. 1274C]

the seed which the first origin created;  
God makes it enduring and governs it by multiplication.

§ IX. “For it has already gone before us. There is no remembrance of former things,” etc. (vv. 10–11)

There is no recollection of deeds done in the past,  
nor will those who come after see our present things.  
Behold, the years are silent about what tyrants committed,  
and forgetfulness breaks even magnificent pomp.  
Foolish inscriptions are buried with foolish flesh—  
the tetrarchs, praetors, and monarchs of the world.

The kings of their patrician [perhaps: illustrious ancestral] line lie beneath the *claxendix* of silence.

[Note: [Col. 1273D] Perhaps *patriciorum*, “of their patrician or illustrious ancestors.” *Claxendice*. Du Cange, in his Latin Glossary, says that *claxendix* means a military call or trumpet; thus in the Life of St Wilfrid, ch. 25:

> The claxendix sounded; the eager king increased his retinue.

It can also mean the covering of the trumpet itself. Hence Priscillian, book V: “A claxendix is a shell by which a signal is directed.” In the same place Du Cange cites a manuscript gloss from Saint-Germain-des-Prés, which reads: κλασσένδιξ, as though καλασσένδιξ, from καλέω, “I call”; or “the guard of the trumpet,” that is,

[Col. 1274D]

the shell with which the trumpet is covered, or the small banner attached to it. Thus, as we think, these verses might be understood:

> Foolish inscriptions are then buried with foolish flesh.

That is, the memory of a fool is buried with the man himself; nor are even tetrarchs, kings, and the rest exempt from this forgetfulness. Like their forebears, they are consigned to oblivion, so deeply silent as though beneath a *claxendrix*, that is, ultimate oblivion, that in the course of time no memory of them remains.]

Their dust is more worthless than the marsh-grass on riverbanks;  
a bird that does not hunger despises such things.  
Thus he rightly pronounces all worldly things vain.

[Col. 1274D]

Therefore the royal judgment stands as a general one.

§ X. “I, Ecclesiastes, was king over Israel in Jerusalem” (v. 12)

After his father David, Solomon reigned as king,

1224 as the documentary record notes in its account of events.

[Col. 1275A]

God endowed him from heaven with exceptional wisdom beyond human capacity,

[Note: [Col. 1275D] Perhaps: “with exceptional wisdom beyond human capacity.”]

and enriched him also with the world’s goods.  
Pleasant things always flowed to him in abundance.  
Great in intelligence and great also in rich wealth,  
he surpassed all who wore the diadem.

§ XI. “And I set my heart to seek,” etc. “This most evil occupation” (v. 13)

When the king does not know whether the things done in the world’s  
marvellous circuit occur by divine decree  
or by unforeseeable chance, he strives wisely to know:

Why does the anger of a demon bind tender limbs  
at the very time of birth, or weary them by tearing them apart?  
Why does the just suffer the same calamity as the wicked,  
and the devout perish in shipwreck, as though by another lot?  
Why, O God, do you pour pure souls into these bodies,  
through which they become disgraceful and blotched?

[Note: [Col. 1275D] That is, perhaps “stained,” a compound word formed from *vari rorum*, said to mean spots disfiguring the face.]

[Col. 1276A]

No human being dwelling in the flesh will investigate these worldly matters  
or matters comparable to them,  
for they remain enclosed beneath that seal of the Godhead.  
If he who governs all things decides that they shall occur,  
they come in true measure, number, and weight.  
If chance is believed, supreme providence is denied.  
Attending to such matters, and in this respect as though reproving himself,  
a person learns within himself that everyone is wearied by this task  
when he sees himself unable sufficiently to penetrate these matters.  
Soon he restrains the one who tries to comprehend all such things.  
He curbs the bold who attempt to be capable of them,  
since such presumption is a most evil and penal thing.  
God, offended, by permitting it gives reprobate minds  
to those who persist in investigating such things.  
You are to be detested if you seek to know such matters.

FROM THE NEW TESTAMENT.

[Col. 1275]

§ I. Why Christ chose to be born of a betrothed woman (Matt. 1:20)

(In the Gemmetic manuscript.)

[Col. 1275B]

Why did Christ choose to be born of a betrothed Virgin?  
The reason was that, if an unmarried woman were pregnant,  
she would immediately be stoned, and in giving birth would lack a companion [the transmitted text reads *clientis agebat*; perhaps *consortis egebat*].  
And lest the Virgin’s childbirth be manifest to demons,  
she was betrothed; and so that Scripture might recount  
the line of descent through Joseph, not through the mother.

§ II. The meaning of the Magi’s three gifts (Matt. 2:11)

(In the Gemmetic manuscript.)

The magus gives gold, incense, and myrrh: the king receives gold;

[Col. 1275C]

God, incense; he who was to die, myrrh.  
We give incense by praying, gold by wisely seeking things above,  
myrrh when we mortify the work of the flesh.

1225 § III. Seed falling in different places (Matt. 13:18)

Rock receives the seed, the path, thorns, and good soil;  
it withers, birds eat it, thorns choke it, it bears fruit.  
The word is the seed; the field, the world; the rock, one who begins well  
but has no root, whose moisture fails and who withers.  
It is the path when the word comes to the heart and immediately passes on.  
Birds eat this; the wicked spirit takes it away.  
Thorns choke the seed when anxiety about riches  
takes God’s word from the breast.  
The chaste union bears thirtyfold fruit for the Lord;

[Col. 1275D]

the widow’s is sixtyfold, virginity’s a hundredfold.

§ IV. One reward for those labouring in the vineyard at various hours (Matt. 20:8)

(In the Gemmetic manuscript.)

God’s cultivated vineyard is the people. Childhood is morning;

[Col. 1276B]

the flame of youth is, as it were, the third hour; the ninth is  
manhood now growing cold; and we understand the eleventh to be old age.  
When a boy becomes a cultivator in the morning, a young man in the heat,  
a man about the ninth hour, and an old man at evening,  
one reward is given: everlasting life.

§ V. What the two blind men of Jericho healed by Christ signify (Matt. 20:29)

Christ leaves Jericho and gives light to two blind men.  
Jericho is the world. By dying and leaving  
the world, Christ gives the light of faith  
to Jew and Gentile, whom ignorance had made blind.

Otherwise, on the same subject. (From Gemmetic.)

Christ leaves Jericho and gives light to each

[Col. 1276C]

blind man. By dying he left the world; to each  
he gives faith’s light—to Gentiles and Israelites.

§ VI. The meaning of the coin offered to Christ (Matt. 22:20)

(In Gemmetic.)

What metal it is, what weight, and whose image it bears  
are asked concerning a coin. Likewise, in a teacher: the metal  
is speech; the image, the Father’s intention; the weight, uprightness.

§ VII. The meaning of one, two, and five talents (Matt. 25:15)

The master gives his servants one, two, and five talents.  
Five talents signify the five senses; two signify  
both action and understanding; in one is  
understanding. Everyone skilled in understanding  
sins when he gains nothing himself through doctrine.

[Col. 1276D]

He who gives his own goods to the poor, who has prepared the five  
senses, brings the master profit from five talents.  
He who benefits others by word and life brings profit from two.

§ VIII. Why Christ, when about to pray, took three disciples with him (Matt. 26:37)

[Col. 1277A]

When the Son, taking three with him, prays to the Father three times,  
he teaches that we must pray concerning three things:  
past, present, and future sins,  
which an evil mind, tongue, or hand has incurred.

1226 Therefore be prudent and strong; attribute nothing to yourself—  
indeed, attribute everything that has been given to God.  
Peter, recognizing this; James, supplanting; and he whose name  
grace commends [John], accomplish this.

[Note: [Col. 1277D] That is, John.]

§ IX. The meaning of the field bought for thirty pieces of silver in the Lord’s Passion, for the burial of strangers (Matt. 27:7)

(Gemmet.)

The field purchased at the price of blood signifies the Church.

[Col. 1277B]

It was bought by God’s blood and given for burial.  
Thus the field is for strangers: one who leaves the world is a stranger  
and dead to the world; such a one rests beneath the altar  
of the Church, buried as regards outward things.

§ X. The meaning of the white and flashing angel (Matt. 28:3)

The angel bears whiteness in his bearing and lightning in his face,  
signifying that he whose life the angel announces will come gentle to the righteous,  
terrible to the wicked.

§ XI. The meaning of the apostles’ fishing (Mark 1:17)

The Father is the fisherman; the world, the sea; the Son, the hook;

[Col. 1277C]

the flesh, the bait; the Godhead, the iron;  
Christ’s generation, the line. When Leviathan the fish devours the bait,  
killing the flesh, he is caught and held by the Godhead.

§ XII. The meaning of grain and seed received (Mark 4:26)

In Egypt the people received grain for seed as servants,  
but for food as free persons. This matter deserves notice.  
Free is the one to whom many things are permitted and whose rule is lax.  
If he is fed with the sacred word, he will receive grain freely for food;  
if he seeks the seeds of the word  
and becomes a teacher, he must be the Lord’s servant.

§ XIII. The meaning of casting off the linen cloth (Mark 14:52)

He who leaves worldly [Note: Gemmet: “human”] things for religion,

[Note: [Col. 1277D] Gemmet: *humanas* (“human”), and immediately afterwards *hostes evadit* (“escapes enemies”) in place of *effugit hostes* (“flees enemies”).]

escapes enemies naked, having cast off the linen cloth.

§ XIV. The meaning of the turtledove and dove in sacrifice (Luke 2:24)

(Found in Colbert manuscript no. 1367.)

[Col. 1277D]

The offering of turtledove and dove is a mystical matter.  
The turtledove is chaste, and the dove simple in modesty.  
Let your mind be a turtledove; let it be a dove in simplicity.  
Thus faith is acceptable to God, thus a holy sacrifice.

§ XV. The empty excuses of those invited (Luke 14:20)

An estate, oxen, and a wife shut the invited from the supper;  
the world, care, and flesh shut the reborn from eternity.

1227 § XVI. The meaning of the sheep and drachma recovered (Luke 15:4)

[Col. 1278A]

The shepherd seeks the sheep; the woman seeks the drachma  
with the light of an earthen lamp,

[Note: [Col. 1278D] That is, a clay lamp.]

and each rejoices in what he or she has found.  
The shepherd is light; the lamp, the woman; the Word made flesh.  
The redeemed human being is both sheep and drachma.  
Therefore heaven rejoices, for by the recovered and restored human being  
the ruin is seen to be filled up.

§ XVII. The different outcome of the lives of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:21)

The rich man possesses, the poor man asks, the rich man refuses: both depart—  
the rich man to destruction, Lazarus to rest.  
The latter asks for a crumb, the former for a finger; but the crumb is refused,  
and therefore his tongue receives no refreshment.

[Col. 1278B]

Purple and fine linen surround the one who will burn;  
behold, the bosom of life receives the other naked.

§ XVIII. What it signifies that the disciples recognized the Lord in the breaking of bread (Luke 24:35).

Bread signifies Scripture; to break bread  
is to expound the Scriptures. From this  
Christ is recognized when the spiritual meaning is opened.

§ XIX. What the six wedding jars signify (John 2:6).

The jars are minds filled from the fountain of doctrine.  
The historical sense is water; the spiritual sense, wine.  
When we carry history back to allegory,  
then water becomes wine. Since the world  
runs through six ages, John writes that these jars are six.

§ XX. What the Samaritan woman’s five husbands, and the sixth who was not her husband, signify (John 4:9).

[Col. 1278C]

Jesus relates that the Samaritan woman had had five husbands  
at the well; and, he says, the sixth is not your husband.  
You may understand the five husbands as the five books of Moses,  
Israel: she was first subject to him.  
But while you seek the carnal meaning, O Judaea,  
this sixth can no longer be your husband.  
That good teacher and author was saying this to you,  
bestowing the gifts of life-giving water upon his own.

If, reader, you seek the moral meaning in these matters,  
take the five husbands as the five bodily senses.  
If you believe yourself governed by these as rulers, you err.  
This error too is a sixth, but it is not that husband.

§ XXI. The five loaves multiplied (John 6:9).

God gives five loaves and two fishes to five thousand men,  
[Col. 1278D] and satisfies them, and indicates something further.  
The five books of Moses are the five loaves; the Prophets  
and Psalms are the two fishes; the five thousand represent  
perfect men, who restrain their five senses  
1228 lest they sin through them. The Hebrew people bear the loaves, and bear the Law; yet they bear neither the loaves nor the Law for themselves. With material bread the crowds are fed, but we with spiritual bread.

§ XXII. What the blind man healed and sent to Siloam signifies (John 9:7).

The blind man goes away, washes, and sees: what is signified?  
[Col. 1279A] Anointed with eye-salve, he is sent to Siloam.  
Earth, saliva, flesh, the Word, baptismal water—  
the spring of Siloam; the blind man is one lacking the light of mind.  
By handing on faith you anoint him; by immersing him beneath the water  
you wash him; there you grant him the lamp of righteousness.

§ XXIII. What Lazarus and his tomb denote (John 11:59).

Evil death is death within; an evil deed is death expressed outwardly;  
the tomb, the girl, the boy, Lazarus signify these things.  
I have said what the tomb of the four-days-dead man signifies;  
I shall say what each individual day of the tomb signifies.  
The first day: Adam’s sin; the second: the law of reason;  
the Old Law is the third; the New, the fourth.  
While I transgress three laws, born in sin,  
Lazarus is in the tomb for four days.

§ XXIV. Peter’s threefold denial, threefold confession (John 21:15).

[Col. 1279B]

Three times the Lord asks Peter whether or not he loves him.  
Three times Peter declares that he loves the Lord utterly.  
This was not without purpose: as a threefold denial  
had condemned him, so a threefold confession made atonement.

Gemmeticensis has the first two verses differently:

The Lord knows, yet asks whether he loves him.  
Peter—he asks three times, and Peter three times confesses love.

Not without purpose, etc.

§ XXV. What the three dead persons raised by the Lord signify, and what the four days of the four-days-dead man signify.

(Gemmeticensis.)

[Col. 1279C]

“Evil death,” etc., as above, §23.

§ XXVI. You are the temple of God (1 Corinthians 3:16).

The foundations are faith; the wall, twofold love;  
the roof, hope: they make the temple of the heart.

1229 OTHER THEMES OF VERSES.

(From the same manuscript of St. Marianus.)

§ I. The Church of God is the mystical paradise.

The fragrance of flowers breathes forth; touched by their breath,  
though not weary, yet here I wish to halt my steps,  
that I may refresh my sight by wandering through this paradise.

Paradise denotes the Church; and in paradise  
is the tree of life, Christ in the Church.  
The other trees are righteous men; their fruit, good action.  
[Col. 1279D] Four rivers fall from one spring.  
Thus there are four books of the Gospel; by their teaching  
we are governed and made fruitful.  
The tree through which Adam knew what things are good and evil  
is called the freedom of our will.

§ II. On the proper administration of justice.

When a judge administers justice to me for a fee,  
he performs what is just unjustly. But when he administers  
justice for justice’s sake, without a fee, he performs  
what is just justly. Two things are commended in him,  
intention and deed: God approves the intention, the people the act.

§ III. On interior judgment.

(From two manuscripts of Jumièges.)

[Col. 1280A]

There are four persons in a judgment: one  
is the accuser; another, the accused; the third, the witness;  
the fourth, the judge. The executioner’s hand punishes crimes.  
I see these persons in myself: I myself am the accused;  
reflection is the accuser, conscience the witness;  
the mind—reason—is the judge; the terror of hell tortures me.

§ IV. What the division of Christ’s body into three parts signifies.

The three portions of Christ’s body signify: the first,  
his own flesh; the second, the saints already buried.  
Or: the first, the dead who have been purged; the second,  
those still being purged; the third, the living. The portion  
[Col. 1280B] dipped in blood is martyrdom’s portion.  
The faithful taste the cup of martyrdom in the flesh.

It is also found in Colbert manuscript 1367, but more briefly, as follows:

The three portions made from Christ’s body signify:  
the first, his own flesh; the second, the saints buried;  
the third, the living: this one is dipped in blood.  
The faithful taste the cup of “martyrdom” [read: *martyrii*, “of martyrdom”] in the flesh.

§ V. What the various stations at the altar signify.

What a station at the right, or on the left side,  
or what the central position at the altar signifies,  
let whoever can know; but let what is known afterwards be useful.

The right signifies that in the beginning the Lord made us blessed,  
and that we remain there only briefly.  
1230 We yield, sin leading us, to the left side.  
[Col. 1280C] Here the evangelical order is set forth for believers.  
Again, through the middle our Mediator, pouring out  
his own blood for the city once half-ruined,  
leads his fellow-servants to be placed on the right side.

§ VI. The old Adam conquered by three things.

Gluttony, pride, and vain desire conquered the old Adam.  
When he eats what was forbidden, gluttony conquers; pride, when he wishes  
to be like God; desire, when he wishes to know all things.

§ VII. What makes us sin.

(Jumièges.)

Four things make one guilty: first suggestion,  
delight, consent, and defence. The devil  
suggests, and the flesh takes delight; the spirit  
[Col. 1280D] consents to it; an insolent tongue defends the fault.  
Thus the serpent suggested; the woman took delight;  
Adam consented, striving to defend the fault.  
[Note: These two little verses, not yet published, are found in manuscript no. 115 of Tours.]

§ VIII. What clerical tonsure signifies.

(It exists in Colbert manuscript 1367.)

As the shaving of the head shows [Colbert: teaches], the cleric  
is both king and priest: the bishop wears a mitre, the king a crown.  
What is shaved at the crown of the head is understood as the mitre;  
the hair remaining below is the crown itself.

§ IX. Why the Easter season is celebrated for forty days.

Feasts are customarily celebrated for at most eight days;  
[Col. 1281A] Easter for four tens. Why this is so is asked: listen.  
For forty hours Christ gave himself over to death,  
both on cross and in tomb; and for as many days  
we celebrate the feast of his resurrection in his honour.

§ X. What it signifies that the solemnity of Easter is celebrated for forty days.

Although feasts are usually completed in the days appointed,  
why do the Easter solemnities fill forty days?  
Christ was dead for forty hours; for as many hours  
as the disciples had been sad over his death, when he rose  
he gladdened the hearts of his servants for as many days.

§ XI. Noah, Job, and Daniel signify three orders in the Church.

(It is also found in Colbert manuscript 1367.)

Job, Daniel, and Noah are the saved, the prophet testifying;  
[Col. 1281B] the threefold order in the Church is represented in these.  
Job signifies married persons, Daniel those mortifying themselves,  
Noah rulers. Job was a husband;  
[Col. 1282A] Daniel mortified the flesh; Noah was ruler in the ark.  
“Pristinum” [read “pistrinum,” mill], bed, and field are assigned to these same  
orders; the mill signifies worldly life,  
the bed repose, the field the people; the mill is for spouses [Colbert: “a bed is given  
to contemplatives, farming to teachers”].  
Each order includes two persons, one reprobate and one faithful.  
1231 One is left behind, snatched away for punishment; the other receives a crown.

§ XII. The Jews, preferring Barabbas to Christ, strain out a gnat.

When the Jews demand that Barabbas be released and Christ killed,  
they strain out a gnat and swallow a camel.  
Understand Barabbas by the gnat, because he wounds; and, as  
[Col. 1282B] a gnat wounds by its mouth, Barabbas by the sword; the camel  
1232 signifies Christ: this one bears a burden, and Christ bears the sins of the world.

§ XIII. On the Nativity and Passion of the Lord.

Herald, maiden, God, flock, shepherd, star, Sabaean:  
brings, bears, turns about, is astonished, hears, leads, adores.  
Here the Mother, Joseph, Christ, Nicodemus the friend:  
sees, takes down, carries away, draws away, here mourns—  
the newborn child, the teacher, the cross, the nails, the sorrowful friend.

[Col. 1281]

BOOKLET OF CHRISTIAN INSCRIPTIONS BY THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT, BISHOP OF LE MANS

First published from manuscript codices no. 117 (modern numbering) and 164 (old numbering) of the twelfth-century Library of Tours, by J.-J. Bourassé, canon of Tours. (G)*

1232 I. The eternity of God.

[Col. 1281C]

The majesty of the Lord is not subject to an end;  
it knows not how to end, just as it knew not how to begin.

II. Adam’s sin.

Man, exiled from his happy home, fed wickedly on an apple;  
by the desert of his fault he came to destruction.

III. What it signifies that the Lord said to the serpent: “You shall crawl upon breast and belly.”

The ancient serpent crawls upon my breast if I think  
something lustful; upon my belly, if I carry the thing into effect.

IV. The patriarchs of the Old Testament.

The leader in the waters of the Ark first, and the other patriarchs,  
are marked out each in the order in which they were born.

V. The holy man Job.

There was a man in the land, Job by name, a man without strife.

VI. Moses strikes the rock in the wilderness.

[Col. 1281D]

The leader and prophet struck the flint twice with his rod.  
The leader’s two blows are the two beams of the cross.

VII. The rod of Jesse.

[Col. 1282C]

Though dry, the rod bears a flower, and the flower fragrance.  
So God began to exist carnally from Jesse.

VII bis. On the Virgin Mother of God.

Virginity gave birth; but if anyone asks how,  
it is not for me to know; but I know that God is able.

VIII. Angels announce to shepherds that the Saviour is born.

The voice of those above makes the bands of shepherds rejoice.

IX. Christ an infant in the manger.

A manger, narrow enough, contains the Virgin’s offspring.

X. On Christ’s twofold nature.

The divinity is reported as united to our nature;  
thus in Christ there are at once the rich and the needy.

XI. Christ as an infant is nursed by the Virgin.

A new thing: he who rules above the heavens is nursed.  
[Col. 1282D] The Maker became man—let every human being rejoice.

XII. The Magi come from the East.

The Nabataean kings come to God’s manger.

XIII. The Magi adore Christ.

[Col. 1283A]

The threefold gift is made: man, king, God; hence the One is made manifest.

XIV. The Magi before Herod.

The kings are forbidden to visit the lawless king.

XV. Shepherds adore the Saviour.

This band of fellow-disciples, marvelling thus at the King of heaven,  
praises, trembles, and reveres him.

XVI. Blessed Elizabeth greets Mary.

Hail, stock of Jesse: God wills to become your offspring.

XVII. The Blessed Virgin Mary visits Elizabeth.

The child leaps when the Virgin greets his mother.

XVIII. The Pharisee and the Publican.

I boast, lifted up; I go down made low.  
Alas, wretch that I am! I am worn away upon the wheel; joyfully I am borne aloft.

XIX. The narrow way that leads to heaven.

[Col. 1283B] Steep is the path beneath which lies a golden valley.

1232 ** XX. Christ forgives the sins of the woman caught in adultery.

The fountain of mercy spares the woman’s sins.  
Let severe fathers learn to pity the wretched.

XXI. Christ heals the sick: the pool of Siloam.

In this pool medicine is given to the infirm.

XXII. The paralytic healed by Christ.

Through you, Christ the King, this paralytic rises,  
whom, healed by you, you commanded to carry his bed.

XXIII. Lazarus rises from the tomb.

God weeps, and by weeping calls Lazarus from the monument.

XXIV. Christ triumphantly enters Jerusalem.

The crowd, revering the Redeemer and celebrating in his honour,  
with a great voice cries repeatedly: Hosanna.

XXV. Christ feeds the Apostles with sacred communion in the upper room.

[Col. 1283C]

Here God is given in bread; here he ministers to his servants.

XXVI. Christ in the upper room washes the disciples’ feet.

He who drinks and eats me lives because of me;  
you have no share in me, Peter, unless I wash you.

XXVII. Christ is betrayed by Judas.

Under the sign of peace Christ, through malignant envy,  
is betrayed by a servant to the Jewish people.

XXVIII. Christ’s Passion.

Bonds, spittle, threats, insults, blows, wounds, thorns—  
for you I endure these, lest you die, O man.

XXXI. Women at Christ’s tomb.

[Col. 1283D] Women carry ointment to the tomb.

XXX. By his death Christ frees humankind from eternal death.

The nails through which I washed your wounds are witnesses  
that in the punishment of the cross the chain of death was broken.

XXXI. Death conquered by Christ’s death.

The one King dies, a life-giving corpse, for all;  
and by divine power death becomes the medicine of death.

XXXII. Where Christ’s image is painted.

The image which you see before you is neither God nor man,  
but the sacred image represents him who is God and man.

XXXIII. The Virgin Mother of Christ standing beside the cross.

“Tell me, dear son, I pray: why do you hang thus?”  
“I hang thus, Mother, that the black serpent may be despoiled.”  
[Col. 1284A] Mother: “Why, son, do you weep?”—“Because I am separated from you.  
Henceforth who will be comfort to me, or who relief?”

XXXIV. On Christ hanging upon the cross.

Upon the cross he bore our infirmities and pains,  
he who is condemned thus lest his creature die.

XXXV. Humankind redeemed through Christ’s death.

Why do you wonder, O man? I die lest you die.

XXXVI. The cross drenched in Christ’s blood.

This blood washes away what the serpent defiled in Eve.

XXXII. Christ to redeemed man.

When I formed you, I did not place you in this abode.  
Return to my kingdoms, because by dying I redeemed you.

XXXVIII. On the Messiah, the Virgin’s son.

Born of the Virgin Mary, he restored us.

XXXIX. The lion of the tribe of Judah prevailed.

[Col. 1284B] The lion from David’s line conquered death by death.

XL. He reconciled sinners to God.

God himself, a merciful victim, reconciled us to God.

LIX. Christ, Son of the eternal Father.

Born from the Father’s heart, the Messiah created all things.

XLII. On Christ’s cross.

Adam’s bite impressed harsh death, a fate under judgment,  
upon his children and all his posterity.

But, pitying the death of his first-created ones,  
God tasted death and emptied death of its power;  
and through the death of the cross he carried us over to the courts of light.

This wood of the cross displays a wondrous sign,  
through which life is given and death emptied of power.

XLIII. Beneath Christ’s image.

Christ’s majesty, to which no power is equal,  
[Col. 1284C] is portrayed in a small circle in a wondrous order.

XLIV. The twelve apostles.

Twelve disciples, to whom God’s law has been entrusted.  
They are twelve stones which the King bears in his diadem.

XLV. Christ to the apostles.

“We who have stripped ourselves of everything and followed your commands—  
what reward awaits us? Tell us, King, who restrain all things.”

“Before my face, when nothing shall remain unpunished,  
you shall administer my just judgment over all.”

XLVI. The saints in paradise.

In heaven life is lived in harmony and without envy.

XLVII. On the Eucharist.

This flesh which you eat saves you, if you believe rightly;  
but if you believe wrongly, you eat judgment.

XLVIII. On sacred communion.

[Col. 1284D]

A spring from the rock was given to the people without a measure;  
abundant salvation comes from the whole body of the Lord.  
Cups of life: therefore, you who thirst, come.  
But God himself commands that the guilty person not drink from it.

XLIX. On sleep.

What lacks alternating rest is not enduring.

L. On old age.

Long age consumes me, made by a hand.

LI. Against evil habits.

Even neglected fires are apt to gather strength.

LII. On confidence amid dangers.

Whatsoever the bow threatens will not always strike.

LIII. Modesty in dress.

Adornment of the mind does not lie in clothing.

LIV. On the human condition.

[Col. 1285A]

We are ash and dust, made from dust,  
sprung from Adam’s stock and touched by his wound;  
we endure exile, overcome by the stain of vices.

We are a wicked shoot; we lead no upright life—  
dregs, stench, worm, a vile, empty, helpless thing.  
Beneath this worthless garment let us take care with manly mind  
that, for a short spring, we do not lack a long April.

Love of this world is brief and calls us downward into the depths.  
As hay, so passes the world’s loveliness.  
With no doubtful mind I believe that the person lacks reason  
who hopes to remain long with the world’s flower.

(After this follows the Life of St. Thais.)

1232 *** LV. From the sayings of blessed Gregory.

When a judge administers justice to me for a fee,  
[Col. 1285B] he performs what is just unjustly. When he administers  
justice for justice’s sake, without a fee, he performs  
what is just justly; two things are commended in him,  
intention and deed: God approves the intention, the people the act.

LVI. On the conception of blessed Mary.

(Unpublished, from Tours manuscript no. 117.)

Trusting the promise, the Virgin conceived the Word,  
which she received in her ear through the breath sent from heaven.  
God enters the flower-bearing breast, hidden by the Virgin;  
he enters the handmaid because the King had made her fitting.  
Within her womb his majesty is enclosed:  
a new thing—nature loses its carnal laws.  
She who knows no intercourse swells, a virgin without seed.

Rejoice, made fruitful, abounding in the gift of divinity;  
[Col. 1285C] in your womb you bear offspring whose light surpasses the sun.  
Let your mind rejoice, for he whom you bear within is acknowledged  
as Son and Father; you are daughter, you are mother to him.  
And through this Word the fierce enemy lost the claim  
which the cruel bite of mother Eve had incurred.

O blessed birth, which does not press upon the mother’s limbs:  
as a ray of the sun, such is the child’s coming forth.  
Rejoice, Mother Mary, in this holy offspring!  
Rejoice, star of the sea: while you are blessed by divinity,  
you give birth without labour, and after birth are proved a virgin.

O with what vows the office of piety exhorts us  
to rejoice at these gifts: that the counsel of divinity  
has taken us, by the first deeds of our parent,  
out of our torments and from the fates, through the mother of virginity.

Hence let hymns resound; hence let all offer earnest service  
[Col. 1285D] for so great a nativity, which frees servants  
from destructive punishment and gives the pleasant joys of light.

Behold, Isaiah’s prophecies are now fulfilled;  
the chaste womb of Mary has given the fruit of joy.  
Now let the guilty Hebrew be wholly confounded,  
saying that the sacred temple of the Mother was violated,  
that Joseph fathered this Christ from his seed while she was giving birth.

Guilty people, where are you being led? Why do you not fear crimes?  
What madness of mind is this? Why do you think wrongly of the Virgin?  
You are permitted to know the truth: he for whom nothing is impossible  
can be born of a maiden-mother without a father.

Yet believe by an example, that, convinced, you may withdraw:  
see Elizabeth barren and her husband aged.  
Age had closed the bounds of nature for these persons;  
[Col. 1286A] yet a child is begotten from a barren woman and an aged father.  
And whereas it is customary for one giving birth to bear pain,  
by the reversed order a Virgin gives birth without pain.

Let the wavering of mind believe through these arguments:  
God, who gives both, crowns with integrity  
his entrance into the mother, being born without the father’s seed.  
Since the summit of this birth is singular,  
the lofty things are nevertheless proved by these lowly things displayed.

Hence, rebellious Judaea, receive faith in him:  
the barren woman is made fruitful; the lordly birth does not oppress  
the mother’s limbs; he comes forth without a father’s seed.  
Thus by divine power three miracles occur.

May this faith of Christ live in us, from which the impious people exclude themselves—  
Christ whom you, holy Virgin, bore.  
May this birth draw us to the harbours of life,  
[Col. 1286B] he who brought healing to this world  
for its ancient sickness. Mother, be present to those revering you;  
by your suppliant prayer render your Son favourable to us.

O rose of spring, flower surpassing all others,  
royal Virgin, way of spiritual life,  
before God become such that the judicial inquiry  
may be merciful, forgiving evils.

LVII. Hildebert’s verses to blessed Mary.

(Manuscript 3550, Imperial Library, Paris.)

Holy Mother, flesh free of stain and of sweet fragrance,  
star of the sea, than whom none equal in beauty has arisen.  
Worthy to be worshipped, Queen of heaven, imperial flower,  
chamber of God, mirror of faith, peerless Virgin;  
flowing with honey, renowned for mercy, overflowing in sweetness,  
[Col. 1286C] cherishing the wounded, removing diseases, healing the sick,  
hope of pardon, way of joy, renowned stock of Jesse:  
deign to be present to the suppliant prayers of your servant.

Since the black dragon entangles me in infernal snares,  
bound by grievous sins, look upon me, merciful Mother.  
Free the guilty man; labour to lighten my burden,  
that I, guilty though I am, may find pardon; pray for me, I beseech you,  
lest the camps of Stygian wickedness become known to me;  
rather, may I deserve through God’s mercy to be borne above the stars.

Here it should be noted that the preceding hexameter verses are also adorned with rhyming syllables and can, moreover, be read as follows:

1.

Holy Mother,  
flesh free of stain  
and of sweet fragrance;

[Col. 1286D] 2.

Star of the Sea,  
than whom none equal  
in beauty has arisen.

3.

Worthy to be worshipped,  
Queen of heaven,  
imperial flower.

4.

Chamber of God,  
mirror of faith,  
peerless Virgin.

5.

Flowing with honey,  
renowned for mercy,  
overflowing in sweetness;

6.

Cherishing the wounded,  
removing diseases,  
[Col. 1287A] healing the sick.

7.

Hope of pardon,  
way of joy,  
renowned stock of Jesse;

8.

To the suppliant  
prayers of your servant  
deign to be present.

9.

Since in infernal  
snares the black  
dragon entangles me,

10.

Bound by  
grievous sins,  
merciful Mother, look on me.

11.

Free the guilty man,  
and labour to  
[Col. 1287B] lighten my burden.

12.

That I, guilty,  
may find pardon—  
pray for me, I beseech you.

13.

Lest the camps  
of Stygian wickedness  
become known to me.

14.

Rather, through God’s  
mercy may I deserve  
to be borne above the stars.

LVIII. Jerome, in the Hebrew annals, on the fifteen signs during the fifteen days before the Day of Judgment.

Such knowledge of the universal end will occur  
for all things during fifteen days, three times five;  
and one day, showing the world’s death to behold,  
[Col. 1287C] having so many witnesses of horror and dreadful terror,  
is to be displayed as fearful through fearsome signs.

I.

The sea will swell and overflow the mountains,  
rising fifteen cubits higher than them,  
not covering them, but reaching the heights with its waves.

II.

Again the sea, lowered, will sink beneath the abyss,  
so that one can scarcely see where its course and wave are borne.

III.

And thereafter its ancient state will be restored.

[Col. 1288A] IV.

Whatever is covered by waters and possesses life and sensation,  
the seas will expose, and they will sound with an uncertain voice.

V.

Leaving the air and gathering in the fields,  
birds will lament in their own voice and will not touch pasture.

VI.

Lightning, repeatedly falling from the sun’s setting,  
will pass across the shining east.

VII.

The stars will burn and flash with long hair.

VIII.

The earth will quake: no animal will stand on its feet.

IX.

A force will split the rocks; one part will cleave another.

X.

The trees of living groves, every kind of green wood,  
will all sweat a dew like blood.

XI.

The mountains will dissolve like dust and become—  
whatever labour has wrought, whatever labour lately built,  
will then be confounded, then reduced to nothing.

[Col. 1288B] XII.

Every kind of wild beast hidden in the forests will flee,  
resounding with fear to come and with the common death.

XIII.

When tombs have been shattered and wholly opened,  
the bodies held enclosed will strive to rise.

XIV.

People will hasten out from the cities and go  
everywhere lamenting, bereft of reason and saying nothing.

XV.

After these things will come the final day of all things and days,  
on which all who live will die; and immediately will rise again  
those dead from the world, and likewise all from the beginning—  
some to be saved, some tortured forever.

Who could tell its terror and its travail?  
The heavens, earth, and sea, disturbed by so many portents,  
[Col. 1288C] will show it approaching, giving much greater evidence  
of sorrows. Let us fear its horror; let us love the honour  
in which he will plainly offer himself to be harmed and be seen  
by the righteous. Nothing hidden will remain  
which is not seen and known in the Godhead;  
in it those who shine with a pure mind will rejoice,  
and will rejoice well, because their joys are without end.

[Col. 1287]

VERSES OF THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT, BISHOP OF LE MANS, ON HOLY SUSANNA.

(From a manuscript codex of Marmoutier more than 500 years old, and another belonging to the distinguished Jacques Dupoirier, physician of Tours, 400 years old.) (G)*

[Col. 1287D] 1232 **** Thus far the grace of beauty has smiled upon Susanna;  
thus far her honour has flourished among the people.  
Her fame was bright, but clouds having formed  
scarcely allow the lamp of renowned praise to shine.  
[“They extinguish her fame and do not allow it to shine.”]  
[Note: In Migne, the words in square brackets are printed above the preceding words.]

For you draw a slight radiance from the lamp of fame  
if you have no oil of morals within.  
[Col. 1288D] Or what fruit will there be if the flowers of reputation adorn you  
and your life reaps no fruit of goodness?

I do not call gold everything that boasts of brightness;  
[“Not everything that glitters receives the name of gold.”]  
[Note: In Migne, the words in square brackets are printed above the preceding words.]

Nor do I call a honeycomb  
[“Nor is everything that tastes in the mouth accustomed to be honeycomb.”]  
[Note: In Migne, the words in square brackets are printed above the preceding words.]

If the nobility of gold clothes a muddy pot,  
[Col. 1289A] it does not follow that it is any less mud.  
So too, if the brightness of fame gilds Susanna,  
it does not follow that she is any less guilty.

It has become known to us [“has shone forth”] that she is adulterous and wicked:  
[Note: In Migne, the word in square brackets is printed above the preceding word.]  
adulterous, she scorned her husband; wicked, she injured God.  
She preferred vice to virtue, shameful things to purity,  
enticement to the law, deceit to faith.

This matter, this deed, this crime burns us grievously:  
a shameful matter, a lamentable deed, a sad crime.  
For it is our duty to root out such plants,  
lest the wicked tree bear evil fruits.

Small [“wicked”] things indeed soon bear fruit, but a fertile tree  
[Note: In Migne, the word in square brackets is printed above the preceding word.]  
always has wearisome nettle growing.

Therefore the law and the case demand that our avenging [“judicial”] axe  
[Col. 1289B] go to the root of this tree.  
[Note: In Migne, the word in square brackets is printed above the preceding word.]  
But until everything becomes clear to us,  
our vengeance has granted a short delay of punishment.

Therefore let the matter be unfolded in due order, and let the rein  
of the listening ear guide the wheel of the running tongue.  
When the sun was balancing yesterday’s time, and the balance  
of our office had long weighed the city’s cases,  
we rose and went out; Joachim’s garden received us,  
a flowering place, to refresh our weariness.

The place delights us and smiles upon our labour.  
These four things make the place smile:  
tree, earth, fountain, bird. The tree is green,  
the earth blooms, the fountain chirps, the bird makes music.  
[Col. 1289C] The tree is green with foliage, the earth buds with shoots,  
the fountain chirps with murmur, the bird plays with its throat.  
The flower feeds the eyes, nard the nostrils, the bird the ears:  
this pleases, that smells sweet, the other gives melody.

Here then we sat beneath a tree, deceiving the sun,  
that our old age might grow a little younger.  
And while the wandering of our gaze surveyed the place,  
by chance our eyes fell upon Susanna.

She knocks at the back door; the door struck, it obeyed; she enters  
the open doorway, moves forward, and hastens her crime.  
And such cheeks as wanton desire seeks  
she offered to her hidden lover.

For she enters girded with deceits, unattended by maidservants,  
painted on the cheeks, bare-footed, beautiful in her hair.  
[Col. 1289D] Having shut out the maids [“companions”], she was encountered without a witness: no one  
[Note: In Migne, the word in square brackets is printed above the preceding word.]  
who commits sin likes the eyes of a witness.

She painted her face with art, because polished beauty  
is wont more swiftly to plunder the breast of a lover.  
Her affected dress displayed foul love  
and was witness and hostage to a shameful stain.

By signs and tokens, if not by voice,  
these things could speak the guilt of an impure mind.  
Her brow starred with roses; wantonness in her embroidered girdle;  
neck and heart swelling; an earring gleaming at her mouth.  
[Note: Perhaps “a jewel shining by her lips.”]

Her foot light, her garment marked with proud folds,  
and hair, its mistress disdaining to endure bonds.  
[Col. 1290A] Why so? That she may please more and burn the lover more.  
Therefore she pleased more, and the lover burned more.

He burned and sprang up; he seizes her. Hand is joined to hand,  
mouth to mouth; shame forbids following everything in order.  
We run; they flee; we follow; he flies outside.  
She stands; he rushes away; she was slower.

1233 We arrive; she is stunned. We speak; she blushes. We threaten;  
she grieves. We seek the cause; she is silent.  
Susanna, as though mocking us with a proud eye,  
passes over the alleged crime with a deaf ear.

Yet by brow or mouth she herself indicates guilt.  
Her brow reddens: behold shame; her mouth is silent: behold fear [perhaps: “favour”].  
[Col. 1290B] It becomes clear who Susanna is, nor did God’s anger,  
the anger of the judge [alternatively, “avenger”], allow this crime to remain buried.

Nor does the common saying, so worn upon people’s lips, deceive:  
until a pot feels a crack, it floats.  
This woman would not have felt the shipwreck in the world’s waves  
[“She who now would not know shipwreck, if she had been earlier”]  
[Note: In Migne, the words in square brackets are printed above the preceding words.]  
if she had followed the morals of her husband.  
[“If, as bride of faith, she had followed her husband.”]  
[Note: In Migne, the words in square brackets are printed above the preceding words.]

But a pious husband and a wicked wife differ greatly from each other:  
the husband faithful to his bride, the bride deceitful toward her husband.  
Yet Joachim should not be tortured because of his wife’s fault in this;  
behold, he incurs no stain at all thereby.  
He is not guilty because he is her husband,  
for oil suffers no harm if it is joined with water.

The case has been stated and needs no witnesses; therefore  
[Col. 1290C] let deserved vengeance torture and torment the guilty woman.

DEFENCE OF DANIEL.

What whirlwind has disturbed the crowd? What sound  
has shaken the city? Whence does this crash thunder, whence this grief?  
Stop, men! Torture the guilty; acquit the innocent woman.  
Their own fault binds them; her own case aids her.

Susanna’s case was weighed on an unequal balance.  
The lying scale of old men did not fear to lie.  
Even grey hair knows how to lie, and white old age  
does not always keep faith bright white.  
Therefore age can be angry at its own habits,  
which is astonished that old men have not grown old in old age.

White in their temples, black in their morals:  
their grey temples equal snow, their deceitful hearts pitch.  
[Col. 1290D] I marvel at old lovers, fat as calves,  
and mad—heavy in body, light in mind [“heart”].  
[Note: In Migne, the word in square brackets is printed above the preceding word.]

Their rank marks them out, but their life has depressed them:  
their honour reaches the highest steps; their life, the lowest.  
Both are presbyters, but neither offers a way to anyone;  
both see, but not according to God’s law.

[Note: The verses enclosed in brackets are absent from the Marmoutier manuscript.]  
Though they govern others, the summit of so great an honour  
remains starved of sweetness of character.  
They leaf out in words, but there is no fruit in deed;  
they rain from their mouth upon others, but have no dew for themselves.

[Col. 1291A] They teach by mouth, not by example, but by precepts;  
a golden tongue does not redeem evil morals.  
He who teaches and sins is a lyre, but a mad one;  
a stream, but impure; or a rose—yet a rose.

While the lyre delights you, while the stream rains forth speech,  
while the rose caresses you with the scent of praise—  
[Note: These six verses are absent from the manuscript of Dupoirier.]  
because it sins, it is as though mad, as though foul,  
and as though the rose-coloured heart has a worm within.

Each such man teaches, harms, anoints, pricks:  
you know that each does more harm and less good.  
Though they teach others, they do not exhort themselves, and, like  
a candle, they make a light to their own harm.  
It benefits others; it fails only itself.  
They benefit others and fail themselves.

[Col. 1291B] To close what has been said in a briefer style, there follow  
[“Do you wish the foregoing to be depicted for you more briefly? There follow”]  
[Note: In Migne, the words in square brackets are printed above the preceding words.]

wine-skins—or bellies; casks—or deceits—  
that they may squeeze the people’s purses of coins.  
Alas! each sells deceits to the people.  
They care not for altars but money-chests; not truths but bronze;  
not what is just but horses; not the poor but wealth.  
They cling to vanities, wines, or poisons;  
1234 they seek vanities, cultivate wines, spit poisons.
