They read over pounds, not books; they obey coins,  
not admonitions; they help everyone by price, not prayer.  
They know not how to belch “alleluia,” but “garlic”:  
they read more in Solmona than in Solomon.

Therefore let our faith grant no favour to such men [perhaps: “let not our faith incline to favour them”],  
[Col. 1291C] not because the deceitful have not deserved belief;  
they invent what they pour into your ears. This is not  
the order of reality which men [printed: “thing”] taught.

But my voice will weave nothing from the thread of falsehood;  
I shall follow the matter briefly, but without a cloud of deceit.

It was hot; the heat pressed; the flaming sun  
had commanded the waters to forget their coldness.  
The stream that playfully wanders in Joachim’s garden  
had been warmed by the force of that same lamp.

The baths invite Susanna there; she rises,  
hastens there, and does not know that deceit lies in the place.  
She tests the water and praises what she has tested; naked, she goes in.  
Both old men saw her, praised and naked.  
They saw and grew hot; her two cheeks are fuel for the flame conceived  
[Col. 1291D] in each old man.

On this side beauty, on that hope; here love, whence loveliness;  
here colour, whence colour burns each old man.  
[“They seized the hearts of the old men.”]  
[Note: In Migne, the words in square brackets are printed above the preceding words.]

Eyes, fiery light, a milk-white neck,  
golden hair, and the glory of her brow give force to the fire.  
O wondrous thing! An old man loves; extinct ash burns,  
[“A new thing! Bold love rules men worn out by age, with fire”]  
[Note: In Migne, the words in square brackets are printed above the preceding words.]  
an old thorn smells sweet, a dry plant grows green.  
[“Bloodless stalks supply new nourishment.”]  
[Note: In Migne, the words in square brackets are printed above the preceding words.]

Boy and old man do not err with a like guilt:  
[Col. 1292A] a boy errs by loving; an old man rages [“as”] by loving.  
[Note: In Migne, the word in square brackets is printed above the preceding word.]

[The flowering age excuses the crime of young men; it is not
The old men’s desire is worthy of pardon by comparison.  
[Note: [Col. 1291D] These two verses are not in the manuscript of D. du Poirier; in their place are the following four, which are absent from the manuscript of Marmoutier.]

> The old men’s flame does not obtain the dew of this forgiveness.  
> A furnace cannot be cooled without a spring.  
> More readily does youthful guilt deserve to be extinguished;  
> a new flame may be subdued by a little dew.

Why say more at this late point? Beauty enslaves the elders; they are drawn by enticement and swiftly fly to their desires.

Therefore they pour out prayers; therefore they offer gifts; therefore they threaten. Neither prayer, nor gifts, nor threats prevailed.

And when they could catch nothing with these nets, they assailed innocent ears with these words:

“If the outcome does not smile upon our love,

[Col. 1292B] we shall invent a new charge to your ruin.

“We shall confess that you violated your marriage-bond; our speech [variant: *querela*, ‘complaint’] will spread this report among the crowd.” [Note: In Migne, *querela* is printed above *loquela*.]

Susanna sways [*fluitat*; variant: *nutat*, ‘wavers’], weighing and fearing; her well-aware mind supplies hope, while the deceitful tongue supplies fear. [Variant: *Spem divinus amor*, ‘Divine love [supplies] hope.’ Note: In Migne, each bracketed reading is printed above the preceding word.]

Her mind is drawn by the sail of hope and the wind of fear; following hope and fear, she swims between the two.

And, her devout mind flying heavenward, she directed to the old men words overflowing with tears:

“Where will a ship driven by twin storms flee? Here is no safety for me; here is no escape.

“Fleeing, my little boat will strike the Syrtes, Charybdis; and in guarding against my fate, I shall be borne into my fate.

“Shall I sin? Hell’s wrath will punish me for sinning. Shall I cry out? The old men’s wrath will punish me for crying out.

“But because your hands, old men, will rage against me, flesh worn by the lash will soften the wrath of hell.

“May my shipwrecked life accept the loss of flesh, that it may gain the soul and purchase the heavenly harbour.

“If flesh serves spirit, if Hagar serves Sarah, the suffering of flesh will be profit to the mind.”

1235 She spoke and resisted. Thus one woman prevails over two savage men: a gentle, righteous woman over guilty men.

Those whom they seek to convict do not overcome her, because this hooked hammer can harm no diamond. [Lacuna.]

“Let the place separate these men, and let reason judge the old men’s deeds, so that my word may be worthy of the people’s belief.

[Col. 1292D] “Tell me, shameless old man: tell me, what was conscious of your burning love?” He answers: “I think it was a pine-tree.” [Note: Perhaps, ‘which tree was conscious of the love?’]

1236 Let the other man, to whom this speech had not been directed, also say what tree it was. He says: “I think it was a mastic-tree.”

Why say more? Their own speech condemns [variant: *convincit*, ‘convicts’] the guilty men: this one states what that one denies; this one denies what that one states. [Note: In Migne, *convincit* is printed above *condemnat*.]

Nothing remains but the cross: let their own punishment recoil upon them; and let each teacher be beaten with his own rods.  
[Note: [Col. 1292D] Thus the poem on Susanna ends in both manuscripts.]

[Col. 1293]

## On the Maccabees

(From the same manuscript of Saint Marianus of Auxerre.)

### Brief Notice

Among the poems of Marbod, bishop of Rennes, there is found a poem on the same subject, entitled *The Contests of the Seven Maccabean Brothers*. It begins thus: “The king’s command, abolishing the law of old.” It ends thus: “Greater in contest.” It is, however, wholly distinct from this poem of Hildebert.

[Col. 1293A] [Note: [Col. 1293C] See 1 and 2 Maccabees.] The kingdom of the Persians, which for so many centuries had flourished widely in fortunate nobility and renown,

after the Macedonian shattered it and subdued Darius, fell in its lofty ambition upon the peoples of the East.

Suffering no delay, and with little effort, he returned by the Illyrian shore, having mastered the East; he consulted Ammon; then, returning to Babylon,

he departed from life after accomplishing so much, so swiftly.

And when death was near, when no remedy could now help him and nothing but death remained,

the illustrious hero summoned to himself the boys whom he had reared [perhaps: with him].

To them he spoke thus: “I know that life is leaving me. The gods above wish to preserve our power among the stars:

they bear me above the stars, because they seek to place me in the stead of Jupiter.

[Col. 1293B] Perhaps Jupiter feared assaults and the dreadful returns of Typhon, and therefore summoned me above the stars.

“If you, nobles, since my illustrious heir, being of tender age, cannot hold the kingdoms,

you whose valour places me in the citadel of the heavens, I appoint as heirs.”

And immediately he divided the seats and rights of the kingdoms that each was to hold.

First, Egypt is granted by him to Ptolemy; he ordered Lysimachus to govern the kingdoms of Thrace.

Moreover, he gave Syria of the Pontus to Laomedon. The greater part of Phrygia fell to Antigonus as a gift.

Cassander received Caria, and Menander Libya.

[Col. 1293C] The unknown peoples of Cilicia yielded to Philotas; Phylo received the kingdoms of the great Illyrians.

Tropatus received the greater Medes, Perdiccas the lesser Medes, and his own attendants and closest servants.

The son of Antipater yielded Macedonia to his brother; and he ordered Seleucus, foremost of commanders, to be commander,

giving him command of the army and of his cavalry, and adding to these gifts the kingdom of Babylon as well.

From him descended wicked Antiochus; from him came the man who committed such numerous and great evils:

the root of sin, unequalled in impiety, the sword of heavenly wrath, the plague of the Jews.

The impiety of this man knew no bounds. Whatever was inhuman, harsh, shameful, or profane,

[Col. 1294A] whatever day might be able to produce or experience might know,

he ordered to be done against the Jewish nation, fearing none of these things; and, commanding the Law to be abolished,

he burned the books. His impious law ordered that those should be sought out who, if they could be found,

had hidden the Law; the concealer of the Law should fall like a victim from the flock,

and the just Law should be burned by an unjust law.

But from what causes, or by what cruel undertakings, Antiochus the king came to reject the Law,

the Temple, and the land, it is fitting to recount, and I have warmed to the task.

A certain Simon, betrayer of his country and enemy of Onias,

secretly committed many grievous wrongs by fraud.

Under the high priesthood of Onias, peace prevailed among the citizens,

Jerusalem was prosperous, and in those days illustrious in many resources.

[Col. 1294B] But ungrateful Simon considered this peace a torment; that repose was labour to the informer,

joy sorrow, and pious vows shame in the highest degree.

Seeing that he could not overcome Onias, while Onias avoided his various frauds,

he spoke with the governor of Phoenicia and enemies of his homeland, miserably arming, for his country’s destruction,

the very care by which a good citizen restrains such great evils.

He therefore reported to a certain governor of King Seleucus that the Jews had accumulated no small wealth,

and declared that, according to ancient custom, much wealth, and much that was superfluous, was gathered in the Temple;

if these things were taken away, it would benefit the king and not injure the Law, since they did nothing.

[Col. 1294C] Everything he had said became known to the king in due sequence; Simon gained favour, but religion suffered loss.

The king, greedy for treasure, summoned Heliodorus. He declared and showed the direction of his purpose:

he was to know himself in the king’s displeasure unless he immediately brought the money.

Heliodorus departed, yet would return empty-handed.

When he came, he declared the reason for his journey to Onias.

Onias, bewildered, said: “It is clear that these funds deposited in the Temple are not for such uses, but are consecrated to God.

The common poverty possesses the resources stored there; they are kept for weak communities, throughout the world and the city,

and religion sufficiently forbids their being thus expended.

“Alas, what grief, if this wealth is now plundered—the hope of orphans, the food of widows and the poor!

Both citizen and foreigner will feel this crime.”

He spoke; but Heliodorus persisted in threats and fixed a definite day for plundering

[Col. 1295A] and dispersing everything found.

At these reports Onias and the elders quickly resorted to the arms of piety.

1237 The high priest, prostrate on the ground, was himself the first to punish sin, and with laments begged pardon of the Almighty,

that the wicked multitude might not now violate the ancient glory;

that He might not allow the Temple to be trampled or violated,

or the common good to come under the rule of lions.

Day had come, a day of mourning. The profane man arrived, led by tyranny, bringing armed hands with him.

But the colour of his face had changed, and its expression was different;

from the man’s bearing one could discern what lay within him.

Clear signs of fear appeared outwardly in his face—signs of a mind afraid of some great thing.

Yet, struck in mind, he still gave impious orders,

[Col. 1295B] his anxious mind hanging upon the outcome of events.

But pious God opposed Heliodorus’s error.

As soon as He approached him, He checked him with such power:

they marvelled at a horse of terrible aspect, coming amid sudden tumult. Upon it was a rider, and with him two striking youths, ready to serve.

The rider’s weapons flashed with marvellous brilliance, so that no one knew who he was or whence he came.

He harmed none of those standing around, but only the author of the crime, whom hope of money had armed.

They handed him over, trampled down and torn by those youths whom he had brought with him, to be beaten.

Thus, prostrate upon the ground, he paid the penalty of his guilt.

The people, who had before seen him full of such strength, now saw him, though the treasury was safe, without sight and without sense.

[Col. 1295C] Then Onias, averting the king’s hostility—which would be stirred if so great a man died—

and unwilling to incur the causes of more serious anger, lest matters become worse, interceded for his life.

As soon as he did this, the wrath of the avenger subsided.

Life and health returned to the wretched man, and he departed healed.

Then the rider said to him: “Remember this day, and do not be ungrateful to Onias for your own life.”

Accordingly, Heliodorus came with the whole choir of the people to the memorable Temple, as an example of praise;

giving thanks to God, he washed away his impieties with tears.

He begged them to pray for him and confessed his guilt; he promised from that hour to do better things.

Thus, having bade the people farewell and fulfilled his vow,

[Col. 1295D] he joyfully returned through Coele-Syria to Antioch.

He reported to the king what he had done and how; how he had escaped, and urged him to fear the Temple.

Smiling, the king said to Heliodorus: “Tell me, I pray: whom is it fitting that I should send? Whose life do you wish to lose?”

“And whoever offends, let such a man be your messenger,” he replied.

At this Simon raged, nor had he yet ceased from deceit. He attacked the good high priest, defender of Law and country,

with the weapons of treachery; with false accusations he disparaged and defamed him, crying out at every crossroads

that everything done against the country was done through Onias.

But when Onias saw laid for him the snares of such great enmities and so many plots,

and that he could now defend the Law only through the king,

the defender of his country went to Antioch;

[Col. 1296A] there he lived privately, and lived blessedly.

They say that he had brothers—two, indeed—but unequal to him in merit, and not such men

as their father Simon had formerly been, nor as their brother now was.

Already sharing Greek extravagances, and already blinded in mind,

they gave themselves Greek names. Contrary to the laws of their homeland, Onias was called Menelaus;

the elder, formerly called Jesus, dared to call himself Jason, rejecting his fortunate name.

An enemy of nature, he was the origin of future disaster and the cause of the city’s impending ruin:

through him came so many slaughterings, the destruction of the sacred seat,

polluted laws, and a people and place without safety.

He rejects and changes, refusing the health-giving name.

1238 The changed name was a sign and, as it were, an omen

[Col. 1296B] that in Jason’s time religion would be changed.

There was an ancient custom, most evil and unjust:

that apostates from the Law should seek the aid of kings,

so that, since they could not overturn perverse matters by themselves,

they might overturn kings in order thus to overturn laws.

Occupied with such plans, deceitful and bloody Jason, when he learned that King Seleucus had died

and that his brother had succeeded him and had become king—

Antiochus having been made king—then finding the worst [variant: best] opportunity,

collected a vast sum through friends on every side.

Having gathered it and weakened the standing of the laws,

he informed the king that he wished to abandon the Law.

He asked that this permission be put into writing under the royal image,

and begged that the Jews be compelled to these reproaches

[Col. 1296C] and condemned to death unless they lived as Greeks,

so that, as they had the same king, they might also have the same law.

When this was granted him, the wretch, putting shame aside,

made a theatre contrary to the decrees of the Fathers.

Moreover, sporting in the games with naked bodies,

so that he would not be seen circumcised among the ranks of youths,

he concealed and covered himself by artifice; and the people did what he had done.

The matter of the covenant, especially given to this people,

which no tyranny had violated in all the years,

perished under the worthless apostate’s youthful excess.

Moreover, he added an *ephebeion*, a youth-training establishment, and after the Greek fashion,

whichever boys seemed suitable for these practices were immediately seized

and shut indoors for shameful uses—alas for shame!

[Col. 1296D] What will he not dare? What dreadful thing will he truly fear?

Or what does he judge shameful who does not reject this as shameful?

To what sins will one who dares this crime close the gates of his heart?

If you believe lawful the unions of Jupiter and Ganymede, think all things lawful; except nothing, refuse nothing,

flee nothing, fear none of the marriages of the first-created race;

do not reverence cattle; do whatever you wish, almost blind.

We know that this too was done, and that no one was struck by lightning;

we read that a father was killed and a mother violated,

yet the vengeance of the Pentapolitans did not thereby strike the guilty,

nor did Mycenae perish for the crime of a shameful banquet.

But it is clear—and you know—what happened to the Sodomites;

it is evident that Busiris’s altars were ignorant of lightning.

For fratricide the wrath above rages against Cain:

[Col. 1297A] yet he did not burn alive; rather, he became a fugitive.

Lot, guilty of grave incest, did not endure Sodom’s heat:

the belly of the man lately fleeing from fire foams for lust unlawfully, yet he does not perish like the Sodomites;

he alone is saved, through whom his daughters’ womb swells.

Hence it is plainly evident how grave this desire is,

in comparison with which that impiety became a pious act.

What rain of sins was like their rain? Or what sword, of whom, was like that of the Sodomites?

They alone are worthy for the guardian of nature, by law firm through the ages,

to destroy with sulphur and fire.

The contagion of the lustful had increased so much

that, as if by decree, abandoning nature’s law,

each person’s pleasure drove him to headlong acts.

Therefore no one was good unless inclined to evil,

[Col. 1297B] wanton wickedly and living shamefully and wickedly.

“You are a good citizen”: it is an honour to crave harmful things.

They conform themselves to foreign obscene practices.

Jerusalem owes nothing in song to Athens.

A brothel-cell is honoured more solemnly than altars.

There was not a great enrolment there of distinguished boys, but it was filled only with a company of young men.

Yet each old man makes himself one and presents himself as an Antiochene.

This is the sum of the evil, the cause why Jerusalem, under such a hostile king, was handed over to vile reproach.

For this reason the hope and path of pardon were shut off;

when the city had been polluted, exceedingly grievous wrath followed,

and Antiochus was given one by whose sword he might be struck.

1239 Jerusalem, having lived after this man’s example, experienced his faithfulness: he commands this and punishes the same.

[Col. 1297C] Of all kings who will be, now are, or have been,

this king was more cruel and less faithful;

by frauds and deceits alone he sought the glory of conquest.

Feigning peace, as if a friend of his nephew, he came to see Ptolemy at Memphis,

whose famous mother was the sister of this Antiochus.

He was born of Philometor and Antiochus’s sister, and by custom reigned for his father.

The child’s strength was ill-suited to affairs so great;

an age suited to a king is not good and just for a king.

But the boy’s uncle sought to be accepted as his guardian,

and, with a treacherous heart, gave words much like peace:

he swore that he would provide for the boy, be a father to him,

and defend his nephew’s kingdom with all his strength.

[Col. 1297D] The authority of Ptolemy’s nobles yielded to him;

he was admitted to the child’s kingdom, but the fraud was exposed.

For, having attained his desire, he prepared arms and death for his nephew;

when the fraud was discovered, open war was prepared against him.

He bitterly endured being repelled in war from Pelusium; had he captured it, all would have submitted to him.

Excluded by deception, he turned to the operations of war:

he besieged the child. But while he remained in the siege, a Roman envoy came from the Senate:

“Rome, the saving head and defender of the world, commands you to be content with the borders of the land granted to you,

and to do no harm to the besieged people.

“You offend against us unless you leave us and what is ours alone; and you injure Rome unless you depart at once from there.”

“I hear what you say,” the king replies; “but what answer ought to be given you about my allies—

[Col. 1298A] that must be discussed.”

At once a circle is made in the sand with a staff; he encloses the king with it and sets him this condition:

“If you cross this before giving an answer, you will perish.”

The king reflected briefly: “Then I shall withdraw.”

And after these words he fled, abandoning the siege.

He returned to Jerusalem because he feared, and because he believed

that, once affairs were known, he would become contemptible to his compatriots,

that Jerusalem might for this reason be closed against him

and the Jews might thus yield to Ptolemy’s kingdom.

But, on the contrary, he saw them rejoice at his return and meet him at the gates, native slaves of death.

Therefore, received and having attained all that he desired,

the terrible destroyer, never to be feared except in peace—

whose threats are gentle, peace war, and gifts plunder—

[Col. 1298B] returned to his usual manner and inborn frenzy.

Forgetting the treaty, as soon as he gained the city,

he showed what he was and what, at last, he now sought.

He prepared arms against citizens, though he had pretended to be a citizen;

he raved in slaughter and stripped men of their possessions.

He ordered his attendant to take up arms against the unarmed

and to slaughter anyone whom he saw displeased him.

The slaughter was violent; no house was without mourning.

Slain bodies and severed limbs lay in the streets.

Religion, piety, Law, duty, place, age—

none protected them, moved them, or bent them.

Nor did this profane man hold his hand back even from the Temple precinct;

but with an armed force he rushed upon the consecrated places,

burning the doors and seeking the inner entrances.

And whatever splendid wealth he thought was there,

[Col. 1298C] he divided as plunder, as though it were common property.

Having stripped away everything, with the rich vessels of the table,

he fortified the citadel and returned to his kingdom,

leaving the people as though conquered, beneath a grievous law.

To defend it he left there a certain man, named Philip, a native of Phrygia,

acceptable to Antiochus because he was no slight criminal:

a Phrygian by nature, Phrygian in character and appearance,

worthy of his king because deceitful and malignant.

Again he took care to interrupt the course of treachery.

1240 The king, as was his custom, broke the reins of shame;

wishing to destroy the people and the powerful place,

he assigned this horrible crime to Apollonius to carry out.

Having adequately equipped him in the practices of impiety

with armed thousands—six, five, and four—joined together,

[Col. 1298D] he sent him to destroy that small remnant which had scarcely escaped him, thus renewing grief by grief.

The wicked king sends a wicked man to destroy what remains.

This man, pretending benevolence and censuring the king’s crime,

addressed the people with falsely peaceful, rather mild words,

and gave them hope of life, initially ordering nothing harsh.

Nothing further was imposed, but he remained quiet by thus enduring,

lest the nation stir until the festival day returned.

The seventh day returned; pretended piety departed.

The impious attendant attacked, sword in hand, those unarmed by the Law;

the savage crowd, intent upon the festival, with wicked hands

dragged them away and slaughtered them, cruelly tormenting them with various evils.

And, while the Jews customarily observed rest

[Col. 1299A] in honour of their solemn day and in fear of God,

they, mad and foolish, perished gratuitously and unavenged:

their Sabbaths became, for the blind, their just cause of death.

To these and other evils imperial frenzy added the impious commands of the old man whom he had sent from Athens.

First, he ordered a statue of Jupiter to be set up upon the altar.

He ordered incense to be offered to him in the Temple, and himself [perhaps: “and God”] to be called by his name.

By edict, abandoning the Fathers’ tradition, he ordered the books of the Law to be burned at the king’s pleasure;

he shattered the Sabbaths and rejected the feast days.

What had been unclean he commanded henceforth to be made clean.

Let the Law exist as though it did not exist; let circumcision cease;

and an altar to the gods of Antiochus stood in every street.

He wished everyone on appointed days to sacrifice there from forbidden things;

[Col. 1299B] and those who refused such practices and dreaded commands so shameful he slaughtered.

Those of noble birth, eager for honourable praise,

whose minds were strong, steadfast, and manly,

who followed virtue rather than the safety of the flesh;

who, following the customs of their fathers and their former fathers,

regarded sinners and the honours of this age as of no account, indeed rebuked them—

such men, cast aside because they could not be bent wickedly, were killed;

but for this reason, under the cruel old man, they deserved to be carried above heaven to the palaces of heaven.

Nor do those endure, but are slight of heart, who in the world are like chaff or reeds,

exult in novelties, and are driven by every whirlwind;

[Col. 1299C] who have no root and wither when the sun burns.

These, quickly changed, yielded to impiety;

made Gentiles, sometimes willingly and sometimes under compulsion,

they became Gentiles—apostates, base throughout the ages.

Nor does the frenzy and madness of rulers permit the evils of the Law thus oppressed to remain only in cities:

this storm resounds through hamlets and fortresses.

For such purposes they appoint officials abroad,

who with great care search every countryside,

seeking in villages the Law or friends of the Law.

One day Apellenus, a judge full of the devil, came to the village of Modin, Mathathias’s village.  
[Note: [Col. 1299] “The village of Modin, Mathathias’s,” that is, where Mathathias lived.]

And because Mathathias was the foremost among the village’s leading men,

he summoned and urged him to offer his incense to Jupiter.

Mathathias, detesting these uncleannesses,

[Col. 1299D] smiled and said: “Although every man abandons the Law, I shall not abandon it.

I do not value life so highly that I should preserve it by keeping these abominations.

You will worship images, but neither I nor my offspring will.”

This man, burning with zeal for piety together with his sons,

wept daily that Jeremiah’s days had come,

over the loss of religion and the sudden ruin of country and Temple, with its few good men.

As an honourable citizen, he brought them manifold benefits;

but although they promised him supporters, friendships, and honours,

1241 they moved him no more than stones.

A certain wretched Israelite, fearing for his life,

[Col. 1300A] stood at the altar and wished to worship Jupiter.

When Mathathias saw him violating the laws of his fathers,

he opposed the offence and struck the wretch with the sword;

in renowned praise, he slew upon the altar the man offering sacrifice,

and some of the sacrilegious, together with the king’s judge,

at the same time breaking the false images of false gods.

With these exhortations he strengthened the people’s spirits:

“Whoever cares for honour, for the Law, and for living rightly,

let him henceforth join me and follow me and mine.”

At these words he rushed out, abandoning possessions and country;

and, leaving home [lacuna],

many strangers gladly joined themselves to the old man.

When those who governed the Samaritans heard these things,

they summoned everyone, including the Solomite leaders,

and, greatly angered, came to avenge this disgrace

[Col. 1300B] upon the small people, exhausted by recent toil

and afflicted in foreign places by so many punishments for many causes.

At that time they had no strength to endure war against so great and powerful a nation.

Therefore they scattered and fled; having opened their caves,

about a thousand leaders shut themselves in there from that time onward.

The enemy came upon those discovered there, and finding them there,

while they observed the Law and refused to violate the Sabbath,

he compelled them to die by fire and gave them a better life.

After their death a law was later given to all

not to observe Sabbaths when such evils raged against them,

but to resist wars whenever they wished,

and to fight for their own cause on feast days.

Thus they first dared to break the lawful ordinance of the Hebrew holy day for the Law’s sake.

[Col. 1300C] Mathathias, again recalling the remnants of the people,

destroyed, mourned, and decreed that the Sabbaths must be observed;

yet they considered labour necessary if war were required,

and allowed warfare: they changed times according to circumstances.

Following the example of their fathers, let them retain the footsteps of their brothers,

so that to die for the Law might be judged the highest honour,

and equal glory be returned to heaven for equal zeal.

Then all the strong men, because of the twofold misfortunes of the nation, hastened daily to join Mathathias.

Love of piety within them and fatherly love had made them so strong, secure, and hard

that, despising rest and living on a poor, scanty diet,

each regarded his country as the highest good, the land of lions.

There was no food; their home and bed were wild-beasts’ caves.

[Col. 1300D] They considered rainwater glorious nectar.

Their flesh is blackened by the sun; thirst is immense; water is scarce;

their hair is scorched, now by sun, now by the night’s frost.

The Law’s friends are tortured by many punishments;

yet from none of these arises a sorrowful complaint,

and no one murmurs wickedly in a blasphemous heart because of evils:

blessed patience, an antidote, heals everything.

Mathathias therefore taught the people such paths;

while he lived, he did such things, and taught that they must be done.

1242 Breathing his last, at the end of his days,

he left the chief affairs to his sons, whom he first instructed concerning the worship of piety

and recalled to these examples.

“The whole mass of evil looks toward us, my offspring!

[Col. 1301A] Chaste love of the Law stirs kings’ wars against us.

When kings are enraged, have confidence; do not fear: God, a mighty warrior, is your helper.

My people, do not despise the rites and laws of your fathers.

Survey the ages: then you will know that no one trusts in God in vain, nor departs from His Law.

Abraham was tested, and proved by testing.

Joseph was a beggar, yet patient and tranquil;

he rejected sin, and thereby his glory grew.

You know of Phinehas, because he was the enemy of lust,

how the priesthood was confirmed to him.

Jesus [Joshua], strengthening the people and bringing back rest,

lived longer than the others and fixed the sun by his prayer.

Because he trusted rightly, Caleb saw all things come to pass.

The piety of Elijah, destroying false prophets,

[Col. 1301B] while zealously defending the veil, deserved to ascend to heaven.

Esther shows in the books who your God is; the piety of women of old lives on.

Instructed by these examples, my dear pledges, my sons,

be ready to suffer every hardship for the Law.

I grant the primacy of good counsel to Simon,

and let my chosen Maccabee wage fierce wars.”

His affairs arranged and his days completed,

the righteous man died and was buried beside his father.

When the guardian of the Law had been buried amid great lamentation,

[Col. 1302A] Judas arose and ruled the people in his father’s place:

sacred in religion and fierce, renowned in war;

strong in body and handsome in countenance;

a despiser of death, redeemer of his people and country,

who, as we read, first gave hope that resurrection was possible.

Girded with the arms of warriors in the fashion of giants,

he took up the breastplate and, threatening, laid low and overwhelmed the hostile nation,

and wiped away his country’s reproaches.

His life was short but vigorous and without blemish;

it carried his father’s name eternally to the stars.

When wicked Apollonius first learned of his undertaking,

he moved his camp against him, hoping suddenly to destroy Judas with his people.

Judas foresaw it, prepared his people, and went to meet him;

battle was joined, and swords struck on both sides.

[Col. 1302B] But God and God’s soldier Maccabee prevailed.

The greater part of the evil men was slain, including their leader,

whom Judas struck down and stripped of his sword;

and thereafter the leader began to fight with it.

Sorrowful Seron, commander, judge of these successes,

having joined to himself all neighbouring peoples by prayer or payment,

hastened to win glory from the death of the illustrious leader.

When he had drawn near Beth-horon and pitched camp,

Judas and his people rose to meet him on high.

[Col. 1301]

## Here Begin the Verses on Saint Vincent

(From a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Marianus of Auxerre, of the Premonstratensian order, about five hundred years old.) (G)*

[Col. 1301C] From his criminal deeds you may learn how exceedingly mad the governor Dacian was.

Among the Spaniards, while reviving profane rites,

he had ordered inquiry to be made whether there might perhaps be found

those who believed in Christ and did not withdraw from this error.

He had commanded that these be severely punished and quickly bent [perhaps: “or” bent].

A law concealed is nothing; it has force when it is seen,

and when it is more generally predominant and in the midst of the people.

Vincent was a light of the world. He judged concealment shameful and wicked,

and therefore refused to hide.

God wished to be called thus, as the name of a friend.

For he truly conquered, as his passion relates,

when, though worn down enough, he gave up life without blood,

and from a soft bed deserved to be carried above heaven.

Valerius had imparted knowledge of Christ to him;

[Col. 1301D] under this good teacher, guide, bishop, father, and patron,

he learned to conquer the world which he afterwards conquered.

Renowned for learning, wise, and therefore beloved,

having accepted charge over ecclesiastical law,

he supplied for the old man what failed in the old man.

Caesaraugusta, which by ancient religion retains honour for its founder,

[Col. 1302C] flourishes, defended by patrons so great and so good.

Therefore, summoned as the frenzy of the raging man commanded,

both father and youth hastened to meet their punishments.

When they were presented, the judge of impiety said:

“So you are those through whom this new plague has come,

and the world wanders confused by the diseases of crimes?

Then he said to his men: “Quickly drag them both away.

Let a heavy chain bind them, and let a long journey tire them;

let Valencia keep for us in prison those who dared this crime. Preserve what I order you:

lest, fearing a lighter punishment, they perhaps die,

let them not be worn out by the weight of chains and the excessive hardship of travel

unless they are first tortured long.”

He mounted swiftly and proceeded thither with his soldiers.

At his arrival the mad frenzy of raging men joyfully displayed itself

[Col. 1302D] and presented them as he had ordered.

When he saw them, he said: “Whoever abandons our gods and worships one put to death, I see, does not wish to live.

Be certain, therefore: unless you are willing to sacrifice,

you must die by whatever death I can make more grievous.

But while you are as yet able and while it is still permitted,

[Col. 1303A] come to the images of Jupiter, the author of life.”

Then the pious bishop said: “You shall answer in resistance.

My son Vincent, vigorous in youthful strength,

has the highest ardour of faith within him; but I am hindered in speech,

my flesh exhausted, old age ruling the flesh.

To you has been given the charge of so many ministries;

you can and know how to speak. Say what answer may be given to the enemy.”

Then Vincent, wholly rejoicing, began thus:

“You have urged us, servants of Christ, to violate the faith

and burn grains of incense before your images.

But this is wholly in vain, since it is clear that it is profane

to hope for the gift of salvation in mute statues.

I prefer to stones Him whom the vault of heaven cannot contain.

Tell me, judge, I pray: by what reasoning shall I abandon,

by what reasoning shall I deny, the King who reigns in heaven,

[Col. 1303B] and follow error, praying to or worshipping stones?

“Give such exhortations to anyone you please; for in behalf of religion

we are willing and prepared to suffer your commands.”

Then the sorrowful judge said: “We are despised by these men.

We achieve nothing by words; they must be tortured by grievous and bitter penalties.

They will not be moved except by the rod.

Let this wretched aged man, an exile superstitious in speech,

bear the misfortunes of decrepit life.

And let the old man’s disciple henceforth be fitted to punishments.”

Stirred by anger, he ordered him to undergo tortures.

First suspended and stretched in every limb,

while he was being tortured and suffering quite grievously,

he cried: “O torturer, I urge you: torture me more cruelly!

Why do you delay? What are you doing? There remains room and flesh for blows.

I beg you, do not stop. Would that you were stronger now!

[Col. 1303C] Strike more fiercely, lest perhaps you wish to spare me.”

The governor grew pale; his anxious mind did not know what to do.

Dacian marvelled that the sufferer, though tortured, had conquered the torturer,

and saw the executioners’ hands grow weary.

He said: “Where is your strength of mind and manly right hand?

What is this weakness of yours? I grieve and am deeply distressed

that this wretch sees that we are conquered and laughs at it.

But take breath now, that your anger may be stronger.

Delay and wait, until, with your strength restored,

you compel by blows what you ask through words.”

To complete the course, they rose again to their blows;

and, with his ribs broken, the enemy penetrated into his entrails.

The unconquered spirit, which nevertheless did not fear these blows,

remained secure in the athlete, his mind tranquil.

[Col. 1303D] Then he rebuked the craftsman of evil in this manner:

“Dacian, I now see you utterly confounded.

For just now, though exalted, you who scorn are acting in the depths;

standing above the world, I despise the world’s abyss.

Exercise whatever you please; restrain me by doing whatever you wish.

You who will torture me will now see that I have greater power than you.”

To him Dacian, mad with rage, replied such words.

Again the commander spoke, gnashing like a bear:

“Stop answering a ruler in this way, Vincent.

Do not set your mind against a mighty torrent.

The Roman axe will quickly free me from these cares;

my sword meets offences and punishes them.

But I have taken thought for you and chastised you with mild warning.

I spare your youth, unwilling to employ harsher means.

[Col. 1304A] While I deal mercifully, let Jupiter’s image be exalted:

make a vow to great Jupiter, whether with incense or a lamb.

But if you scatter salutary words of one who spares you to the winds,

worse things must be done to you without delay.”

The martyr replied: “In vain, Dacian, is it repeated so often

that I should change my resolve through fear of your tortures, contrary to right and salvation.

This has never been the outcome for a strong combatant.

As I have lived, and as I have told you that I live,

so I expect to die, yielding to no pain.

For in exchange for a good death there remains for me an honourable crown [variant: *habenda*, ‘to be possessed’],

which surpasses your laurel and is above gold— [Note: In Migne, *habenda* is printed above *restat*.]

a crown which you now despise; but for you there is everlasting punishment.”

The leader of wickedness paused a little, considering these words.

[Col. 1304B] While he debated in a thousand directions what he should do,

1245 he finally chose what seemed stronger and final:

to burn him alive, placed upon iron plates, with flames.

To complete the course, an iron engine was again made,

with its ribs serrated, as the enemy had commanded;

and they piled brands and devouring flames beneath.

The judge ordered him to be loosed and rolled there;

but first he afflicted him with salt, which he pressed into the wounds.

We read that he, so treated, was born while his father was a consul.

Neither the flower of youth nor the glory of nobility

led him into the snares of crimes, nor abundance of wealth.

Wisely restraining the flesh while still an adolescent,

he renounced the world and turned his heart and eyes from it,

preferring to follow the teaching of all righteousness

and to become naked, so that the enemy might not hold him.

[Col. 1304C] Amid the conflicts of the flesh he cast off garments;

he escaped the enemy’s hands sound, without a garment.

But luxurious flesh, though born of an illustrious father,

keeps the seductive garment; it preferred to suffer these things

rather than, with body subjected to vain prosperity,

endure in the abyss of fire.

Behold, now men torture a man, and do not shrink back;

the bloody flame rages, the flesh crackles, the salt snaps and burns;

yet he remains unmoved, wholly above the sky;

and, with all the strength he can, yearning toward heaven in prayer and gaze,

he shows by his bearing whose minds are heated with passion,

and gives thanks to God amid these afflictions.

Meanwhile the judge asks what is to become of the martyr,

whom those returning to Dacian report to be unharmed.

[Col. 1304D] Moreover, still endowed with such strength as before,

because he not only does not cease but is still more resolute,

he is astonished and says: “He is a magician who has overcome such things;

but there remains for the magician a vast abyss to be overcome,

a Tartarean lake, a foul and dark prison,

which knows no light, where day never dawns without night.

Within is a devouring worm; this is another labyrinth of mine.

Let him be kept here, he who would now die more advantageously.

Let him live, and let no help whatsoever be afforded him.

Let food and drink be absent; let mankind be far away and removed.

To live thus is a grievous kind of death: only let him be strong.

I would always have our rebel endure in this place;

for the life of one living thus is nothing but his own death.

Let cruel power add unusual potsherds,

[Col. 1305A] by whose fragments the wounded flesh of the recumbent man may suffer,

and, whenever he changes his side, let a blade be ready on every side.

Ordered to be shut up there, hear what he sees and hears.

This hated place immediately becomes Paradise,

and its disgraceful entrances shine with heavenly light;

there is an angelic assembly; the place is filled with brightness.

At their service, while the pain of evils flees,

he hears these words sung by the angelic choir:

‘Look, Vincent, by whose mighty power

steadfastness of mind has been granted you amid these torments.

He who gave you strength and salvation amid punishments

promises the palm to the victor and an end to your labor.

Be secure: behold, he will be our companion.’

The terrified guard leaps up at so great a song;

but, uncertain in mind whether the door had been opened,

[Col. 1305B] they hasten in, and, seeing what it was, worship.

The place of horror becomes a house of faith, a hall of beauty.

Crowds gather, faithfully, from the whole city.

Love scatters them abroad; the cry of praise strikes heaven.

They burst through the doors; but those who come nearer

rejoice, with tears, to fix their eyes upon the crevices;

and, as they watch and desire to see more closely,

the saint addresses them thus: “God works these things.

What was a place of punishment is now a delightful dwelling.

Instead of its oppressive stench, we are filled with a sweet fragrance.

Here violets bloom; my light is brighter than the sun.

The heavenly court, as you may now know,

1246 remains here, dwells here, serves me, and enriches this place.

Therefore I command that these things concerning me be reported to the wicked tyrant.

[Col. 1305C] Let him now devise; let him keep watch lest he be overcome.

The more fiercely he burns, the more my praise and glory will increase,

so that none of it may diminish; whatever he can do or possesses, let him add it.”

The command is carried out at once; in order everything is reported to him:

how great a light shines there, and what the martyr says to them.

At this speech the judge says: “I know that I am now conquered.

Yet let him be brought back to a bed, and, when restored there,

after the pleasant gifts of rest we shall subject him to punishment.

Let a little recovered repose soften him,

and let the flesh to be tortured again rest, so that pain may increase.”

Why, blind mind, do you rage, anxious with deceitful cares?

Why do you deliberate with yourself, heart blinded from all light?

Why do you sigh wickedly? What madness has driven you to this wrath?

You promise harsh things; but God, being gentle, promises mild things.

You make him a mangled corpse; but the Triune and One does not so will.

[Col. 1305D] For, when rest has been granted and he has been released by blessed death,

our most celebrated hero is raised to the heights.

Thus the athlete of God, granted passage from respite into rest,

deserved to be raised above the sky from a soft bed.

When these events were published abroad, the whole country rushed there

with zeal of excessive devotion and with a devoted mind.

What breast, however hard, would not be moved by such sweet effects?

Whose mind would not be bent by love for this flock?

One comes to weep; another delights to touch his wounds.

One standing near weeps; another, guilty in conscience, prays at a distance.

The devout love of one pressing close gives kisses to his feet.

Another snatches a little from his garment in hope of relics,

thinking it should be preserved as a treasure in gold;

what blood had stained, devout care made sacred for itself.

[Col. 1306A] Who could now set forth in words the judge’s horror

and excessive grief over these things? What favorable wind could carry me?

A heavy gale swells; flee, lest you perish, my ship.

Keep to familiar shores, lest, if the reins are let loose,

the waves, heavier and deeper, prevail.

A small alder-wood boat endures less than an iron pine ship.

I, who cannot endure the waves of the sea, cling to land.

Let my small skiff run close to land;

lest I offend more grievously, I shall leave greater matters behind.

I shall say what remains; the harbor nearby gives me hope.

Now he does not know what to do, nor does the judge yet rest.

Hideous and bloodless, like a serpent with broken teeth,

the wretch rages here and there, since madness burns him.

With distorted countenance he fills all the halls with tumult,

and, roaring horribly, the madman resounded with such words:

[Col. 1306B] “Wretched me! What shall I do? Who inflicted the wound I bear?

I restored him, to be given to death, with drink and food;

moreover I added this, and caused him to rest on a bed;

and what he possesses as a praiseworthy corpse is my gift.

What was this mind of mine? Alas, wretched, foolish, mad man that I am,

I do not know what is fitting—I honor what the law condemns.

And I have done what is never granted by my law.

With what face shall I behold one willingly dead?

The moderation of the laws condemns every sacrilegious person.

I who know the law have wickedly fostered what is against the law.

But because these gifts were not given him with good intention,

and because all this happened to me contrary to my wish,

it remains for me to show toward what favorable Jupiter I am tending.

It would be inhuman to bury this profane body.

[Col. 1306C] Therefore let him be food for dogs, to delight Dacian.

Let a beast carry off the man excluded from earth for the use of its belly.

Though our law permits ravens there to fasten their beaks;

let him endure nightly dew and the heat of day;

and when the flesh has decayed, let a beast seize his torn entrails.

Let a harsh smell betray the wretch whom a beast gnaws;

and let the attentive wolf, whatever wind promises him,

1247 direct his course here; let a lion tear him, a bear scatter him.

Anything whatsoever is permitted, since dead flesh will say nothing;

it will yield in any direction, having lost its skill.”

Why, wretch, do you rave? This madness is deceitful and empty.

Why do you devise evil, evil mind devoid of reason?

Why do you wickedly hope to endure what you cannot?

He commands the stars, against whom you wish to be rebellious.

He calls the things that are absent and sees them as though present.

[Col. 1306D] He commands the beasts, whom you do not now revere.

God the Maker uses his creation according to his rights.

He turns the rage and hunger of lions into every good.

The raven, servant of his servants, is accustomed to be their servant.

That which lacks reason is subject to him and obeys him;

yet you resist, though reason has preferred you to these things.

He who wages war against God seeks in vain

to make His servants serve ungovernable rage and anger;

for the divine hand quickly changes whatever Dacian prepares,

and whatever he thinks he will do.

And he heaped honor upon the body exposed outside.

Behold, the raven that harmed the world washes it clean a second time;

formerly a server of the righteous, now also their guardian.

For this bird, sitting near and not departing thence,

[Col. 1307A] is given as a guard: it serves, fears, and reveres;

it grieves over the saint and makes something like a lament.

And terrible wild beasts feared the fragile raven.

He terrifies them with his wings—spiritual guardianship.

A monstrous wolf, driven by an empty belly,

as soon as it saw the head, turned its jaws far away from it;

and, bowing its head in the manner of one rendering honor,

contrary to nature, it cared for the body.

1248 But the faithless mind, the mind of the criminal, cannot endure this,

nor does it favor this course, but attributes everything to magic.

And since it can no longer sustain a struggle with earth,

it prepares a war of water, to be conquered in each conflict.

Earth had been made illustrious by signs, air, and the fury of fire;

[Col. 1307B] water is the fourth element remaining to wash away the limbs.

He must be confounded through each of the bodies of the world,

so that the universe may leave nothing unavenged against the fool.

He orders him, weighed down by a heavy mass, to be placed aboard a ship

and the dead man’s body to be buried in the sea,

so that, since neither ravenous nor beastly rage can prevail,

[Col. 1308A] perhaps even sea-monsters may achieve more with divine aid.

But it does not proceed thus, for the sea does not obey him;

and, sunk in the deep, he returns earlier and more swiftly

than the ship, which wind helps and youthful strength propels.

That the man could do this after death I do not think wonderful,

since, if heavenly power is the wind, he is the sailor of the ship.

Its crime accomplished, the wicked little vessel hastened,

gliding to land as though to report great joys.

The executioner exults; but here too the martyr is victor,

whom he thinks swallowed up, though he already knew his harbor.

Woman, a fragile thing, is often manly in faith.

A rustic, warned in a dream, was bidden to seek the shore

and give the martyr’s bones burial in a humble grave;

but he fears and hesitates, and avoids the business of faith;

fearing that he is unworthy to lift the venerable pledge,

[Col. 1308B] the martyr stands before a matron of powerful religion,

appears, teaches her what to do, and she obeys.

What the man does not dare, the devout woman gladly seeks.

In the dark of night she comes to the sea with watchful care,

seeks, seizes what she has found, and gives it a tomb.

[Col. 1307]

# The Passion of Saint Agnes, Virgin and Martyr, Begins

(From the aforementioned manuscript of Saint Marianus of Auxerre.) (G)*

# Brief Notice

It is found printed at Frankfurt in 1624, namely by the Wechel press, with Daniel and David Aubry and Clement Schleich. It appears in book thirty of the *Adversaria* or miscellaneous commentaries of Caspar Barth, folio 1448, but more fully than it survives in the manuscript of Saint Marianus of Auxerre. Of the eleven chapters into which it is divided in Barth, nearly the last two chapters are lacking in that manuscript; these we have appended to this Saint Marianus text. Moreover, Barth states that he received this poem from the most learned Jesuit priest Heribert Rosweyde, who maintained that its author was Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans. This may rightly be confirmed from the manuscript of Saint Marianus. Therefore, the fact that this poem is appended at the end of the works of Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, published at Douai in 1630, should not prevent its attribution to Hildebert; for several other poems are likewise inserted there which, on the evidence of many manuscripts of the highest authority, are unquestionably Hildebert’s, and which are specifically attributed to him in several manuscripts of the highest authority.

1249 # Chapter One

[Note: [Col. 1307C] In Barth’s edition this poem is divided into twelve chapters. We have thought it proper here to note the variant readings of Barth’s edition [Col. 1308C] from our own text, taken from the Marianus manuscript.]

[Col. 1307C]

May holy Agnes gild the pen of her writer,

and drench my tongue with nectar-bearing dew.

[Note: “Her.”] I endeavor to portray her martyrdom in metrical

[Col. 1308C] flowers, so that her holy passion may teach faith.

The city of Rome flourished at the birth of the maiden spoken of before,

and, as if by this mirror, the whole world shone.

The girl arose and sprinkled Rome with a new light,

[Col. 1309A] illustrious in lineage, lovely in face, beautiful in faith.

As the radiant flashing of the moon buries the stars,

so the virgin surpasses her companions by rosy beauty.

Nature’s favor poured so many gifts upon her

that, after its gifts, it was as though a beggar.

She imitates, displays, and equals stars, privet-blossoms, and roses:

fiery in brightness, clear in brow, red in cheeks.

Her eyes shine forth like stars, her head like the rainbow,

her brow like snow, her face like a rose, her teeth like ivory.

Beyond all these shining mirrors of gifts, glorious to all,

the nobler jewel of faith blessed her:

a virgin in sex, a man in deed, golden-haired,

gray in judgment, small in body, great in faith.

# Chapter II

For the title of faith, when her Passion crimsoned Rome,

[Col. 1309B] it was the third year after the tenth [Note: “Decius,” incorrectly].

When, after completing her studies, she prepares to return,

the prefect’s son fixes his gaze upon her; she pleases him.

The flower of her face, the light of her eyes,

the fleece of her brow, the purple of her cheek, and ivory of tooth entice the youth.

This beauty strikes back the young man’s gaze, strikes him within;

thence love takes nourishment for itself.

Love’s murmuring of cares creeps into his breast;

[Note: “The light of reason, darkened with dust, is dulled.”] his mind, frustrated by its wound, is dulled in reason.

Armed with deceits, words, and gifts, the lover tries

to pluck the lilies of virginal flesh.

He tries her with prayers, approaches with gifts, wears her down with craft;

neither prayer, nor deceits, nor love’s skill has any force.

[Note: “He promises estates, boasts of beauty and lineage.”] He promises rewards, boasts of beauty, extols his lineage;

[Col. 1309C] rewards, beauty, and lineage found no place. [Note: “Estates.”]

He loves; she hates. He begs; she resists.

He gives; she scorns. He desires; she refuses.

Every frenzy conspires [Note: “unworthy”] to injure chastity;

but that blooming chastity remains without stain.

Chastity stands unmoved; the lover’s love is mocked:

she had rejected hearing sounds such as these.

# Chapter III

“O storm of peace! O leader of death! O shame of the world!

Stop your words, break off delay, depart far away.

1250 What do you give? What do you [Note: “hope? What do you foolishly sow?”] look for? What do you foolishly seek without gain?

Your hopes are gifts without substance; your labor is toil without harvest.

Another lover binds me, whom the nobility of lineage,

the grace of beauty, and the height of wealth [Note: “will prefer”] set above you.

[Col. 1309D] From whose fingers I claim gems for myself,

from whose eyes light, from whose mouth honeycomb.

In his bridal chambers, at his tables, in his halls,

his lyres sing, honey flows, [Note: “stars.”] purple gleams.

Flower, incense, and bird smile, breathe fragrance, and sing in his gardens:

the flower smiles, the incense gives fragrance, the bird plays the lyre.

He is he at whose beauty the orb of the moon, the circle of the sun,

and the flame of the stars are accustomed to marvel.

[Col. 1310A] This radiant one surpasses the moon’s rays, the sun’s brilliance,

and all heaven’s lamps.

All the splendid necklaces of the stars receive,

from his mirror, whatever honor they possess.

He has adorned my arms with bracelets, my breast

with crystals, my neck with a torque, my cheeks with beauty,

my limbs with a cyclas garment, my hand with gems, [Note: “the head with jeweled garlands.”] my head and ears

[Note: “with papyri.”] with sapphires, my table with nectar, my bed with flowers.

He is the one who enriched heaven with stars, earth with grass,

the air with birds, and the sea with fish.

Whose fragrance, whose touch, whose [Note: “beauty.”] beauty heals the sick,

raises the dead, and surpasses the stars.

To him [Note: “I dedicate myself and owe betrothal.”] I dedicate myself; to him I owe betrothal; to him I subject

my mind, render service, and keep faith—

he who does not blacken snow-white chastity with any blemish.

[Col. 1310B] Rather, with chaste love he preserves chaste beauty for the chaste.

O celebrated condescension of a chaste bridegroom! His kisses are chaste,

his touch sacred, his love honorable.

I follow him, confess him, and seek him by night and day;

I follow with the mind, confess with the mouth, seek with prayer.

# Chapter IV

Her words ended; madness torments the youth, anxiety constricts him,

grief tortures him, [Note: “deceit acts; the virgin’s love burns him.”] and love for the virgin burns him.

He yields, goes away, feigns illness, and the lover disguises

the entire enticement of his frenzy under the name of fever.

His breast, cheeks, and eyes feign fever:

his breast pants, his cheek is pale, his eye dim.

His father learns everything through medical counsel;

he soothes his son, probes his heart, promises help.

[Col. 1310C] He rises and goes, pouring prayers into the virgin’s ear [Note: “ear”],

and seconding his prayers with golden gifts.

By giving and beseeching, the prefect’s contrivances gain nothing:

the gifts lack weight; the breeze carries away the prayers.

The virginal purity refuses to violate itself—

the token of a compact owed to its first lover.

1251 # Chapter V

The prefect asks a servant who is the lover whose love

Agnes [Note: “extols.”] struggles against; he instructs him.

He tells how the maiden has been deceived by so great a fraud

as to think that she has entered into a compact with Christ.

At these words the judge is altogether delighted, and suggests to her parents

that she is guilty of death.

For, because the virgin’s parents shone with a famous name,

[Col. 1310D] he fears to use unlawful violence against her.

There was a law by which the Roman sword punished Christ’s servants;

by this artifice the judge cloaks his crime.

Therefore madness ordered her to be brought before him; she smiles at the command.

[Note: “He joined in and smiles; the virgin is summoned and present.”] She is summoned and present.

He softens and rebukes her; now he flatters, now terrifies her;

now he rains down entreaties, now thunders threats.

But neither does the dew of entreaties corrupt her sincere ears,

[Col. 1311A] nor does his thunder shake her mind.

The judge, finding that he was ploughing the shore, and seeing that

he was lying to the Lord, brings forth these seeds:

“If your chastity wishes to preserve this chastity [perhaps “brightness”],

you must celebrate the sacred rites of renowned Vesta.

Vesta seeks those whom blooming purity adorns;

the virgin’s altar seeks virginal hands.”

[Note: “The virgin replied thus.”] The virgin said to this: “I do not pray to stone,

I do not venerate wood; I do not know Vesta; I despise gods.

Your Vesta is indeed a stone, whom a golden form falsely represents

to you as a goddess by name.

No distinction consecrates her as divinity;

no life supplies any perception to her.

She lacks the touch of hands, the sound of a tongue, hearing of ears,

[Col. 1311B] sight of brow, and smell of nostrils.

She neither feels through flesh, nor sees with brow, nor smells

with nostril, nor hears with ear, nor speaks with mouth.

# Chapter VI

The judge says in reply: “Your childish age pleads for you

and postpones punishment.

But why do we deceive time with barren speech? Behold,

there are two things which I command; do whichever you choose.

Either you will perform the prescribed sacred rites, or, made a prostitute,

you will incur the stain of chastity, wholly consecrated to criminals.”

With this reply she wounds the man’s mind:

“You are mistaken and plough the shore with barren naming.

Neither the coal of the altar defiles faith’s brightness,

nor does any lover defile the flower of the flesh;

[Col. 1311C] Christ consecrated both to himself, body and faith,

keeping the body from stain and faith from the enemy.

This one is indeed my husband, my guardian, and my author:

husband of my mind, guardian of my body, author of my riches.

For Christ [Note: “is hope and light and”] is the hope, light, and medicine of his own:

hope for the wretched, light for the blind, medicine for the guilty.

With him as my leader punishment does not break me,

nor does the sword frighten me, deceit conquer me, or storm shake me.

He is the one who enriches light with Phoebus’s lamp

and honors night’s journey with the mirror of the moon.

[Note: “Who with saffron-colored...”] 1252 He purples the smiling gardens with saffron-colored flower,

makes the grove ripple with foliage, crowns the fields with harvest.

To portray him for you [Note: “To portray him briefly...”] in brief words: he knows

[Col. 1311D] all things, orders each thing, and can do all things.

How vast the field of his titles is, tongue cannot unfold,

mind cannot know, right hand [Note: “pen.”] cannot write.

Since this my Jesus shines with the gold of so many gifts,

no grace ennobles your gods.

Your gods neither live in mind nor move in body,

nor breathe with life nor shine with divinity.

They lack motion, not feet; perception, not body; touch,

not hands; words, though not mouth.

# Chapter VII

The peace of this speech kindles the prefect’s anger into flames;

[Col. 1312A] anger drove his hand to crime. [Note: “the man.”]

Anger orders Agnes to be mocked, handed over to procurers,

scourged, and stripped of garments.

Preparations are made; an impious hand strips the girl’s clothing:

yet, naked, the girl deceives the man’s gaze.

Such grace poured itself forth in her virginal hair

that her hair shadowed her whole body with honor.

So famous a marvel could not soften the madman’s mind,

nor does the chaste cause move him.

But, adding new spurs to his commands, he incites his servants,

heaping threats upon the orders already given.

Therefore the result follows the threats: the chaste virgin begins

to be dragged to the enclosure of an impure house.

At her entrance the wicked cell pours forth and expels

[Note: “It wholly emerges.”] darkness and the stench of filth.

[Col. 1312B] Christ makes the cell serene with angelic brightness;

the light demonstrates that the Author of light is present.

Here is an angel, there light, there fragrance:

the angel consecrates the cave, the light illuminates it, fragrance fills it.

The virgin pours out prayers; her vows do not fail her as she prays

that her sacred limbs may be covered: [Note: “a robe.”] a shining mantle is there.

It corresponds so precisely to the measure of her body

that you would think an angelic hand had fitted it on.

O happy condescension of Christ! Under whose guidance that chastity

swims across such shoals of lust.

No lover violated her; but, worshipping the flashing rays

of light, each returned praying.

# Chapter VIII

[Col. 1312C] Now the love of the young men had grown numb, when the instigator of the crime,

the young man, flies hither swiftly to fulfill his desires.

Entering the place, he separates himself from his companions and enters the cave

alone, armed [Note: “by the art of song.”] with artifice, fury, and deceit.

He had scarcely begun to use his eyes at the entrance of the light,

when the image of sacred light strikes his sight.

The lover despises so great a beauty and grants

that singular brilliance no title of honor.

Ignorant of delay, he rushes into the abyss of the intervening brightness

and commands his hand to proceed nearer.

And when lust wished to touch the sacred flesh with his hands,

death carried him off, avenging the crime.

The companions’ hope for the young man’s return is disappointed: he

does not return; the Fates hold him in their own fetter.

1253 Why the young man’s return is delayed so long, one

[Col. 1312D] of his companions investigates; he enters the cell.

And while he surveys the cell with wandering eyes,

he sees the corpse, summons his companions, and begs help.

All the lustful young men flock hither [perhaps “hither”], and a cry

arises; murmurs resound; hearts [Note: “by the art of song.”] resound [perhaps “are stunned”].

Report of the strange event wounds the father’s ears; terrified,

he flies [Note: “he flies hither”] hither, with the city following the man.

His eyes give way to tears; grief troubles his heart;

his cheek is soaked with rain; his hair is torn by the nail.

His mouth, place, and mind are pierced through; tear, tongue,

[Col. 1313A] rage, falsehood, sounding and heavy [Note: “grief poured forth”] aid him.

The father’s tearful voice ascribes the extinguished flower

of the young man’s body to Agnes’s deceits.

He imputes the death to her, as though the virgin

had used her deceits to bring the young man to death.

Agnes said this: [Note: “O, if by lots...”] “You err if you believe

that our hand used lots to bring you harm.

Why the avenging angel harvested this man alone

from so great a harvest of young men has an appropriate cause.

This light struck the minds of the young men; but the honor of this light

[Note: “Not the mind.”] did not touch his mind.

When he wickedly tried to touch me with an impure hand,

[Note: “A worthy vengeance expelled the crime.”] worthy vengeance cast out the wickedness.”

The governor replied: “If you restore my son to me alive,

this deed will give weight to your word.”

[Col. 1313B] The virgin replies: [Note: “After these things, according to merits...”] “I do not owe this work to your merits;

such grace differs from your faith.

But because the time has come for Christ’s bright power

to come forth into light, receive what you ask.

Therefore now let that company of young men withdraw from the cell,

so that I may be more earnest in my prayers.”

She spoke: at this word the whole flower of young men immediately flies outside,

and the blessed virgin pours forth prayers.

The grace of her wishes smiles upon her prayers; the dead man rises,

affirming divinity worthy of a torch.

Jesus sounds upon his tongue; Christ is

honeycomb in his mouth, light in his heart, melody in his mouth.

# Chapter IX

The novelty inflames the worshippers of the temples; care excites

their minds, fear shakes them, anger burns.

[Col. 1313C] All [Note: “All ... alone.”] conspire against the one woman; they cry

that she deserves death and is guilty of magical arts.

The joy of his son’s safety assails the father’s mind,

and the savage winter of grief is calmed.

Now rage grows numb; now [Note: “the wave.”] the anger of threats subsides;

now he wishes to grant pardon, now prepares to be merciful.

He wishes to spare the snow-white flower, unless law, the mob,

and the band of priests oppose him.

Piety is overcome and broken by the storm of so many things,

and the kindly mind does not bring its work to completion.

[Note: “Yet no one departs hence.”] Yet a clamour departs from here, burdening and honoring

[Note: “Aspasium with the dew of laws.”] Aspasius by the law and in his proper place.

Bending the reins of law to the people’s nod,

[Col. 1313D] he unjustly performs the office of governor.

While popular madness presses him concerning the virgin’s death,

1254 he orders her to be given to the flames.

[Note: “The priest girds himself to accomplish the sacred crime...”] The priest girds himself to accomplish the crime; he kindles the fire;

[Col. 1314A] [Note: “Dry wood kindles the pyre of straw.”] she is given amid the flames.

The hungry fire feeds upon sulphur’s aid;

the bloody flame boils and overflows excessively.

# Chapter X

O crime! That flesh which had moved no fire

of enticement is given as food amid fires.

Yet the present burning accomplishes nothing against her;

the flame, forgetting its strength, does not know itself.

It does not dare employ its own strength against the virgin,

but seems rather to sympathize with and pity her.

Yet a fiery globe envelops in its own jurisdiction

certain men who feed the flame with sulphur.

Two things there amaze me: a wicked leader and a devout fire;

the judge was unjust, the flame just.

[Col. 1314B] The priest burns with desire to punish the virgin; the fire

is cold and inert, and has no heat.

[Note: What follows is supplied from Barth’s edition, mentioned in the summary of this poem, and from the Douai edition of 1630 mentioned above.] In the midst of the flame, sprinkled with a cloud of heavenly

nectar, Agnes spoke these words:

“Christ, to you I proclaim praises; I fulfill my vows,

offer thanks, and pour forth prayers.

Your sweetness, your love, and your grace

fortify, cherish, and preserve me from my enemy.

With you as guide I despised the torturer’s cords, the Charybdis

of lust, the force of flame, and the threats of young men.

For you, Christ, I endured so many bitter things; but behold,

just rewards worthily correspond to my labor.

Now I see what I hoped for, hold what I loved,

touch what I desired, and receive what I purchased.”

The virgin mouth’s voice flies to Christ,

[Col. 1314C] filling his nostrils with the fragrance of its incense.

At her voice all the cruel violence of the flame

grew numb, so that the fire’s odor no longer lived.

The fire, therefore, not daring to breathe, lays aside

its fury, loses its power, and lowers its threats.

# Chapter XI

The new grace of the sign disturbs the crowd. The people see the sign,

envy it, and raise a roar.

The people press Aspasius to crime; therefore he orders

the sword to drink innocent blood.

The torturer’s hand hastens the crime; hungering for punishment,

the sharp point arms the hand.

The virgin makes the executioner’s sword drunk with her blood;

the purple of poured-out blood paints the ground.

[Col. 1314D] A threefold distinction adorns Agnes’s merit with beauty:

a pure body, rosy suffering, steadfast faith.

Agnes claims for herself the Lamb who took away the world’s sin

by these titles of virtues.

[Col. 1315]

# On the Finding of the Holy Cross

(Nowhere published. From the aforementioned manuscript of Saint Marianus of Auxerre, the sole manuscript in which we have found this poem.)

[Col. 1315A] 1255 The gentle Emperor Constantine, not made slothful by honor,

when he felt hostile troops near, courageous in body and spirit,

and when he was almost perishing from fear,

beholds in sleep that through which all fear flees.

A most excellent heavenly vision is shown to the sorrowful;

a heavenly victory follows as witness to what it is.

A shining cross flashes in heaven, a cross without concealment:

for he sees this sign as light, not as wood,

and written above it: “By this you shall be victorious in battle.”

Awakening, he speaks to his servants; a small cross is prepared,

borne before the army; the enemy flees, and victory is won.

Having experienced the power of the cross, but uncertain what it was,

he commands inquiry and summons Helena concerning it.

Thus Constantine’s devout mother is made anxious

[Col. 1315B] for the cross and nails, though the place is not known to her;

she takes neither food nor sleep, and glory is unknown,

nor does she receive rest until Jerusalem is reached.

She burns with desire and searches whether she may deserve what she seeks.

Then the scribes are sought, and experts in the Law;

while the question is debated, those thought to know disclose it.

Thus Judas is brought forward; he denies what is asked.

Helena is troubled: she thunders threats, while he deliberates;

he is silent, she speaks; he pleads, she threatens.

Since he fears little the resounding thunder, she threatens

that he shall be handed over to destruction and orders him shut up without bread.

This man, a Jew skilled in their law,

inherited their rites with his blood—not to mention their morals.

The straight line of his fathers, while his mind was ignorant of his mothers,

gave him the ability to understand where the hidden cross lay.

[Col. 1315C] But Christ wished to glorify his wounds,

placing them in the middle of the world to stand as a light.

Therefore Judas, worn out by hunger, made true confession.

He is drawn out and eats; ordered to seek the sacred things, he obeys.

He goes and investigates the holy places, praying to the God of Jacob:

“If you justly and devoutly desire Mary’s offspring to reign,

reveal today to your own the highest secrets of wisdom.”

Praying thus he weeps; weeping, he labors by digging.

While tears flow with sweat, he is refreshed by a wondrous fragrance,

which gives him strength, as though by a liquid.

If you should compare balsams, flowers, or anything breathing fragrance,

you compare earthly things with heavenly.

From the cross and nails flows that sweet fragrance;

that breath gives hope and relief by its scent.

That it may at once be a sign of the standard and strength to him,

[Col. 1315D] he learns the power of the cross when the earth trembles beneath it.

Like one believing before faith, he cries out there,

declaring that he who was earlier slain, this crucified man,

is the true God, whom the machinery of the world serves.

The queen stands seeing this, trusting that she will see greater things;

she praises believing Judas and herself marvels at the marveling man.

[Col. 1316A] He finds three crosses together, lifts them, returns, and hesitates

which is the Lord’s cross. Now joyful, now almost grieving,

he seems not to possess Christ’s standards, though he holds them.

He prays that it may show which is Christ’s and which the thieves’;

and Christ’s mercy completes the gift of the cross.

Why delay? Without delay, at that very hour

1256 a dead man is seen being carried, and all the people run together.

Then he speaks, and weeps: “The occasion has come for your sign,

Christ, to be glorified—reverend, sweet, benign—

the sacred treasure, for which, when gold is despised,

you may reveal yourself to the devout, so that love may burst into songs.

[Col. 1316B] Weapons by which you once conquered the strong one, sin, hell, and death:

let there be praise to you, and strength to this.”

When he has spoken these words, while the bier stands and hope stands firm,

while the dead man lies, as before, beneath the two crosses,

the third, Christ’s, brings him life and glory to itself.

Praise is offered jointly to Christ; hope is restored;

love grows warm again; the shout strikes heaven more deeply;

and without delay the author sounds from every mouth.

They render the praises due, recount the deeds,

condemn unbelief, and acclaim Mary with her offspring;

the Son is honored above all, the Mother loved.

They call these life, praise them, bless them.

The cross, sanctified by the Lamb, had earlier conquered him;

therefore the same cross, glorified by so many signs, tortures him.

[Col. 1316C] That venomous one, hating Christ and the cross,

grieves that the latter is revealed and the former magnified.

Troubled by the cross, the enemy of the cross cries aloud,

taking on no visible form but hanging in the air:

“By Judas I formerly achieved victorious destruction;

now, through you, O Judas, conquered, I suffer destruction.

After Constantine, I shall set up an alien to the faith,

whom I wish to act; but he will be harsh to Christ and to you.

He will subject you to himself; a beast will be your leader.

He will treat you cruelly, strike you, torment you—

the plague of wickedness, worst to himself, enemy of all.”

Thus he rages; thus he threatens Judas harshly,

promising a tyrant instead of a great king.

What is Helena to do, now that her second wish is fulfilled?

When she sees her wishes, there is no one to make her know

[Col. 1316D] what she desires by what she sees; she is as if in Paradise,

so that the taste of love reveals itself outwardly through signs.

Now she stands, now prays, now worships the signs of salvation;

now contemplates, now sings psalms, now weeps.

She weeps and applauds together; now joy closes her tears;

she applauds everything she herself sees or hears.

[Col. 1317A] As she loves Christ, or prefers him above all,

so she praises what is praised, or loves what is loved.

At the queen’s expense a vessel for life-giving medicine is made,

which the brilliance of silver covers with fitting workmanship.

Judas the Jew—if you strip the covering from the name—

changing his surname, now fulfills the omen of his name,

by believing in Christ and confessing the mother with her child.

Thus he is baptized, thus rejoices, thus renewed.

When he was born he was Judas; but when reborn,
you would call him not Cyriacus, but Quiriacus.

Nor did he merely wash away the stain of impiety in the font,

but cultivated piety in study, work, and desire.

For why should I recount his uprightness? His sobriety?

His poverty? His weeping? His gravity?
