He crucified the flesh with its vices together with the Crucified One.

[Col. 1317B] A living sacrifice of God, he dies to himself and lives in him;

he hangs with Christ hanging, suffers with Christ suffering.

Since, remembering the Crucified One, he has a heart as though pierced through,

he bears the cross in the flesh; but love offers consolations.

Christ’s light yoke, Christ’s light burden, becomes light to him through love,

1257 while he wipes away the ash and clears the cloud from his heart,

and restrains wandering impulses beneath a fixed law.

He embraces these, removes those, governs others;

he judges some worthy, some worthless, some evil.

The people marvel at him, praise him, revere him;

all both love him and proclaim him worthy of the bishopric.

At last he becomes father of the city and nourishes it,

while, made bishop, he regulates a bishop’s conduct.

What he does he urges others to do; what he forbids, he threatens against;

[Col. 1317C] for you build less if you say what your conduct denies.

Helena, anxious but partly fulfilled in her desires,

asks about the nails, since none has yet been found.

Him whom she previously compelled by a threatening voice,

she now asks for help with gentle prayers, thus addressing Quiriacus:

“Since by the cross you enlarge my joys, for the cross I render

innumerable thanks; but I still seek the fastenings.

I now possess my wish concerning the cross, but not the whole cross.

The nails are no small part of the cross; but add, father,

the nails, stars of light; let the mother possess her pledges.

While the nails are lacking, I have denied myself full joy.”

The bishop, persuaded by these words and compelled by excessive devotion,

bringing back good hope and seeking the fastenings with himself,

finds them and shows them to Helena, for which she repays him.

[Col. 1317D] A fitting service—if you ask what kind—was gracious.

Giving kisses, she weeps; falling down, she worships utterly.

Thus the pious queen, having obtained her vows,

grew more in goodness, despised herself more, and despised all things more.

She no longer indulges herself; she now prefers hardships to soft things.

She bears it as unworthy that she should be in a palace, that she should be in the fire;

she tramples upon queenship, to which the Fates promise ruin;

she humbles imperial majesty, which she perceives burdened with cares;

she scorns dominion, she who sees the deaths of kings;

she shudders at the summit by which the exalted mind swells.

Her honour is to seem lowly to all, fear without fear,

to become praise patiently endured, freedom restrained by law.

She calls herself unworthy, foul, and wicked,

to weep before the Cross, to touch holy things, to behold the sacred signs.

Thus pious, thus humble, thus splendid, and thus manly;

[Col. 1318A] thus guilty, thus barren, thus lowest, and thus contemptible to herself;

thus she condemns what she praised, rejects what she loved,

spurns adornment not prepared by virtue,

puts away the delights by which Eve destroyed all;

gold becomes worthless, the brilliance of gems is darkened,

sweetness turns bitter, beauty is abhorrent, downy softness grows stiff,

glory becomes foul, mourning pleases, action increases;

she restrains her tongue, governs her mind, knows no leisure;

her body wastes away, her flesh grows cold, her mind grows warm.

Christ grows sweet; beneath Christ’s love she rests;

shameless care is silent; that inward tumult falls.

While sense or desire lies buried away from things to be fled,

Eve yields to her husband, and does not harm her companion but obeys him;

the pious mind goes before, the flesh follows, conflict withdraws;

all things are pacified; mind and flesh are reconciled:

[Col. 1318B] thus life is lulled, thus dead to the world.

She who formerly wept in fear of hell and death

now languishes in love of the King of kings, now in love of the kingdom;

she burns to embrace and to break the bonds of flesh;

nor does she receive the physician unless she contemplates her friend.

The merciful Maker calls her at last; the mad one calls them chains.

Thus in a good lot she rejoices in a better crown.

By the queen’s merits and her piously repeated prayers,

the grace of the Trinity converted Constantine’s heart.

Thus, his sins and leprosy having been left behind at the font,

with the newness of his skin he is renewed by the garment of salvation.

That the Church’s peace, its eminence, and its glory increased—

this man laboured, this one contributed, that one brought to fulfilment:

for that same king granted Rome

[Col. 1318C] to the pontiff Sylvester, gave him the kingdom, and himself withdrew.

If you wish to know how this was done,

you seek volumes about the king contrary to the present purpose;

let the king be dismissed; let the praise of Quiriacus be resumed.

1258 If you seek a sign, he drives away diseases and malignity;

if you prefer life, under the bishop he leads the life of a hermit.

Cruel Julian seizes and confines this man, so great and such as he is—

a Catholic, a saint—himself an apostate and profane man.

What he wickedly undertook, he took up again as vomit after sacred things;

enlarged by demons, a demon made under a demon.

This raven insinuated himself beneath Constantine’s fleece of sheep;

this one is a wolf, that one a lamb; this one a pious king, that one a tyrant;

this one was given as a battle for the faith, a scourge for chaff:

once promised to grain, now sent to thresh it.

[Col. 1318D] For the dragon in Judas, formerly promising battles,

foreshadowed him, bore him, and spurred him on.

Entirely compounded of vices and nourished by crime,

he is now almost a portent, now a monument of the devil.

Prelacy gave him arrogance, glory nourishment,

abundance heat for his vices, and power to do evil gave him frenzy.

He disturbs the peaceful, oppresses the just, praises the unjust;

to the innocent criminal he gives honour, to the guilty he gives what is his;

he sees sad things as joyful, and rejoicing laughs at sorrowful things;

he loathes what should be pursued, follows wickedness, hates what should be loved;

and what is pious he punishes, punishes himself with blood shed [variant: *fortifies himself*].

Indeed, like a wild beast, he retains the habit of thirsting for blood—

he whose evils, set beside the good, shine forth, and those of Nero [variant: *Nero’s*],

[Col. 1319A] marvellous to say, make every inwardly wicked man appear preferable.

He disparages God, while praising the sacred rites of the gods;

and, himself wickedly submerged, he wishes to submerge the good of others.

He destroys Christ’s worshippers, restoring the cult of idols;

while he holds darkness, he flees the rays of light.

Blinded in face, he desires to blind those who see,

and, having gone out, forbids others wishing to enter.

Deprived of light, cast down from on high,

he wishes to overthrow those who stand and to darken the shining stars.

A portion of the serpent falling from the citadel of the heights,

he vainly seeks companions and prepares bread for them.

An extinguished coal, desiring to extinguish a living coal,

he prefers offerings to the gods to faith.

Now he commits horrors, now promises vain honours;

now by flattering words, now by harshness, he tries to bend men.

[Col. 1319B] Why are you troubled? Why do you gnash your teeth? Why are you enraged?

Why do you devise evils? Why, faithless man, do you seek empty things?

Though you may inflict a thousand deaths upon the man, with dreadful trial,

lest he be given over to death, he cherishes life and confesses it with his mouth.

A soldier cannot be separated from his leader, nor joined to another;

he calls this one king, proclaims him, blesses him.

He brings forth the inner lamp and places it beneath the light;

a bushel does not obscure it, but it shines from a height.

Flatteries and threats, causes of ruin to some,

do not touch his heart or break his strong breast.

He rejects low things for high, vain things for true;

he exchanges neither light for darkness nor Christ for a demon.

Established on a strong vein, not on sand,

founded on rock, he scorns tears with the flood.

If, Julian, you threaten waves of sea or weapons,

[Col. 1319C] his tranquil mind simultaneously scorns both.

If the flesh is beaten, the grain is stripped of chaff;

if it is burned, rust is thought to be removed;

if the old man is corrupted, another man is renewed;

strength weakens the one, suffering strengthens the other.

You can mutilate the body with the sword, burn it with fire,

but by tortures you do not penetrate the inner sanctuary of the mind.

Though all the elements prepare every torture with you,

while they accomplish nothing, all things become as though already nothing.

You cannot inflict as much as endurance can bear.

Carried away by hope of the prize, he is equal to every punishment;

he fears neither roasting, nor beating, nor being torn apart.

He hastens to punishments who hopes for joys through punishments;

he strives toward the prize which the goal of the race repays;

1259 contending in good hope, he hopes to rejoice in the crown.

[Col. 1319D] Whatever you do, torturer—by salt, flames, serpent, or blows—

inward hope recalls it all to honour and to the object of desire.

While you torture the saint, you turn tortures back upon yourself;

and because pressure is sweet to him, let it be hard to you.

He endures coals being placed beneath him as though you were giving dishes.

Pouring salt over the fat and promising severer things,

you support him with two offerings, that the victim may be acceptable:

seasoned more strongly by the force of salt, such a sacrifice tastes better.

Thus a field is made more acceptable and fertile—not foolishly fat—

for crops, if the ground is often ploughed;

if neglected, it bears brambles instead of fruit.

The torn field of flesh bears fruit a hundredfold;

flesh not afflicted bears guilt instead of virtue.

Brief is the anguish which an hour or a lifetime ends,

[Col. 1320A] and punishment is, as it were, light compared with that which vengeance prepares for the cruel.

Compared with the force of the heat that was to ravage you for ever,

Etna lacks heat; I think Vesuvius full of dew.

This is dreadful to the dreadful, fearful to the fearful;

this is due to you, if the cruel man deserves cruel things.

Thus invincible strength, while it scorns flames and blows,

afflicts its afflicter by suffering, and burns the one who burns it.

He grieves at the fires; he grieves that the martyr overcomes pains.

Let the punishment of hell be thus to see punishment scorned [variant: *itself*].

He rejoices in punishments; he is exhilarated by terrors;

by reason he conquers the one terrifying him, by faith the one striking him.

On the one hand considering punishments, on the other the pleasant seats of light,

he judges the slaughtered body to be nothing in comparison with paradise.

While he tastes good things beforehand, while the saint adores the rewards,

he neither feels punishment nor labours in enduring hardships.

[Col. 1320B] Within is a fire which vows foster without wood,

by which he thinks the burning of the flesh a dew without cold.

The fire of love first conquers the strength of burning,

which does not consume that upon which it acts, though it burns it.

Sighing to be relieved of the burden of bodily mass,

he burns to behold face to face the face of his Maker.

To cast nets before the sight of birds—what is it but laughter?

The light mind flies upward, free from the bird-catcher, toward its course.

The good athlete stands firm, constant in his quiet mind;

hope exults at the voice, and the voice resounds with praise.

As stretched strings are accustomed to give a better sound,

so, stretched by punishments, he renders the full honour of praise;

and as the furnace tests an earthen vessel by making it firm,

as by being crushed you know the heat and force of mustard,

and as through burning frankincense pours out fragrance everywhere,

[Col. 1320C] so both wound and fire become a distinguished fragrance.

But Julian is corrupted, tortured,

rages, pants, and is overcome—

this inhuman man, this most wicked man, this Julian.

What the wolf is to the Lamb, he becomes to Anne, mother of the martyr.

In like example, while she contends with manly mind,

the strong woman, first hanged or burned,

afflicted yet victorious, anticipates the peaceful goal.

That a mother might prepare blessed places for her approved son,

she, blessed, goes before him on high, to exalt him who is to be blessed.

Thus Ammon, that chief magician of the great tyrant,

when he sees this saint break the strength of those who inflict death,

and considers the gods to be nothing, and greets the faith,

confesses Christ and is beheaded for Christ.

[Col. 1320D] His mother crowned, Quiriacus, his hope made firm,

is strengthened more, rejoices more, and is more encouraged.

Therefore, shut up until the appointed hour, he reproves the torturers’ delay,

as though they were at fault in leaving him and the scourges.

Because he so fully presses fire, weapons, and poison,

because he fights in this way, all is thought a phantom.

The guilty mind, referring the matter of praise to the crimes of deceit,

is blinded by light and slain by the scent of virtue.

Thus he regards the signs as though they were produced by evil art,

1260 and thinks one fortified by the Cross skilled in magic [variant: *art*].

Now let the contest be touched on briefly;

now let the victor be appended in brief.

His right hand is cut off, he drinks lead, he is burned with fire,

[Col. 1321A] he is tormented by scourging, he crushes serpents, and then is killed.

Thus he deserved to become a martyr, thus to be held victor over the world,

thus to be exalted, thus to be glorified.

To him we owe that we possess the signs of salvation,

that we rejoice in the Cross, that we behold it and its nails.

He first raised up Christ’s banner, beneath which we go to Jerusalem,

coming through it to Him.

He showed to all the pearl so greatly and so long desired,

the shining gem, the gem that enriches the needy,

for which the pious man sells all things.

He scattered through the world that treasure, richer than a treasure of gold,

which an envious people had buried in the earth.

Through him the highest praise is bestowed; Virgil doubts

whether it can be worthily rendered in words by such great praises.

As he deserved to find the wood of wondrous power

through poverty, sweat, hunger, and piety,

[Col. 1321B] so through uprightness, hardships, anxiety,

and poverty we gain the benefit of the Cross.

No one returns to paradise through pleasure, arrogance, or frivolity;

none through laughter or riches.

We who fall through pride return to the heights through humility;

having eaten, we lost what we recover by the path of hunger.

This finder of the Cross, upon which our Redeemer was fixed,

healed wounds and, dying, gave us life.

The Cross took away the sword of the slain one; the Cross, the gate of paradise;

the Cross, the bite of Erebus, the death of death—not without entirely [MS reading: *fluminis orsus*, “the river’s beginning”].

The Cross, by no means obscure, stripped the greedy one of his spoils.

The Cross of happy destiny holds the courts of the conquered strong one.

[Col. 1321C] The Cross, tree of life, a vine more sober than life,

brings forth the fruit of virtue and the harbour of salvation.

The Cross is peace, the Cross a harbour, the Cross the rising of true light.

The Cross is, as it were, an antidote to vices; the Cross is wholly good.

If you should bring Socrates back to penetrate the power of the Cross,

[Col. 1322A] neither Socrates nor the poet-prophet Virgil could unfold it.

The Cross made the draught sweet and prepared drink;

the Cross broke the rock and compelled waters to come forth.

By the serpent bearing signs of the Crucified,

the Cross healed the wounded and put the wounders to death.

If it fortifies doorposts, it drives disaster and enemies away;

if it touches the forehead, it breaks things hostile to the joyful.

The Cross, fulfilling the Law, bore the glorious King of kings.

Under Heraclius the Cross renewed very many signs,

and, restoring the sick, gave life to the dead.

The Cross restrains the guilty, rendering a weapon harmless.

The Cross opens the veil of the Temple together with heaven’s hinge.

The Cross, removing shadow, lifted up [variant: *abolished*] the legal signs.

The Cross filled up the number and homeland of the angelic flock.

[Col. 1322B] The Cross removed the Cross’s reproach, the Cross the crime of the wood.

The Cross redeemed us from sin; the Cross redeemed us from death.

The Cross became the entrance; the Cross is the medicine of sorrows.

The Cross is the way of righteousness; the Cross is the restoration of character.

The Cross is the step to things above, the ladder prepared for the faithful.

The Cross confers merit, hope, and the rewards of heaven.

The Cross restored miserable human beings to heavenly rights.

Every good thing flowed to us, with blood, from the Cross,

which displays length, breadth, height, and depth,

and by effect and form draws and occupies the whole world.

Form, power, wood, and weight: all things of the Cross are worthy—

sweet to the believer, but bitter to one who devoutly remembers it.

O wondrous Cross! O splendid Cross! O venerable Cross!

Cross to be embraced! Cross to be borne in heart and outwardly!

[Col. 1322C] Marked out with rosy flower, with sacred blood,

like a pearl, so are you adorned about your limbs.

O Cross distinguished by the Crucified One, by form, by signs,

preserve the servants in whom are strength and wisdom! Amen.

[Col. 1321]

1261–1262 **HERE BEGINS THE LIFE OF BLESSED MARY OF EGYPT.**  
[Note: [Col. 1321] Published by Bollandus, 7 March. In the manuscript of Saint Marianus at Auxerre it begins thus:] Here begins the Life of fortunate Pharian Mary.

(Compared with the manuscript of Saint Marianus, Victorine manuscript no. 272, and Évreux manuscript no. 19. Moreover, in the Évreux manuscript this poem is divided into several cantos, which we have thought should be marked here for the reader’s convenience.)

## CANTO I

[Col. 1321D]

As winter does not burn the laurel, nor the pyre gold,

so neither riches nor worldly glory burned the boy Zosimas.

These things, swiftly passing away and teaching every harm,

he despised, renounced, and put away by mind and hand.

And, made a monk, he watched over monastic deeds;

[Col. 1322D] and, proposing to follow the teachers of law and justice,

he began to restrain the rule of his years.

He began; and in a short time, changing the habits of his age,

the teacher surpassed the habits of his teachers.

When weak childhood had passed the limits of boyhood,

his gifts increased, and at the same time his very crown increased.

[Col. 1323A] Nothing was more burdensome to him than to wish to be cherished in rest [Évreux: *membra*, “limbs/body”];

nothing more unwelcome than not to punish guilt.

His scant sleep, rough garment,

food, and bed bore witness—now his glory, then his torment.

The monk’s complexion and his flesh unfamiliar with Bacchus bore witness:

not flesh but skin—thin, pale, worn by scourges,

trained to resist itself and to serve the spirit.

In these torments, the melody of his sacred mind

sang psalms to Christ whenever his tongue was silent.

From the filth of the grave his mind, conscious always of justice,

did not remove itself; God knew these things, man the rest.

While in such ways he devoted himself to psalms and hymns,

he saw the secrets of heaven, being destined for them;

he saw and learned by what hope he conquered so many battles.

Taken captive by hope, Zosimas thus grew in holy deeds,

[Col. 1323B] as a pool grows by a stream, or a dormant fire by olive-oil.

And mindful to guard against favours that might benefit his character [corrupt reading: *ad meoeores*],

while he fought well, he took care lest fame should fly abroad.

The more he guarded against it, the more it flew,

and, against his wish, reported all that was praiseworthy.

Countless people came there to be taught;

as place, age, and rank demanded, he taught them,

surpassing his elders as the moon surpasses the lesser stars.

While Zosimas became accustomed to these things, pride grew.

And he said to himself: “Whatever order or justice commands,

I choose, pursue, and love; I proclaim that these things must be learned and kept.

Great labour and narrow sleep [Évreux: *food*] waste my limbs.

As a boy I chose these things; as a boy I accomplished these things and more.

Already then the order of the flock, already the oar and anchor of the law,

already worthy of heaven, holy in deed, mind, and speech,

[Col. 1323C] alone I fought with the world to the final end.

The people, clergy, and flock of monks, admiring these things,

seek me, hear me, love me, and perform what my voice commands.”

While Zosimas thus boasted and reviewed his merit,

a certain one interposed, to whom the Spirit disclosed these things:

“You have fought well; as far as you could, you have conquered well.

Nothing resists you: the flesh serves and the mind rules.

Yet the end of this contest remains uncertain;

and, when you can be overcome, you ought not say, ‘I have conquered.’

For who is conquered or conquers is proved by the end.

The rewards of victors hang at the end of labours;

as Scripture says, the end, not the contest, crowns.

When you fight well, when you think all things subdued,

pride remains to be conquered, which later attacks you.

[Col. 1323D] Unless this is conquered, the promised crown is denied.

Alas! By these weapons the faithful person is often conquered;

under this leader, the rose is sometimes changed into a willow-herb.

Remember, pray, to stand against this portent,

and do not presume either to call yourself alone holy

or yourself, before the holy, deserving of the promises of the Thunderer.

There are many who surpass you in the test of life;

that you may know them, seek the banks of the Jordan.

There a flock of monks worships the King of heaven.

Live among the monks; do what they do, and avoid the rest.

Go out; hasten: delay is great ruin.”

He goes out, departs quickly, knocks, and the doors are opened.

[Col. 1324A] Then, greeted by the abbot, he spoke a few words.

“Tell why you have come.” Zosimas says: “I desire to be taught

and to have the burden of my sins revealed to me.

The austerity of your observance, the graciousness of your appearance,

the signs of a sacred mind have helped the desire of one who seeks.”

The Father answered: “No one, dearest brother,

no one washes the soul from illnesses [Évreux: *raises it from illnesses*] except the Creator of the world;

ask Him that evil be restrained and good be taught.

But if this community pleases you, or this tranquil place itself,

if you wish a great palm to be joined to humble tamarisks,

stay; see whether humble use of the sheepfold will benefit you;

and choose to share with us the food of this wintering-place [Évreux: *hibercum*],

1263 the highest Shepherd will feed us with his own food—

food nourishing the mind which afterward hungers for nothing:

nothing satisfies the soul more than to feed on His sight.”

[Col. 1324B] Zosimas indeed assented to these words and stayed there.

He stayed, and in the cell beheld, praised, learned, kept, and loved

a new life and most sacred battles,

growing both by the flock’s exhortation and by the working of the loom [Évreux: *taeda*, “torch”].

The care of this flock was love of the supreme flock;

to hear the teachers of the Law and teach the younger men;

not to indulge the flesh, to render justice, to use laws;

to speak nothing rashly, to avoid anger like deadly poisons,

envy, quarrels, curses, arrogance,

salt, fish, wine, stew, bedding, and linen:

they did not touch these things, to use which they regarded as a sin;

they had neither taste for vegetables, nor possessions, nor mention of possessions,

nor arranged hair, nor thought for expenditure.

No one, through costly clothing or an unequal table,

envied the Father, nor finally did brother envy brother.

[Col. 1324C] Food and dress were equal; tumult was far absent [variant: *was absent*] from there.

Their drink was the river, their more festive food beans;

haircloth was their garment, harsh ropes their girdles instead of soft ones;

the return of the fallen was joy, their error grief.

Their reading was the lives of the Fathers, their instruction the concord of brothers.

In their words was God, or the sacred deeds of the pious.

By watchful custom leisure was far away, a psalm in the mouth,

flesh worn down by many crosses, with little fuel;

and by frequent tears each published deeds done in secret.

Reports of the populace, marketplaces, lawsuits, external affairs,

the changing course of conduct—none of them knew these.

The cause was the hidden place, the shut gates,

a stern gatekeeper, a flock and pastor, both severe.

[Col. 1324D] These cloistered men had neither fixed officials

nor, if you remove the pastor, any prior.

If a matter required anything [Évreux: “What justice required”], or the Father himself saw it,

each person’s concern was to obey both the matter and the Father.

The pastor indeed indicated what had to be done, and did it himself,

more ready to serve all than to preside over them;

he was no more accustomed to exhort than to minister.

He was the glory of the blessed and mirror of monks,

light in darkness, enclosed there yet celebrated everywhere,

chief exemplar of morals, school of law, rod of guilt,

a cross to himself, a model to the flock, the way of life, glory to the law;

knowing how to rejoice with the rejoicing and grieve with the grieving.  
[Note: [Col. 1323] Évreux: *Gnarus gaudenti*; Victorine: *Nautas gaudenti*, erroneously.]

[Col. 1325A] Severe toward these, gentle toward those, he became all things to all.

## CANTO II

The subject requires that I relate certain things which the flock was accustomed to do.

At the time when the people, purified by the sacred washing,

began, for forgiveness of sins, to tithe the full number of days,

they went out from the cell to new battles;

but first, each having confessed his sins to the abbot,

strengthened beforehand his mind and aided his body

with the tasting of the sacraments and the healing food.

Then the customary blessing was sought and given.  
[Note: [Col. 1325] The practice of blessing among monks when leaving the monastery.]

They exchanged kisses; then at last the enclosure was opened.

And now, having taken leave of the community and left the place,

the flock went out together and, divided, entered the wilderness.

A part, as custom itself required, remained at home

to preserve the goods appropriate against the thief;

[Col. 1325B] but so that the cell might not lack holy offices,

it was prepared for sacred studies and washings of the soul,

poor in festive adornment but rich in honourable things.

Having left the buildings, they disclosed their retreats and their purpose,

1264 and went separately, each wherever choice led.

Each, with equal desire and no witness present, strove

to sing psalms prostrate, to blot out sins with tears,

to please you, Christ, by punishments of torn flesh,

to rejoice in you as companion, guide, end, and rest.

They held you before them, gave you, awaited you, possessed you

as defence in battle, witness, crown, and help.

They persevered in these pursuits, and alike nourished

their holy hearts with words, their flesh with roots or herbs.

A small part carried bread; another refreshed itself with

[Col. 1325C] fruits of palm-trees in place of the luxuries of tables;

in place of festive food, an acorn or wild olive.

These things they took in the desert at a fixed time,

and at set hours took rest and a little sleep.

[Note: [Col. 1325] Évreux: *Talibus*, “with such things.”] When thirty-nine days had thus been completed,

the cell was sought again; they returned when the Christ-worshippers’ canonical observance was celebrated

with palm branches.

## CANTO III

Zosimas, admiring these things and prepared to endure them,

thought nothing holier than the rite of this observance [Évreux: *more satisfying*].

As soon as the cycle of time called him [Évreux: *brought him*], he departed;

he departed and set out from the cell for new battles.

He crossed the Jordan, carrying bread for the time,

and thus, entering the hiding-places and recesses of the wilderness,

paid vows to God and turned new songs over in his breast.

[Col. 1325D] He lives alone; his holy deeds prove him a hermit.

From dawn he presses on his journey; at night he rests.

Lying on the ground, he weeps, seeks and prays for a companion

who might comfort his cares and suffer with him,

instruct him in deeds, and, by conquering, teach him to conquer.

What he seeks, he obtains: a companion of the road is found.

For while at the customary hour he sang psalms with longer delay,

he saw one like a runner, but without clothing,

and was afraid, because he thought it a phantom.

[Col. 1326A] Disturbed by the sight, he recovered himself with the sign of the Cross.

Gathering strength from this, he follows the path of the one going;

he runs, and labour, age, and the haunts of wild beasts hinder him little.

Holy old man, hasten: you shall see better things in hope;

the footsteps you observe and follow are a woman’s.

A woman goes before, who yields to you in no way as a woman:

as in foot, so in life this hermit surpasses you.

She has deserved that, though in hiding, she should now be celebrated everywhere;

in hiding she learned well to conquer the world, and conquered it:

weather-beaten, darkened by the sun, bent by old age,

with her hairy private parts exposed and those that should be covered uncovered;

her small, snowy-white hairs bristle,

scarcely reaching her shoulders, scarcely covering her neck,

[Note: [Col. 1325] Évreux: *implexi*, “entangled.”] uncombed, sparse, accustomed to wander without restraint.

[Col. 1326B] Formerly wholly woman, now she wholly despised all of womanhood;

all flesh long ago rebellious to itself, now wholly rebellious against it.

The woman, rightly disdainful of mortal companions,

flees Zosimas, encountered by chance, with swift step.

Zosimas follows her and begs her to stop; nonetheless he proceeds.

He cries more loudly than usual: “Go more moderately [Évreux: *moderately*],

whoever you are; wait—I am prevented by labour and age from going further.

Wait for one who is weary. I am not a wild beast; check your steps.

I am indeed a small thing, but a human being, a sinner, and likewise

1265 a confessor of Christ, frequenting monastic retreats [Évreux: *and of monks I frequent …*].

Here I sigh for pardon for my sins.

Do not flee; stop a little. Do not fear the haunts of wild beasts,

by the name of Christ, by the rewards you have deserved.

Servant of God, remain; bless me, grant what I ask.”

[Col. 1326C] “Do you live in this desert for Christ? Have you not heard

even for the name of Christ?”

She fixed her step and, covering herself with her hands, said:

“I am a woman, Zosimas, foremost in the mass of sins;

I am ashamed to appear before men without clothing,

nor does shame allow my face to turn, because my groin is not covered.

But because I know you to be Christ’s servant, what you have asked

shall be done, if you give me something with which I may cover a woman’s shame [Évreux: *limbs*].

Would you have me speak or stay? Throw your garment back to me.”

Then he gives her his hood; covered by it, the woman says:

“Why, Father, do you pursue the retreat of a wretched woman?

Why, or whither, is your course? Here the lion roars, the bear growls.

What good can you hope for in a region of lions?”

While she says these things, the monk prostrates himself and asks

[Col. 1326D] to be blessed; but she too, prostrate, asks:

the woman, “Holy Father”; the monk, “Most holy mother.”

Each cries out; each repeats, “Bless!”

This was the subject of their dispute, this the sole dispute of hermits;

the rest of their life was harmonious and without dispute.

While they thus contend, the holy woman speaks as follows.

## CANTO IV

“My Father, you err unless you consider the matter in due order:

[Col. 1327A] you err indeed, when, being a man, you seek from a woman

that which a man ought to give a woman.

Let it be granted that one speak truth: he is held a transgressor of law

who asks for things to be given which may lawfully be denied.

You are a man, long a monk, and likewise a priest;

by these three things you are compelled to obey a woman’s request.

That you bless me, a sinner, not that you be blessed,

is prescribed by the customary office of the hand anointed with oil; this office is the reason for this gift.

[Note: [Col. 1327] The purpose for which this office exists.]

The Father replied: “It is sufficiently evident, O holy mother;

it is clear, holy mother, how great your merits are.

For though I was unknown and far distant,

and though you had not been told what life or order I followed,

you knew everything; you did not keep silent even about my name.

These things show how great you are and how pleasing to the Thunderer.

Therefore, you who are so pleasing, bend Him; make Him favourable to me.

If you ask, He himself will give; ask, and life will assist your prayer.

The life of the blessed supports their petitions:

God heeds it and repays worthy rewards.

No distinction comes to Him from the difference of sex,

nor is a crown given or taken away on account of a person;

grace or merit gives each person the gift requested.”

[Col. 1327B] The woman yields to these words and obeys the petitioner’s tears.

They rise; and after a few preliminary words she asks

what peace the holy Churches enjoy, what their condition is,

with what zeal of kings the sanction of the laws is maintained,

with what care the people keep mortal laws.

He reports, through her merits and blessed prayers,

that Christ’s worshippers are joyful and quiet in festive peace,

and that the faith flourishes. After this he urges her

[Col. 1327C] to pray that what now flourishes may never wither,

and by the antidote of prayers to strengthen and stir up what is right

in the rulers of the venerable Churches.

He says more besides; she obeys, falls down, and prays:

1266 her mind rises to the stars, her silent mouth gives thanks;

in secret the mind knocks with a quiet cry,

and movements, not sound of mouth, give the signs of crying.

While she prays thus, Zosimas marvels and reveres

her mouth, hair, face, having much of piety [Évreux: *cultivation*; Angers: *face*],

and her pale cheeks, now full of the omen of death.

Whatever is seen bears witness to virtue;

all things are proofs of blessed men’s works [Évreux: *labours*].

But things more wonderful than those related followed sufficiently;

for while she prolonged in many ways the hymns of her divine breast,

[Col. 1327D] she hung as though suspended

in the air, now wholly lifted far from the earth,

as though unwilling to bear earth’s contamination.

Her purified body then stood raised aloft.

Thus before the monk, for a time, the woman’s body was a guest of heaven,

soon to be joined eternally to the dwellers above.

Zosimas was alarmed by these things and thought it a prodigy,

or truly something discordant with womanhood.

But she shows that he is mistaken, and wins her brother back:

he, badly troubled, returns to himself, recalled thus:

“Alas! Whither are you carried away? What are you doing, Father? Whence are you moved?”  
[Note: [Col. 1328] Évreux: “Alas, whither are you carried away?”]

[Col. 1328A] “What stupor of mind is this? I perceive well that you perceive wrongly:

you sinned against me when you thought me a phantom.

I am a woman of wretched lot, more guilty than woman;

I am mortal flesh, palpable, material,

which, if you do not know, lives by a soul and needs food,

is changed by time, and threatens corruption and ashes.

This is what I am now; this I can promise of myself.

But what you saw, at which you stood almost dumb in astonishment,

must not be ascribed to me: God works it.

Whatever honourable thing there is comes from heavenly help,

and comes from above whether you act well or meditate.

We are a light shadow; we are smoke in a whirlwind of deeds;

we are grass of the field, first flesh, afterwards mud.

[Col. 1328B] The form of things perishes; another is given with each passing day.

While we are thus changed, we too bear silent witness

to what the world promises, where nature sends us back,

what we are or shall be, whither we tend, whence we come.”

## CANTO V

Afterward Zosimas reckoned nothing rashly about the woman;

he recognizes his fault and asks pardon in supplicating prayer.

He presses her with tears and deep sighs

not to conceal anything from him, but to reveal what she is and whence she comes,

on what food she is sustained, and who accompanies her.

The Father adds: “Tell me, most holy mother:

it will help to be heard; Christ wishes these things to be disclosed.

He suggested this journey to the old man; under His guidance I came.

He gave me little fear in a region of wild beasts,

[Col. 1328C] guided my step, strengthened me when weary,

softened cold, taught me to endure heat.

Who, unless God had helped, could have endured things so hard?

I came for a special good through the haunts of lions;

let it be brought back, by which Christ may be glorified.

Let this torch, this famous gem, come forth from hiding.

God does not wish the illustrious lights of the world to be concealed,

at whose rays the winter of souls melts away.

Therefore recount what you did to Christ’s praise.

How well a story is told by which one’s neighbour is edified!

It is truly a crime to keep silent about examples of character.”

He speaks thus and returns with abundant tears to his requests;

the woman raises him as he lies down and addresses him when raised.

1267 “Alas for me! How many tears am I asked to remember?

[Col. 1328D] What sequence of crimes and what contagions of deeds,

my Father, do you examine? You labour to learn crimes by which I shall not fail to offend you, if I recount a shameful life that ought to be kept silent,

a life that feared no sin.

What ears can you offer for the disgrace of a woman?

Or who, mindful of decency, can bear these reminders of shame?

What shall I pursue, or what shall I do? I am ashamed to show this wound.

But if it is concealed, the medicine for the wound will be lost.

The buried praise of Christ is lost through a grievous danger!

[Col. 1329A] When evils are healed, unless thanks are offered for them,

guilt surely returns to an ungrateful head.

That I may not thus offend, I shall recount my shameful life

and the ointments with which God washed the wounds of my mind.

It is fitting that I be put to shame before a monk for a time,

lest I be put to shame before the saints in the presence of the Thunderer.”

She says this, and weeps; she blushes and fears to tell it.

She looks upward and nods; shame changes her face,

modesty binds her lips, and abundant sweat flowed everywhere.

If one part is begun, scarcely does one reach the final parts.

At last, briefly recounting the sins of her former life,

she spoke thus, her face covered, in poor dress.

## CANTO VI

The land of the Nile bore me from no humble stock,

but after I grew up, I erased the titles of my lineage.

[Col. 1329B] Often my father brought me, in tender life, the precepts of a strict life  
[Note: [Col. 1329] Évreux: “Often he brought me the precept of a moderately strict life.”]

and, on the other hand, my censorious mother.

My mother, as is customary, rehearsing the decrees of modesty,

taught me to unlearn gain which honour does not commend;

and with added threats said: “Be equal to the Sabine women;

let a matronly severity rule even in your tender face.

No one learns too early to guard against harmful things;

every age ought to strive for uprightness.”

I remember my parents, standing by, giving these counsels;

but I gave both parents’ admonitions to the winds [Évreux: *mind*],

and from my twelfth year modesty began wickedly to be despised.

From then my bones drew unseemly heat;

from then I turned away from the marriage of a settled bridal chamber,

and deemed it a delay that modesty had not yet perished,

[Col. 1329C] to bear without payment the losses of virginity.

And lest my parents’ opposing wishes should delay me,

I leave my homeland and set out for Alexandria.

There I found a place in which vice was held in common;

nor was that enough, because whenever a man was lacking to me,

I wandered through houses and, asked by none, asked no one.

Infamous in attire, roving in eye, wanton in face,

an imposture to those who looked, crime and enemy of nature,

my broken gait and speech professing a procuress

proclaimed me outside—shame forbids me to remember this shamelessness;

my gesture proclaimed it, and this madness was no less excessive [Évreux: *too much*].

Thus forgetful of myself, guide and path of ruin,

I spent every day in histories of crimes,

confessing the unhappy day when perhaps I was reminded of honour,

[Col. 1329D] since every time I broke it, I celebrated the feast more lavishly.

Songs which drew toward crime and taught incest

I loved, learned, and surpassed mime-actresses in singing [Évreux: *mimes*].

And when I could no longer arouse exhausted or elderly lechers,

who, worn out, were already disgusted by every lust,

I flattered new ones; I bought these at any price,

and divided every possession among companions in crime,

1268 which needle and spindle had granted for the needs of life.

By these instruments the hand of a needy woman supplied itself;

by these, house, food, and clothing were sought;

[Col. 1330A] by these I was given a partner and heir of guilt according to my desires.

[Note: [Col. 1329] Évreux: “How wickedly, indeed …”] How great, for I remember it, was my delight in abundance of wine?

How eagerly was food sought by which lust is aided?

And since sex and age are two great enemies,

drunkenness was added to these as a third enemy.

With these diseases in me—and through me the world corrupted—

it never could, nor can, be burdened with an equal stain.

Whoever multiplied evils erred less than I;

and to me was wrongly granted the palm for always doing evil.

When I no longer knew whom I could surpass in crime,

by multiplied crime I surpassed even all others and myself.

For, having first dared error and then madness,

*[The supplied source ends here, mid-sentence and incomplete.]*
Whatever exceedingly wicked sins I committed, I justified;  
[Note: Col. 1329, Ebr.: “I multiplied them.”]

Nor did advancing age set limits to my crime.

Hateful in the eyes of the Thunderer for such and so great deeds,  
[Col. 1330B] I spent three times three years and twice four besides.

Behold, on a certain day—yet how shall I tell this to you?  
How wretchedly I fell!—I saw young men upon the shore;  
I saw them and sought them out; I asked where they wished to go.

Smiling, the first said: “We are going to Jerusalem.”  
I ask whether they would allow me as a companion. He added:

“If you provide a sailor, the vessel is open for passage; you may sail.”

Then I: “In place of payment for the ship, I have prepared myself as sailor for you;  
if you seek payment, you shall obtain me as the payment.  
I have nothing but myself; but, if it please you, use me.  
I have nothing better: take the benefit of this gift.  
From this one fortune I shall make enough for all,  
if from the common provision sustenance comes to me alone.”

Having said this, the young man set his steps upon the sand  
and, as though despising the frivolity of my words,

[Col. 1330C] urged on the sailors, called his companions, pressed that they should go.  
I myself bind up my hair, paint my face for sin,  
cast away my distaff, gird myself for the journey;  
I follow them aboard the vessel; the sea promises prosperity.

The wind flatters us; the young men skillfully make use of the wind;  
and within a few hours we reach the desired shores.

Alas for me! What labor is this? In what tongue shall I recount the rest?  
Forgive the wretched woman: shame requires these things to be hidden,  
and it is horror that draws me merely to remember such madness.  
[Note: Col. 1329, Ebr.: “error,” but “horror” is better.]

So she spoke and wept; blush filled her shamefaced face.  
Zosimas consoles her as she weeps and begs her to continue the account.  
She obeyed, and at last thus resumed her answer to the petitioner.  
[Note: Col. 1329, Ebr.: “continued.” Col. 1329, Andeg.: “followed.”]

## CANTO VII

[Col. 1330D] My father, upon the ship I multiplied my crimes.  
There I did nothing except what is contrary to the law,  
and every thought of justice was far from my cares.  
Having cast it aside wickedly, I turned the sailors to shameful acts;  
I rouse the sluggish and call out reproaches to those ashamed of them.

Whoever finds crime pleasing, I consider brave; I declare him blessed.  
Taught to serve a man’s desire with my whole body,  
my concern, upon the guilty sea amid a thousand dangers,  
was to flatter crime, to fear nothing except honorable conduct,  
to wallow in lust, to dissolve again and again in wine,  
to swell with food, to vary the tunes of singing,

[Col. 1331A] to employ all things hostile to salvation.

Believe me: I greatly marvel that that crime went unpunished,  
that neither sea nor wind shattered the deed of the wicked.  
I marvel that the ship submitted to these base disgraces;  
that the wrath of the Thunderer did not withstand so many and such great evils;  
that shore, south wind, and heat endured incest;  
among nearly a thousand deaths, wickedness remained safe.

1269 But the Lord Jesus, who knows how to spare when offended,  
though offended spared me, and by sparing urged me to return.  
Even then the fountain of mercy freely showed me  
that, although angered, he delays punishing guilt,  
and strikes unwillingly, because he seeks to spare the guilty.

## CANTO VIII

Lest you be wearied by a long account of my lust,

[Col. 1331B] I am carried to the harbor; I, a harlot, enter the new holy walls.  
Joined to a light-minded crowd, I linger in the city as both guest and enemy.  
I go about the streets, hunting wicked embraces;  
both citizen and stranger are compelled to sin.

While I ensnare these men and, madly evil, fit myself  
for such great wickedness, the Exaltation of the holy Cross,  
which was then approaching, summoned the citizens to the churches.  
A crowd of fathers goes before; the devotion of mothers follows.

The city, almost emptied, compelled me to go and see,  
to ask what drew the people and what pleased them in the shrine.  
I went seeking a deadly companion for myself;  
and I am ashamed, yet I shall tell it, who would subject the wicked woman.  
[Note: Col. 1331, Ebr.: “what.”]

[Col. 1331C] But the event turned out otherwise, and heavenly mercy restrained  
the incentives of lust and the heat of my passions.

For though I wished to enter the doors and see the sacred things,  
I was not permitted to enter them or see those things.  
The open gate received the arriving people;  
a heavenly power cast back me, a sinner.

Since I supposed this happened through feminine weakness,  
I struggled with all the shamelessness I could;  
yet even then I could not enter the open gates,  
although those before and behind me entered.

I marvel and am indignant that I should be turned back from the sacred building;  
I thrust myself among the crowds, hoping to be helped by their pressure;  
I strain forward and put my hands upon the pressing people.  
But none of this benefits one desiring to enter:  
guilt wears out and enfeebles even these attempts,  
[Note: Col. 1331, Ebr.: “holds.”]

[Col. 1331D] nor does sin allow the sacred threshold to be touched.

When I understood this within myself, I said: “It was not fitting  
that those temples, venerable through the titles of blessed sufferings,  
should stand open to me, a wretched woman.

Here is the sorrowful covenant of death broken;  
here the Author paid for our deeds, made a sacrifice;  
here he was condemned, here he died, here he was buried;  
from here he rose again and restored life through death.

Daring to come to places of such wondrous sweetness,  
I bring neither the dew of olive oil nor the fragrance of incense,  
[Note: Col. 1331, Ebr. and Andeg.: “of olive oil.”]  
nor a pure mind, more pleasing than all these.

[Col. 1332A] A stench that bears witness to disgrace is prepared instead of incense;  
instead of the inscriptions of virtues, I bear a crowd of crimes,  
and whatever befalls the wretched sex of women.

Alas! What have I attempted? Whither, what sort of person, and from where have I come?  
A harlot from a miserable brothel have I approached Christ’s table,  
burdened by these evils—such a woman to such places.

This blocks an entrance that I have often sought in vain.  
God hates the disgraces of the brothel and excludes them from his altars,  
and the filth of the mind from life-giving food.

Then I stifled my voice and withdrew no farther;  
but standing before the gates, I was drenched in rising tears.  
Rejected three times, I lament; grief weighs down my moaning face.  
[Note: Col. 1331, Ebr.: “moist,” and Andeg.]

My feelings are divided; confusion assails my heart;  
I begin to remember my conduct and to be ashamed of my evils,

[Col. 1332B] 1270 and, though late, seek to rise again after being buried.  
What I rightly seek is granted, and Lazarus is brought out from the tomb.

## CANTO IX

By chance there was nearby a beautiful image of that exceptional woman  
painted under the name of Mary,  
who bore the Savior, as a star bears brightness.  
As I look upon her, I am made new within and become another person.

Drawing nearer in tears, I beseech her countenance;  
[Note: Col. 1331, Ebr.: “I sigh.”]  
and, bending my knee, I importune the Mother of the Father with this prayer:

“To you, holy Virgin, sacred Virgin, Virgin Mary,  
I come, a virgin of a new condition, yet a woman of death;  
a woman shamefully common, filthy, and of the tavern;  
one who wept only when I had done what deserved tears;  
when I committed shameful acts, I laughed as though made illustrious by disgrace,

[Col. 1332C] and many a paramour made my sorrowful face cheerful.

And many a paramour made my sorrowful face cheerful.

Night was, in dreams, whenever every man came to me as a man;  
and I considered it a crime only if I had not been joined by much crime,  
rejoicing in forbidden intercourse and in a husband shared by the people.

Thus I completed the course of my wretched life;  
thus I passed it, and now condemn what I did wickedly.  
I repent of my error; the sewer of madness disgusts me;  
nor will I endure or love condemned guilt,  
if the barrier by which I, a sinner, am held is loosened,  
if I, wretched as I am, may see the life-giving wood.

Through you I hope for this; through you I seek to succeed.  
For though angered, the Son will yield at your intercession;  
he will yield, since he is both Father and Son.  
A double affection will draw his entreatable heart;  
[Col. 1332D] each will be bent to every gift, yet they are one.

Therefore, upon this covenant, grant me what I rightly seek;  
be witness of the covenant and avenger also of its breach.  
[Note: Col. 1331, Ebr. and Andeg.: “of the deed.”]  
I do not wish to be spared if the crime is repeated.”

Raised by these words, with my vices now abandoned in mind,  
I turn my step back; good hope accompanies me to the church.  
Impatient of delay, I am borne within, without difficulty,  
[Note: Col. 1332, Ebr.: “within.”]  
and rejoice to be admitted, ask forgiveness for my sins,  
weep for pardon, and adore the standards of salvation.

The crimes of my mind keep me from the sacraments.  
Having offered these things, I return to the Mother of mercy

[Col. 1333A] and give due thanks for benefits received, praying fittingly  
to be taught what she commands me to do, where I should go.  
I seek the way of moral life; I beg the Mother to guide it.

While I thus urgently knock at the doors of life,  
this answer is given—nor did I know who spoke,  
[Note: Col. 1333, Ebr.: “what he was saying.”]  
but I knew only that someone had spoken thus:

“If you cross the Jordan, you shall obtain rest.”  
[Note: Col. 1333: “you shall find rest.” Andeg.: “you shall obtain it.”]

Then astonishment crept over me; when it had passed with time,  
I went out swiftly, thus believing myself instructed.  
The road by which the Jordan is reached is sought and taken.

As I hurried, a certain man, suitably for the occasion,  
offered and secretly gave me three coins.  
With them I bought three loaves; leaving the city walls,  
I press on, am carried away, and flee from the crowds.

[Col. 1333B] It was evening. I entered the church of John the Baptist,  
past which the named river flows in a tranquil course.  
There, confessing my guilt amid tears and groaning,  
I approached the mysteries with a contrite heart.  
After taking bread, I crossed the aforesaid river  
and sought a manner of life by which I might condemn my former crimes.

Then I deprived myself of pleasures; then of the luxury of the flesh;  
then I redeemed the time of wickedness by a better pursuit.

But perhaps you are weary of my words,  
1271 and the sun flies in its swift course, unwilling to be held.

“Therefore depart, Father.” Then he said: “Most holy mother,  
tell what follows; nothing more fitting is disclosed here.  
Speak, handmaid of God; a great part of the day remains.  
Nothing better fulfils my wish than to tell everything.  
Speak, then, if you remember, what hardships you suffered there,

[Col. 1333C] whence you had food, who provided clothing and whence;  
whether any temptation rebelled but did not overcome you;  
whether the once-hostile heat of the flesh cooled.”

Moved by the old man’s prayers, she sat upon the sand  
and, dripping with tears, added these words to the former:

“My father, I completed eleven years and four times nine  
after the fall of my mournful life,  
yet I washed away my crimes only through grievous conflict.

For I am tempted again: after sacred vows there returns  
the longing for cups of perfume and the luxury of foods.  
The fish of Egypt and desire for abandoned wine  
touch and afflict me, wretched woman, all the more violently  
because I had devoted myself more intensely to feasting and drinking.

When moderation disgusted me and drunkenness pleased me,

[Col. 1333D] vice, learned in cities and abroad, is unlearned with difficulty.  
The enemy of good conduct enters everywhere despite one’s resolve.  
The mere memory of evil delights presses and attacks hearts insufficiently firm;  
Eve rages and troubles the man.  
Eve desires the food of death in the gardens of life.

Alas for me! For some things I am ashamed to state, but I shall state them.  
Learn that nothing is safe except one first released from the flesh:  
there will always be at hand something both to press upon and obstruct honorable conduct.

With the fever of longing to marry and the desire to sing

[Col. 1334A] melodies and songs of accursed loves,  
I burn; and forbidden embraces, a thousand husbands,  
return to my mind as it turns back to sobriety.  
Kisses are sought; my desires wander toward marriage;  
virtue is a burden; I am ashamed to remain bound by the rule;  
I am weary of the continual yoke and put serious things behind trifles;  
[Note: Col. 1333, Ebr.: “continual water.”]  
I prefer crowds to solitude, city gatherings to the desert.

These phantoms batter uprightness unto collapse,  
and the image of madness chokes the seed of good conduct,  
until, turning in prayer to exceptional Mary,  
I called back from temptations the eyes of my mind.

Therefore I come here, groan, weep, become a sacrifice;  
[Note: Col. 1333, Ebr.: “I come to this in mind.”]  
I seek to be reformed; I pray that what has grown old may be made new.

After the burnt-offering of prayers, the good mind returns and stands with itself;

[Col. 1334B] after the heart’s weeping every thought of filth flees.  
By these remedies the breasts of the mind were calmed,  
and the frying-pan of revived crimes,  
which had wickedly boiled, was altogether accustomed to grow cold.

Moreover, as I wept and lay miserably,  
a radiance shone around me and covered me wholly,  
sent to call back the wandering, lift up the falling,  
bestow good hope, give strength, and reveal the crown.

Thus three periods of three years and two of four years passed;  
rough things were mingled with gentle, savage with mild.  
But the Virgin Mother, after I had wept well,  
wiped and washed away new wounds; then came salvation, then I rested.

For nearly two lustra, two loaves were my food,  
which I had carried with me when I withdrew here from the city.

[Col. 1334C] They had dried and hardened, lost their own color,  
and ceased to give strength;  
yet from them I used, very sparingly, to relieve hunger.  
What I should drink when failing, I could scarcely find.

After the loaves had been consumed over a long time,  
my mind clinging to the Lord cast away vain cares;  
[Note: Col. 1333, Ebr.: “wiped away.”]  
1272 from then until now the old temptation has subsided;  
from then until now sense obeys reason;  
until now my outward food is grass with leaves;  
until now my inward food is heavenly words.

The clothing I had was torn and worn away by age;  
thereafter naked, I endured regions scorched by the sun,  
in which I suffered excessive cold and excessive heat  
by night and by day,

[Col. 1334D] making satisfaction for the crime and losses of my former life.  
[Note: Col. 1333, Ebr.: “I make up for the former life.”]

I exchange jokes for hymns, cleanse laughter by sorrow;  
punishment redeems pleasure, thirst drunkenness,  
poverty luxury, toil ease, gravel spiced wine,  
[Note: Col. 1333, Ebr.: “poverty.”]  
the cross a soft bed, holy devotion guilt.

I endure nearly as many torments as disgraces have gone before.  
Whatever the flesh sinned, the victim of the flesh has washed away.  
What conflicts of punishments I suffer,  
how many crosses are alike renewed night and day,  
God knows, witness and rewarder of these labors.

Often beneath the burning Crab, or in the rigid winter,

[Col. 1335A] I freeze with nightly cold and burn with daytime fire,  
and nowhere lie safe, as though released by death.  
To this punishment is added the force of dust and the heat of sand.

Nor is the severity of these things alleviated by the nature of the place;  
for, as you see, the place lacks tree, mountain, and cave—  
things by which a dog-day heat is warded off or winter avoided.

You surely know that a human being does not live by bread alone,  
nor withstands the winds by clothes or dwelling.  
God is food to all, all clothing to all;  
the King of heaven governs heaven and is present to the faithful.

When the wind rages outside, the heat of love subdues the wind;  
neither snow nor winds chill the devotion of the mind.  
No hope of the starry realm is arduous for the good.

[Note: Col. 1335, Ebr.: “For I.”] And I, ill acquainted with the world, wickedly betrothed myself to the world.

[Col. 1335B] Scripture was not dear to my heart, nor reading my concern,  
nor even the sacred teachings of the mind.  
My one devotion was the fall of lovers  
and shamefully gratifying the people of the brothel.

If I recall anything of honor, morals, piety,  
or the memorials of divine books,  
behold, it is given from heaven: God teaches and accomplishes these things.  
The Spirit immediately fills the mind and instructs the mouth;  
there is no labor in learning, none in being instructed.

Thus the periods of my former life passed away;  
the time remaining offers me hope of reward—  
the reward of solemn death, because the reward is everlasting life.  
[Note: Col. 1335, Ebr.: “reward.”]

## CANTO X

I have set in order all that I did, badly or well,

[Col. 1335C] and was not ashamed to uncover what I did most shamefully.  
Nothing remains of the work; why do you linger here longer?  
The shadows lengthen, evening comes, the stars shine;  
night, by its accustomed course, commands return: therefore return.

Do not disclose what I have entrusted to you alone.  
[Note: Col. 1335, Ebr.: “And what henceforth [I have entrusted] to you alone.”]

When the cloistered brethren leave the monastery  
and together enter the river Jordan,  
[Note: Col. 1335, Ebr.: “cross.”]  
you yourself shall remain at home, held by an illness  
which nevertheless you will escape through the Lord’s aid.

When restored whole, go out without delay,  
and remember to bring with you the food of the altar—  
that which I hope for in heaven and seek to receive on earth.  
I hope for the true thing, request the thing and its image:

1273 nourished by this food, I shall go more safely where I am bound.  
Here are my escort, carrier, way, homeland, and fruit.  
[Col. 1335D] With this guide, take the road; you shall meet me, my father.

One day will bring you again before these eyes;  
it will bring you, and I shall tell certain things useful to the brethren.  
Then, yes then, I shall see you for the last time.”

Having bidden Zosimas farewell, she fled, leaving him behind.  
He follows her retreating form with his gaze, though she does not look back even at prayer;  
when he sees her thus borne away in swift flight,  
[Note: Col. 1335, Ebr.: “effort.”]  
and vainly recalled, he turns his steps, returns, and departs from the retreat.

The cell lies open to him as he returns; the woman clings to his mind.  
The woman turns in his heart, and scarcely can it be believed

[Col. 1336A] that a woman’s condition is equal to such heavenly things.  
So unlike a human being are her condition, face, lowliness, and ashes.

This almost alone he recalls, and that he saw her taken away;  
[Note: Col. 1335, Ebr.: “This and almost alone.”]  
Zosimas sighs over this equally night and day.  
[Note: Col. 1335, Ebr.: “This Zosimas.”]

He longs for the time when the sacred flock will depart.  
Behold, the time returns; the community leaves the church.  
But Zosimas, struck by illness and compelled to remain,  
gladly gives thanks, because what the prophetic woman  
had told him is fulfilled. He lies ill, but will follow in due time.

Whoever hopes for lofty things willingly endures hardships.  
Hope comes to the sick monk lying in bed;  
it aids him, plays with him, restrains groaning and tears,  
checks anxieties, lightens cares, and makes his face serene.

Nor is he disappointed in hope, because his former health is restored,  
and before long the weakness of feeble old age

[Col. 1336B] does not hold him back. He goes out; the desired labor begins.

And as a woman might delight in sauces or varied foods,  
though she fears their names alone,  
he carries with him a vessel full of boiled lentils,  
[Note: Col. 1335, Ebr.: “full.”]  
carefully adding covered dishes of life.

At the evening of the full sacred meal, he takes the road;  
swift in hope and faith, he hastens to reach the shore.  
When he set foot there, he sighed and said:

“Alas for me, who vainly follow and traverse these wastes!  
Either she hides, forgetful of the old man, or is delayed in the sands;  
or she came earlier but, disappointed in hope, withdrew;  
and while I weave delays, she has gone to the regions where she lives.

Perhaps she will come; but what means shall I then have  
either to give the sacrament or to speak with the woman?

[Col. 1336C] The Jordan stands in the way; effort to proceed on foot is futile:  
there is no ford anywhere, nor bridge, nor boat.”

After uttering many complaints, the old man casts his sorrowful gaze about;  
he looks intently, for his mind speaks though his mouth is silent.  
[Note: Col. 1335, Ebr.: “is not silent.”]

Behold, in hurried step, barefoot, late in the evening,  
as she had promised, she comes and visits the old man.  
Pausing a little, as though weary from the labor of the journey,  
she raises her mind and serene face to heaven  
and, weeping, makes the sign of the fruitful cross upon the water.

Thus, like a marvel, with dusty foot  
she crosses the expanse of the intervening waters.

To one who believes himself dead to the world, the world obeys;  
the elements know how to favor a sincere mind;  
one who delights in good things dares to ask any good thing.

[Col. 1336D] He seeks nothing in vain who sacrifices himself without wound.

The moon shone and did not allow the deed to remain hidden;  
in its rays, with the sight of this woman made clear,  
it draws and elicits from the old man songs of many kinds.

Behold, with pious vows and all circumlocutions set aside,  
woman and man apply themselves to sacred prayer and appease the divine powers;  
they moisten their faces with tears and exhaust words in sobbing;  
they pray for the rejected and adorn words with examples.  
The woman sincerely rejoices in the old man, the man in the woman;  
the sum of their words is God, or instruction in morals.

When these things had been done, she comes to the cup of mercy,

[Col. 1337A] 1274 and, having confessed before touching any part of it,  
she wholly sacrifices herself with tears and receives the cup.  
Then, kneeling, she is given the marriage-gifts of life,  
and by this offering is joined to Christ, the head.  
Giving commands to her companion, she speaks thus:

## CANTO XI

“My father, examine the returning brethren for their faults.  
Some among them reject instruction in morals  
and, as though unaware by what fraud they labor to deceive,  
neglect the enemy who seeks the door of the mind.  
By subtle craft the wolf lies in ambush for the sheepfold.  
If any sheep wanders, it perishes, overwhelmed by some wound,  
and is exposed to the bite while looking backward.

May the care of Abbot John resist these harms,

[Col. 1337B] and urge the flock not to despise the monk’s rule.  
The law makes the brother who sins equal to the father who is silent;  
because guilt binds both, equal punishment likewise afflicts both.

Thus Eli fell, grieving the King of heaven.  
Let no such judicial transgression befall him;  
through vigilant care may the Father root out what is harmful.  
Let him keep watch before the gates, endure labors with an even mind,  
search hearts, strengthen those desiring honorable conduct,  
rouse the negligent, restrain those who profess immoderately,  
rebuke and exhort; let him do what he preaches.

Let him soothe while stern, announce hard things while gentle;  
let him prick some before others, but now join stripes to words;  
let him wash the wounds of sins, or pay for them as their author.

Though a man who follows evil may be safe and happy here,  
God inflicts a harsher judgment for the boldness of such a one,

[Col. 1337C] and his severe mercy continues prosperity for the wicked.  
He who is tormented now does not know how great a gain he makes.  
When God once rages and strikes, he seeks to spare,  
intending to repay these things, and yet to return here once more.

Go, revisit the flock, command them to reverence the rule,  
and, standing at the altar, pray for the sinful woman.”

So having spoken, she returns; the wave obeys her return,  
and, bearing witness to the handmaid of the Thunderer, she walks above  
with dry soles; Zosimas, astonished, departs.

He himself comes swiftly home and, though far from the woman,  
is her companion in sincere prayers and remembers her.  
This thought besieges his mind, wholly occupying him as he wonders  
why such a great one should allow the year to pass slowly.

At last the year passes; the Father goes out and seeks her again.

[Col. 1337D] Having gone beyond the gates, he bears hardships without hardship  
and, as far as his strength allows, searches on foot where passable and elsewhere by sight,  
explores everything, weeping and praying these and further words:

“Christ, image of the Father, Father and sole offspring of the mother,  
hear one weeping; guide, I beg, one following the waste places.  
Show to the old man her for whose sake I came, led by you—  
her whom I desire, whom I seek, through whose prayer I hope for heaven;  
she who, though now serving in the heavenly camps, sits among the stars,  
and already companion of the heavenly beings despises the slippery things of the world;  
already joined to God, she seeks fruit from this marriage:  
fruit long-enduring, fruit that lasts forever.

Woe to me, wretched man! I seek in vain through trackless places  
one whose house is made famous by its hiddenness and its sole inhabitant;

[Col. 1338A] whose hut, desert, bridal chamber, is an uncovered cave;  
whose veil is modesty; whose companion, angel; whose halls, heaven.

Where shall I go or what shall I do? Shall I follow the tract burned by the star?  
1275 Many punishments—old age, thirst, heat, sands—  
oppose these undertakings and delay my wishes.”

Thus Zosimas laments, casting his sorrowful gaze about.  
He does not know whether to hurry and, uncertain what to choose, hesitates;  
he cries out and listens: neither voice nor echo answers,  
no sound is heard and no trace of feet found.

As he wandered about and scanned all things with his eyes,

[Col. 1338B] a ray shone down upon limbs grown cold and deprived of soul,  
as a guide and forerunner to him.  
Rejoicing in the omen and worshiping the Lord God,  
he runs there and finds her whom he seeks by prayer and foot;  
but now dead, now in fact joined to Christ,  
now among the camps of heaven, shining more brightly than the stars.

The flesh, to be glorified, purer than refined gold,  
lay covered as befitted a woman.  
What sorrowful complaints were the monk’s! What heat of heart!  
What groans of a wounded mind! What words were spoken?

Now he sighs, now circles her whole body with his gaze;  
now he turns his eyes to heaven, now applies his mouth to lamentation.  
Prostrate, he mourns and reverently clings to her feet;  
he weeps over them and divides pious kisses among the holy soles.

[Col. 1338C] Lest he return, he prays in vow and voice,  
thinking it a great gift to accompany a funeral with a funeral,  
to live and be buried together in a like death.

While he grieves and wavers uncertainly concerning her name,  
the name found in the sand raises the old man’s eyes,  
and the clouds of his mind dissolve through these instructions:

“Holy Father, I beg you, bury the bones of Mary of Egypt;  
let earth cover earth; let ashes be added to ashes.  
As soon as you gave me Christ’s body and cup,  
I, conqueror of the world, passed from the first to the second world.

When the evening meal full of mysteries was completed,  
heavy night stole on, because the sun had withdrawn with the sun.  
[Note: Col. 1337, Ebr.: “crept over.”]  
At last Zosimas learns from these words both her name and the day of her death. Who was the author of this?

[Col. 1338D] For he knew that the woman had read none of these things,  
learned none of them, nor even remembered studies.

From this he learns also that, after the sacred gifts had been administered, Mary  
was conveyed there in a moment and immediately released,  
to the place to which he had come worn out after twenty days completed,  
having earned his food by labor.  
[Note: Col. 1337, Ebr.: “and food.”]

Displaying new wounds of mind through lamentations,  
he sits beside the lifeless body, drenched in abundant rain of grief;  
angered at fate, he devotes himself to the office of piety,  
applauds with praises, covers the limbs, closes the eyes;  
now he embraces the footprints, now venerates  
face, hair, and features. These had received no care of adornment;  
their majesty was neglect, squalor, poverty.

[Col. 1339A] 1276 The woman, sufficiently cleansed by tears summoned by piety,  
is freely washed, because she is almost equal to the glorified.

He attends to burial; this occupies him, this is his care.  
But he does not know what to do: the hard earth is frozen.  
Much breaks the old man; labor, heat, and thirst afflict him.  
Strength yields to years; his arms are bound in wrinkled folds;  
there is no spade at hand, nor any hoe.

While he grieves and groans, a new event takes away his sighs:  
his eyes are dried, because better things are prepared by hope.

For a lion, resembling one in mourning and honoring the funeral,  
promising service and laying aside rage and wildness,  
comes with lowered head and humbled pride

[Col. 1339B] and humbly adds its tongue to lick the holy feet.

Astonished at so remarkable and devout a companion,  
he attributes it to the woman’s merits: that the beast is gentle,  
that the lion is mild, that her name clung to the sand,  
that light shone upon her and led him as a light before him;  
that no beast or bird attacked her, abandoned without a guardian and unburied,  
nor tore her, nor did great heat dissolve her, nor a whole year consume her.  
Already he pictured what glory awaited limbs  
lying incorrupt beneath hot winds.

Having experienced so many and such great gifts of the Thunderer at once,

[Col. 1340A] he remembers all and rereads what he is to say everywhere,  
giving commands to his companion in this address:

“My companion, we are pressed and commanded to bury her  
whom the world does not know, though no second is greater in the world.  
If you have come sent in Christ’s name,  
if you are to serve, dig the tomb, then return.

Cast off fear; unlearn your accustomed rage.  
What you do for this woman shall turn to the praise of Christ.”

Before he had finished these words, the lion, having set aside wildness and threats,  
walks more gently and readily obeys him;  
ignorant of delay, in the fleeting moment of an hour  
it fulfils the command, completing the work swiftly.

Meanwhile the monk prostrates himself beside the sacred body.  
No garment covered him but a worn and old cowl,

[Col. 1340B] battered and scarcely clinging to him.  
With these coverings he wraps the limbs of the dead woman—  
that immense treasure, now bearing  
something of splendor, something of solemn fragrance,  
something radiant from the nectar of the dwellers in heaven—  
a woman blessed by the reward of saints’ labors.

She is carried to the tomb and buried with the beast serving.  
Then the old man retraces his way and orders the lion, his servant, to depart.  
At home he recounts what he saw and does not spare faults:  
he rebukes, exhorts, promises good things, and threatens hard ones.

Thus, when he had completed twenty lustra, he rested.

[Col. 1339]

1276* **THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT, BISHOP OF LE MANS: LAMENT OF A SINFUL SOUL.**

(From manuscript no. 656, new numbering, and 222, old numbering, of the Tours library; first edited by J.-J. Bourassé, canon of Tours.)

[Col. 1339B] When the day of death comes,  
when death begins to press hard,  
then laughter will fail me;  
then, too late, mourning will arrive.

Why do I, wretched man, laugh now?  
Why do I rejoice thus at present?  
Why do I not always mourn?  
Why do I not weep for my sins?

What good shall I bring to Christ?  
What shall I report that I have done?  
I despised the heavenly life  
and loved instead a wretched one.

I spurned divine commands;  
I always did unlawful things;  
my mind, willingly subject to evils,  
has become—alas!—ruined.

Never did I keep myself chaste,  
but I polluted myself far too foully;  
I wished to be thought a virgin,  
but did not wish to be chaste.

I desire to be called fasting,  
but I stuff my belly too greatly;  
with excessive food and drink  
I nourish the flesh beyond measure.

Anger so drove me to rage  
that it often bore away a trophy,  
[Col. 1339B] struck me with dreadful weapon,  
and took my mind from me.

What shall I say of sadness?  
What shall I complain of concerning envy,  
which, together with her mother Pride,  
overthrows every good thing?

Since through so many harmful faults  
I have fallen into vices,  
what rewards can I await  
except great punishments?

Though I do these things,  
though I serve sins,  
yet I shall end this life  
and come to the day of death.

Then I shall be unable to do anything  
by which I might escape punishment,  
but shall be consumed into ashes  
and dissolved into dust.

The bitter day will come  
when the righteous Judge will come,  
through whom everyone shall receive  
according to what each now does.

A trumpet sounding from heaven  
will command all to rise,  
to come before the tribunal,  
and disclose deeds done and spoken.

[Col. 1340B] All will hear that trumpet;  
they will immediately come forth from tombs,  
behold what they have done,  
and reveal all their acts.

Then that highest King,  
who now is most merciful,  
will be the most righteous Judge  
and serene of countenance.

A tempest will precede him,  
and a great fire go before,  
which will end the whole world  
and cannot be quenched by water.

There the assemblies of angels  
and choirs of archangels  
will stand before the highest Judge,  
the stern avenger of evils.

There prophets will be present,  
nor will patriarchs be absent,  
and they will preside over those to be judged  
who now forsake worldly things.

Thrones are set for all  
precious martyrs,  
Christ’s confessors,  
and holy virgins also.

Then tribes and peoples will rise—  
old men, children, little ones—  
[Col. 1341] and each will set forth before all  
what sin he has committed.

No one will be able to hide;  
every human being will be present,  
whoever has been born  
or has died in the womb.

What then will you say, little man?  
In what refuge will faith be found?  
None will come to your aid,  
certainly no one to your defense.

Spare laughter now, now;  
apply yourself to frequent tears;  
renounce wicked acts;  
devote yourself to good works.

For whatever you do here,  
whatever you think,  
whatever you do with shame,  
will then be open to others.

Then surrounding multitudes of men  
will see your harmful deeds  
and your disgraceful secrets.

If someone now stripped you  
and saw you naked,  
although he saw nothing foul,  
you would nevertheless be greatly ashamed.

What confusion then will there be?  
What desolation, do you suppose,  
when every nation will laugh  
at your disgrace?

For your lust,  
your burning envy,  
and ruinous pride  
will then be known.

Then you will clearly know  
how foully you now live,  
how many evils you now commit,  
and in how many ways you defile yourself.

You will see the monastic choir  
among the angelic choir,  
exceedingly glorified  
and distinguished from the host of the judged.

You will see yourself cast far away,  
thrown among the damned;  
no share of the kingdom will be given you,  
no honor of the monastic life.

You will see them shining brightly,  
yourself growing foul;  
them joyfully singing together,  
but yourself sadly groaning.

They will be in glory;  
you in unceasing misery.  
To them joys will be given;  
to you grievous torments.

The judgment will end,  
and each will bear his own body with him  
to the prize,  
or to everlasting punishment.

If then you are condemned,  
if—may it not be!—you perish,  
you will weep that you were born,  
that you lived even one hour.

Then late repentance,  
vain laments,
