and frequent sighs  
will at last crush your heart.

You will be food for demons  
and fuel for dragons;  
you will be gnawed by serpents  
and consumed by worms.

On one side you will see flame raging,  
on the other water freezing;  
if you wish to flee from this side,  
you will be compelled to rush to that.

You will have exceedingly savage  
torturers in hell;  
then you will see deadly beings  
[Col. 1341] whom you now believe honey-sweet.

You will feel cruel torments  
and swiftly desire to die;  
yet you will not end your life  
nor obtain what you seek.

On one side, most frequent missiles;  
on the other, densest night pressing down;  
there blackest flame,  
here foulest water.

Then by dogs’ barking,  
lions’ roaring,  
and bulls’ bellowing  
you will be slain with terrors.

One will strive to crush you by biting,  
another to dig you up with his foot,  
another to strike you down with his horn;  
all will labor to destroy you.

Then, with the hooks and nails of the Devil,  
the eyes of those will be driven from their foreheads  
who now wander openly  
through the various ages of the world.

Then they will seek to cut off hands,  
tear away legs,  
and remove all limbs  
that now move to sin.

Intolerable stench,  
unspeakable mourning,  
horrible lamentation will be there,  
but useful to no one at all.

The sun never shines there,  
light never gleams there,  
the moon gives no light,  
nor is bitter night absent.

There are no joys there,  
but everlasting sadness;  
no consolations whatsoever,  
but cruel torments.

Weeping and gnashing of teeth  
hold dominion there.  
“Alas, alas!” is the cry  
of all who perish there.

“Woe, woe! Why were we born?  
Why did we live for one hour?  
Why did we not fear the clergy?  
Why did we love to sin?

“Alas, alas, you vices,  
once so sweet to us—  
how grievous you are to us now,  
how cruel you now are!

“Woe! Why did we trust you?  
Why did we not avoid you?  
Why did we satisfy you?  
Why did we wish to follow you?

“What now is pride to us,  
or what does boasting profit?  
All things have now passed away  
which were then pleasant.”

Each will cry these things;  
the peoples will rehearse them  
while they bear the Devil’s punishments  
as the reward of sin.

What then, sinful soul,  
what then will you say, most wretched one,  
when you are made so sorrowful,  
seeing such harsh evils?

If then you could rise again  
and resume this life,  
you would greatly correct yourself  
and no longer wish to sin.

And you would promise God,  
if you believed it could help,  
that you would never again commit  
what would offend him.

Yet you will desire this in vain,  
for you will accomplish none of it;  
but you will receive what you do,  
nor will you escape torments.

[Col. 1342] Nor will infernal punishments alone  
torment you,  
but also the glory of the saints  
and the joys of Paradise.

1276 You will weep for these things laid upon you,  
for those goods set so far away;  
subdued by great evils,  
you will grieve for blessings lost.

For who could describe,  
or what mind comprehend,  
what splendor is in heaven,  
what is the condition of the city above?

This city is called Zion;  
in it God the King is seen;  
in it life is eternal;  
it is inhabited by the saints.

Death has never entered it;  
life has never departed from it;  
none who possesses it has died;  
everyone lacking it has perished.

The enemy does not enter it;  
the citizen does not leave it.  
Whoever obtains it  
is made a child of God.

This is the heavenly city,  
in which everlasting brightness,  
perpetual blessedness,  
and eternal joy endure.

There you will never hunger;  
there will be neither cold nor ice,  
no distressing aspect,  
nor any kind of inclement weather.

There is no sadness there,  
no envy at all,  
but everlasting joy  
and unending glory endure.

There is abiding prosperity there,  
abiding cheerfulness remains,  
sure and constant security,  
secure perpetuity.

There are no hatreds there,  
no quarrel or discord;  
equal peace alone governs all,  
and harmony binds all things together.

Everything harmful is driven away;  
whatever is beneficial is admitted.  
The gate is shut against adversity;  
the place is given over to delights.

There is perpetual light there,  
and a day that never sets;  
the gate always stands open,  
and one always goes out to pasture.

There are green meadows there  
which bear roses and lilies,  
among which the thousands of saints  
pass their welcome leisure.

The radiant Lamb goes before;  
behind follows the shining choir;  
a flowering field is added,  
and now beneath the field is bright.

Whoever drinks from this fountain  
will never be able to thirst;  
whoever possesses this field  
will lack no good thing.

From here the chariot of the sun is sought,  
its form is beheld;  
the course of the moon is displayed,  
the stations of the stars are revealed.

Such play, with joy,  
takes place in the palace of heaven;  
by such pursuit  
the divine host is refreshed.

It always follows the Lamb,  
is nourished by his praise,  
refreshed by his sight,  
and delights in his love.

But, O mind most limited,

[Col. 1343] what great goods do you recount,  
when you speak only most briefly—  
do not speak except of the final things?

Little is whatever you may say;  
brief is whatever you may conceive;  
mean is whatever you may describe;  
nothing is whatever you may report.

O happy and renowned city,  
endowed with heavenly light,  
founded in gems and gold,  
and subject to God alone!

You shine with diverse stones,  
with holy spirits,  
and with chosen human beings  
who devote themselves to good deeds.

Within you is the angelic choir,  
your hymn-singing choir;  
within you is the apostolic flock,  
truly belonging to you.

You are made red by martyrs,  
you blossom with confessors,  
you are made white by virgins,  
and you shine with all alike.

Within you there is no occupation  
that turns into weariness:  
this is the whole office—  
to praise the King of all.

This alone satisfies all,  
and at the same time makes them drunk;  
and the more it satisfies them,  
the more they burn to advance.

They always behold God;  
they always thirst to praise him;  
by thirsting they advance;  
though satisfied, they hunger.

Each rejoices as much in another’s glory  
as in his own;  
with envy entirely absent,  
a wondrous joy burns brightly.

O Zion, holy city,  
in which charity burns so greatly—

[Col. 1343] how great is your blessedness,  
how great your tranquility within yourself!

O, what will he lack now  
who has attained you?  
What he does not wish will be lacking to him;  
what he truly wishes will be present.

O, if I do not come to you,  
if I do not see you, Mother,  
if I am exiled from you—  
alas, alas, then for wretched me!

If you shut your gate against me,  
if you scorn me when I knock,  
alas, I shall soon be plunged  
into the deep prison with the wretched.

Then my pain will be final;  
then my lamentation will be greatest;  
for the prison is most foul,  
and its torturer most cruel.

There will be no hope of escape,  
no entrance into the kingdom,  
no end to punishments,  
no end of destruction.

But you, King of mercy,  
withdraw the hand of justice;  
grant time for repentance;  
bestow on me hope of pardon.

I have sinned greatly, I confess;  
I greatly fear condemnation.  
Yet I am restored by this hope:  
that I behold you as merciful.

For humankind’s salvation,  
you entered the Virgin’s womb  
so that you might take away  
the prey of our race from cruel masters.

For us you bore mockeries,  
the insults of spittle,  
and also the punishments of the cross,  
by wondrous grace.

Nor did you delay, Lord, to die  
for the relief of slavery;  
and, after death’s threshold was broken,

[Col. 1344] you save us by your blood.

May that Passion, Christ the King,  
become my redemption,  
the forgiveness of sins,  
and restoration to Paradise.

For it will profit me nothing  
that you have freed the world,  
unless you also save me  
and give me life.

Hear, therefore, most loving one;  
hear, most merciful King;  
hear the prayers  
of a most wretched and sinful soul.

I beg you, do not spurn me;  
do not turn away your face;  
nor refuse to receive one  
who wishes to flee to you.

Grant pardon for things committed;  
guard me against things to come,  
so that I may both escape punishments  
and reach the kingdom.

But if I am unworthy  
of the heavenly dwellings and seats,  
grant at least that I may rest  
at the threshold with the lesser ones.

Grant at least the smallest place,  
or even the last rank;  
for I shall think myself very rich  
if I see myself even as the least.

May this be granted by the unbegotten Father,  
and his only-begotten Son,  
and also the Holy Paraclete,  
who is Maker, not made,

that I may be with all the saints  
and with the holy virgins  
in the dwellings of Paradise,  
or even at the feet of the saints.

Whoever reads this little sheet,  
whoever sees this song,  
remember me also  
when you say the *Our Father*.

Here ends the lamentation of the sinful soul.

[Col. 1343]

# HISTORY OF HILDEBERT, BISHOP OF LE MANS, CONCERNING MUHAMMAD

(Thus in a manuscript codex about five hundred years old, formerly of Elnone, or Saint-Amand in Pabula, now Royal manuscript no. 274, which alone among the manuscripts we have seen contains this History.) (G)*

## A BRIEF NOTICE

[Col. 1343] **1277–1278.** A history—or rather, a wholly poetic narrative—fabricated as if for an academic exercise rather than an accurate relation of events such as history ought to be. For, apart from the fact that the author has fallen into a striking anachronism by suggesting that Muhammad’s sect, and the defection from the Church of the remarkable hypocrite—namely, as we suppose, the apostate Sergius—occurred about the time of Theodosius and Saint Ambrose, what he relates here concerning a calf secretly reared in a cave, afterwards grown into a raging bull, and cared for by Muhammad in order that he might become king—since absolutely nothing about this is found in writers who have treated Muhammadan affairs—has the entire flavor of nothing but a fable. Hildebert, perhaps then a young man, still occupied with humane letters rather than serious studies and not yet very experienced in history, seems to have devised and composed it as an exercise in hostility to the Muhammadan sect. Thus we came close to omitting this history or fable, had the excellent Elnone manuscript—from which we otherwise extracted many serious and highly worthy things to be read—not so expressly borne the name of Hildebert. Since it has been our purpose to publish all his works

[Col. 1345] that we could discover, whatever their quantity, we judged that we were not permitted to withhold even the smallest part of them.

[Col. 1345A] Alas, how many fools lie buried through pitiable deceit,  
having despised the knowledge of God!

They scorn Christ, whose miracles they behold,  
Christ, the sole Lord, before whom all the earth trembles.

Thus the foolish nations condemn themselves all the more,  
for they laugh at Christ while they behold his kingdoms.

For those who saw him suffer and could not  
believe thereby redeem their sins with folly.

But lest I sin, because I have just spoken thus,  
and lest, by defending the guilty, I be guilty among them,  
I maintain that to have scorned Christ was a crime;  
but for one who was ignorant, it was thus pardonable.

But it is an immense crime not to believe in you, Christ;  
and, to speak without danger, I do not consider it pardonable.

For who would believe that such a deed—  
so hard, so capital—was worthy of merciful pardon?

[Col. 1345B] The lowest Hell, the insatiable Avernus,  
will seize and greedily carry off these wicked persons,  
deserving eternal death;  
and scarcely can what they suffer there be written.

Fire scorches them—at the sound of it my skin already shudders;  
a thing terrible to hear, terrible to contemplate.

A fiery force assails those wretches  
and harasses them in turns,  
and then the rigor of cold.

For they are condemned so as now to suffer cold,  
and in alternating turn sulphur mingled with pitch.

The worm gnaws them, whom almighty God hates,  
and severe punishment is multiplied for the wicked.

There is dense fire there, which the foul abyss rolls about:

[Col. 1345C] there is never a welcome day there, no rest.

Why do I reserve the final thing? One matter is added to this mass,  
far more lamentable than all that has been said:

to mourn forever, for torments to have no end—  
this is truly more grievous and more miserable.

Since no one can recount or enumerate these things,  
why do I number them, when they lack number?

But if this disastrously secure nation, doomed to perish,  
wasting away in unbelief and possessing no reason,  
could know that it must perish in this manner,  
I think it would abandon this course and provide for itself.

It would leave error, following you, Christ, who are better,  
and would provide for itself by offering vows to you.

But there are pagans who are deceived by empty hope,  
who worship as divinity whatever they desire.

[Col. 1345D] Nor is that people drawn away from error by a lesser error [perhaps: “is led astray”],  
about which I have proposed to write as best I can.

It denies that the deep world belongs to Jupiter’s brother,  
takes from Pluto his Stygian power,

and considers Juno and Diana an empty thing,

[Col. 1346A] nor does it regard Pallas’ wisdom as remarkable.

It says that Mars along with Venus lacks divinity,  
and denies that Proteus and Nereus are gods.

Whatever ancient deceit there once was everywhere  
has become worthless among this people under these names.

They curse these things and those who worship them;  
they also refute these people and regard them as wretched.

They say that people live like beasts eating hay,  
and hold Jews and Christians equally guilty.

They say that they themselves are wise, but that we lack reason;  
and we in turn call them guilty, as they call us.

Thus they call us senseless and themselves blessed,  
saying that they truly worship the Lord,  
who, being God in heaven, governs all things by righteous weapon [perhaps: “zeal”];

but this wretched people in truth does not worship him.

[Col. 1346B] If one asks who this person is whom it so worships,

**1279.** His name is Muhammad; trusting in this leader, it swells with pride.

The worship of all gods has yielded to him,  
who holds as his own the throne of unbelief.

This new error has driven out earlier errors,  
and to Muhammad alone have been given the kingdoms of deceit [perhaps: “of the heavens”].

But you, Godebald, mirror of the greatest men  
[Note: [Col. 1345D] Who this Godebald was is not clear.],

ask what was the beginning of the crime,  
and what first cause brought about such great evils.

You command me to explain it; you command it, and I shall do so.

If God deigns that the undertaking be carried through,  
while I follow your commands, I pray: read in this spirit.

## CANTO I

As you know, a domestic enemy harms more than all else,

[Col. 1346C] and the matter itself teaches how he harms.

For a certain man, badly devoted though washed in baptism,  
lived in the Church, full of treachery.

By magical deceits he sought human praise for himself,  
so that through his efforts the Church might collapse.

While he hid and carefully dissembled this,  
like a wolf he sat in ambush for the churches.

[Note: [Col. 1345D] This description of a hypocritical and most crafty man could not implausibly apply to Sergius—not Sergius I, Patriarch of Constantinople, who was himself a Monothelite and made Emperor Heraclius a Monothelite and protector of the Monothelites, as some have wrongly thought [Col. 1346D]—but another Sergius, an Armenian pseudo-monk and apostate from his order. Infected with the errors of the Arians and Nestorians, he adhered so closely to the impious Muhammad, then planning to establish his sect, that the utterly wicked pseudo-prophet employed him in compiling his Qurʾān.]

With sweet speech and a feigned religion  
he flatters the people under the title of faith.

A false witness had joined him: a hideous plague,  
flesh rarely nourished with food, withered on bread;

fleeing far from play, he went barefoot,  
speaking everything with his head ritually bowed.

As he walked before people, he moved his lips,  
so that whoever saw him might consider him holy.

[Col. 1346D] But, sighing, if at any time he raised

his downcast eyes, in order to stir up the people,  
then he lifted his hands and raised his voice,  
not mourning for himself but pitying the people.

For, secure regarding himself, he spoke only a few words,

[Col. 1347A] praying only for the people with trembling heart.

Thus the holy people, long admiring his faith,  
were almost captured by his deceits in Jerusalem.

For when the Father of that city had passed away  
and suddenly gone to heaven, his body laid out,

then this magician, greedily desiring to be elevated  
and made bishop, nevertheless said timidly  
that he would do this only if he knew it would cause no harm  
should he become bishop, since God so wished.

“Nothing indeed is heavier than the burden of this office;  
to this weight,” he said, “God himself draws me.”

But God, examiner of the heart and righteous ruler,  
being merciful and knowing, provides better.

For what the aforementioned wicked man desired  
displeased Christ and could not happen.

[Col. 1347B] Then the unconquered and blessed king Theodosius  
[Note: [Col. 1347D] This is a manifest anachronism, which casts a certain mark of suspicion upon the poem; for Theodosius and Saint Ambrose flourished about the year 392, whereas Muhammad did not begin to devise his absurdities until about the year 620.],

enemy of unbelief and son of the Church,  
was the greatest of kings; under him the holy authority of laws  
flourished while pious Ambrose preached.

When he had learned that so great a bishop had died,  
he hurried to the place where that Father had died.

And when at last the Father had been buried amid great mourning,  
he consulted Christ with supplicating prayers  
that Christ might show him whom he should worthily appoint bishop.

**1280.** To him a voice thus sounded and warned him:  
“Do not trust the crowd: the enemy lies hidden in the city like a serpent.”

When the voice fell silent, the king stood silent in astonishment.  
He wondered what it meant, yet reverenced it in amazement  
and repeated its warning, thus bewildered.

[Col. 1347C] But soon the crowd resolved what the king considered doubtful:  
for, simple-minded, it carried off the madman  
and dragged the wicked man with it, as though unwilling,  
before the king’s doors. While this ill-advised tumult  
of the simple flock raged lawlessly,  
the king asked what this unusual uproar wanted.

Someone said to him: “The people ask that you come out.”  
As requested, the king immediately went forth.

When the magician saw him come out, he was stunned, and turned back—  
for he truly then wished to flee.

I do not know what he saw, for which he was afraid;  
this is clear: he looked unwillingly upon him.

For the mark of pallor gave signs of fear in him;  
hence he would gladly have fled, had the people permitted it.

[Col. 1347D] To him, struggling while it held him, the crowd said:  
“Though you struggle, you shall be Father of the city.”

When they had pulled him back, they demanded him as bishop,  
indeed praising his words and the man’s faith.

While the court, according to custom, loudly resounded with favor for him,  
a sudden and extraordinary clamor roared.

For it was not with human howls but rather unholy ones:  
when the people fell silent, the building itself roared.

For all the demons throughout the world  
had come there, a crowd allied with the magician.

When the people heard so great a murmur of shouting,  
they fell down and lay silent in astonishment.

[Col. 1348A] The king signed them and restored them with the sign of the cross,  
and prayed to the Lord to restore their senses.

He cleansed the hall and restored the people to God;  
then he addressed the ill-omened magician in these words:

“What does your deceit now accomplish, treacherous pest?  
These deeds are your disease.

Whoever knows you to be harmful and deceitful,  
when he examines you will strike you severely.

And so that the true God himself may be more severe toward you,  
I spare you now; but there you shall suffer  
perpetually, when you are deservedly tortured by fire,  
from which you will desire pardon and nevertheless find none.

Go far away, cruel creature, most worthy victim of Dis;  
flee hence into the distance. Unless you do so now,  
I wish you then to learn what the judgment of our courts is.”

[Col. 1348B] “Therefore flee quickly.”

Then he said to his attendants: “I command that this man be carried away.”  
Accordingly he was immediately seized and dragged outside.

Thus the ancient deceit, the pest and wicked enemy,  
could not deceive those whom it had wished to deceive.

Yet, dragged away and compelled to go farther,  
he pronounced this curse upon the Church:

“I shall return, and not merely so: I shall repay you a hundredfold.  
Though your Church is now outstanding,  
it shall suffer our destructions [perhaps: “threats”], suffering destruction,  
when its posterity, conquered by me, pays me  
the full penalties it deserves and which I desire.”

In this the magician was, alas, prophetic.

[Col. 1348C] If you seek a witness, look at the pagan plague,  
whose wickedness leaves signs even today.

**1281.** For the people that hates Christ, the destructive people,  
the people obeying Muhammad and devoid of reason,  
still zealously strives to defend its foolish worship—  
why it perishes, I know, in everlasting punishment.

This particular magician was the cause of such evil,  
whom the Church expelled because of his treachery.

Driven out, blazing with fierce rage,  
he seethed and went, steeped in swift destruction.

Like an impious bear, he turned his course into Libya.  
At that time the Church flourished in Libya;  
Africa prospered and offered vows to Christ,  
but, alas, it quickly abandoned the one whom it had rightly worshipped.

For now the aforesaid magician came, having left the city,

[Col. 1348D] and likewise raged against this pious Church.

Here indeed he pretended, as before, to live a holy life;  
while skillfully counterfeiting good, he accumulated evil.

For, plotting slaughter of souls, the enemy entered the consul’s house as a guest;  
the consul received him.

He rejoiced in the guest, since he reverently regarded  
all Christians as citizens of heaven.

Accordingly he cherished the magician, whose fasts he knew,  
and saw his rites and sacred garb.

For the wicked man lived with such a simple life,  
appearing simple and as though free of bitterness,  
that he was called the flower of those churches.

[Col. 1349A] For no one could know what sort of magician he was.

Therefore the aforesaid wealthy man honored him all the more;  
he loved and feared him, and regarded him as pious.

## CANTO II

This wealthy man, who trusted him well, had a slave  
named Mamutius, whose office it was  
to manage his master’s affairs and attend to them.  
This was Mamutius’ duty and responsibility.

He provided for him and, beyond all else, took care  
to serve the aforesaid magician in this way:  
to give him everything he wished, deny him nothing,  
and immediately do all that he commanded.

Embracing him more closely and binding him to himself in friendship  
by many flatteries and poisons,  
the magician bound him captive, because he saw Mamutius fit

[Col. 1349B] to become material for the intended crime.

Thus he cast out these words in an arrogant voice:

“Ask confidently to choose whatever pleases you.  
Choose, and I shall give what you have chosen and multiply what you request;  
whatever you seek, you shall receive through my gift.”

When the magician had promised these things, Mamutius stood astonished,  
asking what he should desire and what might suit him.

At last he said: “Father, at your words my spirit has revived.  
If what I ask can be done,  
I ask surely for nothing else through you  
than to be made free by swift assistance.”

To this the accursed man replied:  
“You shall obtain what you seek as this gift.

But you know me poorly, since you ask for such gifts:  
is what is easiest to me difficult?

It would indeed be easy to give anyone this gift to you;

[Col. 1349C] but truly I wish to do more for you.

For since gifts ought to correspond to the recipient’s person,  
small things suit the humble, great things those like myself.

Through me you shall be a consul. I have almost told you  
the other things that I have proposed to give, but I had better keep silent;  
yet it shall come later, and what I have told you shall happen.”

Mamutius promptly replied:

“If I am to be your servant, I seek no other gifts;  
for I shall be truly free if I serve you.”

But when the magician learned this, he immediately set his tricks in motion,  
and struck Mamutius’ innocent master  
with illness and burned him with such pains  
that death would have been lighter for him and life more grievous.

[Col. 1349D] **1282.** And because he lingered and did not die so quickly—  
because death was not ready—he suffered more.

He said to himself: “Unless he dies immediately,  
I cannot prevail; but I know what I shall do.”

Having said this silently, he immediately uttered murmurings of wickedness,  
as though righteous, under the appearance of righteousness.

Rising at night, he skilfully removed the lights  
so that darkness might conceal such a notorious crime,  
and he bound everyone in orderly fashion as though dead in sleep.

When this was done, he himself, the closest accomplice in the crime, proceeded;  
and, baring his arms up to the shoulders,  
he crushed the sick man with hands and feet.

Without delay he also stopped his mouth with his nostrils,  
thus taking away his breath; nevertheless  
he broke his throat and compelled him to undergo death,

[Col. 1350A] repaying good gifts with such gifts.

Then he returned rejoicing and said, applauding himself:  
“Now that the crime has been done, I think I am advancing.”

But after Phoebus shone and restored  
to the world the office of light,  
the consul’s death was discovered by the servants.  
When it was made known to many, color fled from their faces,  
and unfamiliar grief overwhelmed them all.

One weeps and beats his breast;  
another tears his hair; grief consumes each.

Here one groans, there one laments: a single grief afflicts all.  
Then the pitiable death of their good patron  
moved not only all his clients to weeping;  
widows also wept unceasingly.

And above all the destitute populace, full of mourning,  
and every church, grieved devoutly.

[Col. 1350B] The entire company of monks with the clergy of the saints,  
the prince and the humble populace, were then in tears.

The aforesaid wicked man also came among them,  
soaked in tears and abandoning himself to grief;  
he became an example of weeping and sorrow,  
and therefore no one believed him guilty.

But after the honored man had been buried  
and the grief had subsided, each recovered his mind.

Then the magician pressed more vigorously upon his foolish enterprises,  
affecting and deceiving the consul’s wife in such a way  
that she could scarcely endure unless she hastened  
to take her own slave Mamutius as husband, though unwilling.

Concerning this she consulted the prescient magician,  
who, as if prudently, gave this cautious reply:

[Col. 1350C] “If you did this, you would provide for yourself.  
You have begun well, if you do this as you wish,  
with God as author and by my counsel.”

She returned rejoicing, daring this crime  
so long as she could have Mamutius as husband.

Impatient of delay, she immediately gave Mamutius  
the honor of freedom; she removed  
his servile office and rendered it lordly for him,  
and made her slave her master.

Indeed, under the marriage-torch and by the rite of wedlock,  
she gave herself to him—alas, because she was put to shame.  
Yet although I say this, I confess her to have been chaste  
and to have rightly been a good matron.

But the ancient deceit, the wicked magician, deceived her;  
nor had it been terrible for him to put her husband to death.

## CANTO III

[Col. 1350D]

Thus, when the blessed consul Mamutius now shone in the honor of high rank,  
wealthy and distinguished,  
he summoned his condemned, wicked dependant  
and addressed him thus:

“Behold: through you Mamutius openly enjoys  
the things promised. I am called consul, yet I deny that I am one.

Now you exercise our honor in the manner of a lord;  
our honor is yours, because yours is mine.

You, Father, shall prescribe and set down what must be done,  
and I shall obey your command immediately.”

“The greater honor,” said the magician, “you shall have through me  
if you do as I advise the things I command.

Take for yourself a calf not yet weaned, but only now born

[Col. 1351A] from its mother; let the matter remain hidden from the people.

We shall shut it up when taken and have it fed,  
so that no one may know where the calf is concealed.

Yet, so that the matter may truly remain hidden without a witness,  
my skill is needed: a pit shall be made,  
unknown to all and removed from the light,  
so that neither sun nor moon may know what is done there.

Let the calf be placed there; but lest it be seen,  
let it lie hidden there alone and see no one but us.

And lest some sudden calf-like cry disclose it,  
it must be dug deep down.

And the chief concern must be that it is dug so far down  
that the calf’s voice does not strike the people’s ears.

We two shall feed it and shall be the only ones who know;  
the affair will be of no use if the wandering crowd knows it.

[Col. 1351B] But if a fifth eye sees the calf inside,  
after that fifth eye you may think the people know it.

Therefore see that you conceal it and reveal these words to no one;  
you yourself must profit from your cunning.”

Mamutius stood ready to answer,  
but the magician restrained and forbade him to speak.

“It is not for speaking now,” he said, “but for doing.”  
Therefore Mamutius hurried away at once.

Now he said nothing; he merely acted and planned  
to carry out diligently, in proper fashion, every detail  
which the magician had ordered to be prepared and arranged.

He sought a calf; the matter remained unknown to the people.

He dug a cave such as, I think, had never existed:  
blind, terrible, fit for demons,  
near to hell and remote from heaven,

[Col. 1351C] a place of earth dreadful in Stygian fashion.

The newly born calf, condemned to such a prison,  
was confined and frequently fed in darkness.

The magician and Mamutius fed it;  
it was known only to them, hidden from the others.

They alone fed the calf and alone knew  
that the former calf had now become a bull.

If you saw it, you would scarcely think it a calf;  
rather, you would say: “It is the companion of a demon.”

For it did not possess a bull’s form but that of a foreign,  
new monster, not comparable with an ox.

Horrible in horns, more to be feared than a rhinoceros,  
the fiery light of its eye was terror to the people.

The very shape of its cheeks bristled as though with thorns;

[Col. 1351D] no beast had nostrils comparable to its own.

Its breath was terrible; its mouth had a gaping opening,  
whose black maw had the appearance of the abyss.

Its crest was crested and maned in equine fashion;  
its neck was splendid in form and terrifying.

Its breast stood out with swelling muscles of fine appearance,  
and there it scarcely resembled itself.

Alas—shall I set its back, or its other limbs, apart:  
back, breast, legs, and feet?

It was, I think, equal in size to an elephant standing among woods;  
and, if anyone asks, such was the beast.

## CANTO IV

Meanwhile a thing occurred to be lamented and mourned:  
the king of Libya, son of the Church, died.

While he lived, his realm flourished in peace;

[Col. 1352A] there was no wickedness there, but pious justice.

No age had known what impiety was;  
it guarded against the vice of unbelief as against destruction.

This had been brought about by the rigor of law and the king’s resolute mind;  
under his reign the pious Church flourished.

**1284.** Like a guardian defending the righteous on every side,  
he was an enemy of impiety wherever he could be.

He was the hope of bereaved widows,  
embracing the wretched as his own children.

He was their consolation, their relief,  
considering all humble persons like himself.

Thus this good man, good toward the good and a lover of religion,  
by dying became an object of mourning in the pious land.

O true piety! Grief scarcely sets bounds for itself.  
The strength of young men weeps, and the frailty of old men weeps;

[Col. 1352B] mothers’ affection weeps, fathers’ reverence mourns,  
and tender children weep together with their fathers.

Africa mourned, as though everyone grieved for himself:  
every Christian, soldier and farmer alike.

Equal too was the grief of slaves and masters.  
Rich and poor grieve; grief is not usually

such. For the clergy, the stern company of monks,  
and every person who rightly worshipped God, grieved.

For this good patron’s life was a protection;  
when he died, the pious Church fell.

Thus, with continual tears, the unhappy fates  
of both king and pious Church are mourned everywhere.

Therefore, when the king had been buried with excessive lamentation,  
they inscribed amid the tumult words under this heading:

[Col. 1352C] “Three causes of grief lie enclosed beneath this marble:  
the king, glory of the Church, highest honor of the country.”

## CANTO V

But when the torrent of so many tears had passed,  
Libya established a council amid uncertainty,  
in which it was debated which noble should be appointed,  
who should be king of Libya, the country’s worthy salvation.

Thus, while among the nobles an heir to the kingdom was sought,  
Mamutius’ companion said to him:

“Go, I pray, and hurry more swiftly than usual;  
seek the council, uncertain in its counsels.

When you have permission to speak, ask that I be called,  
for I know that I shall truly benefit you in this way.

I would say more, unless perhaps it might be harmful;  
even as I give this advice, I detain you too long.”

[Col. 1352D] Mamutius immediately did everything he said, word for word;  
he hurried thence quickly, hastening more than usual.

He waited for nothing but flew as a fugitive,  
until he came into the midst of the council,  
where the murmur of dreadful strife had already begun to rise.

Since every noble desired the summit of power,  
the quarrels of cruel conflict would soon have grown  
had Mamutius not quickly come between them.

For after the preliminary words of bitter strife,  
when men were taking up arms and the camps resounded  
among maddened peoples rushing to arms,  
Mamutius sprang swiftly into their midst.

Thus he calmed and reconciled the nobles.  
When he had settled them and the people were silent,  
after a brief hesitation he is said to have spoken thus:

[Col. 1353A] “I praise the past quarrels now settled;  
yet I by no means boast of what I have done.

I wish it known that I have come to speak without deceit.  
I rejoice to have come, but more to have reconciled you,  
through whom justice flourishes in this land,  
through whom the height of your honors stands and increases,  
through whom Libya flourishes in outstanding peace.

It truly becomes such men as you to uphold every undertaking,  
and each of you is fit for exceptional authority.

But custom demands that one man bear the office of kingship;  
one house does not allow twin masters.

For a king alongside a king is what crimes are to law;  
sovereignty has no concordant partner.

Yet, if you wish one king to be properly made without strife  
by swift counsel,

[Col. 1353B] **1285.** I shall show this, and after counsel prove  
that nothing is better or more useful.

I know a certain man, not one of venerable appearance  
but contemptible, resembling a wretch;  
yet he is full of religion, poor,  
simple and wise, and knowing all future things.

I think him wiser in speech than Solomon,  
for his counsels are prophecies.

Let him be sought, that he may judge and declare  
what ought rightly to be done and what ought wrongly to be done.

He had finished speaking and was preparing to say more;  
he would have wished to speak more, if the people had allowed him.

But both parties cried out alike:

[Col. 1353C] “Let Mamutius be silent; let the proposed thing please us.”

Then the misguided senate, approving these words,  
no longer doubted whom it should send.

They immediately asked Mamutius to go  
for the man of wondrous virtue; but he asked his companion—  
to whom the choice among a thousand nobles was given—  
and that man selected one who was foolish and freeborn.

Therefore they departed and sought the magician together;  
they entreated and urgently begged him  
to come with them, that he might judge what was fair for all  
and govern the council. But the magician refused to go,

saying that he did this, yet did not wish to teach it;  
indeed, that he would be silent if anyone taught him.

He said these things also and repeated them many times:

[Col. 1353D] that he, a wretch, knew nothing among the crowd of nobles.

Yet when beseeched and repeatedly begged,  
he yielded as though unwilling, as though distressed to go.

And, although his evil mind was glad and accustomed to deceit,  
he wholly concealed it beneath mournful clothing.

When he saw a saddled, harnessed horse prepared for him,  
the wicked man said: “What have I to do with trappings?

Who prepared a horse for me? Do not trust him together with me.  
Let every horse be far away; no such honor is for me.

Either I shall be carried on these two feet, or, if by strangers,  
I shall be carried on twice two feet, like the Lord’s ass.”

Accordingly, the envoys, following the wicked man’s word,  
endeavored promptly to do what he ordered.

They sought an ass for him and set him upon it;  
when this was done, they returned and went swiftly away.

[Col. 1354A] But the magician, forewarned by his own wickedness, had meanwhile  
released the bull from the cave before  
his aforesaid companion Mamutius, summoned to the council,  
set out hurriedly to seek it.

He had encircled the bull’s forehead with a golden inscription;  
thus leading it into unfamiliar light,  
like a beast frightened by novel brightness and roused to war,  
it leapt, bellowed, and fled like the wind.

Thus, after little delay, it quickly crossed the neighboring fields,  
showing mercy to none and crushing everything.

It spared no one: it trampled people and lands,  
and alike brought down sheep and mighty oxen.

Swollen with rage, it leveled crops and trampled meadows beneath its feet;  
nor could it remember that it was a bull.

## CANTO VI

[Col. 1354B] Thus, destructive and monstrous to many,  
it drew an innumerable crowd to the spectacle [that is, the show].

When the aforesaid magician, born a dire man,  
entered the council to which he had hurried,

there stood in the midst of the nobles a confusion of affairs—  
an enemy of justice, an embodiment of wickedness.

Humble in countenance and remarkable in poor clothing,  
he was silent like a sheep, which pleased the people.

Then they asked him to speak,  
and for this sole deceiver to choose the king.

**1286.** And when he seemed about to speak, silence fell everywhere  
so that the wicked man’s voice might be heard.

First, groaning, he drew sighs from the depths  
of his breast, suddenly weeping in his usual manner.

[Col. 1354C] Raising his hands, the profane man carefully turned  
his murmurings in his mouth, speaking a few words silently.

Then he bent the knee; his treacherous mind wove snares  
so that he might be believed under the appearance of faith.

The simple people wondered and wept with him,  
and, unaware that he was guilty, praised him.

After he had been drenched with tears, he proceeded sadly  
to his remaining words, ready to speak weighty things, and said:

“I care every day for each of your affairs;  
today and every day you are my concern.

I pray for you; I labor to benefit you.  
I shall always be yours in every way I can.

But in these present affairs you have consulted  
a lowly person, one like wretched me.

[Col. 1354D] I disgrace myself if I alone give counsel;  
if I alone decide, I shall be justly arrogant.

Therefore I now reveal to you something made known from heaven;  
my own mind will not give this, but God.

Whoever yokes the bull shall reign worthily—  
one who has not borne yokes and does not know how to bear them.

Whomever God chooses, let man love and revere;  
for whoever loves him appeases God.

Why, however, this election should have an appropriate sign,  
I shall explain briefly, if it pleases you.

This people is likened and compared to a bull,  
for this race of men scarcely tolerates a master.

But let him rule Libya firmly and powerfully  
who subjugates the bull more successfully and more easily.

[Col. 1355A] He will strengthen and establish justice;  
he will change harmful things and bestow every good.

And because he will reign, he will henceforth drive away every evil;  
and Libya will flourish under him in pious peace.”

## CANTO VII

He had spoken, and great tumult followed his words:  
the young men applauded, nor were the old men silent.

Youthful strength considers this easy for itself;  
but old age, to which prudence has given intelligence,  
said within itself: “Mature wisdom is with me;  
the strength of young men is defeated by the old man’s skill.

Why should I despair? Why should I not seek the kingdom?  
If old age forbids this, let intelligence urge it.

Skill will compensate for what my small strength denies me;  
sure reason shall govern all that I do.”

[Col. 1355B] Thus you might see all the nobles hoping for the kingdom:  
the young men through their own strength, the old through cunning.

Now the whole region was stirred by such great terror:  
one part fled in fear, a great part hid in dread.

But those who had fled came before the assembly  
so that the council might bring them help.

They said that what they fled in trembling  
was a terrible monster, almost like an ox,

sparing no one, scarcely yielding to any crowd,  
destroying everything wherever it rushed in flight.

At this the entire assembly was afraid; even the young men  
were terrified of the monster, and trembled in fear.

Then he urges more strongly that they should go to this monster,  
and, as the magician wished, the crowd rushes to meet it.

[Col. 1355C] Seeing from afar the huge bull coming,  
they shuddered; yet, in hope of an extraordinary sovereignty,  
each man who seeks it made himself wholly ready for the task.  
And now the magnificent and terrifying bull  
stood in the middle, surrounded everywhere by a wondrous ring.  
1287 But when the crowd had halted, the magician repeated this:

“Come now, whoever wishes to be king, only take up the sceptre:  
behold, you can obtain the gifts of rule.  
Whoever yokes this bull, let him, in my judgment, gain the crown;  
and, at God’s command, let this land be beneath his sway.”

At these words applause is given, but none dared  
come near; each was afraid for himself.  
But the bull stood there, bellowing and uncertain within itself  
what it ought rather to do, whom it should first attack.  
For it believed that all whom it saw were enemies.

[Col. 1355D] Looking about at them, it yielded to its thirst among them;  
it rages against itself and often turns in a circle.  
For it stood uncertain where it should rush first.

## CANTO VIII

Here is something which I think ought by no means to be left unsaid.  
A brave, unbridled young man leapt forward.

He said to the bull: “Unless, conquered, you grant me the crown,  
I shall die nobly and thus obtain renown.  
To die struck by you will bring me great honour;  
no praise belongs to your ferocity, but to my courage.”

Then, moving sideways so as to deceive the savage beast,  
he quickly tried to seize it by the horn.  
And I think he would have caught it, had the beast not been wary;  
but when it was nearly captured, the crowd rushed forward to meet it.

[Col. 1356A] And as though rejoicing to have found a certain enemy,  
with the bloody aspect of deceit it gaped at this man alone.  
When the young man saw it, he blushed as if struck  
by a gentle breath of wind, yet he was not afraid.

Although he knew that he could not escape  
unless he fled more swiftly and provided for himself,  
he stood fearless; such strength of spirit did he possess  
that he preferred to fall rather than flee cowardly.

Thus, though lacking weapons, yet conspicuous in strength of heart,  
he gladly returned to the arms nature had given him.  
And so he undertook warfare, fitting his limbs for battle:  
his right hand was a sword; his left hand, a shield.

Behold him, his savage left hand bare and without covering—  
what things he endured, what things he did not fear!  
He stood without a sword, yet, though unarmed, still did not hesitate.

[Col. 1356B] O wondrous man, wondrous in courage!  
I think scarcely anyone can ever be named with equal praise—  
he to whom death was welcome while he was able to live.

Therefore he preferred death to yielding to fear,  
but rejoices to become such a spectacle for the people. [Or: “a spectacle.”]

Then the deadly wild beast, as if wings aided its course,  
rushes upon the young man, by whom the wretch is crushed;  
and, quicker than speech, he falls beneath the fatal blow.

When the bull saw that the young man had fallen,  
it raged against him as though saying to the conquered man: “Go now,  
and have it written that I yielded to you;  
thus through long ages you shall enjoy my trophy.”

But the young man, stripped of life, thus—  
alas for grief!—expires; the vile beast turns him about,

[Col. 1356C] playing with him as a lion plays with an enemy [perhaps: “a sheep”].

But the various peoples, seeing this, said:  
“This beast truly came from heaven,  
and whoever yokes it will rightly rule.”

But when the bull looked upon the wretched young man,  
now wholly torn to pieces, it bent its horns about;  
and by chance it saw its two masters.

When it saw those known to it standing at a distance,  
it went swiftly in that direction; but the people began  
to flee from that side, grievously deceived by magical art.

Then Mammutius, that companion of the magician,  
advances joyfully from the troop, fearing nothing,  
and comes forth alone—fraud, crime, deceit itself,  
the crime of treachery. The panting bull was now present;

[Col. 1356D] it repeatedly licks with its mouth the hands extended to it,  
hands that had often been offered before,  
and more often circles round its master,  
whom Mahomet held as he wished.

Cunningly, therefore, he orders a hard yoke to be brought;  
it was offered, and he placed it upon the bull’s neck  
as its conqueror. Patiently the bull endured  
the touch of the friend whom it feared as its master.

While Mammutius thus tames its wildness,  
the trembling, astonished nobles soon approach.  
They read the writing, at which they were more astonished still;  
for the brow of the bull was inscribed with strange signs,  
glittering with gold, and bore a new inscription.  
Those who saw it report that it was as follows:

“God has chosen this man, to whom he has compelled me to serve.  
Thus by God’s mercy I have been sent to him.”

[Col. 1357A] When the nobles saw what had been written,  
they seize Mammutius and make him their lord.

## CANTO IX

Then a din resounds in the camp as though war were thundering in the sky.  
Not even civil war has produced such a sound.  
You would have said that the very floodgates of heaven were broken;  
if all things were collapsing, they would roar no otherwise.

Such was the indiscriminate voice of the frenzied people  
when they appoint Mammutius their lord.

He resists, indeed protesting aloud:  
“You act unjustly, and I think you have no sense.  
I have never sought nor desired to hold a kingdom.  
You act unjustly; why do you seize me thus?  
But if you persist in using force against me,  
I shall not enjoy the sovereignty that I desire.”

[Col. 1357B] Therefore, seized all the more, he is fitted for the royal sceptre;  
he alone is acclaimed, and so the crown is bestowed.  
Mammutius becomes king after the sacred law has perished.  
By such an order came the origin of evil.

His own craftiness had bestowed this arrogance upon him—  
he through whose treachery Libya, wounded, weeps.

When the wicked man had begun to reign and rule,  
the magician approaches him thus and speaks:

“It becomes you to remember my services,  
if you remember what you are and what you were.  
You will give me gifts, and, unless I am mistaken, you will love me;  
and, as I hope, I shall not be of little account to you.

“Now therefore, if you wish every man to favour you,  
do what I advise: thereafter you will be equal to God.  
Thus I shall give you the highest things; thus I shall raise you above the stars.

[Col. 1357C] For me, it is too little to give kingdoms of the earth.  
Through me you will be supreme; through me you will be made God,  
if you perform, as I command, what I counsel you.

“The law of the Gospels, which must be changed, is harsh:  
it considers us devoid of sense and foolish,  
because it forbids us to commit adultery and indulge in lust  
and itself destroys the marriage-bed even of relatives.

“It forbids many things by its commands and confirms worthless things,  
which you shall condemn when you give rules more suitable.  
For you shall decree that adultery is to be committed and Venus served.  
Let the household be luxurious, and let Venus be unrestrained.

“But you must enclose your decrees within this limit:  
that whatever had been forbidden shall now be permitted.  
Thus, without law, you can win the greater favour of the people,  
if you heed my words.

[Col. 1357D] “Nothing is more burdensome than to be held by a strict law;  
therefore ensure that all things which please may be allowed.  
You can be taught by subtle reasoning how this may be done,  
if you obey me.

“Attack the faulty sayings of earlier writers,  
and correct better now what was formerly badly written.  
Hand down for reading what is free from error and blame;  
ridicule the rest as not worthy of faith.

1289 “We ought rightly to believe that scripture  
which is rightly accepted and lacks arbitrariness.  
Conversely, I rightly despise a scripture  
which gives a harmful law, for it injures free choice.

“Free choice, created broad under liberty,  
you immediately nullify if you establish a law.

[Col. 1358A] “Thus not everything is permitted which liberty tells me,  
for under law it does not possess its own choice.  
Therefore it befits a king to give only such a law  
that whatever pleases may also be permitted.

“Thus, yes thus, you will be great; thus you will enjoy enduring peace,  
rightly pleasing the people by this title of your deed.”

The king, returning thanks for such great counsels, replied:  
“Your counsels are extraordinary.  
And your teaching, wholly foreign to us,  
is known to you alone from heaven’s citadel.

“Through you divine medicine shines upon the world;  
for, I see, you speak with God teaching you all things.  
Therefore I pray, prostrate, that I may now be pleasing to you,  
as I was before when I had less power.

“You made me lord; you gave me kingdoms;

[Col. 1358B] but now you enlarge and multiply your gifts.  
Stand with me thus, and further, Father, instruct me  
so that I may appear to do nothing rashly.

“Therefore advise me, and impart to me each thing that must be done;  
make yourself my mirror, make yourself my eye.  
As you know, I have always done whatever you wished;  
if I now neglect what you command, may I perish.

“Africa will obey what your tongue teaches,  
and the whole people will be your disciple.”

## CANTO X

The king, following every abomination at the magician’s prompting,  
as he had promised, and with equal diligence,  
completed all things: he abolished the sacred laws  
and declared permitted whatever pleased him.

He added this crime as well: those unwilling to revere this decree

[Col. 1358C] were to be deprived of their property and subjected to punishments.

At these decrees the ill-rejoicing mind of the stars  
rejoices and raves, singing what should grievously be lamented.  
The more licentious generation, multiplying joyful voices,  
is glad that many things are written as permitted to it.

Now a chorus of young women and popular applause  
proclaims only [lacuna]ammutium as excellent.

The ever-favourable breeze, a friend to evils,  
had exalted the man as sacred, as marvellous.

O confused people, miserably deceived by magical doctrine!  
O people fit to be joined to beasts! O pitiable people, you perish!  
“You say, ‘I am free.’” May this freedom befall our enemies,  
and may it, I pray, flee from us.

Such freedom will be fatal to you;  
it will condemn you and consign you to punishments.

[Col. 1358D] While you think, O people, that provision is being made for you—  
foolishly—by that which you joyfully embrace, singing, you die.  
While you now exult, you pile up many penalties for yourselves  
and, as you deserve, make for destruction.

Therefore the itch of Venus becomes the origin of crimes,  
while Africa is rashly defiled by Venus.  
Unbridled desire rushes to seduce married women;  
nor was there a virgin able to marry.

The wandering woman, scorning the bed of lawful marriage,  
believes every adultery to be holy.  
All burned with passion; husband and wife did the same;  
blind was the lust of the young, blind the lust of the old.

Therefore wicked Venus often confounded both sexes  
and made sex uncertain.

[Col. 1359A] Thus humankind lost the ordered use of reason,  
doing no differently from every brute beast.  
Nothing was human unless it came to be profane.  
1290 He who feared these things less was the holier man.

When crime entered, honour and reverence departed,  
for these could not be mingled with crime.  
Therefore every union forbidden by sacred law  
began to be praised and celebrated.

While every woman, making male subdue male,  
robbed nature of its rights,  
and, against custom, a brother himself presses his sister,  
a married sister becomes a victim for her brother’s abyss;  
a child commits incest with its mother, a daughter with her father:  
thus by the new law whatever pleased was permitted.

[Col. 1359B] Alas! How many prudent people became foolish  
and favour wickedness and do not fear evil laws.  
The king’s terror drew some, but public error  
drew more, through vices, to destruction.

A few remained steadfast and served God alone;  
while they taught better things, to call the people back,  
they confirmed by example what they taught.  
Though they might often be tested by punishment, prayer, or bribery,  
they could by no means be overcome.

Exposed at once to various punishments,  
they despised the many penalties which they endured.  
Some overcame the world through beatings; some through prisons;  
some perished beneath lashes; one suffers hunger; another dies of thirst.

Some are mutilated; others are burned with fire;

[Col. 1359C] this man is pierced with bars or boiled in oil.  
That man is crowned because he is flayed alive;  
this one perished when cut to pieces, and thus ascended to the stars.

That man triumphed because he fed ravens on a cross;  
this one endured a swift shower of stones.  
Some, offered to tigers or hurled down,  
others, overcame by the punishment of the sword.

Some, leaving all things and following the Lord,  
while they fear human beings cruel toward them,  
wander the trackless forests; the rage of wild beasts  
leaves unharmed those whom humans persecute.

Those who thus live only for the living Almighty  
obtain everlasting rewards through their death.

## CANTO XI

[Col. 1359D]

Thereupon the Lord, mindful that vengeance belongs to him,  
strikes Mammutius suddenly, and deservedly;  
for because of his evil deeds an epileptic affliction seizes him,  
tormenting the wretch in proportion to his crimes.

And though God scourged him in order to call him back,  
he could not come to his senses because of excessive crime.  
But as an unbridled horse is not restrained by reins,  
so, because of punishments, he goes further into vice.

Thus Christ, angered, is accustomed to punish sins;  
while he punishes a man thus, that man rages more fiercely.

Therefore, when the magician sees this condemned criminal,  
he groans inwardly and grieves deeply.  
Yet, lest he seem saddened in these circumstances,

[Col. 1360A] he prudently conceals what stings him.  
While he conceals it well, he aspires to a greater crime.  
He prepares the way to this wickedness in such fashion  
that whenever the king fell and lay unconscious,  
or whenever he was overcome by illness, he might draw crime from it.

Certainly, it will not be considered strange, however strange it may seem,  
if it is ever read. Therefore let us commit to writing  
by what art the magician did this—  
a man whose wickedness was nothing but wickedness.

For whenever the king suffered, he behaved as though applauding,  
thereby duly multiplying praises to God,  
because God had looked upon the people, over whom he had set  
a magnificent king, angelic in character,

who was thought to have died whenever he was carried up  
1291 into heaven, as often as God might deal with the highest matters

[Col. 1360B] of the kingdom or create new laws.  
For he said that God accomplished all things through him.

Therefore he warned the deceived and foolish peoples  
to restrain their tears and not grieve;  
rather, to rejoice and revere the king more greatly  
when they saw that he had pleased God.

But the polluted people, quickly following magical doctrine,  
turned it to their own destruction.

For, according to his custom, when his pain returned  
and he suddenly fell by force and lay unconscious,  
the seduced populace changed mourning into joy;  
where it had previously grieved, there it now fell silent.

It believed the man’s mind had been taken up to heaven,  
to give laws to the earth and govern the sky.

## CANTO XII

[Col. 1360C] The people thus rejoiced and, as I say, sang gladly;  
but meanwhile the magician considered things in the heavens.  
Since he knew beforehand the time when the illness would depart  
and the king’s ordinary life would be restored,  
he then excluded everyone and remained alone,  
pretending to celebrate a holy mystery.

And when the pain had departed and the king had recovered,  
the magician immediately instructed him, as was his former custom;  
the dreadful man instils his own poison into himself,  
so that the wretched people may perish by a pestilent contagion.

Then the king came forth, his pallor declaring his illness,  
and began in this manner, speaking to the people:

“People most choice, rejoice with festive praise;  
your favours have proved pleasing to those above.

[Col. 1360D] You have accomplished this; you have truly deserved  
that I should please all heavenly beings so greatly.  
And whenever I direct my course upward,  
blessed people, it is fitting that this be ascribed to you.

“But because you wept whenever you thought I was suffering,  
learn how welcome that condition of mine is.  
When you see me as if mad and in pain,  
I am carried up to heaven, and suffer not at all.

“Then I enjoy conversation with the holy beings above  
and possess delights worthy of God.  
There Paradise delights my eyes;  
I glory in the hymn-making praises of angels.

“Now I am borne in a chariot; now thence I slip back to the South,

[Col. 1361A] which the fiery zone makes hot though it is cold.  
Then I behold the shining and very numerous stars,  
and with them what road and path there is to the South Wind.

“When it is carried into heaven, my mind marvels  
how the heavenly beings can remain stable,  
so that they neither revolve together nor move.  
When I see such things, do you think that I suffer?

“Here I now languish, but there I rest rejoicing—  
there where rest is without conflict, day without night.  
Yet when I must return to this world,  
then indeed I grieve because I return so soon.

“For, leaving the good of such great delights,  
I can scarcely endure my return to the destruction of the flesh.  
Therefore I would refuse return and not come back,

[Col. 1361B] nor seek the world, unless I loved you.  
You are the cause of my toil; you are the cause of my pain.

“Therefore, my people, attend carefully  
to what I saw when I had been carried to the heights,  
and, faithful person, learn what I proclaim.

“We condemn the world if we first receive you;  
if we receive you, we despise all things.  
The human race, being unsound, does not know what it worships;  
1292 it does not know what it does, though it does many things.

“You are a chosen race; you do nothing but what is right;  
you have true understanding, limbs of the sacred head.  
They bind themselves with laws, fashion them for themselves,  
and create new laws in which they also perish.

“You are pleasing to those above; you are blessed with liberty;

[Col. 1361C] God considers you innocent and his own.  
They would now have been removed and rejected  
had my counsels not intervened.

“For when the peoples due to be condemned had to be healed,  
my tongue spoke thus, as was fitting:

‘Heavenly assembly, since you cannot fail to know  
what the magnificent Libyan religion is,  
you yourselves know and, I think, can observe  
that this people has newly learned the path of salvation.

‘In order that you may recognize the honour of sacred novelty:  
when it has scarcely touched the outermost edge of Libya,  
how could it so quickly spread to the ends of the world?  
What no one has taught, who could have learned?

‘Therefore I ask that this people, lacking a sound teacher,  
be given still some time in which to redeem its fault.

[Col. 1361D] ‘But, I think, they will laugh when they see our sacred rites;  
unless they quickly repent, let them perish with me as judge.  
And let them be condemned so that they may be tortured forever.’

“Here I fell silent, and thus I pleased those above.  
A place of rest without end has been decreed for me,  
so that whenever I return I may hold the sceptres of heaven.

“Through the ages I am equal to the conquering Almighty,  
with whom I alone govern all things that must be governed.  
Therefore rejoice and keep our commands  
with great diligence; for, beyond doubt,  
I shall exalt you and make you like myself  
if here you are made like me by your merits.

“If a mortal can scarcely be wholly pure,  
because of the burden of the flesh, while unable to be good,  
no one can ever be free from stain beneath this burden;

[Col. 1362A] therefore I know that we are subject to some vice.  
Accordingly, for the polluted this is the first path of salvation:  
that after sins each person be washed with water.

“For this element will give the sacrament of pardon—  
yet let such a washing truly be sacred.  
Whoever rightly wishes to be cleansed and purified  
should sanctify himself thus and repeat this four times:

‘Mahomet, cleanser of sin, I pray you,  
wash away whatever wrong I have committed through this sacred water.’

“To those thus washed I shall give the highest gifts of salvation:  
always to enjoy the honour of an everlasting kingdom.  
I would instruct you in more matters if I now had time;  
but while the speech is prolonged, the day is taken away.

“But remember, my people, with attentive heart,  
each thing that I have taught as I determined.

[Col. 1362B] Thus you may avoid the loss of liberty,  
so that each person may be free in his own choice.  
For if you wish thus to persevere in your own observances,  
after death of the flesh I shall give what I have promised.”

After he had said these things, the simple people thundered forth  
melodious praise, with applause immediately added;  
and so great a shout struck the sky like thunder  
as even Juno’s love beneath Jupiter does not know.

## CANTO XIII

What are you doing with these counsels, chief of crimes, victim of Dis,  
while you strive to ensnare the brutish and uncultivated?  
But, cruel and impious robber, I think you fear  
lest you perish alone—which you need not fear.

For you will not go alone and unaccompanied;

[Col. 1362C] indeed, your crowd will not be small.  
Nor will your anger serve many years of tyrannies,  
nor will the life you seek be everlasting.

While you rejoice, divine and unexpected vengeance  
will now overtake you and strike no lightly blow.  
Thus you will suddenly fall, a universal and singular disaster,  
now also worthy, by your deserts, of Dis’s hall.

Void chaos will swallow you, limb of Satan,  
and all Tartarus gapes as though it thirsts for you.  
Come, rejoice, since you will cease to heap up  
for yourself fruitful groans after death.

And for you, foolish people, much confusion remains,  
nor will joy always be your companion.  
For the span of life runs swiftly through its brief course,  
after whose end it goes to destruction.

[Col. 1362D] And when you, Mahomet, become Pluto’s victim,  
you will receive the rewards of your error.

## CANTO XIV

When fraud had now increased, deceit had grown strong,  
and impiety set no bounds to crime,  
then came the cries of the destroyed churches.

But the Lord Mahomet, seeing the crime,  
rages against the author of the crime and pursues such fury  
with deserved punishments. Therefore,  
alone at dawn, at the first hour of light,  
the king silently goes out, by chance without a companion.

He went meditating, considering what doctrines he should write  
and what he should teach on the morrow to please his followers.  
But death stood over him, denying that he would live till tomorrow,  
and forestalling today the doctrines of treachery.

[Col. 1363A] For while the king considered what words he should give the people,  
his customary sudden affliction seized him.  
Bloodless, he falls, numb like a faithless serpent,  
and he could not be harmful as he wished to be.

A great pain, constricting his entrails, burns within:  
it burns inwardly, nor less outwardly.  
Everything was numb; hands, mouth, feet, and tongue were stiff;  
his whole body grew rigid; he lay wholly inert.

His throat closed against his tongue, denying the use of speech;  
his eyes stood empty of their light.  
Why linger? Immense pain had robbed him of his senses,  
and his nearly subdued tongue was ready to fail.

This was foreshadowed by the foam which stiffened his mouth,  
and by his continuous, laboured, and scant breath.

While, in the magician’s absence, the image of death held him thus,  
a fitting plague suddenly came running: swine;

[Col. 1363B] this swift herd, as though scorning that he was king,  
all rushes upon him and tears the wretch apart.  
What remained of life still sustaining the wicked man  
it lightly drains away; he groans heavily.

At last he dies; Styx opens for the dying man,  
and the Stygian robber is turned into the abyss.  
And because he condemned souls and overthrew bodies,  
sparing neither soul nor body,  
now a pig devours his body and Orcus his soul,  
and he is transformed into the filth of his own corruption.

Rightly condemned, suffering torments in both,  
he endures kinds of punishment corresponding to his crimes.

## CANTO XV

When the magician heard that the king had gone out alone

[Col. 1363C] and prolonged his return beyond his custom,  
he follows him alone; and as he goes more swiftly,  
the king is seen to have fallen in the middle of the road.

The avenging herd still stood there and tore the king apart,  
as though he had been given to it by a law of food.  
But at the magician’s arrival the swinish gulf withdrew  
and left the chief of crimes mangled.

1294 Then the magician, source of sin, quickly approaches  
the torn body, uncertain what he should do.  
But what could he do except weep and grieve while weeping?  
So, weeping, he groaned and grieved deeply.

But when this grief perceived that it was departing fruitlessly  
and that his weeping would result in nothing,  
he said to himself: “When a father wept for Hector,  
did tears help him? Not at all.”

[Col. 1363D] Therefore, since mourning produced no fruit for him,  
he grieved in heart, but ceased to weep.  
You too, for a similar reason, lay aside mourning:  
henceforth you do not redeem this man by tears.

Armed and restored by such counsels,  
the magician composed his face and restrained his tears.  
He brought back the body and placed it upon a bed,  
tending its torn limbs, though with tardy art.

To it he adds whatever seemed able to avail:  
the juice of spurge-laurel and the tender flower of the violet.  
Frankincense, balsam, nard, and amomum filled the house;  
from these he had made an unknown antidote.

After he had anointed all the royal limbs,

[Col. 1364A] he adorns the body with garments, for he lays a snare  
by which to capture the minds of the deceived people,  
rejoicing in a fraud that would not last for him.

Once the king had been adorned, by his customary wicked practice  
he summons the royal servants and the people  
and addresses them thus:

“This day is held sacred, on which the king of Libya  
today has sought the heavens.  
For the king faithful to us is received into heaven,  
and he calls you, his children, to the heights above.

“Although his dominion is enlarged,  
he will nevertheless be no less our lord.  
Indeed, he will guard his Libyans not as slaves but as friends,  
protecting them by confirming them and ruling by cherishing them.

“But why is your heart disturbed while it reflects  
and seeks the reason why this father gave  
his all-too-venerable limbs to be gnawed by pigs?

[Col. 1364B] This lowly death teaches how worthless flesh is.  
To demonstrate and openly signify this,  
he chose to suffer it himself and instructed us through it  
how frail we are. But although we perish in flesh,  
after death there is nevertheless some hope remaining.

“For death itself becomes the salvation of our souls,  
and when we die, then we follow Mahomet,  
who will exalt and join to himself all  
who wish to fulfil his commands in deed.

“To his commands we add this: beware  
of defiling yourselves rashly with swinish contagion.  
I do not think it need be stated why this must be done,  
when what sufficiently teaches it is evident in itself.”

From this, that people, scorning pork,

[Col. 1364C] considers anyone who eats pig to be defiled.  
And because a herd of pigs gnawed their king,  
a fabricated superstition arose from this aversion.

Then the magician, delighted that his commands had been accepted,  
believed the deeds done insufficient  
unless he completed the crime and, as it were, sanctified it.  
Being full of crime, he prepares to accomplish this as follows.

## CANTO XVI

He built a shrine—no shrine, rather a profane place—  
before whose doors an inscription carved in marble  
was displayed, as follows:

“Here what is rightly sought through Mahomet shall be given.”

In this construction nothing appeared without care;  
the entire building gleamed with cost and craftsmanship.  
Every visible wall shone white with marble;

[Col. 1364D] 1295 but the varied workmanship surpassed Parian marble.  
For if the work had lived and been able to speak,  
it would have said to its maker: “I have conquered my material.”

Thus the shrine had been adorned and prepared.  
But if anyone asks how large the building was:  
when one stands far from it, it seems to be a golden mountain,  
so great is the extent and cost it contains.

You would marvel more if perhaps you entered;  
for the brilliance of the stones would stupefy you.  
Thus, thus it was adorned with gems and varied with gold,  
like the shining starry night-sky.

Thus a lofty structure, made solely by a magnet,  
stood in the middle like an arch;  
under it Mahomet is carried and placed in a tomb,

[Col. 1365A] 1296 which, if anyone asks, was made of bronze.  
And because such large masses of bronze truly attract one another,  
the tomb in which the king lay was lifted up.  
And thus it hung, because of the force of the stones.

Therefore, when the unlearned people saw  
the marvel of the tomb, they took the thing for a sign,  
wretchedly believing it performed through Mahomet.

[Col. 1366A] That a heavy thing should hang without a chain,  
nor any support hold the tomb.  
When the fools saw this, they worshipped Mahomet—  
what magical art had done among the Libyan people.

Since we have spoken thus far of the causes of these errors,  
let the Muse stay her hand, and let Mahomet perish.

[Col. 1365]

# THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT’S BOOK CALLED *MATHEMATICUS*

(From manuscript codex no. 274 of the former monastery of Elnone, or Saint-Amand-en-Pévèle, now in the Royal Library, at least five hundred years old; it alone among the manuscripts contains this poem, which immediately follows the History of Mahomet.) (G)*

## BRIEF NOTICE

[Col. 1365] Since Hildebert, the author of this story, names no person to whom it might apply, and since, after reading their histories, we have been unable to discover to which Roman noble it might apply, we could suspect nothing else than that it was a gratuitous fiction invented by him as an academic exercise, in mockery of judicial astrology, as it is called. Perhaps he wished to turn away the people of his time, who were excessively devoted to it. Moreover, this narrative seems to have so great an affinity with the story of Oedipus that, had Hildebert not named Rome so expressly, we should have judged it to be that very story of Oedipus; certainly nothing comes closer to its imitation. From it, furthermore, the discerning reader may observe that Hildebert excelled not only in rhythmic verse but, whenever he was allowed to escape the constraints of rhythm, was exceedingly practised in verses of every kind. Therefore we judged this poem, drawn from the Elnone manuscript of at least five hundred years and placed immediately after the History of Mahomet, not unworthy of public light.

## CANTO I

[Col. 1365B]

The laws of the human condition have it that people are always found fortunate in some respect.  
There was at Rome a soldier, honourable in arms and rich in possessions,  
powerful in the city, happy in his wife, distinguished in his ancestors.

In speech, hand, and appearance he was eloquent, generous, honourable—  
a wise man, steady in time, mind, and faith.  
His bride was not lower in lineage than her husband, nor unequal in morals,  
not older in age, nor different in faith.

Ready, modest, reverent—not, as so often happens,  
a beautiful woman imperious toward her husband.  
Though the luxury of wealth slopes toward harmful acts,  
it had not caused her good morals to degenerate.

Although frivolity is usual in youthful years,

[Col. 1365C] this beautiful and powerful woman did no frivolous deed.  
She was chaste and lovely—a virtue rare in the beautiful  
and usually rarer in the frail sex.

She avoided fickleness, the vice of feminine nature,  
and the faults of inborn wickedness.  
She restrained light emotions under a certain weight  
and was able to forget her sex.

Thus upright, beautiful, joined to a handsome husband,  
clever to a sensible man, religious to a pious one,  
fortune smiled upon them and nature favoured them. They were blessed  
in all things except the gift of offspring.

[Col. 1366B] In this one respect they were less than perfect—if lack of children  
is a diminution of complete prosperity.  
Thus the hope of offspring, frustrated through many years,  
prevented all nature’s other gifts from giving pleasure;

it diminishes other successes, obscures other honours,  
and makes fortune guilty in all things.  
They weep and grieve the more; for neither does nature resist,  
nor does weakness [perhaps: “a weaker force”] impede them.

1297 She cannot blame the cold years of an old husband,  
nor can he blame the cold body of his wife.  
Trusting in her age and in heavenly favour,  
the woman alone carries hope in her prayer.

Wishing to be more certain beyond doubtful hope  
what order of fate had in store,

[Col. 1366C] she consults an astrologer,  
who could derive from the stars the concerns of the gods above,  
the mind of the Fates and Jupiter’s counsel,  
know nature’s causes and hidden secrets,  
and what fates wished to proceed under what laws.

Trained in the studies of mathematical art,  
he predicts by numbers; numbers move the stars.  
By the logic of number he investigates the wandering planets,  
carefully noting their points and degrees.  
He gathers the precise moment of the hour consulted  
and weighs in these both the matter and its measure.

[Col. 1367A] “There is,” he says, “behold, I see for you a son; behold, your husband  
will fill your barren womb with fruitfulness.  
In face he will bear Paris; within, Achilles;  
neither virtue nor beauty will make him proud.

“Croesus will be poorer, Ulysses less learned than he.  
Reason will place reins upon affairs and intellect.  
Among the fated advantages of a happy life,  
he will be lord and father of the city of Romulus.

“He will kill his own father—but I say no more, unless you press, question, and insist—  
with fate driving matters thus.  
It will be so; trust it. Such is Jupiter’s fixed will.  
Nothing that I have foretold contains uncertainty.

“The Fates promise it to you, the gods promise it, the stars promise it;  
a thing is certain when stars, fates, and gods promise it.”

## CANTO II

[Col. 1367B] Uncertain whether to rejoice or grieve at these destinies,  
the woman returns, knowing heaven’s counsel:  
Rome, she will bear you a king and her husband death;  
glad in sorrow, sorrowful in gladness.

Her husband perceived her wasting away in anxious, wakeful care  
and asked the reasons; she told him.  
He hears, and with attentive, grieving ear  
the soldier takes in the prodigious fates of his own death.

“This,” he says, “is why the gods regret granting my prayer;  
therefore Jupiter is evil to me, and therefore good.  
I sought a child; a hostile son has been given me;  
by the fulfilment of my desire I suffer its loss.

“Therefore, I pray you, my wife, my love, my only delight,  
the other part and half of my soul,

[Col. 1367C] when the offspring conceived under an evil genius  
and your womb has brought forth its mature burden,  
forget loving affections, forget that you are a mother,  
and do not hesitate to kill your child.

“If you allow him to survive, then, when I am to die,  
this seeming piety will be impiety.”

He had finished; both wept. Without delay, on the following night  
they lie together; she conceives and grows swollen.  
Fulfilling the months of pregnancy by nature’s laws,  
she gave birth at the fixed time of her count.

In the newborn was an image of such great divinity  
that he could scarcely be believed a material human being.
