As wife she loves her husband, as mother her child; she hesitates,  
uncertain whether to spare the child or the husband.

[Col. 1367D] The beautiful, snow-white child compels himself to be loved;  
he softens his mother and forbids her to be cruel.  
Beautiful, and seeming to the angry parent  
like one begging not to die,

his beauty destroyed his father’s pleas;  
the grace of her lovely child cast the man from her mind.  
She who was preparing to be a Medea to her own offspring  
began to know what maternal love was.

1298 Fierce in her pity, she spares him and gives her son  
a longer span of life, but her husband a shorter one.  
Feigning his death, she sends him far away to be raised,  
and silently deceives the unhappy father by art.

## CANTO III

Happy in exile, the boy, suckling alien breasts,  
is reared with devoted care.

[Col. 1368A] The glory of his appearance grew as flourishing age increased;  
such beauty could have been praised even by an enemy.  
His name was uncertain, but he is called “father-killer” (*patricida*);  
his clever mother secretly commands  
that the youth may shudder often at so great a crime,  
at such rage, whenever he hears his own name.

As raw infancy received its first perceptions  
and the inner man drew the force of reason,  
his mind shone forth as capable as if he were already adult,  
his days mature even before their full time.

Ascending the stages of apt and ready youth,  
he made it his study to be a close companion to philosophers.  
For he learned how God first gave seed and matter  
to the stars and to the world;

what order there was in things, what cause in their creation;

[Col. 1368B] what connections and what changes the elements possess;  
from what source numbers flow, by what law they are bound,  
and by what arrangement, disposed, they agree with one another;

by what number or proximity music joins  
and associates dissimilar sounds;  
at what distances the seven planets are separated from the stars,  
having measured both poles and both seas;

the courses of the stars, human fates beneath the stars,  
and how Hercules, weary, supported the heavens.

Wishing also not to be ignorant of rhetorical figures,  
he learned to speak concisely and clearly.  
Examining the natures of genera with a more exacting file,  
he enclosed divine Aristotle in his breast.

And whatever can assail human limbs—  
pain or disease—he knew how to drive it away.

[Col. 1368C] Thus he made his capacious breast and profound mind  
a broad lodging for the seven liberal arts.

Repose suspected of Venus and leisure close to vices  
had now become causes of fear for the young man.  
Fearing the tranquil years of a wanton age,  
he passes to the burdens of armed military service.

He devoted himself to continual wars and earned favour,  
nor did arms lack success for him.  
Surpassing Caesar’s titles and Hercules’ deeds,  
he was the sole glory of the Roman race.

His uprightness and valour had raised him so high,
He would be the standard-bearer of the Ausonian empire.

But amid the riches of the world and the highest summits of earthly things,

the power of heaven strives to set the man above them.

[Col. 1368D] Lachesis strives toward this; Fortune labours for it; Jupiter himself here confirms his own powers.

And because the fated order demands that it be so,

the Fates have granted him this path to kingship.

## CANTO IV

Carthage, rival of the Roman name, had by chance brought arms within the Ausonian borders.

Therefore the Quirites set the Eagles and their ill-omened standards in motion, and an unlucky hour carries off the enrolled Fathers.

For the Carthaginian had hidden a force beneath the shadow of his ships for your destruction, royal Rome.

Thus the senate fell into ambushes and unforeseen missiles, and could then have been captured without battle.

The king is captured, and the tribune is captured; nor can the trapped crowd retreat.

[Col. 1369A] 1299 The nations of Aeneas’ descendants are led away, with the power of the Latin people and the honour of Alban nobility.

Nowhere else could Rome better learn that the world possesses uncertain fortunes.

But when better fortune led the patricide by a better road, at the head of the standard-bearing legion,

he, seeing from afar the confused dust of battle, immediately understood that his own men had been overcome.

Accordingly, he meets and forestalls the advancing enemy and blocks the way with soldiers placed before him;

and, entering the hostile masses under more favourable fates, he conquers the Carthaginians and protects the Ausonians.

Blind Fortune turns about the ridiculous labours of mankind; our ages are sport and plaything to the gods.

[Col. 1369B] With roles reversed, Africa lies defeated and Rome triumphs; they feared those called their victors.

And, as though the sacred order of the gods feared Rome, it immediately relieved the losses with swift assistance.

Thus Fortune could earn pardon, since after evil fates it granted a good outcome.

The report of disaster had exhausted the city with grief, and the losses were those of a greater humiliation.

The joyful news that came after the preceding sorrow could be more welcome because of the evils themselves.

First it is told in what valley or what hiding-places the treacherous Carthaginian band had stood;

how great a fury of war had blinded the Latins, so that they could not beforehand see the silent snares;

how savage Africa had thrust the august Fathers and Rome’s very heart

[Col. 1369C] into its traps;

how the patricide, with a small force, had crushed the enemy and restored your people to you, Rome.

Thus the patricide, splendid and renowned for his deeds, sounds constantly and repeatedly on the lips of the populace.

## CANTO V

When the king had gathered the spoils that victory brings—though he was master of the gain, not its author—

he turned his course toward Rome, and a letter to be read by the venerable Fathers was sent. The letter was as follows:

That the laurel due to him for conquered Carthage, and the honour earned in the Latin fashion, might be granted.

The Romans deliberate for a long time, exercising and agitating keen counsel about what decision should be made on these matters.

After weighing all things on every side with the sharpness of reason,

[Col. 1369D] they see that none of the king’s deeds contains merit—he who, disgracefully adorned with darkened Roman glory, had been conquered in war and made an idle spoil.

Yet, lest he should grieve at a shameful rejection—for the heavy anger of commanders bears contempt badly—

a document is sealed whose ambiguous sense can signify either granting or denying.

“Royal Rome opposes no one’s merits, ever ready to serve her conqueror.

For him to whom victory has earned laurel-bearing chariots, Rome will not refuse what he has deserved;

he who conquered the peoples of Carthage, we confess, ought to mount the triumphal horses.”

The letter, falsely promising good hope by its deceptive appearance,

[Col. 1370A] could at first make the commander glad.

Soon, when he considered it in his mind and ran through the whole of it, taking every word according to its meaning,

being a discerning man, he was not moved to anger. “I perceive,” he said, “the ambiguity of the doubtful expression.”

Then he addresses the patricide—for the kingly mind does not bear another’s praises with distress:

“O young man, if any strength implanted by the stars exists in you, the hour of your birth saw a fortunate star;

and Fortune, favouring you lest she afterwards be called blind, has shaken off the accusation and burden of her fault.

In your face all proofs of mighty Nature are apparent; your beauty is the praise of a goddess.

Through you—I do not blush to say it—I return rescued from the enemy, restored to my wife and my delights.

[Col. 1370B] Behold the day which, proceeding in the sequence of fate, will render worthy rewards to your valour.

Your labour, I confess, has earned sceptres. Receive the sceptres, and possess the government of city and world that you have earned.

You conquered the Carthaginians: use, with my peace, the chariots and processions Rome has prepared for you.

Rome sees justly, and the straight line of right has been preserved; in my own rejection this is more pleasing to me.

Nor can this be called my shame or injury; it may rather bear the name of justice.

Therefore I do not envy you: a worthy crown, foreknowing the future laurel, will come to your hair.

Therefore I do not envy you: you will be borne in a shining chariot, and joyful Rome will raise your name to the stars.

I call the triumph Rome grants you a great merit,

[Col. 1370C] which I judge to be a gift greater still.

I set you above the Roman and all my other kingdoms; the sea and broad land are my gift.”

The young man was astonished and—rarest of virtues—was saddened by the honour conferred upon him.

While he refuses obedience, they behold the processions arriving in order: the people from one side and the Fathers from the other.

The king places the diadem from his own head upon the youth’s brow, though he himself resists, and puts the sceptres in his hand.

Thus, clad in the trabea and possessing all that pertains to a king, he was offered; Rome received him as offered.

High upon snow-white horses, amid the applause of the senate, he is led as far as Capitoline Jupiter.

## CANTO VI

His affectionate mother had heard—for the recorder of deeds did not fail [variant: *had not failed*]—

[Col. 1370D] of the empire of her son.

Piety, love, and nature moved the parent to this; she could almost have perished from joy.

Yet her devout joys burst into tears—the tears which grief and losses more commonly produce.

When the mother had sufficiently applauded her kinsman’s honour, she restrained her smiles at their proper limit.

As though her heart’s secret had been received into an inner sanctuary, she is silent and consults her intelligence as to what she should do.

She is amazed at the astrologers’ prediction and at the order of events, and perceived that the stars had proved true.

From the past she now draws evidence for the future, and believes that the remainder will proceed in the manner foretold.

Therefore, since the event confirmed the prophecy concerning her husband’s death,

[Col. 1371A] the wife is compelled to admit real fears.

But, looking on her son’s glory and her husband’s death, she becomes joyful and troubled by alternating turns.

Whenever she holds before the eyes of her mind her husband, or anything that had been dear to her husband,

care and grief claim lodgement in the breast exhilarated by happy successes.

When the patricide returns, maternal love presents him as such and so great that anger finds no place.

But when marital love and her husband’s bond come to mind—her integrity of life and fidelity not violated—

she wishes she had not borne him; her son and her son’s power displease her, and she altogether ceases to be a parent.

At times her harshness softens and she puts on the guise of a tender mother: the son himself conquers the husband.

[Col. 1371B] She grieves and rejoices alternately, and, miserably happy, weighs sweet fates against evil chances.

Anxious, torn apart, and most wretched in her divided wish, she wavers; mother and wife wage war within her.

If she could forestall the Fates’ eternal course, she would wish to undergo destiny in place of her lord.

But sad Lachesis and inexorable Fate have power only to proceed along their prescribed paths.

Meanwhile her husband, preoccupied by cares, attends to the sick woman; then he was wakeful over her fate.

And, looking upon the husband whose near doom she saw, the true Sabine groans with pious emotion.

The tears long held back at last flow, as though released in a massed advance, with freer course.

The husband was struck dumb by the violently rising tears;

[Col. 1371C] he sensed that some great evil lay beneath them.

He runs into her embrace, presses sweet kisses upon his dear wife, and asks why she grieves.

But she discloses nothing to him. He, insistent, clings to her, presses upon her, and multiplies his entreaties.

The more the sorrowful woman is silent, the more suspicious it seems that she hesitates to speak under so great a burden.

He asks, and by their pledged faith and the sacred marriage-bonds, asks whose grief this is and from what causes it has flowed.

If a matter for counsel will reach safe ears, or if it is a crime, her loving husband may know it.

## CANTO VII

Compelled by the law of the marriage-bed and by marital faith to confess things that might better and more advantageously have been concealed,

[Col. 1371D] she says: “There is reason for me to complain of you, creative Nature, who never bring anything fully to completion.

Although you have given much, that I was born a woman is a deficiency; in this respect your favour failed me.

Mine is the sex that detests what is honourable and claims as its own whatever is criminal.

If it were permitted by the gods, let the unjust race of woman be overthrown; let man now live in his own world.

A harmful breeze, a swelling wave of the sea, and angry battle do not kill your number, dreadful woman.

Plant or tree has seeds by which it may extend itself into time; each preserves its race perpetually.

Woman likewise contains within herself the root of crime, the seed of evil, and its material.

[Col. 1372A] If the times of ancient simplicity should return and the clever spirit of ingenuity fall,

woman would suffice to restore the arts of harming, and perhaps would add a new work of treachery.

In time lions become gentle after laying aside their ferocity; in time tiger and bear are accustomed to be softened.

Woman alone stands firm-footed in crime and never changes her malignant nature.

If any woman has wholly deserted her sex, she has been more prodigious than a snow-white raven.

But why should I assign the burden of this crime to nature’s fault or to inborn character?

That I have made myself evil, worthless, cruel, ruined—I disgracefully refer it to my sex.

[Col. 1372B] For the reason shines clearly by which my fault may colour itself, and my crime has nowhere to hide itself.

O husband long deceived! You trusted a wife who was no wife to you, but rather an enemy.

Perhaps, by dutiful service and flattering attentiveness, you thought you had won my heart.

From my earliest steps you were my sole ardour, sole affection, sole concern.

If my good deeds did not answer ill to your wishes with an equal return of merit,

we repay service with harms, love with hatreds, praise with reproach, and fidelity with treachery.

Seek, husband, some new kind of punishment: draw the sword, pour out my entrails to the sun, tear my limbs apart with wheels.

[Col. 1372C] I deserve these evils—evils which the guilty crowd suffers by Rhadamanthus’ judgment in the Tartarean house.

But because you are held in suspense by my ambiguous speech, hear where my words tend and what they mean.

Long ago, if you remember, I bore the one whom the stars promised would be king and hold the sceptres of aged Numa.

They promised—but it is more lawful to weep than to speak it—alas! that he would be the author of your death.

Terrified by the prophecy, you ordered the mother armed against her own heart and the offspring crushed.

But Nature, more powerful than every threat and warning, could not abandon her part.

I lie: you believe him extinguished; rashly you believe it. But the boy had the aid of another’s milk.

[Col. 1372D] Thus, whether you wish it called fault or crime, this day is lived for that boy.

He is your son, whose keenness of mind you are accustomed to admire in his actions and approve in his words.

He is your son, whom the whole world praises, and every land lying under the sevenfold climate.

He is your son, concerning whom even envy and hostility—concerning whom even Fame herself—fears to lie.

He is your son, whose triumphs neither Carthage nor Hannibal’s nation could blush for.

He is your son whom you see, seated upon the honoured throne of kingship, holding sceptres in his hand.

Except that your own fate remains, you see all the astrologer’s words fulfilled to their certain [variant: decreed] end.

[Col. 1373A] The stars running in their fated order will bring on, and hold fast, your fixed doom.

## CANTO VIII

The man was astonished and for a long time could not believe the things [variant: words], whose outcome [variant: of which] was prodigious.

Troubled, and long silent, with all his heart he withdrew into the inner chambers of his mind.

Prudent reason is consulted, and the whole man, gathered inwardly within himself, keeps watch.

Examining each point, he realized that he ought to rejoice and began to love even his own ruin.

He therefore conceives high honour for his lineage, and, despising his own destruction, says:

[Col. 1373B] “Dear companion, holy love, gracious and harmonious with me, cease your complaint; restrain your tears; put aside fear.

I have not imputed your acts to fault: you please your husband by beautiful deceits and beautiful treachery.

Do not fear to be brought before severe judges; so pure a cause defends your act.

Though you yourself are silent, Nature will speak for you; right and piety are your advocates.

You have no need to bring rhetorical colours to cover your cause; you possess no slight strength.

You were a mother: maternal love and piety compelled you. You avoid Medea and rival Penelope.

I might rightly fear hands ready to bring death even upon my own pledges.

But the ruler both of city and world had to be redeemed by the easy destruction of one old man.

[Col. 1373C] Like an old tree whose surviving shoot is reborn from its stock, I myself perish when cut down.

The branch prolongs its mother into long ages; my son perpetuates my own existence.

A wondrous novelty indeed: a joyful grief, a useful loss—these two things you see in my fortune.

Fortune thinks that it has rendered service to us both, so that one protecting the sceptres may arise from our seed.

It is not fitting to be ungrateful for a divine gift; a joyful mind touches the generous gods.

Great things do not come to a man except through great labour; the stars were won for Jupiter by the Phlegraean war.

That I may deserve to be called both father of a king and lord, I buy the name of so great an honour with my death.

[Col. 1373D] Yet dying I shall not die, but shall wholly survive, wholly reborn in such offspring.

Do not say that what descends from the fated origin of things occurs through your fraud or skill.

Fate destroys me; Fate saved the same man whom you think you saved. All things proceed according to law.

While Lachesis suffers our threatening threads to be broken at any moment, she draws them out with weary thumb.

I wish to address him while he is present and see more closely the one whom the gods have appointed head of affairs.

If I embrace my son once, if I join kisses to him once, that boundary of life will suffice me.

More joyfully I shall come to the Elysian fields, the buried peoples, Chaos, and the pale realms of Stygian Jupiter.”

## CANTO IX

[Col. 1374A]

Thus each ascends, by winding steps, the palatine citadel of the Tarpeian height.

There, sitting with the venerable patrician Fathers, the patricide deliberates concerning the common good of his city:

that the laws may not perish, the order of the senate not fall, nor Rome’s majesty and the splendour of empire decline.

Those entering might have been held by the splendour of the palace, had a lesser or lighter cause given occasion for their coming.

They proceed with gravity and utmost effort toward the king, for the crowd of bystanders was exceedingly dense.

Having penetrated the masses of the commons, they reach the very seats of the leading men and the throne of empire.

At his mother’s approach—the father was not recognized by him—the patricide king rises from his throne.

[Col. 1374B] Casting aside imperial pride and majesty, he wholly submits himself to maternal service.

He follows her, supports her as she walks with a gentle hand, speaks to her more mildly, and listens more affectionately.

And, not forgetful of his own nature, equitable power plays the role of a servant’s condition.

His mother says to him: “Yield the place, and graciously condescend to your mother; I wish to say a few words.

Give a little of yourself to me, my son; sometimes withdraw yourself [variant: *furare*, “steal yourself”] from arduous labour; let the senate transact its business.

Let the care owed by your mind in governing the world relax its burden at least in some measure.

Let Rome watch over itself, using its own strength; let it sometimes learn to do without its king.

[Col. 1374C] This I ask, this I command: I ask the king, I command my son. A loving mother has right over her offspring.

Therefore avoid the crowd and the turmoil of the crowd. Counsel is not well conducted in public.

Lofty matters wish to lie hidden beneath their own majesty and do not safely come into common public view.”

## CANTO X

Accordingly they withdraw to a place that lay silent in long peace, given over to secrets and counsel.

What is there resolved—silent, lofty, deep—is taken away from your ears, malicious Rumour.

The king of kings and the private place of the senate alone hear it, and bury it beneath eternal night.

Both parents sit, and the son between them.

[Col. 1374D] 1304 The woman begins the course of what must first be said:

“Son, whose wealth, wisdom, beauty, and power have been signified to me by the stars’ tokens,

when I recall your merit and the splendour of your life, I rejoice for you, my son; I rejoice for myself, my son.

If pride could steal upon me in any respect, surely I should be proud of your future praise.

Through you the ancient liberty of Romulus’ descendants returns, daring to lift its own head upon earth.

Long ago you were destined, by the decrees of the eternal laws of time, for the rule of this age.

You justify our times and restore the ages to their former gold, permitting them not even to bear the name of iron.

Nature’s far-reaching hand extended itself to the world and bestowed all things in a single gift;

[Col. 1375A] reserving nothing more useful for later ages, the lavish giver nearly remained poor.

Now let Justinian no longer marvel at the censor; nor let Rome boast of her Cato.

If the people lived happily in the years of Augustus, our time possesses no lesser divinity.

You were said to surpass even the Greeks in intellect: you do surpass them; to prevail in war: you do prevail; to hold sceptres: you do hold them.

But though you raise your lofty head beneath the stars, king and disposer of the human race,

one thing was still lacking to the fully completed wealth of your prosperity: that you did not know your father.

But Fortune, bound to your wishes, labours that no part of your glory may be lesser.

This man is your father—this man is your father. Know him; look again upon him,

[Col. 1375B] who granted you existence from his own flesh.”

The son rises, the father rises, and they join kisses; neither restrains his tears.

Long enfolded in tight embraces, they cling together; sacred love soothes their kindred hearts.

## CANTO XI

But the father, not satiated with the beloved sight, clings to him and keeps his eyes fixed upon the young man.

Looking therefore upon the marvels of so great a beauty, either astonished by these things or rejoicing, he says:

“Special glory of warfare, unmoved boundary and perpetual tenor of reason and equity,

my son—though perhaps I usurp a father’s name; he who is a cruel father ceases to be a father—

my son, for I shall confess it: your mother bore you in her womb,

[Col. 1375C] and at that time you were ordered to die.

You were ordered to die; I gave the order, wishing, in years of full strength, to anticipate your mother’s days [the syntax is uncertain].

Punishment is prepared for one whom no error had condemned, and a father’s word passes judgment beforehand.

But the eternal order and predetermined connection of things disperses the vain work of human contrivance.

The boy is preserved who may gently govern the world and rule the Roman walls made by Romulus’ hand.

If a man of harsh savagery governed Rome, he could overturn everything utterly from its foundations.

Provident Jupiter’s care set you over Latium, a friend of simplicity, lest the world perish.

You transform the sword of empire and freedom to do harm

[Col. 1375D] into the work of one gentle and merciful.

Gentle in Latium, imperious in mind, you rule; and for that reason you hold more rightly the name of king.

You conquer the man you bear; you strive by law to restrain the wandering impulses of evil flesh.

You restrain yourself; an old man alive in youthful years, you act not with discrimination merely, but wisely.

You have wished to live within the bounds of nature, while holding the reins of a freer curb.

Neither removed from your purpose nor swollen with beauty nor loosened by riches,

you keep firm the steps proposed by reason.

The broader one’s right and the greater the licence of desire, the more one passes life within a shorter limit.

[Col. 1376A] Hence it comes that the gods, leaving aside in part the concerns of heaven, incline more readily to your words.

The very Father of the gods, whenever you ask even great things, fears to be too slow, though hastening.

When Jupiter bestowed upon you the manifold ornaments of beauty, he moved both hands in giving.

Lest foolish man should say and set against it that nothing solid can stand in human affairs,

among your successes and the joys of prosperity there will be one other unhappy event.

My son, you will kill me; the fixed threads of the sisters established this crime from eternity.

The law and force of destiny, ordered long ago, will use your hands against my life.

You will offer your right hand, not your mind, to fury, my son; another spirit will guide your weapons.

[Col. 1376B] By the force of the firmament and the heavenly courses of the divine stars you will be compelled to do wrong.

You will be compelled to do wrong; and the gods’ guilt is manifest where you cannot be gentler toward your father.

The steadfast sequence of the Fates and fixed necessity simply contain the crime of our killing.

You, my son, are not guilty; for I do not think guilty one who harms because he could not avoid harming.

You are called patricide not without qualification and not without cause; attend to what your name signifies.

“I forgive you, my son, my death.” When he wished to speak of death, no voice followed his tongue.

The sentence of his broken utterance would have been incomplete, but a pious tear supplied what his heart intended.

The moisture lodged above the eyes is released into tears,

[Col. 1376C] and tender piety supplies such resources as it can.

Yet, since they knew that the cares and burdens of kingship were governed by the patricide’s skill and counsel,

fearing to sin against the good of Latium, they shortened the welcome delays of their conversation.

Thus, about to depart, they weary the son with kisses, alternate their efforts, and share the man between them.

In turn the patricide offers himself to their alternating embraces and deliberations.

He is pulled apart: he leaves one, is seized by the other, and comes as a public prize to his two masters.

It was a sight to see the sorrowful yet loving parents; so ill does even sacred love govern itself.

## CANTO XII

[Col. 1376D] Considering with how great disgrace and shame the Fates intended to stain his life,

the patricide groaned more deeply and felt his fortune decline and his glory diminish.

He knows the fragile, rapid wheel of wandering revolution and the ambiguous countenance of blind divinity;

and that no glory of the world, however great one wishes it to be, can stand long with secure step and fixed course.

Fearing sorrow after happiness and ruin after pleasant things, he turns over many thoughts in his anxious heart.

The harsh laws and malignant ways of Fortune redouble his cares and redouble his fear.

He often measures his resources, gathers into account his honourable acts and all his deeds with care.

Conquered Carthage comes before him, and the subjugated kings,

[Col. 1377A] and he grieves as he sees how great a height he will fall from, and whence.

Fortune punishes and taints long successes and long favours with a worse evil.

The father’s death casts a shadow upon his merits and praises: one fault remains amid manifold good.

He was to become, under the stern law of fate, the condemner of his dear father’s life.

He wishes it bought by his own death, so that the end might be like the beginning in the same colour.

“If it be permitted with the stars, if it be permitted to deceive the Fates, we shall forestall the fate and death of my father,” he says.

Rome will see that I am called a patricide but am not one, and the meaning of this name will be false.

What is our mind more akin to than the heavenly stars,

[Col. 1377B] if it must endure the sad necessity of harsh Lachesis?

In vain do we possess a mind divine in nature, though destined for patricide, if our reason cannot guard itself.

Thus God made the elements, thus the fiery stars, so that man would not be subject even to the stars.

Thus greater ingenuity is given to pure intelligence, that what is lesser may go out to meet the obstacles set before it.

## CANTO XIII

From there he comes to the Capitoline seats into which the Albula flows, and occupies the noble ivory of empire.

By royal edict he commands that the assembled people and the united gathering of elders present themselves together.

Jurists, purple-bordered Quirites, Albans, Fabii, the patrician race,

and enrolled Fathers, by whose governance the world

[Col. 1377C] is constrained and compelled to proceed in fixed measures.

Thus all the nobility and purple had come, and many thousands of the assembled people were present.

There too were the dictator, the tribunes ordered to sit, and both consuls with their standard-bearers.

He rises from his throne, signals silence with the majesty of his hand, and finally speaks:

“Blood of Julius, offspring of Mars, Quirites, from this you derive your strength, from that your lineage.

Know—and I shall not keep you in doubtful suspense—what moves your patricide and what he wishes.

My request demands an uncertain gift: whatever it may be, Rome, offer it to your king.

Let no circumspection or deliberated reasoning intervene; let a lavish hand give as though in abundance.

[Col. 1377D] Delay blackens the giver’s merit; gifts made quickly have greater praise and greater favour.

By the gods above, by whatever reverence for me remains, Rome, offer your king whatever it may be.

Offer it, if I have deserved it; if no error, even a slight one, has found a way into the inward depths of my heart;

if my whole life is lived sincerely by me; if I have taken nothing from the world’s mire;

if Venus, who is accustomed to overthrow the hearts and pride of kings, has not made me weak and headlong;

although there be no mention of character or of a life unshaken through many years.

[Col. 1378A] At least my entreaties and repeated requests cannot have failed to touch the pious people.

No such cruelty oppresses Romulus’ race that it rejects a suppliant’s prayer with deaf ear.

I should think a gift largely despised when face, expression, and a persuasive tongue request it.

It is shameful for friends to hesitate over gifts, and delay in giving involves no slight fault.

Let the author [variant: maker] of a pleasing gift forestall the petitioner; gratitude will be greater for swift service.

My labour has also benefited Latium, nor has gratitude been deaf to good merits.

I have promoted Latin laws and honoured the senate; my honour has not been harmful to the people.

What Marius? What Sulla? What Caesar can say:

[Col. 1378B] 1307 ‘None has been under my rule, and none injured by me’?

The victor over lofty Carthage and destroyer of African wealth has not deserved nothing.

My voice does not arrogate to itself deeds falsely claimed: look—the walls of the Carthaginians lie broken;

they lie broken. I shall pass over the captured commanders and the spoils, lest I seem to celebrate my own praises.

By the gods above, by whatever reverence for me remains, Rome, offer your king whatever it may be.”

## CANTO XIV

The people blushed to see the commander cast down and speaking pitiably; the Fathers blushed as well.

For the worthy man, good repute and merit plead, and do not allow a ruler’s prayers to be fruitless.

[Col. 1378C] To ask is for commanders a forceful form of commanding; the powerful man supplicates, as it were, with his sword drawn.

“Let it be given,” say the people, the sacred order, and the tribunes. One voice from all was: “Let it be given.”

Therefore they grant without distinction whatever he asks, even if he demands all the wealth of the Latin city.

Your chaste bed is not excepted, Lucretia, nor the pyre of the sacrificer Numa is to be hurled down.

[Note: [Col. 1377D] *Sacrifici* (“of the sacrificer”) is Hildebert’s word.]

When the patricide sees that his prayer will be granted and feels that all things are coming under his will, he says:

“See, Roman crowd, for what gift I have been eager and what you have given me.

I desire, indeed, to add nothing to my treasures; my abundance has found its limit.

Neither rich Latium nor the broadest world possesses anything

[Col. 1378D] by which my honour can grow greater.

Not a work of Maro, nor a citadel of living marble, but rather that which I think can be granted by a harsh enemy:

that I may be permitted to procure my own death and cast down the wretched day of my life.

This is the form and sum of my wishes; for these gifts my speech was persuasive.

The emperor whom you, Rome, had created for yourselves and to whom you had given the public laws of your people

wishes to have freedom over his own death only if the people or the consenting senate grants it.

Rome, my death is your gift: unaware, you behold it, and clouded error defends your act.

[Col. 1379A] The people’s simplicity and the senate’s deceived piety cannot be guilty of my blood.

But do not solicit me with flatteries, Quirites, nor multiply vain prayers.

My reason cannot recoil from its resolution or be moved from what it has begun; it remains fixed in itself.

I have sought gifts, and now neither can I have not sought harmful gifts nor can the people have not granted them.

While it was permissible for a pure mind to exist under a pure body and not be drawn to the destructive things of crimes,

a happier use of innocent life pleased me. In that time it was a crime to wish to die.

Now, because I am compelled to be defiled by shameful guilt, I am torn away from the simplicity of my life.

It is permitted to separate the ethereal [printed *Ethaeros*; corrected *Aethereos*] soul and the mortal part, the body, from one another.

[Col. 1379B] The learned astrologer, judge of far-reaching intellect and former fame, proclaims prodigies.

For he says that the threads and spindles of the three sisters turn in such a way, and the stars run their courses in such a way,

that the patricide will kill his father, shed dear blood, and shamefully begin to be guilty.

Whether Scorpio watched my natal hour, or the feared star of the aged standard-bearer,

or grievous Saturn clung to one of the two stars, or the martial star poured out its poison,

a driven sword will penetrate the hiding-places of the soul, and the blood which is life’s chief cause will flow.

[Col. 1379C] The steel will disrupt the harmony of mind and flesh, their concordant interchange and harmonious faith.

It will disrupt it, I say; for my mind would not dwell in a bodily house participating in fault [variant: with a participant in fault].

For as contraries struggle in opposed front, so my spirit takes up arms against vice.

My mind, born from heaven and kindred to the stars, remembers its nature and origin.

And because the daughter of radiance—namely reason—understands the pure sources of first things, it recoils from the work of night.

It recoils from the work of night; and the spirit, the head of lofty reason, fears to descend to the unstable things of flesh.

My mind is not thus enslaved to unjust flesh; it has not thus deserted and grown stiff,

[Col. 1379D] so that it might break its noble breast upon its son, or sluggish guilt dissolve its firm senses.

Therefore, while the mind is holy in a holy body and groans at nothing beyond the body’s condition,

let the life-giving companion and ethereal radiance depart from its clayey house and fleshly darkness.

Earthly flesh to earth; mind, fire to fire. Let each portion return to its own form.

My mind, safe by its merits, does not tremble to depart from the blind enclosure of the unseen body.

Upon leaving the flesh it will move to the heavenly poles,

[Col. 1380A] to be restored to the number of its star.

Why does it refuse pleasant and happy death? Or why does Rome begrudge me the Elysian fields?

When the body’s burden has been laid aside, I shall revisit the kindred stars, where, enjoying a freer life,

I shall look gladly upon affairs, watch over the City, and undertake the duty of greater diligence.

## CANTO XV

The Quirites are moved by his arguments and perplexing words.

They wish, by art, to reject what they had granted.

It neither becomes nor became the stern and sacred senate to speak with argumentative cunning.

The enthymeme sounds forth, induction sounds forth; Varro carries his words through wandering windings and brings them back again.

[Col. 1380B] He attempts silently to conclude some great point and gradually binds me with logical reasoning.

But this is not the language of clever sophists such as can remove me from my undertaking.

Pollio speaks and gilds the expression of his discourse; he deploys the weapons of an eloquent heart.

He persuades, embellishes, acts; by art he changes the modes and powers of the orator, colouring them.

That charm [that is, elegance] or grace of elaborated speech is not such as can overturn my resolution and my dying.

Camillus was as rustic in speech as in dress, yet pleasing to the gods by his rusticity.

The stern Catos did not please through painted trifles; their speech was plain and unadorned.

[Col. 1380C] Greece taught rustic Latium how to speak attractively, intricately, and grandly.

O grievous day on which simple, rough truth became contemptible, and ornate sounds pleased more!

Would that the sea had rendered Athens inaccessible; Rome would not have been harmed by eloquence’s brilliance.

Who, or by what means, will grant, if this our Rome herself holds her own prayers in such slight contempt?

I who was their own lord, and of fallen Latium, brought the captive Eagles back victorious from the enemy;

I wiped away the stains and crimes of everlasting disgrace, and Rome is clothed once more in its adornment [variant: colour].

[Col. 1380D] If the Ausonian purple, when entreating, moves no one, and grace for my person dies deaf,

yet the decrees of the laws support me, and the ancient letter gives consent to my wishes.

Justinian has from long ago been my advocate; a dead tongue pleads the cause of one still living.

I rely neither upon an imposing advocate nor upon impoverished speech; he was the greatest judge in the whole world.

“Let the victorious leader of the people have the gift he asks.” I am leader; I am victor; I ask gifts: grant them.

But because your king exercises the gifts of your honour, he therefore ceases to be your king.

Swiftly I lay aside the purple-bordered robe; swiftly I put off your king; free and released, I am my own according to my wishes.

[Note: [Col. 1379D] Thus this poem ends in Hildebert himself; it appears either unfinished, or at least not fully copied by the scribe, since it does not relate what was ultimately the outcome of this catastrophe—something the subject itself required and which every reader could rightly desire.]

[Col. 1381]

# MISCELLANEOUS POEMS OF THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT, SACRED AND MORAL; OR, THE LITTLE BOOK CALLED *THE FLORID COUNTENANCE*

(From a manuscript codex approximately five hundred years old, belonging to the distinguished Jacques du Poirier, doctor of medicine of Tours.) (G)*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1381A]

A wealthy humble man is found only as a rare kind of example; this example applies to you, venerable bishop,

[Note: [Col. 1381C] Hildebert perhaps here means William, bishop of Winchester, who, as appears from Letter 30, Book III, had asked him to write out his little works and send them to him; in that letter he indeed promises that he will send them.]

because, although you soar above and surpass the distinguished marks of your fellow associates in the prerogative of learning, abundance of possessions, and eminence of rank, nevertheless—what is exceedingly rare—I see the lily of humility flowering in you amid such thorns. This is shown in the present instance, illustrious man, by your request: you, a lord, have deigned to ask something of your servant; you, a rich man, of a poor man; you, worthy, of one unworthy—when you ought rather to have commanded. You ask that whatever I can recall of verse from antiquity that excels in a more elegant style be gathered into a single volume and sent to your devotion.

What you requested has been done; and although no delightfulness of rhythms recommends this little book,

[Col. 1381B] nevertheless in many places you will be able to find—saving the author’s humility—the weight of thought and distinction of expression. For I have attempted, in whatever style I could, to touch upon both splendour of language and truth, keeping in view the proverb: “Beautiful things please; precious things benefit”; 1311–1312 and that saying of Horace:

[The supplied source ends here, with the quotation incomplete.]

*He wins every point who blends the useful with the pleasant.*

Since these flowers have flowed together from diverse material into one whole, I judged it fitting that this little work should, in keeping with its character, take its title from that beginning and be called *The Flowery Aspect*, because by the charm of its blooming appearance it draws the minds of all readers to read. Nor without reason have I ennobled the beginning of the page with the dignity of so festive a title [Col. 1381C], since it graciously alludes to this playful work and, by the splendor of its own name, colors and adorns the very gateway of the writing; [Col. 1382A] a worthy title, I say, to stand before it, but worthier still the page which follows—one that in some places sparkles with the majesty of its thoughts and in others shines and glows with the golden brilliance [supplied] of its expression.

## I. On the Nativity of Christ

Olympus distils nectar-like dew upon the earth;  
Rivers of honey sprinkle all the ground.

The golden rose of the saints, from the meadow of paradise,  
Fell into the Virgin’s lap and rested there.

Within virgin splendor, within the enclosure of chastity,  
The Virgin’s chamber gathers the angelic rose.

A rose-like flower, an angelic flower, this blessed flower  
Is turned into hay: may our God become flesh.

The Word of the Father is turned into flesh; yet without injury  
The Virgin is turned into a mother, but without a man.

[Col. 1382B] Power remains in its fullness in him who is born;  
Virgin splendor blooms in her who gives birth.

A new thing, a famous thing, a thing worthy of every wonder!  
Both chastity and childbirth coexist without conflict.

Four things commend the Virgin’s childbirth: gold,  
Gabriel’s voice, the Spirit’s work, the Father’s shadow.

The Virgin is silent; Gabriel speaks; the Spirit perfumes  
Her lofty womb, and the Father’s power overshadows her.

There the Virgin’s ear was wife; Gabriel’s word was her husband;  
The kindly Spirit, her dowry; the Father, her shadow.

The sun is covered by a cloud, the flower by hay, the grain by husk,  
Honey by wax, purple by a sackcloth, God by flesh.

As the kernel is joined to its shell, honey as it were to wax,  
Or silver to gold, so flesh is joined to God.

[Col. 1382C] Therefore, if you rightly distinguish each thing,  
You will at once say that the honeycomb is electrum: that is, God and man.

[Col. 1383A] For two joined together make a nut; two joined together make a honeycomb;  
Two joined together make electrum; two make you, Christ Jesus.

A star bears the sun; dawn bears the day; a rock bears a spring;  
A daughter bears God the Father; a virgin woman bears a man.

These are, as it were, the clasp of heaven and earth,  
Binding discordant realms in the holy embrace of a covenant.

O blessed condescension of the chaste Mother! Through her mediation  
Heaven bends itself down to earth.

She is that holy mother whose name is a honeycomb  
In the heart, a sweet melody of honey in the mouth.

She is she whom God, the painter of heaven, painted within and without  
And adorned with an angelic dowry.

So far as it is lawful to believe, the whole Godhead shone upon her  
And came, as it were girded up, to this work.

[Col. 1383B] For it washed her mind and refined her flesh, so that  
Her mind might be sincere within and her flesh clean without.

Festal splendor claims her wholly for itself,  
In whom every ivory of beauty shines preeminently.

The beauty of her adornment reflects the mirror of angelic light;  
Toward her the whole heavenly court directs its gaze.

All the instruments of heaven play the lyre in praise of her titles;  
Heavenly music sports for her.

She is the spacious chamber where the overflowing honey of divinity  
Fully drenches her with the rain of its gift.

Star of the sea, ivory of brightness, mirror of paradise,  
Fountain of pardon, gate of life—Virgin, hail.

Good ladder of heaven, school of peace, clasp of incense,  
Little rod, cell of spice—Virgin, hail.

The bright insignia of so many praises shine forth from you; none knows  
[Col. 1383C] How much higher so lofty a summit of honor may rise.

Every form of virtue and every perfume together  
Sprinkle you with the fragrance of their incense.

You are a ray without failure, a flower without thorn,  
A day without cloud, a mother without stain.

Why do I speak? Your praise gains no increase from this;  
A torch shines in vain when I attempt to help the day.

No tongue can confine within any bundles of praises  
The expanse open to your virtues.

## II. On the Virgin Birth

Aaron’s rod and the Virgin of God are said to have borne offspring:  
That one, nuts of a tree; this one, God of heaven.

The rod lacks seed and bears fruit without seed;  
The Virgin knows no man and conceives without a man.

The dry rod bears nuts without a root, without the use of seed;  
The intact Virgin bore God.

That rod blossomed and yielded fruit, and from it came a nut;  
This woman conceives and gives birth, and from her God is born.

From the rod a nut arises; from the Virgin, Christ;  
The rod was Mary; the nut was Christ-Man.

In the shell, indeed, human nature is signified;  
In the kernel, divinity; in the nut, Christ-Man.

Divinity lies hidden in the shell; flesh dwells  
With the kernel in the shell, as flesh with divinity.

The kernel tastes sweet; that flavor delights the palate;  
Divinity tastes sweet; that flavor rules the heart.

## III. On the Sale of Joseph

[Col. 1384A]

When nature had blessed Jacob with twelvefold offspring,  
In the boys there was perhaps much grace.

Outshining the faces of the rest with the splendor of his serene countenance,  
Joseph deserved to be Lucifer among them.

The sun’s brilliance eclipses every star;  
So the boy surpassed them all with his rosy face.

Having expended less vigilant labor upon other faces,  
Nature gave this one all the wealth it possessed.

So lavish was she with beauty upon the boy’s face  
That, after this gift, she almost remained poor.

Thus with polished nail she had smoothed away every blemish,  
So that no stain of fault might mar the work.

The boy’s beauty is commended by his rosy mouth and blooming cheek,  
[Col. 1384B] His sparkling eye, pious mind, and pure flesh.

His mouth, his brightness, and his teeth imitate, reproduce, and equal  
The lily, the star, and snowy ivory in their shining purity.

Nature labors wholly to praise the boy  
And marvels that her own hand has labored so earnestly.

If perhaps she had done too little in any respect—far be it!—  
This loss can be redeemed by the honor of his garment.

Dress honors nature’s gift in the boy,  
Whose praise adds support to the praises of his beauty.

A dye had steeped the garment in a rosy color;  
The garment was drunk with purple blood.

A father’s devoted care bestowed it upon the boy;  
Its border plays about his feet and kisses the ground.

Although the father is bound to his other sons by love’s glue,  
His fatherly love clung more firmly to this one.

[Col. 1384C] This fact breeds envy among the brothers; Joseph’s dreams,  
When related, provide nourishment for the evil.

What sleep revealed, he carried to his brothers’ ears;  
Such was the vision he made known to them:

“The matter is this: we go into the field; our hands attend to the sheaves;  
The sickle harvests the field; each is drawn by his own hope.

Your portion bows its head down before my sheaf  
[*gelima*; French *gerbe*, ‘sheaf’—so Martinius in his *Lexicon* and Du Cange in his *Glossary*],

Supplicating, and bearing certain signs of entreaty.”

The faint spark of speech wounds their hearing;  
A second vision adds to the brothers’ crime.

Explaining his dreams, the boy again brings these words  
Before his father and his brothers’ ears:

“Sleep contains all things; one color clothes the world;  
Joyful dreams play before my eyes.

[Col. 1384D] The sun bows its head; the circle of the moon supplicates me;  
The ring of eleven stars asks my aid.”

This speech stirs jealousy among the brothers,  
Provokes anger, torments their hearts, and nourishes crime.

The childish speech does not wound the father’s mind;  
He maintains that the words will fail of their effect.  
[Note: Perhaps: “He wished these words to fail of their effect.”]

Fraternal envy pants for the boy’s death;  
Circumstances answer favorably to their crime.

When the brothers had been sent to pasture without Joseph,  
The boy presents himself before his father; the father speaks thus:

“If your brothers’ fortune smiles favorably, go and see.”  
He obeys, departs, and makes inquiry at Shechem.

The places are silent and deaf to the boy; he stands still and lingers at that  
[Col. 1385A] Threshold [variant: *limine*, “threshold”]. A man learns what he seeks and tells him.

A rustic comes forth among them: “Inquire concerning the place, Dotahim.” He replies:  
“What are you seeking?” The boy tells him the place; he believes and departs.

The brothers fix their eyes upon the boy, and exchange  
Words with one another, saying:

“Look: Joseph, whose fortune to his own honor  
Promises that dreams will give him all they possess.

Let a brotherly spear drink his innocent blood,  
Lest the visions he has seen bear their fruit.

Our rage shall hide itself beneath the name of a wild beast;  
A beast’s guilt shall defend our crime.

Impiety and affection fight within their hearts;  
The one gapes after crime, the other restrains wickedness.

Faith makes war with deceit, virtue with crime,  
Crime with piety, frenzy with reason.

[Col. 1385B] That which now wishes to destroy the boy, now to spare him, may rightly  
Be called impious piety, sweet crime.

Impiety, a stranger, drives pious affections from the heart;  
Love leaves the mind as an exile.

The brothers, forgetful of a brother’s name, press on,  
Hasten their crime, and strive toward their purpose.

Lest he ruin himself and turn his brother into an enemy,  
Reuben, to prevent the crime, speaks thus:

‘Let reason’s rein restrain your madness,  
And let no wave of blood stain your clean hands.

The beauty of the boy’s face pleads with us for him;  
Right, pity, and love are his advocates.

Simplicity asks pardon, should he have done wrong;  
A life ignorant of evil excuses the boy.

So many good things strive to soften our hardness;  
[Col. 1385C] So many prayers can break hearts of stone.

Let this old cistern, which long use of time  
Has compelled into age, conceal Joseph.

For this crime will become sweet: a pious impiety; our frenzy  
Will sin justly by this mercy.’”

The speech carries weight; the cistern receives the boy  
And its image commends this guilt as a good deed.

Reuben rejoices and departs; the others break their fast;  
Food restrains hunger and water relieves thirst.

Scarcely had hungry fasting tasted its first food  
When a band of travelers came to the place.

Judah uttered these words: “See, fortune answers  
Well to our prosperous wish: behold, a new merchant.

Let the boy be spared; let him be sold and serve in exile.”  
[Col. 1385D] They obey; a buyer is present; therefore Joseph is sold.

This matter is hidden from Reuben; he had departed. Returning thence,  
He asks the pit about the boy; it is silent.

He imagines that fraternal swords are guilty of blood  
And believes that loyalty has forgotten itself.

Moved by this feeling, pity sighs; pious grief  
In his heart gives his tongue these words:

“Alas, what shall I do? The boy is dead! O cistern, conscious  
Of madness and fraternal evil, give Joseph back.

Alas, what shall I do? The boy is dead! O madness! What has he done  
Worthy of death? Nothing—but because he was righteous.

Alas, what shall I do? The boy is dead—that boy, that boy  
On whom his father’s whole love depended.

Alas, what shall I do? That boy is dead: that blood, that  
Lucifer, that milky complexion, that Joseph.

[Col. 1386A] The terrible rush of speech stopped, choked by sobbing;  
A coming tear restrains the tongue’s anger.

Grief wets and furrows the face with tears and nails;  
Tears wet the face, nails furrow the hair.

The fatness of compassion flowed from his heart through his eyes;  
The shed tear speaks his pious affection.

The hearts of the remaining brothers watch over their deceit;  
Their deceits did not lack their effect.

Joseph’s garment, smeared with goat’s blood, serves the deceit  
And is sent to the unsuspecting father.

Displaying blood as witness of the boy’s death,  
It tells the father that Joseph now exists no more.

The color of goat’s blood disguises all the artifice,  
Condemning the innocent [variant: *justos*, “the righteous”] and justifying the guilty.

This matter deceives the father’s eyes; he concludes that a bloody  
[Col. 1386B] Beast is guilty of the blood.

This fear excludes hope; the cause troubles his heart.  
Here the savage winter of grief freezes his spirit.

With tears, cries, and nails, he washes, defiles, and scratches  
Face, place, and hair.

The pain of this disaster flashes inwardly in a whirlwind;  
Outwardly anger thunders in such sounds:

“Woe to me, woe to you; woe to me, a father; woe to you, a son.  
O madness! O frenzy! O wild beast, give Joseph back.

Deafer than the sea, fiercer than an asp, more wicked than a serpent,  
More dreadful than a monster—wild beast, give Joseph back.

More treacherous than Styx, fouler than a sow, viler than a goat,  
Rougher than brambles—wild beast, give Joseph back.

Harder than an anvil, blacker than pitch, harder than an enemy,  
Worse than a tigress—wild beast, give Joseph back.

[Col. 1386C] Sweeter than honey, more glittering than fire, more fitting than shade,  
More useful than brothers—woe to you, little boy.

Milder than a lamb, purer than gold, brighter than a star,  
More radiant than jasper—woe to you, little boy.

Simpler than a dove, more welcome than springtime shade,  
Nobler than violets—woe to you, little boy.

Pure as glass, sparkling as Jupiter’s star,  
White as ivory—woe to you, little boy.

Hurry here, old men; let blooming youth gather here;  
Boys, weep for the boy; old men, weep with the old man.

Beat your breasts, pour forth tears, lament the funeral;  
Boys, weep for the boy; old men, weep with the old man.

Let a fountain flow from your eyes; let your nails rage against your garments;  
Boys, weep for the boy; old men, weep with the old man.

[Col. 1386D] In us the hailstorm of the whole tempest is wintering;  
Boys, weep for the boy; old men, weep with the old man.

With its nail withdrawn, the anchor of our ship drifts;  
Boys, weep for the boy; old men, weep with the old man.

Alas, boy! That complexion of yours is my grief; that form  
Is our loss—woe to you, pure boy.

That nose of yours is my downfall; the glory of your face  
Is our sobbing—woe to you, pure boy.

Your lovely likeness is harsh fate to me; your cheeks are punishment to me;  
So new a fate is my death—woe to you, little boy.

That comely face is now my madness; your pure flesh  
Is harsh fortune to me. Death, give me back my Joseph.

My sweet entrails are my wounds; your tender limbs [variant: *umbra*, “shade”]  
Are our tempest. Death, give me back my Joseph.

[Col. 1387A] Your destruction is my end; that speech of yours  
Is our lament. Death, give me back my Joseph.

That rosy blood is my frenzy; that robbery  
Is our ruin. Death, give me back my Joseph.”

## IV. On Job, Noah, and Daniel

(From the Tours manuscript and others.)

Heaven receives three—Daniel, Job, and Noah;  
With its threshold shut, all the rest of the crowd begs outside.

If reason rightly considers the weight of all things,  
That figure of three will express the elect.

Daniel’s life represents the conduct of the chaste;  
Uninjured chastity flowered in Daniel.

Job signifies those whom the bond of marriage entices;  
Job fulfilled the work founded in love of offspring.

Noah shows those whom the ship of the Church obeys;  
[Col. 1387B] The ark followed Noah and was safe beneath Noah.

Those who live chastely are Daniel; those who fulfill  
The duties of marriage are Job; those who rule hearts well are Noah.

He who marries turns upon the millstone; he who teaches sweats in the field;  
He who loves to live chastely dwells in the bedchamber.

To this man belongs the mill, to this the field, to this the bed: the mill is the world,  
The field is the subject people, and the bed is a life of rest.

There I see three ranks: this man grinds [supplied: “rules”], that one lies  
In hope of offspring, another for his brother’s profit, another for the love of God.

God wills this one, calls that one, snatches away another; this one is occupied with offspring,  
That one feeds the flock, another hungers for God.

This man is tender, that strong, another gentle; one feeds as it were  
[Col. 1387C] On milk, another on bread, another on honeycombs.

A demon attacks this one, grieves over that one, envies another;  
This one he subdues, that one he wounds, another he kills.

A field holds this one, a hill that one, a mountain another;  
This one walks, that one runs, another flies.

This one guards against every sin, that one fears it, another flees it;  
This one longs for good things, that one strives, another abounds in them.

This one is pure in hand; that one is holy in speech and hand;  
Another is whole in heart, voice, and hand.

Why do I mark these? This one serves, that one rules, another rests:  
This is the good, this the better, that the best rank.

These three float in the world; yet this one suffers danger  
For a little while, that less, the other none.

[Col. 1387D] So that this one may cross the sea, he makes a ship with his arms;  
That one prepares a vessel; another builds himself a bridge.

The motion of hands helps this one, a ship helps that one, a bridge the other;  
This one swims, that one rows, another leaps across the strait.

This one buys thirtyfold fruit; that one reaps double;  
To the other a hundredfold honor owes its rewards.

## V. On the Three Gifts of the Magi

What incense signifies, what myrrh shadows forth, what gold  
Expresses, I ask; the sacred page teaches.

These three are clothed with sacred figures and carry weight;  
These three have more worth within than they have outwardly.

Shell, stone, and wax are what the words tell you outwardly;  
What lies hidden within is kernel, water, and honeycomb.

[Col. 1388A] The shell will yield its kernel, the stone will vomit forth water,  
Wax will press out the honeycomb, if you observe all things rightly.

In myrrh Christ is signified as dead; in gold as king;  
In incense as God: three things, the form of three.

You offer him myrrh, believing him dead; gold, believing him king;  
Incense, worshipping him as God.

Draw out the sense still hidden within the words;  
Once more the honeyed liquid will flow forth from them.

By myrrh is signified flesh mortified; by gold, doctrine;  
By incense, the tearful voice of prayers.

He gives myrrh who mortifies himself; incense, he who prays  
With tears in lamentation; gold, he who acts wisely.

## VI. On the Three Dwelling Places of Man

The righteous man has a threefold house: the first is made in the air; the second  
Lies under the earth; the next stands above the stars.

[Col. 1388B] This house is a home, this a tomb, that one heaven;  
This passes away, this fails, that one remains.

A builder prepares this, a digger that, Christ the other;  
Stone builds that one, worm this one, and works of piety the other.

The lot of the three differs: this falls, this lies, and that stands—  
The first full of evils, the second filthy with dust, the third supported by good things.

Here there is labor and pain; there neither: this dwelling  
Belongs to storm, that to death, the other to delight.

Man lives in this, sleeps in that, reigns in the other;  
Here he is mortal, there earth, there blessed.

Here he is joined to the living, there to the dead, there to Christ;  
Here is passage, there death, there everlasting life.

[Col. 1388C] Here he chews food, there worms, there praises;  
Here he tastes tears, there gall, there balm.

Here he has something, here nothing, there everything that he desires;  
Here he is wretched, here naked, there accounted rich.

In the home there is dew, in the tomb ashes, in paradise a flower;  
Here is smoke, there foam, there emerald.

Life inhabits the home, flesh the tomb, the spirit heaven:  
It goes forth sighing, enters dead, begins joyfully.

Living, he sighs in the home; dead, he rots in the grave;  
Exulting, he reigns in the city of God.

The first two brought about this last one:  
The fault of the first father, and God’s grace alone.

## VII. In Praise of Samson, Archbishop

[Note: [Col. 1387] Perhaps Archbishop of Rheims, for we read of no other archbishop of this name in Gaul at about this period.]

Touch the pen, my hand; paint Samson’s triumphs,  
[Col. 1388D] Whose titles make the soil of Gaul bloom.

Make yourself several small bundles from these flowers;  
From them a great garland may be woven.

Glory of the Church, palace of virtue,  
Line of law, clasp of discordant things—Samson, hail.

By your deeds you show that you are strong, as your name promises;  
Our age marvels that Samson lives.

May his honor, praise, and fame pour serene light  
Upon the lands; live, I pray.

In whose chambers every glory of things rains down,  
To whom every stream of riches has flowed.

In whose fingers gold sets gems,  
While, O ring, your file hollows out your side.

[Col. 1389A] Three things smile upon one man—fortune, nature, and wisdom—  
And strive to give you all that they possess.

Fortune lavish, nature prudent, wisdom flashing bright:  
The first pours out wealth, the second shapes character, the third teaches honorable things.

Fortune herself came white in a sincere countenance,  
So girded with every good that she almost remained poor.

Nature, polishing character with her refined fingers,  
Left there no mark of any defect.

Sprinkling the mind with the dew of honeyed taste,  
Wisdom gave you knowledge of all that lies hidden in art.

In you no wind of any storm spends its winter,  
For in you the virtues have the season of spring.

Among the virtues whose pomp crowns you,  
Virginity holds royal scepters in you.

Virginity surpasses the honeycomb in sweetness, privet in whiteness,  
[Col. 1389B] A star in radiance, a rose in fragrance.

Virginity is fragrant as incense, glowing as a star,  
Pure as glass, white as ivory.

Why do I mark these things? Gold of learning enriches you,  
The gem of faith endows you, the ivory of chastity refines you.

Mind, tongue, and hand commend you: the first  
Thinks, the second speaks, the third accomplishes good.

Within, the splendor of virtues gilds the mind;  
Without, the refined tongue silvers the name.

## VIII. On the Four Evangelists

Touch the stylus, Muse; put off ornate adornment;  
Let the majesty of things clothe this work.

Ornament is unnecessary here; rather, let rich meaning gild it:  
Precious things have greater value, beautiful things less.

[Col. 1389C] Let your chariot, Christ, be the boundary of this poem; from this  
Matter, Muse, weave your song.

Enclose the body of the subject within a small compass;  
Strive to be brief, yet take care to be weighty.

What yokes or wheels shall I recount, what reins, what axle,  
What man, what calf, what lion, what bird?

I see four rivers of paradise running meanwhile;  
I see Amminadab going upon four wheels.

The first wheel marks you, Matthew; the next, you, Mark;  
The third, Luke; the fourth, you, beloved friend of Jesus.  
[Note: [Col. 1389D] John the Evangelist, namely he whom Jesus loved.]

A different lot draws the wheels: the first goes, the second hastens,  
The third runs, the fourth flies.

Where the axles are excellent, the reins noble,  
[Col. 1389D] And the driver skilled, there the yoke is gentle.

The twofold Law is a bird; discernment is the rein; Christ  
Is the charioteer; your commands, O God, are the yoke.

Grace distributed its own gifts to each: this one flows,  
This one fans, that flashes, and that one thunders.

Matthew’s page learned the Hebrew tongue;  
The other three undertook to speak Greek.

Matthew’s pen is water; Luke’s writing is wine;  
Mark’s page is milk; John’s work is honey.

This one tastes as earth; that drips as myrrh;  
This one smells as a flower; that thrives as spice.

This one ploughs the field; that sows in the furrow;  
This one covers the seed; that waters what has been covered.

[Col. 1390A] Each of them teaches; one resounds to the world,  
One thunders, one sounds the trumpet, one sings.

The first has cymbals, another bears drums,  
The third employs the plectrum, the fourth plays the organ.

As they pour radiance into minds, this one is as a lamp,  
This as a candle, that as Lucifer, that as day.

Consult the Scriptures: this is an iron style, that bronze,  
This silver, that golden.

I mark four things: the face of a man, the form of an ox,  
The face of a lion, the image of a bird.

The man signifies Matthew, the ox Luke, the lion Mark,  
The bird the disciple who was without stain.

Consider the titles of the writers and the reasons for the titles;  
You will find that what I say has its own weight.

[Col. 1390B] A human appearance is given to Matthew because, both in what he writes  
And in his title, he indicates what God did as man.

The ox’s face declares Luke, who took a special  
Subject from your cross, O Christ.

A lion portrays Mark, whose writing cries out  
How great was the power with which your flesh rose, O Christ.

The eagle’s form signifies the chaste disciple,  
Whose voice flies beyond clouds to the stars.

Christ is man; Christ is ox; Christ is lion; Christ  
Is bird: in Christ you may observe all things.

He is man while he lives, ox while he dies, lion  
When he rises, bird when he seeks the heights.

The fountain still drips: consult the veins of the words.  
Every righteous person can be these four things.

[Col. 1390C] Vigorous in mind, he becomes man; mortifying carnal things, ox;  
Taming hard things, lion; pursuing the heights, bird.

## IX. On the Virgin Birth

The sun, cloud, and water make  
The rainbow of heavenly light; these signify the Virgin’s childbirth.

The sun is divinity, the cloud the form of flesh, the water the Holy  
Spirit; the rainbow is Mary, star of the sea.

## X. On Christ’s Nativity

The king is born and seeks us;  
The chaste Virgin knows no stain;  
The shining star gives light;  
The exulting angel declares joys;  
The faithless enemy loses his rights;  
Redeemed man worships God.

## XI. On Christ’s Baptism

The Savior is sprinkled with dew;  
The Father cries out;  
The water is sanctified;  
The dove is present;  
Faith is made firm.

## XII. On Christ’s Offering

[Col. 1390D]

The Law is fulfilled;  
A turtledove is offered;  
The Mother rejoices;  
The Son is borne;  
Anna marvels;  
The old man prays.

## XIII. On Christ’s Passion

He bears reproaches;  
He sets the guilty in motion;  
He condemns Christ;  
Christ in flesh;  
The devil in fury;  
The Pharisee by the cross.

## XIV. On Christ’s Resurrection

The devil weeps;  
Death seeks;  
The abyss is bereft;  
Christ rises;  
Galilee is visited;  
The faithful pray.

## XV. On the Lord’s Ascension

The Savior ascends;  
The brethren sigh;  
The angel rejoices;  
The low places are left;  
Heaven is reached.

## XVI. On the Coming of the Holy Spirit

[Col. 1391A]

The flock awaits gifts in faith; the Spirit fills hearts in mind;  
Fervor drives out fear by warmth.

## XVII. On Christ’s Judgment

The Judge will distinguish deeds by justice; heaven nourish the good in repose;  
Styx burn the reprobate in fire.

## XVIII. On Christ the Lord

Born of a Virgin, pure from fault, man in reality, mighty in power, rising in flesh, light in ascent, inwardly in divinity,  
He takes a body, sanctifies waters, bears punishment, presses down death, raises himself, enters heaven, and fulfills all things.

## XIX. On Aaron

Aaron bears tablets of the Law stained with rust;  
Our Aaron polishes them with the gold of the Gospel.

## XX. On the Virgin Mary

[Col. 1391B]

The star-studded image of the Virgin Mary glows more truly  
With gems and reflects a mirror of gold.

## XXI. On the Ark of God

The ark of God, leafy with diverse figures of things,  
Which Christ’s blood perfumes, represents the altar.

## XXII. On the Altar

The glory of a festive countenance makes this altar purple;  
Thus you see shining forth whatever the old altar prefigures.

## XXIII. On Majesty

This is not the craftsman, but the work; not the king, but the royal  
Image, which plays before our eyes in gold.

## XXIV. On the Synagogue

The garment of the Law veils the forehead of the Synagogue.

## XXV. On the Church

[Col. 1391C] The Church puts on a shining crown studded with stars.

## XXVI. On the Gospel

A wife, an estate, and oxen shut the invited from the feast;  
The world, anxiety, and flesh shut the blessed from eternity.

[Note: [Col. 1391D] From this epitaph it is evident how falsely that celebrated letter is attributed to Hildebert, in which Blessed Robert is reproached for that new kind of martyrdom allegedly imposed upon him by Geoffrey of Vendôme through excessive familiarity with women. For who could believe this concerning a man whom Hildebert, in this epitaph, describes under so many titles as a most bitter enemy of the flesh?]

## XXVII. Epitaph of Robert of Arbrissel

(From the Elnonensis, or Saint-Amand, manuscript, now Royal manuscript no. 274, about five hundred years old.)

A cultivator of the stars and of God harvests stars and God:  
Stars and God are the good man’s place and reward.

This man, good and better than the good—of the better  
I say nothing—is best; to be good suffices for praise.

His work was to strengthen faith, heal the mind,  
Add spurs to virtue, and give hope to the guilty;

To uproot crime, not uproot criminals,  
And reconcile the head, Christ, to his members.

[Col. 1391D] He did not forestall hunger with bread, thirst with drink,  
Cold with clothing, or work with rest.

He did not join luncheon to supper with drink;  
He put reins on gluttony—gluttony did not put reins on the man.

[Col. 1392A] A hauberk wore down his side, parching thirst his throat,  
Harsh hunger his stomach, wakeful care his eyes.

He rarely allowed himself rest, more rarely food;  
He fed his throat with grass and his heart with God.

He thirsted for water, but thirsted more than water:  
Christ and water were the cause of his twofold thirst.

The flesh was worn down under the laws of its mistress, reason;  
For both, there was one savor—and that savor was God.

Life made him equal in heart to Peter, who presided over the flock at Poitiers;  
Death made him equal in merits.

By merit there is given to those who have earned it what grateful God gives and receives  
For each; and each is grateful to God.

## XXVIII. Epitaph of a Bishop Who Ever Performed His Office with Constancy of Mind and at Last Died in Exile for Justice

[Note: [Col. 1391D] This was certainly none other than Peter, bishop of Poitiers, and the duke likewise none other than William, duke of Aquitaine—at once extremely powerful and at that time extremely wicked. Peter tried in vain, with pastoral gentleness, to bring him to better conduct; at length, however, with incomparable zeal, he did not hesitate to strike him with an anathema, when the sword was drawn and threatened death, already almost hanging over the bishop’s head. Thus the most fervent bishoply dissuader from incest, assailed with six hundred insults by the incestuous prince infected by the serpentine hissing of a little harlot, and finally driven into exile, fell as a martyr in a glorious end. See Malmesbury, *History of William II*, books IV and V, and Baronius, under the year 1130.]

(From the Évreux manuscript no. 19, and the Tours manuscript.)

[Col. 1392B]

Peter, you built upon the rock, and not in vain;  
There also you raised towers by which you made a path to the stars.

Winds blew, rain fell, rivers rose, and hail descended;  
Yet none of these ever shook them.

You wholly frustrated so many storms from every side,  
Yielding neither to adversity nor relaxing in prosperity.

You, a chosen vessel, a pure vessel, a vessel unto honor,  
Pouring forth the nectar of character and the honor of life.

You grieved, like a physician, over the duke’s wounds;  
After vain caresses, you piously applied the iron.

He had driven out a bride from her bridal chamber and her seat;  
By force, mistress, and disgrace, he had burdened temple, marriage-bed, and homeland.

Often you warned him to restore himself to himself;  
But, grieving, you handed the scorner over to Satan.

[Col. 1392C] Hence, more grievously sick, he burned with hidden fires,  
And his inward parts, badly wounded by the poison of envy, tore at him.

Jezebel endured Elijah, and Herodias John;  
Thus both earned everlasting titles.

A like sex and an equal madness drove you from the city;  
Thereupon sacred things were defiled by palace dogs,  
The death of the outcast was brought about, right was broken, law violated;  
And the clergy were assailed [variant: *constrictus*, “bound fast”] and torn by them.

Those who hasten freely to crime; to good things no one, though asked:  
[Note: A Hildebertine expression, as appears from Letter 17, book II, where he says of the wicked: “Those who run freely to crime, [do not run] to honorable conduct even for payment …”]

You nevertheless endured all these great things unmoved,  
A bishop in exile, having confessed our mortal condition;  
Now returned to the lofty kingdoms, pray for us.

## XXIX. Epitaph of Peter, Bishop of Poitiers

(From the Tours manuscript.)

[Col. 1392D]

The virtues whose famous distinction smiled upon Peter’s  
Character I gather in brief praise.

A lyre-player of the Muses, standard-bearer of virtues, vine  
[Col. 1393A] Bearing the keys, this man was the Church’s Lucifer.

Dew of counsel, flower of intellect, whetstone of eloquence,  
Mouth of Pallas, dowry of character, honor of Helicon.

Beyond so many titles in which he shone,  
The ivory of chastity flourished in his uninjured flesh.

No coal marked the whiteness of his flesh;  
The snowy flower of allurements was without stain.

Having borne away from his own flesh the standards of praise,  
As conqueror he possesses the golden rewards he earned.

He was a fisher of men; and the fish were caught  
In the fifth [supplied: month], when fate fished for the man.  
[Note: Supplied *mensis*, “month,” that is, May, in about which month Peter, bishop of Poitiers, is reported in *Gallia Christiana* to have died.]

## XXX. Epitaph of Master Anselm

(From the Elnonensis manuscript, now Royal manuscript no. 274.)

In this tomb sleeps that most renowned master,  
Anselm—  
[Note: He may have been Anselm, cantor of the holy and most glorious Sepulchre of our Lord Jesus Christ, among the Parisian canons, and probably himself a canon, whose two letters to Galon, or Walon, then bishop of Paris, and to his clergy, concerning an outstanding portion of the Holy Cross sent to him by Anselm, are recorded in the *Gallia Christiana*. That Galon, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, is said to have died on 23 February 1114. — There was also an Anselm, canon of Laon.]

—whose fame and praise were gathered from every quarter  
[Col. 1393B] Throughout the expanses of the world by sound faith, ample learning, reverence of manners,  
A chaste life, a generous hand, careful action,  
Pleasing speech, vigorous discipline, gentle correction,  
Wise counsel, and a prudent, sober, merciful mind.

But the black month of July, against the Ides, dissolved  
The gifts which God’s lavish grace had gathered;  
The grace in which he flourished alive accompanies him dead.

## XXXI. On the Death of the Count of Flanders

[Note: It seems probable that this count of Flanders was none other than Baldwin, called Hapkin, who, while fighting against the English in support of Louis the Fat, was severely wounded and died among the Flemings on 15 June 1119, in the flower of his age. He left behind a great longing for himself among all good people because of his exceptional virtues, especially his exact administration of justice in the punishment of crimes. Hence he was called Hapkin, because in the Flemish language *Hapkin* means a kind of axe with which offenders were struck. He was endowed with such piety that he wished to die and be buried in monastic dress; hence Hildebert here:]

Almost at once the count is a monk, and the monk a corpse;  
Be companion, O God, both to the count and to the monk.

(From the same Elnonensis-Royal manuscript.)

Death’s same tomb turns those divided by their merits,  
And, excessively impartial, weighs them in equal balance.

The rhetor is not defended by his tongue, nor the horseman by arms;  
Strength does not redeem the brave, nor beauty the handsome.

[Col. 1393C] Death alone triumphs over the count’s fall; in him  
It envies manhood, not the old age of man.

Death marvels at an old age which age had not yet produced:  
“This man,” she says, “is old; cease, Life, to make him old.”

Almost at once the count is a monk, and the monk a corpse;  
Be companion, O God, both to the count and to the monk.

## XXXII. Epitaph of a Certain Worthy Man

[Note: Who this man was is noted neither in the manuscript nor known to us, since in Hildebert’s time there were almost countless persons to whom this eulogy could be applied.]
