(From the same Elnonensis-Royal manuscript.)

A venerable man dies; yet if surviving fame compels anyone  
To live after death, he has not died.

He was wholly piety, wholly concord, wholly  
The height of dignity, wholly abundance.

He was grave and pious, and took care to be  
[Col. 1394A] Grave with piety and pious with gravity.

He was gentle, but also stern; yet gentle and stern:  
In neither was he excessive or lax.

With moderation as guide, he held the middle between vices,  
Knowing how to stand in the mean between more and less.

Yet great as he was, and moderate in all things,  
In preserving measure he took care not to possess measure.

## XXXIII. Epitaph of Milo, Slain in Prison

(From the same Elnonensis-Royal manuscript.)

Milo, you were worthy in life; your death was worthy of an anathema.  
An honorable enemy of deceit, you were conquered by an enemy through deceit.

A guilty crowd, pressing one free man, one just man bound,  
Thus freed the soul from prison, thus freed the man.

Threatening anger ground its teeth; frenzy stood stiff; the torch roared;  
[Col. 1394B] Crime is committed, and this crime expiates every crime.

The sixth day of May confessed grief through darkness:  
“Night,” she said, “I suffer the horses whom I rule to be without their king.”

## XXXIV. Epitaph of a Certain Wealthy Countess

[Note: Perhaps Adela, Countess of Blois.]

(From the Tours manuscript.)

After her ashes, three things labor to confer life upon her:  
A humble mind, gracious speech, and a kindly hand.

Mirror of example, rose of her country, lamp of her ancestors,  
She forgot the limitations of the female sex.

Flourishing in delights, festive in countenance, radiant—
Illustrious in examples, renowned in titles, flourishing in lineage.

Thus Nature refined her mind within and her countenance without,  
so that her mind was without fault and her face without blemish.

A rare kind of example: this woman conquered herself,  
having in herself nothing of feminine frivolity.

[Col. 1394C] Since a woman of faith is rarer than a white raven,  
yet this faith flourished in her sex.

Apollo held the sign of the balance in an equal scale,  
when the unjust hand of death harvested this flower.

### XXXV. Epitaph for a Certain Thomas

(From the same manuscript.)

Death, hostile to him whom Nature had painted with zeal for character [the transmitted *unguis*, “nail,” is uncertain], dyes him with its own ink.

No ice of any vice ever wintered in this man,  
in whom the virtues established their spring.

If the glory of virtue made him well-proportioned,  
no force of wind compelled his gaze in any direction.

The nobility of his character surpassed the origin of his blood;  
by his character this man ennobled nature.

[Col. 1395A] A good mind ordered, speech taught, … [the hand acted].

Thus he was good in one respect, better in another, and best in yet another.

The third day of February was at hand, when a third fever—  
the messenger of death—came, commanded to destroy Thomas.

### XXXVI. Epitaph for Master Theobald

Paint, Thalia, the man in the festive honor of praise;  
gather into his titles whatever resources you possess.

Chosen of faith, painter of words, foster-child  
of the Muses, he was a river of nectar.

He bore sparks in his heart and a honeycomb in his mouth;  
thus his name was “incense,” and his work was a flower.

He knew how to paint books with the flower of shining eloquence,  
not with pigment, not with ink.

[Col. 1395B] The writings he produced sparkle in varied color;  
honeyed words flow from his study.

This man knew how to nourish his bees with the honey of wisdom;  
he knew how to weave a garment with a delicate needle.

His fluent and free style engraved, painted, and gilded  
every work that he produced.

While he lived, the place of Dervent flourished; with him removed,  
the fragrance of this name withers.

Untimely death blackens a bright name;  
wounded fame no longer shines with its accustomed day.

When the light of Andrew was pouring itself over the earth,  
he, enriched with much honey, left his bees behind.

### XXXVII. Epitaph for a Certain Man Named Clarus

(From a Tours manuscript.)

Anchor of those who had fallen, ray of faith, brightness of the world,  
[Col. 1395C] flower of his homeland, rule of morals: Clarus has died.

By a bright deed he fulfilled the radiance of his famous name:  
his name was *Clarus* (“Bright”), and bright was his action.

Why should I make this known? He was bright in reality, bright in name,  
bright in example, bright in teaching, bright in his ancestors.

Distinguished, powerful, generous, devout, abundant—  
in character, intellect, service, heart, and good deeds.

He offered, instructed, scattered, rejected, purchased:  
an example, brothers, losses, things to avoid, heaven.

As the sun rose for the fifth time in September,  
this Lucifer was compelled to suffer his setting.

### XXXVIII. Epitaph for a Certain Master

(From a Tours manuscript.)

The stars grow dim, deprived of their serene ray;  
[Col. 1395D] Gaul sighs, stripped of its bishop.

The lesser stars received light from this sun;  
with the sun fallen, the heavenly brightness grows pale.

To confess the truth: he was a sun among stars,  
a laurel among thickets, a spring among waters.

The sun is dull, the stars lament, the laurel lies fallen, buried thickets  
sigh, the spring dries up, and the water diminishes.

### XXXIX. Epitaph for a Certain Abbess

(From a Tours manuscript.)

The feminine article does not suit her; this masculine one does.  
She put on the man, employing a man’s character.

By the strength of her mind she abandoned feminine actions,  
[Col. 1396A] and deserved to be stronger than her sex.

The honorableness of her character veiled nature’s defect;  
displaying nothing womanly, she was wholly manly.

Thus virtue claims what nature denied her:  
she was feminine in sex, but masculine in character.

She avoided stain, sought God, loved him—just,  
whole, pure, worshipping in body, mind, and faith.

The birth of the starry Virgin granted her birth;  
that one is born in heaven, this one is born to God.

### XL. Epitaph for Berengar

(From printed editions and from the Évreux, Beauvais, and other manuscripts.)

He whom the world now admires, and will always admire,  
Berengar, who is not to die, dies.

Him who held the highest summits of sacred faith,  
[Col. 1396B] the fifth day of January carried off, daring the crime.

[Note: From Book III of William of Malmesbury’s *History of the English Bishops*, where in the fifth verse the erroneous reading is: “Now the fifth day”; nor is the Lyons edition better: “Now then the fifth day.” But the Beauvais and Évreux manuscripts rightly read: “the fifth day of January.”]

That day—ruinous and treacherous to the world—  
on which its glory and the supreme ruin of things occurred!

What standing of the Church! What hope! What glory of the clergy!  
What a guardian of law fell when law itself was falling!

Whatever philosophers wrote, whatever poets sang,  
yielded to his intellect and eloquence.

A holier and greater wisdom, undertaking greater things,  
filled his sacred breast and mouth with God.

When his breast willed, his voice uttered, his action performed:  
each thus devoted itself to its Maker.

A sacred and wise man, whose renown grows by the hour—  
beside whom every other man, however great, is lesser—

whose judgment produced and preserved the honors he won;  
[Col. 1396C] to whom a poor man was preferable to a rich man, and right to gain;

whom great wealth made neither idle nor luxurious,  
and abundant and lofty honor did not make proud;

who turned his eyes neither toward silver nor toward gold,  
but grieved whenever someone was absent to whom he might give.

He did not cease to support the ruins of the needy,  
until by giving he himself became needy.

His concern was to follow nature, observe laws,  
deny vices to the mind and deceits to the lips,

set virtues before riches, truth before falsehood,  
say nothing empty of meaning and do nothing so,

not harm excessively, benefit everyone, and drive  
favoritism and popular profit from mind and hand.

His clothing was coarse enough to cover him; he never had  
[Col. 1396D] drink before thirst, nor food before hunger.

Modesty made its dwelling in him, and afterward he overcame  
lust, which overcomes the incestuous.

When Mother Nature gave him to the world, she said:  
“Others regenerate him; this one is born for me.”

He enclosed within his sacred breast justice,  
which had wandered and almost abandoned the world.

Sacred from childhood, he who surpassed the world in reputation  
governed his own reputation as much as reputation surpassed the world.

Though fame flies through the whole world, less than his merits,  
and though it always grows, it will nevertheless not be equal to them.

A devout and grave man, so moderate in both respects  
[Col. 1397A] that envy could gnaw at him in neither.

Envy laments the man it had formerly assailed; and it did not so much  
assail and hate him then as it now praises and loves him.

As it formerly groaned at his life, so now it groans at his death,  
and complains that his days passed too swiftly.

A truly wise man, blessed in every respect,  
who entrusted heaven to his soul and earth to his body.

After death, may I possess life with him, repose with him,  
and may my lot not be better than his lot.

### XLI. Epitaph for Count Geoffrey

(From Baluze’s papers.)

Flower of the kingdom and father of his homeland, glory of the world, and likewise  
the world’s love, glory of his race, honor of his people:

Count Geoffrey, here too soon carried off by hostile forces—  
loss beyond loss, grief beyond grief!

[Col. 1397B] His name the commonwealth loves, remembers, and venerates;  
his work the commonwealth adores.

While he restrained the wicked, upheld the laws and the good,  
there was peace, and abundance increased by the aid of peace.

How great in counsel, how great in courage and arms,  
what brilliance of eloquence and rigor of judgment,

how steadfast, how generous, what grace of appearance,  
how great in learning and in intellect!

What enemies he subdued or what strongholds he overthrew,  
events prove, and the report of peoples sounds from mouth to mouth.

This pinnacle of integrity, this glory of our age,  
while still flourishing, died before his time.

The world grieves collectively for a common death:  
though the death was of one man, it was not one death alone.

[Col. 1397C] All lived, all die in one man;  
thus in him one man and every human being dies.

Therefore the grief is public, because so great are the public  
losses of sorrow; all grieve what is public, each person what is his own.

The seventh of September took the world’s glory from the world;  
the kingdom lacks its flower, the homeland its father.

[Note: In the longer notes of R. P. Mabillon on St Bernard’s Letter 266, this epitaph for Suger is reported as published by François Chifflet, S.J., and as composed by Simon Capra-Aurea, canon of St Victor, though with some slight differences. There it begins with *decidit* (“fell”), not *occidit* (“died”); it has *viris* instead of *suis*, and *viris* instead of *juris*. Two verses of this epitaph drawn from the manuscript of Saint-Marian are absent from the Victorine manuscript; we have supplied from the Victorine manuscript the final two verses, absent from the Marian manuscript. It reads as follows:]

### XLII. Epitaph for Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis

(Published by R. P. Mabillon in the notes on St Bernard, now from the manuscript of Saint-Marian at Auxerre.)

The flower, jewel, crown, column,  
banner, shield, glory, light, and pinnacle of the Church has died:

Abbot Suger, model of virtue and equity,  
grave with devotion, devout with gravity;

great-souled, wise, eloquent, rich, honorable,  
[Col. 1397D] conspicuous in his deeds [Vict.: “judgments”], present in body and self-possessed in mind.

[Col. 1398A] Through him the king wisely governed the affairs of the kingdom;  
he governed the king, and the king was as though king of a king.

And while the king prolonged his stay overseas for many years,  
this man governed the realm, acting in the king’s place.

What scarcely any other could unite in himself, he united:  
good to his men [*viris*], and good to God.

He adorned the noble see of the Church, repelled its losses, and enlarged its choir by praise, strength, and laws [variant: “men,” *viris*].

Short in body and birth, constrained by a double shortness,  
he refused to be short in his own shortness.

The seventh day after Theophany took away his light;

[Note: “The seventh day after Theophany took away his light; true Theophany gave true light to the man.” From this it is inferred that Suger died on the seventh day within the octave of Theophany, or Epiphany, which falls on 12 January, that is, at the beginning of 13 January. Our learned R. P. D. Michael Félibien assigns this date to Suger's pious death in his recently published distinguished history of the royal monastery of Saint-Denis, p. 573.]

True Theophany gave true light to the man.

### XLIII. Epitaph for William de Ros

(*Literary History of France*, vol. IX, p. 331.)

Rich toward the poor and abbot of the sacred name,  
[Col. 1398B] William, cultivator of the earth only in body,

returned free from Egypt and left the wilderness;  
now, victorious and rejoicing, he possesses Jerusalem.

Having contracted hatred of vices and an everlasting friendship  
with good character, he was steadfast in both.

On the grievous day that preceded the sixth of April by too little,  
his spirit was restored to his homeland, his bones to the soil.

### XLIV. Epitaph for Gualo, Bishop of Paris

[Note: Perhaps the nephew of that Bishop Gualo, bearing the same name, addressed to Gerbert, bishop of Paris, his immediate successor.]

Gualo to the bishop who succeeded his uncle.

[Note: Royal Elnone manuscript no. 274 gives this heading: “Gualo to the bishop who succeeded his father.”]

Father and shepherd, your son and sheep wishes you health;  
receive, father, the prayers of your son, shepherd, of your sheep.

And be a father to me, since that good father—indeed, the best  
of fathers—has ceased to be a father.

I remember what that father used to say to me about you:  
“Gualo is strong; he surpasses other men.”

[Col. 1398C] I entrust this father to you; I share in his possessions,  
and I am burdensome to him in this one respect: I spare his own.

“I am going to Rome; farewell.” He pretended that he was going to Rome;  
but he might better have said: “I am going to die.”

Death, falsely kind to the man and lessening his labor by rest,  
cut short his light by night and his road by delay.

“I do not wish the man,” it said, “to sweat over the frozen Alps;  
rather, let him stand, remain, and die.”

The vessel of faith, vessel of justice, vessel of simplicity  
has fallen; these, when their vessel fell, fall with it.

But I hear that you have placed yourself beneath the fallen vessel  
of justice; if this is so, then though no one else exists, you do.

### XLV. Epitaph for Bruno

[Note: There can be no doubt that the author meant Saint Bruno, founder of the sacred Carthusian order, who in fact died on the sixth day of October 1101.]

(From a Tours manuscript, supplied by C. D. Dupoirier.)

[Col. 1398D] The worshiper and companion of the Most High withdrew to those above,  
commending to earth what belonged to earth: Bruno.

[Col. 1399A] He despises light burdens and the world that plays Proteus,  
having gained eternal riches as a poor man.

I suppose that here the angelic companies rejoice,  
and the citizens of heaven applaud their new fellow citizen.

It was the sixth day of October when Bruno, having professed  
nature, went unburdened to those above.

### XLVI. Epitaph for Elias, Count of Maine

[Note: This is the same Elias who so persistently opposed Hildebert’s election, but who in time, honoring his merit, formed an intimate friendship with him; when Elias finally died, Hildebert himself rendered him honorable funeral rites and buried him in the Church of St Peter of La Couture.]

(From the same manuscript.)

Upholding the laws, loving peace, and greatest in arms—  
Elias, censor of crimes, patron of what is honorable,

justice and all that the world admires in a prince—  
has died; and together peace and the glory of city and world

have fallen: Elias, the homeland’s father, alas, taken from affairs.

### XLVII. Epitaph for a Certain Simoniac Who Died under Excommunication

(From Royal Elnone manuscript 274.)

[Col. 1399B]

Here lies one whom nothing became except disgrace, and whom  
nothing ashamed except what he believed to be honorable.

A man prompt for evils, even more prompt for the worst;  
not good, indeed evil; not evil, indeed evil itself.

Dregs of humankind, wholly fraud as a man: he took care that the owl  
should perform funeral rites at night, and dogs by day for one who called.

Alas for me! How I fear that fraud, the man, may rise by fraud,  
that the deceitful man may be able to deceive death.

Press down his limbs, stone; confine his soul, shades,  
lest the man be made whole by union with these.

Tartarus, consume your punishments upon your own,  
unless you wish to spare your own: he was yours.

[Col. 1399C] Earth alone conceals what deceit is; this man is good only  
in death, by which he ceased to be evil.

This is that criminal than whom none is more simoniacal; this is he  
beside whom every wicked man is better, or less wicked.

A pig in life, a dog in office, a little fox in mind;  
a brute, scarcely knowing himself, scarcely God.

He took hope from the wretched, property from the rich, weapons from the strong,  
the Church’s resources—and himself—from the Church.

Arming his hands for thefts and his tongue for quarrels,  
he believed it a shameful crime to avoid a shameful crime.

### XLVIII. Verses on a Certain Poor Man Recently Raised to the Episcopate

Often a mournful day is followed by golden light; often  
a cheerful day begins after rains.

What the letter of the preceding writing sighs for,  
[Col. 1399D] this man now shows: formerly a drop, a spark.

With his permission I speak: previously he was not distinguished  
by so great a name, but was a wretched, poor exile.

Then neither mitre adorned his head, nor jewel his hand, nor virtue  
his mind; rather, he was as though no one.

Leaven, not wheat; dew, not rose; iron,  
not gold; no one—not yet anyone at all.

Neither flourishing in riches, nor renowned in ancestors, nor endowed  
with honor, nor shining in distinguished integrity,

then like a kernel within a shell, like a flower within a salt marsh,  
[Col. 1400A] like honey in wax, he still lay hidden.

Certainly not bright with the gold of any virtue,  
this man long lay foul beneath the lead of vice.

Fortune played with the wretch for a long time; at last, knowing  
that she had sinned, she pitied the man.

And as if seeking pardon for herself, gently smiling,  
she raises the poor man upon her wheel.

Snatched by Fortune’s chariot from dust to the citadel  
of the summit, he flies to a bishop’s mitre.

Yet, that the true tenor may remain intact,  
having become another man, he no longer thinks himself his own.

Made happy from miserable, bishop from poor,  
he is changed into a flower, though formerly grass.

He who grieved rejoices; he who lay down stands; he who grew old is renewed:  
this man is not what he formerly was.

[Col. 1400B] Formerly grass, now flower; formerly spark, now drop;  
then bronze, now gold; then cabbage, behold, a rose.

Then like a candle begging light from fire;  
now like a sun from which all else has light.

Thus Fortune’s fault could deserve pardon,  
since she now supplied what she formerly gave too little of.

### XLIX. Verses of a Certain Poor Man

(From a Tours manuscript.)

While your expertise governs all things, it touches the stars;  
while it subdues the swollen, softens the harsh, and breaks the strong.

It is moved neither by hatred, nor payment, nor entreaty;  
the rigor of justice and strength of faith are impartial toward all.

He who gave gifts brought no payment for assistance;  
nor did the one who could do nothing harm, nor did he who gives possess influence.

[Col. 1400C] Hence my one hope was to undertake the laws of the city,  
and, like a brute, disputes made me enter in safety.

May your mind be teachable and accommodating toward me, I pray.  
Perhaps the source of my complaint is open in these words, yet hidden here:

a harmful plague, a letter as witness, a rich miser.  
How bitter, how evil an enemy the rich miser is,

I feel beyond measure; yet you know him well here:  
greatest in body, blackest in character, that Pilate,

that spectator of gods, ready to burn their temples  
with fires and scatter all the members of the senate.

Born for destruction excessive to us and to you as well,  
he strikes me cruelly and has inflicted sufficiently harsh injuries—

harsh and grievous injuries, trivial to him but great to me.  
For I sustained a few cattle and sheep in hope of milk;

[Col. 1400D] from them I scarcely had food and clothing.

The envious man wept whenever he saw them going and returning,  
going gladly, their udders filled with milk.

When he saw this, his spirit failed because he lacked it,  
though he possessed a thousand thousand.

Led by the desire to possess, he demands that I sell them to him.  
I do not wish to sell, by force, entreaty, gift, or fear.

Therefore the impious arrogance of the rich man, stirred to rage,  
began to speak shameful things, and all were full of disgrace.

Then he threatened me with blows and impious harm to the flock;  
[Col. 1401A] by craft he blocked their paths as they went and returned.

That is, the sole road by which the animals could reach the courts  
was closed; thus fodder failed both flocks and owner.

What was I to do? Allow myself and the animals to perish?  
Great hunger compelled me to visit the rich man’s courts.

For I know it is safer to sell badly than to perish.  
Then I do what reason proves necessary for me to do.

I sell to him, since he prevents me from keeping them;  
may I deserve bees, whose food he cannot prevent.

When the envious man sees these too, he envies them; so that they might die,  
he scattered bitter cups of death among the gardens.

On the following morning, under the fresh sun, wearied by labor,  
my bees leave their waxen courts for love of honey.

The king hastens, as is fitting, first to their familiar places;  
[Col. 1401B] then the leaders—alas, never to return—and now the entire court.

They return as they were accustomed, not without song;  
and, as they settle on the ground, they die from its odor alone.

What bodies, what hearts then perished!  
Strong companies—alas for grief!—all fell.

Many in body, greatest in heart: a terrible heap.  
What did the little bee, heaven’s offspring, do to you?

Thus he stripped me of cattle, bees, and food;  
nor did he hesitate to injure you too and despise the laws.

What am I to do, wretched man? Shall I flee? If I flee, I have  
no livelihood; nor, if I remain, bread or clothing.

Ah, children of a wretched father, what will you do?  
You move my heart inwardly with grief again and again.

Nor does the aged mother give scraps of bread even to your tender, torn bodies; her hands are empty, and her empty belly [read: *alvus*] is numb.

[Col. 1401C] But though I, a wretch, reveal these things, he is unmoved.  
I grieve more, suffer more losses, and he is judged happier.

Therefore, I beg you, do not despise what is now being done to me;  
with a devout judgment assist a wretched man who has been wronged.

For unless the rich man’s impious arrogance is restrained,  
he will not fear to utter shameful, or even more impious, things.

Let it not harm me that he grieves to see a poor man loved;  
rather, let him weep because he does not see himself blessed in this respect.

I do not entice you by payment, but I have gained you by affection,  
and thought that you should be retained by pious service.

For you know that friends are kept by merits,  
and these are to be helped and loved, not treated as enemies.

As one outwardly becomes inwardly blind in light,  
[Col. 1401D] so one who remains fair to enemies as to friends—

I am indeed stronger and more powerful than a poor man,  
but I am not therefore guilty or more impious.

He lays upon me whatever he wished to have perish through me;  
he says that I stole his bees, cattle, and food.

I would have stolen them had I wished, but I did not take them away;  
when money was given and the agreement ratified, he sold them and I bought them.

I possess nothing except by my right; do not be silent.  
He had the money, the property was bought: who ought to possess it?

This is the favor now: that our road lay open to his livestock,  
and that his flock committed many shameful acts in the courts.

I pass over the fact that his bees made honey from my flowers  
and were accustomed to bear off the innermost lilies, tender fodder,

and afterward make waxen goods and honeyed gifts.  
He cultivated neither vine nor rich soil with diligence;

[Col. 1402A] no field bore him barley, nor vineyard wine.

Therefore, deservedly, I do not doubt, the wretch went hungry,  
and, in the manner of the reprobate, grieved at the gains of the upright—

especially when he saw my possessions, to his sorrow.  
Why I kept livestock, I have shown by the fact that the bees perished.

Finally, if someone scattered seeds of death in his gardens,  
why did he utter a bitter word against me, a poor man, and blaze with anger?

I have lilies, meadows, rose gardens, fruits, and trees:  
shall I not be forbidden to sell everything, to destroy each thing?

I have grasses—I do not know their names—and a thousand possessions: why should he forbid me, above all, to scatter harmful substances upon them?

His bees came into my pastures. If he could prevent them,  
why did he not choose to avert his own losses?

But I see that he pleads with you so tearfully,  
[Col. 1402B] and strives in every way to repair his own losses.

While he speaks, complains, and colors his words,  
he pleads most eloquently from hatred of us.

Therefore, unless the poor man’s impious license is restrained,  
he will not fear to speak shamefully and invent falsehoods.

### L. Verses of the Bishop of Le Mans on Money, or a Satire against Avarice

(From the former Elnone manuscript, now Royal manuscript no. 274.)

The world’s ornament, the glory of things, virtue, will abandon the earth—  
virtue said to deny death to mortals.

No flower of natural excellence ever promises this in anyone.  
Do you know nothing? Is there piety? Is faith anything but a shadow of its name?

If heaven stood still, if the sun refused to shine,  
if snow were hot and flame cold,

I would not grow so pale, nor stand so astonished in wonder,  
as if I should now see any devout person anywhere.

That a woman gave birth to a calf, a cow to a lamb,  
that a vixen’s daughter once suckled a horse,

would not deserve greater belief when narrated,  
than if you say that anyone now possesses faith.

Now each person lives for himself; one will  
does not know how to dwell in another’s breast.

Each seeks his own; alone, each is friend to himself;  
there is no burden that weighs upon another.

When you are prosperous, you are surrounded by many friends;  
let prosperity change—look around, and you will be alone.

Those whom present fortune joins, fleeing fortune dissolves,  
proving that it values wealth, not people.

[Col. 1402D] The shrewd follower of fortune casts his bait;  
the sting of the bee separates those whom honey has as companions.

No one can truly say of another:  
“This man is mine, my other self; we two are one mind.”

Let anyone despair that hereafter there will anywhere be one  
who is yours, while you are no one’s; one who belongs to himself, no one’s to you.

After hoary Faith, abhorring what once flourished everywhere,  
abandoned the world along with piety and innocence,

she had scarcely left impressions of her footsteps in one person—  
if there was one at all; but I think there was none.

Embracing faith and giving himself alike to all, one belonging to none, he is not his own [read: “he does not allow himself to be his own”].

Like a rare bird [sc. Icarus], worthy to be watched  
[Col. 1403A] as, they say, he balanced his wings in the air, he perished by shipwreck.

Whom do you now hear, in any region of the world,  
bringing forth a new equal of sweet friendship?

Who is now a brother to his brother, as Pylades was to Orestes?  
Who is a Theseus to anyone, as, Pirithous, he was to you?

Telamon desired nothing except what Meleager shared with him;  
such was your mind, Patroclus, and that of Achilles.

For if the underworld restored to the world those whom it had sent out,  
each of the two would be discordant, or have no one of his own.

If Polyneices returned to life, no one would be another Tydeus [read: Theseus] to send to Thebes on his behalf.

Now, now the friends of this age die while alive;  
the dead Scipio still lived for Laelius.

With heaven as witness, Pollux shares life with his brother;  
[Col. 1403B] but many brothers now do to their brothers what yours did to you, Remus.

The shade of Phaethon had succeeded in the river to his sisters;  
now many women empty their household through the death of brothers.

Alcestis had applauded the prospect of earning the Fates for her husband;  
behold, many women are a Clytemnestra to their husband.

Indeed, one born without himself goes upon the sea with his one son; now many a mother … to her sons. [The surviving text is defective; no name is supplied.]

He who, fearing only for that burden, carried his father on his neck  
through a thousand dangers,

rescued him from death; under like praise Lausus  
went forward rejoicing beneath the lightning sword for his father.

These rejoice that they deserved to die while their father survived;  
now a long old age of fathers torments some.

I call parents themselves a sacred natural pair,  
[Col. 1403C] because they have become material for their children’s crime.

Pharnaces and Orestes are certain witnesses against themselves:  
the latter deadly to his unhappy mother, the former to his father.

Domestic fraud, forged in the human breast, surpassing  
nature itself, rises into every wickedness.

This fraud places fire beneath ashes and aconite in honey,  
with it come idle luxury and swelling pride.

Madness that exceeds the bounds of hatred, thorny hostility—  
alas, they have subjected the divine human being to themselves!

Whose mind now, tell me, does not delight in being criminal?  
What man does not turn over every wickedness in his heart?

Night has not so many stars, the sea’s wave so many storms,  
the harvest so many grains, as crimes have kinds.

Every crime in this age serves avarice;  
[Col. 1403D] frenzied gain now infests [read: *infestat*] the world.

Confounding right and wrong, it mixes sacred things  
with profane, caring not whence it takes, but only how it may seize.

More inactive than lightning’s fire, rushing through weapons and flames,  
dread Celaeno seizes everything that meets her.

Thirst burns more fiercely in one who acquires more and desires more,  
as dropsy burns more intensely when its waters are drained.

For that man thirst is kindled by drinking; for this man by possessing:  
by being cured, each one’s disease grows.

Water does not boil white in a whirlpool so pitch-black  
as your breast, miser, smokes with the fire of gain.

The burning *dipsas* [sic] scorches those whom it harms with its bite, [Col. 1404A] afflicting them with so great a thirst that they are parched.

By this heat every moisture drunk becomes less;  
nor does it become a remedy for such burning thirst.

But this kind of pest, this new heat in the thirsty person,  
kills the dried body by swift death.

And the end of this illness comes when the body is dead:  
what harmed while living harms nothing when lifeless.

But desire, pleasant to mind and provident flesh,  
fondly nourishes those whom it scorches while alive.

When the flesh has returned itself to earth,  
behold, desire becomes fuel for the Stygian pyre.

After the end, there will at last be flames there without end [read: “a demon”]; and this one [read: “he”] is not sufficient for the soul.

Let desire burn in desire, when desire is thus food for Styx;  
[Col. 1404B] I shall say that no thirst is drier than fire like this.

O monster of gaping jaws, never able to be satisfied,  
always devouring while agape, always agape in order to add more!

Let all the gold the world possesses flow into this abyss:  
the maw of such a Harpy will thirst.

Let Pactolus and Hermus flood it, drinkers of gold;  
Tantalus burns in the midst of waters.

Burning Vesuvius extinguished flames, so they say;  
the fire of avarice does not know how to be extinguished.

A naked face that touches gold will lack it; it lacks no less what it has than what it wishes to have.

But you whom abundance bathes with such a full horn, ask that a worn tunic cover you naked.

Though you begged such a man with a just prayer that rocks might soften, you would sooner snatch a mouthful from a wolf with a dry face.

[Col. 1404C] Thus virtue departed, Astraea left the earth,  
piety turned its back, giving place to crime.

Law, justice, royal majesty, curule office, tribunal—  
they have yielded to money; money alone will be everything.

Money is the public hope; now it will be more powerful than a king:  
when present it raises up; when fleeing it casts down.

Money is nobility; money is wisdom, which now  
surpasses all under a disguise; there the poor man lies.

If you wish to flourish, surround your side with money;  
it will exalt you, bringing whatever you desire.

Money, growing from every crime, bears the scepter;  
it alone possesses all rewards of virtue.

If any good hope of advancement apart from money animates you,  
[Col. 1404D] you feed on a vain hope, and rage more than Orestes.

If the path of virtue promises you the summit of honor,  
you rely upon a reed, a staff that bends.

If, supported by Pegasus and conquering a hundred Chimaeras,  
you reduced them to ash, you would still now be poor.

The twelve labors that formerly made you famous  
would now, though you had endured a thousand, cover you in poverty.

Every poor person is without glory, though virtue herself  
should more worthily lift him in her present hands.

Fish belongs to water, honey to the bee, grapes to vines,  
cheese to milk; glory, Money, belongs to you.

A shadow attains splendor from the sun’s brightness, and splendor from money’s brightness;  
without money, the shadow perishes.

[Col. 1405A] Money alone is now considered virtue’s foster-child;  
it alone is loved; it alone is still worshipped.

Your court, Money, is crowded with a numerous senate;  
how ashamed one would be, gracious one, not to bend the knee to you!

Though the altar of Money’s temple has not yet been raised,  
it is nevertheless worshipped with divine religion.

Though people do not swear by money, who now shrinks  
from becoming sacrilegious for money’s sake?

Once it belonged to philosophers to despise monetary gain;  
now Plato, unless moneyed, would be a fool.

When love of philosophy compelled Theban Crates,  
stripped of the enticements of the body,

to desire to enter learned Athens in order to be taught,  
having first duly made himself a philosopher by the deed itself,

the prudent man carried with him in a ship gold  
[Col. 1405B] which [read: “by which”] he had sold whatever he possessed on that occasion.

When, with a favorable wind, the ship was already being carried on the deep,  
he threw the gold he had brought into the waves:

“Go,” he said, “cruel desire, seek the lowest deep,  
lest you sink me badly; I sink you well beforehand.”

When Diogenes, lying in bed and resting his limbs,  
had bags of coins placed beneath his head

and heard a thief digging in the hope of money,  
he immediately threw out the purses he possessed to him:

“Take,” he said, “the coins you seek, with your mind satisfied, so that you may free me from the care that troubles me;

that certainly we both may be able to rest—  
you having what you seek, I no longer fearing it.”

[Col. 1405C] When Greek Aristippus, in Libya, compelled slaves burdened with a heavy load of gold  
to proceed more slowly along the road,

he, indignant at the gold, ordered them relieved of the burden  
and bade them cast such evil away in the middle of the road.

By trampling gold, these men proved themselves philosophers;  
now he whose purse is empty is without judgment.

Now to contemplate money is to philosophize;  
no one without wealth is now held in esteem.

Pythagoras the wise, who was to give you, Music, your form  
from the strokes of craftsmen’s hammers,

would now be cheaper than a discarded little hammer  
if there were nothing in his purse; Mathematics is now a joke.

What is now the art of the abacus, a portion most contemptible to the heel?  
Now ravenous usury itself calculates for itself.

Behold, the creditor reports more readily than any abacist  
[Col. 1405D] what profit returns daily to the principal.

By proving falsehood to himself with an easy sophism,  
Money would now render Aristotle speechless.

Money taught you, most eloquent Tully, as you plead causes,  
to urge the cases entrusted to you, because you are money’s mouth.

Money, in any fool you now flow with abundant wit;  
only the poor man’s intelligence raves.

May the money that gilds a lawyer’s tongue perish;  
the mouth of the poor will flow with a more meager vein.

Though she bore the Gorgon in her breast, Minerva, born from Jupiter’s head,  
would be foolish without money.

Whoever pleads will win if money makes his cause honorable;  
[Col. 1406A] whoever relies only on justice will plead as a fool.

Let the laws stand with you; let honor plead for you:  
if you wish to win, draw justice from your purses.

Let the case condemn the accused, let the judge’s wrath outlaw him,  
let his neck throb under a fastened noose:

make Money the mediator, and it will swiftly undo the high matter [read: “the proceedings”], at once snatching the accused from the very jaws of death.

The praetor himself will acknowledge that he dictated falsehood,  
nor will he then be ashamed when the accused is absolved.

### LI. On the Birth of the Blessed Virgin

(From the manuscript of the Church of St Gatianus at Tours, the Évreux manuscript, and many others.)

The sun, crystal, and water give whatever figure they may  
[Col. 1406B] to the virginal birth, and establish faith.

If crystal is dipped in water and set beneath the sun,  
that unbroken stone gives forth sparks.

If you carefully observe everything, water, sun, crystal, and fire  
are the Spirit, Word, Virgin, and God the child.

The Spirit corresponds to water, the Word to the sun, the maiden to the gem,  
and the offspring in some respect to fire.

The Spirit is water because he washed her; the supreme Word  
is sun because he does not violate her, yet enters her.

The Virgin is stone because a Virgin gives birth; the only Child is fire,  
for he flashes with power and fills hearts with light.

Thus, by the Spirit’s overshadowing and the Word’s celibate entry,  
the Virgin becomes a mother, and the offspring is at once flesh and God.

[Col. 1406C] They make a new plaster, through which life returns to the buried,  
and through power and mind the order of character returns.

[Note: In the Elnone, or Royal 274, manuscript, the following four verses occur, which are absent from most copies:

“This opens tombs, this restores the sacred ranks,  
this makes good the fall of earth, hell, and heaven.

By this they will leap to heaven, whose bones and marrow …; this will restore the soul to the flesh and God to both.”]

### LII. Why God Became Man

What fitting victim could remove Adam’s sin?  
Could it be a human being? But he too is guilty—how could he make satisfaction?

An angel? Or crops? Or a cow? But such a victim,  
different in nature and lesser in value, would be ineffective.

The same nature that had displeased had to make satisfaction,  
and it had to possess something by which it might make peace.

[Col. 1406D] Therefore a human being had to be sought who, beyond that  
which belongs to a pure human being, possessed something by which he might please.

God is united to flesh, and the redeeming nature  
is equal to humanity because truly human, yet nobler in origin,

unlike humanity in guilt, and likewise more powerful by divinity.  
Because pleasure, born from the Fall, did not generate him,

he acts justly for the fallen and, slain, pleads for them.  
A sufficient sacrifice, by which heaven was filled with a citizen,

by which offended wrath fell and grace increased;  
a blessed antidote by which our wounds are healed.

The angel rejoices, the human being is glad, Tartarus mourns.

### LIII. On the Three Parts of Christ’s Body

Three parts signify Christ’s body: the first,  
[Col. 1407A] his own flesh; the second, the saints who have been buried;

or, the first signifies the dead who have been purified; the second,  
those still being purified; the third, the living. Blood

is the portion of martyrdom. Steeped in blood in the third portion, the faithful taste in their flesh the cup of martyrdom.

### LIV. To Bishop G.

[Note: Perhaps Gualo, then bishop of Paris.]

When Nature created you for the glory of the Church,  
she said: “Be free from vice; possess everything else.”

Created slow toward what is forbidden and swift toward what is permitted,  
you allow nothing but virtue to belong to you.

### LV. On the Virgin Mary

I nurse the Creator; believe my chastity safe for me.  
A new thing: a Virgin is a mother, and flesh lacks a father.

### LVI. Upon the Cross

The Cross: the end of the Law, the way of life, the King’s suffering,  
[Col. 1407B] to which grace, not merit, gave death.

### LVII. To the Bishop of Bayeux

[Note: Perhaps Odo, brother of William the Conqueror, duke of Normandy and king of England. Hildebert composed this epigram before he himself became bishop: for this Odo is said in *Gallia Christiana* to have died in 1096, whereas Hildebert was consecrated bishop only in 1097.]

This ring lately mourned, shut away in its casket;  
the stone too was dim, and, as it were, sorrowful.

But after I said, “You shall go to Bayeux, and shall bind  
the finger of a greater bishop with your circle,”

more gladly the jewel displayed its rays  
and scattered bright flashes, rejoicing in your eyes.

From you it gains this recompense for its lord;  
the bishop adds more to the stone than the stone adds to itself.

### LVIII. The Source of Evil

(From a manuscript also of Colbert, no. 6327, Ebr. 19, and others.)

Why do you ask whence evil comes, when all things were created good?  
The evils that are evil arise from their own defect.

Although the root lacks fault, yet through itself and of itself  
fault more readily draws forth sweet fruits.

[Col. 1407C]

### LIX. To a Nephew

A pattern of life is at hand for you. Speak little;  
let moderation, usefulness, and rectitude be your constant companions in both respects.

Rise sober from the table, chaste from the bed.  
Persist in services, so that they may ask rewards on your behalf.

As is fitting and profitable, so love and hate alike.  
Standing, fear a fall; cast down, hope; and protect him

whom you honor when eminent, miserable, and cast low.

### LX. To Odo

[Note: It is probable that this Odo was none other than Odo, or Otto, who, from being a disciple of St Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and his monk, then prior of Cluny, was raised to the supreme pontificate and called Urban II. While he was Hildebert’s fellow pupil under St Hugh, Hildebert was on familiar terms with him; and in these verses, as to a fellow brother and companion, he familiarly disclosed what he thought about the corruptions of the world, especially the common contempt for humane letters. See the Cluniac Chronicle under St Hugh, *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 1641, col. 1.]

Though you surpass others in character, learning, faith, and a heart fit for heaven,  
yet, Odo, you are foolish.

For you believe that the people love eloquent verse,  
and think that you please them by character, learning, and faith.

[Col. 1407D] Once sacred poets pleased by such pursuits,  
and talent gave them estates, renown, and wealth.

Now the age is different, and manners differ with the age;  
now virtue is hated, wealth earns sceptres.

Learning counts for nothing, pure faith for nothing, eloquence for nothing,  
[Col. 1408A] the wellspring of talent for nothing, integrity without wealth for nothing.

No poor man is wise; where wealth is, there is abundance of sense.  
Riches are wise; a poor man will be nothing but poor.

Nor now do the rich conceal their crimes under a name;  
rather, what the law condemns, the favor of wealth absolves.

Hence the people, worshipping gold as a divinity,  
dare of their own accord to enter unknown wickedness,

and, in hope of gain, repeatedly endure to exceed law and honor,  
and now count the practice of law a thing to be had for nothing.

1334 Law collapses, order perishes; it pleases men to sell their lips and hands to crime,  
and the poorer a man is, the more ashamed he is to be upright.

It is therefore no wonder if some perverse and senseless man  
thinks the divine poets of no account.

True wisdom abandons the man whom riches accompany,  
[Col. 1408B] ever unattended by unstable goods.

### LXI. On the Fall of the World

You do not judge well, you who prefer low things to heavenly ones,  
nor is it enough with you that you subject what is just to things.

For what is silver? What is beauty? What a retinue of clients?  
What famous estates? The glory of the world is a brief festival.

There is no faithfulness in it: today evil, tomorrow worse there.  
It is expedient to use this, but not to prefer it to salvation.

### LXII. To Queen M.

[Note: Namely, Matilda, daughter of Henry, king of England.]

(From several manuscripts.)

Matilda, born more august than august forefathers,  
you summon eloquent mouths to every kind of praise.

But in vain, since no one can render you the praises  
[Col. 1408C] that lineage, character, and fair beauty demand.

One tongue alone can speak of you: you who alone provide  
to every tongue the material of abundant praise.

In your countenance there is a queenly presence; your unstudied gait  
breathes of the Sabine woman, and your beauty is not artifice.

Neither sacred character through learning nor maidenly modesty  
passes you by; both blessings flowed from your ancestors.

You possess all that belonged to your mother, who, enclosed in the tomb,  
illuminates the English realms by her merits.

And lest the glory of the female sex should fall at once,  
she gave birth to you, renewed wholly in your birth.

Placed alongside God, she sees how all that remains is nothing, as though she were destitute while her daughter holds kingdoms.

I think that, secure concerning you, she thus petitions you  
and solicits her own Creator:

[Col. 1408D] “Great God, I have not yet been received wholly into the heavenly seat;  
I enjoy a half-blessed rest.

One part lies in the tomb; one rules the English kingdoms;  
court, tombs, and heaven hold me divided.

Help her whom the court holds; restore her whom the tomb encloses;  
[Col. 1409A] hear her whom heaven holds, and be a crown to all three.”

### LXIII. On Rome

(From several manuscripts.)

Rome, nothing is equal to you, though you are almost wholly ruin.  
Broken, you show how great you were when whole.

Long time has destroyed your splendors; the citadels  
of Caesar and the temples of the gods lie in marshland.

That labor, that labor has fallen, by which the dreadful Araxes  
both trembled while Rome stood and grieves that she has fallen;

she whom kings’ swords, the senate’s provident laws,  
and the gods established as head of the world;

whom Caesar desired more to possess alone through crime  
than jointly, and to be a dutiful father-in-law.

[Note: The following two verses are inserted here in Homeyer.]

He who, growing through three pursuits—enemies, crime, and friends—  
[Col. 1409B] subdued the first by force, cut down the second by laws, and purchased the third by wealth.

While earlier generations took care to make Rome thus,  
devotion aided the work, and a guest’s water aided the site.

Leaders expended treasures, the fates their favor,  
craftsmen their zeal, and the whole world its wealth.

Alas! the city has fallen. While I behold its ruins,  
I weigh its former state and am accustomed to say, “Rome was.”

Yet neither the succession of years, nor fire, nor sword  
could wholly abolish this splendor.

So much still remains, so much has fallen, that neither the standing part  
[Note: [Col. 1409D] Another reading: “excellent”; but “standing part” is better.]

can be equaled, nor the ruined part rebuilt.

Bring together wealth, ivory, marble, and the favor of the gods;  
let craftsmen’s hands be vigilant over new works.

Yet no structure can be made equal to a standing wall,  
[Note: [Col. 1410D] Another reading: “so great”; but “standing” is better.]

[Col. 1409C] nor can ruin alone be restored.

Human care was able to construct Rome so great  
as divine care was unable to destroy.

Here the gods themselves marvel at the forms of the gods,  
and desire to be equal to the fashioned faces.

Nature could not create gods with that countenance  
with which man created the wondrous images of gods.

These divinities have faces, and are worshipped more  
for the craftsmen’s skill than for their own divinity.

Happy city, if that city lacks even rulers,  
or if it would be shameful for rulers to lack faith.

### LXIV. The Same Author Again, on Rome

While images and vain divinities pleased me,  
I was lofty in soldiery, people, and walls.

But once I overthrew images and superstitious altars  
[Col. 1409D] and served the one God,

citadels yielded, palaces of the gods fell,  
the people became enslaved, the knighthood degenerated.

I scarcely know what I was; I scarcely remember Rome’s Rome;  
my downfall scarcely permits me even to remember myself.

This loss is more welcome to me than those successes.  
Fallen, I am greater poor than I was rich while standing.

The standards of the Cross gave more than eagles, Peter more than Caesar,  
an unarmed common people more than mailed leaders.

Standing, I subdued lands; ruined, I drive out hell.  
Standing, I rule bodies; broken and fallen, I rule souls.

[Col. 1410A] Then I commanded a wretched people; now the princes of darkness.  
Then cities were my kingdom; now heaven is my kingdom.

Lest I seem to owe this to Caesars or to arms,  
and lest the appearance of things draw me and mine away,

that force of arms perishes; the high glory of the senate falls;  
temples collapse, theaters lie low.

The rostra are empty, edicts silent; rewards are lacking  
for veterans, laws for the people, fields for the farmer.

The harsh knight, the rigid judge, and the people once free  
seek, love, and endure leisure, gain, and the yoke.

These things lie fallen, lest perhaps my citizen place his hope in them  
and make void both the hope and the benefit of the Cross.

The Cross promised other dwellings and other honors,  
granting heavenly kingdoms to its soldiers.

Under the Cross the king serves, though bound by the law he is free;  
[Col. 1410B] and, though he wears a diadem, he trembles at commands and loves.

The avaricious man pours out wealth, yet abounds; he lends at interest,  
yet keeps well; and, placing himself above the stars—

what Caesar by the sword, what consul by anxious care,  
what rhetorician by speech, what commander by force

gave me such things? By their studies and laws  
I obtained lands; the Cross alone gave heaven.

### LXV. On Jacob’s Variegated Rods

That a greater offspring may multiply its rewards,  
behold prudent Jacob arranges rods before the flocks.

Some he strips by removing their bark; some  
1336 he leaves clothed in their garment of bark.

That you may reap greater joys in Christ, shepherd, instruct the sheep  
by the straight words of Scripture.

[Col. 1410C] The brightness of mystery is not to be sought in those words;  
the veils do not delight in their outer bark alone.

The inward brightness is mystical instruction;  
the bark can be called the letter alone, the outer layer.

### LXVI. On Original Sin

Almost the whole world is subject to the diseases of so many sins [printed *siderum*; read *scelerum*],  
so that not even the smallest child is free from contagion.

These evils are owed to the serpent and to him who rules it,  
who urged the eating of what the Lord forbade.

From that time the dreadful dragon strives to pour out poison,  
removing what is good and fostering what is wicked.

### LXVII. Names of the Seven Sages

(From Gemmetic.)

Pittacus of Mytilene, Solon of Athens, Plimon the Spartan,  
[Col. 1410D] Cleobulus of Lindus [printed “Clodolus Laccius”], Thales of Miletus, Periander of Corinth, Bias of Priene.

### LXVIII. Their Maxims

[Note: [Col. 1410D] The capital letters appended to these verses are absent in manuscript 77.]

What is the highest good? A mind conscious of its own rectitude. P.  
What is the greatest ruin for a human being? Another human being alone. S.  
Who is rich? He who desires nothing. Who is poor? The greedy man. P.  
What is the fairest dowry for married women? A modest life. C.  
Who is chaste? She of whom even rumor fears to lie. T.  
What is the work of the prudent person? When able, to refuse to harm. P.  
What is characteristic of the fool? To be unable, yet to wish, to harm. B.

### LXIX. In How Many Ways We Are Tempted by the Vice of Gluttony

(From the Gemmetic manuscripts.)

[Col. 1411A]

It is known that gluttony condemns the eater in five ways:

when one eats too much, or anticipates the hour of eating;  
when one desires and takes food with excessive eagerness;  
when one seeks delicacies, or prepares with excessive refinement  
even that which is not itself delicate.

That these things may be distinguished more clearly, examples follow.

Bread in abundance was the cause of sinful Sodom.  
The people fast; Jonathan breaks the fast.  
Hungry Esau desires food and sells his honor.  
A great quantity is given: the fastidious people demand meat.  
From the sacred offering the boy Hophni asks for a raw portion;  
thus he carefully prepares it according to his own desire.

[Note: [Col. 1411D] The Beaugendre edition adds the verse, “What the gifts of the Magi signify”; these are already given at col. 1275 of the same edition.]

### LXX. Disputation between the Roman Pontiff and Ulger, Bishop of Angers

(From the manuscript of St Gatianus at Tours and others.)

[Col. 1411B]

**ANG.**

He who lacks reason knows neither how to be ruled by love,  
nor by justice, nor by law, nor does he obey the Lord.

Our Nero was full of these diseases; he was the terror of the world.  
But by God’s grant an ant becomes a lion.

**ROM.**

This I, Rome, can do; but I see that a trophy is lacking:  
[Col. 1412A] for I do not wish my guilty man to remain with me.

Therefore I wish him to yield, or by delay declare what he wants;  
I do not want him to repent, but to depart far hence.

**BISHOP.**

If you judged well, if you did not lack reason,  
the cause I maintain would not be at fault.

Delay is a great honor; I try to resist you, Rome.  
I do not yet repent, nor do I yet fear you.

The pope will end our delay only at the hour of death;  
the obsequies of a bishop will restore me to my homeland.

**ROM.**

Another will be appointed while he lives, and will follow him;  
but you will accomplish nothing and gain nothing.

**BISHOP.**

Although he trusts in the present and enjoys life,  
[Col. 1412B] when it fails, he will accomplish nothing through him.

**COUNCIL.**

Shall I proscribe him? He is guilty; it is lawful to proscribe such a man,  
but it is no virtue to drive out one who is old.

**JUDGE.**

Let him be deprived of the mitre; this seems both lawful and honorable:  
thus in his deeds to condemn a young man by an old man.

### LXXI. A Most Devout Prayer to the Three Persons of the Most Holy Trinity

(From the same Ebr. manuscript. Published by Ussher, *On Creeds*, and in the Supplement of R. P. Homeyer and in several manuscripts.)

[Col. 1411B]

#### To the Father

Alpha and Omega, great God,  
[Note: [Col. 1411D] Reg. 4103 and Victor.: “my God.”]

Eli, Eli, my God,

whose power is to be able to do all things,  
whose understanding is to know all things,  
whose being is the highest good,  
whose work is whatever is good.

Above all things, beneath all things;  
outside all things, within all things.

Within all things, yet not enclosed;  
outside all things, yet not excluded;  
above all things, yet not raised up;  
beneath all things, yet not supported underneath.

Wholly above, by presiding;  
wholly beneath, by sustaining;  
wholly outside, by embracing;  
you are wholly within, by filling.

Within, you are never confined;  
outside, you are never extended;  
above, you are supported by none;  
beneath, you are wearied by none.

Moving the world, you are not moved;  
holding place, you are not held;  
changing time, you are not changed;  
making unstable things firm, you do not wander.

External force  
[Note: [Col. 1411D] Homeyer: “alternating force.”]

or necessity does not alter your being.

Our yesterday, tomorrow, and long ago  
are always to you a present and the same.

Your today, O God,  
is undivided and everlasting.

1338 In this you foresaw all things;  
in this you appointed all things at once,  
according to the pattern of the supreme mind,

[Col. 1411B] giving form to the elements.

#### Prayer to the Son

Son, equal with the Father,  
consubstantial with the Father,  
splendor and image of the Father,  
maker made a creature,

you put on our flesh,  
you took up our cause:

eternal, temporal;  
destined to die, immortal;  
true man, true God;  
God and man without mixture.

You were not changed here into flesh,  
nor diminished  
[Note: [Col. 1412D] Reg. 4103 and Vict. 72: “taken up.”]

because of flesh;

here humanity was assumed into God,  
not consumed because of God.

Equal to the Father in divinity,  
lesser by the reality of flesh.

God the Father is only the Father of God;  
but the Virgin Mother is also Mother of God.

[Note: [Col. 1412D] The same manuscripts: “The Virgin Mother is also indeed Mother of God.”]

In so new a union  
both natures so remain

that each preserves whatever it was,  
having become something which it was not.

This one is our mediator;  
this one is our giver of the law.

[Note: [Col. 1412D] Homeyer: “legislator.”]

Circumcised, baptized,  
crucified, buried,

he slept and descended,  
rose again and ascended.

Thus raised into heaven,  
he will judge, having been judged.

#### Prayer to the Holy Spirit

Paraclete, uncreated,  
neither made nor born,  
sharer with the Father and the Begotten,

you proceed from both  
so as not to be less in power  
or distinct in quality.

[Col. 1412B] As great as those two, so great is this one;  
such as those two are, such is this one.

The Father is distinct by begetting;  
the Son distinct by being born;  
the Spirit by proceeding from them:

three are one in subsisting.

Each of the three is fully God,  
yet not three gods, but God.

In this God, the true God,  
I affirm both three and one,

assigning unity to the essence  
and Trinity to the persons.

Among the persons none is prior,  
none lesser, none greater.

Each is always itself,  
so constant and fixed

that it is neither varied in itself  
nor changed into any other.

This is orthodox faith;  
here error is not harmless.

As I speak, so I also believe;  
1339 nor do I yield to a perverse side.

From this comes, good God,  
that I do not despair though guilty:

guilty of death, I do not despair,  
but in death I seek life.

To appease you I offer nothing  
but the faith which I defend.

[Note: [Col. 1412D] Reg. and Vict.: “display.”]

You see the faith; this I implore:  
lift the burden under which I labor.

Through this sacred poultice  
let the sickly creature recover,

now carried outside the gate,  
now foul-smelling, buried.

A bandage binds it, a stone weighs upon it;  
but if you command, it will rise.

Command: the stone will be rolled away.  
Command: life will burst forth.

He who is to come forth knows no delay  
once you cry, “Come forth!”

[Col. 1413] On this sea my little vessel  
is attacked by pirates;

from one side assault, from the other waves;  
from both sides death and grief.

But come, good sailor:  
restrain the winds, calm the sea.

Make these pirates depart;  
bring the vessel safely to port.

My barren fig tree,  
whose branch is a dry branch,

will be cut down and burned  
if you pronounce what it deserves;

but let it be spared this year;  
let it be manured and dug about.

And if it still gives no answer,  
I say this weeping: then it will burn.

The ancient enemy rages in me;  
he drowns me in waters and burns me in flames.

Thus sick and afflicted,  
I am left to you alone,

that the sick man  
[Note: [Col. 1413D] Thus Reg. and Vict., not “the infernal one,” as Ebr.]

may recover,  
that this enemy may vanish.

Grant the sick man the strength  
to fast; grant him the strength to pray.

Through these two, Christ being witness,  
I shall be freed from this plague.

Free my mind from this plague;  
make it devout and repentant.

Give fear, so that, once it is cast away,  
I may make no conjecture concerning salvation.

Give faith, hope, and charity;  
[Col. 1413] give discerning piety.

Give contempt for earthly things,  
desire for heavenly things.

God, I hope wholly in you;  
God, from you I seek everything.

You are my praise, my good;  
all that is mine is your gift.

You are consolation in labor,  
medicine in sickness;

in grief you are my lyre;  
in anger you are relief.

In constraint, you are liberator;  
in falling, revealer.

You grant motion  
[Note: [Col. 1413D] Reg. and Vict.: “fear.” Ebr.: “motion,” which is better.]

in advancement;  
you preserve hope in failure.

If anyone harms me, you repay;  
if anyone threatens, you defend.

What is doubtful, you resolve;  
1340 what should be concealed, you cover.

Do not allow me to enter  
the infernal workshops,

where are sorrow and fear,  
where are stench and weeping,

where shameful deeds are disclosed,  
where the guilty are confounded,

where the torturer continually strikes,  
where the worm continually devours;

where all this is everlasting,  
because the death of Gehenna is perpetual.

May that Zion receive me—  
Zion, David’s peaceful city,

[Col. 1414] whose builder is the Author of light,  
whose gates are the wood of the Cross,

whose keys are Peter’s tongue,  
whose citizens are always joyful,

whose walls are living stone,  
whose guardian is the festal King.

In this city is solemn light,  
eternal spring, perpetual peace.

In this is fragrance filling heaven;  
[Note: [Col. 1414D] Reg. and Vict.: “order.” Ebr.: “fragrance,” better.]

in this is ever festive melody.

There is no corruption there,  
no failing, no complaint;

none maimed, none deformed;  
all are conformed to Christ.

Heavenly city, blessed city,  
set upon the rock;

city in a sufficiently safe harbor,  
I greet you from afar.

I greet you, I sigh for you,  
I long for you, I seek you.

How greatly those within rejoice in you,  
how festively they feast;

what affection binds them,  
or what gem adorns the walls—

what chalcedony, what hyacinth—  
those who are within know.

In the streets of this city,  
joined to the pious throngs,

with Moses and Elijah  
may I sing a devout Alleluia.

Amen.

### LXXII. In Praise of the Holy Spirit

(From the manuscript of Évreux, no. 19; first published here.)

[Col. 1413A]

#### Prose

Holy Spirit, gracious Paraclete,

love of Father and Son, bond of begetter and begotten;

goodness and charity of both, and purity of the essence of both,

kindness, sweetness, delight.

A bond joining God to man; a power uniting man to the divine—

not that he himself might become the seed of offspring,

but that the Author might create flesh from the flesh of the Virgin—

God, forming all things before day,  
Lord, governing created things by day—

a gift abiding in the Giver’s eternity,

[Col. 1413B] having nothing less than his equality.

Your procession precedes time;  
your outpouring was made in time.

There is the fountain of powers, the river of graces;  
here, their giver and the light of souls.

Going forth from that glorious, luminous day,  
making this day among us renowned and joyful.

To you alone, worthy to be worshipped with the Father and the Son,  
may continual worship and abundant honor always be offered,  
you who proceed from both, in vow and voice, here and everywhere. Amen.

You are our salvation; you are our glory;  
life and reward, end and joy.

You are the power compelling guilt to acknowledge itself,  
the law readily prepared to forgive.

[Col. 1414A] Night and destruction flee before you;  
for you are the finger of the right hand of the Most High.

Subtle and teachable, sublime and humble;

gentle and cheerful, lovable and praiseworthy;

cleanser of vanity, lover of purity;

giver of holiness, rectitude, blessed fullness,  
and complete blessedness.

Sweet voice of sorrowing exiles; melody of rejoicing citizens.

To these, consolation lest they despair of you;  
to these, assistance that they may sigh for you.

Comforter of the devout, inspirer of the good, counsellor of the sorrowful,

purifier of errors, teacher of the unknown, expositor of perplexities.

[Col. 1414B] Raising the weak, gathering the wandering, correcting the erring,

you sustain the falling, advance the striving, perfect the loving;

you lead the perfected person forth; from the pit of dregs and misery

you lead him along the path of peace and joy;

you bring him beneath the cloud into the hall of wisdom.

Here free charity opens the entrance;  
here savage perversity closes the return.

Pardoning faults to those who turn back; reserving punishments for those who turn away.

But if, upon the scale of your equity,  
you weigh our mass of perversity,

then, to confess what I fear, I behold the penalties of death,

and perhaps, at your judgment,  
[Col. 1415A] the condition of life will give righteous consolation.

And behold, our righteousness before you is like a menstruous cloth.

Thus you wish us to serve in fear,  
not knowing who is worthy of wrath or of love;

one thing is certain: under your protection  
we who are wholly yours are safe from the storm.

**YOU ARE THE FINGER OF GOD’S RIGHT HAND,**

in whom are the splendor of all counsel and all hope of consolation,

relief from weariness, and the pledge of eternal joy.

Innocent, unquestionable—than whom nothing exists more beautiful,  
and nothing sweeter,

more honorable, more useful, or better.

Free, fearless, eager, most ready.

Foundation of holiness, nourishment of chastity.

[Col. 1415B] Ornament of gentleness, solace of poverty.

Supplement of generosity, defense of uprightness.

Refuge of the wretched, aid of captives:

most fitting for the former, most prompt for the latter.

Spirit of truth, bond of brotherhood,

sent by him by whom you were also promised.

You are believed to be judge of all, because you are believed to be maker of all,

honoring the well-deserving with reward,  
1342 burdening the undeserving with punishment.

While you are more generous toward those holy ones,  
you wish to be more sparing toward these guilty ones.

Everywhere your mercy overcomes you,

[Col. 1415C] for your nature is nothing but goodness.

You breathe where you will and when you will; you teach whom you will and how much you will.

You fill and instruct the certain in doubtful matters;  
you strengthen in sudden trials, rule in lawful things.

You are order beautifying all things; beauty ordering and adorning all things—

words, deeds, thoughts:

words by truth, deeds by honor, thoughts by purity.

You, the anointing that teaches concerning all things,

granted on earth, yet this divinely.

Illuminating with the charity of divinity  
those whom identity of charity has illuminated in you.

Good gift, perfect good,

giving understanding and also affection;

[Col. 1415D] directing what is right, shaping affection, strengthening progress,

and crowning the beloved at the gates of paradise.

Let our bishops fear this Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 1415D] This conclusion wholly savors of Hildebert’s genius, for with unwearied zeal he always attacked the simoniacs of his age who were disfiguring the Church. [Col. 1416D] That this Prose is a genuine work of his is proved by the word *sacrifex* (“priest-maker” or “sacrificer”), singular and characteristic of him.]

Let them be holy sacrificers for the guilty,  
not cruel executioners of the guilty;

diligent shepherds of the weak,  
not foul predators of the sheep.

Let them cast the sacred net for the capture of souls,  
not for money;

lest, while sinning remissibly  
[Col. 1416A] against the Son and the Father alike,

they sin indelibly against the Spirit.

### LXXIII. On the Nativity of the Lord

(From manuscripts and printed editions.)

#### Prose

Heavenly grace fulfills  
the joys promised to the world  
on this day.

In the Virgin, fruitfulness;  
in the offspring, divinity shone  
on this day.

Begotten in heaven without a mother,  
in this valley he was born without a father  
on this day.

The flowering rod of Jesse gave fruit;  
[Col. 1416B] dew moistened Gideon’s fleeces  
on this day.

Pressed beneath a woman’s foot,  
the crushed serpent was broken  
on this day.

Elisha went forth,  
and came by the fruit,

following the staff  
on this day.

The heart of the Most High uttered  
the good Word which it begot  
on this day.

Man ate  
the bread of angels  
[Col. 1416C] on this day.

The sower went out to sow the true seed;  
the Ancient of Days began to be new  
on this day.

The King went forth for spoil,  
1343 and set his tent in the sun  
on this day.

The earth brought forth a worm,  
through which Jonah lost  
and mourns his shelter  
on this day.

The lamp that the woman lit shone;  
the electrum which Ezekiel sees flashed  
on this day.

Truth from the earth, Emmanuel from Zion,  
[Col. 1416D] arose, sent for the salvation of Israel  
on this day.

The faith of the Virgin Mother,  
the overshadowing of the Spirit,

the power of the Word and of light  
prepared a poultice  
on this day.

By this the wretched breathe again,  
hell is despoiled,

the heavenly powers yield to us,  
the order of things is renewed  
[Col. 1417A] on this day.

So many benefits  
the holy Church began  
on this day.

Glory be to God,  
by whose grace  
we hope for heavenly things. Amen.

### LXXIV. Verses on Faith in the Holy Trinity

[Note: R. P. D. J. Mabillon printed this Prose at the end of vol. V of the *Works of St Bernard*. In a marginal note he says that, in the Speyer edition of 1501, it was attributed to Bernard, the mellifluous doctor. But since in the Paris edition of 1548 it is attributed to Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, under the title “On Faith in the Holy Trinity,” though we have seen it in no manuscript, we judged that it should be published, lest it perish, or placed among doubtful works, although it differs in some respects from Mabillon’s version.]

[Note: [Col. 1417] In the preface, p. XIII, Beaugendre writes: “We must note an error of wording which escaped us in the note on the *Verses on Faith in the Holy Trinity*, when we said that they should be placed among doubtful works. From this someone might perhaps infer that the other works which follow are doubtful works of Hildebert; this we did not at all intend, nor ought we to have intended, since nothing is more certain than that the book *On His Exile* is genuinely his work, as are the other poems, whether preceding or following, which we have recovered from the best manuscripts. Therefore, in place of the words ‘among doubtful works,’ one should read: ‘although doubtful, and it alone among the unquestionably Hildebertian poems which we publish.’”]

God is that which exists from itself, through which existence is given;  
what does not exist from itself does not possess divine being.

God is the being to whom true existence belongs.  
To him alone belongs that which belongs to no other: to be.

Before God there is nothing that can be earlier than him.  
After him there is nothing that can be later than him.

[Note: [Col. 1417] Mabillon’s version: “Before God there is nothing that can be later than him.”]

Above him there is nothing that I can call higher;

[Note: [Col. 1417] “Above him there is nothing that I can believe broader.”]

[Col. 1417B] Outside him there is nothing that I can call more extensive.

[Note: [Col. 1417] “Outside him,” etc.; this verse is absent there.]

Everything that is is his work; he gave being to all things;  
and without him nothing is, or was, or can be.

His majesty, disposing all things in itself,

[Note: [Col. 1417] “Through itself.”]

as it never began, so it never ceases to be.

Nothing that is, was, or will be can be equal to him.  
Apart from him alone, another god has no being.

[Note: [Col. 1417] “Can have being.”]

For truthful reason denies that to be a true god  
which stone and a human hand brought into being.

But almighty God is he to whom no human being gave existence—  
indeed, he who, making man, restored him to being.

[Note: [Col. 1417] “Brought him to being.”]

This one is truly God, and this one cannot fail to be God.  
God himself is believed to be God above all gods,

1344 wholly possessing all things, and by right willing to preside over all.  
[Col. 1417C] Creating all things, he wills all created things to be subject to himself.

God, wholly everywhere, does not alter his own being.

[Note: [Col. 1417] “Everywhere at once.”]

He who is believed to be now no different from what he was before  
changes all things, yet cannot himself be changeable.

Eternal God has eternal being.  
Though great, he cannot be greater or lesser.

In whom there always was being, in that same being he remains.

[Note: [Col. 1417] This verse is absent.]

It befits him to be what he is, but it does not befit him to be by necessity.

[Note: [Col. 1417] “It does not befit him to be anything else.”]

[Col. 1418A] Indeed, through him every good human being can even exist;  
no goodness alien to him makes him good.

From his own goodness he is known to be good.

[Note: [Col. 1417] Here are absent two verses found in Mabillon’s version:

> Therefore let the creature know the Creator to be God,  
> to whom wondrous being belongs in a wondrous way.

“Orthodox faith,” etc., occurs below.]

Orthodox faith proves that there are three persons  
in the Godhead, but denies that there are three gods in the three.

God the unbegotten Father begot the begotten from himself.

[Note: [Col. 1417] “The unbegotten God gives being to begotten generation.”]

Yet this Father did not exist before the Begotten.  
The gracious Spirit proceeding from them has equal being.

One substance, however, is believed to be in these three.  
Coeternal being belongs to the persons.

Thus equal majesty and equal power are said to reside in them.  
What the Father is, the Son is; this is also said of the Spirit.

For the one God contains one being.  
Yet he who is Father cannot also be Begotten.

[Col. 1418B] He who is begotten cannot be the Spirit.  
As in one we say that three persons exist,

so in three persons we believe one to exist.

Therefore let the creature know the Creator to be God,  
to whom wondrous being belongs in a wondrous way.

Though Sabellius babble that this is nothing,  
the orthodox believer holds and affirms that it is so.

[Note: [Col. 1417] “Thus the orthodox believer holds.”]

Unhappy Arius, because he did not believe it to be so,  
deserved to be subject without end to Tartarean flames.

[Note: [Col. 1417] “He deserved necessarily to be subject without end to Tartarean flames.”]

Thus lofty faith reasons concerning true being.  
Thus, I think, it is necessary that all believe.

And unless we believe and confess this  
firmly and rightly, we cannot be saved.

### LXXV. Hildebert’s Book on His Own Exile

[Note: [Col. 1417] The manuscript of St Marianus reads: “On Fortune.” Tours: “On the Fall of This World.”]

(Thus Trithemius. From the manuscripts of Évreux, no. 19; Saint-Victor, no. 272; and St Marianus of Auxerre, at least 500 years old; published in Homeyer’s Supplement.)

[Col. 1418C]

Recently I was wealthy and blessed with many friends,  
and favorable fates smiled upon me for a long time.

Generous Ceres, the Arcadian god, and Bacchus filled  
my granaries, roofs, pantry, with grain, sheep, and wine.

Garden, bees, maidservants enriched abundantly  
my meals with food, my vessels with honey, my house with tapestries.

[Col. 1419A] My right hand labored with gems, my orchards with fruit;  
the meadows overflowed with grass, the flocks with milk.

A heap of wealth,

[Note: [Col. 1419] Évreux and Saint-Victor: “field of wealth.” St Marianus: “heap of wealth,” that is, a collection, an accumulation; this is better.]

quiet repose, and many friends gave  
pleasures, sleep, and counsel.

Why recount the rest, things consoling sorrowful faces?

[Note: [Col. 1419] Tours:

> Why should I recount individual things attesting happy circumstances?  
> All belonged to captive prosperity.]

All belonged to prosperity held captive.

You would have sworn that the gods were contained within my wishes,  
and that my possessions had unlearned how to suffer decline.

I marveled that you, Fortune, were thus faithful to me;  
[Note: [Col. 1419] Tours: “Finally I marveled thus at you, Fortune.”]

I marveled that you were stable, who are accustomed to be fickle.

Often I said to myself: “What is the purpose of such prosperity?  
What does so great and so swift a heap of wealth mean?”

If I can place no trust in things, they have no constancy.  
Things themselves teach by their instability what they are.

[Col. 1419B] A light throw of the dice turns human affairs and human beings from hour to hour;

[Note: [Col. 1419] Tours: “shores.”]

and utter ruin comes from the highest position.

All mortal things hang beneath a twofold hazard,  
and by their own instability promise flight.

Whatever you have today may perhaps leave you tomorrow,  
or even now, while you speak, cease to be yours.

Fortune plays these turns, and does not allow proud kings  
or humble slaves to remain long as they are.

That deceitful companion, faithful only in fickleness,  
does not favor without penalty or crush without end.

Once she flattered me with a serene smile;  
then, made cloudy, she changed her countenance.

And as though intent upon my everlasting destruction,  
she takes even the hope of joy away from me.

[Col. 1419C] She, openly confessing deceit, submerged, overthrew, and burned  
my crops, homes, and vines by rain, fire, and frost.

Moreover she exhausted, shook [variant: scattered, *discussit*], and weakened  
granaries, fruit, and flock by enemy, *noto*, and diseases.

[Note: [Col. 1419] Saint-Victor: *notho*, that is, by the whirlwind of a violent wind.]
