To these losses there was added that new and grievous tyrant,  
under whose rule in Le Mans law perished.

[Note: [Col. 1419] That is, the ruler of the city, the mayor of the town.]

His ancestors were ashamed to have produced a patron of crimes,  
a man equal to Fortune in fickleness and deceits.

That disgrace of his homeland drove me from my homeland,  
because I did not defend the laws of justice with impunity.

Then I board a ship and entrust my life to storms;  
the [read: sails, *vela*] swell wet, the boat is aided by twofold power.

The harbor was far off when a stronger wind stirred the sea  
[Note: [Col. 1419] Homeyer printed “drove into”; both manuscripts read “stirred.”]

and the south wind ploughed the waters into mounds.

The storm increases, the blast drives the ship, the gaping wave rages;  
[Col. 1419D] the sail is drenched with rain, black night covers day.

Winds, sea, whirlpool, wave,  
rocks encountered, and the very sky with its fires command despair.

The whole world almost heaps its angers upon the fragile pine vessel,

[Note: [Col. 1419] Évreux: “almost heaps its angers.” Saint-Victor: “almost distributes its angers.”]

and everything that can harm is an enemy.

[Col. 1420A] While the storm rages thus, while even the captain grows pale,  
is stunned, and fears that he will become food for fishes,

behold, a rapacious whirlwind, raising waves to the stars,  
drove the now rudderless ship to shore.

Thus, wretched and fortunate,

[Note: [Col. 1419] Saint-Victor: “Thus, miserably fortunate.”]

with shattered ship and possessions taken away,  
I escaped winds, sea, rocks, and Jupiter.

Behold what belongs to a human being, what he may rightly call ancestral;  
over what endowment can that wretched man congratulate himself?

This is, this is the human condition: always to slip with time,

[Note: [Col. 1419] Tours: “It is human always to flow and to slip with time.”]

1346 and always to die by a certain condition.

It is human to be born naked and return naked  
to one’s mother, unable to take one’s possessions along.

It is man’s lot to rot in the earth and to acknowledge hunger [or: “the end” (*finemque*)],

and, by wretched stages, to be reduced to ashes.

[Col. 1420B] Man is heir to that prosperity, and no estates await him more certainly as their master.

Possessions and riches are bestowed upon him; they serve him only for an hour,

and rich in the morning, he will be poor in the evening.

No one can assign to things a right of permanence,

for they have not learned to follow human nods.

God assigns them their law and ordains that they be bound

by laws, and stand still or move at his own will.

He alone, at one and the same time, both foresaw and wrought

all things; nor did he see them otherwise than he works them.

As he saw them needing to be made, so he makes them; he rules without effort.

He distinguishes them by forms, time, end, and place.

He measures out to things their impulse to grow, and directs them

by hidden laws [Note: [Col. 1419] Tours: “He measures out their course by distinct decrees and directs them by laws.”], himself remaining unchanged.

Remaining unchanged while he moves all things, he provides for suffering mortals

[Col. 1420C] and teaches where hope ought to be placed [Note: [Col. 1419] Tours: “He provides, and teaches where it is.”].

If it is permitted to believe that you can either do or be anything,

O Fortune, what are you? What power you have, he himself gave.

With your leave, Fortune, I shall speak: flatter or threaten;

yet you will do nothing for which I might complain, or rejoice unduly.

That mighty one—the mild order and harmony of things—

whatever he shall dispose concerning me [Note: [Col. 1419] Tours: “bring forth”], I shall be his.

## LXXVI. Hildebert’s elegiac letter to a friend overseas, or English, as may be inferred from its words

In this letter he asks him not to despise or abandon him in his misfortune; perhaps when he was being so harassed by William Rufus or Henry I that he was compelled to seek Rome, namely on account of the towers of his church, which he always refused to demolish with steadfast resolve. This friend may perhaps have been Roger, or Roger, bishop of Salisbury, to whom Hildebert wrote the twelfth letter of Book II.

(From the Colbert manuscript, no. 3019, on the penultimate folio, in a wholly ancient hand and at least five hundred years old.)

[Col. 1420D]

Shameful indeed to say, but if only we confess the truth,

the crowd judges friendships by usefulness.

Concern for what is advantageous comes before concern for what is honorable,

[Col. 1421A] and faith stands and falls with fortune.

Among many thousands you will not easily find one

who thinks virtue its own reward.

The very beauty of right conduct, if rewards for deeds are lacking,

does not endure, and one regrets being upright for nothing.

It is kinder to place a finger beneath the chin of one who has fallen

than to immerse the face of a swimmer in clear water.

You rebuke, as you ought, the faults of your foolish friend,

and grieve that I suffer evils less than I deserve.

What you say is true, but your reproaches for my fault come too late;

1347 withdraw harsh words from one who has confessed to you.

When I could have passed the Ceraunian Mountains under a favorable sail,

I ought to have been warned to avoid those savage rocks.

Now, after shipwreck has occurred, what benefit is it for me to learn

by what route my little boat ought to have sailed?

Rather, arms should be extended to the exhausted swimmer,

nor should one be reluctant to place a hand beneath his chin.

It is shameful to turn back one’s step and not stand firm;

shameful to abandon a struggling ship;

shameful to follow fortune and believe oneself a friend,

and, unless a man is fortunate, deny that he is one’s own.

My letter wishes first to greet you [Note: [Col. 1421] Here a pentameter is missing, which may be supplied thus: “And it wishes you safety for many years.”],

then follows its desire to hear how you fare;

and now, whatever you do, let care for me be yours.

Nor do I doubt that it is; but fear itself, born of misfortunes,

often compels me to entertain needless anxieties.

Grant pardon, I pray, and forgive my excessive fear:

even calm waters terrify a shipwrecked man.

A fish once wounded by a deceitful hook

thinks hooks lie hidden beneath every bait.

[Col. 1421C] Often a lamb flees a dog seen at a distance, believing it a wolf,

and, unaware, avoids her own aid.

Limbs, unaccustomed to touch, fear even a gentle touch,

and an empty shadow stirs fear in the anxious.

Thus I, pierced by the weapons of hostile fortune,

conceive nothing but sorrow in my heart.

Now my pain has become a habit; and just as rocks are hollowed

by falling waters, and by repeated blows [or: “by a repeated blow” (*percussu*)],

so I am wounded by fortune’s unceasing stroke,

and scarcely is there now room in me for a new wound;

nor is a ploughshare worn thinner by continual use,

nor are hives more worn down by curved wheels,

than my heart has been touched by the succession of evils

[Col. 1421D] for which I have found nothing that could bring me help.

Many seek glory through liberal arts;

I myself have perished through my gifts, unhappy man that I am.

The presence of someone helps amid hard circumstances;

his absence overwhelms the head with a vast storm.

Whom would not even the anger of a silent Caesar overwhelm

[Note: [Col. 1421] Perhaps King William Rufus, or Henry I, or Louis the Fat. See Letter 45, Book II.],

when harsh words are added to my punishments?

A temperate climate aids both body and mind;

the land of the Sarmatians stiffens under perpetual cold.

There is a not unwelcome pleasure in fresh water;

[Col. 1422A] when mixed with sea-salt, the marsh is drunk.

Everything fails; yet the spirit conquers everything:

it even makes the body possess strength.

Hold fast, I beg you, to what you have begun; do not abandon the ship at sea,

and preserve both me and your own judgment.

Hear the voice of a suppliant, most gentle of young men,

and bring what help you can to an exile—for you can.

Fortune has handed me over to you; in this alone, because I do not complain of her,

she has not been hostile to me.

If Jupiter lends deaf ears to one who prays,

then a victim struck down will fall before Jupiter’s temple.

If he grants me no peace at all as I go,

why should I bring vain offerings to Neptune?

Yet although we are separated by the whole breadth of the world,

you may nevertheless know that I remember you.

[Col. 1422B] And I would sooner send this soul back into the empty air

than let gratitude for your merit prove vain.

I call it a great kindness: the tears with which you wet your face

when mine was dry, hardened by grief.

I call it a great kindness: that you gave consolation to my sorrowing mind,

1348 alike to me and to yourself.

Add that you faithfully carry out the charge entrusted to you concerning one absent,

and do not think any burden grievous to bear.

You ask what you should do. Seek this, certainly; you will find it,

if you truly wish to find it.

To will is too little: where you may regain possession, you must desire,

and let this care make your sleep brief.

Fortune exposed me to the people to be seen,

and gave me more notoriety than I had before.

If there is any place for the small among such great names,

[Col. 1422C] my ruin too makes me conspicuous.

Had he erred less, Ulysses would have been less known;

it does no harm to put the spur to a horse once mounted.

Thus it is fitting that by its own excellence our present age should not be surpassed

by ancient times in the praise of chastity.

From the very applause of the people and their joyful favor,

any talent might have grown warm.

And I took courage from such acclaim

as a raw soldier does when he hears the trumpet-call to arms.

Neither the names of commanders nor the names of places were known to me;

my hands had no material.

The more I delight in this, you ought to forgive me

if anything was mistaken or omitted by me there.

And as eyes fear the sun’s light after it has been inflicted on them,

[Col. 1422D] so my sluggish mind was unready for joy.

For although water brought to one is sweet to taste,

water is drunk more pleasantly from the spring itself.

And it is more pleasant to pluck an apple from a bent branch

than to take it from an engraved platter [Note: [Col. 1421] A word used elsewhere by Hildebert, as in Letter 1, Book I, to William of Champeaux.].

I can subtract nothing from the punishment I endure,

if I were compelled to be the judge of my own deed.

And while others slip away and leave the battered sails,

you alone remain the anchor of my torn vessel.

Your compassion, therefore, is welcome; we pardon those

[Col. 1423A] who turned their backs in flight along with fortune.

When lightning strikes one man, it does not terrify one alone;

the crowd joined to the stricken man is accustomed to be afraid.

And when a wall has given signs of impending collapse,

the very place becomes empty from anxious fear.

For who among the timid would avoid the contagion of a sick man,

fearing that some neighboring evil might be drawn thence?

You are the better part, though few, who in difficult circumstances

think that no help at all is to be brought to me.

Theseus too died, and he who accompanied [or: “accompanies,” *comitatur*] Orestes;

yet each lives on in his own praises.

Your late descendants too will often praise you,

and your glory will be bright in my writings.

Your lineage is suited to your spirit; for you possess a noble

[Col. 1423B] heart, and simplicity as its heir [Note: [Col. 1423D] The manuscript reads *h’edèe*.].

Envy, a sluggish vice, does not rise to elevated characters,

but crawls like a hidden viper upon the deep earth.

Your lofty mind rises above lineage itself;

you have no name greater than your talent.

Therefore let others harm the wretched and desire to be feared,

and bear darts dipped in biting gall.

But your house is accustomed to help suppliants:

I pray that you may wish me to be numbered among them.

Those who are strong stand firm by themselves and seek no Machaonian aid

[Note: [Col. 1423D] That is, they need no physician; for Machaon, son of Aesculapius, is reported to have been a famous physician.];

the uncertain sick man flees to medical help.

Writings please after cruel death because envy is wont

to harm the living and gnaw them with an unjust tooth.

When strength is lacking, the will is nevertheless praiseworthy;

[Col. 1423C] by this I prophesy that the gods are satisfied.

This is why even a poor man comes welcome to the altar,

and why a ewe pleases no less than a slaughtered ox.

We have sometimes seen those struck by a thunderbolt survive,

1349 and be restored, Jupiter not forbidding.

Believe me: the heavenly powers care for the wretched,

nor do they always and endlessly crush the injured.

Jupiter hurls rash thunderbolts against many

who have not deserved to suffer punishment for any fault.

But in punishing, our prince is no more restrained;

he tempers the powers of justice by his own [Note: [Col. 1423D] Several more verses follow in the same manuscript, but have no connection either with what precedes or with one another. We therefore judged them to be omitted, since they would benefit neither the convenience nor the enjoyment of any readers.].

## XXVII. On the unfaithfulness of Fortune and worldly love

(From the manuscript of Saint Marianus of Auxerre.)

Love is faithful to no one, Fortune faithful to no one;

[Col. 1423D] neither dispenses its honey to anyone without gall.

Fortune raises up her own and casts down those same persons;

and those whom she favors, she does not favor for long.

Love burns, flatters, delights, and burns;

and from the very source whence it pleases, it wounds more deeply.

Time, love, and fortune accompany the moving wheel;

chance belongs to the wheel; Fortune moderates its force.

[Col. 1424A] While the wheel stands, Fortune favors; when it falls, it crushes her;

time succeeds, but love changes.

Love nourishes groans; Fortune produces fear;

joy is the beginning, pain the end, for each.

She plays out changing turns and accompanies both,

turning day into darkness and darkness into day.

The more Fortune pleases, the more she brings pain from that source;

and what is sweetest she swiftly steals away.

Love does not indeed always delight. Love always

keeps some hidden sorrow in reserve beneath itself.

Cares accompany Fortune, cares accompany love;

hence thirst, hence groans, hence labor, hence tears.

Love mixes snares with milk and poison with honey;

[Col. 1424B] and Fortune adds very many harsh evils to good things.

Thus love is not faithful, thus Fortune is not faithful;

thus Fortune breaks, and love breaks likewise.

## LXXVIII. On the instability of human affairs

(From the Évreux manuscript.)

All human things hang by a slender thread,

and what has flourished collapses by sudden chance.

Divine power plays amid human affairs,

and the present hour scarcely possesses assured trust.

## LXXIX. On the sacrament of marriage

(From Royal manuscript 4103, Vict. 272, Évreux 19, and other Colbert manuscripts.)

[Note: [Col. 1424D] This summary, absent from the Évreux manuscript, has been supplied from Royal manuscript 4103 and Vict. 272.]

In order that marriage might unite kindred and relatives,

it was necessary because the first offspring were few.

In order that marriage under grace might increase charity,

sacred marriages passed over to outsiders.

The first marriages did not take relatives or blood-kindred; neither a single offspring nor a single person did so.

Eve was the wife of one man, Adam the husband of one woman.

Blessing preceded intercourse; grace preceded offspring.

The bride who followed was not so situated, whom the wicked abundance of men

joined to a relative, a blood relation, or a brother,

not only because no woman could find her equal,

but because offspring destined to bear the Messiah were pleasing [or: “went before,” *praeibat*].

You, mother of Isaac, foreknowing the Christ to come,

patiently endured a companion in marriage.

Before the Law was given, Jacob married Rachel and Leah.

Under the Law Elkanah took two wives at the same time.

[Col. 1424D] If you wish to consider the marriages of that age,

offspring was sought, not pleasure affectedly pursued.

The matron satisfied not herself but her line;

thereby she looked ahead to the Redeemer who was to come.

Thus many women clung together to one husband, not one woman to many husbands,

as very many vines to an elm.

For one woman did not suffice for many men in order to produce offspring;

[Col. 1425A] one woman did not need many men in order that she might conceive.

Thus holy women bore the people of the Lord,

from whom their Redeemer and heir was to be created.

His coming restored the original marriages;

thereafter neither a relative nor one near in blood married.

For those descended from the same stock are bound

by their nearness and made dear to one another;

their embrace contributes nothing to honorable love.

It is enough that he is a brother and that she is a sister;

therefore let no marriages be joined between those

whom devotion to their lineage and grace attend.

God wishes those who are not born friends to become friends;

he wishes men to call others their own rather than kinsmen.

He wishes those women to be wives, these men husbands,

both sought from foreign peoples,

[Col. 1425B] whom their descent separates but the good of marriage unites.

Marriage makes treaties among peoples, binds cities, fortifies walls.

Thus love spread abroad; thus the commonwealth grew;

thus the discordant world rested in the peace it sought.

That sacred love might be extended under Christ,

a woman is thus commanded to marry under Christ’s law.

## LXXX. On the two Jameses

(From the manuscript of Saint Marianus.)

Let no one henceforth dispute concerning the Jameses:

one was born of Alphaeus, the other of Zebedee.

The one whom you heard first, remember to declare Christ’s brother;

we read that he is buried at Jerusalem, often visited,

and commonly honored on the Kalends of May.

But the latter was brother of the author of Revelation,

[Col. 1425C] and rejoices to have the soil of Galicia as his resting-place.

Anna, wife of Joachim, bore you, Virgin Mary,

from whom true Wisdom proceeded without seed.

After him, by Cleophas, she bore you a sister, O Virgin,

who bore Joseph and James the Less to Alphaeus.

When Cleophas too had died, Anna was joined to a certain Salome,

from whom the mother of Zebedee’s children was born.

Thus one Anna bore three Maries by three husbands.

## LXXXI. Why we omit Alleluia in Septuagesima

(From Colbert manuscript no. 6101.)

As long as the king of Babylon had subjected the Israelites to himself,

the company could not sing Alleluia,

but endured a grievous punishment for sixty years;

hence Septuagesima is observed by Christians.

When captive man feels sin rule over him,

[Col. 1425D] he prefers to weep in sorrow rather than rejoice.

But when divine mercy spares his guilt,

he rejoices and exults, resounds and sings for joy [Note: [Col. 1425] In Beaugendre’s edition of 1708, the section “Why three Masses are said at Christmas” followed. But the editor had already printed the same little verses in the Book on the Sacred Eucharist, p. 1155.].

## LXXXII. On the manifestation of the Lord

[Note: [Col. 1425D] That is, the Epiphany.]

(From the same manuscript.)

As I have learned, this light is celebrated for a threefold event:

water becomes wine; baptism is consecrated through the boy [Note: [Col. 1425D] That is, the servant—namely John the Baptist.];

three persons worship the threefold Lord with a threefold gift.

[Col. 1426A] He is known from bronze [Note: [Col. 1425D] Perhaps “gold,” or money.] because he ought to hold the scepter;

myrrh proves him mortal, and incense priestly.

## LXXXIII. On receiving the sacred Eucharist

(From the same manuscript.)

Jesus gives Jesus; though eaten by all, he remains whole.

He is chewed unharmed, drunk without being cut by a wound.

A beautiful mystery: the cross is the altar and the chalice the tomb;

the sacred body is grain, the blood becomes grape, water becomes washing.

## LXXXIV. Repentance necessary for the proper administration of the Eucharist

[Note: [Col. 1426D] From the same Colbert manuscript 6101, as are the items that follow down to no. 106.]

Standing at the altar, devout mind, rejoice to weep;

while offering, take care to be offered; while consecrating, to be consecrated.

Devour the Lamb in weeping; weeping, wash body, heart, and mouth.

[Col. 1426B] As you approach this great mystery, be a lamb in the Lamb;

about to receive the Lamb, be pure from every sin.

Do not receive him until, weeping, you become a victim.

First feed yourself with mourning, then with life’s fruit:

tears give laughter, erase evils, and purchase Paradise.

## LXXXV. Christ on the cross

I conquered death,

I trampled the serpent,

I loosed sin,

I shattered hell,

I restored the human race.

## LXXXVI. Addressed to an image of Christ crucified

The image you see before you is neither God nor man;

but he whom the sacred image represents is God and man.

## LXXXVII. When the angel comes to Mary

At Gabriel’s “Hail,” the Virgin bears the sweet seed,

[Col. 1426C] whom the heavens cannot contain, yet the Virgin receives through her faithful ear.

## LXXXVIII. When Mary bears Jesus

The virgin mother, lacking a consort, holds the Almighty.

Thus in her pious heart, as in her womb, she bears him who bears all things.

## LXXXIX. When Mary gives birth to Christ

The star bears the sun, the mountain the mountain, the unwedded woman offspring.

Thus the Maker becomes a made thing, the Word flesh, the cedar hyssop.

## XC. When John baptizes Jesus

The Baptist trembles, the Father himself thunders, the water is astonished.

Christ cleanses the waters; his flesh is not cleansed by the waters.

## XCI. When he enters Jerusalem upon a little ass

If you overcome war, if you restrain the little ass of the flesh,

you enter Jerusalem, bearing the special palm.

## XCII. When he washes the disciples’ feet

[Col. 1426D]

A pattern is given us when the king serves his servants;

what God shows to these, brother likewise owes to brother.

## XCIII. When [Christ] is handed over to the Jews

Gladly the leader goes to death, he who hands himself over for the flock;

he is handed over by the dear Father, and by Judas the avaricious.

## XCIV. When he is crucified

Here Jesus teaches you, when injured, not to seek to injure,

nor to fear suffering punishment, though innocent of guilt.

## XCV. When he has been crucified

[Col. 1427A]

Consider, man, what things I suffered, who I am, and why I suffered them.

Though a joyful king, dying I drink grievous things, lest you die.

I am fixed by nails; be crucified with me in your will.

Despise the evil life. Have you sinned? Rise; I shall forgive.

## XCVI. When the women are before the tomb

Swift women seek Jesus’ tomb in the morning;

the angel says to them: “Life is not here; he has risen.”

## XCVII. When he rises from the tomb

A rod is given to Christ; cross is driven away by cross, death by death;

light appears, Eve returns, Adam stands, the dragon weeps, the lion yields.

## XCVIII. When he appears to Mary Magdalene

He rises, and when the sun has risen, the Sun is seen in the garden,

[Col. 1427B] saying to Magdalene alone: “Do not touch me.”

## XCIX. When Thomas touches Jesus’ side

By touching the side Thomas was made certain;

by believing, you will see what he believed by living.

## C. When Jesus ascends into heaven

The King enters heaven; his mother’s longing heart rejoices.

Thus he will come, say the heavenly ones; the fathers look on.

## CI. When the [Spirit] descends upon the apostles in the form of fire

A fiery tongue is given; the given fire is marked in fire;

it cheers the witnesses, fills the heart, and equips the mouths.

## CII. Inscription on the cross

The King of the Jews breaks the old bond on the cross

and JESUS NAZARENUS—the Nazarene—redeems the human race.

## CIII. When Jesus is born

[Col. 1427C] The Virgin bears the flower, the flower the fruit, the fruit the fragrance.

The Virgin, bearing the Creator, transcends nature.

This mother surpasses a mother and virginity.

She is the Father’s mother, through whom your king is your brother.

The Virgin bears a boy: a new thing, the greatest thing of all things.

1353

## CIV. When Simon Magus offers money

When Simon seeks to purchase God’s gifts for a price,

he condemns himself and his like to a lamentable death.

## CV. When he spares the woman caught in adultery

The fountain of mercy spares the woman’s sins;

let stern fathers learn to pity the wretched.

## CVI. On the three dwellings of human beings

(From the Évreux manuscript.)

Threefold dwelling is prepared for us: home, tomb, and heaven.

[Col. 1427D] Timber prepares the home, the spade the sarcophagus, devotion heaven.

At the home, decline is its companion; in the urn, the worm;

in heaven, the angel. Home is called the place of punishment, tomb of sleep,

and heaven, by a differing lot, of joy.

Sin gives the first two; grace alone gives the highest.

## CVII. What a chaste life is

(From the same.)

You breakfast into the night, Turgidus, and dine into the daylight,

and soak yourself in wine in many ways, night and day.

Though you devote yourself to the belly, you do not wish to marry.

When asked why you do not wish it, you say: “A chaste life pleases me.”

Turgidus, you lie: this is not a chaste life.

Do you wish me to say what a chaste life is? Moderation.

## CVIII. How dangerous intimacy with women is

(From the same.)

[Col. 1428A]

[Note: [Col. 1427] Here he speaks in the person of a young man converted to a better life.]

Treacherous woman, filthy woman, worthy of chains;

a mind conscious of evil, fickle, impious, full of poisons;

most wicked viper, deepest pit, stirred-up pool:

you receive everything, deceive everything, are one thing to all.

Foul owl, public doorway, well-worn path:

your life is more ravenous than fire, more cruel than an asp.

For one who wishes to trust you, many evils are prepared for himself.

O miserable, insatiable, unsated woman!

Stop writing; stop sending flattering poems—

shameful poems, soft poems, scarcely fit to remember.

I have resolved neither to send nor to write to you;

I no longer court you, no longer desire you; I give you back to yourself.

To live for myself and rest in peace are my desires.

[Col. 1428B] I have taken thought for myself; take thought for yourself, be wholly your own.

Choose, gather, love whomever you please: let there be a thousand for you.

Let this man or that be dearer or more precious to you.

Your mind is glassy, leaden, stony, iron, wicked.

It thinks it right to fashion, deceive, betray, and destroy.

May supreme power utterly destroy everything first,

before they endure to take or touch what is mine.

## CIX. On a perverse woman

(From the Tours manuscript.)

Woman takes away, shuts in, deceives, strips, gives, burns;

she deprives, reveals, possesses, despoils.

To the first living man she gave Paradise; to Joseph, prison;

to Judas, adornment; to the strong man, his hair;

to Uriah, death; to David, adultery; to Solomon,

[Col. 1428C] religious apostasy; to Peter, a devilish voice.

## CX. How harmful woman, avarice, and ambition are to holy men

(From the same Évreux manuscript and Colbert manuscript 1050.)

Although very many things are accustomed to overthrow sacred morals,

woman, wealth, and office overthrow them more deeply.

Woman, wealth, and office—the fuel and tinder of evils—

draw hearts and hands toward crime and swords.

1354 Woman is a frail thing, never steadfast except in wrongdoing,

never ceasing of her own accord to be harmful.

Woman is a devouring flame, ultimate madness, an intimate enemy;

she both teaches and learns whatever is accustomed to harm.

Woman is a cheap marketplace, a public commodity born to deceive.

She thinks she has succeeded when she is allowed to be guilty.

[Col. 1428D] Woman is a grievous yoke, a complaint against law and equity.

She thinks it shameful whenever she commits no shameful acts.

Woman is the heavier enemy because the more private.

She invites crime by gift, voice, and hand.

And while consuming men, she is consumed by every vice;

having preyed on men, she herself becomes prey for men.

She enfeebles, plunders, and torments bodies, wealth, and minds;

she supplies, arms, and nourishes weapons, hands, and hatred.

She overturns, agitates, and burns cities, kingdoms, and houses,

and alone seizes [or: “conceives,” *capit*] the hope of so many things, restrains arms.

Woman endured that John be condemned by the sword,

Hippolytus to death, Joseph to prison when she was spurned.

[Col. 1429A] Woman with equal intent deprived Uriah of life,

David of piety, and Solomon of faith.

Woman governs in mind, approves with tongue, fulfills in deeds

that toward which law, people, and she herself together rush.

(After the words ending “arms, and nourishes,” Colbert manuscript 1050 reads:)

Woman deprived Paris of mind, Uriah of life,

David of piety, and Solomon of faith.

Woman endured that John be condemned by the sword,

Hippolytus to death, and Joseph with chains.

Woman conceives in mind, approves with tongue, fulfills in deeds

that toward which law, people, and she herself together rush.

Nor does gold less alter the powers of the mind

[Note: [Col. 1429D] Colbert manuscript 1050: “Gold does not less alter minds, or tear them out.”],

nor does it less show the unlawful path to be pursued.

There is scarcely anyone ashamed to pervert justice for gold,

[Col. 1429B] or reluctant to be guilty for any price.

Gold accomplishes whatever is wrongly sought,

and no one asks vain things with a fee held out beforehand.

Gold, moving hearts, prey of holy eyes,

arms and drives pure hands to crime.

By gold virtue often slips, and so does the strength of those

whose hearts God praises and whose other qualities man praises.

And he whom you would have sworn would lay down his neck for justice

thinks, in hope of a modest profit, that everything is permitted.

A savage enemy, a grave judge, and a harsh torturer,

in hope of reward relax battles, laws, and hands.

Gold stations camps, equips a fleet, draws swords;

it teaches men to scorn force, winds, seas, and weapons.

It dissolves marriage, breaks down the barriers of modesty,

[Col. 1429C] stains sacred hands with bloodshed and mouths with deceits.

[ [Note: [Col. 1429D] These two verses are absent from Colbert manuscript 1050.] By gold Polymestor became perjured, Danaë adulterous,

Tarpeia treacherous, Eriphyle cruel.]

Crassus died through gold; Amphiaraus fell through gold;

through gold camps, commanders, law, and peoples fall.

But him whom neither possessions nor woman can break,

ambition conquers and makes the devout criminal.

Ambition turns conduct toward what is forbidden and does not allow anyone

to be guilty beneath his own capacity.

Its work is to disturb rulers, alter crowns,

prepare death for the innocent and scepters for the guilty;

to prepare destruction for cities, ruin for temples,

to strike patricians down with swords, homes with fire;

to expose kings to mockery, kingdoms to plunder,

mothers to disgrace, and old men to destruction.

[Col. 1429D] 1355 To offend nature with vices and the gods with ritual,

to spare only when it is unable to harm.

As soon as someone is seized by the contagion of so great a disaster,

he thinks everything permitted while he prepares kingdoms for himself.

He endures to bear swords against his father, and never

are mind, hand, or mouth free from deceit, bloodshed, and trickery.

(In Colbert manuscript no. 1650, after the words “mind, hand, or mouth are free,” the following four lines are added:)

I glory when exalted; I descend when brought to death.

[Col. 1430A] Ah, wretch! I am worn down on the axle, joyfully borne upward.

Like a wheel, the unmoving order moves men,

raising the humble and crushing the high-minded.

## CXI. After Hildebert first lamented the various disasters of different churches, he congratulates a certain church because it has acquired a most watchful shepherd, able by his prudence to protect it from those disasters

This church may not implausibly be identified as the Church of Salisbury, whose bishop-elect Roger was chosen about A.D. 1102. To him Hildebert wrote the twelfth congratulatory letter of Book II.

(From Évreux manuscript no. 19.)

Now storms have arisen against as many churches

as no records have ever contained, whether in number or greatness.

So many things sink them, so many oppose their happiness,

[Col. 1430B] that scarcely one can hope for a harbor of peace.

Peace, liberty, and reverence have passed away;

war, plunder, servitude, and contempt have succeeded them.

A raging multitude of robbers oppresses and despoils those

whom the care of holy fathers once raised up and tended.

Those which in earlier years smiled under holy fathers

[Note: [Col. 1429D] That is, churches that once gloried in holy bishops.]

now weep, subjected to Simons [Note: [Col. 1429D] That is, simoniacs.] and tyrants.

Hence, hunting the favor of kings and dukes for themselves,

they do not fear to loosen the rigor of the law against them.

Thus, plundering milk and wool from the sheep for themselves,

they loosen the reins for wolves, silently providing escape.

For hope of gain they pretend that crime and things to be avoided are lawful,

although they have learned to beware whether things are lawful or unlawful.

[Col. 1430C] Thanks be to you, Christ, who calm us through this father,

who governs the Church, the law, and the reins of law;

who has learned to be a shepherd, not a hireling;

who, when a robber is present, does not know how to leave the sheep;

who so recalls those who stray and so serves the needy

that for these there is sustenance, and for those gentle correction.

May eternal rest be prepared for him, after the years of *pilii* [perhaps *praelii*, “battle”],

as he deserves by deeds, mind, and speech.

## CXII. On a man who is both abbot and bishop

[Note: [Col. 1429D] This perhaps concerns Bruno, bishop of Segni, who, not long before, had been elected abbot of Monte Cassino and was forbidden by Paschal II—as Peter the Deacon reports, Book IV, chapter 44—to remain both bishop and abbot at once. Though the monks strove in vain to retain him, he returned to his bishopric and, after some years, rested in a holy death, renowned for miracles after his death. See Baronius under the year 1104.]

(From Évreux manuscript no. 19.)

Art placed a mare beneath an ass, and the mixture

produced a prodigious, lustful offspring: a mule.

So rank is mixed in you; and from abbot together with

bishop, I know not what sort of grade is called by that name.

## CXIII. On the incestuous rape inflicted by Amnon upon his own sister Tamar (2 Samuel 13)

(From the same.)

[Col. 1430D]

The sickly boy Amnon lay down as though dying;

he was pierced by the dart of forbidden desire.

His unsuspecting father asks him to disclose the cause of his illness.

The boy gave this answer to his father’s words:

“Look,” he says, “look, I am dying; I shall die unless there comes to me

your daughter Tamar, joined to me by blood.”

One asks; the other complies, complying with him as with a dying man,

[Col. 1431A] indulgent toward an illness that conceals a crime.

The royal virgin Tamar, with flowing hair adorned,

comes at her father’s command to serve her brother.

Stop your steps, maiden, lest your enemy overpower you

and you become barbarous prey to your own brother.

She does not know it; but carrying food and prepared drinks,

she entered the first threshold of the ill-fated house.

Her brother seizes her and confesses his wretched love,

and himself places the trembling girl upon his bed.

The lover presses her and prepares the crime while the maiden cries out,

but wickedly he gathers up the pleas of the one crying out.

“Amnon, spare Tamar; brother, pity your sister.

Let something foreign succeed your marriage-bed.

Flee unlawful impulses and the cause of crime,

and your father’s hatred, he who sent her to you.”

[Col. 1431B] Neither piety nor the bond of blood comes to his aid,

for the lamb lies subject to the wolf that prevails wickedly.

He dared violate the badges of virginity;

she grieves deeply, robbed of her flowers.

The virgin returns in misery, lamenting her wounded modesty;

her torn purple garment was proof of the deed.

## CXIV. On the secret prudently kept by Papirius Praetextatus, still a boy, from the Roman senate

The men held council and the senate sat;

a public matter occupied a long day.

The state’s business is conducted, the fathers’ private deliberations;

the boy Papirius gathers them with his young ear.

Still immature, yet already prudent and mindful of honor,

and there was more of the man in him than of the boy.

When the case had been argued, his mother eagerly receives him

[Col. 1431C] and boldly asks what Rome is discussing.

The more she found him difficult, the more insistently

she added threats to maternal prayers.

The boy conceals the truth because of his parent’s importunity,

and devises an invention with new cunning.

Rome, bereft of its fathers, like one without a soldier,

can scarcely maintain its own realms, scarcely seek foreign ones.

In its early age it subjected the whole world to itself;

therefore it fears the plots of the whole world.

But the leaders thought, in hope of multiplying offspring,

that one woman did not suffice for any one man.

Yet they hesitate, and the case is still before judgment:

whether one man should have several women, or one woman two men.

The tale is believed and spreads widely through the city,

[Col. 1431D] and rumor stirs the hearts of the matrons.

The following day dawned; the citizens assemble under the law;

an unfamiliar clamor resounds throughout the city.

Not otherwise do the daughters-in-law of Bubacus fill the broad fields with cries

at your festivals, Lyaeus.

The people ask what and whence this tumult may be;

the tumult was among the matrons.

They burst out together into words: “Desist, citizens!

The cause of our common country moves us too.

Let one woman have two men, because one woman suffices for two;

with such help Rome will be everlasting.”

For a long time the citizens sat attentive, astonished

by so great an uproar of madness.

They reconsider the difficult case with greater zeal;

they ask what is the sum and origin of the matter.

[Col. 1432A] They discover that the boy had thus mocked his mother

1357 and concealed the truth by a novel fiction.

Rome gave him a lasting memorial, *Praetextatus*,

and endowed his family with the name of its garment.

## CXV. Dream concerning the lamentation of the Church of Poitiers

(From a manuscript codex, formerly of Saint-Amand, now Royal no. 274, about five hundred years old.)

One night, weary from travel,

lying upon a bed, pressed down by sleep,

in the darkness of dense night,

I saw the church of Poitiers

in the form of a person,

under the appearance of a matron.

Her appearance indeed was

[Col. 1432B] one of venerable countenance;

but a harm worse than every harm

had troubled her brow.

Yet it stands so amid ruined circumstances

that from the contrary condition you might judge

how great she was in those years

when she had suffered no harms.

That youthful color was gone;

there was none—whence the grief;

there was none, but upon her face

bruising stood in place of color.

A little crown clings to her hair,

very much broken; in place of its jewels

is a gnawing troop of moths.

[Col. 1432C] The signs of hunger are upon her belly,

which her torn cloak displays;

through it, indecently exposed,

appears the place of the belly, not the belly itself.

This is the cloak, this the dress,

which many a year has worn away,

from its outermost hem,

stiff with frost, wet with rain.

The antiquity of this garment

testifies to its former newness,

suggesting with what care

this fabric had been made.

Now it holds itself together by a thousand knots,

entangled in a hundred ways.

As she stood thus, drenched with tears,

[Col. 1432D] setting before me the cause of her weeping,

she spoke among other things

about herself in figurative language,

never ceasing to accuse

ship, sailors, winds, and sea,

so that from her words it might be known [or: “not known,” *nesciretur*]

what she was saying or why.

Then fixing her face upon heaven,

she poured out these complaints:

“My God!” she cried,

“what whirlwind has suffocated me?

What power [has made] me powerless?

What force presses me while I lie fallen?

Whence fear? Whence sorrow?

[Col. 1433A] Whence have I come, or where am I borne?

Who or what kind of pirates are these

who attack my sunken vessel?

What storms, or what winds,

rise so against one rising again?

Good sailor, a way for the good,

using the oar of reason,

how foolishly, how heedlessly

my sailors conduct themselves!

Indeed, they should not be called sailors,

who offer their hands to Fortune;

nor do they behave like helmsmen,

who are ruled and do not rule.

To men as blind as they are incompetent

the ship’s helm has been entrusted,

[Col. 1433B] a ship which the outrageous force of pirates

has shortened on one side;

nor have the sailors brought aid

against the blows of those striking.

Those by whom such things ought to be governed

fear things that men ought not fear.

That people of Fortune fears

the movement of a leaf, the shadow of the moon,

if they allow me, blind, to wander

over a blind sea.

Far from my neck is its necklace,

far from my side is its bed;

I am held cheap by my husband,”

Forced to this bed against my will.

For three years I have endured the night;

[Col. 1433C] I am borne over the sea in a battered ship.

Night has not been banished by daylight,

Nor error by a good guide.

1358 For three years drink has not banished thirst,

Nor food hunger;

In place of drink, in place of bread,

Hope filled me—but empty hope;

For for three years, like a fool,

I await the river’s flow,

Yet the river slips away

And cannot be drawn even for an hour.

With mast broken and sail torn,

At last I gasp for breath.

The wind has not yet softened its wrath,

[Col. 1433D] But comes from the direction of the harbour;

It blows from east toward west,

Not toward the harbour, but away from it.

Steward, who distributest

Boundless goods among private persons,

Ordering all things well, nothing unjustly—

Thus everywhere as though nowhere—

Whose rising is the concern

Of all creatures

Whom thou didst create, though not created,

Never made, yet begotten;

Who canst know nothing so great

As that thou canst not be unable to do more.

[Col. 1434A] Thou who art great without division,

Prince of peace without Mars,

Without motion, without place,

Thou grantest motion and rulest place.

Thou who art good—indeed, Goodness—

Whom few are fit to embrace,

Whom it is not easy to address,

Whom not to know is human:

Good Son, good Father,

Good Virgin, yet also mother;

A mother, I say, immortal,

Yet perishable, yet mortal:

Hear him whom you hear,

And do not will what I do not will.

It is plain to you that this is my desire:

[Col. 1434B] that these storms should not torment me;

That I should no longer be thought ruled by fortune,

Though betrothed to the King of kings.

King, bow down those who injure me,

Lest those who rejoice in plunder

Should find their plundering

To be plunder unto ruin.

Keep wolves and pirates away,

Lest the vessel despair of reaching harbour.

Hear, shepherd who rulest me;

Give the flock a learned shepherd,

One ruling himself by reason,

Turning aside from Simon,

Who may so fight in strength

That riches be not inadequately secure,

[Col. 1434C] And so administer them; and when this was said,

Sleep departed, leaving me behind.

### CXVI. On the city of Poitiers and a certain bishop of it

*(From the manuscript of Saint-Marien.)*

If we count all the cities below the Alps,

One among them, Poitiers, has raised its head.

A prince, a very great populace, an honourable clergy,

A mass of wealth, many towers, and the site itself adorn her.

Greater glory than these is added to her: her bishop  
[Note: [Col. 1433D] That is, Bishop Peter.]

A noble city was worthy of such a bishop.

But since virtue is held of greater worth in a bishop,

I should like to relate a few things about his virtue.

His body, wealth, zeal, manners, austere and scanty food,

[Col. 1434D] Reading, reproaches—he subdues, prunes, nourishes; they flee.

He cherishes virtues, cuts off faults, and increases fruit.

He protects law, hates lawsuits, and loves peace.

If genus and species were endowments in a bishop,

In this man endowments themselves would be both genus and species.

Unwillingly he bestows punishments; gladly, rewards:

The former more sparingly than merits deserve, the latter more lavishly than his own merits.

He burns with justice, yet is softened by simplicity;

Severe in strictness, kind in nobility.

O man of wondrous gravity! His mind, tongue, and hand

Think, utter, and do nothing but what is honourable.

O man of wondrous piety! He is not proud in honour,

1359 Nor yields when injured, nor oppresses by ruling.

[Col. 1435A] He bears with the wretched, grants pardon to the sinner,

And preserves unfailing help and continuing faithfulness for his friend.

His mind, on the wings of virtues, lifts him heavenward,

And now he enjoys his own peace in beholding G-od.  
[Note: [Col. 1435D] The end of these verses is missing through a tear in the leaf; we have completed it, as best we could conjecture from the final letter. Let the reader judge whether this has been done successfully.]

Yet he seeks the stars in such a way as not to leave earthly things behind.

Diligent concern recalls the shepherd to his flock.

He ascends in contemplating God; he descends into the deepest

Care for the people committed to him: each is good.

In mind he is free for Mary, but in action Martha labours.

Martha attends to the flock; Mary to God.

Thus with him God reigns within, his neighbour without:

God by desire, his neighbour by service.

He loves Rachel, nor refuses to bear Leah;

Like the new Jacob, he has taken each as wife.

He loves the face of the one and delights to gather the fruit of the other,

[Col. 1435B] Since Rachel is fair, but Leah more fruitful.

### CXVII. On the city of Poitiers and its king

*(From the manuscript of Saint-Marien.)*

Long depressed beneath a servile yoke and buried,

Poitiers, now made free, raise your head.

Liberty returns to you late: rise from the dust,

Cast off the yoke, wipe your eyes, clap your hands.

Led astray by your consuls, you have provided for yourself:

Behold, your king is present for you, gentle and fierce.

Most gentle toward those subject to him, fierce toward enemies:

It profits the royal city to be ruled by such a king.

While that saving day-star rises in the east,

The bloody star of Mars seeks its setting.

Peace flourishes, arms lie still, toil dies, leisure lives.

[Col. 1435C] By law deceit ceases; by fertility, famine ceases.

The city is free of robbers  
[Note: [Col. 1435D] The beginning [Col. 1436D] of these six verses is absent from the manuscript because of a tear in the leaf; we have supplied it, as we think, in accordance with the author’s intention.],

The road of murders, the fields of plunder,

The gates of a snarling enemy’s siege.

The citizen does not grow pale with fear when the dogs are driven off,

Nor does the rabble fill the forum with sedition.

Rewards return to soldiers, gold to citizens,

And each man’s own undiminished honour remains inviolate.

Freedom for slaves, protection for weary peasants,

Hope for the wretched, laughter for those who weep, anger for the wicked.

### CXVIII. On the Nativity of the Lord

*(It is found somewhat differently and at greater length in Royal manuscript Elnonensis no. 274, about the year 500.)*

Today two suns have appeared to us:

This one is the work, that one the maker; this one fleeting, that one abiding.

This sun commands the stars; but, that it may command them, the other commands it.

[Col. 1435D] This one commands the day to go; that one commands command itself.

The sun rises with God the Sun, light with light;

Light with light, day with the maker of day.

The Virgin bears day without night, fruit without seed;

She becomes pregnant without a man; a father comes to be without a father [perhaps *preparing*].

This thing is greater; it is the greatest of all things;

In it is a greater light, the greatest king of all things;

The burden becomes more spacious than its own place.

That night is almost a day, second to no day,

On which God is clothed in flesh, and flesh in God.

[Col. 1436A] The uncreated, made, enters on this night into covenant with the created.  
[Note: [Col. 1436D] Royal manuscript: “and the created, made.”]

The Sun precedes the dawn, and day the day-star.

The true Sun, I say, true Light, and serene radiance:

That one and that one are God, just as that one too is God.

[Note: [Col. 1436D] These two verses are absent in the Royal manuscript.] The Virgin bore God; but if anyone asks how,

It is not mine to know; but I know that God is able.

### CXIX. On the Visitation of Blessed Mary to Elizabeth

*(From the Royal Elnonensis manuscript 274.)*

If an unmarried woman is pregnant, it is a new thing and a heavenly power.

She is pregnant: therefore a new and starry blessing comes to pass.

One pregnant through the Word gives kisses to a pregnant woman; the unmarried woman to the bride:

Though each is pregnant, the one does not know a man.

### CXX. Christ speaking of himself

*(From the same manuscript.)*

[Col. 1436B]

Sea, land, and sky are subject to me; I alone am King.

Alone from eternity I create all things; I govern what I have created.

I am the way of virtue, hope of life, gate of salvation;

You who make for the homeland of life, behold: come.

### CXXI. That adversity befalls the good, and prosperity the wicked

*(From Colbert manuscript 3019, fol. 78.)*

Sometimes prosperity comes, lest one be overwhelmed by adversity.

Adversity comes in order to wash away stains and to prove a man by troubles.

Sometimes prosperity comes to the wicked, that he may be struck more grievously.

Adversity comes, that he may return—as this man does—and suffer what he now suffers.

### CXXII. On the ten plagues of Egypt

*(From Colbert manuscript 3019, fol. 80; Ebroicensis no. 19.)*

First, the reddened water; frogs and corruption, second;

Then the grievous gnat; afterward the fly, more harmful than these;

[Col. 1436C] The fifth struck down cattle; the sixth produced blisters;

Then hail comes on; afterward the locust with its dreadful tooth;

The ninth covers the sun; the last afflicts the firstborn.

### CXXIII. On Joseph

*(From the same manuscript.)*

When his father summoned Joseph, he came; his father commanded him:

“Go to Shechem, and inspect your brothers and the flocks.”

He comes to Hebron and enters Shechem, but there he finds

Neither flock nor brothers. A countryman sees him wandering through the fields

And asks what he is seeking. Joseph answers:

“I seek my brothers; tell me, if perhaps you know where they are.”

“I do not know,” he replies; “yet I remember that they said

This: ‘Let us lead the flock to the pastures of Dothan.’”

Joseph hastens there; and while he is still far away,

[Col. 1436D] He is seen by his brothers. Seeing him, they take counsel

To kill him. Thus they speak of their brother:

“Look, Joseph is coming, the one who saw dreams; come,

Let us kill him; thus surely we shall discover

What his dreams portend, or what good his dreams will do him.”

Reuben, one of the brothers, opposed this: “Far be it

That brothers should kill a brother; rather let him be cast

Alive into this pit.” He had pointed out the pit to them.

While they hesitate, uncertain what to do, they propose differing courses.

They see certain men going by; seeing them go,

[Col. 1437A] They all approve this together: “Let him come; let him be sold to these men.”

It is said at what price Joseph is sold; and they

Pay the price and place Joseph in their wagons.

### CXXIV. On four goods and four evils

*(From Colbert manuscript 3019, fol. 78.)*

To despise the world, to despise oneself, to despise no one,

To despise being despised: these are four goods.

To seek deceit, to seek display, to seek praise,

To seek to be sought: these are four evils.

### CXXV. Words of Christ on the cross

*(From the same manuscript.)*

You have wandered long enough from the homeland of life: return.

Those whom I purchase thus—my death is public life.

The cross is the end of the law, the way of life, the King’s passion,

[Col. 1437B] To whom grace, not merit, gave death.

1361 ### CXXVI. Heavenly things to be preferred to earthly

*(From Colbert manuscripts nos. 1050 and 3019, and Ebroicensis 19.)*

You do not judge rightly if you prefer lower things to heavenly;

Nor are you sufficiently at one with yourself if you subject what is right to things.

For what is silver? What is beauty? What a retinue’s array?

What are famous estates? The world’s glory is a brief festival.

There is no reliability in it: today it is bad, tomorrow worse for you.

It is fitting to use this, but not to prefer it to salvation.

### CXXVII. On the various acts of the soul

*(From the same manuscript, 1050.)*

The soul claims for itself . . . seven acts:

It gives life, feels, embraces various arts,

Corrects excesses, applies itself to virtues; upon itself

[Col. 1437C] It directs its gaze toward the Godhead and rejoices in it.

The first is also present in seeds; brute animals

Share another; two belong to our own nature.

Three are also those of the heavenly beings; yet the heavenly are preferred.

By its proper activity bodies are nourished and grow;

Then vigour, connection, composition, motion,

Rest, form, and a certain harmony proceed.

By another it touches, sees, hears, tastes, and smells;

It hates and loves, seeks things suited to itself, avoids contraries,

Dissolves into sleep and wanders in dreams in mind;

It remembers the past, attends to things to come, and does

Many things that are done by sense, not by reason.

The third traverses the liberal and other arts,

Whatever talent or instruction supplies,

[Col. 1437D] Gathers them, and by varied progress adheres to minds.

The fourth recalls from unlawful things and teaches idle sinners

To renounce guilt; from then on

One begins to know oneself and is taught to strive and pass into newness.

From the fifth we learn to be restrained by nature’s law,

To avoid forbidden things through love of virtue,

And even to forgo certain permitted things without a witness.

The sixth draws the stainless soul into the sight

Of the sun and of heavenly light, almost equal to the heavenly beings.

The seventh binds it fast, yokes it with enduring love,

And joins it side by side with God, that it may now contemplate what dowry,

What bridal chambers [perhaps: *which bridal chambers*], what adornment, what feasts may make glad

Her to whom someone shall say: “Come, beautiful one.” The blessed

And greater souls have spoken; yet before this they had neither virtue

[Col. 1438A] Nor the language by which they might be permitted to disclose these things.

The hidden reward exceeds sense and merit.

### CXXVIII. On the twelve patriarchs allegorically designated by the stones of the high priest’s breastpiece

*(From the same manuscript, 1050.)*

Reuben, first in birth, and jasper in the sanctuary,

Signify the beginnings alike of virtues and of faith.

Simeon in birth, sapphire second in the sanctuary,

Suggest a sorrowful heart whose conversation is heaven.

Chalcedony, third among those set in place, with gentle growth,

Figures the increase of good, though still hidden.

Judah by birth, and emerald fourth in the sanctuary,

Are mouths professing faith and the struggles of faith.

Dan, fifth in the order, and sardonyx,

Recall those prepared for judgment, humble and pure in heart.

[Col. 1438B] Sardius, joined with Naphtali in birth, sixth,

Signifies martyrdom and the fires of twofold love.

Chrysolite in the temple; Gad, seventh son

Of his father, mark those girded for war and gleaming with standards.

Then beryl and Asher, each eighth, figure

Now the rest of the mind and those blessed by the splendour of their deeds.

Topaz ninth in the structure, Issachar by birth,

Figures contemplatives and those who pray in hope of reward.

Then Zebulun tenth, and chrysoprase,

Recount those strong in battle and restored by the brightness of their reward.

Hyacinth, eleventh by its placing, Joseph by birth,

1362 Figures those who add to their vows and become all things to all.

Then Benjamin and amethyst alike, each last,

Figure the modest, humble, and those who merit, by long

Martyrdom, the Father’s right hand and embrace.

### CXXIX. On manifold truth

*(From the same manuscript.)*

[Col. 1438C]

What is the highest good? A mind always conscious of what is right.

What is the greatest ruin of human beings? Another human being alone.

Who is rich? One who desires nothing. Who is poor? The greedy person.

What is a matron’s fairest dowry? A chaste life.

Who is chaste? She of whom reputation fears to lie.

What is peculiar to a fool? To be unable, yet to wish, to harm.

What is the work of the prudent person? When able, not to wish to harm.

### CXXX. On the seven canonical hours

*(From the same manuscript.)*

The full day is enclosed within twenty-four hours;

Seven of these are consecrated to the service of the Lord.

The hour at which the solar sphere is first seen,

[Col. 1438D] **PRIME.**

We appoint Prime. The sun, made and set

In heaven, provides us with different uses.

At this hour praise must be rendered to the Lord,

Who illuminates the world with so great a lamp; then prayer must be made

That he may not allow us to be wrapped in the darkness of sins.

**TERCE.**

Terce shines exalted with manifold light.

At this hour man was made, the old Law given; at this hour the Synagogue

With its mouth crucified the Redeemer; the gracious Spirit

Taught the disciples at the hour when we began to exist.

Let the vessel praise its potter, and by prayer strive to merit

Not to savour of the old Adam, but to bear him about.

Let him who then suffered wrong pray for help

Against vices and for a fire friendly to good morals.

[Col. 1439A] **SEXT.**

At the sixth hour man sinned; Christ suffered on the cross;

The noonday enemy rages against the human race.

Whoever you are, redeemed at this hour by the death of the crucified one,

For so great a gift, after the foregoing praises, pray

That the dragon, who at this hour gained triumph over the first father,

May not cast you beneath himself. But may God, made a victim, act

So that you yield neither to the flesh nor to the noonday enemy.

**NONE.**

At the ninth hour guilty man went forth from Paradise;

At the ninth Christ gave up his spirit and then revisited those faithful ones

In [perhaps: *from*] darkness, in order to lead them back.

Made a participant in hope, let man devote himself to praises

Of their so joyful lot, and pray for return to Paradise,

Which was closed at the ninth hour and then will be opened at the ninth.

[Col. 1439B] **VESPERS.**

Scripture recounts that in the evening the moon was made

With the host of stars and placed in the firmament.

Let the author of so great a light be glorified in them,

Who painted heaven’s lights with diverse lamps

And illumined heaven’s darkness as was fitting.

It was evening when Adam, now wretched and condemned to labour,

Astonished, saw the setting of a sun

He had never seen, and, fearing the darkness,

Is reported to have prayed that divine consolations might not fail him.

He too who boasts that he has been reborn in the sacred font,

After rendering praises, should pray in mind and voice

That the sun of justice may not set upon his boldness.

**COMPLINE.**

[Col. 1439C] No fixed time is prescribed for Compline;

Yet the Lord must be praised and entreated by prayers

That grace may forgive whatever each person has sinned

During the day now past, and that the same grace may grant

That Satan or phantoms not interrupt the night’s repose.

**MATINS AT MIDNIGHT.**

The flood burst forth at midnight and, bearing

The form of baptism, washed away the contagions of sins.

At this hour Moses, when Pharaoh and his men had been submerged,

1363 Crossed the Red Sea rejoicing; David rose

For hymns; fire will divide the wicked from the just.

In these things are set before us example, mercy, and judgment,

By which we are called to better things.

David is the example of prayer; Moses led

[Col. 1439D] Through the waters, of mercy; to be overwhelmed by waves or punished by Christ the Judge is the judicial sentence.

In these things praise should be rendered to the Creator of all things,

Who makes them work salvation for us.

Example instructs, mercy grants pardon,

Judgment terrifies; mindful of these things, let every faithful person—

**LAUDS.**

At the appointed time let him rise for the Lord’s Lauds,

Seeking by praises and prayers to escape the night

In which hope of salvation has been removed by surrounding darkness.

### CXXXI. On the tonsure of a cleric

*(From the same manuscript.)*

As the tonsure of the head teaches, king and priest,

[Col. 1440A] Cleric and bishop wear the mitre, while the king wears the crown.

It is understood what the mitre is: the part shaved at the crown of the head;

The hair remaining below is the crown itself.

### CXXXII. On the evangelical vineyard

*(From the same manuscript.)*

The vineyard was cultivated; the labourers seek rewards;

Their labour is unequal, but they seek equal rewards.

He who came last, when the steward called,

Receives just as much as he who had come first.

### CXXXIII. How many years there are from Adam to Christ

*(From the same source.)*

Twice ten times ten hundred and fifty years, less one,

Are from the first father to Christ.

### CXXXIV. On the three orders in the Church

*(From Colbert manuscript no. 1367.)*

[Col. 1440B]

A threefold order flourishes in the Church, known in these figures.

Job signifies married persons, Daniel those mortifying themselves, Noah rulers.

The former was a husband, Daniel mortified the flesh, Noah was ruler in the ark.

The mill [perhaps: *prison-mill*], bed, and field are assigned to these same

Orders: the mill signifies worldly affairs, the bed repose,

The field the people. The mill is given to spouses, the bed

To contemplatives, and cultivation of the field to teachers.

Each order contains two kinds, reprobate and faithful.

The one is carried off to punishment; the other receives a crown.

The heaven made a firmament is a mystical matter:

For heaven is the good angel who afterward was made

A firmament, strengthened so that he could no longer

[Col. 1440C] Fall; for this one stood firm, while the other fell away.

Noah’s ark was narrow above but broad below.

It was completed in a cubit; below, brute creatures are placed;

Then humans after them, and birds above. The ark figures

The Church: we know that many within it are

Irrational; thus it is broadened in them.

There are human beings within it, but few who seek what is their own

And avoid sin; thus it is narrowed in them.

Within it are rare persons whose mind is set on despising the world.

Like birds, they are lifted to the stars on the wings of virtues:

They dwell near the cubit in the upper part,

For their places are rightly distinguished according to their merits.

The cubit signifies Christ; the hope of the Church strives toward him,

And, arriving there, desires nothing further.  
[Note: [Col. 1439] In the edition of Dom Beaugendre there follows “The Offering of the Turtledove and the Dove,” which see above, p. 1226.]

1364 ### CXXXV. On communion and post-communion

*(From a Tours manuscript.)*

[Col. 1440D]

Holy communion confers joys upon Christ’s holy people,

In which the Lord’s true body is prepared under bread,

And his blood is granted to be present under the appearance of wine.

The devout priest receives this sacrament by mouth;

May he always perform this with a pure and steadfast mind.

### CXXXVI. On thanksgiving

*(From the same manuscript.)*

Thanks are given to Christ for so great a gift.

The people entreat the Lord and repeat praises;

Then, after their praises have been offered, they return to their own homes.

“The dismissal is made; go home, faithful people: praise Christ.

[Col. 1441A] The dismissal is made; go home, all you faithful, rejoice.”

Thanks be to God. Amen.

### CXXXVII. On a certain kind of people, namely those who behave deceitfully in all things

*(From the manuscript once at Elnon, now Royal manuscript no. 274.)*

There are persons whose love so disgusts our love

That enmities are preferable to friendship with them.

By service they earn injury, by favour contempt,

By flatteries quarrels, and by love hatred.

Their lying countenance deceives even stern Catos;

Their deeds accuse them, their life proves them knaves.

In them are concealed a needle, bait, flame, and spark:

The trusting visitor is pricked by the one and burned by the other.

One pack [perhaps: *law*] of deceit confounds for them lawful and unlawful things,

So long as it conceals fraud beneath peace and veils harsh things with blandness;

[Col. 1441B] It whitens gall with milk and smears even a sword with honey.

Though not soon perceived, it quickly poisons and quickly pricks.

Their throats are armed with eloquence, their hearts with poison;

Sweet in the mouth, a bastard; in the breast, many a Celaeno.

Their throats are honeyed, yet bitter nectar is in their mouth.

Their deed betrays the tongue and robs words of flavour.

Speech tastes of nectar, but the mind has turned to vinegar.

Trusting crowd, beware: beware birdlime and virtue.

The asp has poison; the shameless Siren has birdlime.

The mouth equals the Siren, the heart poison, the mind the basilisk.

Piety hates these people; what is honourable opposes them—

[Col. 1442A] Those who count nothing dishonourable except honour itself,

In whom speech is not the messenger of the hidden mind,

In whom deceitfulness is a virtue, the practice of deceiving well.

### CXXXVIII. On the brief continuance of man

*(From the same manuscript.)*

Tell me, man: answer what man is, why he is, and whence he is.

Tell me, man, what man is—but first, whether he is at all.

Do you think that to be which, as soon as it is, hastens not to be,

Which, having scarcely stood, slips away—indeed, perishes?

Do you think that man stands, when death from his origin

Proclaims his end: “He is mine,” and repeats, “He is mine”?

Death has a long hand; death is stronger than strong Hector.

Men conquer city walls; death conquers men.

Rome, which conquered all else, has learned to endure death.

Death, queen, is born for you here and everywhere.

[Col. 1442B] What, by right, is life but signs of death to come?

Flesh that has arisen dies; flesh that has died does not arise.

### CXXXIX. On death

Amid wealth, delights, and the people’s favour,

Let the mind remember this and let your tongue proclaim it:

Death makes master equal to slave, sceptres equal to hoes,

Drawing unequal persons under an equal condition.

### CXL. To an avaricious man

If a thing is given well, though what is given is always counted as given,

No great glory belongs to a gift held back.

[Col. 1441]

## Some miscellaneous poems of the Venerable Hildebert

1365 ### I. To Rome, on its decline

*(From Royal manuscript no. 274.)*

[Col. 1441C]

Guilty Rome, openly teaching examples of wrongdoing,

Rapacious Scylla, capacious pit, greedy to retain:

If I compare you now, broken, with yourself in former times,

It is clear that ancient Rome has been reduced to ashes.

Rome is now a thing without measure, a thirsty hollow,

A rich beggar, ruling all things yet unable alone to rule herself.

If you ask how great you once were—you who have fallen—

You were divine power, you were head of the world, while you were Rome.

On these wings the swift wheel bore itself along;

Giving enough, it itself had nothing greater than its gifts to give.

Much knowledge, little pride, a rule of morals,

The tongue of Cicero, the life of Cato, concern for the good,

Power in arms, all-conquering achievements—

[Col. 1441D] These, as is clear, set you as head over all cities.

Thus this moving wheel was useful and all was well with you,

So that it could do nothing higher or more fitting.

India too saw the threatening missiles and standards confronting standards,

And the sluggish zone, farther removed from the fire of heaven.

Africa is conquered; the many Punic wars yielded their harms.

Gaul gives herself to you, and conquered Greece, with all that they harmed.

[Col. 1442C] You conquer, and are enemy and terror alike to all enemies,

Skilled in resistance, ready to repel every forceful attack.

Then money, and soon pride, are conceived—

Two shameful companions, following one another.

Stop believing that you conquer yourself while you believe

That by conquering brave things and harming the conquered, you harm yourself.

Former wars supplied the first seeds of madness;

Money, the first of evils, infects everything seized.

Moderation stands and perishes, and greed raises its head.

You will have a heap of bronze, a larger house, a more numerous retinue, and a slave.

Worn palaces and rich temples—a richer age

Desires to rise for itself, no longer knowing how to set limits for itself.

The royal structure strives to take away from those below,

The stars from birds in flight, the sea from fish, the fields from farmers;

Its table is now more capacious than before and gleams with bronze;

[Col. 1442D] It scorns even to possess an earthen vessel, as though useless.

Thus a city given over to shameful expenditures has been ruined,

And, broken, stands above all things that previously stood through its deeds.

### II. To Countess A.

[Note: [Col. 1441D] Perhaps Countess Adela of Blois.]

*(From a Tours manuscript.)*

Offspring of Augustus, exalted in the succession of your forebears,

I pray that these trifles sent to you may please you.

[Col. 1443A] I do not wish hands made for sceptres, or a neck suited to a crown,

To bend to my gifts; favour them in your mind.

As it is enough for a people to have earned the favour of the gods above,

When a small sacrifice falls before great gods,

So your favour fulfils my prayer. I err beyond humanity

If I seek more than to have pleased you.

1366 ### III. To the queen of England

[Note: [Col. 1443D] Perhaps Queen Matilda, not yet married to Henry I, king of the English; he had formerly preached before her and praises her highly for the outstanding endowments of her mind and body. [Col. 1444D]]

*(From Ebroicensis manuscript 19.)*

He who is usually more eloquent than Cicero before men

Is less fluent when he comes before gods;

Thus, though I speak eloquently before the common crowd,

Before your face I could say little.

I was struck dumb by your majesty, and, surveying your whole form

With wandering eye, I thought that I beheld a goddess.

Nature, less generous in polishing other girls,

[Col. 1443B] Deferred being lavish until your endowments.

Upon you she poured out her riches, and, seeing the marvellous work,

Wondered that her own hands had been capable of it.

She made [perhaps: *was able to make*] gods in countenance and parents in mind,

Whom men thereafter have never had as gods.

And, what I marvel at more, she created you beautiful and chaste,

Than which this sex can possess nothing greater.

Although sex, wealth, birth, age, and beauty exert their claims,

Nothing delights you as queen except honourable things.

Though a virgin and alone, you conquer countless enemies.

You conquer what no virgin can conquer.

And because no man had been worthy of so great a spouse,

God, himself a virgin, joined you, virgin, to himself as bride.

Let it not shame you, queen, that I speak your praises,

[Col. 1443C] And permit yourself to be called my lady.

### IV. In praise of England, its king Henry I, and his future bride, the queen

*(From the same manuscript.)*

England, fruitful land, lasting peace has given you rest,

And rich commerce abundant luxury.

You are neither constricted by excessive frost nor burning beneath the star;

You please by your mild sky and temperate climate.

When mother Nature bore things forth, and with varied favour

Distributed her gifts among all places,

She chose the better part for you and, declaring herself your mother,

Said: “May you be a wealthy island, full of peace.

Whatever luxury loves, whatever use desires,

Will arise from you or come to you from elsewhere.

[Col. 1443D] For a fortunate ship will seek and find you with merchandise,

Though you lie hidden beneath the western sun.

The time will come when Henry shall govern the sceptres promised to you,

No less a king than his grandfather or his father.

Under this king peace will belong to the Church, reverence to law,

Judgment to vice, glory to worthy deeds.

Under this king the robber will fear even to remember robbery.

Under this king nothing but honourable conduct will be safe.

Hence I purpose to provide him a partner of the bed, in whom I prepare

Whatever virtue recognises as its own in a woman.

And lest she draw a stain from fault or from her parents’ stock,

She will have the blood of kings, with a just parent on either side.

[Col. 1444A] She will be one whom purple and court will seek,

1367 To whom modesty, driven from the world, will flee for refuge.

She will be one whom the king and royal offspring will seek,

Whom Caesar will applaud as wife, mother, and mother-in-law.

She will be one who lives and devotes herself to honourable things;

She will bear few pledges to a husband, many to God.

She will be one who will enliven crown by majesty,

Sceptres by her hand, gems by her gleaming mouth.

With cheeks suffused by that spirit which the world adores,

She will bear spring in her face; her breast will contain laws.

With these rulers I shall make you blessed, England;

What remains I do not wish to reveal to you.

### V. On England and its prince

England, now lowly, once glory of lands,

Tosses and lies sunk with her helmsman sunk.

[Col. 1444B] She who shone with titles of praise throughout the whole world

Suffers eclipse, abandoned by her sun.

With his death she dies; while he was safe she passed her days

In safety; standing while he stood, she falls when he falls.

By laws he restrained frauds, by arms hostile foes,

Gentle with the appeased, mastering the untamed.

Happy in command, he used it happily enough,

A lover of peace, renowned in generosity, mighty in war.

At his death honour died, and there perish

Leisure, the peace of laws, sanction, rights, and faith.

Now seas lack ships, forums laws [perhaps: *ships*], fields farmers,

The common people protection, the clergy honour.

Now the judge renews [perhaps: *repeats*] perjuries, the tyrant wars,

[Col. 1444C] The thief his dagger, the robber his weapons, and the *cylix* [Note: [Col. 1444D] That is, pirate.] his ship.

Therefore England mourns the fall of so great a man,

And, cast down by his headlong fall, falls headlong herself.

### VI. On Matilda, virtuous queen of the English

*(From the aforesaid manuscript of Saint-Marien at Auxerre.)*

Daughter of a past king, wife of a present king, mother

Of a future king: this distinction is yours.

Hardly, or never, is a woman found who is at once

Daughter, wife, and parent of kings.

Your nobility neither began with you nor

Will end in you; after you it will live, as it existed before.

Nor do you degenerate: truly a daughter of your mother,

She bore you such as she herself was.

Chaste, she bore a chaste daughter; beautiful, a lovely one; prudent, a cautious one;

Generous, a generous one; religious, a devout one.

[Col. 1444D] A rose comes from the root of a rose; from religion,

Religion; from piety piety flows.

From a star comes splendour, and from a great name something greater.

One kingdom belonged to your father; two belong to you.

The English venerate you as queen; the people

Of the Normans as countess; each nation calls you lady.

You do not come untrained to sceptres; your birth confers experience.

To reign is yours; the realm is your paternal possession.

You reign by nature; all the rest of the crowd by fortune:

These grant you a kingdom; fortune grants it to others.

No woman is more powerful in the kingdom; none is your equal

[Col. 1445A] In beauty; all are your inferior in religion.

Thus, queen, you order your morals and actions,

That in them there is nothing more or less than what is just.

Can you harm? You do not wish it. Are you offended? You forgive freely.

Do you see sad things? You sympathise.

Do you wish to give? You do not delay. Do you wish to live sparingly? You do not know how.

If you speak, your speech has the weight of merit.

If you are silent, there is gravity; if you smile, your smile is honourable.

Do you pray? Your cheeks are wet with a suppliant’s tears.

Do you fast? You rejoice. Do you eat? You will never be satisfied.

Whatever you do, you have the bridle of sobriety.

Within, simplicity adorns your mind; without, dignity adorns

Your face: each is pleasing, and together more pleasing still.

1368 ### VII. He praises a certain virgin highly skilled in verse, and asks her to console him, placed in exile, with the gift of her poems

*(From Ebroicensis manuscript 19.)*

[Col. 1445B]

Ancient times boasted ten Sibyls,

And yours was a sex of great glory.

The present age delights in the genius of one woman

And is not altogether without a virgin prophetess.

Even now there are certain exchanges between mortals and gods;

I think—and do not err—that they speak through a virgin’s mouth.

The gods have placed their awe-inspiring sanctuary in your mind

And established you as their sacred prophetess.

Whatever comes from your mouth surpasses the wakeful labours of the ancients

And is inferior only to the gods.

Whatever you breathe forth is immortal, and the world

Admires your work as divine.

[Col. 1445C] You surpass in talent renowned bards and poets,

And both sexes marvel at your eloquence.

As I repeatedly read over the poems sent me,

I marvel and think them come from the inner sanctuaries.

It is not human to be able to produce labours so sacred.

I believe not that you speak, but that divine powers speak through you.

The weight of your words, the depth of meaning, order, and grace

Bear the countenance of divine knowledge.

While I marvel at the majesty with which they protect themselves,

I remember less keenly the sad burden of exile.

Perhaps you do not know it; but while I defend what is honourable,

While I uphold the duties of the sacred order, I am driven into exile.

You can lighten the cares of exile and the harsh weight of my labours,

Virgin, by your poetry.

[Col. 1445D] I pray you, lighten them, and do not yourself, as companion,
