Wish to abandon to fortune one whom fortune has abandoned.

Do not deny me words; I can ask for nothing lighter,

And I hope for nothing from you if you deny me words.

Unless perhaps you refuse the service of an exile,

As an exile I strive everywhere to serve you.

### VIII. On the birth and death of a certain monstrous child

*(From a Tours manuscript.)*

While the wife of Tiresias swelled with a full womb,

She consulted the gods about what the swelling was destined to be.

Phoebus said, “It will be a man”; Venus said, “It will become a woman.”

Neptune said, “No: a girl and a boy.”

The event answered their words: she conceived, and a child—

Woman, man, neither—was born, everything at once.

He or she was—I know not what thing—two while alone.

[Col. 1446A] Neither, both, child, woman: nothing more.

Before this child had yet left the flowering years,

He himself consulted the gods about his death.

Venus foretold that he would perish by a noose, Mars by a weapon,

Neptune by water. Each prediction carried weight.

A pine was host to water; the child climbed up; a sword

Which he carried slipped by chance, and he himself slipped with it.

His foot became prey to the branch, the sword pierced his breast,

The water submerged his head: one person dies three times.

There are three causes of death: branch, sword, and water.

What the one holds binds; this kills; that one weighs down.

His hanging foot, pierced side, and submerged head remain fast:

The branch holds him, the point pierces him, the stream kills him.

The strap binds his breast, the hook his head, the point [binds] his side in the flood:

The branch, blade, and stream bind, enter, and act.

### IX. On the death of a man, a beast, and a serpent

*(From the same source.)*

[Col. 1446B]

By chance a man was traversing a wood; by chance a well-fed beast was returning;

By chance a hidden serpent lay on the ground.

The rustic directed his eye and spear together at the beast;

The hand recognised the arrow once it had been shot.

The spear strikes down the beast; the beast crushes the serpent; the serpent

Pours forth poison; by that poison the man is killed.

By devouring bones, trampling the ground, and vomiting venom,

The man by javelin, the boar by foot, the viper by poison, inflicts harm.

Wounded, crushed, struck by missile, foot, and venom,

The beast, viper, and man are cast down, wither, and die.

### X. Epitaph of Seneca

*(From the same source.)*

[Col. 1446C] Care, labour, merit, honours received as recompense,

Go and trouble other souls after this.

God calls me far from you; depart, your business completed.

Farewell, earth, a stranger to earthly things.

Yet receive my body in your greedy bosom;

For we render the soul to heaven, the bones to you.

### XI. On the hermaphrodite

*(From the same source.)*

While my mother bore me, pregnant, in her womb,

She is said to have consulted the gods as to what she would bear.

Phoebus said, “It is a boy”; Mars, “a girl”; and Juno, “neither.”

Now that I was born, I was a hermaphrodite.

When I asked about death, the goddess said: “He will die by weapons”;

[Col. 1446D] Mars said, “by a cross”; Phoebus, “by water.” Each fate proved true.

A tree shades the water; I climb it; a sword slips,

Which I had brought with me by chance, and I myself slip through toil.

My foot caught in the branches, my head fell into the stream; and I underwent,

Man, woman, neither, waters, weapons, and a cross.

### XII. On opposites

*(From the same source.)*
Turbulent winter spoils the flower, night the light, a phantom beauty;

dryness the dew, death life, the raven the swan.

Sadness laughter, labour leisure, Styx Paradise,

the owl the peacock, the wolf the lamb, Davus Adonis.

## XIII. To Hugh

Whenever you write to me, you are accustomed, Hugh, to beg me in humble entreaties not to reveal your written words to anyone.

Do not be afraid: through me your secrets shall never be disclosed;

when I reread them, I cannot tell what they themselves mean.  

[Col. 1447A]

## XIV. + On Lucretia

When Lucretia pierced her chaste breast with a sword,

and a torrent of blood was flowing out, she said:

“Let my blood, before my husband, bear witness that I did not yield to the tyrant;

let my spirit, before the gods, bear witness.

How rightly shall the two, brought forth by me after my death, speak:

the one among the shades below, the other among those above!”

## XV. On the Miserly Promiser

(From Royal manuscript Ebr. 274.)

You burden everyone with promises, man, but only a few with gifts;

though your hand is miserly, your tongue is lavish.

Your mouths open wider with promises than your right hand with gifts;

how much better to give much and say little.

You promise what you possess, what you do not possess, and what you never will possess;

[Col. 1447B]

1370

you give anything, everything, to anybody—and give nothing.

This man asks for this: you promise this; that man asks for that: you promise that.

“This I keep for myself,” you say; “take all the rest for yourself.”

You either promise three things to one person, or one thing to three;

yet the three, or the one, have nothing.

What you promise three times, you do not give even once; yet you yourself

give to three and to yourself: the thing to yourself, the words to the three.

You will be an idle slave: you do not lift your mind from your chest;

the chest becomes the narrow measure of a mind fixed there.

Your right hand distrusts your left hand,

and keeps the suspect left from taking what is its own.

You set the left hand crookedly against the right and the right against the left,

dividing your eyes between alternating watches.

## XVI. Riddle

(From the same Royal manuscript.)

[Col. 1447C]

Abundance advanced three men with a threefold honour;

thus advanced, it joined the three in a threefold love.

[Col. 1448A]

Thus the three were one, because one love united the three;

thus love unites the three, so that nothing but death may separate them.

In them the third life becomes the model of the other two,

and, in reverse, shines by the light of those two.

They are mirrors to one another and offer reciprocal examples,

and the three owe to one another, in turn, that which they are as three.

Happy are those for whom, in a better zeal,

the third life warms the other two, and honour does not decay through honour.

Honour serves them well, because none serves honour;

rightly does he hold the staff for whom the staff is no object of fear.

Happy is he whose honour swells because of its possessor,

when glory yields, not to him, but from him.

## XVII. Conclusion of Hildebert’s Metrical Works; Perhaps Composed When He Was About to Cross from England into France

(From a manuscript codex, formerly of Saint-Amand [Elnone], now Royal manuscript no. 274, approximately five hundred years old.)

[Col. 1448B]

Thus far, O Muses—enough of sleep, and enough of being employed—

I pray you, breathe favourably as we enter the sea.

May the sky be free of cloud; smooth the sea; raise the sail;

mast and breeze, do not begrudge the ship its making.

May the wind fill the sails; may the pine-built vessel float on a placid sea—

she who, trusting too little in herself, entered the peril of the waters.

Every firm hall rests upon its own columns.

The chariot’s course is made surer by the charioteer’s skill.

The vine touches the ground if it ceases to touch the elm.

I am the ship and the vine; be you the elm and the sailor.

Be you my road, my wall, my south wind, my Palinurus.

Raise the trumpet, Clio; Calliope, entrust to me your offices;

sweat and breathe upon me with all your divine power.

[Col. 1448C]

Behold, we enter the waters. Come then, you two sailors:

I beg you, distribute your tasks, cautiously directing each thing.

Come, most learned Clio, sound the horn;

and you, touch the strings with your fingers, and then with song.

[Col. 1447]

# SUPPLEMENT TO HILDEBERT’S POEMS (G)*

## + I. Verses on the Destruction of Troy

(Edited from a manuscript codex of the Pauline Library at Leipzig by Polycarp LEYSER, *Historia poetarum medii aevi*, p. 398. Halle and Magdeburg, 1721, octavo.)

[Col. 1447C]

In wealth, kingdom, appearance, valour, and triumphs,

King Priam was illustrious in his famous city.

While the king, while the nobles, while Troy’s Pergamum stood—

she who was the glory, beauty, and head of the world—

the king took Hecuba as his consort, equal to him in nobility,

omens, beauty, wealth, love, and throne.

By her he received sons. Among them was Hector,

the greatest, and in war like a thunderbolt.

Fiercer than a wild beast, fiercer than a bear, fiercer than a lion;

[Col. 1447D]

thus was he, almost beyond all beasts, fiercer than beasts.

O fortunate king in his sons! O fortunate husband!

Had she not also borne Paris for him.

In him she bore not a pledge, but weapons and fires—

evils for herself, for Priam, and for all their people.

By this son falls the father, the mother, the company of brothers, and Hector;

[Col. 1448C]

by this son also falls Troy, the glory of the kingdom.

When his mother was about to bear Paris, she saw in dreams:

instead of a boy, she saw herself give birth to a torch.

When the king then perceived the meaning of the sign, he shuddered

that he was preparing to be impious toward his own offspring.

For, by the king’s command, servants taking up the newborn child

prepared to kill him on Ida with the sword.

But as the child looked upon the glittering, flashing sword,

he smiled at the blade, unaware of death by the sword.

When the man about to strike saw this, his heart and his blow were softened;

at once both savage and striker he ceased to be.

He left him alive beneath the leaves; a wandering shepherd

found him, as he had lately been covered with leaves.

Seeing him sound, alive, and handsome,

[Col. 1448D]

he drew him out, looked upon him, nourished him, adopted him, and kept him.

When, grown up, he tended the shepherd’s sheep as a shepherd,

Juno, Minerva, and Venus came to him.

They seek Paris’ judgment as to which is the fairest.

They also promise him each her own gifts.

Juno offers splendour; Pallas strength; Cytherea a maiden;

[Col. 1449A]

but he granted victory to Venus, conquered by her.

When the king one day saw him so distinguished and so handsome,

and learned the truth from servants confessing the truth,

he restored Paris to equal honour with his brothers.

Moved by love, the father either regards his mother’s dreams as vain

or strives to turn their truth to a favourable meaning.

Thus neither counsel, nor events, nor royal power,

nor gods above nor human beings, can alter fate.

But Venus, repaying blame for the praise she had received,

warns him, drives him, burns him with a new fire.

“What is this, Paris? Why do you change colour together with your heart?

Thus the lover stands, thus speaks, thus meditates.

Venus’ promise moves you, and Helen’s beauty,

[Col. 1449B]

whom she will give you as a reward, but a reward for praise.

Her beauty, rank, bloodline, and age have moved you.

Yet she does not merely move you: she binds; indeed, she does not merely bind: she draws you.

You desire her, burn for her, seek utterly to possess her—

her whom law, the Danaans, and your fates deny you.

Why a woman joined to a husband? Why a royal wife?

Why one unknown to your people? Why does a Greek woman please you?

Why not rather a pleasing young maiden? Why not

Venus herself, whom you judged beautiful?

Why do you thus wholly degenerate, though born into arms?

That you may not so degenerate, remember Hector.

Do you not, wretch, reckon it wretched? Do you not feel shame

[Col. 1449C]

that you alone should belong to Venus rather than to Pallas?

Let soft love yield to love for your country’s valour.

Weapons alone become Hector’s brother.

Therefore follow the spirit and arms of your spirited brother:

love what he loves; do what he does.

First conquer Venus, if you wish to be a manly knight:

no one can give himself to both arms and Venus.

It is neither glory, worth, nor honour to overcome a girl;

but to overcome Venus’ vice is a work of praise.

Do not now seek Venus in vain, but Minerva’s camp.

She teaches; the other rages. She helps; the other harms.

Come now to your senses, Paris, and leave the ships prepared.

Obeying counsel, come now to your senses, Paris.

[Col. 1449D]

Since love is forbidden, the act of forbidden love is evil.

If it is evil, it harms; if it harms, flee it.

Its beginning is crime, its middle fear, its end fire:

flee, reject, and guard against it through fear.

But, conquered by conceived desire, you cannot avoid

preparing, whatever you plan, a ruin equal to it.

Your fates draw you so that you cannot abandon your undertaking;

your deeds draw you so that you may carry off Helen.

Such is every lover: he despises himself and everything—

counsel, reputation, treaties, laws, gods.

This love, so headlong, blind, impetuous,

and devoid of reason, knows no measure.

This love is mad, hostile to others and to itself;

it is not love, but crime—or rather, not crime, but madness.

[Col. 1450A]

Therefore he equips ships, crosses the sea, and seeks his beloved.

He carries her off, enjoys her, and wickedly keeps her in security.

The guards, overcome either by force, gift, or prayer,

or by death, concealment, or fear, perish.

When King Menelaus heard this, raging with anger,

he scarcely restrained his hand from striking with the sword.

He weeps, thunders, raves, gnashes his teeth, groans, boils, burns;

he accuses the gods above, the walls, fate, and the sea.

For he hates life and, at once, life’s consolations:

wealth, rest, pleasures, sceptres, food.

He would rather die himself than have the adulterer not die;

thus he reckons himself nothing without what is his.

He devises, sets in motion, and yearns for Troy’s destruction,

because he judges Paris’ death alone too little.

He regards as enemies all the friends of his enemy,

[Col. 1450B]

and everything whatever that belongs to Paris.

Sending envoys, therefore, he gathers forces from every side;

everyone able to bear arms prepares to obey him.

The injury to the king touches high and low alike,

and everyone judges it his own.

Though they suffer both from the king’s grief and their own,

shame at the woman’s abduction presses them more than grief.

All Greece conspires against all Phrygia,

so that Paris may perish together with his country.

With joined troops and companies of infantry,

the spirited king orders an advance against Paris.

Leading a thousand ships, he makes for Ilium, besieges it,

rushes on, resolved quickly either to conquer or to die.

Trojan youth bravely resists the Danaans,

[Col. 1450C]

and on each side they inflict and receive savage slaughter.

While sure victory hangs in uncertainty,

for a long time fortune flies as though equal between the two.

Now these, now those, in reversed turn seem to endure

ambushes, blows, wounds, losses, and flight.

Beyond the common hazards, the Achaeans suffer

many things: hunger, rain, cold, heat, thirst.

The haughty Aeacid asks Philoctetes for his mighty arrows,

that Pergamum may be able to be taken.

Accordingly, on the prophets’ counsel, the Danaans seek them for themselves;

by these Hector’s fury falls, and by these Paris himself falls.

The Trojans’ fortune in war stood better while Hector stood,

for he was the city’s hope, shield, and strength.

But when the fierce Aeacid came and conquered Hector,

the Trojans’ strength was conquered when its defender was conquered.

[Col. 1450D]

How great the Aeacid was, what manner of man he was, and whence he came,

many pages of the author’s work reveal and teach.

If you ask after Achilles’ strength, mind, and wars,

let me teach it in few words: he was greater than Hector.

In the Danaan camp Palamedes, Nestor, and Ulysses

are commanders more by counsel than by valour.

The Aeacid, Ajax, Diomedes, Pyrrhus, and the Atrid:

these are the flower, light, and summit of excellence.

What of Sthenelus? What of the son of Testor? What of Protesilaus?

Why should I recount more, whom their own fame recounts?

Who can enumerate the Dolopes, the Myrmidons, or finally all

the nobles of the Greek-born peoples?

At last the king of the Danaans takes Troy by force, by deeds, and by that

[Col. 1451A]

Palladium, after two periods of five years.

Once it has been taken, by deceit, skill, and arms,

they kill Priam and the sons of Priam alike.

And lest the city’s glory remain, they ravage everything else:

the sword destroys men, the battering ram walls, fire houses.

Yet Troy’s capture, conquest, and overthrow were wholly accomplished

by the craft of Sinon and a little wooden horse.

Famous Troy, through the Danaans’ strength, craft, and threats,

after twice five years is made a pyre and ashes by the Greeks’ ruin.

A noble city, now thickets, by the violence of fire and the whirlwind of smoke,

settled upon the ground—though not deserving to be consumed thus.

By Juno’s nod, the fraud of treacherous Sinon,

and secretly given gifts, she was stripped of her goods.

Penelope’s husband, after enduring sea and Cyclopean monsters,

[Col. 1451B]

carried Laomedon’s wealth away to the Dolopes.

Paris, the conflagration of his country, and Troy, head and flower of Phrygia and Asia, lie fallen because he judged goddesses’ beauty.

When the shepherd obeyed Venus, he offended Juno;

when he sat as judge, he gave you so many disasters.

Ruined Troy teaches men to beware of loving rashly:

through Paris’ crime she becomes almost nothing.

The shattered houses of Priam’s sons and of kings fell.

Where now are the countless towers? Beneath ashes.

Where there were temples and houses of armour-bearing Pallas,

ivy stretches out its arms into woodland haunts.

The wrath of the Atrids was kindled by the abduction of Tyndareus’ daughter,

and Paris’ love brought war upon the descendants of Dardanus.

The beauty of the obscene Lacedaemonian mistress stirred

[Col. 1451C]

the hearts of the Trojan-born to unrestrained crime.

Thus Helen’s beauty was the end of the lovely city:

her hair, neck, cheeks, and all things finely adorned.

How love makes men bold and reckless to their own harm!

It hungers after biting cares and flames.

While you, Helen, wickedly please and your enticing nods seduce,

though you yourself are flames, Ilium thereafter lies in flames.

O fateful thing, destructive to all!

Alas, such a woman was the cause of such evils.

More worthy to perish at sea and be burned in flames

than that so many should be deprived of light and given to wild beasts.

The king, proclaiming the time of war among the Danaans,

burns to separate the bed shared by the two.

The fame of offended chastity aids and increases the avenger’s cause:

[Col. 1451D]

it complains that the abducted woman lies in the bed of her abductor.

This matter moves Peleus’ son to accompany the Atrid;

the same moves the Aeolids against Paris.

The Greek-born swear; Mycenae swears to wage war;

the camp is full of young men and old.

Hector by counsel, divine Tritonian Pallas by her nod,

Peleus’ son by the sword, bring the Phrygians into exile.

A faithful defence of the city stood in Hector; while he

stood, the strength of the Dardanians was mighty.

When he fell to Peleus’ son’s spear, Ida was at once deprived of him;

the Dardanians then pursued battle in trembling.

The city of Assaracus falls, delivered to devouring flames;
the life of [Rhesus] the Thracian is taken by the Ithacan’s tricks. [The supplied *Vita res, o Thraci* is grammatically damaged; “Rhesus” is a contextual conjecture.]

It would have stood, had death not overcome the Thracian;

and, lying fallen, the royal city would have obeyed commands.

[Col. 1452A]

Indeed, the art of Cytherea cannot prevent the ruin of Ida’s realm,

nor can the house of Aeneas remain safe through the goddess’s favour.

Nor could Greek force break royal majesty,

but deceit did, and the horse brought inside the walls.

While Sinon begs pardon and colours his words,

he is unbound; he explores and bores through gates and doors.

Those whom he knew were outside he admits; while he labours at crime,

and investigates the matter, flame devours the walls.

With pasture taken away and guards slaughtered,

the city, grievously miserable, yielded to fate.

A city all too miserable—indeed rich in abundant resources,

famous and lofty—became one of the least.

O unrestrained madness! Neptune’s Troy lay exposed to punishments,

betrayed to the Greek-born by a young man’s deceit.

Then flame casts down the dwellings and palaces of kings.

[Col. 1452B]

From one side cavalry rushes to slaughter; from the other infantry.

One can scarcely credit how many thousands the Atrid,

Ajax, the son of Tydeus, Pyrrhus, and Achilles’ son laid low,

while they press on savagely with the sword, as Troy shines with flames,

putting leaders to death who had endured chains and crosses.

Every armed man lies open to the first impiety.

By the sequence of fate, they are commanded to suffer so many evils.

Boys, young men, and stern old men are slaughtered;

every crime, whatever crime is, is permitted.

The race of Assaracus, the race of Ilus, lies under hostile violence.

Its household gods lie in a lowly place, amid swift fire.

Then you might see gems, ivory, and purple cloth become ashes;

then you might see Danaans swift to crime.

Seeing so many little children, so many women,

so many nobles, and so many aged men slain—

[Col. 1452C]

the king of kings’ heir perished together with Hecuba, sorrows enough to tear one’s body apart. That you may grieve, surpass them [reading uncertain].

I should be another Homer, or greater than Homer himself,

if I could write the number of so many fleets.

As the matter shows, Phoebus had laid the foundations,

and the ploughshare, marking out the walls, had traced the site.

The famous work which the king had built becomes a haunt of waters,

a lair of lionesses, and a forest scarcely safe.

The halls of kites, the place and den of wolves,

are the temples, theatres, and forum; the grazing-grounds are for cattle.

Because the hooks of Cypris increase the vice of the marriage-bed,

brambles and reeds hold Priam’s kingdom.

Because glory was accorded to the ridge of Ida,

thus the anger of the god brought destruction upon it.

While you, Troy, fall in the crisis of so great a disaster,

[Col. 1452D]

you entrust Aeneas, yourself, and a ship, and depart.

And provident Venus withdrew this offspring from the ruin.

No deceits harmed this house alone at all.

A long age had promised you the borders of Hesperia.

Your piety preserves you, that you may seek new kingdoms.

By the violence of a storm, when your companions had been thinned,

the transmitted reading says that Paris carried you by fate over long seas [the reading is problematic].

And, when you emerge from the straits and have completed your voyage,

you seek from a wise woman the resting place that has been won.

The Cumaean Sibyl, a stranger driven by unhallowed impulses,

sings the fates owed to the Trojans:

how great the preparations of the Rutulians will be, how great the glory of Iulus will rise,

what royal titles, kingdoms, and peoples there will be.

Therefore, firm in hope, faithful Achates,

[Col. 1453A]

you steer your broad ship toward the fields of Hesperia.

You wage very many wars while seeking places due to you;

but, trusting in the gods above, you crush all that opposes you.

When Turnus, proud and threatening fate to you and yours,

fell prostrate as you pierced his side with the sword,

the royal maiden for whom war was waged is declared yours,

and peace is restored when she is given to you in marriage.

From this union came those who founded Rome;

as they wage war, they accomplish every brave deed.

They made for themselves a name that they raised to the stars,

as those who wrote ancient deeds report.

And Rome, greatest of things, lifts up her turreted head,

both by the gift of the gods above and by the endeavours of her nobles.

Thus Roman trophies grow from Aeneas.

Thus the Roman race rises from the race of Hector.

## + II. Verses of a Husband against His Wife

(From the edition of the works of Philip, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance. Douai, 1621, folio, p. 799.)

A certain merchant, travelling in hope of profit, left his wife at home; she was taken into a sharing of the bed by another trader. She refused him; then, because of her chastity, he loved her so greatly that, when he was overcome by death, he made her heir to his property. But on returning, her husband suspected adultery and brought her before judges on a charge, speaking thus:

[Col. 1453B]

Nothing is rarer on earth than a woman conscious of rectitude;

no known mark identifies one faithful to her husband.

I see none who is either pure as snow in cleanliness,

bright as a mirror of faith, or without stain.

[Col. 1453C]

And though a woman should cast off her womanly sex,

she will not, nevertheless, cast off the tunic of deceit.

For neither will a washed crow lay aside its colour,

nor will a washed brick be without mud.

This woman proves in deeds what I proclaim in words:

she is a crow, she is a brick, and cannot be washed.

I have always tried to wipe away her habitual filth,

but the accustomed smell always clings to the vessel.

I cut off the head of one vice, but two arise;

the hydra becomes more fertile through its own loss.

So great a crop of vice springs from this hydra

as not even Hercules’ sword could mow down.

“But,” you say, “her simple appearance pleases.” I answer:

water without movement is accustomed to be treacherous.

[Col. 1453D]

This is the simplicity that conceals deceit: outwardly

it flatters with its face; secretly it nourishes fraud.

And lest the affair and method of fraud be concealed from you: behold,

I shall portray to you both the thing and the method of deceit.

The purple of violets had woven a garment over the meadows,

and the proud forest had curled its own hair.

The rose had already begun to prepare to burst out from its leaves,

and the bird sang in the green foliage.

To speak briefly: spring smiled with rosy face,

and the breeze had begun to flatter my ship.

I depart; I prepare ships, purchase merchandise, gather treasures,

bind packages, and plough the sea.

I am tossed on the sea; my wife, my companion, is absent; I sweat, she rests;

I trade, she commits adultery; I swim, she spins; I wander, she lies in bed.

I entrust my vessel to you, wave; my bride to you, marriage-bed:

[Col. 1454A]

may this preserve my life, and that preserve her fidelity.

O strange thing! The wave lacks deceit; my wife lacks fidelity:

safe at sea, I am shipwrecked at home.

My bride violated faith: iron bars do not protect beautiful women,

nor can beauty be safe even in a fortress.

Another Jupiter rained gold into Danaë’s lap;

she brought another Jupiter down to earth.

The adulterer is present and draws her after him in golden nets,

but she first drew the young man to herself by love.

She captures the young man by beauty; the young man captures her by gold;

and the woman becomes the prey of her own prey.

In a strange reversal, prey preys upon prey, the burned burns,

the captured captures, the injured injures, the desired desires.

Nor am I surprised if the adulterer fixed his eye or love upon her:

beauty is accustomed to plunder eyes.

Who, having seen Helen’s cheeks, would refuse to be Paris?

Who, having seen the Gorgon, would delay in becoming stone?

Love and beauty are companions, shame the enemy of both;

where shame is, love is—but shame, an exile, is absent.

What more? She received the adulterer under her roof and into her bed;

[Col. 1454B]

the adulteress strives to prepare house and bed for the guest.

Lest you think that my allegation wavers without a witness,

this will stand as the firm pillar of my case.

I have with me witnesses: the adulterer and adulteress. Marked

by these marks in each, each establishes the charge.

He was deceptive, rich, generous, and a trader;

she alone was beautiful, rapacious, and fickle.

He practised deceit by guile; as a rich man, he brought gold;

as a generous man, he poured out wealth; and as a trader, he bought her.

A witness firmer than all others is added: a written

page, inscribed by the adulterer’s hand, indicating the fact.

There the adulterer declares: “While my affairs are flourishing,

let this woman take the place of my heir.”

Would he have permitted her to flourish in his own affairs

if he had seen his own hope withering?

But I know that the young man ploughed not the shore but the bed:

he sowed and reaped in my field.

Therefore I complain; I beg for aid. Court,

with the healing finger of counsel, wipe clean my wound.

## + III. The Wife’s Reply

(Found in the same place, p. 800.)

Slander brands the titles of chastity with a charge of guilt;

thus injured modesty appeals to you, judge.

[Col. 1454D]

A new case summons me; I come; accusations assail me;

I clear myself; guilt wounds me; I resist the stigma.

I plead a case that deserves belief; I am tested though deserving praise and protection;

I am wounded: that harms me, that burdens me, this oppresses me.

My husband prosecutes; my companion defames; my friend wounds:

hence deceit, hence shame, hence crime.

In a husband, devotion had pledged a husband’s love;

but unforeseen fraud breaks faith already broken.

I am astonished at this wound, but more astonished at the striker;

the charge harms me, but the author of the charge harms me more.

Beneath laurel, yew; beneath fig, poison; beneath hope,

I find groaning; beneath devotion, deceit.

Nor is it surprising: the simple dove is often snared,

and the simple turtle-dove falls by the fowler’s art.

[Col. 1455A]

Yet if the scab of this accusation defames me,

this man will suffer public harm from my illness.

Therefore he injures, condemns, and crushes himself

when I am called a she-wolf, a harlot, violent.

But lest the truth be darkened by this rust,

I make it plain, crush the accusers, and suppress falsehood.

When spring first began to grow young,

this man entrusted his property, his life, and his ship to the sea.

He leaves me, but does wrong because I am left alone;

he ploughs the sea, but sins because I alone am sought.

A woman, married, fearful, a suppliant, I am left widowed;

a man, husband, guardian, guide, companion—he flees away.

I live a woman, but no Thaïs; a wife, but no adulteress;

a suppliant, yet chaste; bereft, yet serene.

While the babbling breeze murmurs in my husband’s sails,

[Col. 1455B]

my care then sickens with wretched fear.

While he swims, I fear shipwreck; while he has endured sorrows, I fear disaster;

while he sings, I fear, shipwrecked, sorrowful, falling.

While I am troubled, a young foreigner desires a beautiful woman left alone;

the beautiful woman pleases, is sought while alone, and, when sought, refuses.

That I shine beautiful is nature’s fault; that I am desired, the lover’s fault;

that I alone am sought, this man causes.

He approaches: I flee. He flatters: I refuse. He promises:

I fight him; he offers: I condemn; he labours: I depart.

Though a woman, I am not overcome as one lowly; though a wife, I do not comply;

though beautiful, I do not commit adultery, I do not yield; therefore he is amazed.

He wishes, but does not violate; he desires, but does not possess; he dares,

but does not rejoice. Hence he departs, he dies, and goes into his house.

When fate oppresses him, he seals us as his heirs,

either because I pleased him or because I was chaste.

[Col. 1455C]

Wealth is given: should I flee? Estates are given me: should I refuse?

If I flee, I am cowardly; if I refuse, I am known as foolish.

I do not flee gifts; I do not refuse what has been given, for to refuse

what is given is held to be insane modesty.

Thus I mourn alone, am sought because beautiful, reject when solicited,

possess happily; yet these things do not harm me.

But if I am denied truthfulness, my truthful neighbour, as witness,

will swear that my fidelity did not fall.

Sighing modesty is expiring; but under your guidance, judge,

may it breathe again and flourish, and may the honour of law flourish under your guidance.

## + IV. The Judge’s Reply

(Found in the same place, p. 800.)

The truth is clear: the sentence of law reveals the truth.

She prevails: let her flourish. He is defeated: let him fall.

## + V. Epitaph of a Bishop of Sens

(Ibid., p. 801.)

[Col. 1455D]

Religion adorned his life; discernment his mind; the light of deeds his reputation;

reading his zeal; moderation his speech.

Law adorned his judgment; severity his justice; beauty his face;

piety his heart; the staff his hand.

Pope, count, and Christ advanced him, deprived him, and received him in exile—

in rank, in see, and in heaven.

Stripped of possessions, held by force, driven from his city,

the bishop endured poverty, chains, and exile.

Now rich, free, secure, he attains, follows, and possesses Christ as his reward:

this Peter reaches the stars.

## + VI. Epitaph of the Kings of Jerusalem

(Ibid., p. 802.)

With the nations expelled, the first brother and the second,

[Col. 1456A]

each a brave king in Jerusalem,

accomplished much: the former, but the latter more in his time;

for the brother was king briefly, this man long.

To enemies they were like lightning; to friends, like a wall;

within, peace and the strong sword prevailed.

In war enemies gave their backs; for peace they paid tribute;

the land did not follow greater men.

Churches were filled by clergy, the city by people, the countryside by farmers,

granaries by crops, and storehouses by wine.

## + VII. Epitaph of the Abbot of Clairvaux

(Ibid.)

The valleys are bright, but the abbot brighter than the bright valleys

gave them a bright name throughout the world.

Bright in ancestors, bright in merits, bright in honour,

still brighter in eloquence, and more so in religion.

[Col. 1456B]

His death is bright, his ashes bright, and his tomb bright;

his spirit rejoices more brightly before God.

## + VIII. Verses on Fortune’s Wheel

(Ibid., p. 803.)

I contemplate each thing, dwell on it, and mark its sum;

the marked sum teaches what each particular may be worth.

First good things follow, and with pleasing success

invite the man; he rejoices and enters.

To the man who enters, all things succeed with a kindly face,

and tranquillity, foster-child of the mind, flatters him.

That he may know, prevail, and live, the Fates labour;

you might suppose that the gods had conspired to fulfil his wishes.

Life approves, fortune prepares, nature supplies

sense, kingdoms, lineage: three furnish all things in three ways.

He binds, gathers, and fills

[Col. 1456C]

vines, fields, and houses; he sells, buys, seeks, finds, desires, possesses.

Gold plays upon his finger, and the finger is proud

of gold; each rejoices in the other.

He is at leisure in these things, clings to them, and seals his mind in gold;

evil love presses and forms the mind it burns.

Care burns the heart. Certainly I deem wretched those whose hearts

it burns; but this man is burned; therefore he is wretched.

Joy or grief, hope or fear—each augury

suggests, awaits, stands, and falls, miserable man.

Thus Fortune’s quivering reed toys with the mind;

she plays and cheats it, extending and withdrawing her hand.

Fortune promised her hand, lies, and takes everything away;

she becomes guilty, but is not ashamed to be guilty.

What was becoming grows pale; what flourished withers; what was green dries up;

what was is no more: the man departs.

## + IX. That the Arts Avail Little without Money

(Ibid.)

[Col. 1456D]

Though you surpass others in character, art, faith, and a heart worthy of heaven,

you are foolish nevertheless, Odo.

For you think that the people care for eloquent verses,

and suppose that you have pleased them by character, art, and faith.

Formerly sacred poets pleased by these gifts,

and talent gave rewards, name, and wealth.

Now the age is different and, with the age, morals different:

now virtue is hated; wealth earns sceptres.

Nothing are the arts, nothing pure faith, nothing the glory of speech,

nothing the spring of talent, nothing integrity without property.

No poor man is wise where wealth and abundance of possessions exist:

wealth is wise; the poor man will be nothing but poor.

[Col. 1457A]

The crimes of rich defendants do not take away their rank;

those whom the law condemns, wealth makes equal to gods.

Hence the people, worshipping gold as though it were a god,

often dare to enter unknown crime.

And the hope of profit has so often carried men beyond law and honour

that it is now advantageous to be guilty for nothing.

[Col. 1458A]

Law perishes, order perishes; men prefer to sell face and hand to crime,

and are as ashamed to be upright as they are poor.

It is not surprising if some wicked and senseless man

thinks that divine poets are of no account.

True wisdom has abandoned him whom riches accompany,

always unaccompanied by unstable goods.

# MARBOD, BISHOP OF RENNES

[Col. 1457]

## SHORT PREFACE TO THE LATEST EDITION OF THE SMALL WORKS OF MARBOD, BISHOP OF RENNES

Dom Antoine Beaugendre has related the country, origin, rank, life, and writings of Marbod, Bishop of Rennes, in the preliminary notice to the new edition of his small works. We have resolved to add nothing except a few very brief words concerning the notes and additions to this latest edition.

1. After the letters comes the *Book on the Three Enemies*, from P. Hommey’s *Supplement*, pp. 546–551.

2. After the *Life of St Magnobodus, Bishop of Angers*, and before the metrical *History of Theophilus*, we have added from the Bollandist source:

1. The *Life of St Walter, or Gautier*, abbot and canon of Stirp in the diocese of Limoges in Gaul. (BOLLANDISTS, 11 May.)

2. The *Life of St Florentius*. (Ibid., 22 September.)

3. Among the miscellaneous poems, and after the poem *On the Rape of Dinah*, we have appended certain pieces not previously published, extracted from manuscript codex no. 117 in the new catalogue and no. 164 in the old catalogue at Tours:

I. Commendation of Learning. II. Do Not Trust a Woman Too Much. III. The Theft of a Cock Proved by a Cock. IV. On a Certain Hervaeus. V. On a Leopard. VI. The Paternal House. VII. On Abbots Who Are Too Indulgent. VIII. On Aristotle. IX. Guarmundus. X. Poetic Trifles. XI. A Broken Vessel. XII. Eulogy of Milo, monk of Saint-Albin at Angers, later Bishop of Palestrina under Pope Urban II. We extracted the latter from the *Annals of the Benedictines*, vol. V, appendix, p. 670.

4. To *On the Ornaments of Words*, § I, *On Repetition*, after the two verses:

> You are to me king, law, light, guide, avenger;  
> I worship you, praise you, glorify you, and applaud you.

[Col. 1459]

We added six other unpublished verses from manuscript codex no. 117 at Tours. They are elegiacs, and in our codex immediately follow the foregoing verses.

5. In manuscript codex no. 222 of the old Tours catalogue and no. 656 of the new, the *Lapidary* is inscribed under Hildebert’s name as follows: “The booklet of Lord Hildebert, Bishop of Le Mans, on the various natures of stones.”

That codex, once belonging to the metropolitan church and now to the library of the city of Tours, is entered in the catalogue by Guillaume Jouan and Victor d’Avannes, canons of Tours, as an elegiac work. Hence the learned authors of the *Literary History of France*, vol. XI, p. 394, conjecture that Hildebert’s work *On Stones* differs from Marbod’s *Lapidary*. We, however, carefully compared the two works and found that the poem in the metropolitan Tours codex is not elegiac but hexametric, and agrees wholly with Marbod’s work published by Dom Antoine Beaugendre.

Our codex, unknown to the Benedictine editor, is of excellent authority and considerably fuller than the Majoret codex which he used. Thus, in chapter 30, *On Gerachite*, we found two verses not yet published. In chapter 19, *On the Magnet*, Dom Beaugendre incorrectly prints:

> *Est cui naturae vicinum tollere ferrum*  
> “There is one whose nature is akin to lifting iron,”

whereas the manuscript correctly reads:

> *Et vi naturae*  
> “And by the force of its nature.”

For chapter 1, *On the Diamond*, we supplied a note from Theophilus the monk, by which certain ambiguous or perhaps rather obscure words are readily explained.

Finally, after Marbod’s *Lapidary*, we supplied three charters. The first is drawn from the manuscript *History of Marmoutier near Tours*, by Dom Edmond Martène, vol. II, p. 58; the second from the papers of Dom Morice, vol. I, p. 516, of the *History of Brittany*; the third—which Dom Beaugendre obtained only after the edition of Marbod’s small works had been completed—he placed after Dom Loyauté’s notes, p. 59.

I. Marbod, Bishop of Rennes, gives to Marmoutier the church of Aienciac and half the priestly benefice of the church of Martiniac. II. Letter of Marbod, Bishop of Rennes, for the monastery of St Sergius at Angers. III. Charter of Marbod, Bishop of Rennes, by which, after expelling the irregular canons living there, he grants the church of St Mary at Vitré to the monks of St Melaine, establishing Benedictine monks in the canons’ place, together with several other churches and possessions.

At Tours, 13 September, on the feast of St Lidorus, Bishop of Tours.

J.-J. BOURASSÉ, canon of the Metropolitan Church of Tours.

[Col. 1459]

## PREFACE OF DOM BEAUGENDRE

1371–1378

It is fitting, benevolent reader, that we should give you an account of this new edition of Marbod, Bishop of Rennes, which we present. Our original purpose had been only to restore the works of the venerable Hildebert, insofar as our powers and resources allowed, in a more corrected form to that light which they had once enjoyed.

We were advised not to proceed further both by the inconveniences of advanced age and by the rarity of Marbod’s manuscripts; and, to confess frankly, an octogenarian old man may reasonably be pardoned for desiring to devote so small a rest to preparation for another life.

But, while comparing the works of our Hildebert with more than forty manuscript codices, we found some pieces intermingled in certain of them which belonged to Marbod; and conversely, since we were repeatedly compelled to examine Marbod’s small works and separate them from Hildebert’s, so many gradually and imperceptibly came into our hands that, on the one hand, we should have borne it only with great difficulty if they were lacking to the republic of letters through our negligence; and, on the other, some hope arose that it might perhaps be welcome to many learned persons if, whether from the few manuscripts of Marbod that we succeeded in finding or from a collection of those of his small works which various authors had published here and there, we attempted to produce an edition somewhat more accurate and fuller than that which had formerly issued from the Rennes press in old type, copies of which had already become extremely rare and almost wholly unobtainable.

And indeed, this plan of ours was not merely approved by men holding the foremost rank among the learned; rather, by their kindly encouragements they greatly stimulated us to carry it into effect. Chief among them was the most learned and most illustrious in so many titles Abbot Bignon, who for so many years has stood at the head of both royal Academies, to the astonishment of the world. When, with the kindness natural to him and the goodwill toward all students inherited from his forefathers, he received and deigned favorably to receive our efforts to publish Hildebert’s works, he also so graciously congratulated our undertaking to make public Marbod’s smaller works that he gave us no small encouragement, even when we hesitated, to embark upon it. Therefore, with such diligence as we could command, trusting in God’s help and likewise in the assistance of friends—whom we hoped would not refuse us a helping hand—we set ourselves to seek out everywhere Marbod’s works, whether published or unpublished. [Col. 1461]

We found copies of the published works collected together to be so rare that—strangely enough—we could not find even one in the very city of Rennes, whence they had first appeared. From the Paris libraries themselves, or even from the better supplied ones which we searched, we found a single copy of the aforesaid Rennes edition, in the library of the Mazarin College. Its most learned keeper, M. Collau, doctor of the Sorbonne, most courteously lent it to us. It contains only the metrical works and six letters at the end; and we took care to edit all these according to the authority of five manuscripts, which we scarcely obtained from various places. Yet none of these manuscripts contained all Marbod’s smaller works, but some items appeared in one and some in another. Accordingly, no small labor was imposed upon us in editing them, since for the correction of the texts we were often compelled to turn over and over again a single manuscript. Yet we noticed only a few textual variations in them, or at least scarcely any of importance; the chief were those found in the little book *On the Ornaments of Speech*. It is probable that this little book was composed by Marbod for the instruction of his pupils, while he was publicly teaching eloquence at Angers, long before he had been consecrated bishop.

Moreover, in the Rennes copy only the examples of the precepts were given in verse, not the precepts themselves. We took care to supply these from the manuscripts of Angers, Jumièges, Bec, and Tours—the last of which came to us from the distinguished church of Saint-Gatien. The eminent M. Davannes, doctor of the Sorbonne, canon and librarian of that same metropolitan church, a man born for the advancement of sound learning, graciously deigned to lend it to us through our friend Dom Edmond Martene. From it we gathered several items not to be despised which we had not seen in other manuscripts: for example, the epitaph of Master Lanfranc, the epitaph of Anselm, master at Laon, the Sibyl’s verses on the Day of Judgment, and many other lengthy pieces. These we have added to the works hitherto published and to those recovered from other manuscripts.

Among Marbod’s other works, the book *On Sixty Gems or Little Stones* has always been held in high esteem among the learned. It appeared with the others under his name in the Rennes edition of 1524; shortly afterward, in 1531, Pictorius of Willingen illustrated it with his scholia published at Freiburg, and in 1539 Alardus of Amsterdam with his commentaries. In the manuscripts which we were permitted to see, however, we found it so uniformly attributed to Marbod, bishop of Angers, that we were not a little astonished that the most learned Moréri had identified another Marbod—neither a bishop nor from Angers, but a citizen of Le Mans—as the author of that book.

Since he asserted this without proof, we judged that we ought to adhere to the authority of the manuscripts and the old edition, and especially to the distinguished manuscript of Saint-Victor, contemporary or nearly contemporary, which expressly attributes it to the bishop of Angers. There not only is the Latin text read, but also its French translation, for the most part almost line by line, though in that old French idiom which was then in use among our forefathers. Added also is Marbod’s own ingenious moral application of each stone and its virtue, which we have seen in this Victorine manuscript alone and nowhere in any other. We had intended indeed to publish only the first verses of this translation, as a specimen of the idiom of that age; but, moved by the advice of several students of antiquity, we decided that it should be presented in full alongside the Latin, 1381–1382 since they considered it a genuine monument of ancient, though obsolete, speech, to be entrusted to posterity.

To the foregoing we have also added several Lives of saints written by Marbod in prose and published by various authors. From these the discerning reader will clearly perceive that he was no less skilled in unmetrical than in metrical composition, and that the title of famous and most celebrated master, with which the encyclical letter of the monks of Angers on his death adorned him, was not undeservedly attributed to him.

What kind of man Marbod was, and how great, is especially evident from several charters preserved in the archive of the monastery of Saint-Albin at Angers. Our learned Reverend Father Dom Pierre Cosson, subprior of that monastery, generously provided us with copies after a most diligent and exact examination of them. From these it is established that Marbod was born in the county of Anjou, or even in the city of Angers itself, into a family already numerous at that time. This is clear from an old charter by which Robert Pellicier—also called *Paramentarius* (“clothier”) in another charter—Marbod’s father, in the presence of his wife, together with his two sons Hugh and Solomon and with several of his sisters, all consenting, transfers to the monks of Saint-Albin a certain water-descent, under specified conditions. Since Marbod, being younger, had not been present at this transfer, when he became older he ratified it.

Ulger, bishop of Angers, seems to suggest the nobility of his family when, in the funeral eulogy which we shall give below, he declares:

> He was born of those who were the glory of the Angevins.

Although no offspring of that family sprang from Marbod himself, who from his youthful years devoted himself to God and the Church, nothing prevents us from supposing that many children were born to his lay brothers Hugh and Solomon. From them their numerous family may have been propagated; and because of Marbod’s remarkable fame, it was perhaps known by the name of the Marbods rather than of the Pelliciers, after brothers otherwise obscure.

And certainly, if our conjecture has not deceived us—that is, if we rightly inferred that Letter 35 of Book II of Hildebert’s letters was addressed by Hildebert himself to Marbod, not yet bishop but then only a canon (a dignity with which the Sammarthani brothers in the *Gallia Christiana*, under Eusebius, say he was invested, as do others)—it will be clear that Marbod’s family was already most distinguished at that time. For, as Hildebert testifies in that letter, “fear of Marbod and his people had already fallen upon the canons of Angers, and the whole body of his kindred was suspected by them.” From this family it seems not improbable that, through ancestors and forefathers, there sprang the most illustrious family of the Marbods, commonly called de Marbœuf, who even now exercise the highest magistracies in the supreme court of Upper Brittany with the utmost integrity—ministers always devoted to the king’s service and most ardent defenders of their country, often even at the risk of their fortunes.

Nor is the public teaching of eloquence, by which Marbod became renowned at Angers, inconsistent with the distinction of this Marbodian family. That art, foremost among the liberal arts, has always been esteemed even by the greatest men. By it arms have very often yielded to the gown in swaying the minds of peoples and citizens; nor have kings and princes found anything more effective or more successful for calming bloodless popular disturbances and checking seditions than the gentle strength and sweet charm of eloquence.

[Note: [Col. 1461] On the family of the Marbods, see also what Beaugendre observed in his notes on M. Loyauté, above, col. 125.]

Accordingly, because of the celebrated reputation which he had gained from this excellent and fitting power of expression, Marbod was raised to the mastership of the schools of the Church of Angers. According to Burdigné and Hiret, [Col. 1463] historians of Angevin affairs, he had established the public schools of Angers, after the fashion, as they say, of a kind of university; and he was judged worthy to preside also over the sacred schools of the Church. Ulger, bishop of Angers, seems to indicate that the University of Angers was founded by Marbod when he says in his funeral poem:

> 1383–1384  
> He brought learning here; he brought talent here.

That he discharged this office of scholastic excellently for a full fourteen years, namely from 1067 to 1081, is clear from two charters of the distinguished cathedral church of Saint-Maurice at Angers.

[Note: [Col. 1463] From the cartulary of Saint-Maurice, fols. 34 and 36, and from the same, fol. 43.]

In these he is expressly called “scholastic of the Church of Angers.” He afterward obtained its archdeaconry. In that dignity, too, various charters of the same church show that he conducted himself so distinguishedly under three bishops of Angers—Eusebius, Geoffrey I, and Geoffrey II—that at last, his merits demanding it and Pope Urban II commanding, at the Council of Tours in 1096, as Ulger says in his funeral poem,

> Here he was made bishop, though unwilling and compelled,

and was consecrated bishop of the Church of Rennes by solemn rite. Having governed that church for twenty-eight years, always piously and most wisely, he at length yearned for his heavenly homeland. He voluntarily resigned the episcopate and entered the monastery of Saint-Albin at Angers, where, having professed himself a monk under the Rule of Saint Benedict, he lived for some time according to the Rule and died most holily, full of days and good works, on the third day before the Ides of September [11 September] in the year 1123. He was about eighty-eight years old, as is clear from the letter of the congregation of Blessed Albin, bishop of Angers—that is, of the monks who there in his monastery served God under the Rule of Saint Benedict—by which they announce to all the children of the Church the most holy death of Marbod. We have judged that this letter, as a monument of his holiness more lasting than bronze, should here be appended in full for the edification of the diligent reader.

## Encyclical Letter of the Monks and Convent of Saint-Albin at Angers on the Death of Marbod, Bishop of Rennes and Subsequently Monk of Saint-Albin

[Note: [Col. 1463] From the archive of Saint-Albin at Angers and from the copy printed at Rennes in 1524 by order of Yvo, bishop of Rennes, preserved in the library of the Mazarin College.]

“To all the children of the one most holy Church, the humble congregation of Blessed Albin, bishop of Angers: complete victory over the enemy, and the crown consequent upon victory.

“Apostolic authority teaches us that, praying for one another, we should bear one another’s burdens and so fulfill the law of Christ. Therefore, we servants of Christ, striving with devout concern to fulfill the law of Christ, announce to you the death of the lord Marbod, venerable bishop, ever to be remembered with praise: eloquent in speech, outstanding in religion, illustrious for uprightness of character, most learned in literary knowledge. His discourse was always seasoned with salt, and from his mouth flowed speech sweeter than all honey. And although at that same time all Gaul resounded with various studies, he, the king of orators, occupied the citadel of Gallic eloquence.

“For on the third day before the Ides of September, in the year of the Lord 1123, weak in body but stronger in spirit, departing from this world while living in Christ, he bereaved us of his presence and, having wounded us with the dart of his love, overwhelmed us with intolerable grief. After long exercises in the liberal studies, flourishing far and wide, in which he shone most effectively in the city of Angers, where he was a famous and most celebrated master, he was chosen by the most reverend Pope Urban at the Council of Tours and, God consenting, ordained bishop of the holy see of the Church of Rennes. Girded with the sword of the Holy Spirit, he governed that dignity—or rather burden—for twenty-eight years happily and prudently, though among barbarians armed with a certain natural ferocity. He subdued the necks of the proud by the censure of justice; by rebuking, entreating, and reproving, he made the discordant peaceful. 1385–1386 At last, worn out by extreme old age, full of days in his holy profession, as stated above, he rested in the Lord.

“Having therefore entered upon the way of all flesh and sensing that death was near, he laid down the episcopal burden, assumed the habit and humility of the most holy Benedict, professed himself a monk, and gave himself to Blessed Albin. Thus unburdened, he himself poor followed the poor Christ. Formerly, like Martha, he had been anxious and occupied with many things; now, like another Mary, recognizing that one thing is necessary, he chose the better part, which shall not be taken from him.”

To so authoritative a testimony of Marbod’s virtues, it will not be inappropriate to append what Ulger, his contemporary, successor in the archdeaconry of Angers, and finally bishop of Angers, recorded concerning him for posterity. Ulger had seen him alive and knew his character very well; he also attached this poem to his tomb. In both the published Rennes edition and several distinguished manuscripts it bears the following title:

## VERSES OF MASTER ULGER, BISHOP OF ANGERS

> If anyone asks to know how great Marbod was,  
> He asks what I deny that I can tell.  
>  
> In all the world, though one travel through it,  
> No single man equal to him in name and achievement can be found.  
>  
> We saw all eloquent men rank second to him;  
> None was his equal in talent or in speech.  
>  
> Cicero yielded to him; Virgil joined with Homer yielded:  
> To put it briefly, he surpassed them alike.  
>  
> Throughout all the bounds to which his age extended itself,  
> Nothing pleased him except what was fitting.  
>  
> Seeking to become one who breathed virtue,  
> He brought learning here; he brought talent here.  
>  
> Thus Christ’s judgment gave him, well known as he was,  
> The throne of bishops—yet without his desire.  
>  
> Made bishop here, though unwilling and compelled,  
> He made better what had previously all been good.  
>  
> Measuring every law by an equal measure,  
> He was gentle with the peaceful and stern with the swollen-proud.  
>  
> [Col. 1465] He prayed continually, fasted, kept vigil;  
> And what he withheld from himself he bestowed upon the poor.  
>  
> So worthy of praise, so worthy of love,  
> Falling to the lot of humankind, he passed to the Lord.  
>  
> All persons in religious life  
> Groaned exceedingly in lamentations and tears.  
>  
> The nobility wept, nor did the common people cease from weeping:  
> As they recall his virtues, so they groan and mourn.  
>  
> Through all the years this death will be new to the Bretons,  
> Whom while living he held, nourished, and taught.  
>  
> Rennes especially, deprived by the death of its own protector,  
> Lies as though sick and, made mute, is silent.

## FURTHER VERSES ON THE SAME SUBJECT BY THE SAME ULGER

> Marbod’s life, endowed with the shining light of learning,  
> Shone upon the world, fruitful in profound understanding.  
>  
> He was born of those who were the glory of the Angevins;  
> Afterward he presided over the crowds and clergy of the city of Rennes.  
>  
> While he lived devoted to learning, he spoke very many useful things.  
> The bishop died; this occurrence makes us sorrowful:  
> But may God aid him and join him to rest.

The outstanding virtues of this holy bishop were, to use the very words of the most learned Sirmond in his notes to Letter 14, Book III of Geoffrey of Vendôme’s letters, besides being described by Ulger in these verses, also set forth by Rivallon, archdeacon of Rennes:

> Talent made him wise; speech, eloquent;  
> His mind, retentive; concern for the flock, vigilant;  
>  
> Long age made him old; graciousness of character, pleasant;  
> His rank, a bishop; religion, holy;  
>  
> Sobriety made him sparing toward himself; generosity, lavish  
> Toward the poor; the rule of justice, upright.  
>  
> This foundation of the Church bore its weight, at once  
> An ox in gentleness and a lion in fierceness.

It is therefore no wonder if the most glorious testimony of the most illustrious bishop of Toul, André Du Saussay, should form the crowning conclusion of these eulogies. He did not hesitate to enter our Marbod in the sacred annals of Gaul. Thus he writes in his Gallican Martyrology:

> **THIRD DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF SEPTEMBER (THAT IS, 11 SEPTEMBER), AT RENNES IN ARMORICA: SAINT MARBOD, BISHOP AND CONFESSOR. TWELFTH IN SUCCESSION ON THIS SEE, HE BORE THE NAMES OF THE TWELVE APOSTLES OF THE LAMB, AS A LIVING STONE, HAVING BEEN DIVINELY ENDOWED WITH AN OUTSTANDING IMITATION OF THEIR VIRTUES; WHENCE, RAISED TO THE HEAVENLY ZION, HE WAS NUMBERED AMONG THE PRECIOUS STONES WITH WHICH IT GLEAMS.**

Thus, not in the notes, but in the very body of the Martyrology.

We shall not swell this preface further, since we shall relate Marbod’s other illustrious acts when occasion presents itself in the course of his smaller works.

[Col. 1465]

# LETTERS OF MARBOD, BISHOP OF RENNES

## FIRST LETTER

This letter is full of complaints, but just ones. Marbod, bishop of Rennes, having gone to Rome to secure confirmation of Raynald as bishop of Angers, was meanwhile, through the accusation of certain persons, stripped by the very man whose business he was conducting of all his ecclesiastical goods and, besides, declared an exile. He says that this befell him deservedly at the hands of an ungrateful man because, contrary to law and piety, against the judgment of the metropolitan and his own conscience, he had labored to promote to the episcopate a most frivolous young man. At last he exhorts him to repentance and to a more restrained manner of life.

[Col. 1465A]

**MARBOD, least of bishops, to R., glorious bishop [Col. 1466A] of the Angevins: not to be high-minded, but to associate with the lowly.**

[Note: [Col. 1465A] Otherwise, “river” and “by a river,” but erroneously; for the correct expression is *fulmine afflatus*, “struck by lightning,” not *flumine*, “by a river.”]

“Lightning, according to the saying of a certain wise man, is where anger dwells together with power.

[Note: [Col. 1466A] R. designates none other than Raynald de Martigné, bishop of Angers. Hildebert especially, Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, and other serious men opposed his election so vigorously because it was tumultuous and contrary to the canons. On this, see Hildebert’s Letters 4, 5, and 6, Book II, and our notes appended there; see also Letter 11, Book III, of Geoffrey of Vendôme, addressed to Raynald himself, and several other letters of the same author concerning that election, with the notes of the most learned Sirmond, which it would weary the reader to copy here. Yet Marbod favored this improper election to such an extent that, believing Raynald—though a youth and lacking the order prescribed by the canons—would someday be fit for episcopal rule, he devoted his whole self to defending it and even went to Rome for that purpose. While going there, he was treacherously seized by Stephen, dean of Angers, and, as he notes, even cast into iron chains. [Col. 1467D] Soon afterward, however, having escaped, he came to Tours and persuaded Archbishop Ralph to consecrate Raynald. Ralph did so, with Marbod, one of the assisting bishops, taking part in the rite. Marbod then went again to Rome and obtained from Pope Paschal II confirmation of this consecration.

“Marbod nevertheless paid fitting penalties for all these and such great labors spent in a bad cause. Raynald, unmindful of his benefits and soon stirred up against his benefactor by hatred, for what reason is unknown, stripped him of everything, disgracefully drove him from Angevin territory, and as it were devoted him to curses. But afterward, repenting, Raynald himself condemned his ungrateful disposition and returned so sincerely to favor with Marbod that, when Raynald went to Rome and remained there for some time, he amicably entrusted Marbod with the government of his Church of Angers. Our Dom Pierre Cosson was the first to observe and establish this circumstance of their sincere reconciliation. He informed us that he had learned it from a charter of Fulk Richin preserved in the cartulary of the distinguished church of Saint-Maurice, from which it is gathered that Marbod performed all episcopal functions at Angers in 1109, when Raynald was absent from his diocese.

“That charter, by which Count Richin grants to the church of Saint-Maurice whatever he possessed at Plaissiacum and Ruigniacum, reads as follows: ‘Gift of Count Fulk [namely, count of Anjou] concerning Plaissiacum and Ruigniacum, or Grammarium. Whatever, therefore, he possessed at Plaissiacum of Grammarium (French: Crammoire), with all its appurtenances, and likewise at Ruigniacum, with its appurtenances, he generously and freely gave to it; and he placed the gift, with a staff, in the hand of the lord Marbod, bishop of Rennes, who at that time, while Raynald II, bishop of Angers, was staying in Rome, administered the bishop’s affairs.’ We have noted the witnesses who attested it, whose names the appended record gives: Marbod, bishop of Rennes; Ermengard, countess of Brittany; etc.

“This assumption by Marbod of what was, as it were, the administration of another’s diocese proves the sincerity of his Christian spirit: reconciled with an enemy who had inflicted so many wrongs upon him, he rendered every service that he could have rendered to his closest friend. See on this the notes of M. Loyauté in the Appendix to Hildebert’s Letters, p. 25.]

Although, therefore, I understand that it will be dangerous for me—having already been struck by this lightning—if I try to address you with somewhat greater freedom, I shall nevertheless say what my mind and reason dictate to me. Nor shall I attach such value to the terror of the fortune which now favors you, 1389 that I fail to maintain with myself the truth of justice’s cause. For fortune is glass: it shines in such a way that it can easily [Col. 1467A] be broken; but the assertion of truth is stable and unshaken. If you should prove violent toward me according to your accustomed manner, then you will establish my persecution most fully by persecuting me.

“I ask you, therefore, religious bishop: what cause so powerful kindled the fury of your indignation against your brother and fellow priest—not to say your father and consecrator—

[Note: [Col. 1468D] **Consecrator.** For at Raynald’s consecration Marbod had been one of the bishops assisting Ralph of Tours, who performed the consecration.]

—that, pursuing me with invincible hatred, after cruelly inflicting losses and disgrace upon me and mine, you have at last condemned my lowly person unheard and unexamined, judging me unworthy of conversation with your clergy and not allowing me admission even into the presence of your majesty?

[Note: [Col. 1468D] He uses this word ironically.]

“For if I had sinned against you, ought I not first to have been privately corrected, and then, if I proved incorrigible, ought two or three others not to have been brought in? Yet behold: when none of these things had occurred, you have, contrary to the rule given by Christ—the primary rule—laid a complaint before your Church concerning one absent. Then, treating me as a heathen and a tax collector—wherein the injury is not mine but that common to all priests, not mine, I say, but Christ’s own—you have not so much overturned the order of ecclesiastical correction established by the Lord as plainly shown that the perverse and headlong impulse of turbulent anger rules you. 1390 For I was not allowed either to excuse, deny, or acknowledge the charge, so that either the defense of one offering an excuse might be received, or the purgation of one denying it might be justly admitted, or mercy might be graciously granted to one confessing it.

“In this judgment, therefore, you have abandoned all the ways of the Lord, [Col. 1467C] because you have followed neither mercy nor truth. [Col. 1468A] ‘For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth to those who seek his covenant and his testimonies’ [Psalm 24:10]. For even if, acknowledging my sin, I had sought forgiveness, it would have been fitting for your humility first willingly to forgive of your own accord, and to hasten to the grace of reconciliation, even if Christ had not said that a sinning brother must be forgiven seventy times seven [Matthew 18]. Indeed, even among the philosophers of the Gentiles, a more modest confession of sin holds the place nearest to innocence; they declare it the mark of great strength to disregard one who injures one, and they think that to have been able to take vengeance is vengeance enough, and that a greater kind of vengeance is to forgive. But they judge the seeking of retaliation to belong to a weak and womanish spirit, as may be gathered from this saying alone, as the satirist says:

[Col. 1468B] “Revenge—a pleasure in which no one delights more than a woman.” —Juv., Satire 13.

But what fault, after all, was there, which you judged worthy of punishment by destruction? Plainly this: that, before the lord pope, while excusing my delays, I dared among other things—as was true—to write that Angevin malice had been an obstacle to me, diminishing my resources very greatly. This had been known since the preceding year both to the pope himself and to the Roman Church; nor can Angevin malice itself deny it. [Note: Angevin malice. Namely, the malice of Stephen, dean of Angers, who had Marbod treacherously seized and thrown into prison.] From him, therefore, by whom truth is imputed to me as a crime, falsehood may consequently expect its reward; and since he stripped of office the man who had procured honor for him, it is no wonder if he exalted with honors his own destroyers and assailants. This is the [Col. 1468C] recompense of the wicked, which the Lord does not acknowledge, by which [Col. 1469A] evils are returned for good deeds. Of the same kind is that by which good things are returned for evils [perhaps: “by which evils are returned for good deeds”], when it is done continually by the same person—not through the fickleness of favor, but through the perverse malice of his nature.

But perhaps I ought to have written “kindness” instead of “malice,” so that I might say that Angevin kindness had then hindered me. Yet in that way, either, while attempting to excuse myself, I would accuse myself by calling an obstacle good; or, if I were thought to speak by antiphrasis, the matter would not change. Therefore I had to put forward the true cause of my excuse, known to all, since I had absolutely no other. In this you think yourself injured: you understand yourself to be Angevin. But if you do not understand this, neither ought you to consider yourself injured in it. For I did not name the bishop when I spoke of Angevin [Col. 1469B] malice. Angevin malice is manifold; it has many Stephens and many Williams. Would that the whole matter rested in the head of one of those two: perhaps there would be peace between us and unbroken concord.

But I return to my fault, which you think alone sufficient—or rather, not think, but desire others to think—so that I may appear deservedly deprived of the recompense for so many labors which I undertook for you. If it is no fault, it should be passed over in silence; if small, it should be forgiven; if great, it should be outweighed by comparison with greater services. For I suffered prison and chains on your account, when, summoned to you at the beginning of your election, I hastened there—through the contrivance of that Stephen who now pleases you—as though Fortune already then foresaw and warned me to desist from an ill-fated undertaking. [Note: Prison and chains. I would not hesitate to understand this literally. Such was the savagery of those times that not only those accused of the gravest crimes were bound in iron chains, but if anyone, driven by hatred, had made an enemy captive, he immediately thrust him, loaded with irons, into the depths of prison, and often tore him with tortures. Hildebert experienced this twice. Though guilty of no crime, he was thrown into prison by William Rufus for the rights of the Church and, for a whole year, loaded with iron and repeatedly worn down by many tortures; and again, betrayed into prison by Rotrou along with his dean, he was bound in iron chains and subjected by Hubert, Rotrou’s steward, without any reverence for his rank, to many torments in order to secure his ransom—a thing he always regarded as unworthy of his priesthood. Elias himself, count of Maine, suffered this when, captured in war by Henry I, king of England, he was afflicted at Rouen with six hundred tortures. See the *Life of Hildebert*.] And I endured many mockeries, not only in words but also in [Col. 1469C] deeds. Indeed, the grave indignity inflicted upon my own body made the loss of my possessions seem light to me.

Yet, though I escaped, I did not cease—as I then thought, steadfastly; as I now understand, obstinately—to press on with my purpose, and to maintain the grounds for your promotion against the best of the clergy, who for several reasons disapproved of an election made by the populace without their consent: because it had been made below the canonical age and outside the orders, and because it had been fabricated rather than made by the tumult of the people. The metropolitan himself had already yielded to the opponents; and because he was overcome by argument, he had determined to reserve the matter for the pope’s judgment—not so much to be decided as annulled. Yet by great exertion, much travel, and earnest petitions, I finally obtained from him that you should be consecrated. When Stephen, together with certain men—whom afterward, having, as they say, arranged my overthrow, you made friends from most bitter enemies—cried out that this was unjust, I, foolishly indeed and imprudently, but led astray by excessive favor toward you, devoted myself: “Let this [Col. 1470A] injustice be upon me,” I said. You yourself took care, as soon as it was possible, that I had not said this idly. Pouring that same injustice back upon my own head, with a new and unheard-of kind of affection: namely, that the very man for whose deeds and honor another had invoked it upon himself should inflict disgrace and loss upon his friend.

Would that, as soon as you had obtained your office through us and been enthroned, you had stripped me of honors, as you had conceived in your mind, rather than deciding to conceal your intention for a time, until you had made use of my services to drain the danger that remained at Rome. My travelling provision would have remained safe, by which I served you at my own expense; safe too the many and great labors of that very long journey; safe the prayers and tears which we poured out for you before the pope; safe the money which, though necessary to me as one going farther onward, I nevertheless advanced for your use as you were setting out. [Col. 1470B] After I had been expelled by you, when I claimed back part of it, I scarcely at last deserved to receive it, and only with difficulty; your shrewdness retained part as compensation for the horse which I had borrowed from you and worn out in your service.

After we had returned, therefore, and you realized that you had been confirmed, once a party of our common adversaries had been reconciled to you alone, as I mentioned above, you immediately attacked me at their counsel while I suspected nothing, and deprived me of all the honors and benefices which the generosity of your predecessors had conferred upon me. Nor could I obtain from you by any prayers or appeal to my former services even a reprieve of six months, in which, preserving my honor, I might pretend to leave rather than to be expelled. So far was it from being enough for you [Col. 1470C] to burden a friend with loss unless you also heaped upon him the reproach of disgrace.

And when I complained that I had been treated unworthily, you at once summoned me to the pope’s hearing: a man already stripped by you of the means to appear, recently exhausted in expenses for you, worn out in labors through you, now old in years and gasping with fevers—while you yourself were young, strong, wealthy, and glorious in newly acquired office—so that, compelled by you, I might plead my case there, where voluntarily in that same year I had shed tears for you. You indeed believed that you had contrived all this cleverly; but I perceived that you had contrived it maliciously and cruelly, as if, armed and whole, you were challenging a wounded and unarmed man—not an enemy, but a friend—to battle. For what might have helped me before [Col. 1470D] all others to obtain compassion, you alone turned into an opportunity to uproot me altogether. And what would have softened others—the very things that call for mercy—rather provoked you.

Having returned from Rome, therefore, after receiving authority to do what you had already done, lest anything should be lacking to your hatred, you broke out into an effort to erase [Col. 1471A] my name from the Catalogue, pursuing first everything of mine, even my syllables. Would that you had also inscribed: “With unjust hatred I hated him!” Such a trophy would have been worthy of your title. If you answer that you did this from zeal for justice, because canon law forbids a cleric to be enrolled in the churches of two cities, [Note: XXI, question 1, canon 1, “In Two Churches,” etc.] Sicarius refutes you, and Stephen refutes you: the one previously enrolled in the Church of Le Mans, the other in that of Tours.

But while I recount these things, not as weaving a history but as weaving an injury, perhaps your exaltedness is indignant, angry, inflamed, and, measuring my weakness by its own strength, prepares to exercise vengeance. Do not, I beg you, consider what you can do, but reflect upon what you ought to do; do not attend to the powers of Fortune, but to the consideration of common justice. [Col. 1471B] For as much as you have been able to do against me, so much are others able to do against you; and Fortune has advanced no one so far that she does not threaten him as much as she has permitted him. A fall harms the exalted man far more easily. Therefore, mindful of the human condition, restrain the impulse of ardent youth, and draw in sails too greatly swollen by the wind of prosperous fortune, lest perhaps the very speed of your favorable course become the cause of your striking the rocks.

You have not yet acquired long experience through age, nor has your mind yet been matured by being boiled down in the variety of misfortunes. “With the aged,” says Scripture, “is wisdom, and in length of days prudence” (Job 12:12). And elsewhere: “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deut. 32:7). If reverence, due before your years to those more advanced [Col. 1471C] in age, has come to you, do not ascribe it to your own powers, which either did not exist or were certainly unknown; for Fortune often prevails more than counsel, as we have frequently experienced both in this matter and in others. Rather you should fear that saying of the Wise Man: “An inheritance hastily gotten at the beginning shall lack blessing in the end” (Prov. 20:21).
