And this: “Substance hastily gotten shall be diminished” (Prov. 13:11).

The opinion of some people concerning you—would that it were false!—must also be refuted: they think that your disposition has not so much been changed by prosperity as revealed by it. For the vices of many, which lie hidden through weakness while they lack the means to unfold their wickedness, are uncovered by prosperity when their own strength has become pleasing to them. Thus a deadly serpent is handled without fear while it is stiff with cold: it does not then lack poison, but its poisons are numb. That this may not rightly be applied to you, you must labor with utmost effort; and you must take care not only that the benefits of Fortune do not expose you, but also that they do not make you worse. “If riches increase,” says the Psalmist, “do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61:11).

Therefore summon wholesome counsels when life’s prosperity smiles upon you. Then you will hold and check yourself very firmly on slippery ground, and will not give yourself free rein—if, that is, you look around to see where you are going and how far. Do not place yourself upon a higher thing, from which, once standing there, you must either descend in terror or fall. I say this not that henceforth you may become either more indulgent or more generous toward me, both of which I have long despaired of from sure signs; but lest, using wrongly the authority which the Lord granted you “for edification, and not for destruction” (2 Cor. 13:10), you proceed from my example to the ruin of many.

For although at present I have escaped the Apennines, where you were, with sufficiently insolent praise, dedicating a tomb for me among my predecessors—Melanius and Moderannus, I mean, whom I confess myself unworthy to join—I am now nevertheless dead to labors, and, by the Lord’s granting, having attained the measure due to me, I ought to await a tranquil end of life rather than to occupy myself further with superfluous services. “The time past,” as the Apostle says, “is sufficient [Col. 1472B] for fulfilling the will of the Gentiles” (1 Pet. 4:3), so that henceforth we may live no longer for ourselves but “for him who died for us and rose again” (1 Thess. 4:13).

## LETTER II. That the unworthiness of a minister does not impede the truth of the sacrament.

MARBOD, least of bishops, to INGILGERIUS, solitary servant of God, and to the brethren living the solitary life with him: “To call the light day, and the darkness night” (Gen. 1:5).

Among the many good things reported concerning your holiness, we have heard that you have zeal for God against unworthy priests, but not according to knowledge. [Col. 1472C] For it is said that not only are you unwilling to take part in their offerings, but that you even teach the laity not to receive any sacrament through them. If this is true, dearest brethren, it must be greatly feared lest perhaps the devil—who, with God preserving you, cannot draw you into manifest crimes—cast your souls, God forbid, into perdition through the hidden snare of this error. For what else is the old heresy of the Novatians? What else is the new error of those called Patarines [Note: Patarines, or Paterenes. On them see Matthew Paris, *Greater History*, under Henry, year 1236, and the Lateran Council under Alexander III, chapter 23.] than that the sacraments of the Catholic Church are held cheap because of the unworthiness of their ministers? How contrary this is to the truth is shown by the authorities set forth below.

Augustine, in the tenth tractate on the Psalm against heretics: “What,” he says, “has Christ done to you, who bore his betrayer with such patience that he gave to him, first among all, the Eucharist consecrated by his own hands and commended by his own mouth, just as he gave it to the other apostles? What has Christ done to you, who sent that same betrayer, whom he called a devil, who before the betrayal could not keep faith even with the Lord’s money-bags, together with the other apostles to preach the kingdom of heaven, in order to show that God’s gifts come to those who receive them with faith, even though the person from whom they receive them is such as Judas was?” [Note: See Augustine, chapter 11, book II, *Against Parmenian*.]

Elsewhere the same writer says: “The sacraments of the Church [Col. 1473A] can be performed neither better by a good man nor worse by a bad man; for whatever the outward person may be, the Holy Spirit works inwardly.”

Likewise, from the Register of Pope Nicholas, in the letter to the Bulgarians: “You ask whether you ought to support and honor, or drive away from you, a priest who has a wife.” We answer: Although such priests are very blameworthy, you should nevertheless imitate the Lord, “who, as the Gospel testifies, makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:45). Therefore you ought not to drive them away, [1396] because the Lord did not cast Judas out from the number of disciples, although he was a deceitful disciple. But you must neither judge priests nor investigate anything about their life; rather, whatever the matter is must entirely be reserved for the judgment of bishops.

The same authority says in the same work: “You ask whether you ought to receive communion from a priest who either has been caught in adultery or has merely been stained by common report of it.” We answer: No one, however defiled he may be, can defile the divine sacraments, which are remedies cleansing every contagion; just as a ray of sunlight, passing through sewers and privies, cannot draw from them any contagion. Therefore, whatever kind of priest he may be, he cannot pollute the holy things. Consequently communion must be received from them until they are rejected by the judgment of bishops, because bad men, by administering good things, injure [Col. 1473C] only themselves; and a wax torch, when lit, indeed harms itself, but gives light to others in darkness.

Augustine, in the letter to Vincentius: “The good are not to be forsaken because of the bad, but the bad are to be tolerated because of the good, just as the prophets tolerated those against whom they spoke such great things; nor did they abandon communion in the sacraments of that people, just as the Lord himself tolerated the guilty Judas until his deserved end.”

The same writer, in the book *On the Words of the Lord*: “How many things, and how vehemently, did Jeremiah rebuke among the sinners and criminals of his people! Yet he was among them: he entered the one temple with them, celebrated the same sacraments, and lived in that congregation of criminal men. But he went out from it by crying aloud. This is to go out from it; this is not to touch the unclean thing: not to consent in heart, and not to spare with one’s mouth.” [Col. 1473D]

There are also many other passages of holy authority bearing upon this same matter which I could append; but if these do not suffice for someone, neither would more suffice. Farewell, beloved brethren, and pray for us.

## LETTER III. Evil priests are not to be avoided except after canonical judgment.

The least of bishops to INGUNGERIUS, venerable priest, and the brethren who serve God with him: greetings.

I received the letters of your holiness, responding to the little letter previously sent from my own smallness; [1397] and, after reading them, I rejoiced exceedingly, [Col. 1474A] since I perceived that you think and preach only what does not depart from Catholic truth. For who does not know that all heretics generally must be avoided and detested? The sacred canons also show that fornicating priests must be deposed. Yet this is not to be done indiscriminately or disorderly. For holy Church, which is the body of the Head who is Christ, has a distinction among its members and a difference among its offices, so that one may not with impunity usurp what belongs to another. Are all members an eye? Do all members speak?

Our Lord Jesus answered one who cried out to him, “Master, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me”: “Man, who appointed me a judge and divider between you?” (Luke 12:14). [Col. 1474B] Thus many members ought not to judge or speak, since even the tongue and the word themselves may not speak except according to order and appointment. This appointment and order of judgments is such that, even though certain things are true, they are not to be accepted by a judge unless they have been publicly presented in judicial order. In every judgment there must be four persons: accuser, defender, witnesses, and judge. And you have in the Decrees that no judgment is valid unless it has been conducted in due order. For, apart from the general judgment concerning those who are to be condemned, contained in the rules, the particular examination of individuals is nevertheless required by the particularity of persons.

Who, then, would dare to disturb this established order? Or who would dare to usurp a license to judge that has not been granted to him? For, according to the testimony of Scripture, the danger of the judge is greater than that of the person judged. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged” (Matt. 7:1). And the Apostle: “Do not judge before the time” (2 Cor. 4:5). Hence we read of blessed Martin: “Judging no one, condemning no one.” And the Lord Jesus told some who trusted in themselves as righteous and despised others the parable of the Pharisee and the sinner, and added: “This man justified rather than that one” (Luke 18:1). [Col. 1474C]

Are you also—whom foolish and unlearned people, deceived by error, chatteringly call heretics—to be rejected before a hearing? Far be it! Therefore, most beloved sons and brethren, do not condemn and abominate sinners; rather, rebuke them with gentleness and pray for them that God may convert them. Or, if it is more expedient, accuse each one before his own judges, so that, once convicted or having confessed, they may be justly condemned. For at this time, by God’s favor, there is a great fear that anyone, as you say, should openly defend his iniquity or contend that these great evils—simony and fornication, I mean—are good. But, as I understand, you will be able to obtain this more by prayer than by disputation. May almighty God hear your holiness as you pray for us.

## LETTER IV. He urges Vitalis to arrange for the admission into a monastery of a suitable but poor girl.

The least of bishops to VITALIS, servant of God: perseverance in good work.

[Col. 1475A] We have heard that your religious devotion zealously applies itself to gaining souls, seeking not its own interests but those of others, that they may be saved; so much so that, God cooperating, you are said to have established a monastery of women, so that your compassion may not be lacking even to the weaker female sex. Therefore, dearest brother, I humbly entreat your holiness that you may deem worthy of reception in that flock of yours a certain orphan girl who desires to serve God in virginity and is at present deprived of human assistance. Her earthly father has become a convert in a monastery and renounced the world; but her mother, because of her poverty, cannot aspire to obtain a place for that girl in wealthy monasteries. For although the girl herself has learned letters in part, a corrupt custom has prevailed in the old monasteries [Note: “But a corrupt custom.” Thus already at that time had prevailed that corrupt custom, transmitted down to our own age, by which the richer the monasteries are, the richer dowries they demand from girls who seek admission. How unjust this is is evident from the fact that devout and honorable but needy girls, who desire with their whole heart to devote themselves to God’s service, find that the divine calling does not suffice unless they abundantly satisfy the disordered greed of superiors—or even of nuns—by enormous sums of money extorted through contracts either explicit or at least tacit. This is certainly more unjust in proportion as the monasteries are more wealthy.] among [Col. 1475B] us: money is preferred to learning. Therefore I thought it necessary to take refuge in your religious devotion in this petition, since I did not doubt that you are free from this contagion. Do, then, what I ask, sweetest brother, not so much for love of me as for love of him who is Father of orphans and Judge of widows—on this condition, however, that I too shall gladly grant you whatever you may think fit to request of my lowliness.

## LETTER V.

The least of bishops to AGENOBIDIS, handmaid of Christ.

To enter with the Bridegroom into the wedding feast after the cry at midnight: “Grace is deceitful and beauty vain; [1399] a woman who fears the Lord, she shall be praised” (Prov. 31:30).

Dearest daughter, I heartily rejoice that this saying of wise Solomon has been proved by you and confirmed [Col. 1475C] not so much in word as in deed. For you have despised as nothing, for the love of God, not only the charm of your beauty, but also the glory of riches and the pleasures of the world—and, what is greater among all these, the affection of husband and children. If therefore, according to the saying of the Savior, whoever loves temporal things more than himself is not worthy of God, you have surely begun to be worthy of Christ, whom you have loved more than the world.

But because not beginning but bringing to completion is praiseworthy—for the former sometimes proceeds from fickleness of mind, whereas the latter always proceeds from strength of soul—you must strive with the utmost effort and exert all your powers, not only to retain what you have already attained [Col. 1475D] but also always to seek to attain, by new increases, what must be retained. Such is the condition of our mortality that it cannot preserve the same state for long, but begins at once to fail where it has ceased to desire progress. Therefore you must live each day as though you had begun only that very day; that is, you must believe that you have made no progress while anything remains to be corrected. “Brethren,” says the Apostle, “I do not reckon myself to have attained; but I pursue, if perhaps I may attain” (Phil. 3:13). And elsewhere: “Forgetting those things which are behind, and stretching myself toward those which are before, I press toward the goal” (ibid., 14).

If, then, the holy Apostle, having received such great grace from God that he knew even the secrets of heaven, did not reckon himself to have attained so long as, of course, he was away from the Lord, what mortal person, however holy, can trust that he has attained anything? For, as it is written: “When a man has finished, then he will begin” (Ecclus. 18:6). And the Lord, speaking to the disciples, says among other things: “When you have done all these things, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done” (Luke 17:10). This means: if we pay to the Lord only what we owe, we confer upon him no benefit from our own [Col. 1476B] resources. “For what have you that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

Dearest one, I say these things not to instill in you the weariness of despair, but to summon you to the preservation of humility, lest perhaps, while the world follows your first beginnings with worthy praises, the spirit of pride should secretly creep upon you—God forbid!—as though you alone among noblewomen of this place or time had fulfilled the evangelical command by renouncing all that you possessed, so as to follow Christ naked. For this reason many already declare you blessed and say that, together with the world, you have conquered the devil.

But you must think very differently, as [1400] I believe you do think. Everyone who casts off the works of the flesh and enters upon the religious life does not thereby at once conquer the enemy whom he provokes; rather, [Col. 1476C] only then does he begin to experience the stratagems of that most wicked foe, when he has proclaimed open warfare against him. For an athlete, when he has thrown off his clothes and anointed his limbs with oil, is not immediately secure of victory; on the contrary, the more ready he is for combat, the nearer he comes to the uncertainty of danger. So too one who, stripped, prepares to cross a stormy river has indeed become better suited to swimming, but is not yet certain whether he can swim across.

The same holds for you and those like you, who, casting aside the impediments of secular life, have come forth naked to wrestle with a naked adversary and have prepared bare arms to overcome the rivers of Babylon. A severe conflict awaits you; no small danger hangs over you; and if you relax mind or hand even a little, there looms the fear of shameful ruin, or certainly of a most wretched death. For the ancient enemy does not cease, laying snares for you not only from things to come but also stirring up battle from things past. He recalls former pleasures to memory, in hope that the recollection of past allurements may sweetly soothe a mind wearied by present hardship. The cunning one knows how to take material for temptation from virtue, and from the abstinence of saints he is accustomed to kindle a desire for feasting. [Col. 1477A] At his instigation the people once murmured in the wilderness, longing for the pots of meat which they had left in Egypt (Exod. 16:3). By those meats we ought certainly to understand not so much rich food for the body as the bubbling desire of carnal pleasures.

He knows how to arouse weariness from the future and to frighten the traveler’s mind by the roughness or length of the journey: as though one might have prolonged life longer amid the pleasant places of pleasures and enjoyed the goods of youth, and then at last, in old age—which is a time more suited to religion—earn rest by brief labor. With suggestions of this kind he never ceases to trouble recruits in the religious warfare. But you, handmaid of Christ, protect yourself against all these things with the shield of faith, and, forgetting what lies behind, stretch yourself, as has been said, toward higher things. Put your trust in him to whom you have committed yourself, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear, but will make with the temptation also the way out, so that you may endure it (1 Cor. 10:13).

For the Lord of all, who has adopted you as his daughter and has deemed you worthy to be betrothed to his only Son, our King, himself embraces you in his gentle bosom and addresses you in sweet words: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty, because [1401] he is the Lord your God, and they shall worship him” (Ps. 44:11). Forget, therefore, the people of vices whom you loved; abhor the works of the devil which you performed. For he is the father of evil-doers, as the Lord says to the Jews: “You are from [Col. 1477C] your father, the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father” (John 8:4).

Hear words of consolation from the Law, lest you incur the danger of condemnation through the suggestion of sin. When you hear them, you will say: “The wicked have told me fables, but not according to your law; all your commandments are truth,” etc. (Ps. 118:85). With the discerning eye of the mind, see how great is the vanity in temporal things and how great the sweetness in love of eternal things. Hear, I say, daughter, and see, because the world neither hears nor sees. “For he who does not have these things,” as the apostle Peter says, “is blind and groping with his hand, having received forgetfulness of the cleansing of his former sins” (2 Pet. 1:9).

Let us suppose, then, if you please, by way of example, some woman whom the world thinks fortunate: powerful in nobility, exceptional in beauty, abounding in pleasures, fruitful in offspring, happy in her husband’s love. Let us moreover grant her a long span of life, in which she may indulge herself and enjoy every kind of pleasure. [Col. 1477D]

Yet what true happiness will you find in all these things? For, to pass over the other disadvantages necessarily mixed with false goods—namely anxiety and labor, sleepless cares and fear, lawsuits and business, without all of which these things cannot here be managed, and which unquestionably interrupt and defile that very delight of the world—at last, certainly, all things end in death. Except that those who lived more luxuriously in the world will feel sharper punishments; and when the causes have perished, the accounts of the causes will remain without end. For it is established by nature that each person fears death and torment in proportion as he has known more pleasures in life.

“Do not,” therefore, “be envious of evildoers, nor be jealous of those who do iniquity; for they shall quickly wither like grass and soon fall away like the green herb. Hope in the Lord, and do goodness; dwell in the land, and you shall be fed by its riches. Delight in the Lord” (Ps. 36:1), because “how good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart” (Ps. 72:1). Therefore, handmaid of Christ, have an upright heart, and let not your feet be moved; do not be jealous of the wicked when you see the peace of sinners. Do not listen outwardly with the world. Incline your ear and hear the truth inwardly from Christ. [Col. 1478B] Enter into the sanctuary of God and understand their latter end; then you will say: “How they have been brought into desolation; they have perished because of their iniquity. Like the dream of those who awake, O Lord, in your city you will bring their image to nothing” (ibid., 19).

For temporal goods are imaginary and possessed as in a dream, as he says elsewhere: “They slept their sleep, and all men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75:6). Hear also something from the wisdom of Solomon: “If,” he says, “a man should live many years and rejoice in them all, he must remember the dark time and the many days which, when they have come, will prove the past to have been vanity” (Eccl. 11:8).

Finally hear our Lord and God himself saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11:29). Thus it is sweet to serve God, but laborious to serve the devil, as the wicked, repenting too late in condemnation, will say: “We walked difficult ways and were wearied without cause” (Wis. 5:7).

You have seen, therefore, from reason and from the authority of sacred Scripture, the vanity of secular glory with its troubles. See also from both the true sweetness of humble and religious life. What is sweeter than to be content with necessities, for which nature is satisfied by few and small things, and not to be wearied over superfluities, which are immense and innumerable? For nothing is enough for desire, which is more provoked when it is fed. And in how many difficult [Col. 1478D] hardships and labors are those entangled who pursue earthly desires, in order that they may be able to attain what they desire? Conversely, those who despise these things are free from as many distresses.

“For godliness with sufficiency is great gain,” according to the Apostle. “For we brought nothing into this world, and neither can we take anything away. But having food and clothing, let us be content with these. For those who desire to become rich fall into a snare and into the temptations of the devil, and into many useless and harmful desires which plunge human beings into destruction and perdition. For [Col. 1479A] desire is the root of all evils; some, seeking it, have wandered from the faith and entangled themselves in many sorrows” (1 Tim. 6:6).

Those who lack earthly desire, therefore, also lack sorrows and labors: they are not tormented by envy, lifted up by pride, or stretched out by anxieties; rather, as the apostle Peter says, they rejoice “in the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest spirit, which is rich in the sight of God” (1 Pet. 3:4). What outward riches can compare with inward wealth from a good conscience? Of this the Lord says to his disciples: “No one shall take your joy from you” (John 16:22). And the apostle Paul says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12).

Dearest one, I have taken care to write these things for consolation, delighted by the fragrance of your good reputation, [Col. 1479B] which I have learned from those who have examined your life more closely. But lest, while occupied with greater and more useful studies in God’s service, you should perhaps not have leisure to reread all these things often, since they are rather lengthy, I have thought it good to compose at the end of this letter a shorter rule of life from the sayings of the ancients. Return to it frequently, at least as to a mirror, so that if from examining it you discover anything in yourself that ought to displease, you may immediately restore and shape it according to the rule of uprightness. For even while you loved secular life, you corrected the appearance of your dress and face in a mirror.

Accordingly, the aforesaid rule of life consists, to summarize briefly, [Col. 1479C] in the observance of four virtues, which are customarily called by different names. The first of these is prudence; the second, greatness of soul; the third, self-control; the fourth, justice.

If, therefore, you desire to follow prudence, you will live rightly if you first assess and weigh everything, and assign worth to things not from the opinion of the multitude but from their own nature. Do not marvel at transitory things, nor regard as great what is perishable. If you embrace prudence, be the same everywhere, and accommodate yourself to the time as the diversity of circumstances and times requires; do not change yourself in anything, but adapt yourself, like a hand which remains the same whether it is extended into a palm or clenched into a fist. It belongs to the prudent person to examine [Col. 1479D] counsels and not to fall quickly through easy credulity; to foresee what is coming and to set before the mind all that may happen. The prudent person will never say, “I did not think this would happen,” because such a person does not merely doubt, but expects; does not merely suspect, but guards against it.

Do not entertain wandering thoughts, like dreams. Let your thought be steadfast and certain. Let your speech not be empty, but let it either persuade, move, console, or instruct. Praise sparingly; blame sparingly, lest you incur suspicion either of malice or of flattery. Seek what can be found; learn what can be known.

But if greatness of soul, also called fortitude, is in your mind, you will live freely and fearlessly, with great confidence; you will never judge that an insult has been done to you. Of an enemy you will say: “He did not harm me, but he had the intention [Col. 1480A] of harming me.” And when you see such a person in your power, you will think revenge to consist in having been able to take revenge. For know that it is a noble and great kind of revenge to forgive. It is a great good of the human mind to remain constant to itself and not to tremble, but to await the end of life fearlessly. Greatness of soul alone bestows this good.

But if you possess self-control, also called temperance, you will remove superfluities and narrow your desires within strict bounds. You will consider how much nature requires and how much desire demands; you will put a bridle upon lust and reject everything that flatters. You will eat without cruelty [perhaps “without rawness,” *cruditatem*], and drink without drunkenness. You will neither cling to present luxuries nor long for absent ones. Your nourishment will be easily obtained, and you will approach food not for pleasure but [Col. 1480B] for sustenance. Hunger, not flavor, will awaken your palate; and thus, shaped as far as possible after the divine exemplar, you will draw yourself away from the body toward the spirit.

If you love self-control, flee shameful things before they occur, and fear no one more than yourself. Believe everything endurable except disgrace. Abstain also from shameful speech, because license in such speech nourishes shamelessness. Let your urbanity be not buffoonish but pleasing; let your wit be without a sting, your jokes without vulgarity, your laughter without cackling, your voice without shouting, your walk without bustle. Rest will not mean idleness for you; and while others play, you will occupy yourself with something holy and honorable.

In clothing you will preserve moderation, so that your garments are neither splendid nor mean; for, as Jerome says, the one smells of luxury, the other [Col. 1480C] of vainglory. Philosophers discuss justice in various ways and maintain that it is the virtue which renders to each person what is their own. You will be able to perform its duties, insofar as they concern your religious vocation, if you subject your spirit to God and your body to the spirit. For it is unjust and perverse for lower things to resist higher. If you wish to injure no one, if you desire to benefit everyone—since you yourself wish no injury to be done to you and wish all to benefit you—if you show everyone the reverence due according to differences of age, condition, office, and merit; finally, if you impute to yourself every evil that is in you, but attribute whatever good there is to God: then it will come about that you will harm neither another through injustice nor [Col. 1480D] yourself through self-exaltation. May Christ preserve your religious devotion, praying for us, most beloved sister.

## LETTER VI

The least of bishops, to Robert, servant of God.

It is fitting not only to offer rightly, but also to divide rightly.

Whenever I hear concerning your brotherhood something befitting Christian religion, and something whose imitation by your followers may redound to your reward, I rejoice not only in your name but also congratulate Christ our head, whose good fragrance is, by his own gift, spread far and wide through you. But when certain things are reported to be said and done by you which accord neither with sound teaching nor with an honorable life, I am confounded by grief and fear together: lest the crafty enemy, God forbid, introduce among your good works some contrary matter; or lest you yourself fail to set your good works in their proper place through a certain simple and undiscriminating confidence. For even in building walls, account must be taken not only of the materials but also of their suitable arrangement. Otherwise, things good in themselves begin to displease when badly arranged.

So too in words, the skilled speaker attends not only to what kind of things are uttered, but also to how, when, and before whom they are uttered. It befits your profession, dearest brother—you who have set forth in your own person an example of the most vigorous philosophy—to display in word or deed nothing that can be found contrary to sacred authorities, or by which those who might be edified may be offended. For the Apostle says: “Be without offence to Jews and Gentiles and to the Church of God” (II Cor. X, 32); and elsewhere: “Therefore let not our good be blasphemed” (Rom. XIV, 16). Therefore examine your life and speech with careful attention, so that you give the adversary no occasion for slander. [Col. 1481B]

You ought to remember the heavenly living creatures, among whose number you are counted, which are described as full of eyes before and behind. For you too, bearing about the Gospel of Christ, have mounted upon the chariots of Amminadab. Take heed, therefore, son, lest, while you place too much confidence in your holiness, you become a stumbling-block or scandal to weaker members, and the weak brother perish in his conscience, for whom Christ died. But lest I seem, by pursuing matters generally, to rebuke in you not so much things to be noted as things that ought to be rebuked in anyone, I shall identify specifically the things concerning you which scandalize many. Thus, if you recognize fault, do not neglect to correct it; but if not, dissolve the error of the contrary opinion by a reasonable defence.

You are said to be especially fond of cohabitation with women—a kind of fault in which you once sinned—as though, [having incurred] the contagion of former iniquity, you were striving to atone for it in the same matter by an example of new religion. “For, as they report, you share a common bed with these women at night, while the band of disciples likewise reclines, so that, lying between the two groups, you lay down for either sex the rules of waking and sleeping.” They say that these are the attendants of your pilgrimage and sit constantly beside you while you dispute. Moreover, they assert that in diverse places and regions you have no small number of women distributed among hospices and lodging-houses, whom—mingled with men without safety—you have assigned to the service [Col. 1481D] of the poor and pilgrims. How dangerously this has been done, to say it briefly, the cries of infants have revealed.

Accordingly, many condemn your manner of life in this respect—not only ecclesiastical persons but common people as well—since both divine and human laws openly protest against this association. For the beginning of sin came from a woman, and through her we all die; therefore, if we wish to avoid sin, we ought to cut away from ourselves the cause of sin. For, as Scripture testifies: “He who loves danger will fall into it” (Ecclus. III, 17).

And when you cast your nets for a catch, you enclose an abundant multitude of fish; but you are said to draw in, along with the fish, serpents also, which cannot readily change their deadly nature. You cannot handle them with impunity; their sight cannot be harmless; in seeing them, not fear but desire is generated. Of them Scripture says: “Aspids hiss diseases, and woman pours forth the pestilence of desire.” Solomon compares her in this way, saying: “From garments comes moth, and from woman the iniquity of man” (Ecclus. XLII, 13). Again: “A woman captures the precious soul of a man.” Take care, therefore, lest she capture you.

It is not safe for long to sleep near a serpent. And if you answer that you are awake and keep untiring watches concerning your own guardianship, such serpents are accustomed to inflict a wound even upon those who are awake. For by their mere sight they pour a seductive poison deep into the marrow and stir the hidden recesses of the mind with an insatiable itch. Remove, I beseech you, such arrangements, which, even if they do not wound your soul through consent, nevertheless without doubt stain your reputation and disgrace religion. Hence Augustine: “It is worse than adultery to possess a criminal continence and make holiness infamous.”

But how can we know whether this association does not harm you also? For, as Jerome says: “She whose face you frequently observe ministers to you dangerously.” And again: “You ought not to trust in past chastity, because you cannot be holier than David nor wiser than Solomon, whom we know to have fallen through women.” Even if you do not commit fornication in body, living among women you cannot remain chaste for long. For you are not of that impassible kind of eunuchs who were so born, who indeed have no reward; rather, you strive to be among those who made themselves eunuchs [Col. 1482C] for the kingdom of heaven, of whom it is said: “I will give them a named place in my house and within my walls, and a name better than sons and daughters” (Isa. LVI, 5). These, then, have a contest, and scarcely can overcome the unlawful desire of the flesh, even when women are absent, without great labor.

What if fire should approach straw? It will kindle a harmful blaze for sin, or at least will aggravate the burden of the contest. But, Augustine testifies, it is most absurd for someone to wish to be constrained to labor when victory is offered more easily. For if anyone sets before himself and says, “I wish to have something to overcome,” this is to say, “I desire to live beneath a ruin.” Why did he take a woman to himself who disdained to take a wife? [Col. 1482D] He who does not eat flesh, why does he fill his dwelling with the appurtenances of flesh? And he who does not drink wine, why does he enjoy the delight of wine? As though, often by possessing without tasting, the mind were not fed by an abundance of food, and desire not frequently stirred by the fragrance of wine alone.

Why does he wish, by hypocrisy, to be called abstinent by people, while in secret he is filled with meats and drunkenness? Many possess riches which they deny to their own use but keep for desire’s sake; if no desire clung to them, they would not possess the emblems of desire. But because they are possessed by desire, they enjoy in mind what they do not touch in use. Thus one who has despised the bond of marriage is bound in another way by women’s bonds: although he mingles in no intercourse, he is nevertheless always bound by desire, sight, conversation, [Col. 1483A] and association. For if he had no desire for a woman, he would never take a woman together with her delights. Indeed, the man who has taken an unlawful woman and rejected a lawful wife has given me additional reason to suspect an unlawful pleasure. Unless I am mistaken, he has argued publicly to people that he promises chastity, and yet in secret he cannot be without a woman.

These two proofs, of holiness and of lust, are remarkable from opposite sides. We think these observations on the first heading that we proposed may suffice.

Furthermore, many think that you should be rebuked for the extravagance of your ragged attire, because it seems suitable neither to the canonical profession under which you began to serve nor to the priestly order to which you have been promoted. For every profession and order has a certain appropriate and fitting distinction of dress, and if it is altered, it offends public judgment. The wise person will not disturb public customs or draw the populace’s attention to himself by novelty. Let us therefore see whether those things by which we wish to gain admiration are ridiculous and hateful.

Thus even in cheap and humble clothing, common sense and the authority [perhaps “accepted authority,” *autorisatae*] of received custom must be taken into account, and measure must be observed. It is one thing to go about adorned in splendid dress; another to be clothed neatly. The latter seems to belong to decency, the former to vanity. Likewise, there is no small difference between cheap, dirty clothing and dirty, torn clothing. The former befits religion and modesty; the latter shows rather folly and an undiscriminating mind. For [Col. 1483C] just as to desire luxurious things is luxury, so to avoid ordinary things which can be procured at little cost is madness. Let the garment not shine, but neither let it become filthy.

It is far more praiseworthy to be humble in silks than to boast in rags. Jerome, writing to Nepotian: “Avoid dark garments just as much as white ones.” Adornment and filth must alike be avoided, because the one smells of luxury and the other of vainglory. It is praiseworthy not to go about without a linen garment, but not to possess costly linen garments.

How then can it be fitting for you, dressed in a mean garment, with a hair-shirt worn next to the flesh [the printed text is corrupt: “with the garment covered next to the flesh by a worn hair-shirt”], a worn and perforated *birrus*, one leg half-naked, a long beard, hair cut round at the forehead, to walk barefoot among the crowd [Col. 1483D] and offer the spectators a novel spectacle, so that they say that only a club is now lacking from your costume to make you a lunatic? This gains for you not so much authority among the simple, as you are wont to say, as a suspicion of madness among the wise. For if you appeared unexpectedly to some people, what human feature in you would they see without being compelled to ask: “Where is the man?”

Return, therefore, to common sense, and do not strive to be a solitary example in holiness, since the Wise Man says: “Woe to one alone; for when he falls, he has no one to lift him up” (Eccl. IV, 10). But if you propose John the Baptist for imitation, first fulfill the measure of confessors, fulfill the measure of apostles, so that you may consequently be able to rise to him than whom none greater arose among those born of women. For reason teaches that, just as one must not fall back to low things, so one must not begin from the highest.

Moreover, in the sermons by which you are accustomed to teach the common crowds and unlearned people, you not only rebuke the vices of those present, as is proper, but also enumerate, criticize, and tear apart the crimes of persons of rank, which is improper. This seems to me like mixing poison with an antidote, or, contrary to the order of nature, as the apostle James says, causing sweet and bitter water to flow at once from the same opening (Jas. III, 11). For this is not preaching but detraction.

What usefulness there can be in censuring absent persons, or what spiritual fruit can result from it, I do not see at all. Rather, you seem in a certain fashion to give ignorant hearers license to sin, when you set before them examples of their superiors, whose authority they may invoke in their own defence. For this is the condition of superiors: whatever they do seems to be a command. Those absent, however, can be more indignant and complain rather than be summoned to amendment by your detraction. Perhaps, indeed, it benefits you that, once the whole order of the Church has been cheapened in popular opinion, you alone together with your followers may be held in esteem. There are not lacking those who interpret it in this fashion. But such cunning speaks of the old man; it is earthly, animal, devilish. It does not befit your profession, does not befit this pilgrimage, does not befit these rags.

We see needy priests deserted by their flocks, as though unworthy of persons to whom they may present themselves, to whose prayers they may commend themselves, from whom they may receive the imposition of penance, to whom they may pay tithes or first-fruits [Col. 1484C]—all of them considering themselves condemned by your judgment. We see crowds flowing to you from every side and rendering to you and yours the honors they owe to their own pastors. Yet, as is clear, they are led not by love of religion but by the curiosity always familiar to the multitude and by a desire for novelties. For their lives do not appear improved. Thus the losses of others serve your gain.

Moreover, by what reasoning can that be defended: that men and women of every condition and age who, as commonly happens, are temporarily pierced with compunction while you preach, you indiscriminately receive and immediately compel, untested, to profess the religious life? Yet the Apostle says: “Test the spirits, whether they are from God” (I John IV, 1). Pope Gregory likewise says concerning those not to be received rashly into conversion: “Since it is serious to join one untried to the service of men, who can say how much more serious it is to apply untested persons to the service of God?”

It has thus happened that very many, relapsing into their former deeds, incur a double condemnation. For no discipline restrains them; rather, you leave each one to his own will, either content merely with the invocation of your name over them, or greedy for new gains, lest by lingering over those already acquired you suffer loss of time. For, as is reported, you say it suffices for you if you prevent sin even for one night. Such an intention indeed proceeds without limit: neglecting those who came before, you concern yourself with those who follow. But in this way, as the number of disciples grows, so great will be the destruction of those neglected. [Col. 1485A] You must fear that you will share in it, according to what the Lord says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who travel sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he has been made, you make him a son of Gehenna” (Matt. XXIII, 15). But if this is due to those who make one proselyte, what is due to one who makes very many such persons? For if one person’s condemnation condemns many, much more does the destruction of many redound upon one.

The number of your proselytes is so great that we see them wandering in bands through the provinces, conspicuous for barbarous length, clothed in blackest garments. In the fields, they are said to walk shod; but in cities and villages, barefoot. If the reason is asked of them, they answer that they are “men of the master,” and do not usually add whose master they are, so that the unqualified answer may proclaim your eminence. And it is sufficiently clear that these men are men and walk according to man. But far be it from them to have this from your teaching: to act or speak in such a way as the world knows. For we preferred their faults to be imputed to your negligence rather than fortified by your authority.

I say nothing of the young women whom, as I said, you immediately confined in separate cells after admitting them to profession without examination and changing their dress. Their beginnings were much to be feared, even if they had been enclosed under regular discipline. The pitiable outcome demonstrates the rashness of this deed: some, driven by childbirth, escaped after breaking their prisons; others gave birth in the prisons themselves. This certainly would not have occurred had your prudence measured the outcomes of things—or rather, had you attended carefully to the Lord’s words, by which he teaches that in imposing burdens one must measure the strength of those who bear them, showing this by a fitting comparison: [Col. 1486A] “No one,” he says, “puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst and the wine is poured out. And no one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment; otherwise the new patch pulls away from the old, and a greater tear occurs” (Matt. IX, 17).

Thus it happened also to these wretched little women. Not yet stripped of their old life by long experience, you suddenly entrusted to them the precepts of a new profession. When their wombs swelled, their garments were torn; with the precepts scorned, the rupture of their souls became much worse. When childbirth was delivered, their wombs burst; with the command disregarded, the wineskins perished. For their old condition could not contain the new fervor of so great a virtue. Therefore your religious undertaking is blamed also for this outcome, because at its beginning discretion, the mother of virtues, was not observed.

Thus, brother, taught by present dangers, you must henceforth exercise greater diligence in such matters, directing your devotion especially toward God with supplication, that God himself and Lord may “guard your coming in and your going out, from this time forth and forevermore” (Ps. CXX, 8).

The final heading of the accusation against you, as it is thought, yet not differing from the first, concerns your profession of canonical life, the stability of your former place, and the care of governance undertaken over the brethren professed there—all of which, it is said, you have despised because of the sisters. On this matter we ask either for a reasonable answer from your brotherhood, or we fear for you a certain condemnation. In this part there is indeed an abundant supply of things to be said against you, but we have preferred to await what may be said on your behalf. [Col. 1486C] May Christ preserve your holiness, praying for us, most beloved brother.

## NOTE ON THE PRECEDING LETTER

[Col. 1485]

[Col. 1485C] This is that famous letter which some of the most distinguished among learned persons judged to have been addressed by Marbod to Blessed Robert of Arbrissel, the most devout founder of the celebrated royal monastery of Fontevraud. Others, no less perceptive among them, judged it spurious. Far be it from us to dare to settle their controversy definitively. Yet the kindly reader will not disdain to receive what we have been able to learn concerning it.

There were indeed some who held that it should be attributed to our Hildebert, chiefly because it is found among the Hildebertine works in Victorine manuscript no. 272, though they adduced no other reason for their opinion. It should nevertheless be observed that it is placed absolutely last, after all the others; and that there is no word written at its head, nor any notation from which one may conjecture who its author is, nor even any that indicates the name of the person to whom it is directed. For it begins directly with the title: “He rebukes someone whose religious profession was held suspect.” Then it begins as follows: “To the servant of God: it is fitting not only to offer rightly, but also,” etc. There appears there no name at all, nor a mark of a name, which is nevertheless almost never absent from the other letters. Hence it is not easy to guess either who writes or to whom it is written. I therefore do not see why it is attributed to Hildebert, nor do I perceive why it should be considered addressed to Robert rather than someone else.

Accordingly, I would with good reason suspect that it was freely appended to the Hildebertine works by a copyist, and added with all the greater plausibility because Hildebert certainly always cultivated an unbroken friendship with Blessed Robert. From the beginning he fostered Robert’s holy order through his own patronage and that of his friends; he was desired and obtained as patron from Pope Honorius II by Petronilla, the first abbess of Fontevraud; he earnestly commended Robert’s affairs and business to Henry I, king of the English; and he secured Robert’s rights with more than forty diplomas subscribed by himself, which are diligently and religiously preserved in the archive of Fontevraud itself. [Col. 1486C]

The controversy, however, seems to be settled by that elegant epitaph with which Hildebert wished the memory of Blessed Robert to be adorned. This is from Royal manuscript no. 274, formerly belonging to the celebrated monastery of Elnone, or Saint-Amand, about five hundred years old and of excellent authority; we reproduced it in full above among Hildebert’s poems, p. 1320. In it he describes Blessed Robert as a most vehement enemy of the flesh, whose

> A hauberk crushed his side; dry thirst, his throat;  
> Hard hunger, his stomach; wakeful care, his eyes.

[Col. 1486D]

> He seldom granted himself rest, food still more seldom;  
> He fed his throat with grass, his heart with God.  
> The flesh was worn down beneath the laws of mistress Reason;  
> And they had one savor, and that savor was God.

Who would suspect even slight incontinence in a man accustomed to mortify his flesh with so many austerities? Or who would suspect him guilty of that new martyrdom which Geoffrey of Vendôme—if his letter is genuine—reproached him with? Hildebert did not hesitate in the same epitaph to compare this holy man with Peter of Poitiers, who, in exile [Col. 1487A] for the house of God, was crowned with martyrdom:

> Life made him equal in heart to Peter of Poitiers,  
> Who ruled the flock; death made him equal in merits.

Far be it, then, from us to attribute that letter to Hildebert. Having searched for it with the greatest diligence, we have been able to find it in only one out of the twelve and more manuscripts that we examined; there it is the last of all, without the author’s name or that of its addressee, and thus ambiguous in every respect and at least suspect.

As regards Marbod, I would not think the letter should be attributed to him without hesitation either, since we found it in none of his manuscripts, which are very rare. We saw five in number: one from Angers, two from Jumièges, one from Bec, and one from Saint-Gatien at Tours. In all of these there is not one iota or one stroke concerning this letter. It is found only in the Rennes edition of 1524; but that edition cites no manuscript from which it drew the letter. Nor do we think much trust should be placed in an edition published with such carelessness that a grave error and an anachronism strike the reader’s eyes on its very title-page: it reports that Marbod died in 1180, whereas the circular letter of the monks of Saint-Aubin at Angers, announcing Marbod’s most devout death—which occurs there on the reverse of a single folio—establishes that he died in 1123. Nor did this edition win much esteem for its editors, since in it sacred and profane works are generally found mixed together without order, with such negligence that one may suspect the printer set Marbod’s works in type as they were indiscriminately presented to him, making no, or certainly very little, selection and no inquiry into their sources. [Col. 1487B]

I know that some learned persons thought it probable that this letter might be attributed to Marbod because, among the Hildebertine letters, there is another letter of complaint from Marbod to Raynald, bishop of Angers, nearly of the same style, in their judgment, as this letter to Robert. The very learned Reverend Father Soris, visitor of Fontevraud, sincerely informed us of this in learned observations which he was kind enough to provide for us on the matter; accordingly, he thought that both letters might be ascribed to the same author. And indeed the letter to Raynald is found among the Hildebertine works. But I do not see why, unless because Hildebert and Marbod were the closest friends, and a third friend, wishing to commend Marbod’s just complaints to posterity, thought those letters should be mixed with Hildebert’s letters. Yet this occurs only in the printed editions: in none of the more than twelve manuscripts we examined—of the others I make no assertion—did we see that letter of complaint.

But if, as some thought, Marbod had any ground to complain of Blessed Robert because of his deposition at the Council of Poitiers, certainly he would not have been silent about him in that letter, just as he was not silent concerning “Angevin malice,” that is, Stephen the dean, by whose plots he had been seized, loaded with chains, and thrust into prison. Nor was Marbod the sort of man who, if he had any complaints against Blessed Robert, could not prove his own innocence and Robert’s wrongdoing; nor would he have undertaken any other argument for diminishing Robert’s reputation than the matter treated throughout this whole letter, in which no trace at all of Marbod’s indignation against Blessed Robert appears. [Col. 1488A]

Led by these arguments, we cannot avoid regarding this letter, if not wholly spurious, at least as suspect, and as nothing other than a mere contrivance of spiteful people against a most zealous preacher of the Gospel. By his sermons he attacked the public and notorious incontinence of the clergy of that time, just as the whole Church attacked it in its councils through its canons. These persons, by the venomous pen of the heretic Roscelin, contrived to cast their own disgrace back upon a holy and most continent man. They attempted to strike him with the same weapon and under the same pretext of instructing pious women toward Christian perfection by which Saint Jerome and other most holy men had formerly been assailed by utterly depraved and heretical people; and by which Origen was driven to employ means, even at the peril of his own temporal and eternal salvation, to avert calumny—means which, although he may perhaps have been Catholic, made him an exile from the Church.

Meanwhile, let no reader suppose us to be persons who constitute ourselves judges in so grave a controversy. We set forth our opinion. We compel no one to subscribe to it, apart from truth, which lies hidden in a very deep well; nor do we wish to bar the way of those [Col. 1488C] to whom it especially belongs to persist in refuting what we regard as this false accusation with stronger arguments.

Since this letter has been among the most celebrated Marbodian works throughout the learned world, we thought that, lest we be accused of carelessness in examining it, it would not be unwelcome to the studious reader to append here its variant readings between the printed Rennes edition and the unique Victorine manuscript.

[Note: [Col. 1487] The following manuscript versions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1487]

There: “A woman has captured the precious soul of a man. Take care, therefore, lest she capture you.”

[Col. 1489A] “Remove, therefore, such arrangements.”

Hence Augustine: “It is worse than adultery to possess criminal continence.”

[Note: [Col. 1489D] *Byrrhus*, or *birrus*, is a kind of garment, according to Martinus, which by imperial constitutions was forbidden only to soldiers’ servants (Pithoeus, *Adversaria*, bk. I, ch. 16). Paul the monk and Pontius, deacon of Saint Cyprian himself, who elegantly described his martyrdom in the *Acts*, report that blessed Cyprian was clothed in this *byrrhus*, or *birrus*—which amounts to the same thing—when he was led to execution; Pontius calls the cloak in which the holy martyr was clothed a *byrrhus*. This seems to accord sufficiently with the following phrase, “one leg half-naked,” so that the sense is: the *byrrhus* was so perforated, so torn, that through its rents a half-naked leg could indecently appear to anyone.]

“May Christ preserve your holiness, praying for us.”

### Marbod Printed at Rennes, 1524

[Col. 1488D]

“It befits your profession, dearest brother—you who, by the very novelty of your unusual dress, have turned everyone’s eyes toward yourself, [and who] beyond cloak and sandals have set forth in your own person an example of the most vigorous philosophy—to display in word or deed,” etc.

“Take heed, therefore, dearest son, lest, while you…”

“Brother, on whose account Christ died. For thus the Apostle says: ‘By sinning and striking their weak conscience, you sin against Christ.’ But lest I seem, by pursuing matters generally, to rebuke not so much things to be noted in you…”

“As though formerly…”

You therefore deem them worthy, they say, not only of a common table by day but also of a common bed by night, with the whole company of disciples likewise lying down together, so that between the two groups …

And you indeed, casting out your nets for a catch, enclose an abundant multitude of fish; but among the fish you are said to draw in serpents also, which by their nature …

Hence elsewhere: “A woman captures the precious soul of a man.” Take care, therefore, lest your own catch capture you.

[Col. 1490A] Remove from yourself, I beseech you, temptations of this kind.

How great a sin this is Augustine shows in his book *On the Singularity of Clerics*, saying: “Continence is worse than adultery,” etc.

You cannot remain chaste in mind for long.

It will certainly kindle a harmful fire.

Under ruin. But why should we be reluctant to continue here some small portion of the argument of the aforesaid author, by which alone the whole bosom of this blameworthy cohabitation may be torn open? “Why,” he says, “has the man who disdained to take a wife admitted a woman to himself? Why does everyone who has not eaten flesh fill his dwelling with the furnishings of flesh? And he who has not drunk wine, why does he enjoy the delight of wine?”

To argue publicly before men, promising holiness, and in private not to be without a wife: these are two arguments, of holiness and of lust, marvellous on either side. And he adds many further things of this sort, which plainly disclose the purpose of this dishonourable [Col. 1490B] fellowship. Thus much concerning the first chapter.

Very many people think, and not without reason, that you ought to be rebuked.

It will win them over by the newness of its life. For we ought to act, as Seneca says—for it is lawful to borrow moral maxims from the philosophers of the Gentiles, as golden and silver vessels from the Egyptians. We ought therefore to act so as to follow a life better than that of the crowd, not a contrary one. Otherwise, those whom we wish to correct we drive away from ourselves and turn aside. This is the first promise of philosophy: common sense, humanity, and fellowship; from that profession difference will not separate us. Let us see that those things by which we wish to procure admiration, etc. 1416 Between cheap and durable dress.

Jerome, writing to Nepotian, says: “Your clothes are battered …”

Therefore, with your regular habit cast aside, clothed next to the flesh in haircloth, with a worn and perforated cloak …

Return, therefore, I beg you, to common sense; and do not strive to be alone in holiness [Col. 1490C] without example, since the wise man, etc.

It has one who raises it up. The prophet likewise exhorts us not to devise novelties, but to follow the footsteps of those who have gone before, saying: “Stand upon the ways, and see, and ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is, and walk in it; and you shall find rest for your souls.” But if this is to be imitated, etc.

You are accustomed to teach: not only do you rebuke, as is fitting, the faults of those present, but you also enumerate, censure, and tear apart the crimes of absent churchmen—not only of ranks but even of dignities—which is unfitting.

These rags. Even if you deny that they were sought after, you cannot deny that this result followed. We see needy priests.

They complain that they have been condemned by prejudice.

You compel those not approved to make profession.

The blessed Pope Gregory also, writing to Bishop Fortunatus concerning those not rashly to be received [Col. 1490D] into conversion, says among other things: “Since it is serious …”

Condemnation. For you exercise no further care over certain persons, whom you restrain by no discipline of a rule, but permit each to follow his own judgment—whether content, as some think, with the invocation of your name alone over them, or, as you assert, eager for new gains, lest, by lingering over those already acquired, you suffer losses through the passage of time.

Wandering about, clad in variegated (*bigerricis*) garments, conspicuous for their barbaric length, they walk, as they say, shod through the fields, but barefoot in cities and villages.

[Col. 1492A] Women who have professed religious life without examination.

Others gave birth in the very cells.

Showing that greater precepts do not suit lesser persons: “No one,” he says, “puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst, and the wine is spilled. And no one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment,” etc.

May Christ preserve your religious devotion as you pray for us.

[Col. 1491]

# THE BOOK OF MARBOD, BISHOP OF RENNES, ON THE THREE ENEMIES

(Hommey, *Supplement to the Fathers*, pp. 546–551, octavo.)

## TO THE READER

Hildebert’s eulogy of Marbod, celebrated in verse and placed by us at the beginning of this *Supplement*, was followed in the same manuscript by the present little work which we append. We therefore concluded that it should be ascribed to the same Marbod, whom the other surviving monuments of his genius testify to have been the foremost poet of his age: the *Book on Stones*, of which we have handled very many manuscript copies in different libraries, though it has been printed—see Gesner in the *Bibliotheca*; commentaries on the *Song of Songs*, which we do not despair of recovering from a certain library—on these see Sixtus of Siena. All contemporary writers testify to this: Hildebert, Geoffrey of Vendôme, book III, letter 14; Sigebert; Trithemius; and so forth. In Mabillon’s *Analecta*, vol. III, in Hildebert, Bishop Ulger of Angers therefore ventures to assert among other things in his epitaph:

> Cicero yielded to him; Virgil, joined with Homer, yielded:
>
> To say it briefly, he conquered them alike.

## THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 1491]

### CHAPTER I. On the same three enemies in general

[Col. 1491B]

Although very many things commonly turn sacred morals aside,  
Woman, wealth, and honour turn them aside more deeply.

Woman, wealth, and honour—the kindling and torches of evils—  
Draw hearts and hands into crime and into swords.

### CHAPTER II. On women, how prone they are to evil

Happy is he who has learned by experience what a woman is,  
And by some art has escaped her snares.

Woman is a fragile thing, never constant except in wrongdoing,  
Never of her own accord ceasing to be harmful.

Woman is a devouring flame, utter frenzy, an inward enemy:  
She both teaches and learns whatever is wont to harm.

Woman, a cheap marketplace, a thing born to deceive the commonwealth,  
Thinks she has succeeded when she is permitted to be guilty.

Woman, a grievous yoke, a grievance of law and equity:  
[Col. 1491C] She thinks it shameful whenever she commits no shameful deed.

Woman is all the more grievous an enemy because she is more private;  
She invites crime by gift, voice, and hand.

And, consuming men, she is consumed by every vice;  
And she herself becomes the prey of the men whom she preys upon.

She weakens, plunders, and afflicts body, wealth, and spirit;  
She supplies, arms, and nourishes weapons, hands, and hatred.

[Col. 1492B] She overturns, shakes, and burns citadels, kingdoms, and homes;  
And she crushes the hope, head, and arms of so many kings, she alone.

Woman dared to condemn John’s neck,  
Hippolytus to death, and Joseph, though he spurned her, to prison.

Woman, with like purpose, deprived Uriah of life;  
And David of piety, and Solomon of faith.

Woman conceives in her mind, approves with her tongue, and accomplishes by her arts  
That toward which law, people, and she herself together rush.

### CHAPTER III. On avarice

Gold no less emasculates inward powers,  
And no less shows the unlawful path along which to run.

Hardly is there anyone ashamed to pervert what is right for gold,  
Or reluctant, for any price whatever, to be guilty.

By gold is accomplished whatever is unjustly hoped for,  
And no one asks vainly when a gift is held out.

[Col. 1492C] Gold moves hearts, a robber of holy eyes;  
It arms and drives pure hands into crime.

By gold the virtue and labour of those often falter  
Whose hearts God praises, while men praise the rest.

And he whom you would swear would lay down his neck for what is right  
Thinks all things lawful for hope of a small profit.

A fierce enemy, a stern judge, a bloody torturer:  
[Col. 1493A] Hope of payment loosens hands from battles and from law.

Gold stations armies, prepares a fleet, draws swords;  
It teaches men to despise force, winds, seas, and weapons.

It dissolves marriage, breaks through the barriers of modesty,  
Defiles holy hands with slaughter and mouths with deceit.

For gold Polymnestor was perjured, Danaë adulterous,  
Tarpeia faithless, Eriphyle savage.

For gold Crassus died; for gold Amphiaraus fell;  
For gold armies, leaders, strength, and peoples fall.

### CHAPTER IV. On ambition

But the man whom neither wealth nor woman can break,  
Ambition conquers and makes the devout man criminal.

Ambition turns conduct toward what is forbidden, and does not allow anyone  
[Col. 1494A] to be a criminal below the level of his power.

Its work is to disturb leaders and change crowns,  
To prepare death for the innocent and sceptres for the guilty;

To prepare destruction for cities and ruin for temples,  
To lay patricians low with swords and homes with fire;

To offend nature with vices and the gods by ritual,  
To spare only when it cannot do harm;

To expose kings to mockery, kingdoms to plunder,  
Mothers to disgrace, and old men to exile.

Whomever the contagion of so great a calamity seizes even once  
Thinks all things permitted while he obtains kingdoms for himself.

Such a man endures to carry swords against his father; nor ever  
Are mind, hand, and mouth free from fraud, bloodshed, and deceit.

# [LIFE OF ST LICINIUS]

[Col. 1493]

## NOTICE ON THE LIFE OF SAINT LICINIUS, BISHOP OF ANGERS

1417–1418 This Life of Saint Licinius, composed by Marbod, appears in the Bollandists under 13 February. It is preceded by another, somewhat more extended Life, issued by an anonymous author of Angers. Marbod himself, at the request of the canons of the Church of Angers, abridged it, reshaped it into a better form in a more elegant style; and we judged it superfluous to place that earlier version before this one, since the curious reader may refer to it if he wishes. In return for this work, the aforesaid canons of Angers promised that, while he was still alive and finally after his death, they would offer certain prayers for him.

The original act recording this promise, in the cartulary of the monastery of Saint Sergius at Angers, differs somewhat from that seen in the Bollandists. For there Marbod calls himself archdeacon; in the autograph of Saint Sergius he calls himself a priest-deacon. This, I think, comes to the same thing, except that, as often happened, archdeacons were sometimes not priests. From this promise, moreover, some have concluded that Marbod was not a canon of Angers, since he contracted with the canons as though an outsider. I would not readily subscribe to that opinion, since in prominent chapters nothing is more customary than foundations of this kind, which individual canons make from their own property and by which, under specified conditions, they bind their fellow canons to offer certain public prayers for them after death.

This is so true that, while writing this, in the obituary book of the distinguished Church of Paris which happened to come into my hands, I noted, in January alone, as many as seventeen foundations of this sort, and likewise in the other months. What is customary in Paris is most commonly received practice in Chartres and the other more celebrated churches. Nor, as it seems to me, should it be concluded from this that founders of this sort were not canons of the same church. Nor therefore do I think it may be inferred from the aforesaid act that Marbod was not a canon of Angers, since here too he expressly calls the aforesaid canons his brothers—a designation which seems fitting only for a canon.

[Col. 1493]

# LIFE OF SAINT LICINIUS, BISHOP OF ANGERS, BY MARBOD, ARCHDEACON OF ANGERS AND LATER BISHOP OF RENNES

(From two ancient manuscripts; in the Bollandists, 13 February.)

## AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

[Col. 1493B]

1. Desiring to set forth the life and deeds of the blessed Bishop and Confessor Licinius, we wished to invoke the Lord God, from whom is all wisdom, so that, through the intercession of that same saint, he may open to us a door of speech, and we may say things that are true, not superfluous, and beneficial to our hearers. We think this can be done only if, omitting none of his deeds, we wholly cut away, from the material collected from the earlier [Note: [Col. 1493] Marbod polished the earlier Life of Saint Licinius at the request of the canons of Angers.] version, the various additions and repetitions which bear the mark either of prolixity or display, and bring more weariness to the reader than ornament to the writing.

For this was especially the reason that moved our brothers to impose the present work upon us: in the earlier work, the importunate verbosity of superfluous speech seemed to diminish the dignity of the subject. For frequent recurrence of words concerning the same matter indicates, in some measure, a lack of things to say. Yet we were not moved by levity of mind or any vanity, as though, posing as correctors of another’s work, we wished by a display of our effort to catch popular rumours; 1419–1420 rather, we were overcome by the prospect of eternal reward and by the prayers of worthy persons, so that we would not refuse a labour greater than our strength. For we place confidence not in ourselves but in divine help.

Accordingly, with Christ’s aid, we shall relate, as far as we can, what must be said, preserving fidelity to the facts, for the praise of the aforesaid saint and the glory of God, seeking the benefit not only of ourselves [Col. 1495A] but also of all readers. For he gains a great fruit from his labour who, by writing things through which readers are edified, serves the advancement of many. We shall therefore take care to employ language that is moderate and restrained, so that gravity may not produce obscurity, humility may not impair usefulness, nor prolixity produce weariness. The reader’s part will be to receive these things attentively and faithfully, lest by neglect he turn to his own ruin that which has been prepared for salvation. But now let us begin the narrative.

## CHAPTER I. Saint Licinius’s studies, court offices, and profession of a holier life

2. Licinius, then, born of a most illustrious family—for he counted kings of the Franks among his ancestors—and endowed by nature with every good quality of soul and body, crowned his good fortune with devotion to virtue. From childhood his manner of life was such that there shone forth in him the appearance of a certain future perfection and an unusual example. For besides the excellence of his outward appearance and the modesty of his countenance, by which he charmed the minds of beholders with some hidden grace, this was remarkable in the boy: the vices that seem inborn in tender age and, as it were, rule everyone by natural right, he already despised, having been forestalled by God’s grace.

He was neither excessive in play, nor importunate in eating, nor talkative in speech. He did not rashly gather anger, nor did he rage among his peers with arrogant violence. Nor was he, through fickleness of mind—the instability proper to childhood—immediately carried off in different directions, so as eagerly to scorn at once what he had begun. In short, many marks of manly constancy were visible in the boy.

3. Therefore, when, after the first elements of learning, he had been placed, as children of nobles commonly are, under literary instruction, there the generosity of his noble nature and his receptive intelligence shone out. What he heard from his teachers he easily understood and retained in memory. It was not fear of the rod, as often happens, that forced his attention, but love of learning that kindled it. He knew how to show reverence to his teachers, obedience to his tutors, goodwill to his fellow pupils, and humility to all. He was neither offended by another’s slowness nor proud of his own sharpness.

[Col. 1495D] He so abhorred not only shameful actions but shameful words that he did not allow them to pass unreproved even in others. Already, plainly, the boy was feared by his companions as a censor if they dared anything unlawful. He bore the enmities of rivals with equanimity and swiftly brought them to an end. He conquered anger by patience and pride by humility. He lent neither ear nor tongue to his companions’ slanders. Insults cast against himself he disregarded; those cast against others he softened. In short, while professing to be a pupil, he had become a teacher of morals.

4. When the years of childhood had thus passed in these studies, and by his own industry he had added no small amount to his teachers’ learning in sacred and secular letters, he was compelled, at the command of his father—who held the foremost place in the palace after the king—to renounce philosophy. He was transferred from leisure to business, from study to military service, and from academic pursuits to court offices. King Chlothar gladly received him, both on account of kinship by blood and because of the dignity of his excellent appearance and the elegance of character that shone in the young man. Soon afterwards, having honoured him with the military belt, the king began to count him among his friends, recognizing him as wholly worthy to deliberate with concerning great matters and the administration of the kingdom.

For he lacked neither prudence in counsel, nor trustworthiness in keeping confidence, nor vigour in execution. Nor did he lack ready eloquence or love of justice; therefore he seemed most useful both in pleading cases and in the exercise of jurisdiction.

5. Furthermore, as guardian and cultivator of perpetual chastity, he enhanced, in the judgment of all, the reputation of his own intimacy with the king. Toward his fellow soldiers he behaved in such a way that he strove to earn the goodwill of each by some service. He showed himself approachable to everyone; he met everyone’s needs, if not with aid, then with counsel. He grieved at every person’s misfortune; in his own gains he counted the prosperity of all. At court he advanced the interests of those whom he could; and he could do so for all whom he wished. Thus no one was left to whom some benefit of his had not come.

He praised the brave deeds of each individual, though apart from Licinius himself no one was silent about his virtue. In short, among the retainers of the court he performed the part of a steward. Thus, at the request of all, the king made him tribune of the soldiers, an office now called in our usage Count of the Stable. He administered this office so that he was judged worthy of a greater dignity. Yet amid these things his spirit was always watchful toward God, to whom without ceasing he poured forth pure prayers that God might rescue him uncorrupted from the present evil world.

As often as he could, he devoted himself to sacred reading, by whose constant practice he might kindle his desire for the things above more strongly. He did not so much extinguish as forestall the ardour of youth by frequent fasts, lest through luxury and licence the human mind should grow insolent. He so abounded in the bowels of mercy toward the poor and afflicted that he let no opportunity of place or time pass in helping them. Plainly, he bore a monk in the soldier and a contemplative in the active man; he fulfilled both so that neither impeded the other, nor was he delayed in passing from either to the other.

6. Meanwhile, as prosperity succeeded prosperity, both his ancestral estate having already come to him by hereditary right and his enjoying the most ample honours through royal generosity—for he had also been made Count of Angers—he became betrothed, at the urging of friends and of the king himself, to a virgin from a most illustrious family. This was contrary to the vow of his heart, by which he had long resolved to lead a celibate life and, having renounced honours, to devote himself to God. But when he was already preparing to bring her home—marvellous to tell!—he found that she had been stricken with leprosy in the solemn assembly. Thus he was freed, by a misfortune he welcomed, from the necessity of marriage imposed on him by his friends’ counsels.

7. Nor did he seek to erase his embarrassment by hastening to another marriage. Rather, understanding that God’s providence accorded with his vows, he turned the event into an opportunity, so that he would not be forced again to attempt what, when previously attempted, had turned out otherwise. Therefore, strengthening his resolve, so as no longer to postpone what he had long pondered, he immediately sought his discharge, laid aside the military belt, renounced transient honours, gave himself wholly to God’s service, and received clerical tonsure together with his profession.

Oh, how great a joy he gave his brethren through himself, filling every mouth with praises of God!
