How many hearts he moved to compunction, how many eyes he opened to tears, when they saw this scion of a most noble stock, exalted by offices and wealth, pre-eminent in beauty and outstanding in glory, despising all things, bending his noble neck beneath Christ’s yoke, and by a voluntary exchange becoming poor from rich, weak from powerful, a servant from a master! This is indeed rare and worthy of the highest praise: when such things are present, to despise without difficulty those things whose mere hope scarcely anyone abandons even amid adversity.

But the servant of God considered the glory to come, beside whose beauty every earthly thing grows foul. It was good for him to cling to God and place his hope not in the uncertainty of riches but in the Lord God.

8. Moreover, how greatly he advanced in the clergy may be estimated from what has gone before. All the industry that he had previously spent upon the functions of the world he turned to the benefit of his own soul and of the brethren with whom he lived. He who had sufficed for both with a divided attention, now, gathering his powers, sufficed supremely for the latter. The glory of high birth never tempted him to refuse submission to the services of the lowliest. His learning never mocked the simplicity of the unlearned. While fasting, he did not disparage others’ meals; while keeping watch, he did not despise those asleep. He hastened to recall the discordant to peace and the undisciplined to order. He set before himself the good qualities of all for imitation, their evil qualities for caution. And though all loved him as a father, he revered all as masters.

## CHAPTER II. Saint Licinius’s episcopal functions

9. In accordance with Christ’s command, invited to the Church’s banquet, he had taken the lowest place. When, therefore, the time had come for the Lord to say to him, “Friend, go up higher” (Luke 14:10), it was also said to the bishop of the see of Angers, as illness assailed his body: “Give this man place” (ibid., 9). Thus, when Audoin had died [Note: [Col. 1497] Grandimus: Audouyno; Gazetus: Andouino; Saussaye and Chesne, vol. I of *Francica*: Audouino; Claude Robert: Audoeno and Audonino.], he who had formerly seemed to govern the Church of Angers, and the reputation of the holy man had already spread far and wide, Licinius was sought, seized, and ordained by the acclamation of both orders and with the king’s most ready assent. He who had chosen to be lowly in God’s house was compelled, unwilling and weeping, to preside. Most fittingly, that the good things he had long amassed in himself in retirement he might at last pour forth for the benefit of many through administration.

[Col. 1498A] 10. Having assumed the government, he judged that not honour but a burden had been added to him. As though he had achieved nothing hitherto by all that he had completed, he then began anew; and he who had long surpassed all others in holiness of life undertook to conquer himself, the one task remaining. But because no virtue seemed lacking in him, he had no way to grow except to add quantity where number could not be increased. He therefore extended his vigils, enlarged his prayers, prolonged his fasts, wore down his flesh with haircloth, and tortured his body with cold. And he who had nothing in himself to expiate transferred to himself, after Christ’s example, the sins and infirmities of those committed to his care.

He poured forth almsgiving so lavishly that crowds of poor people, summoned by his fame, hastened to him even from distant provinces, for he omitted no form of generosity. He clothed the naked, fed the hungry, provided medicine for the sick and burial for the dead; he offered hospitality to pilgrims, consolation to the sorrowful, ransom to captives, protection to orphans, and advocacy to widows. He washed the poor’s feet with his hands, wept over them with his eyes, kissed them with his mouth, and dried them with his hair. In a word, he exercised as many mercies as human life endures miseries. Nor did his liberality extend only to the poor, but to all ranks, even to certain bishops.

11. Meanwhile he performed the office he had undertaken no less diligently, celebrating daily the mysteries of the sacraments and publicly preaching the word of God: threatening sinners with the terrors of punishments and setting before those who mourn the joys of rewards. “Mercy and judgment will I sing to thee, O Lord”: judgment for rebels, mercy for suppliants. Such grace was poured upon his lips that no one disliked what he said. He noted the faults of individuals discreetly, rebuking the sin, not the person. Though each person recognized himself in what he said, no one could recognize anything said insultingly about himself.

Nor was he ever lacking material when teaching, because he used his own life as a book. Whenever he needed to consider what to say, it was ready to hand for him to remember what he did.

12. In severity he pursued faults but spared nature: hating vices, he loved people. He reproved offenders with justice and received penitents with gentleness. Thus he tempered zeal with indulgence and indulgence with zeal, so that the latter did not corrupt and the former did not wound. In synodal deliberation he argued at greatest length for mercy and, insofar as reason allowed, exercised his mind and tongue in defence of the accused; he especially protected priests under accusation. In showing regard for persons he considered not rank but character, so that he gave each the greater deference the more he perceived that person to love God.

He went about the churches and visited monasteries. Wherever he turned, spiritual joy was born. He refreshed souls by his word and bodies by food. [Col. 1499A] Everywhere he uprooted vices and planted virtues; driving out diseases, he restored health. Indeed, he regarded both sorts of fortune with the same countenance and spirit, so that prosperity did not exalt him and adversity did not break him. In dress and bearing he observed moderation; in the number of attendants, necessity; in their quality, respectability. In short, he administered public affairs as though he despised private matters; he cared for private matters as though he did not concern himself with public ones. Nor, as most people do, did he fall from brilliance into smoke; rather, he passed from splendour to splendour, from a lesser virtue to a greater.

13. By now his radiance had illuminated all Gaul, and on the report of him alone many nobles, despising wealth, followed Christ in poverty. From this one may judge how much gain he won for the Lord in person, since even where he was absent he converted very many. By now the hopes and resources of the king of the Franks and the magnates depended chiefly upon his authority; and even among the bishops he was held great and wondrous. All, thirsty as though for a fountain, had recourse to him in their necessities. Each drew from him what he desired. In short, he seemed to everyone a kind of human angel, or rather an angelic man. For beyond the incomparable holiness by which he exceeded the measure of a human being, he shone with such power of miracles that no one doubted that apostolic grace dwelt in him.

We shall recount some of his miracles, from which the reader’s faith may judge the rest. For from few things many, from lesser things greater, and from manifest things hidden things are commonly inferred.

## CHAPTER III. Saint Licinius’s buildings, pursuit of retirement, and miracles

[Col. 1499C]

14. When, during a solemn fast, a great crowd of people had assembled in church—as indeed, following their pastor’s institution, they most devoutly did—behold, a woman possessed by a demon burst into the gathering with frenzied cries and mad gestures. Running through the church, she began to perform theatrical antics and, with wandering words such as drunkards commonly utter, to move the people to laughter. The holy man understood the devil’s design, whose constant endeavour is, insofar as he can, to hinder God’s service.

He commanded silence, briefly admonished the people on the immediate matter as the occasion required, and ordered the possessed woman brought to him. After prayer had been poured over her, while the people watched and awaited the outcome with minds held in suspense, he immediately expelled the enemy by the power of the cross and sacred adjurations. Having recovered her mind, the woman gave thanks and, by a public confession from her own mouth, magnified the great miracle before all. For she testified that she had previously had seven demons. I would not believe that anyone there was silent concerning God’s praises; I would suppose that none was silent concerning the priest’s merits. For truly the form of the head shines in the member, and the disciple represents the master in the image of his virtue. Christ cast seven demons out of Mary; Licinius, Christ working through him, cast the same number out of this woman. For although a servant cannot be compared with the Lord, in this miracle quality answers quality, sex sex, and number number.

15. Again, while during the solemnities of Mass on a Sunday he was exhorting the people according to his custom, a certain blind man named Ghiso, standing among the congregation, raised his voice and broke the silence. He implored the bishop, who drove away the darkness of minds by the word of his teaching, to drive blindness from his eyes by his holy prayers. The holy man replied that this was not the place for interruption and that he should not make a disturbance out of season, because the people’s attention would be disturbed. “Do not ascribe this, most holy prelate,” he said, “to importunity, but to faith. For I do not doubt that I shall immediately recover sight through your merits. For in a vision last night it was revealed to me that this grace was reserved for you. I was therefore ordered to hasten to you, that you might grant me what I desire.”

When the bishop heard this, and did not at all doubt the effect of the promised power, yet preferring it to be attributed to the prayers of the whole Church rather than to his own merits, he ordered a common prayer to be made for the blind man. When the office of Mass had ended, he dismissed the people—not because he begrudged them the grace of the coming miracle, but because he himself avoided popular glory. Then, taking the blind man aside in secret, he anointed his eyes with holy oil and sent him home seeing and joyful.

16. As crowds of sick people flocked to the fame of Blessed Licinius’s virtues, and his mind devoted to contemplation suffered inconvenience from the common throng, the servant of God feared lest the favour won by the greatness of his miracles might perhaps diminish his reward with God. He resolved no longer to expose himself to the crowds who rushed together. Shut within a secluded little cell, he began to meditate upon angelic repose, content with only one cleric and two servants. But since he could not even so exclude the tumult of those knocking—for they stood at the door, burst in with their voices, and many by their importunity wrung from him the help they desired—necessity compelled him to leave the place.

From that time he began to seek release from the king and the bishops of the province, so that, once another had been substituted in his place, he himself might hasten to the wilderness. All protested against this petition. For who could doubt that Christ’s flock, deprived of its pastor’s presence, would become prey to ravening wolves? They objected that in this matter he would have more loss than gain in the other; moreover, they contended that it was contrary to the law of charity—which seeks not its own interests but those of the many, that they may be saved—to prefer private advantage to public benefit.

At last, overcome by the prayers and reasoning of his fellow bishops, he abandoned his purpose of solitude. As though beginning anew, he turned himself wholly to carrying out the administration entrusted to him. He began to provide what was necessary for Christ’s household and hastened to compensate for the loss of interrupted contemplation through the gains of fruitful activity. Thus he deserved greater grace from God because he had devoted himself wholly to the benefit of his neighbours. And, that this might be evident to the world, the Lord thereafter adorned him with greater and more frequent miracles. Some of these must be recounted, though their fewness, by their magnitude, may equal a multitude in number.

17. The holy man had begun to build a monastery outside the city, not far from the walls. Later, richly endowed with goods and possessions, he dedicated it, as he had wished, in honour of Saint John the Baptist. Once, as he was going to inspect the work, accompanied only by one disciple very dear to him, he encountered a crowd of poor persons who began to ask him with importunate cries for aid in alms. Among them were twelve who, we have learned, were some blind and some lame.

When the bishop gave them no answer, since the attention of his mind was carried away even while walking by continual prayer, they assailed him with repeated shouts and gave him no opportunity to ignore them. Moved for a moment, he stopped and, as if in his own defence, raised his right hand against the importunate crowd and made the sign of the cross. Immediately lameness and blindness recoiled before the holy man’s zeal; every illness was driven away, and the power of the cross brought healing.

The healed persons followed the physician, who had already gone on, in order to give him the thanks they owed. Magnobodus—this was the disciple’s name—looked back first, recognized the miracle, and cried out in alarm to his master, who was walking ahead. Licinius also looked back and, seeing the grace he had unknowingly merited, gave abundant glory to the Creator for the manifold gift. At once, through the same disciple, he summoned the workmen whom he had been going to inspect, sought out the place from which he had made the sign, and ordered a church to be founded there in honour and remembrance of the holy cross. It remains to this day and represents the ancient miracle to believers. [Note: [Col. 1501D] Marbod himself mentions this in the Life of Saint Magnobodus, 16 October: “In the suburb of his city he began to build a monastery, evidently following the example [Col. 1502D] of his blessed master and predecessor Licinius.”]

## CHAPTER IV. Other miracles of Saint Licinius; his illness, death, and burial
18. As has been said, it was the custom of the holy bishop personally to visit the dioceses of his episcopal jurisdiction, and with devout concern to investigate the needs not only of each district but also of each person, lest perhaps through any negligence of his own or of the priests the flock committed to him should be endangered. Everywhere he scattered the seeds of God’s word, and strengthened the people by confirmations and blessings [Col. 1501D]. Moreover, from his own resources he supplied the want of the needy, and at all times shared his table with guests.

It happened, then, that among other poor persons he received into hospitality a leper, whose distinguished bodily stature and elegant proportion of limbs made the misfortune of his disease seem all the more grievous. When the saint had refreshed him with his own food, he withdrew into the oratory and, with the man standing beside him, passed the coming night without sleep, tirelessly entreating the merciful Lord in prayer for the wretched sufferer. When morning had come, he exorcised water, washed the sick man, and, at the touch of his holy hands [Col. 1502A], the leprosy disappeared more swiftly than words can tell.

> [Note: [Col. 1502D] He uses blessed water and, after prayers, heals the man by washing him.]

O man of prophetic dignity! O new example of ancient power! Let not the people of old glory in miracles, as though to prefer the Old Law to the New Testament. The Lord of both is one, and his power is equal in each. We have water, we have a prophet, we have a leper: Naaman, Elisha, and the Jordan are present for us also. But in this respect our cleansed man was better: he did not return again to his former manner of life [1428], nor did he endure to depart from his Elisha. Instructed by him in the divine writings and formed in the practices of Christian discipline, he changed his dress and cut off his hair. Thus, after being tested over time through the lesser grades, he at last deserved to attain the dignity of the priesthood. His commendable life, never departing from the footsteps of his master [Col. 1502B], afterwards supplied many with a pattern and example for living well.

19. As the bishop was passing by the city gate, those held in the prison adjoining that gate, learning that he was going by, called aloud to him with tearful voices. Moved by their distress, he resolved not to leave the place until he had first freed the wretched men; for he regarded himself as bound in those whose chains he took upon himself through compassion. He therefore sent messengers to appeal to the keeper, offering ransom money for the captives. But when the latter’s obstinacy could be bent neither by entreaties nor by payment, the faith of the avenger turned where it was accustomed to turn, so that what it could not obtain from a man’s wickedness it might obtain more wondrously from insensible matter [Col. 1502C].

He made the sign of the cross upon the prison door; and immediately—marvellous to tell!—the iron fastening of the bolts sprang apart. The customary hardness of the chains’ nature could not remain where a stronger faith had laid hold. Their bonds therefore being loosed, all leapt forth; strengthened by the holy priest with words and provisions, they returned joyfully to their homes. There are many other deeds of his no less worthy of record; but for brevity’s sake let these suffice. For a faithful mind desires nothing further, while an unbelieving one would not receive even more. Let us now hasten to his passing.

20. God’s servant had now fought the good fight, completed the course, and kept the faith; there remained for him from the just Judge the reward, the crown or prize of victory. To the soldier, now discharged from service, there was due a good field [Col. 1502D], the land of the living; to the labourer who had borne the burden and heat of the day, the denarius of eternal rest was due.

Seized in the month of August by violent burning fits of an acute fever, he was brought to hope that he was now about to be released, and most joyfully awaited his end. But when after some time the blaze subsided, he understood that the illness was chronic; saddened that he had been delayed and, as it were, driven back from the nearby harbour, he groaned. For, judging the present life to be a shipwreck, he sought with all his strength the homeland to come. His longing grew through delay, and because of the frequent distress caused by the recurring fever he relaxed none of the practice of his former abstinence [Col. 1503A]. He did not therefore lie upon softer bedding [1429], nor improve the quality of his food or drink. Indeed, now much more intent upon the entrance of the Lord who was already knocking, for as long as he survived he continually withdrew his mind from the body, thinking only of where he was going and forgetting all that he was leaving.

21. The fourth month was now at hand, and the furnace of tribulation had sufficiently tested Christ’s most pure gold. Thus, being in every respect worthy to be laid up in the eternal treasures of the Lord, the most holy bishop departed from the body on the Kalends of November, 1 November. He was magnificently buried, amid a great gathering of the orders, in the monastery of St John the Baptist, which he himself had built from the foundations and in which he had established a community of monks continually devoted to God’s service.

At his funeral, all who were present perceived that angels stood by [Col. 1503B], for they were suddenly suffused with so unusual a fragrance that they compared no earthly sweetness whatsoever with it. There too the consolation shown through signs wiped away the grief of all who mourned the absence of their shepherd. For on that very day two blind men and several sick persons were healed at his tomb. Nor, in the times following down to our own age, have divine gifts ceased in that place, gifts pertaining to the health of souls and bodies. There remission of sins is granted to those who ask faithfully; the desired remedy is granted to the sick; support for this present life is granted to the needy.

22. Here, through the merits of the present patron, so great a miracle was shown that it rightly deserves to be called more than a miracle. For if it is a miracle that the extinguished light of the eyes should be restored [Col. 1503C], it is plainly more than a miracle where the eyes themselves, which had never existed, are created. And if a blind man is one who possesses eyes but lacks sight, one who lacks the eyes themselves is more than blind.

Accordingly, a man more than blind, yet illumined by remarkable faith, as the outcome demonstrated, for a long time persevered at the saint’s tomb in constant prayers and devout supplications. In him there appeared so extraordinary a deviation from nature that he had neither eyeballs nor even sockets; rather, in what seemed like a monstrosity [Col. 1504A; 1430], his face descended flat from his eyebrows. Many came together from all sides to view this spectacle, so that afterwards the fame of the unheard-of miracle might spread all the more widely, because previously the novelty of so great a monstrosity had escaped no one anywhere.

As this man continually knocked upon the saint through prayer, suddenly before the saint’s body he received both eyes and sight; and what the defect of nature had taken from him, the effect of divine grace, through the saint’s merits, restored.

23. We have placed this especially at the end of the work as a kind of epilogue, so that, because it is recited last, it may occur first to memory, not being buried under the mass of intervening narrative. From this one event alone it is certainly established—that which indeed the whole purpose of our work aims to show—how well the supreme Lord is served [Col. 1504B], and how nothing ought to be despaired of by the faithful, since not even nature’s impossibility stands in the way of divine grace; through Christ our Lord, who with, etc.

24. I, Marbod, unworthy archdeacon of the Church of Angers, wrote and revised the Life of the blessed bishop Licinius at the request of the canons of that same church. For the recompense of my labour they promised and gave me a share in, and communion of, all prayers and good works that shall be performed in that church at any time: while I live, every day one Collect in the morning Mass, *God, who justifiest the ungodly*; but after my death, the whole service performed for one of the canons in prayers and Masses, and each year the observance of the anniversary of my death, as for one canon. In addition, every day, except feast days, until the end of the age, after Prime, while they go to chapter, they are to sing for me the psalm *Out of the depths* (*De profundis*), with the chapter verse, *Eternal rest*, and the Collect, *Absolve, O Lord*. Of this agreement between me and the canons, may my lord St Licinius be mediator, witness, and guarantor. Amen.

[VITA S. ROBERTI.]

[Col. 1503]

## NOTICE ON THE LIFE OF ST ROBERT, FIRST ABBOT OF CASA DEI, PUBLISHED BY MARBOD, BISHOP OF RENNES

1431–1432. For a preface to this work of Marbod, we judged nothing more suitable than the remarks made to elucidate it by our fellow members, the Reverend Fathers Dom Jean Mabillon and Thierry Ruinart, in the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Our Holy Father Benedict*, century VI, part II, p. 183. Their preliminary observations are as follows.

Such was the reputation of blessed Robert’s holiness among all people that, shortly after his death, steps were taken to institute a feast in his honour and to render him public veneration. This occasioned the writing of his Life. The task was undertaken by Gerald of Vienne, a monk of Casa Dei, who, as the blessed man’s chaplain, had for the most part been personally present at the deeds and miracles he performed. We learn this from another Life of the same saint:

> [Note: [Col. 1503] This is the one composed by Bernard and called the *Tripartite*, which immediately follows this one in the aforementioned *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*.]

There, in distinction 2, chapter 6, occur these words: “Gerald of Vienne, disciple and chaplain of blessed Robert, described his life and miracles,” etc. He then went to Rome and, having recounted before the supreme pontiff and the cardinals the virtues of blessed Robert, obtained the celebration of this most holy man’s feast.

[Col. 1505] Yet even if nothing but what was certain and beyond doubt had been contained in Gerald’s work, some disliked the fact that, as Marbod says, it was written in a difficult and prolix style, and therefore caused weariness to readers. Marbod himself, at the urging of the abbot and monks of Casa Dei, therefore set his hand to composing another account—or rather, to recasting into a better and more polished form what had already been written. When he had sent it, contained in one little book, to the monks of Casa Dei, the work pleased the abbot so greatly that he immediately compelled him, as Marbod himself says, by frequent requests to perform the same service for Gerald’s second booklet, entitled *On the Virtues of Blessed Robert*.

Marbod, then archdeacon of Angers and afterwards bishop of Rennes, fulfilled the abbot’s desire and dedicated this little book to that same abbot in a separate epistle prefixed to the work. Yet the manuscripts vary in naming this abbot: some call him Stephen, others Seguin. The initial letter S, which alone appeared in older manuscripts, gave occasion for the error: some expanded it into the name Stephen, others into Seguin, since both held the office of abbot of Casa Dei during Marbod’s lifetime.

But anyone wishing to investigate the matter somewhat more carefully will readily discover that Seguin’s name should be retained. Although most manuscripts give Stephen’s name, the older ones indicate Seguin; such is the manuscript of Sainte-Marie de Breteuil in Picardy, which we possess. Our colleague Pierre Laurent informed us that the same reading occurs in an old manuscript of St Cyprian at Poitiers, and he supplied us with many observations on this Life. The testimony of Bernard, namely the monk of Casa Dei, supports it. In the second distinction of the *Tripartite* he expressly relates that Archdeacon Marbod recast the Life of blessed Robert into a better form. Speaking of the vision of a certain Ralph, he says: “Master Marbod, archdeacon of Angers and afterwards bishop of Rennes, related this in the second book, which he wrote on the miracles of blessed Robert.”

Indeed, the style of the dedicatory epistle does not sound like that of a bishop addressing an abbot. But if Marbod wrote this Life while still archdeacon, it necessarily follows that it was dedicated to Seguin, not Stephen. For Stephen was elected abbot of Casa Dei in 1108, that is, twelve years after Marbod had ascended the see of Rennes; for he became bishop in 1096.

Thus speak the editors of the above-mentioned *Acts* concerning this Life of St Robert compiled by Marbod. They also maintain there that several other Lives were composed by various authors; for brevity’s sake we refer the reader who wishes to examine this more carefully to that place. On p. 184 they also discuss very learnedly the year in which St Robert died, and prove by irrefutable arguments that it was the year of Christ 1067—arguments whose transcription here might perhaps weary the reader.

[Col. 1505]

# LIFE OF ST ROBERT, ABBOT OF CASA DEI, BY MARBOD, BISHOP OF RENNES

## AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

[Col. 1505A] 1433–1434. 1. With God’s help, we shall attempt to set forth in plain and brief language the Life of blessed Robert, which one of his disciples—

> [Note: [Col. 1505B] Namely Gerald of Vienne, monk of Casa Dei.]

—related, as we believe, truthfully indeed, but in a difficult and prolix style; so that a brief narrative may banish weariness, and a simple mode of expression may permit easy understanding. This is not because we detract at all from that writer’s talent, but because we give the greatest weight to the religious devotion and authority of those who impose this task upon us. Reason itself seems to have led them to command it. For since the deeds of the saints are committed to writing in order that all who read or hear may be stirred to imitate them, the writer must take the greatest care, so far as possible, not to exceed anyone’s capacity in a matter intended for everyone’s benefit.

Otherwise, the whole undertaking is frustrated of its proper end, if the charm of the deeds invites people to listen but the unwelcome difficulty of the writing excludes them; or if the writing admits them in some fashion but needless prolixity makes them weary [Col. 1505B]. Therefore neither unfamiliar or exotic words should be cultivated, nor should the reading be extended by varied explanations. We need not fear that poverty of expression will exhaust the riches of the subject; rather, we should hope that the deficiency of a poor tongue will be enriched by the abundance of the subject—in so honourable a kind of work, that is—where, if every covering is removed from the material, its dignity sustains itself.

2. We therefore invite the reader’s goodwill and attention alike, since we shall obtain the greater reward insofar as, with God’s cooperation, our labour pleases more people. For it will benefit those whom it pleases; and what benefits them will greatly please us. Thus our labour will serve another’s advancement, and another’s advancement will serve our reward. We, for our part, shall take every care, to the extent of our ability, that it may please: applying ourselves, as we have said, to brevity—not so as to deprive the work of what is necessary, but so as to cut away what is superfluous—and likewise to clarity, not so as to diminish the dignity of the subject, but so as to provide the capacity for understanding.

But if readers dislike the style because it is insufficiently polished [Col. 1506B], let at least the writer’s ready devotion please them; let the truth of the account please them; let the recent memory of holiness please them. For although at every time the faithful find the recollection of good deeds pleasing, what is, as it were, set before their eyes affects the hearer more strongly, since supporting evidence frees it from the suspicion of falsehood. But since enough has been said about these matters, let us come to the narrative.

## HERE BEGINS THE FIRST BOOK OF THE LIFE

[Col. 1507]

[Col. 1507A] 3. Robert, an Auvergnat by birth and free in condition, was born to Christian parents: his mother Raingard and his father Gerald, who, it is believed, traced his ancient descent from the stock of blessed Gerald of Aurillac. Certain signs showed from his earliest infancy that he would be God’s servant [1435]; and it does not seem inappropriate to insert them into the narrative.

For, when his mother was pregnant with him and, as the time of birth drew near, was making for a certain castle, she gave birth in a wilderness through pressing necessity, and not without God’s providence. Clearly he was to be a lover of solitude, and to regard this life in which he was born as a road, not a homeland. From there he was carried with his mother to the castle and, as often happens, entrusted to a certain woman to be nursed. When she put him to her breast [Col. 1507B], he would not take it, not so much abhorring the taste of the milk as the horror of the nurse’s concealed sin [Boll.: “latentis,” concealed]. This immediately became clear, since he gladly sucked his mother’s breasts and, when the former woman was again offered to him for the sake of testing him, rejected her once more.

That woman was a prostitute; and therefore the infant, in refusing her milk, condemned sin. He did not, of course, know what he condemned, but God’s power works even in those who do not know.

4. Thus divine mercy grew with the child. When he had become a boy, he was entrusted to instruction in the town of Brioude, at the church of the martyr Julian. There he became a cleric and was assigned among the canons; afterwards, as time went on, he advanced through the ecclesiastical orders as far as the priesthood. He passed the years of boyhood in such a way as to escape unhurt from those evils with which tender age is commonly infected either through its own fault or through that of others [Col. 1507C]. Rather, meditating innocence from the very beginning amid its first experiences [variant: “vices”], he imbued the pure vessel of his heart with the fresh savour of virtues, so that, prevented by God with the blessings of sweetness, he could admit no bitterness of vices.

Already then, full of faith in eternal things and despising all temporal matters, he had placed all his hope in the Lord and loved him, though little himself, with no little affection. For he often kept vigil throughout whole nights in the church with tears, to the astonishment of those who found him so, since he was unknown even to the guards themselves. He prayed and read very frequently, so that in the one he might commend God to himself, and in the other himself to God. He pursued humility [Col. 1507D] and obedience, by which he so dealt with people that he did not incur God’s offence. He followed the poor and afflicted with the bowels of mercy, giving aid as he could and compassion to all.

More than once, while others recoiled, he touched with his hands the ulcer-covered bodies of the sick [Col. 1508A] and washed their hands, patiently bearing their outward filth because he thought rather of inward gain. Hence it was believed that illness was often driven away by the gracious touch of his hands.

5. A better youth followed such a childhood, as he employed increases both of possessions and of strength in God’s service. For the danger that often befalls people at the fervent threshold of that age [1436]—when the wind of a new temptation assails the mind and they suffer the alluring shipwrecks of modesty—he had prudently anticipated. Long before, he had drunk deeply of the love of chastity, so that no shameful thought could trouble a heart steeped in virtues. Thus he added virtues to virtues and unceasingly built the tower whose foundations he had laid in childhood. The trees [Col. 1508B] he had planted in his heart grew and bore fruit unto eternal life.

Day by day divine grace shone more manifestly in him, and not a few were stirred to live well by both his word and example. He fasted more earnestly and prayed; and, to the extent that he could, he distributed generously to the poor. Indeed, he built an alms-house in the town, so that by continually ministering to the poor there he might be exercised as in a training-ground of holiness. It is certain that, when he had distributed all things to the poor, he often added his cloak or mantle for their use. He plainly recognized Christ in the poor; thinking little of his own needs, he hastened to cover Christ’s nakedness. Thus Martin once divided his cloak with a poor man and deserved to see Christ clothed in that same garment. Though I do not dare compare this man with Martin [Col. 1508C], I do not fear to compare deed with deed.

6. Meanwhile he carried out the priesthood diligently, attending the church at the appointed hours and frequently offering sacrifices to God for the salvation of the Christian people, whom he bore altogether as one person in the broad embrace of charity. He invited sinners to repentance, sometimes instilling fear of punishments, sometimes setting forth the joys of rewards; teaching that no one ought to despair of pardon who, duly converted, had groaned in repentance. He further promised the assistance of his prayers and thereby continually won many for God.

Even when his voice was silent, his life spoke; although when his voice spoke, his life remained silent. For while he displayed in himself a model of good living [Col. 1508D], he did not display himself at all. His face bore the gravity of his character; his gait and dress revealed the modesty of his mind. He showed himself affable to all, yet presented to each person an affection suited to the diversity of condition, age, and character. By this discernment [Col. 1509A], the prudent man provided for everyone’s salvation, persuading all as though more nearly and familiarly, because he had assumed within himself the person of each. Finally, though he surpassed everyone in merit of life, he wished to be judged inferior to all.

Amid these things he burned with love of contemplation, since he always wished to join better things to good, and the best to better. He had tasted, as if in passing, how sweet the Lord is, and with all the marrow of his heart [1437] desired to be free for God alone, that he might drink with the full throat of his mind the sweetness he had, as it were, sampled beforehand.

7. He therefore resolved to change his place and, leaving everything, to follow Christ. He had chosen the monastery of Cluny, moved by the fame of that place’s religious life and discipline. Taking with him only one companion for the journey, not for counsel [Col. 1509B], he unexpectedly set out, fearing—as indeed happened—that, if his plan became known, he would be held back from his undertaking. For who would have wished to lack such a patron, who had so often met the needs of so many? He was an eye to the blind, a foot to the lame, clothing for the naked, food for the hungry, husband and father to orphans and widows, release to prisoners, a bed to travellers, medicine to the sick, burial to the dead.

When it became known that he was departing secretly—the household, astonished at their lord’s solitude and silence as he set out, had shortly afterwards publicized the matter—all quickly pursued the fugitive, as if concerned for public safety; they seized him and brought him back. The holy man was ashamed; grieving that his intention had been not so much thwarted as made public, he fell ill from distress of mind. When he began to recover [Col. 1509C], he understood that by God’s will he had been recalled from the place to which he had been heading, perhaps because he might make greater progress elsewhere. He tried whether he could fulfil his desire among his own people. But since none of his household accepted his salutary counsels, his resolve pressing on irrevocably, he went to Rome, that the apostles’ intercession might obtain from God the guidance he desired.

What he desired was this: that, withdrawn from the crowd of people, he might build a monastery in solitude, where under a religious habit he might live the canonical life with two or three others, professed to God alone. Returning from Rome, he awaited without hesitation in faith what he had asked for. He was delayed for a while, I believe, so that desire might grow through delay.

[Col. 1509D] 8. Meanwhile a certain knight, pierced with compunction by divine inspiration, approached the man of God to seek counsel as to how he might erase by worthy satisfaction the greatness of his sins, by whose awareness he was tormented. He declared that there was nothing so arduous that he would not undertake it in order to recover God’s favour. The saint instructed him to leave all things and enter Christ’s soldiery. When the knight replied that he would indeed do this if he could do so with him, and most gladly, the man of God understood that this man had been divinely appointed to him as a companion and minister of his purpose.

Therefore rejoicing greatly, he opened all the secret of his desire, promised him companionship, confirmed the agreement, and dismissed the man gladly, charging him to seek a place suitable for this purpose [Col. 1510A; 1438] and, if possible, to enlist a third companion. He described the suitability of the place: some little church in the wilderness, even if deserted and ruined, but one with parish rights, where some sort of livelihood might be procured by manual labour or roots of herbs. It was to have parish rights, I think, so that if they established a new oratory on another’s territory, they might not appear to injure older foundations. For what they intended to undertake solely for the sake of heavenly reward ought not to be darkened even by the shadow of any earthly greed.

The knight, now full of faith and steadfastness, resolved to go to Anicium, to the shrine of the blessed Virgin, so that God’s mercy might prosper what he had begun. He knew that nothing would be more effective for obtaining his request than to use the mother’s patronage with her son. As he hastened there [Col. 1510B], behold: by God’s ordering, he found on the road ready what he sought—a certain ancient church, surrounded by vast solitude and corresponding in every respect to his wishes. Before the prayers, his devout desire had been heard; and through the saint’s merits, the result anticipated the servant’s petition.

He nevertheless continued to the place for which he had begun his journey, in order to render thanks at the place of prayer. He added prayers also, that God’s mercy might bring to completion what it had begun in them. Returning to his master, he announced what he had found, setting forth the solitude of the place and its other hardships suitable for strict living. The man of God rejoiced with him, gave thanks, and urged the brother diligently to pursue the remaining matters.

9. One thing was lacking to their wishes: that they might find a third companion for so great an undertaking. For among two, a third is customarily a kind of bond of charity; and under this number they seemed more fittingly to serve the triune and one God in unanimity [Col. 1510C]. What was lacking soon came about, as divine grace attended the knight’s diligence. For when he had returned to his own people and was considering, as has been said, obtaining a companion, and did not conceal in his face the condition of his changed mind, a knight who was his familiar asked why he appeared more thoughtful than usual.

“I would tell you,” he replied, “if I knew that you would faithfully keep what was entrusted to you.”

The other immediately gave the assurance requested and heard in order what he wished to know. As he listened, he conceived a love of virtue; stirred by the example of his companion, he was vehemently inflamed to undertake a purpose of such perfection. At last, with humble entreaties [Col. 1510D], he begged his companion to introduce him, a sinner, to the man of God, and not to judge him unworthy of fellowship in so great a praise. He offered himself not as a companion but as a servant, and promised under pledge of faith that he would never depart from the observance of this profession.

Thus the first knight, having gained the second, returned joyfully with his companion to the master. The latter rejoiced at this spiritual increase [1439] and, commending to God in prayer the fruits of the seeds he had sown, addressed the recruits of the divine soldiery:

> “I congratulate you, my sons, on your ready devotion. Conscious of my own weakness, I desire you as companions and supporters upon the way of God, which he himself declares narrow and exceedingly arduous. Yet I understand that we must greatly fear lest we rashly bind ourselves to a most laborious warfare while thinking only of its rewards. For it is not beginning a good work but completing it that is praiseworthy; it is not a good undertaking but perseverance that receives praise. The former sometimes happens through impulse, but the latter always through virtue. Moreover, not aiming at the highest is tolerable because of human frailty; but falling away from one’s purpose is damnable because it is a diabolical transgression.
>
> “Therefore consider diligently, and consider again and again among yourselves, lest, while you aim at the summit of perfection, you become, God forbid, the cause of greater condemnation for yourselves. While you are still free, set before your minds all the comforts you intend to forgo; and, on the other hand, the many and great hardships to which, in bidding farewell to the world, you deliver yourselves: hunger, thirst, cold, nakedness, vigils, labour, abasement, insults [Col. 1511B]. In short, pursue everything that people flee; take care lest, while these things pursue you, you flee from them.”

He said such things not to deter them from their salutary undertaking, but to prepare them against every future event and thereby make robust for endurance those whom no variety of temptation would find unprepared.

10. But they, in no way moved from their purpose—indeed all the more encouraged by the holy man’s words—promised, with Christ’s help, that no adversities would break them and no recollection of pleasures make them waver. They said it was enough that they had sufficiently experienced the difficult paths of sin and understood that they had wearied themselves without cause. Henceforth they wished to serve as soldiers of Christ, whom one cannot serve without reward, since not serving sin itself is a great reward [Col. 1511C].

Moreover, they said that God had wholly provided for their weakness and ignorance by giving them such a master, by whose word they could be taught and by whose example strengthened; for he knew both how to set forth what ought to be done and how to do what he set forth. They would therefore cling to him and serve him devotedly in all things.

To this the holy man, attributing everything to God and nothing to himself, said:

> “God is able to make the wavering steadfast and to instruct the ignorant. Nor should those protected by the supreme power fear an attack of contrary power in any respect. And he undoubtedly protects you as you serve him, since he is accustomed to protect those who do not serve him in order that they may serve him. Therefore, if you have resolved firmly to cling to God [1440], you have me as either companion or servant—would that I may be as useful as I am devoted. But beware the inconstancy of the human mind; and, if it is not burdensome, go now to the church and, through the intercession of blessed Julian the martyr, implore God to provide what is more beneficial for us.”

They entered the church, prayed prostrate, and returned strengthened.

11. He had sufficiently tested their faith; the time had now come for their departure. Only this remained: that the place granted them by God should also be transferred to them by its earthly lords. Taking one of the two, he therefore went to Anicium, where two noble brothers lived, both canons, one also an abbot. One was named Arbert, the other—according to Manuscript 1—Rostagnus. Abbot Arbert was himself afterwards a disciple and monk of the blessed man. From these men he easily obtained what he wanted, since the fame of his holiness could not be hidden from them because of the nearness of the places [Col. 1512A].

All things therefore being prepared as they wished, on the appointed day he sought the wilderness with two disciples, of whom the first was called Stephen and the second Dalmatius. They found thorns and briars, horror and solitude alike—in short, a place lacking every good thing, except that it was good for them to lack every good thing. For the farther they withdrew from human beings, the nearer they believed themselves to God; and the more temporal goods they lacked, the more eternal goods they expected to receive.

The wickedness of their neighbours added to the difficulties of the place. Like wild beasts in the savagery of their conduct, they harassed God’s servants—whom they ought to have supported—with insults and threats. Judging them mad because they had begun to inhabit a sterile place which the neighbours would not have tolerated even had they brought provisions, they inflicted upon them whatever troubles they could [Col. 1512B]. Certainly, those who had entered into combat against the devil were now being attacked by his members.

We think that the troubles they felt and endured there are better expressed by silence than by speech, for silence often indicates the whole when talk can scarcely unfold even a part. Yet they resisted adversities by enduring them, and conquered their attackers by not resisting. The third strengthened the minds of the two, like a veteran among recruits in battle, teaching that if they overcame the enemy’s first attacks, they would overcome the later ones much more easily. For as greatly as fear increases in the defeated, so greatly does confidence increase in the victor. Thus he not only made them victors in the present, but also more ready for future struggles.

If afterwards a fiercer temptation pressed upon them [Col. 1512C], he declared it most shameful that those who had overcome in the first encounter should yield in the second—men whom experience of battle had made wiser and victory stronger. In this way the man skilled in spiritual weapons [1441] strengthened the untrained and failing spirits of his fellow-soldiers. Thus, as it were by an art, he fostered in them endurance of labour: he used hope of succeeding victories to bring earlier battles to completion, and remembrance of completed battles to gain succeeding victories.

He also instructed them from the holy authorities, so that they might choose rather to be afflicted for a little while with the people of God than to possess the temporal pleasure of sin, since eternal condemnation follows the one part [Col. 1512D], and everlasting blessedness the other. Therefore they should look to the recompense; “they should look to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising shame” (Hebrews 12:2).

With these and other such things he sometimes restored the spirits of his wearied companions, though neither the shared burden of labour nor the particular responsibility of brotherly care wearied him. In a short time he made them so steadfast and perfected that they not only bore every hardship joyfully, but even prayed for their persecutors.

12. Therefore, having made a cell beside the church—of branches and leaves, I suppose—they divided the household duties among themselves: the others were to work with their hands for their food, while he was to devote himself to reading and prayer. They laboured with their hands in work [Col. 1513A]; he too laboured, often bending his knees. Their exercise in work drew forth sweat; contrition of heart bathed him in tears. Rest relieved their weariness; reading refreshed his exhaustion. What each did benefited all; yet what the third did benefited the other two more: for by the instruction of reading he made God known to them, and by persistence in prayer he commended them to God. Thus, when he sowed spiritual things among them, it was no great matter if he reaped their bodily things. In the oratory, which they had repaired as best they could, at fixed hours by night and day they poured forth common prayers; together they took a scanty, dry meal with thanksgiving, the greater part of which was reserved for poor people and travellers, should any happen to turn aside to the place. It was their custom [Col. 1513B], if they possessed anything, to give it to anyone who asked; and the blessed man had trained his companions so that they would without hesitation give even everything, taking no thought for the morrow.

13. One day, when the brothers had gone out to work and he remained alone in the church—where it was his practice daily to offer continual tears together with prayers—he heard the voice of someone asking for alms. He rose quickly, entered the cell, and gave all that he found. This entire store was a portion of bread left over from the previous day’s supper, yet sufficient again for three at table, whose meal was, indeed, scarcely removed from hunger. 1442 When they returned from work, there was no food; and when Dalmatius took this badly, the holy man quickly checked the complaint by bringing forward Christ’s words: “Do not be anxious,” he said, “about your life, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ For your Father knows that you need these things” (Matt. VI.31). The event immediately confirmed this saying, not without marking the imperfection of the doubting brother by a miracle. Abbot Arbertus, who, as was said above, had granted them possession of that place, was not unaware that the voluntary poverty of the saints was distressed by the barrenness of the wilderness; he sent them three pack animals loaded with bread and wine. The messengers accordingly presented two to the blessed man and announced that the third had collapsed on the way, in some unusual manner. For it had neither been weaker than the others nor previously shown any signs of failing. At this the holy man gave thanks; and, as he was always simple and ready in speech that built others up, he turned cheerfully to the brothers [Col. 1513D]:

“Let our beloved Dalmatius learn,” he said, “to hesitate no longer in faith in Christ, since our confidence has received its immediate recompense, and he sees that for his murmuring he has been punished with a penalty small indeed, but plain and sufficient for correction. For let him know that the portion which remains is his: it has not been taken away, but delayed, so that he may not doubt that the faith which failed him is to be restored.”

O how great is the power of faith, the lack of which even beasts of burden perceive!

14. By frequent use of these and similar words, he not only instructed his companions, but also softened the former savagery of the inhabitants; gradually stripping them of brutish habits, he made human beings, as it were, out of wild beasts [Col. 1514A]—certainly a greater miracle than if, as one finds in fables, he had transformed human bodies into beasts. He raised the eyes of their minds to acknowledge the Creator of all things, and, by recounting the labours and dangers of worldly life, readily convinced them that apart from him there is no rest for souls. Thus it came about that some, laying aside the belt of military service and attaching themselves to his holy fellowship, bound themselves there forever to Christ’s service. Some also of the clerical order, taught by his instruction, preferred the solitary and needy life to domestic comforts.

As the number of disciples increased, so too did the observance of religious life grow—an observance produced not so much by the severity of discipline as by the perfection of charity. For besides those things established in common for all [Col. 1514B], each person offered something beyond requirement from his own resources; and in that poor little flock of Christ there was a remarkable commerce in holiness, each adding [variant: employing] to his own virtues whatever he saw worthy of imitation in another. Since poverty itself sufficed for those who possessed nothing for Christ’s sake, they were troubled only by an insufficiency of holiness. For what the dishonourable love of money commonly effects among the avaricious—causing them to despise whatever they have acquired while they crave only new acquisitions—that the most honourable love of righteousness effected in them: a certain insatiable, if one may say so, avarice for religious devotion. Their striving was led by a standard-bearer and teacher of such great perfection, who, forgetting what lay behind and stretching himself toward what lay before, pursued the goal after the manner of the Apostle [Col. 1514C], until he should grasp it; and the disciples’ readiness to follow was strengthened by his example.

15. Thus the reputation of this most holy manner of life stirred the neighbouring regions far and wide to praise God. Such power of miracles was added to the merit of his life that in those places no one any longer doubted that the holy man had plainly received from God the grace of healing. He faithfully dispensed it to those who sought it, while guarding humility, and attributed divine benefits not to his own merits but to those of the holy martyrs Agricola and Vitalis, in whose church he served. Nor did demons keep silence concerning his merits when, at his command, they were expelled from possessed bodies.

The faith of friends brought to him for healing a demoniac woman, the wife of a certain peasant. Hardly had she been brought into the church where the saint was praying when, held by the enemy who possessed her, she began in a terrifying voice to hurl threats and insults at him:

“Robert, Robert of Casa Dei, why do you, a stranger, seek to drive us from our dwelling places? Rather, we shall soon trouble you and yours, increasing with fire the intolerable hardships which you will suffer here. Nor will your associates—Agricola of Bologna, Symphorianus of Autun, Marcellus of Die, Privatus of Mende, and Julianus of Brioude—whom you are preparing to join with yourself in fighting us, be of any help to you.”

The devil saw what was to come: namely, that a foundation would be established there called by the new name Casa Dei, and that relics of the saints whose names he had listed would be brought there. Though unwillingly he foretold future blessings, he nevertheless lied, as he wished, that they would not be beneficial. Of future events, the one thing he gladly predicted was that the place would be consumed by fire; but even in this he did more good by predicting it than later harm by bringing it about. By foretelling it he prepared the saints’ patience; by inflicting it he tested it.

Meanwhile, the woman raged through the church in leaps and rushes, then with a sudden assault turned toward the altar, as though about to lay hands upon its sacred spoils. The holy man, pitying the madness of the unhappy woman, temporarily deferred his prayer, came out to meet her, and lightly struck her with the rod he held, rebuking her more sternly. Then, turning to the demon, he said: “In the name of the Lord I command you: come out of her [Col. 1515B], give glory to God, and, once expelled, do not return again.”

At these words the woman fell down; and, when the enemy departed, she immediately fell asleep, exhausted. Soon awakening, now sound in mind but still weary in body, she asked for bread to be brought to her. She eagerly received it when blessed by the man of God; thus restored unharmed, she returned home. She also lived for a long time afterward, carrying about with her an example of living power.

16. Likewise, a peasant named Constantius [Bollandists: Constantinus], living near Saint-Victor, was so filled with a demon that, sparing no one, he attacked even himself with his teeth; yet he openly declared that he feared only the presence of the man of God. His people brought him, bound in chains over his whole body and carried on a bier as though dead, and presented him, exceedingly frightened and resisting, to the same saint. The saint prayed over him and, raising eyes and mind to heaven, adjured the enemy by God’s name and commanded it to depart. The hostile spirits already knew the power of his words, and it was unlawful to transgress what he commanded. Therefore, frightened at the first voice of his command and compelled to release its captive vessel, the adversary made the man, insofar as it could, weak and tormented. After a little while the man recovered; having received the blessed bread which the saint offered, he returned home healthy and rejoicing.

The report of these events spread abroad and drew many from their homes. Nobles mingled with common people and came together from every quarter to see a new example of ancient power. He received them quite fittingly and kindly [Col. 1515D]. Since in the wilderness he did not have bodily food sufficient for so great a crowd, he set before everyone the word of God, by which, as by bread, wine, fish, and diverse dishes of delicacies, he fattened the souls of believers. All marvelled at the modesty of his countenance and at the spiritual eloquence of his speech, suited to each person. By these things he so changed some hearts that, suddenly despising the pleasures of the present life, they burned only with love for future blessedness.

But since many proposed to serve Christ only under his direction, and the multitude of applicants was considerable, while both the remoteness of the place and the diversity of their pursuits seemed to preclude the cohabitation of many, a new plan arose from necessity, in service of divine providence and under pressure from circumstances: namely, that a monastery should be built there [Col. 1516A], 1445 in which those whom God gathered might dwell unanimously, like a flock in the Lord’s sheepfold, under regular and monastic discipline. The devotion of not a few faithful people opened the way for its construction; eagerly competing with one another, they voluntarily contributed estates and money for these purposes. Seeing that God had divinely prepared an opportunity for so great a good, and knowing truly that it concerned the peril of his own soul if, for the sake of his personal quiet, he failed to provide for the salvation of so many, the servant of God took counsel with his brothers on this matter. With the assent and counsel also of Rencon, bishop of Auvergne of blessed memory, he undertook the laborious administration and began to build the monastery, with the greatest rejoicing and support of all, beside the little dwelling in which he had formerly lived. Long before, he had desired a solitary life with few companions, and determined to accept no money or property from anyone. But when he had attained these things, and more fruitful results [Bollandists: more favourable results] followed from the abundance of divine generosity, he completed the work successfully from the offerings of the faithful, whether made spontaneously or at his urging, lest he seem ungrateful for heavenly benefits.

17. At that time Henry ruled the Franks, and Leo IX occupied the apostolic see. The aforementioned bishop therefore approached the pope, and the holy man the king of the Franks; each sought the strengthening authority and suitable privileges for the stability of the new foundation [Col. 1516C]. Both obtained what they desired. The king not only confirmed the grants made or to be made to the same monastery, but also honoured the house of God and the holy man with royal honours and gifts. The pope, moreover, strengthened the plan by apostolic decrees and further commanded that the man of God—whose reputation for holiness he had heard—be placed over the brothers, though unwilling and resisting. This was done; when the monastery had been dedicated amid the rejoicing of all, the blessed man received the monastic habit and governance with a blessing, compelled both by the brothers’ prayers and the bishop’s authority. Otherwise, he judged it safer to be governed than to govern, and to render an account only of his own life rather than that of many. Yet God’s help proved sufficient for both tasks [Col. 1516D], although he had presumed upon his own strength in neither.

18. How great, after he took up the burden of leadership, was the vigilant energy he showed toward those under him and the simplicity of mind he showed toward God, is attested both by the frequent manifestation of signs and by the spiritual increase of his labours. For, besides a considerable multitude of laypeople whose souls he won through the word of his preaching, the example of his life, and the aid of his prayers, he gained nearly three hundred monks. He also restored to God’s service about fifty churches after prolonged desolation. Yet this is clearly the chief thing: he poured into his disciples a likeness of his own singular simplicity and charity, and appears to have left to the place whose founder he was [Col. 1517A], as an inheritance in place of an outstanding endowment, hereditary holiness.

19. Of his miracles we touch upon only a few, trusting the testimony of those who declare that they saw them. Yet his whole life on earth was a great miracle. Still, for those more readily moved by outward signs—not because these are greater, but because such persons have less capacity and are more often led by the wonder of bodily senses—there is no lack even in this respect of material by which the benefit of such people may be served.

A knight from Mont Gascon, named Bernard, had suffered continuously for three years from an ailment of the kidneys, which physicians call *nephresis*. As the saint prayed devoutly over him with the sprinkling of holy water, he not only freed him from the bodily affliction [Col. 1517B], but afterward dedicated him, once made a monk, to Christ’s military service. Likewise, he restored by the laying on of his holy hand another man suffering from dropsy through the corruption of tainted blood, whose natural warmth had already been submerged and who was about to be overwhelmed by an excess of superfluous fluid. By the same power, with the efficacy of prayer and the laying on of hands, he healed a demoniac boy deprived of the use of feet and tongue, the son of a certain peasant who lived beneath the place called Mount Calcis. In a threefold miracle in the same person, he restored speech to the mute, movement to the lame, and freedom to the captive.

Likewise, when a demoniac was presented to him and he extended holy bread to the man at the very threshold of the church, the enemy, unable to endure the power of such faith, departed with a dreadful sound and intolerable stench [Col. 1517C], leaving the man unharmed. A woman whose limbs were entirely disabled was brought—she was attending the sacred mysteries while he celebrated Mass, being carried, of course, not on her own feet but in the hands of others. Faithfully hearing his discourse to the people on the praises of the ever-Virgin, on the feast of her Annunciation, she was immediately restored to health. Nor did the effect of such power escape those present: a crack issued from the shock of her sinews and struck the bystanders with sudden fear, as if a roof had collapsed [Col. 1518A].

20. Let it suffice briefly to have recalled these few miracles of this saint, so that the assurance of the more advanced may not be burdened and the faith of the simple may be strengthened. For, apart from mention of such powers—which, as is said in legal cases, are a commonplace, since they do not always occur to the good and sometimes occur even to the evil—the constancy of the saints’ life alone supplies to prudent people both proof and example; and no one but a good person could attain it.

For what can ever be more worthy of a miracle than to preserve an unmoved disposition of mind amid such variety in worldly affairs [Col. 1518B]? This blessed man maintained it so firmly by divine gift that neither the diversity of ages, places, times, nor fortunes could move him from his holy purpose. He had asked one thing from the Lord, and this also he sought: everlasting dwelling in the house of the Lord. In view of it he reckoned as nothing any pleasure or hardship of the present life. Thus it came about that, through the course of a brief labour—for everything that passes is brief—he attained the prize of eternal rest, gaining heavenly things in happy exchange for earthly ones.

He is believed to have foreknown the day of his death.

> [Note: [Col. 1517] Having foreknown his death, he died on 24 April, in the year 1067. On him see *Acta Sanctorum*, century VI, part 2, in the notes on this Life.]

Having summoned the brothers to himself, after words of exhortation by which he instructed them with divine admonitions, he kissed each one and bade farewell. Then, turning to God [Col. 1518C] and commending himself and them in prayer, full of days he fell asleep in Christ. He was buried on the eighth day before the Kalends of May [24 April] at the new Casa Dei, which he himself had built, in the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## BOOK II

[Col. 1517]

[Col. 1517D] To the truly holy lord and abbot Stephen, uniquely to be embraced in the members of Christ: Marbod, a sinner.

Most often you ask, excellent man—or rather, under the form of a request you command and compel much more urgently—that I append to the earlier little book, which I composed in plain style concerning the life of blessed Robert, wishing that it might be as effective as it was willingly written, a subsequent work on his virtues according to the headings of the first writer. The charge imposed by your repeated kindness honours my smallness, but the undertaking of so weighty a labour burdens my weakness. For if the first work had displeased you, you would not so insistently demand another from me; nor, again, can that which pleases be polished without labour and care. Yet I am not so foolish as to arrogate to my own powers anything good that I do, rather than to him from whom all good things proceed; nor so faithless as to despair of divine assistance in honourable and pious labours.

I therefore rejoice, Father, that that little work pleased you and the holy brothers, and I give thanks to the divine grace through which it pleased you. But what remains I undertake relying upon the same divine help—a help promised to me not by presumptuous confidence in my own merits, which are evil or nonexistent, but by the intercession of the blessed Patron concerning whom this work is undertaken, and by your holiness. Therefore, whatever is erroneous will be imputed to me; whatever is right, to heavenly grace. And, I pray, let the unworthiness of the writer not prejudice the dignity of the subject undertaken [Col. 1519A], since honour is often paid even to base servants for the sake of their masters. Let the faithful reader attend not to how things are said, but to what is said, because true things are often discussed thinly through an orator’s ability, and false things copiously. Wholesome food is served in earthenware, while deadly poison is sometimes mixed in golden cups.

2. Since I am about to recount the saint’s virtues, it seems to me not inappropriate first to oppose the blasphemies of certain people, upon whose foreheads and sacrilegious mouths the mark of the dragon and the beast is undoubtedly recognized. Of the beast it is written: “It will open its mouth in blasphemies against God, to blaspheme his name, and his tabernacle, and those who dwell in heaven” (Rev. XIII.6). Thus those who vainly devise calumny against this saint undoubtedly prove themselves to belong to the number of that beast.

For they say—and I do not shrink from setting out, as before judges, the intention of their crafty malice, which must be refuted—“This new saint has overturned for us the ancient order of holiness. For whereas all others who faithfully raise their hope on high with love arrange ascents in their heart and always begin the higher things from the lower, this man alone, after first setting his foot upon the summit, gradually afterward slipped down to lower things. He had established himself far from earthly and laborious tumults, his lofty peak rising above the clouds, to gaze with the tranquil sight of his mind only upon divine and heavenly things; and behold, little by little he turned aside to active labour and human affairs, and finally to the care of building works. He began as an amphora; he ended as a jug. He reversed the customary order of marriages, and contrary to ancestral custom and the testimony of ancient history, before Leah’s marriage-bed he gained the embrace of Rachel; having known both, he preferred the beautiful-faced woman to the bleary-eyed one, rejecting the latter and clinging steadfastly to the former. Or rather, having attempted both, he was rightly rejected from both, like an unworthy suitor. He set Martha before Mary and, contrary to Christ’s judgment, which declares Mary’s part the better, blasphemed, if not in word, then—in what is graver—in deed. He is also convicted by the assertion of his own voice, since he declares damnable what he himself later did. For when about to seek the wilderness, he addresses his disciples thus: ‘Not to set one’s aim on the highest is tolerable because of human frailty; but to fall away from one’s purpose is damnable because of diabolical transgression.’ Either, therefore, the writer is not to be believed, or the man whom his own words accuse of transgression is sanctified not by his own merit, but by another’s error.” O calumny full of bitter envy and proud contention!

3. In this too the holy man does not differ from the lot of the blessed: he is attacked by the curses and hatreds of the wicked because of the name of Jesus Christ—indeed because of Christ’s name, although the curses are nominally directed against him. For unless Robert had served Christ outstandingly, and unless the fame of his holiness had grown so greatly through diverse regions, these sons of pride would surely not even judge him worthy of their detraction. But since they themselves do not fear to claim praise for religious devotion through hypocrisy, they consider whatever is added to another’s praise a loss to their own glory. Hence they strive with all the resources of their learning to erase Robert’s name, misusing spiritual weapons and divine authorities against the spiritual servant of God. Christ has nourished them in his camp as enemies within. So too their elders, whom pride—the mother—bore from the father, the devil, once dared to reproach Martin because, burned by the blaze of fire, he had anxiously sought the protection of flight under the threat of death. Then, at Christ’s command, Sulpicius pleaded Martin’s cause and, after his opponents were confounded, imposed silence as victor by the judgment of the reader. Now too Christ is able, through the service of our humility, either to confound or teach pride that is unlearned and vainly applauds itself for learning.

Come then, whoever you are, most vehement assailant of this new holiness: truly hostile to the new man, you still utter with your mouth and bear in your mind the image of the old man. Come, I say, conspicuous exhibitor—indeed, notorious exhibitor—of obscure diligence: while arrogating lynx-like eyes to yourself, you have fallen back to mole-like ones. What then seems to you the ancient rule of holiness? Is it that each person should first exercise active labour, by which charity, anxiously compassionate, comes to the aid of neighbours’ necessities; then, always raising himself higher by fresh progress in virtues, should finally attain as victor the citadel of contemplative sweetness, in which he may delight in the insatiable love of divinity alone? And once he has reached it, is it thereafter unlawful to look down toward lower things? As was absurdly said of a certain man, so it may aptly be said here: “Let him marvel at the hinges of heaven, caring no further for human beings.” Thus, author of a new doctrine and inexperienced in both, you divide the two lives of the Church, each within its own bounds, and with such confused error of mind maintain that they are unmingled [Col. 1520C] that for one who has once attained the higher life it is damnable to return to the lower: that is, one who has fully loved God cannot also love a brother.

4. You introduce a new rule of cruelty in the name of religion, so that talkative Greece will now tell a far more humane tale: Orestes and Pylades, exiles from their country, driven by a storm to a foreign shore, were captured and placed at the altar of Scythian Diana, where the cruel goddess was ritually propitiated with a stranger’s blood. A law was given that only one should die; and for a long while the two gave the barbarians a pious spectacle of friendly contention, as each tried to redeem the other by dying in his place. Yet you urge that Christians should act more brutally than idolaters.

If a most gentle father, standing on the brink of a pit, called with tearful voice to children long shut up in a deep and dark prison, lowered a ladder, and encouraged them to climb the worn rungs; and then, while the others despaired and were troubled in their unteachable minds, one of them with more eager effort and firmer experience attempted the steep ascent—if that one, after joyfully emerging above, turned away from his little brothers as they vainly begged for brotherly help, and refused to guide them easily by the familiar footholds; and if he lied that he did this from paternal love while the father, pitying the afflicted children, never ceased to urge him with pious affection to give assistance—would he appear to you perfect?

Likewise, if someone, in an amphitheatre, saw his brother fighting under threat of death with a most fierce gladiator whom he himself had already conquered and whose tricks he knew, and could instruct him but did not—if, unconcerned for his brother’s danger, he sat retired with the watching father and wished to delight in his untimely kisses—would he not be judged by everyone, and by the father himself, a wicked and cruel man, an impious fratricide through neglect of his brother? “But,” you say, “the fiery love of God devours and consumes every concern for mortal things.”

If that is so, a new and monstrous division arises within the very kingdom of charity; and the mysteries of the whole Christian faith consequently collapse, torn by civil—indeed more than civil—strife between “the two commandments on which hang all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII.40). To compress broad arguments into a brief conclusion: if the most burning love of God, in which the summit of contemplative life consists, devours and extinguishes brotherly love, which is the chief or greatest cause of active life, then in extinguishing the latter it extinguishes itself as well, and no part of charity remains. “For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John IV.20). Again: “Whoever sees his brother in need [Col. 1521C] and closes his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John III.17).

Therefore one who loves God will also love his neighbour; or, despising his neighbour, he will despise God as well. Further, if he loves his brother together with God, he will provide according to his ability the necessities of the needy person; whether he does so by deed or, lacking the means, by will alone, he will undoubtedly engage in the business of actions [perhaps: deeds]. Conversely, brotherly love will be idle—indeed, nonexistent—unless the intention is raised to God through merits. The invincible necessity of reason drives us where it ought. Thus, although the two lives are distinct from one another by their respective merits, they can nevertheless be possessed reciprocally under the same law. And when one returns to the interior life from necessity, it is not a fall but a descent; not transgression but compassion. To accuse the holy man of transgression on this point is therefore, as has appeared, a transgression more deserving of rebuke than words can express.

5.
