As for your assertion that he overturned the ancient order and, before Leah’s marriage-bed, vainly sought Rachel’s beauty after the example of an imprudent suitor: it is strange, unless you saw this while dreaming. For the clear and orderly narrative of his deeds cannot, I think, have escaped even your blindness, since it does not pass over his earlier almsgiving. Moreover, your accusation that, contrary to Christ’s teaching, he preferred Martha to Mary is altogether frivolous and empty. If this preference is referred to temporal order—which is certainly not beyond the foolishness of a careless accuser—the fluent calumny refutes itself, since you now accuse him of doing what a little earlier you accused him of not doing. For above you complain that he did not marry Leah before Rachel; here you complain that he preferred Martha to Mary. Yet Leah and Martha are mystically the same, as are Rachel and Mary. Therefore he could not have preferred Martha to Mary in order if he did not prefer Leah to Rachel.

But if the preference is understood as one of dignity, your emptiness as an objector is likewise evident, since you assert a judgment concerning another’s mind that you do not know. For so far as could appear from that holy man’s words and deeds, he truly placed Mary before Martha in dignity, even though he ministered to the brothers for the love of God. In that compassion he proved himself not a backward violator of a lofty purpose, but the most pious imitator of all the elect and of the Head himself. This is the rule of holiness, ancient, present, and future alike, which the ready devotion of Christ’s servants never ceases to traverse, between the two banks, marked by the distinguished steps of virtues, until the end of the age.

6. We think enough has been said against what is said by those who judge it unlawful to mingle the active life with the contemplative, so that they may cast calumny upon blessed Robert, whose holiness they envy. Yet, separately, lest someone reject us as putting forward these points on human reasoning apart from the authority of the Scriptures, we wish to illuminate our judgment by sacred testimonies. We do not think it foreign to the purpose of this work if, for the edification of readers, we show that the present servant of God was conformed to the ancient saints in this virtue of discernment [Col. 1522C].

Thus, when the patriarch Jacob, weary, slept with his head resting upon the mystical stone, he “saw the Lord standing upon it, and angels of God not only ascending through divine contemplation but also descending through human compassion” (Gen. XXVIII.12). The same patriarch also enacted this mystery in his marriage: after the embraces of the more beautiful wife, he more often returned to intercourse with the more fruitful spouse. Had the rashness of his rivals noticed this, they would by no means have believed divine history supported their foolish calumny.

For what else do the ancient Scriptures say? What else does the most sacred page of the New Testament declare? To offer only a few examples from each: Abraham, father of faith; Isaac, son of promise; and Jacob, the chosen one of spiritual grace, who prefigured in themselves especially the mystery of the blessed Trinity—did they not often speak with God while nevertheless administering household affairs? This alternation shines most clearly in Jacob: after he had seen God face to face, and therefore named the place Phanuel, he immediately, pressed by the needs of the journey, turned to arrange his household, dividing maidservants and wives with children and flocks into companies.

So also Moses the lawgiver remained alone with the Lord on the mountain, then returned in turn to the people entrusted to him. He did not always dwell in the secret place of the divine tabernacle; rather, going out, he resolved the turbulent cases of the weak, often with no small labour [Col. 1523A]. Nor does this seem far removed from the present understanding: “Achsah, sitting upon an ass, asked her father for the upper water-course and the lower water-course; she asked for neither without the other” (Josh. XV.16). Likewise Christ’s apostles Peter and John went up into the Temple at the ninth hour of prayer, a number signifying the angelic summit of contemplation; and, immediately upon going out, they conferred benefits in Christ’s name upon those who asked.

Paul also, foremost of teachers, caught up into paradise more than once and exploring the secrets of the third heaven with the clearest gaze of mind, nevertheless again adapted himself not only to the measure of human beings but even of carnal human beings. With benevolent compassion, he permitted even some indulgence in pleasure to those who lacked continence: “Because of fornication,” he says, “let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband; and let the husband render the debt to the wife, and likewise also the wife to the husband” (1 Cor. VII.2). See what the perfection of charity, which ought to be imitated, accomplishes: a little before, he was secretary of heaven; behold, he becomes attendant of marriage-chambers. He also diligently exhorted the Corinthians concerning the collections made for the saints, to prepare the promised blessing. Thus, through the fullness of twofold charity, he was at once exalted and lowly, heavenly and earthly: whether his mind was carried beyond itself to God, or whether he was sober for our sake. Nor did Christ’s other disciples depart from this rule of holiness.

To attach to this argument the individual distinguishing marks of each would be both very long and not very necessary. The Son of God alone, Jesus Christ, suffices us as an example [Col. 1523C]. From his fullness all have received; his whole earthly life was a discipline of conduct. Jesus now goes up the mountain alone to pray; now comes to the disciples whom he sees labouring amid the waves; now distributes the word of God to crowds; now grants gifts of healing. He is transfigured upon the mountain and shows his glory to a few; returning to the crowds, before many he hears the distress of a father pleading for his son. At one time rejoicing in the Holy Spirit, he gives thanks to the Lord of heaven and earth; at another, troubling himself, he weeps for the death of a friend. He teaches in word what he shows by example, when he exhorts us not only to pray to the Father with the door shut, but also to help a brother who asks in open beneficence.

The contemplative Church also proves the same in the Song of Songs, lamenting that, when the bridegroom calls, she is compelled from the bed of inward rest to the outward care and office of preaching which she had laid aside:

> “I sleep, but my heart keeps watch. The voice of my beloved knocking: ‘Open to me, my sister, my beloved, my dove, my undefiled one; for my head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.’ I have taken off my garment; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them? My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my inward parts trembled at his touch. I rose to open to my beloved” (Song V.2).

7. From all this we judge it sufficiently established and evident that contemplatives are changed to active life not only lawfully but often by necessity, and suffer no loss of their former merit; for if inwardly beautiful barrenness is deprived of anything, outwardly bleary-eyed fruitfulness fully compensates for it. But since the demonstration of this matter extends so widely that time would fail me sooner than an abundance of examples, let what has been said suffice all the more because there is no lack of matters still to be said. Therefore, since truth rebukes falsehood and charity has instructed envy, “let deceitful lips be silenced, which speak iniquity against the righteous in pride and contempt” (Ps. 30:19). Indeed, because we intend rather to build up than to conquer, let envy yield to charity; let impiety be redeemed from its accursed blasphemy by the publicly proclaimed praise of true confession, so that in a spirit of love and peace we may together proclaim the merits of the blessed man. For the miracles by which, through the Lord’s generosity, the tomb of his sacred body is made illustrious are sure proofs of his merits for those who doubt. Thus we meet these objections, both of believers and ill-disposed persons—if any remain such as those mentioned above—as far as the Lord has granted us; let them answer us in accordance with the tenor of this little work, so that, just as, according to the Apostle’s witness, tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, so conversely signs may be a tongue not for believers but for unbelievers.

8. On the very day on which the blessed man’s body lay awaiting burial, one of his older disciples, while the rest were busied with the pious funeral rites, had withdrawn alone to one side, as one who, because of long familiarity, felt the sudden loss of his master more intimately. Exhausted by the excessive anguish of grief and crushed in spirit, he sat down; and, as often happens, sleep stole upon him through sorrow. Then behold: by divine revelation of the mind’s light, he saw a fiery globe descend from heaven and stand above the place where the holy body lay, its luminous radiance shining with special intensity upon the neighboring places. While he stood astonished and terrified at so great a vision, there appeared a woman of incomparable beauty, attended by heavenly legions, whose own brilliance rivaled the splendor of the light that had preceded her; from the majesty of her face and bearing it was clear that she was a queen. Standing above the bier upon the fiery globe, she stretched out her hand, took the right hand of the one lying there, and with gentle speech urged him to rise and ascend with her. Thus, their hands joined, they advanced straight toward heaven, with the light accompanying them; and when they seemed already to be touching the boundaries of the ether, a mighty right hand was extended from above, heaven opened, and they were received within.

Let no one doubt that this was the Lord’s Mother, who brought the devout soul into heavenly joys, Christ receiving it, after it had duly completed the labors of this present life. For after Christ the holy man had especially devoted himself to her service, and while living in the flesh he loved her spiritually with such ardent affection that he could not refrain from her praises even when another subject was under discussion; so that, even asleep, his mind kept watch at her remembrance.

> [Note: The material enclosed between these brackets is absent from the Poitiers manuscript and from Labbe; nevertheless it is present in the Britolensis manuscript and in Bollandus.]

He bore deeply impressed upon his heart the image of Christ and Mary. [Col. 1525A] This he cherished in the rejoicing bosom of his mind as a unique and sweet treasure. He had bound within his heart these two pearls—different indeed, but each of inestimable value—to which at every hour he turned the eyes of his secret love with insatiable desire. Christ and Mary, chastity and mercy, were always upon his lips. He called Mary, using varied names for delight: the gate of heaven, star of the sea, sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, refuge of the wretched, rose of modesty, lily of chastity, jewel of virginity. If anyone wished to win Christ’s grace, he considered that one must first seek the Mother, as though she were another mediator between God and human beings, since the Son had entrusted to her a secondary role in reconciliation, and himself commends to the Father those whom his own Mother has commended to him. The devotion of the disciples still today proves and represents this fervor of their master: following his ordinance, they render together and gladly, in the monastery of Casa Dei, the daily office of praise to the glorious Virgin. Therefore it must not be doubted that the blessed soul was brought especially into joy by her whom, with the divine prerogative preserved, he had especially endeavored to serve. Nor was the authority of the whole divine Trinity absent from the vision described above: in the fire the ardor of the Holy Spirit, in the right hand the strength of the Son, and in the appearance of heaven the majesty of the Father were distinctly displayed.

9. Likewise, a certain inhabitant of the territory of Velay suffered from quartan fevers continuously for two years. Desiring to obtain health, he had long wandered about visiting many shrines of saints; but when his efforts had been wasted in vain, he had increased his dangerous illness by the hardship of untimely travel. He was not deceived either by a fault of his own unbelief or by the powerlessness of his patrons, but was, as afterward became clear, divinely reserved for the merits of blessed Robert. For on the very day of Robert’s burial, news of his venerable death having spread everywhere brought him, amid the mixed crowds hastening thither, before the place of the sacred body. There he lay prostrate on the ground and long implored a remedy, not without firm confidence that health would be granted. While praying, he fell lightly asleep, sleep descending from heaven; meanwhile, through the hidden mercy of God and the merits of the blessed man, the channels of his veins were warmed, the harmful force of the long-standing sluggish chill began to dissolve, and feverish sweats flowed forth simultaneously through the pores opened over his whole body. While asleep, nature, thus relieved, perceived the remedy; and the man, suddenly freed from every affliction without the burden of medical treatment, seemed, when he awoke, to rise as another man, wondering at himself. How great were then the thanks he gave God for recovered health, with what cries he invoked Robert—only one who has measured joy by the preceding suffering can estimate it from his joy. For just as one who has escaped the greater danger rejoices more, so one who rejoices more gives greater thanks.

10. The report of so great a miracle, spread swiftly through the neighboring regions both by the mouths of those who had seen it and by those who believed their accounts, drew crowds of sick and infirm people to the sacred tomb of the blessed man, as to a newly publicized and freely dispensing workshop of healing for all who were ill. Among them, the anxious wife of a miserable old man—upon whose misfortune the grievous and altogether dreadful burden of blindness had been added to the twofold affliction of old age and poverty—placed him at the confessor’s tomb. There, for three days, the blind man fixed the eyes of his mind upon Christ with tireless devotion, repeatedly uttering the name of Robert, in whose patronage he trusted, and never relaxing for even a moment from prayer.

The woman, offended by what seemed to her the importunate chattering of her husband, said: “At least stop troubling those present, if you are not afraid to disturb one who rests. For when you think that you will not be heard by the saint unless you cry out more shamelessly, while begging for your lost sight you insult the hearing that you assail in this way; and you do not deserve to obtain what you ask, since you, though blind, reproach him as though he were deaf. Wait rather in silence and pour out your prayers in the chamber of your heart.”

He recoiled from these words with such indignation that he judged them to be not so much the simple speech of a woman as the deceitful hiss of the serpent. “Spare us,” he said, “spare us, woman, such foolish speech, and do not cloak impious blasphemy with the appearance of faith. Do you suppose the saints’ ears so delicate that you think them wearied by excessive cries? On the contrary, instructed by the divine teaching of Christ, we know that what they often do not give to a friend who asks, they finally grant to an importunate knocker.” Then, turning at once to the saint, he began to cry out the pious name more insistently, imitating the blind man of the Gospel, whom the crowd, rebuking him to be silent, only stirred up more strongly to pray.

The compassion of the priest, already moved, had obtained from God the power to restore sight to the blind man; but he tested the petitioner’s faith by delaying the gift requested, and at the same time made the more desired benefit more welcome. As the man persisted in prayer, hidden power gave a visible effect: the dense cloud of darkness began to be torn away, so that, as though at some distance, his astonished eyes could perceive their blindness although they did not yet see the light—just as though one placed a veil before eyes that see. The man hastily brought his hand to his throbbing eyes and, wonderfully, touching nothing, wiped away whatever obstructed them. A marvelous light shone upon the sockets long buried in darkness and immediately made the whole substance of his body, now illumined, brighter. Joy, unable to contain itself, broke silence; and the fitting herald of the new miracle wrought in himself began suddenly throughout the whole basilica to resound with mingled praises and thanksgiving.

Who then among those present could keep silent about God’s praises, who did not sing the merits of blessed Robert? For by manifest proofs the unquestionable power was established, when the blind man, now presented with various objects, identified each by its distinct name as proof of his sight, so that he was not deceived by the difference of any color or shape. Let biting envy, if it can, find here an opening for slander, and try from hatred to invent something to corrupt at least what cannot be denied. But when it discovers that all its efforts fail in entirely fruitless labor, let it believe for its own sake what perhaps it scorns to believe for ours, and, following the example of that mad prophet, rebuked by his own ass—that is, by its own folly—let it at last come to its senses, though more shamefully.

Will it perhaps maintain that the whole effect of this wondrous power should be attributed not to the merits of the holy man but rather to the petitioner’s faith? Yet this was the petitioner’s faith: that he could obtain, through Robert’s prayers, the sight he had lost. That is why he repeatedly invoked Robert’s name. Therefore, either he obtained what he asked through the merits of that same saint, or the very faith by which he asked did him no good for obtaining it. For previously he had often implored, certainly with Christian faith, for lost sight at the tombs of other saints, and yet nowhere had he deserved to be heard. Finally, if the entire bestowal of benefits were to be credited to the faith of those asking, no thanks would be rendered to Christ, who, though he often bestowed various remedies upon sufferers, nevertheless did not pass over the merit of faith in silence: “Your faith,” he says, “has made you well” (Mark 10:52)—that is, it obtained that you should be made well, not by giving me power, but by earning grace from me. Therefore the petitioner’s faith neither removes the power of the giver nor the merit of the patron.

11. Behold another evident proof of wondrous sanctity. A miserable woman from the district of Limoges, ravaged for nearly twenty years by frequent attacks of an evil spirit, was finally brought by faithful persons to the blessed man’s tomb. The hostile power had not been accustomed to afflict her with continuous torment, as is usual, but, like a chronic illness, to torture her more grievously at intervals. Thus, as she stood before the place of the sacred body, like an accused person awaiting before a merciful judge the sentence of her release while all present waited in suspense, she suddenly began to be convulsed by such violent tremors throughout her body that the dreadful aspect of the torment [Boll.: “of the suppliant”] suggested that death rather than recovery was to be expected. The spiritual wickedness trembled, unable to bear the presence of some invisible majesty; and while, terrified by an unexpected arrival, it hastened to abandon the substance it had wickedly invaded, it found the exits closed, ran about on every side, and shook its prison in trembling.

For judgment restrains the robber for a time in order to torment it, and at the same time the miracle of the imminent cleansing is made more commendable because the great horror of the pestilence has been displayed before the eyes. After she had for some time offered the bystanders, in this foul appearance, a pitiable spectacle of her own calamity, the woman suddenly burst into speech and, repeatedly crying out, began to invoke the aid of Saint Robert. Meanwhile the custodian took water of the sacred sprinkling and sprinkled it into the mouth of the shouting woman; and, as though a shower had been sent from heaven, he suddenly extinguished the entire fire of the savage affliction.

O wholly wondrous merits of the pious confessor, who even through the ministry of a humble servant drives away the enemy’s power! This is plainly an indication of remarkable virtue, such as cannot commonly fall to the lot of every saint. Christ gave this to the apostles: that in his name they should command evil spirits. The apostles often did this themselves, but rarely through others to whom they gave orders. Long ago the great and wonderful Elisha presumed to do this: by the touch of his sacred bones a man’s corpse rose again (4 Kings 13:21); nevertheless, the servant sent in advance with the staff could not, by Elisha’s command, raise the dead son of the great woman. This was not because confidence in his merits deceived so great a prophet, but because even perfect persons are not always granted grace in such overflowing abundance. Yet those to whom it is sometimes granted cannot at all be doubted to be perfect.

The woman therefore collapsed onto the pavement and lay senseless for some time, so that to all she appeared plainly to be nothing other than dead. Nor would it have been difficult for the saint, by his life-giving merits, to raise the dead, if perhaps that which appeared so was indeed the case. When soul or consciousness returned after an interval, she opened her eyes and calmly sat up, like the ancient Tabitha; and for recovered health of mind and body she rendered such thanks as she could to Robert, the servant of God. Then those present, who had long stood stunned awaiting the outcome, at the sight of so great and manifest a miracle vied with one another in sounding God’s praises with devout cries. The woman too returned unharmed to her homeland and spread abroad the example of the marvelous power which she herself had experienced.

12. Likewise, a native of the territory of Forez had a son who for a long time had been afflicted with contraction of the sinews, so that he seemed unable to walk but only to crawl. The father brought him to the blessed man’s tomb in order to pour out pious prayers for the health of this child of his; and there, persisting for a week in tears and vows, he faithfully awaited the aid of divine mercy. Meanwhile, one day, while the brothers were celebrating the offices of Mass, the boy began to be shaken by sudden movements of his sinews; and, as he tried to stretch his legs, long stiffened, [he seemed, as it were, to be prompted by the impulses of reviving nature. He tried, as though hesitating, what he was moving:] and behold, with a certain force and a cracking sound, the sinews were stretched, so that even if he had tried he could not have stopped. Without doubt a heavenly power was breaking the too-tight bonds of nature long held captive, and what was taking place was not in the man’s power. Immediately the lame boy rose upon feet unused to standing, and at first was compelled to walk with an unsteady gait. Those who saw him ran up at once, weeping with joy, and, laying hands upon him from every side, brought him upright to the altar with God’s praises. Such joy arose among all as the manifest proof of heavenly presence deserved. Yet above the praises of everyone, the father’s rejoicing voice resounded more festively, because, being more deeply disposed to joy, he supplied greater material for exclamation. Thus, returning home with his son, whose foundations were strengthened and who was no longer lame, he brought a great miracle into his native region.

13. In the town called Ceresium, a man of no low rank had a daughter who, her face hideously swollen and both eyes long since deprived of sight, was weighed down by the heavy burden of a double affliction. After some time it seemed good to the father, who grieved in his sorrowing heart over the girl’s misery, to send her to the holy man’s tomb, where widespread report had already proclaimed that many recovered health. The blind girl, her face disfigured by ghastly swellings, was brought to the saint; and soon she returned seeing, restored to the former beauty of her face. For while she assiduously knocked upon God with such prayers as the affliction of her contrite heart dictated, and repeatedly appealed to the name and merits of blessed Robert, one of the brothers, the keeper of the church, gathering the petitioner’s feeling from her joyful expression, bent his ear also to her words and immediately sighed, moved by compassion. Swift in feeling, he hurriedly brought wine with which the holy body had been washed and sprinkled it over the whole face of the trembling girl. But when she felt the helpful drops of the consecrated liquid, she repeatedly begged that this be done to her again. After this had been done for several days, the woman received complete health. She returned to her people with a face made bright, which she no longer needed to be ashamed to have seen, nor did those who saw her need to avert their eyes. The father rejoiced at seeing his daughter’s recovery; the household rejoiced with the neighbors; and the whole town exulted together in God’s praises with common prayers. Nor did they keep silent about the praises of blessed Robert, who, according to his custom, had vigorously taken up the cause of the miserable woman as intercessor.

14. There is a village which the natives call Monasteriolum. A knight lived there who had a daughter violently tormented in pitiable ways by a savage spirit. She showed her madness not only by a foul-sounding roar, horrible gestures, or most obscene words, but attacked with bites whoever she could; nor did she spare even herself whenever no opportunity was given her to attack others. She did not recognize even the man who had begotten her as her father, except that, at the prompting of the hidden enemy, she assailed him with greater insults than the rest. But the more grievously she struck him with injuries, the more deeply her father’s compassionate heart was moved toward the unhappy girl. The wretched man beheld his own punishment in his daughter’s body and was, in a sense, tormented with more grievous tortures. For he, being of sound mind, felt what he should mourn, whereas in her madness had swallowed up awareness even of her own pain. She fiercely [Boll.: “calmly”] rolled her grim countenance and eyes made blood-red by frenzy; grief had made the sorrowing parent’s cheeks pale and his eyes wet with abundant tears—a pitiable sight. The terrifying gaping mouth, furious foam, winding turns of the twisted neck, horrible disheveled hair, and whatever else appeared lamentable in the body of one who knew nothing—all this the father’s pious compassion took upon itself.

Meanwhile, since no way of remedy was open, despair itself of recovery aggravated his fierce grief all the more. But as he was tossed upon such waves of sorrow, a favorable breeze of saving counsel suddenly blew from his friends: he should send the girl to the holy man’s tomb, where no petitioner’s faith was cheated of its just desire. Immediately raised to firm hope that this was the salvation of his daughter—the sole way, as it were, of reaching shore—he prepared servants and a maid, ordered necessary provisions, and commanded that the girl, placed upon a vehicle, be hurried to the saint, though with all her limbs restrained lest, leaping out in her customary manner, she wound anyone she encountered.

The river Loire divided midway the route by which they were traveling; even sound-headed people are accustomed to fear its swift currents. There, though bound, she began already to be better and addressed her companions with tranquil face and gentle words. Clearly this was a remedy of power, not of nature, in a place where especially a mind distraught could have been more terrified. “Why,” she said, “have you wrapped me in cloths as though I were dead? Release me, I beg you, exhausted as I am, and do not wish any longer to restrain me bound.” Once released, she at once remained peacefully of sound mind throughout the rest of the journey. But when she was brought to the sacred tomb, as it were to a place of judgment, the one hidden within could not remain silent. As violent examination searched out the recesses of remote sinews that were to be cleansed, the foul pest began to gnash its teeth, rage, and vex her in every way as it was about to lose its possession shortly afterward. For after three days the deceit was expelled and carried away with it every cause of trouble. Nature, gradually restored, returned to its former state of health, and soon she herself returned to her father’s house more than well, marveling at her own strength. What joy she brought, what vows—this we leave the reader to estimate; for I should not believe that even strangers, moved by the simple affection of a common human nature toward the miserable girl, refrained from divine praises. How much more did paternal affection rejoice, urged on by both common and personal suffering! Nor without reason did all extol with many praises the holy confessor of the Lord, to whose glorious merits such great miracles were divinely granted. And lest these perhaps appear doubtful to anyone, it pleased us to recount last what happened in this matter.

15. When the fame of such powers had increased in the Maritime Alps and inflamed the hearts and tongues of the peoples in praise of Saint Robert, the archbishop of that province—a man whose character matched his rank—thought it unworthy that pontifical gravity should immediately give credence to popular rumors. He determined not to leave unexamined what evidently concerned either public error or merit. While the blessed man lived in the flesh, the archbishop had long known him and had been closely joined to him by love of like pursuits. Therefore, having made suitable preparations for the journey as the matter required, he set out—not with the intention of an unbelieving tempter, but rather in a desire to test the truth. He came with a retinue, following the example of the queen of the South, to the place: as she had tested Solomon’s wisdom, so he would test Robert’s power. He was hospitably received, as befitted him, and when he thought the time opportune, he asked leave to enter the monastery. This was immediately granted as he requested; the doors of the church were barred, and he remained alone inside.

There, wholly given over to prayer, he cast himself upon Saint Robert’s tomb and, melted into tears by the fire of fervent love, invoked from the marrow of his heart the true Light, that it might deign to reveal to him more clearly whether divine power had truly and without any ambiguity of suspicion bestowed upon the blessed man so great a grace of miracles, unheard of in the present age. Turning also toward the saint, he spoke many things, as his soul laboring in prayer suggested; he did not cease to invoke the Virgin Mother, nor did he pass over the angelic spirits. Meanwhile, as he added prayers to prayers, a divine answer was immediately manifested—not formed in the elemental sounds of words, but firmly established by evident signs.

A girl whose whole body had long been contracted, whom, as he had requested, they were bringing to the saint’s tomb, was followed by a people gathering from every side with common prayers. At their knocking, the doors were opened, and the accompanying multitude entered. Hardly had she been properly laid down and touched the pavement when the knots of her sinews were loosed and the skin behind her knees burst; she rose to her feet and, walking through the whole basilica, joyfully exercised the first movements of her new gift. The people raised their voices to heaven, and all things resounded with joyful tumult. The bishop stood apart in amazement; and the scruple regarding his former devotion was overcome not only by the harmonious testimony of many, but by the evidence of his own eyes. Silently he also recognized the grace he had sought and marveled that he had been heard so quickly.

Yet lest any occasion for perverse suspicion remain, the miracle was immediately confirmed by a second one, so that the lawful number of witnesses, as it were, should not be lacking. For hardly had the tumult from the first joy subsided when, behold, a boy blind from birth, attended by no small crowd, was brought in and turned upon himself the minds and faces of all who were present. Without delay he was placed at the tomb; the people prayed for him; and the darkness was immediately expelled, while an unknown light penetrated his astonished eyes. Joy arose again, voices again resounded. The bishop marveled at the repeated miracle, whose power over a similar condition alluded to the blindness of his own former state of mind. Blindness was set before the doubter, and illumination answered his faith. No room for ambiguity remained, and amid such evidence no Thomas could doubt further. Therefore the advance of strengthened faith burst forth into speech, and a true confession sounded in everyone’s ears: “Here I see more than I heard, and report is far inferior to the truth.” The prelate returned to his own country, bringing back the riches of a precious confession and giving glory to the God of heaven, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

# [Life of Saint Magnobodus]

[Col. 1531]

# A Short Notice Prefixed to the Life of Saint Magnobodus, Bishop of Angers

1463–1464 We judged that this Life of Saint Magnobodus, written by an anonymous author, should be placed before the other composed by Marbod: both so that this monument of antiquity should not be lost to the diligent reader, and because Marbod did here what he had done with the longer Life of Saint Licinius—namely, following its model, he abridged this work also, which was longer, and recast it into a better form. We judged, however, that it should be inserted here rather than the earlier Life of Saint Licinius, because this work, written by an anonymous author and recovered by Bollandus from two ancient manuscripts, immediately precedes the Life composed by Marbod, to which the reader may accordingly have recourse if desired; whereas this work, so far as I know, is found nowhere else. It is published from Mabillon’s papers.

[Col. 1531]

# Life of Saint Magnobodus, Confessor, by an Anonymous Author

## § I

[Col. 1531C]

Thus the glorious and distinguished bishop of Christ, Magnobodus, nobly born in the district of Angers under preceding divine signs, shone with great privileges of miracles. Before he possessed bodily strength and skill in speech, admirable gifts of virtues were bestowed upon him from heaven, as his praises, everywhere to be commemorated, testify. According to the genealogy of human descent, his parents held a very distinguished and not insignificant rank among their fellow citizens, living under the rule of Lothair, son of Chilperic. While Lothair, still within the years of adolescence, was engaged in conflict with his kinsmen, namely Theuderic and Theudebert, amid storms of hostilities rising everywhere [or perhaps: “amid the hailstorms of conflicts”], his aforementioned parents, under Christ’s auspices, rejoiced greatly at his birth and delighted in its various, and not insignificant, portents.

For, as we have learned through careful investigation, the beginning of his life occurred on the very day of the Epiphany, [Col. 1532C] on which the Author of life, born of the fruitful and undefiled Virgin, wished to be adored by the Gentiles under the guidance of a star and honored with offerings of gifts; likewise to be washed in the Jordan’s baths, and to change the liquid of water into the taste of wine. And at the very sound of the cockcrow by which, without doubt, the little flame of day is announced, his mother’s womb brought forth the holy child into the world, so that it might be clearly shown that he would be a lover and herald of light, whose birthday was adorned at his birth with such signs.

## § II. On the storm whose waves were divinely calmed

Accordingly, when the aforesaid parents sought to bring him to the laver of regeneration to wash away the contagions of original sins, the Loire River, narrowed into a channel that afforded passage to the basilica, lay between them. When they wished to cross that river by the aid of a boat, a storm suddenly arose and nearly took away all hope of their safety. Storm-clouds rose; an immense whirlpool of the waters threatened to dash the boat to pieces. The oars were battered, and the oarsmen, struck by the force of the waves, were discouraged from hope of escaping the danger. All were infected by the horror of fear, and only the image of death was dreaded before their eyes. The vastness of the waters and the quicksands of the whirlpools denied the sailors any way to act or effort by which to seek help. Suddenly, however, as we believe, at a divine nod the blasts of all the winds were stilled, and unexpected, longed-for calm came over them. Those who had feared being swept away to destruction by the threatening peril were, with marvelous and indescribable speed, freed from every fear; filled with joy in spirit, they reached the shores of the river and the harbor of safety. Having completed all for which they had come, and fulfilled the customary rites, they returned cheerfully to their own home.

## § III. On the cutting of his hair and his youthful character

As he grew older, his aforementioned parents, seeing the noble disposition of their son, arranged for him to be instructed in the sacred studies of letters. Entrusted to the school’s teachings, he gave himself with all the attentiveness that his age allowed to divine exercises. Whatever he had learned before, he diligently sought to retain within the recesses of his heart by capacious effort. When he had passed through the courses of infancy and childhood, and was now approaching maturity with increasing years, Saint Licinius, bishop of Angers, cut off the hair of his head and established him in the services of the holy Church. Raised to the honor of orders, he was commended to the utterances of the sacred order. Among his contemporaries he possessed remarkable diligence, supreme obedience, unfeigned charity, humble kindness, spent the whole night in prayer, freely devoted to vigils, distinguished by the practice of frugality, adorned with the privileges of holiness, instructed by abundance of learning, enlightened by lamps of wisdom, endowed with honeyed keenness of speech; he continually bore Christ’s yoke, which appears bitter to those who bear it, and unceasingly carried his burden, which is judged light by those who shoulder it.

## § IV. On the honor of his leadership

[Col. 1533C]

Therefore Saint Licinius, the bishop mentioned above, seeing Magnobodus’s industry and the admirable application of his mind, decided to establish him in a somewhat higher rank and keep him beside himself, so that he might be his helper in all things and the rest might become imitators of his example. Accordingly, he appointed him father over the holy community serving Christ in the monastery of Colonetum, so that, like a lamp placed upon the top of a lampstand, he might more greatly illumine the others by the brightness of his light and provide the obedient with a model of divine instruction.

## § V. On the mission he performed at Rome and what he did there

When Licinius himself, the bishop mentioned above, wished to dedicate in the suburb of the city of Angers a basilica constructed with remarkable workmanship in honor of Saint John the Baptist, he summoned Magnobodus, a man of memorable sanctity who had been advanced to the ministry of ecclesiastical order, and sent him to the city of Rome, where the relics of the apostles are commemorated with due veneration. He was to obtain relics from the supreme pontiff, by which Licinius might consecrate the basilica, newly furnished for worship. Obeying his commands, Magnobodus hastened on his journey. Coming to the blessed pope of the City, he explained the reason for his mission; received graciously by him, he spent some time in his company.

At the pope’s command, following custom, Magnobodus celebrated the divine offices and solemnities of the Mass. It happened that he came with the pontiff to Matins and took part in the melodies of psalms and hymns. When the time came for lessons to be read aloud from the pulpit according to the rite of the Roman Church, he rose with the pope’s blessing and undertook the reading. As he was detained in it for a long time and continued at the work begun without interruption, certain persons seated around him, inflamed by the torches of envy, undertook—an impious thing to say—to extinguish the lamp serving the man of God’s sight. But seeing the opposition brought against him by his rivals, he became more steadfast. Without the lamp’s aid, he nevertheless completed from memory the work which he had begun for some time with its light, reading through the page of the book; thus he showed that by the grace of the Almighty he flourished not only in the bodily light visible outwardly but was also fully ablaze with spiritual light, shining inwardly by the divine breath.

Having obtained from the most blessed pope the precious relics of Saint John for which he had gone, Magnobodus returned by a prosperous journey to the venerable Bishop Licinius at Angers, bearing the welcome pledge. Licinius received it joyfully and, placing it as he had intended within the newly built oratory, dedicated it with solemn consecration. There he gathered a resident community of monks and established them in life according to the rule of their holy profession; he assigned many estates for the needs [editorial supplement: “of worship”] of those serving God there, and arranged for hospices, foundling homes, and various dwellings to be built.

## § VI. On the death of the bishop of Angers and Magnobodus’s ordination
With these deeds accomplished and after the passage of many years, when almighty God wished to release the bishop of Angers from this troubled and transitory life and establish blessed Magnobodus as pastor in His Church, the bishop, compelled by illness, [1467] began to fail in his natural strength. Summoning the assembled brethren to himself, he asked for the viaticum; and, having received the Eucharist of Christ’s sacred body, he was committed to the earth by his disciples with the utmost care, to rise again in glory.

When he had thus been taken up, the people of Angers, clergy and laity alike gathered together, with one mind and with the consent of the illustrious king of the Franks Dagobert, son of Lothair, began unanimously to acclaim Magnobodus as their pastor. Only two priests of eminent rank were found who, in excessive obstinacy, sought to overturn this orderly election and the people’s decision [Col. 1534C]. One was called Leudobaudus, the other Ambrulfus; they opposed the merits of the holy man. But the general decision prevailed against their crooked contrivances. Moreover, divine judgment blazing forth marked them with such punishment that each visibly lost his right eye, and they never deserved to regain hope of their former health. Thus both their crafty guile was punished and the election of the man of God was hallowed, by God’s will, through preceding signs.

## § VII. How he conducted himself after attaining the height of government

But blessed Magnobodus, having received the priestly mitre in accordance with the people’s assent and with the approval of all, was raised to the episcopal throne. Once he had undertaken the burden of the flock, he immediately began, as a good shepherd, to keep watch for the sheep entrusted to him. [Col. 1534D] He admonished the unruly to amend themselves; he encouraged the good to advance day by day toward greater improvement. What he taught in words, he demonstrated in deeds.

Seeking nothing on earth for himself, but providing what would benefit others, he brought help to the sick and furnished aid to those in danger. He visited the poor, consoled the needy, attended to monks, clerics, and consecrated women, and diligently cared for widows and orphans. Against the guile of enemies he persisted in prayer and strove to soften them by the bond of charity. Distinguished in speech, serene in mind, armed with piety and mercy, fortified with the shield of justice and uprightness; strong in adversity, humble in prosperity; he could neither be intimidated by threats, broken by gifts, nor seduced by flattery. He was prudent in counsel, energetic in action, and discerning in every moral virtue; devoted to fasts, lavish in almsgiving, inclined toward the evangelical precepts, unwearying in psalms [Col. 1535A] and hymns, a singer of sacred song, [1468] and mindful of the whole sequence of the divine Scriptures. Daily he made himself a whole burnt offering to the Lord and offered himself upon the altar of a contrite heart as a sacrifice, so that he might become an unblemished victim and enter the living temple of God.

Adorned with these and similar gems of virtue, Magnobodus, appointed bishop, thus governed the citizens of Angers. Whoever desires to know the admirable character of his acts will find it set forth without the varnish of falsehood in the following account.

## § VIII. On prisoners whom he divinely released at Paris

Accordingly, when blessed Magnobodus had been distinguished by so evident an approval and by the affirmation of all at the summit of the episcopate, the aforesaid King Dagobert, who held the monarchy of the Frankish realm, learned of his reputation for goodness and ordered him summoned to Paris, where he was then residing. Obeying his commands, Magnobodus proceeded there without delay. [Col. 1535B]

As he entered the city and passed through its gates, men detained in prisons because of their crimes, having learned of his arrival, loudly and insistently called out, asking for the holy man’s assistance. When he heard the mournful wailing of the miserable and their lamentable plight, moved with compassion, he pressed on with the journey he had set out upon, going to the basilica for prayer. Approaching the judge with a humble mind, he began to ask that pardon be granted to the condemned and that they be allowed to depart freely. But the judge, being cruel, opposed the holy man’s desire with a harsh reply and sent him away without accomplishing anything.

Spurned by that baleful man, he entered the church toward which he had been proceeding and prayed to Christ’s mercy that He would grant the guilty leave to go and rescue them from the cords of their chains. While he persisted in prayer, their fetters were suddenly shattered, their manacles broken, and the prison doors opened to the captives, with no barrier impeding them. They sprang out and hurried to the feet of the holy bishop, offering thanks. He prayed for their safety to the prince’s [Col. 1535C] clemency and obtained the release they desired; he also forbade them, with threats, ever again to be caught in so grave a crime.

## § IX. On a blind man illuminated within the basilica

At the same time, a certain man who had lost the sight of his eyes, having heard of the illustrious man’s powers, resolved [1469], with a guide leading him, to travel to the city of Angers, trusting in full hope to recover through his aid the former health of his eyes. Upon entering the city to seek the bishop’s cure, he was told that Magnobodus was within the enclosure of the basilica, occupied in divine offices and celebrating the solemnities of Mass. Having learned this, the man went with the guide by whom he had come to the church and found the blessed bishop, as he had been told, engaged in the sacred mysteries. Calling out insistently, he begged him to restore the lost light.

The blessed bishop, taking pity on his complaints, poured out prayer for his recovery; and, when the office of Mass had been completed, he placed in the man’s mouth, with a blessing, a portion of the sacred Body. [Col. 1535D] Immediately all blindness was driven away, and the sight of the eyes—which for the course of many years had been assigned to darkness—was restored to him. Giving thanks to Christ’s power, he returned joyfully, in mind and body, to his own home.

## § X. On a priest healed of flux of the belly

Nor do I think that what happened to a certain priest devoted to good works ought to be passed over in silence. Suffering from a flux of the belly, his intestines seemed to be wasting away and tortured by an internal disease even to the destruction of his life. By whatever effort he could manage—perhaps *nisu*, “effort,” rather than the printed *visu*, “sight”—he ordered his servants to go with all speed to the man of God and bring him the eulogiae, blessed bread, which he had decided to send. Obeying their master’s commands, they brought with the greatest haste what he had ordered. Received kindly by Magnobodus, they presented what the sick man had sent; and he, immediately understanding the matter, [Col. 1536A] blessed bread, gave it to the returning bearers, and ordered the sick man to partake of it without delay.

They returned at a swift pace and brought their master, who was afflicted by illness, the bishop’s gift. When he received and ate it, all pain in his intestines at once departed, the fibres of his internal organs were restored, and he returned to his former sound condition, giving thanks to the bishop who had rescued him from such a destructive affliction.

## § XI. On the prodigy displayed because of boys’ mockery

The man of highest holiness, travelling through the diocese entrusted to him in order to enlighten and admonish it, came to a certain estate commonly called Quartiniacum. A crowd of talkative boys, gathered in the street [1470] and advancing together to meet him, did not fear to provoke him with jeering laughter and clamorous abuse, hurling wicked insults in play. As he looked upon them, one of the boys among those playing was suddenly snatched up with all violence and borne through the vast air like a ball of dust, here and there. [Col. 1536B]

Then his companions and parents, overcome with grief and fear, pursued him by every byway and searched the winding tracks of cliffs and valleys, but achieved nothing except the weariness of their toil; the unheard-of and sudden occurrence deprived them of any idea what to do. At last, driven to despair and exhausted on trackless, thorny paths, they found the boy half alive among dense thickets, scarcely drawing a faint breath. With great lamentation his parents wrapped him in a cloak—for nearly all his limbs had been torn apart—and placed him before the holy man. Bending their knees, they began to entreat him to deign to pity their son’s sufferings.

He ordered them to lay the boy within the church enclosure and to implore the Lord’s mercy for him. But when the crowd had withdrawn and the grieving parents returned again to the church, they found alive the boy whom they had expected to be dead. [Col. 1536C] Then the man of God took the boy’s hand and raised him from the entrance of the portico, restoring him healthy and vigorous with life to his parents, returning good for the mockery inflicted upon himself. Joyfully they fell at his knees, made their vows, and returned to their own homes.

## § XII. On a certain Theudegisilus healed

A certain man named Theudegisilus suffered from the trouble of a severe illness, which neither physicians’ skill nor wholesome fomentations could restore to complete health. When, worn down by disease, he had lost all hope of recovering his former health, remembering the assistance of the aforesaid bishop, he tearfully asked to be brought into his sight. Seeing him weakened by the swelling of a grievous illness, Magnobodus turned to Christ’s aid and strove with all earnestness to offer the offices of prayer for him. Thus, with divine mercy favouring him, Theudegisilus was freed from every bodily affliction and recovered health. He who had been carried on another’s bed returned to his own home by his own gait and free power. [Col. 1536D]

## § XIII. On a little boat brought to him without a helmsman

It is worthwhile also to recount the miracle which [1471] many affirm. The venerable bishop, returning with a company of disciples from a village called Othonense toward the walls of his own city, came to the bank of a river. By a divine occurrence, as must be believed, there was no boat available by which they could safely cross the river channel. A boat could indeed be seen moored on the opposite side of the river, but no one was present who, attending to their need, would attempt to bring it to them.

Having recourse, as usual, to the help of prayer, and remaining a long while in supplication, he saw the prow suddenly leap from the place where it was fastened. Without a helmsman and without any one impelling it, it swam to the bank where he was waiting, yielding to the wishes of all. Giving thanks to almighty God, who fulfils the will of those who fear Him [Col. 1537A] and hears their prayers, he embarked with all his noble company and arrived joyfully, by a prosperous voyage, at the place toward which he was travelling and his wish directed him.

## § XIV. On Mummolus freed from fevers

Meanwhile there was a sick man named Mummolus, severely afflicted by the type of a quartan fever and long distressed by the suffering of emaciation. This cruel pestilence miserably tormented him, weak and languishing, every day; since he could obtain no remedies whatsoever, the pressing disease began to drive him to the confines of death. Now at the very end of life, he sent intermediaries to ask the man of God to deign to take pity on him. Moved by compassion for his incurable suffering, Magnobodus sent him oil sanctified by a sacred blessing and ordered him to be anointed with it. When he received it and was anointed, every cause of his sickness was put to flight; he was restored to health and lived again for many years.

## § XV. On the girl Baldetruda restored to sight

[Col. 1537B] In the same district of Angers there lived a girl named Baldetrudis, who was so deprived of the light of her eyes that, abandoned to every despair, all hope of ever seeing seemed forever denied. Her parents, grieving at her blindness, placed her before the sight of the merciful father Magnobodus and humbly begged him to deign to grant healing assistance to their daughter.

Hearing their petition and seeing their faith, he turned to the defence of prayer and humbly besought the Lord [1472] to restore the girl’s sight—He who had healed the man born blind from the beginning of his birth. While Magnobodus persisted thus in prayer, the girl gradually began to blink with her closed eyes, until, all blindness driven away, she obtained complete sight and reached her parents’ door by her own unaided means.

## § XVI. On the withered hand of Domniolus

Among these events, a certain man named Domniolus, afflicted by a long-standing illness, was accustomed to carry about a withered hand, almost useless for any work. The mere form of the limb remained, but its effective strength and sensible vigour were absent; it clung to him like the burden of some lifeless matter. Presented to the notice of the most eminent man, the latter blessed an application of oil and ordered the man with the withered hand to anoint himself with it. Once anointed with the wholesome medicine, strength immediately began to return to the limb, its veins becoming vigorous and its sinews growing firm. Restored in every joint to soundness and accompanied by health, he returned home rejoicing. [Col. 1537C]

## § XVII. On coins multiplied during the feeding of the poor

What should I say of the ineffable miracle which the grace of the Almighty deigned to work through him? For once, when famine was pressing and crowds of poor people, as was customary, flocked from all places to the man of God, he, according to his usual practice as a generous giver, prepared an agape-meal without delay and distributed necessities. Though he had supplied no small number of coins for their provisions, the supply did not fail; all were fed to satiety.

When they had departed joyfully, the bishop’s servants examined the sum of money which had been distributed for the food of the needy and found that the amount they had spent in giving was doubled. Astonished with wonder, they approached him and reported the matter as it was; indeed, they found more than one hundred and fifty coins beyond the amount counted out and distributed for the expense of the needy. [Col. 1537D] But he was not lifted up by this as a ground for self-exaltation, nor did he ascribe it to his own merits. Attributing it to God’s mercy and giving thanks from the innermost chamber of his heart, he ordered the matter to be kept wholly silent, for he guarded against the vice of boasting.

## [1473] § XVIII. On a paralysed woman healed

Once the prodigy had thus disclosed the merits of the man of God, another miracle followed. A woman afflicted with paralysis was brought on a bed to the aforesaid bishop by acquaintances. All her joints were so dissolved that, with every function lost, only the vital breath seemed to draw breath without effort. The man of God, seeing her, was moved with compassion and strove to offer prayers to the highest King for her recovery. Once these had been completed, he approached the woman, took her hand, and ordered her to rise from the ground. [Col. 1538A] Without delay she stood up; all languor was driven away, she was restored whole, and she returned to her own home, needing no assistance and filled with unexpected joy.

## § XIX. On Lodovaeus restored to sight

Not long afterwards, a certain blind man, Lodovaeus, entangled in the bonds of the darkness of blindness, lived a miserable life tending toward ruin. Overwhelmed by such deprivation, he urgently demanded with all his might to be brought without delay before the bishop. His relatives, wearied by his persistent cries, were compelled to bring him to the physician to be healed by the most salutary remedy. The bishop gave himself to prayer for him; and, his face bathed in a shower of tears, the night of blindness was dispelled. With the coming of the sun, he restored to the blind man the longed-for gift of life. [Col. 1538B]

## § XX. On the archdeacon of the Church of Poitiers

Moreover, an archdeacon of the Church of Poitiers, a man of great simplicity named Agericus, enjoyed the special patronage of the blessed man because of the privileges of his holiness. Secretly approaching the bishop while suffering severe pain in his teeth, he disclosed in a mournful account the extent of the danger that he endured within his mouth. Taking pity on his suffering, the oft-mentioned bishop traced the venerable sign of the holy cross upon the cavities of his teeth and freed his mouth from every pain.

Thus secured in health, he returned joyfully from illness to the place whence he had come. In the end, through the intervention of the reputation of his merits, he was chosen by all as bishop of the people, to be adorned with the height of the episcopate and to govern the condition of holy mother Church, as a later [1474] event, worthy of God and conspicuous in deed, declared. [Col. 1538C]

## § XXI. On a man healed from torment

At roughly the same time, a man called Nannenus, born on the estate of Vermentense, was for a long time tormented by the assaults of demons. Bound at all times by a mass of chains and bonds, and deprived of his mind, he was brought to the man of God. Seeing Christ’s creature, redeemed by His blood, so oppressed by the enemy’s fraud, Magnobodus groaned deeply and fled to the help of almighty God, humbly begging that the obstinate enemy might not exercise the power of his foul domination over the man for whom Christ, coming to earth, had not shrunk from undergoing death.

Why delay with many words? When the prayer was finished, the holy man immediately commanded the hostile spirit that was raging in the body to depart swiftly from God’s image. At once, its deceptions reduced to nothing, the demon departed from the possessed man’s mind. Having recovered complete health, he returned with the bishop’s blessing. [Col. 1538D]

## § XXII. On a girl whose right hand was restored

Nor do I consider it right to pass over in silence what happened to a certain girl from a district commonly called Cabariense [variant: *Cabariacensem*]. As was well known to all who survived at that time, she had lost her right hand through illness. Having borne this injury to her limb for a long period, she was brought, at her request, to the often-mentioned blessed bishop. He ordered the girl’s right hand to be anointed with oil endowed with the gift of a sacred blessing. Freed by it from the bonds of all infirmities, she was enabled, by the bishop’s command, to return home in health, magnifying Christ’s power and the faculty of this kind granted by the Lord to the holy man.

## § XXIII. On the practices he performed daily

[Col. 1539A]

If we wished to recount all, each and every miracle performed by the holy man Magnobodus while he lived in the body, they would not yet exceed the bulk of a small book. Yet we have judged it proper to set forth briefly, to the extent permitted by the scantiness of our feeble spring [1475], only those deeds known through the report of many. For, shining inwardly and outwardly with the flowers of virtues, he possessed great privileges of learning. He was solicitous for the sheep entrusted to him, lest the flock of Christ—for which Christ Himself had shed His precious blood—should suffer any loss through the opening made by the ancient enemy. Against the snares of the swift lion, seeking someone to devour, he watched diligently and leapt over all his traps with wakeful vigilance.

Set in the house of the master, distributing to his fellow servants their entrusted measure of wheat, he kept watch diligently through the night for the welfare and increase of the flock committed to him, so that, when the Lord announced His coming, He might find him watchful rather than asleep. [Col. 1539B] Therefore, devoted with great earnestness to the support of prayer, he prayed unweariedly that the condition of God’s holy Church might be preserved.

Among the other works which he practised continually, offering sacrifice to the Lord was his particular work. Therein, sacrificing himself without ceasing upon the altar of a contrite heart, he became a living victim to the Lord. Making commemoration of the holy Mother of God and of all the saints, and receiving the gifts of the holy Eucharist with humble prayer, he thereby gave healing to many sick persons and safety to those in danger; and no obstacle of cold, travel, or any necessity whatsoever caused him to omit this. He was so devoted to the harmonies of psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs at both daytime and nighttime hours that he appeared to undertake no work without them. Nor was he forgetful of the Pentateuch and all sacred history; with keen intelligence he retained the sequence of the divine Scriptures.

Distinguished by fasting and observances of frugality, [Col. 1539C] he enlarged the rule of abstinence. During the days of Lenten observance, he shut himself alone in a cell, content with bread and water alone and taking even these in a measured weight; he lived in great privation. Thus he subdued his flesh by such severe want and hunger that, continually clothed in haircloth, he wore a rough covering.

He was diligently mindful of the poor, needy, and pilgrims. Orphans called him their father; wards and fugitives proclaimed him their comforter. They were nourished by his provisions, sustained by his resources, and covered by the support of clothing. If anyone oppressed by debt, overtaken by the lack of necessities, or any unfortunate person was compelled to seek his assistance, that person deserved to find, without delay, what was needed. Care for the sick clung to him above all else, and he renewed his concern for them with a watchful mind. If anyone, with death pressing, had reached his end [1476], he strove to attend the funeral; and, if necessity required it, the person was committed to burial at Magnobodus’s own expense. [Col. 1539D] And what more need be said? He became all things to all people, that he might gain all. But the order of the narrative requires that, in explaining hidden matters, we return the pen to its course.

## § XXIV. On a consecrated woman freed from illness

A consecrated woman named Procula had contracted a grave illness, so that she confessed herself almost given over to the danger of death. On account of her religious profession, she was well known to the man of God and repeatedly requested that she might deserve to be visited by him. Assisting her by his prayers, he decided, after the evening synaxis, to visit the handmaid of God, and he poured out prayers to almighty God for her recovery. Once these were completed, at the holy man’s command every disease and infirmity immediately departed from her, so that afterwards she lived in health for many years.

## § XXV. On the plot of Abbot Eracleus

There are very many people so ensnared by envy, malice, and rancour that, where they ought to take an example of good conduct and a rule of life, they become worse to their own destruction through the burning thorns of their wickedness. To explain this more plainly: a certain man, surnamed Eracleus, held the office of abbot, although he did not discharge the care of that office as was fitting. Seeing the distinguished virtues of the blessed bishop Magnobodus, he was caught by the bitter draught of envious poison and attempted to kill him. Corrupting men who were privy to his wicked crime, he ordered a cup of secret death to be offered to the man of God. [Col. 1540A]

When Magnobodus saw them coming to him, divine providence showed him their deadly deception. Remembering the evangelical command, “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5:44), he showed them every kindness in food and drink. After the meal he summoned them to himself and began to give them admonitions of salvation, seeking to persuade them to turn away from such wicked and avoidable deceit, lest, like fratricides producing sins of equal kind, they should be punished in the abyss by the sword of eternal curse. [Col. 1540B] With these and similar persuasive words he exhorted the deadly-minded men, admonishing them not to imitate the serpent’s guile but the dove’s simplicity; then, giving them the kiss of peace, he sent them away unharmed.

[1477] But they, overcome by shame and fear, returned to the person who had sent them and reported the affair as it was. When he understood that his crooked frauds had been exposed, shaken by sudden alarm, he fled to the thresholds of blessed Martin, seeking concealment. But because the traitor was repeatedly accused by truthful persons and his deeds became publicly known, he declared under oath that he was innocent of this accursed crime. Thus, falling into a double guilt—namely the crime of homicide and the fabrication of perjury—he incurred the vengeance of divine judgment. Struck by a dreadful ulcer on his forehead, he wasted away so long that no skill of physicians could provide healing remedies; and, having long suffered this foul wound, he deserved to meet an unexpected death—the man who had lain in wait against the life of the holy bishop. [Col. 1540C] Thus, when Magnobodus had been freed from his enemy, Christ’s mercy favouring him, the power of his gifts of virtue was manifested by prosperous outcomes.

## § XXVI. On a girl healed from the city of Rome

After these events, a girl of the city of Rome, born of most noble parents, suffered intolerable torment from an attack of fevers for three years. Since this dreadful pestilence seemed incurable by all and she had almost declined to death, she heard of the miraculous signs which Christ’s power performed in Gaul through the holy Magnobodus, bishop of Angers. She began to cry out in lamentation that she might deserve to be brought to the man of God to be healed. Her relatives, unable to endure her insistent complaint, undertook the long journey; crossing the Pennine Alps and making their way over a dreadful and rugged road, they came to Gaul.

When they learned that the holy bishop was residing at Angers, [Col. 1540D] they hastened to him at speed and found him engaged in the divine solemnities of Mass. At once, worn out by their journey, they explained the reason for their travel. Receiving them kindly, he placed in the girl’s mouth the mystery of the Lord’s Body, which he was handling with holy hands. Without delay, the poison of her long illness was laid aside, and she was restored to her former health; joyfully she returned with her companions to the city of Rome from which she had come.

## § XXVII. On the abbot of the monastery of St Albinus

In these days there was an abbot named Niulfus, who strove to govern according to the rule of holy [1478] religion the monastery in which St Albinus, formerly bishop of Angers, rests in body. Afflicted everywhere by the dreadful disease of gout, he remained incapable of every use of his hands. Therefore his brethren and dependants, surrounded by grief, did not know how to relieve the afflictions of their father. When the priest learned of this, [Col. 1541A] he proceeded, as was his custom, to visit the sick man. Seeing him in great distress, he completed a prayer and urged the sick man to receive sacred eulogiae adorned with a blessing. As soon as Niulfus received them in faith, every affliction that had assailed him immediately departed, and he experienced complete health. Giving thanks to the bishop, he thereafter presided for many years over the aforesaid monastery, serving the Lord with devotion.

## § XXVIII. On the illness of a certain Dodo

Not long afterwards, a man named Dodo, seized from early youth by an indescribable illness, had long been afflicted by ulcerous suffering. When he had become so wasted away, he remembered the things daily performed by the holy bishop Magnobodus. Summoning one of the household servants belonging to his parents, he ordered him to hasten to the bishop and urged him, by the sight of his own suffering, to reveal the cause of his illness and bring back the gift of the bishop’s blessing. The servant travelled quickly to the man of God and explained the business of his coming. Receiving from him bread consecrated by a blessing, he returned without delay and brought his master the healing gift for which he had gone. When Dodo ate it, he immediately felt the divine power present: the long-standing illness departed, his strength returned, and henceforth he was fortified by more joyful health. [Col. 1541B]

## § XXIX. On the deacon Romulus

At the same time, a certain man of archdeacon’s rank named Romulus, born in the region of Aquitaine, had been closely bound for six years by the distress of a certain disability. Since no hope of attaining health smiled upon him, at last, prompted by God, he learned of the far and wide spread fame of the distinguished bishop. He did not hesitate, with undivided purpose, to go to him at Angers. Weeping copiously, he begged the bishop to deign to take pity on him. Compassionating his anguish, as he was wholly devoted to mercy, Magnobodus urged him to seek health from the Lord, without whom [1479] human medicine could not help. For three days he himself persisted in prayer with him, celebrating the divine mysteries daily for the infirm man and communicating him with the Eucharist. [Col. 1541C] When this had been done, every inwardly lurking impurity of disease was put to flight, and Romulus joyfully returned by the way from which he had come, giving thanks.

## § XXX. On a miracle performed by Abbot Martin

Great are the things mentioned above, but still greater things must be added. For when the exceedingly celebrated fame of the man of God was spread everywhere, nobles and others eminent in the height of holiness, seeking his patronage, revered him with intense affection. If some necessity of travel or unexpected misfortune overtook them, they carried with them, as if they were weapons, the eulogiae of his blessing received from him, trusting that they would be protected.

It happened, therefore, that the father of a certain holy monastery, named Martin, concerned for the needs of the monastery entrusted to him, travelled by water for business to the district of Bordeaux. Seeking lodging, he chose to stay at the home of a certain woman worn down by the blindness of darkness. Seeing the woman’s deprivation and remembering the benefit of her hospitality, he gave her, when evening was approaching, a gift of bread which, as we have said, he had brought with him as a blessing. He ordered her to receive it with devotion. [Col. 1541D]

Having received it, she kept the night awake with him in prayer. When the dawn of day shone forth, the hidden darkness of her eyes fled together with the night’s gloom, and with the brilliant radiance of day the light of sight likewise shone openly. Seeing this, the household, astonished by the novelty of so great a miracle, raised the greatest commotion, praising Christ’s power and the gracious physician of their guest. Such, then, was this man whom we have often described in this careful account without false embellishment: such when absent, and such when present in bringing aid.

## § XXXI. On the girl Baudomella healed

[Col. 1542A]

Let the marks of miracles therefore be added, to be inserted on the page. A girl of tender age named Baudomella, from an estate commonly called Cabariacense, had had the light of her eyes covered by an incurable darkness. Brought to the blessed bishop with another’s assistance, she was the subject of prayer that he might deign to grant his merciful aid. [1480] Invoking the ineffable mystery of the Holy Trinity and making upon her the sign of the Cross’s trophy, with heavenly aid favouring him, he restored to the girl a clearer light than she had possessed at any time since the first tokens of her birth.

## § XXXII. On Godolena likewise illuminated

Next follows another similar miracle that must be related, concerning a young woman named Godolena. Though she had reached the years of puberty, she was held fast by blindness, and the sharpness of her sight was darkened; she endured the night of darkness. Brought by acquaintances before Christ’s priest, she was catechized by the anointing of oil alone and the image of the cross, and without delay received the clear sight which had been hidden through the course of many days. [Col. 1542B]

## § XXXIII. On another woman, named Goda

A little later another miracle was made manifest by clear report. A woman named Goda was greatly afflicted by the same black blindness. Immediately, therefore, using another’s assistance, she was brought before the glorious bishop Magnobodus. With cries she began urgently to beg that the eminent confessor would take pity on her. Moved by her complaints, he anointed the circles of the woman’s eyes with the liquid of blessed oil. Once they had been anointed, the darkness was expelled, with the coming of the day of unexpected light.

## § XXXIV. On a young man rescued from a demon

At the same period, a certain young man, mature in the flower of youth, was seized and severely tormented by the ancient enemy lying in wait—the one who deceives the hearts of human beings “through a thousand …” [lacuna]. Bound everywhere in knots of chains and bonds and deprived of his mind, he was brought to the man of God. Seeing Christ’s image invaded by the robber and wishing to recover it from destruction, Magnobodus ordered him to remain beside the cell in which he lived in prayer. [Col. 1542C]

Keeping him with himself through the whole Lenten season, and praying and entreating the Lord for him, the man was healed through the aid of the Lord’s power; the obstinate enemy was put to flight. Having recovered his mind and gained sound understanding, he returned of his own accord to the home from which he had been compelled to come.

## § XXXV. On a disabled girl healed

[1481] Let us add another well-known miracle which he afterwards performed. From a village called Cornaliacum, a girl who had completed three five-year periods of her life had suffered such bodily injury that she was deprived of the natural use of hands and feet. The aforesaid limbs, having lost the power of moisture and strength, were withered like wood and unfit for use. Brought before the holy man, she began to be healed of every affliction by oil sanctified with blessing. Her sinews and veins recovered their power; by the bishop’s command, she returned to her homeland knowing how to go and walk, and thereafter lived by her own guidance. [Col. 1542D]

## § XXXVI. On a boy both healed and tonsured through admonition
But I do not think that what must now be related ought to be passed over in silence. In the district which the common people call Gerciacus, a certain inhabitant had begotten a son who, from the very beginning of his birth, being weak in hands and feet, could move only with the aid of crawling. His parents, unwilling to be overwhelmed by this dreadful misfortune, received, through the comforting providence of God, at the untimely midnight hour, a certain man of handsome appearance, who said to them: “Carry the child whom you have lately received so weak [Col. 1543A] to Bishop Magnobodus, and ask that he may be initiated into the sacred mysteries by him, vowing to dedicate him to the religious life.” Awakened by this vision, they pondered together what they had heard in sleep; and, when dawn broke, they rose and offered the child to the Church to become a priest, so that, when his age had strengthened, he might flourish as a servant of sacred worship. When this was done, all weakness of his limbs was immediately removed; strengthened in bodily vigor, he was presented before the bishop, who cut the hair of his head, as was customary, and, when he grew up, placed him over the divine mysteries, serving the Lord from the whole depth of his heart, who had called him into this order.

### § XXXVII. Of a Girl Named Leta

What shall I say of a certain woman named Leta, who carried her right hand so withered that she was known to be fit for no domestic task? With every affection of her mind she approached the blessed man and made known in mournful complaint what she suffered, [Col. 1543B] and the hopeless condition of her disabled limb. He granted her petition; invoking the aid of the Almighty and making the sign of the cross, he restored her right hand sound like the left. All its joints, strengthened by a firm structure of power, again spun and twisted thread.

### § XXXVIII. Of the Blind Man Named Kariulphus
