It must also be mentioned what, through the working of heavenly grace, he did for a certain man, Kariulphus. For, when a dense darkness of blindness came upon him, he was afflicted with blindness. Using a guide, he hastened to the man of God, disclosed the peril of his bodily condition not without great sorrow, and begged him to show mercy. For this man’s misery, the bishop poured out prayers to the Lord and impressed upon his eyes the wondrous sign of the cross. The night of darkness was put to sleep; the pall of blindness was driven away; and light burst forth in the sight of his pupils.

### § XXXIX. Of the Sick Woman Marcia

[Col. 1543C] I also judge that what is widely known concerning a certain woman called Marcia ought not to be passed over in silence. She was so tormented by an attack of fevers that no rest by day or night was granted her. Thus, afflicted by such severe distress, she was compelled to come into the presence of the holy bishop. Anointed by him, according to custom, with the sacred unction of oil, the deadly affliction at once departed; and she was restored to such sound health that she who had come by another’s assistance returned under her own protection.

### § XL. Of the Two Girls Necteria and Theodechildis

Therefore, if what we have learned from another’s account is to be accepted as true, surely what we have seen with our own eyes ought not to be judged insignificant. To explain more fully: two maiden sisters, one called Necteria and the other Theodechildis, of distinguished lineage according to human genealogy, whether through sins of their own committing or entangled in the crimes of their parents—which we consider should by no means be judged—or in order that the merits of the often-mentioned bishop might more fully be displayed, having lost the light of their eyes, directed their steps by the help of another. Brought into his presence, as soon as their pupils were anointed with the pure application of oil together with the aid of prayer, all blindness being driven away and natural brightness shining forth, they returned to their own home, safeguarded by their own unaided walking.

### § XLI. Of the Basilica Which He Built, and Other Buildings

Thus, while such great signs of the holy man’s powers shone everywhere and the lights of his deeds increased far and wide, his prudent mind began to consider what manner of service he should render to the worship of divine religion, and by what increase he might gather servants of Christ for the proclamation of the rule of the holy Church of God, for his own advancement and the salvation of others. With the favor of Almighty grace upon this concern, [Col. 1544A] he resolved to build a basilica in honor of the glorious martyr Saturninus, first bishop of the city of Toulouse, and in honor of all martyrs and very many saints.

Accordingly, fulfilling in deed what he had conceived in mind, he built a monastery with the highest magnificence and took care to gather men devoted to a holy purpose. There he also built *synthochia* and *brephotholia*—houses for the sick and foundling-houses—and accommodations for pilgrims and many others. So that those living there in a regulated common fellowship should lack no food, he accumulated every necessity, assigning very many estates and a great quantity of possessions. He commanded that, after the end of his earthly sojourn, his body should be committed to the earth there, to await the final day of its restoration.

### § XLII. Of the Daughter of a Certain Theudebald

When these things had been completed with great elegance, and all the small buildings had been constructed as he had vowed in his mind, a very powerful man named Theudebald had a daughter grievously afflicted, whom no remedy could cure. Weeping and lamenting, he caused her to be brought to the holy bishop, begging on bent knees that he might deign to bring help to his daughter, besieged by the enemy.

The blessed man replied that this was not his work, but the work of perfect Fathers, who could obtain such a thing from the Lord by their own spiritual power. Yet overcome by the prayers of the suppliants, he placed relics of the saints upon the girl’s neck, together with the blessing of oil and the sign of the cross. When this was done, the wicked robber, driven away with his deceptions, left the vessel which he had unjustly seized; [1484] the girl, her senses and mind restored, was returned whole to health. Thus the blessed man, adorned by so great an outcome of miracles, was honored by all and praised by everyone. The parents, with their daughter, returned rejoicing to the home from which they had come in sorrow.

### § XLIII. Of the Woman Prisca

By this miraculous sign, celebrated by the blessed man, he again shone forth more wonderfully. A woman named Prisca, blind from the beginning of her birth, had remained in this miserable blindness through six cycles of five years. Offered to the priest, she immediately felt divine power displayed over her. For, when the name of the holy cross was traced by his right hand upon the place where the functions of sight were thought to be located, she at once merited to behold the light of the sun, which she had never seen anywhere before.

Immediately the cry of the people rose up, and many rejoicing said that the holy bishop had done something like the Son of God, who healed a man blind from the beginning of life.

### § XLIV. Of the Young Man Vinciemalus

At the same time, a certain young man named Vinciemalus had contracted such a bodily affliction that, his light being darkened, he lost his eyes. Coming to the most serene bishop, he was anointed on the pupils with consecrated oil; and immediately, as the darkness withdrew, he received the strong light which he had lost while sick.

Thereafter, enjoying good health, he was walking upon the top of a wall when he fell by accident from the height to the ground below. Yet, through the cooperating power of the consecrated oil with which he had been anointed by the blessed bishop, according to the testimony of very many persons, he was found so unharmed that he seemed not to have fallen at all.

### § XLV. Of a Man Sick for Five Years

Again another man was presented, who had been held for the course of five years by a disabling illness. The excellent Shepherd, moved by mercy, anointed him with the liquid of oil endowed with the gift of blessing and poured out prayer. Immediately the strength of his limbs began to flourish; thus the vastness of his pain being cut away, the man who had arrived bedridden went back upright, glorifying the generosity of the eternal King, who, wonderful in his saints, works such great deeds through them.

### § XLVI. Of the Deaf Man Chidoald

[1485] As the course of time turned, a certain man named Gidoaldus, as a prolonged illness grew worse, lost the power of hearing. Brought before the venerable bishop, he earnestly begged, as best he could, to obtain remedies. The aforementioned blessed man approached him, put his fingers into his ears, and at the same time poured in a drop of oil. Immediately a flowing discharge burst forth from them with a horrible stench, so that those standing around could not endure it. Thus the deaf man experienced hearing, and, endowed with a double gift, joyfully hastened back upon his own path.

### § XLVII. Of the Woman Whose Eyes Closed

It should also be committed to memory what happened to a certain woman from the village called Volense. As she related, she was burdened by such an impediment that whenever, through the needs of her household, she was occupied with some task, her eyes grew dim and were closed in blindness for long periods of time. Therefore, following the custom of other sick people, she hurried to the venerable man of God and described the condition of her misfortune [Col. 1545B] and the hardship of her state. Invoking the ineffable mercy of Christ, he made firm and stable the wandering light which the woman possessed uncertainly; having scattered the darkness, he sent her away rejoicing.

### § XLVIII. Of the Woman Restored to Sight

Let us also tell what we can testify and establish without the fabrication of falsehood. A woman, likewise born in the village which is commonly called Verciacense, was compelled, by an intervening accident, to lose the ever-desired light of her head. She was called Alloucia. Brought to the most gracious man, he was bound by the prayers of those standing around to pour out prayer on her behalf. Not refusing the requests of those praying, he invoked the aid of the Almighty and, by healing anointing, restored the woman’s sight. She then returned cheerfully to the place from which she had come.

### § XLIX. Of Another Paralyzed Woman

[1486] We do not judge that what took place in our own presence should be omitted. A certain woman, Carigundis by name, had similarly lost the windows of light; moreover, deprived of all strength and coordination of her limbs and robbed of the use of speech, she had entirely lost hope of recovering her powers. From the village of Conflentis, where she remained secluded, she was brought to the man of God. After prayers were poured out to the Lord for her during three days, he restored her whole; and, with hands and feet completely strengthened, she needed no other person’s assistance in returning.

### § L. Of a Plunderer of His Church

Therefore, when the holy man had been made illustrious by the manifest proof of so many powers, opposition from the wicked also grew hot against him. But he who had swelled up as an enemy of piety was punished. To relate the matter more plainly: a certain man dwelling within the royal court, bent by the winding malice of greed, as the event later proved, rashly seized a beast of burden which provided for the needs of the Church and assigned it to his own uses.

When this was reported to the bishop, he preferred to conceal it in silence rather than intensify the complaint. But on the following night divine vengeance struck the man. As soon as he gave himself to sleep, he saw himself in a dream surrounded by balls of fire and severely rebuked by the bishop’s threats. Awakened by these threats, he began to cry aloud that he was being tormented by the blessed bishop and begged to be granted a visit from him. The bishop did not refuse to go; when he visited him, he warned this adversary not to become a plunderer of God’s holy Church, but rather to honor Christ’s servants and abstain from their provisions. Then, after prayer had been offered, he restored him whole and commanded the damage which he had inflicted upon the Church to be repaired. Without delay the man obeyed his commands, restored what he had unjustly taken, and departed free and safe.

### § LI. Of His Death and Funeral

The oft-mentioned holy bishop had now governed the Church of Angers entrusted to him by the Lord for many years, with great honor in evangelical preaching and outstanding devotion to mercy. During that time he converted a multitude of people to the holiness of the Christian faith by Catholic doctrine. Love of the heavenly country burned in every breast; on appointed days the people flocked to the bosom of the holy Church; everywhere the assembly of clergy resounded with hymn-like songs; the Christian religion increased in exact measure; the marks of vices were cut away; the growth of good works was added.

While the holy Church of God flourished everywhere through these and similar sparks of virtues, the most devout shepherd, as the natural event hastened him toward the boundary of death due to him and the late hour of age was already pressing on, began to draw near. Summoning to himself the brethren whom he had educated in holy doctrine, he announced the dissolution of his body and declared that he would pass from this prison-house of the world. Soon afterward, when the weakness of fevers came upon him, his bodily strength began to fail.

At his departure clergy and people gathered together and attended upon their patron with every devotion they could offer. With such strength as he retained, he admonished and instructed them, exhorting them to take care to avoid the snares of sins; in all things, mindful of the Lord’s commands, to obey his will; to pursue justice; and to cultivate the bonds of charity together with the tranquility of peace. Thus, when the time of their calling from this miserable life drew near, they might not be found sluggish and idle, but might stand ready, watchful in good works.

Having finished the charges by which he instructed his spiritual children, he raised his hands to heaven and diligently invoked the Lord amid the words of prayer. On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of November [15 October], he gave up his spirit to the Lord in their hands and left his body to the earth. His soul, as we truly profess, was taken up by angelic companies, presented before the divine presence, and rejoices in glory.

Many people from villages and fields attended his funeral, filling the air with weeping and groans. [Col. 1546C] His most holy body, borne in a bier and carried by clergy and people into the basilica which he himself had dedicated with great care, was laid with the highest honor in a sarcophagus-tomb. There also rest, held worthy of great veneration, the bodies of very many faithful persons, awaiting the day of their renewal and the judgment to come.

In that place, with the Lord’s cooperation, many great deeds occur: the blind are enlightened, the lame healed, lepers cleansed, demons driven from possessed bodies, paralytics raised up, and countless other things which it would seem burdensome to recount. Of these, one which comes to mind we judge should be inserted into this page.

### § LII. Of the Two Captives from Le Mans

After the death of the man of God, two men from the territory of Le Mans—one called Vualdo and the other Bodecharius—were captured by chance by their enemies, the men of Angers. Bound in fetters [Col. 1546D] and handcuffs, they were afflicted with cruel suffering. Shut within a dreadful prison, surrounded by poverty, hunger, and lack of bread, they were made a spectacle for mockery and laughter.

While they were thus fastened with straps and led through streets and walkways in poverty and for the sake of disgrace, it happened by divine regard that, under heavy guard, they came to the threshold where the body of the memorable bishop lay. When they approached the tomb of the aforesaid bishop, their bonds were immediately untied and the fastenings of their chains removed: those thought to be bound appeared free. Seeing this, their jailers, struck with fear by the astonishing novelty of the miracle, made it known to everyone by spreading the report here and there.

When the matter reached the notice of the leading men of the city, attributing it to the merits of St. Magnobodus, they granted freedom to the prisoners whom they had confined among themselves in the manner of enemies and allowed them to go. Free from every troublesome impediment, the two men returned unharmed to the land of their residence, praising the power of Christ and the merits of St. Magnobodus [Col. 1547A], who had delivered them from so great a danger.

When these things had been spread abroad among the people, greater veneration for the tomb of the holy bishop began to grow. From distant and foreign lands people afflicted by various diseases were brought there; keeping vigil in that place, they were delivered from every trouble of sickness. His memory was celebrated everywhere; his merits were recounted everywhere without interruption, while people heard and saw the ineffable miracles performed day by day by the glorious bishop.

Therefore, with devout mind and supplicating prayer, let us beseech the mercy of his loving-kindness: that, as while living in this present life he sought to favor the petitions of those who prayed, so he may not disdain to be an intercessor for the sins which daily accumulate upon us. Thus, cleansed from every crime of defilement, may we be able to be freed from the destruction of Gehenna and enjoy eternal joy and glory with the saints, through the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and power with the Father and the Holy Spirit, through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

Christ the Lord Jesus, who glorifies those who glorify him, also deigned, through his most precious bishop Magnobodus, to call back from the dead a little boy, for the praise and glory of his name. One day, when the bishop was proceeding to the aforesaid basilica to celebrate Mass amid the greatest rejoicing of clergy and people, a certain woman came with the son of her womb so that she might share in the blessings of the holy bishop. When she had entered within the enclosure of the church and her little child had gone away from her, he went toward the church doors and began to play in the street beside that church.

Suddenly a herd of mares came from Valleia and, heading toward an island commonly called Mons, passed through the same street at a swift gallop. Since the aforesaid boy could not turn to the right or left, and, as I believe, the enemy of the human race lay in wait, he was torn to pieces by the herd and died. When the holy bishop had completed the solemnities of Mass, the woman, forgetting her son, was returning home. Passing through the street, she found her son torn to pieces; with great grief of heart she lifted him from the ground, immediately cried out that she was wretched, filled the air with loud cries, and could in no way restrain her tears.

But when she recalled the things that had long been performed by the holy bishop Magnobodus, she hurried swiftly as far as the basilica; for the holy bishop had not yet departed from it. The aforesaid woman laid the body of her suffocated son before the holy man, saying: “Holy man, restore to me this son, you who are acknowledged as father of the people.”

As she said these and many similar things, the man of God, overcome by the woman’s prayers, resorted to his customary weapons. Before the people watching, he prostrated himself on the ground. Why delay with many words? The priest lay in the dust until bishop and boy rose together: the bishop from prayer, the boy from death. Thereupon the surrounding people were shaken with no small astonishment at beholding the unheard-of miracle, and a cry rose on every side. Praises were offered on high to the Creator, and the true voice of Truth was fulfilled, promising and saying: “He who believes in me will also do the works that I do” (John 14:12). The mother, rejoicing, returned with her son to the home from which she had come.

[Col. 1547]

# The Life of Saint Magnobodus, Bishop of Angers, by Marbod, Bishop of Rennes

*(Our Reverend Father Mabillon supplied us with this Life of Saint Magnobodus, which he had in his archives, copied from an old manuscript of the collegiate church of Saint Magnobodus at Angers.)*

## The Prologue Begins

[Col. 1547C] Those who committed to writing the deeds of brave men—I mean the pagans—seem to me chiefly to have followed a threefold purpose: either that they might receive some reward for their labor from those living in their own time; or that they might perpetuate among posterity the memory of their talent and effort; or, indeed, with the more commendable intention that they might set before readers or hearers a model for imitation.

But we—that is, Christians—who are forbidden to seek earthly things, and are commanded to pursue not enduring fame but eternal life, retain only the last of those three reasons and exchange the other two for a more profitable recompense. For our present labor we expect a future reward; and from our effort we seek not human favor but God’s praise, from whom both works are supplied to those who perform them and words to those who write them.

Therefore I, Marbod, least among bishops, intending to write the Life of the holy bishop Magnobodus, ask first of my hearers that the obscurity, perhaps, of an unpolished style should not prejudice them against the brightness of the truth. Rather, weighing each matter according to its merits, let them criticize the slenderness of the wording in such a way that they do not reject the dignity of the deeds. For not everything said elegantly is immediately to be accepted, nor, conversely, is what is said without ornament to be rejected as useless. Poison is sometimes offered in a golden vessel, while healthful food, on the other hand, is served in earthenware.

“For the Apostle also, preaching the kingdom of God not in wisdom of speech but in simplicity of discourse, says that he possesses this treasure in earthen vessels” (cf. 2 Corinthians 4:7). Thus I shall attempt to set forth, in simple style, as though in an earthen vessel, the riches of God’s goodness manifested in one saint, so that holiness, as if dulled by no outward brilliance, may shine more purely when considered in itself. True virtue, indeed, content with its own manifestation alone, does not require the artificial recommendation of words; rather, those things which lack natural grace desire to be made bright by ornaments sought from outside. But enough of this. Let us now come to the beginning of the narrative.

## The Life of the Holy and Glorious Confessor Magnobodus, Bishop of Angers, Begins

[Col. 1549A] Magnobodus was a native of the territory of Angers, during the reign among the Franks of Lothar, son of Chilperic. His Christian parents were exalted among their fellow citizens by distinguished birth and the dignity of honors. From his very infancy divine grace so cherished and nurtured him that even then there could be no doubt that something exceptional and illustrious, beyond the common lot of those born, was foreshadowed in him.

When he reached boyhood—the age at which it is customary for the children of nobles first to be given to instruction—he was entrusted to a teacher of letters. For his parents’ faith, stirred by certain signs, had determined that he should be devoted to divine service, while the order of heavenly providence was preparing that he should be set over the Church of Christ.

The boy, of keen intellect and singular memory, accompanied by divine favor, soon exceeded the measure of his contemporaries and began easily to equal those more advanced in years. Not long afterward, rivaling even the learning of his teachers, he quickly attained the summit of instruction. Nor is it surprising that wisdom advanced him with such rapid growth, since from the first beginnings of his tender age, having conceived a love of holiness, he admitted none of the enticements of worldly vanity. Rather, while still young, he strove to anticipate the purity of his heart with the sweet blessings of virtues.

It therefore came about that, through the merit of holiness, he also obtained the privilege of understanding, as the Psalmist says: “I have understood more than the elders, because I have sought your commandments” (Psalm 118:100 [119:100]). When he became a young man, he began to exercise himself in fuller studies of virtue. He did not allow the age inclined toward worse things to be corrupted by shameful luxury or idle sloth, but subjected himself to the strict laws of abstinence, granting nothing to his belly or sleep beyond what the necessity of nature demanded. He gave himself continually to prayer or reading, allowing no interval of time to be lost without spiritual progress.

When these things became known to the blessed bishop Licinius, whose remarkable holiness was at that time esteemed among the bishops of Gaul, he rejoiced in the abundance of divine gifts. Having summoned the young man, he gave him the ecclesiastical tonsure according to custom; assigning him to clerical duties, he ordered this recruit, already of proven virtue, to serve in the camps of Christ.

Soon afterward, as time advanced, he promoted him through the ecclesiastical ranks as far as the priesthood, judging him worthy to share the burden of his own care and to resolve, by his counsel, the uncertainties of emerging difficulties. For he lacked neither the prudence by which to assess the outcomes of affairs nor the steadfastness by which fearlessly to carry out what had been well provided for.

Outstanding in chastity, exalted in humility, overflowing in charity, he could offer to his inferiors instruction in conduct even with his tongue silent, through a life that spoke. [Col. 1550A] Nor did he lack sweetness of eloquence or abundance of expression, by which he might turn the hearts of his hearers from love of this age toward a greater desire for heavenly things.

For these reasons the holy bishop entrusted to him the government of the monastery of Colonetense, so that the flock of brothers, stirred by the example of its ruler, instructed by teaching, and kindled by exhortation, might advance toward better things; and so that he himself, as though rehearsing in lesser matters, might be rendered more practiced and more capable through experience for the greater tasks later to be arranged.

In this administration he showed himself so faithful and prudent that he sufficiently supplied the household of the Lord set over him with what was necessary for body and soul, and, from its holy advances, claimed not his own praise but the glory of the Lord himself. [Col. 1550B] It no longer remained doubtful to anyone that he would be suitable for carrying out any great undertaking, since fortunate diligence directed every act he performed.

Accordingly, at his bishop’s command, he undertook an embassy to the Roman pope, for a matter which we shall briefly explain. The blessed bishop Licinius had built from the foundations, in the suburb of his city, a splendid church of costly and illustrious workmanship, now called by his own name. In it he had determined to establish a community of monks to serve God. Desiring to dedicate it in honor of Saint John the Baptist, he requested relics of that saint from the bishop of the Apostolic See.

For this purpose Magnobodus was sent to Rome. He readily obtained from the pope what he sought, since the pope could not fail immediately to perceive the sanctity and ability in which the envoy excelled. Delighted also by his modesty and character, he ordered him to remain with him for some time. At last, enriched with the apostolic blessing and with his petitions granted, Magnobodus was sent back joyfully to his own country, carrying the sacred pledges—that is, relics—of Saint John the Baptist.

But while he remained with the pope, I think it should not be entirely omitted what happened to him, since it appears to contain both a rebuke of malice and an example of diligence to be imitated. During the offices of the night, to which the pope admitted him familiarly, he was, by the pope’s command, reciting a reading from the lectern, as was customary. Certain palace clerics, moved by envy—as human perversity is wont to be, since a foreigner had obtained before their lord a role belonging to members of the household and, as it were, had seized their service—contrived to extinguish the candle by whose light he read, so that, his purpose frustrated, he might withdraw ashamed and seemingly struck dumb.

But he was not disturbed in the least. In the same cadence in which he had begun, he completed the passage from memory. Thus what they had planned for his disgrace was turned instead to glory.

Having received the relics which Magnobodus brought, Saint Licinius gave no small thanks first to God, the giver of all good things, and then also to his disciple. With that same disciple he celebrated, as he had desired, the joy of the dedication of the new church, placing there with due honor the sacred relics of the forerunner of Christ.

Thus Magnobodus, proved and known at home and abroad, as we have said, was held not only most dear to his master but also venerable and most worthy of praise to all good and honorable people. By dishonorable people, however, he could neither be praised nor ought to have been; for to be praised by the base is as bad as to be praised for base things.

After the death of the blessed Licinius, nothing, it must be believed, delayed his immediate elevation to the bishopric except that he himself declined the honor. Judging it safer to cling to the leisure of contemplation than to become entangled in the business of government, he secured the appointment of another. But after that man too died by God’s dispensation, it was sufficiently clear that this man was being demanded by divine judgment.

Therefore, by the common wish of all, with the assent of King Dagobert, to whom the succession of the kingdom had by then descended, he was elected. Compelled according to God’s ordinance to preside over the Church of Angers, two priests, nevertheless, prominent above the others in rank—Ambrulfus and Leobaldus—moved by the spurs of ambition and envy, dared to oppose him, so that material might not be lacking for divine judgment in confirming the decision of the election. Both were immediately deprived of their right eye, and by this manifest punishment were convicted of having resisted with their left sense.

What manner of man he showed himself in the episcopate can be doubtful to no one, since even before he possessed the title, he already possessed the reality of the title. But now, applying himself especially to his task, he heaped upon himself still greater increases of virtue. For a greater burden had to be lifted by greater strength, and a greater honor deserved more earnest diligence.

The learned man could not be ignorant that a pastor’s own holiness does not suffice unless he also heals the sins of those subject to him; nor that only those are reckoned in the most miserable condition to whom the errors of all are imputed, while, conversely, those who are rewarded for the merits of all are deservedly judged most blessed. Therefore, allowing no time and no place for idleness, he watched carefully over the Lord’s flock, lest any sheep entrusted to him, wandering too negligently, should be ravaged by the bites of the wolf that lay in wait.

He ministered to all, in due season, the food of God’s word, according as he saw it suited the capacity of each. Like a good commander, for whom it is insufficient merely to encourage soldiers by words unless he also courageously performs by hand what he has urged them to do by words, he showed in his character and life how what he taught ought to be done.

In accordance with the apostolic command, “he rebuked the unruly, comforted the fainthearted, supported the weak, and was patient toward all” (1 Thessalonians 5:14), adapting himself to the needs of each so that no one’s salvation might be neglected. And, as another apostle says, he was “not lording it over the clergy, but becoming from the heart an example to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3).

He abounded so greatly in the inward feelings of compassion and mercy that he wept with those who wept, was ill with those who were ill, burned with those who were scandalized, and was afflicted with those who were afflicted. Nor did he judge others’ prosperity less than his own: he rejoiced with those who rejoiced, was raised up with those recovering strength, applauded those made glad, and was refreshed with those restored.

He gave especially great care to the poor, most often ministering food while hungry and drink while thirsty. In short, neglecting his own concerns, he served the needs of all others. Filled with the sweetness of charity, seeking not what was his own but what belonged to others, he frequently visited communities of monks, nuns, and clergy. Immediately uprooting whatever harmful growth had sprung up among them, he sowed seeds of virtues that would bear fruit unto eternal life.

For the severity of justice was vigorous in him, by which he struck the faults of offenders; and he displayed the gentleness of pardon, by which he did not deny forgiveness to those corrected. An unconquered lover of justice and a fervent detester of bribes, he knew how to depart from the path of truth neither through flattery nor through threats. In adversity he was raised up by constancy; in prosperity he rejoiced in humility.

Yet amid these most fruitful occupations of ecclesiastical action, he did not cease also to perform the duties of contemplation. Frequently keeping watch through whole nights in church, he delighted in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; offering pure prayers to God with tears, he obtained from heaven protection and peace for the people entrusted to him. For he could not fail to be heard for his people, since he had also made that people worthy to be heard. By continual practice, instructed in words and examples, he had turned them to the love of goodness; and, as upon matter already softened and ready to receive forms, he had impressed upon his subjects the image of his own religion.

Therefore there was nothing for which thanks should not deservedly be given to the author of grace: the skill of the strong farmer was proved by the abundant sowing, and the fertility of the field was praised by its good yield. For, according to the saying of Solomon, “Where there are no oxen, the manger is empty; but where there are many crops, there is manifest strength of oxen” (Proverbs 14:4).

Thus, filled with such and so great gifts of virtues, he spread far and wide the good fragrance of Christ and stirred the minds and tongues even of those far away to praise him. To the merit of his life was added also the power of miracles, so that those unwilling to be led by the example of his merits might be convinced by the display of signs. We shall relate some of these, by which the others also may not be disbelieved.

Magnobodus, bishop, having been summoned by King Dagobert, came to Paris. Prisoners whom a punitive prison held tightly bound in iron, as their crimes deserved, learned that he was passing by and implored the holy bishop’s aid with piteous cries. Moved at once by their misery, he turned aside from the road leading to the church, in order to bend the judge’s mind, by whatever prayers he could, to pity the accused. [Col. 1553A] But when he could not soften that man’s hardness, he entered the basilica and turned to the Lord, praying and supplicating that divine mercy might grant what human wickedness denied. Immediately, by divine power, the bonds of the chains were loosed; the prison doors opened of themselves for those shut within; and, no one hindering them, they came out and fled to the church where the saint was praying. Falling at the blessed man’s feet, they gave thanks for their deliverance. He, having obtained from God their release, also secured their complete discharge from the ruler; and, corrected by fitting rebukes, he dismissed them in peace.

At about the same time, a certain blind man, having heard of the saint’s powers, asked to be brought to him. When he reached the city of Angers, he found the bishop [Col. 1553B] celebrating the sacraments in church. Immediately, raising a cry, he urgently demanded in untimely shouts that his lost sight be restored. The bishop, not at all offended by his importunity, calmly completed the mysteries and offered prayer for the petitioner’s healing. Then, after he had poured the Eucharist into his mouth, the blind man immediately received the light he had long desired, and joyfully and gratefully returned home.

> [Note: [Col. 1553D] From this word it could be concluded with considerable probability that at that time the Eucharist was given to the faithful under both kinds; for nothing is poured into the mouth except that which is [Col. 1554D] liquid, whereas what is solid is put in or handed over.]

Likewise, a certain devout priest was afflicted by persistent dysentery. As the disorder of his intestines tortured him and violent pain had exhausted the sufferer’s strength and was already tearing apart the very seat of life, the afflicted man’s faith nevertheless gathered itself into speech. Calling his servants to him, he commanded them, with whatever effort he could, to carry bread [Col. 1553C] to the bishop, ask him to bless it, and bring it back to offer him as a sure remedy. When this was done, the sick man consumed the blessed bread (*eulogiae*) and immediately recovered; he himself, a competent witness, proclaimed the miracle performed in him.

At another time, while travelling through his diocese, he came to an estate called Cartiniacus. There he encountered a crowd of boys at play, who, stirred by the devil and behaving insolently, did not cease to taunt him with malicious words and laughter, as though he were another Elisha. Suddenly—marvellous to relate—one of them, who pressed the mockery more impudently than the rest, was lifted into the air in a dusty whirlwind and was horribly carried through empty space. At last he fell from on high among brambles [Col. 1553D] and was picked up with nearly all his limbs 1497 bruised and torn. His most unhappy parents carried him with groaning and lamentation into the holy bishop’s presence and begged him to have mercy upon him. He ordered the boy to be laid down in the church porch and told them to withdraw for a little while. When they returned shortly afterward, they received him sound whom they had left despaired of.

He likewise restored without delay, by the power of prayer, a certain Theudegisilus, wasted by a long illness for which no medical remedies had availed, when he was brought to him in bed. Thus he was carried home on his own feet [Col. 1554A], though he had been brought in the hands of others.

Returning from the village called Othomensis, the same holy man, accompanied by many disciples, came to the river-crossing where his journey was interrupted. But since the ferryman was absent and the little boat lay moored on the opposite bank, there seemed no means of crossing. He, however, as was his custom, cast himself down in prayer; and, before all who saw it, by the hidden power of virtue he drew the vessel to himself. Entering it with his companions, he was carried across by the same power in a favourable passage.

Mummolus also—for that was the sick man’s name—received from the same holy bishop a remedy of divine power. For a long time he had been consumed by the slow fires [Col. 1554B] of quartan fevers; and, with the purity of his blood nearly exhausted, the weight of melancholy was bending his afflicted limbs toward death. Through messengers he begged the saint not to deny him the mercy which he bestowed upon all. The bishop, immediately pitying the afflicted man’s distress, gave the messengers consecrated oil and ordered them to anoint the sufferer with it. When this was done, the sick man at once rose healed.

A girl named Baldetrudis, deprived of the light of her eyes, likewise supplied the blessed man with an occasion for his power. Her parents presented her before his holy gaze and did not cease humbly to intercede for her. Moved both by their prayers and by the girl’s misery, the bishop prayed, kneeling upon the ground [Col. 1554C], to Christ, the true light, who enlightens every person coming into the world. Meanwhile the thick darkness gradually began to thin, and an unfamiliar light spread forth as though through a delicate membrane. At last, all blindness having been completely driven away, the girl received the clearest light.

There was also a certain Domolus, widely known because of the loss of a withered hand. Miserable as he was, he carried it about—not for use but as a burden 1498—already dead, hanging like something foreign from the frame of the living body because its sinews had failed. When he was brought before the holy man, the latter blessed oil and ordered the withered hand to be anointed with it. This was done; and immediately, the veins being filled and the sinews restored, the hand came to life and served the necessary uses of the body no less than the other hand [Col. 1554D].

Nor do I think it should be omitted that this seems to represent the power of the Lord Christ himself, according to his saying: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and will do greater than these” (John 14:12). For in a time of famine, when an innumerable multitude of poor people had gathered around the aforesaid bishop, the cheerful giver ordered a considerable sum of money to be spent for their refreshment. When it had been distributed and all had eaten to satisfaction, his stewards found twice the money in their purses. Surely he who in a similar case had multiplied five [Col. 1555A] loaves also gave increase to coins. For although the materials differ—bread and silver—the same power is recognized in both. Something similar occurred long ago under Elijah, when the jar of oil and the vessel of flour did not fail (3 Kings 17:14). For in such matters Christ is the same yesterday and today and unto ages of ages (Hebrews 13:8).

Christ also deigned to restore through him a paralysed woman deprived of every use of her limbs, when the faithful brought her on a couch before the blessed bishop. After kneeling, he mercifully poured forth prayers for the unhappy woman; then, taking her hand, he immediately raised her sound at Christ’s command.

As the report of these powers spread everywhere [Col. 1555B], crowds of sick and infirm people hurried to him from every quarter, plainly as to a physician of proven efficacy, especially because he bestowed divine benefits freely and without difficulty upon each person. Among them was dragged a wretched blind man named Lodovarus, who had extorted from his relatives, with excessive importunity and loud cries, that he should be taken there. When the holy man saw him brought before him, moved by compassion—for he was wholly sympathetic—he shed tears and gave himself to prayer for the unhappy man. Immediately blindness was driven away, and restored light made joyful the face that had long been sorrowful.

The aforesaid holy man had as a familiar friend Agericus, archdeacon of the Church of Poitiers [Col. 1555C], a man of good simplicity and unfeigned religious devotion. Later, by the merit of his holiness, he was raised as worthy bishop of the aforesaid Church. This archdeacon suffered unbearable toothache. When the bishop learned of it with concern, he made the sign of the cross upon the painful places, and at once 1499 all pain was quieted and extinguished.

From the estate of Vernantensis, a certain demoniac named Nannenus was brought to him, bound with straps and iron lest he attack those who met him. Him too, by exorcisms, supplications, and the marvellous power of prayer with which he was accustomed to heal others easily, he cleansed.

From the district called Caprariensis, a girl was brought to him deprived of the use of her right hand; and immediately [Col. 1555D], anointing her with holy oil, he freed her from the affliction of disability.

Likewise, a nun named Procula, lying ill with a prolonged sickness, feared the danger of death. Known to the bishop through her religious profession, she sent messengers entreating him to deign to visit her. He did not disdain to come to her, and, in his customary manner, asked Christ to deign to show the power of his aid upon the sick woman. This done, the woman was immediately restored to health and lived many years afterward.

But since the preceding matters have sufficiently shown that the saint of whom we speak possessed the grace of healing, and this will still be shown by many things that follow, [Col. 1556A] let us insert one instance by which it may be proved that he was not altogether lacking in the spirit of prophecy. For prophecy is divinely given knowledge to a human being not only of future things but also of present and past secrets.

A certain pseudo-abbot named Eracleus, for reasons otherwise unknown but certainly inflamed with the torches of envy and hatred against the bishop, could neither dare nor manage openly to attack him. He therefore prepared to destroy him by hidden plots. He enlisted men privy to his wickedness, gave them poison, and, sending them under the appearance of service, instructed them how to offer it to him to drink. When they arrived, the holy man knew their deceit through revelation of the Spirit. Yet concealing this for the moment, he ordered them to be received with care. After they had been refreshed, he summoned them and secretly rebuked them for the evil they had conceived [Col. 1556B]. He warned them, under threat of punishments, not to presume upon any such thing further; then he kissed each of them and dismissed them in peace. Covered with shame, they returned and told their patron the whole affair in order. Immediately he, terrified by a troubled conscience because the crime had been exposed, took flight and sheltered in hiding for some time at the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours. But there too, when report made him repeatedly hear himself called “traitor,” and when he excused himself on oath and added perjury to the crime of murder, divine vengeance did not permit him to live long. For struck on the forehead by an incurable ulcer, he wasted away, visibly condemned by a manifest punishment for his hidden crime 1500.

[Col. 1556C] Let us now return to the gifts of healing. But because they are not few in number, I shall briefly comprise very many of them, as if in short chapters, lest a detailed account of each in order should produce weariness in the hearer.

He freed a girl of Roman nobility, whom the fame of his powers had drawn to him over a difficult and long journey, from fevers by pouring the sacred Eucharist into her mouth. These fevers had afflicted her continuously for three years; he sent her back rejoicing to Rome with her companions.

> [Note: [Col. 1555D] Observe again the expression “pouring the sacred Eucharist,” which he used above.]

He immediately healed Niulfus, abbot of Saint Albinus, suffering from chiagra, a gouty disorder of the hand [*chiagrico*, or *chirurgio*], by giving him blessed bread (*eulogiae*) as an antidote.

He healed a certain man called Dodo, already worn out by a long-standing scabies and running with foul ulcers [Col. 1556D], likewise sending him blessed bread.

He restored Romulus, an archdeacon confined by illness for a full six years, through his prayer and power and through communion in the body of the Lord.

He restored sight, though he himself was absent and far away, to a blind woman in the district of Bordeaux through a certain abbot Martin. This abbot, travelling there on business of his monastery, had carried with him blessed bread received from the holy bishop for a blessing, as many others customarily did, like provisions for a journey. When he faithfully offered it to his hostess, she received sight at dawn after the interval of only one night.

[Col. 1557A] By making the sign of the cross, he wiped away the dimness that had long covered the eyes of a girl called Gaudomella, from the estate of Cabariacensis.

He freed another woman named Godolena from a similar night of blindness by anointing her with holy oil and making the sign of the life-giving cross.

He likewise freed another woman, called Goda, from the same affliction by the same remedy.

At about that time, by persistent prayer he cleansed a young man possessed by a demon, having kept him with himself throughout the whole Lent.

From the settlement called Corniliacus, a girl was brought to him who, though now in her fifteenth year, had as yet no use of hands or feet. Having anointed her limbs with consecrated oil, he immediately restored her.

[Col. 1557B] The Lord restored, through the merits of the bishop, a boy condemned from birth to the same disability, from the settlement called Jerziacus. His parents, warned by divine revelation, brought him to the bishop and easily obtained that, once healed, he should be dedicated to clerical offices.

A woman named Laeta was distressed by the misfortune of a withered right hand. Invoking God’s name, he also restored her through the power of the cross.

He restored sight to a certain blind man, Carrulfus, by praying over him and making the sign of the cross upon his eyes.

He healed a woman named Marcia, weakened by prolonged fevers, by anointing her with holy oil.

Two twin sisters of noble birth, one called Necteria and the other Theodechildis [Col. 1557C], both condemned to blindness, he made radiant with restored sight at one and the same moment, through the aid of prayer and the remedy of oil.

Having rapidly and briefly sketched these matters, we shall deal somewhat more fully, in their proper place, with the few that remain, lest the uniformity of narration itself produce the weariness from excessive length which we feared above.

Yet amid these so frequent and magnificent signs of miracles, the holy man subjected himself to such humility of mind and body that no entry was open within him to vanity or self-exaltation. Ever clothed in haircloth, worn out by fasting and vigils, he bore the appearance of a poor and suffering person. For, through compassion, he took upon himself the sins and [Col. 1557D] miseries of others and offered himself to the Lord for the sheep entrusted to him. Having no abiding city here, he sought with all his strength the city to come. Judging that he had made no progress so long as anything remained to be advanced, he always strove for new increases, forgetting what lay behind, as the Apostle says, and stretching himself forward toward what lay ahead (Philippians 3:13). Thus advancing daily and becoming stronger than himself, he enlarged, with ever-renewed efforts, his habitual generosity, humility, abstinence, and piety, mindful of Scripture’s saying: “When a person has finished, then he begins” (Ecclesiasticus 18:6). Although he allowed himself no time free from holy labour, he nevertheless spent the days of holy Lent [Col. 1558A] in the strictest abstinence. At that season he remained alone, shut up in his cell, intent upon prayers and tears, and daily, with the offering of the sacraments, sacrificed himself to Christ as a living victim. During these days he tasted nothing but bread and water, and even these he took in a small measured quantity. He was refreshed more by weeping than by food or drink. For to him, thirsting for God, the living fountain, his tears were bread by day and night; and, as one reads in another psalm, lest God should be angry at his prayer which he poured out for the people, 1502, he fed himself with the bread of tears and gave himself drink in tears by measure (Psalm 76:6).

Not considering it enough to do good only while alive [Col. 1558B], he planned to extend the merit of his holiness even beyond life. Having therefore considered the suitability of place and time, he began to build a monastery in the suburb of his city, following the example of his most blessed teacher and predecessor Licinius. There he would gather as many servants of God as he could, assigning them sufficient necessities from his possessions and revenues, so that, since he could not perpetuate the life of this body contrary to nature’s law, he might prolong through many ages a succession of his religious life that would live after him. Having built, as he desired, a church in honour of Saint Saturninus the martyr—the first bishop, that is, of the city of Toulouse—he not only richly endowed it with goods and estates, but also took pains to adorn it with the greatest beauty and elegance, within and without [Col. 1558C], so that he could fittingly say with the Prophet: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Psalm 25:8). For he covered the inner walls of the church in alternating spaces with mosaic and plaster, bearing painted images and flowers. Traces of this marvellous work still remain in it even after so many destructions down to our own times, from which one may clearly infer how great was the beauty of the new work, whose very antiquity appears wonderful. Outside, moreover, he surrounded the entire church with porticoes and columns; he built dwellings necessary for brothers living a common life, and others suitable for receiving guests and for restoring the sick, so that nothing could be thought lacking for the ministry of good works [Col. 1558D]. All things having been completed as he desired, he began to dwell in that place more familiarly, as better suited for private prayers and more fitting for works of mercy toward the poor. For he had resolved to end his life there and to rest there in body after death, as indeed happened. Therefore divine grace did not cease to make him illustrious there also, showing by miracles that both the life and the death of its saint were precious.

Finally, a certain Theudebaldus, a very powerful and distinguished person, came humbly to him, begging with tears and groans that he might deign to provide a remedy for his daughter, who was tormented by a demon. “For many,” he said, “have tried this very thing in vain; but I trust that for you [Col. 1559A], by the power of almighty God whose servant you are, nothing is impossible.” The saint excused his own insufficiency and replied that this should rather be sought from holier and more perfect persons. But when the man and those present persisted in their prayers, the most gentle bishop, overcome, placed holy relics upon the girl’s neck and made upon her, with consecrated oil, the sign of the holy cross. When this was done, the demon immediately fled; the girl regained a sound mind and departed healthy and joyful, while her parents gave thanks and praise.

Not long afterward, a woman named Prisca was offered to him by the faithful to be cured. Blind from her mother’s womb, she had passed thirty years beneath one night, living a life like death [Col. 1559B]. The blessed bishop, compassionating her misery, invoked God’s name over her and marked the places of her eyes with the power of the cross. With no delay intervening, light entered and opened the doors long shut, to the astonishment of all present. How great were the praises then sung by the people to the Lord, and with what acclamations they exalted the priest, we leave to the reader to judge. For what had once been wondrous, with Christ himself acting, now seemed far more wondrous when Christ acted through his disciple.

At about the same time, a young man named Vinciemalus was afflicted with so severe an illness that, because of its long duration, he was even deprived of sight. When he was presented to the bishop, and the latter poured holy oil into his pupils [Col. 1559C], he received sight and health at the same instant by a twofold power. A third miracle was also shown during that same short interval, confirming the two preceding ones. For, rejoicing in the health restored to him, he walked carelessly along a wall, fell headlong, and was believed to have been crushed throughout his body; yet he appeared so unharmed as though he had not fallen at all.

Another sick man was brought to him, who had lain ill with a continuous disease for five years. By the power of prayer and the anointing of consecrated oil, he healed him also and sent him rejoicing back to his own home.

Likewise, a certain Gidoaldus, exhausted by a prolonged illness of his whole body, and especially of his head, had become entirely deaf because the passages of hearing were blocked [Col. 1559D]. Presented before the blessed bishop, he begged him in a tearful voice to have mercy upon him. The bishop put his fingers into his ears and, not without holy prayers, instilled liquid holy oil. When this was done, matter burst forth with a foul smell, and the deaf man—the same sick man—received hearing and health.

A woman, not altogether unknown, from the settlement called Volosesisis, suffered from a most troublesome vertigo of the head. Whenever she attempted to bend down for any household work, her eyes were suddenly struck blind; darkness intervened and cut off her ability to perform it. When she had described the course of her affliction to the holy bishop, not without complaint and tears, after [Col. 1560A] he had invoked the Lord’s name over her in his customary manner, the woman no longer felt any distress from her former sickness.

Likewise, a woman named Alloicia, from the possession called Verchiacensis, begged the holy bishop—joining to her own the prayers of many—that he might restore her lost sight. He did not reject their prayers, but prayed for the blind woman; then, anointing her eyes with consecrated oil, he restored her sight without any delay.

Another woman, Caricundis by name, from the suburban settlement called Confluentum, was blind, mute, and paralysed, and wholly deprived of every hope that her health could ever be restored. The same holy man, by marvellous power, restored her to complete soundness of limbs and senses [Col. 1560B]. For he persisted in prayer for her for three days, as though assigning each day to one of her illnesses; at length, by effective prayer, he freed her altogether from every disability.

A courtier, as often happens, in military arrogance despised ecclesiastical rights. He boldly carried off a beast of burden which served the brothers’ needs and, as he supposed, subjected it instead to his own service. When this was reported to the blessed bishop, he preferred for the time being to overlook the matter rather than undergo the trouble of a lawsuit. But on the following night, as the presumptuous man gave himself to sleep, the bishop appeared to him in a vision, terrible with balls of fire and flashing flames, and uttered grave threats because he had sacrilegiously usurped church property. Startled by these terrors, the man called his servants with immense [Col. 1560C] cries and said that the bishop was tormenting him because of the crime he had committed. They were to go quickly and ask him with many prayers to come to him. This was done; for the kindly bishop did not disdain to come to the suppliant. The wretched man began to beg the bishop to remit the penalty for this sin, whose repentance he showed. He promised firmly that he would immediately return the stolen animal with restitution, and that henceforth he would honour Christ’s servants and ecclesiastical property. Thus the holy man prayed over him; and in that same hour he received back the beast of burden and restored health to the corrected offender.

Persevering in this grace of holiness and power of miracles, blessed Magnobodus reached old age and rejoiced that the spiritual fruits of the seeds [Col. 1560D] he had sown among the people entrusted to him had sprung up abundantly. Already he was seen as a victor in the arena and confidently awaited the crown of righteousness laid up for him by the supreme emperor and just judge. Meanwhile, when the Lord knocked at the door of his body through the distress of sickness, the wakeful and most diligent servant understood that the day of his departure was near. Ready therefore immediately to open to the one knocking, he summoned his sons and brothers, whom he had nurtured in Christian religion, and announced that the desirable time of his dissolution had come. Then immense grief seized them all, and the tearful cry of those lamenting their bereavement sounded from every side. But he comforted them with many words and urged each and all [Col. 1561A] to persevere in faith in Christ and in good works, and above all to preserve among themselves the bonds of peace:

> “For in holy love,” he said, “consists the whole of the divine law and the sum of all commandments. The Lord Christ, teacher and master of all, gave this as his final and greatest commandment to his disciples, declaring that by it, as by a special mark, his own should be distinguished and recognized from strangers. Therefore I too, little children, as I am about to speak my final farewell to you, impress and commend love upon your hearts above all things. In it and through it, living soberly, justly, and piously until the end, may you deserve to be separated by the supreme shepherd and just judge from the unhappy goats and placed among the most blessed sheep at the right hand of glory.”

After saying these and similar things, he raised his hands toward God and, lifting his eyes and mind to heaven, yielded his spirit to God amid the words of holy prayer and amid the hands of his grieving disciples, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November [16 October]. He was honourably buried amid a great multitude of people gathering from every quarter, in the chapel beside the basilica of Saint Saturninus the martyr, which, as was said above, he himself had built, there to rise unto glory among the most illustrious confessors. The Lord made his funeral illustrious by a manifest miracle, so that it might be clear to all that he now lived most fully after his departure and could now much more aid the needs of petitioners before God, since his spirit, free, could no longer be hindered by the burden of flesh. For while the venerable funeral procession was being conducted, two prisoners [Col. 1561C], one called Gualdo and the other Bodecarius, long afflicted by the squalor of prison, were being dragged publicly in fetters and chains under guard in order to collect [Col. 1562A] brushwood. When they approached the saint’s bier, the bonds of their chains loosened of themselves, and they suddenly appeared free before the guards. When this came to the knowledge of the city’s leading men, they were granted freedom by the common decree of all. For the honour of God and in memory of the most holy confessor, they returned to the district of Le Mans from which they had been captured, not keeping silent about the Lord’s mercy shown to them through the merits of the holy confessor. Thereafter honour and fitting reverence increased around the saint’s tomb, so that those who come even from distant regions obtain, for the various needs of their desires, the result they seek, through the favour of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

> [Col. 1562B] [Note: On reading this conclusion, we were surprised to find it exactly the same, and expressed in precisely the same words, as that which we had read and noted at the end of the immediately preceding Life of Saint Licinius. Nothing else occurs to us except that this very devout and pious man seems to have omitted no opportunity of securing for himself, whether living or dead, the suffrages of the Church. By them he considered that his pious labours for the saints’ glory were well recompensed, if he obtained the reward of spiritual work as beneficial to himself for eternal salvation. Therefore, the suffrage which, while archdeacon of Angers, he had secured for himself from the canons of Saint Maurice of Angers for the Life of Saint Licinius, he boasts in this very conclusion that, while bishop of Rennes, he obtained from the canons of the collegiate church of Saint Magnobodus, under the same conditions and in precisely the same words, by the same design of piety. How firm a faith Marbodus seems to require from the devout reader in this Life of Saint Magnobodus is evident from the utmost diligence with which he took care to report most exactly even the names of common persons in whose favour God worked so many and such great miracles through Saint Magnobodus, as also the names of individual, though less well-known, places where they occurred.]

I, Marbodus, bishop of Rennes, have written the Life of the blessed Bishop Magnobodus at the request of the canons of that same church. In return for my labour they have promised and granted me a share and communion in whatever prayers and good works shall at any time be done in this church. Throughout my life, every day, they shall say one collect for me in the morning Mass: “O God, who justifies the ungodly.” After my death, they shall perform for me the entire office said in prayers and Masses for one of the canons, and every year shall observe the commemoration of my anniversary as for one canon. Moreover, every day, except feast days, until the end of the age, after Prime, when they go to chapter, they shall sing “Out of the depths,” with the beginning, “Eternal rest,” and [Col. 1562C] the collect, “Absolve, O Lord.” In this agreement between me and the canons, may my lord Saint Magnobodus be mediator, witness, and guarantor. Amen.

[Col. 1563]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT GUALTERIUS OR GAUTERIUS, ABBOT AND CANON OF ESTERP, IN THE DIOCESE OF LIMOGES IN GAUL. BY MARBODUS, ARCHDEACON OF ANGERS, LATER BISHOP OF RENNES IN ARMORICAN BRITTANY.

(*Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, May, vol. II, 11 May, p. 701.)

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 1563] 1. Geoffrey, monk of the monastery of Saint Martial at Limoges and prior of the monastery of Vigeois, in book I, chapter 12 of his *Chronicle*, describes the transfer of the English kingdom to William the Conqueror in the year 1067, and adds that in that century three men illustrious in holiness flourished. The first named is Saint Odilo of Cluny, who died in 1049 and whose Acts we gave on the Kalends of January [1 January]. Then follows “Gauterius of Esterp, for whom, while he was ill during the winter, divine mercy prepared desired strawberries contrary to the season.” A third is afterward added: “Robert, who built La Chaise-Dieu,” whose Acts we illustrated on 24 April. The same Geoffrey, in chapter 15, discusses the saints more eminent in the bishopric of Limoges, where among other relevant matters he reports:

> “The people of Esterp honour Gauterius, who in recent times appeared glorious in deeds and miracles”—

that is, in the period after the death of Saint Gualterius, when Geoffrey the writer flourished.

Other matters concerning Saint Gualterius are read in the *Chronicle of Saint Maxentius*, or Malleacensis. First, concerning his death, it records:

> “In the year 1070, Lord Gauterius, abbot and canon of the Church of Saint Peter at Esterp, fell asleep in eternal peace, on the fifth day before the Ides of May [11 May].”

Then, for the year 1091, it has:

> “In the same year the church of Saint Peter at Esterp was blessed, and the feast of Blessed Gauterius was established to be celebrated on the anniversary of his death.”

In the *Life of Blessed Israel*, canon of Le Dorat in La Marche, published by Philippe Labbe among the Lives of Saints relating to Aquitaine, these words occur:

> “A disciple of this most holy man was Saint Gauterius, a man abounding in works of piety and mercy. While he was a canon of the Church of Le Dorat, he was appointed by God abbot of Esterp.”

Blessed Israel died “on the second day before the Kalends of January [31 December], in the year of the Lord 1014.”

2. From what has been related thus far, the time of his life and death is first made clear. He appears to have been born about the year 990, and to have reached the age of twenty-four around the death of Blessed Israel. He then lived for some time longer in the said Church of Le Dorat, flourished afterward in the college or monastery of Esterp, and was there made abbot, rector, or provost in 1034. In that office he lived thirty-eight years; and at last, having been blind for seven years, he died in the year of Christ 1070, an old man full of days and merits, about eighty years of age.

Second, it is established from the *Chronicle of Saint Maxentius* that Saint Gualterius died “on the fifth day before the Ides of May,” and that his feast of departure is celebrated on the same day. The Sammarthani confirm this from the Chronicle of Limoges in volume IV of *Gallia Christiana*, p. 850, where they treat of the monastery of Esterp, situated in the diocese and territory of Limoges. John Collinus likewise indicated this day of veneration to us in the catalogue he submitted. In the supplement to the Gallican Martyrology, Saussaye seems to have had very scant information about this saint, since on the third day before the Ides of May [13 May] he has only:

> “In Aquitaine, Saint Galtherus, abbot.”

Furthermore, “Saint Galtherus, abbot of Esterp in the diocese of Limoges, a man of outstanding holiness,” is entered under 13 April in a manuscript calendar of the Order of Saint Benedict preserved among the Premonstratensians at the monastery of Saint Michael in Antwerp. But this calendar is neither ancient nor compiled with great judgment and learning.

Gabriel Pennotto, in his *History of the Order of Clerics Regular*, book II, chapter 23, no. 14, makes two monasteries from one alone when he states that “in the bishopric of Limoges there are monasteries of canons: the first of Saint Galterius, or of Stupeno; the second, Saint Peter’s of Esterp.” They are one and the same. Claudius Robertus and the Sammarthani cited above likewise state that it is still an abbey of the Order of Saint Augustine: commonly called l’Esterp, in the Limousin Marche, six leagues from Le Dorat and eight from Limoges. There is also, within the boundaries of the diocese of Bourges, above the River Creuse near Argenton, a parish and town bearing Saint Gualterius’s name, where I believe he is honoured as patron.

3. These are the items which, so far, we have found published concerning this saint; to them we add another treasure, hitherto hidden. We possess a parchment codex containing several Lives of saints composed by Marbod, archdeacon of Angers—therefore before the year 1096, when he was made bishop of Rennes—and they are listed in this order: the Life of St Florentius the martyr, to be given on 22 September; that of St Licinius, bishop of Angers, illustrated on 13 February; that of St Magnobodus, likewise bishop of Angers, to be published on 16 October; that of St Gualterius of Stirps, which we now give; that of St Robert, abbot of Chaise-Dieu, printed on 24 April; the Passion of Saints Felix and Adauctus, to be given on 30 August; and then various poems by the same author are added, some of which are mentioned by Sigebert in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 158. This codex is very ancient, so that it seems either to have been carefully written in Marbod’s own time, perhaps under his supervision, or at least not long after his death. In the Prologue he cites “the earlier writer of the Life of St Gualterius,” from whom he selects “those things which seemed to him relevant to the dignity of the subject”; just as he polished the already published Lives of St Licinius and St Robert. Perhaps someone will obtain that earlier Life and, should it seem worthwhile, publish it. In this work he is called Gualterius; by others, Gauterius, Galterus, and Galterius.

## THE LIFE BEGINS

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1565A]

1. I have undertaken to write the life of blessed Gualterius, not indeed through confidence in my ability, which is slight, or in my merits, which are none; but rather from regard for obedience and charity: so that I may neither fail the request of devout brethren nor withhold service from the benefit of many. And in this I do not doubt, with Christ’s help, that I too shall have a share in the reward, if from my labour both honour comes to God and some benefit to readers. For it cannot be that no one is edified by frequent hearing of good things; and it may happen that, through this account, fruits of holy imitation may reach many in generations present or future. Indeed, the bosom of brotherly love ought to extend itself in this too: that we should wish to benefit strangers, and wish to benefit those not yet born. With this intention, therefore, I have accepted the task offered to me. To accomplish it I need the help of the prayers of this same saint, so that I may be able to set forth what must be said briefly and clearly, yet not altogether without elegance.

For if eloquence in speaking commonly wins the minds of hearers even in invented or trifling matters, much more must care be taken in matters true and necessary, lest the unworthiness of faulty speech—God forbid!—diminish the dignity of the cause undertaken. Who would strive to please by rusticity of expression? I shall therefore endeavour, as far as I can, to maintain this mean in speaking: that the discourse may appear neither low nor excessively laboured, since each extreme gives equal offence. Moreover, it must not be superfluous or obscure: the former commonly produces weariness, the latter hatred. [Col. 1565B–C]

But I wish to obtain from readers, through their prayers, this indulgence: that they approach this work in a kindly spirit—that is, not as slanderers or hunters after words, but rather as defenders of truth and friendly interpreters of language. And if, through either inexperience or weakness, I happen to fulfil my promises less adequately, let them not find it difficult to pardon me; for human condition excuses my weakness, and the aforesaid devotion to obedience excuses my inexperience.

Nor have I judged that everything found in the earlier writer of this Life should be included, but only those matters which seemed relevant to the dignity of the subject. Whoever occupies himself with worthless little burdens appears to do so through want of better things, especially when even some good things must be passed over where there is an abundance of better choices. Some matters, however, I shall explain more briefly and others more fully, according as each seems to carry more or less weight. Let no one suppose that in the latter case I act contrary to the principle of brevity; for the law of brevity excludes not necessary things, but only idle ones. If this is sufficient, let us hasten to the narrative. [Col. 1565C–1566A]

## CHAPTER I. Birth; cultivation of virtues and learning; removal to Stirps

2. Gualterius, then, an Aquitanian by nation and of senatorial lineage, was born to honourable parents: his father Raymond and his mother Gualburga. Her maternal great-grandfather, descended from Frankish nobility, had governed three not insignificant cities of Aquitaine. She is said to have practised such abstinence that, though she occupied the married estate, she seemed to differ from a purpose of holy widowhood only in outward dress. She took the expenditures, adornments, and luxuries of matrons and applied them rather to the cultivation of the inner person, wisely considering that temporal glory brings no profit to those who perish. Therefore, from temporal goods she reserved for herself only what nature required, and more gladly spent all the rest for the use of the poor.

Whenever she was drawn to render the marital due—solely, that is, through desire for offspring—she expiated the offence done to her inborn delight by tears and prayers immediately following. Hence it came about that, visited by God through an angel in sleep, she conceived, according to the desire of her heart, an heir not so much of possessions as of holiness. That the same angel was appointed to guard him from his mother’s very womb was afterwards made clear by an evident miracle, which it does not seem inappropriate briefly to recount. [Col. 1566A–C]

3. For while her husband was escorting her with a mounted company to the place which she had selected as suitable for giving birth, both the length of the journey and the slowness of their progress had already wrapped the travellers in night’s darkness. The horse upon which the matron sat, following at a lively pace the road it knew, was the first to mount the bridge over the river Taurion.

> [Note: [Col. 1565D] The Taurion is a small stream rising in Limousin and joining the Vienne—still itself no great river there—one and a half leagues above the city of Limoges. Maps show it crossed by four bridges. Let those acquainted with the region determine where it can so spread into a pool as to require a very long bridge such as is described here.]

Having crossed some portion of the very long bridge, it reached an unknown precipice, recently produced where the swift whirlpool of the flooded river had torn apart and scattered the planks. Wonderful to relate: it crossed with such ease that the unsuspecting mind of the pregnant woman suffered not even the least distress from fear. The inhabitants of the place had joined the sections after a plank half a foot wide had broken; but the crossing, passable to no four-footed animal, admitted only pedestrians, and those not without caution and fear of danger. The retinue, following shortly afterward, examined everything, recognized the peril, and, believing their lady swallowed up, cried aloud with mournful wailing. But when she made known by answering cries that she was safe, they were filled at once with joy and amazement. Then, driving their unburdened horses into the deep water, they themselves barely crawled across by the narrow passage and brought the horses over with difficulty by swimming. [Col. 1566C–1567A]

4. Thus this sign, commending beforehand the birth of the holy child, brought joy to many and a foretoken of some great good to come. If anyone should prefer to ascribe it to the merit of the pregnant woman, we nevertheless believe that the grace of the enclosed pledge was thereby commended also: for those whose danger would have been common also share in the miracle of deliverance. Yet the cause appears greater in the latter, since nothing of this kind had happened to the mother before conception. And the progress of his later life, because it surpassed even his mother, seems to claim the preceding miracle for himself.

For, to begin from his earliest years, he spent childhood itself and the years of youth in such a manner that even then he could serve as an example to the old. When, after the tender upbringing of infancy, he had been sent, as most children of noble birth are accustomed, to the study of letters, the singular quickness of his intelligence and the refined sweetness of his character could not remain concealed. Easily grasping obscure meanings, he entrusted them to a tenacious memory; and, not content with the authority of the teacher alone, he consulted reason’s judgment about every point. Before long, exceeding the measure both of his elementary instruction and of his age, he sought out many similar matters from the example of his fellow students; so that, if I may put it thus, he learned more than he was taught. [Col. 1567B–C]

Nor, as often happens, did he ever need to be restrained by the rod, since his spontaneous love of learning increased his zeal for study all the more. Play or childish trifling did not draw him away from devoting himself to books or writing tablets. Meanwhile, under the profession of a pupil, he exercised a certain mastery of conduct, thinking it exceedingly shameful to learn rules of speech while remaining ignorant of rules of life far more useful. He therefore avoided shameful things not only in deeds but also in words, and readily uttered nothing in which he did not perceive some usefulness. He had already learned to abhor anger and envy, and pride, the mother of both; and he denied both ear and tongue even to the slightest detraction against anyone. He submitted himself to inferiors in both birth and learning, and won the affection even of all who rivalled him. It was already sufficiently clear to all that such conduct in a child was ordered not by nature but by grace.

Hervaeus of Tours perceived this—

> [Note: [Col. 1567D] This seems to be Hervaeus, treasurer of St Martin’s, who rebuilt the church of St Martin which St Perpetuus had built and which had been burned in 903, as we stated in the Life of St Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, 8 April, no. 4.]

—whose reputation for holiness was then flourishing. As he happened to pass through the place, he told those present what potential for imitable perfection lay hidden already in that little age.
