For, to infer greater things from the smallest, the boy concealed himself beneath the bench against which Hervaeus had leaned in order to pray, laudably stealing, as it were, the form of holy prayer from the mouth of so great a man. But, as was later learned from the saint’s own report, without any sound of words that holy man prayed much more effectively by tears and groans—a form which we have learned that Gualterius later followed. In this intention of the little child, therefore, there already appears something not to be lightly esteemed: while the unrestrainedness of the other boys made use of the venerable guest as an occasion for play, he alone, with mature judgment, did not let even the brief presence of a religious man pass him by without benefit. [Col. 1567D–1568A]

The Church of Scotorensis rejoiced in so happy a foster-child, and anticipated that the one it had undertaken to educate would become an excellent teacher for itself.

> [Note: [Col. 1567D] This seems to be called the Church of Dorat in the Life of Blessed Israel cited above, where he is said to have been its disciple and a canon of Dorat. Geographic maps mark the place Dorat, not far from the right bank of the Vartampe, where it receives the river Seva. Perhaps the author, from a certain affectation of antiquity, adopted an obsolete name from I know not where.]

5. Having passed his childhood in this pursuit, and entered the more vigorous years of youth, he began to plan greater exercises of virtue. Nor, as most people do, did he surrender an age inclined toward worse things to idleness or luxury. Rather, he armed limbs now fit for the labours of Christian warfare with the weapons of righteousness, intending to fight bravely against spiritual wickedness. And lest some stealthy attack of the cunning enemy harm him, he joined prudence to courage; by prudence he would avoid not merely unlawful deeds but would utterly cut off from himself every cause and occasion of sin, wisely understanding that recruits in the spiritual camp should seek a safer rather than a more glorious victory.

For it is one thing to devote oneself to life, another to glory. Although it is noble, when sin is at hand, to avoid it and refuse to commit it when one can, it is nevertheless safer to flee the very power of sinning. This caution has never deceived anyone; in that experiment, however, very many have fallen. By this course, therefore, he easily overcame the most evil shoots of vices. He extinguished the ardour of lust—which especially endangers youth, when bodily impulses previously unexperienced fix the stings of alluring suggestion in unsuspecting minds—by the chastening of fasts, persistence in prayer, and love of perpetual chastity; he quenched it, so to speak, in its very conception, before it could arise. Blessed indeed is he who held and dashed the little ones of iniquity against the rock. [Col. 1568B–C]

The desire for money and the filth of disgraceful avarice—a vice from which scarcely any is more alien to human dignity—he not only never deigned to admit into himself, but also wholly uprooted or crushed in others by the example of his own generosity. He displayed pure love toward all the brethren with whom he lived and regarded nothing belonging to them as alien from himself. He strove to imitate each person’s distinctive virtues, gathering in himself, as into one storehouse, the good qualities of all. And he made progress not only from the virtues of others but, remarkable though it may seem, even from their vices: the former he set before himself for imitation, the latter for caution. [Col. 1568C–D]

6. Those driven by the goads of impatience and uncontrolled in a spirit of rage he either calmed by tranquillity of mind and sweetness of speech or endured. Thus it happened that, when he sought gently to appease the abbot of the place—

> [Note: [Col. 1569D] That is, some successor of the aforementioned Blessed Israel.]

—who, with beastlike savagery, raged too excessively against the brethren, he instead inflamed him further. The too-obstinate fury of the wretched old man construed the simple correction of the holy young man as contempt for himself; he did not cease to lay snares for him and sought vengeance upon an innocent man as though upon a rebel.

Thinking that he must yield to the times, Gualterius left the place and moved to the fortress called Confluentium, where the nobility of his family was then especially prominent.

> [Note: [Col. 1569D] There is a very accurate map of the government of Orléans. At the confluence of a certain stream with the Vienne it marks a place popularly called Confoulens, from the Latin name Confluentium, only one league west of the abbey of Stirps.]

Living there for a time, he quickly became known not only to household members and townspeople, but also to many neighbours, by the holiness of his life and his pre-eminence in learning. Therefore the clergy of the Church of Stirps, near the aforesaid fortress and owed to him by divine providence, delighted by his frequent conversation, repeatedly begged him to enter the fellowship of their community. They cherished the hope that, should anything happen to their abbot by the lot of humanity, they would unanimously ask for him as their father and teacher. Having been enrolled in their fellowship, he behaved toward every individual with such discernment that, although all loved him with a common love, each considered that he had received the greatest benefit from him. [Col. 1569A–B]

## CHAPTER II. Pilgrimage to Jerusalem; miracles performed on the journey

[Col. 1569C]

7. Meanwhile, as he grew older and virtues followed one another in increasing measure, although he regarded himself, even among his own people, as a stranger and pilgrim—as did all the ancient Fathers—he nevertheless resolved, led by longing for the holy places, to make a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. He wished to fulfil bodily what he had often sung spiritually concerning Christ: “We shall worship in the place where his feet stood” (Psalm 131:7). At the same time, since the circumstances of the age denied him, for faith in Christ, suffering and death at the hand of an executioner, he sought through the necessities of the journey, amid tribulations and hardships, to find for himself a kind of martyrdom. Thus it came about that he who had resolved to suffer graver things for the Lord deserved greater grace from the Lord.

No small or few miracles testify to this, which Christ displayed for him or through him on this pilgrimage. We shall recount some of them, from which the rest may be judged. While he was sailing with his fellow travellers over the Adriatic Gulf, where passage lies open for those bound for Jerusalem, so great a storm suddenly arose that for three continuous days they were tossed by winds and waves in despair of life. But after the urgency of prayer had driven away the imminent danger, they barely gained the shore; scattered in every direction, they sought the necessities of whatever food they could find, for they had been exhausted by prolonged fear of death, worn down by the violence of the storm, and wasted also by long hunger. [Col. 1569C–1570A]

Yet the region was so desolate and the sands so barren that neither human labour nor nature’s fertility produced anything edible in those places. When the efforts of the others had failed and all were again terrified by the storm of hunger, the constancy of his faith alone received a miraculous answer. For behold: a bird of unknown appearance glided in gentle flight to the place where the saint was standing alone and laid an enormous fish at his feet. Unable to lift it by himself, he enlisted one companion standing nearer him and, giving thanks to the Lord, carried this provision of divine bounty to the ship. His companions marvelled at the fish’s size; but, when they learned what had happened, the greatness of this unusual order struck them with still greater astonishment. For truly, by wondrous merits and contrary to custom, fresh spoil from the sea had rained from heaven upon a hungry man through a bird.

But he who once, for those under the Law, wondrously rained down a bird, now more wondrously rained down a fish for his servant under grace. It seems less strange for a bird than for a fish to fall from the air. Those present, astonished at the sight of so great a power and judging the merits of this remarkable man from the remarkable event, bent their knees to the ground and worshipped. Him whom until then they had regarded as holy they now regarded as illustrious and great; nor without reason did they compare him to the ancient Fathers, in whom they saw the likeness of an ancient miracle shining forth. The Lord once fed Elijah through a raven; now he fed both this man and his companions through a bird in a repeated example. And though this man is far inferior to Elijah, in this one deed the likeness of each answers to the other. [Col. 1570A–C]

8. Again, on another occasion, while they were walking through waterless plains and, worn out both by the heat of day and the labour of the journey, suffering the unbearable distress of thirst, the holy man, secure about his own danger, began to fear more for the safety of his companions. At once, after pouring forth prayer with tears and turning to the Lord in complete confidence, he struck the earth with the staff he held. Immediately there followed wholesome, clear waters, sufficient not only to refresh the thirsty but also to bubble forth continuously as the stream of a new spring. For, lest forgetfulness erase the memory of the deed, those who have seen it report that the name of Gualterius was given to that spring and remains to this day.

O how great is the power of faith, against which not even nature’s impossibility can prevail! If we consider the ancient miracle performed through Moses in the wilderness, then—while preserving the majesty of the mystery—the comparison of similar things may seem not far unequal. Certainly, in different times and under two dissimilar Testaments, the same Lord of both works similar things. Let water be compared with water, staff with rod, rock with dry ground; let the thirsty answer to the thirsty, stroke be joined to stroke, and the likeness of causes and places correspond mutually. [Col. 1570C–1571A]

9. Not many days later, when by chance the companions were eating meat on a Friday contrary to custom—for the demands of their daily labour had made them disregard the distinction of days—he suddenly came upon them and rebuked their negligence: why, occupied solely with external necessities, had they not observed reverence for the holy day? But seeing them all ashamed and declaring their heartfelt repentance through tears, he was moved by brotherly compassion.

“Do not be too deeply distressed,” he said, “for what you did unknowingly is pardonable. The merciful Lord has provided for your ignorance, since the present feast excuses whatever fault there was. For know that today the feast of the most blessed confessor Martin is celebrated. Therefore, in confidence of holy charity, I urge you to partake fearlessly of the meal you have begun.”

Having said this, he himself tasted the meat set before them, so that the authority of his own act might strengthen their fear. All the others therefore obeyed without hesitation; only one person resisted, not so much from love of religion as from the obstinacy of superstition, and could by no reasoning be brought to agree. But the consequence of his rebellion was marked so that all might clearly see how great charity was. That very day he lost all the gold that he carried with him for provisions. Clearly this was done by the just judgment of God: he alone had rejected the food of charity, and alone was deprived of the price of necessary sustenance.

But after the warning of this loss had corrected him, he acknowledged his fault and confessed that he had sinned. The holy man consoled his sorrow with gentle words and told him to continue his journey safely with his companions, promising that he would soon restore all that he had lost. Finally, Gualterius alone retraced the journey for some distance and, without delay, found the money by God’s will and returned it to its owner. [Col. 1571A–C]

10. It also pleases me to recount a fourth miracle, which does not seem much inferior to those already mentioned. When, as night came on, the travellers had decided to make their resting-place in sand beside the sea, the sky was suddenly disturbed and a storm of clouds raged, so that even had they been sheltered in houses, tiles could scarcely have repelled the assault of the falling rain. This most patient man, while each of the others looked after himself as he could, remained in the place where he had stayed and protected himself with his accustomed shield of prayer. At his request, a leaf of unheard-of size and unknown kind was sent from heaven—whether of a plant, a tree, or perhaps of neither, was uncertain. To the astonishment of all, he not only defended himself from the rain but also prepared for himself from it a very soft bed.

Nor could there be any suspicion of a chance occurrence in so unprecedented a divine gift, especially since the barrenness of that sandy soil supplied nourishment not even to small plants or trees. These and other deeds, after those who had seen them returned and made them known, soon made the name of the most holy man famous throughout all Aquitaine. [Col. 1571C–D]

## CHAPTER III. Governance of Stirps and remaining deeds, with his holy death

[Col. 1572A]

11. At about the same time, the ruler of the Church of Stirps had died. Therefore its clergy and the prince of the region, Amardus, a man of outstanding virtue, repeatedly begged Gualterius to undertake the care of that church. But as he stubbornly resisted and they nevertheless did not cease their entreaties, he fixed a day on which he would answer them after deliberation, lest he dismiss them utterly disappointed.

On the appointed day, as he returned intending humbly to excuse himself, some clergy and soldiers travelling with him disagreed, because they preferred that he consent. Suddenly a little bird, pursued by a bird of prey called a sparrowhawk (*nisus*), fled to him in order to escape death. He gladly took it up and freed it from imminent danger. Then they seized upon the occasion and pressed him more forcefully, affirming that God had manifestly judged in favour of their view: by this sign, they said, it was openly proved that he ought not to fail those in danger. Thus, little short of being compelled by the clergy of Stirps and the aforementioned prince, he accepted the requested care, lest he seem to oppose the divine will, to the joy of all.

> [Note: [Col. 1571D] In the year 1038, as is clear from the date of his death and the years of his governance.]

12. Once placed in office, what manner of man he showed himself can scarcely be described by anyone in words. For his pre-eminence was not turned, as commonly happens to some, into arrogance; nor did he claim for himself anything more or better in clothing or food because of his rank. Indeed, he was now much more sparing and modest: the greater liberty he had acquired, the less he understood himself to be permitted, because, among those set in high position, virtues profit more people, but vices harm more people.

“Not therefore as lording it over the clergy,” but, according to the Apostle, “becoming from the heart an example to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3), he urged his subjects to virtuous conduct more by love and kindness than by terror or punishments. He judged voluntary devotion more pleasing to the Lord than compelled servitude: the former proceeds from free charity, whereas the latter is extorted by servile fear. Yet zeal was not lacking when needed, nor fitting severity toward rebels. But he employed these at last and only from necessity, as one uses iron and fire, lest some neglected part of corruption spread more widely and infect sound parts.

What human perversity, indeed, would serve the Lord unwillingly under so great a leader, whose teaching dispelled ignorance, whose life provided an example, and whose prayer furnished assistance? These three things the best of fathers provided for the flock entrusted to him: that, instructed by preaching, stirred by example, and aided by prayer, they might know, will, and be able to fight against the ancient enemy. [Col. 1572B–D]

Moreover, he watched over each person with such attentiveness that he applied an appropriate care to everyone according to each one’s nature, age, or condition—like an excellent physician who knows that what helps one person harms another, and that what heals this person may endanger that one. Thus he provided what was fitting for all and each; he became all things to all, and, so to speak, made as many versions of himself as he showed different responses to different persons. He distinguished vice from nature with such subtlety, and separated one from the other in the same individual so well, that by sparing the latter he did not foster the former, nor by pursuing the former did he crush the latter. He overlooked the need of no one, even the lowliest; he was absent from none who asked assistance. Through compassion he made all others’ misfortunes his own; through charity he counted the prosperity of all among his own gains. [Col. 1573A]

13. Amid these things, a most resolute practitioner of abstinence and most lavish distributor of alms, he refreshed the hungry while fasting, clothed the naked while cold, provided lodgings for those without shelter, and gave wages to hired workers. Kind toward all others, he was severe toward himself alone; the service he expended upon all others, he denied to himself alone. Indeed, as though he had not long since been a great conqueror of the body, he continually wore down his flesh with haircloth. And, what seems more unusual, rising at the dead of night, he exposed his stripped body in church to blows—not because any rebellion of his afflicted flesh was felt, but lest any might become capable of being felt. In order that this might be done secretly and frequently, he hired for payment a torturer faithful to him.

Nor did he supply only bodily necessities to the needy, as has been said; but, much more concerned for the salvation of souls, he laboured to win to the Lord as many as he could. The just man rebuked sinners with mercy and received penitents with forgiveness. For, in accordance with the merit of his holiness, he had received from Victor, bishop of the Roman See—

> [Note: [Col. 1573D] This is Victor II, who sat from the year 1054 to the year 1057.]

—the authority also to judge crimes and, at his own discretion, to close or open the Church to penitents.

> [Note: [Col. 1573D–1574D] This authority to absolve excommunicated persons or excommunicate the obstinate seems to have been extraordinary and entirely personal. Not only did it not pass to successors, but a question was raised concerning its ordinary exercise, as Ivo of Chartres mentions in Letter 60, addressed to Gualterius, provost of the Church of Stirps. He complained bitterly that the bishop of Limoges had forbidden all regular clerics both the governance of parishes and the hearing of penitents’ confessions. Ivo wrote this when already bishop of Chartres, having been consecrated by Urban in 1091—that is, twenty-one years after the death of St Gualterius, who, on account of the aforementioned Gualterius, is incorrectly written Galterus and Galterius.]

He used this authority for the salvation of many. By it he raised very many who already despaired under the heavy burden of their crimes, imposing a bearable penance and lifting them, as though dead, from tombs. Others, sluggish through negligence and presuming too greatly upon forgiveness, he terrified by the same authority as persons to be separated, and awakened them as sleepers from sleep.

He was the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord had appointed over his household: faithful indeed, because he sought not his own gain but his Lord’s; he considered not his own praise but his Lord’s honour. Faithful indeed, because he did not hide the money of the Lord’s truth but freely preached the Lord’s commandments to all; and, from fear of punishment or love of reward, he did not flatter any powerful or wealthy person in that person’s iniquities. Moreover, an unconquered defender of the Catholic faith, by the authority of the Spirit speaking within him he quickly imposed silence on heretics and Jews. He was prudent also because in teaching he considered not only the person but also time and place. [Col. 1573B–1574A]

14. His great long-suffering and constancy amid adversity are proved by hostile devastation and the conflagrations of war. Through the dissension of princes, not only was the church itself destroyed by sacrilegious burning, but a great part of the people, together with almost the entire clergy, was consumed in the same fire. For the prince of the land, named Gordianus, despite the resistance and remonstrance of the blessed man, had wickedly fortified the very precincts of the church and, having posted a garrison of armed men, devastated neighbouring districts with frequent raids. This was why a place undeserving of punishment was burned by enemies on account of the deserving wicked.

But even then the aforementioned prince did not abandon his evil purpose. He rebuilt the fortifications and practised his former sacrileges among what had once been sacred walls. At last, however, divine terrors drove him out through dreadful visions of the night. He summoned the saint, who was hiding not far away with the few disciples who had survived the fire and was awaiting divine mercy; the prince swore that he would undertake nothing of the kind thereafter and restored the cleansed walls to the blessed man.

Gualterius transformed the misery of the calamity suffered not into a cause of despair but into an occasion for proving merit. He zealously undertook the work of restoration, although certain bishops opposed him, maintaining that a place polluted by blood and slaughter could no longer be consecrated. At last the sound judgment of the blessed man prevailed, approved not only by a synodal decree of bishops but also confirmed by apostolic letters. He therefore vigorously completed the work begun, invited the bishops of neighbouring cities, and celebrated the feast of dedication with the highest splendour. Then, having substituted clergy for those who had been destroyed, he increased the former state of the church both in number and merit, taking from tribulation material for virtue. Thus the misfortune that had occurred to the greater glory of the place was deservedly considered fortunate. [Col. 1574A–C]

15. Proven in adversity and prosperity—in the latter cautious and humble, in the former strong and steadfast—he showed himself worthy of imitation in both by the merit of holiness. He was a cedar of Lebanon, firmly fixed by roots. He was a house of the Lord, well founded upon solid rock. The flood came, the wind struck, and it remained unmoved. In this course, with the Lord’s help, he governed the Church entrusted to him for thirty-eight years, so that no changing course of events delayed him, but he always added better things to good things and best things to better.

Neither the weakness of old age nor the affliction of blindness, by which his patience was tested for seven years before his death, prevented him from observing the disciplines of his former abstinence. Nor did the long course of prosperity or the frequent display of signs, by which he shone broadly and long in the world, tempt his mind with any vanity. Rather, always humbler amid miracles and more fearful amid prosperity, he crushed the snares of the enemy with Christ as his guide. [Col. 1574D–1575A]

16. I have touched upon some of his outward miracles and deliberately pass over others: the possessed woman whom he cleansed at Vézelay in the church of Mary Magdalene, before the people, on holy Easter Day;

> [Note: [Col. 1575C–1576C] Verzelliacum, otherwise Vezeliacum, in Burgundy. How Odo, the first abbot of that place, is said to have brought there from the territory of Aix the body of the saint, taken by pious theft, will be related on her feast-day, 22 July, under the year 849.]

and likewise another noble and devout matron whose death, though far away, he learned by revelation. I pass over these, lest I seem to have placed the whole substance of his sanctity in such things.

But the miracles he worked spiritually must neither be passed over, because they are most worthy, nor can they be explained, because they are innumerable. For if, just as there are diseases in the body, so vices are known to exist in the soul, then he who corrected innumerable vicious persons certainly drove away innumerable diseases. And if a more dangerous illness makes the cure more glorious, then the healing of vices deserves so much greater praise as the danger to the soul is known to be graver than that to the body.

Therefore the holy father especially strove to banish spiritual illnesses and especially bestowed spiritual healings: humility on the proud; chastity on the wanton; thrift on the prodigal; generosity on the avaricious; gentleness on the wrathful; abstinence on the luxurious; and he restored charity to the envious. But why should we delay over each individual case? Let the person who can number misfortunes enumerate the remedies; or let the one who cannot number illnesses not imagine that he can number healings. [Col. 1575B–C]

17. Now let us come to his passing. The good soldier had already dwelt in the Lord’s tabernacle even unto old age; having entered without blemish and wrought righteousness, he was worthy to receive his discharge and rest upon His holy mountain. Stricken, therefore, with longed-for fevers, he perceived the approach of the Lord who was calling for him; and, having summoned his disciples, he joyfully foretold to them the imminent day of his death. He comforted those who mourned and exhorted them toward better things; and, so that he might show the manner of dying to those to whom he had given a pattern for living, he first requested that the priests be brought in to administer the sacred anointing to him. Then, having received the Eucharist with the utmost humility of heart and body, he removed his linen garment and uncovered the hair-shirt which he always wore against the flesh. When those standing by asked the reason for this act, he said: “One who is naked must wrestle with one who is naked, lest he have anything by which he may be held.”

Thus borne by the brethren into the church and laid before the altar of the Mother of the Lord, he awaited his end in ashes and haircloth, with the eyes of his mind raised to the Lord. Those present wept silently and prayed, while the sacred reading, as he had commanded, sounded in his ears. And when the reader came to the final conclusion of the book, where it says: “Let us all together hear the conclusion of the discourse: Fear the Lord and keep his commandments, for this is the whole of man” (Eccl. 12:13), by an altogether fitting event, with the end of the speaking the holy man made an end of living. And he departed

> [Note: Col. 1576C. In the year 1070, on 11 May, as proved above.]

to the Lord whom he had truly feared and whose commandments he had kept—the end for which, beyond doubt, every human being is known to have been created. But with what zeal for reading and prayer, think we, had he clung while living, when not even in dying could he refrain from them? Or when did he cease from preaching, who even at his departure uttered sayings suited to edification? His body was honorably buried, amid a great concourse of people, in that same church, where it rests to this day. At his tomb many miracles occur, and many who faithfully ask receive benefits, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages.

# On the Life of Saint Florentius, Priest and Confessor, at Mount Glonna in Gaul. A Sermon by Marbod, Bishop of Rennes.

*(Acta Sanctorum of the Bollandists, September, vol. VI, day 22, p. 410, from a very ancient parchment manuscript codex.)*

[Col. 1577]

# Preliminary Observations

[Col. 1577] **1.** Mount Glonna, called by others Gloma and Glomo, is a place which, as we read in the *History of the Monastery of Saint Florentius of Saumur* in Martène, *Collectio amplissima*, vol. V, col. 1084, lies “in the furthest parts of Aquitaine, set apart not far from the bank of the Loire. In this place the most blessed confessor of God, Florentius, serving God for a long time, brought a happy life to completion by a still happier end, and most happily passed over to Christ. This place is said to be situated in the furthest parts of Aquitaine because that kingdom formerly extended as far as the Loire and therefore included Mount Glonna. For a similar reason the place of Saint Florentius’s death is assigned by some to the territory of Poitou: namely, because the province of Poitou, formerly a great part of the kingdom of Aquitaine, likewise had the Loire as its boundary in that region and included Mount Glonna and other places which today belong to the duchy of Anjou. Therefore, speaking according to the present division of territories, the place of the saint’s death lies in the duchy of Anjou.”

In the course of time there was founded there “a certain noble monastery, formerly called Mount Glonna” (these are the words of the history just cited), “a nursery of a remarkable community and beautiful charity, a model of religious life and an example of every uprightness.” It was dedicated to the same saint and is still called Old Saint-Florentius, in order to distinguish it from the renowned New Monastery of Saint-Florentius, subsequently built near the town of Saumur.

**2.** In accordance with the manner just explained, Usuard announces this saint on this day as follows: “In the territory of Poitou, Saint Florentius, priest and confessor.” Belinus, Galesinius, Baronius in today’s Roman [Martyrology], and other more recent writers followed this guide—for in the more ancient sacred calendars I have not found our Florentius recorded. He is mentioned in precisely the same words in our manuscript *Florarium*, but the following is added: “By his prayers he restored to life a certain drowned boy, performed many miracles, and died at the age of one hundred and twenty-three in the year of salvation 402.”

Maurolycus, however, assigns the saint to Lyons: “At Lyons,” he says, “Saint Florentius, priest, who, after driving away the serpents, lived in a cave on the bank of the Loire during Constantine’s reign.” He was probably moved by the authority of Peter de Natalibus, book VIII, chapter 107, who says: “Florentius, priest, flourished in the time of the emperor Constantine . . . [and was] buried near Lyons, renowned for miracles.”

**3.** Benedictus Gononus likewise described this account concerning the place of burial in his *Lives of the Fathers of the West*, p. 154. Saussay, however, in the *Gallican Martyrology*, embraced the same opinion and further added a reason why the saint went to Lyons and died there:

> “At Lyons, Saint Florentius, priest, a native of Poitou, whom Saint Martin consecrated, conspicuous for heavenly signs and miracles. Departing from him, lest he should receive the distinction of honor for a dignity unwillingly accepted, he fled to a place remote from the crowd and came to the bank of the Loire, where there was a cave full of serpents; these he drove away by prayer. There, remaining fixed upon heaven, he devoted himself to Christ’s service through prayers, fasts, and vigils. But when he had restored alive to his grieving mother a boy suffocated by the river’s waters, fearing lest the fame of the deed bring him a paltry reputation [the printed reading *vigili* is uncertain], he left his station and hastened to Lyons in order to hide himself. There, having departed from the course of death, summoned by the heavenly King to the eternal homeland that he sought, he died, indeed worn out by old age but—in accordance with the meaning proclaimed by his very name—greatly flourishing and adorned in merits.”

I cannot discover whence Saussay learned these things, or whence Peter de Natalibus derived his account of the city of Lyons. Be that as it may, just as their authority did not apparently seem sufficient to Theophilus Raynaud to grant Saint Florentius a place in his *Index of Saints of Lyons*, so it does not suffice us to form a serious doubt concerning the truth of the contrary opinion, which is almost universally held and established by stronger authority. Add that Saussay himself, under 2 May, places Saint Florentius’s tomb in Anjou and says that a noble monastery was afterward built there.

**4.** [lacuna]

> [Note: Col. 1577. That is, after the Acts of Saint Florentius written by an anonymous author in the ninth century, which we have omitted. —ED.]

I shall next append the elegant sermon of Marbod, archdeacon of Anjou, upon the same Acts, recited by the author himself on the feast day of Saint Florentius and probably in a church consecrated to him. I infer this from its first period, which, after the title, “Here begins the sermon of Marbod on the Life of Florentius the Confessor,” runs thus: “On the solemnity of this holy father of ours, Florentius, although a feeble discourse can by no means suffice to set forth his virtues, nevertheless it is not fitting for us to be altogether silent.”

I shall transcribe it from our remarkable parchment manuscript codex, of so ancient a script that our predecessors, who praised and occasionally used it in this work, rightly considered it either to have been carefully written in Marbod’s own time and perhaps under his supervision, or at least not long after his death.

**5.** This sermon appears to have been delivered by Marbod when he was archdeacon of Anjou, that is, before 1096, when he held the bishopric of Rennes in Armorican Brittany. This is so both because, in the *Life of Saint Licinius, Bishop of Anjou*, which immediately follows the sermon and occupies the first place in the codex, he explicitly calls himself archdeacon “of the church of Anjou”; and because, in the sermon itself, he clearly indicates that he is speaking in the diocese in which Saint Florentius is venerated as patron. For in no. 24, exhorting his hearers to imitate the saints’ examples, he concludes as follows:

> “Let us take an example from nearby. Before our eyes we have a special patron provided for us by God, so that we need not borrow something to imitate from elsewhere; and although the same things may be found in others, it gives greater pleasure to draw equally sweet waters from a nearby than from a distant spring.”

Now in the diocese of Anjou there are two monasteries of which our saint is the principal patron: Glonna, or Old Saint-Florentius, and the monastery at Saumur, or New Saint-Florentius, distinguished by the same saint’s name.

Otherwise, however learned and scholarly this author was, he did not notice our biographer’s anachronism. He associated Florentius with Florian and, in the remaining deeds, followed the same biographer closely, referring the hearer in no. 2 to him for clearer understanding: “Read,” he says, “the little book of his life, that is, of our saint.” For this reason I hesitated whether to publish this sermon together with the Acts, since nothing more certain can be determined from it than from them. I decided that it should be published: first, because our predecessors had promised it; secondly, because it is learned and devout, and so rare that, to my knowledge, no one but those same predecessors and persons following them has mentioned it until now, much less published it in print—although Antonius Beaugendre, a religious of the Order of Saint Benedict, took great pains to have the collected minor works of this same Marbod printed in 1708; and finally, because it will show from this alone how great was the veneration of Saint Florentius in the eleventh century.

[Col. 1579]

# Sermon on the Life of Saint Florentius

## Part I. Saint Florentius: a martyr in desire and an outstanding confessor in every exercise of virtue.

[Col. 1579A]

On the solemnity of this holy father of ours, Florentius, although a feeble discourse can by no means suffice to set forth his virtues, nevertheless it is not fitting for us to be altogether silent, lest, fearing rebuke for presumption, we be judged more justly for distrust or negligence. For our God, to whose praise is referred whatever praiseworthy thing is proclaimed in His saints, is pleased not so much by variety of speech as by truth of things; and the pure minds of speakers are more pleasing to Him than the many-colored purple of elegant words.

Therefore, for the praise of Him who is glorious in His saints and for the edification of readers, let us attempt to say something about the merits of this saint in plain speech but with manifold devotion. Thus we shall both render to our patron the service due on his feast day and stir up the minds of the faithful to praise God; and we shall set before ourselves a pattern of virtues. If we wish to imitate it—and indeed we ought to wish—we shall without doubt proceed by a straight path to heaven, whither, as we believe without hesitation, he arrived whom we set before ourselves to follow.

The way is indeed steep and the ascent difficult; but divine help cannot fail those who undertake the journey to God, with that same blessed man interceding, to whom it belonged to say: “Help is from you, O Lord, who has set ascents in his heart in the valley of tears, in the place which he has appointed” (Ps. 83:6). Following his footsteps, therefore, “we shall go from strength to strength, and we too shall see the God of gods in Zion” (ibid.).

**2.** Therefore, desiring to provide for our own salvation and that of others, we take courage from charity in undertaking a discourse about him whom we can neither speak of worthily nor ought to keep wholly silent about. For he is such and so great that he alone is sufficient for the praises of many, although the praises of no one are sufficient for him alone. Indeed, he alone is, so to speak, a multitude, in whose person the perfection of many is found.

For if you seek a martyr—not one merely of ordinary endurance, but one poured from the renowned cup of a certain impatience of spirit and a virtue intoxicated, as it were, so that he seems to provoke injuries as though he could not feel them—behold Florentius voluntarily seeking punishments for suffering, revealing himself to the guards, pressing himself upon tribunals, and finally pursuing death with as great an eagerness as others customarily flee it. Read the little book of his life, how willingly he ran to Lauriacum,

> [Note: Col. 1579. Lauriacum (Lorch), once a city of Noricum, now a village in Upper Austria, not far from the River Enns.]

a place so named, where the governor Aquilinus, cruelly beneficent, bestowed the victorious laurel. And what will you see in Florentius except the ranks of armies? For he threw himself against hostile swords with such cheerfulness and constancy that he could be thought not one soldier but a whole army. Hence his burning desire for martyrdom was reckoned to him as martyrdom, and he was judged worthy before God of a long life because he diligently sought a swift death.

**3.** Therefore, being reserved for the benefit of many, released from his chains through angelic intervention, he was withdrawn from suffering by an oracle of divine command. He was somewhat constrained and torn in two, wishing on his own account to be released and to be with Christ (Phil. 1:23), yet understanding that it was necessary for others that he remain in the flesh. Still, the companionship of his most delightful colleague and brother in Christ, Florian, with whom he had both lived in unanimity and wished to die magnanimously, increased his longing for a glorious death.

He reflected upon the happiness soon awaiting his brother Florian, whom he saw on that very day, bearing the triumphal palm, about to be received into the heavenly palace; while many labors remained for himself, no few dangers had to be undergone, and he himself was to be suspended from the refreshment which he had already conceived in his mind by the martyrdom of a more protracted life. For this reason, if it could be, he wished to receive and drink the cup of salvation with his brother, that through the sorrow of the cup he might quickly pass with him to the joy of eternal salvation.

Oh, how extended was that conversation for so brief a time, and yet, for the greatness of their love, how exceedingly brief! The guards having been lulled to sleep, Florentius, awakened by an angel, awakened Florian and disclosed to him the command of that divine will.

> [Note: Col. 1581D–1582D. Marbod, a man celebrated for learning and piety, plainly declared these things in accordance with the account of the Life written by an anonymous author in the ninth century; that he himself possessed this Life, or certainly another very similar to it, is suggested by the *Deeds of Saint Florentius* which he incorporated into his sermon.]

**4.** A great affection of mutual love breathed from those words, but in each man a greater worship and reverence toward God was apparent. Each wished to live or die with the other, yet in such a way that neither wished to offend God. Florentius would therefore willingly have suffered, had not the living God preferred that he live. But he who had denied himself and was to live neither for himself nor die for himself, after perceiving that his emperor, to whose service he had sworn, so willed it, did not dare to fight against the command as against an enemy. Yet he did not obey the order unwillingly, since he well knew that the proud transgressor of a command was liable to no lighter penalty than the fearful deserter of an emperor.

Nevertheless he was certain of the crown of righteousness laid up for him, which the Lord, the just judge, would render to him. Indeed, the crown of righteousness has already been given to his holy soul; but it must at some time also be given to the body in which, while living, he bore the cuts of saws and the scars of wounds—the stigmata of Jesus. For, as we believe, not all the household of that valiant woman, by whom the Church seems to be signified, have yet been clothed in double garments; but each has been given a white robe, and they have been told to rest for a little while longer, until their fellow-servants are fulfilled, so that those who are clothed individually in fine linen in the soul may all together be clothed in purple in their bodies. Then, therefore, we do not doubt that the just Judge will render to him the unimpaired reward of a martyr; before Him a perfect will for the deed is, as it were, the deed of a perfect will. Thus far concerning the martyr.

**5.** But if you wish to behold a confessor discharging the offices of tranquil peace—giving counsel to the troubled, acting as advocate for the accused, sustaining the weak, healing the sick, rejoicing with those who rejoice, weeping with those who weep—you have the same Florentius: as though transformed from a soldier into a civilian advocate, from one clad in armor into one wearing the toga, displaying no less diligence in the leisure of peace than courage in the business of war.

For who is found more active in the aforesaid works of mercy? After he was commanded to leave his land and kindred and come into this land, he willingly lived in exile; for he had no continuing city here but sought the city to come. Therefore, after, without losing the reward of his earlier labor, he was transferred, as it were, from military service to farming, he did not cease, as far as he could, to labor in the Lord’s vineyard: a most skilled pruner of vices, a propagator of virtues, making known by words what ought to be done and commending by deeds what he had made known.

**6.** Clearly, that delightful exhortation of the heavenly Bridegroom seems fitting for this blessed soul: after the winter of unbelief and the rain of persecution, at the season of pruning the vines, He invites His beloved:

> “Arise, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come; show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears. For your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful” (Song 2:13).

“Arise,” He says, “my friend Florentius: your persecution has passed and departed; martyrdom has not been granted you. Come into the land which I shall show you, that is, into the regions of Gaul, where I shall show you the place of your dwelling. There show me—that is, show my people—your face, namely your works: ‘for whatever anyone does to one of my least ones, he does to me’ (Matt. 25:40). Let the voice of your preaching sound in the ears of mine; for your voice is sweet and your works are beautiful. After the time of planting comes the time of pruning. For all things have their time, and everything under heaven passes through its appointed seasons. Martin planted a vineyard for me, and I chose you as its pruner. Join Martin in the share of labor, that you may deserve to share with him in the reward.”

**7.** From these things, therefore, we think it manifest that the man of whom we speak must also be numbered among the holy confessors, to whom, though courage to fight for the assertion of truth even unto death had not been lacking, the divine will granted a bloodless victory over the enemy. And lest you doubt what place of dignity he holds even among confessors, look to Martin, the jewel of the bishops of his time. When Florentius is directed to him by divine revelation, he is certainly shown worthy of the companionship of so great a man.

Moreover, an angelic forerunner reveals the arriving saint to Martin in a vision; and so that he may readily be recognized when present, he presents an image of the absent man’s face. He also commands that Martin advance the man, long since priestly, into the order of priests. Does not all this establish the confessor’s dignity of the blessed man? It certainly does. For if the testimony of approved men in doubtful matters usually carries the weight of unshaken authority, much more does a threefold authority concur in commendation of this priest: first divine, then angelic, third human. He is chosen by God, presented by an angel, consecrated by Martin.

**8.** Rightly, then, was he alone called a multitude, since in him alone the dignity both of martyr and confessor is found; moreover, through compassion he bore in himself as many persons of the wretched as human life has miseries. For the most righteous man strove to fulfill the law of Christ, “who himself bore our weaknesses and carried our sins in his body upon the wood” (Isa. 53:4), paying what He had not taken; mindful of the Apostle’s exhortation: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2).

[Col. 1583A] Nor was he burdened only by others’ burdens; he also rejoiced in their honors. Nor was he more saddened by his neighbors’ adversities than he rejoiced in their prosperity. Finally, if it is lawful to say so, he was more favorable to others than to himself: just as he loved God more than his neighbor, so he loved his neighbor more than himself.

**9.** For he who was easily broken by others’ misfortunes bore his own with such evenness of mind as those bear others’ misfortunes evenly who are easily broken by their own. Thus, while he bestowed a motherly affection upon others, he treated himself, as regards the body, in some manner as a stepmother. Likewise, he so rejoiced in others’ prosperity while making little of his own, as those commonly rejoice in their own prosperity who make little of that of others—except that such people refer their joy to temporal pleasure, whereas he directed both joy and sorrow toward spiritual profit.

In a certain manner, therefore, he loved himself more sternly than his neighbor. In himself he was so steadfast and firm, so unmoved by every wind, that he could neither be bent by the terrifying north winds of persecutions nor dissolved by the soothing south winds of flatteries. Rather, making every fortune material for virtues, steadfast amid adversities, cautious and humble amid prosperity, like some aromatic tree—or rather, like a garden of delights—he spread more widely the fragrance of sweetness at every blast of winds, receiving with equanimity both good and evil from the Lord’s hand. He knew that both were sent by God to the saints for their glory. For the Lord commands the winds and they obey Him: “Arise, O north wind, and come, O south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song 4:16).

**10.** These, then, are the spices of virtues which we ought to gather from this garden, and by which we ought to take delight as in most pleasant food or seasoned drink. The Lord Himself, glorying as though refreshed by these varieties of foods and drinks, exhorts His own friends to eat and drink these same things even unto intoxication. For He says thus in the Song of Songs:

> “I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, friends, and drink, and be intoxicated, beloved ones” (Song 5:1).

Clearly He would have said the same thing more plainly in this way: “I have visited a man fruitful in good virtues, in whom I found and approved the precious myrrh of chastity, by which the bodies of those who are dead to the world and live to God are kept unharmed from the corruption of lust. I found there too other spices of virtues; and I was pleased by the discriminating character of his teaching. For, while he concealed spiritual understanding in the letter—that is, honey in the wax—he knew, according to the capacity of each, to offer wine to the strong and milk to the weak.

“Imitate these good things also, all of you who wish to belong to my friendship. If you wish to be most beloved by me, drink these things and become intoxicated: become intoxicated from the abundance of my house. For house and garden are the same; but it is an aromatic garden and an ivory house, itself fragrant with various spices. For ‘myrrh and stacte and cassia breathe forth from ivory houses’ (Ps. 44:9).” Therefore, invited to such delightful feasts, and invited not by any other but by the Lord Himself, let us recline with grace.

**11.** With this table set before us, as though laden with the most exquisite variety of foods and drinks, let us pluck what is most pleasing, eat and drink, and diligently endeavor to obey the divine exhortation which we have heard. Let us eat unto fullness and drink unto intoxication. Let us hear and believe, love and act; otherwise, the word heard is of no use unless mixed with faith, while “faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:20).

If, however, it is difficult—and indeed it is truly difficult—for any one person now living to imitate all the virtues of this blessed man, let each choose some among them, according as each is delighted by particular virtues. “For each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (1 Cor. 7:7). We have been invited so abundantly and magnificently that nothing which anyone may choose can be lacking; indeed, all may rather be uncertain what they should choose. But whether better things are chosen from among good things, or the best from among better things, in none is there harmful surfeit, since in all there is manifest healthfulness—not as in bodily feasts, which make fullness suspect lest fullness produce illness.

## Part II. The Saint Most Adorned with the Cardinal Virtues and Those Flowing from Them

**12.** Certainly, it is well established that this man of God of whom we speak lacked none of the virtues by which he conquered not only contrary vices in himself but also those in others. But because it would take long to go through them one by one, we shall show that the four principal virtues, which all the others attend as handmaids, were present in him: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. From these it will manifestly appear that he who retained the whole possessed an abundance of the parts.

We shall show what we have promised in this way. If prudence is the knowledge of things both good and bad, who is found more vigilant than this man in such discernment? There are four ways in which imprudent people are customarily deceived: they think either that what is good is bad, or that what is bad is good; again, they think that what is neither good nor bad is either bad or good; or that what is bad or good is neither bad nor good. In none of these four ways—or rather, these four disorders—did the prudent man err.

He judged the pleasure of earthly goods, which people consider good, to be evil; while he judged the happiness of future goods—which, because they are not seen, are even grievously heard of by some—to be the highest good. Rejection, poverty, and insults, which deceived mortals regard as especially to be avoided, he not only did not flee but gladly embraced as praise, riches, and glory, choosing rather to be afflicted with the people of God than to have the enjoyment of temporary sin. For he looked to the recompense: “he looked to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising shame” (Heb. 12:2).

[Col. 1585A] **13.** He understood that one who leans upon a reed staff is foolish, and likewise that one who builds upon sand is foolish; for that staff pierces the hand of the one who leans upon it, and that house, shaken by winds and waves, often involves its builder in an equal ruin. Therefore the prudent man “built his house upon the rock” (Matt. 7:26), “and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4); and he leaned upon the wood, and that wood was the cross. Hence peoples recount his wisdom, and the Church proclaims his praise.

Moreover, in matters of the middle kind, which are neither good nor bad, the judgment of one who retained full knowledge of good and evil could not be deceived. For if he knew what was good, he certainly knew what was not good. If anyone knows what a human being is, certainly, when he sees something other than a human being, he knows how to distinguish it from human nature. Nor is the case otherwise in the knowledge of good and evil. From these facts it may not inappropriately be inferred that prudence was perfect in him, since no portion of imprudence is found in him.

No less was temperance present in him: by it he repelled evil things when they flattered, restrained them when aroused, and made them firm when unstable, distinguishing them from good things through prudence.

**14.** Temperance is the firm and measured rule of reason over lust and other corrupt impulses of the soul. He exercised this rule over vices so broadly and forcefully that, after first extinguishing in himself everything unlawful, he also pursued desire and the other disordered motions in others, put them in chains, suffocated them, proscribed them, and banished them forever.

For after hearing his disputation against vices—a disputation which, while displaying truth, in no way displayed itself—after hearing his speeches, more useful than witty and more upright than accommodating, who, I say, would not immediately conceive some love of virtue and thereby learn in consequence to restrain his own vices, to overthrow them once restrained, and to eradicate them altogether once overthrown? This was especially so because he saw that the teacher’s life in no respect differed from sound doctrine.

Thus he transferred his own temperance into certain others—namely, those “who, hearing and retaining the word, bore fruit in patience” (Luke 8:15). Nor did he restrain others’ vices only through a word of exhortation to the people, but also through the power of prayer to God. By these two means, therefore, he carried the banners of victorious temperance far and wide.

**15.** Fortitude follows temperance in due order. For as through temperance we abstain from evils that allure, so through fortitude we do not fear things that inspire terror. In these two the whole range of evils is contained. Pleasant things generate desire; terrible things generate fear. Fear or desire produces every sin. Hence the Psalmist says, “Burned with fire and dug down” (Ps. 79:27), signifying fear by “dug down” and desire by “burned.” Temperance is therefore necessary against desire, fortitude against fear.

This fortitude, which is also called greatness of soul, may rather be sought in the question how great it was in the holy man than whether he possessed it; indeed, it cannot be doubted that he possessed it in the highest degree. We think both points undeniable and especially clear from the fact, briefly stated above, that he was so contemptuous of dangers and labors that the fear of death could not prevent him from publicly bearing witness to truth. For what could he fear, when he had long since cut away from himself every cause of fear? Nothing makes the mind cowardly except consciousness of a blameworthy life. A wise man could not fear bodily death, for it is foolish to fear what cannot be avoided. Finally, the person who first sacrificed his vices goes to death secure.

He feared death so little that he voluntarily offered himself to the executioner and gladly heard the cruel sentence of death pronounced against him.

**16.** Someone may perhaps speak as follows: “If he was great-souled, he would neither seek dangers as a rash man does nor dread them as a timid man does. Certainly fortitude dwells between rashness and timidity. Can anyone rightly call strong or great-souled, rather than foolish and rash, one who voluntarily throws himself into a flowing river through excessive contempt for death?”

Yes, I say, if someone throws himself in without deliberation, such a person is rash and not strong. For fortitude is the considered undertaking of dangers and the enduring of hardships. But one who, for the assertion of truth, not only undertakes and bears dangers and hardships but even anticipates and embraces them, must be called not merely strong but most strong. For the difference of causes makes the judgment concerning effects different. Therefore, even if the rash man and the strong man are brought to their end by the same kind of death, we believe and confess that the latter deserves praise and the former blame.

Accordingly, this saint’s wish to meet death for the law of his God must not be attributed to rashness but to most fervent charity. Let us therefore praise this most courageous man—or rather, his courage—and refer the praise to the Lord: for “the Lord is his strength and his praise, and has become his salvation” (Ps. 117:14).

**17.** It remains for us to show that he was also just, since we consider that it has been briefly shown that he possessed the other virtues. We place justice last in the order of virtues because it seems to be the perfection of the other three. Justice is the virtue that gives to each person his due dignity. If anyone lacks it, then, even if he prudently distinguishes good from evil, courageously and temperately resists pleasant and harsh things, he shall nevertheless, like one ploughing in salt ground or cleansing seeds from barren sand, not eat the fruit of the labors of his hands.

For, being unjust and wrongly attributing to himself what belongs to God, though he has nothing which he did not receive, he will boast as though he had not received it (1 Cor. 4:7). In his own sins, moreover, turning to excuses as words of wickedness, by accusing the weakness of nature he will dare to lay the blame upon its Creator. But this is the first justice of a human being: to attribute whatever good one has to divine grace, and whatever evil to one’s own fault.

[Col. 1587A] **18.** Justice indeed produces humility, whereas injustice generates pride. Pride is a certain bitter root, which is accustomed even to sprout in the hearts of saints; it is a most savage beast, accustomed to devour even some of the perfect. For whereas the other vices arise only from vices, this monster alone sometimes derives its origin from virtues, as though from a dissimilar stock.

The patriarch Jacob knew this most savage beast when he said: “A most savage beast has devoured my son Joseph” (Gen. 37:33). Humility, however, is a most effective remedy both for preserving and restoring the health of the soul. It preserves saints in goodness, and it unquestionably justifies sinners; indeed, humble and modest confession of sin is not far from innocence.

Justice therefore overturns through humility the iniquities which injustice heaps up through pride. Justice completes through humility the virtues which injustice destroys through pride.

19. Therefore this holy man of ours must, together with his other virtues, have possessed justice, lest he seem to have built a body without a head or a house without a roof. But who could doubt that he was just, having learned what has been related of him above? For to render the Creator the reverence due to him through service is no small part of justice. To preserve fellowship with the human race in such a way that fitting affection is bestowed on all collectively and upon each individually seems to belong to another part. He conducted himself toward God and human beings in such a manner that he became neither inhuman for the sake of religion nor irreligious for the sake of humanity. Indeed, amid the very distinctions among people created by sex, age, or social condition, he so maintained the dignity of justice that he showed deference to superiors, indulgence to inferiors, goodwill to equals, mercy to the weak, and equity to all.

20. Finally, he lived soberly, justly, and piously in this world (Titus 2:12): the first with respect to himself, the second with respect to other people, and the third with respect to God. Here sobriety should not be understood merely as that by which the appetite for bodily food and drink is restrained short of gluttony and drunkenness, but especially as that which spiritually restrains the mind from every enticement of unlawful things. For only thus did he live soberly, if he preserved the integrity of sobriety. There are indeed those who eat sins like bread and drink iniquity as though it were wine. And this is the worst and most to be shunned kind of drunkenness: when, intoxicated by lust, avarice, pride, or some other poisonous draught, the mind can neither distinguish truth with the eye of reason nor firmly set the foot of action upon the path of God’s commandments; but, as though dissolved, enervated, and staggering toward restless and miserable pleasure, it continually complains that something or other is lacking.

[Col. 1588A] Eternal condemnation follows this drunkenness, as the angel revealed to blessed John when he spoke to him: “Come,” he said, “I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot”—that is, of the harlot nation—“who sits upon many waters,” while finding satisfaction in things fluid and transitory, “with whom the kings of the earth committed fornication, and those who dwell upon the earth were made drunk with the wine of her prostitution” (Rev. 17:1). And shortly afterward: “Babylon the great has fallen, has fallen” (Rev. 14:8)—that is, she has fallen twice, namely in body and soul; she has been crushed by a double crushing and clothed “as with a double garment in her own confusion” (Ps. 108:29). Since the blessed man knew that this condemnation was prepared in the future for the lustful, he lived soberly in every respect in this world, so that he neither tasted the wine of vice nor exceeded moderation in tasting wine from vines.

21. Toward other people he observed that justice which Christ sent upon earth, “fulfilling and abbreviating the word in equity”: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. 4:16; Luke 6:30; [Col. 1588B] Matt. 7:12). If this is properly understood, it displays perfected love of neighbour, since it not only restrains one from inflicting injury but also urges one to confer benefits. For the preceding saying also establishes this, although the words do not expressly state it: do not withhold from another what you wish to be done to yourself. For if you withhold it, you are already doing what you do not wish done to yourself; for no one wishes assistance to be withheld from himself in his need.

But if anyone should be so perverse as not to wish some good thing done to himself, or even to wish some shameful thing done to himself, he must not suppose that this commandment forbids him to do good to others, or commands him to do evil to them. Rather, he should know that this commandment, given to human beings, has nothing to do with him, since he himself does not belong to the human condition: through his own vice he has degenerated into an irrational nature, following, in what he seeks and avoids, a beastly judgment, if such a thing can be called judgment. “Woe to that person, because he calls good evil and evil good, makes darkness light and light darkness” (Isa. 5:20). He is no less deranged than a traveller in haste who lifts his feet toward heaven with his head fixed upon the ground, or who, while walking backward, thinks himself to be moving forward.

[Col. 1588D] This commandment, however, was sent to those who wish for themselves nothing but holiness and reject nothing except iniquity; who are so ordered within themselves that they may now extend themselves toward others; and who through sobriety become worthy also to attain justice. Such, beyond doubt, was the holy man of whom we speak. Therefore he rightly observed the commandment toward others, wishing neither to inflict any evil upon his neighbour nor to withhold any good.

22. He also lived piously, because he lived soberly and justly for the sake of piety: he observed the two for the sake of the third, loving himself and his neighbour for the love of God. Thus he lived soberly, justly, and piously in this world (Titus 2:12). Accordingly, secure in part through expectation and in part already through possession, he awaits the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God; he stands without spot before the eternal throne, one of the “harpists playing upon their harps” (Rev. 14:2).

For unlike many, he did not speak well and live badly; for that is nothing else than playing another person’s harp. Today everything is full of such harpists: their life gives no response worthy of hearing, yet they never cease to dictate another’s music. “This and that,” they say, “is reprehensible in him; this person and that transgress badly here.” Perverse and foolish people: unable to play their own harp, they presume to play another’s, and they will surely receive as great a condemnation as good harpists receive a reward—or rather, a condemnation greater by as much as they add presumption to wickedness. The Lord marks such people in the Gospel: those “who lay burdens impossible to bear upon the shoulders of men, but will not touch them with one of their fingers” (Matt. 23:14); or those “who, carrying a beam in their own eye, rebuke their brother’s eye for a speck” (Matt. 7:3), and though themselves utterly blind, do not shrink from presuming to lead the blind.

23. The saints of God did not merit eternal fellowship in the kingdom in this way; nor, to say nothing of others, did this blessed Florentius leave us such an example. More by living than by speaking he corrected those who erred, and more by his deeds than by discourse he prescribed what ought to be done. Yet neither did he fail to instruct by speech; he employed each in its proper order, first acting and then teaching.

Certainly this just man rebuked sinners; but his rebuke breathed sweetness, not bitterness; mercy, not envy; earnest desire, not hatred. He tempered rebuke with gentleness and gentleness with rebuke, so that the latter did not discourage and the former did not relax. Wicked and foolish people, when they attempt falsely to imitate this and labour to join together what nature has separated—good and evil, I mean—make monsters of themselves: from the same fountain of their own heart they pour forth a good word and an evil deed, sweet and bitter water, which nature does not allow; and, though they are barren fig trees, they feign the fruitfulness of grapes.

## PART III. Imitation of the saint: a remedy against every sin

24. But we, brothers, imitating the wisdom of this blessed Father of ours, should flee the folly of such people; or, if any of us are such people, let us flee ourselves, lest, if we do not flee ourselves, others rightly flee us. Let us learn either not to commit what deserves rebuke, or not to rebuke what others have committed. For to rebuke and yet to be open to rebuke is to be a physician and yet fall ill.

Let us imitate our patron in this as in his other good qualities, if we wish to celebrate an acceptable and solemn service in his honour. For the virtues of the saints are remembered especially in order that their hearers may be stirred by good example. Let us take an example from nearby: before our eyes we have a patron especially provided for us by God, so that we need not borrow something fit for imitation from another. Although the same virtues may be found in others, it is more delightful to draw equally sweet waters from a nearby rather than a distant spring—especially from a spring whose unfailing stream, without loss to itself, indeed to its own increase, suffices to refresh all. The waters of this spring are so health-giving that they can quench every heat and fever of sick souls, however varied.

[Col. 1590A] 25. If anyone, unhappy at another’s happiness, thin at another’s abundance, grows pale with envy and thinks whatever has been given to others has been taken from himself, let him draw a full cup of fraternal charity from this spring. At once he will escape not only this plague, but also another that follows from it and, though different, is no less deadly: the belief that whatever has been taken from others has been bestowed on himself. What fruit, then, will he receive from restored health? Namely, that regarding all others’ possessions as his own, he will even turn others’ losses into gain for himself. For grief and rejoicing at a neighbour’s gain and loss have equal recompense with God.

Does some person, maddened by anger, foam forth insanity? Let him come here and drink patience. He will immediately put off the beastly expression together with his rage; restored to himself, he will marvel how far he had wandered, be ashamed of his madness, and the memory of his violent sickness will furnish matter for caution.

26. Whoever sows discord among brothers is like one scattering wormwood in honey. After drinking peace from this spring, he will reunite what he had scattered and uproot what he had sown. He too will regret his former error, and henceforth will reckon the losses of fruitless labour compensated by a more useful exercise.

Some suffer poverty not of property but of judgment: the flame of greed so ravages their inmost being that the more they acquire, the more they desire. This happens because they take not remedies for satiety but stimulants of desire: whoever wishes to quell avarice with money is trying to extinguish a blazing pyre with oil. Let such people therefore drink a full cup of the sufficiency of generosity, lest they remain in the eternal poverty they flee. For equally poor are the person who does not possess enough, and the person for whom what he possesses is not enough.

27. There is another kind of sickness, indeed quite common in our times: that of people who weigh their own offences lightly and those of others heavily, and conversely who judge their own virtues great and make little of others’ virtues. In their virtues they do what fraudulent merchants do with merchandise; but in their vices they act in the opposite manner from those merchants. Yet both are abominable before God. For “weight and weight, measure and measure, both are abominable before God.”

Would that they at least sinned in the other direction: that they judged others’ evils lighter than their own, and their own goods of less weight than those of others. The former would be almost excusable because of humility; the latter is truly condemnable because of pride. Yet both are blameworthy, because unbending justice requires that things of equal weight, whether another’s or our own, be weighed on the same balance of judgment. These people too can easily escape their contrary sickness if they draw from this spring of our patron’s imitation a vessel full of equity. From it let the proud draw humility, the prodigal frugality, the lustful chastity, and the gluttonous abstinence.

But who could enumerate every kind of spiritual sickness? For the praise of the present patron it is enough truthfully to say this: there is no kind of vice to which he did not possess the opposite virtue. Although they are not all individually recorded, some may nevertheless be inferred from others. For from the parts we judge the whole, from greater things lesser things, and from what is manifest what is obscure. Although he concealed his own virtues, as others conceal their vices, so many and so great virtues are recorded of him that there is no need to desire more or greater ones.

28. Finally, the frequent display of signs makes clear how great his merit was before God. To pass over those miracles which, because of their multitude and magnitude, require both more than a brief span of time and the ability of a modern writer—those, I mean, which he wrought wonderfully after his blessed passage to heaven at various times and places—who could adequately match in dignity of narration even the miracles he performed while still burdened with mortal flesh?

To mention briefly, by way of example, a few among many and small among great things: questioned, the Rhône answers for his power; the river Vigenna bears witness; his native Loire proclaims it. For he crossed the Rhône’s swiftest waves and dreaded whirlpools in an old, broken-down boat, with faith alone as helmsman—perhaps by a greater miracle than if an apostolic traveller had crossed that fierce river with bold foot, treading upon its waters. In the latter case he alone would have been preserved by the miracle; in this case the very broken-down age of the preserved little vessel seems to double its power. It was not the ship that conveyed him, but he that conveyed the ship.

And in order to adorn the banks of that famous river also with gifts of his customary powers, he was moved by mercy to cleanse a demoniac whom he encountered immediately at the conclusion of that recent miracle, whose bonds testified to his madness; he loosed him from spiritual and bodily chains. Swiftly and in the midst of his journey he performed these two miracles in succession, as he hurried to Lyons on the Lord’s Day for the solemn celebration of Mass.

29. These things, and many others besides, happened during that journey in which, leaving his native land, he was coming to our place after being warned by a divine voice. The Vigenna too experienced a miracle not distant in place, though performed at a widely different time; its channel and banks were likewise made notable by a twofold power. For when the holy man, after having lived for some time in the place of his dwelling, was visiting blessed Martin according to annual custom, he obtained from God the son of a poor blind woman, who had been swallowed by the aforesaid river some days before. To the woman, sitting and weeping on the bank and doubly bereft, he restored light together with her son.

The Loire too raised a double trophy upon its banks: in one place, where he himself lived, by expelling a multitude of serpents; in another, anciently called Murus, by expelling one serpent—not one among many, but one which, because of its size, was itself like a multitude. Moreover, those who came to him as sick people to a physician—blind persons, lame persons, demoniacs, and people afflicted by various maladies—he gave light, raised up, cleansed, and healed. For all these eagerly frequented the place which he had believed would provide a secluded retreat for contemplation, once his holiness had quickly become known.

30. Finally, if miraculous power is desired, what is more worthy of admiration than to preserve steadfast constancy of mind amid such great instability in mortal life? This is truly to be placed in fire and not burn, or to be immersed in a river and not be overwhelmed. He lived 123 years. What variety of events, we may suppose, assailed him during so long an interval, when human life scarcely remains in the same condition for a single day? Yet the blessed man had so prepared himself for everything, so provided in peace for the necessities of war, that no change of fortune found him unprepared.

He had resolved to omit no good thing, even if it were harmful, dangerous, or laborious; and, conversely, to admit no evil, even if it brought profit, pleasure, or security. Thus this good man, perfect and complete—whom no force and no necessity could make commit evil—like gold most thoroughly tested or any precious pearl, worthy of being stored in the Lord’s eternal treasury, was translated into heaven and reckoned among the children of God, an inhabitant of that blessed city whose wall is built of precious stone, while the “city itself is of pure gold and has no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God has illuminated it, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Rev. 21:13).

31. Therefore, brothers, if we wish to share in that brightness—and who is so mad as not to wish it?—let us cast off the works of darkness. If we love eternal peace and rest, let us renounce the burdensome and turbulent cares of the world. For many, what is worse, the freer their bodies are from business, the more troublingly their minds conduct business; and they waste upon desires for business the leisure they ought to devote to worthy pursuits.

Let us cast away everything that stirs tumult in the soul, shakes the mind’s tranquillity, and tears the distracted heart into many pieces—things which, if they could not otherwise be driven out, would require, as Seneca says, that the heart itself be torn out with them. Let us maintain inwardly what we promise by outward appearance. For to conceal an irreligious mind beneath a religious face or habit is to wear a sheep outwardly and a wolf inwardly; and this is far worse than if one displayed a wolf and concealed a sheep within.

Let us cleanse the conscience from dead works and make ourselves square by means of the virtues mentioned above. For no stone enters the building of that holy city unless it is living and squared; the city itself is set in a square, its length, breadth, and height equal—which is nothing other than to be firm and squared. Therefore let us make ourselves firm and square in conformity with this most blessed Father, whose annual feast we commemorate, that we too, as living and squared stones, may deserve to be built together into God’s heavenly dwelling in the Holy Spirit. Amen.

[Col. 1593]

# The Metrical History of Theophilus, by Marbod, Bishop of Rennes, as Is Believed

## Notice concerning the following Life
