We have considered nothing else necessary to preface this Life except what might establish that this poem may be judged a genuine offspring of Marbod. This was judged and proved by the most learned and discerning Fathers Bollandus and Henschenius in their preliminary Commentary on this Life in prose, published by Eutychianus. In their work this precedes the Life rendered in verse by Marbod; and in volume I, under 4 February, they write:

> We have a manuscript codex in which the following works are contained in various heroic verse, and in this order: the Passion of St. Lawrence; the Life of St. Alexius; the Penance of the vicedominus miraculously saved through the Mother of God; the Passion of the Holy Theban Martyrs; the Poem on Gems; an extract from the writings of Solinus; and so forth. No author is named; we suppose him to be Marbod, formerly archdeacon of Angers and later bishop of Rennes, created by Pope Urban II in the year 1096 at the Council of Tours, held in March during the third week of Lent.

The same Bollandists there proved the truth of this history—which some critics have considered fabulous—by so many distinguished monuments that I have judged it less fair, even less pious, and less worthy of the supreme authority of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, exercised toward her Son on behalf of sinners, to doubt it. I have not thought it appropriate to transcribe those proofs here, lest we appear to be doing a thing already done and to have wished to swell our volume with other people’s observations. From them the diligent reader may also learn what dignity the *vicedomini* formerly possessed in the Church—such as Theophilus was—or stewards (*oeconomi*), and how great their authority was in administering ecclesiastical affairs.

# Chapter I. Theophilus’s Life Piously Begun; His Fall into Crimes after Renouncing Christ and Holy Mary

[Col. 1593A]

There was a certain *vicedominus*, a man of great merits,  
Theophilus by name, who fulfilled the omen of his name.  
For he avoided evil and loved the worship of the Godhead;  
Wholly devoted to the Church’s affairs, wholly to contemplation,  
Wholly to active works, so that every poor man rejoiced in him as a father,  
And no needy person remained in want through him.  
He sustained bishop, clergy, and people—the public hope  
Of all their affairs—and devoted himself to every holy work [conjecture: *vocabat*, “called”; main reading *vacabat*, “devoted himself”].  
Then the bishop died and was mourned; an assembly was held  
To choose a successor, one worthy of that honour.  
The holy man remembered above was approved, as he deserved, for this office;  
But he refused, fearing the heavy burden of the episcopate.

[Col. 1593B]

Though he was sought, he did not comply; the whole body went forward:  
He was elected because he was loved, and known to be worthy.  
Sound counsel came to the metropolitan,  
Who ordered him to come, so that confirmation might take place.  
The *vicedominus* was compelled; he offered excuses and refused to go.  
But he could not prevail, because the people wished to raise up the gracious man;  
As was fitting, he bore this, and he did not fail also to say the psalm.  
Then the supreme bishop kindly entreated him  
To bend his mind, praise the Almighty more highly,  
Change his decision, and not refuse the episcopacy.  
The clergy also came and pressed him with the same exhortation;  
The people said the same, yet their judgment did not overcome him.  
But one man stubbornly resisted all,  
Saying that he had no need to undertake greater burdens,  
But that it was enough for him to hold well the office entrusted to him,  
And that he must not attempt what he feared he could not carry through.

[Col. 1594A]

Therefore they dismissed him, resisting and not obeying the Fathers’ commands,  
And substituted another in his place.  
When that man had entered office and been anointed in the rite of a bishop,  
He administered and took account of the Church’s affairs;  
But through the swelling of envy and the Devil’s cunning  
The bishop was stirred against him, as many observed  
That in every respect greater honour was accorded to the *vicedominus*,  
And that his authority was exceedingly exalted.  
Unless he were deprived of it, anyone would soon discover  
That the episcopal dignity would thereby be shamefully diminished.  
Broken by these arguments, the bishop examined the *vicedominus*’s actions,  
Denounced them as though accursed, and removed him from office;  
He promoted in his place a worse successor.

The affairs of Theophilus, now deemed worthless, were held in contempt,  
By a reversal unlike and unstable, because all things turn.  
While his abundance and former favour had remained secure,  
Wealth and power had attended him alike.  
Where resources fail, strength immediately withers;  
Fortune gives servants, and favour follows authority.  
Remembering this, the aforesaid *vicedominus*  
Groaned in misery and grieved that he had been stripped of office.  
He then repented that he had passed over the episcopate.  
What earlier pleased him, when he had flourished supported by prosperity, displeased him;  
Now he was needy and was a reproach to the people, as though a fool.

1509

Thus he was stunned, thus he lost his senses through his evil lot—  
He whom the deceit of demons injured and robbed.  
Now a certain pestilent man, a magician as well,  
A Hebrew by race, himself full of a demon’s prompting,

[Col. 1595A]

Saw him afflicted and, as it were, out of his mind.  
He came at once and urged him to relate the pressing sorrow;  
Perhaps telling it might help, while silence could do no harm.  
The other sadly recounted in order the causes of his complaint:  
How great his wealth and how great his former esteem had been;  
How, deprived of office and brought to nothing, he had become contemptible;  
And that he would either recover it or soon perish.  
Made happier by these words, the magician promised counsel;  
And he swore this as part of the agreement: if Theophilus took care to ensure it by swearing faith to the agreement he would give him,  
He could thus recover the rights of his former position  
So as to hold the *vicedominatus* even above the episcopate,  
Supreme among the supreme, much more among inferiors.  
Theophilus pledged faith, only warning him not to make vain  
The promises of these benefits or waver in slackness of mind.

[Col. 1595B]

“Now,” he said, “listen in faith to what I command you in detail.  
My king is Satan; he is not accustomed to give empty gifts,  
But is accustomed to assist the miserable, giving also the observances  
Which must be kept by those whom he deems worthy of love.  
He supplies these people with goods and enriches them with possessions and honour.  
At night, beneath darkness, remember to keep the appointed time.  
I shall present you to him; but do not be alarmed  
By this splendour, I forewarn you: he will come with a shining triumphal display.  
Only stand believing, and do not make the sign of the cross,  
By which sign you would be unable to find him favourable.  
Then you will experience him as a good patron according to your wishes.”

Thus the wretched man, rejoicing and relying on this consolation,  
Promised to obey the commands and not lightly disregard them;  
So the magician sent him into his own service.

Then, through the terror of night, while all things on earth  
Were given to sleep and no star or moon  
Shone with any light, the said wretched man and the magician together  
Came to the place appointed for their meeting.

[Col. 1595C]

At the magician’s summons Satan the king, the image of death,  
Came, bearing his emblems and accompanied by an evil crowd:  
Himself foul and dark, yet gleaming with the fire of the abyss,  
And somewhat bright, as befits the king of darkness.  
He arrived and sat on high. The magician addressed him:

“Behold, father, with what special concern I strive  
That your praise, honour, and dominion may increase.  
It is fitting to serve lords and obey their commands;  
It is to serve lords well to strike their adversaries.  
The glory of great men is the numerous people who are theirs.  
Therefore I gain your party by every art,  
Withdrawing Christ’s own people from him, as you see in this man.  
Stripped of power, he seeks assistance from you;  
I pray that you favour one so grievously injured with your accustomed aid.  
Led by his example, profit will come to you,  
And it will increase whenever anyone follows your gifts.  
Grant this now out of pity, reverend father:  
If you have pity, you will be his everlasting lord.”

[Col. 1595D]

“Son,” fierce Satan said, “he sins greatly  
Who kindly favours the unworthy with due gifts,  
And, as you know, harms himself who serves his enemy’s interest.  
This man too is my enemy, and it is not right that he should receive my gifts.  
It is not lawful for those marked with Christ’s brand to stand before me;  
I can give them nothing, because I hate them intensely.  
But if this man wishes anything to be granted or wishes help for himself,  
Let him renounce Christ together with Christ’s baptism and Christ’s mother;

[Col. 1596A]

let him depart from them and freely believe in me.  
Then let him rejoice in me as his prince, when he enjoys  
The lot of my kingdom in the everlasting dwelling of the underworld.  
When he delights with me, let him endure torments;  
Let him gladly bear worms, fires, and weeping.  
On these terms any person may become my fellow-citizen.  
Then he shall receive my gifts, if he clings faithfully to us.  
1510

But this faithless sect of Christ’s worshippers is exceedingly suspect to me,  
Because each of them obeys me, broken by adversity and attaining his desires,  
Then departs from me and serves Christ again—  
Christ, who forcefully crushes my rule and, by recalling him, cherishes the one  
Whom gracious loving-kindness compels to save all things through love.”

[Col. 1596B]

Theophilus said:

> “Him whom the people crucified—Christ, together with Christ’s baptism and Christ’s mother—I renounce. I believe in you, Satan.”

Satan immediately ordered such a pact to be written, and received it when Theophilus had signed it. When this had been done, both departed in triumph.

The demon then displayed his deceit, being pleased not merely to restore his former state but to add still more, as the prince of this world who dispenses the world’s delights. Without delay the bishop, pierced with remorse, and the whole people likewise proclaimed that they had sinned in rejecting him before, neither lawfully nor in proper order, and restored the *vicedominatus* to him. Theophilus, immediately lifted up by sudden pride, exercised the rights of rule, changing whatever he wished.

[Col. 1596C]

All obeyed him; all feared him.  
The magician visited him frequently, for fortune had so smiled upon him  
That he congratulated him as one acquired as a companion in death.  
He reminded him of the compact made with Satan the prince,  
Lest he forget his gift and patron;  
Rather, in return for the gift, he must in every respect obey his patron.  
The wretched man attended to these warnings and gave thanks;  
He swore that the commanded pact would remain inviolate.

# Chapter II. The Repentance of Theophilus

Thus ensnared and possessing the flower of prosperity,  
The fool exults: now that Lazarus is buried,  
Now he lies despairing, fetid, and bound.  
But the true physician says: “My friend sleeps;  
My power shall awaken him.” O sweet grace of Christ!  
He does not will the sinner’s death, but that the sinner,  
Turned toward the endeavour of a better life, should live rightly.

[Col. 1596D]

He did not despise the good works of Theophilus’s former life:  
How through living endeavours he had assisted every needy person;  
How he had been accustomed to administer well what was entrusted to him;  
How useful he was in every matter, provident for himself and for the Church.  
God regarded these things and repaid them a hundredfold—  
Truly merciful, who looked upon Peter and looked upon this man’s heart,  
Touched it, and planted his arrows in it.  
He planted them: for the wretched man returned to his heart,  
Immediately expressed the sorrow of his heart, stood astonished, and redoubled his grief.  
For he began earnestly to remember his former condition.  
Confused, he considered how cruelly demons had toyed with him,  
How he had fallen from the summit, when it profits nothing  
To begin blessedly but to lack a blessed end.

[Col. 1597A]

He also remembered at once the eternal torment:  
The unquenchable fire resounds within the abyss;  
The gnashing of the damned and the lament of the guilty;  
The foul stench and the worm that does not die.  
Grieving from the depths of his heart, he pondered these things;  
He endured sleeplessly and no longer cared for his former delights.  
The immense fear which had earlier swollen his mind  
Cast him down in affliction, like one stunned by a blow from a wound.  
He thought himself ruined. Then he turned over such thoughts in his mind:

> “Behold, through the crime I have committed—alas, wretch! Alas, what am I?  
> When I stood secure, into what have I fallen by falling?  
> Where shall I go? What shall I do, I who bear a deadly wound?  
> There is no saviour except you, God the Creator himself.  
> 1511
>
> Therefore, since I have renounced God’s Son together with you, his Mother,  
> Who will save me and reconcile me to the faith?  
> What profit are the honours gained through the wicked tricks of the demon,  
> And reliance thus upon the prince of demons?

[Col. 1597B]

> Behold, I have become a servant; behold, I have covenanted to be forever  
> A citizen of Satan for the sake of an empty name,  
> And I have written a pact which binds me by delivering myself to him.  
> Alas for me! Who is stronger, to tear from him what I have written?  
> O that I had not known, that I had never consulted  
> That detestable magician, to be tormented in the abyss—  
> He who ought long before to have been condemned as a criminal by the Judge!  
> Why is one who betrays you, why is whoever hates you, O God,  
> Thus exalted and enlarged with honours?  
> What has it profited me that I obtained what pleased me from the enemy?  
> For what shone in the morning flows away; what I desired in the morning passes away.  
> Only a venial fault wears away, and no fault perishes unless it has been venial;  
> But my own particular fault strikes me.  
> Judgment, not escape, remains for me at last.  
> For who will grant me help or counsel  
> When my case summons me guilty before God?  
> And since my crime is mine, no hope will expiate it.

[Col. 1597C]

> Since I know that my case deserves no pardon,  
> What shall I do, when no hope seems able to offer me a way?  
> There each person considers how he may cleanse himself,  
> Yet scarcely can he avail himself; there fear oppresses all the righteous.  
> No one will stand for me when I am joined with the wicked.  
> Woe to me then in my misery: then mourning will come too late!  
> This pain is eternal, nor does Avernus end lamentation.  
> There are savage faces; nothing is heard but “woe, woe.”  
> He who is tortured is restored only in order to suffer there;  
> And while he prays to be received, to be rescued,  
> No one is helped, no one relieved; the punishment is renewed.  
> Death rules; it neither pities nor is satisfied.  
> Alas, defrauded, I am stripped of God’s light,  
> Covered with enticements and surrounded by darkness!  
> Therefore I am mad, a betrayer of myself and of my faith;  
> For one who denies the Almighty loses his mind.  
> Alas, how I have sinned, I who have killed myself!

[Col. 1597D]

> Most deeply, wretched man that I am, I have entangled myself in the soul’s vices,  
> And it is not granted at all that tears should come. But if abundant tears  
> Should come, they would not suffice to wash away such great evils.  
> Rather they would stain more deeply and make evils sting the heart.  
> I fell willingly and did not fear to submit myself to filth.  
> Wretchedly I lost my senses, so that evil things seemed sweet to my heart.  
> It is granted that I be guilty; alas, it harms me to be harmful,  
> To be pitch-black, Tartarean, while I live;  
> Thereafter an everlasting existence is prepared in the fire of Gehenna.  
> O my God, what shall I do? How shall I become Christ’s portion,  
> That I may be joined to the righteous and restored to the merits of faith?  
> Alas, where have I come, fallen into the depths of mire?  
> It is not lawful to rise; it is wicked not to wish to rise.  
> Yet I shall attempt this; I shall beg each person’s aid.  
> Although I have sinned, although I have denied you, Christ,  
> And your Mother, reigning through the ages,

[Col. 1598B]

> Yet I shall go at once, seeking her help,  
> Asking without end the aid of the heavenly Queen.  
> I shall take neither food nor drink nor rest;  
> My food shall be weeping and unceasing sorrow,  
> As with all my mind I pour forth my groaning prayers to God.  
> Yet, I think, even to dare this is an addition to my crime,  
> Since the prayer of a sinner’s mouth is foul.  
> The offended one is provoked all the more when he is petitioned.  
> And if I presume, with what sort of beginning shall I begin?  
> Will heavenly vengeance burst my words apart?  
> Will avenging fire thunder upon my unworthy voice?  
> Both punishments are grievous for the wicked: to pray and to be silent.  
> Terror dissuades; hope wills; and groaning becomes error.  
> Yet I shall pass beyond what is lawful; though rash, I shall go.  
> 1512
>
> As best I can, I shall act, knocking and beseeching Mary.”

[Col. 1598C]

Thus the aforesaid *vicedominus*, having exhorted and strengthened himself, went and lay prostrate in the church of the Mother of the Lord, the Consoler of the world. Fasting, weeping, and praying by night and day without sleep, he remained unmoved for fourteen full days, wholly contrite in heart.

# Chapter III. The Rebuke of the Appearing Holy Mary, and the Hope of Obtaining Forgiveness Given to Theophilus

Then the compassionate Virgin Mary stood before him and said:

> “Why are you so tormented, man, and do not moderate your weeping,  
> Afflicting me, the Mother of the Son whom you denied in writing?  
> And do you seek this through me, when you have betrayed me together with him?  
> Or is it customary for an enemy to be appeased through an enemy?  
> Rather, he will be offended, and his case will be made more grievous.  
> Why, then, do you ask those whom you acknowledge that you have so rashly offended?  
> Yet, since you call upon me as Mother of Mercy,  
> It cannot happen that I should be unable to show mercy where I can.  
> For the race of Christ-worshippers is by no means unpleasing to me.  
> Whoever freely recalls my lights above all others,  
> And remembers my name with a heart of abundant faith,  
> Him I graciously undertake by every means to save—  
> Raising, restoring, admonishing, and guiding him.  
> But it is difficult to approach my offended Son;  
> Indeed, his offence moves me also.  
> Yet now I shall approach him, and, having embraced him, I shall not withdraw
> Until I appease him, once he has relented, and bring you the peace that has been sent.

[Col. 1599A]

> He is indeed a merciful judge, but also a most just one:  
> He gives what is due, afflicts some, and has mercy on others.  
> He strikes and forgives, as both justice and grace require.  
> It is therefore fitting that every guilty person, leaving crimes behind,  
> Diligently occupy himself with how he may appease him.  
> But if the remedy is proportionate, it heals the wound well:  
> A milder pain heals some; fiercer burning is fitting for others.  
> Now ointments are needed, now strong remedies:  
> Cauterization often calms swellings which ointment cannot;  
> Cutting, not dressing, often heals pains;  
> Rebuke improves those whom persuasion does not;  
> A blow corrects some, mercy directs others.”

She had spoken. Encouraged, the man replied:

> “Illustrious Queen of heaven, salvation of peoples,  
> Glory of the saints and mirror of their beauty,”

[Col. 1599B] Most chosen, most exalted mother of honours,

Most merciful Virgin, you are the surest hope of the wretched,

You who bring the higher purpose and counsel,

Protection alike in shipwreck and in every kind of hardship.

I have sinned, Lady, exceedingly, and this ruin weighs upon me;

Ah, how I have sinned, who denied you and the Lord!

I confess that I am pitiably held fast by sins;

And I fear that, as I deserve, behold, I shall be carried off to be burned.

Indeed, this crime, my holy Mary, lacks pardon;
Yet sufficiently many [read *multa*, “many,” for *inulta*, “unavenged”] examples of mercy bestowed have been given,

To those who sinned and fell miserably.

Thus the Ninevites prolong the span of their lives.

Thus Rahab too is saved and joined to Israel.

Thus mighty-handed King David stained himself with a sin of death,

[Col. 1599C] Which he aggravated by adding a greater one;

But by weeping for what he had sinned he restored his standing;

Thereafter renowned alike in prophecy and psalmody.

If I may speak, my fault may be compared

With Peter, steadfast though he denied the Lord twice and thrice:

When the Saviour looked upon him, he immediately went out,

1513 Worthy by weeping to make satisfaction and to behold the Lord,

Thereafter chief of the Church and exemplar also of pardon.

Mary Magdalene too is granted pardon;

For, weeping well, she wiped away the stains of her sins,

Now pleasing to the Lord, now celebrated throughout the ages.

Thus, when called by the Lord, the guilty Zacchaeus becomes pleasing to him.

Thus the grace which cast Saul down established Paul.

Corinth saw such a man who had fallen grievously.

[Col. 1599D] Hence Paul writes that such a one will perish in the flesh,

So that his spirit, saved, may live more worthily.

Such too had been Cyprian the insane magician.

[Note: [Col. 1599D] Not indeed Saint Cyprian, bishop and martyr of Carthage, but Cyprian, formerly a magician and only a martyr, together with the martyr Justina; their feast is celebrated on 26 September.]

As many filths as he had, so many hairs he had—not by chance.

For he had practised malice and joined himself to demons;

He violated sacred things and killed little children in the womb.

At last, pierced with remorse, he returned and was joined to the Church

Through Justina, changing his beastly mind.

Then made a bishop, he corrected the deeds of others,

Worthy of martyrdom. The gracious God did these things:

He acts as he wills, as he foreknows—he knows nothing except what I know not.

[Col. 1600A] The examples of such great men also raise me up,

Lest I despair wickedly, since in despair I should remain;

For the Lord is able to have mercy on wretched me.

Thus, holy one, pray, if you can compel your Son to spare me.

For he will spare for your sake; I beg you, compel him to spare.

Your Son will do your will: command, and it will be done.

For it is within your right to extend your hand to those who are falling.

Since a special natural mercy belongs to you,

A conditional one, and grace of such a kind belongs to you,

That you help the misfortunes of the human race

As protectress, mother, and mediatrix.

God himself is certainly man for us through you.

Therefore, presenting Mary as mediator between God and man,

The Father gave you to him, whom the whole world obeys.

To this one it is permitted for you to speak and to pray to your Son.

[Col. 1600B] And since eloquence in speaking to your child alone belongs to you,

Entreat the holy womb of your beloved offspring.

Then the Virgin said: “Son, now return in manly fashion

To your former good deeds; believe what must be believed;

And with the voice of sincere faith and mind confess

That Christ, born from me and denied in your writings,

Is truly the Son of the ever-living almighty Father,

Who knows no end;

And who is to come and render judgment

Upon those who will live with him, and likewise upon those who will perish apart from him.”

Drawn by such words, the trembling man replied:

“How can I dare, in confessing the Lord and God,

Now to open a mouth so foully defiled—

A mouth which I wickedly defiled when I denied you, most holy one,

And him born from you, and also the rite of the sacrament,

[Col. 1600C] By whose grace baptism saves each person, and the cross?

For the whole salvation of man lies in these two things.

Renouncing them, I despised them; thus I revived to my own destruction,

Exalted by dignities, but cast down by sin.”

“Let a doubting mind be far from you,” replied Saint Mary.

“Only come steadfastly; believe what must be believed,

And confess again the former good things of salvation.

For God, mighty in mercy and altogether merciful,

Will receive you as you weep and thus make satisfaction.”

He replied: “I believe; I give my whole self also to you,

And I confess baptism and the trophy of the cross;
That the Godhead of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit

Has equal majesty, and a power that is not unequal but one.

Neither knows beginning or end,

[Col. 1600D] Yet each is both beginning and end,

Through whom the elements subsist, and none resist.

Hence the eternal offspring of the Father, from the heavenly seat,

Coming at the end of the age, having assumed the nature of true flesh,

1514 Came forth from you, pure Virgin:

You of beauty, you of royal lineage, you of merit beyond what can be said.

You who search the reins and prove the hearts—

You bore him; you pleased him, woman of Christ.

Thus God was made man, having mercy on humankind,

Suffering mortal destinies except for sin.

Hence, dying, after breaking the gates of death in the underworld,

[Col. 1601A] He shone forth, desired by the saints; thence he brought back

With himself the captive people, and soon revealed himself alive again

To his disciples. Hence, victorious, he ascended to the stars,

Where he sits at the right hand, sharer in the Almighty Father;

And thence he is to come and render judgment

Upon those who will live with him, and likewise upon those who will perish apart from him.

With no one accusing or justifying,

Here the fire will test every work by sure signs.

For the mind conscious of its own deeds, whether just or evil,

Will here accuse or justify them,

Giving to each his own due, condemning or crowning.

Believing these things in my heart and confessing them, I therefore first seek

Thereafter your patronage above all others, Mary:

That I may be helped, relieved, and preserved in this examination;

Piously offer me, as a suppliant, to the goodness of your Son.

[Col. 1601B] Nor let it be hard for you, what my impure mouth asks.

Rather purify it with its own utterances,

Lest my greatest sins impede my words.

And you, Mother of God, make black Satan restore

The bond that I wrote, the memorial of my crime;

For such a written security terrifies me as deadly.

I beg you, as you know, remove it, since you can do so from the enemy.

For he to whom opposing power yields gave you this power.

Exercise your power, my hope, defence, and shield;

Exercise it by showing yourself a good patroness.

I shall perish or be saved according as I am accounted yours.”

Then the pious mother of the mercy that precedes humankind,

Having compassion on one speaking thus and making satisfaction, said:

“As I said, you worshippers of the Crucified—

One faith, chrism, and spiritual grace—

[Col. 1601C] Whoever duly professes these, sacred worship makes them my friends;

Such are especially those who have been specially worshippers.

Therefore I shall humbly speak to my Jesus on your behalf, however grievously you have injured him;

And, falling at his feet, I shall beg

That you may be restored from the degree to which you have fallen.”

When she had uttered these words, she disappeared and departed.

## Chapter IV. Theophilus’ sins forgiven; the written bond restored; his death

Then the moved man trembled all over at this speech.

And he remained there for three days, occupied with prayers,

Bathing his face in tears and striking the holy places;

Nor did he turn his eyes away from the image he loved.

Again the Virgin of gentle countenance stood before him,

And, comforting him, said: “Your steadfastness has now prevailed,

[Col. 1601D] So that the Saviour, truly merciful, pardons you,

Granting forgiveness for your misdeeds through me, Mary.

Preserve this pardon, therefore; do not heap up evils anew;

May your end be happy, through the good course of your life.

The work is fixed by its end: each shall reap endlessly what he has done.

Do not yield, therefore, since everyone who yields is struck

More shamefully from behind; therefore fight and do not yield.”

He replied: “Certainly, my holy one, to God and to you

I vow my whole self; may your grace strengthen my vow.

With you as guide, with you as companion, may I be governed to life’s last hour.

1515 There is no hope other than you, holy Mary;

You are the first to watch over the lot of the human race.

No one has hoped in you in vain; no one has called upon you in vain.

You save those who seek you, and hear those who ask.

[Col. 1602A] I entrust myself to you alone; do not despise me.

May care for me belong to you, as I follow your laws.

And there remains something still, something that troubles me greatly:

I mean the parchment formerly given to the enemy,

By which I am held tightly, by which my mind is struck and beaten;

Make it be restored, for my mind is tortured by it.”

Repeating this, he wept, prostrated himself again, and prayed

That the document of his proscribed pledge might be returned to him.

Again, on the next day, the radiant figure of Mary

Presented the bond in sleep to the steward,

Secured with wax sealing it, as it had been before.

But when he awoke, he trembled at this sign of the new reality;

Excessive joy, as often happens, overwhelmed him with astonishment.

He leapt up; then hope, which had instructed him, composed songs,

[Col. 1602B] Songs that testify to great deeds:

“O Wisdom, who governs all things that are created,

Whom magnificence and highest power accompany!

You call the unworthy, and therefore appoint leaders of Churches,

Giving your covenants and also gifts of righteousness,

You prepare in sacred power those ordained for souls.

Let this be revered, glorified, magnified.

Therefore on the day set apart for rest to the Lord,

A great crowd, following pious observances, gathered at the churches;

And while the praise of the sacred offices was being celebrated,

He delayed no longer, but, prostrate before the bishop,

Made known all that had happened:

How, through magical arts, he had entrusted himself to the enemies,

And had been deceived while seeking the joys of the world;

[Col. 1602C] How he had sworn to the enemy and denied the Lord;

How he had written the compact, sealing this criminal transaction;

And how thereafter, pierced with remorse and reunited to the faith

Through the Mother of Christ, she had restored the document to him.

The document too was shown to all; he asked that it be read.

It was read; once it was read, the deeds were disclosed.

Immediately the praise which the people composed touched heaven.

And the pious bishop himself, leader of this song, said:

“Hear, all of you, and come to see

What the Lord has done; he has done great deeds, as he knows how:

The mighty one has done great things and restored the weary soul.

Indeed, he has brought to life the one whom savage death had cast down.

Therefore exult, and rejoice in the Lord God,

Whom you see thus unwilling that the sinner should die.

For, calling him back, he moves him and cherishes him with his accustomed mercy,

[Col. 1602D] And gives him as a pious companion to the saints and to blessed life.

Seeing these things, astonished by these things, glorify him;

Magnify such gifts and mercies so compassionate.

Observe, behold, how this man shines who repents.

Consider the power of fruitful tears.

For by tears swelling is removed from minds and wounds are healed;

By their stream hearts washed from sin are warmed.

By this medicine all things that need relief receive relief.

Thus sick, filthy, swollen, and wan things are abolished;

And the penalty of the avenger and anger of the judge are escaped,

Which true compassion or remission follows.

Deserved pain and destruction are removed by tears.

Through groans and tears they deserve a return above the stars.

[Col. 1603A] Therefore it does not suffice to wonder and venerate,

Nor can it be narrated or equalled by praises,

What wisdom, what patience belongs to the Almighty,

What compassion and love belong to him who has mercy

Upon sinners and those enslaved to crimes.

1516 But now I see the traces of former signs;

For Moses, sacred giver of the Law and mediator

Between the people of the forefathers and the commanding Lord,

When for forty days he abstained from food and other things

And devoted himself to prayer, appeased the Lord,

Angry with the people; and he deserved the Law a second time.

By a like example this pious man, strong in mind,

In the temple of Jesus’ mother, without bodily food,

Completed the same number of days in tears,

[Col. 1603B] So that he might render propitious the one whom he had previously denied,

Mary the pious one favouring and also mediating.

Let us praise, venerate, and glorify him who grants such things,

Who also voluntarily calls back the fallen;

And let us praise his mother, because she restored her brother:

She is the fount of light, the bridge to the courts of light,

Who cherishes the afflicted, conquered by the storm of sin.

She lifts up the weary, weighed down by the burden of vices.

She is hope for the despairing and gives the help of goodness,

The gate of God, opposed to the gates of death,

Accustomed to be open to the prayers of a sincere mind;

All who make their way through her and humbly ask her,

She admits and sends back to the Lord and to heaven.

We knock at her gate and raise our eyes and hearts;

We knock humbly at her gate and ask for entrance;

[Col. 1603C] We cry to her in our souls and keep vigil in prayer;

We cry to her, lest we remain shut out.

May she strengthen us as she wills and as is fitting.

May she protect us and remember us;

And may she grant that we remember her, through manners pleasing to her,

And rejoice by unceasing effort in her service.

May she grant that we are able, and grant us both ability and will.

[Col. 1604A] For if she despises us, in whose service do we perish?

We seek her whose praises we know,

To whom we flee, since we cannot avoid fleeing to her.

For through her we see that this brother has been rescued

From destruction and has moreover attained merit.

Because of this the Father rejoices, and that good one declares:

“Let the ring and robe now be ready in festal fashion,

Let his feet be shod; let the slaughter of the fat calf

Grant us feasting, rejoicing, and banqueting.

For this guilty brother of yours, O Christ, had ceased to live,

But now after death he lives.

And he was found, though held under destruction.”

What, then, can we say, since we are unequal to these things?

Yet we fear vengeance if we are silent;

Therefore now, weeping in spirit instead of sweet song,

[Col. 1604B] Let us sigh forth what we cannot utter.”

The holy bishop sang these words joyfully. When he ended,

The steward, prostrate on the ground, rose and asked him

Not to preserve the document, but to burn the wicked parchment.

And as it was being burned, praise was repeated by the people,

And “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*); the Canon of the Mass also
Was completed in order. Refreshed by the sacraments,

The steward, in the power of God, shone in the brightness of his face,

No less radiant than the glowing sun.

All marvelled at these things and, trembling, venerated them.

With hymn-like applause he was led to the church of Christ’s Mother;

There, after his former griefs,

Though his body was now changing through illness, he nevertheless greeted

The familiar places and signs with constant, devout prayer and hope.

He endured for three days and no longer cared for mortal things.

[Col. 1604C] And after he had greeted the brethren and distributed what remained

Of his possessions among Christ’s servants and the poor companies,

He died blessedly without end.

He who had formerly lain prostrate now lies buried in these places,

Where God is praised, where he works miracles,

Granting help to righteous prayers. Amen.

[Col. 1603]

# Poems on the Seven Maccabean Brothers

(This poem is found among the printed works of Marbod, bishop of Rennes, published at Rennes by the bookseller Jean Macé at the command of Yves, bishop of Rennes, in the year 1524. A copy exists in the library of the Collège Mazarin at Paris.)

[Col. 1603D] 1517 When the command of the king, abolishing the law of old,

Sought to compel the Israelites to unlawful acts,

Seven brothers, refusing the commands of the profane man,

Together with their noble mother, to whom the greatest crown must be given,

Provided examples of true courage to all others,

Pouring out their own blood for their ancestral custom.

The first, scorning torments with strength of mind,

Provokes Antiochus, hurling these darts of speech:

“Inventor of crime, why do you seek to overthrow us [read: *nos*],

When eating pork is plainly ruin?

We are prepared to suffer savage blows and exile,

And to have our limbs cut off rather than transgress the Law.”

Soon the wrath of the angry king commands the tongue of him who uttered this

[Col. 1604D] To be cut out, and likewise the extremities of hands and feet;

Then, his scalp stripped away but his mind unconquered,

He is cast alive into a frying-pan boiling with fire.

Holding fast to faith, he remains the same through all things,

And, dying worthily, shines like gold in fire.

His mother praises the contests of her afflicted son,

Her naturally manly spirit ready for like punishments.

The pious company of brothers who follow sees the torture

And learns in advance how to die, not yielding to pain;

Thus, willing to perish, it conquers even in the death of the first.

The first leaves the world; the second comes to the torments.

Like the first, after all the skin had been stripped from him

From the top of his head, the hope of salvation was offered him,

[Col. 1605A] If he would take food of pork flesh.

He utterly refuses to touch the forbidden bites

And prefers death to life in this crime.

Because he had the same disposition as the first,

The king commands him to be killed after suffering the first man’s tortures.

But, strong in heart, when his flesh was already near death

And was being consumed by pains, lest truth then too should be silent,

He rebukes the mad tyrant with such speech:

“Impious king, in vain do you devise the wicked purpose

Of destroying by torments the lawful observances of our people;

For the rite of the Law has been established by God.

Through these punishments we gain pleasant dwelling-places,

Which the fathers who went before deserved long ago.

You inflict harsh things cruelly, but hope of a better life

[Col. 1605B] Enables the faithful to overcome cruel punishments by suffering them.”

Having spoken thus, he too dies unstained by guilt.

The third approaches and does not depart from their lot,

Whom he prepares to follow in death in hope of a just reward.

Therefore he stretches out his hands and offers his tongue to those demanding it,

And prefers to perish rather than, living, yield to blows.

“These limbs,” he says, “which fleeting life leaves behind,

I give for the Law of God, in hope of perpetual rest,

In hope of receiving them back again from the Judge of all things.”

The great-souled young man, whose mind does not know how to yield to torments,

Gives horror to his enemies and the honour of a victor to himself,

As he follows in death the earlier combatants.

After him the fourth exposes his limbs to torture,

1518 And begins to die, not yielding in mind to pain:

“This brief death,” he says, “and every bodily suffering

[Col. 1605C] By which you torture a people following the Law’s commands,

Is a passage into life established for ever,

Which knows no groaning and does not grow old, conquered by time;

There restored flesh will shine with clear light,

Knowing no blemish and remaining through ages without end.

You who now drive us on will yourself rise again in doom,

To be tortured with endless groaning according to the merit of your crime.”

When he is thus extinguished, blows pass to the fifth.

Though afflicted as though he did not feel the strokes,

Standing with cheerful countenance, he does not cease to speak brave words;

By the force of speech he bears the weight of the contest,

And addresses the author of evil in this utterance:

“Since the ordinance of the Law obeys the nod of the King,

Whom we serve while, as you slaughter us, we perish,

[Col. 1605D] Do not imagine that the power granted you, with which you assail us,

Will not be condemned by heaven’s judgment,

Or that heaven will allow its own worship to be despised unavenged;

For it will make those laid low for its sake blessed in death.

It will destroy you as ungrateful, after you have first been tortured,

Nor will your descendants escape the ancestral punishments.”

The fifth dies victorious. The executioner wounds the sixth,

Who, his entrails twisted, standing upon death’s threshold,

Utters words and refutes the cruel king:

“You err grievously, mad minister of crimes,

Because you hurl a weapon against heaven to wound it,

In giant-like fashion, while justice prevails in triumph.

While we pay the penalty for sins committed, the Lord forbidding,

We enter life by dying.

But your hard heart will not go unpunished,

[Col. 1606A] O hand of the enemy, destined to undergo double punishment:

First in this world, then in the deep abyss.”

When the sixth is dead, the seventh stands in the linked order.

Though youngest of all, he nevertheless resists the wicked commands.

No less armed to endure grievous torments,

As a champion of God he desires to share the trophy.

Because he still remains, the king’s flattering voice troubles him,

Swearing especially that he will love him

And give him many splendid things

If he will transfer himself to the unfamiliar rite.

But while the youth, shuddering at the crime, rejects this,

The king summons to himself the victorious mother of her sex,

And urges her to consult both the young man’s welfare and her own,

And by persuasion make her son blessed.

She seizes upon the ambiguous word and, mocking his pride,

[Col. 1606B] The avenger-mother of noble offspring promises

That she will advise her son and give him counsel.

Therefore, blessed and wondrous mother, three and four times over,

Full of God’s gifts and crowned with seven crowns,

Victorious in the contests of her sons so many times—

To you alone we assign every reward, each one to a child—

Looking upon her son ready to enter the contest,

She exhorts him thus not to fear brief punishment:

“Son, receive the excellent words of your counselling mother,

Who carried you in my body for ten full months,

Whose labour-pains afflicted the limbs of my body,

From whose breasts you sucked milk for three years.

Look up, my son, I beg you; behold heaven and earth,

Look upon the air; encompass in your mind the expanses of the sea.

These are God’s work, made of diverse matter,

[Col. 1606C] Each thing full of the good things of divine creation.

For heaven contains the glorious fires of the stars;

Earth produces fruits which man is accustomed to gather;

Water bears the race of swimming creatures, air that of flying ones.

He who governs all these things subdued them to serve you,

So that, while you bear your limbs, you may devoutly serve him.

Therefore, subject to him alone, do not yield;

But do not prove unworthy heir of your brothers’ blood.

For the Lord, my son, bear the scourges with manly heart;

Bear the horror of death; pour out all your blood for him,

Lest any part of me lack the reward of that day

On which we who are now such shall receive new bodies.

Lest, losing you, I suffer loss—conquer the tyrant.”

Meanwhile the young man, whose mind had long been dedicated to suffering,

[Col. 1606D] Desiring the scourges, broke the silence with these words:

“What are you waiting for, king? Is it that you may bend our resolute hearts?

Break off your sluggish delays; you labour in vain by hesitating.

I have subjected body and mind to the Law, not to the king;

You delay too long in punishing a rebel more than I wished;

You trouble me when you defer, but when you punish you confer rewards.

For the hope remaining to us gives us consolations;

Hope of life through a perpetual age is gained through brief pain.

Supported by this hope, I fear no terrors;

Relying on this hope, I gladly challenge your blows;

Strengthened and secure by this hope, I seek the threshold of death,

Praying for the rest, that they may not be joined to the wicked,

And that, mindful of the fathers’ blood and appeased by the brothers’ blood,

God may now begin to have mercy upon our race.

[Col. 1607A] May the almighty hand compel you amid torments

To confess aloud the renowned mighty deeds of the true God.”

Then the deceived king turns to his customary practices

Of cruelty, since he achieved nothing by promises;

The more his hope hung frustrated, the more it inflamed him.

Burning with anger, he inflicts dreadful blows upon the young man,

Whom he prepares to tear more than he had torn the rest.

With iron, flames, whip, frying-pan, metal plates,

[Col. 1608A] Clubs and thongs, all the force of rage tears him apart.

Thus the tortured young man’s dead flesh yields to punishments;

His spirit hastens to run to the joyful assembly.

In the brotherly flock he shines with heavenly brightness,

Endowed with the gift by which the first, the middle, and the last are enriched.

Their mother, added last to her prostrated sons, shines,

All the more splendid in proportion as her contest was greater.

[Col. 1607]

# Verses on Saint Lawrence

## Notice

[Col. 1607] From a manuscript about five hundred years old, formerly of the monastery of Saint-Amand at Pabula, or Elnone, now in the Royal Library, no. 274.—Although this poem is attributed to Hildebert in the manuscript of Saint-Marien at Auxerre, we assign it to Marbod as his work: first, because in the Elnone-Royal manuscript it immediately follows the Passion of Saint Victor, expressly and by name attributed to Marbod; secondly, because it is found in the 1524 Rennes edition of Marbod’s Works. Sigebert, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 158, recognizes Marbod as the author of this poem; Trithemius, Possevinus, Vossius, Pithoeus, and others followed him.

[Col. 1607B] Sixtus, seized by Decius and slain by the raging sword,

Shone in heaven, joined among the martyrs;

With him two deacons, having gained the rewards of life,

Repaid by praise of the Creator the loss of their blood.

Lawrence, weeping and glad, gives himself tears that bring them joy,

And asks that he too may be slain by the sword in an equal lot.

When he hastens to suffer, he grieves at his postponed perils,

And laments that he has been left bound by three days;

Not, however, as one defeated was left by those three days,

But the more he burned for those whom he wished to precede in death.

Yet, as a youth whose age was suited to punishments,

And who was to contend better and become greater,

The prophetic voice of the old man, whose reins he obeyed,

Had said to this weeping man, eager to suffer with him:

“Cease, dearest son, to weigh yourself as worthless.

[Col. 1607C] What you do not suffer now, you will suffer after three days,

And the gains of punishment will compensate for the loss of delay.

1521 Why do you seek to be joined to old men, to fulfil the task

Of weary age? Young man, undertake greater things.

Let the aged hope for rewards in a light contest;

Let youth seek its profit by enduring punishments.

Let weak old age now obtain its goal by the sword;

[Note: [Col. 1607] Elnone: ‘of the mind.’]

The furnace tests the strong, burned by slow fires;

It is not the will of a strong man to be struck once by the sword,

Nor is it strength to seek a companion

[Note: [Col. 1607] Elnone: ‘of fate.’]

in death.

[Note: [Col. 1607] These three verses are absent in Elnone.]

Let him be joined to the crowd who intends to yield;

He who wishes to fight alone does not offer his back.

[Note: [Col. 1607] This verse is absent in the Rennes edition.]

Undertake the wars, strong in faith, of a more grievous death.”

I indeed go before, but leave you the material

For a greater punishment; after punishment, for a pleasant dwelling.

[Col. 1608B] Behold, my appointment entrusts to your care,

Which will have no companion, my resources to be expended.

What I entrust to you, do by distributing it to the poor,

As you know best, lest it serve the greedy enemy.

Hasten to give, lest, if late delay

Hesitates to scatter it everywhere, the king obtain what has not been scattered.”

After these words of the old man, the blessed deacon was seized and chained,

And brought before Decius, either to show the treasures or

[Note: [Col. 1607] Elnone: “to perish.”]

to die.

The Caesar seeks to bend him, present before him but not fearing his words,

[Note: [Col. 1607] Elnone: “trembling.”]

Now by dreadful terror, now by gentle speech, as he speaks in this manner:

“The goods of the condemned, whose crimes have been disclosed,

Belong to my right, as every inhabitant of my land knows;

For whomever the judgment of the laws condemns as sacrilegious,

[Col. 1608C] It lawfully commands that his goods be enrolled in my treasury.

Thus whatsoever belonged to Sixtus will altogether be mine,

Whom the law condemned and my sword beheaded.

Why does the public property subject to me lack my commendation?

[Note: [Col. 1607] Elnone: ‘Why is it not free of litigation?’]

But although this is so, these goods have not yet been reclaimed.

Thus far I forgive what has not been returned;

[Note: [Col. 1607] Elnone: ‘now,’ but contrary to the sense.]

now I demand it.

If you return it, you shall live, dear to me and rich in my favour.

Now it is not my wish to take the whole estate;

For property virtually preserved,

[Note: [Col. 1607] Elnone: ‘I grant you a share of the preserved property.’]

I grant you a share freely.

If you deny what is demanded and reject the laws you know,

Death is scarcely a punishment. Under a now graver charge,

[Note: [Col. 1607] Elnone: ‘More greatly.’]

Such transgression is greater than a capital offence;

Contempt of the emperor adds to contempt of the law.

A single vengeance does not suffice for a double crime.

[Note: [Col. 1607] These five verses are absent in the Rennes edition.]

Against my will, I am compelled to punish the rebel beyond what I would wish.

[Col. 1609A] If it is the crime of a thief alone, the black axe strikes;

But one who adds wickedness deserves a greater punishment.

Therefore let the punishment of a doubled sin be twofold,

Since these sins are committed by two penalties and are expiated by death.”

Strong in faith and burning with desire for death,

Counting terrors as nothing and rejecting flattering words,

[Note: [Col. 1609] Elnone: “flattering.” The Rennes edition has the same.]

He gave no reply, despising the proud king,

[Note: [Col. 1609] Rennes edition: “Giving no answer, he scorned the proud man by silence.”]

Wishing to provoke him and refusing to spare himself.

Then he was handed over to the mad prefect Valerian,

And ordered to endure punishments that he should not frustrate,

Unless he wished to offer incense to the enraged gods and return the estate.

But he was unwilling either to return the estate or bend his mind to idols,

Because he worshipped the sacred things of Christ;

Had he wished this,

[Note: [Col. 1609] Elnone and the edition: “which.”]

there would no longer have been anything that he could give,

Since, following the old man’s commands, he had given everything to the needy.

[Col. 1609B] At last Hippolytus undertook the same charge

At the prefect’s command.

[Note: [Col. 1609] The Elnone manuscript reads: “of the prefect of lesser jurisdiction.”]

By authority of the prefect of lesser jurisdiction, he bound in prison

The man shut up as though he had dared a capital crime,

Together with many who had been consigned to a penal death.

[Note: [Col. 1609] Elnone: “night.”]

Night and prison were rest for him, and daylight was brightness.

There he found a certain blind man sitting in prison with him,

Who had been blinded through excessive weeping.

His name was Lucillus. Having first taught him

To believe in his heart the sacred truths of the true God and confess them,

[Note: [Col. 1609] Elnone: “with the voice.”]

He washed him in baptism and restored his sight,

Giving him inward light also through the stream of washing.

Likewise he healed there other blind men,

Who had been brought thither from various places because of the report of this deed.

[Note: [Col. 1609] Elnone: “law.”]

Moved by these signs and also by the words worthy of a martyr,

[Col. 1609C] Hippolytus began to abandon the rites of the Gentiles

[Note: [Col. 1609] Elnone and the edition: “to despise.”]

And to wish to maintain the worship of true faith.

Soon, more fully instructed in all the sacraments of the teaching that followed,

[Note: [Col. 1609] Elnone: “certain.”]

He underwent in the usual order the waters

Of the divine font, which wash away the sinner’s crimes.

[Note: [Col. 1609] Elnone: “cleanses.”]

Cleansed in it, he shed tears and prayed

That his household likewise might be worthy to be washed.

Thus his entire household too was washed in baptism.

Ten put off the dregs of sins through sacred rites,

[Note: [Col. 1609] Elnone: “pious rites.”]

And three times three cast off the sin that was their own and their fathers’.

Later, when seized and bloodied by Caesar’s sword,

The crown joined them all to Hippolytus and adorned them.

A command from the prefect, immediately full of rage,

Ordered that Sixtus’ disciple be quickly brought before him.

He addresses him thus: “Decius threatens you cruelly,

[Col. 1609D] Unless you disclose the hidden treasures,

[Note: [Col. 1609] Elnone: “pay.”]

Which many witnesses prove by manifest indications that you possess.

Therefore these treasures will be demanded of you [the construction of *Has igitur peteris* is uncertain],
[Note: [Col. 1609] The Rennes edition prints *Has igitur poenas et dis*, literally “These therefore punishments, and to the gods …,” an incomplete construction. The manuscripts have the better *peteris*, “you are asked [for these],” in place of *poenas*, “punishments.”]

and you will be ordered to offer incense to the gods.

[Note: [Col. 1609] “What you are to do, etc.” This verse and the following are absent in the Rennes edition.]

There are two things you must do; neither is burdensome, both are profitable.

[Col. 1610A] If you obey them, you will enjoy life and property;

Believe my words and prefer sweet things to bitter,

And willingly obey by believing those worthy of belief,

Lest you, guilty of imperial wrath, die amid evils,

[Note: [Col. 1609] “First, etc.” This verse is absent in the manuscript of Saint-Marien.]

First tortured by unheard-of torments,

Instead of deservedly being called happy as a friend of the law.”

The saint replies: “He who prefers harsh things to gentle ones

Is wholly without sense; he despises reality and seeks emptiness.

If you think that I prefer to suffer the bitterness of death

Rather than to live in a blessed lot, you reject true things for false.

Now let your ear hear what I shall say concerning the treasures.

[Note: [Col. 1609] These three verses are absent in Elnone.]

True necessity compels me to disclose them, nor shall I deny them

Further, since denial does not tear me apart.

Hidden treasures, supported by a weight unknown,

Which I have kept and nurtured at great interest,

[Col. 1610B] I ask you for these; now I also ask you royally.

[Note: [Col. 1609] Elnone: “I seek them from the king; I beseech you also royally.”]

If it were possible, I would wish to preserve what I have acquired;

Delay in a loss so great may be pardonable:

Who could rashly wish to be without such riches?

But your majesty and Caesar’s lofty power

Both rightly outweigh the loss of property.

Moreover, to wish to undergo the twofold loss of life and wealth is madness;

If I am distressed by the loss of one, then,

When life is lost, I cannot retain what I desire;

But retaining life, I lose the desired thing more lightly.

It is better for me to abandon one of the two than retain neither

[read: *derelinquere*, “to abandon,” for *retinere*, “to retain”].

But because I have distributed this estate, so great in amount,

Throughout many separate places,

[Note: [Col. 1609] Elnone: “through safe places.”]

[Col. 1610C] I must be given three days to gather it together.”

[Note: [Col. 1609] Elnone expresses the two verses thus:

“Deceived, understanding little of the appearance of things,

The prefect rejoices, etc.”]

The answer, scarcely understood, deceives the greedy man,

And, deceived by the appearance of things, he does not reach the truth.

The prefect rejoices, carried away by swift greed,

And reports these things to Decius; frivolous hope makes him rich as well.

But Christ’s soldier, proving these things worthless to himself,

Seeks beggars through hedges, crossroads, and streets:

The deaf and mute, the blind, and those disabled in their limbs.

[Note: [Col. 1609] Elnone: “those whose limbs are enfeebled.”]

Having quickly found a very great crowd of them,

He himself, leading the flock in front,

[Note: [Col. 1609] Elnone: “draws.”]

brings them to the king’s tribunal.

The king awaited them and prepared lap and hand;

The prefect too, standing beside him, was ready,

And, expecting full bags, he set needy people before them instead.

Thus he eludes the expanded gullet and empty bite of starving greed, beginning thus:

[Col. 1610D] “These are treasures more valuable than mountains of gold;

Precious fleeces of wool plainly yield to these.

[Note: [Col. 1609] This verse is absent in Elnone.]

Precious stones cannot be compared with these;

Thieves cannot carry them off, nor mice gnaw them.

[Col. 1611A] What you give to temples, you ought rather to give to these,

Whom God, the faithful protector, preserves in heaven.”

[Note: [Col. 1611] This verse is absent in Elnone, which has the following instead:

“When he had spoken this word, the governor rages with proud countenance.”]

When he uttered this speech, fierce anger shook the king.

When he uttered these words, the governor raged with proud face:

“Then has the king seemed to you an occasion for laughter,

And do you devise a spectacle full of crime against me?

Thus you show that you make light of my commands;

It is clear that we are a mime and mockery to you.

But why do you hesitate? Why do you make so many evasions?

The altars are ready: offer incense and worship the gods.”

He, filled with God and serene in radiant countenance,

[Note: [Col. 1611] “He replied, etc.” This verse is absent in Elnone.]

Replied safely, freed from fear of death:

“Do not, deceived, believe idols worthy of worship;

Do not think it lawful to venerate wood,

[Note: [Col. 1611] Elnone: “which you know is rightly subject.”]

which you know is subject to fire,

Or the hand of an artisan.

[Col. 1611B] Nor is an image of bronze any more worthy that you should venerate it;

You deceive yourself when you offer incense to metal.

[Note: [Col. 1611] This verse is present in the Elnone manuscript and absent from the Saint-Marien manuscript.]

No sacrifice is lawfully given to any created thing.

He who created all things reserved it for himself alone.

1524 He does not seek merely the corpse and blood of an animal;

Both food and drink are remote from divinity [source *deitate*; conjecture *divinitate*, both meaning “divinity”];

The manner of his worship is to live purely,

To hold faith in him who remains one and the same,

And to burn with unflagging hope in desire for the kingdom

Which, when it comes, God will be all in all to everyone.”

When he heard this, the impious king burst into dreadful rage.

[Note: [Col. 1611] The Rennes edition has:

“Impatient of delay, he rushes on with swelling speech.”]

“Bear the tortures,” etc.] Thus, raging in his customary manner, the Dacian thundered in threatening speech:

[Col. 1611C] “Quickly bear the tortures, executioner, and strike without delay.

“Let the bull-hide force the blasphemer to breathe his last.”

[Note: [Col. 1611] Eln.: “Why does he, the blasphemer,” etc.]

Straightway stripped, he was torn with thongs;  
but the violence of the torture gave joy to his mind.

“Your right hand fails,” he said, “and does not strike well.  
To the weary executioner: add to your fury all that you can.

“You will not compel me, cruel attendant,  
to lay aside, through outward lashes, the inward dignity of the man.”

The enraged king commands every kind of torture  
to be brought forth immediately: leaded scourges, iron chains,

thistles, hooks, clubs, and beasts’ claws,  
a gridiron, metal plates, rods, and finally flames—

so that by these torments he might either bend  
the heart of the fearful man, or, if he despised them, tear his body.

“These,” he says, “are due to you, Lawrence, because you refuse to sacrifice;

[Col. 1611D] if you sacrifice, they shall be removed.”

But the saint, in reply: “Far be such madness from me  
as to spurn the worship of the Lord and the ancestral law,

[Col. 1612A] and to kindle offerings of incense for beings without perception,  
or dishonour myself by pouring out the blood of cattle.

“To him who stands upon the citadel of heaven, to the King alone, I shall offer gifts;  
what I say—to him alone—do not perversely distort in vain.

“The sky shines by the sun, but the sun alone does not rule all things.  
Do not suppose that I wish to offer libations to a star.”

[Note: [Col. 1611D] That is, of slaughtered animals.]

“Therefore much less shall I offer them to any buried body;

[Note: [Col. 1611] Eln.: ‘the entrails to one buried outside.’]

and least of all to material things of a single nature—  
stones and wood—which it is fitting that I subject to myself,

not that I subject myself to them, since such things are not after—or behind—me.”

[Note: [Col. 1611] Eln. and the Redon edition: “before me.”]

“Therefore I seek to give fitting gifts to the true God:  
not the caul of a pig, nor the entrails of sheep,

nor the fat of an ox, nor incense, nor goat’s flesh,  
but my own flesh, that I may become a more welcome victim.

[Col. 1612B] “What pleasing sacrifice shall I make from the gore of cattle?  
The victims of Orcus are those who slaughter the inward parts of a pig.

“No sheep cleanses itself by blood, by any wound;  
he who gives an ox’s fat incurs the ruin of his mind.

“He who gives his own limbs to God cannot lack triumph;

[Note: [Col. 1611] Eln. and edition: “trophy.”]

he shall live eternally, wearing the heavenly diadem,  
having gained a great talent through a brief torture.

“For the King of heaven is the great reward of his own.  
Considering these things with myself and greeting such great rewards,

I count every kind of punishment—though it be grievous—as light.  
Since I was destined to die, why should I not seek thus to live?

1525 “We wisely desire whatever we are unable to avoid.

[Note: [Col. 1611] Eln. and the Redon edition:

‘Who would labour to endure a punishment, whatever it may be, not for gain?’]

“Who would think of enduring what was punishment without gain?

[Col. 1612C] “It is therefore advantageous for me to die for a better life,  
and, by offering sacrifice, to deserve torments due to sin.”

While he spoke such words, while uttering such things he was tortured,  
and he rejoiced in suffering as though he were not suffering:

the heated plates and clubs dripping with blood—  
while, lest perhaps he suffer through fear, he prayed

[Note: [Col. 1611] Eln.: “that he may be spared.”]

that God might release him and pay him his rewards.

A voice fell upon the ears of the king and of those standing by,  
and of those who administered the scourges: “A greater punishment crowns you;

let constancy of mind overcome this suffering which you now feel,

[Note: [Col. 1611] Eln.: “All the remaining things.”]

and all that remains, the many things which bring you still greater rewards.”

The impious mind of Caesar, mad with the heats of his heart,  
thinking the heavenly voice a witness for the true martyr to be that of a demon,  
and changing brightness into darkness:

[Note: [Col. 1611] Eln.: “into a dark cavern.”]

[Col. 1612D] “You achieve nothing thus,” he said; “your cunning shall yield to blows.  
Though by magical arts you constrain these and those,

[Col. 1613A] you shall not deceive me: unless you sacrifice, you shall become a victim.  
And whatever you sinned in speech by reviling

the worship of the sacred things shall not be left unavenged.  
You shall suffer bitter strokes for your proud words.

“Renew the punishments; take the reins, faithful attendant.  
Strike this naked man—stripped and stretched tight by compulsion—with mighty blows.”

“See with what arrogance he scorns us and cunningly disdains us;  
we sing to one deaf and make a blind man resplendent.”

[Note: [Col. 1613] Elnon.: “and glorify, as it were, one blind.”]

Stretched out and beaten, as though wounded by no blow,  
the martyr gives thanks. The iron gridiron delights him,

toward which he was tending, which awaited him after these things;  
he desires greater things still, preferring flames to lashes.

A soldier of Caesar, seeing him endure the shameful punishments inflicted  
and not fear those prepared,

and considering with himself the truth of the words  
which this same man had earlier woven,

[Col. 1613B] and seeing a deed equal to his words,  
Roman by name, he at once ceased to be profane;

and himself confessing God, he won the trophy by dying.

[Note: [Col. 1613] Eln.: “by dying.”]

Caesar’s anger roars because Christ has taken this man also from him.  
He charges the saint with having deprived him of so great a soldier;

and his impious mind, impatient of delay and full of fury,  
lest there be any pause, as though there were room for fault,

changes Jupiter’s temples three times over—those which he judges less suitable—  
for the night-time, as though that were more favourable than the day.

He commands that the athlete of Christ be brought before him without delay;  
and, seated before the tribunal, speaks as follows:

“Setting aside magic, hostile to the gods and to us,  
say who you are and from where you were born.”

[Note: [Col. 1613] Eln.: “Tell, if you please, from where you were born?”]

The blessed man replied: “If you seek my country, I am of Iberian blood,

[Col. 1613C] brought up at Rome, skilled in the law of faith,  
which whoever observes would not wish to surrender in exchange for life.”

1526 Caesar replied: “You observe a vain and profane law,  
since you do not acknowledge the gods and do not fear my torments.

“Change your resolve, and do not refuse to sacrifice.  
Spare your life: let a victim rightly fall on your behalf.

“Unless you give incense to the flames, it remains that you yourself be burned.  
Choose to slaughter rather than be slaughtered, to burn rather than be burned.

“Reject what pricks; take what flatters and anoints.  
Why do you endure fiery flames of the gridiron for nothing?”

[Note: [Col. 1613] Eln.: “Why do you endure?”]

“Though you have suffered much, you have not yet been roasted by flames.  
Whatever you have endured is unequal to this punishment.

[Col. 1614A] However grievous a punishment may be, it becomes sweet beside this.  
Unless you wish to die this very night, go by the better way.”

The martyr, smiling, spoke in an undertone [perhaps *subjunxit*, “added”], confident amid harshness:  
“My night contains nothing dark; in the light shall be

whatever you do, though you seem to wish to lie hidden.”

[Note: [Col. 1613] “Whatever you do,” etc., is absent from Elnonensis.]

“What you do in darkness public report shall proclaim.  
Caesar commands that the mouth daring to speak thus be stoned;

and the savage enemy orders a bed with three crossbeams  
to be fitted like a gridiron to the blessed man’s limbs.

At once stripped, remaining as though mute even in voice,  
he is laid out for punishment—for himself a delight, for himself a feast.

With coals placed underneath, the gentle victim is burned;  
he is confined by forks, as though he intended to escape—

he who would rather be stripped of life than pulled from the gridiron.

[Col. 1614B] “Why do you rage in vain? Why do you torment one who has endured all things?  
Why, cruel minister, do you heap up burning coals?

“Believe that he will endure whatever harsh thing you can add.  
The executioner, though he stands untouched, is nevertheless not shaken.”

[Note: [Col. 1613] Eln.: “He who is touched by such great things.”]

The faithful servant of the Lord receives these as a gift;  
these too are the cause of his trophy.

Having endured fire and been pressed by flames and tongs,  
laughing he rejoices, and rejoicing speaks thus:

“Worshipper of error, whom God the avenger shall strike,

[Note: [Col. 1613] Eln.: “Worshipper of Cecrops.”]

you who now roast me and do not shudder at an unheard-of crime,  
add crime to crime, and do not fear to be seen;

night covers crimes; the place has driven away suitable witnesses.  
Devour the roasted entrails: it is a crime, but you commit worse deeds.

“You who roast a naked man, as though you were unwilling to eat him raw,

[Note: [Col. 1613] Eln.: “if you are unwilling to chew.”]

behold, if you prefer, you may gnaw a roasted rib.

[Col. 1614C] “Learn at last, miserable man, to inflict a great punishment upon yourself,

[Note: [Col. 1613] Eln.: “to hand over.”]

but upon me a reward, to which I compare no slaughter.

“By this punishment I earn the delights of the heavenly kingdom;  
you, the punishments of the abyss and infernal chains.

“Rest has been won for me; you shall become a victim of death.  
You who despise Christ are awaited by fire, cold, stench,

worms, torturers, weeping, crushing pressure, and pains.

“I give thanks to you, Christ, because I have deserved to be enrolled  
in the long and greatly desired book of life.”

With these words he is taken up, leaving the earth, above the stars;  
and having gained the rest for which he was made a victim,

he rejoices eternally, beholding the heavenly King.

## Passion of Saint Victor

[Col. 1613]

## Brief Notice on the Following Poem

[Col. 1613] 1527–1528 We have brought this poem to light from two manuscripts of the highest authority: one, namely, a royal manuscript about five hundred years old, no. 274, formerly belonging to the library of Elnone, or Saint-Amand; the other, an older manuscript of Saint Gatianus of Tours, almost contemporary with it. In both, the Passion of Saint Victor and the Passion of Saint Maurice follow continuously under Marbod’s name; and we collated the Redon edition against both. Therefore, although it is found among Hildebert’s works in the manuscript of Saint Marianus of Auxerre, we judged that it should be assigned to Marbod.

From this Passion of Saint Victor, moreover, the curious reader—and one interested even in a less elegant or indeed obsolete antiquity—may observe how great a craving for preserving, so to speak, a resonant rhythm had taken hold even of the sacred poets of that age in their verses. When words sounding in the required manner were unavailable to them, they invented other words, new ones or even meaningless ones, and for this reason sometimes disregarded grammatical rules. Thus in this poem the author, although otherwise most skilled in humane letters, used *iliu* so that it might rhyme with *diu*, *libi* so that it might chime with *tibi*, and *sitibit* instead of *sitiet* so that it might suit *ibit*, and other such forms.

[Col. 1615]

# Passion of Saint Victor, Martyr

[Col. 1615]

## Marbod of Angers’ Prologue to the Passion of Saint Victor

[Col. 1615] Since the devil strives to bring war upon the saints,

[Note: [Col. 1615] Tours: *Palaemon*.]

and now rejoices only when he deceives and lays snares,  
we must press on, lest by any art of that wicked one

the deceived mind fall, through which it may hand over joys to him.

Lost and sorrowful, he is always occupied with these arts;  
he fights and incites, seeking where to fix his arrows.

For he has many sufficiently fiery arrows,  
which, because the fool does not see them, he despises like dreams.

They are despised; and, when they have been despised, the final part dies in death,  
and while he grieves over life, he grieves that he did not know this to be an arrow.

If it were possible, he promises that he would now know well;  
he grieved in vain because he defiled his last years.

How well this martyr knew you, Christ,  
his death proves; this suffering is not the vow of one unknown to you.

Had he not made the vow, there would not have been in Victor  
so celebrated a courage, which the shaggy torturer recoiled from.

To conquer Victor denotes the honour of a palm;  
nor would he be Victor if the executioner could conquer.

The prologue must be completed, because a heavy mountain must be climbed.  
Therefore let no hostile pest detract from my deeds.

You, God, keep it away; if I insert anything inadequate, pardon me.

[Col. 1615A] When the madness of insane Maximian had reigned,  
and his colleague Diocletian was no less insane,

as their majesty was equal and their power in each equal,  
so their spirit was one in bringing about the destruction of the saints.

One purpose too gave free rein to punishments.  
And as they urged temples and gods upon everyone,

so all these men forbade everyone the name of Christ.

1529 Such was the terror, such had error now increased,  
that it allowed no worship of the faith to go unpunished anywhere.

For one prince, whose concern thereafter no one had  
for the destruction that would result after sacrificing,

writes to Marseilles: “Whoever refuses to sacrifice shall perish.”

[Note: [Col. 1615B] Tours: “He writes.”]

He commands this to the crowds, but especially to the city’s citizens:  
that they diligently seek out those who breathe contempt for the divinities.

[Note: [Col. 1615B] Perhaps: “who despise the divinities.”]

[Col. 1615B] He writes that it must not remain hidden, because, if necessary, he himself will come.

Therefore, arriving and casting all other matters behind him,  
he orders those called by Christ’s name to stand before him.

The man of whom I labour to compose an account is brought into the forum;  
neither of the two tribunes yet knows what the other will say:

“Why, dull Victor,” they say, “ought you thus to despise

[Col. 1616A] Roman laws and introduce vain matters?  
Do you not know what kingdom is due to the enemy?

Or what gifts he will bear who adheres to our laws?  
Moreover, see that your devotion now endures.”

“You greatly offend, Victor; I grant what you say.  
Nor are we ignorant that we ought thus to entreat you.”

“Victor,” says the governor, “unless your reply fails,  
why do you stand idle before those present,

here, where there are altars, instead of sacrificing with us?  
For thus you would appease the prince’s dreadful anger,

and it would not be uncertain that the king would rightly pity you.”

The holy Victor replied: “How many and how frequent laments  
have I wept for them; with how many pains my heart has been distressed,

remembering those whom it is plain are so small-minded,

[Col. 1616B] that they submit their minds to miserable shrines—rather, indeed, profane shrines—  
bringing gifts through delusion.

“Can you, if you turn the light of your mind to this divinity,  
when you see that the very thing you take for a god is plaster,

believe that what comes into a house through you is God?  
Do you not remember that it rests upon altars through you?

[Col. 1617A] First it was mud; now it is first among the gods.  
Whether it was cheap bone, or skin, or a necklace,

from some beech-tree came this image of Divinity;  
and now it receives manifold hymns through you,

is formed through you, valued through you,  
made solemn through you, and gains enduring renown through you;

and by your gift the people think this thing their patron.

“To speak plainly: if it could be God in any way,  
it could sooner know even your gods;

it does not know what you give it; blind, it receives your gifts.”

[Note: [Col. 1617] Tours: “your gifts.”]

“If you make this vow, it is right to impose action upon it;  
hence you take pains in vain to fulfil what you swear to it.

“There is one to whom we owe ourselves and all that we have:  
namely, the Creator, who, sparing not his blood,

[Col. 1617B] endured death first rather than that we should be withdrawn from honour,  
from whom our grieving parents fell.”

The governor: “By delaying matters, you declaim as though in an orator’s voice,  
and rejoice greatly because such abundance

flows from you in words, and perhaps for this reason you are proud.  
But though clever, you have declared your own losses.

“If you worship one slain, that devotion provokes laughter;  
if one suspended on a cross, it is clear that you have lost your senses.

“What dies passes away. Whatever was in Jupiter has remained.  
Of Jupiter there is sure proof: if you gave a hundred wounds,

would Jupiter’s life be dissolved by any wound?  
Now that you see the matter, why do you reject libations?

“If you consent to me, you will come to the powerful one’s temples;  
and, when you stand before his household gods as his priest,

appease him whom you have despised and to whom you have denied due rites,

[Col. 1617C] with an ox or a cow for so great a crime.”

The saint replied: “I shall believe certain things, but not all these things.  
Of Jupiter I am certain that there is no one found in the world

1530 through whom Jupiter’s life might be dissolved by any wound.  
What is not considered to subsist—what could it suffer?

Just as the Chimera never truly existed,  
so Jupiter reigns in heaven only by name.

“In worshipping one suspended, I do not lose but increase my understanding;  
that my slain Lord moves you to laughter

comes from immense fury and disturbance of mind.

“Let matters be perplexing: let the mind strive and see for itself  
what lies hidden; yet it will not do so unless it often turns things over, and unless

[Col. 1617D] it grants what it sees and believes it.  
While you distinguish matters, unless you disdain to believe, you will see.

“To give a slight sign, examine the wooden form of Jupiter:  
for the people’s care, the sacred image itself lies hidden.

Whether it really exists or not, nevertheless I grant that it lies hidden.  
This lofty thing now rules, as it were, the lower regions;

if, by chance, it falls and crashes upon the pavement,  
once it is broken, all of Jupiter’s affairs are finished.

“So it was in Christ, just as you grant in this idol:
