though the flesh was scourged, the Divinity remained unharmed.

Death and opened skin were remedies of salvation,  
and the blood drawn out washed away polluted deeds.

[Col. 1618A] What existed still exists; neither death nor wound prevents  
his resurrection after three days, when the prince of death has been broken.

The King reigns in heaven in his Divinity, with himself as sole ruler.  
Turn your mind toward him who can move mountains,

lest, on account of crooked sin, he overthrow you in your wickedness.”

The governor replied: “I rejoice that you are foolish.  
You furnish enough words, but they are of no use.

By a similar event you hope this can be proved:  
that the divine part did not suffer ruin;

and thereby you finally wish us to confess the same power  
in Jupiter and Christ, as though Jupiter were equal to him.

Jupiter is an eternal god; that one of yours is recent.  
Jupiter is borne in heaven on a dancing camel;

your King, about to suffer in war, led a little ass.

[Col. 1618B] Golgotha is the mountain of death. If his right hand were so strong  
as to move mountains or to destroy sinners,

why was he not removed, or why did Pilate himself  
not pay this penalty by some kind of chain?

Now cease what you say: you do not know to whom you say these things.”

Victor: “You, cease; let your voice be checked by death,  
you who think good things evil and reject them by perverting them.

Every person is permitted by reason  
to defend a true purpose with true speech.

Do you suppose that he was borne through heaven on a dancing camel—  
he whom the tale of Danaë plainly reports to have committed adultery,

as the book of the author defames him with the filth of his sister?  
May the adulterer be punished with scourges, if he lived only so much;

yet perhaps there is something which nature has left remaining as existent.

I reject whatever you do, even if I receive a hundred blows;

[Col. 1618C] while you tear me apart, I shall say: ‘You lose nothing in Jupiter—  
except only this: that he who forgives sins

condemns eternally whoever even thinks this is a matter of today.’

“My King mounted the little ass humbly for battle,  
that, being borne in humility, he might be shown

to suffer death willingly under Pilate’s jurisdiction.

“And now [lacuna] flight thus, and the frivolity that goes before.”

[Note: [Col. 1617] This verse is absent from the Tours manuscript, but is placed in its lower margin.]

“If you flee from battle, you will not sit upon the ass willingly.  
Finally, if he had wished, none could have resisted his power.

If anything had harmed him in the full brightness of day,  
he could either have hidden himself or lifted himself above the stars;

he could also have taken vengeance, because he could have attained this:  
that he might enter the heavenly assembly, supported by its aid.

[Col. 1618D] He did not touch the sinner, nor was there concern to move the mountain;  
God bore all these things with willing purpose.”

The governor: “Unless you despise and sacrifice what you discuss,

1531 within a few days, as I suppose, you shall become Jupiter’s victim.  
You, who might now gird a discus with us,

as befits an athlete sharing a banquet with the King—  
then, if you wished, he would give you gold, cloaks, and furs;

and after receiving the gift you might now be a tribune.  
By our doubled counsel he would clothe you in purple [the text has *comeret*; perhaps *ornaret*, “adorn”],

make you his counsellor above every equal.  
Yet you reject these things and resist the King and the gods.

Having become a pleader, drawn back by persons I know not whom,

[Col. 1619A] you despise every sacred thing by commending some washing.  
You say that one is cleansed, as though immersed in a deep river.

“By Jupiter’s shrine, by King Maximian,  
and by all the assembled companies of the gods above:

if you persist and prepare thus to conquer us,

[Note: [Col. 1619] Tours: “hope.”]

ask your god for ladders and the wings possessed by an angel,  
to which you hasten; he will soon be ruined.

“What should a sailor say concerning so cautious a matter?  
Stop, or finally seek shore and take up an oar;

let this quarrel meet the familiar storms of wars.  
You will go to hell, avoiding ancestral law.

“This was the custom of a father: unless he kept working at the ploughs,

[Note: [Col. 1619] Tours: “when he served.”]

when the dull rustic sat down to ancestral practices,  
he became foolish and applauded, pouring himself out toward everything he heard.

What he had forgotten, he thinks himself skilled in law,

[Col. 1619B] ready to run up and repeat whatever anyone whispers.  
Rise, call upon the gods, and taking a hoe by its handle,

call back from the flock whatever you love; and by doing this  
you will regain clear sight, and your error shall go unpunished.”

Victor replied: “Sailors arrange all things carefully;  
many governors are foolish in governing.

Thus, though my birth be lowly or my livelihood poor,  
these two things take nothing away if my inward parts have strength through laws.

Such is the character of the title of heavenly honour:  
if it sees someone living well, it does not despise the needy.

Nor is it fitting that I should be sad if I was once a servant  
of shore and sea, though you speak it reproachfully;

for as the sea is, so is the world, a sufficiently deep gulf;  
through many deaths it slays many companies.

[Col. 1619C] Would that, restored to ancestral laws, I knew how to conquer these fruits,  
so that I might exclude you.

“Behold, I call God to witness: I am troubled not so much because of the death  
which I am about to suffer, as because you are about to die.

You do not flee this pool; you do not leave this great sea.  
But I, who foresee storms through the stars,

while pursuing my gains, accustomed to cross the sea,  
will show, if you please, what course you should believe ought to be taken.

“Let not a swift and sound ship be sought like a bird;  
nor let our delay be burdensome when the favourable breeze has come.

The harbour is near, where there is a spring and a flower-bearing garden;  
a good man is the host; the dwelling is quite safe.

He gives all things freely and himself rejoices with those who have arrived;  
the fragrance of many apples perfumes the world in that home.

[Col. 1619D] If you cannot partake by mouth, you are healed by scent alone.  
There is no sickness of the mind there, no anguish of the body.

There are persons there; a thousand crowns hang there.  
There are governors there, and honours are conferred there.

“This we show you. But if you do not believe, let us go.  
If anything is lacking, I wish to pay the penalty … say what it is.”

The governor replied: “I approve; if I could see it, I would applaud.  
I have strong cedar ships, swift hulls.

I have purple cloths to serve as strong sails.  
Say where we should steer; when the south wind blows, let us go.”

[Col. 1620A] Victor replied: “If your mind has revived with your voice,

1532 first raise the sail of your mind upward to heaven;  
from above the breeze will blow, by which your prow will fly.

Because of your excessive concern, I set forth such an image.  
Let your mind be the ship; let the spirit be the sweet breeze.

Let him govern the mind that wishes to cross the world,  
and lead it to Christ, who possesses this harbour.

Let him immerse it in the washing by which he wipes away your crimes;  
and let hunger and thirst be removed by those same waters,

the savage gluttony which Eve once endured  
when, listening to sin, she bent her husband.

Who could describe the governor’s rage and the movements of his fury,  
or transfer its likeness into that of this one?

As a lioness rages in the arena after three days without food,

[Col. 1620B] wearing the face of a wolf when she seeks to seize prey;  
as is the assault of a bear when it sees a man:

such was the not dissimilar bearing of this man, grim toward the martyr.  
He ceases from words and attends to bitter punishments.

There are those there who inflict punishments as though composing songs;  
but, as from a file, they make the first suspension.

The weighers strive to inflict excessive pains;  
but the physician of heaven makes the faithful man not feel them.

When he was hanging on the wood, sighing with a gracious heart,  
he spoke thus: “O nations lacking reason of mind,

[Note: [Col. 1619] Tours: “of men.”]

unrestrained and brutish, pursuing death not merely thus far,

[Note: [Col. 1619] Tours: “thus far.”]

now that I am suspended, I ask you to suspend your minds  
from such a pursuit, than which none is more destructive.

“You see me stretched out; but turn your thought to this:  
why should I suffer myself to be suspended, why stretched in every direction?

[Col. 1620C] Why should I despise you, governors, why your honours?  
Why should I die for nothing, as you entirely deny,

if this worship of mine were not newly mature,  
nor certain, nor previously found in the laws?

“What law rightly teaches anyone to pray to calves?

[Note: [Col. 1619] Tours: “to teach.”]

What hope, what cause of salvation lies in many divinities?  
Minds capable of greater things are compelled to this by themselves.

“What you carve with your hands is now a lion, in the evening a fox;  
tomorrow a man; poured four times, it is formed as black Cerberus;

when the mud is changed, it is immediately Pluto in an image.  
As you multiply your art, you will see Mars arise there.

“Inquire what God is: it is great knowledge to know  
what god exists, or what god withstands being.

“If you address things and speak to each one,

[Col. 1620D] though called sacred, it will tell you: ‘I am not God.’  
If it is silent, it is thereby evident that what is God is not present there.

“This is sufficiently clear and hidden from no soul.  
If this were God, speech would never be lacking to it.

Speech is lacking: it is evident that what is God is not present there.  
Is it fitting that the One should divide himself?

Ever and hitherto speech and God have been one;  
and add no less that he now transcends the ages.

“He who takes nothing from you ought to take himself away from you.  
Thus eternal God,

[Note: [Col. 1619] Tours: “fatherly.”]

serene in face and countenance,

[Col. 1621A] is not the Father’s companion; but, as there is kindling in light,  
mind, power, and understanding through which the Father has measured all things,

he breathes forth words through spiritual principles.

Thus from himself he offers pure water to those who thirst;  
whoever drinks it no longer thirsts;

and will receive the faith by which he shall worship the same One.

“But if you knew that you have a gift from him,  
and how mercifully a womb bore him without seed,

that, having become flesh, he might remove fleshly deeds;  
and that he might free those who were captive, no longer restored to life,

[Note: [Col. 1621] Tours: “And you.”]

after breaking down the gate and binding the bound enemy,

1533 it would be fitting no longer to serve impure images;  
and it would be right that Jupiter’s shrine be burned,

and that, according to the rule of faith, the form of divinity be destroyed.”

[Note: [Col. 1621] Tours: “rule.”]

[Col. 1621B] Moved in his inward parts by these pretexts, the governor  
thrusts him into prison, there to accomplish his trophy through death.

He tortures and confines the outer man, while the mind is lifted up;  
he tries to weaken it, but the less anxious mind burns more strongly.

He strengthens and dishonours the man who cries out against shrines and gods.  
Entering joyfully, he judges himself to be at rest.

In prison he is stronger in facing his own death;  
he wept and prayed and called upon the Lord and God,

speaking thus: “O God, who are Creator! O you who  
hold the kingdoms above! Wise in what law you restrain

the courses of the stars, raising them through their periods again,

what your air brushes from the constellations, and your fire—  
from which the earth renews the seeds it can bear;

and you make the swelling, impatient sea calm,

[Note: [Col. 1621] Tours: “you immediately.”]

spreading the waves to pour them forth, and drawing them together again.

[Col. 1621C] Hell fears you; through you that fatherly destruction  
of death is idle, its threshold-gates broken.

You who once perform these things, King and rule of peace,  
rule me, I pray, with my affairs—but grant them full days.

Here I behold nothing full, nothing lovely.  
The unstable world passes away, and death shall call us from the world.

I consider the setting sign sufficiently fitting for me.  
I am like a falling star, but you urge me to rise.

Thus I pray: hold me in such a chain,

[Note: [Col. 1621] Tours: “bind.”]

the chain with which you hold a mind often falling into vices.

“Yet, that I may earn hope, let your fire come, that I may burn;  
and when set afire by it, let my mind at last be warmed.

Grant that my soil bring forth such seeds and fruits

[Col. 1621D] as may be rewards for my sorrow.

May I irrigate and wash it, so that it may remove the poppy from the harvest  
and make wholesome grain come forth;

and I pray that you may become for me like the sea,  
so that, well lulled to sleep, I may beware of crossing the shore,

and that the deep place of infernal Avernus may carry me [the text has *frear*; perhaps *ferat*, “may carry”];

lest it despair of me, whom it would possess if you did not spare me.

“If you thus have mercy, why does this life of mine not depart?

[Col. 1622A] Shall I not, living beneath this sun, see nothing  
that is the love of a mind desiring to reign with you?

Is there not beneath this moon one thing among many  
which does not delight whoever sees it in any order?

[Note: [Col. 1621] Tours: “will turn aside.”]

May the ruddy sun reveal distinctions among things.

[Note: [Col. 1621] Tours: “reveals.”]

“My sun, appear; fountain of light, shine upon me.  
I am a thing of night; you are light and daylight.

Scatter my mind, seated in darkness and death;  
and grant me, I pray, as I look and love, the gift

which you promise: although it bears the name of death,

[Note: [Col. 1621] Tours: “although.”]

in experienced reality it is rather certain quickening.

“For beneath the open sky it is enough for me that what I now live  
is a passage; but in dying I shall fall away even from this.”

Thus he spoke; and, when sleep came, his words ceased.  
The prison is fragrant with perfume; light runs through the prison’s interior,

[Note: [Col. 1621] Tours: “caverns.”]

[Col. 1622B] and a resonant angelic choir entered with praise,  
sounding forth and, as it uttered a gracious psalm, awakening him.

It awakens him and conveys through us [lacuna].

[Note: [Col. 1621] Elnone and Tours: “The Lord returns to you.”]

“The voice for which you pray assigns you only a few hours,

1534 and the time shall be short, as your Passion requires.  
For you will soon depart; you will soon proceed to the dwellings

in which, once you are there, you shall enjoy enduring peace,  
and you shall live life as a good Israelite.”

It spoke and departed; shadow returned and restrained fear.  
Such a vision moved the men; a wondrous song is sung in the air.

When the choir departs, the guard now believes  
that the matter is heavenly. He asks the witness to explain this:

what and whence is the sound? “It is praise,” he says, “which that patron  
once performs, and performs once, twice, and three times,

[Note: [Col. 1621] Tours: “choir.”]

a divine song, through which the voice heard instructs us  
to believe in the Trinity, and through which the Trinity crowns us.”

[Col. 1622C] Once the vision had been explained, with all watchful zeal  
he desires the hope he heard, rejoicing to set aside life,

[Note: [Col. 1621] Tours: “to put forward.”]

if by deserving death he might become a companion of that company.

When the guard perceived that his feelings were inflamed with piety,  
he burns with love of death—if, nevertheless, death takes this from him:

that the crime of error may remove from him the gift of honour.

When the martyr learned that his guard knew what he had vowed,

[Note: [Col. 1621] Tours: “vowed.”]

wishing those converted through him to be immersed,  
he seeks a Baptist who knows this matter well;

he seeks him and, finding him, instructs him in the teaching of faith.  
This man instructs, proceeds, teaches, anoints, and immerses them in the sea.

[Note: [Col. 1621D] “In the sea,” that is, in the baptismal vessel in which people were formerly immersed in baptism, and which was called a “sea.”]

For the joyful martyr, producing such offspring,

[Col. 1622D] through whom from the first depths of the prison  
he was made a father, fruitful through chrismal waters.

When this sacred rite was completed, the martyr and they rejoicing,  
he returns to his seat; they return to the prison-building.

Night passes, and the light of the rising dawn had long scattered its dawn,

[Note: [Col. 1622D] *Iliu*: a license for rhythmic sound, used for *illius* after *diu*.]

when at the first hour the governor, sending an envoy,  
orders the blessed man to come before him.

He commands, and they go there. Seeing their minds burning  
with the sacred doctrine, he thinks them full of wine;

[Col. 1623A] but whose minds? The guards’, not others’.

“Tell me, guards,” he says, “what, pray, do you mean?”

“Do you ask about these?” they reply. “But now, pray, do not make such a request” [the wording is uncertain].

“Why?” he says. They add: “Because the sacred chrism  
of doctrine anoints us; but you worship a stone as a god.”

“Are you joking, or do you report these things for certain reasons?”

One says: “We do not admit as brothers those whom God rejects—  
not you, even if you bark for Jupiter.

“This messenger himself smells of the covenant of Christ.  
This is not the scent of our people; it is not the scent of our gods.”

He spoke and added: “Who, I ask, anointed you thus?  
Who was their maker? Victor taught you such things.”

Then sufficiently angered, delaying no longer in the dispute,  
he commands them to leave and go wherever they should go.

[Col. 1623B] He commands, and they depart, rejoicing because they believe  
their blessed destinies are near, and blessing the hour of death.

They arrive at the forum; already there are a hundred thousand people  
waiting together to see whether death or blows will bend

the heart of so great a faith when Victor comes before them.

[Note: [Col. 1623] Tours: “why.”]

The ruler [the text has *rector*; perhaps *praetor*, “governor”] himself comes and first softens him by gifts;  
when he refuses the gift, he afterwards promises death.

But neither gift could change the patron.

Peoples gather, rushing now from this direction, now from that,  
and shake the place with the diverse whirlwind of their voices.

1535 A great uproar arises. The king asks, “Whence is this tumult?”  
He asks, and when he learned, he angrily entered the forum at once.

When the crowds see that the king advances from the city,

[Col. 1623C] they immediately change their bearing, fear the king, and greet him.

The king went in and, sitting down, orders the murmur to be suppressed;  
fear of imperial power restrains the assemblies on every side.

Then he says to the people: “If, my people, you owe me anything  
of sound counsel, if you wish my commands to be reconsidered,

that I may be less angry and not feed upon your blood,  
now weigh out for this villain a punishment—but a just punishment,

yet such a punishment as he may feel to be destructive.

“No one has yet so despised laws, no one kings;  
nor has this ever been the custom among men toward the highest powers:

to say what he has said. As though by a single wound he has pierced  
both us and the race of gods—no one does this unless full of a demon.

By a like lot he has endeavoured to despise death.

[Col. 1623D] This hanged man began to pervert minds;  
turning to the peoples, he turned minds toward Christ.

He said to them: ‘There was a just law among the Thebans,  
by whose rule I myself formerly killed more than six thousand.

Nor afterwards did I see anyone worship Christ,  
until we have now seen this man.

“It has been reported to me that you held this man bound,  
and that my faithful *pagidi* held the keys.”

[Note: [Col. 1623D] Perhaps *paganos*, “pagans,” or subject citizens.]

“I do not know whether he deceived them by words or by herbs,  
but now, if they love anything, they cry out outside the divinities [perhaps *contra numina*, “against the gods”].

“Jupiter and Juno, whom we believe born of one offspring,  
are made vile by these people for the name of I know not what Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1623] Tours: “name.”]

If new doctrines increase and the old practice disappears,

[Note: [Col. 1623] Variant: “and the new practice.”]

Jupiter will reproach all those in whose hands are the laws of the gods.

“But because slow vengeance does not suit kingdoms,  
let our sentence be carried out in deed and word.”

When he had spoken these words, believing this now more useful,  
he commends the matter, as it were, to the crowd as to a single tribune.

While the entire crowd is silent, though divine power is held cheap,  
the governor says to the king: “There is no need to punish what I have done.

Phoebus cries aloud from heaven that he is being destroyed from the earth over trifling matters,

1536 matters which you refer to as needing silence.”

[Note: [Col. 1623] Tours: “to be retained.”]

[Col. 1624B] “Both father and guardian: if I judge it grievous to destroy  
things which I employ for some purposes, I do not think it pleasing to the gods.

Therefore warn the man, lest it be surprising from the prince  
when you are first present, if you hasten these matters,

that he be beaten, so that he may believe. He has uttered new things;  
let a new punishment and new pain harm him. Thus I console you, thus the gods.

If nothing else opposes him [the text has *oblectat*; perhaps *objectat*, “opposes”], let his conversion move you.”

If he acts as he did before, have him led naked

Through the forums, through the streets; and let whoever beats him

Be set among his friends, since he believes neither in the gods nor in you;

His mind counsels you worse than punishments do.

The king accepts and approves. Victor comes and seems almost to applaud;

He appears more joyful, because now his suffering is made clear.

[Col. 1624C] Then Augustus said: “If you defer your vow until you have only been beaten and burned,

The whole thing will prove useless,

And whatever is done through you will be judged shameful;

Nor will Jupiter accept this, however much the victim may smoke.

If martyrdom, Victor’s hope, offerings, and prayers

Have prompted laughter, I think they are rightly cut short.

In short, you will ruin us, even if much remains besides;

Afterward no rewards will be recorded for you.”

Augustus had said: “If you defer your vow until you have only been beaten and burned.”

Victor said: “May I be sacrificed; I do not know what I should discuss with you.

When [Note: [Col. 1623] E. Tur.: “When you are wise, you see.”] … and you see whether by such means you overthrow

My hope and faith, though you yourself remain unchanged,

My worship, even when I am buried;

If I am burned and beaten, there is a part where I am not injured.

[Col. 1624D] Nor do I fear so greatly the furies and words of those who threaten

That I should value them at nothing, or seek such support,

So that Jupiter may accept this, if any victim of mine gives off smoke:

We are his image; let my suffering be smoke for him.

Martyrdom, Victor’s hope, offerings, and prayers,

If they have provoked laughter, do not think them rightly cut short;

Offer everything you say to your servile friends;

There is no need of gifts where the contest of struggle is prepared.

It is enough that I be sacrificed; I reject your gifts and yourself.

[Col. 1625A] Let them be displayed to those who, reciting your choruses,

Then deceive you the more when they chant their songs to you.”

The king said: “Depart, repulsed from our dwelling,

[Col. 1626A] And do not feed your mouth before you pour libations to the gods.”

Then he said to a certain man: “I shall sell you at a heavy whipping,

And I do not wish you now to grow fat, even if you should eat any foods whatever.”  
[Note: [Col. 1625] This poem seems incomplete, since its author did not treat the final episode of Victor’s martyrdom. Therefore in the manuscript of St. Gatianus at Tours, after this final verse, there follows one written in red, as follows:

“Here is written only part of the Passion of Saint Victor.”

Thus it is understood that it was not described in its entirety.]

[Col. 1625]

## THE PASSION OF SAINT MAURITIUS AND HIS COMPANIONS

[Note: [Col. 1625D] Sigebert, *On Illustrious Men*, says that Marbod, bishop of Rennes, committed to writing the contest of Saint Mauritius and his companions. [Col. 1626D]]

(Edited from the Tours manuscript, the royal manuscript of Elnone, and the Rennes edition of 1524.)

[Col. 1625B] While Maximian was preparing to restrain the Gauls, whom he had gathered together,

So that diverse peoples might not also have diverse minds,

He ordered the ranks to join hands, helping one another by mutual treaties

And pouring libations to the gods.

The rest of the crowd sacrifices; it avoids neither treaties nor rites.

The Theban legion considers this a crime, and therefore refuses.

1537 Three times two thousand, with twice three hundreds [Note: [Col. 1626D] That is, 6,666, the number of which the legion consisted.]

And also three tens and four times nine,

Observe the sacred rites of Christ and therefore refuse to offer rites to the gods.

Together they flee to Octodurum, where another part

Burns incense to the gods, swearing that it would not yield.

Soon, as they go around the pleasant meadow that surrounds the heights,

Flight, which had wearied them, refreshed these fugitives from crimes.

Near the Rhône is a place called Agaunum,

[Col. 1625C] Which granted rest to the weary and monuments to those who suffered.

When he hears that the legion is pursuing an unfamiliar rite,

That the decree of the treaty is despised and the camp abandoned

Lest they worship idols or be seen sacrificing to others,

The king’s madness laments contempt for the law

And therefore contrives to recall them to himself,

Admonishing gently in speech, but threatening harsh things fiercely:

“What my decision decrees, my people despise,

And my soldier dares call the gods worthless.

He is guilty both toward the gods and toward the Lord, under a double charge.

Let punishment restrain them, lest transgression grow.

Let them learn my power, or regain their senses by obeying orders.

Let them be compelled to the rites, or, if they refuse, be struck down.

Let them turn back here, lest wounds punish their fault.

It is better to return to Octodurum and not despise the customs [Note: [Col. 1625] Tours: “of their ancestors.”] of the pious,

[Col. 1625D] Than to worship I know not what,

To follow ancient practices rather than be slain for novelty.”

The messenger reports this, but the pious flock avoids impiety,

Despising what the king urges and what he threatens.

[Col. 1626B] It stands strong in faith, free from fear of death,

Preferring heavenly joys to earthly penalties.

So that it may reign while afflicted, it declines to live while conquered,

Deserving through brief death the rewards of eternal life.

How great must suffering be to make such a condition collapse?

Where hope is such, what can imperial fury accomplish?

This wall of faith is not ever [f. “ever”] going to fall.

They therefore answer: “It is plainly clear to us

That demonic error is no friend to Christ;

Because we love him, we cannot love what he despises.

Therefore we consider it wicked to worship the temples of the gods,

And through a Salian rite to violate the baptismal washing of faith.

Indeed, we flee temples; nevertheless, we have come to your [Note: [Col. 1625] Tours, Elnone, and the Rennes edition read “commands.”] camps,

Giving what is due to God, and not denying, king, what is due to you.

[Col. 1626C] [Note: [Col. 1625] Elnone: “Then the step.” Rennes edition and Tours: “Whence the step.”] It is no crime to refuse to turn our step, but to be punished in body;

[Note: [Col. 1625] Elnone and Rennes edition: “The task is not lighter for you.”] And the task is lighter for us than suffering is for us.”

When the envoy reports this, the king gives vent to his anger in words such as these:

“Shall I then allow a legal command to be violated,

And my orders to pass without vengeance upon my own men?

Those who persist in such deeds will not escape unpunished.

I affirm that commands are to be given and sacred rites must not be refused.

Let suffering restrain [Note: [Col. 1625] Rennes edition: “restrain.” Elnone and Tours: “compel.”] those whom exhortation cannot.”

“Yet it is not my wish to punish the whole flock.

Who would wish rashly to destroy these men all together?

Let the lot decide whether to destroy or spare a number.

Go: preserving the others, kill every tenth man,

So that the wickedness of the rest may pay [f. “be weakened”] through the death of a few.”

But when the royal command, sent [Note: [Col. 1625] Tours: “reported.”] to the saints,

[Col. 1626D] Reached Saint Mauritius, who was leader of this flock,

He strengthened the cohort for death with this speech:

“Because we worship Christ and do not submit to wicked commands,

1538 The king, goaded by anger, orders our ranks to perish.

Put away fear, I pray; gladly choose death.

[Col. 1627A] For no earthly thing can be exempt from death,

Which either disease brings about or some end removes.

If Caesar allowed the worship we follow to go unpunished,

Even were he to let us live, death would prevent us from enduring long.

Who would not wisely seek to lose what lasts only a little?

For he is well sacrificed who gains the heavenly kingdoms.

Honor is won for him who devotes his limbs to Christ.

If the flesh is made worthless, the breath shines above the stars.

For it knows no funeral, but possesses, without visible form, a gift

Which mouth cannot utter, eye cannot see, mind cannot contemplate.

Therefore let the hope of this pious crowd be in the starry city,

And know that a triumph [Note: [Col. 1627] Elnone, Tours, and Rennes edition: “trophy.”] is being prepared for God the Victor.

Let fear now depart, lest so great a glory depart.

Let the executioner now come; let the decimation now take place.

Though we bear weapons, I beg that we should not [Note: [Col. 1627] Tours: “strike back.”] return the blow.

[Col. 1627B] Let the hand be unwarlike; let voice and spirit be defiant.

Let bodies yield to swords; let weapons not resist.

The faithful man must conquer by blood, not missiles.

He who stands patiently beneath blows is unconquered though conquered.”

Encouraged by these words, they resolved to suffer.

Without delay fury draws its sword against the legion.

They give every tenth man to punishment, sparing nine parts.

O [Note: [Col. 1627] So also the Rennes edition; but Elnone: “Although cruel, faithful mercy is mingled.”] how cruel is this mercy! O faithful conflict!

The soldier spares in order that he may kill; he slaughters while showing pity;

And the pious man, that he may live, deprives himself of the gift of life.

One strives to transfer the suffering of clay to breath;

The other, through the labor of clay, to serve the salvation of breath.

That man postpones death; this one offers [Note: [Col. 1627] So also the Rennes edition; but Elnone: “offers himself.”] himself to swords.

This man goes before his companion, lest the choice of death generate dispute,

And each grieves who is denied a share in death.

[Col. 1627C] Whoever stands after the ninth thinks he receives a great gift.

After three times three have been selected, death suffers no [Note: [Col. 1627] Rennes edition and Elnone: “gentle.”] delay.

But he exults whom decimation presently punishes.

If it were possible, every man desires to be accounted the tenth.

Those who perish as tenth come first to the rewards.

When six hundred, twice nine hundred, and twelve four

Have been killed, the part remains, not frightened by what it has seen.

Caesar supposes that, broken as it were and shaken by fear of death,

It wishes to be preserved rather than imitate its companions.

He orders that his command be followed,

Or, if they resist, that every tenth man again be killed. [Note: [Col. 1627] Elnone: “he orders that the tenths be [killed].”]

Then Exuperius, the legion’s sole standard-bearer,

Bearing the imperial standards, but seeking not those [Note: [Col. 1627] Rennes edition, Elnone, and Tours: “battles.”] rewards,

Gives the portion that remains strength for wounds.

[Col. 1627D] While he thus exhorts them not to fear punishment,

Because constancy of mind does not yield to tortures:

“You have heard enough; now you have deserved to see;

And behold [f. “Behold”] your companions have deserved to become your teachers.

Do not wish to degenerate from their merits.

But retain faith, that the same end may befall you.

I urge you not to resist, though you bear arms.

Who would rather seek revenge than obtain kingdoms?

[Col. 1628A] [Note: [Col. 1627] So the Rennes edition. But this verse, “Those things which are man’s,” etc., is absent from Elnone.] Those things which belong to man are happy, knowing no end.

I do not say with what trophy God adorns our ranks;

What reward is given, what honor, what palm is prepared;

What this blood brings forth, [Note: [Col. 1627] Rennes edition, Elnone, and Tours read “when Mauritius recalled”; this makes no sense.] when the spirit climbs heaven:

These things are learned more by experiencing than by recounting.

1539 Such things are experienced by those who die for the Lord.

Therefore I think that it must be embraced, not fled,

That which gives rest to the dying and crowns them.

Are we prepared to suffer harsh things under uncertain fortune

In obedience to a king, yet do we fear wounds and death?

Who, to whom everlasting glory is promised,

Miserably excuses himself, miserably refuses these torments,

When God declares those laid low for himself blessed?

For he preserves himself who, O God, hates himself for you,

And joyfully reaps, weeping, the seeds he sows.”

[Col. 1628B] Supported by pious words, the crowd does not obey proud ones,

Nor does it deem the sacred rites worthy; therefore it is decimated again.

Six hundred men endured this force of torment.

[Note: [Col. 1627] “When the lot had twice been exacted,” etc. This verse and the following two are absent from Elnone, but not from the Rennes edition.]

“When the lot had twice been exacted, the remaining part was not subdued;

Its resolve remained established by the example,

And the commander invites the survivors again to the sacred rites.”

If his command is scorned, he threatens harshly.

But the champions of faith, judging rewards great

And Caesar’s threats and whatever bodily disasters

To be cheap, because they exchange penalties for joys,

Desire therefore to follow their companions and wish by dying

To deserve to become participants in an equal reward.

And lest they delay long, they dare to die together without a lot,

So that the honor of martyrdom may come alike to first and last.

When Caesar sees the entire band hastening to death,

[Col. 1628C] Not wavering from its accustomed worship through any tumult,

And desiring more to die by arms than yield to fear,

He does not prepare to count those whom he had vainly counted twice.

But because equality of faith belongs to the whole battle-line,

He decides that all should be put to death under equal terms,

The lot having been set aside.

Giving reins to anger, as though ordering them to go to battle,

He orders cohorts loyal to himself and to the gods to the deaths of their companions.

And lest they hesitate at the crime or avoid civil warfare,

He orders the slayer’s reward to be the plunder of the fallen.

Soon fury loosens its reins for punishing their comrades,

Despising the crimes of slaughter for hope of reward.

Though they bear arms, since they do not seek escape,

No one shields himself with a buckler, nor does anyone aim a weapon;

[Col. 1628D] But mute endurance, like that of cattle, submits to fury,

Their shields cast aside and their throats exposed [f. “uncovered”].

They do not merely owe the swords the wounds they offer themselves,

But adapt their throats to the blows [Note: [Col. 1627] Elnone: “by presenting.”] and press upon the sword.

The hand is eager for crime, willing to spare no one;

It passes over neither the flower of youth nor the dignity of old age.

He willingly endures these things who hopes for heavenly rewards,

[Col. 1629A] And, intent on gain, knows that no sword spares anyone.

Thus the pious multitude falls, but triumphantly goes to the stars [Note: [Col. 1629] Elnone: “above the heavens.”].

Let this place rejoice to see such sacred slaughter.

Let the river, its waves covered by so sacred a [Note: [Col. 1629] Elnone and Rennes edition: “blood.”] stream, rejoice.

1540 Caesar’s impiety does not know how to set limits for itself.

He looks upon the bodies of the slain and rivers of blood.

And, that he may see the same sight repeatedly, he lingers there,

Delighting in the spectacle and daring to feast amid it.

Thus the same field is amazed at slaughter mingled with feasting.

For one part lives; the other has learned how to live.

The sword has laid this part low; abundant food has satisfied that one.

This part drinks the grape-bearing dew; that one vomits blood.

The road brought here an old man named Victor,

And, as both [Note: [Col. 1629] Tours: “both.”] those wondering and those eating approached,

The army offered the righteous Victor food unfit to eat,

[Col. 1629B] Honoring his gray hair and years,

Asking why [Note: [Col. 1629] So the Rennes edition; but Elnone: “Asking why he does not eat, nor withdraws from this error.”] he ate and did not turn from this horror.

As he applauds, he hears the words of someone:

“You see a sacrilegious people, worshipping I know not what rites,

Despising ours and not following the king’s commands,

Laid low and mangled by our swords.”

At this Victor laments, and violent grief afflicts the old man;

He curses the banquet and speaks thus:

“Alas! Why did I delay? Why did I not hasten my journey,

That weak old age might equally have earned its goal?

[Col. 1630A] For though the service of a soldier is excluded by old age,

And my body is weak in strength and worn out,

What prevents me from being among so great [f. “being”] men?

Either flight from sacred rites, contempt for demons,

Or service of Christ would have joined me to this band,

That I might become a companion both in punishment and crown.

I indeed desire punishment, destined to earn delightful rest.

When he who now weeps shall applaud, he who now rejoices shall weep.

Impious man, why do you shout over the slaughter of this phalanx?

These, well laid low, are now placed above the stars [Note: [Col. 1629] Elnone: “raised up.”].

God smiles upon them; each shines in a diadem.

You rejoice wickedly, but at last you will receive

The fruit of wickedness: darkness, fires, grief.

For the merciful pardoner, [Note: [Col. 1629] Elnone: “and yet God, then a just avenger.”] and yet the just avenger, God,

[Col. 1630B] Protects what is his and punishes what is hostile.

May his love accomplish that I too may be made so by our service,

Lest long delay deprive me of the good of the legion.

Let it be granted me to follow after, when I am denied going together with them,

And let equal punishment make me a companion in like faith.”

While he says these things and intends to say more,

The executioner cuts him down. Thus Victor climbs to the stars

And finds the flock whose fellowship he seeks,

[Note: [Col. 1629] Elnone: “Rejoicing in death.”] By a deadly gift to which nothing can be compared;

And because he had confessed the same, suffering an equal wound,

He bears the same rewards, adorned with the same palm.

[Col. 1629]

## THIS IS THE LIFE OF SAINT THAIS

(From the Angers manuscript and that of St. Gatianus at Tours.)

[Col. 1629C] 1541 I shall tell in verse the life of a certain woman,

So that those attached to worldly things may not despair,

But may learn through her that God desires them to repent;

Nor does he hold those who repent cheap because of their crimes,

Nor will those who have committed no crimes be worth more to him,

But he commands both alike to be blessed with equal reward.

In heaven life is lived harmoniously and without envy.

Long ago there was an exceedingly beautiful girl named Thais,

Notorious throughout Egypt for her crimes.

For she despised God, by whose gift she lives.

That beauty of body gave her heart also to impious deeds;

She prostituted herself as Satan’s snare to those who were perishing;

For shameful purposes she sold her lovely limbs.

She passed sleepless nights while receiving everyone;

So great was her thirst for lust, and so great for gain.

[Col. 1629D] She mixed ages and despised blood relationships;

She judged adulterous intercourse equal to permitted unions.

She was difficult for no one, except one who brought her nothing.

[Col. 1630C] That monster’s house was open to all, without bolt.

Many nobles, supported by very rich wealth,

Were made beggars while giving their property to the harlot.

While Mars disturbed marriage, they stained the threshold with blood.

Mutual slaughter occurred before her doors,

And streams ran with the blood of rivals.

She, reclining on a couch blessed with gems and gold,

Rejoices that she was the cause and prize of quarrels,

And considers the streams of blood witnesses to her beauty.

Moved by this report, holy Abbot Paphnutius,

A hermit mighty in distinguished life and miracles,

Became sorrowful, wept, and poured grief from his breast:

“Alas for me! By how many diseases, amid how shameful things, the world perishes!

What an image of hell has risen in my district!”

Immediately taking off his clothing, he put on lay dress,

[Col. 1630D] Concealing what he was while seeking her who was lost to Christ.

He took a weight of silver for the purposes he knew,

[Col. 1631A] And sought the famous house of the unspeakable girl.

As there was opportunity to enter, so he was granted opportunity to speak.

He produces silver and offers the price of lust.

She, captivated by the man, said: “Let us hasten inside,”

And draws him to the bed, not having set out to do these things,

Where, lying down quickly, she said: “Come, my dear.”

The hermit answered her: “Let us not do it thus,

For this place is open; it is right for us to seek a hiding-place.”

Thais replied: “God sees within and without;

The coverings of night are to him as naked day.

If you fear him, trust in no [Note: [Col. 1631] Tours: “concealment.”] covering;

But if, fearing men, you seek more inner hiding-places,

You do not know what you seek, because you do not fear what ought to be feared.

Disregard human sight, trusting in a wall.”

[Col. 1631B] The monk responded, following the woman’s words:

“If God is witness of crime, as you yourself confess,

And no hidden place can shut out his sight,

Then this wall is set in place to no purpose;

Let every judge be far from human eyes,

Yet you will not escape when the final calamity comes;

For the avenger of crimes becomes their witness and judge.

1542 O woman beloved by God, image of the heavenly King!

If you know the Lord, why do you serve his enemy?

Why, with so many buried together with you,

Will you deservedly be tortured in eternal fire?

You should not trust in life; you should not trust in beauty;

We are all earth; life swiftly flees, smoke swiftly vanishes.”

Terrified at once by such true words, Thais

Said: “Woe is me, woe!” She pressed kisses upon the old man’s feet,

[Col. 1631C] And shedding tears and striking her breast with her fists,

She gently begged the man, uttering sighs,

That he would wait outside the city for her three hours;

And, appointing a place, he broke off their exchange of words.

Then she seizes treasures, perfumes, necklaces, gems,

Garments, silver, tripods, bowls, and gold,

And whatever she had gained by her body,

And carries the wealth of her vices into the middle of the forum,

Which was found to amount to four hundred pounds.

Having kindled a pyre, she said: “I shall first burn these in fire

Rather than be burned in the black fires of hell for preserving them.

And I shall altogether first lack a partner in my bed

Rather than be plunged into the abysses of hell for my deeds.

O wretched citizens, from whom I am wickedly made rich,

[Col. 1631D] You who bought sin and sought it with payment [Note: [Col. 1631] Tours: “perished.”],

Come and behold the fruit of my former life.

The display of the proud returns here, and the gains of evildoers;

Fire will consume whatever corruption begets.

Repent with me, you whom equal sin defiles;

Participants in guilt, share in its deserts.”

Weeping, she uttered these words and compelled all to weep,

When she saw everything at once fall into warm ash.

Without delay she flees, cursing her former deeds,

And follows the saint, desiring heavenly things only.

He came to the enclosure of holy maidens,

Whose religious life despised pleasures,

[Col. 1632A] And could offer her consolations should she fail.

He thrust his rejoicing friend into a small cell,

And shut it from outside, showing examples of severity.

Yet he ordered that a small opening be left in one side,

Through which a restricted allowance could reach her:

A small measure of water and bread for each day.

For black lust is quenched by cold drink,

And she dies to the world while living on the second bread.

He orders the nuns to give her such fare,

And threatens sternly that nothing be added.

He prepares to return after fulfilling his purpose,

When the pitiable girl cries from the cell:

“My father, listen, for I do not intend to say much.

I beg you, do not depart until you grant what I ask.

Briefly tell me how I should pray to the Maker of the world.”

[Col. 1632B] He said: “The name of Christ, of which you have never been worthy,

Is not safe to bring forth through a polluted mouth;

Let the divine name be foreign to your mouth.

Do not even presume to raise your hands to heaven,

Hands which long, by beguiling fraud, handled abominable things.

Only sit sorrowful, and do not depart from this saying:

‘You who formed me, have mercy, I pray, on me [Note: [Col. 1631] Tours: “on one who prays.”].’

Turning your head and mind toward the east,

Though your mind be weary, never cease to say this.”

After speaking these words, the patriarch departed weeping.

Thais, in darkness intent only on things to come,

Enjoying the bright light, sacrifices herself upon the altar of her heart;

And now she had afflicted herself with great hardships for three years,

1543 When that compassionate Father, pitying her labors,

[Col. 1632C] Seeks to learn whether Christ has granted her forgiveness.

Then he seeks Antony [f. “Then he seeks Antony”], no one of whose religious equal,

From the world’s furthest limits to its utmost bounds, was living.

He tells what he seeks; afterward he learns what he seeks.

For Antony orders all the brothers on the coming night

To strike the ears of the Thunderer with sleepless tears,

Humble care, and holy prayers,

For learning the matter for which Abbot Paphnutius had come,

That God might deign to open to anyone the cause which was closed.

Yet he does not disclose to them what he seeks to learn.

Then Paul, called the Greater, surpassing the rest,

In ecstasy of mind, his course fixed above heaven,

Sees a couch gleaming, adorned with gems,

[Col. 1632D] Spread with purple and altogether delightful to behold,

Which three maidens guarded as though it were a star.

As he marvels, he says these things to himself alone:

“Father Antony, I believe this rest is laid up for you.”

A voice answered, leaving nothing doubtful:

“It is not for him whom you name, but for Thais the harlot.”

1544 When these things had thus been discovered, excellent Paphnutius,

You turn your steps toward Thais; soon you command that she,

Shattered by long suffering in the broken prison, be led out.

As she resists and wishes to cherish her hiding-place,

You console her thus: “Peace be with you; life be with you;

Weep no longer, for you have finished your labors.

[Col. 1633A] Know that all your offenses have been forgiven.”

She answered the Father: “During the time of that dark prison,

In which I always wept, I counted nothing long or burdensome,

In comparison with the number and weight of my sins.

This oppressed me so that it never departed from my mind:

As I bore breath in my nostrils, so I bore guilt in my mind.”

Then the Father said: “This leaves you no punishment,

[Col. 1634A] Because you have repented perfectly with a sorrowful heart;

For a troubled spirit is more pleasing to God

Than flesh perpetually tormented by bitter suffering.

He approves a heart more that is contrite and established in goodness

Than if you continually restrain yourself from every food.”

She lived fifteen days after this,

And thus rested with Christ from this world.

[Col. 1633]

## THE PASSION OF THE HOLY MARTYRS FELIX AND ADAUCTUS

[Col. 1633B] Felix in faith, Felix in deed, a certain Felix by name,

Born and raised at Rome, and a priest by rank,

When persecution had arisen against the Christian name,

Was brought bound before the emperor Diocletian.

Dracus was then prefect, a most wicked idolater,

Who, by command of the king, tortured the bodies of saints.

This charge had been assigned to him on account of his cruelty,

As one who would spare no one and do nothing half-heartedly.

Brought before him by Caesar’s command, holy Felix

Stood before the savage tribunal free from fear.

He alike despised the man’s deceitfully flattering words

And his repeated, terrifying threats.

At length commanded to offer incense to the statue of Serapis,

Whose temple stood beside the prefect’s residence,

When he was thought to be about to offer prayer as a suppliant to the idol,

[Col. 1633C] Prayer which he ought to offer to no one except the Lord alone,

He blew upon the face of the stone image

And overthrew all that had been consecrated to the demon.

Thus he showed false that which the pagans worshipped,

Since their gods fell when a Christian breathed upon them.

Again he was led to the temple of swift Cylenius [“swift Mercury”],

Supposed to be a more powerful god, born of great Jupiter.

For Serapis, born in Egypt, was an alien god,

And was thought less powerful than the Roman deities.

Felix laughed at the caduceus, the sleep-inducing rod;

He laughed also at the winged sandals and golden tiara.

“Let us do,” he said, “what is fitting to Jupiter’s messenger;

Let him be protected neither by the aid of wings nor of rod.”

[Col. 1633D] Therefore the saint blew upon Mercury’s idol,

And by his breath caused the cast statue to fall.

Wonderful to tell! He broke its bronze thigh-bases [f. “and the bronze bases”]

And reduced the abominable image to fragments.

A third time he was led into Diana’s sacred shrine;

He blew upon it as before and overturned the statue,

Broke the bow and arrows, and did not spare the quiver

With which the goddess-huntress ought to have defended herself.

What better thing remained for the attendants to await?

Indeed the remaining gods had more to fear.

He would have overthrown a thousand gods had he blown a thousand times;

Neither armed nor unarmed demons would have escaped.

[Col. 1634B] They return to the prefect and report the events,

And the more they speak to him, the more they arouse his fury.

Felix stands cheerful and calm, with undaunted face,

Desiring to be tortured or sacrificed for the Lord.

Then he is seized and beaten, and mounted upon the rack.

Stretched out, he is torn apart at the prefect’s pleasure.

“Tell me, foul man, tell me, impostor: by what magic arts

Did you destroy the venerable statue of Serapis,

The offspring of Maia’s son, of Jupiter, and Latona’s daughter,

Through whom Rome possesses the monarchy of the whole world?”

“It is not as you say, most foolish prefect,” he answered.

“Rome does not rule through those, nor should you worship them.

For Serapis and Burbastis [Note: [Col. 1633] Perhaps Hercules, called Buraicus from Bura, a city of Achaea in which he was worshipped.] and ruined Osiris

Are plunged deep in hell to be tortured;

Jupiter, Maia’s son, and Latona’s daughter,

[Col. 1634C] Are tortured eternally because of their crimes.

Christ alone, who reigns with the Father and with the Spirit,

Whose power is confined neither by place nor by time,

Must be loved and worshipped as Creator of all,

Through whom Rome holds dominion over the whole world.”

Then the magistrate orders the saint taken down from the rack,

Giving orders to his men according to a silent plan:

“On the Ostian Way, at the second milestone,” he said,

“There is a tree at which sacrifice is made according to the ancient rite.

Let him be led there; and let him persuade himself of one easy matter:

If he scorns our gods, let him worship the tree.”

Felix was led by attendants to sacrifice to the tree

That stood near the temple of a certain image.

Seeing the crowd of unbelieving people gathered round,

[Col. 1634D] He invoked, kneeling, the name of the highest Lord.

Soon he rose and turned toward the abominable tree,

Breathed upon it as was his custom, and drove away the demon:

“Tree, too tall, upheld by hard oak strength,

In the power of Jesus Christ, be uprooted at once;

Falling, break the temple before you, the altars, and the image,

And let human minds no longer be deceived through you.”

Hardly had he finished these words when the huge tree fell

And crushed the temple, tables, altars, and idol.

They return to the prefect, and sad news is announced.

Felix, the accused, is brought forward; a judgment is sought.

1545 Prefect Dracus, cruel dragon and bloody beast,

[Col. 1635A] Groans, twists his jaws, and hisses such words:

“Let the criminal be led back to the tree’s ruins,

And let him stain its roots with the stream of guilty blood;

Let him feel what the wrath of an insulted judge can do,

Receiving in reverse an omen from his own name.

Let birds and beasts devour his beheaded body,

And let him be unworthy of burial, since he refuses to worship the gods.”

The saint was therefore led out to be struck by the sword,

A curious populace rushing together, as is usual.

Behold, a certain Christian came to meet them.

He saw the crowd, saw the bound man, and asked for an explanation.

One of the pagan people recounts what he asked,

Thinking that the spectacle of blood would delight him:

“This priest of Christian superstition,

Despising the gods, the prefect, and the Caesars alike,

[Col. 1635B] Is being led to undergo capital sentence

Before the temple that he overthrew by blowing, through magical art.

Come see; feed your mind upon wicked blood,

Unless [Note: [Col. 1635B] Perhaps *dirum*, “dreadful,” or something similar, is missing.] he can evade the sword’s stroke.”

Hearing this, the Christian cried out boldly:

“I too worship Christ, as does that priest;

I worship your gods no more than unclean cattle,

Nor do I observe the commands of abominable rulers.

May I become a partner in his guilt and a partner in his punishment;

Let not torment separate those united by a like cause.”

Meanwhile he too was seized by impious attendants

[Col. 1636A] And was dragged with Felix to the roots of the tree.

When both stood there, with swords already drawn,

They requested that a short delay be granted them.

Then, lifting their hearts to heaven with knees fixed upon the ground,

They interceded with Christ for their executioners.

Soon rising, they armed themselves with the sign of the cross

And gave each other the kiss of charity.

Thus each prepared his throat for the executioner,

And, their heads cut off, they obtained the prize.

Their bodies, left to beasts and birds,

Were buried by the faithful at night in pits

Which the uprooted great trunk of the tree had excavated,

And which, by God’s will, had opened graves for the saints.

When in the morning some pagans learned this,

1546 They tried to demolish the martyrs’ tombs.

[Col. 1636B] But all who presumed to lay hands there

Were immediately seized by a violent demon.

Thus, at the first time when peace was restored to Christians,

A basilica was made over the bodies of the saints

From stones of the shrine that had been destroyed,

So that God might fulfill what he had ordained.

Here the memorial of the two martyrs is celebrated,

Who obtain many benefits for those who ask.

The first was called Felix; the other lacks a name.

But Christians afterward called this man Adauctus,

Giving him a fitting name from the event,

Because he joined Saint Felix in martyrdom.

[Col. 1635] The Passion ends.

## PRAYER

[Col. 1635C] Holy Felix and Adauctus, precious martyrs,

Who through faith overcame the cruel rulers of the world,

Obtain for me forgiveness of sins,

You who are accustomed to give rain to thirsty earth.

Twice I saw crops dying in drought,

Fields split by thirst, and people despairing.

After your most holy pledges were brought forth,

At once the desired rain came from above.

Again I saw fields swimming in great rains,

Bent crops oppressed by harmful weeds.

[Col. 1636C] After we brought forth your most holy relics,

At once the serenity obtained from heaven shone forth.

You have power to close heaven’s gates

And again, whenever you wish, pour forth abundant rains from them.

Irrigate, I pray, my thirsty soul,

Not with rain but with that grace which cleanses me.

My unworthy pen has served you;

Through you may the Savior of the world be gracious to me.

Amen.

[Col. 1635]

## THE LIFE OF BLESSED MAURILIUS, BISHOP AND CONFESSOR BEGINS

### BOOK ONE

[Col. 1635D] What my Clio attempts to say of Maurilius

Has love as its cause, and ventures beyond her strength;

She hopes for the help of the saint, whom she knows to have pleased the Thunderer.

[Col. 1636D] Let pardon be deserved, because she unfolds the hymn she can,

While she thinks it good to celebrate her patron in verse,

[Col. 1637A] Whose bones the illustrious place of this see covers,

Which he governed with righteous reins for thirty years:

A magnificent bishop, friend of the highest Deity.

Born at Milan while Julian ruled,

Of a distinguished family, but more distinguished in character,

He was given to you, Martin, for discipleship,

And as a boy was keen of intellect in sacred books.

His young, untrained, tender age, remaining in a cell,

Under such a master’s rod and special instruction,

Was imbued with the good things of divine tradition.

1547 He drank none of the filth of worldly allurements,

But, like a pure vessel, like a vessel destined for honor,

He baked into the earthen vessel the sap of honorable virtue.

But the hostile party of the erring crowd, opposed to Catholic Martin,

Now drives him from the city previously mentioned.

[Col. 1637B] The boy, wishing for the same reason to accompany him,

Is held back by the loving prohibition of his parents.

Ambrose, a bishop, seeing in the boy proofs of good character,

Orders him to join the clergy and promises him the superior rank of reader.

But not long afterward the boy’s father died,

Whose force had opposed this young man’s efforts

Lest he sooner undertake what he had long turned over in his heart.

Now free, now having obtained a fitting time,

He leaves his father’s house and does not think of his mother’s kisses.

He scorns worldly wealth, forestalled by zeal to depart.

He rejoices to possess little, because he is weary of riches.

He desires to be poor, because he has broken harmful bonds.

He bears Christ in his mind, and seeks nothing for himself apart from him.

And while he changes his location, he greets no one from his people.

[Col. 1637C] His noble heart rejects carnal affections,

And judges the undertaking of following Martin a matter of equal weight,

Martin now made metropolitan because of his renowned life.

Through mountain ridges and snow he hastens, rich in constancy

Of exceptional mind, though lacking means and food.

He crosses the Alps and reaches the territory of Tours.

Martin rejoices, for the pilgrim was known to him,

Long before made his companion by similar deeds.

For similarity of character binds the hearts of two;

From differing lives springs the discord of conflict.

Wisdom, guardian of life, reconciles the just,

And the wicked agree among themselves in a destructive alliance.

Therefore, pleasing to God, he remained with you, Martin,

Standing fast in commands and in the service of piety.

As time passed, with the unceasing progress of virtues,

[Col. 1637D] He climbed steep heights while always tending toward the furthest goals.

He advances without delay who tends toward inward things,

Thus commended and proved by the tenor of his life.

At the proper time, raised from the lowest steps,

he who as a boy had previously advanced through two ranks,

now, promoted by Martin in the fifth order,

with the seventh office, his full charisma increasing,

was made a priest—though unwilling, and compelled.

Therefore, now endowed with the priestly rank, with all

his strength he hastens to attain the highest coin [i.e. reward],

bearing burden and heat for the gain of that coin,

and digging God’s vineyards from the morning of day.

Nor does he think this enough: he bids you farewell, Martin,

and gives forth groans, departing weeping from one who weeps.

[Col. 1638A] But, fleeing the turmoil of the world, he desires to be hidden,

captivated by the sweetness of the contemplative life.

For great is the labor of enduring worldly tumults,

which he wholly does not know who rests in contemplation.

Therefore he goes down to the neighboring people of Anjou,

that, divinely made an exile, he might become their bishop.

At Calonne stood every kind of image;

there is a place by the Loire called by this name,

made famous by an ancient shrine in profane fashion.

There a foolish people, a nation ignorant of true worship,

offered impious incense, with salvation lost,

to deaf and mute things, and sacrificed with the blood of cattle.

Saint Maurilius, apostle of this region,

when he learned that the shrine and its profane rite remained,

lest the worship of faith, in which he now rejoiced as mature,

[Col. 1638B] should still be corrupted there by the old impiety,

went thither; at once he took up his accustomed arms:

he preaches to the mad, that they should refuse to believe in vanities;

he fasts, weeps, keeps vigil, prostrates himself, and prays.

Soon divine fire serves his worthy prayers,

falling from heaven’s height like hail or like a missile

which, launched, flies and flies back through the cleft air.

Immediately the ancient sanctuary lies burned out.

1548 Avenging flame devours all that the gentile worships.

The divinities of the shrine are mingled with Vulcan’s divinity.

Through heaps of ashes the molten bronze rolls.

Jupiter and Juno are turned together in one stream.

Phoebus and the moon roll together over the ground,

and Venus with her adulterer is dissolved in equal fire.

Mulciber punishes bed-thefts while joining the adulterers.

[Col. 1638C] The remaining accursed images of false gods

deserve a similar ruin under the same lot.

Therefore he cleanses the place, lest extinguished deceit rise again,

and sprinkles the fields to be purified with holy waters;

and there he soon founds a church of God, of no contemptible appearance,

and consecrates it at the people’s request.

He is said to have remained there as inhabitant for twelve years.

All the good deeds he performed there cannot be written.

Yet I shall set forth certain wonders among many miracles.

To a certain Saturninus, who for a long time

had lived with both hands withered, though otherwise sound,

a voice said in a dream: “Aid is at hand for the injury to your hands;

behold, power is granted you to bear them full rather than empty.

A holy man of Italian blood, inhabitant of the village

called Calonne, will remove every kind of your affliction from you,

[Col. 1638D] will sign your hands, and you will immediately be well.

Now hasten on your way, setting aside tardy delays.”

The man rises quickly, desiring to obtain what was promised,

and comes to the saint. He not only speaks prayers,

but pours forth tears; nor does he withdraw his withered limbs.

He recounts the words spoken to him from heaven, and further asks

that, as the sign had said, he may impress upon him the sign of the cross.

Maurilius, not doubting, but always avoiding

the deceit of merit—that is, receiving worldly praise

for what he could presently grant the petitioner—

gives himself no credit, but postpones it until the next day,

unwilling to seem able to give an immediate result.

Throughout the whole night he does not cease to pour out prayers.

In the morning he touches the hands and thus drives out every affliction;

[Col. 1639A] he touches the hands in the morning, and the sick man is immediately healed.

By the merits of the saint pouring out vows to the Thunderer,

through Christ’s standard the illness departed from him.

There is another sign worthy to be celebrated in song,

and after it many more wonders will be related like this one.

A certain woman, given as prey to a savage demon,

was living under twofold punishment, weighed down with chains;

and, beneath this burden, deprived also of both lights [her eyes],

she is led to the saint, dragged by the hands of those entreating him

to cleanse the wretched woman whom the demon’s assault presses.

As soon as he sees her, the terrified demon immediately departs.

Then, touching and signing the blind woman’s eyes, behold:

by the power of the cross the gifts of light are restored

to closed eyelids and to the darkness of the pupils.

Thus in one person he performed two miracles,

[Col. 1639B] while he drives away the hostile being and by prayer restores sight.

While a keeper of sheep, vigilant through the nocturnal hours,

was traveling with companions, he was struck by a serpent’s bite.

The dreadful snake had poured venom into him with the wound;

his diseased skin drew swelling in the manner of wine-skins,

and the pus poured in took away the body’s use.

The devoted faith of his companions presents the half-dead boy

to the saint, whom the distressed crowd now throngs.

He protects each limb of the boy with frequent signs of the cross,

where the wicked pestilence had corrupted the swollen veins;

and, with a cross and with spittle healing together, he loosens

and soothes the mouth of the wound; immediately the cruel infection ceases.

For—marvelous to say—the venom enclosed in the veins

seeks the wound in the act of piercing and is poured back out.

The shepherd goes away joyful, changing tears into gladness.

[Col. 1639C] The womb of a matron from a neighboring district,

long shut, had disappointed the hope of offspring,

forcing the sad pair to sleep in a barren bed.

Both were sufficiently wealthy and of no small nobility;
the husband lacked an heir to succeed him;

1549 she, however, was very diligent in the worship of the Deity,

that by the Lord’s good pleasure she might become fruitful for her husband.

For many five-year periods she had persisted vainly in prayers.

Therefore with vows she knocks at the merciful heart of the priest,

and with a sorrowful heart addresses Christ’s servant:

“What does the light of dawn profit me, servant of God?

What the course of night, when anxiety tortures me anew?

For whom, rising in the morning, do I toil about the marriage-bed?

What are house and servants? What the abundant yield of the field?

[Col. 1639D] What is the value of silver’s splendor to one lacking an heir?

You, holy man, who are accustomed to obtain by prayers

whatever great things you ask, cause a male child to be born to me,

born for the Creator, soon to be given back to his Giver.

Be to me an Eli; let the child be to me as Samuel,

while as a boy he will soon begin to serve at the altar.”

Maurilius, moved by her vows and tears,

prays and obtains her prayer. The woman becomes pregnant and goes into labor;

she bears a boy, and returns to you, Christ, the one she had borne,

to remain all his life, in accordance with his mother’s vow.

Report says that this gift was Renatus,

who afterward held the aforesaid episcopate.

Those who went before us tell wonders concerning him,

which I think ought to be reported, nor do I deny that they were true;

but when the time comes. The earlier order calls for what follows:

[Col. 1640A] There is a place called Prisciac Hill from ancient time,

so named because of the charge it had incurred:

images full of evils of demonic worship

were deceiving some of the uncultivated people.

While the Lord’s soldier sought to win his master’s gain,

desiring to overthrow the deception for Christ’s praise,

he takes with him as many as he judges fitting to lead,

and hastens to the hill which the hostile party had filled.

At once the opposing voice of imprisoned demons

raises an outcry and complains: “Is no place found

where, Maurilius, we may hang you cheaply?

Where may we defend ourselves, since we are put to flight at your coming?

From here too you drive us out—fierce, violent, rebellious man!”

Against them he casts the cross with his avenging right hand;

immediately every superstitious thing, driven out, flees,

[Col. 1640B] and as the phantom host flees, its trumpet bellows.

The stench testifies that the foul crowd is put to flight.

The saint orders the idols gathered and then burned.

Then he cleanses the place; immediately he founds new halls,

and orders the church of God to be the sign of victory.

The harshness of a quartan fever shakes Clement’s body

with repeated chills on the fourth day,

and so each fourth day wears down his tormented limbs,

that for three days he cannot repair the harm done.

For illness of the stomach rejects Ceres’ gifts and Bacchus’ offerings,

and all food has become loathsome to him.

For three years the monk, ravaged by these afflictions,

lies rolling in bed, unable to go beyond the roof;

his limbs wasted, hope of recovery is already removed,

and his neighbors’ sole expectation is the end.

[Col. 1640C] Remembering doctors, the friends of the languishing monk

carry him, bed and body, into Maurilius’ presence,

whether for one who would live badly or perhaps soon die.

Maurilius, more swiftly than speech, conquering illness or death,

postpones funeral rites while he bestows blessed bread,

making the sufferer from quartan fever sound through a divine gift.

A trader, for the sake of profit putting aside all that is honorable,

desiring to gain by any means from a matter of equal chance,

a Croesus through usury and selling everything at a higher price,

had gone to purchase captive Iberian boys.

One of their number, inexperienced and unable to endure labors,

making his way, fled for refuge into the holy church,

where the gentle man was pouring forth tears with prayer.

[Col. 1640D] Trusting in the holy man’s renown, he believed he could either not be claimed,

or might be released by a plea, or redeemed for a price;

for the priest’s fame, known in remote lands,

could appear precious even to the boy’s master.

1550 Therefore he begs weeping and adores him prostrate,

that in whatever way he wishes he may free him from this knot.

At this the saint laments, because the distress that afflicts him

shows, through a familiar language, that he is his fellow-countryman.

He offers silver, desiring to free him by ransom.

The man dear to God supplicates, implores, and labors much and long;

the greedy merchant refuses. At last he orders the captive,

as a fugitive, to be beaten, and, by cruel command violating the sanctuary, led away.

[Col. 1641A] The saint grieved, and such zeal came upon him

because the temple’s violation was an exceedingly grave example,

that the ardor of zeal sought heaven’s heights.

For as soon as he turned his mind to the Almighty

and, lying upon the ground, gave forth a groan and prayed,

an impious death, witness to heavenly wrath,

fell upon the violator, a manifest avenger of his rage;

and so that wretched man fell by sudden destruction.

The rest of the trembling crowd asks the saint mercifully

to spare him and grant the lifeless man to see life’s threshold—

twice condemned, by death and by guilt.

Fearing lest the man’s soul be submerged without end,

he stretches himself bent upon the ground, to loose death’s bonds by prayer.

I tell a marvelous thing, but one consonant with truth:

[Col. 1641B] powerful prayer, overcoming the dominion of death,

by the Lord’s nod recalls one already released from flesh.

The saint rises from the ground; the body rises from death.

The captive rejoices, free and restored to life together;

joyfully they give offerings for the crime of having spurned the temple.

While a sailor, bearing a great and enormous burden,

strives to propel a vessel toward Angers—

labor which is customarily unceasing on the Loire—

behold, a dreadful storm stirs troublesome causes:

the sky darkens; gradually the heavy wave swells;

the wind bears down; the crew trembles among the benches;

the united force of sail and ropes cannot restrain the wind,

and mast and broken yards are carried away by the river.

The master’s hand can no longer command the tiller;

[Col. 1641C] now the wave has nearly swallowed the hull full of water;

the whirlwind spins the craft; fear breaks every heart.

Only Maurilius is called upon by the mournful voice of those at sea,

and, summoned, he who is pleasing to God hastens to be present.

Standing outside on the riverbank, he signs them with his right hand.

The storm ceases: manifest is the power of the cross.

At faith’s command the serene hour of day returns;

the ship rises, and at once a sweet breeze blows,

bringing to harbor and to a new beginning from death’s threshold

all whom but lately you could have mourned as almost dead.

It was the custom of this saint whose praises I sing

to visit all the sick through villages and fields,

or to recite sacred homilies in churches,

and faithfully to serve the Lord of heaven by the word.

[Col. 1641D] And lest he be less able to do this or fall silent, exhausted by labor,

since constrained by the need for modest sustenance,
he kept a colt of a she-ass for the service of the saddle;
[Col. 1642A] he knew nothing of controlling hard mouths with gilded bits.

High upon proud horses’ backs he scorned

the resisting quadrupeds,

preferring to ride a colt with no pride at all,

surely taught in this by Christ’s example.

When an accursed thief tried to steal it by night,

seized by a demon, the fool knows not where he is going.

For while he believes himself moving forward, he returns in circles;

and—marvelous to tell—he cannot escape this circuit.

In the morning, after labors prolonged through the night, he stands before the doors,

forced before the holy threshold to disclose his crime.

He presents the stolen animal, and, mad, tries to depart,

trembling lest he who is held captive should be cured.

To him, though unworthy, after first driving out the hostile evil one,

1551 Maurilius pardons the crime and then gives three coins,

[Col. 1642B] believing that poverty compelled him to this deed.

What good mercy of the saint grants to one committing wickedness,

multiplying the enemy’s crime with compounded interest:

the thief, giving back the ass, receives threefold for the single animal,

enriched with gold, safe and free of guilt.

Physicians said that a certain Amelina could by no means be helped;

her friends were grieved, and anxious concern for burial had already grown.

She was exalted by a line of proud ancestors,

rich in possessions, mistress of her own person, yet powerless over her body.

For already twelve years she had been ill,

so that the more was done, the more medicine harmed her.

The sorrowful household wept because she lay in despair.

[Col. 1642C] Then it came to her mind that he who performed wonders was not absent,

and, trusting in the man’s prayer, that she could obtain health.

“Your art,” she says to the physicians, “leaves me without hope;

but now, though late, I seek better aid.

Go,” she says to her people, “for extinguished hope has revived.

Run swiftly, I beg you; tell the gentle patron

that he may deign to visit one afflicted and abandoned without any helper,

because he often heals by visiting.

He who is accustomed to visit everyone—will he not visit me?”

That I may not be made dull through empty prolixity:

they run, summon him, and soon return with him as he comes.

He prays lying on the ground; he rises after not many prayers;

he hastens to the bed, and the sick woman now hopes for better.

The physician anoints her; immediately the cruel illness flees.

Anointed once with consecrated ointment, she rises from the couch.

[Col. 1642D] Thus far I have written what Maurilius did before he received the episcopate;

may it be pleasing to him, I pray.

The rest should be reserved for a better writer.

# BOOK II

[Col. 1641]

[Col. 1641D] While I sing Saint Maurilius in a rich poem,

my reed, as if a marsh reed, recounts the praises of the illustrious man.

But because he is devout and I have the right to sing to him—

namely, as his own child, whom he deigned, from boyhood,

to nourish after joining me to the clergy and to raise by teaching me as a young man—

[Col. 1642D] at least I offer you the rich service of my tongue;

may it repay affection in place of a gift, as I reckon what is hidden.

If I could do better, I would be ashamed of this offering.

While the confessor’s renowned praise shone everywhere through frequent miracles,

in no virtue inferior,

[Col. 1643A] by divine will he was taken from the people of Anjou,

compelled to depart in death.

Crowds gather, as happens in a city made widowed.

The sacred order, the people, and the senate

deliberate in seeking a replacement bishop,

who among the clergy may be judged worthy.

One favors age; another favors nobility;

this man recommends a clientage, that one eloquence;

someone extols riches in unjust words;

but no one, at last, morals or spiritual qualities.

Thus, when many interests collide,

praise is not granted to one person by common vote.

But at last Saint Martin, hastening to the same cause,

the metropolitan, decides the disputes.

As the crowd murmurs, he settles the parties thus in speech:

[Col. 1643B] “Why do you, beloved brothers, wish by foolish wishes

to change a settled matter? Heavenly things cannot be bent.

God rejects human praise as vain.

The King who rules all things has already chosen a bishop for himself.

Maurilius is appointed bishop of this see.”

Heaven’s decree at once restrains the assembly.

One voice of approval follows the judge’s word.

Without delay the envoys hasten to the blessed man’s dwelling,

presenting one snatched away as fit for the sacred altars.

At his entrance a white dove, gliding in gentle flight,

gave signs by settling upon him.
