1552 Again, at this sign, the people acclaim him worthy of the office,

purified by so great an indication of the Holy Spirit.

The supreme Father once did the same at the gentle Jordan’s water

in the Baptist’s time, O Christ—

what the King of Heaven himself does now for his own faithful servant.

Thus consecrated to the height of episcopal office,

he remained more humble while continually advancing to better things.

How many signs the Almighty’s favor then exalted him by,

and how great they were, no voice of recitation can tell.

For to give sight to the blind, by prayer strength of movement to the lame,

speech to the mute, power to loosened limbs to the paralyzed,

to open the passage of voice to ears deprived of it,

and, cleansing the skin, to grant healing from leprosy—

these were as easy for him as bestowing a present gift

[Col. 1643C] from the rich treasury of his own merits.

Bodies dead to their former life were restored.

Yet I shall relate a few, seeking to dispel tedium.

Returning in the morning from Saint Peter’s basilica,

where, watchful, he had passed the whole sleepless night,

he met a man blind from birth, who begged

that he give the use of light to his sightless eyes.

Unfamiliar with delay, though his face was flushed,

because he did not wish to be acclaimed by popular voice,

as soon as he signs him, the cross unseals his closed eyes:

a new sun shone, because night fled with blood.

On the following day, while he performs the sacrament,

standing at the altar where it is customary to offer sacrifice,

behold, a mother, with tears born from fear of death, standing there,

prays for her son, suddenly overcome by illness,

that after the font he may seal his brow with chrism.

[Col. 1644A] Lest grace be lacking to the stricken child,

he, intent upon the altar, wishes to continue the sacred rites;

and while he makes delays, cruel death strikes the boy.

When the sacred rites are completed, sorrow follows joy:

for who could fail to weep thus at the boy’s fall?

He groans and grieves more than the woman who wept for her own child.

He does not wish to consider such guilt pardonable to himself,

although it could have been excused by his devotion to the Mass.

Amid these anxieties he decides to depart secretly,

an exile and pilgrim, that he may more greatly expiate this deed.

Alone he hastens to Ocean and the British shore,

bearing the keys of holy relics.

Waiting, therefore, for the winds by which England is reached,

[Col. 1644B] he inscribed a few things in metrical characters upon a stone:
who he was and whither he hastened to direct his journey.

God in his providence willed this inscription to be placed on the stone,

that the fugitive might be more clearly known, in whatever nation he lay hidden.

Now he boards the vessel; now the wind spreads the sails;

now he cuts through the deep sea; now his course leaves the lands behind,

when the deceit of the ancient evil one, never ceasing,

adds a burden to his first tears through the misfortunes that follow.

For while the fugitive asks himself why he had carried the keys,

and reflects, turning many things over in his mind,

the grievous keys slip into the waters as he weeps.

Then, truly sorrowful, he binds himself with these words:

“I shall not turn my course, nor see my places again,

until the keys sunk in the waters are returned from there.

The lost key has closed Angers’ gates against me;

[Col. 1644C] when the key returns, then our return will take place.”

Now, after the sea-course had been completed and harbor reached,

the fugitive bishop considers how to remain concealed,

with clothing changed and his rank also disguised.

He places himself in service to one of the nobles,

to please his lord by humble service at table.

He becomes keeper of vegetables, fleeing lofty things,

glad to tend vegetables so that he may live alone,

1553 standing far from the crowds and acquaintances of the city.

The man of holy lot rightly occupies himself in gardens,

that there may cleave to his mind a memorial of this place,

from which he who raised himself above the heavens arose.

While he thus lay hidden as an exile in distant lands,

the people of Anjou groan with immeasurable lamentation,

[Col. 1644D] like prey delivered to wolves or a ship without a helmsman.

But the supreme Shepherd gives help in their desolation,

restraining the wolves’ savagery.

Meanwhile, an image shown in sleep to many

threatens the town with destruction by night,

unless the saint returns bringing relief from their mourning;

it orders that he be sought until he can be found.

The assembly of nobles obeys the command.

Four are chosen and judged fit to depart from the city.

They seek their patron and traverse regions’ places,

nor do they bring their undertaking to an end until their father is recovered.

With the people’s assent, expenses are allotted to the young men.

They fly through lands, avoiding neither hard nor rough places;

they search cities and wander through fields and villages,

yet he whom they seek does not appear where he lay hidden.

[Col. 1645A] They had sought almost all Europe in pursuit of their desire.

Now the fruitless labor of the journey had occupied six years;

the seventh year orders them to go to Ocean, to Britain,

that they might cross the sea if perhaps they found the man.

But why prolong delay? They come to the shore,

and find the writing which, as we said above, he had left.

They rejoice in sure hope, as though the drachma had already been found;

they board the ship and make for the English by sea.

Suddenly a fish leaps from the water into the air

and falls into the ship, carrying the key in its belly.

Whereupon, rejoicing, they draw the keys from the cut-open fish’s belly,

and become sad again,

thinking that he for whom they had changed places so often had perished;

for they recognized the keys and therefore mourned him as if dead.

[Col. 1645B] But a vision confirms their minds, fearing vainly,

urging them neither to doubt nor desist from their undertaking,

but to seek until they find him without doubt.

Made cheerful by this, soon driven across the sea by waves,

they come directly to the famous house of the nobleman

to whom Maurilius rendered welcome service,

giving gifts of vegetables each day after the meal.

When the envoys catch sight of him coming,

they leap forth, cast themselves down, and, eyes and hands raised,

embrace his feet and fill the house with these words:

“Best of shepherds, at last have pity on your own!

Why do we endure punishment? Why does the neglected people perish?

For what sin of your own will you not see your own threshold?

Your sorrowful city groans because misfortune has taken you from it.

Since you are gentle, do not despise such great tears.

[Col. 1645C] Now, holy bishop, let the sorrowful receive consolation;

restore to your people the laughter cut off by your departure.

Return, holy one, to your own; restore yourself to your empty see.

By angelic guidance, with the sea’s wave also serving,

Christ’s command has brought us to this land.

And lest you choose to doubt, receive the signs of the faithful word:

behold the lost keys; we return them to you.”

When they had spoken thus and openly laid down the keys,

and related what had been said or done,

the blessed man, overcome by so many signs, consented.

Those present weep as they behold the unexpected sight,

and marvel that so great a man should be sought in such poverty.

Report summons the peoples dwelling throughout the surrounding places,

frequently recounting in speech the praises of the man found:

[Col. 1645D] that a great bishop had lain hidden, small and exiled.

With gifts, the people of the whole region run together;

even the king of the land hastens to bring presents.

All desire to see the man hitherto unknown.

Thus, rich in gifts, he accompanies the citizens to the sea;

and, after the sea has been crossed, he is worthily received

far away by the people’s meeting and regains his former home.

1554 What a throng, what cries of joy then arose,

what thanks they gave—no poet can tell.

Yet he did not first set foot in his own dwelling

before he sought the tomb that held the boy’s limbs.

Trusting in the Lord, who had appeared to him in dreams and said:

“Permission is granted you to recall the buried one,

for whom you have mourned so justly through seven harvests after death.”

The earth-bank having been cast down with picks and the tomb uncovered,

[Col. 1646A] he prays prostrate and lingers long in prayer.

At last the boy rose and came forth from the tomb,

bearing from the mausoleum the trophy of victory over death.

He orders that the one anointed with chrism be called Renatus, “Reborn,”

lest frail age be able to set bounds to the deed.

Thus we believe that the lives of a thousand thousand men who have died

are restored even after a thousand years.

What fruits he afterward bore at the Lord’s command when restored,

what evils he suppressed, or what miracles he performed,

no mouth can utter, for they cannot be numbered;

I note a few, known beyond doubt.

A peasant dared this, whom greedy avarice had filled,

at the solemn season to cut down wood with a two-edged axe;

desiring profanely to free his bound hands,

[Col. 1646B] he was held fast by the avenging wood in deserved punishment.

When the saint learned, after five months of groaning, the force of this torment,

he removed it by healing touch,

restoring the contracted sinews to their former functions.

A man of Belgium dared the same thing and felt the same at the same season,

how grievous it is to violate God’s feast of Easter.

For on the holy day, devoted against right to fieldwork,

he compelled his servants to go and clear the crops.

Immediately God’s wrath blinds the man who violates the law of the day,

because he sins with a blind heart.

Tortured by these punishments for thirty-six months,

at last he is compelled to seek the same remedy.

He orders his friends to bring him the bishop’s garment;

when he is quickly touched with it, his eyes are made bright.

This too can rightly be numbered among the miracles:

[Col. 1646C] that by the bishop’s merit the harmony of peace

bound the people of Anjou throughout the whole time he lived.

Prosperity too was so established in his life

that the price of a measure of grain did not rise by a bronze coin,

and a measure of wine could always be had;

the fertility of the year, joined with enduring peace,

filled the people’s granaries from bountiful fields.

Moreover, retaining a trophy against the enemy,

the village of Comonicus learned what the Lord’s friend could do.

On a high rock stood an infection of ancient rite:

there was a grove of Mars, which the people had been accustomed to celebrate

for many years after wine with mad slaughter,

turning the guilt of quarrel and killing into destiny.

When the saint learned this, he hastened to the grove;

[Col. 1646D] and while he prayed to the Lord during one fasting night,

at cockcrow he drove away the hosts of demons.

The odor of the fleeing beings makes the bystanders’ nostrils sad.

In the morning he orders the wood cut down, and that no one depart

until fire set beneath the logs devours the oaks.

Then a church of God promptly rises in place of the trophy;

the place, purified by flames, is called Chaste Rock.

At the same time, returning to the city of Le Mans,

he performed great miracles to the Lord’s praise.

There is a bridge not far away; the neighborhood calls it Leuge.

There a boy of pitiable appearance was presented to him,

his limbs contracted and forced by illness’s rigidity

to have his twisted body in the form of a sphere.

After the holy man spoke, God uncoiled him,

and the bonds of torment were loosened by powerful prayer.

[Col. 1647A] As the saint thereafter came to the harbor of Lydda,

no boatman was present, and the river had filled its highest shallows.

A third cause of delay: boats were held far off

on the farther bank. Suddenly they moved themselves,

with ready service, without oar and without pole,

1555 and, having received the man—more marvelous still—

returned, carrying him and his companions by themselves.

Yet, out of gratuitous kindness, he orders the fare to be repaid

to the boatman, who was preparing it a little later.

While he was staying at Gerziac, on an estate

which he had bought for the use of the brethren,

he drove away, by sacred power, a demon changed into the form

of a dark raven from a horned ox,

forcing it, by the cross’s constraint, to come out bloody.

The heifer returns sound and harms no one thereafter.

[Col. 1647B] Carried along the river as he travels after departing the city,

he lies in the boat and sleeps a sweet sleep,

wearied by vigils and by fasting endured.

Suddenly, the river released into conflict,

the threatening Mayenne stirs war against peace.

Waves rise; crash and tumult arise;

a great terror of winds infects the men’s faces.

Though strong, the saint is shaken by fear of death and wakes;

for disturbance, lamentation,

and the force of shouting broke the secrecy of his sleep.

Having signed the river and taken consecrated liquid,

he sprinkled the waves and repressed the storm;

liquid was poured from a flask, and the tempest was conquered.

A certain pitiable child of grieving parents,

already catechized but not yet reborn at the font,

[Col. 1647C] alas, lay dead outside and damned within.

One part had yielded to the bier, the other to the abyss.

When the sad bishop learned of this misfortune,

he runs swiftly to undo the sudden funeral.

Arriving at the bed, he orders all to leave the house;

kneeling, he strives by tears to bring back the breath taken away

from the very jaws of Erebus.

[Col. 1648A] Nor was there tardy delay: scarcely had an hour passed

when the return to life restored both the body to the bier and breath to it.

Therefore, after mourning, he gives joy to all,

the youth returned from death, washed in holy baptism.

A little later, likewise, the same most holy man orders twin persons

defiled by leprosy to go away cleansed by his word.

An ancient village, Saponaria, lies near the Loire.

When, having departed from it, he sought to return, weary, to the city walls

after visiting all the districts around,

whose welfare had been the reason for his journeys,

behold: his sad neighbors, mindful of his destiny,

weep the final death and lament the misfortune of the stranger.

The confessor’s praise had previously called him, renowned for holy life,

out of his native region,

that he might become better when he saw the bishop’s old age;

but the Fate envied him and cut the threads of life.

[Col. 1648B] The holy bishop is present while the dead exile is mourned;

standing nearby, he pays the dead man his due rites,

and with solemn prayer offers vows to the eternal Lord.

Suddenly, the known law of fates removed,

the buried man raises his face as the people watch,

and the guest for whom he had come sees him safe.

The crowds cry out that no greater shepherd in the world

should be judged equal to Elisha, God himself bearing witness.

Distinguished by such and so great signs at the Thunderer’s preceding nod,

a man worthy of psalm and hymns,

and abundantly enriched with the fullness of a pure life,

when he had already reached ninety years,

at the completed time when what is owed yields to death,

he committed to earth what mother earth had produced.

His vital breath, a spiritual substance,

[Col. 1648C] on the Ides of September, stripped of mortal limbs,

did not know death but lives forever in heaven.

The grace of miracles accompanies him freed from flesh:

two blind from birth were restored by touching the bier

at the sacred funeral, and one paralytic.

Nor is any suppliant disappointed who prays

at his shrine, if only he asks a just thing.

[Col. 1647]

# VARIOUS POEMS OF MARBOD, BISHOP OF RENNES. (G)*

## I. First Hymn concerning Magdalene

[Col. 1647D]

Mary, mother of the Lord, and Mary, Lazarus’s sister,

are two patronesses bestowed from heaven upon the faithful.

The handmaid is unequal to the Lady, but shines with an equal name.

This one is the model of repentance; that one the mother of pardon.

That one is the virgin of virgins, chief of all saints;

this one, conscious of sins and favorable to criminals.

Mary gave birth to the feet which the other, weeping, held.

Because she loved exceedingly, she is cleansed from the stain of sins.

[Col. 1648D] Most wretched, clinging to the ground, she embraces the footprints;

the streams she poured from her eyes she dries with devout kisses.

A wondrous dignity accrued to her merit:

she poured ointment of genuine nard upon the Lord’s head.

The praise of this deed will live as far as the world’s boundaries,

in agreement with the Gospel, the Lord himself bearing witness.

The risen Lord first revealed himself to her,

making a woman once infamous an apostle.

Praise be to the unbegotten Father and to his Only-begotten,

[Col. 1649A] with the Paraclete Spirit, neither begotten nor unbegotten.

## II. Second Hymn concerning the Same

All who are unclean, run: the fountain of pardon stands open.

Let none despair of forgiveness who observes repentance.

The Son of God showed sinners an example:

Mary, a vessel of filth, full of sevenfold disgrace,

once none more shameful, now scarcely any holier,

who washed Christ’s feet and soon afterward anointed his head.

Christ abhors no one; God does not despise a human being.

Let us give him thanks by pouring forth devout tears;

let us dry with our hair the feet which the Lord bares;

from our superfluous wealth let us minister to the poor.

[Col. 1649B] He who grants pardon will increase grace for us.

May our Church be fragrant with our perfume;

may this most holy sinner drive our sins away;

may her prayer be for us an abundance of virtues.

Praise be to the unbegotten Father, etc.

## III. Third Hymn concerning the Same

A certain sinful woman, the last of the Church,

freed from the burden of flesh, ascends to heaven today.

Let those who celebrate her departure recount her entrance,

to the praise of the highest Lord, who bestows so much upon mankind.

God clothed as man was sitting with Simon;

grieving and weak, she approached the physician’s footsteps.

From great longing came this boldness,

[Col. 1649C] that the harlot should touch him whom the Virgin Mother bore.

What she wished she kept silent in speech, but expressed in tears;

with kisses and hair she prayed for her sins.

She interceded with ointment when she did not dare to do so with speech,

giving offense to the Pharisee but sacrifice to God.

For this she departed, loosed from the bond of all sins,

he himself granting pardon, who had pronounced the sentence.

Praise be to the Father, etc.

## IV. Prayer to the Father

Uncreated Lord and Ruler of all creation,

first source of the movements of things, blessed and immortal,

one power, one splendor, in whom there is neither more nor less,

one God, three persons, a threefold name, one being,

[Col. 1649D] who from mud made the first father, and from the father the first mother,

and then from these two propagated the whole human race,

and breathed down into them minds from heaven,

so that they might know what ought to be followed and follow what they knew:

Grant me, my God, my Maker and Restorer,

that, mindful of its origin, my mind may follow you, good guide,

and may run gladly after you, drawing the body after itself;

may it walk in your commandments, so that it may never fall utterly.

Therefore I ask for a sound mind and one loving discipline,

[Col. 1650A] and, together with mental health, bodily soundness.

You, shaper of both, give what is fitting to each.

We are inclined to sin, and earth returns to earth.

Support our fall by your sweet mercy.

1558 What is man, Adam’s offspring, a shoot of death worthy of destruction?

What is man but a worm, a weak thing, a defenseless thing?

Do not deign to be angry with one who cannot be born clean.

Do not, God, condemn one who cannot avoid sinning.

It is not just to judge the creature; it is not fitting for you;

miserable man is not of such worth that he should answer to the Thunderer.

[Col. 1650B] Like shadow, like smoke, like grass we have been made.

Have mercy, triune God; have mercy, have mercy.

## V. Prayer to the Son

Jesus Christ our God, good shepherd and teacher,

you who, though you were in the form of God,

equal to your Father,

for humankind’s salvation put on the garment of flesh

and came forth from the virgin womb as a bridegroom.

Thus you lived in the old condition of flesh without stain,

so that you might both fulfill the work and give us an example.

The work, I say, of mercy, surpassing the disposition of the mind:

harassed by insults and lifted upon the cross,

by your death you destroyed the laws of universal death;

you slept, you rose, you ascended above the heavens.

From there you will come at the end to judge what you made,

rendering what is deserved for deeds with the restoration of flesh.

[Col. 1650C] God-man Jesus Christ, have mercy on the wretched;

God-man, king of heaven, have mercy on the wretched.

Though guilty and transgressing, the confessor of this faith

twice entreats you, Jesus Christ, name above every name,

that, as you yourself teach and command, you may forgive these sins

to one confessing them and grant those virtues to one who longs for them,

as you yourself teach and admonish—[the supplied source ends here].

To gird up our loins and keep our lamps burning.

When you command that virtues be sought, which you call the kingdom of God, grant that we may seek what you command, and so command what we are to do.

Among all that I ask, there is one thing for which I sigh, which I desire especially and request by name:

[Col. 1650D] Against the corruption of the flesh I beg from you a remedy; through your mercy grant me chastity, and knowledge both of myself and of you, insofar as human capacity allows.

To those from whom you willed that I should be born according to the flesh, and to all their ancestors reckoned backwards, grant, rich God, life among your citizens. Make my brothers and sisters sharers in these gifts.

Save all my kindred joined to me, merciful God; make all who live faithfully, or have died faithful, enjoy everlasting rest without fear of its end.

Let there be praise to the eternal Father, and to the coeternal Son; to you, the Spirit of both, let equal praise be given with each of them. Amen.

## VI. Prayer to God

[Col. 1651A]

When I remember with what care I pursued things that perish, and how harshly death, under its rule, exercises its rights, in my inward self—which lies open to God alone—I roar like a lion and weep for my sins.

When I remember that I must pass through the hard path of death, and what will become of me after that pure examination, anxious in the turmoil of a mind lacking the cultivation of virtues, with sad heart and sorrowful face I pour out prayers with sobbing;

1559 With sobbing I pour out prayers, bend my knee, beat my breast, speak with trembling mouth, and cry to you from the depths.

[Col. 1651B] Jesus Christ, Son of God, consubstantial with him, maker of night and day, I beg you: have mercy on me. Through the bite of the first parent I fell, and thereafter the sins we commit individually weigh down our backs.

Through the second mother, the restorer of the world, reverse the ancient condition, washing the body and [read: the mind] . . .

Let there be praise to Christ, praise to the Father, and praise also to the eternal [read: eternal Spirit] . . .

May they protect us from the black punishments of the abyss.

## VII. Prayer to Saint Mary

O holy Virgin of virgins, who bore the Lord,

[Col. 1651C] the conqueror of the devil, the restorer of the world: I, a most sinful man, ask you for a remedy. Be patroness, salvation, and defense to one in misery.

Enemies press upon me from every side, seeking the death of my soul: perverse human beings without, malignant demons within. Already many wounds have been inflicted upon me, O Lady! Unless you heal them, they will be the cause of my death.

I consented to enemies urging me toward mortal sin; for this I am held guilty, and I confess my fault. For the five senses of the body have become gates of sin: desiring beauty through sight, loving what is pleasant through touch, I gladly heard shameful things and joyfully told frivolous ones; I repeatedly filled my nostrils with unlawful scents; I delighted too much in sweet food and drink.

[Col. 1651D] I sinned through pride and vain glory; I was polluted by perjury and defiled by idleness; through unjust lying I deceived my neighbor [often]; and from the plunder of the poor I amassed most wicked profit.

I served anger and avarice as though they were my mistresses; in body or soul I committed every crime. For what the body could not accomplish, the mind wished to perpetrate.

A shameful thought, a pestilent utterance, guilt for my deeds, and the wickedness known to my conscience condemn me. These things I now confess to you, holier than all saints! Take up my cause; rescue one deserving punishment.

[Col. 1652A] Entreat your Son to give me a remedy. Born of your flesh, he will favor your prayers, and can deny nothing to the mother who bore him.

By his birth, by his fast, by the harsh insults, scourges, spittings, and blows which he freely endured, he who offered himself for us; by the scarlet garment and the crown of thorns;

by the nails, by the cross, by the scars of the wounds, by the opening of the side, by the stream of sacred blood; by the holy Eucharist and the grace of baptism; by the sacraments of faith which I have learned while believing with my heart: I implore you, most merciful one, to obtain pardon, that Christ’s Passion may be remission of my sins, and his Resurrection an increase of virtues. Amen.

## VIII. Prayer to the Mother of the Lord

[Col. 1652B]

[Note: [Col. 1651D] Note here the exact repetition of rhythm at the beginning, middle, and end of the verses.]

Star of the sea, who alone bear offspring without a spouse, the bright sun of righteousness, surpassing all things in beauty;

a fitting jewel, a newly born rose perfect in loveliness,

1560 honey enclosed in hollow combs, transformed in taste:

your nourishing fragrance surpasses every kind of odor [Note: [Col. 1652D] Perhaps a metrical or sonic license: *odos* for *odor*.];

your grace exceeds the flowers which spring unfolds.

God conceived bodily floods you, chaste one; rising, suffering, and dying, he cleanses us of sin.

That he might draw the wretched to the heights, the exalted one came down to the depths; while death dies, the first created being is delivered.

This was an exceedingly extraordinary thing for you, holy woman: the Father’s image came forth through your virginal womb.

[Col. 1652C] This sex ordinarily feels shameful embraces, so that from equal seeds it may bring forth beings destined for tears.

But you, pregnant in your womb while preserving modesty, bring forth the Lord of light and giver of life.

Mother of the child who bears light, the world adores you; devotedly it honors you with prayers and songs.

After the Lord, you are the hope of human beings: remove the punishment of Gehenna from the mind conscious of sin, which is defiled through Venus’s contagions; grant that the devout may dwell forever in the Elysian fields.

## IX. On the Twelve Patriarchs

Judah stands first in order, “confessor” or “praise”; Reuben, “seeing the son,” is called second; Gad, “girded” or “temptation,” is third;

[Col. 1652D] Asher is fourth, whose name itself means “blessed”; Naphtali, the son, we must put fifth; Manasseh is sixth, “forgetfulness” or “compelled”; Simeon is placed seventh, called “dwelling”; Levi, the eighth name, means “addition”;

Issachar is “reward,” whom you ought to place ninth; Zebulun is tenth, called “strong dwelling-place”; Joseph is eleventh, worthy of the name “increase”; Benjamin is “son of the right hand,” and is last.

## X. Hymn on Priests

While the faithful celebrate the venerable feasts of priests with solemn worship,

[Col. 1653A] this honor redounds to your praise, supreme Priest.

By your gift the saints were able to mock the world’s pride and fleeting riches, and the tenacious snares of pleasures.

Nor could adversities move from the sure tenor of your faith those whom the steadfast hope of future rewards enlivened.

Therefore, when the labors of their frail life have been duly completed, having attained their native dwelling-places of heaven, blessed, they enjoy enduring peace.

## XI. M., Bishop of Rennes, to H., Bishop of Le Mans

[Note: [Col. 1653D] That is, Marbod, bishop of Rennes, to Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans.]

[Col. 1653B] When, reading your writings, I turn my eyes back to our own, I seem to behold earth lying beneath heaven. Yours soar above the clouds in lofty flight; ours do not cling to earth, creeping with a lowly step.

Often reread, yours are clear [variant: pleasing] to wise persons alone, compressing hidden meanings into few words.

As a very great gem is scarcely enclosed in a small amount of gold [Note: [Col. 1653D] Homeius, variant:

[Col. 1654D] “As though a great gem were set in a small amount of gold.”],

so these are accessible in appearance [variant: approach] to the unlearned and the learned alike, being plainly less exact in the craftsman’s preparation and flowing lightly from a common vein.

Your Muse frequently bends herself through antithesis, practicing returning turns in a winding figure;

[Col. 1653C] 1561 for us it is enough to proceed along a straight path, even if we weave words with a rather coarse Minerva, lest we be struck by the subtle shuttle of Arachne [Note: [Col. 1654D] Homeius, variant:

“Nor do we prepare to contend with subtle Arachne.”].

## XII. Commendation of Chastity

As a flower in the meadows, so is the grace of virginity in a good woman; for men likewise it is the foremost crown.

The next praise belongs to the virtue of those whom no pleasure draws toward corrupt things, who, having once experienced them, do not wish to return to foulness.

The third condition is not like the first or the second; yet it is a part of virtue and a cause of salvation—namely, for those who, after grave and habitual evil deeds, withdraw their heel from sin.

O good Messiah, born of the Virgin Mary! How happy are those to whom, most merciful one, you will say:

[Col. 1653D] “Let your portion be among the virginal dances, with whom it is fitting for me to be, whom it is also fitting to go on with me.”

The principle of recompense will likewise separate from the goats those whose clean life is an adornment in the second rank.

O may the final rank steer our ship to the harbor of life, that is, the garden of paradise! There the blessed people rejoice amid eternally springlike grass; with them, if I am not a rose, may I be a wild thyme.

## XIII. Commendation of Virtues by Comparison

Virginity is a flower and the virgin’s golden dowry;

[Col. 1654A] sexual intercourse is dregs, and its own most wretched recompense is death;

drunkenness is a torch; drinking water is peace;

anger is a savage lion; patience is the light that goes before;

devouring envy is a cross and a guide to impious Tartarus;

true faith is snow; fraud and deceit are pitch;

a humble mind is incense; swollen pride is pus.

## XIV. To a Virgin Dedicated to God

In place of the corruptible bed full of pain, by which brief and blameworthy pleasure stains married women—pleasure not sufficiently moderated even for the sake of posterity—and by which the day of childbirth wastes tortured limbs,

you have received a marriage-bed which neither pressure of pain nor fear troubles, and which no foul guilt pollutes. In it lies the King of kings, and his glory is with you; in his embraces there is no corruption of sex. He makes you fruitful, and his grace cleanses you.

[Col. 1654B] From him, when you give birth, come new joys, not torments, as you produce the offspring of virtue, with the reward of salvation. He knows no old age; before him the imparted light grows dark; the sun marvels at him and the moon reveres him in awe. He made heaven and laid the foundations of earth; the element of the great sea is his creation; at his command the brightness of this air came into being.

O exceedingly happy woman, if you recognize yourself to be faithful to so great a marriage, whose praises I sing.

I owe not as much as I ought, but only as much as I am able; I beg you, do not desire the joys of a child you are to bear; nor await a husband who may perhaps have no heir, whose death—even if he is dear—may cause you grief, or whose life, if he is not loved, may afflict you as though it were death.

[Col. 1654C] Joined now to chaste choirs, you are called the court of modesty; the angelic company joyfully keeps gifts for you; the powers of heaven desire to bring you greetings. All who serve the Bridegroom marvel at his bride. The very mother of Christ, whom you have willingly followed, beholds, loves, and venerates you.

1562 Do you, after despising these things, cast your rewards to the winds? [read: Learn not to cast your rewards to the winds.] And do not—may that ruin be far away—become, instead of a queen, a concubine amid carnal foulness, under the miserable condition of a person of low rank. Would you rather become a demonic prey than purchase the kingdoms of heaven at the price of moral excellence?

## XV. To a Devoted Virgin

Brighter than a star, simple and pure maiden,

[Col. 1654D] chosen by God and subdued by no lust: continue as you have begun in what displeases this world. Spurn light cares and attend to things to come. Learn to please the supreme God, and you shall obtain the trophy.

Let nothing present be lovable to a chaste mind, and let nothing quickly perishing be hard for you.

Among human affairs labor is exerted in vain; nor does one who hopes for what the wicked man attempts rejoice for long.

What now flatters leads by that very means to grim places; what now makes sad is later far from weeping.

O wretched laughter by which a human being loses paradise!

[Col. 1655A] O happy tears which long eternity rewards!

## XVI. A Dissuasion from Venereal Love

An excellent face, supported by a little plumpness, whiter than snow, redder than a spring rose; starry eyes, a smile promising delights; fiery kisses from slightly swelling lips; shining teeth, small and set in a row; limbs full of vigor and manners good without pretense—these belong to the girl who seeks union with me.

This distinguished youth, whose beauty is my flame, loves her, courts her, and adapts himself to please her. Yet she, rejecting the youth, wants me and bids me, “Hail!” She flatters me; because I reject her, she almost dies.

Had an ugly woman long ago done the same to me,

[Col. 1655B] I would have been wholly turned by lust toward Venus. But now, hard-hearted, I care neither for words nor kisses—kisses full of the sweet ruin of wantonness; by whose allurements the pursuer of loves is captivated; words, sweetest and charming, entering the heart, so powerful that they bend a mind made of stones and iron.

But while my madness grows, it does not know how to bend. While I spurn kisses, still, though spurning them, I behold the kisses and the flattering words, whose sounds might move the spirit of a eunuch; though I see them, I cannot help but spurn them. Harder than iron is the weapon by which, wounded, I go astray.

The tinder of one vice conquers [read: has conquered] the powers of this one and kills it. O thing worthy of notice: love gives contrary desires!

[Col. 1655C] Through the vice of lust, behold, I become most chaste; that which softens the hard takes softness away from me.

What, I ask, does it mean that Venus herself displeases one wounded by the spear of love? What moneylender would scorn interest? What merchant would scorn gains? What farmer would scorn crops?

Nature reversed changes its former laws, if food makes one unfed and lust chaste, if fear makes one bold, if a secure mind makes one flee.

There are many bonds of this kind of knot; but discord plainly troubles Satan’s kingdom, and it tears itself apart when one sin repels another sin. Harmony keeps the kingdom of virtues safe, and it does not know how to be dissolved while it grows together in its own peace.

Therefore it is better that I join myself to the camp which its own peace fortifies, rather than to that which discord punishes—

[Col. 1655D] that which will remain standing rather than that which wavers and is about to fall.

1563 ## XVII. Repentance for Wanton Love

Recently I was bound by the cords of mad love, caught by birdlime; but now I am ashamed and come to my senses. That frenzy fails, and I burn less and less; my mind and color return, while pallor and madness depart.

O good Savior, how every lover deceives himself! He considers shameful things beautiful and changes black into white. He believes the stench of filth to be the smell of perfume; he declares bitter things like gall sweet as honey. While he eats a stone, he thinks that he is enjoying bread; he drinks serpentine poison as though it were wine.

[Col. 1656A] While I cherished vice, I did not know what I now know. I was altogether blind, with a heart empty of virtue. Deceived, I thought I had obtained great rewards if at any time I had earned a few kisses by pleading.

Then the scent of her mouth seemed like the scent of a flower, though now it is proved otherwise. As a rose mingles whiteness and redness together, so then did her face, which now is buried in pallor, seem to me—not because the beloved scent or face has changed, but because I have changed; what was once dear to me I now reject.

For my mind then erred and approved what was reprobate. My mind erred, mad with the heat of lust, no less inflamed than a furnace melting stones.

What of the fact that he or she was dearer to me than the apple of my eye,

[Col. 1656B] yet would scarcely consent to speak when aware of being loved? If the heart of a lover is not tortured by so many and such great things, this very disdain is enough to make me [read: I prefer] live chastely.

Therefore remain outside, winged boy, author of love; let there be no place for you in my house, O Cytherean goddess! The embraces of either sex indeed displease me, but the one which departs further from law harms me more.

Let all the offenses of my former life remain outside. For I have rejected everything and wept greatly and in every way; I changed my countenance and wept greatly over everything. If I return to wine once rejected, let it become vinegar to me; and let bread be filth, flesh a worm, and milk poison. Instead of a crane, may I eat a toad; instead of a fish, a dragon.

## XVIII. On an Abbot Usurping Pontifical Insignia

[Col. 1656C]

An abbot wearing only the insignia of a bishop—namely, a ring, gloves, sandals, and mitre—since he is above an abbot and below a bishop, can be neither; or, if he is called both, I think him a two-formed monster like a centaur. If he imitates a bishop but remains an abbot, then he remains an ass hidden beneath a lion’s skin, or, as on the stage, wears another person’s mask.

## XIX. Concerning Majesty

[Note: [Col. 1655D] Perhaps a more suitable title would be: “On the Incarnation of the Word.”]

This is not the form of the Father, nor is the Father’s form the form of the Son; yet it is the Son’s form, but the form which he took from the Virgin.

O great sign! The angel fears and worships the Lamb, and earth fears the fleece set above the heavens;

[Col. 1656D] for the Lamb is God, and to serve him is salvation.

The sheep’s fleece signifies the divine body. Twice the leader and prophet strikes the rock with his rod; the leader’s two blows are the two beams of the cross. From the rock a spring was given to the people without measure; abundant salvation for humankind comes from the Lord’s body.

The twelve disciples to whom God’s law was entrusted are the twelve stones which the king wears in his diadem.

1564 ## XX. Praise of the Monastic Life

*(Reported by R. P. Sirmond from the manuscripts of Angers and of Saint-Gatien of Tours as by an uncertain author, in the notes to Geoffrey of Vendôme’s Letters, book IV.)*

Happy flock of people who, following Christ’s teaching,

[Col. 1657A] despise riches and hold nothing as their own.

They are restrained by a holy rule under the direction of one person; none of them acts by his own judgment.

Their hearts are one and their will undivided; all have equal clothing and similar food, yet each receives whatever he seems to need, as frailty of age or weakness requires.

All luxury is absent; opportunity for sin is rare, because all fear one another’s eyes.

The common rule requires faults seen to be revealed at once, so that the punishment which follows may cut off the vice as it is born.

They flee idleness; useful labor occupies them all, lest harmful thoughts overtake idle minds.

Nothing is confused where all things are done in order; everything is cared for and nothing neglected.

[Col. 1657B] There is not only an ordered manner of life but also an established order of speech: they distribute great matters and small alike fairly.

No one speaks or keeps silence except as prescribed; each stands, sits, and walks according to his own rule.

They frequent the threshold of the church night and day, and assist themselves and their own people with holy prayers.

Why do I delay and try to unfold every individual detail in words? Whatever they do is work of body or soul.

Moreover, they live so that the very site, arrangement, and number of their dwellings are sacred and sufficient to themselves.

The domestic structure presents a square form: courts made famous by four porticoes.

Enclosed by three houses, which bodily need requires, and by the fourth house, which is the house of the Lord,

[Col. 1657C] they give the monks movement, life, and station, so that, like sheep in folds, they may be contained.

The first of these houses stores drink and food; the second, adjoining it, refreshes them with these. The third cherishes limbs wearied by daily labor; the fourth continually resounds with God’s praises.

I pass over very many things worthy of similar description; but I shall say briefly: nothing is superfluous or lacking.

Therefore I compare these leaders, this senate worthy of praise—small in outward appearance, outstanding in morals—to ants, whose industrious troop of workers conveys a burden larger than its body; so that they may be able to maintain a common life, they establish small storehouses beneath the same roofs.

I compare them to divine bees, which in a small body possess

[Col. 1657D] mighty and excellent spirits. In hexagonal cells they store flowing honey, performing a wondrous and useful work; they observe discipline and domestic laws, and are at once nourished by their ingenious house.

I compare them to the stars by which the heavenly court shines, which light the dark air at night. They preserve through the ages the law once imposed upon them, and pursue their accustomed courses and measures.

I compare them to the heaven that solemnly revolves all things; furthermore, I compare them to angelic powers, who continually answer “holy” with repeated voice.

[Col. 1658A] On earth the monks sing what the cherubim sing in heaven; cherubim abiding in heaven and monks on earth render one service to the one Lord.

## XXI. Marbod to Bishop Samson

[Note: [Col. 1657D] Perhaps bishop of Worcester or Winchester, whom Henry of Huntingdon calls most illustrious, *Sacred History of England*, part II, p. 700.]

The wave of the ancient sea begrudges me my friend; Ocean’s boundary separates minds united in affection.

There is no bridge upon the sea, nor are there shallows passable with a pole, as a boat driven along is wont to travel on the Loire.

Yet I judge it neither prudent to entrust oneself to the winds nor, disregarding oneself, to commit one’s fate to the sea.

The waters are granted only to the race of swimmers, the earth to walkers, the air to fliers. As the choir of stars preserves the vault of the poles, the fourfold matter bears just as many kinds.

Neptune’s realm thus belongs to one race alone;

[Col. 1658B] but our recklessness ventures into forbidden things.

Hence I hesitate, whether, cautious, I should avoid danger, or, foolish, become so for friendship’s sake.

I greatly desire, my bishop, to see your face and embrace in old age the old man whom I honored in youth; to join my aged hand to your consecrated hands, and to enjoy conversation with you, sweet friend.

What labor it would be to recount to you in writing the loyalty of hospitality and the gifts exchanged long ago—lest I seem an ungrateful father, though I am ready to serve you, and even if I gave myself to you, would still not be your equal.

But my chilled breast and old age wearied by labor prevent me from making the journey across the depths of the sea.

If your borders could be sought by a pedestrian road,

[Col. 1658C] my feet, friend, would carry me to your dear dwelling. But you, vigorous and accustomed to scorn the winds, do not fear to be borne about on the waves of the sea. In the fashion of your people, which undertakes anything difficult, you can visit our shores whenever you wish.

On this side you have salvation; here your father was born. May it be permitted you to enter the sea on the way to your native soil. Here are your house and estate; this place is first, that second. This place educated you, for which that place is renowned.

To return to your homeland, dare to break through the sea’s bounds; for in those regions you act as bishop and exile.

In these lands, too, you possess the fitting summit of honor: your father has obtained the city which bore you. Here you stand as bishop, though you are bodily distant from here;

[Col. 1658D] for I govern the city which my other self governs.

Therefore you may arrange a return here, unless you do not wish to see us, whenever it pleases you. Or, if you summon me, I shall hasten to Bayeux; that city suffices as the seat for three bishops. Or if this displeases you, if you disdain to travel there, say where I am commanded to go—but take care that I do not perish.

## XXII. M., Bishop, to R., Archdeacon

[Note: [Col. 1658D] Perhaps Marbod to Rivalon, archdeacon of Nantes; concerning him, see the notes of D. Loyauté above.]

I embrace, dearest son, the verses sent by you, favorable signs of your talent. I embrace the praises reported by spreading fame, which proofs of your natural ability obtain for you.

[Col. 1659A] I rejoice in the auspices of your life and good conduct, which Christ, who had given them, now receives in you. I rejoice that you have been joined to the army of the Church, though until now you were a soldier under the world’s ruler.

Do not repent as though you had followed worse things, because you have quickly become untrained after being an old soldier. For, having been cast down, you choose [read: choose rather] to be a great prophet than to follow the wicked camp of sinners.

Yet Christ’s favor toward you did not permit you to become lowly in an inferior station. Soon elevated to the honor of the archdeaconry, without labor you attain what labor obtains.

But let it not displease the rulers of churches that they received one inexperienced, something which would have been appropriate for a veteran.

[Col. 1659B] This does not prejudice the authority of the canons, since moral excellence cannot be confined by law. Virtue perfected in a short time compensates for many years and, deservedly, anticipates what it seeks.

You fill a high office with the gifts granted you; by your conduct you adorn the office you have undertaken. Report declares you just and chaste; you are good in speech, ready in service, so that there can be no doubt that you are of noble stock,

1566 one whom nobility of spirit thus commends.

The king desired you, my most beloved son, as David desired the service of Uriah’s wife. Christ, having overthrown the devil, joined you to himself, so that through you the royal offspring may increase.

You were Saul; now you will be Paul, and at Christ’s command

[Col. 1659C] you will later receive the summit of episcopal office. This is our hope concerning you, noble Riallon; labor night and day that we may not be disappointed in it.

You will always find me accommodating and ready, so that nothing I can possess will be lacking to you. May I be to you a fellow-servant of the Lord [the printed text has *conservus Dominus*, read *conservus Domini*], patron, friend, and grant whatever you may justly ask, whether more or less.

## XXIII. M., Bishop, to Countess E.

[Note: [Col. 1659D] Ermenegard, daughter of Fulk Rechin, wife of Alan called Fergent, duke of Brittany.]

Daughter of Fulk, glory of the Armorican region, beautiful, chaste, graceful, fair, illustrious, youthful: if you had not entered marriage and endured the labors of childbirth, in my judgment you could be a Cynthia.

But because one joined in marriage cannot be equal to a chaste virgin,

[Col. 1659D] the honor of virginity is yet greater.

Among the flock of married women you may be believed to be one of the goddesses, first among the foremost, O woman of surpassing beauty! Yet this beauty of yours—born of a prince and wife of a prince—will pass away like smoke and soon become earth.

Or, if your days run on with death deferred—alas, dreadful fate!—you will become an old woman. A beautiful face is praised and precious, but death or old age will destroy this value.

The gleaming eyes that wound those who look upon them, and blond hair, will both become ashes. Fame reports that no woman before you is powerful in eloquence or skillful in counsel.

[Col. 1660A] These too will fail and become only a tale. A tale also recounts eloquent sages of old.

A garment of purple cloth is food for moths; a heap of gold fears thieves. To every wise person all such things are like gusts of wind: gusts pass away, and these perish no less.

What does the softness of a bed covered with purple contribute? No glory of a couch takes away death [read: “can cause its pleasures to die”].

Regard table delicacies as cheap dishes, since what is dear is changed into worthless nothing.

Whoever possesses servants, maidservants, towers, towns, and estates while living will leave them behind when dying. What title of praise do the skins of ermine and an ornamented retinue give you after the tomb?

[Col. 1660B] Why should I hasten to enumerate all the goods of sea and land which seem to enrich and supply you? Such riches are everlasting for no one: they go with the world, and fall with the falling world.

But that you love Christ, despise this world, and are clothing and food to the poor—this makes you beautiful and precious to the Lord; neither death nor old age will destroy this value.

## XXIV. To the Queen of the English

[Note: [Col. 1660D] Perhaps Matilda.]

It is worthwhile to have attempted the perils of the sea and feared the threats of uncertain fortune. It is pleasant to have seen a queen whom no one can equal in beauty of body and face.

Yet she alone seeks, with the veil of loose clothing and a new modesty,

[Col. 1660C] to conceal what she has; but what shines by its own light cannot be hidden, and the sun penetrating clouds sends forth rays.

It is more pleasing to remain silent about outstanding morals and words flowing with honey than to say less than they deserve.

Other women strive to acquire what nature has denied them, painting purple cheeks with snowy white cosmetics; their treated face assumes artificial colors, distinguishing marks through the deception of art.

Some bind their protruding breasts with a band; their tight-drawn garment fashions a long flank. Others partly uncover their hair with an unbound forehead and seek to please with curled locks.

But you, queen, though beautiful, fear to appear beautiful—

[Col. 1660D] possessing freely the gifts that others purchase.

It is better to possess openly what nature has bestowed upon you; you would be ungrateful to God if you denied his gifts. You seek to conceal a lamp alight under a bushel; what you possess is not your own gift but the gift of the Lord who gives.

Even a modest virgin wishes to appear beautiful, and a fair form befits a chaste mind.

O wife of a king, descended from kings in your forefathers! Great things cannot be concealed; small things are accustomed to lie hidden. Your fame will live as long as my poems live, and whoever reads my writings will sing of you.

## XXV. On the Annunciation of the Lord

Gabriel, sent to noble Mary, brought these words:

[Col. 1661A] “Hail, ever-unwed one, lovely flower, sweet being; you shall bear Christ in your womb, blessed above women. He whom your womb saves will alone be safe. From you shall be born he who will rule David’s scepter; from his fruit shall come the hope of this offspring. Now and forever he bears the paternal diadem; he shall be called Jesus, king blessed above all.”

O happy fruit, turning sorrows into joys! O holy offspring—never was there such a one, nor one so great.

Having heard such words, the gentle maiden speaks: “How shall I conceive, or how shall I become a mother, who, as I have vowed, neither know nor have known a man? Conception and childbirth follow violated limbs; how can the womb of one who knows no intercourse swell?”

Thus, when the Virgin had spoken, the divine voice answered:

[Col. 1661B] “The offspring of Jesse is God, who commands this to be so, and who, commanding it to be, makes it necessarily be by commanding. The eternal Spirit and the Father’s favor will overshadow you, chaste one, within, and make your womb pregnant.

The very Son of God, sower of night and day, ruler of the heavens, God and Lord of lords, of twofold nature, without beginning and without end, last and first, long and short, high and low, little and great, great lion and little lamb,

will be mortal from you, as an ordinary father would have been mortal [Note: [Col. 1661D] That is, such as an ordinary father would have been—namely, mortal.], but such from the Father. And you, Star of the Sea, will be helper to the wretched, hope of sinners, blessed queen of the heavens; on earth you will be called loving, holy, and the object of every prayer.

Mother of the Sun of righteousness, bearing offspring without seed, do not wish to doubt. Already Elizabeth, barren in her aged womb,

[Col. 1661C] has been given a great child by her failing old husband, in miraculous order. Her breast, swelling with milk, now learns to exist in old age; the old woman rejoices in her child, and the old man too rejoices in his child.

Your kinswoman’s offspring is lesser and differs from yours; judge and herald are not weighed in an equal balance. Yet, as the birth of a servant proves like that of a master, so, if a barren woman is pregnant and a Virgin has the power to bear, whoever believes the one is not injured by the other. Therefore strengthen your faith: the same God performs two miracles.”

Trustingly she replied: “May he who promised such great things through you, so as to save the world, grant that your words be fulfilled in me.”

1568 ## XXVI. On the Epiphany

Among God’s feasts shines the origin of this day,

[Col. 1661D] on which the newborn, lately given from the Virgin, God, was honored with three gifts by three foreigners. A bright star, sent before the Chaldeans by which he had directed them, led the men, shining most greatly in heaven, while standing still it pointed out the house in which Christ lay.

A matter exceedingly wondrous, unknown to the first “seats” (*sedis*) [read: ages (*saeclis*)]! A star showed the sun lying beneath a roof. O newness of events, coming in the latter days! He who established the earth lay in a stable. He through whom the sun shone sucked his mother’s breasts. The cradle deserved to confine the maker of the moon.

[Col. 1662A] Not earth alone, not only ox and ass, were astonished at this work which nature had not created, but sea, abyss, humankind, and every created thing; the powers of heaven beheld this trembling.

The lesser enclosed the greater, and what was born afterwards enclosed what was earlier. The sun was in a star; God was in a pregnant girl.

Therefore the star showed forth this sun, the offspring born without seed, the sun of righteousness born from Mary’s womb, the hidden sun concealed under a cloud of flesh. Three kings approached the cradle of the little king, bearing three mystical gifts. With gold they honor him as reigning; with incense, as thundering; myrrh is offered as suited to his future burial.

The Sabaeans consecrated the first fruits of faith,

[Col. 1662B] signifying that the nations would come to Christ. The Israelite race, bringing forth the author of life, does not recognize him; the Gentile, believing, worships him.

For this reason, then, today’s feast is celebrated and precious, called the feast of Epiphany; the origin of nascent faith is deservedly made famous.

A second reason exists for which this day is noble. As the Savior began to enter his thirtieth year, he sought the waters of the Jordan and John’s baptism, not disdaining, though created without stain, to be joined on equal terms with common crowds.

He who had no need to be cleansed wished to be immersed in the stream; washed, he washed the waters and sanctified baptism.

And so that the power concealed in flesh might be made manifest, a sweet milk-white dove without gall came,

[Col. 1662C] and, when it settled upon him, gave a sign that he was filled with a certain holy breath [read: “filled with the Holy Spirit”] amid that great crowd.

Soon a trustworthy voice was heard from heaven, testifying that the Son was pleasing to the Father above all things. This voice terrified the river and John himself; it terrified those standing by, who thought thunder had sounded.

The river was afraid to touch so great a divinity. Jordan, fleeing backward, turned back its course; for that was the Father’s voice and the terror of divinity, sanctifying the waters for cleansing the nations—not by the old washing, but by sacred baptism, which the threefold Person and simple substance sanctify: the Begotten [read: Son], the Unbegotten, and the spotless Spirit;

[Col. 1662D] and which does not wash merely the outward person, but cleanses minds and floods the believer’s heart.

Moreover, God performed a sign in Galilee on this very day, as the yearly cycle returned, by which he showed that he who renews things created them. For the maker of forms changes the species of things and varies forms—he alone who created them.

With the other guests, the unwed mother attended the wedding feast, and the teacher with his disciples. When the wine failed and the minister of the cups ceased, Christ ordered six vessels to be filled with water, each holding two or three measures.

[Col. 1663A] Then, at God’s command, the water was changed into wine [read: *lĭaeō*, “wine”],

1569 and, when tasted, the new law surpassed the old flavor.

Wine grapes are normally pressed in the winepress; by this new power, wine did not flow from a single [read: immediately flowed from the water] stream. Thirst was overcome by wine, but not wine from the vine’s shoot.

Even when a fertile year occurs, human labor scarcely draws out wine by art through varied processes; at the divine command the water jar suddenly reddens with wine, and without delayed interval water at once becomes flavorful. Grace surpasses nature; command surpasses effort.

When the wine had been tasted, its flavor pleased the steward. By so many sacraments, the one almighty God was recognized today, and he himself as Mary’s only son.

[Col. 1663B] The star, the dove, and the wine alike testify that this is true.

It is also fitting to weave in a fourth sign, which he afterward performed in due order after the year’s course: he had fed five thousand men—a wonder like the others—from five loaves and two little fishes, and four times three baskets remained over.

More remained than there had been five loaves;

Twelve baskets remained, full of fragments.

When God wills, heavenly abundance flows into food.

Thus from the fragments, O Christ, you could give to three hundred

Thousand people, and three hundred baskets would still remain.

Whenever we eat these, we cannot restore what has been consumed;

But whoever devours diminishes the whole by eating,

And whatever remains is less, while it supplies very much.

[Col. 1663C] O brief human power, subject to limits!

Unable to extend its care beyond nature.

But the Lord’s power is not subject to an end.

The Author of nature does all things by his own right.

For it is worth observing what manner of eating there then was:

Without the labor of a mill, the bread increased in the mouth;

It increased also in the hands, although broken into pieces;

It did not increase in number, but the mass made good the loss.

Whatever there was in this meal is marvelous to tell.

The loaves filled the crowds, though there were five;

Not more in number, but more fruitful in weight.

The same use of those eating bestowed increase upon the fishes,

Which did not fail until the crowd had refreshed itself.

Thus from the five books of the old Law, wisdom

[Col. 1663D] Refreshes crowds of peoples through the mouths of teachers;

Nor does the hearer grasp all that the teacher can impart.

O how great a feast, how noble, how manifest!

XXVI. On the Hypapante of the Lord.

It delights me to write a matter that may move devout hearts,

And it is pleasing to recount for the good the deeds of the old man Simeon.

God was born under the Law from his mother’s body,

A true man, not in the manner of a man, without the Father’s seed.

Although his mother most certainly knew that he was God,

And could not pay to God what must be paid on behalf of a guilty person,

Yet, according to the customary law concerning the first offspring,

She prepares to bring with her new child two offerings to the Temple:

[Col. 1664A] Namely, a young pigeon, or two turtledoves;

By these the birth of the firstborn child was commanded to be redeemed.

Therefore the parent, though free from stain, bore these gifts;

That good child, God himself, was her burden.

When trembling Simeon, old and likewise most righteous,

Saw him and recognized God, as the High-Thunderer had formerly,

Prophesying, told him that he would not die

Until the person of God had been given him to carry.

Stretching out his hands, the gray-haired man receives the sacred pledge,

So that he holds as an infant him who rules above the heavens’ stars.

Therefore what is seen is marvelous to the world,

To the dwellers in heaven and on earth, and to the abyss of hell.

He is received whom no region of places can contain,

And he is carried through whom the lofty house of the poles is sustained.

O most happy old age! You have borne well;

[Col. 1664B] Now the presence of Christ shines forth, satisfying you.

1570 Behold, the Savior of the peoples is set before the altars;

In his body is hidden the light that reveals all things.

Tell us, old man—than whom none is better or sweeter—

What does that little God, who sees hearts, give you?

Wearied, he says: “This spirit scarcely draws along its limbs.

I have awaited what I did not deserve: to see you, Christ.

Now it is enough, and nothing remains except to enjoy

The peace of rest and to repose in the mansions of your kingdom.

O most radiant light, to be veiled by no darkness,

Bright with glowworms [Note: [Col. 1663D] a kind of worm that glitters by night at harvest-time], close to the starry heavens!

With what praise shall I bear you forth, you who bear wax on behalf of the Virgin,

Wax shining with light, itself nourishing light from itself?

As the Mother gave nourishment to the thundering Infant,

Therefore crowds in our city sing,

[Col. 1664C] And when wax bearing light is brought in procession,

At once melody sounds to Christ and Mary.

Every sex and age offers joyful thanks;

No one is silent, nor does any woman or man sing out of tune.

The innocent flock of tender children themselves

Meet the hurrying Infant, celebrating the feast;

And the melodious virgin choir, O Virgin Mary, gives you

A pleasant song, together with Simeon’s assembly of old men.

Anna leads the final choir of chaste widows:

“Hail, bright day, deservedly you shall be most celebrated,

Until holy wisdom reigns in the Church.

Farewell, departing light, ornament and special glory of the feast.”

XXVII. Christ’s Triumph in His Ascension.

The destroyer of death, giver of life, mighty lion,

[Col. 1664D] After he rose again, while Thomas doubted, revealed

The nail-marks before the flock of disciples,

And gave them his side to touch; he drank and ate,

Lest they suppose that what they saw was a bodiless shadow:

“A spirit,” he said, “after it leaves the limbs,

Is without bones, and is not one whom you can touch;

But you see that I truly have flesh and bones.”

By these proofs he wiped away the wounds of the mind;

By such great evidences he strengthened the doubter’s heart.

Moreover, appearing more than once in Galilee,

He made himself known, removing every cause for doubt.

Phoebus had driven the stars away for forty days,

[Col. 1665A] When he prepared to return, after completing his commands,

To the seat [variant: throne] of the eternal Father and the heavenly kingdom.

Then taking to himself six witnesses at once,

Through whom these things might be spread throughout the regions of the world,

He went out from the city to the slopes of the nearby mountain,

The Mount of Olives, which they had been accustomed to climb.

When he had ascended it, he stretched his hands toward the stars;

With those with whom he had lived, he blessed them as he departed.

And, concerning the state of the kingdom that would endure by perpetual right,

Or concerning the promised one who proceeds from the Father and from himself,

After speaking much, he was lifted from the earth;

And with the trumpet’s voice he is borne cloud upon cloud through the clouds,

God surpassing the gods upon the wings of the winds,

Leading back captive thousands of former saints

[Col. 1665B] Whom the mighty lion had rescued from the gates of death.

The harmony of the highest heavens sings in welcome;

The angelic choirs resound with no lesser praise;

The bright stars rejoice with the triumphant Thunderer.

The astonished flock of the eleven disciples

Receives with eyes and mind the heavenly dances,

When suddenly two men stand nearby, clothed in snowy brightness,

Sent from heaven by a divine gift; and the faithful company hears:

“Why do you stand stunned? Why do you raise your eyes to the stars?

Behold, the Son of God seeks the heavens, men of Galilee:

In this body, which you saw and touched by hand,

He shall come from the stars with the hosts of heaven as Judge.”

Having spoken thus, they again direct their course toward the stars.

Those clinging to earth desire to carry their hearts to heaven;

[Col. 1665C] 1571 Thus Christ taught all his disciples, joined to him in fervent faith,

As a royal bird bears her young in flight,

Lifted from earth, into the heavens,

That eagles may gather where the Lord’s body is found.

But what mortal, I ask, or with what wings,

Can strive after the heights and be established at the highest pole,

Since we are an earthly mass, offspring of flesh,

And guilt, pressing upon our backs, holds us downward?

The first father brought this burden of disease upon the world,

That first father with whom we perish by sinning.

The second took away this burden by conquering death.

If we love him, through him we return from death.

A mind subject to flesh deserved the punishments of hell,

[Col. 1665D] Its rational acuity effaced by perverse order;

Let flesh, which ruled, be subjected again

To the rule of a mind vigorous in pure reason;

Let everlasting life be regained on the wings of virtues,

Whence, weighted by the burden of sin, we slipped down.

And since Father and Son abolish ancient offenses,

Trusting in this help, do not withhold your own efforts:

The almighty hand will conquer the grievous thing you feel.

Now a member of Christ, though formerly of the devil,

Aspire to the Head, to receive marvelous rewards.

XXVIII. Discourse on Vices and Virtues.—[Note: [Col. 1665D] How excellently those ancient poets versified when they were not constrained by rhythm is evident from this and from many freer poems [Col. 1666D] of equal worth.] That Solitude Must Be Sought.

My uncle has a country place in the woods; there it is often my custom,

[Col. 1666A] Having cast aside the filth of cares and those things

That torment humankind, to withdraw into the countryside’s delights.

Green grass, silent woodland, the gentle and cheerful breath of the breeze,

And a living spring in the grass refresh my weary mind,

Restore me to myself,

And make me remain within myself. For who in the anxious city,

Boiling with varied tumults, stands firm

Without being carried outside himself and spending his time,

Bereft of himself, on vain things?

Here love presses, there hatred; here fear, there desire;

Different from one another indeed, yet under one law,

They subject minds ignorant of truth to falsehood.

The whole army of vices follows these four.

There is scarcely anyone who does not think they should be pursued,

[Col. 1666B] Or, thinking that they should be fled, nevertheless follows them;

For the very force of the rushing multitude drags along one who resists.

And it presses from behind like a downward slope of evils.

Therefore the first thing is to escape the crowds, and thus

To plant one’s step on firm ground and hold one’s course.

Only then should one hasten back to the lofty rewards

Of abandoned virtue, if one has any concern for salvation.

But perhaps one thinks it hard, because, having followed steep descents,

One cannot again undertake the heights without labor.

Let him think it harder to plunge into the sheerest precipices,

Whence either to draw back one’s foot, or remain there without end,

Is the greatest labor; the latter is the worst of fates.

Therefore we must first undertake what is lighter;

If nothing light remains, let us undertake what remains.

If you are wicked, do not become worse or most wicked;

[Col. 1666C] But if you are even utterly wicked, gradually seize [variant: carry off] your heart for a better condition;

For it is the greatest praise to overcome a most difficult thing by the greatest labor.

If you despise yourself, you may despise this praise.

But that man is too impious and perverse

Who anxiously tends his possessions and despises himself.

For you vainly hunger after profits, vainly cultivate a field,

If you yourself fail through the loss of an uncultivated mind.

For if you do not perceive the gains or losses of the mind,

Devoted only to what bodily use indicates,

1572 Since you lack understanding, a most desperate invalid,

You are no longer rightly called a human being, but earth or beast.

[Col. 1666D] Here a disease arises from a deadly habit,

Like lethargy; yet some have escaped even from this,

Snatched from death’s very jaws.

Adverse fortune sometimes awakens them,

Striking and stirring their sluggish hearts; for in adverse events

The instability of things becomes apparent,

And pain itself, which comes from fleeting things, shows

That no one can become happy through what flees.

Now a single favorable success in affairs, and anxiety itself

Lest things now possessed be lost,

Rouse them, showing even this; it urgently stirs effort [printed: *imparce*; corrected: *impense*],

So that they may see by how great a languor they are burdened,

[Col. 1667A] But not to be able to drive away the causes of the languor.

Whoever suffers or fears is shown not to be happy.

Whoever loses what he loves, or loves what he can lose,

Suffers or fears; but there is no pleasure

Among temporal things that cannot quickly be lost.

Therefore no pleasure makes anyone happy;

Double fortune demonstrates this to the one enjoying it:

Sadness over things lost, or anxiety about retaining them.

The same lot afflicts all the covetous: both the man

Who, though he has nothing, greatly desires to have,

And him who desires more though much already remains to him.

When these things have thus been recognized and the mind’s sleep banished,

Seek escape from the disease; for a perverse wish to perish

Condemns a fevered person, of his own accord, in the physician’s presence.

[Col. 1667B] Do not delay help for yourself, because delay in treatment

Sometimes kills the sick person by sudden death.

The present hour is more suitable for coming to one’s senses

Amid so many cares and endless labors.

Consider how brief is our life: death’s image has consumed

Every period of life already past.

The image of death likewise possesses all the future.

That tiny, short, and very slight span

In which you live in the present already becomes past and absent.

These things and more I am permitted, and delight, to meditate upon

While I remain beneath rural foliage at my uncle’s country place.

XXIX. Contempt for the Present Life.

(From a manuscript of St. Gatianus of Tours.)

If I compare the joys of the present life with winds,

Since neither lasts, let no one think to reproach me.

[Col. 1667C] Everyone trusting in this world is like a reed,

Which the wind tosses and the river at the same time shakes.

The evils of the human condition are mingled with its goods

In unequal measure, because more evils are mingled with its goods.

He does not rejoice well for whom a cause of weeping is prepared.

No one stands secure who totters and is soon to fall.

Thus this life cannot give anyone a happy state,

Since it is unequal, now bright, now rainy.

Even if it could perhaps give one, death would nevertheless annihilate it,

Taking away whatever life has given when life departs.

These are approximately the words of Job, lamenting the brevity of present life:

“Man, born of woman, appears like a flower; heat comes, and immediately he withers.”

Therefore despise the swift life and choose the long one;

[Col. 1667D] Seek, through brief labor, the rest of everlasting age.

Let the abundance of fragile fortune become cheap to you;

Unless it becomes cheap, it ensnares in vain the person whom it will leave.

While your goods are yours, scatter them generously among the poor;

And let not your heir concern you, O one who must die.

XXX. A Warning against Worldly Avarice.

You who love goods that you cannot retain,

And do not love what you know to be eternal,

1573 Hear the lament of human life; come,

That you may thoroughly know how worthless is what you love,

And come to your senses, lest you perish with Satan.

The beauty of girls, the deception of their minds,

And the faces of young men, bearded yet grown,

Whom frivolity of character entangles in the snares of love—

In a moment of time they perish, as things equal to the wind;

[Col. 1668A] The corpse becomes earth, and wicked smoke seeks Tartarus.

Loved ones weep for them, yet cannot help them by weeping.

You who wretchedly feast, fearing to empty your purses,

And spare not yourself while you fill new money-bags,

Do not know for whose use you heap up what you keep.

The gold you know may perhaps be kept for an enemy.

Death will seize what you have, and your flesh will become decay;

You will not take with you purses full of rust.

The unhappy soul will pay eternal punishments.

Perhaps he too is wept for here; but youth vanishes amid weeping—

Clothed in purple, its head crowned with gems,

Drinking splendid drink, eating choice delicacies,

Holding the right of the sword and lapsing into every crime,

A despiser of law, abusing the law with impunity.

He who burdens and oppresses those whom Christ redeemed from the enemy,

[Col. 1668B] When the hour comes falls wretchedly and goes to Tartarus;

And if he is wept for, is he helped by weeping?

The tongues of the eloquent, who pursue worldly gain,

Blacken white things and whiten black things by their speech;

When they are dissolved, they speak neither black nor white.

A long torment awaits us in the valley of the silent;

The punishment of those who suffer is not made less by their tears.

Why should I recount individually the pitiable labor of life,

In which the mad are tormented by vain pursuit?

The whole remainder is made known by the resemblance.

O miserable lot: to seek death by living!

O evil fortune, which one syllable destroys [namely, *mors*, “death”]!

XXXI. That Bodily Death Is Not to Be Feared.

[Col. 1668C] The Lord God had planted in Paradise trees of pleasure fit for the blessed,

With Adam provided for.

“Eat the rest,” he said, “but withdraw from this as from an enemy.”

And he touched the fig tree: “It will be very unjust,” he said,

“If because of a fig you make me your enemy.

If you taste it, it follows at once that you shall die.

Whoever wishes to die by death, let him bring figs to his mouth.”

By chance, one day his wife came to Adam—

The woman fashioned from his rib, but an enemy—

With a composed countenance, coming to please her husband,

So that she might quickly persuade him of what she advised.

He lay upon the ground, where the fruit could be taken

Hanging from the tree—the beginning of our grief.

Then Eve, reclining in her husband’s embrace,

Her breast now full of venom from the serpent’s mouth, began:

[Col. 1668D] “O my man,” she said, “do you see what grace lies in the apple?

Do you see what tasty food it offers us,

Promising hidden delights of flavor through its outward appearance?

Furthermore, why would God wish to forbid you alone

These apples, among the fruits that bear fruit,

Unless this food gave what God himself refused to give?

Happily hasten to eat the fruit of the tree

Whose portion I give you.” The woman, deceived by the devil’s craft,

In turn deceived her unsuspecting husband.

Because of the sin of both, as the number of evils increased,

The whole offspring was exiled from Paradise’s region,

And cries: “Woe, woe to Eve’s lamentable succession!”

Thus it is no more surprising that everyone dies

Than that a Breton eats butter,

[Col. 1669A] That the Norman-born [Note: [Col. 1669D] Perhaps more correctly: “that the Fleming-born are satisfied by drinking oats.”] are satisfied by drinking oats,

Or that the men of Poitou fear our swords [Note: [Col. 1669D] He speaks here in the manner of the Angevins, with whom, and with the people of Rennes, there had formerly been an enduring and almost natural [Col. 1670D] hostility.].

1574 XXXII. That One’s Resolution Must Not Be Suddenly Changed.

Certain men of good intention, after a crown has duly been made for them,

At proper times, as is customary among those brothers,

Receive their cowls on the condition

That their conversion may not be merely momentary.

Before witnesses they promise that they are converted for the hour,

Whatever those promise who renounce the pleasures of the flesh.

Afterward, finding the unfamiliar life burdensome,

They cast off their garments after three or four years,

And, made wanderers, run through the byways of the district,

Now despised by the world because of monastic causes.

Then ashamed, because they are the world’s mockery,
