[Col. 1669B] When expelled, they return where they did not wish to go back,

Now despised by monks, like a soldier who has deserted his king.

Therefore, since scarcely anyone remains the same

Who changes his dress without first considering these things,

Such a person is rash, and misfortune is likely to befall him.

XXXIII. On the Many Punishments of the Damned.

The devil’s invention of wickedness comprises a hundred thousand offenses,

By which he drags this world into the penal abyss,

Where those who are confined die because they are unable to die.

For they would wish to die, because death is no part of pain [Note: [Col. 1670D] Perhaps *pax*, that is, a diminution or postponement, of pain.]

For the wretch whom everlasting flame burns.

Forehead, eyes, nostrils, neck, the region of the ears,

Mouth, throat, breasts: there they become food for flame.

[Col. 1669C] Back, side, belly burn without failing;

The thighs do not grow cold, nor the penis conscious of guilt.

O how sad is he who is delivered to these fires!

How mournful he who is given as food to serpents,

Who scarcely endures the force of the stench at every hour,

Whom a cruel torturer beats on every side with thongs!

Indeed, harsh vengeance is inflicted in every dreadful respect;

Yet there is a distinction among their punishments,

Which are weighed thus: greater crimes endure greater

Punishments, lesser crimes lesser ones.

XXXIV. Prayer of a Penitent Who Has Often Fallen.

(Found in the Colbert manuscript, no. 3019.)

What shall I do, wretch that I am? I bear beneath my breast a wound,

The wound of foul and inveterate sin,

As though I bore death beneath that same breast.

[Col. 1669D] As often as I have washed it, as often as I have bound plasters upon it,

The remedy has as often been defeated by corruption.

I applied a thousand bindings, none of them effective;

The skin is always torn, there is always no path to salvation.

Hence my mind is full of fear at every hour [variant: “hence at every hour is my mind”];

For it fears that life may suddenly depart,

And dreads the flames by which vengeance burns sins,

The eternal flames and infernal caverns.

Yet when I meditate upon these things, I strive in vain to rise,

For I cling to mud and sink through habit.

[Col. 1670A] I have violated the commands of the Thunderer in so many and such great ways

That I almost despair of becoming better, because it is late;

Yet though late, I seek help—

Not human help, certainly, for that has long been known to me;

I must be saved by divine medicine alone.

To you I sigh, you who are not subject to heaven’s circuit.

Highest of priests, I lay all my weakness before you.

Let your saving right hand adhere to this creature,

And not renew the furrow, as a gaping ulcer is wont to do.

Christ, Word of God, who despises every proud person,

Exalts the humble and lifts the lowly from the dust,

Fashioner of things, true light from light,

Apply your hands here, as the Samaritan did.

Wash away hunger [printed: *famen*; corrected: *crimen*, “sin”] with divine wine and blood;

[Col. 1670B] 1575 And while I live, pour oil upon the wound,

That, washed with wine, it may be healed wholly by ointment.

O greater than heaven! I reveal to you all that pains me;

I acknowledge my faults and ask that my debts be remitted.

Do not despise me because I have sinned against you alone,

Nor give me over to death because I have done evil before you.

Savior of the world and lover of our salvation,

At whose nod eloquence fills the mute,

At whose divinity blindness receives light,

Restore sight, that it may see [printed: *vitiet*; variant: *videat*] all good things,

And make the mute tongue free for good words.

You who heal the feeble, fill hollow places, level rough ones,

Straighten what is crooked, turn death into rising,

Be forgiving to me, full of these and other evils.

[Col. 1670C] Virgin mother of Christ, reconcile to me him whom you bore.

Hear me, beloved of God, you who were born of Zebedee.

Peter, noble inhabitant of Rome, intercede for me;

And you, holy Paul, spiritual and keen man.

All the elect, compel the Lord by prayer to be moved.

XXXV. To a Slandering Monk.—That No One Is to Be Despaired of While He Lives.

I do not think you wish it, nor do I greet you, Geoffrey;

For since you are pure and perhaps about to become an abbot,

You recoil from us as exiles from the heavenly kingdom.

But those who are weighed down by an excessive burden of sin,

If they are converted, are not merely relieved of the burden,

But are richly endowed with an abundance of pure life.

God’s abundant mercy knows no bounds to set for itself;

Without consulting you, he has mercy without punishment on whom he wills;

[Col. 1670D] He hardens whom he wills; without you God orders all things.

And, since both righteous and perishing people are under his jurisdiction,

He controls rewards and punishments with certain reins.

But because we do not know, until we are without the body,

Whom God intends to place at his right hand and whom outside it,

No one lives secure concerning his final end.

No one is secure about the side on which he will be;

For since penal transgression is universal,

He forgives whom he wills and demands debts from whom he wills,

Truthful and merciful, condemning sins and pardoning them.

The thief was worthy first of the cross, then of the abyss;

[Col. 1671A] Full grace gave him rewards in place of punishment.

An unnamed hermit is said to have led an angelic life,

Having worn no clothing for many years,

And, marvelous to tell, living on neither bread nor water;

Yet at last he fell once into a great sin,

Justly condemned, with punishment accompanying his offense.

Therefore spare, I pray, while you yourself are carried over the sea,

The vessel tossed by winds of words [variant: *vanis*, “vain”]; do not tear it with your words.

XXXVI. On the Fall of the First Man.

[Note: [Col. 1671D] Reciprocal verses.]

Man is burdened by death; but the man burdened by death,

Though he could have lived, loved that he might be unable to live.

Man laments wounds; but the man who laments wounds

Committed the forbidden wound with a biting tooth.

[Col. 1671B] Adam bit the apples; but Adam, who bit the apples,

Experienced death for the bite and wounds for the wound.

Eve deceived him; but Eve would not have deceived him

Had she not herself been deceived: the serpent had deceived Eve.

The woman urged the deed; but the deed the woman urged,

The man ought to have forbidden her. Had the man forbidden her

To eat what she wished, he would have wished to eat what he mourned having eaten.

Man rightly dies; but the man who rightly dies,

By weeping deserves help; yet if he repeats sins,

He repeats what destroys sins.

1576 XXXVII. On Life and Death.

The earth is exile, since heaven is our homeland;

To be born is to be condemned, to end life is to be blessed;

[Col. 1671C] Therefore let us call dying “being born,” and being born “dying,”

Fitting names to differing things.

For death is a harsh sound and an uncultivated syllable,

Precisely because the thing it denotes is harsh.

But “life” is an agreeable and pleasant expression;

The name commends the thing signified.

Therefore we ought to seek the nature of things,

So that from it we may discern the truth concerning the name.

How full of evils is this present thing called life

Is proved more by things themselves than by our speech.

We are taught not so much by books as by hard experience

How great is the harshness under which we living people are burdened here.

Hunger, cold, heat, thirst, illness,

Labor, plagues, and the rest are witnesses for me:

[Col. 1671D] Ought something oppressed by such great evils to be called life?

Will you concede that to live is to be tortured?

If every word derives harshness from things,

So many hard and bitter things demand a dreadful name.

Therefore these should fittingly be designated by the name of death,

Lest the name of life be dishonored by harshness.

Conversely, bodily death can be called life,

Since our faith is that a person is blessed through death—

I mean *hic* [or *hunc*], “this person,” whom Christ’s grace saves,

Not those such as you were, first-created man.

It pleases me to call those not human beings but earth and beasts,

[Col. 1672A] Who, rejecting reason, plainly devote themselves to flesh.

For neither present nor future life is assured to them,

Whom the harsh sentence of death oppresses here and there.

But to those who lament themselves as wretched in the valley of tears,

The Paradise of delights is due.

For these death is birth; for these death is life’s gate,

Whom the diadem blesses and the splendor of embroidered garments.

Eye has not seen, nor has mind been able to conceive,

Hearing cannot contain, nor can the tongue recount,

How great are the rewards which the Lord prepares above the heaven for the saints

Who fear, love, and keep the commands of the Thunderer.

May we deserve to attain their lot,

We who always die while weighed down by the mass of flesh.

XXXVIII. Commendation of the Jerusalem Expedition.

In all the world there is no man equal to Bohemond [Note: [Col. 1671D] namely, the Duke of Apulia, who conducted himself so illustriously in that expedition that he was raised to the principality of Antioch. [Col. 1672D] BARONIUS, under the year 1099.],

[Col. 1672B] Of whose deeds you can know a few things,

Surpassing a great number by the weight of their accomplishments.

He, foremost of leaders—unless we wish to relate falsehoods—

Moved peoples against the mighty Turks.

Originator and example of taking away the temple by force,

He had formerly conquered Constantinople, overcoming its duke;

He would also have conquered it now, had his people permitted it.

Yet the king pays him a great tribute at his command.

Then the martial hero attacked fierce enemies;

He shattered Nicaea and subdued the Turks in war.

He led strong cohorts into the walls of Antioch,

Which would have fallen had they not yielded.

Syria serves him; the Sabaeans send new gifts;

Parthian, Arab, and Mede desire to join alliance with him.

The magnificent king of Babylon, the Sultan, appeases him with gifts;

[Col. 1672C] Persia fears him and flees his swords;

Africa is afraid and, submissive, gives him a gift.

Bari and Taranto honor his coming,

And it would take far too long to recount how much land does so.

Yet he has not ceased even now from undertaking brave enterprises

Toward the West, at the urging of most just wars.

For plainly, unless he bears the name in vain,

A soldier devoted to God ought to fight against the gentiles.

1577 God invites the man who avoids domestic wars;

War is unlawful where there is no opposing party:

Men of one sect cannot rightly fight each other.

For these reasons, and for so many and such great exploits,

Loud-reporting fame bears Bohemond’s name through all the world,

And let the world echo because Bohemond does such great things.

XXXIX. To the Messenger of Death.

(To the manuscript of St. Gatianus and the Redonensis edition.)

[Col. 1672D]

The owl—a savage name, a dire omen for mortals—

As Maro testifies when, singing, he threatens fates.

Every kind of bird condemns its song,

And with a like wish drives this crime from the whole air.

Therefore it inhabits nights, since it does not desire daylight;

It appears at night, because if it flew by day,

Its hated head would by now have been cut off by many a claw,

Its limbs with its feathers divided and scattered among the bushes,

For every bird would wish to tear them apart—

A bird so dire, worthy to undergo an evil fate.

Therefore, away with that foul bird; and likewise, depart far off,

[Col. 1673A] Bearer of the funeral notice [Note: [Col. 1673D] that is, the person who invites people to funerals], condemned to darkness,

Who in the owl’s manner never report anything joyful,

Always sing mournfully, never to depart empty-handed.

For since you bring nothing but sadness, nothing but deaths,

You seek well-filled feasts with an annoying voice,

And, lest you grow weary, you ask for shoes and demand food;

On account of the deceased we give sandals and provide ointment.

Twice you sadden us: giving evil news, you receive these things.

Thus importunate, you sell me a funeral as a gift.

Wicked man, go outside! Why do you defile [printed: *pollius*; variant: *polluis*] the upper world?

What have you to do with the living, most foul citizen of the abyss,

Household slave of Pluto, embassy of destruction?

Why do you assail us by repeating troublesome words?

“Let the gathering assemble; give groans, pour out tears;

[Col. 1673B] Beat the bronze and cry out like Corybants;

Offer mournful songs with funeral dances;

Give sad poems, mark your places and the day;

Provide an outlay, set a plentiful table before me.”

Gulf of foods, why do you harass us with so many such demands?

You who command us to weep, weep yourself; rain down like a dripping cloud.

Drink the draught of sorrow; feed on the bread of grief.

Since evils delight you, may all evils punish you likewise;

Allow us to rejoice and pray to Christ and the Father

That the Three-and-One may grant us life’s gift.

Unless you obey these things while seeking the comforts of your belly,

You will be filled with clubs and iron, worst of buffoons.

XL. Consolation of Mourners, Namely Mary and Martha.

(To an Angevin manuscript.)

[Col. 1673C] Mary, accompanied by her sister, anxiously implores Christ’s aid with a sad face

From Bethany,

That he may recall her brother’s spirit from the dark abode

And restore him healthy though four days dead and stinking.

The gentle mercy of Christ feels compassion for the sorrowing woman;

Troubled, he wept and spoke thus:

“Lazarus, rise quickly; living, return from death.”

When the Maker said this, the creature called came back to life,

And each sister received her brother, healthy though four days dead.

O mercy of Christ! First you wept,

That you might instruct us to have a merciful heart because you wept;

Then you restore the life which you yourself [Note: [Col. 1674D] Perhaps the word *ipse*, “yourself,” is missing.] had made.

You are proved the Creator of air and sea,

You who commanded rivers to bear the earth’s mass,

[Col. 1673D] To whom alone the countless stars of heaven are known,

So that, once tears are wiped away, life may be restored,

And whoever steadfastly clings to you may hope for life.

Therefore the devotion of Christ’s worshippers, following Christ,

Should sorrow in such a way that it is not thought to despair.

1578 Let consolations, moderating fear by hope, wipe away tears.

Let compassion for these things move the mind that considers them;

Let the hearts of groaning persons who consider them breathe again.

To grieve at the funeral of a loved one is a pious thing,

But the trumpet will sound which shall call the dead bodies,

And in an instant they shall all rise from the tomb,

That each may receive what life and faith deserve.

[Col. 1674A] You can bring these consolations to sorrowful circumstances.

XLI. Prayer for the Faithful Departed.

Christ, great king and Lamb of God the Father,

Who gave himself, fixed to the wood, over to death,

Made a propitiatory sacrifice for our deeds,

Tasting gall and vinegar before his death,

That he might rescue us whom hostile power held

On account of a certain tree, whose forbidden taste faithless Adam touched,

Tasting it through the deceiver.

Therefore it was fitting to set wood against wood,

And thus just to set tasting against tasting.

This is at last the physician to whom the enemy is subject,

As are death, sickness, cold, heat, and hell;

May he profit this person for whom you wish it, and the other buried persons.

XLII. Another Prayer for the Departed.

[Col. 1674B] Highest Father of Christ, who always are and have been,

And always shall be, neither increasing nor diminishing,

Grant, O God, to the abbot the promises of the blessed kingdom.

Christ, Son of the Father, whom this world has believed

Equal to the Father and despoiler of the abyss,

Preserve the abbot for whom this company prays.

Life-giving Spirit, bond of Father and Son,

Not less than either, since you proceed from both,

Grant the abbot feasts that do not fail,

Throughout the world, where by common vow

The Three and One are served as the Son has commanded.

O living one, truly living! Have mercy on the departed;

May the gracious mother and virgin Mary be with them;

Most merciful Cephas, forgive them every sin;

Paul, together with Peter, gatekeeper of the heavenly hall;

[Col. 1674C] Thomas, Matthew, Luke, Barnabas, Philip, Matthias,

Simon, Thaddaeus, John, Bartholomew,

Peter’s brother, and first and second James,

Disciples of the Lord and possessors of Paradise,

Grant them the gifts of rest in joyful dwellings.

All saints, male and female, who have pleased the Thunderer,

May they grant the kingdom of heaven to their souls.

XLIII. That One Must Not Weep for the Death of a Christian.

We to whom a promise of future life has been made,

Who do not fail to know that, when we are born, we depart,

And do not fail to know that, by dying, we return,

Must not weep together at a loved one’s funeral;

Nor is it right to rejoice together at the non-funeral of a loved one.

To die is but a word; spare your weeping for empty grief.

[Col. 1674D] The first all-parenting human being was spirit and clay;

The first all-parenting human being is spirit and clay.

What has been is, and shall be; why does he seek vainly to lament it?

Death did not lay low this man, from whom it annihilated nothing.

What if by death two things were made separate,

Which soon will again be as they formerly were together?

Why should anyone care to weep for this, when each portion endures?

By the example of the first, let the middle and the one [perhaps: *imi*, “the lowest”] be considered:

Every human being is ashes, and also a mind ignorant of an end,

Both while he lives and after he has ceased to live.

What place is there for tears where nothing is either less or more?

For at the funeral, he who was formerly one becomes two.

[Col. 1675A] 1579 Count it among your gains to commit beloved bodies to tombs,

For whoever increases through death knows no loss.

XLIV. Censure of Superfluities in the Epitaph of Abbot John.

That John’s life endured for many years,

And that, while he lived, concern for his own good did not grow cold,

But, joining better things to good and the best to better,

He zealously founded and more zealously built

A tower of virtues by which he might climb heaven’s heights;

That he ruled speech well, adapting himself to the occasion,

Anointing and pricking, joining harsh things to gentle;

That he kept God’s commands in hope of rest;

That, for what he kept, his lot is joined with the blessed—

All this we read because we know it to be useful;

[Col. 1675B] We also praise it and approve it as worthy of praise,

For that is rightly praised by which the reader is edified.

If a good person reads these things, he rejoices because he has done what he reads;

If a bad person, he grieves that he is bad and wishes not to be so.

But what remains gives the reader weariness,

And he wanders away, nor is the reader edified.

For what purpose does it tend, or, I ask, what useful result follows,

That the month of February was for him like a death-bearing sword,

That he departed when Phoebus entered the Fishes?

You could add in this way whatever superfluities you knew:

When heaven stood above and earth below,

When the Loire flowed, when water swelled under the winds,

When fishes swam, when little sparrows fluttered,

When a woman spun, when a little daughter cried.

If every branch standing on a tree became a pen,

[Col. 1675C] And whatever provides a draught for all should become ink,

If all flat bodies became parchment,

If all living and dead persons wrote such things,

Such matters would weary all living and dead persons.

XLV. On the Difference of Merits and Places

Heaven, earth, and chaos—the threefold division of places—  
receive souls according to the judgments of their merits.  
For to those exceedingly good, abiding existence in heaven is given;  
and to those outstandingly evil, the wrath of Gehenna is swiftly rendered.  
To those who are neither, but nevertheless stand between the two,  
some manner of purgation is assigned upon earth.  
For some are tormented in gloomy dwellings by cold,  
while I believe the sins of others are scorched by flames.  
[Col. 1675D] Through sea and through lands unceasing toil drives these restless souls;  
to some of them an assembly is accustomed to appear.  
If anyone doubts that these cannot be greatly aided by prayers,  
he may prove it by this reasoning:  
the torment of hell cannot be removed by prayer,  
nor can one placed above the stars be improved by prayer.  
It remains, therefore, that we should commend in prayer only those  
whose sins we know are being purged through punishments;  
and since this blessed man was not among their number,  
may he himself rather cleanse our offences by his prayers.

XLVI. The Shipwreck of Jonah the Prophet

You who do not know, now learn concerning the Ninevites;  
learn from Jonah, the prophet fleeing from the Lord,  
how he was submerged and how he returned from thence.  
You who flee the Lord enter into the peril of the deep,  
[Col. 1676A] where the whale swallows living fugitives from God.  
You who weep for sins possess great consolation;  
do not despair, because sorrows will yield to joys.  
You who offend, you who forsake offences,  
draw two lessons for yourself from the Book of Jonah.  
Let the reading of these deeds be a delight—or rather a guidance—of morals for you.

The immense city of Nineveh, most renowned for its many citizens,  
1580 rich in wealth and powerful through the diadem of its kingdom,  
by its disgraceful life moved the Lord to anger.  
But God, though angry, postpones the punishment of offences;  
he wishes pardon to be sought; though offended, he wishes to show mercy.  
Therefore he calls Jonah and instructs him to announce ruin  
to the city which had deserved it by the foul crimes of its life.  
“Arise, my prophet, and leave your own home;  
[Col. 1676B] hasten to Nineveh and report to them my own words.  
Cry through the streets, terrifying my enemies:  
‘The city shall be overthrown sooner than anyone fears;  
the impure citizens shall perish after a short time.’”

Jonah arose, but turned his journey by devious paths;  
he went down to the sea as he intended to travel to Tarshish.  
This was not what had been commanded, yet he desired to go to Tarshish;  
but the waves of the sea detained the fugitive of the Lord.  
O mind of the prophet, of wondrous simplicity!  
He thinks that the Lord is far from him when he changes places.  
For nothing can be remote from him who fills all things.  
Should he flee to hell or to the heavenly kingdom,  
God stands behind him; let the fugitive therefore cease.

But it is pleasant to consider what was the cause of his flight.  
[Col. 1676C] Perhaps, fearing his fate, he did not go to prophesy.  
For, because he would bear a message burdening the hearts of the people,  
as a herald of destruction he might well be battered on every side,  
laid low by the sword, or perhaps burned by fire.  
But he is not brave who so fears the end of death  
that he puts love of life before the ability to die well;  
nor does he believe the Lord who does not obediently entrust himself to him.  
Therefore this cannot have been the prophet’s reason for fleeing.

Rather, he knew the Lord: that he labours to call us back  
and swiftly forgives if anyone abandons former evils.  
For why does he give warning beforehand? Why does he not immediately punish sins?  
Why does he lie, as it were, before his threats, unless he wishes to give remedies?  
The physician frightens the sick man so that he may seek a draught for himself.  
[Col. 1676D] This the messenger feared, whom the abyss preserved:  
that he might prove false unless the outcome followed the prediction.  
He would say that those were to be overthrown whom he knew could turn back,  
and who, if they learned of it, would by no means perish.

Knowing God, therefore, he flees the presence of the gracious countenance;  
he descends to Joppa and hastens to board a ship.  
He leaves the shore, as though he were safer thus upon the sea.  
But he does not know that the sea, swelling on every side in its waves,  
can disturb the fugitive’s course with the fury of the wind.  
The storm carries off the sail; the lofty vessel touches heaven;  
then it falls again into the depths and enters fearful waters beneath.  
The air lacks light: neither sun nor Cynthia appears;  
nor do the stars shine, but that night was a storm.  
No safety appears; the broken mast lies in the ship.  
The oars burst apart; the hour of final disaster comes.  
[Col. 1677A] The sailors groan, surrounded by such great perils.  
The master of the ship abandons the steering of the helm.  
On every side there is sad thunder; the crash crowns all heaven.  
Frequent lightning flashes, as though all things together were saying:  
“O fugitive, return and obey the command of the Thunderer!”

Jonah does not know this and rests oppressed by sleep.  
The inner part of the vessel has become the prophet’s bedchamber.  
But a sailor approaches him, assails him with voice and foot:  
“Arise! What are you doing? Most worthy of many blows,  
you sleep securely when shortly you are to perish.  
Perhaps at this very hour the prow, overwhelmed by waves, is perishing.  
With prayer add tears; let intercession drive away death,  
if it can happen; if not, it is not fitting to bewail the last things.”

Meanwhile, amid the winds and the raging swelling sea,  
[Col. 1677B] the helpless ship had entrusted everything to the fates.  
Whatever was thought to weigh it down is cast into the sea,  
yet the anxious pine-wood vessel fears no less to be submerged.  
1581 For the ship remains burdened by sin, not by weight;  
nor, because guilt weighs it down, does he who removes weights lighten it.  
Now it is sufficiently apparent, though it had caused such evils,  
that the vessel is being assailed by divine wrath.

Therefore the mission of the lot seeks out one guilty of death,  
and the verdict seizes Jonah and draws him to punishment.  
He is sent into the waves; the sea falls, and the tumult falls.  
The fate of one man given up appeases Neptune’s anger.  
The prow, previously heavy, immediately raises itself;  
the just submersion of the fugitive becomes the cause of peace.

[Col. 1677C] O God, deeds of your mercy greatly to be remembered!  
You spare when you strike, and in striking show mercy;  
you are accustomed to cherish us, as though humankind were your offspring.  
In the region of the sea, gracious power, you rule;  
and, as is plain, death itself, trembling, obeys you.  
For who would think that one sunk in the sea could be recalled?  
Who would imagine one swallowed by a fish returning to daylight?  
Behold, a whale comes, accustomed to cut through the sea’s depths—  
a fish equal to a mountain, the most savage monster of the deep—  
and as though prey, it snatches and swallows the prophet.  
But, as though entrusted with him, whether it wishes or not, it will give him back;  
and unwillingly it will carry to a useful shore the one whom it captured.  
Thus for three nights, and for as many days,  
the prophet, shut in the belly of the beast, expiates the boldness of his grave sin.

[Col. 1677D] After this, the innocent monster vomits forth the one allotted, or cast into the sea by lot.  
[Note: That is, the one assigned, or sunk by lot.]  
and, immediately cast forth, he reaches tangible land;  
the light of day, despaired of, shines again upon him.  
He leaves the shores, which he had sought with longing mind,  
and, condemning his own punishment, condemns sea and sand.  
Then warned anew, he does not dare to turn aside from his course,  
but swiftly makes straight for the dwellings of Nineveh.  
And, to make up for the delay of sailing by the measure of travelling,  
a journey suited to three days is run in one day.

Having entered the walls, he says these things to sinful men:  
“Citizens, I proclaim to you Nineveh’s destruction.  
The cry of your crimes reaches heaven,  
nor will God any longer endure these things unavenged.  
[Col. 1678A] After six weeks an impious destruction awaits the city.  
I speak to you the words of the God of heaven with a faithful mouth.”

Terrified by these words, the people are pierced with compunction, anxious and sad;  
each laments the evils which he had redeemed by no good deeds.  
Great and small, clothed in sackcloth,  
fasted and offered tears and prayers.  
The king too did what they did: he cast off the badges of pride.  
For before great evils imperial splendour gave way;  
disturbed by recognition of his guilt,  
in a rare example he did not disdain to descend from his splendid throne:  
he mourned and wept.  
Then before Jonah the lofty crown is laid aside,  
and ashes are placed upon his head, in remembrance of the end;  
purple is cast away; the king is clothed in haircloth.

[Col. 1678B] Meditation upon punishment removes the pleasures of the banquet,  
and the force of grief drives away delight in fragrance.  
The earth, which knows not how to bend itself, became the bed’s feather mattress.  
In place of the sound of the lyre were mournful sighs,  
and in place of spices, the wretched contrition of the mind.  
The court of nobles bears a similar affliction.  
Courtier and soldier imitate their lord’s mourning.  
Ashes are everywhere; none lacks haircloth.  
They lie in mourning, if perhaps sleep might please them.

Then the herald’s voice, flying through the places of the region,  
by royal command admonishes all in this order:  
“Let every human being mourn; let anxious grief constrain every heart;  
let food and drink be removed from every flesh.  
While the mother grieves, no infant shall suck the breast.  
A shrill voice will sound from the cares of those fasting.  
[Col. 1678C] 1582 A new care will deny fodder to the feeding beasts of burden.  
The flock itself will be kept from the streams by the staff of one weeping,  
so that every beast may cry out and equal toil may weigh upon all.  
Who knows whether a gentle judgment may spare those worn down,  
lest it shake the shattered, lest it inflict wounds upon those already suffering,  
or moreover destroy those whom their own care destroys?  
The gentle one does not delight in afflicting the wretched with punishments;  
the merciful one is not made glad by the blood of the miserable.”

By such great lamentations the wrath of the Almighty yielded,  
sparing punishments and driving far away the crime of death,  
and thus giving pious examples from the Scriptures for those to come.

XLVII. Before the Book of Ruth, after an interval, four verses without a title follow, separated by spaces as follows:

[Col. 1678D]

A fixed crown in the heavens casts rays rivaling the sun,  
a star to be beheld in serene heaven, sevenfold—  
at whose centre shines the author of this threshold,  
[Note: That is, “of this threshold.”]  
a star, mother of offspring, nevertheless rivaling the sun.

At the beginning of the manuscript of Saint Gatianus the following verse, painted in red, is placed as a title: “Marbod relates in these verses the history of Ruth.” THE BOOK OF RUTH BEGINS.

We shall sing deeds performed in the time of one judge,  
set forth in the plain speech of an earlier writer,  
which it is pleasant to recite, so that the account of events may become  
clearer by being fashioned anew and polished once.

[Col. 1679A] A certain Elimelech, born of Judaean stock,  
fleeing with his marriage-partner and two sons  
when dreadful famine was ravaging towns and fields,  
went over to the Moabites, fertile in food.  
When he died shortly afterward, Naomi remained widowed.  
But the two brothers, led by vain hope of offspring,  
marry Ruth and Orpah, sisters, I believe.  
This one was called Chilion; that one was named Mahlon.  
Their life in exile there lasted twice five years.  
Thus they yield to fate without offspring.  
Bereft of her two sons, Naomi the chaste woman mourned with her daughters-in-law,  
remembering that she was oppressed by a hard lot.  
And now exhausted by the destructive misfortunes  
both of fortune and of that dreadful land, she prepares to return to her former home;  
for she had heard that food was now there.

[Col. 1679B] She laments having lived among the idolatrous Moabites,  
and now sets out on her return, accompanied by the tears of the two women.  
She stopped and thus addressed the sorrowful girls:  
“What advantage, O daughters, approved in the devotion of faith,  
is there in accompanying the steps of an old woman? I beg you, return.  
Fortune oppresses me; disaster has also taken hope from me.  
O my beloved ones! There is now no hope for my old age;  
the hand of the Almighty has taken from me the fruit of my womb.  
Even if you could have husbands born from me—  
if I should now conceive and become a mother again—  
while the boys grew and your bodies grew old,  
feeble age would prevent you from becoming fruitful.  
Those who have experienced it know how grievous it is  
to have left one’s home and despised one’s own countrymen, and how sweet to return.  
Go home, dear ones; the cause which bids me return is this:  
[Col. 1679C] that my native soil may give me a grave as dowry.  
My desire is to die; a better lot befits you:  
that in happy childbirth you may be called mothers by a husband.  
Live and fare well; hold as a grave pledge for my sake  
the bodies of my sons, dead with their wives.”

1583 Having said this, weeping, she pressed kisses upon those who wept;  
then, turning, she takes the road, frequently uttering sighs.  
Orpah, unwilling to leave the gods of her fathers and her paternal home,  
departs, seeking again what she believes prosperous.  
Ruth accompanies her mother-in-law and counts these losses as gain,  
while she desires to become an Israelite proselyte  
and to be numbered with God’s people in equal recompense.

Her mother-in-law says to her: “Behold, your kinswoman has left you  
[Col. 1679D] and returned home, led by devotion to her parents.  
You too, daughter, return and obey the words of one who advises you.”  
Having heard such words, Ruth the Moabite replied:  
“It shall not be so. Rather, let my life be with you;  
let death be shared; let us remain in the same households.  
Let my portion be with you while I live, and your portion with me.  
What you worship I shall worship; I shall not venerate idols.”

O rock of the desert, unwilling to return to what you had abandoned!  
What reward do you think will come to you for leaving your own things?  
The stranger whom you follow lacks provisions and needs money.  
Deprived of silver, what, I ask, will she provide for one in need?  
But the King of heaven pleases you more than the multitude of gods;  
you follow him and seem to wish to please him.  
He to whom you entrust yourself will give you more than what you have left.  
He himself—powerful, great, ruler of earth, and the Lamb—  
[Col. 1680A] will be sent forth from here. From you a king will come forth  
in the fourth generation, the lyre-playing great-grandfather of Mary.

The mother-in-law did not dare resist so steadfast a mind,  
possessing the cause of goodness, nor so pious a companion.  
Joined to her, and receiving fitting consolation,  
she hastens to the borders of Judah, whence she had departed.  
The city of Bethlehem gives rest to the weary at harvest time.  
Without delay the speech of women spreads from mouth to mouth:  
“This is that Naomi, celebrated at home and abroad.”  
“No,” she says, “I am not worthy to be called by such a name—  
I whom God has afflicted, whom he has wounded with many a blow.  
Once full of goods, behold, now I return empty.  
What is beautiful for me now, except perhaps to enter the grave?  
Therefore call me Mara, whom bitter death has devastated;  
the prey of so great an evil, I ought not be called beautiful.”

[Col. 1680B] These arrangements having been made, Ruth the Moabite, dwelling there,  
addresses her mother-in-law: “If you wish, I shall go into the field,  
where I may find merciful reapers,  
so that I may gather the ears remaining in their tracks.  
Whatever has been left will help our livelihood.”  
Her mother-in-law agrees; the diligent daughter-in-law immediately goes out.  
O blessed daughter-in-law, from whom a king will arise!  
Behold, you pluck ears of grain mingled with foreign girls;  
to feed a widow, you have resolved not to spare yourself.  
Like an ant, you seek food for your friend;  
not even blazing summer forbids you, though necessity compels you.  
You do not know what greatness is being prepared for you, you for whom sun and moon obey.  
Behold, among the citizens is a man powerful in virtue and rich:  
Boaz, owner of many possessions, was heir to these fields after Elimelech’s death,  
[Col. 1680C] and was related to him by blood; Boaz came to inspect the work of his reapers.  
Having greeted them, according to the measure of his goodness,  
and having received their greeting in return, he said this to one man:  
“Boy, I do not know this woman, but I am anxious to learn who she is.”  
He spoke and heard: “She recently came to Bethlehem,  
though born among the Moabites, unwilling as they were,  
with her mother, desiring to remain under a husband’s law;  
and she fled a people pretending to worship abominations.  
Lest she worship idols, she clings to those who worship better things.  
And from the whole day she has not withdrawn anywhere;  
the sun has already set, yet she has not ended her fasting.”

Boaz said: “Daughter, let there be no hesitation for you;  
but safely join my girls in the field,  
so that you may follow the ears before the sickle of the reaper;  
[Col. 1680D] I wish you not to cease gathering until the threshing-floor grinds the harvest.  
1584 Seek gain diligently; you shall suffer no annoyance.  
I shall command the boys that you may not be troubled in any manner.  
Indeed, whenever you thirst, you may hasten to refresh yourself  
from the waters by which the boys too are refreshed.  
And lest you grow weary, take food with the reapers.”

Falling forward upon the ground, she prepares to return thanks  
and worships him whom she now knew as lord of the region.  
“Whence,” she said, “has so pleasant a hope shone upon me,  
that in your goodness you grant such great things kindly to one unworthy,  
and console the heart of a foreign woman—  
lowly and unknown, far from her own land,  
scarcely worthy to belong to the band of your maidservants?”

[Col. 1681A] “We know,” he says, “how you have done all things rightly:  
how after your husband’s death you submitted yourself to your mother-in-law,  
and how greatly, fleeing peoples who worship images,  
you despised the rites in which you had been brought up.  
Nor did the sweetness of your parents hold you back in sorrow;  
rather, you chose to be preserved beneath the Lord’s wings, even amid evils.  
We have believed true reports: you are deemed a woman of virtue.  
May the King, who judges most justly, recompense these things to you;  
may he who possesses heaven’s dwelling give you reward.”

He spoke, and turning to the boys, the nobleman commands:  
“Reap where she wishes, and let no one hinder her.  
I also wish you to overlook some of your sheaves.  
Let her prudently gather portions which she may lawfully collect;  
let no one inquire into this; let no one take pains to spare me [read: obey me].”

[Col. 1681B] Therefore Ruth sat with the reapers and ate;  
and, not consuming the delicacies of the meal,  
she judges it right to keep them with her and give them to her mother-in-law.  
Then, setting out, she returns after harvesting barley as before;  
and from her labour, gathered with daily diligence,  
she beat it with a rod and brought together the cleansed grain:  
a measure of an ephah, which would yield three bushels.  
She carried these to her mother-in-law with the remaining portion of food,  
and related what had happened and repeated Boaz’s words.

The woman gives thanks and adds, as a provident prophetess:  
“O sole hope left to me after so many have been buried!  
I think much how provision may be made for you,  
lest excessive labour become an unjust burden for you  
and anxious poverty, which you are determined thus to overcome,  
sink your bent and fragile sex beneath its weight.

[Col. 1681C] Therefore, with my troubled heart, I now command you  
to set out quickly, so that you may become happy through a husband,  
who may make you fruitful and through whom bread with wine  
and unfailing salt may always abound for you.  
When Boaz comes to inspect the servants measuring the heaps,  
resplendent in festive dress and with a composed countenance,  
mark carefully where he lies at night upon his bed.  
When he is already snoring, approach him with silent step  
and, having awakened him, remind him of the requirement of the law:  
that, in place of your departed husband, he ought to be yours  
and restore the familial seed through his kinsman,  
he who through a barren fate lacked a fruitful marriage-bed.”

Why do I delay and attempt to proceed in slow verse?  
The harvest was ended; the threshing-floor was distributing portions to the weary.  
Ruth, obeying the words, with the boys left here and there,  
[Col. 1681D] quietly seeks the supports of the better man’s bed,  
and, having awakened him, tells him what the law commands him to grant her.  
At first suddenly alarmed, but soon steady in heart,  
he answers timidly: “Most chaste daughter, in faith,  
you shall receive all that you ask, if a certain heir before me  
does not render you what the rule of the law requires.  
But now wait, that the proceeding may take its proper course;  
it is not customary here to anticipate the right of the first.  
He must be consulted whether he will consent or fail you.  
Tomorrow it will become known to whom you shall join your marriage-vow.  
Now be quietly at ease and preserve a chaste bed.”

When he had finished these words, the secure girl rested.  
In the morning Boaz rose and, pressing forward what he had conceived,  
commands the woman to return home swiftly and secretly.  
[Col. 1682A] As a pledge he gives the girl ears of grain in her cloak:  
1585 six measures of grain, lest she return empty-clad—  
a suitable pledge from the country and token of what was to come.  
For heavenly grace lies hidden in the grains of bread,  
which he who was born from Mary’s flesh gave to the Church;  
he is believed to be signified by this strong man,  
as the daughter-in-law represents the Church and the mother-in-law portrays the Synagogue.

Then, having summoned the kinsman in the presence of the people  
and asked the elders of the city to sit before the gates,  
he addresses his cousin with these words through this mediation:  
“Elimelech’s field—which, as I must tell you, is yours by right—  
must be bought by you, Naomi the widow selling it;  
for we know that you are first in order of blood.  
If you retain it, wishing to extend your boundaries,  
[Col. 1682B] by the law of her husband you must also take Ruth as wife,  
performing for your dead brother the duties of a father in his stead.  
But if you are unwilling—you who appear to be first—  
the estate is now mine, since by lot I am second to you.”

The young man answered: “I have no desire to become a father to another’s offspring;  
I want you to be the first brother.  
I yield my right; what was mine I give to you.  
Untie the binding of your foot, if you yield your right to me.”  
He unties it and immediately gives him the removed shoe.  
It was the custom of the ancients and an almost fixed law among kinsmen  
that the first heir, transferring his rights to the next,  
should do what I have said, so that the cession might have force.

This solemn customary arrangement having been performed,  
Boaz says to the assembly of people and elders sitting there:  
“The shoe is a witness; you too are witnesses,  
[Col. 1682C] that behold, I take possession of Mahlon’s goods and marriage.”

The elders and common people answered,  
asking that good things may be multiplied for the woman  
whom God has taken from the nations and joined to you,  
that she may be fruitful in offspring, like Leah,  
beloved in Rachel’s place and faithful to her husband,  
and surpass the women of Bethlehem in virtue.  
Thus, having offered their auspicious wishes, they depart.

Boaz has a wife, better than whom no one has;  
and not long afterward he receives offspring from his wife.  
For Obed is born, completing his father’s joy.  
He is the father of Jesse, whom we know to be the father  
of the psalmist king, from whose seed, O Christ,  
we worship you as born, hoping for a blessed end. Amen.

XLVIII. On the Rape of Dinah (Genesis XXXIV)

(To the Angers and Tours manuscripts.)

[Col. 1682D]

Learn to endure enclosure, you who spare your chastity,  
and not to put forth your foot or leave your dwelling.  
The foolish little girl who hates hiding places exposes herself;  
whenever she does not avoid public places, she invites violation.  
Let the life of Mary, the Virgin without equal,  
whom nevertheless it is lawful to imitate, be for you a model of chastity.  
She was not mingled with dances in the streets;  
to her, in seclusion, the angel brought that “Hail,”  
which she would not have heard had she not been enclosed.

Dinah, Leah’s very beautiful young daughter,  
while wandering outside, suffered new losses of modesty;  
she would have remained intact had she not gone out.  
[Col. 1683A] But while she goes forth, while her lovely appearance is adorned  
with nature’s gifts, surpassing the brides of the region,  
there was no lack of fuel for so great a fire.  
For the prince of the land cannot endure these flames.  
The son of Hivite, astonished by the novelty of her face,  
the youth Shechem, bears cruel wounds in his veins;  
impatient of delay, he carries her off and despoils her of chastity.  
Having violated the virgin, the ravisher receives grateful kisses,  
comforting the sorrowful girl and reconciling her with gifts.

But Dinah’s levity was for him the cause of ruin,  
and the violence of desire found a fitting end.  
Her brother Simeon, not intending to leave the foolish youth unavenged  
for the abduction, deferred the affair through deceit;  
and, against the adulterer, because he thought deception just,  
he prepares by craft to kill the man who had dishonoured him by force.

[Col. 1683B] 1586 For a short while Levi’s dissimulated indignation is silent,  
mingling the disgrace of his sister with the blood of her ravisher.  
These two brothers, thirsting for the death of the profane men,  
address the foolish youth, restraining the tumult of their hearts:  
“You corrupted the woman and did not fear us, young man.  
If you desire to retain our sister as wife,  
make a firm peace, removing contentious quarrelling,  
and swiftly enter into a pact; swiftly end the wars that threaten.  
Let us be one people, ruled under one law;  
let us live as one and cultivate common fields.  
Let the law of our marriages be shared.  
It is not lawful for Hebrews to abandon their true sect;  
you may pass over to the required rite  
and, in order to join the peoples, you must lay aside foreskins.

[Col. 1683C] Let the party conscious of deserved guilt be conscious of punishment;  
let every man dwelling in the city be circumcised.  
Let the honour of this deed be testimony to the compact;  
let the removal of the skin be an acceptable vengeance to the girls,  
when you yourselves expiate your crime in blood for your sins,  
and when your people together with you undergo a just punishment.  
If you do the things mentioned, the covenants of peace shall be ratified;  
but if not, the seizure of Dinah remains unappeased,  
and we shall take her away, although we grieve for what she has suffered.”

This youthful love accepts these terms, and so does his father Hamor;  
the whole people, moved by the father’s and son’s request, accepts them.  
Immediately the loss of skin is made by all;  
nobles and commoners alike are cut short in their manhood.  
The third dawn, bringing greater pain,  
[Col. 1683D] had opened the city gates to the weakened crowds.  
Behold, the brothers’ rage, raging over the crime previously committed,  
breaks through the gates and brings wounds of death.  
Nor is it enough for their wrath to strike the guilty man with the sword;  
vengeance rages also against a people lacking guilt.  
The harmful sword runs wild in immeasurable slaughter;  
it distinguishes no one, but strikes down old men with youths.  
The funeral of a people results from one man’s offence.  
He himself lies laid low beneath the fate of his own guilt,  
and his father also, as though a partner in this crime, falls.  
After the deed had sufficiently satisfied Simeon’s sword,  
and Levi’s right hand, weary from slaughter, had rested,  
and no blood remained for anyone to shed against anyone—

[Col. 1684A] having avenged the ravisher, they brought back their sister.  
But Jacob’s sons, imitating the twin brothers,  
having poured into the walls, easily used their strength.  
The city, stripped of men, lay open to plunder without warfare;  
each takes what he encounters, and no one resists him.  
One seizes flocks of livestock; another, the treasures of houses.  
This man carries off nursing infants and widowed mothers;  
having searched every single thing, they lay all waste.  
Finally, the zeal of the unjust victors, leaving nothing remaining,  
also strips the bodies of the slain men;  
the end of their devastation was to spare only corpses.

Thus, because of the violation, the city became a place of burial—  
because Dinah, by wandering and casting off restraint, incurred that violation.  
Thus Dinah’s levity was the origin of this ruin.

Therefore, since this is so, let the consecrated virgin,  
the companion of public life and one to be blessed by heaven’s trophy,  
[Col. 1684B] sit in her cell if she wishes to be a modest girl;  
she who is about to admit males loves encounters with the populace.  
Yet let no one think that these things are to be recited for girls alone;  
we have written them so that both sexes may be instructed.  
Let our mind not, as it were, be poured out through the world’s pathless places,  
but hold to the law of its mother and the commands of its father,  
equally cherishing the heavenly camp night and day.  
For, if we wish to fit the correspondences together,  
what is a son of the Church except a daughter of Leah?  
Shechem will be the devil, who seeks to corrupt us;  
we then slay him when we subdue our shameful members,  
when the whole people of vices is overcome with him,  
and when the power of threefold faith becomes the cause of his ruin,  
[Col. 1684C] so that the third light gives the ravisher of the harlot to night.

+ XLIX. Commendation of Learning  
[Note: The verses that follow, from no. 49 through no. 60, are unpublished.]

Since medicine makes no progress without learning;  
nor are sails stretched upon the sea without learning;  
nor does any ship seek harbour without learning:  
listen to learning, if you wish to avoid ruin.

+ L. Do Not Trust a Woman Too Much

Whoever you are who trust a woman’s fidelity,  
believe me: if you trust her, you will be deceived.

+ LI. A Thief’s Theft Proved by a Cock

A widow had a cock, and a thief ate the cock.  
She charges the thief with theft; he denies it.  
While he clears himself by oath, the cock sang in the perjurer’s belly,  
and thus the matter was proved.

+ LII. On a Certain Hervaeus

[Col. 1684D]

The people’s counsel, the voice of the commons, the tongue of the senate—  
here lies Hervaeus, a great ruin to his own people.

+ LIII. On the Leopard

Neither lion nor panther: I draw my name from these, leopard.

1586* + LIV. The Paternal House

Rejoice in the narrow house acquired for you by the praise of your ancestors.

+ LV. On Abbots Excessively Indulgent

It is abbots’ custom never to punish wrongdoing;  
but when they depart from the world, they seek rewards.  
Therefore let us say the “Our Father” three times for them.

+ LVI. On Aristotle

Supreme Aristotle, weighing the heights of things,  
[Col. 1685A] divided into two whatever existed in the world.

+ LVII. Guarmundus

The world lacks Guarmundus, and Guarmundus lacks a diadem;  
the bereaved world groans at Guarmundus’s death.  
When death came to Guarmundus, grief immediately came to the world,  
because dreadful death carried off Guarmundus, the ornament of the world.  
Death to you, Guarmundus; grief and lamentation to you, world;  
peace with Guarmundus, because scarcely anything is good in this world.

+ LVIII. Poetic Trifles

A high mountain; a firm bridge; a free brow; a glassy spring.  
A nut-tree; a holy cross; a fierce lion; good light; a watchful leader.  
White snow; black pitch; a fried man; the water Styx; a screech-owl.  
A fertile countryside; corruption, pus; and a sow friendly with mud.

[Col. 1685B] A long leg; a crane bends; a mouse gnaws; incense smells sweet.  
There is a biting tooth, a mindful mind, a people of one’s homeland;  
a city’s populace, hope of virtue, every thing, a foot walks.  
Force compels; strife disturbs; *glis* [“dormouse”] is equivocal in three senses.  
A dowry enriches; a flower blooms; dew drips; a whetstone sharpens.  
A sister-in-law, a brother’s wife; an ox lows; custom draws all things.  
Fate gives; death takes away; a voice resounds; night conceals thefts.  
The law of flesh, the power of a ruler, and the law of law are each a *ius*.

+ LIX. A Broken Vessel

There is a portico in Rome, where, as I take a walk,  
seeking novel things, I found a vessel of sapphire.  
An unknown dealer, selling incense with sapphire,  
our companion bought incense for three denarii three times;  
and I, extravagant, bought the vessel for three and a half solidi.

[Col. 1685C] While I anxiously take care to carry it unshaken,  
I pay the price for a clean wicker basket.  
The vessel is put inside whole; afterward, I remember,  
it is taken out cracked; then I am sad, wretched beyond measure.  
Among great guests this vessel would have been of great value,  
if it had been brought as it had then been put away.  
But the bearer crushed it—may no day be prosperous for him!

+ LX. Eulogy of Milo, Monk of Saint Albinus, Afterwards Bishop of Palestrina under Urban II, from Marbod

(From the manuscript codex of Saint Albinus of Angers.)

Rome, exceedingly blessed, which has grown so from low beginnings  
that now it is called, and deservedly regarded,  
the light of the Church and the world’s highest summit,  
sending forth royal and pontifical light,  
by whose teaching our ruin is supported—  
seeing the Church troubled by simony,  
[Col. 1686A] it sent through the Gallic kingdoms an approved legate;  
it commanded Milo to fight against Simon.  
He is ordered to assist the oppressed and fallen Church:  
to give protection to the oppressed and, by granting remedy, to the fallen.  
With the sword of Peter the leader attacks the ranks of the foul enemy;  
the bishopric is taken from unworthy men who obtained it by payment,  
and an illustrious see is given without payment to those worthy of it.  
Because of sellers, purchasers are not excused.

His coming was useful, as the situation required;  
for there are prelates attentive to profit,  
who make gain from God’s manifest gifts  
and sell Christ, while others do not rebuke them.  
Some endure them through fear, others through favour:  
no bishopric is bestowed without payment.  
If a hand is stuffed with money, that boy will become a dean;  
[Col. 1686B] and those well supplied with coins are immediately made canons.  
Wealth is promoted; understanding, without a name, is worthless.  
A purse filled with money is full of understanding.  
Riches overcome every teaching of wisdom,  
and the words of the learned yield to the wealthy fool.  
Giving gifts is more powerful than proving falsehoods by truths.  
In the highest sacred offices money rises everywhere;  
the gifts that speak are condemned by no decrees.  
Silver has more power than Gregory’s teaching.

Now the whole state of religion consists in gifts;  
they are now shepherds of mouths, not of souls.  
A secret gift, if you wish, enables a bridegroom  
to dismiss his wife if he wishes to marry another, more noble one.  
If you wish to be good to your companions and faithful to your lord,  
you will begin to become the clergy’s greatest object of mockery;  
[Col. 1686C] but the persecutor of his companions, the lover of fraud,  
is feared and revered by everyone.  
The whole Gallic world is filled with these vices;  
but Milo penetrated to its inmost parts with the spear of faith.  
Neither gifts nor affection bent the good champion;  
his mind was strong, though bodily strength was lacking.  
I saw purchasers cut down by the sword of his word,  
and filthy Simon fell ashamed beneath him.  
How great were the joys which that virtue of Milo gave to the good;  
and it would have given us far greater things,  
and he would have been unconquered, but death took away his blows.  
Mind too secure and rigidly following Peter,  
now, faithful servant, you receive your rewards in heaven.  
Now placed above the stars, now crowned with a diadem,  
hear our prayers by remitting our offences.

[ON THE ORNAMENTS OF WORDS]

[Col. 1685]

A BRIEF NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK

1587–1588 This manuscript book has been extracted from codices: namely, from the Angers manuscript, at least 600 years old; from the somewhat more recent Bec manuscript, no. 98; from the Gemmeticum manuscript, approximately 400 years old; and finally from the Redon edition of 1524. In each it is found variously inscribed and entitled. The Angers manuscript, indeed the oldest of all, has no title and begins without introduction: “To one about to compose verse,” etc. At the head of each article it has a summary of each precept, followed by an example composed in verse. The Gemmeticum codex likewise has this, but under the title: “Marbod to his pupil, On the Ornaments of Words. To one about to compose verse,” etc.

The Bec manuscript has a title, but it has been so erased and obliterated that it wholly escapes sight; nor can the author be determined from it. Only from the ending, where it reads: “The little book of Marbod on [Col. 1687] the ornaments of words ends,” can this be known. It has summaries of the precepts only in the margin, while the examples are on the page of the book itself with the title of each article. Finally, the Redon edition of 1524 has no summaries at all, but only the title of each article together with its example composed in verse. At its beginning it reads: “Prologue of the little book On the Ornaments of Words.” Having considered all this, we have judged that the edition of this book which would be more convenient for the reader should be presented as follows. Moreover, from the prefixed Gemmeticum title it may be inferred that Marbod composed this little book for his pupils while he was still teaching humane letters and rhetoric at Angers, long before he had been elevated to the see of Rennes.

[Col. 1687]

MARBOD TO HIS PUPIL: ON THE ORNAMENTS OF WORDS

PROLOGUE OF THE LITTLE BOOK

For one intending to compose verse I take care to hand down  
certain figures of speech celebrated by the study of earlier writers,  
which are no less beautiful in prose as well.  
If you can use them like gems and flowers,  
your work will become splendid, like a garden of delights,  
where the fragrance of diverse scents breathes forth,  
nor will there be lacking fruit drawn from the seed of flowers:  
the listener’s mind is persuaded by the brightness of ornament.

But if, perhaps, you are untrained and scarcely yet fashion commonplace things,  
since every capacity requires many things for itself,  
first learn the elementary matters, so that you may become fit for these;  
having been instructed in small things, you will safely attempt great ones.  
Therefore, because in this way a matter is well explained by examples,  
I have displayed each one and set out each individually,  
[Note: Thus also the Bec manuscript; but the Redon edition has *praetitulavi*, “I gave titles beforehand,” as does the Angers manuscript.]  
with names and glosses by which you may recognize these figures.

§ I. REPETITION.—Repetition occurs when beginnings are taken in similar and different matters with one and the same word; as follows:

[Col. 1687A]

You are to me king, to me law, to me light, to me leader, to me avenger;  
you I worship, you I praise, glorifying you, I applaud you.

[Note: Bec: “are contained from one and the same [word].” Angers: “are contained from one up to the same [word].”]

[Note: In manuscript codex no. 164 old numbering and no. 117 modern numbering of the municipal library of Tours, after these two little verses the following are read:

+ Receive the sweet “Hail,” by which the name Eva [Eve] is reversed;  
you shall become the ladder of heaven, Virgin bearing God.

The pious forerunner of Christ rejoices at Mary’s coming;  
her womb receives him; he perceives God’s presence.

For the sin of the world, God as an infant cries in confinement.]

Through whom you may return and hold the spacious realm of heaven.]

Woman brought forth justice; woman brought forth guilt. [Note: [Col. 1687] Two verses are lacking here, which occur in the Bec manuscript.]

Woman gave rise to life; woman gave rise to death.  
Woman sinned; woman washed away sin.

1589 § II. CONVERSION.—Conversion is that figure by which, unlike the preceding one, we repeat a word not at the beginning but return to it at the end [Note: [Col. 1687] Bec: *continentur*, “are contained”]; thus:

[Col. 1687A]

You alone are God; you are good, you are pious, you are wise;  
You bear the earth, you bear the sea, you bear the stars—  
You whom neither sea nor earth nor sky nor air can bear.

§ III. COMBINATION.—Combination is that which embraces both ornaments: the one just explained, by which we repeat the same word often and frequently, and also return to the same word at the end; thus:

[Col. 1688A]

Who are they that fight boldly? The men of Anjou.  
Who are they that overcome their enemies? The men of Anjou.  
Who are they that spare the conquered? The men of Anjou.  
Therefore let envy deny that the men of Anjou are excellent.

[Note: [Col. 1687] This section is absent from the Anjou manuscript, but occurs in the Bec manuscript and the Rennes edition.] § IV. TRANSLATION.—Translation is the figure which makes the frequent use of the same word not merely fail to offend the mind, but actually render the discourse more harmonious; thus:

If in life nothing is more pleasant to you than life,  
You will live an unseemly life, virtue having been abandoned.

Why do you care for him who gives you many cares?

[Col. 1688B] I should always wish to love, if there were nothing bitter in love. [Note: [Col. 1687] Thus Bec; but the Rennes edition has: “but I am weary of bitter death.”]

§ V. ANTITHESIS.—Antithesis is produced when discourse is composed from contrary things; in this manner:

[Col. 1689A]

In mourning you laugh; amid feasts you grieve.  
In the morning you seek your bed; in the evening you leave your shelter.  
There is peace: you rage for arms; in war you pray for peace.  
When you ought to cry out, you are silent; when you ought to spare, you cry out.  
You desire the city while in the country; in the city you praise the country’s blessings.

§ VI. EXCLAMATION.—Exclamation produces an expression of grief or indignation by an address to a person, city, or any other thing; thus:

O flower of Asia, mighty Troy! O what glory now  
You lie fallen into ashes! Where is the royal offspring,  
Born of Hecuba, of Priam’s seed, of the gods? [Note: [Col. 1689] Anjou and Rennes: “blood.”]

1590 O Hector, once Troy’s bravest champion—alas, in vain—

[Col. 1689B] Before the eyes of your wife, and of your dead parents, [Note: [Col. 1689] Bec: *defectorum*; more correctly Anjou and Rennes: *defunctorumque*, “and of the dead.”]  
You stained your hostile chariot first with blood!

That ruin of your fatherland, faithless shepherd,  
Was brought in by ships—your pleasure, accursed by the gods!

§ VII. REASONING.—Reasoning is the figure through which we ourselves demand from ourselves the reason why we say something, and frequently seek from ourselves an explanation of each proposition.

The rich miser is poor. How so? Because, when need requires it,  
He fears to touch what he has acquired. Why? Lest his heap diminish. [Note: [Col. 1689] Bec: *acutus*, “sharp.”]

Why does he fear diminution? Because he prefers increase. Why?  
It would not be a fault if it did not lack reason.

[Note: [Col. 1689] In the Anjou manuscript the example of this precept and the precept of the following example are absent; both occur in Bec, as in Gemmeticum.] § VIII. MAXIM.—A maxim is a statement which briefly shows either what something is, or what it ought to be in life; thus:

He to whom what he has is enough is certainly possessed of enough.

[Col. 1689C] He to whom what he has is not enough is certainly in want.  
Therefore virtue, not abundance, makes one self-sufficient;  
And not poverty, but the gaping appetite of the mind, makes one needy.

§ IX. THE CONTRARY.—The contrary is that which, from two different things, briefly and easily confirms one by the other; thus:

How will one who does not spare himself spare me or you?  
Do you think that one who publicizes his own disgraces will conceal yours?  
Now you will fear the sick man whom you despised when healthy. [Note: [Col. 1689] Anjou, Bec, and Rennes: “Will you fear?”]  
Will you yield alone to one whom you overcame with an ally?

§ X. CLAUSE.—A clause of discourse is a brief, complete expression, without the demonstration of the whole thought, which is then taken up again by another clause of discourse; thus:

[Note: [Col. 1689] Anjou and Bec: “But nothing for you,” which is more correct.] You were harming me, and you were profiting greatly,

[Col. 1689D] And thereby you were gladdening our enemies.

§ XI. ARTICLE.—It is called an article when individual words are distinguished by intervals in a discourse broken into pieces [Note: [Col. 1689] Anjou and Bec: *caesa*, “cut”]; thus:

Rich in arms, fleet, and provisions, you sought disastrous camps;  
Alone, unarmed, destitute, inglorious—behold, you returned.

1591 By sword, plague, and famine you were consumed, and perished. [Note: [Col. 1689] Anjou and Bec: “you were consumed.”]

§ XII. LIKE CASE-ENDINGS.—Like case-endings occur when two or more words in the same construction are similarly construed in the same cases [Note: [Col. 1689] Anjou and Bec: *efferuntur*, “are expressed”]; thus:

[Col. 1690A]

Make your own fortune; hasten to break the moon,  
And let care make you happy against fate. [Note: [Col. 1689] Anjou: “will make.”]

§ XIII. LIKE ENDINGS.—Like endings occur when, although the cases are not the same, the words nevertheless have similar endings; thus:

You seek to become rich in wealth, to be emptied of virtue.  
But you will not become rich while you lack virtue.  
You speak softly; you plot deceitfully.  
You inquire gently; you wickedly betray what has been entrusted to you. [Note: [Col. 1689] Anjou: *promis*, perhaps *promissa*, “things promised.”]

§ XIV. MIXED FIGURE.—The mixed figure is one in which two figures placed together concur; thus:

It is the fashion of crime to arrange one’s appearance, to despise reputation,  
To pursue a prostitute, to be called a *miracimmum* [meaning uncertain]. [Note: [Col. 1689] Bec manuscript: *Miracrimium*; Anjou: *Miracocinium*.]

[Col. 1690B] This man, who wishes to seem great-hearted and brave,  
Has the heart of a hare. Though he terrifies with a lion’s mouth,

[Note: [Col. 1689] This verse is added from Anjou, Bec, and Rennes.] Like a doe he flees; like an ox he bellows when wounded.

[Note: [Col. 1689] The following is absent from Anjou, but occurs in Gemmeticum, Bec, and the Rennes edition.] § XV. PARONOMASIA.—Paronomasia occurs when a word or noun is approached by changing or adding one letter or several letters, or when similar words are applied to dissimilar things; thus:

The court, mother and nurse of cares and evils,  
Makes the just equal to the unjust, the honourable to the dishonourable.

The valour of Alcides, overcome by no labour,  
About to enter untamed houses, the unspeakable depths, [Note: [Col. 1689] Perhaps *profanda*, “deep places.”]  
Did not fear misshapen shapes, and despised the dark  
Halls dreadful for Cerberus’ barking.

1592 § XVI. SUBJECTIO.—Subjectio occurs when we question our opponents, or ourselves ask what they can say against us, or we against them; then we add what ought or ought not to be said, what will assist us, or what will harm us; thus:

[Col. 1690C]

What cause had you for flight? Was it perhaps the lash? None was given.  
Was it labour? Yet you were accustomed to soak yourself in play and sleep.  
Was it perhaps hunger like a wild beast’s? You received dishes of food. [Note: [Col. 1689] Bec and Rennes: “perhaps.”]  
Was it cold? You changed clothes on a working day.

Therefore a mind conscious of guilt was driving you.

What should I have done when caught? Should I have fled? But an enemy  
Mounted on horseback would catch a footman. Should I have begged pardon?  
But he was cruel. Should I have fought? He was stronger.  
Thus it remained to deceive the greedy man by promises.

§ XVII. CLIMAX.—Climax is that figure in which one does not descend to the following word until one has ascended to the preceding; thus:

[Col. 1690D]

Whatever this man sees he desires, and whatever he has desired  
He attracts. What he has attracted he corrupts; what he has corrupted he betrays.

Had virtue not produced praise, and praise envy,  
Androgeus would have returned safe to the Cnossian kingdom.  
But virtue produced praise, praise generated envy;  
This party, overcome by the darts of envy, killed him. [Note: [Col. 1689] Bec: *hunc*, “this man.”]

§ XVIII. DEFINITION.—Definition briefly and absolutely embraces the proper powers of a thing; thus:

[Col. 1691A]

The generous man differs from the miser just as the prodigal does.  
The prodigal, through a fault of mind, squanders what ought to be kept;  
The generous man willingly spends reasonably.  
The thrifty man keeps whatever need does not demand;  
He who greedily keeps what need demands is a miser.

§ XIX. TRANSITION.—Transition briefly indicates what has been said and briefly proposes what follows; thus:

You have heard what a man this fellow showed himself to be toward his father;  
Now hear, in turn, what sort of father he himself was,  
So that he may seem worthy neither of son nor of father.

1593 § XX. CORRECTION.—Correction removes what has been said and puts in its place what appears more suitable; thus:

[Col. 1691B]

When the lover saw—or rather, more truly, the madman—  
Her being handled and willingly caressed,  
Like a wolf—or rather, a lioness bereft of her cubs—  
He flies at the man’s face; he seizes her, he tears her apart:  
Clearly forgetting propriety—indeed, rather, propriety itself.

§ XXI. OCCUPATION.—Occupation occurs when we say that we are passing over, do not know, or do not wish to say precisely what we are then chiefly saying; thus:

What shall I recount? With how many crimes your youth  
Has been stained? How often you have suffered public beatings?  
I pass over murders, perjuries, thefts, robberies.  
I hasten to the end. Who, [Note: [Col. 1691] Bec and Rennes: “For who?”] if he wished to recount  
Or even touch on everything, would offer ears to be wearied?

§ XXII. DISJUNCTION.—Disjunction occurs when either both or each one of the things of which we speak is concluded by a definite verb; thus:

[Col. 1691C]

The Roman people conquered the Gauls under Caesar.  
Under Pompey as leader it subdued the kingdoms of Mithridates.  
By Scipio’s name it broke Hannibal’s forces.  
Either illness brings beauty low, or age withers it.

§ XXIII. CONJUNCTION.—Conjunction occurs when, by the interposition of a verb, both the preceding and following parts of discourse are comprehended; thus:

Either age wears away the beauty of form, or illness does.

§ XXIV. ADJUNCTION.—Adjunction occurs when the verb by which we comprehend the things is not interposed, but placed either first or last; thus:

By illness or old age the beauty of form is effaced.  
Either illness or old age extinguishes beauty. [Note: [Col. 1691] Bec: “youth,” but erroneously.]

1594 § XXV. REDUPLICATION.—Reduplication occurs when, for the sake of amplification or pity, one word or several words are repeated; thus:

[Note: [Col. 1691] Bec: “to amplify, or by pity for that same one,” but erroneously.]

[Col. 1691D]

Did you, cruel daughter, kill your father with the sword?  
Did you kill your father—for whom you should have undergone death?  
Do you flee the light, filth and contagion of life?  
Do you flee? If the judge had wished to spare you,  
Would you not have been bound to take death upon yourself by your own hand?

§ XXVI. INTERCHANGE.—Interchange occurs when two discordant propositions are so expressed by transposition that the latter, contrary to the former, proceeds from the former; thus:

[Col. 1692A]

To speak nothing that ought to be silent, or to be silent about nothing that ought to be spoken—  
What wise person would command either, when each exceeds us?  
Or who can wisely command, when he himself cannot do what he commands?

§ XXVII. DOUBT.—Doubt occurs when the speaker seems to inquire which of two things, or what above all of several things, he ought to say; thus:

You compare yourself to me, man: by what name shall I call you?  
I hesitate. If I call you most filthy, it will not be fair.  
If I call you a crime, that is too little. Whether you are more deformed  
Or more wicked, I do not know. Neither this nor that pleases me.

§ XXVIII. ASYNDETON.—Asyndeton is that which, with connecting turns of words removed from the middle, expresses its parts separately; thus:

[Col. 1692B] Love your kindred; honour your dear parents.  
Be subject to God; obey the commandments of the law.

§ XXIX. BREAKING OFF.—Breaking off occurs when certain words have been set aside [Note: [Col. 1691] Bec: *dictis*, “said,” more correctly], and what one began to say is left to the judgment of the hearers; thus:

It is not fitting for you to enter into contest with me,  
Because the people … but I do not wish to say it,  
Lest, speaking grandly, I seem to breathe arrogance upon anyone.  
But the people marked you with blows and disgrace.

Do you now dare these things? You who lately, in the sacred building,  
On the solemn day … but it is better to spare words,

1595 Lest, speaking what you deserve, I offend the judge’s ears.

§ XXX. CONCLUSION.—Conclusion is that which, by a brief argument, follows at once and necessarily from the things already said or done; thus:

[Col. 1692C] If the oracles declared that Troy could not be taken  
Without Philoctetes—by whose arrows Paris himself was slain—  
And those arrows did Troy no greater harm than Paris’s death,  
Then surely Paris’s death was Troy’s destruction.

## EPILOGUE

Of many things I first gave you these few, lest many things be burdensome—  
1596 Like choice dishes—  
Distinguishing each and setting each down in easy brevity.  
That they might be plain, I thought they would be more pleasing.

If, once tasted, they please, and further tastes are sought,  
The remaining things will be given under my dispensing.  
But first you must turn these matters over in frequent study,  
So that, as it were, you may entrust the rest to a mind emptied by these.

Meanwhile, you who wish to write natures truly, keep the poet as a mirror and model,

[Col. 1692D] Him to whose example anyone who eagerly desires to fashion well  
May fit his first work, as one learning to paint.

Art, proceeding from nature at reason’s call [Note: [Col. 1691] Rennes: *cicute* (apparently corrupt)],  
Strives to retain the form of its own beginning. [Note: [Col. 1691] Bec: “preserve.”]

Therefore, whoever wishes to gain praise for himself by writing  
Must strive to describe distinctly sexes, ages, dispositions, and conditions, [Note: [Col. 1691] Bec: “of condition.”]  
As they are in reality. [Note: [Col. 1691] Bec: “as the laws are.”]  
He who despises this will be a Baius; [Note: [Col. 1691] Bec: *Bavius*; Rennes: *Bamus*.] he who observes it will become a Homer.

[Col. 1693]

# HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF BISHOP MARBOD IN TEN CHAPTERS

## CHAPTER ONE: ON THE FITTING MODE OF WRITING

*(From the Rennes edition of 1524.)*

What I wrote as a young man, now that I am old and reconsider more things,  
I regret; and I wish that I had neither written nor published certain pieces—  
Both because their subject matter seems shameful and trivial,  
And because the manner of expression could have been more fitting.

Thus, being neither precious in invention nor in verbal art,  
They ought either quickly to have been destroyed or not published.

But because a word once sent forth goes out irretrievably,  
And it is unlawful to correct a former error,  
It remains for me henceforth to be more cautious in my work,  
That I may produce nothing unadorned or useless;  
Especially because there can now be no place for pardon  
Such as there once was, when foolish, rough,  
[Col. 1693B] And frivolous youth could be regarded as tolerable in its fault.

Now a longer experience alike of life and study  
More keenly awaits the judgment of a stern critic.

Therefore let it be my purpose neither to write trifles  
Nor to soothe ears with melodious words;  
Not because I praise an unadorned account of serious subjects,  
But lest, neglecting what is prior—the weight of things—  
We pursue sweet-sounding verses and well-joined words.

It is indeed a laborious faculty, granted to few,  
To preserve the force of things under the rule of words  
And make the music of words abound beneath the subject matter;  
Yet this was what I seemed once to seek through unceasing study.

But riper age now advises me better:  
It ought fittingly to be content with easy usefulness  
[Col. 1693C] And strive to avoid superfluous labour.

There is another reason why I think it absurd to continue  
Melodious verses: one colour everywhere  
Creates nothing varied; nor is it called a painting,  
But rather a smear, because varied and rare things  
Are accustomed to delight the beholders; abundance becomes cheap.

Therefore we think that employing diverse colours in writings  
And varying one’s style bring greater praise.

Yet a poem does not consist in being praiseworthy for this reason alone;  
For the law of right writing demands three things: that it be  
Clear, free from fault, and flourishing in figure.  
He who achieves this is at once sweet and useful,  
And can hold the minds and ears of readers.

This, therefore, is the kind that I henceforth intend to pursue,  
In which I believe there is more praise and less labour.

Nor do I altogether regret having pursued those things
