[Col. 1694A] In which, exercising my mind, I used to sweat;  
For a harder labour seems more suitable to a young man,  
And the passage from difficult things to easier ones is swift.

Moreover, it suited a young man to sing playful things;  
Clear reason teaches that these are denied to an old man,  
Whose words ought to be seasoned with moral savour  
And oppose vices with a stern countenance.

Therefore, keeping the measure of a moderate style everywhere,  
I shall now attempt, while writing serious things,  
To use words neither elaborate nor commonplace:  
The latter makes a thing cheap, the former odious.

Nor shall I wish to be judged either brief or excessively prolix:  
The one produces obscurity, the other weariness.

1597 Let it not be lawful for me to attempt the highest poets,  
Nor let me too abjectly rank myself among inferior ones.

[Col. 1694B] First we shall speak of the lot of human life  
And of the causes affecting human beings, why time runs on;  
In this we believe there will be no small usefulness,  
That every person may know whither he ought to tend  
When he complains that he was born under a harsh lot.

I send these things to be considered by you, most learned bishop, [Note: [Col. 1693C] He perhaps addresses his friend Hildebert.]  
Whose judgment neither deceives nor is deceived.  
If, when considered, you approve them, I shall take courage for the rest.  
If otherwise, I shall rise to later work with slow endeavour:  
In these matters, you shall put either rein or spurs upon me.

## CHAPTER II: ON TIME AND AGE

My sixty-seventh year is now running,  
Since, poured forth from the enclosure of the womb, as from a dark prison,  
[Col. 1694C] Into this light, I first began to utter cries—  
My weeping thus bearing witness to the labours that were to come.

This I infer from the common law of those born,  
Remembering absolutely nothing of that age;  
For the mind, newly buried in the clay of fluid flesh,  
Lies numb, as though weighed down by Lethean sleep.  
Shaking this off only gradually through the use of time,  
It learns to distinguish the present causes of things  
And to weigh some future things from those past.

Nor does the full keenness of reason at once appear:  
A stronger age succeeds the age of boyhood,  
And mounting heat strengthens youthful limbs,  
Making a human being capable alike of virtue and vice.

Now life, hitherto simple and conducted in a straight course,  
Is furrowed by a divided path,

[Col. 1695A] As the letter Y now marks with its divided summit:  
The right-hand part it has marked with chalk, the left with charcoal;  
The steep path represents virtue, the downward path vice,  
Sending many by an easy descent to Tartarus.

But it is a heavy labour to raise one’s steps toward heaven,  
Where burning virtue cannot climb except for a few.

The age called manhood follows youth,  
Because it fills the human body with solid strength.  
This is the standing point, as it were the centre, of mortal life,  
From which its orbit rolls downward in headlong fall;  
Failing heat dulls the senses and dissolves them,  
Giving the falling limbs over to old age and death.

Behold, I have extended time through five ages;  
Yet if earliest infancy is a part of the ages,  
It should rather be called the beginning of life than life itself.

[Col. 1695B] And now my unsightly old age loosens my limbs,  
Hastening into decrepitude and leading me to death’s final limits.

What does it profit miserable me to have lived through so many years?  
What, to have passed happy days and pleasant times?  
Since the fleeing hour has carried away whatever pleased,  
Yet has not taken away what torments the mind; for, when  
Joys have passed, the punishment of deeds remains,  
Torturing guilty hearts with hidden blows.

Nor is the reckoning of punishment feared any less thereafter,  
When the wretched spirit departs from this body.

And if I wished to recall the labours of my past life,  
Its various sicknesses, the sad fates of my parents,  
Heavy miseries, a thousand dangers of circumstances,  
And cares keeping wake in an anxiously troubled breast,  
A greater measure of sorrows

[Col. 1695C] Darkens and veils the joys of fleeing life.

I pass over the lowly beginnings of bloody birth.  
I pass over the cradle; I leave aside the foulness of swaddling-clothes.  
I despise infants’ cries and nurses’ labours.

I hasten to the tears of the boy whom an angry master  
Compels with cruel beating to repeat dictated verses,  
Teaching him to unlearn the things poets have invented:

1598 Jupiter’s unspeakable debaucheries, or Mars’s adulterous acts,  
Reciting lustful young men and shameful girls  
Whom a mutual but detestable pleasure joined.

The crude tale imbues an untaught heart with a similar fault;  
And the boy, forestalled by the scent of burning vice,  
Already longs by the gods’ example to commit foul deeds.

[Col. 1695D] Therefore, when the limbs burn with their first generative heat  
And lust, goading it, strikes the heart of the young man,  
With no one restraining him he loosens the reins of chastity,  
Running by a downward path to sinister deeds.

And if, after sin, shame stirs his mind  
And he wishes to resist, stained by vice, upon the right-hand path,  
Sin holds back the slippery footprints fixed in mud  
And prevents one accustomed to evil from turning his steps aright.

Thus pitiable youth is carried over the precipice,  
Adding crimes to crimes, or deaths to deaths.

Why recount the kinds of wickedness: perjuries, thefts,  
Sacrilegious daring, murders, incest, robberies?  
I pass over very many things that do not even seem fit to mention,  
In which this age wallows with blind mind.

But even when he has become a man, he does not readily reject  
[Col. 1696A] The digested disgraces of pleasures, except that he seeks  
To indulge himself more cautiously, fearing loss of reputation.

Now zealous for wealth, zealous for empty honour,  
He cannot by the power of judgment overcome the depraved habit of sin  
To which he freely submitted himself.

Thereafter evil habit troubles old age;  
And though the pleasure of intercourse has been withdrawn from him,  
Since cold blood confines his inner parts,  
Still insatiate desire itches beneath his heart  
And seeks in affection what does not proceed to action.

Nor is desire for wealth usually less in old men,  
Nor is any age more ambitious for the things mentioned above;  
Indeed, it is marked by the stain of graver avarice,  
Since, destined to live less long, it desires more anxiously to save.

What evils old age brings—the age nearer to death—  
[Col. 1696B] The ravings of the decrepit can prove,  
For its feeble activity returns to the life of infants.

For humankind’s setting and rising are nearly alike:  
As one comes forth into this life, as though from nothing,  
So from this life one departs, as though into nothing.

What then in this life pleases sickly mortals,  
Whose labour is displayed from its rising to its setting,  
And in no part of which there is freedom from many troubles?

What then pleases those who pursue only perishable things?  
Sexual intercourse? But that pleasure suits horses.  
Food and drink? Cattle too seek such things.  
The favour of the people? But nothing is swifter than a breeze.  
Wealth? But we cannot take it hence.  
The beauty of appearance? But it withers through age or sickness.

[Col. 1696C] Or rather, do these long spans of life please?  
But the first part of an hour does not wait for the second,  
And it cannot rightly be called whole unless it has passed away.

If a long period is proved to be nothing long,  
What difference then does it make whether one has lived a perishable life  
For few or many years, after those years have passed?

They say that little creatures are born in the river Ganges,  
Whose limbs the rising dawn shapes out of mud;  
The rising sun gives them life; the second hour makes them move;  
The third grants play and leaps to creatures now vigorous.

But after radiant Phoebus stands at the summit of his course,  
Their bodily strength too reaches its full measure.  
Then, when the sun bends his descending chariot in its circuit,  
They begin to move more sluggishly as play ceases,

[Col. 1696D] And strength gradually abandons their exhausted limbs.  
When evening comes, their skin gives them the wrinkles of old women,  
And heavy old age bends their tottering limbs.

But as soon as the sun plunges its rays into Ocean’s waves,  
Their brief life together departs into the thin air,  
Extended only through the span of a single day.

Do we not seem like those animals,  
1599 Whom the brevity of life, however long it may be, confines?  
For whatever is called long under any measure of time,  
When compared with what is eternal, is proved a brief point. [Supplement: “when.”]

Indeed, not even a point; for when a thousand years  
Have passed, the point remains, but those years are nothing.

What, I ask, did the wise Maker of the world intend,

[Col. 1697A] He who himself abides forever, when he made transient things?

If the human race has been created under this law,  
That whatever we do in the time of fleeting life  
Passes away, and at last we ourselves perish together,  
The craftsman seems foolish and deserving of blame,  
Whose vain work passes away like a clay vessel.

Thus an idle artisan is blamed for an inept work,  
And a tottering structure reproves its builder.

Nor does our lot seem better than that of cattle  
If an equal destruction takes away humans and beasts.

If anyone begins a work in order that it may end, or enters  
A house in order to leave it,  
He seems justly foolish and worthy of ridicule.

If we too are born only in order to die,

[Col. 1697B] We are shown to have been born in vain and to have lived fruitlessly.

But since he who created us is wise—indeed, Wisdom itself—  
And marked the mind with his own image,  
Entrusting to it the governance of limbs fashioned from clay,  
We must not believe that we shall perish utterly.

Rather, it is certain that not even our flesh will perish,  
Once wondrously joined in order to the eternal mind.

For the Almighty fused two things into one human being,  
So that, made from contrary elements, he might have a contest  
And by his own choice might be conquered or conquer;  
That victory might grant a palm to one who fights well  
And judgment prepare a worthy punishment for the conquered.

Thus what the best Creator made would be eternal—  
He who knows no end, whom no times constrain,  
Whose possession is wholly peace and unchanging identity.

[Col. 1697C] I think times were made, whose variation produces time;  
From varied things discord produces struggle;  
Then the pursuit of struggle is followed by victory, and if victory  
Were removed, both reward and punishment would perish.

Nor would there be a place for the justice of the Omnipotent,  
By which recompense is returned to each according to merits.

Therefore it was necessary to fashion varied motions  
And to join diverse things into one world,  
So that, as in a stadium, there might be contest in a long struggle,  
While the human race stretches through time toward eternity,  
Until the Judge, arranging each matter by a just examination,  
Pays penalties or rewards to the contestants.

Alas, wretch that I am! What torments will that day prepare for me—  
I who always followed the downward left-hand way,

[Col. 1697D] Who, with the mind overcome, devoted myself to the enticements of flesh;  
Whose intent ran readily toward every wickedness;  
Whose deed no virtue redeemed from crime!

If God is only just, mercy being removed,  
There is no hope of pardon for me, no hope of salvation.

But because mercy is part of the Lord’s justice—  
For by his own right he exacts what is his, or freely remits it—  
I, a guilty suppliant, betake myself to the Lord’s mercy,  
Who can justly condemn and spare whom he wills.

I pray that he may be willing to pity me, half-dead,  
Whom a demon tore apart, whom a savage viper bit,  
Whom a robber struck down with wounds after stripping him of clothing;  
The Levite despised me; the priest despised my wounds;  
And no one brought help to one lying near death.

If you too pass by, most gentle guardian of humankind,

[Col. 1698A] Who will care for me, or who will bind my raw wounds?

You who gave abundant grounds for hope of pardon,  
Set judgment aside and grant pardon to one who asks.  
For who can contend with you in judgment?

I have no confidence in merit. Yet if you desire,

1600 Since you are pious, a merit by which you may rightly show pity,  
Let the contrition of my sorrowful heart be my merit;  
Let my tears be my merit; let my words and prayers be my merit.

Peter’s denial is said to have been washed away by tears.  
The thief is believed to have gained Paradise by his merits.  
A seven-day hunger is said to have amended the king’s adultery; the same king atoned for the murder  
Of a righteous man by the same means.

Mary, cleansed by weeping from a sevenfold demon,

[Col. 1698B] Was the first to deserve to recognize Christ risen again.

There are many examples by which you have provided certain  
Confidence of pardon for the fallen, to be recalled,  
Lest anyone despair when he knows you to be kind.

Therefore, kind Father, deal kindly with me in your accustomed manner,  
That I may deserve to rest with you among the saved.

May your praise, Holy One, always dwell in my mouth,  
And may confession live in this writing of mine.

Amen.

## CHAPTER III: ON THE PROSTITUTE

Among the countless snares which the crafty enemy  
Has spread over every hill and plain of the world,  
The greatest is woman, the gloomy source, evil stock, vicious offspring,  
And scarcely anyone can avoid being deceived by her.

[Col. 1698C] She produces very many scandals throughout the whole world;  
She stirs up lawsuits, quarrels, and harsh seditions,  
Sets old friends at war, separates affections, and incites children against parents.

I speak of small matters: she removes kings from their thrones and tetrarchs;  
She clashes nations, shakes towns, destroys cities,  
Multiplies murders, mixes deadly draughts;  
Raging through villas and fields, she casts firebrands.

In short, no kind of evil ranges through the world  
In which woman does not claim some share for herself.

The sex is envious, frivolous, irascible, greedy,  
Excessive in drink and greedy in appetite;  
Rejoicing in vengeance and always panting to conquer;  
Desiring through right and wrong alike to accomplish what it seeks,

[Col. 1698D] To whom nothing that is sweet seems forbidden.

She walks radiant in face while concealing secret filth,  
Lying and shameless, not free from the crime of theft;  
Here gaping after profit, there burning with the fire of lust,  
Talkative, fickle, and, after so many evils, proud.

Armed with these evils, woman overturns the world;  
Woman, a sweet evil, at once honeycomb and poison,  
Coating the sword with honey, she pierces even wise hearts.

Who first persuaded the parent to taste what was forbidden?  
Woman. Who compelled the father to violate his daughters?  
Woman. Who killed the strong man after he was shorn of his hair?  
Woman. Who cut off with the sword the sacred head of the just man?  
Woman—she who added crime to her mother’s crime  
And marked incest with a more grievous murder.

Who seduced holy David, who wise Solomon

[Col. 1699A] With sweet enticements, so that the one became an adulterer,  
The other sacrilegious, if not alluring woman?

I pass over many whom sacred Scripture recounts:  
Unspeakable Jezebel and Athalia, who dared a wicked deed,  
And more women whom it is unnecessary to enumerate.

I pass over many women whom poets and histories  
Are accustomed to count: Exiphyle and Clytemnestra,  
Belides and Procne, and the prostitute born of Leda  
For whom the lands contended in a ten-year war,  
And those others whom tragedians customarily recite to the people.

As an image of this grave and dangerous monster,  
Ancient wisdom fashioned the terrible Chimera;

1601 And not without reason is she said to have been given a threefold form:  
Her first part is a lion, her last a dragon’s tail,  
And her middle parts are nothing but blazing fire.

[Col. 1699B] This image plays upon the nature of the prostitute:  
That she may snatch prey, she displays a lion’s face,  
Feigning something distinguished, as it were a marriageable countenance.

By this appearance she burns in love’s flames those whom she has captured;  
In this love there appears no solidity, no weight,  
But only light, irrational, burning desire,  
Whose final parts are stuffed with deadly poison,  
Since death and damnation end its pleasures.

Restless Charybdis bears a woman’s form,  
Swallowing up and drawing to death whatever is nearest her.  
She is also the Siren who, singing sweetly,  
Allures fools; having allured them, draws them; having drawn them,  
Drowns them in the deep to destruction.

Ulysses avoided this by blocking his companions’ ears  
Against the notorious songs and also restraining himself by force,  
[Col. 1699C] Bound fast with cords to the mast of the fleeing ship.

Likewise he avoided Circe’s perniciously sweet potions:  
Those who drank them assumed bestial forms,  
Made like dogs and muddy swine.  
By them are denoted people who have become debased and softened,  
Living the life of cattle under the dominion of lust.

O human race, beware honeyed poisons,  
Sweet songs, and the pull of the fierce whirlpool;  
Let not the grace of a composed face seduce you,  
But fear burning flames and the savage dragon.

If a beautiful woman calls you, seeking to deceive you,  
And, trusting yourself, you hasten to enter the contest,  
Despising hostile weapons with a strong heart,  
You are deceived in ignorance: this contest’s

[Col. 1699D] Law is not such that you can conquer in close combat.  
It is better to flee and procure safety by your feet.  
If you flee, you will escape; if you engage, you will be captured.

But I warn you not to look disdainfully on her, because whoever is numbed by lust  
At the sight of the Gorgon is turned into stone.

Whoever crosses the waves of the world in the ship of the Church  
So that he may attain the desired harbour of his homeland  
Must, avoiding sweet-sounding songs and flattering dangers,  
Fortify his closed ears with lawful doctrine,  
Bound to the wood by the rope of divine fear.

The wood of our salvation is the cross, like a mast in a ship;  
Nor does it lack yards, which are the two arms of the wood.

## CHAPTER IV: ON THE MARRIED WOMAN

Among all things which, by God’s gift, seem granted  
For human use, we think that nothing is more beautiful,

[Col. 1700A] Nothing better, than a good woman. She is a portion of our body,  
And we are in turn a portion of her flesh.

By the law of nature, which rightly compels us,  
We love her as a social good even when she harms us;  
For since we are the same, we live under the same condition,  
And there is nothing that we do not hold in common,  
Alike in all things, save for the distinction of sex.

Our law and birth are equal; we use the same nourishment;  
We are equally clothed; we are moved to weeping and laughter  
By similar feeling; by equal sense we distinguish  
What things are good, what evil, what is just, what unjust;  
And mutual thought proceeds in like speech.

Among those like ourselves we know how to return favours in turn,

[Col. 1700B] To earn reciprocal gifts by services,  
And to give counsel by which harmful things may be removed.

Man and woman can do all these things together  
Which are certainly denied to brute animals.

Yet many people desire and acknowledge as lovable  
Things that lack reason but nevertheless live and move:

1602 Things joined to us in nature’s second rank, [Correction: *Stantque gradu*, “they stand in rank.”]  
Herbs, flowers, and every green thing of earth,  
Which heat mingled with moisture nourishes and cherishes,  
Giving them growth and the power of bearing fruit.

People think these beautiful, though they do not fail to know  
That they lack soul; yet they move by growing.

Therefore the third rank teaches that these things deserve less approval than  
[Col. 1700C] Clothing, silver, gems, gold, and everything  
Which lacks motion yet is desirable to the sight,  
Although far, far removed from us. [Correction: *lateque*, “widely.”]  
For these hold the fourth place by nature’s law.

They also regard as admirable things to which these are denied.

Therefore, since woman is more worthy than all these things,

More beautiful than silver, more precious than yellow gold,

More splendid than gems, because these lack the light of reason,

We think it certain from what has been said above

That she is more to be admired, or rather more to be loved.

Although we are joined to these things by the just bond of natural love

For these reasons alone, arising from their order,

Yet both sexes share them equally,

And they are no less fitting for men than for women.

[Col. 1700D] But there are many things in which womanly care

Takes precedence, and woman gives the world its proper cause;

Remove her, and the entire human race will perish.

For, if the field be lacking, tell me, what use are your seeds?

Who could be a father, if woman the mother were lacking?

I pass over the harsh and lengthy labours of pregnancy;

I pass over the anxious hours of the agonizing birth

By which the most sorrowful mother brings us into the light,

Soon forgetting such great pains for the price of her offspring.

Who, I ask, repays this service with worthy love?

Who can say that he has not had a mother?

Many lesser things indeed, yet such as common life requires,

Woman alone supplies you in its service.

For who but a woman will undertake a nurse’s care,

[Col. 1701A] Without which no one born can preserve life?

Who will draw wool and flax? Who will turn the spindle?

Who will render the allotted work, or endure to weave?

These things are done for our use, done with such advantage,

That, if they fail, the dignity of life is diminished.

Moreover, very many things which domestic care requires

Woman more readily performs with her particular solicitude,

And she endures many things which our pride passes over.

She tends the sick person more gently, more diligently

Stands by the bed, and carefully supplies food and drink.

She loves more, and more quickly can be moved by instruction,

And, like soft wax, be bent into the form of goodness;

She is shown to be more subject to discipline.

But the hard mind of man resists with stiff neck,

And scarcely bears the yoke while refusing to call itself inferior.

[Col. 1701B] Add that, in the frailer sex,

The pursuit of virtue is more praiseworthy, transgression more pardonable;

Yet virtue has often not been found less in the inferior sex,

Nor transgression greater.

For what most wicked woman surpasses Judas in crime?

Or what man can equal the merit of Mary?

Yet, with this single exception, since the matter is established,

We read that not a few women have possessed men’s minds,

Or even surpassed men, and with brave heart

Have borne a reward worthy of their merit and praise.

Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, Esther, Judith, Anna, Noem [Naomi],

Like seven stars whom ancient ages brought forth,

Are read to have equalled men or exceeded them.

For Judith performed a notable deed which no man

[Col. 1701C] Had dared: returning after Holofernes had been slain,

She gave salvation to the city of Bethulia,

And drove the enemy, repulsed, away from the other cities.

Everlasting fame commends Queen Esther,

Who, like a lamb married to a cruel wolf, a tyrant,

Did not fear, at the peril of her head, to enter the threshold

Which none who entered unbidden came out from;

She set her own safety against that of her people,

And turned the edict of the people’s death against their enemies.

I pass over Ruth, who alone accompanied her chaste mother-in-law,

And deserved to transmit offspring into the royal line,

When for the sake of faith she fled country and parents.

Or, under the new law, after the praise of chastity

Shone forth celebrated in a virgin birth for the world,

The times are full of countless maidens

[Col. 1701D] Who compensated for chastity with the loss of life,

And, overcoming the enemy, gave men proof

That virtue of mind knows not how to yield to punishments.

Among their number, not inferior in merits,

Agnes, Faith, Agatha, Lucy, Cecilia, and Thecla

By outstanding virtue conquered savage tyrants.

I could also recall pagan maidens

Famous for contempt of death and chaste modesty.

Lucretia won everlasting fame by dying,

Voluntarily following the violation of her chastity with swift death.

Alcestis refused to behold the light of beauty [*decoris*, perhaps a corrupt reading];

Yet they also recount that, under the harsh condition

By which cruel fates demanded one or the other head,

She saved the life of her royal husband by her own death.

[Col. 1702A] The chaste Pethē had pierced her own breast with a sword,

Desiring to precede the fates of her condemned husband;

When she handed it to her beloved, she said: “Receive this:

The wound I have made does not pain me; but the wounds, Pethē,

Which you will make, will pain me even after death.”

By these examples, and by those arguments

Which we set down at the beginning of this poem,

It is clear that a woman must not be blamed merely because she is a woman,

Nor should anyone be made glorious merely because he is a man;

Rather, vice is altered in each sex alike,

And virtue equally deserves praise in both.

## CHAPTER V. ON OLD AGE

Many inconveniences afflict old age,

[Col. 1702B] Which arise from the mortal condition

Of the human body, weakening its frame

As it prepares the limbs to be dissolved in death.

For the living mind, not enclosed by the body, does not grow old,

And, once free from the body, knows no end of life.

These, then, are approximately the troubles of most old people:

Individual limbs are often assailed by new pain;

Now the head or breast aches, now the heart or side; now

An oppressive injury of the loins forces groans.

Now the whole body is contracted by excessive cold,

And can scarcely be warmed, heaped with many garments;

The weight imposed soon oppresses the weary limbs,

And bids the troublesome pile be removed more quickly.

[Col. 1702C] Yet the wretched man must endure either burden or cold,

But can bear neither; he is weighed down by both:

There is labour on either side; rest is denied on either side.

At times, seized by sudden fever, he burns;

Cold and weight are present, but unjust heat torments him.

A cruel cloud covers his dimming eyes,

So that he can scarcely distinguish the faces of servants,

Or envious light wholly deserts his wide-open eyes.

Another laments molars shaken from their roots

As he turns moistened bread in his bare mouth,

And is compelled rather to swallow than chew his food.

Food sustains him, but gives no pleasure to the eater,

And tasteless food deceives his palate, numb in taste.

[Note: [Col. 1701D] Perhaps *insipidus*, “tasteless”; compare *cibus*, “food.”]

1604 Even speech is deformed in the toothless mouth,

And the tongue, struck against a light lip, stammers.

[Col. 1702D] For some, the blocked passage of the ear is now shut off,

And they can scarcely be stirred even by a loud voice.

The nostrils of others are deprived of the sense of smell,

So that the fragrance of incense differs not at all from stench;

Neither stench grieves them nor perfume delights them.

Nor does sleep so sweetly relax the limbs of old men,

Nor does gentle sound so softly enter aged ears;

They are not thus refreshed by the summer breeze when tired,

Nor do drink or food afford a similar taste.

They carry out undertakings begun with slow effort,

And, whenever need requires, speak through matters in slow speech.

Eager for gain, they hoard what they have acquired tenaciously,

And fear to use what is present lest it fail;

Though the very little remaining of life requires very little of them,

[Col. 1703A] They vainly preserve not a few superfluities in hope of a long life.

But what sane man prepares long provisions for a short journey?

Does not he act foolishly who, the shorter the road remaining,

The more anxiously takes up heavier travelling provisions?

More foolish is he who increases what he does not use.

Why? Because he is always in want. Why? Because he spares his hoard.

Why does he spare it? Lest his comforts fail him. What comforts?

Lodging, clothes, food, and varied household goods.

But these will fail if he spends that from which they are procured;

And lest they fail, they fail by this very reasoning—

A thing whose folly is plain even to fools. Therefore

Let him take and spend, and procure things for use.

But the old man’s cold blood constricts his outward parts;

He fears expense and is in want lest he be unable to be in want.

Therefore advancing age takes away pleasures,

[Col. 1703B] Which many number among the body’s advantages;

Among these sexual intercourse is said to be perhaps the greatest,

Whose use age, late and lacking heat, cuts off.

For this reason old age is commonly blamed by old men themselves;

And although all wish to attain old age,

All accuse and detest it once attained,

When they no longer have the same sense of pleasures.

But many things which a longer age confers please me,

And I do not deny that it is blameworthy in certain matters alleged against it.

Thus youth too has not many praiseworthy qualities,

And is no less subject to certain vices.

I praise old age because it is known to drive away shameful impulses

And to preserve the body from worldly desire;

Then because older people possess greater prudence in affairs,

And because they seek and love tranquil repose.

[Col. 1703C] Wanton frivolity is driven away by the gravity of age;

Then because they often avert public disasters

By giving salutary counsel in doubtful matters

And recall those in discord to covenants of peace;

And not because most suffer from the disease of avarice,

Especially because they defraud even themselves through wicked expenditure

And reserve for death what the needs of life demand.

For the fact that strength grows weak in an aged body,

Or that the assault of diseases afflicts the wretched,

I blame no more than the fact that an infant cannot stand

By his own strength, or a boy use youthful strength,

Or that their own diseases weary youths and children—

[Col. 1703D] The distinct characteristics, that is, of the ages.

He who turns the law of nature into blame condemns it,

Because deceptive forgetfulness darkens the old man’s mind,

And he is apt to forget suddenly what has just been done.

I think this belongs to age, not to a failing defect,

But rather happens through the fault of an uncultivated mind.

Those whom luxuriant youth gives over to idleness

Dull, foolish, hateful old age receives;

Those whom their earlier age exercises in honourable studies,

We see flourish as pleasant and distinguished old men,

Who with remembering heart and eloquent tongue recount

Recent events and the deeds of their forebears worthy of imitation.

1605 Conversely, we see certain youths and boys

[Col. 1704A] Scarcely remember today what was done yesterday.

Hence it is clear that the cause of folly must be attributed

Not to the times of youth or old age, but to character;

For wicked luxury harms every age,

And moderation preserves, adorns, and helps every age.

I remember, when old, that as a young man I endured many reproaches

In words, because I did not follow my contemporaries’ frivolity,

Those occupied with untimely feasts and games,

While sober concern for learning held me back.

I now see some of them enduring a wretched old age:

A dull mind and a body deprived of its very senses

Show the foul traces of their former excess.

But I now gather the sweet fruits of my studies

When I read, meditate, write anything useful,

Or instruct those entrusted to me with moral words.

[Col. 1704B] By these exercises old age becomes pleasant to me;

And if age deprives me of bodily strength,

My intellect and mind are vigorous and grow with time.

Nor has maturer age brought me contempt;

Rather, greater reverence has grown for my grey head.

Therefore I will not cease to give thanks to the Creator,

Who, pitying me, has brought me to this age,

In which nature’s wanton heat has now cooled,

And at last allows the senses to rest in peace.

Let youths delight in ranging through wide fields,

Pursuing hares, roe-deer, and birds in flight;

Let feasts, games, shows, and songs delight them.

My mind delights me, as I lie reading and pondering such things.

## CHAPTER VI. ON FATE AND NATIVITY

[Note: [Col. 1703] By *genesis* the author intended nativity, that is, the time and exact moment of each person’s birth.]

[Col. 1704C] Popular opinion maintains that all things are ruled by fate,

Those who assert that Fortune’s gifts are established more

At the hour of birth than by nobility of parents.

Nor are there lacking some who bear the name of learned men

Who seem able to demonstrate, by a certain reasoning,

That the force of nativity directs our actions,

So as to affirm that whatever we do is necessary.

Nativity is the determining point of the hour of birth,

Which they assert is held under the law of the stars;

Their positions provide everything to those born.

For they say that the seven stars move backward through the twelve signs,

Yet that some move quickly and others slowly

At fixed times and intervals.

Therefore astrologers claim that through the influence of the seven stars

[Col. 1704D] All prosperity and adverse events are given,

According as they join one another in individual signs,

Or withdraw from one another by short or long distances,

Yet in such a way that some proportion joins whatever rays.

They attribute to these not only external causes,

But also believe that they disclose people’s characters at birth.

For Venus, remaining with Mars in a certain configuration,

When the sun’s ray looks upon her in a square aspect,

Compels those born to commit the crime of adultery,

And compels disgraceful incest to be performed.

[Col. 1705A] From this they suppose is drawn what the poetic Muse tells:

That the Sun marked the adultery of Mars and Venus.

Mars likewise, looking upon Saturn in a square configuration,

While no favourable star looks upon it,

Makes people bold, gladiators, murderers,

Demon-possessed, thieves, and full of every lust.

Venus joined with Jupiter produces every joy for everyone,

Provided no malign influence opposes them.

Hence Maro recalls that Jupiter, kissing his daughter beforehand,

With serene face drives away every ill omen.

Fierce Mars stirs up wars; therefore he is called god of war.

Saturn’s star is thought the worst of all.

Their art assigns its respective actions to Mercury and the Moon,

Giving the stars power over human life and death:

[Col. 1705B] To these they assign profits and losses, healthy or sick bodies;

To these all virtues and every crime;

To these causes they ascribe poverty and riches.

I remember having once read these things among astrologers.

Firmicus strives to prove them by weak arguments,

And his horoscopes seem false to me.

For, according to the investigation which he approves for observation,

I should affirm that my own constellation is false,

As I once proved while engaging in this study—

Unless I fear that someone may rather think that I deceive,

Or that I could have been mistaken in a difficult calculation—

If I do not refute these matters by a reason known to all.

First, if this false assertion could possess plausible arguments

And be instilled among peoples—that nativity compels whatever is done—

[Col. 1705C] What benefit, I ask, would this persuasion bring the world?

Plainly, that no one would avoid any wicked act whatever,

But, using the defence of a related star,

Each would wish to justify his own crime by this reasoning.

Why after this should any judge try to impose blame upon me

And decree an unjust punishment against an innocent person?

Let punishment strike the one who compels; let its judgment spare the compelled;

Or rather, let it praise whatever delights the agent,

Since all crimes are acknowledged to descend from heaven.

Therefore, once fear of punishment, which restrains those wishing to sin,

Has disappeared, every wicked man, his reins broken,

Will rush into crime, doing whatever he pleases.

See how wide a window is opened to wicked crimes:

The thief, robber, sacrilegious man, plunderer, perjurer, adulterer,

[Col. 1705D] And every impiety punished throughout the world

Will now rush into forbidden acts as though they were lawful.

But if no punishment is shown to be owed to the guilty,

And, conversely, no rewards are owed to the just,

Hope and fear perish; paradise and hell perish;

Freedom of choice perishes; compulsion constrains everything.

Thus laws are futile; thus judicial law is futile;

Counsel is futile; prudence of mind is futile;

God’s temples are futile; humble prayer is futile;

And all things that help the wretched are futile.

Therefore it does not harm an ignorant man to remain idle without labour,

Nor does it benefit the farmer to plough with many oxen,

If an evil star makes a good man, or a good one an idle man.

Yet one is needy while another abounds in wealth.

What is more: such an opinion condemns the Creator,

[Col. 1706A] Upon whom the blame for the stars plainly falls.

Therefore either nativity must be wholly rejected,

Or, if nativity stands, nothing is shown to stand secure.

I think these arguments sufficient for impious error to yield;

Yet if anyone seeks more after these,

And asks that nativity be struck as though on the opposite front,

We can prove it false by another argument.

There are certain peoples whom no discord stirs,

Whom they call Bragmans and Seres, and who would prove true things.

There is no plunderer there, none spreading fires,

No one knows adultery, no one perjury;

They shun incest and commit no murders.

Do Venus or Mars have any jurisdiction among them?

Or is no one born under their hour?

[Col. 1706B] Conversely, there are others among whom incest is customary,

Whose people are accustomed to live by plunder,

To whom human bloodshed is cheap,

Who avoid neither adultery nor other crimes—

People whom we are moved by not through report but sight itself.

Does a favourable star prevent even these from sinning?

Or can none of them be born under such a star?

1607 Finally, among the Jews wherever they dwell,

Their private members are cut on the eighth day,

And blood flowed from every tender body.

Who would madly imagine that all were born in one hour,

At which bloody Mars made wounds for those born,

So that all suffered a wound in one member?

Therefore it is proved that the choice to take the left or the right at a crossroads

Belongs to will, not to a star.

[Col. 1706C] Nor is it less clear that will is often changed by fear

Or hope, and flees what it formerly sought:

Thus, if someone wishing to walk along a level path

Suddenly sees a chasm in the split earth,

Fearing destruction, he avoids the dangers set before him;

And likewise, unwilling to make for a rocky way,

If he suddenly sees gold of no small weight,

Hastening in hope of gain, he weighs the labour against the reward

And enters the road on which he had formerly feared to travel.

Let Mars, Venus, and Cupid impel a youth

To intercourse with a woman whom he desires likewise;

but let the anger of a man bearing swords and hostile weapons

Come upon them when both are now ready,

And, with his hand held back, leave the deed unperformed by those about to die:

Will not, at the point when death threatens both,

[Col. 1706D] All will to sin, conquered by fear, flee,

And is not fear, forbidding the crime, stronger than the stars?

Likewise we see peoples who fear the decrees of kings,

Who are accustomed to punish the guilty and restrain offences,

Living gladly in perpetual peace:

They neither commit plunder, nor are fires kindled by them,

Nor dare they shamefully violate another’s marriage-bed,

Nor inflict mutual wounds upon themselves with hostile weapons.

Therefore fear, not a star, causes crimes not to be committed.

But where no authority hostile to vices governs,

Or threatening enforcement of law or right restrains,

You may see men raging among themselves in bloody slaughter,

Accustomed to disturb peace with repeated robberies,

And wanton licence joins them in forbidden intercourse.

[Col. 1707A] Therefore will, devoid of fear, commits every crime;

But we think all good things come to pass through hope of reward,

Since this too is a reward: escaping punishment itself.

Yet hope and fear are in proportion to faith:

Undoubted faith produces undoubted hope,

And sure fear is accompanied by sure faith;

But with wavering faith, hope and fear will waver.

Hence the frequent sins of those of slight faith;

For those who perfectly believe in punishments and rewards,

Fear to sin lest they suffer punishments,

And always do good that they may merit the kingdom.

I thought these things should be written briefly against nativity.

Yet, lest I reject fate and nativity altogether,

I declare that my fate is the Word of the highest Father,

By whom all things must be governed, as all must confess;

[Col. 1707B] And I call the inborn principle of reason my nativity,

And the freedom by which I can direct myself wherever I will,

Freely doing good or freely doing evil without a star.

Therefore, if will is joined to reason

In the sign of Libra, with Christ looking upon me,

All things prosperous will happen to me here and everywhere.

This is the good nativity of all worshippers of Christ.

## CHAPTER VII. ON PLEASURE

Greece had philosophers following differing paths,

While each, pleased with himself, condemned others’ doctrines,

Since shame makes it hard to lay aside a position once adopted.

On the principles of the world and the blessed life

They laboured to weave many thousands of words,

[Col. 1707C] 1608 Using subtlety in intellect rather than in truth,

And composed more things plausibly than truly.

They had many followers of their error,

Captured by the attractive skill of their speech.

Among these Epicurus holds no low place,

Declaring the world’s mass to consist of atoms.

He defines pleasure to be the highest and perfect good,

By enjoying which each person lives blessed,

Rejoicing in himself without anxiety—

That is, believing either that souls perish with bodies,

Or that after death no merit remains.

His disciples are more numerous than the Pythagoreans,

More numerous than the Socratics; nor could any philosopher

Find so many followers for his own sect.

[Col. 1707D] Who could number the regions, towns, villages,

Cities, and households following Epicurus’ doctrine?

Yet I too would not doubt, if any bodily pleasure

Could accomplish this—that, anxiety expelled,

I might live out my life in perpetual joy—

That I should extend my hands to Epicurus amid delights.

But if it is established that destructive lust weakens the body

And dulls the keenness of the mind,

Reason must prevail: pleasure is to be shunned.

First, even Epicurus the teacher could prepare adequate delights

Only by being anxious himself.

But, for the sake of argument, let us anxiously provide him

Every comfort, which he may enjoy freely,

[Col. 1708A] And let us see whether, luxuriating, he is happy.

Let us not give him merely things sweet to taste;

Let things most beautiful to behold feed his eyes also,

And let every other sense have its proper pleasure:

“Boy, spread the couches; prepare three couches with four places on each;

The festive arrangement of the dining-room requires this number.

Adorn the house with curtains and painted tapestries;

Scatter fragrant flowers over the floor.

Let the prince himself, glittering with gems and proud in purple,

Recline upon a couch covered in precious Tyrian purple;

Let coverings or linen garments adorn the guests;

Let a crowd of servants be clothed in fitting attire.

Then set out tables, white cloths, and napkins;

Bring forth bread made of snow-white finest flour;

In due course add honeyed cakes,

[Col. 1708B] Set out shining cups and polished dishes;

Bring in courses seasoned with diverse flavours;

The flesh of four-footed animals which household care feeds,

And those which the barking of dogs is accustomed to drive in forests;

Every kind of bird which a royal table frequents;

Bring fish from the sea and river waters,

Chosen fruits from every tree,

And whatever edible thing the earth produces for humankind,

So that you may overcome distaste for the fare of the cheap stomach;

And, that the refined palate may take pleasure,

Fill skins with varied drinks no less:

Let Caecuban and Falernian wines not be lacking;

Serve cups flavoured with spices and honey.

For these things a baker, cupbearer, cook, and server

[Col. 1708C] Must be at work, with a lesser crowd of attendants,

Lest, should sluggish activity perhaps prolong delays,

The king be miserable from hunger before being happy in eating.

Meanwhile, lest pleasure be cheated of any part,

A flautist, trumpeter, female lyre-player, dancing-girl, mime,

Cymbals, psaltery, lyre, drums, pipe, voices,

And whatever kind music may furnish more sweetly,

Let each delight the ears with festive songs.

Let the joyful house be fragrant with the precious scent of nard;

Let balsams breathe forth; let galbanum and incense not be absent.

After this, when the happy man’s entrails are already full,

Baths, barbers, strigils, ointments, and *silotrum* [uncertain cosmetic],

With which cared-for skin may shine, should duly be prepared.

Thus every colour, sound, taste, and smell—

[Col. 1708D] 1609 The bodily senses enjoy these for a moment—

If they make anyone happy while the enjoyment is present,

Soon leave him miserable when they depart.

Nor does he who enjoys a thing he knows will quickly perish

Rejoice securely; nor does any anxiety suit the happy person,

Yet without anxiety no one enjoys perishable things.

For when they are lacking, he desires and strives to enjoy them;

While he enjoys them, he fears that the fleeting things will leave him;

In turn fear and desire tear the miserable man apart.

Therefore, while awake, he cannot but be pricked by anxiety;

He is driven to and fro [*ansatur*; reading uncertain; see note],

[Note: [Col. 1707D] Perhaps *arctatur*, “is constrained,” unless *ansatur* is better: that is, he is made *ansatus*, like a man who staggers from drunkenness on both sides and is, as it were, seized by two handles, driven and repelled now this way, now that.]

and, buried in deep wine and sleep,

Desiring nothing and fearing nothing, he may perhaps be happy

[Col. 1709A] Since he does not perceive that he is happy.

Or indeed, if he is miserable unless he sleeps all the time,

He will sleep eternally, lest he become miserable by waking.

This is excessively ridiculous; and that too seems absurd:

For drunkenness and surfeit burdening the body

Torment it inwardly and burst the swollen entrails,

While the heavy stomach cannot digest immoderate food,

And the abundance of foul-smelling belches exhales badly;

The breathless lung scarcely breathes beneath this mass,

And the brain made mad by wine pounds against the hollow temples.

What rest, I ask, can there be in such a storm?

Indeed, immoderate pleasure produces diseases,

Relaxes the nerves, obstructs the courses of the veins,

[Col. 1709B] Generates excessive fevers from corrupted blood,

And makes the limbs tremble when their strength is exhausted.

Finally, it cuts short the span of life;

In the end, nothing can so extinguish the mind’s spark

And submerge the waking senses.

By contrast, sobriety, a sparing measure of food,

And moderation in luxury preserve the senses lively

And strengthen the body with natural vigour.

They provide sweet sleep and every healthful thing,

Awaken the intellect, preserve the mind’s keenness,

Multiply days, and prolong the years of life.

What place, I ask, is there for virtue where foul pleasure reigns?

Can anyone, with lust ruling, be called prudent,

[Col. 1709C] Or just, self-controlled, or brave?

Why does the importunate hand of robbers murder a man?

Plainly, that wicked pleasure may be redeemed by plunder.

Why does brother hasten brother, why do parents—holy names!—

Hasten their children toward death with eager wishes?

That wicked pleasure may fall to successors.

In short, pleasure becomes the cause of every crime.

Therefore pleasure is certainly not to be considered the highest good,

Nor even a moderate good. The sophist himself who rejects the highest

Denies that it is the least; but we deny both,

For the nature of good cannot be opposed to good,

As we often see vice clash with vice.

But pleasure is accustomed to be hostile to all goods;

It is plainly the greatest evil because it destroys every

[Col. 1709D] Form of virtue, and produces and nourishes every vice.

Therefore reject the foolish doctrines of Epicurus,

If you desire someday to attain the blessed life;

Scorn pleasures hostile to philosophy,

Unless you prefer to be deemed fat among a herd of pigs,

Destined to suffer the axe against your hardened forehead.

1610 ## CHAPTER VIII. ON TRUE FRIENDSHIP

What the law and measure of friendship among honourable people are,

And what sweet fruits true affection produces,

I do not have sufficient power fully to encompass in words.

Yet I shall try to touch upon certain matters concerning them.

For the doctrine said to have pleased certain philosophers—

That the wise person should live content with self-love

And not join to himself through friendships the foreign burden

[Col. 1710A] Of an afflicted friend’s misfortunes, by which he is tortured,

And so rob himself through anxiety of a blessed state,

Which he cannot attain except with a secure mind—

This doctrine, I say, is abominable to everyone.

How inhuman it is appears from nature herself as judge:

Nature binds children and parents in generative love,

Joins blood-relations in a social covenant,

And keeps the faith of spouses in an indissoluble bond.

This force also holds together peoples and great cities,

And makes the exchange of services mutual;

It makes people of one mind dwell beneath the same roof.

By a kind of shared instinct it likewise gathers together

Dumb animals that belong to the same kind;

Under nature’s guidance, each seeks what suits itself,

And pleasing harmony joins kindred souls.

[Col. 1710B] Therefore the voice eager for novelties achieves nothing,

When it invents friendships hostile to philosophy.

For what is so splendid, what so worthy of a wise person,

As to rejoice in the blessings of a friend who rejoices with him,

To bear adverse circumstances with equal feeling,

And to help one another with joined resources and counsel?

For when one supplies what another lacks,

Both rise more strongly to virtue’s burden;

And, as if one person were bound from two,

Each sees an image of himself in the other.

Therefore the absent friend is present; though needy, he abounds;

Though weak, he is strong; though silent, he speaks through his friend.

And, what is more wonderful, while he is at once another and the same,

After death he lives—surviving, that is, in himself.

[Col. 1710C] What is so pleasant, or what pleasure so true,

As a companion of one mind, to whom you may relate your joys

So that he rejoices with you in you as you do yourself,

Mourns with you likewise, helps you, and raises you when fallen?

If there should come to anyone what can scarcely come to one person—

All things at once, though they are given singly to many:

Glory, riches, eloquence, beauty, power,

Fortune’s gifts, each of which seems great—

Even so he is miserable if deprived of a friend.

This power has been implanted by nature in mortals:

Rejoicing in what is like, it rejects all contrary things.

Thus first arises affection for companions,

Which good deeds foster and the regular course of services nourishes,

When these have been mutually rendered with cheerful face.

This gift, so divine and useful to all,

[Col. 1710D] Has a most wretched lot for those who do not receive it.

Yet if anyone is so iron-hearted and without sap

That he trusts no one and can love no one,

Whom can we call an enemy of the human race,

While content with himself he labours to benefit no one,

I think any robbers preferable to him,

Though a perverse community of crimes joins them;

And cattle live better socially in a herd,

Whom common affection drives joyfully, as their play reveals.

He who lacks this impulse, so that he cannot attach himself

To one like himself or love one who loves him,

Will live a life most like a log or a stone.

But although we may wish to distribute our good deeds

1611 Among many, or, if it could happen, among all,

[Col. 1711A] Yet this precaution is needed in making friendships:

Let not anyone who feigns friendship with flattering appearance

Immediately seem worthy to be loved by you,

Nor open the thresholds of your closed mind to him too quickly.

Fear attracts some; hope of advantages attracts others;

Their crowd is numerous, yet not to be driven away so completely

That you should trust no one in anything or at any time,

Since we sometimes make good use of false friends.

For this dubious kind, ready to flatter,

Does not fear to deceive, because it seeks not you but what is yours.

They are companions of fortune and friends of prosperity:

While it remains, they remain; when it flees, they depart with it.

But those whom a virtue emulous of our own virtue draws,

And a beloved harmony of good character,

[Col. 1711B] Who do not regard a friend as they would a beast,

So as to value more highly whoever will yield greater advantage,

But judge that we should be loved for our own sake and freely,

Just as everyone is demonstrably bound to love himself for his own sake—

This is the kind with whom we should hold all things in common,

To whom we should refuse nothing, and who should refuse us nothing,

And with whom a firm covenant endures through the ages.

For we establish this law for true friends:

They should neither ask nor do, when asked, anything shameful;

Nor should they wait to be asked for what ought to be rendered,

But rather of their own accord should reciprocally give one another whatever is fitting.

Therefore the wise man should first choose whom he will love,

And cautiously strive to know beforehand by sure signs

One who will be of one mind with him and like in disposition.

[Col. 1711C] A man intending to buy a horse first tests its powers,

Lest its foot be tender, its legs slender,

Lest it be overcome in open ground by too slow a course,

Or, resisting the bridle, refuse to obey the reins;

And will you not test the friend to whom you entrust yourself?

Therefore we must choose one serious, just, and faithful,

Who cannot put expediency before honour—

If indeed anything can be expedient which is not honourable.

To him we shall safely open our hearts,

In which he will recognize whatever he has recognized in himself,

Provided we are such as we have described him.

For unless both are cultivators of virtue,

Discord may arise between unlike persons,

Which will never be able to trouble true friends,

[Col. 1711D] Since virtue is never contrary to virtue.

But the agreement of the vicious often wavers:

For instance, if one is excessively grasping and the other prodigal,

Or another discordant vice tears the two apart;

Such a man is thereby shown not to be a true friend.

From this it follows that only the compacts of the good

Rightly deserve the name of friendship;

For a harmonious but unjust will joining wicked people

May rightly be called a pretence or a conspiracy.

Therefore one ought not rashly or by chance

To enter into particular friendships with just anyone.

For Fortune supplies many ordinary acquaintances;

But give the foremost place to those first tested,

And use the rest as is appropriate for various purposes.

Should it happen that we are deceived in our judgment,

[Col. 1712A] Or that those we love change their former character—

For slender Fortune keeps some people modest,

Whom wealth or honour, if it should smile upon them, makes proud,

Or many other causes make them defect—

They must not immediately be rejected from affection.

Gentle, mild reproof must first be employed;

Then, if the matter requires it, harsh rebuke,

Which, striking vice, may spare the friend little by little.

If it is established that he cannot be drawn away from vice,

Then, lest association with the foul man stain us,

Care should gradually withdraw the covenant of friendship,

So that it may seem unstitched, not torn apart.

Nor should we suddenly undertake war or quarrels

1612 Against one whose will was once joined and identical with ours.

[Col. 1712B] For what is more shameful, what more often recounted among people,

Than those formerly of one mind contending in harsh hatreds?

But if grave fault disturbs the public interest,

Or threatens us with loss of life or reputation,

We are compelled to determine that he who was lately a friend is an enemy,

And to drive back with force the exceedingly foolish designs of the insolent man.

Happy is the lasting harmony of companions,

Which stands equally in adversity and prosperity;

Yet experience now proves very few faithful,

Since the world’s ruin slopes toward worse things,

And nothing belonging to you is shown sufficiently secure without faith.

We must also endure suspect friends,

Since the needs of life require even such unworthy people;

But let us not harbour unfaithfulness in our own hearts,

[Col. 1712C] Or become like them in deceptions.

Rather we must take care, and act without pretence,

How the false friend may depart from vice,

Rebuked by the example of our simplicity,

Which prudent cunning nevertheless preserves from harm.

For even if you can find no faithful person,

Can life be pleasing without any sort of companion?

From this it sufficiently appears how precious a true friend is,

And how delightful one is whose very shadow delights.

But those whose virtue has reconciled their minds to one another,
The pursuit of virtue preserves true friends,

which God commands above all things after himself to be cultivated,

and without which a true friend is never found.

Therefore the Godhead holds the first place above all things;

virtue stands next; after it let a friend be counted.

[Col. 1712D] For we think that after those two nothing is better.

## CHAPTER IX. ON THE GOOD OF DEATH

A grave and universal complaint of humankind is

that the harsh decree of death spares no one;

every age and both sexes recoil from it.

Rich and poor alike detest it,

the young man with the boy, the man with the old man, the healthy and the sick.

The unlearned man judges it the greatest of evils,

because it removes, together with life, all life’s advantages.

It makes man equal to a beast in respect of the body,

when it dissolves the flesh of each by a like corruption.

And why say more? If death’s violence were absent,

freedom restored would seem perfect to the world.

For fear of death, believed to be the greatest of fears,

[Col. 1713A] hangs at every hour over every neck;

under it stand kings and every perishable power,

and it darkens whatever delights in life itself.

A certain Damocles, guest of a Sicilian tyrant,

formerly learned this by experience, though ignorant of such matters.

For while, extolling the happy lot of his patron,

he often recounted the advantages of a fortunate kingdom—

enumerating gold, garments, engraved vessels,

royal banquets, games, and a crowd of dependents,

and finally the freedom to do whatever pleased him—

calling the tyrant fortunate in every particular,

as one who, fearing no one, was an object of fear to all:

“Therefore,” said the tyrant, “if this condition seems so great to you,

you may experience the advantages of our fortune:

let royal purple, sceptre, diadem, tribunal,

[Col. 1713B] and the authority of my rule be granted you.

Behold: I shall be what you were; what I was, you shall become to me.”

Having taken up the fasces, the servant is placed aloft,

conspicuous upon an ivory throne; a table is furnished

with festive equipment; a throng of nobles stands around him as he sits,

1613 eagerly hastening to fulfil the commands he gives.

At last, whatever royal banquets possess in sumptuousness,

the king himself, now a servant, presents and serves in full.

He had begun to pass a joyful day amid so many delights,

when he sees, hanging from the ceiling by a slender thread,

the sharp point of an unseen sword,

already threatening a deadly fall upon his brain.

Trembling, he is quickly driven from the ivory throne,

and condemns the unwelcome dangers mingled with delights,

[Col. 1713C] having learned by experience that fear of death hangs over kings.

Therefore death seems hateful and harmful to all

who lament the end of fragile life as a loss.

It is an irrational popular opinion that leads them;

for whatever mighty Nature commands must necessarily be,

and whatever provident order distinguishes by its appointed spaces,

you act foolishly, whoever attempts to censure it.

Who, being sane, complains that darkness succeeds daylight,

which the sun measures out by setting and rising?

Who complains that, by the changing turns and return of the sun,

winter night occupies the space of three days,

while at the season of the Crab daylight becomes equal to three nights?

Who complains that the year runs through four seasons:

that fiercer summer disturbs spring’s temperateness,

that it is soon driven away by autumn succeeding it,

[Col. 1713D] and that autumn is expelled by icy winter’s violent cold?

Spring opens the fruits which burning summer ripens;

autumn gathers them mature, but winter stores them away,

closing the year; and, most like cold death,

it shakes the withering leaves from the dry tree

and prevents the constrained fields from putting forth grass.

It is Nature’s law that past time can be restored by no one;

that future things will pass away; and that the present

can scarcely await the speaker.

Who, I ask, would wish such great flight to be everlasting?

Rather, one ought to desire to reach the goal of one’s course.

When a tiny infant comes forth from its mother’s womb,

like a beast, ignorant what it is, whither it tends, and whence it comes,

then it begins to set its first steps in the race-course;

it runs, and by growing reaches the years of childhood.

[Col. 1714A] But the boy passes through flowing time into a young man;

then he becomes a man; afterward afflicted old age comes on;

this yields to decrepitude, and death, the final thing, ends decrepitude.

The hours pass by, and there can be no return

to what came before, except insofar as the mind recalls deeds done.

Why, then, do you grieve more that old age yields to death

than that mature old age has yielded to decrepitude,

or that stronger age has yielded to old age,

before which youth had yielded in turn,

though childhood’s preceding years had ended in youth,

and infancy had recently preceded those years?

For you will seem to condemn man’s first beginnings

if you condemn the final stages of fleeing life,

which the same Creator orders by an equal principle.

Since the mortal drama of natural life has been well described,

as though by a learned poet,

[Col. 1714B] once the first act has been praised, let the last also be praised;

when it is now finished, let the reader say: “Applaud!”

The remaining stages of life are closed by their end,

and as many ages as there are, so many deaths must be undergone.

The last, most dreadful of all, will lack an end,
for the longest road already shakes the weary limbs.

For if the life of a wretched old man remained without end,

for whom, I ask, would it not be burdensome—burdensome even to itself?

Therefore it is better for old persons to die than to lack death.

But if death swiftly cuts short life’s course,

as we often see, without awaiting old age,

even so no just cause for complaint is given you.

One should rejoice instead that, by death’s short-cut,

[Col. 1714C] the labour of life, which had to be endured, is shortened.

Nor does an importunate will henceforth harm by sinning,

nor is the affliction of death, through which you are torn, to be repeated.

1614 Death alone gives a human being the inability to die,

and no longer to be afflicted by punishments or fear savage wounds.

How can that which confers so many goods be judged an evil?

Or why should that which removes so many evils not be held good?

Is it because, after death, the wicked suffer punishments?

But this is shown to be the fault not of death but of life.

For if death could end their pains,

then, though life were grievous, death would be desirable;

indeed, nothing is more grievous for them than to be deprived of death.

Death, therefore, is rest for the good and an end of evils;

[Col. 1714D] for the wicked, the cause of punishment is not death but a wicked life.

Finally, if every thing returns to its own origin,

and fountains call back their streams so that they may flow again,

as pleased the learned king who wrote mystical things,

than whom scarcely anyone wiser lived in the whole world,

who would take it badly, or rather not judge it just,

if earth receives a corpse born from earth,

and the spirit returns to the first principles of its ancient dwelling?

Finally, unless death restrained wicked desires,

there would be no rule for preserving peace in the world,

nor would anyone avoid committing whatever crime he pleased.

For although they feared punishments and losses of possessions,

the firm hope of life would make fear empty;

for fear of death aggravates every punishment,

while hope of life makes every loss seem less.

[Col. 1715A] It is therefore better that mortal limbs be dissolved,

and that the wicked be held by this fear as by a harsh rope,

than that, fear having ceased, they prolong their life through the ages

and, their reins broken, rush headlong into every crime.

But as to those who complain of life’s brevity,

when I consider what their complaint is, I see that it lacks reason.

For if long periods of living are sought for this reason,

lest pleasure be lost, cheated of its allotted time,

it is beneficial that what an evil mind entertains be brief; for certainly

prolonged desire deserves greater punishments.

But if swift death prevents the actions of one living well,

the full reward of the righteous desire remains after death.

Therefore the shortening of fragile life does not harm the good,

and it seems to benefit the wicked by making them fear punishment.

[Col. 1715B] Hence it is clear that neither has any cause left for complaint.

## CHAPTER X. ON THE RESURRECTION OF BODIES

What lay hidden from the ancient sages of this world,

who measured the regions and times of heaven and earth

and thought that they had comprehended the natures of things,

sure faith, proved by sight, reveals to us:

he himself who destroyed death testifies

that new human bodies shall rise after ashes,

and restored flesh, now knowing no end, shall rise.

Christ, the first fruits, leader and head of the devout,

by first ascending to the right hand of the Father, raised himself,

and at last shall place his revived members in heaven.

And lest anyone deny that these things could happen to others,

he who alone was free from sin,

[Col. 1715C] both God and man, master of life and death,

had commanded the dead to return to life’s offices,

while he was still mortal, mingled with mortals,

in order to testify to the people that spirit and flesh,

as they were able to be joined before they had been joined,

so also can, after death, be restored after their separation;

nor is the labour harder for the Omnipotent in either case.

The widow’s only son, whom God raised from the bier while the crowd watched, teaches this to his mother.

Lazarus proclaims it when he leaps from the tomb,

1615 with his face covered and his hands and feet bound;

the winding-sheet does not hold him, against whom a stronger command stands.

And lest the frailer sex also despair of such things,

the girl shut indoors truly attests that she has returned to life;

each parent is witness, and the household crowd is witness.

[Col. 1715D] This, therefore, is the hope; this the sole expectation

that consoles the many and great labours

amid which wretched people live in this present time.

It removes from the faithful the fear and punishment of death,

and excuses them from thinking that the Lord’s image

is reduced to nothing and created in vain,

if our end is ashes and worthless cinder.

The holy prophets hand these things down to us as objects of belief.

Job also, the patient man and contemplator of the future,

with this hope consoles the wounds of his stricken flesh:

that his own flesh, skin, and bones shall rise from the tomb,

and that, himself restored to life, he shall see the living Lord [read: “the living God”].

Paul too, once and twice caught up to heaven’s secrets, affirms the same,

[Col. 1716A] declaring in faithful speech that the last trumpet

will give a sound terrifying to the world;

without delay, the dead will rise when the earth is torn open,

and one part, meeting God, will be borne aloft,

while the other will be dragged captive down into the world.

Why should I hesitate to believe that what has been shown possible will occur?

And why should I not believe future that which sacred Scripture reports accomplished,

on which rests the greatest force of our faith?

Nature itself whispers this to me without speech,

having accomplished its office and being a type of the same thing:

every day, oppressed by sleep as by an image of death,

and rising again when I awaken as though from death:

“After sleep you awaken; after the time of death you shall live.”

The same world cries this, and provident Nature of things,

[Col. 1716B] which God created so suited to human uses

that certain things can signify future events to humankind.

The moon changes its phases and, when its light has died, is born again,

taking increase through the monthly periods.

1616 The sun also, as though buried beneath the earth during night,

rising new in the morning, represents a return from death.

The revolving heaven, turning its circuits,

signifies the same, separating the air into darkness and following light.

Earth itself, our mother, which receives our bodies,

keeps in trees an image of life and death,

and preserves a similar form in revived plants:

branches stripped of leaves in winter time,

and trunks as though dried beneath death’s image,

[Col. 1716C] leafy summer restores to their proper appearance;

the fresh grasses which winter destroyed rise again in spring

and at fixed seasons repair their former losses.

Seeds cast by hand die when covered in furrows,

but, as though from tombs, quickly rise enlivened,

so that their own labour may begin to gladden the farmers.

The same hope and restoration of life awaits us,

by which the same body shall grow green again, but incapable of dissolution.

Has renewal been granted to things placed beneath me,

and does the whole world, bearing back this form, serve me,

while irreparable loss presses upon me alone?

And what cause will there be why I, living for a short time—

the best part of the world and image of the giver of life—

should perish after a little while, deprived of hope of return?

[Col. 1716D] Should the world made for me endure through the ages,

do you not think it more fitting that inferior things perish irreparably

than those proved more excellent?

Yet those things remain; therefore these things shall remain still more.

Moreover, what reasoning permits that the good Creator,

whose intention was to grant us immortal bodies,

suited to fill the gaps caused by the angelic fall,

should either be thought to have failed

or, as though fickle in mind, to no longer will what he then willed?

Let both thoughts be far from God, whose will

toward the good things once begun is so fixed, and whose power is complete.

Therefore no reason remains why we should now doubt

that, together with our bodies, we shall enjoy everlasting life.

[Col. 1717]

# VARIOUS POEMS OF MARBOD, BISHOP OF RENNES (G)*

## I. M., Bishop of Rennes, to R., Bishop of Lincoln

[Note: [Col. 1717D] Perhaps Robert, called Bloet, who is named in the charter by which Henry I transferred Ely Abbey into a bishopric in 1108. *Anglia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 681.]

[Col. 1717A]

It was not fitting that words should be given me, nor that you should give words;

it is shameful for me to be deceived, but more shameful for you to deceive.

For just as the giver is more commended than the recipient,

so one who promises, unless he gives, is held more worthless.

## II. Description of Spring’s Beauty

Spring’s grace prevents me from having savage manners,

and from the elements I borrow a form for my mind;

I rightly, as I think, rejoice with Nature herself.

A thousand varied colours distinguish the flowers.

The earth has put upon itself a grassy fleece.

We see the grove green with leaves and bearing fruit.

Golden orioles [read: little birds], blackbirds, jackdaws, woodpeckers, nightingales

[Col. 1717B] vie in equal praise to modulate their varied songs.

For some, a nest stands in a tree, not without chicks,

and in bushes a new offspring without feathers lies hidden.

When the rose comes forth, the gardens are beautiful.

Add to these the field which bristles with ears of grain.

Add vines, grapes also, and later nuts.

You may count the dances of brides and mothers,

the games of young men, and the festival and bright day.

Whoever sees so many beauties and is neither moved nor smiles

is intractable, and strife lies in his breast.

Whoever does not wish to recount the beauty of the earth with praise

envies its Creator, for whose honour serve

rigid winter, summer, autumn, and the loveliness of spring.

## III. To an Absent Friend

If you cherish in the city something that you love and would not wish to lose,

and cherish it faithfully, let the court not concern you.

Break off every delay; your loss increases hour by hour.

But this loss is great because it cannot be repaired.

You will postpone everything that makes you a Calonne.

In this country house you will lose more than you gain in that place;

for what is of such value as a boy who is kind to his lover?

He who is kind now, if delay occurs, will become unkind.

For he is tempted by many flatteries,

and one who is tempted is in danger of being deceived.

Therefore return quickly if you wish to retain what you love.

Leave the little castle if you wish to keep the little citadel.

## IV. Satire on a Lover of a Boy, in an Assumed Persona

[Col. 1717D] Horace composed an ode about a certain boy

who, with his beautiful face, could sufficiently be a girl.

His hair flowed over his ivory neck.

[Col. 1718A] His brow was white as snow and his eyes black as pitch;

his beardless cheeks were full of pleasing sweetness,

while blush bloomed amid the brightness of their whiteness.

His nose was well formed, his lips fiery, and his teeth beautiful.

His appearance was fashioned for the mind in a becoming proportion.

Whoever seeks what body lay hidden beneath clothing

should fit to it one corresponding to that face.

This radiant beauty of countenance, full of loveliness,

kindled the spectator’s heart with love’s flame.

But Nature had fashioned so handsome and exceptional a boy,

an incitement to all who beheld him,

as cruel and stern [the text reads: “Say/Nature,” perhaps *Hunc* or *Sic*],

so that he would rather die than consent to love.

Harsh and ungrateful, as though born of a tigress,

[Col. 1718B] he only laughed at the tenderest words of supplicants;

he laughed at cares that would have no effect,

and he laughed at the tears of a sighing lover.

He laughed at those whom he himself made die;

that impious one indeed, cruel and likewise impious,

who prevents the body from being beautiful through vice of character.

A beautiful face seeks a good and patient mind,

not one that is foolish, but one prepared for both these things.

The little flower of youth is swift and of excessive brevity.

Once it withers, it falls and does not know how to grow green again—

this flesh, so soft, so milky, so without moles,

so good, so beautiful, so smooth, and so tender.

The time will yet come when it will become ugly and bristly;

when dear boyish flesh will become cheap flesh.

Therefore, while you flower, put on mature manners.

## V. Epigram on a Wooden House

[Col. 1718C]

A house built of timber can become food for fire;

if fire does not feed upon it, it nevertheless soon goes, for it grows old.

1618 But what would it profit if its wall were iron,

when harsh death would nevertheless find a hole for it?

Therefore one who endures only a little while should not care

how long his dwelling lasts, even if he worries about such things.

## VI. To a Restless Smith

Lipari is said to have the workshops of the Cyclopes,

whom hard labour exercises by night and day,

yet in such a way that they take some share of sleep and food,

and a small pause refreshes their weary hands.

You, detestable smith, are wearied neither by work nor flame

from pressing the anvil with the glowing mass.

[Col. 1718D] You have no rest; the neighbourhood feels none,

since your labour plagues everything near at hand.

Would that the shared wall were as high as the Alps,

[Col. 1719A] or that Etna were a furnace for your fires!

I do not think you were created from human stock;

a sleepless dragon could have begotten you.

Yet, though descended from gold, you have sunk to iron

and, degenerate, apply yourself to an inferior occupation.

Golden splendour held your father; an iron mass holds you.

May dark sleep, may death, press down your eyes.

## VII. To a Friend as Guest

Returning to these parts after five harvests,

you wish a few verses to be written for you by me.

You desire verses few indeed, but sweet;

like mixed food, you ask both things of me.

Behold, we give what you ask, because we love what you ask:

that a poem may run briefly along an easy road.

[Col. 1719B] Whatever you wish, I wish; what you do not wish, I also do not wish;

and what I do not wish, I wish you also not to wish.

With death delayed, fare well through long years,

and may the fates grant you a swift return.

## VIII. Verses Inscribed on a Fan

The troublesome swarm of flies is frightened by a fan,

which is wont to be a nuisance at tables for no reason.

It is wont to be a nuisance when limbs are given to rest,

and it is wont to be a nuisance when we read.

It is wont to be a nuisance when we write or meditate,

and it is wont to be a nuisance in other ways.

## IX. To Faustinus

While, Faustinus, I consider the part of your little book

[Col. 1719C] where the mute page of blank parchment lies,

I judge the part that speaks more empty than you;

for a page full of superfluities is empty.

Hence I conclude that the whole book is empty:

one half contains trifles; the other nothing.
