## X. On a Bird Trampling Grass

While a bird walks with its feet, it damages fresh grass.

Wherever it wishes to fly, let it fly, lest it violate the grass.

## XI. To Scaevola

Though you reject lesser gifts in order to bear greater ones,

Scaevola, you sometimes lose great things.

For once the giver has been excluded and does not yet return,

you receive nothing and are deceived by your own cunning.

O crafty man! O prudent man! While you always seize at the greatest things,

[Col. 1719D] great things become nothing through your cleverness.

1619

## XII. Against an Envious Man

Someone, dear Julius, is consumed with envy

because Rome reads me; he is consumed with envy.

He is consumed with envy because I am a witty friend,

because I am a frequent dinner guest; he is consumed with envy.

He is consumed with envy because I have a pleasant country place near the city

and a small house in the city; he is consumed with envy.

He is consumed with envy because, everywhere, a crowd

always points at me with the finger; he is consumed with envy.

He is consumed with envy because I am loved and approved.

Let whoever is consumed with envy be consumed.

## XIII. On a Beautiful Girl

Nature, polishing other girls more sparingly,

postponed being generous with her gifts.

Upon you she poured out her wealth; and, beholding the wondrous work,

she marvelled that her own hands could have accomplished this.

## XIV. Two Friends to Three Friends

Marbod and Hugh say to William: “Fare well”;

but each says to Thomas alone: “Fare well.”

To William and Thomas, Samson being joined: “Fare well, all of you”;

and may there be a threefold well-being for three, or one well-being for three.

## XV. On Avarice

By the fault in its name, *avitia* (“avarice”) ought to be corrupted [source *vitiari*, “to be corrupted”; conjecture *vocitari*, “to be called”].

Certainly, *avaritia* (“avarice”) is said to derive from *vitium* (“fault”).

## XVI. In Defence of Avarice

I judge it to be named rather from *vita* (“life”) than from *vitium* (“fault”).

Therefore avarice ought not to endure a fault.

## XVII. Consolation of Mourners

[Note: [Col. 1719D] Another work, wholly distinct from this one though bearing the same title, is printed above at col. 1673.]

[Col. 1720B]

As everything which the lowest place produces returns to one,

and ash cannot be a free end,

so what comes from above seeks the ether again,

that what God himself creates may remain forever.

God himself produced souls; parents produced the body.

The body perishes in death; the good soul shall always remain.

At last it shall come and resume the same flesh,

so that what has gone may return and what was before may be again;

but let it return in holiness, happier than before,

that it may live better and fall no further.

If you know these things well, there is no reason why you should wish to weep:

for how does that which shall be again perish?

## XVIII. Prose—The Sinner’s Compunction

(From the manuscript of St Gatianus, Tours. Unpublished.)

[Col. 1720C]

When I remember with how much care

I have pursued perishable things,

and how harshly death exercises

its rights in my inward being,

1620 which lies open to God alone;

roaring like a lion,

I weep for my sins.

When I remember that I shall pass

through death’s hard road,

and what shall become of me

after that pure judgment,

anxious in my mind’s tumult,

which lacks the cultivation of virtues,

with sad heart and sad countenance,

[Col. 1720D] I pour out prayers with sobbing.

With sobbing I pour out prayers;

with bent knee I beat my breast;

speaking with trembling mouth,

I cry to you from the depths:

Jesus Christ, Son of God,

consubstantial with him,

maker of night and day,

I beseech you, have mercy on me.

Through the bite of the first parent

we fell down here below.

The sins which we committed separately

weigh down our back.

Through the fruitful Mother,

[Col. 1721A] renewer of the world,

turn back the ancient condition,

saving the body and Shechem [reading uncertain: *Sichem*].

Let there be praise to Christ our Lord,

praise to his holy Mother,

who may protect us from the dark

punishments of the abyss.

Amen.

## XIX. Epitaph

[Note: [Col. 1721C] This Bruno, bishop of Angers, is the same person who is called Eusebius Bruno in the Sammarthani brothers’ *Gallia Christiana*. As they say, after Hubert, bishop of Angers, had died, he was appointed to the episcopate in 1047. His epitaph, composed by Marbod, is reported together with, and not distinguished from, the epitaph of Geoffrey I, called bishop of Tours, which immediately precedes it. Since the version in *Gallia Christiana* is longer than the one here by two verses, we have judged that it should be presented here for Geoffrey I in the same form and sequence in which it is found there, together also with the epitaph of Geoffrey the singer. Thus these three epitaphs are continuously joined:]

Father Bruno, gracious old man, gentlest bishop,

whose heart was compassion, whose tongue honey and milk:

if it was a fault in you that you wished to harm no one,

what was your merit, when the fault was good?

What should clergy and people pray for you, dear Father?

May the Lord be to you what you were to us.

[Col. 1722C] Here lies Geoffrey, bishop of the city of Angers,

[Col. 1722D] if the dead flesh of a bishop has a name.

But if we prefer to apply this more fittingly to the spirit,

the bishop does not lie here, but sits above the stars.

But if a position can be attributed only to bodily things,

he neither stands, nor reclines, nor sits above the stars.

Carnal glory flies away on swift wings.

The glory which prepares the world has an end.

Geoffrey the singer, noble star of singers,

rich in lands, houses, dependents, and wealth,

prudent, famous, upright, diligent, ingenious,

passes like smoke; in this soil he becomes soil.

[The pleading of cases, the civil exposition of law,

in which he had fixed his talent (*ingenio*; variant *ingenium*) and study. These final two verses are the first two verses of the immediately following epitaph of Robert the dean, where, however, the reading is *vixerat* (“he had lived”) … *studio* (“study”).]

Father Bruno, gracious old man, gentlest bishop,

whose heart was compassion, whose tongue honey and milk:

if it was a fault in you that you wished to harm no one,

what was your merit, when the fault was good?

What should clergy and people pray for you, dear Father?

May the Lord be to you what you were to us.

## XX. Epitaph of Geoffrey, Bishop of Angers

[Col. 1721B]

Here lies Geoffrey, bishop of the city of Angers,

if the dead flesh of a bishop has a name.

But if we prefer to apply this more fittingly to the spirit,

the bishop does not lie here, but sits above the stars.

But if a position can be attributed only to bodily things,

he neither stands, nor reclines, nor sits above the stars.

Carnal glory calls forth [read: “flies away”] on swift wings.

The glory which prepares the world has no end.

## XXI. Epitaph of Geoffrey the Singer

Geoffrey the singer, noble star of singers,

rich in lands, houses, dependents, and wealth,

prudent, famous, upright, diligent, ingenious,

passes [read: “passed”] like smoke; in this soil he becomes soil.

1621

## XXII. Epitaph of Robert the Dean

[Col. 1721C]

[The pleading of cases, the civil exposition of law,

in which he had lived with talent and study.]

To Robert they had given the office and name of dean,

that he might be the brothers’ shield through his eloquent tongue.

But neither wealth nor honourable standing was lacking to him,

so that so many gifts might benefit our needs.

For all these things he deserved punishments or rewards: may the Almighty

take away the punishments and multiply the rewards.

## XXIII. Epitaph of Robert

A certain Robert, neither a rich man nor poor,

[Col. 1722A] neither very wise nor excessively foolish,

neither very well known nor remote from every praise,

neither too holy nor quick to vice,

when suffering shook his face with sobbing,

fell and diminished our number.

Angers nourished him; Orléans lost him:

that city was his mother; this one his stepmother.

Alas, Robert, boy welcomed by the wishes of your people,

how grievously, dear nephew, has your thirst been defeated!

Thirsting for learning, pitiable one, you drank the Loire.

May Christ give you drink from the fountain of everlasting water.

## XXIV. Epitaph of Anselm of Laon, Master and Dean of Laon, a Distinguished Teacher of Theology in His Age, Instructor of Abelard and Other Scholars of That Era, Who Died in 1117

Buried [Col. 1722B] at Laon in the church of St Vincent. Concerning him, see *Gallia Christiana*, under the deans of Laon.

(From the manuscript of St Gatianus, Tours. Unpublished.)

Prince of teachers, flower of the clergy, glory of poets,

Anselm has passed away through unavoidable fate.

The glory of his integrity, derived from a most chaste life,

had been an indication of how great an Israelite he was.

Law, Gospel, psalm, or matters wrapped in cloud—

God granted these to be unfolded through Anselm.

England, the kingdom of the Franks, all Pannonia,

the Ligurian people, the population of Apulia, distant Judaea—

formerly entangled in the many darknesses of error—

received the teachings of the man, blessed teachings.

Under his leadership, welcome wisdom had flourished in learning,

but now withers, bereft of its teacher.

[Col. 1722C] The labours of grammatical art have wholly perished;

Aristotle’s forms and the rigours of study have ceased;

rhetorical colour and Cato’s legal cases fade away;

Plato’s natural philosophy lies desolate.

Number is debased; concern for arithmetic is silent.

With its guide removed, the principles of geometry lie fallen.

Mourn your poet, assembly of bereaved clergy:

there is no one who can worthily uphold your laws.

City of Laon, grieve: that poet of yours has fallen.

At once your praise and your happy times have perished.

1622

## XXV. On the Finial Surmounting the Tomb

[Note: [Col. 1722D] “Majesty,” that is, the ornament or finial which rises above the tomb.]

France, which in my judgment surpasses the whole world,

[Col. 1723A] will not have another second Anselm like him.

## XXVI. Lament of an Afflicted Captive

[Note: [Col. 1723D] Perhaps of Marbod himself, who in his letter to Raynald of Martigné, whose election he had unjustly supported, complains that he suffered prison and chains at the hands of that ungrateful man. See Marbod, epistle 1, and the note [Col. 1724D] on it, p. 1391.]

The darkness, cold, and hunger of a narrow prison,

and thirst, wakeful fears, threatening spectres,

and savage monsters breaking the wretched man’s brief sleep;

besides, the weight of iron and double chains,

by which the emaciation of cramped legs is eaten away;

then the grievous misery of a bed, upon which the frequent knot

chafes the weary limbs of one lying down, and its shortness constrains them;

and terrible threats and sad torments,

whose names or forms horror forbids one to enumerate;

the position of foulness and the filth of a wet, stinking place—

behold, for forty nights and days now

I endure these intolerably and live buried alive.

## XXVII. Warning against Sailing for Profit

[Col. 1723B]

Whoever wishes to know the threats and storms of the sea,

let him hear and learn how greatly the sea’s wave yawns open [read: *dehiscat*],

how it makes its course upward as though toward slopes,

how scattered storm-spray makes the stars wet,

how the torn sea opens a fearful abyss.

Let him hear these things, and many others much worse than those related;

let him hear them, I say, but never experience them.

Let him believe the narrator, whose rewards are not so great

that for profit he should become food for the birds of the sea,

or, for hope of profit alone, food for swimming creatures.

He whom my warning offends will trust himself;

he delights in the use of foreign riches.

Led by hope of these, he will strike the waves with his oar;

the waves will strike him, he will prove true what I say,

[Col. 1723C] and then he will believe, not words, but bitter realities.

## XXVIII. Against a Seditious Mob

Since Wisdom earned her heavenly seat,

Peace, born of the highest Father, joined to Jupiter’s household,

Bacchus, stirred by envy, fights with Pallas.

The conflict begun in heaven fell to earth;

neither Semele’s son nor Minerva lacks armies.

To follow two such different things is not a matter of equal weight.

Every good man seeks the one; the mob seeks the other:

the latter is devoted to pleasure; the former to labour.

Therefore more defend Bacchus’ camp—

that is, pour out wine—than fight for Pallas.

Hence it is no wonder if the drunken mob rages fiercely

against those unlike itself, judging us most contemptible because lowly.

1623

## XXIX. Invective Admonition to Those Besieged in a Castle

[Col. 1723D]

Though adamantine fortresses rise round about,

though ninefold strong walls flow around,

though a molten river of swift metal sends up smoke;

though at the gates lies a dragon, braced upon its tail,

and the hideous rage of a fire-breathing Chimera roars:

yet you infamous, murderous band, you robbers,

shall in no way escape the punishment of your crime.

Not because dreadful engines should strike terrifying crashes

against the fortifications and break their woven defences,

[Col. 1724A] nor because sickle, ram, slings, lead-weighted missiles, and moles

bring deaths from every side in many forms;

but because the hand of the Almighty fights for the widows,

whose tears distress us more than the siege.

For a fearsome enemy threatens outside, while within,

a conscience aware of itself wages an implacable war.

## XXX. Instruction of a Boy Pupil

If concern for my instructions remains with you,

spare, boy, your trifles while I cultivate the country at harvest-time;

I shall set before you limits such as your age requires.

If you transgress them, you will deserve ill from your adviser.

Despising your bed, rise early in the morning,

and spend time reading until the fourth hour [the text has *taxat*; perhaps *tardat*, “delays”].

Take food at the fifth hour; drink wine, but moderately;

[Col. 1724B] after breakfast, sleep briefly or play a little.

After you have slept, let it be your custom to meditate.

Do not be reluctant to commit to tablets what you have meditated.

I hope someday to see the things which you must unlearn.

Send some of them to me here, that I may believe the rest.

After this, go to bed; when you have read, go to eat.

After taking food, if the hour now bids, rest.

If time remains, it is beneficial to play after supper.

Within such a limit your whole regimen is established.

## XXXI. On Correcting Boys

He who spares a boy stuffs his light heart with fat.

He who continually applies the lash makes a fat heart lean.

## XXXII. To Odo, Both Bishop and Count

Marbod to Odo: the benefits of the true good in the Lord.

You bear the twofold title of bishop and count,

[Col. 1724C] [Note: [Col. 1724D] Perhaps better in accordance with the author’s meaning: *Indiciis et vos cum proficiatis utrisque*: “and since you prosper in both respects.”]

and, distinguished, may you be perfected in both,

serving equally clergy and military service,

with a shared office, but one which each side treats as though it belonged to itself alone.

For each thinks himself alone to be honoured,

that gifts are offered to him alone,

and that nothing he wishes is to be denied him.

Since fortune has given you all that a man seeks for himself—

treasures, years, noble rank,

a tongue that knows how to speak, a mind that knows how to reflect,

uprightness of character, and the favour of people and fathers—

yet I dare to write a few things to you, as a renewal,

lest you be one who does not wish to remember,

if it is permitted to say so, your particular friend:

not because I am such a man as to be particular to you,

but because I know you to be one whom I may make particular.

[Col. 1724D] Nor does it matter to me what you may give: I love you more than what you possess.

I love what you have also, but I do not demand those goods.

I do not wish gifts to be given me, but, being poor, I wish to be loved.

It is sufficient as a gift if one love binds us.

1624

## XXXIII. M. to His Walter, Greetings

When I wish to send my Muse, accustomed to the crowds

and luxury of a rich city, and thus blunted, to the countryside,

she draws back and does not believe it will be safe

to be seen by you, Walter, poet to be feared.

For you enjoy a place where, as you yourself confess,

[Col. 1725A] the charm of the countryside invites you, free from cares,

while the lyre answers and you sing wondrous poems.

This frightens her: lest, if she delivered something badly commanded,

you should give her lashes, or savagely burn her with fire,

or send her back shamefully, her tunic torn.

“He,” she says, “is by no means devoted to the country estate—

he to whom you now wish to send me, ignorant and alone.

Though he lives in the countryside, he avoids everything rustic.

For a book stands beside him through a great part of the day;

indeed, even after supper he is accustomed to summon the Muse,

and, free from cares, to dictate things to be read by those to come.

If I say anything unpolished, anything not plainly expressed,

I shall, by the poet’s judgment, be charged with rusticity.

By his censure I shall receive many an erasure,

for my errors could not easily escape his notice.

[Col. 1725B] Or indeed, if I speak many things elegantly,

yet because of a few faults he will make a great hole in me.

Send Coturnicus to greet his friend by voice,
one of the household servants from the ancestral home: the journey is not long.”

Having used these words, I answered my Muse thus:

“Do not fear,” I said, “for I shall not abandon you,

if this man should do anything sad to you—which I do not think he will.

Indeed, go gladly, to see the country nymphs,

and to see the chorus of sisters—which you ought to wish—
The sight of your offspring will be a source of pleasure to you,

Whom, though you have never seen him, you hear to be worthy of praise.

Clio, not distrustful, obeyed my command,

And, whatever she may send, thus nevertheless greets you:

May you live as many years as slip away in threats.

### XXXIV. Likewise to the Same Poet

[Col. 1725C]

By sweet songs, dearest one, you delight me so,

As a man living in the countryside is delighted by water babbling over pebbles,

Or by a wordy bed giving his limbs to sleep,

Or by draughts of a living stream one who is thirsty,

Or warmth one who is cold, or food one who is hungry.

For this I give you great thanks, most eminent poet;

And that you may long continue singing, I and my Muse, praying,

Sing with you—not answering in equal measure,

But as a harsh goose intrudes upon the voice of a swan with a hoarse sound.

For no bird’s voice surpasses your song;

Among songbirds I am like a chattering bird.

For in praising me, you illumine darkness with light,

Proclaiming that my poems are spread throughout the regions of the world.

You say this the more to draw me along by friendly words

[Col. 1725D]

Than because it is true in the balance of facts, unless I am mistaken.

Yet, since you delight in laying these praises upon me,

May just Jupiter grant you immortal glory.

You do not know envy, you who apportion honour to me,

You who almost alone possess this quality; it is not the jealous wasting sickness,

Which praises no one and cheats some even of their name.

What is more: you are so eager to exclude harsh contention

From our sportive verses that you would rather have me write in bare words,

And fashion verses devoid of salt, than injure the reader’s mind

By the cause of wit. How gentle you are is shown by your avoidance of dispute.

[Col. 1726A]

Therefore Clio yields to you; Clio willingly obeys you.

Let her too take no care for those figures which you do not care for.

Let her write without ornament, since this is what you require of her.

For me to turn a poem into the tasteless beat of a lyre

Is far preferable to writing in polished verse.

Therefore I abandon wit; I send you verses such as these,

In which there seems to be enough simplicity.

### XXXV. Epitaph of King Charles the Great

(From manuscript no. 164 of Saint Gatian at Tours.)

Guardian of wealth, avenger of crimes, bestower of honours,

Charles, the glory of the world—and the world’s grief itself.

While it was permitted, while your power, Martel, remained strong,

Fraud lay hidden, great peace prevailed, integrity reigned.

Ruler of Laon, a Cato to citizens and a Hector to enemies,

[Col. 1726B]

Equal in countenance to Paris, he lies beneath this stone.

### XXXVI. Epitaph of Master Lanfranc, Archbishop

(From the manuscript of Saint Gatian. It is found at greater length in the final volume, part II, of the *Acts of Saint Benedict*, as composed by Saint Anselm.)

Lanfranc undertook not the riches or honours

Of the archbishopric, but its cares and labours.

Born in Italy, in the region of Pavia,

Of distinguished citizens and honourable rank,

He was monk and prior of Bec; then abbot

Of Caen; afterwards primate-prelate of Canterbury.

He was restorer of the whole English Church,

And likewise helper of the Normans.

The greater part of the world had experienced his learning,

And he was a common consolation to widows and orphans,

[Col. 1726C]

To the lame, the crippled, lepers, demoniacs,

The deaf, the blind, and also the vicious.

After exhortation, he did not disdain to bring relief;

And although his meals with drink were luxurious,

And his garments soft and costly,

He himself was clothed in the garb of austerity,

Always living on cheap and poor fare.

A true, not false, cultivator of the order of justice,

He was a most upright and pious avenger of wickedness.

Harsh toward the proud, supplicant to none for a gift,

Harmless toward the good, and never two-faced.

Chaste, he aided the unchaste by sparing them;

Just, he corrected the unjust by bearing with them.

Thus, caring for others, he performed a shepherd’s work.

[Col. 1726D]

Thus preserving himself, he pleased the Lord in all things.

This man, so wise and strong in this struggle,

Could not at last escape the snares of death.

Oh, how many sorrows the wretched then found!

And how many honours the English people lost!

### XXXVII. On the City of Rennes

[Note: [Col. 1725D] At first we had intended altogether to suppress these verses, lest we should seem to have wished to offend the native people of Rennes, now distinguished by so many titles and virtues. But since they occurred in several manuscripts—namely, the Tours and Angers manuscripts—and in the Rennes edition itself of 1524, we feared that we might be accused of rashness if, on our own authority, which is none at all, we erased from Marbod’s works verses also reproduced in the recently published *History of Brittany*. And indeed the learned author of this very distinguished history seems to think that they are not Marbod’s, because each verse is endowed with a threefold rhythm. But this does not prove that they ought to be denied to Marbod, since among his poems many can be seen resounding in this same threefold manner—for example, in the prayer to the Mother of the Lord, col. 1652:

> Fair jewel, fresh-born rose, perfect in beauty,  
> Honey enclosed in hollow combs, transformed in flavour,

and so on for twenty verses. We could cite many other unquestioned poems of Marbod of this kind. More truly, or at least more probably, we think that Marbod, an Angevin by birth, composed these verses in youthful ardour while the people of Angers and Rennes, as often before, were agitated by various dissensions among themselves. We suppose that they are among those verses of which Marbod himself says at the beginning of the book of ten chapters:

> What I wrote as a young man, while as an old man I revise more things,  
> I regret, and wish that some things had not been written or published.

Whence he says:

> They ought either to have been quickly erased or never published.

For it does not seem probable that a bishop otherwise most holy and loving toward his flock would have wished to commend to posterity its blemishes and defects in so savage a poem.]

(From a Tours manuscript of Saint Gatian, about the year 600; from the Rennes edition of 1524; and from the recently published *History of Brittany* by our Reverend Father Dom Alexis Lobineau.)

City of Rennes, stripped of goods, bereft of inhabitants,

[Col. 1727A]

Full of deceits, hateful to the heavens, without the sun’s light,

It idles in darkness amid enticements and delights in hiding-places.

It judges idleness excellent and despises wisdom.

It calls every law of the Fathers black; it itself deserves the abyss.

By means of false advocates it acquits the wicked;

It condemns truthful and peace-loving friends.

Every good man is considered a burden and cannot be a patron.

It provokes wars and will not cease, because it will become most wicked.

No one raised there knows how to keep faith.

Why should I describe this savage people, this cruel Megaera?

Those who live in the countryside alone are oppressed by armed men.

Death runs about, because the robber rages and burns the villages.

The wrath of God does not hinder one filled with fury.

Whoever goes his way is stripped and beaten with fists.

[Col. 1727B]

Food is lacking for the poor; wounds are their swelling.

### XXXVIII. How Money Is Served

(From the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatian. Unpublished.)

Since honour is bestowed by money and money is loved by many,

That deceiver deceives those who honour it, and deceives those who love it.

Prince, prelate, monk, senate of the people,

Cleric and soldier, woman and the male sex,

Rejoice in money and serve its commands.

1627 Everyone applauds it. Whatever it commands, he promptly obeys.

What it pleases is carried out; what displeases it is forbidden.

While money speaks, the voice of all others is buried.

It is preferred to justice, though the case be pleaded at great length.

When speeches avail nothing, when arguments avail nothing,

When no advocate avails and no friend helps,

Money arrives, and the whole dispute departs.

[Col. 1727C]

What was unjust becomes just when money is judge.

Everything worldly that you have known is subject to it.

At its pleasure every request is granted.

It softens the angry and sets the reconciled at variance,

Exalts the lowly and weakens hard men in their strength.

It perverts morals, grants kingdoms, changes honours,

Corrupts law, setting up a king through bribes.

What it once made, it in turn destroys.

Whomever it oppresses is constrained; whom it loves is helped.

It loves this man, torments that one; money breaks marriages.

The court of pontiffs judges as incest what the law commends as honourable,

Though this seems unjust; it separates what is just and joins what is forbidden through gifts.

When the matter comes to gifts,

[Col. 1727D]

The majesty of kings and the power of prelates plainly lie.

Money surpasses kings when it proffers gifts.

Money, standing highest among all else, surpasses pledge,

Honour, understanding, birth, and integrity.

### XXXIX. How One Who Serves Money Is Deceived

(From the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatian. Unpublished.)

[Col. 1728A]

Alas! Why is law rashly corrupted by worthless money?

Why, man, are you deceived? Why are you held by the world’s praise?

Why, man, do you harm yourself? Why do you depart from piety?

When you despise law, you see with darkened sight.

Consider, mortal, what praise, what glory,

What sort of fruit the world possesses: in it there is nothing but grief.

For, like hay, the delightful world withers.

Live for God alone; do not entrust yourself to the world.

Whoever trusts the world is disappointed in the end.

Why do you serve money? Why does heap cling to heap?

When age has drawn you on to life’s limit,

Alas for you on your last day: from rich you will become poor.

Why then do you seek things which you will no longer be able to possess?

[Col. 1728B]

You acquire freely where there is no usefulness.

O how badly he rages who has accustomed himself to live thus!

Usury begets a grim kind of death through usury.

He who heaps up usury breaks and enfeebles his body.

A double toil afflicts the avaricious man ignorant of burial.

He boils over in pursuit of gain, burdened by great exertion.

He is never secure as to how his property may be preserved.

Now locks, now walls become obstacles to the thief.

See: the desirous man is shut in and fears thieves.

Thus he is tortured by the pains of a double death that has arisen.

Alas, what shall I say to you? Why do you seek an unjust death?

While you live, you die, because you are reckoned a worshipper of death.

The life now granted is death; it is not judged life.

Living, you are punished; dead, you will obtain death.

Why, wretch, are you mad? This labour seems vain.

[Col. 1728C]

The more you gain, the more you are tortured by desire.

It will not suffice you, though abundance become very great.

Atone for this sin; unlearn your habitual guilt.

Remember that the end hastens with a moment’s brevity,

And that, though possessions be manifold, fate cannot be resisted.

### XL. Parable concerning the Trick Played by a Wolf upon a Shepherd

(From the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatian. Unpublished.)

It is reported that a wolf here played this trick upon a shepherd.

A certain wolf often seized many of the shepherd’s sheep

As they wandered through broad pastures.

After the shepherd could not harm the ravager by force,

He sought to ensnare him by deceit.

For with such effort he bends a rigid oak

That its head can touch the ground;

[Col. 1728D]

And a noose is fastened to the bent top,

So that a movable stick may hold the noose;

But he places the stick against the ground in such a way

That whoever moves the stick will perish by the noose.

[Col. 1729A]

And the head of a lamb is inserted in the middle of the noose,

So that whoever seizes the head will move the stick.

Then the shepherd goes away; the wolf seeks out the contrivance

And at once snatches the lamb’s head in his mouth.

But when the stick is moved, the noose immediately binds his neck,

And the stiffness of the oak raises the wolf on high.

When the shepherd sees the robber hanging captive,

He throws stones at him, hastening his death.

He inflicts a thousand wounds, so that the wolf may die by stoning;

But that evil spirit cannot be driven out.

To torture him still further, he finally brings him down from on high,

And, raising a club, speaks these words to the wolf:

“The stones accomplish nothing. I shall now smash your brains with this club

And offer you as a funeral sacrifice to my lambs.”

The wolf immediately cries: “Have mercy, most pious shepherd,

[Col. 1729B]

And, I pray, hear the few things I have to say to you.

If you deign to grant me life,

I shall restore a hundredfold all that I have carried off.

But I have nothing here; if you allow me to go away,

Take a useful pledge, lest I deceive you.

My little wolf will be a suitable hostage; I shall hand him over to you,

So that I may return on the day you appoint.

If I never return, you suffer only a very small loss

If the young one dies in place of the worn-out old one.

He can do harm; I shall do no harm even if I live,

And if I die, I shall offer you no benefit.

Take my hide: it will not suit you for a boot.

Take my flesh: it will not suit you for food.

I do not know why you wish to scatter my wretched body,

When it will be of no use to you in either respect.”

[Col. 1729C]

In short, when the hostage was received, the credulous shepherd

Allows the wolf to return as quickly as possible.

The wolf, planning an artifice by which to deceive the shepherd,

On his way back finds a monk and a servant.

“My father,” he says, “hail! Do not despise the words of a suppliant,

Nor, because I have sinned, be willing to reject me.

I repent of my error; I am weary of taking the world’s goods,

And I am ashamed to have slaughtered innocent livestock.

It profits nothing to indulge one’s body with continual pleasures

If no hope of pardon is available to me.

Strike me with a rod, or beat me with any lash;

Only restore this soul, holy man, to God.

Cutting my long mane, I beg, shave a broad tonsure,

And, once I am thus shaven, give me a monk’s tunic.

[Col. 1729D]

Do not think that you undergo so much labour for nothing:

Since none has been given to me, I give you a sheep as a gift.

If dishes of sheep’s flesh do not please you,

Give the flesh to your servant; keep the fleece for yourself.”

When the monk receives the highly welcome gift,

He takes scissors and immediately shears him;

And, shaving his head, he takes pains to make such a tonsure

That the circle extends from ear to ear.

He further instructs him what rule ought to be observed,

1629 Then orders the cowled wolf to depart.

The day had come on which the hostage ought to be restored,

The day on which the wolf had promised he would return.

Then he returns; but the shepherd can scarcely recognize him,

For he who had been tawny now appears black.

“What were you like?” he says. “You are greatly changed from the one

[Col. 1730A]

Who, a ravager of sheep, was caught in the noose.”

Bowing his head, after saying “Bless me,”

Bathing his face in tears, he speaks these words:

“Worn down by the wounds from the stones which you gave me,

I was lately sick, and a physician came.

Feeling my vein, he sensed that my pulse was running badly,

And said to me: ‘You will not live, but will die.’

Meanwhile a monk came to visit the sick man

And urged me at last to repent of my crimes;

He taught holy hope: no one is lost

Whose life was evil if his death proves good.

Finally he persuaded me to despise the world utterly,

And, having thus shaven me, gave me this habit.

Once I abandoned my old customs and former food,

Though I had been sick, I immediately recovered.

[Col. 1730B]

Now, because my hostage was to lose his life,

I seek to give up my own so that my son may not perish.

Returning here, as I had proposed to return,

I possess nothing of my own with which to repay you.

I do not wish to break faith: if you wish to spare me, spare me.

If you prefer that I die, kill me quickly.

This right hand of mine,” says the shepherd, “will never harm you;

But because it harmed you, I ask that you forgive it.

If I killed a monk, I should become a double murderer.

Your hostage shall go free, and you return home.”

Then they go back joyfully and remain safely in the field,

When the hungry wolf tells this to his young wolf:

“Believe me, son, sheep’s flesh is exceedingly dear,

And cheese and beans will be harsh food.

I shall not undertake a burden that I cannot bear.”

[Col. 1730C]

He spoke, and began again to carry off sheep as before.

But shortly afterward, while the ravager was eating a lamb,

The shepherd sees him and rebukes him thus:

“You are well and a monk; you ought not to feed on flesh.

The holy rule of Basil does not command this.”

Then the wolf replies: “The order of the good is not simple;

Now I am a monk, and now I am a canon.”

And so the wolf went leaping through the woods.

The shepherd realized that he had been badly deceived.

### XLI. On the Monastic and Ecclesiastical Order

(From the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatian. Unpublished.)

The monastic order used to be ecclesiastical,

When it cultivated harsh food throughout the rural countryside.

No money, no business hindered it.

[Col. 1730D]

It atoned for our capital sins as well as venial ones.

Reduced from capital crimes to venial losses,

The monastic order is forcibly ecclesiastical

When it powerfully acquires every ritual gift.

The monastic order is fruitless ecclesiastical order.

It enters sheepfolds through upper doors, not without grief.

The monastic order is senseless ecclesiastical order.

It values all spiritual things at a rich price.

The monastic order is ecclesiastical without cause.

It knocks at spiritual doors now closed to it.

Why is the monastic order called ecclesiastical,

When it is likened to the grasping and rapacious?

But I do not wish to identify two crimes by their names,

Which wisdom or reverence does not know how to love.

A wound more concealed is reckoned the more harmful enemy;

[Col. 1731A]

A pleasant sickness seems incurable.

To speak more plainly is more dishonourable; it will disclose itself of its own accord.

Who will hear of his own accord? Who will understand of his own accord? It will disclose itself of its own accord.

Land, money, churches, great palaces are acquired,

Whence pride and power are magnified.

What does vain pride accomplish by its empty sport?

Lucifer was exalted, and God expelled him, and he is tormented.

But may my Lord, almighty God, creator of all,

Helper of the foolish and the wise,

In his mercy remove these things and grant good things, so that they may deserve

To seek spiritual pastures, lest they die.

### XLII. Sibyl’s Verses on the Day of Judgment

(From the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatian. Unpublished.)

The sign of judgment: the earth will be drenched with sweat;

A king will come from heaven, destined to reign through the ages—

[Col. 1731B]

Present in the flesh, indeed, in order to judge the world.

Therefore unbeliever and believer will see God

On high with the saints, when at the very end

Souls together with flesh will be present, whom he himself judges.

When the world lies uncultivated in dense brambles,

Men will cast away idols and every treasure.

Fire will burn lands, sea, and heaven,

Seeking to break down the gates of grim Avernus.

But a free light will be granted to the whole flesh of the saints;

The guilty everlasting flame will burn,

Revealing hidden acts. Then each person will speak

Secrets, and God will open hearts to the light.

Then there will also be weeping, and all will gnash their teeth.

The radiance of the sun is taken away, and the choir of stars perishes.

Heaven will be dissolved; the moon’s brightness will fail.

[Col. 1731C]

He will cast down hills and raise valleys from their depths.

There will be nothing lofty or high among human things;

For mountains are levelled with plains, and the blue waters of the sea

Will all cease; the shattered earth will perish;

Likewise springs, torrents, and rivers in the fire.

And when the trumpet sends forth its mournful sound from the lofty

Sphere, lamenting wretched crime and diverse labours,

The gaping earth will reveal Tartarean chaos,

And before this Lord kings will be set, one and all.

A river of fire and sulphur will fall from heaven.

### XLIII. On the Fall and Restoration of Humankind

(From the same manuscript. Unpublished.)

The serpent, making promises, deceived the woman, credulous toward the apple; she favoured the man; he violated God’s commands.

Deceit despised justice; death assailed life; the proud man cast down the king; hope hurled down those who stood; the citizen lost heavenly things; each guilt broke the law. Hence guilt subjected us to itself.

Deceits were crushed, the hated one cast down, life given, death extinguished, and paradise opened.

By right, by power, dying, victorious, in mercy,

Foretold by the Law, at last born of a Virgin,

Last, first, God and man, highest and lowest,

Infant, great man, little one, lion, worm, and lamb,

King, sun, mountain, peace, flower, law, guide, light, hope, hut, spring, dowry

Of kings, of justice, of virtues, the true [dowry] of Mary,

Of the order of the Church, of goodness, welcome wisdom,

Of the life of the saints, strength of the homeland, gate of the heavens.

[Col. 1732A]

The only offspring of the Father, whom the mass of the world serves:

Praise, law, honey, torch, lot, mind, salt, dew, part, *mna* [a weight], man, art, death

Of things, of conquerors, bright [death] of mercy, of the pious,

Of the Father, teacher, Gideon, of angels,

Of warriors, of the widow, of heaven, of the reprobate.

Since he is God, it is fitting that we applaud and sing psalms to him.

### XLIV. Canonical Verses

(From the same manuscript. Unpublished.)

The matter and the time urge me to describe the grievances of the brethren.

Princes of the Church, bishops and leading clergy,

You who judge rightly, who wish to live honourably,

Turn here the eyes of your heart, here the ears of your mind.

Let every man hear: youth, boy, unmarried maiden,

[Col. 1732B]

And trembling old men—what the clergy’s complaint may be.

Whatever the pen records flows from the stream of truth.

Whoever doubts the truth, let him know the deeds of the superiors.

From the fruit he will be able to know what a viper is.

Between the superiors and ourselves the rule differs.

The matter is weighed badly, while the balance is not held even.

One rule is for superiors, another rule for us.

They may with impunity do whatever they please.

They strip the altars: the execrable power approves;

They despoil the saints, while the silent guardian says nothing of it all.

If they break chalices or sell curtains and hangings,

We may not murmur. Who would be mad enough to blame such things?

Who would now dare to defame such robbers?

One guilty of theft is given a great gift.

Do not condemn theft if you fear the blow of a lash.

[Col. 1732C]

The avenging rule condemns those who condemn thieves.

He sins no little who relates public crimes.

Every kind of crime will live unpunished without a judge.

Do you wish to live richly? Remember to praise robbers.

I am poor because I often rebuke thieves

In deed. But I prefer always to live needy

Rather than be the accomplice of thieves, the slave of riches.

Poverty is best when integrity of mind enriches it.

I have no treasures increased by thefts, plunder,

Fraud, prejudgment, perjuries, faction, or profit.

One rule is for superiors, another rule for us.

We are the lowly people, an unmemorable rabble,

A hired populace, for whom all household goods are food;

If we rightly complain why we live so badly,

[Col. 1732D]

Why our goods are ruined, why they are not made common property,

In the midst springs forth the image of a hideous spectre,

Enemy of honour, betrayer of religion,

Fountain and source of evil, violator of holy sanctuary,

Destroyer of laws, no pretended lover of deceit,

A witness to wickedness, whose concern is perjuries,

Who suddenly belches a thousand lies from his mouth,

Leader of murderers, hope and protector of thieves.

This sweet voice of an ass brays these songs to us:

“Say, rulers, bid the clergy’s leaders pronounce judgment.

What sudden madness is this? What such rash daring

Has come among this people? What insanity arises?

Why does it rage with such clamour? Why does it proudly become so frantic?

The author of this murmuring will not go unpunished.

He shall live as an example to many for so great a crime.”

[Col. 1733A]

The whole troop follows the teacher’s words.

At the spectre’s command, each gives his judgment.

Relentless Burburus, a sphinx always fond of bloodshed,

Cruel beast, savage arbiter, impious pest,

Whom Pluto sent to us from the Stygian waters,

First belches forth these lessons of madness:

“He who wishes to contend in words is like a fool.

We administer laws; we teach the laws that must be observed.

If we commit theft, we wish it always to be unpunished.

The sentence of law depends on the king’s desire.

He barks in vain who blames the crimes of thieves.

By merit of theft a thief has sought the heights of heaven.

It is right for superiors to forgive their own faults,

Nor may one note their thefts, even though truthfully.

The king and superiors are to be restrained by no law.

[Col. 1733B]

If the king steals, the law remains unquestioned.

For the king’s fault, the page of law sleeps.

Although they are thieves, the powerful are revered everywhere.

His office of superior covers the infamous robber.

1632 Deceitful speech becomes a shield of wickedness for me.

He who speaks truth will become an enemy of the superiors.

Thus the censure demands; thus law and rule promise.

He who contradicts will undergo the rods’ lashes.”

The master’s flayer approves the Burburean [read: “purple”] words—he who stripped the sides and altars of the saints.

He who suffers sickness very often tends the sick.

A sacrilegious thief may give excellent testimony.

Let a thief support a thief, as a prostitute supports a prostitute.

By praising a thief, I thus increase my own praise.

[Col. 1733C]

If I condemn a thief, I defile myself with like theft.

Rhadamanthus springs forth in the midst with a thick voice:

“You judge splendidly; numbers make weapons feared.

Let those whom crime stains and makes equal be allowed to stand together.

Catulus praises this, and so do Clodos and Manichaeus.

This number of thieves completes twice three and one.

But since discourse has now begun concerning Catulus,

I shall set down who he was in youth, what he became, and whence he came.

As he begged, naked, seeking food,

Before the burning wheel of the summer sun, he gave way.

Thereupon his trembling skin, full of black blood [read: colour],

Bursts and disfigures his limbs with foul poison.

Like an Ethiopian, he comes without a covering of skin,

Poor, destitute, naked, girded with linden bark.

[Col. 1733D]

Such was he at first who now bathes himself in gold.

Whom Fortune’s wheel suddenly carried up to the stars,

Now, a stern Cato, he thunders laws at us.

The nobles marvel, flourishing in probity of morals.

Now an ass commands leopards; now a hoopoe commands swans.

Yet if the precarious little hide should roll headlong,

Then, though unwilling, the little ass will submit to leopards,

And the exceedingly haughty little Cato will leap from the cliff.

He who stands often falls; he who runs injures his feet.

Thus, thus, Fortune, you play with uncertain movements.

One rule is for superiors, another rule for us.

We, a worthless populace, are often read at the lecterns.

Let superiors sit; let them not compel us to sing psalms standing.

Laughter will feed them; a long chant will weary us.

[Col. 1734A]

The flock sings the Gradual *Alleluia* in the customary manner.

The superiors contend with words and laughter.

This is their zeal; this the profit of the elders.

And as if a blind man held his eyes wide open,

Seeing nothing of the light, though living with eyes open,

So likewise such men, splendid in face but not in mind:

To stand in choir is beautiful, but not very useful.

One rule is for superiors, another rule for us.

It is not permitted to divide the table’s dishes equally.

Let a small meal without complaint suffice for us;

For the superiors, little chickens; for me, the thinnest rib.

A bare mouth will be given me if I reject the gift of a rib.

If I wish to murmur, I shall be fed on frequent blows.

For superiors let the portion be threefold; for us, single.

After a thin rib we eat no roasted meat.

[Col. 1734B]

The superiors triple their dishes with tender chickens.

If we fast on a few days from time to time,

Let cheese mixed with eggs suffice us,

Or beans, which make warm figs grow green again.

If once a month we happen to have fish,

Crayfish, eels, Tiber fish, spring fish, and sewer fish

Defile the tables—fish worn down by long age.

Let the superiors alone be filled with fresh fish.

One portion is for superiors; another is given to us.

We unfortunate people do not know the scent of wine.

The superiors have wine; we taste vinegar.

We rise from table, but not without angry murmuring.

Sick thirst shakes this man; stomach trouble shakes that man.

Long hunger of the stomach rarely becomes a friend to rest.

Those who belch with stretched throat blame this on the Lord.

[Col. 1734C]

One rule is for superiors, another rule for us.

We are forbidden to set foot outside the cloister;

1633 But the lords of the chamber may return to their own houses.

A pyre is made in the midst, and Bacchic revels are celebrated.

Cups filled with foaming nectar are drained.

Then they recite laws; there we are all proscribed.

The sentence of law totters beneath a worthless tail.

One rule is for superiors, another rule for us.

One steals mills, another our fields.

One exacts tithes from estates, another defrauds revenues.

One sells woods, another takes green meadows.

Not all our income is transferred to our use.

Moreover, they force our churches to sell themselves to them.

This is the work of wickedness, not of honourable poverty.

Burburus made this gift without the approval of good men.

[Col. 1734D]

Exopici [read: Exotici, or “foreigners”] mice, thus stealing our goods,

Gnaw away all the brethren’s possessions as a mouse gnaws grain.

They give us straw and fill their own houses with marrow.

Nor are they ashamed to take tithes together with fourths.

Hens, chicks, tender lambs with their mothers,

Fleece of wethers, beans, lentils, hemp, flax,

And the tithe of livestock: all belong to the superiors.

It is a very foolish thing if the brothers cry out such things.

The troop of superiors rises to answer:

“You know neither how to card wool nor weave fine cloth,

Nor how to wind linen twisted from the spindle.

Let the superiors or masters of works do such things,

And let our tithe be their wages.

[Col. 1735A]

Tell me: what sin do I commit if I seek my own advantage?

Who, bad to himself, will ever, tell me, be good to another?

If I hold a manor for the profit of denarii,

Let the whole be my portion; I do not know how to divide money.

Let food and a share of income suffice you.

Everything that remains becomes the superiors’ treasury.

Thus the canons decree; thus the elders have treated matters.

Thus we will, thus we approve, thus we command it to be.”

Alas, grief! Alas, mourning! O detestable age!

Alas, astonishing crime! Why such great power of thieves?

Say, where are king, law, justice, and the avenging rule?

Fraud overcomes laws; gifts blind kings.

Rule and law sleep while the judge is a thief;

Because of the head’s defect, the image of the limbs grows pale.

Under a ruinous prince the ecclesiastical order falls.

[Col. 1735B]

He has made an end; but why has his spectre remained?

Cruel Verres, Ulysses, brother of Simon,

Infamous thief, why does he live surviving in the world?

O God! Why do you delay? Why do you not strike him with lightning?

All the temple’s dignity has perished under such a judge.

What had been firm falls, torn up by his struggle.

He has thrown everything into confusion and does not yet cease to purge it.

Why does he hold power? Why does he wish to be a master?

And why does he oppress doctors and priors beneath himself,

He who ought from his ancestors to lead an ass out of the woods,

Even if he has sucked the honey of wisdom on Mount Pegasus?

Let one mingled with the Muses tell me what a letter is,

1634 Or what a superior, a cleric, or a steward is.

He will not explain these to me unless someone whispers them murmuringly.

Such an ornament of life, such a shining jewel of wisdom,

A lamp of the Church, which gives darkness instead of light,

A tasteless teacher, foolish lover of fools,

Rules here briefly; Pluto will openly seize him

And make him superintendent over the bands of thieves.

There let him rule sceptres, and thus here break perjuries.

### XLV. Proverbs of Cato the Philosopher

(From the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatian. Unpublished.)

Let the wise man give ear to useful counsels.

Let neither happy events puff up the mind nor sad events break it.

[Col. 1736A]

The manner of life differs; death is one for all.

Beware of entrusting anything great to a timid heart.

The wounds of a deformed reputation are never healed.

A cursed woman is the shipwreck of her husband’s property.

If you are ruled by mind, you are a king; if by body, a slave.

Be near the good if you cannot be the best.

No one is so frugal as one prodigal from another’s resources.

He hears what he does not wish who persists in saying what he wishes.

I do not like anyone who greatly pleases himself.

Give obedience to law if you wish to be held free.

Practice teaches either to despise good things or to endure bad.

As smoke rises from fire, so reputation rises from crime.

Let him who mocks the wretched know that all the future is uncertain.

The greater you are, the more moderate be.

High things fall through hatred; low things are raised through love.

[Col. 1736B]

Boldness secure in pardon for a crime grows.

Indignation makes any coward brave.

Riches tremble; poverty is a free thing.

A man is blameworthy when he has fallen into crime.

Do what befits you, not what another deserves.

Voice, face, life, and will are unlike in all persons.

The envious man himself torments you [read: himself] and takes revenge on you.

Poverty always increases the gain of the very rich.

A memorable deed is accomplished at great risk.

The earth is humankind’s homeland, where we are born and buried.

Things hard to endure become pleasant to recount.

We desire more keenly new things which we already hold in part [read: have acquired].

A good deed slips from the mind; an injury endures.

[Col. 1736C]

Remove witnesses to evil, and we shall bear our evils more lightly.

A steadfast man labours to complete whatever he has begun.

Often grief dries tears, and joys pour them forth.

He is unjust who thinks good the things that he himself does.

I shall be afflicted more heavily by sorrows if I remember happy things.

Long age consumes everything made by hand.

The examples of others will teach you what you should cautiously avoid.

Pretended vanity will remain for no length of time.

Hunger seasons dishes; to those who are full, everything is insipid.

Learning is the sweet fruit of a bitter root.

## BOOK OF STONES

[Col. 1735]

## Notice on the Book of Gems

[Col. 1735] 1635–1636 We have learned from the Colbert manuscripts 4181 and 6609, and from the Parisian Victorine manuscript no. 905, that this book—printed at Rennes in 1524 among Marbod’s other shorter works—is a legitimate offspring of his. In the latter manuscript a French translation in the old idiom, copied in the same hand as the original itself, may also be seen. Bollandus speaks of it thus, on 4 February, p. 82, col. 2:

> “Gesner reports in his *Bibliotheca* that the poem *On Gems and Stones*, by Marbodaeus or Marboldus (for the name is written in various ways), has often been printed, and that it is sometimes cited by Vincent and Albert and other such authors under the name *Liliarius* or *Lapidarius*, and sometimes also under that of Evax—not because Evax was his surname, as Bale, Pits, and others assert, but because of the poem’s opening, which is:
>
> ‘Evax, king of the Arabs, is said to have written to Nero.’”

“This,” Bollandus says, “we judged worthy of public light because of the weightiness of its sentiments and language.”

Further, at the head of the Victorine manuscript, which appeared to us older than the others, being at least six hundred years old, we read—though in a much more recent hand:

> “The author of this book is Marbod, bishop of Rennes, who before becoming bishop taught humane letters at Angers, and was finally raised to the bishopric of Rennes because of his exceptional learning. According to Trithemius’s calculation, he flourished in the year of the Lord 1060.”

We have collated this poem against the manuscripts of Saint Victor at Paris, no. 905, and of the Greater Monastery at Tours, although the latter is defective toward the end; and against the first Rennes edition of 1524, as well as the recent Leiden edition of 1695, prepared by Abraham Gorlaeus, with the scholia of Jacob Gronovius.

It bears different titles in different copies, but all amount to the same thing. In the Victorine manuscript it is entitled: “Here begins the Book of Stones”; and we have retained this title as the older one. In the Rennes edition: “Here begins Marbod’s Book of Sixty Stones.” The Tours manuscript, defective and incomplete at the end: “The little book of Lord Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans” (but this, as is clear from all the other copies, is wholly erroneous), “on the diverse natures of stones.” Concerning this book Peter the Deacon, in his *On the Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino*, while enumerating his own works, says in chapter 47, the last: “He translated the book of Hevax, king of the Arabs, concerning stones.” For the variant readings, the reader should note that V signifies the Victorine manuscript, T the Tours manuscript, R the Rennes edition, G Gorlaeus’s edition, and M after G a marginal note in Gorlaeus’s edition. At the end of the latter are found two letters of Evax, king of the Arabs, to the Emperor Tiberius, serving as a kind of preface to the Book on Gems. Although Gorlaeus does not say whence he drew them, we judged that they ought to be appended, lest anything be lacking; likewise the following verses, which he declares had never been published anywhere.

As for the translation, our first intention had been to reproduce merely a few opening verses in that old French language, by way of specimen. But several learned men and students of antiquity thought it preferable that this not unworthy monument of antiquity should be printed whole, as it stands, for readers’ benefit and pleasure. We did not dare to oppose their judgment, especially since, in their view, works composed in that old French idiom in the eleventh or even twelfth century are exceedingly rare, and this French rendering of the poem has proved so felicitous that, in most of its sections, what was transmitted in Latin has been faithfully rendered in French, almost line for line.

+ The manuscript of the Church of Tours is now kept in the library of the city of Tours, under old no. 222 and modern no. 656. It was written, I think, at the beginning of the thirteenth century. In the same codex are read: 1. The *Life of Charlemagne*, by Turpin, Archbishop of Reims; 2. Miracles of very many saints; 3. Various works of ascetic piety; 4. The history of Dares, king of the Trojans, translated from Greek into Latin by Cornelius Nepos; 5. finally, “The little book of Lord Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, concerning the diverse natures of stones.” At the end one reads: “Here ends the Lapidary.”

We carefully collated the Tours codex word for word with the text published by Dom Beaugendre (Paris, 1708), and found many things less than correct, or even mutually inconsistent. Certain verses, though few, cannot stand metrically, although in the Tours codex they are by no means defective. In chapter 30, “On the Gerachite,” we found two verses omitted by the Benedictine editor and therefore unpublished until now. Some words are transmitted incorrectly, which are here for the first time printed correctly. Thus, in verse 9 of chapter 19, “On the Magnet,” the printed text reads: “It is one whose nature is to draw iron”; but the Tours codex has: “And by the force of its nature,” etc., which is correctly said of the magnet-stone.

[Col. 1737]

## HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF STONES, BY MARBOD, BISHOP OF RENNES

[Col. 1737] 1637–38  
[Note: These four verses occur in the Tours manuscript before the prologue; here they are printed at the end.]

The ancients gave gems their name from gum,  
because they shine through like translucent gum.  
Yet by either name the species is denoted as a stone;  
therefore this book is entitled *Of Stones*.

## PROLOGUE

[Note: [Col. 1737A]

## PROLOGUE

Evax was a very rich king;  
he ruled the kingdom of the Arabs.  
He was wise in many matters  
and learned in many languages.  
He knew the seven arts and was their master.  
He was powerful and of noble character.  
He possessed great treasures of gold and silver  
and was generous to all people.  
For his great wisdom and prowess,  
[Col. 1738A]  
which he possessed, and his great liberality,  
he was known and much loved,  
renowned in many lands.

Nero had heard of him;  
and because everyone praised him,  
he loved him greatly in his heart  
and sent him a wise messenger.  
Nero was emperor of Rome  
at the time when this king lived.  
He commanded the messenger  
[Col. 1739B]  
through his embassy to make known to him  
his wisdom and courtesy,  
and that he sought no other possession.

Evax wrote him a book,  
which he himself made with his own hand,  
concerning the natures of stones,  
[Col. 1739C]  
their powers and their properties:  
whence they come and where they are found,  
in what places and in what countries;  
their names and their colours,  
what powers they possess and what virtues.

Many of their virtues are hidden,  
but their aids are manifest;  
physicians find in them great help.  
Those who know their powers  
find in them great skill  
for making medicines.

No wise person ought to doubt  
that stones possess great virtue;  
not so many proven virtues  
are found in herbs.  
God made them very glorious;  
therefore they are called precious.  
And I tell you this truly:  
[Col. 1739D]  
nothing can possess virtue  
unless God wills and grants it,  
and unless it descends from him.

### § I. THE ADAMANT (or rather, the diamond)

We shall first speak to you of the stone  
which is called the adamant.  
The *annas* is such a stone;  
it is clear as crystal,  
and brown as iron in colour.  
It is found in Greater India.  
Neither iron nor fire can work it  
[Col. 1740B]  
unless it is tempered in the hot blood of a buck.

Then it must be moistened while it is hot,  
and afterwards broken with a hammer  
upon an anvil into little pieces,  
which fly apart in fragments.  
[Col. 1740C]  
Other gems are cut  
and finely fashioned.  
It is no larger than a small nut.

This stone I have described to you.  
From Arabia comes another kind,  
which is neither so hard nor so fierce.  
It is broken without the blood of a buck;  
it is not so beautiful nor so prized.  
It is larger, but worth less;  
it bears the name “diamond.”

One is found in Cyprus; the remaining wording is uncertain.  
A fourth is found in Greece, less prized.  
All these have such a nature  
that they draw iron to themselves.

This stone is of great value  
to those who practise enchantments.  
Whoever wears it may acquire strength;  
it gives him power and protection.  
It defends him from grievous dreams  
[Col. 1740D]  
and likewise from phantoms;  
from poisons and deadly potions,  
from quarrels, anger, and madness.  
A madman is far better than a bad physician.

Whoever wears it will never be harmed  
by any of all his enemies.  
It ought to be set in gold or silver  
and kept honourably;  
it should be worn upon the left arm.  
So, according to the writing, it ought to be.

### § II. AGATE

This is called agate  
from a river where it is found,  
which bears that name.  
Within it may be seen many figures  
formed there by nature.  
One sees in it the image of a king,  
which is naturally within it,  
or the likeness of another beast:  
such is its appearance.

Another agate is found  
and brought from Crete.  
It bears the image of coral,  
and grains of gold are naturally painted in it.  
It is so opposed to harmful poisons  
that where it is, they can do no harm.

Still another is found  
which is likewise called agate.  
Trees are painted upon it,  
[Col. 1741D]  
and thickets are carved there.  
Whoever wears this upon himself,  
no harm shall ever befall him.  
But whoever looks at it too often  
loses his sight thereby.

There is yet another kind  
which, when burned, has the odour of myrrh.  
There is another that is spotted  
as though touched by drops of blood;  
and another of great worth,  
which has the colour of wax.  
Because it is not very plentiful,  
a man is apt to prize it highly.

But its power is great:  
it protects a person and makes him strong.  
It gives him a ruddy colour  
[Col. 1742C]  
and makes him a good counsellor.  
It causes him to give counsel to friends  
and makes him feared by his enemies.

### § III. ALECTORIUS

They esteem the alectorius highly.  
It grows in the belly of a capon  
that has been castrated after three years  
and lives until it has passed seven years.  
They find in its belly the stone,  
which is very precious and dear.  
It is as large as a bean  
and resembles glass in colour,  
or crystal-like glass.  
The stone is very spiritual.

Whoever keeps it and holds it in remembrance,  
it gives him power and great victory.  
It takes away all declining good fortune;  
he will not be defeated in battle.  
It gains a man good friends  
[Col. 1742D]  
and makes him overcome his enemies.  
It makes him loved and eloquent,  
delivers a woman of her child,  
and causes him to be loved by his lord.  
It should be carried in the mouth.

### § IV. JASPER

Jaspers are very good and dear,  
and there are seventeen kinds of them.  
They occur in many colours  
and grow in many lands.

But the best and strongest  
is green and very shining,  
and possesses the finest virtues.  
It sustains and comforts a person well;  
whoever keeps it chastely  
receives from it great security.

[Col. 1743B]  
It removes fever and dropsy  
and aids a woman in labour.  
It protects a person and makes him strong,  
[Col. 1743C]  
loved, and very valiant.  
It takes phantoms from all people.  
It should be worn in silver.

### § V. SAPPHIRE

Sapphire is beautiful and fitting,  
bright and resplendent.  
It resembles the sky when it is pure  
and without clouds, when it is not dark.  
No gem has a greater virtue,  
greater beauty, or greater worth;  
it is good and beautiful.

It is found in the gravel  
of a river in that country  
which is called the Syrtes,  
after a very ancient people  
whom they call Syrians.  
But that is better and worth more  
which comes from the eastern land.

[Col. 1743D]  
This one is not very shining,  
but possesses worthy and excellent virtues.  
It is called the gem of gems.  
It is very valuable to men and women;  
it gives great comfort to both,  
keeps the limbs sound and strong,  
removes envy and deceit,  
and frees a person from poison.  
It possesses very great power.  
Whoever wears it will have no fear.

It reconciles those at odds,  
and whoever wears it will not be dismayed.  
It is good by nature.  
It bears within itself the image  
of something that is not known  
[Col. 1744B]  
or recognized by any person.

It is of great use in medicine.  
It cools one who is excessively hot,  
[Col. 1744C]  
who has too great an inward heat  
and sweats excessively from pain;  
and if it is dissolved in milk,  
it is good for healing wounds.  
It removes filth from the eyes  
and great pain from the head;  
it destroys evil of the tongue  
and makes everything go downward.

It should be worn very chastely  
and kept very honourably.  
Whoever thus keeps it  
will not be constrained by poverty.

### § VI. CHALCEDONY

Chalcedony is a yellow stone,  
intermediate between jacinth and beryl.  
It is greatly loved and prized  
and well renowned among rich people.  
If it is worn hanging from the neck,  
it brings many things into one’s sight;  
[Col. 1744D]  
and whoever wears it on his finger  
will be able to overcome all things.  
It is sent from Ethiopia  
and is found in three colours.

### § VII. SMARAGDUS [i.e. Emerald]

The emerald, by its colour,  
surpasses all things in greenness,  
and there are six kinds of it.  
They are very precious and dear.

One is found far away in Scythia,  
and another comes from Bactria.  
Another is brought thence,  
the *linilo*, which comes from Paradise.  
[Col. 1745C]  
There is another well renowned,  
called chalcedony,  
greatly loved and prized,  
sent from Scythia.

The Arimaspians, that people,  
love them more than gold or silver;  
and they take them from griffins,  
great and long-winged birds.

The very clear kind is truly better,  
for one can see through it.  
The other is darker and more deeply coloured.  
It has this nature:  
it does not change its beauty  
through sun or brightness,  
nor through shade or light,  
which may obscure it in its own fashion.

The flat kind is good for a mirror.  
Nero greatly loved it.  
[Col. 1745D]  
He had a mirror of it  
in which he watched his entertainments by day.

This stone makes known through water  
things that are to happen in the year,  
if one asks it properly; it cannot fail.  
It grants great riches  
to whoever keeps it very chastely.  
It makes a person eloquent  
to those who wish to honour him.

It heals violently the fever  
which has brought many a person death;  
it is called *emitheus*.  
Many a person will recover  
when this sickness keeps him alive,  
[Col. 1746C]  
if the stone is hung about his neck.  
It is effective against falling sickness.  
Whoever always has it upon himself  
will guard his eyes unharmed;  
it removes tempest and lust.  
Whoever has it ought to be of good disposition.

And if he wishes to make it greener,  
he should wash it well and soak it,  
then anoint it with virgin oil.

### § VIII. SARDONYX OR SARD

Sard is composed of two stones,  
made from sard and onyx.  
Of these two it bears three colours:  
white, black, and red.  
The white is set upon the black,  
and the red laid upon the white.

It is said to be of five kinds.  
It is neither too large nor too small.  
That which has the three colours  
[Col. 1746D]  
well distinct and not mingled  
is plainly the most prized.  
It should have neither wax-like nor airy matter.  
A humble and chaste person ought to possess it.  
Of other virtues I know none truly,  
for elsewhere nothing is written of them.  
It is said to come from Arabia and India.

### § IX. ONYX

Onyx causes grievous dreams,  
contentions, and phantoms to be seen;  
it also makes children drool  
and become angry and troublesome.  
These stones come from Arabia and India  
and are said to be of five kinds.

[Col. 1747C]  
If it is bound with sard,  
onyx will never harm you.

### § X. SARD

This is called sard  
from an island where it was found.  
It is red and has great virtue,  
except that it stops bleeding.  
It kills worms, and whoever has it  
will suffer no harm from onyx.

### § XI. CHRYSOLITE

Chrysolite makes one lovable  
and has the appearance of clear glass.  
It has a grain of gold in its midst  
and shines like fire.  
Whoever wears it will have no fear.  
The stone possesses great power.

Whoever pierces it and then puts  
an ass’s hair through the hole  
and hangs it from his left arm,  
[Col. 1747D]  
the devil will not await him.  
This very precious and dear stone  
comes from Ethiopia.

### § XII. BERYL

Beryl is found in India  
and is formed with six angles.  
It is of great brightness  
and likewise of great beauty.  
It makes men and women agreeable,  
and whoever wears it beloved.

[Col. 1748C]  
If one holds it tightly in the hand,  
it binds the hand that holds it.  
It heals diseased eyes  
with the water in which it has been washed.  
If one bathes in this water  
who suffers heavy bleeding,  
it will remove his grievous distress;  
it also takes away every pain.  
Its power is such against fever.

Certainly there are nine kinds of it.  
They are very precious and dear.

### § XIII. TOPAZ

Topaz is found on an island  
which is also called Topaz.  
It is of two kinds;  
few are found, and they are very dear.  
One resembles a mirror;  
the other seems clearer to me.  
The one resembles the light of the day.

It has great power against boiling:  
[Col. 1748D]  
it makes boiling water cease to boil.  
Once it senses it, it will boil no more.  
If you see a scorpion in one place,  
make a circle around it with the stone:  
it will not be able to leave the circle;  
there it must die.  
This is proof of the stone.  
It comes honourably and dearly from Arabia.

### § XIV. JACINTH

Jacinths are of three kinds  
[Col. 1749B]  
and are very precious stones.  
One is garnet, another citrine,  
and the third is pale-blue; all are medicinal.  
All strengthen by their power  
and remove vain thoughts and sadness.

Those who are somewhat good lapidaries  
hold the garnet more dear.  
It has the fairest colour;  
therefore they deem it best,  
[Col. 1749C]  
and therefore esteem it greatly,  
because they do not find it abundantly.

The pale-blue does not lose its brightness,  
however greatly it may be darkened.  
They love most that pale-blue kind  
which is neither too bright nor too dark,  
but of a temperate colour,  
purple and of great coolness.  
Whoever wears it  
will not have great heat in his mouth.

Because of its hardness,  
it will not be carved  
unless it is worked with a fragment  
that has been split from adamant.  
The citrine inclines to paleness  
and is less valuable because of its colour.

Whatever jacinth one wears,  
hung about the neck or on one’s finger,  
one may travel in great safety.  
[Col. 1749D]  
Evil will fear him greatly.  
When he comes to a dwelling,  
he will be received loved and gladly;  
and whatever he asks reasonably,  
will not be foolishly refused him.  
This kind is brought from Ethiopia.  
It is very good and honoured.

### § XV. CHRYSOPRASE

[Col. 1750B]

Chrysoprase comes from Greater India.  
It has the colour of leek juice,  
with a drop of gold extinguished in purple.  
It has no other virtues here.

### § XVI. AMETHYST

Amethyst has a purple colour,  
like a drop of wine.  
Another kind is like a violet,  
[Col. 1750C]  
or like a clean, pure rose.  
One inclines somewhat toward whiteness;  
another has red mixed with wine-colour.  
This stone comes to us from India  
and is easy to carve.

Whoever has it upon himself will not become drunk,  
nor will wine make him dizzy.  
It would rightly be held very dear  
if it were not so plentiful;  
otherwise it would have to be very expensive.  
There are five kinds of it.

### § XVII. CHELIDONIUS

Chelidonius is good, though not beautiful.  
It grows in the belly of the swallow.  
It comes from precious powers.  
They say it is of two kinds,  
found in two colours:  
one tending to black, the other red.

The red removes the disease  
[Col. 1750D]  
that comes upon a person through lunacy,  
by which he falls and becomes mad.  
It heals the languishing and the insane.  
It makes its possessor eloquent  
and beloved by all people.  
It should be wrapped in linen cloth  
and worn on the left arm.

[Col. 1751B]  
In the same manner  
the black stone should be worn.  
It helps accomplish great things  
and protects a person from adversity,  
against the wrath of princes and kings.  
[Col. 1751C]  
It gives aid and protection.

Water in which this stone has been washed  
heals inflamed eyes.  
This stone should be set  
in linen dyed with saffron.  
It removes fever and evil humours.  
It relieves those who suffer great pains.

### § XVIII. GAGATES OR JET

Jet grows in a country  
called Lycia. It is scarcely a gem, this stone.  
It is shining, black, and light.  
It also grows in Great Britain,  
in a land far away.

When one rubs it somewhat,  
it grows hot through the rubbing.  
It draws chaff strongly to itself,  
and is extinguished in water or oil.

It heals a person of the dry disease,  
[Col. 1751D]  
of swelling between skin and flesh,  
and greatly cures intestinal swelling.  
Washed in wine, it heals the teeth.

If a woman steams herself over it,  
the stone restores her courses  
if it is cast into a fire.  
Whoever suffers from the falling sickness,  
when he smells its odour,  
falls in such a way that he feels no pain.

When it is burned, it is very marvellous:  
it drives away serpents and destroys devils.  
It turns the womb and cuts through poisons.  
It destroys all malignity  
of evil spells, sorceries, and poisons.

[Col. 1752B]  
It tests a woman’s virginity.  
Water in which it has been thrown for three days—  
if a pregnant woman drinks it—  
[Col. 1752C]  
will immediately deliver her without hindrance  
of her child, if she is in labour.

### § XIX. MAGNET

The Troglodytes find the magnet  
in India, and it is called precious.  
It resembles iron and draws it,  
just as the adamant does.

Circe loved it greatly,  
she who used it for enchantment,  
that marvellous sorceress.  
She made an experiment with it  
which is proved from afar,  
if one wishes to know the truth  
whether his wife loves another man.

He shall put the stone upon her head  
while she sleeps unaware.  
If she is chaste in her sleep,  
[Col. 1752D]  
she will seem to embrace him.  
But if she is not, the wicked woman  
will draw away to the other side of the bed  
and come shamefully,  
as if she had been foully driven away.

This stone gives such an odour:  
it harms the wicked and benefits the good.  
A thief who has it holds it very dear.  
He makes powder from this stone.  
In the house he intends to enter  
when he wishes to steal,  
he takes live coals from the fire  
and sets them at the four sides  
[Col. 1753B]  
of the house, toward the four directions.  
The smoke rises from them like incense.  
All who are in the house,  
when they smell the smoke around them,  
[Col. 1753C]  
flee away in great fear,  
and he takes what he wishes of theirs.

It gives love between man and woman  
and grants great force of speech.  
To all who wear it, it is good  
against dropsy caused by drinking.  
Its powder is good for burns  
and every scalding.

### § XX. CORAL

Coral grows in the sea like a tree.  
It grows green and is much loved.  
When air touches it, it becomes hard;  
by nature it becomes red.  
It is half a foot in length.

Whoever has it upon himself will have no fear  
of lightning or storm.  
The house where it is in great abundance  
will suffer no damage  
from hail or other tempests.

[Col. 1753D]  
It causes fruit to multiply,  
turns aside all phantoms,  
gives a good beginning  
and likewise a good end.

### § XXI. ALABANDINE

Alabandine is found in Asia,  
in the country of Alabanda,  
and resembles sard;  
they differ only slightly.

### § XXII. CORNELIAN

[Col. 1754B]

Cornelian is a dark stone  
and has great virtue by nature.  
It removes anger and rancour,  
[Col. 1754C]  
and causes a person to speak by reason.  
That is of the better kind  
which resembles washed flesh.  
It stops blood that flows too much  
and cures a woman of her secret ailment.

### § XXIII. SCARBUNCLE [i.e. Carbuncle]

The carbuncle sends forth rays from itself;  
there is no stone more fiery.  
With its brightness it shines at night,  
but by day it shows nothing.  
It grows in the land of the Troglodytes,  
and twelve kinds are described.

### § XXIV. LIGURIUS

Ligurius grows from the urine  
of a fierce beast,  
which sees through stones  
just as one sees through glass.  
It is called a lynx and is very beautiful.  
[Col. 1754D]  
The beast urinates the stone into gravel.  
It greatly wishes it to remain hidden  
and covers it lest it be found.

Theophrastus, who knew this well,  
said that it resembled amber  
and drew chaff to itself.  
Without fail, it removes pain of the belly  
and grants healing from jaundice and madness.

### § XXV. ECHITES

[Col. 1755C]

Echites is held among the dearest  
when numbered among other stones.  
When the eagle is greatly distressed,  
it carries it from a very distant land  
for its chicks, to defend them,  
and cherishes it in its nest.  
There is another stone within this one.

A pregnant woman who has it upon herself  
need not fear for her child;  
it greatly aids her in childbirth.  
Hung from the left arm, it is highly praised
