for one who wishes to remain alive.  
Whoever wears it will never become drunk.  
It frees a person from great distress,  
increases riches, makes one beloved,  
conquers enemies, and wins a people’s praise.

If someone is under suspicion  
of sorcery, venom, or some other poison,  
[Col. 1755D]  
he must be compelled to eat with it.  
Put the stone beneath his food:  
he cannot swallow the food;  
remove the stone, and he eats it at once.

It governs young women and boys  
and restrains sciatica and pains of the joints.  
This stone is red in colour.  
It comes from Ocean and is very dear.  
It is found far away in eagles’ nests,  
or in the region of Persia.

### § XXVI. SELENITE

[Col. 1756C]

Selenite has a beautiful colour,  
resembling jasper in greenness.  
It is sacred and grows with the moon;  
as the moon wanes, it likewise wanes.  
It gives love and keeps the body sound.  
It grows in Persia and comes from there.

### § XXVII. GAGATROMAEA

Gagatromaea is very good.  
It is a spotted stone  
like the skin of a kid.  
If one wears it in battle,  
he will be able to drive away his enemies;  
none will dare touch him.

Alcides knew its value well,  
for he wore it in many conflicts.  
In every battle in which he had it,  
he could never be defeated;  
and when he did not have it upon himself,  
[Col. 1756D]  
he was defeated in the very first encounter.

### § XXVIII. CERAUNIA

Ceraunia is a very beautiful stone.  
It falls with lightning and is very dear.  
Whoever wears it chastely  
will suffer no harm from lightning.  
Where it is, no house will perish  
from lightning or storm.

It conquers in battles and is good in litigation;  
[Col. 1757C]  
it gives good, fair dreams.  
It has two colours, though the wording is uncertain:  
one is coloured like crystal and tinged with blue.  
It is obtained in Germany.  
Another resembles parchment.  
It fears neither fire nor flame.  
This stone comes from Spain.

### § XXIX. HELIOTROPE

Heliotrope is a stone  
of very virtuous character.  
Set it opposite the sun  
in a vessel, if it makes the vessel red,  
the person holding it will think  
that a new eclipse is occurring.  
In a short time it will cause  
the water in the vessel to boil.

When it is soaked in abundant rainwater,  
it gives good repute and great health.  
It destroys poison and stops blood.  
[Col. 1757D]  
It conquers deceit and does no harm.

There is an herb, very precious,  
which bears the same name as the stone.  
If one can possess them both,  
no one will be able to see him if he wishes.  
It comes from Ethiopia and Cyprus  
and is found in Africa.

[Col. 1758C]  
It wholly resembles emeralds,  
except that it has drops of blood.

### § XXX. GERACHITE

Gerachite is black in colour,  
but possesses great power.  
If one has washed one’s mouth with it  
and placed it beneath the tongue,  
one will be able to divine  
what another thinks of him.

Whoever wishes to test its virtue  
should anoint a man with honey and milk,  
have him stand out in the hot sun  
where there are many flies,  
and hold the stone in his mouth:  
not even one fly will touch him.  
Remove the stone and leave him without it:  
then they will hurt him greatly.

### § XXXI. EPISTITE

[Col. 1758D]

Epistite is pleasing,  
beautiful and brightly shining.  
It is red, and its virtue is so precious  
that it makes a pot boil.  
It drives birds from their nests,  
and locusts, caterpillars, and grasshoppers.

It safely removes quarrels;  
[Col. 1759C]  
whoever wears it honourably prospers.  
Put it in the sun’s rays:  
it will make bright fire red.  
It should be worn on the left side,  
as the writing says it ought to be.

### § XXXII. HAEMATITE

There is another, haematite,  
whose virtue is not small.  
It naturally staunches blood  
and properly heals sick persons.  
When it is powdered with wine  
and mixed with egg-white,  
it removes roughness from the eyelids  
and gives brightness to the eyes.

Whoever spits blood, if he has the stone,  
should rub it upon a potsherd  
in juice tempered from wild apple  
and give it as a drink  
to the sick person;  
[Col. 1759D]  
it will keep him sound always.

It is of great benefit to a woman:  
it restrains the menses when they are excessive.  
It staunches a wound and, by healing it,  
brings recovery.  
It destroys poison when drunk;  
when a serpent has bitten, it makes the wound sound.  
With honey it greatly benefits the eyes  
of old people and children.  
It removes a stone from the bladder.

It comes honourably from Africa;  
[Col. 1760C]  
it is brought from Ethiopia  
and is also produced in Arabia.

### § XXXIII. ASBESTOS

Asbestos comes from the country  
of Arcadia, where it is found.  
This stone has the colour of iron  
and such great power  
that if one part of it is taken by fire,  
it will never thereafter be extinguished, however much it burns.

### § XXXIV. PAEANITE

Paeanite has such properties:  
if it is struck against another stone within,  
it is called female; whatever it may be worth,  
it aids a woman in childbirth.

### § XXXV. SADE

Sade is found with great difficulty;  
it is born in the land of the Chaldeans.  
It is found swimming in that sea,  
but it is difficult to catch.

[Col. 1760D]  
If it adheres, it will not fall  
until it has been cut;  
it has great love for wood  
and bears the colour of prase.

### § XXXVI. MEDE

Among the Turks grows a stone  
called *medus*, and it is very fierce.  
It gives death and life:  
to one it does harm, to another aid.

Whoever wishes to make medicine from it  
should soak it thoroughly with a whetstone  
in a woman’s milk—  
of a woman who has borne only a boy—  
and it restores sight  
to those who have long not seen.

[Col. 1761C]  
And similarly, crushed in the milk of a ewe  
which a male lamb has suckled,  
it will heal a person of the disease of the eyelids.

The Nephritian people make from it  
a very precious ointment  
to remove great pain from the kidneys,  
which afflicts them every day.

It should be kept in a silver vessel,  
or in another very beautiful and elegant receptacle [uncertain reading].  
Whoever wishes to shame his enemy  
should soak it thoroughly with the whetstone.  
If he washes that man’s forehead  
with the water in which it has been rubbed,  
within a day he will lose  
[Col. 1761D]  
his sight permanently.

If one gives him a drink of it in a potion,  
he will vomit all his lungs.  
The stone is black in colour  
and possesses great force and power.  
It is truly black to those whom it kills:  
it leads them to a black death.

### § XXXVII. GELACIA

Gelacia is a very beautiful stone  
and of such hard nature  
that it cannot be broken  
by heat or by any force.

### § XXXVIII. HEXACONTALITHOS

Hexacontalithos is coloured,  
[Col. 1762C]  
dyed with sixty colours.  
It has its colours in small portions;  
it grows in Libya among the Troglodytes.

### § XXXIX. CHELONITES

In India the *nocium* bears  
a stone called chelonites.  
Whoever has washed his mouth with it  
and then placed it upon his tongue,  
from morning until the moon’s increase,  
until midday appears,  
can divine without failing  
what will happen to him during the waxing moon.

During the waning, before daybreak,  
until prime, it has a sure virtue;  
when it is prime, its power lasts all day,  
and has the fifth essence in its nature.  
It fears neither fire nor flame.  
It grows in India and comes from there.  
It is very beautiful and fair of aspect,  
[Col. 1762D]  
all purple and variegated.

### § XL. PRASE

Prase is beautifully green,  
but its virtue is not especially prized:  
no virtue comes from it  
except that it is suitable for setting in gold.  
One sort has three white spots, certainly;  
another is not so green.  
It has no virtues or medicines,  
except that it prevails against bloody flux.

### § XLI. CRYSTAL

Some say that crystal  
is natural ice,  
hardened by cold through the years;  
[Col. 1763C]  
by cold it changes its nature,  
and it retains the pleasure  
that in the hand it is not without coldness.

It conceives red fire  
when one holds it in the sun’s ray.  
And certain people say that,  
if it is often touched,  
it is good for a nurse,  
because it gives the milk with which she feeds the child.

### § XLII. GALACTITE

A woman who has galactite  
will have much milk for her child.  
She ought first to give suck,  
and afterwards use it before eating.  
Whoever pierces it and puts through it  
a thread of wool from a pregnant ewe,  
and hangs it about the nurse’s neck,  
will give her a great abundance of milk.

A woman labouring with child  
[Col. 1763D]  
should bind it before her thigh;  
she will not fail to obtain relief,  
but will immediately have her delivery.

If it is dissolved in water  
and an almond-tree is watered with it,  
the sheep will have enough milk  
and will not become ruinous.

This stone has the colour of iron  
and is of very great worth.  
The ancients say truly  
that whoever can possess this stone  
finds in it as many virtues  
as though all the others were present.

### § XLIII. ORYTES

Orytes are of three kinds,  
[Col. 1764C]  
very precious stones.  
One is naturally black and round;  
it is very valuable against bites.  
If it is crushed in rose oil  
and carried against serpents,  
one will suffer no bite from them.

Another tends toward green.  
If a person wears it upon himself,  
no cruel beast can harm him,  
nor can he fear evil or adversity.

Another is white laid over black;  
it is much loved and prized.  
The third orytes is marvellous:  
one side is very rough,  
the other solid like another gem.  
If a woman wears this upon herself,  
she will never bear a child on any day  
[Col. 1763] [will not bear a child],  
and if she is already pregnant, she will lose it.

### § XLIV. HYENA

[Col. 1764D]

Hyena is born in the pupil  
of a beast; it is a very beautiful stone.  
They call the stone by the beast’s name,  
for the beast is called a hyena.  
If one has washed one’s mouth with wine  
and placed it upon the tongue,  
one can divine, provided that one keeps  
the stone upon the tongue.

### § XLV. LIPARAEA

Liparaea grows in Libya.  
Whoever has it upon himself in the heat,  
no beast will flee from him;  
he may take whatever he finds.

### § XLVI. ENHYDRUS

Enhydrus, of short duration,  
[Col. 1765C]  
like a flowing spring,  
has a nature difficult to grasp.  
As the year passes it becomes smaller  
by as much dew as it gives forth;  
no one perceives or restores it.  
Taken in water, it harms  
the contrary and the calcareous [uncertain reading].

### § XLVII. IRIS

In the Red Sea grows a stone  
called iris, not very dear.  
Whoever holds it in the sun’s ray,  
the rainbow appears upon the wall;  
its reflection becomes so bright  
that it seems to be crystal.

### § XLVIII. ANDRODRAGME

Androdragme is formed  
somewhat square in shape.  
It has the colour of silver and is very beautiful.  
[Col. 1765D]  
It is found in the gravel  
of the Red Sea. Whoever has it upon himself  
will never be angry there;  
it grants him a good heart,  
and whoever wears it suffers no harm.

### § XLIX. OPAL

Opal is of such a nature  
that because of its virtue it ought to be dear.  
It removes disease from the eyes,  
greatly aids thieves,  
and whoever wears it  
will see with clear sight.

[Col. 1766C]  
But those who are around him  
must yield this advantage to the thief:  
without difficulty they may be robbed,  
their house despoiled.

### § L. PEARLS

In India, in a fish,  
grows a stone called pearl.  
It is called *unio* because it is single,  
and the fish is called a mussel.

Wise men say that when the molluscs  
open their mouths against the eastern wind,  
they receive the dew of heaven  
and conceive pearls from it.

Pearls are white and bright;  
the most beautiful come from the young.  
Whichever has more dew in its body  
produces the larger stone.

If it thunders in that country  
[Col. 1766D]  
when they receive the dew,  
they flee from the light and the pearl perishes,  
though conceived beautiful and dear.  
It may be half an ounce in size;  
no one will ever see a larger.

It grows in India and in Britain  
[Col. 1765] *Brittany*,  
which is called the first.  
It is good against bodily gout  
and against a spot that grows on a person;  
it is by nature good against pain in the teeth.  
The clear is worth more than the dark;  
the older lapidaries  
judged the round to be better.

### § LI. PANTHER

[Col. 1767C]

The panther is black, red, and green,  
pale purple and rose-coloured,  
having all these colours together,  
which would seem never to have seen the day.

The panther is a cruel beast  
and has diverse colours;  
beasts flee it because it is so fierce.  
The stone takes its name from it.

### § LII. ABSICTE

Absicte is black and heavy,  
with veins red as blood.  
When it is heated next to a fire,  
the following phrase is uncertain: “on a dry day it is found coloured.”

### § LIII. CHALCOPHANE

Chalcophane is a black stone.  
When one strikes it, it sounds and rings.  
[Col. 1767D]  
Whoever wears it honourably  
will be able to sing very loudly  
and will have a sweet and good voice,  
such that he will never grow hoarse.

### § LIV. MELOCHITE

Melochite has a deep green colour,  
the colour of an emerald.  
By its nature it protects children  
from great misfortune  
and guards them, keeping them in strength,
[Col. 1768C] This stone comes from Arabia.

§ LV. THE GEGOLITE.

Gegolite is dun-coloured,  
and has a cloudy appearance.  
If anyone heats the stone,  
he removes the gravel with it.

It is very quick to heal a man;  
in appearance it resembles the lowly olive.

§ LVI. THE PYRITE.

Pyrite is tawny in colour;  
whoever grips it feels heat.  
If he wishes to touch it gently,  
it will burn his nose.

§ LVII. THE DIACODE.

He who possesses a diacode  
will be able to divine by water;  
it separates the pure from the impure above.

[Col. 1768D] No stone is worth more.  
If it contends with a dead man,  
it loses its power but not its sheen.  
The stone is holy and hates death  
when it touches it closely and knows it well.

§ LVIII. THE DIONYSIA.

Dionysias are wholly black,  
and have drops of blackness.  
Whoever stirs it with water  
will smell wine;

[Col. 1769B] and will neither fall nor stumble,  
for it protects a man from drunkenness.

§ LIX. THE CHRYSOLECTER.

This stone is called chrysolecter;  
it is gold in colour and resembles amber.  
At the third watch it changes colour,  
and afterward its beauty flees the day.  
Nothing catches fire more quickly:  
if fire touches it, it immediately ignites.

§ LX. THE CHRYSOPRASE.

[Col. 1769C] This stone comes from Ethiopia;  
it is called chrysoprase, and is very dear.  
At night, as though it knew, it grows bright;  
by day it conceals itself in golden yellow.  
Therefore its nature changes:  
for day is bright and night dark.

§ LXI. OF THE RING AND THE GEM.

Some there are who do not believe  
that stones possess such powers.  
They are such as will never fail  
if those who have them do not sin;

[Col. 1770B] and whoever goes astray from himself  
cannot fail to value them less.  
There will be great deception  
in buying wares that are sold.

The fool thinks a thing good  
because of the beast which he believes it to be.  
There he is deceived by its beauty,  
for such things have no value.

He knew very well what they were worth  
and what powers they had,  
who first made a book of them  
and gave an account of them.

[Col. 1770C] In many places and in many lands  
their powers have been well tested.

It is well established and known,  
and plainly perceived by many,  
that God made the stones  
and placed great powers within them.  
And whoever does not know their powers  
will learn them from these books.

A hundred men carry them, and have them,  
who do not know what they do.  
They are asses in merely bearing them;  
they do not know how they work or how to keep them.

[Col. 1737A]

King Evax of the Arabs is said [Note: [Col. 1737] G manuscript: “is reported.”] to have written to Nero,  
who reigned second in Rome after Augustus,  
how many kinds of stones there are, what their names and colours are,  
what country belongs to each, and how great the power of each.

[Col. 1738A] Taking up this work [Note: [Col. 1737] R: “This.”], I judged it fitting to compose  
a little book, suitable for its wearer, in a briefer form,  
which might be accessible chiefly to me and to a few friends.  
For he diminishes majesty who divulges mysteries,  
and secrets do not remain secret when a crowd becomes privy to them.

[Col. 1739A] [We decree that this be given to three friends, however great its value.] [Note: [Col. 1739] V: “When.”]

For this number is sacred [Note: [Col. 1739] “He who makes the gift is sacred, and makes us so.”], and we disclose sacred things to them.

[Note: [Col. 1739] This verse is absent in Victorinus and occurs in Redonensis, Gorlaeus, and Turonensis.] Who fittingly honour God’s secrets by keeping them,  
whom gravity of character and uprightness of life commend.

For to know the hidden powers of stones—  
whose concealed cause produces manifest effects—  
we wish it to appear something excellent and rare.  
Clearly, thereby the diligent care of physicians is aided,  
skilled through the aid of stones in driving out diseases.

Authors for whom these matters are said to have been examined also declare  
that no less the benefits of specific [Note: [Col. 1739] G manuscript and V: “all.”] things are granted from them.  
Nor should it seem doubtful or false to anyone  
that gems possess a power divinely implanted in them.  
Great power has been granted to herbs, and the greatest to gems.

1639–40. § I. OF THE DIAMOND.

In the Gorlaeus manuscript the work is not divided into sections, but all the verses follow one another immediately.

[Col. 1739B]

Farthest India produces the chief kind of diamond,  
born and derived from crystal ores.

Its crystalline origin makes it shine so brightly [Note: [Col. 1739] G: “image.”]  
that it never ceases to be of an iron-grey colour.

[Col. 1740A] Its hardness, wholly solid, does not know how to yield,  
despising iron and being conquerable by no fire.  
Yet it gives way when heated in goat’s blood [Note: [Col. 1739D] + The monk Theophilus, *Treatise on the Various Arts*, book III, chapter 34, “On Polishing Gems,” sets out more fully the method of grinding gems which was once commonly believed: “If you wish to carve crystal, take a goat two or three years old, bind its feet, make an opening between its breast and belly at the place of its heart, and place the crystal there so that it lies in its blood until it becomes warm. Then take it out at once and cut it in whatever manner you wish, as long as that heat lasts. When it begins to cool and harden, put it again in the goat’s blood; when warmed, take it out once more and cut it. Continue thus until you complete the carving.” Theophilus is said to have lived in the twelfth century.].

By the damage done to an anvil and the labour of those striking it,  
gems are carved with sharp fragments of this stone.

But it is not found larger than a hazelnut.  
Arabia produces a diamond of another kind,  
not so invincible, for it is broken without blood.  
Its brilliance is not equal, and it is considered less valuable,  
although it may be greater in weight and enormous in size.

Cyprus, an island of the sea, yields a third diamond.  
A vein of iron-producing land at Philippi produces a fourth.  
Yet all have an equal power to draw iron;  
the magnet too can do this when the diamond is absent,  
for, when the diamond is present, it takes from the magnet what the latter draws.

[Col. 1740B] This same stone is considered suitable for magical arts,  
and by wondrous power makes its bearer unconquerable.  
It drives away the phantoms of night and vain dreams.  
It banishes black poisons and changes [Note: [Col. 1739] G: “calms.”] quarrels and disputes.  
It cures madmen and repels fierce enemies.

Let this stone be carried enclosed in silver or gold,  
and let a shining bracelet thence encircle the left arm.

§ II. OF AGATE.

[Col. 1741A]

As they report, agate was first found  
on the banks of a river called by the same name.  
This river [Note: [Col. 1741] V: “is.”], rich in treasure, flows along the Sicilian shores.  
Though the stone itself is black [Note: [Col. 1741] Turonensis: “with veins.”], it is marked with white bands.

This stone [Note: [Col. 1741] R: “these.”] is said [Note: [Col. 1741] G: “reported.”] to possess innate figures;  
a face traced among its native veins  
now presents forms of kings, now images of gods.

King Pyrrhus [Note: [Col. 1741] V: “King Purus.”] is reported to have worn on his finger an agate

1641–42 whose flat surface [Note: [Col. 1741] G: “full.”] bore the nine Muses;  
Apollo stood in their midst, touching the lyre—  
a work of nature, not art, marvellous to tell.

Crete also produces one resembling coral [Note: [Col. 1741] R: *corallio*; G: *coralio*.],  
whose flat surface is struck through with golden [*chryseis*; Note: [Col. 1741] G: *chrycis*.] veins.

[Col. 1741B] This, indeed [Note: [Col. 1741] G: “nopa.”], drives away poison and what the viper pours forth.

India produces an agate that gives back diverse appearances [Note: [Col. 1741] V: “species.”]:  
now the foliage of groves, now the forms of wild beasts.  
This is thought to allay thirst and strengthen sight.  
There is also one which, when kindled, breathes the scent of myrrh.  
Another is said to have blood-red spots.  
Another has a waxen appearance, and, because it is common, is held cheap.

Agate protects its bearer [Note: [Col. 1741] T: “a gift for the bearer.”], supplies strength,  
and makes him eloquent, agreeable, and of good complexion;

[Col. 1742A] [Note: [Col. 1741] This verse is absent in Gorlaeus.] persuasive also, and pleasing to the world and to God.  
With this aid Anchises’ son overcame dangers.

§ III. OF THE ALLECTORY.

In the stomach of a cock deprived of its testicles [Note: [Col. 1741] G: “stripped”; manuscript: “despoiled.”],  
after it has become a capon and lived at least three years,  
there is born that stone, whose praise is not the least;  
during the following four years it increases,  
yet as it grows it does not exceed the size of a bean.

It is like crystal or water when it appears clear.  
The ancients gave it the name allectory [Note: [Col. 1741] G: *allectorium*.].

This stone makes whoever wears it unconquerable,  
and, when received in the mouth, quenches the thirst of the sufferer [Note: [Col. 1741] Turonensis: “the thirsty person.”].  
For under its protection Milo defeated the Crotonian boxers.  
By it many kings also overcame battles.

[Col. 1742B] It is prompt to restore those who have been expelled [Note: [Col. 1741] G: “cast out.”],  
and acquires [Note: [Col. 1741] G: “restores.”] new honours and renews old ones.  
It makes an orator eloquent in speech,  
making him steadfast and altogether agreeable to all.  
It stimulates the powers of Venus.  
It is useful to a wife who wishes to be pleasing to her husband.

That it may grant so many benefits, it is carried enclosed in the mouth [Note: [Col. 1741] At this point Gorlaeus places ten verses on geranite, which will be seen below substituted for those on gerachite.].

§ IV. OF JASPER.

They say there are seventeen kinds of jasper.  
It is known to have many colours,

[Col. 1743A] and is reported to be born in many regions of the world.  
The best is translucent and green,  
1643–44 and is proved to possess the greatest power.

When worn chastely, it drives away fevers and dropsy [Note: [Col. 1743] G: “it flees fever and wards off dropsy”; manuscript: “it wards off dropsy.”].  
Applied to a woman in labour, it helps her,  
and is believed to be a protection for its bearer [Note: [Col. 1743] R: “of the bearer.”].  
For when consecrated, it makes one acceptable and powerful,  
and, as they report, drives away harmful phantoms.  
Its power is thought [Note: [Col. 1743] T and G: “proved.”] to be stronger when set in silver.

§ V. OF SAPPHIRE.

The species of sapphire [Note: [Col. 1743] G: “sapphire, or syrtite.”], especially suited to royal fingers,  
shines excellently and is most like the pure sky;  
in powers and beauty [Note: [Col. 1743] T: “colour.”] it is inferior [Note: [Col. 1743] G: “lower.”] to none.

This stone is also called *syrlites* [Note: [Col. 1743] R: “consircites.”] by many,  
because, mingled with Libyan sands near the Syrtes,

[Col. 1743B] it is found when the waves have been driven away and the sea is raging.

But the best is that produced by medicinal earth,  
which is said never to transmit sight.  
Powerful nature has endowed it with such honour  
that it is deservedly called sacred and the gem of gems.  
For it quickens the body, preserves [Note: [Col. 1743] G: “preserves it vigorous”; V: “quickening”; R: “preserves it vigorous.”] the limbs, and keeps them sound.  
No bearer of it can be harmed by any deceit [Note: [Col. 1743] R: “that.”].  
He overcomes envy and is moved by no fear.

[Col. 1744A] This stone, they say, draws prisoners from prison;  
it opens barred [Note: [Col. 1743] G and V: “hidden.”] doors and loosens chains when they are touched.  
It renders God [Note: [Col. 1743] R: “the Lord.”] appeased [Note: [Col. 1743] T: “peaceful.”] and favourable to prayers.  
It is said also to be good for restoring peace.  
Hydromancy [Note: [Col. 1743] T: “necromancy.”] loves this gem more than all the rest,  
so that through it it may obtain divine answers [Note: [Col. 1743] G manuscript and V: “be moved.”].

It cools inward heat,  
checks sweat flowing in an excessive torrent [Note: [Col. 1743] V: “terror”; Turonensis: “terror.”],  
when crushed and smeared upon milk [Note: [Col. 1743] G manuscript: “the side.”], it heals ulcers [Note: [Col. 1743] T: “smeared around.”],  
and removes defilement from the eyes and pain from the brow [Note: [Col. 1743] T: “and pains from the brow.”].  
In like manner it heals defects of the tongue.

But whoever wears it is commanded to be most chaste.

1645–46. § VI. OF CHALCEDONY. [Note: [Col. 1743] V: “chalcedon.”]

[Col. 1744B] Chalcedony is a stone shining with a dull pallor,  
intermediate between hyacinth and beryl.  
If it is pierced and worn on finger and neck [Note: [Col. 1743] V: “carried.”],  
its bearer is said to win his case.  
This kind of stone is found only in three colours.

§ VII. OF EMERALD.

The emerald surpasses every green thing in its verdant form.  
They report twelve kinds of it.  
For there are Scythian, Bactrian [Note: [Col. 1743] G: “Bractanian”; marginal addition: “Bactrian.”], and Nile varieties.

[Col. 1745A] Some are said to arise in veins of copper,  
which the flawed nature of the metal marks with spots.  
There are Chalcedonian [Note: [Col. 1745] G: “Carthaginian.”] kinds; it is tiresome to enumerate the remaining ones [*residos*, i.e. “the rest”].  
The Scythian kind has the chief honour and greater renown [Note: [Col. 1745] G: “glory.”].  
The Arimaspians take these from the griffins [Note: [Col. 1745] G and T: “Gryphilus.”] that guard them [Note: [Col. 1745] T: “Erimaspians.”].

Those through which sight can penetrate are held in higher repute;  
by their green light the neighbouring air is tinged [Note: [Col. 1745] G manuscript: “touched.”].  
Neither sun nor bright lamp nor shadows alter them.

Those with a level surface or a concave form  
reflect the face of a beholder like still water [Note: [Col. 1745] G: “shades.”].  
Report testifies that Nero used such mirrors  
when he wished to watch gladiators’ combats.

The best of these are those whose bodies are flat.  
This stone is said to be useful to those investigating hidden things  
when they wish to foreknow and divine the future [Note: [Col. 1745] R: “through water.”].

[Col. 1745B] This stone increases the wealth of one who treats it reverently,  
giving persuasive speech in every cause [Note: [Col. 1745] V: “gives.”].

[Note: [Col. 1745] G alone has this verse.] As though the force of eloquent speech resided in it.

Suspended from the neck, it drives away severe *erutriceum* [Note: [Col. 1745] G: “hemitritaeum”; T: “ermitleum.”],  
and can likewise heal epileptics.  
It refreshes weary eyes with green soothing treatment [Note: [Col. 1745] G and T: “medicament.”],  
and is thought able to turn aside storms.  
It is also said to restrain lustful impulses.  
Washed with wine and anointed with green olive oil,  
it develops into a greener and more perfect colour [Note: [Col. 1745] G and R: “beauty.”].

1647–48. § VIII. OF SARDONYX.

[Col. 1746A]

Two names, sard and onyx, make “sardonyx” [Note: [Col. 1745] G: “sard and onyx.”].  
This single stone contains three colours in pairs.  
White rises from black, red from white [Note: [Col. 1745] G manuscript: “thence.”].  
Masters divide it into five types.

But those that retain the three pure and unmixed colours  
so that they are separated by a distinct boundary [Note: [Col. 1745] T: “when.”]  
have greater honour, and their appearance [Note: [Col. 1745] V: “renown.”] is approved.  
The denser and clearer it is [Note: [Col. 1745] R and T: “rarer.”], the more beauty [Note: [Col. 1745] T: “colour.”] it is said to possess.  
Of stones, it alone cannot tear wax away.

It befits the humble and chaste person, modest in countenance [Note: [Col. 1745] G: “and the countenance.”].  
I have not been able to discover its other powers.  
Arabs and India send it to our regions.

§ IX. OF ONYX.

But onyx, suspended from the neck [Note: [Col. 1745] G: “from the neck.”] or bound upon the finger,

[Col. 1746B] presents phantoms and every sad thing in sleep [Note: [Col. 1745] G: “all these.”].  
It multiplies lawsuits and stirs up quarrels everywhere.  
It is also said to increase children’s excessive salivation.  
The Arabs give us this gem, and India also gives it.  
It too is said to have five kinds.

[Note: [Col. 1745] This verse is absent in R and T.] But if *Sanlius* is present with you, onyx does not harm you.

[Note: [Col. 1745] The following four verses are added in Gorlaeus and are not transmitted in Victorinus.] It derives its name from the nail in Greek usage.  
For those things which we call nails in our own language,  
he is accustomed to call them *ὄνυξ* (*onyx*) in his native tongue.

[Col. 1747A] But if sard is present with you, onyx does not harm you.

§ X. OF SARD.

Sard takes its name from Sardis, where it was first found [Note: [Col. 1747] T: “received.”].  
It is usually red [Note: [Col. 1747] G: “ruddy.”] in colour.  
It is proved [Note: [Col. 1747] G: “thought.”] to be most useful among gems,  
although, apart from its brilliance, it has no beneficial power,  
except that onyx cannot harm when it is present.  
The diligence of antiquity likewise assigns it five kinds.

[Note: [Col. 1747] R through G.] § XI. OF CHRYSOLITE.

Chrysolite [Note: [Col. 1747] *Grisolitus*.] shines like gold and sparkles like fire.  
It resembles the sea and suggests a certain greenness.  
Set in gold, it is said to be a phylactery [Note: [Col. 1747] Φυλακτήριον, “a protective amulet.”],  
a strong protection against terrors of the night [Note: [Col. 1747] G: “strongly wards off nocturnal [terrors].”].

If pierced and strung on the bristles of an ass [Note: [Col. 1747] T: “struck.”],  
it frightens demons and is thought to drive them away.  
It is fitting to wear it, when strung, on the left arm [Note: [Col. 1747] G: “wear.”].

[Col. 1747B] 1649–50. We read that the Ethiopians send us this gem.

§ XII. OF BERYL.

A six-sided shape makes beryls conspicuous.  
Unless it becomes dull [Note: [Col. 1747] G, R, T: “because it.”], they seem to possess pallor.  
Knowledgeable antiquity holds that they are outstanding, like oil [Note: [Col. 1747] G: “the finest violet.”] or sea-water.

This stone comes to our regions from India.  
It is said to bear the love of marriage,  
and is reported to magnify its bearer.  
It is said also to burn the right hand of one gripping [Note: [Col. 1747] T: “wearing.”] it.

Water in which it lies heals weak eyes;  
when drunk, it removes both belching and sighing [Note: [Col. 1747] G: “when drunk, [it removes] belching …”].  
It is said to cure all pains of the liver.

[Col. 1748A] Masters have wished [Note: [Col. 1747] G manuscript: “said.”] it to have nine kinds.

§ XIII. OF TOPAZ.

An island named Topazion produces it;  
the rarer it is [Note: [Col. 1747] G: “the rarer it is.”], the more precious it is.  
It is said to have only two kinds.  
One is nearer in colour to pure gold;  
the other is found brighter and more delicate.

The same stone is said to help haemorrhoids [Note: [Col. 1747] T: + “haemorrhoid.”].  
What is more marvellous, it is thought to perceive the moon.  
It is also said to calm boiling waters.  
The land of the Arabs, richest in gems, also produces it.

§ XIV. OF HYACINTH. [Note: [Col. 1747] R and V: “jacinth.”]

Learned men say that there are three types of hyacinth [Note: [Col. 1747] G: “hyacinths.”]:  
for there are garnet-coloured, citron-coloured, and Venetian kinds.  
All are thought to have strengthening power  
and to banish sorrow and groundless suspicions.

[Col. 1748B] Every expert in gems prefers the garnet-coloured kind.  
They are reddish [Note: [Col. 1747] G manuscript: “rough.”] in colour and are more rarely found.  
The Venetian kind is blue, immediately reflecting the air:  
cloudy in overcast weather, bright red and clear in fair weather.

The best shade is that which neither a denser, darker [Note: [Col. 1747] G manuscript: “lower.”] substance obscures  
nor a sparse one renders transparent.  
Rather, a purple flower blends the two.

It is also thought to be more cooling when put into the mouth.  
Its solid hardness resists cutting and carving;  
yet it can be overcome by fragments of diamond [Note: [Col. 1747] G and R: “by fragments only.”].

1651–52. A pale appearance proves citron-coloured stones inferior.  
But whatever kind you can suspend from the neck  
or wear upon the finger, you will travel lands in safety,

[Col. 1749A] nor will the climate of a pestilential region harm you.  
Indeed, you will be judged more worthy of honour by hosts;  
and if you seek any just thing, you will suffer no rejection.

The Ethiopians send us this gem also,

[Note: [Col. 1749] G alone has this verse.] together with many others for the use of ordinary life.

§ XV. OF CHRYSOPRASE. [Note: [Col. 1749] Thus R.]

India, the home of stones, sends chrysoprase [Note: [Col. 1749] G: “and chrysoprason.”].  
It resembles the juice of a leek and is mingled in colour [Note: [Col. 1749] G manuscript: “and a mingled colour.”];  
with little golden drops it gleams like purple dyed [Note: [Col. 1749] G: “shines”; manuscript: “glitters.”].

I have not yet been able to learn what powers it possesses;  
yet I think it has them, and it is not permitted to know everything.

§ XVI. OF AMETHYST.

Amethyst is purple and violet in colour,  
or appears like a drop of neat wine or a pure rose [Note: [Col. 1749] G: “which”; T: “because.”].

[Col. 1749B] Some are duller, as though fading toward white,  
so that they seem to have the blush of wine diluted with water.

[Note: [Col. 1749] In Victorinus the following two verses and their French interpretation are inserted here, in a much later though somewhat old hand:

“This stone keeps one wakeful  
and removes evil thoughts;  
it gives good understanding to the stone-worker.”

“This stone makes one keep watch well,  
and casts evil thoughts out,  
and gives good understanding.  
It certainly possesses these powers.”]

India, greatest nurse of gems, sends it.  
Easy to carve and opposed to drunkenness,  
it would deservedly be prized if it were rarer [Note: [Col. 1749] V: “if it were found rare.”];

[Col. 1750A] but now it is neglected because [Note: [Col. 1749] G: “when.”] it is common.  
The ingenuity of the ancients also gives it five kinds.

1653–54. § XVII. OF CHELIDONIAN. [Note: [Col. 1749] V: “celidonian.”]

But [Note: [Col. 1749] G: “and.”] chelidonian is a stone produced by the swallow,  
carrying in its belly a treasure for which it itself might rightly be killed.  
This stone should not be counted among brilliant ones.  
It is small and shapeless, but inferior to none in power;  
in usefulness it surpasses certain illustrious stones.

It has two kinds and two colours,  
for a black and a red stone are taken from a cut-open belly.  
The red, when worn, relieves lunacy.  
It also cures madmen and prolonged illnesses.  
It makes people eloquent, agreeable, and pleasing to many [Note: [Col. 1749] T: “greatly.”].

It should be wrapped in a cloth made of linen  
and thus carried enclosed in the left claw [*chela*; Note: [Col. 1749] G manuscript: “under.”].

[Col. 1750B] But the black stone, worn in cloth under the same arrangement,  
brings undertakings to a worthy end,  
resists threats, and softens the anger of kings.  
Dissolved in water, it heals failing eyes  
when enclosed in a saffron-coloured linen cloth.

[Col. 1751A] The stone itself, when placed thus, is said to extinguish fevers  
and to check [Note: [Col. 1751] G: “expel.”] every harmful humour.

§ XVIII. OF JET.

Jet, a stone near to a gem, is born in Lycia;  
but distant Britain produces [Note: [Col. 1751] G: “fruitful”; G: “sends”; T: “begets.”] an excellent variety.  
It is bright and black, smooth, and exceedingly light.  
When warmed by rubbing, it draws neighbouring straws.  
Washed in water it burns; anointed with olive oil it is extinguished.

When worn, it benefits dropsical swelling under the skin;  
dissolved in water, it strengthens loose teeth.  
By fumigation [Note: [Col. 1751] G: “whose smoke”; manuscript: “fumigation.”] it restores menstruation to a woman.  
When ignited, it reveals epileptics by the stench of its smoke [Note: [Col. 1751] G manuscript: “benefits.”],  
and by the same means drives away cruel water-snakes.  
It is likewise thought hostile to demons.  
It aids displaced wombs and distended entrails.

[Col. 1751B] It defeats deceptions [Note: [Col. 1751] R: “deceptions.”] and undoes deadly spells,  
and, as they report, is accustomed to reveal virginity.  
A pregnant woman may drink water in which it has been immersed for three days,  
and she who was suffering will quickly give birth free from labour.

[Note: [Col. 1751] Here ends, and proceeds no further, the Turonensis manuscript sent to me. [Col. 1751] The Turonensis codex, mentioned above, contains sixty-one chapters; hence I suspect that Dom Beaugendre did not see the genuine work, but only a reworking of it, and that an unfaithful and incomplete one; or rather, as is clear, the Majoretanus codex was not of the same character as the codex of the metropolitan church of Tours.]

1655–56. § XIX. OF THE MAGNET.

The magnet was discovered among the Troglodytes [Note: [Col. 1751] R: “Tragodites.”],  
though India, mother of stones, sends it as well.

[Col. 1752A] It is known to be iron-grey in colour  
and by nature has the power to lift nearby iron.

The magician Deendor [Note: [Col. 1751] R: “Deendon”; G: “Dorendus”; manuscript: “Decedon or Edendon.”] is said first to have used it,  
knowing that nothing was more powerful in magical art.  
After him the famous sorceress Circe  
is said to have used it especially in magical tricks.

Thereupon [Note: [Col. 1751] V: “here.”], when its use had reached the Medes,  
the experience of magicians revealed the stone’s powers.  
For anyone wishing to know whether his wife is adulterous  
should place the stone beneath the head of the snoring woman.  
Straightway the chaste wife, waking, seeks to embrace her husband;  
the adulteress, however [Note: [Col. 1751] G: “yet.”], falls from the bed  
as though struck by a hand, compelled by a sudden stench  
which the stone emits as the indicator of a hidden crime.

[Col. 1752B] If a thief enters a house filled with goods and treasure,  
places burning coals about the place,  
and scatters fragments of magnet over the coals,

[Note: [Col. 1751] This verse is absent in Redonensis.] then all who remain in that house are driven out,  
as the vapour of smoke rises high in a square [Note: [Col. 1751] G: “tetragonal.”].  
Maddened in mind, as though ruin were impending,  
all who dwelt there flee in every direction,

[Col. 1753A] and the thief safely carries away whatever he wishes.

The stone can reconcile husbands to their wives  
and conversely [Note: [Col. 1753] G: “converted.”] restore married women to their husbands.  
It bestows favour, and its *dela* [reading uncertain] through it:  
grace of speech and ability in disputation.  
Given with mulled wine, it dissolves dropsy that needs purging;  
sprinkled over burns, it heals them.

§ XX. OF CORAL. [Note: [Col. 1753] R: “coralium.”]

Coral [Note: [Col. 1753] G: “coralius.”], while alive in the sea, is a twig.  
Torn from the nets or cut with the point of iron,  
on contact with air [Note: [Col. 1753] G and R: “having touched”; G manuscript: “having been touched.”] it grows hard and turns to stone.  
What had been green becomes purple-red.  
It appears like a little branch of a shrub,  
and is scarcely found longer than half a foot.

From it are made ornaments useful to many,

[Col. 1753B] for it is proved salutary to those who wear [Note: [Col. 1753] R: “carry.”] it.  
According to Zoroaster, it possesses marvellous power;  
and, as Metrodorus, an excellent [Note: [Col. 1753] G manuscript: “greatest.”] author, writes,

1657–58 it repels lightning, typhoons, and storms  
from ship, roof, or field, wherever it is carried [Note: [Col. 1753] G: “worn.”].

But when scattered in vineyards and among olive trees,  
or cast by farmers into fields with seed [Note: [Col. 1753] G: “fields.”],  
it wards off the hostile missiles of hail,  
multiplying fruit so that the crops overflow with fertility.  
It drives away demonic shadows and Thessalian monsters.  
It gives easy entrances and favourable outcomes.

§ XXI. OF ALABANDINE.

[Col. 1754A]

There is [Note: [Col. 1753] G: “but.”] a region of Asia called Alabanda  
which produces alabandine. Its brightness, rival to that of sard,  
deceives the uncertain judgement of one judging it by name.

§ XXII. OF CARNELIAN. [Note: [Col. 1753] R: “Of carnelians.”]

Nor would it be tedious to mention carnelian stones [Note: [Col. 1753] G: “carnelian.”],  
which, although they seem to have a dark colour [Note: [Col. 1753] G: “redness”; manuscript: “colour.”],  
are nevertheless believed to have an inherent power not to be despised.

For when this stone adheres to the finger or neck of its wearer,  
it calms rising anger in litigation.  
And one which appears fit for washing flesh [Note: [Col. 1753] G: “good.”]  
stops the flow of blood from any limb,  
especially when a woman suffers such a discharge.

§ XXIII. OF CARBUNCLE.

Carbuncle surpasses all burning gems,

[Col. 1754B] for, like a fiery coal, it casts rays in every direction,  
from which it seems to have derived the cause of its name.  
But in Greek the same stone is called *anthrax* [Note: [Col. 1753] G manuscript: “carbuncle, or anthracite.”].

Darkness cannot extinguish its light,  
but, flashing flames [Note: [Col. 1753] V: “blazing shadows.”], it gleams in the eyes of beholders.

It is born in the region of the Libyan Troglodytes [Note: [Col. 1753] faulty reading: “rogloditarum.”],  
and it is said to have nine kinds, three times three.

§ XXIV. OF LIGURIUM. [Note: [Col. 1753] V: “Of ligirium and ligirium.”]

What drips from the loins of a lynx turns into stone.  
They call it ligurium [Note: [Col. 1753] G: “lynnorium.”], and it is a precious little stone [Note: [Col. 1753] G: “yet this stone is precious.”],  
for they believe the lynxes themselves perceive this.

[Col. 1755A] They immediately strive [Note: [Col. 1755] G: “hurry.”] to cover the discharged liquid,  
heaping the weight of accumulated sand upon it,  
doubtless out of envy, lest it come to our use.

Theophrastus says that it resembles amber in colour  
and draws straws in the same way.  
He considers it able to relieve pain of the stomach,  
restore the former colour [Note: [Col. 1755] R: “vigour”; G: “warmth.”] to jaundiced persons,  
and check the fluxes of a disordered belly.

§ XXV. OF THE EAGLE-STONE.

Among the chief stones is counted the eagle-stone [*ethites*; Note: [Col. 1755] G: “actites”; Turonensis: “echites.”],  
which Jupiter’s bird seeks from the farthest ends of the world,

1659–60 to serve as guardian and defender of its nest,  
so that it may avert uncertain dangers from its young.  
This stone contains another little stone, as though pregnant.  
It is therefore believed powerful to assist pregnant women,

[Col. 1755B] lest they miscarry or suffer in childbirth,  
when suspended, as usual, from the left arm.  
Moreover, it gives sobriety to its wearer.  
It increases riches, compels people to love its possessor,  
makes him victorious, and adorns him with popular favour.  
It enables boys and girls alike to live unharmed,  
and is said to check [Note: [Col. 1755] G: “report,” or “calm.”] epileptic seizures.

If you suspect someone of poisoning  
and wish to test whether his intention is evil,  
admit the person whom you fear to share your table.  
When food has been set out, if an eagle-stone [Note: [Col. 1755] G: “actites.”] has been placed beneath it,  
then, if deceit is in his heart, he will be unable to swallow as he tries;  
remove [Note: [Col. 1755] G: “if you remove.”] the stone, and he will greedily devour what he had tasted.

This stone is said to be purple-red in colour  
and to be found hidden on ocean shores,

[Col. 1756A] or in eagles’ nests, or in the land of the Persians.  
The twin brothers Pollux and Castor are said to have borne it.

§ XXVI. OF SELENITE.

Nor is it right to pass over selenite [Note: [Col. 1755] G: “nor”; R: “selenites.”] in silence.  
Like a green herb, and a gem rivaling jasper,  
it observes the movements of the moon and the monthly periods.  
For it grows as the moon grows, and becomes smaller as the moon wanes,  
as though troubled by celestial losses.

For this reason many call it a sacred stone.  
It is said to be powerful for bringing about love.  
It is also thought to help the weak and consumptive [Note: [Col. 1755] G: “phthisical.”].  
When worn throughout the whole period of the waxing moon,  
and no less throughout [Note: [Col. 1755] V: “of the whole.”] all its waning,  
it grants marvellous effects and many benefits.  
They report that this gem is born in Persia.

§ XXVII. OF GAGATROMAEUS.

[Col. 1756B]

But the variegated stone called gagatromaeus  
is said to resemble the hide of a roebuck.  
Whoever wears it as a leader going to battle against an enemy  
will drive that enemy away by land [Note: [Col. 1755] G: “by land and.”] and sea.

By this stone’s help Alcides overcame many dangers;  
whenever he was defeated, he had not carried this stone.

1661–62. § XXVIII. OF CERAUNIAN.

When the air seethes in turmoil with the rage of winds,  
when it thunders terribly, when the fiery sky flashes,  
this little stone falls from heaven when clouds collide [Note: [Col. 1755] [lacuna], “struck forth”; R: “mocked.”].  
Among the Greeks it has a name from lightning.

It is thought to be found only in places  
known to have been struck by lightning;  
therefore it is called *ceraunius* in Greek speech:

[Col. 1757A] for what we call lightning, the Greeks call *ceraunon* [Note: [Col. 1757] κεραυνόν, “thunderbolt/lightning.”].

Whoever wears this chastely will not be struck by lightning,  
nor will the house or villa in which the stone is customarily kept.  
Nor, if he is carried in a ship across river [Note: [Col. 1757] G: “rivers.”] or sea,  
will he be sunk by storm or struck by lightning.  
It also benefits lawsuits and battles that must be won,  
and grants sweet sleep and sweet dreams [Note: [Col. 1757] R: “and supplies happy dreams.”].

It has two kinds and as many colours.  
Germany is said to send one like crystal,  
but marked with blue and reddish [Note: [Col. 1757] R: “reddish.”] colour.  
Spain, dwelling in the Lusitanian region, also sends one,  
which despises flames and resembles pyrope in colour.

§ XXIX. OF HELIOTROPE.

The gem heliotrope [Note: [Col. 1757] G: “heliotropia.”] has a name derived from its effect:  
when placed in water in a *vacillo* (basin) beneath the sun’s rays [Note: [Col. 1757] R: “batillo.”],

[Col. 1757B] it makes the sun blood-red by changing its light  
and compels a new eclipse to spread over the earth.

Then shortly afterward you will see the vessel boil  
and a shower of sudden spray scattered outward,  
as happens when the troubled air drips with rainclouds.

[Note: [Col. 1757] G has this verse, absent in Victorinus and the printed Redonensis.] It calls down rains from heaven and restrains fair weather.  
It grants its bearer much power of prophecy  
and the knowledge [Note: [Col. 1757] G manuscript: “foretelling.”] of certain future things.  
It adorns those to whom it is given with praises of good reputation,  
preserves them unharmed, and prolongs their span of life.  
It checks bleeding and drives away poisons;  
nor can one who wears this stone be deceived.

So many benefits have been granted by divine gift to this gem;  
yet its power is said to be greater [Note: [Col. 1757] G: “to them”; R: “a greater power is said to have been granted to it.”],

[Col. 1758A] if the herb of the same name [Note: [Col. 1757] R: “herbs.”] is joined [Note: [Col. 1757] G: “girded.”] to it,  
consecrated by a lawful incantation, by a powerful word [Note: [Col. 1757] “and by a word.”]:  
it withdraws from human eyes whoever wears it.

Now Ethiopians, now Cyprus and Africa, send this stone,  
sprinkled with drops of blood and resembling emerald.

§ XXX. OF GERACHITE.

But ancient experience commends the gerachite. [Note: R. and G.: “And geranite”; Ad. ms.: “hieracite.” In the Gorlaean manuscript gerachite is placed between allectorius and jasper.]

Though black in colour, it surpasses colour in power;  
if anyone, after washing his mouth, first tastes it,  
he will at once be able to tell what another is thinking of him. [Note: In the Tours manuscript the following two verses are also read:

> It likewise always possesses the power of obtaining requests,  
> so that no woman can refuse anything to one who asks.]

Its power is said to be capable of being tested thus:  
if the naked body of one who wears it is exposed to flies,  
and anointed with a mixture of milk and liquid honey,  
you will marvel to see it left untouched by the eager swarm.

[Col. 1758B] If you remove the stone, they will gather in a flock and drive in their stings,  
and suck the saturated skin through a thousand wounds.

## 1663–64. § XXXI. ON EPISTITE

In Corinth, prized above its bronze, born between two seas, [Note: “Bimini,” perhaps for “bimari”; see Baudran’s Dictionary.]  
is found the reddish, ruddy stone called epistite. [Note: G. ms.: “hephaestite, or epistite.”]  
If it is thrown into a boiling cauldron,  
after first leaping amid the flames, it is immediately checked by water,  
which shortly becomes cold through the stone’s power.

It is said to keep locusts, birds harmful to crops, from the land,  
as well as barren mists and destructive hail.  
Neither blows nor whirlwind will harm those whom it protects.  
Set in the sun, it emits rays like fire, [Note: G.: “and.”]  
dazzling the astonished eyes with flashing brilliance.  
It also restrains inflamed seditions,  
and keeps safe the wearer when fortune is uncertain.

[Col. 1759A] Yet we ought to hold firmly in mindful heart  
upon what part of the body these stones are to be worn. [Note: R.: “here.”]

## § XXXII. ON HEMATITE

Hematite [Note: G.: “Haematites.”] took its Greek name from blood,  
a stone created to serve human nature,  
whose astringent power is proved in many ways. [Note: The supplied main reading *typica* literally means “typical” or “figurative”; “astringent” follows the contextual sense of G.’s *Stiptica*. R. has *Stipica*, apparently a defective form of the same word.]  
For, rubbed upon the roughness of the eyelids,  
it heals dim sight by driving away the cloudiness.

If its scrapings [Note: G. ms.: “filings.”] are mixed with the white of an egg,  
and diluted with the juice yielded by pomegranates,  
as though upon a medicinal whetstone for eye-salves, [Note: G.: “like eye-salves.”]  
or dissolved in water, it helps those who cast up  
bloody foam from the mouth, and heals ulcers. [Note: G.: “which, when it is applied, it heals.”]

It restrains the flow suffered by a woman when drunk;  
the power of this powder suppresses proud flesh in a wound,

[Col. 1759B] and immediately checks a flowing belly,  
when diluted in old wine and frequently drunk. [Note: R.: “fruenter,” that is, sparingly.]

It excellently cures the bite of a serpent, or the wound made by an asp,  
when dissolved in water and applied. [Note: G.: “heals”; G. ms.: “cures.”]  
Mixed with honey, it can heal sore eyes.  
When drunk, it is said to dissolve a stone in the bladder.  
It is marked by a rusty or reddish colour.  
Africa sends it, as do the Ethiopians and Arabs.

## § XXXIII. ON ABESTON

The land of Arcadia produces the stone abeston, [Note: G. ms.: “ebeston.”]  
iron-coloured and marvellous in natural power:

[Col. 1760A] once kindled, it retains the fire it has caught,  
and cannot be extinguished, shining with everlasting flame.

[Note: The following two verses occur only in the Gorlaean manuscript:

> Hence among the Greeks it is called *abeston*,  
> because, once kindled, you could no longer extinguish it.]

## 1665–66. § XXXIV. ON PEANITE

In the region of the Machedi [Note: R.: “Machetum”; perhaps the country of the Machicores in Madagascar; see Baudran under *Machicolium*.] the stone peanite is produced,  
opening, by imitation, the labours of the female sex. [Note: R.: “changing”; G.: “provoking”; G.: “afflicts.”]  
For, when conception and birth are doubtful as to their cause but certain as to time,  
it assists women in childbirth,  
whom the final hour of a doubtful crisis presses hard.

## § XXXV. ON SADA

Above all gems, sada is difficult to find. [Note: R.: “Sada, difficult to find above all gems.”]  
It would never be known unless it offered itself to be found.  
For this stone, born in the midst of the deep, [Note: G.: “unwary.”]  
by a certain power seeks ships passing from that region,

[Col. 1760B] and, clinging to the planks of a gliding keel,  
is carried to harbour, merchandise given to unsuspecting sailors. [Note: R.: “ships in a certain [way]”; G.: “is drawn.”]  
But it is fixed to the plank with so tenacious a bite  
that it cannot be torn away without a portion of the wood being scraped off.  
Its colour is leek-green; its region, the Chaldaean land. [Note: G.: “Its colour is orange.”]

## § XXXVI. ON MEDUS

But in the region of the Medes there is found  
a stone which they call Medus, the giver of death and of health.  
For, dissolved upon a whetstone in the milk  
of a woman who has once borne a male child, it cures by application  
those deprived of sight, blind for a long time.

The medicinal whetstone is usually green in colour, [Note: R. corruptly: “whom.”]

[Col. 1761A] dissolved in the milk of a ewe that has once borne a male lamb.  
In like manner it expels chronic gout, [Note: R.: “equally.”]  
and restores exhausted limbs beneath a panting breast;  
with this ointment the kidneys of nephritic sufferers are healed.  
It ought to be kept mixed in silver or glass,  
and given to one fasting; thus the medicine is beneficial.

But, dissolved in water and mixed with fragments of its whetstone,  
then offered to an enemy whom you intend  
to wash his forehead with it as though with a remedy,  
it will cover his wretched face by extinguishing his sight.  
If you give it to him to drink, he will die by vomiting up his lungs.  
It is wholly black, but its power is not wholly black. [Note: G.: “black”; G. ms.: “unpleasant.”]  
Let the white be called beneficial, the black harmful.

## 1667–68. § XXXVII. ON GELACIA

But Gelacia is a gem that bears the whiteness and shape of hail,  
unconquered by innumerable blows; [Note: G. and R.: “of every kind.”]  
its natural force is proved to be so great  
that it is cold at every time and is warmed by no fire.

## § XXXVIII. ON EXACONTALITE

Exacontalite [Note: G.: “Execontallite.”] is a stone deriving its name from its property:  
within its small circumference it bears sixty colours,  
and makes up by number for its small bodily size,  
while a single little gem bears the colours of so many gems.  
This stone is found in Libya among the Troglodytes. [Note: G.: “Troglodytes”; R.: “Tragodytes.”]

## § XXXIX. ON CHELONITE

The Indian tortoise yields the stone chelonite,  
pleasing, bright with purple and varied colour.

[Col. 1762A] If anyone, after washing his mouth, carries it beneath his tongue,  
magicians believe that he can foretell things to come,  
from the dawn of day only until the sixth hour.  
At the time when the disk of the moon is seen to increase,  
the aforesaid power of the stone at the first moon  
is said to last through the space of the whole day;  
the periods of the fifteenth moon agree with those of the first. [Note: G.: *luna*, “moon”; G. m.: *primae. decrementi*, “of the first … of the waning,” as punctuated in the supplied note. *Quintae post decimam* means the fifth after the tenth, that is, the fifteenth.]  
But throughout the time of lunar waning,  
that power remains in the stone only until noon.  
This stone is also subject to no fire.

## § XL. ON PRASUS

The conspicuous prase [Note: G. and R.: “prasius.”] is usually counted among gems,  
but it is not costly: content with its beauty,  
it provides no usefulness except that it is green and suits gold.

[Col. 1762B] One variety is marked with bloody drops. [Note: G.: “veins.”]  
A third is inscribed with three whitish figures. [Note: G.: “strokes”; R.: “letters.”]

## § XLI. ON CRYSTAL

Crystal is ice hardened over many years,  
as seemed good to certain learned men who wrote thus;  
it retains the coldness and colour of ancient hail. [Note: G.: “hail.”]  
Others deny this, and maintain that in many parts of the world  
crystal is produced which no force of cold,  
nor icy winter, has ever been proved to have affected.  
But all agree, and it is doubtful to no one,  
that this stone, exposed to the sun, catches fire,  
and from this is accustomed to kindle tinder placed near it.

[Col. 1763A] 1669–70 Some also administer it, ground with honey,  
to mothers charged with nursing infants,  
believing that this drink fills their breasts with milk.

## § XLII. ON GALACTITE

They likewise say that galactite, resembling ash,  
when ground with honey-wine, increases milk in one who drinks it.

If, however, after baths and before food it is taken,  
or if it is fitting to draw a thread from the wool of a pregnant ewe  
through the pierced stone and put it round the neck,  
then it fills the breasts of its wearer with milk.  
Bound in the same manner to the thigh  
of a woman labouring in childbirth, it gives easy delivery.

But if, mixed with salt and water at the rising of the sun, it is sprinkled around a cleansed sheepfold,

[Col. 1763B] the sheep are filled with milk and scab is driven away from them. [Note: G. and R.: “and malignant scab is driven away.”]  
Moreover, the ancients adorn it with such great praises  
that they think it alone supplies to its wearer  
all the benefits which, united, other stones would give through their power.  
But if it melts within a closed mouth, it disturbs the mind.  
The Nile sends it, and the Achelous produces it.  
When ground, it yields a milky juice and the taste of milk.

## § XLIII. ON ORITE

Black and round orite perfectly heals deadly bites  
inflicted by a wild beast’s horn or savage tooth,

[Col. 1764A] when mixed with rose-coloured oil.  
It preserves unharmed those travelling through vast deserts among wild beasts,  
driving away diseases [Note: G.: “bites.”] caused by beasts.  
Another orite is green and has white spots. [Note: G.: “which.”]  
When carried, it everywhere resists adverse accidents.

A third orite, more celebrated, is asserted:  
one part of it is exceedingly rough with many projections,  
the other smoother, like a plate of hard iron. [Note: G.: “hard.”]  
When hung upon a woman, it prevents her from becoming pregnant;  
or, if she is pregnant, [Note: G.: “or so that if”; R.: “that she may be”; G.: “quickly.”] it causes a miscarriage.

## § XLIV. ON HYENA

From the eyes of the hyena is taken a stone worthy of exaltation,  
called *hyena*, which the ancients, if it is credible,  
declare to impart prophetic power to its wearer,

1671–72 so that, imbued with it, he may foretell all future things,

[Col. 1764B] if it is held beneath the tongue in the whole mouth. [Note: G.: “wholly.”]

## § XLV. ON LIPAREA

In Scythian regions there is a stone called liparea,  
to which every kind of wild animal of its own accord hastens,  
the animals which hunters’ toil is accustomed to drive out.  
Therefore one who carries this stone while searching woodland glades  
needs neither the running of dogs nor skilful care:  
it is enough to raise hunting-spears against the prey to be laid low.

## § XLVI. ON ENHYDROS

Enhydros [Note: G.: “Enydros.”] distils with tears of perpetual weeping,

[Col. 1765A] which flow as though from the spring of a full fountain,  
and the cause of whose nature is difficult to discover.  
For if the substance of the stone runs away, why  
does it not become smaller, or melt altogether?  
If external dew descends into the interior [Note: G. and R.: “but if.”]  
so that it may always flow back out, why does it not obstruct itself,  
since what enters must clearly oppose what goes out?

## § XLVII. ON IRIS

The Arabs provide iris, but the Red Sea produces it,  
a stone like crystal, whose six-sided form,  
glittering with clear light, gives the reason for this name.  
For if, under a roof, it is exposed to a ray of sunlight,  
the nearest wall is coloured and paints in varied colour  
the form of each heavenly rainbow. [Note: V.: “it paints both forms of the heavenly rainbow.”]

## § XLVIII. ON ANDRODRAGMA

Androdragma [Note: G.: “Adrodramanta.”] is a stone shaped like a square die,  
said to display the gleam of silver. [Note: V.: “colour.”]  
Its hardness is like the hardness of diamond.  
It is found mixed with the sands of the Red Sea itself;  
a magician asserts that it has such great power  
that it can at once calm angry friends.

## § XLIX. ON OPTALLIUS

Optallius, which turns away every disease of the eyes, [Note: R.: “ophtalius”; G.: “ophtalmius.”]  
is said to be the safest patron of thieves.  
[Note: This verse is absent from G.]

For it preserves sharp sight in its wearer,  
but dulls the bystanders’ vision with an overcast cloud,

[Col. 1766A] so that robbers may plunder houses with impunity.

## 1673–74. § L. ON PEARLS

A remarkable kind is taken from marine shells,  
called *unio* because one is taken [Note: G.: “born.”] from one:  
never are two or more found together.  
For its ornament its white appearance is praised,  
since it suits garments and likewise suits gold. [Note: G.: “because.”]

At fixed seasons the shells are said to open,  
gaping toward the sky to drink the descending dew,  
from which shining little spheres are conceived.  
The pearl is brighter when made from morning dew;  
evening dew ordinarily produces dark offspring.  
But young shells yield whiter pearls. [Note: G. ms.: “of pearls.”]  
The greater age of shells darkens their offspring.  
The more they have drunk of the dewy air,  
the larger a pearl the condensation produces.  
Yet none is thought to grow beyond half an ounce. [Note: Main reading *semuncem*, “half an ounce”; G.: *Semi nucem concrescere*, “to grow into half a nut”; G. m.: *sed crescere*, “but to grow.”]

But if the lofty vaults mingle thunder with lightning,  
the shells flee in sudden fright and close.  
Thus, the draught having been interrupted, conception perishes,  
and what had begun to be created becomes abortive.  
India produces outstanding pearls, the spoils of the sea,  
and ancient Brachmania [Note: perhaps Britain.] produces outstanding pearls as well.

## § LI. ON PANTHER

Panther is attested to have many colours:  
it appears black, red, green, pale,

[Col. 1767A] purple and rose-coloured at once; it has these colours scattered about  
and blooms with a variegated pattern.

It is beneficial to see it as soon as the sun has risen,  
so that you may emerge victorious in every undertaking:  
for on that very day no one will be able to defeat you.

It is clear that the panther is a wild beast of varied colour,  
which India produces; frightened by its voice,  
the fury of lions flees, and every beast trembles.  
After its likeness this stone has received its name.

## § LII. ON ABSICTUS

Absictus [Note: G.: “apistus.”] is no mean gem of black colour,  
marked with red veins in an attractive appearance.  
It equals a larger body in weight;  
when it has once received heat from a fire brought near it, [Note: G.: “once”; G.: “if it begins with fire.”]  
they testify that it remains hot for seven days.

## § LIII. ON CHALCOPHANUS

[Col. 1767B] Chalcophanus [Note: G.: “calcophonus.”] when struck gives back bronze-like ringing sounds.  
If it is handled reverently by a chaste body, [Note: “If it is handled reverently by a chaste body.”]  
they say it confers the sweet melody of voice upon its wearer,  
and protects clear throats from becoming hoarse.  
This stone too is said to be black in colour.

## 1675–76. § LIV. ON MELOCHITE

By its power melochite protects the care of infants [Note: G. and R.: “cradles.”]  
and drives away every sinister accident,  
lest any evil power harm their tender limbs.  
Power joined to beauty gives the stone its worth:  
green like prase, it is accustomed to resemble emerald. [Note: G. and R.: “thick.”]

[Col. 1768A] The peoples of Arabia are said to have discovered it first.

## § LV. ON GEGOLITE

Gegolite [Note: R.: “Cegoto tecolithos.”], said to resemble an olive stone,  
is cheap in appearance but precious in natural force.  
For, dissolved in water and drunk by those who need it,  
it is said to have power to dissolve stony kidneys  
and at the same time cleanse the gravel of a painful bladder.

## § LVI. ON PYRITE

Pyrite, yellow in colour and named from fire, [Note: R.: “pirithe”; G.: “pyrites.”]  
will not allow itself to be clasped or handled closely.  
It wishes to be touched lightly and held in a timid hand;  
for if squeezed too tightly, it burns the fingers of its holder.

## § LVII. ON DIADOCHUS

Diadochus [Note: R.: “diadochus, diadoches.”] is said to be suited to those seeking answers through water,

[Col. 1768B] displaying various images of demons.  
There is no other stone that evokes shades more powerfully;  
but if someone should perhaps apply it to a dead person,  
it is immediately said to lose its customary powers.  
For it is a sacred stone and abhors one whom death has struck.  
They further say that it resembles beryl in brightness.

## § LVIII. ON DIONYSIA

Dionysia glitters black, strewn with red drops.  
When it is crushed in water, they say that the water smells of wine,  
yet drunkenness is driven away by its odour.  
In this, nature proceeds in no customary order:

[Col. 1769A] for the stone produces from water the smell of wine,  
and drives away drunkenness, which wine ordinarily creates.

## § LIX. ON CHRYSELECTRUS

Chryselectrus [Note: V.: “crisolectrus.”] is described as resembling gold,  
its colour seeming to incline toward amber.  
It is more pleasant to look upon in the morning hours, [Note: G. ms.: “to hear.”]  
but afterwards presents a different appearance to those who look at it.  
Its substance is said to be very quick to catch fire,  
for it soon burns when seized by a neighbouring flame.

## 1677–78. § LX. ON CHRYSOPACION

The land of the Ethiopians produces the stone chrysopacion, [Note: G.: “chrysopassion.”]  
which darkness reveals [Note: G.: “destroys.” This is the ninth article in the Gorlaean manuscript.] and daylight conceals.  
It glitters with fire at night, but vanishes in daylight,  
lying without shine, buried in the pallor of gold.  
Here too the order of nature is seen to be reversed:

[Col. 1769B] for what night normally conceals, daylight reveals. [Note: G.: “daylight suddenly conceals; blind night reveals.”]

## § LXI. ON THE RING AND THE GEM

Prometheus is said first to have made use of a ring,  
so that a gem might be fitted for the finger:  
they relate that he enclosed in iron the shining fragments  
of the Caucasian rock [Note: G. ms.: “scruple.”] and wore them set upon his finger.

[Col. 1770A] A later age bound precious metals together,  
added costly stones and, further, art,  
and clothed an unaccustomed hand with threefold honour.

But, since human fraud leaves nothing untouched  
—while envious art imitates nature—  
it is difficult to distinguish true gems from false,  
which ingenuity learned to counterfeit with deceptive glass  
while the adulterous form feigns a true appearance.

Hence it comes about that the power of gems is thought nonexistent,  
whenever an ignorant test deceives those who make it;  
but if their kinds are genuine [Note: G.: “but genuine kinds.”]—if they have been properly consecrated—  
marvellous effects unquestionably attend them.

[Note: With these verses the author concludes the poem with which he had begun; in the Tours manuscript they stand at the head of the poem and before the prologue, as we too have placed them.]

The ancients gave gems their name from *gum*,  
because they shone through like glittering gum;  
those which do not shine through they wished to call opaque.

[Col. 1770B] Yet both kinds are denoted by the name “stone,”  
and for that reason this book is entitled *Of Stones*.  
Let these names, selected from innumerable gems,  
collected by our labour, suffice to be retained,  
which are clearly distinguished in sixty little headings. [Note: These three verses are absent in the Gorlaean manuscript. The Victorine codex ends thus: “Here ends the book of Marbod [R.: Morbod], bishop, *On Stones*, containing seven hundred and thirty verses and sixty stones in itself through sixty-one chapters, counting among them the chapter on the Ring and the Gem.” — Moreover, in the same manuscript the following prose and moral explanation of the aforesaid stones are appended. We have not doubted that Marbod himself was their author, since the properties there ascribed to the gems or stones and drawn into a moral or mystical sense are precisely the same as those which he recounted in the preceding poem. This prose and explanation are absent from the Rennes edition of 1524 and the Gorlaean manuscript.]

[Col. 1771]

# PROSE OF MARBOD, BISHOP OF REDON, ON THE TWELVE PRECIOUS STONES PLACED IN THE FOUNDATION OF THE HEAVENLY CITY (Rev. 21:19)

(From St Victor manuscript no. 905. Never published.) (G)*

1679

Citizens of the heavenly homeland,  
sing together to the King of kings,  
who is the supreme maker  
of the heavenly city,  
in whose building  
this foundation stands.

Jasper, green in colour,  
displays the greenness of faith,  
which in all the perfect  
never wholly withers,  
and by whose strong protection  
the devil is resisted.

Sapphire has an appearance  
like the heavenly throne;  
it signifies the heart of the simple,  
who await with certain hope,  
whose life and conduct [lacuna] [Note: Perhaps: “shine brightly also with virtues.”]

Pale chalcedony  
has the likeness of fire:  
it reddens in public,  
it gives brightness in darkness,  
and bears the virtue of believers  
who serve secretly.

The very green emerald  
gives an olive-green light:  
it is most upright faith,  
open to every good,  
which never knows how to fail  
in the work of piety.

Sardonyx is composed of three colours;  
it signifies the inward person:  
humility makes him black,  
chastity makes him white,  
and martyrdom too makes him red,  
to complete his honour.

Sardius is crimson,  
its bloody colour displaying  
the glory of martyrs  
who contend lawfully:  
sixth in the catalogue,  
it adheres to the mystery of the Cross.

Golden chrysolite  
sparkles like a furnace;  
it represents the character of men  
of perfect wisdom,  
who shine with the sacred splendour  
of sevenfold grace.

1680 Beryl is watery,  
like the sun in clear water;  
it figures the vows of minds  
of keen intelligence:  
the mystical door [perhaps “occupation”] of supreme rest.

The dearer [perhaps “the rarer”] the topaz,  
the more precious it is,  
appears with a grey gleam  
and ethereal aspect:  
it supplies the solid office  
of the contemplative life.

Chrysoprase imitates  
the purple assembly;  
it is interspersed with  
a certain mixture of golden drops:  
this is perfect charity,  
which no ferocity overthrows.

Hyacinth is blue,  
of a middling brilliance;  
its beautiful appearance  
changes as the weather changes:  
it marks the angelic life,  
endowed with discernment.

Amethyst, chief among stones,  
is violet in beauty;  
it emits golden flames  
and purple markings:  
it represents the heart of the humble  
who die with Christ.

These precious stones  
signify fleshly persons;  
the diversity of colours,  
the multiplicity of virtues.  
Whoever flourishes in these  
will be able to be a fellow-citizen.

Peace-bearing Jerusalem,  
these are your foundations:  
happy and near to God,  
may the soul be granted to you.  
The guardian of your towers  
does not sleep for ever.

Grant us, holy  
King of the heavenly city,  
after the course of this fleeting life,  
fellowship in the world above,  
that among the ranks of the saints  
we may sing songs to you.

Amen.

[Col. 1771]

# MYSTICAL OR MORAL APPLICATION OF THE PRECIOUS STONES DISCUSSED IN THE PRECEDING PROSE, BY MARBOD, BISHOP OF REDON

(From the same St Victor manuscript no. 905. Never published.)

[Col. 1771A] 1681 § I. Jasper is the first foundation of the Church of God and is green in colour. Whoever has it upon himself will not be harmed by a phantom. It signifies those who always hold the faith of God and never depart from it or wither away, but always remain green in it and do not fear the deceits of the devil.

[Col. 1772A] § II. Sapphire has the colour of heaven. It signifies those who, though still placed on earth, attend to heavenly things and despise all earthly things as though they were not on earth, according to the saying: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

§ III. Chalcedony does not shine so long as it is in a house; [Col. 1773A] it shines *sub diva*, that is, beneath the open sky. It resists those wishing to cut and carve it. Heated by the rays of the sun or by rubbing with fingers, it draws straw to itself. By this are denoted those who conceal their goodness and do good works in secret, including fasting, almsgiving, and such things, according to the saying: “But when you fast,” etc. (Matt. 6:27). But when they are compelled to go out among people, their goodness then appears and they shine. If anyone wishes to flatter them or give them praise—which is like carving or painting—they do not receive empty praises, but resist them strongly, not yielding to them. Yet, breathed upon by the ray of the true sun, that is, Christ, or handled and heated by fingers, that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, by the word of their preaching and the example of their goodness they draw straw—that is,

[Col. 1773B] sinners—to themselves, unite them to themselves, and urge them to persevere in good works.

§ IV. Emerald is of extraordinary greenness. It surpasses all gems and herbs by its greenness. It is born only in a dry and uninhabitable place. Because of the cold, none dwell there except griffins, beasts like lions with wings like eagles, and one-eyed *asinaspi*, who fight with them. By the gem, that is, the emerald, we mean those who are greener in faith than all others and surpass unbelievers by the greenness of faith; unbelievers are cold and dry in charity, which they do not possess. The griffins which guard them signify demons, who envy people possessing faith—which is a precious pearl and gem—and attempt to take it from them. They are rightly compared with griffins,

[Col. 1773C] as earthly beasts and birds: they are plunged into hell for their deserts and, flying through pride like birds, fell from heaven. Against them fight the one-eyed, that is, those who do not walk in two ways, do not have a double heart, and do not serve two masters; but always possess their intention and the gem of faith, which demons seek to wrest from them, overcoming the demons with God’s help.

§ V. Sardonyx has three colours: beneath it is black, in the middle white, above red. It represents those who endure in their hearts the sufferings of the Passion for Christ’s name, and who are inwardly white in soul, that is, without hypocrisy, provided that they despise themselves

[Col. 1773D] and see themselves as black—that is, as sinners.

§ VI. Sardius is wholly red; it signifies martyrs who pour out their blood for Christ.

§ VII. Chrysolite shines like gold and sends forth burning sparks: it represents wise and charitable people who show to others in deed and word what they know. *Chrysos* (Χρυσός) means “gold,” and by gold are understood wisdom and charity, which are more perfect than all virtues, just as gold is more perfect than every metal.

§ VIII. Beryl shines like water struck by the sun and warms the hand of its holder. It signifies those who are frail, but, struck by the ray and grace of the true sun, that is, Christ, shine in good works and warm those

1683 who associate with them by the warmth of charity and the example of a good life.

§ IX. Topaz is found rarely and is therefore considered more precious. It has two colours, one like gold and the other brighter. It surpasses all gems in brilliance,

[Col. 1774B] and no thing is more beautiful to behold. It signifies those who love God and neighbour. Those who love their neighbour shine like gold; cleansed from the filth of this age and always intent upon heavenly things, they become brighter and more beautiful.

§ X. Chrysoprase is purple, dotted with golden drops. It signifies those who spend their life always in tribulation and the labours of suffering, while always remaining in charity.

§ XI. Hyacinth changes its colour with the appearance of the sky: if the sky is clear, it shines; if it is dark, it does not shine. It signifies those who strive in understanding with the wise, so as to adapt themselves to the capacity of their hearers, as the Apostle says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2:6).

[Col. 1774C] To those who knew little he said: “I could not give food to you as to spiritual persons, but gave you milk to drink as to carnal persons, not food” (1 Cor. 9:22). This Apostle was a hyacinth and so accommodated himself to all, that he might be all things to all, saying: “I became all things to all, that I might gain all” (1 Cor. 9:22).

§ XII. Amethyst is wholly red and sends forth certain rose-coloured flames. It represents those who, for God, endure the torments of suffering and emit them from themselves as a flame of charity, praying for those who kill them. They grieve more over the sins of those doing evil to them than over what they themselves suffer. And it is rightly placed last, because it signifies those who pray for enemies. For the virtue of virtues is to pray
