[Col. 1774D] for persecutors. Few are found to have done this; nevertheless, two are found in the Old Testament, namely Moses and Samuel, and two in the New, the Lord Christ and Stephen.

[Col. 1773]

# FURTHER, BY THE SAME AUTHOR, ON THE NATURES OF STONES

(From the same manuscript. Never published.)

[Col. 1773D] 1684 Jasper benefits those who possess it against lightning and thunder. [The supplied *se haben ibus* is read as *se habentibus*, “those who possess it.”]

[Col. 1774D] A consecrated and bound chalcedony stone cures lunatics. Moreover, whoever carries it will never

[Col. 1775A] drown or be afflicted. It also makes its wearer handsome, faithful, powerful, and able to accomplish everything. One ought to carve armed Mars and a veiled maiden, clothed in a flowing garment and holding a laurel, with perpetual consecration.

Aristotle says in his book *On Stones*: “An emerald hung around the neck or worn on the finger protects against the danger of an epileptic seizure.” Therefore we command noble persons always to hang it around their children’s necks, lest they fall into this infirmity. Emerald has efficacy for every divination; carried in every undertaking, it increases one’s substance, both in body and in speech.

Sardius weighing twenty grains of barley, if hung about the neck or worn on the finger,

[Col. 1775B] will cause its wearer not to see terrifying or fearful things in dreams; nor will he fear incantations and sorceries.

Chrysolite drives away every kind of serpent; it is a dense, shining stone like gold. Applied to gold filings and washed, it is a most safe protective amulet [perhaps *tutissimum*] against nocturnal terrors. Passed through donkey bristles and tied on the left arm, it conquers demons. For it is above . . . and of love and justice. [Note: The manuscript’s reading is corrupt: “e eni. sup. ipam qi TTIS est ocul’7. amoris 7 justicie.”]

It makes a stranger welcome, eloquent, gracious, and lovable to those who see him, and opens everything to him. It also helps against inflammation of the eyes.

Beryl is a large and bright stone. Carve upon it a sea-locust and beneath its feet a little crow; under the gem place *herbina* enclosed in a little gold,

[Col. 1775C] consecrated; wear it . . . [Note: The manuscript reads “TO cuing.”] It makes one victorious over every evil and gives complete health against defects of the eyes. If you put this stone in water and give someone a drink from that water, it will heal a person seized in spirit and short of breath, and free him from pain of the liver. It is useful when worn; whoever has this stone upon himself will emerge victorious while fighting against enemies. It is found in India, like emerald but paler.

[Note: Since among the many interpretations of these characters and words which either persons more skilled in divining them, or we ourselves, could devise, none occurred to us that approached the author’s meaning, we preferred to offer them, graphically represented—as also the following two words—to the acumen of a more fortunate reader, rather than to supply something not understood.]

Topaz, when carried by anyone, permits no enemy to harm him. It is good to keep this in the house for averting sorceries.

1685 If anyone has hyacinth hung around his neck or on his finger, then, should he enter a plague-ridden region, he will not be harmed,

[Col. 1775D] but rather will be honoured by all, and his requests will be fulfilled.

If amethyst is washed in water and given to a barren woman, she will immediately conceive.

Agate helps a woman having a miscarriage and compels the child to come forth quickly.

[Col. 1776A] Sardius is good when worn and is loved by women. Carve upon it a vine and entwined ivy.

Whoever has onyx will be able to interpret a vision he sees.

Carnelian, worn around the neck or on the finger, mitigates anger and contention.

Casteis is suited to freedom. [Note: Thus exactly in the manuscript.] For whoever consecrates it and performs what ought to be done with it will altogether obtain freedom. The stone, once acquired, must be prepared as follows. Carve a scarab upon it; then, beneath its belly, standing afterwards, let it be extended lengthwise; and, consecrated with a golden clasp and placed in a prepared and decorated place, it will display the glory which God has granted it.

[Col. 1776B] In jasper, therefore, is denoted the greenness of faith; in sapphire, the heavenly height of hope; in chalcedony, the flame of inward charity is represented; in emerald, the strong confession of that same faith amid adversities; in sardonyx, the humility of saints amid virtues; in sardius, the venerable blood of martyrs is expressed; in chrysolite, spiritual preaching amid

1686 miracles; in beryl, the perfect activity of preachers; in topaz, their burning contemplation; in chrysoprase, together the work and reward of blessed martyrs; in hyacinth, the heavenly raising of teachers toward high things and, on account of the weak, their humble descent to human things. In amethyst is denoted the constant remembrance of the heavenly kingdom in the mind of the humble (Rev. 21:19). Therefore individual precious stones are assigned to individual foundations,

[Col. 1776C] because, although all those by whom the city of God is adorned and founded upon his holy mountain are perfect, they nevertheless shine with the light of spiritual grace.

There then follow sixteen verses, written in the old French idiom, by the same hand and in the same style of writing, as follows:

> Here are named the twelve stones  
> held to be the dearest:  
> Jasper, Sapphire, Chalcedony;  
> Emerald, Sardonyx, and Sardius;  
> Chrysolite, Beryl, and Topaz;  
> Chrysoprase, Hyacinth, and Amethyst.  
> They bear the figure of holy men,  
> who serve God without fear,  
> in every kind of holiness,
[Col. 1776D] They have a human form,

Who shall wish to serve God,

Like precious stones, bright in their brilliance,

They shall be set in the City of God,

And well assigned in its foundation;

They shall rest in the vision of peace,

In which they may rejoice without end.

Then, on the following leaf, this is found: “Here are inscribed the names of the precious stones whose powers and natures are explained in this Lapidary. First it is said:”

[DUBIA.]

[Col. 1777]

[NOTICE.]

[Col. 1777B] The following verses have been excerpted from Abraham Gorlaeus’s *Dactylotheca*, printed at Leiden in 1695 with the explanations of Jacob Gronovius. Near the end is found a book on gems under this title: *The Poem on Gems, or Precious Stones, of Marbod, an Ancient Gallic Poet*. Yet neither Gorlaeus nor Gronovius identifies any manuscript from which it was taken. Before the poem itself, however, there are found in the same place, as if in place of a preface, two letters of Evax to the Emperor Tiberius, whose wording is as follows.

[Col. 1777]

[LETTERS.]

Evax sends greetings to Tiberius.

[Col. 1777C]

Since you desire that the mysteries of all stones which seem useful to humankind, that wise race, should be written down for you by me, it was not right to refuse you. You, therefore, must guard with the utmost diligence the mystery of the supreme and most high God. For this mystery, unknown to the other nations but known to the Egyptians, you must not hand over either to the *allophyloi*—foreign peoples—or to other enemies, lest Egypt ever be reduced to barrenness in this knowledge; and lest it be consumed through some person, perish in a conflagration, or, when kings are brought into Egypt, make slaves of all who rule over the Egyptians. For it is not to be handed over to others; and lest others hold it in their power, it must be kept under perpetual guard. I swear to you by the supreme [Col. 1778C] God that Egypt possesses no book equal or superior to this. The supreme God is witness to this oath. For I shall send the good—that is, the name—of the book, by which its kind will be known. Therefore let it be guarded perpetually among us. For it is of great benefit in every undertaking, through the individual hierarchies, as the Greeks call them, of all stones. Farewell.

Evax sends greetings to the Emperor Tiberius.

I have received your splendid gifts through the centurion Lucinius Fronto, as he is called, whom you deigned to send to me. And I in return have sent you whatever most precious account of remedies from all stones exists upon the earth in the regions of the East. Farewell.

[Col. 1777]

SOME VERSES OF MARBOD, OR RATHER OF AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR, HITHERTO WANTED.

(From Gorlaeus’s Leiden edition of 1695, with Gronovius’s notes at the end of his *Dactylotheca*.)

[Col. 1777C] Capnitis, a most excellent gem, crystalline in appearance,

Makes its bearer eloquent and powerfully cures dropsy;

Great is its power and healing for those who wear it.

[Col. 1778C] It makes one beautiful and softens every anger.

It also drives away fears, as grace accompanies it.

[Col. 1779A] Ophtalmius is proved to bring great benefit to the eyes.

But thieves use it, and those whom no one can hold

When it is present; let its author know why this is so.

The obsian stone is one that can always drive away

Uncertain dreams; secure with it as companion,

He who can sleep is not deceived by dreams.

Ignites is a stone whose colour appears

Glassy and clear; it is accustomed to check

Every flow of blood, provided only that it be bound upon the forehead.

This gem also prevents the sick from speaking another’s words;

It drives away warts and moles, and keeps malignant *striges* (blood-sucking witches)

Away from children, whose blood they thirst to draw.

You may perhaps see fires consuming houses;

Yet, if you apply this stone, the fires subside of themselves.

Diadochos, in appearance and colour like beryl,

Displays the images of those looking into it better than any mirror;

And no stone heals burns so greatly.

Where this is applied to the dead, it is said to halt [corruption];

when it loses its power, it becomes dull and does not soothe burns.

[Col. 1779B] Exebenus is a white stone, sufficiently handsome.

While this gem brightens gold in the hands of goldsmiths,

They value nothing more highly, nor is anything dearer to them than it.

It is good for the stomach, if powder made from the broken gem

Is sprinkled with wine or water.

The mad and insane, too, know the powers of exebenus.

It preserves childbirth and quickly delivers the woman in labour,

If it is fastened to her right thigh.

If a pregnant woman wears lingurum, the child will possess lingurum,

So that, according to its nature, it may be less afraid.

The king’s disease is overcome by drinking lingurum,

If you grind the gem’s powder mixed with wine.

Excellent daphnius causes every frenzied person,

When it is present, immediately to deserve restoration to health;

Daphnius is accustomed to give rest to the possessed.

Daphnius is good for flux and restrains dropsy.

Mennonius drives away diseases, illnesses, and swellings,

[Its] power [or “poison”] driving off every evil and repelling enmities;

1689 It makes each of its wearers eloquent, steadfast, and faithful.

Kings have conquered battles;

Those accused in capital cases have escaped death,

With mennonium as their protector; whoever wears it escapes wrath.

A sailor never fears shipwreck while it accompanies him.

Nature herself has called the stone galactite,

Drawing the name from milk in both Greek and Latin,

For the one name conveys milk in each language.

[Col. 1780A] For in Greek *galaz* means milk, as we say in Latin;

A woman lacking milk can make milk flow for herself

Through this gem, when she takes its powder with mead.

If a woman rejects a draught of the crushed stone,

Let her bind the fleece of a pregnant ewe around her neck;

Then galactite sprinkled upon the wet fleece

Will soon enable a child to suck milk from full breasts.

If any hunter has the odontes stone,

Or if a thief or robber wears that stone,

Their wishes will succeed. Yet, though he lacks

The offices of piety, the God of nature and stones

Will not be blameworthy—he who makes nothing in things

Without a cause, and whose every creation remains subject

To the law of weight and number.

The brow of a wild ass, or more commonly an ass’s brow, when swollen,

Sometimes bears its stone, which is said to restrain

Poisons when drunk and venomous bites.

Scrape it into water, and, when you see the water grow pale,

[Col. 1780B] 1690 do not delay in giving it to the patient who is soon to recover.

You will see it larger than a walnut, with a wrinkled shape

And a pale surface, not shining.

The three-coloured stone has imitated the heavenly rainbow;

By its threefold name it makes its wearers learned in law,

And is therefore fitting for the fingers of kings.

The Phrygian stone is born in Phrygia, but is like pumice,

Though heavier than pumice. When wine is poured upon it,

It is said to be burned by the power of fire blown through bellows

From a distance, and to glow or redden as though ignited;

It is said to be extinguished only when drenched in nectar.

This stone is said to be useful for dyeing cloth,

And particularly suited to the Phrygian fullers.

Sarcophagus is a stone said to be capable

Of consuming dead bodies in nearly forty days.

A very abundant vein of it is found near Troy.

Many stones of the same kind have been found,

Which even eat away living bodies by touch

And pay little heed to whatever corpses they enclose.

[Col. 1780C] Abundance makes this remarkable reflective stone cheap:

Spain first sent this stone forth to the world;

Now we read that it is found in many regions.

When dug from the earth, it is split into such thin layers

That any inlays are seen to be thinner than all glass,

And you can no longer believe it to be anything but glass.

[Col. 1779]

CHARTERS GRANTED BY MARBOD.

I.

(*History of Marmoutier*, manuscript, edited by Dom Martène, vol. II, p. 58.) Marbod, bishop of Rennes, gives to Marmoutier the church of Aienciac and half the priestly benefice of the church of Martiniac.

[Col. 1779D]

Because time slips away in swift course and remembrance of things past perishes in silence, it is necessary that what we wish to be remembered should be committed to the written record. Therefore I, Marbod, by God’s grace bishop of Rennes, having regard for my soul and in need of the prayers of the righteous, write to my successors that I granted—indeed, gave—the church of Aienciac and half the priestly benefice of the church of Martiniac to the brothers and friends of our church, the monks of Marmoutier, in whose prayers I trust. A certain priest, Guingenoius, had held them by hereditary right, and, at his death, had given them to those monks, saving canonical reverence and episcopal right, and likewise saving the customary revenues of the holy mother Church of Rennes. But after Abbot William had been invested with possession of those churches, he granted them back to our archdeacon Roger, to hold freely and peacefully for as long as Roger himself should live; on the condition, however, that Roger should pay all the churches’ revenues to the bishop and should give the monks absolutely no share. The witnesses to this transaction are, among the monks: William the prior, Gilo son of Ansquitil, Andrew of Gomez, Milo, and Evenus the bailiff. Among the canons: Biso the archdeacon, Rannulf the captain, Rainulf the provost, and many others.

II. LETTER OF MARBOD, BISHOP OF RENNES, FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT SERGIUS AT ANGERS. (A.D. 1108.)

[MORICE, *Memoirs Serving the History of Brittany*, vol. I, p. 516.]

[Col. 1781]

[Col. 1781A] I, MARBOD, by God’s grace bishop of Rennes, make known that we did not delay in assenting to the petition of Lord Walter, abbot of Saint Sergius, at the request of Lord Reginald, bishop of Angers. Therefore, with the chapter’s consent, we granted to him and his successors all the churches which the monks of Saint Sergius possessed and still possess in our diocese: namely, Gena, Briellas, Monasteriolum, Tosleia, and Breellum, saving the right of our church. But concerning Brello, which was only a chapel, the abbot and I established and confirmed that each year he and his successors should pay to us and our successors an annual rent of three solidi; and thus that church shall be free and quit from all other customary dues, and also from the charge of sacrilege, saving canonical right.

[Col. 1782A] Done and confirmed at Rennes, in our chamber, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1108, indiction 1, epact 6, on the Ides of May.

These present persons saw and heard this: Baudric, archbishop of Dol; Reginald, bishop of Angers; Judicael, bishop of Alet; William, abbot of Saint-Florent; Gervase, abbot of Saint-Melaine; Fulk, abbot of Beaulieu; Count Alan and Countess Ermengard.

Among the canons of Blessed Peter: Piscis the archdeacon, Roger the archdeacon, and Joscius the treasurer.

Among the canons of Saint Maurice of Angers: Stephen the precentor, William the archdeacon, and William Musca.

III. Charter of Marbod, bishop of Rennes, by which, having expelled the disorderly canons dwelling there, he grants the church of Saint Mary at Vitré, in whose place he installed Benedictine monks, to the monks of Saint-Melaine, together with many other churches and properties. (A.D. 1116.) [Hildebert’s *Works*, ed. Beaugendre, p. lix.]

[Col. 1781B]

I, MARBOD, by God’s grace bishop of Rennes, judged it fitting to put in writing for the knowledge of those to come what it is useful for both the holy see of Rennes and the church of Vitré to retain in memory. Since canons had from ancient times been established in the church of Vitré, and that order had continued until our time, the canons surviving in our day, conducting themselves more carelessly than honourably, fell, as their sins required, to such a state that they were hateful to the princes of the land and incorrigible to us. Thus the order was thrown into confusion, the Church’s resources dissipated, and the number of clerics reduced so greatly that only three remained in the church. Therefore, after taking counsel with worthy persons, both ecclesiastical and secular, lest so great a church should any longer be deprived of its ministry, and also at the request of the lords of the castle, Andrew and his sons, and the other barons of the castle, I gave, as a perpetual alms, that same church—with its resources, lands, boroughs, and possessions—and all the revenues of the churches which the canons held: namely, the church of Saint Martin in the same castle; the churches [Col. 1782B] of Balazé and Mecé; Saint Desiderius; and the church of Saint Symphorian in the town of Rennes, to our religious and beloved sons, the monks of Saint-Melaine, saving in every respect the right and dignity of the holy church of Rennes. Conan, duke of Brittany, son of Alan Fergant, and his mother Countess Ermengard approved, desired, and carried out this gift of mine on their part. Our archdeacons Mainus and Roger, and the unanimous assembly of our canons, likewise approved and confirmed my gift. Their names are these: Mainus the cantor, Joscedus the treasurer, the two provosts Radulf, Withenocus the bishop’s chaplain, Radulf Gertranni, Mainfinitus Hugonis, William, Alan, and Peter. Afterwards the monks established with Lord Andrew, and confirmed in the presence of the count and myself, that everything which he held in his lordship, in obediences and possessions, should be transferred to the church of Saint Mary, so that a community and religious order might be maintained there.

Done in the chapter of Blessed Peter at Rennes, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1116, indiction 9, during the pontificate of Pope Paschal II, the reign of Louis [namely VI, son of Philip], king of the Franks, and the countship of the aforesaid Conan.

Place of the seal.

[APPENDIX TO HILDEBERT OF LE MANS.]

[Col. 1783]

SUPPLEMENT TO HILDEBERT’S CHARTERS. (After col. 324.) Confirmation by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, of the donation of the church of Saint Mary of Mayenne, made in 1125 to the monks of Marmoutier by John, priest of Mayenne.

(*History of the Lords of Mayenne*, by J.-B. Guyard de la Fosse, priest.—Le Mans, 1850, 12mo. Proofs, p. X.—Charters of Gehard.)

[Col. 1783A] Let all present and future persons know that a certain John, priest of Mayenne, moved by love of God and Saint Martin, approached Marmoutier together with Walter, then prior of Mayenne. There, in the presence of Lord William the abbot and the entire chapter, he most willingly confirmed the gift of the church of Saint Mary of Mayenne, which Robert Pavo, lord of that church, had long before made to the monks of Saint Martin, as the charter drawn up concerning it attests. He promised, to the best of his ability, to establish the claim of, defend, and secure that gift for Saint Martin against all adversaries. He also received from the lord abbot of Saint Martin the priestly benefice of the same church, which he had hitherto held from Robert Pavo, to possess and hold henceforth, entirely saving [Col. 1783B] his fealty and agreement with Robert Pavo. The agreement is as follows: for as long as Robert Pavo holds the aforesaid church in his own hand, Robert and John shall divide its revenues equally between them. But when Robert becomes a monk or dies, and that church comes into the monks’ hands, John shall confine himself solely to the priest’s share, namely: the monks shall receive two-thirds of the tithes and first-fruits, and John one-third. Throughout all the remaining time, however, John shall receive the whole offering, as is customary for other priests. Further, the lord abbot granted to John that, if he should have a son or clerical nephew who after the father’s death performed the office of the priestly benefice, that man, by the bishop’s counsel or out of favour for John, should hold for life from the monks the aforesaid church with its lands, houses, and other buildings pertaining to it. But if that kinsman were not a cleric but a layman, he should have only the land of Brionis, which belongs by right to the church; everything else—that is, the church with its appurtenances—would belong to the monks. Thus far concerning these matters.

Likewise, a dispute arose concerning the cemetery of the chapel of Mayenne between the monks of Saint Martin and the aforesaid John. The following settlement of peace and concord was reached. John, acknowledging that he had made an unjust claim against the monks concerning the aforesaid cemetery, willingly granted that the whole household of the lord of Mayenne—both knights and servants living from his bread and maintenance—provided that they reside in the parish [Col. 1784B] of Saint Mary, that is, have hearth and home there, shall, without any objection, receive from the monks’ chaplain all their due rites of confession and communion while living, and, when dead, shall be carried for burial to the chapel cemetery. Likewise, any other persons from all the surrounding parishes outside the parish of Saint Mary the mother church may have themselves carried to the chapel cemetery and buried without any claim being raised. But if any parishioner of Saint Mary comes to the aforesaid cemetery and asks to be buried there, then, preserving the due right of the mother church and with no one opposing, that person may have his wish fulfilled.

I, Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, have granted and signed this.

Judgment. In every judgment four persons ought to be present: accuser, defender, witness, and judge, 1397. Sinners are not to be condemned or shunned by private judgment, 1397. God preferred to prove the sin of the Sodomites rather than judge it, 376. At the last judgment there will be three ranks of persons: those to be judged, those judging, and those already judged, 284. Either by God at the judgment, or by ourselves in this life, we must be judged, [Col. 1802] 300. As each person is found at death, so that person will be judged, Section 107. A judge more readily pardons a few punishable offenses than many, 85. The more abundantly wicked will be punished more abundantly, 52. If we wish to be judged mercifully in respect of many evils, the judge ought to be softened by some good deeds, 18. At judgment an account will be required of three things: the image of God, redemption by Christ, and each person’s dignity, 218. Whoever assumes the person of judge, or even of adviser, must put off both friend and enemy, 971. We judge others’ affairs better than our own, 964. How rash judgment must be avoided, 112.

To swear. One who does not swear is farther from perjury than one who even swears justly, 165.

Law. Hildebert began, but did not finish, his Exceptions of Law, 124. It is probable that Ivo of Chartres borrowed them from him and subsequently completed them, 124, 161. Justification is twofold: the first makes a person just; the second is performed by a just person, 429. There are more justified persons in the Church than just persons, 580. Christ is just and justifying, not justified, 447. Justice is the constant and perpetual will to render to each person his due, 234. Justice is moderation in the desire for advantage, 1074. Justice is better than courage: its duties and degrees, 987. The two pillars of justice are courage and temperance, 962. Justice has two opposite vices, brutality and negligence, 974. God’s justice sometimes rages even against the elect, 323. The just person cannot be tranquil so long as he struggles with the flesh, 536. Above all, the just person ought to be peaceable, 799. The just have three blessednesses against the unjust person’s three deaths, 843. One who fears anything cannot be just, 965. Not even robbers can live among themselves without justice, 965. Justice is divided into severity and liberality, 965. A judge is condemned when a guilty person is acquitted by him, 966. As rewards proposed for virtue profit, so punishments proposed and threatened for crime profit by example, 131. The soul of the just person is God’s house, 656. How God, who is essentially everywhere, is truly said to be in the soul of the just person, 657.

## L

How great the power of tears is, 319. Their origin is fourfold: one’s own sins, the sins of others, exile from our homeland, and longing for it, 360. Tears are also to be shed in charity for one’s neighbors, 510. Tears of penitence are a second baptism, 510. They are equivalent to martyrdom, 552. The gift of tears should be sought from God, 846. One may rejoice on the way, but always between hope and fear, 479. Epitaph of Lanfranc, 1625. Christ’s death would have profited either thief, had they been willing, 370. The thief sought paradise in the very hour in which Adam departed from paradise, 370. On the cross the thief turned punishment into martyrdom, 318. In Christ’s Passion the thief was stronger than Peter, 482. The side signifies the union of flesh and soul, 581, 583. Praise. To be praised by the shameful is as disgraceful as to be praised for shameful things, 1493. Marbod’s poem on St. Lawrence, 1520. Monastic readings were formerly held in common in the cloister, 556. Why Christ touched the leper though he was unclean, 289. An ingenious comparison between the leper and the centurion, 292. The faith of both surpasses that of Lazarus’s sisters, 292. Leta cured by St. Magnobodus, 1481, 1501. Leudobaldus, priest of Angers, 1467. The old law was given to the Jews as the new law was given to the apostles, 487. Christ took up the legal observances so that, when these had been fulfilled, he might substitute the Gospel for them, 513. Neither natural law nor written law could save human beings, but Christ’s grace alone could, 557, 596. Christ’s law is the Christians’ mirror, 690. The new, or evangelical, law is commanded not to one people but to all, 1101. In the old law there were three things: promises, sacraments, and commandments, 1102. Some commandments were natural, others figurative, 1102. “Deliver us from evil,” that is, from the corruption and burden of the body, 584. What liberality is, 966. Excellent precepts for doing good, 966. An unwelcome word: “I ask,” 966. What harms the recipient should not be given, 966. You imitate God if you give even to the ungrateful, 967. God does good especially to the ungrateful, 967. Discernment is necessary in distributing benefits, 968.

[Col. 1803] Human freedom is threefold: that of nature, grace, and glory, 225. What free will is, 1078. Four matters to be considered in free will, 1079. Freedom is threefold: from necessity, from sin, and from misery, 1080. In what respect free will has been weakened by sin, 1082. A multitude of books distracts; it does not instruct, 997. The best method of reading books, 997. Through license we become worse, 992. Life of St. Licinius, commonly St. Lezin, 1417. And his miracles, 1424 ff. Moral allegories of the tree, 631. How carefully the tongue must be restrained, 434. The tongue’s various sins: in speaking evils and in keeping silent about good things, 577. We speak evils in six ways, 577. We speak good things in three ways, 577. One should be readier to listen than to speak, 985. God opens mouth and ears for good things; the devil, for evil things, 622. The monk has his tongue crucified, which Christ did not have, 823. The monastery of Lérins devastated by barbarians, 174. Hildebert alone among writers related this devastation; Baronius and Spondanus relied on his testimony, 172. Lawsuit. St. Magnobodus preferred to suffer loss rather than bring a lawsuit, 1504. The use of litanies in processions against Henry the heretic is defended, 114. Ingenious description of monastic places and moral application, 549. Lodevaeus is miraculously cured of blindness by St. Magnobodus, 1473. Lodovarus, the same person, 1498. Base gain must be avoided, 984. Recreation should be indulged in no otherwise than sleep and rest, 983. Two kinds of joking: refined and vulgar, 983. Luxury is the vice of a beast, 614. Humility and study preserve one from it, 615. How difficult victory over luxury is, 644. Luxury is most disgraceful in an old man, 983.

## M

Maccabees. Verses on the Maccabees, 1235, 1520. St. Mary Magdalene, Sermon 69. An outstanding prosopopoeia in her person addressed to Christ, 574. She is the woman from whom Christ cast out seven demons, 575. She appears to have doubted Christ’s divinity and to have loved Christ as a man, not yet as God, 579. Blessed Virgin Mary and Blessed Magdalene are for us the star of the sea, 580. How effective Magdalene’s intercession is for penitents, 580. Blessed Magdalene did not love many things greatly; rather, she loved one thing greatly. Therefore many things were forgiven her, 833. The Magi were not sorcerers, but Chaldean philosophers, 274. The duties of magnificence are partly peaceful and partly military, 998. Life and Miracles of St. Magnobodus, bishop of Angers, 1463. Another Life of the same by Marbod, 1490. A metrical history of Muhammad, 1277. God’s majesty and love of the world do not agree well, 534. Reginald, monk of Blessed Augustine, composed the history of Malchus, which does not survive, 180. Evil. Even evil persons approve better things, 962. Evil is of three kinds: one is fault; another is punishment and not fault; another is neither fault nor punishment, but leads to punishment, 1091. Christ’s commandment is called new because it extends to love of enemies, 420. Hand. What it means to swear by the seventh or eighth hand, 143 n. Encomium of Marbod, 1381. Marbod seems to have sprung from an illustrious family, 80. Perhaps the noble family of Marboeuf derives from him, 80. His quarrel with Raynald, bishop of Angers, 80. Most skilled in poetry, 113. Passion of St. Maurice and his companions by Marbod, 1535. To Matilda, queen of the English, 1534, 1567, 1566. Marbod’s verses that the death of the body is not to be feared, 1573. By the same, On the Good of Death, 1612. That one should not weep over the death of a Christian, 1578. On the difference of merits and places, 1579. Marbod’s verses on a prostitute, 1600. And on a matron, 1601. Blessed Mary was entirely cleansed from sin; in her the tinder of sin was wholly weakened, 1045. The Immaculate Conception of Blessed Mary is implied, 538. Blessed Mary is the rod; Christ, her son, is the flower, 263. She was a virgin before childbirth, in childbirth, and after childbirth, 264, 503, 523. [Col. 1804] When Hildebert was transferred to the see of Tours, he urged Guy, his successor in the bishopric of Le Mans, to celebrate Blessed Mary’s Assumption more solemnly, 524. Blessed Mary was assumed into heaven in body and soul, 527. Formerly, on the Assumption of Blessed Mary, the Church said a prayer other than the one it now says, 527. It was formerly customary to kneel at the name of Mary, 518. Blessed Mary gave birth to Christ without pain, 538. Her greatest joy in childbirth, 538. Mary’s betrothal is twofold: as mother of the Lord and as mother of the Son; of humanity and of the Church, 537. Mary, the gate closed forever, 370. Blessed Mary commends herself for humility, not for other virtues, 540. The higher Blessed Mary is, the humbler she is, 830. She was the model of holy virgins, especially nuns, 830. Metrical Life of Blessed Mary of Egypt, 1262. The monastery of Marsinay was founded for women by St. Hugh, 919. He brought there the arm of St. Agnes and other relics, 919. The royal church of St. Martin was adorned with many privileges from supreme pontiffs, 154. Formerly a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, 154. Hildebert commends it to the supreme pontiff, 134, 135 n. Abbot Martin miraculously heals a blind girl, 482, 1101. Martyrdom. All ought to be prepared for martyrdom at least in intention, but monks especially, 551. Therefore blood and water came forth from Christ’s side, 552. The shedding of tears is equivalent to martyrdom, 552. St. Germanus was a martyr in will, 552. Not even martyrdom itself avails one who hates a brother, 508. The marvelous battle of unarmed martyrs, but their victory more marvelous still, 565. Faithful martyrs can be killed, but cannot be bent, 607. No one becomes a martyr without great merit of virtues, 614. Martyrdom without charity is nothing, 630. There are two kinds of martyrdom, hidden and manifest, as also of sacrifice, 766. The Mathematician against astrologers, 1295. Matilda, the most devout wife of King Henry I, consecrated queen by St. Anselm, 15, 38. The story of her cursing her children is rejected, 38. She died in 1118, 124. Another Matilda, thought to have been the wife of William, son of Henry I, who was drowned, and afterwards an abbess, 43. Matildis or Mathilda, daughter of Matilda, wife of Henry I, king of the English, 153. Educated among the nuns of Winchester, 153. Called “most excellent and most Christian” by Aelred of Rievaulx, 153 and 179. Hildebert’s verses to Matilda, queen of the English, 1334. Medicine, commerce, and architecture are honorable arts, 983. The subject of meditation is fourfold: what one was, so that one may hope; what one is, so that one may grieve; what one would be, so that one may fear; what one will be, so that one may rejoice, 584. The identity of the bishop of Memoriensis praised by Hildebert is considered, 124. Liars are children of the devil, 685. Four kinds of tables in Holy Scripture, 553. Daedalus, inventor of the table, 553. Elegant denunciation of superfluous luxury in tables, 564. These are immense things rather than tables, 564. Moral and ingenious explanation of superfluous tables, 554. What *meridae* and *margaritae* signify concerning the holy Eucharist among the Greeks, 96. Merit. A good will suffices for merit if the ability to act is lacking, 163, 342. What the merit of the foundation is, and how certain lukewarm persons are saved by the merit of the foundation, 313. The widow and Zacchaeus have equal merit because their wills are equal, 341. No one merits except while in the body, 773. What are the arms of Christian warfare, 792. To be unable to show mercy belongs to beasts, 159. God’s mercy must not be abused, 217. There are seven bodily works of mercy, 428. God’s mercy is in part great and in part small: what their daughters are, 428. The same mercy is great, greater, and greatest, 428. Daily celebration of Mass in Hildebert’s time, 597, 706. Those for whom prayer is offered in Mass, 1117. No one should sit during Mass; all should stand, 1118. With what intention the faithful should offer their temporal goods to priests for Mass, [Col. 1805] 1118. A priest ought not celebrate alone, 1118. Certain words which were in the old Canon but are not in the new, 1118. The sending of the Word into the world, 247, 252, 261.

Monk. How severe the temptations that assail a good monk are, 34. Outstanding description of pseudo-monks, 35. Reform of monks is difficult, 91. Monastic perfection is not acquired without much labor, 196. Remembrance of the monastic profession is a safe refuge against temptations, 196. How dangerous for a monk is the recollection of past pleasures, 196. Many monks bear the cross, but, like Simon of Cyrene, under compulsion, and therefore without fruit, 352. How dangerous curiosity and excessive diffusion toward outward things are to a monk, 397. Praise of monastic life and denunciation of monastic failings, 430, 570, 660. Ingenious description and moral application of cloistral or monastic places, 549. Every Christian, but especially a monk, ought to be prepared for martyrdom at least in intention, 551. The various illnesses of monks caused by their exercises must be endured for merit, 570. Especially those caused by standing in choir, 570. Monastic failings are described, 570. But especially their murmuring against one another, 570. Various temptations of monks, 571. How they must be repelled, 572. Their ambition is reproved, 572, 584. The regular exercise is fourfold: divine, weekly, intermittent, continuous, 584–585. Praise of monastic life, 579. Like Peter, the monk ought to have three names, 579. The various ailments of monks from their exercises and from their prolonged standing in choir, 579. Monks’ murmuring against one another, 579. The monk’s four occupations: reading, prayer, meditation, and regular exercise, 584. A monk is bound by two chains: profession and love of his Order, 584–585. The lukewarm monk is Simon of Cyrene, compelled to carry the cross, 585. Monks ought to merit not for themselves alone but also for others, especially their benefactors, 647, 653. Samuel, first patriarch of cenobites, 652. Monasteries are sometimes located in cities for the benefit of laypeople, not monks, 660. Dialogue between a layman dissuading a monk from his profession and a monk persevering in it, 605. How great is the happiness of cenobites or monks already in this life, 797. Among monks nothing is more disgraceful than litigation, 800. Above all, a monk ought to be peaceable, 799. Monks ought to forget earthly things and long for heavenly things, 800. A professed monk may not turn back, 806. Monks who are poor by compulsion rather than in mind are by no means blessed, 806. Constrained monks are Cyrenians who carry the cross only in anguish, 807. How dead Benedictine monks ought to be to the world, 811. They should not excuse themselves from regular exercises, 812. What the exercises of true monks are, 812. The three sources of monastic tears: one’s own sins, neighbors’ sins, and longing for the heavenly homeland, 812. It is not place but action that makes a monk, 818. Hildebert addresses black monks, 818. But whom could these then be except Benedictines? 818. Monasteries are God’s gardens, in which he walks, 820. Four virtues are necessary to the monastic order: charity, humility, obedience, and discipline, 827. It is abominable for pride to lurk beneath a black—that is, humble—garment, 831. Four mountains surround the Church, 601. What delay is, and what it is to delay, 546. The derivation and meaning of *mora* and *morari*, 548. Our body is a horse to be tamed, 794. By continual mortification of the senses, the saints are finally unmoved by sensory pleasures, 872. How necessary mortification of the flesh is to every Christian, 480.

Death. Dead. Each person’s death is that person’s day of the Lord, 344. How the dead bury their dead, 391, 414. Christ raised three dead persons, in different ways and places, signifying three kinds of persons dead through sin, 391, 412. Why Christ did not wish to raise a fourth dead person, 413. The wicked person dies amid a mass of vices; the just person, amid a mass of merits, 429. One who brings death upon oneself wrongs God, 581, 585. As each person is found at death, so that person will be judged, 773. Each person’s death is, for that person, the day of the Lord, 346. We and all that is ours are owed to death; therefore we ought wholly to entrust our life to God, 971. A human being enters life on the condition of leaving it; therefore death is not to be feared, 976. In necessity, death must be preferred to disgrace, 976. One who reaches the furthest limit of fate dies old, 977. “We are all driven toward the same end . . . sooner or later the lot must come forth,” 988. We die daily, 990. Death is due to the flesh of sin, 1084. Moses philosophized with God on the mountain for forty days and forty nights, 584.

[Col. 1806] How dangerous familiarity with women is, 1353. Contempt for the world cannot endure without courage and temperance, especially without humility, 8. This world is a true dung-heap, 232, 600. How vain this world’s prosperity is, 757. There are three things in the world to be hated, 769. In this world there are four reasons for groaning, 798. Love of the world is sweet at first and bitter at the end, 76. Love of God, conversely, 76.

Nannersus is freed from a demon by St. Magnobodus, 1474, 1499. There are four modes of birth: without a mother, like Eve; without father and mother, like Adam; from father and mother, like all people; from a mother without a father, like Christ, 420. Christ’s Nativity is the Church’s marriage feast, 259. Hildebert’s verses on the Nativity of the Lord: “The sun [is] today for us,” 1359. Idleness destroys nature’s good; diligence restores it, 697. The sisters Nederia and Theodechildis are freed from blindness by St. Magnobodus, 1482, 1501. Negligence, a vice opposed to justice, 974. What its causes are, 974. The occupations of business are diverse, 983. What befits prelates and what private persons, 983. The church of St. Nicholas at Angers was dedicated by Urban II, 661. Hildebert preaches there, 661. Christ’s commandment concerning love is called new because it extends even to enemies, which was not so in the old Law, Sermon 34. Threefold night in this world: the devil, the present life, and sin, 270. Coin. How one serves coin, 1626. How one who serves coin is deceived, 1627. Marriage. ## O

How great a good obedience is, 407. It is the shorter path to perfection, 481. Through obedience, the crucifixion of the whole person ought to take place, 481. Description of monastic obedience, 481. Obedience is sometimes to be preferred even to one’s vow, 49. More pleasing to God than sacrifices themselves, 104. Disobedience has often involved the innocent with the guilty in punishment, 104. To Odo, bishop of Bayeux, 1333. Marbod’s verses to Odo, simultaneously bishop and count, 1623. Office. How dangerous negligence concerning the divine office is, 509. Oil. Even what is promised to the elect by God is obtained only through prayers and merits, 36, 58.

[Col. 1807] What a good prayer is, 217. True prayer is a bitter groan with compunction, 217. One who does not cease to love does not cease to pray, 217. Confession should precede prayer, 459. Prayer without fasting and almsgiving is not true prayer; for these are its two wings to heaven, 460. How the heart’s cry is made in prayer, 462. One must ask urgently and perseveringly, 462, 466. One who does not cease to do good does not cease to pray, 462. How the four kinds of prayer are distinguished, 465. A mind accustomed to wander among external things returns to itself only with difficulty in order to pray, 466. For prayer to obtain its request, it must have three things: asking, seeking, and knocking, 466. One asks wrongly who asks for things not conducive to salvation, 467. To ask for an enemy’s death is mad prayer, 467. Forgiveness of injuries is the chief condition of prayer, 467. Origin of Rogation Days, 461. How the four kinds of prayer—supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings—are distinguished, 465. God awaits and requires our urgency or perseverance in prayer, 465. For prayer to obtain its request, three things are necessary: prayer, a good life, and perseverance, 465. Prayer is a sweet vehicle on the way, a faithful forerunner to God, 499. The seven hills by which we reach God are the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer, 499. Prayer ought to be modest, pure, ample, and devout, 584. A louder voice is not necessary for prayer, 1114. Why there is a secret prayer in Mass, 1114. Let the heart be raised upward, lest it rot upon the earth, 1115. Why those praying turn to the east, just as the feet of the dead are turned, 822. Ask nothing of God that you could not ask openly, 971. Hildebert’s prosodic and most devout prayer to the three Persons of the most holy Trinity, 1337. Three prayers of Marbod: to the Father, to the Son, and to God, 1557. His prayer to St. Mary, 1559. Prayer of a penitent who has fallen often, 1574. Two prayers for the dead, 1577, 1578. Why one ordained offers a candle with both hands to the pope who ordains him, 677. Origen’s error is noted and refuted, 213, 304. Evil external adornment is an indication of an evil mind, 189. Ostropius, count of Angers, or Austropius, 896.

## P
Palatine clerics, 1493. The palm in Scripture, a symbol of victory, 387. Procession of Palms on Sunday, 385. Why Christ on this occasion alone employed the equipment of beasts of burden, 389. Four kinds of differently baked bread were offered in the Law: what they signify, 361. Why the pope wears a red mantle, 804. The earthly Paradise: where it was located, 1070. Why the tree of life is so called, 1070. On the Virgin’s Childbirth: the Sun and water, 1332. The ancient, or Jewish, Paschal rite compared with the Christian Passover, 455. Great things may be understood from small ones, 1996. Pastor. A pastor who censures the vices of others while neglecting his own is guilty, 115. It belongs to a good pastor to be ashamed at the shame of his subjects, 106. In pastoral government, it is neither lawful to seek those who do not call, nor lawful to cast aside those who do call, 159 n. At judgment pastors must render account to God for three things: their faith, their ministry, and their office, 663. The hired pastor demands two things from the sheep, milk and wool: milk, by which he feeds himself rather than them; wool, that is, the reverence which he ought not to seek, 666. Pastors should imitate Christ in caring for the paralytic lowered before him through the roof, 667. The pastor should provide opportunely for those willing, and importunately for those unwilling, even at risk to his temporal goods and his life, 668. Good pastors become more glorious through insults and injuries, 671. The hired man is impatient of labor, 671. Good pastors should cultivate discriminating severity, 672. [Col. 1808] They must consider four things: dignity, duty, caution, and steadfastness, 673. The remarkable dignity of pastors and their remarkable danger, discussed at length, 274. How great the diligence of a good pastor must be in difficult matters, 675. A pastor stretches out his hands to God in vain if he does not stretch out his hand to the poor, 676. Let them not love to be feared, except by those who do not fear God, 694. Let them be equal to the good and rule over the wicked, 694. Nature did not set human beings over human beings, but fault did, 694. A pastor must mingle gentleness with severity and severity with gentleness, 695. How culpable pastoral negligence is, and how vain its excuse, 696. Pastors are the luminaries of the Church, 853. Among them are the greater luminary and the lesser luminary, 853. What was the error of the Patarines or Paterenes, 1393. God’s patience must not be abused, 217. What patience is and what its duties are, 981. ## Q

God is to be sought not elsewhere but within ourselves, 777. The five outward senses must be guarded most diligently in order to preserve innocence, 305.

Rabetius, bishop of Séez, 102. Saint Radegund: her lineage and homeland, 887. She is taken captive, 102; her upbringing, 888. Even as a child she was merciful to the poor; a cleric assigned to her to carry a cross before her, 889. She had no artifice in her countenance, 889. She longs for martyrdom, 889. Married to King Chlothar, 890. She lived for virtue and the kingdom, not for pleasure, 890. Her charity toward every sort of poor person, 890. She especially venerates priests, 890. She establishes a hospice of the altar, where she herself ministers to the poor, 890. How piously and chastely she preserved herself in marriage, 891. She restrains lawful pleasure by voluntary suffering, 891. How austerely she spent Lent, 892. She provides magnificently for sacred altars and attends most devoutly upon the mysteries, 892. She is illustrious for miracles, 903, 905. By prayer she raises a dead woman, 905. Her remarkable poverty and humility are compensated by a miracle, 906. By divine revelation she foreknows and foretells her death, 907. She dies happily, 907. The miracle of the oats, which are said to have suddenly grown when the holy queen hid herself: highly doubtful, 908. Radulf, dean of Tours, is accused by the mutilated Nicholas, 143 ff. He is cleared, 144. Nicholas, who had appealed to Rome, is murdered on the road while going there, 144. Raingarolis, mother of Saint Robert, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, 1433. Ranulf or Randulf, bishop of Durham, promoted by William Rufus, king of England, 169. Reason presides over all virtues, 5. Raynald of Martigné, illegitimately elected bishop of Angers, 81. His inauguration is called not consecration but execration by Hildebert, as also by Geoffrey of Vendôme. Saint Bernard used the same word in a similar case, 82 n. Hildebert writes to him on this matter: Epistles 5 and 6, book 2, pp. 83, 85. Hildebert summons him back to attend Raynald’s consecration, 83. He tries, but in vain, to deter him from his election, 85. Raynald is consecrated by Ralph, metropolitan of Tours, against the canons, 81. Eventually Raynald becomes Hildebert’s friend, 103, 173. He is praised by Hildebert, 178. Various ways of departing from God, 309, 323. A mind accustomed to wander among outward things returns to itself and gathers itself together only with difficulty, 466. Six ways of returning good for evil, 592. Reginald, a regular canon, is called by Hildebert a monk of Blessed Augustine, 180. He wrote a history of Melch, which does not survive, 180. Hildebert’s closest friend, 180. The region of dissimilarity, 19, 222, 268, 277. Its prince is the devil, 309. On it, 311, 312, 417, 768, 772, 779, and elsewhere passim. Against offenders, example is more effective than the sword, 38. What religion is and its various duties, 971. True religion consists in two things: compassion and innocence, 227. In religious persons, secular people attend to the dung placed around the fig tree, not to its fruitfulness, 804. Relics of saints employed for the dedication of churches, 1446, 1493. History of Saint Renatus, raised from the dead after seven years by Saint Mauricius, bishop of Angers, and later bishop of Angers himself, 1552. Rencho, monk and first procurator of Menat, appointed by Saint Hugh, 919. Some things are for enjoyment, others for use: things for enjoyment, such as God, belong to the blessed; things for use make blessed those who are tending toward blessedness, 1027. According to Plato, things have three principles—matter, form, and maker; according to faith, one only, namely God, 1053. Spiritual and bodily creatures were created simultaneously by God, 1054. [Col. 1812] King, Queen. The duty of a good and just king, 6. An outstanding example of a perfect queen, 5. Clemency is especially becoming to kings, 5. The duty of a Christian and most excellent ruler, 49. He must punish rapacious ministers, 49. With what reverence kings must be reproved, 136. How reverently Hildebert himself complains of a king who had not offended him, 138. An excellent method, used by Hildebert in adversity, of appeasing kings, 136. A royal hand is more splendid through a gift than through a sceptre, 93. Under the Old Law kings and priests were anointed, but as a figure of Christ, 713. Origin of the Rogation Days, 462. Abstinence from meat during them, 463, 468. Reason for their institution, 462. Their origin in a decree of the bishops assembled at Vienne, to restrain plague, curb the madness of wolves, and so forth, 469. Roger or Rogerius, bishop of Salisbury, called “the Great,” 91. A multiplicity of ecclesiastical dignities is wrongly attributed to him, 91. He is justly praised by Hildebert, 93. He attends the Council of London, 1102. Although only invested, 1102. Holy Saturday: why it was free from the station, 382. How lamentable are priests entangled in temporal affairs, 69. The threefold table in Sacred Scripture: Law, Gospel, heaven, 395. Scripture is a mirror, safeguard, and table, 400. In the Scriptures the book is fourfold, 217. # ORDER OF THE MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

[Col. 1819] THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT, BISHOP OF LE MANS.

Dedicatory letter, 9. Preface to the new edition, 17. Preface of Dom Beaugendre, 45. Life of the venerable Hildebert, 63. Deeds of the venerable Hildebert, 89.
