# HILDEBERT’S LETTERS

## BOOK ONE
EP. I.—To Master William of Champeaux.—He congratulates him on his conversion from secular to Christian philosophy, the perfection of which he promises him, provided only that he fears nothing and hopes for nothing; meanwhile he urges him not to cease from fulfilling the office of master or preacher. 141

EP. II.—To Archbishop A.—He sends his friend a fan, whose mystical meaning he ingeniously and devoutly suggests to him. 143

EP. III.—To Countess A.—He praises Countess Adela for her outstanding prudence in governing the peoples entrusted to her by her absent husband, and especially commends to her clemency toward them. 144

EP. IV.—To a Certain Countess.—This letter appears to be addressed to Countess Adela, wife of Stephen, Count of Blois, who, after her husband’s death, consecrated herself to God by a monastic vow. Applauding her, Hildebert offers excellent counsels against the temptations threatening her on every side; and, that she may deserve to obtain the grace of perseverance in the struggle she has undertaken, he especially commends humility to her—“the consummation and crowning conclusion of the other virtues,” as he says. 145

EP. V.—To an Illustrious Widow.—He congratulates her because, abandoning her plan of pilgrimage to the Lord’s tomb, she preferred, having renounced all things, to take up Christ’s cross in a monastery rather than visit his tomb. 148

EP. VI.—To Countess Adela.—He congratulates this widow, formerly brought up amid the delights of court, on her marriage to Christ—undoubtedly by monastic profession. Hildebert most kindly exhorts her not to lose heart because of her former, perhaps somewhat freer, life in the world; for he maintains that penitents can please God as righteous persons, and widows as virgins. He also supplies her with various Scriptural counsels against the temptations threatening her. 149

EP. VII.—To Queen M. of the English.—He congratulates Princess Matilda on her marriage to the king of the English—undoubtedly Henry I. He urges her to render sincere thanks to God, the giver of all good things, and to use temporal goods the more moderately because the righteous Judge will demand a stricter account of them. 153

EP. VIII.—He deals with a friend, apparently recently appointed to some ecclesiastical dignity, concerning the seriousness and dangers of avarice; and gracefully commends him because, generously refusing gold, silver, and other gifts offered for God’s sake, he has presented God with a most pleasing sacrifice. 156

EP. IX.—To Queen M. of the English.—Matilda, queen of the English—the very same woman mentioned in the preceding letter—had sent Hildebert as a gift two finely wrought golden candlesticks. He praises her generosity; and, thanking her, ingeniously indicates both how meritorious it is for each person, according to his or her condition, to cooperate in the divine mysteries, and what spiritual benefit he himself derives from so precious a gift. 160

EP. X.—To Widow A.—He congratulates a certain illustrious widow on her contempt for the world; offers her various means both for overcoming temptation and for spiritual progress; and raises her spirit to perseverance by hope of eternal rewards. 162

EP. XI.—To the Monks Who Refused to Receive the Bishop of Chartres.—Hildebert first teaches them that even the more rigorous exercises of monastic life profit nothing without humility and mercy—virtues which, he laments, they lacked when they refused to receive the bishop of Chartres as a guest, though they ought not merely to have invited him, but even to have drawn him in by the expenditure of sacred furnishings. He then magnifies by the examples of Lot and Abraham the merit of hospitality, and exhorts those monks more diligently to practice it.

[Col. 1820]

168

EP. XII.—To King Henry.—He consoles Henry, namely Henry I, king of the English, concerning the grievous drowning of his children, and by an excellent description of the truly wise man strengthens his mind for constancy. Further, he elegantly proves that true human happiness lies not in things around a person, but in things within that person; to cling to and reverence these alone is to reflect God’s image in us. 172

EP. XIII.—To a Certain Converted Girl.—With exultation he warns a nun steadfast in her holy purpose to beware of flesh and woman, as of accumulated weakness, and likewise of certain women whose proximity, he says, is a bold enticement. 178

EP. XIV.—To the Queen of the English, That Since She Lacks Children She Should Make Christ’s Poor Her Heirs.—Adela, wife of Henry I, king of England, had earnestly requested Hildebert to make her a participant in the prayers and pious works of the Church of Le Mans. He permanently granted this to her as a daughter of that Church, warning her, in place of the children she lacked, to adopt Christ’s poor; and not to cease, as she had begun and had done, to support the monks dedicated to her in the monastery of Saint Vincent. 179

EP. XV.—To the Count of Anjou.—Hildebert does not indeed disapprove of sacred pilgrimages, but he places them, even when undertaken by vow and under whatever pretext, far below the duties imposed upon each estate by divine providence. Accordingly, he dissuades this count from the then already very celebrated distant pilgrimage to Saint James, maintaining that it would be far more useful, setting that pilgrimage aside, to devote himself wholly to governing according to right the peoples subject to him. He supplies him with altogether excellent means of fulfilling this office properly. 181

EP. XVI.—He sharply reproaches a certain wealthy but unscrupulous courtier for his abuse of riches and power, and attempts, by setting divine severity before his eyes, to call him back to repentance. 183

EP. XVII.—A Letter of Consolation.—To a friend who, after becoming extremely powerful at the royal court through the king’s favor, was later reduced to the greatest distress by the king’s displeasure. 186

EP. XVIII.—In this letter Hildebert greets Adela, wife of Henry I, king of England, as she is preparing to cross from Normandy to England, and consoles her concerning barrenness, maintaining that no remedy is more effective for her than charity and generosity toward the poor. 189

EP. XIX.—Consolation to a Nun, That in Adversity She Should Glory in Her Conscience.—He consoles a nun attacked by calumnies from certain persons of utterly bad character and, apparently, unjustly expelled by them even from her own monastery. He raises her mind to endurance through the testimony of a good conscience and the example of holy women, meanwhile pledging himself to be the advocate of her innocence before the supreme pontiff, namely Innocent II. 191

EP. XX.—He congratulates the monks of Saint Cuthbert of Durham that their ways and pursuits are becoming good; meanwhile he requests their prayers, offering his own for them in return at the altar where, he says, the Son is sacrificed to the Father. 192

EP. XXI.—To Athalisa, a Recluse.—He congratulates her on her purpose of virginity, the praise of which he elegantly develops; and he maintains that this state is far superior to that of married women or widows, provided that it is supported by humility. 193

EP. XXII.—To William, Abbot of Saint Vincent.—William, having been made abbot, lamented that the best part of contemplation had been taken from him. Hildebert consoles him as a friend with numerous testimonies from Scripture, especially the examples of Rachel and Leah, proving that it is no slight good alternately to pursue contemplation and action; meanwhile he laments the idleness of those who strive to attend to neither—something he himself humbly deplores of himself. 197

EP. XXIII.—A certain archimandrite had consulted Hildebert concerning a most grievous temptation of the flesh, by which a demon harassed one of his monks, especially during prayer. In this letter Hildebert explains what he thinks of this temptation and what remedies he judges should be used. 203

EP. XXIV.—To a Certain Friend, Perhaps a Benefactor of His Church.—That brute animals in some manner accuse the ungrateful. 205

EP. XXV.—He teaches his friend the difference between love of God and love of the world. 206

## BOOK TWO

EP. I.—To Archdeacon G.—That no woman may marry a man whose brother she previously married, even if no carnal union occurred. 207

EP. II.—Hildebert urges the bishop of Sées not to permit the marriage mentioned in the preceding letter to be completed. 207

EP. III.—To a Bishop.—A certain canon had requested Hildebert’s assistance with the bishop of Anjou, so that he might be allowed to substitute his nephew in his canonry. Hildebert informs him what he had done on his behalf and what obstacles he had encountered in this affair; at the same time, he instructs him by what means he can obtain this favor from the bishop and canons opposing him. 209

EP. IV.—To the Archbishop of Tours.—He advises the archbishop not to consecrate a young man who was not canonically elected. 210

EP. V.—To R. of Anjou.—He attempts to dissuade Raynald, elected bishop of Anjou contrary to the canons, from accepting the episcopate. 211

EP. VI.—He continues to deter the same Raynald, bishop-elect of Anjou and now about to be consecrated, from receiving sacred anointing. 213

EP. VII.—To the Bishop of Sées.—He praises the bishop of Sées for stoutly defending the right of asylum in the Church, which, on the testimony of Saint Augustine, ought to be kept inviolate. 213

EP. VIII.—To John and Benedict.—Hildebert excuses himself before John and Benedict, cardinals of the Holy Roman Church and legates of Pope Paschal II, for being unable to attend the council summoned by them at Poitiers, being overwhelmed by excessive calamities inflicted by the consuls of Le Mans. 215

EP. IX.—To Archbishop Anselm.—At the Council of Bari in 1098, in the presence of Pope Urban II, Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, had excellently refuted the Greek error concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. Hildebert asks him not to disdain committing to writing, for the Church’s benefit, the arguments he had presented orally in the disputation. 216

EP. X.—To the Prior of Chartres.—He congratulates him on reforming for the better monks who had fallen away from their original zeal for regular observance, and movingly exhorts him diligently to complete what he has commendably begun. 217

EP. XI.—From Saint Anselm to Hildebert.—Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, to Lord Hildebert, his venerable fellow bishop of Le Mans: temporal and eternal salvation. 218

EP. XII.—To Roger, Bishop of Salisbury.—Hildebert congratulates him, apparently recently promoted to the bishopric of Salisbury, and commends to him the outstanding gifts for service to the Church of Guy, who later succeeded him in the Church of Le Mans. 219

EP. XIII.—Hildebert thanks Saint Anselm for undertaking the treatise *On the Holy Spirit*, which he had requested from him in the preceding letter. 220

EP. XIV.—To the Archbishop of Rouen.—Hildebert denies that any marriage can be legitimate, under whatever pretext, between blood relatives or relatives by marriage. 221

EP. XV.—He attempts to recall a certain abbot, excessively devoted to an overly elegant style, to a simpler mode of speech, and likewise from an ancient custom received in his monastery, whereby Eucharistic bread was offered to communicants only when dipped. 222

EP. XVI.—To C., Bishop of Palestrina.—He congratulates the bishop of Palestrina, namely Cardinal Conon, legate of the supreme pontiff throughout East and West, on his unconquered integrity in ecclesiastical affairs, and exhorts him to perseverance. 224

EP. XVII.—Although Hildebert movingly sets before all the children of the Church the injury inflicted upon the Church by the treacherous imprisonment of his own person by Count Rotrou and his steward Humbert, he nevertheless declares with apostolic vigor that the liberty of the Church, which he judges would be harmed by a monetary ransom for himself, must be preferred to his own life. He maintains that it would be unworthy for him, redeemed once by Christ’s blood, to be redeemed for any price. 225

EP. XVIII.—He complains, in friendly but moving terms, to the bishop of Sées that he abandons him in chains without comfort; and urges him to strike Hubert, steward of Count Rotrou, who variously torments him in prison, with the sword of anathema. 227

EP. XIX.—To R., Bishop of Anjou.—He remits to the bishop of Anjou, namely his own bishop, for punishment a priest who had consecrated ordinary bread owing to lack of unleavened bread—rather for scandal than for the offense itself.

[Col. 1822]

228

EP. XX.—Having repeatedly and gently urged an ecclesiastic to reform his conduct and discharge his office, he had sung to a deaf man. In this letter he reproaches him more sharply for negligence and hardness of heart, and threatens to deal more severely with him unless he repents, lest he himself be accused of having placed a cushion beneath his elbow. 229

EP. XXI.—In this letter to a friend, he bitterly laments the injuries inflicted with extreme violence by Henry V, emperor of the Romans, upon Pope Paschal II, the entire Roman clergy, and people, when, after imprisoning and cruelly tormenting the pope with all the clergy, he unjustly and violently extorted from him the right of investitures. 232

EP. XXII.—Taken by force and deceit by Emperor Henry V, Paschal II at first stoutly resisted the emperor’s attempt, by whatever threats, even of death, to exact the right of investitures. Yet, moved by the prayers of the cardinals and leading men of the Roman people detained and cruelly tormented by the emperor, he unwillingly conceded that right to him. But as soon as he recovered his freedom, he revoked in its entirety whatever had been extorted from him by violent force. Hildebert relates this in this apologetic letter. 233

EP. XXIII.—In this letter he attacks a certain heretic who, like Vigilantius of old, assailed the invocation of saints. He pursues him all the more fiercely because this heretic had more shamelessly dared to assert that Hildebert shared his opinion. 237

EP. XXIV.—Cyprian and Peter, clerics, had imprudently adhered to Henry, a notorious heresiarch. When they repented and, at Hildebert’s persuasion, returned to sounder doctrine, he commends them to all the clergy as sincerely Catholic. 242

EP. XXV.—He describes to Gerard, legate of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Angoulême, the corrupt condition of the monastery of Évron near Le Mans, caused by the incompetence and stupidity of its abbot, and asks what should be done under Gerard’s authority for its reform. 243

EP. XXVI.—To R. of Anjou.—He warns the bishop of Anjou concerning a certain Lisiard, unjustly struck by him with anathema for the alleged abduction of Geoffrey’s daughter. Since that abduction is not even plausible, he proves rather that a lawful marriage took place between them, because the free consent of both was present. 244

EP. XXVII.—To the Bishop of Memoria [possibly uncertain].—To a certain bishop, thought to have been English, who had commended the soul of a deceased queen to Hildebert’s prayers, he promises not to fail in the duty of gratitude and charity. He also promises to send him the excerpts from decrees which he had begun to collect as soon as he had put the finishing touch to them. 245

EP. XXVIII.—To Bishop Gerard.—William of Longeio, or Lonleio, having communicated with a certain Hugh excommunicated by Gerard, had fallen from Gerard’s favor, but through Hildebert’s intervention had returned to it. Nevertheless, fearing that Gerard, not forgetting the forgiven injury, might again harass William, Hildebert earnestly requests confirmation of the pardon granted. 247

EP. XXIX.—He congratulates the bishop of the Church of Clermont on bestowing the archdeaconry upon William, an outstanding man; and he expresses astonishment that hereditary succession in ecclesiastical dignities and canonries had gained force there. He urges him to root it out entirely as wholly contrary to the precepts of law and grace. 248

EP. XXX.—To Pope Honorius.—Shortly after his translation from the bishopric of Le Mans to the archbishopric of Tours, Hildebert, striving to eradicate various abuses discovered in Armorica, which was subject to him as metropolitan, summoned a council at Nantes in 1127 with his suffragan bishops. He earnestly requests Pope Honorius to confirm its statutes. 253

EP. XXXI.—In this letter Pope Honorius II confirms all that, by the preceding letter, he had learned was done by Hildebert and his suffragans at the Council of Nantes. 254

EP. XXXII.—Hildebert intercedes with Pope Honorius II for the canons of Saint Martin, who had incurred his displeasure while defending the rights of their church. 255

EP. XXXIII.—In this letter, which seems almost an encyclical since it is addressed to no one by name, Hildebert complains that, while he is variously harassed by the king of France for the Church’s rights, all abandon him without help or comfort—especially those whose office obliged them to defend those rights with him. Yet he judges that what is just should be represented to the king neither harshly nor obstinately, but gently and with reverence due to royal dignity. Moreover, he says that in his afflictions he will cast his care upon the Lord, whose help, as in the cases of Joseph and David, he will never despair of receiving. 256

EP. XXXIV.—He beseeches the apostolic legate to endeavor to reconcile him to the king of France, from whom he has suffered much for the Church’s rights.

[Col. 1823]

257

EP. XXXV.—He petitions the supreme pontiff not to grant the pallium and its use to the bishops of Dol, namely his suffragans, since it had most recently been granted personally by the pope to Baudry alone, now deceased, and not to the Church of Dol. 258

EP. XXXVI.—He informs Pope Honorius II of a grave affront credulously as well as shamefully inflicted upon his canon; tells him what he has done in the matter; and asks him what the supreme pontiff himself judges should henceforth be done. 259

EP. XXXVII.—He announces that, at the supreme pontiff’s recommendation, he has restored to a penitent named Bracerius the prebend which he had lost through the enormity of his fault. He also reports what he himself has again done in the case of Dean Ralph and Canon Nicholas, and what Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the Roman Church, has decided; asking the pope finally to put the finishing touch, by apostolic authority, to this affair, which had grievously disturbed the Church of Tours itself. 260

EP. XXXVIII.—He again complains before the supreme pontiff that he is variously harassed by the king of France, especially because, by episcopal right, he had provided his church with a dean and archdeacon other than those named by the king, on account of their unfitness. He further relates what he did in the dispute between Dean Ralph and Canon Nicholas, who, as he asserted, had been shamefully mutilated by the dean’s brother and on the dean’s advice. 262

EP. XXXIX.—Hildebert earnestly commends to his friend Ralph, dean of Tours, unjustly harassed by certain wicked men. 263

EP. XL.—Hildebert excuses himself before Pope Honorius II for being unable to complete the affair concerning the marriage of Hugh of Crécy entrusted to him, both because one party resisted and because the king of France summoned him to his son’s coronation. 264

EP. XLI.—With truly episcopal freedom but the greatest reverence, Hildebert explains to the supreme pontiff how dangerous it is to the Church and good morals for all appeals whatsoever to be indiscriminately admitted at the Roman curia. 265

EP. XLII.—As patron of the monastery of Fontevraud, Hildebert requests Pope Honorius II to confirm a certain alms granted to it by Henry, king of the English, and payable yearly from England. 267

EP. XLIII.—Hildebert judges that it is not lawful for a priest to kill a robber intending to kill him, even when the latter actually attacks him with armed hand; but he states this in such a way that, in a like case, he judges it safer to consult the supreme pontiff. 267

EP. XLIV.—From Saint Bernard to Hildebert.—This letter of the most holy abbot proves how highly Saint Bernard esteemed Hildebert and what weight he judged his support to have in the Church’s greatest affair. In it he movingly and effectively calls upon him, as a great pillar of the Church, to support the cause of Innocent II against Anacletus. From this the reader will also perceive almost at a glance how affectionately Saint Bernard dealt with Hildebert. 268

EP. XLV.—Jerome disapproves of a virgin’s leaving her monastery anywhere, especially alone, and above all on feast days, when crowds of people are generally greater. He sharply attacks those women who seek lodging with lay people in order to live more freely without overseers. 269

EP. XLVI.—To Henry, King of the English.—Hildebert familiarly explains the state of his health to Henry I, king of the English, and thanks him because, at his recommendation, the king of France had restored to him, though with great reluctance, a certain provostship of the Church of Tours which the French king had held for four years. 272

EP. XLVII.—Before the supreme pontiff he complains bitterly, though affectionately, that the pope had absolved clerics justly excommunicated by him without consulting him, and had restored them to lost dignities. Meanwhile he beseeches him to allow him freely to possess and exercise his episcopal right in his diocese. 273

EP. XLVIII.—To Archdeacon William.—He suspends from an order wrongly received a cleric who had simoniacally obtained the diaconate, and forbids him to receive the priesthood. 273

EP. XLIX.—To an Abbot, That He Should Be Merciful toward Brothers Seeking Mercy.—To obtain mercy for penitents, he takes occasion from the imminent celebration of Easter and from the examples of Peter and Magdalene, who, repenting, obtained from the Lord pardon for their guilt. 274

EP. L.—To Abbot G.—That a wandering sheep should be recalled to the fold through mercy.

[Col. 1824]

275

EP. LI.—He rebukes a certain regular superior because, too lightly wearied by the disorderliness of some of his subjects, he had renounced the government imposed upon him, to the detriment of the good; and because, without consulting them, he had substituted another, less suitable person, even against their wishes. 275

EP. LII.—To Priest G.—He rebukes a certain priest, whom he calls Sacrifices, because he had cruelly tortured for disclosure a person suspected of theft committed against him. Such a course, he says, is lawful for a secular court, not for the Church. 277

EP. LIII.—Or Rather.—Preface of Saint Hildebert, archbishop of Tours, to his *Excerpts from Ecclesiastical Rules*, concerning the manifold kinds of divine commandments. 278

## BOOK THREE

EP. I.—He writes to Ranulf, bishop of Durham, on behalf of a certain Robert. 283

EP. II.—He reminds Countess Adela of a chasuble promised him by her, and asks her to give it to him. 284

EP. III.—That one buys a friend too dearly when one obtains something from a friend only by entreaties. Meanwhile, he excuses himself for having sent late the history of the miracles of the Church of Exeter, because its first copy had been lost. 284

EP. IV.—To S., Bishop of Sées.—He excuses himself before the bishop for delaying, being detained by necessity, to send him a small [work] intended for him; meanwhile, as he is about to depart for Rome for a council, he commends himself to the bishop’s prayers. 286

EP. V.—To Bishop R.—He asks his friend to inform him of the contents of the apostolic letters he has received. 286

EP. VI.—To Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury.—He urges his friend to send letters either more frequent or more lengthy, as being most welcome to him. 287

EP. VII.—He thanks the abbot of Cluny because, returning from Rome through the abbot’s prayers, he escaped many and most grave dangers. He says that he would have thrown himself into the abbot’s bosom if, through the Roman pontiff, he had been permitted to shake off the burden of the episcopal office; meanwhile he commends to him the bishop of Anjou, whom he calls a novice of Saint Benedict. 287

EP. VIII.—He asks Adela, countess of Blois, to provide him, as she had done for the bishop of Chartres, with safe-conduct as he departs for a council. 288

EP. IX.—He thanks the bishop of Beauvais for services kindly rendered in his city to a certain member of Hildebert’s household. 289

EP. X.—To S., Returning from Rome.—Since all things ought to be shared among friends, Hildebert says that he has endured with this friend, over whose return from Rome he rejoices, all the discomforts and dangers of the journey. 289

EP. XI.—He congratulates Matilda, queen of the English, on good health, which he maintains is necessary for the observance of laws and very beneficial for the Church’s welfare. 289

EP. XII.—To Queen M.—He promises Matilda, queen of the English, an inviolable affection of charity and prayers, although separated from her by the whole expanse of the seas. 290

EP. XIII.—To King H. of the English.—To Henry I, king of the English, whom he extols with great praise, he warmly commends the younger brother of the bishop of Anjou. 290

EP. XIV.—To M., Daughter of King H.—He asks Matilda, daughter of Henry I, king of the English, to deign personally to inform him what is happening in England, and especially what her father’s disposition is concerning the affront inflicted upon his daughter. 291

EP. XV.—He thanks Reginald, monk of Saint Augustine, for sending him the history of the monk Malchus written in verse by Reginald. Accordingly he promises to enter with him into a closer friendship that will never end, which he wishes to foster through mutual products of their talents; and he indicates certain works published here by himself. 292

EP. XVI.—To Bishop G.—He asks a certain bishop to show favor to a cleric named William. 292

EP. XVII.—To Subdean A.—After exalting the virtue of hospitality with praises, Hildebert thanks his friend for the hospitality which, without even being asked by him, he showed to three of Hildebert’s clerics. Yet he does not approve of his friend’s attempt to conceal or disguise this good work under the pretext of avoiding vainglory. 293

EP. XVIII.—To the Abbot of Clairvaux.—Moved by the fame, spread throughout the world, of Saint Bernard’s holiness and learning, Hildebert elegantly and earnestly requests admission to the sanctuary of his friendship and familiarity. Meanwhile he commends to him Gebuin, archdeacon of Troyes, as a man outstanding in character and letters. 294

EP. XIX.—This is Saint Bernard’s reply to Hildebert’s preceding letter; he returns the praises, while attributing nothing to himself of the praise offered. 295

EP. XX.—He beseeches Henry I, king of the English, to deign to protect and honor with his patronage a certain monastery of nuns and its abbess.

[Col. 1825]

295

EP. XXI.—To William, Abbot of Saint Vincent.—In the dispute concerning the churches of Scoda and Cortegam involving the monastery of Jumièges—or Gemegense, as he calls it—Hildebert testifies that, during his episcopate, the monks of Jumièges had raised no lawsuit or complaint. 296

EP. XXII.—To Archdeacon R. of Nantes.—He promises his dearest friend unfailing fidelity and services, especially now that he is in exile. Meanwhile, he congratulates him that, even in exile and amid arms, he devotes himself to letters, especially poetry; and he marvels that he is Caesar in arms and Virgil in verse. 297

EP. XXIII.—To Dean F.—It is the duty of a true friend to anticipate a friend’s petitions with good deeds; Hildebert says that he has done this, and promises to do so, for the imprisoned friend of the person to whom he writes. 297

EP. XXIV.—He commends his friend Simon to a certain official of the Roman curia and beseeches him to arrange that Simon become a member of the household of the Roman Church. 298

EP. XXV.—To a friend asking what the Lord Jesus wrote on the ground when the adulterous woman was brought before him, he explains what he has learned concerning this from Saint Ambrose. 298

EP. XXVI.—He promises a friend inviolable constancy in friendship. 300

EP. XXVII.—He rejoices with a friend over his prosperity and well-being, meanwhile offering him from his heart everything that is his own. 300

EP. XXVIII.—Hildebert thanks a certain bishop, his friend, for services most kindly and unsolicitedly rendered to some members of Hildebert’s household, storm-tossed while traveling. 300

EP. XXIX.—Afflicted, Hildebert mourns the death of one who had become, from an enemy, his dearest friend. 300

EP. XXX.—He frankly confesses to William, bishop of Winchester, that he was most pleased that William had requested his little works to be sent, which he very modestly promises to send him. 301

EP. XXXI.—He thanks a certain bishop, his closest friend, for episcopal sandals sent to him; explains their form as observed in the Gallican Church and the reason for it; and shows why the Gospel text is offered open to the bishop and closed to the others. 302

EP. XXXII.—To Brother R. O. 302

EP. XXXIII.—To Brother Fr. Fr. O. 305

EP. XXXIV.—Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, to Urban II, concerning the cemetery of Saint Vincent. 307

EP. XXXV.—He assures Thurstan, archbishop of York, of his friendship toward him, and that he has never done, nor will do, anything that could in any way oppose him in his disputes with Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury. 307

EP. XXXVI.—That married persons who have voluntarily vowed continence together may not withdraw from their vow. 310

EP. XXXVII.—How one should understand the statement that God sometimes punishes sin in the fourth and fifth generation. 310

EP. XXXVIII.—To a friend to whom Hildebert had commended both Stephen and Ralph, dean of the Church of Tours. 312

EP. XXXIX.—To a certain unknown person, concerning faithful and grateful remembrance of benefits. 312

## DIPLOMAS GRANTED BY THE VENERABLE HILDEBERT

I.—On behalf of the monastery of Saint Albinus of Anjou, concerning the church of Saint Audoin near Le Mans. 311

II.—On behalf of Marmoutier, concerning the church of Lupiniacum. 314

III.—Authorization of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, concerning the church of Saint Mary of Mayenne, and the gift of Robert Pavo. 314

IV.—Confirmation granted by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, of all the rights and possessions of the monastery of Évron. 315

V.—For the monastery of Saint Vincent of Le Mans. 317

VI.—For the monastery of Saint Vincent of Le Mans. 318

VII.—Gift of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, concerning the church of Saint George of the Wood. 318

VIII.—Letters of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, concerning the churches of Mayenne and Saccio. 319

IX.—In what cases only the ornaments of the Church may be pledged. 320

X.—Instrument concerning the agreement made between the canons of Saint Julian of Le Mans and the monks of Saint Vincent. 320

XI.—Diploma of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, for the monastery of Saint Victor of Le Mans.—He confirms churches granted to the monks by laypeople. 321

XII.—Charter of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, for Marmoutier.

[Col. 1826]

322

XIII.—Confirmation by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, concerning the church of Torciacum, commonly Torcé. 323

## LETTERS

Letter I.—A letter full of complaints, but justified ones. Marbod, bishop of Rennes, having gone to Rome in order to secure the confirmation of Raynald as bishop of Angers, was meanwhile, through the accusation of certain persons, despoiled by the very man whose business he was conducting of all ecclesiastical goods; moreover, he was declared an exile. He says that this had deservedly befallen him from an ungrateful man, because, contrary to law and piety, apart from the judgment of his metropolitan and against his own conscience, he had exerted himself to promote to the episcopate an utterly frivolous young man; he finally exhorts him to repentance and to a more restrained manner of life. 1465  
Letter II.—That the wickedness of a minister does not impede the truth of the sacrament. 1472
